# Preface to the Reader.

->To the Reader Eager for the Sacred Sources<-
->Much Greeting in CHRIST JESUS<-
->from<-

## JOHANN HEINRICH MICHAELIS, D. <note>original: "D." for Doctor.</note>

<margin>Introduction.</margin>
It has already been fifteen years <note>original: "Tria iam lustra"; a lustrum was a Roman period of five years.</note>, benevolent and learned Reader, since we promised the publication of this biblical work in a public announcement; a) at 그당시 not yet foreseeing all the delays, various and most serious, which we have experienced from then until this very day. Thus now, after an interval of many years, necessity demands that—in order to remove the unfair judgments of certain people—we set forth a few things regarding the occasion of this undertaking and its progress. We must also address the obstacles encountered, and the resulting changes to our plans, before we come to explaining the rest in this preface. I shall do this briefly through five chapters, so that I may: I. set forth the history of our labor, II. speak of the Hebrew and Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaico." In this period, the Aramaic language used in the Bible was commonly called Chaldean.</note> text, III. deal with the various readings <term>variant readings</term> within it, IV. discuss the Masorah <note>The traditional system of notes and rules intended to preserve the precise letter-for-letter text of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, and V. discuss our own annotations and other matters which must be noted. I am prevented from explaining more at length not so much by a lack of things to say, as by weak health and a shortage of time.

---

a) Published in the year of Christ 1705, in the month of March, with a Latin title for the work, and—because of the constant inquiries from friends—an appended account of our undertaking in the vernacular <note>referring to German.</note>; this was afterwards also shared with those abroad in French, in the Netherlands.

<vocab>Johann Heinrich Michaelis, Preface, Hebrew text, Aramaic (Chaldean), Masorah</vocab>

## CHAPTER I.

->Concerning the<-

### OCCASION AND HISTORY OF THIS WORK.

->§. I.<-

<margin>The occasion of this work.</margin>
The primary occasion for this labor was provided by the ORIENTAL THEOLOGICAL COLLEGE <note>The *Collegium Orientale Theologicum* was a small, elite circle of students at the University of Halle dedicated to the study of Biblical languages and textual criticism.</note>, established in May of the second year of this century [1702] by my venerable colleague, AUGUST HERMANN FRANCKE. He is a man who has earned the highest merit from this academy—and indeed from the Church of Christ. The College was instituted for this purpose: that together with their Inspector, the late <note>original: "B." for *Beatus*, meaning "blessed" or "of blessed memory," a standard way to refer to the recently deceased.</note> Johann Tribbechow, twelve or more students of the sacred letters b) might be prepared as teachers for the needs of the church. This was to be achieved through a more accurate cultivation of the individual parts of Sacred Theology and instruction continued over four or more years, so that they might handle the Sacred Scripture with logical demonstration <note>original: "apodixi," from the Greek *apodeixis*, meaning a clear, certain proof or manifestation of the truth.</note>—that is, as the Apostle says in Titus 1:9, "both to exhort with sound doctrine, and to convince those who contradict." Here are the names of the young men, arranged in alphabetical order:

Master Lucas Gottfried Backmeister, *of Stuttgart, Wurttemberg. †* <note>The cross symbol indicates the student had died by the time of publication.</note>

<header>TO THE READER.</header>
<sig>a 5</sig>

...men of the church, schools, and academies, who have performed—and by God’s grace still perform—the most serious duties with no small amount of success. And although the structure of this institution has experienced some change in the following years, partly due to illnesses and partly through other causes, the core mission remained. Consequently, through counsel and support, those talents considered suitable were assisted toward that same end. Nor do we abandon the hope that the Man born for the public good <note>Likely referring to August Hermann Francke, the founder of the Pietist movement in Halle.</note> will return to restore it to its original form, once those matters which have hitherto hindered it <note>original: "sufflaminarunt," literally "clogged" or "put a brake on."</note> are settled. This is especially so now that even more colleagues are present who, aided by divine grace, will work alongside him in every way so that in the future, young men will be ready and prepared for every good work. May God grant it success!

<margin>Collation of Manuscripts</margin>
§. II. Just as all things in that college were arranged so that its designated members might draw a solid knowledge of the sacred scriptures from the very Hebrew and Greek sources themselves, it did not seem foreign to our purpose if, in our spare time, a <term>collation of manuscripts</term> <note>The systematic process of comparing different copies of a text to identify and record variations in the wording.</note> of the Hebrew texts—especially handwritten ones—were carried out under my guidance as Professor of Oriental Languages. From this work, a new edition of the Hebrew Bible was to be prepared. To that end, we sought out not only the more excellent printed editions, as many as came into our hands, but also five parchment manuscripts <note>original: "membranaceos," meaning written on vellum or animal skin rather than paper.</note> owned by the library of the venerable Evangelical Ministry of Erfurt. These were acquired under honorable conditions and lent to us with the greatest kindness toward the autumn of the year 1702; we have long since restored them all in good faith and with due thanks. Because the most reverend Master *Abraham Kall* d) learnedly described those manuscripts—and sufficiently for our purposes—in his dissertation *On the Hebrew-Biblical Manuscripts, especially those of Erfurt,* held under my presidency in 1706, we will not repeat here what was done then. Instead, we refer every eager reader to that praised dissertation, especially since more things are explained there which would otherwise have had to be discussed more extensively here. However, lest anyone search for those details in vain, we shall provide them through the printers after our more abundant annotations on the <term>Hagiographa</term> <note>The "Holy Writings," the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible, which includes books such as Psalms, Job, and Proverbs.</note> are finished.

§. III. In the meantime, so that the reader may be somewhat certain of those manuscripts, and also the printed volumes which we have examined, we will briefly list them all here in the order in which they are most concisely cited or compared by us by number alone. Thus, the number

1. in our selected variant readings signifies the first...

---

*d)* Our former associate, as we just mentioned, and now a most faithful Minister of the Divine Word at Charlottenburg in the vicinity of Berlin: to whom we also owe the greatest part of the notes on the prophecy of Ezekiel.

1. *The Erfurt Manuscript*, in two large volumes, featuring the *Targum* <note>original: "Targum, f. versione Chaldaica"; an ancient Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> placed beneath each verse, including in the books of Chronicles. It also contains the little and large textual Masorah <note>The Masorah refers to the traditional system of notes used to ensure the precise preservation of the biblical text.</note>.

2. *The second Erfurt Manuscript*, a complete codex of the Old Testament including the Masorah and the Aramaic translation of the Pentateuch by Onkelos <note>The standard Aramaic translation of the first five books of the Bible.</note>, contained in one large volume.

3. *The third Erfurt Manuscript*, in medium folio size, containing the text of the entire Old Testament with the *Masorah*; however, there is a large gap from Jeremiah 44:26 to Ezekiel 8:3.

4. *The fourth Erfurt Manuscript*, damaged at both the beginning and the end. **e)**

5. *The fifth Erfurt Manuscript*, though very incomplete; it begins with the book of Joshua and ends after the Prophets with the book of Psalms. In the prophecy of Jeremiah, there is also a gap from chapter 14:17 to chapter 24:7; thus the number—

6. Indicates **DANIEL BOMBERG’S** *Hebrew and Aramaic Bible*, with Rabbinic commentaries and the preface by *Felix Pratensis*, printed in Venice in 1517 in a large folio format. We obtained a copy of this edition from the Marien-Library of this city <note>Referring to the library in Halle, Germany, where the author worked.</note>. From this edition, our Codex 9 was produced, and from that, Codex 20.

7. The fourth edition of the same work, the *Venetian Bible* in large folio, Venice, 1618.

8. **JOHANNES BUXTORF’S** *Hebrew-Aramaic and Rabbinic Bible*, widely available, Basel, 1620.

9. *Daniel Bomberg’s* Hebrew Bible in quarto format, Venice, 1518.

10. **ROBERT ESTIENNE’S** <note>original: "Roberti Stephani"; a famous French printer known for his scholarly editions.</note> edition in quarto, Paris, 1543, which displays everything transposed and jumbled by the printer due to a notable error from Hosea 5:8 to chapter 6:8.

11. The Royal *Antwerp Bible*, or the **PLANTIN** edition, in large folio, 1571.

12. The *Plantin* Bible in quarto format, Antwerp, 1566.

13. The Hebrew Bible with a Greek version and a double Latin version, also with notes by *François Vatable* in large folio, from the Saint-André workshop, 1587.

14. - - *Elias Hutter’s* in folio, Hamburg, 1587.

15. - - The *English Polyglot*, London, 1657. <note>A massive scholarly undertaking featuring the Bible in many different languages side-by-side.</note>

All these latter parts are without the Aramaic translation.

<margin>How the work was done.</margin>
§. IV. As the foundation for our comparison of manuscripts, we used the Hebrew Bible of the most Reverend and Celebrated **DR. DANIEL ERNEST JABLONSKI**, published in Berlin in 1699 in both octavo and quarto formats. We reviewed the text of this edition from beginning to end, not merely word by word, but syllable by syllable, including every vowel point and accent mark. In our selection of variant readings, we cite this edition under the abbreviation *Ber.* or *Berol.* <note>Short for Berolinensis, meaning "of Berlin."</note>. This labor of comparing the texts began on October 9, 1702, and continued for over fifteen months, concluding at the start of 1704. I devoted three or four hours each day to this task, assisted by twelve fellow students. Although it was quite tedious to focus so intensely on nearly superfluous details and often empty signs, the exhaustion was easily wiped away by the usefulness we occasionally discovered and the successful progress of the work. While our strength was still fresh, all the fellow students worked together eagerly on their assigned tasks. I personally filled the roles of both reader and scribe; I would pause briefly not only at every word, but at every consonant, vowel, and accent, as well as the critical marks, so that each student could accurately inspect his own copy and alert me and the whole group if any variation was found. In this way, within the space of a year and three months, a substantial volume was finally compiled from these many small variations.

<margin>Examination of the Masorah.</margin>
§. V. Up until this point, the work proceeded according to our wishes, and it seemed to us that we had completed a large portion of the preparation for our edition. However, we were then led to a much more tedious, indeed "iron" labor: the revision of the <term>Masorah</term> <note>The traditional system of notes and rules intended to preserve the precise letter-for-letter text of the Hebrew Bible.</note> based on our manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8, as well as a specific manuscript of the Masorah written on paper in a large quarto format—

---

f) This edition—prepared with great diligence but with a less elegant typeface under the care of the celebrated **Dr. Johannes Meyer**, a Professor at Harderwijk—reached us while we were printing Deuteronomy chapter 5. Among other things, it is unique because the editors provided Italian explanations for the Hebrew words, just as we provide Latin ones in our margin. For example, at Genesis 1:2: **היתה תהו ובהו** <note>original: "era vana e vacua"; English: "was empty and void."</note>; **מרחפת** <note>original: "dibateua"; English: "fluttering" or "moving."</note>; verse 6: **רקיע** <note>original: "firmamento"; English: "firmament."</note>; verse 9: **יקוו** <note>original: "fian adunnate"; English: "let them be gathered."</note>; **ותראה** <note>original: "e apparisca"; English: "and let it appear."</note>; verse 10: **ולמקוה** <note>original: "all' adunamento"; English: "to the gathering" etc.</note>. However, the preceding edition (number 21) usually does not print either of the distinguishing marks for the letter *Shin* <note>The Hebrew letter ש can be pronounced "sh" or "s" depending on a dot above it.</note>, as if the editors wished to suspend their judgment on the matter.

[...from the] former [task], **g)** had to be undertaken for the sake of perfecting our current edition. We also employed the critical books of the Hebrews, such as: 1) *En Hakkore* <note>Hebrew: "The Fountain of the Reader," a grammatical work by Rabbi Jekuthiel</note> from the margin of our first manuscript... 2) *Elias Levita’s Masoreth Hammasoreth* <note>Hebrew: "The Tradition of the Masorah," a foundational 16th-century work explaining the system of notes used to preserve the biblical text</note>, Venice, 1538... 3) The dissertation of *Rabbi Moses the Punctuator* <note>Originally: *R. Mosis Hannakkedan*; a specialist in adding vowel points and accents to the text</note>... 4) *Shaar Hanneginoth* <note>Hebrew: "The Gate of the Melodies," a treatise on musical accents</note> found at the end of the Venice and Buxtorf Bibles... 5) *Rabbi Judah son of Jacob’s explanation of the Masorah*, Amsterdam, 1650... 6) *Solomon ben Melech’s Michlal Yophi* <note>Hebrew: "The Perfection of Beauty"</note>... and 7) *Rabbi Menachem de Lonzano’s Or Torah* <note>Hebrew: "The Light of the Torah"</note>, Amsterdam, 1659... which deserves the highest praise.

This labor was much more tedious than the previous one. While the earlier work dealt with the actual words and sentences of the prophets, this task required us to hunt down and examine the often empty observations of the Masoretes <note>Scholars who worked between the 6th and 10th centuries to standardize the Hebrew Bible</note>, or rather the trivialities of more recent masters **h)**—immature follies packed together with obscure diligence. Furthermore, other obstacles were thrown in our way, which did not seem so great at the start but proved to be significant later on.

First, by the singular providence of God and the most merciful will of the Serene Founder of the Academy <note>Likely King Frederick I of Prussia, who founded the University of Halle</note>, in 1704, "Royal Tables" <note>A charitable system of subsidized meals</note> were established for the support of poor university students. I was appointed by royal decree to the *ephoria* <note>The administrative oversight or "inspectorship"</note> of these tables, alongside other highly esteemed men, despite being the youngest in rank and age at the time. I performed this duty with as much faithfulness and skill as I could, but it is hard to describe how much weariness and trouble arose for me in the following years **i)** from this inspection. Indeed, while I was serving those tables, the printing of our Bible was nearly brought to a standstill, until matters were finally settled and a new Inspector took over those duties.

<margin>And many more obstacles.</margin>
§. VI. Yet it was not only this task that kept me hindered; soon another event occurred that disrupted the entire scholarly circle. In the summer of that same...

**g)** Which we call the *Masorah of Erfurt* in our collection of variant readings; its work was of great use to us in this section.
**h)** For there are other, more recent critics, and then there are those ancient "pre-Talmudic" Masoretes so highly commended by Buxtorf and other learned men. This is clearly shown both by manuscripts (interpolated by different hands at different times) and by printed books. In almost every one of these, something has been written in Hebrew in the margin by editors, which then commonly goes by the name of "Masoretic notes." We would have preferred that this superfluous diligence had not been applied (despite what Elias Levita argues), especially by those who displayed little seasoned judgment and much rashness in these matters.
**i)** Especially in the year 1708, after the sudden death of the Blessed Johann Friedrich Ruoppius, Assistant of the Theological Faculty and most worthy Inspector of the Royal Tables.

# TO THE READER.

[At the beginning] of the year 1704, many young men and Greek **monk-priests** <note>Original: *hieromonachoi*; monks who have also been ordained as priests</note> arrived from Greece and Constantinople, drawn by the fame of our new Academy. Some of them $k)$ were well-versed in Greek literature; however, for the most part, the others were ignorant of ancient Greek, and every one of them was a complete stranger to and unrefined in Latin and German letters and affairs. Since these men coming from the Eastern Church joined our college, it was necessary for three or four members of our college to instruct and assist them in the Latin language and other subjects so that their time here would not be in vain. Consequently, the portions of labor which those colleagues had previously sustained could not help but fall more heavily upon me and my other fellow-workers. Meanwhile, quite prematurely, friends from elsewhere were urging us through frequent letters to begin our edition after a delay of only a year or two (as they interpreted our labor with good intentions, yet not enough foresight). Their wish was finally granted, and the printing of the book was begun toward the end of the year 1704, even though the laborious review of the **Masorah** <term>Masorah: The traditional system of notes used to preserve the exact text of the Hebrew Bible</term> had not yet been brought entirely to an end. And, as if it were not enough to manage the care of one edition, a double edition—another in a smaller format and with smaller type—had to be started at the same time. However, out of necessity, as will appear later, this second version has so far ceased after the completion of the **Pentateuch** <note>The first five books of the Bible</note>. Then, in order to free ourselves from writing so many letters, we issued that **Announcement** <note>Original: *Programma*; a formal prospectus describing the project</note> which was mentioned above in Section I.

<margin>increased labor,</margin>
§. VII. But I must not pass over in silence here that, although from the start of our work I had nothing else in mind but an edition of the Hebrew Bible—purified as much as possible from faults and errors (especially those in the accents arising from ignorance) through the examination of various books and the entire Masorah—and $l)$ adorned with new headings and a selection of variant readings; yet soon, at the constant requests of friends, it was required that we also add parallel passages of Scripture (both thematic and verbal), the "core" of the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> or the Greek and Oriental versions, and then certain **scholia** <term>Scholia: Brief explanatory notes or comments written in the margins of a text</term> or short notes. In this matter, since I had complied with the desires of my friends $m)$ without enough circumspection and being unaware of what was to come, such a great [burden] fell upon me from that point, even with suitable assistants...

---

$k)$ *Above all, a young man of exceptional talent, Michael Anastasius of Macedonia, became better known through a Greek formal speech delivered publicly among us.*

$l)$ *For, as Blessed Augustine says in "On Christian Doctrine," book 2, chapter 14: "The diligence of those who desire to know the Divine Scriptures should first be watchful in correcting the manuscripts."*

$m)$ *Those who promised themselves and others more benefit from "tasting the core of Scripture" than from our laborious review of letters, vowels, and punctuation marks, and especially the Masorah itself. And it is indeed true that the fruit of that great labor which we spent on the comparison of the manuscripts and the Masorah does not immediately appear to those unskilled in these matters; nevertheless, we have served the sacred text well in that its true...*

# PREFACE

Having been left behind by others, the mountain of labor increased, which would have ruined not only my health but my very life, had not divine mercy preserved me. For our printing had not yet reached the end of the **Pentateuch** <term>Pentateuch: The first five books of the Hebrew Bible, also known as the Torah</term> through the combined efforts of my associates when, behold, almost all my fellow soldiers began to be entangled in and weakened by various diseases—especially by a fever combined with **purpura** <note>original: *febri cum purpura*; likely referring to a type of "spotted fever" or typhus characterized by purple skin spots</note>. The rest, who still seemed healthy, were burdened with even more work alongside me. Finally, I was the last to fall ill, and all the more severely the longer I had resisted that ailment. Consequently, our printing ceased for several months during the years 1705 and 1706. Moreover, the greater part of my colleagues, having finished their three or four-year terms as they had agreed, departed—either due to ill health, to return to their families, or because they were called to public offices. Since it had not been possible to train new students through other means to succeed those who were leaving as reinforcements in this labor, barely two or three remained for the printing of **Isaiah**. Soon, these were to be reduced again, so that afterward, for the **Hagiographa** <term>Hagiographa: The "Holy Writings," the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible, including Psalms, Job, and Proverbs</term>, only one remained: my relative, and now most close colleague, the **Renowned Christian Benedict Michaelis**, of whom more will be said below.

<margin>delayed once more,</margin>
§. VIII. While these things were being done, it further happened that in the year 1707, the most deserving Professor of History and Eloquence in this academy, the Renowned and **Blessed Christopher Cellarius**, passed away. Among his other duties had been the oversight of the university library. Therefore, when this care was entrusted to me by the common vote of the Academic Senate, a new distraction arose from it, joined with a great loss of time. For although I had cataloged and organized the university library for two hours daily during 1707 and 1708, the same labor had to be undertaken from scratch in 1709, when, by the generous legacy of the Most Illustrious Lord **Daniel Ludolph von Danckelmann**, etc. etc., his numerous library had to be transferred here from **Berlin** and coordinated with the university collection. And, lest I pursue more details to the reader's annoyance, when in that same year of 1709—by the singular grace of Almighty God and the **King of Prussia**, our most merciful Lord—the highly reverend and most deserving Senior of the Theological order, **Dr. Joachim Justus Breithaupt**, was appointed Abbot of the Bergen monastery near **Magdeburg**, by that same royal decree, the roles of Ordinary Professor of Theology were also most mercifully entrusted to me, which I was to fulfill through public lectures on ecclesiastical history. And thus, being pulled in various and different directions...

<column-break/>

...the writing and punctuation in many places, we have restored not from our own cleverness, but from several **Codices** <note>ancient manuscript volumes</note> compared with one another. Nevertheless, we show the alternative reading in the selection of variations, mindful of that precept of the masters: **lest it should be by conjecture** <note>Hebrew original: *le-vilti hayetah mi-sevarah*</note>, that nothing in these sacred texts should be corrected based on guesswork.

# TO THE READER.

...lest I be too distracted by these labors; what I had to do from the beginning due to a multitude of business later became a habit, so that I spent nights entirely without sleep. I suffered miserably from continuous sweats, toothaches, and a general wasting of the whole body <note>original: *cachexia*; a physical wasting syndrome involving loss of weight and muscle atrophy</note>. At last, after the office of Pro-Rector of this Academy had been successfully administered through the grace of God in the years 1712 and 1713, I felt my physical health so weakened that I would have succumbed, had not God moved the mind of **OUR MOST SERENE AND POWERFUL KING** <note>Referring to Frederick William I of Prussia</note> to most kindly grant me some space to breathe. Therefore, at the beginning of spring in 1714, I was dismissed for a time to attend to the recovery of my health. I found a harbor with the Most Illustrious Lord **KARL HILDEBRAND, FREE BARON OF CANSTEIN, LORD IN CANSTEIN**, etc. *n*) under whose care I waited for a year and six months for the recovery of my lost strength. As much as my health allowed, I wrote notes on the **Psalter** <term>Psalter: The Book of Psalms</term>; because these became quite extensive, they have now been published separately along with the rest of our notes on the **Hagiographa** <term>Hagiographa: The "Holy Writings," the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible</term>.

<margin>The work resumed and completed.</margin>
§. IX. From there, around the autumn of 1715, having returned to the Academy and being somewhat firmer in health, I devoted myself entirely to the project. Aside from the ordinary labors of my post and my duties as Dean *o*), and several dissertations held in public, I worked with my distinguished relative and the most learned young man **JOHANN JAKOB RAMBACH** of Halle *p*). Our goal was to finish our biblical notes on the Hagiographa and to finally bring to light the third part of the Hebrew Codex, which had remained unfinished since the twelfth year of this century. However, our friend Rambach was not present for the labor of printing and the correction of the proofs due to a weakness of his eyes; he set out for the Academy of Jena toward the autumn of last year. At this very time, while we are engaged in this, he was decorated with the honor of a Master’s degree by the most distinguished Philosophical Faculty. Consequently, the roles of first and second corrector for the **Pentateuch** <term>Pentateuch: The first five books of the Bible</term> were undertaken by members of our College, and after their departure, by various others. My distinguished relative undertook the third review, and I performed the fourth or final revision.

<margin>Many obstacles passed over in silence.</margin>
§. X. I have willingly kept silent about many troubles and bitter misfortunes with which I had to struggle during almost the entire time of this labor. But those things which have been mentioned, I have brought forward for this purpose: so that those who, by some vain persuasion, believe we were given over to leisure and a life...

<header>PREFACE</header>

...they claim to revel in comforts here; or *they dare to seek the work of years in a few days*, as Blessed Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> writes in his *Preface to the Commentary on Matthew*. May His holy name be blessed by me and by all, now and forever!

### CHAPTER II.
->CONCERNING<-
### THE HEBREW MANUSCRIPT ITSELF, AND ITS DIVISION AND INTEGRITY.

#### §. I.

<margin>The Hebrew naming of the Sacred Codex.</margin>
We proceed now to the Hebrew manuscript itself—the canonical Scripture of the Old Testament, or the sacred books containing the revelation of Christ—to be briefly described here for the benefit of beginners. Among the Hebrews, by a broader use of the word, it is called תּוֹרָה <note>original: "Torah"</note> i. e. *Law* or *Doctrine* revealed by God; also תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב <note>original: "Torah she-bi-khtav"</note> *Written Law*, but commonly, based on the number of books, it is called עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָ <note>original: "Esrim ve-Arba’a"</note> *twenty-four*. *a)* Formerly, however, it was distributed into twenty-two books *c)* according to the number of Hebrew letters or consonants *b)*, as is certain from *Josephus's Against Apion, book 1, p. 1036; Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History, book 3, ch. 10* with the notes of *Valesius* p. 47; *Jerome’s Helmeted Preface*, and many others. It was written in the Hebrew language *d)* as the first of all and the patriarchal language, the native tongue of the people of God until the Babylonian captivity; with the exception of Daniel 2:4 through 7:28, Ezra 4:1 through 6:18 and 7:12–22, which are expressed in the Chaldaic <note>Aramaic</note> or Babylonian dialect. Compare the introductions in the *Fuller Annotations on Daniel*, § 29.

#### §. II.

<margin>Tripartite division.</margin>
All these books of the Old Testament are distinguished among the Jews first by a tripartite division *e)* into:

->I. תּוֹרָה <note>Torah / The Law</note><-

---

*a)* While they count the five books of the Pentateuch with us, they assign eight to the Prophets and eleven to the Hagiographa <note>The "Sacred Writings," such as Psalms and Proverbs</note>, as will be clear from what follows.
*b)* That this number of letters was established long ago is clearly proved by the acrostic poems of Holy Scripture, for example, Psalms 25, 34, and 119; Proverbs 31:10 and following; also Lamentations chapters 1, 2, 3, and 4.
*c)* In this arrangement, the book of Ruth was attached to the book of Judges, and Lamentations <note>Latin: Threni</note> to the prophecy of Jeremiah.
*d)* With two Chaldaic <note>Aramaic</note> words interspersed in Genesis 31:47 and an entire verse in Jeremiah 10:11; and more frequently with Chaldaic forms and endings, e.g., Psalms 116:7, 12, etc.
*e)* Compare Luke 24:44; also our various readings on Jeremiah 1:1, and the prologue of Sirach <note>The Wisdom of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus</note>, where two or three times they are called "the Law and the Prophets and the other ancestral books" <note>original Greek: ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάτρια βιβλία</note> or "the Law and the prophecies and the rest of the books." <note>original Greek: ὁ νόμος καὶ αἱ προφητεῖαι, καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ τῶν βιβλίων</note>

<margin>Concerning the Law,</margin>
I. תּוֹרָה <note>original: "Torah"</note> **LAW** specifically so-called, or חֲמִשָּׁה חֻמְשֵׁי תוֹרָה <note>original: "Hamisha humshey torah"</note> the *five-fifths* or five books of Moses, named after their first emphatic words: so that בְּרֵאשִׁית <note>original: "Bereshit"</note> denotes *Genesis*, שְׁמוֹת <note>original: "Shemot"</note> or וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹת <note>original: "Ve-eleh shemot"</note> *Exodus*, וַיִּקְרָא <note>original: "Vayikra"</note> *Leviticus*, בַּמִּדְבָּר <note>original: "Bemidbar"</note> *Numbers*, and דְּבָרִים <note>original: "Devarim"</note> or אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים <note>original: "Eleh ha-devarim"</note> the book of *Deuteronomy*:

<margin>the Prophets,</margin>
II. נְבִיאִים <note>original: "Neviim"</note> **PROPHETS** or eight books written by prophets; these are subdivided into the רִאשׁוֹנִים <note>original: "Rishonim"</note> *former* prophets, namely the four historical books: *Joshua*, *Judges*, *Samuel*, and *Kings* f) and the same number of אַחֲרוֹנִים <note>original: "Aharonim"</note> *latter* prophets: *Isaiah*, *Jeremiah*, *Ezekiel* g) and the Δωδεκαπρόφητον <note>original: "Dodekapropheton"</note> or "Twelve-Prophet" book, in Hebrew שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר <note>original: "Shneim Asar"</note> or in Aramaic תְּרֵיסַר <note>original: "Treisar"</note> or תְּרֵי עָשָׂר <note>original: "Trei Asar"</note>, that is, the twelve minor prophets: and

<margin>& the Holy Writings.</margin>
III. כְּתוּבִים <note>original: "Ketuvim"</note> f. **HOLY WRITINGS** <note>Also known by the Greek term Hagiographa.</note> numbering eleven. These include three "metric" or poetic books: *Psalms*, *Proverbs*, and *Job*, which are distinguished by the musical laws of poetic accents; and five מְגִלּוֹת <note>original: "Megillot"</note> f. small volumes or *scrolls*; h) one prophetic book of *Daniel*; i) two historical books, *Ezra* and *Nehemiah*, which were formerly joined; and one book for the two of *Chronicles* <note>original: "Paralipomenon"</note>; just as they formerly considered the two books of *Samuel* and *Kings* as one each.

<margin>Division of the Law into several sections,</margin>
§. III. Next, the Pentateuch <note>The "Five Books" of Moses.</note> was long ago divided by the Jews—from the time of Ezra, as they say—into פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת <note>original: "Parashiyot"</note> or **SECTIONS**, consisting of 53 or 54 large portions. k) These are again divided into smaller ones according to the diversity of the subject matter. These sections, both large and small, are either פְּתוּחוֹת <note>original: "Petuhot"</note> meaning *open*, which start at the beginning of a line; or סְתוּמוֹת <note>original: "Setumot"</note> *closed*, which begin within a line. The larger sections are marked in printed editions either by three large פפפ <note>The Hebrew letter Pe, for "open".</note>, as in Genesis 6:9, 12:1, etc., or three ססס <note>The Hebrew letter Samekh, for "closed".</note>, as in Genesis 44:11; l) the smaller sections, however, are marked by a single letter.

---

f) Written by Joshua, Samuel, and subsequent divinely inspired men <note>original: "θεοπνεύστοις"</note>, especially Jeremiah, as the Jews pass down by tradition through divine suggestion and other monuments of those times. Compare our Prefaces to the more abundant notes on the books of *Ezra* and *Chronicles*.

g) However, they are not in the same order in all manuscripts; compare the Various Readings for *Jeremiah* 1:1, etc.

h) These are usually added by the Jews to the five books of Moses like an appendix, and are read publicly on the more solemn festivals: 1. *Song of Songs* at the Passover festival, 2. *Ruth* at the feast of Pentecost, 3. *Lamentations* <note>original: "Threni"</note> on the 9th day of the month of *Ab* (July/August), on which the Temple was burned, 4. *Ecclesiastes* <note>original: "Coheleth"</note> at the feast of Tabernacles, and 5. *Esther* at the feast of Purim (the festival of lots).

i) Regarding this, see the preface to the Psalms, § 1, and more extensively the prolegomena to *Daniel*, § 21, 22.

k) These 53 or 54 sections are read through in the Synagogues on the Sabbaths of their intercalary year; in other years, they join two shorter ones together twice. Each of these takes its name from its first or nearest word, for example: the first is *Bereshit*, the second *Noach*, the third *Lech Lecha*, the fourth *Vayera*, etc. In our editions, these names are placed above the column, after the book name and before the chapter number. To each of these major sections, there corresponds in the Jewish Synagogue the הַפְטָרוֹת <note>original: "Haphtarot"</note> or prophetic readings, compare Acts 13:27 and 15:21. They trace the origin of these to the times of Antiochus Epiphanes. See *Buxtorf* on Hebrew Abbreviations, p. 281 ff.; *Pfeiffer's* Sacred Criticism, p. 10, 23, etc.

l) In manuscripts, they are also marked by one large פ, or by three arranged in this manner פפפ, or by writing "Parash" <note>An abbreviation for Parashah.</note> in the margin, or by some other sign or method.

§. IV. Furthermore, the same sacred books of the Old Testament—within the Law, the Prophets, and the Holy Writings—were anciently distributed by the Hebrews into certain <term>סדרים</term> *orders*, or *Sidras* <note>meaning larger segments or chapters</note>, as the Masoretic notes in our Codex at the end of Genesis, Exodus, etc., demonstrate. However, since they are no longer in use in our books and manuscripts today, we do not provide a catalog of them here to avoid wasting paper. Those who enjoy such things may find them in the frontispiece of Buxtorf’s Bible. For the same reason, we have not added a separate <term>לוח הפרשיות</term> & <term>ההפטרות</term>, that is, a table or index of the legal sections <note>Parashot</note> and prophetic sections <note>Haftarot</note> <gloss>m)</gloss>; this is because we have very little use for them, and the Jews are unlikely to admit our edition into the Synagogue due to the added Latin annotations. If you wish, see the index of *Parashot* <note>weekly Torah portions</note> in Buxtorf’s *On Abbreviations*, page 286 and following.

<margin>Division of books by Chapters;</margin>
§. V. A more common practice today among both Jews and Christians is the division of books into chapters, called <term>פרקים</term> <note>Perakim</note> or <term>קפיטולי</term> <note>Capituli</note> by them. This system was introduced by Christians around the 12th or 13th century and was subsequently received and approved by the Jews as well; see *Buxtorf’s Preface to the Hebrew Concordance* and *Pfeiffer’s Sacred Criticism, page 8*, to name but a few. In this division and the starting points of chapters, however, the Hebrew manuscripts sometimes vary—not without inconvenience—just as much as the Greek, Latin, and other codices. Furthermore, the division was not always made in the most appropriate place. We think it necessary to mention this here so that no one incautiously presses that human division more than is right; rather, one should draw arguments for the coherence or lack of coherence of the subject matter from the very "innards" of the text itself. This is also something to be observed occasionally in the New Testament and the Holy Apocalypse. Compare the *Preface to the Richer Annotations on Daniel, §. 26*. In our edition, we have followed the division of *B. Clodius* <note>Johannes Bartholomaeus Clodius, a 17th-century scholar</note>, even if it is not the best in every instance (such as Exodus 21:37, etc.), because of the many citations made from it; however, we have noted the differences in other editions among the Various Readings in their proper places. As for the Psalms, in the Hebrew codices they are 150 essentially separate short works; in their present order, they have no connection or coherence with what precedes or follows them, except what their own material and subject matter might suggest: on which see the *Preface to the Psalms, §. 8*.

<margin>The distinction of chapters by verses and accents is authentic [divine],</margin>
§. VI. We must say and establish something altogether different regarding the *distinction of the Hebrew text* by <term>פסוקים</term> <note>Pasukim</note>, that is, commas or verses, and likewise regarding the <term>נקודות וטעמים</term> <note>Nekudot and Te'amim</note> or the system of *vowels and accents*—that is, the sacred musical and structural pauses. For weighty reasons, and having long and maturely weighed the arguments on both sides, we cannot help but acknowledge these as divine and authentic. It is not permitted here—

<margin>Commended to students.</margin>
§. VII. Although it must be granted even to those who disagree (as all experience proves) that a student who is not entirely lazy may profit quite successfully from the instruction of a skilled master—and the living voice of a teacher usually conveys more than knowledge drawn from merely re-reading writings—nevertheless, one who is ignorant of the analogy of the Hebrew points and distinctions <note>The system of vowels and musical accents (cantillation marks).</note> will never attain the sense of Holy Scripture as easily, certainly, or evidently as one who is equipped with a solid knowledge of them. For **Melanchthon** <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a German reformer and collaborator of Martin Luther.</note> truly said elsewhere: *Scripture cannot be understood theologically, unless it is understood grammatically;* and as has been proven more fully elsewhere, the accents of the Hebrews are signs for distinguishing or connecting parts of speech, according to the requirements of sense, emotion, and elocution.

-># PREFACE <-

From this, it is easy to understand how much those people hinder themselves who—whether occupied by the prejudice of malice or of ignorance—despise these divine aids <note>The Hebrew vowel points and accents discussed on the previous page.</note> and either indulge their own wandering wit in sacred matters, not without danger and loss, or else enslave themselves only to the eyes or the faith of others. <margin>o)</margin> *For the duty of a commentator, or rather an interpreter, is to set forth not what he himself wishes, but what the author whom he interprets thinks; otherwise, if he says the opposite, he will not be so much an interpreter as an adversary of the one he strives to explain.* And since today there is a short and open path to learning these things with little effort, we cannot help but studiously recommend to each and every person that they learn these things before they judge them, and experience them before they rashly cast any of them aside. We certainly praise what **Solomon ben Melech**, following the example of **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), also known as Radak, a foundational medieval Hebrew grammarian and exegete.</note>, commands the student of Holy Scripture in the Epilogue of his *Perfect Beauty* <note>original: "Michlal Iophi"</note>: <gloss>that he be a keeper of the connection of that passage, a keeper of the vowel points, and a keeper of the accents</gloss> <note>original: להיותו שומר קשר הפרשה ההיא להיותו שומר הנקוד ולהיותו שומר הטעמים</note>; *that is: that he observe, 1. the context, 2. the system of vowels, and 3. the series of sacred accents or distinctions:* just as we also, according to our small measure, direct our mind to both grammar and sacred matters in our annotations.

*b*) **Louis Cappel**, who deserved well here—though otherwise poorly regarding the "Hebrew truth"—writes as follows in his apologetic letter to **James Ussher**, Archbishop of Armagh (p. 110), against Bootius:
> *The divine care and providence regarding the sacred books appears all the greater and more illustrious because it has so guided all their scribes in all places and ages that in every single one of their manuscripts, and in the various translations of those books, all the momentous and necessary truth which He willed to be revealed to us is contained whole and unimpaired. The devil snarls and gnashes his teeth against it in vain; he could do nothing against it, except to introduce a harmless and most tolerable variety of multiple readings into those books through the blameless infirmity of the men who transcribed them. This infirmity, without a perpetual, grand, and extraordinary miracle, could not be so corrected and amended that manifest traces of it would not remain in that manifold variety. This is more wonderful and more suited to blunt the blasphemy against those sacred books than if the original <term>autographs</term> <note>the original manuscripts written by the biblical authors themselves</note> of the writers had been preserved for us until these times. For those might be more easily called into suspicion of fraud or substitution than so many different manuscripts, transcribed by so many different men, at such different places and times, and so many translations made from them, which so unanimously agree in essential and necessary matters, and differ so little in various lighter readings of almost no importance.*

# TO THE READER.

...of his crime on pages 1 and 2, and in K. 1, he dared to mark the words of Psalm 29:1–2 as impious, even though they are read elsewhere in the Holy Scriptures. The same man is more than futile when, in that same place on page 2, he explains the word <term>be-oni</term> <note>original: "בעוני"; traditionally "in my iniquity" or "in my affliction"</note> in Psalm 31:11 as referring to a shameful lust or excessive sexual desire. Nevertheless, these ideas have so delighted some incautious people that I must confess they were part of the reason I undertook the labor of collating many codices. I wished to dispel the variations of reading—which he had so invidiously pointed out—through actual use and experience. How inappropriately also that man, otherwise most learned, Jean Le Clerc <note>A famous 17th-century biblical critic known for his rationalist approach</note>, exercises and commends his "critical art" here; we have had to warn of the truth throughout our more extensive notes on the <term>Hagiographa</term> <note>The "Holy Writings," the third section of the Hebrew Bible including Psalms, Proverbs, etc.</note>. Far be it from us that our diligence should provide anything to satisfy itching minds. **"For the foolishness of God is wiser than men"** <note>original Greek: "ὅτι τὸ μωρὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ σοφώτερον τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐστί"; 1 Corinthians 1:25</note>.

<margin>Various sources of different readings.</margin>
§. V. Furthermore, just as the various readings of the Old Testament are not all of one kind (as we partly indicated above in section 1), so too their sources are varied, from which they flowed into the Hebrew codex itself. For:

1. The biblical books themselves vary among one another, as they were written at very different times and had different authors. For example, the first of all, the book of Genesis, and the last in our codex, <term>Paralipomenon</term> <note>The book of Chronicles</note>; compare Genesis 10:3, 4 etc. with 1 Chronicles 1:6, 7 etc., where our Codex 22 has noted the difference in the margin. Compare also the more extensive notes we have made in that place.

2. Observe that the occasion for diverse readings was given by letters whose shapes have some similarity, such as:
**Bet (ב) and Kaf (כ)**; and **Nun (נ)**;
**Dalet (ד) and Resh (ר)**;
**He (ה) and Het (ח)**;
**Vav (ו) and Zayin (ז)**;
**Yod (י) and Vav (ו)**;
**Final Mem (ם) and Samekh (ס)**;
**Sin (שׂ) and Shin (שׁ)** *k)*.
This is especially prone to happen in proper names; if the writing becomes somewhat ambiguous, the genuine reading cannot be gathered from the context, whereas in common nouns it usually can be. Take for example 2 Kings 22:14, where our manuscripts 1, 2, and 5, and of the printed editions 6, 9, and 20, have **Harham** <note>original: "חרחם"</note> instead of **Harhas** <note>original: "חרחס"</note>. So in Jeremiah 15:14, instead of **ve-ha’avarti** <note>"and I will cause to pass"</note>, manuscripts 1, 3, and 8 have **ve-ha’avadti** <note>"and I will cause to serve"</note>, which is also how the ancient <term>LXX</term> <note>The Septuagint (Greek translation)</note>, <term>Chaldee</term> <note>The Targum (Aramaic translation)</note>, Syriac, and Arabic versions interpreted it here. Nor is this variation to be entirely despised, for it is read that way in Jeremiah 17:4. Similarly, in Isaiah 44:4, instead of **ke-vein** <note>"like among"</note>, several books have **be-vein** <note>"in among"</note>, just as the Septuagint renders it **"as in the midst"** <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἀνὰ μέσον"</note>. In Ezekiel 30:18, instead of **hashakh** <note>"it shall withhold," specifically its light</note>, one Erfurt manuscript and some printed editions have **hashakh** <note>"it shall be darkened"</note>, which is how the Septuagint, Vulgate, Chaldee, and Syriac rendered it. In Jeremiah 4:16, instead of **notzrim** <note>"watchers" or "besiegers"</note>, the Chaldee—as noted by <term>Kimchi</term> <note>David Kimchi, a famous 12th-century Jewish commentator and grammarian</note> on this passage—seems to have read **metzurim** <note>"siegers"</note>; for he rendered it "the armies of the peoples who plunder, like grape-gatherers." In Psalm 71:3, instead of **ma’on** <note>"dwelling"</note>, one manuscript and several others have **makhon** <note>"established place" or "foundation"</note>...

---

*k)* The book **Tanchuma** <note>An ancient collection of Jewish homilies (Midrash)</note> shows right at the beginning (folio 1, column 1) with many examples how great a difference in meaning the addition of a single point or tip can sometimes produce in similar letters.

3. **Letters with the same or similar pronunciation**: For example, in Job 20:22, instead of <term>his sufficiency</term> <note>original: "שִׂפְקוֹ"; pronounced with an 's'</note>, two manuscripts and several printed editions have <term>his clapping</term> <note>original: "שִׁפְקוֹ"; pronounced with a 'sh'</note>. Compare also Psalm 139:23 and Proverbs 23:10.

4. **Confusion of diacritical signs**: For instance, <term>Metheg</term> and <term>Merca</term> <note>marks used to indicate stress or musical chanting in Hebrew</note>, etc. For the sake of brevity, consult the Most Reverend Mr. Jablonski’s Preface to the Berlin Bible, section 17, and our own dissertation on Manuscript Codices, section 15.

5. **Displacement of accents**: For example, <term>Tiphcha</term> and <term>Merca</term> <note>types of musical accents</note> in the domain of the <term>Silluk</term> <note>an accent marking the end of a verse</note> in 1 Samuel 14:41, Habakkuk 2:4, and quite frequently elsewhere.

6. **Different verse beginnings**: Not only in those fifteen places marked by a <term>Piska</term> <note>original: "Piſka"; a break or space in the middle of a verse in the Masoretic text</note>, such as Genesis 35:22, but also in many others, as our various readings will indicate in their proper place.

7. **Synonyms**: When, for example, the divine names <term>LORD</term> <note>original: "יהוה"; YHWH</note> and <term>Lord</term> <note>original: "אדני"; Adonai</note> were frequently swapped.

8. **Not only ignorance**, especially in the poetic books, but also a presumed or imaginary analogy in the sequence of accents. Thus, for example, in Ezekiel 31:15 on the word <term>I caused to mourn</term> <note>original: "הַאֲבַלְתִּי"</note>, in verse 18 on <term>trees of Eden</term> <note>original: "עֲצֵי עֵדֶן"</note>, in 2 Chronicles 22:11 on <term>and she stole him</term> <note>original: "וַתִּגְנֹב אֹתוֹ"</note>, and in chapter 30, verse 6 on the name <term>LORD</term> <note>original: "יהוה"</note>, common codices mistakenly have a <term>Zakeph Katon</term> accent instead of a <term>Rebia</term> or <term>Geresh</term>. This is because their scribes or editors thought that the preceding <term>Pashta</term> accent could not stand otherwise.

9. **Identity of initial and final words**: We have a notable example of this in a passage which we have rescued from unjust exclusion against our common codices using evident reasons, namely Joshua 21:36–37. Compare what we noted there in the various readings, and the famous Jablonski in his Preface, section 27, note *t*. He rightly conjectured that the scribe, deceived by the similarity of the word <term>and from the tribe of</term> <note>original: "וּמִמַּטֵּה"</note>—which is the starting word of both verse 37 and verse 39—made a jump from the first to the latter, a common error <note>Known as "eye-skip" or homoeoteleuton, where a scribe's eye jumps between two identical words, skipping the text in between</note>. Without doubt, an error flowed from this same source when, in the second Frankfurt edition of Clodius’s Bible, verses 5 and 6 of Ezra 8 were transposed by a sufficiently obvious and large blunder.

10. **The ambiguity and confusion of the Masora itself**, by which it not infrequently contradicts itself; *l*) for example, in Numbers 5:13, they double the <term>L</term> in the word <term>and it be hidden</term> <note>original: "וְנֶעְלַם"</note> with a <term>Dagesh</term> <note>a dot in a Hebrew letter indicating it is doubled or emphasized</note>—

---

*l*) Due to the ambiguity and confusion of the **Masora** <note>The body of traditional notes on the text of the Hebrew Bible</note>, that leading man in these letters, the most learned **Buxtorf** <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a massive figure in 17th-century Hebrew studies</note>, not only frequently omitted many things but also erred, both in his key to the Masora and in his corrections of it. This could be demonstrated with many examples if I chose to do so. However, we do not approve of the character of those who observe nothing in great men except their defects and blemishes. Therefore, I mention this only so it may be established that these matters would have been better settled long ago if his successors had not been persuaded that everything had already been fully worked out by the labor of that one most industrious man.

§ VI. ->### PREFACE<-

...labor, begun with incredible zeal by the ancient Hebrews, had come down to posterity and even to our own times whole and intact. For in that case, many more things could undoubtedly be obtained from a safe and whole **Masora** <note>The traditional system of notes and rules used by Jewish scholars to preserve the exact text of the Hebrew Bible</note> than from its torn and confused parts, which might establish the genuine and ancient reading in ambiguous passages. Now, however, since the previous discussion has revealed not only its merits to the learned but also its flaws or defects, we must see to it that we act prudently—neither praising nor blaming it too much. In both directions, people tend to err toward extremes; he who holds the middle ground here will walk most safely.

**§. II.** In order for this to be a bit clearer for the students for whose benefit these words are written, the **Masora** $a)$ is a critical doctrine of the ancient sages or scholars among the Hebrews $b)$ concerning the sacred text and its **verses**, $c)$ **words**, $d)$ and **elements**, i.e., consonants, $e)$ **vowels**, $f)$ **tone**, $g)$ **accents**, $h)$ and **diacritical marks**, $i)$ for the purpose of preserving its genuine reading. For this reason, they also call it the <term>Hedge of the Law</term> <note>original: "סייג לתורה" (Seyag la-Torah); a metaphor suggesting that these notes act like a fence protecting the core text from being changed or corrupted</note>. See the summary on this in *Johann Benedict Carpzov’s Introduction to Jewish Theology, page 77 and following.*

**§. III.** However, its form and arrangement were different in the past than they are now in manuscripts and printed editions, and only a very small part of it is found in our current and other common editions of the Bible. The ancients presented it separately in various sheets or several books $k)$, as our **Erfurt Masora** (praised above in Chapter 1, §. 2) also teaches. Later, they linked it to the text itself, so that the <term>Compendium of the Masora</term> <note>original: "קצור המסרת" (Kitzur ha-Masoret)</note>—which we call today the **Small Masora** or **Intercolumnar Masora**—was written at the side using numerical and symbolic letters, referring to the words of the text marked with a small circle; $l)$ the rest was written above or below the column, and sometimes even in the margi- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the word "margin" on the next page.</note>

---

$a)$ Also called **Masoreth** <note>original: "מסורת"</note> by the Hebrews, from the word **masar** <note>original: "מסר"</note>, meaning "he handed down" or "transmitted."
$b)$ For **Buxtorf**, in his work *Tiberias*, has placed it beyond controversy that the ancient **Masoretes** <note>The scribes and scholars who compiled the Masora</note> flourished long before the **Talmud** <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, compiled roughly between the 3rd and 6th centuries CE</note> was written.
$c)$ See, for example, in the Masoretic notes after the end of Genesis, Exodus, etc., the **number of verses and the middle verse of the books**. To this also refer the **Piska** <note>original: "פסקה"; a space or break in the text</note>, or empty space, as in Genesis 35:22, Numbers 25:19, Deuteronomy 2:8, etc., which indicates the beginning of a verse in the middle of a verse from another manuscript; compare Chapter V, number 6 of the preceding chapter.
$d)$ These indicate variant readings where the vowels placed under the <term>Ketiv</term> <note>original: "כתיב"; the "written" form of the word in the text</note> signify the <term>Qere</term> <note>original: "קרי" (written here in Greek as "τὸ Kri"); the "read" form of the word found in the margin</note>, as in Genesis 8:17; or the vowels appear alone in the text with the **Qere** in the margin, as in Judges 20:13, 1 Samuel 14:32, 2 Samuel 8:3, chapter 16:32, chapter 18:20, etc. Or a Masoretic note confirms the genuine reading, as in Genesis 9:29, or indicates a different notation, as in Genesis 18:3; compare chapter 19:2, 18 and chapter 35:7.
$e)$ For example, **large letters** in Genesis 1:1, Leviticus 11:42, and **small letters** in Genesis 2:4, and others.
$f)$ As in Genesis 6:19, chapter 11:3, 11, chapter 18:13, etc.
$g)$ As in Leviticus 15:29, Numbers 24:17, 22.
$h)$ For example, a **double accent** on one word, and how it is to be pronounced in Genesis 5:29.
$i)$ For example, a **Dagesh** <note>a dot indicating a stronger pronunciation</note> after a **Shureq** <note>a vowel mark for the "u" sound</note> in Genesis 2:25, or the letter **He** without a Dagesh in Genesis 4:4.
$k)$ For, as **Buxtorf** reports in his work *On Abbreviations, page 438*, there are countless **manuscript books of the Masora**; from these various sources, a book was once extracted, named **Ochlah ve-Ochlah** <note>original: "אכלה ואכלה"; one of the earliest and most important collections of Masoretic rules</note> from its opening words, and praised by **Rabbi Elias Levita** in *Masoreth Ha-Masoreth, page 7*, but it was never printed.
$l)$ These, however, must not only be reconstructed from the textual **Large and Final Masora**, but very often must be supplemented from the manuscript books of the Masora.

->### TO THE READER<-

...were noted in the margin, which would constitute the Great Masora, and what is called the textual Masora. This arrangement, while it would have been most convenient for the reader's use if everything had been properly organized and applied in its place, conversely became the primary occasion for the mutilation and confusion of the Masora; for unskillful scribes wandered completely from the goal and turned the educational system into a picture.

<margin>Mutilation and confusion of the Masora.</margin>
**§. IV.** For after they no longer prioritized transcribing a perfect Masora and presenting it to their readers, but rather aimed to make the columns of the manuscript more elegant and uniform through various images, flowers, and ornaments—which frequently occur in manuscript codices, especially at the beginning of books, as mentioned in our dissertation, § XVII—they were often forced, whenever space was lacking, to shorten the text of the Masora. Conversely, where space remained, they would adopt something from the Masora elsewhere that did not belong there; yet they made no mention of this later in the appropriate place. From this, complaints later arose among Jews and Christians from those more recent and corrupt copies, involving those who had a more correct understanding of the Masora’s purpose. Specifically, the first compiler of the Masora edited by Bomberg <note>Daniel Bomberg, a famous 16th-century Christian printer of Hebrew books in Venice</note>, *Rabbi Jacob ben Chaiim*, an *African from Tunis*, complained greatly about this corruption of the Masora in his Preface to the Masoretic Bible, column 7. Likewise, *Rabbi Elias Levita* in *The Tradition of the Masora* <note>original: "Masoreth Ha-Masoreth"</note>, page 7; *Abraham, son of Eliezer*, the corrector of the Buxtorf Bible, in the Preface after the title of the work; and *Johannes Rittangel* in his notes to the book *Yetzirah* <note>The Sefer Yetzirah, or "Book of Formation," a primary work of Jewish mysticism</note>, page 34, not to mention many others.

<margin>A remedy attempted in vain.</margin>
**§. V.** The aforementioned *Rabbi Jacob ben Chaiim* did indeed wish to apply a remedy to these omissions and this torn-apart Masora, adding by a new arrangement to the printed Bibles what they call the *Great or Final Masora*: which was intended to supply, by way of an index—albeit one rather confusedly patched together—what had been excluded elsewhere. For this reason, *Elias Levita* not undeservedly gave him considerable praise in the passage cited, though it was quite limited; as did the previously praised *Rabbi Menachem* throughout his *Light of the Torah* <note>original: "Or Torah"</note>, mentioned above in chapter 1, § 5. For in truth, that remedy was only attempted, not perfected by Rabbi Jacob, nor did the matter reach completion <note>original: "ad umbilicum pervenit" - a Latin idiom meaning to reach the end of a scroll, indicating a finished task</note>; whether he felt himself alone unequal to such a burden, or whether he dealt with a printer who was more hurried and pressing than was right. Certainly, the Great Masora would have been much better served if the first editors had arranged it in the manner of concordances with an index of places, having first restored it through a comparison of various codices and manuscripts. In that way, if a doubt arose about any matter, one could immediately return to it and seek a decision; whereas now, given the current state of the Masora, this can only be done with a great—and yet often vain—expenditure of time. For the celebrated *Daniel Jablonski* <note>A German court preacher and scholar who published a notable Hebrew Bible in 1699</note> judged most correctly in his Preface to the Berlin Bible, § 31, that *the Masora, as it appears printed today, is so mutilated and tangled in many places...*

->### PREFACE<-

...in places it is clearly erroneous, in many parts it is suspect, and it is frequently inconsistent both with itself and with manuscript codices everywhere, so that it would truly require a labor of Hercules <note>A reference to the Greek hero's nearly impossible task of cleaning the massive, filthy Augean stables of King Augeas in a single day</note> for anyone attempting to purge this "Augean stable."

<margin>
Example of a corrupted Masora
</margin>

**§ VI.** Lest someone inexperienced think this is said without cause, let us demonstrate it with a single example. Specifically, in Genesis 22:2, at the first word of that verse, **And he said** (**ויאמר**), the *Small Masora* <note>Brief notes found in the side margins of the Hebrew Bible</note> notes very concisely: **14 [times] with the accent** (**יד בטעם**); that is, it correctly warns that this word occurs fourteen times with that specific *Paser* <term>Paser: A Hebrew cantillation mark or "accent" that indicates a distinct pause and musical phrasing; its shape resembles a small vertical line with a hook</term> accent. However, in the textual *Great Masora* <note>More extensive notes usually found at the very top or bottom of the page</note> at that location, nothing of the sort is found. 

Therefore, if you desire to know these locations, you must either undertake the incredible labor of searching through hundreds—no, thousands—of entries in a Hebrew concordance; or rather, you must patiently endure your curiosity and continue reading the entire Masora until you reach the second of those locations, namely Genesis 27:33. There, you will find written in the margin the faulty note: **14 with the accent pur** (**יד בטעם פור**), when <gloss>"</gloss> it should have been written again; yet you will still search in vain for the list of locations. 

Thus, when you reach the third location where **And he said** (**ויאמר**) appears with the *Paser* accent in Genesis 27:36, even if you have not yet learned where those 14 places are, you will find a completely new and different observation recorded in the textual *Great Masora*: namely, that there are seven verses in which **And he said** is first read as *Milel* <term>Milel: A Hebrew word accented on the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable</term> and then as *Milra* <term>Milra: A Hebrew word accented on the final syllable</term>, the locations of which are said to be listed in the *Final Masora* <note>The "Masora Finalis" is an alphabetical appendix of Masoretic notes found at the end of many Rabbinic Bibles</note>. 

Led away by this reference from looking for those 14 places, now search with new zeal, my reader, to find where these seven places of this latter observation are hidden in the confused baggage of the *Final Masora*. For if you suspect that Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a famous Christian scholar of Hebrew and the Masora</note> noted anything regarding these places in his corrections, you will find your inquiry was in vain. Turn, therefore, to the *Final Masora* from the beginning up to folio 9, and you will find nothing of this there. So, proceed to folio 10; after tiring yourself out on column 1 to no avail, you will finally find, in the middle of column 2—in place of the promised index of locations for either or at least the latter observation to which the Masora of Gen. 27:36 referred you—these words written: **And he said, 14 with the accent and the signs** (**ויאמר יד בטעם וסימני'**) <gloss>m)</gloss> **transmitted in the section Ki Tisa** (**נמסר פרשה כי תשא**): *that is, **And he said** occurs with the Paser accent in 14 places, which are reviewed in the textual Masora in the Great Section of the Law, number 21, which begins at Exodus 30:11 and ends at chapter 34:35.* 

Now, therefore, read through all the Masora for those four chapters according to this indication from the *Final Masora*; or, if that seems too long or troublesome, look up at least 20 or so places starting from Exodus 30:11 with the help of a Concordance. Thus, you will seem to have achieved your wish when, at Exodus 34:9, you read not only the note in the *Small Masora* **14 with the accent pur** (**יד בטעם פור**) but you will also find the same in the *Great Masora* above the text, and furthermore, this addition: **And the signs: Take now your son; and thus he called his name; and if now I have found favor; and David was heard; and he said, let me go, for a sacrifice; and David was heard by him,** <note>These Hebrew phrases (simanim) serve as mnemonics or "catchwords" to help a scholar identify the specific verses across the Bible where the word appears with this specific accent</note>

<note>
m) For which "in the section" [b'parashah] should have been written.
</note>

**§ VII.** Indeed, so many detours were necessary to properly complete that single investigation of the 14 locations where the word **And he said** (**ויאמר**) occurs with the *Paser* <term>Paser: A Hebrew cantillation mark or "accent" that indicates a distinct pause and musical phrasing; its shape resembles a small vertical line with a hook</term> accent. However, what the Masora at Genesis 27:36 asserted regarding **And he said** (**ויאמר**) and **And he said** (**ויאמר**) occurring together in 7 places has not yet been so thoroughly investigated, but must still be sought from elsewhere. I wished to produce only one example here, from which the learned reader will easily judge regarding many other cases what remains for him to do, should he wish to undergo the labor of restoring the Masora in its entirety. For our own firsthand observation <term>αὐτοψία: "Autopsia" - the act of seeing something for oneself rather than relying on reports</term> bids us doubt that anyone has yet achieved this; and our variant readings will everywhere provide many more examples of the Masora contradicting itself.

<margin>The means of repair are shown.</margin>

**§ VIII.** Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a famous Hebraist and scholar of the Masora</note> long ago wisely advised a century ago in his *Masoretic Commentary* (p. 72, at the end) that manuscript books of the Masora must be consulted in the future. If this could have been done by him, or at least done by others, more things would undoubtedly have been edited more accurately; for that most industrious man left behind a huge "gleaning" of corrections. Manuscripts that have Masoretic notes added to the text are indeed not to be despised for this purpose, for they often successfully supply what is missing in the printed version, and vice versa; nevertheless, the Masora books written separately contribute more here, as we have learned through use from the *Erfurt Masora* <note>A famous 13th-century Hebrew Bible manuscript with extensive Masoretic notes</note> already praised above; although even it is not infallible <term>ἀנאמאrtētos: "Anamartetos" - without error or sinless; in this context, it refers to a text being free from scribal mistakes</term> and has been interpolated in places with more recent notes. It was our intention to show you a specimen of it, and at the same time a demonstration of repairing the Masora from our collated books; but we are prevented by the narrowness of the paper. Therefore, to him who, moved by the public good, [seeks] to end otherwise useless disputes, this difficult task...

<page-num>24</page-num>
<header>PREFACE</header>

to undertake this province and wish to take up the correction of the Masorah <note>The Masorah is the body of traditional notes and rules used to preserve the exact text of the Hebrew Bible.</note> fully and fruitfully, we would wish for them: leisure for this one work alone, uninterrupted for several years; tireless study; complete strength of mind and body; a judgment no less sharp; the most excellent and numerous manuscript copies of the Masorah; and assistants no less eager than they are faithful and patient in labor. For in this way, it would be entirely possible that not only might the "Small and Textual" Masorah <note>original: "parva & textualis Mafora"; these are the brief notes found in the side margins of Hebrew Bibles</note> come forth far more perfect and corrected, but also the "Great and Final" Masorah <note>original: "magna & finalis"; the more extensive notes and lists usually found at the top/bottom of pages or the end of a volume</note> might be restored to the learned world in one fitting—and not even that large—volume, arranged by way of a Concordance <note>An alphabetical index of words</note> with an added index of locations. And even if the manuscript and printed books of the Masorah themselves cannot perhaps be brought into total harmony regarding "full and defective" spellings <note>original: "plene & defective"; referring to Hebrew orthography where certain vowels are either written with a letter (full) or left out (defective)</note>, the salvation of the Church and divine truth will not depend upon that, as we have said above. The places and copies of disputed readings can be openly designated without damage or prejudice to the truth.

# CHAPTER V.

->Concerning<-

## OUR EDITION ITSELF, AND THE NOTES ADDED TO IT.

### §. I.

<margin>Transition.</margin>
We have already given above in Chapter 1 the history of our labor regarding the occasion and progress of the work and its obstacles. It remains for us to advise the reader even more specifically regarding one or two of its particular points. Indeed, I feel how many things I have passed over in the preceding pages which ought to have been said, and I seem to enter once again into a most wide-open field here; but a commanded brevity compels me to complete the remaining course of the preface more concisely.

<margin>Concerning the Hebrew text of the present edition.</margin>
§. II. As it pertains, therefore, to this edition itself, we have no doubt that it could be compared with the best, if it were permitted by one or two obstacles that could not be removed by us. For with all our zeal, as much as was in us, we gave our effort to ensure the Hebrew text would come forth as unblemished as possible. For this reason, with great care and concern, we have reviewed the copy from which the printing was made—not from our own whim or conjecture, but according to the manuscripts we compared: *a)* and on that occasion, we noticed very many errors <note>original: "sphalmata"; from the Greek for "slips" or "mistakes"</note> in even the most excellent editions, sometimes quite serious ones. These could have been pointed out if it were greatly to our reader's advantage. But we do not wish to reproach well-deserving men for anything that might be attributed to human imperfection.

---

*a)* On the other hand, things that were not manifestly faulty in the common versions, we have displayed among the variant readings, as was already said above in Chapter 1, Section 7, note *m*.

# TO THE READER #

...we ourselves have experienced proofs of <note>The Latin 'imperfectionis' is implied by the context of human error.</note> imperfection in this matter. For it is easier in these [Hebrew] letters to notice the past slips of predecessors than to be eagle-eyed enough amidst so many difficulties to prevent a new error, especially if one is distracted by many cares. Surely no one’s labor thus far has been immune from every stain—least of all his, who not long ago reproached others for such things quite immodestly and not without new 
<margin>And the flaws of this edition.</margin>
error of his own. Thus, a blemish or two has been sprinkled upon our edition, not only through the inexperience of the typesetters at the beginning of the work, but also—and most especially—by the insurmountable inconsistency of the types themselves. This was particularly true for the <term>Iod dageschati</term> <note>A Hebrew letter 'Iod' containing a 'dagesh' (a small grammatical dot). The author explains that these tiny marks often failed to print correctly or consistently.</note>: which, during the repeated reviews of the printing work, eluded all our industry until a better type for it was finally found and a remedy for this evil was prepared. Likewise, in the crowded meeting of several vowel points, accents, or <term>diacritics</term> <note>Marks added to letters to indicate pronunciation or musical cantillation.</note>, especially in a shorter word or syllable, the position of each could not always be observed with perfect precision by our type. Occasionally also, due to a flaw in either the type or the printing, the letter <term>He</term> (ה) appeared instead of <term>Het</term> (ח), and vice-versa, as was seen later in some copies. If anyone should happen to observe more such things in some copies than we have noted in the list of errors, let him not find fault so much with our diligence as with the defects of the types, the printer, and sometimes even the paper itself—indeed, let him blame the imperfection of all human things. Meanwhile, let him use the Divine Word itself with a heart grateful to God as the highest benefit. **Eusebius** <note>A 4th-century Christian historian.</note>, in his *Life of Constantine*, Book 4, Chapter 36, page 543 and following, praises the pious care of that great prince, by which he provided for the uses of the church by preparing **FIFTY VOLUMES OF SACRED BIBLES**, which were *easy to read and convenient to carry for every use* <note>original Greek: εὐανάγνωστά τε καὶ πρὸς τὴν χρῆσιν εὐμετακόμιστα</note>. But what was that gift—though most splendid for the conditions of those times—if it were compared with the so many examples which have come forth in our age in various forms and incredible numbers, and even in various languages, by the benefit of the art of printing? We are poorly grateful to God if we do not worthily employ this great aid, or if we do not highly value the most precious thing itself because of minor <term>sphalmata</term> <note>original Latin: 'sphalmata'; scribal or printing errors.</note>.

<margin>Concerning the Summaries.</margin>
§. III. The second point to be discussed here are the <term>Lemmata</term> <note>Summaries or headings placed in the margins to help readers find their place.</note>, or summaries of the sacred text. We initially added new ones to the inner margin of our volume so that no one could complain that anything had been taken from them. However, we later exchanged these for our own *Scholia* <note>Explanatory notes or commentaries.</note> at the persuasion of friends, because it seemed that more utility would flow to students from the latter than the former. And as I later applied my mind to writing the annotations far more attentively than was possible at the beginning, these easily occupied all the space. We began to compensate for the lack of summaries in the Prophets by another method, showing not only the connection and coherence of individual chapters with those preceding, but also the parts...
