# PREFACE #

...also by indicating those things pertaining to the first verse; this was especially observed in the <term>Hagiographa</term> <note>original: "Hagiographis"; the third section of the Hebrew Bible, including books like Psalms, Proverbs, and Job</note> right through to the end.

<margin>And about our annotations.</margin>
§. IV. In the third place, therefore, we must deal with our *<term>Scholia</term> <note>Brief explanatory notes or commentaries on a text</note> and annotations.* The primary occasion for these was discussed in Chapter 1, Section VIII. However, there are also other reasons which persuaded me that I should comply with the requests of my friends. For instance, there is what the illustrious *Leibniz* <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), the famous German philosopher and mathematician</note> is reported to have said to the celebrated Feller in *Hanoverian Leisure*, page 309:
> *I would wish that notes as brief and as solid on the sacred scriptures existed, such as Gothofredus produced for the Body of Law:* <note>original: "Corpus Iuris"; Jacques Godefroy (Gothofredus) was a famous jurist known for his concise and definitive legal commentaries.</note>
I myself have often wished for this same thing when I applied my mind seriously to these sacred studies, being destitute of any living guidance in this part of the holier doctrine; but I also discovered that other most famous men held the same in their prayers. Thus, among more recent scholars, *Dr. Johannes Fechtius* in his Preface to *Dorsch’s* Analysis of Isaiah, after other well-said points, speaks thus:
> *Since massive books easily deter the reader, it would be desirable that, by a shorter method, the rising boredom could be countered, and every obstacle thus removed.*
Indeed, we also thought to consult the needs of our impoverished students, most of whom lack the resources to acquire a large apparatus of books. These students felt themselves helped not a little in their rapid reading of the Old Testament by the <term>parallelism</term> we indicated and our brief declaration of the words.

<margin>Concerning parallel passages.</margin>
§. V. For the *parallelism* of Scripture, of which I just spoke—if it is applied with attentive consideration of the context itself (b)—is absolutely among the most certain means of understanding it. It is, without doubt, the best and safest commentary of all, while the divine matters and words, which seem to be spoken more briefly or obscurely in one place, are proposed more clearly or more fully elsewhere by the Holy Spirit Himself. And this one aid, used alongside pious prayers and attentive inspection of the passages, has afforded us as much help in correctly understanding more difficult matters and words as almost any other, even if those other helps are not to be despised. Hence, in our notes, the primary care was given to parallelism: both *verbal parallelism*, when the root, related and derived forms, or neighboring synonyms, or even opposites and contraries are compared to more correctly recognize the genuine significance of a word and its emphasis; and *real parallelism*, when the subject matters themselves are compared, as noted in our preface to Isaiah, section 14.

<margin>On the core of the Oriental and Greek versions.</margin>
§. VI. Nor should we despise the use offered by the collation of the *ancient and Oriental versions*, especially the Greek <term>Septuagint</term> <note>original: "LXX Interpretum"; the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. This was treated specifically in a particular Dissertation recently revised and reprinted by our once most beloved collaborator <note>original: "συνεργὸς" (synergos)</note>, and now most deeply missed, Glau...

---

(b) *No other commentary will explain the truest and most genuine sense of the phrases used in sacred scripture to the pious and attentive reader as perfectly and sufficiently as the most diligent estimation of those contexts in which they are found, and the accurate comparison of the preceding and following parts,* says Wolfgang Franzius in *On the Interpretation of Scripture*, page 72.

# TO THE READER #

Deacon *M. Georg Johann Hencke* of the Glaucha church <note>Glaucha was a district in Halle, Germany, famous for its Pietist institutions where many of these scholars worked</note> has, in these very days while we write, passed away in a premature but blessed death. However, what we have brought forward from the *Eastern* versions <note>original: "Orientt."; refers to ancient translations such as the Syriac Peshitta or the Arabic versions which help clarify the Hebrew text</note> can serve as an example to students of how much more could be expected from them by someone who can devote some study to those versions after properly learning the *Hebrew* sources. Nevertheless, we have often been prevented from including more from them by other more necessary matters and by the narrowness of the space.

<margin>Doubts are addressed.</margin>
**§. VII.** Furthermore, two things must be discussed here before I proceed to the rest, which might perhaps offend our reader: 1. that our annotations appear so rare and thin in the first part of *Genesis*, and 2. that some things are nevertheless written there which might not seem entirely commendable. I respond therefore to the first point: that when we undertook this task, those delays soon occurred (according to what was said in Chapter 1, Section 5 and following), by which our study was hindered, and almost all the enthusiasm—which is most powerful in conducting business—was shaken out of us. For the magnitude of the varied and laborious work stole all our time, so that these annotations were then only a sort of <term>overweight burden</term> <note>original: "hyperpondium"; an additional load added to an already heavy task</note> of our occupations; they could certainly have been presented more fully and more polished if it had been possible through other means. You will forgive, therefore, kind reader, a meager beginning, and at least you will not be angry with us that our zeal and attention did not decrease thereafter, but was increased more and more; so much so that many things which had already been usefully written had to be deleted again because the space on the paper would not admit them. Our purpose was to keep the same pages unchangeably aligned with the editions of *Athias (edited by Leusden)*, *Clodius*, and the *Berlin edition* <note>Famous 17th-century printed editions of the Hebrew Bible that the author is using as a layout template for the convenience of scholars</note> to help the memory, until it was absolutely necessary to depart from those limits at the beginning of *Isaiah*. Would that fuller annotations had been published separately then, in the same way as was done for the <term>Hagiographa</term>! <note>The "Holy Writings," the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible, including books like Psalms and Job</note> However, when we included certain things from the ancients at the start of this work which we ourselves do not simply approve of, we did so partly because we had to hurry, and partly so that they might only provide an opportunity for us to instruct our students more correctly and fully by voice concerning that kind of interpretation—for example, at *Genesis 2:25*. Yet, because this could be a stumbling block to beginners deprived of a teacher’s living voice, we have not easily admitted such things in the following parts without adding our own judgment or warning.

# PREFACE #

...reasons, which you will see described more fully in the more extensive notes on the **Hagiographa** <note>original: "Hagiographos"; the 'Sacred Writings' or *Ketuvim*, the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible including books like Psalms, Proverbs, and Job</note> books. From these it will at least be clear that those passages of Scripture are not at all **irreconcilable** <note>original Greek: "ἀδιάλλακτα"</note>, provided that one brings to them that modesty which is due to any sensible and serious writer: that he does not rashly dictate to the sacred authors what he himself wants, but is ready to learn from them what they actually wrote.

<margin>**CHRIST is the general goal of Scripture.**</margin>
**§. IX.** Especially in the prophecies of the prophets and other sacred texts, we have made it our goal that student readers should not lose sight of **CHRIST**, the center and nucleus of all Scripture. For every pious interpreter, along with the **Blessed Luther, Schmid, Cocceius**, and others, will strive to confirm with clear reasons that what is cited from the Old Testament in the New Testament as being spoken about Christ should also be understood literally of Him, and was once so understood by the ancient Jews. This is better than the mistaken opinion of others who think these passages should be understood as referring to Christ only through a later "application." According to our small measure, we have followed this diligently, though more could be shared at another time and noted by the industrious reader. However, those curious searchers will look in vain in our notes for "novelty-seeking" views or rash opinions. Instead, those who love the **truth that leads to godliness** <note>original Greek: "τὴν κατ’ εὐσέβειαν"; a reference to Titus 1:1</note> and the simple sense of the divine word, if they apply due diligence themselves, will perhaps find more here for the confirmation of the truth through actual use than they had promised themselves at the start. In cases of notable disagreement among interpreters, we gladly use the words and authority of the **Blessed Sebastian Schmid** <note>"Blessed" (Latin: *Beatus*) was a traditional honorific for deceased scholars</note> to soften any hostility, using the very brief note **S.** or **Schm.** We have done this in such a way that we have frequently, for the benefit of beginners, added scriptural passages to which he was silently referring. This has also often been observed in the words of other authors.

<margin>**The more specific goal of the annotations.**</margin>
**§. X.** As we already hinted above in Section 4, we have especially sought in our annotations to be a help to those beginning their reading of the **Hebrew** <note>original: "Ebraicorum"</note> sources. We by no means thrust or commend such things to learned and erudite men. They will have their own means by which they can not only compensate for this meager equipment—prepared more concisely for the sake of the poor—but even far surpass it. Nor should students of sacred literature think that the depths of the sacred text are so exhausted by our notes that nothing remains for them to seek in it. Those who think so will be utterly deceived. The knowledge that is born from the constant reading of the sacred sources themselves and from one's own meditation always differs from the concepts formed only in passing from the sayings of other interpreters, just as a firm habit differs from its first beginnings. Since all the questions and difficulties that arise in the reading of Holy Scripture have not yet been fully untied even in large and proper volumes, it would be the mark of a thoughtless mind if someone, with the briefest annotations...

# TO THE READER #

...presumed that everything could be exhausted by these means. Since our condition has varied according to Chapter 1, it will not be surprising if more things must be supplied from time to time, either from living instruction or from one's own meditation and reading. Thus, for example, the more abundant notes on **1 Chronicles chapter 1** will clearly show that more things are to be observed in **Genesis chapter 10** than were written down there during that first haste. **Blessed Augustine** <note>original: "B. Augustinus"</note> says beautifully in his letter to **Volusianus** <note>Augustine’s Letter 137, written to a Roman official around 412 AD</note> not far from the beginning: *“So great is the depth of Christian writings that I would be making progress in them daily, even if I tried to learn them alone from early childhood until decrepit old age, with the greatest leisure, the highest study, and a better wit. It is not that one reaches such difficulty in those things which are necessary for salvation; but when someone has grasped the faith there—without which one cannot live piously and rightly—so many things remain to be understood by those making progress, and so many things are obscured by multiple shadows of mysteries; and such a depth of wisdom lies hidden, not only in the words in which these things are said, but also in the matters which are to be understood, that for the oldest, the sharpest, and those most burning with the desire for learning, this happens which the same Scripture has in a certain place: **When a man has finished, then he begins.**”* **Sirach 18:6.**

<margin>Concerning the method of Hebrew study.</margin>
**§. XI.** In the meantime, however, it was not at all bad for the sake of beginners <note>original: "tironibus"; literally "recruits" or novices</note> that the observations on the sacred text were written more sparingly at the beginning, more richly as the work progressed, and again more abundantly at the end. For beginners must proceed by degrees, and it will be enough from the start if—after the foundations of the **Hebrew language** are briefly but solidly grasped—they learn the words, phrases, and idioms of the sacred text in **Genesis**, and in that matter, they make use of the living and faithful instruction of a teacher. Then, indeed, if they have also solidly learned the system of the sacred **accents** or "distinctions" <note>original: "interstinctionum"; referring to the cantillation marks in Hebrew which also serve as punctuation</note>, either from our guidance or from that of others, they will proceed more easily in the following parts, many obstacles having been removed here which could have delayed a beginner's progress. However, he who has diligently listened to a teacher going before him will establish a "cursory" <note>rapid or flowing</note> reading of the entire sacred book more easily and solidly, nor will he regret his labor at the end; compare the **Preface to Isaiah §. 13. note d**.

<margin>The authors of the annotations.</margin>
**§. XII.** Just as I have written the annotations from the beginning of the sacred Book all the way to the end—except for **Jeremiah, Amos, Obadiah, Micah, Zechariah, Lamentations, and Daniel**, which acknowledge the famous relative <note>original: "Cl. Cognatum"; likely referring to Christian Benedict Michaelis</note> **C. B. MICHAELIS** as their author (whose performance I would prefer you learn by reading, for example, his **Preface to Jeremiah**, rather than through my praise)—so he also corrected the text throughout the entire Book where it was necessary, and recorded a **selection of variant readings** <note>original: "selectum variantium lectionum"</note> which are placed beneath each column, after I had led the way by example in the first few leaves. Among these, the very first of all, written at **Genesis 1:1** only for the sake of an example, is quite forced; nor does it deserve the name of a "variant reading," compare **Chapter III. §. I. note b** above. Sometimes, however, given the opportunity, something was reviewed among those small details...

...which has more importance for the illustration of truth; for example, Exodus 34:6, Deuteronomy 6:4, Joshua 21:36, 37, etc.

<margin>An Excuse.</margin>
**§. XIII.** For the rest, just as there were various judgments regarding our labor before any part of it was published, so I do not doubt that there will now be many who will either find many things lacking in it or will find fault, because some parts were occasionally produced in haste and are therefore less refined, etc. Indeed, just as we ourselves find more things lacking in these writings of ours than perhaps any critic might, we are far from hoping that we have satisfied everyone else. Many things occur here that require very accurate, long-lasting, and fixed meditation, as well as a careful comparison of matters. I frankly confess that I have not had enough natural talent for this, nor enough leisure in a most laborious kind of life. Nevertheless, to those judges who are perhaps a bit unfair, I respond not with my own words, but with those of that pious and serious theologian and most excellent interpreter of the <term>Sacred Scriptures</term> <note>original: "Scræ. S." (Sacrae Scripturae)</note>, **Blessed Johannes Brenz** <note>original: "B. Io. Brentii." Brenz (1499–1570) was a German reformer and theologian. "Blessed" (Beatus) was a common honorific for deceased respected scholars.</note>, from his own preface to the second book of Samuel, Volume II, page 200: *“I am not ignorant of how variously this kind of writing of mine is judged; one person desires brevity, another elegance of discourse. There are those who say that such writings contain more ostentation than the building up of the Church. Others cry out about other things, I know not what. But if it were enough simply to be displeased, what thing, I ask, would you undertake to do that would please everyone? And if nothing were to be approved unless it were perfect in every part, what writing would ever be worthy of the light of day? In publishing these things, I have followed the will of my friends more than my own. If this is ostentation, I do not know what kind of duty would not incur some suspicion or even blame. I have written these things not for the learned, but for those like myself, nor does any official decree exist by which anyone is forced to read them. If there be anyone,”* <note>The following is a quote from the Greek poet Hesiod.</note> **who perceives all things by himself, considering what will be better even in the end** <note>original Greek: "ὃς αὐτῷ πάντα νοήσει, φρασσάμενός τὰ κ' ἔπειτα κ' εἰς τέλος εἶσιν ἀμείνω"</note>, *“let him use his own gift for the benefit of the Church, and bring into the open what might be better. I will not only favor him, but I will also give thanks both in my own name and in the name of the Church of the Son of God. If nothing else, certainly this labor of mine will bear witness that the will to deserve well of the Church was not lacking in me.”* At the very least, good and sensible readers will not disapprove of our attempts; they will deem us worthy of pardon wherever we have slipped, if they respect our zeal to serve the studious youth. It will not grieve me—as **Blessed Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Western Church Fathers.</note> beautifully says again in *On the Trinity*, book 3—**to seek where I hesitate, nor will I be ashamed to learn where I err.** <note>original: "sicubi hæsito, quærere; nec pudebit, sicubi erro, discere."</note> And just as it is to be wished, so it is also to be hoped that God will continue to raise up learned and pious men who will devote themselves entirely to explaining the Sacred Scriptures soundly, and who will illustrate the truth from the Scriptures **spiritually** <note>original Greek: "πνευματικῶς" (pneumatikos)</note> and powerfully against the empty conjectures and corruptions of others.

<margin>An exhortation to the studious youth.</margin>
**§. XIV.** And here, before the face of God and His Church, I also exhort and warn you, most beloved students of sacred letters! Especially you who have heard us teaching, or who read these refined works for your own benefit. See again and again at what price you hold these sacred oracles! For by the grace of God, there are those among your number who receive the word of God and heavenly truth with a [sincere] 
<meta>catchword: heart</meta>

<meta>Continuity: Following the author's defense of his work's quality and his acknowledgement of potential flaws, he now addresses the reader directly regarding the spiritual attitude required to benefit from biblical study.</meta>

->### TO THE READER. ###<-

...with a good and upright heart, who give us hope that our labor will not be in vain in the future. However, there are also those who, through their own fault and to their own detriment, are blind to the most clear light of <term>evangelical truth</term> <note>original: "evangelicae veritatis," referring to the truth found in the Gospel</note> set forth from the Word of God. They do not act so that they themselves might first be instructed toward salvation through faith in Christ Jesus; rather, they only act so that they might have something to occasionally recite to others in the manner of parrots, seeking from the Word of God not what is Christ’s, but what is their own. Indeed, there are even those who either completely neglect these divine studies or apply them only to empty and useless questions with which they might disturb the church. <note>original Greek: "τὸ δὲ τέλος τῆς παραγγελίας ἐστὶν ἀγάπη..."</note> *But the goal of our instruction is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and a sincere faith. Some, having missed these, have turned aside into meaningless talk, wanting to be teachers of the law, yet understanding neither what they say nor the things about which they make confident assertions,* as the divine Apostle teaches in 1 Timothy 1:5–7. Therefore, *let everyone who calls on the name of Christ depart from impiety,* 2 Timothy 2:19, and *strive to be pure, you who carry the weapons of the Lord,* Isaiah 52:11. That is to say, let each person turn with a humble and upright mind to Him through whom the grace and truth of God have been revealed to us, and in whom all the treasures of divine wisdom are found hidden. And since a person cannot rightly set their path toward heaven by any other means than according to the divinely given Scriptures (comparing Psalm 119:9), do not neglect any opportunity that God offers you to know the truth from them. <note>original Greek: "Καὶ γὰρ ἐντεῦθεν τὰ μυρία ἐφύη κακὰ..."</note> *For from this source countless evils have arisen: from ignorance of the Scriptures. From this, the great pestilence of heresies has sprouted; from this, neglected lives; from this, fruitless labors. For just as those deprived of light cannot walk straight, so those who do not look toward the rays of the divine Scriptures are forced to sin much and continually, as they walk in the most difficult darkness. To prevent this, let us open our eyes to the brightness of the apostolic (and prophetic) words,* as **Blessed Johannes Chrysostom** <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his powerful preaching.</note> weightily and eloquently emphasizes in his preface to the Epistle to the Romans, page 2. Read them indeed with a sincere mind, ready and prepared to obey divine warnings, John 7:17. For he who does not wish to admit the Spirit of God into his breast must blame himself for the fact that he does not reach a successful understanding for his own salvation and that of others—unlike the pious and faithful searcher of the divine Word, whom the Holy Spirit leads into all necessary truth through diligent reading. <note>original Greek: "Ἡ γὰρ συνεχὴς ἀνάγνωσις..."</note> *For the continuous reading of the divine Scriptures leads to the knowledge of them. For He is truthful who said, "Seek and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you,"* as **Theophylact** <note>Theophylact of Ohrid (c. 1055–1107 AD), a prominent Byzantine commentator on the Bible.</note> has it in his preface to the Epistle to the Romans. The nature of the present undertaking prevents me from bringing forward more points that could be said here and which might have no small power to persuade.

**evangelical truth, salvation, faith, parrots, 1 Tim. 1, 2 Tim. 2, Isa. 52, Ps. 119, Johannes Chrysostom, John 7, Theophylact**

<margin>Conclusion</margin>
§ XV. To You indeed, eternal and highest **GOD, <term>T. O. M.</term>** <note>original: *Te Optime Maxime*, a title meaning "To You, the Best and Greatest." While originally a Roman address to Jupiter, Christian authors used it to honor the supreme majesty of God.</note> to whom these words and writings belong, I give immortal and never-ending thanks. Above all, I thank You that through Your Word and by the grace of the Holy Spirit, You have made me to know You, the one and true God, and Jesus Christ whom You sent as Redeemer; and that until now, in all my weakness, You have stood by me with Your help. From my heart, I acknowledge and openly profess that I am unworthy and less than all the mercies which You have shown to Your servant. For You have sustained the afflicted health of my body, and amidst many adversities, You have kept my mind tranquil in Your peace. Now, also, You have granted the long-desired end of this labor. Forgive, most Merciful **GOD**, all my failings, and do not allow the truth of Your Word to suffer any harm with any reader through my unworthiness. Rather, grant that I, and all who read these Your oracles with me, may always profit from them, from faith to faith and from virtue to virtue—until we attain that which will be perfect in that blessed and immortal life with You. Truly, for all Your grace and truth, *not to us, **LORD**, not to us; but to Your name be the praise, honor, and glory* <note>original: "non nobis, Domine, non nobis," a reference to Psalm 115:1.</note> through all ages. Amen!

verse 16. **the lights** <note>original: הַמְּאֹורֹת (Ha-Me'orot)</note> written "full" <note>original: plene; meaning written with the letter 'vav' to indicate a vowel.</note> in source 2 because it varies from others in verse 15, but our reading is proved by the Masorah of Buxtorf and Erffurt. verse 19. **fourth** <note>original: רְבִיעִי (Revi'i)</note> so source 2 and 3 usually place the *Metheg* <note>A small vertical line under a letter used as a secondary accent.</note>. **bird** <note>original: עֹוף (Oph)</note> is "defective" <note>Written without the 'vav' placeholder.</note> according to Buxtorf, Stephanus, Plantin, Vatablus, etc.; but many others and the Old Testament folio 2. a. l. write it "full." verse 24. **after its kind** <note>original: לְמִינָהּ (Le-minah)</note> source 2 and 3 place a *Mappik* <note>A dot in the letter 'he' to show it is a consonant and not a silent vowel.</note> under the 'he', also in the following verses. **and it was so** <note>original: וַיְהִי־כֵן (Vayehi-khen)</note> without the *Metheg* according to Ben Naphtali <note>A 10th-century Masoretic scholar.</note>. verse 26. **man in our image and in our likeness** <note>original: אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ וּבִדְמוּתֵנוּ</note> thus the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>; the elders preferred to change it; see above at verses 1, 6, 21, 7. verse 29. **and [the fruit]** <note>original: וְאֶת</note> marked with *Tseré* <note>a vowel mark</note> and *Darga* <note>a cantillation mark/musical accent</note>. **it shall be** <note>original: יִהְיֶה</note> here the *Metheg* is in 1, 2, 3, and the Bomberg edition at verse 30.

<note>This section contains technical Masoretic and grammatical notes for scholars.</note>

*v. 2. g)* **And God finished on the day** so in the Hebrew and Samaritan versions, and so the 72 elders <note>The Septuagint</note> changed it, as above in chapter 1, verses 1 and 26. *v. 4.* **Generations** Why here and in Ruth 4:18 it is written in the full form <note>with the letter Vav</note>, see <gloss>as in the Tanchuma, folio 1, column 4, near the end.</gloss> **When they were created** <gloss>small He</gloss>—here it is equal to the other letters, but with a note on the **He** in versions 1, 2, and 3 of Bomberg and the Erfurt Masorah; and thus without a note in Stephanus and Plantin versions. *v. 6.* **All of it** [is written] with the vowels Tsere and Metheg according to Ben Asher. *v. 7.* **The ground** Metheg instead of Munach in versions 1, 2, 3; likewise in v. 9. **Garden** *v. 8.* with the mark Merca in 1, 2, 3; with the vowel Kamets in 3. *v. 9.* **And the tree** with Merca in 1, Buxtorf, etc., but the Great Scheph marks it as O.T. folio 2, side a. *v. 14.* **And the name** with the mark Kadma in 1, 2, 3, Barol, etc., but with Makkaph in the O.T. *v. 16.* **Of every tree** 1, 2, 3; so also Ben Naphtali and Bomberg.

### Critical Notes on the Hebrew Text
*verse* 18. **לֹא** (Not) — with a <term>Metheg</term> <note>a vertical stroke indicating secondary stress</note> in the Berlin editions 12, 17, 18. | *verse* 19. **וַיִּצֶר** (And He formed) — with a doubled <term>Tlisha</term> <note>a specific musical accent</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and almost always in following words where the stress is on the second-to-last syllable. | **אֶל־הָאָדָם** (to the man) — <term>Metheg</term> instead of <term>Munach</term> <note>a different accent</note> in manuscript 2; likewise in Chapter 3:22, etc. | *verse* 20. **לֹא** (Not) — without a <term>Metheg</term> in manuscripts 2, 3, 15. | *verse* 22. **הַצֵּלָע** (the rib) — thus with a <term>Kamets</term> <note>vowel sign for 'ah'</note>, correctly in Berlin manuscripts z, 6, 9, 12, 17, 18. Other versions use a <term>Patach</term> <note>short 'a' sound</note> and similarly a <term>Raphe</term> <note>a soft-breathing mark</note> over the letter Kaph in manuscript 1. Also in manuscript 2, it appears with a <term>Dagesh</term> <note>a dot indicating doubling</note> preceded by a <term>Metheg</term>. | *verse* 23. **לֻקֳחָה** (she was taken) — with the explicit Ara Masorah <note>marginal notes on the Hebrew Bible</note> in manuscript 1 and Erfurt 50. T. | *verse* 23. **לָקַח** (He took)... | *Chapter III, verse 3.* **אֱלֹהִים** (God) — with a <term>Sakeph-katon</term> <note>a specific pause accent</note> in manuscript u; so also in manuscript 1, contrary to other Old Testament texts. | **בּוֹ** (in it) — with a <term>Mercha</term> <note>a connecting accent</note> in manuscripts 1 and 3. | But there is a <term>Maqqeph</term> <note>a hyphen connecting words</note> in the margin of manuscript Aleph (^א). | *verse* 6. **כִּי** (that) — with a <term>Maqqeph</term> in the Codex Crispini 1 and 2, and in printed editions. | **הוּא** (it/he) — as found in the <term>Kethiv</term> <note>the written text, as opposed to what is read aloud</note>.

<note>The following notes are technical details regarding the Hebrew text's punctuation, accents, and spelling used by scholars and scribes (the Masoretes).</note>

\* verse 10. **Your voice** (קֹלְךָ) is written in the "full" spelling (plene). Verses 10, 13, 14. \* **Naked** (עֵירֹם) has a "suspended" letter Ayin: according to Masora 1. — \* verse 11. **And he said** (וַיֹּאמֶר) has a Rebia accent in margin 1. **You ate** (אָכַלְתָּ) has a Patach vowel; so in Masora 4. — \* verse 13. **The woman** (הָאִשָּׁה) uses a Munach accent in place of a Metheg in several manuscripts. — \* verse 14. **God** (אֱלֹהִים) uses a Pashmunachatum accent; so in the Old Testament. — \* verse 15. **He** (הוּא) has a Maqqef (hyphen). — \* verse 16. **Greatly** (הַרְבָּה) is without a Dagesh (emphasis dot) in some versions, contrary to the standard Old Testament. **I will greatly multiply your pain and your conception**. — \* verse 17. **You shall eat it** (תֹּאכֲלֶנָּה) has a simple Sheva vowel in some traditions (Ben Naphtali) but a Chateph-patach in others (Ben Asher). — \* verse 19. **You** (אַתָּה) is stressed on the last syllable in some versions, but the Masora prefers the penult. — \* verse 20. **The man** (הָאָדָם) has the prefix removed in one manuscript. — \* verse 22. **She** (הִוא) written with a 'vav' instead of a 'yod' as is very frequent. — \* verse 24. **To guard the way of the tree**... with a Metheg accent according to the "En Hakkore" grammarians.

**Technical Notes on the Hebrew Text:**

Verse 2: **And in all** <note>Hebrew: "u-ve-khol"</note>—The letter *Vav* is written with a *Metheg* accent according to the scholar Ben Asher. Verse 3: **Which is** <note>Hebrew: "asher hu"</note>—In verse 2, it is noted as such in the first margin. **Behold, I** <note>Hebrew: "hin'ni"</note>—In verse 9, marked with a *Mercat* accent in the Ber. manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9; but the others, including the Old Testament <note>likely referring to a specific edition</note>, use a *Darga* accent. Verse 11: **And there shall not be** <note>Hebrew: "ve-lo yihyeh"</note>—Written without a *Metheg* accent in manuscripts 1 and 2. Verse 12: **This is the sign** <note>Hebrew: "zot ot"</note>—Marked with a *Mahpach* preceding a *Munach* accent. Verse 12: **Which** <note>Hebrew: "asher"</note>—Marked with a *Pik munach*; many printed editions go against the Old Testament standard here. **Which for generations** <note>Hebrew: "asher ledorot"</note>—In verse 13, the word **with you** <note>Hebrew: "it'chem"</note> goes against the Masora <note>traditional scribal rules</note>. **Everlasting** <note>Hebrew: "olam"</note>—In verse 12, this is lacking in manuscript 1. Verse 14: **In my clouding** <note>Hebrew: "be-an'ni"</note>—The letter *Nun* is marked with a simple *Shuva* in Bevol 3 and the Midelianus manuscript; but all others, including the manuscripts in the Old Testament, write it with a *Chateph-patach* vowel. Verse 15: **Shall be** <note>Hebrew: "yihyeh"</note>—Marked with a *Makkaph* in manuscript 3. Verse 17: **I have established** <note>Hebrew: "hekimoti"</note>—The syllable *Ki* is written in full in some printed editions, but is deficient <note>spelled without the letter Yod</note> in the rest and the Old Testament according to the Masora of Leviticus 26:9.

### CRITICAL NOTES ON ACCENTS AND READINGS

Verse 19. **The sons** <note>Hebrew: B'nei</note>: thus in all manuscripts except the Berlin and 3rd editions, which have the Munach accent. Verse 23. **Not** <note>Hebrew: Lo</note>: with the Merca accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, etc.
Verse 26. **The God of** <note>Hebrew: Elohei</note>: with the accent on the last syllable <note>Milra</note> in 10, 13, 14, contrary to the Masorah. Verse 27. **In the tents of** <note>Hebrew: Be-oholei</note>: with the Munach accent on the second-to-last syllable <note>Milel</note> in edition 3. Verse 28. **And he lived** <note>Hebrew: Vayechi</note>: with the Merca accent on the last syllable in edition 3. Verse 29. **Three hundred** <note>Hebrew: Shelesh Me'ot</note>: with the Munach accent and Maqqeph <note>hyphen</note> in edition 3. Verse 29. **And he was** <note>Hebrew: Vayehi</note>: in the singular in Berlin manuscript 7, 11, 17; thus also in 1, 2, according to Masorah 1, 7, 8, and the Erfurt manuscript, as well as the Old Testament fragment 3.a and the printed Masorah on Genesis 5:23. The others read **And they were** <note>Hebrew: Vayihyu</note> in the plural; thus in the margin of edition 2. CHAPTER 10, Verse 2. **And Tubal** <note>Hebrew: Ve-Tubal</note>: written with the full vowel <note>plena</note> in 1, 2, 3 and the H. volume. Verse 3. **Gomer**: with the Sakeph-Qaton accent preceded by Munach in 1 and formerly in 2. **And Togarmah**: written with the full vowel in 1, 2, 3. Verse 5. **The coastlands of the nations in their lands**: with the accent on the last syllable in 2. Verse 5. **Every one according to his language**: with the Rebia accent in 1, 2, 3, 15. Verse 7. **Cush**: with the Munach accent in several printed editions, but the Pascha accent is preferred in 1, 2, 8 and the Old Testament. Verse 8. **Nimrod**: written with full spelling with a note in 1; thus in the Masorah Magna on Genesis 11:14. Verse 9. **And he said**: Munach instead of Metheg in 1, 2. **Like Nimrod**: with the Sakeph-Qaton accent in 6, 8; Merca in 1, 3. Verse 9. **Mighty**: with the Maqqeph and Metheg in 3, 6, 7, 8, etc.; with the Merca accent in Berlin, 1, 3, Erfurt 1, 17, 8.

Critical notes on the Hebrew text: In verse 14, Pathrusim and Casluhim are written "plene" <note>with extra vowels</note> in two manuscripts. In verse 16, several manuscripts add "and the Girgashite and the Amorite" but with a Patach <note>a short 'a' vowel</note> in verses 17 and 18. Regarding the "Arkite" in verse 17, the letter He has a Kamets <note>a long 'a' vowel</note> in our printed editions, which was also observed by other scholars. In verse 19, "Admah" is written without a prefix in three sources. The word "Zeboiim" appears in the main text of two manuscripts and once in the Masoretic notes as a <term>Keri</term> <note>the traditional reading versus the written spelling</note>. In verse 20, the order is "by their families, by their tongues, in their lands." Verse 32 notes "according to their generations" is deficient in two or three volumes. In Chapter 11:2, "and it happened" and "they found" are joined by a Makkeph <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in certain traditions. In verse 5, the phrase "to see the city" has a word transposition in one manuscript.

Verse 29. **Nahor**: written without the letter *Vav* in manuscripts 1 and 2, following the *Masora* <note>The tradition of notes protecting the biblical text</note> in 1, 2, and the Erfurt manuscript. **Sarai**: The letter *Resh* is marked with a *Patach* vowel in Berlin manuscripts 6, 9, 17, 18; the rest use a *Kametz* vowel according to manuscripts 1, 2, 3 and the Erfurt Masora. **Avi** (Father of): without a *Metheg* <note>a secondary accent mark</note> in 1 and 2. Verse 30. **Valad** (child): the letter *Lamed* has a *Patach* vowel according to its Masora in 1 and 2, and the Erfurt manuscript. Verse 31. **Sarai**: a *Patach* vowel under the letter *Resh*, contrary to the Masora in manuscripts 7 and 8; this is approved in the *Or Torah* folio 3b. Verse 32. **In Haran**: written with an "inverted *Nun*" in manuscript 8 with a note; manuscript 7 has this too. This is the view of Rashi and Rabbi Shimshon in *Or Torah* folio 3b, although that work itself does not approve of it. CHAPTER 12, verse 7. **To your seed**: with a *Metheg* in manuscripts 2 and 3 and in the margins of 1 and 8. Verse 8. **To Bethel**: written as one word in 1, 2, and 3. Likewise **Bethel** here and in chapter 13:3.

**Philological Notes:**
Verse 7: **all of** marked with Merca and Tifcha accents beneath the Aleph, as noted by Buxtorf etc., contrary to the Old Testament folio 4. a. 1. **the Amorite** with a Metheg accent instead of a Munach.
Verse 8: **he** marked with Munach in editions 2 and 3.
Verse 10: **and they fell** with a Metheg accent before the Patach vowel in editions 1 and 2.
Verse 12: **and they took** marked with Grahaim in edition 2. **his property** spelled fully in 2 and 3, contrary to the Masoretic text.
Verse 13: **that** with a Merca accent preceding a Maqqaf in edition 1.
Verse 15: **against them** without a Pasek in Buxtorf, but contrary to the Masoretic text and the Erfurt manuscript.
Verse 16: **the property** spelled fully in 2 and 3, contrary to the Masoretic text.
Verse 19: **Possessor** with a Segol vowel in 1, 2, and 3; and in Verse 22, **Possessor** spelled fully in edition 3.
Verse 20: **and he gave** but with a Metheg accent in 1 and 2.
Verse 23: **and even to a strap** in 1, 2, and 3.

\* V. 14. **And he went out**: accented on the penultimate syllable in Buxtorf and Berlin editions; all others accent the final syllable. V. 15. **who are found**: spelled fully with the letter Vav. V. 16. **And he lingered**: there are variants in the writing; a Metheg <note>a small vertical stroke used as a secondary accent</note> is placed under the Vav by Bomberg etc., under the Yod by Leusden, and under the following Mem with a Chateph-patach vowel. Three versions lack the Metheg. The ending **-mah** is without a Mappik <note>a dot in the letter He indicating it should be pronounced</note> in two versions. The Masorah and Erffurt manuscripts, following Kimchi and Spanish codices, use the Kametz vowel; Leusden and the Berlin edition use the Patach vowel. It is correctly written with a Psik mark in Bomberg and others, although the Masorah argues against the Psik, a point sharply refuted by other scholars. V. 17. **as they brought them out**: spelled with a Dagesh <note>an emphasis dot</note> in the letter Kaf in several versions. V. 21. **to him**: marked with a Zakef-Katon accent in the Bomberg and Berlin editions; others use a Revia accent. **My overthrowing**: with a Dagesh in the letter Kaf in multiple manuscripts and the Masorah.

<note>The following are technical notes on the Hebrew script and variations found in different historical manuscripts.</note>
v. 6. **To me** <note>Hebrew: "li"</note> with a *Dagesh* <note>a grammatical dot</note> in the Berlin manuscript, but others are without it, and with a *Raphe* <note>a line indicating a soft sound</note> in copies 1, 2, and 3. v. 7. **She nursed**. v. 10. **And she saw** with a *Munach* <note>a musical accent</note> and **Sarah** with a *Rebia* <note>another accent</note> in copy 3. **Mocking** with the letter *Chet* having a *Segol* vowel in copy 2; thus also in the *Masora of Erfurt*. v. 15. **And she cast** with a *Paschta* accent in copies 1 and 2. **The shrubs** as in copy 2. **Like bowshots** <note>a spelling variation</note> in the Bomberg, Stephens, and Hutter editions. v. 16. **In the death** in copies 1 and 2; written **defectively** <note>missing a vowel letter</note> in the Stephens, Plantin, and Hutter editions. v. 17. **Her voice** contrary to the *Masora* of the others.

v. 1. *to him* [אֵלָיו] with the accent <term>Tbhir</term> preceded by <term>Darga</term> in two [sources]. v. 2, 3, 17, 18. The Berlin [edition] and the Old Testament folio 5. a. have this; the others have the accent <term>Kadma</term>.
*for you* [לָכֶם] in v. 5 with the accent <term>Tbhir</term> in [manuscripts] 8, 11, 15, 16, instead of <term>Merca</term>, which the [standard] Old Testament requires. v. 7. *here I am* [הִנְנִי] with the <term>Maqqeph</term> [connecting hyphen] in 6, 7, 8 etc., contrary to the Old Testament.
v. 8. *And he said* [וַיֹּאמֶר] with <term>Munach</term> in 1. *God* [אֱלֹהִים] with <term>Zaqeph Gadol</term> in 1, 2, 6, 9; but with <term>Revia</term> in the margin of 1. *He will provide* [יִרְאֶה] with the <term>Metheg</term> [stress mark] in all printed editions, and thus found in the margin of a certain manuscript by Menahem in the Old Testament; but without <term>Metheg</term> in all [other] Old Testaments and our manuscripts. v. 9. *and he arranged the wood and he bound Isaac his son and he placed him*... thus also in v. 11, but instead of the Name [the LORD] it has "God" without vowel points in two [manuscripts]. v. 13. *and behold* [וְהִנֵּה] with <term>Munach</term> in 1. *caught* [נֶאֱחַז] with <term>Zaqeph Gadol</term> in 1, 2, 3, 17, the Berlin [edition], and the Old Testament; the others with <term>Qamets</term>. *In the thicket* [בַּסְּבַךְ] with <term>Qamets</term> in 8, 11, etc. and the <term>Masorah</term> in 7, 8, against the Old Testament.

**Critical Notes on the Hebrew Text:**

**Verse 9.** <note>original: "בְּכֶסֶף מָלֵא"</note> "for the full price" marked with a Munach accent; <note>original: "מָלֵא"</note> "full" has a Rebia accent in manuscripts 7, 8, 10, 13, and 14, though the Old Testament [scholarly edition] rejects this. <note>original: "בְּתוֹכְכֶם"</note> "in your presence" is written defectively (missing a vowel letter). **Verse 11.** <note>original: "שְׁמָעֵנִי"</note> "hear me" has a Rebia accent in the margin of manuscript 1; also in verse 15. **Verse 12.** <note>original: "עַם הָאָרֶץ"</note> "the people of the land" has a Merca accent in manuscripts 2 and 3. **Verse 13.** <note>original: "אַךְ אִם־אַתָּה"</note> "if only you" uses a Merca accent; <note>original: "אַתָּה"</note> "you" has a double Maqqeph [hyphen] in manuscript 1. **Verse 17.** <note>original: "עֶפְרוֹן"</note> "Ephron" is written defectively in manuscript 3, as noted by the Masora to Genesis 50:13. <note>original: "אֲשֶׁר בַּשָּׂדֶה"</note> "which was in the field" in verses 17 and 18, and the Berlin manuscript; others have <note>original: "אֲשֶׁר"</note> "which" with a Munach. **Verse 18.** Instead of <note>original: "בְּכֹל"</note> "in all," manuscript 3 has <note>original: "לְכֹל"</note> "to all," but this contradicts the printed Masora for verse 10. **Verse 19.** <note>original: "עַל־פְּנֵי"</note> "before/facing" is preceded by <note>original: "אֲשֶׁר"</note> "which" in manuscripts 2 and 3, against the printed Masora and the Erfurt manuscript. **Chapter 24, Verse 2.** <note>original: "בְּכֹל"</note> "in all" uses a Munach in manuscript 1, following the 'En Hakkore' [grammatical treatise]. **Verse 3.** <note>original: "וְאַשְׁבִּיעֲךָ"</note> "and I will make you swear" has a Rebia in manuscript 3 and in the margin of 1. <note>original: "אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי יוֹשֵׁב"</note> "among whom I dwell" [is written thus]. **Verse 4.** <note>original: "אִשָּׁה לִבְנִי"</note> "a wife for my son" appears thus in manuscript 2.

<note>The following are technical grammatical notes regarding the Hebrew Masoretic text (the traditional Hebrew notation system).</note>
verse 41. **from my oath** [mialati] contains a Metheg <note>a small vertical line used as a stress mark</note> instead of a Munach <note>a music/accent mark</note>. **not** [lo] has a Paschta accent and **they give** [yitnu] has a Munach. verse 46. **and she lowered** [vattored] is written defectively <note>missing a letter usually present</note> contrary to the Masorah <note>tradition of scribal notes</note> at verse 38. **and also** [ve-gam] has a Merca accent contrary to the Masorah at verse 14. verse 47. **and I placed** [va-asim] is written fully in the Stephens and Hutter editions contrary to the Masorah. verse 49. **and if not** [ve-im lo] has a Paschta accent but a Sakeph-gadol <note>a major pause mark</note> is in the margin. verse 50. **from the Lord** [mi-Yehovah] is without a Shva <note>a vowel sign indicating a very short sound</note> under the Yod in the 3rd and Bomberg editions. verse 52. **and it was** [vayehi] has a Rebia accent. verse 54. **and they drank** [vayishtu] has a Sakeph-katon accent.

### Scholarly Notes on the Hebrew Text

<margin>verse 9. **The Hittite**: marked with a Munach accent instead of a Metheg in the editions of Bomberg, Buxtorf, and Stephanus, though this contradicts other Masoretic traditions.</margin>
<margin>**And he dwelt** verse 11: uses the Darga accent, and **Isaac** uses the Tebhir accent, as noted in the margins.</margin>
<margin>verse 14. **And Dumah**: written with an Aleph at the end in the Venice and Buxtorf margins according to other manuscripts, though this is cited as incorrect in other Masoretic notes.</margin>
<margin>verse 15. **Hadad**: uses a Kametz vowel. Note that the final letter is a Daleth in many editions (Leusden, Clodius, Berlin), as well as the Samaritan, Arabic, and the Greek Complutensian Polyglot. Others read it as a Resh, including the Chaldean (Targum), Syriac, and Latin Vulgate.</margin>
<margin>verse 16. **Princes**: written in full form (with a Yod), contradicting the Masorah on Genesis 17:20. verse 22. **Why am I thus?**</margin>

**Textual Notes:**
In verse 10, the word for "almost" (*kim'at*) has a Revi'a accent in 3 sources. In verse 12, the word for "that" (*hahu*) is written with a Yod in 2 sources and several printed editions, contrary to the Great Masorah fol. 5 b. In verse 16, there is a Munach accent on the first word; the word "from us" (*me'immanu*) has a Munach instead of a Metheg in 2 sources. In verse 18, "wells" (*be'erot*) is written in the full spelling (*plene*) contrary to the printed Masorah; verse 18 is also written this way against the Masorah in manuscript and print. In verse 22, the phrase "for now" (*ki 'attah*) follows Ben Asher. In verse 24, "and I will multiply" (*ve-hirbeti*) is in the defective spelling in 3 sources, against the Masorah and the Erfurt manuscript. In verse 25, "he pitched" (*vayet*) has a Tsere, Metheg, and Maqqeph; but at the end of the Metheg in 14, 17. By Merca in 3, 3; the rest by Segol and Maqqeph. "His tent" (*oholeh*) is written with a 'He' at the end in sources 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 15, and 16. The Meserethic books also vary, and this place in the Great Masorah could be marked with a Vav. In verse 26, "his friend" (*mere'ehu*) has a Munach instead of a Metheg in sources 1 and 2.

**Technical Textual Notes:**
verse 11: The word for "hairy" <note>original: 'sa'ir'</note> is written plainly here, against the Masoretic tradition. verse 14: "and he went" uses a specific musical accent <note>Munach</note>; "he loved" and "as" also have specific traditional accents. verse 15: "the great/eldest" is written against the usual Masoretic printing. verse 18: "and he said" does not have the expected accent mark. verse 19: "for the sake of" is missing a letter compared to other Masoretic versions. verse 21: "come near" and "that I may feel you" have specific accents. verse 25: "in order that" and "may bless you" have specific accents; "and he brought" is accented on the last syllable according to the grammarian *En hakkore*. verse 26: "and kiss" — the first letter has a specific vowel mark in most books according to the Masoretic note on Genesis 2, 12. verse 28: "and he shall give" has a specific accent in other versions. verse 29: "be [lord]" has a specific vowel mark in various Spanish and Jerusalem manuscripts.

The text includes extensive scholarly notes on Hebrew accents, vowels, and ancient translations like the Targum Jonathan.</summary>

Verse 31. *to his father* [la-aviv] marked with Sakeph-Katon accent. *you may bless me* [tevarakhani] with a Dagesh at the end. Verse 32. *and he said* [vayomer] marked with Sakeph-Gadol accent. Verse 38. *and bless me* [u-varkheni] with a simple Shva vowel. *The blessing* [ha-berakhah] with a Kamets vowel. Verse 37. *What* [mah]. Masorah mentions Exodus 34, 9. Marginal note for verse 42 mentions *and she sent* [va-tishlach] against the Masorah. Verse 41. *he blessed him* [berakho]. Verse 40. *his voice* [qolo]. Verse 46. *I am weary* [qatzti] with a minuscule Koph; manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, etc., do not have it in the text, yet most note it as required by the Masorah of Leviticus 1, 1.

<summary>This page lists the births and naming of Jacob's first eight sons (Reuben through Asher), explaining the Hebrew wordplay behind each name as a reflection of the mothers' rivalry. It also begins the narrative of the mandrakes, a plant believed to aid fertility, which Rachel trades to Leah in exchange for time with Jacob.</summary>

Following the birth of Leah’s first four sons, the text now details the births of Issachar and Zebulun, Leah’s daughter Dinah, and finally Rachel’s first son, Joseph. The second half of the page marks a shift in the story as Jacob completes his fourteen years of service for his wives and begins negotiating a new contract for his own wages, focusing on the speckled and spotted livestock.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the account of Jacob’s service to Laban. On the previous page, Jacob and Laban negotiated a new wage: Jacob would keep all the speckled, spotted, and dark-colored animals born from the flocks. This page details Jacob’s clever—if controversial—breeding techniques to ensure his share of the flock became the strongest and most numerous, leading to his immense wealth and the subsequent jealousy of Laban’s sons.</meta>

v. 35. *the speckled* <note>original: "ha-nekuddot"</note> spelled deficiently <note>referring to Hebrew spelling without certain vowels</note> in Manuscript 1 and its Masorah, which Masorah 2, 7, and 8 contradict. The Erfurt Masorah contains both, but by a different hand. * v. 37. *in them* <note>original: "ba-hen"</note> with the vowel Segol in Manuscripts 3, 12, 17, 18 and the Berlin manuscript; but the rest have Tsere according to Masorah 2 and the final Masorah. * v. 40. *and he gave* <note>original: "wa-yitten"</note> with the accent Tifcha-katanna in Manuscript 1. * v. 41. *that they might breed* <note>original: "le-yachmennah"</note> the letter Mem has the vowel Tsere without a following Dagesh in Manuscript 1, consistent with Masorah 1, 2, Erfurt, and the Old Testament. Some in the Mikraot Gedolot prefer Segol. * v. 42. *and when they were faint* <note>original: "u-be-ha’atiph"</note> <note>The letter 'Pe' (פ) is printed larger in the original.</note> A large letter Pe is found in Manuscripts 3, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 16, 19 according to the printed Masorah for Genesis 1:1, but unlike the others, Masorah 1, 2, 3, and Erfurt do not have it here; nor does the initial Masorah of 1 Chronicles 1, nor twelve other manuscripts in the Old Testament. * v. 43. *and he increased... and menservants and maidservants*—so in Manuscript 2. It places the masculine term first as being more worthy. CHAPTER XXXI, 2. *as before* <note>original: "ki-temol"</note> spelled deficiently in 1, 7, 8, etc., with Masorah 1, 7, 8; but the rest spell it fully according to the Old Testament. * v. 5. *to them* <note>original: "la-hen"</note> with the vowel Tsere in 1, 6, 9, contrary to the Masorah for Ezekiel 23, 36.

*℣. 10. "And they conceived" with the Kamets vowel in manuscripts 2 and 3. "And they were weak" with the Sakeph accent preceded by Munach under v. 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, contrary to the Old Testament folio 5. b. "The rams" written in full spelling in manuscript 2, contrary to the Masorah of Erffurt. "And the livestock" adds the prefix "and" in 3. "To come" in defective spelling in 1 and 2. ℣. 24. "And he came" thus in ℣. 29 with the prefix "and" in 3; which, conversely, was omitted in the following verse in "and he overtook." ℣. 25. "And he went down."*

<note>This section contains technical scholarly notes on the Hebrew text variants found in different historic manuscripts.</note>
* Verse 7: *Vayira* ("and he feared")—Ends with a *Metheg* <note>a secondary accent mark</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, and 3. Verse 11: *Katonti* ("I am small")—marked with a *Revia* accent in manuscripts 2 and 3, and in the margin of 1. Verse 16: *Va-ayarim* ("and foals")—here the letter *Ayin* has a *Shva* vowel in manuscripts 2 and 17, and according to the Ben Hayyim and Michaelis editions, following Spanish codices and Kimchi's grammar. Furthermore, the word is spelled "defectively" <note>missing a vowel letter</note> in manuscripts 7 and 8, but "plene" <note>full spelling</note> in 1 and 2. Verse 18: *U-fegashcha* ("and he meets you")—here the *ga* syllable lacks a *Metheg* in manuscripts 3, 7, 10, through 15, 19, and the Berlin and Ben Asher editions; but it has a *Metheg* in 1, 2, 6, 8, 9, 17, 18. It appears with a double *Metheg* in 1, 6, 9, 17, 18. The letter *Gimel* is marked with a *Rafe* or lacks a *Dagesh* <note>a dot indicating doubling or hardening</note> in several sources. Verse 20: *Gam et-kol* ("also all")—appears with the prefix *ve-* ("and") and a *Pashta* accent in manuscript 3, contrary to the Masora. The word *Ha-holchim* ("those walking") has a *Metheg* instead of a *Munach* accent in 17, 18. *Bimtzacha-chem* ("when you find") is spelled fully in manuscript 2.

<note>Translator's notes on textual variants:</note>

Verse 21. "And afterward": כך is written this way in sources 1, 2, 3 and the Halle manuscript. Verse 22. "And he": marked with a <term>Makkaph</term> <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in the text, but noted as <term>Tbhirt</term> in the margin. Verse 27. "And he said": instead of the <term>Munach</term> accent, it has a double <term>Pashta</term> in source 1. Verse 30. "This": written with a <term>Dagesh</term> <note>an emphasis dot</note> in sources 2, 3, 6, 9; the Berlin manuscript correctly follows the Old Testament format. Verse 31. Before "there," source 1 places the word "the" <note>Hebrew: *et*</note>, contrary to the Masorah; after "the place," source 2 and the Erfurt manuscript add "it is," but without vowel points. CHAPTER 33. Verse 1. "And behold": has a <term>Munach</term> accent in 1, 2, 17 and the Berlin manuscript; others use a <term>Makkaph</term> except source 3. Verse 4. "His neck": written with the letter <term>Yod</term> in source 2, against the Masorah. Regarding "and he kissed him," source 2 has seven three-toothed marks instead of dots; the Old Testament requires six dots, one for each letter, which according to Hiller (p. 153) signifies a variant reading of the entire word. Verse 5. "To you": has a <term>Dagesh</term> in 1, 2, 17, 18 and Berlin; others omit it against the Old Testament.

**Textual Notes on the Hebrew Verses:**

**v. 5. held his peace:** written in full <note>meaning with the vowel letter *yod* included</note> in 17 manuscripts and the Berlin edition; the second future form, against the Masorah. Elsewhere, our 4th Manuscript begins here.
**v. 7. were grieved:** written without the *Metheg* accent in the 3rd manuscript.
**v. 11. her brothers:** the letter *Aleph* is marked with a *Kamets* vowel in manuscripts 3 and 4; so expressed.
**v. 14. to them:** written defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> in manuscripts 3 and 4; second future form, against the Masorah in this place and at the end of folio 8, column 7.
**with us:** i.e., written in full in manuscripts 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15 and the Halle edition; second future, against the Old Testament folio 6. a. 2. and the Masorah 7, 8 in this place and in Genesis 24:60.
**v. 15. only:** marked with a *Merca* accent in manuscript 1 and 3.
**if:** marked with a *Makkaph* <note>a hyphen-like connector</note> in manuscripts 2, 3, 4, 6, 9. Marked with *Makkaph* and *Ithibh* accents.
**to be circumcised:** written in full in manuscripts 3 and 4, against the Masorah in this place and at the end of folio 45. d.
**v. 17. to be circumcised:** the final Masorah on folio 45, column 4, requires the defective spelling, undoubtedly confusing this place with verse 15; this is against the textual Masorah in 1, 7, 8 and the Erfurt manuscript.
**v. 19. honored:** marked with a *Patach* vowel in manuscript 3, against the Masorah.
**v. 20. and they spoke:** the letter *Vav* prefix is marked with a *Metheg* accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, etc.
**v. 21. behold, [it is] large:** so it is, namely: "broad-handed."

v. 16. The word **she had hard labor** <note>Hebrew: *Vatekash*</note> is marked with the *Tiphcha* accent following *Zakeph-katon* with *Munach* in manuscripts 1, 2, and 4.
v. 12. The word **And they were** <note>Hebrew: *Veyihyu*</note> is marked with the *Revia* accent in manuscripts 7 and 8 and many printed editions; so it was in 3, but this is against the Masora of Erfurt and 4 in this place, and against the printed Masora as well as the manuscript at Genesis 10:19; likewise against the Older Testament, folio 6a.
v. 22. The word **that** <note>Hebrew: *Haha-hi*</note> is marked with *Zakeph* and also *Segolta*, and the preceding word **Israel** has *Pashta* and *Zarka* in a certain Spanish codex in the Older Testament.
The name **Reuben** is correctly marked in manuscripts 1, 2, and 17 according to the Older Testament; but in 3 (which also has simple accents in the following words) and 4, it has the *Revia* accent; the rest have *Zakeph*.
The name **Israel** is correctly marked in 2, 4, etc. (with manuscript 14 adding the *Sof-pasuk* [end-of-verse] mark). The doubling of accents seems to have arisen from the diversity of codices, some of which made one verse and others two verses out of this passage, as noted by the famous Hiller in his Preface on the *Keri* and *Ketiv* <note>Traditional variants in how the Bible is read vs. written</note>, and the Older Testament in the cited place.

**Critical Apparatus:**
<note>This section notes technical variations in the spelling and vowel markings (niqqud) found in different historical manuscripts.</note>

v. 27. **He-Arba** <note>original: "הארבע"</note> written with the vowel *Kamets* in manuscripts 1, 3, and 4; with the *Metheg* accent in 2, 3. Verse 4, but **Abraham** <note>original: "אברהם"</note> in verses 6, 9.

CHAPTER 36, 1. **Toledot** <note>original: "תלדות" — "Generations"</note> thus according to most following the Masorah <note>The traditional scribal notes for the Hebrew Bible</note> 7, 8 in this place and at the end of Chapter 35, column 7. This seems supported by the Erfurt manuscript, but written as **Toledot** <note>original: "תולדות"</note> in 3, 4, etc. according to Masorah 4. Finally, the Masorah 1 & 2 placed it twice without the vowel letter *vav* (**תלדות**). v. 7. **Rekush** <note>original: "רכוש" — "Wealth"</note> written defectively [missing a letter] in the margin of 7, 8, against the Old Testament [textual tradition]. **Miknehem** <note>original: "מניהם" — "Their livestock"</note> written defectively with the letter *Yod* erased in 1, Halle 3, against Masorah 7, 8, which however observe it is found that way in other books. v. 10. **Eliphaz** <note>original: "אליפז"</note> with a *Kamets* in 3, 10, 14, etc., against Masorah 1 and Erfurt. v. 14. **Vayalam** <note>original: "ויעלם"</note> thus in 2, 8, 13, 15, against the standard text. v. 15. **Teman** <note>original: "תימן"</note> thus in all manuscripts, also 6, 9, 17, 18, etc.

**Linguistic Notes on the Text:**
v. 21. "and Dishan" here and in v. 25 is written in full <note>meaning the vowel letter is present</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4 and the Halle edition; likewise v. 30 in 2, 4, and Halle. v. 27. "and the sons of" contains a <term>Gaiah</term> or <term>Metheg</term> <note>types of musical/accent marks</note> before the <term>Shva</term> <note>a vowel representing 'e' or silence</note> in 1 and 3, and after the Shva in 2; manuscript 3 and 4 use a <term>Munach</term> accent instead of a Metheg. * v. 34. "Husham" has a <term>Dagesh</term> <note>a dot indicating a stronger sound</note> in the letter Shin in 1 and 4; so does 4 in the following verse. v. 35. "and he reigned in his stead" is found in all except 17, 18, and the Berlin edition, which use the <term>Zakef Katon</term> accent with Munach. "Bedad" is written with a <term>Kametz</term> <note>an 'ah' vowel</note> in 2, 4, 6, 9. * v. 37. "from Rehoboth" is written defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> in 1, 2, 3, 4 and the Meir Codex in the Old Testament folio 6a; all others, including other Old Testaments, write it in full. v. 39. "Baal" uses a <term>Maqqef</term> <note>hyphen</note> and Metheg in 1, 2, 3, 4. "Hadad" is with Kametz in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 through 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16; the rest use <term>Patach</term> <note>a short 'a' vowel</note> according to the Old Testament.

**Chapter XXXVII.**
The History of Joseph. His innocent youth, dear to his father, hated by his brothers, especially because of divine dreams foreshadowing his dominion over them.
</margin>

<margin>
**CHAPTER XXXVII notes:**
v. 1. l) Targum Jonathan adds: "in tranquility." m) Compare verse 14; chapter 35:27; chapter 36:7.
v. 2. n) Chapter 35:23. Specifically regarding Joseph. Arabic and Persian versions: "The history of Jacob," as in chapter 25:19. "Their bad report." Root word (1) from Song of Solomon 7:10.
v. 3. p) "Son of old age," meaning he was born during his father's old age. Chapter 21:2, 7. Just as Benjamin was after him, chapter 37:12. Onkelos <note>An early Aramaic translation</note> translates this as "wise son." q) "Of many colors," or made of various threads. (s) Verse 23, 32; 2 Samuel 13:18. Greek Septuagint: "a multi-colored tunic." <note>original: "χιτῶνα ποικίλον"</note> Jonathan and Jerome: "a figured tunic." Similarly, Jonathan in verses 23 and 32. But the Syriac version says: "a tunic with fringes." The Arabic and Persian versions call it: "a silk tunic, specifically of Italian style, woven with gold." Similarly in verse 23.
v. 4. v) Exceedingly. Verse 34; chapter 44:20. s) Verse 11; Acts 7:9. t) "To speak with him." u) "For his peace and welfare." Compare chapter 43:27; verse 15. x) That is, "they hated him even more." Verse 8.
v. 7. y) Gathering. z) Bundles or sheaves. a) For the fulfillment of this, see chapter 42:6; 44:14; 50:18.
v. 10. b) "He rebuked him," or spoke sharply to him. Compare Zechariah 3:2.
v. 11. c) Compare verse 4. Greek: "they were jealous of him." <note>original: "ἐζήλωσαν αὐτὸν"</note> Acts 7:9.

1 And Jacob dwelt in the land of his father’s sojournings, in the land of Canaan. 2 These are the generations of Jacob: Joseph, being seventeen years old, was shepherding the flock with his brothers; and he was a youth with the sons of Bilhah and with the sons of Zilpah, his father’s wives; and Joseph brought a bad report of them to their father. 3 Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age; and he made him a <term>coat of many colors</term> <note>Hebrew: "ketonet passim." While traditionally "many colors," it may refer to a long-sleeved or ornamented garment worn by royalty or overseers.</note>. 4 And when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him. 5 And Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it to his brothers; and they hated him yet the more. 6 And he said to them: "Hear, I pray you, this dream which I have dreamed: 7 For, behold, we were binding <unclear>sheaves</unclear> <note>The text here is obscured by a burn/stain.</note> in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your <unclear>sheaves</unclear> came round about, and bowed down to my sheaf." 8 And his brothers said to him: "Shall you indeed reign over us? Or shall you indeed have dominion over us?" And they <unclear>hated</unclear> him yet the more for his dreams, and for his words. 9 And he dreamed yet another dream, and told <unclear>it</unclear> to his brothers, and said: "Behold, I have dreamed yet another dream; and, behold, the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowed down to me." 10 And he told it to his father, and to his brothers; and his father rebuked him, and said to him: "What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow down to the earth before you?" 11 And his brothers envied him; but his father kept the matter in mind.

**v. 40.** "Timnah" uses the Patach vowel in manuscripts 1, 3, and 4. "Alvah" has a Metheg mark in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, and 9. (Manuscript 1 has a soft 'r' sound). **CHAPTER XXXVII.** **v. 1.** "In the land" — so read all our manuscripts, except 17, 18, and the Berlin codex, which incorrectly use the Merca accent. **v. 2.** "Generations" — spelled fully in most according to the Masorah 2 and printed editions here and at the end of the chapter; but spelled shorter in manuscript 3 and 4 with its own Masorah. Compare chapter 36:1. **v. 4.** "Peaceably" — spelled fully in manuscripts 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, and 19. **v. 7.** "And [they] bowed down" — all have the Metheg mark under the first letter, except 3, 17, 18, and Berlin. **v. 8.** "Or [shall you] indeed have dominion" — includes the prefix 'and' in manuscripts 2 and 3. **v. 10.** "To bow down" — with Metheg under the 'He' according to Ben Naphtali in the Selden codex. **v. 11.** "And [they] envied" — Metheg under the prefix 'Vav' in 1 and 3; under the 'Kof' in others. The 'Nun' has a Dagesh dot in 4, against the Masorah, but manuscript 1 marks it with a Raphe (softener).

<note>Footnotes describing textual variants and Masoretic notes.</note>
V. 45. **Pharaoh**: written with a regular *Munach* in several manuscripts (Berlin and Spanish codices); others use a *Merca* accent as required by the small Masorah here. **Paneah**: the letter *Ain* has a *Chateph-pathach* vowel in most manuscripts. **Poti-Phera**: some divide the name into two words without a hyphen (Makkaph), following the Masorah of Erfurt, while others use a hyphen or write it as a single word. V. 48. **Field**: written with a *Metheg* or *Merca* accent in different traditions. V. 50. **Was born** <note>original: "יֻלַּד" (Yullad)</note>: written with a *Kamets* vowel by all according to the Masorah, except for a few manuscripts and Ben Asher, who use a *Patach*. **Poti-Phera**: similar variations in accents and word-joining as in verse 45.

*v. 54.* "To come" (*lavo*) is written defectively <note>Missing a letter common in standard spelling</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, and Hal. "The lands" (*ha'aratzot*) has a Metheg instead of a Munach <note>Hebrew musical/grammatical accents</note> in all our copies except 10, 17, and 18.
*v. 56.* "Upon all the face" (*al kol pne*) — so in 7, 8, and others, against the common printed editions of Chapter 42:1.
The Berlin manuscript requires a Munach according to the common edition folio 6b.
*Chapter 42:1.* "Grain" (*shever*) — a certain Masoretic author <note>The Masoretes were scholars who preserved the traditional text of the Hebrew Bible</note> requires a Tsere vowel under the letter Shin in the margins of 7 and 8, but this is without the agreement of the remaining manuscripts.
*v. 3.* "Brothers of" (*achei*) — so with a Metheg in 3, 6, 7, 9, etc.; others without it.
*v. 7.* "To them" (*alehem*) is written defectively in 3 and others, against the Masorah of this place. Conversely, it is written fully in Hal. 12, 14, etc., against Masorah 2 and the Erfurt manuscript, and likewise against the common edition.
*v. 11.* "Sons of a man" (*bnei ish*) — in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4. So also in verse 13.

**Philological and Scribal Notes:**

v. 16. **The truth** <note>original: "הָאֱמֶת"</note>: Correctly written with the interrogative <term>Patach</term> <note>A short 'a' vowel mark</note> as **הַאֱמֶת** in many manuscripts, as required by the *Minchat Shai* and the *Massorah* <note>Traditional notes on the Hebrew text</note> (codices 3, 4, 7, 8 and the Erfurt manuscript). v. 18. **To the opening**; but written with a <term>Kametz</term> <note>A long 'a' vowel mark</note> in codices 10, 13, 17, 18, 19 and the Berlin manuscript. v. 20. **And they did so** with the <term>Tiphcha</term> <note>A musical accent mark</note> in codex 3. v. 21. **And they said**: so in codex 2, but the Grafschaim manuscript follows the *Massorah* in codices 1, 4, 7, 8 and the Erfurt manuscript at this location and at Genesis 11, 3. Also found in printed editions at 1 Samuel 11, 9. **In his pleading**: The letter *He* has a <term>Metheq</term> <note>A small vertical line used as a stress mark</note> according to Ben Naphtali <note>A 10th-century scholar of the Hebrew text</note>. The letter *Nun* has a <term>Chateph-patach</term> <note>A very short 'a' vowel</note> in codices 1, 2, 6; but written with a <term>Dagesh</term> <note>A dot indicating a doubled consonant</note> without a preceding <term>Metheq</term> in codex 3, contrary to the *Minchat Shai*. v. 24. **And he wept**: with a simple <term>Sheva</term> <note>A vowel sign for a very short neutral sound</note> in codices 6, 8, 11, 16, contrary to the *Massorah* and the Old Testament (folio 7, a). v. 25. **And they filled**: The letter *Mem* is without a <term>Metheq</term> in codices 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9. v. 27. **And look**: with the <term>Merca</term> <note>A musical accent mark</note> in codices 3 and 4. v. 30. **As spies**: The prefix *Ke* has a <term>Metheq</term> in codices 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, and follows Ben Naphtali.

*v. 26.* "And they prostrated themselves" <note>original: וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲוּוּ</note> thus with the accent *Merka* in manuscripts 3 and 6; but both with *Maqqeph* and *Merka* in 7 and 9. *v. 27.* "And he said" <note>original: וַיֹּאמֶר</note> with *Zakeph gadol* in 1, 2, 4, 6, 9; but with *Rebia* in the others. *v. 28.* "And they bowed" <note>original: וַיִּקְּדוּ</note> without the *Dagesh* in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9. *v. 29.* "And they prostrated themselves" <note>original: וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲוּוּ</note> thus with the vowel *Shurek* in the text of 1 and 3; yet 1 also has *Kibbutz* placed below. *v. 32.* "Because" <note>original: כִּי</note> with *Tifcha gadol* in the margin of 1. \*. 8. **we brought back** so in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 4. \*. 10. **innocent** written in full spelling <note>plene</note> in manuscripts 2, 4, 9, and the first Erfurt edition; contrary to the Masoretic text. \*. 11. **and they lowered** written with a missing letter <note>defective</note> in manuscript 2 and 4. A "Setumah" <note>a "closed" paragraph break in the Torah</note> section is found in manuscripts 3, 17, 18, and the Berlin edition. A "Petuchah" <note>an "open" paragraph break</note> is found in 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 12, 14. Manuscripts 7, 8, and 19 use the general term **Parashah** <note>portion</note>. \*. 18. **speak** the letter *Daleth* has a *Dagesh* <note>a dot indicating emphasis</note> in manuscripts 7, 8, 10-15, 19, against the standard text. \*. 19. **is there** manuscripts 1, 4, 10, 13, 14, 59. \*. 21. **bring him down** written in full in manuscripts 4 and 6, against the standard Masorah for this passage and Genesis 39:1.

**v. 14.** Benjamin [written] with full spelling <note>term: plene — using extra letters like 'yod' or 'waw' to indicate vowels</note> as in v. 12 and according to Ben Asher <note>a famous medieval scholar of the Hebrew Bible text</note>, against the Masorah <note>the traditional body of notes on the text</note> on Genesis 35:18. Metheg <note>a small vertical line mark used to indicate stress or a pause</note> in the second-to-last syllable in manuscripts 1, 2, 4, 7, 37, 18 and the Berlin edition of the Old Testament. Metheg is in the last syllable in manuscript 6; however, others have none, except for 3 and 9, which have a Merca <note>a musical accent mark</note> preceding the Metheg. **v. 14.** "And he wept" in manuscript 1 according to the Erfurt manuscripts. **v. 15.** "Upon them" written with full spelling in 3, Halle 10, 13, 14, 19, against the Masorah. "And they spoke" — thus it is written together with the Silluq <note>an accent mark indicating the end of a verse</note> with a double accent in 1, 2, 4, 9; but with a Metheg instead of a Munach <note>another type of accent mark</note> in manuscript 3. **v. 16.** "Saying" — the redundant Metheg under the letter Lamed, which is present in most, is omitted in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 9. **v. 18.** "Your households" — all include the Metheg except 3, 4, and the Berlin edition. **v. 19.** "Take" — a Munach accent instead of a Makkaph <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in 2, 4, and in the margin. **v. 22.** "Three" — here with a Makkaph in 1, 4, 6, 9, but others have a Munach.

### Scholarly Notes on the Hebrew Text

**v. 26.** The word **still** <note>original Hebrew: "עוֹד" (od)</note> is written defectively according to the first Masora <note>Scribal notes on the text</note> and the Erfurt manuscripts in this place; the second Masora on Genesis 8:22 agrees, though other Masoretic traditions differ. **v. 27.** **that he spoke** <note>Hebrew: "אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּר"</note> follows manuscripts 1 and 2. **v. 28.** The word **much** <note>Hebrew: "רַב" (rav)</note> has the *Sakeph gadol* accent in manuscript 2 and in the margin of manuscript 1; others use the *Tiphcha* accent. **CHAPTER 46, v. 3.** **Egypt** <note>Hebrew: "מִצְרַיִם"</note> appears without the final *He* in the margins of manuscripts 7 and 8, following a certain "Correction of the Scribes," though this contradicts the standard Masora. **v. 5.** **In the wagons** <note>Hebrew: "בָּעֲגָלוֹת"</note> is written with a *Qamatz* vowel under the *Bet* in most copies; manuscripts 3, 4, 6, 17, and 18 use a *Patach* vowel. **v. 6.** **Their livestock** <note>Hebrew: "מִקְנֵיהֶם"</note> is written defectively in most copies according to the second Masora; however, it is written in full <note>plene</note> in manuscripts 1, 4, and twelve other manuscripts, noting that the Masora varies. **v. 11.** **Kohath** <note>Hebrew: "קְהָת"</note> appears with a prefixed *Vav* in the margins of manuscripts 7 and 8, which goes against the standard Hebrew Bible. **v. 13.** **And Puvah** <note>Hebrew: "וּפֻוָה"</note> is without the *Dagesh* <note>a dot indicating a stronger sound</note> in manuscripts 1-4, 6, and 13, but the majority include the *Dagesh* following the authorities David Kimchi and Rabbi Meir Ha-Levi. **v. 16.** **Arodi** <note>Hebrew: "וַאֲרוֹדִי"</note> is written defectively in manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 10, and 15.

\* **v. 17.** *Serah* is written with the letter *Samech* in 4 manuscripts; others agree with the Masoretic text. *Heber* is written with the letter *Chet* instead of *He* in several versions. **v. 20.** *Asenath* has a *Munach* accent instead of a *Metheg* <note>types of musical/grammatical marks in Hebrew</note> in some texts. \* v. 17. **בְּכָל־מִקְנֵהֶם** (for all their livestock) spelled fully in 4 manuscripts. v. 19. **וְתֶן** (and give) written with the vowel *Tsere* without a *Metheg* in manuscripts 6-9, 11-16, and 19. v. 24. **בְּבָתֵּיכֶם** (in your houses) thus with a *Metheg* in all, except manuscript 3 and the Berlin edition. v. 28. All recognize a major Section here, the twelfth in number <note>This refers to the start of Parashat Vayechi</note>; however, the more accurate scribes, following the rules of the Old Testament and all manuscript codices (including Maimonides and Rabbi Elias the Oriental), leave no space except that of a single letter. According to these, the beginning of this section is joined to the end of the preceding verse, whether it ends as a *Sethuma* (closed) or *Pethucha* (open). In the margin, however, manuscript 1 places a large letter *Pe* and manuscript 2 places the word **PARASHA**. Manuscript 17 has the Hebrew note as in the Berlin edition. Furthermore, the Rabbis discuss in *Bereshit Rabbah* and in the *Zohar* why this section is not distinct like the others. But Rabbi Abraham in the book *Tseror Hammor* brings this reason: That this Portion is the key and seal not only of Genesis, but of the entire Law and the Prophets, and contains the universal fate of Israel hidden in the blessing of Jacob until the time of the Messiah; because it cannot and should not yet be understood by anyone, therefore this Portion continues without a greater distinction from the preceding one, being **סְתוּמָה** (*sethuma*) or "closed."

<note>The following notes are technical details regarding the Hebrew text's vowels and accents in various historical manuscripts.</note>

v. 30 **I will do**: The letter *Ayin* uses a simple *Shva* <note>a vowel sign indicating a very short 'e' or no vowel</note> in manuscripts 7 and 8 and Spanish books of the Old Testament. 
Chapter XLVIII, 1. **And it was**: The letter *Vav* has a *Metheg* <note>a stress mark</note> in manuscripts 6 through 19. 
v. 3. **Appeared**: without a *Metheg* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 4. 
v. 4. **Behold me**: The letter *He* is without a *Metheg* in all, except 17, 18, and the Berlin manuscript. 
**And I will multiply you**: written "defectively" <note>shorthand spelling</note> in 1 and 2; written "plene" <note>full spelling with extra letters</note> in 1, 2, 3, and 4, but both go against the Masorah and the printed edition. 
v. 5. **Two**: with a *Munach* accent in 1, 2, 3, and 4. 
**They are mine**: *Munach* instead of *Makkaph* in 1, 2, 3, and both in 6 and 9. 
v. 7. **She died**: thus with a double *Tiphcha* accent in 1, 2, and 4. 
**There**: The letter *Shin* has a *Dagesh* <note>a dot indicating emphasis or doubling</note> in 4, 9, Berlin, and others, while the rest are without it. 
v. 9. **And I will bless them**: The letter *Resh* has a simple *Shva* in 1, 3, 4, 6–12, 14, 15, 16, 19, against the Old Testament. The suffix **them** uses a *Tsere* vowel in 3, 4, 17, 18, Berlin, and Spanish books, but the others have the *Segol* vowel required by the Masorah of Erfurt and the printed edition.
