<note>Footnotes describing textual variants and vocalization:</note>
v. 18. **The firstborn** [Ha-bechor]: spelled fully in manuscripts 1 and 3, Halle 6 and 9. v. 19. **He shall be** [Yihyeh]: with a double Metheg in most versions, except 1, 2, 3, 4. Ben Ascher; but Ben Naphtali has it simple, yet on the latter syllable. v. 20. **And he blessed them** [Vayvarechem]: Dagesh in manuscripts 1, 12, 14, 15, 16. The 'Ain' has a Patach vowel in 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 15, 19. v. 20. **May he set you** [Yesimcha]: Vav with Metheg in 1, 2, 18. Resh with a simple Shua in 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9. Suffix has a Segol in 1, 6, 9, 10, 14. v. 22. **His head / and in their self-will**: Rebia accent in 2, 4. CHAPTER XLIX, 4. **You shall [not] have preeminence**: with a Kamets in 14 and Masorah 1. v. 6. For the phrase **and in their self-will etc.**, the Seventy-two Elders <note>The Septuagint translators</note> wrote to King Ptolemy: "and in their self-will they uprooted a manger"; as found in the Talmud, Tractate Megillah folio 9a.

**Scribal and Textual Notes:**
<note>These notes record variations in the Hebrew script, accents, and punctuation found in different medieval manuscripts and the Masora (the tradition of scribal corrections).</note>

v. 14. "To the man" (*le-ish*) uses the accent *Rebia* in Manuscript 4 and in the margin of Manuscript 1. v. 17. "And he saved them" (*vayoshi’an*) is written with full spelling in the Halle manuscripts 13 and 14, and Frankfurt 4, contrary to the Masora and the Old Testament manuscript 7b. v. 23. No small section break is made here by manuscripts 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, and 19, contrary to the standard Old Testament text. CHAPTER III, v. 1. "Shepherd" (*ro'eh*) is marked by the *Darga* accent in manuscripts 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, and 16, contrary to the standard text. v. 3. "The great" (*ha-gadol*) is written with full spelling in manuscripts 3 and 4, and Frankfurt 1, contrary to Masora 1 and the Erfurt manuscript. v. 4. Joined by a *Makkaph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in manuscripts 1, 3, and 4. *Makkaph* and *Munach* accents appear together in manuscript 2. "Moses, Moses" appears with an interposed *Pasek* <note>a vertical line indicating a pause</note> in manuscript 4, but Masora 1, 2, 7, 8, and the Erfurt manuscript command it to be absent. Rabbi Yehuda ben Jacob, in his explanation of the Masora, adds the reason why it should be absent: "because his prophecy never ceased" <note>original Aramaic: *dela fasek neviuteih*</note>, playing on the name of the *Pasek* mark (which means "stop" or "cut"). v. 5. "Put off" (*shal*) has the *Mahpach* accent in manuscripts 1, 2, and 3, and Frankfurt 4, but manuscript 1 has a *Makkaph* in the margin. The words "your feet" and "your sandals" are both written without the dual *Yod* letter in manuscript 1 and its Masora, though Masora 7, 8, and the Erfurt manuscript contradict this.

<note>This final section contains Masoretic and scholarly notes on the Hebrew text, comparing different manuscripts (codices) regarding specific vowel points and accents.</note>

v. 18. **נלכה** (Let us go) - The letter Lamed requires a specific vowel mark based on Old Testament folio 7.b. v. 19. **לא** (Not) - The first instance has a Munach accent in some versions, but Ben Asher and Selden’s codex differ. v. 20. **נפלאתי** (My wonders) - Many use a Patach vowel; the Berlin codex has it expressed, but others use a Kamets according to the Masora. **ל' אעשה** (which I will do) - The letter Ain uses a simple Shua in Spanish manuscripts. v. 21. **העם** (The people) - Most of our codices write it this way, but some place a Metheg accent under the letter He. Chapter IV, v. 3. **השלכהו** (Cast it) - Written defectively (missing a letter) in several codices (2, 7, 8, etc.) against the Masora. v. 8. **והאמינו** (And they will believe) - Has a Sakeph-katon accent in some codices, while others have a Metheg. v. 9. **האחת** (The one) - Twice defective in some versions against the Masora. v. 10. **אנכי** (I am) - The Aleph is without a Metheg according to the Masora here and in Genesis 3:19.

<note>
This section contains technical notes on the Hebrew text (the Masorah).
verse 3. **נִקְרָא** [He met with us]: Written with the letter *He* at the end according to some traditions, though the Masorah of Erfurt disagrees. **נֵלֲכָה** [Let us go]: The letter *Lamed* has a short *a* sound (Chateph-patah). **פֶּן** [Lest]: Written with a connecting mark (Maqqeph) and a musical accent (Kadma) in some versions (4, 6, 9, 11), but omitted in others. verse 5. **עַם** [People]: Marked with a hyphen (Maqqeph) in various manuscripts. verse 7. **תֹּאסִפֿוּן** [You shall continue]: Marked with a specific accent (Rebbia) in the margin. **כִּתְמוֹל** [As before]: Written in full form in some Berlin and older manuscripts, contrary to the standard Masorah for Genesis 31:2. **יֵלְכוּ** [They shall go]: Uses a specific rhythmic pause (Metheg) instead of a Munach accent in some copies. **וְקֹשְׁשׁוּ** [And gather]: The letter *Shin* has a short *a* sound in certain codices like that of Hammeiri, though this is rejected by other ancient texts. verse 8. **אֲשֶׁר** [Which]: Marked with a hyphen. **כִּי** [For]: Uses a specific accent (Ithibh). verse 11. **אֵין** [None]: Uses a specific musical sequence (Darga and Psik) for emphasis in some traditions.
</note>

### SCHOLARLY NOTES ON THE TRANSCRIPTION

Verse 14. **Alehem** <note>upon them</note> is written "full" <note>plene—using extra letters to indicate vowels</note> in sources 10, 14, and 19. This matches the usage in Genesis 45:15. **Tachmol** is written "defective" <note>lacking vowel-helper letters</note> in sources 2 and 4 according to the Masorah <note>the tradition of biblical text transmission</note> for Genesis 31:2, though other books write it full. Verse 15. **Ta'aseh** <note>you do</note> has a simple *Merca* accent in sources 10, 12, 13, and 14, contrary to the Masorah for Numbers 32:42. **Koh** <note>thus</note> appears with a *Dagesh* <note>an emphasis dot</note> in source 18, but other manuscripts use a *Raphe* <note>a mark indicating a soft sound</note>. Verse 16. **Vechatat** <note>and the sin</note>: the letter *Chet* has a *Patach* vowel followed by a *Dagesh* in source 4, though others treat it as a feminine verb. CHAPTER VI. Verse 4. **Heqimoti** <note>I established</note>: the "Ki" syllable is written full in sources 1, 2, and 4. Verse 6. **Emor** <note>say</note>: most follow the Masorah here, but source 3 uses a *Munach* accent.

**Verse 25:** The name <term>Phinehas</term> is written "defectively" <note>spelled without the vowel-letter yod</note> in several manuscripts. **Verse 27:** The word "those who spoke" <note>original: המדרבים</note> appears without the Metheg <note>a small vertical line used as a secondary accent</note> in the Ben Asher tradition. **Verse 29:** The presence of a new paragraph marker here, which might seem inconvenient or misplaced, is also noted with wonder by the scholar Aben Esra in his commentary, though he reaches no certain conclusion. <note>Critical footnotes at bottom of page regarding the Hebrew script:</note>
\* Verse 13. The letter *Beth* in the word "with his staff" contains a *Dagesh* <note>a dot indicating a harder pronunciation</note> because the preceding *Mahpach* accent functions here as a separator. But see our notes on such a "light" *Dagesh* at Genesis 39:19. The word for "lice" is written defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> in some manuscripts. \* Verse 15. The word "the magicians" is written in full <note>with all vowel letters</note> in certain versions, though the Masoretic text and others differ. The word for "heart" includes a *Metheg* <note>a vertical line used as a stress marker or to ensure a long vowel</note>. \* Verse 17. In the word "and upon your people," a *Metheg* is almost always placed between the *Kamets* vowel and the *Dagesh* so that the vowel is not mistaken for a short 'o' sound. \* Verse 18. The word "I will set apart" is written defectively. The word "swarm" is written in full.

**Critical Apparatus:**
Verse 27: *The Swarm* <note>original: הָעָרֹב</note> appears thus with a *Munach* <note>a Hebrew musical/grammatical accent</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 4, and the Berlin manuscript, but the others have a *Metheg* <note>a small vertical stroke used to mark stress or slow the reading</note>. CHAPTER IX. Verse 3: *And on the camels* <note>original: וּבַגְמַלִּים</note> with the prefix "and" in manuscript 3.
Verse 4: *The Lord* <note>original: יְהוָה</note> with a *Rebia* accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, but a *Sakeph* is more appropriate. Verse 5.
*And the Lord set a time* <note>original: וַיָּשֶׂם יְהוָה מוֹעֵד</note>—this is the reading in 2 and 4, which is much more suitable if you look at the words according to our way of punctuating; but this is an almost constant anomaly in the sacred book, that the infinitive *to say* <note>original: לֵאמֹר</note> is joined to the preceding word by the accents. Verse 6: *On the next day* <note>original: מִמָּחֳרָת</note>—the second letter *Mem* is without a *Munach* in manuscript 1 (which has a *Metheg* in its place) and manuscript 3; thus it appears in the Spanish books of the Old Testament, folio 8, column a.

[The following section contains technical notes on the Hebrew spelling and accents found in specific historic manuscripts.]

Signature mark: G 5

**Verse 7:** The word "the men" <note>original: הָאֲנָשִׁים</note> has the accent Munach instead of Metheg, appearing only in the Berlin manuscript. **Verse 9:** "and with our old" <note>original: וּבִזְקֵנֵינוּ</note> is spelled fully (plene) with the letter Yod in the Halle, Berlin, Egyptian, Jerusalem, and Hillelian manuscripts, and all Spanish editions; also Rabbi Meir Hallevi in the "Or Torah" (folio 8a). However, our other texts have the shorter (defective) spelling according to the Masora. **Verses 7 & 8:** "and with our daughters" <note>original: ובבנתינו</note> is defective in Halle and others, against the Masora. **Verse 11:** "so" <note>original: כן</note> has the Gerschaim accent in several manuscripts. "seeking" <note>original: מבקשים</note>—the letter Koph has a Dagesh [emphasized dot] in many manuscripts against the "Or Torah." **Verse 14:** "was" <note>original: היה</note> is accented on the last syllable (milra) in several manuscripts. "there shall not be" <note>original: לא־יהיה</note>—so in all, except one manuscript and the Berlin, which join the words with a hyphen (Maqqeph). **Verse 15:** "so" <note>original: כן</note> appears without a Dagesh in many texts, though some use a Psik accent. "reeds" <note>original: סוף</note> without a Dagesh in some texts. **Verse 16:** Instead of "to call," one manuscript reads "and he called." **Verse 19:** "The Lord" appears with a Psik accent in one manuscript. "reeds" [Suph] without a Dagesh in others.

<note>Scholar's Note: Regarding verse 31, the word "go out" (tse'u) is written without a dot (dagesh) in many manuscripts, contrary to the Masoretic notes. Regarding verse 37, the word "besides" (levad) has a specific vowel mark (Kamets) noted in the Masorah, but some scholars believe this was applied incorrectly as it doesn't appear in our primary codices. Regarding verse 39, "cakes" (ugot) is also debated in the Masorah. Most importantly, regarding verse 40, the Samaritan Hebrew text and its translation add "and in the land of Canaan" after "Israel," suggesting the 430 years covers their entire journey since Abraham. The 72 Elders (the Septuagint) also added "in the land of Canaan and in the land of Egypt" to the text preserved in the Megillah scroll.</note>

<note>Critical and philological notes on the Masoretic text and variants.</note>
*v. 11. yevia'cha* [brings you] is written with a *Vau* in the text according to the marginal *Keri* in manuscripts 4, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16, 19. But the *Or Torah* (f. 8. b.) says this written form (*Kethiv*) is false, because it is not found in the Masoretic list of similar examples (as in 1 Chronicles 1). *v. 12. ve-ha'avarta kol peter* [you shall set apart every firstborn], so in 7, 8, 10-16, 18, 19. But our reading, besides 1, 2, 3, 4, and the Berlin codex, is also approved by *Or Torah*. *v. 13. ve-kol bechor* [and every firstborn] uses the *Makkaph* (hyphen) and *Kametz-chateph* vowel in 1, 2, 3, 4. *v. 14. yad* [hand] uses the *Revia* accent in 6, 9, and *Or Torah*. *v. 15. YHWH* [the LORD]: a *Pasek* (dividing line) is added in 6, 7, 9; that it should at least be understood is hinted at by the *Dagesh lene* (softening dot) inscribed in the following *kol* [all], which all codices have consistently here. *mibechor* [from the firstborn] is written fully in 4, 10, 12, contrary to *Or Torah* and the Masora for chapter 12:29. *v. 18. Elohim* [God] is with a *Pasek* in 4, 7, 8, 10-16, 19, contrary to Masora 1 and the Erfurt codex, as well as *Or Torah*. *vachamushim* [and in five ranks]: thus *Schit* without a *Dagesh* in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, Berlin, and also the Spanish and Jerusalem books in *Or Torah* according to the Masora of Erfurt; but the rest have the *Dagesh* dot.

* **4.** "And I will harden the heart" <note>original Hebrew: וְחִזַּקְתִּי אֶת־לֵב</note> so in 1. 2. 3. but the <term>Makkaph</term> <note>a horizontal connecting line in Hebrew</note> on the word "heart" [lev] is proved by the <term>Minchat Shai</term> <note>a famous 17th-century commentary on the Masoretic text</note>. Regarding "in Pharaoh" [be-Pharao], all our copies (except 18.) constantly have a <term>Dagesh lene</term> <note>a dot indicating a "hard" pronunciation of a letter</note> for the sake of euphony: examples of this kind exist elsewhere, e.g., v. 17. 18. Leviticus 25, 53 in "with rigor" [be-ferech]. * **6.** "And he made ready" [vayye'esor] with a <term>Chateph Segol</term> vowel; preceded by a <term>Metheg</term> <note>a vertical accent mark</note>, in 3. contrary to Minchat Shai & the <term>Masora</term> <note>the traditional system of notes on the Hebrew Bible text</note> for Genesis 42, 24. Written with a doubled *Samech* in 1. 2. according to their Masora, which was nonetheless misunderstood by the scribes and applied much more unhappily. * **10.** "And behold" [ve-hinneh] has a <term>Makkaph</term> in 1. 3. 4. and simultaneously with a <term>Metheg</term> in 6. 9. 11. 12. 14. 15. 16. * **11.** "Is it because" [hamibbli] - the letter *He* requires a <term>Gaiah</term> <note>another name for the Metheg accent</note> according to Minchat Shai, with a <term>Patach</term> vowel followed by a <term>Dagesh</term> in the margin of 1. Thus Rabbi Jonah cites from the Jerusalem codex according to David Kimchi, who nevertheless in all other books found a <term>Chateph-Patach</term>. Compare Minchat Shai on v. 12. Makkaph in 1. 3. & Ben Naphtali. One truly has both Makkaph and <term>Munach</term> <note>a musical accent mark</note> in 4.

The form of this Song, as it is expressed here, is prescribed by the Masorah <note>The body of tradition concerning the correct text and layout of the Hebrew Bible</note> on page 8, and more extensively in the Old Testament, folio 9. a.

**v. 1. I will sing to the LORD** with the letter Lamed having a dagesh <note>a grammatical dot indicating emphasis or doubling</note> in editions 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10. **He has triumphed** without the dagesh in 3, 6, 7, contrary to the Masorah. Such an extraordinary dagesh, appearing several times in this Song, seems to be for emphatic pronunciation and is approved by the Masorah, as in **v. 13. [Who is] like you** .11. **You have redeemed** .16. **As a stone** . **v. 1. He has triumphed** &nbsp;**v. 7. Those rising against you** with the Kametz vowel in 1, 3, 4, contrary to the Masorah. **v. 8. They were gathered together** thus in 4, 6, 9, 17, 18, and the Berlin codex; but others omit the Maqqeph <note>hyphen</note> and indeed place the accent on the last syllable in 3, 15, 16. However, under the letter Nun, others place a Munach accent. **v. 10. As lead** with the letter Caph having a Patach vowel in 3, 10, 13, 17, 18, 19, the Berlin codex, and Spanish codices in the Old Testament; but the rest use a Kametz. Furthermore, it is defective in 1, 2, 4, according to the Halle Masorah in Number 31, 22; though the Masorah in 4 cites another example from Zechariah 5:7 in place of this. **v. 11. [Who is] like you** thus without a Pesiq accent in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, and 17, according to the Old Testament. **v. 17. Sanctuary** with the letter Kaph having a Raphe <note>mark indicating soft pronunciation</note> followed by the letter Vav in 10, 14, contrary to the Old Testament folio 7. b. and Masorah 3 and the Brescia editions.

<column-break/>

**v. 2. For salvation** l) I will honor him. (2) Habakkuk 2:5. Compare Jeremiah 6:2; Psalm 93:5. m) **I will glorify him.** <note>original Greek: "δοξάσω αὐτόν"</note> So say Hierosolymitanus, Jonathan, and the Syriac. But Onkelos says: "I will build him a sanctuary." m) Chapter 3:6; Genesis 31:29, 42. **v. 3. n)** A warrior. Psalm 24:8. o) Chapter 6:3; Compare Revelation 1:8. **v. 4. p)** The choice of his captains. Chapter 14:7. q) They were drowned. Psalm 9:16. **v. 5. r)** It covered them. Chapter 14:28. s) Targum Jonathan 2:4; Nehemiah 9:11. Compare Jeremiah 51:62, 63, 64; Revelation 18:21. t) It is magnificent, and it has shown itself great. Verse 10, 11. **v. 6. u)** Shatters. Judges 10:18. **v. 7. x)** Destroys. Psalm 28:6. y) Those rising against you. Deuteronomy 33:11. z) Isaiah 5:24; Malachi 3:19. **v. 8. a)** Job 4:9. b) They were heaped up. (1) Compare Song of Solomon 7:3; 2 Chronicles 31:6 and following. c) A heap. Joshua 3:13, 15; Psalm 33:7. d) Judges 5:5. e) They were congealed. (3) Zephaniah 1:12. Used of cheese in Job 10:10. <note>The following notes are technical observations regarding the Hebrew manuscript traditions (Masora) and vowel points (Niqqud).</note>
v. 1. **vayis'u** <note>they journeyed</note> Grafchaim 3. v. 3. **zeh** <note>this</note> without Dagesh <note>a grammatical dot in a letter</note> 3. 7. 11. 12. 16. contrary to O.T. f. 9. b. v. 6. **sham** <note>there</note> with euphonic Dagesh 1. 4. without Pasek <note>a vertical line separating words</note> 1. 2. 6. with Pasek 4. v. 7. **ve-al** <note>and upon</note> with Kadma <note>an accent mark</note> 2. 6.—16. 19. **vayiqchu** <note>and they took</note> v. 12. Mercha-Miltra 3. 4. **bo** <note>coming</note> written fully according to the Erfurt Masora and other Masoretic books, as noted in Masora 7. 8. on Ezekiel 33, 22. v. 14. **zekher** <note>remembrance</note> with Tsere <note>a vowel mark</note> 2. 7.—16. 19. v. 16. **kes Yah** <note>Throne of the LORD</note> thus found as two words in all our books according to the Erfurt Masora. However, Rabbi David Kimchi in his Lexicon under the root **ksh** states it should be a single word **kesyah**, which is extensively refuted by the O.T. f. 9 & 10 from all Spanish, Catalonian, Mauritanian, Hillel, Egyptian, and German codices and from the Masora; although he admits that German Masoretic books establish a variation <note>Hebrew: "pelugta"</note> here, and <unclear>accentes</unclear>, that Rabbi Nachman held these words to be a single one, etc.

<meta>Translator notes regarding textual variations and Masoretic notations found at the bottom of the page</meta>

**v. 1.** *And he heard* <note>original Hebrew: "וַיִּשְׁמַע"</note> with the **Rebhia** <note>a Hebrew accent mark</note> 3. contrary to the **Masorah** <note>traditional Hebrew text notes</note> on Genesis 31:1. However, the **Rebhia** is found in the **Sinai Codex**, as noted by the **Masorah** in this place, and by **Elias** in his **Masoreth**, folio 78.
**v. 5.** *To the wilderness* <note>original Hebrew: "אֶל־הַמִּדְבָּר"</note> thus in manuscripts 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 10. **Bakephgadol** <note>a large accent/spacing mark</note> with the rest of our sources; the aforementioned **Sinai Codex** notes it likewise in 7, 8 in the margin, and **Elias** in the **Masoreth**, folio 78.
**v. 8.** *Reasons/Account of* <note>original Hebrew: "אֹדוֹת"</note> twice defective in manuscripts 2, 3, and **Halle**. But "אֹדוֹת" is full in 4. Both, however, are rejected by the **Enbakbore**.
**v. 8.** *Which* <note>original Hebrew: "אֲשֶׁר"</note> in 1, 7, and 8 in this place; and **Masorah** 1 on Genesis 21:11. "אֲשֶׁר" with a **Maqqeph** <note>Hebrew hyphen</note> instead of a **Munach** <note>accent</note> in 1, 2, 3, and printed edition 4.
**v. 8.** *Met them* <note>original Hebrew: "מְצָאָתַם"</note> with the letter **Tau** having a **Qamets** vowel and the **Mitra** accent 3, contrary to **Masorah** 7, 8. But as **Milel** <note>accent on the penultimate syllable</note> with **Qamets** in 4 and 18, contrary to **Masorah** 1 on Genesis 21:32.
**v. 10.** *The LORD* <note>original Hebrew: "יְהֹוָה"</note> here with **Bakephk.** <note>small spacing mark</note> correctly in 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, according to the **Quarto Text**, folio 10a. The rest use the **Rebhia** accent. *Hand* <note>original Hebrew: "יד"</note> with the **Mercha** accent in 1, 3, 4.
**v. 14.** *Until evening* <note>original Hebrew: "עַד־עֶרֶב"</note> thus with the letter **Waw** prefixed in 3 and **Halle**.

Chapter XX. verse 1. q) Nehemiah 9:13. This "God" is the Glory of the LORD and the *Shekhinah* <note>the Divine Presence</note>, the One who sits between the Cherubim (1 Chronicles 13:6), who is nonetheless worshiped and adored alongside the LORD as one (compare John 5:23). He is the God of Bethel (Genesis 31:13), the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Exodus 3:6), and the "Goodness of the LORD" which passed before Moses (Exodus 33:19; 34:6). He is the "Face of the LORD" (Exodus 23:17), according to Rabbi Bahya <note>R. Bechai, a medieval commentator</note>. See Deuteronomy 5:6 and following.

<note>The following footnotes discuss the Masoretic text—the precise traditional system of spelling and musical accents used in Hebrew Bibles. These notes compare different manuscripts (like "Erff." or "Hal.") and early printed editions (like "O. T.") to identify the most accurate reading of the Ten Commandments.</note>

Verse 21. **לראות** (to see) - This word is spelled defectively here according to certain Masoretic traditions and manuscripts. While some observe it this way, others reject it as an error based on Kabbalistic interpretations.

Verse 24. **ויאמר** (and he said) - Discussion of variant verse numbering and manuscript traditions (manuscripts 3, 6-9, etc.) which sometimes conflict with older printed editions.

CHAPTER XX. verse 2. **עבדים** (slaves) - Most manuscripts place a certain musical accent (Rebia) here, but some (manuscripts 3 and 13) substitute a stronger pause (Atnach). The note observes that even accurate scholars like Menachem sometimes struggle with the complex double-accentuation system of the Decalogue (the Ten Commandments), leading to confusion in many of our codices.

Verse 4. **תעשה** (you shall make) - Comparison of different musical accents (Munach vs. Merca) found in various manuscripts. The editor argues that some versions go against the grammatical rules of the language.

Verse 10. **ובנך** (and your son) - Notes whether this word is joined to the next with a hyphen (Maqqef) in manuscripts 1-4 and 6. For **ועבדך** (and your servant), there is a note regarding a specific graphical mark in the Halle manuscript.

The extensive scholarly notes explain the identity of the Divine Speaker and clarify technical details of the Hebrew text's accents and spelling.</summary>

**Masoretic Notes:**
**v. 6. *God (Elohim):*** The *Metheg* <note>a small vertical line used as a secondary stress</note> is used instead of *Munach* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 17, 12. 
**v. 8. *Not (Lo):*** The written form (*Kethiv*) using the letter Aleph is as valid as the read form (*Keri*) using the letter Vav, meaning "to him"; for the Masora does not mark the spelling as an error, but observes the substitution of Aleph for Vav, as noted by Hiller. 
**v. 10. *He shall take (Yikach):*** Written without *Metheg* in manuscript 4 and the Berlin edition. 
**v. 18. *Men (Anashim):*** With the *Rebia* accent in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9. ***And he strikes (Ve-hikah):*** With *Merca miltra* in 1, 2, 3, 4. 
**v. 19. *And he walks (Ve-hithallech):*** So in Ben Naphtali, as observed by Masora 7 and 8. 
**v. 21. *Punished (Yukkam):*** With the *Kametz* vowel in 1, 2, 3; correctly according to the Masora on Genesis 4:15, but against the Masora on this specific passage. 
**v. 24. *Tooth for tooth, hand for hand:*** So in manuscript 1 and following in 4.

**v. 29.** **And it kills a man or...** So read in version R. **v. 31.** **It has gored** with the vowel <term>Kamets</term> in various manuscripts including Erfurt. **v. 33.** **Ox** without the dot <note>Dagesh</note> in manuscripts 3, 7, 8, etc., contrary to the Masoretic text. **v. 35.** **And it strikes**... the accent <term>Darga</term> is required here as in Leviticus 11:22. **v. 36.** **From yesterday** written deficiently <note>missing a letter</note> in several manuscripts. **v. 37.** CHAPTER 22 begins from this verse in many manuscripts including 6, 8, and 11. **If [a man] steals** written with the <term>Metheg</term> mark in most sources; others use the <term>Chateph Kamets</term> vowel. **And four** written with the connecting <term>Makkaph</term> in version 27. **CHAPTER 22, 4.** **His beast** written deficiently in the Bero manuscript.

<note>
**Technical Scribal and Masoretic Notes:**
v. 29. The word "so" (ken) appears with a Metheg <note>a small vertical line used for stress or rhythm</note> according to Ben Naphtali.
CHAPTER XXIII, v. 2. "to pervert" (lehattot) is clearly marked in several manuscripts (1, 2, 3) against the Masora of Erfurt.
v. 3. "And the poor" (ve-dal). The letter Tau has a Metheg in most manuscripts, but manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 lack it.
v. 5. "help" (azov) is placed after the Makkef <note>a hyphen connecting words</note> in manuscripts 2 and 3, contrary to the Masora for verse 4. Most manuscripts include a Metheg, except 3, 4, 8, and 1 (where it was deleted).
v. 15. "I commanded you" (tsivvitikha). Manuscripts 3, 4, and Halle provide the full spelling as required by Rabbi Hammari, though this is refuted by other authorities like Rabbi Meir Habeni.
v. 16. "at the going out" (be-tzeit). Seven books are said to have this reading in the margins of manuscripts 7 and 8.
</note>

<note>The following are technical philological notes regarding Hebrew spelling and manuscript variations.</note>
*v. 2.* **אשר** (which) Makkef 3. su. 4. - *v. 5.* **אילם** (rams) written defectively in 4, but fully in 3 and 4. Both are noted against the Masorah of Genesis 32:14. - *v. 6.* **למאור** (for the light) written fully in 2 and 4. - *v. 10.* **קומתו** (its height) written fully in 4. - *v. 12.* **לו** (for it) without the Dagesh <note>a dot indicating emphasis or doubling</note> in 1, 3, and 7. - **האחת** (the one) the masculine form **והאחד** is found in version 4. - *v. 15.* **הארן** (the ark) Munach instead of Metheg in versions 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6. - *v. 16.* **אשר אתן** (which I will give) thus in version 1. - *v. 17.* With this verse, versions 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, and 10 begin a "Setumah" (closed) section. - *v. 19.* **תעשו** (you [plural] shall make) instead of **תעשה** (you [singular] shall make); some had the singular in 1, 2, 3, 11, and 12, but corrected it. Version 1 adds a note: "Every structure you shall make... whoever wrote the singular is considered to have corrupted the books of Moses." - **קצותיו** (its ends) written defectively in 1, 3, and 4, contrary to the Masorah of Erfurt.

15 And you shall make the **boards**<sup>r</sup> for the Tabernacle of shittim wood <note>Shittim is acacia wood, known for its durability.</note> standing upright.<sup>s</sup> 16 **Ten** cubits shall be the length of a board, and a cubit and a half shall be the width of each board. 17 There shall be two tenons<sup>t</sup> [literally "hands"] for each board, joined<sup>u</sup> one to another; so you shall do for all the boards of the Tabernacle. 18 And you shall make the boards for the Tabernacle: twenty boards for the south side<sup>x</sup> southward. 19 And you shall make forty sockets of silver<sup>y</sup> under the twenty boards: two sockets under one board for its two tenons, and two sockets under the next board for its two tenons. 20 And for the second side of the Tabernacle, on the north side, there shall be twenty boards, 21 and their forty sockets of silver: two sockets under one board, and two sockets under the next board. 22 And for the rear<sup>z</sup> of the Tabernacle westward, you shall make six boards. 23 And two boards you shall make for the corners<sup>a</sup> of the Tabernacle in the rear. 24 And they shall be doubled<sup>b</sup> from beneath, and they shall be coupled together<sup>c</sup> at the top of it into one ring; and you shall overlay the bars with gold.<sup>k</sup> 30 And you shall rear up the Tabernacle according to the fashion<sup>l</sup> thereof which was shown to you on the mountain.<sup>m</sup>

<note>The following are technical Masoretic notes regarding specific Hebrew word spellings and accents in this manuscript.</note>
\* v. 13. **Upon** [Al] with a *Munach* accent in 4 [manuscripts] and in the margin of 1.
\* v. 14. **Covering** [Mikseh] with a *Tsere* vowel in 17 [manuscripts] and the Berlin manuscript, against the Masorah.

\* v. 25. **And their sockets** with *Paschta* accent in 3.
\* v. 29. **And the** (the first instance) with a *Ga'ya* mark in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 19.

<note>Philological apparatus at the bottom of the page regarding specific Hebrew letter markings and variant readings.</note>

v. 31. **Veil**: The letter Pe has a <term>Dagesh; a dot indicating a harder pronunciation</term> in manuscripts 4, 8, 11, and 14, and in the Beverly manuscript, but others do not have it. v. 33. Instead of **the clasps** <note>Hebrew: hakkerasim</note>, manuscripts 1 and 2 have **the boards** <note>Hebrew: hakkerashim, using the letter 'Shin' instead of 'Samekh'</note>; some ancient versions read it this way too, namely the Greek Septuagint, the Syriac, and the Aramaic Targum in our second manuscript. **It shall divide**: stressed on the second-to-last syllable in manuscript 3 and 4, contrary to the Masorah <note>the traditional system of notes on the biblical text</note>. v. 37. **Bases of**: joined with a <term>Maqqeph; a Hebrew hyphen</term> in manuscripts 7 through 16 and 19. CHAPTER 27, v. 3. **Its pots**: without a Dagesh in 7, 8, 11, 12, 15. v. 5. **From beneath**: The letter Teth lacks a Dagesh in 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 12, and 15, contrary to the standard Masoretic text.

<margin>
**Textual and Masoretic Notes on Spelling and Manuscript Variants:**
v. 21. **Signet** <note>original: "חתם"</note>: Written "defectively" <note>shorter spelling</note> in 4, 6, and 9 manuscripts. Follows the second Masora for verse 11, but contradicts Masora 1 and the printed edition for this location.
v. 24. **And you shall put** <note>original: "ונתת"</note>: Without the additional *He* <note>original: "ane ה paragog."</note> in 2 manuscripts. Likewise in verses 25 and 27, and others; but everywhere else Masora 7 and 8 require it, as in Exodus 25, 21.
v. 26. **The Ephod** <note>original: "האפוד"</note>: Full spelling <note>with the letter Vav</note> in 17 and 18 manuscripts and the Berlin codex. Similarly in 3 others according to Spanish books and the manuscript Masora in the Old Testament, folio 12a. But all others are defective.
v. 27. **The Ephod** <note>original: "האפד"</note>: Defective spelling in 1, 7, 8, 10–15, and 19 manuscripts. This contradicts the Masora here and in Chapter 28, 4, as well as the Old Testament text.
v. 28. **To be** <note>original: "להית"</note>: Defective in 2 and 4 manuscripts. Similarly in 3 others, perhaps from a Masoretic note applied here from Chapter 19, 16, which others correctly referred to Chapter 39, 21. For the full spelling is required here by Masora 7 and 8.
v. 33. **Pomegranates** <note>original: "רמני"</note>: Marked with the Kadma accent in manuscripts 7, 8, 10–13, 15, 17, 18, and 19.
v. 35. **His sound** <note>original: "קלו"</note>: Defective spelling required by Masora 7 and 8 at Genesis 27, 38. But full spelling is required by Masora 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 and the Erfurt manuscripts here, and also by Masora 1 and the Erfurt manuscripts at Genesis 45, 2.
v. 36. **Plate** <note>original: "ציץ"</term>: Written with a Dagesh <note>a grammatical dot</note> in 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 13, 17, and the Berlin codex according to the Old Testament. Furthermore, Masora 1 requires a small letter here, but this is without the text's actual writing or support from any codex.
</margin>

v. 39. "And you shall weave the tunic" so in manuscript 1. v. 40. "tunics" with the letter Caph marked by a Dagesh <note>a dot indicating emphasis or doubling</note> in manuscripts 7, 11, 12, 13, 15, contrary to the standard Hebrew text in verse 9. 
v. 12. "Them" with a simple Sheva <note>a vowel mark</note> in manuscript 3 and many Spanish codices. In the standard text, "not" is written fully in 7, 8, 10–16, 19, contrary to the standard Masorah.
"And head-bands" is written defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> according to Masorah 3, but against the Masorah in 7 and 8. "And they shall minister" v. 41. The Merca accent is used without a Maqqaph <note>hyphen</note> in 1, 2, and in the codex of Ben-Naphtali according to Selden: to which must be added the Spanish codices which the standard text says have the Gaiah (which is also sometimes called Merca elsewhere) under the Nun, not under the Caph. v. 43. "And to his descendants" so in 1, 4, 7, 8, 10–16, 19, but this division is incongruous and was corrected in the standard Hebrew text. CHAPTER 29, v. 1. "Which" with a Kadma accent in 1, 2, 4, and together with a Maqqaph in 6, 9, but in most books it is written with a Kadma without a Maqqaph; in some, the standard text notes it is written with a Maqqaph and a Metheg. v. 9. "Head-bands" written fully in 3 and 4, according to the Erfurt Masorah.

<note>The following are technical scribal and grammatical notes regarding the Hebrew text variants found in different ancient manuscripts.</note>

*. 11. "And you shall put" with a paragogic He at the end. *. 13. "And you shall take" with a Munach accent. "And the appendage" thus with a Makkaph [hyphen].
verse 15. "Aaron" written fully in 1, 2, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 19 with the Masorah 7 and 8, which however the Old Testament refutes.
f. 12. a. with both all Spanish codices and from Rabbi Meir Halleni, who writes: "In the whole Torah [Pentateuch] this name is found defective [missing a letter]." verse 17. "And the ram" with a Kadma accent in 3, 17, 18 and the Berlin codex, but the logic of the Sakeph accent requires it. verse 21. "Which" with a Makkaph and Metheg in 3rd edition, 4th. Munach, however, which regularly serves Sarka, is in the 4th, but the Masorah requires Merca here and in Genesis 30:16. verse 22. "And the appendage of the liver" read thus. verse 22. "His garments," the prefix "and" was erased in the 2nd.

v. 31. **Holiness** <note>Hebrew: *Kodesh*</note>: The *Geresh* accent is present. v. 32. **And in its composition**: The *Kadma* accent is placed over the second prefix. v. 34. **Stacte**: without *Pasek* mark, contrary to the Masorah on Deuteronomy 8:15. **Onycha**: The letter *Chet* is written with a *Segol* vowel in various copies. v. 38. **A man**: Marked with the *Zakeph gadol* accent. CHAPTER XXXI, v. 4. **To work**: written in the "defective" form (missing a letter), as the Masorah requires for chapter 35:1. v. 6. **Behold**: The *Pasek* is coupled with a *Munach* accent. **And Oholiab**: written with a *Tsere* and *Munach* in Berlin and Spanish manuscripts; others have *Segol* and a hyphen. **I have commanded you**: written in the "full" form in many manuscripts according to the Masorah, though others use the "defective" form. v. 8. **And all its utensils**: The word "all" is included in some manuscripts against the Masorah on chapter 30:27.

# EXODUS. CHAPTER 32.

<margin>verse 8. v) compare chapter 19:8; chapter 24:3; Acts 7:53. S) Jonathan's Targum: and they proclaimed before it.</margin>
"They have turned aside quickly from the way which I commanded them; they have made for themselves a molten calf, and have worshipped it, and have sacrificed to it, and said: 'These are your gods, O Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt.'"

<margin>verse 9. t) I have seen and experienced. Genesis 6:5. u) stiff-necked <note>original: "durus ceruice"</note>. chapter 33:3; chapter 34:9. A metaphor drawn from oxen who refuse to receive the yoke with a stiff neck.</margin>
And the Lord said to Moses: "I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people."

<margin>verse 10. x) leave me alone <note>original: "permitte mihi"</note>. Hosea 4:17; Psalm 106:23. y) Genesis 12:2; chapter 17:4; chapter 21:18; etc.</margin>
"Now therefore, let Me alone, that My wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them; and I will make of you a great nation."

<margin>verse 11. z) but he entreated <note>original: "sed deprecatus est"</note>. 1 Samuel 13:12. a) Numbers 14:13; Deuteronomy 9:18, 25. a) chapter 33:14, 15.</margin>
And Moses implored the face of the Lord his God, and said: "Lord, why does Your wrath wax hot against Your people, whom You have brought forth out of the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand?"

<margin>verse 12. b) Numbers 14:13; Deuteronomy 9:28. c) with evil intent <note>original: "ὁ κᾷ πονηρίας"</note>, with a bad spirit. Syriac: for their own evil. d) between the mountains, specifically of Arabia Petraea, where they were then. e) let it repent You <note>original: "pœniteat te"</note>. verse 14; Genesis 6:6. Greek: be merciful <note>original: "ἵλεως γίνδ"</note>. Hebrews 8:12. f) Targum Onkelos & Jonathan: concerning what You spoke that You would do to Your people. from verse 14.</margin>
"Why should the Egyptians speak, saying: 'For evil did He bring them forth, to slay them in the mountains, and to consume them from the face of the earth'? Turn from Your fierce wrath, and repent of this evil against Your people."

<margin>verse 13. g) Of Abraham. Deuteronomy 9:27; Nehemiah 5:19; Psalm 136:23. h) Genesis 22:16. i) Genesis 15:5. k) Genesis 13:7. l) which I will give to it <note>original: "ὃ κατεξέσω αὐτὴν"</note>. Matthew 21:38.</margin>
"Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, Your servants, to whom You swore by Your own self, and said to them: 'I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven, and all this land that I have spoken of I will give to your seed, and they shall inherit it forever.'"

<margin>verse 17. q) chapter 24:13; chapter 33:11. r) in his shouting or when he shouted. Micah 4:9. Jonathan's Targum: when they were jubilating with joy before the calf. s) the tumult of battle. Jeremiah 50:22.</margin>
<margin>At their shouting <note>A note on the Hebrew word "Be-re'oh"</note></margin>

<margin>verse 18. t) The sense is: It is neither the cry of the warrior nor of the conquered people, but of those celebrating a festival. Arabic, Persian, & Ethiopic versions: it is not a voice indicating victory, etc. Greek Scholia: instead of those winning, or those fleeing. Samaritan version: no longer a voice of responding with courage, and still a voice of responding with defeat. u) of responding, specifically of singing alternately. <margin>verse 20. c) Immediately he destroyed it, armed with divine zeal. cf. Psalm 69:10; John 2:14. d) and having burned what could be burned. e) and he ground the rest as much as he could. \*. 8. **You have commanded them** <note>Hebrew: "Tzivvitem"</note>: written fully in 4 manuscripts, against the Masoretic text of Erfurt. But "Tzivvitem" with a Qametz <note>a vowel mark</note> means "you commanded them," which is how the Greek (Septuagint), Vulgate, Samaritan, and Chaldean versions read it. Finally, defective in 3, 10, 19. \*. 11. **And he entreated** <note>Hebrew: "Vaychal"</note>: the letter Chet is silent in 2 manuscripts, but without the consensus of other codices or the Masora. \*. 12. **And to consume them**: the Kadma accent <note>a musical notation for chanting</note> is placed over the Lamed in 1, 2, 4. \*. 13. **And You spoke**: the letter Zain has a Metheg in 1, 2, 6, 9; a Munach in 4; a Kadma in 7, 8, 10–16, 19; but the Kadma is rejected by other texts. **As the stars**: defective in 2, 6–16, 19. Furthermore, a Mercha instead of a Metheg with a Tipcha is found in 6–10, 14, 19. \*. 17. **At their shouting**: without the Keri <note>a marginal reading suggesting a correction</note> in 1, 2, 4. \*. 20. **The calf which they had made**: so in 1, 2, 3; also in 4, but our accents were placed in the margin from the En Hakkore <note>a grammatical/masoretic treatise</note>.

*verse 19.* **I will show mercy** <note>original: "ארחם"</note> The Sagol vowel under the letter Chet requires a specific emphasis. *verse 20.* **To see** <note>original: "לראת"</note> this is written defectively <note>missing a letter</note>, as argued at length against another Masoretic note in Masora 7, 8 on Exodus 10:5. **CHAPTER 34.** *verse 1.* **The words** <note>original: "אֶת־הַדְּבָרִים"</note> thus in manuscripts 2 and 17, and Genesis Section 9. But others place the Kadma mark over the word "et," except for manuscript 3, which does not have it at all. *verse 5.* **And Yahweh** <note>original: "וַיהוה"</note> thus in 1, 2, 13, 17, 18. The others use the Merca mark anomalously. Furthermore, the *Pfik* <note>a vertical line used as a musical or textual separator</note>, which all have here near the *Sakeph-Katon*, is entirely emphatic, as the Jewish teachers themselves observe. Rabbi Yehuda ben Jacob in the Explanation of the Masora says: "Of this *Pfik* it is said in the Mechilta: 'The prudent one will understand and see' <note>original: "המשכיל יבין ויראה"</note>; for he who understands, let him understand and be silent, for a great mystery is signified." And Bechai <note>Rabbi Bahya</note> says that from this interposed *Pfik*, we learn that he who makes no distinction between **Yahweh** and **Yahweh** will one day pay the penalty. We do not doubt that the holy and venerable mystery of the Trinity is being pointed to here, since Bechai himself explains the name **Yahweh** repeated three times as: 1. referring to the **Crown** <note>original: "כתר"</note>, 2. referring to **Wisdom** <note>original: "חכמה"</note>, and 3. referring to **Understanding** <note>original: "בינה"</note>, which are three in the essence of God: *and the three of them are the essence of the Name* <note>original: "ושׁלשם הייהם עצמותם של שם"</note>.

<margin>
*Chapter XXXV. The observance of the Sabbath is emphasized.*
</margin>
<margin>
*v. 34. s) Greek: thereafter, etc. 2 Corinthians 3:16. Namely, as often as Moses entered the sanctuary before the Mercy Seat or the Ark of the Covenant to receive the laws delivered to him by God—speaking from the midst of the Cherubim—he removed the veil from his face, and did not put it back on until he had reported those same laws to the whole assembly of Israel. Thus, with an open face, he both perceived what was dictated by God and spoke while reporting it to the people. This is contrary to what is commonly thought, that Moses had the veil on when he reported the words of God to the people, whereas the Hebrew text clearly teaches the opposite. Maius, "Treatise on the Urim and Thummim," page 29. See also Bechai, folio 116. b.*
</margin>
**And Moses assembled** all the congregation of the children of Israel, and said to them: 1 **Chapter XXXV.** "These are the words which **Yahweh** has commanded you to do: 2 Work shall be done for six days, but the seventh day shall be a holy day for you, a **Sabbath** of rest to **Yahweh**; whoever does any work on it shall be put to death. 3 You shall kindle no fire throughout your dwellings on the Sabbath day."

<note>Philological and Masoretic notes regarding scribal variations and spelling</note>
*v. 30. "And they were afraid" is spelled deficiently in manuscript 1, contrary to the Erfurt Masorah. — v. 31. "The rulers" is spelled fully in manuscripts 3 and 4, but the Masorah requires it to be deficient. — v. 32. Omit "all the children of" in the Halle manuscript; the same was deleted in the codex of Rabbi Joseph the Punctuator, as witnessed by a marginal note in manuscript 1. — v. 33. "And Moses finished speaking" so in 1, 3, 17, 18. Revol. and Spanish codices; in the Old Testament folio 12. b. manuscript 4 corrected it, but the rest have "speaking" preceded by the accents Tiphcha with Merca. — CHAPTER XXXV, v. 1. "Children of" linked by a Maqqeph <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in manuscripts 7, 8, 10–16, 19, against the common Old Testament reading. — v. 2. "He shall be put to death" with a Patach vowel in manuscript 2, as required by the Erfurt Masorah. — v. 9. "And onyx stones and stones" so in Saphphando! found in 3, formerly 2 and 4. — "For the ephod" spelled deficiently in 1, 2, 3, formerly 4, against the Masorah at chapter 28:4 and Question 39, 24.*

*v. 12.* **The Ark** — written with the prefix "and" in several manuscripts (3, 1, 4), contrary to the Masorah of Erfurt.   *v. 16.* **The Laver** — spelled fully in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, contrary to the Major Masorah at chapter 30:18.

<note>The following notes are technical corrections regarding the Hebrew text and its traditional markings.</note>

v. 35. **in all the work** with the prefix *be* [in] in line 3. further 2. Furthermore, the Pesk adds it, and against this they place it after **craftsman** 2. 4. 7. 10. 11. 13. 19. against the Old Testament folio 12. b. **and in scarlet** with the prefix in line 3. further 4. except for the Masorah 2. and Ess.

CHAPTER XXXVI, v. 1. **to do** written fully in row 3. against the Masorah: at chapter 35, 1. The prefix *vav* [and] is added again in this place. 3.

v. 2. **who stirred** thus the Pronoun is held by a Maqqeph [hyphen] in line 2. 3. v. 4. **each man** thus in line further 4. v. 6. **voice** thus through Mercha [accent]: 2. 6. 7. 8. 9. etc. according to the Masorah at Genesis 30, 15. but others use a regular Munach [accent]. **they shall do** through Mercha: mibra, followed by Tiphcha, line 3. 4. 6. 9.

<note>The following notes are technical scholarly observations regarding variations in ancient Hebrew manuscripts and the Masora (the tradition of preserving the biblical text).</note>

Verse 10. The word *curtains* is written "defectively" (missing a vowel letter) in manuscripts 2 and 8, which goes against the *Or Torah* commentary, though that commentary contradicts its own Masoretic notes for verse 9. The letter *Beth* is written with a *Kamets* vowel in several lines according to the Masora. In verse 12, the word *corresponding* has a full spelling in manuscript 2; this variation is noted in the Masora Parva for Exodus 26:5, though the Masora usually requires the shorter spelling. Verse 13. The word *and he made* has a specific musical accent (Merca) in manuscript 3. Verse 15. The word *by the cubit* uses a Munach accent instead of a Metheg in manuscripts 1, 2, and 4. Verse 23. A new section of the *Setumah* (closed paragraph) begins with this verse in manuscript 3.

verse 29. **doubled** <note>Hebrew: to'amim</note>. Written defectively <note>Missing a letter, a common variation in Hebrew scribal tradition</note> in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 according to the Masorah, but the full spelling is required by Masorah 1 and the Erfurt manuscript for this passage and chapter 26:24. Similarly, it is printed in chapter 39:24 with the letter "mem" written fully in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, though this is contrary to the Old Testament folio 12b. For **together** <note>Hebrew: yachdav</note> it has the same word but with a variation found in manuscript 1. Regarding this diversity (as is the custom among Hebrew critics), the marginal note sharply objects with these words: **"The fools were writing and they turned away from the true writing"** <note>original Hebrew: ha-bo'arim hayu kotvim... natu</note>. He says they are foolish who write this way and wander from the path of truth. verse 36. **and he cast** <note>Hebrew: va-yitzok</note>. The letter Yod is written with a dot <note>term: Dagesh - a pronunciation mark</note> here and in chapter 37:3, 13 in manuscripts 10, 14, 16, 17, 18, and the Berlin manuscript; but others among ours are partly without the dot and partly with the horizontal mark <note>term: Raphe - indicating a softer pronunciation</note>, which is also required elsewhere in the Old Testament, for example in chapter 38:5 and Genesis 28:18.

# EXODUS. Chapter 38.

<margin>
x) its base. cf. chapter 39:39. 
y) from the mirrors. <note>original: "ex speculis"</note> (1) for this meaning cf. Job 37:18. Made of bronze, specifically for ease of use. Greek: "of the mirrors" <note>original: "κατόπτρων"</note>. cf. 2 Corinthians 3:10. The Hebrew letter 'Bet' very often denotes the material from which something is made, as in 1 Kings 7:14. 
z) of the women assembling in troops. So says M. I. <note>likely referring to a medieval commentator like Maimonides or a specific manuscript</note> cf. chapter 35:22; and see the same word in 1 Samuel 2:22 regarding women. But Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century theologian</note> translates: "of the ministers, who ministered before the door." cf. Numbers 8:24, Job 7:1, Luke 2:37. Onkelos <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> and the Syriac: "of the women who came to pray at the gate of the tent of meeting." Josephus: "of the modesty of the women." **v. 8.** "and its base" <note>original: "וְאֵת כַּנּוֹ"</note> so in manuscripts 1 and 2. **v. 11.** "and their bands" <note>original: "וַחֲשֻׁקֵיהֶם"</note> written fully in manuscript 2; missing letters in 1 and 3. According to the Masora <note>The tradition of biblical text preservation</note> applied here, which according to others belongs to v. 12. **v. 12.** "in the cubit" <note>original: "בָּאַמָּה"</note> without the prefix in 1. But manuscript 2 has the letter Nun in the text, though the Dagesh <note>a dot indicating letter doubling</note> and Kamets vowel are deleted; 3 has the letter Bet with points above and below, just as the Syrians write their "Ptocho" vowel. "and their bands" written defectively in 1, 2, 3, 4. Hal. <note>likely the Halle edition</note> notes this against the Masora for ch. 36:38. **v. 19.** "and their posts" written fully in 1, against the Masora for ch. 27:17. The Munach accent instead of Paschta in 1, 2, 4. **v. 21.** "the Testimony" <note>original: "הָעֵדֻת"</note> written fully in 4, against the Masora of Erfurt. **v. 23.** "in blue and in purple" <note>original: "בַּתְּכֵלֶת וּבָאַרְגָּמָן"</note> thus in manuscript 2.

<meta>Scholarly apparatus with textual variants and grammatical notes.</meta>

*v. 10.* **And they filled in it** <note>original: וַיְמַלְאוּ־בוֹ</note> without the *Kadma* accent in manuscripts 3, 7, 8, 11 through 16, and 19, which is contrary to the usual grammatical analogy. *v. 11.* **And a diamond** <note>original: וְיָהֲלֹם</note> the letter *Iod* is written with the *Kamets* vowel in Spanish codices in the Theta T. manuscript, folio 12b. *v. 12.* **And an amethyst** <note>original: וְאַחְלָמָה</note> accented on the last syllable (*milra*) in 3, 6, 9, and similarly in the first and second editions. *v. 13.* **And jasper** <note>original: וְיָשְׁפֶה</note> thus in 3. It is also found with the *Segol* vowel in 1, 2, 4, 6, 9. **Golden settings** <note>original: מוּסַבּוֹת זָהָב</note> thus in 1, following the *Tebhir* accent, perhaps for *Merca*, with the word **settings** <note>original: מִמשְׁבְּצוֹת</note> omitted. *v. 19.* **Inward** <note>original: בָּיְתָה</note> thus in 1. *v. 20.* **Two** <note>original: שְׁתֵּי</note> with the *Makkaph* connector in 1, 2, 3, 4. **From above the waistband** <note>original: מִמַּעַל לְחֵשֶׁב</note> thus in 1. *v. 21.* **From its rings** <note>original: מִטַּבְּעֹתָיו</note> the *Mem* has a *Metheg* in the Ben Naphtali tradition; but a marginal note in 1 orders it to be absent. **Shall be loosened** <note>original: יִזַּח</note> written in full in 1 according to the Massorah 7, 8 at verse 24, unless this perhaps refers to the suffix *-tiv* as found in the Erfurt manuscript at this location. Furthermore, they write **the breastpiece** <note>original: חן</note> deficiently in the text but read it <note>Kri</note> as **the breastpiece** <note>original: חן</note> in 4, Halle 8, 10 through 13, 15, 16, 19, contrary to Theta T.

### Philological Notes

**v. 25.** **The pomegranates**: spelled defectively [missing the letter 'vav']. The Masora notes this occurs only once. **v. 27.** **The tunics**: spelled fully [with 'vav'] twice according to the Masora and the Erfurt manuscript, though the Masora elsewhere requires the defective spelling in 7 or 8 instances. **v. 28.** **And the turban**: here with a Maqqeph [hyphen] and a Segol vowel. **v. 29.** **And**: with a Gaiah or Metheg [vowel stress mark] following Ben Asher. **v. 30.** **Writing**: with a Qamets vowel in the absolute state, a reading approved by the Masora and the Erfurt manuscript. **v. 33.** **Its hooks**: with a Pashta accent. **Its bars**: spelled defectively in many manuscripts, against the Masora and the Erfurt. **v. 35.** **The Testimony**: spelled fully, as found by Rabbi Hammeiri in his codex; however, the Masora and other ancient texts require the defective spelling. **v. 37.** **And the lampstand**: with the reading of the Halleni codex. **And its lamps**: again with the Halleni reading. **v. 40.** **For the tent**: thus in our marginal notes, though the text itself reads **in the tent** with the letter 'Beth'.

\*v.\* 20. **And he took**: The <term>Bible</term> <note>referring to specific manuscript traditions</note> has it twice: "And he took and he put the mercy seat," so it is read in the margin. \*v.\* 29. **entrance of the tabernacle**: so the <term>Masora</term> <note>The traditional system of notes on the Hebrew biblical text</note> 1, 17, 18. and the **Aramaic Version** in 4. ->**Be Strong**^h<- 
<note>original Hebrew: *Chazak*. It is a Jewish tradition to exclaim "Be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened" upon completing a book of the Torah in the synagogue. Here, the printer uses it to mark the conclusion of the book.</note>

---

<margin>
i) See after Genesis. k) ch. 22, 27.
l) Isaiah 66, 1. m) Psalm 19, 3.
n) Psalm 37, 31. o) Psalm 20, 3.
<note>The marginal notes here provide the biblical sources for the mnemonics used in the Masoretic summary below.</note>
</margin>

The sum of the verses of the book "And these are the names" <note>The Hebrew name for the Book of Exodus</note> is one thousand two hundred and nine; the mnemonic is **Arat**^i <note>A mnemonic is a word where the numerical values of the letters add up to the total. Aleph=1000, Resh=200, Tet=9</note>.
Its midpoint is "You shall not revile God" <note>Exodus 22:27</note>.
Its portions are **11**^k; the mnemonic is: "What is the house that you would build for me?"^l <note>Refers to the 11 weekly Torah portions contained in Exodus</note>.
Its sections <term>Sedarim|The Seder is a division of the biblical text used in the ancient Land of Israel for a three-year reading cycle</term> are **29**; the mnemonic is: "Night to night **declares** [**yechaveh**]^m knowledge."
Its chapters are **40**; the mnemonic is: "The law of his God is in his **heart** [**be-libo**]^n."
The count of the "open" paragraphs <note>Hebrew: *petuchot*; sections that start on a new line</note> is sixty-nine; and the "closed" paragraphs <note>Hebrew: *setumot*; sections separated by a space on the same line</note> is ninety-five.
The total is one hundred and sixty-four paragraphs; the mnemonic is: "**May He send** [**yishlach**]^o your help from the sanctuary and support you from Zion."

---

The manuscripts vary in establishing the number of verses. For codices 6 and 9 count 1,290; however, codex 3 counts **1,159** (written as A' K' N' T'). But codices 1, 4, 7, 8, 12, 17, 18, and the Berlin codex agree with us. Instead of the symbol for the 11 Portions (**11**), some use the word **Chag** (Festival), which equals the same numerical value. However, codices 7, 8, and 12 count 11 sections and 29 portions erroneously and in a confused order. For the symbol **Yechaveh** (29), some substitute **Kadah**, which is equivalent in value. Finally, these add: "And the verse-divisions are sixteen, and their mnemonic is **Kadi**."

<note>Critical notes on the Hebrew text at the bottom of the page.</note>

* **v. 1. And he called [Vayikra]** This word contains a small letter *Aleph* <note>The final letter of the first word is traditionally written smaller in the Torah</note> according to the Masorah. In some manuscripts (7, 8, 12, etc.) it is noted as such. The illustrious Hiller conjectures (p. 175) that this small *Aleph* might be a symbol of a variant reading between "Vayikra" (and He called) and "Vayikar" (and He happened upon), a phrase used when God appeared elsewhere (Exodus 5:3, Numbers 23:3). * **v. 8. The priests** Certain manuscripts (4, 17, 18) place a *Munach* accent under the letter Caph, while others use a *Metheg*. * **v. 8. The pieces** Manuscripts 7, 2, 10, etc., use this form against other editions. * **v. 9. Offering by fire** The Masorah requires a *Merca* accent here, though some Erfurdt manuscripts use *Tebhir*. * **v. 11. On the side** Three manuscripts use a hyphen (*Makkaph*) here. * **v. 13. It [Hu]** A *Zakef-Katon* accent is found here in several manuscripts.

*   **v. 16.** *The Altar*: written with a simple *Pashta* accent in various Spanish manuscripts and the Berlin codex. This is required wherever no other consonant comes between the tonic letter and the *Patach-gnupha*.
*   **v. 17.** *By its wings*: The letter *Beth* has a *Dagesh* in several manuscripts (6, 11, 13-16, 19) because of the preceding substitute accent; however, the Masora requires it to be soft (*raphatum*).
*   **Chapter II, v. 1.** *When*: Uses a *Munach* accent instead of a *Maqqeph* in some copies. **v. 2.** *The Priest*: Has a *Geresh* accent in several Spanish books, while others have a *Mahpach*.
*   **v. 8.** *The Grain Offering*: Uses a *Zakef-katon* preceded by a *Pashta*.
*   **v. 10.** *And the remnant*: Written defectively (missing a letter) in some manuscripts, against the Erfurt Masora but in agreement with the printed text at verse 3. **v. 12.** *Them*: Some read "it" (feminine singular) referring specifically to the *Mincha*.

**1** And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

*   **verse 11.** *and all* — The prefix *vav* <note>The Hebrew letter 'and'.</note> was removed in manuscript 3, contrary to the Major Erfurt manuscript.
*   **verse 12.** *and he shall burn it* — Thus with the accents *Zakef Katon* and *Munach* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, and 20.
*   **verse 13.** *and it is hidden* — The letter *Ayin* is written with the vowel *Hatef-Segol* in manuscripts 2, 3, 6, 9, and 20.
*   **verse 17.** *before* — Marked with *Merkha* and *Tzere* in manuscript 4; but with the accents transposed in 7, 8, 10–13, 15–19.
*   **verse 18.** *horns* — Spelled fully (with a *vav*) in manuscripts 3, 4, and the Halle edition; but in the Masora <note>Traditional notes on the text of the Hebrew Bible.</note> that appears at chapter 4:7, this word is not listed among those spelled fully.
*   **verse 19.** *and [the fat]* — Manuscripts 1, 2, 4, and the Berlin edition have a *Maqqef* <note>A Hebrew hyphen.</note>; but all others have the accents *Merkha* and *Tzere*.
*   **verse 20.** *for the bull* — Uses the accent *Revia* instead of *Zakef Katon* in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 20.
*   **verse 24.** *and he shall lay* — Manuscripts 3 and 4 add the particle *et* without vowels; but manuscript 1 deleted it after it had been included.

# LEVITICUS. CHAPTER 5

<margin>
**Concerning him who swears in vain, and how he is atoned for.**
</margin>

**4** Or if a person swears, speaking rashly with their lips to do evil or to do good—whatever it is that a person may speak rashly in an oath—and it is hidden from them, but then they come to know it, and they become guilty in one of these matters.

**5** And it shall be, when they are guilty in one of these matters, that they shall confess that in which they have sinned.

**6** And they shall bring their guilt offering <note>Hebrew: *asham*, a sacrifice specifically for restitution or perceived guilt</note> to the LORD for their sin which they have committed: a female from the flock, a lamb or a female goat, for a sin offering; and the priest shall make atonement for them concerning their sin.

**7** But if their hand cannot reach enough for a lamb, then they shall bring as their guilt offering for that which they have committed two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the LORD; one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering.

**8** And they shall bring them to the priest, who shall offer that which is for the sin offering first, and pinch off its head from the back of its neck, but shall not divide it asunder.

**9** And he shall sprinkle of the blood of the sin offering upon the side of the altar; and the rest of the blood shall be drained out at the base of the altar; it is a sin offering.

**10** And he shall offer the second for a burnt offering, according to the ordinance; and the priest shall make atonement for them for their sin which they have committed, and it shall be forgiven them. 

**11** But if their hand cannot attain to two turtledoves or two young pigeons, then they shall bring for their offering for that which they have committed the tenth part of an ephah <note>An ephah is an ancient dry measure; a tenth of an ephah is roughly 2.2 liters or about 9 cups</note> of fine flour for a sin offering; they shall put no oil upon it, nor shall they put frankincense on it, for it is a sin offering.

**12** And they shall bring it to the priest, and the priest shall take a handful of it, the memorial portion, and burn it on the altar, upon the offerings made by fire to the LORD; it is a sin offering.

**13** And the priest shall make atonement for them concerning their sin that they have committed in any of these things, and it shall be forgiven them; and the remainder shall be the priest's, as a grain offering.

</margin>

**14** And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:

**15** If a person commits a breach of trust <note>Hebrew: *ma’al*, implying a "trespass" or "sacrilege"</note> and sins unintentionally in the holy things of the LORD, then they shall bring as their guilt offering to the LORD a ram without blemish out of the flocks, according to your valuation in silver shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary, for a guilt offering.

**16** And they shall make restitution for that which they have done wrong in the holy thing, and shall add the fifth part to it, and give it to the priest; and the priest shall make atonement for them with the ram of the guilt offering, and it shall be forgiven them. 

**17** And if a person sins, and does any of the things which the LORD has commanded not to be done, though they did not know it, yet they are guilty, and shall bear their iniquity.

\* 1. **וזאת** [And this] By the accent Tiphcha followed by Munach... which the Targum <note>Aramaic translation</note> also retains in this way.  
\* **הכליות** [The kidneys] Written fully <note>including the letter 'yod'</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, and the Hillel codex according to Masorah 1, 2, and Erfurt; but the Masorah 7 and 8 requires it to be written defectively <note>missing the 'yod'</note> here and in Chapter 3, verse 10.

\* 5. The Hillel codex was corrected in this way, with the Masoretic note added: **חג חסרין** [missing the letter 'gimel'?], as Menachem reports in his Old Testament work, folio 13b, who nevertheless approves the full spelling based on Rabbi Meir Halevi, author of the tract *Halachot*.  
\* 8. **עלה** [Burnt offering] shortened in manuscripts 7, 8, 10, 12 through 16, 19, and 21, contrary to the standard Old Testament.  
\* **תאפה** [Shall be baked] The letter Pe has the vowel Tsere in the Hillel manuscript according to the Masoretic information. **מחבת** [Pan] has the vowel Kamets under the letter Beth in manuscripts 3, 4, 5, and 21, contrary to Masorah 1, 2, and Erfurt.  
\* 10. **וחרבה** [And dry] The letter Beth has a Patach vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 8, 9, 12, 13, 15, 19, and 21 according to Masorah 1, 2, 7, 8, and Erfurt; but it has a Kamets in our other manuscripts, including the Spanish, Hillel, and Jerusalem codices; nor is this instance listed in the Masorah of words with Patach at the accent Atnach, as observed in the Old Testament.

<note>The following are critical notes on specific Hebrew letters and accents from various manuscript codices.</note>
\* v. 36. **אֲשֶׁר** (*Asher*) - The accent *Tlischaktana* is found in codices 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 9. 20. and the Berlin codex; but the others have *Gdola*. \* v. 38. **קָרְבְּנֵיהֶם** (*Korbaneyhem*) - The vowel *Kamets* is under the letter *Beth* in codices 7. 8. 10. 12. 13. 15. 16. 19. and 21. CHAPTER VIII. v. 7. **הָאֵפֹד** (*Ha-Ephod*) - The accent *Metheg* instead of *Munach* is in 6 through 21. The "Middle of the Law" regarding the count of verses is noted in our margin as **ו ון** in 1. 2. 6 through 9. 17. and the Berlin codex. \* v. 9. **נֵזֶר** (*Nezer*) - The letter *Nun* has the vowel *Tsere* in 2. 7. 8. 10. 13. 14. 15. 16. 19. 20. 21. \* v. 11. **וַיַּז** (*Vayaz*) - The letter *Yod* has the vowel *Tsere* in 1, and *Chirek* in 3; both are against the Masoretic tradition. \* v. 12. **וַיִּצֹק** (*Vayitzok*) - The letter *Tsade* is without a *Dagesh* in 4. 6. 7. 8. etc., with an explicit *Raphe* in 2; others have it with a *Dagesh*. Compare what we noted at Exodus 36:36. \* v. 13. **כֻּתֳנֹת** (*Kuttonot*) - thus in 1 and Berlin. **מִגְבָּעוֹת** (*Migba'ot*) is written defectively in 3 and 4, according to the Masorah for Exodus 28:40, but against the printed versions there and here, and the Erfurt codex.

v. 15. **קַרְנֹת** (horns) is written deficiently in manuscripts 3, 4, and 5, contrary to the <term>Masorah</term><note>The traditional system of notes on the text of the Hebrew Bible used to ensure its accurate transmission.</note> on chapter 4:7. v. 21. **נִיחֹחַ** (pleasing) is written with a double <term>Paschta</term><note>A Hebrew cantillation mark or accent.</note> by most of our sources; but with a single one in 3, 14, 17, 18, and the Spanish books in the Old Testament folio 13b and elsewhere. v. 23. **וַיִּשְׁחָט** (and he slaughtered) lacks the <term>Pesiq</term><note>A vertical line used as a musical or logical separator in Hebrew text.</note> in 3 and 5, contrary to the Masorah. A <term>Patach</term><note>A vowel sign representing the 'a' sound.</note> under the letter Chet is found in 3 and 4, but the Masorah itself requires a <term>Qamets</term><note>A vowel sign usually representing a longer 'a' or 'o' sound.</note> in 4 for this location, as do the printed editions at verse 15 and the *Minchat Shai*. v. 26. **הַחֲלָבִים** (the fats) has a <term>Metheg</term><note>A small vertical stroke used as an accent or to indicate a vowel's length.</note> instead of a <term>Munach</term><note>A common conjunctive cantillation mark.</note> in 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 19, and 20. v. 27. **הַכֹּל** (the whole) was corrected with a <term>Rebia</term><note>A diamond-shaped accent mark.</note> in 1, but "all that he gave" is found in 4, 6, 9, and 20; this was also the case in 1, which now refers to our reading in the margin.

**verse 29.** **למשה** <note>original: "for Moses"</note> marked with the accent *Pishla* followed by *Munach*... and the Targum... which was amended in the text according to our reading. **verse 30.** **ועל בגדיו** <note>original: "and on his garments"</note> with the prefix *Vav*... the Masorah wants this removed... but it is added again in several manuscripts... **verse 31.** **אהל** <note>original: "Tent"</note> with the connector *Maqqeph*... **צויתי** <note>original: "I commanded"</note> with the vowel *Kibbutz* in the passive form (as it follows in verse 35) is found in the old Basel edition... and so the Septuagint, Latin Vulgate, Syriac, and Chaldean read it; but the Masorah requires the vowel *Chireq* in the active voice. **verse 32.** **והנותר** <note>original: "and the remainder"</note>... **CHAPTER 9. verse 5.** **אשר** <note>original: "which"</note> has a *Maqqeph* in some versions... but a *Munach* in others.

Verse 3. The word "He" [hu] is marked with a <term>Telisha Gedola</term> accent in manuscripts 1, 2, and 5. *Verse 4. The phrase "and to Elzaphan" [ve-el-Elzaphan] uses a <term>Maqqef</term> (hyphen) in place of a <term>Munach</term> accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9, and 20. Verse 5. In the word "in their tunics" [bekuttonotam], the letter Tau has a simple <term>Shva</term> in most manuscripts, including the edition of Hipp. in the Old Testament, folio 14b; David Kimchi also notes this in the Masorah, though he found a <term>Chateph Qamets</term> vowel in one corrected manuscript. *Verse 6. The word "your heads" [rasheichem] has a <term>Munach</term> accent in manuscripts 1, 5, 6, 9, and 20. *Verse 10. The word "And to distinguish" [ve-lahavdil] is written thus with a <term>Zaqef Qatan</term> and <term>Metheg</term> in all our texts... whereas elsewhere a <term>Zaqef Gadol</term> would be required. *Verse 12. "And to Eleazar" [ve-el-Eleazar] appears with a <term>Maqqef</term> in many manuscripts (1, 3, 4, 5, etc.). However, others use a <term>Munach</term> in the text... For "and to Ithamar" [ve-el-Ithamar], some call for a <term>Merca</term> with <term>Kadma</term>... while others omit the <term>Kadma</term> entirely against the standard Old Testament text.

CHAPTER XI. 2. d) Compare Deuteronomy 14:4 and following. Note: Some of these precepts seem to have had natural causes, based on good or bad nutrition, as Maimonides <note>The famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and physician</note> observed; or because humans naturally shrink from some, such as venomous lizards etc.; nor should it be dismissed, as others have argued, that it was established so that the Hebrews would live apart from other idolatrous nations, based on Leviticus 20:24, 25, 26. # LEVITICUS. CHAPTER 11. <note>The Hebrew header correctly identifies this as Chapter 11 (יא), though the Latin text mistakenly reads Chapter 2.</note>

<margin>
v. 11. **u)** you shall abhor them. 
v. 13. Deuteronomy 7:26. 
v. 13. **x)** the eagle. Deuteronomy 14:12. 
**y)** the bone-breaking eagle <note>original: "aquilam ossifragam"</note> from the root *paras* (פרס), to break bones. Micah 3:3. 
**z)** a powerful or black eagle. <note>original Greek: "άλιαιετον" - sea-eagle</note>. 
v. 14. **a)** the kite, named for its flight. cf. Deuteronomy 28:49. 
**b)** the falcon or hawk, a bird of very sharp sight. Deuteronomy 14:13; Job 28:7. 
v. 16. **e)** "daughter of crying," i.e., a noisy bird or owl. Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar</note> identifies it as the female ostrich. 
**d)** Bochart identifies this as the male ostrich because of its neglect of eggs and chicks; others say the swallow. 
**e)** <note>original Greek: "λαάγυ"</note> the gull; a sea bird that is extremely lean. 
**f)** the hawk, from the root *natsah* (נצה) meaning "to fly." Job 39:26. 
v. 17. **g)** The Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> calls it an owl; Bochart calls it a pelican. Psalm 102:7. 
**h)** a diver bird <note>cormorant</note>. 
**i)** a small owl, named from *neshef* (נשף), meaning "darkness." Isaiah 34:11. 
v. 18. **k)** the screech owl. cf. verse 30. 
**l)** the pelican. Isaiah 34:11; Psalm 102:7. 
**m)** a species of vulture, named for its mercy and care toward its young <note>from the Hebrew root *racham*, mercy</note>. 
v. 19. **n)** the stork. Jeremiah 8:7. 
**o)** the heron, named for its anger. Bochart calls it a genus of eagle. 
**p)** the moorhen, or otherwise the hoopoe. 
**q)** the bat. Deuteronomy 14:18. 
v. 20. **r)** specifically types of bats and flies. 
v. 21. **s)** those which have two longer legs in addition to four feet, such as locusts. cf. verse 23. 
**t)** for leaping. Job 37:1. 
v. 22. **u)** a wingless locust <note>original: "attelabum"</note>, a species of locust, from the Chaldean root *salaam* meaning "to consume." 
**x)** another species of locust. The Arabic root suggests "being joined in a long series." According to Golius <note>a Dutch orientalist</note>, this word in Arabic signifies a species of wingless locust, called *dromaron* by the Greeks. 
**y)** another species of locust; the Arabic root notes "to cover," because they veil the sun. Numbers 13:33. <note>original Greek: "άκερίδα"</note> Matthew 3:4. 
v. 24. **z)** Chapter 5:2.
</margin>

<margin>
*On permitted or forbidden birds and creeping things.*
<note>Hebrew: לו קרי - Read as "to it" (lo)</note>
v. 26. **a)** see verses 3 and 7. 
**b)** namely, when dead, as in verses 24, 27, 31. 
v. 27. **c)** not having hooves, but toes, such as the dog, cat, etc. 
v. 29. **d)** regarding creeping things, or smaller four-footed animals; similarly regarding birds in verses 20 and 23. 
**e)** The Mole, from "sweeping" or "digging out." 
**f)** the mouse. 1 Samuel 6:4.

**i)** The *Coach* lizard. 
**k)** The *Letaa* lizard.

<note>Translator's Philological Notes:</note>
Verse 12: A small section break is made here in manuscripts 1, 3, 4, 5, and Hal. and 21. 
Verse 14: **And the kite** (ואת־הדאה) - so the Kadma accent is placed over the Aleph in manuscripts 1, 6, 9, 20, and similarly in manuscript 4. 
Verse 15: **And every** (ואת) with the prefix Vav in manuscripts 1 and 4, contrary to Masoretic manuscript 1 and Erfurt. 
Verse 20: **Four** (ארבע) with a Kamets vowel in manuscripts 1, 3, 4, 5, and also in the following verse. 
Verse 21: **Which to it** (אשר-לו) has a Kadma accent instead of a Maqqef in 4, 6, 9, 20. The written form (*Ktiv*) with the letter Aleph (לא) instead of Vav (לו) is to be explained as affirmative, just like the reading (*Kri*), according to Hiller, page 65-66. For **in them** (בהן), which is approved by the Masorah on Genesis 30:26, as well as the printed editions and Erfurt, manuscripts 3, 5, and Hal. have **in them** (בהם - masculine), and so in manuscripts 1 and 4. 
Verse 24: With this verse, Hal. 7 and 8 begin a new section, contrary to the Old Testament folio 14. b. 
Verse 26: **To every** (לכל) without a Gaia accent in 21 and Berlin. 
Verse 30: **And the wall lizard** (והלטאה) - they have a large Lamed in manuscripts 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 16, 17, 19, 21, which according to Hiller (page 173) is a symbol of a variant reading; but this is rejected by the Old Testament <note>likely referring to a specific codex or tradition</note>.

℣. 32. **יפל** (falls) with Metheg and Makkef in various manuscripts. Spanish books also note a Munach accent in the margin. **מהם** (of them) without Paseq in several manuscripts, contrary to other editions.

℣. 42. **גחון** (belly): contains a <term>Vav Rabbati</term> <note>A "large Vav," an oversized letter in the Torah scroll.</note> as noted by Buxtorf in *Tiberias*, citing the Talmudic tractate *Kiddushin*. It is written larger to warn the reader that this letter is the middle of the entire Torah. Compare *Cosri* Part III. However, Hiller considers it a symbol of variant spelling. The *O.T.* advises that while the Vav should be large, it should be slightly shorter than a final *Nun*.

v. 24. **burning** (*Mikvat*): Thus written with a <term>Metheg</term> <note>a small vertical line used as a musical or stress marker</note> in manuscripts 6 and 9 according to the Masorah of Erfurt. v. 26. **and it** (*ve-hi*): written with the letter *Yod* in manuscripts 1, 2, and 4, contrary to the Masorah on Genesis 38:25. — v. 28. **it** (*Hu*): Thus written with the letter *Vav* in 1–5, Halle 17, 18, and Berlin according to the Old Testament folio 14b, while others write it with *Yod*. v. 30. **deep** (*Amok*): Written "plene" <note>using a vowel-letter instead of just a vowel-point</note> in 2; likewise in verses 25, 31, 32, 34; but everywhere contrary to the Masorah of Erfurt for verse 3. v. 32. **hair** (*Se'ar*): The letter *Ayin* is written with a *Patach* vowel almost always in this context in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 4. v. 33. **and he shall be shaven** (*ve-hitgallach*): A large letter *Gimel* <note>Gimel maiusculum</note> is used in 2, 3, 4, Halle 7, 8, etc., as required by the Masorah here and at Genesis 1:1 and 1 Chronicles 1:1. The Talmudists note in the tractate *Kiddushin* (30a) that this is the middle verse of the Torah. However, the scholar Hiller (p. 166) suspects this large letter might symbolize a variant reading *ve-hitnallach*, following the form of *vayitpallel* in Judges 21:9. Furthermore, the letter *Lamed* is written with a *Patach* vowel in manuscripts 1–3, 7, 8, etc., contrary to the Masorah.

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
2 This shall be the law of the leper on the day of his cleansing: he shall be brought to the priest.
3 And the priest shall go out to the outside of the camp, and the priest shall look, and behold, the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper.

10 And on the eighth day he shall take two **lambs**<sup>f</sup> without blemish, and one ewe lamb in its first year without blemish, and three **tenths**<sup>g</sup> of fine flour for a grain offering mixed with oil, and one **log**<sup>h</sup> of oil.

11 And the priest who cleanses shall **present**<sup>i</sup> the man to be cleansed and **them**<sup>k</sup> before the Lord at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.

12 And the priest shall take one lamb and offer it for a **guilt offering**<sup>l</sup> and the **log**<sup>m</sup> of oil, and **wave**<sup>n</sup> them as a wave offering before the Lord.

13 And he shall slaughter the lamb in the place where he slaughters the **sin offering**<sup>o</sup> and the burnt offering, in the holy place; for like the sin offering, the guilt offering belongs to the priest; it is **most holy**<sup>p</sup>.

14 And the priest shall take some of the blood of the **guilt offering**<sup>q</sup>, and the priest shall put it on the **lobe**<sup>r</sup> of the right ear of the person to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.

15 And the priest shall take some of the **log**<sup>s</sup> of oil and pour it into the **palm**<sup>t</sup> of the priest's left hand.

16 And the priest shall **dip**<sup>u</sup> his right finger in the oil that is in his left palm and **sprinkle**<sup>x</sup> some of the oil with his finger seven times before the Lord.

17 And of the rest of the oil that is in his palm, the priest shall put some on the lobe of the right ear of the person to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot, **over**<sup>y</sup> the blood of the guilt offering.

18 And what remains of the oil that is in the priest’s palm he shall put on the head of the person to be cleansed; and the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord.

19 And the priest shall offer the **sin offering**<sup>z</sup> and make atonement for the person to be cleansed from his uncleanness; and afterward he shall slaughter the burnt offering.

20 And the priest shall offer the burnt offering and the grain offering on the altar; and the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be clean.
