22 and **two turtledoves**<sup>d</sup> or two young pigeons, such as his means allow; one shall be a sin offering and the other a burnt offering.

23 And he shall bring them on the eighth day **for his purification**<sup>e</sup> to the priest, to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, before the Lord.

The ritual mirrors priestly consecration by applying blood and oil to the right ear, thumb, and toe of the cleansed individual.</summary>

**v. 41.** **And they shall pour out** with the Mahpach accent in manuscripts 1 and 3. --- **v. 42.** **And other dust he shall take and smear** thus in 1 and likewise in 4. **And he shall smear** with the Pasach accent in 3, 4, 5, contrary to the Masora and manuscript 1. --- **v. 49.** **And hyssop** written defectively in the Halle 17, 18 manuscripts and the Berlin manuscript according to the Old Testament folio 14. b.; all others write it fully. --- **v. 51.** **Wood** with a Munach accent in place of a Makkef in 1, 2, 3. **The hyssop** thus with Gerashaim and Mesh in 2, 3. --- **v. 52.** **The house** has a Rebia accent in 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11, 12, 15, 16, 20. --- **v. 56.** **And for a swelling** with a "raphatum" (soft) Shin in 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9, 17, 18, 20 and Berlin manuscript; but it is marked with a dagesh (hardened) in the rest. --- **v. 57.** **This is the law** thus in 4.

# LEVITICUS. CHAPTER 16.

<margin>
**o)** *inside the curtain.* <note>original Latin: "intra velum"</note> Verses 12, 15. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> reads: "further inside the curtain" <note>original Greek: "esōteron tou katapetasmatos"</note>. See Hebrews 6:19 and compare with Exodus 26:31.
**p)** *before the mercy seat.* <note>The "mercy seat" or "atonement cover" was the gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant.</note> Verse 14. The Septuagint reads: "at the face of the propitiatory" <note>original Greek: "eis prosōpon tou hilastēriou"</note>. See Exodus 25:17.
**q)** See verses 1 and 13.
**r)** Both inside and outside the tabernacle. Exodus 40:34 and following; Numbers 9:15, 16.
**s)** With this thing, or victim, he shall enter into the sanctuary, not without blood. Hebrews 9:7.

**u)** The holy linen tunic. See Exodus 28:40, 42.
**x)** And linen undergarments. See Leviticus 6:3; Ezekiel 44:18.
**y)** With a sash. Exodus 28:4.
**z)** He shall clothe himself, cover, or dress. See Exodus 22:18.
**a)** Scripture teaches that the High Priest, who serves in the inner sanctuary, is a "type" <note>A symbolic foreshadowing or model.</note> of the ministry that takes place in the heavenly sanctuary. For the High Priest of the earthly sanctuary, dressed in four linen garments during his service, was a model of the camps of the Shechinah <note>The Divine Presence of God.</note>, or the sacred living creatures with four wings and four faces. So they also say in the Midrash Vayikra Rabba <note>An ancient Jewish homiletic commentary on Leviticus.</note>: "What is the heavenly service like? Answer: There is one man (Michael) in their midst, dressed in linen" (Ezekiel 9:2). Thus, also in administering the earthly service, a linen tunic is required. According to Bahya <note>A reference to the medieval commentator Bahya ben Asher.</note>.
**b)** His whole body. Verses 24, 26, 28. Not just hands and feet, as in Exodus 30:19.

Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Hebrew grammarian.</note> explains most simply: "for the goat that goes away" into the desert (verse 21) or to freedom, like the second bird in Leviticus 14:7, 53. The Septuagint translates it as "the one sent away" <note>original Greek: "tō apopompaiō"</note>, meaning the emissary or the "averter" who drives away evils. Bochart <note>A 17th-century scholar of biblical animals.</note> believes it is a plural Arabic name for "recesses in the desert." Clericus thinks it is a compound Arabic word meaning "precipitation" or "casting down." We omit further conjectures. Verses 10, 26.
**Verse 9. i)** That is, from the vessel in which the lots were gathered. Joshua 18:11; compare chapter 19:10. The Rabbis believe the lots were drawn by the High Priest; others say they jumped out by shaking the urn.
**Verse 10. k)** For the transgression of the people.
**l)** Clericus: "to the solitudes in the desert." Verse 8.
**Verse 12. m)** A fullness, i.e., a full censer. Chapter 2:2.
**n)** Leviticus 10:1; Numbers 17:11.
**o)** Exodus 9:8, 10.

**Technical Notes on the Text:**
In verse 18, the phrase *which-before* <note>original: "asher-lifne"</note> is written this way in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 14, 20. The word *The goat* <note>original: "ha-sa'ir"</note> here and in verse 21 is written in "defective" form [missing a letter], which requires a Masoretic note. Verse 21: *upon the head of the goat* is accented with a double Munach in manuscripts 6, 14, 19, 20, 21. Verse 22: *cutting off* <note>original: "gezirah"</note> is spelled with a silent letter *Yud* in manuscripts 1, 3, 5. Verse 26: *And the one who sends* <note>original: "ve-ha-meshalleach"</note> has a *Chateph-patach* vowel under the letter *Mem* in most Spanish codices. Verse 29: *among you* <note>original: "be-tochechem"</note> is spelled with a *Chateph-patach* in manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 20. Verse 30: *For* <note>original: "ki"</note> has a Munach accent instead of a Makkaph [hyphen] in manuscripts 6, 9, 20.

<margin>
**h)** Reasons for so severe a prohibition: 1) because the soul, that is, the life, is in the blood. verse 11. And so that they would not learn to hunger even for human blood. Genesis 9:4 and following. 2) Lest blood be profaned by ordinary, common use. verse 11. This also 3) so that the price of Christ's blood might be foreshadowed, which alone is truly our propitiation and atonement. Acts 20:28. Colossians 1:14, 20. 1 Peter 1:19. 1 John 1:7. etc.
Just as it was signified while the symbolic tabernacle or temple was still standing that the way into the holy places was not yet manifest (Hebrews 9:8), so also while the law concerning the prohibition of blood was instituted and enduring, the Holy Spirit signified that He had not yet come into the flesh, who truly sanctifies men by the shedding of His blood. But after He arrived; not only was the law against eating blood repealed, but Christ Himself offered His own blood for us to drink. Matthew 26:27, 28. John 6:53 and following. For, as for the fact that the Apostles commanded the Gentiles to abstain from blood (Acts 15:29), it was not a perpetual law, or a means by which they would be saved, but an ordinance instituted for a time, and a bond of charity, by which they might more gently unite with the weak Jews. Just as for the sake of a friend who is nauseated by cheese, a friend abstains from the same.
**v. 11. i)** chapter 4:25, 30, 34. **k)** "for the soul." Numbers 35:33. Hebrews 9:22. <note>original Greek: ἀνטὶ ψυχῆς</note> "instead of a soul." Matthew 26:28. Gusset <note>Jacques Gousset, a 17th-century Hebrew scholar</note>: "through the soul," that is, by the power of the soul, consisting in that blood. Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum of Pseudo-Jonathan</note>: "for the blood of the sacrifice atones for the guilt of the soul."
**v. 12. l)** chapter 7:26, 27. **m)** Arabic Pentateuch: "nay, not even the stranger."

**v. 20.** Here a new small section is opened by manuscripts 2, 3, 4, 5, and the Halle edition. The word "and the man" <note>original Hebrew: וְאִישׁ</note> has a small <term>Tifcha</term> accent in the text; but in the margin it is a great one. The word "and she" <note>original Hebrew: וְהִיא</note> is written with a 'yod' by manuscripts 2, 4, 7, 8, 12, 13, 15, 16, and the Halle edition; but the Old Testament requires a 'vav'.
**v. 24.** The word "fourth" is written "plene" <note>using a vowel letter to indicate pronunciation</note> in 2, 3, 4, 5, against Masoretic manuscript 1 and the Erfurt edition.
**v. 25.** "The fifth": Written with the <term>Revia</term> accent in all except 17 and the Berlin manuscript, which use <term>Zakef Katon</term>. Furthermore, the word "to me" is written "plene" in 2, 5, Halle, 6, 9, 17, 20, and the Berlin manuscript; thus it appears in the first edition, second edition, and the Old Testament, while others use the "defective" <note>shorter</note> spelling. The word for "disfigure" is written defective without the 'yod' in 2, 6, 9, 17, 20, and the Berlin manuscript; thus in the first edition, but others write it plene. Finally, the letter 'Shin' is doubled with a strong <term>Dagesh</term> mark in 4, 8, 11, 12, 14, 15, 18, 21, against the Old Testament.
**v. 31.** "Do not seek": The letter 'Kuf' has a <term>Dagesh</term> in 3, 6, 9, 11, 12, 20, against the Old Testament.
**v. 33.** "Shall dwell": Uses the <term>Merca</term> accent in 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 20, against standard grammar.

**Verse 4.** *to profane himself* [le-he-challo]: Thus the accent *Tiphcha* appears with *Silluk* in the same word in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15, 16, 19, 20, and in the Berlin edition according to the printed Masorah and the Erfurt manuscript; but others have *Metheg* instead of *Tiphcha*, or neither. **Verse 8.** *And you shall sanctify him*: without the *Kadma* accent in the Spanish books of the Old Testament, folio 15. **For the [fire-offerings]**: thus with a *Makkeph* [hyphen] in manuscripts 1, 3, 5, and the Spanish. According to the Masorah in the margin of manuscript 1, which holds this, but others distinguish the word *for* with a *Tevir* accent. **Verse 12.** *Crown*: with a *Makkeph* in manuscript 3; but without accent or *Makkeph* in 1, 2, 6, 9, 20. Manuscript 4 and the final Masorah require the *Paser* accent. Manuscript 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 20, and 4 use the *Tiphcha* accent, as the Old Testament seems to require. **Verse 14.** *In her virginity*: The *Dagesh* [dot indicating emphasis] which some have in the prefix *Kaph* is rightly ordered to be absent. **Verse 20. Verse 19. Verse 1.** *A spot*: written fully in manuscript 1 according to its Masorah and the Erfurt manuscript, but a later hand wrote a note there.

<note>The following are technical notes on specific Hebrew word forms and manuscript variations.</note>
Verse 19. **for your acceptance, a perfect male**: so it appears in manuscripts 2 and 5. Verse 20. **for**: marked with the *Tevir* accent in manuscripts 2, 4, and 5. Verse 21. **in it**: The letter *Beth* is written without a dot (*raphatum*) in manuscripts 3, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 18, 19, and 21, contrary to other editions. Verse 25. **for**: joined by a *Makkeph* [hyphen] in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5; however, manuscript 1 has a different mark in the margin. Verse 27. **it shall be accepted**: marked with the *Tevir* accent in 4 and 5. Verse 29. **you shall sacrifice a sacrifice**: so in 3 and 4, contrary to the Masoretic traditional text. Verse 32. **and [they shall] profane**: written with a full spelling and a *Dagesh* [dot] in manuscripts 4 and 5. CHAPTER XXIII, verse 2. **to them**: The Erfurt Masora requires a full spelling, but none of our manuscripts agree except for manuscript 1. **convocations**: accented on the penultimate syllable (*milel*) in manuscripts 3 and 5, and so in verses 2 and 4. The same is observed in verse 37.

**25** And the Lord spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, saying: 
**2** Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When you come into the land which I <gloss>g</gloss> give to you, then the land shall keep a Sabbath to the Lord. 
**3** Six years you shall sow your field, and six years <gloss>h</gloss> you shall prune your vineyard, <gloss>i</gloss> and gather in its fruit. 
**4** But in the seventh year <gloss>k</gloss> there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the Lord; you shall neither sow your field nor prune your vineyard. 
**5** <gloss>l</gloss> That which grows of its own accord from your harvest you shall not reap, and the grapes of <gloss>m</gloss> your unpruned vines you shall not gather; it shall be a year of solemn rest for the land. 
**6** And the <gloss>n</gloss> Sabbath of the land shall be <gloss>o</gloss> food for you: <gloss>p</gloss> for you, and for your male and female servants, for your hired worker, and for the stranger who dwells with you. 
**7** And for your livestock and the beasts that are in your land, all its produce shall be for food. **[Section Break]**
**8** And you shall count <gloss>q</gloss> seven Sabbaths of years for yourself—seven years seven times—and the days of the seven <gloss>r</gloss> Sabbaths of years shall be forty-nine years for you. 
**9** Then you shall cause the trumpet <gloss>s</gloss> of sounding to pass through in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month; <gloss>t</gloss> on the Day of Atonement you shall cause the trumpet to pass throughout all your land. 
**10** And you shall sanctify <gloss>u</gloss> the fiftieth year, and proclaim <gloss>v</gloss> liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants; <gloss>x</gloss> it shall be a Jubilee for you, and you shall return every man to <gloss>y</gloss> his possession, and every man to his family you shall return. 
**11** <gloss>z</gloss> That fiftieth year shall be a Jubilee for you; you shall not sow, nor <gloss>a</gloss> reap that which grows of itself in it, nor gather the grapes from <gloss>b</gloss> its unpruned vines. 
**12** For <gloss>c</gloss> it is a Jubilee; it shall be holy to you; you shall eat its produce directly from the field. 
**13** In this year of <gloss>d</gloss> Jubilee, every man shall return to his possession. 
**14** And if you sell <gloss>e</gloss> anything to your neighbor or buy from your neighbor's hand, you shall not wrong one another. 
**15** According to the number of years after the Jubilee you shall buy <gloss>f</gloss> from your neighbor, and according to the number of years of crops he shall sell to you. 
**16** According to the multitude of years you shall increase its price, and according to the fewness of years you shall diminish its price; for he is selling to you the number of the crops.

<summary>This page introduces the laws of the Sabbatical Year and the Jubilee Year, emphasizing that the land belongs to God and must rest every seven and fifty years. It details the social implications of these years, including the release of debts, the return of ancestral property, and the prohibition of overcharging for land based on the time remaining until the next Jubilee.</summary>

18 You shall observe My statutes and keep My ordinances and perform them, so that you may dwell upon the land in safety. 19 And the land shall yield its fruit, and you shall eat your fill, and you shall dwell upon it in safety. 20 And if you should say, "What shall we eat in the seventh year, since we may not sow nor gather in our harvest?" 21 Then I will command My blessing upon you in the sixth year, and it shall produce a harvest for three years. 22 And you shall sow in the eighth year and eat of the old harvest until the ninth year; until its harvest comes in, you shall eat the old. 23 And the land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is Mine; for you are but strangers and sojourners with Me. 24 And in all the land of your possession, you shall grant a redemption for the land.

25 If your brother becomes impoverished and sells some of his possession, then his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what his brother has sold. 26 And if a man has no one to redeem it, but his own hand acquires enough and he finds the means for its redemption: 27 Then let him calculate the years since its sale and return the remainder to the man to whom he sold it, and he shall return to his possession. 28 But if his hand does not find sufficient means to return it to him, then that which he sold shall remain in the hand of the buyer until the year of Jubilee; and in the Jubilee it shall go out, and he shall return to his possession.

29 And if a man sells a dwelling house in a walled city, then its redemption shall be until the end of the year of its sale; for a full year his right of redemption shall last. 30 And if it is not redeemed within the completion of a full year, then the house that is in the city which <note>Marginal note: Read as "has" (לו) though written "not" (לא)</note> has a wall shall be established in perpetuity to the one who bought it throughout his generations; it shall not go out in the Jubilee. 31 But the houses of the villages which have no wall around them shall be considered as the fields of the country; redemption shall be available for it, and it shall go out in the Jubilee. 32 As for the cities of the Levites, the houses in the cities of their possession, the Levites shall have a perpetual right of redemption. 33 And if one redeems from the Levites, then the sale of a house or a city of his possession shall go out in the Jubilee; for the houses of the cities of the Levites are their possession in the midst of the children of Israel. 34 But the field of the suburbs of their cities shall not be sold, for it is their perpetual possession.

<summary>This page details the divine promise of abundance to sustain the Sabbatical year and the laws governing the permanent sale of land. It establishes that land belongs to God and creates a system where property in walled cities can be permanently sold, while rural land and Levitical property must always return to the original family in the Jubilee year.</summary>

verse 17. **Your enemies** [Hebrew: *shone’echem*]: The letter *Beth* has a *dagesh* <note>a dot indicating emphasis or doubling</note> in manuscripts 5, 11, 17, 12, and the Berlin codex, which contradicts the rules. **And they shall rule over you** [Hebrew: *v’radu bachem*]: thus written in full in manuscripts 7, 8. **d** 10–16, 19, 20, 21. contrary to the Old Testament, folio 15. b. verse 18. So also in the 3rd section according to the printed Masora, but against Masora 1 and the Erfurt manuscript.

33 And I will scatter you among the nations, and I will unsheathe the sword after you; and your land shall be a desolation, and your cities shall be a waste.
34 Then the land shall enjoy its sabbaths all the days of its desolation, while you are in the land of your enemies; then the land shall rest and enjoy its sabbaths.
35 All the days of its desolation it shall rest, the rest that it did not have on your sabbaths when you were dwelling upon it.
36 And as for those of you who are left, I will send faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies; and the sound of a driven leaf shall pursue them, and they shall flee as one flees from the sword, and they shall fall when no one pursues.
37 And they shall stumble over one another as if before a sword, though no one pursues; and you shall have no power to stand before your enemies.
38 And you shall perish among the nations, and the land of your enemies shall devour you.
39 And those of you who are left shall waste away in their iniquity in the lands of your enemies; and also because of the iniquities of their fathers they shall waste away with them.
40 And they shall confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers in their treachery which they committed against me, and also that they walked contrary to me.
41 I also will walk contrary to them and bring them into the land of their enemies; or then their uncircumcised heart will be humbled, and then they will accept the punishment for their iniquity.
42 Then I will remember my covenant with Jacob, and also my covenant with Isaac, and also my covenant with Abraham I will remember, and I will remember the land.
43 And the land shall be left by them and shall enjoy its sabbaths while it lies desolate without them, and they shall accept the punishment for their iniquity, because—even because—they rejected my rules and their soul loathed my statutes.
44 And yet for all that, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject them, nor will I loathe them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them; for I am the LORD their God.
45 But I will remember for them the covenant of the ancestors, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt in the sight of the nations, that I might be their God; I am the LORD.
46 These are the statutes and the rules and the laws which the LORD made between himself and the people of Israel at Mount Sinai by the hand of Moses.

*d)* Namely, those who, when the signal sounded, were bound to go out from the camp to the place designated by the Leader. Among various nations, such as the Romans, men of every age were compelled to answer to their names; and, if it seemed right to the supreme power, to be ready for the Leader on the appointed day to follow him. From this, one can understand how it was possible for the Kings of Judah and others to have such large armies at times; those who judge by our modern customs, where no one is forced to give their name for military service, can scarcely grasp this. — *Le Clerc* <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Swiss theologian and biblical scholar.</note>

*v. 21. e)* those numbered of the tribe of **Reuben** were 46,500. So also in chapter 2:11. Compare chapter 26:7.

*v. 22. f)* Regarding the children of **Simeon**. — *Schmidt* <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian and Hebraist.</note>. Compare verses 26, 28, 30, 32. *g)* those reviewed of that tribe (the tribe of Simeon). *h)* See verse 2.

*v. 23. i)* those numbered of the tribe of **Simeon** were 59,300. So also in chapter 2:13. Compare chapter 26:14.

*v. 24. k)* Of the descendants of **Gad**. Gad is joined to Reuben and Simeon because he used to pitch camp together with them on the southern side. See chapter 2:10 and following. — *Le Clerc*.

*v. 25. l)* those reviewed of them, namely the tribe of **Gad**, were 45,650. So also in chapter 2:15. Compare chapter 26:18.

*v. 27. m)* those numbered of the tribe of **Judah** were 74,600. So also in chapter 2:4. Compare chapter 26:22.

*v. 28. n)* These are also placed here because of the order of the encampment. See chapter 2:5 and *Ibn Ezra*.

*v. 22.* **by their polls** <note>Hebrew: *legulgulotam*</note> *A note in the margin: The final Lamed* [ל] *requires it to be drawn like a saw* (**as a saw**) <note>Referring to a scribal tradition where the tail of the Hebrew letter Lamed is jagged or serrated.</note>, *because it stands out and is raised above the other consonants, yet with a truncated top: this is to mark the fornication of Zimri (Genesis 48:19, 20), father of the prince of the Simeonites, which he committed among the Israelites with an uncovered head and an erect posture (see chapter 25).* <note>The scholar is connecting a specific scribal flourish to a moral lesson about the tribe of Simeon's later sin with the Midianites.</note> *But Ibn Ezra, compare above on the Erffurt Masora* <note>The Masora is the tradition of notes on the Hebrew text to ensure its accurate copying.</note>, *requires this figure on the Lamed in the middle of the word: just as he found it in another German book. Rabbi Menachem in the Old Testament, folio 16a, notes however that in the Hilleliano* <note>A famous and authoritative lost manuscript of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, *the Jerusalem, the Spanish, and other Western books, nothing of this sort of stroke was observed by him; except that in the margin of a certain most excellent codex it was written:* **the Lamed of the tradition is more saw-like than every other Lamed**, *which Menachem understands not as a serrated shape, but as one more prominent and made in the manner of a channel or a pipe.*

b) They shall therefore keep the charge, that is, they shall take care. Chapter 18:3; as will be said in chapter 3.
Chapter II, verse 2. c) by his banner. <note>Original Greek: ἐχόμενοι αὐτῷ (echomenoi autō)</note> order / rank. <note>Original Greek: τάγμα (tagma)</note> verses 5, 7, 17, etc. Mark 1:38.
d) with their signs. Each banner had its own unique sign, and indeed, as the ancient Rabbis hand down, on the banner of **Reuben** was the figure of a **Man**, on the banner of **Judah** the figure of a **Lion**, on **Ephraim's** the figure of an **Ox**, and on the banner of **Dan**, the figure of an **Eagle**; so that they corresponded with the chariot of Ezekiel, Chapter 1:10. According to Bechai and Ibn Ezra. Compare also Jonathan.
e) from a distance. Genesis 21:16. It signifies an approach or joining, but not from close up. Cocceius. <note>Johannes Cocceius was a 17th-century Dutch theologian.</note>

**Critical Notes on the Hebrew Text:**
**v. 20.** Pedah-zur: Manuscripts 1, 3, and 4 separate this name with a Makkaph <note>A Hebrew hyphen-like connector</note>.
**v. 24.** And eight (v’shmonat): Manuscripts 5, 7, and 17 place a Metheg <note>A vertical stress mark</note> under the letter Nun.
**v. 25.** Ammi-shaddai: Written as two separate words in manuscripts 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 12, 19, 20, 21, and the Halle edition, contrary to others and the Masorah <note>The tradition of biblical textual preservation</note>.
**v. 31.** For the camp (l’machaneh): Manuscripts 1 and 4 place a Munach <note>A musical accent</note> below; manuscripts 3 and 5 use a Makkaph. Last (la-acharonah): Manuscript 1 and 5 use a Sheva under the Lamed, contrary to the Erffurt Masorah.
**v. 32.** Counted (pekudei): Written defectively <note>Missing a vowel-letter</note> in manuscript 3 and the Halle edition.
**v. 33.** And the Levites (v’ha-Leviyim): Marked with only a Pashta accent over the Mem in manuscripts 1, 3, and 5.
**v. 34.** Son (ben): Marked with a Munach in 2, 3, and the margin of 1.
</note>

\* v. 2. **The firstborn** — The emphatic *Pasek* mark <note>a vertical line used in cantillation or to separate words</note> was deleted in 4 manuscripts.
\* v. 4. **And Abihu** — with the *Pasek* added in manuscripts 6, 9, 20, and in the margin.
\* v. 4. **Before** — joined by a *Makkaph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in 1, 4, 5, 6, 9, 20. **When they offered** — written "fully" <note>with extra vowels</note> in 1, 5, 7, 20. Thus also in 4, against the Masorah <note>the traditional system of notes on the biblical text</note> on this passage and Leviticus 2:4.
\* v. 9. **And you shall give** — with a paragogic ending <note>an extra letter, usually 'He', added to the end of the word</note> in 2, against the Erfurt Masorah.
\* v. 12. In place of **From the children** (which is recorded in the margin from another codex), manuscript 'r' has in the text **Among the children**.
\* v. 13. **Because** — joined by a *Makkaph* in 3 and 5.
\* v. 21. **For Gershon** — with the cantillation marks *Zakef Katon* and *Kadma* in 4; but with *Revia* in 3, 6, 9, 20, and another codex cited in the margin; however, the *En ha-Kore* <note>a medieval work on grammar and cantillation</note> approves *Munach* and *Sakeph* in the margin.

39 All those numbered of the Levites, whom Moses <insert>and Aaron</insert> <note>In the Hebrew text, the word "and Aaron" is marked with dots above each letter, known as *puncta extraordinaria*, indicating a textual tradition that the word might not belong there or has special significance.</note> numbered by the mouth of the Lord by their families, every male...

**v. 27.** "The Amramite": This requires a *He* with a *patach* vowel according to the Old Testament folio 16b. "The Uzzielite": Written with a *Kibbutz* vowel in some manuscripts (3 and 5), contrary to the standard Old Testament and the marginal note which proves a *Kametz-chatuph* is used in all the best codices. "The Kohathite": Here and elsewhere (verses 2, 6-16, 19-21, and chapter 4) the *Koph* has a *Chateph-Kamatz* vowel; however, the Spanish manuscripts everywhere prefer a simple *Shua* according to the Old Testament. **v. 35.** "On": written with a *Makkaph* (hyphen) in manuscripts 1, 3, 5, and chapter 4. **v. 37.** "And their pegs": written fully (plene) in various manuscripts (1, 6, 7, etc.), contrary to the standard Old Testament. **v. 38.** "Meeting": with a *Pesik* (separator mark) in manuscripts 2, 5, 17, and the Berlin manuscript, following the Old Testament, though others are without it. **v. 39.** "And Aaron": The extraordinary dots <note>These are special marks used by Masoretic scribes to flag words they were uncertain about or that were missing in some ancient manuscripts.</note> which the Masora requires in this place are missing in manuscripts 2 and 20. Furthermore, we favor the opinion of the famous Hiller, who states on page 153 that these dots are a Masoretic symbol for a whole word not found in other codices. Indeed, the Samaritan Pentateuch does not have the word "and Aaron" here, and it is also omitted in the parallel verses 14 and 16.

NUMBERS CHAPTER 3 & 4

<margin>
Compare chapters 1, 2, 6.

"The sum" or "the total." <note>original Greek: τὸ κεφάλαιον</note>. Likewise in chapter 31:26 and Hebrews 8:1.

**v. 3. e)** compare verses 23, 30, and chapter 8:24. **f)** regarding the service [at the entrance], see Exodus 38:8. "The one serving." <note>original Greek: ὁ λειτουργῶν</note>

47 You shall take five shekels <note>A shekel was a standard unit of weight and currency</note> apiece for each head; you shall take them according to the shekel of the sanctuary—the shekel being twenty gerahs. <note>A gerah was a small unit of weight, about 1/20th of a shekel</note>

48 And you shall give the money to Aaron and his sons as the redemption for those who are in excess among them."

49 So Moses took the redemption money from those who exceeded the number of those redeemed by the Levites.

**v. 7.** *The jars* <note>Hebrew: ha-menaqiyot</note> is written with full spelling in codices 2, 10, 14, 19, 20, 21, contrary to the Masorah and the Old Testament folio 16. b. Further, a strong dot <note>Dagesh forte</note> appears in the letter Mem in codices 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. **v. 8.** *And they shall spread a cloth* — so in codex 1, according to the En Hakore. *Its lamps* — uses a Metheg accent instead of a Munach in codices 2, 6, 9. **v. 9.** *Its lamps (and they shall take)* — <gloss>corrected by codex 4</gloss> using a Great Tifcha accent. **v. 14.** *Which* in codices 1 and 2, but *which they serve* in codices 1 and 4. Codex 1 notes in the margin that manuscripts vary greatly here, but its reading follows Rabbi Simon and Silveira. **v. 15.** *Aaron* — so in 1, 2, 4; using a Merca accent in 6, 9, 20; Maqqeph <note>hyphen</note> in others. *And the meat hooks* — with the prefix "and" in codices 1, 3, 4 and Halle, against the Masorah for Exodus 37:16. **v. 15.** *Aaron* — so in 1, 2, 4; using a Merca accent in 6, 9, 20; Maqqeph in others. *And after that* — using a Grashayim accent in 1 and 2. **v. 18.** *The Kohathite* — so in 3, 17, 18 and Berlin according to the Old Testament; but others almost always have a Chateph Qamets vowel under the letter Qoph. **v. 19.** *To the holy* — thus instead of "with the holy" in 3 and 5. So also in 2 and 4, against the Masorah.

### NUMBERS NASO 7 . CHAPTER 7 . 7

<margin>
**The Gifts of the Princes, which each offered on individual days.**
</margin>

<margin>
*If it had been said* that all the families had offered together, the text would not have needed to repeat the list twelve times; saying it once would have been enough. But the simplicity of the ancients did not shy away from such repetitions, even among the most refined nations. This is evident in the works of Homer, where many repetitions occur that are not found in the works of more recent poets. Brentius <note>Johannes Brenz, a 16th-century reformer</note> observes regarding these matters the duty of Princes: they are to be the "nourishers" of the Church and must aid the true worship of God in whatever way they can.
</margin>

**v. 13.** <term>mizraq</term> <note>sprinkling bowl</note> is written here and in the following verses with a *Patach* <note>a short 'a' vowel</note> according to manuscripts 3 and 4. This is the spelling in M.I., although it is noted that in the Jerusalem manuscript it is written with a *Kamets* <note>a long 'a' vowel</note>. However, the *Kamets* is approved by O.T. (folio 16b) based on the Masorah <note>the traditional system for preserving the biblical text</note> and the readings found in Spanish manuscripts. 

**v. 18.** From this verse until verse 83, the scribes of German manuscripts and the early Hebrew printers often omitted the vowel points to save labor. They did this because the words are repeated almost exactly, with only the names of the offering Princes changing. However, O.T. praises the Spanish manuscripts, which are so meticulous that not a single point of any letter is missing. 

**v. 24.** <term>Helon</term> is written "fully" with the letter *Vav* in manuscripts 4 and 5, which goes against the Erfurt Masorah.

v. 51. m) See Leviticus 1:3 and following. Regarding this, Franzius <note>Wolfgang Franz (1564–1628), a Lutheran theologian known for his "Sacred Zoologist" works which interpreted biblical animals allegorically.</note> writes: "We ought to offer morally, and provide for burning in the mortification of the flesh—on the day of penance—the fierceness of the ox, the wicked inclination of the goat, and the dullness of the sheep. We offer a calf when we conquer the luxury of the flesh; a young goat when we avoid lewdness; a dove when we strive for simplicity; a turtledove when we are chaste; unleavened bread when we walk pure, sincere, and honest; salt when we are constant; and oil when we are mild and gentle. Thus we are rendered as burnt offerings pleasing to God, presenting our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, which is our reasonable service <note>A reference to Romans 12:1</note>. Similarly, let our heart be displayed as the altar: let the burnt offerings be prayers, good works, and every exercise of piety; the fire is true faith with unfeigned love for one's neighbor; the wood is the consideration of divine benefits. Therefore, whenever someone notices new benefits from the Lord toward himself or others, he ought out of love for God and neighbor to offer prayers upon the altar of his heart; and these prayers will also be an offering of a soothing aroma to Jehovah." God himself confirms this observation of Franzius in Hosea 6:6: "For I desired kindness <note>original Hebrew: חסד (chesed), meaning mercy or steadfast love</note> and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings." <note>original Hebrew: כי חסד חפצתי ולא זבח ודעת אלהים מעולה</note>

v. 3. *ten*: So in manuscripts 1, 3 with the *Merca* accent; 4, 5 with *Munach* and *Maqqeph*; 6 and others with *Maqqeph*. *day*: with the *Tifcha-khattanna* accent in manuscript 1. *In the month*: Manuscript 1, 2, 3, 4 have a *bet* with a *dagesh* [indicative of 'the' month], and so in the Halle edition. v. 7. *And they said*: Manuscripts 1 and 3 have the *Revia* accent, but 2 has *Gereshayim*. v. 8. *To them*: written in full in 4, 6, 9, and 20. *The Lord*: thus here with the *Munach* accent in 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, and 20; the rest have *Merca*, except the Berlin manuscript which has *Maqqeph* and *Metheg*. *Distant* <note>original: "rechokah"</note>: The extraordinary dot sitting over the letter *He* denotes a variant reading *rechoq* in the masculine gender without the *He*, because the preceding noun *derech* (way) is of common gender [masculine or feminine]. **Textual Notes on Verse 10:**
For **your gladness** <note>original: שמחתכם</note>, it is thus marked with the *Merca* accent in manuscripts 6, 9, 20, and corrected in 4, as required by the Masora to Genesis 30:16. However, others have the regular *Munach* accent. For **your months** <note>original: חדשיכם</note>, it is written in full (with the letter Vav) in manuscripts 1, 3, 4, 5, Halle 6, 9, 12, 20. Thus also the Jerusalem Hillel codex and the Egyptian books; but it is written "defectively" (without Vav) in our remaining copies, which, besides the printed Masora in this place, are also confirmed by O.T. f. 17. a. from nearly all Spanish and German codices, two Masoretic copies, the Talmud, and Rabbi Meir Hallevi.
**Verse 15:** For **and over the army** <note>original: ועל-צבא</note>, it is written with a *Shateph-gadol* (large vowel mark) in 1, 2, 3, according to the Masora of 1, 7, 8, and Erfurt. The same is found, but with a *Kadma* accent added above, in 7, 8, 10, 13, 15, 19, which is against analogy. In others, it is written differently in manuscripts 4, 5, 6, 9, 11, 12, 14, 16, 17, 18, 20, 21.
**Verse 21:** A paragraph space is placed before this by 2, 3, 4, 5, Halle 6-10, 12, 19, 21, and two old codices, although this division is rejected by the authority of Maimonides and Spanish codices.

### CHAPTER XI.

1 And the people were as those complaining of evil in the ears of the Lord, and the Lord heard, and His anger was kindled; and the fire of the Lord burned among them, and consumed at the edge 2 of the camp. And the people cried out to Moses, and Moses prayed to 3 the Lord, and the fire subsided. And he called the name of that place Taberah <note>meaning "Burning"</note>, because the fire of the Lord burned among them. 4 And the mixed multitude that was among them lusted with desire, and the children of Israel also turned and wept, 5 and they said: "Who shall feed us meat? We remember the fish which we ate in Egypt for free; the cucumbers, and the melons, and 6 the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic. But now our soul is dried up; there is nothing at all, except our eyes are toward the manna." 7 And the manna was like coriander seed, 8 and its appearance was like the appearance of bdellium. The people wandered and gathered, and ground it in mills or pounded it in a mortar, and cooked it in a pot, and made it into cakes; 9 and its taste was like the taste of rich oil. And when the dew descended upon the camp at night, the manna descended upon it. 10 And Moses heard the people weeping by their families, every man at the entrance of his tent; and the anger of the Lord was kindled 11 greatly, and in the eyes of Moses it was evil. And Moses said to the Lord: "Why have You done evil to Your servant? and why have I not found favor in Your eyes, that You put the 12 burden of all this people upon me? Did I conceive all this people? Did I beget them, that You should say to me: 'Carry them in your bosom,' as..."

From each ancestral tribe send one of its leaders."** 3 **So at the LORD’s command, Moses sent them out from the Desert of Paran. All of them were leaders of the Israelites.** 4 **These are their names:** 5 **from the tribe of Reuben, Shammua son of Zakkur;** 6 **from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat son of Hori;** 7 **from the tribe of Judah, Caleb son of Jephunneh;** 8 **from the tribe of Issachar, Igal son of Joseph;** 9 **from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea son of Nun;** 10 **from the tribe of Benjamin, Palti son of Raphu;** 11 **from the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel son of Sodi;** 12 **from the tribe of Joseph (that is, from the tribe of Manasseh), Gaddi son of Susi;** 13 **from the tribe of Dan, Ammiel son of Gammalli;** 14 **from the tribe of Asher, Sethur son of Michael;** 15 **from the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi son of Vophsi;** 16 **from the tribe of Gad, Geuel son of Maki.**

***

**v. 12. Trustworthy** <note>Hebrew: Amen</note> The <term>Masora</term> <note>the traditional system of notes on the Hebrew biblical text</note> notes here that this is a <term>Tikkun Ezra</term> <note>an emendation of Ezra</note> or a reading left and approved by Ezra. However, other Masoretic notes and the Erfurt manuscript call it a <term>Tikkun Sopherim</term> <note>Scribal Emendation</note>, a reading prepared by the scribes who are said to have been colleagues of Ezra, so that no one would dare to read or write it otherwise. Concerning these Emendations, see Pfeiffer’s *Sacred Criticism* and others. **His flesh** This too is a Scribal Emendation according to the Masora. **v. 14. After** written without the prefix "and" <note>the Hebrew letter Vav</note> in the Berlin manuscript. Likewise, David Kimchi in his Commentary testifies that he saw the "and" erased in a certain corrected codex. Note 18 and the Berlin manuscript say that the "and" is a <term>Ittur Sopherim</term> <note>Scribal omission/embellishment</note>, or according to the reading handed down by the scribes it ought to be absent, based on the Talmud (Nedarim, chapter 4). But all our remaining manuscripts have the "and," and Rabbi Menachem found the same in all German, Spanish, and Catalonian manuscripts. He refers the Talmudic saying instead to chapter 31:2. Finally, the Masora also requires the "and" at the end of Numbers 10.

### Text-Critical Notes

v. 16. **וַיִּשְׁחָטֵם** ("and he slaughtered them") *written with a large letter Chet in manuscripts 3, 4 and Halle, but against the Masorah* <note>The traditional system of notes on the Hebrew biblical text</note> *of Genesis 1:1 and 1 Chronicles 1:1.*
v. 17. **יִגְדַּל** ("let [it] be great") *written with a large letter Yod. According to Hiller (p. 172), this is a symbol for a variant reading.*
v. 19. **סְלַח** ("pardon") *so in 2, 17, 18 and Berlin manuscripts, but others have* **סְלַח**; *however, Spanish books place a Metheg* <note>a stress mark</note> *under the Lamed.*
v. 24. **וִירָשֶׁנָּה** ("and [he] shall possess it") *written fully in manuscripts 6, 9, 12, 15, 26, 21, against the Masorah of this place.*
v. 27. **תְּלֻנּוֹת** ("grumblings") *written fully in 6, 9, 20, according to the Erfurt Masorah here and Exodus 16:12, but against other Masoretic notes and printed editions.*

3 ...to fulfill a vow, or as a freewill offering, or at your appointed feasts, to make a soothing aroma to the Lord, from the herd or from the flock. 4 Then he who presents his offering shall present to the Lord a grain offering of a tenth of an <term>ephah|a dry measure</term> of fine flour mixed with a fourth of a <term>hin|a liquid measure</term> of oil. 5 And you shall prepare a fourth of a hin of wine for the drink offering with the burnt offering or for the sacrifice, for each lamb. 6 Or for a ram, you shall prepare as a grain offering two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of oil. 7 And for the drink offering you shall present a third of a hin of wine, a soothing aroma to the Lord. 8 And when you prepare a bull as a burnt offering or a sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or for peace offerings to the Lord, 9 then he shall present with the bull a grain offering of three-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with half a hin of oil. 10 And you shall present for the drink offering half a hin of wine, as an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the Lord. 11 Thus it shall be done for each ox, or for each ram, or for each lamb of the sheep or the goats. 12 According to the number that you prepare, so you shall do for everyone according to their number. 13 All who are native-born shall do these things in this way, to present an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the Lord. 14 And if a stranger dwells with you, or whoever is among you throughout your generations, and would present an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the Lord, just as you do, so shall he do. 15 One statute shall be for you of the assembly and for the stranger who dwells with you, a perpetual statute throughout your generations; as you are, so shall the stranger be before the Lord. 16 One law and one ordinance shall be for you and for the stranger who dwells with you.

17 And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: 18 Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When you come into the land where I am bringing you, 19 then it shall be, when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall lift up a contribution to the Lord. 20 You shall lift up a cake of the first of your dough as a contribution; as the contribution of the threshing floor, so shall you lift it up. 21 Of the first of your dough you shall give to the Lord a contribution throughout your generations.

22 And if you err and do not perform all these commandments which the Lord has spoken to Moses, 23 all that the Lord has commanded you by the hand of Moses, from the day that the Lord commanded and onward throughout your generations.

\* v. 2. **זרה** (scatter): Manuscripts 3, 4, 9, and 10 have the *Munach* accent, but manuscript 6 has both *Makkef* and *Munach* together. \* v. 3. **הקריבם** (they offered them): written with a *Shurek* vowel in manuscripts 7 and 8, but this contradicts the Masora. \* v. 5. **למען** (so that): with the *Tifcha Ktanna* accent in manuscripts 1, 4, 6, 9, 12, 20, and 21. **וכעדותו** (and like his company): Many manuscripts (1, 2, 3, 6-10, etc.) have a *Metheg* mark in place of a *Munach*. \* v. 6. **ממחרת** (on the next day): Thus with a *Munach* in manuscripts 4, 6-16, etc., but the Spanish books have a *Metheg*. \* v. 10. **הרמו** (get away): The letter *Mem* is without a *Dagesh* (doubling mark) in manuscripts 1, 6, 9, and 10. \* v. 11. **ותן** (and put): with a *Tsere* vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 5, etc., whereas the Masoretic rules for this verse and Psalm 18:4 require a *Segol* vowel.

v. 19. **yirimu** (they shall offer): Manuscripts 6, 9, and 20 have the *Munach* accent, which is more regular, but it goes against the Masora on Genesis 30:16. v. 19. **hi** (it/she): written with both points (masculine and feminine) in manuscripts 6, 9, 11, and 20, undoubtedly from variant source codes. Manuscript 1 and 8 have it in the masculine according to Masora 1 on Exodus 29:28, where this passage expressly requires the *Shurek* vowel. Some books even write **Hi** with a *Vav* in the Old Testament, but all Spanish and German manuscripts read it with the standard feminine points, as does the Masoretic codex of the Old Testament (folio 10a) and the Erfurt Masora. v. 20. **To Aaron... and the LORD said**: Thus in manuscript 2 and in the margin of 1; also in manuscript 4, against the printed Masora for chapter 3:40. v. 24. **Ma'aser** (tithe): Written with a simple *Sheva* in manuscripts 1 and 2, according to Masora 1 and the Erfurt Masora here, and Masora 1 on Deuteronomy 12:17. v. 26: All use the *Munach* accent except for manuscripts 17, 18, and the Berlin codex, which have the *Makkaph* (connector) according to the Old Testament.

<note>Translator's Critical Notes: The text below documents minor variations in the Hebrew letters and vowel markings (Masoretic notes) found in different historical manuscripts like the Berlin or Erfurt codices.</note>

\* v. 19. **To them**. Thus most of our scholars mark it with a *Mercha* accent, as required by the Masora to Genesis 30:15, but manuscripts 1, 3, and 4 (Berlin) have a *Munach* accent, and manuscript 2 adds a *Pasek* mark. \* v. 21. **And he refused**. The *Pasek* mark is omitted in manuscripts 4, 5, and 14, contrary to Masora 1. v. 29. **The assembly**. Marked with a *Metheg* instead of *Munach* in manuscripts 3, 6, 9, 20. CHAPTER 21, v. 1. **Arad**. The letter Resh has a *Patach* vowel in manuscripts 1, 3, 4, 5. **And he took captive**. No *Pasek* in manuscript 4, contrary to Masora i, 7, 8, and the Erfurt manuscript. \* v. 3. **To the voice**. Some amended this from "at the voice." v. 4. **To go around**. The letter Beth lacks a *Dagesh* (emphasis mark) in manuscripts 6, 8, 9, 10-16, and the Ben Ascher codex, and also the book **Mahzor** cited by Elias in Masoreth f. 77.

<note>Footnotes regarding textual variants and Masoretic notes</note>

*. v. 24. *Arnon*: Written in full [plene] in codices 1, 2, 3, 5. *Strong* (Az): written with a Kamets vowel in 1, 3, 4, 5, as required by the printed Masorah on Genesis 49:7; but others have a Patach. *. v. 28. *Ar*: v. 28 written with a Patach because the word is in the construct state with the following word "Moab" in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 20; and so the Masorah requires; others have a Kamets. *. v. 29. *Fugitives*: written defectively [short spelling] in 1, 2, 4, 5. *. v. 30. *And we laid waste* (Vannashim) and *Their lamp/dominion* (Niram): Cantillation marks in 1, 3, 4, 20. *Which* (Asher): An extraordinary dot resting over the letter Resh according to Hiller (p. 156) is a symbol of a variant reading for "until Nophah-ah shar," while maintaining the same sense. CHAPTER XXII, v. 5. *Beor*: defective spelling in 5, 7, 8.

*   **v. 23.** In the word "The donkey" (<note>Hebrew: הָאָתוֹן</note>), the Metheg <note>a stress mark</note> is used instead of a Munach <note>a musical accent</note> in manuscripts 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, and 20.
*   **v. 26.** The word "left" (<note>Hebrew: וּשְׂמֹאול</note>) is written without the silent letter Vav in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, and also in 4 and the Halle edition, contrary to the Masora <note>the traditional system of Hebrew text preservation</note>.
*   **v. 28.** The word "Because" (<note>Hebrew: כִּי</note>) uses an Ithibh accent in manuscript 4. In "you struck me" (<note>Hebrew: הִכִּיתַנִי</note>), the letter Tau has a short 'a' (Patach) in manuscripts 1, 3, 6-16, 19, 20, and 21; but a long 'a' (Kamets), which the rest of our manuscripts have, is approved by the Old Testament folio 19. b. from Spanish books.
*   **v. 33.** The Masora printed at Leviticus 10, 17 requires a "defective" spelling <note>spelling without vowel letters</note> for "and her" (<note>Hebrew: וְאוֹתָהּ</note>), though none of our manuscripts agree with this.
*   **v. 35.** In "the men" (<note>Hebrew: הָאֲנָשִׁים</note>), a Metheg is used in place of a Munach in manuscripts 1 through 4.
*   **v. 36.** Manuscripts 6 through 19 and 21 use a Munach accent.

<note>The following notes provide technical details on Hebrew grammar, vowels, and chanting marks (accents) found in ancient manuscripts.</note>

Verse 37. **Indeed** <note>original: "Ha-omnam"</note>: The accent marks *Munach* and *Sakeph-katon* are correctly placed in manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 20; but others have the *Metheg* mark instead of *Munach*.

CHAPTER 23, Verse 3. **I have arranged** <note>original: "Arakhti"</note>: Written in full with the letter *Iod* (a vowel marker) in manuscripts 1, 3, 6, 9, 16, 20. So also in the Hal... against the Masorah on Leviticus 9, 7. The word **He will meet** <note>original: "Yikkareh"</note> is found written with the *Tsere* vowel in some books.

Verse 4. **The** <note>original: "Et"</note>: With *Tsere* and *Munach* marks; corrected in manuscript 4.

Verse 7. **From the mountains** <note>original: "Me-harerei"</note>: With the *Chateph-patach* vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9.

-> **v. 15.** *ammot* Thus 1–5, 17 and Berlin according to the Old Testament folio 21 a. But the others have *Sakeph-katon*. **v. 18.** *Makkef* lines 2, 4, 6, 9, 20. *davar-peor* thus with *Makkef* 3, 6–16, 19, 20, 21. *hamukkuh* thus 8, 17, 18 and Berlin according to the printed Masorah at verse 15, but others have *Mercha*. *davar-peor* with *Makkef* 3, 17, 18 and Berlin according to the Old Testament; the others have *Mercat*. **v. 19.** All have the *Piska* or space after the *Atnach* [accent mark], which although it seems to introduce an inconvenient division or some kind of gap, is rather a symbol of a different punctuation observed from various codices. Specifically, some referred the words "And it was after the plague" to the beginning of the next chapter (just as codices 10–16 begin Chapter XXVI with these same words); their symbol is the *Atnach*. But others, assuming a *Silluk* in place of the *Atnach*, referred them to the end of Chapter XXV (as almost all our other books do), so that the sense is: "And this (God's command to attack the Midianites) was done after the plague." Their symbol is the *Piska* or space, which separates two propositions of different meaning. Compare variant readings at Genesis 35:22. <-

Verse 9. *And their grain offering*. According to Mercator, thus in manuscript 4; but the *Zakef* with *Kadma* <term>cantillation marks used for chanting the Hebrew text</term> is proved by the Old Testament, folio 21, b. Verse 11. *Sin offering*. Six dots <note>special vowel or scribal marks</note>, one for each letter, are placed by manuscript 4 and Hammeiri <note>Rabbi Menahem Meiri, a famous 13th-century Catalan scholar</note>; but the Old Testament requires only one over the last letter, which symbol signifies another reading of the word: *ve-isaron* <note>meaning "and a tenth"</note>: written defectively <term>defective writing: a Hebrew spelling style using fewer vowels</term>, etc. See Hillerus <note>Mattheus Hiller, a 17th-century German orientalist</note>, page 156.
Verse 17. *And on the second day*. So in manuscript 2 and 4, but against the Masora <term>the authoritative tradition of the Hebrew text's transmission</term>. Verse 20. *And on the third day*. So manuscript 3 in this place, and in verses 23, 25, 29.
Verse 21. *for the rams*. written defectively in verses 6, 8, 9, 11, 15. Written in full in manuscripts 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 15, 20, here, and in verse 27; but both are against the Old Testament.

4 ...and she bound a bond <term>issar</term> <note>a binding obligation, usually involving self-denial</note> in her father's house in her youth; 5 and her father hears her vow and her bond by which she bound her soul, and her father remains silent to her, then all her vows shall stand, and every bond by which she bound her soul shall stand. 6 But if her father prohibits her on the day he hears it, none of her vows or her bonds by which she bound her soul shall stand; and the Lord will forgive her, because her father prohibited her. 7 And if she should be married to a man, and her vows were upon her, or an utterance of her lips by which she bound her soul; 8 and her husband hears it on the day he hears it and remains silent to her, then her vows shall stand, and her bonds by which she bound her soul shall stand. 9 But if on the day her husband hears it, he prohibits her, then he shall make void her vow which was upon her and the utterance of her lips by which she bound her soul; and the Lord will forgive her. 10 But the vow of a widow or a divorced woman—everything by which she has bound her soul—shall stand against her. 11 And if she vowed in her husband's house, or bound a bond upon her soul with an oath; 12 and her husband heard it and remained silent to her and did not prohibit her, then all her vows shall stand, and every bond by which she bound her soul shall stand. 13 But if her husband should utterly make them void on the day he hears them, then whatever proceeded from her lips concerning her vows or concerning the bond of her soul shall not stand; her husband has made them void, and the Lord will forgive her. 14 Every vow and every oath of a bond to afflict the soul, her husband may establish it, or her husband may make it void. 15 But if her husband remains completely silent to her from day to day, then he establishes all her vows or all her bonds which are upon her; he has established them because he remained silent to her on the day he heard them. 16 But if he should utterly make them void after he has heard them, then he shall bear her iniquity <note>He takes on the spiritual guilt of the broken vow if he waits too long to nullify it</note>. 17 These are the statutes which the Lord commanded Moses, between a man and his wife, between a father and his daughter, in her youth, while in her father's house.

**Notes on the Hebrew Text:**
v. 6 The name **Phinehas** is spelled "defective" <note>lacking the letter 'yod' as a vowel marker</note> in manuscripts 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 20, and 21. Use the Geresh accent mark in 12, 16, 20, 21, though this is incorrect; Grafchaim has it in 3. **And the holy instruments**: so it appears in manuscript 2 and what follows here. v. 14 The printed Masora <note>traditional notes on the Hebrew text</note> for this location is confused; it notes that **among the little ones** appears twice with these accents (specifically the Tebir and Mercha accents found in verses 7 and 8). In the other location cited, Numbers 3:31, it is found with Sakeph-katon and Munach. v. 8 **And the kings of**: so in 1, 6-16, 19, 20, and 21, against the Old Testament manuscript folio 21b. v. 9 **And every** with the Segol vowel and a connector (Makkeph) in 1, 3, 4, 5. **Their livestock** spelled fully in 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 9, 20, contrary to the Masora here and in Genesis 34:23. v. 16 **Behold** with an added Psīq mark in 4. **The matter** with the Munach accent in 1, 2, 3, 4. v. 18 **The little ones** (Tet) with the Kamets vowel in 2, 3, 4.

**Manuscript Notes:**
v. 43. *And seven*: with the prefix "and" in manuscripts 1, 5 and Hale. v. 47. *From the half of the children*: so in manuscripts 1, 3, 6, 9, 20. v. 49. *They raised (took count)*: Not with the euphonic Dagesh in manuscripts 1, 2, 4. **Critical Notes:**
Verse 21. **Until** [עַד]: According to the *Maqqeph* <note>a Hebrew horizontal connecting line</note> in versions 3 and 5, so also in 4. And the word **driven out** [הוֹרִישׁוֹ] is found in version 2. Verse 22. **Blameless** [נְקִיִּם]: Written fully <note>with the letter 'yod' included</note> in version 3, contrary to the Erffurt Masorah <note>traditional Hebrew scribal notes</note>. The phrase **and you shall be blameless** [וְהִייתֶם נְקִיִּם] is also in version 2. Verse 24. **Build** [בְּנוּ]: Marked with the *Kadma* accent in versions 2, 4, 6, and 9. Verse 25. **They will do** [יַעֲשׂוּ]: The letter 'Iod' appears with a euphonic *Dagesh* <note>a dot indicating emphasis or double consonant</note> in versions 2 and 4; the same is also found in verse 27 in the word **they will cross** [יַעְבְּרוּ]. Verse 26. **Our livestock** [מִקְנֵנוּ]: Written fully or with the plural 'Iod' in versions 2 and 5, and in the Halle version, against the Erffurt Mischnah. Verse 28. **And** [וְאֵת]: This reading is held by most according to the *En hakkore* <note>The Reader's Eye, a grammatical treatise</note> in the marginal note; but with the *Rebia* and *Tsere* accents in version 2 and in the margin. Verse 29. **Reuben** [רְאוּבֵן]: Without the *Psik* <note>a vertical separator mark</note> in versions 4, 9, and 20, contrary to the Masorah and Erffurt versions. Verse 32. **Our inheritance** [נַחְלָתֵנוּ]: Written fully with the letter 'Iod' in versions 1, 2, and 5, and in the Halle version and 4, against the Masorah and Erffurt. Verse 33. **And to half** [וּלְחֵצִי]: Without the *Psik* mark in versions 4, 6, 7, 9, and 20; with the *Mercacoloco* <note>an accent mark</note> in Man-n. 6, 7, 9, 20, and 21.

<note>The following are technical notes regarding the Hebrew spelling (orthography) found in specific historic manuscripts.</note>
Verse 16. *Kibroth*: Written "Plene" <note>with the full vowel letter 'vav'</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, and the Halle edition; likewise in verse 17 in manuscripts 1, 2, 4, contrary to the Erfurt Masorah. Verse 30. *Moserot*: Written "Plene" in manuscript 3 and the Halle edition; but "Defective" <note>lacking the vowel letter</note> in 1, 2, 3, 4, and Halle. Verse 38. *The Fifth*: Defective spelling, with a *Dagesh* <note>a grammatical dot for emphasis</note> in the letter *Shin* in 3, 4; but at the end with a *Dagesh* in 2 and Halle, contrary to the Erfurt Masorah. Verse 39. *And Aaron*: Thus with a *Munach* accent and *Zakeph-katon*, which most of our texts have correctly; but with a *Metheg* instead of a *Munach* in manuscripts 3, 5, 17, 18, and the Berlin edition. Verse 46. *Almon*: Written "Plene" in 1, 2, 3, 5, here and in verse 47.

->**BE STRONG!**<-

The sum of the verses of the Book of Numbers is one thousand, two hundred and eighty-eight; the sign is *Appah* <note>The Hebrew letters totaling the verse count</note>.
Its midpoint is "And it shall come to pass, that the man whom I shall choose, his rod shall blossom" (Numbers 17:5).
Its weekly portions are ten; the sign is "The Lord alone shall lead him" (Deuteronomy 32:12).
Its sections are thirty-two; the sign is "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Psalm 51:12).
Its chapters are thirty-six; the sign is "O that they were wise, that they understood this" (Deuteronomy 32:29).
The number of "Open" sections is ninety-two, and the "Closed" sections are sixty-six. The total is one hundred and fifty-eight portions; the sign is "I am your portion and your inheritance" (Numbers 18:20).

Hal. fu. 1. Against the Masorah of Erfurt. \* v. 9. **In his inheritance**: Munach in place of Metheg in 7, 10–19, 21. v. 11. **Their uncles** [Dodeihen]: with a large letter Nun in 3, 4, and Hal. v. 13. **In the plains of** [Bearvot]: written in full [plene] in 2, 6, 9, 20, contrary to the printed Masorah. **Critical Notes on the Hebrew Text:**
*V. 30.* The word "did" (*asah*) is marked with *Merca* accents in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, and similar in 4. *V. 31.* "Until you reached" (*ad bo'achem ad*) appears thus in manuscript 1. *V. 35.* The word "among the men" (*ba'anashim*) has a *Patach* <note>a short 'a' vowel</note> under the letter *Beth* in manuscripts 4 and 5, but this goes against the *Masora* <note>the traditional system for preserving the biblical text</note> in 1, 2, 7, 8 and the Erfurt codex. "The evil" (*hara*) has a *Patach* under the *Resh* in 1, 2, 3, 4, against the Masora and other texts. *V. 36.* "And to him" (*v'lo*) uses a *Kadma* accent in 2, 3, 4. "Which he walked" (*asher-darach*) appears thus in 1, 5, and 4, against other texts. *V. 38.* "He shall enter" (*yavo*) is accented on the penultimate syllable in 1, 2, 4, 13 and the Berlin manuscript, as required by the Masora. *V. 41.* "To go up" (*la'alot*) is written in full spelling in 1, 2, 3, 5, and 4, against the Masora here and in Exodus 19:23.

### Chapter II.
1 Then we turned and journeyed into the wilderness by way of the Sea of Reeds, as the Lord spoke to me; and we circled Mount Seir for many days.
2 And the Lord spoke to me, saying:
3 "You have circled this mountain long enough; turn yourselves northward.
4 And command the people, saying: 'You are passing through the border of your brothers, the sons of Esau, who live in Seir; and they will be afraid of you, so be very careful.
5 Do not provoke them, for I will not give you any of their land, not even a foot's breadth, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession.
6 You shall buy food from them for money, that you may eat; and you shall also buy water from them for money, that you may drink.'
7 For the Lord your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands; He has known your walking through this great wilderness. These forty years the Lord your God has been with you; you have lacked nothing."
8 And we passed over from our brothers, the sons of Esau, who live in Seir, away from the way of the Arabah, from Elath and Ezion-geber. Then we turned and passed by way of the wilderness of Moab.
9 And the Lord said to me, "Do not harass Moab, nor provoke them to war, for I will not give you any of their land as a possession; because I have given Ar to the sons of Lot as a possession."
10 (The Emim formerly lived there, a people as great and numerous and tall as the Anakim.
11 They are also accounted as Rephaim <note>giants</note> like the Anakim, but the Moabites call them Emim.
12 And in Seir, the Horites formerly lived, but the sons of Esau dispossessed them and destroyed them from before them and lived in their place; just as Israel did to the land of their possession which the Lord gave to them.)
13 "Now rise up and cross over the Zered Brook." So we crossed over the Zered Brook.
14 And the time that we traveled from Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the Zered Brook was thirty-eight years, until the whole generation of the men of war had perished from the midst of the camp, as the Lord had sworn to them.

v. 16. All our manuscripts have a space <note>original: "Spatium sessionis"</note> at the end of the verse. Therefore, according to this division, verse 16 is not to be joined with the following verse 17, but is to be joined in explanation with the preceding verse 13, so that the sense is: And that (meaning the crossing of the Zered valley, which ended the period in the desert, verse 13) was not done before the men were consumed, etc. Thus verses 14 and 15 would be in a parenthesis. verse 18. <note>The following notes represent technical Masoretic and philological observations regarding specific word spellings and accents in the Hebrew manuscripts used for this edition, such as those by Rabbi Asher or the Erfurt Masorah.</note>
v. 26. The Name [יהוה]. With *Pfik* v. 27. And to the north [וצפונה] written fully 4. 7. 8. 10. 12 -- 15. 19. ... contrary to the Masorah in this place and Genesis 28:14. "For not" [כי לא] thus 1. 5. and Rabbi Asher, against the Erfurt Masorah. CHAPTER IV. v. 3. "You have seen" [הראת] both syllables defective 1. 3. 5... according to the Masorah, but against the printed edition. They have *Munach* instead of *Metheg* 1. 2. 4. 6. 9. 20. v. 5. "To do so" [לעשות כן] thus 2., 3. 5. 17. 18. Berlin edition, and thus corrected in 4, which the Old Testament folio 22. a. far prefers to our others, which have "to do so." v. 8. "Righteous" [צדיקים] ending in *kim* written fully 1. 4. 10. 21... against the Old Testament and the marginal Masorah 7. 8.

Rabbi Bechai <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi</note> in his Commentary, folio 193. c. Thus far Bechai. See the same in Megillah folio 9. b.

<note>This section contains Masoretic notes regarding technical aspects of the Hebrew text across various manuscripts.</note>
**verse 2.** "Our God": Thus in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9, 20. However, the others have the *Revia* [accent mark]. **verse 4.** "Face": without a *Psik* [vertical separator] in 20. Like 1, but the following has a *Zakeph-Katon* [accent]. **verse 6.** An "Open Section" [Petuchah] is found in 4, 6-10, 14, 19, 20, 21, contrary to other editions. Furthermore, in this whole verse, only simple accents derived from *Silluq* are found in 3 and 4, as required. However, in the place of the *Revia* under "slaves," it wants an *Atnach* [major pause mark] to be placed. **verse 7.** "The LORD": most without a *Maqqef* [hyphen], as ordered. This results in fewer manuscripts having a *Dagesh* [dot] in the word "Not." **verse 8.** "You shall [not] make": Thus in 22, according to the tradition, also 17, 18. Except these add a *Munach* accent along with the others who have *Munach* and *Mercha* without *Maqqef*. "Not": without a *Dagesh* in all except 17, 18. "Idol": a *Psik* is added in 3, 17, 18, 21, 22, but the others omit it. "Likeness": the letter *Vav* is marked with an extraordinary dot in 3, with the note: "it is dotted above and disputed." "And what is in the waters": thus 2, 4 through 22. **verse 9.** "To them": verse 10 in 18. **verse 14.** "You shall not do any work": thus 17, 18. **verse 15.** "Slave": thus 1 through 5, 7, 17, 18. **verse 16.** "Your father upon": thus 1, 7, 8, 11, 22, 15 through 18. **verse 12.** "As": through *Mercha* and *Munach* accents together in 2, 4, 5.
</margin>

**Verse 20.** z) hornets <note>original Latin: *crabrones*</note> (3) Exodus 23:28. Joshua 24:12. a) Those in hiding, specifically those who fled into the forests and mountains; those living under the open sky could be severely infested by harmful insects. Similarly, in Congo, a kingdom of Africa, there are most destructive flying ants, fatal to humans and livestock: they fly in such numbers that they can only be repelled by fire. Dionysius de Carli, a missionary to that kingdom, testifies that he was nearly devoured alive by them. In Angola, this occurs frequently, so much so that whole swarms attack cows and consume them to the bone in a single night. Ludolf, *Commentary on the History of Ethiopia*, p. 193.

<margin>
...Exodus 22:7; chapter 37:24.
"Of your vows," that is, the choicest victims which you have vowed; for otherwise it was not permitted to vow. Leviticus 22:20, 23.
Furthermore, before the Law, it was permitted for all men to offer sacrifice everywhere in faith to God, and thus to commemorate the covenant of God and the hope of reconciliation. But God, through the Law of Moses, restricted this liberty when He gave the priesthood to Aaron and his sons. He willed that those sacrifices not be considered valid unless they were offered in one place. Compare Exodus 20:21 (and notes on Leviticus 17:4).
By this very thing, God shows that He is not delighted by a multitude of sacrifices, but by faith and the one Priest; and that He would recognize only the one Priest and the one sacrifice that brings completion. Therefore, this precept was a preparation for the eventual abolishing of sacrifices through the destruction of the earthly sanctuary. Daniel 9:26, 27, etc.

*Verse 1:* The word "all" has a *Kadma* accent over the letter *He*. <note>Technical notes on the Hebrew cantillation marks and vowels used to ensure precise liturgical reading.</note>
*Verse 5:* The word "there" is marked with a *Munach* accent. The word "He shall choose" has a *Raphe* mark <note>A small horizontal line over a letter indicating it should be pronounced softly, without a Dagesh/hardening.</note> in the *Hikilian* codex, according to David Kimchi in the *Michlal* and Elias in the *Masoreth* (page 78). This is supported by the *Masora of Erfurt*, which suggests a *Raphe* on the letter *Lamed* as required by analogy. However, others show it with a *Dagesh* [hardening dot].
*Verse 12:* The word "you shall vow" is marked with a *Munach* accent in several editions.
*Verse 14:* The phrase "there you shall offer" is formatted according to the Spanish manuscripts and the *Masora*, though some editions place a *Makkeph* [hyphen] and *Kadma* together here.

### Critical Notes on the Hebrew Text
*v. 14. The suffix on the word "commands you" lacks a Dagesh <note>a grammatical dot signifying emphasis</note> in the second letter, contrary to the Masora <note>the traditional scribal system for preserving the text</note> found in manuscripts and printed editions. v. 15. The word "only" was corrected via the Tischagdola <note>a type of cantillation or scribal mark</note> in source 4. "Which he gave to you?" v. 17. The word "not" uses a Munach accent in sources 2, 3, and 4. The word "your wine" appears without the prefix. v. 18. "In the place" uses the Tischakt accent. The word "your hand" is written "plene" <note>fully</note> or with a plural 'Yod' in many manuscripts (1, 3, 7, 8, etc.), which goes against other ancient Masoretic traditions. v. 20. "Your God" uses a Munach accent in sources 1, 2, and 3, contrary to the Masora on Genesis 30:16. "Your border" is written fully with a Shurek vowel in sources 2 and 3. v. 21. "I commanded you" is written fully in many sources, against certain Masoretic traditions. "And you shall eat" uses a Munach accent in several sources, contrary to others. v. 23. The word "be firm" appears thus in sources 1–6, 9, and 22, which is correct according to the Masora, though others use the Zakef Katon accent.*

v. 26. **בבקר** (in the cattle) The euphonic Dagesh <note>A dot in a Hebrew letter indicating doubling or hardening</note> is omitted in manuscripts 5, 16, 19, 20, 21; and with a Raphe mark <note>A horizontal line over a letter indicating a soft pronunciation</note> in 3. A metaphor drawn from a path, from which it is not permitted to turn aside without danger of wandering. Moses grants such power of pronouncing the meaning of the laws regarding civil causes to the priests and judges here, that it could not be greater; because no republic can stand without such power. But Moses does not give the Priests or judges the power to judge in the same way concerning matters pertaining to religion: for he would have conferred on them the power of changing religion by the same effort, than which nothing more contrary to his laws can be imagined. <note>Commentary by Clericus.</note> God does not demand that they do everything which they themselves say in their own name, but the word of God, the doctrine, the law, the demonstration, the judgment, for discerning right from wrong, which they have spoken: and which they could not reject except through stubbornness of the matter. <note>Cocceius Lexicon, page 944.</note>

# DEUTERONOMY CHAPTER 18 & 19 .CAP. 18. 19.

<margin>
Signs and punishment of the false prophet. <note>original Latin: "Pseudo-prophetæ indicia & pœna"</note>

...in My name,<sup>u</sup> even that which I have not commanded him to speak, or who shall speak in the name of other gods; that prophet shall die. <margin>u) as if by my command and authority. See verse 5; Jeremiah 14:14, 23:31, 29:9.</margin>

And if you say in your heart,<sup>v. 21. x</sup> “How shall we know the word which the Lord has not spoken?” <margin>x) how? Chapter 12:30.</margin>

When a prophet speaks<sup>v. 22. y</sup> in the name of the Lord, if the thing does not happen or come to pass, that is the thing which the Lord has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously; you shall not be afraid<sup>z</sup> of him. <margin>y) It was not indeed a certain sign of a divine mission if what was predicted by a Seer came to pass, as Moses taught above in chapter 13:2, 3. But it was certain that it was *not* predicted by God's command if it did not happen, provided the prediction was absolute, i.e., without any condition; such as was in Jonah's prediction concerning the Ninevites. <term>Clavis</term> <note>Likely referring to a 'Clavis' or 'Key' to the Bible, a type of scholarly reference book</note>: He who teaches what God said in His word needs no sign or miracle; just as one who preaches repentance, and the judgments of God toward repentance, such as God has threatened. But he who speaks of good things to be expected, if they do not happen, is a false Prophet, nor should he be feared so as to yield him obedience. Thus Jeremiah explains in chapter 28:8, 9. <term>Cocc. Lex. p. 461</term> <note>Reference to the Lexicon of Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century theologian</note>. z) Chapter 17:12. a) Chapter 1:17; Chapter 32:27; even if he threatens God's wrath.</margin>

**Critical Notes on the Hebrew Text:**
Verse 9. **And it shall be** — with a specific grammatical accent. **When they finished** — written in full spelling in several manuscripts. Verse 14. **And all its spoil** — includes the prefix "and" in several copies, contrary to the standard Masoretic text which omits it. **You shall plunder** — written in full spelling. Verse 15. **The distant** — plural feminine form, written in full spelling. **The nations** — marked with a specific stress marker (Metheg) in all our copies. Verse 20. **Until** — written with a specific vowel (Kametz) in some manuscripts. CHAPTER 21, verse 1. **In the land** — written with a Kametz vowel in many listed manuscripts, while others have a Patach. **Known** — written in a defective (shortened) spelling according to the Masorah and the Erfurt manuscript.

**Textual and Philological Notes:**
v. 19. "And they shall take hold": The *Makkef* <note>Hebrew hyphen</note> and *Metheg* <note>stress mark</note> are found in manuscripts 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 20. "His place" is written fully in manuscripts 4 and 5, though this goes against the Masorah of Erfurt. v. 23. "Curse": found in manuscripts 1, 2, and 22. 
**Chapter 22:** v. 1. "Not": written with the *Munach* accent in manuscript 2 and further in 1 and 4. v. 2. "Until": with *Makkef* in manuscripts 1, 3, 6, 9, 20. "Him": written this way in further manuscripts 2 and 4. The Zohar requires it to be written fully, but this is against the evidence of all codices and critics of the Old Testament. v. 5. "Whoever does": with *Makkef* and *Metheg* in 6, 9, 20. The letter *Sin* is written with the *Segol* vowel in 1, 3, 5, 10, 14, 16, 17, 18, and the Berlin manuscript; however, you may see it written with *Tsere* in chapter 12:12, 25:16, and elsewhere. v. 6. "If": with *Makkef* in 1-6, 9, 20. "The mother": written defectively in 1, 3, 4, 5, and 2, against Masorah 2, 3, and Erfurt. The same should be noted regarding the following word "the eggs."

2 You shall take of the first of all the fruit of the ground, which you shall bring in from your land that the Lord your God is giving you; and you shall put it in a basket, and you shall go to the place which the Lord your God shall choose to cause His name to dwell there.
3 And you shall come to the priest who shall be in those days, and say to him: "I declare today to the Lord your God, that I have come into the land which the Lord swore to our fathers to give us."
4 And the priest shall take the basket from your hand, and set it down before the altar of the Lord your God.
5 And you shall answer and say before the Lord your God: "A wandering Aramaean was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there with a few people; and he became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous.
6 And the Egyptians treated us ill, and afflicted us, and laid upon us hard bondage.
7 And we cried out to the Lord, the God of our fathers, and the Lord heard our voice, and saw our affliction, and our labor, and our oppression.
8 And the Lord brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with great terribleness, and with signs, and with wonders.
9 And He has brought us into this place, and has given us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey.
10 And now, behold, I have brought the first of the fruit of the ground, which You, O Lord, have given me." And you shall set it down before the Lord your God, and worship before the Lord your God.
11 And you shall rejoice in all the good which the Lord your God has given to you, and to your house, you, and the Levite, and the stranger that is in the midst of you.

<margin>
D

Tithes to be paid in the home city; for otherwise, they were to be carried to Jerusalem, or the money made from them. Clericus. To better understand this, one should observe the following from Selden’s *Dissertation on Tithes*, chapter 2: From the fruits of the soil or from livestock, the following were offered to the Priests: (1) First fruits, Exodus 23, 19, etc. (2) *Trumah*, or the heavy offering of the produce, Numbers 15, 19. Then, from what remained, there were paid (3) the first tithes to the Levites serving at the Tabernacle or Temple, Numbers 18, 21; who themselves paid a tenth of these tithes to the Priests; ibid. verse 26. (4) From the remaining nine parts, a second tithe was taken, which (or its value) was to be carried to the sanctuary and consumed in feasts. Deuteronomy 12, 18; 14, 23. This second tithe, however, every third year, they divided within the walls of each town for the poor and the Levites.

**Textual and Masoretic Notes:**
v. 19. **על** (Upon): Connected by a <term>Makkaph</term> <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in manuscripts 3, 17, and 13; and so it was in 4. **דבר** (Spoken): The letter Beth has a <term>Segol</term> vowel in 17, 18, and 22; but all others have a <term>Tsere</term>. **CAP. XXVII, 2. והיה** (And it shall be): The printed Masorah for Exodus 12:25 requires a <term>Ga’ashayim</term> accent, but none of our manuscripts support this here. **גדלת** (Large): Written deficiently <note>missing a letter</note> in 2, 3, and 4, contrary to the Masorah in 1 and the Erfurt manuscript. v. 3. **אשר יְהוָה** (Which the LORD): With a repeated Makkaph in 3; thus corrected in 2 and 1 from the *En Hakkore* <note>a medieval grammatical work</note>. v. 7. **שם** (There): Without a <term>Dagesh</term> <note>a dot indicating emphasis</note> in 3, 4, 5, 7, 11, 21, and 22. v. 8. **באר** (Clearly): Has a <term>Patach</term> vowel in 7, 13, 15, 17, 18, and 22, which the *Or Torah* approves against the others who have a <term>Qamets</term>. **הסכת** (Take heed) v. 9: The <term>Psik</term> mark is omitted in 3, 5, 6, 9, 14, and 20, contrary to the Masorah. **נהיית** (You have become): Read with a <term>Segol</term> in many manuscripts. **לעם** (For a people): Written with a <term>Dagesh</term> in 17 and 18, but without it in the others.
