v. 15. The word "the work of" is spelled defectively <note>missing a letter usually present</note> in some manuscripts. [The Lord will send upon you] in every undertaking of your hand which you shall do, until you are destroyed and until you perish quickly, because of the evil of your deeds by which you have forsaken Me. And your carcass shall be food for all the birds of the air and for the beasts of the earth, and no one shall frighten them away. The Lord will strike you with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart. Your sons and your daughters shall be given to another people, and your eyes shall look and fail with longing for them all day long, and there shall be no power in your hand. The fruit of your ground and all your labors shall a nation which you do not know eat up; and you shall be only oppressed and crushed continually. And you shall be driven mad by the sight of your eyes which you shall see. The Lord will strike you with evil boils upon the knees and upon the legs, from which you cannot be healed, from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head. The Lord will bring you and your king whom you shall set over you to a nation which neither you nor your fathers have known, and there you shall serve other gods [of wood and stone].

# DEUTERONOMY. CHAPTER 28 & 29. כט

<margin>
**v. 7-8)** See Chapter 3, verse 12. 
**v. 8. 1)** "that you may act prudently and that it may turn out successfully for you." Compare Joshua 1:7, 1 Kings 2:3, and Psalm 19:8. Both meanings (acting wisely and being successful) easily agree, because he who desires success in his affairs must act considerately and prudently. <note>The note refers to the Hebrew root 'S-K-L' which implies both wisdom and success.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 68. c)** "By ships," namely those of the Sidonians or Tyrians, who carried slaves bought from the Assyrians, Babylonians, or other neighboring nations into Egypt to be sold. Among these slaves were many Hebrews, according to the scholar Le Clerc. See also Joel 4:4, 6 and Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 7, Chapter 44. 
**d)** See Chapter 17:16. 
**e)** Le Clerc translates as "you shall be set out for sale"; Schmidt translates "you shall be sold." Indeed, out of extreme poverty, you will even offer yourselves for sale. <note>The Hebrew verb is in the 'Hithpael' form, indicating a reflexive action where one sells oneself.</note> 1 Kings 20:20, 25; 2 Kings 17:17. 
**f)** "But no one will buy you," because you will be held in such great contempt.
</margin>

**68** ...which you shall see. And the Lord shall bring you into Egypt again in ships, by the way whereof I said unto you, "You shall see it no more again"; and there you shall be sold^e to your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen, and no man shall buy^f you.

<margin>
**v. 69. g)** "To cut" or "to strike." The rituals of the covenant were repeated shortly before the Hebrews entered the land of Canaan to remind them of what they or their fathers had previously promised. <note>In the ancient world, "cutting a covenant" referred to the ritual of walking between the halves of sacrificed animals.</note> See the note on Chapter 29:13 regarding the meaning of these rites.
</margin>

**69** These are the words of the covenant which the Lord commanded Moses to make^g with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant which He made with them in Horeb. <note>Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, where the original Ten Commandments were given.</note>

***

### CHAPTER XXIX

<margin>
**Chapter XXIX.**
**v. 9. u)** "Standing," "staying," or "remaining." See Numbers 16:27.
**v. 10. x)** "And the stranger," meaning those who had come out of Egypt with them. Exodus 11:38. 
**y)** "From the one who fells your wood," etc. That is, not even those who perform the most menial tasks were excluded, such as the Gibeonites later became. Joshua 9:21, 27.
**v. 11. z)** "That you should pass into the covenant." This phrasing is drawn from a common ritual. Those making a covenant used to pass through the pieces of a dissected animal or a slaughtered bird. Compare Genesis 15:10 and following, and Jeremiah 34:18-19.
**a)** "And into His oath." They took a sacred oath to God, promising they would obey Him, calling Him as a witness to their promises and as an avenger if they did not stand by them. See Ecclesiastes 8:2 and Nehemiah 10:29. 
**v. 12. b)** See Chapter 27:9.
</margin>

<margin>
**Chapter XXIX, v. 1. h)** See Chapter 5:1. 
**i)** See notes on Chapter 11:2 and Exodus 19:4.
**v. 2. k)** See Chapter 4:34 and 7:19.
**v. 3. l)** "The Lord has not given." Moses expresses his grief and sorrow with this phrase. By denying the act, he denies its effect and outcome (cf. 2 Timothy 2:25), even though God Himself earnestly desired it (Chapter 5:26) and wished to achieve it through all His care and miracles. See verses 1, 2, 4, etc. Truly, God "did not give" it because you were unwilling (Matthew 23:37). Yet He hoped for better things eventually (Chapter 30:6) through Christ (Jeremiah 31:31). Le Clerc reads this as a question: "Has He not given...?" but this is forced because the phrase "until this day" follows. 
**m)** Isaiah 6:10, Jeremiah 5:21, Ezekiel 36:26.
**v. 4. n)** Chapter 8:2; see note on Numbers 33:1. 
**o)** See Chapter 8:4 and Nehemiah 9:21.
**v. 5. p)** See Chapter 8:3.
**v. 6. q)** Chapter 2:30, Numbers 21:23. 
**r)** Chapter 3:1, Numbers 21:33.
</margin>

**1** And Moses called unto all Israel, and said unto them: "You have seen all that the Lord did before your eyes in the land of Egypt unto Pharaoh, and unto all his servants, and unto all his land; **2** The great trials^k which your eyes have seen, those signs, and those great miracles: **3** Yet the Lord has not given^l you a heart to perceive, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, until^m this day. **4** And I have led you forty years in the wilderness^n; your clothes^o are not waxen old upon you, and your shoe is not waxen old upon your foot. **5** You have not eaten bread^p, neither have you drunk wine or strong drink: that you might know that I am the Lord your God. **6** And when you came unto this place, Sihon the king of Heshbon^q, and Og the king of Bashan^r, came out against us unto battle, and we smote them: **7** And we took their land, and gave it for an inheritance unto the Reubenites, and to the Gadites, and to the half-tribe of Manasseh. **8** Keep therefore the words of this covenant, and do them, that you may prosper in all that you do."

**v. 68.** The name "Jehovah" <note>original: יהוה</note> was corrected by a later hand in the Berlin manuscript following the printed Masorah <note>The Masorah is the traditional system of notes on the Hebrew text</note>. However, this reading rests on the testimony of only one Masorah, so we found it too harsh to admit into the main text.

<meta>This page continues the renewal of the covenant in the land of Moab. On the previous page, Moses reminded the people of God’s care during the Exodus. Here, he formally establishes the covenant not only with those present but with future generations, warning against the "poisonous root" of idolatry and the devastating destruction that follows the breaking of this divine oath.</meta>

<margin>
**v. 13. f)** Compare John 17:20; Acts 2:39. **g)** The making of a covenant is called the <term>Cutting of the Covenant</term> <note>original: "Foederis sectio"</note>, following the legal ritual that God initiated in Genesis 15:10, 17, and which was observed by the people in Jeremiah 34:10. By this it is noted: (1) that a covenant is made with God through sacrifice (Psalm 50:5). Indeed, God can receive no one into friendship except through the intervention of a "brother priest" who, by the power of an indestructible life, can act as a guarantor for sinners (Hebrews 7:15, 22; Chapter 9:14). This priest earns life for his brothers by obeying (Ephesians 49:5-6; Chapter 53:10; Psalm 16:2-3) and decrees it through his grace (Romans 5:15; Luke 22:29). This bears a resemblance to a Testator who ratifies a final will by death (Hebrews 9:16). Thus, his own blood is called the "blood of the covenant" (Zechariah 9:11; compare 12:10; Chapter 13:7; Matthew 26:28; Hebrews 10:29), corresponding to its symbol—the blood with which the first covenant was initiated (Exodus 24:8). That blood could not actually take away sins or sanctify souls (Hebrews 10:5-6; Psalm 40:7), but was a shadow of the blood that "speaks better things" (Hebrews 9:23; Chapter 12:24). (2) It notes that those who despise the covenant will be <term>cut in two</term> <note>original Greek: "διχοτομηθήσεסθαι"</note> (Luke 12:45; see notes on Chapter 28:65).
</margin>

<note>Critical notes regarding accents and Masoretic readings:</note>
Verse 14: "And with him." **f)** Thus in versions 2, 4, 6, 9, 10. Verse 15: Marked with the *Ithibh* accent in version 3. Verse 21: "Your children." The *Kadima* accent is found in versions 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 19, 20, 21, 22; however, this is done poorly and goes against the Q. T. f. 25. a. Verse 22: "And its sicknesses." Here, versions 7, 8, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, and 22 make the first *Yod* vocal and the second silent. But this is contrary to the usual Masoretic system; compare for example Genesis 14:2, 8. Furthermore, Hiller (page 252) conjectures that there is a variant reading for "Zeboiim" without the letter *Vav*. Verse 23: "What [means] the heat." In version 3, it appeared with the prefix *Vav* ("And what"), and the marginal note in versions 7 and 8 observes that it is found written this way in certain books.

<margin>
**v. 26.** The Israelites, yet in such a way that the greatest part of them was left under other kingdoms. Then, however, God will circumcise our heart to love Him, just as it is written in Ezekiel 36:26, and thus what is promised in this place will be fulfilled. See Rabbi John 11:51-52. Thus Rabbi Bechai <note>Rabbi Bachya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish commentator</note> refers these things to the mission of the Messiah, the son of David, that is, to the final redemption. folio 210b.

**v. 4. b)** They are driven out. See Isaiah 27:13; Ezekiel 34:16; Micah 4:6; Zephaniah 3:19.

**v. 6. c)** See chapter 10:16; 29:3; Jeremiah 4:4; 32:39; Ezekiel 11:19; 36:26; Romans 2:29; Colossians 2:11.

**v. 8. d) You shall walk** <note>original Greek: περιπατησετε</note>, being purified: the conscience from evil affections. Acts 15:9; Hebrews 9:14; 10:2, 22. Namely, the cutting away of the foreskin of the heart, which is evil desire. For one who indulges in evil desire is called "uncircumcised." Jeremiah 9:26. But he who renounces his desires is said to be "circumcised in heart." Therefore, this is that New Covenant of which Jeremiah speaks in 31:31 and following. These are the words of Bechai, folio 220c.

**q)** namely, to the Hebrews. Compare chapter 4:19. Others: "which He had not assigned to them as their portion." Compare chapter 18:14.

**v. 27. q)** He uprooted them: Schmid: "So much so, that He cast them away." 1 Kings 14:15.

**v. 28. r)** Schmid: "The hidden things also are known to Jehovah our God." Chapter 32:34; Romans 11:33; 2 Corinthians 2:7. Compare Job 28:12–28. So also Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan</note>.
**s)** Schmid: "but the revealed things are spoken to us, etc." Compare Psalm 25:14; Psalm 147:19-20. Perhaps the leaders of the Hebrews asked whether their descendants would truly sin against God to such an extent that they would incur the mentioned punishments? To which question Moses answered most wisely: that events of this kind, lying hidden in the darkness of the future, are to be left to the knowledge of God alone, since they pertain in no way to the duty of men; but His revealed laws must be obeyed. Clericus. See also Luke 13:23-24 and the open response in Deuteronomy 31 and 32. But Brentius says: "The mysteries of God, which are the Law and the Gospel, have been revealed to the Israelite people." Therefore, they will be punished all the more severely for idolatry, the more clearly the word of God is preached to them, as it says shortly after in chapter 30:11 and following.

**11** For this commandment which I command you today is not too hidden <note>or "too difficult"</note> from you, nor is it far off.

<margin>m) It is not a miracle <note>original Latin: mirabile</note> that exceeds your grasp, or is unknown to you (chapter 17:8; Psalm 131:1). That is, after the revelation has been made; for outside of revelation, it far surpasses all human intellect. —Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note>.
n) Nor is it far removed, such that you must seek it from a distance or require an anxious search. See the expansion of this saying in verses 12 and 13.</margin>
<margin>12</margin>
**12** It is not in heaven, that you should say, "Who will go up for us to heaven and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?"

<margin>13</margin>
**13** Nor is it beyond the sea, that you should say, "Who will go over the sea for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?"

<margin>o) It is not hidden by God in the heavens. Compare Isaiah 45:19.
p) That you might say.
q) Beyond the sea, from the farther shore which is by the sea. Numbers 32:19; Joshua 14:3.
r) Through a difficult and dangerous voyage. According to the Apostle [Paul] in Romans 10:6 ff., to obtain Christ, we do not need our own ascent or descent to bring Him down from heaven or back from the dead. Christ Himself descended from heaven for our sake to be joined to us, and returned from the dead to make Himself manifest to us: thus by His descent and return He earned all grace for us, and ensured that the word of faith is near us, along with the salvation and life we obtain through it. —Calovius.</margin>

He commends the written Law to the Levites and the Elders of the people.

**Note on Verse 14:**
From 1 Kings 2:3, we understand that for every human, their days for living are appointed. God either fulfills them in full number (Exodus 23:26; Genesis 48:29; 1 Kings 2:1), or prolongs them out of grace (2 Kings 20:6), or finally cuts them short as a punishment (2 Kings 1:16). ### Critical Apparatus (Textual Variants)

**Verse 5.** "According to all the commandment" (**ככל־המצוה**): Thus read manuscripts 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 20, and the Berlin manuscript; but others place the accent *Kadma* on the prefix *He*.
**Verse 9.** A minor section space is placed before this by the Halle manuscripts 2-6, 9, 10, 12, 19, 20, 21, contrary to other Old Testament manuscripts.
**Verse 12.** "And the little ones" (**והטף**): The letter *Tet* is written with the *Kames* vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, and 22.
**Verse 13.** "The land" (**האדמה**): Manuscripts 17, 18, 22, and the Berlin manuscript have the *Munach* accent instead of *Metheg*.
**Verse 15.** "To" (**אל**): For this, manuscript 3 reads "unto" (**אֶל**) and so also manuscript 2.
**Verse 16.** Manuscripts 1, 2, 3, Halle 6-10, 12, 19, 20, 21 begin a minor section with this verse.

**Technical Notes on the Hebrew Text**

**Verse 16:** The letter <term>Nun</term> in the word for "foreign" is written with a <term>Segol</term> vowel mark according to the second <term>Masora</term> note. Several manuscripts (1 through 5) have a <term>Maqqeph</term> (hyphen) in place of a <term>Kadma</term> accent on the word "which."
**Verse 17:** "My anger" is written with a <term>Maqqeph</term> in manuscripts 1, 2, 4, and 5. The word "found him" uses a <term>Zakef Gadol</term> accent in manuscript 2, contrary to the marginal note of manuscript 1.
**Verse 18:** "And I" has a <term>Telisha Gedola</term> accent in manuscript 1.
**Verse 20:** "And they provoke me" has a <term>Zakef Gadol</term> accent with a <term>Meteg</term> in manuscripts 1, 3, and 5; but a <term>Zakef Katan</term> with a <term>Meteg</term> in 17 and 18.
**Verse 23:** On the word "which," manuscripts 17, 18, and the Berlin manuscript have a <term>Munach</term> accent instead of a <term>Maqqeph</term>.
**Verse 25:** Manuscripts 5, 6, 9, 20, and 31 begin a "minor section" (paragraph break) here.
**Verse 26:** The word "the" is written with a <term>Segol</term> and <term>Maqqeph</term> in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.

-ation of the world, and proceeding from there, he concludes his oration with the days of the Messiah. This is according to Bechai <note>Rabbi Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century commentator</note>, folio 223, column c. This song possesses authority (and is confirmed) by the Prophetic and Apostolic writings; its subject matter is the rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles into the church of the people of God. It consists first of an introduction, in which attention is stirred by calling heaven and earth to witness, and praying that this assembly and song might bear fruit; namely, that it might keep at least some Israelites, if not all, in the duty of piety. Then it consists of the contrast between the benefits of God and the wrongdoings of Israel. After this, the punishment of Israel is recounted, namely their blindness and rejection, so that they are no longer the people of God. Finally, at the end, it contains the calling of the Gentiles. So writes *Brentius* <note>Johannes Brenz, a German Reformer</note>. The scope of the Song is to assert the faith of the Divinity of the future Redeemer. See van Til on this passage, page 8. *Augustine* rightly advises in his 9th Tractate on John: *Read the prophetic books without understanding Christ, and what will you find so tasteless and foolish? Understand Christ there, and not only is what you read flavorful, but it even intoxicates.* Compare Acts 10:43; 3:18, 24; Revelation 19:10, etc. **Verse 2. a)** *For it shall flow down*, or *it shall trickle* (2). Chapter 33:28. Compare Ephesians 45:8; also Ezekiel 21:2. Others read it in the <term>optative</term> sense: *let it trickle*. Moses desires that his words be heard and fixed in the hearts of the listeners, with such an effect as is usual for rain, which fertilizes the earth to produce sprouts and plants, etc. Isaiah 55:10, 11. Bechai folio 223, column d. **b)** See Job 29:22, 23. **Compare** Deuteronomy 11:11; Isaiah 55:10; Psalm 72:6. **c)** my doctrine, received from God, and worthy of all acceptance. Numbers 22:20; Isaiah 29:24; Proverbs 1:5. Compare 1 Corinthians 11:23; 1 Timothy 1:15. **d)** let it flow. Schmid reads *it shall trickle*. Numbers 24:7; Isaiah 55:10, 11. **e)** Hosea 14:6; Proverbs 19:12. **f)** *trickle* (1). Rain in frequent and thin drops, which when seen falling, presents the appearance of hairs to the eyes. Others: storms with tempests. **g)** tender herb. Genesis 1:11. **h)** many little drops, thinner rains (6). Psalm 65:11; Psalm 72:6; Jeremiah 3:3; chapter 14:22. **i)** Micah 5:6. **Verse 3. k)** and the Son of God, from the following and Exodus 3:2, 4; chapter 23:21, etc.; Jeremiah 23:5, 6. **l)** I will proclaim. Schmid reads *I will preach*. Exodus 33:19; chapter 34:5, 6. **m)** give therefore magnificence. Chapter 9:26; Psalm 29:1, 2; Psalm 96:7, 8; Psalm 145:3. **n)** whom a perverse generation does not recognize as God. Psalm 45:8; Psalm 47:1, 6; 1 John 2:23; 2 John 9. **Verse 4. o)** Schmid reads: *He is the Rock*. Specifically, while proclaiming, Moses points his finger at this Rock, as it were. <meta>The following text consists of critical apparatus notes in a smaller typeface discussing manuscript variations.</meta>

* Verse 28. "And I will bear witness" — Margin notes are found in manuscripts 17, 22, and Berlin, but no one observes the instruction itself in writing, except for the Halle manuscript, which places this word first at the start of the column.
* Verse 29. "Evil" — Manuscripts 1, 5, 6, 9, 20, 21 have the letter Resh with a Qamets vowel.
* Verse 30. "The words of the song" — Thus in manuscript 1, and so in manuscript 21.
* Chapter 32. Regarding the visual form of this Song, which he wants scribes and printers to observe, Rabbi Menachem is extremely concerned in the *Or Torah*, folios 25 and 26. From which we give the more important points. Namely, some Spanish codices describe the whole Song in sixty-seven verses or (as they now call them) lines, by the order of Rabbi Maimonides in three manuscript copies and Hammeiri; in such a way that in three places they are forced to reduce two lines of our printing into one, which happens in the tenth, sixteenth, and thirty-eighth lines, which are therefore longer than they should be and without a space in the middle. But other Spanish books, as well as the Hillel and Jerusalem manuscripts, complete the writing with seventy lines, as we do, following the instructions of the same Maimonides in different copies (one manuscript and several printed ones). This is also required by Rabbi Israel in *Kethibhath HaSopher*, the Talmudic tractate *Sopherim*, and with them Rabbi Menachem himself, alleging that the previous method cannot be done because, as Hammeiri admits, it is necessary that a vacuum be left in the middle of the lines as large as the space required for a *sethuma* section. Rabbi Menachem arranges the lines with us in the order prescribed by the printed edition of Maimonides, except for line 23 in verse 14, which see. Verse 2. "As the dew" — Qamets vowel in manuscripts 1, 3, 4, 20, 21.
* Verse 4. "The Rock" — written with a large letter Tsade in manuscripts 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 16, 19, 21, contrary to the *Or Torah*.

at Babel, and men were scattered throughout the world, God provided for the children of Israel, and established distinct boundaries for certain peoples as He foresaw would be convenient for them, so that the care and providence of God toward the Israelites might be celebrated. The reason for this providence is given in verse 9. (According to Galovius). **Verse 9.** s) A Portion, taken from among the rest of the nations (Acts 14:16). Chapter 7:6; 10:15. In Arabic, *El-tihu* specifically denotes that great desert between the Red Sea, Palestine, and Egypt, which they also call the "Desert of Israel." The root *Taha* means "he wandered through the land astonished and erring." a) howling (i) namely, of wild beasts. cf. Isaiah 13:22. b) of the solitude. Psalm 68:8. c) He surrounded him. Psalm 26:6. Jonah 2:4. cf. Psalm 34:8. like a wall of fire, Zechariah 2:9. Psalm 147:19, 20. e) He guarded him chapter 33:9. Psalm 12:8. f) like the blackness or the pupil (4) Proverbs 7:9. Psalm 17:8. Zechariah 2:12. A proverbial expression for the greatest care. **Verse 11.** g) see Exodus 19:4. h) he excites the nest to fly, that is, his brood. see Bochart’s *Hierozoicon* Part II, book 2, chapter 3. i) Genesis 1:2. k) Genesis 1:2. Jeremiah 23:9. This comparison most aptly describes the cloud hanging over the camp of the Israelites, by whose movement they were stirred to set out, and which always hung suspended over them like an eagle that flies around its nest with outspread wings. (According to Le Clerc). l) thus the Lord spread out His wings, as it were, and took him up. m) see chapter 1:31. Isaiah 63:9. n) wing or the stronger feather of the wing. Isaiah 40:31. Psalm 55:7. **Verse 12.** o) chapter 33:28. p) He led him. Psalm 78:53. Psalm 80:2. see Exodus 13:21. chapter 15:13. Numbers 9:17. following. q) verse 39. ---

*   **Verse 6.** הַ לְיהֹוָה. All our sources (except for 4. II.) follow the <term>Masora</term> here in having a "Large He" [He-maiusculum], as also in Genesis 1:1. But there is a strange variety in its separate writing. For according to the *Or Torah* and the Masora, the Western and Spanish books write it as one word [הַלְיהֹוָה]; the Nahardians write it separately [הַ לְיהֹוָה] (as if it were the Arabic *Hal* [a question particle]?); and finally the Eastern scribes write it in this manner [הַ לְיהֹוָה], which the *Or Torah* approves from all the best Hebrew critics, from Tanchuma and two very ancient Jerusalem codices. Although it may be admitted that the Westerners are elsewhere to be preferred to the Easterners when a reading is controversial, the analogy of the writing and the authority of a certain manuscript Masora in the book *Hiss.* favor the Easterners in this place. Next, as to the vowel points, [manuscripts] 1. 2. 3. 4. 6. 9. 20. 21. place a <term>Metheg</term> under the *He*. The *Lamed* is without a <term>Sheva</term> (which however the *Minchat Shai* and *Or Torah* require) in 2. 11. 13. 16.; but with a <term>Patach</term> and a Metheg in 3. Furthermore, it appears with a Sheva in 2. 4. 5. 11. 13. 16. 18., and David Kimchi in the *Minchat Shai* wants it to be voiced in reading, though he warns nothing about the writing. Finally, for the reading of this word, compare the various and equally uncertain opinions of David Kimchi, Rabbi Menachem in *Or Torah* folio 26, 27, and Hiller page 213 and 171.

*   **Verse 7.** "And he will tell you" [וְיַגֵּדְךָ] has the accent on the last syllable in 1. 2. 4. 6. 7. 8. 9. 20. The letter *Gimel* has a <term>Segol</term> vowel in 3. 4. 6. 8-16. 19. 20. 21. contrary to the *Or Torah* which has [וְיַגֵּדְךָ]. **Verse 10.** "He surrounded him" [יְסֹבְבֶנְהוּ] has a <term>Daghesh</term> in the letter *Beth* in 1. 2. Likewise the *Nun* in the following word "He instructed him" [יְבֹונְנֵהוּ]. "He guarded him" [יִצְרֶנְהוּ] has the *Tsade* without a Daghesh in 1. 3. 4. 5. 11. 13. 15. 16. 22., against *Or Torah* folio 27. a. **Verse 11.** "He flutters" [יְרַחֵף] has a Segol instead of a <term>Tsere</term> in 2., undoubtedly from a misapplication of his Masora and the Erfurt manuscript, which has "L and Patach." **Verse 13.** "High places" [בָּמֳתֵי] has a Metheg and a <term>Makkaph</term> in 1. 2.

*   **Verse 14.** "And rams" [וְאֵילִים]. Maimonides wants this word to be placed at the end of the preceding line (as they call the verse), as written in the Jerusalem codices. But our order is upheld by the *Or Torah* because of the distinction of the accents and the consensus of the Hillel codex and others.

k) that is, *red wine.* <note>See Genesis 49:11; 1 Maccabees 6:34.</note> l) *pure wine* (2) <note>Isaiah 27:2.</note> wine that has fermented and passed from being must. Root in Arabic: *to ferment*.

*contempt; (treating God like a wicked scoundrel who committed a crime, chapter 28:21; Joshua 7:15, worthy of becoming a corpse, chapter 21:23.) Micah 7:6; Nahum 3:6. Compare Proverbs 1:26 and following. r) Proverbs 6:14; compare above at verse 5. s) truth, faithfulness. Psalm 12, 2.* $\quad *v. 21. t) See verse 16. u) 1 Corinthians 8:4, 5; chapter 12:19, 20. x) they have done wrongly to Me. Verse 16; Jeremiah 8:19. y) Jeremiah 14:22. Compare Matthew 15, 9. z) This metaphorical phrase is taken from the nature of lovers: where a lover, noticing that his love is not returned equally, turns his own love elsewhere. In the sight of the one by whom he feels despised, he takes another, and to make the first burst with envy, he heaps favors upon the new one. In this manner of lovers, God is conceived as wanting to act with the Jews, who broke the marriage covenant; since He wished to return the favor to the ungrateful and faithless bride, He decided to transfer His love to the nations, and from them to adorn a chosen bride for Himself, and in the sight of the Jews to accumulate every kind of benefit upon her, so that the Jews might burn more intensely. Surely if a husband divorces an adulterous wife and, while she watches, marries a servant girl or a beggar in her place, giving her the jewelry taken from the first, it cannot fail to affect her deeply. Just as when Ahasuerus, having divorced Queen Vashti, joined Esther to himself in her place, who was brought from the captive Jews. Tillinghast, p. 100. a) See the key in Romans 10, 19. The calling of the nations is a singular character of Christ’s kingdom and an infallible sign. b) insofar as the Gentiles were destitute of the true knowledge of God. Compare note on chapter 4:6.* $\quad *v. 22. c) chapter 4:24; Psalm 52, 3; Psalm 97, 3. d) it is kindled (5) Ephesians 50:2. e) as happened to Sodom. Chapter 29:22. Compare Numbers 16:30; Psalm 86:13. f) and it inflamed the foundations. Malachi 3:19; Psalm 83:15; Lamentations 4:11; Psalm 82:5; 2 Peter 3:7, 10 and following. There is no need to imagine a hyperbole here; rather, the fire of divine wrath is understood, which both destroys men eternally and burns through the inner parts of the earth. For it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. Calvin.* $\quad *v. 23. g) I will accumulate, I will consume, or I will cause all evils to be consumed upon them. <term>Hiphil</term> verb form. (1) Genesis 18:24. See note on Numbers 32:14. h) hunger, pestilence, slaughter by enemies, incursions of beasts. Verses 24, 25. For the evils sent by God are called His "arrows" in Psalm 38:3, Psalm 91:5; Job 6:4. i) I will spend them against them, having become their enemy. Isaiah 63:10. Compare Revelation 18, 8.* $\quad *v. 24. k) consumed. Ibn Ezra: scorched, from the root <term>Mazah</term> in Daniel 3:19. Others: burning heats. For hunger burns like a flame and feeds on the vital spirits. Compare Lamentations 5:10. l) chapter 28:48, 53. m) consumed. Proverbs 4:17. n) with a carbuncle, a burning plague that exhausts all moisture and leaves nothing behind: for that is what the Arabic root signifies. Others understand it as lightning. See Song of Solomon 8:6; Habakkuk 3:5. o) with destruction, plague. (3) Ephesians 28:2; Psalm 91:6. p) with bitterness (1) Compare 1 Samuel 15:32. q) see Leviticus 26:22; Ezekiel 14:21; Revelation 6:8. r) with venom. Psalm 58, 5. s) of the serpents of the earth. \* v. 14. "And blood" found in Merca 3. 6. 9. 20. 21. v. 16. "They provoked Him" found in 4. 5. 10. 13. 14. 19. 20. 21. contrary to the Masoretic and Old Testament. "feared them" <note>Hebrew: se-arum</note> - Noram has "se-arum" in 17. 18. 22. and reversed at T. & Masoretic Erff. they place a contrary note "lo" (not). <meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the "Song of Moses" (Deuteronomy 32). The previous page likely concluded with the descriptions of Israel’s rebellion and the beginning of God’s decree of judgment. This page focuses on the total devastation of the people (v. 26-27), the spiritual blindness of the nation (v. 28-29), the source of their military defeat (v. 30-31), and the corrupt nature of their "vine" or character compared to Sodom (v. 32-33).</meta>

# DEUTERONOMY. Chapter 32.

<margin>
**v. 26.** y) Leviticus 19:32. A description of the most extreme slaughter. Compare chapter 20:16, 17.
z) Schmid: "I would have said," or "I might have said."
a) "I will cut them off to the corners," leaving nothing remaining <note>original Latin: "ad angulos usque excidam eos, nihil relicturus"</note>; (r) see the term in Leviticus 19:9 and compare Exodus 32:10, Numbers 17:10, etc.
b) By the total abolition of the nation. Compare Exodus 17:14, Job 18:17.
**v. 27.** c) Of the enemies, that is, even of the Devil himself, Psalm 8:3.
d) Chapter 1:17.
e) "Lest they estrange," or attribute to others. Clericus compares Jeremiah 19:4; see Isaiah 42:8, chapter 48:9. Gussetius: "Lest they be ignorant" that I am the one striking the Israelites; compare Job 21:19.
f) Chapter 9:28, Exodus 32:12, etc.
g) Exodus 14:8; compare Isaiah 36 and 37.
**v. 28.** h) For the Israelites are a nation lost in counsel. This is the reason for verse 26. So too verse 32. Others say the Gentiles, the enemies of God and the Church.
i) Ludolffus, from the Ethiopic, "foolish"; so Jeremiah 4:9.
k) They care for nothing—neither wrath, nor grace—nor do they notice, so as to hold their affairs before me; the presumptuous imagine me to be favorable to them when I am angry; therefore they do not think to consult for their own welfare. —Luther.
**v. 29.** l) The words of Moses or the servant of God, from verse 31. Compare Luke 19:42.
m) Jeremiah 9:11, Psalm 2:10, Psalm 107:43, Hosea 14:10.
n) Verse 20, Psalm 73:17.

**v. 30.** o) How could one of the enemies pursue, or how would he have pursued, a thousand of the Israelites? See Leviticus 26:8, Joshua 23:10. p) Compare Judges 3:31, chapter 20:10 following, 1 Samuel 14:13 following. q) "Is it not?" or "Unless." r) The Rock, that is, the God and Savior of the Israelites. v. 4, 15. s) As if He sold them, that is, He abdicated and permitted them to the tyranny of the enemies. Compare chapter 4:42, and see Judges 2:14, Psalm 44:13. t) Chapter 23:16, Lamentations 2:7.
**v. 31.** u) For otherwise. Genesis 48:14. x) Concerning which, see verses 4, 15, 18, 30. y) "Is their rock," namely of the enemies; that is, the Devil and their gods. z) Even with the enemies as judges; for they are forced to acknowledge the greater power of our God. Compare Exodus 8:15, chapter 14:25, 1 Samuel 4:8, chapter 5:7, chapter 6:5. a) Judges/Arbiters. Exodus 21:22.
**v. 32.** b) Refers back to verse 30. Compare verse 28. c) Chapter 29:28. d) Compare Psalm 80:9, 15; that is, they have shoots from the Sodomitic vines. A proverbial expression to signify that the Hebrews imitate the Sodomites and the inhabitants of other overthrown cities. Compare Isaiah 1:10, chapter 5:2, Jeremiah 2:21, Ezekiel 16:46, 48. Others think this refers to what various authors report about the fruits of plants in the vicinity of the Asphalt Lake <note>The Dead Sea</note>, for example Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 5, chapter 5. The fruits are similar in color to edible ones, but in the hands of those picking them, they dissolve into smoke and ashes. Compare Wisdom of Solomon 10:7. e) "And from the fields," 2 Kings 23:4, Isaiah 16:8. f) Genesis 40:10, 11. g) They are poisonous grapes. Verse 33, chapter 29:17, Jeremiah 8:14, Hosea 10:4. h) Of bitternesses. Job 13:27, chapter 20:14. k) "They have for them," that is, instead of the sweet fruit of piety, they produce the worst fruits of all impiety, worthy to perish just as Sodom did.
**v. 33.** l) Poison. Verse 24. m) Exodus 7:12. n) Is their wine (their harmful doctrine. Compare Isaiah 55:1, 2) and the venom of asps. Verse 32, Psalm 58:5, Isaiah 11:8, Job 20:16. p) Atrocious, cruel. Jeremiah 39:14.
**v. 34.** q) It is laid up in store. r) With me. God speaks. That is, the things done by the Hebrews and their enemies are all preserved with me as if recorded on tablets, to be inspected in their own time, and punishments taken from the sinners. —Clericus. s) Sealed. Compare chapter 29:28 and see Job 14:17, Jeremiah 32:11, 14. Bechai: "Sealed, but to be unsealed in the end times." Daniel 12:9. t) In my treasures. Chapter 28:12. Here it signifies archives or chambers in which royal papers are kept. See Ezra 6:1.
**v. 35.** u) "To me" (the Judge of all the earth, Genesis 18:25) belongs vengeance (verse 41) against the faithless Hebrews and their impious enemies. Isaiah 61:2, chapter 63:4, Psalm 94:1, Romans 12:19, Hebrews 10:30. x) And retribution. Compare verse 41, Judges 1:7. y) At its own just time, in which their foot shall stumble. Psalm 38:17, Psalm 94:18; compare Leviticus 25:35. z) For the day of their destruction is near, even when they think those things are most remote. a) A cloudy and dark state. Compare Genesis 2:6, Proverbs 24:22, Psalm 18:19, Job 21:30. b) "And it hastens" (for just as Genesis 1:14, etc.) all things hurry. Isaiah 8:1, Habakkuk 1:8, Psalm 119:60, 2 Peter 2:3. c) The things that are to happen or are prepared for them. Esther 3:14.
**v. 36.** d) For the Lord will judge His people, which can be understood as for their good (as in Psalm 54:3, Psalm 72:4) or rather in this place concerning punishment and vengeance (as in Genesis 15:14) according to the diversity of the citizens of His people. So Paul in Hebrews 10:30, 15:29. Genesis 6:6. Gussetius: "He will comfort Himself by exercising vengeance on enemies"; see Isaiah 1:24, Ezekiel 5:13, Genesis 27:41, Psalm 90:13, Psalm 135:14. g) "When He sees." Verse 19, Exodus 3:7. h) "That it has gone away, vanished," like consumed bread. 1 Samuel 9:7. Or water which flows away and does not return. Job 14:11. i) Their strength or hand, in which the strength of men chiefly resides. Daniel 12:7. k) "And there is nothing shut up or left"; or: "it has gone into nothing." Isaiah 40:17. l) A man shut up. Nehemiah 6:10. Or that which was shut up as something precious, or left and neglected as something vile. A proverbial expression by which total overthrow is signified. See 1 Kings 14:10, chapter 21:21, 2 Kings 9:8, chapter 14:26; compare Ezekiel 6:12, Micah 5:9 following.
**v. 37.** m) Schmid: "When it shall be said." Compare chapter 15:2. This, some attribute to the Lord mocking the faithless Israelites (Judges 10:14) or according to others, to the enemies of the Church and their idols (compare Isaiah 21:9, chapter 46:1, Jeremiah 50:2, chapter 51:44). Others, however, attribute it to the impious themselves and the heathen mockers of the servants of God. n) Joel 2:17, Micah 7:10, Psalm 42:4, Psalm 79:10. o) To whom they fled for refuge. Psalm 2:12, Proverbs 18:10.
**v. 38.** p) Who are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. q) Compare in the sense of the New Testament, Romans 12:1.

\* **v. 26.** The word *Me-enosh* ("from man") has a dagesh [a grammatical dot] in versions 1, 2, and 4. \* **v. 27.** The word *Lulei* ("were it not") is written with *Grafchaim* [an accent] in 2 and 3. The word *Yanivu* is written fully in 1, 3, 4, 5, etc., contrary to the Masorah. \* **v. 32.** The name of the Lord [Y-H-W-H] is noted in 3, 4, 5, 17, 18, 22... while others use *Munach*. The word *Invei* ("grapes of") lacks a dagesh in the letter Nun in 3, 5, 13, 14, contrary to the *Minchat Shai*. \* **v. 34.** The word *Halo* ("is it not") has a *Merca* accent in 3, 17, 18. Several versions write it fully, and it was corrected in 1 according to the Masorah of others, but against the *Or Torah*. Even the printed Masorah here and in Numbers 14:3 refers to this among examples of doubtful spelling. The word *Be-otzerotai* ("in my treasures") is defective in many manuscripts... corrected in 2 and 3 according to manuscripts and printed editions here and in 2 Kings 20:13, but against the *Or Torah*. \* **v. 35.** The word *Atidot* ("things to come") has a *Patach* vowel in 1, 3, 4.

<summary>This page analyzes Deuteronomy 32:26-38, interpreting Israel's military defeats as a divine "selling" of the people due to their spiritual corruption, which is compared to the poisonous "grapes of Sodom." The commentary emphasizes that God keeps a record of these deeds in His "treasures" to be addressed in the day of judgment.</summary>

m) **Let him take hold of it for judgment,** or, My hand shall take hold of judgment. (Compare Job 23:11, Ecclesiastes 7:18, Psalm 45:4-5, Revelation 19:11).
n) **Then I will return vengeance to My enemies.** (Verses 35, 43; Leviticus 26:25, Psalm 149:6-7).
o) Verse 34; compare Ezekiel 20:5, Luke 19:27, Revelation 17:14, 19:15.
**Verse 42.**
p) **I will inebriate,** I will make as if drunk. (Genesis 43:34; compare Isaiah 34:5, Jeremiah 45:10).
q) See verse 23.
r) Isaiah 1:20. **War is, as it were, a monstrous beast, devouring everywhere.**
s) **With the blood of the pierced.** (Chapter 21:1).
t) **Even of the captives themselves.** (Chapter 21:11). Thus, none are spared: just as God commanded concerning the Canaanites. (Chapter 20:16; compare Numbers 31:17, 1 Samuel 15:32-33).
u) **Concerning the head.** (Compare Psalm 68:22, Psalm 110:6, Habakkuk 3:13). But Schmid interprets it as "from the bitterness of the enemy's vengeance." (See verse 33).
x) **The vengeance of the enemy** (taken from the enemies) shall thus happen and begin. (2) (Judges 5:2; compare 2 Thessalonians 2:8).
**Verse 43.**
y) **These are the words of the Prophet.** Schmid: "Sing therefore! Shout for joy, O nations!" (So Psalm 32:11, 81:2, 67:5). The Septuagint reads it as in Romans 15:10; compare Revelation 12:10, 15:3. But the Zurich translators <note>A reference to the *Biblia Tigurina*, a Reformation-era translation.</note> say: "Stir up His people to jubilee, O nations." (See Psalm 65:9, Job 29:13). However, the first interpretation is more common and better fits the theme of the whole Song.
z) **Now His people,** by apposition. (See verse 21).
a) <note>original Greek: "μετὰ τοῦ λαοῦ αὐτοῦ"</note> **"With His people."** From this comes Romans 15:10.
a) Compare Genesis 4:10, Psalm 9:13, Matthew 23:31, 34-35.
b) **Of the sincere worshipers and Martyrs.** (See verse 36).
c) See verse 35, Luke 18:7, Revelation 6:10, 18:20, 19:2.
d) See verses 35 and 41, Psalm 58:11-12.
e) **To His enemies,** whether they be from the Jews or from the Gentiles. Properly, however, in this Song the "enemies of God" are Israel according to the flesh (verses 15, 16, 21). For this entire Song aims to teach, on the one hand, God’s faithfulness in perfectly fulfilling His promises; and on the other hand, the ingratitude of that Israel in their defection and stubborn rebellion, and thus the avenging justice of God in their abandonment and rejection, in order to substitute another Church, chosen from the Gentiles. (Gussetius, p. 795).
f) **And He will expiate.** (Leviticus 16:32). Because the ransom <note>original: "lytrum"</note> has been paid, He will wipe away the debts and be propitious <note>Kind and forgiving.</note>. A metaphor from Genesis 6:14.
g) **His whole land.** (Psalm 24:1). Also Palestine, which was struck with a curse under Titus. (Malachi 3:24).
h) **His people of hope,** gathered from Jews and Gentiles. (Romans 11:25-26). Note especially that this very Song will be the greatest instrument for the conversion of the Israelite people at the end of days, according to Deuteronomy 31:21, compared with 2 Corinthians 3:16, Romans 11:15, and Revelation 11:15. (Till. in Cant. Mos. p. 207). For God provides in this Song the method and arguments by which the apostate Jews are eventually to be called to repentance. (Ibid. p. 188).
**Verse 44.** i) Chapter 31:30. k) See Numbers 13:8, 16.
**Verse 46.** l) That is, attend diligently. (Haggai 1:5, 7, 2:15). m) In which I have testified to you. (Chapter 31:28). n) Chapter 6:7, Genesis 18:19.
**Verse 47.** o) It is not empty, or it is not in vain. (Genesis 37:24). The Septuagint reads it as in Ephesians 5:6. p) For you, so that you might hear and do it. Compare a similar Hebraism in Genesis 32:11, Isaiah 7:13. q) See chapter 30:15, 20.
**Verse 49.** r) See Numbers 27:12. s) Chapter 34:1; compare Numbers 32:3.
**Verse 50.** s) Chapter 34:5. An emphatic command for the future, as in Genesis 12:2, chapter 20:7, Psalm 37:27. t) Genesis 25:8, 17.

<meta>The final lines contain technical Masoretic notes regarding spelling variations and accents in specific manuscripts (labeled 1-21).</meta>
Verse 40: "Forever" <note>Hebrew: *le'olam*</note> is written in full in manuscripts 5, 6, 9, 20. Verse 41: "I sharpen" <note>Hebrew: *shannoti*</note> is written defectively <note>Missing a vowel letter.</note> in manuscript 2, as required by the Erffurt Masorah. Several manuscripts (3, 4, 7-11, etc.) place the accent on the penultimate syllable. Verse 43: "And he will expiate" <note>Hebrew: *vekipper*</note> is defective in 1, 2, 4. Verse 46: "And he said to them: Set your hearts" in 2, 3. Verse 47: "This" <note>Hebrew: *hazeh*</note> with specific punctuation in 5, 8, 12, etc.

<meta>The following notes provide a deep philological and theological commentary on the text of Chapter 33, explaining the poetic descriptions of God appearing from the mountains.</meta>

from the vicinity of Idumea, where Mount Seir is (chapter 2:1ff). Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius, a 17th-century theologian</note>: He rose for them from Mount Seir when, after many were wounded by the bite of serpents, He provided help through the bronze serpent; for this happened as they bypassed Mount Seir (Numbers 21:4ff). l) He shone forth. Psalm 80:2, 94:1. m) from Mount Paran. Habakkuk 3:3. The Israelites came there after three days' journey from the desert of Sinai (Numbers 10:12, 33). It is near Kadesh, on the border of the Idumeans. Calovius: He appeared from Mount Paran when He gave the quails and appointed the 70 judges (Numbers 11:16, 32). So say Brentius and others. But perhaps he is not wrong who, following Ibn Ezra <note>A medieval Spanish biblical commentator</note>, understands this whole verse as referring to the station of the Israelites at Mount Sinai and the glorious arrival of the Lord on that mountain: thus, that terrible storm (also seen in Judges 5:4, 5; Habakkuk 3:3; Psalm 68:9, etc.) first arose for the Israelites toward Seir, and shone more fully from Mount Paran, until finally it settled on Mount Sinai. The mention of the "Law" must be understood as the giving of the Law. n) "He came," I say. verse 21. Isaiah 21:12. o) from the myriads of holiness, or holy ones, to the myriads of Israel (Numbers 10:36). p) namely, from heaven, where truly innumerable Angels and Saints serve and adore Him (Daniel 7:10), and the Apostle Jude calls them "holy myriads" (Jude 15). Psalm 68:17 refers here; see also Job 33:23. p) Schmid: from His right hand (cf. Habakkuk 2:16) was given the fire of the Law to them. It speaks of the Law given in lightning—to show it terrifies men no differently than celestial fire. (Vatablus). q) see chapter 4:11, 36. r) Esther 1:8, 13, 19, etc. s) "for them" instead of *lahem* as in chapter 32:32. This refers to the holy myriads, i.e., the Angels; it carries the same sense as the saying that the Law was given through Angels (Acts 7:53, Galatians 3:19, Hebrews 2:2). Thus two Cherubim were placed on the Ark to hint that the divine Law was given through the mediation of Angels. (Abarbanel). v. 3. t) Yea. v. 20. u) He loves (t). Very common in Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic: so the sense is that God... [refers to Psalm 89:51, John 13:1]. Cocceius: the Son of God, when He promulgated the Law together with the Father and the Holy Spirit—the Law which works wrath (Romans 4:15)—did not lay aside the will and love of the Sponsor, by which from eternity He asked for the nations to be given as His inheritance... (Hebrews 7:22, 9:14). x) Some understand "the peoples of Israel" (v. 19, Judges 5:14), but see our previous notes. y) all His holy ones, the help of Jehovah the Son... (Psalm 16:3, 50:5, Hebrews 2:11). But Onkelos <note>Author of a famous Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> and others: the holy ones of the house of Israel. z) "in your hand they are" from God! John 10:29. a) they fell down. Schmid: they were prostrate at your feet. From the Arabic root meaning "to recline." Compare Exodus 24:1, 10, Acts 22:3. 4) Schmid: he shall receive of your words. Each one; or: he was receiving from your words what was commanded to Moses. Compare John 3:32, 8:26. verse 4. c) John 1:18, 7:19. d) inheritance, that is, it was to be their own perpetual possession (Ezekiel 11:15), not just as shadows but as the substance of things (Hebrews 10:2, Psalm 119:111). e) congregation (Nehemiah 5:7). verse 5. f) Schmid: And He was King in Jeshurun (Israel. v. 26). He understands God Himself, whose gracious Presence was in Israel (Numbers 23:21, Song of Songs 7:6, Psalm 24:9, 10). Under the Judges... God (the Son, Psalm 2:6, 45:1) alone was considered King. To Him alone the Hebrews paid tribute. Clericus; see note on Numbers 23:21. g) when they gathered themselves. At the time the Law was given (Exodus 19:7, 17) and so on under Moses and the Judges. verse 6. h) i.e., let him never perish from the tribe. i) [Note on the negative particle]. k) his men (chapter 2:34). l) number (chapter 4:27). Furthermore, it is strange that in this blessing no mention is made of the tribe of Simeon, which seemed to need it more than others, being greatly diminished in the desert (Numbers 26:14). Therefore, the Septuagint (LXX) supplies it here... joining it with Reuben: "and let Simeon be many in number." Zebulun and Issachar are joined later. Others think Simeon is included under Judah's blessing, within whose borders they received their inheritance (Joshua 19:1). verse 7. m) and bring him into his people, i.e., into the place he must occupy after the current inhabitants are expelled (Judges 1:4). n) Schmid: with his hands he shall be contending for himself; but Clericus: his hands shall be sufficient for him. o) and may You be a help against the enemies (Psalm 60:13).

# DEUTERONOMY: AND THIS IS THE BLESSING, CHAPTER 33.

**v. 8.** p) see Exodus 28:29, 30. <note>original: "vid. Ex. 28, 29. 30"</note> Schmid adds: "O Lord! they shall be." Others understand this as: "O Israel!" q) To your holy one. This refers to Aaron, who was consecrated to the priesthood by God's command in Exodus 28:36. Though he indeed sinned in Exodus 32:4 and Numbers 20:12, he was nevertheless received back into grace and truly strove for holiness; compare Malachi 3:4 and following. Furthermore, the entire Levitical worship was nothing but a shadow of Christ. (Brentius). In a specialized sense, it is said of Christ in Psalm 16:10, "the Holy One." <note>original: "ὅסιος" [hosios]</note> Thus also in Hebrews 7:26. r) whom you tested, O Israel, and whose authority or office you called into doubt. See Exodus 17:2, 7. s) you contended with him. Compare Numbers 20:2, 13.

x) Verse 17. y) they shall observe. Chapter 32:10. **v. 10.** z) they shall teach, according to their office. Chapter 17:9 and following; Chapter 24:8; Leviticus 10:11; Malachi 2:7. a) they shall place: incense in your nostrils. Exodus 30:7, 8. Compare Paragraph 26:18. b) Leviticus 6:15, 16. Those who would snatch the priesthood from them, as in Numbers 16:3 and following. g) and those who hate him. Chapter 32:41. h) Schmid translates: "so that they do not rise." Thus the word "from" <note>original Hebrew: "min"</note> would be negative before a future verb, which is without a parallel example; however, before nouns and infinitives it is not infrequent, for example 1 Samuel 15:23; Hosea 6:6. But Cocceius's Lexicon (p. 441) understands "from the time that" <note>original: "asher"</note> they rose up, as in Psalm 45:9. **v. 12.** i) To or concerning Benjamin. See verses 7, 8. After Levi, he blesses Benjamin, because the temple was to be built in his portion. (Calovius). k) beloved (?) Psalm 5:1. l) Schmid: "The beloved of the Lord" (as he was once to his father in Genesis 44:20). According to Calovius, this is understood as the tribe of Benjamin, which would dwell confidently in the Lord because it had God with it in His temple and dwelling place. Indeed, not only was the city itself situated in this tribe (Joshua 18:28), but also the most important part of the Sanctuary. However, some part belonged to the tribe of Judah (Psalm 78:68), and therefore the city is also reckoned to them in Joshua 15:63. But Cocceius's Lexicon (p. 291) says: "The beloved of the Lord," etc. He speaks of Him whom he later calls in verse 16 "the one dwelling in the bush": and in Isaiah 48:14 "whom the Lord loved," of whom Ephesians 5:1 and Jeremiah 11:15 speak. It is He, I say, of whom it can be said that He protects the Church and dwells in her midst: namely, "the Son of His love." <note>original: "ο υιος της αγαπης" [ho huios tēs agapēs]</note> Solomon was also called Jedidiah (2 Samuel 12:25), but not in the same way, and he was loved for His sake; compare Psalm 60:7, Psalm 127:2. m) the Lord will be protecting him. n) and between his shoulders He shall dwell, or remain. That is, in the very bosom and lap, so to speak, he shall be cherished by God. Compare Isaiah 49:22. Luther: perhaps Moses says this because the tribe of Benjamin dwelt between the tribes of Judah and Ephraim—both royal and powerful—and had the Temple in its own tribe. But Cocceius: "The beloved of the Lord shall dwell between his shoulder blades," that is, in a way between the sides of Benjamin: for in the division of the land, "shoulder" is often used to mean the side of a city and similar things, e.g., Joshua 15:8, 10, 11, etc. **v. 13.** o) Blessed by the Lord she shall be; compare Genesis 26:29. p) excellence or a precious gift. (7) Song of Solomon 4:13, 16. Arabic Root: "Glory surpassed, excelled in honor." q) and the abyss lying below, i.e., subterranean waters and springs by which plants are nourished. Chapter 8:7; Genesis 49:25; Ezekiel 31:4. **v. 14.** r) The produce of the sun; things that come by the sun's benefit, or according to Clericus, things that come forth only once within a solar period (i.e., a year). s) of the protrusion (thrusting forth), perhaps of lunar fruits, which are gathered every month, or after some lunar periods have passed, such as hay, vegetables, etc. Compare Revelation 22:2. **v. 15.** t) and from the summit. Genesis 8:5. u) of the eternal mountains (Psalm 68:34) which have been from the beginning; but Schmid understands "from the first fruits" also of the mountains of the East. x) of the perpetual hills. v. 23. Psalm 5:13; Psalm 51:20. a) of the one inhabiting the bush, who is called the Lord and the Angel of the Lord in Exodus 3:2 and following; in which Angel Jacob also prayed for a blessing upon the sons of Joseph. Genesis 48:16. The Angel of the covenant of grace (Malachi 3:1) and the Son of God, from whom and in whom is every blessing (Genesis 12:3; John 1, 17; Ephesians 1:3). The Greek Septuagint as in Acts 7:30, 35. b) Let it come, I say, all this good. There is emphasis in the double suffix; compare Job 22:21. c) Genesis 49:26. Schmid: "Nazirite." But Clericus: "Of the Prince." Compare Exodus 29:6 and Nahum 3:17. **v. 17.** d) Schmid: "Just as to the firstborn of his ox, honor is his"; such could be the sense and context. He seems to understand the horns, which are the beauty of oxen. (Clericus). e) Psalm 22:22. Bochart: the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. f) Bochart: of a two-horned wild goat. See Numbers 23:22. g) he shall gore the peoples together. Exodus 21:28. See Joshua 17:17 and compare 2 Kings 22:11, Psalm 44:6, Daniel 8:4. h) even to the boundaries; understand the word "upon" <note>original: "al"</note> (Psalm 59:14). i) those, namely, the horns, are. k) verse 2. Compare 1 Samuel 18:7. l) Compare Joshua 17:14. Ephraim is placed before Manasseh, as in Genesis 48:19, 20. m) Compare Judges 6:15; Micah 5:2. **v. 18.** n) see chapter 28:6 and compare Judges 4:10. It seems to signify voyages or commerce, etc. Compare Genesis 49:13. (Clericus). o) staying at home, and occupied in cultivating the fields. Compare Genesis 25:27; chapter 49:14, 15. **v. 19.** p) see verse 3. q) to the mountain of the Temple, namely. Compare Exodus 15:17. r) they shall call together; by their example and by the offering of peace sacrifices, they shall invite other guests. s) i.e., legitimate and holily offered. Compare chapter 16:18; Leviticus 19:36; Psalm 4:6. t) abundance, an overflowing. Compare Job 22:11. u) they shall suck. Isaiah 60:16; chapter 66:11, 12. i.e., they shall abound in merchandise brought to them by sea, and in fish. (Clericus). x) and covered. y) of hidden things, or hidden treasures. Joshua 7:21, 22. z) sand, i.e., according to Clericus: in the very sand of their shore, from which glass is melted, they shall find hidden treasures. Grammatical Notes: v. 15. The word for "mountains" <note>original: "harere"</note> has a He with a Metheg in manuscripts 1 and 4, but with a Munach following a Chateph-pathach. The word for "hills" is defective according to the Erfurt Masorah, but against the printed edition at Genesis 49:26. v. 17. The word for "wild ox" <note>original: "re'em"</note> has a Resh with a Metheg followed by a Chateph-pathach in manuscripts 1, 2, and 22. But the Erfurt Masorah requires a simple Shva. v. 19. uses a Munach in several manuscripts (3, 6, 9, etc.). The word for "hidden" <note>original: "temune"</note> is defective with a Kibbutz in manuscript 2 according to its Masorah, but against the Erfurt version.

**h)** However, "He came" appears in verse 2; compare Proverbs 1:27. **i)** He will come: for the Prophets, viewing what is to come as if it were already past, frequently speak in this manner. **i)** *With the heads of the people:* that is, with the remaining tribes they shall cross the Jordan, even at the beginning or the front of the army. **CHAPTER 34, v. 1. f)** Some suggest this final chapter of the book was not written by Moses; for it narrates how he died and was buried by the Lord; that is, by Michael (Jude verse 9) or by Christ, who was to bury the ceremonies of Moses. Lightfoot, *Chronicle of the Old Testament*. However, Abarbanel denies this in his commentary and contends that all things in the whole Pentateuch were written by Moses, based on a comparison of chapter 31:9, 24 and chapter 4:25; 30:1; 31:16. **g)** Numbers 22:1. **h)** chapter 32:49. **i)** chapter 3:17; Numbers 21:20. **k)** chapter 3:27. **l)** Numbers 26:29. **m)** An anticipation (prolepsis), as in Genesis 14:8; chapter 19:22. Since this chapter is not by the hand of Moses, it is no wonder that a more recent name of the city is read here. Le Clerc. It was called Leshem in Joshua 19:47 and Laish in Judges 18:29. Compare also Genesis 14:14, where the name of Dan comes from the other source of the Jordan, according to Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 1, Chapter 11. **v. 2. n)** as far as the western sea. See chapter 11:24; Zechariah 14:8; Joel 2:20.

**v. 21.** *Vaitetha*: written with a double Segol according to various manuscripts. **v. 23.** They begin a new section here with a space provided. **v. 24.** *Bashemen*: The letter Caph is without a Dagesh (the strengthening dot) and with the Raphe mark (the line indicating a soft sound). **v. 25.** *Min'aleka*: Written in full according to most codices, contrary to the Masorah of Erfurt. **v. 27.** *Me'onah*: For this, another codex had *Ma'on* [dwelling]; see Lightfoot on Matthew 5:18 and Jacob ben Hayyim in the Preface to the Rabbinic Bible. **v. 29.** *Ve'attah*: With the Qametz vowel, contrary to the first hand and the Masorah.

* **v. 7.** f) Chapter 31:2. g) His eyes had not grown dim, as in Genesis 27:1. h) Nor had his life-force—or vigor—fled (1); compare Genesis 30:37.

Brentius <note>Johannes Brenz, a Lutheran reformer</note>. See the notes on chapter 18:15 and Numbers 27:21. n) Indeed, whom the Lord knew. John 10:14; 1 Corinthians 8:3; 2 Timothy 2:19. o) As if turned face to face. Chapter 5:4; Exodus 33:11. Rabbi Joseph Albo speaks beautifully on this passage in book 3 of *The Roots* <note>original: "Ikkarim"</note>, chapter 20, as cited by Meier in the notes to *The Order of the World* <note>original: "Seder Olam"</note> page 975: It is impossible but that there should arise eventually a Prophet similar to Moses, or greater than him; for the King Messiah will be similar to him, or greater. These words should be explained thus: "none arose like him"—not as if no one similar would ever exist for eternity, but that none arose similar in some particular quality; or that in all the time following the prophets until the cessation of prophecy, none arose like Moses, but thereafter one will indeed exist who is similar, or rather, greater than Moses.
* **v. 11.** p) Greek <note>original: "ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς σημείοις καὶ τέראσιν"</note>: "in all signs and wonders." Compare John 15:24; Joel 3:1.
2) Chapter 14:15. q) Chapter 19:10. x) Psalm 118:27. y) Proverbs 12:17. z) Psalm 111:1. a) 1 Samuel 2:8. b) Isaiah 30:26. c) Leviticus 8:8. d) Song of Solomon 4:16. e) Numbers 30:14. f) Deuteronomy 8:9.

# BE STRONG

->The sum of the verses of the Book of Deuteronomy is nine hundred and fifty-five; its mnemonic is "The Vulture" <note>Hebrew: Ha-Netz, numerical value 955</note>.<-
->Its middle point is: "And you shall act according to the word which they tell you" (Deut 17:10). Its weekly portions are 11; its mnemonic is "Bind the festival sacrifice<-
->with cords" <note>Psalm 118:27; Hebrew "Isru Chag" refers to the 11 portions</note>. Its sections are 27; its mnemonic is "Her beauty is faith, he tells of righteousness" <note>Numerical value of "Yafyah" is 27</note>. Its chapters are 34; its mnemonic is "I will praise<-
->the Lord with all my heart" <note>Psalm 111:1; Hebrew "Odeh" is 34</note>. The number of "Open" sections is thirty-four, and the "Closed" sections are one hundred<-
->and twenty-four; the total is one hundred and fifty-eight sections; its mnemonic is "He will grant them<-
->a throne of glory" <note>1 Samuel 2:8; "Kise" is 158</note>.<-
->The sum of the verses of the entire Torah is five thousand eight hundred and forty-five; its mnemonic is "And the light of the sun shall be sevenfold" <note>Isaiah 30:26; "Shiv'atayim" is 700, but here used for a larger total</note>. Its middle verse is: "And he put<-
->the breastplate on him, and in the breastplate he put the Urim and the Thummim" (Lev 8:8).<-
->The number of "Open" sections in the whole Torah is two hundred and ninety; its mnemonic is "Let my beloved come into his garden and eat<-
->his choice fruits" (Song 4:16). And the "Closed" sections are three hundred and seventy-nine; its mnemonic is "Or binds<-
->an obligation on herself by an oath" (Num 30:14). Thus the total number of all sections, both Open<-
->and Closed, is six hundred and sixty-nine; its mnemonic is "You shall lack nothing in it" (Deut 8:9).<-

**Column 3 Notes**
* **v. 3.** o) The south of Judea; see notes on Numbers 13:17. p) The plain; Genesis 13:10, a part of which was the Valley of Siddim; Genesis 14:3. q) The valley of Jericho. That was a most blessed region, about which Josephus, among others, says in *The Jewish War* book 5, chapter 4 (27): The spring of Jericho permeates a plain 70 stadia long and 20 wide. It nurtures the best and densest parks, and various kinds of irrigated palm trees, differing in both flavor and name. The fattest of these, when pressed by the heels, emit a great deal of honey, not much inferior to other honey, though that region is also a breeder of bees. It also produces balsam <note>original: "opobalsamum"</note>, which is the most precious fruit of those that are there, and cypress, and myrobalan; so that he who calls that region divine would not be in error. r) Judges 1:16; 3:13; 2 Chronicles 28:15. s) Genesis 19:22.
* **v. 4.** t) Genesis 12:7, etc. u) Chapter 1:37.
* **v. 5.** x) Thus he died there being 120 years old. y) Compare notes on chapter 1:3. z) Joshua 1:2, 7, 13; Psalm 18:1. a) As he had said in chapter 17:11.
* **v. 6.** a) And he buried him. See notes on verse 1. He [God] saw to it that he was buried without the work of men. Le Clerc <note>original: "Clericus"</note>. b) In the valley; Numbers 21:20; Jude verse 9. Josephus in *Antiquities* book 4, near the end: When, after mutual embraces, he had said farewell to Eleazar and Joshua, and while he was still speaking with them, he was suddenly surrounded by a cloud and snatched into a certain valley, and became invisible. c) Chapter 3:29. d) Lest, for example, people should go to his monument to worship. Le Clerc. e) It does not say "his sepulcher" but "his burial," i.e., the manner in which he was buried; whether Moses was left there under the earth, or whether he was truly transferred from there to another place. So says Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and commentator</note>, in a pointless distinction.

<note>This section of the Bible, the "Former Prophets," consists of historical narratives that the Jewish tradition views as being written with prophetic inspiration. They chronicle the history of Israel from the crossing of the Jordan River under Joshua’s leadership to the eventual exile to Babylon in the Book of Kings.</note>

# THE BOOK OF JOSHUA
### In Hebrew: *Yehoshua*

->This book describes the introduction of the Israelites into the land of Canaan: its occupation, then its distribution; furthermore, the dismissal of the auxiliary tribes, and finally Joshua's last speech and his final days. It contains a history of seventeen years, which, although nowhere expressly determined, are nevertheless well-gathered by Lightfoot in his *Chronotaxi* <note>A chronological arrangement of Scripture</note> on this passage from the years of the Judges and Kings, to complete those 480 years mentioned in 1 Kings 6:1.<-

But others have the *Munach* accent instead of *Merca*. **המה** <note>they</note> instead of this, some have **הם** in 1, 3, 5, and in the margin of 6, 9. **להם** <note>to them</note> instead of this, some read **לכם** <note>to you</note> in 3, 12, 2, 5, and in the margin of 6, 9; contrary to the Masorah in this place and Numbers 11:21. **אתה** <note>you</note> deficient in 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 19, and in the margin of 6, 9. **ויענו** <note>and they answered</note> thus with a *Zakef-Katan* and an anomalous *Metheg* in all, except 3, which has a *Mercha*: which was also in 5. **כל** <note>all</note> with the prefix "and" in 3, 2, and in the margin of 6, 9. **וְאל** <note>and to</note> with a *Tsere* in 2, 3. **ככל־אשר** <note>according to all that</note> thus in 3 and in the margin of 6, 9. **דבריך** <note>your words</note> instead of **את דבריך** they have **את דבריך** in 1, 3 and the margin of 2.
**CHAPTER II, v. 1.** **חרש** <note>secretly</note> with a *Sin* in 5, 17, and the margin of 6; but doubtfully with a double point. **ירחו** <note>Jericho</note> written deficiently in 2, 27, and "Ber." Hebrew and **v. 3. בית** <note>house</note> with a *Munach* in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 20, 21. **v. 5. ולא** <note>and not</note> with the prefix "and" in 3, 1, 2, and 5.
</note>

**Left Column**

<margin>
g) under the stalks of flax or wood. It is doubtful what this refers to. The Greek Septuagint <note>original: "ἐν τῇ λινοκαλάμη"</note> says "under the flax-stalk," referring to flax from which the fiber has not yet been separated from its stalk—that is, the bark and husks have not yet been stripped away. Others interpret this similarly but with a reversed construction. Thus the Syriac: "the stalks of flax." The Targum of Jonathan: "bundles of flax." But the Arabic: "among the wood of the cotton plant." To Schmid, these are called "wood of flax" to distinguish a certain wood similar to flax that was used for fuel and kept for that purpose. However, it does not seem absurd to Masius if we consider it to mean "wood-flax," also known as cotton <note>original: "Xylinum"</note>, of which Pliny writes in his Natural History, book 19, chapter 1.
</margin>

* v. 7. *the pursuers* written in full in manuscripts 5, 6, 9, 10, 12, 14, 16, 20.
* v. 10. *how* [et] with the Tileschak accent in 1, 2, 5... and others... following Masoretic traditions.
* v. 13. *and my sisters* thus in 1, at the end of the "Kri" or "Ctiv" <note>Technical terms for "what is read" versus "what is written" in the Hebrew tradition</note>; also in 3, 5.

* v. 14. *the men* with the Sakeph-katon accent in 6, 9... others report the Rehia accent from different books in the margin.
* v. 15. *and in the wall* written in full in nearly all listed manuscripts (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, etc.).
* v. 16. *until* [ad] with a Makkaph in 2; also in 5. *return* [shuv] written in full in 1, 3, 6, 9... against the Masorah.

* v. 17. & 19. *guiltless* written in full in 3; also in 2, 5 and the margins of 6, 9, though both cases are against the Masorah and M. I.
* v. 19. *and it shall be* with the Gaia accent required by the Erfurt Masorah; with a Makkaph and Kametz-Chatuph in 1, 2, 3. *on his head* with the Darga accent in 7, 8, 10... and others.

### CHAPTER 2 & 3. JOSHUA II, III

<margin>
**19.** u) Compare Deuteronomy 4:42. 
u) Compare Matthew 27:25 <note>original: "His blood be on us and on our children"</note>.

</margin>

And it shall be, that whosoever shall go out of the doors of thy house into the street, his blood shall be upon his head, and we will be guiltless: and whosoever shall be with thee in the house, his blood shall be on our head, if any hand be upon him.

**v. 20.** y) This business of ours. Verse 14. 
z) See verse 17.
</margin>

c) See verse 18.

<margin>
**v. 22.** d) They were sent out on the sixth day of the month of Nisan, and they escaped from Jericho that night. On the seventh day they stayed in the mountains; on the eighth they returned to the camp. These three days are counted in exactly the same way as the three days of the burial of our Savior. (John Lightfoot <note>A 17th-century English Hebraist</note>).
</margin>

And they went, and came unto the mountain, and abode there three days, until the pursuers were returned: and the pursuers sought them throughout all the way, but found them not.

<margin>
**v. 23.** e) Which had happened to them. Exodus 18:8.
</margin>

So the two men returned, and descended from the mountain, and passed over, and came to Joshua the son of Nun, and told him all things that befell them:

<margin>
**v. 24.** f) Schmid: "Certainly he has given." 1 Samuel 10:19. Others understand it as "let us go, because..." 
g) He has given it, provided we take hold of it. (Schmid).

**Textual Notes:**

\* **v. 4.** A leading space is found in manuscripts 7, 8, 10, 17, 18, and the Berlin manuscript; the rest omit it.

\* **v. 5.** Manuscript *ab* adds "the Lord" at the beginning, and the word "children" from chapter 3. "Covenant" — other books do not have this word in the margin.

\* **v. 6.** Manuscripts 6, 9, 10, 13, 19, 20 make the text longer with "tomorrow to their fathers, saying." Our reading is noted in the margin of 6 and 9 from other codices.

\* **v. 7.** "The Jordan" with the *Rebhia* accent, preceded by the servant accent *Munach* in manuscript 2. In "when he passed over," the *Ayin* is written with *Qamets* and *Metheg* in 1 and 2, and corrected in 5. Several books in the Erfurt Masorah have the same, though a certain corrected copy lacks the *Metheg*. <note>Hebrew note: "This is how it is in most, but in one precise [manuscript] it was pointed 'be-av-ro' [without Metheg]: thus it is finished in the manuscript."</note>

\* **v. 8.** "And they lifted up" with the *Tlisha Qetana* accent.

\* **v. 13.** "Jericho" written deficiently <note>spelled without the final 'vav'</note> in 17 and Berlin.

**v. 1.** Circumcise again. Compare Psalm 71:20. This foreshadows that we cannot enter or occupy the land of eternal happiness unless we are circumcised, that is, entirely sanctified. We are sanctified, however, through JESUS Christ our Lord. — Brentius. <note>Johannes Brentius, 16th-century Reformer.</note> **e)** a second time, or again, namely by a solemn and general circumcision of the whole people before the Passover (verse 10), as had been done before the departure from Egypt. Verse 5, compared with Exodus 12:44, 48. Just as God held the Egyptians in three days of darkness so they could not move from their place, so now He strikes the Canaanites with terror so they do not dare move to harm the people while they are incapacitated by pain. Circumcision also seals the deed to the promised land of Canaan; therefore, as soon as they set foot in it, they had to be circumcised. The 11th, 12th, and 13th days of the month of Nisan were spent on this task; on the 14th day they celebrated the Passover; and thus they enjoyed both of their sacraments. Exactly 40 years had now passed since the exit from Egypt. — Lightfoot, *Chronot*. <note>John Lightfoot, 17th-century Hebraist.</note>

**CHAPTER VII, v. 1. m)** But they transgressed; knowing the will of the Lord, they nevertheless sinned. 1 Chronicles 2:7. **n)** Specifically, according to Schmid, Achan committed the act of theft itself, while the rest were guilty through negligence and failure of duty; compare v. 11. **o)** A sin against conscience. Cf. Leviticus 5:15, 20; Numbers 5:12. **p)** v. 11, 12; cf. Deuteronomy 13:18. Additionally, [in Greek]: "or one [who] abstained from the devoted thing." Compare Acts 5:2–3, Titus 2:10. **q)** For he subtracted [from the total], against the express command of God. Chapter 6:18, 19.

**v. 17** "who is with her" [Hebrew: *asher itah*] has a *Makkef* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in manuscripts 1 and 11, but manuscript 2 omits it. The word "she hid" [Hebrew: *hechbi'atah*] has a *Pataḥ* vowel sign in manuscript 2 according to its Masorah and the Erfurt manuscript, as required by the *M.I.* [Minchat Shai] which also cites the Masorah. **v. 18** "the devoted thing" [Hebrew: *ha-cherem*] has a *Segol* vowel sign under the letter Chet in manuscript 3 according to its Masorah and the Erfurt manuscript; the same should be observed in chapter 7:1 in the word "in the devoted thing" [Hebrew: *ba-cherem*]. **v. 20** "shofars" [Hebrew: *shofrot*] is written defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> in manuscripts 1 and 3 according to Masorah 1 and 2 and Erfurt, though a more recent hand in manuscript A added it, requiring the full spelling. "The city" [Hebrew: *et ha-ir*] appears this way with the particle *et* in the margin of manuscript 2, but in the main text, it omits the *et*. **v. 23** "and they came" [Hebrew: *vaya-bo'u*] appears with an irregular *Gerashim* accent in manuscripts 6, 9, 11, etc. "And they brought out" [Hebrew: *vaya-tsi'u*] is written defectively in manuscripts 1 and 5, and corrected in 3 according to the printed Masorah on Numbers 15:36. **v. 24** "And all" [Hebrew: *v'chol*]—manuscript 2 has "And [the particle] all" [Hebrew: *v'et-kol*] instead. **v. 25** "Joshua" [Hebrew: *Yehoshua*] is written defectively <note>missing a letter</note> in manuscript 17 and the Berlin manuscript here and in verse 26.

* v. 11. **The valley**: spelled with an Aleph at the end? So in manuscript 5, contrary to the <term>Masora</term> 1 and the edition at this place, and the printed version at Deuteronomy 34:6.
* v. 12. **And they encamped**: thus punctuated in manuscripts 1 and 5. **Them**: written "full" <note>original: plene — meaning with helper vowels</note> in 17, 18, 22, the Berlin edition, and in the margins of 1, 2, 5, 6, 9. But almost all others are "defective" <note>original: defect. — missing helper vowels</note> except the Masora at chapter 5:7. **Between**: with a *Merca* accent in 1, 3, 6, 9, 14, 20, contrary to the Masora at Exodus 21:25. **Bethel**: thus the *Eastern* tradition <note>original: Orientales — the Babylonian manuscript tradition</note> reads, but in the text they write **Beth-Aven**, which the Masora follows. **To the city**: thus written and read in the text of 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 14, 20, 22. In fact, manuscript 22 adds the note <gloss>written/read</gloss> contrary to the Erfurt Masora, although a later hand wrote: *The Easterns read and write* **To Ai**.
* v. 13. **All of**: thus the Eastern tradition reads, but in the text they write **All the** in manuscript 1 with the *Qere* <note>The tradition of how the word is read aloud versus written</note> of verse 26. But the Easterns write and read it twice in this verse. **And he went**: instead of this, the margin of manuscript 9 and manuscript 5 have **And he stayed the night** (<gloss>pernoctavit</gloss>).
* v. 18. **The city**: Manuscript 2 has **Ai**.
* v. 19. **As he stretched out**: with the prefix "K" in manuscript 5 and the margin of 6. **And they set on fire**: thus with the *Munach* accent in 1 and 2, but the rest have it with *Metheg*.
* v. 22. **To them**: Manuscript 5 and the margins of 2, 6, and 9 have an alternative.

**v. 27.** **They took for themselves** [bizu] with a *Chateph-patach* vowel in manuscripts 5, 6, 9, 14, 20, and 22. Instead of **Israel**, manuscripts 3 and others write **The children of Israel**, as do the printed edition 1, 2, and 5; this is also noted in the margin of 6 and 9. **v. 28.** **Heap** [tel]: the letter Tau is without a *Dagesh* [dot] in 6, 9, 10, 14, 20; and with an explicit **Raphe** [bar above] in 1. However, 9 has a *Dagesh* in the margin from other books. **v. 29.** **And as it came** [ukeboa] is spelled defectively in 2 and 5, according to the Erfurt Masorah on this passage, but against the printed Masorah here and in Deuteronomy 23:11. **And they took down** [wayuridu]: the letter *yod* is missing in 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 12, 14, 15, 20, 21; however, it is spelled fully in the margin of 6 and 9. **v. 32.** **The [sign of the accusative]** [et] with a *Segol* and *Maqqeph* in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 20, and edition 5; but 6 and 9 have a *Rebia* with a *Tsere* in the margin. **v. 33.** **And its officers** [weshoteraw]: manuscript 2 writes **And his officer** with a singular suffix. **Standing** [omedim] with an added *Pasek* mark in 6, 9, 11, 12, 16, 20, 21, 22. **Ebal**: the letter *Zain* <note>Translator's note: Likely a typo in the source Latin referring to the Hebrew letter in the context of vocalization</note> without a *Dagesh* in 1, 5, 10, 13, 19, and with a *Raphe* placed over it in 3. **v. 34.** **The Law**: for this, others read **Moses** in the margin of 6 and 9. **v. 35.** **And the little ones** [wehataph] with a *Qamets* vowel in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 14, 20.

**8** And they said to Joshua, "We are your servants." And Joshua said to them, "Who are you, and where do you come from?"

**9** And they said to him, "Your servants have come from a very distant land because of the name of the Lord your God; for we have heard the report of Him, and all that He did in Egypt,

**10** And all that He did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan—to Sihon king of Heshbon, and to Og king of Bashan, who was in Ashtaroth.

**11** Therefore our elders and all the inhabitants of our land spoke to us, saying, 'Take provisions in your hand for the journey, and go to meet them, and say to them: We are your servants; and now, make a covenant with us.'

**12** This bread of ours was hot when we took it as provision from our houses on the day we came out to go to you; but now, look, it is dry and crumbly.

**13** And these wineskins, which we filled when they were new, look, they are burst; and these our garments and our sandals are worn out from the very long journey."

**14** And the men took of their provisions, but they did not ask the mouth of the Lord.

**15** And Joshua made peace with them, and made a covenant with them to let them live; and the leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them.

**16** And it came to pass at the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, that they heard that they were their neighbors and lived in their midst.

**17** And the children of Israel traveled—

<margin>
**verse 13. (c)** verse 4.
**verse 14. (k)** The leading men therefore took from their provisions. There is a kind of opposition here: they took the Gibeonites' bread into their hands and trusted their own eyes, rather than questioning the mouth or oracle of the Lord. <note>From the commentator Andreas Masius</note>. **(l)** Genesis 24:57; Ephesians 30:2. **(m)** "with too much trust," see chapter 7:10.
**verse 15. (n)** chapter 11:19. **(o)** He accepted them into surrender, so that they might be subjects to the Israelites. See 1 Kings 9:23. <note>Grotius</note>. **(p)** verse 18, 19; 2 Samuel 21:2. For they thought they would more safely occupy the other kingdoms of the land of Canaan if they had peace with the neighboring regions. <note>Brenz</note>.
**verse 16. (q)** see verse 7.
**verse 17. (r)** Schmidt: "For when they set out."
