*   v. 4. **ויצטירו** <note>original Hebrew: "And they disguised themselves"</note> Written this way with a *Daleth* (which is also marked with a *rafe*). It means they equipped themselves with provisions.
*   v. 5. **ומטלאות** <note>original Hebrew: "And patched"</note> Written in full in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12, 14, 19, 20, 21. **יבש היה** <note>original Hebrew: "It was dry"</note> thus in 3, 5. v. 6. **הגלגלה** <note>original Hebrew: "To Gilgal"</note> with the added *He* in 1; also in 2, 3, and later in 5. **מארץ** <note>original Hebrew: "From a land"</note> 10. **רחוקה מאד** <note>original Hebrew: "Very distant"</note> the accent varies in 3, with a <term>merca</term> <note>a Hebrew musical/grammatical accent</note> added from verse 9.
*   v. 8. **ויאמר אליהם יהושע** <note>original Hebrew: "And Joshua said to them"</note> thus in 3. v. 10. **בעשתרות** <note>original Hebrew: "In Ashtaroth"</note> spelled defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> in all, except 2, 3, 17, 18, 22, Berlin, and in the margins of 6, 9. v. 11. **זקינינו** <note>original Hebrew: "Our elders"</note> The unnecessary *Iod* after the *Kaph* is omitted in 3, 5, and in the margins of 6, 9; thus amended in the text of 2, against the *Minchat Shai*. v. 13. **אשר** <note>original Hebrew: "Which"</note> with a <term>makkaph</term> <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in 1, 2, 3, and later in 5. v. 16. **קרובים** <note>original Hebrew: "Near"</note> spelled fully with a *Vav* in 2, 3, and in the margins of 6, 9.

**Textual variants and Masoretic notes:**
**v. 20.** The word *otam* (them) is written in the "defective" form here and in v. 26 in several manuscripts. **v. 21.** The word *vayihyu* (and they were) contains a specific musical accent (Tlisha gedolah). **v. 22.** The word *alehem* (to them) is missing in some versions. **v. 24.** There is a debate about the vowel for *vanna'aseh* (and we did), whether it should be a Segol or a Tsere according to the Masorah of Erfurt. **v. 25.** The word *hinnennu* (here we are) has a double-emphasis mark (Dagesh) in the letter Nun in certain codices.

<note>Critical footnotes regarding Hebrew orthography and Masoretic notes</note>

v. 16. **בְּמַקֵּדָה** (at Makkedah): The letter Beth has a short 'a' sound (patach), followed by a doubling dot (Dagesh); this is found in manuscripts 6 and 9 in the margin. v. 17. **וַיֻּגַּד לִיהוֹשֻׁעַ** (and it was told to Joshua): So in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 12, 14, 16, 19, 20, 21, 22. **בַּמְּעָרָה** (in the cave): The Mem is without a doubling dot (Dagesh) in 1, 2, 8. v. 20. **וַיְהִי** (And it happened): With a specific musical accent (Tishagda) in 6, 9, 20. **לְהַכּוֹתָם** (to strike them): Written "full" (with extra vowel letters) in 1, 5, and in the margin of 6 and 9, according to the Masorah for Numbers 15:36; all others also have it full. **גְּדֹלָה** (great): Missing a vowel letter (defective) in 7, 8, 11, 13, 15, 17, 18, and the Berlin manuscript. v. 23. **וַיֹּצִיאוּ** (and they brought out): manuscript 10 is defective; so are 1, 2, and Berlin. v. 24. **וַיִּקְרְבוּ** (and they came near): All use a specific accent (Zakeph-katon) on this single word. **מֶלֶךְ עֶגְלֹון** (king of Eglon): Linked with a hyphen (Makkaph) in 10, 15, 17, 18. Doubling dot (Dagesh) in 17, 18, 21, and Berlin. v. 26. **וַיְמִיתֵם** (and he killed them): This is how the Eastern (Babylonian) tradition reads it, but in the text they write **וַיַּמִיתוּם**. v. 25. **תֵּחָתּוּ** (be dismayed): The second Tau is without a doubling dot. **וַיִּקְרְבוּ** (and they came near): The Tau has a Dagesh in 1, 7, 8, 17, and Berlin. v. 27. **וַיַּשְׁלִכֻם** (and they threw them): defective in 1, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, 21, 22. **וַיָּשִׂימוּ** (and they placed): written "full" in 3, 6, 9, 12, 20; also in 1 and 5, though this goes against the Masorah here and in Genesis 43:32.

* v. 28. **its king** <note>original Hebrew: מַלְכָּהּ</note> So in manuscripts 1, 3, 5, and in the margin of 6, 9. **utterly destroyed** <note>original Hebrew: הֶחֱרִם</note> written fully in 2; and thus the margin of 6, 9 has it, against the Masorah. Elsewhere, for the infinitive **to utterly destroy** <note>original Hebrew: הַחֲרֵם</note>, manuscript 3 reads it as such. **them** <note>original Hebrew: אוֹתָם</note>; for this, manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 5 have **it** <note>original Hebrew: אוֹתָהּ</note>, and so in the margin of 6, 9. **Jericho** <note>original Hebrew: יְרִיחוֹ</note> is defective in 17 and Ber. here and in verse 30; likewise in several other chapters, but everywhere against the Masorah at Joshua 16:1. * v. 29. **with him** <note>original Hebrew: עִמּוֹ</note>; for this, manuscript 2 reads **he went up** <note>original Hebrew: עָלָה</note>. * v. 30. **he left no** <note>original Hebrew: לֹא הִשְׁאִיר</note>; omitting the particle **in it** <note>original Hebrew: בָּהּ</note> are manuscripts 1, 3, 5, against the Erfurt Masorah and printed editions. * v. 33. **to help** <note>original Hebrew: לַעְזֹר</note>; the letter Ain has a simple Sheva without a preceding Metheg in 2, 6, 9-15, 20, 21. * v. 35. **and** <note>original Hebrew: וְאֵת</note> with a Maqqeph and Segol in 1, 2, 5, and in the margin of 6, 9. * v. 37. **and they struck it** <note>original Hebrew: וַיַּכּוּהָ</note> with a Munach accent instead of Maqqeph and Metheg in 2, 3, 5, 21. * v. 39. **and he took it** <note>original Hebrew: וַיִּלְכְּדָהּ</note>; the plural **and they took it** <note>original Hebrew: וַיִּלְכְּדוּהָ</note> with a Geresh accent is in manuscript 3. **its king** <note>original Hebrew: אֶת מַלְכָּהּ</note> without the prefix "and" in 2 and 5.

->**CRITICAL APPARATUS**<-
**v. 42.** The Makkaph <note>A Hebrew hyphen-like mark.</note> is present. But Rebia is in verse 3. He amended **fought** (*nilcham*) with a Patach vowel. **Chapter 11, v. 1.** Instead of **Shimron**, some read **Shimran**. **v. 2. From the north** (*mitzephon*), the letter Tsade has a Qamets vowel in some manuscripts, and so it is held in the margin. Contrary to the Masoretic text, the Nun in **Chinneroth** is doubled with a Dagesh in many editions, against the Erfurt Masorah on chapter 12:3. **v. 4. Many** (*rav*) appears with a Qamets in several manuscripts. Others read it with a Patach. Finally, instead of **many** (*rav*), some read **until** (*ad*) in the margin. **v. 5. Met together** (*vayivva'adu*) has a Rebia accent. **v. 6.** Makkaphs are present in various manuscripts. **Their horses** (*suseyhem*) appears with a Pashta accent. **v. 8. The LORD** (*YHWH*) is marked with a Pesiq. In **Mizpeh**, the letter Pe is vocalized with a Qamets.

# CHAPTER 11. JOSHUA 11.

**v. 19. g)** refers to a city that behaved peacefully and offered peace. Compare Chapter 10, verse 4. This means one which had believed the word of the Lord. <note>original: "quae credidisset verbo Domini"</note> **Brentius.** <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a German Reformer and theologian.</note> **h)** See Numbers 32:12. **i)** Chapter 9:15, 18.

**v. 20. k)** **Schmidt** <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian and Hebraist.</note>: "so that they might watch their own hearts." See notes on Exodus 4:21; Joshua 17:13; 9:12. For this people, from the very origin of their race and from their first patriarchs Ham and Canaan, had lived impiously, grown up in impiety, and now grew old in it. God therefore permits, as a punishment for their wickedness, that they should be hardened against Israel and be slaughtered while resisting. **CHAPTER XII, v. 1. b)** Slain by Moses (v. 1–6) and by Joshua (v. 7 and following). **c)** This chapter is a recapitulation <note>original: "ανακεφαלאίωσις" — a rhetorical summary</note> and a summary of all those victories that were previously described. This is done so that by commemorating them, first, the unbelief of those who perished in the desert might be rebuked; and second, that faith in the truth of God might be confirmed. To be sure, such a physical land of Canaan and such military victories are not promised to us today, but by this example God declared that nothing is more certain than the word of His promises. **Brentius.** <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a German Lutheran reformer.</note> **d)** Compare verse 7 and the note on Deuteronomy 1:1. **e)** Numbers 21:13; Deuteronomy 2:24; Judges 11:13, 18. **f)** Verse 5; Chapter 11:3; Chapter 13:5. **g)** Deuteronomy 1:1.

**v. 23.** *According to their divisions* <note>original: "כְּמַחְלְקֹתָם"</note> - Written with the prefix *Beth* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 11, 13, 20. Contrary to the Erfurt Masora. <note>The Masora refers to the traditional system of notes on the biblical text to ensure its accurate transmission.</note> Compare chapter 12, verse 7.

**CHAPTER XII, v. 1.** *And as far as* <note>original: "וְעַד"</note> - with the prefix *Vav* in manuscripts 1, 2, 5. — **v. 2.** *The one dwelling* <note>original: "הַיּוֹשֵׁב"</note> - written in full in manuscripts 1, 2, 22, according to the Erfurt Masora and printed editions at chapter 16, 10. **v. 3.** *Sea* and *Sea* <note>original: "יָם & יָם"</note> - both with the vowel *Patach* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and in the margin of 5 and 9. *Chinnereth* <note>original: "כִּנְרוֹת"</note> is required by the Erfurt Masora, but the letter *Nun* has a *Dagesh* <note>a grammatical dot emphasizing the letter</note> in manuscripts 6, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 18, 20, 22. *Beth-jeshimoth* <note>original: "הַיְשִׁמוֹת"</note> written in full in 1, 3, 9, 14, 20, 22; written deficiently in 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 19, 21. But the Masora for this place and Numbers 33:49 disagrees with both. **v. 4.** *And in Edrei* <note>original: "וּבְאֶדְרֶעִי"</note> - the letter *Resch* has the vowel *Tsere* in manuscripts 1 and 3. **v. 5.** *The border of Sihon the king* <note>original: "גְּבוּל סִיחוֹן מֶלֶךְ"</note> - thus in 1 and corrected in 5. **v. 6.** *Possession* <note>original: "יְרֻשָּׁה"</note> - the letter *Schin* is without a *Dagesh* in manuscripts 3, 6, 9, 20, 22. **v. 7.** *The one going up* <note>original: "הָעֹלֶה"</note> - the Erfurt Masora requires the full spelling here and at chapter 11:17, but all our manuscripts disagree. *According to their divisions* - with the prefix *Beth* in 3, 6, 9, 14, 20, 5; against the Masora.

<note>Footnotes/Critical Apparatus</note>

**v. 20.** Meron: written thus with a <term>silent Aleph</term> <note>original: "Aleph otioso" — a letter that is written but not pronounced</note> in most of our copies, as in the word "fear ye," etc. But written with a <term>silent Vav</term> <note>original: "Vau otioso"</note> according to the form of "Samuel" in 2, 22. Hartmann. Indeed, they write Meron with a <term>double Cholem</term> <note>a vowel mark representing the "o" sound</note> in 5, 11, 14; and finally, manuscript 3 omits Meron entirely, contrary to the Masorah <note>The authoritative tradition of the Hebrew text</note> in this place. **v. 21.** Taanach: with a <term>Qamets vowel on the letter Nun</term> in manuscripts 2, 3, 6, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 20, 21, 22. **v. 23.** "For the region": plural with a <term>Cholem</term>, and indeed written defectively <note>without the letter Vav</note> in manuscript 1. The Erfurt Masorah requires this, though it is written fully with a Vav in manuscript 3. **v. 24.** Tirzah, one. **CHAPTER XIII, v. 1.** "You have grown old": without the <term>additional He</term> <note>original: "He paragogico" — a suffix added for emphasis or style</note> in manuscript 3 and the Oriental tradition; against Masorah 1 and the printed editions. "You have come": with the <term>additional He</term> in manuscripts 1, 2, and 5.

# JOSHUA CHAPTER 13 יג

<margin>
m) This had been assigned to the half-tribe of Manasseh in verse 11, but the Israelites were unwilling to expel its inhabitants as noted in verse 13. Therefore, even in the time of David, it had its own King, whose daughter David married (see 2 Samuel 3:3 and the note on Joshua 12:5).

n) verse 3. 1 Chronicles 13:15. The Nile is so called [Shihor] because of its blackness; in Greek, *melas*, which means "black," because it carries water made turbid by silt from the fields of Ethiopia. See Job Ludolf’s *History of Ethiopia*, Book 1, chapter 8, number 5. It is clear this refers to the Nile from Jeremiah 2:18, for its relationship to Egypt is the same as the Euphrates to Assyria. It is divided into such various streams that solutions to difficulties flow from them. Gousset <note>Jacques Gousset (1635–1704), a French Hebraist.</note> page 849. Another Shihor is found in the tribe of Asher, Joshua 19:26.

o) verse 3. These are cities of the Philistines in the tribe of Judah (chapter 15:45, Judges 1:18, 1 Samuel 5:10), where Baal-Zebub was worshiped (2 Kings 1:2, 3, 6). Yet they were to be made for Christ according to Zechariah 9:7.

q) Satraps or Princes (Judges 3:3). 
r) Chapter 10:41. 
s) Judges 1:18. 
t) Chapter 11:22.

**Textual Notes:**
**verse 3.** * "The Ashkelonite" [Ha-Ashkeloni] contains an Aleph with a Patach vowel in codex 3. "And the Gittite" [Ve-ha-Gitti] includes the prefix in codices 6, 9, in the margin, and thus in the text of 3 and 1, 2, 5. **verse 4.** "As far as Aphek" [Ve-ad-Aphekah]. **verse 4.** * In codices 6, 9 in the margin, "Aphekah" is accented on the last syllable [milra]. **verses 20, 23.** * "Mountain" [Har]. **verse 5.** * marked by a Munach accent in 1, 2, 3. **verse 10.** "Sihon": the syllable "chon" is spelled defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> in codices 3, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 19. **verse 12.** "Until the border" [Ad gevul], so in codices 6, 9, 12, 16, 20, 21, 22, 23. "Children" [Bnei] with a Mercha accent in 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 15, 19. **verse 11.** "And the border" [U-gevul] with a Pfik-munach accent in 6, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 20, 21, 22, 23. **verse 13.** "And Maachath" [U-Maachat]: the letter Caph has a Patach-atnum in codex 1 and in the margin of 6 and 9. **verse 14.** "Moses did not give" [Lo natan Moshe]: so it is read with the name "Moses" added in the margin. **verse 15.** "To their families" [Le-mishpechotam] spelled defectively in 1, 3, 5, 12 and in the margin of 6 and 9. **verse 16.** "Bank of the river" [Sfat-nachal], so in 6, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 20, 21, 22. **verse 17.** "Dibon": thus the "bon" is defective in 2, 5, 6, 9, 20, 21, 22 according to the Erfurt Masorah. **verse 18.** "And Jahazah" [Ve-yahzah] is accented on the last syllable [milra] in 1, 2, 5. The letter Iod has a Kamets vowel in 6, 9, 14, 20. The letter He has a Chateph-patach in 1, 3, 7, 8, 10, 13, 19, 5. **verse 20.** "And the slopes" [Ve-ashdot] is spelled defectively in codex 1 according to its Masorah and the Erfurt Masorah.

**Textual Notes:**
Verse 21: *Kingdoms* <note>original: "mamlĕkôt"</note> written with a Cholem in the plural in manuscripts 3, 6, 9, 20, contrary to the Great Masora <note>The marginal notes in the Hebrew Bible that safeguard the text.</note>. Verse 23: *Border* <note>original: "ugĕbul"</note> with a Kibbutz vowel. Verse 26: The Masora notes this verse as the "half of the book" in manuscript 2 and the Erfurt manuscript. Verse 27: *Rest* <note>original: "yeter"</note> with a Mahpach accent. *Kingdoms* <note>original: "mamlĕkût"</note> with a Zakef Katon accent to avoid an anomaly in the order of accents, though it makes the sense very awkward. Verse 29: with a Patach vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 3 and the margin of 6, 9. *And their villages* <note>original: "wĕḥaṣrêhem"</note> with a feminine suffix in 6, 9, against the Masora and the Erfurt manuscript. Verse 30: *Their border* <note>original: "gĕbûlām"</note>—the editor of the Masora says he saw the word "all" <note>Hebrew: "kol"</note> before this in an old codex. Verse 31: *And all* <note>original: "wĕkol"</note> with a prefix in 1 and 2. CHAPTER 14, Verse 3: Manuscripts 6, 9, 16, 20 add the word "to her" after "Moses."

Chapter XV, verse 1.
f) To Judah, the royal tribe, the first seat was attributed. (Lightfoot). It might seem that this chapter, and others written about the lots of the tribes of Israel, are useless for us to read. But nothing in Scripture is so lowly or irrelevant that it does not bring its own utility with it. And first, indeed, the description of the lots was necessary for the Israelites, so that they might know what the boundary of each tribe was. Second, it is useful to those who read the Scripture. For in the Prophets and other books of Scripture, mention of these places is made very often. In this chapter, therefore, it is found where their location is, and in which tribe, etc. (Brentius). Various things are also set before the eyes parabolically. (Cocceius).

\* verse 1. "And it was": written fully in copies 1, 3, and above in 5. \* verse 2. "And it was": with a Patach vowel in 1, 2, and in the margin of 6, 9. \* verse 3. "Zin": [The letter] Nun without a Dagesh in 2, 5, 6, 7, 9, 13, 15, 16, 19, and with the Raphe mark placed above in 3. \* verse 4. "Azmon": written defectively in 1, 3, according to the Masorah 1, but against the Erfurt copy. \* verse 5. "The sea": with a Patach in 1, 2, and with a Makkaph in 3. \* verse 6. "Bohan": with the letter Chet in 23 and in the margin of 6, 9. \* verse 7. "The Gilgal": with the Pasek-Munach accent in 1, 3, 6, 9, 20, 22, 23, so also in the Berith against Masorah Genesis 30:16. "Asher" [which] he took for "collected" and "v'alah" [and it went up] in 2, in the margin. \* verse 10. "And it circled": with Nishgadh erroneously in 3, 6, 15, 17, 23, and above in 5. "Chesalon": thus read in 1, 3. \* verse 11. "Timnah": in place of this has "Timnathah," thus in 5; but the Chaldee [Targum] in 1 reads "Timnah." \* verse 12. "Shikkeron": with the letter Beth in place of Caph in 2, 5. \* verse 13. "The Anak": the letter Nun with a Cholem in 2, and above in 5. \* verse 14. "Three": written defectively in 3, 10, 19, 20, so also in 1, 2, 5, against the Masorah.

<meta>Footnotes and Critical Apparatus</meta>

v. 47. **The border** <note>original Hebrew: "Ha-Gvul"</note>: in place of this, manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 write and read **The Great** <note>original Hebrew: "Ha-Gadol"</note>, against the Masoretic notes of Erfurt and M. 1. v. 48. **And Socoh**: The *Keri* reading omits the letter *Vav* in manuscripts 5, 6, 9, 20, 21, and 22. v. 50. **And Eshtemoh**: with the added *Keri* reading **And Eshtemoa** in 1, 2, 5 and the Erfurt Masorah. v. 51. **And Gilo**: thus the Eastern tradition reads, but in the text they write without the prefix *Vav*. **And Giloh** with the *Keri* **And Gilo** in 1 and the Erfurt Masorah. v. 52. **And Rumah**: The letter *Resh* has a *Patach* vowel in 1, 3, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 21, and 22. In 5, a *Resh* is used instead of a *Daleth* <note>changing the name to Dumah</note> in 1, 5, and 3. This was also the reading of the Latin Vulgate, the Syrian, the Greek in codices 11, 13, and 15, and the Chaldean in 11. v. 54. **And Humtah**: The letter *Mem* has a *Dagesh* <note>an emphasis dot</note> in 1, 2, and 5 according to the Erfurt Masorah. v. 55. **Maon**: The *Pasek* mark is omitted in 2, 3, and 5, against Masorah 1 and Erfurt. **And Juttah**: Thus the letter *Tet* is doubled by a *Dagesh* in 1, 2, 5, 10, 13, and 19 according to Masorah 1, 2, and Erfurt, just as in chapter 21:16 many codices double it; but others in this place do not have the *Dagesh*. v. 59. **And Ar**: defective spelling in 1 according to Masorah 1, 2, and Erfurt. **CHAPTER XVI, v. 3. And it went down**: accented on the penultimate syllable in 3, 6, 7, and 21. v. 7. **And it went down**: for this, other books read **And it passed over** in the margin of 2.

# JOSHUA. CHAPTERS 16, 17

<margin>
v. 10. u) chapter 13, 13.
f. 17, 13. Judges 1, 29.
It was shown above that God, though not all the peoples in Canaan were yet defeated, commanded Joshua to divide the land by lot. After the land was divided, Joshua died. Therefore, after the death of the Leader <note>referring to Joshua</note>, the Israelites soon sinned and forsook God, worshipping idols, as written in Judges chapters 1, 2, and 3. Thus, because of their impiety, the Israelites were unable to immediately cast out the remaining nations. And so, the remnants of these nations remained until the time of David. — Brentius <note>Johann Brenz, a 16th-century Protestant Reformer and commentator</note>.
x) v. 3. chapter 21, 21. y) chapter 4, 9. Indeed, until Solomon’s time, when they were cut off by Pharaoh (1 Kings 9, 16), an event which is added here in the Septuagint version <note>original Latin: "LXX. versione"</note>. z) that is, a working slave, serving in servile works. chapter 17, 13.
</margin>

...of Manasseh, all the cities and their villages. **17** And the lot fell to the tribe<sup>k</sup> of Manasseh<sup>a</sup>, for he was the firstborn of Joseph<sup>l</sup>: to Machir<sup>b</sup>, the firstborn of Manasseh, the father<sup>c</sup> of Gilead<sup>c</sup>, because he was a man of war<sup>l</sup>; therefore Gilead<sup>d</sup> and Bashan<sup>d</sup> were his. And there was a lot for the rest of the sons of Manasseh according to their families: for the sons of<sup>e</sup> Abiezer, the sons of Helek, the sons of Asriel, the sons of Shechem, the sons of Hepher, and the sons of Shemida; these were the male children of Manasseh son of Joseph<sup>f</sup> according to their families. But Zelophehad, son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, but only daughters; and these are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. And they came near<sup>g</sup> before Eleazar the priest, before Joshua son of Nun, and before the leaders, saying, "The Lord commanded Moses<sup>h</sup> to give us an inheritance among our brothers." Therefore, according to the word of the Lord, he gave them an inheritance among their father's brothers<sup>i</sup>. And ten portions<sup>k</sup> fell to Manasseh, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan which are across the Jordan. For the daughters of Manasseh<sup>l</sup> received an inheritance among his sons, and the land of Gilead belonged to the rest of the sons<sup>m</sup> of Manasseh. And the boundary of Manasseh<sup>n</sup> was from Asher to Michmethath<sup>o</sup>, which is before Shechem<sup>p</sup>; and the boundary went along to the right, to the inhabitants of En-tappuah. The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh<sup>q</sup>, but Tappuah on the border of Manasseh belonged to the sons of Ephraim. And the boundary went down to the Brook Kanah<sup>r</sup>; southward of the brook, these cities belonged to Ephraim among the cities of Manasseh; and the boundary of Manasseh was on the north side of the brook, and its limit was at the sea. Southward it was Ephraim's and northward it was Manasseh's, and the sea was its boundary<sup>s</sup>; and they reached to Asher on the north and to Issachar on the east. And Manasseh had<sup>t</sup> in Issachar and in Asher: Beth-shean and its towns, Ibleam and its towns<sup>u</sup>, the inhabitants of Dor<sup>x</sup> and its towns, the inhabitants of En-dor<sup>y</sup> and its towns, the inhabitants of Taanach<sup>z</sup> and its towns, and the inhabitants of Megiddo<sup>a</sup> and its towns—the three heights.

v. 2. *Manasseh*: With the *Merkha* accent in manuscripts 7, 8, 10, and 13, 19, but contrary to the Masorah on Genesis 30, 16. * v. 4. *The leaders*: written defectively in 8, 11, and in the margin of 6, 9. *By the hand of Moses*: 1, 2, and 5 read this previously; likewise 3. *verse 9. Shiloh: Some add a 'vav' at the end. verse 10. For "to the children" <note>Hebrew: libnei</note>, other codices write "before" <note>Hebrew: liphnei</note> in the margin. "According to their divisions" <note>bemachlekottam</note>: spelled with a Beth instead of a Caph in various manuscripts. verse 11. "And between the children": the order is reversed in some versions. verse 12. "Toward the wilderness": spelled with a Kamets vowel under the Beth in several codices, though the Masorah requires a Patach vowel here and in Isaiah 16:1. verse 13. "Beth": written with a connector mark <note>Makkaph</note> in most versions. verse 14. "To" <note>el</note>: some read as "upon" <note>al</note>. verse 16. "Mouth" <note>pi</note>: written with an additional 'he' in some margins. verse 17. "The Ascent": with a prefixed 'lamed'. "Bohan": spelled with a 'chet' instead of a 'he' in some margins. verse 19. "Endings": some read in the text without the 'yod'.*

1 The LORD also spake unto Joshua, saying,

3 That the slayer that killeth any person unawares and unwittingly may flee thither: and they shall be your refuge from the avenger of blood. 4 And when he that doth flee unto one of those cities shall stand at the entering of the gate of the city, and shall declare his cause in the ears of the elders of that city, they shall take him into the city unto them, and give him a place, that he may dwell among them. 5 And if the avenger of blood pursue after him, then they shall not deliver the slayer up into his hand; because he smote his neighbor unwittingly, and hated him not beforetime. 6 And he shall dwell in that city, until he stand before the congregation for judgment, and until the death of the high priest that shall be in those days: then shall the slayer return, and come...

*verse 39. b)* Even if in the recounting of the names of the places assigned to these tribes, Scripture seems to do nothing of worth for us; nevertheless, the enumeration was necessary for its own time, and the Holy Spirit has His own purpose in why He proposes these names for posterity to read. — The Holy Spirit lingers and halts, as it were, on each one, looking at us to warn us of the certainty, possibility, and ease of the fulfillment of God's promises. *etc. Brenz.* <note>Johannes Brenz, a 16th-century theologian</note>

* verse 10. **The Kohathite:** The letter Qoph is written with a reduced Kametz vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 20. <note>This refers to the specific Hebrew vowel pointing for "ha-Kehati"</note>

* verse 23. **And from the tribe:** With the Munach accent below in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5.

v. 31. <term>חֶלְקַת</term> <note>Helkath</note>. The letter Kaph is written with a Pattach vowel in various manuscripts (17, 18, 22). Regarding verses 36 and 37: We have judged that these two verses (which some have compressed into one) should be restored to the text, even though they are missing in some books. They are found in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9–16, 19–23, as well as the Venetian edition of Justinian, Ben Israel, the commentary of Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508) was a famous Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note>, and a Bible printed in Spain in 1508. However, Rabbi Kimchi in his commentary does not recognize them as genuine here because: (1) he saw them missing or marked as doubtful in corrected manuscripts; (2) Rabbi Hai, when asked about these cities, replied that if they aren't counted in Joshua, they are in Chronicles. The printed <term>Masora</term> <note>The Masora is a collection of traditional notes on the Hebrew text to ensure its accurate transmission.</note> adds another "weighty" argument: (3) the particle <term>אֶת</term> <note>"et" - a grammatical marker</note> appears 28 times in this chapter; if these verses were included, it would appear 30 times. Some editors follow these reasons. But others argue that Kimchi's proof is insufficient. Other manuscripts oppose his; and Rabbi Hai's testimony is conditional. The Masora, while noting the omission, is not so authoritative that we should follow it over stronger arguments, as Masoretic counts often contain errors. On the other hand, several reasons favor including these verses: (1) verse 7 explicitly states that cities were given by the Reubenites, which would be inconsistent if they weren't listed; (2) the total of 12 cities for the Merarites (v. 7 and 40) would be wrong, as only 8 would remain; (3) the grand total of 48 cities (v. 41) would be short by four; (4) nearly all ancient versions include them: the Greek Septuagint, the Latin Vulgate, the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, and Jerome. Even some Chaldee <note>Aramaic Targum</note> manuscripts include them.

CHAPTER XXII. v. 1. q) Then they called them, namely, when the war was finished and the neighbors were pacified. Whether the two and a half tribes returned home immediately after the land rested from war (which happened in the seventh year), or whether they remained until the land was divided and the people were settled in their places (which required a much longer time), it is not worth examining, because it cannot be defined. However, this chapter is placed in its proper and just position, because it was right that the entire history pertaining to the conquest and possession of the land be treated together before any other narrations or emerging cases might break it off. <note>Reference to John Lightfoot’s "Chronicle of the Times of the Old Testament."</note>
</margin>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion of the tribes' inheritance, moving into the dramatic confrontation in Joshua chapter 22. The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh have completed their military service in Canaan and are returning to their lands east of the Jordan River. Upon reaching the border, they build a massive altar, which is immediately misinterpreted by the western tribes as an act of apostasy or rebellion against the central sanctuary at Shiloh.</meta>

**Chapter 1, verse 1. a)** namely, that which follows. This connects with the book of Joshua. Compare 1 Samuel 12:7–8; Sirach 46:11; Acts 13:19–20; Hebrews 11:32. The sacred history is continued in this book, first for a certain and then for an uncertain period (chapters 17–21, which according to Lightfoot should be placed after chapter 2, verse 10) from the death of Joshua to the death of Samson, or to Eli the Priest, spanning three centuries and more, or according to Lightfoot's Chronology <note>original: "Chronotaxin"</note> for 299 years under the twelve Judges, including the years of Israel's oppression.

<meta>This page continues from the conclusion of Judges chapter 2, transitioning into the specific accounts of the individual Judges. It follows the theological framework established in the previous section: that God left certain nations in the land to test Israel's faithfulness and to teach new generations the art of war.</meta>

# JUDGES. CHAPTERS 2, 3.

<margin>
**verse 22. b)** Therefore He left <note>original Latin: "Reliquit ergo"</note> them (cf. chapter 3:1; 1 Kings 19:3). It was beneficial—not indeed due to any merit of the Israelites, but by God’s kindness—that some nations were left in Canaan. First, so that the land would not become uncultivated and full of serpents if all Canaanites were immediately destroyed (Deuteronomy 7:22). Second, so that the Israelites would have practice in fighting and resisting enemies (see Judges 3:2). Finally, this act foreshadows what happens in a person reborn through the Holy Spirit. Just as the Israelites leave some adversarial nations in Canaan for the exercise of war, whom they nevertheless make subjects for tribute; so the Holy Spirit, in regenerating a person, does not make them entirely holy all at once, but leaves remnants of the flesh, so that the person may have the exercise of fighting against the lusts of the flesh. Let us only take care that the flesh does not prevail, but becomes tributary, etc. See Brontius on Joshua chapter 16. Compare Galatians 5:16 and following.
</margin>

<margin>
**verse 3. a)** chapter 16:5; Joshua 13:3.
**p)** Exodus 15:14, 15.
**q)** ibid. 15.
</margin>

# CHAPTER 4. JUDGES

<margin>
Initially, Jael acted toward Sisera with sincerity and from the heart, without any fraud, pretense, or lie, though not without error and the sin committed against the Israelites when she received Sisera into her tent with the best of words and helped him for a time. Nor did God suggest or approve of that deception or lie to her. <note>Schmid refers to Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century theologian who argues Jael's initial hospitality was a mistake, but her later killing of Sisera was a divine "instinct."</note> Then, led by repentance and confirmed by divine instinct, she undertook and performed the praiseworthy act of slaughter. When God incited her to this, His instinct was most just, as it was through this that Jael was called back from an unjust peace and the receiving of Sisera to her duty, which she owed to God and the Israelite people. **Schmid.** **u)** with a thick and shaggy rug. <note>original Latin: *stragulo denso & villoso*</note> (i) a covering. <note>original Greek: *επιβολαιω*</note> **Tig.** <note>The Tigurina Bible, a 1543 Latin translation.</note> with a certain covering. Cf. Bochart's *Sacred Geography* p. 748.
</margin>
<margin>
Accent on the last syllable. <note>Hebrew: *Milra*</note>
</margin>
<margin>
Led by repentance and divine instinct.
</margin>
<margin>
Missing the letter Aleph. <note>Hebrew: *Chaser Aleph*</note>
</margin>

<margin>
*v. 12.* **s)** see verse 5.
*v. 13.* **f)** see verse 10. **g)** that is, scythed chariots. <note>original Latin: *falcatos*</note> chapter 1:19. For in earlier centuries the Medes, Syrians, Arabs, and all Asians used chariots in this way, just as the Cyrenaeans do now. Three hundred fighting chariots provide three hundred [drivers], but require one thousand two hundred horses. Cyrus abolished this method of driving chariots and instead equipped chariots better suited for war, with firm wheels so they would not be easily broken, and long axles so that everything carried would be less likely to overturn. He built a seat for the drivers like a tower out of firm wood. The height of these reached to the driver's elbows, so the horses could be guided by reins above the seats. He armed the drivers themselves entirely in breastplates, except for their eyes. Furthermore, he attached iron scythes two cubits long to the axles on each side of the wheels, and others below the axle facing the ground: as if they were to make an attack with these against opposing chariots. Thus **Xenophon** in *The Education of Cyrus*, Book VI. See also **Curtius**, Book 4, chapter 15. **h)** verse 2. 16. **i)** verse 7; chapter 5:21; 1 Kings 18:40.
*v. 14.* **k)** see verse 6. **l)** Exodus 23:23; chapter 32:34; 2 Samuel 5:24. **m)** verse 6. 10.
*v. 15.* **n)** He threw into confusion. <note>original Latin: *Conturbavit*</note> Joshua 10:10; Esther 9:24. **o)** Psalm 83:10.
*v. 16.* **p)** Genesis 14:14. **q)** verse 2. 13.
*v. 17.* **r)** verse 11. **s)** a peace of abstinence from offenses, not a sworn peace. We prefer to say it was done on Jabin's part according to the law of nations, by which it was fair that when there was a dispute over the ownership of lands, foreigners who possessed nothing in the lands should be spared, unless they voluntarily joined the warring parties. Since Heber did not do this, he remained at peace with Jabin. **Schmid.**
*v. 18.* **t)** Withdraw for now. <note>original Latin: *Secede modo*</note> Genesis 19:2.
</margin>

# JUDGES CHAPTER 5

<margin>
**Chapter V.** verse 1. <note>note n</note> verse 3. Exodus 15:1. He uses the feminine form because Deborah was the primary leader in this work, just as Miriam was in Numbers 12:1. **Masora Illustrata. <note>note o</note>** concerning the tribe of Naphtali, chapter 4:6. Hence they compare this to Genesis 49:21.

**verse 2. <note>note p</note>** for avenging <note>original Latin: *pro ulciscendo*</note> according to Chaldean usage. **Masora Illustrata.** That is, for the fact that the LORD (Chapter 4:14, 23) has avenged with vengeance. **Schmidt. <note>note q</note>** Deuteronomy 32:42. **<note>note r</note>** We translate "in Israel" so the location is indicated. For the enemies previously dominated the land of Israel itself, and now they are struck down. **Schmidt.** Compare verses 7, 8, and 11. **<note>note s</note>** while the people so readily offered themselves, verse 9; see chapter 4:10. We interpret the verb here, placed without an object, as: to drive oneself to act by a free and noble movement of the heart; especially to present oneself and one's members as a living sacrifice to the enemy, etc. Romans 12:1, compared with Psalm 110:3 and Song of Solomon 6:12. **Cocceius.**

**verse 3. <note>note t</note>** Princes, Psalm 2:2. **<note>note u</note>** for as for me, Genesis 24:27, according to the accents. **<note>note x</note>** I will sing praises, 2 Samuel 22:50.

**verse 4. <note>note y</note>** when You went out long ago in a miraculous storm with whirlwind and tempest. See the note on Deuteronomy 33:2 and compare Exodus 19:16. **<note>note z</note>** when You marched, Psalm 68:8, Habakkuk 3:12. **<note>note a</note>** it trembled, Psalm 18:8. **<note>note b</note>** they dropped, Psalm 68:9, compare Psalm 114:7.

**verse 5. <note>note c</note>** they flowed down and failed with rains, Exodus 15:8, Isaiah 64:2, Psalm 97:5. **<note>note d</note>** Sinai itself, Psalm 68:9.

**verse 6. <note>note e</note>** Chapter 3:31. Now she describes the misery of the land and the people of her time. **<note>note f</note>** which concerns the noble Sisera, verse 24, chapter 4:18. He joins Jael to the account to equate her with Shamgar; for although they provided some salvation, it was not yet perfect. **Abarbanel. <note>note g</note>** the ways, that is, those making a journey on the roads. **Masora Illustrata.** All paths were made dangerous for travelers because of the enemy's incursions. **<note>note h</note>** winding or crooked paths <note>original Latin: *tortuosis*</note>, Psalm 125:5.

**verse 7. <note>note i</note>** the villages, towns, and hamlets, verse 11, compare Deuteronomy 3:5. **<note>note k</note>** Chapter 4:4, 9. Deborah’s judgments were not only about right or wrong between men, but especially about faith in God. She therefore corrected the Israelites.
</margin>

<margin>
**Chapter V.** because of their exposure by God, like a mother's children, she was birthing them into the image of God. Galatians 4:19. **Cocceius.**

**verse 8. <note>note l</note>** he chose—that is, when Israel chose new gods, according to the Chaldean accents, the Septuagint, **Masora Illustrata, Schmidt,** etc. **<note>note m</note>** that is, fictitious ones, recently made. Deuteronomy 32:17. **<note>note n</note>** war <note>original Latin: *debellatio*</note>. Then also occurred the capture of the gates by the enemies and the greatest calamity. **Schmidt.** Then they had war in the gates. **Masora Illustrata. <note>note o</note>** compare 1 Samuel 13:22. **<note>note p</note>** she speaks of the 40,000 of Israel who were struck down by the Benjaminites in chapter 20, as if neither sword nor spear had been among them. **Lightfoot** on chapter 21.

**verse 9. <note>note q</note>** my heart is toward the governors, verse 14, who were so ready for war with their people. **<note>note r</note>** verse 1, Nehemiah 11:2.

**verse 10. <note>note s</note>** Chapter 10:4, chapter 12:14. **<note>note t</note>** white, off-white, in which redness is mixed with whiteness. Compare Ezekiel 27:18. **<note>note u</note>** **Schmidt.** properly from Job 15:61. So also **Masora Illustrata. <note>note x</note>** meditate.

These things with the praise of God, Psalm 105:2. **v. 11. <note>note y</note>** because of the voice of those dividing (**Cocceius** says "counting") their sheep <note>original Latin: *oues fuas*</note>, Proverbs 20:27, Job 21:21. **v. 1.** The letter *Schin* has a *Kamets* vowel <term>Kamets: a long 'a' vowel mark</term>. **v. 6.** "In the days of" has a *Kadma* accent <term>Kadma: a musical/grammatical chant mark</term>. "They walked" lacks the prefix *Vav*. **v. 7.** "They ceased" has a double *Lamed* with a *Dagesch* <term>Dagesch: a dot indicating a doubled or 'hard' consonant</term> according to the **Masora Illustrata. v. 8.** "War" has a *Tsere* vowel <term>Tsere: an 'e' vowel mark</term> under the *Lamed* in some versions, against the Masora of Erfurt. **v. 9.** "Bless" has a simple *Shua* <term>Shua: a very short vowel or neutral sound</term>. **v. 11.** "They shall give" is spelled deficiently (missing a letter) in some manuscripts. **v. 12.** "Utter a song"—the *Schin* has a simple *Shua*, but the **Masora Illustrata** requires a *Chateph* followed by a *Metheg* <term>Metheg: a vertical line indicating a pause or secondary stress</term>. **v. 15.** "And Issachar" is written this way in version 1.

v. 29. (a) The wisest of her princesses answered her. The "wise" ones here are the shrewd, prudent, and judicious women who judge events with insight. The "princesses" are the chief attendants of Sisera’s mother, who was like a Queen, if not from the royal family itself. **Schmidt**. (b) Each one answered her. compare Exodus 19:19; Habakkuk 2:11. The discrepancy in number <note>original Latin: "discrepantia numeri"</note> indicates a distribution of speakers, as in Deuteronomy 32:35. (c) Indeed, she even returned her own words to herself, with which she vainly consoled herself, saying with the rest:

CHAPTER VI. v. 1. (p) Chapter 4:1; 10:6. (q) See verse 13; chapter 2:14. (r) Of the Midianites. Numbers 25:17, 18. <note>Footnotes from bottom of the page regarding textual variants and Hebrew accents</note>
v. 7. The word "And why" <note>original Hebrew: וּמַדּוּעַ</note> is marked with a *Rebia* accent in some manuscripts, but with a *Gereshayim* in others (including copies 6, 9, 13, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, and the Berlin edition); however, it is marked with a *Geresh* in the remaining copies according to the Masora 3 and the printed editions. The word "now" <note>original Hebrew: עַתָּה</note> is stressed on the last syllable (*milra*) in copies 6 and 9-14, 16, 20, 22; but in both places the accent is placed sometimes on the second-to-last (*milel*) and sometimes on the last (*milra*) in copy 5. v. 8. The word "and you shall be" <note>original Hebrew: וְהָיִיתָ</note> appears with an additional letter 'He' at the end in copy 2 according to its own note, but this goes against the printed Masora for the following verses. q) The word "And now" <note>original Hebrew: וְעַתָּה</note> is marked with a *Tebhir* accent in copy 3; likewise in copy 5. v. 16. The word "when they came up" <note>original Hebrew: בַּעֲלוֹתָם</note> is written defectively (without a vowel letter) in copy 2, according to the Erfurt Masora. v. 17. The word "messengers" <note>original Hebrew: מַלְאָכִים</note> omits the dot (*Pik*) in copies 9, 20, 21. "Edom" <note>original Hebrew: אֱדוֹם</note> adds a dot in copy 2. The particle "Please" <note>original Hebrew: נָא</note> was marked with a deletion sign (obelus) in copies 2 and 5 as if it were redundant; and in copy 3 it has an added note: "it ought to be so" <note>original Latin: ita fieri debere</note>.

**36** And she said to him, "My father, if you have opened your mouth to the Lord, do to me according to what has proceeded out of your mouth, since the Lord has taken vengeance for you on your enemies, the people of Ammon."

<margin>

<margin>
**v. 39. s)** See verse 31; namely, that which is immediately added. According to Abarbanel: **t)** She therefore did not know a man. Others say: she had not known one. **u)** According to Schmidt: "it became a statute in Israel," namely, that which follows. But according to Gussetius: "and it was a custom in Israel," specifically of dedicating girls to God. Thus Abarbanel—though I do not know by what reasoning—believes she was removed from the company of all people, not just men but also women, and remained secluded in separate houses for her whole life; he attempts to derive the origin of Christian nuns from this, though he proves neither point. <column-break/>

Thus, for eighteen years, they had taken their refuge with the Ephraimites, and were thus snatched away and defended by them. Now, after they survived by their benefit, they despised them and did not call them to the alliance of war; (to which we add this) and so they secretly slipped away from them again like fugitives, and for such they are rightly held among the Ephraimites and Manassites. For the Genitive case which follows the word "fugitives" <note>original: פְּלִיטֵי (peleyte)</note> in a construct state always denotes elsewhere either the people from whom, or the boundary and danger from which, someone has escaped by flight. See verse 5, chapter 45:22, Ezekiel 6:8, 9, and Obadiah verse 14.

**Scribe's Critical Notes on the Hebrew Text:**
\* **34.** *To Mizpah:* Written with a paragogic He <note>An extra letter at the end of the word</note>. \* *With dances:* The Masora <note>Traditional notes on the Hebrew text</note> and Breithaupt on Exodus 15:20 require this to be written "defectively" (missing a letter) in two places. However, the same Masora on this passage requires the last syllable to be written "fully." \* **35.** *You have brought me low:* The letter Tau is written with a Patach vowel here. \* **36.** *My father:* Notated with a Paschta accent in various manuscripts (1, 2, 5, etc.). \* **39.** *Two months:* Manuscript 2 has a marginal note for a variant spelling as required by the Masora. \* **40.** *Yearly:* Written without a Pesk divider in several copies. \* *Four:* Marginal note in manuscript 2 suggests a different grammatical gender for the word "four." **CHAPTER XII, v. 2.** *And I cried out:* Uses a minor Tishir accent in many manuscripts. Some suggest a spelling change from the letter Zain to Tsade in the margin. \* **3.** *And I put:* Written in the main text without a special marginal instruction <note>original: Kvi aut Cthibh (Keri or Ketiv)</note> in almost all major manuscripts and the Masora. \* **5.** *And it was:* Includes a Gaiah accent according to the Ben Naphtali tradition.

**v. 6. m)** *Shibboleth*, that is, according to the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note>, an "ear of grain," as seen in Job 24:24 and Genesis 41:5. Others translate it as a "flood" or "flowing stream," as in Psalm 69:3, 16. However, it is clear enough that the test concerned the pronunciation of the word, not its specific meaning. *Schmid.* <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century commentator</note>

**(o)** Thus those whom the cruelty of their enemies could not reform now perish by the sword of their own brothers. Compare verse 1 and chapter 10:7–10. <note>Critical annotations at the bottom of the page:</note>
**v. 5. And they said.** Manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, and 10 connect these words with a *Makkaph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note>. **The Ephraimite.** The interrogative *He* here takes a *Patach* vowel in manuscripts 1, 3, 6, and 9, according to the Masora of Erfurt and grammatical analogy; others use a *Kametz*. **And he said.** A *Pasek* <note>a vertical dividing line</note> is added in 1 and 3, according to the Masora. **v. 6. And they slaughtered him.** Thus written deficiently with a *Mercha* accent in 1, 2, and 3, according to the Masora, though the printed editions disagree. **CHAPTER XIII, v. 1. Into the hand.** With a *Mercha* in 1 and 2. **v. 3. And you shall bear.** So in the margin of manuscript 2; however, the text of 2 and 3 uses the participial form "And you are bearing," though this is contrary to the printed Masora at verse 5.

<note>Textual Criticism & Variations</note>
*. 14. **And out of the strong**: Manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 5 have a Kamets vowel under the letter 'Ain. **And not**: Manuscripts 2 and 3 show this more regularly; the others use the Merca accent. *. 15. **Your husband**: marked with a Rebia accent in MSS 11, 12, 13, 14, 17, 18 and the Berlin edition. **To disinherit us**: MSS 5, 6, 9, 10, 12-16, 19, 20, 21 and Furtado 2 write a Kamets Chatuph under the Yod; MS 3 notes this in the margin while the text has "you called us." **To disinherit us** [another form]: stressed on the penultimate syllable in MSS 1 and 2, and corrected in 5. *. 16. **Only**: with a Mahpach accent in 1, 2, 3, 5. **You told**: The letter Gimel is voweled with a Kamets in MSS 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 20, and Furtado 5. *. 18. **Strong**: voweled with a Kamets in 1, 2, 3 according to the Masorah in 1 and 2, and in the Ef. edition here and Genesis 49:7; the rest use a Pathach. **For them**: with a Zakef-Katon accent in 17, 18 and Berlin; the rest have a Rebia.

# JUDGES CHAPTER 15

**v. 3. s)** *beautiful.* **Genesis 6, 2. t)** *but this marriage would have been incestuous, and no safer than with the previous woman.* <note>referring to the Timnite's offer of his younger daughter</note>
**v. 3. u)** *I am pure, that is, innocent.* **Jeremiah 2, 35; Psalm 19, 12.** As if to say: "Up to this point I had some cause, but now I have truly found a just cause for a public war." — Schmid.
**v. 4. x) y)** *they captured, both he himself and through others.* **chapter 7, 25; Job 5, 13; Amos 3, 4. etc.** Nor was it necessarily in one day or week, or in one place. **y)** Some wonder at the number of three hundred foxes, since they judge it by the conditions of our own land, where foxes are very rare. But commentators rightly note that the land of Canaan abounded in foxes, which is gathered especially from **Song of Solomon 2, 15**, from which place it is simultaneously learned that they knew how to hunt them. — Schmid. Bochart adds in his *Hierozoicon* (part 1, book 3, chapter 13, page 855) that the name "foxes" could also have included jackals <note>original: "thoes"</note>, an animal very similar to the fox and very frequent in Judea, especially in Palestine and around Caesarea (cf. the "land of foxes" in **1 Samuel 13, 17**). Jackals are so gregarious that it is reported by Bellonius (and an eyewitness friend confirms this to us) that sometimes two hundred jackals gather in one pack; thus, many could be captured with no trouble. Other doubts usually raised are likewise removed by the most learned Bochart, so that we think it is by no means necessary here to flee to a new meaning for the word "foxes," against the consensus of all commentators and antiquity, and especially against the clear phrasing of the text.
**v. 4. z)** *foxes.* **Ezekiel 13, 3; Psalm 63, 11; Lamentations 5, 18; Song of Solomon 2, 15; Nehemiah 3, 35.** Root in Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopian: *to cough*; also in Arabic: *to be white on part of the tail.*
**v. 4. a)** *torches.* **chapter 7, 15. 16.** and he...

<meta>The following are technical notes regarding specific Hebrew word forms and manuscript variations.</meta>

**v. 14.** *and he pulled away* <note>original: וַיִּסַּע</note> Iod with a Patach vowel in the Hiphil form; likewise in source 3 and source 5.
**v. 15.** *How can you say* <note>original: אֵיךְ תֹּאמַר</note> thus in source 3 and also in source 5.
**v. 16.** *and she urged him* <note>original: וַתְּאַלְצֵהוּ</note> Lamed with a simple Sheva vowel in sources 1, 2, 3, 5, 21.
**v. 18.** *to her* <note>original: לָהּ</note> instead of this, source 1 writes **to me** <note>original: לי</note> in the text without any note, and likewise in source 5, against the Masorah of Erfurt. But source 3 writes **to us** <note>original: לן</note> with the marginal correction "to me," also against the Masorah of Erfurt.
**v. 20.** *and I will shake myself* <note>original: וְאִנָּעֵר</note> Aleph with a Segol vowel; but in the margin with a Chirek vowel from "other books."
**v. 23.** *they gathered* <note>original: נֶאֱסְפוּ</note> with a Kadma accent according to Berlin alone; likewise in source 1 and 5. But all others have a Pashta accent, appearing anomalously in place of the former Rebia, as in Deuteronomy 20:20 and elsewhere. **into our hand** <note>original: בְּיָדֵנוּ</note> in the plural in sources 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, 21.

Verse 7. **Dwelling**: Manuscripts 6, 9, 20, 22, 23 add a *Pesiq* <note>a vertical line used as a musical or logical separator in the Hebrew text</note>. **Securely**: via the *Tlisha Qetana* accent in 6, 9, 10, 20, 21. **Quiet**: without the *Pesiq* in 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 20. Verse 9. **Arise!**: Instead of the singular, manuscripts 6 and 9 have the plural "Arise!", and 3 and 8 note it in the margin. **Which**: written with a *Maqqaph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in 10. **And now**: found in 1, 2. Verse 12. **Camp**: marked with the *Munach* accent on the penultimate syllable in 6, 9, 14, 20. Verse 13. **Mount**: marked with the *Munach* accent in 1, 2, 3, etc. Verse 14. **Know!**: Thus they transpose the accents in 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 17, 18, 19, 22, 23. Verse 19. **To him**: The letter Lamed has a *Dagesh* <note>a dot indicating emphasis or doubling</note> in 2 and 5, following the Masora printed for Genesis 19:2 and Rabbi Obadiah... but others appear without the *Dagesh*.

# JUDGES. CHAPTER 19.

<margin>
**v. 18. b)** See Noldius, *On Particles*, page 114. <note>original: "Et ad domum Iehovæ ego eo"</note> "And I am going to the house of the LORD," compared with Proverbs 22:25. This refers to Shiloh, where the Tabernacle and the Ark of the Covenant were located; see chapter 18:31, Joshua 18:1, and 1 Samuel 1:3. This is the view of the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, as well as the Arabic and Syriac versions, Rashi, and many other interpreters. However, the scholar Schmid thinks the phrase should be translated: "and I walk with the house of God," meaning, "I am a Levite." It is as if he is saying: "The Lord deems me worthy to serve Him as a Levite in His house, yet there is no one among the people of God who deems me worthy to receive me into their home." See Cocceius, *Lexicon*, page 73. **c)** See verse 15.

\* v. 2. **drew [the sword]** <note>original: "sholef"</note> So it appears in manuscripts 1, 2, and 5, as the rules of grammar require. The last syllable is supported by a *Metheg* accent mark because of the stress on the preceding syllable. In the manuscripts, this mark is so similar to a *Merca* accent that they are hard to distinguish except by grammar rules. This is why other books mistakenly write it with a different mark. For more on such examples, see Jablonski's Preface to the Berlin Bible, section 17. See also verses 15 and 17. **sons of their brothers** <note>original: "benei acheihem"</note> so in manuscripts 2, 3, 17, 18 and the Berlin edition.

\* v. 15. **drew [the sword]** <note>original: "sholef"</note> so in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9, 11, 12, 14, 16, 17, 20, 22. In manuscript 5, one must note that printers mistakenly used a *Merca* accent because the *Metheg* mark was ambiguous. However, manuscript 3 and the Berlin edition use only a *Munach* accent; the same is found in manuscripts 7, 8, 10, 15, 19, and 23, though with a *mikel* variation.

<note>The following notes are technical details regarding the Hebrew text’s grammar and accents used by scholars to ensure accuracy.</note>

v. 17. **Drew** <note>original: "שֹׁלֵף"</note> - So in most copies; "so it is in all the good books." However, the Berlin edition and 3 others have a different stress on the last syllable.
v. 18. **And the LORD said: Judah.** A pause <note>Piska</note> after the accent <note>Athnach</note> is required by the Masorah <note>tradition of the text</note>, but it is found here without the agreement of the others.
v. 19. **The children of Benjamin** - so in manuscripts 6, 9, 11, 12, 20, 21, 22.
v. 22. **They set in array** - Stressed on the last syllable <note>Milra</note>, following a connecting mark.
v. 25. **To meet them** - without the pause mark <note>Pfik</note> in manuscripts 3, 6, 9, 20, 21, contrary to the Masorah.
v. 26. **And they wept** - with the accent *Paschta* in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9, etc.
v. 26. **And they fasted** - with the accent *Tobir* followed by *Merca* in 6, 9, 14, 20.
v. 28. **And Phinehas** - thus in 1 and 2, which is correct; all others use the accent *Tifcha*. **Stood** - so in 7, 8, 13, 17, 18; the others are without the pause mark.
v. 31. **As at [other] times** - without the pause mark in 1, 5, 6, 9, 20, 21.

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the Book of Samuel, specifically the famous "Song of Hannah" in 1 Samuel Chapter 2. # 1 SAMUEL CHAPTER 2

**v. 3.** <gloss>o</gloss> "Do not multiply your words!" An emphatic omission of conjunctions, and an address to those swollen with worldly wisdom. <gloss>p</gloss> i.e., "very high things," arising from dull presumption. Psalm 12:4, 5; Psalm 73:8; 1 Corinthians 3:21; Philippians 3:3. <gloss>q</gloss> "Let it no longer go out," repeating the negative particle **אל** <note>Hebrew: "al", meaning "not"</note> from the preceding phrase. (M.I.) <gloss>r</gloss> "Hard things," as in Jude verse 15; or things commended under the pretext of antiquity. 1 Peter 1:18. Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note>: "blasphemies." Syriac: "calumny." <gloss>s</gloss> To whom all things are intimately known, and who alone is wise. Ephesians 3:10, 20; 1 Timothy 2:17. <gloss>t</gloss> And by Him actions are weighed. See Ezekiel 18:25, 29; chapter 33:17. Arabic: "nor do arts profit before Him."

**v. 4.** <gloss>u</gloss> Regarding the bow of the mighty. A similar construction to Job 15:20. <gloss>x</gloss> The mighty are broken in spirit and terrified along with their bows. Verse 10; Jeremiah 46:5; chapter 50:2. See Ezekiel 39:3; Luke 1:51, 52. <gloss>y</gloss> And those faltering. Zechariah 12:8. <gloss>z</gloss> Psalm 18:3; Ephesians 6:10.

**v. 5.** <gloss>a</gloss> Full of bread. Thus indicated by the accents. <gloss>b</gloss> Forced to serve for wages due to a lack of bread. In the Niphal <note>a Hebrew verb form</note> (1) Judges 18:4. See Luke 1:53; Amos 8:11, 12. <gloss>c</gloss> And the hungry cease—that is, they cease to be hungry or such as they were. See Isaiah 55:1; chapter 65:13; Matthew 5:6. Arabic: "the hungry indeed are filled, and there was abundance left for them." <gloss>d</gloss> According to Schmid and others, the number seven represents a multitude, as in Proverbs 24:16. Compare Isaiah 54:1 and following; Galatians 4:27. Augustine, however, signifies by it the perfection of the Church's understanding. See Proverbs 9:1; Revelation 1:4, 12. <gloss>e</gloss> She who had many children languishes and is rendered barren. Jeremiah 15:9; Joel 1:10, 12.

**v. 6.** <gloss>f</gloss> Deuteronomy 32:39; Job 5:18; Wisdom 16:13; Tobit 13:2. <gloss>g</gloss> Genesis 37:35; Psalm 116:3. See Matthew 11:23; chapter 16:18; John 11:25, 26.

**v. 7.** <gloss>h</gloss> He makes poor. See note on Numbers 22:38. <gloss>i</gloss> Proverbs 10:22; see Psalm 107:41. <gloss>k</gloss> Psalm 147:6. <gloss>l</gloss> Psalm 75:8.

**v. 8.** <gloss>m</gloss> Psalm 113:7, 8. See 1 Samuel 18:14, 51, 18.

**v. 3.** **hadellu** <note>ceased</note> with a Dagesh in the Lamed in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 16, 22, 23. Thus required by M.I. See notes on Judges 5:7. **v. 9.** **hasidav** <note>His holy ones</note> thus in 1, 2 according to its Masorah and Erffurt; but 3, 5, 6, 9, 17, 18 and others have a Kamets, yet with the Dagesh in the Mem omitted. **v. 16.** **yaktirun** <note>they shall burn</note> thus in full in 3, 6, 9, 22, 23. Thus also in 1 according to the Masorah and Erffurt. **ve-kach** <note>and take</note> with a Pashta accent in 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 16, 23. **v'omar** <note>and he said</note> without a Pesik in 2, 11, 12, 16, 20, 21, 23, against Masorah 1 and Erffurt; but 3, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14, 15, 19 have a Mercha with Pesik. **lo** <note>to him</note> thus with the Keri **lo** <note>no</note> in 2, 3, and 22 according to the Masorah, Erffurt, and M.I. in this place, and the printed Masorah at Isaiah 9:3. But from the Keri **lo** they make a **Sevir** <note>a scribal opinion</note>, that is, it falsely seems that it should be written "not" in 7, 8, 17, 18. Others note nothing in the margin, except 1 and 3, who require it to be written as "not" and read as "to him." **lo** without a Pesik in 1, 6, 9, 12, 13, 14, 15, 19, 20, 21, against the Masorah.

From this it appears that even the holiest things can lead to a person's total destruction if they are used irreverently or against the will of God. —Frankius. **a)** so that the earth was moved, that is, all the people were stirred up. <note>Critical footnotes at the bottom of the page</note>

* v. 13. **to them/for them** <note>Hebrew: *lahem*</note> This is a "Correction of the Scribes" <note>Tikkun Sopherim</note>, as noted in various Masoretic manuscripts.
* v. 15. **the vision** <note>Hebrew: *ha-mareh*</note> written with a Segol vowel in some manuscripts, but this contradicts the Masora <note>traditional Hebrew textual notation</note>.
* v. 16. **to me** <note>Hebrew: *elai*</note> Some manuscripts have "to me" instead of the standard "to."
* v. 17. **may [God] do** <note>Hebrew: *ya'aseh*</note> marked with a Kadma accent in certain codices.
* v. 21. **in Shiloh** <note>Hebrew: *be-shiloh*</note> with a traditional reading <note>Keri</note> variant in some manuscripts.
* CHAPTER IV, v. 1. **the Help** <note>Hebrew: *ha-ezer*</note> The letter Ain is written with a Tsere vowel in many early editions.
* v. 4. **[direct object marker]** <note>Hebrew: *et*</note> marked with specific grammatical accents in various codices.
* v. 5. **and they shouted** <note>Hebrew: *wa-yari'u*</note> written in full spelling in a corrected manuscript margin.
* v. 6. **voice/sound** <note>Hebrew: *kol*</note> the second instance is written with a Kadma accent in several manuscripts, which is against the usual rules of grammar.

<note>
**Verse 19. r)** near to giving birth. A contraction for *lalaedet*; as *meschavarat* for *meschavarat* in 1 Kings 1:15. **q)** the report; compare the use of the word *el* in chapter 1:27. **r)** which turned upon her. See Daniel 10:16. **s)** most take this as "pains" or "her boundaries," as in Isaiah 13:8 and chapter 21:3. Thus the Arabic: "and that, because the pains of birth had seized her due to the vehemence of fear." But because in Proverbs 26:14, the word *tzir* undoubtedly signifies the "hinge" of a door, Gussetius (page 713) suggests: The sense is (as in Daniel 10:16) the hinges or the heads of her bones had slipped out of the socket; the tendons being loosened by the dissipation of the spirits, the joints of the members were dissolved, resulting in extreme weakness and inability to retain the fetus in the womb, which therefore fell out, and thus she gave birth.

**Textual variants:**
* **Verse 7.** The word "No" (*lo*) is used here as in 3:5 and Ben [Asher] according to analogy; but all others use the *Merca* accent, except for manuscript 2 which has it otherwise. * **Verse 13.** For "hand" (*yad*), manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 write and read *yad* in the text; so too in 5. But manuscript 2 writes *yad* and reads *yad* in the margin; both of which go against M. I. and the Erfurt Masorah. "And the man came" (*ve-ha-ish ba*)—so it is in manuscripts 1, 6, 9, 11, 20, 22. * **Verse 15.** The word "set" (*qamah*)—so the Easterners write it, but they read *qamu* (plural) in the margin. * **Verse 16.** The second "and he said"—manuscript 2 uses a *Sakeshpg* accent. * **Verse 17.** Instead of "before" (*lifnei*), the margin of manuscripts 6 and 9 has "from before" (*mipnei*). The second "and also"—manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 11, 12, 16, 20, 21, 22 use the *Tifcha* accent.
</note>

# 232 I SAMUEL. CHAPTERS 8 & 9.

<margin>
**11. a)** See verse 9; also chapter 10:25 and Deuteronomy 17:14 and following. It points out that a kingdom was granted by God. See Pfeiffer in *Dubia Vexata* <note>August Pfeiffer was a 17th-century Lutheran theologian; this book title translates to "Troublesome Doubts."</note> on this passage. But this must be understood as being restricted by the Mosaic law; the divine law allows for no other interpretation. Therefore, this is the meaning intended by God and Samuel: "Since you, elders of my people, demand a king for yourselves according to the custom of all the neighboring nations, hear also what the royal right <note>original: "ius regium"</note> is according to the custom of those same nations." Indeed, this right should be exercised not according to the whims of the kings of the nations, but according to the divine law in Deuteronomy 17:6 and following. Meanwhile, not only the root of it—some splendor of royal majesty—but also specific royal rights will remain by virtue of your petition, as long as they do not contradict the divine law. Here you see not only that your status under kings will be much harsher and more burdensome than it was under the Judges, but also how easy it is for a king to fall into tyranny or to abuse royal rights. Therefore, it is time for you to consider the matter more maturely while there is still room for repentance. Once a king is chosen, repentance will be too late. Schmidt. <note>Sebastian Schmidt was a prominent 17th-century Hebraist and commentator.</note>
**d)** He will appoint them as his charioteers in his chariots. See Genesis 41:43; compare Exodus 33:22. **e)** *Among his horsemen.* In Arabic, *Pharas* denotes a horse, and *phara* a horseman. Compare also 2 Samuel 1:6; Isaiah 21:7, 9; and 28:28. **f)** 2 Samuel 15:1; 1 Kings 1:5.

***

**v. 13. *And which you asked*:** Thus with the prefix *Vav* <note>The Hebrew letter 'and'.</note> in manuscripts 2, 3.
**v. 14. *Which*:** indicated by the *Munach* <note>A Hebrew musical/grammatical accent.</note> in 7, 8, 10.
**v. 15. *And against your fathers*:** written "defectively" <note>An abbreviated spelling style in Hebrew.</note> in 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 22, 23; and corrected in manuscript 2 according to the Masorah <note>The tradition of textual notes that ensures the accurate transmission of the Hebrew Bible.</note>.
**v. 17. *Your wickedness*:** thus with a double accent according to Ben Naphtali <note>A famous 10th-century Masoretic scholar.</note>.
**v. 24. *Fear*:** spelled one way instead of another in manuscripts 2 and 3; thus also in 5, though this goes against the printed Masorah and the notes on Joshua 24:15. Manuscript 22 notes in its margin that it has a "quiescent Aleph" <note>A silent letter used as a vowel marker.</note>.
**v. 25. *You shall be consumed*:** thus with the accent on the last syllable in 2, 17, 22, and according to Ben Asher <note>The most authoritative Masoretic scholar.</note> in 5; but the rest place the accent on the second-to-last syllable.

<summary>Samuel delivers a powerful warning to Israel, using a miraculous out-of-season rainstorm during the wheat harvest to demonstrate God's displeasure with their demand for a king. The text transitions into Chapter 13, introducing the start of Saul's formal military reign and the famous textual difficulty regarding his age.</summary>

<summary>This page captures the dramatic confrontation between the prophet Samuel and King Saul, where Samuel delivers God's rejection of Saul's kingship due to his failure to fully eliminate the Amalekites. Saul attempts to shift blame to the people and offers excuses of religious piety, which Samuel famously rebukes by stating that obedience is superior to ritual sacrifice.</summary>

**27, 4. Genesis 38:26.)** l. "He visited him," meaning as he used to do previously, to instruct him as a King who was pleasing and acceptable to God. **v. 26. n)** Lest he should seem to revoke or disapprove of the divine rejection. (Schmid).
**v. 27. o)** But Saul persistently and urgently grabbed him. 2 Samuel 1:1. **p)** The "wing" or hem; one of the four corners of the outer garment. See Deuteronomy 22:12; 1 Samuel 23:1. **q)** So that it broke. Exodus 28:32. This was an unlucky omen.
**v. 28. r)** He cut it off. Chapter 28:17; 1 Kings 11:30, 31. **s)** Not necessarily from you yourself immediately, but certainly from your house and your posterity.

**v. 30. z)** He finally confessed his sin, though unwillingly. See verse 24. **a)** Compare Job 5:44; John 12:43.
**v. 31. b)** So that it would be clear to the people that as long as he lived, he would remain king, and was not entirely excluded from divine worship or the community like a pagan. (Schmid).
**v. 32. c)** Interpreters vary. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a Dutch theologian</note> suggests "in delights," i.e., cheerfully, either preferring death or hoping Samuel would spare his life. **v. 33. e)** Made childless. Genesis 32:46. **f)** She shall be made childless above all women. Genesis 27:45; Isaiah 49:21. **g)** He butchered or cut him apart. <note>Footnotes describing Masoretic notes and textual variants</note>

**v. 2. q)** He did not refuse, but desired to be taught how he might escape certain danger to his life. Compare Luke 1:34. For, as Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, legal scholar and theologian</note> correctly noted, if he had gone to anoint a new King without God's command, he would have incurred the crime of Lese-majesty <note>treason against the crown</note> and been liable to death, as Saul was still in power. (Schmid). **r)** Isaiah 7:21; Deuteronomy 21:3. **s)** That is, "with you." Compare chapter 14:34; 21:9. **v. 3. t)** Verse 5; chapter 9:13. **v. 4. u)** They were troubled. Chapter 13:7; 21:2; 1 Kings 17:18; Hosea 11:10, 11. **x)** One spoke in the name of the rest. Numbers 32:25.

**v. 27. A minor section break**, preceded by a *space*, is opened here by manuscripts 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 19, 20, 23. **v. 30. "Now" (attah)** according to Schmid; **h)** whose accent marker *Zakeph Gadol* was corrected by manuscript 5. **"Before" (neged)** marked with *Merka*, followed by a *Maqqeph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in **"the elders of" (ziqne)**. **v. 33. "Samuel" (Shemuel)** see manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10. However, the *Zakeph* is confirmed by the final Masora. **CHAPTER XVI, 1. 2. "And he will kill me" (ve-haragani)**. A *Piska* or space is found in manuscripts 1, 2, 17, 18, and also required by the Great Erfurt manuscripts. Others omit it. **v. 4. "And he said" (vayyomer)**: from this, manuscript 3 made a plural **"and they said" (vayyomru)**, as did manuscripts 1 and 2 originally; but the Masora requires the singular here. **v. 5. "With me" (itti)**: written as *itti* without a *Psiq* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 21. **"Sanctify yourselves" (hitqaddeshu)**: so in manuscript 1, and with a *Munach* instead of *Kadma* in 6, 9, 12, 20, 23. Others use a *Metheg* with an irregular *Zakeph Gadol* on the same word.

<margin>p) chapter 16:1; Micah 5:1; Matthew 2:6. q) chapter 16:10. But in 1 Chronicles 2:13, only seven sons are listed. Rashi <note>the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note> responds that the eighth died without children, and therefore was not listed in Chronicles. Others say the eighth was by another wife, perhaps an adopted son, or a grandson. Finally, Schmidt counts Jesse himself among them, comparing Genesis 46:8, to which one might add Shecaniah and his sons in 1 Chronicles 3:22.</margin>

v. 1. **Socoh**: The *Keri* <note>the traditional "read" version of the text</note> is **Socho**, added by the Erfurt Masorah <note>tradition of biblical textual notes</note>. v. 7. **Spearhead**: without a *Keri* in manuscripts 2, 10, 14, 15, 20. For the *Ctibh* <note>the "written" version of the text</note> has its own value and signifies the pole or shaft of the lance just as much as the *Keri* **wood**, which the Erfurt Masorah confirms. v. 9. **And I kill him**: clearly in 2, 3, 5, 22, and thus corrected in 1 according to the Masorah. v. 11. **And they were dismayed**: Thus in manuscripts 1, 2, 5, 22, 23. Others differ, but without the <term>Metheg</term> <note>a secondary accent mark in Hebrew</note> under the letter *Yod*, which is perhaps an error. **And they feared**: thus with a compensatory <term>Metheg</term>, which Berlin omits, correctly in 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, and others; for the letter *Yod* is missing from the spelling of "they feared," according to Masorah 1, 2, 3.

b) verse 15. x) Arabic version: "And when Saul was occupied with waging war, David returned to feed the sheep, etc." So says Maius in *Economy*, p. 741. Because Saul was only troubled by the evil spirit at intervals, and David’s divine music restrained the affected spirit, David returned occasionally to his household duties and served his father and brothers faithfully. Yet, in the meantime, he did not neglect matters concerning court service or other works by which he became more and more famous, whenever the King and the opportunity provided by God required it. However, Schmid establishes a <term>prothysteron</term> <note>a literary device where the chronological order is reversed</note> in chapters 16 and 17; he writes in his *Commentary* (p. 539, 546, 576) that both the anointing of David and his calling to the court occurred after the fight with Goliath. He contends on p. 590 that this is clear from chapter 16:19, 21, 22 and chapter 17:55, 56.

**verse 28.** The <term>Dagesh</term> <note>a grammatical dot in Hebrew</note> is omitted in manuscripts 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 19, 20, 21, 22. **verse 29.** "Is it not a word" <note>Hebrew: Halo davar</note> is written thus in manuscript 5. **verse 34.** "And he carried away" <note>Hebrew: ve-nasa</note>... Genesis 19, 20. **verse 30.** a) *perversely*. from the root 'awah'. Job 8, 3. or *perverse things* from the root 'awah'. Proverbs 12, 8. b) *rebellion* (1) c) "you are a partner/partisan." Luke 5, 7.

**verse 19.** The letter 'Shin' is without a 'Dagesh' <note>a grammatical dot</note> in codices 7, 8, 10--14, 19, 20, 21, 23, and with an explicit 'Raphe' in 3. **verse 20.** "To send" is marked with a 'Merca' accent on the last syllable in 1, 2, 3. **verse 21.** "Behold you" is marked with a 'Merca' regularly in 3, 5; others have a 'Munach'. "Take it" is marked with a 'Psik' in 1; so also in 5, according to the Masorah in 1 and Erff. **verse 24.** "Upon" is thus in the text with a 'Patach' vowel, and in the margin it is "To." in 6, 9. but in the text "To" without vowels, and in the margin "Upon" in 3. both are against the final Masorah... **verse 25.** "As at [other] times" without a 'Psik' in 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 20. **verse 27.** "David" has a 'Piska' <note>a space or pause</note> after the 'Atnach' accent in 2, 5, according to the Masorah of Erff. "Wherefore" requires 'Grashaim' according to the Masorah of Erff. **verse 29.** "And he said" uses 'Sakeph' in 8, 17, 18, and Ben Asher, against the Masorah of this place and the printed edition 34. 19. For the word "to him," they double the letter 'Lamed' with a 'Dagesh' in 1, 2.

**31** your mother: for as long as the son of Jesse lives upon the earth, neither **you nor your kingdom** shall be established. Now therefore, send and bring him to me, for he is a **son of death** <note>original: "בן-מות" - a Hebrew idiom meaning "he is as good as dead" or "he deserves to die"</note>. **32** And Jonathan answered Saul his father and said to him: **Why should he be put to death? What has he done?** **33** And Saul **threw his spear** at him to strike him; so Jonathan knew that his father was determined <note>original: "כלה" - literally "finished" or "completed," meaning the decision was final</note> to kill David. **34** And Jonathan rose from the table **in fierce anger** and ate no food on the second day of the month, for he was grieved for David, because his father had treated him with such shame.

**35** And it came to pass in the morning that Jonathan went out to the field at the **appointed time** with David, and a small lad was with him. **36** And he said to his lad: Run, find now the arrows which I am shooting. The lad ran, and he shot the arrow so as to pass over him. **37** And when the lad came to the place of the arrow which Jonathan had shot, Jonathan called after the lad and said: **Is not the arrow beyond you?** **38** And Jonathan called after the lad: **Hurry, make haste, do not stand still!** And Jonathan’s lad gathered up the arrow and came to his master. **39** But the lad **knew nothing**; only Jonathan and David knew the matter. **40** And Jonathan gave his weapons to the lad who was with him and said to him: Go, take them back to the city. **41** The lad went, and David rose from beside the south side and fell on his face to the ground and **bowed three times**; and they kissed one another and wept with one another, until David exceeded <note>original: "הגדל" - David's grief was the greater or more expressed</note>. **42** And Jonathan said to David: **Go in peace**, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the Lord, saying: The Lord be between me and you, and between my seed and your seed forever.

And he arose and departed, and Jonathan went into the city. **21:1** And David came to **Nob**, to **Ahimelech the priest**; and Ahimelech was afraid at meeting David and said to him: **Why are you alone, and no man with you?** **3** And David said to Ahimelech the priest: The king has commanded me a matter and said to me: Let no man know anything of the matter about which I send you and which I have commanded you...

**CHAPTER XXI, v. 2. f)** The same as **Nob** (chapter 22, 19) with the locative "h" suffix. It was a **city of priests** in the tribe of Benjamin (Nehemiah 11, 32). The **Tabernacle of Moses** was there at the time, having been moved there from Shiloh, just as it was later moved to Gibeon (1 Chronicles 16, 39; 2 Chronicles 1, 3). Scholar Sebastian Schmidt considers it probable that Nob was among the suburbs of **Kiriath-jearim**. David came there intending to **consult God** through the **Urim and Thummim** as to whether he should proceed on his journey.

The word **"shall know"** is marked with a special musical accent <note>cantillation mark</note>.

<note>
**Critical Notes on the Text:**
**v. 2.** The word "creditor" <note>original Hebrew: "נֹשֶׁא"</note> is written with the letter *Sin* incorrectly in some editions (1, 7, 19), but with the letter *He* in place of *Aleph* in the margins of others (6, 9).
**v. 5.** "Go and come" <note>original Hebrew: "לֵךְ וּבָאתָ"</note> appears this way in editions 1, 2, and 5. "Into the land" <note>original Hebrew: "אֶרֶץ"</note> is written with the prepositional particle "to" <note>original Hebrew: "אֶל"</note> in edition 2.
**v. 6.** "Under" <note>original Hebrew: "תַּחַת"</note> is noted by Mun. 1, 2, 5. For "to his servants," edition 3 uses a slightly different preposition.
**v. 8.** "Against my servants" was read by the Eastern traditions, but this goes against the printed Masora <note>the traditional system of notes on the Hebrew biblical text</note>.
**v. 10.** The name Goliath is written with a *Kametz* vowel under the letter *Yod* in several editions (7, 8, 10–13, etc.).
</note>

**Textual Notes:**
Verse 12. *And they turned back*: So they read in the Niphal <note>passive/reflexive verb form</note> in manuscripts 6 and 9 in the margin. Verse 14. *And he flew upon*: The letter 'Ain' has a Kametz <note>vowel mark</note> in manuscripts 1, 6, 9, but 'Yod' has a Patach in manuscript 3. Verse 17. *Our master*: singular without the letter 'Yod' in manuscript 3. Verse 18. *Parched grain*: thus with a paragogic Aleph in manuscript 2. Verse 19. *Behold I am*: thus in manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 14, etc. Verse 22. *Light*: This word is omitted in manuscripts 5, 11, 15, 16.

<note>Critical Apparatus/Footnotes</note>

\* **verse 20.** **The partridge** requires a full spelling according to the Erfurt Masora. **verse 23.** **His faithfulness** with an Aleph by a <term>Chateph Segol</term> <note>a composite vowel mark</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 14.
