# 1 SAMUEL 28 .CHAPTER 28.

<margin>
Regarding verse 15, it should be understood as a result of Saul's false persuasion; he wrongly believed that Samuel was actually present. These matters are reported more extensively by Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and commentator</note> on page 132 and following, where he argues against the literal sense of the text. He notes that Ralbag <note>Levi ben Gershon, a medieval philosopher</note>, along with Maimonides and others, believed none of this actually happened in reality, but was all in Saul's mind or imagination, conceived out of terror and the memory of divine threats. Abarbanel himself eventually concludes (p. 133, col. 3) that while Samuel's soul was certainly not summoned from the dwellings of the blessed by a medium, an evil spirit was stirred up by magical arts, took on the form of Samuel’s corpse, and predicted the future. He concludes that the "corpse of Samuel" is rightly called by his name, comparing this to Genesis 49:31. We gladly embrace and approve our own opinion, which is established in the Sacred Commentary on page 913 and following.
</margin>

**a)** Leviticus 20:27, Deuteronomy 18:10-11. **b)** "You set a snare," i.e., you lay an ambush. **(5)** Psalm 9:17. 
**c)** See Hosea 4:15, Ezekiel 20:39. Saul was like an adulteress here, who while she prostitutes herself to another, yet swears by the life of her husband. <note>From Vajjikra Rabba, a midrashic text, chapter 26</note>. **d)** Numbers 11:23. **e)** "Iniquity," or the punishment due to this iniquity (chapter 3:14, Lev. 26:41). The Greek Septuagint uses "unrighteousness"; compare Revelation 2:11.
**f. 11)** The superstitious opinion was that souls were truly led out. See verse 13. But according to Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a 12th-century grammarian</note>, these were "mere illusions." Interpreters raise various and perplexing questions here, the full review of which this narrow space cannot hold. Indeed, the Talmudists handed down that he was raised, but according to Rabbi Saadia and Rabbi Hai, he was raised not by the woman’s spells, but by the power and will of God. This opinion is found not only among the translators of the Septuagint (1 Chronicles 10:13) and Sirach (46:20), but also among the Church Fathers, as Abarbanel himself observed on this passage. However, Abarbanel attributes another view to Augustine (which matches our own), and rejects it, but without sufficient reason. Kimchi refutes the opinion of Saadia and others, primarily because no reason can be given why God would not answer Saul through the Urim and Thummim, or through dreams and Prophets, yet would seemingly assent to diabolical plays. He thinks it was the mere trickery and fraud of a deceptive woman, who, in the opinion of Rabbi Samuel ben Chophni, produced nothing under Samuel's name except what was already known to all the people or easy to guess.
</margin>

<note>
* This section contains a technical scholarly apparatus regarding the Hebrew text. It notes variant readings and Masoretic accents (like Paschta, Makkaph, and Sakeph) across different manuscripts (numbered 1 through 23). For example, it notes that in Verse 23, some manuscripts write "urged" differently. In Verse 5, it mentions that "David" has a specific musical accent in many copies, and that the word "thousands" is written "fully" (with all its vowels) in manuscript 22. These notes ensure that the translator or printer is using the most accurate version of the holy text.
</note>

**v. 11. f)** Indeed, when they heard it, they were attentive to him. <note>Compare Genesis 16:11.</note> **g)** These were the people Saul had liberated from a heavy siege and disgrace at the beginning of his reign (chapter 11:1 and following). **v. 12. h)** Judges 3:29; chapter 20:44. **i)** And they burned them, or those corpses. This was unusual and done in haste so that the enemy would not recover them and treat them with further indignity. <note>Gussetius, p. 889.</note> The burning of spices at a funeral was different (Jeremiah 34:4, 5; 2 Chronicles 16:14; 21:19). The Aramaic Targum <note>original: "Ion:" referring to Targum Jonathan.</note> translates: "And they burned over them just as they burned over Kings." But the Arabic version translates: "And they lit lamps for them, just as lamps are usually lit for Kings."
**v. 13. k)** 1 Chronicles 10:12. Just as among the Romans, the gathering of bones was done from the funeral pyre. **l)** Chapter 22:6. That is, under some oak tree in a place (compare 1 Chronicles 10:11) where they would not easily be found by enemies. **m)** As was customary in solemn and public mourning (2 Samuel 1, 12; Judges 20, 26, etc.). **n)** Genesis 50:10; Ezekiel 3:15.
</margin>

Compare Genesis 16:12. But Schmidt suggests the spear was "thrown behind the back." l) The Latin Vulgate translates this as "in the groin" or "the abdomen." See Chapter 3:27 and 4:6, which agrees with the Ethiopic translation.

<margin>The **Keri** <note>a traditional reading that differs from the written text</note> is 'Tachtav' (in his place/under him)</margin> which here signifies the womb or female parts. See Job Ludolf’s Ethiopic Lexicon, column 31. Schmidt translates this as "at the fifth rib," a dangerous and fatal location. m) "In the very place where he was." Exodus 16:29. n) Those who were coming from Joab's army, whom Asahel had outrun.

**Notes on the Latin Glosses:**
b) "let them play before us" f) "let them perform a prelude for us." That is, let them begin a light skirmish, which in respect to a proper battle is like a game. Schmidt and others: "let them perform a sport." Compare 2 Samuel 6:5, 16; Proverbs 8:30. c) [Joab agreed] lest he should seem more timid.

**v. 15.** d) They came forward from the battle lines arranged on both sides to begin the fight. e) Equal in number. Compare Deuteronomy 25:2, Ephesians 40:26. f) As mentioned in verses 12, 13, and 17.

**v. 16.** g) Lest he should escape. h) Truly remarkable stubbornness, or perhaps courage. i) Therefore it was called [the Field of Flints]. k) A portion of the field. Jeremiah 12:10. l) Of the edges, or of the sharp swords. See the note on Job 5:2. But Schmidt, following Kimchi and others, translates "of rocks" <note>original Latin: 'petrarum'</note>, referring to men who were as immovable and unconquered as rocks. See 2 Samuel 1:19, Deuteronomy 14:5, 1 Chronicles 12:8. For their wonderful speed, see Bochart’s *Hieroz*.

**v. 19.** x) He outran his own men and followed Abner through his speed of foot. y) Verse 21, Numbers 20:17. z) Seeking him, if he might kill him. # III

<margin>
CHAPTER III. v. 1. a) After that first fierce battle and the subsequent truce (Chapter 2:17, 26 ff.), the state of war did not entirely cease, but there was a sufficiently long contention over the kingdom of all Israel, even if they did not meet in a hostile battle line. Just as the event showed those plots of the Philistines were in vain, so David, by the prophetic Spirit, foresaw and predicted a similar outcome for the Antichristian nations. **Chapter VI, verse 1.** Then he gathered, from *asaf* as in Psalm 104:29. Manuscript 3 does have a space, under the express name <term>פ</term> **Petucha**, but in place of an **Atnach** <note>a mid-verse accent</note> it has a **Silluk** with **Soph Pasuk** <note>the end-of-verse marker</note>. **Into your hand** is plural in 6, 9, 14, 20, 23. **Verse 20.** **David** with a **Munach** instead of a **Mercha** <note>different types of musical/grammatical accents</note> in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 14, 20, 23, contrary to the printed Masorah. Regarding Exodus 6:6. **And he struck them** thus with a **Segol** followed by a **Makkef** <note>a hyphen-like connector</note>. **Verse 24.** **The marching** with the prefix **He** in 3, and in the margin of 2. **Chapter VI, verse 3.** **And they carried it** with a **Zakef Gadol** in 1 and 3; so also in 5; thus with the rest of our manuscripts 6, 9, and in the margin according to the Masorah of 1 and the printed edition; but they write with a **Pashta** at the end in 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 21, 22. **Abinadab** with a **Munach** instead of a **Metheg** in manuscripts 5–10, 12, 14–23.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of King David in Jerusalem. Having successfully brought the Ark of the Covenant to the city, the text transitions from David’s conflict with his wife Michal—who despised his humble display of devotion—to his desire to build a permanent temple for God. This marks the beginning of the "Davidic Covenant," a pivotal moment in biblical history where God promises an eternal dynasty to David’s line.</meta>

### SECOND SAMUEL. CHAPTERS 6 & 7.

<column-break/>

**21** And David said to Michal: "It was before the Lord, who chose me over your father and over all his house, to appoint me as ruler over the people of the Lord, over Israel; and I will celebrate before the Lord. **22** And I will be even more lightly esteemed than this, and I will be humble in my own eyes; and with the maidservants of whom you spoke, with them I shall be honored." **23** And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child until the day of her death.

->**AND IT CAME TO PASS, WHEN THE KING DWELT**<-

**1** In his house, and the Lord had given him rest from all his enemies all around. **2** And the king said to Nathan the prophet: "See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells within the tent-curtains." **3** And Nathan said to the king: "All that is in your heart, go and do, for the Lord is with you." **4** And it happened that night, that the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying: **5** "Go and say to my servant, to David: Thus says the Lord: Would you build me a house for my dwelling? **6** For I have not dwelt in a house from the day I brought up the children of Israel from Egypt until this day, but I have moved about in a tent and in a tabernacle. **7** In all the places where I have moved with all the children of Israel, did I speak a word to any of the tribes of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying: Why have you not built me a house of cedar? **8** And now, thus shall you say to my servant, to David: Thus says the Lord of Hosts: I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people, over Israel. **9** And I have been with you wherever you have gone, and I have cut off all your enemies from before you, and I have made for you a great name, like the name of the great ones who are on the earth. **10** And I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant them, and they shall dwell in their own place and not be disturbed anymore; and the children of wickedness shall no longer afflict them as in the beginning. **11** And from the day that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel, I will give you rest from all your enemies."

**l)** <note>original: "quæ detectus fuit"</note> He was uncovered and showed himself to be seen, stripped of all Royal ornament (v. 14). Compare Genesis 31:7; 1 Samuel 14:8, 11. Kings in the East rarely showed themselves to be seen by the common people. Hence, familiars and intimate counselors are called "those who see the face of the King" (2 Kings 25:19; Jeremiah 52:25; Esther 1:14; compare Matthew 18:10). **m)** Of vain or empty men (Judges 9:4; 11:3; Proverbs 12:11). The proud woman seems to sting the Levites, whose attire and humble devotion of this sort she thought did not at all suit royal majesty.

<meta>This page continues the text of 2 Samuel 7, following God’s message to King David through the prophet Nathan. On the previous page, David expressed his desire to build a house (temple) for God, but God responded by promising to build a "house" (a dynasty) for David instead.</meta>

### SECOND SAMUEL. CHAPTER 7.
**Kk 5**

<margin>
h) Although these listed benefits are the greatest, God indicates even more to you. i) A house far more noble than you would have made for Him; whose architect is God Himself (Hebrews 11:10). k) verse 27. Through the Messiah; whom the Holy Spirit teaches everywhere is the primary goal of the prophecy, both in the figure of Solomon and in his own person and mystically in his members <note>that is, the Church</note> (for example, Acts 2:30, 3:24, etc.). And some Jewish interpreters agree that the discourse here is also about the Messiah, such as Rabbi Alschech in his Commentary on this passage (folio 66. c.), and Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century statesman and philosopher</note> reports this opinion as well (folio 158. d.) and offers nothing against it. Therefore, those who think only of Solomon is meant here are not to be approved; yet it is also not proven that nothing pertains to Solomon as a figure, but everything must be understood only of Christ. This is refuted by Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmid, a 17th-century theologian</note> (page 324). It seems some things pertain to Solomon in his person, and some to the person of the Messiah; to Solomon, however, only through his offspring, who is the Messiah himself. A similar explanation applies to the promises made to Abraham in Genesis 12:3, which did not pertain to Abraham except through his offspring, the Messiah (Genesis 22:18). Compare Galatians 3:8, 16.

<note>Annotations on Verse 12:</note>
z) verse 12. a) The time for the Messiah to be raised up. b) Deuteronomy 21:16. h) 1 Kings 2:10, Acts 13:36. i) This does not fit Solomon, because he was not born *after* David <note>in the sense of after his death</note>, but rather while he was still living he was chosen and anointed king. Compare the figure in 1 Kings 2:20. p) 1 Chronicles 17:11. q) Mediately, as in Genesis 25:23; even though Solomon was not yet born when this promise was made (compare 1 Chronicles 21:9). r) Isaiah 9:6, 1 Samuel 13:13. Greek: *anastēso* <note>I will raise up</note> (Acts 15:16). t) Compare Psalm 89:4, Psalm 132:11.

<note>Annotations on Verse 13:</note>
t) Solomon and Christ; the former as a figure, the latter in truth. u) 1 Chronicles 22:9.

<column-break/>

<note>Annotations on Verse 16:</note>
g) Stable. It will be firm (Isaiah 22:23). h) verse 13. Psalm 72:17, Psalm 89:37, John 11:34. i) This is fulfilled while Jesus, having been taken up to the right hand of the Father, reigns, while David watches from the heavens where he is blessed (Grotius). For David the King of Israel still lives and remains, as Alschech writes.

<note>Annotations on Verse 17:</note>
k) The vision. l) Isaiah 22:1, 5. m) Faithfully and exactly.

<note>Annotations on Verse 18:</note>
m) The Arabic version adds: "into the house of the Lord." He was so rejoiced by the divine promise that he came in. n) Remaining long in prayer and humble thanksgiving (compare Exodus 17:11). o) 1 Chronicles 17:16. Rashi: "before the ark." p) The family of descendants or ancestors (1 Samuel 1:21). q) Even to the royal dignity; the Arabic version says "to such great magnitude" (compare Genesis 32:11).

<note>Annotations on Verse 19:</note>
r) And it was yet little. s) 2 Kings 19:25; the promise looking to a time still far remote. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan</note>: "into the world to come" (compare Hebrews 2:5). For this vision was great, and David also said: "you have spoken also concerning the house of your servant in the distance," hinting at the Messiah, the son of David (Abarbanel). t) And this is by the "law" or order of men, who are mortal and miserable, whose mortal state you are to undergo without sin for the sake of redeeming them (Schmid). u) Schmid, with the Septuagint and Vulgate, reads this as a calling out: "O Lord GOD!"

<note>Annotations on Verse 22-23:</note>
x) On account of the promise already made to your servant. y) Without any merit of my own. z) This greatness or supreme benefit. a) The Arabic version says: "Therefore I say you are great in mercy, from which alone these promises were made" (compare Psalm 48:2). b) Deuteronomy 3:24, Mark 12:29. c) From our ancestors. David continues to praise God's mercy by recalling the benefits given to Israel. d) Deuteronomy 4:7. e) Concerning Israel (Deuteronomy 4:34). f) To redeem whom the Triune God went (compare Genesis 1:1, 3:22). Alschech understands this as the Shekhinah <note>the Divine Presence</note> and the heavenly family with the angels. i) A famous and glorious name (Isaiah 63:12). k) O Elohim, Triune God. l) While you drove out the nations of Canaan and their gods.

<note>Annotations on Verse 24-25:</note>
m) Under Christ and his kingdom. z) Genesis 17:7. n) In these verses David asks for the fulfillment of the promises, not through his own merits, but through divine truth. p) Concerning Christ and his eternal kingdom.

<note>Philological Notes:</note>
Verse 16. s) Aleph with a simple Sheva. Verse 21. *Ha-gedullah* (The Greatness): The letter Lamed is doubled with a Dagesh. Verse 22. "Lord GOD": The Arabic version and others write *Adonai Yahweh*. Verse 23. *Lecha* (To you): The Lamed is written without a Dagesh in many manuscripts.

<note>Continued annotation from Margin d:</note>
...they serve directly under the King, not through intermediaries like the Levites; thus they were second only to the King. And just as the Arabic *Cahen* refers to administrators of another's business, they performed the father’s duties when the situation required and carried them out by his command, like Vice-Regents. For what else were the priests of the Old Testament but representatives <note>Latin: "Vicarii"</note> of the High Priest, the Son of God? (Compare the note on Leviticus 17:4.) Just as in the New Testament, ministers of the church act as ambassadors for Christ (2 Corinthians 5:20).

<margin>
Extra *Aleph* **v. 4. o)** As if to say: a coming, or understand "a man," as in Psalm 109:4. A Traveler. **(z)** 1 Samuel 14:26. In the Talmudic Tractate *Succah* (folio 52b), the Rabbi says: depraved lust is called here first a "traveler" <note>Hebrew: *helech*</note>, then a "guest" <note>Hebrew: *oreach*</note>, and finally a "man" <note>Hebrew: *ish*</note>. **1** And the Lord sent Nathan to David. And he came to him and said to him: "There were two men in one city, one rich and the other poor.
**2** The rich man had very many flocks and herds.
**3** But the poor man had nothing at all except one little ewe lamb which he had bought. And he nourished it, and it grew up with him and with his children together; it ate of his own bread and drank from his own cup and lay in his bosom, and it was to him like a daughter.
**4** And there came a traveler to the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd to prepare for the guest who had come to him; but he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him."
**5** And David's anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan: "As the Lord lives, the man who has done this is a son of death! <note>meaning: he deserves to die</note>
**6** And he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing and because he had no pity."
**7** And Nathan said to David: "**You are the man!** Thus says the Lord God of Israel: 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.
**8** And I gave you your master's house and your master's wives into your bosom, and I gave you the house of Israel and of Judah; and if—'"

---

What then do you think of that man? **v. 5. t)** by a hasty but just judgment. **u)** 1 Samuel 20:3. **x)** Genesis 20:3. The matter is one of death, namely eternal death in the divine court, such unjust and violent robbery. **v. 6. y)** in the human court he shall restore fourfold according to the law in Exodus 21:37. Others think David, because of the cruel violence of the robber, thought of a doubled legal penalty and understood eightfold; indeed, Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan</note> says fortyfold, but incorrectly; for this dual formula does not signify a number, but that the thing itself is multiplied by that number. Thus "sevenfold" <note>Hebrew: *shibatayim*</note> does not mean twice seven, but sevenfold. Genesis 4:15, 24; Proverbs 6:31, etc. **v. 7. a)** David. Philemon v. 19. **b. 7. b)** and much more are you guilty of death, you who have sinned far more atrociously. **a)** 1 Samuel 16:13, 14. **b)** see 1 Samuel 23:14. **v. 8. c)** Whether they were the daughters of Saul or his sons' wives. Schmid notes that this is said not because (as Abarbanel observes) the wives of Saul belonged to David, but because they were in David's power, so that he could have married them if he wished, with no one hindering. For no one but a King ought to marry the wives of a King according to Oriental custom. Hence Adonijah incurred such a great penalty in 1 Kings 2:22, and such a great quarrel arose between Ish-bosheth and Abner in 2 Samuel 3:7. **d) v. 3.** As if to say: if you certainly did not wish to be chaste, you would not have lacked for wives whom you already had. God does not approve of polygamy here, but exaggerates David's crime. <note>Schmid, p. 557</note>

**Textual Notes and Variants:**
**8.** ***And if too little***: thus in manuscripts 1, 2, 5. But according to Munster, in place of the *Kadma* accent and with a *Makkaph* at the end... all have only the *Zakeph-katon* accent.
**To you** (*lecha*): Lamed with a *Dagesh* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 21, 22. **As much again** (*ka-hennah*). **v. 9. In his eyes**: with a *Kamets* vowel according to the *Qere* (read as) **in his eyes**. Found in 6, 9, 14, 17, 18, 20. But manuscript 2 writes it with the *Qere* reading. **With the sword**: The letter Beth has a *Dagesh* in 3, 17, 18. **13. To the Lord**: The *Piska* (pause) required by the Masora and Erfurt manuscripts is missing in 1, 2, 6-16, 13-23.
**v. 15. The Lord**: with a *Revia* accent in 1, 3, 5, 10, 13, 19. **And he became terminally ill**: thus with an Aleph in 1, 2, 3, 5, 22, according to the Masora. Manuscript 22 has a marginal note: **Because it must be according to the Masora.** All others write it with a He. **19. And he saw**: with a *Revia* accent in 2, 5, 6, 9, 21.

# CHAPTER 13. II SAMUEL 13.

<margin>
**v. 13.** However, by his royal power, he [David] could grant a dispensation for her and give me to you, just as God sometimes granted dispensations against the law of Moses. <note>original Latin: *tamen pro regia sua potestate de ea dispensare...*</note> Some believe Tamar said this out of an error or ignorance of the law; others think she spoke this way only as a pretense to preserve her chastity.

**v. 14.** **f)** By force. **g)** See the law cited at verse 13.

**v. 15. h)** Immediately after the crime was committed, when he felt the stings of conscience, he began to hate her against whom he had sinned through lust, whereas he ought to have hated himself. **i)** And that hatred was insane and diabolical.

**v. 16. k)** A difficult passage, and there is great disagreement about this particle. The Septuagint, the Chaldee Targum, and others took it to mean "on account of" (עַל), a noun frequently joined with others elsewhere, such as in Genesis 21:11. Hence, the scholar Cocceius in his Lexicon (p. 14) suggests two possible readings exist: one written with the letter *Ayin* (עַל) and the other read with the vowel of *Aleph* (אֶל).
</margin>

**6.** So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, "Please let <margin>d) so that she may prepare cakes (or "liba," heart-shaped cakes). **(2) v. 8.** e) just two little cakes, which are "heart-refreshing" (liba cordialia). **(3) v. 8, 10.** f) so that I may eat from her own hand. **(5) v. 5, 10; c. 12, 17.**</margin> my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand."

<meta>The transcription contains technical Masoretic notes (the Masora) regarding the spelling and accents of the Hebrew text. It notes the presence of the *Metheg* (a secondary accent) in verses 6, 7, 8, etc., and discusses the spelling of "Amnon" and "Tamar." It also notes grammatical variants like the *He paragogicum* on "they shall wear" in verse 18. These details were vital for scribes to ensure the text was copied without a single error.</meta>

*v. 21. n)* David was altogether more indulgent in this business: he could have rightfully rejected both Joab and the woman of Tekoa with indignation, because they wished to deceive him with a fictional case. Schmidt, p. 673.

*v. 13.* The word "you thought" <note>original: "חָשַׁבְתָּה"</note> does not have the paragogic 'He' in manuscripts 6, 9, 14, 20, 21. This follows verse 1 and 2, against the Masorah and the printed editions. *v. 19.* For the word "ish" <note>original: "אִשׁ"</note>, manuscripts 6 and 9 have "man" <note>original: "אִישׁ"</note> in the margin. Manuscript 5 corrected it to "man" (in which sense the Masoretes, Jonathan, and many others also take the word "ish" in this place), but both are against Masorah 1 and 2, the printed edition, and the Erfurt manuscript. *v. 21.* The word "you did" <note>original: "עָשִׂיתָ"</note> is read as "I did" <note>original: "עָשִׂיתִי"</note> according to the <term>Keri</term> in manuscripts 2, 5, 6, 9, 12, 18, 21. Berlin and a more correct book in the second place of the Masorah Esther, and a note in the margin <insert>A</insert> which says: "The Masorah did not record it, yet it is so." Although it is found nowhere in the Masorah, it is correct. However, manuscripts 7, 8, 11, 13, 16, 23 write "you did" <note>original: "עָשִׂיתָ"</note> (but with the Keri "I did," which is against the nature of the Keri and <term>Ketiv</term> [the written tradition]). Finally, they write and read "I have done" <note>original: "עשתי"</note> in verse 22. David Kimchi and M. J. follow this, more appropriately than the others. For this reading was expressed by the ancient versions: Greek, Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic; and the Editor of the Masorah in the margin of manuscripts 7 and 8 says that he found that Keri and Ketiv in many codices, but hardly in one in a thousand.

**Textual Notes:**
**v. 3**. "Your words" (*Debareka*): The Eastern scribes write this without the letter *Yod*.
**v. 5**. "In drawing near" (*Bikreb*): Many of our texts have the *Metheg* mark under the *Beth*, which the Masora also requires. *Lo* [to him]—some have *Ben* [son] instead.
**v. 7, 18, 19, 22, 23**. and Ber. <note>likely referring to the Berlin manuscript or a specific edition</note>.
**v. 7**. Some include a space before this; others omit it.
**v. 8**. "He will bring back" (*Yashiv*): Thus written with a *Cholem* vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 8, 4, 13, 15, 16, 19-22; and thus corrected in 5 according to the printed Masora and Index 7:3. But 17 and 18 write *Yashuv* [he will return]. 7, 14, and 21 have neither vowel point.
**v. 12**. "Counselor" (*Vaya'atz*): with the added letter *Vav* in various manuscripts. "From Giloh" (*Miggiloh*): spelled with a *Ki* in 1 and 2.
**v. 13**. "Heart" (*Lev*): with a *Segol* vowel and without *Mech* in many manuscripts.
**v. 16**. "The" (*Et*): with a *Segol* and *Makkaph* (hyphen) in several versions. "Concubines" (*Pilagshim*): written in full in some; the letter *Lamed* is written without a *Dagesh* (emphasis dot) in all except a few specified manuscripts.

y. 18. **at his feet**: so it is written in the text, with the tradition <note>original: "Kri"</note> reading **at his feet** according to the Masoretic Effect. y. 19. A space is placed between this and the preceding verse in codices 1, 5, 6, 9, 10, 19, 20. y. 20. **I should make you wander**: without the *Psik* <note>a vertical musical accent</note> in codices 1, 2, 6, 9, 10. y. 21. **which**: with a *Maqqeph* <note>Hebrew hyphen</note> in codices 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 14, 20. y. 23. **from his place**: with a *Maqqeph* in place of a *Meteg* <note>a stress mark</note> in codices 5, 10, 12, 18. y. 26. **and if**: with a *Maqqeph* in codices 6, 9, 14, 20, 21, 22. And it is corrected thus in y. 27. **return**: all our manuscripts mark this with a *Milel* <note>accent on the penultimate syllable</note> stress, as required by Hannagid in M. I., though his authority denies that *Milel* is found in corrected codices, stating it should be thus in the Masoretic exemplar. y. 30. **by the ascent**: the letter *Beth* has a *Dagesh* <note>a dot indicating emphasis</note> contrary to standard grammar in codices 1, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10 through 12, 15, 17 through 19, 21, 23. **going up**: without the *Psik* in 1, 2, 5 through 9, 14, 15, 20. **weeping as they went**: with the traditional reading **they went up and wept** in codex 2 and the Masoretic Effect.

The text and its extensive marginalia emphasize the spiritual and symbolic weight of David's ascent of the Mount of Olives.</summary>

<margin>
o) he was strangled, and by a noose he brought death upon himself out of a bad conscience (z) <note>original: "strangulatus est"</note> Nahum 2:13. "he hanged himself" <note>original Latin/Greek: "ὁ ἀπήגξατο"</note> Matthew 27:5. Gussetius (p. 271) and others take exception to this interpretation because the Hebrew word is not in the <term>Hithpael</term> <note>a reflexive verb form</note> but the <term>Niphal</term> <note>usually a passive or middle-voice verb form</note>. Therefore, I would not say he strangled himself, but that he was "strangled"—that is, his throat was constricted and his breath cut off, a physical symptom arising from mixed grief and anger, as others understand Job 7:15. But Schmid (p. 796) responds that he was strangled—that is, suffocated—not directly by himself but by the noose he tied around his own neck. Furthermore, the meaning of the <term>Niphal</term> conjugation is often reciprocal or <term>deponential</term> <note>acting like an active verb despite its form</note>, as is taught in grammars, for example: <unclear>was guarded</unclear>, <unclear>leaned</unclear>, <unclear>swore</unclear>, etc. So also above in verse 13.

<meta>This page continues David’s Song of Deliverance, a poetic masterpiece found in both 2 Samuel 22 and Psalm 18. The translator’s notes here focus on the minor linguistic differences between these two versions, treating the passage as a vivid description of a "theophany"—a visible manifestation of God’s power through a terrifying storm.</meta>

### II SAMUEL. CHAPTER 22.

<margin>
**verse 7.** a) but when I was in distress, I called out. Deuteronomy 4:30. compare (25, 4. 4) to God, I say, to Him. chapter 12:9, 14:4 etc. b) compare 1 Samuel 1:9 and following. c) Exodus 2:23. 1 Samuel 5:12. d) He heard with His ears. compare Psalm 18:7, it came to Him.
**verse 8.** e) Then indeed it was shaken or moved. (Psalm 18:8). f) compare Psalm 18:9, 1 Samuel 14:15, Joel 2:10. g) compare Job 26:11. foundations of the mountains, Psalm 18:8. h) they were moved, chapter 19. i) Isaiah 13:13. as if heaven itself were about to fall. Specifically, God’s help and the battle against the enemies are described in the manner of a terrifying storm. i) all things, I say, moved themselves, Jeremiah 5:22, 25:16. k) when anger blazed for Him. Genesis 4:5-6. Psalm 2:12.
**verse 9.** l) Psalm 18:9, Isaiah 65:5. m) fire breaking out from His mouth. Symbols of one who is vehemently angry and burning with a desire for vengeance. compare Revelation 9:17, Job 41:11-12. n) coals, verse 13, chapter 14:7, Proverbs 25:22. o) they burned. Numbers 11:1, 3.
**verse 10.** p) He bowed the heavens and descended. Psalm 18:10, Psalm 144:5. q) Deuteronomy 33:11. r) [interpretation of the Hebrew word for "feet"]. compare Deuteronomy 33:26, Isaiah 19:1. s) compare Exodus 25:18, 22. Psalm 99:1, Isaiah 3:1, 10:31. t) He was seen; He appeared to be present. Psalm 18, verse [7]. u) Psalm 104:3.
**verse 12.** x) you consider them thick and dark clouds, as in Deuteronomy 4:11. y) pavilions, in which He Himself, being angry, as if lay hidden. z) others derive it from an Arabic root meaning "collected" or "gathered." A gathering or a constriction. Others, by switching the letters, suggest "darkness of water," comparing Psalm 18:12. So also Tiz. "dark waters." compare below at verse 16 with Psalm 18:16. a) thick clouds. Exodus 19:9, 1 Kings 18:45. b) of many clouds. Deuteronomy 33:26.
**verse 13.** c) Psalm 4:5, Ezekiel 10:4. d) verse 9. The eruption of the storm is now described.
**verse 14.** e) He thundered. 1 Samuel 7:10, Psalm 29:3, Amos 1:6, 18:8. f) specifically the thunder, compare Amos 1:2.
**verse 15.** g) lightning bolts, that is, He made lightning. h) and He scattered the enemies. Jeremiah 13:24. i) He sent out lightning. Psalm 144:6. k) and He threw them into confusion. Exodus 14:24.
**verse 16.** l) channels, Joel 1:20.
</margin>

verse 16. **אֲפִיקֵי** <note>original: "afikei" (channels)</note> written "defective" <note>term: Defective spelling (chaser) occurs when a vowel-indicating letter, like Yod, is omitted in the written text.</note> in 6, 9, 22. <note>
verse 33. The word "my fortress" [Ma'uzzi] is "defective" [missing a letter], using a Kibbutz vowel followed by a Dagesh mark. Verse 34. "My feet" [Reglay] is without the letter Iod in the text. "And upon" [Ve-al] has the Marca accent in various manuscripts (1, 7, 8, etc.). "My high places" [Bamotay] is written "plene" [with full letters]. These technical notes refer to the Masora (the tradition of the Hebrew text) and the Erffurt codex.
</note>

**Critical Notes:**
**verse 37. g)** 1 Chronicles 11:39. A Dagesh <note>a grammatical dot emphasizing a letter</note> in the letter Yod is found in manuscripts 3, 12, 17, 18, and Berlin. **verse 38.** The Masorah <note>the traditional system of notes on the Hebrew biblical text</note> requires a "Piska" or Space here between *Gareb* and *the Ithrite*, and in **verse 39** between *the Hittite* and *all*. **CHAPTER XXIV. verse 3.** *Ve-yosef* <note>"may He add"</note> uses a different vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 5, 8, 9, 20. **verse 5.** The Masorah requires a specific spelling for *Aroer* at 2 Kings 10:33, but without support from the manuscripts. A *Gimel* vowel is requested by the Masorah here, though it notes that a *Kamets* vowel is found in some books. **verse 9.** Manuscript Berlin alone has a specific musical accent [Munach] on the word for *drawing [the sword]*. **verse 10.** *The people* lacks a space in many manuscripts. **verse 11.** *In the morning* lacks a space in several manuscripts. **verse 13.** *Years* lacks a space in some, contrary to the Masorah.
</insert>

Rashi <note>A famous medieval Jewish commentator</note> describes them thus: It is a sharp wooden instrument, or cut all around and heavy, which they pull continuously over the straw so that it is chopped up, making chaff for the cattle's food.

<margin>
r) 2 Samuel 23:16. s) see Numbers 12:26.
v. 14. t) Chapter 1:26, 1 Samuel 28:15. u) of a father, specifically a chastising one, Hebrews 12:9. But not of an angry one, into whose hands it is terrifying to fall, Hebrews 10:31. Arabic: It will be best for you that the Lord our God should take us to chastise us. John <note>likely a reference to the Targum of Jonathan</note>: into the hand of the Word of the Lord. compare Exodus 3:1 & 7.
x) Psalm 103:8, 13; Sirach 2:18. For enemies are cruel. y) Isaiah 47:6.
v. 15. z) until the time of the assembly, when men come together for sacred rites, Acts 3:1. Jonah <note>Targum Jonathan</note>: until the time when the continual sacrifice was burned. Syriac & Arabic: until the sixth hour of the day. Bochart (Hieroz. P. I. lib 2. c. 31) understands it as the evening time, the first plague of the day. Others think the pestilence raged until that three-day period (v. 13) had passed. But it is more correctly thought that the evil was shortened (Matthew 24:22) because immediately here in v. 16 it is added that God repented of the evil. Now, God does not "repent" of evil, i.e., of punishment already inflicted, but of that to be inflicted (Jeremiah 26:3, 13, 18, 19). Not that God is changeable, but because He revokes what He had decreed under a certain condition (namely, if David and the people did not repent). Nor would God be said to have restrained the Angel if the Angel had already fulfilled whatever was his duty. a) Because David wished to pride himself on the multitude of the people, therefore God punished him with the reduction of the people. Schmid. Yet the people were not entirely innocent; see v. 1 & 17.
v. 16. b) at the suppliant prayers of David and the people. compare Jonah 3:10, 1 Chronicles 21:16. c) Judges 21:5. d) Exodus 12:23. e) Deuteronomy 1:6. f) 1 Chronicles 21:15, Nehemiah 9:9. g) in visible form, compare v. 17, 1 Chronicles 21:15 following. h) v. 18, ch 5:6.

v. 14. "Please" (Na) with Dagesh in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 15, 16, 19, 20, 21. v. 16. ## OF KINGS,
Hebrew:
# מלכים א

The history of the church and the Israelite republic is continued in this book under the Kings for 118 years: of which 40 years belong to Solomon (chapters 1–11), and the remainder to his four successors in Judah: Rehoboam (chapters 12–14), Abijah, Asa, and Jehoshaphat (chapters 15–22), as well as eight Kings of Israel.

<summary>This page details King Solomon's consolidation of power by executing his brother Adonijah, banishing the priest Abiathar, and ordering the execution of the general Joab at the altar, fulfilling divine prophecies and securing his throne.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative from 1 Kings chapter 2. Following Solomon's decision to execute Adonijah for his political maneuvering, the king now turns his attention to the remaining conspirators and those who posed a threat to his father David’s legacy, specifically Joab and Shimei.</meta>

<summary>This page describes the consolidation of Solomon's kingdom through the execution of Joab for his past murders and the conditional house arrest of Shimei. It concludes with Shimei breaking his oath to stay in Jerusalem, leading to his final confrontation with Solomon.</summary>

--- Page 604 ---
<meta>This page concludes the administrative purges of Solomon’s early reign and transitions into his legendary request for wisdom. It follows the execution of Shimei, which solidified Solomon’s internal control, allowing him to focus on international alliances and the centralizing of religious worship.</meta>

46 [The kingdom] shall be established before the Lord forever. And the king commanded Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he went out and struck him <note>referring to Shimei</note> down, and he died. And the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.

# CHAPTER 3.

1 And Solomon made an alliance by marriage with Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he took Pharaoh’s daughter and brought her into the City of David, until he finished building his own house, and the house of the Lord, and the wall of Jerusalem all around. 2 Only the people were sacrificing at the high places <note>Hebrew: *bamot*; these were local outdoor altars</note>, for a house had not yet been built for the name of the Lord until those days. 3 And Solomon loved the Lord, walking in the statutes of David his father; only he sacrificed and burned incense at the high places. 4 And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place; a thousand burnt offerings did Solomon offer on that altar. 5 At Gibeon the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night; and God said, “Ask what I shall give you.” 6 And Solomon said, “You have shown great kindness to your servant David my father, as he walked before you in truth, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart with you; and you have kept for him this great kindness, and you have given him a son to sit on his throne, as it is this day. 7 And now, O Lord my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father; and I am but a small youth; I do not know how to go out or come in. 8 And your servant is in the midst of your people whom you have chosen, a great people, that cannot be numbered nor counted for multitude. 9 Give therefore your servant an understanding heart to judge your people, to discern between good and evil; for who is able to judge this your heavy <note>original: *kaved*, meaning both numerous and burdensome</note> people?” 10 And the speech pleased the Lord, that Solomon had asked this thing. 11 And God said to him, “Because you have asked this thing, and have not asked for yourself long life, nor have you asked riches for yourself, nor have you asked the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to hear judgment; 12 Behold, I have done according to your words; behold, I have given you a wise and understanding heart, so that there has been none like you.”

<summary>This page records the final establishment of Solomon's throne and his famous dream at Gibeon where he requests an "understanding heart" rather than long life or wealth. The scholarly marginalia debate the morality of his marriage to Pharaoh's daughter and the legality of using high places for sacrifice before the Temple's completion.</summary>

¶ 4. For "statute" <note>original: חֲקַת</note> manuscript 1 has "my statutes" <note>original: חֻקַּי</note> in the margin. * verse 15. The word "and he awoke" <note>original: וַיִּקַץ</note> has the letter Qoph without a Dagesh dot in manuscripts 2, 3, 21 and the Berlin edition; manuscript 1 has it with a Raphe mark; the others have a Dagesh. The name "Lord" <note>original: אֲדֹנָי</note> is thus in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 20 according to the final Masora of 3; the rest have "Yahweh" <note>original: יְהוָֹה</note>. Verse 18: "besides us two" <note>original: זוּלָתִי שְׁתַּיִם</note> in 3, 6, 9, 14, 20, 21, 22. Verse 20: "sleeping" <note>original: יְשֵׁנָה</note> written in full by the Westerners, but lacking a letter by the Easterners according to Masora 1 and the Erfurt manuscript. "And behold" <note>original: וְהִנֵּה</note> in verse 21: Munster uses a Makkaph <note>hyphen</note> in 1, 8, 9, 12, 14, 15, 20, 23. Verse 24: Manuscripts 2, 5, 10, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23 leave a space before "Fetch me" <note>original: קְחוּ־לִי</note> as found in 3, 7, 8, 10, 13, 17, 18, 19 and Berlin; but others use a Makkaph. Verse 25: A marginal note in 17 and Berlin is superfluous. * Verse 26: "They said" <note>original: אָמְרוּ</note> with a Zakef-Katon accent in 1, 2, 5. <summary>This page contains the biblical account of the Judgment of Solomon, where the king identifies the true mother of a child by proposing to divide it in two, demonstrating his God-given wisdom. The accompanying scholarly notes provide textual variants and cross-references to theological interpretations of Solomon's intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the spiritual gift of wisdom Solomon received at Gibeon to the practical organization of his kingdom. It lists the high-ranking officials of the royal court and the twelve governors responsible for the logistics of the monarchy, demonstrating how Solomon’s "understanding heart" was applied to the complex administration of a flourishing nation.</meta>

**Chapter IV.**
**What we owe.** In Hebrew, these are said to be *upon us*. 2 Samuel 18, 11.

# 1 KINGS. CHAPTER 5.

<margin>
**v. 17. k)** see 1 Chronicles 28:3 and the note on 2 Samuel 7:1. **l)** with which enemies surrounded him from the beginning of his reign. See a similar construction in Psalm 109:3. **m)** until the Lord gave [the land], chapter 17:14. **x)** Malachi 3:21; Romans 16:20. Compare Joshua 10:24.

...to build a house for the name of the Lord his God, because of the wars which^k surrounded him^l until the Lord put them^m under the soles of his feet^n. **18** But now, the Lord^o my God has given me rest on every side^p; there is no adversary^q <note>original: "Satan"</note> and no evil occurrence^r. **19** And behold^s, I intend to build a house for the name of the Lord my God, as the Lord spoke to David my father, saying: "Your son, whom I will set upon your throne in your place, he shall build the house for my name."^t

<margin>
**v. 20. t)** see verse 13; Ezra 3:7. **u)** God had granted the inhabitants of Tyre and Sidon a sharp, lively, and versatile intellect. Arithmetic and Astronomy flowed from them to the Greeks—but their chief fame came from the mechanical arts. The mixing of purple dye at Tyre, and glassmaking and the weaving of fine linens from the thinnest flax at Sidon, are said to have been first invented there. Solomon greatly praises the skill of these craftsmen. Through these arts, their wealth grew immensely in a short time, as they were able to devote themselves to them during long periods of peace. Compare Judges 18:7; Bochart, *Phaleg*, page 343 and following.
</margin>

**20** Now therefore^u, command that they cut for me cedars from Lebanon; and my servants shall be with your servants, and I will give you wages for your servants^x according to all that you say; for you know^y that there is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians^z.

<center>

# 7

1 <gloss>g</gloss> **But Solomon was building his own house for thirteen years, and he finished all his house.**

2 <gloss>h</gloss> **He built also the House of the Forest of Lebanon; its length was a hundred cubits, and its breadth fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits, upon four rows of cedar columns, with cedar beams upon the columns.**

3 **And it was paneled with cedar above the side-chambers that were upon the columns, forty-five in number, fifteen in a row.**

4 **And there were window frames in three rows, and light was against light in three ranks.**

5 **And all the doors and doorposts were square, with the windows; and light was against light in three ranks.**

6 **And he made a porch of columns; its length was fifty cubits and its breadth thirty cubits; and the porch was before them, and the columns and the thick beam were before them.**

7 **Then he made a porch for the throne where he might judge, even the Porch of Judgment; and it was covered with cedar from one side of the floor to the other.**

8 **And his house where he dwelt had another court within the porch, which was of like workmanship. Solomon also made a house for Pharaoh's daughter, whom he had taken to wife, like unto this porch.**

9 **All these were of costly stones, according to the measures of dressed stones, sawn with saws, within and without, even from the foundation unto the coping, and so on the outside toward the great court.**

10 **And the foundation was of costly stones, even great stones, stones of ten cubits and stones of eight cubits.**

11 **And above were costly stones...**

Ezek. 37:12. d) see v. 23. e) like a lily flower v. 19. 22. f) two thousand baths <note>A 'bath' is a liquid measure of about 22 liters; 2,000 baths equals roughly 44,000 liters</note> ch. 5:2. Ezek. 45:11. Namely, at its maximum it could contain three thousand baths (2 Chron. 4:5), but it was not usually filled except to two thousand. Whence it could be called a "Sea" because of such a great abundance of water, which flowed into it perpetually from the spring of Etham, and again flowed out through the outlets brought out through the mouths or heads of the oxen, of which two rows surrounded the sea. Thus it was a fountain of perennial water, from which the Priests, about to approach their ministry, daily washed their hands and feet, etc. Compare the spiritual type in Eph. 2:3, Zech. 13:1, & Maius's *Economy* <note>Johann Heinrich Maius, Lutheran theologian</note> p. 833. g) it held, contained v. 38. Eph. 40:12.

**43** ...and pray toward this house: You shall hear in heaven, the place of Your dwelling, and do according to all that the foreigner calls to You for, so that all the peoples of the earth may know Your name to fear You, as Your people Israel do, and to know that Your name is called upon this house which I have built.

**44** When Your people go out to war against their enemy, by the way that You shall send them, and they pray to the Lord toward the city which You have chosen, and the house which I have built for Your name:

**45** Then hear in heaven their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause.

**46** When they sin against You—for there is no man who does not sin—and You are angry with them and deliver them before the enemy, and those who take them captive carry them away to the land of the enemy, far off or near:

**47** And if they take it to heart in the land where they were carried captive, and repent and make supplication to You in the land of those who took them captive, saying, "We have sinned, and we have acted perversely, we have done wickedly":

**48** And they return to You with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies who took them captive, and they pray to You toward their land which You gave to their fathers, the city which You have chosen, and the house which I have built for Your name:

**49** Then hear in heaven, the place of Your dwelling, their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause:

**50** And forgive Your people who have sinned against You, and all their transgressions which they have transgressed against You, and grant them compassion before those who took them captive, that they may have compassion on them:

**51** For they are Your people and Your inheritance, whom You brought out of Egypt, from the midst of the iron furnace.

**52** That Your eyes may be open to the supplication of Your servant and to the supplication of Your people Israel, to listen to them in all for which they call to You.

**53** For You did separate them to Yourself for an inheritance from among all the peoples of the earth, as You spoke by the hand of Moses Your servant, when You brought our fathers out of Egypt, O Lord God.

**54** And it was so, that when Solomon had finished praying all this prayer and supplication to the Lord, he rose from before the altar of the Lord, from kneeling on his knees with his hands spread out toward heaven.

**55** And he stood and blessed all the assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying:

**56** Blessed be the Lord, who has given rest to His people Israel, according to all that He promised; not one word has failed of all His good promise, which He promised by the hand of Moses His servant.

<meta>
Translator’s critical notes:
* v. 43. "and pray" appears with the prefix Vav in the 3rd person future in several manuscripts (1, 3, 5) against the final Masoretic reading.
* v. 44. "which" appears later with a Makkaph (hyphen) in sources 1, 2, 5.
* v. 48. "which You gave" is repeated in manuscripts 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 19, 21.
* v. 49. "Your dwelling" is vocalized with a Segol in sources 1, 2, 3, 22; compare verse 39.
* v. 52. "in all for which they call" is recorded thus in 1, 2, 3.
* v. 54. "spread out" follows a Tipcha and Merca accent in 2, 3.
* v. 56. "word" is vocalized with a Tsere in 2, 3, 5, 22, etc. Masorah Magna on Joshua 14:10. Others use a Segol.
</meta>

Note: Deuteronomy 17:16. **i)** 2 Chronicles 1:16. Interpretations vary widely, and we touch only on the most significant. Bochart (*Hier.* P. But Schmidt, Cocceius, and others understand it as "yarn," the Vulgate as "fine linen." Gousset (p. 735), however, understands it as "market" where horses gathered (Jeremiah 3:17, Exodus 7:19, etc.), in this sense: as for the market, the merchants paid a certain price to Solomon so they might be allowed to hold a market for themselves and thus sell horses to the kings of the Hittites and Aramaeans, who could not get them from elsewhere. v. 29. **k)** chariot, or a four-horse team. Compare Ezekiel 23:20; 2 Samuel 8:4. Each chariot cost 600 shekels, for four horses were joined together for each chariot, and 4 men sat in it for fighting; see note on Judges 4:13. **l)** the merchants brought them out by their hand. **CHAPTER XI.** v. 1. **m)** compare 1 Peter 2:11. **n)** v. 8. **o)** compare note on Deuteronomy 17:17. **p)** Noldius: "and that besides." So in v. 25. **q)** a legitimate wife, chapter 3:1. **r)** so that they remained in their pagan superstitions. v. 2. **s)** <note>original Greek: "ὁ' ὡν ἀπέπει-"</note> 2 Corinthians 4:2. **t)** compare Exodus 34:16; Deuteronomy 7:3.

<margin>
**v. 3. z)** Princesses and primary wives. Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note>: "queens." Compare Isaiah 49:23. **a)** Compare note on 2 Samuel 5:13. It is well known that it was the custom among Eastern Kings for wives or concubines to be taken and brought into the women's quarters <note>original Latin: gynæceum</note>, even if they were never intimately known in a matrimonial sense. Thus Abishag, in chapter 1:3, was a concubine of David whom he never "knew." Thus Esther was taken into the royal women's quarters in the third or fourth year of King Ahasuerus, but was only brought to the King in the seventh year, and over several years she was "known" by him only once (Esther 1:3; 2:16). We say this to show that the objections of certain people [regarding the high number of wives] are foolish. *Schmid*. **b)** Compare Nehemiah 13:26.

Kimchi proves this from Ezekiel 37:19, 22, 24; likewise Ralbag and Abravanel. Vatablus observes that this was fulfilled in Christ Jesus our Lord, who sat upon the throne of his father David, according to Luke 1:32. But because the Jews expect a worldly kingdom of the Messiah, Schmid (in his notes on this place, page 67) preferred to say that this must have been fulfilled before the captivity of the ten tribes, though a certain time cannot be defined. But just as the promise made to Jeroboam was conditional, so is this appendix about the return of the kingdom to the seed of David. Meanwhile, from this promise, the right to reclaim the kingdom remained with the house of David, etc. Compare Hosea 8:4, 2 Chronicles 13:5, 6, 7.

Verse 40. i) Compare 1 Samuel 19:1. k) To the one who had succeeded Solomon's father-in-law, see chapter 14:25. l) Here he began to oppose Solomon...

**11** And a certain old prophet was living in Bethel; and his son came and told him all the deed that the man of God had done today in Bethel, the words which he had spoken to the king; and they told them to their father. **12** And their father spoke to them: "Which way did he go?" and his sons had seen the way the man of God who came from Judah had gone. **13** And he said to his sons: "Saddle the donkey for me." And he said: "I am." **15** And he said to him: "Come with me home and eat bread." **16** And he said: "I cannot return with you or go with you, nor will I eat bread or drink water with you in this place. **17** For a word came to me by the word of the LORD: 'You shall not eat bread or drink water there; you shall not return to go by the way you went.'" **18** And he said to him: "I too am a prophet like you, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying: 'Bring him back with you to your house, and let him eat bread and drink water.'" But he lied to him. **19** And he returned with him and ate bread in his house and drank water. **20** And it was, as they sat at the table, that the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back. **21** And he cried out to the man of God who had come from Judah, saying: "Thus says the LORD: Because you have rebelled against the mouth of the LORD and have not kept the commandment which the LORD your God commanded you, **22** but you returned and ate bread and drank water in the place where He said to you, 'Do not eat bread and do not drink water,' your corpse shall not come to the grave of your ancestors." **23** And it was, after he had eaten bread and after he had drunk, that he saddled the donkey for the prophet whom he had brought back. **24** And he went, and a lion found him on the way and killed him; and his corpse was cast on the way, and the donkey was standing...

**c)** ...so that he would not meet anyone who had seen him before, and thus enter into conversation with him again and be delayed. But God knew the mind of this Prophet—that he would rather have stayed—and so He pressed him more firmly with this command. And indeed, the lukewarmness of his zeal is evident from what he said in verse 8: "If you were to give me [half your house]" etc., as if to say: "I would gladly stay and eat with you, but I am not allowed." See verse 16. How cold this is! S. <note>Schmid</note>.

**v. 11. d)** But there was a certain Prophet. The Arabic and Jonah <note>likely referring to the Targum of Jonathan</note>, and Rashi, add: false or lying. So also in verses 25 and 29. It seems clear enough that he had become an idolater and wicked (or at least a hypocrite) and was deprived of the prophetic gift, however much he might have possessed it before. Schmid. **e)** who had come from Samaria. 2 Kings 23:18. Intending to look out for his own advantage there. Schmid. **f)** which (he said) he did today. A mixture of speech from the words of the writer and the son reporting it. S. **g)** and these things the rest of the sons also narrated.

**v. 12. h)** by which [way]? 2 Kings 3:8; Job 38:24. **i)** they had seen indeed. But the Arabic and Syriac, from the *Hiphil* <note>a Hebrew verb form indicating causative action</note>, translated it as "they showed," which Luther followed. Vatablus: they saw, that is, they searched out. S. And when they had seen. So compare 1 Samuel 23:22.

**v. 13. k)** verses 22 and 27. **l)** for the old man could not catch up with the other on foot. Compare 2 Samuel 19:27.

**v. 14. m)** Hypocritically, he intended to insinuate himself into his familiarity, as if he strongly approved of his Prophecy, and as one to whom Jeroboam's impiety had always been displeasing. We believe, however, that his conscience truly rebuked him. But he entered upon a way of repentance that was not true, but hypocritical, by veiling his sin. And he would have perished, had he not reached a sounder repentance through the fall of the Prophet, as seen below.
</margin>

...violently, before you return to your homeland, you shall perish. See verses 24, 29, 30. See also chapter 14:13. **v. 23. c)** S. The old man prepared [the donkey] in verse 13. **v. 24. d)** Chapter 20:26. **e)** verse 25. Although severe, this judgment was nonetheless just: by which we are taught that not even the smallest of God’s commands are to be neglected, as Theodorete holds here. Compare Matthew 5:19; James 2:10. Furthermore, by this very punishment inflicted upon a prophet who was otherwise holy, God wished to deter idolaters from wicked worship, thus taught how fearful it is to fall into the hands of the living God—from whom it was right to demand punishments so much heavier as they sinned more gravely. *Bochart, Hierozoicon Part I, page 207.*

->**Philological Notes on the Hebrew Text**<-
Verse 10: "which" <note>Hebrew: *asher*</note> with a joining mark <note>Makkaph</note> occurs in versions 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 20. Verse 11: "God" <note>Hebrew: *ha-Elohim*</note> without a pause mark <note>Pshik</note> in 1, 3. Verse 13: "to him" <note>Hebrew: *lo*</note> with the *Pashta* accent. Verse 17: "you shall eat" <note>Hebrew: *tokhal*</note> with the accent on the penultimate syllable <note>milel</note>. "And you shall not return" with the prefix *Vav*. Verse 22: "which" <note>Hebrew: *asher*</note> with a joining mark <note>Makkaph</note>.

# I KINGS. CHAPTER 13. 14. יג יד

<margin>
**f)** Compare verse 28. Rabbi Levi rightly asserts that this was a great miracle <note>original: "magnum miraculum"</note>. For it was contrary to the nature of a lion that it did not touch the corpse, nor attack the donkey, nor the travelers passing through there; it abstained from prey so obvious and available. It was also against the nature of the donkey that, upon seeing the lion, it was not terrified, nor did it seek safety in flight. Furthermore, the lion not only spared the corpse and the beast of burden, but even protected them, as if stationed as a guardian, so that the miracle would be more illustrious and not believed to have happened by chance. But God also wished to honor him as a Prophet, whom He had punished as a transgressor (Bochart). Without doubt, the slain Prophet repented. Hence Josiah also held his tomb in honor, as that of a holy man; and God vindicated the truth of His words. S. <note>Sebastian Schmid</note>

# CHAPTER XVII.

**1** And Elijah the Tishbite, of the inhabitants of Gilead, said to Ahab, "As the Lord God of Israel lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, except at my word."
**2** Then the word of the Lord came to him, saying:
**3** "Get away from here and turn eastward, and hide yourself by the Brook Cherith, which flows into the Jordan.
**4** And it shall be that you shall drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there."
**5** So he went and did according to the word of the Lord, for he went and stayed by the Brook Cherith, which flows into the Jordan.
**6** The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening; and he drank from the brook.
**7** And it happened after a while that the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land.

---

> v. 1. "The Lord lives": a word brought forth by God’s command, whatever others may falsely claim. At my imprecations the evil will begin, and at my prayers it will end (Grotius, compare James 5:17). This famine, lasting three and a half years (cf. chapter 18:1; Luke 4:25; James 5:17) in the idolatrous kingdom of Ahab, is a type of the scarcity of saving food in the Antichristian kingdom for three mystical years and a half (Revelation 11:2, 3, 6). q, r, s, t) "to the torrent" (chapter 15:13). x) properly so in verse 5. Some think this is the same as the "Brook Kanah" <note>the brook of reeds</note> (Joshua 16:8; 17:9) from the abundance of reeds in which Elijah hid. See also Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, Part II, page 216. y) "before the Jordan," into which it eventually flows.
> 
> V. 4. z) "and the ravens." So the Septuagint, Jonathan, Syriac, Vulgate, and Western versions, as well as Josephus, Jerome, most Hebrews, and all teachers of the Church. The same Hebrew word signifies "merchants" (Ezekiel 27:27) and "sureties" (Proverbs 22:26) or those exchanging something (Nehemiah 5:3); but always with an addition indicating that meaning. When placed alone (unless it is a proper name, as in Judges 7:25), it altogether denotes "ravens," as in verse 6, Proverbs 30:17, etc. Because this seems absurd to some rational minds (as Bochart notes), some have believed it refers to others: Kimchi mentions some who think "nobles," others "merchants," others "Arabs," and others "Orehim" as a name of a tribe or family; others explain it as "citizens of a city" (but specifically Orbo). Thus in the Talmud (Tractate Chullin, chapter 1, folio 5a), three opinions are recorded: 1) regarding literal ravens; 2) regarding two men so named, like Oreb the prince of Midian (Judges 7:25); 3) regarding men from a place—that is, following Rashi's explanation—called from the "Rock of Oreb"; however, the spelling would have to be different, as both the Gemara and marginal notes point out. Similarly, in *Bereshit Rabbah*, the Rabbis disagree. Rabbi Judah says: it was a small town on the borders of Beth-Shean whose name was Orbo. The commentator *Mattenot Kehunnah* agrees; well enough, if only they could prove what they confidently conjecture according to their custom! Therefore, Rabbi Nehemiah immediately objects there that literal ravens are to be understood. And Kimchi, Rabbi Levi, Abarbanel, Ben Melech, and Ibn Ezra defend this literal view with good reason. For this is not a new opinion recently adorned in a French pamphlet, but one long ago defended by the most learned Bochart and other moderns (*Hierozoicon*, Part II, book II, chapter 13, page 214). Lightfoot also mentions that fictional town in his *Chorography* (Mark, Chapter VII, section 7). But he approves of Kimchi's contrary objection: God commanded Elijah to hide himself so that no one would know he was there. We see that Ahab sought him everywhere, etc. a) Kimchi correctly notes: "I have put it into their minds," as in verse 9. To command brute animals is to use their instincts to execute His decrees (see Isaiah 5:6; Amos 9:3; Jonah 2:11; 2 Chronicles 7:13; Psalm 33:9; Isaiah 23:8; 28:6). b) through a miracle, as in verses 14, 15. God wanted this service to be performed by ravens—which an Angel performs in chapter 19:5, 6—to teach that all creatures are under His command (Bochart, chapter 5). c) see verse 3. d) see verse 4. e) from wherever God willed. f) which he ate skillfully, because God so commanded (Rabbi Levi).

</margin>

w. z. x) Here Gilgal, verse 1; compare verses 4, 6, and 1 Kings 12:12.

d) Bethel was a school of the Prophets, who asserted and defended the worship of the true God with all their might. **v. 7.** *Nishyeki*. Thus the Shurek point (as the method of the *Keri* and *Ketiv* requires) is expressed in the text in 3, 8, 28; compare Acts 5:3, 16. 39 One went out into the field to gather herbs, and he found a wild vine and gathered from it wild gourds, his garment full. He came and sliced them into the pot of stew, for they did not know what they were.
40 Then they poured it out for the men to eat. And it happened as they were eating the stew, they cried out and said, "There is death in the pot, O man of God!" And they could not eat it.
41 But he said, "Then bring flour." And he threw it into the pot and said, "Pour it out for the people, that they may eat." And there was nothing harmful in the pot.

<margin>compare Esther 3:13; chapter 8:10; 2 Samuel 11:14. m) that is, with him. Genesis 24:10; chapter 43:12; etc. n) see 2 Samuel 12:30. o) S. 6000 pieces of gold, or gold coins.</margin>

->**Prophetic Reading for Tazria**<-
<note>original Hebrew: "Haftarat Tazria"; this marks the selection from the Prophets read in the synagogue alongside the Torah portion of Tazria (Leviticus 12-13), which deals with skin diseases and purification.</note>

<margin>v. 42. k) Rashio <note>Baal-Shalishah</note> is the name of a province. see 1 Samuel 9:4. l) see note 1 Samuel 9:7. m) compare Numbers 18:12, 15. n) Judges 7:13. Greek Septuagint as in John 6:9. o) green fruit <note>fresh ears of grain</note>. see Leviticus 2:14; 23:14. p) S. in its husk. Tigurine Bible: in its little bags. Jonathan, Syriac, Arabic: in his garment. Vulgate: in his pouch (1) Gousset says the same as "basket" <note>original Hebrew: "tene"</note> in Deuteronomy 26:2.</margin>

<margin>Understanding "shekels" of gold, as in Numbers 7:13. p) changes of garments. verse 22, 23; Genesis 45:22; Judges 14:12, 13. These "changeable garments," which they possessed and desired in such numbers, are to be understood according to the custom of the Orientals—now among the Moroccans and those long ago descended from the East—where it is the custom to wear white, soft linen garments layered over other clothes for the sake of ornament; and because they easily lose their exquisite brightness, they change them often. <note>referencing the scholar Gousset, p. 263</note></margin>

42 A man came from Baal-Shalishah, and he brought the man of God bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh grain in his sack. And Elisha said, "Give it to the people, that they may eat."
43 But his servant said, "What? Shall I set this before a hundred men?" He said again, "Give it to the people, that they may eat; for thus says the Lord: 'They shall eat and have some left over.'"
44 So he set it before them, and they ate and had some left over, according to the word of the Lord.

1 Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Aram, was a great man in the sight of his master and highly respected, because through him the Lord had given victory to Aram. He was a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper.
2 Now the Arameans had gone out in raids and had taken captive a young girl from the land of Israel, and she served Naaman’s wife.
3 She said to her mistress, "Oh, that my lord were before the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him of his leprosy."
4 So Naaman went in and told his lord, saying, "Thus and so spoke the girl who is from the land of Israel."
5 Then the king of Aram said, "Go now, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel." So he departed and took in his hand ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of clothes.
6 He brought the letter to the king of Israel, which said: "And now, when this letter comes to you, behold, I have sent Naaman my servant to you, that you may heal him of his leprosy."
7 When the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and said, "Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man sends to me to heal a man of his leprosy? Only consider, and see how he is seeking a quarrel with me."
8 But when Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, he sent word to the king, saying, "Why have you torn your clothes? Let him come now to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel."

***

<margin>from 1 Kings 20:7. a) let him seize an opportunity. Psalm 91:10; compare Judges 14:4. Greek Septuagint: "He seeks a pretext." Compare John 15:22. 20. Chapter 4:25. c) verse 7. As if to say: Why do you not finally at some point recognize Jehovah and His true worship, having cast off idolatrous worship and persistent impiety? d) a true prophet, and a true God. verse 15.</margin>

v. 40. **and they said** <note>Hebrew: "Vayomeru"</note> thus with a *Pashta* accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20; but others have a *Kadma* accent. *v. 41.* **and take** <note>Hebrew: "Ukchu"</note> without the prefix "and" in manuscript 1. *v. 42.* **twenty** <note>Hebrew: "Esrim"</note> with a repeated *Munach* accent in 1, 3, 6, 9, 20. *v. 43.* **the God** <note>Hebrew: "Ha-Elohim"</note>... **and he said** in 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 13, 14, 15, 19. *v. 8.* **and he sent to the king** thus in 2, 5. <note>These notes refer to variations in musical accents and spelling found in different medieval Hebrew manuscripts.</note>

9 So Naaman came with his horses and with his chariot, and stood at the door of the house of Elisha.
10 And Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, "Go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh shall be restored to you, and you shall be clean."
11 But Naaman was wroth, and went away, and said, "Behold, I thought, 'He will surely come out to me, and stand, and call on the name of the Lord his God, and wave his hand over the place, and recover the leper.'"
12 "Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? may I not wash in them, and be clean?" So he turned and went away in a rage.
13 And his servants came near, and spoke to him, and said, "My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, 'Wash, and be clean'?"
14 Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
15 And he returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and came, and stood before him: and he said, "Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel: now therefore, I pray thee, take a blessing <note>original Hebrew: "berakhah," meaning a gift or present</note> from thy servant."
16 But he said, "As the Lord liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none." And he urged him to take it; but he refused.
17 And Naaman said, "Shall there not then, I pray thee, be given to thy servant two mules' burden of earth? for thy servant will henceforth offer neither burnt offering nor sacrifice unto other gods, but unto the Lord."
18 "In this thing the Lord pardon thy servant, that when my master goeth into the house of Rimmon to worship there, and he leaneth on my hand, and I bow myself in the house of Rimmon: when I bow down myself in the house of Rimmon, the Lord pardon thy servant in this thing."
19 And he said unto him, "Go in peace." So he departed from him a little way.
20 But Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, "Behold, my master hath spared Naaman this Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought: but, as the Lord liveth, I will run after him, and take somewhat of him."
21 So Gehazi followed after Naaman. And when Naaman saw him running after him, he lighted down from the chariot to meet him, and said, "Is all well?"
22 And he said, "All is well. My master hath sent me, saying, 'Behold, even now there be come to me from mount Ephraim two young men of the sons of the prophets...'"

**v. 6.** <term>V’Adonai</term> ("And the Lord") is written with a "moving Aleph" in various manuscripts. The Masorah <note>The traditional notes on the Hebrew biblical text</note> of the first printed edition of Genesis 19:24 directs that it be written as <term>V’Adonah</term> here, contrary to the second printed edition and the Erfurt manuscript. Likewise, the name <term>Yehovah</term> is found without the vowel point on the letter *Vav*. Regarding the phrase "and the sound like," some books include the prefix "And." **v. 7.** <term>ka’asher</term> ("as/when") is written with a *Maqqeph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note>. The word <term>hi</term> ("it") is written with a *Vav* in the text of many manuscripts, though others have <term>hu</term> ("he/it") in the text and <term>hi</term> in the margin. **v. 8.** <term>Ha-metzoraim</term> ("The lepers") is written with a *Dagesh* <note>a dot indicating a double or hardened consonant</note> in most manuscripts. **v. 9.** "And they told the house" is marked with a *Zakef Katan* <note>a specific musical/grammatical accent</note> in several editions. **v. 11.** The word "And he called" was corrected to "And they called" in many manuscripts and the Berlin edition. **v. 16.** <term>Solet</term> ("fine flour") is written with a *Dagesh* in the letter *Samekh*. The word <term>asher</term> ("which") is written with a *Kadma* accent.

1 Now Elisha had spoken to the woman whose son he had restored to life, saying, "Arise and go, <gloss>read: you</gloss> and your household, and dwell wherever you can dwell; for the Lord has called for a famine, and it is coming upon the land for seven years." 2 So the woman arose and did according to the word of the man of God; she went with her household and dwelt as a stranger in the land of the Philistines for seven years. 3 At the end of seven years, the woman returned from the land of the Philistines and went out to appeal to the king for her house and for her field. 4 Now the king was speaking to Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, saying, "Please tell me all the great things that Elisha has done." 5 And it happened that as he was telling the king how he had restored the dead to life, behold, the woman whose son he had restored to life was appealing to the king for her house and for her field. And Gehazi said, "My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is her son whom Elisha restored to life." 6 When the king asked the woman, she told him the story. So the king appointed a certain official for her, saying, "Restore all that was hers, and all the produce of the field from the day she left the land until now."

#### Textual Notes:
\* 25. **Year**: Manuscript 20 omits this word, and it is missing in the text of chapter 9. \* 26. **And his mother's name was Athaliah**: So in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5. \* 29. **When he fought**: Written with a *Caph* instead of *Beth* in manuscripts 6, 9 in the margin. **He went down**: With the accent *Tilcha* in 1, 2, 5. **He was sick**: Voweled as *milel* in 2, 30. **CHAPTER IX, v. 1. And you shall come**: Masoretic note printed at Numbers 28:26, and found in manuscripts 1, 2, and the Erfurt manuscript here. For similar accents, compare Genesis 8:18; Ezekiel 7:25; chapter 10:13; 11:18, etc. **v. 3. to/over**: Manuscript 5 and 20 use "upon" instead of "to," as does the text of chapter 9 and likely manuscript 2. **The door**: With the accent *Sakeph-katon* in manuscripts 1, 2, and likely 5. **v. 7. And you shall strike**: With the accent *Sakeph-gadol* in manuscript 5. **v. 10. Jezebel**: Incorrectly marked with *Gerashayim* in manuscripts 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 21, and Berlin. **And Jezreel**: With a *Segol* vowel in manuscript 23; here in manuscript 1.

<margin>1</margin> In the seventh year of Jehu, Jehoash began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. **v. 28.** *And his might:* Thus in manuscripts 2 and 3, and likewise in 5; but with a Pashta accent in 1. *He warred:* with a Patach vowel in 1, 2, 5, 23. According to the Masorah in 1, 2 and the Erfurt manuscript, but contrary to the printed Masorah in this place; likewise in the printed text for Judges 9, 17. **CHAPTER XV, v. 2.** *In Jerusalem:* with a Munach accent in place of a Metheg in 3, 6, 9, 11, 14, 16, 20, 21; but manuscripts 1 and 2 write it as a single word. **v. 10.** *Before the people:* Thus the letter Kuph has a Chateph-Qamets vowel without a Metheg in 6, 9, 11, 14, 16, 20, 21; but 1 and 2 write it as one word: *Kabal-am*. In 3 and 5, it sounds like a proper name of a man according to those who read *Keblaam*. **v. 13.** *Of Azariah:* instead of this, some have *L'Azaryah* (just as the same king is called in verses 1, 2, 3); thus in 1 and 5, and thus the Vulgate and Jonathan read.

<note>TEXTUAL NOTES AND VARIANTS</note>

*. 26. **Shebna** spelled with an *Aleph* in three manuscripts, and in the margins of six others, contrary to the Masoretic and Erfurt traditions; compare verse 18. *. 27. **The wall** [Ha-chomah] thus with the *Munach* accent in most; but with *Metheg* in manuscripts 2, 3, 6, 9, 14, 16, 20, 21, 22, 23. *. 29. **Shall deceive** [yashi] defective in 1, 22. According to Masorah I. — **From his hand** [miyado] thus in manuscript 3, but with the traditional reading (Qere) "from my hand" [miyadi], which is how the Eastern tradition writes it in the text. *. 31. **Make** [asu] with the *Maqqeph* joining mark in 7, 8, 10, 13, 14, 19. *. 32. **And honey** [u-devash] with the *Kametz* vowel in 2, 3, 6, 9, 14, 16, 20, 21, 22, 23. *. 33. **Has [it] delivered** [ha-hatzel] with the *Chirek* vowel and defective spelling in 1, 22, 23 according to Masorah I. *. 34. **Samaria** [Shomron]; in place of this, another codex has "their land" [artzam] in the margin of 2. *. 37. **The words** [et divrei]; in place of this, some have "the specific words" [et ha-divrei] without the marker in 2, 5, and in the Western tradition. CHAPTER XIX. *. 2. **And he sent** [vayishlach] with the *Tifcha* accent in 1, 2, 5. *. 3. **To him** [alav] with the *Zakeph-Katon* accent in 17, 18, 20 and in the Berlin manuscript.
