<note>
**v. 20.** "Concerning Sennacherib": Others read "against Sennacherib." The Eastern manuscripts have a different preposition.
**v. 22.** "Voice": written without a *Dagesh* [a grammatical dot marking emphasis] in several manuscripts. The text varies between the written form and the traditional reading across different codices.
**v. 23.** "With the multitude of my chariots": In some versions, it is written as "With the chariot of my chariots." There is a significant discussion among scholars (like Hiller and Erf) about whether the *Ketiv* [written text] should imply "with my chariots and chariot-drivers," meaning the entire military force. "His end" is also noted as a variant in several marginal readings and specific codices.
**v. 25.** "Have you not": Marked with a specific musical accent (*Kadma*) in several early printed editions. Regarding the word for "ruining," there is a note that a letter is missing in some manuscripts, a point debated by medieval commentators like Kimchi.
**v. 27.** "And your rage": Thus it appears in several major manuscripts.
**v. 29.** "In the year": Some manuscripts use the definite article ("in *the* year") while others omit it.
</note>

<summary>God responds to King Hezekiah's prayer through the prophet Isaiah, mocking the pride of the Assyrian King Sennacherib and promising that Jerusalem will be miraculously spared without a single arrow being fired. The text includes a promise of a "remnant" that will survive and thrive once the siege is lifted.</summary>

Furthermore, it is noteworthy that this history is also read in Herodotus, but corrupted by the Egyptian priests; who, envying the God of Israel for the glory of the Assyrian defeat, attributed it to their god Vulcan <note>The Roman name for the Greek Hephaestus</note>. For he writes in Book II that a multitude of field mice poured out upon the enemies at night, eating their quivers, bows, and the handles of their shields, so that the next day the enemies, stripped of their weapons, fled with many losses. And for this reason, that King Sennacherib now stands as a stone statue in the Temple of Vulcan, holding a mouse in his hand, and saying these words through letters: <term>εἰς ἐμέ τις ὁρέων εὐσεβὴς ἔστω</term> <note>original Greek: "Let whoever looks upon me be pious."</note>.

<summary>This page records the miraculous destruction of the Assyrian army by an angel and the subsequent assassination of Sennacherib by his own sons. It also details King Hezekiah’s terminal illness, his successful plea for longer life, and the astronomical miracle of the sundial shadow retreating as a divine sign.</summary>

# II KINGS. CHAPTER 25.

<margin>
**verse 22. g)** Regarding the people who remained. Compare chapter 24:18; 2 Samuel 4:10. **h)** See verse 12. **i)** He appointed (see verse 23; chapter 7:17). **k)** Whose fates are described in more detail in Jeremiah 40:5 and following.
**verse 23. l)** See verse 15; 1 Kings 15:20. See the plural in Jeremiah 40:7 and following. **m)** Mizpah in the tribe of Benjamin (1 Kings 15:22) or of Gilead (Judges 11:11, 29, 34; Joshua 13:11). <note>Mizpah was an important administrative center north of Jerusalem.</note> **n)** Especially that Ishmael mentioned in verse 25. **o)** 2 Samuel 23:28, 29. **p)** Jeremiah 40:8. **q)** Compare 2 Samuel 23:34.
**verse 24. r)** Compare Jeremiah 40:9. **s)** "That it may be well," or "it shall be well with you" (Jeremiah 38:20). Although the face of the Judean Church was sad after the city and the sacred house were occupied and overturned, it should rightly be considered a great benefit that they were able to hear and read the Divine Word, to live securely, to have the necessary supports of life, and to enjoy the protection of Gedaliah who was left in the Holy Land. Nor should it be considered a small gift that the Prophet Jeremiah lived among them, from whose mouth they could always be taught and instructed concerning the will of God and their duties toward God and neighbor. See Jeremiah 40:2 and following. But in truth, they did not show themselves worthy or sufficiently grateful for so many and such great benefits; indeed, they were far worse than those who lived in the midst of enemies in Babylonia, as Jeremiah predicted in chapter 24. When they could have lived securely in Judea under the leader Gedaliah, etc. See following and compare Maius’ *Economy of the Old Testament*, page 1024.

# ON THE PROPHET ISAIAH
## PREFACE.

->$\S$. I.<-

<margin>Order of the Biblical books and the Prophets.</margin>
Having completed the books of Moses and several historical books *a)*, we come to the Prophets. Among these, the "Major" works are placed first, followed by those considered "Minor," which the Hebrews call the <term>תרי עשר</term> <note>original: "Trei Asar," meaning "The Twelve"</note> and we call the *Minor Prophets* *b)*. However, the ancient Rabbis have handed down a memory that a different order existed in some ancient codices: in that arrangement, *Jeremiah* was first, *Ezekiel* second, and only then *Isaiah*. For more on this, one may consult our various *readings at the beginning of Jeremiah* and the *Dissertation on Manuscript Codices of the Bible*, section 5.

<margin>Isaiah is the first among these.</margin>
Nevertheless, *Isaiah* deservedly holds the very first place among the Prophets. This is not contradicted by the chronology of his time, as his recorded prophecies either preceded the others or were at least contemporary with them *c)*. We say this even without emphasizing the more eminent prophetic gift found in *Isaiah*, or his royal lineage—though *Isaac Abarbanel* <note>A 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> stresses both points in *column 1 and 2 of the first page of his Commentary*. Abarbanel notes that Isaiah began his work *near the start of King Uzziah's reign*, and thus entirely before Hose-

---
->)(<-

*a)* These are the books which the Hebrews call the *Former Prophets* <note>original: "Prophetae priores"</note> to distinguish them from the divine writers we call the *Latter Prophets* <note>original: "posteriores"</note>. The book of *Daniel* is referred to the third category, the *Writings* <note>original: "Hagiographa"</note>, though without a just reason.

*b)* *Augustine* <note>The influential 4th-5th century theologian</note> says in *The City of God, Book 18, chapter 29*: *“They are called 'minor' because their discourses are brief in comparison to those called 'major,' who are so named because they produced extensive volumes.”* Likewise, *Abarbanel* in his *Preface to Isaiah, page 1, column 2* says: *“Because those twelve Prophets are small in bulk, they were collected into a single volume.”*

*c)* This is true unless you except that oracle of *Jonah* mentioned in *2 Kings 14:25*, which is no longer extant elsewhere. For the mission of *Jonah* to the *Ninevites* seems to have been of a slightly later age, as we noted at *2 Kings 15:20*. Compare *Ussher’s Annals of the Old Testament, page 78*, *Lightfoot’s Chronicle, page 96*, and *Maius’s Economy, page 895*.

It also clarifies the distinction between the "Major" and "Minor" prophets based on the length of their writings rather than their importance.</summary>

d) For nothing hinders Isaiah from having been able to write down later things that were already performed by Uzziah before he began his prophetic duty, as Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval rabbi and grammarian</note> cleverly noted in his preface to Isaiah. Yet the entirely opposite conjecture of Abraham ibn Ezra <note>A 12th-century scholar</note> is not supported by a firmer foundation; at the beginning of his *Commentary on Isaiah*, it seemed most probable to him that Isaiah began to prophesy before the death of Uzziah. This is true regarding the vision in the sixth chapter, but not regarding those preceding it. And although it is difficult to indicate which among the contemporaries—Isaiah, Hosea, and Amos—prophesied first, second, or third; yet it is mere conjecture that makes Isaiah the last among them in age. Also, when Saint Jerome, writing on Isaiah 1:1, says (correctly): "We know from the Kings listed in the title that Isaiah, Hosea, Joel, and Amos prophesied at one and the same time," he then writes: "But the beginning of the word of the Lord was in Hosea the son of Beeri"—this relies on a presumed explanation of the words in Hosea 1:1.

§. III. Regarding the origin of our prophet, if we trust the consistent historical 
<margin>family</margin>
tradition of the Hebrews, l) he was born not of an obscure family, but of the most illustrious and royal house of David. His father was not **Amos**, the third among the Minor Prophets—as several, including even learned Church Fathers, mistakenly believed due to their ignorance of the Hebrew script m)—but **Amoz** <note>original: אמוץ (Amots)</note>, Isaiah 1:1. The Jews constantly affirm from the tradition of their ancestors that this Amoz was the brother of Amaziah, King of Judah (2 Kings 14:1). See Abraham Zacuto’s book *The Book of Genealogies* <note>original: Sefer Juchasin</note> page 12a; Rabbi Gedaliah’s *The Chain of Tradition* <note>original: Shalshelet Ha-Kabbalah</note> page 18b; likewise the commentaries of Rashi <note>Rabbi Solomon</note>, Kimchi, Abarbanel, and others on the Book of Isaiah n). Because of this, many Christians are convinced that the Messiah is called by the name of his "Cousin" <note>original: Patruelis</note> by Isaiah in chapter 5:1. See Dr. Pfeiffer’s *Troubling Doubts* <note>original: Dubia Vexata</note> regarding that passage, page 671, etc.

k) Thus Abarbanel judged, and not poorly, in his *Preface to Ezekiel* page 153, column 4, whose words we will present in our own *Preface to Ezekiel*, §. 2.

l) Briefly and frankly, David Kimchi writes on Isaiah 1:1: *“We do not know his lineage or family, nor from which tribe he came; except that our Teachers hold by tradition that Amoz and Amaziah were brothers.”* Likewise Rashi: *“This has been handed down to us by our ancestors: that Amoz and Amaziah were brothers.”* Rabbi Levi says the same in the *Scroll Tractate* <note>original: Codice Megilla</note> chapter 1, page 10, column 2; and Abarbanel emphasizes the same in his *Preface*, page 1, column 2.

Likewise an uncertain author on the *Lives of the Prophets*, found among the works of Epiphanius, Volume II, page 235 and following. Among the Latin writers of the 4th and 5th Centuries, Augustine is somewhat hesitant, though leaning toward the better opinion, in *The City of God*, Book 18, chapter 27: *“Amos also writes that he prophesied in the days of King Uzziah... as did Isaiah, the son of Amos—either the aforementioned prophet, or, as is more commonly held, another man who was not a prophet but had the same name.”* 

But Jerome, in his *Preface to the Prophet Amos* addressed to Pammachius, rightly judged: *“The prophet Amos, who follows Joel and is the third of the twelve Prophets, is not the same man whom we read of as the father of the prophet Isaiah. For the former [Isaiah's father] is written as **Amoz** <note>original: אמוץ</note> with the first and last letters of his name being Aleph and Tzade, and it is interpreted as 'strong' or 'robust'; but this prophet [the minor prophet] is **Amos** <note>original: עמוס</note> with Ayin and Samekh, and is interpreted as 'a people torn away'”* (Jerome would have more correctly said "Burdened"). *“The middle letters, Mem and Vav, are common to both. Among us, however, who do not have such a great distinction of vowel letters, nor of the letter S (which is triple among the Hebrews), these and other names seem to be the same; among the Hebrews they are distinguished by the diversity of their elements and their own properties.”* The most learned Father Jerome repeats the same things on Isaiah 1:1: *“But Amoz the father of Isaiah is not, as many claim, the third of the twelve prophets, but another; and they are written with different letters among the Hebrews. ... The former, according to some, is interpreted as 'strength' or 'robustness,' while the latter is 'harsh and heavy to the people,' about which we have spoken more fully in [the commentary on] Amos.”*

§. IV. This is clearly testified <note>original: "liquido testatur"</note> by the title and inscription, as well as the most reliable division of the entire book in chapter 
<margin>Division of the book.</margin>
1, verse 1, and the account of those Kings during whose times Isaiah performed his prophetic duty *o)*. First, from chapter I to V under *Azariah son of Uzziah*, who reigned for 52 years in Judah (2 Kings 15:2). Then chapter VI under *Jotham* for 16 years (2 Kings 15:33). Furthermore, chapters VII through XIV, verse 27 under *Ahaz*, for 16 years (2 Kings 18:2); and finally, from chapter XIV, verse 28 to the end of the book under *Hezekiah*, who presided over the kingdom for 29 years (2 Kings 18:2). ...the works of Jerome <note>original: "Opera Hieronymi"</note>, volume 4, Basel edition, page 76. *Isaiah was a most noble man among his people, who is reported to have been the father-in-law of King Hezekiah.*) Jerome himself writes in his Commentary at the end of Isaiah chapter XX: *The Hebrews hand down the tradition that Isaiah was the father-in-law* (that is, as Cornelius a Lapide explains in his commentary on Isaiah page 43, the *grandfather-in-law* or *father of the father-in-law*) *of Manasseh, the son of Hezekiah, King of Judah.* But this is a very weak tradition, which neither found support among his tribesmen nor deserves our faith.

o) How much weight the first verse of Isaiah carries was most brilliantly stated by *the Blessed Luther* in his German Preface, which we recommend here above all others to all students again and again. Similarly, *Saint Jerome* near the beginning of his Commentary on Isaiah says: *That which is placed in the title—that he prophesied under the kings of Judah Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah—is not to be understood confusedly, as in other prophets, where we might not know what was said specifically under which king; rather, the writing should be referred to the end of the volume, showing what was revealed to him by the Lord separately under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah.* However, some matters from earlier times seem to have been related to the final part of the book for serious reasons, which we shall discuss in their proper place.

p) *Exactly how many years Isaiah lived or taught*, however, remains uncertain and cannot be accurately defined, since nothing is explicitly determined in Holy Scripture concerning either the end or the beginning of his life or office. *Abul-Faraj* <note>A 13th-century Syrian scholar also known as Bar Hebraeus</note> in his *History of the Dynasties*, Arabic page 67, Latin page 43, described *his age as one hundred and twenty, and his prophetic office as a span of eighty-five years*. *John Lightfoot* <note>An English churchman and rabbinical scholar</note>, however—following the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, specifically as it is noted in Scaliger’s *Treasury of Times* page 112 after the 22nd year of Uzziah (others, including the Latin edition of Eusebius’s works, note it from the 17th to the 26th year of Uzziah)—places the beginning of the prophetic office in his *Old Testament Chronicle* page 97 at the year of the world 3223, the twenty-third year of Uzziah, and on page 110 places its end at the death of Hezekiah in the year of the world 3310. This results in an intervening span of eighty-seven years, which nearly agrees with Abul-Faraj’s sum, even if he counts differently, as we shall soon say. *Seth Calvisius* <note>A German chronologist and astronomer</note> in his *Chronological Work* page 264, has it thus: *In the year of the world 3192, before the birth of Christ 756, the Prophet Isaiah, born of royal seed, saw the Lord sitting on a throne in this Sabbatical year.* From this it is clear that he began his prophetic office earlier. He taught under five (perhaps read: four) kings: under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, for nearly ninety years (Isaiah 1 and 6). Indeed, even more...

ON ISAIAH.
)( 3
<meta>Catchword: then</meta>

<margin>The Authority of Isaiah</margin>
This man of God was truly venerable for his holiness, and especially for his admirable faith in the most difficult times and the power of his prayers (see chapters 36 and 37). He held great authority with King Hezekiah; however, he was not held in the same esteem by King Ahaz and other impious leaders, priests, and commoners. Instead, he experienced the same fate as all truly godly people (as noted in 2 Timothy 3:12 <note>original: "All who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution."</note>). He indicates this himself in several places, for example, chapters 7:13, 28:22, 30:10, and 57:4. Blessed Martin Luther also warns of this with great weight in his preface.

<margin>His fate</margin>
<margin>& death.</margin>
### §. V.
According to some, he ceased to prophesy and died during the reign of Hezekiah <note>note q</note>; or rather, as is commonly believed, under the de-

> generate Manasseh. He taught for many years, if you listen to Cornelius a Lapide <note>a 17th-century Jesuit scholar known for his encyclopedic biblical commentaries</note>. For he says in his work on Isaiah (page 44): *“Therefore, if we say that, following the custom of the Hebrews like Christ and John the Baptist, he did not begin to prophesy before his thirtieth year, it follows that he lived to a decrepit old age, up to the year 126 and beyond. For Manasseh killed him, and that was not immediately at the beginning of his reign (for he himself began to reign as a boy of 12) but when he had already become older and more wicked.”* Yet many things are stated here recklessly, and difficulties are increased without necessity. Let us also hear from the Hebrew scholars: Rabbi Solomon <note>Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note>, who writes on Isaiah 1:1: *“In the year that Uzziah was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:19), the Shekhinah <term>Shekhinah: The visible or felt presence of the Divine</term> came upon Isaiah, and he prophesied throughout the time of those kings, until Manasseh rose up and killed him.”* If you ask in which year of his reign Uzziah was struck with leprosy? The Jews repeatedly say it happened in his twenty-seventh year, along with a horrible earthquake mentioned in Amos 1:1 and Zechariah 14:5, to which they also relate Isaiah 6:1 and 6:4. However, how could Amos have begun to prophesy two years before Isaiah? (Compare again Amos 1:1). But Abarbanel <note>Don Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> responds in his Preface to Isaiah (folio 1a): *“Although Amos may have prophesied two years before that earthquake, he did not therefore precede Isaiah. For Isaiah perhaps began to prophesy near the beginning of Uzziah's reign, whereas that earthquake occurred in his 27th year; and Uzziah reigned 52 years in total.”* Furthermore, Eastern Christians believe that Isaiah lost the gift of prophecy for 28 years, and thus claim Uzziah was struck with leprosy in the 24th year of his reign. So reports Herbelot <note>Barthélemy d'Herbelot, a French Orientalist</note> in the *Oriental Library* (page 500 ff.). Abul-Pharagius <note>also known as Bar Hebraeus, a 13th-century polymath</note> agrees with this account in his *History of the Dynasties* (page 39, Arabic 60). Truly, what we think of such circumstances, we shall say in the following sections.

->§. VI.<-

Others, however, argue that *Isaiah* prophesied under *Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah*, but not under *Manasseh*. He certainly would not have neglected to mention Manasseh in his opening verses if he had lived into those times and survived until the king had grown older and more wicked. For this reason, *Abulensis* (Alfonso Tostado) <note>a prolific 15th-century Spanish theologian</note> did not hesitate to contradict that tradition in his commentary on the 4th book of Kings [2 Kings] chapter 21, question 17. He argues that this story was drawn from no other source than "Jewish pits" and the Babylonian Talmud. Even Jerome, although he calls the tradition "most certain" at the end of his 15th book of Commentaries on Isaiah, makes it appear suspect due to the little fables with which it is packed—not to mention that the reasons they give for the prophet's killing carry no likelihood. But see what we remark on these matters in the note immediately following.

->ON ISAIAH.<-

<margin>Isaiah’s audience</margin>
§. VI. Isaiah delivered those sermons of his—specifically the ones God commanded him to record in writing for all generations (as seen in Isaiah 30:8 and 8:1)—to the Jews, primarily in the royal city of Jerusalem. This took place while the prophets Hosea and Amos were performing the same prophetic duties among the Israelites in Samaria or Bethel. Later, Joel and Micah joined them as additional witnesses, prophesying in Judah at nearly the same time as Isaiah; however, we will not add more about them at this present time.

### §. VII. Orosius

<note>Paulus Orosius was a 5th-century Christian historian.</note>, page 161. *George Cedrenus in his Synopsis or Compendium of History, page 110. The Paschal Chronicle (also known as the Sicilian Annals), edited by du Fresne, pages 118 and 155. The Roman Martyrology for July 6th, page 373, with notes by Baronius,* and many others. We will, however, add one more testimony from *Abul-Faraj* <note>also known as Bar Hebraeus, a 13th-century scholar</note> from the 13th century, in his *History of the Dynasties, Latin version page 43, Arabic version page 66 and following.* He writes: *This Manasseh committed every forbidden and illicit act—and Isaiah, who tried to restrain him from his wickedness, he bound between two planks and sawed through with a saw.* Nor do the *Muslims* themselves deny this, even if they introduce new errors in their typical fashion. See regarding them *Herbelot in his Oriental Library, page 500 and following, under the entry "Ischaia."*

We follow a middle path here. We do not yet see sufficiently heavy or convincing reasons to stop agreeing with the ancient Christians and Jews that *Isaiah* was removed from this world by the impious King *Manasseh*, along with other pious and just men. We do, however, grant to the skill and observation of others that certain details drawn from the Jewish imagination have been added to the history, to which more recent writers have added even more. 

Nevertheless, the objections previously raised by *Abraham ibn Ezra* <note>a celebrated 12th-century Jewish scholar</note> and *Abraham Calovius* <note>a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> against the common opinion do not necessarily follow: 

(1) They argue that in the title of the book, *Manasseh* is not mentioned, and therefore *Isaiah* did not reach his reign. However, it is enough—in fact, no more was required—for the title to indicate those Kings under whom these recorded prophecies of *Isaiah* were published. *The Scripture does not mention Manasseh because soon after he began to reign, Isaiah ceased his prophetic office and was killed by him, just as the Rabbis have handed down in their records;* so says *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century statesman and commentator</note> in his commentary on *Isaiah 1:1, folio 4a.* 

(2) Nor can one argue from his repeated or "special" calling (described in chapter 6) that his *first* calling must have been there; it is rightly assumed to have happened at chapter 1 and following, unless you wish to follow certain Rabbis who try to pass off Isaiah’s sixth chapter as his first. This view is rightly rejected by *Kimchi* <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Hebrew grammarian</note>, *Abarbanel*, and others. 

(3) Nor is the objection based on *Isaiah’s* supposedly "incredible" longevity any more solid. There is no shortage of other examples from those times: it is enough to produce one, *Jehoiada*, who flourished in the time of *Joash* (the father of *Amaziah* and grandfather of *Uzziah*). For it is explicitly written of him in *2 Chronicles 24:15*:

> *And Jehoiada grew old and was full of days, and finally he died: he was one hundred and thirty years old when he died.*

Nothing could be clearer for our case than this example. Even today, public reports—especially from France—frequently confirm what was said by *Lactantius* <note>an early Christian author</note> in his *Divine Institutes, book 2, chapter 12, page 101*: that humans very often reach their hundredth year, and that reliable authors record people reaching 120 years. Thus, in *Socrates’ Ecclesiastical History, book 7, chapter 6, Dorotheus, the Arian bishop of Constantinople, passed away under the Emperor Honorius when he was 119 years old.* And so that a more recent example is not lacking, we think we should mention here what was recorded about the great-great-grandfather of the famous historian *Christoph Hartknoch*, named *Stephan Hartknoch*, in the *Leipzig Acts of the Learned* in the month of June

For the corrupt life and faith of his entire nation <margin>demonstrated by the subject matter</margin> he approached with a courageous heart <note>t</note>: he most sharply rebuked the hypocrisy and vices of the princes and priests no less than those of the common people. He spoke of Christ's death and resurrection, and our redemption; likewise, he spoke of His spiritual and glorious kingdom, which would at last triumph over all enemies. In this way, he nurtured those on the "way of the cross" with the most abundant hope of eternal light and glory. Thus, to Blessed Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note>, Isaiah seems not so much a Prophet as an Evangelist. ON ISAIAH

He exalts the majesty of Christ far and wonderfully above all human things; so much so that he considers the terrifying enemies of the Church—even the most powerful Kings of the world and vast empires—to be scarcely comparable to a locust, a small drop of water, or a tiny speck of dust when set against the power of God (see chapters 10, 37, 40, etc.). He burned with a most holy love for God and the Savior and was gifted with prophetic light more abundantly than others. Thus, he does not only point out those things that concerned the Jews of his own time in a direct and literal sense, but he often looks forward in the very same sermon to the time of Christ and through all the ages of the world—even to the Church triumphant in heaven—frequently using symbolic and typical expressions for that purpose <note>x</note>.

<margin>from a divine disposition.</margin>
To stir the emotions of the listener—which is the greatest skill of an orator—he does not use a manufactured eloquence or the empty "persuasive speech" <note>original Greek: πιθανολογίᾳ (pithanologia)</note> of rhetoricians. Instead, armed with divine zeal, he rises up entirely against the hypocrisy or treachery of his people. With the words and phrases that the Holy Spirit taught him (1 Corinthians 2:13), he does not merely bend every teachable and attentive reader toward the obedience of faith, but he draws and seizes them. He lets no one go without some benefit, unless they are stubbornly wicked and hopelessly malicious. Certainly, there is such gravity in Isaiah's style, such sweetness and elegance in his speech, and such vivid images of things, that we have never seen anything similar produced even by the most skillful orator <note>y</note>. As our Blessed Luther best said regarding Isaiah 1:2 (Tome III, Jena Latin edition, leaf 286b): *“If anyone could look deeply into the heart of the Prophet, he would see in every single word furnaces of fire and the most vehement heat.”*

->PREFACE<-

<margin>*The origin of his figurative style.*</margin>
§. IX. From this source of sacred passions, therefore, we must derive those features which occur so frequently in the style of Isaiah: the tropes and *figurative* patterns of speech. From this source come those frequently employed *similes* or *comparisons, exclamations, questions, apostrophes* <note>direct addresses to an absent person or personified object</note>, *paronomasia* <note>wordplay or puns</note>, *asyndeta* <note>the omission of conjunctions between parts of a sentence</note>, or concise expressions. From this also comes the frequent substitution <note>original: enallage</note> not only of persons, genders, numbers, and tenses, but also changes of speakers and *mimesis* <note>imitation or representation of another's speech</note>, etc., as if his writings occasionally presented a living dialogue to you. *For he wishes the matter he is treating to be set before you as if you were hearing it directly from his mouth; and he often does not so much speak it as act it out with specific gestures and emotions, representing it as if in a living play*, as the Blessed Wolfgang Franzius <note>a 17th-century Lutheran theologian known for his work on biblical interpretation</note> well observed in his *Interpretation of Holy Scripture*, page 501.

<margin>*The praise given to Isaiah by the son of Sirach.*</margin>
§. X. Isaiah is therefore rightly called the Great and Faithful Prophet <note>original: Sirach 48:22</note>; for such he truly was, and is, whether you look at his subject matter, his style of speech, or the truth, quantity, order, and majesty of the things he prophesies. And because, after David, there is no prophet besides Isaiah who explains the mysteries of the whole kingdom of God more eloquently or more clearly, we agree with Brentz <note>Johann Brentz, a Protestant Reformer</note> that he holds the chief place among the interpreters of heavenly and truly saving doctrine; just as in the New Testament, God the Father, Christ, the Angels, the Evangelists, and the Apostles very frequently used his testimonies to confirm divine truth.

<margin>*The emotions of Isaiah to be observed and adopted in reading him.*</margin>
§. XI. Furthermore, just as all Holy Scripture is not a matter of *one's own interpretation* <note>original Greek: ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως (idias epilyseos); 2 Peter 1:21</note>, so also it is not for just anyone to interpret the prophets—owing to the extreme intensity of their emotions—unless they have the Holy Spirit as their teacher, as Luther most correctly warned in the same place cited above.
"Yet it would also be of great benefit for a true understanding of all Scripture, and thus of Isaiah, to be well-acquainted with the various cases, movements, and conditions that occur in the human soul: whether they arise from our own malice or frailty, such as various and depraved passions, or of desires, or of fear; or from a wicked spirit, testing, sifting, and afflicting us in various ways; and then also from the Spirit of Con-

->ON ISAIAH.<-

> ...forth. Therefore, just as one must observe the changes of times and persons in the Scriptures, so it is also worthwhile to observe the frequent *changes of emotions and passions*, according to the alternating movement of the Holy Spirit as He comes and goes, visiting the human soul in manifold ways. It contributes much to the understanding of the Scriptures if the reader considers whether certain things are said with a mind that is questioning or inquiring, or with one that is marvelling, or praying, or giving thanks, or mourning over sins. You read Scripture profitably if you clothe yourself in the emotion of each holy speaker; as Matthias Flacius <note>a prominent 16th-century Lutheran reformer and scholar</note> rightly writes in his *Key to the Scriptures* <note>original: "Clave Scripturae"</note>, Part II, page 43, section 21.

### §. XII.

<margin>Parallelism to be observed in historical accounts.</margin>Furthermore, the *historical books* must be compared before all else, and especially the history of those Kings who are expressly mentioned in the title of this book <note>referring to Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah mentioned in Isaiah 1:1</note>. For as *Isaac Abarbanel* <note>a famous 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> advised in his commentary <note>original: "b) Comment. in Prophetas posteriores fol. 1. a."</note>, the *later Prophets are like branches of the earlier ones*; and in Isaiah and the rest, all those things are presupposed which were treated in the earlier books—whether by the Prophets or the historians—concerning the state of both the commonwealth and the church. <margin>The state of Judah in the time of Isaiah.</margin>Therefore, to provide for the convenience of beginners, we wished to subjoin here a succinct *description of the state of Judah in the time of Isaiah*, collected by Dr. Augustus Varenius <note>a 17th-century German theologian</note> in his *Introduction to Isaiah* <note>original: "Prodromo Iesaiano"</note>, page 13 and following, from 2 Kings 14–21 and 2 Chronicles 26–32.

<margin>under Amaziah,</margin>1. *The kingdom of Judah stood, of course, glorious under AMAZIAH, the conqueror of the Edomites. But when he, with a heart made arrogant by so many victories, raised the signal for war and provoked the King of Israel (who was advising better things), the battle went most unhappily. It seemed as though the scepter of Judah was not far from its end. The capital city itself was captured, the walls were torn down over a wide area, treasures were snatched from both sacred and profane places, and countless people were killed. The King himself was murdered not long after by conspirators in Jerusalem.*

<margin>under Uzziah,</margin>2. *King AZARIAH succeeded him, under whom that mournful state gradually began to shine more gloriously, and soon the royal splendor stood at its peak. This King, UZZIAH <note>The text notes he is also called Azariah</note>, having conquered the Arabs, Philistines, Ammonites, and other nations in war, and having stormed the highest fortresses of those peoples, became a magnificent conqueror. The terror of his name and arms was carried even through Egypt, and he became the commander over many tributary nations. He took great pains to ensure that the calamity Jerusalem suffered under his father was marked by a wonderful improvement of the times. Towers were built in Jerusalem; stupendous fortifications...*

# PREFACE

...civil and military skill. Outside the holy city <note>Jerusalem</note>, the greatest effort was spent on strengthening fortifications and very strong castles here and there, to block off similar approaches to any future enemy. Everything was flourishing. Furthermore, there was an abundance of men incomparable in the arts of peace and war. In the camps were numbered (besides 600 leaders; see 2 Chronicles 26:12, 13 <note>original: "2 Par 26,12.13." Paralipomenon is the Greek/Latin name for Chronicles</note>) three hundred and seven thousand five hundred (307,500) warriors. Thus, the state of the kingdom and the King was at the pinnacle of worldly glory. And indeed, the state of the kingdom remained illustrious for a time, but that of the King himself became mournful; while destined for the scepter, he insolently intruded upon sacred things <note>original: "sacris"</note>. Having even threatened the most holy monitors <note>the priests who warned him not to offer incense</note> with a raised hand, as he prepared to be a priest himself, he became a leper and was driven from the temple with a roar, remaining impure until death.

3. Nevertheless, the *Lion of Judah*, or the kingdom itself, remained in bloom under *Jotham*, the successor to *JOTHAM* <note>likely a scribal repetition or referring to him succeeding the era of Amaziah and Uzziah</note>, who was a King no less in piety, war, or the glory of the kingdom. The *Ammonites* were preparing a rebellion, but they were brought back into order everywhere by the successful arms of *Jotham*. In further building up walls, towers, palaces, and cities, or in founding or enlarging castles, the King acted so that if he did not surpass his father’s praise, he certainly equaled it. Thus, here too, things were splendid and held as glorious for that age, in the highest degree.

<margin>under Ahaz,</margin>
4. *AHAZ* succeeded *Jotham*, a king second to none in impiety, and with him came a great new calamity. *Rezin* and *Pekah* struck a social alliance for war; the former was the King of *Syria*, the latter the King of the *Ephraimite* kingdom, that is, *Israel*. Although he had been king in a kingdom that was turbulent until now (through the massacres of Kings and bloody successions without law, except that which parricide armed), he was nevertheless successful in arms against *Judah*. A huge slaughter and ruin occurred throughout all *Judah*. One hundred and twenty thousand (120,000) warriors from the camps of *Judah* fell in a single battle, consumed by the sword. A mixed number of widows (for war had made them such), boys, and girls, reaching 200,000, were captured; however, by the compassion of the victor and the counsel of a prophet, they were sent back home. The holy city was besieged. Cruel decrees were then made in the camps concerning the uprooting of the *Davidic* house and the appointment of another successor. King *Ahaz*, in a desperate situation (for so it seemed, with the Prophet fruitlessly insisting upon the faith of *Immanuel* <note>meaning "God with us," a reference to Isaiah's prophecy to Ahaz</note>), worshipped the *Assyrian* gods as helpers, offering gold and silver from the royal treasures and

...taking up sacred things without distinction. Damascus is captured by the Assyrian <note>King Tiglath-Pileser III</note>, and the Syrian <note>King Rezin</note> is pulled back. But while Ahaz goes to Damascus to congratulate his "helper" <note>original: "opitulatori"; referring to the Assyrian king who helped him against Syria</note>, he becomes a sacrilegious profaner of the Temple and a most wicked reformer of worship. He does this by means of a Damascene altar and the most profane Uriah <note>the high priest who complied with the king’s pagan innovations; see 2 Kings 16</note>; for the priest was ready for any crime.

<margin>Under Hezekiah,</margin>
5. A King more worthy of the scepter succeeds him—one who was, up to this point, the closest to David in character and greater than all the others. He was a new corrector of the times: **HEZEKIAH**. He inaugurated his reign with a solemn reformation and publicized the celebration of the Passover. He even summoned the remnants of the kingdom of Israel <note>the Northern Kingdom</note> through speakers and envoys. He provided such an example of piety and holy governance as none of the Kings before him had ever shown. In this way, the glory of a sufficiently splendid external state returned easily. This would have remained so, had there not intervened the lamentable spectacle of the capture of Samaria in the sixth year of Hezekiah by the Assyrian Shalmaneser, the defeat of the last King Hoshea, and the deportation of the Israelites. The causes for this are made known in "God’s Manifesto," as if in a public proclamation, in 2 Kings 17:7–24.

A new calamity followed, although in its outcome it was suffered by the very one who brought it. Hezekiah did not want the scepter of Judah to be bound in vassalage to the Assyrians, a condition his father <note>Ahaz</note> had agreed to. Interpreting this as a cause for war, the Assyrian Sennacherib marched against the Jews in the 14th year of Hezekiah, with the same intent his predecessor had shown toward the Ten Tribes of Israel a few years earlier. Judah rushed down from its high peak. *Everywhere there was sad fear and many an image of death.* <note>The author quotes Virgil's Aeneid (Book 2, line 369), "ubique pavor, et plurima mortis imago," comparing the Assyrian invasion to the fall of Troy.</note> Hezekiah went to meet him with talents of gold and silver, even with tears, hoping to plead with and turn away the tyrant; but that shrewd man accepted the gold while remaining equally implacable. He sent five blasphemous speakers to the city. *Nothing of weapons, except the duty of prayer, remained.* In these prayers Hezekiah was totally poured out. He experienced, through the interpretation of Isaiah, that as long as such intercessors remain, the city is unconquered. The tyrant would not be the victor; instead, with the joyful shouts of the daughter of Zion, he would be immediately removed by a superior hand. An angelic slaughter occurred. A single Angel struck down 185,000 enemy warriors. 

Hence followed the triumph of Jerusalem and the already-captive Israel. Favor followed favor, miracle followed miracle: Hezekiah was healed, his years of life were increased, and a sign was given <note>the shadow moving backward on the sundial</note>. In this one thing he was unhappy, showing how wretched a man is when left to himself: he indulged too much in human affection toward the congratulators from the city of Babylon. For this reason, he finally had to be informed by our Isaiah concerning the hitherto secret judgments of heaven. This Isaiah,

*The Orator before Kings noted in the Scriptures <note>original: "Orator apud Reges"; likely referring to Isaiah's role as a prophet speaking to the Judean court</note> ends here.* We also finish, intending to show the use of this title in what follows. It is enough to have pointed out one example: without those things we said in Thesis 1, no one can understand the first chapter of Isaiah; and without those things we said in Thesis 2 and 3 being properly understood, no one can understand chapters 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. The same logic applies to what follows. Thus far the words of Varenis <note>Augustus Varenis (1633–1684), a Lutheran theologian known for his work on the prophets</note> and the description of Jewish history taken from the books of Kings and Chronicles <note>original: "Paralipomenon"; the traditional name for the books of Chronicles in the Latin Vulgate</note>.

However, we must not neglect the Prophets who were contemporaries <note>original Greek: "σύγχρονοι" (synchronoi)</note> of Isaiah—as we said above in Section VI—or those who came later. These prophets sometimes report things that were not specifically mentioned by Isaiah, such as that horrible *earthquake* among the terrifying judgments of GOD (Amos 1:1, Zechariah 14:5), the destruction by locusts (Joel 1 and 2), likewise the calamity of fire (Amos 7:4), and a very great drought (Joel 1:20), with which were mixed terrible flames falling from heaven—as once occurred in Egypt (Exodus 9:23)—through which certain cities were overturned, just as Sodom and Gomorrah (Amos 4:11, Isaiah 1:7, 9, etc.). Indeed, not only are the preceding historical books of Kings, Chronicles, Joshua, Judges, and Samuel to be compared as the foundation for what is said in the Prophets, but also
<margin>Moses</margin>
the writings of Moses must be kept constantly in mind and before one's eyes. For from these, as from an ocean (Sirach 24:23 ff.), all other things are drawn. Thus, Isaiah most evidently looks back immediately in chapter 1:2 to Deuteronomy 4:26, and in chapter 32:1 to Exodus 4:22, to omit many other instances. No less must the subsequent Prophets and the remaining books of the Old Testament be read, as just stated: for they show that all those things happened to the Jews which were predicted by Isaiah in the name of the Lord. In-
<margin>In the Old and New Testaments, or the universal Scripture:</margin>
-primis <note>Latin: "Inprimis" (Especially)</note>, the New Testament must also be diligently compared with Isaiah, as it very frequently refers back to him and provides the final fulfillment of his and the other prophecies in the Holy Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>. *For the principal aim* <note>original: "Scopus enim principalis"</note>—both of the whole Scripture and of Isaiah—is CHRIST (Acts 3:24, 10:43), through whom all things were made, and to whom all things are referred as the head and foundation of His Church.

<margin>Difficulty in the prophetic books.</margin>
§. XIII. From this, everyone will perceive along with *the Blessed Jerome c)* how much labor it is to understand the Prophets; and how necessary it is, as *the Blessed Luther* used to advise, to pray for the grace and help of the Holy Spirit. *For by the same Spirit that the Scriptures were made, by that Spirit they desire to be read, and by Him they must be understood, etc.*—as the golden saying of Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux</note> goes.

### ON ISAIAH.

The counsel of Abbot William <note>William of Saint-Thierry (c. 1075–1148), a Benedictine abbot and mystic</note> in his letter to the brothers of Mont Dieu, page 1749: "From this, no one will be able to easily judge a true interpretation, except one who through the Spirit of Truth has properly understood divine matters, has been more than lightly practiced in the Scriptures and the Hebrew language, and has a mind disciplined by actual use." Therefore, we greatly urge students beginning the school of Isaiah that, after a thorough reading of his version in the vernacular <note>The student's native language, such as German</note>, and after a diligent study of the Hebrew Sources in the books of Moses and the historical books, they should look around for a teacher—like that Eunuch in Acts 8:31—who may pave the way through difficult passages with a living explanation of words and phrases *d)*, and briefly illuminate the very matters which Isaiah treats by pointing out the parallelism of Scripture and a careful observation of the Church’s constant practice.

<margin>A warning regarding our notes.</margin>
§. XIV. In accordance with the nature of our undertaking, we have noted in our scholia <note>brief explanatory notes or comments on a text</note> not so much those things which the most excellent commentators—such as our own **B. Luther, Brentius, Varenius, Dorscheus, Calovius, and Schmidius** <note>These are prominent Lutheran theologians and commentators from the 16th and 17th centuries</note>, etc.—were able to supply in abundance, to say nothing of the ancient and Oriental writers whom we have touched upon more sparingly here; but rather what a diligent reading of the text and a comparison of the scriptures suggested. However, we have not included everything we possessed, but only what the narrowness of the paper permitted. In this comparison of parallel places (for some refer chiefly to words and phrases, while others exhibit the same matter and phrasing), one must carefully observe how the same material, treated elsewhere in the Scriptures, agrees with Isaiah: whether it is a history narrated or cited elsewhere, a sentiment found elsewhere, a type <note>a person or event in the Old Testament seen as prefiguring something in the New</note> or symbol with its antitype <note>the fulfillment of a type</note> explained elsewhere, a parable with its exposition made elsewhere, or a prophecy with its fulfillment described elsewhere, and vice versa. Thus, those who are willing to enter the same path of diligent scrutiny with us will easily perceive the divine virtues of this most holy prophet and the most abundant fruit of his labor, progressing from strength to strength through him. Then, having become in a sense familiar with the sacred orator himself, for the confirmation of the truth,

> *d) Jerome, Epistle 103 to Paulinus, chapter 2: "The living voice <note>original: "viva vox"</note> has a certain hidden energy, and sounding from the mouth of the author into the ears of the disciple, it resonates more strongly." Pliny, Book 2, Epistle 3 to Nepos: "You will say, 'I have people here whom I may read who are no less eloquent.' True: but there is always an opportunity for reading; there is not always an opportunity for hearing. Furthermore, the living voice affects one much more, as the common saying goes. For although what you read may be sharper, those things which the pronunciation, the face, the bearing, and even the gestures of the speaker fix in the mind sit more deeply." — All of which tend toward this: that you should hear Isaiah; or even for this reason alone, that you might say you have heard him.*

# CHAPTER 1. ISAIAH 1

Exodus 25:4. **e)** *like wool* to wit: white or clean, as Targum Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary of the prophets.</note> adds. See verses 14 and 16. In this verse, they think it refers to a Jewish rite, namely that scarlet piece of wool that was placed between the horns on the forehead of the scapegoat (about which see Leviticus 16:8 and following) and at the door of the Temple porch. If it turned white after the goat was sent out, they rejoiced greatly, and it was a sign to them of the remission of sins. They themselves record in the Talmudic Tractate Yoma, folio 39b, that this ceased, along with other signs, forty years before the destruction of the Temple (to wit: from the death of Christ). See also Buxtorf's *On Abbreviations*, page 218 and following; Lundius, page 1038, and others.
</margin>

> ...always devoted to magic, as well as predictions, and burned with the greatest desire to know the future, believing it could be foreknown. John 3:29. e) an allegorical song. cf. Deuteronomy 31:19. following. f) of my beloved. Song of Solomon 1:12. following. Others translate as "cousin" or "my kinsman," as in Leviticus 10:4, collected with Hebrews 2:14; and because Isaiah was born of the family of David. See our Preface, section 3. The Messiah himself also recited this song to the Jews in Matthew 21:31, Mark 12:1, Luke 20:9. g) concerning his vineyard. chapter 3:14. Psalm 80:9. following. Jeremiah 2:21. John 15:1. (following. h) cf. chapter 27:2. Matthew 20:1. following. chapter 21:28. following. i) on a horn, that is, on a ridge of mountains or on a slope, which is most suitable for vineyards, Psalm 80:11. As this name in Syriac denotes an extremity, for example of a garment (Matthew 9:20) and a linen sheet (Acts 11:5), so it is not only a tract and extremity of land, but also the peak of a mountain, likewise a small hill standing out from others, or a part of a mountain divided from others, which we think fits here above all else, comparing Exodus 15:17, Deuteronomy 33:11, Psalm 68:16, 17. k) that is, in a mountainous place indeed, yet not sterile, but in a very fertile spot <note>Latin: pinguissimo loco</note>. cf. ### CHAPTER V.
**1** ^e Let me sing now to my beloved a song of my loved one regarding his vineyard. ^f My beloved had a vineyard on a horn ^g in a fertile place. **2** And he dug it up, ^h and cleared it of stones, ^i and planted it with a choice vine, ^k and built a tower ^l in the midst of it, and also hewed out a winepress ^m in it: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, ^n and it brought forth wild grapes. **3** And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, and men of Judah, judge now between me and my vineyard. **4** What ^o more could have been done to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? why, when I looked that it should bring forth ^p grapes, did it bring forth wild grapes? **5** And now I will show you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away its hedge, ^q and it shall be eaten up; and break down its wall, ^r and it shall be trodden down: **6** And I will lay it waste; ^s it shall not be pruned, nor hoed; ^t but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain ^u upon it. **7** For the vineyard ^w of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, ^x but behold oppression; ^y for righteousness, ^z but behold a cry.

<summary>This page contains the Hebrew text and philological commentary for Isaiah 4:2-6 and 5:1-8. It focuses on identifying the "Branch of the Lord" as the Messiah and interpreting the parabolic "Song of the Vineyard" as a metaphor for the divine judgment of Israel.</summary>

This page transitions into a series of "woes" (denunciations) against specific social and moral sins such as greed, hedonism, and the perversion of justice.</meta>

<summary>This page contains Isaiah 5:8-24, known as the "Woes of Isaiah," which condemn the social injustices of the ruling class in Judah. The translator provides extensive philological notes comparing Hebrew accents, vowel points (Kametz, Cholem), and ancient measurements (Bath, Homer, Ephah) to other biblical and classical sources.</summary>
<keywords>Isaiah 5, Woes of Isaiah, social justice, Hebrew philology, Masoretic notes, weights and measures, Sheol, biblical commentary</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the Book of Isaiah. Having concluded the "woes" against Israel in the previous verses, it now details the resulting divine judgment (the "outstretched hand") and transitions into one of the most famous passages in the Bible: Isaiah's vision of the divine throne room in Chapter 6.</meta>

<header>ISAIAH CHAPTER 5 & 6</header>

# ## Chapter VI.

1 In the year of King Uzziah’s death, I saw the Lord sitting on a high and lofty throne, and the hem of His robe filled the Temple.
2 Seraphim stood above Him; each had six wings: with two he covered his face, with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew.
3 And one called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory."
4 And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the House was filled with smoke.
5 Then I said: "Woe is me! For I am ruined; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips."

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Isaiah’s ministry during a time of national crisis. Having been commissioned by God in the previous chapter, Isaiah now confronts King Ahaz of Judah. The context is the Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 735 BCE), where the Northern Kingdom of Israel (Ephraim) and Syria (Aram) have allied against Jerusalem. The commentary provides deep historical and linguistic analysis of the famous "Immanuel" prophecy.</meta>

<header>ISAIAH 7. CHAPTER 7.</header>

<margin>
Finally, the total mixing of the remnants of Israel with other nations who were introduced into Samaria by Esarhaddon <note>The King of Assyria who succeeded Sennacherib</note>. See 2 Kings 17:24 and Ezra 4:2, 10. This blending was so complete that the few remaining Israelites (Amos 5:3; cf. also 2 Chronicles 34:33, 35:18) were no longer regarded as a distinct people from the other nations. Most were extinguished by plague (Amos 4:10), the sword (Hosea 9:13, 16; Amos 4:10), and famine (Hosea 8:7, 9:2; Amos 4:6), or had slipped away in flight (Amos 2:16), besides those who had long ago been carried away into exile (2 Kings 17:6, 23). Another opinion, however, which the Hebrews commonly follow, begins from the time of the prophecy of Amos against the Syrians (Amos 1:3-4) and the Israelites (Amos 2:6, 3:1 etc., 4:1 etc.) in the 22nd year of Uzziah, two years before the earthquake (Amos 1:1; Zechariah 14:5), and ends with the destruction of the kingdom of Israel in the 6th year of Hezekiah (2 Kings 17:6). This is approved by Noldius and others. The former view, which Glassius judges more consistent with the Hebrew phrasing, is supported by Tremellius, Calvin, and others.
</margin>

Their fury and power will soon end. r) Exodus 11:2. s) Rezin and Syria or the Syrians. v. 1. s. 8. t) namely Pekah, verse 1.
</margin>

Designed to designate His divine and human nature, and His almighty help. cf. John 1:1, 14; Romans 9:5; 1 Timothy 3:16.

*v. 9. n)* There is great disagreement concerning this word, and the meaning is found with difficulty. **Luther** in the German version: *mali estote* <note>original: "mali estote"</note> "be evil," from the root *ra'a* <note>רעע</note>, and so also **Gussetius** p. 799, according to the form *bo'u* <note>באוּ</note>, comparing Jeremiah 15:12. But that root is not yet proven, especially as used in the *Kal* <note>the simple active verb form</note>. **Vatablus**, therefore, along with Abraham Ibn Ezra and Kimchi and others, translates it "shatter" or "shake" from the root *ra'a*, comparing Psalm 2:9. But this does not fit well with the following "gird yourselves," nor does Isaiah express the *effect* of the enemies by this address, but rather their *attempt*.

It expresses the outcome. Better, therefore, with Targum Jonathan, Rashi, and Abarbanel, and the Vulgate: "be gathered" or as **Schmidt** and **Tremellius** translate: "Associate yourselves" <note>original: "consociamini"</note>. And thus **Cocceius** in his Lexicon p. 820, from the Pyal imperative, from the root *ra'a*, comparing Judges 14:20, Proverbs 22:24. Truly, because the Pyal imperative is quite unusual, and the accent is on the second-to-last syllable, we prefer to take it as the Kal imperative from the root *ra'a*, comparing Proverbs 18:24, just as the forms *shwach*, *shoch*, and *shomem* are mixed with the same meaning. **o)** the enemies: Israelites, Syrians, and Assyrians. <term>A closed Mem in the middle of a word</term> <note>original: "Mem stumah be-emtza teivah." In Hebrew scribal tradition, the letter Mem has a final form (ם) that is usually only used at the end of words. Here, it appearing in the middle of a word is a significant scribal anomaly.</note>

Chapter 22:22; 1 Samuel 10:9. **d)** He took the law upon himself to keep it. Compare Galatians 4:4, 5. So this "government" is not only an honor but also a burden; see *Luther* on this passage. He himself governs the entire kingdom, present and powerful everywhere, knowing all things (Matthew 28:18; Ephesians 1:21; Hebrews 1:3), not relying on the help of counselors in the manner of earthly princes; but He is King Himself, and all in all. In a similar phrase, *Cicero* in his *Speech for Flaccus* said to the judges: *In this judgment, you uphold the entire Republic on your shoulders—on your shoulders, I say.* And *Pliny* in his *Panegyric to Trajan*, chapter 10, when the Father had abundantly experienced how well the empire sat upon his shoulders—that is, it was so composed that it remained constant and stable, as noted by *B. Cellarius*. **b)** And his name is called. Used impersonally, as in Joshua 7:26; Judges 15:17. **c)** A real name, used almost as a title, as in Chapter 7:14. Compare Genesis 32:30. So also where he is called *Shiloh* in Genesis 49:10; *A star coming out of Jacob* in Numbers 24:17; *The LORD our Righteousness* in Jeremiah 23:6; *The one Shepherd* in Ezekiel 34:23; *The Man named Branch* in Zechariah 6:12 (collected with Ephesians 11:1); *The Desire of nations* in Haggai 2:7; *The Sun of Righteousness* in Malachi 3:20; *The Most Holy* in Daniel 9:24; and *Solomon* in Song of Solomon 3:11. **d)** Judges 13:18. Compare Revelation 19:12; Psalm 72:18; Proverbs 30:4. He is not only wonderful, but <term>preeminently</term> <note>original: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν"</note> a Miracle (Isaiah 25:1): God by Himself, and by the personal union, the <term>God-man</term> <note>original: "Θεάνθρωπος"</note>. *Glassius*, page 675. Furthermore, observe that these and the following names are by no means names of the one who bestows the name, as the Jews treacherously devise against the accents, as if the sense were: *And the LORD—who is Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of Eternity—called the name of the child 'Prince of Peace'*; this last title is the only one they leave to the child, and they ignorantly (see Chapter 7:14) refer it to Hezekiah; see *Rashi, Kimchi, Abarbanel* and others. But as *Ibn Ezra* rightly taught in his commentary on this place—and even the blasphemously harmful *Abarbanel* cannot deny—all these are titles of the named child, as the constant use of this grammatical construction invincibly demonstrates. For example, Genesis 4:25, 26; Chapter 5:3, 29. **d)** Judges 16:11; Chapter 27:36; and in the Hebrew Concordances under **his name** <note>original: "shemo"</note> many more. **e)** Micah 4:9; John 1:18; Revelation 3:18. The power and wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24. This name looks back to the counsels of eternity. *Dorscheus*. **f)** Chapter 10:21; 11:2; 12:2; Zephaniah 3:17; Psalm 24:8; 45:4. **g)** Father of eternity, Chapter 45:17; Job 20:4. He is not only the possessor of it (as among the Arabs "father of beauty" signifies one who is beautiful, etc.), but also the author of it for us: He who fathered and gave this happiness to us, that we might be children of that age (Luke 20:35; cf. Hebrews 1:2; 2:5; and below Chapter 63:16). **h)** Prince of spiritual and eternal peace (Romans 5:1; cf. verse 6; Genesis 49:10; Psalm 72:3, 7; and Song of Solomon 3:11). However, how poorly this name and its force (explained in verse 6) suit Hezekiah—as the Jews desire—is shown by 2 Kings 18:8 and following. **Verse 6. i)** To him who multiplies this government, and multiplies peace. Thus it would be a participle, as in Leviticus 11:42. But others take it as a noun: "To the multiplication" or "To the abundance of the government, and to peace there shall be no end," in the forms of *mar'eh* or *machseh*; just as *mashkeh* is taken sometimes as a noun, sometimes as an adjective. As for what mysteries both Christians and Jews seek in this closed **Mem** (ם), see what others have written. *Abarbanel* thinks the Messiah is hinted at here, whom Hezekiah resembled in many ways. **Verse 4. l)** For to further explain the manner in which it shall happen. **m)** Just as in that Midianite war, every charge and clash of the enemies **(l) n)** rushed in and collided. **(l) o)** With a terrible noise or crash (Jeremiah 10:22; Chapter 47:3; Nahum 3:2), not only of Gideon and his allies, but of the enemies themselves (**Judges 7:20 and following**) with **m)** trembling (Ezekiel 12:18; Job 39:24). So also it shall be in the battle of Christ. Cf. below Chapter 63:3; Revelation 19:13. Others: with a shaking or earthquake, as in Amos 1:1; Zechariah 14:5; so compare Matthew 27:51, 54; 28:2, 4; Hebrews 12:26; Revelation 6:12; 11:13; 16:18. **p)** So that the garment of the enemies is rolled and stained. Psalm (l) 2 Samuel 20:12. **q)** With the blood of the enemies themselves. Compare Zephaniah 1:17; and the Epistle of Jude verse 23. **r)** Chapter 64:10; Numbers 19:6. Cf. Ezekiel 39:19. **s)** Food or fuel for the fire. **(2)** Verse 18.

**Verse 5. t)** The child <term>God-man</term>. Luke 2:12, 21, 27; Hebrews 2:14. That promised seed of the woman in Genesis 3:15. **u)** A man born of a virgin mother, Chapter 7:14; Galatians 4:4. **x)** To us, for our good. Luke 2:10, 11; Romans 5:25; 8:32, etc. **y)** The eternal Son of God, of whom Psalm 2:7 and Proverbs 30:4 speak, was given to us (John 3:16; Romans 8:3). That this passage must be understood as referring to the Messiah is proved not only by every word of the text, but also by Jonathan, the Chaldean Interpreter (who poorly divides the names of the Child), and other ancient Jews testify to this. Thus in *Devarim Rabbah* on Deuteronomy 2:4, to prove that the Messiah must be raised from the descendants of Jacob, they appeal to these very words: *A child is born to us.* folio 287, column 1, Amsterdam edition, 1679.

---

->**Variant Readings**<-

**Verse 5.** **Avi-ad** <note>Father of Eternity</note> is written as one word in manuscripts 1, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 20, 21, 22. **Verse 6.** **Le-marbeh** <note>To the increase</note>: Hillerus (page 139) recognizes nothing under the closed **Mem** (ם) except a variant reading, **Mah rabbah** <note>How great</note>, with the **Lamed** (ל) entirely removed and omitted; as expressed in the Vulgate Version: *His empire shall be multiplied*; **luna** "his dignity shall be increased"; Arabic with all Greek versions: *Great is his government.* And so Eliu in the Masoreth (page 52), except he prefers it to be **lam rabbah**, which is grammatically poor, instead of **la-hem rabbah**, "it shall be multiplied for them." However, he observes this against most books (which in the margin call the closed **Mem** in the middle of a word "lam rabbah"), and according to the *Kethiv* <note>the written text</note> it is more correctly divided into **la-hem rabbah**, as explicitly required by our manuscript 22 and the printed Masora for 2 Chronicles 34:61.

<summary>This page analyzes the prophecy of the birth of the Messiah in Isaiah 9, focusing on his divine titles and the textual anomaly of the "closed Mem" in verse 6. It defends the Christological interpretation against contemporary Jewish views that applied the text to King Hezekiah.</summary>

**CHAPTER XI, verse 1.** a) It shall go forth. <note>original: "Prodibit"</note> See Gen. 1:13, Job 31:40. This happens after a long series of years and at a time defined by God; long after the Assyrian enemy has been destroyed. See ch. 10:33, 34. b) A rod or staff. (z) Prov. 14:3; compare with ch. 4:2 above. Hence the Chaldean root "to strike with a staff." This staff will be a scepter, as spoken of in Num. 24:17. This refers to the Messiah, whose person and office are described here in verse 3 and following, along with the gathering and expansion of his kingdom or Church, with his enemies either destroyed (v. 4) or converted (v. 6 and following). a) From the trunk, the stem having been cut down. (3) ch. 40:24, Job 14:8. 6) d) A sprout or offspring. (4) ch. 1:1, 9; ch. 60:21, Dan. 11:7. g) The Messiah. Compare Matt. 2:23 and John 1:46, 47. e) From the roots of Jesse (v. 10) and of David. See Matt. 1:1, Luke 2:4, Acts 13:23, Heb. 7:14. The Targum of Jonathan says: "from the sons of his sons he shall be propagated." Thus in v. 10. d) He shall be fruitful; he shall increase with spiritual offspring. ch. 53:10, Ezek. 17:23. Compare Gen. 1:28, ch. 9:1, 7; ch. 35:11, Ezek. 1:7. The Messiah is understood here throughout, as the Chaldean paraphrase correctly notes here and in v. 6, based on the whole context. This is Immanuel, of whom the Prophet has spoken since chapter 7 as the foundation of all hope and salvation; it is by no means Hezekiah, who had been born long before (see note on ch. 7:14), nor was the family of David a "stump" then, but was still flourishing in its royal dignity.

(4) Amos 5:8; Job 9:9. Most think that *Orion* is so called from the inconstancy and changeability of the air which it brings. From which they also conjecture the month of *Kislev* was named, from the cold, which the Arabic root denotes. Others think *Bootes* or the constellation of the *Bear* is meant, or *Arcturus*, by which word the Vulgate expressed our text in Job 38:31. But our Hillerus, in *Names of the Bible* <note>original: "Onomasticon Sacrum"</note> page 56, best derives it from "confidence" or "hope," Psalm 78:7; Job 31:24. Thus it is called *Cynosura* or the *Little Bear*, a constellation in which confidence and hope were placed by Phoenician sailors, as Cicero witnesses in *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 2, page 47: "With this leader the Phoenicians trust the night on the deep," etc., from Aratus. o) they shall not cause to shine or glitter, verse 20; chapter 14:12; Job 31:26. (1) compare chapter 22; Jeremiah 23:2. It deals with Babylon, into whose shadow many had withdrawn as if into a very safe fortress. According to Bochart, these are <term>wild cats</term>, from the Arabic. **b)** Schmid calls them <term>Ochim</term>; creatures named from their "associating" or "howling together," according to Dr. Neumann. But their exact kind is uncertain to us. The Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic translations have "echoes," with which Bochart contends (in his *Hierozoicon* I, p. 865) that it refers not to a species of animal, but to the howling of wild beasts that makes the desert ring. **c)** chapter 34:13; Micah 1:8. <term>Female ostriches</term> according to Bochart (*Hierozoicon* II, p. 218). **d)** hairy <term>apparitions</term> <note>original: spectra</note>, or a species of shaggy goat. Compare Leviticus 17:7. **and even demons** <note>original Greek: ό κἀι δαιμόνια</note>. So the Jonathan, Syriac, and Arabic versions. See Revelation 18:2.

**v. 22. e)** And they shall answer, howling in competition. Compare chapter 27:2; 1 Samuel 21:12. **f)** Jeremiah 50:39. <term>Jackals</term> <note>original: thoes</note>, as Bochart teaches at length, whose specific trait is that they answer one another with alternating howls (*Hierozoicon* I, p. 842). **g)** in its ruins; because elsewhere this word signifies a <term>widow</term> (compare chapter 47:8), some here understand it by antithesis as "palaces" (chapter 32:14) that are "widowed"—that is, deprived of their inhabitants. However, Guffetius (p. 96) thinks it should be rendered: And they shall answer...

<note>Notes continued from the bottom of the source page:</note>
...proverbial expression. Compare chapter 11:1. **s)** A viper or basilisk. Compare chapter 11:8. Bochart argues in his *Hierozoicon* (vol. 2, p. 399) that a basilisk is meant. He explains the sense thus: All you Philistines, who once exulted because of the death of King Uzziah—who had punished you severely—and who dared to rise against us under Ahaz, do not rejoice anymore. For from the root of the serpent (the lineage of Uzziah, who bit you like a serpent) comes another serpent, and a most grave one: Hezekiah, the basilisk, whom you will find even more dangerous than Uzziah to your great misfortune. Others suggest that because the Messiah will come from the descendants of Jesse, his works among you will be like flying serpents. **t)** Numbers 21:6. A "prester" or "hydrus" [water-snake], as Bochart proves (vol. 2, p. 421). He notes that the hydrus and chersydrus differ little; the water-snake that lives in marshes in winter is forced to live on dry land in summer, becoming a "chersydrus." In hot regions, its venom becomes far more acute, burning whatever it touches or even killing with its pestilential breath. **u)** A flying hydra, chapter 30:6, which has membrane wings like a bat.

**v. 30. n)** Then they shall graze. **x)** The firstborn of the wretched; most afflicted Israelites, sacred to God (Exodus 4:22). Just as the firstborn of Egypt were killed, the firstborn of the poor shall be saved. **y)** The afflicted and needy. **z)** Leviticus 25:18. Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> adds "in the days of the Messiah," like the typical reign of Solomon. **a)** chapter 11:7. **b)** Hosea 9:16. **c)** Your enemy Hezekiah (v. 29) or the Assyrian (v. 31) will kill them.

**v. 32. o)** Multiple difficulties occur in this short verse. Schmid asks: What will the ambassadors of the nation answer? He takes "nation" to mean the Israelites. But Jonathan asks: What will the messengers of the *peoples* answer? The Vulgate asks: What is answered to the messengers of the nation? We agree with Schmid that these are messengers of the Jews, announcing Hezekiah's victory over the Philistines or the city's liberation. However, we also take this text with the Aramaic paraphrase as referring to Christ and his kingdom. The "messengers" are the Apostles sent from the Jews into the whole world. This is the surest defense in dangerous times: to know that God is favorable to you in Christ. **p)** This they will answer: that the Lord himself, whose promises do not fail, has done this. **q)** He has founded it upon an invincible foundation and a rock never to be moved: the Messiah himself, his Son, the Savior of his Church. See chapter 28:16; Psalm 87:1; and the words of Christ in Matthew 16:18.

Jonathan <note>original: "Ion." — referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase</note> calls it the *Burden* of the cup of cursing, to be drunk by the *Moabites*. They became apostates from God (Num. 21, 29; Judg. 11, 24; 1 Kings 11, 7) and were excluded from the congregation (Deut. 23, 3, 4; Neh. 13, 1). They were bitter enemies of the Israelites (Num. 22, 2; see also ch. 25, 1 and following; Ps. 83, 7). They were tributaries to Solomon (1 Kings 5, 1) and the Kings of Israel until they rebelled under Ahab or his son Joram (2 Kings 1, 1; ch. 3, 5). From then on they were troublesome to the Israelites (2 Kings 13, 20). Consequently, they were to be devastated and diminished by the Assyrians under Shalmaneser or Sennacherib after three years (Isa. 16, 14; Amos 2, 1 and following), and further broken in the fifth year after the destruction of Jerusalem (according to Josephus, *Antiquities* X. 11) by Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonians (Jer. 27, 3; ch. 48, 1 and following), whom they had helped in attacking the Jews (2 Kings 24, 2). Finally, they were reduced by Judas Maccabeus (1 Macc. 5, 35, 56) and others to such distress that they long ago ceased to be a distinct people, according to the prophecies (Jer. 48, 42; Zeph. 2, 9). x) Because. y) by night, in which it was devastated. ### CHAPTER XVII.
*. 1. a) A funeral oracle <note>original Latin: "Onus funebre," often translated as "The Burden"</note>. chapter 13:1, 14:28, 15:1. b) Of Damascus (chapter 7:8) and its allies the Israelites, verse 3 and following, and even of the Assyrians, verse 12, the enemies of Judah, verse 14. Otherwise, the city of Damascus itself was not long ago captured and plundered, and its citizens stripped by Tiglath-Pileser the Assyrian; just as was predicted above and in 2 Kings 16:9. Likewise we read it fulfilled in Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 9, chapter 12. But filled again with new inhabitants, it was then destroyed under the Assyrian empire (see note on 2 Kings 24:2) and a little later by the Egyptians (ibid verse 7) who had taken possession of Syria, 2 Kings 23:29.
</margin>

# ISAIAH 19:20. CHAPTER 19, 20.

**k)** * They shall bind themselves to the Lord by oath and religious worship. However, the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> has "City of the Sun" <note>original Latin: *urbis solis*, as if the text read *Ir ha-Cheres*, comparing Judges 8:13; this is the same as *Beth-Shemesh* in Jeremiah 43:13</note> shall one be called. This stood for over 300 years, until the time of Vespasian, as Josephus reports in *The Jewish War*, Book 7, chapter 37 (Latin chapter 30). ### Chap. XX.

<margin>
**Chapter 20. a)** In the year that he came; compare a similar construction in chapter 6:1; Ezekiel 38:12; and 2 Kings 18:13, 17. Others prefer to understand this as Shalmaneser, and yet others as a certain third king between Shalmaneser and Sennacherib; see the scholar Schmidt on this passage. Indeed, Marsham in his *Canon*, page 514, contends it is Esarhaddon, but this goes against the timeline. **c)** and he fought against Ashdod; see 2 Samuel 12:26, 29. Ashdod was a strong city of the Philistines (Joshua 11:22), situated on the furthest borders of Palestine and Judea toward Egypt near the sea (Joshua 15:46, 47). It was dedicated to the worship of Dagon (1 Samuel 5:2), taken from the Philistines and fortified by Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:6), but lost by Ahaz with other cities (2 Chronicles 28:18), and recovered not long ago by Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:8). It was not only captured by this Assyrian general, as Amos also predicted in chapter 1, but not long after also by Psammetichus, King of Egypt and father of Necho, after a 29-year siege, as Herodotus reports in Book II. Finally, it was also captured by Judas Maccabeus (1 Maccabees 5:68) and again burned by his brother Jonathan (1 Maccabees 10:84). **d)** Joshua 10:32, 39; this must have happened before the year of Hezekiah in chapter 36:1, when it was subjected to the Assyrian (chapter 37:36). For after Hezekiah threw off the Assyrian yoke (2 Kings 18:7), Sennacherib occupied most of the fortified cities of Judea, among which was Ashdod again. **verse 2. e)** In this 14th year of Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:13), Isaiah predicted the capture three years in advance, as appears from verse 3. (Dorscheus) **f)** to the Jews, so they might learn to be ashamed of their vain reliance on the Ethiopians and Egyptians against the Assyrian, and trust in God alone as their protector (verse 5). **g)** that is, by means of. Exodus 9:35; Hosea 12:11. **h)** now loosen. Chapter 5:27; 1 Kings 20:11; Isaiah 32:12. **i)** Chapter 37:1, 2; 1 Chronicles 21:16, where Isaiah was clothed like a preacher of repentance (below chapter 22:12); therefore Jonathan has: "gird sackcloth upon your loins." **k)** you shall take off. Deuteronomy 25:9.

> <note>Additional commentary notes on verses 21-25</note>
> **v. 21. a)** Then He shall be made known. Chapter 66:14; Psalm 9:17. **b)** compare Exodus 5:2; 1 Samuel 2:12. **c)** verse 23; Exodus 13:5. Jonathan: "and they shall worship (the Lord) with the sacrifices and offerings of their enemies." **d)** compare Psalm 51:21; Malachi 3:3; 1 Peter 2:5. **e)** see Psalm 50:14.
> **v. 22. f)** So He will indeed smite. Exodus 12:23, 27. **g)** but again by healing them. Chapter 6:10; Hosea 6:1. Septuagint, as in Matthew 13:15. It was not so done of old, when the firstborn were smitten and died (Exodus 12:29, 30). **h)** Genesis 25:21.
> **v. 23. i)** see verses 18, 19, 21. **k)** chapter 11:15; 40:3. **l)** so that the converted Assyrian comes into Egypt, and likewise the Egyptian into Assyria. For there shall be concord among those converted to Christ, and a mutual communication of the acknowledged truth. Otherwise, as Dorscheus notes, there is a dispute about the fulfillment. Most refer all these things to the times of the New Testament, which I do not resist. For it is certain that there was a wonderful gathering of Egyptians into the kingdom of God in the primitive Church. But also those who interpret these things concerning the great light of truth existing in Egypt and Assyria even before Christ do not seem to be rejected. For it is known from Jewish history that a great number of Jews were in Egypt and Assyria long before the coming of Christ, and that they established illustrious schools everywhere. From there, they undoubtedly won many proselytes from both nations to the true God; which must be numbered among the benefits of God. Compare Acts 2:10. Thus these two opinions can be joined. So far the words of Dorscheus. **m)** Tigurine Version: "and the Egyptians shall worship the Lord." Verse 21; Deuteronomy 6:13. So Varenius, and the same sense in Schmidt: "and they shall serve." **n)** with the Assyrian. So Tigurine, Varenius, and Schmidt from the context. But other versions—Septuagint, Vulgate, Jonathan, Syriac, Arabic—say "and the Egyptians shall serve the Assyrians": certainly because this word <note>Hebrew: *et*</note> with this verb <note>Hebrew: *avad*, to serve</note> almost constantly denotes the object which is served or worshipped, e.g., Genesis 14:4; 27:40; 31:6; Exodus 14:12, etc. If anyone thinks this is to be preferred here, this verse must be connected with the preceding thus: "the Egyptians shall serve the Assyrians under Nebuchadnezzar," which Jeremiah also predicted (Jeremiah 27:7-12) and Ezekiel (Ezekiel 29:18, etc.). There are, however, other places besides this one where the particle *et* after the verb *avad* is rendered differently than as an object marker; see Judges 9:28 and our notes there.
> **v. 24. o)** verses 18, 19, 21, 23. **p)** chapter 10:20; Romans 9:5; Galatians 6:16. **q)** a third. Chapter 15:5; namely, the land or region to which they shall flow. Chapter 2:2, 3. **r)** and thus it shall be a blessing. Genesis 12:2, 3; Ephesians 1:3. **s)** in all the earth. Chapter 10:23; Psalm 74:12.
> **v. 25. t)** for. 1 Samuel 3:23; or, since. Joshua 22:31. **u)** he blessed each of them. Genesis 27:27; Numbers 6:24; Psalm 67:2. **x)** compare chapter 52:15; 65:1; Hosea 2:1. **y)** chapter 60:21. **z)** see above, chapter 11:6 and following.
