The night which the Babylonians had consecrated to pleasures. Dorshe. y) Joel 1:7. z) into terror (1 Samuel 14:15; see Daniel 5:5, 9, 30; and compare Jeremiah 50:43). For this prophecy can refer to a double fall of the Babylonians, though it looks primarily to Cyrus. Namely, Belshazzar lost his life on that night which he had destined for pleasures (Daniel 5:30), and Darius the Mede then received the kingdom (who is called Nabonidus by outsiders). In the 17th year of his reign, after the Babylonian army was defeated and slaughtered before the city and the outer walls were destroyed, Cyrus finally—in the second year—diverted the Euphrates through channels into the marsh (Isaiah 44:27, 28; Jeremiah 50:38). While the Babylonians were intemperately celebrating the feast of the Sacaea (Isaiah 21:5; Jeremiah 51:39), he arrived unexpectedly through the riverbed from which the water had receded and which cut through the city. He took possession of one part of the city while the other part was still unaware of it; the prefect of the city only learned of it later through messengers (Jeremiah 51:31). See Herodotus (Book I, page 49) and Xenophon (*The Education of Cyrus*, Book VII, pages 190 and following) narrating these things more clearly. verse 5. a) while by preparing, the table is prepared. Psalm 23:5. b) by watching, he watches. See Leviticus 6:7; Judges 7:19; 1 Kings 3:15; and chapter 21:6. c) a watch (1). But the Babylonians standing on the wall, ignorant of what Cyrus was doing, mocked the siege; later, even after the city was occupied, the guards of the palace gates, drinking by a bright fire, were unexpectedly overwhelmed by the Persians. Xenophon, as cited above. d) while by eating they eat, and by drinking they drink. See Daniel 5:1 and following; so Xenophon, as cited: "And the ditches indeed," he says, "had already been dug. But Cyrus, when he had heard that a certain feast was being celebrated in Babylon, a day of the sort on which all the Babylonians would drink and revel all night long," etc. Compare 1 Thessalonians 5:3. e) namely, a messenger comes who says: "Arise, princes!" See Jeremiah 51:31. f) anoint the shields—namely, so that the hides do not crack. But Gusset (page 483) suspects that for the sake of a good omen, shields were accustomed to be anointed before battle as a kind of consecration. For this word is not used for every anointing, but for a solemn one used for consecration. Compare 2 Samuel 1:21. Jonathan: "Arise and polish the weapons."

Compare 2 Kings 19:18. **Verse 10.** h) *my threshing!* <note>original: "tritura mea"</note> Babylon, which previously threshed others, is now herself subject to threshing. Dorschem. Compare chapter 25:10; chapter 41:15. Micah 4:13. i) *and the son of my threshing floor*, like grain in my floor to be threshed and shaken out. Compare Jeremiah 51:33. Micah 4:12. Thus "son of stripes" is one to be beaten (Deuteronomy 25:2); "son of death" is one to be handed over to death (1 Samuel 20:31); "son of the kingdom" is one destined for the kingdom (Matthew 8:12); "son of Gehenna" is one to be cast into Gehenna (Matthew 23:15). k) Those things which I have heard from the Lord (Obadiah verse 1), and thus most certain, I have declared to you. Compare Jeremiah 51:62. These are the words of the Prophet, as Jonathan adds. **Verse 11.** l) verse 1; chapter 17:1. m) Dumah, perhaps Idumea [Edom]. Compare chapter 34:5, 6. The name is a wordplay or allusion, as in Micah 1:10 and following; as if to say the noisy insolence of the nation is to be reduced to silence <term>Dumah</term> <note>The Hebrew name "Dumah" sounds like the word for "silence" (*dumah*)</note>, collective Psalm 94:17; Psalm 115:17. Others understand the descendants of Dumah, the son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:14), a people of Arabia; the city of Judah (Joshua 15:52) does not belong here. Moreover, the Idumeans, having been subjected by David, obeyed until the time of Jehoshaphat (1 Kings 22:48), but then became rebels (2 Chronicles 21:10) and revolted from his son Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20; Genesis 27:40); though conquered by Amaziah (2 Chronicles 25:11), they prevailed again over Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:17). They impiously rejoiced at the calamities of the Israelites and Jews (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah verse 10 and following; Lamentations 4:21, 22), and therefore they were not only to be punished by Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 25:21; chapter 27:2; Lamentations 4:21, 22), but further even by the Jews (Ester 11:14; Numbers 24:18; Ezekiel 25:12 and following; Obadiah verse 18). Through Judas Maccabeus (1 Maccabees 5:3) and Hyrcanus (Josephus, *Antiquities* book 13, chapter 17), they were subdued, and finally with the Jews themselves they were conquered and extinguished by the Romans. Compare Jeremiah 49:7; Ezekiel 25:12; chapter 32:29; chapter 35:2; chapter 36:5; Obadiah verse 1. n) toward me, and in my hearing, someone was crying out. o) from the mountains of Seir. Genesis 36:8, 9, 20. p) O watchman, the Prophet. See Maius's *Economy* page 919. But according to Schmidt: the Prophet speaks as if stationed in a vision, in which he had heard both the voice of the one asking and the one responding. q) what remains of the night, of miseries (Micah 3:6)? etc. Schmidt. r) Psalm 130:6. s) what news do you bring and announce concerning the coming night? Jonathan: and the punishment for the wicked. z) If therefore you wish to inquire (5) chapter 30:13; chapter 64:1. a) inquire sincerely and seriously. Obadiah verse 6. Compare Jeremiah 4:1. According to Gousset (page 137) it notes a soul boiling with vehement affection, comparing Exodus 9:9. As if to say: you boil, then boil; i.e., if you are moved by a sincere and fervent desire to know the will of God, be moved more and more. b) namely, be converted (chapter 31:6; Jeremiah 3:14, 22; Ezekiel 14:6) and repent (Matthew 3:2; chapter 4:17; Mark 1:15). c) and come to Christ through faith (chapter 56:9; compare John 5:40; chapter 6, 37, 45). Therefore the calling of the Idumeans and their return to the Church is predicted here, which Josephus testifies occurred almost a whole century before the reign of Herod, when they became Jews (*Antiquities* book 13, chapter 17). Hence in the time of the New Testament they had the opportunity to recognize and embrace the light that appeared to them also. Maius, *Economy* page 919. **Verse 13.** d) A burden, or a heavy prophecy. verse 1, 11; chapter 22:1. e) pronounced in or against Arabia. This land, from a mixture of peoples and in opposition to Kedar or Arabia toward the East (Job 1:3; Genesis 25:5), was also partly called Erech (1 Kings 10:15; Jeremiah 25:20, 24, etc.). It provided a home for various nations: namely the descendants of Joktan (Genesis 10:26), Lot (Genesis 19:36, 37), Ishmael (Genesis 21:2; chapter 25:12 and following), Nahor (Genesis 22:21), and Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1 and following), also Esau or Edom (Genesis 36:6 and following), the Midianites and Amalekites, etc. However, this prophecy primarily regards Arabia Petraea and the Kedarites, who within a year lost all their glory (below, verse 16); whether they suffered this from Sennacherib—whom Herodotus explicitly calls the king of the Assyrians and Arabs—or from Nebuchadnezzar, whose yoke they bore along with their neighbors. See Jeremiah 25:23; chapter 49:28 and following. Compare also above chapter 13:21 and chapter 15:7. f) in the forest in Arabia you shall hereafter spend the night, O troops of Dedanites: namely because the towns and villages which otherwise provided a convenient lodging have been wasted and desolated. g) Genesis 37:25. h) of the Dedanites, merchants (Ezekiel 27:15, 20) descending from Dedan, the son of Abraham (Genesis 25:3). **Verse 14.** i) Compare Genesis 21:16, 19; 2 Samuel 17:29; Exodus 15:22; Psalm 107:5. k) Imperative: bring; others, the past tense in Hiphil: let them bring. Compare Jeremiah 12:19; and the root in the preceding verse 12.

<summary>This page concludes the oracle against Kedar, predicting its downfall within a year, and begins the "Burden of the Valley of Vision," a multifaceted prophecy concerning the siege and spiritual state of Jerusalem. The commentary debates whether the "valley" refers to Jerusalem's geography, its spiritual status as a place of prophecy, or its future state of lamentation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Isaiah 22. Having described the military preparations and the spiritual failures of Jerusalem, the text now focuses on the individual fates of two high officials: Shebna, the proud steward who is to be deposed, and Eliakim, who is raised up as a faithful successor and a prophetic type of Christ.</meta>

<header>CHAPTER 22. Isaiah 22.</header>

<margin>
Compare Saint Jerome on this location. 
The Prefect of the royal palace (chapter 36:3; 1 Kings 18:18). 
Otherwise, Shebna here—described as an old hypocrite and an adversary of the reforms of the time, <term>Kometz Batra</term> <note>original Hebrew: קמץ בטרא; likely a reference to a specific Talmudic or rabbinic designation for a type of official or a specific character trait</note> (see notes on 2 Kings 18:18)—serves as an emblematic figure for vile and entirely carnal leaders, Epicureans <note>followers of Epicurus, here meaning those pursuing pleasure and denying divine providence</note>, swollen with pride and arrogance, such as would appear among them around the time of Jesus Christ. 
In Eliakim, however, we see depicted Jesus Christ, who was to be substituted for those princes and prefects of the people of God (whom Paul calls "authorities and powers") and raised to the highest dignity—

The Targum Jonathan says, "let us fell bulls and slaughter sheep." z) chapter 5:11, 22. a) "it is for eating and drinking," that is, they say this, as the Septuagint correctly supplies (compare verses 15, 16 and chapter 14:8). b) chapter 56:12, Wisdom of Solomon 2:6. (1) compare 1 Kings 1:2, also Exodus 15:11. l) toward chapter 10:3. m) Shebna, who is called a scribe below, meaning the king's secretary for letters and records; thus he is thrown down from his rank of honor and prefecture because of his arrogance, pride, and ungrateful spirit toward God—

<column-break/>

—and raised up over the breach of the whole house of God; while the rest were to be cast down from their rank, and after the Republic was overturned by the Romans and the Temple destroyed, they would perish miserably and be driven into a shameful and calamitous exile. (Vitringa on Revelation 1:20, page 74 following).
v. 16. n) "What is here to you?" again, understand before this verse the word <term>le-mor</term> <note>saying</note>, he says to him (compare verse 13). p) compare chapter 52:5. q) "you have hewn" (chapter 5:2, chapter 51:1). The Septuagint uses the term "you have cut out" (Matthew 27:60). r) he is hewing for himself with pride of spirit, or "he caused a royal monument to be hewn for himself." Note the extra letter "yod" at the end (as in Genesis 49:11). s) "on high," in a high rock (compare Habakkuk 2:9). t) "engraving" or "designating" (chapter 49:16, Ezekiel 4:1).
v. 17. u) "hurl you with a throw." (1) x) "with a hurling." (1) y) "O man!" The Syriac version correctly calls him this. z) "wrapping, he will wrap you" (chapter 59:17, Micah 3:7, Song of Solomon 1:7). The Targum Jonathan: "shame shall cover you" (compare Esther 7:3).
v. 18. a) Cocceius's Lexicon, page 718: "he will roll you roundly"; Gousset: "he will mass you together" and "pack you into a round shape." (3) Leviticus 15:4. The Arabic root means to arrange, compose, or distinguish a thing into various types and forms. b) "in a massing." (1) c) "like a ball." (2) (chapter 29:3). d) chapter 33:21, Genesis 34:21. e) "they shall be a shame to your lord's house" (Hosea 4:7), as it will be said: "Behold, here is that prince of the king of Judah, who previously rode in a magnificent chariot." (Saint Jerome). f) 1 Kings 18:8.
v. 19. g) "thus I will drive you away" (Numbers 35:20, 22, Jeremiah 46:15). h) "from your station" (Joshua 4:3, 9). i) "and from your place" where you stand (1 Kings 10:5). k) "He will overthrow you" (Isaiah 22:5). Although it is not clear from history at what time or on what occasion these threats were fulfilled, the outcome is not to be doubted. Some speculate he was taken into captivity with Manasseh and died miserably in Assyria.
v. 20. l) chapter 36:3, 2 Kings 18:18.
v. 21. m) Genesis 41:41, 42, Daniel 5:29, Esther 6:8, 9. n) "with your belt" (Exodus 28:4). o) "I will strengthen him" (chapter 33:23, chapter 41:7, Nahum 2:2). p) chapter 39:2, compare Genesis 45:8. q) compare Esther 8:2. r) Genesis 45:8, 2 Kings 6:21.
v. 22. s) "Keys." (3) (Judges 3:25, 1 Chronicles 9:27). "The house of David." The grammatical sense of these words is that Eliakim, because of his piety, modesty, and faithfulness to God, and the loyal service rendered to Him, is to be substituted in the highest dignity of the prefecture of the royal palace with such authority and power that all things should be arranged according to his judgment; without his opinion and counsel, nothing should be done in the royal court, and all care of affairs should devolve upon him. The insignia of that dignity were the keys, which are said here to be placed "upon the shoulder" because, as I believe, they hung from the shoulders by a belt of more ornate craftsmanship, much like swords among the ancients. (Vitringa on Revelation 3:7, page 177, 8; compare chapter 9:5). u) Job 12:12, 14, Revelation 3:7. In chapter 5:2 and following, the phrases are to be understood absolutely regarding Christ, and in a limited sense regarding Eliakim (Dorscheus). Just as Shebna bore the figure of the prefects of the Jewish Church (see note at v. 15), so Eliakim, as Prefect of the palace of David, bore the figure of Jesus Christ, the Supreme Head of the Church, which is the house of God. For His is the supreme power in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18) and the supreme authority in the Church. He, as a Son, is over the house of God, which house we are (Hebrews 3:6). In His hand are the keys of the kingdom of heaven, which He dispenses by His authority (Matthew 16:19, etc.; Vitringa as cited, page 178).
v. 23. x) "And I will fix him" (verse 25, Judges 4:21). y) "like a nail" (Judges 16:14). z) verse 25, 2 Samuel 7:16.

<margin>
**CHAPTER XXIII. verse 1.** 
*q)* chapter 13:1; chapter 17:1; chapter 21:1. 
*r)* Of Tyre, Joshua 19:29. Its devastation is predicted here, carried out by Nebuchadnezzar, followed by its restoration, verse 15 ff., and its conversion to Christ, verse 18. The name is derived from the rocks [Hebrew: *Tzur*]. It was the most famous city of Phoenicia, and after Sidon, the largest and most ancient; Strabo, *Geography* book 16, page 504. It was founded by the Sidonians before the Trojan war, and 240 years before Solomon's Temple, on the mainland; Justin, book 18, chapter 3; Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 8, chapter 2. It was called *Palaetyrus*, or "Old Tyre," according to Bochart’s *Canaan*, book 2, chapter 17, page 861. It was the marketplace for almost the entire world—Asia, Africa, and Europe; see verse 3 of this chapter and Ezekiel 27:3 ff. It was unsuccessfully besieged by Shalmaneser (Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 9, chapter 14), then by Nebuchadnezzar (verse 13) for 13 years, and after a most severe siege (following the fall of Jerusalem, Ezekiel 26:2) it was captured and destroyed; Jeremiah 25:22; chapter 27:3; Ezekiel 26:7 ff.; chapter 29:18; Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 10, chapter 11 and *Against Apion*, book 1, page 1046. This gave rise to "New Tyre" on the island, which Alexander the Great, in the seventh month after the siege began,
</margin>

<margin>
captured and destroyed in a horrific manner. See Curtius, book 4, chapters 1, 2, 3, and 4.
</margin>

<margin>
**CHAPTER XXIII.**
Yet, it was restored again, though subject to various subsequent disasters, and was finally converted to Christ, as seen below in verse 18; Zechariah 9:2; Psalm 45:13; Psalm 87:4; Acts 21:3–4. It is clearly evident from the parallels in Revelation 18:23 that Tyre served as a type <note>a prophetic symbol</note> of the mystical Harlot. Compare Gualther’s *Prophetic Theology*, page 719. More details pertaining to its more recent history, and how it was occupied by the Saracens and Turks, may be found in the works of other authors. 
*v)* verse 6, 14.
</margin>

**c)** The pouring out upon him. Ezekiel 15:3.

**e)** of the offspring, others say: of the grandsons. 
**(1) f)** of the basins or bowls. 
**(3)** Exodus 24:6; Song of Solomon 7:3.

Chapter 13:6. **s)** chapter 2:16; chapter 60:9. Those carrying on trade with Tyre. Ezekiel 27:12, 25. Compare the note on 1 Kings 10:22; the Septuagint translates this as *Carthage*, as they do in verses 10 and 14. Indeed, the Tyrians founded Carthage and always honored it as their mother city. Compare chapter 24:10; 1 Samuel 25:27. **z)** *The Chittim* verse 12. Most understand this to mean the Macedonians, who under Alexander's leadership besieged and devastated Tyre. And the writer of the book of Maccabees properly thought the Chittim were Macedonians, 1 Maccabees 1:1; chapter 8:5. However, Bochart in other scriptural passages—for example Numbers 24:24; Ezekiel 27:6; Daniel 11:30—identifies them as Romans. But in this specific place, he argues in his *Phaleg* (pages 179 and 182) that it should be understood as the Cuthaeans (2 Kings 17:24) or the Cissians, inhabitants of Susiana near Babylon, based on the context of this prophecy. **a)** *this will be revealed to them.* chapter 22:14; chapter 40:5; Daniel 10:21. **v. 2. b)** *Be silent.* Psalm 4:5. See note on Joshua 13:3. **k)** *the harvests of the Nile.* chapter 19:7; Genesis 41:1 ff. **l)** this was the revenue of Tyre, Genesis 47:24. Not because it grew in Tyre, but because grain was carried in abundance to Tyre from Egypt by sea. (1) a threat against the land, city, and people. (2) a promise concerning the remnants in verse 13 and following, and a gracious visitation in verse 23, and concerning the kingdom of Christ in verse 23. The chief difficulty is that they do not have a title indicating who they are about, or which land is to be understood. Some, with Saint Jerome, understand the whole world, and refer this prophecy to the end of the world. Others join together the lands about which the Prophet has spoken thus far. Grotius understands the Ten Tribes; Dorsche, Schmid, Ion, and others primarily the Judean land, though not excluding the neighboring region, comparing Jeremiah 25:9 and following. We also subscribe to this opinion, yet in such a way that we think the newest judgments of God narrated in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> are simultaneously indicated by these chapters. For as we already observed above at chapter 6:9 from Dorsche’s fourth rule, prophets, because of their great light, extend their oracles to many things that will happen at clearly different times. Thus the prophecy concerning the first destruction of Jerusalem also involves the last, because they involve the world itself (Matthew 24, etc.). And Rule V: Often it is given, he says, whether the prophets speak of the type or the antitype, as in Isaiah 45 where he speaks of Cyrus. Here a double antitype must be observed; 2) the literal sense is adapted to the type as far and as long as it can be; and the mystical sense, which exhausts the force of the words, is subjoined. Thus the Holy Spirit taught in the New Testament. Compare 2 Samuel 7:14, 1 Kings 8:20 with Hebrews 1:5. Hence also Dr. Maius, in his review of these chapters, looks primarily to their final fulfillment in the *Economy of the Old Testament*, page 922 and following. **h)** About to evacuate; according to Neumann, about to overturn. **CHAPTER XXIV.** **Verse 2.** **Nasak** <note>original: "נשך"</note> spelled with *He* in manuscripts 5, 10, 14, 20, 21 and in the text of 6, 9. <summary>This page concludes the cosmic judgment of Isaiah 24, interpreting the "host of the high" as either celestial bodies or fallen angels, and transitions into the hymn of praise in Isaiah 25. The commentary identifies the "fortified city" destroyed by God as Babylon, viewing it both as a historical city and a mystical symbol for the enemies of the Church.</summary>

**s)** verse 7, 10; chapter 24, 23; Hebrews 12:22-23. **t)** The Gospel feast and the wedding banquet; compare Psalm 22:30; Proverbs 9:2; Matthew 8:11; chapter 22:1; Luke 14:16; chapter 22:30; Revelation 19:7, 9. **u)** of fatty dishes; chapter 28:2, 4; compare Deuteronomy 32:14; Nehemiah 8:10; and Romans 14:17. **x)** of the dregs <note>Hebrew: *shemarim*</note>. (4) Psalm 75:9. That is, according to Dorscheus <note>Johann Georg Dorsche, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> and others, dregs that are not retained but purged; hence, wine purified from its dregs. According to Schmidius <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a notable 17th-century biblical scholar</note>, it refers to sweet and fragrant wine that sits upon its dregs and properly retains its aroma and flavor; compare Jeremiah 48:11; Zephaniah 1:12. Simplicius and others interpret this in a negative sense (see the note at the end of verse 5), and Varenius refers it to the pains of hell, comparing Matthew 25:31, 41, 42. **y)** as if to say, full of marrow, (1) compare chapter 5:17; Job 21:24. **z)** purged—that is, pure and unmixed. (7) Elsewhere used for metals purified by smelting; Malachi 3:3; Job 36:27; 1 Chronicles 28:18, etc. From this, Schmidius conjectures it refers to "burnt wine" (brandy) which is made from dregs distilled by fire, etc., but this is less likely.
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 18. i)** *We conceived* indeed, and were in labor (verse 17; Micah 4:10). This refers to the *hope of spiritual* offspring and freedom emerging from that most heavy affliction. **k)** *But we have brought forth as if wind, and consumed our strength* in vain. Compare below, chapter 33:11; 49:4. **l)** *Help and salvation*. Chapter 33:6; Psalm 74:12. **m)** *We have not done*, nor were we able to provide for the earth, so that the enemies would fall. No appearance of salvation seemed to show itself to us amidst our calamities, nor was there hope that our enemies would fall. *Dorscheus* <note>Johann Georg Dorsche, 1601–1659, a Lutheran theologian</note>. **n)** *They were falling*. Numbers 14:32; 2 Samuel 1:12, 19. **o)** See verse 9; chapter 18:3.

**v. 19. p)** *But now your dead live or shall live.* Many difficulties and questions occur in this verse, of which we will touch only the most important. For (1) to some, these are the words of the Prophet; however, Vavenio on Isaiah Part II, p. 288, and Maio in *Economy* p. 925, see them as the words of Christ to the Church; but to Schmidio and to us still, like the preceding verses, they are the words of the Church to God and the Savior. (2) Concerning the *proper and final resurrection*, by whose blessed hope the Church consoles itself under afflictions; Jonathan, Schmid, and many others understand this text in this way; others, however, *as Dorsche does, understand it as a tropical [metaphorical] death and resurrection*, that is, concerning liberation from misery and restoration to a former state. Others finally (as we shall soon hear from Vitringa) understand it *as a figurative and symbolic resurrection of the Martyrs*, when their cause is solemnly vindicated and justified by God, and those who were considered holy but treated as heresiarchs and rebels are now recognized as holy Martyrs of Christ: an example of such a resurrection occurred around the time of Constantine the Great. (3) Others understand the beginning of the verse in this way: *They live to God (Matthew 21:32), having died in the faith of the Savior (John 11:25, 26), and finally they shall also rise in the body.*
</margin>

and the diabolical beast of Revelation 11:7-8, who slaughtered them for the confession of truth (Revelation 12:11) throughout all time (Psalm 44:23; Psalm 79:2, etc.). Regarding these dead, Schmid says: "We understand those whom the Church buried in her long-lasting affliction or calamity." **r)** *They shall rise again*, namely, to a better and eternal life, according to Schmid, as we just said. But *Dorscheus says: The exit from calamities is described as if from a grave, a phraseology taken from the article on the resurrection of the dead, just as in Ezekiel 37. It is therefore not a resurrection properly speaking, but rather a restoration to a state of happiness, both spiritual and civil.* Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa, 1659–1722, a Dutch theologian</note>, on Revelation 20:4, p. 1159, says after other things: *This is the resurrection of the Church, along with the Prophets, Apostles, Martyrs, and distinguished ministers of Christ, which this prophecy mentions as figurative and symbolic; such as John himself gave us to see in the resurrection of the two witnesses (Revelation 11:11). Isaiah also, dealing with the same time of the Church in this place, depicts it under this emblem; similar examples exist, to be referred here in a spiritual sense, in Hosea 6:2, Ezekiel 37:1 and following, and Daniel 12:1-2. Compare also Luke 15:24 and Romans 11:15.* **s)** *Awake.* See note on chapter 23:3. **u)** *Like the dew of herbs.* (2) 2 Kings 4:39. Like one who refreshes herbs that are withered and as if dead. **x)** *It is Your dew, O Savior, poured out by You.* Compare Deuteronomy 33:2; Hosea 6:3. **y)** Schmid in his version: *but the land of the Rephaim <note>The Rephaim were an ancient race of giants, often associated with the spirits of the dead in the underworld</note> You shall cast down: for which, according to the accents and points (which nowhere put 'earth' [va-aretz] in the construct state, see for example chapter 65:17, Proverbs 25:3, etc.), it should be read: 'but into the earth, You shall cast down or throw down the Rephaim,'* as Vatablus and Tremellius translate. Therefore also in his commentary Schmid has: *and the earth shall make the Rephaim fall, shall cast them out; (for 'tappil' [shall cast down] is either 2nd person masculine or 3rd person feminine)* and he thinks the Church is looking toward the region of the giants, which has, as it were, vomited them out because of their crimes. See Leviticus 18:25, 28; chapter 20:22. **v. 20. z)** *Meanwhile go, my people.* A prophetic warning to the people of God concerning withdrawal into patience and hope toward God. *Dorscheus*. **a)** *Enter the chambers, or inner rooms.* Genesis 43:30; 1 Kings 20:30; chapter 22:25. *Schmid, with Gerhard and others, takes this to mean the chambers of the graves; yet he confesses that the other exposition, concerning chambers of solitude, prayer, and silence, does not displease him. To Dorscheus, 'cheder'* <note>Hebrew for chamber</note> *notes any place of refuge and retreat which those in calamity seek out of pressing necessity; just as one overwhelmed by a storm retreats into a cave or a hollow tree. To Bochartus <note>Samuel Bochart, 1599–1667, a French biblical scholar</note> in Hierozoicon Part I, p. 610, this text seems not badly to allude to Exodus 12:22-23 [the Passover].* **b)** 2 Kings 4:4; Matthew 6:6. **c)** Genesis 7:16. **d)** *Hide under the shadow and divine protection.* Judges 9:5; compare Habakkuk 3:4. **e)** *As if for a small moment.* Chapter 27:3; chapter 54:7. <note>original Greek: *mikron hoson hoson*</note> "A very, very little while." Hebrews 10:37. **f)** *Until the wrath of God against the enemies has passed and been finished.* Chapter 10:5, 25. And your full liberation approaches. *They shall rise* etc.

**CHAPTER XXVII, v. 1. q)** *In that day*, verses 2, 12, 13; chapter 24:21; 25:9; 26:1. Namely, in the time of those miseries which were deplored in the previous chapters: where the pious in the Church were considered dead and mourn in their inner chambers, and indeed always whenever that one [the dragon] tries to swallow the Church (Revelation 12:4). Therefore, the day of the last judgment is not meant; for after this day the Church will flourish on the earth (verse 2, etc.). *Dorscheus*. Almost all interpreters grant that the previous prophecy or Song continues here, announcing judgment against the enemies of Christ’s kingdom: the Devil, the infernal serpent, and the Antichrist, to be slain by the hardest, greatest, and strongest sword of the Word (verse 1), comparing 2 Thessalonians 2:8 and Revelation 20:10, where the double Leviathan (and the Dragon in the sea) is explained as the devil, the beast, and the false prophet. Maius in *Economy* p. 925; though *Schmidius* understands the Babylonian and Egyptian kingdoms here from verse 13, following *Luther*, because he refers everything in this prophecy primarily to the liberation of the Jewish people from the Babylonian captivity. But compare notes on chapter 24:1, 22. **r)** See chapter 26:14, 21. **s)** Chapter 25:6; 26:21; Hebrews 3:8. The Son of God, the Avenger of the Church and Judge of the world (Genesis 18:25), to whom the spiritual vineyard described above in chapter 5 belongs: whose glory was seen in chapter 6, mother described in chapter 7, kingdom delineated in chapter 8, birth indicated in chapter 9, whose anointing was narrated in chapter 11, etc., to whom the Father gave judgment (John 5:27; compare John 15:1). *Dorscheus*. **t)** Compare chapter 34:5-6; Psalm 45:4; Ephesians 6:17. **u)** *Hard.* Verse 8; compare Jeremiah 23:29. **x)** Compare Revelation 6:4. **y)** Compare chapter 40:10; Exodus 3:19; chapter 6:1; Hebrews 4:12; Revelation 19:15, 21. **z)** *Leviathan.* Job 3:8. That *crocodiles* are called so in Job 40:25 and following is less doubtful, and the consensus of the learned with *Bochart* is more certain, as *Ludolf* affirms in *Commentary on the History of Ethiopia* p. 159. But as the synonymous word *Thannin* signifies a dragon, so it is often transferred to whales and marine beasts because they reflect the form and coil of dragons in some way; so that you may see whales and baleen whales called by the name *Leviathan* in various places, as here and in Psalm 74:14, Psalm 104:26, etc. For this very reason, crocodiles are signified by both names *Thannin* and *Leviathan*, because crocodiles are in the likeness of a dragon. *Bochart, Hierozoicon Part II, p. 770.* Furthermore, not only the proper and literal meaning, but also the tropical or figurative meaning must be considered here. Dorscheus reconciles the various opinions (some of which we have already cited) this way: *Most, he says, immediately understand Satan and refer this whole thing to the New Testament; we broaden it, and under this metaphor understand the Kingdom of devils and the impious, stirred up against the Church by the ancient serpent (Genesis 3:15; Revelation 12:3); and thus also the temporal and visible enemies of the Church, as well as the spiritual and invisible ones (Ephesians 6:12). And among the temporal ones here, primarily the Assyrian and Babylonian kingdoms, which loomed over the Church in the time of Isaiah, which therefore needed consolation.* Compare Glassius, *Sacred Rhetoric* p. 1787.

so that the method of extracting grain, the second and third [ways] alluded to in this text, may be a little more fully understood by the reader, we will add the words of Edward Pococke on Joel 3:14, page 334 onwards, who says: Truly, such threshing as we call it by our custom—done with sticks or flails—is not meant; but that which was done by the help of a certain instrument which broke and *cut* the straw and the husks, and thus pushed out the grains. Even today there are two kinds of these instruments: one is made of very heavy wooden planks into which are fixed very sharp stones or flints; these, drawn by beasts over the grain arranged in rows, extract the grains in one turn, break the husks, and cut the straw or crush it into tiny pieces like chaff, which serves as fodder for the beasts. — The other kind of this instrument is made of iron, consisting of two iron wheels marked with cut notches and very sharp teeth, like iron, which are connected to each other by a wooden axle. When this is drawn through the grain on the threshing floor, it achieves the same result in extracting the grains and breaking and cutting the husks and straw as the one described before. r) *is threshed or extracted*. Passive form <note>original: "Hoph."</note> (1) compare v. 28, chapter 25:10. s) *poppy*. v. 25. t) *either a wheel*, or nor a wheel. Exodus 14:25, Proverbs 20:26. The negation is repeated from the preceding as above in chapter 23:4. u) *wagon* or small cart, which we just described. x) see v. 25. y) *is turned around, is led around*. Passive form <note>original: "Noph." for "Hoph."</note> (1) compare 1 Sam 5:9-10. z) *it is shaken out*. chapter 27:12. a) *a rod*. compare chapter 10:5, 24; 2 Sam 23:21. w. v. 28. b) Scholion: *Afterwards it is crushed into bread*. Passive form (1) compare Exodus 30:36, 2 Kings 23:6. c) *for not forever*. 2 Sam 2:26. d) *by threshing*. Infinitive of the simple verb <note>original: "Inf. Kal"</note> (1) e) *he threshes the grain*. see v. 27. f) *and though he drives [the wheels] over it*. Jer 51:34. g) *the wheel*. (1) compare chapter 5:28. h) *of his small cart*. see v. 27. i) and *horsemen* or his horses. chapter 21:7, 9. see note on l) *1 Sam 8:11.* k) *yet he does not crush it*. chapter 41:15, Deut 9:21, but only threshes it. l) *This also, namely, the moderation of punishments and direction toward a saving end.* m) chapter 1:24. n) *Gen 24:50.* o) *he made it to be wondered at*. compare chapter 29:14, Judges 13:18-19, and Job 38:2. p) *counsel*. compare chapter 9:5, Jer 32:19. q) *he showed great [wisdom].* 1 Sam 12:24, Joel 2:20-21. r) *wisdom, by the truth of the matter, and by proceeding through suitable means to the goal set for Himself.* Micah 6:9. **CHAPTER XXIX. v. 1.** s) *Woe!* chapter 1:4. This 29th chapter deals with the Jews, and primarily the detestable condition of Jerusalem (both physical and spiritual v. 9 onwards), their punishments, and the destruction of the city. (2) the causes or merits of the punishments v. 13 onwards. (3) the remnants of the Jews and the outcome of the punishments v. 22 onwards. However, it by no means deals with the siege of Sennacherib, as some think, nor even with the conquest by Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonians (discussed in chapters 22 and 39), but with the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, based on the context, in which everything fits the New Testament more correctly. The Prophet predicted punishments for the mockers of God's word in his own time (as Scholion notes) in chapter 28:17 onwards; then he exhorted them in the same place v. 22 so that the Jews would at least abstain from mockery in the future, lest after the Babylonian captivity the chains would become stronger at the time of the consumption to be made under the New Testament; and he promised hope of pardon to those looking back in v. 23 onwards. But soon, seeing in the spirit that the Jewish people under the New Testament would neglect that most faithful exhortation, he predicts for that reason as a punishment the *total overthrow of the city and Jerusalem*, for very grave reasons. These things persuade us to take the whole chapter as being about the siege and destruction by the Romans and the times of the New Testament. t) *Ariel, Ariel!* as if to say *Lion of God, Lion of God!* There is much dispute about what that mystical name means in this place. It is said indeed (1) of the two most valiant Moabites in 2 Sam 23:20. (2) of the Altar of burnt offering in Ezekiel 43:15-16, whose fire, according to Bochart in *Hierozoicon* Part I, page 717 and others, being perpetually lit, devoured and consumed the burnt offerings like a lion; which Hiller, however, prefers to be called something like the "crib of God." (3) it is said here because of the altar itself, by a synecdoche <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note> of the part for the whole; that is, because of similarity, of the city of Jerusalem itself, comparing v. 2. As if to say, according to Gousset page 64: You, O city, are the altar through the consumption of your people within you, and the slaughtered corpses around you. But Scholion understands by it immediately the tribe of Judah, and thus primarily its metropolis Jerusalem; and he thinks it is not inconveniently taken from Genesis 49:9. As if the Prophet said: *Woe to you, O Judah!* who are indeed the lion of God, and like a lion and a King among your brothers, appointed by God Himself! who dwell in the city of Jerusalem, in which David encamped. Gurtler, however, in *Typics* page 15 says: although David fixed his seat and tent with the ark of the covenant. Num 1:51, Nahum 3:17. At the same time, there is an ellipsis of the relative here, as in the Psalm; compare Daniel 9:26. x) *The Septuagint and others: "which he fought against":* but Jonathan and many others more correctly: *in which he encamped*, that is, resided. In which, because the same city had given birth to his throne, which was placed in Jerusalem. Whence the prediction must have seemed a much more terrible and unexpected sense. compare 2 Sam 7:1 onwards. Dorsch. x) *just add [years]*, instead of *your highest security, year upon year*, as an Imperial reproach. Root: Gousset, others **saphah**, compare chapter 30:1, 1:13, 15, Num 33:14. a) *let the moveable feasts* be defined, or determined by their calculation. (compare Amos 5:21, Nahum 2:1) as if to say: just write your calendars for many years, and determine the feasts in them, in which you may rejoice. But let them slaughter the festive victims, comparing Psalm 118:27. b) *let them fall, let them be killed* (3) chapter 10:34. Therefore, security/complacency is censured in this place. Dorsch. v. 2. c) *I will indeed [bring] distress to Ariel,* or I will prepare distresses for Ariel, Deut 28:53, namely, through the Romans, your enemies v. 7, whose multitude (v. 5), speed (v. 7), and audacity (v. 8) are described. compare above chapter 5:26. d) so that there is nothing there but grief and sorrow. (2) Lamentations 2:5, compare Matthew 24:21. e) for it will be to me *like the Altar (the crib of God)* Ezekiel 43:16. see note on v. 1. But Scholion and Dorsch say: I will treat the most fierce city and people like the lion of God, which God attacks, or who opposes himself to God; compare Judges 14:5-6, 1 Sam 17:34 onwards; so that the Genitive (Lion of God) in verse 1 is of the possessor and lover, but here of the adversary. As above in chapter 3:14, Matthew 10:21. v. 3. g) *For I will pitch camp.* 2 Kings 25:1, Jer 52:1. h) *as a circle* or in a circle. (2) Isaiah 22:18. So that he is surrounded by a siege. see 2 Kings 25:4. The Arabic root in the 10th conjugation is *to make round*, in the 1st *to go around*, in the 2nd *to hope*, which for the Hebrews means *to turn, to drive in a circle*. i) Deut 20:12. Septuagint as in Luke 19:43.

**k)** an earthwork or rampart. <note>original: "aggerem, vallum"</note> Judges 9:36; compare below, chapter 37:33; 2 Samuel 20:15; and indeed a wall, according to Josephus’s *The Jewish War*, Book 7, chapter 3 and 7. **l)** siege engines or the fortifications of those besieging. <note>original: "machinas bellicas"</note> Deuteronomy 20:20. Thus Josephus writes in *The Jewish War*, Book 7, chapter 1, when he speaks of the construction of the second ramparts and the devastated suburbs of Jerusalem: "The face of the land was miserable; for what had previously been adorned with trees and gardens was then a desert, seen with trees cut down everywhere (to erect ramparts). Nor could any foreigner who had formerly seen Judea and the beautiful suburbs of the city, seeing its solitude then, contain their tears or not groan at the change, seeing how much its former beauty had been stripped away. For war had deleted all marks of beauty; nor would one who arrived suddenly, who had known the place before, recognize it, but would ask about the city while standing within it." **o)** compare chapter 15:12; 25:5; 47:1; Nehemiah 3:34. **p)** it will be very low. "Because you did not know the time of your visitation." <note>original: "ἀνθ' ὧן οὐק ἔγνως τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς σου"</note> Luke 19:44. **f)** with a shaking, or with thunder. <note>original: "cum tonitru"</note> Psalm 77:19; Job 39:25. **g)** with an earthquake. Chapter 9:4; 1 Kings 19:11, 12; Amos 1:1. Compare above, chapter 5:25 and Luke 21:25, 26. **h)** compare Exodus 19:16. **i)** as if with a storm. <note>original: "cum procella"</note> Chapter 17:13; Amos 1:14. **k)** and a whirlwind. Chapter 40:24. **l)** with flames of fire. Chapter 30:30; 66:15; compare above chapter 6:4 and the Septuagint with 2 Thessalonians 1:8. **m)** chapter 33:14; Deuteronomy 5:22; chapter 4:24. Verse 7. **n)** and this will happen to you so suddenly and unexpectedly, just as a dream comes unawares. Compare Judges 7:13; Daniel 1:12. **o)** or a nocturnal vision. <note>original: "visum nocturnum"</note> Job 4:13; Daniel 2:19; chapter 7:2. **p)** so, I say, the multitude of enemies shall suddenly be present (verse 5). Or this verse can be connected with the following, so that it completes the comparison begun in verse 8. And it shall be as in a dream or a vision of the night, the multitude of all nations that fight against Ariel, the entirety of those attacking her and her fortifications and distressing her. It shall be, I say, most greedy and insatiable. Verse 8. **q)** which were under the Roman empire. **r)** those fighting against Ariel. Verse 8; compare Numbers 31:7; Zechariah 14:12. **s)** see verse 1. **t)** all, I say, fighting against her. **n)** he conquered, as in 1 Samuel 25:8. **u)** and her fortifications. See note on verse 7. **z)** the hungry. <note>original: "famelicus"</note> Chapter 58:7; who went to bed hungry. **a)** as if, behold (Genesis 41:1–6), he were eating. **b)** but when he awakes. Chapter 26:19; Ezekiel 7:6. **c)** then it is still empty. 2 Kings 4:3; Nehemiah 5:13. **d)** chapter 32:6. That is, the appetite is not yet satisfied. **e)** he is faint, as happens from thirst. Compare Genesis 25:30; Deuteronomy 25:18; 2 Samuel 16:14; chapter 17:29. **f)** the "nutritive soul," as in Matthew 6:25. **g)** it is still longing. Psalm 107:9. **h)** Thus the multitude of nations (verses 5, 7) that will fight against Mount Zion and Jerusalem will be greedy and insatiable; always, as it were, hungering and thirsting for the blood of the Jews, and they will not be moved from the siege even by the most difficult labors. Others think these words are said to the Jews themselves, understanding the imperatives as permissive. Chapter 41:23; 10:19; 16; compare Ecclesiastes 11:8. **m)** and cry out in astonishment! Chapter 22:5; 58:9. **n)** the Jews are drunk. Genesis 9:21. **o)** but without wine. Chapter 51:21. **p)** they waver and stagger. Chapter 24:20; Lamentations 4:14. So that they are neither in the faith (Romans 11:20) nor can they go from strength to strength. If they are accepted as being from God, they are to be interpreted as divine permission. **x)** see verse 15. **y)** princes. Deuteronomy 1:15; chapter 29:9. **z)** who boast of themselves as seers. Verse 11. **b)** whence it has happened to you Jews, the people, teachers, and princes. **c)** the vision of all and of the entire Scripture. Chapter 21:2; 28:18. **d)** chapter 8:16; Daniel 12:4. See Acts 13:27; 2 Corinthians 3:14, 15; Revelation 5:1, 5. However, Prophecy or Scripture is not such from the beginning... but from the outcome and the disorder of the recipient. The book of Scripture is not sealed for those who accommodate themselves to the divine order (Acts 13:48); but as the Holy Spirit speaks in 2 Peter 3:16, it is so for the unlearned and unstable. Note this against the arrogance and imaginary wisdom of the Rabbis. For they cannot deny that this passage deals with their own nation.

**v. 17.** x) **Exodus** 17:4; **Jeremiah** 5:33; **Hosea** 1:4. s) and it is a tiny amount. (q) **Chapter 10:25; 16:14; 24:6.** x) and it shall be converted. **Psalm** 73:10; **Psalm** 94:15. **v. 13.** The word *nagash* <note>approached</note> is spelled with the letter Sin. (Cocceius's Lexicon, 470, translates it as "is driven," suggesting they are of a servile nature and do nothing of their own accord.) 17. **Beveridge** and in the margin 6, 9 and in the notes; and other manuscripts in **M. I.** and in Kimchi’s commentary on this passage; likewise the Masora of Erfurt, where it appears three times. This is how Jonah reads it, who translates it as *v’it-harar*, which means to act like a prince or Lord. **Ephesians** 60:17. Furthermore, 22 reads it as *nagash*, but the Italian Gloss explains it as "was oppressed." And Rabbi Nathan in the Concordance refers to this place in both ways, under *nagash* and *nagas*. But we follow the reading of the majority, which the Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint, and Arabic versions have expressed, and which is confirmed in the **New Testament** in **Matthew** 15:8 and **Mark** 7:6. Kimchi in his commentary and the **M. I.** prefer this, on the authority of Rabbi Jonah and according to the Masora. It does not appear again in this book; however, *nagash* appears once more in **Isaiah** 53:7. The Erfurt Masora is also deceptive here. (h) It should be written with the letter Sin here. It is found more than three times; compare **1 Samuel** 13:6; **chapter 14:24; Isaiah** 53:7. (16) The word *haphkechem* <note>your turning upside down</note> is noted in various manuscripts (1, 2, 5, 7, 8, etc.). The word *asinu* <note>we have made</note> is noted in manuscripts 1, 7, 10, 14, 20, as well as in **S.**, in text 1, 9, and the Erfurt Masora.

# ISAIAH. CH. 29. 30.

**v. 22. h)** Therefore, namely on account of that promise given in verse 19. **i)** **Leviticus** 27:27; compare **Genesis** 48:16. **k)** Chapter 54:4; **Joel** 2:26. **l)** The true and spiritual progeny of Jacob. Compare above chapter 8:12; and **Hosea** 3:5; **Psalm** 2:11; **Hebrews** 12:28.

To those despising the counsel and help of God. Chapter 1:23; chapter 65:2; see **Deuteronomy** 21:18, 20. This chapter contains: 1) A rebuke of the Jews, especially those of the south (v. 6), for their misplaced trust in the Egyptians. 2) Consolation and prophetic promise made to the faithful (v. 18 ff). As Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), English churchman and Hebraist.</note> well observes in *Chronicle*, page 108: (for it is very important to know the chronology of this chapter, Dorsch page 97). The oppression and terror of the Assyrian armies so disturbed Judea that they turned their eyes to the arm of flesh, the "reed of Egypt." (Chapter 36:6). The Prophet severely taxes this carnal confidence in this and the following chapter; however, for the sake of the faithful, he promises liberation and predicts vengeance upon the Assyrian. Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), German theologian.</note> and others refer this to the defection of Zedekiah from Nebuchadnezzar (**Ezekiel** 17:13, 15; **Jeremiah** 37:5, 7; **2 Chronicles** 36:13), but others rightly refer it to the time of Hezekiah being attacked by Sennacherib because: 1) this danger was imminent (see ch. 36:1 ff), specifically 2) from the Assyrian (v. 31; ch. 31:8), not from the Chaldeans or Babylonians; 3) because this enemy was not to be destroyed by human hand (ch. 31:8, 9); 4) because everything fits the siege of Sennacherib: immense danger, sudden liberation, and maximum joy. Thus Dorsch. Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmid (1617–1696), Lutheran theologian.</note> adds that in Hezekiah's time, an embassy was sent to Egypt to obtain help, which is evident from the facts in chapter 36:6, 9 and **2 Kings** 18:21. **h)** Chapter 1:24. **i)** and to pour out a molten image. Verse 22. Namely, the Jews were making and casting idols in which there was no Spirit of God (Schmid). But Dorsch and others, following Vatablus, say "to cover themselves with a covering" (ch. 25:7), namely for defense, and according to the Septuagint, through treaties with the Egyptians. **k)** to add (Septuagint), so that sin accumulated upon sin destroys you. Thus **Numbers** 32:14; **Deuteronomy** 29:18. **v. 2. l)** Who depart. Not all departed, but they sent their messengers and princes to seek help, as verse 4 has it. **m)** Chapter 20:5, 6; chapter 31:1. Compare **Jeremiah** 2:18; 37:7; **Ezekiel** 17:15. **n)** **Joshua** 9:14. Meaning the words of my Prophets. **o)** to strengthen or fortify themselves. **Judges** 3:10; **Daniel** 11:12. **p)** Verse 3; chapter 17:10. **q)** **Psalm** 36:8. **r)** See chapter 36:6; **2 Kings** 18:19. **v. 3. s)** into blushing or shame. Verse 5; **Jeremiah** 2:26; **Ezra** 9:6. **t)** and a refuge. **u)** into ignominy. Chapter 45:16; **Psalm** 4:3. **v. 4. x)** For, referring back to verse 3. When his princes were in Zoan, and his messengers reached Hanes: everyone will be ashamed. **y)** See chapter 19:11, 13; **Ezekiel** 30:14. **z)** Compare **Ezekiel** 17:15. **a)** as far as Hanes: this seems to be the same as Tahpanhes, or Taphnis or Daphne. **Jeremiah** 2:16; chapter 43:7, 8; **Ezekiel** 30:18. **b)** they arrive. **1 Samuel** 14:19. **v. 5. c)** Vulgate: All were confused. Tigurine: they shall be ashamed; and thus they feel they have worked in vain in reconciling a people who will not benefit them. Compare **Jeremiah** 10:14; chapter 48:20. **d)** who will not profit them. Verse 6; **Jeremiah** 2:36. **e)** For the Egyptians will not be a help to the Jews. Chapter 20:6; chapter 31:1. Compare **2 Chronicles** 28:21. **f)** Chapter 44:10; chapter 48:17. **g)** See verse 3. **h)** Chapter 41:1; **Jeremiah** 14:9. **v. 6. i)** Compare chapter 13:1; chapter 15:1; chapter 17:1; chapter 19:1. This is not a new prophecy in matter, but in words: namely, there are two sermons on the same subject, which are joined so that the latter confirms the former. Or, as the former was general, this specifically concerns the southern Jews. **k)** of beasts. **Joel** 1:20; compare **Psalm** 32:9. We prefer this reason from the text: that the southern Jews are called "beasts" because they did not hesitate to hand themselves over with all their wealth into a condition of slavery to obtain help from the Egyptians. Thus, for example, in **Genesis** 49:14, Issachar is called a donkey because, as verse 15 explains, he bowed his shoulder to bear and became a tributary. Perhaps a clear enough argument is from **2 Kings** 19:8, 9. For why did Tirhakah come out, if not to help besieged Libnah? Who would believe he would have come out unless help had been sought from him? —S. p. 273 & 275. **m)** In the land, or into the land, compared with "in the south" in chapter 11:14; 19:4, 23. Namely, of Egypt. The construction of the following words is difficult, and the sense a bit intricate. Attention is needed here. **n)** of anxiety and distress. Chapter 8:23; **Proverbs** 1:27. Compare **Zephaniah** 1:15. Namely, that by which the Egyptians once oppressed the Israelites (**Exodus** 1:13, 14; 2:23; 3:7; 6:9, etc.) or by which they themselves were to be afflicted by the Assyrians. See note on **2 Kings** 19:35, 37 and above at chapter 21:13. **o)** from where or from which Egyptians the lion, or according to Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), author of Hierozoicon.</note>, the lioness (see chapter 5:29; **Numbers** 23:24; **Ezekiel** 19:2; and compare **Job** 4:11) often comes forth. The root of this name in Arabic... means to low like a cow... Thence according to Bochart is the name of the lioness, whose milk is thicker like colostrum. *Hierozoicon* P. I. page 719. However, the relative "from which" is understood, as in verse 5, chapter 28:16, **Exodus** 4:13, to be constructed with the following "from" in Hebrew. **p)** and the fierce or most ferocious lion. (3) **Proverbs** 30:30; **Job** 4:11. **q)** from which Egyptians lions and serpents, properly and improperly so-called, often come and fly across into Judea.

# CHAPTER 30. Isaiah 30.

<margin>
**Ayirim** <note>original: "עירים"</note> is the reading. **Hab** and **Rib** or **Errib** (which are the same, as *Nachas* and *Neser*, *Nachal* and *Nilum*; see notes on Numbers 34:5) properly signifies the "Egyptian Pear," or that part of Egypt whose lower regions are widened in the shape of a pear <note>A reference to the triangular shape of the Nile Delta.</note>. However, in Scripture, it is taken by synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note> for the whole of Egypt. **h)** S. in sitting still. See 2 Samuel 23:7 and others. By sitting or resting. Deuteronomy 1:6, 1 Samuel 7:2. Gousset <note>Jacques Gousset (1635–1704), a French Hebrew scholar.</note> p. 829: the Egyptians are a strength that leads to rest—that is, they will rest vigorously while the Jews vigorously hope they will bring help. Compare Jeremiah 37:7.

### Masoretic and Grammatical Notes:
*   **v. 15. lo** (not) marked by *Merca* in various manuscripts (7. 8. 12. 17. 18) and *Ber.* against the rules of accents.
*   **v. 16. Vatomeru** (And you said) thus with a double accent in 5. 9. 13. 19. 20. but **Vatomeru lo** in Habakkuk 1, 2.
*   **v. 18. Velachen** (And therefore) marked by *Rebia* in manuscripts 6. 9. 10. 14. 20. 21. 22. 23.
*   **v. 21. Taamenu** (You shall turn) defective spelling according to its Masorah.

...indeed there would be a coherence with the following Chapter 32. **CHAPTER 32, v. 1.** **i)** Behold indeed! Chapter 33:17, chapter 55:4, 5. This chapter is connected with the previous one, as we noted at its end; and it contains (1) a notable prophecy regarding the King Messiah and His spiritual kingdom. (2) A threat against idle and proud women and daughters, according to Jonathan, against cities and villages that feel secure (v. 9ff). **k)** Or, toward justice. See chapter 11:4, 5; Psalm 45:8; Psalm 72:2. Beyond the manner of reigning, the effect is also denoted: that He will not only reign justly, but by reigning He will establish righteousness, both of imputation <note>Righteousness credited to a believer</note> and of sanctification <note>Inward holiness</note>. S. **l)** A King shall reign, namely the Messiah. Chapter 33:17, 22; chapter 44:6; Psalm 2:6; Psalm 72:1; Psalm 145:1, etc. The Jews generally understand Hezekiah here, but erroneously. For this King is described as (1) one yet to come; whereas Hezekiah was already sitting on the royal throne as the successor of Ahaz (chapter 14:28). (2) As <term>sinless</term> <note>original Greek: ἀναμάρτητος</note>, but Hezekiah fell into sin both before and after the destruction of Sennacherib (2 Chronicles 32:25). (3) As insuperable and invincible (v. 2). Hezekiah could not be adorned with such a title. (4) This King opens the eyes, ears, and hearts (v. 3), which does not apply to Hezekiah. See Dorsch and S. It is most frequent for the Prophets, and especially Isaiah, to look forward from their own times into the times of the Messiah, and to comfort the calamity of their own times with the happiness of the Messiah's times. S. **m)** Or, as far as the Princes are concerned. See Psalm 45:17, Psalm 68:28, and thus compare Numbers 12:7, Proverbs 25:3, etc. But the Zurich Bible <note>original: "Tig." for Tigurinus</note> along with the Vulgate: "And the princes themselves shall preside over judgment," as the Nominative case indicates, not without emphasis. 1 Chronicles 3:2, collected with 2 Samuel 3:3. By "Princes" are understood primarily the Apostles, as well as other Teachers of divine truth. However, the leadership of the Teachers of the Church is spiritual, not worldly, etc. S. **n)** According to judgment and spiritual discernment. Or, the prescription of the divine word. And thus also elsewhere "a man" <note>Hebrew: אִישׁ, Ish</note> is understood to denote "each one"; see for example Genesis 41:12, Numbers 25:5. **q)** As a hiding place or a covert. * 20. **e)** How much more blessed are you! (Psalm 128:2). Teachers of the Gospel, according to Luther. Compare the note to verse 1. **f)** sowing. (Psalm 72:16, Luke 8:5, 6, 8, 11; John 4:36, 37; 1 Peter 1:23). **g)** beside all waters, that is, according to Luther on this passage: among all nations, etc. **h)** for plowing, or threshing, according to Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), author of *Hierozoicon*, a study of animals in the Bible</note> (Hierozoicon book 1, page 186). That is: you who plow and sow irrigated fields using the labor of oxen and donkeys. Cf. note on Chapter 30:24. But Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note> says: "Blessed are you, O righteous ones, for you have performed good works for yourselves, because you are like those who sow in a well-watered place: who send out oxen to thresh and donkeys to gather." Cf. note on Chapter 28:27.

CHAPTER 33, verse 1. **i)** Woe to you! (Chapter 1, verse 4; Chapter 5, verses 11, 18). According to the mind of Saint Isaiah, this chapter contains: the devastation of the Assyrians predicted by the words of the Prophet in verse 1; obtained through the prayers of the Church in verse 2; and hastened by God's mercy because of the misery of His people in verses 7 and following, and verse 10 and 11. It also contains the removal of the stumbling block taken from God’s supreme justice, and the restoration of the Church in verses 14 and following. This is not through the happy state of the former ones, where the previous chapter ended; here the status of the Church’s enemies is contrasted. (Matu Oeconomia, page 932 and following). **k)** O devastator! (Chapter 16:4, 21:2). The Church Fathers correctly judge that through this, not only the Assyrian (Sennacherib and his successors, up until Nineveh and the destruction of the kingdom, which Nahum describes) but any persecutors of the Church are to be understood, as is clear from the progress and end of the chapter. Truly, this is a discourse about a notable devastator of the Church, who was successful for a long time and thought that happiness would be perpetual. This fits the Antichrist best, to whom devastation is therefore predicted, when he shall have finished, by divine permission, his own devastation in the Church with judgment. Dorsche understands "the Assyrian" in the Holy Scriptures specifically as Sennacherib, because the Prophet has dealt with his tyranny up to this point.

Chapter 35:2, 65:10, Song of Solomon 2:1. It is a plain region (Joshua 12:18) around Joppa and Lydda (Acts 9:35), one of the three places in Judea best for grazing cattle (1 Chronicles 27:29). <meta>This page transitions from the peaceful depiction of Zion in Chapter 33 to the dramatic and terrifying vision of universal judgment in Chapter 34. # ISAIAH. Chapter 34.
### Page 356

<margin>
**o)** verse 7. Revelation 14:20.
**p)** 4. **q)** They shall also waste away. <note>original Greek: δ</note> Psalm 38:6.
The atrocity of divine wrath, to be poured out upon the nations, is described here; so great, in fact, that even the heavens themselves will seem to tremble, and their entire host will waste away. Similar metaphors are found in Isaiah 13:10, 4:23, 15:9, Ezekiel 32:7, Amos 8:9, Micah 3:6. Indeed, in reality they will finally collapse and be folded together when the final slaughter of the enemies and the seizure of the ungodly for eternal damnation occurs. Regarding the Last Day, this prophecy cannot be understood as happening immediately, as proven by the fact that this rolling up of the heavens is followed by the devastation of many regions in verse 10 and following. Dorsch, p. 40, 26. Psalm 103:27. <note>original Greek: αἱ δυνάμεις τῶν οὐρανῶν</note> "The powers of the heavens." Matthew 24:29, Mark 13:25, Luke 21:26. **r)** and they shall be rolled up. <term>Niphal</term> <note>a Hebrew passive verb form</note> (2 Peter 3:10). **s)** In great storms (from which this emblem is taken) the sky is covered with clouds and entirely veiled, so that it seems to have utterly disappeared, and nothing of its elegance and admirable order, constructed by the wisest Architect, is seen in it: nothing of the "letters" or "figures" <note>referring to constellations as signs</note> from which astronomers make their calculations. It is therefore like a rolled-up book, in which nothing can be seen, nothing read, and from which nothing can be gathered or learned. Vitringa on Revelation 5:14, p. 380. But the heaven here is compared with a book not in terms of the writing, but of the folding; and it refers to the rolling of volumes or books used by the Hebrews. Scripture expresses the creation of the heaven by comparing it to the extension of a skin (Psalm 40:22; Psalm 104:2), whence it is called the "Expanse" [Firmament]; on the contrary, by the folding of the heavens is to be understood their destruction and annihilation. Pfeiffer in *Difficulties Explained* on this passage. Although it is true, as S. <note>likely Sebastian Schmid</note> says on this passage, that calamities are signified in Scripture by darkness, the failing of the sun or moon, and the obscuring of the sky and stars, yet no other "rolling up of the heaven" is shown to be used metaphorically for calamities.
</margin>

<margin>
<note>original Hebrew: קמץ בּוֹק</note> <note>Masoretic grammatical notes</note>
Wherefore another [view] seems more worthy of approval...
</margin>

Isaiah 2:20, etc. and see Revelation 14:11; 19:3. **h)** it shall be devastated. **i)** chapter 13:20. Psalm 9:7. **k)** compare chapter 33:8; 60:15. The devastation of the land is horrible and irreparable; like the overturning of Sodom and Gomorrah. S. **v. 11. l)** That is: the pelican and the heron (differing only in beaks), especially the bittern, as Bochart proves in *Hierozoicon* II, p. 292, etc. to which, although they are aquatic birds, a seat in desert places is not inconveniently assigned, since not every desert is waterless. **m)** the hedgehog or porcupine. (3) see chapter 14:23. Zephaniah 2:14. **n)** and the night-owl or great owl. (3) Leviticus 11:17. It is usually joined with the raven, and is a bird of ill omen and inauspicious, and in both names it has something dire and ominous. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* II, p. 281, etc.

The commentary links these images to the destruction of Sodom, the final judgment in Revelation, and historical-mystical interpretations identifying Edom with Rome or the Antichrist.</summary>

*Hierozoicon* I. p. 643 and following. Likewise volume II. p. 829. Understand these as apparitions rather—phantasms of goats—rather than real goats. **o)** shall cry. Chapter 6:3. Jonathan: and one of the demons shall play with the other. Compare also Matthew 12:45. **p)** indeed, also, verse 15. Leviticus 23:27, 39. **q)** shall rest. Deuteronomy 28:65, Ruth 3:1. **s)** the screech owl, a nocturnal and harmful bird. **(t)** We have shown that by the name of the "Hairy One" <note>Satyr</note> is meant the devil appearing in the form of a goat. From this, you might conclude with great probability that the **Lilith** is also a kind of specter, but a female one, as the ending is feminine and the name is derived from "night" (*layla*), which is the primary time for such apparitions. They translate it as "Lamia" and "screech-owl": these are likewise winged women or nocturnal birds to the poets. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* II. p. 832. **s)** Genesis 8:9, Deuteronomy 28:65, Ruth 3:1. **v. 15. t)** shall build a nest. **(u)** Jeremiah 22:23. This is most characteristic of birds: but it is also attributed figuratively to other living things, e.g., to man in Sirach 36:26, compare Job 29:18, Numbers 24:21, etc. Thus to the lion, the pig, the porcupine, the crocodile, worms, the gnat, etc. In this place, to the snake, even according to Cicero, etc. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* II. p. 413 and following. **u)** The Septuagint: blackbird. Tigurinus: vulture. Others: hedgehog. **(1)** but according to Bochart, it is more correctly the *acontias* or arrow-snake, so called because it moves with the force of a dart. In Arabic it is called *Kipphaz* from "leaping," and the Arabic root means "to rush with force." Among the pests of Africa, none is worse than this snake; from its bite comes intense pain and a hot ulcer over the whole body, and from that, death. Nor is this "weapon" avoidable, since it bursts from ambush with such force that it outstrips all flight. From these things it is understood that the places fertile with such a pest must be utterly vast and uncultivated. *Hierozoicon* II. p. 408 and following, with many illustrations from secular authors on this passage. **x)** and shall lay. The Septuagint: shall lay eggs. Compare chapter 66:7. **y)** and shall hatch; i.e., shall bring forth chicks by the breaking of the egg. Compare Job 28:10, Psalm 74:15. **z)** and shall gather; i.e., shall cherish the chicks with maternal heat. **(2)** Jeremiah 17:11. **a)** in its shadow. Compare chapter 51:16. The Prophet would rather say "under its wings" or "under the shadow of its wings" if it were about a bird, as they claim. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* II. p. 415. **b)** indeed also, verse 14. **c)** they shall be gathered. Verse 16, chapter 43:9, Joshua 10:6. **d)** black vultures. **(2)** Deuteronomy 14:13. This is different from the *milius* vulture. **e)** The Septuagint: each one with its companion, or one with the other. Verse 16, Exodus 11:2, Jeremiah 9:19.

**v. 16. f)** Seek, or rather, inquire after the truth. Chapter 1:17, Deuteronomy 13:15. **g)** from the book in which it is written. Compare the particle "from" after the verb "to seek" in 1 Kings 14:5, 2 Chronicles 18:7. Or, compare the book of Jehovah. Now God or the Prophet speaks in prophecy with those who were to live at that time when all these things predicted about the Edomites were to be fulfilled. This passage hints that these terrible signs are to be sought and read in the book of the Lord, because the Prophet foresaw that many would neglect the fates of the Church—both the sad and the prosperous—and would live carelessly for the day. That these things are most certain and irrevocably decreed by God will be evident from this. Maius, *Oeconomia* p. 936. **h)** By this "book of Jehovah," some understand Genesis, others the Pentateuch, others the Psalms, others Jeremiah; others specifically refer back to Deuteronomy 28:15 and following. But with Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a major medieval Jewish commentator</note>, he understands the book of Isaiah itself, together with the rest of the Canonical Scriptures, i.e., the entire Holy Bible. **i)** Chapter 29:11-12. **k)** either one of those decrees, or one of those beasts and birds mentioned in verse 13 and following. You will find that not even a letter remains that has not been exactly fulfilled. **l)** shall not be missing or fail. Chapter 40:26, 1 Samuel 30:19, 2 Samuel 17:22. The Arabic root... among other things means used as an excuse, or was missing, or did less than he ought. **m)** one shall not lack the other. But he says: one and another shall not lack. See verse 15. **n)** Chapter 26:16, 1 Samuel 20:6, chapter 25:15. **o)** He added the reason: for my mouth has commanded. Compare chapter 1:20. **p)** Psalm 33:9. **q)** and his spirit, i.e., of my mouth; Kimchi, comparing Psalm 33:6. Others think the Prophet speaks again, comparing 2 Samuel 23:2. **r)** he has collected, i.e., gathered those beasts and unclean birds. See verse 15. **r. 17. s)** See Joshua 13:6, chapter 23:4, Proverbs 1:14. **t)** he divided it, namely Idumea <note>Edom</note>. See Joshua 13:7, Ezekiel 5:1. **u)** to them, namely the wild beasts, hyenas, satyrs, etc. verse 14. **x)** as if by a line or measuring rope. Verse 11, Psalm 19:5. See Joshua 17:5; compare also 2 Samuel 8:2. What was said in verse 16 is illustrated here by the casting of lots and the laying of the plumb-line (I would prefer "measuring rope"); as if God in his decree had so certainly devoted them to destruction as if the lot were already cast and the line drawn. Dorsch.

### CHAPTER XXXV, verse 1.

**y)** They shall be glad. Chapter 61:10, 66:14. Concerning those things said in chapter 34. Let them think on these things with a joyful heart. The suffix shows the connection of this chapter with the preceding one. Namely, the happiness of the Church in the kingdom of Christ is expressed, especially of the Jewish Church, which was turned into a wilderness by its enemies, especially the Edomites; now in turn it shall rejoice over the devastation of Edom, and shall blossom joyfully, and see the glory of Jehovah and the King of Glory, in the highest glory and majesty. Matthew 24:30, chapter 26:64, of which they also will become participants. Maius, *Oeconomia* p. 935. Schmidius <note>Sebastian Schmid (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian</note> observes three things in this chapter: (1) The promise of the Messiah’s coming in verses 1 and 2. (2) His preaching in verses 3 and 4. (3) The effect in verse 5 and following. Namely, the miraculous works of the Messiah tending toward spiritual effects in verses 5 and 6, the new state of the Church in verses 6 and 7, and its propagation through the Way, in which access is given to all who repent in verse 8, etc. Thus the object of the promise in verses 1 and 2 is the Jewish Church oppressed under the Old Testament, therefore called a wilderness and solitary place in verse 1. The object of the preaching is the "weak hands," etc. in verses 3 and 4 (those contrite in spirit and disturbed by the sense of sins, etc.). Chapter 32:15, 40:3, Jeremiah 12:10. The wilderness of Judah, Joshua 15:61. The wilderness, i.e., the Jewish Church, which the Prophet had previously predicted would be turned into a solitary place by the Assyrians and Babylonians, while the Edomites rejoiced. Psalm 137:7-8. **z)** and a place of parched ground. Chapter 41:18. **b)** and shall exult. Psalm 21:2.

Instead of "my mouth he," some have "his mouth." **CHAPTER XXXV, v. 1.** "They shall be glad" so in some manuscripts according to the Masorah.</note>

# ISAIAH 35, 36. CHAPTERS 35. 36. 36.

<margin>
The slaughter and miracles involving the liberation of the Jewish people (which otherwise exists described in almost the same words in 2 Kings 18:13 and following, where see our notes; see also 2 Chronicles 32:1 and following) were inserted by Isaiah into his prophecies by divine inspiration. This account is not merely historical, but also prophetic. It serves (1) to assert the invincible and everlasting firmness of the Messiah’s kingdom upon the throne of David; (2) to demonstrate the terrible confusion and refutation of the enemies of the Church through an evident example; and (3) to provide an understanding of many preceding prophecies—for example, concerning the "hired razor" <note>Referring to Isaiah 7:20</note> and the "divine whistling" to be called forth, etc. See Isaiah 7:18; 8:7 and following.
</margin>

Matthew 16:18; Romans 16:20. **d)** <note>original: "λελυτρωμένοι"</note> The redeemed ones. 1 Peter 1:18.
</margin>

**CHAPTER XXXVI, verse 1.**
**q)** "And it came to pass." Since Isaiah has prophesied more than once in the preceding chapters about the land of Judah being laid waste by the Assyrians, and about the liberation of Jerusalem, he now adds the history in which the fulfillment of those prophecies is exhibited. At the same time, the credibility of the intermingled predictions concerning future times and especially concerning the Messiah is established; as if to say: there now follows the history from which not only the truth of the previous matters can be clear, but also what God spoke and did further through Isaiah. **S.** For this slaughter of the Assyrians, etc.
</margin>

Scaliger, in book 5 of *The Emendation of Time*, page 217, strives to prove that year was a Sabbatical year, in which fields were not to be gathered. But Salian rightly notes at the year of the world 3321, no. 64, that it was not a Sabbatical year. For the fact that the field was not sown, nor the vineyard planted, was not done because of a Sabbatical year, but because Sennacherib's army was devastating everything and standing in the way so that sowing could not be done; so indeed thinks Blessed Dorsch. Yet Scaliger's opinion is altogether more probable, which Lightfoot also holds in *Chronicles of the Old Testament*, page 109, and the Chronological Tables of Wasmuth prove it.

<summary>This page contains God's response to Hezekiah's prayer, mocking the pride of the Assyrian king Sennacherib and comparing his eventual retreat to a beast being led away by a hook. It concludes with a prophetic sign of survival for the Judean people, promising that they will eventually return to normal agriculture after two years of living off the land's natural growth.</summary>
