<margin>
**CHAPTER XL, v. 1. p)** Comfort ye. See chapter 61:2. The Targum of Jonathan supplies "O Prophets!"; others (with the Septuagint at verse 2) suggest "O Priests." Luther says "O Apostles!"; others say "all you who read these things!" Individually, each should comfort himself and his neighbor; publicly, the Priests and those entrusted with the office of public teaching. **S. <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century theologian</note>** For although the descendants of Hezekiah and the Jewish people were to be led into exile in Babylon (39:5-6), they were not to be left forever without solace, but were most certainly to be liberated and redeemed through the Messiah, according to the unchanging will and promise of the Almighty God. There are two things in this chapter: (1) A notable prophecy concerning the coming of the Messiah and his forerunner (v. 1-11). (2) A discussion of the trials of the faithful (v. 12 and following, compared with v. 27). Indeed, since Isaiah in chapter 39 predicted the Babylonian captivity and other evils to be brought upon the Jews by the Babylonians, from chapter 40 onward he provides abundant comfort for that misery, drawing arguments primarily from the happiness of the times of the Messiah, who is surely coming; thus the state, however much it is pressed, will not perish before his arrival, as it might seem under tribulations. The power of this argument also pertained to the times after the Babylonian captivity, when the Jewish Church was repeatedly and most severely afflicted. But after the coming of the Messiah, the Church is most richly instructed through this same prophecy in the knowledge of the Messiah and his kingdom, so that it may rightly be called a doctrine for all times. **S.** **q)** "my people," nearest to the Jews (compare 39:6-7) and thus to any who are afflicted. Compare Micah 4:10. **r)** so he speaks through the Prophet. **s)** The Messiah, "your God" (v. 3, 9), who will keep the covenant made with the Fathers and will fully provide redemption.
</margin>

**THE FLESH**

but not about the earthly one, except insofar as it was some spiritual dwelling place. **Dorsch <note>Johann Georg Dorsch, a Lutheran theologian</note>**. See the note at verse 1 and Ephesians 2:22. **x)** and shout to her words full of comfort and the Gospel. verse 6. **y)** "that she has completed her service." Compare Genesis 29:21, 27; 1 Samuel 18:26. Or that her warfare is fulfilled and finished, in the same sense, and not contrary to Grammar, because the following noun is more frequently Masculine (as in 1 Kings 22:19; Isaiah 8:12; 2 Chronicles 18:18), though more rarely Feminine (as in Daniel 8:12). **z)** "warfare" [militia] and the servile condition and its labors under the law. Compare Numbers 8:25; Job 7:1, 10:17, 14:14; and Galatians 4:3-6. The Septuagint translates: "her humiliation is filled" <note>Greek: ἐπλήσθη ἡ ταπείνωσις αὐτῆς</note>. **a)** "that it has been expiated by the gracious sacrifice of the Messiah." Compare below 56:7 and Leviticus 1:4, 19:7. So Rashi <note>the famous medieval Jewish commentator</note> says on this passage: "it is accepted," that is, "it is expiated." We do not doubt, says Schmid, that the finger here points to the perfect sacrifice of the Messiah. Compare Ephesians 5:2; Hebrews 9:8, 14, etc.; and notes on Leviticus 16:34, 17:4, etc. Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan</note> says: "that her sins are forgiven her." Others, such as Gousset (p. 590) with Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, medieval Hebrew grammarian</note> on this passage, say: "that the punishment inflicted on her for sins has been accepted as sufficient," comparing Leviticus 26:41, 43; in which sense it would still refer to Christ's satisfaction, comparing below 53:5, 6, 11; Acts 4:12; Romans 4:25; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13; 1 Timothy 2:5, 6; 1 John 2:2, 4:10, etc. For the ending of the legal warfare and the expiation of sins are proposed in the prophetic style as past things, yet they were still future benefits at that time; compare above 5:13, 9:2, 13, 37:22, etc. **b)** "for." We take this particle here as explanatory, to be translated as "because," not "that": and "double" we understand not as a doubling of punishments, as others wish; but with Blessed Luther, we understand it as the two promised benefits: the ending of warfare and the remission of sins, etc. **Schmid...** **c)** she has received from the most liberal hand of the Lord. Jonathan: "because she has received the cup of comforts (Jeremiah 16:7) from the Lord." Compare below 51:17. **d)** "double." Chapter 61:7; Zechariah 9:12; Job 11:6; 1 Timothy 5:17. That "double" simultaneously refers to the right of the firstborn in Deuteronomy 21:17, we do not reject, says Schmid. Thus: the Lord is read in Job 42:10 to have returned all his goods double to Job, his strenuous soldier, who possessed his soul in patience after all temptations were conquered and overcome. Isaiah also alludes to this in 61:7: "In their land they shall possess double." This refers to those Jewish firstfruits who received the firstfruits of the Spirit and constituted the primitive Church (of which Hebrews 12:23 speaks), etc., from Salmeron in Dorsch on this passage. **e)** "for all her sins." Compare Romans 5:20; Ephesians 2:5; 1 John 4:10, etc. Others, like Ludolf in his *Commentary on the History of Ethiopia* (p. 205, n. 19), translate from the Ethiopian meaning: "in all her defects." **v. 3. f)** "A voice crying" was presented to me through a prophetic vision, or the voice of God crying, as in 1 Samuel 3:4, 8. The Septuagint, as in Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4, John 1:23. We assume, therefore, that this text speaks literally, not merely allegorically or typically, about the New Testament and the prediction of John the Baptist. As if to say: these things predicted about the New Testament and Christ's benefits are so true that the Lord revealed to me even the forerunner of the Messiah himself in the spirit. He is the "voice of one crying," that is, one crying something with a clear voice. For regarding the construction, the sense is not diminished. If it is a "voice crying," he is crying; it is also the "voice of one who cries," etc. **S.** However, the latter construction, which the Septuagint has and the New Testament repeats often, can again be conveniently illustrated from the Ethiopian language. For among the Abyssinians, the "Voice of the King" or Prince is commonly called the Messenger or legate of the King (see Ludolf's *New Ethiopian Lexicon*, col. 190). Thus John the Baptist would be called by this phrase the messenger (Malachi 3:1, Matthew 11:10, etc.) of the One crying—that is, of God calling the Jews to repentance and faith. Compare Luke 3:2 <note>Likely refers to Luke 3:3-4</note>. **g)** "in the wilderness" of Judea. Chapter 35:1. Most connect this with the preceding words, yet I can hardly disagree with Tremellius, who observed that this phrase should be referred [to the following words]. The accents of the Hebrew codex and the balance of the words urge this. For just as the latter half-verse wants the way made straight in the desert plain, so the first wants the way prepared in the wilderness. Meanwhile, the common version has nothing against the Prophet's meaning. For this voice certainly cried there, where it commanded the way to be prepared for the Lord. **h)** See chapter 57:14 and Malachi 3:1. **i)** of the LORD, the Messiah (v. 9; Psalm 24:7; Luke 1:17), that is: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" <note>Greek: μετανοεῖτε, ἤγγικε γὰρ ἡ βασִλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν</note> (Matthew 3:2). **k)** and then also "make straight," level it. Chapter 45:2, 13. **l)** "in the desert plain" (chapter 33:9) of the nations (chapter 35:1, 6; Psalm 68:5). **m)** Chapter 19:23. **n)** of the Messiah, "our God." v. 9, 10, 28. **v. 4. o)** "Every valley," that is, the humble man who submits himself to Christ. See below chapter 57:15. **p)** "shall be raised," or "will be raised." Chapter 2:2, 14; 30:25; see James 1:9. **q)** "And every mountain and hill." See above chapter 2:14, 41:15; Psalm 97:5; also Luke 18:9 and Colossians 2:18. He continues the metaphor from verse 3 and warns everyone to remove obstacles, erroneous opinions, self-righteousness, and boasting in external things, etc. And because he was preaching in the wilderness, he forms his speech according to those things that are in the wilderness, as if pointing his finger at the mountains and hills and saying: "You, who are like these mountains and hills, humble yourselves," etc. **S.** **r)** See chapter 2:11; Ezekiel 17:24. **s)** "the crooked shall also become" [straight], that which trips up the heel or feet of those walking. Psalm 56:7; Jeremiah 17:19; see below chapter 42:16. **t)** "into a plain." Zechariah 4:7. **u)** "and the rough places," others say "entangled with thorns." Compare Psalm 31:21 and the root in Exodus 28:28. **x)** "into a level place between mountains" or an "unobstructed valley." Chapter 63:14. **v. 5. y)** "For it shall be revealed." Chapter 53:1; Psalm 35:2; Exodus 15:10. Christ (Luke 3:6; Hebrews 1:3; 1 Corinthians 2:8) and his divine glory (John 1:14-15, 2:11). **a)** **S.** and they shall see that glory, because, etc. Chapter 35:2, 66:18; Psalm 97:6. But others, according to the accents: "they shall see and know that," etc. (compare chapter 52:10, 62:2; Deuteronomy 28:10, etc.). **b)** that is, all men. Verse 6; chapter 66:23; Daniel 2:11; Psalm 145:21. **c)** Psalm 42:15. Not only Jews, but also Gentiles. See chapter 49:6. **d)** Chapter 1:20, 58:14. The Septuagint as in Luke 3:6. **v. 6. e)** Furthermore, a heavenly voice, or the voice of God, as in Genesis 3:8. **f)** "saying" was to that voice crying in verse 3, the forerunner of the Messiah. See Luke 3:2 and following; compare John 1:33. Here, however, Isaiah speaks as if in a vision presented to him. **S.** **g)** "Cry," or preach freely, O Forerunner! Chapter 58:1. **h)** "And the Forerunner said" (Jonathan: "responded"), "What shall I cry?" Then she <note>the voice</note> said, "Cry: All flesh," etc. See our Preface to this book, §. 9. **i)** "All" people in the whole world. See verse 5 and John 3:6. Although these words speak primarily of the corruption of bodies, they also insinuate the corruption of the mind, because from this the other arises. Romans 5:12 and following, and 6:23. **Dorsch.**

verse 27. l) Why then do you say, O Jacob? Here at last is the actual trial of the Jews, which he has begun to rebuke, as it greatly offends the divine majesty. For although the words do not sound so crude, the Jews imagined that God had completely deserted them and deliberately withdrawn Himself, so that their way was hidden from Him; yet from this follows a most grave denial of divine majesty as a necessary consequence. From here to the end, He shows them that He is a far different God than one who deserts those who hope in Him. Therefore, one must hope and acknowledge that evils occurred because faith and hope in God were not kept. *S.* m) compare chapter 41, 9. 14; 49, 14; 55, 6, 7, 8; 54, 4, 5. **CHAPTER XLI. verse 1.** s) *Keep silence therefore toward me.* chapter 36, 21; 42, 14. Genesis 24, 21. t) *islands.* verse 5. chapter 40, 15; 49, 1. u) chapter 34, 1. x) Septuagint: *let them renew their strength.* chapter 40, 31. y) *let them approach.* Joel 4, 9. z) *let us approach into judgment.* Numbers 27, 21. Malachi 3, 5. compare above chapter 1, 18. Truly, after the comfort given to the Jewish people in the appearance of the Messiah in chapter 40, **Isaiah** now returns to the judgment of the enemies of the Church, and summons the islands and peoples to it. While **Dreschem** observes parts in this chapter: I. An exhortation to the Israelites to conceive the firmest confidence in their God, see verses 10, 13, 14. II. A challenge to the nations to hear the nothingness of their predictions, verse 21. But **Schmidius** sees: I. The conversion of the nations to Christ, verse 1, etc. II. The confirmation of the Jewish Church, verse 8, etc. and III. The refutation of the boasting of the nations and Babylonians against God and the Church, verse 21. But the former seems simpler. **verse 2. a)** *Who raised up.* verse 25. Jeremiah 51, 11. namely the Jewish people, about whom and to whom the Prophet spoke in the preceding chapter, whom God chose from all nations, and therefore stirred up from the east and called in the Patriarch **Abraham**, Genesis 12, 1. etc. Thus it truly refers to the departure of Abraham. Jonathan says: *Who publicly brought Abraham, the chosen of righteousness, from the East!* etc. The Rabbis and many others refer this to **Cyrus**, and with them **Varenius** on Isaiah III. page 57, comparing chapter 46, 11 below. But, as **Dorsch** judges, this is against the purpose, which is to challenge the islands into judgment over past deeds, so that later persuasion can be made about future ones. b) *He called him in righteousness.* chapter 42, 6. Hosea 2, 21. or *to righteousness* Psalm 40, 10. Daniel 9, 24. so that he might learn its true nature. Genesis 15, 6. But **Cocceius** on page 788, in the Nominative: *the righteousness of Christ met him* Genesis 42, 4. etc. *at his foot* i.e., wherever he went. etc. and he understands here the Apostles departing from Palestine toward the west. c) *at his own foot* and to follow his footsteps, compare 1 Samuel 25, 42. d) *who gave the Canaanite nations to be slaughtered before him?* see Deuteronomy 1, 8. chapter 7, 2. 23; 31, 5. Judges 11, 9. e) and *to Kings.* see Joshua 12, 1. etc. Others refer this to the victory of **Abraham** against the eastern Kings, Genesis 14, 1. etc. f) *He made him to rule.* <term>Hiphil</term> <note>a causative verb form in Hebrew</note>. compare **Niel** on Judges 5, 13. g) *for God gave*, or, so that Israel might render those enemies so. compare chapter 40, 23. Lamentations 1, 13. h) *as dust.* 2 Kings 13, 7. Zephaniah 1, 17. i) *by his sword.* (as some also in Job 40, 19, understand a prefix) compare chapter 27, 1; 34, 5; 66, 16. Deuteronomy 32, 41. 42. others in the Dative: "to the sword of Israel." k) chapter 40, 24. l) *driven by a strong wind.* chapter 19, 7. Psalm 1, 4. Leviticus 26, 36. m) *by his bow.* Psalm 7, 13. **verse 3.** n) *Abraham pursued*, Genesis 14, 14. and Israel in Joshua 10, 19, pursued their enemies. o) *and passed through* various nations. Exodus 15, 16. Psalm 141, 10. to occupy the promised land. p) *safe and in peace.* see Joshua 10, 21. and compare 1 Samuel 25, 6. q) *by the way* or *by the path.* Job 16, 22. r) under the guidance of the Son of God Himself, see Exodus 13, 21, Numbers 10, 11, 33. and compare Exodus 11, 8. Judges 4, 10. 2 Samuel 15, 18. s) which neither he nor anyone else had entered before: namely through the sea and the Jordan. **verse 4.** t) *Who has devised and done all these things?* Micah 2, 11. Habakkuk 1, 5. Psalm 58, 3. u) *calling also the generations.* chapter 46, 10. Ecclesiastes 1, 4. so that the human race is preserved through continuous generations. x) *from the beginning of the world.* verse 26. chapter 40, 21. Certainly no one else performed it but me. Jonathan: *I the Lord created the world from the beginning, and the ages of ages are mine: besides me there is no God.* y) *I am the first.* chapter 44, 6.

**v. 26.** **מִלֶּךְ** <note>Hebrew: millel (accented on the penultimate syllable)</note> see manuscript 5, and so in the margin 6, 9. **v. 28.** **עוֹלָם** <note>Hebrew: "eternal"</note> without the <term>Pesiq</term> <note>a vertical line musical/textual mark in the Hebrew Bible</note> in manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 10, 20. thus in manuscript 5, against the Basel Index folio 60, column 6. **v. 31.** **וְקוֹיֵ** <note>Hebrew: "and those who wait"</note> thus with a mobile <term>Yod</term>, lacking the plural <term>Yod</term> in manuscript 22. And so **Kimchi** in his Commentary and M. I. But others write **וְקוֹיֵי** in manuscripts 1, 3. and thus also in manuscript 5, where the Masora and Erfurt notes mark it as such. Compare more in the Preface of **Jablonski**, section 13 d. **CAP. XLI. v. 2.** **כֶּעָפָר** <note>Hebrew: "like dust"</note> with an anomalous <term>Tzere</term> vowel in manuscripts 1 and 2, according to their Masora and the Erfurt manuscript, and so **Rabbi Chaiim** in the final Masora, folio 17, d.

**verse 25. a)** I have raised up <note>original Latin: "Ego excitaui"</note>, see verse 2, and chapter 45:13, or "I will raise up." See note b. 37:22. **b)** Others understand this to be Abraham with his descendants, as in verse 2; others the Assyrians, comparing chapter 37:26; others the Babylonians, comparing 2 Kings 24:2; others Darius and the Medes, enemies of the Babylonians, comparing Jeremiah 50:3, 41. Schmidius, however, takes this text—which speaks indefinitely—to refer to the gathering of the church from all parts of the world: which proves that Jehovah is the one supreme and true God. Likewise, Dorches predicts here the wonderful gathering of a new people from all regions of the world against idolatry, comparing Matthew 8:11. This people is described as a single individual, as below in chapter 42:19, 25 and 43:21. **y)** and he comes. verse 5. **z)** verse 2, chapter 43:5, 10. I will raise up not only Cyrus, whom some take this to refer to (comparing chapter 44:28 and 45:5), but many more, comparing chapter 59:19, Malachi 1:11, Psalm 50:1, Psalm 113:3, Revelation 16:12. **q)** who shall call upon my name. Joel 3:5, Zechariah 13:9. **i)** Or: for the leaders shall come, Jeremiah 51:28, standing as stable as clay. But others: he shall come against the Babylonian and Antichristian leaders, in both the political and ecclesiastical states. See Varenius volume III, page 79, and compare a similar construction of the word without an intervening particle in Ezekiel 32:11, Psalm 35:8, 35:12, Proverbs 10:24, Job 20:22, etc. Thus Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note>: "I have openly brought a strong king from the northern region, and he shall come, as the sun goes out in its strength, from the East; I will strengthen him in my name, and he shall come and trample princes and the people, as they trample dust, and like a potter who prepares clay." **c)** chapter 10:6. **d)** chapter 14:4, 63:3, Nahum 3:14. **e)** 2 Samuel 22:43, Micah 7:10, Zechariah 10:5.

—announcing <note>referring back to verse 22</note>. **n)** *nor indeed one hearing, or one who might hear your words: but you must be silent, and the matter is settled.* Compare verse 28, chapter 42:17. **verse 27. o)** And I am the first, verse 4. **p)** behold, behold all those things (supplied from the preceding verse) I am announcing: which things were determined by God from the beginning and from antiquity, indeed from eternity. **CHAPTER XLII, verse 1. f)** Behold! chapter 32:1. As if He wished to present the Son in the flesh right now. For the discourse continues, established in chapter 40 for the comfort of the Jews and brought forward to this point. S. <note>likely a reference to a commentator like Seiler or Starcke</note> In this chapter there is: I. The presentation and commendation of the Messiah. II. His calling and appointment in verse 5. III. An instructional application in verse 10. And IV. A corrective application in verse 18. Dorcheus observes two things: 1. the promise of the Messiah, 2. the threat against the ungrateful Jews in verse 18. S. however, makes five parts: 1) the commendation of the Messiah. 2) His celebration in verse 10. 3) His coming in verse 13. 4) The consolation of the blind in verse 18. And 5) The raising up of the desperate in verse 22 (but see notes on verse 18 and following). **g)** God the Father speaks of the Son, the Messiah, as in verse 5, and calls him His servant in respect to His voluntary pledge and obligation to obedience and satisfaction for the human race. Compare chapter 43:10, 52:13, Psalm 69:18, Galatians 4:4-5, Philippians 2:7-8. **For it is not (as the Septuagint translation has it) about the people of Israel, who is here given as a servant of the covenant in verse 6, nor about the Prophet Isaiah (as Grotius wrongly thought with Abraham Ibn Ezra), who announced him but himself never filled the measure of these praises; much less about Cyrus, as Saadia Gaon wished; but it is to be understood of Christ in this place, as Matthew 12:18 and the whole context clearly teach. And so Jonathan expressly says: "Behold my servant the Messiah," etc. So says Kimchi, and with him Abarbanel on this passage, who judges all those other interpreters to be struck by excitement because they did not observe that this text cannot legitimately be explained as anyone other than the Messiah, the Son of David.** **h)** *whom I sustain;* S. compares Matthew 12:18. *in whom I am well-pleased,* namely as one whom He supports, I will support him and rescue him from death again. Compare chapter 33:15, 41:10, Ezekiel 17:12, Psalm 41:13, 63:9, Proverbs 28:17. It denotes a special sustaining, regarding which see John 3:2, 8:29, Acts 10:38, 2 Corinthians 5:19. Dorcheus. **i)** *my chosen.* The Mediator, and most singularly beloved son. chapter 43:20, 2 Samuel 21:6, Psalm 106:23. **k)** S. in whom my soul has good pleasure, Jeremiah 14:10. See Matthew 3:17. Because of his generation from eternity, Psalm 2:7, his incarnation, and the expiation of men through the offering of his body. Psalm 40:8-9, 110:4, Ephesians 5:2, comparing Leviticus 1:3-4, etc. **l)** *Jonathan: My Holy Spirit.* see chapter 11:2, 61:1, John 3:34. **m)** verse 3, 4. compare chapter 2, 4; 4, 4; 28, 17; 32, 16; 33, 5; 40, 14; 51, 4. "Justice" <note>original Latin: 'iudicium'</note> in this place, says S., is the order of salvation established by God, according to which the Messiah exercises his judgment both in the Church and on the last day, that is, the Gospel itself. Romans 2:16. **n)** *not only to the Jews, but also to the nations.* verse 4, chapter 49:6, etc. **o)** *he will bring out, that is, bring forward through the preaching of the Gospel.* verse 3. Or as Jonathan says, *he will reveal,* as a mystery hidden from the ages. Romans 16:25-26. **verse 2. p)** He will not cry out contentiously, compare Matthew 12:19. **q)** nor with secular noise or pomp will he lift himself up, or his voice, as seen at the end of the verse. Compare verse 11, Numbers 14:1. **r)** chapter 30:30. **s)** compare chapter 24:11, 33:11. **t)** Compare Proverbs 1:20 and Matthew 11:28-29. Namely, Christ did not wish to sharply rebuke his adversaries, but calmly dismissed them, Matthew 12:14 and following. Sometimes, however, he drove the mockers to silence with divine answers. Gurtler, Prophetic Theology, page 88 and following, comparing Isaiah 29:14, 44:25, 45:9, 49:2, Psalm 45:6, Job 5:13. **verse 3. u)** *A bruised reed,* a crushed stalk. chapter 36:6, 58:6. **x)** he will not completely shatter it. chapter 14:29. **y)** *and the flax (wick).* chapter 43:17, Exodus 9:31. **z)** *contracted, dim, and smoking.* chapter 61:3. **a)** *he will not extinguish.* compare chapter 40:11, 43:17, 2 Samuel 14:7. Jonathan: "The humble, who are like a bruised reed, shall not be broken, and the poor, who are like a dim wick, shall not be extinguished." So Dorcheus and others on this passage: consciences terrified by the mass of sins and brought into distress are depicted by the bruised reed and the smoking wick. Compare Matthew 9:12-13. But Gurtler (cited above, pages 389 and 70) says it is commonly understood that the bruised reed and smoking wick refer to weak faith which is not rejected by the Lord; but this is contrary to the intent of Isaiah and Matthew: because here it is not about receiving those weak in faith, but about tolerating for a time the Jewish enemies of Jesus Christ, who were very near to destruction. Compare verse 2.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Isaiah 42, transitioning from the call of the Messiah to His active, forceful intervention in the world. The previous page established the Messiah’s humble character; here, the tone shifts to a "man of war" who breaks His long silence to bring judgment and light. The commentary continues to debate the identity of the "blind servant" in verse 19, weighing the views of the Rabbis against Reformers like Luther and scholarly contemporaries like Dorscheus.</meta>

Interpreters differ greatly about this servant of God, because he is called both blind and deaf, and yet also perfect. (1) The Rabbis want this to be said mockingly by the wicked Jews about Isaiah himself, compare Jeremiah 5:12; Hosea 9:7; but this is outside the context. But (2) Luther and Brentius, as well as Varenius, Dorscheus in his analysis, and Maius, judge that the stupid and blind people of Israel themselves are noted; while by the "messenger of God" they understand the teachers of Israel, the Priests and Levites, who ought to have been perfect, or were perfect in their own opinion. Others (3), among them Carpzov, think that the blasphemies of the Jews against the most holy Savior are shown, who was regarded by them as if blind and foolish; he who is called the "servant of God" not only from the beginning of this chapter but also elsewhere quite often, for example, chapter 43:10; 52:13. 
In this diversity of opinions, either the third or rather the second seems preferable. For the doubts moved against it can be removed without difficulty. The main objection is that the text speaks in the singular of the "blind and deaf yet perfect servant of God," and that a collective meaning for the names "servant" and "messenger" in the singular cannot be proven by examples. But see the name "servant of God" used for the Israelite people in chapter 41:8 and chapter 44:1, 2, etc., and the name "angel" or "messenger of God" for the priests in Malachi 2:7—to omit other examples for the sake of brevity. x) verse 18; Psalm 38:14. y) of the Priests, Malachi 2:7; of the Prophets below chapter 44:25; of Christ chapter 63:9; Malachi 3:1. z) whom I send or will send, or who at least boasted that they were sent. Jeremiah 23:21, 31, 32. compare Micah 5:4. a) compare Matthew 19:20; Luke 6:40; or regarding Christ, Hebrews 7:26.
</margin>

...at least in the future (chapter 41:23). x) So that they may be converted to God through serious repentance. **v. 24.** c) For who indeed delivered them? d) See verse 22. g) See chapter 45:7; Amos 3:6. h) Chapter 43:3. i) Isaiah 3:25; Daniel 9. l) Deuteronomy 8:6. n) Verse 20. **v. 25.** o) Therefore He poured out. p) A burning heat, that is, fury. q) Namely, of His anger. r) And the force or violence of war s) carried out by the Romans <note>The commentator links the biblical "strength of battle" to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem</note>. t) It inflamed or kindled him with His anger (Deuteronomy 32:22). u) Everywhere, on all sides. x) But he did not notice (Psalm 82:5). z) Nor yet did he attend to it or call it to mind and care for it.

**CHAPTER XLIII. v. 1.** a) "But now" — this is the opposite of the past time of God's wrath. It is as if to say: it will not be as before. The punishment of blindness and rejection (42:18, 24) will not be eternal, but a place for grace remains. God now declares and confirms this with the promised redemption, calling, adoption, and preservation in various tribulations. The theologian Dorsheus <note>Johann Conrad Dannhauer, a 17th-century scholar</note> observes here: 1. A medicine for present dangers, and 2. An abundance of future benefits. The scholar Schmidius <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a Lutheran Hebraist</note> sees four parts: 1) The divine promise; 2) The assertion of divine glory (v. 2 ff.); 3) The repetition and fuller explanation of the promise (v. 14 ff.); and 4) The motivating cause of all those benefits (v. 22 ff.). b) The one speaking here as "Jehovah" is God the Father, calling His Son as a witness (v. 10). c) He calls Himself this to signal His majesty and dominion over all creatures, in whom one can safely trust. f) This immediately refers to the Israelite people, then placed in the greatest difficulties and near destruction; but ultimately and by extension, it refers to the Church Militant in general. g) That is to say: do not fear your destruction. h) Schmidius and Brentius refer this to the exodus from Egypt. But Dorsheus says: "I do not deny that by 'redemption and salvation' (v. 3) is meant that which is from Egyptian servitude and other temporal afflictions; but it also refers to spiritual redemption, of which the former was a type." <term>I have redeemed you</term> <note>original Greek: "ο ελυτρωσαμηן σε"</note> (Luke 24:21; Titus 2:14).

**v. 2.** l) When you cross over. m) A proverbial expression for passing through water and fire. Dorsheus says: "We do not understand the water, rivers, and fire literally, but metaphorically as the cross and tribulation, specifically the Babylonian captivity." n) Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note>: "Because in the beginning, when you passed through the Sea of Reeds, my Word was your help... and so when you are again among peoples who are strong like fire, they shall not prevail against you." p) They shall not overwhelm or inundate you, just as when you once passed through the Red Sea (Exodus 14:29) and the Jordan (Joshua 3:16). r) You shall not be burned. This was even literally fulfilled in Daniel 3:23.

**v. 3.** y) Your Savior (v. 11, 12). I have not only liberated you from the servitude of the Egyptians and others, and will lead you out of Babylon (v. 14), but I will also regather my own from all parts of the world (v. 5, 6), and without any merit of your own (v. 22 ff.), I will make you eternally safe from spiritual captivity and misery. <term>The one who saves you</term> <note>original Greek: "ο σωζων σε"</note> (Matthew 1, 21).

Regarding the fulfillment or the time of this prophecy, interpreters differ. ### CHAPTER 44. Isaiah 44

...of drawing near and approaching, which includes both a substantial presence and the bestowing of gifts, partly extraordinary <note>Referring to the miraculous gifts of the early Church, such as tongues or prophecy.</note> (Acts 2:3, 10:45; 1 Corinthians 12:3, 14), and partly ordinary (Ezekiel 35:25, 39:29; Titus 3:6). Both are suggested in this passage and in Joel 3:1. Thus says Dorsch. <note>Johann Georg Dorsch (1597–1659), a Lutheran theologian.</note>

<gloss>Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation.</note>: Because just as waters are given upon a thirsty land and flow over the dry ground, so I will give my Holy Spirit upon your children, and my blessing upon your children's children.</gloss> **x)** "Offspring of Jacob" signifies all descendants; not exclusively, but inclusively and in the right order. For in the first and most notable outpouring of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2), it was poured upon the Apostles from the seed of Jacob, but then also upon the Gentiles. **y)** Compare Ezekiel 34:26, Psalm 68:10. The Holy Spirit is also called a "blessing" because he seals the promise of Abraham (cf. Galatians 3:14) for all believers (Ephesians 1:13). **z)** chapter 22:24; 34:1. **verse 4. a)** From which they will sprout abundantly and joyfully. Cf. chapter 41:9, 43:19; Psalm 85:12. The effect of the poured-out Holy Spirit is spiritual blossoming and growth in heavenly gifts. For they shall grow under the *Zemach* <note>Hebrew: "Branch," often a title for the Messiah.</note> (Zechariah 6:12). From this emerge the fruits of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22; John 15:1ff). Thus Dorsch. **b)** in the midst of the sprout or among the herbs. Cf. chapter 66:14; Job 5:25. **c)** or like salices (willows). Chapter 15:7. **d)** by the rivers. Cf. chapter 30:25; Jeremiah 17:8. The comparison is twofold: as both grass and willows grow quickly and then increase themselves, so the Church among the Jews grew quickly after the first outpouring of the Spirit and soon spread and multiplied among the nations. **verse 5. a)** "I am the Lord’s!" To whose glory and service I have consecrated myself in humble obedience, and I profess this by mouth, gesture, and deed. Cf. chapter 43:7; Revelation 14:1; Exodus 32:26. <gloss>Jonathan: I am among those who fear Jehovah.</gloss> This is the second effect: the adoption of the name of God and Jacob. It is as if the Prophet said: countless people will desire to be "Jehovians," "Messianics," "Jacobites," or "Israelites." Thus Dorsch. Simply put, this is the Christian profession, by which a Christian declares (1) that he belongs to the Lord, i.e., the Messiah, and (2) that he is a member of Jacob, i.e., the Church. **f)** this one shall call himself, or be called by the name of Jacob. Chapter 48:1. **g)** that one. Others say he shall enroll himself to the Lord with his own hand. By "this one," "that one," and "another," a great influx of people is noted, especially from the Gentiles. For if they were already from Jacob and Israel, there would be no need for them to name themselves after Jacob and Israel. **h) i)** by the name of Israel. Cf. Revelation 3:12. **i)** he shall take the name. Chapter 45:4; Job 32:21, 22. **verse 6. k)** Following is the doctrine of spiritual liberation (chapter 43:16ff) and a corrective application against idolaters, from here until verse 20. **l)** verse 2; 32:1; chapter 43:15. **m)** and his avenger, i.e., his redeemer. Verse 22, 24; chapter 47:4, 59:20. Regarding the emphasis of this name, Gussetius <note>Jacques Gousset (1635–1704), a French Hebrew scholar.</note> is worth consulting (p. 157ff). Namely, by the force of its own meaning, which the use of the root shows, it involves not only a snatching away or liberation from misery or physical evil, but most especially the liberation of us as persons to be vindicated from the guilt and punishment of sins, and the vindication of a heritage to be acquired for God, and the payment of a debt made by our kinsman. Thus, God cannot be called our <term>Goël</term> <note>The Hebrew term for a "Kinsman-Redeemer," a relative who buys back a family member or their property.</note> properly and fully, except in Christ His Son, who through birth put on our nature, and by giving Himself to the punishment of death, became the <term>ransom</term> <note>original: "ἀντίλυτρον" (antilytron)</note> for us; and this was necessary, because we were to be redeemed from the hand of a just detainer—not the devil, who is a mere executioner, but the most just and powerful Judge and His avenging justice—so that we might afterwards live free in the <term>relationship</term> <note>original: "σχέσει" (schesei)</note> of Christ our Redeemer, and as a heritage returned to Him at such a great price, we might be His eternal possession. **n)** chapter 41:4, 42:12; Revelation 1:8, 11, 17; 22:13. **o)** i.e., eternal from before and after. Not as if He ever began or will have an end; but because He was before all things as the beginning, and will be after all things without end, even if all things should perish. Others interpret it to mean that all those other gods will cease, while He survives. **p)** verse 8; chapter 43:11. **q)** verse 8; chapter 45:21, 22. **verse 7. r)** For who is like Me? Chapter 46:9. **s)** will proclaim such a thing (Zechariah 7:7) or call (cf. Romans 4:17). **t)** will indicate it as something certain to happen. Cf. chapter 42:9, 43:9, 12. **u)** and will set it in order for me, so that I may see and acknowledge it. Cf. Psalm 50:21; Job 23:4. **x)** and that not just now, but from the time I established it from the beginning of the world. Cf. Proverbs 8:29. **y)** it is said: "the people of eternity." This is a hyperbolic formula among the Hebrews, by which they designate as "from eternity" those things which are very ancient and existed long before us. Cf. chapter 58:12, 61:4; Ezekiel 26:20; Amos 9:11; Psalm 143:3; Proverbs 22:28; Lamentations 3:6. For this properly belongs to God, as above in chapter 40:28. But Dorsch thinks the Prophet is referring to the divine power exercised over empires and the boundaries of nations in all ages everywhere on earth, by which He also chose the Israelite people for Himself as a special possession and will defend them forever, unless they defect from God by malicious desertion. **z)** and the subsequent or imminent things. Chapter 41:23, 45:11. **a)** chapter 41:22. **b)** let them indicate or announce. Chapter 43:8. **c)** for themselves—that is, in their own honor—or for those who worship them. **verse 8. d)** Therefore, do not fear, O my people! the carved images and their Babylonian worshippers. Chapter 12:2. **e)** and do not be terrified or afraid. Among the Arabs, *rahia* signifies one who has formed a weak plan in his mind, or was feeble, sluggish, slow, inconstant, and wavering. **f)** from that time—that is, long ago. Chapter 16:13, 48:3, 5, 7; Psalm 93:2. **g)** chapter 42:12, 48:5, 6. **h)** chapter 43:12, 45:21. **i)** for you are my witnesses. Chapter 43:10, 12. **k)** Is there a God? The question strongly denies it, as in Psalm 18:32; hence it is immediately followed by a negation: "there is no rock." **l)** verse 6.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the folly of idolatry (Isaiah 44) into the specific prophecy naming Cyrus as the instrument of God’s will, leading into the first seven verses of Isaiah 45. # ISAIAH CHAPTER 44, 45.

<margin>
**a)** <note>original: "ad flumios tuos"</note> regarding your rivers; compare Isaiah 11:15, 19:5, 6, 8.
**b)** compare chapter 42:15.
**c)** These things are to be understood here in reference to Babylon.
**d)** The scholar Schmidt says this refers to the drying up of the Red Sea <note>original: "maris Suph"</note> and the Jordan river. However, the literal sense of the words also holds true. For Cyrus, in order to capture Babylon, divided the Euphrates, and after drawing part of it away into a lake, he entered the city through the old riverbed. This is as we have taught above regarding chapter 21:4, citing Herodotus and Xenophon. Compare also Revelation 15:12.
</margin>

**27** [I am the one] who says to the deep, "Be dry," and I will dry up your rivers. **28** Who says of Cyrus, "He is my shepherd," and he shall fulfill all my pleasure; even saying to Jerusalem, "She shall be built," and to the temple, "Your foundation shall be laid."

**2** I will go before you and make the crooked places straight; I will break in pieces the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron.

<margin>
**CHAPTER XLV, verses 1, 2)**
What began concerning Cyrus at the end of the previous chapter is now more fully explained and **I.** confirmed: not only the most certain liberation of the Jews from Babylonian captivity through Cyrus, but also the spiritual liberation of mankind through Christ in **verse 8.** **II.** A corrective application is made against the rebellious Jews in **verses 9 and 10.** **III.** The promise of liberation from Babylon is repeated in **verse 11**, along with the most happy spiritual liberation in **verse 14.** **IV.** There follows a teaching application for refutation in **verse 20** and for instruction in **verse 22.** Or to put it briefly: it contains: **(1)** A fuller explanation of the prophecy regarding Cyrus in **chapter 44:24 and following.** **(2)** An exhortation to the people, ranging from joy to impatience. **(3)** The majesty of the Messiah as through the Prophe-...
</margin>

—anointed ones are types of Christ (as Dorsch says), and there is no power except from God. Romans 13:1. For otherwise it is not established, as the scholar notes, that the Kings of the Persians were physically anointed as the Scripture testifies concerning the Kings of the Jews. Therefore, they rightly note that the Hebrew custom and its underlying reason are being referenced here. And since among the Hebrews anointing was not unique to Kings but also to Priests, we must seek the common reason, which was the destination and authority of the Most High God himself. Cyrus also had the clearest signs of divine favor and governance in his most successful outcomes. Compare also 1 Kings 19:15. **9)** Chapter 44:28. 2 Chronicles 36:22. **v)** Whose right hand I have taken and will strengthen. Chapter 42:6, Psalm 73:22. **5)** The scholar notes: for subduing, for casting down. (4) Judges 19:11, 1 Kings 6:32, Psalm 144:2. The Hebrew form <term>lerad</term> is the infinitive of the simple verb. Jeremiah 5:26. **t)** The nations: Medes, Ionians, Babylonians, etc. **u)** I will loosen, I will ungird. Chapter 5:27, chapter 20:2. All these terms are taken from the belt of a soldier; for the conquered were ungirded. (Dorsch). **x)** That I may open before Cyrus. Deuteronomy 20:11, 2 Kings 15:16. Compare Revelation 3:8. **y)** Compare 1 Corinthians 16:9, 2 Corinthians 2:12, verse 2. **z)** I, the Messiah. Verse 1 of Jonah: "My Word shall go before you." **a)** <note>original: "inaequalia, tortuosa"</note> The uneven, the crooked. (1) **b)** I will make straight or I will level. Chapter 40:3. Jerome and the Vulgate: "I will humble the glorious ones of the earth." **c)** Chapter 48:4, Psalm 107:16. **d)** Compare chapter 43:14, Amos 1:5, 1 Kings 4:13. **e)** I will shatter. Chapter 9:9, Psalm 75:11, Psalm 107:16. So that nothing can delay your most successful progress. **Verse 3. f)** *Treasures of darkness*, that is, the most hidden treasures and wealth of the Babylonians, even if they were hidden with the greatest care. **s. g)** And hidden riches. (1) Compare Jeremiah 41:8. **h)** From the hiding place. Jeremiah 49:10. **i)** Not so that you become insolent or attribute this to yourself, but *so that you may acknowledge that I am Jehovah*, the God of Israel, who called you by such a name long beforehand. Indeed, Josephus, in the place cited above at chapter 44:24, records that Cyrus obtained knowledge of this prophecy, and marvelling at its antiquity, decided from a consideration of it to grant the Jewish people their liberty. This is not unlikely, for Daniel flourished in the court of Cyrus (Daniel 6:29) and lived in Susa (Daniel 8:2), where Xenophon teaches in the 8th book of the *Cyropaedia* (page 233) that Cyrus used to spend the springtime. Hence it becomes probable that Daniel showed the scroll of Isaiah to Cyrus. Compare Ezra 1:1 and following, 2 Chronicles 36:23. **Verse 4. k)** Above all, it should be observed here that the Church is of the highest care to God, such that he even overturns kingdoms for its sake. (Schmidt). **l)** Chapter 44:1. **m)** Chapter 43:20. **n)** Therefore, I say, *I have called you by name* (verse 3, chapter 44:28). **o)** *And I have titled you* (chapter 44:5). **p)** When as yet you did not know me (Psalm 139:16, Job 22:16). **Verse 5. That is**, out of mere favor and my singular good pleasure, I have destined the kingdom for you, O Cyrus, and expressed your name in the sacred book, so that you, who otherwise ignore me, may confess that I am the omnipotent God who foreknows all things, and that you may release my people from the captivity in which they are unjustly held by the Babylonians. **Verse 5. q)** Verse 6, 14, 17. **r)** Besides me (verse 21, Hosea 13:4, Deuteronomy 32:39). **s)** Verse 21, 22, chapter 44:8, 2 Samuel 22:32. **t)** *I will therefore gird you* (Psalm 18:33, 40). **u)** See verse 4. **Verse 6. x)** So that all nations through all parts of the world may also know (2 Chronicles 33:13, chapter 59:19, Psalm 50:1, Psalm 113:3, Malachi 1:11). **z)** Chapter 43:5. **a)** That *there is no God* (verse 14, chapter 40:17, chapter 46:9) **b)** besides me (Genesis 41:44). **c)** Verse 5, 14. **Verse 7. d)** *Forming* (verse 13) *light*, that is, the day (compare Job 26:10, Habakkuk 3:4, Psalm 139:11). By light, they usually understand happiness and liberation in this place, and by darkness, they understand unhappiness and the imminent Babylonian captivity; and it can be said fittingly enough that light and darkness are to be taken literally, but are placed here for the sake of comparison, and not without the argument that God also sends peace and evil. As if to say: just as *I once formed the light and created darkness*, so I form and am able to form peace and evil also. etc. **e)** God is said to *create darkness* through the removal of the opposite light; otherwise darkness, because it is a privation, is not strictly "created" (Dorsch). Yet God created darkness when He so established the earth and water that they have no light of their own, and even block light by their positioning, as we see in eclipses of the moon. (Schmidt). **f)** Job 38:2. **g)** Chapter 42:24, chapter 48:7, Amos 3:6, Numbers 16:30. Compare Lamentations 3:37. **h)** That I say, I am *Jehovah* (verse 6). **i)** Chapter 44:24. And that this is my work and office.

# CHAPTER 45. ISAIAH 45

<margin>
**v. 8.** Let its inhabitants bring forth the fruit of salvation, or produce fruits that correspond to the salvation granted through Christ.
Others say: let heaven and earth bring forth the fruit of Salvation, namely that Righteous Branch and Savior (compare Jeremiah 23:5, 6; 1 Corinthians 1:30).
**An active verb** is used, as in Deuteronomy 29:17. For the noun, compare below in chapter 51:5, 61:10, 62:11; Psalm 85:10. q) compare Jeremiah 23:5. r) compare chapter 42:9; 2 Samuel 23:5; Psalm 85:13. s) "I was created and wonderfully produced," see verse 7; chapter 43:5. Targum Jonathan: "I created it."
</margin>

# 8. Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness; let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together; I the Lord have created it.

<margin>
**v. 8. k)** "Shower down," <note>original: "Rorate"</note> "distill." (s) Job 36:28; Psalm 65:12. Compare the related term in Deuteronomy 32:2. Most commentators state that this verse speaks of the goods or benefits to be granted to the Jewish people through Cyrus (though it is not Cyrus himself who is distilled from heaven, but justice and salvation; see Dorssh on this passage and Gusset p. 717, and others). However, the words are too magnificent to seem applicable only to Cyrus. Furthermore: (1) It is not the Prophet or the Church speaking, but Jehovah the Messiah himself, as seen from the end of the verse. (2) This is a prophetic imperative (as above in chapter 23:2, 26:19; or a certain promise as in 2 Kings 5:10), meaning the following words are in the future tense; nothing else is here but a promise of the Jehovah-Messiah, as if to say: the heavens will drop down from above, and the clouds will drip righteousness; the earth will open itself, etc. (3) This verse does not speak immediately of the birth of the Messiah nor his conception in Mary's womb through the "overshadowing" <note>original Greek: ἐπέλευσιν (epeleusin)</note> of the Holy Spirit, as others think; rather, the Messiah describes things external to his own person. For he himself, as stated, is the one speaking here. We say the happiness of the New Testament is described by comparing it with the present state of the world, as if the entire machine of the world is to be renewed; so that the clear sky drops down not water, as it has until now, but righteousness; the clouds drip not drops of water, but righteousness, etc. Thus elsewhere the state of the New Testament is compared to a new heaven and a new earth in Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22, a state which is to be fulfilled in eternal life. S. l) from above, Exodus 20:4. m) clouds, Deuteronomy 33:26; 2 Samuel 22:12. n) let them drip or flow, Jeremiah 9:17; Job 36:28. o) the earth will open itself, compare Psalm 67:7. p)
</margin>

# 9. Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! A potsherd among the potsherds of the earth! Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, "What makest thou?" or thy work, "He hath no hands"?

# 10. Woe unto him that saith unto his father, "What begettest thou?" or to the woman, "What hast thou brought forth?"

# 11. Thus saith the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, and his Maker: Ask me of things to come concerning my sons, and concerning the work of my hands command ye me.

# 12. I have made the earth, and created man upon it; I, even my hands, have stretched out the heavens, and all their host have I commanded.

# 13. I have raised him up in righteousness, and I will direct all his ways; he shall build my city, and he shall let go my captives, not for price nor reward, saith the Lord of hosts.

# 14. Thus saith the Lord: The labor of Egypt, and merchandise of Ethiopia and of the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over unto thee, and they shall be thine; they shall walk after thee.

**v. 9. f)** Woe, therefore, to the impious and stubborn Jew (see v. 10, v. 1, 4). ñ) Litigating or contending, Judges 11:25. x) with his fashioner or founder, chapter 64:7; Genesis 2:7. y) a potsherd, as in chapter 30:14. z) with the other potsherds of the earth, compare Lamentations 4:2; 2 Corinthians 4:7. a) see chapter 29:16. b) to his potter, chapter 64:7; compare Jeremiah 18:6; Romans 9:20. c) "O your work!" O impious litigator (chapter 45:24), can it say of you? d) "he has no hands," namely, "to my maker." Surely those litigating ones were accusing both the wisdom of God, by saying "What are you doing?" and His omnipotence, by saying "He has no hands." As if God should not have permitted the Babylonian captivity, or could not have averted it, or rescued them from it. S. **v. 10. e)** Woe is denounced upon those denying these greatest mysteries and benefits, since they accuse God's wisdom and power and act absurdly. This is a second comparison, in which these stubborn Jews are compared to an insolent son who mocks his parents or argues with them about his own birth. **v. 11. f)** Chapter 41:14, 21. g) Referencing the mystery of the incarnation (v. 9 and 10), which is explained on page 156 using the words of Jerome <note>original: Hieronymi</note>, which in his Commentary on this passage say: "Woe to those who contradict God, and do not think Christ will come, as if the clay and the potsherd should contradict its potter. Or who says to the almighty Father, 'Why do you beget a son?' and to the holy woman Mary, 'What are you about to bring forth?'" etc. But while Jerome explained not only this but another view regarding Cyrus, *Luther*, *Brentius*, and *Schmidt* hold our view based on the context. f) "What do you beget?" I do not take "What" adverbially for "why," but pronominally for "what kind of thing do you beget?" This again rebukes those accusing both the wisdom and omnipotence of God and His work, as if it were not well made. The speech is with the Israelites, of whom God is accustomed to call Himself the father and mother, not of the gentiles. S. g) Chapter 26:17; 66:7. **v. 11. h)** The Messiah, v. 15, 17, 21; chapter 1:4. i) Chapter 43:7, 21. k) things to come, chapter 41:23. l) "Ask" or "Inquire of Me," chapter 7:11, 30:2, 41:28, 58:2; not other gods or your impious counsels, because I alone can judge and provide for your future. See chapter 42:9, 43:9, 12, etc. m) Chapter 43:6. n) Chapter 5, 12, 19. o) "Command ye me," that is, you Jews and Israelites; now you Gentiles, act and ask of me! For I will recount to you (if only someone asks seriously and it can be done) my future and past works, not so much those I already completed in creation, but those I will yet complete in my sons, in the people of my Church: so that it may be clearly seen that divine majesty belongs not to the gods of the nations, but to me alone, and that I alone am the Savior of the Church. *Brentius*. Jehovah the Messiah had said in v. 9 and 10 that they do wrong who accuse His wisdom or power. Now, therefore, he wishes to further convince them that nothing of wisdom or power is lacking in Him. S.

<note>This section contains detailed cross-references and philological notes for the verses above.</note>

Chapter 37:16. **o)** Who formed. Verse 7; Jeremiah 10:16. **p)** And who made it. Compare Jeremiah 32:2; Psalm 95:4, 5. **q)** Who Himself prepared or formed it. Deuteronomy 32:6; Psalm 24:2; Psalm 119:90. **r)** See Genesis 1:2. **s)** But rather for it to be inhabited by men. Chapter 44:7; Acts 17:26. **t)** Thus I am still the same Jehovah, who does good to men, and specifically promised to Israel that it would not be in vain if they seek me. Verse 19. **u)** Verses 5, 6, 21. Verse 19. **x)** Chapter 48:16; Deuteronomy 13:7; Jeremiah 37:17. **y)** "In secret" <note>original: "en kryphē"</note>. Ephesians 5:12; John 12:20. Compare Deuteronomy 30:11. **z)** In a place of the land of darkness. Compare Job 10:21. By this, you have looked only to the deceptive oracles of demons among the gentiles, which spoke from hiding and from the earth itself with obscurity, ambiguity, and great deceit. So says Schmidius. Compare above, chapter 29:4. Verse 25. See chapter 41:8, etc.; chapter 44:3. **a)** Emptily and in vain, chapter 41:29; 19:4. As it truly is when the gentiles seek their oracles. Compare above, chapter 8:19. **b)** Seek me, Zephaniah 2:3; Psalm 27:8. But I surely hear those who call upon me. Compare Hebrews 11:6. **c)** Speaking righteousness; that is, whatever I speak, promise, and have promised, it is infallible, certain, and such that my justice appears from it; as I have promised, so shall I do; thus I announce right and indubitable things. So says Schmidius. Compare verse 23; chapter 33:15; Proverbs 16:13; and the opposite in Psalm 101:7. **d)** Indicating, as in chapter 42:9. **e)** Right things. Chapter 33:15. <note>The following notes provide a deep dive into the specific Hebrew words used in the verses above.</note>

**v. 2.** Compare the related word in Exodus 26:6, which signifies curved loops. The Tigurine version says "he collapsed"; others say he "fell on his nose" or was "prostrated on his face," like Dagon in 1 Samuel 5:3-4. The Targum has "he was cut down"; or simply from the Chaldean usage of our word: "he was split, pulled apart, or crushed." Compare chapter 21:9 above. **e)** "Nebo" was a god of the Chaldeans, named by Hiller for "height." He is not mentioned elsewhere, though the name remains in "Nebuchadnezzar," "Nebuzaradan," etc. For the name of the Moabite city, see chapter 15:2 above, which once belonged to the Reubenites (Numbers 32:3, 38); Mount Nebo was nearby (Deuteronomy 32:48-49; 34:1), and another town of that name exists in Ezra 2:29 and Nehemiah 7:33. **f)** "Their idols were" or "became"; specifically, they became a load or "for a load," as shown at the end of the verse. **g)** Chapter 10:10; 2 Samuel 5:21. Many apply these suffixes to the Babylonians, but S. and others refer them to the gods Bel and Nebo. **h)** "To the beast and the cattle," Leviticus 25:7, etc. Thus they are placed on animals to be carried away into Persia. Kimchi notes here that even female camels are used for carrying loads, like elephants. **i)** Bochart (in *Hieroz.* I, p. 220) translates this as "your burden-bearers," meaning the animals that carry you or your loads. He argues that passive participles can signify action when used as nouns (citing Proverbs 28:17 and Jeremiah 9:7), though these examples do not fully prove the rule. Hence, Tremellius translates "your carriages," and S. says "your things to be carried," namely the pieces of the idols. For having spoken of Bel and Nebo in the third person, the prophet now addresses them in the second person to mock them more bitterly. The Targum says "their burdens." Compare verse 2 and Genesis 45:23. **k)** Placed on as a burden to be carried. See verse 3; Genesis 44:13; Nehemiah 4:11. **l)** "They are a burden," verse 2; chapter 22:25. **m)** "Weary" or "tired" beasts, chapter 32:2; Jeremiah 4:31. It is as if he says: "You gods are such a burden that you even tire out the animals carrying you away!" What "excellent" gods you are! Truly, God the Messiah—having promised Israel's liberation and its unshakeable certainty—now illustrates this with a symbol: predicting the fall of the Babylonian idols under Cyrus (verses 1-2). He then contrasts Himself, the true God of Israel, who is not carried but instead carries His worshippers from the womb to old age most faithfully, delivering them most powerfully (verses 3-4). He warns the stubborn Jews (verse 12; chapter 45:9-10) that He should never be compared or equated to these powerless idols, which are laboriously and expensively cast by men (verse 5). **v. 2. n)** "They were destroyed" and "stooped together," Bel and Nebo (verse 1) and the other gods of the Babylonians (chapter 21:9; 2 Chronicles 32:13). **p)** "To snatch away and deliver" from enemies, verse 4; 2 Samuel 19:10. **q)** "The burden," that is, their own idols, placed on beasts to be carried away (verse 1). **r)** "And their soul," which according to Kimchi means "themselves" (compare chapter 5:14; Psalm 105:18), a common way for Arabs to speak. Similarly, the <gloss>Greek term</gloss> *autoi* <note>original: "αὐτοὶ"</note> is used for "themselves," meaning the <gloss>Greek term</gloss> *aichmalōtoi* <note>original: "αἰχמάλωτοι"</note> "captives" who were "led away." But it is a very sharp irony when "soul" is used for a wooden trunk, to mock the fact that they have no other soul or spirit; as if to say: "And so it appeared how 'great' those gods are, being led into captivity—lifeless idols who have no soul beyond that heavy trunk." **s)** Deuteronomy 28:41; Jeremiah 30:16; Nahum 3:10. Bochart (in *Hieroz.* I, p. 357) recognizes here the custom of ancient generals who triumphed not only over conquered nations but also over their gods. Compare Jeremiah 48:7. **v. 3. t)** Verse 12; chapter 42:1, 12, 16. **u)** Chapter 2:5; 44:1. **x)** "Carried by me" (see verse 1) "from the womb"; see chapter 44:2, 24. **y)** "Borne," referring back to verse 1. **z)** "From the womb," Numbers 12:12; Jeremiah 1:5; chapter 20:18. The Targum says: "Who are loved above all peoples, and dear above all kingdoms." **v. 4. a)** "For even to old age," Psalm 71:9, 18. **b)** "I am the same," chapter 43:10. As He is immutable in essence, so He is immutable in His will and mercy regarding His promises. **c)** "And even to gray hairs," Psalm 71:18; Genesis 15:15; chapter 25:8. **d)** "I will carry you," verse 7; chapter 53:4, 11. **e)** Referring back to verse 2; see Jeremiah 39:18. The Targum says: "Indeed, even forever I am the same, and to the ages of ages my Word persists. I created all men; and I scattered you among the nations; I also will forgive their sins and pardon them." **v. 5. f)** See chapter 40:18, 25; and compare 41:7; 44:9. **g)** "And make me equal," chapter 40:25; Lamentations 2:13. **h)** "And to whom, as an example, will you compare me?" See chapter 14:10; Job 30:19. **i)** "So that we might agree or be similar," comparing myself with me. Psalm 144:4. As if to say: "You certainly cannot compare me to anyone, let alone to such rotten idols." Therefore, the Targum adds: "That we might be similar in truth." **v. 6. k)** Wasteful idolaters pour out [gold]. (2 Lamentations 1:8. **l)** "From bags" or "from the purse." (3 Micah 6:11; Proverbs 1:14. **m)** "A scale"; generally it denotes a stalk or reed, as in Genesis 41:5; specifically a marsh reed (Isaiah 19:6; 36:6), a sweet cane (chapter 43:24), a measuring reed (Ezekiel 40:4-5), the shaft of a lampstand (Exodus 25:31), and here, the "beam of a scale" or the "balance-bar." **n)** "They weigh," chapter 55:2; Genesis 23:16. **o)** "They hire for wages," Genesis 30:16. **p)** Chapter 40:19; Judges 17:4.

**CHAPTER XLVI, v. 2. ולא** with the prefix *vav-aleph*... **v. 5. ותמשלוני** with the vowel *Shureq*... according to the Masorah. **They are poured out.**

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Isaiah, moving from the collapse of the Babylonian idols (Bel and Nebo) in chapter 46 to the personified downfall of the city of Babylon itself in chapter 47. # CHAPTER 47. ISAIAH 47

<margin>
I will rush <note>Latin: "irruam"</note> against other men, compare Exodus 5:3. But I will take full vengeance <note>Hebrew: נְקָם, *neqam*</note> on myself; as Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase</note> translates: "I will arrange your judgment from the sons of men." He is also called simply "The Holy One" in Psalm 16:10 and the "Holy of Holies" in Daniel 9:24. From the New Testament, compare Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34; Acts 2:27; 3:14; 1 John 2:20; Revelation 3:7. The reason why the Messiah was so frequently marked with the name "Holy One of Israel" in the time of Isaiah and the later Prophets is that at that time there were great doubts regarding the promise of that Holy One, arising from the diminishing of the Israelite people and the devastation of the holy land where He was predicted to be revealed; indeed, from the impending exile of the remaining tribe of Judah into Babylonian captivity. These doubts had to be countered by the frequent repetition of the title "Holy One of Israel." Compare <term>Dorsiheus</term> <note>likely a reference to a specific scholar's work</note>. Truly, because the liberation of Israel is joined with the fall of the enemies (which was the subject of chapters 46 and 47), Jehovah the Messiah now explains the cause of that liberation, which is nothing but the glory of the divine name, excluding all merits of the Israelites, whose unworthiness he indicates from the very beginning. He calls them 1. nominal only and carnal, insofar as they came from the waters or the seed of Judah: 2. those dedicating themselves to God by external profession, but lying, and not truly or sincerely worshipping Him (verses 1, 2, etc.). From Maius's *Economy*, page 95. Schmidt observes two parts in this chapter: I. The complaint of the Messiah concerning the Jews in the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, II. The complaint concerning the same in the liberation of the New Testament (verse 16 and following). He declares the continuity with the preceding chapters thus: Hitherto from chapter 40, Jehovah the Messiah has spoken of the destruction of Babylon and the liberation of the people of Israel; but while in the earlier chapters he consoled his people for the sake of the weaker, yet sincere ones, in chapter 46 he began to chastise the unbelieving and hypocrites among his people. In this chapter, turning to the ingratitude of the Jewish people under the New Testament, he more severely rebukes the beginning of that vice, which began at the time of the liberation from Babylon, grew thereafter, and reached its peak in the New Testament. Schmidt adds: It is useful to observe this continuity, so that it is not hidden in what manner the Son of God approached the New Testament, which is treated intentionally in the following sections until the end of the book. **r)** chapter 2:5, 6 and 44:1. **s)** who are called by the name of Israel, chapter 43:7. 3. 4. But S. *and before the day*, that is, things which were in eternity, you did not hear them. o) see verse 5.

Here the Messiah shows the true cause of the liberation from Babylon, destroying all merit of their own, and commending the glory of His name. S. z) *I was deferring it for a long time, and further I will thus defer my anger.* Numbers 14:18, Psalm 106:45, Proverbs 19:11. a) and *for my glory.* chapter 42:8. b) *I was sparing,* and *I will spare you.* (1) Cocceius Lexicon p. 327. I was containing myself, and he derives this with the Rabbis from the Chaldean <term>chotem</term>, meaning nose, or anger. as if to say *I was containing my nose,* lest the breath and fiery vapor should go out from it, which would consume them. compare Isaiah 65:5. Others: I was containing and as if muzzling your enemies for your sake; from the Arabic root *he struck on the nose, he muzzled a camel, horse, ox.* c) cf. Deuteronomy 32:26.

Judges 17:4, Psalm 26:2, 66:10, Zechariah 13:9, Malachi 3:3. e) *but not for silver,* that is, for free, without any price or merit of yours. cf. chapter 52:3, 1 Kings 21:6, Micah 3:11, 1 Chronicles 21:22. as if to say: Purifiers of gold and silver purify for silver [payment] without reward; but I purified you indeed, but for free, not for your merits. And thus God the Messiah did not exceed the manner of purifying, but the reason for purifying. f) *I will choose you as one tested.* chapter 41:8, 9. g) *in the melting pot or furnace of affliction.* (8) Deuteronomy 4:20, Proverbs 17:3. cf. Wisdom 3:6, 1 Peter 1:7, Hebrews 12:11, 1 Corinthians 3:13, 15.

The question strongly denies, as if to say: for in no way will I allow my name to be profaned. — For the name of God would have been profaned, and He would have given His glory to another incidentally, if He had not liberated the Jews: because the gentiles would have ascribed that work to the power of their idols, and would have blasphemed God, as if He had been unable to liberate His people. S. Compare Numbers 14:15, 16, Deuteronomy 9:28. l) chapter 42:8.

Zurich: *the palm is a measure;* others: *he fitted or stretched or sustained with the palm.* (2) Lamentations 2:22. cf. Isaiah 40:12. t) *I call them.* chapter 46:11. **v. 14. y)** chapter 45:20. z) who among the Babylonians and their gods judged and predicted these things? Chapter 45:21. a) *he loved him.* It is asked, whom? Cocceius refers it to Christ, as we noted on Deuteronomy 33:12. Many refer it to Cyrus, but without context. <summary>This page contains a detailed philological and theological commentary on Isaiah 48:3-14, emphasizing God’s sovereign prediction of events to counteract Israel's stubbornness and idolatry. The author interprets the "caller" as the Messiah and explains the refining of Israel in the "furnace of affliction" as an act of grace intended to preserve the glory of God's name.</summary>
<keywords>Isaiah 48, Messiah, Babylon, Chaldeans, original sin, furnace of affliction, divine glory, biblical philology, Sebastian Schmidt, Targum Jonathan</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Isaiah 48, moving from the prediction of Cyrus’s conquests to a deeper, mystical revelation of the speaker's identity—interpreted here as the Messiah—and a call for the people to depart from Babylonian captivity, both physical and spiritual.</meta>

<margin>
**v. 16. k)** *Come near to me,* the Son of God, see verses 12, 13, 15. Here is the chief difficulty: who is speaking? S. says it is not God the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, as is clear from the end of the verse. Most think these are the words of Isaiah speaking of himself. But Dorschæus rightly concludes these are the words of Christ speaking of his mission with the Holy Spirit and others; (1) because in the preceding verses no other person is named than Jehovah, v. 12 seqq. (2) because he who invites them to "come near" here is the same who in verse 14 invited them to gather and hear. (3) because no other has spoken indefinitely to the Israelites from the beginning until now except the divine person in verse 16. (4) Because the most ancient Doctors of the Church interpreted it thus: Eusebius, Athanasius, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, etc. **l)** *Hear these things,* regarding what follows about my mission in the flesh, compare verse 1. For after the Son of God extensively excuses the future unbelief of the Jews. S. **v. 19. l)** *It would have been as the sand.* compare 1 Kings 4:20. **m)** *and the offspring of your bowels* chapter 49, 1. Genesis 15, 4. **o)** *like the pebbles or grains of sand.* (1) **p)** chapter 55, 13. **q)** Deuteronomy 28, chapter 28:20, 24. 1 Kings 15, 27. **r)** chapter 14, 22. Jonathan: "the name of Israel." **v. 20. n)** *Go out therefore at last from spiritual Babylon,* and flee from the Chaldea of spiritual malice. Jeremiah 51:6, 45. Revelation 18:4. 2 Corinthians 6:17. These words are commonly interpreted as the release from the Babylonian captivity: see Sanctius at length on this passage, who also reviews many authors, but admits others take them as referring to Christ; which we also hold, all the more because verse 21 does not fit the Babylonian captivity. Although they try to pull it there with Abraham ibn Ezra, David Kimchi not undeservedly casts this aside on this passage: "If this prophecy was spoken about those returning from the Babylonian captivity, as it indeed seems, it is a wonder how it is not clear in the Book of Ezra, where he narrates the exit from that captivity, that these miracles happened for them—that the Lord split the rock for them in the desert." This certainly aids our opinion. If you say these things are to be understood metaphorically: I reply, the magnitude of the event far exceeds those metaphors, so that even authors of the contrary opinion are forced to flee to hyperbole. But in Christ, the magnitude of spiritual benefits and their abundance is so great that these metaphors shadow it most aptly, though they cannot perfectly reach it. **s. t)** chapter 14, 7. chapter 35, 10. Psalm 47, 2. Psalm 118, 15. **u)** *with the voice of joy announce* verse 6. chapter 45, 21.
</margin>

**n)** *not in secret* (chapter 45:19. Septuagint: as in John 18:20) but openly and clearly I have spoken, verse 15, concerning the redemption of the human race. **o)** as if to say: for I did not then first begin to exist when I was made man and appeared in the flesh among mortals, but from the time when it was decreed by God that I should be sent, I was there among the persons making the decree. The meaning of the word looks back to "and him" <note>original: ואתו</note>, which demonstrates the mission of the Son of God in the flesh; existence here is to be understood not in physical reality, but in the divine decree, as is frequent; "time" however is used here in a broad sense and denotes eternity itself. S. Compare Proverbs 8:30. Romans 16:25. 2 Timothy 1:9. Titus 1:2. **p)** *there I was already present.* compare Proverbs 8:22, 27. John 1:1, 2. chapter 2:8, 58. namely, as your surety and sponsor; which the ancient Jews also acknowledge in the *Yalkut* <note>Yalkut Shimoni, a medieval midrashic compilation</note> Part II, folio 56, column 2 seqq. For they teach there not without emphasis that the Messiah is to be understood by "that coming light" of Isaiah 60:1, compared with Psalm 36:10 and Genesis 1:4. And that God, even before the creation of the world, looked toward the times of the Messiah and his works, and established that light for the Messiah himself and his age under the throne of His glory. Compare Colossians 3:3. John 17:5, etc. Then they proceed with these words: *“When God created the Messiah, He entered into a covenant with him and spoke thus: These men, whose iniquities are hidden with you, will put you under an iron yoke and reduce you to the state of a calf whose eyes grow dim, and they will distress your soul with perversity. Indeed, because of their iniquities, it will happen that your tongue cleaves to the roof of your mouth <note>Psalm 22:16</note>. Do you then acquiesce to this condition? The Messiah answered: Lord of this universe! Will this affliction last many years? God answered: By your life and the life of your head! One week <note>Daniel 9:27</note> I have decreed upon you. But if your soul grieves for this reason, I will immediately destroy them. But the Messiah said: Ruler of the world, with joy and gladness of heart I take these demands upon myself, so that not one of Israel may perish, and that not only those who live in my days be saved, but also those hidden in the earth; and not only the dead of my days, but all who have died from the first Adam until now; and not only they, but also the stillborn; and not only these, but also those You have decided to create but have not yet been created. Thus I agree with You, and thus I take Your stipulation upon myself.”* Furthermore, the Ancients said: in that week when the Son of David comes, they shall bring iron beams and place them on his neck until his straight stature is bent. And he himself will cry out so that his voice ascends to heaven, and he will say before God: Lord of the world, how great is my strength? what is my spirit, and what is my soul? what are my limbs? Am I not flesh and blood? (And because of that hour David also wept and said: *My strength is dried up like a potsherd,* Psalm 22:16). But God answered him: Ephraim, Messiah, my righteousness! You yourself have already taken this upon yourself from the creation of the world, etc. **q)** *but now* in the fullness of time, Galatians 4:4, 5. **r)** God the Father. **s)** *has sent me* in the flesh, chapter 61:1. compare Zechariah 2:13, 15; 4:9; 6:15. **t)** *and His Spirit* chapter 63:10. In a short verse (says Jerome in his Commentary on this passage) the mystery of the Trinity is shown to us. The Father sends the Son according to both divine and human nature; but the Holy Spirit sends according to the human nature, by which Christ was born of Him, Matthew 1:20, Luke 1:35, and by the same was anointed, Isaiah 11:2, 42:1, 61:1, Psalm 45:8, Luke 4:18. The Son speaks not as one to be incarnated, but as if already incarnated, and of the matters of the New, not the Old Testament. For it is not unknown that in the Prophets future things are represented as if already present, so that how and what they will be may be indicated more clearly. S. Compare notes on 5:13, 9:2, 13, 10:28, 16:4, 37:22, 42:17, 45:16. **v. 17. u)** Furthermore, thus says Jehovah the Son; the same who spoke in verse 16. For often these words, *thus said the Lord*, are placed parenthetically among the Hebrews, like the Latin *inquil* <note>he says</note>. see chapter 7:7, 30:12, 15. S. 43:14, 16, 44:2, 6. **x)** chapter 41:14, 49:7, 26. compare Hebrews 9:15, Colossians 1:14. **y)** chapter 41:14, 47:4, Daniel 9:24, 1 Corinthians 1:30, chapter 6:11. **z)** *I the Messiah am Jehovah your God.* chapter 45:13. **a)** *most faithfully instructing you* according to my Prophetic office. compare chapter 2:3, 63:1, Psalm 25:4, 5. **b)** not with vain words that do not profit you if you follow them, or empty promises I cannot fulfill, like the gods of the nations; but for your greatest benefit, if only you believe. chapter 30:5, 44:10, Jeremiah 2:8, 11, Zephaniah 3:5, Matthew 16:26. **c)** *leading or directing you* Psalm 25:5, 9, Proverbs 4:11, through the word of the Gospel, which is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. Romans 1:16. **d)** *in the way of salvation* which you ought to go. Psalm 32:8. **v. 18. e)** Oh, if only you would turn your ears and mind, chapter 28:23, 42:23; 1 Samuel 15:22, Psalm 81:14, Revelation 3:15. **f)** Exodus 15:26, Psalm 119:131, Nehemiah 9:29. **g)** S. for it would have been *like a river* chapter 59:19. The Septuagint: as in Acts 9:15; compare 1 Chronicles 7:40, 9:22. **d)** In His quiver (chapter 22:6; Jeremiah 5:16). **f) verse 3.** My servant, chosen and beloved (chapter 42:1; Philippians 2:7; Hebrews 2:14 and following). A singular servant is understood here, which is proven by the works soon indicated in verses 5 and 6. **g)** Tremellius: "Israel, of whom I am to be made glorious." This version, as Schmidt indicates, gives the best coherence and indicates among whom the Messiah would administer his office in the flesh, namely in Israel, to convert them (verse 5; add Matthew 10:6, 15:24; Acts 13:46, 28:25 and following). But the Zurich Bible: "You are Israel, in whom I will glory." Or as others: "You are that true Israel, of whom I said: In you all the nations of the earth shall be blessed" (Genesis 28:14). Dorscheus says: Christ is called "Israel" after Jacob, his type, who represented him as the victor and reconciler of God the Father. Thus Maius in *Oeconomica*, page 959. **h)** chapter 44:23, 60:21; John 17:4. **verse 4. i)** I, the Messiah, said this out of consideration for the incredulity of the Jews, discussed in the previous chapter. There is an elegant parallel between "He said to me" (v. 3) and "I said" (here). **k)** for nothing (chapter 30:7, 65:23; compare chapter 26:18, 53:1; Proverbs 1:24; Luke 17:31). **l)** I labored (see chapter 43:24). **m)** in vain (chapter 45:19). **n)** and uselessly (chapter 30:7; Job 9:29). **o)** I consumed my strength (Psalm 22:16, 71:9; compare John 4:31, 46; Matthew 23:27). **p)** Nevertheless (chapter 40:7, 53:4). **q)** My right and my judgment (compare Psalm 35:23, 37:2). **r)** Is with the Lord. Jonathan: "It is manifest before God," to those who will judge my cause and vindicate me from adversaries (compare John 8:50). **s)** And the reward of my works (Leviticus 19:13). **t)** Is with my God, who will not let me labor for nothing (compare verse 5; chapter 48:17). **verse 5. u)** Genesis 45:8. **x)** Who formed me from the womb (verse 1; chapter 44:2; Psalm 22:11). **y)** Into a servant for Himself (verse 3; chapter 52:13). **z)** That I might convert (verse 6; Jeremiah 30:19). **a)** Jonathan: "the house of Jacob" (compare chapter 43:1). **b)** To Himself. Jonathan: "to His worship." **c)** "And that Israel to Him"—Jonathan: "might be brought to the fear of Him." See Matthew 15:24; John 11:52; and compare above chapter 9:2, also 63:9, and the variant readings to Leviticus 11:21. Others read it negatively: "and that I might not convert Israel to Him, who are not gathered, like sheep having no shepherd" (Matthew 9:36), understanding a relative particle as in chapter 10:30. **d)** Schmidt: "now precious," others "glorious," from chapter 43:4 (compare John 1, 14, 2:11, 17:1, 5). **e)** verse 4; Zechariah 11:4; chapter 12:2. **verse 6. f)** Schmidt: "Nay, He said" (compare chapter 22:10, 39:7; Habakkuk 1:8). **g)** Schmidt: "It is a light thing that you should be to me." As if to say: it would be a small and slight thing to be a servant only of the inhabitants [of Israel] (compare Ezekiel 8:17; 1 Samuel 18:23; 1 Kings 16:21; 2 Kings 20:10). **h)** verses 3, 5. **i)** To raise up and restore (verse 8; Amos 9:11). **k)** The tribes of the Jacobites (chapter 63:17) lest they perish. **l)** And to bring back and gather the saved of Israel (verse 8; Ezekiel 6:12) who for a long time refused to be gathered (see above verse 4; Matthew 23:37), but will finally be converted (Romans 11:25-26; Maius, *Oeconomica*, page 959). But the Zurich Bible, Lyra, and others: "to bring back" or "to restore the desolations." The root <term>נצר</term> <note>N-TS-R</note>, says Dorscheus, has both meanings: preservation and destruction. It may be thought that such an ambiguous word was used intentionally; for even in the midst of vastation and desolation, those who belong to the <term>λεῖμμα κατ’ ἐκλογὴν χάριτος</term> <note>remnant according to the election of grace</note> (Romans 11:5) were guarded and preserved, whom Zechariah 9:12 calls "prisoners of hope." But then a different origin of the form must be sought, as we showed above at chapter 1:8. **m)** Compare Matthew 12:6, 15:24. **n)** Compare Jeremiah 29:10. For the greater fruit of Christ's mission was the conversion of the Gentiles. **o)** "But I will also give you" (verse 8; chapter 42:6, 55:4). **p)** chapter 9:1, 42:6-7, 51:4; Luke 2:32; Acts 13:47. Reference is also made to this in John 15:7 and following, 3:19, 8:12, 9:5, 12:46. **q)** That you may be, or that my salvation may become open (chapter 51:6, 8). **r)** To the ends of the earth (chapter 48:20), so that the whole world may be filled with your glory (Ephesians 6:3; John 11:52, 12:41). Moses Haddarsan correctly understood this of the Messiah, according to Raymond Martini in *Pugio Fidei*, page 828.

<summary>This page concludes the exhortation to flee Babylon in Isaiah 48 and begins the profound 'Servant Song' of Isaiah 49. The commentary identifies the Servant as the Messiah, whose mission begins with the restoration of Israel but ultimately expands to bring salvation to the Gentile nations and the ends of the earth.</summary>
