**verse 7. b)** According to the mind of Musculus <note>Wolfgang Musculus, a 16th-century Reformer</note>, this is a dialogue with the oppressed Church. So says Musculus in his *Divine Economy*, page 960. But Jerome says in his *Commentary on this place* that the interpretation concerning Christ is better. With him, Krentzius, Varenius, and Schmidius also accept all these things as spoken by God the Father to Christ. See verse 16, chapter 41:14. A little before in chapter 48:17, these titles were attributed to the Son of God; now they are attributed to God the Father, so that you may know that even if the Father and Son are two persons, they are nevertheless one essence and divinity, according to Brennius. Compare 1 Timothy 1:1, Titus 1:3, and chapter 10:17. **x)** Specifically regarding the "despising of the soul"; that is, that I should promptly pour out my soul and my life, comparing chapter 53:10, 12, Matthew 20:28, and John 10:17, 18. **y)** "To the one abhorred," he who detests the impious nation. Amos 6:8, Deuteronomy 23:18, Psalm 106:40. Compare above verse 4, which is the foundation of this. **z)** Philippians 2:7, 8. **a)** Chapter 11:5, 28:14, 52:5. Referring to Pilate, Herod, and the High Priests. **S.** For although He is the Lord not only of kings and princes, but of all creatures, He was nevertheless made a servant of lords on this earth, indeed a servant of servants, comparing Matthew 20:28 (Brentius). **b)** Kings also in verse 33, chapter 52:15, shall see Him and acknowledge His glory. Chapter 41:20, 52:8, Psalm 48:6. **d)** Specifically: "and they shall stand firm." **Vatablus:** "And they shall rise up" for the sake of honor, compare Exodus 33:10, Leviticus 19:32, Esther 5:9. **e)** "Princes," that is, they shall see. **f)** Verse 23, Genesis 27:29, Zephaniah 2:11, Psalm 22:28, 72:11. **g)** And this will certainly happen because of Jehovah, who is faithful in keeping His promises. See **S.** on this place. **h)** Deuteronomy 7:9. **i)** Specifically: because He chose and loves the Messiah. Chapter 42:1, 43:10. **k)** He who chose you, Israel, justified you, and will finally glorify you. Thus Musculus on this place, comparing Psalm 45:10 and following, Romans 8:28 and following.

**verse 8. l)** John 11:41, 42; Hebrews 5:7. However, these prayers are to be understood not only as the final ones of Christ, as in John 17:1 and following, or Psalm 22:2 and following, but those which He poured out throughout His whole life. **S.** **m)** Chapter 41:10. **n)** I will keep you (verse 6, chapter 27:3, 42:6). **p)** See verse 6. **q)** Chapter 42:6. **r)** **S.** For restoring the earth (verse 6) which was subjected to the curse (Genesis 3:17, 5:29). **s)** For distributing (Joshua 1:6, Zechariah 8:12, Proverbs 8:21). **t)** Heritages (Joshua 19:51). **u)** Desolate (verse 19, chapter 54:1). **verse 9. x)** Tigurinus version: "that you may say." **y)** To the bound, see chapter 42:7, 61:1. **z)** **S.** To those who are in darkness (chapter 47:5, Micah 7:8; compare above chapter 9:2, 50:2, Acts 26:18, Ephesians 5:8). **a)** Come forth into the light (compare 1 Samuel 14:8). **b)** Compare chapter 35:8 and following. **c)** Chapter 30:23; compare John 10:9. **d)** Chapter 13:2, Numbers 21:3. **e)** There shall be their feeding or pasture. (**10**) Jeremiah 10:21, Hosea 12:1. **verse 10. f)** Compare chapter 65:13, Proverbs 10:3, John 6:33. **g)** Chapter 18:28, John 4:14; compare Psalm 23:1, John 10:9. **h)** **S.** Neither shall He strike them (Isaiah 49:10). **i)** Heat. (1) Chapter 35:7. The Chaldean and Syriac root means: it was dry, it burned, it was scorched.) **k)** Or the sun (Psalm 121:6). **l)** He who has mercy on them (verse 15, chapter 54:10). **m)** Chapter 33:4. **n)** Chapter 35:7, 55:1, Revelation 7:17. **o)** Chapter 40:11, Psalm 23:2. This alludes to the custom of the Orientals, where after the morning feeding, all are led to the waters at the fourth hour of the day (which is our ten o'clock), then to the shade and midday rest, from which they go again to the waters. After this, they fed again until evening and sunset. For in hot regions, unless the cattle were led to shade and water in the midday hours, they would waste away from the day's heat and fall into dangerous diseases. Compare Ezekiel 34:13, 14, 15; Song of Solomon 1:7; and Bochart’s *Hierozoicon*, volume I, page 519. **verse 11. p)** Chapter 40:4, 32:34, 14. **q)** Chapter 35:8, 42:15, Zechariah 4:7. **r)** And my fortified ways (chapter 33:8, 52:10). **s)** They shall be exalted in marshy places, compare chapter 40:4, Proverbs 15:19. **verse 12. t)** Verse 2, chapter 43:6, 60:4, 9. **u)** Chapter 41:25, 43:5, 6; compare Revelation 11:13, 16. **x)** Sinim (Genesis 10:17). Some, like Bochart in his *Analysis*, understand the Sinae or Chinese in the far East; others, like Pfeiffer in his *Difficulties of the Text*, along with Jerome on this place, understand the inhabitants of Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:1), comparing the desert of Sin (Exodus 16:1). Bochart elsewhere and Hiller in his *Sacred Onomasticon* suggest the Pelusians of Egypt: for whom 'Sin' is the name of the city (Ezekiel 30:15, 16). In Chaldean and Syriac, this means the same as the Greek <term>pēlos</term> <note>original: πηλός, meaning mud or clay</note>, from which Pelusium gets its name. See Strabo’s *Geography*, book 17. **verse 13. y)** Let the heavens therefore sing (chapter 44:23, Jeremiah 51:48; compare Psalm 96:11). **z)** Chapter 41:27. **a)** Chapter 1:17, 54:1, 55:1. **b)** Verse 10, chapter 12:1, 13:10, 66:13. **c)** His sighing people (Psalm 114:7). **d)** Chapter 14:32, 41:17, 54:11. **e)** Chapter 14:3, Micah 7:19. **verse 14. f)** Zion indeed says (chapter 52:1). According to Jerome, this is the Church at the beginning of the New Testament, gathered from the remnants of the Jews. Compare chapter 51:3. Zion is the name given to the Church primarily consisting of Jews, as is known from the Old Testament. Concerning that church, the Messiah already predicted in chapter 48 that the greater part would not receive Him; indeed, in verse 4 of this very chapter, He complained that He labored in vain among the Jews. Therefore Zion herself is introduced here as one who sees that deplorable decrease of hers and complains as if the Lord has completely forgotten and deserted her, and that she will soon perish entirely. But just as above in verse 5 and following, God the Father consoled the Messiah complaining of the vanity of His labor, saying that the defection of the Jews would be abundantly compensated by the gathering of the nations: so Zion here receives the same consolation—that this decrease, by which she was made like one desolate, will be abundantly compensated by the immense multitude of nations who are to be gathered to her, so that she will not be empty and void but so populous that the space will be too narrow (Schmidt). Others refer this to the captives in Babylon (as above in 40:27); others, like Gurtler, refer it to the hope of the repenting Church toward the end of this age. **g)** Chapter 41:17, 54:6, 7, Numbers 10:31, Psalm 13:2, 71:11; compare Judges 6:13. **h)** Compare chapter 40:17, 50:1, Genesis 40:23. **verse 15. i)** Her infant, the nursing child (chapter 65:20). From the Arabic root meaning "to nourish." **k)** That she should not have mercy (verse 10). This word signifies that natural affection and compassion of parents toward children. See 1 Kings 3:25, Genesis 43:16. **l)** Specifically: Even if these should forget. The plural refers to the sense, and "woman" in the preceding parts is taken collectively for the whole sex. **m)** Compare Psalm 37:28, 77:10, Lamentations 5:20, John 14:18. **verse 16. n)** Compare Song of Solomon 8:16, Varenius. Compare Job 20:25, 27. **o)** He inscribed (chapter 12:25, 30:8). The sense is that God has a type and sketch of the spiritual city of Jerusalem as if engraved and drawn on the palm of His hand, and He continually contemplates it as present before Him. Compare Exodus 13:9 and Revelation 21:1.

**Jeremiah 17:13. b)** Ch. 1:2; Ch. 51:18. **c)** Daniel 9:8. **d)** "Where then were these?" Genesis 37:16; 1 Samuel 19:22; 2 Samuel 9:4.

**verse 22. e)** This is a most clear and distinguished promise concerning the calling of the nations. **f)** The Messiah. verse 1 and following. **g)** To summon the nations by the word of the Gospel. **h)** Ch. 65:2. "The embassy of hands" is <term>Cheirotonia</term> <note>original Greek: Χειροτονία - the laying on of hands or ordination</note>, through which the Apostles were sent to preach the Gospel, as in Acts 10:41. **Dorjch.** **i)** Ch. 5:26; 11:12; 13:2; 18:3; 62:10. **k)** verse 17; Ch. 60:9. To Christ, Mark 10:13. **l)** **S.** "in the bosom," **Tig.** <note>The Tigurinus Bible</note> "in the lap." Others "in the arms" (3). Nehemiah 5:12; Psalm 129:7. The root in Arabic and Ethiopic means "to give milk, to nourish, to cherish one's offspring"; also "to take into the arms and embrace an infant," etc. **m)** Ch. 60:4. **n)** Ch. 46:7; compare Deuteronomy 33:12. **o)** compare Ch. 60:4.

**verse 23. p)** verse 7; Ch. 60:2, 10; Psalm 72:10, 11; Revelation 21:24. **q)** "Your foster fathers," compare Ch. 60:4; Esther 2:7; Numbers 11:12. **r)** "And their princesses, the beloved ones." compare 1 Kings 11:3; Esther 1:18. Some understand "kings" as the kingdoms and empires of the world, and "princesses" as the major cities and republics. compare Lamentations 1:1. **s)** "Your nursing mothers." **t)** 2, 7; 2 Chronicles 22:11; compare Genesis 32:16. **t)** "Indeed, they shall prostrate themselves with their faces to the earth." Genesis 19:1; Ch. 42:6; 1 Samuel 24:9. **u)** verse 7; Ch. 45:14. **x)** "They shall lick" (Numbers 22:4; Psalm 72:9). This was the highest demonstration of reverence: to prostrate the whole body on the ground. Where that was not possible, the head was lowered even to the feet, and a kiss was fixed upon the feet—or even the right hand, lowered to the sole of the foot, was moved back to the mouth. This is alluded to in Ephesians 60:14. A notable example is Matthew 28:9. See **Vitringa** on Revelation 4:10. **y)** "That you may know by experience that I, the Messiah, am Jehovah." verse 25; Ch. 60:16. **z)** Ch. 45:17. **a)** Ch. 40:31; Psalm 25:3. **Ion.** <note>likely the Targum of Jonathan</note> "The righteous, who wait for my salvation." compare Psalm 2:12.

**verse 24. b)** "Shall it be taken away?" verse 25; Ch. 52:7; Genesis 12:15. The question here is an affirmation, as in Jeremiah 31:20, by which the Messiah (or according to S., the Prophet) answers the objection of Zion in verse 14. It seems scarcely credible that what was promised in the preceding verses would be fulfilled, or that nations—bound so tightly by idolatry and a heap of sins—would join the Church. The Son of God confirms in verses 25 and 26 that this will indeed happen. **c)** "From the strong one," compare Genesis 10:8, 9. The "mighty" one here is the Devil, sin, and the world. **S.** compare Luke 11:21; John 14:30; 2 Corinthians 4:4; Ephesians 2:2; Ch. 6:12. **d)** "A captive" or "prey"? verse 25; Numbers 31:11, 12, 27, 32. **Vitringa** on Revelation 12:2, page 694, proposes an example: "Can it be that the Dragon, presiding over the Roman Empire, should be cast down from his seat, and that empire be claimed for CHRIST?" So also in the following verse. **e)** "Whether?" Ch. 27:1; Ch. 50:2; Jeremiah 31:20. **f)** "Captivity" or "captives." **d)** verse 25; Ch. 20:4; Numbers 31:1. **g)** "There is some difficulty here," as **Schmidius** rightly says. With others, he takes "the captivity of the righteous" passively, so that it is the "captivity of the righteous captives," i.e., the nations, who are called such not because they were already righteous, but by the outcome—namely, that they were to be converted and justified by Christ. Just as in verses 17 and 22, and again in verse 23, they are called "children of the Church" because they would become such. But this opinion does not seem approved because of the symmetry with the following verse; for he who is called "righteous" here is shortly called "terrible" or "dreadful" in verse 25. Hence **Varenius** on Isaiah Part III, page 260, says the "captivity of the righteous" is said in respect to divine judgment or the justice of God himself, as the principal one holding them. And **Gussetius** (p. 509) says the "Righteous" is God the Father as judge, from whom the other person, namely God the Son/Messiah, delivers us. He also takes <term>Aritz</term> <note>terrible/tyrant</note> in verse 25 as referring to God (p. 646), comparing Jeremiah 20:11. But even this does not remove every doubt for readers. **Luther** understood the Law of Moses, especially the ceremonial law; **Brentius** understood the tyrant kings and princes of the nations, from whose empires the Gentiles were to be spiritually led away to the kingdom and Church of Christ. Simpler and better than the others seems the opinion of those who take these words as a comparison to the tyrant Satan, to whom—as the enforcer of the avenger of justice—the human race was captive because of sin (Hebrews 2:14, 15). For the Devil is compared to a military leader who retains under his power by right of war those whom he has overcome and made captive. So says **Carpzov** in his local homilies Part I, p. 496. And **Jerome** on this place: "The devil is the strong one and the Giant," he says, "who had subjected all nations to his empire, daring to say to the Savior: 'all these things have been delivered to me, and I will give them to you, if you will fall down and worship me' (Matthew 4:9; Luke 4:6)." For the world is seated in wickedness (1 John 5:19), which none of the righteous could conquer, nor take the prey from the mouth of the lion (compare Amos 3:12). **h)** verse 25; Ch. 20:6; Ch. 37:38.

**verse 19. f)** **S.** "For as for your ruins..." Ch. 51:23; 44:26. **g)** verse 8; Ch. 61:4. **h)** "And the land of your overthrow" or "overturned." (1) compare verse 17; Amos 9:10. **i)** "By an oath, I say, I promise you that now..." verse 18. **k)** "You will be too narrow to contain the inhabitants." compare Genesis 32:8; 1 Samuel 30:6. **l)** "Far off from the sight of your eyes..." compare Ch. 54:15. **m)** 2 Samuel 20:20; compare above verse 17.

**verse 20. n)** i.e., in the hearing of. compare Ch. 56:11. **o)** "Children of bereavement," i.e., born to you from the nations after your bereavement; namely, when through the defection and unbelief of the Jews, the Church seemed bereaved of almost all her children. **S.** (1) compare Ch. 14:12; Genesis 37:3. **p)** "It is too narrow for me." Ch. 28:20; 2 Kings 11:19. **q)** compare Zechariah 10:10. **r)** **S.** "Withdraw from me," but properly it is "approach me," as in Genesis 19:9; Ch. 27:21, 26. **q)** i.e., "Join yourself to others for my sake." compare below Chapter 65:5. **Gussetius** (p. 496) thinks it should be translated: "Join yourself to me, that we may more easily dwell in our narrow place."

---

**verse 18.** The word "bind them" [וּֽתְקַשְּׁרִ֖ים] has a Shin without a Dagesh <note>a grammatical marker in Hebrew</note> in manuscripts 6, 9, 10, 20. **verse 21.** "In your heart" [בִּלְבָבֵ֗ךְ] with the accent Sakeph in mss 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 22. "Give me space" [גְּשָׁה־לִּ֥י]. "And I was bereaved" [וַאֲנִ֥י שְׁכוּלָ֖ה] so in ms 2. "Exile" [גֹּלָ֣ה] without a Resh in mss 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 20, 22. **verse 22.** "They shall be carried" [תִּנָּשֶֽׂאנָה] irregularly with a Tsere vowel. compare mss 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 22. **verse 23.** "Your nursing mothers" [מֵינִֽיקֹותַ֔יִךְ] spelled deficiently in mss 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 22 according to the Masora and Evss. Others spell it fully.

**CHAPTER 50, verse 1, g)** Thus further says Jehovah the Messiah, the same who has spoken until now. He indeed, in chapter 48:4, 8, 18, predicted the rejection of the Jews in the New Testament; in chapter 49, the Messiah complains of their unbelief (v. 4), and Zion, mourning the small number of her citizens left (v. 14), received the promise concerning the gathering of the nations to the Church (v. 6, 18 sqq.). Now, therefore, the Jews, thus rejected, argue with the Messiah about their repudiation. Paul discusses this same matter systematically in Romans 9:1 sqq.

Deuteronomy 24:1, 3, Jeremiah 3:8. A "bill of divorce" <note>original: "libellus repudii"</note> is understood here as one given without a just and sufficient cause. **k)** i.e., your Church or Synagogue; so say Jonathan and Kimchi. compare Hosea 2:4. Paul in Romans 11:1 calls her the *people*, i.e., the greater part of the people, in which the people "according to the flesh" are said to consist. For God did not reject the true Church, but only separated her from unbelieving Israel. **l)** by which I might have dismissed her by My own will or fault. chapter 27:8, Jeremiah 3:8. compare above, chapter 49:14, Romans 11:1 seq. **m)** or which of my creditors or moneylenders is it? chapter 24:2. compare 2 Kings 4:1. **n)** to whom I might have sold you. compare chapter 52:4, Deuteronomy 32:30, Judges 2:14, and 1 Kings 21:20. The question is emphatic, by which Christ vehemently denies that a bill of divorce was given by Him to the Synagogue, and demands that it be produced; since they cannot do this, He absolves Himself and attributes both the dismissal and the sale into the power of enemies to their own most atrocious sins. Indeed, He rather complains that He was rejected by the synagogue, which thought that appearing in the form of a servant, He could not complete the work of redemption as that blind nation dreamed. **v. 2. **CHAPTER 51, v. 1. t)** compare verse 7, chapter 46:12, chapter 49:12. At the end of chapter 50, a promise and exhortation were made simultaneously to all who fear the Lord (verses 1–8). However, a severe threat followed in verse 11 for the impious and rebellious. Now, therefore, the Messiah returns to those who truly fear God in this chapter, comforting them: first, with certain confidence in himself and the expansion of the Church (verses 1–8). Second, the spiritual Church (Zion), burning with desire, seeks its promised salvation (verses 9, 10). Third, having been tested in its hope and expectation, it is raised up and confirmed by the Messiah (verse 12 and following). **u)** following. Proverbs 21:2, Psalm 34:15, Romans 9:30, 31, 1 Timothy 6:11, 2 Timothy 2:22. **x)** true righteousness (verses 5, 7). compare chapter 55:1, Matthew 5:6. This righteousness is the righteousness of the Messiah, or righteousness in Jehovah; hence it is immediately added, "you who seek Jehovah," to show that Jehovah, or the Messiah, is that righteousness, according to Schmidius. Compare Jeremiah 23:6, 1 Corinthians 1:30. **y)** compare chapter 50:10, chapter 55:6, Zephaniah 2:3, Psalm 9:11, Psalm 24:6. **z)** look back. verse 2. **a)** to the rock from which you were cut; that is, to Abraham, from whom you were born (verse 2), from his "dead" body, just like stones cut from a cliff by the hand of Almighty God. So also Schmidius, who nevertheless adds: "We shall not condemn it as absurd if someone refers the 'rock' and 'cistern' to Jehovah the Messiah himself," as if saying: Look to me, Jehovah, as the rock from which your being comes. Compare Deuteronomy 32:15, 18. "Christ is the rock of salvation, from whose side, as from the opening of a cistern, the church flowed out. For the birth of the church depends on the blood of Christ" (Cocceius). **b)** verse 9, chapter 22:16. compare Matthew 23:9. Ellipsis of the relative, as in chapter 50:11, etc. **c)** Schmidius: "and to the digging." Likely referring to that hammer <note>Latin: 'malleum'</note> which signifies the Almighty hand of God, as in chapter 44:12, Judges 4:21. Hence others: "Look to that hammer or the Almighty hand of God." **d)** 2 Kings 18:31. **e)** from which you were dug out or brought forth. 1 Kings 11:2. **v. 2. f)** Look back, I say. verse 1. **g)** Deuteronomy 31:18, Psalm 51:7. **h)** for he was unique and without children. Malachi 2:15. **i)** chapter 41:9, Genesis 12:1. **k)** but I will bless him and multiply him. These futures can be retained if they are referred to the primary fulfillment of blessing and multiplication in the New Testament, according to the Apostle in Romans 4:11, etc. (Schmidius).

The people, of whom it was said, they shall be multiplied like the stars of the heavens: to perfect the church, of whom it was said, they shall be multiplied like the sand of the earth. **e)** To which people therefore <note>original Greek: "τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note> the oracles of God were entrusted (Romans 3:2), so that it might be a seed-bed for a new heaven and a new earth, and for the elect people of God; that people will certainly attain the promised freedom. <meta>This page transitions from the calls for comfort in Isaiah 51 to the triumphant call for Jerusalem to awaken and be redeemed in Isaiah 52. The commentary continues to blend philological analysis with a Christian theological interpretation, linking the liberation of Israel from physical exile (Egypt, Assyria, Babylon) to a spiritual liberation through the Messiah.</meta>

# ISAIAH. CHAPTERS 51. 52.

<margin>
*. chapter 50, 6.
**CHAPTER 52, verse 1.)** This seems to refer back to chapter 51, verse 9, where it was said, "Awake, awake, put on the strength of the arm of the Lord." In this verse, the response is: "Awake, even you in your turn, and clothe yourself in your strength," which the strength of the Lord's arm works within you. <note>Scholar "S." likely refers to Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century theologian.</note> After the longing of Zion was explained in chapter 51:9, and she was confirmed in her sorrow by the promise of a better state under the New Testament in chapter 51:12 and following, now the Messiah rouses her again. He calls her to put on the strength prepared by Him through true faith, to fight bravely against the prince of darkness, to overcome him, to adorn herself with the garments of salvation, to cleanse herself from all defilement of the flesh, and to "perfect holiness in the fear of God" (2 Corinthians 7:1). Thus, she may truly be the holy city, which no "spiritually uncircumcised" or "impure" person shall enter. *The parts of this chapter according to Schmid are three:* I. The repeated spiritual restoration of Zion (v. 1). II. Her address by the watchmen (v. 7-10). III. Instruction on the proper way to depart (v. 11 and following). b) chapter 45:24, chapter 51:9, compare Ephesians 3:16, chapter 6:10 and following. c) chapter 49:18. d) The garments of your beauty; chapter 3:18, chapter 61:10, Ephesians 4:24. e) This beauty is the truth, or the truest internal beauty of the Church, foreshadowed in the Old Testament by the external cleanliness of those serving and worshipping God. Compare chapter 51:10, Revelation 6:11, chapter 19:8, 1 Peter 3:3-4. e) Spiritual Jerusalem; chapter 51:17. f) chapter 48:2, Nehemiah 11:1, Matthew 4:5, Revelation 21:2. Compare below, chapter 60:21, Ephesians 5:25 and following. g) For he shall not add to enter, meaning: he shall enter no more. Compare chapter 51:22, Hosea 1:6, Nahum 2:1, Proverbs 23:35. <term>Asyndeton</term> <note>A stylistic device where conjunctions are omitted.</note>, as above in chapter 3:11. h) "Uncircumcised in heart," see the note on Deuteronomy 30:6, and compare Ezekiel 44:9, Acts 7:51. The Jews themselves observe uncircumcision in man in other ways: (1) of the flesh, Genesis 17:14; (2) of the mouth, Exodus 6:12; (3) of the ear, Jeremiah 6:10; and (4) of the heart, Deuteronomy 10:16.
</margin>

Romans 2:28-29, Colossians 2:11, Titus 2:14. \*. 2. k) *Shake yourself* (Judges 16:20). l) From the filth and dust into which you were thrown through devastation (chapter 51:23; compare chapter 29:4, chapter 25:12, chapter 26:5, chapter 47:1, etc.). m) <note>original: "Ion." — The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation.</note> *Sit* on a throne of glory, like a queen or a bride. n) *Loose* or unfold yourself (chapter 51:14). o) *From the chains* (3) (chapter 28:22). p) *O captive* (1) *This refers indeed to the imminent state when the commonwealth was to fall into the gravest danger of the Babylonian captivity, in which the Church also lived; meanwhile, it looks toward the entire calamitous and miserable state of the Church, which, as if always shut in prisons, can be said to be in the dust.* <note>Scholar "Dorsh." refers to Johann Dorsche, a Lutheran theologian.</note> q) chapter 1:8, chapter 62:11. He commands her to shake off the intolerable yoke of the Law, of the Antichrist, and of tyrants, and to aspire to Evangelical liberty. <note>Scholar "Mail." refers to Johann Mai's 'Economy of Scripture.'</note> page 963. verse 3. r) The Prophet confirms that this will most certainly happen, speaking from the mouth of Jehovah, who says... s) Namely, the Messiah, who also spoke above, just as you were sold "gratis" and without just cause in respect to the oppressors (v. 5, Psalm 35:19). u) You were sold and reduced to slavery by your oppressors. Compare chapter 45:13. y) Through myself as a *ransom* <note>original: "ἀντίλυτρον" — Greek for a ransom-price.</note> for all (1 Timothy 2:6), you shall be redeemed. verse 9, Ephesians 41:14 <note>likely error for Isa 41:14</note>. The <term>LXX</term> <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> compare with 1 Peter 1:18-19, who seems to have looked back entirely to this place. verse 4. z) For this action of recovery is illustrated (1) by the example of the Egyptian captivity, into which the people of God came through no merit of their own, at least regarding the Egyptians: for they were granted the right of hospitality, but were afterwards oppressed through tyranny; finally, they were reclaimed by the great strength of God and given liberty for free. (2) By the example of the Assyrian captivity. In respect to the Assyrians, the Church of God was undeservedly brought into it; therefore, she is also to obtain the liberty promised before. From this he concludes: by the same reasoning, the Messiah in His own time will liberate His Church and restore it to God. <note>Dorsche.</note> a) Into Egypt (Genesis 46:6, Exodus 1:1). b) At the beginning, or formerly (Genesis 13:4). c) Genesis 47:4; but later he was oppressed without cause by the Egyptians and reduced to slavery (see Exodus 1). d) Then the Assyrian Shalmaneser (2 Kings 17:3). We do not wonder, says scholar S., that others preferred Nebuchadnezzar; for they thought the speech here was about the liberation from Babylon; whereas it is the liberation through Christ, who redeemed not only the Jews oppressed by the Babylonians, but all of Israel, etc. e) Undeservedly and for nothing (chapter 41:12). f) Oppressed him here (see Jeremiah 50:33). verse 5. g) And now. The Messiah passes from the Egyptian and Assyrian captivities to another. h) What must I do here? (compare chapter 22:16) namely, according to S., in the Babylonian captivity; about which much was said in the preceding parts, and therefore it should not be omitted here. The Jews, however, interpret it as their present exile. But Brentius <note>Johannes Brentz, a Protestant reformer.</note> interprets it as the spiritual captivity into which the Scribes and Pharisees snatched the people with their impious traditions: which was much heavier and more destructive than those two former ones. As if to say: my people were previously heavily afflicted by the Egyptians and Assyrians, and will also be heavily afflicted later by the Babylonians; but see, what has happened to Me now at this time among My people? etc. We understand both the Babylonian calamity and whatever followed it for the Church, according to the notes on verse 1 from Dorsche. i) chapter 24. k) because he is snatched away (Jeremiah 48:46). l) see verse 3. m) Her Babylonian rulers, and then the domestic ones and apostates (chapter 14:5, chapter 28:14, chapter 49:7). n) They make him wail (chapter 15:2; compare the form in 1 Samuel 17:47). o) chapter 52:13, Habakkuk 1:17. p) chapter 28:22, chapter 65:2, 5. q) My name is despised or blasphemed by both impious Jews and by the Gentiles and Babylonians—for example, Belshazzar in Daniel 5—as if I cannot provide the long-promised salvation. Compare above, chapter 1:4, chapter 5:24, Deuteronomy 28:58, Ezekiel 36:20, Psalm 74:18, Romans 2:24. verse 6. r) He shall finally know by true faith and experience (chapter 49:23, chapter 60:15, Isaiah <note>likely citation error</note>, Matthew 1:22). s) My name as Messiah (v. 6, 7; chapter 29:23). Which truly seems to happen in "Immanuel" (chapter 7:14, chapter 8:10) and "Jesus" (Matthew 1:21). t) Therefore, I say u) in that day or time (about which v. 1, 2, etc.) my people shall know my name. x) Because I myself (chapter 51:12, chapter 44:6, chapter 48:12) y) who speak or have spoken these things (compare chapter 43:19, chapter 45:19, chapter 46:11, chapter 48:15-16, chapter 63:1). z) Behold, I am present or will be present for the salvation of my own. <note>original: "πάρειμι" — Greek for 'I am present.'</note> Compare above, chapter 40:9. verse 7. a) How heavy or pleasant they are to the pious and faithful (Psalm 93:5, Song of Solomon 1:10). Here begins the II. part of the chapter, and the addressing of Zion by the Prophet, who predicts and describes the watchmen of the New Testament. b) chapter 40:9. Targum: upon the mountains of the land of Israel. c) The feet of the one bringing good news, or those bringing good news (chapter 41:27, chapter 60:4, 9, Acts 7:51). The Jews themselves say that the words are to be taken collectively, so that a company bringing good news and announcing peace is understood. Most rightly, however, these words are understood first and immediately of Christ, who himself went about with his own feet on the mountain of the Church and preached the gospel (Acts 10:38); and afterwards, from that power which he had, he also sent out other evangelists and heralds of peace. Compare Matthew 10:1, chapter 28:19, Luke 10:1, John 20:21. And here the Apostle looks back in Romans 10:15, where he uses this passage of our Isaiah specifically to prove the calling of the Gentiles, etc. <note>Dorsche.</note> d) chapter 26:3, 12, chapter 32:17, chapter 54:1, 13, Colossians 1:20. e) compare chapter 2:10, 1 Kings 1:42, Philemon v. 6.

from there. This and what follows, *go out from the midst of her*, some restrict to Jerusalem in verse 9 and to the stubborn Jews, whose communion and cohabitation the believers are commanded to desert and retreat to a safe place, lest they be caught up in the common judgment with them; see Hosea 2:2; Malachi 3:20; Matthew 24:16, 20; also Revelation 18:4. *Schmid*, however, refers these to the *ends of the earth* in verse 10; and understands a *spiritual exit from paganism* to embrace the <term>regeneration</term> <note>original Greek: παλιγγενεσίαν</note> of Christ along with *Dorsche*, see 2 Corinthians 6:17. These are *spiritual priests and soldiers*, such as all Christians ought to be in the New Testament. Compare Ephesians 6:11, 23; 1 Peter 2:5; Revelation 1:6. v. 12. l) arguments follow for the commanded purification. m) *not with haste* Exodus 12:11, 39; but shown spiritually, says Schmidt. It looks back to the manner of the liberation from Egypt, which was first hurried (Exodus 12:33) and then also a flight before Pharaoh (Exodus 14:5). *Dorsche.* n) and *with flight*, (2) Leviticus 26:36. o) *Jehovah the Messiah.* See Hebrews 12:2. Again, the manner of the leading out from Egypt is referenced, concerning which see Exodus 13:21, 22; compare 1 Corinthians 10:4, 9. *Dorsche.* q) and he will gather you in the rearguard, he will lead your first and last line of battle, and will return you safe from enemies. Compare Numbers 10:25; Joshua 6:8; and Matthew 28:20. r) Chapter 29:23. v. 13. s) For behold, that I may confirm that liberation through the Messiah will certainly happen. Almost everyone commonly begins chapter 53 from this verse, as if this does not fit conveniently with verse 12, but begins a new speech by God the Father. But according to Schmidt, the Heavenly Father here continues his speech begun in verse 11; and after he said in verse 12 that Jehovah the Messiah would be the leader and gatherer of the Church, he now instructs the same as to what kind of leader he would be, and what is to be hoped for regarding him—namely, that he would act prudently, and as a victor would have great glory. t) *he shall act prudently and successfully*; although to corrupted reason and to the foolishly preconceived opinion among the later Jews he seems to act stupidly (1 Corinthians 1:23, 24). This word is excellently suited, as it is used for military leaders (as in Joshua 1:7, 8; 1 Samuel 18:5, 30) and likewise for kings (1 Kings 2:3) and for the King Messiah himself (Jeremiah 23:5). Schmidt. u) *That servant of mine*, namely the Messiah, as above in chapter 42:1; as even *Iz.* <note>possibly Isaac Abarbanel</note> expressly adds in this place, even if in other matters he recedes too far from the text. Thus the *Jewish Authorities* from *Tanchuma*: <term>This is the King Messiah</term> <note>original Hebrew: זה מלך המשיח</note>. *And thus with great consensus the ancient Jews referred this to the Messiah.* Moses *Alshech* <note>a prominent 16th-century rabbi</note> is a witness, who in his commentary on this place says, "Behold, our Teachers of blessed memory establish with one mouth, and have received from their ancestors, that the speech is concerning the King Messiah." *Aben Ezra* and *Abarbanel* confess the same regarding their ancestors in their commentaries on this place, as do *Rashi* (as cited by *Raymundus Martini* in Part II of the *Dagger of Faith*, chapter 9, and Part III, distinction 1, chapter 10) and others; who nevertheless turn themselves to anything else rather than acknowledge the manifest truth. For some understand this text as being about Abraham, others about Moses, others about Josiah, others about Jeremiah (which *Grotius* also poorly chose), and most indeed understand it as the Jewish people vexed among the nations. To us, however, along with Dr. *Pfeiffer* in *Difficulties Vexed* <note>original: 'Dub. Vex.'</note> regarding this place and others, it is most evident—not only from the infallible exposition of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament (see verse 15 and chapter 53:1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12) and the testimony of Jewish Antiquity (which is also clear from the frequent allegations in the New Testament to have been everywhere confessed)—but also from the collation of the text itself: (1) that the Prophet speaks not of a people, but of a certain individual, who is always and most expressly (chapter 53:8) distinguished from the people. (2) It can be applied to no one of all those whom the Jews imagine, since none of them suffered those things which all and singular fit our Savior well. Thus also the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>original: 'Midrasch Tillim', a midrash on the Psalms</note> on Psalm 2:7 (folio 4, b) cites this verse concerning the Messiah. Compare also for the Commentary on this place what you have in the *Yalkut* <note>original: 'I-lkut'</note> on Isaiah 60. x) *he shall be exalted* 2 Samuel 22:47; Psalm 21:14. To the state of humiliation <note>original: 'exinanitionis'</note>, expressed by the name of "servant," the Heavenly Father immediately subjoins the state of exaltation (Philippians 2:8), indicated by three emphatic words and the particle "greatly," doubtless in respect to the degrees of: 1. resurrection, 2. ascension, and 3. sitting at the right hand of majesty. Everywhere humiliation and exaltation are signified even to the point of astonishment, and are soon explained somewhat more fully, but in summary in verses 14 and 15. *Maü Oecon.* p. 965. The *Yalkut* moreover illustrates these three words thus: *The Messiah shall be higher than Abraham, more sublime than Moses, and more exalted than the ministering Angels,* which compare with Hebrews 1:4. y) Chapter 33:10; 57:15. z) Chapter 5, 16. v. 14. a) and following. *Just as they were astonished.* Jeremiah 2:12. b) and following. *at you, O Israel*, that is, my church. Compare verses 4, 11. Thus *Tarnovius* in his paraphrase of this chapter. Others say *at you*, my beloved and chosen servant, so that they understand the whole verse as being about Christ; compare Matthew 11:6; Luke 2:34. *But the change of person*, although not infrequent in Scripture, is nevertheless to be avoided where it can conveniently be avoided, as Schmidt rightly advises. c) *So disfigured* (in the lack of form of his passion and ignominy) *shall his appearance be, more than men.* For in verse 13 God the Father had said of his servant *that he shall act prudently*; now therefore he explains in what that prudence consists: namely, that having been made like men, he underwent persecution and contempt, which the church and any of the faithful are forced to undergo by the impious world, so that in this way he might redeem the church and the whole human race. A most elegant figuration supplying the image of Christ in the Church, concerning which see Romans 8:17; Philippians 3:21; 2 Timothy 2:11; also 2 Corinthians 5:21. Schmidt. The name *Mishchat* <note>original: 'Mischchat'</note> itself, appearing only in this place, *Kimchi* <note>David Kimchi, 13th-century grammarian</note> takes for an adjective. For others it is a noun, "corruption" or "a corrupt thing." So in *Cocceius' Lexicon*, p. 884: "his form was so corrupted compared to a man, his appearance was so miserable, that he did not seem like a man who was in any position of eminence." Compare John 19:5, 6.

The arm of the almighty Lord will be revealed to them, so that they may cling to him in faith. However, the Jews, who had seen and heard the Messiah in the days of his flesh, did not believe; a fact which Isaiah prophesies, wonders at, and laments, both in his own name and in the name of the Savior himself and all those bringing good news to Zion, chapter 53:1. <note>Miss. Oecon. page 965</note>.

**CHAPTER LIII, 1. q)** *Who or how few?* Malachi 3:2. Especially from the Jewish nation, chapter 49:4; John 12:37, 38; Romans 10:16. The question is not entirely negative, but one of wonder at the small number of believers. Compare above chapter 9, chapter 10:22, with Romans 9:27, 29; Micah 7:1. **r)** *believes*, certain and not at all wavering in mind. chapter 7:9; chapter 28:16; chapter 43:10; Genesis 45:16. **s)** *our report*. chapter 28:9. That is, the gospel, clearly set forth and announced by us Prophets and Apostles, so that not only the Jews but also the nations heard it, chapter 52:15. This is the Prophet's complaint regarding the stumbling block of the Jews, which they encountered through their own fault and malice due to the Messiah's self-emptying, 1 Corinthians 1:23. Moreover, this chapter contains: I. the removal of that stumbling block (verses 1–7). II. The celebration of the Messiah's exaltation, that is, the majesty given through his exaltation (verse 8 and following). **t)** *the arm of the Lord Messiah* chapter 51:9, which he bared in the sight of all nations, chapter 52:10; that is, his almighty power which he demonstrated in the work of redemption. chapter 59:16. **u)** upon whom, or to which of the Jews, after the veil of Moses was removed (2 Corinthians 3:14, 15), *has it been revealed?* Elsewhere the following verb is constructed with <term>על</term> <note>al: upon</note> or <term>ל</term> <note>le: to</note> as in Genesis 35:7; 1 Samuel 2:27; chapter 3:7, 21; chapter 14:8, II; and Job 38:17; Daniel 10:1. **x)** chapter 40:5; chapter 56:1; Colossians 3:3, 4. Indeed, the Jews think they have a just cause for loathing the Messiah; for they see his humble origin and object to his contemptible appearance. Compare Matthew 13:55 and following; Mark 6:3; John 7:27; chapter 9:29. 

**v. 2. y)** The occasion of the stumbling block. For he does not go forth like a <term>ארז</term> <note>erez: cedar</note> or stand out; but *he grows up* (Genesis 41:5) like that word of God mentioned above in chapter 52:13. **z)** like a tender plant, or a shoot, from a tree or trunk in dry ground, newly born, drawing juice from it; the root <term>יונק</term> <note>yoneq</note> means *to flow*. It is properly used of infants in Numbers 11:12; Deuteronomy 32:25; 1 Samuel 15:3; but metaphorically it denotes a small plant or a tender branch. See Hosea 14:7; Job 8:16; compare also above chapter 11:1. **a)** before that proud and unbelieving people, who were fascinated by the idea of a worldly kingdom that the Messiah ought to establish, so that they do not see or recognize the bared arm of God in Christ. verse 1. **b)** <term>כשורש</term> <note>kashoresh: like a root</note> so from another root it metonymically means a sprout or twig growing from the root. Compare chapter 11:1, 10. But the root here is not considered in the category of relationship (insofar as a sprout is born from it, the root being its origin); but in the category of quality, regarding its state. A root is a lowly thing, and it sends out sprouts slowly and small and less successful in dry ground. Thus Christ seemed to begin his kingdom too contemptibly. **S. <note>Sebastian Schmidt</note> e)** chapter 41:18. **d)** he had no singular beauty chapter 52:14. **e)** nor, because of the form of a servant he assumed (Philippians 2:7), was there *splendor or majesty* in him, such as the Jews imagined for themselves in their fictional Messiah. For although the faithful and enlightened saw his glory (chapter 2:10; chapter 33:2) and recognized it from his sermons and miracles which breathed divine majesty (John 1:14 etc.), most Jews were blind and attributed such things to Satan rather than to God. **f)** "We did see him," say the foolish Jews. **g)** "but no visible beauty appeared that could have carried us away into some love or admiration of him." chapter 52:14. Compare 1 Samuel 17:42. **h)** "why then should we have desired him (chapter 1:29; Song of Songs 2:3) and eagerly received him as the promised King and Prophet?" John 1:11. For regarding the Priestly office of the Messiah—that he must suffer and die, and thus redeem us—most Jews did not even think, and still do not think: even though Scripture clearly revealed it, for example in Zechariah 6:12, 13; Psalm 40:7; Psalm 110:4; etc. We have rendered this clause *interrogatively*, as suggested by the preceding accent, which others have rendered in various ways, and some as "that we should despair." This interrogation, as S. observes, emphatically expresses the vehement attitude of the Jews, according to which they think they have the best right to repudiate Christ. Compare a similar interrogation to be understood after the prefix <term>ו</term> <note>vov: and</note> above in chapter 37:11; 1 Samuel 24:20; chapter 25:11; etc.

**v. 3. i)** For he was *contemned* (chapter 49:7; Psalm 22:7) and *despised* by the High Priests, Pharisees, and our learned men, etc. Compare Mark 9:12; Luke 16:14; chapter 23:11. **k)** <term>חדל</term> <note>chadal</note> ceasing or leaving off. **l)** Ezekiel 3:27; Psalm 39:5. **l)** *of men plural.* (3) Psalm 141:4; Proverbs 8:4. He is indeed "ceasing from men" according to S., who will end sooner with all his affairs and efforts than any of men. According to Tremellius, *the most abject of men*, from whom all those conspicuous in authority and wisdom cease and desist (John 7:43, 49), or who will quickly cease to be counted among humans or men. **m)** *a man of sorrows or of sicknesses and hardships.* verse 4. Subject to all kinds of sorrows, both in soul and body. Psalm 38:18; Psalm 69:27. Compare a similar passive meaning in Proverbs 29:1. **n)** <term>וידוע</term> <note>vidua</note> and *known*. (3) Deuteronomy 1:13, 15. **o)** *by infirmity or infirmities*, which he underwent and sustained, in the praetorium and on the cross, so that no one can deny or excuse them; he was even marked by a famous name because of them. *Choli*, which they translate as disease, signifies not only a disease arising from natural weakness, but also infirmity from wounds and blows, and indeed the most severe kind. Compare 1 Kings 22:34; Jeremiah 6:5; chapter 10:19. But the gospel history graphically depicts for us the most severe wounds of the Lord's passion. S. **p)** S.: *from which there was as it were a hiding of faces from him*; I would prefer "as something that makes one hide the face from it," namely, a thing so foul and abominable that men cover their faces and turn away because of it, for example, from leprosy or a leper (Leviticus 13:45). Compare the verb below in chapter 59:2 and the matter from the New Testament in John 7:3, 4, 5; chapter 19:15; etc. Indeed, God himself seemed to have abandoned him of his merciful countenance when he was forced to cry out, *My God! My God! Why hast thou forsaken me?* Psalm 22:2; Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34. Compare also Psalm 88:5, 6, 16; etc.

by the affection of the flesh and the sense of blind reason; to which the mystery of the Lord’s passion is nothing but foolishness, even if it is overcome by the faithful. 1 Corinthians 1:23, 24. b) *we esteemed him* (v. 3). Genesis 38:15; Job 19:15. The Prophet includes himself, as in Daniel 9:5, etc. c) not afflicted for his own or another's sins, but for his own. Psalm 73:14; Psalm 38:12. Or afflicted by divine plagues, such as leprosy. Leviticus 13:3. Thus the Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> says: *as if a leper*: which is how the ancient Jews also thought the Messiah would be called in the Talmudic Tractate Sanhedrin, Chapter 11, folio 98b, where they prove the sufferings of the Messiah from this place and chapter; these are narrated even more fully in the Yalkut on Isaiah, Chapter 60. d) and divinely (smitten by God for his own crimes). However, the fact that the ancients and the Papists have translated this phrase as "smitten God," and try to prove from it not only the humanity but also the divinity of Christ, is against the grammar and construction of the Hebrew. Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:14; Colossians 1:20. n) *it was upon him*, or it lay upon him as the Guarantor. Genesis 27:13; Judges 19:20; 2 Samuel 18:11; Chapter 19:39, etc. o) and *in his bruise or stripe*, inflicted by whips or some other way. Chapter 1:6; 1 Peter 2:24. p) *healing happened* or effective medicine was given to us (Chapter 6:10) against the poison of sin and the sting of death. Cf. Hosea 13:14; Revelation 22:2; and above, Chapter 1:6. *Jonathan* <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note> renders these two phrases thus: @ in his teaching peace shall be multiplied upon us; @ when we obey his words, our sins shall be forgiven us. The rest they perverted, as noted in Chapter 52:13.

**Verse 6. q)** All of us, both Jews and Gentiles. Psalm 14, 3; Romans 3:9, etc. **r)** cf. 1 Kings 22:17; Ezekiel 34:5; Zechariah 10:2; Matthew 9:36; 1 Peter 2:24, 25. **s)** *we wandered from the way of salvation*. Psalm 58:4; Psalm 95:10; Psalm 119:176; Ephesians 4:17, 18. **t)** *each one of us*. Chapter 47:15. **u)** having left God, each to his own way, which he thought he should enter (1 Kings 1:49), even if it plunged us into the abyss and eternal destruction. Proverbs 14:12; Chapter 15:25. **x)** *we looked*. Chapter 56:11; Acts 14:16. **y)** but the Lord (v. 10), God the Father, not wanting any to perish, but for all to come to repentance (1 Timothy 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9), by his kindness, by which he wished to consult well for each and every one. Ephesians 1:9, 10; Colossians 1:20. **z)** made it fall upon him. Exodus 5:3; Numbers 35:19; Judges 8:21; 2 Samuel 1:15. Since he had presented himself as the surety (see at v. 4) and the Father had accepted his pledge, and thus justly imputed both the guilt and the punishment to him. Cf. 2 Corinthians 5:21. **a)** *the iniquity of us all*, v. 5, 11; Psalm 40:13, which also brought death upon him; as the emphasis of the preceding word suggests. We ourselves (says Gousset <note>Jacques Gousset, a 17th-century French Hebraist</note>, page 663), while practicing iniquity, did not rush upon him: for in the time of the Prophet, Christ was not living on earth, nor is he living now, to be attacked by the wicked men of that age or this age. What then? Our iniquity itself rushed upon him, as the words of the Prophet express. How so? Only insofar as it was laid upon him to bring about his death, imputed to him so that he might pay its penalties in our place.

**Verse 7. b)** Or, from here and there he sustained exaltation. Or: *From here the payment of iniquities was demanded.* For the word is constructed with the debt and the debtor. Chapter 3:5, 8; 9:3; Chapter 58:3; Exodus 5:6; Deuteronomy 15:2; 2 Kings 23:35, etc. **c)** and he himself, as the security and guarantor for the sins of the whole world. 1 John 2:2. **d)** *he was afflicted and he humbled himself*. Verse 4; Chapter 58:10; Ezekiel 10:3; Psalm 119:107. Becoming patient and obedient unto the most shameful death of the cross (Philippians 2:8), so that what he did not steal, he might thus pay (Psalm 69:5), and give himself as a ransom and divine blood (v. 10). Matthew 20:28; 1 Timothy 2:6. Since the blood of bulls and goats could not appease the angry Deity and prepare mutual reconciliation. Hebrews 10:4, etc.; Colossians 1:20. **e)** so that he did not even open his mouth against his mockers and torturers. Cf. Matthew 27:14; 1 Peter 2:23. **f)** like a small beast, for example, the Paschal lamb or kid (Exodus 12:3, 5) or the lamb sacrificed daily (Exodus 29:38; Numbers 28:3, etc.), which types Christ thus fulfilled. Cf. John 1:29; Revelation 5:6. **g)** to the slaughter. Chapter 34:2; Chapter 65:12; Acts 8:32. **h)** he is led. Chapter 22:7; Jeremiah 11:19. One who does not struggle, nor gnaw or bite the one leading or killing him, but follows gently; so also in all that time in which he was sought, seized, and led to his killing, he showed no sign of impatience or avenging anger, but from his bloody circumcision until the last breath of his life, he was an example of the highest mercy, gentleness, and patience. <note>From Maius’s *Economy of the Covenants*, page 969.</note> **i)** and like a *weak sheep (4)*. Genesis 31:38; Chapter 32:15. **k)** *before its shearers*. Genesis 38:12. **l)** *is silent or mute*. Ezekiel 3:26. **m)** thus, I say (Proverbs 10:23), the Messiah also did not open his mouth, but allowed himself to be stripped and spoiled (Psalm 22:19), so that he might clothe us with the garments of righteousness, which we lost (Romans 3:23). Below v. 11; Chapter 61:10. It was fitting for the Messiah to suffer all these things, just as God announced beforehand through the mouth of all his Prophets, and especially Isaiah in this place (Acts 3:18). But because it was impossible for him to be held by death (Acts 2:24), God released the guarantor from prison, the ransom having been paid in full; he crowned him with honor and glory (Psalm 8:5), which the Prophet now adds in the following verse 8, and explains the exaltation after the emptying.

**Verse 8. x)** *From constriction or distress*, and all torment of mind and body. (3) Psalm 107:39; Proverbs 30:16. Gousset, page 631. **e)** in the midst of the firmness and force of his adversaries; according to Cocceius, from the power of Pilate. But according to Dorsche, *from constriction or distress and from judgment* (in which the Messiah was a curse <note>original: "κατάרה"</note>, Galatians 3:13) is the same as if he had said: from the judgment that constricts and, like a winepress, crushes him even to a bloody sweat. Luke 22:42, 44. **o)** and *from the rigid judgment of God* (Psalm 143:2) to which he, as our Guarantor, had submitted himself, having been made sin and a curse for us. 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13.

---

Verse 4. After **ומכאבינו** <note>Hebrew: "and our pains"</note> there is a small circle, and in the margin the note: **הוא קרי ולא כתיב** that is, "**he** [hu]" is to be read, even if it is not written in the text. Verse 9, 11, 21, 23. The Eastern manuscripts clearly have **ומכאבינו**. Verse 5. **שׁלוֹמֵנוּ** <note>Hebrew: "our peace"</note> is written fully in verses 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16, 21, and in the margin of 6 and 9.

<margin>
(p) After he satisfied justice, he was taken away, and for our justification was raised [Romans 4:25], and taken up into heaven to the right hand of majesty. Compare Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:3, 9; Psalm 73:24. (q) His age or life [Isaiah 38:12] shall not be ended by any ages; see below verse 10 and Hebrews 7:24. Christ entered this life after his death [Luke 24:26], so that he dies no more [Romans 6:9]. But because the Hebrew word *dor* <note>original: דּוֹר</note> very frequently signifies a generation or people living at the same time and those following them [Exodus 1:6; Numbers 32:13; Deuteronomy 2:14; Ecclesiastes 1:4], others gather from this the fruit of Christ's exaltation: namely, the procreation of offspring and an innumerable spiritual generation. For although, after the manner of earthly kings, he did not procreate another successor or leave one behind, he will nonetheless have a copious spiritual seed [verse 10], and such a great series of many generations succeeding him that no one can easily grasp or think of it, much less declare it. Thus says Dr. Maius in his *Economy*, page 970. (r) Who? The question indicates the difficulty of the matter, as in Psalm 106:2. (s) Pondered or meditated [Psalm 143:5; compare Judges 5:10; Psalm 77:4, 7, 13; Job 7:11]. (t) Because he was cut off [Psalm 88:6; Lamentations 3:54] by a violent death [1 Corinthians 15:3]. Christ is the tree of life [above verse 2; Chapter 11:1; Luke 23:31] without hope of a sprout or root reflourishing [Psalm 41:9], so that we, who are by nature dry and dead trees [Ephesians 2:1], might be grafted in and draw the sap of life from him [John 15:1-8]. (u) On account of transgression [verse 5; Chapter 43:25]. (x) Of my people: the words of the Prophet. (y) On account of the stroke [Genesis 12:17; Exodus 11:1; Deuteronomy 17:8; Psalm 38:12]. (z) To be inflicted upon them [Chapter 44:15], but he himself was struck with the wounds.

Compare above Chapter 23:1; 30:5; 43:8; 44:7; etc. Nor do the examples cited by *Noldius* in his *Concordance of Particles* [page 513] prove the contrary. **verse 9. a)** *And he gave*, that is, he appointed—either the Messiah or God the Father. This verse is "most vexed" <note>extremely difficult to interpret</note>, says Schultens, and there are so many varying opinions about it that they cannot all be reviewed here. See, if you wish, the *Vexing Doubts* of Pfeiffer, Dorsch, and other commentators. We shall propose what seems simplest and most fitting to the words and context, agreeing in essence with Brentius, Dorsch, Schmid, Maius, and Glassius in his *Sacred Philology* [page 534, new edition]. Then we shall also touch upon one or two other views, but only briefly. **b)** *The wicked* and those condemned by the law of God, as all people are by nature [Romans 3:9 and following]; or according to Glassius, "wickednesses" from the singular *Resha*. However, the plural of this noun is not found elsewhere, unless you refer to Job 24:26. **c)** *In his grave* or "in the grave of him." **d)** We understand "with" here, because in the following phrase **in his deaths** <note>original: בְּמֹתָיו</note> it is expressly present. **e)** So that they, being buried together with him, might rise again free from sins by the power of his merit [Romans 6:4, 8; Colossians 2:12; Galatians 2:20]. For we rightly judge, as Paul teaches in 2 Corinthians 5:15, that if one died for all, then all have died; since the iniquities of all the wicked were imputed to Christ [above verse 6]. The burial of Christ, says Glassius, is the final act of his state of humiliation (*exinanitionis*), in which he bore our sins and made satisfaction for them.

Therefore, the Scripture, wishing to express the full satisfaction for sins and their "putting away" <note>original Greek: άθεσιν</note> [Hebrews 9:26], says they were buried with Christ and remained, as it were, in the grave. And **d)** *the rich*—the Father made him rich [see verses 11 and 12]; or **f)** Christ himself made man (the impoverished human race) rich [Romans 3:23; 4:25; 2 Corinthians 8:9; Ephesians 1:18; 2:7]. But *Maius* in his *Economy* interprets *the rich* as the "unjust, greedy, or harsh," as this meaning of the word is common in the Arabic language. **e)** *In his deaths*, that is, in a most bitter death, which was preceded by many passions and tortures like so many deaths. The plural is also found in Ezekiel 28:10. Others interpret it thus: the wicked soldiers assigned him to his grave, and the rich (Pfeiffer understands the "thief," others "Joseph of Arimathea") in his deaths, or his "high places." Compare Pfeiffer's *Vexing Doubts* and Wasmuth's *Inaugural Dissertation*, etc. But Cocceius in his Lexicon [page 729] says: "My people gave his grave with the wicked on the cross, and with the rich in the tomb of Joseph, sealing and guarding it." Similarly, *Gurtler* in his *Prophetic Theology* [page 403] writes: The Jews desired Jesus to be buried like a dead man among the wicked, hidden forever in the grave; but by divine fate, it happened beyond their wishes that he was buried honorably in the tomb of a wealthy man of high authority [Matthew 27:57 and following]. *Gussetius* [page 730] also points to this, comparing John 19:31–38. **f)** *Because*, understanding the relative particle *asher* as in Psalm 119:136. **g)** *Nothing of violence* [Chapter 59:6; 60:18; Genesis 6:11]. **h)** *He did*, though he was crucified with thieves; for he himself was most holy [Daniel 9:24; Luke 1:35] and separated from sinners [Hebrews 7:26]. **i)** *Neither was fraud or deceit* against God, Caesar, or other men [Genesis 34:13; 2 Kings 9:23]. **k)** *Found in his mouth* [1 Peter 2:22; 1 John 3:5]. He never sinned in deeds, words, or thoughts. For if Christ had done iniquity or committed sin himself, he would have had to enter death and his grave alone, and could not have atoned for the sins of others. But now, because he committed no sin—neither in heart, word, nor deed—but is perfectly just and holy, he therefore atoned by his death and abolished the sins of others by his burial. Thus it is rightly said that he led the wicked and unjust with him into death and his grave. *Brentius*.

**verse 10. h)** Therefore Jehovah the Father [verse 6], out of his benevolent will toward the fallen human race [John 3:16; Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:9], so that he might be just and the justifier of those who believe in Christ [Romans 3:26], **m)** *willed* [Job 13:3; 33:32] and decreed by eternal counsel [Ephesians 1:5, 9] **n)** *to crush and afflict him* [verse 5; Job 6:9]. This does not always mean crushing into small pieces, but a vehement pressure and affliction, as in this place. **o)** He involved him in various calamities and tortures greater than any grave disease, and made him weak. [Hiphil form, see Hosea 7:5; Micah 6:13], just as was said above in verse 4. Not for the purpose the Jews intended—to satisfy their unjust hatred—but so that he, as the Mediator between God and men [1 Timothy 2:5, 6], might fulfill the covenant for the redemption of the human race. It is well understood here to insert "saying" or "by saying" before what follows: "if he should lay down," etc., as in Chapter 14:8; 22:13; 45:14; etc. **p)** *If he should lay down* or give [John 7:19; Job 17:3] **q)** *a guilt offering* <note>original: אָשָׁם - Asham</note>. This signifies an "offering for a fault." For it means a fault in such a way that it also denotes the sacrifice upon which the fault is imputed. See everywhere, especially Leviticus 4:3; Chapters 5, 6, 7, 16; 7:1; etc. Compare Psalm 40:7; Romans 8:3; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13; John 1:29. *Rashi* correctly comments on this place: *Asham*, he says, signifies the satisfaction or ransom (*lytron*) that one pays to another whom he has offended—a *Gullice Amande*, that is, a fine. As it is said of the Philistines in 1 Samuel 6:3: "Do not send the ark back empty, but by all means return to him a fine or satisfaction." Compare Job 33:20; Matthew 20:28; 1 Timothy 2:6. For the law, by enjoining upon sinners sacrifices for sin and guilt as a fine and satisfaction, shows that without satisfaction sins are not remitted, or the accusation of sin is not removed [Hebrews 9:22]. But the blood of beasts cannot be a satisfaction [Psalm 50:13; Hebrews 10:4]. That alone is the true satisfaction which the *soul of the Just Servant of God* places—that is, exhibits to God and grants to men. Compare the notes on Leviticus 16:34 and Numbers 35:25. **r)** *His soul* [verse 12; compare Mark 10:45; John 10:11, 15, 17], and thus by his blood he has sprinkled the nations [Chapter 52:15; Matthew 26:28]. **s)** *Then, having been raised*, he shall see a spiritual seed from Jews and Gentiles, an innumerable offspring [Psalm 22:31; compare Psalm 110:3 and above Chapter 11:10]. Regarding the Jewish objection, see *Gussetius* [page 234 and following; compare Genesis 3:15]. **t)** *And with that seed of his*, he shall prolong his days into all eternity, and obtain an eternal kingdom and priesthood with ineffable joy. See verse 8 and compare Psalm 16:11; 21:5; 110:4; Hebrews 7:24; 12:28. **u)** *And the will of Jehovah*, that is, his burning desire for the salvation of men [John 3:16; 1 Timothy 2:4; compare above Chapter 44:28; 46:10; 48:14] **x)** *by the hand* and ministry of that most wise Servant of God [Chapter 52:13; compare Genesis 39:3; Jeremiah 27:8; and above Chapter 30:2] **y)** *shall be happily perfected* and shall prosper exceedingly [Jeremiah 13:1; Psalm 118:25]. Nor shall the Messiah labor in vain, as it seemed [Isaiah 49:4], nor shall the Church be left by God or destitute of children [Chapter 49:14, 21; 54:1 and following]. **verse 11. z)** Thus, *from the labor of his soul* [verse 10], of which see also Chapter 43:24. Compare Judges 10:16; Psalm 73:5; 125:18. The preposition "from" signifies the order by which he shall ascend to that royal vision on the divine throne. Compare Hebrews 2:9, 10. **a)** *He shall see*, namely the seed and fruit of his labor [verse 10]. But according to *Dorsch*, "vision" here is taken absolutely and is not restricted to a certain object (as in verse 10), but extends to all objects subject to his kingdom—indeed, it reaches even to those things which are within God [Matthew 11:27], and thus it is clearly a divine vision. Hence it is also "satisfying," because it lacks any emptying [Philippians 2:7] and has all fullness [Colossians 1:19; 2:9], and that not only for indwelling but for the fulfillment of all things [Ephesians 4:10; Philippians 3:21]. Hence also he shall fill the earth with the saving knowledge of faith [Isaiah 11:9]. **b)** *And he shall be satisfied* with all good things forever [Psalm 16:11; 17:15], and with him all those adhering to him by true faith [Psalm 22:27].

(l) The most powerful enemies, as in Deuteronomy 4:38; Chapter 7:1; 9:1; 11:23; Joshua 23:9; Psalm 135:10. Namely, Satan with the evil angels, the tyrants and the Antichrist [Matthew 12:29; Ezekiel 39:18 and following; Ephesians 6:1 and following], death [1 Corinthians 15:26], and hell [Revelation 20:14]. (Maius). But Sebastian Schmidt interprets it as "that he may divide the spiritual spoil, righteousness and eternal life, with the strong," meaning those strong in faith. Concerning these, compare Ephesians 6:10; 1 John 5:4; Psalm 18:3. (m) He himself as victor will distribute the prey. Compare Chapter 9:2; Genesis 49:27; Exodus 15:9; Psalm 68:13; Proverbs 16:19; and Luke 11:22. (n) For the reason that. 1 Samuel 28:21; Deuteronomy 21:14. Not as if Christ had earned anything for himself, but in terms of the exchange and with respect to us, for whom he properly earned it. (Dorsch). Compare Psalm 68:19: "you have received gifts for men." (o) Totally, like water to be poured out [Psalm 22:15] and of his own accord [John 10:18]. He poured out—that is, he emptied himself. Compare notes on Chapter 32:15 and Psalm 141:8. (o) <note>original Greek: ἀנθ' ὧν παρεδόθη εἰς θάνατον ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ</note> "Because of which his soul was delivered unto death." Romans 4:25. (p) Even unto a cursed death. Philippians 2:8. (q) His soul and all its powers. Verse 10. Compare the prefiguration of Christ in 2 Samuel 24:17. (r) With the wicked and the covenant-breakers, or rebellious sinners. See 2 Kings 1:1; 3:5, 7; and compare Mark 15:28; Luke 22:37; 23:33. (s) He was counted among them. Chapter 65:12. (t) He himself, not only in the judgment of the world, but also by divine imputation. Verse 6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13. (u) Sin and the punishments of sin [Leviticus 19:17] of the whole multitude of men. See verses 4, 6, 11; Hebrews 9:28. (x) He bore it and by bearing it took it away. See verses 4, 11; John 1:29. The Septuagint translation matches 1 Peter 2:24. Compare Leviticus 22:9; Numbers 18:22, 32. As a type, see the goat for the Israelites in Leviticus 16:21, 22, and Aaron for the people in Exodus 28:38. (y) Indeed, even for the rebels [Chapter 46:8; 66:24; Psalm 68:19], who not only failed to recognize him as their King or teacher but even drove him to an ignominious death [Chapter 1:2; Luke 19:14, 27; John 19:15]. How much more then does he intercede with a special prayer for the faithful [John 17:9]. (z) He will intercede. Chapter 59:16; Genesis 23:8; Jeremiah 7:16; 27:18; 36:25. And thus he will satisfy in every part the office of Priest and universal atonement. See Luke 23:34; and if you take the word in the future tense, compare Romans 8:34; Hebrews 9:24; 1 John 2:1.

->**CHAPTER LIV,** verse 1. (a) Sing therefore—that is, shout for joy. Chapter 12:6; compare Colossians 3:16. Ionathan adds: "Jerusalem," namely the mystical or heavenly Jerusalem of Galatians 4:26.<-

Since the Prophet [Chapter 53:1] and the Church herself [Chapter 49:14, 21] had complained about the fewness of believers among the Jews, especially at the beginning of the New Testament, God had foretold that this scarcity of Jews would be made up by a multitude of Gentiles [Chapter 49:22 and following; 52:15]. And in this 54th chapter, the Messiah himself confirms this, to whom the nations are given as an inheritance [Chapter 53:12; Psalm 2:8; 72:8]. He stirs up his Bride to praise and joy, having promised: I. the multiplication of the Church [verses 1-10], II. its adornment [verse 11 and following], and III. its defense [verse 14 and following]. (b) You who seemed barren [Chapter 49:21], like Sarah and Rebekah of old [Genesis 11:30; 25:21; compare Psalm 113:9]. (c) The omission of the relative pronoun and the change of person are well resolved by Ionathan: "you who were like a woman who did not bear." This is read again of Sarah in Genesis 16:1. Paul also cites this verse of Isaiah in Galatians 4:27 and compares it with the type of Sarah and Hagar; by this, he simultaneously indicates that Isaiah also had these two women in mind. And from that passage of Paul, the sense of Isaiah is best understood. (d) Burst forth into praise and song. Sebastian Schmidt: "sing in person." Chapter 14:7; 44:23; 49:13; 55:12; Psalm 98:4. (e) And shout for joy. Chapter 10:30; 12:6; Jeremiah 5:8; Psalm 104:25. (f) Ionathan: "you who were like a woman who did not conceive," or labor. Chapter 23:4; 66:8. (g) For through the gathering of the Gentiles [Chapter 49:22; 52:15] they shall be more. Compare Psalm 87:4, 5. (h) The children of the desolate one [Chapter 49:8; Lamentations 1:4, 13], which, because of the great unbelief and apostasy of the Jews, seemed almost entirely devastated and solitary [Chapter 49:21], as if she had no husband or children. Compare 2 Samuel 13:20. (i) Than the children of the married woman [verse 5; Chapter 62:4; Genesis 20:3]. That is, the Synagogue, which (because of having many children, but only according to the flesh and born for slavery from Abraham, and thus existing under the curse of the law [Galatians 3:10; 4:23, 24, 25]) seemed to herself still to live in a mystical marriage with God. Compare above Chapter 50:1; John 8:33, 37, 39, 41; also Romans 7:1, 4.

**verse 2. (k)** Enlarge, therefore, or dilate. Chapter 30:33; 57:8. (l) The place of your tent for receiving the Gentiles. For the Church will not be enclosed only within the narrow boundaries of Jerusalem or Palestine, but will be extended to the ends of the earth. Compare Chapter 49:20; Zechariah 10:10. (m) Sebastian Schmidt: "those who [extend] the curtains." Exodus 26:11. (n) of your tabernacles. Chapter 32:18. (o) Let them extend [Chapter 31:3; 2 Samuel 21:10], namely, the teachers of the Gospel, the Apostles, and their fellow-workers. (p) Do not prohibit it. Chapter 52:1. For the Messiah clearly foresaw that believers from among the Jews would hardly be satisfied with this extension, as they had not yet laid aside their zeal for Moses. (Sebastian Schmidt). For the Jews could scarcely grasp that the Gentiles should also become co-heirs and participants in the promise [Ephesians 3:5, 6]. Compare Acts 10:47; 11:3. (q) Prolong, or make long. Chapter 53:10; 57:4. (r) Your ropes. Exodus 35:18; see the note on Numbers 3:26. (s) And your pegs or nails. See Chapter 33:20. (t) Strengthen [Chapter 33:23]—that is, fix them firmly so they cannot be pulled out; by which the perpetuity of the New Testament Church is indicated. (Sebastian Schmidt).

**verse 3. (u)** For here the reason is given why the tent of the church must be extended: because she will have many children in the whole world, so that a narrower tent cannot receive them all. (Sebastian Schmidt). (x) To the right and left, and toward all quarters of the world. Compare Chapter 9:19; Zechariah 12:6.

<column-break/>

(e) And by the knowledge of him—not by which he himself knows, but by which he himself is known through true faith and trust as the Propitiator <note>One who makes atonement or reconciles</note> [John 17:3; Romans 3:22, 25]. Compare Jeremiah 9:23; 24:7; Hosea 4:1; 5:3. (f) The suffix in this place has a passive or objective meaning, as in Chapter 56:7; Psalm 35:4; Lamentations 3:59. (d) He will give righteousness, he will justify. Chapter 5, 25; Philippians 3:8, 9. (e) That righteous one. 2 Samuel 23:3; Jeremiah 23:6; Zechariah 9:9; 1 Peter 2:18, 19; 1 John 2:1. Christ is called righteous even after his passion, to show that his righteousness was not overcome by our sins, but rather that his righteousness prevailed. (Sebastian Schmidt). And thus he brought back eternal righteousness [Daniel 9:24; Hebrews 9:12]. (f) To many, or the many—as many as receive the offered righteousness by true faith [Habakkuk 2:4; John 1:11; Romans 1:16]. For he acquired it for all, and thus for many, not few, because he bore the iniquities of all [verses 6, 12]; although, if you look at the outcome, not all arrive at righteousness through their own fault. See the note on Chapter 52:15 and compare John 1:9; Romans 5:13, 18, 19; 1 Timothy 4:10; 1 John 2:2. (g) for their iniquities. As if to say: (h) See verse 4; Lamentations 5:7; John 1:29. (i) <note>original Greek: ἀנוίσει</note> "He shall bear up," and in verse 12 <note>original Greek: ἀνήנהγκε</note> "he bore," as in 1 Peter 2:24. Justification, therefore, according to Isaiah, is founded on the carrying of sins completed by the righteous Servant of God. (Dorsch). Compare 2 Corinthians 5:21. Christ is said to have carried and taken away our sins because by carrying them, he removed them. (Gurtler, *Prophetic Theology*, p. 409). This is truly a remarkable exchange: Christ justifies men by giving them his righteousness; and in turn, he took upon himself their sins, so that he might atone for them and reconcile them to God the Father. (Sebastian Schmidt).

Indeed the Messiah, that is, the Son of God, because of the incarnation and redemption, is the Bridegroom of the Church, who betrothed her to himself in an eternal covenant, Hosea 2:21, 22; John 3:29; 2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25. However, God the Father and the Holy Spirit are not to be excluded. For we are also reconciled to God through the death of the Son, Romans 5:10. Furthermore, *Boel* <note>original: בֹּעֲלַיִךְ - 'your husband/master'</note> in this place signifies a husband rather than a ruler; for the circumstances of the text require it. For the Church in the preceding and following verses is compared to a woman, whose counterpart is a husband. Compare also verse 1, Jeremiah 3:14, Hosea 2:18. This is the best connection and a most serious argument for consolation. The Church seemed to itself to be repudiated and a widow: but the Lord responds that the matter is not so; for He Himself is her husband. And since she was in distress and needed her husband’s help, He consoles her with the fact that He is the Lord of Hosts, and the God of the whole earth, who can rescue her from every difficulty. r) Chapter 22:11, Psalm 149:2, Job 35:10. s) Chapter 8:13, 51:15, Psalm 24:10. t) Chapter 48:2. v) verse 8, Chapter 41:14. u) see Chapter 2, 4; 30:11; 47:4. x) Chapter 52:6, 7. y) he shall be called and shall be. <header># CHAPTER 54. Isaiah 54</header>

<margin>
See I. c. or in the compendium of Maius’s supplement to Cocceius’s Lexicon p. 97. s) g) I will found you. c. 14, 32. c. 28, 16. compare 1 Peter 2:5 and Revelation 21:18 and following. t) Ezekiel 28:18. Song of Solomon 3:14. Revelation 21:19.

Behold the reading <note>original Hebrew: "הנה קרי" — referring to a variant scribal reading</note>

The spiritual beauty of the church is described here using most elegant metaphors. Compare the symbolic pattern in 1 Kings 5:31 and 7:10.

<margin>
n) & perfection <note>original: "perfectionem"</note> tossed by storms. Tigurinus <note>The Zurich Bible</note>: driven by tempests. The adjective form denotes one who is plundered or exhausted. Isaiah 18:2, 7. 2 Kings 2:10, and elsewhere. A participle in the simple active voice, as in Jonah 1:11, 13; see also Hosea 13:3. o) destitute of consolation, having found no comfort, compare Isaiah 51:18; 66:13. p) behold I, the almighty Lord and your God. verse 5. q) I will lay down <note>original: "consternam"</note>. S. <note>likely the scholar Schultens</note>: I am the one arranging, as if to say "I will cause to be hollowed out." Isaiah 13:20. r) Tigurinus: in paint. S.: with (or rather in) stibium <note>original: "stibio" — antimony, a black mineral powder used as eye-makeup</note>. Jonathan <note>The Targum</note>: I will set the stones of your pavement in stibium. So also Symmachus and Theodotion, etc. Jerome says on this passage: All except the Septuagint translated it similarly: "I will pave your stones in stibium," in the likeness of a well-adorned woman who paints her eyes with stibium, to signify the beauty of the city. See 2 Kings 9:30, Jeremiah 4:30, and 1 Chronicles 29:2. For sapphire is not found there. However, because "stones of stibium" are mentioned at the end, others thought gems were meant here. Hence the Septuagint and many others place "carbuncle" here, the Syrian version "beryl," the Arabic "hyacinth," and Gussetius (p. 668) "gypsum" in place of sanded lime. But since the Hebrew <term>פוך</term> <note>puk: antimony or eye-paint</note> without doubt denotes paint or stibium—called <term>Cohul</term> <note>Kohl</note> in the East—a mineral used in the Orient not only for ornament but also for eye medicine, the Blessed Ludolfus in his Ethiopian History (p. 107-110) thought one should not flee from the accepted meaning to an unknown one. He understands it as the powder of Kohl prepared from mineral stone and raised in the pavement for the health of the eyes. In 1 Chronicles 29:2, he conjectures that David, among other precious things, also provided the priests with items pertaining to the healing and health of the body. See his work.
</margin>

**v. 12. n)** Tigurinus: *crystal*. Vulgate: *Jasper*, etc. (2) Exodus 27:16. **x)** *your windows*: others: *your looking-glasses* (1) named after the *Sun*, which admits light through them. y) compare chapter 60:18. Revelation 21:21. z) *carbuncles*, S. *pyropes* (1) a flaming or glowing gem. a) & *all your borders or boundaries*. Deuteronomy 19:14. Jeremiah 5:22. b) S. *stones of desire* i.e., *Vulgate: desirable and precious stones*. compare the construction in Malachi 3:12. Ecclesiastes 12:10. **v. 13. c)** *And all your children*, whether born again from the Jews or from the Gentiles, chapter 43:6; 49:17, 22; 60:4, 9. also the child in Christ, 1 Corinthians 3:1. d) they shall not remain in ignorance, but shall be *taught and instructed* (6) chapter 2:8, 16; 50:4. Jeremiah 2:24. e) by Jehovah. A genitive of the agent, as in chapter 53:4, etc. *Taught by God* <note>original: "Theodidacti"</note>, John 6:45. Not indeed without means, as others wrongly conclude; but through the *Word of God*, which is set before everyone, and with which the earth shall be so filled with the knowledge of God (Isaiah 11:9) that individuals may recognize that one necessary thing, and like Mary, prefer these better concerns over all others, Luke 10:42. Compare also Jeremiah 31:34; 1 John 2:27. Jonathan well says: *And all your children shall learn in the law or word of the Lord*. Psalm 1:2. The means (says Dorf h.) through which men are led by the Holy Spirit to believe is ordinarily the Holy Scripture, John 5:39. Christ willed that all nations be taught, Matthew 28:19, and that all come to the knowledge of the truth, 1 Timothy 2:4; Matthew 23:37. But the *effect* does not follow in some; not because of a lack of teaching grace, but because of the stubbornness they set up, by which *the counsel of God is rejected*, Luke 7:30, and *the Holy Spirit is resisted*, Acts 7:51; Matthew 23:37. This passage is cited in John 6:45 to prove the necessity of the *divine drawing* mentioned there in verse 44; this drawing is not by an absolute decree, but through means—the Word and Sacraments. Compare John 12:32, where that drawing happens through the passion. Christ died for all men (see above on chapter 53:6, 11) even for those who do not follow the one drawing them, who break the *cords of the drawer* (Jeremiah 31:3). Psalm 2:3. **f)** *and great shall be the peace*, chapter 26:3, 12; 27:5; 52:7. Romans 5:1. g) compare chapter 11:9. **v. 14. h)** chapter 1:27; 5:16. This *Justice* is the justice of divine promises, or the mercy of God itself in Christ. This is the Church's consolation and causes it not to fear. S. Compare chapter 63:1. i) you shall be established, Proverbs 24:3. k) S. be far off, chapter 49:19. Ezekiel 11:15. Jehovah-Messiah commands the church through this imperative to be of good courage, and wills that it should not entertain thoughts as if it were to be oppressed. S. l) chapter 30:12; 59:13. m) for you shall not fear, i.e., you shall have no cause for fear, and it is your duty not to fear. S. see verse 4, chapter 40:9. Zephaniah 3:16. n) *and from terror or consternation*, Jeremiah 17:17. o) Psalm 91:10.

**v. 15. p)** *Behold!* chapter 50:1, 2; 52:13. q) S. *dreading he shall dread*. compare Deuteronomy 1:17; chapter 18:22. Psalm 22:24.
