<meta>This page transitions from the architectural and structural restoration of the Church described in Chapter 54 to a universal invitation to spiritual refreshment in Chapter 55. It focuses on the "Covenant of Grace" and the identity of the Messiah as the "Second David."</meta>

# ISAIAH. CHAPTER 55.

<margin>
CHAPTER 55, verse 1.)
**Ho:** <note>original: "Heus"</note> Zechariah 2:10. (11.)
Since in the preceding chapters the Church has received consolation through remarkable promises—especially concerning the gathering to herself not only of Jews but also of Gentiles—now, so that it may more clearly appear that these promises are both true and serious, the Messiah is presented by God the Father. All people, both individually and collectively, are invited to Him, especially the Gentiles (as even the Jewish interpreters acknowledge), regarding whom those promises were made. Thus, in this chapter there is:
**I.** The presentation of the Messiah before the world (verses 1–5).
**II.** A serious exhortation to accept Him (verse 6 and following). 
The scholar Saint Gussetius, in his *Prophetic Theology*, explains the argument of this chapter in these words: *God the Father,* he says, *calls men, who were buying spiritual goods from the Antichrist with money, to Christ, who imparts salvation by grace* (verses 1–5); and *the Prophet commands them to repent* (verses 6–9) because of the fruitfulness of the Gospel (verses 10–13). 
Truly, the one inviting (who speaks from verse 1 to 5) is altogether God the Father: because He **(1)** promises the presentation of the "mercies of David" in verse 3; **(2)** speaks of the Messiah as a witness, leader, and teacher of the nations in verse 4; **(3)** proposes the Messiah as the Holy One of Israel, who will be an ornament for His people in verse 5. 
Christ, however, in John 7:37, makes these words of the Father His own because of their supreme identity (John 10:30). Dorsch; compare also Matthew 11:28, John 4:10, 13, 14, and Revelation 22:17. 
**n)** All and each, Jews and Gentiles, whoever is stirred by my grace and promises (for by himself, man is spiritually dead, Ephesians 2:5, and does not thirst for those things which are of the Spirit of God, 1 Corinthians 2:14, Romans 8:7). You acknowledge your misery...
</margin>

<margin>
...and you desire to be admitted to the communion of such great goods. For all and each are able to receive grace upon grace from the fullness of Christ, as if from an open and inexhaustible fountain of salvation (Isaiah 12:3, Zechariah 13:1; John 1:16).
</margin>

**v. 1.** *x)* thirsting or those thirsting spiritually, that is, the soul. **verse 2, 3; chapter 44:3.** Matthew 5:6. *y)* Come now, approach. **verse 3; chapter 2:3, 5.** These imperatives are not "legal" ones, which give nothing of what they demand; rather, they are "evangelical" imperatives, which give and extend that which they require—just like the miraculous imperatives in **Luke 7:14 and John 11:43.** *Dorsch.* For Christ teaches that the word "to come" includes a divine drawing, **John 6:44.** *z)* to the waters, by which thirst and all spiritual poverty are extinguished. **chapter 12:3; 49:10; 65:13.** Gushing up into eternal life, **John 4:14.** Namely, Christ, with all His benefits and gifts, is described thus figuratively. *Dorsch says: "The spring of that water, wine, milk, and fatness consists in the wounds, stripes, and afflictions of the Messiah in chapter 53."* *a)* and to whoever has no silver, that is, who has no money, or no righteousness of his own, or merits; which describes all men without exception, **Romans 3:23.** *b)* come to me. **verse 3.** and to the fountain of salvation. **verse 1, 3, 4.** *c)* buy. **Genesis 41:57; 42:2, 5, 7.** *d)* eat. compare **Proverbs 9:2, 5; chapter 24:13, 14; Song of Solomon 5:1.** the bread of life, **John 6:35, 48.** *e)* come, I say. **2 Samuel 22:7.** *f)* **Genesis 43:4, 20; Deuteronomy 2:6.** *g)* without (Numbers 35:22; Jeremiah 22:13) silver. compare **John 1:16; Romans 3:24.** *h)* and without price. **chapter 45:13; Proverbs 17:16; compare also Revelation 22:17; Romans 11:35; Ephesians 2:8, 9.** *i)* **Proverbs 9:2, 5; Zechariah 9:17; compare also Matthew 26:28; John 6:55.** *k)* and milk. **Joel 4:18; Song of Solomon 4:11; 1 Peter 2:2.** 

The Targum of Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> puts it thus: *Ho everyone who desires to learn, let him come and learn; and those who have no silver: come and learn, without price and without money, a doctrine better than wine and milk—namely, the doctrine of the Gospel, or of Christ.* 

**v. 2.** *l)* Why in vain! <note>original: "frustra !"</note> **chapter 40:27; Ruth 1:11.** *m)* **chapter 46:6.** *n)* The scholar Schultens notes this is used for that which *is not*, compare **Jeremiah 2 (1:11); Psalm 104:14, 15.** So that men might run more promptly, the excellence of the gifts offered for free and the empty labor of idolaters (who spend everything in vain) are placed side by side. **Maius.** *p)* **chapter 45:14.** *q)* for that which is not, as just before. *r)* to satiety <note>original: "ad satietatem"</note> **chapter 23:18; compare Zechariah 9:17 and Romans 9:31, 32.** *For whatever things are put forward for a human price in the business of salvation, as usually happens in false religions, they are deceptive and useless. Dorsch.* *s)* **Zechariah 6:15.** *t)* to me, God the Father, the giver of the Son. **verse 3; John 3:16.** Jonathan: Obey my word. The means of obtaining these goods are a diligent hearing of the evangelical word and a faithful approach. **John 6:40, 45; Romans 10:17; Hebrews 11:6. Maius.** *u)* compare **chapter 1:19.** *x)* Schultens: so that it may be delighted. The Zurich Bible: let it delight itself. **chapter 58:14; 65:11; Psalm 37:4.** *y)* in that abundance and fatness **Psalm 36:9; Psalm 63:6.** compare above **chapter 30:23; Romans 14:17.** *z)* in the kingdom of grace and glory, compare **chapter 65:13; 66:10, 11; Psalm 34:9; Matthew 8:11; Luke 22:30; Ephesians 3:16, 17.**

**v. 3.** *aa)* Incline your ears therefore **Joshua 24:23; Psalm 78:1.** *b)* to me, the Father, see **verse 2.** and to Christ **Matthew 11:23; compare note at verse 1.** *c)* Jonathan: obey, I say, my Word, as in **verse 2.** *d)* so that it may live eternally **Psalm 22:27; John 6:33.** *e)* **verse 2. compare Psalm 143:6.** *f)* The Vulgate: *and I will strike a covenant with you*. Schultens: thus I will cut for you. **chapter 61:8; Jeremiah 32:40; Ezekiel 34:25; 37:26.** *g)* a covenant or an eternal pact, namely of grace, not of works or merit (verses 1, 2), which will save into eternity and will never be abolished as happened with the legal pact. **Schultens; compare chapter 54:10; 61:8; Jeremiah 31:31 and following; Daniel 9:24.** 

This covenant is **(1)** free with respect to the man receiving it (verse 1), and does not base its gifts on the merit of works, as the Law did. **(2)** Its benefits consist in the life of the soul (verses 2, 3). **(3)** It announces the remission of sins, while yet inciting the ceasing of sin (verse 7). **(4)** It coincides with that in **Jeremiah 31:31–34**, and is therefore new: and that novelty certainly agrees with the future-tense verb "I will strike." **(5)** Its substance is those "mercies of David," which are firm and faithful (verse 3). **(6)** It includes the Gentiles, who are indeed to be called (verse 4; chapter 56:3, 6), while meanwhile **(7)** the Jews are rejected (chapter 56:10–12; 57:3) and their slaughter, such as occurred in the war of Titus, is predicted (chapter 56:9), after the pious Jews—such as Simeon, Anna, Zacharias, Elizabeth, Mary, and Joseph—were first taken away by a blessed death (chapter 57:1). **See Gusset, page 581.**

*h)* namely, the mercies of David. This hints at the King Messiah, which the following verse testifies. These are the words of **Abraham ibn Ezra; so also David Kimchi:** *This is the Messiah,* he says, *for He is also called David, comparing Ezekiel 34:24.* Many things should be noted here again, if the narrowness of the paper and the plan of this work allowed. That the kingdom of the Messiah is being discussed in this place is a matter of consensus among Christians, from the whole context and **compared with Acts 13:34.** Even the more sensible Jewish interpreters confess this, as we just saw. The only ambiguity here among Christians is whether the genitive "of David" is passive (meaning the one receiving) or active (the one performing)? That is, should we understand the "mercies of David" as that most excellent and kind promise concerning the Messiah made to David (**2 Samuel 7:12; Psalm 89:29**), as Dorsch and others have it, including Gusset (page 273, comparing Psalm 59:11, Psalm 144:2, and 2 Chronicles 6:42, where the "mercies of David" are not those he himself performed, but those he received as provided or promised by God in that covenant)? Or is it the "mercies" that the *second* David performed—for the Jews also call the Messiah "David" in the Talmudic Tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 11, folio 98b—that is, Jesus Christ, the son and archetype of David, who was foreshadowed by the first David and therefore often called by this very name by the Prophets? See **Jeremiah 30:9; Ezekiel 34:23, 24; 37:25; Hosea 3:5; Psalm 132:10, etc.** 

Gusset prefers this (pages 681–683), where he discusses this passage extensively and learnedly. Forgetting his earlier points, he argues several times that the Hebrew word **חֶסֶד** (*chesed*) always denotes the kindnesses or actions of the one to whom they are attributed. Therefore, we also prefer this view, or at least join it with the first opinion, because of the connection of this verse with the next. Indeed, as **Vitringa** well notes on **Revelation 5:5 (page 272)**: Whatever graces and prerogatives God once indulged upon the family of David, none of them fell to it except in respect to the Messiah, who was to be born, raised from the dead, and to reign for all ages. Not only that, but those very graces and prerogatives were conferred upon the family of David through Him, and He Himself is David’s Rock, King, and Shepherd—names by which David frequently distinguishes Him in his hymns. Indeed, He Himself is David’s savior, and his hope and consolation, etc. 

Thus, as **Gusset observes (page 581)**, it is of the free mercy of Christ that He took up the work of our redemption and beatification, seeing us from eternity in our corruption, misery, and weakness; that moved by such love He put on our flesh, took our likeness in the form of a servant, emptied and humbled Himself even to the death of the cross; that He rose again for our justification, ascended into heaven to perform the remaining duties of the priesthood, intercedes for us, and reconciles us to the Father; He rules the church by His word and spirit; dwells in us through faith; connects us as members to the Head; makes us to be children of God, His brothers, co-heirs, and His bride; conquers our enemies and protects us from them; grants us to persevere; and does not abandon us until He leads us into the supreme inheritance of good, of which He took possession for us by His ascension.

chapter 60, 3 and following; chapter 65, 1; Zechariah 8:20–23; Galatians 4:8, 9; Ephesians 2:12. (x) God, namely of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the Angel from the bush (Exodus 3:15). **v. 6.** (a) Seek the Lord therefore. chapter 31:1; Amos 5:4; Psalm 78:34; Matthew 7:7; Acts 17:27; Hebrews 11:6. The application here is a teaching <note>original: "hit paedeutica"</note> on the preceding verses, in the words of the Prophet, collected also "to our God" in verse 7. This is defended in verses 8 and 9, illustrated by a simile in verses 10 and 11, and confirmed by a happy outcome in verses 12 and 13. Truly, Isaiah now recalls to the memory of his countrymen what God the Father had said in verse 1 and following, and exhorts them to seek and receive the Messiah. For since he foresaw they would be rejected because they rejected the Messiah, and many might suspect from the long duration of their punishment that no place for grace remained or that God's promises would fail, he rouses them to seek and call upon the Lord diligently and seriously, adding the promise that He will be found and is near; and he gives the method of seeking: namely, that the wicked man should desert his evil ways and thoughts contrary to God, as if He were no longer willing to have mercy or had forgotten the covenant entered into. *Maius, Oeconomia,* page 974. Schmidius determines that the prophet is speaking with the captives in Babylon in this and the following chapters 56–59. (b) Schmidius: "while He can be found." Compare Deuteronomy 4:29; Jeremiah 29:13; Psalm 32:6; Song of Solomon 3:1; Isaiah 28:9. Jonathan <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation</note>: *Seek the fear of the Lord while you live; ask of Him while you survive.* (c) Call upon Him (Psalm 50:15). (d) While He is near. (l) Then He will altogether have mercy on him. chapter 27:11; chapter 54:8; Micah 7:19; compare Deuteronomy 4:31; Psalm 103:8. (m) To our God, from whom we have shamefully defected (chapter 59:13), though He otherwise most faithfully keeps His covenant with those who love Him (Deuteronomy 7:9; 1 Kings 8:23; Daniel 9:4). **Chapter 56, Verse 1. Note a:** Thus spoke Jehovah the Son, the Messiah, whose house is a house of prayer (verse 7, Matthew 21:13). He is called the Lord who shall come to His temple in Malachi 3:1. Compare Haggai 2:6, 7, 9. 
**Dorscheus:** This is again a pedagogical application of the previous sections, offering a serious exhortation to a godly life (verses 1–8) and a severe rebuke and threat to the teachers (verses 9–12). Interpreters differ on the historical timing. **Schmid** thinks it refers to the captives in Babylon, as in chapter 55:6. But since so much in this context points to Christ, the rest...

is not the legalistic or physical rest, but a ceasing from sins ᵃ and from our own ways and thoughts (Isaiah 55:7). **(4)** "Judgment and justice" here refer to those things which Christ commands as King and Commander of all peoples (chapter 55:4), ordering those things which pertain to the economy of His covenant and kingdom—namely, to believe with a sincere and living faith, and to repent. This is why in verse 2, the one who does these things is called "blessed." **Gousset**, in his *Prophetic Theology* (page 113), believes this predicts the reformation of the church and the corruption of the clergy. We believe that while these things applied in their own way to the Jews in Babylon and Isaiah's contemporaries, they primarily refer to New Testament times—literally to the corruption of the Jewish Church before Christ's coming, and mystically to the foul corruption under the Antichrist, as gathered from New Testament parallels.

**v. 8. h)** who is to gather. chapter 11:12, chapter 43:5. chapter 54:7. Deuteronomy 30:3. Jeremiah 31:8, 10; chapter 32:37. Ezekiel 11:17, chapter 34:13. Psalm 107:2, 3. **i)** the dispersed of Israel Deuteronomy 30:4. Matthew 9:36, chapter 23:37. John 11:52. **l)** yet others from the nations, John 10:16. **m)** I will gather Jeremiah 23:3. Micah 2:12. chapter 4:6. Zephaniah 3:19. **n)** to Israel itself 1 Kings 11:34. 2 Chronicles 15:7. **o)** namely, to the gathered ones of Israel. Compare Jeremiah 49:15. We establish that there is a new argument in this verse for the consolation of foreigners, etc. S. <note>Likely referring to the commentator Schmidt.</note> **v. 9. q)** All beasts. A great disagreement arises here among interpreters concerning the connection of this verse and its meaning. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> and Schmidius connect it with verse 8, and the latter appeals to the Masoretes <note>Jewish scholars who standardized the Biblical text</note> and Editors of the Bibles, who therefore left a space between verses 8 and 10; so that the invective speech begins only at verse 10. But not all approved printed codes recognize that space, much less the manuscripts, nor, even if they agreed on it, would its authority be so great that we should force the text and words because of it. Our brevity does not allow for many points, so we state our opinion in few words: (1) with the Vulgate, Zurich, Tremellius, and others, we begin the second part of this chapter from this verse, regarding which see verse 1. (2) Symmachus <note>a 2nd-century Greek translator</note> well expressed the words of the text according to the legitimate construction and sense according to the accents, rendering it thus: *All the beasts of the field, come, devour the beasts of the forest.* But if (3) by the beasts of the field we understand the enemies of the Jews—not so much the Babylonians, Greeks, Syrians, or Egyptians in this place as the Romans; and by the beasts in the forest, we understand the reprobate Jews in the forest-like field or vineyard of God; which, following Dr. Maius, could also be referred to any cruel enemies of the Church, tyrants, and the Antichrist, etc. For in order that the nations might be brought more abundantly to the Church of Christ, which was predicted in verse 8, that scandal or hindrance to Christian doctrine—namely, the Jewish state with its superstition and impious worship—had to be removed. Just as frequently in the Prophets, the calling of the nations and the rejection of the Jews are joined together, as in chapter 65:1 and following. Now we will also note a few things on individual words. **q)** beast. The construction is with the "Paragogic Vav" <note>an archaic grammatical suffix</note>, as in Genesis 1:24. Psalm 104:11. **r)** of the field. This does not mean, as some translate, *of my fields*, but is the same as <span lang="heb">שדה</span> <note>sadeh</note>, with the harsh breath changed into a thin one, as Abraham ben Ezra rightly teaches on Psalm 8:8. Compare Deuteronomy 32:13. Jeremiah 4:17. Joel 2:22. Psalm 80:14. Psalm 96:12. Psalm 104:11. Lamentations 4:9. etc. **s)** come. see chapter 21:12. Compare Revelation 19:17. **t)** to devour. see Jeremiah 12:9 and compare below chapter 65:12. *Every beast*. Compare chapter 57:3. Habakkuk 2:17. Daniel 7:3, 7. **w)** in the forest. see chapter 29:17. chapter 32:15, 19. Luke 21:30.

**v. 10. x)** For its watchmen, the leaders and teachers of the Jewish people. chapter 52:8. Ezekiel 3:17. Compare 2 Kings 16:10, 11. **y)** they are blind. chapter 42:18. Matthew 23:24, 26. Here occur first the sins of the ecclesiastics (as in chapter 57:1 and following, those of the whole people), which are ignorance, blindness, fear, laziness, greed, and devotion to the belly: from which the Apostles took their phrases with which they describe false Apostles. Compare Philippians 3:19. 2 Timothy 3:2, 3, 4. Titus 2:3, chapter 3:3. 2 Peter 2:1, 14. Dorsch. **b)** they understand or know nothing, they do not acknowledge the truth. verse 11. chapter 42:16. chapter 44:18. Psalm 82:5. Compare 1 Peter 2:17. Jude verse 13. **d)** they are dumb dogs chapter 35:6. Habakkuk 2:18. That dogs were already long ago used for guarding cattle and keeping wild beasts from the flock is clear from Job 30:1. **g)** who cannot bark, (1) and having neglected their duty, indulge only in sleep and gluttony. For otherwise the duty of shepherds is to watch over the flock, and to betray the wolves, i.e., the enemies of the Church, by barking. Compare Zechariah 11:14. Matthew 7:29. John 10:12, 13. **i)** dreaming <note>original: *son dormientes* - they are sleeping</note>. The Zurich version says "creeping," others "snoring" (1) and so commonly the Hebrews. But Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar</note> in *Hierozoicon* I, page 680: dreaming and raving, from the Arabic root (using *Dsal* in place of the Hebrew *Zain*). It means to rave either through sleep or through disease. Therefore it was not poorly rendered by the Greeks as <span lang="grc">ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι</span> <note>enypniazomenoi</note>, "dreamers," comparing Jude verse 8; and by Aquila as <span lang="grc">φανταζόμενοι</span> <note>phantazomenoi</note>, agitated by fantasies and vain imaginations. For false Prophets are both deluded themselves by vain images of things, and they delude those believing in them. And in this part they are deservedly compared with dogs, who not only dream, as many animals do, but also reveal their dreams either by barking or gesture, at least in part. Cocceius in his Lexicon, page 128, thinks there is a hidden paronomasia <note>a play on words</note> with <span lang="heb">הזים</span> <note>hozim - dreamers</note> and "seers." See chapter 29:10. Ezekiel 13:9. etc. or as it were, with the Vulgate, "seeing vain things." Schmidius, however, seems to have read it as <span lang="heb">חזים</span> <note>chozim - seers</note>, while he renders it "they are only looking"; but with no manuscript or Hebrew interpreter supporting him. **k)** 1 Samuel 26:6. **l)** lovers Amos 4:5. **m)** to slumber chapter 5:27. Compare Proverbs 6:10. Whenever Scripture either reproaches the shepherds of the Lord's flock for sleep or commends vigilance, it alludes to those watches of shepherds, by which it was customary to spend the night in the fields, where they remained within enclosures lest they wander at night. Luke 2:8, etc. Acts 20:31. 2 Corinthians 6:5. 2 Timothy 4:5. Revelation 3:2, 3. Bochart *Hierozoicon* I, page 452 and following. **v. 11. l)** S. Or they are dogs. Compare 2 Samuel 24:13. **m)** as if to say strong, S. obstinate, Septuagint and Arabic: impudent of soul, Vulgate: most impudent. And perhaps that is not bad, since the canine vice is extreme impudence, and elsewhere those who are of a stubborn countenance are called <span lang="heb">עזי פנים</span> <note>azze panim - strong of face</note>, Deuteronomy 28:50, etc. Others render "of greedy soul," i.e., gluttonous and voracious, or with unquenchable voracity, so that these things better cohere with the following, *they know not satiety*. But shamelessness is almost always a companion of voracity; so that you see few gluttons and parasites who are not also extremely impudent. Bochart *Hierozoicon* I, page 688. Compare as to the words, Daniel 8:23. Exodus 23:9. Psalm 27:12. **p)** they know not satiety, or they cannot be satisfied. Compare Jeremiah 6:15. chapter 8:12.

The text completes the promise of joy and acceptance for faithful foreigners in the Temple before shifting into a scathing indictment of Israel’s leadership. The "blind watchmen" and "greedy dogs" mentioned here are metaphors for prophets and leaders who have abandoned their duty to protect and guide the people, seeking only their own pleasure and profit.</meta>

v. 7. q) Compare chapter 35:10 regarding everlasting joy. r) Cited by Christ in Matthew 21:13. s) In the spiritual sense, our prayers and praises; see Romans 12:1 and 1 Peter 2:5. t) Compare chapter 60:7. u) They shall be well-pleasing through the Messiah; see Ephesians 1:6. v) Our altar is Christ; Hebrews 13:10. w) The Church of the living God; 1 Timothy 3:15. x) Malachi 1:11. y) All nations and peoples; John 10:16.

Their **burnt offerings**<sup>s</sup> and their **sacrifices**<sup>t</sup> will be **accepted**<sup>u</sup> on my **altar**<sup>v</sup>; for my **house**<sup>w</sup> shall be called a **house of prayer**<sup>x</sup> for **all nations**<sup>y</sup>.

# 8 The **Lord**<sup>z</sup> **God**<sup>aa</sup>, who **gathers**<sup>bb</sup> the **outcasts**<sup>cc</sup> of Israel, **declares**<sup>dd</sup>: “I will **gather**<sup>ee</sup> yet **others**<sup>ff</sup> to him besides those already **gathered**<sup>gg</sup>.”

v. 10. ll) The Hebrew letter *Tsade* in the word "Watchmen" is written larger than usual in some manuscripts <note>A "Large Tsade" is a scribal tradition used to draw the reader's eye to a significant transition or warning.</note>. mm) Spiritual blindness; Matthew 15:14. nn) Without discernment or knowledge of God's word; Hosea 4:6. oo) Zephaniah 3:3. pp) They have lost the power to warn. qq) <note>original: "hozim" — this word suggests those who see delusions or "raving" rather than true prophecy.</note> rr) Proverbs 6:10.

# 9 All you **beasts of the field**<sup>hh</sup>, come to **devour**<sup>ii</sup>—all you **beasts in the forest**<sup>kk</sup>. <note>This marks a sharp transition. Having promised a house for all nations, the prophet now calls for the destruction of the current corrupt system.</note>

# 10 **His watchmen**<sup>ll</sup> are **blind**<sup>mm</sup>; they are all **without knowledge**<sup>nn</sup>. They are all **silent dogs**<sup>oo</sup>; they **cannot**<sup>pp</sup> bark. They are **dreamers**<sup>qq</sup>, lying down, loving to **slumber**<sup>rr</sup>. <note>A watchman who cannot bark is like a guard dog that stays silent when a thief arrives; they are useless for protection.</note>

# 11 The **dogs**<sup>ss</sup> have a **mighty appetite**<sup>tt</sup> <note>original: "strong of soul" — a Hebrew idiom for being insatiably greedy.</note>; they **never have enough**<sup>uu</sup>. And these are **shepherds**<sup>vv</sup> who **have no understanding**<sup>ww</sup>; they have all **turned**<sup>xx</sup> to their **own way**<sup>yy</sup>, each one to his own **gain**<sup>zz</sup>, from one end of the land to the other.

<margin>
v. 11. ss) Philippians 3:2. tt) Greedy for worldly things. uu) Ezekiel 34:2. vv) The teachers and rulers. ww) Jeremiah 10:21. xx) Philippians 2:21. yy) Following their own desires rather than God's law. zz) Micah 3:11.
v. 12. aaa) A scene of drunken revelry. bbb) Fetching more. ccc) Indulging in wine. ddd) Intoxicating beverages. eee) Proverbs 27:1. fff) Today. ggg) Even more abundant than today.
</margin>

# 12 “**Come**,”<sup>aaa</sup> they say, “let me **get**<sup>bbb</sup> **wine**<sup>ccc</sup>, and let us **fill ourselves**<sup>ddd</sup> with **strong drink**<sup>eee</sup>; and **tomorrow**<sup>fff</sup> will be like **this day**<sup>ggg</sup>, great beyond measure.” <note>The leaders are portrayed as being so confident in their comfort that they believe their luxury and intoxication will never end.</note>

<summary>This page concludes the vision of a universal house of prayer for all nations and transitions into a fierce condemnation of Israel's corrupt leaders, described as blind watchmen and greedy, silent dogs. It highlights the contrast between the spiritual inclusion of foreigners and the moral decay of the established priesthood and rulers.</summary>

**Verse 8.** Following Kimchi and Abraham Ibn Ezra. **n)** Who that King might be is not explicitly stated: "Doubtless the King of Assyria," says Dorsch. So also Kimchi, etc. Compare notes on chapter 7:4, 11 and 2 Kings 16:7, 8. Others understand the Egyptian Kings, comparing chapter 20:4; 31:1, etc. Others mystically understand the Antichrist or the Devil himself. Others collectively: Antichristian Kings. So says Oecolampadius, p. 476, comparing Revelation 13, 17, and 18. **o)** With precious oil, Song of Solomon 1:2; Ecclesiastes 7:1; 10:1; compare Ruth 3:3. **p)** Your ointments. **q)** Compare Ezekiel 23:40. **r)** Your ambassadors/messengers, chapter 18:2. **s)** Even to those who are far off, to the remote. Compare chapter 5:26; 23:7; Proverbs 7:19; Nehemiah 12:43. **t)** Or "humility [debases] you." See chapter 2:9. Others: "You threw yourself down into hell," comparing chapter 25:11; 26:5. **u)** Even to the underworld (*Sheol*). This signifies the most foul and abject flattery, with which King Ahaz especially flattered the King of Assyria so that he would come to his aid; which perhaps even progressed to shared idolatrous worship. Or as in 2 Kings 6:33: "Why should we seek the Lord any longer?" You said: *If I cannot bend the gods above, I will move the underworld* <note>original Latin: "Flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta mouebo" — a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, suggesting that if heaven won't help, one will turn to hell</note>. Compare the note on chapter 7:12. **Verse 10.** **i)** In the "multitude" (chapter 47:9, 12) and "magnitude," comparing 1 Kings 19:7. **y)** Jeremiah 2:23, 33, 36; chapter 4:18. **z)** Chapter 47:12, 15. The Greek Septuagint: "You were weary" (Matthew 11:28). **a)** It is "despaired of," namely, to worship foreign gods and trust in men. This is the voice of one rejecting, see Jeremiah 2:25; 18:12; compare Ecclesiastes 2:20. Jonathan: "I will return." **b)** Life, Ezekiel 7:13; Job 33:8. Others: "A troop," as in 2 Samuel 23:11, 13. **c)** The hand of you, laboring and fatigued. **d)** You found [it] in the help of the Assyrians. Compare 2 Kings 16:9. **e)** Zurich Bible: "Therefore you did not faint." You were "weakened," that is, you did not stop walking and laboring in your evil way; compare chapter 33:24; Judges 16:7, 11, 17; 1 Samuel 30:13; Jeremiah 5:3. The Arabic version: "Therefore you did not care for me," acting unlike a faithful bride, who becomes sick with longing and love for her groom (Song of Solomon 2:5; 5:8). **Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac:** "You did not ask me." He reproaches the Jews because when God, out of mercy, mitigated their punishment so as not to destroy them entirely, they became more ardent in their idolatry. A manifest example is Ahaz in 2 Kings 16:10 and 2 Chronicles 28:22. **Verse 11.** **f)** But whom do you fear so anxiously? Jeremiah 17:8; chapter 38:19. **g)** Or who is so feared in himself? See chapter 51:12; 7:4. **h)** Because or when you so flatter Kings (v. 9) and lie to me (Psalm 78:36). The Greek version: "And you lied to me." Observe the accusative case, comparing Acts 5:3. **i)** For you do not remember me, chapter 17:10. **k)** Verse 1, chapter 42:25. **l)** Have I not been silent out of my long-suffering? Chapter 42:14; Psalm 50:21; Romans 2:4. Or transitively: "Have I not restrained all, even the terrible enemies?" Comparing Nehemiah 8:11. **m)** And that not just recently, but from of old. Chapter 46:9; 64:3; Jeremiah 2:20. **n)** And yet you do not fear me. Jeremiah 5:22; Matthew 10:28. Jonathan: "Have I not given a delay from of old, that perhaps you might return to the law? But you have not turned in my sight." **Verse 12.** **o)** Therefore I will now declare. Chapter 44:8; 48:5; 1 Samuel 3:13. **p)** Your imaginary and false righteousness, upon which you leaned. See chapter 58:2 and compare chapter 64:5; also Luke 15:7. **q)** Your works—the things you actually did! Chapter 58:2; compare 59:6; 66:18; Genesis 20:9. **r)** They will not profit you. Chapter 30:5; Jeremiah 2:8, 11, etc. **Verse 13.** **s)** When you cry out to me, compare chapter 30:19; Jeremiah 2:27; Hosea 7:14; Lamentations 3:8. **t)** I will say, "Let them rescue you." Compare 1 Samuel 12:21; Jeremiah 2:28; Hosea 9:1. **u)** Collectively: "your troop" of gods whom you collected. Compare Judges 10:14. **x)** But all of these, **y)** the wind will carry off. Chapter 41:16; Psalm 1:4. **z)** Indeed, a breath of the mouth will take them away. Psalm 62:10; 144:4; comparing James 4:14. Compare also above, chapter 30:7; 2 Kings 17:15; Jeremiah 2:5; 10:3, 15. **a)** But he who trusts in me (Jonathan: "In my Word," the Son of God) takes refuge in me. Psalm 2:12; 36:8; compare above, chapter 25:4. **b)** Exodus 23:30; Joshua 14:1; Matthew 5:5. Compare also Psalm 107:36ff. Here consolation begins, soon to be narrated more fully. **c)** Chapter 54:3. **d)** Chapter 56:7. **Verse 14.** **e)** "And it shall be said"—namely, according to S., by God the Father whose people they are, about whom the Son also speaks in verse 15. Or translate: "For the same one who has spoken until now, the Son of God, has said." Thus the words of Christ are further presented by the Prophet: see verses 19, 21. **f)** Level it, level it! Or "Heap up the way." Chapter 62:10; Psalm 68:5. Chapter 8:14; Jeremiah 19:14. Compare the word in Hosea 14:10. **i)** So that they can walk with an unstumbling foot. See chapter 35:8, 9. **Verse 15.** **k)** The Most High and Lofty One. The Comforter is described here by the loftiness of His majesty, by eternity, by the holiness of His name, by the height of His dwelling, by His gracious dwelling among the contrite, and by the outpouring of His vindicating wrath. **l)** Verse 17. **l)** "Dwelling in eternity," or "dwelling among my own forever," Revelation 21:3; as formerly among the Israelites in the Tabernacle, Numbers 5:3. **m)** Chapter 9:5; 45:17. **n)** Chapter 1:4; Psalm 111:9; Revelation 15:4. **o)** Indeed the high heaven, chapter 33:15; Psalm 102:20; compare below, chapter 66:1; 1 Kings 8:27. **p)** And that place is truly holy because of my majesty. Psalm 34:19ff; Proverbs 29:23. **f)** Chapter 38:16; Genesis 19:19; 1 Samuel 2:6. **s)** Of the humble. Malachi 2:9; Job 5:11.

**v. 9. m)** Interpreters vary greatly here. The Easterners do not render the words as "safe," but the sense which they thought was inherent. Meanwhile, there is a wonderous [variation], as in the Vulgate. Saadia [Gaon] follows Kimchi. So also: "And you have gone up" is not bad, comparing 1 Samuel 9:7. However, with the Zurich version: "You went straight to the king," Kimchi does this, comparing Ezekiel 23:25; Job 33:27; Song of Solomon 4:8; which places, however, do not certainly prove that meaning. Gastafio therefore, on page 84, was pleased with "You sang," because that is beyond doubt, comparing Exodus 15:1; Judges 5:1; Psalm 7:1.

# CHAPTER LIX.

<margin>

(3) They take hold of the grace of God in Christ the Redeemer through true faith, looking toward Christ (verses 16–19) and toward God the Father, who promises and pledges the work of our regeneration and renewal in the Holy Spirit to His Son (verses 20–21). Schmid still thinks this deals with the Jews in Babylon, as we said at Chapter 55, 6; on the other hand, Gurtler in his *Prophetic Theology* (page 694 and following) thinks this and the preceding Chapter 58 look toward our own times, which can be established thus: (a) because the final section of this chapter, according to Paul in Romans 11, 26, deals with the conversion of the Jews to occur in the last time before the end of the world; therefore the preceding sections look toward prior times. (b) because Chapter 53 deals with the passion and death of the Messiah, Chapter 54 with the calling of the nations, and Chapter 55 with the selling of spiritual goods under the Antichrist. Therefore (he concludes) the following things deal with the fates of the church to be fulfilled until the conversion of the Jews, etc. Since this has not yet happened in Israel according to the flesh, Maius (in *Economy*, page 979) rightly thinks its fulfillment is still to be expected; while others (like Dorsch on verse 20) think the conversion—that is, the turning away of iniquity from Jacob—has happened since the time of Christ and has been continuously propagated until now. However, we cannot deal with this more extensively here. Tremellius and others translate: *for justice*, namely that true justice of which Chapter 45, 24; Romans 9, 31–32; Philippians 3, 6, 9 speak. But Schmid, along with the Zurich version, prefers *in justice*; because he who cries in justice or justly (cf. Chapter 57, 17. Chapter 33, 11; Numbers 23, 21; Psalm 10, 7, 11; Job 4, 8. **g)** verse 6; Chapter 10, 1; Numbers 21, 21. **verse 5. h)** *Eggs*, Chapter 10, 14; Deuteronomy 22, 6; Job 39, 14. **i)** of an asp or a basilisk, Chapter 11, 8; Proverbs 23, 32. **k)** they hatch, Chapter 34, 15. *Basilisk's eggs* are crimes and wicked deeds which, having been conceived in thought, are hatched through works. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* II, page 405 and following. But to us (says Schmid) this is proven along with Brentius: that it still mostly deals with false doctrine, etc. The same false doctrine is understood by the spider's web. **l)** *webs*. verse 6. Concerning the etymology, thus Gusset, page 751: *The spider's web*, he says, this name is unique because in the center, pouring out many threads from itself in every direction, it is an image of a fertile fountain, sending out streams from itself into all parts. However, it can also be compared to the Hebrew *qir* (wall), verse 10, or the Arabic *qur* (a fresh rope); likewise the Arabic root for capturing and circumventing prey from ambush and secretly. **m)** *spider*. Job 8, 14. Which does not weave its nets in vain, since it captures flies and gnats with them, which it eats. Whence many of the ancients refer these words of the Prophet to the subtleties of heretics. But if their webs are useful to spiders, they are nevertheless useless to us. Therefore the Prophet does not compare the impious to spiders, but their works to spider webs, which profit humans nothing. compare verse 6. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* II, page 603. **n)** they weave. Chapter 19, 9. From this the name *arachne* <note>Greek for spider</note> was made according to Bochart.

<summary>This page concludes the discussion on the blessings of the Sabbath (Isaiah 58) and begins Chapter 59, which explains that God's perceived distance is not due to a lack of power but is caused by human sin. The text uses vivid metaphors of vipers' eggs and spider webs to describe the poisonous and fragile nature of wicked deeds and false doctrines.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the description of societal decay and divine intervention in Isaiah 59 to the glorious restoration of Zion in Isaiah 60. The commentary shifts from themes of judgment to the arrival of the "Light," interpreted here as the advent of the Messiah and the inclusion of the nations in the New Testament church.</meta>

# ISAIAH CHAPTER 60.

<margin>
Chapter 60.
**Prophetic Reading**
**Ki Tavo**
<note>Hebrew: "Ki Tavo" (When you enter) refers to the weekly Torah portion (Deuteronomy 26:1–29:8) for which this chapter serves as the accompanying reading from the Prophets in the Jewish liturgy.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
...but we cannot [deny] that even the final fulfillment of these promises refers to the end [of time] (compare the words of Dorscheus in his notes on chapter 6, verse 9) based on a comparison with Revelation chapters 21 and 22, which frequently look back to this passage. Unless...
</margin>

<margin>
(d) Chapter 43:17; 54:10; 55:13; Matthew 16:18.
**CHAPTER 60, verse 1.** (a)
**Arise therefore, O Jerusalem,** which Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note> adds again in this place and in verses 4, 12, and 17, as in chapter 54:1. Namely, the mystical or spiritual [Jerusalem] of Galatians 4:26; see the note above on chapter 51:17. This chapter is immediately connected to the end of the preceding one, and the distinguished character of the New Testament—which was mentioned there—is more fully explained to a repentant Jerusalem. The words are those of a Divine Person: either God the Father, as in chapter 59:20–21, or rather of Jehovah the Messiah Himself (here in verses 7, 9, 10, 13, and 16; compare chapter 61:1). He rouses the Jewish church—which according to Scripture was obscured by the darkness of traditions and false opinions (just as the whole world in verse 3 was obscured by the darkness of idolatry; compare chapter 9:1, Matthew 4:16, Luke 1:78–79, 2:32)—or, according to Maius in *Economia Temporum* page 979, He rouses the Jewish people who have been long without a King or Prince (according to Hosea 3:4), so that they may finally arise from the darkness (Ephesians 5:14) and from their squalor (as in chapter 51:17 and 52:2). According to scholarly interpretation, this chapter describes: I. The light of the New Testament Church. II. The majesty of that same light (verse 17 onwards). Interpreters differ on the time of fulfillment. Schmid concludes from verses 2 and 3 that this refers to the beginnings of the New Testament, because the whole earth of the Gentiles is called dark, and the nations are predicted to flow toward Jerusalem. However, according to the mind of Gusset in *Prophetic Theology* page 1130 and others, the glory of the church in the "last times" is described here, which is clear from verse 11 onwards, where it is promised that the gates of the church will be closed neither by day nor by night, the sun will not lose its light, and the days of misery will be ended. We recognize the benefits of Christ provided to the Church in both views, and we hold to the scriptural sense, yet...
</margin>

1 Arise,<sup>a</sup> shine,<sup>b</sup> for<sup>c</sup> your light<sup>d</sup> has come,<sup>e</sup> and the glory<sup>f</sup> of the LORD<sup>g</sup> has risen<sup>h</sup> upon you.<sup>i</sup>
2 For behold,<sup>k</sup> the darkness<sup>l</sup> shall cover the earth,<sup>m</sup> and thick darkness<sup>n</sup> the peoples;<sup>o</sup> but upon you<sup>p</sup> the LORD<sup>q</sup> shall rise,<sup>r</sup> and His glory<sup>s</sup> shall be seen<sup>t</sup> upon you.<sup>u</sup>
3 And the nations<sup>z</sup> shall walk<sup>a'</sup> to your light,<sup>b'</sup> and kings<sup>c'</sup> to the brightness<sup>d'</sup> of your rising.<sup>e'</sup>
4 Lift up your eyes<sup>f'</sup> round about<sup>h'</sup> and see;<sup>i'</sup> they all<sup>k'</sup> gather together,<sup>l'</sup> they come to you;<sup>m'</sup> your sons<sup>o'</sup> shall come from afar,<sup>p'</sup> and your daughters<sup>r'</sup> shall be nursed<sup>u'</sup> at your side.<sup>t'</sup>
5 Then<sup>x'</sup> you shall see<sup>y'</sup> and be radiant,<sup>z'</sup> and your heart<sup>C</sup> shall throb<sup>A</sup> and overflow;<sup>B</sup> for the abundance<sup>G</sup> of the sea<sup>H</sup> shall be turned<sup>D</sup> to you;<sup>F</sup> the wealth<sup>I</sup> of the nations<sup>K</sup> shall come<sup>L</sup> to you.<sup>M</sup>

...who would want to wrongly assert with some that the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> looks not to the end of the world, but only to the final fates of the Jewish Commonwealth—an assertion which the Apocalypse itself (composed long after the destruction of Jerusalem) and a careful consideration of it do not permit. (f) <term>to enlighten</term> <note>original: "illuminare"</note> 1 Samuel 14:29; Proverbs 4:18. That is, according to Scripture: allow the darkness in you to be dispelled, and do not deny entry to the rising light. And so, according to Jonah and the Syriac: also give forth light. These are evangelical imperatives, as in chapter 55:1. (g) <term>because he came</term> <note>original: "quia venit"</note> John 1:11. Gusset (page 120) thinks Abraham ibn Ezra interprets this to mean "your light has set," comparing it to verse 20 and Genesis 15:12, but this is against the sense of the context. For "Light" here is not the Sun properly speaking, which is said to "set" in the scriptures; but it is Jehovah the Messiah Himself, who is preached here not as setting, but as rising (verses 2 and 3), looking back to the connection in chapter 59:20. (h) **Your eternal light,** verses 19 and 20; that great light of chapter 9:1; and the essential light of John 1:5, 9, 10, chapter 8:12, etc. **Light of Light,** according to the Nicene Creed. The Jews acknowledge that the Messiah is to be understood here in the *Yalkut* <note>Yalkut Shimoni, a medieval midrashic compilation</note> on this passage (Part II, folio 56). In the *Pesikta Rabbathi* (column 36), they ask: **"What is that which is said: 'And in your light we see or shall see light'?"** and they respond: **"This is the Light of the Messiah, as it was said in Genesis 1:4: 'And God saw the light, that it was good,' for God blessed the age and the works of the Messiah even before the world was created."** Likewise in *Echa Rabbathi* (folio 68), Rabbi Biba Sangorianus proves the Messiah is called by the name **"Light"** from the words of Daniel 2:22: "and light dwells with God." Rabbi Abba Serongianus shows the same from this passage in Isaiah and the cited Daniel verse in *Bereshit Rabba* (folio 3). So too the holy Apocalypse [Revelation] 21:23 says: **"its lamp is the Lamb."** (i) **the glory of Jehovah,** the same Messiah, the Son and Glory of the Father. Chapter 4:5; 58:8; Hebrews 1:3; John 1:14. Compare Exodus 29:43; 40:34–35. (k) **having arisen upon you from heaven and manifested in the flesh.** See verses 2 and 3; chapter 58:10; Malachi 3:20; Luke 1:78–79. (l) Chapter 59:2. (m) Chapter 8:22; 9:1; 29:18; 59:9. (n) Chapter 29:10. (o) <term>darkness</term> <note>original: "caligo"</note>, Deuteronomy 4:11; Jeremiah 13:16. (p) Chapter 49:1; 55:4. Jonah <note>Targum</note> translates as **"kingdoms."** As once darkness covered Egypt (Exodus 10:11), so here. (q) See verse 1. (r) Zechariah 9:14; compare Exodus 40:34. (s) 1 Kings 8:10–11. Jonah: **"but the Shekhinah <note>the Divine Presence</note> of the Lord shall dwell in you, and His glory shall be revealed upon you."** **verse 3.** (s) And the nations shall walk, chapter 2:3; Psalm 47:8–9; Ephesians 2:12. No longer, as once, in the vanity of their minds (Romans 1:24; Ephesians 4:17–18), but as children of light (Ephesians 5:8; compare Acts 17:30). (t) To your light (verse 1), so that it may direct them and lead them into the way of salvation. Compare Revelation 21:24. (u) Even Kings. Verse 10, 16; chapter 49:23; 52:2; Psalm 148:11. For the church does not eliminate the royal and all magisterial dignity, but consecrates it to Christ (Dorscheus). (x) To the splendor, chapter 59:10; 62:1. (y) **of your rising**—that is, of the Messiah or that light which rises for you (verses 1 and 2), meaning the light of the gospel (compare 2 Peter 1:19). **verse 4.** (z) To make the promise more certain, the church is brought into the present moment, as it were, so that she may look around and see the multitude of nations gathering to her. Compare chapter 49:18. (a') Compare John 4:35. (b') All those whom I said would come (verse 3). (c') They are gathered from all parts of the world. Verse 7; compare chapter 56:8; Psalm 102:23. (d) Verse 5. Septuagint, as in Matthew 8:11. (e) Verse 9; chapter 43:6. (f) Chapter 49:12. (g) Chapter 49:22; compare Galatians 3:28; 1 Peter 3:7. (h) At the side, chapter 66:12. (i) Zurich Bible: "they shall be cherished." Others: "carried by nurses." Neumann: <term>algebuntur</term>, that is, "they shall be nourished or brought up." Compare Ruth 4:16; 2 Samuel 4:4. Varenius: "they shall be established." **verse 5.** (k) Then you shall see what I now predict will happen. Compare chapter 40:5. Others following Ibn Ezra derive it from the root for **"fear"** <note>Hebrew: yara</note> (though Kimchi rejects this as an error): "then you shall fear" (compare Matthew 2:3). (l) **it shall flow together** <note>original: "adfluet"</note>, that is, you shall go out to meet your sons and daughters joyfully to receive them. Tremellius: "flow together." Compare chapter 2:2; Jeremiah 51:44. Others: "you shall break out like a river," or as Gusset (page 498): "you shall run down like a river into remote regions, copiously and swiftly." Jonah and the Syriac from the Chaldean meaning: "you shall be illuminated" or **"you shall shine"**; however, biblical usage does not support this. Compare Psalm 34:6; Jeremiah 31:12; Micah 4:1. (m) **and shall be amazed** at the unexpected and unhoped-for event. Compare Jeremiah 33:9. (n) **soon with joy and poured-out gladness your heart shall expand.** Psalm 119:32; 1 Kings 5:9; 2 Corinthians 6:11, 13. Compare Genesis 45:26–27 and for the matter Luke 2:52; Acts 10:34–35, 11:18. (o) **because it is converted to you.** 1 Samuel 4:19; chapter 10:6. (p) Zurich Bible: **"abundance."** Tremellius: **"the roaring of the sea."** But most with Ibn Ezra and Kimchi: **"a multitude like the sea."** Compare chapter 17:12 and Genesis 17:4–5. (q) A host, chapter 8:4. Others: "abundance" or "wealth of the nations," as in verse 11; chapter 10:14; 61:6. (r) Verse 4, 6; compare Psalm 87:5–6. **verse 6.** (s) **A troop, a multitude, or a company,** commonly called a **Caravan** (s). 2 Kings 9:17. (t) **shall cover you.** Compare Exodus 8:2; chapter 10:5, 15; chapter 16:13; Numbers 22:5, 11. (u) Most translate as **"dromedaries"** or **"dromedary camels."** But Bochart (*Hieroz.* I page 82), from Arabic usage, says this does not denote a specific species like the dromedary, but a certain age, specifically "younger camels." So also Kimchi, Abarbanel, and Vatablus. Maius notes the Arabic root properly means "to go before." From this meaning, D. Neumann (on Exodus page 165) appropriately derives the meaning of "dromedary" as one that surpasses others in speed. Isidore (*Origins* XII. 1): **"The dromedary is a kind of camel, of smaller stature but faster, whence it gets its name,"** for *dromos* in Greek means "running" or speed. **"It is accustomed to travel a hundred or more miles in one day."** Curtius (Book V, chapter 2): **"Dromedary camels were among the gifts, having exceptional speed."** (x) Of the Midianites and Ephah, descendants of Abraham through Keturah; the founder of these nations was Midian, son of Abraham, and Ephah was his grandson. See Genesis 25:2, 4; 1 Chronicles 1:32–33. Nowhere are camels more frequent than in the land of Midian. See Judges 6:5, 7:12. (y) All. Verse 4. Not as once only one queen with her retinue (1 Kings 10:1), but everyone. (z) From Sheba. Psalm 72:10. Sheba was also a grandson of Abraham and Keturah, from the son Jokshan (Genesis 25:3). Others, however, refer our people to Genesis 10:7, 28.

<meta>This page continues the exegesis of Isaiah 60, focusing on the gathering of the nations and the wealth of the world flowing toward the "New Jerusalem" or the Church. The previous page established the identity of the "Light" as the Messiah; here, the text details the specific peoples (Kedar, Nebaioth, Tarshish) who will submit to this divine kingdom.</meta>

# ISAIAH. CHAPTER 60. D

(a) **gold and frankincense,** compare 1 Kings 10:10; Jeremiah 6:20; Psalm 72:15. (b) **camels will carry,** Genesis 37:25; 1 Kings 10:2. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note> renders this: *they were loaded with gold and frankincense; and those who come with them shall declare the glory of the Lord.* Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish commentator</note> explains it thus: *merchants will bring frankincense and gold for sale on camels, and also as an offering or gift to the King Messiah.* Compare Matthew 2:11 regarding the gifts of the Magi, who came from the East or Persia; whereas the Sabaeans are to the south of Judea. (c) **and the praises of Jehovah the Messiah.** See verse 2; chapter 63:7; Psalm 78:4. (d) Chapter 40:9; chapter 61:1.

**Verse 7. (e)** The Tigurinus Bible <note>A 16th-century Latin translation from Zurich</note> reads: *All the sheep.* The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation</note> reads: *all the cattle*: for this term also includes goats under its meaning. See Genesis 27:9; chapter 38:17; Leviticus 1:10. **(f)** Psalm 120:5; Song of Solomon 1:4. The Septuagint reads: *of Arabia.* Jonathan reads: *of the Arabs.* See the note above on chapter 21:16. Kedar and Nebaioth were grandsons of Abraham, through his son Ishmael, whom he had by Hagar. See Genesis 25:13; 1 Chronicles 1:29. One will not wonder that the livestock of these peoples is praised in such illustrious words in Scripture if they know that the wealth of these nations consisted almost entirely of livestock. Diodorus and Strabo write explicitly about this regarding the Nabataeans, as cited in Bochart’s *Hierozoicon*, Part I, page 535. **(g)** See verse 4. **(h)** **rams.** Genesis 31:38. **(i)** Of the Nabataeans, in Arabia Petraea. Nebaioth was the firstborn of Ishmael, Genesis 25:13; chapter 28:9; chapter 36:3. Secular writers seem to have included the related Kedareans under the name "Nabataeans," whom they frequently celebrate; whereas in Holy Scripture, mention of the Kedareans is more frequent. **(k)** **they shall minister** or **serve you.** Verse 10; chapter 56:6; 61:6. Just as the Septuagint correctly concludes from this description that by the "cattle of the Arabs" we should understand the Arabs themselves; so by the "rams" we also understand the Nabataeans themselves and their leaders or priests. Compare Ezekiel 34:17. **(l)** **they shall be offered,** Leviticus 2:12, or **they shall go up,** that is:

<column-break/>

7 <gloss>a</gloss> They shall come <gloss>b</gloss> gold and frankincense they shall carry, and the praises <gloss>c</gloss> of Jehovah they shall proclaim. <gloss>d</gloss> All the flocks of <gloss>e</gloss> Kedar <gloss>f</gloss> shall be gathered to you, the rams of <gloss>h</gloss> Nebaioth <gloss>i</gloss> shall minister to you; <gloss>k</gloss> they shall go up with acceptance <gloss>l</gloss> upon my altar, <gloss>m</gloss> and the house <gloss>o</gloss> of my glory <gloss>p</gloss> I will glorify.

8 <gloss>q</gloss> Who are these <gloss>r</gloss> that fly like a cloud <gloss>s</gloss> and like doves to their windows?

9 <gloss>t</gloss> For me <gloss>u</gloss> the islands shall wait, <gloss>x</gloss> and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring your sons from afar, their silver and their gold with them, <gloss>y</gloss> to the name of Jehovah your God, and to the Holy One of Israel, for <gloss>z</gloss> He has glorified you.

10 <gloss>a</gloss> And the sons of foreigners shall build your walls, <gloss>b</gloss> and their kings shall minister to you; <gloss>c</gloss> for in my wrath I struck you, and in my favor I have had mercy on you.

it will no longer need the light of the Sun. The sense is: the Church is to be illustrated by divine glory far more splendidly than the Sun and Moon illustrate this vast theater of the world. Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa, a prominent 17th-century commentator</note> on Revelation 21:23. However, according to Schmidt, the Sun and Moon, which shone upon the church before the Messiah began to shine, are the shadows of the Mosaic Law. There was indeed some light in the Old Testament, but it was plainly absorbed by the clarity of the New Testament light. Jeremiah 31:35; Genesis 1:16. (m) and regarding the silence in verses 4-5, by which the moon otherwise shines at night. (n) chapter 13:10; compare chapter 24:23; Genesis 37:9. (o) it will not shine (Genesis 1:15-17) for itself, being equipped with a greater light. Compare above, chapter 30:26. (p) Jehovah the Messiah. verses 1, 2; Revelation 21:23. (q) for eternal light, verse 20; Psalm 84:12. For the kingdom of grace in this earth is to be consummated in the kingdom of glory of the future age, and absorbed by it. Vitringa on Revelation 22:5. (r) verse 7; chapter 52:1. *God is your glory* <note>original Greek: ὁ Θεός δόξα σου</note> compare Revelation 21:11, 23. --- **Verse 20.** (s) It shall no longer set. Jeremiah 15:9; Micah 3:6; Amos 8:9. (t) Your Sun, verse 19. The Sun of Righteousness, Christ (Malachi 4:2), shall not be hidden from your eyes, nor shall any false obscuring of the truth occur. Compare Revelation 21:25; 22:5. (u) And your Moon shall not withdraw itself, or suffer an eclipse. Compare Joel 3:15. Jonathan: Your kingdom shall no longer cease, and your glory shall not be taken away. (x) for, as has already been said in the preceding verse, Jehovah etc. (y) and they shall be finished. chapter 38:12; 1 Kings 7:51. (z) the days of your mourning. chapter 61:2; compare above, verse 18; Revelation 7:16-17. These words persuade us, says Dorsch, that this chapter is to be understood as referring to the New Testament. Nor does any doubt remain about that, but Interpreters disagree on this: whether this text speaks of the church militant on earth, or indeed of the church triumphant in heaven? The latter pleased Jerome and many others; the former pleased Luther, Brentius, and others. Schmidt judges that both opinions can be very well joined here, and that John in Revelation 22 cited this text with respect to its ultimate fulfillment in the kingdom of glory. This is entirely correct: for Isaiah in this place, and John in Revelation 21 and 22, so exhibited the type of the Church—to be adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit on this earth and illustrated by divine glory—that under the same narration, a taste and image of eternal life is also exhibited. For that these places of Isaiah and John cannot otherwise be taken absolutely regarding the church received into heaven, Gurtlerus in *Prophetic Theology* (p. 794 and following) proves thus: (1) because after the glory and illumination of the church, they add a new influx of peoples and nations to it; compare in this chapter verse 3, 11 with verses 1, 2; and chapter 66:19, 23 with verses 10, 11, 12; likewise Revelation 21:24, 26 with verse 1 and following. (2) Here in verse 12, God threatens devastation to those nations which refuse to come to the glorious church; but after the last day there will be no occasion for embracing or repudiating the gospel, nor fear of temporal punishment. (3) John in Revelation 22:10 is forbidden from sealing the words of this prophecy, because the time is near when they must be fulfilled. But in the next life, neither do prophecies have a place, nor are they sealed there; compare 1 Corinthians 13:8, 12. Add to this that according to verse 11 of this chapter and Revelation 21:24, 26, the Kings of the earth bring their glory into the new Jerusalem; but they will not carry glory into heaven, rather the pious Kings will receive it there. Likewise, that this Jerusalem, having arisen from heaven, is to be exhibited on earth (Revelation 21:2, 10), whereas on the last day the righteous are to be transferred to heavenly seats (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Add that verse 22 of this chapter, as Schmidt observes, cannot be taken as referring to eternal life, in which the multiplication of one into a thousand etc. is not given.

# ISAIAH. CHAPTER 61.

<margin>
**CHAPTER LXI, 1. p)** chapter 11:2; 40:13; 59:19; 63:10, 11, 14. **q)** Verse 11. Chapter 7:7. **r)** Compare 11:2; 59:21; 60:22. | Luke 4:18; Colossians 2:9. The Messiah had affirmed in chapter 60:22 that He would fulfill all promises and hasten them in His own time. Now, to declare that He is equipped with sufficient gifts and powers to complete such a great work, He says that *the Spirit of the Lord God—proceeding from the Father and Himself from eternity—is upon Him and rests within Him* (cf. chapter 11:2). He says He is *anointed with immense gifts*, so that He might report this joyful news of redemption from spiritual captivity and blindness, etc. He brings this not only to the Jews in the days of His earthly life, but also to those who would one day turn from transgression (cf. chapter 59:20). He proclaims the *year of favor, that is, of gracious acceptance and forgiveness* (verse 2), according to the covenantal promise indicated shortly before in chapter 59:21. To His enemies, however, He will preach and bring a day of vengeance, thereby most fully completing all those things mentioned so far in verses 1–9. From here, the Israelite Church responds to this illustrious sermon and promise of the Messiah, accepting it with exultant true faith, and gives thanks to God for the magnificent and beautiful spiritual garment (verse 10, compared with verse 3) and for the fruit of righteousness and glory sprouting most abundantly (verse 11). These are the notes from Masius’s *Economy*, page 930. <note>Andreas Masius was a 16th-century Catholic humanist and scholar of Syriac.</note> We have, therefore, in this chapter: I. *The Messiah’s sermon and repeated promise* (verses 1–9). II. *The Church’s response and song or jubilee* (verses 10, 11). Our scholars—Dorsch, Schmidt, and others—prove with many arguments that this chapter is to be understood as referring to no one other than the Messiah alone: (1) from the divine works in verses 1, 2, 3; (2) because it is Jehovah who speaks in verse 8; (3) the speaker is the same as in chapter 60; (4) because Christ Himself in Luke [interprets it so].
</margin>

**CHAPTER LXII, verse 1. h)** For Zion’s sake. chapter 49:14. <meta>This page transitions from the celebratory promises of Jerusalem's restoration in Chapter 62 to the dramatic, investigative dialogue of Chapter 63 regarding a mysterious, blood-stained figure arriving from the land of Edom. It continues the scholarly tradition of interpreting these prophetic visions through a Christological lens.</meta>

<header>ISAIAH 63 .CHAPTER. 63</header>

# **Who is this**$^h$ **coming**$^i$ **from Edom**$^k$ **with crimsoned**$^l$ **garments**$^m$ **from Bozrah**$^n$? **This one who is glorious**$^o$ **in his apparel**$^p$, **marching**$^q$ **in the greatness of his strength**$^r$? **It is I, speaking**$^s$ **in righteousness**$^t$

### CHAPTER LXIII.

<margin>
63. & 66. (2) Because this chapter in the New Testament is clearly referred to Christ in Revelation 19:15, where it is argued by Dorsch and Schmid <note>Johann Georg Dorsch and Sebastian Schmid, 17th-century Lutheran theologians</note> that this is not a mere allusion but a direct citation. They prove this from the fact that the words from Psalm 2:9, cited in the same place, cannot be understood otherwise than as referring properly to Christ.
</margin>

III. The object and subject matter of this prophecy are questioned. Jerome <note>Early Church Father and translator of the Vulgate</note> and other ancients (as we have said) think Christ is represented here ascending into heaven; however, Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a medieval Franciscan exegete</note> rightly disputes this in his commentary on this place. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian known for historical interpretations</note> wrongly takes it to refer to the liberation of the Jews by Judas Maccabeus. Others refer it to the liberation of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity, but this is also contrary to the context; unless, following the Book of Revelation, you understand here "mystical Jews" (that is, true confessors of Christ) and a "mystical Babylon." Others (such as Luther <note>Martin Luther, the Reformer</note> in his commentary and partly Gussetus <note>Jacques Gousset, a Hebrew scholar</note>) refer it to Christ utterly destroying the Jewish synagogue through the Romans; this is much more probable (compare the notes on chapter 34:1). Others, even in Jerome's time, refer it to Christ coming to judgment and destroying the Antichrist, as Lyra does. Finally, others refer it to the suffering Christ, such as Glassius, Dorsch, Schmid, and many others. On this chapter, Pfeiffer <note>August Pfeiffer, a Lutheran orientalist</note> says (in the words of Glassius): "It contains a sorrowful depiction of the passion and death of Jesus Christ, and especially its fruitful resolution: namely, how he, emerging as victor over his enemies—the devil, death, and hell, who were plotting his total destruction—celebrated a triumph by rising from the dead, ascending to heaven, and sitting at the right hand of the Father; and how he still carries a trophy over every adversary until the end of the age, and rescues his Church from them, eventually to destroy the entire hostile crowd with a full excision."

How this expanded view also includes what others want, specifically Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow, a 17th-century theologian</note>, who explains this oracle not as the suffering Christ placating God's wrath through his passion, but as Christ the King of the Church, most powerfully liberating and defending his people from external enemies. Dorsch writes that he proves this because: (1) He takes vengeance on earthly enemies in verse 4. (2) He has a garment sprinkled not with his own blood, but with the blood of the strongest of those he cast down to the ground, and indeed (3) contaminated in verse 3. (4) Because he is said to tread down not the devil or hell, but the "peoples" in verse 6. (5) Because in his passion he did not come from Idumaea <note>The Greek name for Edom</note>, nor from its capital Bozrah (verse 1). (6) Because Christ in his passion felt the Father's wrath rather than supporting himself by his own indignation (contrary to verse 5). (7) Because he does not contaminate us with his blood but purges us. (8) Because the winepress in Holy Scripture signifies vengeance and the power of the one treading (Joel 3:13, Lamentations 1:15, Revelation 14:19, 20). He concedes, however, that this act of Christ toward external enemies faithfully presupposes the act of the passion, as the one by whose power all enemies are conquered. To this we answer: Dorsch asks (1) whether it appears from verse 4 that the speech is about earthly enemies. For it is the day of your redemption, and also the day of vengeance and the time for those to be avenged. Regarding (2), did Christ on the day of his passion have a garment sprinkled with his own blood? The sprinkling arising from the blood of enemies is said metaphorically, whether you understand it as the suffering Christ or the triumphant Christ. For the antecedent is placed for the consequent: the shedding of blood for victory. Thus also the "strongest" cast to the ground is said metaphorically, in which sense Satan himself is said to be cast down to the earth in Revelation 12:9. Regarding (3), the *contamination of the garment* by the blood of his enemies (verse 3) is also said metaphorically, in whatever sense it is accepted regarding Christ. Regarding (4), the fact that "peoples" are said to be trodden down follows from the fact that Christ's enemies are described like an army into which peoples usually flow, and this pertains to the continued metaphor; nor should the treading down of peoples properly so called (insofar as they are enemies of Christ, infected by sin and paganism) be excluded from the act of Christ's passion. Regarding (5), in the passion he did not come from the literal Idumaea and Bozrah, but the spiritual ones. For we have already said that Idumaea and Bozrah mystically denote the entire <term>πoνηρόπολιν</term> <note>original Greek: "City of Evil" or "City of the Wicked"</note>, just as the descendants of Esau are presented as an image of the reprobate in Romans 9. Nor in the liberation of the Church from external enemies does Christ come from a literal Idumaea or Bozrah. Regarding (6), the Father's wrath does not exclude Christ's power and his roaring against enemies, even in the midst of his passion. Regarding (7), the answer is in the response to (2). Regarding (8), it is not contradictory for someone to exercise vengeance and to suffer while being avenged; nor does the metaphor of the winepress contradict Christ's passion if it is explained in the way we have said. This passage speaks of that act in which he was so alone that every subordinate help is excluded. Yet in the liberation of the Church, God very often uses means—which is the argument of Glassius. Tarnovius responds to this with many points, but here Christ is said to be alone, excluding every outsider. Thus far are the words of Dorsch, which we wanted to present in full so that in a difficult question, the reasons for both opinions might be immediately available to the judgment of the prudent reader. See our opinion above at chapter 34 and in the following notes. **i)** Who comes (chapter 62:11) as victor over enemies and Savior of his own. **k)** See chapter 34:5, 6 and compare Psalm 137:7. **l)** *That is, sprinkled*, vibrant, or reddened (1). Thus Kimchi, Mordecai, Pomarius, Aquinas, etc. explain it; also the Greeks and the Syrian. This interpretation is clearly confirmed by verse 2: *why is it red?* etc. (Bochart, *Hieroz. I*, p. 112; compare also notes on Zechariah 6:3). **m)** See Revelation 19:13. **n)** verses 3, 6. Amos 1:12. *By Edom* here, nothing less is understood than what the people of that time called Edom; by Bozrah, nothing less than the capital of Idumaea known by that name around that age. The names of Edom and Bozrah are mystical and hieroglyphical here, to be understood spiritually, as in chapter 1:10 Sodom and Gomorrah. Edom here denotes the kingdom or empire that is the rival and enemy of the Church, opposed to the true kingdom of Christ, which knew and drank the blood of the confessors of truth; an allusion is made both to the thing and to the name אדום <note>Edom</note>, meaning Red, from the drinking of a red-colored liquid. Bozrah here signifies the capital of that empire, extremely well fortified: *Whose officials are the clusters of the vine of the earth* (Revelation 14:18, 19) where God would take vengeance on the enemies of the church, removing them with the shedding of their blood. For there is an allusion here to the true meaning of the word בצר <note>Bozrah</note>, which signifies both a fortification and a vintage/grape-harvest. (Vitringa on Revelation 1:20, p. 69). **o)** That is, here I say, honorable, or decorous, exceedingly excellent (1). Compare chapter 2:10. **p)** Compare again Revelation 19:13. **q)** Entering/marching. (5) chapter 51:14. Jeremiah 2:20. **r)** Deuteronomy 4:37. Jeremiah 10:12. Revelation 5:5. Not at all weary, and surrounded by a great army (Revelation 19:14). **s)** *The Messiah answers.* *It is I.* **s)** Who speak (chapter 52:6).

Namely, not an ordinary angel or legate, but the Son of God himself, the savior of Israel (v. 8, 9) and the Redeemer of Jacob (Genesis 48, 16), who is so from God and comes to men that what he sees, he himself both does and testifies (John 3, 11; ch. 5, 19), and in him God is discerned (John 14, 9), since he is <note>original: "ἀπαύגασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴר τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ"</note> "the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his being" (Hebrews 1, 3); the very "face of God" (Exodus 33, 14, 15), in whom is the "name of God" (Exodus 23, 20, 21), and <note>original: "πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος"</note> "all the fullness of the deity," and thus even the divine essence itself (Colossians 2, 9). He is Jehovah himself (Genesis 16, 10-13; Jeremiah 23, 6) and the Holy One of Israel (Ephesians 1, 4; ch. 30, 11; ch. 47, 4; Psalm 78, 41), appearing to Moses (Exodus 3, 2 seq.) and to Joshua (Joshua 5, 13) and the leader of the people (Exodus 13, 21; ch. 14, 19), etc. Compare the note from Rabbi Bechai on Exodus 23, 20; also the Septuagint in this place. a) v. 8; ch. 43, 3; ch. 45, 21. b) "out of love" without end (ch. 43, 4; Deuteronomy 7, 7, 8; Jeremiah 31, 3; Ephesians 5, 25). c) "and because of his clemency" (1) (Genesis 19, 16), of which Numbers 6, 25. d) this very Angel of God claimed them as his own (ch. 43, 1; ch. 44, 22). e) "and he took them up," as it were. <term>Piel</term> <note>A Hebrew verb stem usually indicating intensive action</note> (1) compare ch. 40, 15. f) "and he carried them" (Exodus 19, 4, 5; Deuteronomy 1, 31; ch. 32, 11; Psalm 28, 9; Hebrews 1, 3). g) "all the days of eternity" or "the age," that is, the most ancient times, which have long since passed away. v. 11; Amos 9, 11; Micah 7, 14; Malachi 3, 4. Properly of God and Christ (Micah 5, 1). Compare note above ch. 44, 7; ch. 46, 9; ch. 57, 11; and 2 Kings 5, 27.
v. 10. h) "But they," most graciously adopted and heaped with benefits (v. 7, 8; ch. 1, 2). i) "repeatedly rebelled" (ch. 1, 20; Numbers 20, 24; Psalm 78, 8, 40, 56). <note>original: "ἀπειθήσαν"</note> "They were disobedient" (Acts 19, 9). Compare Numbers 14, 22; Psalm 78, 57; Psalm 95, 9. k) "and they grieved" (Psalm 56, 6; Genesis 6, 6; ch. 54, 7; 1 Samuel 20, 3, 34). l) v. 11, 14; ch. 48, 16. Paul looked back to this in Ephesians 4, 30. **It is also to be observed here the testimony concerning the Holy Trinity**: for mention has been made of three persons so far: God the Father (v. 7, 8), the Angel of the Face or the Son (v. 9), and the Holy Spirit in this verse. m) "wherefore he was turned against them" (Job 19, 19; ch. 30, 21; Psalm 15, 20). Jonathan [the Targumist]: "And his Word was turned to them into an enemy." n) Compare Job 13, 24; Lamentations 2, 4.

v. 11. p) S. Verse 9. In which he took them up and promised they would be his sons. r) By <term>asyndeton</term> <note>a literary device where conjunctions like "and" are omitted for emphasis</note>, of Moses and his people, looking back to the promises made to them. For one should not think here of any merit of Moses or the people, but only of God's promise. S. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan</note> says, not poorly: "And he spared for the glory of his name, for the memory of his kindnesses from of old," etc. Others, however, take this whole clause as being spoken by the people in this manner: "Even if at last (in distress, see Deuteronomy 30:1, Jeremiah 23:20, Ch. 30:24) Israel remembered (Deuteronomy 7:18) the times of old and God’s benefits (see this full phrase in Deuteronomy 32:4), and him who extracted and rescued his people (as in 2 Samuel 22:17, Psalm 18:17) saying: Where is he now?" etc. So says Gusset on page 482: The Divine Person, he says, is here called "The One Extracting the people" or "The Extractor of his people" from the waters. Yet there is an allusion to the name of Moses (Exodus 2:10), so that God appears as the [God] of Moses himself. s) Where is he now? Verse 15. Jonathan prefixes: "lest they say"; either the Israelites themselves, as in Deuteronomy 31:17, Judges 6:13, 2 Kings 2:14, Jeremiah 2:6; or rather the profane enemies, as in Psalm 42:4, 11; compare Exodus 32:12, 13. t) Who brought them up from the sea? See Exodus 14:29, 30. u) With the shepherd of his flock, which can be understood either of Moses, comparing Numbers 27:17 and Psalm 77:21; or of Christ, as above in Ch. 40:11, Jeremiah 31:10, Ezekiel 34:23, Zechariah 13:7, Psalm 23:1, Psalm 80:2, etc.
