By the arm of Moses; to show that God was the supreme and principal cause, who used Moses as a leader. Verse 13. Ch. 48:22, Deuteronomy 8:2, 15. Others, following the Hebrew: "Who caused the arm of his glory to go at the right hand of Moses." b) I think mention is made of the right hand of Moses with respect to Moses' staff, mentioned in Exodus 4:17. For in his right hand he carried the staff, according to David Kimchi. c) S. [Schmid] and others translate this in the <term>Ablative</term> <note>a grammatical case often indicating "by means of"</note>: "by the arm of his beauty." Others, with the Hebrew, in the <term>Accusative</term>: "the arm of his glory." By which Ezra understands the Angel of the Lord, see verse 9, and we, along with Schmid, understand it as Christ. d) Exodus 14:21, Joshua 3:15, 16, Psalm 78:13, Nehemiah 9:11. e) "to make for himself," see verse 14, Genesis 11:4, 2 Samuel 7:19, 23. f) Verse 14, Jeremiah 32:20, Daniel 9:15; compare also Exodus 32:12, Numbers 14:16, 17, Joshua 2:10, and Joshua 7:9. g) Verse 13. g) Who led them. Verse 12, Jeremiah 2:5. h) Through the abysses of the sea. Ch. 51:10, Psalm 106:9. i) Like a horse. Ch. 30:16; to which Judah is also compared in Zechariah 10:3. k) Through the desert, dry (Ch. 41:18, Jeremiah 17:6) or level (Jeremiah 9:9). "The desert, and he did not stumble," as Jonathan adds. l) Thus the Israelites went through the channel of the sea no less securely, nor did they stumble. Ch. 40:30, Hosea 14:10, Proverbs 4:12, 19. Verse 14. m) Like some beast of burden. 2 Kings 3:9, Nehemiah 2:12, 14. n) Through the valley (Ch. 40:4) or the plain (Genesis 11:2). He alludes here to the descent into the sea, just as he alluded to the descent or departure in verse 11. o) Thus the Spirit of the Lord. Verse 10, Ch. 11:2, Ch. 40:11. p) Made him quiet or led him. Ezekiel 37:1, Ch. 40:2. For cattle and horses, when they descend from a mountain via a slope, are usually led very gently. q) Ch. 49:10. r) See verse 12, Jeremiah 31:10, Psalm 23:1, 2. s) Verse 11, Verse 12, Ch. 63:1. t) S. [Schmid]: "Look down, therefore, even now." Ch. 64:8, Deuteronomy 26:15, Psalm 80:15, Baruch 2:16. u) From heaven. Ch. 66:1, Psalm 102:20; see also 1 Kings 8:30, 2 Chronicles 6:23, etc. That thanksgiving in verse 7 and following is succeeded here by a most burning <term>litany</term> <note>a series of petitions used in church services or processions</note>, by which Israel seeks a gracious liberation and brings forward the reasons that might move God: God's ancient zeal, power, and mercy, his manifest affection (verses 15, 16), the promises given of old, the tyranny of the enemies, and the profanation of the Sanctuary (verses 17, 18), and their own misery and disgrace in their long-term abandonment (verse 19). See Musi, *Sacred Economy*, page 982. x) From the dwelling; 1 Kings 8:13, Habakkuk 3:11. y) Compare Psalm 11:4. z) Verse 12, Ch. 60:7, Ch. 64:10. a) For where is he? Verse 11, Psalm 89:50. b) Ch. 9:6, Ch. 37:32, Ch. 59:17, Zechariah 1:14, Ch. 8:2. c) S. [Schmid]: "your virtues" or "the miracles of your power" done of old. Ch. 33:13, Deuteronomy 3:24, Psalm 106:2, Psalm 115:4, 11, Psalm 150:2. d) The Septuagint, Vulgate, Tigurinus, etc.: "multitude"; Schmid: "for the commotion." See Ch. 13:12, Ch. 29:5, 7, 8, Jeremiah 31:20, etc. e) Your heart <note>literally "bowels"</note>. Ch. 15:11, Jeremiah 4:19. f) Your mercies. Verse 7, Ch. 54:7, 8. g) "They have restrained themselves toward me"; the Tigurinus version: "they are restrained." Ch. 54:11, Genesis 45:1. Verse 15. h) This connects with the whole of verse 15, the sense of which is: "Look down from heaven, stir up your zeal, and do not hold back your compassion, because you are our Father." S. [Schmid]. i) Ch. 64:7; compare Psalm 103:13. In that God is called Father, this looks back to the promise in verse 8: "And he said, surely they are my people, sons," etc. Therefore, these prayers are founded on that promise, and not on the merits of the Fathers, Abraham and Israel, about whom they most rightly say that they "do not know" them. S. [Schmid]. k) By which Father? Ch. 51:2. The Jews boasted in vain of this in Matthew 3:9 and John 8:39. l) This not only denies their knowledge (as in Job 28:7) but also their power of pitying and helping with any weight, and therefore denies all merit. S. [Schmid]; compare Hosea 12:5, Psalm 31:8. m) From whom they had their name. Ch. 48:1. n) He does not recognize us. Ch. 61:9, Psalm 103:16, Psalm 143:5, Ruth 2:10, 19. The Prophet speaks in the person of the faithful among the Jews, deploring the common degeneration of the whole nation from Abraham and Israel, and from their spirit and faith; as if to say: "Abraham does not know such sons of his, nor does Israel know such as most of us are." See above, Ch. 29:22, 23. Cocceius, *Lexicon*, page 294 and 505. Jonathan: "Because you are the one whose mercies are great toward us, like a father toward a son; for Abraham did not lead us out of Egypt, and Israel did not perform wonders for us in the desert." Kimchi, however, says: "Even if Abraham is our Father, he has been dead a long time: a natural father does not know his son or grandson except while he lives. But you, our Father, are living, and you remain from age to age, nor is it permitted for us to invoke any other but you: for in all ages, both past and future, you are our Father, and you are our redeemer from every distress, and from of old your name has been upon us," etc. o) Ch. 41:14, Ch. 59:20. p) Verse 19, Ch. 42:14. q) See Genesis 48:16, Job 19:25. Verse 17. r) Why? This is the cry of those supplicating here, as in Exodus 32:11, Jeremiah 15:18, Psalm 10, 1, etc. s) "Will you let us wander longer?" or according to Schmid: "Will you make us wander?" Ch. 3:12, Job 12:24. You who do not desire impiety, but detest sins most greatly (Psalm 5:5, 6, Proverbs 8:17). Tremellius, Junius, and Piscator explain that "making to wander," as the Vulgate has it, as "permitting to wander." See the permissive meaning of the <term>Hiphil</term> <note>a Hebrew verb form usually indicating causation, but sometimes permission</note> conjugation in Exodus 7:3, Numbers 31:18, Deuteronomy 2:30. t) Ch. 54:4, Exodus 32:8, Job 21:14. Jonathan: "from the way which is right before you," and adds, "like the nations, who have no part in the teaching of your law." u) "You will permit [the heart] to be hardened" or "you will harden" (Job 39:16). <note>original: "ἐσκλήρυνας"</note> "You hardened," Romans 9:18; see also Romans 11:7, 25, 2 Corinthians 3:14. Concerning hardening, Augustine rightly says in Epistle 105 to Sixtus: when he treats this matter, he says, "God does not harden by imparting malice, but by not imparting grace." x) From the fear of you. See Jeremiah 32:40, Deuteronomy 5:26, and above, Ch. 29:13. y) Psalm 90:13, Zechariah 1:16. z) Ch. 52:1, Ch. 65:8; see 2 Kings 13:23.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Isaiah 63 and begins Chapter 64. This page concludes Chapter 63 with a plea regarding the "tribes of His inheritance" and the desecration of the sanctuary, then transitions into the famous prayer of Chapter 64 for God to "rend the heavens" and descend.</meta>

—that what they have prayed for until now will come to pass; as if to say: "Nay, why do we say, 'Would that you would rend the heavens!' Truly, you are going to do that shortly: and when you do it, then it will be *as fire consumes brushwood*." But the blessed man [Schmid] constructs the words thus against the Hebrew distinctions or accents, to which he otherwise often professes to be most devoted. Closer to their mind is Gussetius (page 141), though with another meaning: *As the fire of metal-meltings burns, so the fire will cause the waters to boil to demonstrate your name to your enemies — before you the mountains shall melt away*. 

t) An obscure noun <note>original: "הֲמָסִים", hamasim</note> concerning which the Hebrews have nothing certain. Schmid and most others translate as *stipulas* [stubble] or perhaps *cremia* [brushwood], which are easily dissolved by fire. Others, like Cocceius (Lexicon page 185), take it as the burning fire of liquations/meltings, from the root <term>מסס</term> <note>masas, to melt</note>. By Neumann (from a hypothetical meaning of letters in Exodus, page 374), it is understood as *liquid moisture*, which does not remain present but flows away; however, an application to the text is lacking. The Arabic root with *He* means *to emit a low sound or noise*; to which Ludovicus de Dieu seems to look when, in his Observations on this passage, he rendered it: *As fire makes water boil with a slow, burning heat*. I would prefer to compare the Arabic root with *Hha*: *to be vehement, strong, and constant, also to fry or roast meat*; whence the Arabic name *Hhami*, *Vehement*, also *Oven* or *furnace*; compare Matthew 6:30. 

u) and *makes the water boil*. Neumann (page 185): *fire draws out boiling and bubbling water*. (5) chapter 21:12, chapter 30:23. x) compare chapter 37:20, chapter 45:6, Jeremiah 16:21, Ezekiel 39:7, Psalm 46:11, Psalm 106:8, 2 Chronicles 6:33. y) chapter 26:11, chapter 59:18. z) verse 2, chapter 63:19. a) chapter 32:10, Exodus 15:14, Habakkuk 3:7. 

**Verse 2. b)** in your doing, or so that you would do. Compare Leviticus 4:27, Ezekiel 16:30, chapter 20:44. c) as once in Egypt and at the Red Sea etc., you did such terrifying and terrible things; see Deuteronomy 10:21, 2 Samuel 7:23, Psalm 106:22, 1 Chronicles 17:21, and Psalm 45:5, Psalm 145:6. d) which we did not expect. chapter 25:9, chapter 26:8, chapter 59:9, 11. Ellipsis of the relative [pronoun], as in chapter 62:1. and (often e) would that you therefore also now descend to deliver your people; compare 63:19, Psalm 18:10. f) see "before you." verse 1, chapter 26:18. g) opposing mountains, Zechariah 4:7, would melt. Deuteronomy 32:2, Judges 5:5. 

**Verse 3. h)** For from eternity chapter 45:9, chapter 63:16, 19. i) chapter 52:15. k) chapter 8:9, chapter 28:23. l) *the eye has not seen* Job 13:1, chapter 29:11, nor could such things have entered the mind of man without divine revelation. 1 Corinthians 2:9. The Apostle does not cite the words so much as the sense, and most excellently interprets this concerning the blessings of the New Testament and the benefits of the Messiah: among which, since eternal life is also included, this passage is not wrongly extended to it as well. Meanwhile, the Prophet says these things primarily about the grace of the New Testament. Schmid. Compare Job 28:21, and concerning the mystical wisdom of God (of which Paul speaks in 1 Corinthians 2:9) Matthew 11:27, John 1:18, Ephesians 3:9, Colossians 1:26, 1 Timothy 3:16. 

m) Schmid and most others in the vocative: *O God!* But the Septuagint, Arabic, Vulgate, and Cocceius (Lexicon page 19) take it in the accusative: another God, who could do or provide such things for those waiting for him. n) besides you. chapter 26:13, compare Job 18:10, 24, 1 Corinthians 2:10. o) compare chapter 44:23, Psalm 22:32. p) chapter 30:18, Daniel 12:12, compare Psalm 31:20. 

**Verse 4. q)** For *you met*, and still graciously meet. Genesis 32:2, Exodus 5:20, chapter 23:4, 1 Samuel 10:5. Arabic: For those who work righteousness, you meet with your mercy. v) the one rejoicing, chapter 62:10, concerning you and your meeting. Compare Psalm 145:18, 19, James 4:8. s) and with joy to those doing justice. Compare chapter 51:1, 7, chapter 56:1, Psalm 15:2, Psalm 106:3, Galatians 5:6. t) *1 John 2:29, t)* in your ways 1 Kings 3:14, Zechariah 3:7, Psalm 81:14, Psalm 119:37, 2 Chronicles 6:21. u) who remember or are continually mindful of you. chapter 26:8, 13; perhaps Numbers 15:39, 40, Deuteronomy 8:14, 18, Zechariah 10:9, Psalm 22:28, Psalm 78:35. 

**Verse 5. d)** This has always been your custom: that you would be present for the one who, with a joyful heart for your glory, overcomes the world and endures calamities; and that you would sweetly meet the one who embraces justice and exalt him who walks in your ways. Grant this even now to the godly. Dorsch. x) truly now. verse 8, chapter 50:2. y) you, our most pious God and Father. verse 7. z) *you were angry with us*. verse 8, chapter 47:6. Compare Deuteronomy 1:34, chapter 9:19, Zechariah 1:2, and that most justly. a) for we have sinned, nor have we walked in your ways. chapter 42:24. Compare Numbers 14:40, chapter 21:7, Deuteronomy 1:41, Judges 10:10, 15, etc. b) since in those your ways alone, described in the word of the Gospel 1 Timothy 2:4, c) *eternity* and eternal life are found. Psalm 139:24, Jeremiah 6:16, chapter 18:15, John 5:24, chapter 17:3. Compare above chapter 40:8, Psalm 1:6, and d) so that we may be preserved and saved. chapter 45:21, Matthew 1:21. Varenius: if the world had walked in those ways of yours, we would have been saved. Schmid: because the whole world was in those sins, and yet we were saved. Well said, comparing 1 John 5:19, if only the meaning of "the world" in Hebraism were certain, and the last word did not have the express form of the future; to omit other matters.

<margin>
**m)** A word occurring only once <note>Hebrew: *iddim*</note>, and translated in various ways by interpreters. Sebastian Schmidt: "like a garment of menstruation." Vulgate: "like a menstrual cloth." Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic: "menstruated." This is not incorrect, for in Arabic *Iddah* refers to the status of a woman prohibited from her husband’s embrace due to menstruation. See also a very similar comparison in Ezekiel 36:17. Others: "like a garment of rejection," so Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan</note>, from the root *adah* (Hebrew, Chaldean, Arabic, and Ethiopic: "to pass away," and in the 2nd or 4th conjugation: "to remove"). See Proverbs 25:20. Others: "like a garment of filth or a dirty garment," comparing the Ethiopic *ydan* (scraps, filth), as in Philippians 3:8, implying a dirty rag to be thrown away into the scraps or the dung-heap, to be among the three rejected and filthy rags; especially if you understand it with Gousset <note>Jacques Gousset, 17th-century Hebrew scholar</note> (page 581) as filth wiped from an ulcer, comparing the Arabic root *adah* in the 4th conjugation: "the contagion of disease infected," and *Mo'din*: "contagious." Undoubtedly, however, Dorsch <note>Johann Georg Dorsche, Lutheran theologian</note> rightly says that by these words "the height of uncleanness" is implied: so much so that our own righteousnesses, as they exist in man, cannot endure the rigor of divine justice.
**k)** Directly indeed and by design, this passage does not so much deal with the imperfect righteousness and piety of the regenerate, as with the imaginary righteousness of the impious Jews and hypocrites, relying on which they rejected the true righteousness of God in Christ. See chapter 57:12, Matthew 5:20, Romans 9:31-32, chapter 10:3, etc., about whom the pious complain. Meanwhile, however, it is not incorrectly applied to the righteousness of the regenerate (as those speaking here) and the saints, as is accepted not only by our theologians but also by the ancients, because of the lack of due intensity and degrees of perfection, and because of the adjoining old imperfection. See Dorsch. S. and chapter l) and we fall away or wither. chapter 40, 7. compare a similar form in 1 Chronicles 20, 2.

**CHAPTER LXV, Verse 1. g)** I was sought (after, namely, I first sought them by my grace and word. Romans 10, 14). I, the *Messiah*, the Light and desire of the nations, chapter 11, 10; chapter 42, 6; chapter 60, 1. 3; Haggai 2, 7. For, as Dorscheus well notes (page 209), the response of God which follows here to that representation of the Church’s desires in chapters 63 and 64 is entirely Messianic, and indicative of the New Testament; therefore it is cited in Romans 10, 20; 2 Peter 3, 13; Revelation 21, 1. *Construction* of the word with the following preposition **לְ** [to/for]: compare Ezekiel 14, 3; chapter 20, 3. 31; chapter 36, 37. h) even to those who did not ask about me. compare chapter 30, 2. Deuteronomy 4, 32. chapter 13, 15. and **לֹא** [not] with a following noun or verb as if coalescing into a negative noun, as above in chapter 62, 12; Hosea 1, 9; chapter 2, 1. 25. also with the relative pronoun understood, as in Job 26, 2. 3; 2 Chronicles 13, 9. i) I was found, i.e., according to Abraham ben Ezra, I offered myself to be found. compare chapter 55, 6; Jeremiah 29, 13. 14; Matthew 7, 7. 8. k) even to those who did not seek me (Zephaniah 1, 5). compare above chapter 52, 15; chapter 55, 5. l) compare chapter 58, 9. m) which was not called (Psalm 7; chapter 48, 8, 12). n) by my name. chapter 43, 7. Moses Haccohen <note>a medieval Spanish grammarian</note> (quoted in Abraham ben Ezra) acknowledges that the discourse here is about the Gentiles, and the Apostle teaches this most excellently and certainly, referring verse 1 to the Gentiles and verse 2 to the Jews by an express antithesis in Romans 10, 20. 21. Compare Ephesians 1, 2. 5; chapter 66, 18. 19; Hosea 2, 1. **Verse 2. o)** On the contrary, I spread out my hands as if to summon them with prayers. compare chapter 1, 15; chapter 49, 22; Jeremiah 4, 31; Proverbs 1, 24; Lamentations 1, 17; 2 Corinthians 5, 20. p) every and all day (verse 5; chapter 62, 6). q) to the Jewish people (Romans 10, 21). r) stubborn and rebellious. chapter 1, 23; chapter 30, 1; Hosea 4, 16. This is the opposition: I met the Gentiles scarcely for an hour, and they were without resistance through the direct path of the word; but I met the Jews all day long, and I spread out my hands for a long time, besides what I did in a sufficiently clear word, and yet they maliciously resisted. S. From this is also evident the antecedent and consequent will of God, and the resistible grace of God: likewise that divine converting Grace precedes our wills; as the Council of Orange (Canon 3) rightly concludes from this passage. Compare below verse 12; Matthew 23, 37. s) who walk or proceed. chapter 9, 1; Jeremiah 13, 10; compare Ecclesiastes 12, 5. t) in a way—not physical, but moral—as in chapter 35, 8; Proverbs 6, 12. u) not at all good, but most perverse. 1 Samuel 26, 17; Ezekiel 36, 31; Psalm 36, 5. x) chapter 55, 7; chapter 59, 7; chapter 66, 18. compare Psalm 81, 13; and above chapter 29, 13; Colossians 2, 23. Namely, to the Israelite litany in chapters 63 and 64, the Son of God now responds, and indicates the reasons why He does not sooner hear and free the people: because, to be sure, for a long time He was not only not sought by them, but wickedly despised and provoked to just anger (verse 1 and following). Nevertheless, He promises a place of grace to those who repent (Hosea 3, 5) and the most ample benefits, especially spiritual ones (verse 8 and following), and He illustrates them through antithesis (verse 11 and following). Thus, in this chapter, I. He explains and confirms the rejection and unhappiness of the stubborn Jews as having occurred for most just causes. II. The adoption and frequently promised happiness of the pious and repentant (verse 8 and following). **Verse 3. y)** To the people of the Jews, I say (verse 2). z) who provoke me to anger. 1 Kings 14, 9; 2 Kings 21, 7. 16; Jeremiah 7, 19. a) in my sight, and as if to my face. This refers to the First Commandment of the Decalogue (Exodus 20, 3).

<summary>This page concludes the communal lament of Isaiah 64, describing the people's total unworthiness and the ruin of Jerusalem, then transitions to Chapter 65 where God responds by announcing His availability to the Gentiles while rebuking the rebellious Jews. The commentary emphasizes the contrast between "imaginary righteousness" and divine grace, citing various linguistic and theological interpretations from Christian and Jewish scholars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the divine response to the lament of the previous chapter. While Chapter 64 ended in a plea for God to act, Chapter 65 begins with God explaining why judgment fell—specifically due to the persistent idolatry and hypocrisy of the people. The translation maintains the numbering and scholarly cross-references from the Latin commentary.</meta>

<header>ISAIAH. Chapter 65.</header>

<margin>
**b)** see chapter 49:16; chapter 52:5. **c)** those sacrificing, namely to their idols, as the Jonathan Targum adds; cf. Leviticus 17:5. **d)** in gardens, that is, in the groves of idols, see chapter 1:29; chapter 58:17. Most interpreters recognize the text speaks of the Jews under the New Testament; cf. the note at verse 1 and Revelation 3:9. Therefore, these things should be understood mystically or symbolically regarding them, which in the time of the Prophet, among their ancestors, also occurred literally. See, for example, 2 Kings 21:1–15. Among these ancestors, their descendants (as S. observes at verse 8) were also the most foul idolaters; compare verse 7; Matthew 23:35, 36; Romans 5:12. **e)** verse 7; 2 Kings 16:4; chapter 22:17; chapter 23:5; Jeremiah 1:16; chapter 44:8. **f)** in the ages, i.e., according to Bochart in *Hieroz.* book I, page 700: on the roofs of houses, as idolaters then were accustomed. See 2 Kings 23:12; Jeremiah 19:13; chapter 32:29; Zephaniah 1:5. Others say: on bricks, i.e., on altars constructed of brick, contrary to the command of God in Exodus 20:21, 22. Not offering their prayers and worship to God on the true altar (Hebrews 13:10), but in the name and trust of men; on fabricated altars, in trust of their own counsel, work, and authority. Cocceius *Lexicon*, page 409.
</margin>

* verse 11. y) **But you**, who abandon the Lord and your Savior. (cf. Isaiah 1:4, 28; Jeremiah 17:13; Ezra 8:22). z) who forget. (2) Psalm 9:18. a) Isaiah 2:2; 11:9; 56:7. (Colossians 2:3). b) who prepare, you have furnished. (Psalm 23:5). c) Tigurinus version and Schmidt: **Gadi and Menio**. But Tremellius translates as: to that "troop"—to those "numbers" of idols, which the Prophet points out as if with a finger extended. <note>Greek: *tē daimoniō — tē tuchē*, "to the demon — to fortune"</note>. Jonathan Targum: to their idols and deities, etc. As many as there are learned interpreters, there are almost as many opinions or conjectures regarding these. Luther (also Forerius) thinks **Gad** is Mars, and **Meni** is Mercury, the deity of merchants, comparing Genesis 49:19. He notes that **Meni** signifies "number," comparing the following verse 12. However, Pfeiferus in *Difficulties of the Text* on this passage says: **Meni** is an idol called **Manat** by the Arabs (which was believed to appease the stars that brought rain, as Pococke taught), and **Gad** here is also an Arabic word, from the root *giadda*, meaning "he was happy and fortunate," expressing good fortune, and specifically the star and idol of Jupiter, as Rabbi Moses (Maimonides) suggests in Ibn Ezra and Kimchi. The meaning of "Fortune" was also expressed here by the Septuagint and the Vulgate; compare Genesis 30:11. So also Hiller in *Sacred Names* page 807, though on page 881 he has "a troop of stars" and "a number of planets," as pleases other Hebrews. To Clericus on Genesis 30:11, Gad and Meni are synonyms and signify the Moon; from *ge* (earth) comes **Hecate**, and from *men* comes **Mēnē** (Greek for Moon), the Moon. So Neumann in *Exodus* page 249: Gad is the name of the crescent Moon, joined...

...judged as a youth. Compare verse 15. But **Schmidt** thinks that here, regarding longevity, the Jews are being refuted; he believes that longevity can be understood neither in the sense of temporal history, nor mystically of spiritual things. He agrees with **Sanctius**, who explains the "infant" as someone with infantile habits, and the "old man" who has not fulfilled his years as one who has not reached senile prudence. The verse, says *Schmidt*, should be understood as referring to **spiritual wisdom**, and things will go well.

It says—namely, what is held elsewhere (chapter 54:13; John 6:45)—**"All shall be taught by Jehovah."** In this manner: For the boy, a son of a hundred years, shall die, that is, he shall be cut off and not tolerated by the Lord; and the sinner, a son of a hundred years (that is, an old man who has not yet filled the years of spiritual senile prudence so that he is still a sinner), shall be subjected to a curse. But in this way, the opposition between the "infant" and the "old man" at the beginning of the verse seems to perish, and the context (as we will soon say) and the accents also seem to conflict; these accents require that "a hundred years" be referred not to the subject (the boy or sinner) but to the predicate (shall die or shall be accursed). Otherwise, **Cocceius** in his *Lexicon* (page 422): **"The boy born a hundred years shall die,"** that is, he who dies in childhood will have as much knowledge as one formerly a hundred years old; and **"the sinner born a hundred years shall be cursed,"** that is, he will be as inexcusable as one formerly born a hundred years. **Dorsch,** however, observes that here the extinction of a premature death is simply promised; compare Revelation 21:4. The words and context favor this. So *Schmidt* himself on verse 22: This must be the sense: It shall not happen that they die before the trees planted by them bear fruit, or while they are still bearing; but they themselves shall live as long as the trees planted by them shall flourish, and thus **"my chosen shall wear out the work of their hands; they shall eat, and not others."** These words confirm this: **"my chosen shall wear out the work of their hands"**: which is nothing other than if he said; they shall live so long that the work of their hands wears out along with them. etc. **v. 21.** The propagation of the **Church Militant** <note>The Church on earth, currently struggling against sin and evil</note> is indicated under the metaphor of building houses and planting vineyards. *Dorsch.* Compare chapter 58:12; 61:4. Ezekiel 28:26. **p)** Amos 9:14. See chapter 62:8, 9. By these words, the blessing and prosperity of the faithful are metaphorically indicated. For just as they are blessed and prosperous in the **kingdom of power** <note>The physical world ruled by God</note> for whom the building of houses, the planting of vineyards, and all labor succeeds happily and for their own benefit; so also are they blessed in the **kingdom of grace** for whom spiritual architecture and planting succeed happily; compare 1 Corinthians 3:6, 9. 1 Timothy 3:6. The happiness of the church militant, however, must always be understood with the exception of the cross <note>Meaning earthly happiness is still accompanied by spiritual trials</note>. *Dorsch.* **v. 22.** r) Amos 9:11. Zephaniah 1:13. **s)** chapter 62:8. Deuteronomy 28:39. **t)** Psalm 1:3; 52:10; 92:13. **u)** Long shall be the days of my people. Compare Deuteronomy 4:26, 40; 5:30; 11:9, 21; 32:47. Lamentations 5:21. And to the contrary, Psalm 55:24; 109:8. Also Psalm 102:15; 144:4, etc. **x)** compare chapter 60:21. **y)** *Schmidt:* they shall wear out. others: they shall consume. However, there is a distinction (which was already made in chapter 65:8): the Messiah proclaims that the remnant of the pious among the Jews (verse 5) are not to be confounded with the others, but rather are to be converted to Him by the miraculous and most happy success of the Gospel (verses 7–14). **II.** Just as chapter 65:11 and following illustrated the contrast between the punishment of the wicked and the happiness of His own, so here also are contrasted the destruction of the impious (verses 15–18) and the restoration of the New Jerusalem—that is, the gathering of the entire Church from both Jews and Gentiles (verses 19–21)—and finally its most happy and blessed state (verses 22–23), after the enemies of Christ have been destroyed and eternally condemned (verse 24). **z)** Compare 1 Kings 8:27. ...do they shamelessly claim for themselves the name and benefits of the true Church (Jeremiah 7:4; Romans 2:17 and following), but they do not even think it possible that anyone else, whether man or nation, could think rightly of God unless they subscribe to their own vain opinions. See chapter 52:5; Ezekiel 36:20, 21, 22; Romans 2:24. g) "But we shall see and experience, I and you with me, that they shall be put to shame." Compare verses 14, 24; and above, chapter 5:19; 41:23. But with Kimchi, others say: "The Lord will be seen or will appear for your salvation and joy," as in verse 60:2; Zechariah 9:14; Psalm 102:17. h) "In or with your joy," and that of the whole Church; concerning which see verses 10, 11; chapter 35:10; 51:11; 65:14; Psalm 5:12. i) "When" those impious ones... compare chapter 29:3, 17. k) "They shall be covered in shame," and shall feel themselves deceived by their own vain persuasion. Compare chapter 1:29; 65:13; Psalm 25:3; 40:15; 86:17. Schmid holds another, and indeed entirely contrary, opinion regarding these "brothers" of the pious; he takes this verse as if Jehovah were exhorting the believers among the Jews to join themselves with the converted Gentiles in this way: "Your brothers say—those made brothers from the nations through faith (as below in verse 20)—who before their conversion hated you and excluded you as an abomination; to whom, I say, in their exile He says: 'For my name's sake,' and 'Let Jehovah be glorified over me'" (collecting Acts 11:18; Romans 15:9). "We shall see, therefore, in your joy," that is, "we ask that we may be allowed to become participants in your joy in the gospel" (compare the phrase in Ecclesiastes 2:1), "which will indeed happen." But those worst of sacrificers and mockers (verses 3, 4) will not be participants in your joy (Luke 14:24), but will be put to shame (Matthew 22:13). However, the distinctions or accents clearly teach otherwise, as they are completely opposed to this. <term>*</term> v. 6. l) For there will be a "sound of tumult" (chapter 13:4) from the city and from the Temple: not only through the internal dissensions of the Jews, but also the conquest of the city itself, and the most miserable slaughter of the Jews made by the Romans both in the city and in the temple. It is clear enough that the confusion predicted in verse 5 is further explained here. Luther, Brentius, Varen., and others rightly take this to refer to the final destruction of Jerusalem. Compare above chapter 29:1 and following, and read Josephus, *The Jewish War*, books VI and VII, especially Book VI, chapter 5 and following, and Book VII, chapter 12. While I do not deny that this passage can be referred generally to the wonderful conversion of the nations to Christ which happened through the preaching of the Gospel, I hold that this prophecy never followed a more evident implementation than at the time when the Roman Empire began to be subjected to Christ in its rulers. <meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the final chapter of Isaiah. It focuses on the transition from the judgment of idolaters and hypocrites (verse 17) to the universal mission of God, where survivors are sent to the ends of the earth to gather all nations into a new spiritual kingdom (verses 18-22). This section highlights the inclusion of Gentiles in the divine priesthood and the promise of a perpetual "new creation."</meta>

# ISAIAH. CHAPTER 66.

<margin>
Verse 17. b) **Those who sanctify themselves by the Holy ones**: or as Varinius <note>original: "Varinius," likely a reference to the 16th-century scholar Girolamo Varino</note> has it in Part III, page 185: *those who sell themselves as holy*; yet in such a way that, in what they consider themselves most holy and pure, in that they are most polluted and unclean, because they are idolaters or hypocrites; compare above at verse 5 and chapter 65, 5; Proverbs 30:12. c) Compare Genesis 35:2; Leviticus 14:7-8; Numbers 8:7; Joshua 22:17; Matthew 15:2; chapter 23:25 and following; Mark 7:2-4; John 18:28, etc. d) Jonathan <note>original: "ion." referring to the Aramaic Targum of Jonathan</note> says: *in the gardens of idols*; perhaps *in the groves*, as in chapter 65:3. This means they have left the Temple of God and departed to the gardens; compare the particle "to" <note>original: "אֶל"</note> in chapter 7:3; Joshua 3:3; Ezekiel 18:6. e) The Septuagint <note>original: "S." stands for Septuaginta</note> reads: *behind one tree in the midst*; so also Bochart in *Hierozoicon* <note>original: "Boch. Hieroz." refers to Samuel Bochart’s 1663 work on the animals of the Bible</note> vol. I, page 700. He says you should supply the word *trees*, both because the context requires it and because it is implicitly contained in the Hebrew *bagganoth*, which does not mean just any gardens, but gardens planted with trees—in a word, groves or paradises. However, Carpzov <note>original: "Carpzoui us," Johann Benedict Carpzov, a prominent Hebraist</note> says *behind one* refers to some idol. Jonathan says: *crowd after crowd*; the Syriac: *one after another*. Thus Tremellius, Noldius page 11, etc. But Pfeiffer in *Difficult Passages* <note>original: "Dub. Vex." for Dubia Vexata</note> interprets *after one in the midst* as *imitating one leader in the middle*. Others say: *after* or *besides* (Job 19:26; Nehemiah 5:15) that *one true God Jehovah* (Deuteronomy 6:4), whom they should worship uniquely (Exodus 20:3) and in whom they should seek cleansing (cf. chapter 8:14; 43:24; 44:22; 52:15; 53:5-6; Jeremiah 23:6; 1 Corinthians 1:30; Hebrews 1:3; Revelation 1:5; 7:14, etc.). Deserting Him, they follow that *one Babylonian harlot* placed in the midst, who offers a false way of purification to all (Revelation 17:1 and following; 18:3). These are more defiled than those who eat abominable things once forbidden by divine law, such as swine's flesh, the mouse, etc. So says Mail. <note>original: "Mail." refers to Friedrich Adolf Lampe's "Miscellanea Sacra," sometimes cited as Mail.</note>

...and for their works; by omission of a conjunction; or because of such works and their thoughts, understanding "on account of" <note>original: "עַל vel ב"</note> as in 2 Kings 24:4. Truly, the Messiah predicted here what Paul says experience testifies to in Romans 11:11—that by the fall of the Jews, salvation has come to the Gentiles, and in verse 15, their rejection is the reconciliation of the world. Septuagint o) chapter 65:2. p) The time is coming, or it shall be. Compare Ezekiel 7:10; chapter 30:9. q) I will gather through the word of the Gospel to my church. Compare chapter 56:8; Joel 4:2. r) verse 61:11; chapter 62:10; Zechariah 8:23; compare Genesis 10:20, 31; Deuteronomy 32:21; Romans 11:30. s) Compare chapter 27:13; 35:10; 49:18; 60:4; Zechariah 8:22. t) verse 19; chapter 40:5; 62:2; compare Exodus 16:7; Revelation 15:4; Malachi 1:5.

Verse 19. u) I will set, or I will make (Genesis 4:15) among them, the Jews. Septuagint x) a sign, perhaps a miracle (chapter 7:11; 19:20). Septuagint says through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:2 and following). Others say a sign of gathering, comparing chapter 11:12; 49:12; 62:12. y) and I will send (chapter 57:19). z) from those Jews. Septuagint a) the survivors, rescued from the impenitence and unbelief of the rest and their slaughter in verse 16; compare chapter 4:2; 10:20; 37:31-32; 1 Kings 10:22. d) To Hiller, these are the same as *Put*, that is, Africans at the Atlantic Ocean from Ham’s descendants (Genesis 10:6; 1 Chronicles 1:8). But to Bochart in *Phaleg* book 4, chapter 26, it is *Phila* or *Elephantine*, an island and city on the Nile above Syene, disputed between Egyptian and Ethiopian jurisdiction. e) and Lydia (Ezekiel 27:10). Lydia is otherwise known as a region of Asia Minor at the Maeander river, named after Lud, son of Shem (Genesis 10:22). But here and in Jeremiah 46:9, African Lydians seem to be meant, descending from Mizraim and Ham (Genesis 10:13). f) drawing or stretching bows, that is, archers; compare 1 Kings 22:34; Jeremiah 46:9. Hence Bochart in *Phaleg* page 99, since he proved from authors that Asiatic Lydians were not archers, says those archer Lydians of whom Isaiah and Jeremiah speak are not Asiatic but African Lydians, above Egypt. g) Iberians or Tibareni, neighbors of the Moschi and Colchis. Bochart, *Phaleg* page 204 and following. Compare Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5; Ezekiel 27:13; 38:2. h) and Ionians, that is, Greeks (Ezekiel 27:13, 19; Daniel 8:21; Joel 4:6) named from Javan (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). The Septuagint says: *into Greece* (Acts 20:2). Of those who escape the last devastation of the Antichrist, some will, by God’s providence, come into Greece to purify religion and establish the kingdom of Christ (Gertler, *Prophetic Theology*, page 758). i) even to the most remote regions or islands; compare chapter 11:11; 42:4; 60:9. k) chapter 52:15. l) compare Numbers 14:15; Joshua 9:9. m) see verse 18 and compare chapter 65:1. n) and they shall announce (chapter 42:12).

Verse 20. o) And so the Apostles shall lead them to my church; compare verse 18; chapter 43:5; 16:11. p) all your brothers, spiritual ones, gathered from the nations, and reborn from the same Father and Holy Spirit through baptism and the word of the Gospel (John 1:13; 3:3, 5; James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:3, 23), just like those converted from the Jews, with whom He began to speak in verse 5, 10, and following, according to the Septuagint. Others were brothers in verse 5, called so by the flesh. q) compare verses 12, 18; chapter 11:10; 49:18, etc. Revelation 21:24. r) as a spiritual offering (verse 3; Genesis 4:3; Malachi 1:11; 3:3; Ecclesiasticus 50:7; Romans 12:1; 15:16) consecrated to God through subjection and veneration; compare 2 Samuel 8:2; 2 Kings 8:8; and above, chapter 18:7. s) Jeremiah 17:25. t) Jeremiah 22:4. u) Septuagint: and upon covered wagons <note>original: "rhedis cameratis"</note>; see Numbers 7:3. x) and on mules (2 Samuel 13:29; 18:9; 1 Chronicles 12:40). y) Septuagint, Tremellius, and others: and upon swift couriers <note>original: "veredariis"</note>. This word (which in Arabic also signifies a group of men or a troop) is very ambiguous and of uncertain meaning. Bochart, following the Hebrews, follows those who interpret it as camels or dromedaries (about which see above at chapter 60:6), such as Abraham ben Ezra, Kimchi, etc., because the flow of speech almost requires it to be about camels. For it is unlikely the Prophet would omit such a noble genus of beast so common in the East. They seem to be named from the Arabic *carh*, a strong camel, or from *Cari*, to run or jump vehemently, to which the Hebrew *kirkhar* (2 Samuel 6:14) also seems to allude (*Hierozoicon* vol. I, page 89 and following). z) chapter 2:2-3; 11:9; 56:7; 57:13; 65:11, 25; Psalm 2:6. a) Jerusalem renewed and spiritual (verse 10; Revelation 21:2). b) verse 21, 23; chapter 65:17. c) An offering like the *Mincha*; see verse 3; Leviticus 2:1. d) compare 1 Samuel 21:6; Zechariah 14:20-21.

Verse 21. e) For from them also, namely from the converted Gentiles (verses 19, 20), among whom even excellent teachers of the Gospel have arisen. Septuagint f) He chooses and I will take (Genesis 47:2; Exodus 6:7; Deuteronomy 4:20; 2 Samuel 7:8; Esther 2:7, 15). g) spiritual priests; see chapter 61:6, etc., the Mosaic priesthood having been abolished (chapter 50:7; compare Leviticus 8:2 and following; Numbers 1:1 and following; Jeremiah 31:31 and following; Hebrews 7:11-12). h) and Levites; see Numbers 3:41, 45; 8:6, 16, 18; compare Jeremiah 33:21. i) see verse 20, 22. k) those new heavens which He promised (chapter 51:15; 65:17; Haggai 2:6, 21), that is, my heavenly and spiritual kingdom (John 18:36), which is therefore also called "heaven" in the New Testament (as in Revelation 21:1; 12:1, 3, 4, 7, etc.) and "the kingdom of heaven" (for example, Matthew 3:2, etc.) frequently. Compare also Ephesians 1:3; 2:6.

Verse 19. [Among the nations] without the *Psik* <note>a Hebrew cantillation mark</note> mark 17, 18.
Verse 20. [Your brothers] without the *Psik* (which others have in verse 22); against the final Masorah.

Not only three times in a year as once commanded in Exodus 23:14, nor only at the individual new moons as in Numbers 28:11 or Amos 8:5; but from month to month, or from one new moon to the next—that is, in a continuous solemnity and through all days. Compare Luke 1:75 and Revelation 4:8. See a similar construction in 1 Samuel 7:16, 2 Chronicles 24:5, and the same matter in Zechariah 14:16.

<column-break/>

**Verse 23.** s) Numbers 28:14. These particles "from" and "in its" are not idle; for this denotes the legitimate boundary of time precisely within the month itself, without delay or hindrance. <term>Rabbi Kimchi</term> <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish commentator</note> also correctly notes that a continuity of time is signified: just as "from year to year" in 1 Samuel 1:3 denotes a long and constant custom. And since this continuity here has no expressed end-point, it is to be extended into eternity.

S. v) <note>S. refers to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation</note> Compare Numbers 28:10. The phraseology is taken from the Old Testament, in which the new moons and Sabbaths were celebrated, during which God was also to be worshipped. Therefore, just as in the Old Testament they observed their Sabbaths and new moons in peace at the appointed time—that is, after seven days or every month—so in eternal life they will celebrate their Sabbaths and new moons in the highest peace. In the nature of that life, these are every day—that is, always—and without any hindrance or intermission. 

x) They shall come to that new and heavenly Jerusalem (v. 10 and following; compare 60:3, 4, 11; Revelation 15:4; 22:14). y) **All flesh**: chapter 40:5, Psalm 65:2. This includes both Jews and Gentiles, as seen in verse 15 above, chapter 60:5, Romans 11:12, 25, and Revelation 7:9. In other words, it shall happen that Jews and Gentiles come together. z) The adoration of God will be perpetual. Dorsh. <note>Johann Georg Dorsche, a 17th-century theologian</note> See Zechariah 14:16, 17; Revelation 15:4, 19:4. Compare also Jeremiah 7:2, 2 Chronicles 20:18. u) Revelation 4:10, 5:14, 7:11, 11:16, 14:7, 19:4, 22:3, 4.

**Verse 24.** a) The Lord has said this (v. 20), so it is most certain. Compare chapter 1:20; Revelation 19:9, 21:5, 22:6. b) **And the righteous shall go out**: not in place, but in understanding, says Jerome <note>Early church father and translator of the Vulgate</note> on this passage. S. says: the phraseology seems to me to be taken from the Old Testament, regarding a <term>Sabbath day's journey</term> <note>A distance of about 2,000 cubits, the maximum a Jew was traditionally allowed to walk on the Sabbath</note>. For in the Old Testament, after divine worship was performed, it was permitted for Jews to walk abroad, but not beyond the Sabbath journey. Compare Acts 1:12. Thus we read that the Savior himself went through the grain fields with his disciples on the Sabbath day (Mark 2:23). 

Others add that those walking out from the city usually crossed over to the Mount of Olives and the Kidron Brook (compare John 18:1). Since that deep valley of <term>Tophet</term> or <term>Gehinnom</term> <note>The Hinnom Valley, south of Jerusalem, used as a site for burning waste, which became a metaphor for Hell</note> was nearby, into which corpses, bones, and other unclean things were thrown (2 Kings 23:10, Jeremiah 7:32), they would sometimes stop there and see how eagles, ravens, or other unclean birds would fly into those corpses—which were also swarming with worms—and tear them apart with claws and beaks. 

Indeed, if what the author of the book <term>Cozri</term> <note>The Kuzari by Judah Halevi (c. 1140)</note> says is true (Part I, n. 115), <term>Gehenna</term> was a place near Jerusalem, a valley in which fire was never extinguished, where they burned unclean bones, carcasses, and other refuse. Perhaps they also frequently saw smoke rising with a stench, or serpents and worms crawling in those ashes and funeral pyres. Such a sight could not but move those seeing it to horror and nausea. 

c) **And they shall see** outside that holy city of God (Revelation 14:20, 21:27, 22:3, 15; compare Psalm 58:11). It is a metaphor, says Dorsh., taken from a battle, after which the victors survey the bodies of the defeated. But S. continues: "Thus this scripture means that in eternal life, having performed the worship of their Sabbath, they shall go out as if for the sake of delight and see the condemned." That is, in eternal life the blessed will not only meditate on and sing of God's mercy toward themselves, but also His just judgment upon the wicked. 

Although the pious in this life also discern and understand the unhappiness of the wicked to some extent, this passage speaks primarily of the eternal torments of the ungodly. Christ certainly cites it in Mark 9:44 as referring to eternal death. d) **In the corpses**: chapter 34:3, 37:36. e) **Of men**: of whatever sex, rank, or age. f) Jonathan says: *who rebelled against my Word*. g) **Their worm**: chapter 14:11, Exodus 16:20. **Shall not die**: the Septuagint and Mark 9:44, 46, 48. There are traces of this metaphorical speech elsewhere (Judith 16:17, Sirach 7:17). A worm leaves a corpse when it has consumed it down to the bones, so that nothing remains but a skeleton. But in the infernal regions, there is another worm that never leaves the souls. Most understand the "worm" to be the conscience of sin, which perpetually bites the guilty. Victor of Antioch explains this more clearly and fully than any of the ancients. (See his words in Bochart, *Hierozoicon* II, p. 531). Jonathan says: *their souls shall not die*. 

h) **And their infernal fire**: chapter 50:11, Matthew 25:41, Revelation 14:11. i) **Shall not be extinguished**: chapter 34:10, Jeremiah 7:20, Matthew 25:46, Revelation 19:3. The phraseology is clearly taken from the bodies of the slain which rot and become food for worms or are eventually consumed by fire. Thus, since eternal damnation is the eternal death of soul and body, these are applied such that the worm and fire are the highest, most exquisite, and most shameful punishment of the damned; and not temporary, like for dead bodies, but as the text expressly adds, eternal. Through these two types of torment, the accumulation of infernal punishments to be inflicted on both soul and body is indicated. 

k) **And they shall be a nausea**: or an aversion and horror. l) **To all flesh**: To all blessed men, whether from the Jews or the nations (v. 23). Let us therefore embrace, as <term>Brentius</term> <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a German reformer and commentator</note> warns here, the Gospel of the Son of God with all our zeal: so that, justified by faith and adopted as sons of God, we may receive, because of Jesus Christ our Lord, the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom and everlasting life.

m) Ezekiel 20:41. n) Chapter 33:21. o) Zechariah 14:9.
p) 2 Samuel 10:12. v. 22. "New moons" through the <term>Tishakt</term> <note>Likely a reference to a specific Masoretic or grammatical notation</note>.

u) 2 Peter 3:13, Revelation 21:1, 4. m) **Which I am about to make**: chapter 43:19, 2 Corinthians 5:17, Revelation 21:5, so that the face of the Church will be entirely new. n) **They shall stand**: or remain before me (Psalm 148:6). They shall not be subject to the overthrow of enemies (Matthew 16:18) nor to change, like the prior state of the Church (Hebrews 8:13, 12:27, 28). For the kingdom of grace of this earth will end in the kingdom of glory of the world to come, and thus it must be fulfilled for all time. q) **And your name**: chapter 56:5, 62:2, 65:15, written in heaven (Luke 10:20, Revelation 3:5). According to S., this is to fulfill the promise regarding the seed of the Israelites and their Fathers, that they would not perish but remain before the Lord forever. The firm preservation of the saints is compared with the immutable preparation of the new heaven and earth made for the faithful.

v. 23. r) **And thus it shall be**: chapter 65:24, in that blessed state of the Church when the marriage feast of the Lamb shall be held with the highest spiritual joy (Revelation 19:7), and the kingdom shall be the Lord’s (Obadiah v. 21, Revelation 11:15), the King of kings and Lord of lords (Revelation 17:14), with the destroyers of the earth converted or destroyed (Revelation 11:18). This looks toward the completion of that mystery of which all the Prophets spoke (Revelation 10:7).

# PREFACE TO THE PROPHET JEREMIAH

### §. I.

<margin>Jeremiah’s family.</margin>
Jeremiah the Prophet, to whom our modern editions assign a middle place between Isaiah and Ezekiel, though the ancients assigned him the first place in the volume of the Major Prophets <note>The "Major Prophets" refers to the longer prophetic books of the Old Testament: Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel; some traditions also include Daniel.</note> (see the Various Readings for chapter 1, verse 1).
He was the son of Hilkiah (chapter 1, verse 1). Indeed, not only the Hebrew scholars but also some Christian ones believe this Hilkiah was the High Priest who found the Book of the Law in the temple during the eighteenth year of King Josiah’s reign (2 Kings 22:3, 8). If this could be solidly proven, it would be of no small significance in the history of Jeremiah: for it would show that the splendor of a family provided true prophets with no immunity from mockery and injury. It would mean that Jeremiah, although he was the son of the High Priest, nevertheless enjoyed no privilege against insults, beatings, and imprisonments. He would have shared a similar fate with Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada the High Priest, whom the Jews killed with stones in the temple itself (2 Chronicles 24:21 <note>original: "2 Par. 24, 21"</note>), and with Isaiah, who was born of royal lineage and was sawn asunder (see the Preface to Isaiah, section 3). However, this opinion faces a difficulty: the men of Anathoth (of whom Jeremiah was one) seem to have belonged not to the family of Phinehas, but to the family of Ithamar (compare 1 Kings 2:26 and the note there on verse 27). Furthermore, from the reign of Solomon until the Babylonian captivity, the High Priestly dignity remained with the family of Phinehas—specifically with Zadok and his descendants (compare 1 Chronicles 5:38 <note>original: "1 Par. 5, 38"</note> and following, and the note on Numbers 25:13).

<margin>Lineage.</margin>
### §. II.
If you consider the lineage of our Prophet, he was of the Priests, or the descendants of Aaron, chosen for the holy ministry of God (chapter 1, verse 1). Ezekiel was also of this same order (Ezekiel 1:3). Thus, Jeremiah performed a double office: both the prophetic and the priestly. Furthermore, just as he frequently rebuked his colleagues and kinsmen for neglecting their duties, so in turn the priests—viewing him as a fanatic—most strongly resisted and opposed him (compare chapter 26:7–11; chapter 20:1 and following; and chapter 29:26).

<margin>Homeland.</margin>
### §. III.
His homeland was Anathoth, which Jerome <note>A 4th-century scholar and translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> places at the third mile-marker from Jerusalem toward the north. It was located in the tribe of Benjamin (chapter 1, verse 1; chapter 32, verse 8) but was inhabited by priests, to whom in the distribu- <note>The text breaks here at the catchword "butio-", part of the word "distribution."</note>

->PREFACE<-

[distri]bution of the land formerly fell to them, Joshua 21:18. From which it is easier to understand, when it is said in *Jeremiah* chapter 37, verse 12, that he intended to migrate from Jerusalem to the *land of Benjamin, so that he might receive the portion due to him there (perhaps from his ancestral lands) in the midst of the people.* Nor indeed does *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was a prominent English scholar and clergyman known for using Rabbinical literature to explain the New Testament.</note> conclude without reason that the Prophet at first did not prophesy in Jerusalem, but in *Anathoth*, until his own fellow citizens threatened his very life (chapter 11, verses 21, 22; compare chapter 12, verses 5, 6). And this is made probable even by the fact that Josiah, in the eighteenth year of his reign, is recorded to have consulted *Huldah* rather than Jeremiah concerning the Mosaic scroll of the law, as she was present in Jerusalem (2 Kings 22:14). After this, however, there is little doubt that he spent the greatest part of his time in Jerusalem, not so much for the sake of his priestly duty as for his prophetic office—namely, so that his prophecies might become better known both to all the people and to the kings and priests. Furthermore, the attitude of the people of Anathoth toward their kinsman and fellow citizen Jeremiah is clear from chapter 11, verses 21–23, and chapter 12, verses 5–6. To be sure, he himself also experienced what *Christ* says in Luke 4:24: *That no prophet is accepted in his own country.*

<margin>*His age in relation to the Kings.*</margin>
§. IV. Jeremiah expresses his age himself in chapter 1, verses 2 and 3, when he says he performed his prophetic duty from the thirteenth year of Josiah, and thereafter during the time of *Jehoiakim*, until the *eleventh year of Zedekiah*. In this, however, it should be noted that the times of *Jehoiakim* also include the reign of his predecessor and brother *Jehoahaz*, as well as the reign of his successor and son *Jeconiah*, since both were very brief (each lasting only three months); compare chapter 22, verses 11, 12, 24, and following. Therefore, calculating the 18 years of Josiah remaining after the thirteenth year (for he reigned thirty-one years, 2 Kings 22:1), the *three months of Jehoahaz* (2 Kings 23:31), the *11 years of Jehoiakim* (verse 36), again the *three months of Jeconiah* (chapter 24:8), and the *11 years of Zedekiah* (verse 18), the *total is 40 years and 6 months.* These years, which he spent from the beginning of his office until the destruction of the Jewish Commonwealth <note>The author uses the Latin "Respublica" to refer to the organized Jewish state or nation.</note> by the Chaldeans <note>The Chaldeans were the ruling dynasty of the Neo-Babylonian Empire.</note>, were highly significant for the Jewish kingdom; indeed, it is the probable opinion of interpreters that Ezekiel had these in mind in chapter 4:6, in his definition of the 40 years of the sins of the house of Judah. But even beyond the eleventh year of Zedekiah (which is mentioned in chapter 1:3, either as the specific boundary of the first part, from chapters 1–40, or as the most fatal year of all Jeremiah’s prophecies), he continued his life and prophecies: first in Judea (chapter 40:1 and following) and then in Egypt (chapter 43:8 and following), though how long he was there cannot be determined. From this, it is clear that Jeremiah was called by God to the prophetic office as quite a young man, which he himself hints at in chapter 1:6 (where you may see our note) and is easily gathered from chapter 16:2.

<margin>*and in relation to contemporary Prophets.*</margin>

This means she is mentioned in the biblical narrative but did not leave a written book of her own.</note> (compare 2 Kings 22:14), and probably *Habakkuk*, who already prophesied concerning the imminent Babylonian captivity...

### ON JEREMIAH.

][ 2

...we learn of [Habakkuk's] prophecy from Habakkuk 1:5–6. (2) During the time of Jehoiakim, there was *Uriah*, likewise an *unwritten prophet* <note>original: "ἄγραφον" (unwritten); this refers to a prophet who is mentioned in the biblical narrative but does not have a dedicated book of their own in the canon.</note>, comparing Jeremiah 26:20 and our notes there. (3) Under Zedekiah and in the following times, there were *Daniel* and *Ezekiel*, both of whom prophesied in Babylon (compare Daniel 1:1 and following; Ezekiel 1:2), just as Jeremiah did conversely in Jerusalem. It is clear that **God**, in His kindness and faithfulness toward His people, acted earnestly so that both the Jews in Jerusalem and those in Babylon would be warned of His will and judgments, having sent for that purpose not just one or two, but many prophets. Compare Jeremiah 7:13, 25; 25:4; 29:19, etc. However, his era also had many false prophets (2 Peter 2:1), who boldly tried to tear down what he himself prophesied in the name of the Lord with contrary prophecies; compare chapter 14:13 and following; 23:9 and following; 27:14–15, etc. Specifically named among those in Jerusalem are *Pashhur, son of Immer* (chapter 20:6) and *Hananiah* (chapter 28:1 and following), both priests; while among those in Babylon were *Ahab, son of Kolaiah*, *Zedekiah, son of Maaseiah* (chapter 29:21), and *Shemaiah the Nehelamite* (verse 24 and following).

<margin>The status of the Jewish people before Josiah.</margin>
§. VI. To understand Jeremiah, it is especially helpful to make oneself familiar with the history of the times both preceding and during which he lived and prophesied, as recorded in 2 Kings 21–25 and 2 Chronicles 33–36; for it can rightly be said that *History is the light of prophecy*. We will provide the most significant moments here. Ninety-four years had passed by the time Jeremiah began to prophesy since the ten tribes of the Kingdom of Israel <note>The Northern Kingdom of Israel was conquered by Assyria in 722 BCE, roughly a century before Jeremiah's call.</note> had been deported by the Assyrians because of their sins, and especially because of their idolatry (2 Kings 18:9 and following). Although the Jews in the south had seen this example of divine severity, they had not become any better; indeed, they became worse than the Israelites and the surrounding nations (Jeremiah 3:6–11; Ezekiel 23:11 and following). Under the wicked Manasseh and his son Amon, they had fallen into the most blatant crimes and foulest idolatry, and could not be recalled to their duty by either the voices of the prophets or the judgments of God (2 Kings 21:1 and following; 2 Chronicles 33:10; Jeremiah 2:30). Thus, at last, God decreed the same severity for Jerusalem and the Jewish kingdom as he had for Samaria—total destruction (2 Kings 21:10 and following), to be executed immediately, had not the prayerful humiliation of the very pious King Josiah obtained a delay from God (chapter 22:16–20).

<margin>under Josiah,</margin>
§. VII. Josiah had begun to seek the Lord in the eighth year of his reign, while still a boy of sixteen; thereafter, following in the ways of David, he reigned most excellently and laudably. He eliminated idols not only throughout Judah and Jerusalem, but also in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and the rest of the remnants of Israel (2 Chronicles 34:1–7). He repaired the temple (verse 8 and following), renewed the covenant with God (verse 29 and following), celebrated the Passover most solemnly, and organized the divisions of the priests (chapter 35:1–19). Furthermore, he established justice and right, especially for the poor and the afflicted (Jeremiah 22:15–16; compare Sirach 49:1–6). And the Holy Spirit Himself bears witness to him in 2 Kings 23:25: *There was no king like him, either before or after, who had so turned himself to...*

# PREFACE

->PREFACE<-

...[King Josiah turned to] the Lord **with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his strength**, according to the **whole law of Moses**. It seemed, therefore, that under this King the Jewish people had converted and were reconciled with God; at least they flattered themselves so (compare Jeremiah 2:35). Nonetheless, God **did not turn from the burning of His great anger**, which had flared up because of all those provocations with which Manasseh had provoked Him, etc. (2 Kings 23:26, 27). While Jeremiah insisted on this **paradox**, it could not help but deeply offend the ears of the hypocritical people (compare Jeremiah 4:8, 10). But this was entirely the case: for although the most pious King had eliminated the worship of idols in the twelfth year of his reign (2 Chronicles 34:3 and following), how quickly the people relapsed is understood partly from the fact that Jeremiah, in the very next year—namely the thirteenth (chapter 1:2)—so severely rebukes the idolatry of the Jews (as in chapter 2:11, chapter 7:17, 18, and elsewhere). It is also understood from the fact that in the eighteenth year, when Josiah renewed the covenant between God and the whole people (2 Chronicles 34:8, 29–32), a new purge of idols from Israel was necessary, the people having been forced into the worship of God (verse 33). 

Indeed, impiety and the insane worship of idols had so settled in their minds that, whatever Josiah did, they soon returned to their own nature with the greatest fickleness (compare Jeremiah 3:4, 5, 10); they did not continue faithfully and seriously as they had begun (chapter 4:1–4), but with a conversion faked through **hypocrisy**, they remained turned away from God in **perpetual turning away** (chapter 8:5, 6). They were content with external worship and ceremonies (chapter 6:20) and rashly trusted in them (chapter 7:4), as if these were compatible with any crimes whatsoever, and especially with idolatry (verse 5 and following). Therefore, it finally happened by the just judgment of God that Josiah—an otherwise pious King—was killed in a battle joined in the fields near Megiddo (2 Chronicles 35:20 and following) because he had stubbornly insisted on fighting against Necho <note>Necho II was a Pharaoh of Egypt's 26th Dynasty.</note> after ignoring a divine warning and lacking sufficient cause. The whole people and Jeremiah solemnly and rightly mourned his death (verses 24, 25), for it was no more mournful for the King himself than it was for the Commonwealth, being nearly fatal for it (Jeremiah 22:10).

<margin>After Josiah, under Jehoahaz,</margin>
§. VIII. From that time on, the divine judgments, which had been delayed until then, began to weigh upon the stubborn people under the ungodly sons of the pious Josiah, becoming more severe day by day until they completely overturned the Jewish Commonwealth. First, Necho deported Jehoahaz—also called **Shallum**, a man of fierce character—to Egypt (where he died) after a three-month usurpation of the kingdom. He had unjustly snatched the kingdom from his older brother Jehoiakim with the help of the people and without consulting his father's victor [Necho]. A fine was also imposed on the land (2 Kings 23:30–36; 2 Chronicles 36:1–4; Jeremiah 22:10, 11, 12; Ezekiel 19:3, 4). Thus the "sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes" <note>original: "filii Mempheos ac Taphnes"; these refer to the Egyptian military forces from these prominent cities.</note> grazed upon the crown of the people’s head, as Jeremiah had predicted in chapter 2:16.

<margin>under Jehoiakim,</margin>
§. IX. Jehoiakim, also called **Eliakim**, was substituted for his brother; at first he stood as a vassal and ally of Necho, from whom he had received the kingdom. But when the Egyptian army was broken by the Chaldeans (Jeremiah 46:2), he was finally besieged by them in the eighth year of his reign and driven to...

...so that he might be under the protection <note>original: *in clientela*, referring to a vassal state relationship</note> of Nebuchadnezzar and pay tributes. But when, in the third year after—specifically the eleventh of his reign—he had rebelled, relying on the help of the Egyptians (2 Kings 24:1), he was again besieged by the Chaldeans <note>The people of Babylon</note>, captured, and thrown into chains. This was so that he, along with other Jews (especially those of the royal lineage and the nobles, among whom were Daniel and his companions) and part of the temple vessels, might be deported to Babylon (2 Chronicles 36:6; Daniel 1:1–6; Ezekiel 19:5 and following). However, on the way (as is probable), he was either killed or died, and his body was thrown out like a carcass; he lacked a proper burial, receiving a punishment worthy of his crimes (Jeremiah 22:18, 19; chapter 36:30). He was a man of a fierce and very harsh nature, stubborn, proud, a wicked pursuer of royal splendor and luxury, a lavish builder, greedy, unjust, bloody, and, to say it in a single word, a tyrant (verses 13–17). He was not content to have seized the prophet Uriah from Egypt for slaughter (Jeremiah 26:20), nor did he fear to cast the prophecies of Jeremiah, contained in a single scroll, into the flames (chapter 36:23, 24, 25). He also ordered that Jeremiah himself and the pious Baruch be sought for execution, though they were preserved by a divine miracle (verse 26). The reward for this impiety, among other things, was that he had no son to succeed him in the kingdom (verse 30).

<margin>under Jeconiah,</margin>
§. X. For the Chaldeans led away Jeconiah his son, who had succeeded him (perhaps because he himself had also stirred up a rebellion), after only three months. Along with his mother, the princes, the royal treasures, and the better part of the people and the sacred vessels, he was taken to Babylon. The kingdom was then handed over to his uncle Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:8–17; compare Jeremiah 13:18; chapter 22:24–30). We shall speak below in §. 12 regarding how Jeconiah received a milder judgment because of his voluntary surrender than did Jehoiakim and Zedekiah.

<margin>under Zedekiah.</margin>
§. XI. Zedekiah, otherwise known as Mattaniah, the third son of Josiah (Jeremiah 37:1; 1 Chronicles 3:15), stirred up great hope for himself and his reign within the Jewish Republic (Lamentations 4:20). But, in no way corrected by the sad example of his predecessors, he persisted stubbornly in their footsteps until he brought total destruction upon both himself and his kingdom. Thus, the very fact that he had obtained the kingdom was an argument of God’s wrath and judgment upon the Jewish people—whose impiety was growing daily (2 Kings 24:19, 20)—rather than a sign of divine grace or merit. This was despite how the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the rest who survived in Judah under Zedekiah’s reign proudly boasted against the Babylonian exiles (Ezekiel 11:15). For although Nebuchadnezzar had given him a kingdom worn down in strength, so that he might have less power for new uprisings (2 Kings 24:14), and had furthermore taken from him a sacred oath of loyalty by Jehovah <note>original: *per Iehouam*</note> (Ezekiel 17:13 and following; 2 Chronicles 36:13); and although Zedekiah himself had traveled to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign, undoubtedly to make his loyalty more evident to the Babylonians (Jeremiah 51:59); nevertheless, being solicited by neighboring Kings (chapter 27:3, compare verse 9 and following), instigated by false prophets (verse 14 and following), and finally encouraged by his own princes (chapter 38:4, 22), he despised the warning of Jeremiah...

# PREFACE

...of Jeremiah from the mouth of the Lord <note>original: *ex ore Domini*</note> (Jeremiah 37:2; 2 Chronicles 36:12). Zedekiah rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar with a completely unhappy and destructive outcome. Indeed, in the fourth month of the eleventh year of Zedekiah's reign, the Babylonians captured Jerusalem after an eighteen-month siege (2 Kings 25:1 and following). Help was sought from the Egyptians in vain (Jeremiah 37:5 and following), while famine and plague spread horribly within the city in the meantime (chapter 21:6, 7, etc.). Zedekiah was caught by the Chaldeans <note>The people of Babylon</note> while fleeing and was brought to Riblah, where Nebuchadnezzar was staying. There, the most wretched father saw his own sons slaughtered before his eyes; he himself was then blinded, bound, and deported to Babylon, while the city and the temple were burned (chapter 39:5 and following).

<margin>A more specific historical comparison (1) regarding the guilt and punishment of Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah.</margin>

§. XII. Furthermore, light may be shed on the book of Jeremiah by a more specific pair of historical considerations: (1) that these last kings differed in their degrees of punishment just as they did in their stubbornness; or rather, that a certain proportion can be observed between their defiance and their penalty. 

For Jeconiah, who ruled in the time between Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, did indeed follow wicked ways, for which a deserved punishment was announced to him (chapter 13:18)—specifically, captivity (chapter 22:24 and following). However, because he was quite young (an age that turns easily to either virtue or vice), he had at least this one commendable quality: he surrendered himself voluntarily to Nebuchadnezzar while the king was besieging the city (2 Kings 24:12; Jeremiah 29:2). The more obstinate Zedekiah could not be brought to this same submission, no matter how much Jeremiah urged it by God's command (chapter 38:17, 18, and following). 

Therefore, Jeconiah’s punishment was also the mildest. He eventually emerged from prison (where he likely humbled himself before God) by the grace of Evil-merodach <note>The son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar</note>. He obtained a place of honor higher than the other kings who were in Babylon, along with royal provisions (2 Kings 25:27 and following; Jeremiah 52:31 and following). Likewise, the rest of the multitude of Jews captured with him included at least some pious men, and they received a better and more tolerable exile than those deported later with Zedekiah, whom one might rightly call the "dregs of the people" <note>original: *faecem populi*</note>. Compare Jeremiah chapters 24 and 29 on this, as well as Ezekiel 11:16 and following, and chapter 33:24 and following.

§. XIII. Furthermore, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah were both stubborn princes. But Jehoiakim had a harder and more atrocious nature, a portrait and examples of which we gave above in Section 9. Although he still had some good ministers in his time who advised better things (chapter 36:25), he did not obey them. Consequently, he deserved a harsher punishment and was buried like a donkey <note>Meaning he was denied a royal burial and thrown out like a dead animal</note> (chapter 22:18, 19; chapter 36:30). 

Zedekiah, however, when compared with Jehoiakim, was more manageable <note>original: *tractabilior*</note>; he heard Jeremiah several times and not unkindly. Perhaps he would not have been so bad if he had not been driven off course by the wickedness of his princes (compare chapter 38:4, etc.). Zedekiah was affected by some fear of God, though it was servile and hypocritical; but Jehoiakim was affected by none at all. Hence, Zedekiah’s fate was indeed harsher than Jeconiah’s, since he was not only taken captive but also blinded; yet it was better than Jehoiakim’s, as he eventually died peacefully and was honored with a royal burial.

It highlights Jeconiah's relative leniency due to his surrender, contrasted with the brutal endings of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the final kings of Judah and the escalating severity of divine judgment during the time of the prophet Jeremiah. The previous page discussed how the punishment of these kings was proportional to their stubbornness.</meta>

### ON JEREMIAH.

...was, as many interpreters gather from chapter 32, verse 5 and chapter 34, verses 5 and 6. Meanwhile, it is not surprising that the people’s captivity under Jehoiakim was tolerable, while under Zedekiah it was truly fatal to the State <note>original: *Reip.*, short for *Respublica*</note>. This is because the punishment was proportioned not so much to the sins of the Kings as to the sins of the people. For the number of godly people who remained from the time of Josiah during the reign of Jehoiakim was diminished more and more under Zedekiah, so that God could no longer spare them. And in this way, we understand the saying of the ancient Rabbis in the commentary of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>original: *R. Salomonis*. This refers to the famous 11th-century Jewish scholar Rashi.</note> on chapter 37: *Zedekiah was righteous (by comparison), but his generation was wicked; Jehoiakim, however, was wicked, but his generation (meaning the better leaders, comparing chapter 26:24 and 36:25) was righteous.*

<margin>
(2) Regarding the judgments of God proceeding by degrees.
</margin>

§. XIV. (2) The judgments of God did not break out all at once with a single blow, but proceeded gradually over time, becoming more accumulated and rigid by the day. Thus, the consideration of these events provides an illustrative lesson in both divine patience <note>original: *longanimitatis*</note> and severity. The heavy wrath of God already lay upon the Judeans in the time of Josiah, but it was held back for the sake of this most pious King (2 Kings 22:13 and following; 19, 20). Meanwhile, the prophets frequently and seriously—but in vain—urged the people toward repentance (chapter 25:3 and following; compare 2 Chronicles 36:15, 16). However, the judgment began to show itself in a prelude of drought and sterility—to more effectively warn the people to repent (Jeremiah 3:3; 12:4, 13; 14:1 and following)—breaking out more severely after the death of Josiah. Once Josiah was killed (which was a most mournful event for the State), Necho of Egypt deported *Jehoahaz* (who had presumed to reign) into Egypt, substituted *Jehoiakim* in his place, and exacted a financial fine from the people, etc. See sections 8 and 9. 

In the same way, *Zedekiah* could certainly have avoided a worse evil by this very act of submission, if he had voluntarily surrendered to the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians</note> (chapter 38:17). In that case, the city and the temple would not have been burned by the Chaldeans (verses 18, 23), nor would he himself have been blinded after his sons and nobles were slaughtered (chapter 39:6, 7). But his own stubborn defiance, and that of the people, drew this heap of punishments upon them, far beyond the captivity originally decreed by God. 

Furthermore, when the larger and more powerful part of the people had been led away by the Chaldeans, the King of Babylon, out of divine indulgence, showed favor to the poorer people whom he left in the land (verses 9, 10). He wished for them to grow together again into some form of a State after the city was burned, appointing *Gedaliah* as a local governor over them (chapter 40:11). But the outcome proved they were unworthy even of this benefit, as Gedaliah was killed through the treachery of *Ishmael* (chapter 41:1 and following). For although better things were promised to this remnant even then through the interpretation of Jeremiah—if only they would remain in the land—the people, in their typical stubbornness and blindness, did not obey the command of God at all. They departed for Egypt, where they publicly relapsed into the foulest idolatry (chapter 44). Finally, they were all consumed either by the sword, famine, or plague (chapters 42 and 43), except for a very few (chapter 44:28). Thus, the greater God’s patience toward the Judeans, the worse the Judeans became; but the worse they became, the more severe was the rigor of God they experienced.

# PREFACE

<margin>Jeremiah’s fate,</margin>
### §. XV. You have here the times into which our Prophet <note>The Latin *Vates* can mean prophet, seer, or bard.</note> fell: they were truly lamentable and deplorable (Lamentations 3:1 and following), because, as the Holy Spirit testifies, things had progressed so far that no room for pardon remained with God (2 Kings 24:4; Jeremiah 15:1 and following). So great and so desperate was the stubbornness of the people. Therefore, one can understand, even by guessing, how Jeremiah was received by such a wicked nation. To be sure, he provoked against himself through his sermons not only the tyranny of kings and princes, but also the hatred of the clergy and the entire people (chapter 1:18, 19). He suffered mockeries, slanders, insults, plots, curses, beatings, imprisonments, and the harshest chains (chapter 11:18 and following; chapter 12:5, 6; chapter 15:10; chapter 18:18 and following; chapter 20; chapter 26:7 and following; chapter 32:3; chapter 36:26; chapter 37:13 and following; chapter 38). Consequently, it was not without reason that he himself wished to live somewhere in a traveler's hut in the desert, far removed from the treachery and malice of his people (chapter 9:1 and following). Yet, against all the schemes of his adversaries, **"Jehovah was a bronze wall"** <note>original: *Iehoua murus aheneus*</note> to him, just as He had promised in chapter 1:18. God freed him from dangers and evils (chapter 26:24; chapter 38:13), granted him authority and respect even among his enemies (chapter 15:11; compare chapter 21:1, 2; chapter 37:3; chapter 42:2), and gained for him the favor of Nebuchadnezzar (chapter 39:11, 12). By this favor, it happened that he obtained the freedom to remain in Judea (chapter 40:2 and following). Finally, having been dragged by force into Egypt by the Jews (chapter 43:6), he was no more free from the hatred and contradictions of his countrymen there than he had been in Judea (compare chapter 44:15 and following). What end he eventually met is not sufficiently clear, except for a tradition held by certain Church Fathers that he was stoned to death by the Jews in Egypt.

<margin>Faithfulness in performing his duty,</margin>
### §. XVI. So many and such great afflictions did not frighten the Prophet’s spirit away from performing his duty faithfully, nor from having the most tender love for his people. Indeed, in chapter 1:6, he tries to decline the prophetic office, partly out of fear and partly from a sense of his own weakness and unfitness. However, he did so in such a way that when God urged him and promised him strength, he willingly obeyed despite the objections of "the flesh" <note>The author uses *caro* (the flesh) to refer to human frailty or natural hesitation.</note>. He also experienced human struggles when, in chapter 12:1 and following, he could not reconcile the afflictions of the faithful—and especially his own—with the justice and goodness of God. Likewise, in chapter 20:7 and following, his human nature suggested to him that he should stop announcing the divine Word, which had stirred up so much suffering and shame for him. But by the grace of God, he soon repressed and overcame these temptations of the flesh in that same passage, keeping the final goal in view and being lifted up by divine help. <margin>Love toward his people.</margin> Furthermore, the persecutions by the Jews did not embitter his spirit; rather, he was moved by deep compassion (chapter 8:23) and almost an excess of love for his people. He insisted on interceding for them before God until the very end, so much so that he had to be restrained by God several times (chapter 7:18; chapter 11:14; chapter 14:7, 11 and following). This point can be noted against the slanders of the Princes, who accused Jeremiah of having a hostile spirit toward the people (chapter 38:4; chapter 43:3). Nevertheless, he himself eventually left those who were stubbornly malicious to God’s just judgment, rather than continuing to plead for them (chapter 6:11; chapter 18).

<summary>This page describes the immense suffering Jeremiah endured at the hands of his own people and his steadfast faithfulness despite his personal doubts and fears. It highlights the paradox of his life: being hated by the people he loved and interceded for, while being supernaturally protected by God as a "bronze wall."</summary>
