# ON JEREMIAH

[References to Jeremiah 21, 22, 23, and 20:12]. How much modesty and reverence he showed toward his superiors is made clear by the examples in chapter 26:14–15 and chapter 37:20.

<margin>
*Subject Matter.*

Chapter 1:10.
</margin>

§ XVII. The prophet himself expressed the subject matter of his entire prophecy in chapter 1, verse 10. It consists of two parts: I. **Uprooting, tearing down, and ruining**: this involves threats, both generally against the **nations** and specifically against the **Jews**, regarding **famine, plague, the sword, and the total destruction of the land**, the city, and the temple **by the Chaldeans** <note>The "Chaldeans" refers to the Neo-Babylonian Empire, which besieged Jerusalem.</note> because of the inhabitants' enormous crimes, especially their idolatry, which he harshly rebukes. A brief summary of these threats is presented under a double symbol in chapter 1, consisting of two propositions: (a) that **God is watching to carry out His word** (v. 12), and (b) that specifically **evil is coming from the North**—meaning Babylon—**upon all the inhabitants of the land** (v. 14). II. **Building and planting**, which he does primarily in three ways, by promising: (a) **to the Jews, immunity from the immediate destruction of the city** if they obey the word of God and voluntarily surrender to the Chaldeans; and **to the remnant**—those who survived in the land after the downfall of the Judeans—**safety**, if they are willing to remain in the land; (b) **a return from the 70-year Babylonian captivity** (a promise that Daniel especially looked to in Daniel 9:2, Ezra in Ezra 1:1, and according to some, Zechariah in Zechariah 1:12 and 7:5); and (c) most importantly, **the Coming of the Messiah**, whose person, office, blessings, and kingdom he brilliantly describes (see, for example, chapters 30 and 31).

<margin>Divisions.</margin>

§ XVIII. There are two **General Parts** of the book: I. PROPHECIES TO THE PEOPLE OF GOD, that is, Israel and especially Judah, to be subdivided—

-> ][ ][ <-

* That term of 70 years in Jeremiah is quite remarkable. We have already said some things about it regarding chapter 25:12, to which we now add another calculation, compiled from Holy Scripture with as much diligence as possible. First, let us carefully note that the fourth year of Jehoiakim <note>King of Judah, placed on the throne by Pharaoh Necho.</note> is the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, comparing Jeremiah 25:1. Therefore, if we measure Nebuchadnezzar's times from that point, his years will be 45. Specifically:

| | years | months |
|---|---|---|
| Eight years from the 4th to the 11th year of Jehoiakim (compare 2 Kings 23:36). | 8. | - - |
| Three months of Jeconiah's reign (compare 2 Kings 24:8). | - - | 3. |
| Thirty-seven years of Jeconiah's <note>Also known as Jehoiachin.</note> captivity (compare Jeremiah 52:31). | 37. | - - |
| | --- | --- |
| | 45. | 3. |

Furthermore, let us observe that Egypt was subject to the Babylonians for 40 years (compare Ezekiel 29:11–13). The start of this period does not precede the 27th year of Jeconiah's captivity, or the 35th year of Nebuchadnezzar (compare Ezekiel 29:17ff with 1:2). Let us therefore subtract from those forty years the ten years of Jeconiah’s captivity during which Egypt was subject while Nebuchadnezzar was still alive; thus, 30 years of Egyptian servitude will remain for his successors.

| | 30. | - - |
|---|---|---|
| **Total** | **75 years** | **3 months.** |

We assume now that these years of Egypt extend to the end of Jeremiah's 70 years (compare Jeremiah 25:11, 13 with v. 19). We further assume that these 70 years terminate with Nebuchadnezzar’s grandson, Belshazzar (compare chapter 27:7 and Daniel 9:2, or perhaps 5:30 and 6:1). Counting backward from there, **the beginning of the 70 years falls in the eighth year of Jehoiakim**, which is when he himself began to serve Nebuchadnezzar (compare 2 Kings 24:1).

...to be divided again into those parts which (1) were issued from the thirteenth year of Josiah until the destruction of the city, chapters 1–39; likewise chapter 45, when compared with the book's frontispiece in chapter 1:1, 2, 3. (2) Those issued after the destruction of the city to the remnants of the Jews, partly in Judea and partly in Egypt, interspersed with histories of that same time, chapters 40–44; compare the new inscription of this part in chapter 40:1. II. PROPHECIES AGAINST THE NATIONS, <note>original: "VATICINIA CONTRA GENTES"</note> such as the Egyptians, Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Damascenes, Kedarenes, the kingdoms of Hazor, Elamites, and the Babylonians themselves, chapters 46–51. <margin>The order of the prophecies.</margin>
§ XIX. By God’s command, Jeremiah recorded all these prophecies in writing, both so they might be read to his contemporaries (chapter 36:2 and following) and so they might serve posterity—to whom many of the prophecies pertained (chapter 30:2 and following; compare verse 24). But it is also clear from chapter 25:3 that the very order in which the prophecies are arranged throughout the book comes from Jeremiah himself, even if it is not adapted to a chronological timeline <term>chronotaxis: the arrangement of events in chronological order</term>. While some sort of reason or connection for this arrangement can be found, mostly based on the similarity of the subject matter, nevertheless, according to *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned English Hebraist and clergyman.</note> in his *Chronotaxis*, it is frequently difficult, and in some places almost impossible. <note>original Greek: "αδυνατος" (adunatos)</note> *For it was not the concern of the Prophets,* says Jerome in his *Commentary on chapter 25:1*, *to preserve the chronology that the laws of history require; but to write whatever they knew was useful to those hearing and reading.* Thus in the Psalter and other books of Holy Scripture—and indeed in the very arrangement of the entire Hebrew Code as it stands—one would search in vain for a consistent chronological order.

<margin>The chronology of these same prophecies.</margin>
§ XX. Since a chronological arrangement is entirely helpful for understanding the prophecies more correctly, we will briefly arrange the individual chapters and prophecies here according to those laws for the reader's use.

<margin>Chapters 1-12 belong to the time of JOSIAH.</margin>
Only chapters 1:2 and 3:6 explicitly mention the time of *Josiah*; however, from chapter 1 through chapter 12 inclusive, no trace appears from which one could conclude that the chronological order has been transposed. Therefore, according to Lightfoot, those chapters should be left in the place and sequence in which they were arranged. But in addition,
<margin>Also chapters 14, 15, and 16.</margin>
chapters 14, 15, and 16 seem to be reckoned to the times of *Josiah*. For chapter 14 deals with the drought in verse 1, about which Jeremiah prophesied under Josiah (compare 3:3, 4, 6; 5:24; 8:13, 20; 9:10, 11; and 12:4). The 15th chapter is very closely linked with the end of the preceding one, serving as a response to the Prophet's intercession; nor does verse 4 diverge from the time of Josiah (compare 2 Kings 23:26 and following). Likewise, chapter 16 was issued at a time when Jeremiah, perhaps still a young man, was thinking about taking a wife (verse 2). This could hardly have happened except under the reign of Josiah, contrary to what *Lightfoot* establishes; for the prophet was probably already in his fortieth year at the beginning of King Jehoiakim’s reign (compare 25:3). Finally, chapter 47—issued before Gaza was struck by Pharaoh—seems to refer to the final times of Josiah, or certainly very close to his death; though others prefer to refer this to the times of Zedekiah <note>original: "Tfedekiæ"</note> (compare the note on verse 1).

<margin>Chapters 17, 18, 19, and 20 belong to the time of JEHOIAKIM.</margin>
We do grant, however, that chapters 17, 18, 19, and 20 belong to the times of Jehoiakim; because chapter 17 proves (1) a reliance on Egyptian help in verse 5, and (2) wealth unjustly acquired in verse 11—both of which were uniquely characteristic of Jehoiakim (compare 2 Kings 23:34 and Jeremiah 22:13, 17). (3) Pashhur would hardly have dared to insult Jeremiah so much during the reign of Josiah, as we nevertheless read in chapter 20, which is closely joined to the preceding chapters 18 and 19 by verse 1—although we cannot determine the exact year in which they fell.
<margin>Chapter 22:1-23.</margin>
Furthermore, chapter 22:1–23 pertains to the earlier and more prosperous times of Jehoiakim (compare verse 18), since Shallum (also known as Jehoahaz) had not been deported to Egypt so long before (compare verses 10, 11, 12).
<margin>Chapter 23.</margin>
The following chapter 23 is connected to it, as it is likewise directed against the "bad shepherds" or Kings.

<summary>This page analyzes the organizational structure of the Book of Jeremiah, debating whether the chapters follow a thematic or chronological order. The author concludes that while Jeremiah arranged the book himself, he prioritized spiritual utility over strict historical sequence.</summary>

# ON JEREMIAH

<margin>Chapter 25</margin> ...nations, verse 1, against whom Chapter 22 was written. Chapter 25 follows, published in the fourth year of *Jehoiakim* (verse 1), along with many prophecies against foreign nations—excluding, of course, those that clearly state a different time of publication. For in verse 13, it explicitly calls upon the prophecies against *Babylon* and other nations, with a reference back to the second part of the book, which is titled <note>original: "על הגוים"</note> "Concerning the Nations" (Chapter 46:1). Therefore, you should assign here <margin>Chapter 46:1–12</margin> Chapter 46:1–12 against the *Egyptians*, namely the army of Necho, which was defeated in that same year near <margin>Chapter 48</margin> Carchemish <note>original: "Circasium"</note> by the Chaldeans (verse 2). Likewise, Chapter 48 against the *Moabites*; Chapter 49 <margin>Chapter 49</margin> against the *Ammonites*, *Edomites*, and *Syrians*; and finally Chapters 50 and 51:1–59 against the <margin>Chapters 50, 51:1–59</margin> *Babylonians*: for all of these were introduced previously in Chapter 25. To these we finally <margin>Chapter 26</margin> subjoin Chapter 26, published (it seems) in the same year; for the statement in verse 1 regarding the *beginning of Jehoiakim's reign* can be reconciled with Chapter 28:1 without much difficulty. Furthermore, <margin>Chapter 36</margin> Chapter 36 follows, the beginning of which (verses 1–9) pertains to the *end of the fourth year of Jehoiakim*, while the rest (verse 9 and following) pertains to the *fifth year*, in which an extraordinary fast was celebrated in Jerusalem. This was undoubtedly because, after the defeat of Necho’s army, the danger from Nebuchadnezzar was now looming closer. At that time, the word of the Lord came <margin>Chapter 45</margin> to *Baruch* (Chapter 45, comparing verse 1), whom Jeremiah used to record and read these prophecies. And finally, here follows Chapter 35, occurring <margin>Chapter 35</margin> in roughly the *eighth year of Jehoiakim*, when Nebuchadnezzar was no longer just a threat but had actually made an incursion into Judea (compare verse 11). See § 9 and *Lightfoot’s Chronology, p. 120.*

<margin>*To the times of Jehoiachin: Chapters 13 and 22:24 and following.*</margin> Under the reign of *Jehoiachin* <note>original: "Iechoniae"</note>, which was quite brief, only Chapter 13 was published (compare verse 18 and our notes there) and Chapter 22:24 and following. This latter prophecy seems to be joined to the preceding ones against *Jehoahaz* and *Jehoiakim* because of the similarity of the subject matter—unless you prefer to refer verse 18 to the times of Jehoiakim as in the preceding parts and consider this a "prophetic anticipation."

<margin>*To the times of Zedekiah: Chapters 24; 51:59 and following; 27, 28, 29; 30, 31; 49:34 and following; 21; 34; 37; 32, 33, 38; 39:15 and following; verses 1–14; Chapter 52.*</margin> To the reign of *Zedekiah* should be referred Chapter 24 regarding the *two baskets of figs*, since it was published after Jehoiachin was deported (verse 1), which is referenced in Chapter 29:17 as something that happened previously. Likewise Chapter 51:59 and following, occurring in the *fourth year of Zedekiah*, when he himself had set out for Babylon with his retinue (verse 59). And to this, according to the opinion of *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Likely referring to Rashi, the famous medieval Jewish commentator.</note> and the *Seder Olam* <note>An ancient Hebrew chronological work.</note>, Chapters 27, 28, and 29 are added in order, having been published in the same year and (as is probable) after the return of *Zedekiah* from Babylon. This is based on the inscription in Chapter 28:1, which also harmonizes the timing of the preceding Chapter 27, even though it is inscribed with the fourth year of Jehoiakim—an <term>apparent contradiction: original "ἐναντιοφάνειαν", a Greek term for a surface-level conflict in the text</term> which we resolve in the notes to Chapter 27:1. Chapters 30 and 31 are very fittingly joined with Chapter 29 (which tears down the reckless and premature promises of the false prophets regarding Israel's restoration), for in these chapters, true comfort from the mind of God is substituted. Add Chapter 49:34 and following. Then, when the city began to be besieged by the Chaldeans, the first delegation from *Zedekiah* to Jeremiah occurred (Chapter 21). After Chapter 34 is inserted (for this was published when the siege was lifted and the Chaldeans had gone to meet the Egyptian reinforcements, verse 22; and Jeremiah was not yet shut up in prison, verse 2), there follows the second delegation of the same king (Chapter 37), likewise made during the time the siege was lifted (compare verses 4–5). After this, Jeremiah was cast into prison (verse 12 and following), where he published the prophecies contained in Chapters 32 and 33 (compare Chapter 32:2 and 33:1). From this follow Chapter 38 (compare verse 28) and Chapter 39:15 and following, and only then verses 1–14 of that same chapter, which look to the final days of *Zedekiah*, during and after the capture of the city. Chapter 52 can be added here or reserved for the end, as many parts of it pertain to this time.

<margin>*After the destruction of the city: Chapters 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, and 46:13 and following.*</margin> *After the destruction of the city*, the Prophet preached first in the land of Judah to the remnants of his people (Chapters 40, 41, 42), and then in Egypt, partly against the stubborn Jews and partly against the Egyptians (Chapters 43, 44), to which Chapter 46:13 and following should probably also be referred.

<meta>This page serves as the formal introduction to the commentary on the Book of Jeremiah. It follows the previous page's chronological and historical breakdown of the prophet's work by addressing long-standing scholarly debates regarding the literary quality and grammatical accuracy of Jeremiah’s writing.</meta>

# PREFACE TO JEREMIAH

<margin>Preface to the Commentary on Jeremiah</margin>
The author of the Preface to the Commentary on Jeremiah is of the opinion that the prophet used a style that was less accurate and elegant. He concludes this from the frequent use of ellipses <note>omissions of words</note>, the confusion of the particles <note>original: "אל & על"</note> *el* and *al*, as well as the <term>enallage</term> <note>a grammatical substitution</note> of Gender, Number, Tense, and Person; and finally, from the frequent use of <term>metathesis</term> <note>reordering</note> by means of <note>original: "ὕστερον πρότερον"</note> *hysteron proteron* <note>a figure of speech where the natural order is reversed, putting the "last thing first"</note>. He admits that such departures from ordinary speech are found in the writings of other prophets, but he claims they are found more frequently here. He further argues that the prophet was less skilled in the art of spelling, based on the *Keri* and *Ketiv* <note>original: "Krijan & Cthiban"; these are marginal notes in the Hebrew Bible indicating a difference between the "written" text and the "read" tradition</note>, which are more numerous in Jeremiah than in other Biblical books. He seeks the cause of this in Jeremiah's age, noting that he began to prophesy as a mere youth when he was not yet sufficiently skilled in accurate and orderly speech, citing Chapter 1, verse 6. However, just as the authority of *Jerome* <note>original: "Hieronymi"</note> does not force us to agree, we even less approve of that rash criticism by *Isaac Abarbanel*. For if Jeremiah’s youth caused a defect in his speech, why then did he not acquire a more fitting way of speaking over time, so that under Kings Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, having reached a mature age, he might then speak and write more orderly? Or, if Jeremiah raised his lack of grammatical training as an objection to his divine calling, why would the power bestowed by God **not have been able** to remove that defect (as was promised in verse 9)? As for the substitutions and reorderings that *Abarbanel* cites in Jeremiah, they are of so little importance that he himself does not deny they are common to the other prophets; in their writings, such figures are even more frequent, partly due to accepted Hebrew usage and partly due to a certain prophetic sublimity. Nor does the argument from the multitude of *Keri* and *Ketiv* fare any better. In this, he rashly supposes that the *Keri* are nothing but marginal corrections or explanations *made by Ezra* according to the nature of the language and textual context, specifically in those places where the *sacred writers, because of an insufficient knowledge of the Hebrew language or grammar, wrote erroneously.* This hypothesis deserves to be more fully dismantled elsewhere, as it characterizes all the <term>theopneustos</term> <note>divinely inspired</note> writers (for all of them have *Keri*) as an unlearned rabble, and makes *Abarbanel* himself appear much more learned in the grammar of the sacred language than they were. Indeed, I believe anyone who considers the following will easily acquit our Prophet of rusticity and ignorance of the language: (1) *Anathoth*, his homeland, was only three miles from Jerusalem; (2) it was a priestly city (see § 3). Where would the dialect of the Hebrew language be more pure than in Jerusalem and its neighboring region? And where would it be more cultivated than among the priests? And even if we granted that the Anathothite way of speaking was more rustic, (3) Jeremiah likely spent a larger part of his life in Jerusalem than in Anathoth, and was therefore probably accustomed to the Jerusalem speech. But what can best defend Jeremiah from the charge of ignorance of speech are (4) his *Lamentations* <note>original: "Threni"</note>, about which *Sanctius* says:

> *That Jeremiah possessed an elegant and*
> *grave style is sufficiently shown by the Lamentations, ----- than which*
> *antiquity has held nothing more serious, more rhythmic, or more sonorous.*

Furthermore, if to anyone Jeremiah’s speech nonetheless seems simple, or rather mournful and sad, let them know that the mind and the times of Jeremiah were also sad, such that they shunned the affectation of elegance. Let them also know this: that divine simplicity has more wisdom, weight, and efficacy than all the rhetorical flourishes of all the orators combined.

<margin>Our Annotations.</margin>
§ XXII. After these introductory remarks, it remains for us to guide the students of the Hebrew Codex to the reading of Jeremiah itself. We have endeavored to make this clearer and easier through our notes, explaining the more obscure words and phrases, showing the connection where it seemed more difficult, and clearing away things that could hinder someone striving for an understanding of this Prophet. In this matter, lest we should indulge ourselves or trust too much in our own judgment, we have simultaneously consulted the most excellent interpreters: from the Jewish tradition, *Rabbi Solomon* [Rashi] and *David Kimchi*; and from the Christians, especially *Sebastian Schmidt* <note>original: "B. Seb. Schmidium"</note>, adding here and there the Eastern Versions. Therefore, dear reader, enjoy this labor of ours, such as it is, and enjoy it in such a way that you strive to obtain from God Himself the enlightened eyes of the mind
->to recognize and revere the wonders of the<-
->Law of God. Farewell.<-

**CHAPTER I.** They give *Jeremiah* the first place in the Volume of the Major Prophets, *Ezekiel* the second, and *Isaiah* the third (2. 2. and the Manuscript in the Jena University Library, and the Berlin Manuscript, which consists of four volumes. The same order once prevailed among the Talmudists, compare the Tractate *Bava Batra* folio 14, b. where they say: although Isaiah is prior to Jeremiah and Ezekiel in terms of time, he is nevertheless placed after them. Because the books of Kings end with the description of devastation, and Jeremiah is entirely concerned with predicting devastation, and Ezekiel begins with devastation and ends with consolation, while Isaiah is entirely about consolation: therefore we join the prediction of desolation to the description of it, and join consolations to consolations. Maimonides prescribes the same order again in *The Laws of Tefillin* chapter 7, § 15, page 95, b of the Amsterdam Edition; and Rabbi Elias <note>Elijah Levita</note> says it is found in the books of the Germans and French in his *Preface to the Masorah III*, page 19, 20. However, he, along with David Kimchi in the *Preface to Jeremiah*, testifies that in all Spanish books the order of the major Prophets is preserved according to their times. It would be a long task to weigh the reasons by which Abarbanel, in his *Preface to the Commentary on Isaiah*, rejects that order of the Talmudists; see our Preface to Isaiah §. 2. Meanwhile, Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century scholar</note> attempted to reconcile the citation in Matthew 27, 9 with these same facts, by assuming, as he thinks, that Jeremiah stands for the Volume of the Prophets, in which he once proceeded first; compare Luke 24, 44, where "the Psalms" stands for the entire Volume of the Hagiographa <note>the "Writings" or third section of the Hebrew Bible</note>.

...[binding] their long robes with a belt around their loins, so that their walking or work may be more unhindered. 2 Kings 4:29; Luke 12:35; Ephesians 6:14; 1 Peter 1:13. **a)** <note>original: "ne consterneris"</note> *Do not be dismayed*, see verse 1. **b)** Chapter 17:17, 18; Isaiah 8:3. Psalm 108:11, 13, 19; chapter 32:36. **e)** Which can neither be bent nor broken. He means to say: The Prophet will not be immune to trials, but by God's grace, he will be superior to them. **k)** verse 8; 2 Timothy 4:17.

**CHAPTER 2.** The goal of this chapter is to convince all Israel, and especially the Jews, that they have defected from Jehovah to idols without cause. Compare Micah 6. **verse 2. l)** *by going*, namely to them. Whence the adjective <term>chasid</term> (pious, holy), Psalm 32:6, etc. **o)** your childhood, that is, the devotion you had toward me in your childhood. Leviticus 22:10. Compare Exodus 19:5, 6; chapter 28:36. **r)** like the firstfruits of his produce, or sacred to him. Genesis 25:13. Jonathan: "in the province of the Arabs." **b)** "Behold, whether," chapter 3:1. A Chaldean usage of the particle. Compare Ezra 5:17. **c)** Isaiah 66:8, 11. **d)** "Whether it has changed." Leviticus 27:10; Micah 2:4; compare Micah 4:5. **e)** chapter 5:7; 2 Kings 19:18. **f)** that is, me, whom to have was their highest glory. Psalm 106:20; Romans 1:23. Conversely, fictitious gods are everywhere called "shame." Jeremiah 3:24; 11:13. Compare Bochart, *Hieroz.* Part I, book II, chapter 34. **g)** with that which does not profit, verse 8; Isaiah 55:2, for which they ought to be ashamed.

* **verse 12. h)** *Be astonished:* Isaiah 52:14; Psalm 40:16. **i)** As if to say: the iniquities of the Jews are so great that it would not be a wonder if the Lord moved the heavens to destruction over them. Schmidt; Isaiah 1:2. **k)** *shudder:* Ezekiel 27:35; Deuteronomy 32:17. **l)** *be stunned:* properly "be desolated," like the preceding <term>shommu</term> <note>original: "שֹׁמּוּ"</note>. For he who shudders suffers a kind of desolation of the soul. **verse 13. m)** not a simple sin, such as that of the Gentiles, who, since they are ignorant of the true God, stubbornly cling to idols. Verse 11. **n)** chapter 17:13; compare Isaiah 1:2 and following; Hosea 4:10. **o)** a fountain, which does not give foreign waters like a cistern, but its own; and that not by turns, but continually and without ceasing. Kimchi. Compare chapter 18:14, 15; 17:13; Psalm 36:10; John 4:14. **p)** *by cutting out:* Deuteronomy 6:11. **q)** *cisterns:* for collecting rainwater. 2 Chronicles 26:10; 2 Samuel 17:18. These do not spring water from themselves but receive it from elsewhere. **r)** indeed, broken cisterns, with the stones shattered that usually fortify them; therefore, they frustrate the hope of those seeking water much more. Furthermore (says Kimchi), he thus describes the "good" which Israel expected both from idols and from idolatrous nations (Assyrians and Egyptians). Compare verse 11, 18.

* **verse 14. s)** spoken in wonder. How does it happen, he asks, that one whom God formerly held as a son (Exodus 4:22; Deuteronomy 4:1), whom no one attacked with impunity because he was sacred to the Lord (above, verse 3), is now like a slave and is plundered by all? Compare verse 17. **t)** born at home of a maidservant, i.e., a house-born slave. Genesis 17:12.

* **verse 15. u)** For they roar over him (as over prey, Amos 3:4; Ezekiel 22:25; Isaiah 5:29; Psalm 74:4). **x)** young lions beginning to hunt (Ezekiel 19:3), i.e., the Kings of the Egyptians and Assyrians. Jeremiah 4:7. **y)** Lamentations 2:8. **z)** *Keri* reading: <term>nits’tu</term> <note>original: "נִצְּתוּ"</note>, they are [burned], from the root <term>natsat</term>, chapter 9:9. For the prefix <term>mibbli</term> <note>original: "מִבְּלִי"</note> sometimes in Jeremiah seems not so much causal as eventual. As in chapter 4:7; 9:9, 10, 11, etc.

* **verse 16. b)** Memphis, according to the Chaldean, Syriac, and the Septuagint. See note on chapter 44:1; Isaiah 19:13. **c)** Daphne or Pelusium. Chapter 43:7, 8, 9; 44:1; Ezekiel 30:18. Compare according to Hiller, Isaiah 30:4. But it is a woman's name in 1 Kings 11:19, 20. Let the Egyptians be understood, to whom both these cities belonged. As if to say: those very ones in whom you have now placed the greatest hope of help, verses 18, 36, 37. For the particle <term>gam</term> (also) is emphatic here as in verse 36. **d)** they shall graze upon the crown of your head, making you bald. Compare Isaiah 3:17. A phrase transferred from the business of herding. Jonathan translates: "they shall kill your heroes and plunder your wealth." For the fulfillment, see 2 Kings 22:29–35 and Preface § 8.

* **verse 17. e)** this effects it. i.e., this is the cause of this evil. Chapter 4:18; 20:15; Isaiah 3:9; Hosea 13:9. It is the response to verse 14. **f)** because they fail; the Infinitive is constructed like a noun with a feminine verb, as in 1 Samuel 12:22. Kimchi.

<summary>In this passage, the prophet Jeremiah delivers God's indictment against Israel for their unprecedented abandonment of their Creator for worthless idols. The text uses vivid imagery of a desert journey and the metaphor of "broken cisterns" to illustrate the futility of seeking security in foreign alliances and false gods.</summary>

### CHAPTER 3. JEREMIAH 3

<margin>
Mark 10:4; compare Hosea 2:4.
**Superfluous Yod** <note>A Hebrew scribal note indicating an extra letter in the manuscript</note>
a) I saw, I say, that [she did] not. b) Faithless <note>original: "perfida"</note>. See verses 7, 10, 11. Just like a wife who is faithless toward her husband. Verse 20. c) To go away refers not so much to the start as to the progression; to move forward, to proceed. —Schmidt.
</margin>

<margin>
b) Isaiah 47:10. * v. 3. c) Showers, Deuteronomy 32:2. The "former" rains, which is clear from the contrast with the "latter rain" <note>Hebrew: מלקוש (malkosh)</note>. —Cocceius. See Leviticus 26:19; Deuteronomy 11:17. d) The latter rain. Joel 2:23. See Jeremiah 14:1. e) Ezekiel 3:7. f) Chapter 5:3; Zephaniah 3:5. * v. 4. g) "Now," that is, not so long ago. Isaiah 48:6–7. This denotes the twelfth year of Josiah (see chapter 1:2), since the worship of idols was abolished by the authority of that most pious king (2 Kings 22:2–3; 2 Chronicles 34:3). However, the people and the leaders promoted this reform with little sincerity (v. 10; Jeremiah 4:1); indeed, they gradually slid back into idolatry (2 Chronicles 34:8–33). h) v. 19; see chapter 2:27, 35. i) Proverbs 2:17. Whom I followed in my youth as a leader and a husband. Jeremiah 2:2.
</margin>

3 ...and by your wickedness. Therefore the showers have been withheld, and the spring rain has not come. You have the brow of a harlot wife; you refuse to be ashamed. 4 Have you not just now called to me: "My Father, you are the friend of my youth"? 5 "Will he be angry forever? Will he keep a grudge to the end?" Behold, you have spoken this, but you have done all the evil you were able to do.

6 The LORD said to me in the days of King Josiah: "Have you seen what backsliding Israel has done? She went up on every high mountain and under every green tree, and played the harlot there. 7 And I thought: 'After she has done all these things, she will return to me.' But she did not return. And her faithless sister Judah saw it. 8 And I saw that for all the causes for which backsliding Israel committed adultery, I sent her away and gave her a bill of divorce. Yet her faithless sister Judah was not afraid; she also went and played the harlot. 9 And because the noise of her whoredom was so loud, she defiled the land; she committed adultery with stone and wood. 10 Yet for all this, her faithless sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but only in pretense," says the LORD.

11 And the LORD said to me: "Backsliding Israel has shown herself more righteous than faithless Judah. 12 Go and proclaim these words toward the north, and say: 'Return, backsliding Israel,' says the LORD. 'I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful,' says the LORD. 'I will not keep a grudge forever. 13 Only acknowledge your iniquity, that you have rebelled against the LORD your God, and have scattered your favors to strangers under every green tree...'"

<margin>

v. 10. h) "And yet in all this," meaning "nonetheless." This is an invitation to repentance and a prophecy at the same time. —Schmidt. Indeed, it is also a "Gospel word," offering a kind reception to sinners, just as David ordered his degenerate son Absalom to return (2 Samuel 14:21), or Saul to the exiled David (1 Samuel 26:21). <meta>This page continues the prophetic warnings found in Jeremiah chapter 4. ### JEREMIAH. CHAPTER 4.

<margin>
**m)** *and they shall be devastated*, that is, they shall be stunned. Job 18:20. **n)** *the false prophets*, chapter 2:8. **o)** they will be amazed when they see that things have turned out quite differently than they themselves had predicted. For the fulfillment, see chapter 39:19.

$^6$ ...a leopard is watching over their cities; everyone who goes out from them shall be torn in pieces, because their transgressions are many, and their backslidings are strong. $^7$ **How shall I pardon you for this?** Your children have forsaken Me and sworn by those who are no gods. $^{10}$ **Go up upon her walls and destroy**, but do not make a complete end; take away her branches, for they are not the Lord’s. $^{11}$ **For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have been utterly treacherous** to Me, says the Lord. $^{12}$ **They have lied about the Lord** and said, "It is not He; neither shall evil come upon us, nor shall we see sword or famine. $^{13}$ **And the prophets shall become wind**, and the word is not in them; thus shall it be done to them." $^{14}$ **Therefore, thus says the Lord God of Hosts**: "Because you speak this word, behold, I will make My words in your mouth fire, and this people wood, and it shall devour them. $^{15}$ **Behold, I am bringing upon you a nation from afar**, O house of Israel," says the Lord; "it is a mighty nation, it is an ancient nation, a nation whose language you do not know, nor can you understand what they say. $^{16}$ **Their quiver is like an open grave**; they are all mighty men. $^{17}$ **And they shall eat up your harvest and your bread**; they shall eat up your sons and your daughters; they shall eat up your flocks and your herds; they shall eat up your vines and your fig trees; they shall impoverish your fortified cities, in which you trust, with the sword. $^{18}$ **Nevertheless in those days**," says the Lord, "I will not make a complete end of you. $^{19}$ **And it shall come to pass, when you say**, 'Why has the Lord our God done all these things to us?' then you shall answer them, 'Just as you have forsaken Me and served foreign gods in your land, so shall you serve strangers in a land that is not yours.'" $^{20}$ **Declare this in the house of Jacob...**

---

**v. 14. e)** **mighty**, rapid, breaking through everything so that no one can resist, like a rapid river. (Schmidt). Psalm 74:15. **f)** **ancient** <note>original: "a-saeculo"</note> Genesis 6:4. That is, ancient, which for many centuries past has been famous for the atrocity of its warfare, cf. e.g. Genesis 10:10. **g)** that which increases the gravity of the evil. Deuteronomy 28:49. Primarily because no one can plead with or pacify with words enemies of an unknown language. (Schmidt). **h)** i.e., understand. cf. 2 Kings 18:26. **v. 16. i)** **His quiver**, in which the arrows are stored, ($\beta$) Isaiah 22:6; chapter 49:2. **k)** **like an open grave**, yawning wide. Psalm 5:10; Ezekiel 37:12. Not only because of its size, which holds a great force of arrows, but also its effect, because its arrows will all be lethal. Compare Lamentations 3:13. **v. 17. l)** Leviticus 26:16; Deuteronomy 28:31, 51. Like an evil and monstrous beast that devours everything in its path, whether it be men, beasts, or the fruits of the trees and earth. (Schmidt). Nor did Grotius speak badly here: "Total consumption is usually called 'eating' <note>original Hebrew: "אכל"</note> by the Hebrews." **m)** **it shall impoverish**, deprive of men. Psalm 34:11. Or rather it shall demolish, compare Malachi 1:4. Others by shifting letters (metathesis) read it as "he shall uproot." **n)** Numbers 32:36; Hosea 10:14. **o)** **with the sword**, specifically it shall demolish. For the immediately preceding clause is parenthetical. By "the sword," however, any instruments of devastation are denoted. Compare Ezekiel 26:9. **v. 18. p)** **Yet even**. This is a mitigation of the punishment. **q)** verse 10; chapter 4:27. **v. 19. r)** **you shall say**. He uses the 2nd person by way of communication, meaning: "if your people shall say." **s)** Chapter 13:22; Chapter 16:10. Since at that time only idolatry seemed to have been eliminated. See Preface § 7. **t)** **by the law of retaliation**. For here, foreign gods and foreign peoples, one's own land and a foreign land, are placed alongside each other. **u)** **which is not yours**, cf. Deuteronomy 28:47, 48. **v. 20. x)** as if to say: As many of you as hear these things from me, Jeremiah, speak of them everywhere, that I have spoken this, and indeed in the name of the Lord. An indefinite imperative, as in chapter 11:2.

---

*) **v. 7.** **"And I satiated"**: thus with the letter *Shin* according to our scholars; but Jonathan, Rashi, Kimchi and others interpret it as "and they were satisfied," as if they had read with the letter *Sin*. *) **v. 9.** **"And if against a nation such as"**: thus in manuscripts 1, 2, 3. *) **17.** **"trusting"**: written fully in manuscript 5 and according to the Western tradition; thus specifically in 1 and 2 according to Museum 1 and 2, but missing in the Masoretic Krsf.

<meta>This page continues the prophetic warnings in Jeremiah 6, specifically the people's refusal to listen to God’s "ancient paths" and the resulting announcement of a northern invader. It concludes the chapter with a metallurgical metaphor of judgment and introduces the beginning of Chapter 7.</meta>

->**Commentary**<-

The approach of those coming is marked by both noise and a great multitude. Chapter 50:42. Isaiah 17:12. a) They will have a great cavalry, in which the chief strength of Eastern armies lies. Chapter 50:42. b) As one man. Ibid. Compare Judges 20:8, 11. <margin>v. 24. c)</margin> As soon as we heard the report of his coming (namely the approaching enemy), we lost our peace. Deuteronomy 2:25. d) Our hands have grown slack, that is, we have become dismayed and terrified. Chapter 38:4. Isaiah 13:7. e) Chapter 3:21. f) Chapter 4:31; chapter 22:23; chapter 49:24; chapter 50:43. Isaiah 13:8. <margin>v. 25. g)</margin> Matthew 24:17, 18. h) Terror threatens from every side. Chapter 20:3, 10. Psalm 31:14. Isaiah 31:9. <margin>v. 26. i)</margin> Sprinkle yourself (4). Chapter 25:34. Isaiah 27:30. Micah 1:10. Jonathan: cover your heads. Others: <term>to roll</term>. l) As was customary in the most serious calamities. Joshua 7:6. 2 Samuel 13:19. Job 2:8. m) As if for an only child. Compare Amos 8:10. Zechariah 12:10. n) Of bitterness, that is, most bitter. Chapter 31:15. o) Chapter 4:20; chapter 15:8. p) Isaiah 21:3. <margin>v. 27. q)</margin> A watchtower or <term>watchman</term>. (1) Compare Isaiah 23:12. Others: a tester/prover. So the Vulgate, the Septuagint, Jonathan, and the Syriac. Compare v. 29, chapter 9:6. r) And like a fortification. Chapter 1:18. s) You shall test, therefore. By making a trial, you shall inquire what sort of people they are. Zechariah 13:9. <margin>v. 28. t)</margin> Strictly "those who turn aside," that is, the rebellious; the most stubborn of the stubborn (as Tremellius translates). For the Hebrew roots *SUR* and *SAR* are very close both in letters and meaning. Compare Isaiah 1:23. n) Walking in slander. (6) Chapter 9:3. Proverbs 11:13. x) They are mere <term>bronze</term> and <term>iron</term>; not good silver. v. 30. This alludes to the intractable nature of the persistent Jews. y) Isaiah 1:4. <margin>v. 29. z)</margin> <term>Scorched</term> or burned. From the root *NACHAR*. Isaiah 24:6. Ezekiel 15:4. As if to say: such a great fire was placed under the crucible that the bellows were scorched by the heat. a) The bellows of the furnace (1). b) It is consumed by the fire. Deuteronomy 2:14, 16. c) Lead, which is usually added to silver in a cupel by those who melt metals, for the purpose of protecting the silver from the force of the flame and carrying away its impurities when the fire is applied. d) But he refined in vain; chapter 9:6. Isaiah 1:25. Malachi 3:2, 3. e) The refiner (r) or <term>in refining</term>; for the wicked were not separated. Chapter 10:20. Joshua 4:18; chapter 8:16. Namely, like dross from that metal which was hoped to be good silver. <margin>v. 30 g)</margin> Rejected silver. Psalm 15:4. Compare Isaiah 1:22. h) By their real name. To be "called" often means to "be": chapter 11:16. Isaiah 1:26. Chapter 35:8; chapter 54:5. i) Compare the note on Isaiah 7:15.

<summary>This page covers the conclusion of Jeremiah's warning in chapter 6, where the people's rejection of God's "ancient paths" leads to a decree of judgment via a northern invader. It uses a detailed metallurgical metaphor to describe the people as "rejected silver" that cannot be purified even by the prophet acting as a refiner.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the "Temple Sermon" of Jeremiah 7. It follows the conclusion of Chapter 6, moving from general warnings of a northern invader to a specific critique of the Judeans' false sense of security in the physical structure of the Temple in Jerusalem.</meta>

# JEREMIAH. CHAPTER 7.

<margin>
CHAPTER 7, verse 2.
a) namely the Eastern gate, which was the most famous of all; according to <note>Rabbi David</note> Kimchi and <note>Isaac</note> Abarbanel. But S. <note>likely Sebastian Schmidt</note> understands the great gate of the priests' court, where everyone who usually entered through the various gates of the people's court would gather, both to bring sacrifices and to worship. It was here that their prejudice most needed to be removed (see verse 4). m) Those whom Jeremiah was pointing to with his finger or extended hand. n) Zechariah 14:16.
</margin>

<margin>

Verse 8; chapter 5:31; Isaiah 5. r) while they say—namely, the false prophets; or "so that you say," which Schmidt proves. s) "These are," namely, according to most, the parts of the temple: the Court, the Holy Place, and the Holy of Holies, which the Jews pointed out. As if to say: therefore the Lord will not devastate His temple, nor this city. Compare Acts 6:13 and the note on Jeremiah 26:11. But Schmidt refers this to the false priests and prophets, as if to say: "These are the established ministry of the temple," just as today the Pope and the Prelates claim to be called "the Church."

<margin>
v. 10. l) "We are rescued," namely from imminent evils. Ezekiel 14:15, 18; Amos 3:12. [You think] no danger is to be feared, contrary to what you prophets say. The past tense is used instead of the future to denote a firm conviction of safety. m) "In order that you may do," as if to say: The external worship which you hypocritically offer me is a cloak for your wickedness, used so that under the appearance of religion you might sin more freely. <summary>Jeremiah delivers his famous "Temple Sermon," rebuking the people of Judah for thinking their religious rituals and the physical presence of the Temple would protect them from judgment while they continue in social injustice and idolatry.</summary>
<keywords>Jeremiah 7, Temple Sermon, Shiloh, social justice, religious hypocrisy, Judah, Kimchi, Abarbanel, Masoretic notes</keywords>

--- Page 888 ---
<meta>This page continues Jeremiah’s "Temple Sermon" from the previous page. Having warned the people not to trust in the physical building of the Temple while continuing to sin, the prophet now draws a historical parallel to the destruction of the ancient sanctuary at Shiloh and describes the widespread idolatry occurring in the streets of Jerusalem.</meta>

<header>JEREMIAH 7 CHAPTER 7.</header>

<margin>
v. 14. <sup>h</sup>) With vain presumption, as seen in verses 4 and 8. <sup>y</sup>) This refers not only to the Ark being taken from there by the Philistines (see the note on 1 Samuel 4:21), <sup>i</sup>) but to everything that is currently happening to the people, so that the current captivity of the ten tribes is seen as a continuation of the ruin of Shiloh. Compare verse 15 and 12, according to the commentator Sebastian Schmidt.
</margin>

<gloss>14</gloss> Therefore I will do to the house which is called by My name, in which you trust, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh. <gloss>h y i</gloss>

<margin>
v. 15. <sup>k</sup>) See 2 Kings 17:18, 20, 23. <sup>l</sup>) Meaning the ten tribes, who since the division of the kingdom have been called "Ephraim," because the royal power was held by that tribe. So says <note>the medieval scholar</note> Kimchi. Compare Isaiah 7:2 and Hosea 5:9. But Schmidt prefers: "with all the seed of Ephraim."
</margin>

<gloss>15</gloss> And I will cast you out of My sight, as I cast out all your brothers, even all the offspring of Ephraim. <gloss>k l</gloss>

<margin>
v. 16. <sup>b</sup>) Compare chapter 11:14, 14:11, and 1 John 5:16. God addresses the Prophet as if to say: "Do not intercede with me to spare the people (compare Genesis 18:25 and following) for the sake of a few godly ones or for the sake of the children; for their corruption and malice is universal, involving children, fathers, and mothers." According to Schmidt. <sup>c</sup>) "A cry," used in mournful matters as in Psalm 17:1 and 61:2; though elsewhere it refers to a joyful matter, i.e., a shout of joy. See the note on 1 Kings 8:28. <sup>d</sup>) "Intercede with me." Compare the notes on chapter 27:18, Genesis 23:8, and Job 21:15. <sup>e</sup>) Isaiah 1:15.
</margin>

<gloss>16</gloss> As for you, do not pray for this people, and do not lift up a cry or prayer for them, and do not intercede with Me, for I am not listening to you. <gloss>b c d e</gloss>

<margin>
v. 17. <sup>f</sup>) As if to say: "Just look around you, my Jeremiah, and see what kind of people these are." According to Schmidt. <sup>g</sup>) Compare chapter 2:28 and see the Preface, section 7. <sup>h</sup>) And in all the squares. See verse 34 and compare chapter 11:13 and 44:21.
</margin>

<gloss>17</gloss> Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? <gloss>f g h</gloss>

<margin>
<sup>n</sup>) Instead of "for the work," the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>the ancient Greek translation</note> and the <term>Targum Jonathan</term> <note>the Aramaic translation</note> understand this as "the stars." Compare chapter 8:2 and 19:13. But the <term>Vulgate</term> <note>the Latin Bible</note> and others say: "the queen of heaven" (following the form for "Mistress"). That is, some refer it to the Sun, others to the Moon, or to some particular star. Schmidt, however, considers this and the following word <note>kavanim</note> to be foreign terms, adopted from the places where the Jews learned this worship. <sup>o</sup>) "And to pour out drink offerings." Isaiah 65:11.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 18. <sup>i</sup>) Kindling, as in Exodus 35:3. <sup>k</sup>) With the husbands and sons agreeing—indeed, helping—which is noted here figuratively through the gathering of wood and kindling of fire. Compare chapter 44:15, 19. That is, each and every one commits and promotes idolatry; therefore, they are capable of receiving no mercy or intercession. See verse 16. <sup>l</sup>) Kneading the dough. Genesis 18:6, Hosea 7:4. <sup>m</sup>) <term>Popana</term> <note>original: "popana f. placentas rotundas"</note> i.e., round sacrificial cakes, which were used by idolaters in sacrifices. Suetonius calls this "bread-making" in his Life of Vespasian, chapter 7. Compare below, chapter 44:19. <sup>n</sup>) To the "work of the heavens," i.e., celestial things. Chapter 44:17, 19.
</margin>

<gloss>18</gloss> The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead dough to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven, and they pour out drink offerings to other gods, in order to provoke Me. <gloss>i k l m n o</gloss>

<margin>
v. 19. <sup>p</sup>) According to the Targum Jonathan: "Do they really think they are provoking me?" <sup>q</sup>) "Causing distress?" See chapter 32:30, 1 Samuel 1:6. Since distress cannot properly affect God in His essence, this means that when He is justly angered by human sins, He might be said to suffer some disturbance or loss. Compare Ezekiel 16:42. Kimchi **rightly compares** Job 35:6, 7, 8. It should be understood in a way consistent with God's nature when distress and sorrow are attributed to Him in Jeremiah 8:19, Deuteronomy 32:21, etc. <sup>r</sup>) "Is it not rather themselves?" Compare verse 6 and chapter 25:7.
</margin>

<gloss>19</gloss> Is it Me they provoke? says the Lord. Is it not themselves, to the shame of their own faces? <gloss>p q r</gloss>

<margin>
v. 20. <sup>s</sup>) Resulting in shame. This is not the *intended* purpose, but the *outcome*, as in verse 6, chapter 44:8, and Hosea 8:4. That is: "so that shame happens to them." <sup>t</sup>) To be poured out like a heavy rain. 2 Samuel 21:10. Compare Jeremiah 6:11. <sup>u</sup>) As in Exodus 9:25. <sup>x</sup>) Chapter 17:27, 2 Kings 22:17.
</margin>

<gloss>20</gloss> Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, My anger and My fury will be poured out upon this place, upon man and upon beast, upon the trees of the field and upon the fruit of the ground; and it will burn and not be extinguished. <gloss>s t u x</gloss>

<margin>Haftarah portion: Tzav</margin>

<margin>
v. 21. <sup>y</sup>) As if to say: "Just keep adding them!" Compare Isaiah 29:1. This is not a command of approval or desire, but of rejection; like someone saying to another: "Do whatever you want, it won't help you anyway." So says Kimchi. <sup>z</sup>) Namely, the remaining parts. So Exodus 20:21. <sup>a</sup>) Namely, of the victims. For it was permitted for those offering peace offerings to eat a portion (1 Samuel 9:13, Exodus 18:12). But Schmidt interprets: "Those things which you intend for me as an offering—you might as well devour them yourselves rather than offer them to me."
</margin>

<gloss>21</gloss> Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat meat. <gloss>y z a</gloss>

<margin>The written text says "Bring out" <note>Hebrew: Hotzi'i</note></margin>

<margin>
v. 22. <sup>b</sup>) "For I did not speak so much about sacrifices as I did about..." (verse 23). Compare chapter 26:14-15 and Isaiah 42:19. <sup>c</sup>) Compare Hosea 6:6, Psalm 40:7, 50:8 and following, 51:18. Kimchi well observes that the law regarding bringing sacrifices was (1) not the first law given (compare Exodus 15:25, 26), (2) nor was it the primary or principal law, as no mention of it is made in the words of the covenant in Exodus 19:3–6 or in the Ten Commandments. Those things commanded later (says Cocceius in his Lexicon, column 613) were not given for the sake of righteousness, but were imposed to testify to faith, to confess guilt in servitude, and to present a <term>chirographum</term> <note>a handwritten record of debt</note>. Schmidt adds (3) that sacrifices in this passage should not be understood as they were in their divine institution, but as they were being offered by the Jews. Compare the note on Isaiah 1:11.
</margin>

<margin>
verse 29. <sup>a</sup>) **Cut off your hair, therefore**, as was customary in mourning. See chapter 16:6; Job 1:20. It suggests thick hair, held in too much esteem and value, or perhaps hair left long like that of the Nazirites (Numbers 6:5). According to the scholar Gusset (page 504, column c). But according to Sebastian Schmidt: *tear away your crown*, comparing Psalm 89:40 and the word *gazaz* in Numbers 11:31. <sup>b</sup>) **Upon the high places.** <note>original: "super eminentioribus locis"</note> See the note on chapter 3:21. <sup>c</sup>) **A lament.** See chapter 9:9; 2 Samuel 1:17. <sup>d</sup>) Isaiah 2:6. <sup>e</sup>) **His burning anger**, <note>original: "excandescentia ipsius"</note> directed at those who provoked Him by their sins. verse 30. <sup>f</sup>) Chapter 32:34; Deuteronomy 29:16; Ezekiel 8:5. <sup>g</sup>) See 2 Kings 21:4, 7. <sup>h</sup>) See verse 10.

verse 31. <sup>i</sup>) **Topheth** is the proper name of a place in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, specifically consecrated to Moloch, containing his high places and altars (v. 32; ch. 19:5, 6), and perhaps even a tabernacle (Acts 7:43). Some believe the name comes from *toph* <note>the Hebrew word for drum</note>, suggesting that drums were beaten during the sacrifices so that the wailing of the children would not affect the hearts of the parents. However, the scholar Schmidt observes that the letter *Pe* would then require a dot (Dagesh) from the root *taphaf*. He suspects the name is of foreign origin, adopted from other nations along with the cult itself, or perhaps it was a term for hell used in the Church of God (see Job 17:6; Isaiah 30:33; 2 Kings 23:10). What if it is derived from the Arabic *hafara*, meaning "he cleaned" or "he performed sacred rites," referring to sacred washings? <sup>k</sup>) **In the valley near Jerusalem**, named after the son of Hinnom (though the reason is uncertain). See chapter 19:2, 6; Joshua 15:8. <sup>l</sup>) Chapter 32:35; indeed, I expressly forbade it in Leviticus 18:21. See the note on Jeremiah 19:5. <sup>m</sup>) **Nor did it ever enter My mind** to command such worship. See 2 Kings 12:5. This phrase implies there were those who persuaded the people that this ritual had been divinely instituted.
</margin>

<gloss>29</gloss> Cut off your hair <sup>g</sup> and cast it away, and take up a lamentation <sup>h</sup> on the high places; for the LORD has rejected and forsaken the generation of His wrath. <gloss>30</gloss> For the children of Judah have done evil in My sight, <sup>i</sup> says the LORD; they have set their abominations in the house which is called by My name, to defile it. <sup>k</sup> <gloss>31</gloss> And they have built the high places of Topheth, <sup>l</sup> which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not <sup>m</sup> command, nor did it come into My heart.

<gloss>32</gloss> Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says the LORD, when it will no longer be called Topheth, nor the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter; for they will bury in Topheth <sup>o</sup> because there is no other place. <gloss>33</gloss> And the carcasses <sup>p</sup> of this people will be food for the birds of the air and for the beasts of the earth, and no one will frighten them away. <sup>q</sup> <gloss>34</gloss> Then I will cause to cease <sup>r</sup> from the cities of Judah and from the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride; <sup>s</sup> for the land shall become a desolation.

<meta>This page continues the prophetic lamentation of Jeremiah. On the previous page, the prophet described the people's irrational behavior and their failure to recognize the divine "judgment" (mishpat). Now, the text shifts to the immediate, terrifying sounds of the coming invasion from the north and the prophet's profound personal grief over the impending ruin of his people.</meta>

<header>JEREMIAH. CHAPTER 8. 9.</header>

<column-break/>

a) healing <note>original: "fanationis"</note>, used here for the restoration and return of stolen goods and compensation for evils. According to Schmidius <note>Sebastian Schmid (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian</note>, compare chapter 14:19. f) terror (2) chapter 14:19, compare Isaiah 59:11.
**16.** n) as if at the northern boundary (Judges 18:28, 29) through which the Chaldeans <note>the Babylonians</note> were to burst in (chapter 1:14). h) snorting (1) Job 39:20. In Arabic <term>נחיר</term> <note>nakir</term>, a sound emitted through the nostrils. y) neighing (2) chapter 22:27. z) of his mighty ones, namely horses, that is, steeds (chapter 47:3, chapter 50:11).
**v. 17.** d) Isaiah 14:29. b) royal serpents <note>original: "regios"</note> or basilisks (+) Isaiah 11:8, chapter 59:5. c) against whom no incantation has power; compare Psalm 58:6, Ecclesiastes 10:11, and Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> *Hierozoicon* part II, book 3, chapter 6. These are understood to be enemies who cannot be resisted in any way (Schmidius). d) g) they shall bite you; this alludes to Numbers 21:6, compare Habakkuk 3:7. e) compare Deuteronomy 32:24, Amos 9:3.
**v. 18.** f) My comforting <note>original: "Recreatio mea"</note>. r) a noun with a suffix; compare Psalm 39:14. s) and he takes the words to mean: "O God, who restores me in or over my sorrow." But according to Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and grammarian</note>: "Even if I try to comfort myself over my sorrow, etc." as if to say: "although my comfort should be..." g) faint (3) Isaiah 1:5, Lamentations 1:22.
**v. 19.** h) of the cry (chapter 4:31). i) v. 21, 22. k) the most distant, that is, the remote land into which the captives will be led, presumably Chaldea; compare chapter 5:15. He speaks these things (as Schmidius notes) in the spirit of prophecy, as if to say: "I seem to see before me both their captivity and hear their cries, saying: etc." l) compare chapter 14:19, Isaiah 31:22, etc. m) namely God, Isaiah 33:22, compare Deuteronomy 31:17. n) This is God's response. o) Deuteronomy 31:21. p) causing provocation (3) as in Isaiah 50:2. r) He inflicted his judgments, 2 Chronicles 33:19, 22. s) chapter 10:8, chapter 14:22.
**v. 20.** v) Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation of the Prophets</note> introduces it: "The congregation of Israel says..." t) late harvest, the time of the grape harvest and the gathering of garden fruits (Isaiah).

<column-break/>

**16** "And there is no good for the time of healing, and behold, terror!"
Isaiah 28:4. As if to say: "We indeed hoped, while we were still in our own land, to be liberated from our enemies before the onset of the harvest or autumn; but in vain, alas!" Compare chapter 5:17. Perhaps this refers to the time the city was captured, which fell on the 18th of Tammuz <note>a month in the Hebrew calendar</note> or the fourth ecclesiastical month (chapter 39:1).
---
### Chapter IX.
---
**v. 21.** x) verse 11, chapter 4:6. "I am broken" by grief. (Hophal <note>a Hebrew verb form</note>). t) the Prophet speaks. x) "I am blackened," that is, I am clothed in black, after the manner of mourners (chapter 14:2, Psalm 42:10). y) "astonishment has seized me" (chapter 5:24, Micah 4:9).

---

v. 22. a) "Is there no resin?" <note>original: "refina"</note>. Thus correctly translated by the Vulgate and Arabic. chapter 46:11, chapter 51:8. It refers to the most precious substances used for wounds; compare Bochart *Hierozoicon* part I, book 2, chapter 51. a) since its mountains abound in resinous trees (Genesis 37:25). b) "ascended," that is, as when a dressing is applied to a wound. Compare the name <term>תעלה</term> <note>te'alah, "conduit" or "healing"</note> chapter 30:13, 46:11 and note 30:17. c) "health" (chapter 30:17, Isaiah 58:8, 2 Chronicles 24:11). The word <term>ארוכה</term> <note>arukah</note> signifies the joining or closing of a wound among the Hebrews as well as the Arabs, from the Root <term>ארך</term> <note>arakh</note>: "It held fast," when the flesh joined together with watery and reddish color. Thus the Prophet deplores the incurability of the evil.
v. 23. d) "Who will give my head to be" (that is, "Oh that it were") water, or a reservoir of water, so that tears would be supplied to me, sufficient for mourning such a great evil! e) chapter 3:17, 4:17-19, 14:17, Lamentations 1:16, Isaiah 22:4. **CHAPTER IX. v. 1.**
f) "Who will give me," that is, "Oh that I were" (Job 29:2, Isaiah 27:4). g) in a little hut <note>original: "tuguriolo"</note>, such as is used by a watchman in cucumber fields; compare Isaiah 24:20, 1:8. Elsewhere it signifies a lodging place in general, as in Exodus 4:24. h) of travelers (4) chapter 14:8, meaning such a hut which is made of wickerwork by travelers themselves (when they journey through the desert), constructed of branches and turf, under which they can spend the night, somewhat immune from rain and cold. Or it is a portable tent, such as travelers (according to Schmidius on chapter 14:8) carried with them in Eastern lands so that, wherever night might overtake them, they could sleep under it. i) compare Psalm 55:7, 8, 9. k) chapter 17:9, 23:10, Matthew 12:39. l) a congregation (Amos 5:21). m) Isaiah 24:16. **v. 2. n)** "They bend"; literally "they tread," because the bow was bent by placing the foot on the string (Psalm 7:13, 25:9, 64:4). o) verse 7, Hosea 7:15, Psalm 57:5. p) as if the branches of the tongue were leafy with lies, that is, prepared for vibrating lies like weapons. v. 3. q) for faithfulness (chapter 7:28) both toward men and toward God. r) "they grew strong." They acted strenuously, not for good but for evil (Psalm 12:5), becoming worse, not better. This phrase strongly emphasizes the following contrast: "but out of malice, etc." s) chapter 4:7, compare the opposite in Psalm 84:8. t) "they proceeded," with emphasis, as if to say: "They departed from the true way, and wandered and progressed from evil to evil" (Schmidius). u) verse 23, chapter 4:22, Hosea 5:4. **v. 3. x)** compare chapter 12:6. y) compare Micah 7:5, 6. x) "he circumvented with deceit," namely the other. The Hebrew word does not mean to place the sole of one's foot under a fallen person, but to deceitfully catch someone by the foot from behind so that they are forced to fall down on their face (Gussetius 632). Compare Genesis 27:36. It seems simultaneously to allude to the name Jacob (Genesis 25:26, Hosea 12:4), as if to say: "they are indeed Jacobites, but in a sense far different from their father," who by divine will and without fraud held his brother's heel in the womb, so that as the later he might precede the earlier, and as the younger, the older. a) "he walks in slander" (6); compare note on chapter 6:28, Ezekiel 22:9. **v. 4. b)** "they mock," promising clever things to another, but so far from performing them that they rather do harm, like Laban (Genesis 31:7) and Pharaoh (Exodus 8:28) (Schmidius).

v. 15 "healing" <term>מרפא</term> with an Aleph. 3. 2. and so on... v. 16 "snorting" <term>נחרת</term> with a simple Sheva. 3. 5... v. 18 <term>מבלי...גיתי</term> written separately in manuscripts 1. 5... v. 19 "The LORD" <term>היהוה</term> with Sheva in manuscripts 1. 2... v. 22 "physician" <term>רפא</term> spelled fully in 22. 23 according to the Masorah... v. 21 "I am broken" <term>השברתי</term> with Qamets... v. 22 "the balm" <term>הצרי</term> with a Dagesh... v. 23 Here begins verse IX... v. 2 "their tongue" <term>לשונם</term> without a space... "their bow" <term>קשתם</term> with the prefix Lamed... "Jacob" <term>יעקב</term> with Chateph-Pathach... v. 4 "they mock" <term>יהתלו</term> Lamed with a Dagesh...

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
1 <gloss>Hear</gloss> <note>original: "t"</note> the word which the LORD speaks concerning you, O house of Israel:

(1) That the prefix **f** denotes association, see Leviticus 1:16. "With a foreskin," that is (according to Tremellius and Piscator) *with the uncircumcised*, or (according to Schmidius) *among the uncircumcised* by way of metonymy. So nearly Jonathan: *over all the uncircumcised peoples, and over the house of Israel, whose works are similar to the works of the uncircumcised.* For Schmidius gathers from the following verse, where two classes are placed, that this does not refer to the uncircumcised alone. (2) The Septuagint and the Vulgate take it materially: *those who have a circumcised foreskin*. If so, then all the nations named in the next verse must have been circumcised, though they are distinguished from the Jews there because of the foreskin; or, by "circumcised," the Jews are indeed understood, but in such a way that they are joined to the nations in the next verse because of their common "foreskin of the heart" and their common fate of divine vengeance. Or finally, following Jerome, by "all uncircumcised nations" we should not understand the named nations, but others; though by this reasoning (as noted), the Jews should not have been the only ones opposed to the nations, but also the Egyptians, etc. (3) Cocceius Lexicon 759: circumcised in the flesh but with a foreskin of the heart, compare chapter 4:4. Romans 2:25. By this reasoning, the following verse would be judged the same as just stated.

**v. 25. n)** Herodotus (Book 2, chapter 36) mentions that these people used the rite of circumcision anciently, but whether all Egyptian nations did so always and universally may be doubted; especially because in Ezekiel 31:18 and 32:19, the Egyptians are said to lie among the other uncircumcised. Regarding the Idumeans (Edomites), Josephus (Antiquities Book 13, chapter 17) reports that they were only circumcised after being subjugated by Hyrcanus. Regarding the Ammonites and Moabites, it is not at all clear. Nor is it proven regarding the Arabs, although it is known from Philostorgius that the Homerites adopted circumcision after the birth of Christ. And if any of these nations had circumcision at all in Jeremiah's time, it is credible that it was not religious and <term>sacramental</term> <note>a sacred rite signifying a spiritual reality</note> as it was with the Jews, but instituted for natural reasons, see Ludolf's *Commentary on Ethiopian History*, page 269. **o)** chapter 25:23; 49:32. Jonathan translates as "those shorn at the corners," namely of the head, using the Hebrew phrase from Leviticus 19:27. The Septuagint, Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus, as well as Jerome, interpret this as the clipping of the hair in a circle, leaving only a lock on the back of the head, as praised by Bochart in *Sacred Geography* Part 1, book 1, chapter 6. This is how we also understand the Vulgate's "those shorn into a crest," and the Septuagint with the Arabic: *shorn around the face.* But Cocceius Lexicon 759 suggests "those who have the extremities cut off" as a <term>pejorative</term> term for the circumcised, compare verse 24. And Rabbi Solomon (Rashi) interprets it as "those cut off in the corner of the desert," that is, living most remotely in the desert. **p)** the corner of the temples, that is, the hair around the sloping part of the head (whatever hair is on the head besides the skull, or the upper part of the skull, see Leviticus 19:9, 27). Jonathan: those who dwell in tents in the desert; meaning the Arabs, specifically the <term>Scenites</term> <note>tent-dwellers</note>, see notes on Judges 8:11. For Herodotus (Book 3, chapter 8) is the authority that the Arabs were shorn in a circle, shaving the temples. The Greek Scholiast on Leviticus 19 says the Saracens practiced this until his own time. compare Bochart and Clericus's *Commentary on Leviticus 19:27*. **q)** The Septuagint, Arabic, Syriac, and Jonathan add: *of their flesh.* **s)** chapter 4:4. Leviticus 26:41. Ezekiel 44:7. Romans 2:29.

**CHAPTER X. v. 1. t)** The connection of this with the preceding chapter is this: those to whom he had denounced captivity and God's just vengeance because of their sins, he now fortifies with a certain instruction, so that they do not give in to the Chaldeans who entice them toward superstition and idolatry. compare verse 11 and, among the Apocrypha, the Epistle of Jeremiah or Baruch 6:1, following.

v. 2. a) to the way <note>original: "ad viam"</note>, that is, the ritual or manner of acting, which the Gentiles chose for themselves superstitiously. Leviticus 18:3.
3. Deuteronomy 12:30. At the time when Babylon claimed the empire of the East through Nabopolassar the Father, the conquered nations, following the superstition of the Eastern peoples, undoubtedly all worshipped the Babylonian Bel—that great idol of Babylon—having deserted their own gods; against which scandal of temptation the Jews, to be led away into Babylon, are fortified. Vitringa on the Apocalypse chapter 17:5. page 1024. x) accustomed. chapter 2:24. y) by the signs of heaven, that is, by the stars, especially the sun and moon, comparing Deuteronomy 4:19; or also from the constellations of heaven, from which those nations presume to reveal the fates of men. For no one is unaware that the Easterners were most devoted to judicial astrology, which is situated in the observation of the stars. Herodotus Book II. chapter 32. page 75. edition of Stephanus. Others besides were devised by the Egyptians, regarding which god belongs to which day of the month, and on what day someone was born, what fortunes they will have, and what death they will undergo, and what kind of life it will be. Diodorus, Book I, says similar things. Regarding the Chaldeans, the matter is very well known. See T. Stanley's *History of Oriental Philosophy*, Book I, Section 1.
*. Clericus on Leviticus 19:26. He therefore warns against magical prophecies. Isaiah 10:25. With a superstitious fear, as if they could bring or foretell any evil. a) which it is not proper to imitate. # JEREMIAH. CHAPTER 11 & 12. 

<margin>
**a)** for removing evil or misfortune. <note>original: "pro malo f. infortunio se remouendo"</note> See verse 12 and chapter 2:27.
**b)** What business is there? <note>original: "Quid negotii est?"</note> This is an emphatic question. It is as if to say: You could have requested, as an intercessor on their behalf, that I might at least look upon the house in which my divinity has dwelt until now (compare Isaiah 64:10, Lamentations 1:10), but why should my beloved dwell any longer, etc. Compare especially chapter 12:7 and Psalm 78:60, 61. 
**g)** To my beloved, namely the Son, or Christ (Ephesians 5:1), who dwelt symbolically and typically in the temple between the <term>Cherubim</term> <note>winged celestial beings whose figures sat atop the Ark of the Covenant</note> (Deuteronomy 33:12). For here it is not Jeremiah speaking (as the scholar Kimchi prefers) but **God the Father** himself; this is clear from the attached phrase *in my house*, which could hardly be attributed to the prophet. Diodati says it well: It is most likely that God speaks of his Son of love, who was present in his own person and manifested himself in *word and power*, in the temple **h)** which has been so shamefully profaned. Compare chapter 23:11, Ezekiel 8:39, and chapter 44:7. 
**i)** to those doing that monstrous crime, described in verse 9 and following. Compare Psalm 7:9, 20 and Jeremiah 7:10. The reason for the desertion of the Temple is given; it is as if to say: It is no longer a house of prayer, but a house of crimes and a den of thieves (chapter 7:11, Matthew 21:13). Where it should be noted **(†)** that the infinitive *To Do* can be taken with the subject *Many*, almost like a participle, meaning "while many are doing," similar to Genesis 25:18, "as you come" or *while you come*. **(1)** That suffix is emphatically redundant, as in chapter 27:8 and 51:56. 
**k)** that is, truly holy victims, or rather those that should truly be sanctified to God, according to Schmidt. Compare Haggai 2:12. 
**l)** they shall take away from you (Zechariah 3:4). The <term>Hiphil</term> <note>a Hebrew verb form indicating causative action</note> is used for *they shall remove*, as in chapter 29:8. Or, in the simple <term>Kal</term> form: the holy meats pass away or are taken from you. It means: No sacrifices that truly please God are being offered by you. 
**m)** and when your malice 
</margin>

<margin>
is at its most foul, even then you exult, sinning insolently and with total security. Psalm 94:3. He is addressing the Jewish Church. 
**n)** see verse 16. 
**o)** Hosea 14:7, Psalm 52:10. 
**o)** beautiful in fruit and appearance. Compare Psalm 48:3. 
**p)** He had named it and at the same time brought it to pass. According to Schmidt, for the Lord to speak is for the Lord to act. 
**q)** but at the sound of a great [multitude], such as the sound of an advancing army (Ezekiel 1:24). This refers to the war-like tumult of the Chaldeans <note>the Babylonian forces invading Judah</note>. But Cocceius interprets it as the sound of crackling, as in burning wood. 
**r)** see chapter 21:14 and Lamentations 4:11.
</margin>

...of the malice of those people. **b)** namely, Jeremiah. It is as if to say: He has indeed threatened us with destruction in the name of God, but he will never see it fulfilled. Compare chapter 5:12, 13. **c)** our end or our outcome. Chapter 5:31; Deuteronomy 32:20. But Jonathan, with others: *Our end is not revealed before him.* **v. 5. d)** Jonathan prefixes: *This is the answer given to Jeremiah the Prophet concerning his question.* **e)** When you ran with the footmen (2 Kings 13:7), namely the men of Anathoth, your relatives and those of your own lot. **f)** *and they have wearied you*, so that this goes badly for you, and it afflicts you more grievously that they impiously plotted snares for you. Job 4:2; Isaiah 1:14. **g)** *will you mix yourself* (2) chapter 22:15. Vulgate: *will you be able to contend.* Jonathan: *you think to run.* Cocceius: *you will contend*, for the word used here by the Syriac in the sense of *contending*, but Gussetius: *you will fortify yourself among* the horsemen. **h)** with horses, which are much swifter. Kimchi understands this as the people of Jerusalem with the King and the nobles. The sense therefore comes to this: You wonder why I permitted you to suffer snares from the men of Anathoth? But I would rather you remember your weakness, and how your patience was fatigued, which had to be exercised by these "preludes," as it were, so that you might more strongly endure the greater tribulations pressing upon you. **i)** *And if you only trust in a peaceful land*, where there is no danger to be feared. **k)** *in the pride of the Jordan*, Cocceius in his Commentary and Lexicon notes that this entire region was called the "surrounding area of the Jordan"; which he proves was abundant with savage beasts. Jonathan refers to this, saying: *How therefore do you think to act against the beasts of the field, which are in the pride of the Jordan?* Compare chapter 49:19; 50:44; Zechariah 11:3. Otherwise, it could be taken thus: What will you do if the Jordan (which it usually does at harvest time, Joshua 3:15; 4:18) boils over and overflows? Thus the overflowing of the Jordan would metaphorically signify the greatest and most immediate dangers. **v. 6. l)** He declares more fully what kind of people he should expect the rest to be, since he suffered snares even from his own relatives in Anathoth. **m)** *it is full*, namely of days, chapter 6:12. **7. p)** compare chapter 11:15; Hosea 8:1; chapter 9:8, 15. **q)** chapter 7:21; Isaiah 2:6, 7. **v. 8, 9.** Isaiah 47:6. **S)** *the love (1) of my soul*, Jonathan: *the people*, who were beloved before me. Compare Deuteronomy 33:12; 2 Samuel 12:25. **v. 8. t)** *For my heritage has become to me*, that is, my people. Chapter 10:16. **u)** compare chapter 2:30 and Isaiah 29:1, 2, 7. **x)** It is as if to say: she has let out a roar or a growl with her voice against me, like a lion about to seize its prey. Judges 14:5; Isaiah 5:29. Schmid understands this as fierce disobedience, by which they spoke fiercely both against God himself and his Prophets. On the words and construction, see Ezekiel 27:30; Psalm 46:7; Psalm 68:34; Psalm 104:12. **v. 9. y)** *Is it a speckled bird?* (1) Compare Judges 5:30. Others: *armed with claws*, from the word for finger: as if to say, they are of the most savage character, and like wild beasts, greedy in spirit. **z)** verses 7, 8; chapter 16:18. **a)** *is there a bird of prey all around her?* The question here is an affirmation. It is as if to say: it is absolutely so: my people have taken on the nature of a wild bird, therefore by just retribution other birds of prey will in turn infest her. Compare chapter 7:33; Isaiah 18:6; 1 Samuel 17:46; Revelation 19:17. **b)** *bring them, command them to come*, namely them. From the root meaning "to come." Compare Isaiah 21:14. **c)** *to devour*, namely my heritage. **v. 10. d)** Jonathan: *Kings*, thinking of Nebuchadnezzar with his military leaders. Chapter 6:3. **e)** Nahum 2:3. **f)** chapter 6:1; Isaiah 51:1. **g)** *they have trodden under foot*, namely through their flocks. Isaiah 63:18. **h)** 2 Samuel 14:30. **i)** *into a wilderness of desolation*, that is, most desolate. Joel 2:3; chapter 4:20.

<summary>Jeremiah questions why the wicked prosper while the land suffers, and God responds by warning him of even greater trials to come, using the metaphors of racing horses and the flooding Jordan. The passage also describes God's rejection of His own heritage (Israel) due to their lion-like ferocity and rebellion.</summary>

Compare the cited place and Genesis 3:18. There is no doubt that these things ought to be understood literally; although some interpret them allegorically, compare verse 4:3. For among other preludes to the Babylonian captivity, by which God manifested His wrath from heaven to call the Jews back to repentance (such as the earthquakes, fires sent from heaven, locusts, etc., mentioned in the Prophets), it is established from verse 4, chapter 3:3, chapter 14:1, etc., that there was also a greediness and sterility of the land followed by famine. y) they were weakened, that is, they labored unto weakness and exhaustion in cultivating the fields; but in vain. See note at chapter 10:19. z) Chapter 22:22. a) Therefore, you shall be put to shame by your harvests, which came to you in place of wheat, because of the burning anger of the Lord. Chapter 14:4; Ezekiel 36:32. Compare Romans 6:21.
**v. 14. b)** *my neighbors.* e.g., Egyptians, Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites, etc., whom God Himself calls His neighbors, because they were neighbors to the Holy Land as His own heritage. See Psalm 72:4, 12. c) Jonathan: "who harm the inheritance." See Zechariah 2:12. d) *I am about to pluck them out*, like a plant, chapter 45:4. e) But first I will pluck out the house of Judah from the midst of them, while it is still somewhat safe; for I will begin the judgments with my own people. 14 Thus says the Lord against all my evil neighbors who touch the inheritance which I have caused my people Israel to inherit: Behold, I will pluck them up from off their land, and I will pluck up the house of Judah from among them.

15 And it shall come to pass, after I have plucked them up, I will return and have compassion on them; and I will bring them back, every man to his heritage, and every man to his land.

16 And it shall come to pass, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, "As the Lord lives," even as they taught my people to swear by Baal, then they shall be built up in the midst of my people.
