> ...bring on. Jonathan: "before tribulation comes upon you, and you become like those walking in the dark." Joel 2:2. b) stumble, strike against. Psalm 91:12. c) to the mountains of twilight, or rather the darkness of night. Ecclesiastes 5:11; 59:10. Those who are hidden by darkness, so that their feet stumble on them contrary to expectation; just as it happens to those who travel through mountain regions infested with many large rocks, and cannot guard themselves from a fall. Schmidt. But Cocceius (Lexicon column 387) says: "mountains suddenly taking away the day, bringing an inexplicable <term>aporia</term> <note>original Greek: 'ἀπορίαν'; a state of perplexity or being at a loss</note>, and hindering progress." d) and you indeed expect light or better things, but everything turns for the worse. Isaiah 59:9; Jeremiah 8:15. e) Chapter 2:6; Psalm 44:20. f) according to the reading <note>Kri</note> **yasit** [he will set], I say, and according to the written text <note>Kthib</note> **vesamah** [and he will place her]. g) Isaiah 60:2; Joel 2:2. **v. 17. h)** in secret places, where those mourning love to withdraw, so that they can weep more intensely. Compare chapter 23:24; Genesis 43:30. i) because of the insolence by which you proudly refused repentance. Verses 9, 15, 16; compare Hebrews 12:17. k) will weep (1). l) and my eye will run down with tears: an emphatic hypallage <note>a literary device where the order of words is swapped</note>. As if to say, I will persist in weeping so that my very eye seems to flow away. Chapter 9:17; 14:17; Lamentations 1:16. m) Genesis 14:14. n) compare verse 20; chapter 31:10; Isaiah 40:11; Psalm 78:52.

> **v. 18. o)** Jechoniah <note>Jehoiachin</note>, and to his mother, see chapter 22:24, 26; 2 Kings 24:12, 15. Thus, among others, also Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> and David Kimchi. p) and to the Lady, i.e., the widowed Queen and the Queen Mother, to whom this title is given in 1 Kings 15:13; 2 Chronicles 15:16. Schmidt observes that she is joined to the King because the kingdom of her young son (he was eighteen years old, 2 Kings 24:8) seemed to be placed largely in her hand. q) humbled, i.e., sit on the ground, Isaiah 29:4; chapter 47:1. r) what was on your head, your ornament. 1 Samuel 26:12; chapter 19:13. s) Ezekiel 16:12. **v. 19. t)** of the southern part of Judea. Genesis 13:1, 3; Numbers 13:17; Joshua 10:40. As if to say, the enemies will indeed come from the North (v. 20), but they will pervade to the extreme southern border of Judea. But Schmidt, with Abarbanel, holds that the southern cities are called Jewish in general, in opposition to the northern Chaldeans (v. 20). u) they are shut up, besieged by the enemy, so that no one can enter or leave. Joshua 6:1; compare also Isaiah 24:10. x) an opener: one who frees a city from siege. Schmidt. y) but she was led away captive. Chapter 40:7; 1 Chronicles 9:1. Things that were to be in the future are narrated as if past, for the sake of denoting certainty. For these were fulfilled in part under Jechoniah (Esther 2:6), but more fully only during the reign of Zedekiah. Compare Preface to this book § 10, 12. z) with perfections, i.e., entirely, or (as the Vulgate, Septuagint, Arabic, Syriac, and Jonathan render it) a perfect exile. Compare Amos 1:6, 9. Jonathan, however, in another way: "the retribution for your works has been received," as if it were for retributions. As in Psalm 69:23. # CHAPTER XIV.

1 That which was the word of the LORD to Jeremiah concerning the matters of the droughts.
2 Judah mourns, and her gates languish; they are dressed in black for the land, and the cry of Jerusalem has gone up.
3 Their nobles sent their little ones for water; they came to the pits and found no water; they returned with their vessels empty; they were ashamed and confounded and covered their heads.
4 Because the ground is cracked, for there has been no rain in the land, the plowmen were ashamed; they covered their heads.
5 For even the hind in the field gave birth and abandoned her young, because there was no grass.
6 And the wild donkeys stood on the bare heights; they gasped for air like jackals; their eyes failed because there was no herbage.
7 Though our iniquities testify against us, O LORD, act for Your name's sake.

> **CHAPTER XIV, verse 1.** l) A <term>Hyperbaton</term> <note>a figure of speech where words are out of their natural order</note> for: "The word of the Lord, which was made, etc." (see chapter 46:1, 47:1). m) *of the droughts*, that is, of the withholding of rain. <margin>
**CHAPTER XV,** *verse 1.* x) This coheres most closely with the end of the preceding chapter. For God answers Jeremiah who is interceding for the people. x) the posture of those ministering, verse 19; Deuteronomy 1:38; 1 Kings 17:1. But especially of those praying, Jeremiah 18:20; 2 Chronicles 20:13. As if to say: "even if those two most holy men, as My ministers and prophets, were to intercede for the people." y) each of whom was illustrious for the efficacy of intercession made for the people: Moses, Ezekiel 32:11, 14; Samuel, 1 Samuel 7:6 and following; Psalm 99:6. Compare Ezekiel 14:14, 16, 18, 20. z) "yet My soul would not be toward them," etc., that is, I would not be moved to embrace this people with an affection of mercy and benevolence. Schmidt. Compare chapter 14:19; 6:8; Ezekiel 23:18. a) "Cast them out now," or "command them to go out." The voice of one gravely angry and speaking with command, as if to say: "away with this people from Me, whom I so loathe that I do not want them to be mentioned by you further in prayers or brought into My sight." Compare Genesis 3:23; 2 Samuel 13:17; 2 Kings 23:27; chapter 24:3. God speaks thus (as Schmidt notes) as if the people themselves, whose persona the Prophet had taken on, were present and interceding with the prophet. b) namely, from My face. Compare Isaiah 50:22. "To go out" in this place means to be cast away by God, not to be cared for by Him, and to enjoy none of His help. Schmidt. For the foundation of this severity, see verse 6. *verse 2.* c) as if to say: "where then shall we wretched ones turn ourselves, since You command us to be driven from Your sight?" Compare John 6:68. v. 19. i) According to the second interpretation: **if you return** <note>original: "fi conuerteris te"</note> Jeremiah, or rather "I will cause you to return," chapter 31:18, then before my face etc. Thus it would be like a correction, as in Galatians 4:9. Both words in this place denote a perpetual turning and conversion of the heart to God; just as elsewhere it signifies to go and return or to repeat something several times, Psalm 23:6, Psalm 71:10. Others: **if you return** from distrust and impatience, I will cause you to return so that you may stand. k) That is, you will be my minister. l) Val. well: **you shall have separated.** m) **the precious from the vile.** Lamentations 4:1. This is spoken metaphorically and taken from metals, in which the vile is mixed with the precious when it is dug from the mines, and then a separation must be made. Schmid. That is to say, if you conduct your office such that from the mixed crowd you convert at least some of good mind and who are still correctable, who separate themselves from impurities. If you convert the impious so that they become righteous. n) **as the interpreter of my will and counsels,** compare Exodus 4:16, which cannot but be a great honor to you. 2 Corinthians 5:20. o) That is, see to it that those who have departed from the laws of God comply with you; and do not you comply with them. <meta>This page continues the divine instructions given to Jeremiah regarding his conduct as a prophet during the coming judgment. While the previous page focused on his personal lament and isolation, this page details the specific prohibitions God places upon him—forbidding him from participating in common social rituals of mourning or celebration—to serve as a living omen of the total devastation awaiting Judah. The commentary draws heavily on Rabbinic sources like the Talmud and Kimchi, as well as Reformation-era scholars like Schmid.</meta>

Although this ritual belonged to the Gentiles when mourning their dead, it seems to have been adopted by the Jews against the express prohibition of God in Leviticus 19, 28 and Deuteronomy 14, 1. The root *gdd*: In Chaldean and Arabic it means to cut or incise. Or it should be said with Rashi that incision and baldness are mentioned here merely as examples of mourning. p) "he shall make for himself a baldness on their account." Isaiah 15, 2. Compare Cocceius in his Lexicon.

Most understand this as the funeral feast, which friends, neighbors, and relatives provided for the mourners according to ritual, using contributed tokens. Compare Ezekiel 24, 17. r) **the breaking of bread.** <note>original Greek: "κλασθῇ ἄרτος"</note> Compare Mark 8, 19. Acts 2, 46; chapter 20, 7. r) "the cup of consolations." Compare Proverbs 31, 6.
* verse 8. s) "of a more joyful feast." Proverbs 15, 15. By a most certain sign, just as the mourning in verse 7, so too the more joyful feasts in the Jewish Republic shall soon be no more. verse 9.

<summary>God commands Jeremiah to abstain from social customs of mourning and feasting as a sign of the total withdrawal of divine peace from Judah. The text explains that the coming exile is a punishment for persistent idolatry, but concludes with a promise of a future liberation so great it will overshadow the Exodus from Egypt.</summary>

**CHAPTER XVII, Verse 1.** b) it is written, namely, with me <note>God</note>, not only for memory, but also for vengeance and for punishment to be taken upon them; according to Schmid, compare Isaiah 65, 5; chapter 14, 10; Hosea 8, 13; chapter 9, 9. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* Part II, Book 6, chapter 11. But perhaps more suitably "diamond-like" <note>original: "adamantino"</note> according to the Vulgate; for in Arabic, *Samir* is diamond, the use of which stone is for writing. f) engraved; hence the Greek *charasso*. Verse 2. k) While I record. This hangs together with the preceding verse as a more distinct explanation of it. l) <term>asyndeton</term> <note>the omission of conjunctions between parts of a sentence</note>, of the children themselves (whom they passed through fire to Molech, chapter 32, 35), as well as of their altars, which they built for idols.

<meta>This page continues the philological and exegetical commentary on Jeremiah, moving into the famous metaphors of Chapter 17. It contrasts the "cursed man" who trusts in human strength (likened to a desert shrub) with the "blessed man" who trusts in the Lord (likened to a tree by the water). The translator continues to reference Sebastian Schmid and early modern Hebraists to clarify the botanical and theological imagery.</meta>

### CHAPTER 18: THE WORD

<margin>
CHAPTER XVIII.
</margin>

**1** The word which came to Jeremiah from the **Lord**, saying:
<margin>
v. 2. f) d) **Go down**; verse 3; chapter 22:1. i.e., depart, as in 1 Samuel 29:4 compared with verse 9. The prophet is commanded to "go down" because of the elevation of his starting point—whether it was the Temple or some other higher or northern part of the city—so that from there he had to travel southward. Compare Genesis 12:10 and the opposite in chapter 13:1. g) Deuteronomy 4:10; 1 Samuel 9:27.
</margin>
**2** Arise and go down to the potter’s house, and there I will let you hear my words.
**3** Then I went down to the potter’s house, and there he was, doing work on the wheels. <note>original: "ha-ovnayim," literally "the two stones," referring to the potter's wheel mechanism.</note>
<margin>
"And behold he"
Masoretic reading
</margin>
<margin>
v. 3. h) **And behold he**; according to the *Keri* (spoken reading); the *Kethiv* (written text) includes a suffix which amounts to the same thing. It is as if the finger is pointed toward the wonderful providence of God, who foresaw that at the very time Jeremiah arrived, the potter would be performing his work. i) i.e., he was practicing his craft. 1 Chronicles 22:15. k) **Seat**; Exodus 1:16. Others, following the Vulgate, translate it as **wheel**.
</margin>
**4** And the vessel that he was making of clay was spoiled in the hand of the potter; so he made it again into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to make.
<margin>
p) namely, a more ignoble vessel (of wrath), unless one prefers, with Schmid (as follows soon after), to see an ellipsis <note>A literary omission</note> in the comparison. q) The third point of comparison between God and the potter, Schmid gathers from the second part of the conclusion in verses 9–10, is that something is understood here: namely, that by the same power, if a broken vessel were found unworthy of being remade, it would be utterly cast away and not rebuilt at all.
</margin>
<margin>
v. 4. l) **And the vessel was ruined** (which etc.) **in the hand** etc. A transposition of words due to the intervening clause. m) **Of clay**.
</margin>
**5** Then the word of the **Lord** came to me, saying:
**6** O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter? says the **Lord**. Behold, as the clay is in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel.
**7** At one moment I may speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, to pull down, and to destroy;
**8** but if that nation turns from its evil because of which I spoke against it, I will relent of the evil that I thought to do to it.
**9** And at another moment I may speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant;
**10** but if it does evil in my sight by not obeying my voice, then I will relent of the good which I had said I would do for it.
<margin>
"The evil"
Masoretic reading
</margin>
<margin>
v. 6. r) So that I might make you vessels of wrath and ignominy because of your stubbornness, or make you vessels of grace and honor according to my most free pleasure. Romans 9:20–21; cf. Isaiah 19:16; 45:9–10; 64:7; Wisdom 15:7. This questioning refutes the security and vain persuasion of the Jews; compare chapter 17:15.
</margin>
**11** Now therefore, speak to the men of Judah and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying: Thus says the **Lord**: Behold, I am fashioning <note>original: "yotzer," the same root as "potter"</note> disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return now, every one from his evil way...

---

...I will make you like vessels of grace and honor from my most free pleasure (Romans 9:20–21). The interrogation argues against the Jews’ false sense of security and vain persuasion (cf. chapter 17:15).

**v. 7–8)** *In a moment* (v. 9). This denotes that God's power is so independent that whatever He has decreed, He executes immediately and without delay. He is no more bound to deliberate with men than a potter with clay, nor is His decree suspended until they approve. **t)** *Against a nation*, indefinitely—whichever one it may be. From this, the application is made specifically to the Jews in verse 11. **u)** cf. Amos 9:8. **x)** chapter 1:10. **v. 8. y)** *But if that nation turns itself* (v. 11; Ezekiel 18:21; chapter 33:11). **z)** *From its evil* (v. 11). **a)** *Because of which* I spoke against it, namely in a corrective way, threatening it with destruction (v. 7). The Syriac and Septuagint omit this phrase entirely. **b)** The Syriac reads: *I will turn away the evil from him*. Cf. chapter 26:3; 42:10; Joel 2:13; Jonah 3:10; Malachi 3:7. **v. 9. c)** chapter 1:10; 42:10. **v. 10. d)** *But if it shall have done.* **e)** verse 8. The Syriac reads: *I will turn away the good from him*.

**Rashi:** *I will think another thought.* "Repentance," when attributed to God, does not imply a change in His nature, but rather a change in the circumstances of the subjects. God observes everyone; if neglected, He neither wishes nor is able, despite His kindness, to fulfill conditional promises to men (Genesis 6:6; cf. notes on 1 Samuel 15:11, 35). **v. 11. f)** *Now therefore.* What was said generally in verses 7–10 is now applied specifically to the Jews. **g)** *Fashioning.* This participle, which also means **Potter**, is elegantly used here based on the preceding analogy; as if to say, "I am now like a potter," etc. But if you intervene with repentance, it is in my hand to remake you (Schmid). **h)** namely, concerning uprooting, destroying, and perishing. **v. 7. i)** *Turn back, therefore.* Chapter 3:12, 14, etc.; 35:15; Jonah 3:8. It is as if to say: "This decree of mine depends on no one's will but my own, yet it is not so absolute that it cannot be abolished if you turn; indeed, I announce this to you for the very purpose that you might turn."

---

Chapter XVIII, v. 1. **Which**: Marked with a *Maqqeph* <note>A Hebrew hyphen</note> in manuscripts 1 and 2. **v. 2. I will let you hear**: So read with the *Keri* in manuscripts 1 and 2 and the Massorah. **v. 3. And behold he**: Accented on the last syllable in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 7, 8 according to the rules of the *Keri*; others accent the penultimate. **v. 4. The vessel**: So with a *Revia* <note>A type of musical/grammatical accent</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, 22. The rest use a *Zaqef Qaton*. **With clay**: Using the letter *Kaph* instead of *Beth* in several manuscripts. From this reading, Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century commentator</note> draws the emphasis that the vessel was ruined not by the potter's fault, but by a defect in the clay itself. However, the *Beth* is required by the Massorah in verse 6 and Job 10:9. This was also the reading of Jonathan, the Syriac, and the Vulgate. **v. 10. The evil**: The accent is placed on the letter *Ayin* in manuscripts 2, 7, 8, 22 according to the *Keri*; others place it on the *Resh*.

<note>This section contains technical philological notes referencing various ancient translations.</note>

Isaiah 57:8. 2 Chronicles 32:21. Jonathan, Syriac, Septuagint, and Arabic: you shall take with you some of, etc. as witnesses of what was to be shown and said in verse 10. *. v. 2. e) 2 Kings 23:10. f) near the doorway, Judges 9:35. Vulgate: near the entrance. g) For some, "the solar gate," connecting *Charsith* to *Cheres* (sun) in Judges 8:13, chapter 14:18. That is, the eastern gate according to the Talmudists, or according to others, the southern, exposed to the heat of the sun. Joshua 15:8, chapter 18:16, where the Valley of Hinnom seems to be placed on the southern side of the city. The Vulgate has "earthenware," derived from *cheresh* (potsherd). There is certainly a play on words with verse 1. Jonathan translates it as "the dung gate," where they carried out broken shards; this is supported by Rashi and Kimchi. But the Syriac, Septuagint, and Arabic retain "Harfith" as a proper name, which Schmid also accepts. To us, it seems to be the same as the "Valley Gate" mentioned in Nehemiah 2:13, 15; 3:13, so named because it leads to the Valley of Ben Hinnom. *. 3. h) verse 13. See note on chapter 17:20. i) Namely, the Valley of Ben Hinnom, in which Jeremiah preached these things (verses 2, 4, 6). By association, it also implies Jerusalem, which he had in view (verses 7, 8, 12). k) So that whoever hears it, their ears shall ring. chapter 17:19; 1 Samuel 3:11; 2 Kings 21:12. A Chaldean form for *titzalnah*. *. 4. l) chapter 2:13; 15:6. m) They alienated; they handed over what was my private property to foreign gods, greatly prejudice to my rights. The name Baalim is common to many idols, including Moloch himself. n) 2 Kings 21:6. s) But of those burned, verse 5. Others: of the prophets. compare chapter 22:3; 2 Kings 21:16. *. 5. q) That is, to Moloch. chapter 7:31; 32:35. I specifically forbade it in Leviticus 18:21 and Deuteronomy 12:31. As Schmid observes, this negative phrasing removes the wicked excuse of hypocritical Jews, who claimed that by serving Baal they were ultimately serving Jehovah. Jonathan adds: "in my law." r) Jonathan adds: "by my servants the prophets." u) chapter 32:35. Jonathan: "neither is it pleasing before me." compare note on chapter 7:37.

<summary>Jeremiah is beaten and placed in stocks by Pashhur the priest for his prophecies of doom. Upon his release, Jeremiah renames Pashhur "Terror on Every Side" and laments the heavy burden of his prophetic calling.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded with Jeremiah being placed in the stocks by Pashhur the priest and then released the following day, only to deliver a renewed prophecy of doom. This page captures Jeremiah’s deep internal struggle—his desire to stop prophesying because of the mockery he faces, and the "burning fire" of God's word that he cannot hold back.</meta>

# JEREMIAH. CHAPTER 20. 21.

<margin>
v. 9. a) For I said at some point within myself, out of the weakness and counsel of the flesh: <note>original Latin: "ex infirmitate & consilio carnis"</note> i) I will no longer remember it, nor will I mention it—that is, the divine word, according to Schmidt <note>original Latin: "sec. Schm."</note>; or of God himself, according to Cocceius. Compare Chapter 23:35 and 3:16. k) Psalm 39:4. Compare Job 32:18–19 and 1 Corinthians 9:16–17. x) The fire presses on, shut in: Chapter 33:1. y) I am weary of sustaining it. Genesis 19:11, Proverbs 26:15, Exodus 7:18. That is, I have labored to the point of exhaustion to keep the word of God within me, so as not to speak it; but in vain. z) Malachi 3:2. α) But I could not—namely, keep it in.
</margin>
9 Then I said, I will not mention him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in my heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.

<margin>
v. 10. b) This connects with both verbs "I said" and "I was weary" in verse 9, as the reason why he tried to silence the word of God. c) Slander. Ezekiel 36:3. d) verse 3. That is, words striking terror from every side, such as those that follow here. e) "Defeat him, and we will desert this same Jeremiah"—namely, with false accusations; Job 17:6. As if to say: all are conspiring for my destruction and inciting each other. Compare Chapter 18:18. f) That is, my friends, but false ones. Psalm 41:10. g) They are watchers of my stumbling—that is, of my misfortune. Psalm 35:15, Psalm 38:18. They overlook no opportunity to harm me. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note>: "they lie in wait to do me evil." h) "Perhaps he will be deceived," they say, so that he might do or blurt out something imprudent (Ezekiel 14:9, Proverbs 1:10), providing an opportunity to accuse him. Compare Matthew 22:15 and following; Luke 20:20. i) Compare Chapter 1:19 and 15:20. k) Compare verse 11.
</margin>
10 For I heard the defaming of many, fear on every side. Report, say they, and we will report it. All my familiars watched for my halting, saying, Peradventure he will be enticed, and we shall prevail against him, and we shall take our revenge on him.

<margin>
v. 11. l) But the Lord (the prophet's faith recovers itself) is with me. Chapter 1:8, 19; 15:20. Joshua 1:12, 14. Isaiah 41:10. m) Like a mighty hero. Isaiah 49:25. n) Chapter 17:18. o) Compare verse 10. p) They did not act prudently (and therefore not successfully). For both of these meanings are sometimes implied by this word, as in Joshua 1:7 and 1 Samuel 18:14. Jonathan: "they shall not prosper." q) I say, they shall be put to shame with everlasting ignominy, which shall never be blotted out by oblivion. Chapter 23:40.
</margin>
11 But the Lord is with me as a mighty terrible one: therefore my persecutors shall stumble, and they shall not prevail: they shall be greatly ashamed; for they shall not prosper: their everlasting confusion shall never be forgotten.

<margin>
v. 12. r) He is the just tester. Psalm 7:10. s) Chapter 11:20. t) I shall see; as if to say, I fully trust and am certain that I will see it. In this way, the connection with verse 13 ("sing therefore," etc.) is easier. Others take it as a wish: "Let me see," or "Make me see." u) Chapter 11:20; Genesis 35:7.
</margin>
12 But, O Lord of hosts, that triest the righteous, and seest the reins and the heart, let me see thy vengeance on them: for unto thee have I opened my cause.

13 Sing unto the Lord, praise ye the Lord: for he hath delivered the soul of the poor from the hand of evildoers.

<margin>
v. 13. x) Ezekiel 15:31. y) Chapter 31:7.

## CURSED
14 Cursed be the day wherein I was born: let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed.
15 Cursed be the man who brought tidings to my father, saying, A man child is born unto thee; making him very glad.
16 And let that man be as the cities which the Lord overthrew, and repented not: and let him hear the cry in the morning, and the shouting at noontide;
17 Because he slew me not from the womb; or that my mother might have been my grave, and her womb to be always great with me.
18 Wherefore came I forth out of the womb to see labour and sorrow, that my days should be consumed with shame?

### CHAPTER XXI.
### THE WORD WHICH CAME UNTO JEREMIAH FROM THE LORD, WHEN KING ZEDEKIAH SENT UNTO HIM PASHHUR THE SON OF MELCHIAH (...)

---

v. 14. a) Otherwise (unless I had this defender), I would say: Cursed is that day. Psalm 72:12, Job 5:15. If you take it in this limited sense, both the meaning and the connection with what precedes are easier. Compare 2 Samuel 1:21 and Job 3:3 and following. Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt, 17th-century theologian</note> approaches this view, thinking that Jeremiah here describes his former state—from which he was miserably snatched—a state so afflicted that he even cursed his birthday out of a certain weakness which he suffered in the past, but not at this time. Others, however, believe he lapsed from faith back into weakness at this moment. **v. 15. b)** He refreshed him with good news (as it seemed to him). 1 Samuel 31:9. c) Who, I say, greatly gladdened him with this news. Chapter 31:13. **v. 16. d)** Genesis 19:25. e) Nor did He repent, so as to change His decree about subverting the cities. Compare Jonah 3:9. f) A cry, a wailing. verse 8. g) A trumpet blast and consternation. Compare Micah 4:9. h) Chapter 6:4; 15:8. **v. 17. i)** He—that is, that messenger (v. 15) or the day (v. 11)—should rather have killed me. Compare 1 Samuel 14:13. k) That is, from the moment I received life in the womb. Compare Job 3:11, Judges 13:17, and the note on Isaiah 44:2. Others: "as soon as I had come out of the womb," comparing this with verse 18. l) (Alternatively) That it was not so. m) So that she would have been pregnant with me forever; that is, that she might never have brought me into the light. Others: "that her womb," etc., but the Hebrew word for "womb" <term>racham</term> is masculine. Compare Hosea 9:14, Job 24:20, Chapter 31:15. **v. 18. n)** Job 3:11, 20; 10:18. As if to say: I justly complain in this way, because it would have been better for me never to have been born, than to be born and be so miserable. Schmidt. o) Job 3:10. p) Chapter 45:3, Psalm 13:3. q) Psalm 31:11. r) Psalm 44:16. **CHAPTER XXI, v. 1.** s) In imitation of the pious Hezekiah, envoys were sent from the same orders—one political, the other ecclesiastical—and with the same displayed sign of hope (v. 3). Compare 2 Kings 19:2 and following. There was another embassy from Zedekiah to Jeremiah during the same period, mentioned below in Chapter 37:3. However, this one was earlier in time; compare Chapter 37:11–21 and 38:28. t) Compare Chapter 27:12; 2 Kings 24:17 and following; 2 Chronicles 36:10–19. u) This Pashhur seems to have been one of the princes or courtiers (Chapter 38:4; compare verse 1 there). He is therefore a different Pashhur than the one in Chapter 20:1, who was a priest and the son of Immer. Nevertheless, both were impious enemies and persecutors of the Prophet; and because of this similarity in subject matter, this chapter seems to have been joined with the preceding Chapter 20, outside its chronological order. Compare Lightfoot’s *Chronicle*, page 125, and our Preface, § 19 and 20.

### CHAPTER 21. Jeremiah 21

<margin>
v. 2. x) Not a common priest, but the deputy of the High Priest <note>original Latin: "summi Pontificis vicarium"</note>, who was eventually executed by Nebuchadnezzar (see 2 Kings 25:18, 21). Furthermore, like king, like messengers—that is, they were hypocritical and wicked men. Regarding Zephaniah, see Chapter 29:25; regarding Pashchur, see Chapter 38:1.
y) "Inquire"—that is, through prayers—so that God might make us certain of the outcome of this siege through some oracle (2 Kings 1:3, Ezekiel 20:1, 3). Moreover, what was promised to Jeremiah in Chapter 15:11 is fulfilled here.
z) See Chapter 39:1, Chapter 52:4, 2 Kings 25:1.
a) Isaiah 37:4. To such an extent do hypocrites fail to acknowledge their own lack of repentance that they think themselves worthy of God promising and doing the very best for them. — Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note>.
b) "With us" (as in Chapter 20:11).
c) Such as He performed long ago for our fathers, and specifically for Hezekiah (2 Kings 19:35, 36).
d) By the lifting of the siege (1 Kings 15:19).

f) This refers to those besieging you outside the walls.

**v. 6.** "The man" <note>Hebrew: "ha-adam"</note> appears without the prefix in some manuscripts. **v. 7.** "Judah" ends with a specific vowel mark in certain codices. "Nor shall he spare" <note>Hebrew: "ve-lo ya-chus"</note> includes a prefix in several versions. **v. 9.** "He shall live and it shall be" <note>Hebrew: "yichyeh ve-hayetah"</note> includes a variation in the prefix. **v. 10.** "In the city" marked with a Tissechâta <note>an accent mark</note>.

The prophecy emphasizes that God himself is now fighting against Judah because of their failure to practice justice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Jeremiah’s specific prophecies against the kings of Judah. Having previously addressed the general house of David, the prophet now turns his focus to the tragic fates of Shallum (Jehoahaz) and Jehoiakim, sons of the late King Josiah. This continues the theme of divine judgment for social injustice and the failure of leadership established in Chapter 21.</meta>

# CHAPTER 22. Jeremiah 22

<margin>* v. 10. p) Concerning the dead man, namely Josiah, that most pious King, for whom there was great mourning among the people (2 Chronicles 35:24) and by Jeremiah himself (v. 25). Therefore (as observed by S... <note>likely Sebastian Schmidt</note>), mourning is not simply forbidden here, but rather discouraged by comparison. It is as if to say: Do not weep so much over the dead (for whom there remains a reason for consolation, 2 Kings 22:20) as over the one who has gone away. Perhaps by "the dead" one could understand... Shallum, also known as Jehoahaz, son of Josiah (1 Chronicles 3:15). a) Nahum 3:7, Job 2:11. a) On account of him who goes away (compare Shallum in v. 11, who was deported to Egypt by Pharaoh Necho and died there, 2 Kings 23:33-34). For other specific contrasts regarding the "sons of prophecy," see Zephaniah 1:8 compared with v. 1, and the entirety of Ezekiel 19.</margin>
10 Weep not for the dead, neither bemoan him; but weep sore for him that goes away, for he shall return no more, nor see his native country.

**accents**. compare the notes on 2 Kings 24:8. And yet offspring are attributed to him here and in v. 28, and also in 1 Chronicles 3:16, 17. To be sure, Schmid observes that the phrase is taken from genealogies, in which inheritances, not just names, were recorded. When an inheritance was taken from someone, he was written down as if "sterile" or "barren," meaning a person whose offspring would not receive the inheritance. Thus Jeconiah is said to be "written childless" because while he would indeed have offspring, the kingdom would not belong to them. For his uncle <note>original: "patruelis"</note> Zedekiah, not his son, was substituted for him in the kingdom. And thus the prophet himself explains it shortly thereafter. But Gussetius (p. 545) prefers to take it as a total lack of children, and therefore in 1 Chronicles 3:17, 18, to deviate from the literal meaning of the word "son," or rather to believe that this condemnation was revoked thanks to the repentance of Jeconiah. **o)** v. 2, chapter 13:13, 29:21, 36:30.

**CHAPTER XXIII**
**v. 1 p)** To the shepherds; that is, the false prophets and priests (see verses 9, 11 and following; John 10:8). Or rather, following Schmidt (who connects the first part of this chapter, verses 1–9, to the previous prophecy against the Kings of Judah), it refers to the Kings; compare chapter 22:22. This is also the view of Kimchi <note>Rabbi David Kimchi, a major medieval French Hebrew scholar</note> and others. In this way, the contrast with Christ the King in verse 5 becomes more evident. Unless you prefer, with others, to understand both Kings as well as prophets and priests together here; compare chapter 10:21; 23:30; Isaiah 56:11; Ezekiel 34:2; Zechariah 11:17. 
**q)** Both physically, comparing chapter 22:3, 13, 15–17, and morally, since through their wickedness they were the cause for not only themselves but the entire people to perish with them. *Schmidt.*
**r)** And those who scatter; likewise in a moral sense (verse 2), since they are the reason I have dispersed my people as captives through various regions (verse 3). 
**s)** Chapter 10:21; Isaiah 49:9.

**h)** Chapter 10:2, 21.

<columns>
of David he shall sprout (Jeremiah 33:15; Psalm 132:17; compare Isaiah 11:1, 10; 2 Samuel 23:5). The **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> here and elsewhere uses the word *anatolen* <note>original: "ἀνατολὴν"</note>, perhaps from Syriac usage where the word for "branch" (*tsamach*) means to shine or appear, and the noun *tsamachat* means "splendor" (which the Syriac translator has here); thus compare Luke 1:78 and Malachi 4:2. Or *anatellein* (from which *anatole* comes) signifies more generally to come forth or be born; thus compare Hebrews 7:14. The Targum Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase</note> calls him "the Messiah of the righteous" or (as the Royal Bible more correctly has it) "of righteousness." Many Jewish commentators like Abarbanel and Kimchi also explain this as referring to the Messiah; see verse 6. 
**n)** Since he is to be our righteousness (verse 6), so that he makes people righteous as well (Isaiah 53:11; compare Zechariah 9:9; 2 Samuel 23:3; 1 John 2:1). He will not be a wicked branch, like Jehoiakim and his son, but a righteous one. *Abarbanel.* 
**o)** As a King (Isaiah 32:1; Ezekiel 37:24; Psalm 72:1); and not only of the Israelites, but of the whole world (comparing Zechariah 9:10). *Kimchi.* 
**p)** He shall act prudently, which by extension implies happiness or success (Isaiah 52:13; compare notes on Jeremiah 10:21 and 20:11). 
**q)** Chapter 9:23; Isaiah 61:8; Psalm 45:8. 
**v. 6. r)** Compare chapter 30:7; Hosea 1:7. 
**s)** Chapter 33:16; Deuteronomy 33:28. 
**t)** By which name each of the believers shall call him, or it shall be called impersonally (as in Genesis 11:9; 27:36). But Gusset (p. 753) says "which Judah itself shall call upon." Schmidt, however, says: "which Judah, every faithful person, or minister of the word shall proclaim" (comparing chapter 33:16). 
**u)** This name, which belongs to God alone (Isaiah 42:8), is also attributed to the Messiah; for example, chapter 33:16; Jeremiah 6:3, 5 (comparing John 12:41); 45:24, 25; Hosea 1:7; Zephaniah 3:15; Psalm 24:8. Even Jewish scholars, compelled by the light of this passage, admit and prove that the name of the Messiah is *Jehovah Tsidkenu* <note>original: "יהוה צדקנו" - The Lord Our Righteousness</note>, as seen in Kimchi, *M. l.*, Bechai on the Law, and the Zohar on Genesis (Cremona edition). Also cited in Medrash Tillim, the Talmud (Baba Bathra), Ialkut Jeremiah, Alschech on Isaiah 42, Echah Rabbathi, Albo's Book of Principles, and Abraham Ibn Ezra on Exodus 18:33, where Saadia Gaon rejects any corruption based on the accents. See more in our Discussion on the Divine Names of Christ, § 6 and following. 
**x)** The Lord our righteousness, in whom we are justified and glory (Isaiah 45:24, 25; Daniel 9:24; 1 Corinthians 1:30). Targum: "Righteousness shall be done for us by God in his days." Hence the frequent saying among the Jews: "The Messiah is our righteousness." 
**v. 7. y)** See notes on chapter 16:14, 15. 
**v. 8. z)** verse 3; chapter 8:3. 
**v. 9. a)** As for the prophets. Targum: "on account of the false prophets." So also in verses 15, 16, etc. 
**b)** Compare Psalm 51:19. 
**c)** They were moved or fluttered (3); Genesis 1:2; Deuteronomy 32:11. 
**d)** Whom wine has crossed or penetrated; that is, one completely overwhelmed by wine and hangovers. Compare Psalm 74:4, 5. Targum: "who has become insane from his wine." 
**e)** God's holiness and His most just vengeance against those prophets. 
**f)** His threatening words, which are no less firm than His promises (Psalm 105:42). 
**v. 10. g)** Adulterers, both in the literal sense and spiritual sense (those who break their covenant with God). verse 14; chapter 5:7, 8; 9:1. 
**h)** Because of the curse that lies upon the land due to the violated covenant of God (Isaiah 24:6; compare verse 5; Ezekiel 16:59; 17:19), to which they once bound themselves when entering the covenant, should they transgress it (Deuteronomy 29:11, 13, 18–20). But Targum interprets it actively as "because of a false oath."

<column-break/>

**v. 3. a)** But I will gather together; chapter 29:14; 31:8, 10; Isaiah 43:5; Ezekiel 11:17; Micah 2:12; 4:6. Into one spiritual communion under Christ. *Schmidt.* Compare John 11:52. Certainly the Jewish commentators Abarbanel and Kimchi explain this as the future redemption or the Messiah, as the following context in verse 5 requires. 
**b)** Compare chapter 16:15 and verse 14 with the note there. 
**c)** verse 2. 
**d)** chapter 12:15; 30:3; Zechariah 10:10. 
**e)** To their folds; compare Jeremiah 32:18; Ezekiel 34:14; John 10:16. 
**f)** Genesis 1:32, 28; Zechariah 10:8.

<margin>
**Notes on Verse 10:**
k) See chapter 12, 11; chapter 14, 2.
l) The character of the desert; see chapter 9, 9.
l) Their course; see chapter 8, 6.
m) That is, they rush into crimes with the greatest force, as in Isaiah 59, 7. 
m) Their strength is not right; others translate as "nothing of right." As if to say: they have directed all their powers, but only toward evil. See chapter 8, 6; 2 Kings 17, 9.

**Notes on Verse 11:**
n) As if to say: those very ones who boast of being leaders. See chapter 6, 13; chapter 8, 10.
o) Stuffed with impurity. See verse 15. Compare Jeremiah 3, 1–2, 9; Numbers 35, 33; Isaiah 24, 5. However, Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> argues they practice hypocrisy.
p) "Even" or "indeed." An intensive particle.
q) In my very house, which ought to have been most holy. See chapter 7, 10–11.
r) See chapter 1, 15; Ezekiel 8, 3; chapter 23, 38–39.

**Notes on Verse 12:**
s) Slippery places. See Psalm 35, 6; compare Jeremiah 13, 16.
s) In the darkness, as in Isaiah 8, 22; this exaggerates the evil. For slippery places are dangerous, but in the darkness they are more dangerous still. Because if (as follows in this passage) a push is added from above, a fall will follow without delay and without doubt. *Kimchi.* <note>Rabbi David Kimchi, medieval commentator</note>
u) They shall be driven or struck toward a fall. See Psalm 118, 13.
x) Jeremiah calls it "the year of the visitation" of their sins. Compare chapter 11, 23; chapter 46, 21.

**Notes on Verse 13:**
y) "For in the prophets of Samaria I indeed saw..." etc. But in the prophets (verse 14). The wickedness of the prophets of Jerusalem is explained: (z) by contrast, because it is greater than that of the prophets of Samaria (Hosea 4, 5; chapter 6, 5; chapter 9, 7), and (2) by comparison, because it is as great as that of Sodom and Gomorrah (verse 14, 8; compare chapter 3, 11).
z) Insipidness or folly. See Job 1, 22; chapter 24, 12; compare Lamentations 2, 14. Properly used of tasteless food which lacks salt or other spices for seasoning, as in Job 6, 6.
a) "For they prophesied." An irregular grammatical form for *hitnabbe'u* [they prophesied] as in 1 Kings 18, 29; a similar form appears in Numbers 23, 24; 2 Chronicles 32, 23.
b) See verse 32; Amos 2, 4.
</margin>

<margin>
**Notes on Verse 14:**
c) See chapter 3, 8. 
d) A horror, or something horrendous. See chapter 5, 30; compare chapter 18, 13. 
**[Grammatical Note]** 
*Merei'im* [evildoers]: The vowel is opened in place of a *Qamatz*. 
The distinction between the prophets of Samaria and Jerusalem seems to be this: the folly of the former held more fatuity and ignorance, while the crimes of the latter held more malice. Furthermore, the deception of the former was more obvious, while that of the latter—under the pretext of true religion—was more hidden and hypocritical. 
e) While they commit adultery. See verse 10; chapter 29, 23.
f) "And they strengthen." See Ezekiel 13, 22; Judges 9, 24; Romans 1, 32. That is, they help, instigate, and tell them to be of good courage.
g) So that they do not return. A similar construction is found in chapter 27.
**[Masoretic note]** 
Words of the *Qere* [marginal reading].

**Commentary Continued:**
**v. 14.** h) Deuteronomy 32, 32; Isaiah 1, 9–10; Ezekiel 16, 46, 51.

**v. 15.** i) Verses 9, 16. 
k) With wormwood. <note>original Latin: absinthio</note> Jonathan [the Targumist]: *I will bring upon them bitter distress like wormwood.* See 9, 14; Lamentations 3, 15, 19. 
l) Of gall, that is, of hemlock; chapter 8, 14. Jonathan: *with a cup of evil malediction like the heads of serpents.*
m) Hypocrisy or pollution arising from perfected hypocrisy. See verse 11; Ephesians 5, 6.
n) Compare Micah 1, 5.

**v. 16.** o) Chapter 14, 14; chapter 27, 9, 14. 
p) For they make you vain; see chapter 2, 5; 2 Kings 17, 15. And they delude you with vain hope, promising all the best things; Zechariah 10, 2. 
q) Verse 25. That is, a *vision from their own heart*, originating from it as the first principle, fashioned from the malice of the heart. *Schmidt.*

**v. 17.** r) They say by saying; that is, boldly, openly, and continually. Compare Genesis 8, 7; chapter 19, 9; Joshua 7, 7; 2 Samuel 18, 25. 
s) To those who despise me; Isaiah 1, 4; Psalm 10, 3, 13.
t) As if to say: there is nothing you should fear. Compare chapter 4, 10; 6, 14; 8, 11; 14, 13; 28, 2, 9; Ezekiel 13, 10, 16; Deuteronomy 29, 18. This is undoubtedly the criterion of a false word, since it conflicts with the nature of the true Word to stubbornly promise peace to the wicked. Compare Isaiah 48, 22; 57, 21. 
u) Chapter 3, 17. 
x) Chapter 5, 12; 14, 13; Zechariah 10, 2.

**v. 18.** y) "Because." This connects with verse 16; it gives the reason why they should not listen to those prophets. 
z) Verse 22; Job 15, 8. The question implies a negative: that is, none of them stood in the secret counsel of God to see etc. Therefore, they boast most vainly of those prophecies (verse 15) as if they were participants in God’s own counsels. Compare Isaiah 40, 13–14. Yet the Lord never spoke to them, nor sent them (verse 21).

**v. 19.** a) On the contrary, rather a storm of the Lord. See chapter 20, 23; Isaiah 29, 6; Nahum 1, 3; Psalm 11, 6. It is so far from being true, as they chatter, that there will be peace, that instead there will be a storm. *Schmidt.*
b) In anger; Genesis 48, 7; Isaiah 10, 5; chapter 59, 18. 
c) "Persisting," according to Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 17th-century Dutch theologian</note>, comparing chapter 30, 23, where the word is *mitgorer*; but Schmidt says "threatening to rush in" or "threatening to rush in fiercely to stay."
d) It shall rush in or stay, remain; 2 Samuel 3, 29; Hosea 11, 6.

**v. 20.** e) Signifies a peremptory and irrevocable divine decree, by the force of which He will punish the (stubbornly) wicked. Numbers 25, 4; Job 33, 6. 
f) This will happen in the days of the Messiah; *Kimchi.* See chapter 48, 47; Isaiah 2, 2; Hosea 3, 5. 
g) Chapter 30, 24; compare Isaiah 29, 14 and Matthew 24, 15.

**v. 21.** h) Verse 32; chapter 14, 14 following; chapter 27, 15; 29, 9.

**v. 22.** i) But if they indeed stood etc. as they wish to appear (verse 18), let them then make [the people] hear etc. so that they might be converted etc. which is the duty of true prophets; not, through fabricated lies, to strengthen men in their malice. Compare verse 28 and chapter 27, 18.

# JEREMIAH 23. CHAPTER 23.

<margin>
**Notes on Verse 28:**
a) Concerning the status. As if to say: I do not forbid the telling of prophetic dreams of which I myself am the author, provided they are truly divine, with no lies mixed in. However, Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt, 17th-century theologian</note> understands "dream" in both parts of this verse to mean a hollow dream. As if to say: he who has a hollow dream, let him tell it as a hollow dream; (see Ezekiel 20:39).
b) But he who has my word, etc. In truth, truly; let him speak it as the word of God, as in 1 Peter 4:11, without extra nourishment or inventions. 1 Kings 17:24. For it is opposed to the mixture of wheat and straw (chaff).
c) What does the straw have in common with the wheat? Structured as in Judges 11:12. The Syriac version reads: "Why do you mix straw with wheat?"
d) Genesis 41:25; Joel 2:24; Amos 5:11.

**Notes on Verse 29:**
e) What he said in verse 28 regarding the truth of the divine word, he now explains...
</margin>

If they had stood in my council (s), they would have proclaimed my words to my people, and they would have turned them from their evil way and from the evil of their doings.

Am I a God at hand <gloss>t</gloss>—declares the LORD—and not a God far off?

Can a man hide in secret places and I not see him? —declares the LORD (v). Do I not fill the heavens and the earth? —declares the LORD.

I have heard what the prophets have said who prophesy lies in my name, saying: "I have dreamed, I have dreamed!" (x)

How long <gloss>y</gloss>—is this in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, and the prophets of the deceit of their own heart?

Who think <gloss>z</gloss> to make my people forget my name by their dreams which they tell one another, just as their fathers forgot my name for Baal.

The prophet <gloss>a</gloss> who has a dream, let him tell a dream; and he who has my word with him, let him speak my word in truth. What has the straw to do with the grain? <gloss>b</gloss> —declares the LORD.

Is not my word like fire <gloss>c</gloss>—declares the LORD—and like a hammer that breaks <gloss>d</gloss> the rock in pieces?

Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets <gloss>e</gloss>—declares the LORD—who steal my words from one another.

Behold, I am against those who prophesy false dreams <gloss>h</gloss>—declares the LORD—and tell them, and lead my people astray by their lies and their recklessness; and I did not send them, nor did I command them, and they do not profit this people at all—declares the LORD (i).

And when this people <gloss>k</gloss> or the prophet or a priest asks you, saying: "What is the burden of the LORD?" then you shall say to them: "What burden? I will forsake you" —declares the LORD (l).

<margin>
Exodus chapter 21, 12; chapter 26, 3.
**Verse 23:** l) Am I a God (of a place) who is only near? See 1 Kings 20:23. Not indeed at the same time a God, etc. See verse 24. Men sometimes think God is far away from them and does not see or hear what they do and say. God wishes to refute this fiction here and teach that distance of place does not affect or apply to Him in any way. Schmidt explains: as if to say, I do not only know how to restrain things in a nearby place, and if I am in heaven, I would not know what happens on earth. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 17th-century Hebraist</note> compares this to Psalm 10:5; Ezekiel 8:12; also Psalm 139:2; Acts 17:27-28. Elsewhere, local gods are opposed to the Eternal God, as in Deuteronomy 32:17.
**Verse 24:** m) An inference from the non-locality of God in verse 23. Schmidt compares to chapter 16, 17; Psalm 139:7; Amos 9:2-3. n) I fill; being absent neither from heaven nor earth, neither near nor far (verse 23), but whole everywhere.
**Verse 25:** o) Therefore I have heard, being omnipresent and omniscient (verses 23-24). p) Chapter 24, 14. q) The Jonathan Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation</note> says: "The word of prophecy was announced to me in dreams." The doubling of the word "dreamed" is emphatic. As if to say: nothing but dreams. They chatter them everywhere and as often as they like. Compare chapter 29, 8.
**Verse 26:** r) How long? That is, how long will they speak thus? How long shall I endure this? See Psalm 6, 4; Jeremiah 13, 27. s) Is it in the mind, etc. A new question, which, due to some intervening words, is not resolved here, but only in the following verse (where it is resumed through the synonym *chashav*—"they think"). Thus Schmidt. t) Verse 16; chapter 8, 5.
**Verse 27:** u) Do they think, I say? See verse 26. x) To cause my people to forget. This is in the Hiphil <note>The causative verb form in Hebrew</note> (1). y) Judges 3, 7; chapter 8, 33.
**Verse 28:** z) He who has (or thinks he has) a divine dream. Numbers 12, 6; 1 Samuel 28, 6, 15. a) Add from the following member: "in truth."
</margin>

> ...he now explains by its efficacy and operation. f) Thus, "like fire." Jeremiah 23, 1; Hebrews 4, 12; see Luke 24, 32. g) "And like a hammer" (3) chapter 50, 23. h) "Which causes to shatter." See Job 16, 12. Therefore, the divine word can be distinguished from the human by its effect; for it does not confirm the wicked in their impiety (verse 16) but converts them (verse 22). Or, if they refuse to be converted (as Schmidt says), it utterly crushes, scatters, and casts them into hell. Compare 2 Corinthians 2, 14 and following. **Verse 30:** i) "Stealing." According to Cocceius, this refers to those who intercept the words so that they are not cared for, known, understood, or descend into the heart. Compare Matthew 13, 19. But according to Schmidt, it refers to those who catch from others in conversation what kind of prophecies they desire, and then preach those very things to them. What if it denotes the <term>kakozēlia</term> <note>original: "κακοζηλίαν" - a Greek term for a misguided or perverse imitation/affectation</note> of the pseudo-prophets in imitating the true prophets, such as in their external habits and manners, as well as their ways of speaking? For example, when they repeatedly groaned that phrase "the oracle of the LORD" (*neum Yehovah*) in verse 31. **Verse 31:** k) "Taking" impudently and by their own impulse—not the Holy Spirit—their own tongue. See Job 15, 12. But Schmidt suggests it is a metathesis for "smooth," making their tongue smooth/flattering. l) And you pronounce (just like the true prophets) that *Neum*—that is, the oracle of Jehovah. Isaiah 1, 24. **Verse 32:** m) Verse 17; chapter 14, 14-15; Deuteronomy 18, 20. n) Verse 13. o) By their levity/recklessness (1). Genesis 49, 4; see Zephaniah 3, 4. p) Chapter 12, 13. **Verse 33:** q) "What is the oracle [burden] of God?" See verse 34 and following; Proverbs 30, 1; chapter 51, 1. From *nasa* (to lift up/proclaim), they pronounce. Job 27, 1, etc. The words are good, but the sense of the questioners is sarcastic, directed at the ambiguous word *massa*, which means both "oracle/utterance" and "burden/weight." As if to say: you can only prophesy things that are burdensome and evil. Compare verse 36, where God turns the word back upon the Jews in this sense. But Schmidt suggests "oblivion," i.e., a prophecy to be given to oblivion, from *nashah* (to forget), comparing verse 39. r) What the "burden" is, in another sense, you shall reply to the mockers, hinting that they themselves are a burden to me, to be shaken off my shoulders. s) That is, I will cast you off. Verse 39; 2 Kings 21, 14. It alludes to the preceding word and says He wishes neither to carry them nor to care for them. Cocceius.

### CHAPTER XXIV.

<margin>
CHAPTER XXIV. 1. m) It is the same as if you said: "The Lord showed me in a vision two..." compare Genesis 41:22, Amos 7:1, 4, 7. a) Baskets. Thus all the ancient versions. Compare verse 2, 2 Kings 10:7, Psalm 81:7. Schnurrer <note>Christian Friedrich von Schnurrer, 18th-century orientalist</note> conjectured these were branches heavy with figs, which also appear under this name in Genesis 39:14, 15, 16. e) Chapter 8:13, compare Amos 8:1. β) Appointed or set <note>original: "constituti"</note> as in Ezekiel 21:21. That is, for the purpose of this prophecy, or so that prophecies might be drawn from them.
</margin>

1 The LORD showed me, and behold, two baskets of figs were set before the temple of the LORD, after Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and the princes of Judah, and the craftsmen and the smiths <gloss>the locksmiths/artisans</gloss> from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon.

<margin>
* v. 2. t) Basket. See verse 1. u) Of trees bearing early fruit <note>original: "præocci ferentium"</note>, that is, whose figs ripen among the first, specifically before the summer, Isaiah 28:4. Therefore they are sweeter to those who taste them, not only because of their ripeness but also their rarity, Hosea 9:10. Compare Ezekiel 17:12. The Vulgate reads: "as figs usually are in the early season." The Septuagint, Jonathan, and Syriac: "like the first-ripe figs." Schnurrer explains it slightly differently: "There are various types of figs in Judea, especially those that bear twice a year (cf. Pliny, Book 15, Ch. 18). Those that grew the first time were the best and ripened excellently; those that grew the second time were less good and often did not even reach proper ripeness because the season was turning toward winter." κ) v. 3, 8, because of their immaturity.
</margin>

2 One basket had very good figs, like the figs that are first ripe; and the other basket had very bad figs, which could not be eaten for badness.

Schnurrer. z) Schmidt supplies: "some good, others bad" from verse 2. a) verses 2, 8. Schnurrer supplies: "But I do not know, Lord, what these figs, whether good or bad, signify?"
</margin>

<margin>
* v. 5. c) "Like these good figs," which are pleasing to those who eat them because of their sweet flavor (vv. 2, 3). d) I will acknowledge for good. Deuteronomy 21:17, Psalm 142:5, Ruth 2:10, 19. That is, so that I may have favor in them and bring them back (v. 6). e) The transportation <note>or the body of exiles</note> of Judah. Chapter 28:4, Isaiah 45:13, Obadiah v. 20. f) Which He sent out, 28:16, 29:20, Genesis 3:23. Namely, with Jehoiakim (Daniel 1:1ff) and especially Jeconiah (Jeremiah 20:1ff, 2 Kings 24:15, 16, 25:27).
* v. 6. l) For the beginning of verse 5, he supplies: "Say to the children of Israel." Cf. Ezekiel 11:5.
</margin>

->**Textual and Masoretic Notes**<-

* v. 35. **Thus** <term>Koh</term>—with the Darga accent is more regular according to source 2, but with Makkaph in source 3. — **Upon** <term>Al</term> used instead of **To** <term>El</term> in source 3. This follows a pattern found in Ezekiel 21:14.
* v. 39. **And I will forget** <term>V’nashiti</term>—spelled with the letter Sin in source 1. — Likewise **To lift/carry** <term>Nasha</term> with Sin in sources 6, 7, 9, 10, 20. "As if it were from the root to lift/carry, I will take you away (forget you) by taking away." Thus the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Syriac read it.
**The city**—with the Gerschaim accent in sources 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 16, 20, 21, 22, 23; but with Paschta in sources 8, 13, 15, 19.
* v. 40. **And shames** <term>V’khilmut</term>—in the plural with the Holem vowel in sources 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 23, against the Masoretic standard.

CHAPTER XXIV, v. 1. **Jeconiah**—without the final "yod" (which other books include in the margin) in sources 7, 8, against the Masora and Lufft.

### CHAPTER XXV.

<margin>
He was destined to rebel after three years, and again be besieged by the Chaldeans, captured, and deported to Babylon (2 Chronicles 36:6); yet he would die on the way (Jeremiah 22:19). Most interpreters, both Christian and Jewish, are mistaken and entangle themselves in great difficulties by claiming that the third year of Jehoiakim mentioned in Daniel 1:1 is the same as the fourth year mentioned here. For there (as will be shown more fully at that passage), the calculation starts from the time Jehoiakim's reign was confirmed by the Chaldeans; but here, as in 36:1, it is from the time he simply began to reign. e) chapter 22:18. f) The first year. This circumstance is not idle; compare verse 9, where this very time is an example of a curse, when God had already prepared the rod for striking the unrepentant. Compare 2 Kings 24:12; Jeremiah 52:12. Chapter 29:22 continues this interpretative chronology.

along with the father of Nebuchadnezzar. See note on 2 Kings 24:1; Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 10, Chapter 3. And afterward, they submissively honored the majesty and power of Nebuchadnezzar (compare Guertler's *Prophetic Theology*, page 352 and following). **v. 26 s)** The unique one. **t)** That is, of Babylon, as seen in verses 31 and 41. From where it gets this name, there are various but uncertain opinions among interpreters. The Jews derive it through their <term>Atbash</term> <note>A Hebrew code where the first letter of the alphabet is replaced by the last, the second by the second-to-last, etc. Under this system, the word B-B-L (Babel) becomes Sh-Sh-K (Sheshach).</note>, whom Jerome also follows in his commentary on this passage. To others, Babylon seems to be called this because of the "Sukka" sacred rites and a festival similar to the Roman Saturnalia; while the Babylonians were immoderately celebrating this very thing, the city was captured by Cyrus, as noted in Isaiah 21:4. What if it is formed from *shur*, meaning strength and power, showing valor in war—it shows that it was clothed in full armor; so that with the root doubled in the form *Shoshach*, it was called "the warrior Babylon," as if it would subdue all the aforementioned nations with incredible strength. **u)**

**v. 27 y)** "and be drunk" (Nahum 3:11). **x)** Namely, by the wrath of God, as below in chapter 51:7; Isaiah 51:21; 63:6. **z)** "Vomit," from the word *qua* (Leviticus 18:28). It is an irregular form, as if it were from *qaha* or *qayah*. Compare Isaiah 19:14 and Jeremiah 48:26. **v. 28 a)** Namely, by despising your prophecy as if it were empty, or by opposing Nebuchadnezzar with all their might. Schmid. **b)** Verse 15. **c)** That is: nevertheless, you shall certainly drink, whether you want to or not. Compare 49:12; Obadiah verse 16; Habakkuk 2:16. **v. 29 d)** "I am beginning to do evil" (Zechariah 8:14). Compare verse 18 above; Ezekiel 9:6; 1 Peter 4:17; Leviticus 10:3; Isaiah 10:12. **e)** A voice asking clearly: "Do you think you will be immune?" Namely, will you escape unpunished? (Chapter 49:12; compare 1 Kings 2:9).

**v. 18 And its princes:** written with the prefix "And" (Vav) in verses 2, 5, and (in the text) 6, 9, as well as 10, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 20, 21, 23. This is against the Masora <note>The traditional system of notes on the Hebrew text</note> in final 12, column 5. **v. 22 Kings of the island:** Verses 1, 2, 3 add the word "and all." But David Kimchi advises that this is absent in the corrected codex. **v. 23 And Dedan:** written with the prefix "And" (Vav) in 1, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. **v. 26 The near ones:** written in full in verse 5, according to the printed Masora on Ezekiel 23:5. **v. 27 And vomit:** with a "Vav" in verses 14 and 20 according to the printed Masora on Exodus 39:4. **v. 28 To them:** with a *Sakeph Katon* accent in 7, 8, 14, 16, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23. The printed Masora should be interpreted as *Rebia* instead. For the word "to them" with the preceding "and you shall say" does indeed have a *Rebia* accent, but the *Sakeph Katon* (to which the Masora is wrongly adapted) appears eighteen times. **v. 30 All the words:** so in 1, 2, 3; thus in 5.

k) he was a prophet in verse 20. (v. 32, 3 m) see the note on Micah 3:12. n) shall be plowed, as in 1 Samuel 8:12 and Job 1:14. o) heaps, as in Psalm 79:1. Compare Isaiah 17:1 and Micah 1:6. p) in the high forest, or a wooded place. Compare chapter 17:3 and Hosea 2:14.

**19** Verse 19. q) *By killing,* etc. Compare verse 11. r) *and he besought*, or entreated. Isaiah 32:11, 2 Kings 13:14. This is an example we must imitate in the present. s) just as it can happen to us, if we are willing. Compare verses 13 and 3; 2 Samuel 24:16. t) but we, if we proceed as we have begun: Or as a question following the scholar Schmidius: "Are we then making ourselves guilty?" **20** Verse 20 x) Some (though others have said the contrary) say "there was also a man," etc. So Schmidius suggests that those opposing Jeremiah might oppose the example of Hezekiah with a more recent one of Jehoiakim, who did not allow Urijah’s freedom of speech to go unpunished. Others still suggest these are the words of those defending Jeremiah, as if they wanted to teach what should be avoided by the contrary example of Jehoiakim. But as the omission there is too harsh, so here the circumstances of time are inconsistent; it is not probable that those elders would have wanted to propose the example of Jehoiakim (during whose reign these things were happening, see verse 1) as something to be detested and avoided. Therefore, the scholar Abendana <note>Solomon Abendana, a 17th-century Jewish scholar</note> posits that these are the words of neither the defenders nor the accusers of Jeremiah, but rather a narrative of the history. He suggests it says: Truly, there was a singular providence of God in protecting Jeremiah through Ahikam (verse 24), because, unless he had the patronage of Ahikam and the other princes, he would have undoubtedly experienced the same fate as Urijah under the same king, Jehoiakim, and for the same cause.

**CHAPTER XXVII, verse 1.** l) compare the note on chapter 26:1. m) The Syriac and Oxford Arabic versions have *Zedekiah*; the Greek Septuagint (LXX) omits it entirely: undoubtedly because of the difficulty in verse 3 and chapter 28:1. However, the better interpreters reconcile this by saying that Jeremiah received this word of the Lord at the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign, but it was only to be announced in the time of Zedekiah. See Abendana in *Miclal Jofì*. We must think that these things are announced regarding Zedekiah prophetically, just like those things said about the sons of Nebuchadnezzar, etc., says Lightfoot in his *Chronicle*, page 118. In this way, other prophecies were received long before they were published: compare 1 Kings 13:15, 16 with 2 Kings 8:13, also 2 Chronicles 21:12. Schmidius adds that, although he did not send the yokes to the kings until the time of Zedekiah, nevertheless he himself, from the fourth year of Jehoiakim, not only bore the yoke (compare Ezekiel 4:4 and following) but also preached the word revealed to Jehoiakim and the Jews, which was to be fulfilled under Zedekiah.
**v. 2.** n) bonds, perhaps leather straps, fastened to the yoke. Chapter 5:4. o) Jeremiah 28:10, 12, 13. Nahum 1:13. Bars, that is, a yoke composed of bars. Leviticus 26:13. p) Genesis 27:40, Lamentations 1:14. He was to prophesy not only with words but also with symbolic signs <note>original: "hieroglyphicis signis"</note>, as Isaiah in chapter 20:2–4, Ezekiel 12:3 and 18, Hosea 1:2; and by perverse imitation <note>original: "κακοזηλίαν"</note>, the false prophet Zedekiah in 1 Kings 22:11.
**v. 3.** q) From this, S. suspects that he must have made several yokes to send to the kings, but he only wore one of them. Compare chapter 28:10. But even this is not necessary. For the phrasing could be allegorical, which is not unusual for Jeremiah (compare chapter 25:15), so that the sending of the yoke and straps through messengers to the Kings signifies that servitude is portended for them by this very sign. This is especially so since it is hardly credible that the messengers of these nations (who were themselves enticed by the flattery of their own diviners, v. 9) would have been willing to carry the yokes offered by Jeremiah back to their masters. r) see chapter 25:21, 22. s) coming after some years, according to verse 1; either to congratulate Zedekiah on his kingdom, or, as S. prefers, to entice Zedekiah into a coalition of rebellion against the Chaldeans. Compare the note on 2 Kings 24:20. **v. 4.** t) that is, instruct them with commands to be carried to their masters in my name. Esther 4:5 and 10.

v. 23. *Graves* <note>original: "קִבְרֵי"</note> is written defectively <note>without the extra vowel letter</note>. According to the Masorah of the Erfurt manuscript... they read it as *graves*, but it is written *bury*. v. 24. *Hand* <note>original: "יַד"</note> is read this way, but in the text it is written *by the hand* <note>original: "בְּיַד"</note>. **CHAPTER XXVII, v. 1.** *And it was Josiah* without the unnecessary "and" <note>the Vav</note>. The Marginal Reading <note>Keri</note> adds the name Josiah.

**Verse 5.** The word for "the earth" <note>original: "הארץ"</note> appears with a "paragogic He" <note>a grammatical suffix adding emphasis or direction</note>.
**Verse 6.** The word for "I" <note>original: "אָנֹכִי"</note> is marked by the *Mahpach* <note>a Hebrew cantillation mark or musical accent</note>.
**Verse 7.** The word for "so that" <note>original: "למען"</note> is marked by the *Rebia* <note>another cantillation mark, indicating a pause</note>.
**Verse 12.** The phrase "in the yoke of the king" <note>original: "בְּעֹל מֶלֶךְ"</note> appears in various manuscript traditions (2, 3, 7, 8, 13, 19).

### CHAPTER 28. Jeremiah 28

<margin>
**v. 4. m)** This contradicts the prophecy found in chapter 22:27. **n)** Specifically, those deported along with King Jeconiah (see chapter 24:5 and chapter 29:22). **o)** That is, not after the full 70 years (as mentioned in chapter 27:7 and 25:11), but within a mere two years, as stated in verse 3. **p)** See chapter 23:17, 31. **q)** See verse 2.
</margin>

4 "And I will bring back to this place Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exiles of Judah who went to Babylon," declares the LORD, "for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon."

5 Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Hananiah the prophet in the presence of the priests and in the presence of all the people who were standing in the house of the LORD.

<margin>
**v. 6. r)** "He said," I say (referring back to verse 5; compare the note on 27:21). **s)** This expresses a wish, similar to 1 Kings 1:36. It is as if Jeremiah says: "I myself would wish, out of my love for my people, that it would happen exactly as you have prophesied; but so that I may say what I truly think of your prophecy, listen now to the following" (verse 7). **t)** May he establish—that is, may he fulfill (compare chapter 29:10, 1 Kings 6:12, and 1 Samuel 15:11). The opposite sense is found in Job 21:43 and Jeremiah 22:14.
</margin>

6 And Jeremiah the prophet said: "Amen! May the LORD do so; may the LORD fulfill your words which you have prophesied, to bring back the vessels of the LORD’s house and all the exiles from Babylon to this place.

<margin>
**v. 7. u)** See verse 25. **x)** Compare 1 Kings 22:28.
</margin>

7 Yet hear now this word which I speak in your ears and in the ears of all the people.

<margin>
**v. 8. y)** Specifically the true prophets, whom you would hardly deny should be accepted as authoritative (canonical), since they spoke in the name of the Lord—prophets like Micah (chapter 26:18) and others. **x)** "They prophesied," I say. For a similar use of the term <term>yoke</term> <note>original: "עֹל"</note> see chapter 27:11. **a)** Their message was no different than mine; therefore, I can safely cite their historical consensus in my favor.
</margin>

8 The prophets who were before me and before you from ancient times prophesied against many lands and against great kingdoms, of war, of disaster, and of pestilence.

<margin>
**v. 9. b)** Therefore, the prophet (whether you, Hananiah, or anyone else) who prophesies of peace—and who appeals only to the eventual outcome to prove his point (as you rashly do, ignoring whether the ancient, authoritative prophets agree or disagree)—will only be recognized when his word actually comes to pass. But your disagreement with all the other prophets suggests that no such outcome will follow. Thus argues Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century theologian</note>. **c)** This refers to whether or not repentance is a prerequisite; because Hananiah speaks so rashly, his words are rightly viewed with suspicion (compare chapter 8:11 and 23:17). **d)** That is, when it has been fulfilled (see Deuteronomy 18:22), for that is when a prophet is truly known (compare Psalm 9:17 and 79:10).
</margin>

9 The prophet who prophesies of peace, when the word of that prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that the LORD has truly sent the prophet."

<margin>
**v. 10. f)** Referring to a shameless impostor (see verse 10), similar to those like Ahab and Zedekiah who were in Babylon (chapter 29:21). **g)** This refers to the wooden yoke that Jeremiah had been carrying by divine command until this moment.
</margin>

10 Then Hananiah the prophet took the yoke-bar from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it.

<margin>
...which he had been carrying; 27:2. **h)** See verse 2. There is a shift in gender in the Hebrew grammar here: instead of the feminine word for <term>yoke-bar</term> <note>original: "מוֹטָה"</note>, the writer uses a masculine suffix as if the masculine synonym <term>yoke</term> <note>original: "עֹל"</note> had been used (verse 11).
**v. 11. i)** Compare the note on verse 3. **k)** See 1 Samuel 25:25. Jeremiah leaves, not without sadness and indignation, proving the man's rashness and stubbornness by his own quiet withdrawal (compare Titus 3:10 and Romans 16:17).
</margin>

11 And Hananiah spoke in the presence of all the people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: 'Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon within two full years from the neck of all the nations.'" And Jeremiah the prophet went his way.

12 The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah after Hananiah the prophet had broken the yoke-bar from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet, saying:

<margin>
**v. 13. l)** "Go" <note>original: "הָלוֹךְ"</note>—the same form of the verb as in chapter 2:2. **m)** Hananiah's act was in vain, and indeed, it will prove harmful. **n)** This is a concise expression mixing two ideas: "Hananiah broke your wooden yoke, so you must make an iron yoke in its place; go and tell him: 'You broke wood, but by God's command, iron replaces it.'" (Schmidt). **o)** "The bars of the yoke." This Hebrew term is used sometimes in the plural (referring to the individual parts of the yoke) and sometimes in the singular (referring to the whole object). See verse 13:10.
</margin>

13 "Go and speak to Hananiah, saying: 'Thus says the LORD: You have broken wooden bars, but you shall make in their place bars of iron.'

<margin>
**v. 14. p)** See Deuteronomy 28:48. **q)** Compare the note on chapter 27:6.
</margin>

14 For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: 'I have put a yoke of iron on the neck of all these nations to serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and they shall serve him, and I have even given him the beasts of the field.'"

<margin>
**v. 15. r)** See verse 7. **s)** Compare chapter 14:14 and 23:21, 32. **t)** "You have made them trust"—you have morally influenced the people so that by listening to your lies, they fall into a worse calamity, forced to wear an iron yoke instead of a wooden one. Compare chapter 29:31.
</margin>

15 Then Jeremiah the prophet said to Hananiah the prophet: "Listen, Hananiah, the LORD has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie."

**Textual Notes on Chapter 28:**
Verse 7: The word "But" <note>original: "אַךְ"</note> is noted by the Rabbinic sources. Verse 8: "And they prophesied" <note>original: "וַיִּנָּבְאוּ"</note> follows the Grafchaim manuscript. In several margins, "against" <note>original: "עַל־"</note> is substituted for "to" <note>original: "אֶל־"</note>.
Verse 11: Scholars note this as the "half-way point of the book" <note>original: "חֲצִי הַסֵּפֶר"</note>. Note the spelling of Nebuchadnezzar: some manuscripts use the full spelling while others use a <term>Makkaph</term> <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> to divide the name: Nebuchad-nezzar.
Verse 12 & 15: Variations in the spelling of "Jeremiah" <note>original: "יִרְמְיָה"</note> occur, sometimes ending with the letter 'H' and sometimes with 'Y'.

# CHAPTER 30. JEREMIAH 30

<margin>
a) Jeremiah 6:19; Psalm 69:30.
b) 4. c) These indeed are the words, says Jeremiah, which the Lord spoke and commanded to be written (verse 2). Furthermore, the Jewish scholars Kimchi and others acknowledge that this entire prophecy must be referred to the times of the Messiah, and Abarbanel <note>Don Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century statesman and commentator</note> confirms this with strong arguments: (1) because here and in verse 3, mention is made of the restoration of both Judah and Israel, whereas it is certain that only the Jews (and not even all of them) returned from Babylon; (2) because in verses 11 and 16, all the nations that were enemies to the Jews are said to be consumed, whereas in the devastation of Babylon, only the Babylonians were destroyed; (3) because in verses 9 and 21, King David is promised, whereas during the time of the Second Temple, no one from the family of David reigned; (4) because this liberation happens after a very long time (verses 10, 12, and 24); and (5) because they shall not return to captivity again (verses 8 and 10), unlike what happened after the return from Babylon.
</margin>

<margin>
The greatness refers to the magnitude of the distress (Joel 2:11; Amos 5:18, 20; Zephaniah 1:14), but also great in respect to grace (verse 8; Malachi 3:2 and following). l) "None like it" <note>original: "prae non esse sicut illum"</note> so that there is plainly none similar to it. See the note on chapter 10:6. m) Chapter 14:8; Daniel 12:1. n) "Yet he shall be saved from it." See verse 10 and chapter 23:6.
</margin>

**4** And these are the words that the Lord spoke concerning Israel and concerning Judah:
**5** For thus says the Lord: "We have heard a voice of trembling; there is fear, and no peace."
**6** "Ask now, and see: can a male give birth? Why then do I see every man <term>geber</term> <note>A Hebrew word for a strong man or warrior</note> with his hands on his loins like a woman in labor, and all faces turned pale?"
**7** "Alas! For that day is great, none is like it; it is a time of distress for Jacob, but he shall be saved out of it."
**8** "And it shall come to pass on that day," says the Lord of Hosts, "that I will break his yoke from your neck, and I will burst your bonds; and strangers shall no longer make slaves of them."
**9** "But they shall serve the Lord their God, and David their king, whom I will raise up for them."
**10** "Therefore do not fear, O My servant Jacob," says the Lord, "nor be dismayed, O Israel; for behold, I will save you from afar, and your descendants from the land of their captivity. Jacob shall return, and have rest and be quiet, and no one shall make him afraid."
**11** "For I am with you," says the Lord, "to save you; though I make a full end of all the nations where I have scattered you, yet I will not make a full end of you. But I will correct you in justice, and I will not let you go altogether unpunished."
**12** For thus says the Lord: "Your breach is incurable, and your wound is grievous."
**13** "There is no one to plead your cause, no medicine for your sore, no healing for you."
**14** "All your lovers have forgotten you; they do not seek you; for I have wounded you with the wound of an enemy, with the punishment of a cruel one, because of the multitude of your iniquities, because your sins have increased."
**15** "Why..."

v. 5. c) Namely. d) 1 Samuel 14:15; Jeremiah 21:4; Ezekiel 26:15. e) See Jeremiah 4:31 and 48:29. Without being overbold, we suggest that God here speaks of Himself in the plural because of the Trinity of Persons, as in Genesis 1:26 and 11:7. *Schmidt*.

v. 6. f) "One giving birth" or "one in labor," like a woman. See chapter 28:2. p) "His yoke," namely Jacob's (verse 7), which was placed upon Jacob (1 Kings 12:4), as the same person immediately continues: "And they shall not make him serve," etc. See Jeremiah 9:3. This pertains to that age which was to be partaker of liberty and salvation, the yoke which the fathers had carried being broken. *Cocceius*.

v. 15. b) **Why indeed do you cry out?** This teaches that God, in verses 13 and 14, by way of concession, enumerated the complaints of Israel: as if to say, "It is true what you complain of, that I have treated you very harshly; but in such a way that I have done you no wrong. Rather, I punished you for this end, so that you would not appear innocent to yourself or to others" (compare verse 11). c) see verse 12 and chapter 18, 19. d) And that it is desperate. verse 13; chapter 15:19; Isaiah 1:7, 11. e) He adds the **true cause** of these evils, so that by acknowledging their sins they might humbly submit themselves to divine justice. **Masoretic Notes:**
v. 16. The word *Lachen* ("Therefore") with a *Rebia* accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16, 20, 21, 22, 23 according to the Masorah in this place; but the Erfurt manuscript is against it here, and especially at chapter 7:32.
v. 17. *Arukah* ("healing") with a *Dagesh* in manuscripts 7, 8, against the Masorah.
v. 21. *Mi hu* ("who is he") so in manuscript 1 and following.
v. 22. *Ve-anokhi* ("And I") with a *Zakef-Katon* accent in manuscripts 3, 5.
v. 23. *Ve-sa'arat* ("and the storm") with the prefix *Vau* in the margin.
*Al* ("upon") written as *al* in Masoretic manuscripts 1, 3 and following.

The same word repeated is sometimes taken in a reduplicative sense, as in verse 18: *you chastised me and I was chastised—turn me and I shall be turned*. Rashi <note>The famous medieval Jewish commentator</note> says: Two buildings [temples] happened to you by the hands of men, and therefore they were desolated again; but yet I myself will build you a third time, and you shall remain built forever. *x)* verse 21; chapter 18:15. *y)* you shall take up your ornaments, or you shall clothe yourself. Chapter 4:30; Isaiah 61:10. *z)* your tambourines. Under the Old Testament, the virgins among the people of God were accustomed to handle tambourines and lead dances. Schmidt. Compare verse 13; Exodus 15:20; Judges 11:34; chapter 21:23; 1 Samuel 18:6. *a)* into a dance [chorus]. Zurich Bible: *in choreo*. Verse 13; Psalm 30:12; Psalm 149:3. <margin>* v. 24. d) Namely, in the land of Judah (v. 23). e) The people of Judah, collectively. f) All and every city distributed among them. g) Farmers (chapter 14:4).
