<margin>* v. 29. c) Any longer, as in the past. d) Jonathan translates well: "Our fathers have sinned, and the children are beaten." e) Unripe grapes <note>original: "omphaces"</note> (v. 30, Isaiah 18:5). f) Are blunted or numbed. (Ecclesiastes 10:10). A proverbial expression, as in Ezekiel 18:2, by those who thought they were paying the penalty not for their own sins, but for the sins of their fathers—doubtless from an abuse of Exodus 20:5. Even today, the Jews fall into the same error, thinking the sins of their ancestors committed while the Temple still stood are the cause of such a long exile. See Ezekiel 18, and Cocceius Lexicon 737.</margin>
<margin>* v. 30. g) Each because of his own (not another's) fault. It will be so manifest that I do not desire the destruction of anyone, or to punish children for their fathers, that those who perish will perish by their own fault. h) Jonathan: "He who sins, he shall die." Cf. Ezekiel 18:4, 20.</margin>

m) I called to witness <note>original Latin: "וְאֶעִידָה feci"; referring to the act of securing witnesses for the deed</note> see Jeremiah 32:25, 44 and Isaiah 8:2. o) And I took, as a buyer, into my own power and custody, so that they might testify to the necessity of the matter. <note>Schmidius refers to Sebastian Schmid, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian and Bible commentator.</note> p) A small book or instrument of purchase <note>original Latin: "libellus s. instrumentum emtionis"</note> see verses 12, 14, in duplicate, as follows. q) Namely, signed or fortified with a seal, see Nehemiah 10:1. This is a distributive declaration of the preceding verse. For both the preceding word *Anachus* <note>a technical term for a grammatical pause or distinction</note> and the absence of the conjunction "and" seem to require this. But Schmidius suggests this is an asyndeton <note>a list without "and"</note> and, comparing verse 14, establishes that there were three documents—not separate, but on one parchment with spaces: (1) the purchase document with the contract; (2) the sealed part where the parties signed with seals; (3) the open part where witnesses signed but did not seal. However, one might ask why the other document is said to be made according to the commandment and statutes? r) According to the commandment and statutes, so the Syriac version; that is, with all the rites and precepts of such a contract legally observed. Schmidius: according to the constitution of the law and in the due manner. <note>Ion. refers to the Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary.</note> s) Open, see verse 14. The Syriac says "not signed"; that is, a transcript or copy of the former, which was made according to the formalities of the law, used for proving the purchase while the original was kept more safely.

Verse 14. a) "In taking," that is, "take." Deuteronomy 31:26. It connects thus: "Take these scrolls" (for there were two, verse 11), specifically this deed of purchase, and indeed (comparing 1 Samuel 17:40 and Zechariah 9:9) the sealed one; even the open scroll, though it is of less importance than the sealed one. c) As a jar or made of clay; namely, so that they are preserved from moisture and other damages. <note>This practice mirrors the preservation of the Dead Sea Scrolls in jars.</note> d) That they may endure or be preserved. Verse 17. f) Alas! <note>original Hebrew: "אֲהָהּ"</note> Chapter 4:10. Targum Jonathan: "Receive my prayer." It expresses Jeremiah's humble emotion, by which he seeks a fuller declaration of this promise. This did not displease God, see Chapter 33:1, 3. g) Chapter 27:5, compare Isaiah 44:24, 45:12; Zechariah 12:1. h) Verse 21, Job 40:9. i) And therefore nothing will be too wonderful before You (so as to exceed Your ability). Verse 27, Luke 1:37, Genesis 18:14, Zechariah 8:6, Job 42:2. This is the prophet's excellent confession concerning the attributes and works of God, phrased as a "pre-occupation" <note>a rhetorical term where one anticipates an objection</note> so that it is clear he does not doubt the divine promise, but wishes to be further instructed, as Mary did in Luke 1:34 or Abraham in Genesis 15:8.

Verse 18. k) Targum Jonathan: "Unto a thousand generations." Add: "to those who fear Him and keep Your commandments," from Ezekiel 20:6, Daniel 9:4, Deuteronomy 5:10, Exodus 34:7. l) And repaying with just retribution, Judges 1:7, Deuteronomy 32:35. m) "Into the bosom," see Isaiah 65:6-7, Psalm 79:12, Luke 6:38. n) Add: "of those who hate Him," from Exodus 20:5. Targum Jonathan: "when they fill up the measure of their fathers" (Matthew 23:32, 35) by sinning after them. o) The Strong God, in nature. p) Powerful, victoriously, in the exercise of strength, compare Isaiah 10:21.

Verse 19. q) Great in action, compare 2 Samuel 23:10, Psalm 66:5. "Work" is added to "Counsel" so it may appear that God's counsel, however great, is not powerless or ineffective. (Schmidius). s) You, whose eyes are open, compare Psalm 14:2, 33:18, Job 34:21. t) Chapter 17:10, Psalm 62:13. u) According to the fruit of his studies/efforts, Chapter 17:10, 21:14; Isaiah 3, 10. That is, according to merit, compare Romans 2:6. Unless perhaps "deeds" <note>original: "מעללים"</note> are habitual works and internal character, while "fruit" <note>original: "פרי"</note> are the external acts born from that internal habit.

Verse 11. "And that which was sealed, the commandment" <note>original Hebrew: "וְאֶת־הֶחָתוּם הַמִּצְוָה"</note>. The Eastern tradition places the "and" <note>original: "וְאֶת"</note> first. But others treat "the commandment" as the *Kethiv* (written form) with an added *Qere* (reading instruction) "and the commandment."
Verse 14. "Et" (the direct object marker) with a *Makkaph* (hyphen) in various manuscripts (1, 2, 10, etc.).
Verse 15. "Because/For" <note>original: "כִּי"</note> with a *Makkaph* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3.
Verse 19. "Which" <note>original: "אֲשֶׁר"</note> with a *Makkaph* in manuscripts 1, 6, 9, etc., but with a *Darga* (cantillation mark) in others. "Man" <note>original: "אָָדָם"</note> is written in manuscript 3 with the reading instruction "The Man." There are variations noted between the Eastern and Western traditions here.

<meta>This page transitions from the general rebukes of Chapter 34 to a specific object lesson in Chapter 35. While the previous section condemned the Judeans for breaking their covenant regarding slaves, this chapter introduces the Rechabites—a group famous for their strict adherence to their ancestral laws—to serve as a stinging contrast to Israel’s unfaithfulness.</meta>

# JEREMIAH 35.

<margin>
**CHAPTER 35, v. 1. a)** This occurred around the eighth year of King Jehoiakim's reign. See the Preface, section 20.
</margin>

1 **The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord in the days of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, saying:**

<margin>
**v. 2. b)** Go to them, see verse 13. **c)** See chapter 2, verse 2. **g)** "House," meaning the family or clan, as in verses 3, 5, and 18; compare Exodus 2:1, etc. **h)** Of the Rechabites (verses 3, 5, 18), named for Rechab (verses 6, 8, 14, 19). They were living in Jerusalem at this time (verse 11). Hermann Witsius wrote a detailed dissertation on them. They were foreigners, not Israelites (verse 7). They are also known by the broader name "Kenites" (1 Chronicles 2:55), being of the lineage of Jethro, Moses' father-in-law (Judges 1:16). After Jethro embraced the religion of Jehovah (Exodus 18:9) and was invited by Moses (Numbers 10:29), he remained with the Israelites. His descendants later joined Israel, eventually dividing into two branches: some moved to Kedesh in the tribe of Naphtali (Judges 4:11, 17), while the majority associated with the tribe of Judah (Judges 1:16) and spread to the borders of the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:6). Our Rechabites come from these (1 Chronicles 2:55). That they joined the Israelite religion is clear from this passage (compare verse 19) and from 2 Kings 10:16. **i)** Speak to them—specifically, ask them to come with you into the house of the Lord (Schmid). **k)** A cellar or side-chamber (verse 4, 1 Chronicles 9:26). See Cocceius’ Lexicon, 420. **l)** You shall offer them wine to drink. Compare Amos 2:11–12. This was not because God commanded that they *must* drink, but rather to test their constancy (which God foresaw), providing an opportunity to shame the Jews by the Rechabites' example.
</margin>

2 **“Go to the house of the Rechabites and speak with them, and bring them into the house of the Lord, into one of the chambers, and give them wine to drink.”**

<margin>
**v. 3. m)** This Jaazaniah was undoubtedly their leader and the father of the house (Schmid). **n)** See verse 2.
</margin>

3 **So I took Jaazaniah son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah, and his brothers, and all his sons, and the whole house of the Rechabites.**

<margin>
**v. 4. o)** This was a very suitable place for this act, both because appropriate witnesses were available from among the priests and leaders, and because it was close to where the people gathered to speak (verse 13). **p)** See verse 2. It is doubtful whether this chamber was inside the court of the priests (which the Rechabites, as non-Israelites, would rarely be permitted to enter) or attached to its outer walls.

</margin>

**Schin. q)** The Syriac and Ionic versions say "prophet of the Lord." Compare 1 Kings 13:22; Jeremiah 13:4, etc. **r)** One of the temple leaders (Schmid). **s)** "Keeper of the threshold." The Ionic version says "treasurer." This official was in charge of the temple funds used for repairing damage and purchasing sacred vessels; see 2 Kings 12.

---

1a. Chapter 22:4; Chapter 25:18. See Buxtorf's Talmudic Lexicon, 127. \
\* 5. **l)** "And I set before them." See Genesis 18:8. **m)** Bowls or pitchers (Genesis 44:2). **x)** And cups, which differ in shape from the bowls (Genesis 40:11, 13). **y)** This was an imperative of *offering*, not a divine command or coercion. It was a test of their perseverance in a good tradition, while leaving them the freedom to drink. See the note on verse 2. \
v. 6. **z)** "We are not accustomed to drink," as in Genesis 29:26. **a)** Jonadab was a man of singular holiness and zeal, as well as authority; he was a supporter <note>original Greek: "συνήγορος" (sunēgoros)</note> of King Jehu of Israel (2 Kings 10:15, 23). Consequently, the Rechabites lived by these laws for nearly three hundred years with remarkable constancy (verse 14). **b)** "Our father" here means one of our ancestors (see verse 8, 10; 1 Samuel 20:10). **c)** This lifestyle was neither specifically commanded nor blamed by God. However, the children's strict, spontaneous obedience was praiseworthy, as the lifestyle was not only harmless but useful and suited to their circumstances (verses 14, 18, 19). Schmid suggests Jonadab could be called the "legislator" of the Rechabites, just as other nations or cities had their own lawgivers. **d)** Their practice was somewhat analogous to the Nazirite vow (Numbers 6:3-4; Amos 2:11-12), especially those who were Nazirites for life (Judges 13:5; 1 Samuel 1:11; Luke 1:15). \
v. 7. **e)** Meaning "so that you may inhabit them" (verses 9, 10). They only moved into the city out of necessity (verse 11), which was a permitted exception. **f)** See Isaiah 5:2. **g)** "And nothing of these shall be yours," meaning they shall possess nothing—not a house, nor seed, nor a vineyard. **v. 8. h)** Following the ancient custom of the Kenites (Judges 4:17). Women "in the tent" was a simple way to describe Kenite women (Judges 5:24). This pastoral, nomadic life was modeled after Jethro (Exodus 2:16) and other "tent-dwellers" (Scenites) (Judges 8:11; Jeremiah 49:29; Genesis 4:19; 2 Chronicles 14:14). Crucially, as foreigners <note>term: "sojourners" (resident aliens without land-owning rights)</note>, they did not own land in Canaan (verse 7). Jonadab wanted this simple life, which suited their status, to be preserved. **i)** The scholar Kimchi explains: they lived long and comfortably because houses, fields, and vineyards bring many worries to their owners; and Solomon teaches how harmful wine can be (Proverbs 23:29). Others add: as foreigners, they avoided the envy of the local people by not competing for property. But it is most likely that this refers to the promise of the Fourth Commandment (Exodus 20:12) and had a moral purpose: Jonadab wanted to turn his family away from the luxuries of this life toward heavenly things. For this reason, in 1 Chronicles 2:55, they are called **scribes** <note>original Hebrew: "סופרים" (sopherim)</note> or experts in the law. **k)** See the note on verse 2. \
v. 8. **l)** "And we have obeyed," remaining constant until now out of reverence for our father's command (verses 14, 16, 18).

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Chapter 36. Following the account of the obedient Rechabites in the previous chapter, the narrative shifts to the fourth year of King Jehoiakim's reign. Jeremiah is commanded to document all the prophecies he has received to date—spanning from the time of Josiah to the present—in a written scroll, providing a final opportunity for the nation to repent before the coming judgment.</meta>

### CHAPTER 36. Jeremiah 36

<margin>
**Chapter 36. 1. a)** probably at the end of the year, comparing verse 6 with verse 9. See the notes on chapter 25:1 and the Preface, section 20.
**v. 2. x)** A roll of a book, that is, a scroll prepared for writing. See verse 4, Psalm 40:8, and Ezekiel 2:9. The ancients did not fold parchments like modern books, but rolled them together; see the Lexicon, page 138. Compare Isaiah 34:4 and Revelation 6:14. **y)** Write upon it; so that during the upcoming fast, the collected prophecies might be read to the people (verse 6) and preserved for future generations (verse 28; chapter 30:2; Isaiah 8:1; 30:8; Habakkuk 2:3; compare Psalm 102:19). **z)** concerning Israel, namely the ten tribes. Compare chapter 3:12; 30:3 and following; 31:1 and following. **a)** See the note on chapter 1:5. **b)** from the day I began to speak, or first spoke. **c)** specifically from his thirteenth year (chapter 1:2; 25:3). Thus, all the prophecies issued up to the fourth year of Jehoiakim contained in this book are signified. (Note by Schmid).
**v. 3. d)** See verse 7 and chapter 26:3. Although God foreknew that they would not do so, He indicates by this phrasing that He seriously desires their salvation and conversion (Ezekiel 18:23; Zephaniah 3:5), and that it was still possible then for the Jews to turn back. **e)** especially now with evil looming and causing anxiety (verse 9). See the notes on chapter 25:1 and 46:2. **f)** that is, unless they turned back.
**v. 4. g)** his secretary (verses 5, 8) and a scribe by profession (verses 26, 32; chapter 32:12). He suffered much along with Jeremiah from the Jews (compare verse 26 here and chapter 45:1). According to some, he was also a priest (compare verse 10). **h)** that is, by dictation (verses 6, 19). **i)** See verse 2.
**v. 5. k)** that is, in the following year (verse 9, comparing verse 6). Therefore, that scroll was written in the fourth year, but—

—extraordinary fast mentioned in verse 9, when all Judah was gathered. **r)** Compare verse 9. Because Jeremiah is barred from the Temple, Baruch ben Neriah writes the scroll and reads it publicly during a time of national fasting.</summary>

<margin>
verse 17. α) How? It was indeed clear to them that Baruch had written from the mouth of Jeremiah; but this could have happened in two ways: (1) after a continuous narration by Jeremiah, Baruch could have arranged in his own way what occurred to his memory; or (2) with Jeremiah dictating the words while they were captured by the pen. The first way was harder to conceive because of the size of the writing (all these words), therefore they were eager to find out that it was the latter (verse 18).

verse 2. x) Staying, with the intent of resisting the Chaldeans, so that he is unwilling to go out to them. Schmid well observes that "to stay" is to be understood as spontaneous and by one's own will: for the prophet himself stayed in the city, but under compulsion; nor does he seem to have intended anything else than that the people, setting aside their obstinacy, should promote the spontaneous surrender of the city as far as they were able. Compare the note on chapter 21:9. a) Chapter 27:8, 13. b) Jonathan: *But whoever shall go out and give himself up*. Verses 17, 18, 21. c) *he shall remain living*, not dying by sword, famine, or plague. d) *of his life*. Chapter 4:10. e) for *spoil*; that is, he made. Greek <note>Septuagint</note> and Arabic: *as a find* <note>original: εἰς ἕυρημα</note>, as if something found which was undoubtedly lost, unless he had surrendered to the Chaldeans. Jonathan: *as a rescue*. Similarly the Syriac. But Schmid: like one who in war gains some notable prey, he considers it a thing granted to him by God. Compare verse 17, chapter 21:9, chapter 39:18, chapter 45:5. f) *so that he lives*. Genesis 3:22. Deuteronomy 4:42. verse 3. g) most certainly, chapter 32:4.

<summary>Jeremiah is falsely accused of desertion and imprisoned in a dungeon. King Zedekiah secretly consults him, leading to Jeremiah's transfer to a less harsh confinement in the court of the guard, where he continues to prophesy the city's fall.</summary>

verse 4. h) Likely those who were listed above in verse 1, who have long been hostile to Jeremiah (see chapter 37, verses 14 and 15). i) "Please" <note>original: 'na'</note>; do this for emphasis—not so much as a humble prayer, but as an urgent demand; as if to say, "I beg you, do this very thing which we advised before." k) "Man." Syntax similar to chapter 35, verse 14 and chapter 36, verse 22. l) "Since" or "Because" (see Genesis 18:5). m) "He makes them slack" <note>original: 'merappe'</note>; meaning he makes the men dismayed and fearful (compare Ezra 4:4 and Isaiah 35:3). n) "Of the soldiers" (see chapter 39:4 and 41:3). o) Namely, from the plague, the sword, and the famine (verse 2, chapter 21:7). There is no excessive abundance of these men, so they ought to be encouraged rather than dismayed. p) Also of the inhabitants. q) Namely, those things described in verses 2 and 3, which were undoubtedly narrated to the King by them. r) "He seeks" (that is, he directs his mind and care toward) "peace" or the good for this people (compare verse 22, Job 10:6, Jeremiah 29:7, and Esther 10:3).

verse 5. s) Permitting an innocent man, whom he ought to have and could have defended, to be given to his accusers out of inexcusable indulgence. Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmid, 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note>. t) That is, in your judgment or power (chapter 26:14, Genesis 16:6). u) "The king is not" (that is, "it is not I..." etc., comparing Esther 8:8) "one who is able." This signifies a negation of existence; it cannot be joined here with the future tense unless the word "who" <note>original: 'asher'</note> is understood. Thus say David Kimchi <note>a medieval grammarian and commentator</note> and Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 17th-century Hebraist</note>. x) "Who" (or "so that he") "is able to do anything with you or against you." As if to say: "So much must be granted to your merits that it does not befit the king to resist you, who are men faithful to the Commonwealth and endowed with distinguished wisdom." (Compare Schmid). The Vulgate translation follows this: "For it is not right for the king to deny you anything." The Syriac and Targum Jonathan also suggest he could not answer them.

king" of King Zedekiah (as Jonathan translates), it would have said "the servant" <note>original: 'ha-melekh'</note> with the prefix, or at least his name would have been expressed somewhere. Kimchi. h) Therefore, originally born outside the Israelite community, but later converted. Schmid. i) A eunuch or court official (Genesis 40:7). k) "He himself—of the king." This is a parenthesis. l) See verse 6. m) "The king, however, was then sitting," etc. A new parenthesis, provided to illustrate verse 8. n) Undoubtedly intending to give courage to the guards by his presence (compare the note on chapter 37, 13). o) From those places, namely, from the king’s house to the Benjamin Gate (verse 7). p) "They have done badly—whatever they have done" (Genesis 44:5, Psalm 74:3). q) Those named above in verse 1. It is not probable that they were present right then; but Scripture sometimes uses a demonstrative "these" in place of proper names, especially when they have already appeared in the history. Schmid. So also in verse 4. r) He emphasizes the indignity of the crime with a general particle, even though a specific detail follows (as in 1 Kings 2:44). s) Namely, or (as Schmid says) "especially" because they threw him in (verse 6). t) Rashi <note>a famous 11th-century commentator</note> and Abarbanel <note>a 15th-century commentator</note> interpret it thus: "for (since they wanted him dead anyway) he would eventually have died on his own 'under himself' (that is, in his former prison, chapter 37:21) because of the hunger growing stronger and stronger, and there would have been no need to establish a new cruelty against him." Jonathan also reads it this way. But Schmid interprets it thus: "for already he was nearly killed by hunger and made like a dead man in the court of the guard, due to the small portion of bread given to him, because there was almost no bread left in the city." Truly, it seems to us to be a grammatical shift where the future tense represents the past, suggesting the certainty of a thing about to happen: "He is dying in this pit," etc. (compare verse 10), from which it is clear the King understood these words as referring to the immediate danger of death. u) "In his place," that is, immediately, on the spot (as in 2 Samuel 2:23). x) Not only because of the filth of the prison, but also because of the famine. For we determine, with Luther, Schmid, and others, that the princes in the pit denied him even the bread previously allotted to him. y) Especially since there was no bread remaining; so that, unless he was pulled out of the pit to continue receiving bread from the King's generosity (as before in chapter 37:21), he could not be provided for from anywhere else. z) That is, under your guidance and command (verse 11, Numbers 31:49). a) Namely, from the Benjamin Gate (verse 7), which was quite crowded with guards (chapter 37:13). b) Not only to pull him out, but also to ensure that no one could prevent the extraction by force; for the princes were suspected by the king (verse 1). Schmid. c) Because there is danger in delay (compare verses 9 and 11). d) Those 30 men (verse 10).

<margin>
The word "beneath" <note>original: 'tachat'</note> seems to be considered in respect to the body, so that what is closer to the body is "lower," even if in another respect it is "higher." Thus the rags were applied to the body, then the ropes were added, so that the rags were between the body and the ropes, lest the body be harmed by the ropes. Schmid.
</margin>

Often in a question, that which is to be supplied from the answer is omitted. s) Verse 25; 1 Samuel 3:17.

<summary>Jeremiah is rescued from the pit by Ebed-Melech using old rags to protect his arms from the ropes. He then holds a secret meeting with King Zedekiah, offering a final divine ultimatum: surrender to Babylon and live, or remain and watch the city burn.</summary>

<header>JEREMIAH. CHAPTERS 38, 39.</header>

<margin>
n) Indeed, they are now "immersed." This is a *Hophal* <note>a passive Hebrew verb form</note> as in Proverbs 8:25; compare also verse 6 above and Psalm 69:3. v) "In the mud." Compare Job 8:11. This is a proverbial expression, as if to say: By their advice, it has come to pass that you have fallen into the greatest destruction. p) "They have turned back," namely your feet, into the same mud from which they were trying to emerge; they have shamefully relapsed more heavily and without hope of safety. Compare chapter 46:5, Isaiah 42:17, and Psalm 35:4. But Schmid interprets it thus: "and they have retreated," namely the "men of your peace" <note>your trusted allies</note>. That is to say, they have failed you. Compare Psalm 78:57.
</margin>
<margin>
**Grace**
23. "He gave himself," etc. Compare verse 13 and chapter 37:21. Meanwhile, it is just for him to buy the field and claim it for himself by right of kinship, and by this symbol to create a certain hope of liberation from the impending captivity. See chapter 32:1 and following. i) Compare chapter 39:11 and following.
</margin>

23 "They shall lead out all your wives and your children to the Chaldeans, and you yourself shall not escape from their hand, for by the hand of the king of Babylon you shall be seized, and this city you shall burn with fire."

<margin>
v. 23. q) "All," I say. This is taken up again from the mention of the women in verse 22, so that something further might be added concerning the children, etc. r) "They are about to lead out." Used impersonally for "they shall be led out." See verse 22. s) Verse 18. š) "Into the hand—you shall be taken," that is, being captured, you shall be handed over. This is a "pregnant" expression <note>a concise phrase implying more than it says</note>, more distinctly explained in chapter 34:3. u) "You shall burn" through the Chaldeans; this is the moral cause, because by a spontaneous surrender you could have averted the burning. Compare verses 17 and 18.
</margin>
<margin>
v. 24. x) "Anything about these words." This is a partitive preposition, as in Numbers 11:17 and Psalm 141:4. y) Chapter 11:21. He begins to limit the promise and the oath in some way. —Schmid.
</margin>

24 Then Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "Let no man know of these words, and you shall not die."

<margin>
v. 25. z) a) From this it can be established that although they spoke privately, the King spoke with the prophet not entirely without anyone noticing or seeing. —Schmid. a) Verse 14. b) The words of those using flattery, as if to say: "Be of good courage, there is nothing for you to fear," etc. And the Syriac version has: "so that we do not kill you," phrased as a threat.
</margin>

25 "But if the officials hear that I have spoken with you, and they come to you and say to you, 'Tell us now what you said to the king; do not hide it from us and we will not put you to death; also, what did the king say to you?'"

<margin>
v. 26. c) Compare the note on chapter 36:7. d) The Vulgate reads: "lest you should command me to be brought back." e) Chapter 37:20.
</margin>

26 "Then you shall say to them, 'I was presenting my petition before the king, that he would not send me back to the house of Jonathan to die there.'"

<margin>
v. 27. f) And so they desisted from him in silence. Compare 1 Samuel 7:8, Job 13:11, and Judges 18:2. g) "The word itself," that is, the conversation held with the King; so that they could not have examined the prophet more closely, even if they had relied on some certain foundation.
</margin>
<margin>
k) According to the accents, it connects with the preceding in this way: "For Jeremiah was there, even until he was taken," etc. But according to the *Piska* <note>original: 'piska be-emza pasuk' — a scribal gap in the middle of a verse</note> or the space, it connects with the following.

# 39

<margin>
**CHAPTER XXXIX.**
...in the following: "And so it happened, when," etc. And thus the interpreters also vary.
**CHAPTER XXXIX.**
1. l) Compare chapter 52:4 and following; 2 Kings 25:1 and following; and the notes there. Furthermore, the order of the narrative required that the history of the capture of Jerusalem be placed here, not only because of what preceded, but also...
</margin>

1 In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem and besieged it.
2 In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month, the city was breached.
3 And all the officials of the king of Babylon came and sat in the Middle Gate: Nergal-sharezer, Samgar-nebo, Sarsechim the *Rab-saris* <note>Chief Official/Eunuch</note>, Nergal-sharezer the *Rab-mag* <note>Chief Magician/Soothsayer</note>, and all the rest of the officials of the king of Babylon.
4 And it happened when Zedekiah the king of Judah and all the men of war saw them, they fled and went out of the city by night, by way of the king's garden, through the gate between the two walls; and he went out toward the Arabah <note>the plain or desert valley</note>.

<sig>84</sig>
<meta>catchword: And they pursued</meta>

---

...because of what follows, since the events that succeeded the storming of the city are narrated next. —Schmid. m) Namely, of the ecclesiastical year; compare the note on chapter 36:9. And indeed on the tenth day of its month, chapter 52:4, 2 Kings 25:1. n) Who, however, having returned to Riblah (v. 5), was not present at the storming (v. 3). Compare note (p) at 2 Kings 25:6. o) "They besieged it." Chapter 21:2, 32:2, 37:5. Moreover, on that very day when the siege occurred, the same was indicated by the Lord to Ezekiel in Chaldea, and the destruction of the city and temple (their delight) was predicted to the people through him under the parable of the death of his beloved wife. Ezekiel 24:1 and following. —Lightfoot, *Chronicles*, p. 124. v. 2. p) "On the ninth day of that month." Therefore the siege lasted a year and a half. q) "Broken through," that is, by the enemies, and captured by those forcing their way through the destroyed and breached walls. Ezekiel 26:10, 2 Kings 25:4. v. 3. r) Those who were in command of his army; chapter 38:17, 18, 22. For Nebuchadnezzar himself was at Riblah at that time (v. 5). s) Or "victors and lords," chapter 49:38. Compare the prophecy in chapter 1:15. s) "In the middle gate." Compare Judges 16:29. Kimchi: This was one of the city gates so named. Aben Ezra: the gate of the middle wall between the first and third city walls. What if it were a gate in the middle part of the city which they occupied? Compare 2 Kings 20:4, chapter 22:14. x) According to the accents, four names are mentioned: Nergal-Sharezer, Samgar-Nebo, Sarsechim, and another Nergal-Sharezer. x) Syriac: "prefect of the eunuchs"; a name of an office, as in verse 13 and 2 Kings 18:17. y) A different person from the first one; from whom he is distinguished by the title of office added in this place. x) "Prefect of the Magi" <note>original: 'Praefectus magorum'</note> (v. 13), likely of the priests. For the Persian *Magh* denotes a Priest, as the illustrious Hyde shows in *History of the Religion of the Ancient Persians*. See *Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensia*, 1701, p. 410. The singular number is taken collectively, as in the preceding "prefect of the Eunuch" for "of the eunuchs." v. 4. a) Namely, because they had penetrated so far into the city that he despaired of being able to resist them any longer from the citadel or the temple mount (to which it is inferred the King had retreated with his soldiers when the breach into the city was made). —Schmid. b) Chapter 38:4. c) Lest they be noticed by the Chaldeans. Compare the prophecy in Ezekiel 12:12. d) "Through the gate between the two walls," so called here because it led those exiting between two walls, where the path was more hidden, so that they could be less observed because of the walls. —Schmid. Perhaps newly dug out for this purpose, so they might slip away by a certain stratagem; compare Ezekiel 12:12. e) Toward the wilderness or the plains of Jericho (v. 5). Joshua 11:16. Compare Cocceius, *Lexicon* 642.

# JEREMIAH 39. CHAPTER 39. 39.

<margin>
*. 38, 17. and following. But the extreme stubbornness of Zedekiah, which the outcome very clearly proved, provoked the mind of the Babylonian; they demolished [the walls] on every side. See chapter 52:14 and 2 Kings 25:10.
*. 9. u) 2 Kings 25:11. x) specifically from the plague, famine, and sword, chapter 21:7, both before and after the conquest. y) chapter 38:19. Vulgate <note>The Latin Bible</note>: "those who had defected"; namely, during the siege. z) to him, namely the king of Babylon, verse 6. a) specifically the provincials. For in this passage they are distinguished from the city dwellers. b) he transported.
</margin>

<margin>
**CHAPTER XL, 1. s)** But are these not historical accounts rather than prophecies? Certainly, most commentators refer back to that "Word of the Lord" mentioned in chapter 42:7 and following, to which this historical parenthesis of the time is placed as a precursor or "light" for the subsequent prophecies. But *Schmidt thinks* that a new book of the entire prophetic volume begins here, the previous one having been completed, which Jeremiah intended to end with the captivity of Jerusalem.
</margin>

Compare Isaiah 60:11, or according to others the Arabic **חָזַק** (*hazaq*), *to be narrow or constricted.* **b)** *the captive crowd*. Chapter 29:22. **c)** *those who were to be deported*. Chapter 13:19; compare note on chapter 39:13. **verse 2. d)** *For he took* — Jeremiah from the crowd of captives, among whom he had been led from Jerusalem to Ramah. Verse 1. **e)** Verse 2; chapter 39:9. **f)** Jeremiah. The syntax follows Chaldaic or Syriac forms, as in Job 5:2. **g)** that is, the God whose servant and prophet you are. *Schmidt*. **h)** Compare note on chapter 39:11. **i)** that which is before our eyes, namely the present misery of the city and the land. *Schmidt*. **k)** Jerusalem and all of Judea. **verse 3. l)** that is, He also fulfilled it; compare note on chapter 39:16 and Isaiah 31:2. This confession from a pagan man is indeed very glorious to the God of Israel. Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> elegantly says: "He wants to say: I do not think this thing happened because of the strength of Nebuchadnezzar, his princes, and his armies, but from the providence of Jehovah; not because of the merit of Nebuchadnezzar, but because of the sins and malice of the Jews." **m)** *For because.* This connects with what follows rather than what precedes; according to the accents. **n)** He includes *Jeremiah* only insofar as he belongs to the body of the people, to whom is attributed that which is common to most. *Schmidt*. **o)** therefore this happened to you. **verse 4. p)** "And now," because you are not in the same guilt as the rest, but (as we have learned) you rebuked their sins and their rebellion against the King of Babylon. *Schmidt*. **q)** specifically, that thing. Chapter 14:17. **r)** A change of tense: *untie* [the chains], as in Genesis 14:22 and chapter 23:13. **v. 1. s)** 1 Kings 21:2. **t)** Compare note on chapter 39:12. **u)** *leave off* or "let be." Zechariah 11:12; Job 16:6. Meaning, with complete freedom. **x)** that is, it is open and allowed to you. Genesis 13:9; chapter 47:6. **y)** to a *good* (place), that is, wherever it pleases you to go. Compare Genesis 20:15. **verse 5. z)** This is a difficult sentence. Perhaps the most convenient interpretation is this: When Jeremiah had not yet returned, or had not yet determined to which specific seat in his homeland he would return from the captives (though his face showed that this was more desirable to him than going to Babylon with Nebuzaradan), perhaps fearing that if he declared his desire too clearly, Nebuzaradan might interpret it as him undervaluing the excellent conditions offered in Babylon; finally, Nebuzaradan said, "Return then to Gedaliah," etc. In this way, the first part of the verse is historical, yet concise, so that the reader feels present at the business itself rather than reading a historical description. There is something similar in 1 Kings 20:34. However, *Schütze* suggests: "If that place which seems good to you—namely Anathoth—has not yet 'returned' (that is, if its inhabitants, scattered by the evils of war, have not yet returned there so you can live safely), then go to Gedaliah." Finally, others say: "*Since he* (Gedaliah) *will not be returning here* or to Jerusalem, *therefore return to Mizpah to him*." **a)** He is said to *return* here not in relation to his destination (Gedaliah), since Jeremiah had not been with him yet, but in relation to the starting point (Ramah), to which he had been led shortly before with the other captives. Verse 1. **b)** Verse 6; chapter 39:14; 2 Kings 25:22. **c)** He made him governor. Verse 7, 11; Genesis 39:4, 5. **d)** namely, those left in the land. Verse 6; chapter 39:14. As if to say: "Use the same privileges that they do." **e)** Verse 4. Since he had only given advice, he protests again that he does not want to restrict Jeremiah's freedom even in this case. *Schmidt*.

v. 3. p) *with him, with Gedaliah, I say.* A pleonasm <note>redundant phrasing</note>, as in Exodus 2:6. q) namely, the "men of war" or soldiers (Jeremiah 38:4) who were attached to Gedaliah for his protection, but who at that time (because they suspected no evil and, as Schmidt conjectures, had been drinking wine quite freely) were unarmed and unprepared. We understand this, therefore, with the Church History of Gesenius (p. 292), to mean the ruins of the Temple in Jerusalem, where perhaps some priests had attempted to restore the sacred rites, or as Abarbanel says, these men presumed they had been restored. It is clear from this that this is Mizpah of Benjamin (compare note m, 2 Kings 25:23). d) walking continually and weeping. <margin>
**Verse 8.** k) *were found*, or came to light. l) those who said. m) *hidden* treasures which we promise you in exchange for our lives. (compare Proverbs 2:4). In times of war, people were accustomed to hide grain and produce in this way, which Ishmael had otherwise destroyed. (verse 3). u) the daughters of King Zedekiah, as in verse 1; compare chapter 43:6. v) It is hardly probable that any other "King" would be mentioned without further title than the one who was most recently known in memory <note>referring to the recently deposed Zedekiah</note>. x) those to whom Mizpah was given as a residence, not elsewhere. y) whom he had placed under Gedaliah’s care. **Verses 7-8.** g) from which there was no escape, unlike the open field in verse 5. h) he cast them, these *mastanites* and *mastaros* <note>Latin terms likely referring to the slaughtered men</note> into the pit; compare chapter 39:16 and 2 Kings 10:14. i) the well or pit mentioned in verse 9.

**Verse 9.** n) A "pit" of artifice (verse 7). o) Joshua 10:27. p) *corpses*; chapter 33:5. q) "by the hand of Gedaliah." This should be understood by interpretation to mean the same as "because of Gedaliah," as the commentator Kimchi explains. For had it not been for Gedaliah, against whom such great envy burned, Ishmael would not have killed Gedaliah’s companions or the passing travelers. But Schmidt translates: *under the empire or power of Gedaliah*, that is, those existing under his authority; compare chapter 38:11. This undoubtedly refers to the men who had been with Gedaliah, who are primarily considered here. It was an ancient practice to hide in subterranean places so as not to be found by enemies. It is helpful to compare this with Hirtius, Book V, on the *African War*: "It is," he says, "a custom of the inhabitants in Africa that in the fields and in all villages, they have underground caves for the sake of storing grain, and they prepare these especially because of wars and the sudden arrival of enemies." Likewise, Varro in *On Agriculture*, Book II, chapter 57: "Some have granaries under the earth, like caves, which they call *siros* <note>Greek: σῑρούς</note>, as in Cappadocia and Thrace." See more in Bochart’s *Hierozoicon*, Part II, pages 594–595.
</margin>

**1** Then all the military commanders—including Johanan son of Kareah and Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah—and all the people from the least to the greatest approached. **2** They said to Jeremiah the prophet, "Please let our petition come before you, and pray for us to the Lord your God on behalf of all this remnant. I will not withhold a word from you." **5** Then they said to Jeremiah, "May the Lord be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act according to every word the Lord your God sends you to tell us. **6** Whether it is good or bad, we will obey the voice of the Lord our God to whom we are sending you, so that it may go well with us when we obey the voice of the Lord our God." **7** At the end of ten days, the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah. **8** So he called Johanan son of Kareah and all the military commanders who were with him, and all the people from the least to the greatest, **9** and said to them, "Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your petition before Him: **10** 'If you will truly stay in this land, then I will build you and not pull you down; I will plant you and not uproot you...'"

Indeed, I will do what you ask promptly and willingly. 1 Kings 2:42. o) verse 2, 20. p) I will not prohibit (keep back) any word from you, but will announce it to you. compare chapter 26:2; 1 Kings 22:14. *We* <note>original Hebrew: <hebrew>אנחנו</hebrew></note> - Masoretic note: Read as *we* [anachnu].
v. 5. q) Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation</note>: "The Word of the Lord." v) "as a witness of truth," or a most truthful witness. As if to say: we cite God as a witness, who is neither ignorant of anything (ch. 29:23), nor can He lie (Proverbs 14:25), or tolerate a lie (Psalm 5:7); so that He may convict us of such a foul lie by establishing a just punishment against us if we do not [obey]. s) "and faithful," Psalm 89:38. t) "what (i.e., with which, or because of which) He shall send you"; as if to say: what He gives you in commission to report to us. ch. 43:1. k) Exodus 19:8; Joshua 24:24. v. 6. x) "Whether it seems good or bad to us, nevertheless to the voice [we will listen]." y) *We* <note>The note discusses a Hebrew variant <hebrew>אנן</hebrew> "anan" for "anachnu"</note>. This is frequent among the Rabbis, and perhaps was once more common among the Hebrews: for from this, the ending of the Perfect tense in the first person plural (original: <hebrew>פקדנו</hebrew> [pakadnu]) seems to have arisen. z) "to whom we are sending you." The Vulgate reads: "if staying you remain." So say some; compare Ecclesiastes 30:15. Most, however, translate "by staying" or "by inhabiting": certainly the verbs *to sit/dwell* (original: <hebrew>ישב</hebrew>) and *to return* (original: <hebrew>שוב</hebrew>) sometimes exchange their meanings. compare Psalm 23:6; 2 Samuel 15:8; ch. 19:33. k) and do not go to Egypt, as you intended (v. 13 and following). l) He will increase you with long life, children, wealth, and all good things (ch. 24:6; 31:4; 33:7).

28 And those who escape the sword shall return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, few in number; and all the remnant of Judah, who came to the land of Egypt to live there, shall know whose word will stand, Mine or theirs.

<margin>
Namely, everything that indicates another thing—past, present, or future—which is not yet apparent, and brings it to mind, is called a "sign" <note>Hebrew: *oth*</note>. Even a future event is set as a sign of a present and simultaneously future thing, as in Exodus 3:12; 1 Samuel 2:34; 2 Kings 19:29. In these cases, it signifies those things by which it will be manifest that God spoke and that He truly decreed to do those things. When the event happens after the word is spoken, that is the sign that God spoke and decreed the act. (Thus far Cocceius’s Lexicon 18). Therefore, in this place, the imminent betrayal of Pharaoh Hophra is set as a certain prelude...
</margin>

29 "And this shall be the sign to you," declares the LORD, "that I will punish you in this place, in order that you may know that My words will surely stand against you for harm":

30 Thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hand of those who seek his life, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, who was his enemy and sought his life."

<margin>
**verse 5.** d) "And you alone," in the common calamity of all the people (v. 4). e) so that you should not wish to feel or notice any trouble or adversity. Or see James 5:3. This is an emphatic question, an inference from what precedes: Therefore, you ought not to seek great things—total immunity from sorrow and pain due to dangers, contempt, persecutions, etc. (cf. v. 3). The reason for this inference consists in: (1) because everyone, without exception, is suffering (v. 4); to demand to be excepted by some sort of privilege is against equity, especially since even the pious have contributed something to God's judgments. (2) because it ought to be enough that God promised by special grace to rescue the life of Baruch in every place, whereas he was going to destroy most others. f) specifically "great things," but be content with what I give you, just as you have a sufficiently grave cause to be as others are; for behold, etc. Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a prominent Lutheran Hebraist.</note> compares this to 2 Corinthians 12:8-9. g) verse 4. h) Jeremiah 66:36 <note>Likely a typo in the original manuscript for 46:1.</note>.

> 27. 1. and following: These things said against the nations are only a kind of general precursor, sent forward primarily for the sake of the Jewish people; the fuller narration of them is reserved for this place, cf. chapter 25:13. It is probable that most of these prophecies were issued in the **fourth year of Jehoiakim** <note>Jehoiakim was a puppet king of Judah, reigning 609–598 BCE.</note>, according to 25:1 and 27:1 (cf. verse 2 here), unless a special inscription stands in the way, e.g., 47:1. $\aleph$. 2. k) **Against Egypt**: chapter 25:19. A more specific title. cf. Isaiah 19:1; Ezekiel 29:2; 30:1 etc. l) A most specific title. For there is a double prophecy against Egypt: (1) against its army, outside the borders of the homeland, fighting under Necho (here); (2) against the land of Egypt itself, to be subjugated by enemies under Pharaoh Hophra (v. 13 and following). m) regarding which see the note on 2 Kings 23:29. n) namely, the army. For Necho himself, after three months of this expedition, returned to Egypt taking Jehoahaz with him (2 Kings 23:34, cf. v. 31). o) he was at etc., having already spent four years there, since he set out there in the third month before Jehoiakim's reign. In that interval of time, he conquered not only **Carchemish**, but also all of Syria (cf. 2 Kings 24:7 and 23:33). p) which Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar.</note> and others conjecture is Cercusium or Circesium, in the corner where the river Aboras meets the Euphrates. Formerly it belonged to the Assyrians (Isaiah 10:9) but was taken from them by Necho’s army (2 Kings 23:29, cf. 2 Chronicles 35:20). This happened at the time when the Assyrian kingdom was declining and was about to expire. But with the Chaldeans threatening that very thing and claiming the monarchy of the East for themselves, a war arose for Necho with **Nebuchadnezzar** (just as earlier with the Assyrians), but with an unhappy outcome. q) just as predicted in this very prophecy (v. 6). For the title is more recent than the prophecy itself, added after its outcome. cf. 49:28. The slaughter was followed by the loss of all Syria (2 Kings 24:7) and in the first year of Nebuchadnezzar (25:11), so that the prophecy was fulfilled in the very year it was issued. $\aleph$. 3. a) "Arrange yourselves" for battle (1 Chronicles 12:8). He addresses the Egyptians (v. 5) emphatically through the imperative. He says: Arm yourselves as much as you can, but it will be in vain; you will be defeated by the Chaldeans anyway (so also v. 8, 10, 11). b) "The small shield" and "the large shield" (Psalm 35:2, cf. 1 Kings 10:16-17). $\aleph$. 4. u) "Join the horses," in which the Egyptians were powerful. see Exodus 14:7; Deuteronomy 17:16; 1 Kings 10:28; Isaiah 31:1, 3; 2 Chronicles 12:3. He says: bind them to the chariots (1 Kings 18:44; Exodus 14:6). But Jonathan and the Arabic version say "saddle"; the Syriac "put on the bridles." x) and go up upon your horses, O horsemen (1 Samuel 8:11). y) and "present yourselves," a military term (v. 14). η) in helmets, being helmeted (1 Samuel 17:5; Ezekiel 27:10). a) "Polish," so that the points gleam; these are the sharpenings (2 Chronicles 4:16; cf. Jeremiah 51:11). b) "Breastplates" (chapter 51:3). $\aleph$. 5. q) "But why etc." These questions are usually those of one marvelling at an unexpected and unforeseen thing; Schmidt cf. v. 25. d) in a prophetic vision (1 Kings 22:19). e) and behold, they themselves are dismayed (1 Samuel 2:4); such is the dismay of the conquered in battle when they see they can no longer resist (cf. Ezekiel 31:15). f) "turned backward," the battle line having yielded, forced to leave their station (chapter 38:22; Psalm 35:4). g) "beaten down" (Deuteronomy 1:44). h) and "they flee a flight" (or as much as they can) (v. 21; chapter 48:45). i) nor do they turn their face, i.e., look back (chapter 47:3) to stop the flight (Nahum 2:9). As Jonathan adds, "to take a stand." k) for "terror is all around," i.e., such great fear seized them that they think the enemy is pressing them from every side, and they do not even dare to look back (chapter 6:25, etc.). $\aleph$. 6. l) "Let not the swift flee," because it will be in vain even if he flees (cf. Amos 2:14-15). Therefore the sense is: Let no one presume he will escape by the speed of his flight. m) "nor let him escape," i.e., let him not try to escape, trusting in his strength, thinking he might push back the enemy to give himself the chance to flee; Schmidt cf. Zechariah 2:7. The Vulgate says "nor let him think he is saved." n) For toward the north, near Carchemish, which is north of Egypt (v. 2). o) "along the bank" (Deuteronomy 2:37). p) "they stumbled," pushed by the enemy, and thus fell—both the swift and the strong (v. 12; Psalm 27:2). $\aleph$. 7. q) "Who is this, who etc." The question of one marvelling at the massive tumult and military preparations of the Egyptians, to explain and once again exaggerate their slaughter (v. 10, cf. v. 5). r) "like the Nile," earlier called by this name (v. 8), whose nature is to rise above its banks every year and flood the land (Schmidt). s) "it rises," overwhelming the land with troops, as if with waters (v. 8; chapter 47:2).

From this comes the name of Jupiter Amon. But Hiller in *Onomasticon Sacrum* explains it as "the nourisher from the city of Memphis," that is, Apis, worshipped by the Memphites. Others: "the multitude." cf. ch. 52:15. **p)** From No. Nahum 3:8, where <unclear>that idol</unclear> was especially worshipped. Bochart in *Phaleg* book I, ch. I understands this as Egyptian Thebes, otherwise called Diospolis, as the translators in Ezekiel 30:16 rendered it. Hiller, however, in the cited place, says Memphis, as the same rendered in verse 15. For it is established that the Egyptians, after the Babylonian empire was overturned, shook off the yoke, only to be brought back into servitude by Cambyses, king of the Persians. cf. Ezekiel 29:11-13. Unless it is rather a promise regarding the times of the New Testament, such as is attached to other prophecies against the nations; ch. 48:47, ch. 49:6, 39. **v. 27. u)** "You therefore," etc. As if to say: "If Egypt is finally restored (v. 26), then you ought to fear much less," etc. But Sch. puts it this way: "But you," as if a contrast is made with the Jews who went to Egypt, in this manner: "Those who went to Egypt and trusted in Pharaoh shall perish with Pharaoh; but you remaining Jews and Israelites, dispersed in captivity, shall be preserved from destruction." For the rest, cf. ch. 30:10, 11 and the notes there. **CHAPTER XLVII, 1. x)** cf. ch. 46:1 and the note on ch. 14:1. **y)** cf. ch. 25:20, Isaiah 14:28ff, where see the note on Ezekiel 25:15, 16, Zephaniah 2:5, Zechariah 9:6. **z)** and so at that time, when the war between the Egyptians and the northern monarchy had not yet flared up, nor could anyone suspect that the Philistines would be cut off by those very northerners in v. 2 (who were soon to be allies against Necho). cf. Sch. **a)** Probably Necho (ch. 46:2) who, while moving against the Assyrians, killed Josiah (2 Kings 23:29); in the same expedition he captured Gaza which was in his path and perhaps likewise resisting him. Others, however, like Lightfoot in *Chron.* p. 121, think this happened during the expedition of Pharaoh by which he lifted the siege of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 37:5). **b)** Gaza, one of the chief cities of the Philistines (v. 5, ch. 25:20), closest to Egypt (Joshua 15:47); see the note on Joshua 10:41. Whence it is likely it was captured by Necho as soon as he went to Carchemish on the Euphrates, in passing, to make his rear more secure. Perhaps also Gaza, like Josiah, had denied passage to Necho, and was punished either on the same journey or on the return, after the Assyrians were struck and Syria occupied; so Sch. However, the present prophecy intends another and different slaughter, namely: (1) not only of Gaza, but a universal one of all the Philistines (v. 4); (2) coming not from southern Egypt, but from northern Chaldea (v. 2). **v. 2. c)** metaphorically for the huge and numerous army of Nebuchadnezzar. Jonathan: "Behold, peoples come." cf. ch. 46:7. **d)** They shall be rising, like the waters of some great river, which are said to rise when they swell above and beyond the banks. cf. note on ch. 46:7. **e)** Isaiah 14:31. Namely from Babylonia (Jeremiah 46:20, 24) compared with v. 13. Perhaps he alludes to the waters of the Euphrates, the greatest northern river, on which Babylon was situated. Sch. **f)** flooding everything. Isaiah 30:28. **g)** Isaiah 8:8.

<meta>This page continues the prophetic judgment of the nations from the previous page. Having concluded the oracle against the Philistines, the text now turns to Moab (Jeremiah 48). The commentary focuses on Moab’s historical stability—likened to wine settled on its dregs—and the impending "decanting" of the nation into captivity by the Babylonian forces.</meta>

### CHAPTER 48. JEREMIAH 48

<margin>
**Chemosh** <note>original: "Camos"</note> is the reading. See **v. 12**. 
**v. 24**. cf. Num. 21, 3. C. 31, 7. Deut. 7, 2. C. 20, 16. 17. Jos. 10, 32.

**v. 11. q) q)** 46, 27, Job 30:18. **o)** on his **dregs**, a term derived from "preserving" or "keeping." **r)** Ps. 75, 9. Zeph. 1, 12. cf. Is. 25, 6. And so, up to this day, he is like a certain **wine** that has always rested upon its dregs; **Schmidt** <note>Sebastian Schmidt, 17th-century theologian</note> follows the interpretation: "upon his wealth." But **Kimchi** <note>David Kimhi, medieval Hebrew grammarian</note> more aptly suggests "in his own land," meaning he has never suffered captivity in foreign lands, as follows; although he occasionally felt the calamities of war. **p)** he was **poured out** <note>original: "transfusus"</note> Song of Sol. 1, 3. Because...
</margin>

<margin>
**p)** also you, O Moabite woman, just like Israel and other nations. **v. 16, 27**. But **Schen.** refers this to Morenaium in **v. 5**. **r)** **v. 13, 46**. 1 Kings 11, 7. **s)** **v. 11**. cf. Is. 46, 2. **t)** chapter 49, 3.

**v. 8. c) e)** No city shall escape. There will be a universal slaughter. cf. Nahum 3, 12. Hab. 1, 10. **d)** the **valley**. Ch. 47, 5. The translation of **Jonathan** <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> says: those who dwell in the valley shall perish, etc. **e)** the **plain**, which was the nature of a good part of the Moabite region; compare **v. 21** onwards and Joshua 13, 16. 17. 21. **f)** **Syriac**: "just as"; so also **Kimchi**. cf. Jer. 33, 22. Others: "because"; cf. Gen. 34, 27. As if to say: This will most certainly happen, because...

**v. 9. g)** Give (O enemies! compare **v. 10**) a **wing** <note>original: "alam"</note> to Moab, that is, make him as if he were not there, as if you had given him wings to flee most swiftly; **Schmidt**. So also the ancient scholars cited by **Kimchi**. He says the word *tzitz* means "to fly." Whatever is hanging or prominent on a man or animal is called this: tassels in Numbers 15:38, locks of hair in Ezekiel 8:3, wings here, and in the Targum of Psalm 139:9; even the fins of fish among the Talmudists. I would think it agrees in some way with the following root *natza*, "to fly." **h)** he shall go out by flying; the first word is from the root *natza*, Lamentations 4:15, the second from *yatza* (to go out). These two roots, related in sound and sense, are elegantly combined; for something similar see chapter 42, 10. At the same time, it alludes to the noun *natza* in **v. 9**. That is: I did not say in vain that wings must be given to Moab, since it will altogether happen that he is suddenly forced to go out from his land, as if he had flown away from there. **i)** ch. 46, 19. ch. 51, 29.

**v. 10. k)** Deut. 17, 15-26. Under the penalty of a curse, He binds the enemies to faithfully and precisely execute the work committed to them by the Lord against the Moabites, and not to spare them. **l)** cf. Daniel 8, 27. 1 Chronicles 26, 30. **Jonathan** adds: "against her," namely Moab. **m)** in **deceitfulness**; that is, deceitfully, lazily, like someone doing a job poorly or who...
</margin>

7 <gloss>p</gloss>And in your pride, you also shall be taken; and <gloss>q</gloss>**Chemosh**<gloss>r</gloss> <note>The national god of Moab</note> shall go into captivity, his priests and his princes together.

8 And the spoiler shall come to every city, <gloss>e</gloss>and no city shall escape; the <gloss>d</gloss>valley shall perish, and the <gloss>e</gloss>plain shall be destroyed, as the LORD has spoken.

9 Give <gloss>g</gloss>wings to Moab, for she <gloss>h</gloss>shall surely fly away; and her cities shall be a desolation, with no one to dwell in them.

<meta>This page continues the divine judgment against the nation of Moab. The previous page detailed the initial collapse of Moabite cities and the flight of refugees toward the Arnon river. This section focuses on the silencing of Moab’s joy, the destruction of its religious high places, and the physical signs of extreme mourning among the survivors.</meta>

# JEREMIAH. CHAPTER 48.

<margin>
**Left Margin:**
In this place <note>original Latin: "impr. h. l."</note> the word **shorn** <note>Hebrew: *gerua*</note> appears. Elsewhere, this word means to diminish or take away, as seen above in chapter 26:2. However, here and in the cited passage, it specifically means to shave or remove by scraping, following Syriac usage. Compare the Syriac Version here and in the New Testament at Acts 21:24 and 1 Corinthians 2:6. **Incisions** <note>Hebrew: *gedudot*</note> refer to the ritual of cutting oneself; for this custom, see the notes on chapter 16:6, 41:5, and 47:5. See also chapter 4:8 and 6:26 regarding the sackcloth.
</margin>

<margin>
**Right Margin:**
**v. 33. p)** The destroyer rushes in, as in Job 1:15. **q)** See Isaiah 16:10. **r)** Taken from the fertile field, as in chapter 2:7; see also notes on Joshua 12:22. **s)** From the wine-vats. **t)** No one shall tread the grapes, or the treader <note>Isaiah 16:10</note> will not shout the traditional vintage-cry <term>Hedad: a rhythmic shout used by grape-treaders</term> as in chapter 25:30. **u)** That is to say, such a "Hedad" shout will henceforth be a "non-entity," compared with Isaiah 16:10.
</margin>

33. And joy and gladness are taken away from the fruitful field and from the land of Moab; and I have caused wine to fail from the winepresses; none shall tread with shouting; their shouting shall be no shouting.

<margin>
**Right Margin:**
**v. 34. x)** From the cry of devastated Heshbon, which continues all the way to Elealeh, over which they also cry out as a place destroyed, and from there onwards to Jahaz, etc. Thus interpreted by Schmid. **y)** Numbers 32:3; Isaiah 15:4. **z)** Isaiah 15:4. **a)** See verses 3 and 5. **b)** Jonah adds "great." See notes on Isaiah 15:5. **c)** See notes on Isaiah 15:6.
</margin>

34. From the cry of Heshbon even unto Elealeh, and even unto Jahaz, have they uttered their voice, from Zoar even unto Horonaim, as a heifer of three years old <note>likely a place name, Eglath-shelishiyah, or a metaphor for a crying calf</note>; for the waters of Nimrim also shall be desolate.

<margin>
**Right Margin:**
**v. 35. d)** And thus I will cause to cease, etc. (see verse 33). This is a threat concerning the abolition of the Moabites' superstitious worship, as in verse 7; but it is simultaneously an explanation of one of the causes which, among others, provoked God to such great anger against the Moabites. **e)** Referring to one who offers a burnt offering on a high place. Compare Isaiah 16:12.
</margin>

35. Moreover I will cause to cease in Moab, saith the Lord, him that offereth in the high place, and him that burneth incense to his gods.

<margin>
**Right Margin:**
**v. 36. f)** Regarding this verse, see what we noted on Isaiah 15:5. **g)** Like flutes <note>or pipes</note>. **(S)** Isaiah 5:12. **h)** It sounds loudly; it expresses the trembling motion of the heart, just as mournful flutes and harps emit a trembling sound. See Schmid on Isaiah 15:5. **i)** Abundance, specifically the wealth which Moab acquired for himself; the pronoun "which" is omitted after the noun, as in Psalm 16:3 and Hosea 1:2. Compare Isaiah 15:7. **k)** They have perished, i.e., it has perished. This is a grammatical shift <term>enallage: a substitution of plural for singular</term> which is frequent after collective nouns. Jonah notes: "Therefore their remaining wealth, which they had acquired, shall be plundered."
</margin>

36. Therefore mine heart shall sound for Moab like pipes, and mine heart shall sound like pipes for the men of Kir-heres: because the riches that he hath gotten are perished.

<margin>
**Right Margin:**
**v. 37. l)** This refers to baldness, that is, a bald spot on every head. Baldness is a sign among the Moabites of the deepest mourning, as in chapter 47:5, Isaiah 15:2, and Ezekiel 7:18. **m)** Shaved. **(2)** Also in Isaiah 15:7, where some manuscripts read *gerua* (diminished) written with the letter Daleth against the Masoretic tradition.
</margin>

37. For every head shall be bald, and every beard clipped: upon all the hands shall be cuttings, and upon the loins sackcloth.

<margin>
**Left Margin:**
**v. 38. p)** These are witnesses, regarding which see notes on chapter 19:13. This refers to those places that were not yet devastated but would soon be; thus the mourning here is not only for other cities but for the imminent destruction of their own. See Schmid and Isaiah 15:3; also chapter 22:1. **q)** According to the marginal reading <note>Hebrew: *Ha-nas*</note>, Moab itself is nothing but lamentation, or is entirely poured out in lamentation. See chapter 6:26. **r)** See also chapter 9:20, 22:38, and Hosea 8:8.
</margin>

38. There shall be lamentation generally upon all the housetops of Moab, and in the streets thereof: for I have broken Moab like a vessel wherein is no pleasure, saith the Lord.

39. They shall howl, saying, "How is it broken down! how hath Moab turned the back with shame!" so shall Moab be a derision and a dismay to all them about him.

40. For thus saith the Lord; Behold, he shall fly as an eagle, and shall spread his wings over Moab.

41. Kerioth is taken, and the strongholds are surprised, and the mighty men's hearts in Moab at that day shall be as the heart of a woman in her pangs.

42. And Moab shall be destroyed from being a people, because he hath magnified himself against the Lord.

43. Fear, and the pit, and the snare, shall be upon thee, O inhabitant of Moab, saith the Lord.

44. He that fleeth from the fear shall fall into the pit; and he that getteth up out of the pit shall be taken in the snare: for I will bring upon it, even upon Moab, the year of their visitation, saith the Lord.

45. They that fled stood under the shadow of Heshbon because of the force: but a fire shall come forth out of Heshbon, and a flame from the midst of Sihon, and shall devour the corner of Moab.

***

**v. 39. r)** See the note on verse 17. **t)** See notes on verses 1 and 20. **u)** And they wailed; others translate "wail therefore." Compare verse 20. **x)** He turned his neck to flee, as in chapters 49:8, 24, and 46:5. **y)** And was put to shame, as in verse 13. **z)** See verses 26 and 27. **a)** And into consternation, as in chapter 17:17. That is, according to whether neighboring nations were friends or enemies: his fall will be a joy to some and a source of dread to others. See Schmid. 

**v. 40. b)** That is, very swiftly. See notes on chapter 4:13, 2 Samuel 1:23, Lamentations 4:19, Habakkuk 1:8; compare Ezekiel 17:3. **c)** He shall fly <note>original: "aduolabît"</note> as in chapter 49:22, referring to Nebuchadnezzar. **d)** With wings spread he will hasten to Moab (Job 39:26), or he will spread his wings (meaning his armies) over Moab (Jeremiah 49:22). 

**v. 41. e)** Properly a city name, see verse 24 and Amos 2:2; therefore it is joined with a singular verb. **f)** And each fortress. But according to the Syriac and Kimchi, it is a proper name of a city. **g)** Chapter 50:46. **h)** Of one giving birth, as in chapter 49:22. Compare 2 Chronicles 33:12. The word *tzirim* (pangs) fits the pains of childbirth, as in Isaiah 21:3. 

**v. 42. i)** So that it ceases to be a nation, specifically organized as a public republic. See verse 2. **k)** See note on verse 26. 

**v. 43. l)** Amos 5:19, Lamentations 3:47, and Isaiah 24:17-18, where see the notes. 

**v. 44. m)** Chapter 23:12; 50:27. 

**v. 45. n)** That is, in Heshbon, which they thought would be a shadow for them from the heat of danger and the enemy; see Schmid, verse 2:34, and Psalm 91:1. **o)** They stood still, intending to take rest from the exhaustion of flight, but in vain: because fire, etc. But Schmid says "fleeing," see chapter 46:5. **p)** Gusset adds (p. 931) that they are fleeing so that they cease to have strength; just as in verse 42, "from being a people" means they cease to be a nation. Schmid says they will be fleeing with all their strength (as much as they can). **q)** The meaning: Because the enemies will also capture Heshbon, and from there they shall go forth, etc. And so it will happen again as was told in the ancient history of Numbers 21:27-30, from which these words and the following in verse 46 are drawn. This is a **prophetic parody** <note>a literary device where a prophet reuses an ancient text to show history repeating</note> just as this entire prophecy against the Moabites mirrors Isaiah 15 and 16. **r)** From within Sihon, meaning from Heshbon, which was most destructive to the Moabites from whom he had taken it (Numbers 21:26). Nebuchadnezzar with his army is depicted here to the Moabites as a revived Sihon, breathing fire and flames. The Syriac reads "from the city of Sihon." **s)** The corner, or the extremity of the head (Leviticus 19:27). The Syriac translates as "mustache"; compare the same and Leviticus 21:5.

***

**v. 34.** *Shelshiyah* is written deficiently here and in verse 6 and 9. Thus the Masoretes note in the margin. **v. 35.** *Ma'aleh* is written with the vowel Tsere. **v. 36.** *Kehalilim* (like flutes) is written in full. **v. 37.** *Kol-rosh* (every head) is preceded by a small particle in some texts. *Gerua* (shorn) is corrected in the margins of certain manuscripts. **v. 38.** *Kullo* (all of it) is written with the letter Kaph. **v. 39.** *Rishonah* is written as in verse 26. **v. 41.** *Nitpashah* is read by the Oriental tradition, but others write it differently. **v. 44.** *Ha-nas* (the one fleeing) is written and read thus by the Orientals.

<summary>This page describes the total social and religious collapse of Moab, using vivid imagery of silenced vineyards, ritual self-mutilation for mourning, and the metaphorical "fire of Sihon" to show that Moab’s destruction by Nebuchadnezzar is a repeat of their ancient historical defeats.</summary>

->### CHAPTER XLIX.<-

<margin>
**CHAPTER XLIX, 1. a)** A prophecy against the children of Ammon, the descendants of Lot (Genesis 19:38). They were the most bitter enemies of the Israelites throughout every age (Psalm 83:8-9), though Israel had not harmed them (Deuteronomy 2:19). See also 1 Samuel 11:1 and Jeremiah 40:14. They followed the destruction of the Temple and the Commonwealth—both of Israel and Judah—with wicked joy (Ezekiel 25:3, 6) and taunts (Ezekiel 21:33, Zephaniah 2:8, 10). They occupied the region of Gilead or the Gadites, which they had claimed long ago in the time of Jephthah (Judges 11:13). Now that the trans-Jordanian tribes were deported by the Assyrians, they occupied it unlawfully and with terrible cruelty toward the Israelites (Amos 1:13). Because of these things, a just punishment of devastation is decreed for them, to be inflicted at various times: by the Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 25:21, 27:3, 6), by the Arabs (Ezekiel 25:4), and by the remnants of the Jews under the Maccabees (Zephaniah 2:9; compare Josephus' *Antiquities of the Jews* book 12). Parallel prophecies are found in Ezekiel 21:33, 25:1, Amos 1:13, and Zephaniah 2:8-10. **b)** A serious rhetorical question: Does Israel truly have no sons? Does he truly have no heir?
</margin>
<margin>
**1.** [continued] ...right of inheritance or succeeding to the abandoned property would have belonged to them as the nearest kin.
</margin>

But more probably others say: *Malkam* is the petty god of the Ammonites (verse 3, Amos 1:15). Elsewhere he is called *Milcom* (1 Kings 11:5) and *Molech* (verse 7). Here he is said to have "inherited" (says Schmid) because his worship was introduced into the land. **f)** That is, the Ammonites, just as the Moabites are the "people of Chemosh" (48:46) and the Israelites are the "people of Jehovah" everywhere. **g)** We noted at 48:1 and verse 2 that this was also practiced by the Moabites. **h)** The metropolis and royal city of the Ammonites (2 Samuel 11:1, 12:26-27). **i)** See verse 4, 19 and Amos 1:14. **k)** Into a mound of devastation; that is, it will be so destroyed that nothing but rubble will remain from the ruins (compare Deuteronomy 13:17, Joshua 8:28). **l)** They shall be set on fire (51:58). **m)** He shall inherit by right when—perhaps under the Maccabees (see note on verse 20) or, according to Kimchi, Abarbanel, and Schmid, in the time of the Messiah. **v. 3. n)** A Moabite city (48:2, 45), but due to its proximity to the Ammonite Ai, it is in immediate danger; unless you prefer to think Heshbon was divided into two parts by the Arnon river, acting as two cities, one part perhaps belonging to the Ammonites and the other to the Moabites. **o)** See verse 1. **p)** See 4:8, 6:26, 48:37. **q)** Run about; this is a <term>Hithpael</term> <note>a reflexive Hebrew verb form</note> (chapter 5:1, Job 1:7). **r)** Among the walls of the villages and sheepfolds, bewailing your misery (Nahum 3:17). **s)** See verse 1. **r)** Amos 1:15; compare Jeremiah 48:7. **v. 4. s)** That is, you boast in vain. This is an anticipation of an objection, as if no one would dare to attack the Ammonites, who live in a plain enclosed by mountains and filled with all treasures (compare 9:22). **x)** Compare 21:13. **y)** For your valley shall flow, namely with the blood of the slain (compare Ezekiel 21:37, 35:8). Things are said to "flow" when something flows in them (as in Exodus 3:8). **z)** A turning daughter, rebellious (31:32); always straying and following (Isaiah 57:17). She might also be called "turning away" in relation to her father, the pious Lot. **a)** Chapter 48:7. **b)** By saying: "Who shall...?" (compare 21:13). **v. 5. c)** I am about to make it so that it comes (which you boast in vain cannot happen, verse 4). **d)** That is, the enemies will strike fear into you. This is contrasted with the security and overconfidence of the Ammonites in verse 4. **e)** That is, from every side, so that no part of your borders remains immune. **f)** And you shall be scattered like a dispersed flock (50:17). **g)** Before him, that is, wherever the path lies open, a way chosen not by deliberation but by chance; this indicates headlong flight and the greatest consternation (compare Amos 4:3). **h)** Isaiah 13:14. **i)** To the wanderer, the one fleeing from his land (Isaiah 16:3, Jeremiah 21:14-15); that is, the wanderer will have no one to gather him back from his dispersion. **v. 6. k)** Verse 39, 43:47. **v. 7. l)** Chapter 25:21; compare Isaiah 21:11, Jeremiah 34:5, Ezekiel 25:12-13, 35:2, Amos 1:11, the whole of Obadiah, and Malachi 1:3-5. **m)** An Edomite city or province (verse 20), undoubtedly named after Teman, the grandson of Esau (compare Genesis 36:11, 15, 34); it is used here by way of <term>synecdoche</term> <note>a part representing the whole</note> for all of Idumea <note>Edom</note>, because its inhabitants otherwise claimed the highest praise for wisdom (compare Baruch 3:22). **n)** Isaiah 29:14. **o)** From the intelligent ones. From the root *bin* (Psalm 139:2). Others say: from his sons. **p)** Has it rotted and become useless? A <term>Niphal</term> form (Amos 6:4). **v. 8. q)** Therefore flee. No counsel or help remains for you (verse 30, 48:6). The imperative here does not command, but predicts what will happen (Schmid). **r)** Turn yourselves to flight (48:39). An imperative in the <term>Hophal</term> <note>a passive causative verb form</note>, which is very rare; but Schmid interprets it by <term>enallage of person</term> <note>a grammatical substitution of one person for another</note> as "they turned themselves" in the past tense. **s)** Go deep to dwell, that is, seek out deep places, caves, and pits in which you can be safe from the enemy and hide (Schmid, verse 30; compare Isaiah 29:15).

v. 9. **y)** "If." This condition suggests that Idumæa, in a third point of comparison, will be like either (1) a vineyard at the time of vintage, or (2) a house filled with wealth but plundered by thieves. Thus compare with Canticles 8:9. However, the subsequent question indicates a certain difference for Idumæa in both comparisons. Truly, grape-gatherers harvest a vineyard, but in such a way that they leave some gleanings; thieves plunder a house so that at least they do not take everything, but only as much as is sufficient for one time. But for Idumæa, when it is harvested or plundered by enemies, nothing at all will be left; see verse 10. **z)** Asked as a question: "would they not have left...?" (Compare Obadiah verse 5). According to Schmid: Whether your destroyers come like grape-gatherers, they will leave no gleanings; or whether like thieves (and they shall come in both ways), they will destroy their own insatiable abundance, leaving nothing to you. **א)** Judges 8:2, Isaiah 17:6, Micah 7:1. Compare above (chapter 6, verse 6), "would they not destroy?" (Compare Obadiah verse 5), namely by stealing. Or it is a mixture of literal and figurative speech, such that they destroy...
