"I myself will strip," etc. **e)** I will strip Esau, that is, the Edomites (verse 8; compare Obadiah verse 6). **f)** "I have uncovered" or "I will uncover" (Isaiah 16:3; chapter 22:8). **g)** (chapter 23:24) those places in which he tries to hide (Isaiah 45:3). **h)** And he will not be able to be hidden. Alternatively, according to Jona: that even if they wished to hide themselves, they are unable. Thus it would be the Perfect tense, and understood as an attempt. **i)** From where it shall be devastated (chapter 48:15, 20). **k)** By the same trope by which he called the Edomite people by the name of Esau, he continues to call the individuals of that same people the "seed, brothers, and neighbors" of Esau, meaning indiscriminately all who in any way belong to the Edomites and dwell in their region. **l)** "and his neighbors" (verse 18). **m)** so that he himself is no longer anything at all (Psalm 59:14). **v. 11. n)** "Leave your fatherless children," that is, that people who have no father on earth, and therefore are "fatherless" before you, partly because of your tyranny (compare Psalm 137:7; Obadiah verse 10 and following). Therefore, keep your hand off them; do not afflict them as you have done until now. Thus, the cause of the Edomites' destruction is indicated at the same time. **o)** "whom I will preserve alive," contrary to what you think and desire (Psalm 22:30). **p)** "and your widows," whom you have bereaved of their husbands, or at least consider as deserted; understand this as the people of God and compare chapter 51:5. **q)** "who shall trust in me," receiving security and protection from me in their own time. It is the 3rd person feminine form (Ezekiel 37:7). **v. 12. r)** for whom there was no right, or who, compared with you, ought to have drunk the cup of my wrath less, since they were my people (chapter 25:29). **s)** (chapter 25:15). **t)** Are you then that most wicked scoundrel who, above all, has deserved punishment? According to Schmid, compare 2 Chronicles 28:21. **u)** "shall you go entirely unpunished?" Rather, surely not, etc. (chapter 25:29). **x)** You shall certainly drink, whether you wish to or not (chapter 25:28, 15, 16; compare Obadiah verse 16). **v. 13. y)** See the note on chapter 22:5, and compare Genesis 22:16; Isaiah 45:23. **z)** (chapter 19:8; 24:9; 50:3; 44:12). **a)** (verse 22, Isaiah 63:1; compare note on Jeremiah 48:24). **b)** its smaller cities, which are counted as daughters to the metropolis of Bozrah. **c)** (chapter 25:9). **v. 14. d)** Compare Obadiah verse 1. **e)** "and an ambassador," as in Obadiah and Isaiah 18:2. **f)** He has already been sent, namely, to say, etc. **g)** namely to Bozrah (verse 13) or to all Idumæa (verse 17). **v. 15. h)** Obadiah verse 2; compare Amos 7:2, 5. Abraham Ibn Ezra according to Kimchi: The people of the Edomites were not so great, and their land was not very spacious. As if to say: therefore you did not have a cause to exalt yourself so much. Perhaps this also looks back to past disasters of the Edomites (compare note on Isaiah 21:11). **i)** Compare 1 Kings 14:26. **k)** most contemptible among men (Obadiah verses 1, 2). But Kimchi, Schmid, and others take it for the Future: "I will make you small" or "least," namely when I have called together the nations against you (verse 14). **v. 16. l)** "Your terribleness," which you imagined for yourself (compare 1 Kings 15:13; Isaiah 21:4); this is, according to the Vulgate, your arrogance, as declared by apposition in this very clause. **m)** (chapter 27:9; Genesis 3:13). **n)** the pride, I say, of your heart (1 Samuel 17:28). **o)** "dwelling"; the *Yod* is paragogic here <note>A paragogic Yud is an extra letter added to the end of a word for emphasis or style in biblical Hebrew</note> and in the following word "holding." At the same time, the cause of Edom's pride is hinted at by these epithets; as though it arose from the very fact that they dwelt so high up. According to Schmid. **p)** in the clefts (compare Obadiah verse 3; Canticles 2:14), that is, in high and precipitous rocks. For the region of the Edomites was mountainous, from which it was also called Mount Seir. **q)** "holding." Compare note on chapter 40:10. **r)** Compare 2 Kings 19:23; Habakkuk 2:9. **s)** although you should exalt yourself like an eagle (Obadiah verse 4; Psalm 139:8), which places its nest in the highest and most inaccessible summits of the mountains (Amos 9:2, 3). **t)** your nest (Numbers 24:21). **א)** (Obadiah verse 4; Amos 3:11). **v. 17. x)** (verse 13; chapter 18:16; 19:8). **y)** Compare note on chapter 19:8 and 50:13.

**Textual variants and Masorah notes:**
v. 8. *nusu* with Makkaph in manuscripts 2, 5, 10, 14, 20, 21, 22. v. 9. *yash'iru* written defectively in 22, and similarly in the Masorah of Erfurt. v. 10. *ve-nechbah* with a *Mem* in 1 and 5. v. 12. *nako* with a *Vav* and *nako* according to the Erfurt Masorah. v. 13. *areyah* with a *Zakeph-katon* accent in manuscript 2. v. 14. *shemuah* written defectively according to the Erfurt Masorah. v. 16. *hishi* includes the word *otach* in manuscript 1 and in the margin of manuscript 6, contrary to the printed Masorah.

like dogs, Jeremiah 15:3. **q)** "the least of the flock," referring to the weak and few sheep, chapter 50:45; compare Zechariah 13:7. This refers to my people [the Jews], compare Ezekiel 25:14. For Hyrcanus <note>John Hyrcanus, the Hasmonean ruler (reigned 134–104 BCE)</note>, the son of Simon Maccabaeus, occupied Idumæa; see Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 13, chapter 17. Others understand the "least" as the common soldiers of the enemy; compare Jeremiah 14:3. It is presented as a paradox (like Revelation 6:16-17), a wonderful reversal of fortune: it would happen that the Jews, who were once miserably harassed, would do to the Edomites exactly what they had suffered from them; see verse 2. For it seemed a paradox to the Edomites that they should be overthrown by those whom they had hitherto despised and afflicted as wretched sheep. **r)** the Lord will devastate (Numbers 21:30) their dwelling place over them, chapter 23:3; that is, He will cause their cities and houses, suddenly destroyed by the enemy, to fall as if upon the heads of the Edomites. Prophetic imperatives used for future events. **r)** see note at verse 8. **s)** compare note at verse 28. **t)** see verse 28. **u)** namely, destruction (v. 20). **x)** chapter 11:19, 48:2. **y)** namely, an evil one. The imperatives signify that God, by His admirable providence, will so govern all things that the enemies, led by political reasons as if by divine command, shall go up. **a)** tranquil, without fear. Psalm 23:42 <note>likely 23:2</note>; Job 16:12; chapter 21:23. **b)** compare Judges 18:7; Ezekiel 38:11. **c)** it has no fortified cities; but country towns without walls. Ezekiel 38:11; Deuteronomy 3:5. **d)** solitary. Deuteronomy 32:12. Or they dwell solitary and separately, each in his own home, in profound peace and security; according to Cocceius, not gathered together, but each in their own houses. Deuteronomy 33:28; 1 Kings 5:5. Or separately from other nations, having no treaties or commerce with others. Numbers 23:9; Judges 18:7. **v. 32. e)** compare note at verse 29. **f)** I will winnow by throwing toward every wind or quarter of the world, not otherwise than grain is usually scattered against the wind on the threshing floor. Verse 36; Ezekiel 5:12, 2. **g)** Vulgate: "who are shorn into a mane." Thus almost the Septuagint and Jonathan. See note on chapter 9:25, 25:23. But Schmidt: "so that they may be cut off/exterminated into every corner." Compare Deuteronomy 32:26. **h)** on its parts or sides, namely of the people of the Arabs and Hazor. 1 Kings 5:4. **i)** their calamity. Verse 8; chapter 18:17; Job 21:17. **v. 33. k)** verses 30, 28. **l)** chapter 10:22, 51:37. **m)** or into a devastation. Chapter 9:10. **n)** verse 18. **v. 34. o)** compare note on chapter 14:1. **p)** verse 31; chapter 25:25; Isaiah 22:6; Ezekiel 32:24. The Elymaeans, neighbors to the Medes; which name was sometimes taken more broadly to include several neighboring provinces... Susiana itself (Daniel 8:2). At this time, Schmidt thinks the Elymaeans belonged neither to the Medes nor the Persians, but were a peculiar people, first subdued by Nebuchadnezzar before he approached the Persians with the kingdom of Babel. Indeed, they always had their own kings, says Bochart, whom Strabo also mentions besides Jeremiah. Furthermore, because this nation had joined itself to Babylon against Judah (Isaiah 22:6), it is similarly joined here in the threats against Babylon. Lightfoot, Chronology p. 124. **q)** The "beginning of the reign of Zedekiah" can be understood, as in chapter 28:1, for his fourth year. Ibid. **v. 35. r)** Apposition: "The beginning of their strength," that is, that chief kind of weapon in which they excel. Compare Amos 6:6 and Strabo, book 16. <note>The Elamites were famous as archers.</note>

Certainly, the greatness of the following promises demands this exposition—for example, concerning the eternal covenant never to be forgotten, etc.—which do not fit the times of the Old Testament after the Babylonian captivity. Likewise the distinction of Israel (the 10 tribes) and Judah, as in v. 20 and chapter 30:3, 4 (where see note), which insists that something more be understood by "Israel" than that small portion of Israelites formerly joined to the Jews and returning with them from Babylon, namely the fullness of the 10 tribes (Romans 11:25). Psalm 23:6. r) From one kind of idolatry to another.

<meta>This page continues the prophetic oracle against Babylon in Jeremiah 50. Having previously described the "assembly of great nations" coming from the north and the instruction for the Israelites to flee like he-goats, the text now focuses on the theological justification for Babylon's fall—specifically as a recompense for their destruction of the Temple and their cruelty toward Israel—and the promise of a future restoration for God's people.</meta>

<header>JEREMIAH. Chapter 50.</header>

### 18 Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Behold, I am punishing the king of Babylon and his land, just as I punished the king of Assyria."
### 19 "And I will bring Israel back to his pasture, and he shall graze on Carmel and Bashan, and his soul shall be satisfied in the hill country of Ephraim and in Gilead."
### 20 "In those days and at that time," says the LORD, "the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none, and the sins of Judah, and they shall not be found; for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant."
### 21 "Go up against the land of Merathaim <note>original: *Merathaim*, a name meaning 'Double Rebellion'</note>, go up against it and against the inhabitants of Pekod <note>original: *Pekod*, a name meaning 'Punishment' or 'Visitation'</note>. Slay them and utterly destroy what remains after them," says the LORD, "and do according to all that I have commanded you."
### 22 "A sound of battle is in the land, and great destruction."
### 23 "How the hammer of the whole earth is cut down and broken! How Babylon has become a desolation among the nations!"
### 24 "I laid a snare for you and you were also caught, O Babylon, and you did not know it; you were found and also seized, because you strove against the LORD."
### 25 "The LORD has opened His armory and brought out the weapons of His indignation; for this is the work of the Lord GOD of hosts in the land of the Chaldeans."
### 26 "Come against her from the farthest border; open her storehouses; pile her up like heaps of grain and destroy her utterly; let nothing of her be left."
### 27 "Slay all her bulls; let them go down to the slaughter. Woe to them! For their day has come, the time of their punishment."
### 28 "The voice of those who flee and escape from the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of the LORD our God, the vengeance for His temple."

*A destroying wind*, that is, a harsh, dry, impetuous wind, drying up everything, carrying away and scattering; by which may be understood the evil of war. Compare verse 2 and chapter 4, 11; and the note on Isaiah 27, 8. **verse 2. n)** *Strangers*, see verse 51 and Isaiah 1, 7. But the Vulgate and others say: *winnowers*, as if the word were from the following *v’zeruha*; but this is unnecessary. For <term>paronomasia</term> <note>a play on words</note> among the Prophets does not always declare the etymology. See, for example, Isaiah 5, 7; chapter 13, 6; chapter 32, 7; Zephaniah 2, 4. **o)** *And they shall winnow her*, chapter 49, 36, by snatching away and destroying her inhabitants, both through slaughter and through captivity. **p)** *And they shall empty* the land of inhabitants, chapter 19, 7; Isaiah 24, 1, 3. **q)** *Because they shall be*, namely these winnowers or strangers, against him. 2 Samuel 11, 23. **r)** Chapter 17, 18. **verse 3. s)** The <term>Kri</term> <note>the traditional reading</note>: *Against him who bends, let there be a bender &c.* There is an omission of the relative "who," as in 1 Chronicles 15, 12. The <term>Ktibh</term> <note>the written text</note>: *Against him who bends, let him bend* in turn, whether the archer or the bowman, his bow. Psalm 7, 13. The sense is the same on both sides: for it suggests the law of retaliation in the punishment of Babylon. It is as if to say: the Babylonians have until now stretched their weapons and their bows against the nations, but now the time is at hand for this very thing to be turned back against the Babylonians by the Medes and Persians. Compare chapter 50, 15. But Jonathan and the Vulgate say: *Let him not bend who bends his bow; nor let him go up in his armor*, as if the word *al* with a <term>Segol</term> vowel meant the same as with a <term>Patach</term> vowel <note>changing "against" to "not"</note>, and the sense would be: it will be in vain for the Babylonians to try to resist the enemies. **t)** (thus the archer of the enemy) against him who lifts himself up or is proud. **u)** in his armor, chapter 45, 4. **x)** Chapter 13, 14. **verse 4. y)** that is, many. Judges 9, 40. **z)** *those thrust through*, chapter 27, 10; Lamentations 4, 9. **a)** namely, of Babylon. See chapter 50, 30; Isaiah 13, 15. **verse 5. b)** *is not bereaved* or widowed. Jonathan translates well: "deserted," that is, like a widow bereaved and destitute of a husband. See Isaiah 54, 4, 5, 6; John 14, 18. It is as if to say: Israel is not so widowed that she does not have her husband and avenger, her God, who will avenge the injuries of the Chaldeans. **c)** namely, of the Chaldeans, verse 4, the immediate cause of divine vengeance. **d)** which they contracted from the Holy One of Israel, chapter 50, 29; Isaiah 1, 4, as the object against which they sinned.

<note>
The runners and messengers sent later will meet in confusion and announce to the King that his city is captured. Xenophon, in *Cyropaedia* book 7, page 152, describes it: "When a shout and noise arose, those inside the palace heard the tumult, and the king ordered them to see what it was. When the gates were opened, some ran out. When the Persians saw the gates open, they burst in; and following those who were fleeing back inside, they reached the king, striking them down..." (compare Isaiah 21:5). **x)** "from every side," that is, everywhere. **y)** "The crossings" refers to the fords of the Euphrates, along with the fortifications placed there to keep the enemy from crossing the river (1 Samuel 14:4). **z)** Even the reed-beds or marshes (Isaiah 42:15). According to Rabbi Jonah in Kimchi's commentary, these refer to fortresses and towers; or according to others, wooden fortifications that blocked passage through the marshes to the city. These were set on fire. Kimchi, however, understands "reeds" and very large stalks in the stagnant waters of the Euphrates (compare Isaiah 58:5).

To understand this better, we add the words of the learned Vitringa: "The 'crossings' are the fords of the Euphrates diverted by Cyrus. By 'marshes' he primarily means that great swampy reservoir dug far above Babylon to the north-west. Queen Nitocris had diverted the waters of the Euphrates into it through trenches so she could more easily build her magnificent works in the city. When she finished, she returned the river to its bed. The reservoir, with its water mostly exhausted, became a great marsh filled with reeds and rushes. Cyrus, finding that he made little progress besieging such a fortified city, recalled this plan of Queen Nitocris. He looked at that great burning void and, seeing it was choked with reeds and rushes with old trenches leading there, he set the reeds on fire and cleared the trenches. He then redirected the Euphrates' current into that swampy pit, which led to the destruction of Babylon."

**v. 33. a)** Isaiah 21:10. **b)** The Jonathan and Syriac translations render this well: "The area is like a threshing floor when the time for treading grain arrives," that is, when the grain is soon to be crushed by the hooves of oxen. The infinitive here functions as a noun, meaning "treading" or "threshing." **d)** Isaiah 2:1; Joel 4:13; Revelation 14:15. The grain (the Chaldeans, made ripe for God's judgment by their sins) is to be threshed by the enemies in Babylon as if on a threshing floor.

**v. 34. e)** "He devoured me" (the personification of Zion) or "us" (the people of Zion). The translations rightly preface this with: "Jerusalem said" (compare v. 35). **h)** 2 Kings 4:3; that is, he plundered me so that nothing was left to me.
</note>

**Scribal and Manuscript Notes:**
**verse 46.** The word "ruler" (m-sh-l) appears with the prefix "and" in several manuscripts (1, 2, 5, 6). The Masora <note>traditional notes on the Hebrew text</note> attributes this reading to the "Eastern" tradition, though other Masoretic notes suggest the Easterners simply spell the word with a full vowel. **verse 47.** "Behold" (hinneh) is marked with specific punctuation (Maqqeph and Metheg) in manuscripts 1 and Berlin. **verse 51.** The word "shame" (kelimah) appears in manuscripts 1, 2, 7, 8, 15, 22, and 23. Others read "with shame." **verse 57.** The phrase "says [the King]" appears without the Kadma accent in manuscript 18 and Berlin, but with a manual correction in manuscript 1.

<header>JEREMIAH. CHAPTER 51. 52.</header>

<margin>
**verse 58. q)** See verse 44. Regarding "each of the walls," see verse 57. Others translate as "the wall" in the singular, though expressed in plural for its vastness; just as "salvations" is used in Psalm 42:6 & 43:5. It was indeed of the widest extent, built of baked brick <note>original Latin: *latere coctili*</note>, smeared with bitumen, and 50 cubits high. It was so wide that four-horse chariots <note>original Latin: *quadrigae*</note> passing one another could travel safely. On it were 250 towers, each ten feet higher than the wall itself; there were one hundred bronze gates, and a deep, wide trench surrounding the exterior. (Bochart, *Sacred Geography*, book 4, chapter 13, page 261). **l)** Cocceius's Lexicon, page 645: "It shall be made bare," <note>original Latin: *denudabitur*</note> that is, emptied, or rather taken away, so that only the bare ground is left; compare Psalm 137:7. **m)** See 49:2 and 9:17. **n)** *And thus the peoples shall labor* for vanity, etc. Habakkuk 2:13. That is, the outcome will show that they spent their labor in vain and exhausted themselves—those who constructed the magnificent palaces of Babylon, the widest walls, and the highest gates with great effort—since they were ultimately to be demolished and burned with fire by the Medes and Persians; compare Isaiah 65:23. Scripture sometimes says a thing is being done when it is manifested to be so. Compare Jeremiah 19:11. But the commentator Schmid takes this sense: *And the peoples shall labor in destroying the walls and gates of Babylon to bring them to nothing, and they shall willingly endure exhaustion out of a desire for devastation, if only they may see everything wasted.* **o)** As if to say: "for a sufficiency of emptiness," as in Nahum 2:13 and Job 39:25. **p)** By which all those magnificent works shall finally be consumed.
</margin>

Thus says the Lord of hosts: The broad walls of Babylon shall be utterly leveled <note>original Hebrew: *ar'er tit'ar'ar* (עַרְעֵר תִּתְעַרְעָר); a double verb emphasizing total destruction</note>, and her high gates shall be burned with fire; and the peoples shall labor for nothing, and the nations for the fire, and they shall be weary.

<margin>
**verse 59. q)** This is not so much a specific prophecy against Babylon as it is the conclusion and binding of all the prior ones through the act of Seraiah, commanded by Jeremiah. **r)** Namely, *in the name of the Lord*. **s)** On the mission of Zedekiah; that is, sent there by Zedekiah.
</margin>

<meta>This page serves as the formal introduction to the Book of Ezekiel, following the conclusion of the Book of Jeremiah on the previous page. The translator/author establishes the historical and theological framework for Ezekiel's ministry in exile.</meta>

# PREFACE TO THE PROPHECY OF EZEKIEL.

## §. I.

<margin>
Transition to the visions of Ezekiel:
</margin>

May God, the Best and Greatest, grant a good and happy outcome as we proceed to briefly explain, according to our established plan, the visions of Ezekiel. These visions—which Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and influential theologian</note> called "the most wonderful and sublime of the prophets" <note>original Greek: τῶν προφητῶν θαυμασιωτάτης καὶ ὑψηλοτάτης (tōn prophētōn thaumasiōtatēs kai hypsēlotatēs)</note>—have been universally recognized as the most noble and difficult, containing many and varied discourses. It will not be ill-advised or useless if we first provide several general reminders. By these, we hope to stir the minds of beginners and render them more prepared to consider these wonders of God. However, we will not spend much time repeating what has already been noted elsewhere or regarding the Book of Ezekiel itself; rather, we shall present those matters as a brief summary, while explaining one or two points more fully that could not be easily added to the main text due to the constraints of the page.

## §. II.

<margin>
his Name,
</margin>

§. II. Our prophet received the name IECHEZKIEL, commonly known as EZEKIEL. This name, taken from the invincible power of God and our Savior, means the same as saying, *God will prevail!* <note>The Hebrew יְחֶזְקֵאל (Yeḥezqēl) literally translates to "God strengthens" or "God will strengthen."</note> Indeed, pious parents did not only explain their faith through the names they gave their children; our Prophet himself—like Joshua, Isaiah, Hosea, and others—also proclaimed by his name that CHRIST is the almighty God and most powerful hero. a) He who, having finally overcome all enemies, shall reign forever. By the mere remembrance and meaning of his name, Ezekiel could encourage and confirm himself against any temptations and difficulties in the execution of his prophetic duty. b)

## §. III.

<margin>
Family, and Lineage;
</margin>

§. III. He was the son of BUZI, a priest of the line of Aaron. <note>The "Aharonidae" were the descendants of Aaron, who held the hereditary office of the priesthood in Israel.</note> Regarding what kind of man Buzi was in his life—whether pious or impious—nothing has been preserved in the Sacred Scriptures. However, out of charity and based on his son's name, we presume the better of him. As for the claim that Buzi himself was a prophet (unless you mean the ordinary duty of teaching held by priests in the Old Testament), the Holy Scripture nowhere indicates this. Nor is the uncertain Hebrew rule sufficient to prove it: *that the fathers of Prophets were also Prophets whenever the names of the parents are found recorded in the scriptures.* As Christian interpreters have rightly pointed out for some time, this rule is not absolute. Thus, our prophet was a priest by birth and, according to the administration of the Old Testament, an ordinary minister of God among His people—even though in Babylonia neither the Temple could be maintained nor bloody sacrifices offered. And although at that time (as also later in Malachi 2:8) most priests had turned away from the way of the Lord (Ezekiel 22:26), God nevertheless preserved for Aaron some faithful and holy seed from whom He did not withdraw His grace, and through whom He instructed the people, as is also certain from the example of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:1, etc.).

## §. IV.

<margin>
Homeland, Age, and the place of the visions.
</margin>

§. IV. Ezekiel’s homeland was Judah, or the Kingdom of Judah. He was born and lived there until he was led away into exile by the Chaldeans in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar, along with Jehoiachin and others (Chapter 1:2; 2 Kings 24:12, 14). He was not a child then, as some commonly interpret Josephus in *Antiquities of the Jews* (Book 10, Chapter 8), but rather a "youth" <note>original Greek: παῖς ὢן (pais ōn)</note> of early age. For the Lord not only called him to his very heavy duty in the fifth year after his exile (Chapter 1:2), but four years later, in the ninth year of his deportation, He also made him a widower (Chapter 24:1, 18). The location of his visions was not Jerusalem or his native land (though he was sometimes snatched away to it in the Holy Spirit by divine ecstasy), but in Chaldea or lower Mesopotamia, by the river Chebar, near which a significant number of Jewish exiles lived (See Chapter 1:1 and the notes there). For God, the Lord of the whole world, has bound His spiritual gifts and His kingdom to no specific land or place (which is the Jewish opinion); so that in whatever place we commemorate His name, we may be persuaded that He is present there with Christ and His Spirit. Indeed, as Cocceius c) rightly noted, God did not desert the people, but went as if into exile with them. By a great favor, He gave them Prophets d) even in the midst of the nations, in an impure land, and visions indicating the greatest of things. This did not happen to the Jews dispersed after the final destruction of the Temple. For at that time, prophecy departed from them, and the disciples of Christ preached and prophesied the Gospel to all nations—whom the Jews despised, thus casting the Spirit of God out of their synagogue. Compare the notes on Ezekiel 31:12, Jeremiah 24:5 onwards, as well as the notes on Jeremiah 29:15 and the Preface to Jeremiah, §. 5.

## §. V.

<margin>
The synchronism of true and false prophets.
</margin>

§. V. In the year that Ezekiel began to prophesy in Chaldea, Jeremiah had already completed thirty-four years of his prophetic ministry in Jerusalem. Jeremiah continued in that same office with great labor for at least eight more years alongside our prophet. Since Ezekiel began in the fifth year after his exile and was still prophesying in the twenty-seventh year (as is clear from Chapter 29:17), he sustained his prophetic office for at least twenty-two years. His final vision or prophecy (in terms of chronological recording) is not the one described from Chapter 40 to the end of the book, as we have noted in that place. Among the true prophets, he had Daniel as a contemporary in Babylonia, and in Judah—besides Zephaniah (who sometimes says the same things as our prophet; compare Ezekiel 7:19 and Zephaniah 1:18)—most notably Jeremiah, as we mentioned in the Preface to Jeremiah, §. 5. These true prophets remarkably confirmed the divine truth that Jeremiah was announcing to the stubborn people in Judah through the testimonies of Zephaniah, Ezekiel, and other servants of God. Nevertheless, in that same age, both in Judah and Babylonia, there was no lack of false prophets (2 Peter 2:1) who announced pleasant things to the ears of the common people and flattering dreams, so that they might be dear to all and held in high esteem, as we have noted from others regarding Chapter 12:24 and 22:28. Thus, what the men of God built up by their sermons, these others boldly tore down and destroyed with their lies. There were not only Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah in Babylonia, promising wonderful things to the people and laughing at the gullibility of those who had so rashly been persuaded by Jeremiah's prophecies to leave their homeland rather than attempting the ultimate for its liberty against the Babylonians (Jeremiah 29:20, 21). There was also Shemaiah the Nehelamite, who most audaciously wrote to the High Priest in Jerusalem as if by divine instinct, rebuking him as sluggish and soft for not more severely punishing Jeremiah as a madman or one possessed, and for not restraining him. See the cited place, verse 24. Similarly, in Jerusalem, Hananiah son of Azzur, in the fourth year of Zedekiah, strenuously lied about a divine oracle in the Temple before the priests and the rest of the people against Jeremiah (Jeremiah 28:1 onwards). Regarding all these, compare also our Preface to Jeremiah §. 5 and our notes here on Chapter 22:25. Indeed, even from the female sex, there were not lacking false prophetesses who, with diabolical daring, used the name of Jehovah as a pretext for their insane deceptions. See our prophet at Chapter 13:2, 17 onwards, Chapter 22:28, etc.

<meta>This page continues the preface to the Book of Ezekiel, focusing on the historical context of Zedekiah’s rebellion, the moral state of the Jewish people, the life and purported martyrdom of Ezekiel, and a structural outline of the prophetic book's contents and chronology.</meta>

->### PREFACE<-

...by the most powerful King of the Egyptians, a rival of Nebuchadnezzar, in this very year or the following. But because Zedekiah did this with no piety toward God and with very bad faith toward the Babylonian king, that matter had only a most dismal outcome. Zedekiah had indeed raised great hope among the Jews <note>Lamentations 4:20</note>; he could have lived happily enough under the Babylonian King with his people if he had been obedient to the warnings of God set forth through Jeremiah. But by neglecting the word of God and violating the oath of loyalty which the Babylonian had required of him through the most holy name of Jehovah, he threw off his yoke, rebelled, and joined the side of the Egyptian against Nebuchadnezzar. This gave the false prophets in Judea and Babylonia an opportunity to slander the word of God spoken by Jeremiah in many ways, and it resulted in an insult to Jehovah Himself, by whose name Zedekiah had promised his faith to the Babylonians. Therefore, Ezekiel most severely reproached Zedekiah for this treachery in Babylonia the following year, as we read in chapter 17, verse 15 and following.

<margin>The impiety of the people and the judgments of God.</margin>
§. VII. Meanwhile, the people—both in Babylonia and in Judea (for those in Babylon were better by comparison, as seen in Ezekiel 11:15 and following; Jeremiah 24:1 and following)—for the most part persisted in their lack of repentance and stubborn obstinacy of mind against the divine word. The King, the Princes, the Priests, and the Teachers led the rest by their bad example. Therefore, they are not only frequently called a "rebellious house" <note>original: "familia inobedientiæ" - family of disobedience</note> by God (see chapter 2, verse 5; chapter 12, verse 2; chapter 24, verse 3; chapter 44, verse 6), and harsh prophecies were pronounced against them; but the most severe judgments of God were also hastened. To these judgments, out of His unspeakable mercy, God did not proceed with a single impulse, but with a very slow step, and as if unwillingly. For the most kind God omitted nothing in warning and exhorting them through the Prophets so that they might be snatched from destruction; but <unclear>fated</unclear> to it, most of them—though rendered without excuse—preferred to perish rather than obey the word of the Lord. See Ezekiel 7:2; chapter 21:30; and compare Preface to Jeremiah §. 11, 12, 13.

<margin>Ezekiel’s faithfulness in performing his duty and his fate.</margin>
§. VIII. Amidst this corruption of his people, our prophet—chosen by God from a large assembly of exiles near the river Chebar in Chaldea and brilliantly inaugurated into his prophetic office (chapter 1:1)—showed himself a faithful servant to God. He acted both in uncovering the hypocrisy of the deported exiles among whom he lived, and in rebuking the impiety of the people remaining in Judea, as well as explaining the fates of his own and other nations. From this, at last, if we believe Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for writing about the lives of the prophets</note> (or the writer who recorded the lives of the prophets under his name), he ended his life in martyrdom, killed by the Jews. Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and commentator</note> reports in his Preface to this book (folio 133, column 3), drawing from the *Travels of Benjamin* <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler</note> (page 77), that his synagogue and tomb are still shown today in the East between the Euphrates and the Chebar rivers. We, however, rightly leave this among the uncertain things. See also *The Chain of Tradition* <note>original: "Schalſcheth Hakkab."</note> (folio 96b), Hottinger’s *Monuments* (page 82), Huet’s *Demonstration of the Gospel* (page 437), and Johann Meyer on the *Order of the World* <note>original: "Seder Olam"</note> (page 979).

<margin>Subject Matter.</margin>
§. IX. The subject matter of Ezekiel is almost the same as that of the other Prophets, and specifically Jeremiah, for which our Preface to Jeremiah (§. 17) can be consulted. For Ezekiel deals in his very frequent visions with famine, plague, the sword, and the destruction, captivity, and dispersion of the Jews remaining in their homeland with Zedekiah by Nebuchadnezzar. He describes the glory of God being removed from the Temple and the City by a most just judgment, and the causes of that judgment—namely, the most serious crimes and sins. He especially targets their trust in the Temple and external worship, as well as human defenses (the Egyptians and others), relying on which they arrogantly promised themselves permanent or at least very long immunity from the evils the prophets denounced. Yet he also frequently speaks, for the comfort of the few godly and the whole Church, about the liberation and return of the captives, and about the judgments of God upon neighboring and hostile nations. Above all, and very frequently in suitable places, he inserts discourses about CHRIST, His office and kingdom, the grace of the Gospel, and finally about the restoration of the Temple and the new city. He undoubtedly presents these mysteries to the Church under a certain covering, as Heidegger <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger, a 17th-century Swiss theologian</note> says in his *Handbook* (page 270). Of this, more below in this Preface (§. 15 and 16) and in the notes to chapter 40, etc.

<margin>Aim and Use.</margin>
§. X. The general and principal aim proposed to our prophet was the same as that of Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the others: namely, CHRIST and His kingdom or Church, represented by various images. Therefore (as Calov <note>Abraham Calov, a 16th-century Lutheran theologian</note> writes on this book, page 497), at the beginning, Christ is shown about to drive the chariot of the Gospel and His kingdom through the world; the same glory is presented again in its progress in chapters 10 and 11, verse 23. At the end, through nine entire chapters, the image of the Temple and the City and the spiritual state is sketched. Therefore, even in the destruction of the city, Christ is introduced marking the faithful with a sign so they do not perish together with the rest (chapter 9). The promised liberation from captivity and the return of the people was for the sake of preserving the kingdom of Christ in Judea, until by His advent He might propagate it from there through the whole world. For this reason, the mystical union of Israel and Judah was promised (chapters 11, 20, 29, and 37), along with the remission of sins (chapter 16), the expansion of Christ’s kingdom (chapter 17), and the gracious will of God confirmed by an oath (chapters 18 and 33). Therefore, Christ, that Good Shepherd, is promised (chapter 34), as is the conversion of the nations to Him (chapter 36), the resurrection of the faithful to eternal life (chapter 37), and the destruction of the enemies of the Church (chapters 38 and 39). And indeed, as we indicated above in §. 4, it was a singular goodness and grace of God that while the devil had his instruments or deceivers in Babylonia and Judea who fought with every effort against the divine truth set forth by Jeremiah’s voice and writings, He opposed them with Ezekiel among the captives in a legitimate prophetic office. This was so that those remaining in Babylonia, by following lies, would not miserably perish with those deceivers. Moreover, those in Jerusalem, hearing that Ezekiel’s prophecies agreed in all things with Jeremiah's, could be greatly confirmed in their truth. For it could hardly happen naturally that one in Jerusalem and the other in Chaldea would bring forth their prophecies as if from a single mouth. See Heidegger’s *Biblical Handbook* (page 272).

<margin>Parts of the book.</margin>
§. XI. Interpreters arrange the parts of the book in more than one way; Heidegger, in his *Handbook* (page 273), divides this entire prophecy into twenty-two visions or prophetic sections. More distinctly, after the title of the whole book (chapter 1, verse 1), it treats: **I.** The calling and appointment of the Prophet to his office (chapters 1–3). **II.** The judgments of God against the Jews and the destruction of the city by the Babylonians (chapters 4–24). **III.** Against the nations: (1) the Ammonites <note>Of whom mention had already been made in chapter 27:33 following the occasion of what was said there in chapter 21:24-25</note> (chapter 25:1–7); (2) the Moabites (chapter 25:8–11); (3) the Edomites (chapter 25:12–14; compare chapter 35:2 following); (4) the Philistines (chapter 25:15–17); (5) the Tyrians (chapters 26–28); (6) the Sidonians (chapter 28:20 following); (7) the Egyptians (chapters 29–32). **IV.** Promises and consolations <note>Which others only begin from the 40th chapter</note> follow regarding: (1) God's gracious will toward the penitent (chapter 33); (2) that Good Shepherd (chapter 34); (3) vengeance on enemies, especially the Edomites (chapter 35); (4) the return and gathering of Israel to the kingdom of Christ (chapter 36); (5) the resurrection of the dead and the union of the Israelites (chapter 37); (6) the destruction of Gog and Magog (chapters 38 and 39); (7) the new Temple and city (chapter 40 following), where it treats the restoration of the Temple (chapters 40–42); (8) the worship itself (chapters 43 and 44); and (9) the reformation of the whole kingdom (chapters 45–48).

<margin>Order of the prophecies.</margin>
§. XII. Furthermore, Ezekiel himself committed his prophecies and the visions offered to him by God to writing, as all things in this book show <note>Nor should we listen to the Talmudists, who attributed the composition of this and other books—even Daniel and Esther—to the Men of the Great Assembly (Ezra and his colleagues Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, Zerubbabel, etc.), on the grounds that it was not permitted to write down divine prophecies outside the Holy Land. See Babylonian Tractate Bava Batra chapter 1, folio 15a; and The Chain of Tradition folio 66b and 69b.</note>. In these, he preserved the order of nature and time accurately enough, unless a specific reason required him to occasionally join one prophecy with a previous one, or immediately connect the fulfillment of it from later times. Compare our notes to chapter 26:1; chapter 29:1 and verse 17; chapter 30:20; chapter 31:1. Thus, we do not doubt that the first and following chapters, up to and including chapter 7, refer to the fifth year of King Zedekiah’s reign (or the deportation of Jehoiachin). To the 6th year: chapters 8 to 19. To the 7th and 8th years: chapters 20–23. To the 9th year: chapters 24 and 25. To the 10th year: chapter 29:1–17. To the 11th year: chapters 26, 27, 28; also chapter 30:20 following and chapter 31:1. To the 12th year: chapters 32 and 33:21. To the 13th and 14th years: Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century Hebraist and clergyman</note> in his *Chronology* (page 130) refers chapters 34–39. To the 25th year belongs chapter 40 and following to the end of the book. Finally, to the 27th year: chapter 29:17 following, and according to some, chapter 30:1–20; although this might perhaps better be referred to the 10th year (compare chapter 29:1 and chapter 30:20). See also Lightfoot in his *Chronology of the Old Testament* (page 131).

We will discuss only one here as an example, arising right from the very beginning of the book. The words with which the Prophet begins are these: *Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year...* (chapter 1:1). Here, because he does not indicate

->## ON EZEKIEL.<-
† † 2
<meta>catchword: con</meta>

...indicates, but leaves the starting point from which he counted these thirty years to be gathered from elsewhere; on this, learned men depart into various opinions. For Lightfoot in *Chronology* p. 123, and Maius in *Economy of the Old Testament* p. 1027, and others—along with the author of *The Chain of Tradition* <note>original: "Schalschelet Hakkab."</note> folio page 96. b.—refer it to the age of Ezekiel and the thirtieth year of his life; at which time Levites and Priests otherwise entered upon their ministry, as we read in Numbers 4:23, 30, etc. Just as also Christ our Savior did in Luke 3:23. Others, however, such as Vossius in *Annals of the Old Testament*, and indeed the most celebrated interpreters—Junius, Cocceius, Calovius, etc.—understand it as the thirtieth year from the Law being found by Hilkiah, and the covenant with God and His worship being solemnly restored by Josiah, and the Passover being most solemnly celebrated. So also the Chaldean interpreter, namely Jonathan, adds: "from the time when Hilkiah, the High Priest <note>original: "summus Sacerdos s. Pontifex"</note>, had found the book of the law," etc. 2 Kings 22:8. For Josiah celebrated that Passover according to 2 Kings 23:23 at the beginning of his eighteenth regnal year [h]; and so after that he reigned fourteen years [i], compare 2 Kings 22:1. Moreover, Jehoiakim reigned eleven years, 2 Kings 23:36. Add to these the five years of Jeconiah or Zedekiah from Ezekiel 1:2, and thirty years come forth. While Kimchi counts these from the Jubilee, Rashi—from the *Order of the World* <note>original: "Seder Olam"</note>—joins that opinion with the preceding one, by what reasoning I know not, in his *Commentary on Ezekiel* 1:2. And certainly, the solemn remembrance of such great benefits could easily have supplied the Jews with a new way of counting years; on this opinion, also compare the *Preface to Jeremiah* §. 7. However, we incline more with others toward the era of Nabopolassar, which was then in use and best known in Chaldea, where Ezekiel was writing. See Joseph Scaliger on *The Emendation of Time* book 5, page 218. And Vitringa says: "Ezekiel is to be understood thus, when he himself, recording the beginnings of his ministry, writes 'in the thirtieth year,' and joins it with the fifth year of Jeconiah's deportation in verse 2. For if you subtract two years from the 21 years of Nabopolassar—which are given to him in the *Canon of Ptolemy*—because Nebuchadnezzar reigned with his father, you will find the 19 years you seek, from the beginning of Nabopolassar until the fifth year of Jeconiah's deportation"; in *The Model of Prophetic Doctrine* <note>original: "typo doctrinae proph."</note> page 41. Compare also Aegidius Strauch’s *Chronological Breviary* page 515 and following, Leipzig Edition, 1708.

<margin>Style and method of presentation.</margin>
§. XIV. Furthermore, as pertains to the genius and learning, as well as the speech and style of Ezekiel: his discourse is pure, certain, and grave, having nothing that conflicts with the elegance of the Hebrew language, as Abarbanel rashly judged here (as he also did regarding Jeremiah) in his preface to this place, folio 154, column 1. Rather, as the subject requires, there is a diligent repetition through the most fitting words and phrases, although they are more difficult in our age and not found everywhere in the other Biblical books. It is certainly strange that his style seemed "fragmentary" <note>original: "conetarium"</note> to some, for example in chapter 12:1 and following. But "let someone pronounce all those parts, pausing gradually on each one, and he will see (as the illustrious Cocceius rightly notes on chapter 12, §. 6) that all things were written as they ought to be." Our Prophet was certainly so strong in genius and erudition that—besides being equipped by God with the incomparable gift of prophecy—on account of his most beautiful sentiments, illustrious comparisons, and great knowledge of many things (especially his extraordinary knowledge of military and civil architecture, see chapter 4:1-3 and chapter 40 and following), he is to be compared not with Homer, as Grotius wrongly thought, but with the greatest and highest Prophets. Abarbanel also shows this extensively in his *Preface to Ezekiel* folio 353. See also John Mayer’s *Dissertation on the final chapters of Ezekiel* page 1. 2. Yet he did not set forth the counsel of God only in open words, but also demonstrated very many things through figures, symbols, and types, which would both seize the men of that age with admiration and exercise the minds of all times. For the revelations which he received from God are plainly wonderful, whether you look at the sublime genius of the composition or the sublimity of the meaning; they are not to be understood or penetrated by the strength of any human genius alone without the grace of the Holy Spirit and the Word.

<margin>Example from the first vision in chapter 1, of which is described (a) the image,</margin>
§. XV. This will be clear even by the single example of the first vision, described in chapter 1, with which God deigned to honor him from the beginning of his calling to his extraordinary and prophetic office. For by the consensus of all Jewish and Christian interpreters, no prophetic emblem is more illustrious or noble than this one, but none is more difficult to understand or hides more abstruse meanings. Learned and pious men have always labored to dig these out, though not with equal success by all; as shown by the great disagreement of Jewish and Christian interpreters, which we do not review here for the sake of brevity. See Blessed Jacob Thomasius’s *Dissertation on the Signs of the Four Evangelists*, Leipzig 1667. Most recently, however, after the diligent researchers of these matters—the illustrious Cocceius in his *Commentary* on this book, and the most learned Lightfoot in his *Description of the Temple of Jerusalem* chapter 38, volume 1 of his *Works*, pages 651-658—the most learned Vitringa in book 4 of his *Sacred Observations* has solidly considered this majestic vision in his usual manner. In chapter 1, he carefully examines its image, and in chapter 2, he studiously extracts its sense, namely its mystical significance. The sum of the visual representation of the things presented to the Prophet's mind by God, from the description of that Illustrious Man in the place cited, chapter 1, page 2 and following, comes to this: Ezekiel, about to be initiated into the most grave prophetic office, saw through an ecstasy <note>original: "ἔκστασιν"</note> a stormy wind stirred up from the north; joined to the wind was the brightness of a most glowing fire, surrounded by a cloud; but coming out of the fire was something white-hot and exceedingly flashing, like amber <note>original: "electri"</note>; from which were formed, while the Prophet watched, the likenesses of four living creatures, joined to as many wheels, supporting with their wings [k] a certain high throne, upon which God sat in human form, like a certain King or Emperor. Those living creatures were composed of the likenesses of four excellent animals: a Man, an Eagle, an Ox, and a Lion; [l] each presenting a fourfold face on four sides; the posture of the body otherwise being upright and approaching the human; with feet that were like calves' feet at their lowest part; equipped with four wings; two covering the hands, feet, and less conspicuous parts of the body; and two wings raised upward [m] and joined together supporting the throne of the divine majesty. Present with the living creatures (and supporting their base) were four wheels; four wheels of remarkable height were seen, embracing them crosswise, that is, cutting through them transversely; equipped with rims and furthermore conspicuous with human eyes appearing in them. At the same time, both the wheels and the living creatures flashed with the sharpest brightness, like glowing brass, chrysolite, or coals of fire; and they were simultaneously moved most rapidly in a motion—backward, forward, upward, downward: by one and the same spirit that moved the living creatures, which also drove the wheels themselves. Moreover, they moved straight ahead, so that in moving they never turned toward another quarter of the heaven or changed their position: and this with as much noise as the waves of stirred-up waters, more violent thunders, or great armies drawn up for battle are accustomed to make. These are the primary things which are narrated as seen by Ezekiel at two distinct times (namely in the fifth year of his exile, chapter 1:2, and in the sixth, chapter 10, compare chapter 8:1). Anyone easily sees, without my pointing it out, how wonderful these things are and most worthy of all attention. Thus far are the words of the most learned man concerning the image or prophetic emblem.

<margin>(b) The mystical significance.</margin>
§. XVI. As for its mystical significance, based on certain hypotheses and those learnedly constructed, he himself also shows in the second chapter of the cited work that the one sitting upon the chariot is God; [n] that the throne or his seat, which the living creatures supported, is the kingdom of Christ—both the typical one in the Old Testament and the spiritual one in the New Testament. He understands the living creatures to be not so much ministering Angels (as otherwise Master Doctor Maius also thinks in *Economy of the Old Testament* page 1028), or four Archangels, or only the four Evangelists (which pleased the ancients); nor yet the whole Church of the saints (which Cocceius thought); but the most excellent and extraordinary ministers of God of all ages—in the New Testament especially the Apostles and apostolic men. By the wheels, however, are understood the ordinary teachers of the divine word, whom God uses as instruments in establishing and promoting His kingdom on this earth, represented in the Apocalypse of Saint John by the 24 elders. [o] Since these four animals in that whole vision of John in Revelation chapter 4 [p]...

[k] Or by their heads, verse 22, 26. [l] The Hebrews hand down that the figures of these were also once expressed on the four primary standards of the Israelites. See Abraham ibn Ezra on Numbers 2:2, where his words are: "Our Elders said that on the standard of Reuben was expressed the form of a Man—on the standard of Judah a Lion—on the standard of Ephraim an Ox—on the standard of Dan an Eagle, so that they displayed the form of the Cherubim, whom the Prophet Ezekiel saw." <meta>This page continues the discussion on the identity of the "Living Creatures" in Ezekiel’s vision, debating whether they represent angels, the four Evangelists, or the general ministry of the Church, before concluding the preface with an overview of the commentary's sources and a closing prayer.</meta>

### PREFACE TO EZEKIEL

...they are joined with the assembly of the **Elders** [g] and are not only distinguished from the **Angels**, but are explicitly set in contrast to the angelic orders in Revelation 7:11 and especially Revelation 5:9, 10, 12. In those passages, the entire heavenly assembly standing before the throne is divided into two choirs or classes: one consists of the **Living Creatures** and the **Elders** (verse 8), and the other consists of the **Angels** (verse 11). Furthermore, in the hymn of praise <note>original: "doxologia"</note> attributed to the Living Creatures and the Elders, the Living Creatures—along with the Elders—acknowledge and celebrate that greatest benefit of redemption through the **blood of CHRIST**, which they proclaim has fallen to them (verse 9). This point, along with many others, is urged by that solidly learned man <note>likely referring to Cocceius or a similar contemporary scholar</note> following Lightfoot in the previously cited work (page 656), both in his *Sacred Observations* and in his *Commentary on Revelation 4:6*. While we gladly acknowledge the force and strength of these arguments, everything is nevertheless arranged in such a way that we do not yet dare to pronounce anything too boldly against the ancient writers and others, or to simply reject their opinions. 

For regarding the **Four Evangelists**, it is certain—even in the opinion of that most learned man—that they too are to be referred to the order of God’s excellent ministers. As for the opinion of others regarding the **Four Archangels**, although it is not clear to us from the Scriptures except for the one Archangel, the Son of God [r], it is nevertheless certain from the divine books that there is a diversity of ranks and certain orders even among the angels themselves (compare Ephesians 1:21 and Colossians 1:16), even if it is not our place to define them rashly without divine revelation. And just as Christ, in His Kingdom among men, uses human ministers, so He no less uses the ministry of Angels *in invisible things* <note>original Greek: "en aoratois"</note> (Colossians 1:16). Indeed, they are *ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation* <note>original Greek: "pneumata leitourgika, apostellomena dia tous mellontas klēronomein sōtērian"</note>, as the Apostle teaches in Hebrews 1:14. Nor should the will of God be done any less in heaven than we desire it to be done on earth—especially since not only elsewhere (as in Psalm 18:11, 80:2, and 99:1) is God and Christ our Lord said to ride upon the **Cherubim**, and His glory was supported by the Cherubim over the Ark of the Covenant, but our **Living Creatures** are expressly named "Cherubim" later in Ezekiel 10:20. 

Although the most learned man does not think this hinders his opinion (in *Sacred Observations*, page 35, § 31), arguing that the Cherubim can be—and truly are—symbols of all God’s ministers who execute His commands with the greatest readiness, sincerity, and zeal for divine glory, nothing prevents us from also thinking that through this vision, the Prophet was shown how the will of their Prince is most promptly carried out by the **Angels** and the heavenly host, just as He wishes it to be done by His saints and ministers on this earth. In reality, there is a just analogy and conformity between these groups, as even that learned man does not deny, but proves. Truly, we are persuaded with difficulty that the Angels are not to be understood most directly under the name of the Cherubim. And since Cherubim (or angels) are represented elsewhere as the vehicle of God, as we have proved from the scriptures just cited, what is to stop them from being so here? Certainly, no passage occurs to us in Holy Scripture where the name "Cherubim" is immediately applied to men. Furthermore, the goal and subject of this first and second vision concerns the kingdom of God under the **New Testament** <note>original: "N. T."</note> more directly than the overthrow of the Jews by the Babylonians, though even so we do not deny that the latter was a prefiguration of what was to come. And although the entire Church of the saints may not be figured by the Living Creatures and the **Wheels**—as the celebrated Cocceius thought—nevertheless, no saint or faithful servant of Christ and His members can be excluded from the fellowship of this entire **Four-Horse Chariot** <note>original: "Quadrigæ"</note>, if indeed the Kingdom of Christ was figured by these symbols, as we believe along with that learned man. Indeed, the Blessed Macarius gives a pious and sweet application of this first vision to all pious and holy souls in his *First Homily*, which we rightly recommend to our readers.

<margin>Regarding our annotations.</margin>
§ XVII. As for our annotations on this book, the celebrated and Reverend Master **Abraham Kall** was our assistant in illustrating it; he was formerly our associate from the beginning of this labor, as is evident from the Dissertation he previously presented to the public regarding the Manuscript Codices of the Bible. He is now a minister of the divine word in Charlottenburg, in the vicinity of the royal city of Berlin. To his industry, therefore, are owed many things, but especially the greatest part of what has been noted here from other authors and interpreters: from **Poole’s Synopsis**, **Cocceius’s Commentary**, and **Bochart’s Hierozoicon** <note>A famous 17th-century study of the animals of the Bible</note>. However, the celebrated man stopped at the 39th chapter of this prophecy, hindered from continuing this labor by his call to the pastoral office and other cares. He left it to us to work out some things in the rest, and everything in those final chapters in full. 

For this reason, and also due to a lack of time, we have only noted a few things here and there regarding the mystical meaning of that final vision <note>The vision of the Third Temple</note>. This was partly because it was difficult to clearly show the parts of that whole holy building in an application with few words, and partly so that the minds of those beginning their studies—who are already quite busy enough if the admirable symmetry of that structure is to be observed and conceived in the mind—might not be completely overwhelmed by a multitude of details. For a more abundant application, however, the Interpreters may be consulted, as well as **Haffenreffer** in his special commentary on this Temple. Or, as one's progress in the knowledge and sense of divine truth grows, these things can be better illustrated by comparing passages of Holy Scripture with one another, and then the meditations of others may also be employed. For just as the Church of Christ is the Temple of God, so Christ Himself is the Altar, and He is also the Priest and the Sacrifice, as we have already noted from our **Brentius** <note>Johannes Brenz, a Lutheran reformer</note> on Leviticus 1:3. 

Furthermore, our Kall constantly consulted **Schmid’s Latin version** in his notes, the Bibles of **Junius and Tremellius**, as well as (from Poole’s Synopsis) the posthumous commentary of Junius on Ezekiel. To distinguish this from Junius’s Bible, he cited it as *Jun.* or *Junius*, but the Bible as *Tremell.* or *Jun. & Tremell.* He examined not only Poole’s Synopsis but also the **Sacred Critics** themselves, which was occasionally useful for correcting Poole’s doubts or errors. Additionally, he used Cocceius’s Lexicon and commentary on Ezekiel, **Gousset’s Lexicon**, **Maius’s Economy of the Old Testament**, the **Septuagint** <note>original: "LXX"</note>, the **Targum of Jonathan**, the **Syriac Version**, and the **Rabbinic commentators**, Bochart’s *Hierozoicon* and *Sacred Geography*, **Pfeiffer’s** *Difficulties Vexed*, and **Glassius’s** *Sacred Philology* (of which we cite only the pages from the newest Leipzig edition as a shortcut). 

However, he did not always and everywhere credit the authors whose words were brought in. Where they held easy and obvious points, it was sufficient to express the matter in their words (either retained or partly changed) or in his own, without their name. Nor did he list the names of all the interpreters whom he found agreeing on this or that explanation, but was content with one or two principal ones, very often adding "and others." Sometimes he even rendered into Latin things that might seem easy, in order to connect more difficult points, or to indicate the connection and coherence of the text, or the distinction of times and Hebrew words, and various meanings or connections of the prefixed *Vav* <note>The Hebrew letter used as a conjunction</note> with a certain little word or particle; these things are not always clear to beginners. 

Regarding the various opinions of interpreters which he sometimes brought forward, he wished to advise the **Kind Reader** here that they are often of such a nature that one does not cancel out the other, but they can be aptly joined or subordinated; we have also indicated this in the text itself from time to time. Thus, in such matters, the attentive reader’s mind is so far from being confused by such diversity that meditation is rather assisted. In those things that are entirely discrepant and cannot stand together, we have not infrequently interposed our judgment, yet we have ultimately left it to the choice of the pious and prudent reader to decide which opinion they think they should more rightly rest upon. If, however, one or another of the interpreters we cited should foster or hide their own unique hypotheses under the quoted phrases or words, no fair-minded person should attribute these to our Kall. For when two people use the same word, they do not necessarily say the same thing if their different aim and sense is clear. But it is enough to have advised these things.

<margin>Conclusion of the Preface.</margin>
§ XVIII. May **GOD**, the Thrice-Greatest and Best, and our Lord **JESUS CHRIST**—whose judgments, kingdom, and glory are described here—grant that we may so behold these wonders of His that we do not wander in our minds into vain or useless thoughts. Rather, aided by His grace, may we so consider all these things that we, through true faith and animated by His Spirit, may be led according to His will and perform the same here under grace, and there in eternal glory for all ages. **Amen!**

***

g) In place of which there are **Wheels** here, as we have said. 
r) Although the Jews—as that celebrated Man himself observed—in the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer* <note>original: "Pirke Eliezeris"</note> chapter 4 and elsewhere, occasionally distribute all the Angels into four classes, each having its own Prince: **Michael, Gabriel, Uriel, and Raphael**.

**Verse 7.** y) *to each of them*, or *to their individual selves*. z) *And their feet*. The masculine suffix refers to the preceding subject, not to the grammatical gender of the word "Creatures." (Compare the note on Hosea 10:5). It means each of their legs was straight, not curved or with faltering knees. (Compare Isaiah 35:3). b) *and the sole or plant of their foot*. c) it was like the sole of a calf's foot, namely round and identical on every side: whereas a human foot is extended in length and always faces a certain direction; if a person wishes to turn, it is necessary for the foot to be moved around. <note>referencing Vitringa, *Sacred Observations*, book 4, page 20</note>. And although each *Creature* had the *face of a Lion*, yet it did not have the feet and claws of a lion made for tearing, nor those of an Eagle. <note>referencing Cocceius</note>. d) and they were *glistening*, or *their feet shone*. e) like bronze. See note on verse 4 and chapter 40:3. f) burnished, smoothed, or polished. (Daniel 10:6, Revelation 1:15). 

**Verse 8.** g) *And human hands*; or in the singular, *And a human hand*. See *Hillernum* regarding the "Keri" <note>the traditional reading of the Hebrew text</note> pages 120 and 285. h) *were under their wings*. This signifies human operation, which befits the image of God. <note>referencing Cocceius</note>. Or according to *Maüs*, *hands represent agility and fitness for performing the duties of one's office*. i) *on their four quarters or sides*. k) *and thus their faces and their four wings*. l) *belonged to the four of them and each had them*, as was also said in verse 6. For they had all things <term>isokoma</term> <note>original Greek: ισόκωμα — balanced or uniform in height and proportion</note>. 

**Verse 9.** m) In such a way that their wings were joined. (See verse 11). n) that is, one to another. This was a symbol of concord and union in carrying out the Lord's commands. (Compare Exodus 25:20, 1 Kings 6:27). o) *they did not turn themselves* (verse 12, 17, Luke 17:31). For they were able to go in all directions—that is, forward, backward, right, or left—wherever the spirit moved them. Everything was "forward" to them because they had a face in every direction. p) as they went and moved from their place. (See Proverbs 4:25, Philippians 3:13). q) but each individual. 

**Verse 12.** r) That is, toward the side facing its face; straight ahead, not with an oblique or circular motion. 

**Verse 10.** s) Furthermore, as it pertains to the figure or likeness of their faces. t) the face of a man, or human face, from the front. This is a symbol of humanity, mercy, moderation, and wisdom, by which these Ministers of God commend themselves. <note>referencing Vitringa on Revelation 4:7</note>. u) *and the face of a lion*. This marks that remarkable disposition of the excellent Ministers of Christ, by which—having no regard for the dangers threatening them from every side—driven by the Spirit of God like heroes, with a lofty and noble spirit <note>Hebrew: nadiv — generous or noble</note>, they strongly oppose the world and the devil. <note>referencing Vitringa</note>. (Compare Isaiah 31:4, Proverbs 28:1). x) *on the right*. y) *the four of them had them*. So each individual Creature had four faces, with respect to the four climates of heaven and the four parts of this world in which the seat of Christ's Kingdom would be, where they would fulfill their office. z) *the face of a bull* or *ox*. This signifies that these Ministers of Christ will be constant, diligent, upright, hardworking, and exceptionally prepared for great labors. Thus the horns of an ox denote strength and fortitude (Deuteronomy 33:17). Furthermore, this face is said in chapter 10:14 to have been that of a *Cherub*. From this, *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar of biblical animals</note> concludes that the Cherubim expressed various forms of different animals, but in a way that they more closely approached the appearance of an ox. Be careful, however, not to imagine the figure of an ox here. For the bodies of these Creatures were human and upright (verse 5), except for the soles of the feet, which were like a calf's (verse 7). a) and thus prepared for everything. b) finally, there was also the face of an eagle at the back; a symbol of swiftness, insight, and divine sagacity. (Isaiah 40:31, Matthew 24:28).

<column-break/>

p) the figure or appearance broke forth or was produced. (See verse 10, 2 Chronicles 3:3). q) of the four Living Creatures. These, on account of the variety and excellence of their attributes, are displayed in this emblem in a figure that is wonderful, terrible, and plainly paradoxical. Concerning the mystical meaning, see Preface § 16. The number *four* is also mystical and is the number of universality; it refers to the four quarters of the world, through which the Kingdom of God and the Church of Christ under the New Testament was to be spread. These *Creatures* or *Living Beings* are called *Angels*, or other excellent ministers of God, whom He uses in establishing and promoting His kingdom, because in them there was "life"—the principle of true and continuous activity, which belongs to faith and hope, joined with the affection of pure and most ardent love for God, Christ, and the saints. This life was produced in them by the Spirit of God and was continually nourished. <note>referencing Vitringa on Revelation 4:6</note>. r) this was the appearance or disposition of those creatures. s) namely, the form of a man. t) they had it; so that they expressed the human form by their figure, and were not crouched like beasts, but were upright.

**verse 6.** u) *Nevertheless, each had four faces*: so that these Ministers of God were immediately prompt and ready to take up the Lord's commands in all directions, wherever they were to be done. x) *and four wings*; not six, as in Isaiah 6:2 or Revelation 4:8, because standing here beneath the throne of God they did not...

Everything, after God's long patience, looked toward vengeance, says **Grotius**. <note>Compare 2 Samuel 22:15; Psalm 144:6.</note> **v. 14. b)** *The living creatures* indeed, regarding their movement. **c)** by running (1) this agrees with *ratzo* <note>Hebrew: רָצֹוא</note>, compare Psalm 50:13. **d)** and by returning; namely, they were swift, as **Jonathan** adds. **e)** like verse 13, etc. **f)** of a lightning flash (1) which is suddenly spread very widely. From the Chaldean and Syriac root <term>pazar</term> <note>Hebrew: פּזר</term>, meaning "he scattered, dispersed, or dissipated." Compare Matthew 24:27; Luke 17:24. And thus the Talmudists explain it through the word *pizzur* <note>Hebrew: פִּזּוּר</note>, meaning something scattered. **v. 15. g)** And when I thus saw, or looked more attentively at the Living Creatures, described up to this point. **h)** see verse 4. **i)** *There was one wheel*. Just as in the bases of the bronze basins or shells <note>1 Kings 7:30 and following, from which the image of this emblem seems to be taken</note> the Cherubim were joined with wheels; the wheel being lower, and the Cherubim occupying the higher place, according to **Vitringa**, *Sacred Observations*, book 4, chapter 1, page 11. **k)** *on the earth*. So that you may understand that the Cherubim stood out above the wheels; just as those bases of the shells, showing the same appearances to living beings <note>1 Kings 7:29</note>, were supported on the lower part by four wheels, resembling the wheels of chariots in everything; which were joined to those bases just as the wheels of wagons are usually joined to the boards, and are accustomed to carry and sustain them. (Ibid.) **l)** *beside the living creatures*; to which they were so joined that one body could not be moved or agitated without the other. For those Living Creatures themselves sustained the throne of the Divine Majesty with their wings (or rather their heads, verse 22), not some chariot or carriage distinct from them. Therefore, they were joined to the wheels in the manner of a living being, just as the upper part of a vehicle is usually joined to the wheels; not as a vehicle is usually joined to beasts of burden. (Ibid. page 7.) Ezekiel saw the wheels joined and inserted into some base, as the wheels of wagons are usually joined to boards. Upon that base he saw the Cherubim, closely joined to the wheels, making up that very chariot which is supported and propped up by the wheels. (Ibid. page 18.) **m)** *to its four faces*, namely, of the whole chariot or four-horse team. And so there were four wheels in number; compare chapter 10:9; 1 Kings 7:30. Furthermore, just as he understands by the Living Creatures the most excellent and extraordinary ministers of God, so by the Wheels he understands the ordinary ministers, as the instruments upon which the kingdom of God on this earth rests, and through which the same is promoted; so says **Vitringa**, *Sacred Observations*, book 4, chapter 2, pages 18 and following. And on pages 34 and following, he says: *What are Living Creatures and Wheels in Ezekiel, are Living Creatures and Elders in John (Revelation 4:4, 6, etc.). For John, who does not mention wheels, mentions Elders. By the 24 Elders in John, however, are to be understood entirely the ordinary ministers of the whole Christian Church through all times, related to the 24 orders of priests, who had been the ordinary ministers of the Old Testament Church (see 1 Chronicles 24:18; 25:31); therefore the same is meant by the Wheels in Ezekiel. Since ordinary Ministers of the Church are distinguished from extraordinary ones, it is clear that the Extraordinary ones are designated by the Living Creatures.* **v. 16. n)** *Appearance*, species and color (verses 5, 13, 14) of the wheels. **o)** and *their work or structure*. Exodus 24:10; 28:15; 1 Kings 7:33. **p)** *it was like the species or color.* See note at verse 4. **q)** *Chrysolite* <note>original Latin: "Chrysolithi"</note> chapter 10:9; Exodus 28:20; Daniel 10:6. A gem or stone, shining like the purest gold. **Vitringa**, in the place cited, page 12. It was so named by the Hebrews from the place whence it was then dug out. Compare note at 1 Kings 10:22. **r)** but there was one and the same figure. Verses 5, 10, 13. Compare note at verse 4. **s)** to those four themselves, verse 18; namely, similar in all things to their four sides. Compare verses 8, 10. **t)** *but their aspect or figure and structure* was prepared in such a wonderful way, as if it were <note>Zechariah 10:6; Job 18:19</note> **x)** *a wheel in the midst of a wheel* chapter 10:10. Just as, for example, in some celestial or terrestrial globe the meridian circle is transversely entangled with the horizontal one. Here the Prophet signifies not obscurely that there is something new and unexpected which he catches in these wheels: namely, that they were made in such a way as if one wheel had been entangled with another, and had cut it crosswise as if at right angles; so that the wheels were not of one circle, as the ordinary wheels of chariots usually are; but that they were constructed with a double circle, one inserted into the other, and cutting it crosswise at right angles, they described two circles. **Vitringa**, book 4, *Sacred Observations*, pages 18 and following. **v. 17. y)** *To their four fourth parts*, or semicircles, looking toward the 4 regions of the sky. Verse 8. **z)** when they went, they went without turning. Verses 9, 11. **a)** they did not turn themselves when they proceeded; as in verses 9, 12. I hold it certain, says **Vitringa**, in the place cited, page 19, that the Prophet wanted to say the Wheels were so composed that they could be moved to the 4 regions of the sky, without which the chariot, which was square, would have had to be turned and converted to that region of the sky into which it would be moved. Which certainly cannot be conceived of this chariot unless it had double wheels.

Up to this point the Animals and Wheels have been described; the Prophet now proceeds to the Expanse above the heads and wings of the Cherubim v. 23. and the throne of divine majesty that was placed upon it v. 26. **g)** Ch. 10:1 **h)** Of the Living Creature or Creatures. see note v. 20. **i)** which provided as it were a floor or base for the Throne of Christ v. 23, 25. ch. 10:1. This is either due to similarity, or because crystal is formed from intensely frozen ice; as Pliny records in *Natural History* (book 37, ch. 2): "Crystal is certainly not found anywhere else except where the winter snows freeze most severely: and it is certain that it is ice: whence also the Greeks gave it the name." Therefore those Living Creatures themselves supported the throne of the Divine Majesty with their heads (or summits), just as the wings of the Cherubim supported the throne of God among the Israelites above the Ark in the Holy of Holies, Exodus 25:19 onwards. In the most sacred inner sanctuary of the Temple in Jerusalem, as is commonly known, God was said to dwell like a King among the Cherubim; who, with their wings raised upward, supported the throne of God, as if resting upon them. This same appearance was expressed by God, following the example of this emblem, in Isaiah chapter 6:1, who saw the Lord and Commander of the Jewish people sitting on a high throne in the Holy of Holies, with the hems of his garments filling the front part of the Temple. This same appearance, with slight variation, was shown to John, as is clear from his Apocalypse chapter 4:1, 2. and both those visions agree with this our vision of Ezekiel. <meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Ezekiel’s inaugural vision. Having described the living creatures and the wheels, the text now moves to the sounds they produce and the appearance of the divine throne above them. # EZEKIEL. CHAPTER I.

<margin>
* 24. **a)** And I heard. Until now the Prophet has only described what he saw; now he also reports what he heard. **b)** ch. 10:5. Through this, others understand the prayers and the fervor of the spirit in the Church Militant <note>The Church on earth, struggling against sin and evil</note>; to Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 1603–1669, a Dutch theologian</note> it signifies speech, rumor, fame, and the tumult in the world when the Church is moved. cf. note ch. 3:13. **c)** cf. ch. 43:2. Rev. 14:2, ch. 19:6, & Ps. 18:12. **d)** ch. 10:5. cf. Psalm 29:3 and following. What the Church speaks is the word of the omnipotent God, powerful and effective, etc. Heb. 4:12, Isa. 51:16. Cocceius. **e)** when they went or moved themselves with the swiftest course; the Living Creatures, v. 9, 12, 14, 21. **f)** the voice of a tumult or a very great noise **g)** Jer. 11:16. **g)** like the sound of an army camp clashing. cf. Preface § 15.
