10:1. cf. Rev. 4:2 and following, & Ps. 9:5. Allusion is made to the throne of God among the Israelites, resting on the wings of the Cherubim over the Ark in the Holy of Holies, Vitringa *Sacred Observations* book 4, ch. 1, p. 9. The same in ch. 2, p. 27: By the throne, he says, I understand (1) the Kingdom of grace, which God had among the Israelites, as a type of that spiritual and heavenly kingdom which God would eventually establish in His Son under the New Dispensation; (2) that very spiritual and heavenly kingdom of the new dispensation, which the Father administers through His Son with the highest glory and majesty, with the Son sitting on the throne of his Father. Since this is the fulfillment <note>original: "antitypon"</note> of the former, and thus much more illustrious and excellent, it is undoubtedly primarily intended here by the Holy Spirit, etc. Compare also from the same note to v. 23. **x)** understand Christ, the Son of God, who was appointed by the Father as judge of this universe, Gen. 18:25, Ps. 110:1, Zech. 6:13, Eph. 1:3-4, John 5:22, Acts 10:42, ch. 17:31; he also prefigured the mystery of his incarnation in this way. cf. Dan. 7:13, Zech. 1:8, Rev. 1:13, ch. 4:2, etc., & note Ex. 24:10. **y)** above. v. 11, 22. **z)** I saw moreover. v. 1, 4, 15. **a)** something like the most brilliant. see note v. 4. **b)** Or burning coals, others: electrum <note>a natural alloy of gold and silver</note>, others: lightning, others: mountain brass or glowing gold (3) see v. 4. **c)** and like the appearance v. 13, 14, 26. **d)** of fire. cf. Ex. 13:21, 22; Lev. 16:2, 3; comparing Num. 9:15, 16; ch. 14:14; also Eph. 4:5; & Deut. 4:24, Isa. 33:15, Ps. 50:3, Heb. 12:29; comparing Ex. 32:10, ch. 33:3, 20. **e)** within or between it, the appearance of glowing air. comparing below ch. 41:9, Prov. 8:2. But Danz’s Interpreter p. 36 and following: it was the enclosure of a furnace or a containing place; comparing 1 Kings 18:31. **f)** all around v. 4, 18, 28. **g)** and upward ch. 8:2, ch. 43:15. **h)** and below or downward. 2 Chron. 31:30. **i)** so that the whole was shining v. 4. cf. Eph. 4:5 & Rev. 1:14 and following. **k)** v. 4, 18, 28. **l)** Such as the appearance (v. 27) of the rainbow. Gen. 9:13, Rev. 4:3, ch. 10:1. The rainbow is a symbol of the covenant and the grace of God promised in Jesus Christ. Whence Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, 1583–1645, a Dutch jurist and theologian</note> also concludes here that divine judgments, however severe, would nonetheless not abolish the memory of the covenant made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, comparing Isa. 54:10, Jer. 31:20, 21, 25, 26. **m)** v. 4, 27. **n)** v. 4, 18, 27. **o)** v. 5, 10. cf. note v. 4. **p)** ch. 3:12, ch. 10:4. Therefore, Jehovah was seen sitting on the throne in the appearance of a man, as said in the preceding v. 26. cf. Ex. 16:10, ch. 40:35, etc., & Isa. 60:1, John 1:14, Heb. 1:3. This vision, says Cocceius, was not a glorious thing like the cloud or fire (in Moses' time, in the places just cited for v. 27), but a glorious foreshadowing of the appearance of Jehovah in the flesh with his kingdom, 1 Tim. 3:16. The Son of God was seen here as head and king with his brothers, both the blessed in heaven and the militant on earth, and with his servants and fellow servants of his brothers, sent because of them, namely the Angels. **q)** when therefore I saw it. v. 1, 4, 15. Struck by such majesty, because of weakness, and also for the sake of reverence and adoration, I fell on my face. cf. ch. 3:23, ch. 43:3, Dan. 8:17, 18, ch. 10:7, 8, 9, Matt. 17:6, Acts 9:7, Rev. 1:17. For there is no strength in a sinful man to stand before the most holy God and His purest light, unless he is strengthened by His grace and spirit. cf. Eph. 6:5, Luke 5:8, etc. **s)** yet I heard ch. 2:2, ch. 43:6, Dan. 8:16. **t)** the voice speaking, or of Jehovah speaking ch. 2:1, 2, Isa. 6:8.

**CHAPTER II, v. 1. u)** And he said, namely, the one seated on the throne. ch. 1:26, 28. After that first vision of divine majesty described in Chapter 1, in this second chapter follows: I. The calling and mission of the Prophet v. 1–5; II. the confirmation of the same through words v. 6, 7; & the divine symbol v. 8 and following. **x)** so v. 3, 6, etc. This address is a testimony of the <term>philanthropia <note>original: "Φιλανθρωπίας" — love for humanity</note></term> of Christ, as if to say: I know your weakness, that you are a man, and cannot endure the brilliance of divine majesty. Cocceius: He names him Son of man, he who was seen as a son of man (ch. 1:26), as if to say: my brother! comparing Ps. 22:23, Heb. 2:11, 12. But Rashi says: he calls him thus so that his mind would not be puffed up because of this vision, cf. 2 Cor. 12:7. **y)** Stand, raise yourself. cf. Dan. 8:17, 18, ch. 10:11, Matt. 17:7, Acts 26:16.

**z)** so that He might speak with him.
Chapter 3:22, 27.
**v. 2. a)** And he entered into me. Chapter 3:24.
Compare Revelation 1:17. **b)** The Holy Spirit, who drove the wheels and the living creatures. Chapter 1:20, 21. **c)** and He raised me up. Daniel 8:18. **d)** Chapter 1:28.
A type <note>a symbolic foreshadowing</note> of regeneration. God commands us to rise from the death in which we lie (Ephesians 5:1, 5; chapter 5:14) and at the same time sends the Spirit into us to give us life and make us stand upright. Such is the strengthening in all things. We are commanded to do our duty, and God makes it so that we do it. Cocceius. Compare Philippians 2:13.
**e)** speaking. See verse 1, 3. The Hebrew participle <term>מדבר</term> <note>midaber - speaking</note> takes the same form in chapter 43:6 and Numbers 7:89. Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, 11th-century commentator</note>: The Divine Presence <note>original: "Schechina"</note> was speaking within itself in its glory, while His messengers listened.
**v. 3. f)** Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, 12th-century grammarian</note>: those who were in the Babylonian captivity, comparing chapters 5 and 11. **g)** Among the Jews, this word <note>Goyim - nations</note> was a mark of shame. Although they were one nation, the plural is used because some worshipped the idols of the Ammonites, others those of the Moabites or other peoples. The plural also seems to respect the distinction of tribes and families; Kimchi, comparing Deuteronomy 33:19 and Judges 5:14. By this word, He equates them with the rest of the nations, as a "non-people" (Hosea 1:9). But by what follows, He casts them even lower than the other nations. **h)** those rebels. The article <note>the</note> notes that this is, as it were, characteristic of them. Chapter 20:38; compare 17:15, Nehemiah 2:19. **i)** <term>פשע</term> <note>pasha - transgress</note> <term>παρακιράνοντάς με</term> <note>original Greek: provoking me to bitterness</note>. Cocceius. **m)** Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan</note>: "against my Word." Compare 1 Corinthians 10:9. He who speaks is the one whom he had seen sitting on the throne; the Fathers ought to have recognized Him as King and Lord. **CHAPTER III. v. 1.** **d)** Then he said. There follows in this chapter: I. the eating of the presented scroll, II. the repeated calling and confirmation of the prophet in verse 4, III. his transfer to Tel Abib in verse 12, IV. the second address and instruction of the prophet in verse 16, V. his calling out into the valley in verse 22, and VI. the mandate given there in verse 24. **e)** "you find," namely, held out to you in my hand, chapter 2:9. **f)** verse 3, Revelation 10:9. For the explanation see below at verse 10 and the note on chapter 2:9. The emblem is taken from a metaphorical expression common to almost all nations, by which those eager to know the truth are said to greedily devour, like <term>helluonum</term> <note>original Latin: "gluttons" or "insatiable eaters"</note>, a thing useful for satisfying this honorable desire, and to convert it into their juice and blood. So in Jeremiah 15:16. Thus, what we read in Isaiah 51:16, Jeremiah 1:9, and Matthew 10:20 is expressed symbolically here. **g)** "eat," I say, see chapter 2:8. **h)** and having eaten the little book, go. **i)** Revelation 10:11. 

**v. 2.** **k)** So I opened. compare chapter 2:8, Psalm 119:131. **l)** and he gave it to me to be eaten. see verse 3, Deuteronomy 8:3, Jonah 1. He taught me that which was written in the book. 

**v. 3.** **m)** lest perhaps he should spit the hand out from his teeth. compare verses 1, 2, also Job 32:18, 19, 1 Timothy 4:6. It intimates that a minister of the Church ought not to rest in theory alone, but should convert divine truth into juice and blood, and should be anxious for the treasure of the heart, so that from it he may properly show the way of truth to others as well. compare Matthew 13:52, Luke 6:45. **n)** chapter 7:19, compare Psalm 40:9. For those who eagerly hear the word of God, it enters into their heart and all their inward parts as it were, and becomes a treasure in them, from which they can abundantly draw all necessary doctrine, and it so fills them entirely that without it they think, consult, deliberate, or desire nothing. Cocceius. **o)** so I ate, Jeremiah 15:16. **p)** Revelation 10:10. Knowledge of the word of God has the highest sweetness; for it is the good word, and wisdom, and the life of the soul. Although the contents were lamentations etc., chapter 2:10, and thus bitter to the people, they were nevertheless sweet to the prophet, being offered by God and made sweet, so that he rested in God’s mandates and subscribed to His just judgment. compare Psalm 19:11, Psalm 119:103. **q)** as to sweetness, or into a sweet thing. A noun of the form <term>כְּנֹוֹחַ</term> <note>kenoach - like resting</note> compare Judges 9:11, Proverbs 16:24, chapter 24:13. Some, however, understand the other half of the antithesis: "but in the stomach it was bitter as gall," comparing Revelation 10:10. 

**v. 4.** **r)** Presently he said. **s)** "go" then, see verse 1, Isaiah 22:15. **t)** "with my words." compare note on 1 Kings 13:1, 2. 

**v. 5.** **u)** that is, <term>ἑτερογλώττῳ</term> <note>original Greek: heteroglotto - "of a different tongue"</note>, those who are "deep," that is, obscure and difficult to understand, see verse 6, Isaiah 33:19. **x)** and heavy, difficult, see verse 6, Exodus 4:10. **y)** Jonah, but to. **z)** to men of the same language and already accustomed to those words which the prophet was going to speak; not new and barbarous things, but what Moses and other prophets had already spoken. For here one must think not only of the dialect, but also of the very subject matter of the speech. Cocceius. 

**v. 6.** **a)** <margin>Surely?</margin> compare Judges 21:22, 2 Samuel 23:5, 1 Kings 22:17, 2 Kings 5:26. Others simply: "not," I say, or: "neither to," etc. **b)** numerous and diverse. **c)** see verse 5. **d)** verse 5. **e)** whose words you would not hear, or would not understand.

<meta>This page continues the divine commissioning of the prophet Ezekiel. The commentary draws heavily on 17th-century scholars like Cocceius and medieval rabbis like Kimchi to explain the spiritual psychological state of the people and the mechanics of Ezekiel's prophetic transport.</meta>

I., this is a formula for an oath, using an ellipsis <note>a grammatical omission</note> common in swearing; as if to say, "certainly, if I had sent you to these, they would have listened." Compare Joshua 14:9, Psalm 5:9, Jeremiah 22:6, and Glassius's *Sacred Philology*, Book I, pages 158-159. **g)** *S.* "If I were to send you." Thus the Past tense is often joined with the Future, so that the former, even without a conditional particle, denotes the antecedent, while the latter denotes the consequence. Compare 2 Kings 5:13. But to Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century theologian</note>, the simplest construction seems to be this: "I have not sent you to them (the Israelites); those others (the many peoples of unknown and diverse tongues) would have listened to you, if it were already the time for the calling of the nations; but the time is now for prophets to be sent still to Israel, to whom the Lord Himself was to come, and whose forerunners the prophets were." **h)** "they would be obedient." Although they would not understand your language, and you in turn would not understand theirs, they would nevertheless seek someone to explain your prophecies to them. Clavius and Cocceius: this indicates that the nations of "other tongues" <note>original Greek: ἑτερογλώσσους</note> would eventually be called and would be more prepared to receive the Gospel than the Jews. \*. 8. **p)** "Behold, nevertheless." **q)** compare Jeremiah 1:18, 19; 15:19, 20; Micah 3:8. Grotius: "I will give you courage, by which you may despise their attacks and not be afraid." **r)** hardened, strong, and undaunted. A metaphor taken from animals that butt with their horns, where one prevails over the other in strength. Compare Jeremiah 15:19 and 5:14. **s)** "against." Ecclesiastes 7:14, 2 Samuel 16:13.

Zechariah 7:12. see the note on Jeremiah 17:1. **u)** "firmer than rock." **x)** compare Ezekiel 48:4. **y)** "therefore do not fear." Luke 12:4. **z)** chapter 2:6. **a)** verses 26, 27; chapter 2:5. Kimchi: "For I know that they will resist you when you rebuke them."

\*. 10. **b)** "Furthermore He said." **c)** chapter 2:1. **d)** "all, not just a part." Job 33:1, Acts 20:20, 27. **e)** *S.* "I have spoken." Others: "I speak." **f)** compare 1 Samuel 21:13, Job 22:22. **g)** "and with your ears"—not only the external ones, but also the internal, chapter 40:4. Contrary to Jeremiah 6:10 and Acts 7:51. Cocceius: This is not a <term>hysteron proteron</term> <note>a figure of speech where the last thing comes first</note>. There must be trust in the listener toward the speaker and a desire to hear, so that the ear may do its duty, and thus the word may be instilled and brought into the heart. As long as the heart is absent, the ear hears nothing rightly. Compare Acts 16:14. God truly effects in His own people what He commands. Compare Psalm 55:1.

\*. 11. **h)** verse 4. **i)** "The Exile"—those who are held captive among the Chaldeans, verse 15, chapter 1:1. **k)** that is, to your countrymen, chapter 33:2, 12, 17. Others: "to the children of your people," not Mine; compare Exodus 32:7, 11; Hosea 1:9. **l)** Kimchi: "The same thing is expressed with various words for the sake of emphasis." The sense is that the Prophet ought to say this to them again and again. Cocceius: The prophet's style is not redundantly overflowing. He inculcates everything distinctly and in detail; he wants nothing to be unknown; he is diligent. Therefore, he sometimes repeats what has been said so that he may add something notable not yet mentioned, lest anything should escape or be overlooked. Compare the note above on chapter 1:12. **m)** compare the note on chapter 2:4. Rashi <note>the famous 11th-century French rabbi</note>: "this prophecy, namely, that I should explain it to you." Cocceius: "Let us learn that we must hear before we speak; that listening is useless without the preparation of the heart to receive the doctrine of God; that what we have learned must be spoken without fear to those to whom it is necessary, and that in the name of Christ, as He who is Lord and Jehovah." **n)** "whether they hear." verse 27, chapter 2:5, 7. **o)** Thus far the first vision, by which the Prophet is prepared to undertake his prophecy. Cocceius.

\*. 12. **p)** "Presently He lifted me up," verse 14. Either in ecstasy only (compare 2 Corinthians 12:2, 3, 4) according to Kimchi; or also in terms of the body, following the example of Elijah in 1 Kings 18:12, Christ in Matthew 4:1, and Philip in Acts 8:39. Rashi: "When He had finished His words, He commanded the wind to carry him to where the captives were." **q)** "The Spirit," verse 14, chapter 1:1, 2, and "the hand of the Lord," below in verse 22, chapter 1:3. **r)** see chapter 1:24. **s)** "of a noise, a shaking, a crashing." verse 13, chapter 37:7. Jonathan <note>referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note> adds: "of those who, singing the praises of God, were saying: 'Blessed be,' etc." Cocceius: "That voice is of the Living Creatures, that is, of the faithful, by which they glorify Him who is the glory of God, Christ, in whom all the power of God is manifested." see the notes on chapter 1:5 and 28. But Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch jurist and theologian</note> understands it as a choir of Angels approving God's judgments. Compare Revelation 17:10, 11, 12. **t)** The Syriac adds: "by which he said." Likewise the Arabic: "of those who said." **u)** "Blessed be." Revelation 5:12. **x)** compare Luke 2:14. **y)** verse 23, chapter 1:28. **z)** Cocceius: "The Living Creatures, that is, the Church, desire this above all, that the glory of Jehovah be blessed, not only in the place of His manifestation where He was to be revealed, but also from that place throughout the whole world." Compare Malachi 1:5. Others: "Of the Lord presently departing—by a just judgment—from His place: the temple, the mercy seat, from the midst of the two Cherubim." Compare chapter 9:3. Jonathan: "From the place of His Shekhinah."

Cocceius. *Hiph.* <note>a Hebrew verb form denoting causative action</note> (1) compare the note on chapter 1:9, 11. Jonathan: "clashing against each other." **d)** "of one."

According to some, raw, not yet baked—clay. Others say a square tablet in the likeness of a brick. Truly, there is no need to deviate from the literal meaning. *Münster:* <note>Sebastian Münster, a 16th-century Hebraist.</note> It is taught here that the people remaining in Jerusalem were to be exterminated by war, plague, and famine because of their iniquity; and this is conveyed not only in words but also in pictures and actions, which move the minds of the simple more deeply. Compare the note on Hosea 1:2. Indeed, in this chapter, the sign of the siege of Jerusalem is displayed, and it is also explained in verses 13, 15, and 17. **k)** and engrave, describe, or delineate (chapter 23:14; Ezekiel 22:16; chapter 30:8). **l)** namely Jerusalem, to be besieged after three years by the Chaldeans, and finally captured and destroyed. **v. 2.** **m)** Then you shall place, arrange, or fashion against it (v. 3). **n)** a blockade, i.e., the figure of a siege around the city. For the Prophet, like a civilian, was also skilled in military architecture. Compare the Preface. **o)** Deuteronomy 20:20. **p)** Kimchi: a wooden tower, which they used to build against a city to capture it. Rashi: from which they throw stones into the city. The commentators explore the military terminology and the symbolic "wall" between God and His people.</summary>

**v. 4. e)** *And you shall lie down;* and indeed truly so: for we do not think this was done only through a vision, but in the sight of others (v. 12; compare also v. 8 and chapter 3:25). See chapter 3:20, 25 and the note on 2 Samuel 12:11, chapter 16:10, and chapter 17:14. Here the Prophet carries the persona of the city and of the citizens soon to be besieged and bound; just as above he carried the persona of God and of the besiegers. **d)** *[lon]:* My word is like a bond of ropes; so Rashi and so Glassius: God is said to have applied ropes to the prophet while He constrains him by the authority of His word and confirms him by the power of His spirit, as if ropes were used, so that he would in no way desist from the established type of prophetic action, but openly make the firmness of the divine decree witnessed by a conspicuous sign. He is also told to eat strictly rationed, mixed-grain bread to symbolize the famine conditions of the impending Babylonian siege of Jerusalem.</summary>

Jeremiah 24:9. **v. 14. n)** Schmidt: "When I said." o) "Ah!" an exclamation of one crying out in pain and pleading. 2 Kings 6:5; Jeremiah 1:6; see below chapter 20:2. p) "It is polluted." q) Compare Leviticus 11:24, 44. **ℵ** <note>aleph, possibly indicating a specific manuscript or version</note> "A dead carcass." Deuteronomy 14:21. r) "Or torn apart." Chapter 44:31; Exodus 22:30; Leviticus 17:15; chapter 22:8. By synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note> he means all foods unclean by the law; as if to say, "let me not be forced to use something naturally unclean." s) "So that it did not even come into my mouth." Compare Acts 10:14. t) "Of a rotten and foul taste." Leviticus 7:18; 19:7; compare note on Isaiah 65:4. **v. 15. u)** "Then he said." x) "I permit." Compare verse 5. y) "Dung" or "fuel" <note>Hebrew: *tsfi'ei*</note>. Similarly in Ethiopian *Tseiph* is dung, and the Arabic root means "he excreted waste." z) "Instead of human [waste]." a) "That you may make [it]." **v. 16. b)** "Behold, I will break," etc. i.e., I will send famine upon them and take away bread, which is the support of man; and at the same time I will snatch away the ability to nourish themselves with what bread they might still have. Leviticus 26:26. It often happens in famine that men, though they eat, are never satisfied. See Hosea 4:10; Micah 6:14; Haggai 1:6; compare Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4; Lamentations 4:9. c) "The staff," a support; as if someone had lost the walking stick on which they lean. Chapter 5:16; 14:13; Ecclesiastes 3:1. d) "By weight," that is, weighed out, and indeed sparingly. Compare verse 10; Leviticus 26:26. e) "And in sorrow" <note>Hebrew: *be-de'agah*</note>. Chapter 12:18-19; Proverbs 12:25. They will fear while eating that the bread and water will run out, anxious about future food. f) Verse 11. g) "And with stupor, horror." Chapter 12:19; see the verb in verse 17 and chapter 26:16. **Cocceius:** Among the outcomes of the siege and deportation, "stupor" is listed. For what happened to Jerusalem occurred entirely against their hopes. They seemed to have fulfilled every duty: high places and idols were removed, the Passover was celebrated with great religious fervor, and the covenant with God was renewed; for this reason they were angry with the Prophets who predicted all these evils. — But they maintained the same [wicked] spirit — and worshipped God in hypocrisy. See the Preface to Jeremiah, § 7 and following. **v. 17. h)** "Because of the fact that." But Schmidt: "So that at last they lack." Thus also Vatablus refers this to the beginning of the preceding verse. Compare chapter 12:19; Isaiah 66:11; and Glassius, *Sacred Philology*, page 1129. i) "They shall lack," or "they will be in need of bread and water," i.e., food and drink. Compare 2 Kings 25:3; Jeremiah 52:6; Lamentations 4:9-10; chapter 2:11-12, etc. k) "And they shall be astonished." Verse 16; Jeremiah 4:9. l) i.e., "one with another" or "each one." Compare chapter 24:23; 33:30. m) "They shall waste away." Chapter 24:23; compare Lamentations 2:12, 19; Luke 21:26. Grotius: after long periods of meager food, he will fall lifeless here and there from hunger and thirst. n) "Because of their iniquity." Chapter 3:18; compare Leviticus 26:39. **CHAPTER V, v. 1. o)** Or "Moreover you." p) Chapter 2:1. q) Everything that has an edge and cuts is called this by the Hebrews. Compare the note on Joshua 5:2. Rashi: it prefigures the sword of Nebuchadnezzar. r) "Sharp." Psalm 57:5. s) Or "a razor." Isaiah 7:20; Numbers 6:5. t) "Of barbers." The same word in Chaldean [Aramaic] means this, from the Chaldean and Syriac **galab**, "razor." u) "Which you shall pass over." Compare chapter 14:17. Shaving the hair and beard was a sign of mourning (see Jeremiah 41:5; 48:37) and of inflicted disgrace (2 Samuel 10:4-5). x) Compare Judges 13:5; chapter 16:17. y) "So that none are exempt." Compare Psalm 7:20. z) "Balances of just weight." Chapter 45:10. A symbol of divine justice, which measures out to each what is fair. Psalm 7:13.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the prophetic signs performed by Ezekiel. Following the symbolic siege and the consumption of "unclean" bread, the prophet is now commanded to shave his head and beard, dividing the hair to represent the different fates awaiting the inhabitants of Jerusalem: death by plague/famine, death by the sword, or exile.</meta>

### 471 EZEKIEL. CHAP. 5. 

a) "so that you may divide the cut hair." See Isaiah 7:20. The relative suffix here lacks a direct noun antecedent but is easily understood from the context of the passage. Compare Numbers 7:89, Jonah 1:3, etc. **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> says: This is a second sign, very precise, of future events. The *razor* represents divine vengeance; the *scales* represent His justice; the *hairs* are the Jews; and the *division* represents the specific punishments assigned to each. Indeed, as **Schmid** <note>Sebastian Schmid (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian and Bible commentator.</note> observed, in this fifth chapter: I. A new sign is given to Ezekiel (v. 1-4). II. It is explained in relation to Jerusalem and the Jews (v. 5 and following). III. According to **Schmid**, some promise and consolation is also added (v. 13), though see the notes there.

v. 2, b) "a third part of them." The clearest explanation of this verse is found in verse 12. Compare Revelation 8:7-12 and Zechariah 13:8. c) "with fire" d) "you shall burn." See Nahum 2:14. This refers to the famine and pestilence in Jerusalem during the siege; so says **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note>, as explained in verse 12, for both famine and pestilence burn the body like fire. Compare the note on Deuteronomy 32:24. Others understand it more generally as divine wrath effective in various ways. See Jeremiah 44:6. **Junius** <note>FranciscuS Junius (1545–1602), a Huguenot theologian.</note> takes it to mean the burning of the city. **Raschi** <note>Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> applies it to famine, comparing Lamentations 5:10. e) **Grotius**, **Raschi**, **Kimchi** and others: "which you made for yourself out of clay." See chapter 4:1. f) "when they are fulfilled." Jeremiah 25:12. g) namely the 390 days during which you lay confined at home. Chapter 4:5, 8. h) "then you shall take." i) "and strike," or rather, "cut it into pieces," namely the hair itself. So the Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> uses the Greek *katakopseis* <note>original: "κατακόψεις", meaning "you shall cut down" or "strike".</note>. Mark 5:5. **Kimchi** says: Thus Zedekiah and his entourage, who had left the city, were overtaken by the Chaldeans and struck with the sword, etc. So also say **Vatablus** <note>François Vatable (d. 1547), a French humanist and Hebraist.</note> and **Raschi**. **Grotius** refers this to those who made sorties from the city into the enemy camp; others to the slaughter of the Jews wandering about during the time of the siege.

This signifies that they would flee here and there and wander with no fixed home, like hair or chaff which is

dispersed by the wind. Compare Ezekiel 41:16. m) "yet a sword." Others: "for a sword." n) "I will unsheathe after them." Verse 12, 17; Chapter 12:14; Leviticus 26:33. I will pursue them with a drawn sword so that they are in perpetual fear, exposed to the violence and injuries of everyone. **Kimchi** refers this to those who fled to Egypt with Johanan son of Kareah. Jeremiah 43:5, 6, 7. So also **Vatablus**. Others refer it to those who escaped to other regions or were led away to Babylon. We believe these opinions are better joined together than opposed to one another. Verse 3. o) "Yet you shall take." p) namely, from the third part that shall be dispersed among the nations. q) "some," a specific number. 2 Samuel 2:15. r) "and you shall bind them," that is, the hairs being bound together. Verse 24; Hosea 4:19. This is so that the "holy seed" (Isaiah 6:13) does not utterly perish. **Raschi**: This designates a very small number of those who were kept alive while being deported to Babylon. But according to **Grotius** and **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian.</note>, these are to be understood as the very few who remained in Judea by permission of Nebuchadnezzar, and those who returned from Babylon and lived freely in all lands, especially under the Romans, and fixed their home in the land. All these were very few in comparison with those who perished by so many plagues or remained in the dispersion. s) that is, in the hem of your garment. Compare chapter 7:2; Deuteronomy 22:12; Jeremiah 2:34. Verse 4. t) "Finally, of those bound hairs (v. 3), you shall again take some." u) "fire," namely, of divine wrath. Jeremiah 4:4; Zephaniah 3:8. For example, through civil war between Gedaliah and Ishmael, which is described more fully in Jeremiah 40 and following. **Raschi** compares this for completion to Jeremiah 29:21, 22. x) "from it a fire shall go forth." Judges 9:15, 20. **Grotius**: Those civil unrests gave the Chaldeans the occasion to remove even the lowliest person from Judea, leaving no one behind, as those were the seeds of new rebellions. Compare Jeremiah 52:30. **Cocceius** on this passage says: This signifies that God will make a distinction among those remaining in the land, carrying some in his bosom while burning others—not so much with material fire, but with the fire of His wrath, handing them over to a curse and the perpetual torment of a bad conscience. This fire or judgment and curse would proceed to the whole house of Israel, except for those He retains as if in His bosom. Therefore, this chapter should be taken as referring not only to the first destruction of Jerusalem but also the second; it is a type of both. See notes on v. 9, 10. Verse 5. y) "For thus says the Lord." Here follows the explanation of the preceding sign regarding Jerusalem: and indeed (1) divine favors in this verse; (2) its sins in verse 6 and 7; (3) judgment and punishments generally in verses 7, 8, 9, then specifically in verse 10, and most specifically in verse 12 and following. z) "This," namely this city depicted on the side, is Jerusalem, and those hairs signify the inhabitants of Jerusalem especially. See note on verse 1. a) "among the nations" as if a princess (Lamentations 1:1), placed in the highest honor and love. See below, chapter 16:14; Psalm 78:68; Psalm 87:2, etc. **Grotius**: so that the Egyptians, Syrians, Arabs, Africans, and Greeks might take an example of piety from her, and so others gradually. b) "and around her" various lands and provinces of other nations. Verse 6. c) "But she rebelled." [Grammatical note on the verb *vatemer*]. Compare Deuteronomy 1:26, 43; 9:7, 24; 31:27; Psalm 105:28; Psalm 106:33. d) verse 7, that is, 1 Kings 9:4. e) "into wickedness." Compare Ephesians 5:7; Amos 5:7; Romans 1:25. Others: "she rebelled against my judgments toward wickedness," that is, impiously and stubbornly. f) "more than the nations," even more than the Gentiles, than whom the Jews were worse because they sinned knowingly and willingly. 2 Kings 21:9; Ephesians 2:6; compare Jeremiah 2:10. g) for the Gentiles retain their rites invented by men better than these Jews retained those given by God. **Grotius**. See chapter 20:24. h) chapter 20:13, 16; Jeremiah 8:9; Leviticus 26:43. Verse 7. i) "Therefore:" Here begins the proclamation of divine punishment and judgment. Compare verses 8, 10, 11. k) **Schmid** reads it actively: "Because you have multiplied evils more than the nations." See verse 9; chapter 16:15-48; 23:11-27; also Ephesians 2:5. **Kimchi** reads it passively: "because of your being multiplied," that is, because you became a great people while I multiplied you and increased you with goods more than the surrounding nations, yet you did not walk in my statutes. Compare Deuteronomy 28:15; Hosea 2:10. So also **Gusset** <note>Jacques Gousset (1635–1704), a French Hebraist.</note> on page 215. He correctly argues with **Kimchi** that this is an infinitive from the root *hamon* (to multiply) rather than a related noun *hamon*, as some wish, though a similar construction exists in Job 35:2. [Grammatical explanation follows regarding the vowel change before a suffix]. **Gusset** is wrong, however, in denying that the word *ya'an* (because) can be joined with a noun. See here verse 9 and Haggai 1:9. **Raschi** interprets it: "because you have appointed yourselves to act stubbornly, even more than the nations," from a root meaning "to count/appoint" (compare Daniel 1:5), but this goes against grammar. More correctly, **Rabbi Menachem** <note>Menachem ben Saruq (c. 910–970), a Spanish Jewish philologist.</note> compares it to Psalm 46:7, 4: "because of your being tumultuous," or as **Cocceius** has it: "because you are more turbulent." For both the verb *hamah* and the noun *hamon* signify a multitude, a great crowd, and much noise. See Isaiah 17:12; 31:4; 22:2; Ezekiel 7:11, etc. On this interpretation, **Cocceius** notes: They did not have the righteousness of faith, nor did they place their righteousness in abstaining from evil deeds and in good works and laudable actions, as the more honest among the Gentiles did. Instead, they placed their holiness in those very things by which they were declared impure (Ezekiel 20:25, 26). This is what it means to be turbulent and to mix many things that cannot be mixed and joined. For to confess sin, yet to place righteousness in one's own works, and to attribute the expiation of sin to the blood of cattle, and to consider the observation of those precepts (in which a man does not live) as the fulfillment of the law... and to call God the Sanctifier while not acknowledging true sanctification—this is nothing but confusion, entanglement, and perplexity. l) see verses 5 and 6.

<meta>Note on the Hebrew text: The phrase "and my statutes" appears without the Kadma accent here, similar to Genesis 11, 17, 19. </meta>

<summary>This page explains Ezekiel's symbolic action of shaving his hair and dividing it into three parts, representing the various ways the inhabitants of Jerusalem will perish or be scattered. The commentary explores the linguistic roots of the people's "rebellion" and "turbulence," noting they became more spiritually confused and wicked than the pagan nations surrounding them.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Ezekiel 5, specifically verses 7 through 13. The previous page established the symbolic actions of the prophet (shaving his hair and dividing it). This page provides the divine explanation for those actions, emphasizing that Jerusalem’s punishment will be unprecedented because her disobedience was likewise unprecedented compared to the surrounding nations.</meta>

The Jews imitated the Gentiles, either by defending Gentile opinions or by adopting the rites and sacred things of the nations. But they did not act like the Gentiles, who served their gods with integrity. For the Israelites abused the name of God while still wishing to appear as His people.

See Deuteronomy 28:53, 2 Kings 6:28, 29, Lamentations 2:20, chapter 4:10, and **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> in *The Jewish War*, Book 7, chapter 21. Although we do not read that these things [cannibalism] happened in Jerusalem when it was besieged and captured by the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians in 586 BC.</note>, nothing prevents us from referring this to the final destruction of this city under the leadership of Titus Vespasian [in 70 AD]; for it is not unusual among the Prophets to look toward both immediate events and the most remote events simultaneously. Christ himself provides an example in Matthew 24. See the note on Isaiah 6:9 and chapter 24:1. At the same time, this notes the internal dissensions and mutual slaughters with which the Jews raged against their own kin; compare the note above on verse 4, Isaiah 9:11, 19, 20, Luke 12:35, Galatians 5:19. **c)** Verse 15, chapter 14:21, Ezekiel 6:6, 5. Compare Isaiah 24:11, Jeremiah 18:17, and above verse 2. This is said regarding punishments; however, <term>Messiah</term> <note>original: "מְשִׁיחַ" (Mashiach)</note> is also used in a good sense. **d)** "and I will disperse," chapter 12:14, chapter 17:21, Jeremiah 49:32, 36. **e)** "and into all quarters of the world," verses 2, 12, chapter 12:14, chapter 17:21, so that they will eventually be a people without a republic or homeland. Hosea 3:4, Daniel 9:27. **Kimchi**: Some went to Egypt, others to Babylon, and so also to the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, and into other regions. See 2 Kings 25:26. **v. 11. f)** Jeremiah 4:2. See note on Deuteronomy 32:40, 1 Samuel 20:3. **g)** Numbers 24:3, Isaiah 1:24, Hosea 11:11. **h)** As if to say: "May I no longer be considered a living God by you, if I do not..." etc. Compare Joshua 14:9, Isaiah 5:9, Jeremiah 22:6. **i)** "because," 1 Samuel 15:23. **k)** "you have polluted my sanctuary"; namely, by placing idols in the temple. 2 Kings 21:4, 5, 7. **l)** Isaiah 66:3, Jeremiah 4:1, chapter 13:27. **m)** "with their idols and execrable crimes." Verse 8. **Cocceius**: We must not only understand here the idols they brought into the temple, but also the spiritual harlotry and idolatry they carried into the temple when they wished to appear to worship the true God. Let us, who are from the Gentiles (to whom Jerusalem was meant to be an example, verse 8) and who see the judgment of Israel, learn above all that God is offended by nothing more than the profanation of His name. This is emphatically expressed by these various words. Compare note on chapter 3, verse 11. **n)** "therefore I also," through most just reasoning, verse 8. **o)** "I will diminish," including His benevolence, His word, His blessing, the Spirit, prophecy, the kingdom of God, and the republic from them. **p)** Compare chapter 7, verses 4, 9. **q)** "Even though you see yourself as most miserable." To spare is an act of the mind, but it is attributed to the eyes as the indicators; for these are the leaders in love and mercy. Compare I. chapter 2. 8, 18. **Jonah**. The word <term>to spare</term> <note>original: "חָמַל" (chamal)</note>. See Exodus 23:21. **r)** Jeremiah 13:14. **v. 12. s)** "For a third part of you." See notes for the whole of verse 2. **t)** "by pestilence," which usually follows famine, they shall die. See verse 17, chapter 7:15, Jeremiah 29:17. **u)** "or by famine," see verse 16, 17, chapter 4:16. **x)** Jeremiah 16:4, Psalm 71:13. **y)** See verse 2, 17, chapter 6:12, chapter 11:10. **z)** Verse 2, Jeremiah 12:7. **a)** Future Piel [verb form], verse 10. **b)** "so that with a sword drawn I will pursue them as they flee." Verses 2, 17. **Cocceius**: After the Jews were dispersed among the nations, they lived first for a long time under the fear of the sword of the nations; then they were also killed in great numbers by the sword of Hadrian Caesar. I pass over their other calamities in silence. **v. 13. c)** "so it will be completed," or fully exert itself against them. **Schmid**: "When it is completed, however," chapter 7:8, Deuteronomy 32:23. **d)** "and I will cause it to rest," so that it remains upon them for a long time and does not pass quickly. Chapter 16:42, chapter 21:22, Zechariah 6:8. **e)** Preterite Hithpael for <term>and I will be comforted</term> <note>original: "וְהִתְנֶחַמְתִּי" (ve-hitnachamti)</note>. "And I will comfort myself," as if being upright through consolation, I will forget all the iniquity by which they provoked me to anger. **Abendana** <note>Jacob Abendana (1630–1695), a Sephardic rabbi and scholar.</note>: There will be such peace that God also will finally repent of that [anger]. Compare Genesis 6:6. So also **Schmid**: "it will repent me." For according to Schmid’s version, as well as **Maius’s** *Economy of the Old Testament*, page 1033, and some others, this is a promise of pardon or consolation; according to others, however, it is a threat, so that the sense is: "I will comfort myself through the vengeance taken for the insult received," which seems more consistent with the preceding and following context. Compare Genesis 37:35, Isaiah 1:24, Deuteronomy 32:36, also Deuteronomy 28:63. **f)** "so that they may know," being taught by experience. Chapter 6:10, Hosea 9:7.

**Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi, a 12th-13th century grammarian</note>: [of those] whose whoring heart I have broken <note>original: "quorum fractus sum corde scortante"</note>, comparing this to Genesis 6:6.
**Schmidt** <note>Sebastian Schmidt, 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note>: with those whose [heart] was broken, etc. **Ficinus-Grotius**: [interpreting as] I was broken, that is, I was affected by grief because of their harlot-like heart; compare Jeremiah 23:9 and Psalm 51:19.

Therefore, once led into captivity, they will remember...

**CHAPTER VII. v. 1. n)** v. 6, 1. This is the final prophecy issued in the fifth year of King Zedekiah, comparing ch. 1:2 and ch. 8:1, by which the Prophet expressly indicates that the end of the Israelite or Jewish state <note>original: "reipublicae Israeliticae"</note> is immediately at hand. And to move the Jews toward repentance, he repeats this again and again in v. 2 and following. **II.** He predicts the total consternation of the people and their inability to resist in v. 13 and following. **III.** He explains the cause, especially idolatry, in v. 20. **IV.** He confirms the message with the sign of a chain, showing that the survivors will be bound and led away in v. 23.
</margin>

and visible to everyone. **Cocceius** says: As if to say, the disturbances will appear as if they were committed in a single day, which were actually committed throughout a long stretch of time: so that every person might understand and recall to mind which actions of the Israelites are being refuted and punished by these plagues. Others [interpret] through the omission of the word <term>asher</term> <note>the relative pronoun "which"</note>: "which were perpetrated in your midst." **v. 9. 27. ch. 6:7.** **v. 5. a)** that is, a singular and greatest and most holy [punishment]. **Kimchi**: to which no likeness is given, compare ch. 5:9. **Rashi**: the greatest evil, altogether peculiar and surpassing all others, was the desolation of the Temple. **Jonathan**: evil after evil, as if to say, one after another. **f) v. 6, 10. Jeremiah 10:22.** **v. 6. g)** v. 2, 3. For in the fifth year of Zedekiah, Ezekiel began to prophesy in Babylon to the captives (ch. 1:1), but in the ninth year Nebuchadnezzar surrounded Jerusalem with a siege, which he captured in the eleventh (2 Kings 25:1, 3); see the notes on v. 1. **h)** compare Amos 8:2. **i)** "it has awakened" (Ephesians 29:8). God, as if having broken His sleep; or, "vengeance rushes upon you, being fully awake." Observe the emphatic <term>paronomasia</term> <note>a play on words: here between *qetz* (end) and *heqitz* (awakened)</note>: see Ephesians 5:7, Jeremiah 31:2. **k)** upon you. v. 13; ch. 6:13. **l)** compare notes on Ephesians 3:1, Jeremiah 31:8, Hosea 9:6. **m)** specifically, the evil. v. 5. **v. 7. n)** **Cocceius** in his Lexicon and some with him: "The order" or "the circle has come to you," v. 10, comparing Job 4:5. **Jonathan**: "the kingdom," from Ephesians 28:5. **Kimchi & Abarbanel** <note>Isaac Abarbanel, 15th-century statesman and commentator</note>: a girding or a surrounding of evils sent by God, comparing Judges 9:3. So **Drusius** observes that **Theodotion** interprets this as <term>strophē</term> <note>turning/turning point</note>, that is, the order and weaving together of all evils. Thus, as **Grotius** himself observes, it seems to refer to the Arabic *Dafron*, "plaited work." But **Schmidt** and others: "The morning has come upon you, upon the inhabitant," from the Chaldean <term>tsaphra</term>, "dawn" (referring back to "the morning" in v. 6), which according to Grotius is a sign; for judgements were exercised in the morning, and thus he shakes off the lethargy in which they had become numb, promising themselves perpetual peace as if they would never be called to judgement. v. 12; see note on Hosea 9:7. **p)** ch. 30:3. **q)** "a day, a day of tumult," I say, and of calamity. Zephaniah 1:14, Ephesians 22:5; similar construction below in ch. 40:15, comparing Psalm 133:2. **r)** **Schmidt**: "and not of the vintage-shout"; that is, the song or happy cry of the vine-dressers or grape-gatherers on the wine-bearing mountains. **(i)** For **Cocceius**, it is the interjection "hurrah!" compare the Hebrew <term>hedad</term> in Ephesians 16:9, 10; Jeremiah 25:30; ch. 48:33. **Kimchi**: "This tumult will not be like the cry of the mountains," that is, an echo: "but it will be a voice of crying and noise, a true voice [of enemies], not a likeness of a voice." **Abarbanel**: "glory or beauty will not remain on the mountains," as if it were the same as the word for "majesty" <note>Hebrew *hod*</note> in Hosea 14:7. **Jonathan**: "neither will it be allowed to escape into the steep fortifications of the mountains." **v. 8. s)** For now. **t)** "from nearby," that is, shortly. Compare Deuteronomy 32:17, Job 20:5. **Rashi**: "hastily." **u)** ch. 5:13; ch. 22:31; Lamentations 2:1; ch. 4:11. **x)** ch. 6:12. **y)** v. 3. **z)** "that I may repay upon you." see v. 3, 4. **v. 9. a)** "Neither shall you spare," etc. v. 4. **b)** **Schmidt**: "Your abominations." Others: "and according to your abominations which are in your midst." See v. 4; ch. 6:7, 13. **d)** "striking." He adds this unique detail to the fourth verse repeated here: that this judgement will be such that it is apparent to all that these plagues are not inflicted by chance or some common misfortune, as with other nations, but by Him whom they called their God, yet did not acknowledge nor glorify as their Savior and their righteousness. —**Cocceius**. Compare Ephesians 9:12, Hosea 6:1, etc. **v. 10. e)** Behold, the day is ready! v. 7; Joel 2:1, 2. **f)** behold, the predicted evil arrives. v. 5, 6; ch. 30:9; compare Ephesians 66:18. **g)** it has gone forth, the morning has arisen; that morning spoken of in v. 7. **Cocceius** in Lexicon p. 326: "the wheel has turned, the period has gone out." The measure of patience is finished. The time has come to present past sins in judgement, as a circle returns upon itself.

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the book of Ezekiel. Following the discussion of the "desert of Diblah" at the end of chapter 6, the focus here is Ezekiel 7:10–17, which describes the "day of doom" approaching Jerusalem. The text continues to weigh the opinions of medieval Jewish commentators like Rashi and Kimchi against 17th-century Christian Hebraists like Grotius, Cocceius, and Gussetius.</meta>

of themselves. Others refer this to the Chaldeans in this sense: "These increases of empire and power do not come from them, nor from the multitude of people; nor from the noise and tumult of armies, but from God, who made them your scourge." But **Cocceius** shows that this kingdom is foreign: therefore he says, it is not "from them"; and distinctly, nor "from their multitude"—just as many kings in the ten tribes arose from the multitude—nor from their "noise," by which the capture of the kings of the sons of David is hinted; but another King and other (foreign) lords have gained power over them. **q)** *from their multitude or the common people*. Ecclesiastes 5:14, chapter 31:4. **Kimchi**: *from the multitude of their riches*, comparing Psalm 37:16, Ecclesiastes 5:9. **r)** *from the noise or noises of them*, i.e., according to some, the nobles, who walk with the noise of attendants. (1) root *hamah* of the form *Yephah* or *Kaneh*. Others, using the doubled letters with the pronoun, translate with the Rabbis: *from them*, as if to say: "absolutely nothing will remain of them." So **Schmidt**: *from those living ones*. **Jonathan**: *from their children*; perhaps because they disturb and make a tumult. **s)** *mourning, lamentation* (1) Root *nahah*, Micah 2:4. **Kimchi**: *due to the multitude of distresses, the living will not weep for the dead*. see Jeremiah 16:4-7, 25:33. **t)** *because of them*. Or *in them*. **Cocceius** interprets: "thus the scepter of the house of David and the power of the princes will be taken away; and the freedom to appoint a king for themselves, so that there is no one among them who performs a 'laying out' <note>original: "lectum faciat"</note> or wails, as was customary for Kings in Jeremiah 34:5. For everyone will be forced to hide their grief because of the rule of the Tyrant." But **Gussetius** (p. 498) derives it from the *root* *na'ah*, *beauty, appearance, form*, the loss of all of which is announced, after the preceding verse said they flourished in the practice of their malice and pride. Thus, by analogy from *yan ya'oh*, which **Cocceius** and others derive from the root *na'ah*. see note on Ephesians 12:2; compare also Hiller's *Sacred Onomasticon* p. 251. **v. 12.** **u)** *see v. 7. x) it arrives*. Song of Solomon 2:12, Esther 2:12. That is, it will come most nearly and certainly; a Prophetic Past tense, as in Ephesians 5:13, chapter 9:2, Jeremiah 15:7 and 9. **y)** *buyer*. Proverbs 20:14. **z)** *because he will not enjoy the whole thing, for the Chaldeans will plunder it, and so he will lose his money*. see Hosea 9:1. **a)** *let him not mourn*; namely, because he is forced to sell out of poverty, and for a time, as if not having an inheritance; he lives among brothers (see Nehemiah 5:3, 4.) **s)** *because, even if he had not sold it, he would still have lost it. Thus the lot of the poor and the rich will be the same.* **b)** *for the burning wrath (v. 14) goes out over the entire multitude of the city and region.* **v. 13. 14. c)** *the thing sold* (10) Nehemiah 13:20. **d)** *as used to happen in the Jubilee year*, see Leviticus 25:10, 13. Nor does Jeremiah 32:15 contradict this place. For Ezekiel is dealing with parents and the present; and especially addresses the wicked, excluded from the hope of liberation; while Jeremiah speaks of children and the future, addressing the faithful, so that they might hope for restitution. **e)** *even if it still is. or yet will be. it subsists.* from the preceding with the negation. **f)** *among the living is their life*, i.e., although they will remain alive until the Jubilee, they will not reclaim what was sold, because they will be under the power of others, and they themselves in a foreign land. **Cocceius**: *meanwhile, the life of the sellers will be among the living*, i.e., they will carry away their life as a spoil. Jeremiah 45:5. **g)** see Psalm 143:3, Job 33:18, 28, 36:14. **h)** *prophetic vision*, Ephesians 1:1, i.e., the prophecy or judgment of God shown to me in a vision. see Ephesians 21:2; and observe here again the wordplay <note>term: paronomasia (a play on words)</note> between *chazon* (vision) in v. 13 and *charon* (wrath) in this place. **i)** *to, upon, or against its whole multitude*. **v. 13. k)** *it shall be turned away, retracted by God, nor will it be in vain or return empty, but it will be fulfilled*. see chapter 12:22, Ephesians 12:1, Numbers 23:20, Ephesians 43:13, 45:23, 55:11. Others: *because the vision of the prophets was to all his people, calling them to repentance, yet they did not turn; or, it will not be repeated, but finished in one time.* **l)** *everyone whose life is in his iniquity. An omission of the relative pronoun, as in Exodus 4:13, Ecclesiastes 55:5, 56:2.* **Cocceius** restricts and limits this way what he had said before, that the life of the sellers would remain among the living, namely that whoever's life is in his own wickedness, they will not survive. But **Jonathan**: *everyone who delights in the sins of his soul*. so **Rashi**. **m)** *they will not be strengthened, because they refuse to repent, so that they might stand against the enemies and reduce God's vengeance to nothing. See the following, and compare 2 Samuel 10:12. A plural verb is joined to a singular collective noun for the sake of distribution, as is often done.* **v. 14. n)** *By blowing they shall blow, or let them blow, and sound the trumpet, to go out to meet the approaching enemy*. **Schmidt** takes it as a Proper Name, in *Tekoa*; but to **Cocceius** it is rather an absolute infinitive, used as a noun with the article: since *Tekoa*, the name of a town in the tribe of Judah, is written with a Shua at the beginning, as in 2 Samuel 14:2, Jeremiah 6:1, Amos 1:1, etc. **Gussetius** says this name joined to the verb seems to note the highest exertion: and perhaps it is nothing other than the sound itself. **o)** *by preparing, namely, they shall prepare or let them prepare all things required for war*. see Nahum 2:4, Psalm 7:17, 13. **r)** *see v. 12, 13.* **v. 15. s)** *Outside, in the fields it will be, or it will kill them. Jeremiah 6:11, v. 11, Hosea 7:1. t) inside the city, as follows.* **u)** *chapter 5:12, 6:12. see Lamentations 1:20, Jeremiah 14:12, 15.* **v. 16. x)** *Even if they should escape. Kal (1) Piel more frequently. y) some escapees from among them, chapter 6:8. x) yet they will all and each be s) upon the mountains (chapter 6:12) and rocks, seeking places inconvenient for living, for the sake of preserving their lives. see Judges 6:2, Matthew 24:16. b) like doves of the valleys; which, for fear of the fowler or the hawk, having deserted their natural home, are forced to go elsewhere to look out for their lives. The mountain doves are contrasted with those of the valleys, like wild animals with domestic ones.* **Bochart** <note>Samuel Bochart, 17th-century naturalist and scholar</note>, *Hierozoicon* II. p. 17. **c)** *of the valleys* 1 Kings 21:16. **d)** *moaning* Ephesians 59:11. For there is something plaintive and moaning in the voice of the dove and the turtledove; whence **Virgil** <note>Roman poet</note>: *Nor shall the turtledove cease to moan from the airy elm*. **Bochart**, ibid. p. 12, 13. **e)** *everyone chapter 1:9, f) because of his iniquity.* **v. 13.** Chapter 3:18, 19.

**h) v. 11. m)** *Violence, namely of the Chaldeans, those violent and predatory men*. see v. 21, 24. But **Rashi** and others: *the violence which is in your hand shall rise against you, like a rod of wickedness to destroy you*. see Habakkuk 1:2, 9. **n)** *it rises up, it girds itself.* **o)** *so that it becomes a rod for punishing your wickedness*. But **Grotius**: *against that wicked rod (the tribe of Judah)* is present (the violent Chaldean) to cut it out by the roots. But **Cocceius**: *violence, opposed to love for one's neighbor (Genesis 6:11, 13), grew into a rod or scepter of wickedness, it produces the rule of the wicked over you, after God's scepter and the government of the righteous are taken away, so that you are handed over to the hand of a wicked ruler; so that your own violence leads you to such a kingdom, and this seems to have blossomed from your injuries. That wicked King is Nebuchadnezzar and his successors; the Medes and Persians, Greeks and Romans. see Psalm 125:3, Ephesians 14:5. p)* The interpreters vary. Some refer it to the Jews, so the sense is: "No one will remain among them immune from evil, nor from the multitude..."

It contrasts Jewish and Christian interpretations regarding whether the "rod" of punishment represents Israel's pride or the invading King Nebuchadnezzar.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Ezekiel 7. Having previously discussed the "day of doom," the text now explores the physical and emotional reactions of the people (verses 17–19), the worthlessness of their wealth, and the eventual desecration of the Temple (verses 20–25) by the "worst of nations."</meta>

->### EZEKIEL. CHAPTER 7.###<-
->Ppp 2, 474<-

<margin>
***Verse 17. g)** "They will be weakened out of fear." See Ezekiel 21:12; Isaiah 13:7. **h)** See Ezekiel 35:3; Job 4:4; Psalm 109:24. **i)** "They will turn into water," meaning they will seem to dissolve into water so that they falter and cannot resist the enemies. Just as elsewhere the heart, or even the men themselves, are said to melt from fear and desperation; for example, Exodus 15:15; Deuteronomy 1:28; Joshua 2:9, 24, etc. See notes on 2 Samuel 17:10. **Kimchi** <note>Rabbi David Kimhi, medieval grammarian</note>: "so that there is no strength in them because of the greatest consternation."
</margin>

<margin>
***Verse 18. k)** "They will gird themselves with sackcloth," as was done in the deepest sorrow. Isaiah 3:17, 24; Jeremiah 48:37. **l)** "For it will cover," it will invade them from every side. Jeremiah 51:51; Micah 7:10. **m)** "Trembling, horror." Isaiah 21:4; Psalm 55:6; Job 21:6. **n)** "There will be shame and disgrace." Obadiah verse 10. **o)** "Baldness due to hair being plucked out," a sign of mourning. Ezra 9:3. This was otherwise forbidden to the Jews in private mourning (Deuteronomy 14:1). Thus **Grotius**, e.g., homicides and other crying sins. Jeremiah 36:31. **e)** "The worst and most cruel of nations." See Numbers 34:29; Joshua 13:32; 14:1; 19:51. **k)** "Those who sanctify them," that is, the priests, who hypocritically sanctify the nobles and the people with Mosaic rites, having no regard for dignity or true repentance. (See Isaiah 3:13; chapter 9:15; Micah 3:5; Ezekiel 13:10.) They shall be killed as profane or led away. For truly Jehovah, the Son of God, is the Holy One of Israel (Isaiah 1:4; 30:21; 47:4) and the one who sanctifies Israel (Ezekiel 20:12; 37:28; Leviticus 20:8; 21:8, 15, 23, etc.). Therefore, whatever does not have Him as its author is profane in religion. God. See Psalm 16:4 and notes on 1 Kings 12:32. **Grotius** understands the Temple in the plural number, due to its three parts into which it was divided (see Psalm 68:36; Jeremiah 51:51), which is called "theirs" because God no longer considered the Temple polluted by them as His own. **Cocceius** in the same place: "the things that sanctify them shall be profaned," which separate and distinguish them from the impure nations. **Verse 25. l)** "Destruction," see the verb in Ezekiel 38:12. **m)** Or, "therefore they shall seek peace" (Psalm 34:15) but find it nowhere. See Jeremiah 8:15, 11; 14:19; Isaiah 48:22; 57:21; 59:8; Hosea 5:5. **Piscator** <note>Johannes Piscator, German theologian</note>: "The Jews will seek peace by excusing Zedekiah before Nebuchadnezzar, etc."

<summary>This page analyzes Ezekiel 7:18–25, focusing on the psychological terror of the coming judgment where wealth becomes useless ("unclean") and the Holy of Holies is profaned by "the worst of the nations." The commentary contrasts the Jews' false pride in the physical Temple with the reality of their impending captivity and the withdrawal of the Divine Presence (Shekhinah).</summary>

<summary>This page concludes the warnings of Ezekiel 7, where the collapse of religious and social leadership is predicted, and begins the vivid vision of Chapter 8. The Prophet is supernaturally transported to the Jerusalem Temple to witness the "image of jealousy" that provokes God's departure from His sanctuary.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the vision narrative from the end of Chapter 7. Having described the impending doom of Jerusalem, the text now moves into Chapter 8, where the Prophet Ezekiel is supernaturally transported to the Temple in Jerusalem to witness the specific "abominations"—acts of idolatry—that have provoked Divine judgment. This page covers the "Image of Jealousy" and the secret "Chambers of Imagery" where the elders of Israel are practicing forbidden rites.</meta>

# 475 EZEKIEL. CHAPTER 8

<margin>
**q)** Chapter 43:3. **r)** Chapter 3:22, 23.
**s)** Genesis 13:14; Zechariah 5:5. **t)** The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> version says "northward," as in chapter 40:20, 46. **x)** See the note for verse 3. Others believe this gate was named for Solomon’s altar, which King Ahaz moved from the middle of the court to the northern gate; see 2 Kings 16:14. Others, following **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi, a major medieval Jewish commentator</note>, believe an altar was erected for the idol mentioned in verse 3, and the gate was named for it. **y)** at the entrance. **z)** In this way, the worship of God was hindered, and impious worship was substituted in its place. The location of the crime increases its gravity and exposes their shamelessness. Compare 2 Kings 21:4, 5, etc.
</margin>

**5** Then He said to me, "Son of man, lift up your eyes now toward the north." So I lifted up my eyes toward the north, and behold, northward of the altar gate <margin>x</margin>, this "Image of Jealousy" was at the entrance <margin>y</margin>.

**6** And He said to me <margin>z</margin>, "Son of man, do you see what they are doing? The great abominations <margin>a b</margin> that the House of Israel is committing here, to drive Me far <margin>c</margin> from My sanctuary? But turn again, and you will see even greater abominations <margin>d e f</margin>."

**7** So He brought me to the door of the court <margin>g h i k l</margin>; and when I looked, behold, there was a hole in the wall.

<margin>
* **v. 6. a)** He makes the Prophet a witness and an indicator; likewise in verses 12, 15, 17 and Jeremiah 3:6. **b)** "what they themselves do." The construction is emphatic, as in Exodus 4:1, Isaiah 3:15, and Malachi 1:13. **v)** "abominations etc." verses 13, 15; chapter 8:11. **c)** "so that I may withdraw far away" (using the Infinitive with a paragogic He, as in Exodus 30:18), that is, so that I might abandon the care of this temple and be forced to depart from there. Compare Jeremiah 12:7; Isaiah 65:5; or so that they themselves may finally withdraw; see below, chapter 11:23. **d)** "but furthermore" or "besides." Chapter 20:27. **e)** "again you shall see others," that is, you shall see other outrages. Verse 13; compare Genesis 26:18. **f)** 1 Kings 13:33. **f)** The Septuagint reads: "abominations greater than these." So also in verse 13; compare verse 15. However, **Abarbanel** <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century statesman and commentator</note> thinks that a comparison was not intentionally intended here or in verse 13.
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 7. g)** verses 14, 15; chapter 40:1. **h)** at the door of the inner court, that is, according to **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century scholar of the Temple</note>, at the Eastern gate, which was then the most frequented by travelers, and where the Great Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme council and court of justice in ancient Israel</term> sat at that time. Compare verse 3. **i)** where I saw. **k)** verses 2, 4. **l)** there was a hole there. Isaiah 11:8; 2 Kings 12:10. These were the princes of the people, or rather the priests (for whom this place was designated). According to **Lightfoot's** <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century scholar of the Temple and Hebrew customs</note> *Chronology* (p. 124), they were the heads of the 24 priestly classes and the High Priest himself. It is unlikely, however—as some Jews report from the **Talmudic** writings—that they uncovered themselves toward the Temple or emitted obscene sounds or excrement. **h)** and they were bowing themselves. The Hebrew form is a Chaldean-style construction of a participle and a verb or pronoun; as if the Prophet, speaking of the twenty-five men in the vision, was simultaneously rebuking the people present before him as guilty of the same crime. Where the Jews are mentioned as having sinned with idolatry in that same part. r) of destruction, or of his scattering (1) see Jeremiah 51:20 and following. s) but *one* man. Munster <note>Sebastian Münster, a 16th-century Hebraist</note>: There were six destroyers, and one deliverer. But as to who this man was in terms of his person, the interpreters disagree. Our commentators say *Christ*; others say the *Holy Spirit*. Grotius says an *Angel*; the Jews say *Gabriel*, as we shall soon mention. t) <term>clothed in linen</term> <note>original Hebrew: לבוש בדים</note> (chapter 10:6, 7). Clothed in a garment reaching to the feet <note>original Greek: ποδήρη; see Revelation 1:13</note> made of the finest linen, such as the High Priest wore (Leviticus 6:3, 16:4, 23). This same attire is given here and in Daniel 10:5 and 12:6-7 to the Angel, which is also given to the High Priest; for both are ministers of God (Grotius). The Talmudists, however, in tractate *Yoma* (chapter 8, folio 77) and elsewhere, understand this to be Gabriel; which Rashi confirms there and in his commentary on chapter 10:2, as does Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval rabbi</note> in this place. According to our interpreters, it was rather *Christ* himself, the one mediator and intercessor and Savior of his people (1 Timothy 2:5), the Angel of the Covenant (Malachi 3:1), the Prince of the Lord's army (Joshua 5:14). Hence the other six angels in verse 2 are commanded to follow him. Furthermore, the instruments he carries are not deadly like the others, but life-giving (see verse 4). Nor is it inconsistent for Christ to be foreshadowed by various figures in one vision, just as he was prefigured in sacrifices by the priest, the victim, the altar, and so on. For the offices of Christ are various, and a single thing cannot shadow them all at once. In this way, Christ—the image of the invisible God—sits on the same throne with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and yet, as he is man (as the mystery of the Incarnation is prefigured here) and less than the Father, he receives and executes commands. Compare Junius, Calovius, and Maius. For Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century theologian</note>, however, this man clothed in the long robe symbolically signifies the Spirit of God, marking the faithful (see note on verse 4), and the long robe represents those whom the Spirit carries and holds joined to himself, in whom he dwells and works, who are like his garment. Thus, Salomon van Til on Malachi 3:16: the Holy Spirit himself is depicted having an inkhorn at his loins. u) and an inkhorn (3) verse 3, part II. Which scribes are accustomed to use. So Schmid and most others rightly suggest; although Castellus, without sufficient reason, thinks it is better rendered as a *girdle* or *belt*, along with the Septuagint, Arabic, and Syrian versions, who nonetheless also render <term>the scribe</term> (<term>הסופר</term>) as a sapphire belt, which Cocceius also observed in his Lexicon. x) at his loins, or on one of his loins. See Guiset page 52, folio 4. y) and they entered the inner court. z) and they stood, waiting for the divine nod and command. a) of burnt offerings (1 Kings 8:64) namely according to Grotius, as those who were about to prepare many victims for God. For thus the wicked are often called, upon whom God wishes to take vengeance (Isaiah 34:6, Jeremiah 12:3, chapter 46:10, Ezekiel 39:17). But Cocceius says: a place was given to them at the altar itself, where the atonement for sin was typically made. From this we understand that God decreed this visitation of the city because they had provoked him by offering sacrifices and had accumulated guilt, rather than expiating their sins, seeking righteousness (from the work performed) in the shedding of the blood of cattle. v. 3. b) chapter 10:4. c) it was lifted up, it was being taken up (Exodus 40:36-37, Numbers 10:11). d) from the Cherubim, who were in the inner sanctuary upon the mercy seat; compare Lundius pages 65-66. Upon which the glory of the Lord then appeared to the prophet (above, chapter 8:4). e) upon which it had been before. See Psalm 80:2. f) withdrawing himself to the threshold of the temple (chapter 10:4, 18), to signify that he would now depart from the place because of the impiety of the people, and to draw closer to the ministers of his judgments, and as if sitting before a tribunal, to command that they lay waste the city. g) verses 1, 4. h) chapter 10:2, 6. i) verse 2, part II. v. 4. k) see verse 1. l) <term>Tau</term> (<term>תו</term>), a sign (6). 1 Samuel 21:14. m) a sign; by which those killers might recognize who was to be spared (3). verse 6. Job 31:35. Others think the letter <term>Tau</term> was impressed on their foreheads. So the Vulgate: "and mark the sign Thau." Grotius: the letter <term>ת</term>, from which the word <term>Torah</term> (<term>תורה</term>) begins, signifying they were devoted to the law. So also Jerome on this passage, which however seems frivolous to Cocceius. To others, it is the first letter of the word <term>Tichyeh</term> (<term>תחיה</term>), "you shall live." See Kimchi on this place. "And to come to our own people," says Jerome on this passage, "in the ancient Hebrew letters, which the Samaritans use to this day, the final letter *Thau* has the likeness of a Cross." Thus also others of the Ancients, especially Origen; whose defense against Scaliger was recently taken up from Phoenician coins by the famous Rhenferd in *Phoenician Peril*, pages 5 and 6. See besides the Interpreters, D. Pfeiffer’s *Vexed Doubts* on this passage. n) upon the foreheads (Revelation 7:3, Ezekiel 28:38, see Exodus 12:23). Servants in the Orient had the name of their Lord on their forehead, as witnessed by Hesychius and Caelius Rhodiginus. See Grotius on this place. It marks not indeed the elect, as Junius wished; the Spirit of God causes the upright to be marked on their foreheads, that is, so that they may bear the name of the lamb publicly through confession, so that through confession of every kind their faith may be clear. The Holy Spirit, who is given to the faithful, is that seal (<unclear>original Greek: σφραγὶς</unclear>) and mark by which Christ and his Father recognize their own, and by which, having been marked as his, they are preserved. He who receives another mark (<unclear>original Greek: χάραγμα</unclear>) will hear: "I do not know you, you are not mine, you do not bear the sign of me and my Father" (Cocceius). o) of those groaning (chapter 21:11, 12). p) and deeply sighing. This is more serious than the preceding "to groan" (4) (chapter 24:17, 26:15). Jeremiah, Baruch, Ebed-melech, and whoever else feared God were noted down for the sake of deliverance (Lightfoot).

# EZEKIEL CH. 9. 10.

<margin>
The word is used for the first person, as if to say:

The vision then shifts to the Temple, where the "man in linen" is ordered to take coals of fire from the angelic Chariot to scatter over the city, signaling its coming destruction.</summary>

verse 19. f) verse 16; chapter 11, verse 22. g) *Schmidius*: They moved themselves away, etc. verses 15, 17. h) See verse 2. i) While they were going out from the temple, at whose right side he had initially seen them, verse 3. *Kimchi* <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish commentator also known as Radak</note>. k) Beside them, chapter 1, verses 20, 21; chapter 11, verse 22. l) Thus the living creature stood, i.e., each one of the Cherubim, collectively. See verse 2. He uses the singular because they stood as one. *Kimchi*. Compare the note on chapter 1, verses 7, 20. m) Beside the door, chapter 8, verse 16. n) Of the gate, namely, of the outer court (perhaps the people's court). o) Of the house of the Lord, namely, the temple, which was situated in the eastern part of the city of Jerusalem, and opposite it was the Mount of Olives. p) Eastern, chapter 11, verse 1. *Grotius*: So that the temple might be understood to be completely deserted by divine protection. But *Cocceius*: Because it says the glory stood with the living creatures at the entrance of both the city and the temple after the glory of God was placed on the throne, it signifies that after Christ's ascension into heaven, one must no longer come into the court where the Israelites stood, but that Christ and His Church are immediately found in the open, meeting the nations flowing in from everywhere, without a handmade temple. The glory of the God of Israel is found, I say, upon the living creatures, that is, the called elect faithful, nor is there any need to seek it elsewhere. q) Compare chapter 1, verses 11, 22, 26. Indeed, the Lord leaves His house with such sorrow and slowness, making various stops. Compare the note on verse 4. verse 20. r) This, I say, is that very same living creature, verse 15. s) The Son of God, whom he had called "like a man" in chapter 1, verse 26, and who is the God of Israel. n) chapter 1, verse 3. x) I understood it, however, certainly and distinctly; see John 19:35. y) That they were Cherubim, that is, that those living creatures signified the same thing as the Cherubim in the temple and above the ark (whose form was very well known to him, since he was a priest, chapter 1, verse 3). This observation has this use: that God does not properly dwell among Cherubim made of gold—but among Cherubim who are living creatures <gloss>original Greek: zōa</gloss>, who have life in themselves, eyes with which they see the light of truth and the fire of charity, and those virtues which are signified by the four living creatures as an emblem: the fruit of charity and the life of God in them. God is present to those who glorify Him; He has a temple in which He may dwell, even if that house built of material by the hands of men is destroyed. From these things, one can understand that just as these living creatures correspond to the Cherubim, so He who sits on the throne corresponds to the mercy seat <note>original: *hilasterion*</note> and the floor; He is the "propitiation set forth publicly" <gloss>original Greek: hilasterion protetheimenon</gloss>, not enclosed in a sanctuary, to which all can approach in faith in His blood (Romans 3:25). All these things, so carefully emphasized, pertain to this: that the Israelites might turn their thoughts and trust away from the material temple and the elements of the world, and seek God in Christ, and establish the kingdom of God within themselves through faith in Christ, and not be overly saddened when they heard that the temple was to be destroyed and profaned, etc. *Cocceius*. verse 21. z) Each had four faces, as was said in verse 14. a) Also four wings, with two of which they flew, and with two they covered their lower parts; chapter 1, verse 6. b) Compare verses 7, 8 and see the note on chapter 1, verse 8. The Prophet repeats this often so that the people, destined to live without a temple, might hold the mysteries of the temple in place of the temple itself, and thus be much better prepared for the covenant. *Grotius*. See also the note on chapter 3, verse 11. verse 22. c) And as pertains to the likeness—that is, the form—of their faces. d) They were the same faces e) verses 15, 20. f) regarding their appearances and themselves. As if to say: not only in appearance, but in actual fact, they were exactly the same as those I saw in this second vision as those I saw in the first vision. Thus *Kimchi*: even the face and appearance of them were like the faces which I saw, etc. g) To the region opposite him, chapter 1, verses 9, 12 and following. h) *Schmidius*: Afterward he lifted me up, verse 24; chapter 3, verses 12, 14; chapter 8, verse 3. But *Grotius* says: More correctly, "he had lifted up," that is, he had kept me suspended (comparing chapter 8, verse 16), so that the Prophet repeats the things said there in this place, and continues here the speech that was interrupted to turn to greater matters. *Kimchi* tends toward the same. For also according to Glassius, these four chapters—8, 9, 10, and 11—describe one vision of the prophet and constitute its four parts. Regarding these, see Sacred Philology, pages 455 and following. Therefore, the vision shown to the Prophet in Jerusalem is continued in this chapter and brought to a conclusion: where there occurs I. Prophecy against the wicked princes, verses 1–12. II. Confirmation of the same, and the Prophet's intercession not accepted, verses 13–16. III. Divine promise regarding the return and conversion of the remnant through Christ, verses 17–21. IV. The end of this vision, and the Prophet’s return to Babylonia, and the report made concerning the vision, verses 22 and following.

v. 3. v) *And who will consult:* Giving suggestions to the King and others. 2 Chronicles 22:4.

v. 3. y) *For they say obstinately:* Compare chapter 8, verse 12; Zephaniah 1:12.
x) *Is it not near at hand to build houses?* Thus we take it as a question with S. and others (compare 2 Samuel 23:5, Hosea 4:14, etc.), and in opposition to what God had said through the Prophet in chapter 7, verses 7-8. That is to say: the destruction of the city threatened by Jeremiah and Ezekiel is not near, but far off. Compare chapter 12, verse 27; Matthew 24:48.
a) *Compare Genesis 11:4; Isaiah 22:12.* Others say: One should not build suburban houses near the city, lest the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians</note> use them as tools or as a cook uses firewood to heat this pot. This is military advice, as seen in places fearing a siege, where surrounding buildings are demolished.
b) *For this is the city of Jerusalem:* verse 6. Formerly, see verse 7; 2 Kings 24:3.

c) *And we are the meat:* Just as meat being cooked remains in the pot until it is thoroughly boiled, so we shall remain in the city and die in it rather than surrender to the Chaldeans.
