<note>This section provides expanded commentary on the verses above, citing various scholars.</note>

...a people consecrated and devoted to God, indeed, sacred meat. Therefore, [they believed] God would preserve both the city and themselves, since He has His hearth, fire, and pot there. **v. 4. d)** The prophet [is sent] against them; the prophet, I say. An emphatic repetition, as in Isaiah 40:1 and Daniel 10:19. **v. 5. e)** *It fell therefore,* etc. See chapter 8, verse 1. **f)** The Holy Spirit through the gift of prophecy, previously received and now renewed. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note>: "The spirit of prophecy from before the Lord," as in chapter 1, verse 3 and chapter 3, verse 14. **g)** Schmid explains it well. Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval biblical commentator</note> says: "You have spoken the truth in this proverb or figurative speech—yet not about yourselves, nor as you think—namely, that you would not depart from Jerusalem into captivity," etc. Compare Exodus 10:29, Numbers 27:7. **h)** *Ascensions,* that is, thoughts. Compare chapter 14, verse 3. **i)** Chapter 20, verse 32. **k)** I know each one of them, or every single one. Compare Deuteronomy 31:21, Hosea 5:3, Psalm 139:2, and John 2:25. **v. 6. l)** *You have multiplied* (chapter 24,10) *your slaughters.* verse 7: You have killed very many through deceit and unjust judgments; the city is full of unjust killings; therefore, you cannot but fear the avenging sword (verse 8). Cocceius: He hints that their thoughts in verses 2 and 3 proceed from a bad conscience and a madness for committing all types of outrages. Nor should we think here only of the murders of the pious, but also of the perdition of souls. For the princes of the people ought to have been the masters and teachers of the Church. Since they did not teach men to know, love, revere, and worship God, they were the cause of many thousands dying in their sins. **m)** Compare chapter 7:23, 8:13, 9:9. **n)** Like enemies or savage beasts. Compare chapter 30:11, 19:3, and the Preface to Jeremiah sections 8 and 9. **v. 7. o)** verse 6: The prophets and holy men whom you killed because of their severe warnings; and then others as well. **p)** Compare chapter 24, verse 7. **q)** These, I say, are the ones for whom this city was like a cauldron, as if they were the meat; but for you, it shall not be so. **r)** The pot itself, see verse 3. **s)** But you shall be miserably tormented in remote places. **t)** *By leading out,* that is, I will lead out (verse 9). So the Septuagint and the Syriac. Jonathan: "I will make you migrate." Others: "The enemy will lead out." See notes on Leviticus 6:7, Judges 17:19, etc. **v. 8. u)** verse 5. **f)** Of the Chaldeans. **x)** [Feared] more than Me and My word. Rashi: From where they sent to Egypt to obtain help, compare chapter 17, verse 15. Cocceius: Your conscience dictates to you that you are worthy of the sword coming against you; so it shall be. You only fear those who can kill the body; but God, who can cast both body and soul into Gehenna <note>Hell</note>, you do not fear. Therefore both will happen to you. Your sins will not be forgiven you until you die, Isaiah 22:14. **y)** Therefore I will bring the sword (chapter 6:3, 14:17), that very one which you feared; nor will the King of Egypt rescue you (Kimchi). **z)** The seal of the threat. verse 21; compare Isaiah 1:20, 24; Hosea 11:11. **v. 9. a)** I will lead you out, I say (verse 8); what you thought—that you would remain in the city until you died—will not happen (Kimchi). **b)** From the midst of it, namely, your city. Compare Micah 2:10. **c)** Isaiah 1:7, Jeremiah 30:8. Those who themselves live as strangers to the worship of the true God. See Ephesians 2:12. **d)** So that I may perform. **e)** Judgments and just punishments, chapter 5:10, 15; 16:41. **v. 10. f)** You shall fall by that sword. verse 8; chapter 5:12. **g)** *On the border of Israel:* verse 11. That is, in Riblah, in the land of Hamath. 2 Kings 25:18-21; Jeremiah 52:9-11. For Hamath is the border of Israel, compare 1 Kings 8:65 (Kimchi).

He rebukes their arrogant "pot and meat" proverb, declaring that while they feel safe inside the city, they will actually be dragged out to face judgment and death at the borders of Israel.</summary>

---

If they depart from the Lord, then the people tell those who do *not* depart but act with the Lord: *depart*. This verse (15) shows the corruption of teaching and judgment in Israel. Cf. John 9:22. *l) Be far off:* or "be gone." Chapter 8:6; Isaiah 54:14. For you were unworthy to live in this place. *m) From the Lord:* and from His temple and land. Cf. Jonah 1:3; Jonah 4 regarding the fear of the Lord. *n) To us:* for to us the land is given. Vatablus <note>François Vatable, a French scholar of the 16th century.</note> notes it is as if they were saying: "Those others were to be cast out from this holy land because they were rejected; but we shall remain here forever." This is a Pharisaic spirit <note>original: *spiritum Pharisæicum*</note> (Luke 18:11, 12), which Christ countered in Luke 13:2 and following. Cf. Jeremiah 21:13. 

Cocceius <term>paraphrases</term> <note>original: *παραφראζει*</note> it thus: "We who sit as judges in the land are undoubtedly the heirs and the true Israel. You must therefore agree with us if you wish to share in the inheritance. And our kingdom is perpetual. That one whom you call the Lord is not one of us, nor the heir of the land; therefore leave Him (the Christ)." But the stone which the builders reject becomes the <term>chief cornerstone</term> <note>original: *ἀקרוγωνιαῖος*</note>. Cf. the "head of the corner," Psalm 118:22 (cf. Isaiah 66:5). *o) For a possession:* a hereditary one. Chapter 28:4, 19; Exodus 6:8. — *v. 16. p) Therefore:* because they insult them so. *q) Although:* or "when." Schmidt translates as *altogether*. *r) I have removed them:* I have cast them far away. Jeremiah 27:9, concerning those deported with Jeconiah. *s) Because I have scattered:* them. Deuteronomy 4:27; chapter 28:64; 30:3. *t)* Chapter 6:8; 12:15. *u) But I myself will be:* or "nevertheless I shall be." Others: *Since I have become*—therefore I will gather them (verse 17). *x)* Cf. Psalm 90:1; and what will eventually be in the Jerusalem above (Revelation 21:22). *y) For a sanctuary:* Isaiah 8:14; Jeremiah 17:12. 

By this He teaches that He sanctifies them and will sanctify them by His indwelling. For God's dwelling in the tabernacle which He placed in the midst of Israel signifies the dwelling of the divinity in Christ and His flesh, and in those who are His, both in heaven and on earth. The faithful who were led into captivity heard the words of God even there; they had the Spirit of God teaching in their midst; they approached Christ with their hearts and held Him as the true sanctuary. They did not think that by being removed from the physical sanctuary anything was taken from them but an external pledge, their communion with many believers, and their dwelling in the land to which the Lord was to come. (Cocceius). *z) A little while:* or for that "small number" whom I will not desert, but I will be present with them and hear their prayers, as I used to hear them in that great temple. Cocceius: It is indicated that God will give conversion from the heart to a few in captivity, as promised in Deuteronomy 30:8. This "fewness" is contrasted with the "many" mentioned in Isaiah 53:12 and Romans 8:29. 

The sense is emphatic: These are the first of Israel to whom I have appeared as a sanctuary (for they are sanctified by me without an earthly temple and approach me), and indeed a sanctuary not with a massive population gathered in one place, but such that a few here and a few there approach me, and I approach those few. Therefore I will gather them, and in their midst, I will become a sanctuary for many—first for them and their children gathered from all tribes, and finally for all nations (Isaiah 66:23). Ezekiel describes this sanctuary in a riddle in chapter 40 and following. Because the word **for a sanctuary** <note>Hebrew: *le-mikdash*</note> is not in the construct form, others translate it as "for a little while," lasting only for the 70 years of captivity. Compare Hosea 1:4; Psalm 2:6. Others, following the Septuagint, read "a small sanctuary," by way of comparison and contrast between the splendor of the visible temple and the grace of God, which is hidden from the world. Cf. Colossians 2:3.

**v. 17. a)** Therefore I will gather you; both politically from the Babylonian captivity, and spiritually according to John 11:52. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian who emphasized the "Covenant of Grace" and saw many Old Testament events as types of Christ.</note> says: All Israelites who had never been led into captivity received the liberty to return to the land of their fathers by the edict of Cyrus. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch legal scholar and theologian known for his literal and historical interpretation of the Bible.</note>: They will live without idolatry, led by the excellent men Ezra, Nehemiah, Zerubbabel, etc. Cocceius: Ezra and Nehemiah began to reform the people; but the Maccabees and their brothers removed all idols from the entire land, and indeed even subdued neighboring nations and compelled them to accept circumcision, and cut off those who refused. **v. 19. l)** For I will give to them. Which Paul in Rom. 10:6-10 interprets as the commandment of faith. There is no need here to search for commandments which are of the law of decrees, carnal, weak, and useless, as Paul speaks—For those are not for all time, if you look at the external work; but if you look at the truth and the core, and their essence, they are contained in the commandment of faith and charity. etc. Cf. Rom. 8:1-4; Luke 1:74, 75. **t)** c. 14:11. Hos. 2:22. This name is used here, by which God encompassed all His goodness in the promise of Gen. 17:7. Cf. Judg. 5:9; c. 9:3; 2 Sam. 15:13; Neh. 3:38. Their heart, rebellious and refractory, Jer. 5:21, 23. <meta>This page concludes the vision of the departure of God's glory from Jerusalem and transitions into Chapter 12, where Ezekiel is commanded to perform a symbolic "mime" or prophetic act. Having seen the leadership judged and a promise of spiritual renewal given to the exiles, the prophet now witnesses the final abandonment of the city by the Divine Presence and is returned to his fellow captives in Babylonia to warn them of the impending fall of Jerusalem.</meta>

## CHAPTER XII. <note>original Hebrew: יב</note>

<margin>
**CHAPTER XII.**
...they had obeyed the Prophets, especially Jeremiah, by surrendering themselves to the Chaldeans; then, so that He might relieve and encourage them with comforts, in the hope of a certain better glory for the temple and a holier city, and thus confirm their faith. **m)** all the words...
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 24. n)** But the Holy Spirit lifted me up. v. 1. Ch. 3:14. **o)** and brought me back into Chaldea. In a state of ecstasy <note>A prophetic trance or out-of-body experience.</note>, he seemed to himself to have been taken away to those in Jerusalem, and so now he was brought back to the captives in Chaldea. Ch. 1:1. **p)** that is, in ecstasy, produced by the Spirit of God. cf. Revelation 1:10. **q)** and it thus ascended, ceased, and vanished. cf. Genesis 17:22, Ch. 35:13, Acts 10:16. Junius: <note>Francis Junius (1545–1602), a Huguenot theologian.</note> By the word "ascending," he most elegantly teaches that this vision was heavenly, offered by God, and therefore received back by God in the manner of an ascension (so to speak), so that the truth of the entire matter might be further confirmed. Kimchi: then the Spirit of Prophecy ascended (departed) from me and gave me the power to speak, cf. Ch. 3:27. **r)** Ch. 1:1. **v. 25. s)** Junius: He explained to them the whole counsel of God, which he had perceived by both vision and word. **t)** to the captives. v. 24.

---

**v. 25.** *all things.* **x)** For the word had not been simple, but clothed in external and visible symbols. cf. Jeremiah 24:1; Ch. 38:21; Amos 7:1, 4. 

**CHAPTER XII.**
**v. 1. y)** *Moreover it happened etc.* After the Lord had truly removed His glory from Jerusalem in Chapter 11, now, in order to deeply fix the thought of captivity in the minds of the Jews and to more strongly constrain the stubborn, He uses: 
I. A **type** <note>In biblical studies, a "type" is a symbolic person, object, or event that foreshadows a future reality.</note> or symbol of carrying household goods and its explanation, signifying Zedekiah's nocturnal flight, his captivity, his blinding, and the abduction and dispersion of the Jews (v. 1–16). 
II. A second type, **eating bread with trembling**, signifying the calamities that would happen before the deportation: famine, thirst, and anxiety (v. 17–20). 
III. He again foretells and confirms that divine judgments against mockers and procrastinators will come shortly (v. 21–25, and again v. 26 ff.).

**v. 2. z)** namely, among the Jews in Babylonia, who, seeing Jerusalem still standing and not believing it would perish, were grieving that they had surrendered to the Chaldeans; they discouraged the Jerusalemites from surrendering and wanted to return themselves if they could. cf. Jeremiah 29:8, 21, 28; and the Preface to Jeremiah § 5. **a)** v. 9; Ch. 2:5, 6; Ch. 3:26. **b)** Cocceius: This is a synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note>. For Ezekiel and his brothers and kinsmen—and all in all the tribes to whom the rest were saying, "Go far from the Lord" (Ch. 11:15)—must be excepted as those dwelling with Ezekiel in the midst of a house of disobedience. But these were by far the smallest part of the people. **c)** see Isaiah 6:9, 10; Ch. 42:18; Jeremiah 5:21; Ch. 6:10; Matthew 13:14, 15. **d)** that is, with obedience and faith; because out of stubbornness they do not consider what needs to be done, so that they might believe and repent. **e)** v. 3; Ch. 2:4. The source of blindness is defiance, through which divine light is not admitted. cf. John 12:40, 2 Corinthians 4:4.

**v. 3. f)** You therefore. **g)** act, prepare for yourself the vessels of migration <note>Meaning the necessary bags and supplies for a journey into exile.</note>, necessary for one about to move; pack your bundles. cf. Jeremiah 46:19; Matthew 10:9, 10. **h)** and migrate during the day, in broad daylight. v. 3, 7. Rashi: from day to day, for two or three days. **i)** while they are watching. v. 4, 6. **k)** for perhaps (Jeremiah 26:3; Ch. 36:3, 7) they might see and be moved by these signs, so that they understand how I am going to punish the Jerusalemites. **l)** v. 2. *Because*, or others say *for they are a house of rebellion*, as they are people who despise the word of God and vainly believe the False Prophets, who say things will be better for those who remained in Jerusalem than for the captives.

**v. 4. m)** You shall therefore bring out. v. 5. You shall send your bundles ahead while it is still day, following yourself in the evening. **n)** v. 3, 7. Kimchi: with a sack on the shoulders and a staff in the hands. **o)** That is, you shall go out with those vessels. **p)** to prefigure the nocturnal flight of King Zedekiah. 2 Kings 25:4. **q)** according to the departure (Numbers 33:2) *of migration*; like those who must go out into flight for exile. v. 7. II. Ch. 11:25. Palatinus: *perhaps* it signifies the habit of a migrant; as if to say, you shall go out mournful and indignant. So Kimchi. cf. v. 6, 12.

**v. 5. r)** Surely *in their sight*. v. 4, 6. dig. v. 7; Ch. 8:8. **s)** in the wall of your house, which will represent Jerusalem. **t)** v. 4. so that you may carry out your vessels or furniture through that breached wall. This signified that Zedekiah would flee through the gate of the royal garden, as if through a narrow hole in the wall, and the Jews would not exit freely, but stealthily, snatching themselves from the sight of the enemy through hiding places and in the darkness of night.

**v. 6. u)** Then *in their sight*. v. 4, 5; Ch. 4:12. **x)** v. 7, 12; Isaiah 49:22. **y)** The Syriac version adds: the bundle; others: necessities for food. **z)** in the gloom (a) v. 7, 12; Genesis 15:17. For Zedekiah went out at night. Jeremiah 39:4; Ch. 52:7. **a)** Like those who, affected by shame, do not want to be seen or recognized; cf. 2 Samuel 15:30. Thus it represents the confusion and "blinding" of Zedekiah when he is led into Babylonia. Kimchi compares Jeremiah 9:18. **b)** as it is in Deuteronomy 28:15.

The text focuses on the fate of the "Prince in Jerusalem" (King Zedekiah), prophesying his attempted escape, his capture, his deportation to Babylon, and his eventual blindness.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Ezekiel 12, shifting from the symbolic actions of the prophet (packing for exile) to the psychological state of the people. It addresses the skepticism of the Judeans who believe that prophecies of doom are either for the distant future or will never come to pass. The commentary emphasizes that God's judgments are imminent and that the false, "flattering" prophecies will be silenced.</meta>

in which it is situated. c) *of its fullness* <note>original: "a plenitudine sua"</note> chapter 32, verse 15. It shall be deprived of the multitude of inhabitants and wealth, crops, fruits, livestock, houses, treasures, etc. Compare chapter 19:7, 30:12; Jeremiah 8:16; 1 Timothy 6:5. Others say: *because of its fullness*, because it is entirely filled with wicked men, as the following clause states. d) *because of violence*, which they used by oppressing the innocent, seizing what belonged to others, and persecuting the pious. Compare chapter 7:23, 27; 2:17. **v. 20.** e) For the cities were inhabited and populous. chapter 38:11. f) chapter 8:6; Jeremiah 4:27; chapter 9:11; Micah 6:13. g) Ephesians 1:6; Joshua 8:28. *Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian who emphasized the covenantal progress of redemptive history.</note>:* Truly, where there is no trust in the people, no uplifted spirit, no alacrity (the nursemaid of which is a good conscience), there is no safety; rather, it is necessary that both cities and courts become pots and cauldrons for consuming men, and the lands be laid waste and everything scattered. h) *then you will acknowledge*, or *so that you may acknowledge*, namely you, the people of the land. See verse 19. i) verses 15, 16. *Cocceius:* The judgments of God, with which He chastises His people, are designed so that those who do not know God may come to know Him—that He is holy, and does not wish to be seen as the God of those who are devoid of His holiness and deny His justice. **v. 21.** k) *Furthermore, it happened*. **v. 22.** l) Meaning, *what does it mean?* It is an interrogation of reproach or demand, as below in chapter 19:2. m) a saying, a proverb. verse 33; 1 Samuel 24:13. n) It is even attributed to the Prophet <term>collectively</term> <note>original Greek: κοινωνικῶς (koinōnikōs); implying the prophet shares in the community's identity even when they sin.</note>, though it was most alien to him, because he was one of the body of the people. In this sense, *Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (c. 1160–1235), a major medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian.</note>* also helpfully compares Exodus 16:28; or God (as *Kimchi* adds) tells the Prophet to say to the Israelites: *what does it mean?* etc. o) *in*; others say *concerning* the land. p) *be prolonged*. Read as: *are dragged out* only after many years or will never happen. Genesis 26:8. For the contrary, see following verse 23. *Kimchi* compares chapter 11:3. q) Namely, the punishment or destruction predicted for us by the Prophets. Compare chapter 7:2, 5, 6, 10, etc. r) *and shall perish*, or *will be in vain*, it will vanish into the wind. verse 24; chapter 19:5, 37:11. *Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note>:* Those men were saying: either those things which are predicted will happen long after us, or they will simply vanish. God responds to both parts. But most excellently with *Luther*, *Cocceius* says: *He reproaches* them for the common saying among them: *every vision perishes as the days are prolonged*, that is, the Prophets speak of a future time, and they die, and then nothing happens of what they predicted. For in this way, most of them hardened their hearts against prophetic predictions. While the long-suffering of God should have been a stimulus to them for repentance, they accumulated divine wrath for themselves through continuous security. Romans 2:4-5. Compare the note below at verse 27 and 2 Peter 3:4. s) verse 23. Compare verse 27; chapter 7:13; Habakkuk 3:3. **v. 23.** t) *I will cause to cease*. Prophetic past tense, as in chapter 7:13; Ephesians 5:3. u) verse 22. x) Meaning, *they will not speak*. *Vatablus <note>François Vatable (d. 1547), a French humanist scholar.</note>:* and no longer will they use this following proverb. chapter 16:44; Numbers 21:27. y) *but, rather indeed*. Compare Ephesians 33:21. z) Compare chapter 9:1, 21:12, 24:14; Hosea 1:4. Opposed here to verse 22. a) *and every matter of vision*, i.e., whatever the prophets foresaw and predicted will soon be proven by the outcome. Compare verses 25, 28; Matthew 5:18. **v. 24.** b) *It shall not be*, or it will no longer happen as it occasionally seemed to you to happen by God's permission. *Cocceius:* Many false prophets had arisen among the people, who predicted things pleasing and flattering to the ears, so that they might be honored and loved by men; such men were held in high esteem. Compare 2 Peter 2:1; Micah 3:11. But when they saw that as the days were prolonged, those prophecies vanished, men began to think that every prophecy was empty. Compare 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21. c) *any vision*, due to the preceding negative. Thus chapter 31:14; Exodus 10:15, etc. d) *of vanity*, i.e., empty, false. chapter 13:6, 8; Lamentations 2:14. e) *and divination* chapter 13:7. f) *flattering*, fawning, namely the false Prophets, by contradicting the true Prophets and promising a happy state to the people—a natural inclination toward flattery. g) <term>prophesying things for favor</term> <note>original Greek: μαντευόμενοι τὰ πρὸς χάριν</note>. Compare Hosea 10:2; Psalm 5:10; Proverbs 26:28; chapter 29:5. For I will no longer deal with you with words, but with lashes, with rods already prepared, and swords, and flames. g) *Grotius:* For all those false Prophets will be cast out. chapter 13:23. *Cocceius:* If Jesus came after the Babylonian captivity (as He certainly did) and if He was a false prophet along with His disciples, as the Jews maintain, then this prophecy is not true. But the speech of Christ and His disciples cannot be called a reckless vision (<term>false vision</term> <note>original Hebrew: חזון שוא (chazon shav)</note>) because it obtained its outcome: nor was it flattering divination, because it was contrary to the lust of the Jews and rebuked them from the Law and the Prophets. **v. 25.** h) For I am Jehovah (note the emphatic transposition of the major distinctive with the minor), not false prophets feeding you with empty hope. verse 24.

<summary>This page explains Ezekiel 12:17-25, where the prophet is commanded to eat and drink with trembling to symbolize the coming terror in Jerusalem. It also refutes the popular proverb that prophecies of judgment fail or are only for the distant future, promising that God's word will be fulfilled immediately.</summary>

i) I speak, that which I speak is the word, and it shall most certainly come to pass. This is required by the accents. This is the Niphal [passive] form. l) Compare verse 28 and Ezekiel 13:21. l) According to some: because now. m) While you are still living. Verse 27. r) A vision. Compare verse 23. s) Which that Ezekiel sees; he speaks of it with contempt. Compare verse i. 3. Amos 1:1. t) According to some: it will happen after many days. Others: life is to be prolonged for many days, and it will eventually happen after a long interval of time. Compare Daniel 8:26. u) and for remote times. Compare Daniel 8:17. x) He utters prophecies, he prophesies. Compare Jeremiah 20:7; chapter 32:3. For we do not yet see happening those things which he already predicted in the previous year in chapter 7:2, 7. This rebuke differs from the preceding one: that one was directed at the impudent despisers of God, who rejected and laughed at the threats of God's prophets; this one addresses the hypocrites and procrastinators, who did not laugh at God openly, but pushed the fulfillment of the prophetic word into the future—an attitude of security that easily slides into gross contempt for God. Compare the notes from Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology" and detailed biblical commentaries.</note> on verse 22.

<gloss>s</gloss> "You have not gone up into the breaches, nor built a wall for the house of Israel, to stand <gloss>u</gloss> in the battle in the day of the Lord." <page-num>5</page-num>

by their own judgment, uttering vain and false prophecies. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Prophets.</note>: *according to the pleasure of their own heart.* So also in verse 17. Compare verse 3; Nehemiah 6:8. The *Prefix* does not hinder the construct state of the preceding Name, as in Psalm 2:12; 2 Samuel 1:21; Isaiah 9:2. h) chapter 6, verse 3. **Verse 3.** i) compare Isaiah 1:4; Matthew 23:13 and following. k) Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 32:5, 6. God judges such men, who were swelling and flourishing with the highest praise for wisdom and prudence, yet were devoid of divine wisdom and truth, nor were they students of a good conscience, but rather precipitating themselves into danger, shame, and infamy. *Cocceius*: Let us consider how dangerous it is to follow one's own opinions and conjectures or desires, and not to attend to the promises of God, His word, and His covenant, etc. l) Jonathan: *who walk after the thought of their own heart.* Who indulge their own will, wisdom, and imagination in devising false prophecies, and are not led by the Spirit of God. Compare chapter 11:5; Micah 2:11; Numbers 15:39. m) According to some: and according to that which they have not seen, i.e., since they have had no vision, nor was it made manifest to them by the <term>ἀποσέσει πνεύματος</term> <note>original Greek: "shaking of the spirit," referring to a prophetic trance or divine inspiration</note>. Compare Colossians 2:18, 19; Jeremiah 29:8. **Verse 4.** n) *like foxes*, Judges 15:4; Lamentations 5:18. Cunning, deceitful, elusive, and timid: likewise hungry, who, pressed by want, are carried with greater force toward even the slightest prey. *Bochartus* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French scholar who wrote "Hierozoicon," a massive work on the animals of the Bible.</note>: Foxes excavate and undermine the ground beneath them with tunnels. This is what those Prophets did, when they should have been repairing the ruins of Jerusalem and putting up a fence to meet the imminent evil. The following verse encourages this view. *Hierozoicon* Part I, page 860. They are depicted as shrewd, versatile men, liars who insinuate themselves into houses, who slander the good, and who corrupt the minds of the simple with their <term>εὐλογíαις & χρηστολογíαις</term> <note>original Greek: "blessings and fair speeches," a reference to Romans 16:18</note>. Just as foxes ruin vineyards, so these men subvert the fruit of God's vineyard and cause it to bear no good fruit, *Cocceius*. Compare Song of Solomon 2:15; Jude verse 4. o) *in the desolate places* chapter 26:20; Isaiah 48:21. Compare Matthew 8:20. *Kimchi*: Just as foxes gather in a broken place, in the hedge of a vineyard, and ruin the vineyard, etc. Compare Song of Solomon 2:15. p) *Kimchi*: i.e., they are your prophets, and not the Lord's. q) O Israel! they have become. **Verse 5.** s) An apostrophe [address] to the false teachers. The sense is: you have not looked after the public safety by your prayers and intercession for it, nor do you show the true means through sound doctrine by which the greatest evils, both of guilt and punishment, can and should be removed from the people. t) *in or at the breaches* chapter 22:30; Psalm 106:23. A metaphor from the attacking of cities, where, once a breach is made in the wall, the besieged quickly gather there to drive back the enemy so he does not break through the gap. Where the iniquity of the people has overflowed like a flood, a breach is already made through which the vengeance of God can penetrate. Therefore, those who persuade the people to true repentance are the ones who restore the wall. u) nor did you hedge it in, according to some. *to hedge it*—Syriac: you also did not hedge it in. Compare notes on chapter 11:11. x) the wall or the hedge, compare chapter 22:30; Psalm 58:12. *Kimchi*: namely, through repentance and good works. Jonathan: neither did you perform good works for yourselves, to pray for the house of Israel. Grotius: when the enemy has shattered part of the walls with battering rams, two things are usually done; men are placed to defend the gaps, and the inner parts are fortified. For others, it is a new metaphor from the fortification of vineyards to keep out wild beasts. y) *around the n.* according to some, above. Compare verse 18; 1 Samuel 25:16. z) According to some: that you might stand; others: that it might stand, or the wall or house might be able to stand. *Cocceius*: so that Israel might thus stand—that is, subsist against all temptations. Compare Judges 2:14; Jeremiah 49:19; Nahum 1:6; Psalm 76:8. a) in battle or assault, 2 Kings 14:7; Amos 1:14; Hosea 10:14. Jonathan: to stand, to pray for mercies for them at the time when the warriors came against them in the day of the Lord. b) In the day of the assault which the Lord will make through enemies. Compare chapter 7:19; Hosea 5:9; Zephaniah 1:2, 3; Lamentations 1:12; chapter 2:1, 22, etc. Against Him there is no defense except in repentance and pious prayers, *Grotius*. But *Cocceius*: i.e., when Christ appears. For the day of His appearing is called most <term>historikotata</term> <note>original Greek: "most historically" or "most significantly in history"</note>. Of which day the Prophets speak in Amos 5:18; Malachi 3:2; Joel 2:3, 4. Christ has enemies with whom He must fight, just as those who belong to Christ must fight. Psalm 110:1. He is a stumbling block to many, Isaiah 8:14. Therefore, temptation must be resisted in the days of Christ; one must do battle. Thus, those who expect the day of the Lord ought to be armed and ready for the fight. **Verse 6.** c) They have seen, they have prophesied from made-up visions. Verses 7, 8, 9; chapter 21:24; chapter 22:28. Frequent is the change of persons due to emotion. d) and a divination of a lie. Verses 8, 9. Destitute of the effect which they were boasting. e) according to some: while they were saying. Or: yet at the same time saying. *Grotius*: they add a huge crime to their lie by signing God as the author. Compare note on verse 7.

<meta>This page continues the detailed commentary on Ezekiel. The commentary relies heavily on Rabbinic sources like Kimchi and Rashi, alongside Reformation-era scholars like Calvin and Cocceius.</meta>

Verse 10. i) For the reason that in many ways. Chapter 36:3. Compare notes on Leviticus 26:43. k) They led my people into error. Compare Isaiah 3:12; Micah 3:5. l) Saying all things are safe. Compare Jeremiah 4:10; 1 Thessalonians 5:3. m) When nevertheless they are not safe. Verse 16; Jeremiah 6:14; Isaiah 48:22. n) And when that people, mentioned just before (so Rashi), builds; accumulating evil habits; yet observing external worship <term>ex opere operato</term> <note>A Latin theological term meaning "from the work performed," implying that the ritual works automatically regardless of the person's spiritual state.</note>, and thus dreaming sweetly for themselves of an excellent and flourishing state—or at least one not so bad. Thus Cocceius: It signifies that the people, seduced by their words, placed a false foundation and put their trust in it, instituting their judgment and actions accordingly. The prophets, or teachers of the people, praised such work and, with God's words distorted and reduced to <term>empty sounds</term> <note>original: <greek>ξενοφωνίας</greek> (xenophōnias) — foreign or meaningless voices.</note> and vain noises, plastered it over, calling it righteousness and the fulfillment of the law. It was as if by their praise and approval, a non-foundation could become a foundation, and that which was built upon it could be a solid and established wall. Others say: And when this or that false prophet builds. So Kimchi. An elegant allegory. These false prophets are like wicked builders colluding with each other; if one brings mud from the streets and constructs the form of a wall from water, all with one consent help and consume their effort in decorating and adorning the false wall. Thus they build—or rather destroy—the church of God, they whose job it should have been to stand in the breaches and build a firm hedge. So says Tremellius, whom Glassius praises. Above in verse 5, he had rebuked their negligence in performing the duties of their office. Now he adds that they are indeed busy, pretending to be concerned; but with great effort they achieve nothing, building a wall in appearance, but without mortar, and therefore accomplishing nothing. o) A fence, a mud wall made of mud and material lying in the streets. Tremellius and Glassius. Compare 1 Corinthians 3:12. p) Then behold, those false prophets. q) They are those who smear or plaster it. Leviticus 14:42; 1 Chronicles 29:4. r) With mortar or unmixed plaster. Verse 11; chapter 22:28. Cocceius: "folly." Gusset: "With egg white, by which the plastered wall might shine more, but does not resist the rain better." Jonathan: "And they themselves are like one building a wall and smearing it with pure mud, without straw (without a mixture of straw or chaff)." Grotius: "They wish to make it so the filthiness of vices does not appear, but they take up a useless labor." Compare Matthew 23:27-28. Cocceius: "As if that smooth lime could grant solidity and stability to the wall." Verse 11. s) Thus he says to those plastering with the inept material. Verse 14, 15; Lamentations 2:14. t) That it will fall, or so that it falls. Verse 12. u) It has happened, or it comes. 1 Kings 18:45. "For there shall be rain." The prophetic past tense is used for the future because of its certainty, as in chapter 7:12. Syriac: "Behold I will give a sweeping rain." Allegorically, the divine judgments to be exercised through the Chaldeans, most powerful enemies, against the Israelite people are most gravely described. Compare Isaiah 8:8. x) Invading (verse 13), washing away that deceptive coating, or easily dissolving that mortar. Compare Isaiah 28:2. y) They (the hailstones) shall fall upon you. Thus through intense emotion, the second and third persons are mixed. Yet without necessity; since the verb is equally the second person feminine: "you, O stones of hail, shall fall upon them," through an emphatic apostrophe. Thus Kimchi and Cocceius, who adds: "Since these prophets do not listen, God has stones that are obedient to His word, which fall upon them." z) Of the greatest hailstones. Verse 13; chapter 38:22. So Rashi and Kimchi. Compare Isaiah 32:19; Revelation 16:21. Syriac: "Flint stones (or millstones)." So verse 13. a) O soon-coming whirlwind. Verse 13; compare Isaiah 41:16. b) It will break through, it will burst that wall. Verse 13; Habakkuk 3:9; compare Isaiah 28:17. Verse 12. c) Behold therefore. d) When that wall has fallen. Verse 11. e) The plastering or coating which had given the wall the appearance of a solid wall. f) Which you smeared? Verse 10. So that by this proverb, your foolishness and vanity may be open to all, and a mockery to all. Cocceius: "For God's judgments show that it is not a solid wall which is overturned." Rashi: "When evil comes, it will be said to you: Where is the peace in which you trusted?" Compare Jeremiah 38:22. Verse 13. g) For I will cause it to burst. Verse 11; Habakkuk 3:9. Jonathan: "I will bring a strong King, with a wind of storms." h) Verse 11; chapter 38:22. Jonathan: "And the killers of the people like an invalidating rain shall come in my anger." i) Jonathan: "And kingdoms that are strong (robust) like *algabish* [hail] stones." See verse 11. k) In my fury and heat. Verse 15; chapter 8:18; Psalm 59:14. They shall be, or they shall descend. Verse 11. l) Into consumption. Chapter 11:13; 2 Chronicles 12:11. Compare Isaiah 28:17. Verse 14. m) So that I may destroy. 2 Samuel 11:25; Micah 5:10; Lamentations 2:2, 17.

<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on Ezekiel 13. The previous page discussed the false prophets who built a flimsy "whitewashed wall" of lies. This page addresses the literal and metaphorical destruction of that wall (symbolizing Jerusalem's false security) and shifts focus to the female false prophets—sorceresses who used physical charms and "pillows" to deceive the people.</meta>

# EZEKIEL. CHAPTER 13.

<margin>
**x)** Verse 14. Compare **Ezekiel** 36:13. **Jonathan:** <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Bible.</note> "And I will destroy the city in which you prophesied false prophecies." **Rashi:** <note>A famous 11th-century French rabbi and commentator.</note> This is Jerusalem. Verse 15. **a)** Verses 10, 12. **Job** 6:6. **p)** "And I will cast it down to the earth." **Ezekiel** 25:12, chapter 26:5. **q)** "So that the foundation of that wall is touched, utterly overturned." Ezekiel 30:4; **Micah** 1:6; **Psalm** 137:7. **Cocceius:** <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian.</note> "So that it may appear to everyone that they did not build their house on a rock, but on sand (referencing **Matthew** 7:24ff); that they did not trust in God and the truth—but in their own hearts and the lies of men." **r)** "And when that wall falls," verses 11, 12. **But** because the word and suffix are feminine, and thus the gender has changed, **Tremellius** <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a 16th-century Jewish-Italian convert and scholar.</note> translates: "*it*" (that is, the burning wrath from verse 13). **I would prefer:** "*it*" refers to the hailstones from verses 11 and 13, rushing in. For this use of the verb, see verse 11 and the intensive form in **Genesis** 42:18. **Cocceius** understands the subject to be *Jerusalem*, which is not a bad interpretation. **s)** "You shall be consumed." **Malachi** 3:6; **Psalm** 90:7. **t)** "Then you shall know," verses 9, 23; chapter 6:7.

**14, 15.** **e.** 33, 16. **d)** "Those men," instead of "those women," for its own sake. **e)** "When there is no peace," verse 10. **f)** Verse 8. **Page 17.** **g)** 5. Similarly verse 11. **h)** chapter 6:2. **i)** Against the prophets, or rather the female false prophets; for there were also true female prophets from the later [weaker] sex. Compare the note on **2 Kings** 22:14. **Others** understand "men" to be meant here, called "daughters" out of contempt because they were soft and strong only in their tongues. Compare **Revelation** 2:20. But we prefer the former interpretation. **k)** Verse 2. **l)** chapter 6:3; chapter 25:2.

**Verse 18. m)** *Dictyge* <note>original: "Dictyge", a Latinized Greek term for a hunting net.</note>. **n)** *Woe to those sewing*. **(4) Genesis** 3:7; **Ecclesiastes** 3:7. Appropriately, he attributes "building a wall" to the men's vices, and "making pillows" to the women. **o)** Or *pillows* (λ) verse 20. Septuagint: <term>ἐπιϰεφάλαια</term> (head-cushions). **Mark** 4:38. **Tremellius:** "Since they themselves wanted to signal rest to the Jews, they sewed pillows as symbols of the most stable rest. Since everyone takes the 'wall' metaphorically, it is right to take the 'pillows' the same way; the sense being: they help the Jews with lying words, they applaud their crimes so they may rest securely and softly in them, and not be pricked by any stings [of conscience]." **Cocceius:** "Cushions and pillows are vain speeches, doctrines prepared for seduction, false opinions—uttered either by invoking great names or disguised with poorly understood words of the Law; or even new revelations, whether famous or invented—on which people might securely recline, fearing no evil." **p)** *for* verse 5; chapter 16:11. Or *underneath*. **q)** *cubits*. Or *armpits* (3) chapter 41:8; **Jeremiah** 38:12. **r)** Or *of my hands*, meaning my people. **Thus Tremellius:** "of my hands," as if there is an omission of the word "people" between the noun and the suffix. According to **Rashi, Kimchi, and Glassius** (Grammar p. 1202), it is by <term>apocope</term> <note>The shortening of a word by removing the final sound.</note> for *yadayim* (hands), like *yadai* in **Jeremiah** 22:14. Compare similar forms in **Nahum** 3:17, **Psalm** 8:2, 95:12, and according to some **Judges** 5:15. Also see the note on **2 Kings** 1:4. The "hand" is used by <term>synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note> for the entire arm in verse 20. **But Gusset** (p. 395. A.) interprets it without grammatical anomaly in this sense: "sewing bands over the entire armpits of my hands," that is, hiding the arm and hand of God from men so that, ignoring it and neglecting it, they may cast off the fear of God and the hope of His help, following men and indulging the flesh. **s)** Or *woe to those making*. **t)** *veils*. Syriac: *experiments*. **Kimchi** and others: *pepla* (mantles). Septuagint: <term>ἐπίβολα</term> (coverings), which **Cocceius** judges to be a good translation. Others: cushions on which people might sleep securely (2) verse 21. **Tremellius** in his notes: "To symbolize that the people were most certainly protected and supported by divine help; that this defense would never cease." **Grotius** puts it best: "Thus those female prophets suggested pretexts to the great and small alike to cover their vices." **u)** *Of people of every height or stature*, chapter 17:6; **Song of Solomon** 7:8. Whether great or small, they gratified everyone **without distinction**, as long as a payment was in hand. Others say "stature" refers to the fact that they ordered those who consulted them to stand. Compare **1 Samuel** 28:20. **x)** *to hunt, to catch*, verse 20; **Leviticus** 17:13. So that they may draw souls into their own factions and love, so that those captured may perish. **Jonathan:** *to destroy souls*. Septuagint: <term>διαστρέφειν</term> (to pervert or distort). **Acts** 13:8, 10; **Luke** 23:2, etc. **Rashi:** "They hunted souls toward Gehenna <note>The place of spiritual punishment or purification.</note>, by strengthening the hands of the wicked by divining peace for them, while weakening the hands of the righteous by divining evil for them." **y)** Compare **Proverbs** 6:26. **Cocceius:** "This shows that even women among the Israelite people had reached such a level of impudence that they dared to teach as if from the word of God, which God had not taught them. They did this to make men feel secure, thus practicing a 'fowling' of souls, making a profit from the destruction of men whom they taught to despise the threats of the true Prophets. Such wicked teachers usually have devoted female followers through whom they build a name and reputation, capturing the simple souls of every age. These women stood as types. From this, we must take an example—for superstitious, idle women can act this way at any time, wandering between houses, slandering others, and speaking perversely (**1 Timothy** 5:13)." *Will you hunt souls?* Thus Jonathan, Rashi, and Kimchi. But **Schmid:** *For you hunt souls*. **4)** verse 10; **Genesis** 27:3. 6) That is, the pious. Or *those who belong to my people*. **Tremellius:** "Must you seek a living most wickedly at the expense of the life and souls of my people?" **c)** *and in turn the souls of other wicked people.* **d)** Or *those which are yours*. **Thus Kimchi:** "those which are yours, namely the souls of the wicked." For others, like **Dathe**, it is a dative of advantage: "for yourselves, for gain and reward." Thus **Tremellius** best: "When it is useful for you, you pronounce life for them." **e)** *Will you keep them alive?* or *will you preserve them?* or *you assign them to life*. Verse 19. For among the Hebrews, words of "declaring" are often called by words of "doing," as **Grotius** rightly notes. Compare chapter 43:3; **Leviticus** 13:3, 6, 17; **Deuteronomy** 25:1, etc. **Verse 19. f)** *You profane me, selling your own inventions in my name, saying things to the people that are not holy and are unbecoming of me, thus instilling a bad opinion of me in the people. Compare chapter 20:39; Ezekiel 20:7, etc.* **g)** in **Chapter** 1718; **Proverbs** 30:10. **h)** *for a handful* (3) **1 Kings** 20:10. **Of barley.** **Gusset:** "for a quantity of barley equal to the sole of a foot, that is, for the smallest reward and for the sake of food." A proverbial expression; compare **Hosea** 3:2. Pliny says barley is the most ancient of foods (**Natural History** book 18, chapter 7). **i)** *and for pieces* (1). Compare **Genesis** 18:5; **Leviticus** 2:6; **1 Kings** 17:11; and **Proverbs** 28:21. **k)** *so that you deliver souls to death*, by predicting destruction for pious souls. **l)** *who should not die*. Thus the **Septuagint, Inn., and Syriac**. **m)** *and by promising life, enticing with vain hope and absolving the unrepentant*. See note on verse 18. **n)** *who should not live*.

<margin>
**v. 14. x)** "Thus I will consume," that is, I will pour out all my wrath. Compare chapter 22:6, 12. **v)** See verse 10. **Jonathan:** "And my wrath shall reside in the city and upon the false prophets who prophesied false prophecies in it." **y)** **Kimchi:** "And then it will be said to you." **y)** Or: "neither is there a wall, nor etc." **Cocceius:** "I will sing a <term>ἐπίνιϰον</term> (song of victory) over you; I will triumph over you. I will make known to all that I have condemned the work of the Jews which they prepared so that they might stand by its benefit in the evil day, along with its plastering which the prophets made, and the prophets who plastered it; therefore, I have removed them and they have been overcome by me, and did not stand before me and my wrath."
**v. 16. a)** Or: "The Prophets of Israel." Verse 3. Those who are "prophesying" are the "plasterers," namely the false prophets. **b)** "Prophesying to Jerusalem," verse 2. **c)** Verse 6, 7, 9. Not in reality, but falsely, and as they boasted. Compare verse 12:24; **Jeremiah** 14:15.

The **Arabic root** means "to be of a fearful and small heart," and the noun derived from it means a timid and faint-hearted man. **l)** with a lie. **Jeremiah** 29:9. **m)** "whom I, however, did not sadden," or "whom I did not wish to be harmed or saddened." **Ezekiel** 28:24; **Job** 5:18. **n)** For God does not terrify those who believe and flee to Him, nor does He wish them to be tormented. —**Cocceius**, comparing **Psalm** 2:12; **Matthew** 5:6; **Hebrews** 6:18. **o)** "by confirming," that is, while you confirm the hands of the wicked and give him courage so that he sins more securely. **Chapter XIV. v. 1. a)** Afterward the men came to me—or, the men came one after another, as **Abarbanel** explains the discrepancy in number <note>The Hebrew verb is singular while the subject "men" is plural</note>. According to **Kimchi** and **Rashi**, the singular verb indicates that they all came with one mind—an evil one. The previous chapter dealt with the Prophets and Prophetesses; this one deals with those who consult them, showing that the reason false prophets are stirred up lies within the seekers themselves. (**Cocceius x**) they were there to consult about the future state of affairs. Thus the **Syriac** expressly adds: "to seek from the Lord." **y)** not from the number of those already deported to Babylon, as many think, but rather from those who had remained in Judea and had come to Babylon on some occasion, perhaps with Zedekiah’s embassy, as happened two years before this time (**Jeremiah** 51:59). This opinion is supported by: 1) their impiety is rebuked by God both in themselves and in the whole people over whom the elders ruled; 2) the judgment of God coming upon them (v. 21) is described not as if they were living in Chaldea, but rather in Canaan. It would be out of place for God to reproach the deportees for sins while announcing judgments to those remaining. —**Junius**. **x)** chapter 20:1. * **v. 2. a)** "And it happened," see chapter 20:1. This chapter has two or three parts: I. Prophecy against those who seek the Lord with evil intent (v. 1-8). II. Against prophets who allow themselves to be wrongly persuaded (v. 9-11). III. Against Jerusalem and the survivors in the Judean homeland (v. 12 onwards). * **v. 3. e)** "They have caused to ascend," meaning they carry it in their whole soul. To make something "ascend into the heart" is to give such things a place in one's affection. —**Cocceius**. **d)** their idols—literally, "dung-gods" <note>A derogatory Hebrew term for idols</note>. **Jonathan**: "the worship of their idols." But **Cocceius** translates it as "their excrement"—love for a thing of nothing. Such "dung" is one's own righteousness which comes from the law, not the righteousness of God from faith in Christ; it is the high opinion of one's own works, name, and all external privileges which Israel could boast of over other men. Paul also calls this righteousness "rubbish" <note>original: 'σκύβαλα' (skybala)</note> and "loss" <note>original: 'ζημίαן' (zēmian)</note> in **Philippians** 3:7-8. See **Malachi** 2:3. The **Septuagint** reads: "they placed their thoughts upon their own hearts." **e)** chapter 20:32. **f)** the stumbling block or scandal of their iniquity. These idols were a scandal to their worshippers, causing them to strike against them and fall into all the evils of guilt and punishment.

The reason for equal punishment is that the inquirer comes to the Prophet with a heart full of filth and eyes on a stumbling block; and the Prophet, like Balaam, hunts for the reward of injustice from such people and desires to please them: and thus they commit spiritual adultery together. **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his covenant theology.</note>.

II. III. Nevertheless, He adds IV. a Gospel promise from the covenant of grace already entered into long ago, by virtue of which He is willing to receive back the repudiated woman after she has repented, to atone for her, and to give her spiritual children—not indeed from the legal covenant, but from the evangelical or new covenant. verse 60 and following. # EZEKIEL. Chapter 16.

<margin>
**v. 3. r)** Others translate as: "your dealings," as if from the root *makar* meaning "he sold." Among the Hebrews, it refers to a "habitation" or "dwelling place," from the root *gur*. To us, it suggests the "breast"—the place of formation or digging, comparing the word *kur* in Isaiah 51:1-2. Thus says Guffert (p. 467) and Cocceius in his Lexicon (p. 435), who says: "One who is born from a certain people or from the land of that people is seen as if 'dug out' from metal, or derived from a spring." The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and the Syriac version translate it as "her root." Compare below in chapters 21:30 and 29:14. Root: *’ar*.
**s)** Perhaps it means "colleagues," gathered into one. In the Talmud, the verb in the *piel* stem means "to paint, to figure, or to induce shapes." From this comes *kiyyur*, meaning "figure" or "picture"; and *Kuryan*, meaning "models" or "figures" according to which bronze or clay vessels are formed. **s)** births; or "your generations" (verse 4). See Genesis 11:28, 24:4, and 31:13. **t)** They are from the land of the Canaanites, which was most corrupt in its customs; from them you drank in much more than you did from the virtues of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, your true parents from whom you properly originated. Compare Zephaniah 1:11 and Zechariah 14:21. **u)** The Amorite is mentioned in verse 45. The Amorites were notably evil, as were the Hittites (Genesis 15:16). Perhaps by their names, the remaining nations like the Jebusites and Perizzites are also understood. The sense is: "You imitate their impious customs and idolatry as if you were born from them," just as a person is often called the "son" of another whose character they imitate. See Matthew 3:7, 23:33, and John 8:44. Virgil wrote similarly: <note>original: "Nec tibi diva parens, generis nec Dardanus auctor, Perfide, sed duris genuit te cautibus horrens Caucasus, Hyrcanæque admorunt ubera tigres."</note> "Neither was a goddess your mother, nor Dardanus the founder of your race, you treacherous man; but the shivering Caucasus bore you on harsh rocks, and Hyrcanian tigers gave you their teats." In this vein, Cocceius says: "The inhabitants of Jerusalem, the nobles and teachers of the Israelites and the tribe of Judah, are from Amorites and Hittites." In Genesis 38:2, it is told that Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite man among the Adullamites and took her as a wife; then, he took for his son a wife—
</margin>

<margin>
—surely also from the Canaanites, from whom came Perez and Zerah. Therefore, Amorites and Hittites were ancestors of the Jews. **v)** See verses 44 and 45. **y)** On account of the similarity of their customs. Compare Genesis 27:46.
</margin>

He names the Hittite woman because that nation seems to have been more prone to lust, as seen in verse 45. — **verse 4. z)** *For, furthermore, as it pertains to your birth.* verse 3. **a)** *on which you were born.* Verse 5. Genesis 40:20, Hosea 2:5. Piscator and others apply this to the time when God called Abraham, then an idolater, out of Ur of the Chaldeans (Joshua 24:2). Others more correctly apply it to the times after the death of Joseph until the exodus from Egypt, when the multiplied Israel began to be not just the family of Israel, but a people. So say Kimchi, Grotius, and Cocceius, who compares chapter 20:8. The assembly of Israel (under those Egyptian afflictions) was like an infant cast out upon the face of the field, whose umbilical cord, etc. **b)** *it was not cut off*, (as is customary for newborn infants) from that intestine by which the infant adheres to the mother. **c)** *your umbilical cord.* (2) Proverbs 3:8, Song of Songs 7:3. That which is in the womb is, as it were, the "mouth" of the fetus, through which it draws life, spirit, and nourishment. **d)** *and with water you were not washed;* Proverbs 30:12. As is common for newborns to be purged of blood and the filth of the womb, and so that the limbs, previously contracted in the womb, might be extended and properly formed by warm water. **e)** Cocceius and others: "for my (pleasant) sight" (1) so that you might appear lovely; or "when I looked upon you," as Tremellius has it. **f)** *and by salting you were not salted.* Ezekiel 30:35, Leviticus 2:13. In ancient times, the bodies of newborns were salted, or washed with water steeped in salt, to dry up excessive moisture and remove all uncleanness from the womb, among other reasons. Galen, in *On the Preservation of Health*, book 1, says: "by sprinkling a little salt, the infant's skin is rendered denser and more solid," etc. So say Rashi, Kimchi, and others. **g)** *and by wrapping in bandages.* <note>The Hebrew grammar here uses an "Infinitive Hophal" form, indicating a passive action being performed on the subject.</note> **h)** *you were not wrapped.* Also according to the custom of infants. (2) See Numbers 30:21. 6. and Luke 2:7. There is an allegory in this verse and those following. According to Grotius, Piscator, and others: You were most contemptible. No one was present at your birth to perform the duties of a mother or midwife; but, destitute of law and teacher, you lived unformed, unrefined, in the filth of sin, in idolatry and the other crimes of the Egyptians. No one took care of you to deliver you from your misery and innate sin and to lead you toward eternal salvation. But Kimchi applies all this to the external afflictions of the Israelites and their subsequent liberation from Egypt. Although the Holy Spirit intended to signify by these words how despised the Israelite nation once was, especially while serving in Egypt, yet by this description of foulness, He also depicted the spiritual uncleanness of original sin, which we bring with us into this world from our mother's womb. That must be washed away by the water of baptism, lest it be imputed to us—which allegory is not unfitting, especially since that original foulness is the source and origin of every evil, even those described here properly. (Oliander and Calovius). **verse 5. i)** *He did not have pity on you.* chapter 20:17. No one was found who possessed that charity which ought to be in a redeemer (Cocceius). **k)** *to do to you one of these things.* **l)** by dealing with you with clemency. chapter 11, Ezekiel 9:13. It signifies the harshness of the Egyptians, who ought to have been like parents to them, as Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note> correctly observes here, says Grotius. Yet God does not therefore concede that human infirmity can be cured by man; rather, He feels that man was utterly incurable by nature, and of such great foulness that he was a loathing to all created things, much less could he be cured by any of them (Tremellius). **m)** *thus you were cast out.* Genesis 21:15, Psalm 22:11. **n)** just as exposed infants are usually cast out. **o)** Others: *in the loathing of your soul;* which you caused in everyone by that foulness of yours, or: so that you yourself loathed your own life. (1) compare the verb in verse 45. Leviticus 26:11, 15; Jeremiah 14:19. **p)** for the people were born in Egypt, as we said at verse 4. **verse 6. q)** *But I passed by you.* verses 8, 1 Kings 19:19. He begins now to recount His benefits, to show their ungrateful heart. **r)** compare Hosea 9:10. As if someone in a field happened upon an exposed girl; just as Moses was found by the daughter of Pharaoh as she passed by. **s)** *to be trampled.* Others: *trampled.* Tremellius: "you being present to be trampled," verse 12. namely, exposed to death and all evils leading to death. **t)** *in your bloods,* which clung to you from birth. Tremellius refers this to the blood of the infant, which is exhausted by flowing from an untended umbilical cord. **u)** *I said therefore to you,* (Tremellius). By the power of my word and my promises, I delivered you from most present death, in which you were as much involved as an infant whose umbilical cord is bleeding out. **x)** *in your bloods.* (Tremellius). However much you were submerged in your sins and dead by nature, like an infant with exhausted blood. A. Gusset (p. 190): While Israel was being killed in Egypt in righteous homicides, God made him live in blood (in the midst of slaughter). **y)** *Live!* Also with spiritual and eternal life (Cocceius). Nor does it stand in the way that death is later decreed for the same woman, and that her defection from her God is mentioned. For when it is said she is "righteous to live," that is said on account of the holy fathers; into whose place the degenerate descendants then come. Since this tree or lineage is likened to one woman, contrary things are said of her in different respects. Compare Jeremiah 2:3, 5, 18. **z)** and again I said. Not once, but with promises repeated more often I confirmed it, comparing Genesis 12, 13, 15, and 17. Others: "I said, I say" (Cocceius). The repetition signifies a fixed and certain purpose. By which it is signified to us that our life depends entirely on the grace, purpose, and good pleasure of God. **a)** although foul from blood, I want you to live (Grotius). **verse 7. b)** *Into a myriad;* that is, increased into many thousands. Compare Genesis 24:60, Numbers 10:36, Deuteronomy 33:17, and Exodus 1:7. **c)** *as the sprout, etc.* compare Isaiah 44:3. (Cocceius). It signifies a huge multitude of people, on account of which she began to be remarkable. **d)** Genesis 17:5. **e)** from which you grew, or: "you were thus increased." Genesis 1:28, 35:11, Ecclesiastes 1:10, 12. **f)** *and you arrived at the proper age.* Genesis 25:27, 2 Samuel 12:3. As it would be said of a girl, under whose person the Jewish nation is described (Grotius). Compare Ephesians 1:2. **g)** and you arrived. chapter 22:4.

not a thing for all peoples. *Deuteronomy 4:6, 7, 8.* **Cocceius;** who also adds: From this saying it is perceived why God made the Israelite people so great, namely, so that God's glory and divine truth, and the doctrine of God's justice, true wisdom, and prudence might become known to the nations through them, and God's name would become great in all the earth. **f)** the most true saying of the Lord Jehovah God. *Chapter 11:8.* **v. 15. g)** But you securely trusted in your beauty; *verse 14; Psalm 47:10; Jeremiah 13:25;* seizing material for pride and security from my gifts. **Cocceius:** that is, because she claimed those ornaments and especially the divine indwelling for herself as her own, as if it could not be taken away; she wrongly held those things as arguments for saving divine grace, the remission of sin, and righteousness, rather than as the causes of righteousness and life. Moreover, he now begins to touch upon the ungrateful soul and all the shames of the nations. **h)** both corporally and spiritually. *Verse 16; Psalm 106:39; compare Jeremiah 3:1; Hosea 1:2.* For in both ways it is most true: it is indeed a great form of [lost] modesty. **i)** S. "because of your fame." *Verse 14.* **Cocceius:** you played the harlot over your name, that is, because, having set forth their name (just as harlots used to affix their names to their cells), they invited neighbors from all sides to love and honor that name, and to imitate their deeds, and thus showed themselves friendly and consenting to such minds. Isaiah interprets this in *chapter 66:5,* where this is proposed as a symbol of the Jews: "In my name the Lord will be glorified," that is, it is the glory of the Lord that I am a Jew by name—and those who do this so that they may be named Jews, glorify the Lord. In this way, most Israelites added proselytes to themselves, whom they made children of hell more than they themselves were (*Matthew 23:15*), while they persuaded them that for righteousness and salvation it was enough to be called by name "Jehovah the God of Abraham," as they themselves did, to say "one God," and to use the same institutions with them. Thus they flattered the nations, who estimated their name and imitated their deeds while retaining their pagan opinions and transferring them to God, as if they were partners in the same covenant and heirs of righteousness. **k)** so much so that you poured out, you prostituted your harlotries and lusts profusely. *Verses 20, 22, 33, etc.* **l)** S. "upon every passerby"; you gave the opportunity for your impurity to every traveler, like a harlot who prostitutes herself to every passerby. *Compare Genesis 38:14.* **m)** **Cocceius:** namely, while they imbued all who approached the land of Canaan with such opinions that, having taken up the name of Jews, they were held as members of the same city and people, and in that mixing they might mutually exult, just as those playing the harlot exult in the mixing of flesh. This was to introduce the uncircumcised in heart and flesh into the sanctuary. *Chapter 44:7.* **Jonathan:** <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase of the prophets</note> you associated yourself to worship idols with every passerby. **m)** S. "whoever it might be." Therefore, the superstition of the nations, being more heavy and severe than the yoke God placed on the Israelites, could seem to please God more, as if it honored Him more. **Cocceius** on verse 22. r) to be devoured, *chapter 23:27*, so that the fire might consume them for the favor of those [idols]. **Psat.** s) S. <note>Septuagint</note> "Is this a small thing?" *chapter 14:18.* t) S. A preface to the sentence, to hear which she is summoned as a harlot. l) chapter 6:3; chapter 13:2. **v. 36. m)** Because it was poured out by you, profuse, verse 15. **n)** your brass, your money given to lovers. **Septuagint** by metonymy <note>a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it</note>: "your dross," i.e., according to Tremellius and Cocceius: "the scoriae or filth flowing from you because of the frequency and constancy of your fornication." Thus Gussetius, page 506. He says it alludes to the filth flowing from brass in a furnace, as in chapter 24:11; for it regards this happening from burning lust, and the flow of humors causing dissolution. Compare Jeremiah 3:22, chapter 13:27. Targum Jonathan: "because you uncovered your nakedness." **o)** and your nakedness was exposed; see verses 8, 37. **p)** verses 33, 34. **q)** with (**Septuagint:** upon) your lovers, verses 15, 16, 33; Jeremiah 22:20. **r)** chapter 8:10. **s)** verses 2, 22. **t) Septuagint:** and according to the blood of your children. Verse 20. Targum Jonathan: "and because of the guilt of blood," etc. **u)** see verse 21. **v. 37. x)** "Therefore," I say, verse 35. **y)** gathering them. Compare Hosea 8:10. **z)** verses 33, 35. He is about to punish you through your very lovers (Grotius says: "the Chaldeans with Assyrian helpers"). **a)** to whom you were sweet and pleasant. Psalm 104:34. Syriac: "in whom you delighted." But **Septuagint** reads: "with whom you made a pact." **b)** you were mixed. Compare chapter 27:9, 27. **b)** Isaiah 57:8, Jeremiah 2:25. **c)** together with. **Septuagint:** besides. Genesis 32:12, Exodus 35:22. **d)** Grotius understands the Edomites and Palestinians. But Cocceius says: just as harlots sometimes quarrel with their lovers, so the Jews fell into quarrels with the Assyrians, whom they had hired to wage war against the Syrians. **e)** against you. Compare 1 Kings 11:24. **f)** chapter 23:10. **g)** toward them. Compare Hosea 2:5, 12. "I will expose you to public shame," as a punishment of retaliation, gathering from verse 36, by taking away every ornament and clothing mentioned above. **h)** Lamentations 1:8. That is, your injustice, your infidelity, a heart estranged from God. Whence we conclude that the destruction of the temple and the Babylonian captivity are a testimony of the injustice of the Israelites and their abandonment of God's covenant. Cocceius. **v. 38. i)** Thus I will judge you, chapter 7:3, 8. **k)** with capital judgments. Compare chapter 23:10, 24. **l)** of adulteresses. chapter 23:45; Leviticus 20:10. Such as you were above in verse 32. Compare Hosea 2:4. **m)** such as they were toward their own and godly children, verses 20, 36; chapter 7:23; chapter 22:4. Compare Genesis 9:6, Exodus 21:12. **n)** "and I will give you over to blood," i.e., to the slaughter of my wrath; proceeding from my wrath and jealousy; with which, as a just judge, I boil over against the bloodthirsty, and as a just husband, I am hostile toward the adulterous Jerusalem. **Septuagint:** as the blood of wrath and jealousy. Compare chapter 5:13, 15; chapter 8:3; chapter 14:19. **v. 39. o)** "For I will give you into the hands of enemies," verse 37. **p)** so that they may destroy your mound, your brothel (**Septuagint:** your bed). Verse 24. Grotius: "the temple, of which you made an idol." Cocceius: that is, every place in which the Israelite people boasted themselves as the people of God before the eyes of the nations, and in which, with the boasting of the name of the people of God, they wished to please the nations, and sinned with them—and not to God, but to the false gods of the nations, with whom they contracted friendship and in whose wealth they trusted—they made offerings. **q)** and tear down. **Septuagint:** overthrow. Deuteronomy 12:2; 2 Chronicles 31:1. **r)** verses 24, 25. **s)** they shall strip you of your clothes, chapter 23:26; Genesis 37:23. **t)** and take away, remove. chapter 23:26, 29; 1 Kings 20:6. **u)** verse 17. Grotius: "the vessels of the temple," gathering from 2 Kings 25:13. Indeed, all the gifts with which God adorned you. **x)** they shall cast you down and leave you, chapter 22:10; Isaiah 23:2. **y)** verse 7; chapter 23:29.

**v. 30.** The word for "your mound" is written as <term>בִּבְנֹתַיִךְ</term> but read as <term>בִּבְנוֹתַיִךְ</term> according to the Masoretic notes. **v. 32.** The word <term>הַמְּנָאָפֶת</term> (the adulteress) has a double 'Mem' indicated by a Dagesh. **v. 33.** The word <term>נְדָנַיִךְ</term> (your gifts) is written with the Segol vowel in various manuscripts. **v. 34.** The word <term>הֵפֶךְ</term> (reverse/opposite) appears with the Segol vowel; some manuscripts use the Kibbuts vowel. The word <term>וְאֶתְנָן</term> (and hire) appears with the Kamets vowel, contrary to some Masoretic traditions. **v. 36.** The word <term>וְכִדְמֵי</term> (and like the blood) appears with the Chateph-Patah vowel; some versions read <term>וּבְדָמֵי</term> (and in the blood). **v. 37.** The phrase <term>אֲשֶׁר־עָרַבְתְּ</term> (with whom you took pleasure) includes a Makkaph <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in several key editions.

<summary>This page analyzes Ezekiel's condemnation of Jerusalem's unique depravity: unlike a typical harlot who is paid, Jerusalem paid her foreign "lovers" (allies like Egypt and Assyria) to sin with her. The text details the impending "capital judgment" where these very allies will strip and destroy the city as punishment for its spiritual and literal adultery.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on Ezekiel 16. Following the previous page’s description of Jerusalem's spiritual infidelity and "harlotry," this section details the divine judgment: the gathering of her former allies to act as her executioners. The text moves from the legal punishment of an adulteress (stoning and burning) to a deep genealogical critique, identifying Jerusalem’s "true" family not as the patriarchs, but as the pagan Canaanites, Samaritans, and Sodomites.</meta>

### CHAPTER 16. EZEKIEL 16

<margin>
**v. 42. n)** Septuagint: "until I shall cause my anger to rest in you."

**The 'He' is with a Patah** <note>Hebrew grammatical note regarding the vowel in Ezekiel 5:13</note>. **m)** "And my jealousy—or my zealotry—shall recede from you."

**Singular** <note>Hebrew: *yechir*</note>

**Singular** <note>Hebrew: *yechir*</note>

Compare Isaiah 11:13. This means: "I will no longer hold you as a wife (compare Hosea 2:4), but I will despise you as if you were a stranger (compare Deuteronomy 32:22 and following **x**), and I shall rest." Compare Isaiah 18:4, 61:1.
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 40. x)** Septuagint: "And at last making them ascend over you." Compare chapter 26:3, Isaiah 8:7. **d)** Chapter 23:47. They shall deal with you <note>the Hebrew word used is related to the punishment for adultery</note>, as above in verse 32; compare Joshua 8:5. **b)** Targum Jonathan: "They shall pour out stones upon you." and "they shall transfix/pierce you." Septuagint: "They shall dissect you (1) with their swords." **Cocceius:** These things allude to the siege of cities and especially of Jerusalem. For in sieges, stones were usually thrown by catapults, walls broken by rams, those in the way were cast down, and people were torn by swords. Who can deny that the prophetic Spirit alludes to what actually happened? So says **Kimchi**.

**v. 41. d)** Compare 2 Kings 25:9. **Grotius**: The law commands this to be done to an idolatrous city in Deuteronomy 13:16-17. **e)** "so that they do/exercise." Chapter 11:9. **f)** Chapter 5:10. **g)** That is, of the nations (verse 34). **Targum Jonathan and Kimchi**: of the neighboring and remote provinces, nations, kingdoms, and republics. So that it may be a public example and a mockery to the whole world. Compare Psalm 137:7. **h)** Septuagint: "so I will make you cease." Chapter 7:24, 23:27. **i)** From harlotry, so that you are no longer a harlot, but stop playing the harlot. Compare chapter 34:10. **Cocceius:** That is, so that they become a despised people or multitude, with whom no king or republic would make a treaty or enter into society, and who would have no communion with any nation. Just as the Jews are at this time everywhere. Not because they are any better, or healed from their harlot-like nature; but because they have neither temple nor idols with which to play the harlot, nor can they make treaties with any men, since they have no republic, kings, or princes. Just as **Hosea** prophesied of them in chapter 3. **k)** So that you also give hire no more. Verse 33-34.
</margin>

40. They shall bring up <a> against you <b> a company <c> and they shall stone <d> you with stones <kit: and they shall cut you down> <g> with their swords <h>.
41. And they shall burn <d> your houses <e> with fire <f> and execute upon you <g> judgments <h> in the eyes of <i> many women <k>. And I will cause you to cease <l> from being a harlot <m>, and also a reward you shall no <n> give anymore <o>.
42. So will I make rest <n> my fury <o> in you, and shall depart <p> my jealousy from you <q>, and I will be quiet <r> and not be angry <s> anymore <t>.
43. Because <p> that you did not remember <q> the days of <r> your youth <s>, but you provoked me <t> in all these; and also I <u> behold <v> your way <w> upon your head I have set <x>, says the Lord GOD; and you did not <y> commit this lewdness <z> upon all your abominations <a>.
44. Behold <a> everyone that uses proverbs <b> against you shall use this proverb, saying: As is the mother, so is her daughter <c>.
45. The daughter of your mother <d> are you, who loathes her husband <e> and her children; and the sister of your sisters <f> are you, who loathed <g> their husbands and their children <h>; your mother was a Hittite <i> and your father an Amorite <k>.
46. And your sister <l> the elder <m> is Samaria and her daughters <n> who dwells on your left <o>; and your younger sister <p> than you, who dwells at your right hand, is Sodom and her daughters <q>.
