**n)** "nor will I be incensed with you anymore" as a husband; or toward your enemies for your sake. Compare Deuteronomy 32:21, 27 and Hosea 5:15, 8. **Greek Text:** "I will not care for you" <note>original: "µὴ µεϱιµνήσω ὑµῶν"</note>. Compare 1 Peter 5:7.

**v. 45. d)** Meaning: similar to her by way of character. Compare 2 Kings 6:32. **e)** One who is loathing; she who was loathing and rejecting (Job 31:10) her husband; she violated the faith given to her husband by playing the harlot with others. **f)** That is, God, whom they had learned about from Noah. **Grotius**: compare Isaiah 54:5. **g)** Whom she gave to death in honor of idols. Compare Leviticus 18:21, 24; Deuteronomy 12:30-31. **h)** Septuagint: "of your sisters." **Tremellius**: "as each of your sisters." So verse 52. **Grotius**: similar in nature to those you are related to by blood. **i)** Who loathed and rejected (Leviticus 26:11, 15, 30, 43, 44) their husbands. **k)** Meaning: your mother is a Hittite. **l)** See verse 3. **Cocceius**: Just as the children of Abraham can come from the Gentiles, so from Abraham according to the flesh can come those who are not children of Abraham (Romans 9:7). The Jews have no grounds for boasting that they are the seed of Abraham as long as they imitate the feelings and manners of the Hittites and do not walk in the footsteps of Abraham's faith. **v. 46. m)** "And your elder sister..." Samaria is called the "elder," according to **Grotius**, because she was closer in blood; but according to **Tremellius** and others (which is better), because she was the capital of the ten tribes, whereas only two tribes were in Judah; compare verse 61. Others say it is because she turned away from the worship of God earlier than Jerusalem. **n)** Chapter 23:4. **o)** "and daughters," meaning the smaller cities and her villages; see verses 27, 31. **p)** Meaning: to the north. Compare chapter 4:4-5. A Hebrew idiom: this is said in relation to the Temple, if you were looking from there toward the rising sun in the east. **Grotius**: compare chapter 1:10; 2 Chronicles 3:17. **q)** "your sister, smaller than you": not in age, as she was older; but in the number of citizens and cities. Compare verse 61. According to **Grotius**, because she was more remote in blood. **r)** To the south; compare chapter 16:3. **s)** Compare Deuteronomy 32:32; Isaiah 1:10. Sodom and from there, from the incestuous union of Lot with his daughters, the inhabitants of Sodom arose: the Ammonites and Moabites. **Grotius** on verse 45: the Ammonites and Moabites took the Chaldean gods in place of their old gods, Molech and Chemosh; the Samaritans took the golden calves; yet this profited them nothing. See Jeremiah 48 and 49. **s)** Those other four cities, which **Piscator** (on verse 53) concludes obeyed the King of Sodom because he alone treated with Abraham regarding the spoils (Genesis 14:21). But according to **Grotius**, these are the Ammonites and Moabites as the offspring of Sodom.

<column-break/>

**v. 43. p)** Septuagint: "I will do all these things to you because you did not remember" (verse 22). **q)** That is, your original condition and my kindness, mentioned above in verse 4 and following. Meaning: from how much misery and by whom they were liberated; who it was that addressed them, who made a covenant with them, who was named their Leader and King, and who placed his **Greek: tabernacle** <note>original: "σκηνωϱὴν"</note> among them. **Cocceius**. **v)** "And you were moved/unsettled," or you rioted against me (1 Kings 19:27-28) by indulging in your crimes and not attending to the voice of God and the prophets calling you back to repentance, indeed even treating them with insults and killing them. **Greek Text:** "Did you not grieve me?" <note>original: "µὴ ἐλύπηסάς µε"</note> (Ephesians 4:30). Septuagint: "and you moved me to anger." So **Targum Jonathan and the Syriac**; compare Job 12:6. But **Cocceius** in his Lexicon: "you were angry with me." Compare Psalm 4:7. **s)** From which it also marks a just retaliation, as in verse 52 and chapter 9:10. **8)** "Behold!" (Genesis 47:23). To **Cocceius**, this seems to express the spirit, gesture, and voice of one triumphing. "Aha!" (Lexicon page 191). **t)** Jeremiah 4:18. **Targum Jonathan**: "the vengeance of your way." **x)** Chapter 9:10; 22:31; 2 Chronicles 6:23. **y)** Septuagint: "so that you did not commit a crime." That is, so that you do not add this outrage (verse 29) on top of all your crimes. But **Cocceius** (Lexicon page 204): "Did you not commit that great and incomparable crime (which you know well and I need not recount) above all your abominations?" Meaning (as he explains more fully on page 191 and in his Commentary): that crime which I predicted in my word would come to pass, specifically by you. "Did you not repudiate your Savior, crucify Him?" etc. Others: "And no," "yet not," or "for you did not give thought to all your abominations to repent of them." **Jonathan, Kimchi, and Rashi** follow this. The sense is easy, provided the phrase and word "you did" <note>Hebrew: *asita*</note> occurs elsewhere specifically in a positive sense. **z)** Verse 22, 36, 51.

**v. 44. a)** "Whoever uses parables," Septuagint: "skilled in speaking." Chapter 18:2. **b)** "He shall make a proverb against you," or "he can rightly make one." Chapter 12:23; 17:2. **c)** "As is such a mother, so is her daughter." Like mother, like daughter. The daughter of the worst mother is the worst, equal in guilt and punishment. Compare Acts 7:51. **Glassius** (Philologia Sacra page 165) correctly advises that by "mother," the original inhabitants of the land of Canaan, rebels against God, are understood. So **Grotius**: He calls the Canaanites and other nations who held the same land before "mother." See verse 3, where the interpretation of this passage is to be sought, also from verse 45. Others specifically understand by "mother" the old and pagan Jerusalem, and by "daughter" the Israelite or Jewish Jerusalem. **Cocceius** says it is not safe to live simply according to **Greek: traditions handed down from the fathers** <note>original: "πατροπαϱαδότοις"</note> and to speak words received from fathers.

<note>Continuing the commentary from the margins:</note>
...they persecuted Lot himself with the greatest injury, Genesis 19. **v. 47. c. 18, 12. c. 33, 26. o)** "but I removed them from my sight." Compare Genesis 19:24, 25. **p)** "when I saw their abominations, worthy of destruction." This alludes to Genesis 18:21. **v. 51. q)** The Jews were worse than these, not in the substance of the sin, but in its appearance, quality, and circumstances. They had received more benefits than Samaria: the temple, priests, prophets, several pious kings, a longer-lasting kingdom, and the patience of God in bearing their ways for a longer time. Yet, not warned by the punishments of the Israelites, they did not obey God; instead, though adorned with so many benefits, they showed an ungrateful spirit, with even greater offense to God and exaggeration of their crimes. Especially later, when they both rejected and crucified Christ, and rejected the Gospel, and blasphemed the Spirit poured out from heaven, they surpassed both Samaria and Sodom in many ways. **r)** <note>Schmid:</note> "according to half." A similar exaggeration is found in 2 Chronicles 9:6. **s)** Compare 2 Kings 17:17, 19 and following. **t)** "for you multiplied." v. 25, 26, 29. **u)** more than they, Samaria and her daughters. <note>Kimchi</note>. **x)** "and thus you justified." v. 52. Jeremiah 3:11. This is in a certain respect and comparatively; you caused them to appear innocent and upright compared to you and your works. Thus the <note>Syriac version</note> adds for the sake of explanation: "you polluted yourself more than they, and so they are more righteous than you." **y)** v. 22, 43, 58. **v. 52. a)** "Endure, carry your ignominy." v. 54; Chapter 23, 35; 32, 24, 25. **b)** <note>Schmid:</note> "which you adjudged to your sister"; namely, by saying that Sodom and the ten tribes were justly punished. So <note>Rashi and Michlal Yophi</note>. <term>Piel</term> <note>intensive verb form</note> (4) Genesis 48, 11; Psalm 106, 30. Compare Romans 2, 1; Luke 13, 2. But <note>Gussetius, page 678</note>: "because you were an arbiter for your sisters." And so <note>Cocceius in his commentary</note>: "because you advocated for your sisters" (you absolved them by comparison to yourself, as in v. 51), saying they were not worthy of punishment because you yourself (Jerusalem) sinned more, and yet remain safe. **c)** <note>Tremellius:</note> "to both of your sisters," as in v. 45. **d)** and that for your sins. Or, more according to the <term>accents</term> <note>musical/grammatical marks in Hebrew text</note>: "you were the arbiter or you advocated for them; for through your sins, they are righteous before you." **e)** <note>Schmid:</note> "by which you rendered yourself abominable." Others: "in which you acted abominably beyond them," 2 Kings 21, 26. **f)** <note>Schmid:</note> "since they were justified," v. 51, "before you." But look at what was just said. **g)** "be ashamed." Isaiah 23, 4; Jeremiah 31, 19. **h)** <note>Schmid:</note> "for that which you justified in your sisters." <term>Infinitive Piel</term> with <term>Paragogic</term> <note>an added letter/syllable</note> changed into a suffix, as in Exodus 40, 12. **v. 53. k)** Interpreters vary regarding the sense of this and the following verses; some see a threat, others (simply and more consistently with the context, especially comparing v. 61) see a promise here. In the latter sense, <note>Schmid</note> and others say: "Nevertheless, I will then bring back their captivity." However, we believe this should be understood not so much as a physical return, but as a spiritual liberation—namely, conversion to Christ. Thus <note>Vatablus and Castalio</note>: it says that someday nations similar to Sodom will stand through Christ, though they now lie under Satan's tyranny; just as Sodom and Samaria once stood, though they now lie in ruins. He speaks of Sodom's change from a fallen state to a restored one—what kind of restoration this will be, however, will be known in its own time. Thus <note>Castalio</note>. Compare the same phrase in chapter 29, 14; Jeremiah 30, 3; 48, 47; Amos 9, 14. Others say: "And if I should bring back," as if this were a threat based on an impossible or absurd condition. It would mean: "If I restore Sodom and Samaria, I will also restore you. But that will not happen (since Sodom was overturned and turned into a lake, and Samaria is not to be brought back), therefore neither will this happen." Just as I destroyed them utterly, so I will destroy you, comparing it to a similar expression in John 15, 10. To those who object that he often promises the Jews a return to their homeland—even in Ezekiel himself and other prophets—they respond that the prophets in such threats are addressing the common crowd and the whole body of the people; or that the discourse here is about the impious Jews who existed in Ezekiel's time, and the promises found elsewhere do not pertain to them, but to their descendants. Those who feel this way (though <note>Cocceius</note> judges that the phrase and speech of the prophet portend nothing of the sort, but rather the opposite) only begin the promise with verse 60. **l)** Psalm 126, 1.

* **v. 50.** *watigbehena* <note>they were haughty</note> Defective in manuscripts 1, 2, and 5.
* **v. 51.** *achotayich* <note>your sisters</note> in the text without the extra letter in various editions, against the Masoretic notes.
* **v. 52.** *achotayich* with a <term>Segol</term> vowel in several manuscripts.
* **v. 53.** *shevutayich* <note>your captives</note> thus with the <term>Keri</term> reading in many manuscripts according to the Masoretes.

Hence some understand "Sodom" to mean the two and a half tribes living across the Jordan in Gilead and Bashan: both because of their proximity to the site of Sodom, the similar fertility of the soil, and also because of the similarity of their customs and vices. By Samaria we understand all who fell away from the covenant of God, were led away, and were mixed with the nations. Thus Jeremiah 3:18. Johannes Cocceius <note>A 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> notes: The plural indicates that what was said of Samaria and Sodom was not said of them alone, but of all nations, great and small (compare Isaiah 42:6, 22, etc.). i) Among the children (Isaiah 49:22, chapter 60:4) born in you through the Gospel (compare verse 62, Isaiah 54:1, Psalm 87:5). This sets up an opposition in the sentence, as in Romans 8:11. So says Rashi <note>A preeminent medieval French rabbi</note>, or rather: not from the Old Testament, which you broke, and which made sons into slaves; far from adopting foreigners as sons, it instead points to the new covenant in Christ (Romans 10:4), the covenant of the Gospel, written not on stone tablets but on the fleshy tablets of the heart by the Spirit of the living God (see Jeremiah 31:31, 2 Corinthians 3:3, Hebrews 8:8). See more on this in Cocceius’s Commentary and in Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius, a Lutheran divine</note> on this passage.

# CHAPTER XVII.

<gloss>a</gloss> 1 And the word of the LORD came to me, saying:
<gloss>a</gloss> <gloss>b</gloss> <gloss>c</gloss> 2 "Son of man, pose a riddle and speak a parable to the house of Israel,

v) *The opening of the mouth* (2) chapter 29:21. So that you no longer dare to open your mouth against me, nor have any further cause to complain justly about me, or to excuse or cloak your sins, recognizing that there is nothing in you but the material for damnation; and therefore, by faith alone embracing the atonement perfected by Christ, and giving all glory to God alone, your Savior (compare Psalm 107:42, Job 5:16). z) *Because of your ignominy, or your shame* (verse 61). t) *When I have atoned for and forgiven you* (Deuteronomy 21:8). u) *Everything, or according to everything*. x) See verse 59. y) See verse 14, chapter 11:8. 

**CHAPTER XVII, verses 1, 2.**) Furthermore, it happened. After God in the preceding chapter most severely reproached the crimes of faithless Jerusalem and announced just punishments, eventually adding a promise for the remnant of the godly, there now follows a declaration of judgment against King Zedekiah under another riddle or emblem of grace, on account of his violated oath and rash rebellion against the King of Babylon. Here is: I. The riddle itself, an emblem of two eagles, a cedar sprig, and a vine (v. 3–10). II. Its clear explanation (v. 11–21). III. The promise concerning the spiritual restoration of the kingdom of Israel through Christ, and its expansion to all nations (v. 22 onwards). 

**v. 2. a)** *Propose riddlingly, sharply and obscurely* (4) (Judges 14:12, 13, 16), to make the Jews pay attention as if to something extraordinary that should seriously affect them. b) *A riddle* (Psalm 49:5). Cocceius: The use of riddles is great in Scripture. They seize the listener for consideration; they stick in the memory; they provide great light when understood; they are heard with less offense; they offer teachers a facility <note>original Greek: εὐχερίαν</note> for teaching, and make brothers communicate with one another, occupied together in searching out the meanings of the riddles. c) Or *parabolize a parable* (chapter 16:44, chapter 21:5). d) Concerning (chapter 19:1, 4). e) And specifically concerning their King. 

**v. 3. f)** *That great eagle*, namely the King of Babylon (v. 12; compare Jeremiah 48:40 and 49:22, Hosea 8:1). The reason for the likeness is that the eagle excels in strength and swiftness, has keen sight, an intrepid spirit, and carries a certain royal majesty in its whole body. Hence it is believed to hold empire over birds. Nor is it unlikely that the ancient Kings of Assyria had a golden eagle with outstretched wings as a royal sign, and that Scripture alludes to this whenever it designates them by the name of eagles. Bochart, *Hieroz.* Part II, p. 184. <note>Samuel Bochart, a French Protestant biblical scholar</note>. g) *Large-winged*, that is, having great armies (see Isaiah 8:8, Jeremiah 48:40). An eagle has large wings and extends them as much as possible during flight, by which it is carried most rapidly and with great force (Bochart, *Hieroz.* Part II, p. 169). h) *Long*. It is often used of the long-suffering (see Exodus 34:6, Ecclesiastes 7:8). i) *Wing or wing feathers* (3) (Isaiah 40:31, Psalm 55:7), with which he flew very swiftly from Babylon to the West. Thus the Prophet shows how the Babylonian surpassed the Egyptian, mentioned in verse 7 (Tremellius). Others say *limbs* from the Chaldean, because wings were mentioned previously. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, the famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> suggests it signifies that Nebuchadnezzar ruled widely. k) *Full of feathers* (4) (v. 7, Leviticus 1:16) for defense from oncoming injuries, as opposed to the baldness in Micah 1:16. In early spring, birds of prey are subject to the shedding of feathers (Bochart, Part II, p. 165). By feathers, Vatablus <note>François Vatable, a French humanist scholar</note> understands immense wealth; Grotius understands people of various languages and habits. l) Rashi: *whose plumage was beautiful and patterned*. Or *embroidered*; a Phrygian work <note>Intricate embroidery</note>, which according to Wasmuth denotes the dignity and majesty of the kingdom. Bochart understands the species of eagles called *Asteriae* or starry, having the brilliance of gold and scattered spots, which are the largest of eagles (*Hieroz.* Part II, p. 169). m) *Upon Lebanon*, i.e., according to some, to the Temple or Sanctuary built from the cedars of Lebanon (2 Chronicles 2:8, 13, Zechariah 11:1). But Grotius and others understand both the Temple and Jerusalem or Zion, so called because it consisted almost entirely of the cedars of Lebanon; hence, because Lebanon abounded in cedars, he used "Lebanon" for Jerusalem or Zion. Others say *the land of Judea*, whose notable glory was Lebanon due to its cedars, etc., and its border through which one comes from Babylonia into Judea; so that the Prophet might persist in the metaphor of the eagle, which usually dwells in mountains. Tremellius: *invading the kingdom of Judea*, which is compared to the most excellent forest of Lebanon. Thus Maius in *Oecon. V. T.* p. 1038. Perhaps these opinions are not poorly combined. n) And *took from there* (compare 2 Kings 24:12). o) *The highest sprig or branch. Or little branch*. Cocceius in his Commentary says "downy hair." Others collectively *the highest branches* (5) (v. 22, chapter 31:3, 10). According to Wasmuth and others, it means King Jeconiah (alluding to his tender age, which was 18 years) and the royal line, as well as the princes and famous men, and a good part of the people (see 2 Kings 24:14 onwards). p) *Of the cedar* (v. 22, 23). The kingdom of the house of David before Nebuchadnezzar was like a green, tall, fragrant cedar (Cocceius; compare note on v. 22 and Isaiah 2:13). **v. 4. q)** *The head*, I say, *of the sprigs, or the summit of its foliage*. Verse 4 explains what was said in the preceding verse. r) *Of its tender branches or sprigs* (1) (compare v. 22). s) *He plucked* (5) (v. 22, Deuteronomy 23:26). t) And having torn him from his seat, he led him away, as later he did to Zedekiah (Jeremiah 52:11; compare 2 Kings 24:15).

**verse 7. 25. Jeremiah 11:16. r)** referring to that one, namely the eagle in verse 3, the King of Babylon [Nebuchadnezzar]. Verse 12. The meaning: Zedekiah was a king sufficiently wealthy and fortunate, but was bound to look up to the Babylonian King and revere him, partly as a subject, or as a client. **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian</note>. **e)** "his roots were under it." However, the <term>suffix</term> in **"under him"** can also refer to the *Eagle* (**according to Rashi, Grotius, etc.**) so that the sense is that Zedekiah’s kingdom was firm under the Babylonian king. **Compare verse 7. p)** *Thus, I say, it became a vine.* **q)** Or, where it made branches, or offshoots. **chapter 19:14. v)** and sent out **verse 7; chapter 31:5; Psalm 80:12. s)** beautiful or fruit-bearing branches **(6) chapter 31:5, 6, 8, 12, 13. Compare Isaiah 10:33.** that is, he begot sons (**see 2 Kings 25:7; Jeremiah 52:10**) and had nobles and citizens of the kingdom, or a people that multiplied daily. --- **verse 7. t)** But there was. **u)** another eagle; namely, the King of Egypt **verse 15**, who appears to **Grotius** to have been Apries <note>Also known as Hophra</note>, about whom see **Jeremiah 44:30. x)** also great; yet smaller than the Babylonian eagle. Hence it is not described with words as magnificent as that one in **verse 3. y)** See there, **verse 3. z)** abundant (though not flat) with feathers, as in **verse 3. a)** chapter 1:4; **Isaiah 50:2. b)** described in verse 6, namely Zedekiah and the kingdom of Judah. **c)** The Syriac and **Tremellius**: toward which, behold, this vine applied itself. **Grotius**: it bent. Others: it panted, it hungered. **Gussetius <note>Jacques Gousset, a French Hebrew scholar</note> page 396:** in the manner of those who are miserably in need, it stretched out its roots (1) compare the noun in Job 5:22. **d)** seeking strength and protection for itself from Egypt, having entered into a treaty with him; but having violated the faith which he had given to the Babylonian. **verse 15. Compare Jeremiah 37:5, 7. e)** it sent out to that one **verse 6. f)** to water it, that is, so that it might receive from him auxiliary forces, chariots, and horses **verse 15.** It may be seen as an allusion to the Nile, which waters Egypt, being sent into the fields through ditches, **compare Isaiah 2:18. g)** Syriac: from the garden beds (**namely, sprouting joyfully**) **verse 6. Others:** rather than from the beds of its own planting, i.e., so that the Egyptian might rather cause the state of the Jews to flourish and sustain it, than the garden bed made for it by Nebuchadnezzar in verse 5. (4) **verse 10;** Song of Solomon 5:13, chapter 6:2. I prefer the supplement to **Cocceius' Lexicon page 94:** this name from the meaning of the Arabic and Ethiopic root "to ascend"; as garden beds are accustomed to rise and ascend. But **Gussetius page 642** says: from the rivulets of the place in which it was planted. I would prefer: than the springs of the place in which it was planted, based on the meaning of the Ethiopic root "a fountain gushes forth." **h)** of the place of its planting. **(5)** chapter 31:4. Moreover, we refer the feminine suffix to the word **"vine"**; others to *Egypt*, whose King, like the Eagle, is presented in the masculine gender. **verse 8. i)** Syriac: though it was in a good or fertile field of the land **verse 5. k)** near, by, chapter 13:19. **l)** verse 5. **m)** it had been planted. **verses 21, 23; Psalm 1:3. n)** so that it might produce, might send out foliage. Syriac: a branch. **(7)** verse 21; Leviticus 23:40. **o)** so that it might be a vine of magnificence, or that it might become an extraordinary vine, Zechariah 11:2. **Grotius**: What was said in verses 5 and 6 is repeated, so that from the magnitude of the benefits, the guilt of the ungrateful mind might appear more grave; nor did Zedekiah defect to Pharaoh out of poverty or the oppression of the kingdom, but out of sheer pride, although he was treated benignly enough by Nebuchadnezzar. --- **verse 9. p)** Say therefore **verse 12; chapter 11:5. q)** will it prosper? You shall say to him; Syriac: will he be successful? verse 10; Numbers 14:41; Daniel 11:27. **Grotius**: is it possible that God would give prosperity to one who is both ungrateful and treacherous? Faith must be kept by the law of nations, even toward those whom one has come to through some necessity of war. But Zedekiah, besides his pledge, was also bound by benefits, owing everything he had to the Babylonian. **r) Isaiah 5:24; Amos 2:9. s)** the Babylonian eagle will pull up; that is, he will overturn the kingdom and the state, so that there is no longer a King. **t)** namely, the children of Zedekiah, whom he slaughtered with others in his sight: Rashi, **Kimhi, and Mishlal Yophi.** **u)** he will pluck. Syriac: he will cut off (1) compare the related word **"to cut off"** Deuteronomy 25:12; Judges 1:6, 7. **x)** so that it withers **Psalm 90:6. y)** and as for all its plucked leaves, let them wither. Schmid: and all the leaves shall wither. By "leaves," according to **Grotius and Kimhi**, are understood the princes and common people whom Nebuchadnezzar slaughtered. **z) Gussetius**: designates the foliage of the outermost branches, which are plucked and snatched by sheep and goats, and eaten at the same time. The singular is **Tareph**, or rather **Taraph** (2) **Genesis 8:11. a)** of its sprout. verse 10. Compare verse 6. **b)** and that not (others: "is it not?" so **Cocceius in his Commentary**) by a great arm or power; or according to the **Targum of Jonathan**: they shall not come with a great arm or with a great people.

<summary>This page analyzes Ezekiel 17:4-9, interpreting the allegory of the vine (Zedekiah) turning from the first eagle (Babylon) to the second eagle (Egypt). The commentary emphasizes that Zedekiah's downfall was due to his treacherous violation of his oath to Babylon, driven by pride rather than necessity.</summary>

**e)** See verse 3 and chapter 26:7. **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch scholar and theologian</note>: He will not need to use all the forces of his kingdom against a king so powerless, because the Lord will deliver this man into his hand. **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi (c. 1160–1235), a preeminent medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian</note> says: "With a small people he will uproot it." For Nebuchadnezzar, even if he came himself with his entire army against Jerusalem, did not remain there through all the days of the siege, which were prolonged from the ninth year of Zedekiah until the eleventh; but in the meantime, he went toward Riblah in the land of Hamath, leaving a part of the army under the leader Nebuzaradan. That remaining army captured the city, and having taken Zedekiah, they led him to the King of Babylon in Riblah. **d)** for removing or devastating it. A noun used for an infinitive, as in Numbers 10:2. **e)** by the roots. See verse 7 and the phrase in Job 28:9.

**verse 10. f)** Behold, even if it is so planted, or, though it be so planted. **Grotius**: Therefore, it was well planted in verse 8. **g)** verse 9. **h)** when it has withered (scorched) it. 2 Samuel 12:10; compare Psalm 103:16. **i)** winds. Chapter 1:4. **k)** The East wind. Chapter 19:12. Harmful to buds and plants. Genesis 41:6; see notes on Isaiah 27:8. **Kimchi**: He compares the King of Babylon to this wind; for Babylon is situated to the northeast in respect to Judea. **l)** it shall utterly wither. Verse 9; Isaiah 27:11; Zechariah 11:17. Regarding the doubled verb, see notes on Joshua 7:7. **m)** upon or in the garden beds; that is, according to **Kimchi**: in the very place where it expected the King of Egypt to water it. **Piscator** and **Tremellius** <note>Reformed theologians known for their Latin Bible translations</note>: with the garden beds, meaning the region of Judea itself where it was planted. But **Gussetius** <note>Jacques Gousset (1635–1704), a French Hebraist</note>: over the ripples of its growth; that is, by the streams beside which it sprouted. See notes on verse 7. **n)** see verse 9.

**verse 12. q)** "Say now!" Jeremiah 18:11; Haggai 2:3. **r)** see verse 3 and chapter 2:5, 6, etc. **s)** Compare Zechariah 4:5.

Compare Matthew 21:40, 41; Luke 20:15, 16.

...of which some understand *Grotius*, to whom however the subsequent grand descriptions do not apply. Hence we rightly understand Christ, that is, the *Messiah* (along with others and certain Jewish interpreters mentioned in *Kimchi*), in whom all these things fit perfectly: a spiritual King, descending from Jeconiah through Zerubbabel. Thus *Abarbanel* himself correctly notes that this promise is rather harshly applied to Zerubbabel, since he was never a King in Jerusalem—but rather it should be explained concerning the future, namely, concerning the King Messiah, who in the following verse is said to bear leaves and fruit, becoming a magnificent cedar, as one who will reign in supreme excellence. Because the nations were to cling to Him (Genesis 49:10), he says (verse 23) that *every bird of every wing shall dwell in the shadow of his branches*. And a little later: these things are said regarding the future redemption, when that righteous sprout shall germinate from the house of David. Thus far *Abarbanel*. Furthermore, the sprout is called "tender" because the stem of David from which it arose was greatly worn down and humbled, and because of the lowly beginning of Christ's kingdom, not equipped with human power. See especially Isaiah 11:1 and the notes there. **e)** I will pluck. The Septuagint: "I will cut off." (5) See verse 4 and Job 8:12. This cutting signifies death (Isaiah 53:8, Daniel 2:45, and 9:26). He will plant that soft thing in such a way—that is, Christ Himself will be King, and He will have an ample kingdom in His members, visible in the whole world. (Cocceius) **f)** and I will plant. verses 8, 23. **g)** chapter 40:2; Isaiah 30:25. **h)** and piled up. The Septuagint: "rocky." (1) Junius: *By the mountain he spiritually understands the Church, whose condition is signified here 1. by its location, because like a mountain, it is high; 2. by its care, because like a mountain, it is built up, that is, it is what God cares for and heaps daily with new benefits*. Indeed, the Prophet's phrasing alludes to Jerusalem, which is largely mountainous, especially Mount *Zion*, the type of the spiritual Zion. Compare Isaiah 2:2. Furthermore, this admonition (these are the words of *Cocceius* on verse 24) is conveniently added to this chapter, so that the prediction of destroying David's kingdom in verse 9 would not be without the consolation of establishing Christ's kingdom. **i)** **23. k)** On the mountain of the height of Israel, chapter 20:40, 34:14. That is, on Mount Zion or the mountain of the house of the Lord; which was higher than all the mountains in the whole world because the house of God was only upon it; so it was to be far higher when the King of Kings was manifested in it, the Holy Spirit poured out, and the Holy of Holies anointed. (Cocceius) Compare Isaiah 1:2. **l)** that it may bear leaves. The Septuagint: "that it may lift up a branch." (7) verse 8, Psalm 80:11. **l)** namely, spiritual offspring. Isaiah 11:1, 2. Junius: *He will bring forth members of the Church and will be fruitful in individual members, who are so many creations of God, formed for good works. Ephesians 2:10.* **m)** into a huge or far more excellent cedar; that is, as Jonathan has it, He will be a most powerful King. For the cedar symbolizes Kings and nobles, eminent in authority. Compare verse 3, Isaiah 2:13, Song of Solomon 5:15. **n)** let them dwell under it, that is, under his power and protection. Compare chapter 31:6, Daniel 4:9, Matthew 13:32. **o)** Genesis 7:14; compare Psalm 8:7-9, Psalm 84:4. Jonathan: "And all the righteous shall be invited upon him." **p)** Septuagint: "of every wing," winged in whatever manner, chapter 39:4, 17; Genesis 7:14. Jonathan: "And all the gentle ones shall dwell in the shadow of his kingdom." Cocceius: that is, that all nations are to come to him, I say, as their only refuge; that they shall finally enjoy peace under the protection of that Son, etc. Compare Matthew 13:31, 32. Pradus: *This cannot be understood of Zerubbabel, who was neither a great King, nor did he gather all birds—that is, the inhabitants of the world—nor even all the children of Israel, to himself. Therefore, it must be understood of Christ. Just as in Abendana’s commentary, the Rabbis also refer these things to the King Messiah. **q)** verses 6, 7; chapter 19:11.* **r)** **24. s)** That they may know and experience. chapter 21:10, 29:6; Exodus 14:4. **t)** all the trees of the field; that is, the nations, which were once wild, without Christ, not yet grafted into Him (Romans 11:17 ff.), alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and lacking the covenants of promise (Ephesians 2:12). Cocceius: *the princes and powerful ones of this world, as well as the nobles of the Israelite people. Jonathan: Kings of the peoples; whom according to Kimchi he compares with the rest of the trees of the forest (just as the kingdom of the house of David is compared to the cedar). Compare chapter 31:4-15, Psalm 96:12. **t)** the humble, I have humbled. Compare Isaiah 40:4, chapter 13:11, 35:11-12, 26:5. **u)** Jonathan: the kingdom that was powerful, namely, the worldly kingdom of the house of David, and most recently the kingdom of Zedekiah, who had raised himself up and was proud; likewise the Jews, whom God had exalted, and who flourished in the glory of the Law and the Prophets. Compare Isaiah 5:15. Grotius, however, understands the Babylonians, and Kimchi the King of Babylon; Rashi understands the nations ruling over Israel. Others understand all the world empires and principalities that oppose the kingdom of Christ. **x)** but I exalt, chapter 31:31. **y)** Cocceius: that is, Christ, the son of David, the servant of rulers. So Maius: *the Messiah coming forth and flourishing from the cut-down trunk of Jesse. For the secular kingdom of Israel had to pass into the spiritual kingdom of Christ, the antitype. (Economy of the Old Testament, p. 1039). Others understand the very humble family of David, with Christ arising from that lineage. Jonathan: the kingdom that was weak. Kimchi wrongly explains this of Zerubbabel as King of the Jews; nor is it enough that other Jews understand it of Jeconiah, humbled in captivity (Jeremiah 22:30), but by divine grace brought out of prison by Evil-Merodach and elevated above all other Kings (Jeremiah 52:31, 32).*

**x)** And that I will dry up. See Ezekiel 19:12 and 42:15. **a)** A green and succulent tree, as in chapter 21:3 and Genesis 30:37. Cocceius cites Psalm 1:3, 70:31, 37:34-35, and 92:8, 13-15. **d)** See chapter 22:14, 36:36, and 37:14.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

# 18 CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>
**CHAPTER XVIII.** **e)** "And it was." This chapter deals with the justification of the Lord's ways against the murmuring of Israel regarding the justification of the sinner who sees. Primarily, it refutes the Jewish opinion about the cause of their afflictions. According to the scholar Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmidt, 1617–1696, a Lutheran theologian</note>, it has three parts: **I.** The impious Jewish parable and proverb is rebuked and refuted from verses 1-18. **II.** The first objection of the Jews is dissolved in verses 19-24. **III.** The second objection is resolved from verse 25 onwards. Namely, lest while the Messiah promised in chapter 17:22-24 is coming, the Jews should claim they were being punished most severely and undeservedly for the sins of their ancestors, crushed by such a long exile and many calamities—He refutes this opinion.
</margin>

**x)** "but gives his bread," etc. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note> notes: After the duties of justice, he comes to the duties of beneficence. This is best joined to the preceding: giving to the poor and not taking interest if it is a loan. Christ also joins "lend" and "borrow" <note>original Greek: "δανειζετε" (daneizete) and "δανεισον" (daneison)</note> in Luke 6:30, 35 and Matthew 5:42. He does not want a benefit to be sold. The Law distinguishes between a creditor, who has the right to seek interest in commerce, and one who assists the poor through a loan; to take interest from the latter is oppression. See Deuteronomy 23:20-21, Exodus 22:24, and Psalm 15:5. **a)** interest, an excess of profit. Leviticus 25:36. **b)** verses 13, 17. **c)** from such and all other perversity, verses 24, 26. **d)** withdraws his hand. Verse 17 and Lamentations 2:8. **e)** Zechariah 7:9. **f)** whether an appointed judge or a chosen arbiter. Grotius.

The extensive marginal and scholarly notes provide philological analysis and cross-references to demonstrate how individual responsibility replaces the concept of inherited guilt.</summary>

<summary>This page concludes the theological argument of Ezekiel 18, asserting that God judges individuals based on their current actions rather than their past or their parents' sins. Thus David "made" himself a new heart when he prayed to God to create a new heart in him (Psalm 51:12). — Let our will conspire with the divine; so God makes us to will, so circumcising our hearts He makes us circumcise them; so making a new heart for us, He makes it so that we make a new heart for ourselves. Truly, this chapter has a double lamentation or double allegory: I. <term>Of the lioness and the cubs</term> v. 10-14, 9. v. 2. <term>b)</term> <term>What did your mother the lioness do?</term> - <term>she lay down—she brought up.</term> The exposition is as in ch. 12:22. others say it is the sound of mourning and lamenting, as in ch. 16:30. So <term>Kimchi and M. I.</term> <term>c)</term> <term>your mother.</term> By this, some understand the degenerate royal family of David; others Jerusalem; others, better, the Judean nation. Compare ch. 11:6. * v. 4. <term>p)</term> Meaning: <term>Moreover the nations heard concerning him;</term> as of one fierce and prone to war; perhaps even making excursions into Egypt. Or certainly: <term>But when the surrounding nations heard it against him:</term> for this construction generally implies attentive listening; see for example Exodus 6:9, 12. 1 Kings 12:16. leading to obedience, Genesis 34:24. Exodus 4:13, 23. Judges 2:17. etc. or help, as in Genesis 16:11; ch. 21:17. or even to harm another, as in this place, to capture him. compare note on 1 Samuel 31:11. But Tremellius says: <term>hearing, they ran together against him.</term> Thus Glasfius p. 749. It seems to allude to the custom of men who, when they hear that a lion or some fierce beast is wandering in the field, gather a band of men to kill or capture it. <header>EZEKIEL. CHAPTER 19. 19</header>
<sig>Rrr 5</sig>

<margin>
a) He took another <note>original: "accepit alterum"</note> (Some say: "another one") from her cubs; namely, according to the view of Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian</note> and others, this refers to Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:34, 2 Chronicles 36:4). Or rather, it refers to Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:8, 15) according to Cocceius and Schmidt in their introduction to this chapter and in the commentary on 2 Kings 24:9, p. 281. For this one [Jehoiachin] was made king by his mother, that is, the people (cf. note on verse 2) following the Babylonian insult (see note on 2 Kings 24:8), whereas the former [Jehoiakim] was appointed king not by his mother, but by the Egyptian (2 Kings 23:34). See also the note below on verse 9. Cocceius notes: The reign of Jehoiakim intervenes—his omission seems to be signified by that phrase where it is said that "her expectation had perished." For the Lioness, that is, the people, could have expected a restoration and confirmation of the kingdom under Jehoiakim, because under him Nebuchadnezzar repelled the Egyptian and took from him everything he held from the River of Egypt to the Euphrates (2 Kings 24:7). For they seemed able to eventually recover their strength under the King of Babylon, since he was further away. But when he [Jehoiakim] died and did not have a suitable successor, the boy Jehoiachin was substituted in his place. b) whom she made a young lion (verses 2, 3), a King just as fierce as his predecessors (Genesis 45:9).

v. 6. c) And he [the lion]. For he conducted himself, or as some say: "He walked therefore among the lions"; he lived in the manner of a king, imitating their ferocity and tyranny. Cf. chapter 28:14, 1 Samuel 12:8. Junius <note>Francis Junius, a Reformed theologian</note> says in his Commentary: he lived among men as if among wild beasts—inhumane, impious, and treacherous—and joined in their counsels, etc. d) and thus he was a young lion (verse 2). He became as in verse 3. e) verse 3. cf. 2 Kings 24:9. f) Some say: "especially, he devoured men." See verse 3. Grotius: he himself became cruel, comparing 2 Kings 23:37, 2 Chronicles 36:5 regarding Jehoiakim.

* v. 7. g) He also knew. Some say: "he defiled" <note>original: "stupravit"</note> (Genesis 4:1). "His widow"; that is, of the man or men devoured (verse 6). The singular is used collectively for the plural very frequently, as in Hosea 13:2. The language is mixed because he speaks now without a figure of speech regarding widows (and their strongholds, which lions do not usually enter), but soon returns to the metaphor. Others translate: "he knew," that is, "he claimed for himself."

[He] dedicated (so they compare Genesis 39:6) his palaces, comparing Isaiah 13:22, where see the note. Cf. also Gussetius <note>Jacques Gousset, Hebrew lexicographer</note> p. 312. As for what Grotius and Bochart (in *Hierozoicon* Part I, p. 760) contend—that for "he knew" <note>original Hebrew: "va-yeda"</note> we should read "he destroyed" <note>original Hebrew: "va-yera"</note> with a *Resh*—we do not follow that, although the Chaldean [Targum] renders it paraphrastically as "and he made desolate." Cf. Calovius on this place. h) Isaiah 37:18. He provided the occasion for desolation through his sins, Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius, author of *Philologia Sacra*</note> p. 771, new edition. i) and the land was devastated. (4) chapter 6:6. k) and its fullness (chapter 12:19, 30:12). The "fullness of the earth" refers to the people; these fled for fear of a cruel lord. Grotius. l) Because of the sound of his roaring. Zechariah 11:3, Job 4:10. The antecedent stands for the consequent; for having let out a roar, he leaped upon men and flocks, and devoured them, crushed and torn in a monstrous way. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* Part I, p. 729. Cf. Judges 14:5, Isaiah 5, 29. Cocceius: It is credible that Jehoiachin did these things more abundantly, even if he reigned for a short time; since, as youths usually are, he was reckless, and to stabilize his kingdom, he began to vex the people with exactions, so that many left their homes. For the "voice of roaring" seems to denote edicts. Where the lion roars, all animals flee, and the land is made desolate. Cf. Amos 3:8. v. 8. m) Therefore the nations placed themselves against him. [They spread] their net, as follows. Others: they raised their voice against him, as in Jeremiah 4:16, and rushed upon him with a great shout. So says Vatablus. Others: they set a plan or an ambush. So Schmidt: "therefore they laid wait for him." The Vulgate: "And the nations from the provinces round about assembled against him." Or take the verb impersonally (as in Hosea 12:9). n) in this manner: "And the nations were placed," that is, the Chaldeans set the neighboring nations against him on every side; namely, the Syrians, Moabites, Ammonites, etc., who helped the Chaldeans with their reinforcements and resources, just as they had done in 2 Kings 24:2 against Jehoiachin’s father, Jehoiakim—to whom Bochart (p. 760) and others believe all this refers. But see the notes on verses 5 and 9. n) from the provinces. 1 Kings 20:14. o) chapter 12:13, 32:3. p) Or: "and he was captured in their pit." v. 4, chapter 18:13. v. 9. q) They put him, like a wild beast, r) so to speak, in a enclosure, that is, according to some and Bochart, in a cage (i). s) with hooks. See verse 4. t) and they led him away (verse 4). u) Some say: "they led him into strongholds," Cocceius: "into citadels," that is, according to Tremellius, "into most-fortified Babylon." So Grotius, but regarding Jehoiakim (cf. 2 Chronicles 36:6). However, Jehoiakim did not arrive there (see note on 2 Kings 24:6), but Jehoiachin did; he was a captive there until the reign of Evil-merodach (2 Kings 25:27). Some say: "in nets." (z) verse 29, 7. masculine, Proverbs 12:12. x) so that his voice should not be heard, that is, lest he be a terror to anyone further, as above in verse 7; lest his terrible edicts be heard any longer among the Israelites. Cf. Nahum 2:14. y) on, or over the mountains, where lions are accustomed to roar and strike terror into men and beasts. z) on the mountains (chapter 18:6) and the land of Israel (chapter 6:2, 3; 34:13, 14). v. 10. a) See verse 2. This is a second comparison or allegory pertaining to the same Judean nation; Kimchi and M. I. refer the suffix to Israel. b) she was like a vine. chapter 17:6, Psalm 80:9 ff. c) Some say: "in your likeness" <note>Hebrew: "ke-dimutkha"</note> according to Kimchi and M. I. of the forms *tsadi* and *koph*. Rashi: as if to say, "you are like yourself," whose mother is like a vine planted by the waters. So Jonathan [the Targum]: The assembly of Israel, when it performed the Law, was like a vine. Others, better: "in your vigorous sap or blood," comparing Genesis 49:11, Deuteronomy 32:14, where it is said of the juice of grapes. Cocceius: that is, in which vine that blood, from which you were born, was fruitful for generating shoots and branches. d) as in chapter 17:8. e) fruitful (Ezekiel 32:12, Psalm 128:3). f) and indeed it became leafy (i). Grotius: the people grew and wealth increased. Cocceius: the Israelite people, the tribe of Judah, the family of David, abounded in divine blessing. g) from the waters, or because of many waters, by which it was planted (chapter 17:5, 8). v. 11. h) From which there were. i) a rod of strength, or robust, strong branches (verse 12, Psalm 110:2), namely Princes born of the royal family. k) into scepters of rulers, or men who would hold scepters. Grotius: in the family of David, they came to the kingdom here and there; Kings were taken from them like shoots from a vine. Cf. verse 14, Isaiah 14:5. l) and she was high, some say: "its stature or height lifted itself up" (chapter 17:6, 31:5), specifically the rod or staff, that is, of each King. The masculine suffix refers to the "rod" <note>Hebrew: "matteh"</note> rather than the "vine" <note>Hebrew: "gephen"</note>, which is mostly feminine. Cf. Noldius, *Concordance of Particles*, p. 720. As if to say: the kingdom of Judea stood out above others by the majesty of its Kings, the greatness of its Princes, and the number of its common people. Thus the ancient excellence of the kingdom is shadowed in this verse and the preceding; but its decline and ruin in verses 12, 13, 14. m) above the middle or in the midst (chapter 40:7, Isaiah 44:4). n) of thick branches. Cocceius: even among the leafy trees (chapter 20:28, 31:3). The stock itself grew among its own foliage, so that it appeared from that to be a most powerful monarch. That strong branch does not seem to signify one specific king, but the family and successors of David, or many powerful kings from the house of David. o) so that it appeared, the rod or branch was conspicuous; or according to others, the vine itself. p) because of its height (chapter 31:10). q) chapter 17:6. v. 12. r) But the vine was plucked up; that is, the nation was deported and cast out from its seats; the ten tribes gradually by the Assyrian, the Jews by Nebuchadnezzar. Jonathan [Targum]: And the house of the Shekhinah was uprooted with violence from the land; as God had long ago threatened (Deuteronomy 29:27, 1 Kings 14:15, Jeremiah 12:17, Hosea (1)).

<margin>
The reigning power, surrounded by many lesser princes, became the cause of a new conflagration—Zedekiah kindled this fire, by which the royal power was burned up, along with all the prominence of the court, all leadership and prefecture which usually accompanies a King. So also, what we add shows that this slaughter is not so much to be ascribed to the Chaldeans, but to themselves.
**i)** which consumed its fruit (verse 12).
**k)** so that it exists no more, until the Messiah comes.
**l)** a strong rod (verse 11). Jeremiah 48:17.
**m)** or a scepter for ruling (verse 11). That is, so that there are no more kings from her, but the royal power is abolished. Compare Jeremiah 22:30.
**n)** verse 1; chapter 31:16. **Jonathan:** this lamentation is through the prophetic word, and so it also became a lamentation at the time of devastation and exile. **Schmidt:** therefore it is a lamentation, and has become a lamentation. **Grotius:** This is a prophecy of a mourning that will truly come to pass.

**verse 13. d)** Now therefore she is transplanted. verse 10. But had he not already said she was dried up and burned? **Answer:** It was so as to the greatest part, and with respect to the horrible ruin, and according to common human perception. But that she was planted again commends the mercy of God. 
**e)** compare **f)** in a land of drought. Isaiah 35:2; Psalm 63:2. That is, in Babylonia, which in itself was well-watered and fertile; but here he regards not the nature of the land, but the condition of the people in it. 1 And it came to pass <gloss>p)</gloss> in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, that men from the elders of Israel came <gloss>q)</gloss> to inquire of the Lord, and sat before me.

**CHAPTER XX. verse 1. p)** And it came to pass. Compare chapter 14:1. This prophecy, contained in chapters 20–23, is an appendix to the preceding one, and of almost the same argument, consisting of the reproach of sins and the announcement of judgments. This chapter has three parts according to **Schmidt**: I. God denies that He will give the hypocrites the answer they seek (verses 2, 3, and 31). II. He reproaches them for their rebellions, including those of their fathers (1) in Egypt (verses 4–9), (2) in the desert (verses 10–27), (3) in the promised land (verse 29), with the predicted and inflicted punishments; then their own (verses 29–39). III. He adds a promise concerning the times of the Messiah (verse 40 and following; or according to Schmidt, verse 34 and following). 
**q)** in the seventh year since the deportation of King Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah), and four years before the destruction of the city. Compare chapter 1, 2; chapter 8, 1. 
**r)** in the fifth month, chapter 1:1. 
**s)** on the tenth day, chapter 24:1. 
**t)** certain of the elders of Israel came again, either from the number of the deported; or according to others, ambassadors sent from Zedekiah in Judea. See notes at chapter 14:1. 
**u)** to consult the Lord (verse 3) through the Prophet concerning their affairs, for example: what would happen to them and their brothers left in Judea, and what should be done to escape their present misery. 
**x)** which is the posture of those ready to hear another speaking; hence those "sitting before the Lord" are those who attend to the word of God as the sole teacher. Isaiah 23:18. **Cocceius.**

**verse 2. y)** It came to pass therefore. **verse 3. z)** chapter 2, 1. **a)** see verse 1. **b)** Do you wicked ones and hypocrites dare to come? **c)** chapter 14, 16. **d)** "Am I to be consulted?" or, "having been consulted, shall I answer?" (verse 31). See chapter 14:3; compare chapter 36:37. **Septuagint:** <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> "I will answer." So the **Syriac:** "I will not give you an answer." **e)** chapter 16:14. **Cocceius:** In denying that He will answer them, it signifies that there is neither a promise in all of scripture nor a word hidden with God that would lead to their consolation (as hypocrites). 

**verse 4. f)** **Schmidt:** "Will you not contend with them?" **Cocceius:** "Will you pronounce judgment on them according to my word and rebuke them?" It is understood that the Elders of Israel came to hear justifications, praises, and consolations, as if they were righteous. Hence others translate: "Would you declare them righteous, or patronize them and defend their cause?" By no means; for they are worthy not of intercession, but of rebuke. For the word signifies actions done in courts, whether by the judge, the plaintiff, or the advocate. Compare chapter 22:2; Isaiah 1:17; and above, chapter 9:8. 
**g)** but rather [make known] the abominations of their fathers, which they themselves have securely imitated. Compare verse 18, 27; chapter 5:11; chapter 18:12, 13. **h)** make them to know, or point out to them. chapter 16:2. 

**verse 5. i)** in which I chose and took Israel, or began to act with them as my people, passing over the Egyptians and other nations. Compare Deuteronomy 7:6; chapter 14:2. 
**k)** I lifted my hand: the promise of those swearing, that is, I swore. verses 6, 15. Also chapter 8; Numbers 14:30; Deuteronomy 32:40; Daniel 12:7; Revelation 10:5. So rightly **Jonathan**, **Kimchi**, and **M. I.** Others: I showed my power and help to the Israelites by striking the Egyptians. 
**l)** and I was known through experience, or I became known to them through miracles, by sending Moses to them; and thus in reality I proved myself to be truthful. Compare verse 9; Exodus 6:3, 7; chapter 14:4, 18; chapter 32:16; 1 Kings 18:36; Psalm 79:10. 
**m)** I lifted, I say, my hand. 
**n)** Genesis 17:7, 8; Exodus 3:6, 18; chapter 6:7, 8. **Cocceius:** The sum of all benefits is contained in this, that Jehovah calls Himself the God of Israel. It is clear that this signifies God would do something according to His power and the riches of His grace, for which they could not but celebrate Him—indeed, glory in Him—namely, liberation from wrath and condemnation, from the kingdom of sin and all misery; and on the other hand, the manifestation of His goodness and majesty in them. That promise can signify nothing less than this: I will be to you wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption (1 Corinthians 1:30). 

**verse 6. o)** verses 5, 15, 28. **p)** verse 9; Exodus 12:42; chapter 6:6.

**Chapter 20 verse 1.** "In the fifth" [month]. The letter Shin is without a Dagesh <note>a grammatical mark in Hebrew</note>. See chapter 3:22. This seems to be against the printed Masoretic text.

<meta>This page continues the transition into Ezekiel Chapter 20. <header>EZEKIEL. CHAPTER 20. כ</header>

**q) Cocceius:** <note>Johannes Cocceius, 1 Dutch theologian</note> Observe here that the promise of giving the land is an addition to the better promise already made to them regarding God, etc. **r)** "which I had searched out," that is, provided; <note>original Latin: "exploraveram f. prouideram"</note> as a scout or lookout, looking out for them for a most suitable seat, where they might rest comfortably after their enemies were cast out. Compare Isaiah 13:19. **\*)** Either because that land bore certain excellent fruits denied to other lands, such as balsam; <note>original Latin: "opobalſamum"</note> or because it surpassed most lands in fertility; or rather, because God chose a seat for Himself in that land and determined to manifest His glory to men within it. **Cocceius.** **y)** Compare Jeremiah 2:7. **z)** verse 39; chapter 1:9; chapter 7:16. **α)** idols, to which they lift up their eyes with trust and worship. **Grotius:** Nevertheless, He did good to them because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had been called His own. **p)** verse 14, 44; Isaiah 48:9; compare Psalm 106:8. **q) Schmidt:** so that it would not be profaned, as if I were unable or unwilling to stand by my promises and liberate my people. This is the "Niphal" infinitive <note>a Hebrew grammatical form</note> here as in verse 14, 22; compare Isaiah 48:11; Leviticus 21:9. **r)** verse 14, 41; chapter 5:8. **s) Schmidt:** in whose sight (the nations) I also was made known in their eyes, when I brought them out. Others suggest it is simpler: because I had become known to the Israelites in the eyes of the nations themselves; or in whose eyes (that is, in the presence of which nations) I had become known to them. Compare verse 14, 22. **t)** see verse 5. **u)** see verse 6. **v. 10. x)** Thus therefore I led them out, etc. Verse 6, 9. **y. 11. y) Schmidt:** Where I gave to them. **z)** Statutes <note>term: statutes (Hebrew: chuqqim)</note> are called precepts that have a fixed measure, so that nothing can be added or taken away. For *choq* is a fixed and defined measure. These same precepts are called judgments, <note>term: judgments (Hebrew: mishpatim)</note> because according to them Judgment is established. These words are often joined together, as in Exodus 15:25, 26; Malachi 3:22; and below in verse 25 and following. **Cocceius.** **a)** compare Exodus 20:1 and following; Deuteronomy 5:1 and following. **b) Schmidt:** which if a man does. Verse 13. **c)** he shall live through them. **Jonathan:** <note>the Aramaic Targum</note> adds "eternal life," so also in verses 13 and 21. This is understood if they are used in the proper way (1 Timothy 1:8) and as a tutor leading to Christ (Galatians 3:24); compare Romans 7:10, 8:3, 10:4; Galatians 3:10 and following. They were not to seek life *in* them, but they were to be a type of holiness and an instrument of sanctification for repentance—so that, after they had recognized what righteousness was necessary for life, they might deny their own righteousness. Since the Lord declared that He wanted to sanctify them, they should believe that He, who cannot deny His own law (and therefore added this praise to these precepts: that he who does them shall live in them, to make it clear that the justice of God requires such obedience for life to be given), would provide a sacrifice by which their conscience could be purified, and a priest through whose obedience they could be righteous. Through thanksgiving and the love of their God, they would most zealously perform those precepts and hate and flee from doing the opposite. **Cocceius.** Compare Leviticus 18:5; Nehemiah 9:29; Matthew 19:17; Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12; compare 1 Timothy 4:8. **v. 12. d)** And also my Sabbaths, that is, my festivals. Verse 13, 16, 20, 21, 24; Exodus 20:8 and following; 31:13; 34:21; 35:2; Leviticus 19:3; 26:2. **Menochius:** <note>Giovanni Stefano Menochio, 1575–1655, an Italian Jesuit scholar</note> in the plural, because they recur often, that is, every week. Others establish a three-fold Sabbath: 1. of days, which was properly called the Sabbath; 2. of months, which was the seventh month, a feast for a large part of it; 3. of years, the seventh year and the Jubilee. **e)** that they might be for a sign and a pledge between me and them. Exodus 31:13. In this way Abraham received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith (Romans 4:11), like a petition to God or the confidence of a covenant from God (1 Peter 3:21). Therefore, the resting of the Israelites has the force of a covenant of a good conscience with God, that He might give them that necessary sanctification, etc. Compare Deuteronomy 30:6 and Colossians 2:16. **Cocceius.** **f)** chapter 37:28; Leviticus 20:8; 21:8, 23; 22:9, 16, 32. **Cocceius:** This is, moreover, the sanctification from the guilt and slavery of sin—that is, redemption and purification from the consciousness of sin. Compare Hebrews 10:1-4. **v. 13. g)** see verse 8, 21. **h)** Not only in Egypt, but even when they had already been led out, in the wilderness, and more often and in many ways, they provoked me. **Grotius.** Compare Psalm 106:13 and following. **i)** verse 16, 21; chapter 5:7; 11:12. **k)** verse 15; chapter 5:6; Hosea 4:6; compare Exodus 16:28, 29. **l) Schmidt:** which nevertheless if a man does. Verse 11. **m)** verse 11. **n)** verse 16, 21, 24. This does not mean that they performed work on the Sabbath in a shameless and stubborn manner. For Moses does not record that. Rather, he testifies that when they found a man gathering sticks in the field, they threw him into custody, and after consulting God on the matter, they stoned him according to His word (Numbers 15:32 and following). It is rather to be noted that they did not *use* the Sabbath as a sign between God and themselves, to recognize that Jehovah Himself sanctified them (verse 12). Instead, they thought that keeping the Sabbath or idling was their own holiness and a part of their own righteousness—neglecting the purpose and legitimate use of the Sabbath, etc. **Cocceius**, who may be seen more extensively on this and the preceding verse.

**Grotius:** "I took away their minds, so that being dissatisfied with my laws, they made for themselves laws that were harsh and deadly." Thus **Jonah [Targum]**: "I also, because they rebelled against my Word and would not obey my Prophets, removed them and delivered them into the hand of enemies; and they followed after their own foolish lusts and made decrees that were not right, and laws by which you shall not live." Likewise **Rashi** <note>Shlomo Yitzchaki, medieval Jewish commentator.</note> on this place. Compare the phrase in chapter 36:31; Isaiah 65:2; Psalm 26:5; Exodus 18:27; Nehemiah 5:9 and 9:13. Others, such as **Glassius** in *Sacred Rhetoric*, page 2004, understand these to be divine curses, threats, and punishments; specifically, following **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi, medieval grammarian and commentator.</note>, they understand heavy taxes imposed by their enemies. Thus compare Deuteronomy 30:15, 19 and above chapter 16:43, etc. Others, however, understand the ceremonial precepts of God themselves, which are said to be "not good" <term>synkritikōs</term> <note>original Greek: comparatively</note>, as they do not contain the image of God nor the true holiness of man (hence they were given neither to Abraham nor the fathers before him); compare Ephesians 2:15; Colossians 2:14; Hebrews 7:16, 18; chapter 9:10. Nor were they pleasant, as in Matthew 11:30, but heavy and difficult, compare Acts 15:10; Romans 4:15; Galatians 3:10; chapter 4:1; Hebrews 8:9. Nor do they give life, Acts 13:39, or the "new man," Deuteronomy 30:6; Colossians 2:11, 13. Rather, that better hope was to be expected under those bonds, Isaiah 52:7; Hebrews 7:19; chapter 9:8 and following; chapter 10:1, etc. See Meyer’s *Dissertation on the final chapters of Ezekiel*, pages 67 and 106; Ursinus' *Commentary on Hosea 6:6*, page 109; and more extensively **Cocceius** on this place. Indeed, **Gussetius**, page 544, takes this verse to refer to the law of God itself, and refers the following to Mosaic rites in this manner: "I brought it about that my commandments were not good to them; and as for judgments, that they should not live by them," etc., page 300. "You should take it relatively," he says, "in this sense: I caused my commandments to be evil to them," namely in the kind of evil described in Romans 7:11. And God effects this in the manner indicated in Isaiah 6:10, which is not the place to dispute at length here. See also **Hackspan**, to whom **Calovius** refers on this place. **q)** "by which they shall not live." see verse 11. Ellipsis of [the word] "which," as above in chapter 7:13, etc. **v. 26. r)** "And I declared them impure," all of them, namely the Israelites. **Cocceius**. Others: "but I will pollute them." **Glassius**: "I showed them to be impure, and treated them as impure and rejected them from me." *Sacred Grammar*, page 784; compare Leviticus 13:3, etc.

**v. 30. x)** Having commanded the prophet to speak of the fathers, He now commands him to turn to the elders (v. 1), indeed to the house of Israel, and accuse their impudence, etc. Cocceius. 
**y)** Is it "in the way of your fathers?" (verses 4, 18, 27). An interrogative that implies "yes" with indignation and detestation, as in Isaiah 58:5. As if to say: Have you reached such a point of perversity that you pollute yourselves in the most unworthy ways of your ancestors' sins, and yet you dare to approach my servant to inquire of me through him? 
**v. 31. z)** "You are defiled," or "will you defile yourselves?" (verses 18, 31, 43; chapter 23:7, 30; 11:21). 
**a)** chapter 7:20. 
**b)** chapter 6:9, 14:3. 
**g)** chapter 14:15, 16, 17, etc. 
**v. 31. c)** Or, "And when you lift up," or "offer" (chapter 45:13; Judges 3:18). 
**d)** your gifts. verses 26, 39. 
**e)** when you lead your sons through the fire (verse 26; 2 Chronicles 33:6). 
**f)** Or, "you are polluted" (verse 30) by all your idols (chapter 6:4, 8:10, 14:3). 
**g)** "Yet shall I be consulted," or "shall I give counsel and answer you?" (verse 3). 
**h)** "As I live" (verse 3, 33; 1 Samuel 20:3). 
**v. 32. i)** "That also which ascends." Or: "but that which ascends" (chapter 14:3; Jeremiah 51:50). 
**k)** "into your spirit" or "your mind" (chapter 1:20, 11:5). Vatablus: "that which you think and conceive in your mind." 
**l)** Or: "it shall never happen." 
**m)** which (chapter 14:5). Second reading: "because you are saying." Cf. note on chapter 11:3. 
**n)** "We shall be," i.e., "let us be like those nations." That is, according to Grotius: we will live peacefully and friendly with them by sharing their form of worship. So also Vatablus and others. But to Cocceius, these are the words of despairing Israelites, thinking that in the future there would be no worship of God in the world; and that they too would be like the rest of the nations, worshipping wood and stone; as if God had forgotten his oath to be their God; not believing that Christ would arise from them and preach the Gospel of peace, justice, and liberty among them—for which purpose they were chosen by God from the nations, so that Christ might be manifested among them. 
**o)** Deuteronomy 4:28; chapter 28:36, 64; 29:16; Isaiah 37:19. 
**v. 33. p)** Or: "Against, as I live," etc. (verse 31). 
**q)** chapter 16:14. 
**r)** Chapter 5:11, 27:26. 
**s)** verse 34; Exodus 6:1, 6. 
**t)** Chapter 6:14. 
**u)** verses 8, 13, 21, 34; cf. chapter 21:36.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Ezekiel 20, specifically focusing on the transition from Israel's history of rebellion to God's promise of a "second Exodus"—a forced gathering from the nations for judgment and eventual restoration.</meta>

<header>EZEKIEL 20. CHAPTER 20.</header>

<margin>
Where there are various movements, and as it were a continuous murmur of waves and a tumult, of which Isaiah speaks beautifully in chapter 17:12. Thus Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator, a 16th-century German theologian</note> explains: into Babylon, which will be as troublesome to you as a desert. However, other terrifying and inhospitable places into which they were led are not excluded; for example, into Media, the Caspian regions, Hyrcania, etc., where they were greatly vexed by those various peoples. Compare what was said above in chapter 19:13.
</margin>

-> 34 I will rule over you: and I will bring you out from the peoples and gather <-

<margin>
**x)** By force, and whether you are willing or unwilling, I will be your King; compare Luke 19:14, 27. Not humanely and mercifully as before, but I will subdue you; just as perverse slaves are condemned when they refuse voluntary obedience, condemned either to the mill or to other cruel labors. —**Calvin**.

**v. 34. y)** In order that I may lead you out. Compare verse 6. **z)** Concerning the peoples among whom you were scattered while fleeing the Chaldeans; as if to say: I will pull you back from your flight and deliver you to the Chaldeans. —**Menochius**. So also **Grotius**: I will lead you far away from those with whom you now live mixed, and whose examples you imitate: from the Phoenicians, Ammonites, and Moabites, whose borders you touch. Thus also others: because the final words of this verse seem to suggest a sentence of wrath: *in poured-out fury* (unless you understand these, along with the others, as directed not so much against the Israelites as against the nations). See also verses 35 and 36. Compare chapter 11:9. To some, however, these words seem to declare divine mercy rather than wrath; as if to say: I will not allow you to be held in eternal captivity among the nations; but I will lead you out so that I may be your King. Thus **Schmidius** <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> in his summaries of this chapter thinks that from verse 33 a notable promise concerning the times of the Messiah is given. Compare Ezekiel 6:5, 7:4, 5. **a)** verse 41, 11:17. **b)** Ibid. **c)** See verse 33.

**v. 35. d)** In order that I may lead you. But others say: I will lead you down. Another: Yet I will lead you down first. **e)** into the wilderness of the peoples; the Babylonian empire. Thus **Piscator** on Revelation 17:3, p. 1016. Which same thing (he says) Isaiah meant by his "wilderness of the sea" in Isaiah 21:1, where see the notes. For many peoples and nations, if they flow together into one city, are like a sea, or a confluence of waters, in which...
</margin>

**Cocceius**, however, distinguishes these from what was said before and refers them to those times when Judea became part of the dominion of the <term>Romans</term>, and the Jews lived scattered, partly in the land and partly outside their fatherland, in the midst of the Gentiles. It is called a "wilderness" to the world itself, having no cultivation to bear fruit for God. **f)** And there I will plead, or judge (verse 36, chapter 38:22; Joel 3:2; Isaiah 1:18). **g)** Face to face, openly (Genesis 32:31, Exodus 33:11, Deuteronomy 5:4). **Cocceius** says this means He will come to them so they may see Him and hear Him speaking, and He will argue with them concerning justice, just as in Psalm 82:1. * **v. 36. h)** Just as I contended in judgment (verse 35) with your fathers (see Numbers 14:22, 23). **i)** In the wilderness reaching the land of Egypt. **k)** Thus I will plead (1 Samuel 12:7). **Cocceius** says: no less directly than I spoke with the fathers when they heard His voice saying, "I am Jehovah your God" (Exodus 20:2). Thus the Jews were to hear the voice of God Himself, whom Ezekiel had seen in an emblem sitting on a throne. They had seen God in a cloud; so they were to see Him in the flesh, etc. This signifies that He would find the Israelites, and among them His sheep, when He came to them as they were wandering from the truth, so that He would find it necessary to rebuke them and convince them of their error. **l)** chapter 11:8, 16:14. * **v. 37. m)** Then I will make you pass <term>under the shepherd’s rod</term> <note>original: sub virga pastorali</note>. See Leviticus 27:32, Micah 7:14. Compare 1 Corinthians 4:21. **Bochart**: This does not refer to the counting of livestock done by a tax collector (as **Kimchi** thinks), but that which is done by a shepherd; to show that God has the same care for His people as a good shepherd has for his flock, counting each sheep as it enters the fold by touching it with the end of his rod in the presence of the master or the bailiff; so that He may accurately count and recognize all His own. (Hieroz. P. I. p. 459). Compare Jeremiah 33:13, John 10:14. Others, along with <term>Rashi</term>, understand it as the rod of chastisement. **o)** In the <term>bond of the covenant</term>; (1) from which you now seem loosened. From the root <term>asar</term> <note>original: אסר - meaning to bind</note>, the word <term>masoret</term> <note>original: מסורת</note>, following forms like those in 1 Kings 5:25. That is, I will bind myself to you and you to me by a new covenant. —**Bochart**, as cited above. This was done partly through Ezra, but more through Christ. —**Cornelius a Lapide**. Others with **Rashi**: into the <term>tradition of the covenant</term>, from the root <term>masar</term> <note>original: מכר - Likely a typo for מסר meaning to deliver or hand over</note> (Numbers 31:5, 16). That is, into the covenant which I delivered and offered to you. * **v. 38. p)** And I will purge, I will select, that is, the sheep from the goats; I will separate. Compare 1 Samuel 17:8. —**Cocceius**. Namely, with the winnowing fan of the Gospel of peace, justice, and liberty, preached to the Gentiles and the Jews. For because they are scandalized in Christ and that Gospel, they are cut off from the olive tree through their unbelief, and lie dry and trampled outside the vineyard, excluded from the kingdom of Christ. **q)** chapter 2:3. **r)** chapter 2:3, Isaiah 66:24. **s)** From the land of their wanderings (Genesis 36:7, Exodus 6:4) where they live for a time: namely, from Judea, according to **Grotius**, which they boasted would remain theirs forever (chapter 11:15). Or rather, according to **Kimchi** and others, from the land of their exile among the Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, etc., as in verses 34 and 35. **t)** See verse 34. **u)** He shall not come, no one of those rebels shall return (see Jeremiah 22:27, 44:14). **Cocceius**: that is, they shall not become participants and sharers in the kingdom of God and Christ and the Church among the nations; but, as cursed ones, they shall live in the world outside the society of the saints. Compare below, verse 42. **x)** verses 42, 44; chapter 6:7, 13. * **v. 39. y)** You therefore. **z)** Each man, or individuals (chapter 1:9, 7:16). **a)** Their dung-gods, their idols (chapter 6:4, 8:10, 14:3). **b)** Go ahead and worship. A hypothetical <term>concession</term> <note>original: συγχώρησις - a rhetorical term where one appears to grant a point to an opponent</note>, as in Revelation 22:11. —**Grotius**. Rather, be openly idolaters than to mix my worship, which must be pure, with the rites of profane nations. Compare Hosea 4:17, 15. —**Glassius** (Rhet. S. p. 1515). This is an ironical dismissal and rejection, he says, by which He silently invites them to the opposite of this speech—to true piety and the worship of God. **c)** Even hereafter (Revelation 22:11). **d)** If you do not wish to obey me. Compare Jeremiah 32:33, 44:16. Others connect the word "if" <note>original: אם</note> with the preceding "hereafter" <note>original: ואחר</note> more harshly in this way: after or since you have refused to obey me. But **Schmid** reads: But will you not afterward be obedient to me? So that [God's] name [might not be profaned], because of the connection to the following verse.
