<meta>This page continues the commentary on the transition between Ezekiel chapters 20 and 21. It addresses the "parable of the forest fire" in the south and the Lord’s subsequent clarification that this "fire" is actually a "sword" drawn against Jerusalem and all of Israel, encompassing both the righteous and the wicked.</meta>

<header>EZEKIEL 21. CHAPTER 21.</header>

<margin>
**e)** In the manner I have just announced, compare Jeremiah 1:15.
**g)** A teller of parables <note>original: "parabolizator"</note>; one who speaks in riddles. Compare chapter 17:2. Does he not speak in parables? Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch scholar</note> asks: "Is this man not always speaking in a confused manner?" as if to say he is a madman who has nothing in his mouth but parables that are neither understood nor coherent. Compare Ephesians 29:11 and 2 Corinthians 4:4. It is characteristic of the profane to claim the Scripture is merely parabolic and therefore cannot be understood.
</margin>

<margin>
**Opening with a sigh.**
**\* v. 6. h)** Why it was done. Now it is expressed more explicitly and more openly, whereas before it was said in parables.
</margin>

3 And say to the forest of the South: "Hear the word of the Lord! Thus says the Lord God: 'Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it shall devour every green tree in you and every dry tree; the blazing flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from the south to the north shall be scorched by it.'
4 'And all flesh shall see that I, the Lord, have kindled it; it shall not be quenched.'"
5 Then I said, "Ah, Lord God! They say of me, 'Is he not a teller of parables?'"
6 And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:
7 "Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem, preach against the sanctuaries, and prophesy against the land of Israel;
8 and say to the land of Israel, 'Thus says the Lord: "Behold, I am against you, and I will draw My sword from its sheath and cut off from you both the righteous and the wicked."
9 "Because I will cut off from you both the righteous and the wicked, therefore My sword shall go out from its sheath against all flesh from south to north."
10 "And all flesh shall know that I, the Lord, have drawn My sword from its sheath; it shall not return anymore."'
11 "As for you, son of man, sigh with breaking heart and with bitterness, sigh before their eyes."
12 "And it shall be, when they say to you, 'Why do you sigh?' that you shall say, 'Because of the news; when it comes, every heart will melt, and all hands will grow feeble...'"

---

**\* v. 7. i)** Set [your face] therefore, etc., as in verse 2. **k)** likewise. **l)** against the sanctuaries or the temple; spoken in the plural because of its three parts, according to Grotius; or according to Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 17th-century theologian</note> and Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Hebrew grammarian and commentator</note>, because he prophesies not only concerning the sanctuary of Solomon, but also that of Zerubbabel. Cocceius observes on verse 2 that just as the Israelites in battle or exile turned their faces toward the location of the sanctuary while praying (1 Kings 8:44, 48; Daniel 6:11), so now the Prophet is commanded to prophesy *against* the sanctuaries. This is because the Jews held the temple as their source of confidence (chapter 7:20), as if on account of the temple and the worship performed there, they held God and His grace in their own power. **m)** see verses 2, 14, 19; and chapter 25:2.

**\* v. 8. n)** I will rise up against you. Compare Jeremiah 50:31; chapter 51:25. **o)** verses 9, 10. The Chaldean <note>The Babylonian army</note> is armed, whom I will use like a sword to carry out my judgments. Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a 16th-century Jewish-Italian convert and Hebraist</note>. **p)** so that I may cut off or take away from you and your land. chapter 14:13, 17; 1 Kings 9:7. **q)** the just and the ungodly. verse 9. Without distinction. verse 3. For even the righteous are often involved with the unrighteous in temporal punishments, namely chastisements and hardships. Compare Job 9:22; Ecclesiastes 9:5. Others understand "the righteous" comparatively (see chapter 16:51), meaning those who possess an outward form of righteousness before men, though they are unrighteous before God. Thus Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius, a Lutheran biblical critic</note>, page 1491. But Grotius interprets "I will cut off the righteous and the impious" as taking away the good by sending them into exile, and destroying the bad by an evil death; see chapters 9:4–6 and 18:2 onwards.

**\* v. 9. r)** Since I am therefore about to cut off. chapter 16:43; 26:2. **s)** verse 8; Zephaniah 3:6. **t)** see verse 8. **u)** that is, against all Jews, from Dan even to Beersheba. But others say: "Because I have punished the righteous and the wicked among my own people, how much more shall I punish all others: the Moabites, Ammonites, etc." (compare verse 4, 10; and Jeremiah 25:28, 29) from Jerusalem all the way to Chaldea; those who insulted the ruin of the Israelites and encouraged it. Kimchi and Rashi <note>Solomon ben Isaac, the preeminent medieval French commentator</note> lean toward this view. **x)** see verse 3.

**\* v. 10. y)** That they may know. chapter 17:24; 29:6. **z)** verse 4, 9; Isaiah 40:5. **a)** verse 8, 9. **b)** It shall not return into its sheath until it has consumed everything. Compare verse 4. In this way, he compares this final slaughter with previous ones, in which God—having chastened the people for a time—returned the sword to its sheath. Tremellius. But Cocceius argues: This signifies that from that beginning, God will so prostrate them until He subjects all peoples to Christ; He will carry out almost continuous judgments among the nations resisting Christ and not giving place to His kingdom. Hence it happens that the histories of nations, beginning from the Babylonian wars down to this day, tell of cruel wars and the almost uninterrupted destruction of peoples and kingdoms.

**\* v. 11. c)** But you. Verses 11 and 12 serve as a preface to the following prophecy in verse 13. **d)** Groan or sigh. Ezekiel 2:23. Displaying yourself as a sign of the coming calamity for the Jews. **e)** with the breaking of the loins. Nahum 2:11; compare Deuteronomy 33:11. As those who are bitterly mourning and groaning are accustomed to collapse almost to their knees, as if their loins were broken and unfit for their duty. Grotius: Groan deeply, as those who suffer from pleurisy <note>an inflammation of the lung lining causing sharp pain</note>. Others: with the belt snapped from the weight of grief, clothing loose, flowing, and torn, as if one were most negligent of oneself and most unprepared for any action. **f)** with bitterness: (1) with most bitter weeping and wailing. Compare chapter 27:31; Isaiah 22:4; chapter 33:7; Jeremiah 6:26; 31:15. **g)** chapter 4:12; chapter 12:3, 4.

**\* v. 12. h)** For what reason? Jeremiah 16:10. **i)** verse 9; chapter 9:4. **k)** on account of verse 17; chapter 6:9. **l)** the report, the news of future evil, chapter 7:26. **m)** compare chapter 7:5, 6, 10. **n)** so that every heart melts. Isaiah 19:1; Nahum 2:11. **o)** chapter 7:17; Isaiah 35:3.

-> CHAPTER XXI, verse 11. **Sigh** <note>Hebrew: He'anach</note> with a Qamets vowel. Thus in the 1st, also the 5th, against the Manuscripts of Erfurt and Index Basle, folio 60, column 8. <-
-> **Sighing** <note>Hebrew: Ne'anach</note> thus with a Chateph-Pathach in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 5th, 6th, 9th, 10th, and 20th [manuscripts]. <-
-> verse 12 **Sighing** <-

<column-break/>

**\* v. 3. i)** chapter 8:3; 28:13; 2. chapter 16:35. **112)** I will be kindling. Jeremiah 11:16; Amos 1:4. **n)** in you, Jerusalem, and other towns and villages. **o)** a fire, that is, according to Vatablus <note>François Vatable, 16th-century French humanist</note>: I am prepared to send the greatest affliction. Grotius: This fire does not signify a literal burning only, but everything that consumes, as above in chapter 19:12. **p)** every green tree. This is the same as in verse 8. Compare Luke 23:31; Revelation 9:4. **q)** chapter 17:24. i.e., Princes and subjects, old and young, rich and poor, good and bad; see verse 8. **r)** it shall not be extinguished, that is, the sent evils will not cease until what I will is accomplished; see verse 4, 10. **s)** The flame is a heavy flame; most inflammatory. With a prosthetic "Shin" <note>an additional letter at the start of the word</note> in Job 15:30; Song of Solomon 8:6; more frequent among the Chaldeans and Syrians. **t)** and they shall be scorched by it; namely by shame, hunger, disease, etc. Compare Jeremiah 30:6; Joel 2:6; Lamentations 4:8; chapter 5:10. Whence they shall be burned in it. **(u)** Noun. Proverbs 16:27. **u)** all faces. chapter 7:18; chapter 27:35. Or: whatever is pleasant, beautiful, and remarkable in that region. **x)** from the south of Judah even to its north; from one end to the other. verse 9. Others: from Jerusalem all the way to Chaldea. Thus Cocceius: he notes that since God’s judgments in the land of Israel were carried out by Nebuchadnezzar, then also the sword in verse 8 would pursue the Babylonians; so that from Jerusalem toward Babylon no nation escapes the punishment of the sword.

**\* v. 4. y)** That they may see and know. Isaiah 40:5. **z)** that is, all men to whom these things become known. verse 9, 10. **a)** I have kindled it. chapter 39:9, 10; Jeremiah 7:18. **b)** for it shall not be extinguished. verse 3; Jeremiah 7:20; Ezekiel 30:31. Compare below, verse 10.

**\* v. 5. c)** But I said. **d)** see chapter 4:14. **e)** But they, indeed being rebellious and stubborn. chapter 2:7; chapter 3:7. **f)** they say and will say to me, if I myself [speak] these things...
**v. 12.** rebellious and stubborn. chapter 2:7; chapter 3:7. **f)** they say and will say to me, if I myself [speak] these things...

<summary>This page analyzes Ezekiel 21:3-12, interpreting the "forest fire" parable as a literal sword (the Babylonian army) that will devastate the land of Israel. The commentary explores the theological difficulty of both the righteous and the wicked being "cut off" and describes the prophet's physical act of sighing as a sign of impending doom.</summary>

by which my son, Israel, shall be struck; namely, with a rod of iron, Psalm 2:9. But Schmidius takes it in the nominative case, as we said: "And the rod of my son," etc., which we take as referring to Christ, the Son of God, to whom the Father has handed over all judgment, John 5:22. Thus the speech, as is the custom of the prophets, is interrupted with changing persons, and various speaking persons are introduced. Compare 1 Kings 20:34. 
**i)** **it despises, rejects, and turns away from**, namely <term>shebet</term> <note>Hebrew: rod/scepter</note>, which elsewhere is masculine but here and in verse 18 is feminine. Compare 2 Kings 17:20; 23:27. Jeremiah 3:37; 6:30; 7:29. Hosea 9:17. etc. 
**k)** every tree, according to Grotius; that is, it will spare no man. Compare verses 2, 3. Cocceius: that is, it cuts off everything noble in the world, as if it were vile and of no value or dignity; and especially all that which was prominent in the people of God. Maius: **despising every tree** of the Judean forest, rejecting the tree of life. Compare Isaiah 2:12 following.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Ezekiel 21. Having described the "Song of the Sword," the text now moves into the specific application of this judgment: the sword is "tripled" and directed toward the gates of Jerusalem. The commentary transitions from the poetic description of the weapon to the historical prophecy of the King of Babylon standing at a crossroads, deciding whether to attack Jerusalem or the Ammonites.</meta>

<header>CHAPTER 21. EZEKIEL 21</header>

# THE SWORD IS TRIPLED; IT IS THE SWORD OF THE SLAIN, THE SWORD OF THE GREAT SLAIN ONE
# WHICH PENETRATES TO THEM.
# SO THAT THE HEART MAY MELT AND THE STUMBLING BLOCKS BE MULTIPLIED.

<margin>
Jeremiah 6:21. **a)** against verse 27. **b)** Compare Judges 9:40; 2 Samuel 11:23; Ezekiel 24:12; Lamentations 1:4; 2:9. **c)** He gave it in my decree. S. <note>meaning</note> I will give. Compare notes on chapter 7:12; 13:11. **d)** This word is unusual elsewhere, and so its meaning is uncertain to us; the interpreters render it various ways based on context, of which we bring the better ones:
</margin>

<margin>
**p)** S. <note>meaning</note> "Let the sword be repeated by you," saying, "Aha! the sword is tripled." Others: "A third sword shall come." Others: "For it shall be doubled, indeed the sword shall become triple." Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, 16th-century Hebraist</note>: "For the sword shall be repeated a third time." Some refer this to the three deportations of kings Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah; others to the triple calamity looming in Zedekiah’s time. The first was the capture of Zedekiah, the second the capture of the city, the third the deportation of all the remnants who were with Gedaliah. So says Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius</note>. Others count slightly differently. But Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius</note> says: "We can hardly doubt that this prophecy proceeds further, speaking as much of the sword to be drawn in the last days (as in Deuteronomy 32:41-42) as of the sword by which the disobedient were first struck." **q)** The sword shall be pierced through. Compare chapter 9:4; 32:22. By which many are pierced. See Isaiah 66:16. **r)** This shall be the sword at the same time. **s)** Pierced through. See verse 30. By which not only the common people, but the King himself, the princes, and the nobles shall fall. Others: "The great profane ones," to be handed over to profane men, and especially to the great profane Chaldean. Compare chapter 7:21, 24; Habakkuk 1:6 and following. **t)** Penetrating into the innermost chambers, pursuing them even into the bedrooms. <note>original Latin: *in intima penetralia penetrans*</note> Compare 1 Kings 20:30; 22:25. Others, following Louis de Dieu <note>17th-century orientalist</note>, using the meaning from an Ethiopic root, say: "Which awaits them." See Maius's supplement to Cocceius’s Lexicon, page 35.

Verse 20. *****) "Therefore so that you may melt away, be dissolved." Exodus 15:15; Psalm 46:7; 75:4. An emphatic repetition; for one particle would have sufficed. **x)** "Apportune." See chapter 22:14. **y)** "And so that they may be multiplied." See chapter 11:6; 24:10; Jeremiah 46:16. **z)** Ruins, stumbling blocks—that is, things against which people strike, fall, and perish. Jeremiah.
</margin>

<page-num>21</page-num> **AGAINST ALL THEIR GATES I HAVE SET THE TERROR OF THE SWORD; ALAS! IT IS MADE FOR LIGHTNING,**
**SHARPENED FOR SLAUGHTER. GATHER YOURSELF, GO TO THE RIGHT, SET YOURSELF, GO TO THE LEFT,**
<page-num>22</page-num> **WHITHER YOUR FACE IS APPOINTED.**
**AND I ALSO WILL STRIKE MY HANDS TOGETHER AND I WILL SATISFY**
**MY WRATH; I THE LORD HAVE SPOKEN IT.**
<page-num>23</page-num> **AND THE WORD OF THE LORD CAME TO ME, SAYING:**
<page-num>24</page-num> **AND YOU, SON OF MAN, APPOINT FOR YOURSELF TWO WAYS**
**FOR THE SWORD OF THE KING OF BABYLON TO COME; FROM ONE LAND BOTH SHALL GO OUT, AND A SIGN**
<page-num>25</page-num> **MARK AT THE HEAD OF THE WAY TO THE CITY. MARK A WAY FOR THE SWORD TO COME TO**

---

Translators render this as "reproach," from an Arabic root <unclear>לכח</unclear> meaning he argued, refuted, or severely criticized; as if to say, "I will no longer correct the incorrigible Jews with words, but with the swords of enemies." Others understand it as the "dazzling" of the sword, based on the Arabic *abchah* and 2 Maccabees 15:6. So says Castell’s Lexicon, page 9, and Ludolfus in his commentary on Ethiopian history, page 203. Others, with Louis de Dieu, translate it as "power" from the Ethiopic language, but Ludolfus shows this is less correct. S. <note>meaning</note>, Cocceius, and M. I. <note>Michaelis</note> say "edge." Gussetius <note>Jacques Gousset</note>, page 11, following Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, derives it from the root **נבח** <note>nabach</note> in Isaiah 56:10, meaning "barking." That is, the sound of many swords being swung together with great force, which sound imitates a sharp barking; just as at other times a "mouth" and the action of "eating" are attributed to a sword. Still others want it to be understood as the "clashing" of a cutting sword. We omit other more uncertain interpretations. **e)** Alas! S. <note>meaning</note> Ah! as in chapter 6:11. Others: "brother," "companion," or "similar." See note on chapter 18:10. **f)** The sword is smoothed/furbished. **g)** To lightning. S. <note>meaning</note> into lightning. Verse 15; Deuteronomy 32:41. **h)** Some, with the Vulgate, say "clothed"—that is, wrapped and hidden in a scabbard as if in a garment, lest the edge be dulled. Cocceius: "wrapped up," meaning it is covered with deceits; from the root **עטה** <note>atah</note>. Others, like Tremellius and Kimchi, say "pointed" or "sharpened" like the **עט** <note>et</note> or stylus in Jeremiah 17:1 and Job 19:24. But Maius prefers the Arabic meaning: "It has already been given over or handed over." **i)** For slaughter. Verse 15. **k)** "Woe, join yourself together"—namely, sword to sword. An apostrophe <note>a speech directed to an object</note> to the sword, which should invade the enemies of God as if united with its fellow soldiers. Rashi: "Turn yourself to one side." Others: "Be directed into one." S. <note>meaning</note> "Why solitude?" So M. I. Others: "Sharpen yourself, sharpen." From **התאחד** <note>hitachadi</note> related to "one." Thus the Septuagint, but not correctly. **l)** Turn yourself to the right. See Genesis 13:9. **m)** Prepare yourself, oppose yourself to the enemies. Compare 1 Kings 20:12. **n)** And turn yourself to the left. Genesis 13:9; 1 Chronicles 12:2. Oppose yourself to the enemies, whether they occur on the right or the left. **o)** Where or whither, without a question. As in Joshua 2:5; Nehemiah 2:16. **p)** Wherever your face has been established, destined, or arranged. That is, wherever you are drawn, go and kill. Grotius: "Exercise the vengeance commanded by God in all directions." But Cocceius in his Lexicon asks: "Whither is your face directed? Where do you intend to go, O sword?" As in Genesis 16:8; Zechariah 2:6; 5:10, etc. As if the words are either restraining the sword or indicating its remarkable path. **q)** A grammatical form <note>Hophal participle</note> from the root **עוד** <note>od</note> as in Jeremiah 24:1. But Schmidius asks: "But whither will you turn those wavering faces?" Based on a different root meaning to totter. Verse 22. **r)** "Therefore I also." **s)** I will applaud—that is, I will favor the slayers. See verse 19; chapter 22:13. **t)** And I will cause my burning anger to rest and endure, not suddenly vanish. Chapter 5:13; 16:42; 24:13. A song of victory <note>original Greek: *Ἐπινίκιον*</note>, by which God declares that He will eventually triumph and satisfy His wrath. **u)** "And therefore it shall most certainly be done." Chapter 5:13, 15; Numbers 14:35. Verse 23. **x)** Jerome: "Secondly, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Do you wish, son of man, to know who this sword is, and to learn more clearly the identity of the raging sword? Listen to what I say: set two ways, so that the sword of the King of Babylon may come through them, etc." Verse 24. **y)** "But you." **x)** Set—paint for yourself on a tablet, as above in chapter 4:1. Others: conceive in your mind two ways. **a)** Whence the sword or the Babylonian army might come. **b)** "One"—treating the "land of the Hebrews" as a common gender. Others: "of the one," the Babylonian king. **c)** Both of those ways shall go out. Grotius: From one way that comes out of Arabia, these two ways are divided—one to Jerusalem, the other to Rabbah, the chief city of the Ammonites. The Prophet foretells that Nebuchadnezzar, by God's instinct, will hesitate at that crossroads <note>Latin: *biuio*</note> as to which way he should go. Verse 25. **d)** A place, monument, or sign. See 1 Samuel 15:12. To show the Babylonian which way he should enter. But Cocceius says: "A space where Nebuchadnezzar might stand, performing sacred rites with his army." Compare Deuteronomy 23:13; Isaiah 56:5. **e)** Choose, prepare, or construct. Chapter 23:47. See Joshua 17:15, and the root **ברא** <note>bara</note> above in chapter 20:38. **f)** At the beginning of the way or ways leading to each city. Verse 26; chapter 43:12. Verse 25. **g)** You shall set a way. Verse 24. **h)** By which the sword of Nebuchadnezzar might come;

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Ezekiel 21. Having established the "Song of the Sword" on the previous page, the text now illustrates the sword’s specific destination. The prophet describes the King of Babylon at a crossroads, using ancient divination rituals to decide whether to strike the Ammonites first or turn his full wrath toward Jerusalem. The commentary meticulously details the methods of ancient divination—arrows, household idols, and animal sacrifice—as historical context for the King's decision-making process.</meta>

...superstitions as those of the Chaldeans). Namely, when some great business was to be performed, they would consult three arrows enclosed in a small vessel. On the first was written: *The Lord commanded me*; on the second: *The Lord forbade me*; the third was **unmarked** <term>ἀβάπτιστον</term> <note>original Greek: unmarked/neutral</note>. If the one drawing by hand encountered the first, they proceeded with a cheerful spirit; if the second, they desisted; if the third, they put them back until either the first or the second appeared. See Jerome in his Commentary on this place; Pococke's *Specimen of Arab History*, page 329 and following; and from him Noldius in *Concordance of Particles*, no. 760, page 895; Selden's *Syntagma on the Syrian Gods*, Book I, chapter 2, page 101; Pfeiffer, same work as above, and in the *Select Decade of Sacred Exercises* annexed to *Vexed Doubts*, page 93; Hiob Ludolf's *Ethiopic Lexicon*, column 200 and following. **u)** he asked or consulted, cf. on the construction Numbers 27:21; Judges 1:1; Hosea 4:12. **x) Teraphim** or images, Genesis 31:19; Judges 17:5; 1 Samuel 19:13; 2 Kings 23:24; cf. Zechariah 10:2. **y)** he inspected or will inspect the liver of the sacrificed beast: for this species of divination from the entrails of victims, especially from the liver and heart, was very familiar to the ancients, as is known even from the writers of Roman history. See Struve's *Syntagma of Roman Antiquities*, page 289 and following. Nor do I think it should be doubted, says Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius</note> on this place, that those arts came from the Chaldeans to the Lydians, and from the Lydians to the Etruscans, cf. note on Isaiah 47:12. **v. 27.** <note>Verse 22 in English Bibles</note> **z)** In his right hand, with which he will draw the arrow from the vessel. **a)** the divination will be for Jerusalem. So Kimchi and Rashi. **l)** as if a vain divination or a certain empty divination; they will despise the Chaldean omens as vain, v. 34; Ezekiel 12:24. Others: they will mock this prophecy of yours as a vain, empty, and foolish divination. **m)** although bound by oaths <note>original: "iurate obstricti"</note> to them. Although the Jews made oaths of loyalty to the Chaldeans, the treacherous ones want to fear nothing from them. see Ezekiel 17:13 and following. According to Kimchi: as if the Chaldeans had sworn many oaths to them: repeating the prefix *Caph* from the preceding word. Others take both as nouns: as if there were oaths of oaths to them, with the same sense as the preceding. However, Schuv. puts it this way: "but the oaths of oaths shall be to them"; i.e., those things shall happen which I have often threatened them by oath, and to which they themselves bound themselves to the Chaldeans by oath. **n)** for he, *S.* rather he (Judah) makes to remember; Ezekiel 29:16; Numbers 5:15. Namely, God and the Babylonian; so that he cannot but take punishment from the rebellious Jews. **o)** iniquity; specifically the treachery and perjury of Zedekiah, by which he had violated the faith given to Nebuchadnezzar with the name of God interposed. Tremellius: "this very fact, that they mock you and my prophets, brings it about that the whole iniquity comes into account before me and before the enemies." **p)** that they may be seized v. 29; Ezekiel 14:5. **z)** Zedekiah, Jerusalem, and the treaty-breaking Jerusalemites. For Nebuchadnezzar had kept the faith given by his idols; but Zedekiah had not kept the faith given by the true God. That indeed pertained greatly to the insult of God, and therefore it was fitting for God to avenge it. Grotius. Indeed, Cocceius ingeniously interprets this verse in the following way: "It became to them (Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonians) like a vain omen." The King did not believe it, but held it as a vain and deceptive response: both because the city was fortified (v. 25) and because the temple of God was there, under whose protection that city had always been safe, so that many kings and peoples laying hands on it were put to shame, like Sennacherib among others. There the diviners had sworn and vowed that they were not responding through deceit or fallacy. But then he (i.e., someone) commemorated the sin, that the Jews had defected from their God and sinned against His law, and therefore the King was called by God through those signs, so that from a rebellious people, as if **sold into his hand** <term>venundato</term>, he might exact punishment. But the opinion of Schmidt seems simplest and consistent with both words and context. **v. 29.** <note>Verse 24 in English Bibles</note> **q)** Because you make it to be remembered, v. 28. **r)** namely while they are revealed, uncovered, and become publicly known. These can be read parenthetically up to the Atnach <note>Hebrew cantillation mark</note>. cf. Ezekiel 16:57; Isaiah 22:14; Hosea 7:1. **s)** Ezekiel 18:30, 31. cf. note on Ezekiel 21:11. **t)** so that they appear, your sins are conspicuous. **u)** in all your actions. Ezekiel 20:43. **x)** therefore, I say, because you have come into the mind or memory, with your sins crying out against you. cf. v. 28. This triple repetition of the word does not so much indicate continuity and exaggeration—that the crown of the house of David was not afflicted and corrupted at one time until it was all taken away—as it does the triple slaughter and overthrow of the crown. For wherever a triple repetition of a word is found, the discourse is about three really distinct things. And thus from Isaiah 6, 3, a sufficiently firm argument for proving the Holy Trinity is woven, as **D. Danzius** rightly observed in his *Interpreter* p. 16. following. So **Abarbanel** at this place: He regards (he says) those three Kings, whom Nebuchadnezzar removed from the rule of Judah, namely Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah. Some indeed in **Glassius** p. 548 take the triple repetition for the three more notable slaughters of the Jews, brought upon them by the Babylonians, Antiochus or the Greeks, and finally the Romans; which last one finally brought <term>total destruction (panolethriam)</term> to the people. **q)** I will place, I will make it that crown or kingdom. cf. Jeremiah 6, 8. **r)** even this crown of Zedekiah, as that of Jehoiakim and Jeconiah, or even the same (as Isaiah 65, 4. Psalm 71, 22.) this royal and priestly dignity. **s)** nothing was made, or there will be nothing v. 13. For when he says *also this*, he hints at another besides that which he had already said would be corrupted. **Cocceius's Lexicon** p. 485. But **Schmetau:** even this even this was not done before, until he came etc. **Abendana:** as if to say: Even if I said that Jehoiachin, now humbled, would be exalted; yet he will not have the crown of the kingdom, until he comes from his seed, whose judgment it is, namely the King Messiah. **t)** until he comes as in Genesis 49, 10. Psalm 110, 1. 4. as to the King of Kings and Lord of Lords. Deuteronomy 10, 17. **x)** with him himself relative **שֶׁ** to whom I gave it. or **שֶׁ** I will give this right or judgment to him; compare Joshua 15, 19. Judges 1, 15. see Luke 1, 32. 33. **y)** *S.* You however. **z)** prophet also v. 2, 4) c. 30, 2, 6) regarding c. 13, 16. or c. 19, 1. **c)** the Ammonites, of whom above v. 24. 25. following. For since the Jews took from there matter either of envy against the Ammonites, or of expostulation with God, as if he acted more harshly with them than with others; or the Ammonites matter of congratulation and glorying, because they were freed from their fear; so that he might snatch away that opportunity from both, he announces here the judgments of God against the Ammonites. **Innes** in the *Commentary* in Poole's *Synopsis*. **d)** because of their reproach, c. 22, 4. Psalm 79, 12. Lamentations 3, 61. with which they indeed affected Israel when it was afflicted, (see below c. 25, 3. 6. Zephaniah 2, 8. and note on Jeremiah 49, 1.) and Christ, and the justice of God and his kingdom, sent to the Jews. **Cocceius.** cf. also **Gaertler's Prophetic Theology** p. 231. following. **e)** say, I say. **f)** see v. 14. 19. **g)** it is opened, drawn. <meta>This page continues the prophetic oracles of Ezekiel. It concludes the judgment against the Ammonites (the neighbors of Israel to the east) in chapter 21 and begins a new indictment in chapter 22 directed at Jerusalem, here called the "city of blood." The commentary draws heavily on Rabbinic authorities like Kimchi and the Targum of Jonathan to explain linguistic shifts and historical context.</meta>

For indeed, after the history of the Hasmoneans, no mention is made of the Moabites and Ammonites, etc. **Gurtler, Prophetic Theology** p. 369.

--- Page 1071 ---
<meta>This page continues the indictment of Jerusalem in Ezekiel chapter 22. While the previous page focused on the city's general social injustices and "blood-guilt," this page introduces a vivid metallurgical metaphor—comparing the people to the "dross" or waste produced during the smelting of metals—and specifically condemns the corruption of the nation's leaders, including the prophets, priests, and princes.</meta>

# EZEKIEL CHAPTER 22

<margin>
**g)** this refers to the dross of silver (verse 18; Isaiah 1:22), indicating they have degenerated from their original goodness. It seems to me that the word *sig* <note>original: "סִיג"</note> is not just dross—that is, the refuse or filth of silver—but everything mixed with silver that must be separated from it. I am led to this by the following text and the origin of the word from *sug* <note>original: "סוּג"</note>, which means "to turn away." This is supported by the authority of the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> which translates it as "mixed together," as the scholar Hugo Grotius notes. **h)** The Syriac version favors this view in the following: "for all are changed for the worse; tin, iron, and lead are in the middle of the crucible; indeed, they have become dross instead of silver." Or: "for all who were like false gold-tin, or iron, or lead in the crucible, have now become nothing but the dross of silver." Some explain the point of comparison like this: some degenerated into the impudence of malice and stubbornness (Jeremiah 6:28); others into the flame of fake piety (Isaiah 1:25); others into the iron of tyranny; others into the lead of greed. **i)** "and tin" (verse 20; chapter 27:12), which is usually of less value than bronze in metalwork. There is a progression from bronze down to lead. **k)** glowing crucibles (verse 30, 22; Deuteronomy 4:20). **l)** not silver as before, but only the dross of silver. This follows Jeremiah and the Masoretic reading <note>The authoritative Hebrew text tradition</note> with a similar construction to Proverbs 22:21. Others say "dross for silver," and Tremellius says "dross out of silver." But the Syriac version says: "those things which are mixed with silver." 

**v. 19. m)** verse 18. The Syriac says: "because you are all mixed together." **n)** "behold, I will gather" (verse 20). **o)** compare chapter 24:4.

**v. 20. p)** By a gathering, or "as silver is usually gathered."
</margin>

<margin>
<term>לסוג קרי</term> <note>A scribal note indicating the word should be read as "for dross."</note>

This refers to the return of the punishment (chapter 16:39; Numbers 17:19). **u)** *S.* "so that I may melt [you]" (verse 22; Job 10:10).

**v. 21. x)** "I will gather [you]," I say (chapter 39:28). **y)** "and I will blow upon you" (verse 20).

**v. 22. b)** *S.* "According to the melting of silver"; just as silver...

**18** Son of man, the house of Israel has become $^g$ dross to me; $^h$ they are all bronze, tin, iron, and lead in the middle of a $^k$ furnace; they have become $^l$ the dross of silver.
**19** Therefore, thus says the Lord God: Because $^m$ you have all become dross, therefore behold, I am $^n$ gathering you into the $^o$ midst of Jerusalem.
**20** $^p$ As silver, bronze, iron, lead, and tin are gathered into the $^q$ furnace to $^r$ blow fire upon them to $^s$ melt them; so I will gather you in my anger and in my fury, and I will $^t$ place you there and $^u$ melt you.
**21** I will $^x$ gather you and $^y$ blow upon you with the $^z$ fire of my wrath, and you shall be $^a$ melted in its midst.
**22** As silver is $^b$ melted in a furnace, so you shall be melted in its midst; and you shall know that I, the Lord, have poured out my fury upon you.
**23** And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:
**24** Son of man, say to her: You are a land that is not $^c$ cleansed, $^d$ nor rained upon in the day of indignation.
**25** There is a $^e$ conspiracy of her prophets in her midst, like a $^n$ roaring $^o$ lion $^p$ tearing the prey; they have $^q$ devoured souls; they $^r$ take $^s$ wealth and $^t$ precious things; they have $^u$ multiplied her $^v$ widows in her midst.
**26** Her $^i$ priests have $^x$ violated my law and $^y$ profaned my holy things; they have $^k$ made no $^z$ distinction $^a$ between the holy and the $^b$ profane, nor have they $^c$ shown the $^d$ difference between the $^e$ unclean and the clean; and they have $^f$ hidden their $^g$ eyes from my $^h$ Sabbaths, and I am profaned among them.
**27** Her $^m$ princes in her midst are like $^k$ wolves $^l$ tearing the prey, to shed $^m$ blood...

# EZEKIEL CHAPTER 22 & 23

<margin>
All ranks of the Judean state are accused of the highest corruption. See the note at verse 1. **z)** verse 12, chapter 18:18. Compare Ezekiel 3:5; Jeremiah 9:3; Habakkuk 1:3. **a)** and empty of wisdom. Chapter 18:18; Isaiah 61:8; Psalm 62:11. **b)** the wretched, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
**\*)** for destroying <note>original Latin: "ad perdendum"</note> or by destroying. Jeremiah 23:1. **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note>: One may distinguish between shedding blood and destroying souls. Not everyone who sheds the blood of another also destroys their soul. The Jews killed the Apostles and Prophets, but they did not destroy their souls. On the other hand, a soul can be destroyed even if the body is not killed. This happens when terror and force are used to prevent the truth from being spoken and heard—and when a law of injustice is prescribed to men, and by these things souls are held back so that they do not seek the truth and do not glorify God. **o)** verse 25. **p)** so that they may greedily gain profit from the goods of those killed or oppressed. Verse 12; Jeremiah 6:13; Habakkuk 2:9. **Jonathan** <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note>: so that they might receive the mammon of falsehood or injustice. Compare Luke 16:9, 11.

28 **And her prophets have smeared whitewash for them, seeing false visions and divining lies for them, saying, "Thus says the Lord GOD," when the LORD has not spoken.** <note>The "whitewash" (Hebrew: *taphel*) refers to flimsy or deceptive justifications that cover up the rot of society, much like thin plaster on a crumbling wall.</note>
29 **The people of the land have practiced extortion and committed robbery. They have wronged the poor and needy, and have oppressed the resident foreigner without justice.**
30 **And I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none.**
31 **Therefore I have poured out my indignation upon them. I have consumed them with the fire of my wrath. I have returned their way upon their own heads, declares the Lord GOD.**

**m)** Jerusalem, and by synecdoche <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note> the kingdom of Judah, is *Oholibah*. Thus he explains himself what he had previously said more obscurely.

It is understood that Abraham was called out from that land so that he and his sons would not worship other gods; they were brought into a land where God dwelt in their midst and spoke with them familiarly. Sated by their coupling, she turned again to the Egyptians, so that they were, so to speak, wrenched and broken apart from each other, they who previously seemed to have grown together by a common treaty into one body and one soul. **Kimchi and Rashi:** Jehoiakim and Zedekiah rebelled against them (see 2 Kings 24:1, 7, 20). **Verse 18. a)** **Septuagint:** when indeed she had become so poisonous (compare Isaiah 57:8; chapter 16:8, 37). **b)** her lust and harlotries (verse 7, 19). **c)** so that she might of her own accord thrust into view those things which ought to be hidden (chapter 16:8). In Ethiopic, *naqa'a* means to be broken or split (see **Ludolf's Ethiopic Lexicon**, page 298). Hence you might best translate it: "and she was broken off." **f)** **Glassius:** this metaphorical phrase most excellently expresses the communion of God with the faithful. If the Lord withdraws His grace from these people, who sin intentionally and stubbornly, the Head is, as it were, wrenched and torn away from the putrid members. **verse 32.** **k)** A deep cup <note>original: "Calicem profundum"</note>, see Proverbs 22:14. **l)** wide, see Job 11:9. The severity of the punishment is indicated here. **m)** it shall be; this cup, exhausted by you, will fall to you as a sight; it will expose you to laughter while you are intoxicated, which is what usually happens to those who drain large cups. This seems to be the understanding according to the sequence of the words. Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish scholar also known as Radak</note> tends toward the same view. But Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmid, a 17th-century theologian</note> changes the gender to the second person masculine, from which it becomes: "into laughter and derision, wide for containing." **x) o)** into derision, see chapter 36:4. Because of the greatness of the vengeance that will come upon you, as Kimchi notes. Compare Lamentations 2:5. **y)** for the cup will be very large and wide. **(r) z)** so that it may hold much, see chapter 31:33.

**verse 33.** **a)** Why drunkenness, see chapter 39:19. **b)** sorrow, see Psalm 116:3. You shall be filled, compare Isaiah 51:21. **b)** Namely, with the cup of devastation, see Isaiah 24:12, Jeremiah 19:8. **c)** and desolation. Compare verse 7 and 2 Kings 21:13. **d)** see verse 31. **e)** see verses 9, 10; 2 Kings 21:13.

Jonah 9: "you have cast my fear from your eyes." **r)** therefore also chapter 16:43. **s)** bear your wickedness, and the penalties of your crime. See verse 49, chapter 16:52, 58. **v)** See verses 11, 14, 18, 29.

**verse 36.** **x)** Would you still plead the cause of Oholah? <note>Oholah and Oholibah are symbolic names for Samaria and Jerusalem</note> See chapter 20:4, 22:2. **x)** see verse 4. **y)** rather, declare, see Ecclesiastes 58:1. **z)** Chapter 16:2.

<margin>
**verse 34.** **f)** Namely, which you shall drink. Compare Jeremiah 25:28, 29. **g)** and drain. Namely, sorrow, chapter 39:17, Psalm 75:9. No part of the punishment will remain which you do not taste. **h)** The very shards <note>pottery fragments</note> into which you will break the cup, thrown down out of indignation. **i)** you shall break off, crush into small pieces, or scatter. (2) Numbers 24:8, Zephaniah 2:3. Others, following the Vulgate <note>The Latin Bible</note>, translate: "and you shall devour its fragments," as drunkards sometimes do. **k)** you shall tear, chapter 17:9. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a Dutch theologian</note>: out of rage and pain you will pluck out, break, and tear. As those who have drunk too much are accustomed to want to vomit, and while they vomit, they are constricted. **l)** chapter 5:13, 17:21, 34, 26:5. **m)** chapter 16:14.

**verse 35. n)** Therefore, I say, thus he spoke in verse 22. **o)** chapter 15:8. **p)** chapter 22:12, Jeremiah 2:32, 3:22, Hosea 2:15. **q)** behind the back.
</margin>

...but that which follows, having the *Athnach* <note>a Hebrew cantillation mark acting as a semicolon</note>, is taken improperly. To others, however, along with Raschi <note>Solomon ben Isaac, the preeminent medieval commentator</note>, the latter part contains an explanation of the former in this manner: they committed adultery with their idols. Compare verse 45, Jeremiah 3:8, Hosea 2:4-5. See also verse 45, Ecclesiastes 1:15. They shed innocent blood, and indeed for the sake of false gods; by persecuting the prophets and their disciples, who were champions of the truth. But to Raschi, it is the same as what follows: that they passed their children through the fire, etc. **c)** verse 39, Psalm 106:37. **d)** who ought to have been mine, chapter 16:20. **e)** they passed to idols through the fire, or they offered them, chapter 20:31. The Syriac version says: they burned them with fire for them. **verse 38. f)** chapter 20:27. **g)** chapter 5:11. **h)** see chapter 16:24, 22:8, Isaiah 56:2, 6, Jeremiah 17:21 and following.

**verse 39. i)** For when they slaughtered, chapter 16:21. **k)** see verse 37. **l)** compare Isaiah 1:11, Jeremiah 7:4, 21. **m)** on the same day. Coming from those sacrilegious rites, they approach my Temple. The words that follow indicate this sense. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch jurist and theologian</note>. **n)** and behold! chapter 15:4. **o)** in the Temple itself, where even horrendous idolatry was practiced. See 2 Kings 21:4 and noted above in chapter 8:3. **verse 40. p)** Furthermore, even. Habakkuk 2:5. **q)** because you sent. Namely, in the third person perfect: "besides they also sent," verse 16. **r)** to men. **s)** from a distance, Jeremiah 5:15. **t)** Namely, to whom when a messenger was sent. Compare Isaiah 57:9. **u)** then behold! they came, verses 17, 44. Through emotion, he repeats the same words with a few changes to express and stir up more indignation. **x)** for whom also, for whose sake, **y)** you washed yourself, Ruth 3:3, or you used a bath, O Oholibah. For he transitions here from the two sisters to one; so Cocceius. Or the discrepancy in number suggests a distribution. **z)** you colored your eyes <note>original: "fucasti... oculos tuos"</note>. Compare the note on 2 Kings 9:30 and Jeremiah 4:30. **a)** and you adorned yourself with an ornament, chapter 16:11, 13. According to the custom and habit of harlots, who receive their lovers most kindly and praise-worthily. It signifies that nothing was omitted by them which they thought convenient for winning and keeping lovers—that is, foreign nations. Junius <note>Francis Junius, a Huguenot theologian</note>. Compare Isaiah 57:9. **verse 41. b)** upon a bed, according to the ancient Eastern custom still used today, feasting with guests (and invited lovers). See Amos 2:8, 6:4, Esther 1:6, 7:8, and the writers of travelogues, including Maundrell's description of his journey to Palestine, pages 39-40 of the Hamburg German edition. **c)** glorious, spread with the most ornate carpets and cushions. See Psalm 45:14, Judges 18:21. **d)** Namely, before which a table was arranged; sumptuously and lavishly prepared. Compare Psalm 23:5, Isaiah 21:5. **e)** before that bed. **f)** but my incense and my oil, which I had given you to use with thanksgiving, or which you ought to have offered to me (chapter 16:18), **g)** you placed upon it, the bed. Vatablus says: you perfumed your bed with spices. Kimchi and M.I. teach that this custom existed, where they closed feasts with the sweetest scents and ointments. Travelogues testify that the same is done today. See Maundrell in the place cited.

**verse 34.** The word for "shards" <note>original: חרשיה</note> is written with the letter *Shin* instead of *Sin*, which is incorrect. **verse 41.** "And you sat" <note>original: וישבת</note> is written thus with a double *Pascha* <note>a Hebrew accent mark</note> according to analogy; others use the simple form.

<summary>This page analyzes the metaphorical "cup of judgment" drunk by Oholah and Oholibah (Samaria and Jerusalem) and their grotesque combination of child sacrifice with formal Temple worship. It highlights the use of foreign luxury and cosmetics as metaphors for the political alliances that led to their spiritual downfall.</summary>

**CHAPTER XXIV.**

1 And the word <gloss>f</gloss> of the LORD came to me in the ninth year <gloss>g</gloss>, in the tenth month, on the tenth day <gloss>h</gloss> of the month, saying:
2 Son of man, write for yourself <gloss>i</gloss> the name of the day, this very day; the king of Babylon has leaned <gloss>l</gloss> <note>original: "samakh" - meaning to lean upon, press, or begin a siege</note> against <gloss>m</gloss> Jerusalem on this very day <gloss>n</gloss>.
3 And speak <gloss>o</gloss> a parable <gloss>q</gloss> to the rebellious house <gloss>p</gloss>, and say to them: "Thus says the Lord GOD: 'Set on <gloss>r</gloss> the pot <gloss>s</gloss>; set it on and also pour water into it <gloss>t</gloss>.'
4 Gather its pieces into it, every good piece <gloss>x</gloss>, the thigh and the shoulder; fill <gloss>z</gloss> it with choice <gloss>y</gloss> bones.
5 Take the choice of the flock <gloss>a</gloss>, and also a pile of bones <gloss>b</gloss> under it; make it boil fiercely, and let its bones also be cooked within it.
6 Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: 'Woe <gloss>l</gloss> to the bloody city <gloss>m</gloss>, to the pot <gloss>n</gloss> in which is its rust <gloss>o</gloss>, and whose rust has not gone out of it <gloss>q</gloss>! 8 That it might stir up <gloss>z</gloss> fury <gloss>a</gloss> to take vengeance, I have set...
<meta>catchword: her</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>
**CHAPTER XXIV. f)** *Furthermore, it happened. Since the Prophet had previously predicted the siege and overthrow of the city of Jerusalem many times, now that it was beginning to happen, he is commanded to represent it to his fellow citizens in Babylonia by this parabolic sermon and a new emblem. Therefore, noted are: I. the day the siege of Jerusalem began, v. 1-2. II. a burning pot is proposed, full of meat, water, and bones, as a type of the city to be cut off and burned, v. 3–14. III. The Prophet is forbidden to mourn the death of his beloved wife, as a sign to the people of Jerusalem that they will do the same after the city is overthrown and their wives and children lost, v. 15-24. IV. The confirmation of this prophecy is predicted through the arrival of a messenger escaping from the slaughter of Jerusalem, v. 25-26, until which time the Prophet refrained from further denunciation of that destruction, v. 27.* **g)** *in the ninth year from the deportation of Jeconiah and the fifth of his prophetic office. Compare chapter 1:2, 8:1, 20:1, and the Preface to this book, sections 11 and 12.* **h)** *on the tenth day, Chapter 20:1, 2 Kings 25:1, Jeremiah 32:4 and following.* **v. 3. i)** *write, note for yourself, Jeremiah 22:30.* **k)** *Chapter 2:3, so that seeing in Chaldea [Babylon] what is happening in Jerusalem, you may be believed as a true prophet when the messenger arrives to confirm those things happened on that very day you noted, v. 26.* **l)** *for he has come near, he has approached with an army. Or: he has positioned himself. Compare Psalm 88:8.* **m)** *to, or against Jerusalem. Gusset <note>James Gusset, 17th-century Hebraist</note>: he persists by pressing, stretching toward Jerusalem, or rather all the way to Jerusalem, p. 563.* **n)** *Chapter 40:1, see 2 Kings 25:1 and the notes on Jeremiah 39:1.* **v. 3. o)** *Then tell a parable; and thus signify not only with words, but also with things through allegories, Chapter 17:2.*
</margin>

---

[Notes on the meat and bones]: ...the most prominent citizens, to be slaughtered in the city. **x)** *See the cross in chapter 21:17, Genesis 32:33, and the count in Ezekiel 12:6-7.* **a)** *by choosing bones, v. 5. Ezekiel 37:24 <note>likely 24:5</note>, that is, with choice bones, the best and most solid limbs, which are usually full of bone and marrow, fill it. Compare Isaiah 25:6, Micah 3:3.* **v. 5. b)** *The choicest of the sheep, v. 4, or: from the choicest cattle.* **c)** *by taking, that is, take. Compare Ezekiel 20:8, the pieces and the bones.* **d)** *and also let it be, or let it happen.* **e)** *a pyre or hearth (1) compare v. 9, for boiling the bones.* **v. Kal (2)** <note>Grammatical reference to the "Kal" verb stem</note> *Joel 4:13 [Hebrew numbering]* **k)** *its bones, which are inside it, v. 4, 10. That is, according to Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, medieval Jewish commentator</note>, the most powerful and robust people. Thus, we believe with most interpreters that the punishment to be inflicted on the Jews was most conveniently proposed in these verses allegorically. Junius and Tremellius <note>Calvinist biblical scholars</note>, however, understand what has been said so far not as punishment but as guilt; just as in the previous chapters the Prophet had indicated their abominations to the Jews by word, so now by this visible sign he reproaches their crimes, teaching that Jerusalem—in all its parts and members, highest and lowest, great and small—seethes and boils with wickedness. Ezekiel is commanded to suppress all outward signs of mourning to symbolize the stunned silence of the people when Jerusalem and the Temple fall.</summary>

After the prophecies that look toward the Jews, the prophet proceeds to other neighboring nations, who utterly mocked the Jews and exulted over the destruction of the city and the people. Compare notes on chapter 24, verse 27 and the Preface to this book, section 11. There are indeed four parts or prophecies in this chapter: I. against the Ammonites (v. 2–7); II. against the Moabites (v. 8–11); III. against the Edomites (v. 12–14); and IV. against the Philistines (v. 15, 16, 17).

Some, along with Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch scholar</note>, understand these to be the Chaldeans or Babylonians, who were called "northerners" in respect to Judea. Others, like Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish commentator</note>, think they are the Medes and Persians; others prefer the Arabs, who are frequently called "children of the East" in Scripture (see Judges 6, 3; Jeremiah 49, 28; Job 1, 3), and to whom, as shepherds, the following descriptions aptly apply. From this, Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a Dutch theologian</note> argues: It is established that after the return of the Jews from Babylon, the land of Ammon was possessed in part for a time by the Jews, but soon after by the Arabs, and became part of Arabia. Now the Arabs are the children of the East, and they inhabit those parts...

**Chapter XXVI, 1. f)** It happened further. From the Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites, and Philistines, the Prophet now comes to the Tyrians; so that, according to the opinion of Gautler in *Prophetic Theology* page 235 and 308, he deals in this chapter first with Tyre in general (v. 2–6), then specifically with Old Tyre devastated by Nebuchadnezzar (v. 7 and following). In Chapter 27 he deals with New Tyre (the island city) cut off by Alexander the Great, and in chapter 28 with a restored Tyre. In all these, the mystical significance of Tyre is not denied, to which Cocceius refers many things. Others combine Old and New (island) Tyre throughout. Compare the notes on verses 6 and 14 of this chapter. **g)** in the eleventh year, specifically from the deportation of Jeconiah and the reign of Zedekiah. See chapter 1:1, 2. And thus in the very year Jerusalem was conquered, 2 Kings 25:2 and following, Jeremiah 52:5 and following, which was the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, 2 Kings 25:8, Jeremiah 52:12. For the year in which Jeconiah was deported was the eighth year of the Babylonian King, 2 Kings 24:12. **h)** on the first day. Compare chapter 1:1, 8:1, 20:1, 24:1, 29:17. **i)** that is, of the first month; namely of that eleventh year. Compare chapter 30:20, 31:1. So say Cocceius and Maius, on the very first day of the first month, even before Jerusalem was conquered in the fourth month (Jeremiah 39:2, chapter 52:6). Most interpreters tend toward this view. Nor is it an obstacle that the Prophet introduces the Tyrians here on the first day of the eleventh year as boasting as if the destruction of Jerusalem were already accomplished; for then Jerusalem was pressed by a very heavy siege, and the Tyrians, with an envious and hostile mind, had already anticipated the imminent end of the city as it gasped its last. Gautler, *Prophetic Theology*, p. 239. Others, with Kimchi, understand this to be the fourth month itself in which Jerusalem was taken; he does not name it because it was well known to all and ill-omened, the very name of which he dreaded. But Grotius and Tremellius say: on the first day of the month that followed the capture of Jerusalem, which the following verses imply; that is, the fifth month, in which the Tyrians, having received news of the capture of Jerusalem, proclaimed that glorious confidence which is explained in verse 2. Furthermore, in chronological order, after the revelations made to the Prophet in the ninth year of his exile (chapter 24:1 and following), the prophecy against Egypt should follow, which was made in the tenth year, tenth month, twelfth day, and described in chapter 29:1–16. However, because Tyre had to be destroyed first, and Egypt was to be Nebuchadnezzar's reward for its destruction (chapter 29:18, 19), therefore, to better observe this, the threat of Tyre's destruction—though pronounced later—is placed before the threat of devastating Egypt. Compare Lightfoot, *Chronology of the Old Testament*, p. 125. **k)** undoubtedly, so that the prophet might be fortified with consolation, and through him the other exiles, hearing or about to hear not only the troubles of their countrymen and the mockery of the Tyrians, but also the just and most severe judgment upon them. According to Schmidt, there are two parts to this chapter: I. The prophecy against Tyre to be devastated by Nebuchadnezzar (v. 2–14). II. The lamentation of the neighbors over its devastation (v. 15 and following). **v. 2. l)** Therefore, as in chapter 16:43, 31:10. **m)** because she said or says, hearing the extreme distress and imminent ruin of Jerusalem. See the note on verse 1. **n)** Tyre, chapter 27:2, 28:2, Jeremiah 47:4, Joel 4:4, Amos 1:9. Compare the note on Joshua 19:29 and throughout Isaiah 23:1.

<summary>This page concludes the judgments against Edom and the Philistines for their vengeful behavior during Jerusalem's fall and begins the prophecy against the city of Tyre. It also contains scholarly debates regarding the exact timing of these revelations and notes the "halfway point" of the Book of Ezekiel.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the detailed commentary on the prophecies of Ezekiel. After concluding the judgments on Edom and Philistia in Chapter 25, the author now begins the extensive prophecy against the Phoenician merchant-city of Tyre in Chapter 26. The commentary integrates classical scholarship from figures like Hugo Grotius and Johannes Cocceius with linguistic analysis of the Hebrew text.</meta>

# EZEKIEL. CHAPTER 26.

<margin>
**o)** Aha! <note>original Latin: "euge!"</note> See chapter 25:3.
**p)** Broken, and soon to be cut down by the Babylonians, is Jerusalem. Isaiah 24:10. **q)** The doors, or "the gate of the nations," meaning the city through whose gates a numerous people entered and exited. From the borders and the outer regions: for trade and religion converged there from almost the entire East, and it also held the promise that nations would flow to it. Isaiah 2:1, 3; Jeremiah 17. It was a city that supplied merchandise to all peoples. **r)** It is turned, or transferred to me, namely its commerce. **Grotius:** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note> it turns itself to me, that marketplace of grain, wine, oil, and balsam. Compare the usage in Genesis 19:4, 2 Samuel 3:12, 1 Chronicles 10:14, chapter 12:23. And so now I shall be filled with goods and wealth. Chapter 27:25. **s)** Since, or because she herself is laid waste. Verse 19, chapter 29:12, 1 Kings 3:23. I shall grow from her ruins; **Grotius:** neighboring trade centers are accustomed to take their increase from the ruins of others. **Calov.** <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686) was a strict Lutheran theologian</note>
</margin>

<margin>
Note on Lamentations 3:45. In Arabic, the root *dahada* means to bring down, to take away, or to remove openly; hence, to remove the very surface of the earth. **s)** even its soil. **Grotius:** In Latin they would say: "I will scrape everything away, down to the last speck of dust." Compare 1 Kings 20:10. It is as if he says: Tyre boasts that she will be filled with the wealth of the whole world (verse 2), but I will bring it about that not even dust remains in her. **Tirinus.** <note>Jacobus Tirinus (1580–1636) was a Jesuit commentator</note> It will be so thoroughly overturned that only bare rocks remain.
</margin>

<margin>v. 2.</margin>
"Son of man, because Tyre has said against Jerusalem: 'Aha! The gate of the nations is broken; she has turned to me; I shall be filled, now that she is laid waste.'"

<margin>3</margin>

Thus, we understand here specifically that slaughter which was first carried out by Nebuchadnezzar, repeated by Alexander, and finally completed by **Saladin** in the year 1291 AD, when, after Ptolemais was captured, the Christian inhabitants deserted it out of fear. <meta>This page continues the technical and historical analysis of Ezekiel's prophecy against the city of Tyre. Having established the motivations for the city's downfall in the previous verses, the text now details the specific methods of destruction—trampling horses, plundering wealth, and the total erasure of the city's physical structures—linking these biblical predictions to the later historical conquests of Nebuchadnezzar and Alexander the Great.</meta>

# CHAPTER 26. EZEKIEL 26

<margin>
**verse 12. r)** "They will plunder," see also chapter 29:19. Their wealth, see chapter 29:5; Jeremiah 15:13 and 17:3. **s)** "and the divisions," see verse 5 and chapter 39:10; their rewards. **t)** chapter 28:5, 16, 18. This threat is not contradicted by what we noted below regarding chapter 29:18 and Isaiah 23:6, where Tyre is described as being stripped of its wealth. These passages are to be understood specifically regarding the merchandise and possessions located outside the city, and the remaining goods within Tyre; for it was not possible to carry everything away during the delay. See the work of Gurtler <note>Nicolaus Gürtler (1654–1711) was a Swiss theologian known for his work on prophetic theology</note>, page 237. **l)** See verse 4. **m)** and **the houses of your desire**. Compare Isaiah 2:16 and Jeremiah 12:10. **n)** That is, *their ruins*. According to Grotius. **o)** See verse 10. The events Ezekiel predicts here regarding the ruins of Tyre being overwhelmed by water were fulfilled to the letter in the time of Alexander the Great. This is clearly demonstrated from the histories of Diodorus Siculus (Book 17, chapter 40) and Curtius (Book 4, chapter 2), as noted by Gurtler in *Prophetic Theology*, page 307.
</margin>

According to Grotius.

So great will be the dust from the running of the horses that it will cover the city like a cloud. Grotius. **u)** Compare Jeremiah 4:29; chapter 8:16; chapter 47:3. **x)** chapter 10:13; chapter 23:24. **y)** "They shall come together," or "your walls shall shake." Verse 15; chapter 27:28. Grotius: For houses usually tremble when many chariots and horses run nearby, due to the solid nature of the ground. **z)** "when he enters through your gates." **a)** "according to the entrances of the city," just as men are accustomed to enter a conquered city. **b)** "broken through," 2 Kings 25:4; Jeremiah 39:4.

**verse 13. p)** Or, "I will thus make to cease." Chapter 30:10. **q)** The noise or the multitude of your songs. The signs of joy will stop. Amos 5:23; compare Isaiah 26:9; Jeremiah 7:34; chapter 25:10; chapter 48:33. **v)** Compare Isaiah 23:16; chapter 24:8; Job 30:31. **verse 14. s)** "And I will set you." This refers to Old Tyre <note>Palaetyrus</note>, whose destruction by Nebuchadnezzar is foretold here. Gurtler, page 236. Or, "I will finally give you," see verse 4. **t)** "like the nakedness of a rock," that is, you will be like a cliff. Verse 4. **u)** "an expansion," as seen above. **x)** "of nets," verse 5; chapter 32:3; Ecclesiastes 7:26. **y)** "you shall be." The masculine gender here refers to the grammatical ending of the name of Tyre; see the notes on chapter 22:4; 2 Kings 15:16; Isaiah 23:1; Exodus 10:7. Nothing will remain of you except a rock or a mound on which fishermen will spread their nets. **z)** "nor shall you be built anymore." **a)** See verse 5. An objection is raised regarding Isaiah 23:15, 17, where it says Tyre is to be restored after 70 years; compare Jeremiah 25:11, 22. **The Response:** You shall not be built anymore with that same dignity, elegance, and fame—indeed, not even in the same place where you were before. For that which was later restored in the same vicinity and called "Old Tyre" <note>Palaetyrus</note> was not a city, but a village, and it did not retain the city's splendor or even its traces. Thus Grotius says: You will not return to your former fortune. Indeed, according to Glassius's *Sacred Grammar* (page 779), certain words indicate not just their literal meaning but also a certain quality or condition. For example, "to speak" can mean to speak truly, sincerely, and from the soul (Proverbs 20:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3). "To commit sin" can imply the eagerness, readiness, and persistence in sinning (1 John 3:8, 9). "To see" can mean to see with delight (Psalm 35:21). Understood in this way, the words of the text apply both to the old city destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar and the new island-city of Tyre destroyed by Alexander; for neither, though both were rebuilt in some form, ever emerged again to their original dignity, fame, and size. Indeed, Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian</note> says that while verses 7 through 11 undoubtedly speak of what Nebuchadnezzar did, what is said in verses 12 through 14 need not necessarily be restricted to Nebuchadnezzar and that time alone. "And they will plunder," etc. (verse 12) is stated impersonally, unlike the preceding words which specifically designated who would do the acting. These things flow best if understood as being fulfilled across different times. It is also notable that when Tyre was cut down by Alexander, Thebes—the daughter of Tyre—was also destroyed by him. One might also ask about Carthage, her colony, and other cities; so that it was not only Nebuchadnezzar who killed her "daughters in the field" (verse 6). Maio, in his *Economy of the Old Testament* (page 1044), also says that the destruction by the Chaldeans first, and later by the Greeks, is predicted in this chapter. Abendana <note>Jacob Abendana (1630–1695) was a Sephardic rabbi and scholar</note> holds the same opinion. **verse 15. b)** "on account of the sound," Jeremiah 49:21. **c)** "the fall," or "your ruins," verse 18; chapter 27:26. Abendana specifically refers this to the devastation caused by Alexander. **d)** "when the pierced one groans," and they will tremble with consternation. Verse 10. **h)** "the island," and every maritime shore, or the inhabitants of the maritime regions. Verse 18; chapter 27:7, 15.

<column-break/>

**verse 11. c)** Isaiah 5, 28. **d)** "he will trample." Isaiah 1:12. **e)** Horsemen will run through the town. Compare Nahum 2:5. **f)** verses 6, 8. **g)** The variation in number in the verb notes a distribution of the action. Compare chapter 23:40; Judges 5:29; Isaiah 19:4; Hosea 6:5. "Your strength"; that is, according to Vatablus: statues erected in honor of brave citizens; or according to others, images of famous men by which they displayed the ancient nobility of their race. Grotius: statues erected by the Egyptians for the Kings and other allies of Tyre and enemies of the Chaldeans. For it is customary to cast down the images of those for whom things turn out unfortunately. Others say: statues of the gods, specifically Hercules and Apollo, whom they worshiped; compare Jeremiah 43:13; Hosea 10:2; Micah 5:13. These opinions may perhaps be well combined. **h)** "they will descend to the ground." It will collapse in pieces. Compare chapter 38:20; Isaiah 21:9; Amos 3:14; Lamentations 1:9.

<summary>This page analyzes the prophesied destruction of Tyre, detailing the horsemen's trampling of the city and the looting of its immense maritime wealth. It reconciles the prophecy that the city would "never be rebuilt" with history by suggesting Tyre never regained its former sovereign glory or original location after the Greek and Babylonian conquests.</summary>

**verse 16.) f)** They will surely descend, as in Isaiah 47:1 and Jeremiah 48:18. **k)** from their seat, in the manner of mourners as in Jonah 3:6. **l)** The Carthaginians, Gaditanians <note>People of Gades, modern-day Cádiz</note>, and others descended from Tyre, who were powerful at sea, according to Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and scholar</note>. **m)** chapter 27:31. **n)** their outer garments. referring to the city of Tyre

Cocceius: that is, those who by a heavy and severe rule held and restrained the entire city. For the inhabitants who are in power are distinguished from the rest of the inhabitants, who either live in the city or have the rights of that city in all its colonies. Therefore, for so magnificent a city, whose senators were equal to kings, to perish was miserable. **verse 18. f)** Why they will tremble, Genesis 42:28, 1 Kings 1:49. **g)** by the influx. 15. The ending is Chaldean. **h)** On the day, or in the day of your fall, verse 15, chapter 27:27. **i)** and they will be troubled, Ezekiel 15:15, 2 Samuel 4:1. **k)** because of your most sorrowful departure; your destruction and captivity. **verse 18.** Marsham, in his *Chronological Canon*, page 578, understands this as the departure of the Tyrians when they were driven from their ancient seat and migrated to the Island (where New Tyre was later built), on which see below at chapter 29:18. **verse 19. l)** When I shall give/make, chapter 32:15. **m)** you, Old Tyre <term>Palætyrus</term>, according to Gæsler, pages 306 and following. **n)** desolated, verse 2, chapter 30:7. **o)** which are not inhabited, or are inhabited no more, Jeremiah 22:6. Namely, that which you once were, according to Grotius. **i)** though you are sought, indeed, Psalm 37:36. Men will ask, where is that city now, which sent out so many colonies, which ruled so widely over the sea? according to Grotius. **k)** Isaiah 41:12, Daniel 11:19. What more? Marsham says in his *Chronological Canon*, page 578: Old Tyre was captured and cut off by Nebuchadnezzar, and never returned to its former royal dignity and fortune, etc. Regarding the mystical application of these verses, see Cocceius. **l)** chapter 11:8, 14:14. **CHAPTER XXVII. verse 1. m)** It happened further. The Prophet, living in Babylonia, continues in this chapter to prophesy against Tyre (not yet destroyed, according to Grotius, page 308; see note on verse 2, chapter 26:1). I. He describes its splendor regarding its magnificent buildings, naval affairs, and hired forces, verses 3-11. II. He recounts its market and trade with almost all nations, verses 12-25. And III. He deplores its great ruin and devastation, amplifying it through contrast, verses 26-36. **verse 2. n)** You also, like others in chapter 26:17. **o)** take up a lamentation over Tyre, verse 32, chapter 28:12. Cocceius: These things can indeed be understood regarding Tyre itself, whether when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it, or when Alexander the Great conquered and stormed it. They are, however, also to be understood regarding a certain center of trade of another kind, which is called both Tyre and Babylon, as is clear from Ezekiel 23:1 and following, and the parallel in Revelation 18:13, where the second part is used concerning Babylon, which had been said concerning Tyre in the prophecy of Ezekiel 23:8.

So the pupil of the eye is called the "daughter of the eye" in Psalm 17:8 and Lamentations 2:18, because it is in the eye. An arrow is the "son of the quiver" in which it is enclosed, Lamentations 3:13. He therefore reproaches the Tyrians for immense luxury, because in their naval matters they did not only use things for necessity or convenience, but even shone forth in luxury and delights, since they applied the most precious material, such as ivory (enclosed in boxwood), to the most common parts of the ships. Glassius, from Junius and Tremellius. v. 7. q) Byssus, or rather cotton. Compare Exodus 25:4. r) Or: in needlework, or with Phrygian work <note>elaborate embroidery</note>. v. 11. x) see b. b) Greek: the rest of your army. Latin: with your army, v. 10. Grotius says they were mixed with the city's soldiers. y) upon your walls. Concerning these, Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> says in book 17, chapter 43: "Soon the Tyrians, to make the walls twice as strong, leaving a five-cubit interval in the middle, built another wall ten cubits wide, and filled the empty space between both with stones and heaped earth." d) S. and the Gammadim. (z) That this is the proper name of an unknown nation (perhaps Phoenician) is clear from the connection of the preceding and following verses; since soldiers and foreign peoples are recounted; as Pfeiffer <note>August Pfeiffer (1640–1698), a German orientalist</note> correctly indicates regarding this difficult passage, and Ludolf in *Historical Commentary on Ethiopia* p. 73, 74. For as some interpret them as pygmies or "men a cubit long," others as robust or "strong-armed" men, or with Louis de Dieu <note>Dutch orientalist (1590–1642)</note> from the Syriac as "fierce and audacious men," these interpretations are either fabulous or forced. v. 12. l) due to the multitude of all resources, v. 18. m) Spain abounded in the metals listed here, and the silver in it was most beautiful, according to Pliny, book 33, chapter 6. Opposite Celtiberia are many islands called the Cassiterides by the Greeks, from their fertility in lead, Pliny book 4, chapter 22. q) they gave, they established your markets or trades. (r) verses 14, 16, 19, 22, 27. Gesenius p. 594: your exchanges, i.e., things which one leaves to another for a thing handed over in a contract of exchange. v. 13. f) Ionia. g) i.e., Ionians or Greeks v. 19. Joel 4:6. Named from Javan son of Japheth, Genesis 10:2. 1 Chronicles 1:5. See Bochart *Phaleg* book 3, chapter 3. s) Tubal and Meshech are mostly joined because of kinship, chapter 32:26. 38:2, 3. 39:1. Genesis 10:2. 1 Chronicles 1:5. Tubal are the Tibareni, Isaiah 66:19. Meshech are the Moschi, inhabiting the Moschian mountains, which divide Iberia from Armenia and both from Colchis. Thus Bochart *Phaleg* book 3, chapter 12. t) they were your shopkeepers, they did business with you. v. 15, chapter 17:4. Nahum 3:16. u) with the souls of men, i.e., slaves. Revelation 18:13. 1 Chronicles 5:21. Compare Numbers 31:35, 40. Bochart shows that slaves from Javan, i.e., Greek and Ionian, were in the highest price in the entire East. He also shows that in the regions of Pontus there were many slaves, especially in Cappadocia, of which Tibarenia is a part, and there slaves were once sold for four drachmas. v) most inhabitants were men born for slavery. x) and with vessels of Euboean bronze. Among the Tibareni were the Mossynoeci, whose bronze is praised as most splendid and white. But also in Iberia, part of which the Moschi hold, it is believed the bronze is the most excellent of all. y) which they gave in your commerce. v. 9. v. 14. x) from the house or region of Togarmah chapter 38:6. 1 Chronicles 1:6. i.e., from Cappadocia, as Bochart proves with many points. Indeed, the nobility of Cappadocian horses was always supreme, and likewise for their excellent mules and asses. a) common or work horses, and horsemen or military horses; for the word <term>סוס</term> <note>sus</note> signifies both. Others prefer simply: horses and horsemen. c) slaves who were suitable horsemen. b) 1 Kings 10:25. c) S. in your negotiations. See v. 12, 16. v. 15. d) Sons of Dedan. This is not the same Dedan as in Jeremiah 25:23, an Edomite city, but another Dedan founded by the son of Raamah, today called Daden, not far from the mouth of the Persian Gulf. Ezekiel is speaking of a maritime city with many neighboring islands, from which navigation to India was convenient: for among Indian goods are ivory and ebony, all of which fit Daden. e) v. 17, 22. f) for many islands v. 7. g) negotiation of your hand, i.e., your hands were merchant hands for goods. h) S. horn of ivory. For elephant teeth are considered horns by the ancients. Ludolf thinks the Ethiopians more correctly establish that they are horns of the elephant. See the reasons for both opinions in Bochart. Some call them teeth but acknowledge they have something in common with horns, arising from the skull and drawing nourishment from veins like horns. Others, like Jonah, interpret "horns and teeth" separately as ivory, but this does not fit the grammar well. i) and ebony wood. k) they returned to you in compensation. l) as your gift or price (2) Psalm 72:10. v. 16. m) v. 12. Syrians were great negotiators, as Jerome notes here. n) due to the multitude of your works; to acquire works made with great skill. o) with carbuncle or ruby, others say emerald. p) purple v. 7, 24. r) and fine linen (7) Esther 1:6. s) S. and Ramoth. (2) Job 28:18. Commonly thought to be a species of gem, others say coral; but Castell with Aquila, the Syriac and Arabic renders it "silk." t) and crystal. u) see v. 12, 19. v. 17. x) see Acts 12:20.

# EZEKIEL 27.
### CHAPTER 27.

->### 17 Judah and the land of Israel, they were your traders; with wheat of Minnith <note>original: "Minnit"</note> and Pannag, and honey, oil, and balm, they provided your merchandise.
18 Damascus was your merchant because of the multitude of your handiworks, from the multitude of all wealth, in wine of Helbon <note>original: "Chelbon"</note> and white wool.
19 Vedan and Javan from Uzal <note>original: "Me-Uzal"</note> traded in your wares; wrought iron, cassia, and sweet cane were in your exchange.
20 Dedan was your merchant in precious clothes for riding.
21 Arabia and all the princes of Kedar, they were the merchants of your hand; in lambs, rams, and goats, in these they were your merchants.

Therefore, Tyre is a very clear mirror of those who, though they have come close to the Church, nevertheless seek nothing else but profit, the splendor of life, vanity, and pleasure; and much more of those who, through the Word of God and the handling of spiritual things which they profess, seek to achieve nothing but profit and pleasure.

It was perhaps the same as Aleppo, as the Arabs call it today. That wine was so excellent that the Kings of Persia drank from no other. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* Part I, page 485. 17. **The same Bochart** says that the fame of *Damascene* wool still lasted in the time of Jerome <note>c. 347–420 AD, translator of the Vulgate</note>, who says of Tyre in this place: *To its markets were brought from Damascus the richest wine and choice wool, which we still see today.* But silk and cotton, which are the greatest products of Damascus today, have obscured the fame of its wool. *Ibid. p. 486.* **v. 19. n)** And Dan, that is, the Danites of Israel, Judges 18:29, chapter 20:1. But Grotius says: I believe Taprobane <note>the ancient name for Sri Lanka</note> is indicated here, that is, the island of Ceylon, fertile in fragrant reeds and other scents and not lacking in metals; in which there were cities like Dana and Joganna, etc. o) both wandering, a discourse for the sake of trading. (1) To others it is a proper name, as with Aquila <note>a 2nd-century translator</note> and the Syriac: from <unclear>Uzal</unclear>, which was the capital of the land of Yemen (as witnessed by Abraham Zacuto in the book *Yachasin*), taking its name from <unclear>Uzale</unclear>, the son of Joktan, Genesis 10:27, elsewhere called Sanaa; which could have been added by the prophet for the sake of distinction, lest it be thought to be about the Javanites who are commonly known, that is, the Greeks or Ionians. But the Schwa <note>a Hebrew vowel mark</note> under the letter Bet favors the former explanation, which also has the support of the Chaldean <note>the Aramaic Targum</note> (which translates it as "in groups" or "by caravans") and more recent Hebrew scholars, and even Symmachus <note>another ancient translator</note> among the Greeks. It is therefore the part of a prudent man to embrace either interpretation so as not to exclude the other. Bochart, *Phaleg* 2. 21. Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmid (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian</note>, however, has "going." So says Rashi <note>a famous 11th-century Jewish commentator</note>. p) in leaving they gave to themselves. verses 2, 25.
