k) The Septuagint: "Ships of Tarshish, your troops"; or "coming in troops" were in your market. So the Vatican [manuscript]: "your troops," that is, they went to you in troops for the sake of trading. This is undoubtedly from the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> *shiyara* or *sharah*, meaning a company, army, or troop. Others, however, more simply from the literal meaning of the word, render it: "those singing or praising you." 2 Samuel 19:36.
l) on account of your trade, see verse 9. But Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch Hebraist</note> in his Commentary says: "The ships of Tarshish hold your singers and your merchandise"; so that the joy of the Tyrians poured itself out over the whole sea, and their pleasure came from the whole world, with the Tyrians holding the power over all negotiation.
m) from which you were filled with riches and honors. see chapter 26:2.
n) and honored, or "made glorious." Isaiah 66:5. Job 24:21. Or "rich and opulent," as if you were made heavy or burdened with goods. compare Genesis 13:2, chapter 31:1, chapter 50:9.
o) see verses 4 and 26. Thus far regarding the power and glory of Tyre; the description of which was drawn out more broadly so that the calamity which followed it might now be more rightly estimated and magnified. It shows that those things which cities tend to love most are of no value and mere vanity, having no other final fruit than weeping and wailing.

<header>CHAPTER 27 & 28. Ezekiel 27, 28</header>

<margin>
o) and your merchandise. v. 9, 13, 17, 25.
p) dispersed (Genesis 14:23), namely from the taxes according to Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian</note>.
q) Kings of the earth (Psalm 2:2, 148:11; Lamentations 4:12 according to Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century theologian</note>).
Here and in the following verses, a comparison is made between the time of abundance, in which the city enriched kings, and the time of its destruction, accompanied by the horror of those same kings, etc.
</margin>

v. 34. r) In the time, indeed, when you were broken—that is, when you were shattered and submerged by the waves of the sea. See v. 26; 1 Kings 22:49; Jonah 1:4; and similar passages; compare Jeremiah 49:8, 50:31, 51:33.
s) In the depths <note>original: "in profunditatibus"</note> of the waters (Psalm 130:1).

u) v. 27.

Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian</note> in book 4, chapter 4, writes: Alexander ordered all to be killed except those who had fled to the temples, and commanded fire to be set to the houses. Then, the anger of the King provided a sad spectacle for the victors. Two thousand men, whose slaughter had exhausted the soldiers' rage, hung fixed to crosses along a vast stretch of the shore.

<margin>
v. 35. y) All the inhabitants of the maritime regions and islands (v. 3, 7, 15).
z) they were stunned, or "stunned on account of you." Chapter 26:16; compare Zechariah 9:5, 6.
"They were saddened/gloomy" <note>original Greek: "ἐστύγνασαν"</note>. Mark 10:22; Matthew 16:3.
a) and the kings themselves, compare v. 33.

...of Tyre. (See v. 12, compared with chapter 21:30; 2 Samuel 6:21, 7:8, etc.) Specifically, this refers to Ithobaal II <note>A king of Tyre who reigned during the siege by Nebuchadnezzar</note> according to Grotius. For under him, Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years, as Josephus reports from the Phoenician annals in his first book *Against Apion*, page 1046. Marsham, in his *Chronicus Canon*, page 579, thinks he perished from the prophet's curses, understanding everything as referring to Old Tyre—though others refer these things partly to the island city and partly to a "mystical" Tyre. Gurtlerus, however, in his *Prophetic Theology*, page 308 (as we said regarding chapter 26:1), takes this chapter to refer to the restored Christian Tyre which was captured by the Saracens, and applies several of its verses there; but this seems to us to be by accommodation only. Cocceius, on this passage, says the King of Tyre was a glorious evaluator and admirer of himself, boasting in his own prosperity and that of his city; he was thus fit to become a type and hieroglyphic symbol of one who turns the Church into a marketplace and wishes to reign in it, calling himself the Vicar of God, etc. Compare especially the notes on Isaiah 6:9, chapter 24:1, and 23:1, and Cocceius himself, who most diligently pursues the mystical sense of this chapter, while we study to illustrate the literal and immediate sense.
m) Because of this (chapter 15:8).
n) you have lifted up your heart (v. 5, 17; 2 Chronicles 26:16; Daniel 5:20).
o) so that you say or think (v. 9; chapter 29:3).
p) as if I myself were some god, like Isaiah 14:14 or Acts 12:22.
q) literally: in the habitation; others: in the seat of God—that is, in an inaccessible place, surrounded and fortified by the sea, which no one can harm. Grotius: Just as God is safe from all injury in the heavenly citadel, so the sea defends me. compare 2 Thessalonians 2:4.
r) chapter 27:4, 25, 26.
s) since you are nevertheless a man, subject to every human fate. Isaiah 31:3; compare Daniel 5:20.

u) even though you have set or considered (Genesis 42:30) your heart—that is, your proud mind. compare Obadiah v. 3; 2 Chronicles 25:19.
x) v. 6. While you thought yourself equal to God in wisdom, power, and command over all: as if all things ought to obey you.

v. 3. y) An absolute declaration: "Behold, you are wiser than Daniel"—namely, in your own opinion. So say Vatablus, Grotius, etc. Others read it as a question, following the Septuagint and the Syriac. But the sense is: "As if you were wise before Daniel; they have not hidden from you." Compare Sirach 8:11; Romans 11:15.
z) whose fame, on account of the extraordinary gifts of wisdom received from God, was then celebrated. Compare chapter 14:14 and Daniel 1:7, 2:48, 4:6, 5:1, 6:27.

...mass of wealth, wisdom, glory, and all happiness, such that nothing more seems possible to be added; you possess all things so perfectly and consummately. Others: "sealer of the sum," namely both of the merchandise to be exported and the taxes to be paid to you, and whatever else is of that kind—so says Junius. Cocceius, however, in his *Lexicon* page 273 and *Commentary*: "sealer of the measure," or "signing the measure," with an allusion to the custom of the marketplace. For in marketplaces it belongs to the supreme power to seal measures and coins. Some manuscripts read **חותם** with a *Kamets* in this sense: "you were a signet ring of this form" or "excellently formed," that is, you were most diligently guarded, like a splendid ring of great artistry. So says Grotius, comparing Jeremiah 22:24. t) **the sum,** or the measured amount (z) chapter 43:10. See chapter 45:11. u) **full of wisdom.** See verses 3-4. Namely in your political art, and those things which pertained to the order and splendor of your city and its preservation. x) **and perfect in beauty** and splendor, chapter 27:3. v) 13. y) **In Eden,** as if in a most pleasant region. Genesis 2:8. z) **of the garden of God:** or rather "indeed you were in the garden of God, or paradise," as if in Genesis 2:8, even though you lived in the middle of the sea. That is, according to Jonathan, Kimchi, Rashi, and Michlal Yophi: all things flowed to you; whatever pertained either to necessity or utility, or even pleasure, was abundant; as formerly for Adam in the Garden of Eden, which God had granted to him. In Cocceius's judgment, these things cannot be understood literally of the King of Tyre, but most excellently of the spiritual king of Tyre <note>often interpreted as a reference to the fall of a celestial being</note>; wherefore he also accommodates all things to that. We, however, think the literal sense concerning the King of Tyre should be entirely retained along with other interpreters, not rejecting the mystical sense, which you may see more extensively in Cocceius and others. a) chapter 27:12. b) **is your trial or your covering** (1). That is, according to Grotius and others: "the garments that cover you," or according to others: "the tent or canopy" (under which you, the King, sat) was adorned or interwoven with precious stones or gems of every kind. c) **Or the Ruby.** See the Septuagint: **Sardius.** (3) See Exodus 28:17ff, chapter 39:10ff, where besides the nine kinds of gems which are listed here, three others are found in the breastplate of the High Priest. d) **Or Topaz.** (4) Job 28:19. e) **Or Diamond.** (2) Exodus 28:18. f) **Chrysolite.** Others: **Beryl.** See chapter 1:16, Song of Solomon 5:14. g) **Or Sardonyx.** Genesis 2:12, Job 28:16. h) **And Jasper.** (3) Exodus 28:20. i) **Sapphire.** See chapter 1:26. k) **Or Chrysoprase.** Others: **Emerald.** (4) chapter 27:16. l) **And Carbuncle.** Or **Emerald.** (3) Exodus 28:17. m) **And gold** chapter 27:22. Junius: "you were so softly bound about that the gold was (only) an addition"; which is therefore named in the last place. But others count gold among the gems, because we think it is included with gold as they are usually adorned. So Jonathan simply renders it: "immersed or dyed in gold." For the antitype see Revelation 17:4. n) **the workmanship of your tambourines.** Isaiah 5:12, chapter 24:8. That is, your most laborious and artistic instruments, which he describes here synecdochically <note>using a part to represent the whole</note> through two types: namely those which are struck or those which are blown. — Junius. o) **and of your pipes.** (1) p) **in** or **with you.** See chapter 10:15, "in the river," that is, "by the river," etc. q) **in the day** and "from the day" in which you were created, or formed in the womb and brought into the light, verse 15, chapter 21:35. r) **were already prepared** for your delight or for singing. Psalm (2) 37:23. s) 14. s) **You.** Written in the feminine form out of contempt; or rather through shortening (Apocope). See note on Numbers 11:15. t) **as if you were a Cherub.** See above chapter 10:14 and chapter 1:10. u) **of anointing,** or as "that anointed work" (1). See Exodus 30:26. Schmidt: "the magnificent expansion of the covering one": perhaps because the Chaldean and Syriac root also means "he measured" or "he proportioned." x) **covering** verse 16. As the Cherubim covered the Ark, Exodus 25:10-20, Nahum 2:6. There seems to be an allusion to the Cherubim of the Sanctuary covering the Ark, and that in the holy mountain of God, in the place of the Oracle: and these are in the same system of things as the sparkling stones of the breastplate of judgment. — Gusset page 555. See also Glassius page 1684ff. But Cocceius's *Lexicon* page 453: "The wall of the covering; a wall built by men so that you might be a covering." Whom men hold in the place of Christ, who is the shield of the Church, and for him, through whom and out of whose will God is known, and His light and grace perceived. See also ibid. page 392, 565ff. y) **and I placed [you],** I established, I had established you in such dignity. See verse 17, Genesis 17:5, 6. z) **so that you were as if on the holy mountain of God.** Just as those Cherubim were upon the holy mountain of Zion in the inner sanctuary of the temple, so you were in a place that seemed inaccessible to all force. — Grotius. Maius, *Economy of the Old Testament* page 1044, thus: "It is easily gathered from this that this prophecy also extends to times far in the future, in which the Tyrians could be said to have been on the mountain of God and were to be driven out from there." See what we observed at Isaiah 21. a) **and as if in the midst of stones of fire,** that is, "fiery" or "bright and shining" like fire, verse 16. Such were those which were included in the High Priest's breastplate. See verse 13.

The text identifies the king with a "covering cherub" and lists the precious stones of his "Eden," while philological notes debate the precise meaning of Hebrew terms for jewelry and musical instruments.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER 28. EZEKIEL 28</header>

<margin>
r) Obedient *Cherub*: verse 14.
s) Verse 14.
*. 17 s) For your mind was proud. verses 2, 5; chapter 31, 10.
n) because of your beauty, verses 7, 12. x) you corrupted, you misused [it]. Amos 1:11; compare above chapter 23:11. y) verses 5, 7. The heart of one who is truly wise does not exalt itself because of the goods of this world. — Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a major medieval Jewish commentator</note>. z) because of his splendor (z) verse 7. a) therefore I have cast you to the ground. Jeremiah 22:19. b) compare 1 Kings 8:46. c) I gave, delivered, exposed you. 1 Samuel 1:16. d) for looking upon you; according to Kimchi, this means being "disfigured and stripped of royalty."
</margin>

<margin>
c) *that you might walk* chapter 19:6. Everything in your palace shone not only with gold, but also with the most brilliant gems. Others: *you walked clothed in a garment adorned with brilliant gems*, like the High Priest of the Israelites; but Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch scholar</note>: Just as the High Priest approached the *Cherubim* with 12 flashing stones; so also those who were around you entered with equal adornment. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a theologian known for "covenant theology"</note> indeed interprets this concerning the Antitype <note>the future fulfillment of a symbol</note>: i.e., you walked in the midst of living stones 1 Peter 2:5.
V. 15. d) Perfect, upright (Grotius: perfectly happy), namely among men. Genesis 6:9. e) In [this way] you once were the King of Tyre. f) in your ways and actions, chapter 18:30, establishing wisely adorned things, and with most happy success, holding the path of virtue for a while. g) from the time you were formed, verse 13. h) until it was found, discovered. Jeremiah 2:26. i) greatest perversity, of which see the following verse; compare chapter 26:2. The noun is masculine in verse 18 with a paragogic [added] suffix as in Hosea 10:3, Psalm 92:16, Psalm 125:3.
V. 16. k) Syriac: For through the abundance of your trade, verse 5. l) your citizens or merchants filled the midst of you, i.e., of your city. Similar verb form in chapter 39:26, 1 Samuel 6:10. Syriac: they were filled in the midst of you. Grotius: your inner parts were filled. m) chapter 7:23, 8:17, Genesis 6:11. n) chapter 14:13, since you could easily have made a profit from righteous commerce. Münster <note>Sebastian Münster, a 16th-century German cartographer and Hebraist</note>: Since this was not fulfilled after the Babylonian captivity, when the Jews suffered many tribulations, it is established that it is perfectly fulfilled through Christ—not in the body, since his followers still groan, but in the spirit, which cries out Abba, Father. Thus Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a Jewish convert to Christianity and influential Bible translator</note> likewise notes that this refers to the peace and tranquility of the church of God, begun through the gospel, and to be completed at the second coming of Christ. For this is a gospel promise and properly pertains to the church of Christ, which was prefigured by the ancient church, even though the matter itself is taught and explained through the symbol of the land and allegorical words.

1 In the tenth year, in the tenth month, on the twelfth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying:
2 Son of man, set your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and prophesy against him and against all Egypt.
3 Speak and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great monster that lies in the midst of his streams, that says, "My Nile is my own; I made it for myself."

CHAPTER XXIX, 1. *l) In the tenth year* of the exile of Jehoiachin. chapter 1:2. This was two months before those prophecies concerning Tyre (chapters 26–28), and sixteen years before the one which follows in verse 17, which is connected here immediately because of the similarity of the subject. **Grotius:** These prophecies are arranged not by timing, but by nations; and they begin with those closer to the land of Judah. **Lightfoot** notes in *Chronicle of the Old Testament*, page 125, that Ezekiel prophesies this at a most opportune time: when the pride of Egypt had reached its peak, and those in Jerusalem had placed their trust in it. For now Pharaoh had come forth (or was about to come forth) with all his strength to relieve the siege of Jerusalem, and all of Jerusalem's hope rested upon him. Therefore, at this very time, he announces destruction for Egypt, and for the Jews, the frustration of their hope. compare verse 6. *m)* in the tenth month. chapter 33:21; Genesis 8:5. *n)* on the twelfth day. Ezra 8:31. *o)* chapter 1:3, etc. There are truly two prophecies in this chapter against Pharaoh and Egypt (verse 2). I. Concerning the slaughter and devastation of the Egyptians by the Cyrenean kings and then the Chaldeans, verses 3–12, with some restoration for both under Cyrus, verses 13–16. II. Concerning Nebuchadnezzar, who would receive Egypt as a reward for the destruction of Tyre, verses 17–21. This prophecy against Egypt continues through the following chapters 30, 31, and 32, through five more prophecies; they are arranged more by the logic of the subject matter than by time, the sequence of which Ezekiel occasionally neglects by deliberate design to look toward the connection of arguments, as we have already said and is easily seen from the sequence of the chapters themselves. Compare also **Rashi** <note>Shlomo Yitzchaki, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note>, who observes the same at verse 17. **v. 2. p)** chapter 6:2; chapter 25:2. *q)* this Pharaoh is called *Hophra* (in secular writings *Apries*) in Jeremiah 44:30. He was very successful for many years, according to Herodotus (Book II, p. 97). He carried himself with such pride that he thought no kingdom of gods or men could take his own away from him, as Herodotus explicitly relates (p. 98); he seemed to have established it so firmly for himself. see here verse 3. Although according to others, the prophet here by the name "Pharaoh" perhaps denotes not just one, but several kings of Egypt following in order, as these names are often taken collectively. Compare notes at verse 17; Isaiah 19:1, 2, etc. **v. 3. r)** behold I will be, or, I will rise against you. verse 10; chapter 13:8, 20; chapter 26:3; chapter 28:22. *s)* see verse 2 and what is about to be said. *t)* **dragon**, or rather, a crocodile. <term>great</term> chapter 32:2; Psalm 74:13; Isaiah 27:1; chapter 51:9. **Bochart** <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar of biblical animals</note>: This is not a *whale* in this place, as some wish. For a whale has neither feet nor scales, nor does it dwell in the rivers of Egypt, nor does it ascend from there onto land, nor is it surrounded by a snare of nets; yet all these things are attributed here to the *Thannim* <note>the Hebrew word for monster/dragon</note>. From this it is plain that a whale is not meant, but a Crocodile, which **Scaliger** writes is numbered among the cetaceous fish. Thus it is also called *Leviathan* by Job, with a full and accurate description of it in chapters 40 and 41. (Bochart, *Hieroz.* Part I, p. 52 and Part II, p. 795), where he adds: It is not for nothing that the comparison of Pharaoh with a crocodile is so extensively drawn. The very name of Pharaoh is alluded to here; we learn from Arabic that it signifies a *crocodile*. And so the Prophet would be saying: You, Pharaoh, who enjoy a common name with the crocodile, shall also have a lot equal to the crocodile, which is caught by an iron hook or entangled in iron nets, and thus, willing or unwilling, is dragged from the river to its death. To others, *Pharaoh* in Coptic or Egyptian signifies *King*; **Josephus** <note>1st-century Jewish historian</note> follows this in *Antiquities* Book 8, chapter 2: "Pharaoh among the Egyptians signifies king" <note>original Greek: ὁ Φαραὼν κατ’ αἰγυπτίους βασιλέα σημαίνει</note>. **Hiller**, however, in *Onomasticon Sacrum* (p. 673 and 908), suggests "Vengeance" or "Avenger of Wrath" from Hebrew; or "Dreaded Prince of the people" from an Arabic idiom, following Paul in Romans 13:3, 4. Thus the word would be transferred to the crocodile because it was, as it were, the king among the aquatic creatures of the rivers of Egypt. See Noldius, *Concordance*, p. 989. *u)* crouching, you who lie down. chapter 19:2; Genesis 4:7; chapter 49:9. **Ammianus Marcellinus** says of the crocodile: *resting harmlessly through the waves, by day it feeds on the ground*. Compare Psalm 68:31. *x)* in the midst of his rivers. verse 4. **Vatablus** <note>François Vatable, a French scholar</note>: He understands the Nile (see Genesis 41:1; Exodus 1:22; chapter 7:17, 18), whose waters were distributed into many parts through trenches or streams diverted here and there; and with the Nile, he understands Egypt, because the whole land was washed and enriched by the Nile. But **Cocceius**: He understands not so much the river as the people drinking the Nile, just as the Babylonians are understood by the Euphrates in Isaiah 8:7. It is a metaphorical thing to compare a people with a flood. compare Revelation 17:15. *y)* chapter 28:2. *z)* the river is mine, supplying all things to me in abundance; which no one will dare or be able to take from me or claim for themselves. compare verse 9; chapter 35:10; and the note above at verse 2.

Scholars debate the identity of the "great monster" mentioned in the text, concluding it refers to the Nile crocodile as a symbol of Pharaoh's pride.</summary>

<margin>
a) **I have made it for myself**, etc. That great [river], according to Vatablus, Tigurinus, Piscator, etc. <note>various Reformation-era biblical scholars</note>—namely, so that it might water my region, and that by my own industry and wisdom. Others, however, like Cocceius and Schmidt, following the Vulgate, translate: **he made me**, meaning the King. So Jonathan <note>the Targum</note> in this place and verse 9: "This kingdom (Egypt) is mine, and I have subjugated it." Cocceius says: He thinks of himself in such a way as if he were not a creature of God, but owed his power, his kingdom, and his future state to himself. Compare chapter 28:2; Numbers 13:22; Isaiah 19:11, etc. Regarding (spiritual) Egypt (Revelation 11:8), of which this is a type, see the same Cocceius on this whole chapter.

* v. 4. b) Standard: **Therefore I will put hooks** (Hebrew: *chach*) chapter 19:4, by means of very powerful enemies, specifically Amasis. Amasis, after Hophra (or Apries, see verse 2) was cast down by a rebellion and eventually strangled, obtained the kingdom. See Herodotus in the place cited above at verse 2, and Diodorus Siculus, *Library of History*, Book 1, page 62. Junius <note>Francis Junius, a Huguenot scholar</note> summarizes the matter from these authors thus: The Cyrenaeans, relying on auxiliary Greek troops, had occupied neighboring Libya and stripped King Adricanus of his domain. He fled to Pharaoh Apries for protection. Apries gathered a large army, not of foreigners but of Egyptians, and so nearly exhausted his own people who clung to him like smaller fish resting in the shadow of a whale (crocodile); he led them into the Cyrenaean territory, where nearly all perished, the King narrowly escaping with a few in a shameful flight. Therefore, the offended Egyptians—thinking the King, by an insane plan, was attempting to establish a terrible tyranny over the remaining commoners by destroying the Egyptian soldiers—rose up against him.

26. d) **and I will cause to stick** <note>original Latin: agglutinabo</note>, to make adhere. See chapter 3:26; Jeremiah 13:11. Jonathan translates this to the end of the verse as: "and I will kill the princes of your strength with their mighty ones, and I will deprive you of the kingdom; and all the princes of your strength with their mighty ones shall be killed." e) **your scales**. 1 Samuel 17:5. I interpret the words thus: I will cause you to conscript an army throughout your whole kingdom and lead them out against enemies, but with an unhappy outcome. For when you come into the desert with your troops (v. 5), I will strengthen your enemies there so that they may destroy them with slaughter. See Suilar, *Prophetic Theology*, page 246 ff. f) **I will cause you to go up**, or I will extract you. Habakkuk 1:15. **from your rivers** (v. 3), that is, I will cast you out and strip you of your kingdom. Grotius: "I will take away all dignity from you." g) **So that every fish... clings**, or: "and indeed with every fish that will cling to your scales." For a similar construction of the particle **את** <note>et - the Hebrew direct object marker</note>, see 2 Kings 6:5; Nehemiah 9:19, 32; Joshua 22:17.

\* v. 5. h) **But I will abandon [you]** after being led away and cast out. Chapter 32:4; Isaiah 2:6. i) **into the dry desert**, as the marginal reading <note>Qere</note> says (Jeremiah 31:2), where fish cannot live. The metaphor is continued. Junius: "I will expose you and yours in the Cyrenaean and Libyan desert, like a fisherman exposes fish in a fish market, deserted and as prey." k) **you, I say, and &c.** l) that is, your troops. Jonathan, as in verse 4: "all the princes of your strength." m) Chapter 32:4. n) **you shall fall**, you shall be cut down. Chapter 39:5. That is, your army shall fall. A <term>synecdoche</term> <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note>. For otherwise, Apries himself returned to Egypt and was imprisoned and finally strangled. For this reason, Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius, a Lutheran theologian</note> thinks this refers more correctly to the slaughter of Pharaoh Necho (mentioned in Jeremiah 46:2). But that had already happened in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and thus at least 17 years before this prophecy. And if it is not permitted to take this as referring to the buried corpses of Apries' soldiers, certainly Apries' rival and successor Amasis lacked a burial, according to Herodotus (Book 3, chapter 16). See Gataker <note>Thomas Gataker, English scholar</note>, page 249. o) **you shall not be gathered**. Jeremiah 8:2. p) **nor shall you be collected** chapter 39:17. Vatablus: i.e., according to Jonathan, "you shall not be buried." But Grotius: "you shall not return to the river." Junius: "no troop from the remains of that army can be reunited." Compare Joshua 10:6; 1 Samuel 7:6. q) **for to the beasts of the earth** chapter 32:4. r) 1 Samuel 17:46. s) Chapter 39:4. The meaning: I have given power to fierce and predatory men to strip you of your kingdom, freedom, goods, and finally your life. Grotius. Compare chapter 34:28. **v. 6. s)** **That they may know** v. 10, 16; chapter 17:24. u) Who alone can accomplish all things, while Pharaoh can do nothing. x) Because they were a **staff of reed**, namely a broken one, as Jonathan adds. Compare 2 Kings 18:21—too weak to sustain and help them. Grotius: This is a proverbial expression, fitting for those who harm the ones they ought to benefit. Thus the King, with that boastful pride (v. 3), deceived those who relied on him, just as a reed staff [pierces] those who lean on it. Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, medieval Jewish commentator</note>: The Egyptians were not a support and help to the Israelites, except only for a very little while (for a short time), see Jeremiah 37:5 ff., and for that reason they did them harm instead; for out of trust in the Egyptians, they rebelled against the King of Babylon.

**v. 7. y)** Standard: **For when they held (grasped)** you with the hand; or according to the written text <note>Kethiv</note>, **with your hand**, chapter 30:21; Isaiah 3, 6. When the Jews, conscious of their weakness, procured these allies for themselves. Junius. z) **you are shattered**. Schmidt: "you were shattered." 2 Kings 18:21. You did not provide the promised help to them. a) But rather you made the Jews' situation worse, and you pierced [them], chapter 13:11. b) **the whole side**. Schmidt, v. 18. Grotius: i.e., by synecdoche, "the whole arm." Fragments of a reed are usually sharp; and so, while they work their way into the shoulders or forearms, they wound severely. Vatablus. c) Standard: **and when they leaned** with their whole body. Compare Judges 16:26; Isaiah 10:20; chapter 31:1; Job 8:15; 2 Chronicles 16:7. d) **you made them stand (and labor or serve)**. Compare 1 Kings 22:35; Isaiah 21:6; 1 Chronicles 22:2. Or according to others, ironically: **you thus strain for them** (compare above chapter 2:2; 3:24) **all their loins**, so that there is no help for them from you, but the entire burden of the war finally falls back on them. Rashi, Kimchi, M. I., and Gusset (page 617) lean that way. Grotius: Allegorical meaning: you were the destruction for the Israelites who expected help from you. See the event in 2 Kings 24:7; Jeremiah 37:7; chapter 42:17; chapter 43:10. Others, according to Kimchi, by transposition of letters read "and you make them stagger." Compare Psalm 69:24. e) Compare the place cited and Psalm 66:11. **v. 8. f)** Chapter 26:7. g) First Amasis, or the civil wars (see v. 4), then also the weapons of Nebuchadnezzar, v. 19; Jeremiah 42:16. h) Chapter 21:8. i) Chapter 14:13, 17. Grotius: many men, and many animals.

**v. 9. k)** Standard: **That it may become.** l) Standard: **a solitude**. Jeremiah 12:11; Joel 4:19. m) and **a waste or a desert**. Compare chapter 36:35.

# EZEKIEL. Chapter 29.

<margin>
v. 6, 16. o) Schmidt <note>Erasmus Schmidt, a 17th-century scholar</note> says: "therefore, I say, because." p) **the river is mine**. see v. 3.
v. 10. q) Schmidt says: "therefore then." r) Schmidt says: "behold I am against you" from v. 3 and chapter 30:22. s) Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note>: "and against your kingdoms." See v. 3. t) v. 12; chapter 25:5. u) Schmidt: "into wastes," chapter 36:4. It is constructed here as in Jeremiah 49:13. x) **of waste** (Ezekiel 6:14). **of desolation** Ezekiel 12:20. That is: the greatest and most horrendous desolation. A superlative formed by combining synonyms. Compare chapter 21:15. y) **from the tower of Seveneh** <note>original: Sevenes</note> or **Syene**, chapter 30:6, which everyone knows was a city and the furthest boundary of Egypt toward Ethiopia, which the name itself signifies. See Hiller’s *Onomasticon Sacrum*, p. 672. Hence Stephanus says: "it is a city of Egypt and Ethiopia, as if wavering between them." See more in Bochart’s *Phaleg*, book 4, chapter 2, p. 239, citing Strabo, Pliny, Solinus, and Josephus. z) 1 Chronicles 1:8; Nahum 3:9. **Cush** <note>usually translated as Ethiopia</note> as a boundary of Egypt opposite Syene cannot be Ethiopia (as the Vulgate and others assume here and elsewhere). Rather, it is entirely necessary to understand it as Arabia, which borders the part of Egypt most distant from Ethiopia. This was the opinion of Bochart in the place cited. Contrary to Hiller in *Onomasticon Sacrum*, p. 656. **From Migdol to Syene**, that is, to the border of Ethiopia. **Migdol** or **Magdalum** was a city of Egypt to which the Jews from Jerusalem fled from the Chaldeans, Jeremiah 44:1, 46:14; it was not far from the Red Sea and served as the northern boundary of Egypt, just as Syene was the southern. Those learned in Hebrew know that the "and" <note>the Hebrew letter Vav</note> can be taken to mean "that is," etc.
v. 11. a) Schmidt: "So that it does not pass through it," compare chapter 14:14. b) This is to be understood either in part or comparatively; namely, that in regions suitable for trade, as Egypt was, people—whether out of concern or for the purpose of business—usually flock to them freely. c) Schmidt.
</margin>

<margin>
e) Schmidt: "it shall not be inhabited." Jonathan, the Septuagint, Cocceius, and Tremellius <note>Reformation-era biblical translators</note>: "it shall [not] be inhabited." chapter 36:20; Zechariah 9:5. d) **40 years.** v. 12, 13. This is therefore the Prophet's clearest prophecy concerning the desolation of Egypt for 40 years; but to show its fulfillment from secular history is not so easy. This is because Herodotus <note>the Greek historian</note> has little or nothing sound regarding Egyptian affairs of this age, and he primarily records those things which he received from lying priests who were eager for the praise of their nation and who...
</margin>

> 9 And they shall know<sup>o</sup> that I am the LORD, because he said, "The river<sup>p</sup> is mine, and I have made it."
> 10 Therefore,<sup>q</sup> behold, I am against you<sup>r</sup> and against your rivers, and I will give the land of Egypt over to ruins,<sup>s</sup> to parched<sup>t</sup> desolation,<sup>u</sup> from Migdol<sup>y</sup> to Syene even unto the border of Cush<sup>z</sup> <note>Ethiopia/Arabia</note>.
> 11 No foot of man<sup>a</sup> shall pass through it, and no foot of beast shall pass through it;<sup>b</sup> it shall not be inhabited<sup>c</sup> for forty years<sup>d</sup>.
> 12 And I will make the land of Egypt a desolation<sup>e</sup> in the midst of desolated lands,<sup>f</sup> and her cities<sup>g</sup> in the midst of ruined cities<sup>h</sup> shall be a desolation<sup>i</sup> for forty years;<sup>k</sup> and I will scatter Egypt among the nations and disperse them through the lands<sup>l</sup>.
> 13 For thus says the Lord GOD: At the end of forty years<sup>m</sup> I will gather Egypt from the peoples where they were scattered<sup>n</sup>.
> 14 And I will restore the captivity<sup>o</sup> of Egypt and return them to the land of Pathros,<sup>p</sup> to the land of their origin;<sup>q</sup> and they shall be there a lowly kingdom<sup>r</sup>.
> 15 It shall be the lowliest<sup>s</sup> of the kingdoms, and it shall not exalt itself<sup>t</sup> any more<sup>u</sup> over the nations; for I will diminish them<sup>x</sup> so that they do not rule over the nations<sup>y</sup>.
> 16 And it shall no longer<sup>z</sup> be a confidence<sup>a</sup> for the house of Israel, bringing iniquity to remembrance<sup>b</sup> when they turn<sup>c</sup> after them.

---

...wrapped shameful misfortunes in silence, as Gürtler observes in *Theologia Prophetica*, p. 244. Jeremiah the prophet, however, circumscribes the desolation of Egypt (which he predicted often, noting also that it would be inhabited again, chapter 46:26) within the times of the Babylonian Kings. Just as he indicated in chapter 25:11-12, the nations to be delivered to the Babylonian King (among whom were the Egyptians, v. 19) were not to serve him beyond 70 years. Whether you trace the beginning of these 40 years from Nebuchadnezzar's invasion of Egypt (discussed below at v. 17 and following), or with others from that foul Cyrenaic slaughter (which according to Visser, around 3130 A.M., preceded Nebuchadnezzar's arrival by only three years) and the internal war between Amasis and Apries that followed it—by which regions are most devastated—the end of those 40 years nearly coincides with the end of the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity and the beginnings of Cyrus. Compare Gürtler, cited above, p. 242-247.

v. 12. e) **I will give therefore**, etc. v. 10. f) chapter 12:20; 14:15. g) That is: I will render Egypt desolated, as other regions are desolated, chapter 30:7. h) **wasted**, chapter 26:2. i) See note on v. 11. k) Schmidt: "moreover scattered, I will disperse," chapter 30:23, 26. l) **and I will scatter them** into various regions, chapter 5:2, 6:8, into which they will both be snatched away as captives by enemies and betake themselves out of fear of war.

v. 13. m) **From the end** finally of the 40 years. v. 11, 12. n) where they were dispersed. v. 12.

v. 14. o) **And I will bring back the captivity** or the captives. chapter 16:50; Jeremiah 48:47. p) **into the land of Pathros.** chapter 30:14. Which Nebuchadnezzar had especially struck, as is clear from what is read in Nahum 3:10 concerning the city of No-Amon, which is the Great Diospolis or **Thebes** (Hiller however says Memphis, *Onomasticon Sacrum*, p. 571 ff.), the capital of the region of Pathros, that is, the **Thebaid**. Bochart, *Phaleg*, book 4, chapter 27. Compare note on Ezekiel 11:11. q) **of their formation**, origin, or elsewhere their pilgrimage or habitation. r) <note>Greek: in the land from which they were taken</note>. Schmidt: "of their trade," see chapter 16:3 and 21:35; and compare Jeremiah 46:26. r) **so that they may be a humble kingdom there**, v. 15; compare chapter 17:14. Not rising to its former dignity and power, with the empire of the Chaldeans and then the Persians prevailing. Amasis himself, who succeeded after Apries was killed (as we said at v. 4), and who undoubtedly held the kingdom as a trusted vassal under Nebuchadnezzar (for Herodotus writes he reigned 44 years and Diodorus Siculus 55 years, reaching the times of Cambyses), shows how lowly he judged the height of the Egyptian scepter compared to the Persian. The same Herodotus (Book 3, chapter 1) says: Amasis neither dared to give his daughter to Cambyses as a wife, nor to refuse. For he understood that Cambyses would not keep her as a wife, but as a concubine; and he was weighed down by and dreaded the power of the Persians. See Gürtler, p. 247. It did indeed grow later, as Munster notes, into a great kingdom under the Ptolemies; but it was not independent <note>original: "of its own right"</note>, as it obeyed the Greeks and finally the Romans.

v. 15. s) **Above other kingdoms.** t) It will be lowly for a long time. See note on v. 14. u) **nor shall it lift up**, exalt itself. chapter 17:14. x) **For I will diminish them.** Jeremiah 10:24. y) Schmidt: "so that they do not rule over the nations." Compare Isaiah 14:6.

v. 16. z) Schmidt: "So it shall not be." a) **into a deceptive confidence.** Schmidt: "refuge." Compare v. 6, 7; Proverbs 25:19. Thus the end of the preceding judgments is the calling away of the Church from confidence in human things to the most certain faith in God. Compare Proverbs 14:26; chapter 18:10. b) **which may remind me of iniquity**, chapter 21:28. This is the reason why God is mindful of the other crimes of the Israelites. Vatablus. c) **while they look back**, turn themselves after them, expecting help from them. Compare Psalm 40:5; Isaiah 30:6; Lamentations 4:17, etc.

**v. 18.** Every shoulder. **v. 7.** q) **made bald**. Gousset <note>Jacques Gousset, a 17th-century Hebrew scholar</note> p. 481. qf. polished and shining; from the rubbing of the burden frequently carried. Chapter 21:14, 33. Leviticus 13:40, 41. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> on this passage: a great number of stones from the earth were carried by the nations, by which the shoulders are worn down and the head is made bald. Alternatively: their clothes were worn out by the long siege. r) **and yet there were no wages**. It happened to him and his army at Tyre, for the labor which he performed.

**v. 17** q) **Moreover it happened**, f) **in the twenty-seventh year**, namely from the deportation of Jeconiah <note>King Jehoiachin</note>, as our Prophet is accustomed to calculate. See v. 1. chapter 1:2, etc. But Kimchi, Rashi, and Abendana <note>prominent Jewish commentators</note> say: from the beginning of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, following the *Seder Olam* <note>a 2nd-century chronological work</note>. Therefore, this prophecy was the last of the Prophet in terms of time, compare chapter 40:1, and thus it would also be the last of the entire book. It is woven together with the preceding sections because of the consistency of the subject matter; so that all the prophecies against Egypt might be joined together. See note on v. 1 and the Preface to this book §. 12. Also Lightfoot's *Chronology* p. 131. g) **in the first month** chapter 45:18, 21. h) chapter 26:1. Genesis 8:13.

Jerome's words in his commentary on this passage, p. 582: *When the Tyrians saw that the foundations of the walls were being shaken by the battering of the rams, whatever precious things they had in gold, silver, clothes, and various noble furnishings, they placed on ships and transported to the islands <note>specifically the island that became the seat of New Tyre</note>; so that when the city was captured, Nebuchadnezzar found nothing worthy of his labor. And because he had obeyed the will of God in this part, Egypt is given to him.* cf. note above on chapter 26:12 and Ezekiel 23:6.

Leviticus 19:13. c) **for which price or wages he labored**. v. 18. Genesis 29:18. Namely, which he performed in it. d) **I have given** or **I will give**. v. 19. e) cf. v. 30:10 seqq. f) **because they labored**. Namely, because they performed for me that service (Ruth 2:19) as executors of my will and justice. cf. Ezekiel 10:5, 6. But Kimchi and Rashi: because the Egyptians did evil against me. So Tremellius etc.: I will promote in some way the strength and power of Christ in the house of Israel, so that it does not seem entirely buried and extinct. Cocceius joins all these together. Jonathan: I will bring liberation. Cf. II. Isaiah 13:6. p) **Ah!** Woe! (1) **the day**, namely the unhappy and sad day. Kimchi. namely if you compare chapter 29:17. s) **predefined by the Lord**; in which He also wishes it to be known that He Himself is the one who judges the impiety and injustice of men. t) **a day of clouds**, cloudy with the storms of adverse affairs; a "black day," as the Latins say. cf. v. 18, chapter 34:12, Joel 2:2, Zephaniah 1:14 seqq. u) **it shall be a time of the nations** being devastated, the Egyptians and their allies; as in v. 9, the day of Egypt is the day of its destruction. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Ezekiel 30, shifting from the general prophecy against Egypt to specific allies and geographical regions that will fall alongside it. It maintains the scholarly focus on identifying historical peoples like the Libyans (Phut) and Arabians (Cush/Chub) and uses references from early modern geographers like Bochart.</meta>

<header>EZEKIEL. CHAPTER 30. 5</header>

<margin>
n) And there shall be a bitter and vehement pain, or a torment. (q) See verse 9; Isaiah 21:3. r) in Cush <note>Ethiopia or Arabia</note>. Tremellius, Vatablus, Piscator <note>Protestant biblical commentators of the 16th/17th centuries</note>.
Some understand this as African Ethiopia, neighboring Egypt; others as Chusean Arabia. But by the nature of the matter, and (as Gurtler concludes in *Prophetic Theology*, page 250) because Cush is mentioned twice in verses 4 and 5, it can rightly be understood as both. For both regions are named in the prophecies and were allied with the Egyptians. This latter region (Chusean Arabia), being neighbor to the Chaldeans <note>Babylonians</note> as they marched toward Egypt, was forced to undergo the greatest hardships. Compare notes on verse 9; Isaiah 18:1 and chapter 20:3, 5; Zephaniah 2:12. s) chapter 32:10. b) cf. Isaiah 19:1 following; chapter 20:3 following. q) the calamity of Egypt will be so great that all neighboring nations will tremble. t) and they shall take away (chapter 16:39) the enemies. d) its multitude (chapter 29:19). e) shall be overturned (chapter 38:20). f) chapter 23:14, with cities destroyed. Cf. chapter 36:35, which was also done later by the Persian kings. See Gurtler, *Prophetic Theology*, page 238, and the note below for verse 13.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 5. g) See verse 4; Isaiah 41:3. h) and Phut, or the Libyans, descended from Phut, son of Ham, from whom comes the city Putta and the river of the same name in Libya. See chapter 27:19; Jeremiah 46:9. Most of the Phutites lived beyond the Tritonis marsh, which divided Africa into two nearly equal parts; however, some lived on this side of it and near Egypt, as is gathered from this passage and Jeremiah. Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar of biblical geography</note>, *Phaleg* book 4, chapter 33. i) Bochart makes the Ludim <note>Ludites</note> in this place a people of Ethiopia. See the note on chapter 27:10. For the Africans were also among the allies of Egypt in Jeremiah 46:9, and from this Nebuchadnezzar took a pretext for war in Africa. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note>. k) and all the mixed multitude. Cf. Isaiah 2, 38. Grotius says: mercenary soldiers gathered from many nations. But according to Schmidt, it refers to Syria, and for others, Arabia. Cf. note on 1 Kings 10:25; Isaiah 21:13; Jeremiah.
</margin>

<margin>
Jeremiah 25:20, 24. l) and Chub, whom I think lived around Palirus, a town in Marmarica <note>a region between Egypt and Cyrenaica</note>, because Chub is Palirus in Syriac. Bochart, *Phaleg* book 4, chapter 33. Ptolemy <note>the ancient geographer</note> also places them in Mareotis. m) and the sons of the land of the covenant, that is, the people of the allied regions, or other allies of the Egyptians. So say Vatablus, Munster, etc. Others, like Grotius and Jerome <note>the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note>, specifically understand them to be the Jews, who were involved in the same calamities as the Egyptians after the remnants of them, once Jerusalem was destroyed, had gone into Egypt. Jeremiah 42:22; chapter 44:14.

# EZEKIEL. CHAPTERS 30, 31.

<margin>
**verse 22. u)** See chapter 29, verse 10.
**x)** verse 18, 24. Compare Ezekiel 14:5 and Hosea 7:5. **y)** Both that which is still *strong* and that which is already *broken* (see verse 21), which I will crush further. **o-** I will weaken all of Pharaoh’s forces. Tirinus <note>Jacobus Tirinus, 1580–1636, a Jesuit commentator</note> suggests: *with one arm already broken*, namely the kingdom of Syria, I will now crush his other arm, the kingdom of Egypt. However, Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 1603–1669, a Dutch theologian</note> argues: it is not unreasonable to think of two royal houses; the one then reigning, in which Apries (Pharaoh Hophra) ruled, and the one that would succeed it, which was to be a humble kingdom. The current family was the "intact" arm, while the other kings were the "broken" one. **z)** *I will shake out*, or cause to fall. See chapter 39, verse 3.
**verse 23. a)** verse 26. Chapter 22, verse 15. **b)** verse 26. Chapter 29, verse 12.
**verse 24. c)** Conversely, *I will strengthen*. See verse 25 and compare Hosea 7:15. **d)** verses 10, 25. **e)** Cocceius: These verses teach that God alone gathers and scatters nations; He gives and takes away strength. The sword they carry is *God's sword*. This is not only a hidden governance but a manifest ordering. Thus it happened that God’s sword came into the hand of now this Monarch, now that one; in this place, it is Nebuchadnezzar's. He held not only the highest majesty and power among men but also carried out God’s judgments against the peoples whom God wished to judge as an example of His wrath. Compare Daniel 4:14. **f)** *But I will break*. verses 18, 22. Isaiah 10:15. Jeremiah 48:25. **g)** so that he *groans* <note>original: "ingemifcat"</note>. Job 24:12. **h)** with *groanings* <note>original: "gemissibus"</note>. Exodus 2:24. Chapter 6:5. Judges 2:18. *The mortally wounded*—that is, as a man wounded unto death is accustomed to groan. **i)** In front of him, the Babylonian victor.
**verse 25. k)** Indeed, *I will strengthen*. verse 24. **l)** *but the arms*. **m)** see verse 19. **n)** see verse 24. **o)** *and he shall stretch out*. Meaning *so that he may stretch out*. **p)** that hand. Namely, *that sword*, over the land of Egypt.

**§ I.** The growth of the Egyptian kingdom under God's providence is described (verses 2–9). **§ II.** Its excessive pride and divine *vengeance* (verses 10–14). **§ III.** The great *mourning* over its fall (verse 15 onwards). <margin>**v. 2. a)** Compare the notes from Cocceius at the end of this chapter. **b)** verse 18. Chapter 32, verses 31, 32. **c)** Whom are you like? verse 18. Chapter 32, verse 2. **d)** in your magnitude. verse 7, 18. Ephesians 9:8. Chapter 10, 12. Compare Daniel 4:7 and following. **v. 3. e)** Behold, you are like (verse 2). **f)** To the *Assyrian* king and kingdom. Chapter 32, verse 22. Namely, like the tallest cedar in Lebanon; enjoying the highest power and glory; and hence, equally arrogant in will. But just as he was treated terribly by the Chaldeans <note>the Babylonians</note>, so too will you be treated by them. Others suggest: *Behold, you are like the Assyrian, a cedar, etc.* Others, following Schmidt: *Behold, Assyria was a cedar in Lebanon*; implying *and yet it fell*; how much more will you, who are inferior to it. Thus Pharaoh is terrified by the destruction of the Assyrian, and by this example, his own end is confirmed, according to Cocceius and Gurtler’s *Prophetic Theology* page 202 / 243. See the note on verse 4. However, Marcus Meibomius in his specimens writes: you have become like a straight cedar in Lebanon (which they call a *cedrelaten* <note>a Greek/Latin term for a fir-like cedar</note>, see Pliny’s *Natural History* book 13 chapter 5 and book 24 chapter 5), with a very tall, straight trunk. See Maius's supplement to Cocceius’s Lexicon, page 8. **g)** Like a cedar, as the tallest, most beautiful, most shaded, leafiest, and most vibrant of trees in Lebanon. Chapter 27, verse 5. (*For the cedar loves mountains, and in Syria it is most highly praised*, according to Pliny’s *Natural History* book 16 chapters 18 and 39) because of the height, breadth, and strength of the kingdom. Compare Isaiah 10:34. **Grotius:** Kings are customarily compared to tall trees. Daniel 4:20–22. Ezekiel 17:3. **h)** *beautiful with leaves*. Compare chapter 17, verse 8; chapter 19, verse 10; Jeremiah 11:16. **i)** *and with shoots* or branches. 2 Chronicles 27:4. Isaiah 17:9. **k)** *shadowing*, a cedar making shade; protecting many. Nehemiah 13:19. **Piscator:** with arms reaching out in all directions for the convenience of all. **l)** Meaning *and of high height*. Others: *lofty in its trunk*. verses 5, 10, 14. Cocceius: that is, [above] others. **n)** its summit was elevated, the highest part of its trunk. See verse 10, compare chapter 17, verse 3. Meibomius discusses the meaning of this phrase extensively in his *Specimen* pages 83–88. **v. 4. o)** *Waters*. A great abundance of water, such as in the Tigris and the Nile. This alludes to the waters of the Tigris if referring to the Assyrian; or more likely the Nile and its streams if you apply these and the following verses up to verse 17 to the Egyptian. Most interpreters refer this *to the Assyrian*; they are favored by the frequent use of the Past Tense in the following verses, describing the past fates, power, riches, pride, and finally the crushing defeat and severe punishment of the Assyrians as already accomplished facts. However, it is well known that the Hebrew Past Tense is often used, especially by Prophets, to speak of the future, as we have noted throughout. The Prophet himself later in verse 10 and especially verse 18 expressly applies what was said at length in the preceding verses to Pharaoh and his multitude. Even the Past Tenses are not used consistently but are mixed with the Future (e.g., verses 11, 13), so that the Prophet looks partly at past disasters and partly at the decreed and certain future disasters of the Egyptians. See chapter 30, verses 21, 22. **p)** *had nourished*. Meaning they had made that cedar grow. Isaiah 44:14. **q)** *The Deep*, that is, the subterranean waters and springs that nourish plants. Compare Genesis 49:25; Deuteronomy 8:7; chapter 33, verse 13. Others: *The Nile overflowing is the "deep" for Egypt*. Without this rising at a certain time of year, Egypt would be the poorest of lands: because it is not made fertile by heavy rains like other lands, says Meibomius. See the note on chapter 30, verse 12. **r)** Meaning *it made it, had made it high*. Isaiah 1:2; chapter 2, verse 13.</margin>

**verse 5.** Compare verse 5 and Ezekiel 17:6. **h)** they nested (S) Psalm 104:17. **i)** birds of the heaven, i.e., according to Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, 1583–1645, a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> and others, many nations fled to its protection and were kept in its power. (Compare verse 13, chapter 17:23, Daniel 4:9, 18). **k)** see verse 5. **l)** Grotius: the people grew with a fortunate offspring. Compare verse 12, Daniel 4:9. **m)** and under its shade or bower and protection they lived. That is, cedars of such height were not in the paradise or garden of God. He is compared with other princes and leaders of the world, none of whom surpassed his height, or even equaled the majesty of the kings dependent upon him. (Cocceius) **u)** Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, 1040–1105, the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note>: as if to say, in the whole world, verse 9. The style of speaking is the same as above in verse 2, Ezekiel 28:13. Compare chapter 31:35. Cocceius: Princes are called trees in the garden of God. This world is as it were the garden of God, abounding in divine planting for every use and every ornament. Although all princes are not a planting for bearing fruit to God, as those endowed with the life of God, they are nonetheless a divine planting by reason of the office and power which each has received. They are trees planted in the garden of God so that they may protect men with their shade and feed them with their goods, or provide them with an abundance of all good and useful things; especially indeed of wisdom and knowledge, so that each may live a life most worthy of a human being. Compare Daniel 4:18, 19. **x)** firs, others say pines, Ezekiel 60:13, Hosea 14:9. <summary>This page provides a detailed linguistic and theological commentary on Ezekiel 31, interpreting the allegory of the great cedar (representing the Assyrian Empire and Pharaoh) through Hebrew philology and the insights of scholars like Cocceius, Grotius, and Kimchi. The text explains how the "waters" and "branches" represent the wealth, armies, and subordinate nations that once supported the great empire before its divine judgment.</summary>

# EZEKIEL. CHAPTER 31. 31

<margin>
a) i.e., the Chaldeans (chapter 30:12; compare Isaiah 1:7). b) The most warlike and terrible among the nations (chapter 30:11; 32:12). c) And they shall cast it down, or carry it away; Others: they shall fail (with chapter 32:41). d) Upon the mountains (chapter 18:2). e) And in all the valleys, situated beneath the mountains (chapter 32:5; 35:8). f) Others: the branches fell; alternatively: its foliage (verse 9). g) Chapter 30:8; Isaiah 27:11. h) Its larger branches (verse 13). i) Others: in all the paths (Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Hebraist</note>: in the hollows of the earth where water can be collected and flow, chapter 32:6. Junius <note>Francis Junius, a Reformed theologian</note>: for branches are prone to fall by their own weight from the mountains through the valleys, while the lighter ones are broken by the fall and cast headlong into the channels below to be carried away). k) Others: from where they shall descend or withdraw. l) See verse 6. m) Compare verse 6; chapter 32:9, 10. n) And they abandoned him; the people whom he ruled shall fail him, as well as neighboring and allied nations who trusted in his help. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch jurist and scholar</note>: He mixes the elements of the comparison here, as he and other writers often do.
</margin>

<margin>
31:2, 5. r) Trees of the waters, those rejoicing in much water; i.e., princes and those who abound in riches (compare verse 4). The aim of the whole chapter is concluded in this verse: that by God’s command, the Prophet wrote this vision to warn all Kings and Princes of the world not to be proud or exalt themselves too much because of the power given to them by God (verse 9); and so that the Jewish King would never again trust in the help of the King of Egypt or any other. x) Others: nor let them send out (Tremellius: put forth) a branch.
</margin>

> **12** And foreigners, the most ruthless of nations, have cut it down and left it; its branches have fallen upon the mountains and in all the valleys, and its boughs are broken in all the ravines of the land. All the peoples of the earth have departed from its shade and abandoned it.
> 
> **13** Upon its ruin all the birds of the heavens shall dwell, and all the beasts of the field shall be among its boughs.
> 
> **14** This is so that no trees by the waters may exalt themselves in their stature, nor set their tops among the thick clouds, and that no well-watered trees may stand up to them in their height. For they are all delivered unto death, to the depths of the earth, among the children of men, with those who go down to the pit.
> 
> **15** Thus says the Lord God: On the day when he went down to the underworld <note>original: "Sheol"</note>, I caused mourning; I covered the abyss for him and restrained its rivers, and the great waters were held back. I made Lebanon mourn for him, and all the trees of the field languished because of him.
> 
> **16** I made the nations shake at the sound of his fall, when I cast him down to the underworld with those who descend into the pit; and all the trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon, all that drink water, were comforted in the depths of the earth.
> 
> **17** They also went down to the underworld with him, to those slain by the sword; and those who were his arm, who lived under his shade among the nations.

f. rather his swarm (s) <note>referring to verses 3, 10 and chapter 17:3</note> as the Assyrian had done, and then Pharaoh (verse 2). y) Others: toward the intertwined branches; alternatively: even among the thick clouds (see verses 3, 10). z) Nor should they stand, or persist—in their pride (compare 2 Chronicles 32:26). a) Their strong ones, powerful ones, or princes (verse 11); others: oaks (comparing Isaiah 61:3, Hosea 4:13). But Schmidt says: "over them." Likewise, Meibom in his *Specimen* p. 92: "nor do the trees of the water stand by them," that is, join or assist them by treaty (see variant readings). b) Others: because of their pride; alternatively: when they exalt themselves, having grown to a great height (verse 10; chapter 19:11). c) The oaks/trees drinking water; those rejoicing in much moisture, perhaps those flowing with wealth and riches (verse 16). d) For all those proud trees—or, by comparison, the haughty Kings and Princes, the Assyrian and the Egyptian, and their highest men. e) Compare Psalm 118:18; Isaiah 34:2. f) Into the lower earth (verses 16, 18; chapter 26:20), i.e., into the grave or the lower parts of the earth (Ephesians 4:9). g) Among other sons of Adam, perhaps men (Isaiah 56:2), even commoners or the crowd. For in death, those who were most splendid in life are made equal to the lowliest, those who would not live piously and peacefully but abused their power, attempting everything to the danger and destruction of many. h) To those descending; Grotius: who are cast down into the pit (verse 16; chapter 26:20; 32:18), namely of their grave; or: into the pit of the house of perdition, as Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Bible</note> adds here and in verse 16. These phrases signify destruction, ruin, ignominy, vileness, and dire examples. Cocceius verse 15: i) where he descends. Others: where he is about to flow down into the infernal regions (chapter 30:6; 32:19; Isaiah 14:11). Grotius: when Sennacherib, killed by his sons, descends to the underworld (2 Kings 19:37). k) Others: I will cause to mourn, namely all his friends. (Hiphil verb form). Others, as we noted above, in the past tense: "I brought mourning," and they take all these things to be about the Assyrian, whereas we take them to be about the Egyptians. l) Others: and I will cover over it (or for its sake, or because of him) the abyss (chapter 26:19; Psalm 104:6; Isaiah 11:9), which previously watered that cedar (verse 4). So that the abyss itself mourns, as if covered in sackcloth, and no longer waters it. Or: I will bring the very abyss of evils over Pharaoh and overwhelm him (compare similar constructions in chapter 24:7, 26:19, Psalm 42:8, and Isaiah 8:7-8). m) And I will block its rivers (verse 4; Amos 4:7). I will dry up the fountains of his wealth. n) Others: so that they are closed up (compare Genesis 8:2). o) Those many waters (see verses 5, 7). Cocceius: When people are so foolish that they abuse God's blessings and trust in human strength for luxury, injustice, and wickedness—drinking water but not knowing God, and not expecting true goods from Him—then both Kings and kingdoms perish, are covered in mourning, and God's blessings are taken away and transferred to others. p) But I also made it dark. Others: I will blacken over them, i.e., I will clothe them in black and mournful garments (Hiphil form) (Chapter 32:7-8; compare Jeremiah 14:2; Psalm 35:14). q) Lebanon, in which that highest cedar was (verse 3). Understand by "Lebanon" here the whole kingdom. Menochius <note>Giovanni Stefano Menochio, a Jesuit scholar</note>: But Jonathan says "and the faces of the Kings were darkened because of him." r) Jonathan: kings (or princes) of the peoples (verses 4, 5). s) They shall be a failing, they shall suffer a fainting. Others take it as a concrete noun: they shall be like a failing or dead tree; just as the name *Libhnah*, of the same ending, is the white poplar tree (Genesis 30:37; compare the verb in Isaiah 51:20, verse 16). t) From the sound, perhaps because of the crash of his ruin (verse 13; chapter 26:15). u) It moved. Others: I will make the nations tremble (Isaiah 14:16). x) Others: when I have caused him to descend (verses 17, 18; chapter 26:20). y) To the underworld (verse 17; Isaiah 14:15). z) With those who descended into the pit (verse 14; Psalm 143:7). a) Indeed, they shall receive consolation from this destruction. Others: from which they shall console themselves. ### CHAPTER 32. EZEKIEL 32

According to Calovius. **q)** verse 21; chapter 31:17. **r)** the same applies to the Egyptians and their allies (chapter 6:7). <summary>This page contains a detailed commentary on Ezekiel 32:17-25, describing Egypt’s prophetic descent into the underworld. The text draws parallels between Egypt's fall and the prior destruction of empires like Assyria and Elam, framing their shared fate in Sheol as a divine judgment on their earthly pride and violence.</summary>

<meta>This page marks a significant transition in the Book of Ezekiel. Having concluded the prophecies against foreign nations (chapters 25–32), the text returns to Ezekiel’s role as a "watchman" for the house of Israel. This section mirrors the language used in chapter 3, emphasizing the prophet's individual responsibility and the theme of personal repentance following the fall of Jerusalem.</meta>

### CHAPTER 33. Ezekiel 33:1–10

<margin>
It is contained within its own boundaries, and thus utilized. I believe it is understood this way in Genesis 19:4, 47:2; Numbers 11:1; Judges 18:2; 1 Kings 12:31; Jeremiah 50:26 and 51:31. This is the view of De Dieu, with whom Bochart agrees (Hieroz. l. 356, 357). Compare our notes on 1 Kings 9:10 and the locations just cited.

<gloss>Qamets Nun-Vav-Qof</gloss> <note>A grammatical note regarding the vowel marking and root of a Hebrew word.</note>

m) And they appointed for themselves. verse 7; Deuteronomy 1:15, etc. n) As a watchman. verse 6, 7; 2 Kings 9:17. This is so that he may guard the public interest with the greatest faith and diligence. He compares the Prophet to a military watchman. This is the same sense as above in chapter 3, verse 17 and following, but repeated here due to the necessity of the times.
</margin>

1. And the word of the LORD came to me, saying:
2. "Son of man, speak to the children of your people and say to them: 'When I bring a sword upon a land, and the people of the land take one man from their borders and appoint him as their watchman;
3. And he sees the sword coming upon the land, and he blows the shofar <term>shofar: a ram's horn trumpet used for signals and religious ceremonies</term> and warns the people;
4. Then whoever hears the sound of the shofar and does not take warning, and the sword comes and takes him away, his blood shall be on his own head.
5. He heard the sound of the shofar and did not take warning; his blood shall be upon him. But had he taken warning, he would have delivered his soul.
6. But if the watchman sees the sword coming and does not blow the shofar, and the people are not warned, and the sword comes and takes a person from among them—he is taken away in his iniquity, but his blood I will require from the watchman's hand.'
7. "As for you, son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; so you shall hear a word from My mouth and warn them from Me.
8. When I say to the wicked, 'O wicked man, you shall surely die!' and you do not speak to warn the wicked from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require from your hand.
9. But if you warn the wicked from his way to turn from it, and he does not turn from his way, he shall die in his iniquity; but you have delivered your soul.
10. "Therefore, you, son of man, say to the house of Israel: 'Thus you have spoken, saying, "Indeed our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and in them we pine away..."

<column-break/>

<margin>
CHAPTER 33, verse 1.
f) Furthermore it happened. Specifically in the twelfth year (compare chapter 32:17), after the destruction of the city of Jerusalem; shortly, it seems, before the prophecy that follows in verse 21 and sequence. For there are two prophecies in this chapter, and two parts to each. In the first part (I): a) God recalls the Prophet from the foreign nations back to the Israelites and gravely reminds him of his duty (v. 2–9). b) He refutes the people’s proverb—as if they were destined to perish absolutely—out of His hatred for evil and His grace toward all who repent (v. 10–20). In the second part (II): after describing the arrival of a fugitive, there is a prophecy: a) against the impious remnants of the people in Judea (v. 21–29). b) against the hypocritical and malicious listeners of the Prophet in Babylonia (v. 30–33).

v. 2. g) To your fellow countryman, v. 12, 17. Specifically the Israelites, v. 7, 10, who were deported with you. Just as I commanded you to prophesy against the nations until now, so now you must prophesy again to your own. cf. chapter 24:26, 27. h) To a certain land or region, regarding it. Or: when I have brought the sword upon the land. The antecedent with its redundant relative, as in chapter 14:13. i) Where I have introduced a hostile sword against it. chapter 5:17, 14:17. Grotius notes: "When enemies approach a region, which does not happen without my decree or permission." cf. Amos 3:6. k) And the people of the land, or whoever is in charge of human administration, shall take. l) From their ends. Louis de Dieu: "from their whole community"; just as Jonah says "from their midst," and the Greek Septuagint says "from themselves." I would prefer, however, to say "from the midst of all of them" or "from among all of them," so that the "totality," which is denoted by the Hebrew <note>original: miqtsēhem</note>, is expressed. Properly, this word means the end or extremity of a thing; because the end is the completion of it, it is used here for the "totality" of the thing, which is entirely...
</margin>

---

...contained within its borders. v. 3. o) He shall have seen the sword or enemies, or some other imminent evil (v. 6, chapter 30:4). p) And he shall have sounded the trumpet, to signal the arrival of the enemy. cf. Isaiah 58:1, Hosea 8:1. q) And he shall have warned—one who hears but does not take care for himself. 2 Samuel 17:9. s) And yet, having been warned, he did not take care or heed the warning. Or: he refused to be warned (v. 5, 6). t) And therefore the sword comes and takes him (v. 6). u) His blood (Targum Jonathan: "the guilt of his killing") shall be on his own head. That is: the evil that happens to him shall be imputed to him alone. Thus in verse 5, see Leviticus 20:9. This is a metaphor from expiatory victims, upon whose heads the sacrificers placed their hands, and by that rite imputed guilt to them; see Leviticus 1:4, 24:14, and compare Matthew 27:25. Piscator. v. 5. x) For the voice, etc. y) And yet he did not take care for himself. v. 4. cf. Amos 3:6. z) Therefore his blood shall be upon himself. v. 4. a) But if he had taken care for himself (v. 4, chapter 3:21). b) He would have rescued his soul. cf. 1 Samuel 19:11, Jeremiah 48:6. v. 6. c) On the other hand, the watchman, if he sees (v. 2, 3). d) So that the people were not warned (v. 3); and therefore it comes and takes away (v. 4). e) Some soul, i.e., anyone. Leviticus 4:27, cf. above chapter 18:4, 20. f) He indeed for his own sin (v. 8, 9, chapter 18:18). Grotius: "by his own fault; because those who are in war must constantly be on guard." g) He is taken away (v. 4). h) But I will require his blood from the hand of the watchman (v. 8, chapter 3:18, 20). Even he will be punished, who ought to have roused the negligent. The crime of sluggishness in a soldier is a transgression. If someone appointed by the people owes such great diligence, how much more does he who is appointed by God? (Grotius). v. 7. i) As for what concerns you. Others: this acts as a direct address, as in v. 10, 12. This is the application of the preceding comparison. k) Tremellius on v. 2: "Not the people, nor any human authority, but I myself have appointed you a watchman over my people (chapter 3:17); and although I commanded you to be silent among your countrymen for a time (chapter 24:27), yet now I recall you to your former function." So now, act, attend to your duty, and explain to your people the necessity of fulfilling it. Compare Hebrews 13:17. l) That you may hear a word from my mouth (chapter 3:17). m) And warn them (v. 3–9). Exodus 18:20. n) From me, by my words. Targum Jonathan: "lest they sin before me." v. 8. o) When I shall have said to the wicked (chapter 3:18). p) O wicked man, in dying you shall die eternally (v. 14), unless you repent. For there is a silent condition implied. See v. 11. q) But you have not spoken. cf. Matthew 25:24, 25; Psalm 40:10. r) To warn or discourage the wicked from his way. So that by warning the wicked you might pull him back from his habit. See chapter 3:18. s) Tremellius: "that he may desist from his evil way." cf. Isaiah 55:7. t) Because of his own wickedness (v. 6, 9). u) But his blood, etc. (v. 6, chapter 3:18, 20). cf. 1 Corinthians 9:16. Oecolampadius: "This doctrine pertains to all who have oversight and care of others. Nor does it in no way concern those who are private individuals, who have any <term>apokalypsin: Greek for 'revelation'</term> from God by which they can be useful to a neighbor. Common charity obliges us to seek the salvation of one another." See Jude 21, 22, 23. v. 9. x) But if you have discouraged the wicked from his way (v. 3, 7). y) v. 6, 8. z) chapter 3:19, 21. cf. Acts 20:25, 26. v. 10. a) You therefore. b) Correctly. So say Kimchi and M. I., comparing Numbers 27:7. Others, like the Septuagint and Syriac: "Thus you plainly say." Vatablus: "You are accustomed to say." c) Entirely. Tremellius: "Because—therefore in these things we rot away." d) cf. Isaiah 59:12.

*verse 32.* a love song; such as lovers are accustomed to sing, and profane minds gladly hear. o) that is, with the voice of a beautiful singer, or one who is endowed with a beautiful voice. Others, like the <note>original: "S."</note>, "beautiful in voice or sound," which sounds beautiful. p) or like a harpist, playing most excellently. Isaiah 23:15; Psalm 33:3. q) <note>original: "S. audiunt enim quidem verba tua"</note> for they indeed hear your words. r) but they do not do them. See note at verse 31; Isaiah 5:12, 19. **The Sense:** You indeed delight them, but you do not move them so that their hearts are affected. *Grotius:* "They praise your eloquence, but they do not care for the reality." There are many such in the Church even today (says Jerome on this passage) who say: "Come, let us hear so-and-so, rolling out the words of his preaching with wonderful eloquence," and many join in the applause, and shout, and wave their hands. Junius specifically takes this to refer to the prophecies which he had pronounced against the nations in chapters 25–32, since those did not affect them at all, but only foreign nations, against whom it was pleasant for them to hear him prophesying; while in the meantime, by his silence regarding their own affairs, the prophet seemed to be promising them all favorable things. *verse 33. s)* <note>original: "S. Quum vero id veniet"</note> But when that comes; namely, what you predicted about the utter devastation of the land, etc. (verses 27, 28, 29). Others: "But now when it comes, what you had predicted about the destruction of the city." t) <note>original: "S. ecce, ita veniet, vt sciant"</note> behold, it will so come, that they may know. chapter 30:9. Others, like Grotius, in the past tense: "for it certainly happened, so that they may know," etc. u) then they will recognize. chapter 5:13. x) chapter 2:5. That is, they will not be able to deny that you were a true prophet, and sent to them by me. They will be able to pull no veil of ignorance over their faults. Grotius. **CHAPTER XXXIV.** 1. y) <note>original: "S. Præterea factum est"</note> Moreover, it came to pass, etc. Now that the city has been cut off and the Jews dispersed, God, through the Prophet, commemorates: I. the causes of the destruction, both present and future, especially the lazy negligence and insatiable greed of the shepherds, that is, the leaders of the people (verses 2–6) and announces just punishment for them (verses 7–10). II. To whom He promises Himself as the best shepherd (verses 10–16). III. Through a turning away (apostrophe), He explains more fully the judgments against the wicked goats and rams (verses 17–22). And IV. God the Father describes Gospel benefits through the Messiah, the unique and universal shepherd, in the most ample words (verses 23–31). This promise, therefore, extends most widely, as Cocceius shows here. However, all these chapters (34–39) do not have a certain and determined time. But Chapter 40 refers to the 25th year of the captivity of Jeconiah; therefore, one must think of some interval, and time must be given to them between the twelfth year of the captivity, to which we see Chapter 33 refers (verse 21), and the 25th year, which Chapter 40 bears inscribed, as Lightfoot observes in his *Chronology*, p. 130. *verse 2. z)* against the shepherds, that is, the overseers and governors of Israel, both the political (King, princes, magistrates) and the ecclesiastical (prophets and priests), whom the following things especially fit. Abarbanel, with other Jews, understands this only of the political leaders, but he is refuted by Cocceius, as Grotius is by Calovius on this passage. See chapter 13:2; Jeremiah 3:15; chapter 10:21; chapter 22:22; Zechariah 10:2. a) chapter 13:2; chapter 21:14, 33; chapter 30:2. b) namely, to the shepherds. An emphatic redundancy. c) woe to the shepherds! Jeremiah 23:1 and following; chapter 25:34, 36; Zechariah 11:3 and following. d) Jonah, Kimchi, Rashi, M. I., and others: "who are feeding themselves." So in verses 8 and 10. So Glassius, *Grammatica Sacra*, p. 764. See below, verse 8. e) but should not shepherds feed the flock, not themselves? Should they not feed them, namely the Israelites; or according to Tremellius, "who were to be feeding them"; as if to say, I call them shepherds, not from the fact of how they behave, but from the duty by which they ought to have fed. Just as the words of the Hebrews, denoting an action, often signify a duty or office—those who do this one thing, so that they themselves may grow rich. See Philippians 2:21; 2 Corinthians 12:14; Jude verse 12. But Schmid: "who were feeding—is that the duty of shepherds? I appeal to your conscience." See Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2; 2 Corinthians 12:14. *verse 3. f)* <note>original: "S. atqui vos adipem"</note> but you eat the fat (or the best). See Genesis 31:38; Deuteronomy 32:14; Leviticus 3:16, 17. That is, you snatch the goods or wealth of the people for yourselves. But Bochart says: "The Greeks, Jerome, and the Arab read with different vowels *hechalabh*, you eat the milk (Proverbs 27:27; 1 Corinthians 9:7)," namely, not observing moderation, according to that saying: *This stranger guard milks the sheep twice in an hour, and the life-force is withdrawn from the flock and the milk from the lambs.* Which seems more fitting; because in this way the repetition emerging from the other reading is avoided, as is the manifest <term>hysteron-prologia</term> <note>a figure of speech where the natural order of events is reversed</note>, since the fat of sheep is not eaten unless after they have been slaughtered. *Hierozoicon*, Part I, p. 447. These things, however, are not so important to us that we think the customary reading should be abandoned for that reason. g) and with the wool, that is, by metonymy: with the cloth made from the shorn wool, you clothe yourselves. See Leviticus 13:47, 59. h) <note>original: "S. pinguem onem"</note> the fat sheep. Zechariah 11:16. slaughtered. Deuteronomy 12:15; 1 Samuel 28:24. For your banquets. See John 10:10. Grotius: "you were killing the rich through false accusation, so that you might take possession of their cattle." i) but the sheep, or the flock, you do not feed (verse 2), nor do you have care for them. John 10:13.
