Among the signs of the Messiah’s coming (which you can see summarized in Vitringa's *Typus Doctrinae Propheticae*, p. 141 ff.) is also the state of the Church, which, as for its shepherds, the princes of the people, and the priests, is utterly corrupt. *verse 9. a)* Therefore, I say. verse 7. He breaks off the speech through emotion, and it is only completed in verse ten, but as a new statement rather than a continuous discourse. *verse 10. b)* Behold, I will be against the shepherds. cf. chapter 13:8, 20; chapter 26:3. c) verse 8; Zechariah 9:16; cf. above chapter 33:8. d) That is, I will demand the penalty for the neglected sheep from them. cf. chapter 33:6, 8. e) chapter 16:41. **Cocceius:** This does not imply that the shepherds of that time would perish and others would come in their place to hold the same office and power. For that would not have been a full liberation. Nor does the prophet mean that after those shepherds were abolished, no "wolves" or "false prophets" would arise who do not spare the flock (which Paul predicted in Acts 20:29; cf. Zechariah 11:16). Rather, this signifies that even if such people arise, they are not to be regarded as shepherds; their commands and words can be safely rejected, and one may distance oneself from them. In contrast, under the Old Testament, the people were subject to the shepherds and forced to go to them; one approaching God necessarily had to go to the temple where they sat on the "seat of Moses." The same applies to verse 11. Therefore, he foretells the fall of these shepherds who were to lead the people after the kingdom was abolished; namely, when God was about to visit His people. Thus, he addresses that entire order of priests and judges instituted by Moses, and foretells that they will no longer be shepherds; that is, their office of teaching the people, offering sacrifices, and judging the people according to the tenor of the Mosaic law will cease. f) <note>original: "S. se ipſos"</note> themselves. see verses 2, 8. g) <note>original: "S. atque sic eripiam"</note> and so I will rescue. verse 12; chapter 13:21. h) verse 5. *verse 11. i)* Behold I, I say, I myself will take special care of my own: namely, I will be the shepherd of the sheep and the judge of the treacherous shepherds. **Jonah:** Behold, I will be revealed. So in verse 20. cf. Zechariah 13:7; John 10:11.

<summary>Ezekiel 34:4-11 contains a stinging divine rebuke of Israel's leaders for their failure to care for the weak, sick, and lost sheep of the nation. The text and commentary emphasize that God will personally intervene to rescue the flock and abolish the corrupt leadership order.</summary>

->### 503 EZEKIEL. Chapter 34.<-

<margin>
*l)* I will seek (verse 8). *l)* I will search for them, I will examine them; I will consider and inspect their condition, wherever they are, and I will look out for them (verse 11).

**v. 12. m)** According to the search (1) of a flock in its pasture. <note>References to Isaiah 40:11 and Jeremiah 31:10</note>. Just as a shepherd searches his flock with precision. Compare Luke 15:4. *o)* on the day that he is. *p)* in the midst of his flock or his sheep. *q)* of those scattered; Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a 16th-century Hebraist</note> translates: "of his flock, of his dispersed sheep." According to the search of a shepherd for sheep that are not distinguished. Compare chapter 17:21 and see various readings below. *r)* verse 11. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note>: This is a great consolation for the faithful among the people. Even if they were dispersed into many places, God nevertheless does not abandon them, but cares for them no less than a shepherd cares for his sheep, so that none of God's sheep would perish in that captivity and dispersion which had then occurred. For this reason, He also gave prophets in Babylon itself, specifically so that they might turn to God from the heart. Deuteronomy 30:1, 2. *s)* compare Deuteronomy 4:31; Zephaniah 3:19; Zechariah 10:8. *t)* see Jeremiah 29:14 and compare chapter 8:3, 24:9, 40:12. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch scholar</note>: "I will bring back the Jews from all the places of the Babylonian empire, and indeed from Egypt and elsewhere." But Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius, a Lutheran theologian</note> says: "This did not happen when they were restored from the Babylonian captivity, but in the time of the New Testament, when the Synagogue was rejected and the Israelites were liberated from the yoke of Moses and the abuse of the law." etc. Compare the notes at verses 1 and 10. *u)* which they scattered. verse 6; chapter 38:25. *x)* chapter 30:3. *y)* of thick darkness; in a dark and gloomy time, full of miseries. Joel 2:2. Root: <term>gnophos [Greek: γνόφος]</term> <note>A Greek word for "darkness" or "gloom," used in the Greek translation of the Old Testament and the New Testament</note>. Hebrews 12:18. Cocceius: that is, from the calamities and disasters of the nations to which they had been driven. He is about to rescue the sheep of the house of Israel so they would not perish or be consumed along with those whom God willed to punish for having vexed His people. Clearly, God guarded the house of Israel during the fall of the dominion of the Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians, and Greeks; God visited these nations in their own lands with a "cloud and thick darkness."

**v. 13. z)** For I will lead them out, as formerly from Egypt. Exodus 6:6; 7:4, 5. A certain "leading out" was done through Cyrus—when as many as preferred God the Shepherd to the "impure land" returned to their own land, choosing to live under God rather than under the dominion of the nations. And also *in the final time of the people*, when God poured out His Spirit upon the Apostles, the sheep of God were gathered in Jerusalem from all places. Acts 2:9, 10, 11. Cocceius. **a)** chapter 11:17; Deuteronomy 30:3; Isaiah 56:8; Micah 2:12; John 11:52. **b)** Isaiah 43:5; Jeremiah 3:14; Zephaniah 3:20. **c)** verse 27; chapter 37:21. **d)** verse 14. Compare Isaiah 40:11; Micah 7:14. **e)** on the mountains of Israel. verse 14; chapter 19:9; 35:8. **f)** Tremellius: *at the channels*. Others: *in the ravines*; Cocceius: lower places in which water can be collected and flow down. <term>phagai [Greek: φαγαί]</term> <note>A Greek term for "clefts" or "watercourses"</note>. chapter 6:3; 31:12. Compare note on Isaiah 49:10. **g)** *in all the habitations of the land*, or the whole world. By this is signified not only the future multiplication of the people after their return from Babylon—that they filled the entire land of Israel—but the gathering of the Church throughout the whole world. **v. 14. h)** *In a good pasture*, **i)** by my word, which is to say, a healthy feeding. Compare verse 18; Psalm 23:2; 1 Chronicles 4:39, 40; John 10:10. **i)** verse 13. Compare Isaiah 5, 17. **k)** *and in the high mountains of the heights of Israel*. chapter 17:23. Compare Isaiah 40:9, 10, 11 and 49:11. Cocceius: that is, in those mountains in which Israel used to triumph most, and was eminent above other peoples—such as the mountains of Jerusalem, the holy city. Compare Isaiah 2:2. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note>: "on the holy mountain of Israel." **l)** *it shall be their fold*. Isaiah 32:18; Jeremiah 23:3. **m)** Isaiah 14:30. **n)** *in an excellent fold*. 2 Samuel 7:8; Isaiah 33:20. **o)** Isaiah 50:23. **p)** Others: *they shall feed upon the mountains*. verse 13; Zephaniah 2:13. **v. 15. q)** I myself, I say—the Son of God himself—will feed my sheep. verse 23; John 10:11. **r)** *and I will make them lie down*. Psalm 23:2; Song of Solomon 1:7. Compare Isaiah 49:10. I will give them peace and a quiet resting place. **v. 16. s)** verse 4, 6; Psalm 119:176; Matthew 18:24; chapter 11:15 etc.; Luke 15:4; 19:10. That is: those not cared for by the shepherds, and who desire a true shepherd but do not find him—I will approach them, I will make myself known to them, and I will lead them after me. Cocceius. **t)** verse 4; Micah 4:6. That is: I will lead back those turned away from the good path and seduced; or, as the Gospel says, "I will save sinners" etc. Cocceius. **u)** verse 4. That is: I will comfort those crushed in heart and mourning. Cocceius. **x)** verse 4. That is: those who are fainting and weary of all food, and thus sluggish due to the lack of food that refreshes the soul, I will revive through that Word which will not be nausea to them, but through which they can truly thrive. Cocceius. **y)** verse 4. <term>ischyron [Greek: ἰσχυρόν]</term> <note>Greek for "strong" or "powerful"</note>. Luke 22:32, 43. **y)** *but the fat and the strong*, and therefore the arrogant, the insolent, the wanton, and the headstrong; in opposition to the good, the thin, and the humble. See verse 13. Compare Isaiah 40:30. Thus <term>shamen [Hebrew: שמן]</term> <note>"Fat"</note> and <term>chazaq [Hebrew: חזק]</term> <note>"Strong"</note> are commonly ascribed to vices in Scripture. See chapter 2:4; 3:7; Exodus 7:13; Deuteronomy 32:15; Psalm 78:31; Isaiah 6:10; Jeremiah 5:3, 28. Indeed, it is clear from what follows that these terms are to be taken in a burdensome and hateful sense here, both in this verse and in verse 17, where the words "But as for you, my sheep" etc., teach that other sheep have already been mentioned, namely the stubborn ones; and from verses 18 and 19, which show that the preceding contains not only consolation for the pious sheep but also a rebuke for the impious; and most of all from verse 20, where the "fat cattle" are the evil and stubborn ones. See Glassius <note>Salomo Glassius, a 17th-century biblical critic</note> page 159 onwards. Jonathan: "the impious and sinners." Cocceius: the wealthy and powerful peoples, satisfied in their status, desiring neither the justice of God, nor Christ as the giver of justice, nor His kingdom (which is not of this world, but a kingdom of justification and sanctification in liberty, and thus a kingdom of the spirit). Compare Luke 1:52, 53. The aim of the prophecy, according to Glassius, is to rebuke false prophets but comfort the pious. Just as in verse 4 the wicked shepherds are rebuked for ruling the sheep harshly and tyrannically, so in this verse God threatens "measure for measure" <note>the law of retaliation</note> that He will, in turn, feed those shepherds (whom He now introduces as "bad sheep," the metaphor having changed, as Glassius judges) in judgment. We think that just as bad shepherds and false prophets are not to be excluded here but are themselves numbered among the insolent he-goats, so too we do not exclude other wicked and stubborn people from this threat. **z)** I will destroy. chapter 14:9; 25:7. Compare Luke 1:51, 52. And see Glassius. **a)** For I will feed her (the fat one) with judgment, as is proper; by which is understood not the feeding of grace, but of wrath and destruction. Compare Revelation 2:27 from Psalm 2:9. Glassius. Add 1 Samuel 3:13; Psalm 7:12; 50:6. But Cocceius says: "He does not entirely cease to feed the Jews who are excluded from the kingdom of heaven. For He feeds them with judgment. For He gives them Moses and the Prophets. Nor does He deny them His Gospel; for they are compelled to hear it in almost all nations. But He does not give them the inheritance of the world, and He scatters them through all nations, nor does He give them the word concerning justice, salvation, and the kingdom familiarly in their own native language, but through the writings of the nations and the languages of the barbarians." Compare Isaiah 28:11; Deuteronomy 32:21; Amos 8:11, 12. **v. 17. b)** Others: *But as for you, O my flock!* or: *For as it pertains also to you* etc. so that it connects with what immediately precedes; as if to say: "Do not think that only the bad shepherds are to be censured, while you are all blameless and capable of consolation." Thus, having rebuked the shepherds, God comes to the sins of the people. Compare the note at verse 1.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Ezekiel 34. Having addressed the failures of the human "shepherds" (the leaders of Israel), the text now focuses on God's judgment between the members of the flock itself—specifically how the strong and wealthy have oppressed the weak and poor—before promising the coming of the "One Shepherd," the Messiah.</meta>

->### CHAPTER 34. Ezekiel 34<-

<margin>
They begrudged the poor the harvest and vintage, the gleanings and the leftover grapes. <note>original Latin: messim & vindemiam, pauperibus spicilegium & racematione inuidebant</note> This is not unusual among the prophets, that there is more in the *moral of the story* <note>original Greek: en tō epimythiō</note> than in the *story itself* <note>original Greek: en tō mythō</note>, and those things are attributed to the breeding of livestock <note>original Greek: ktēnogonō</note> which actually apply to the spiritual type. Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, volume 1, page 526. <note>Samuel Bochart was a 17th-century scholar; his Hierozoicon is a famous study of animals in the Bible.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
**e)** Compare Matthew 25:32 and following, where Christ alludes to this passage. **d)** The Hebrew says "I will be judging between sheep and sheep" (verse 20). Targum Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> renders this: "between man and man." **e)** The Hebrew says "between the rams and between the male goats." But Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius, a 17th-century biblical critic</note> says it is better read as: "namely, the rams and the goats." For the identity of the prefixed Hebrew letter *Lamed* shows that these words act as an explanation of the previous term "for the sheep" (*laseh*). By the names "rams and goats," it is not the pious who are meant, but the wicked who are most prominent among the common people. See chapter 39:18; Ezekiel 14:10; Zechariah 10:3. Therefore, Jonathan rightly translates this as "sinners and the impious." So also Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a Dutch theologian</note>: In judgment, God places before Himself on one side the "sheep," meaning the small or weak livestock, and on the other side also "sheep" (the fat and strong ones mentioned in verse 16), as well as the rams and goats; namely, so that He might help the one sheep and be its avenger against the other sheep, rams, and goats.
***
**verse 18. f)** For is it too small a thing for you? The Vulgate <note>Latin Bible</note> reads: "Was it not enough for you?" See chapter 16:20; Job 15:11. **g)** That you robust sheep (verse 16), rams, and goats (verse 17), graze upon the best pasture (verse 14). Cocceius: He rebukes the sheep, that is, those who were considered His people. **h)** "And the rest of your pastures." Joel 3:4. **i)** "You trample with your feet." 2 Kings 7:17, 20. This behavior is more like a wild beast than a sheep; compare 2 Kings 14:9; Daniel 7:7; chapter 8:7, 10. **k)** The Hebrew says: "and the settling of the pure waters"; that is, the pure and most limpid waters, taken apart from the sediment where all the filth settles. (1) compare chapter 32:14. **l)** "You foul them with your feet." Compare chapter 32:2. They begrudge others the use of the same good things, so that nothing pure remains for them. If these descriptions do not fit literal sheep, they certainly fit the "mystical sheep"—that is, the Israelites, among whom many wealthy people, after a full harvest...
</margin>

->my servant<-

***

Compare James 2:6. **Cocceius:** This means they would not allow the true sheep of God to receive the sincere Word of God, which is pure and clean for life and joy (as if eating and drinking), but instead they corrupted and falsified it with their own trifles, fictions, and rash sayings, precepts, and prescriptions, forcing others to attend to these things. Compare Jeremiah 8:8; Luke 11:52. Indeed, I wish all handlers of the Holy Scriptures or sacred doctrine would remember this place, lest they be like sheep drinking the water and fouling the rest with their feet. For if someone takes for himself what he understands (or wants to understand) from the Holy Scriptures, and does not want others to read, understand, or observe those things he perhaps has not read or noticed—making a noise against those who read and share them, and interpreting what he doesn't understand according to his own will, forcing others to approve it and permitting no one to think more sincerely—does he not act like those petulant sheep who drink the pure water and stir up the rest, making it muddy? <margin>verse 19. m) The Hebrew says: "And so"</margin> "My flock," those who truly are my sheep. Verses 12, 15, 22. Note the emphasis of the *Atnach* <note>a Hebrew accent mark indicating a major pause</note>. **n)** "Only that which is trampled." Compare verse 18; Ezekiel 7:25. **o)** "And that which is fouled" (l). **p)** That is, they are forced not to enjoy the sincere Word of God and the voices of the Holy Spirit, but to hear the Word corrupted and contaminated by opinions, conjectures, fantasies, and fables. **Cocceius.**

**v. 20. q)** To the pious and the impious: to the latter for terror, to the former for consolation. **r)** Hebrew: "Behold I, I, I say, will be present." See verse 11. **s)** "And I will judge." Verses 11, 17. **t)** The "fat, well-fed one," concerning which see verse 16. (1) The Greek Septuagint says "the strong." Compare Mark 2:17. **u)** "The lean one" (2) Numbers 13:18. The Greek Septuagint says "the weak." Mark 14:38; 1 Corinthians 9:22. **Grotius** and **Jonathan**: "between the rich and the poor." I will vindicate the latter and punish the former. **Cocceius:** That is, between those who are satisfied and those who are thirsty, or those hungering and thirsting for righteousness.

**v. 21. x)** "Because with sides and shoulders." But **Schmidt** says: "Because, namely, through narrowness and a violent shoulder," having been deceived by a faulty reading. **y)** "You fat or wealthy ones push and drive, and keep on driving." As larger livestock are accustomed to shove and butt the smaller ones. Compare Numbers 35:20; Proverbs 10:3. **z)** "And with strength and power" (so Jonathan), as if striking with your horns like petulant goats and rams. See Daniel 8:4. **a)** "All the weak." Verse 4. **b)** "Until you have dispersed and expelled them." Jeremiah 23:1, 2. **c)** "Outwards," out of their fold or stall. **Cocceius:** This refers to those who did not rejoice with the "strong" ones (who seemed wise and righteous to themselves) and did not admire them or applaud them. Instead, being exhausted by long expectation, burdened by the yoke of the law, and weighed down by the injury of the shepherds and the strong sheep, they mourned and were saddened, hungering and thirsting for the righteousness of God. These the strong ones pursue and drive away as if they were unrighteous, declaring them "expelled from the synagogue" <note>original Greek: aposynagōgōs</note>. Yet these are the very ones whom Christ called to Himself when He came. Matthew 11:28.

**v. 22. d)** Hebrew: "Therefore I will save my flock." Verses 12, 19; chapter 36:25; Zephaniah 3:19. **Grotius:** The same sense as above in verse 13. **Cocceius:** That is, 1) I will make the faithful possessors of their desire, and I will take away their thirst and satisfy them (Jeremiah 31:14). 2) I will make it so they escape the wrath and plagues that hang over the others (Malachi 3:19-20, or chapter 4:1-2 in some versions). **e)** Verses 8, 18. Namely, so that the Word of God is taken away from the oppressors. For when the faithful are no longer bound to the temple, the princes, the city, the politics, or the land, but follow Christ and His Gospel, nothing can be snatched from them, because they wish to have nothing except the Kingdom and the righteousness of God. However, it is specifically hinted here that the power of the shepherds is to be so diminished and broken that they cease to harm the faithful. **Cocceius.** **f)** Verses 17, 20. **Cocceius:** This signifies that from that time on, God will not allow the saints and the hypocrites to be mixed for long, but with His winnowing fan He will separate the chaff from the wheat through His Word and Spirit.

**v. 23. g)** Hebrew: "But I will raise up." **Tremellius:** "For I will raise up." Verse 29; Deuteronomy 18:15. **h)** Verse 15; chapter 37:24; Psalm 23:1; Isaiah 40:11; John 10:11; 1 Peter 2:25; Hebrews 13:20. See also the notes on Isaiah 9:5. This refers to the Chief Shepherd <note>original Greek: archipoimēn</note>, Christ, who had to come: first as a teaching shepherd; second as a shepherd laying down his life for the sheep; and third to be manifested as a prince—so that the promise of God (that He would be a God to the seed of Abraham) would become "Yes and Amen." 2 Corinthians 1:20. **Cocceius.** **i)** "One," without a partner or a vicar. Chapter 37:24. **k)** "Who shall feed them." Matthew 2:6. The gender varies in the Hebrew because "flock" (*tzon*) is of common gender. **l)** Namely, "my servant." See Isaiah 42:1; 43:10; 49:3, 5, 6; 50:10; 53:13; Philippians 2:7, 8. **Cocceius:** Christ is called the "Servant of God" because He was made under the law (also a minister of the circumcision, Romans 15:8) and fulfilled it, so that He might expiate sins and bring in righteousness, and thus be a perfected Redeemer <note>original Hebrew: Goel; original Greek: lytrotēs</note>. Compare Galatians 4:4, 5.

<meta>This page continues the transition from God’s judgment of the "fat sheep" (the oppressive leaders) to the promise of a restoration under a single, faithful Shepherd. The focus shifts to the identity of this "David" and the nature of the "covenant of peace" that brings both spiritual and physical safety.</meta>

->### EZEKIEL. CHAPTER 34.<-

<margin>
**m)** On **David** (v. 24; see also chapter 37:24; Hosea 3:5; Isaiah 55:3; Jeremiah 23:5; Psalm 132:10). This refers to **Christ**, the **Messiah**, who is called "David" because the historical King David was a *type* <note>In biblical study, a "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future spiritual reality.</note> of Him. He is named this by association <note>original Latin: metonymice</note>, because He is of the family of David, and is David’s head and bridegroom. He fulfills the pattern of David as the ultimate Truth, and in Him, David’s kingdom is eternal and without end (Luke 1:32-33). Gussetius (page 683) says that just as there is a "Second Adam" (Christ) of whom the first Adam was a forerunner, in the same way, there is a "Second David" foreshadowed by the first. The Rabbis themselves speak this way in the Talmud, Book Sanhedrin, chapter 11, folio 98.
</margin>

<margin>
...with His blood, He will perform all the duties of a shepherd, for their **preservation** <note>original Greek: peripoiēsin</note> and **refreshment** <note>original Greek: anapsyxin</note> and revival; and He will remain their shepherd forever (Psalm 23:1; Revelation 7:17).
**v. 24. p)** **Meaning:** I, even I...

***

**q)** Jehovah, God the Father. **s)** He shall be a prince (chapter 37:24, 25) and shall be exalted above all things, as the head in their midst (Ephesians 1:22; Micah 5:1; Isaiah 55:4; Luke 1:32; 1 Kings 11:34). The one He first called a "servant," He now calls a "prince." Likewise in Daniel, the Messiah is both "cut off" and a "prince" <note>original Hebrew: nagid</note> (Daniel 9:25-26). Humility comes first, followed by exaltation (Ephesians 4:9). **Cocceius**. <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century theologian known for "Federal Theology" which focused on the covenants.</note> **u)** A **covenant of peace** <note>original Greek: Diathēkēn eirēnēs</note> (Hebrews 8:10; Acts 3:25). **x)** (Compare Isaiah 54:10; Romans 5:1; Colossians 1:20). He promises peace added to them by a covenant—we rightly understand "covenant" as a **testament**; as if to say, "I will make you heirs of peace according to the testament." The New Testament, which brings the forgiveness of sins without the memory of sin, is undoubtedly a **testament of peace**. This peace was to be preached by Christ's Apostles even to the Gentiles, who are blessed in Christ (Ephesians 2:17; Isaiah 56:3-7), bringing liberty from the yoke of the Law and from wrath. Christ, the messenger of peace, also has a law of peace which the nations heed. **y)** He further emphasizes this peace until the end of the verse, noting that God will gradually cut off those who infest the Church so that they may finally live securely among the nations and God's enemies. **z)** **Meaning:** that they may dwell even in the wilderness, in the place of pasture assigned to them in the world. A place was prepared for the Church in the wilderness (Revelation 12:6, 14), after it had wandered for a time seeking a city to dwell in (Psalm 107:4). **c)** **In the woods:** Even the frightening forests will provide every benefit to the godly (Isaiah 10:18-19). Both readings of the text mean the same thing. **d)** I will also grant these things to the faithful, who are my true sheep. **e)** Those who are around my hill, Zion. **Targum Jonathan:** the house of my sanctuary. **Cocceius** says: those who approach my hill from all sides—that is, those who join the Church or allow the Church to live quietly in their midst. The Church becomes a great mountain (Daniel 2:35), but in its beginnings here, it is called a "hill." It is likened to Mount Zion where God dwelt (Revelation 14:1). It is called a hill especially when it is not scattered, but gathered and bound together as one. **f)** **In blessing:** I will heap so many goods upon them that they will be an example of blessing (Genesis 12:2; Psalm 21:7). **i)** Not a meager rain, but every spiritual blessing **in the heavenly places** <note>original Greek: en tois epouraniois</note>; such as can be desired from a blessing God, so that food is never lacking for the sheep. Following the allegory, this signifies the preaching of the Word and the increasingly abundant light of the doctrine of truth. **Colobium** says: this regards the shower of the Word and the rain of the Gospel, which brings true blessing (Isaiah 44:3; Psalm 68:10; Romans 15:29). **l)** **Trees:** Cocceius interprets these as the "princes" or leaders in the Church. **m)** The glosses say the trees will be fertile, which often happens in exhausted soil. But **Maius** more correctly says: the "trees of righteousness" in the Church will grow joyfully and bring forth rich fruit for the praise of God (Isaiah 61:3). **n)** In the land: meaning the humble common people will not lack faith or confession. From both orders (leaders and commoners), there will be those who seal the truth with their blood. **o)** They shall have the world, or a significant part of it, serving them as their own. **r)** The **bars of their yoke** (Isaiah 56:6) refers to the Law and to "Antichristian tyranny." This looks back to Leviticus 26:13. Men will try to impose this yoke on the Church to reduce it to slavery, and many will receive it, but my sheep will not (John 8:36; Acts 15:10).

<margin>
**CHAPTER 35.** ...driven to hunger. Compare Amos 8:11, Matthew 5:6, John 6:27, 35, and Revelation 7:16-17. This section stands in opposition to the earlier judgments in chapters 5:12, 16; 6:11, 12; 17:15; and 21:16. e) "The reproach of the nations" (chapter 36:6, 15), but finally they shall shine with heavenly glory (Matthew 13:43). Vatable says the nations will no longer say to them that God has deserted them. Compare Psalm 115:2, Jeremiah 51:51, and Isaiah 61:7.
</margin>

Others translate: "The nations shall know that..." (v. 27). g) Genesis 17:7, Leviticus 26:12. h) "I shall be with them," as a protector and helper. See Revelation 21:3. Jonathan <note>referring to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation</note>: "My Word shall be for their help." i) They are truly my people, the church of the living God, and the seed of Israel (chapter 36:8, 37:27, Zechariah 8:8, 2 Corinthians 6:16). k) For just as Abraham was, so also Israel is the father of a multitude of nations; Cocceius compares this to Psalm 24:6. l) verse 15, etc. <margin>v. 31. m) S. "You therefore," or "But you,"</margin> my flock (v. 17). n) "Sheep of my pasture" or "of my feeding" (10) <note>Latin: pascuui/passionis</note>. See Jeremiah 10:21, Hosea 13:6, Psalm 95:7. o) S. "You shall be man." It is as if to say: "At last you will be wise and understand that you are human beings; therefore you will stop following lusts, which belong to brutes and not to men, and you will cling entirely to me." Others: "You are men, born for piety, humanity, and justice, not cattle or brutes." Compare Psalm 32:9. It is as if God says: "These things I depicted through the imagery of livestock do not apply to animals, but to men, and specifically to you Jews." See also chapter 36:37-38. Cocceius feels this way: He addresses the Jews by apostrophe <note>a literary device where the speaker addresses an absent person or personified object</note>, who until now were stubborn toward Christ and His church. When this is noted, a very clear sense emerges: that God will have mercy on those sheep whom He once claimed as His own and separated from all nations, to whom He gave the land, the law, and His covenant—since they are human beings—and He will be their God. When the nations recognize who the people of God and the true Israel are (v. 30), then the disobedient Jews will also recognize it; they will tremble before the Lord and His goodness, and before David their King (Hosea 3:5). Compare Leviticus 26:44-45. The cause of this mercy is God's "love for mankind" <note>original Greek: Φιλανθρωπια (Philanthropia)</note> (expressed in "you are men"). Therefore, at the time when God most wishes to show His love for humanity, He will remember them as men and as children of the first covenant. Others: "You are men, weak creatures; yet I will be your God." p) S. "But I." q) See v. 30. r) chapter 11:8, 16:14.

<column-break/>

**CHAPTER 35.** v. 1. s) Furthermore, it happened... <margin>v. 2. t) "Set your face"—with a severe and threatening demeanor, so that the listeners understand you are dealing with a serious matter (chapter 6:2, 25:2, 38:21, 29:2). u) "Against the mountains of Seir," that is, against the Edomites living in the mountainous regions of Seir (Genesis 36:9). Junius says: He includes all enemies of the church under the name of "Edomites," because they were the closest, best known, and most hostile to the Jews. However, for Cocceius, the Jewish people are figuratively signified here under the name of "Edom" and "Mount Seir." He argues that this chapter deals with their abolition, just as chapter 34 dealt with the abolition of the [bad] shepherds, so that the sheep might be under the rule of Christ. For at that time when Christ was to rule, the Jewish people could be called "Edom" by synecdoche <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note>, because Edom was contained within the multitude of the Jews, and the Idumaeans were part of the people—having accepted circumcision and the other rites—and because the [later] kings were of Edomite descent, such as Herod and his successors. Cocceius pursues all of this at greater length in this chapter. As for us, while we believe the text can be applied well in a prophetic and mystical sense to every "Edomite spirit" in every age, we nevertheless understand it most directly and literally to refer to the people of the Edomites, and we will direct our notes primarily toward that. See above at chapter 25:8, 12; Jeremiah 49:7; and the notes on Isaiah 34:1, 5; 63:1. x) chapter 29:2, 38:2. y) S. "I will be against you" (chapter 34:10). z) verses 2, 7, 15. a) chapter 6:14, 25:7, 13; Isaiah 31:3. b) chapter 7:2; Obadiah verse 2. c) chapter 33:28-29. Gurtlerus indicates some fulfillment of this in his *Prophetic Theology* (page 369) from 2 Maccabees 10:17, 23. v. 4. d) Compare chapter 25:3, Isaiah 25:2, Malachi 1:3, Zechariah 12:6. e) chapter 12:20, 14:15-16. f) verses 13, 15; chapter 25:7.
</margin>

### Extended Commentary
[...continued from Column 1] that Israel would do and suffer something through which God, who justifies, would be sanctified. *In you*, that is, by synecdoche <note>using a part to represent the whole</note> in some of you, in your brother, the son of Abraham—Meanwhile, this phrase also carries that emphasis, meaning that obedience and sufferings, and indeed the sacrifice is a <term>ransom</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντίλυτρον (antilytron)</note> for Israel, that is, for the sanctified, because of the union of the guarantor and those to be redeemed, the head and the members—Thus in Christ we are said to be circumcised, crucified, dead, made alive, placed in the heavenly places; because what is done in the guarantor belongs to those for whom he pledged, etc. Others like S. with the Septuagint, Jonathan, the Syriac, and the Arabic read *through the justice of the third person, in their eyes*, as in chapter 38, 16. cf. various readings.

$\ast$ v. 24. a) S. *Therefore I will receive you*. cf. Isaiah 14, 2. b) c. 11, 17. c. 20, 34. 41. c. 37, 21. c) c. 34, 13.

$\ast$ v. 25. d) S. *And I will scatter*. cf. Exodus 24, 6. Numbers 19, 9. 13. etc. e) pure and purifying waters, from the fountains of salvation, that is, Jesus. Isaiah 12, 3. cf. c. 47, 9. & see Isaiah 44, 3. Zechariah 13, 1. Hebrews 10, 22. 23. John 3, 5. c. 7, 38. 39. Jerome: *the clean water of saving baptism*. cf. Titus 3, 6. Cocceius: It must be understood as a thing clean in itself and having the power to remove guilt and filth—This thing is the obedience of the guarantor, that is, the priest offering a sacrifice for sin, and indeed obedience even unto death and the shedding of blood. Its *sprinkling* is its imputation <note>assigning the merit of one to another</note>; which imputation all the sprinklings and washings commanded in the law signified, to which Peter also alludes in 1 Peter 1, 2. see also Cocceius's Lexicon p. 276. f) He alludes to legal purifications, but especially to the waters mixed with the ashes of the red heifer sacrifice for sin. Numbers 19, 9. Thus Jonathan: *I will forgive your sins, just as they are cleansed by the waters of sprinkling and the ash of the heifer of the sacrifice for sin*. g) cf. v. 33. Leviticus 16, 30. Numbers 31, 24. Psalm 51, 9. Acts 15, 9. 1 Corinthians 6, 11. Ephesians 5, 26. Hebrews 9, 14. 15. h) v. 29. cf. Leviticus 16, 16. 19. i) c. 20, 31. k) cf. Jeremiah 33, 8.

$\ast$ v. 26 l) *And I will give to you through regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit.* see c. 11, 19. m) cf. Deuteronomy 30, 6 following. Jeremiah 31, 33. c. 32, 39. 2 Corinthians 3, 3. n) Jerome: *A new heart, so that they might believe in the Son of God, and a new Spirit*; about which David spoke in Psalm 51, 12. cf. above c. 18, 31. Jeremiah 31, 31 following. *Heart* in scripture signifies the soul itself, especially the will. *Spirit* signifies the movement and pulse by which one is incited to do something. Junius and others. cf. above c. 11, 19. o) v. 27. Jeremiah 31, 33. p) *A heart of stone*, which admits no impression of pious and healthy doctrine. Jerome: the hardness of the heart is compared to a stone. Junius: into which, no more than into a rock, can seed be cast. Jonathan: *I will break the impious heart, which is hard like stone*. q) i.e. regarding you, now carnal cf. John 3, 6. r) *A heart of flesh* c. 11, 19. Jerome: i.e. soft and tender, which can receive the Spirit of God into itself, and be inscribed with the letters of salvation. Jonathan: *A heart fearing me to do my will*.

$\ast$ v. 27. s) My Spirit, I say. Jonathan: *adds "holy"*. c. 37, 14. c. 39, 29. Isaiah 44, 3. Joel 3, 1. 2. Zechariah 4, 6. c. 12, 10. t) see v. 26. u) S. *that you might walk*. x) c. 11, 20. y) c. 18, 9. z) cf. Luke 1, 74. 75.

* v. 29 d) Chapter 34:22; 37:23. cf. Matthew 1:21. e) see verse 25.
*Grotius*: i.e., from the idolatrous stains to which the Jews never relapsed afterward. compare note on Jeremiah 3:15. However, this promise is more widely applicable, cf. Titus 2:14.
f) *And I will call for the grain.* *Schmid* <note>Sebastian Schmid, a Lutheran theologian</note>: "and I will command the grain." *Vatablus* <note>François Vatable, a French Hebraist</note>: "I will effect by a word that it should come; as servants are accustomed to gather at a master's nod." cf. the opposite in 2 Kings 8:1 and the note there. g) "grain" refers not only to the physical or natural, but especially the spiritual, cf. Hosea 2:23, 24. Zechariah 9:17. Grotius: "the fields will be fruitful"; but these words are more sublimely fulfilled in Christ, Matthew 14:15. Abraham Calovius <note>A strict Lutheran theologian</note>, page 555: "Though we admit," he says, "that promises about temporal things are mixed in—the return to the land of Canaan, the blessing of trees and fields, and the multiplication of the people of Israel—nevertheless, spiritual benefits of calling, regeneration, justification, sanctification, etc., are primarily promised here. And the Lord promised to bring the people back to the land of Canaan in verse 24 so that divine worship might be restored there, and the Israelites might be a people to the Lord, and He might be their God (verse 28). This is especially because of the kingdom of Christ, which is prophesied to be propagated in the fullness of time, and the sending of the Holy Spirit in verse 25 and following." h) Vatablus: "that is, I will multiply." The prefix "Vau" <note>the Hebrew letter 'and'</note> is explanatory, as in Numbers 31:6. Regarding the word, cf. verses 30, 10, 11, etc.

<meta>This page continues from Ezekiel 36, which concluded with the promise of Israel's spiritual and physical restoration. The commentary now shifts to Chapter 37, the famous vision of the "Valley of Dry Bones," which serves as a prophetic confirmation of the promises made in the previous chapter regarding the return from the Babylonian exile and the future of the Church.</meta>

<header>EZEKIEL 37. CAP. 37.</header>

<margin>
14. Ezekiel, he says, beheld dry bones, scattered across a field, but restored to life by the spirit; a likeness of the Jewish people to be recalled from exile and restored in Canaan. The same author [P. 716] says: The resolution of the Babylonian captivity and the restoration of the Jewish people to their own land is represented by the emblem of the resurrection of the dead.
</margin>

<margin>
**CAP. XXXVII, 1. a)** It came to pass. *Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian known for federal theology</note>: It began to be upon me; *it came over me*. This chapter is connected with the previous one. For since at the end of Chapter 36, from verse 24 onward, He had spoken of the restoration of Israel to its integrity, God wished to confirm that matter here with a certain type and figure. Therefore, in the figure of the dry bones coming back to life, the resurrection of the dead and the restoration of Israel are signified; and by the joining of two sticks, the union of the Jews and Israelites under Christ is signified. The *parts* of this chapter, according to *Schmid* <note>Sebastian Schmid, 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note>, are two: I. The prophetic vision of the dead and dry bones coming back to life (v. 1–10), with the explanation regarding the children of Israel to be brought back into their land (v. 11–14). II. The prophecy concerning Judah and Israel, as if two sticks were being reduced into one under the Messiah, and their future happiness (v. 15–28). **u)** See Chapter 1:3, 33:22, 40:1. *Jonathan* <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note>: "The Spirit of Prophecy from before the Lord." **x)** Not transported in body, but in spirit, i.e., in a vision. Compare Chapter 8:3, 11:24, 2 Corinthians 12:2 ff. **y)** S. <note>likely "Syriac" or a specific manuscript</note> *Jehovah*; Better the Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note>, *Grotius*, & *Tremellius*, etc.: *Jehovah* or *The Lord*, in the Nominative case. The accents suggest this; the term is also more frequently feminine. **z)** And he placed me gently [Chapter 4]. **2. a)** Of some valley (v. 3), as above in Chapter 3:22. **b)** To the bones. The Septuagint and Jonathan add "human." Compare the note on Isaiah 66:14. *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, Dutch jurist and scholar</note>: A people led into captivity ceases to be a people; therefore they are best compared to bones or a dead body. *Vatablus* <note>François Vatable, French Hebraist</note>: Just as there is no hope of future life in dry bones, so the Israelites did not hope for a return to their fatherland; yet their liberation is predicted here (cf. v. 11). Namely, according to *Vitringa* <note>Campegius Vitringa, Dutch theologian</note> on Apocalypse 20:5, p. 1163: The Prophet vaticinates <note>prophesies</note> about the return of the Jews from the Babylonian exile under the type of resurrection. So says Gürtler in *Prophetic Theology*, p. 34.
</margin>

# CHAPTER XXXVII.

-> 1 The hand of the LORD was upon me, and He brought me out by the Spirit of the LORD and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. <-

-> 2 And He led me all around them; and behold, there were very many on the surface of the valley; and behold, they were very dry. <-

-> 3 And He said to me, "Son of man, can these bones live?" And I said, "O Lord GOD, You know." <-

-> 4 And He said to me, "Prophesy over these bones and say to them: 'O dry bones, hear the word of the LORD.'" <-

-> 5 Thus says the Lord GOD to these bones: "Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and you shall live." <-

-> 6 "And I will lay sinews upon you and bring up flesh upon you, and cover you with skin and put breath in you, and you shall live; and you shall know that I am the LORD." <-

-> 7 So I prophesied as I was commanded; and as I prophesied, there was a sound, and behold, a rattling; and the bones came together, bone to its bone. <-

---

And *Dorscheus* <note>Johann Georg Dorsche, Lutheran theologian</note> on Isaiah 66:14 says: *The ancients and moderns alike interpret this as the resurrection—yet immediately it also speaks of the restoration of the church, and its leading forth, as it were, from the cradle.* However, the liberation of the Jews (to speak again with *Vitringa*, p. 1164) from the Babylonian exile was not a type of the benefit that befell the church around the times of Constantine; but of what would befall it around that time when, having been long oppressed by the empire of the *mystic Babylon*, it would finally be vindicated into full liberty. The Spirit thus teaches us that a *mystic* sense underlies this prophecy of Ezekiel, and it is to be referred <term>πνευματικῶς</term> <note>original: "pneumatikos" — spiritually</note> to that great salvation which God would finally grant to the church of the New Covenant after a long time of afflictions and struggle with the empire of superstition and wickedness, fulfilling the faithfulness of His promises. Learned men and interpreters certainly disagree regarding the scope and sense of this so illustrious vision, and its threefold sense is already handed down by *Jerome*, as *Calovius* observed. For some, like *Tertullian* in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 30, explain it as the *universal resurrection*. Another opinion is about the *restoration of the people* from the graves and chains of the Babylonian captivity; which the *Jews (and Grotius)* say was fulfilled under *Zerubbabel*, when a great commotion occurred and the kingdom of the Chaldeans was transferred to the Medes and Persians. Although others still hope for it only in the presence of Christ or their Messiah, whom they think is yet to come. The third opinion is that of *Jerome* himself: who does not deny that it began to be fulfilled in the faithful under Zerubbabel, with the Israelite church gathered again, but refers the completion to the times of the New Testament. Our opinion, says *Calovius* [p. 557], is that the resurrection of the dead was exhibited by the Lord in this illustrious vision; but the occasion, cause, and scope of this vision was the restoration of the Israelite people (v. 11). Not only to show the possibility of this—but also to sketch out by a kind of "hypotyposis" <note>a vivid, lifelike description</note> the condition and state both present and subsequent (especially in the time of Christ): that they are to be raised as if from the dead, when the Ecclesiastical polity would be restored and public worship reinstated. He confirms this with many arguments, especially from the letter of the text (which *Tertullian* also urges, and *Masius* in *Economy of the Old Testament*, p. 1047 ff.) as well as the consensus of *Jerome, Epiphanius, Justin, and Theodoret* [p. 559]. Compare also the note to verse 8 from the same author. *Cocceius* rightly advised: In the explanation of this parable, care must be taken not to refer it to one thing or to one time. For *what God promises regarding the awakening and vivification of Israel, and thus of the dead, has place and implementation at many times. Whenever the church seems to be as if dead, when the faithful seem reduced to a tiny few (Psalm 12:2), yet He will awaken them as if from the dead.* Yet if you look at the condition of that time, this prophecy first concerns the Israelites, who were in captivity like the dead. The same <unclear>Cocceius</uncalled> <note>Correcting "tocc." to Cocceius</note> notes at v. 11: *this parable extends more widely than the interpretation (provided in this place). For it can and should be understood not only of the Israelites (though they are the first example) but also of the nations brought to life from death in sins, and the afflicted church, and of the dead themselves, who in their time will rise in a spiritual body.* Nor does *Tirinus* <note>Jacobus Tirinus, a Jesuit commentator</note> note badly, following *Tertullian and Augustine*, that the future resurrection of bodies is certainly gathered from here; otherwise, a similarity would not be taken from there to confirm the restoration of Israel. For no one confirms uncertain things through things that are not certainly established. **v. 2. c)** *S. Therefore He led me around over them* [Chapter 46:21]. **d)** [Chapter 8:10, 40:5]. **e)** They were very dry or parched, and as if consumed (v. 4, cf. v. 11, Isaiah 66:14). **v. 3. f)** *Will they live, will they come back to life?* Do you think it possible that they might revive? (cf. note on Isaiah 26:19). **g)** See verse 11. **h)** As if to say: There is no reason for you to ask me. This depends on Your divine counsel, etc. *Grotius*: "You are entirely able; what You wish is Yours to know." Great is the faith of the prophet, and an image of Christian faith, which believes in the resurrection from the dead. *Tremellius* <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a Jewish-Italian convert and reformer</note>: The prophet does not doubt the future resurrection of the flesh to eternal life, but the recovery of the present state, which he therefore commits to the knowledge and providence of God. **v. 4. i)** Verses 7, 9, 12. **k)** Dry bones! (v. 2). **l)** Chapter 36:1, 4. *Grotius*: A "prosopopoeia" <note>personification</note>, the more excusable because by bones, captive men are understood. But you should also understand the dead, and compare John 5:28, 29; Romans 4:17. *Cocceius*: Just as God here addresses the bones through the Prophet, so also through the Gospel He addresses those dead in sin and lapses—and commands them to rise from the dead or to repent (Ephesians 5:14). When they hear and understand this and love that truth, and flee to Christ, they live, etc. **v. 5. m)** Into you (v. 6), i.e., into each number of bones belonging to a single body. *Piscator* <note>Johannes Piscator, German theologian</note>. **n)** *The vital spirit* (v. 6, 14), by which *Grotius* understands the restoration of liberty and state. **o)** *And you shall come back to life*. (cf. Isaiah 26:19, 66:14). **v. 6. p)** *S. For I will give. q)* Tendons or nerves. **(7)** v. 8. Genesis 32:33, Job 10:10, 11. **r)** And *I will bring up flesh upon you* (v. 8). **s)** And *I will bring over, I will draw skin over you*: **(2)** v. 8. (cf. Job 10:11). **t)** v. 5, 14. **u)** v. 5, 10, 14. **x)** v. 13, 14. Chapter 5:13. **v. 7. y)** *So I prophesied* (v. 10). **z)** *As I was commanded*. (v. 4, Chapter 12:7, 24:18). **a)** S. *and there was a sound*. (cf. Chapter 1:25). **b)** While I prophesied. Chapter 11:13. **c)** Chapter 1, 1, 4. **d)** *The noise of the bones*, which were moving, and by approaching others, as follows, were striking together. *Schmid*: "An earthquake." (cf. Chapter 3:12, 13). *Indicating* the sound and noise of the Jews, exulting over their liberation and return, and (following the edict of Cyrus) preparing themselves and packing their belongings. *Cornelius à Lapide* <note>Jesuit exegete</note>. Compare the note to v. 8. **e)** *While they approached. S. they approached therefore*. It is the third person plural feminine in the Future, irregular (cf. similar form in Jeremiah 49:11). **f)** *Bone to its bone* (with which it was to be combined), so that they might be bound with sinews (v. 8).

<summary>This page contains the first seven verses of Ezekiel 37, the vision of the Valley of Dry Bones, accompanied by extensive scholarly commentary. The notes debate whether the vision refers literally to the resurrection of the dead or metaphorically to the restoration of Israel from Babylonian exile and the future growth of the Christian Church.</summary>

--- Page 1121 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Ezekiel 37, specifically focusing on the second half of the vision of the dry bones (verses 8–14) and beginning the prophecy of the two sticks (verse 16). The previous page established the bones as a metaphor for the state of Israel in exile.</meta>

<header>598 EZEKIEL. CAP. 37. 36</header>

<margin>
**v. 8. g)** Chapter 1:4, 44:4. **h)** Verse 6. Isaiah 48:4. **i)** *And flesh came up, increased.* Verse 6, Chapter 19:3. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 17th-century federal theologian</note>: *he saw in them sinews and flesh*, that is, he saw them (the Israelites) gradually breathe again and recover their former wealth and strength. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note>: *First the bones are joined with other bones by the bonds of the sinews, then they are filled with flesh, and skin is stretched over them from above for the sake of beauty, to cover the deformity of the naked flesh*, and then they receive the Spirit, which makes them live (verse 10). **k)** *And it was covered.* Cocceius in his Lexicon: *and he brought skin over them.* In his commentary: *he drew skin over them.* Verse 6. That is, according to Cocceius: they began to be a great people, indeed having leaders, and fathers, and priests, and their ornaments, and political liberty itself; moreover, power was even given to them over the neighboring nations on every side. **l)** *Yet the Spirit was not yet in them.* John 7:39. The Holy Spirit was not yet there, because Christ was not yet glorified. They were still placed in servitude, in fear, expectation, and desire, and they were sick; while food indeed was provided as good for all by God, but it was diverted by the shepherds, etc. (Cocceius). But Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius, 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> says (p. 559): In the first part of this prophecy up to verse 10, *the resurrection of the dead is treated according to the letter, and that is the unique sense of that speech.* But lest the immediate cause be hidden from the Prophet as to why God wished to show him this resuscitation of the dead, a second speech follows in verse 11 and following, in which the words of the previous speech are not merely explained, nor is the application of the parable given; but the goal of that preceding vision is shown through the analogy which restoration has with **Corporal** resuscitation.
</margin>

Thus Theodoret <note>5th-century bishop and theologian</note>, etc.

Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, 17th-century Dutch jurist and scholar</note>: It signifies the gathering of the people from all regions. just as in the first condition of man God breathed into his face and he was made into a living soul; so also in the second condition, that is, the resurrection of the dead, they shall be made alive by the breathing of the spirit; compare Psalm 104:30. **v. 10. t)** *When I prophesied.* Verse 7. **u)** Verses 5, 9; compare Chapter 2:2, 3:24. **x)** Verses 5, 6, 9. Cocceius: *It is signified that according to the word of God and the faith, hope, desire, and prayers of the faithful, the Spirit of God shall come from heaven, and without distinction of place, race, or nation, shall animate the Israel of God—so that they may be robust, that their soul may live.* **v. 11. y)** *Then he said.* **z)** Verse 2, 3, etc. **a)** *Those are a type or image of the whole House of Israel.* Cocceius: *The first example of these bones being made alive are the Israelites. The whole house of Israel, not just Judah and Benjamin, but all the tribes. Indeed, the whole church.* **b)** *Who, behold, are saying.* **c)** Compare verse 2, that is: *our affairs are deplored; no hope remains of returning to the fatherland.* Grotius and Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator, 16th-century German theologian</note>. **d)** *And our hope has perished.* Chapter 19:5. **e)** *We are cut off for ourselves. i.e. according to Jonathan: we have perished. Namely, as a limb torn from the body;* Grotius. Compare Lamentations 3:54. **f)** That is, to our evil or our loss (Vatablus <note>François Vatable, 16th-century French scholar</note>). **v. 12. g)** Verses 4, 9. **h)** *I am about to open.* Verse 13, Jeremiah 5:16. **i)** *As if from your graves,* verse 13. That is, according to Vatablus: *from the cities, lands, and prisons in which you are held captive.* Grotius: *I will cause the mounds, so to speak, to be opened for you. I will restore civil life to you.* The Prophet persists in the allegory. Cocceius: *The places of captivity were like graves; because 1. they could not leave them and return to the fatherland at will. 2. in them they were as if dead, rarely having the word of God, and as long as they were in them, deprived of the hope of the coming of Christ to procure salvation—The opening of the graves signifies the permission to depart from all places of captivity.* This opening was made through the destruction of the Babylonian empire and its transfer to Cyrus, the author of the people's liberty, and the building of the city and temple, etc. **k)** *My people!* verse 13. By which name two things are signified: 1. that because of His covenant with the Fathers, and because He had chosen that people in whom He wished to dwell in the land, He would lead them back. 2. that He would lead back those from all the tribes whom He had chosen for this, so that they, or their descendants, would be the first to hear the words of Christ, and see His works and passions, as the people of God, and the preaching of the Gospel would go out from them. For from Jeremiah 3:14, it is clear that God did not absolutely and simply promise a return to the fatherland to all their individuals without exception (Cocceius). **v. 14. l)** Verse 13. **m)** Verses 6, 14. **n)** *When, namely, I shall have opened.* Verse 12. **v. 14. o)** *And I shall have given* etc. Verse 6, Chapter 36:27. Cocceius: *The Apostle calls this the Spirit of the Son in Galatians 4:6. And indeed, He speaks here who showed Himself as one about to come in the flesh, at the very beginning of the vision. See Chapter 1:26.* **p)** *That you may live.* Verses 5, 6, 10; compare Isaiah 26:19, 66:14, Romans 11:15, Luke 15:24. Cocceius: *you shall serve Me with joy. For life consists especially in a good will, in love and joy.* **q)** *And I shall have placed* etc. Isaiah 14:1. **r)** Verse 12. **s)** Verses 6, 13. **t)** Chapter 17:24, 22:14, 36:36. **u)** Chapter 11:8. **v. 15. x)** The second part of this chapter begins. See note at verse 1. **v. 16. y)** Jonathan and Vatablus: *a wooden tablet or writing-tablets. Others, rather with the Septuagint and Arabic versions: a single rod.* Menochius <note>Giovanni Stefano Menochio, 17th-century Jesuit scholar</note>: *rods here signify scepters or kingdoms.* Calovius: *for a scepter, the symbol of a kingdom, was made of wood.* **z)** *That is, with an inscription made to specifically designate which people is shadowed by the rod.* Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, 16th-century Jewish convert and Hebraist</note>. Compare Numbers 17:17, 18. **a)** *For Judah or pertaining to Judah is this tablet or rod.* **b)** *And his companions.* Verse 19, Judges 20:11. By whom are understood, as Calovius notes, those who in the first schism under Rehoboam (1 Kings 12) followed the side of Judah along with the tribes of Benjamin and Levi; such as were some from all the tribes (2 Chronicles 11:16); then those from the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who withdrew to Asa, the grandson of Solomon (2 Chronicles 15:9); as well as those who under Hezekiah joined from the tribes of Asher, Manasseh, Zebulun, and Issachar (2 Chronicles 30:11, 18; 31:1). **c)** Then take also a certain other wood.

<summary>This page concludes the vision of the dry bones coming to life, interpreting the miracle as a metaphor for Israel's political and spiritual restoration from exile. It also introduces the symbolic act of joining two sticks to represent the future unification of the divided kingdoms of Judah and Israel.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Ezekiel 37. While the previous section dealt with the resurrection of the dry bones, this page transitions to the symbolic action of the two sticks, representing the reunification of the divided kingdoms of Israel (Ephraim) and Judah under a single, Davidic ruler.</meta>

<header>CHAPTER 37. EZEKIEL 37</header>

<margin>(the tribes of Israel) to himself! <note>Note on verse 16: connecting the tribes back to the main body.</note>
**His companions** <note>original: "חבריו קרי" — a Masoretic note to read the word as plural</note>; together with that Ephraim, with the stick of Judah. Schin. <note>likely an abbreviation for a scholar or manuscript</note>: I will add them, those who are upon it with the stick of Judah. Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, 16th-century Hebraist</note>: I will arrange these tablets joined to him with the stick of Judah. But Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 17th-century theologian</note>: and I will give them to it, near the stick of Judah (v. 16). s) v. 22. cf. Isaiah 11:13. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note>: into one people. t) so that they might be one Stick or kingdom (v. 17) under my care and protection. This is because many from the ten tribes joined themselves to Judah upon the return from Babylon and coalesced with them into one republic; and primarily, through Christ (v. 22, 24; Hosea 2:2), who removed the rivalry between the Jews and the Samaritans, joined both into one church, and added the Gentiles to the Jews (Ephesians 2:14). Cocceius: it signifies that two kingdoms are to be merged into one. So it was done; and this by such a wonderful and signal power of God, that raising the dead is no more evident a miracle than effecting this; especially because this was done through an effective power upon the wills of many men. — In the land, all the tribes acknowledged one temple and obeyed one senate (cf. Nehemiah 11:1). Thus Joseph and Judah and their companions became one people. Indeed, they all shared the name of "Jews." But this is only a slight preparation for the unity of the kingdom which He clearly promises. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, 17th-century jurist and theologian</note>: This prophecy would have had its full effect in those tribes if they had seriously turned to God; now, because few did so, it profited few. — In all the promises and threats of God, a silent condition is underlying, as Ezekiel himself said (c. 33:13) and Jeremiah (c. 18:7, 8). But Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius, a strict Lutheran critic of Grotius</note>: Grotius rashly makes this prophecy conditional. For there is nothing in the text to teach that what is absolutely predicted should be understood under a condition. Nor is it true that all promises have a silent condition. For there are also absolute promises, such as that regarding the manifestation of the Messiah, the New Testament, etc. Nor are all threats conditional, such as those regarding the extermination of the Canaanites or the Babylonian captivity.</margin>

17 And join them one to another for yourself into one stick; and they shall become one in your hand.

<margin>d) instead of Joseph. Namely, the stick of Ephraim (v. 19). Jonathan: to the tribe of Joseph, which is the tribe of Ephraim, because the kingdom was in that tribe. For Jeroboam, who ruled Israel when the empire was divided, was from the tribe of Ephraim. Vatablus <note>François Vatable, 16th-century scholar</note>. e) For the rest of the house of Israel were companions to Ephraim just as Benjamin was to Judah; Grotius. Thus, by Ephraim we understand the ten tribes, of which Ephraim was the head. Others, however, wish for the Gentiles to be figured here by the ten tribes (since those tribes degenerated into profane nations, and few of them returned to the land of Israel after the Babylonian captivity compared to those who remained), who through faith in Christ are made one people with the true Jews. v. 17. f) S. Afterward join them to yourself. It is an Imperative. So Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, medieval Jewish commentator</note> and M. I. Piel <note>A Hebrew verb form</note> (6) Isaiah 41:21; Hosea 7:6; Psalm 65:5; similar form in Job 36:2. g) one to another (Isaiah 27:12). h) that both may become one.</margin>

<margin>v. 19. Ezekiel 26:6, 11. Cocceius: whether this is to be understood as those two sticks cohering in his hand so as to become one continuous piece of wood; or whether it pertains to this command, that he should hold the two sticks so joined in his hand that they appear to be one stick.</margin>

Hosea 2:2. e) chapter 34:13, 14. Moreover, Grotius is entirely wrong to understand Zerubbabel here; since he is nowhere called "King" (though frequently called *pechah* <note>original: "פחה" — governor</note> or prefect), nor was he such in reality, and he presided over only a few Jews returning from Babylon, and that for only a few years; whereas the King of this place is said to rule over *all* Israelites forever (v. 25, compared with Luke 1:33). See the learned arguments Bochart disputes against Grotius (Hieroz. I. p. 217, 218) and Calovius on this place. Nor can the kingdom of the Hasmoneans <note>The Maccabean dynasty</note> be understood here. For previously in chapter 21:27, 32, it was shown that that crown was not the promised crown. And the following things testify that God speaks of a new kingdom, which is a kingdom of infinity; Cocceius. cf. John 18:36; Romans 14:17. g) nor shall they be divided. Niphal <note>A Hebrew passive verb form</note> (4) 2 Kings 2:8; Daniel 11:4. h) S. further—again. The particle is doubled for greater expression. i) as in 1 Kings 12:19. cf. Zechariah 11, v. 23. k) chapter 14:11. l) chapter 23:30; 36:24. c) chapter 5:11; Ezekiel 6:3. n) chapter 14:11. o) for I will save them. chapter 34:23; 36:29. p) from all their dwelling places (chapter 6:6, 14). Marsh. <note>likely Narcissus Marsh</note>: that is, I will rescue them from all the habitations in which they worshipped idols and were addicted to abominable things; cf. chapter 14:13. Cocceius: it signifies that fruit of Christ's death which the Apostle teaches in Galatians 1:4, namely, that through it they are made free and exempt from this evil age. q) chapter 36:25, 33. r) v. 27; chapter 36:28. s) v. 27; chapter 34:24. v. 24. t) v. 25. see chapter 34:23. Kimchi: that is, the King Messiah who is called David, because he will be of the offspring of David. So also clearly Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, 15th-century statesman and commentator</note>: because he will be of his seed and will walk in the ways of David and imitate his character. Just as all the Kings of Egypt were for a long time called first by the name of Pharaoh, and later Ptolemy; so the King Messiah and all his descendants (so the Jew wrongly says <note>The Christian commentator here disagrees with Abarbanel's view that there would be a succession of earthly kings</note>) shall be called by the name of David. u) A spiritual King shall be over them (v. 22; Ezekiel 37:7; Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 14:9; Micah 4:7; John 18:36). x) S. so that there may be one shepherd. chapter 34:12, 23; Isaiah 40:11; John 10:11. Cocceius: He did not wish to say only this, that Christ, the son of David, would be king and shepherd for them, or would have a kingdom among them in which he feeds his sheep from among them; but that Christ is in the same way the shepherd of all, with the same food, in the same justice and liberty without distinction of slaves and free men, so that all are brothers and do not have their shepherd and their people under another king who occupies his place and prescribes another law for them; and finally that he will be the one shepherd for all—so that he is received by all and receives all as his sheep, etc.</margin>

<summary>This page discusses Ezekiel's prophecy of the two sticks, which symbolizes the reunification of Judah and Israel into a single nation. The commentary identifies the "one king" and "one shepherd" as the Messiah, debating historical interpretations (like Zerubbabel) in favor of a spiritual, eternal reign of Christ.</summary>

CHAPTER 38.

</margin>

Ezekiel, all of which are entirely beyond our strength to resolve, nor should we try through reckless presumption. Indeed, even the most learned interpreters are silent (see Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a Lutheran theologian known for his massive biblical commentaries.</note>, p. 563, etc.) on what is specifically contained in these two chapters, 38 and 39. These matters are such that, until their fulfillment (which, by the connection of these prophecies with the Holy Revelation [of John] and its progression, is still to be expected alongside the final persecution and liberation of the Church before the end of the world), they are like a very difficult riddle to explain.

Others, such as Maius (p. 1048), observe this connection with what precedes: that the profane and pagan nations look with envious eyes upon that happiness promised to the people of God (or the Church) under the Messiah in the previous chapters; and therefore they will try with every effort to disturb the Israelites there; but in vain. They will instead bring upon themselves a staggering slaughter and total destruction. Furthermore, this prophecy of Ezekiel agrees with that found in Revelation 20:8 and following, as will be evident to anyone from a comparison. This prediction is not cited here by mere allusion, but the Holy Spirit indicates that it is to be fulfilled at the end of the age, as Calovius says (p. 571).

The argument of both, summarized by Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a Dutch theologian and expert in prophetic interpretation.</note> on Revelation 20:8 (p. 1176), is: The peoples who are called Gog and Magog will unexpectedly emerge from their confinement with a huge army; this with the plan to unexpectedly invade and overwhelm the Christian peoples living securely in their places and lands, flourishing in peace (both spiritual and external) and wealth. However, these attempts will have no success, because God will show in them a singular example of His severity for the good of the Church. For God will overthrow this great and formidable collection of nations by His tremendous judgments, causing them to be either scattered by storms from heaven, consumed by plague and other evils, or even to turn violently against one another.

Cocceius says: Gog is dealt with as the one who will disturb the peace of the Church, through whose fall the Church will finally reach peace and the full inheritance of the world, so that all kingdoms might serve it; the divided will not be gathered again, and the hardened Jews themselves will be brought to the Church. Moreover, it is clear from verses 8 and 16 that this prophecy looks to the "latter times," as the whole thread of the prophetic text, when compared with the Book of Revelation, clearly proves. Therefore, it is not surprising that the fulfillment in all its circumstances is difficult to define before the event occurs.

Nevertheless, interpreters of sounder judgment willingly concede that the complete fulfillment cannot yet be demonstrated in history, but must be cast into a future time. See Hulsemannus (in Calovius, p. 565), and in the same place (p. 568) Luther, the Magdeburg Centuriators, and Osiander; see also Gurtlerus (p. 747 seq.) and Rabbi Saadia in the book *Emunoth* <note>Saadia Gaon's (882–942) "Book of Beliefs and Opinions," a foundational work of Jewish philosophy.</note> (chapter 8, etc.), though with Christian judgment. For this most August prophecy is not exhausted (to say nothing of other opinions or conjectures, which you will see in Calovius and Gurtlerus) by what some, with Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian who often sought historical rather than future fulfillments for prophecy.</note>, think: that as far as the historical sense goes, it found its fulfillment after the Babylonian captivity through Antiochus, the Seleucids, Demetrius, Nicanor, etc., who afflicted the Jews; or (as others want) through the Goths and Vandals, or through the Ottoman Turks and Tartars, who often most grievously afflicted Christians. Although, by the breadth of the prophetic sense, those things are perhaps not entirely excluded; it could be conceded that those were preludes to the things which will obtain their full completion in the newest times.

And in these and other more general warnings we rest, and do not dare to descend to specifics before the fulfillment of the matter. How successfully others have tried this, each according to his own hypothesis, let him who can judge. If by chance our little notes (mostly excerpted from others) are in some places narrower than the text itself—as they seem to us here and there—we certainly do not wish to detract anything from the breadth and majesty of the prophetic sense.

According to Schmid, there are two parts to this chapter: I. Gog is described with a varied army, at war and plundering the land of Israel (v. 2–13). II. Divine wrath and punishment are predicted for him (v. 14 seq.). Or according to Gurtlerus: (1) Gog's military preparations (v. 2–6). (2) The expedition into the land of Israel (v. 7–17) with great terror (v. 18–20). (3) The slaughter on the mountains (v. 21–23). Because this chapter agrees with Revelation 20:8–9, and chapter 39:17 seq. with Revelation 19:17 seq., some conclude that Ezekiel speaks there of the first visitation of God, and here of the last. This we also leave to the pious meditation of the reader. See the note on chapter 39:1. v. 2. a) see chapter 6:2, 25:2, 35:3.

**b)** *Verse 1. against Gog verse 3, 14, 16, 18; chapter 39:1, 6; Revelation 20:8.* See the notes shortly following. This name, according to Hiller’s *Sacred Names*, signifies "high" or "exalted": to which the prophet also seems to allude on page 477, when he calls him [גָּבֹהַּ] <note>original: "gavoh," meaning high or lofty</note> an exalted or supreme prince, etc. **c)** The land of Magog, according to Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), a German Reformed theologian.</note>, refers to one who dwells in the land of Magog. The land of Gog or Magog is that part of Scythia <note>An ancient region in central Eurasia inhabited by nomadic warriors.</note> situated under the Caucasus. The Scythians are the descendants of Japheth (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). See Bochart's *Phaleg* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant scholar whose work *Phaleg* analyzed the geography of the post-flood world.</note>, book 3, chapter 13. Nothing seems more certain and true than that by Gog and Magog (descendants of Japheth) are understood the northern peoples who occupied the lands between the Euxine [Black] and Caspian Seas, and those further north toward the Tanais [Don River] to the west and Mount Imaus to the east; this is clear from the whole prophecy. Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a Dutch theologian known for his work on biblical prophecy.</note> in his commentary on Revelation 20, p. 1170, says: "The appearance of the passage in Ezekiel is as if Gog were the prince of that land or people called Magog; but in Revelation 20:8, Gog and Magog appear as types of nations." But the prophets play with names and mix mystical things with literal ones. When the Prophet sought a name to designate the prince of the Scythians, he found none more suitable than the name Gog. Meanwhile, it is also well established from Bochart that Gog can be taken as a name of a nation, as he discovered traces of that name in the histories of nations, namely the Scythians who live around the Caucasus mountain. Thus far Vitringa. Others, including Luther, Osiander, Hullemann, Calovius, etc., understand this to refer to the Turks and their allies. However, because others want nothing historical to be signified here, but only something mystical, they view Gog and Magog as nothing other than heretics or leaders of heresy...

Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a pioneer in "Covenant Theology."</note>, after many other things said at length, has this: "Since it is well established that this Gog did not exist before the time of Ezekiel—and this prophecy cannot be explained as referring to Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a Greek king of the Seleucid Empire often associated with biblical villains.</note>, since the Book of Revelation also prophesies concerning Gog after the times of Antiochus; and Ezekiel agrees with Revelation, saying he would be 'in the end of days' (verses 8, 16)—since, moreover, it is certain that Scripture often hides a riddle in the names of cities and nations; and in the final time it is impossible to show either certain origins of nations and families or even the lands formerly occupied by certain nations; we are forced to conclude our thoughts on this prophecy, lest they be mere divinations: At some time, in the end of days, there will be some prince King, a primary one, the head not only of peoples but also of kings and princes. He can be called Gog for a certain reason; and what is said of him is as if he were called Gog. Moreover, the land in which he will be is called Magog... Furthermore, nations or peoples can be called Meshech and Tubal, either by reason of their descent from Japheth, or by reason of their character and customs, because they are barbarians, traders of souls, placing their terror in the land of the living, etc." **d)** Prince, verse 3; chapter 39:1. **e)** The head of Meshech; others: "chief prince," which Vitringa (p. 1170) considers forced and violent; and from here he interprets: the prince of the Russians, Muscovites, and Tibareni. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch scholar and theologian</note>: **Continually** <note>original: "Tamid" (**תמיד**)</note> here means "for a long time," or "throughout the years" according to the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>. Calov <note>Abraham Calov (1612–1686), a Lutheran theologian known for literal interpretation</note>: **y)** "that land," which is perhaps a metonymy <note>a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it</note> for its inhabitants. **z)** "brought out from the peoples." **v. 10. i)** Meaning "it shall truly be." **k)** Verse 14; compare the notes on chapter 24:26 and 29:16. **l)** "words shall ascend," that is, thoughts and plans for afflicting the church shall come into your mind. That is, into a land accessible from every side like villages, where almost nothing is fortified. This is explained in the latter half of the verse.

See 1 John 2:18, Acts 2:2. **e)** "This shall happen." **f)** "That I may lead you," as my scourge, or as a defendant to the place of execution. Compare verse 8, 17. **g)** Jonathan: "the land of the house of my Shechinah" <note>The Divine Presence dwelling among people</note>. **h)** Chapter 39:23. **i)** Jonathan: "the vengeance of my power." **k)** Compare verse 23, chapter 20:41, chapter 36:23. "When I have punished you; in which my holiness and severity shall appear." Calov. **l)** Chapter 36:23, 37:20. **m)** O Gog. Verse 2, 3, 14, 18.

**v. 17. n)** Meaning: "Are you truly he of whom I spoke?" The question affirms more strongly, as if to say: "You are surely the one." **o)** "In days of old," long ago. 1 Samuel 24:14, Job 18:20. **p)** That is, "through my servants." Exodus 9:35, Ezekiel 20:2, Hosea 12:11. **q)** Therefore, other prophets also spoke of Gog before this; either all their sayings were not recorded in writing—like some of Christ's in Acts 20:35—or their writings are not extant—like Enoch's, see Jude verse 14—without compromising the integrity of the Canon. Or rather, in the writings of the prophets that are commonly held, general prophecies against the enemies of the Church are rightly judged to pertain also to Gog, as an enemy of the Church more distinguished than others and the final persecutor. The Jewish masters compare Numbers 11:26; see the note there. Calovius (page 569) compares Luke 1:70, Acts 3:18, 21, 10:43, Daniel 9:10. Others compare Isaiah 27:1, with chapter 26:20, 21, Jeremiah 30:23, 24, Joel 4:1 following, Micah 5:5, 6, Zechariah 14:1 following.

# EZEKIEL. CHAPTERS 39. 40. 529

<margin>
p) **S.** <note>likely Scholia or Syriac</note> "nor will I leave any more of them." Compare chapter 6, verse 8; chapter 12, verse 16. This prophecy, and that of chapter 37 regarding the joining of the two kingdoms (that is, the twelve tribes), has never been fulfilled, but remains to be fulfilled, says Meyer <note>Johann Meyer, a 17th-century theologian</note> in his *Dissertation on the final chapters of Ezekiel*, page 74. And in the section near the beginning of the chapter, he says: This was not fulfilled under the Old Testament—namely, that the Israelites would be brought back from the lands of their enemies with none left behind, and that God would pour out the Holy Spirit upon the house of Israel. Even after the time of Antiochus (whom some wish to identify as Gog), no such return took place; rather, an even greater dispersion of the people occurred throughout all lands. Compare, however, the notes on Hosea 2:1-2; 3:5, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
p) which are found in chapter 39:17 and following. Compare the notes there and the Preface to this book, section 5.

## AND I WILL NO LONGER HIDE MY FACE FROM THEM <gloss>p</gloss> FOR I HAVE POURED OUT MY SPIRIT UPON THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL, SAYS THE LORD GOD.
