<margin>
verse 29. q) **S.** Then I will no longer hide my face. See verses 23, 24. Because that persecution by Gog and Magog, spoken of in Revelation 20, will be the very last before the end of the world—as the connection of these prophecies with the Apocalypse easily shows, and as Jerome and Augustine rightly noted; so says Hulsemann in Calov <note>Abraham Calovius, a prominent Lutheran theologian</note>, page 565.
r) from them. God declares this not merely in respect to a certain few who have seriously repented (as Grotius argues), but in respect to the whole Church and His entire people: "I will not hide my face from them anymore." Calov, page 570.
s) **S.** because. Deuteronomy 3:24; 1 Samuel 7:23. t) I have poured out. **S.** I will pour out my Spirit. Chapter 36:27; Isaiah 32:15, 16; chapter 44:3; Joel 2:28 (otherwise chapter 3:1); Zechariah 12:10. That is to say, because Christians (in reality, not in name only), being illuminated by the Holy Spirit, will conform their lives to the commands of my Word, etc. Osiander in Calov, page 570.
w) This is the seal of the divine promise, as in verse 13; chapter 11:8; chapter 16:14, etc.

<margin>
CHAPTER XL, verse 1. x) In the twenty-fifth year. Therefore, this final vision of Ezekiel, by the reckoning of time handed down in the scriptures, is not the one which...
</margin>

-> 28:1 <meta>catchword: tree</meta> <-

passed from the first stage of the captivity to the second (that is, from the beginning of Jehoiakim's fourth year, when Daniel was led away with his companions, Daniel 1:1, 6, until the eleventh year of Jehoiakim and the reign of Jeconiah, who was king for only three months), it is concluded from this that Daniel and his companions had already spent 32 years in Babylonia when Ezekiel saw the new Temple in the vision, says Gurtler in *Prophetic Theology*, page 41. **x)** at the beginning of the year. Compare Exodus 12:2. **a)** namely, on the tenth day. As in chapter 20:1; 24:1. **b)** namely, of the first month, as **S.** supplies; others say the seventh month. For the beginning of the civil year for the Jews is the seventh month (compare Exodus 23:16), on the tenth day of which falls the solemn Feast of Atonement, Leviticus 16:29; 23:27; 25:9. Thus, the "antitype" <note>The spiritual fulfillment of a symbolic "type"</note> is beautifully shown by the Prophet: namely, the true construction, cleansing, and sanctification of the Holy City and Temple through Christ for those entering it. To this, the faithful Fathers looked, wandering here and there as pilgrims, Hebrews 11:10, etc. *Muis, Oecon.* page 1049. **c)** afterwards, or after which. Joshua 9:16. **d)** the city of Jerusalem had been cut down. Chapter 33:21; which happened in the eleventh year after the captivity of Jeconiah and the reign of Zedekiah, 2 Kings 25:2. **e)** on this very day. Chapter 24:2; Genesis 7:13; Exodus 12:17; Leviticus 16:29. **f)** came upon me. See chapter 1:3; 3:14, 22; 8:1; 37:1. **h)** and led me in the spirit, or seized and transported me through ecstasy. Verse 2; compare chapter 11:24; 37:1. **i)** there, verse 3; namely, to the city of Jerusalem and into the land of Israel, verse 2. Indeed, since the city and temple of Jerusalem had been destroyed, chapter 33:21, and God wished to give the Jews hope of building a new Temple upon their return from exile, He exhibits to the prophet in a vision a certain Temple, as a perfect prototype of the Temple of God, and simultaneously an illustrious type of the Church, in which God would gloriously dwell in the last times. Compare chapter 37:27, 28 and 43:7, 9. He did no differently with Zechariah, chapter 2:5, 6, where under this kind of architecture—which even the more refined nations still admire and cultivate—an absolute model is represented. 2) It is very similar to Solomon’s Temple, 3) yet in truth it was not built, nor was it possible to be built on Mount Moriah (for the outermost area of the Temple was 3000 cubits long and just as many wide, which is almost as large as all of Jerusalem, much less the enclosed Mount Moriah); 4) yet it served as a model for the temple built after the captivity; and finally 5) it is principally a mystical type of the happy Church of Christ in which we live. These are the words of the famous Sturm <note>Leonhard Christoph Sturm, a mathematician and architect</note> in his *Sketch of the Temple of Jerusalem*, pages 13, 15; who with laudable industry both in this *Sketch* and elsewhere (in the larger work of Goldmann on Civil Architecture, published in German, page 42 and following), having provided the floor plan and delineation based on architectural principles, has to a great extent successfully illustrated this otherwise obscure and difficult matter; so that anyone equipped with a solid knowledge of the Holy tongue [Hebrew] will feel himself greatly aided by this labor. It must be confessed, however, that this man, though otherwise accurate and most learned, often hesitates due to a less than exact skill in the Hebrew language, and thus moves doubts against the text itself for the unskillful. We have thought it necessary to advise this candidly, not out of a spirit of contradiction, but lest a most useful writing—and one to be commended above others on this subject—be neglected or used improvidently to establish false prejudices. For the rest, we hold it as certain and indubitable that these prophecies were not fulfilled in the time of Ezra or Zerubbabel under the Second Temple, as Villalpandus and Grotius would have it; as Dr. Jo. Meyer has shown extensively and solidly in a specific dissertation. We do not, however, agree with Meyer when he thinks they have not even begun to be fulfilled under the New Testament, but will only find their outcome in a future time: even if we do not yet perceive every individual part, or if we hope for the final completion of this building in the last times according to the remaining prophecies and the Holy Apocalypse chapters 21 and 22; as Martin Luther advises in his very weighty Preface to this book. Compare 1 Corinthians 3:16; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Hebrews 12:18, 22 and following. For the Jews, who—contrary to reason and the words of Holy Scripture (see Isaiah 66:1, 2; Jeremiah 3:16; Haggai 2:7, 9; Zechariah 14:20, 21, etc.)—expect a material and third Temple to be built under their Messiah, were solidly refuted by the aforementioned Meyer in that same writing. **k)** In divine visions. Chapter 1:1; Genesis 46:2; Numbers 12:6; Daniel 10:16; not in the body. **l)** transported me, verse 1; chapter 8:3, 7, etc. **m)** and placed me, chapter 37:1. **n)** on a very high mountain, quite lofty; such as Mount Zion would be, not physically, but in the eminence of its dignity and evangelical glory, as Isaiah also foretold, Isaiah 2:2. Compare also above, chapter 17:22, 23; Revelation 21:10. **o)** and upon it was something like the structure of a city. That is, the prophet saw the most majestic building of the Temple like a city, as Sturm also thinks, pages 19 and 22. Others, like Munster: those things which pertain to it up to chapter 45, then the land, and finally in chapter 48:15-30 and following, the site and structure of the city. **p)** from the South. Either because the Prophet approached this sacred mountain from Babylonia and from the North toward the south; or because Jerusalem was to the south with respect to the mountain. Compare below, chapter 45:6; 48:15; and Psalm 48:3. **q)** And when he had led me there, verses 1, 2. **r)** then behold! This is a particle for waking one up, for affirmation, and for pointing something out, as in chapter 1:4; Isaiah 50:2; Jeremiah 31:8. **s)** A certain man was there; whom below in chapter 44:2, 5 he calls "Jehovah," namely Christ the <term>God-man</term> <note>original: "Θεάνθρωπον"</note>, the Lord and Architect of His Church, Matthew 16:18. Compare Zechariah 2:5; Revelation 1:13 and following; Hebrews 3:2 and following; 11:16. Others, with Grotius, say an Angel, collecting Revelation 21:9. **t)** like shining bronze. Compare chapter 1:4, 7, 13; Daniel 10:6; and Revelation 1:15. **u)** and a cord of linen for measuring, for example, the circumference of columns, or the length and width of the land; compare chapter 47:3, 13; Joshua 17:14; Zechariah 2:5. Others, following Lyra, understand a cord with lead [a plumb line], which serves for erecting buildings straight.

See verse 3. k) There was a wall, namely the exterior; or, as the Septuagint <note>Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> has in verse 6, a "peribolus" or enclosure, surrounding the whole and separating the sacred square area from the non-sacred (chapter 42:20). This area had 12,000 cubits in its circumference, or 3,000 cubits (500 reeds) on each side. Chapter 42:15. l) Outside the house, i.e., the Temple building. Compare chapter 43:21. m) The Vulgate <note>Latin Bible</note> says: on the outside in the circuit of the house everywhere. See verses 14, 17, 25, etc. n) See verse 3. o) The measuring reed. See there and verses 6, 7, etc. p) Exactly six cubits. Verse 12, chapter 41:1, 3. q) In cubit measure. Exodus 26:2, chapter 36:9, 15. r) But this cubit included a palm: so that each cubit was one palm larger than the common cubit used in Babylonia.
</margin>

The divine Architect with his reed measures: v. 6, 8, 9, 11, etc. (1) The wall or enclosure of the entire holy area, (2) the east gate of the outer court (v. 6), the north gate (v. 20), and the south gate (v. 24). (3) The south gate of the inner court (v. 28), the east gate (v. 32), and the north gate (v. 35). And finally, (4) the vestibule of the Temple itself (v. 48, etc.). Compare Zechariah 2:6, Revelation 11:1. s) In width, v. 6, 7. u) Of that fabric or structure, i.e., this outermost wall mentioned from the start of the verse. t) The enclosure. x) And the height. Exodus 27:18. y) Of one reed. So that the thickness and height were one reed or six cubits, making the wall square. v. 6. z) Then he came, approaching through that great space included within that enclosure, which we call the Court of the Gentiles. a) To the gate, not of the whole circuit, but the gate of the outer court, namely the Court of Israel or of the Women (v. 17). According to Sturm's observation (p. 56), this had sides of 1,000 cubits each. b) The Vulgate: which looked toward. v. 20, 22. c) Toward the East. v. 10, 19. d) And he ascended. Because the floor of this outer court was several cubits higher (12 according to Sturm, though I would prefer 3 or 4) than the Court of the Gentiles; and again, the inner Court of the Priests was higher than the Court of Israel (v. 31); and the Temple itself was the highest of all (v. 49). Lest anyone think they can leap into heaven in one bound, but must continually seek the things above (Colossians 3:1-2), as Dr. Maius observes. Compare also Kopkius's *Dialogue on the Temple of Solomon* and the notes on 1 Kings 6:19. e) By its steps, namely seven, as the Septuagint correctly adds from verses 22 and 26. f) And then he measured with his reed (v. 5). g) The threshold (Judges 19:27, 2 Kings 12:10, ch. 22:4), specifically the outer one; this was the threshold of the eastern gate. h) Again, one threshold; that is, the second, inner one. i) Namely, both the inner and outer thresholds of this gate had a width of one reed, just like the outer enclosure (v. 5). It appears, therefore, that the building here was enclosed along its longer sides by a wall 6 cubits thick; and rightly, indeed necessarily, we derive the same thickness for all the walls of the buildings from the walls of the gates, says Sturm (p. 64). Compare also ch. 41:5. v. 7. k) The Vulgate: And the chamber. So in verses 10, 12. Others call it a guardroom, comparing 1 Kings 14:28. This refers to the rooms or cells, three on each side (right and left) of the gate, hidden within the structure of the wall, 6 cubits long and wide, and separated by equal intervals, as explained more clearly below in verse 10. From one of these, an entrance opened into the next, as Sturm teaches (p. 65). Therefore, there were small windows in the posts, as well as in the inner wall next to the door. See below v. 16 and Sturm (p. 63). l) verse 5. m) And the space between those chambers, i.e., the wall that separated these rooms. Compare chapter 19:11, Leviticus 27:12, 2 Samuel 19:36, etc. n) Five cubits, see Sturm (p. 65). o) The threshold of the gate, inner and outer, as said in v. 6. p) Near, from the side of. ch. 10:16. q) The inner and outer vestibule of the gate (v. 8). Regarding the vestibule, see 1 Kings 7:6-7 and Sturm (p. 60). r) From the house. The Vulgate: from within. So in verse 8. For a vestibule also lay adjacent to this outer gate on the inside, as symmetry required, to which the outer vestibule of the inner gate would be opposed (see v. 23, 26, 31). Sturm (p. 63). s) Which was also the measure of the outer threshold (v. 6). v. 8. t) He also measured the vestibule of the gate itself. Sturm (p. 63). u) From the house, i.e., from within, as in v. 7. x) One reed. Namely, from the outermost wall-column to the outermost free-standing one. See Sturm (p. 71 ff.). v. 9. y) Furthermore, he measured the outer vestibule of the gate. z) Eight cubits in width; namely, from the center of the wall-column to the center of the free one, for without these, the vestibule was only one reed or 6 cubits (v. 8). a) And its columns/pillars. v. 10, 14, 16. They translate and understand this variously: The Vulgate says "its front." The Septuagint says "its thresholds." Cocceius says "the margins of the walls." But Sturm rightly judges that columns are meant. For, he says (p. 71), if we decorate the capital of our column in the Corinthian style with a double row of palms and volutes above, will it not aptly represent a shaggy ram's head with horns wound into a spiral? Let the round columns decorated with palms remain. Compare notes on 1 Kings 6:31. b) Thus he measured the other vestibule of the gate. c) From the inner face of the gate toward the inner court. v. 7, 8. v. 10. d) Regarding the guardrooms or cells of this eastern gate. See v. 7. e) v. 6, 19. f) They were three in number on this side and that, i.e., on both sides. See v. 12, 21, 26, 34, etc. g) ch. 46:23. h) The pillars/columns. v. 9, 14. v. 11. i) Afterward he measured the width. v. 5. k) Of the gateway opening, i.e., the open space in the gate. See v. 13.

# EZEKIEL. CHAPTER 40.

<margin>
l) 10 cubits, as below in chapter 41:2. This is calculated by including the half-columns or posts of one cubit on both sides; otherwise, the gate opening would have been wider than the vestibule, which was 8 cubits (verse 9). m) the length of the gate (verse 18). n) was thirteen cubits. Lyranus, Villalpandus, and others refer this to the height of the gate because it is the larger dimension; however, they are rightly rejected by the famous Sturm (pages 66–67), who considers the number thirteen completely alien and imperfect. He proposes "thirty" (three times ten) instead, though this goes against the construction and phrasing of the sacred text. We must consider another arrangement or admit we do not know the limits of this number. See also Marius’s *Oeconomia*, page 1052.

Verse 12. o) The boundary (or space) was before the side rooms. The Vulgate says: "And the border before the side rooms," derived from verse 11 (see also 43:20). p) See verse 7. q) of one cubit: namely, as much as the columns placed on both sides between the three rooms projected from the wall (see Sturm, page 71). r) And so also on the other side there was a space of one cubit between the columns: so that the gate was twelve cubits wide between opposite walls, but ten cubits between the columns, as stated in verse 11. s) Each side room <term>thalamus; a small chamber or cell</term> (verse 7). t) Six and a quarter cubits (verse 5; 41:1). u) On this side and that, i. e., on both sides (verse 10).

Verse 13. x) Then he measured the width of the whole gate and its buildings from opposite doors of the side rooms. y) From the roof, i. e., from the highest and outermost wall to the outermost wall of the opposite side room (see Exodus 30:3, 37:26). For the rooms did not have a "roof" in the strict sense, being situated under the roof—or rather the ceiling—of the gate, but they had their own paneled ceiling, as Sturm says (page 68). z) Namely, half a cubit for the external wall on each side, half a cubit for the front wall of the rooms, and half a cubit for its foundation.

(page 72).

A calculation of half a cubit is proven: 6 cubits from the furthest column of the vestibule to the wall, 1 cubit of wall projection, 6 for wall thickness, 36 for the interior gate length, 6 for interior wall thickness, 1 for column projection width, 3 to the edge of the inner vestibule column, and half a cubit for the base; totaling 60 cubits. e) And beside the columns (verses 9, 15). f) A court or small area or space within the columns. For everyone will admit that a "court" in the strict sense—an open-air place surrounded by walls—cannot be meant here, as Sturm says (page 72). On page 73, he understands arches or gates built over the side rooms between two columns, which were open and not closed by doors, allowing free access and air, like suburbs of the larger gate (comparing Leviticus 25:31, Isaiah 42:11). We doubt this interpretation, though we dare not determine anything precisely due to our lack of architectural skill. g) And a smaller gate of this kind, by omission of a conjunction (see verse 48) or according to Sturm by apposition: namely, the gate. h) The Vulgate says "all around," i. e., through the entire Greater Gate (see verses 5, 16, 17, 25, etc.).
</margin>

Verse 15. i) Before the face of the gate; namely, the entrance or passage (i) from the root *bo* <note>meaning: to enter</note>. k) A similar construction to 7:7, Joshua 3:14, 1 Kings 22:27, etc. l) unto the inner vestibule of the gate. The first clause marks the starting point, this second clause the ending point. m) We connect this with "vestibule" according to the accents, though others connect it with "gate" (see verses 19, 22, 25, 33, etc.). n) It was fifty cubits, as in verses 21, 25, 29, etc. For the total length of the gate, as we heard in verse 14, was 60 cubits. Thus, if you subtract six and a half cubits for the front and three and a half for the inner vestibule, 50 remains for the rest of the gate (Sturm, page 74). Verse 16. o) And indeed windows. Sturm (page 63) calls them "little windows" meant to light the winding stairs hidden within the wall (see note on verse 7). p) Narrowed or squeezed. The Vulgate says "slanted"; specifically narrower on the inside (see 41:16, 26; 1 Kings 6:4). q) They belonged to the side rooms (see note on verse 7). r) To their columns (see verses 9, 37, 49). s) Inside the gate (1 Kings 6:30). t) Verse 14, 17. u) And so (41:7). x) In the porches (verses 21, 22, 30, etc.). y) Namely, there were windows. z) Inwardly (41:3). b) And at each column (see verses 9, 14). c) There were two palm trees (verse 26, cf. 31, 34 and note on verse 9). Verse 17. d) To the outer court (verses 20, 31; 10:5, 42:1). Namely, the Court of the Israelites and the Court of Women, as we said at verse 6. For the inner court of the priests, see verse 23. e) And behold! the court was surrounded on all sides by splendid buildings (see note on verse 5). f) The Vulgate calls them "treasuries." Others say "chambers" or "small cells" (41:10, 42:4, 7ff.; 1 Samuel 9:22). These were the foundations of the surrounding buildings, which had three stories; they were full of storerooms and attached covered walkways where light came in through ordinary windows. Such receptacles were needed to preserve the temple's revenue, which could not withstand the dampness of underground cells—items like fabric for vestments, veils, and tapestries. Below these were likely deeper cellars suitable for storing wine. Thus, the floor of the buildings was higher than the gate floor, likely resting on very solid arches, upon which magnificent and spacious porches stood for receiving the people who flocked there on feast days (Sturm, page 75). g) And the pavement toward the north and south, and on both sides toward the west, 12 cubits apart, as in 10:12 and 2 Samuel 16:13. o) See verses 11, 15. p) The lower pavement (see note on verse 17 and cf. 41:7). Verse 19. q) Afterward he measured the width of the whole structure around the Court of the Israelites (verse 17). r) That is, from the front of the gate (1 Kings 8:54, Ezra 10:6). The Vulgate says: "from the face of the lower gate to the front of the inner court." s) Beginning most precisely where the outer gate—or "lower" gate due to its lower position—ends inside the vestibule or gate building (Sturm, page 76). The "He" is a paragogic <term>paragogic He; an added letter at the end of a Hebrew word, often for emphasis or direction</term>, and thus a noun of dignity, with a milel accent. t) That is, "unto the face" (46:9). u) Of the inner court, or of the Priests (verses 15, 23; see note on 1 Kings 6:36). x) From the outside or externally (46:2). That is, at the outer wall of the building that surrounded the inner court; for the Architect had not yet entered that building. y) As in 23, 27, 47. z) The Vulgate says "to the east and to the north." Thus, by measuring all quarters from west to east (verse 10) and from south to north (verse 20), the building was 100 cubits long, and the court was a perfect square. Verse 20. a) The Vulgate says: "Also the gate which looked..." (see verses 6, 22). b) Toward the north (see verses 10, 24, 27). c) Of the outer court (see verse 17). d) With the same measurement as he had measured the eastern gate (verse 6ff). Verse 21. e) Likewise its side rooms (see verses 7, 10).

Thus the Architect first measures the face on both sides from the vestibule jamb toward the middle up to the end of the free-standing column, which is five cubits; then also the space between the jamb and the column, which is three cubits. From this, the thickness of the columns is concluded to be 2 cubits. Within the inner row, a wall was drawn around on both sides, so that on all sides around the Temple it was two cubits wide, increasing the thickness of the Temple wall. Thus the Temple wall was six cubits wide, as stated at the beginning of this verse. The pillars closely surrounding it were connected to the wall toward the Temple in such a way that the portico around the Temple remained four cubits wide, and thus the wall surrounding it was six cubits thick where the pillars were, but five cubits thick between them. According to Cocceius in his Lexicon, page 551, it signifies a type of column attached to the walls of buildings and broken through so that they are passable, strengthening the building, etc. Compare Ezekiel 42:6. To Neumann, however, in *Exodus*, it means a chamber, a dining room, or something similar; compare Ezekiel 42:3, where it is expressly said to have been a dining room. However, he leaves what it properly was for researchers of the Jerusalem Temple to discern. The Rabbis also freely admit their ignorance of it. Rashi on Ezekiel 42:3 states clearly: <note>original Hebrew: "I do not know what it is"</note> and David Kimchi on Ezekiel 42:3 says: "I cannot understand these chambers—and I say freely, this section will only be explained by Elijah [the prophet] himself." Nevertheless, he accepts the word as meaning chambers. It occurs in verse 16 and chapter 42:3, 5.

...which is. Furthermore, between those chambers there were two series, one looking toward the inner court, the other looking toward the outer court; these necessarily leave a cruciform <note>cross-shaped</note> walkway between them, as the following verse also confirms.

<margin>**Verse 4. f)** Indeed, before those chambers. Verse 1, 5, 7; chapter 40:17, 41:10. **g)** there was a cruciform walkway. See the note on the preceding verse. The word (*mahalakh*) is found; but elsewhere it denotes a journey, as in Jonah 3:3, 4. For the prefix letter *Mem* in nouns signifies both place and action. **h)** the width of which walkway was ten cubits. **i)** and that walkway led from the outer to the inner chamber, or even the court. Chapter 8:3, 16; chapter 10:3. **k)** Schmidt: the way itself one cubit. Cocceius: but each cell was approached by a way of one cubit. That is, in the mind of Cocceius, between the doors of the cells were square posts, standing out one cubit from the wall. Thus the free walkway had a width of 10 cubits: but with the cubit added on both sides between the posts, before the doors of the dining rooms, it had a width of twelve cubits. To Sturmius, however, in his *Sciagraphia* page 84, this way of one cubit is the threshold itself, or at least the passage through the opening—that is, the door of the wall, one cubit thick. See him in the cited place. **l)** the doors of the innermost dining rooms. **m)** were toward the north. Chapter 40:23.</margin>

<margin>**Verse 5. n)** Schmidt: Furthermore, the highest rooms. Cocceius: the upper cells. Castalio: they were exceeded, etc. Thus we accept the anomalous punctuation of the anomalous verb *yukhalu* <note>original Hebrew: יוכלו</note> in a passive sense as the meaning demands. Schmidt and others in an active sense: because they prevailed. Cocceius, however, along with the Rabbis: they "bit off" from the structure, from the root *akhal* (to eat). See the variant readings below. **r)** the uppermost chambers. Verse 3. **s)** perisylia <note>galleries or colonnades</note>. Cocceius: accessible posts. See note on chapter 41:15. **s)** by them, namely, by the lowest and middle ones, as he soon adds in parentheses. **t)** Verse 6; chapter 41:7. **u)** the structure. Verse 1, 10. Chapter 40:49. **c)** such as were in the porticos of the courts. 12 **This is the law of the house <gloss>e</gloss>: Upon the top of the mountain <gloss>f</gloss>, its entire boundary all around shall be most holy. Behold, this is the law of the house.**

13 **And these are the measurements of the altar in cubits <gloss>g</gloss> (the cubit <gloss>h</gloss> being a cubit and a handbreadth <gloss>i</gloss>): the base <gloss>k</gloss> shall be a cubit high and a cubit wide, with a rim around its edge of one span <gloss>l</gloss>. This shall be the base of the altar.**

14 **From the base on the ground to the lower ledge shall be two cubits, with a width of one cubit; and from the smaller ledge <gloss>m</gloss> to the larger ledge shall be four cubits, with a width of one cubit.**

15 **The altar hearth <gloss>n</gloss> shall be four cubits high <gloss>o</gloss>, and from the altar hearth and upward there shall be four horns <gloss>p</gloss>.**

16 **And the altar hearth <gloss>q</gloss> shall be twelve [cubits]...**

---

...confession of the sacrifice is the celebration of God and His glorification (v. 23). Every worship of the faithful at the altar is pleasing (Hebrews 13:15-16), which Ezekiel also hints at in v. 27. x) By cubits. For Jesus Christ (as Vitringa writes on Revelation 11:1-2) has His own certain attributes, properties, and signs—*gnorismata* <note>Greek: identifying marks</note>—by which He is to be known. These characters are mystically called His "engraving" in Zechariah 3:9. y) Where a cubit is a cubit, it has a cubit and a palm <note>A "long cubit," about 21 inches</note>. The Vulgate says: "in the truest cubit, which had a cubit and a palm." z) The "bosom" or "hollow" (v. 14, 17). Cocceius: Jerome translates this as a "ditch," but it is soon called the "back" of the altar, that is, the structure supporting the altar. It is the base and foundation, called the *Yesod* in Leviticus 4:7. It resembled a bosom because there was a rim on its edge, so that the altar sat in the base as if in a bosom. a) Its height was [one] cubit. b) Its width was also one cubit beyond the altar structure. c) Its border or limit (chapter 43:12), that is, the "crown" or "rim." d) On the edge or extremity of the base. e) It was one span (half a cubit, v. 17). f) And this is the "back" of the altar, supporting it. g) From the "bosom" of the earth or the foundation of the altar. h) To the lower ledge; for there was another higher one. i) It was two cubits. Cocceius: From the base, the altar rose two cubits to a square space where the rest was placed. k) There was a margin or empty space of one cubit. l) From this smaller or lower ledge to the larger and higher space, twelve cubits wide (v. 15). m) Four cubits. n) Again, the width of the empty space or margin was one cubit. Cocceius notes: The height here (7 cubits total) differs from Solomon's altar (10 cubits). This height represents the church of the seven periods, united in one altar. The three regions of the altar (base, lower ledge, upper ledge) signify to me the will of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. o) *Ariel*, or rather *Har-el*, meaning "Mountain of God." According to Hiller, it surpassed other altars in size. Cocceius calls it the "altar hearth." It is called *Ariel*, meaning "Lion of God," because like a lion it consumes the food placed for God with fire. Others suggest it means "God's hearth" or "God's ditch." p) Four cubits. q) From the Ariel itself, the hearth of God. r) upward. s) There were four horns, which signify power and loftiness. t) Of the Ariel or the hearth.

<column-break/>

v. 11. **its exits** — textual variants noted in the Masoretic manuscripts of Erfurt. **its entrances** — written without the letter *Yod* in some versions. **its forms** — follows the grammatical analogy in some manuscripts. **its statutes** — variant spelling in the *Keri* (traditional reading). **the Ariel** — verse 16 uses a different spelling (*Har-el*) in place of the traditional *Ariel* in some manuscripts.

<vocab>Ezekiel: A major prophet of the Exile; Ariel: Literally "Lion of God," referring to the altar hearth; Altar of Burnt Offering: The central site of sacrifice; Cubit: A unit of measure, here the "long cubit" (approx. 21 inches); Span: Half a cubit, the width of a hand; Ledge: The tiered steps of the altar structure.</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the detailed architectural and ritual instructions for the Temple in Ezekiel 43. The previous page established the Altar's foundation; this page details the specific dimensions of the upper tiers and the "Ariel" (the altar hearth), followed by the divine command for a seven-day purification ceremony using the blood of bulls and goats. The commentary by Johannes Cocceius provides a 17th-century Christian typological interpretation, linking these Old Testament measurements to the Apostles and the sacrifice of Christ.</meta>

**(u)** its length was 12 cubits, with a 12-cubit width. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian who famously interpreted the Old Testament as a series of progressive covenants pointing toward Christ.</note>: Twelve cubits signify the 12 witnesses among the tribes of Israel, specifically the agreement of the 12 Apostles; and twelve times twelve (144) is the number of those who belong to Christ and are pleasing and accepted by God (Revelation 14:1). **x)** the Altar stood out as a square (cf. Exodus 27:1, 38:1). **y)** according to its four sides (v. 17; 1:8, 17). Just as he built the height of the altar from the bottom upwards, he now indicates the width and length by descending. —Cocceius.

**v. 17. z)** The space, truly, which enclosed the Ariel <note>original: "Arielem," a Hebrew term for the altar-hearth, literally "Lion of God."</note> or focus. **v. 14. a)** it had fourteen cubits in length and just as many in width: because a cubit is added on each side (see v. 14). **b)** in its four quarters or sides (v. 16). Here, however, he is silent regarding the square measurement of the second or lower space (v. 14) and the foundation (v. 13), because that is plain in itself. For the second space had sixteen cubits, while the base had eighteen cubits in length and width. —Cocceius. **c)** But the border <note>original: "Terminum," referring to the ledge or rim.</note> or the breastwork/crown around the base (v. 13). **d)** was half a cubit. Thus he interprets the term *Asta* (v. 17). **e)** and the hollow or "bosom" <note>original: "sinus f. gremium," referring to the gutter at the base of the altar.</note> for receiving [the blood] was one cubit (see v. 13). **f)** but the steps of the Altar, or its ascent (40:6), which the Hebrews pass down as having been like a gently rising slope; because in Exodus 20:26 <note>original cites 20:23, likely referring to the prohibition of steps to prevent nakedness.</note> they are forbidden from ascending to the Altar by other types of steps. **g)** they were toward the east. Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian.</note> views "Facing the East" as a noun; others as a verbal noun. You will see the mystical interpretation in Cocceius and others.

etc. Cocceius: The power, purity, and freedom of Christ are noted. For no yoke was upon Him when He took up our burden. **u)** in the sacrifice for sin (v. 21, 22; 42:13).

**v. 20. x)** And you shall take some of its blood (Exodus 29:12; Leviticus 4:17, 18). **y)** and you shall give it, or sprinkle it (Leviticus 4:7, 25, 30). **z)** see v. 15. **a)** the corners (45:19; Exodus 27:2). **b)** or "prominences," otherwise called the ledge or the space (see v. 14). **c)** and upon the border, that is, the breastwork or crown all around (v. 13, 17; 40:12). **d)** thus you shall cleanse the altar from sins. Or "so that you may purify it" (v. 22, 23; 45:18). **e)** and you shall expiate or make propitiation for it (v. 26; 45:20). Cocceius: For with the blood of the covenant shed, there is a holy and irreproachable habitation of God among men, and their sanctification and justification (cf. Romans 3:25-26). Compare also Leviticus 16:16, 33 where it is said the Tabernacle must be cleansed from all the impurities of the children of Israel. Similarly, Hebrews 9:23 says that heavenly things are purified with better sacrifices than those by which the figures of heavenly things are purified. By this it is signified that God Himself is contaminated by communion with a sinner, unless peace is reconciled through a most noble sacrifice, in which the holiness and justice of God can be demonstrated—He who wishes through mercy to sanctify and justify the sinner and have communion with him.

**v. 21. f)** Or "Afterwards you shall take the bull." **g)** for sin (v. 19). **h)** and someone shall burn it (cf. Leviticus 4:12, 21; 6:23). Cocceius: An impersonal phrasing sometimes explains what is done by a multitude. The misery of the Church kindles that fire by which Christ was consumed (cf. Psalm 69:9). **i)** Or "in the designated place of the house" (3). Nehemiah 3:31; it denotes a command in 2 Chronicles 31:13. Cocceius: that is, Christ had to suffer in that church which was being guarded for that faith which was to be revealed (Galatians 3:23). **k)** Cocceius: I interpret "outside the sanctuary" here not in the same way as it is prescribed in Leviticus (cf. Lev. 4:12, 21; 8:17; 9:11; Num. 19:3, 5), which signified that Christ would suffer outside Jerusalem (Hebrews 13:11), but rather I understand that Christ, as a servant of the circumcision (Romans 15:8) made under the law (Galatians 4:4), had not yet found the church in that state which is signified by this sanctuary; or even that, when He suffered, He had nothing (Daniel 9:26).

**v. 22. l)** And on the day or second time after the offering of Christ, and so on for the remaining six days. **m)** you shall offer a kid of the goats (v. 25; 45:23; Leviticus 9:3). **n)** v. 23; 45:18; Leviticus 1:3, 10; 3:1, etc. **o)** v. 19. Cocceius: It is not signified here that another sacrifice for sin is made than that which was offered once by Him who was able to offer it (see Hebrews 9:25, 26, 28; 10:10, 12, 14), but rather that Christ is constantly to be brought forward and confessed as the unique Priest and unique victim for sin. **p)** and they shall expiate (v. 20; Leviticus 8:15). **q)** cf. Exodus 29:36. **r)** v. 20.

**v. 23. s)** Or "When indeed you have finished." (1 Samuel 13:10; 2 Kings 10:25). **t)** to expiate or offer for sin (v. 20, 22). **u)** v. 19. **x)** and a ram (v. 25). **y)** v. 22; 46:4.

**v. 24. z)** You shall offer them, I say, before Jehovah (v. 23). **a)** and the priests shall cast (5:4) upon those—or upon them—the bull and the ram (v. 23). **b)** salt (Leviticus 2:13). Cocceius: Salt cast upon them denotes the absence of corruption (1 Peter 3:4). For salt makes flesh *asepton* <note>Greek: "un-rotting" or "incorruptible."</note>. **c)** and they shall offer them (1 Samuel 6:14, 15). **d)** Cocceius: The Burnt Offering signifies the passions of the faithful, consecrating themselves entirely to God, either by love or by the very act, even unto death (cf. note at v. 27).

**v. 25. e)** Seven days (v. 26; 45:23, 25). **f)** you shall perform/make (Exodus 29:36, 38; Numbers 15:8; etc.; 2 Corinthians 5:21). **g)** a goat for a sin offering (v. 22). **h)** daily (4:10; 45:23).

ance v. 28–31. **v. 2. e)** he entered through it; see chapter 43:2. **f)** therefore it shall be closed and remain so. verse 1. Also the gate of the inner court, except on the Sabbath and the day of the new moon; see chapter 46:1 and following. Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned Hebraist and scholar of the Temple.</note> notes in *Description of the Temple* p. 655 that this denotes the eternal dwelling of the Lord's glory in the Christian church, from which it shall never depart, as it departed from the Jerusalem temple. Compare Matthew 28:20 and Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note> on this passage. To Cocceius, however, this passage signifies that where Christ has gone, no one else can go. After Christ, no one comes to succeed him in the priesthood or in the kingdom. See Hebrews 7:3, 24, etc. It is well known that the ancient doctors of the Church wished to see in this closed gate a shadow of the womb of the Holy Virgin and Mother of God, as found in the hymn: *The gate of Christ is made passable, full and overflowing with grace; the King passes through, and it remains closed, as it was, through the ages.* See Augustine, Ambrose, and Rufinus cited by Calovius in this sense. However, this displeases Noldius (in *Concordance of Particles* p. 868, note 27) because the eastern gate was open on certain days not only to the Prince but also to the people; see following verse 3 and chapter 46:3, 10. Nevertheless, Lightfoot thinks the outer eastern gate of the sanctuary was perpetually closed, while the inner one was closed only for six days of the week. **v. 3. g)** Septuagint: "With the Prince." Cocceius: "As for what pertains to the Prince." Compare chapter 20:16. **h)** Septuagint: "That Prince is he, therefore he shall sit in it." Cocceius: In Ezekiel 34:24, it is promised to Israel that God's servant David (the Messiah) would be their Prince, who in verse 23 is also called a shepherd, and indeed the only one. Now, in this vision too, mention is made of a Prince, to whom a certain portion is assigned below in the inheritance of the land for himself and his sons. He is to be distinguished by us from Christ the King, who sits at the right hand of the Father. These things, if I am not mistaken, signify the prerogative or <term>ἀξιοπίαν</term> <note>original: "axiopian," meaning authority or worthiness.</note> which godly Princes, magistrates, and lords have among other believers, who are equally citizens and heirs of the kingdom of heaven. One who succeeds in the priesthood cannot be understood here. For the priesthood was given to the sons of Zadok, and this Prince cannot approach the altar with them—namely, by the name and title of prince, as one having power over the priests, etc. **i)** Compare chapter 46:2, 12. Cocceius: Christ, as often noted, is the gate, and indeed the only gate. Therefore, it is granted to the prince, as if to eat and drink bread with Christ, and to worship—that is, collecting John 4:32, to take pleasure and joy in a good conscience, because he has done the work given to him to do as a Prince. This is not only to provide for the people so they may lead a quiet and peaceful life, but also so they may hear the word of God and offer the sacrifice of confession to God in peace and without fear. Therefore, in chapter 45:17, it is enjoined upon the Prince to provide burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings at feasts, new moons, and sabbaths, and all solemnities of the house of Israel, and to prepare (sacrifices) for sin, etc. When he does this, he is truly a <term>נָגִיד</term> <note>original: "Nagid," a Hebrew word for leader or prince.</note> and a <term>ἡγεμόνης</term> <note>original: "hegemones," a Greek word for governor or leader.</note> (Isaiah 32:8), and then he has a most sweet banquet of a good conscience, and in some way shares with Christ and His work, standing firm for Him and His kingdom. Cocceius discusses these and other matters at length, comparing Isaiah 49:23. **k)** Chapter 46:2, 8; Chapter 40:8, 9. **v. 4. l)** "Afterward he brought me in." Chapter 40:17, 32. **m)** See verse 1. **n)** Chapter 40:20, 35. **o)** Toward the face of the house, or before the house. Chapter 41:4, 14. **p)** Chapter 1:4. **q)** "The glory of the Lord had filled," etc. Chapter 43:5. **r)** "And I fell on my face." Chapter 1:28. **v. 5. s)** "Apply your heart." See chapter 40:4. **t)** Chapter 43:11, 12. **u)** "That you may mark, I say." **x)** "To the entrance of the house." Compare chapter 46:19. **y)** "With all the exits of the sanctuary," that is, and at all its exits. Compare chapter 43:11; chapter 42:11.

...holy garments, that is, according to Cocceius, lest they arrogate righteousness to themselves because of their labors. But Gussetius (p. 315), from the meaning of the word *yaza* <note>sweat</note> as "to be moved," says: they shall not gird themselves in an unstable way, as if to say, with the restlessness of a belt, letting it be loose. Thus this command would be against softness or laziness. Compare 1 Peter 1:13.
l) But when they go out or come forth, ch. 46:10. m) ch. 42:14. n) to the outer atrium, I say, which he emphasizes by repetition. o) ch. 16:16. p) Lev. 6:4, ch. 16:23. q) in which or with which they minister to God, v. 17. r) ch. 42:14. s) ch. 42:13, 14. t) ch. 42:14. Cocceius: By this thing it is signified, not what the Chaldean <note>the Aramaic Targum</note> wants—that they should not mix with the people (for clearly the opposite is achieved)—but that, when they approach any Christian, they should indeed keep those ornaments inwardly, but not boast of them before the brothers, or usurp any prerogative for themselves, but rather that brothers should converse entirely as brothers with brothers. u) nor shall they sanctify the people in those garments of theirs. ch. 46:20. Cocceius: The meaning is not as if they ought not to give effort to the sanctification of the brothers, but that no one should thrust their own name, authority, prerogative, and progress upon others, so that because of those things they would want others to depend on them, and thus "sanctify" them for themselves, etc. Compare Eph. 6:5. **v. 20. x)** *But they shall not shave their head.* Lev. 21:5. **y)** *however, the hair also of the head* Num. 6:5. **z)** *they shall not let grow.* ch. 17:6, 7. in the manner of the Nazirites (1 Sam. 1:11) or of women (1 Cor. 11:15). **a)** *but they shall trim their heads quite decorously.* (1) Compare again 1 Cor. 11:14. Cocceius: It is easy to recognize the sense of this prophecy, that the priests of this sanctuary must abstain from wantonness and softness, nor make themselves an object of spiritual fornication. Compare Rev. 9:8. **v. 21. b)** *Neither shall they drink wine.* See Lev. 10:9, etc. **c)** see v. 17. For the indulgence of the flesh casts clouds over the mind and makes the depravity of the flesh powerful. —Cocceius.

Indeed, even Christ wept in sympathy <note>original Greek: ἐν συμπάθεια</note> at the death of Lazarus. Cocceius. c) Leviticus 21:3. d) Hosea 9:4.

See Psalm 73:17. i) see v. 17. k) he shall offer his sacrifice for sin (see v. 29), namely, that which was offered once for all. Hebrews 9:12, 14, 24; 10:14, etc. l) Ezekiel 11:8; 16:14.

*. 28. m) Scholium: Then it shall be to them for an inheritance. See Psalm 73:17. n) that is, of the priests themselves; or, as Cocceius connects it, because "I am their inheritance." n) See Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 10:9; Joshua 13:14, 33. o) you shall not give them a possession in Israel. See Psalm 73:25; 2 Corinthians 6:10.

*. 29. p) Scholium: The Mincha <note>term: the grain offering</note>. i.e., the sacrifice made from flour. Ezekiel 45:15; Leviticus 2:1. q) Ezekiel 42:13; 45:17. r) the priests themselves shall eat them. Ezekiel 42:13; Leviticus 6:9; 8:31, etc. For he who serves at the altar ought to eat from the altar (1 Corinthians 9:13); and those who benefit the Church by word, labor, and patience—the church ought to share all good things with them; for this is to sow to the spirit. Galatians 6:6, 8. Cocceius. s) also every devoted thing. Leviticus 27:21, 28, 29.

<column-break/>

*. 26. e) Scholium: And after his cleansing, or after he has been purified. See the phrase in Leviticus 13:35. f) they shall count seven days for him. See Ezekiel 43:25; 45:23, 25; and Numbers 19:11–12. The "philanthropy" <note>original Greek: Φιλανθρωπια</note> or kindness of God permits even the sanctified a time of mourning; namely, seven days from the purification—that is, from the time consolation is received in the soul, or the correction of one's weakness—seven days, lest they lack their Sabbath, etc. Cocceius.

*. 30. s) And the firstfruits. Exodus 22:28; 23:19; 34:26; Deuteronomy 18:4. x) of all the firstfruits. See Numbers 18:12 ff; Nehemiah 10:36. See also Exodus 13:2; 34:19. x) of all things, or concerning all things. y) every offering of any kind. Numbers 15:19. z) Ezekiel 20:40; Leviticus 7:32. a) See Leviticus 5:13, 16; 7:6 ff; 14:13; 23:14, 20; 27:21. b) also the first of your dough (4). Numbers 15:20–21; Nehemiah 10:38. c) Scholium: to cause a blessing to rest upon your house. See Malachi 3:10; Proverbs 3:25; and the opposite above in Ezekiel 5:13; 16:42, etc.

*. 31. d) Any carcass <note>original: "morticinum"</note> or torn thing. Ezekiel 4:14; Exodus 22:30; Leviticus 22:8. e) the priests shall not eat. As in Isaiah 65:4, to eat pork or polluted meat is to commune with the impure, with dogs and pigs; so also here, to eat a carcass or what died naturally is to commune with men dead in the uncircumcision of the flesh, and to take pleasure in them. Cocceius.

<meta>This page continues the technical and theological exposition of Ezekiel’s vision. While the previous page focused on the personal conduct and marital laws of the Zadokite priests, this page transitions to the "Holy Portion"—the physical division of the land surrounding the visionary Temple. The commentary engages with the debate over whether the measurements refer to small cubits or much larger "reeds," a distinction that significantly alters the scale of the prophetic city and sanctuary. It continues to feature the insights of Johannes Cocceius and Johannes Meyerus, interpreting these physical boundaries as symbols of the Church’s order under Christ.</meta>

# CHAPTER XLV.

<margin>
**25000.** This refers to the number of reeds <note>original: "calamorum"</note>. Compare with chapter 48, verse 20.
(6) 10,000. For the Persians <note>likely a reference to a specific measurement or historical interpretation</note>. Jerome <note>St. Jerome, c. 347–420 AD, the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> says excellently: He commands that from all the tribes a place be chosen **five [the Keri reading]** which shall have twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth. And because "cubits" was not explicitly written...
</margin>

<margin>
CHAPTER XLV, verse 1.
f) And when you happen to divide the land, you shall distribute it. As if to say: When you cause the land to fall as an inheritance; that is, when you cast lots for the land so that each tribe may see the inheritance destined for it by God, whether nearer or farther from the Sanctuary. See chapter 47:14, 22; chapter 48:29; Joshua 13:6; Proverbs 16:33. Naturally, with the Temple and the more sacred worship established in the previous chapters, here the "new land" (2 Peter 3:13; compare here verses 9 and 14) is to be divided, and a new form of the Church is proposed to be established through Christ. It is expressed in phrases of the old government and worship, but nevertheless, as the matter itself most clearly teaches, something new is denoted, as Cocceius has proven more fully at this passage. According to Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmidt, 1617–1696, a Lutheran theologian</note>, there are four parts to this chapter: I. The division of the land and inheritances for the priests (v. 1-4), the Levites (v. 5), the city (v. 6), and the Prince (v. 7-8). II. The weights and measures are prescribed (v. 9-12). III. The tribute for divine worship to be given to the Prince (v. 13-17). IV. The worship and sacrifices of the festivals (v. 18-25). g) To be possessed by hereditary right (Numbers 34:2; Joshua 13:7; 23:4). h) You shall set aside an offering <note>original: "ablationem"</note>, that is, you shall separate a certain and special portion from the midst of it (v. 6, 13; c. 48:8, 9). i) For the Lord; so that He may dwell in your midst, and that His worship may be established among you. k) As a holy space, separated from the rest of the land (v. 2, 4), between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin (c. 48:8, 23). l) Regarding the length from east to west (c. 48:10). m) The length shall be 25,000 poles or reeds. See verses 2, 3, 5; chapter 48:8, 20. n) But the width (between north and south) of the space to be set apart for the temple and the priests (v. 3, 4). For some believe the width of the entire space—containing the Temple, priests, Levites, and the city—was the same as the length: 25,000.
</margin>

**And it shall be [Keri]** <note>Keri refers to the traditional reading of the Hebrew text where it differs from the written form (Ketiv).</note> a market or feet or ulnas <note>forearm lengths</note>, which is given to be understood.
</margin>

---

This is understood to signify a reed <note>original: "calamum"</note>, because it was in the hand of the Living One. See chapter 40:3. The famous Johannes Meyerus <note>a 17th-century scholar</note> proves this in his *Dissertation on the last chapters of Ezekiel*, pages 42 and following: (1) From verse 2 of this chapter compared with chapter 42:16 and following, where the measure of the reed is most expressly held, whatever others may think differently. (2) Because the sacred Architect here in verse 12 expressed the name of cubits in the last place for the smaller attached number. For if he had wanted cubits to be understood here, the word "cubits" would not only have had to be added to "five" in verse 2, just as "reeds" are added in chapter 42:16, but also a mention of cubits would have had to be introduced soon in verse 1. (3) Because those "five" in verse 2 are joined by an indissoluble bond with the length of 25,000 and the width of 10,000; indeed, with a width of 25,000 reeds in chapter 48:20. From which it necessarily follows that the same measure of reeds is understood in verse 1 as in verse 2, as is designated from the collection of chapter 42:16 and following. And (4) Meyerus solidly demonstrates this by the collection of parts into one sum on the cited pages 43 and following. p) This shall be holy in all its border everywhere. Verse 2. Namely, of that entire space which was to run between the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin, a square middle part 25,000 reeds long and just as many wide was to be dedicated to JEHOVAH; which would contain the Temple (v. 3) and the habitation of the priests (v. 4), the Levites (v. 5), and the city of Jerusalem (v. 6). The remaining portion of that space, adjacent to the sacred square on the east and west, was to be granted to the Prince (v. 7; c. 48:21). V. 2. q) There shall be from this Sanctuary or Temple (v. 3, 4) r) five hundred reeds. See the note on verse 1 and chapter 42:16 and following. s) with five hundred reeds. Compare a similar thing in Exodus 27:18. t) square on every side. (3) Chapter 40:47; compare chapter 42:16-19. u) but fifty cubits. x) shall be an open space <note>original: "pomarium," literally an orchard or boundary space</note> for the Temple round about. Compare chapter 48:15, 17. V. 3. y) Specifically from that measurement of the whole square, concerning which see verse 1. z) you shall measure the length from east to west, as in verse 1. a) of 25,000 reeds. Verse 1, 5, 6. b) and the width (as said in verse 1) of 10,000 rods. c) and within it, namely in its center, shall be the Sanctuary (v. 4) already designated. Compare chapter 48:8. d) that is, the holy of holies or the most holy space. See chapter 43:12; 48:12. V. 4. e) this holy part of the land (v. 1) f) shall be for the priests (c. 48:10) ministering to the Sanctuary. g) who draw near to minister to the Lord. Chapter 40:46; 44:15. h) so that it may be a place for them. i) for houses. For a field is not given to the priests (c. 44:28). k) and a more holy or consecrated place (Numbers 18:29) for the Sanctuary, for the holy structure (v. 3; c. 48:21). A rhetorical repetition <note>original: "Antanaclasis"</note>. Cocceius: The whole portion of 25,000 in width [by] 10,000 is holy (v. 1), but something from it was to be set apart as especially holy for the Sanctuary; the rest is destined for the houses of the priests. V. 5. l) And 25,000 reeds in length, as in verses 1, 2, 3. Here follows the portion of the Levites, having to the north the portion and habitation of the Priests with the Sanctuary, which occupied the middle place in that portion of the Priests (v. 4). m) and 10,000 in width. Thus the Levites occupied more space than the Priests, since the length and width of their portion was as widely extended as the portion of the priests and the Sanctuary combined (v. 1, 3). n) and this shall be the Levites' (c. 48:13). o) Chapter 44:11, 12. p) for them, I say, it shall pass into possession (v. 8). q) that is, with twenty chambers. Chapter 40:17, 38, 44; 41:10; 42:1, 4, 5, etc., in which they would live, so as to be near the Temple. The remaining space served their necessity and convenience. Thus Meyerus on pages 46 and following. But Cocceius says: By apposition, he calls that space "twenty chambers"—because the place or portion of the Levites ought to have 20 chambers built, so that their place could be named from those twenty chambers. However, by "Chambers" or "Rooms" <note>original: "Cellas s. Cubicula"</note> one should not understand small and narrow buildings here, but plainly grand and magnificent ones, furnished with many conveniences. Formerly the Levites were scattered through the twelve tribes, and to them were assigned cities of refuge, asylums. Here the Levites are gathered into one (compare Psalm 133:1), and to them is assigned a notable place for living with twenty chambers or halls, not so much for receiving guests as for receiving many coming from all the tribes to learn the word of the Lord, and as if preparing the offering of all, that it may be sanctified in the Holy Spirit. V. 6. r) And the possession of the city you shall give (v. 7). Here the sacred Architect proceeds to the dimension of the city, which he has gone further into and accurately defined in chapter 48:15–19 and verses 30–35, where its gates and circuit are described. The City was located to the south of the Temple, as we have already said at verse 5, having the tribe of Benjamin to its south (c. 48:22, 23), which can be more clearly seen from the ground plan <note>original: "Ichnographia"</note> of the whole land, such as the famous Meyerus exhibits according to this revelation (with the portion of the Priests and Levites transposed). This prophecy therefore places the Sanctuary outside the City; and yet it joins the city to the Sanctuary, to signify that in the kingdom of Christ, cities and republics are to be given to the people of God, in which, however, the kingdom of God is not taken captive, says Cocceius (compare Hosea 11:9). s) Five thousand reeds in width from north toward south, as in verse 1; compare chapter 48:15. Here again, all that precedes teaches that "reeds" are indicated; and Jerome says on this passage: "The City shall have five thousand reeds in width."

For thirteen portions of land are described in the division in chapter 48, of which the thirteenth is assigned to the Prince between the borders of Judah and Benjamin (48:22), while the remaining twelve are assigned to the twelve tribes. Indeed, the sanctuary was as if attached to the Prince's portion, because it is the duty of godly Princes to provide a place for the Church to dwell and to practice those things that must be done in the assembly of brothers. See Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 1603–1669, a Dutch theologian known for federal theology</note>. p) See chapter 47:20.

q) Chapter 47:18. **v. 8. v)** Regarding the land, this shall be his for a possession (v. 5). s) **And my Princes shall no longer vex** or oppress my people (see 18:7, 46:18), as they did previously in Jerusalem (22:6) and as Ahab did in Israel (1 Kings 21:10, 15) and others (Micah 2:1-2; see also 1 Samuel 8:11 ff.). **t)** Instead, they shall grant the land to the house of Israel. **u)** **According to their tribes** (47:13, 21, 22). These things teach that the Christian people under Princes will not live as if under masters, but as if under fathers or brothers, who have their own portion in the common inheritance. (Cocceius).
**v. 9. x)** **Let it be enough for you** (44:6). **y)** **O Princes of Israel** (v. 8). Jerome: "So great is your power that your possession has received the portion of an entire tribe." (Compare note on v. 7). **z)** Therefore, **violence and destruction** (Jeremiah 6:7, 20:8, Habakkuk 1:3). **a)** **Remove them** (Isaiah 1:16). **b)** **But do what is right and just** (18:5, 19, 21). **c)** **Take away, remove** (21:31, Isaiah 57:14). **d)** **Your extortions, your expulsions** (r). See Micah 2:9. **e)** v. 15, 11:8, 16:14.
**v. 10. f)** **Just scales and weights** (Leviticus 19:36, Proverbs 16:11). **g)** **And a just Ephah** <term>Ephah: A dry measure, roughly 22 liters</term>, a just bushel. See the opposite in Micah 6:10. **h)** **And a just Bath** <term>Bath: A liquid measure equal in volume to the dry Ephah</term>, a just measure of liquids. See 1 Kings 5:2. **i)** **Let it be yours.** For it is the mark of a Christian city both to exercise justice and judgment in every matter, and also in exchanges or commerce (compare 1 Corinthians 6:7-10, 1 Thessalonians 4:6). (Cocceius).

<column>
**v. 11. k)** **Ephahs and Baths** (v. 10). **l)** **One and the same measure** (2) there shall be (Exodus 5:18; compare above 28:12). **m)** **So that the Bath contains** (Genesis 36:7). **n)** **A tenth of a Homer** <term>Homer: The largest Hebrew unit of volume, also called a Cor</term>. See v. 14. **o)** For a tenth part of a Homer shall be an Ephah. See Leviticus 27:16. **p)** And according to the Homer or Cor (v. 14). **q)** **Shall be its measurement** or proportion (s). (2 Chronicles 24:13).
**v. 12. r)** **As for the Shekel** <term>Shekel: The standard weight for currency, approximately 11 grams</term>. Regarding which, see 4:10, 1 Samuel 17:5. **s)** **It shall be twenty Gerahs** <term>Gerah: The smallest unit of weight, 1/20th of a shekel</term>. See Exodus 30:13, Leviticus 27:25, Numbers 3:47. **t)** **Twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels, fifteen shekels**, that is, according to the Rabbis and others, sixty shekels shall make a Maneh <term>Maneh: Also known as a Mina, a larger unit of weight and currency</term> for you. They wish to say that these three parts of the number 60 are mentioned here because each of them constituted a certain and common type of coin: so that one was 20 shekels, another 25, and finally a third of 15 shekels. See Abarbanel on this passage. But Cocceius says: "I cannot be brought to believe that the Spirit here composed the Maneh out of three unequal parts, if He intended to mean that the Maneh is sixty shekels." What if we say that in our passage three types of Maneh are distinguished? A large one of 25, a medium one of 20, and a small one of 15 shekels? etc. **u)** **Shall be the Maneh for you.** (3) (1 Kings 10:17, Ezra 2:69). We translate it "Maneh" (Mina), not because it corresponds exactly to the Greek *minas*, but because of the similarity of the sound, as other interpreters, ancient and modern, have done; so says Clericus on 1 Kings 10:17. From that passage, compared with 2 Chronicles 9:16, it is clear that the Maneh in Solomon's time consisted of 100 shekels. Therefore, the Prophet seems to deliver a new proportion here, just as he innovates somewhat in the sacrifices and other matters. Compare Gussetius p. 472. C. Cocceius rightly advises: "As for what pertains to these measures, they are from the Hebrews, and the Christian people are not precisely bound to their use by this prophecy; but rather that integrity should be observed analogically in every measure and weight." If there were one empire, or a consensus among many princes, perhaps (indeed, easily) it could be achieved that measure, weight, and money would agree everywhere; the disparity of which is a gain to some and a loss to others.
</column>

<note>The following notes are scholarly arguments from the bottom of the page.</note>

u) Cocceius & Starckius: they shall be obligated. Vulgate, Tigurine version: he shall be held. x) toward this offering or collection described in verses 13 and following. y) To the Prince or for the Prince in Israel. v. 7. cf. notes on c. 44, 3. It should also be known (says Meyer in his dissertation p. 56) that this first offering, given to the prince, is not the one they were bound by law to give to the priests. Since the offering mandated by law was not from the flock, but from the threshing floor and the yield of the winepress (Exod 23:19; Num 15:19-20; c. 18:12; Ez 44:30). This, however, was to be given to the prince, partly for his dignified maintenance, and partly so that he might give from it what was required for the sin offering, the grain offering, the burnt offering, and the peace offerings—not for individuals, but the general offerings for the whole assembly. Therefore, the next verse says: "to make atonement for the house of Israel." This prophecy cannot be referred to the times of Ezra and Zerubbabel, compare Neh 5:14-19.

v. 17. z) Starckius: "But it shall be upon the Prince," it shall be incumbent upon him. vid. note 2 Sam 18:11. a) to provide burnt offerings from that offering of the people in v. 13, 16. b) and the sacrifice from flour v. 13. c) and the drink offering c. 20, 28. d) on the feasts c. 45, 11. e) and in the new moons and sabbaths. c. 46, 3. f) in all meetings or fixed days of the house of Israel. c. 36, 38; c. 46, 11. Meyer (loc. cit.): The Prince, he says, is not bound to give the daily sacrifices (as others conclude from c. 46:13), since those were to be bought with the half-shekel given by the whole congregation (Exod 30:13). g) "he himself shall do" i.e., shall provide v. 22. h) sin offering c. 42, 13; c. 43, 19. i) see v. 15. k) see ibid. Cocceius: that is, it is incumbent upon the Prince to provide the proclamation of the divine word, so that the people may know with which sacrifice, or in which priest, it is fitting for them to approach God and obtain remission of sins.

v. 18. l) in the first month. v. 21. m) on the first day of that month. c. 26:1. n) you shall take a bull for the dedication of the Altar and Sanctuary, of which we spoke above in c. 43:18. o) c. 43:22, 23. p) "and you shall expiate the Sanctuary." Some have dared to judge the book of Ezekiel poorly and thought of hiding it with insane counsel <note>referring to early Rabbinic debates about the book's contradictions with the Torah</note>, as Meyer proved at the start of his dissertation. However, Meyer rightly argues here that this prophecy was not fulfilled after the return from Babylonian captivity under the second Temple; and with Cocceius, it is manifest to us that corporal sacrifices are not understood here. For otherwise, according to Moses's institution, they would have to be offered (Mal 3:22). Therefore, as Cocceius writes, we must think of something signified here through an enigma. Namely, from the beginning of the year of grace, as if with the first new light, the sanctification and justification of God dwelling in men would be preached and recognized, made through the offering of the body of Christ, who is compared to a bull of the herd without blemish, etc.

v. 19. q) And the priest shall take of the blood of the sin offering v. 17; Lev 4:7. r) on the doorpost of the house c. 41:21. s) and on the four corners c. 43:20. t) Starckius: the prominence; Cocceius: the ledges of the altar. see c. 43:14, 20. x) c. 46, 1. Cocceius: Since this blood is ordered to be smeared on the post of the house and the four corners of the altar's ledge, and on the post of the inner court gate (which was also not commanded by Moses), it can signify that this is the blood of the testament, both the blood of the Son of God and the blood of those in whom God dwells, and of all who enter the inner court.

<margin>
**v. 21. b)** "In the first month." <note>See verse 18; Genesis 8:13.</note> **c)** "the fourteenth day." <note>Exodus 12:6.</note> **d)** "the Passover." <note>Exodus 12:11.</note> **e)** "of weeks" <note>Jeremiah 5:24</note> of days. According to the commentator **Abarbanel**, the Passover is called a feast of weeks because they ate unleavened bread for seven days <note>Exodus 12:15</note>. However, **Rabbi Solomon (Rashi)** believes it is because they would count seven weeks from then until Pentecost <note>Leviticus 23:15; Deuteronomy 16:9–10</note>. **Gussetius** argues that "weeks" is used in the plural here because it refers to the institution of Passover as an annual festival to be celebrated many times over the centuries. **f)** "it shall be eaten with unleavened bread." This should be understood primarily according to the Apostle’s interpretation in 1 Corinthians 5:7–8, which **Cocceius** explains more broadly. Furthermore, Ezekiel’s commands for Passover and Tabernacles differ significantly from the Mosaic laws; therefore, these should not be applied to the time of Ezra (who restored the cult exactly according to Moses), as **Meyer** has proven.
</margin>

**v. 7.** *rams.* Notably, in the Law of Moses, there were only two bulls, one ram, and seven lambs <note>Numbers 28:19</note>. **o)** "without blemish." <note>See verse 18; chapter 45:4, 6.</note> **p)** "for each day." <note>Ezekiel 43:25.</note> **q)** "for a sin offering." <note>See verse 22.</note> **r)** <note>See chapter 43:22, 25.</note> **s)** <note>Chapter 4:10.</note> **Cocceius:** Here again a male goat is required daily for a sin offering. There is no other sacrifice for sin but one. While it is being prepared for the yoke, it is called a "goat," just as it is elsewhere called a "serpent" or a "lamb." **v. 24. t)** "And a grain offering." <note>See verses 15 and 17.</note> **u)** "An ephah." <note>See verse 10; chapter 46:5.</note> **x)** Here, the grain offering for a bull and a ram is made equal, whereas they differ in Numbers 28:20. **y)** "and a hin of oil for each ephah." <note>See chapter 46:5, 7, 11.</note> The Mosaic Law in Numbers 15:6 prescribes two-tenths of fine flour and a third of a hin of oil for a ram. In verse 9, for a bull, it requires three-tenths of an ephah and half a hin of oil. **Cocceius:** The gift of flour and oil is added because in the house of God there must be food, the sharing of all good things, and the cheerfulness and joy of the Holy Spirit. **v. 25. z)** "In the seventh month, on the fifteenth day." <note>See Leviticus 23:34; Numbers 29:12.</note> **a)** "at the festival of tabernacles." The prophet Zechariah <note>Zechariah 14:16</note> also prophesied about the true celebration of this feast. **b)** "he shall offer" the same sacrifices as at Passover. **c)** including the sin offering, **d)** the burnt offering, **e)** and the grain offering and oil. **Cocceius:** Passover signifies Christ’s crucifixion; the Feast of Tabernacles signifies what is called "the last hour." **Chapter 46. v. 1. f)** This chapter follows with rules for the Sabbath, the New Moon, festivals, and daily life, for both the Prince and the people. **Schmid** divides it into five parts: I. Entry and worship for the Prince and people (v. 1–3). II. The Prince's sacrifices on the Sabbath (v. 4–5), New Moon (v. 6–7), festivals (v. 11), voluntary offerings (v. 12), and the continual offering (v. 13–15). III. The manner of exiting (v. 8–10). IV. The Prince's inheritance and gifts (v. 16–18). V. The kitchens (v. 19–24). **g)** "The gate of the inner court." <note>Chapter 45:19.</note> **h)** "facing east." <note>Verse 12.</note> **i)** "shall be shut." <note>Chapter 44:1.</note> **k)** "during the six working days." <note>See Exodus 23:12.</note> **Cocceius:** There are times for work, but work should not lack dignity; it should be lawful and useful. However, we should not labor and sweat perpetually, handling earthly things; we must take days to fully enjoy the rest God prepared through Christ and devote ourselves to communal edification and the sparking of charity. **l)** "on the Sabbath day." <note>See verses 3 and 4.</note> **m)** "and on the day of the New Moon." **n)** "it shall be opened." **Cocceius:** This signifies that when a person devotes time to meditation and the study of sacred scripture, the path is opened through which Christ enters the Church and each believer, making them his temple. **v. 2. o)** "And the Prince shall enter." **Maius** notes that the "Princes of the people" are all believers <note>1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 5:10</note>. Through Christ, the gate of heaven is opened to them, and they always offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God. They have food prepared <note>Matthew 22:4</note>, which is the flesh of Christ <note>John 6:33, 51</note>. **p)** "by way of the porch" or through the gate’s vestibule. <note>Verses 8 and 9; Chapter 44:3.</note> **q)** "from the outside." <note>Chapter 40:19.</note> **r)** "and shall stand." <note>Compare 2 Chronicles 6:12.</note> **s)** "by the doorpost of the gate." <note>Chapter 41:21; 43:8.</note> **t)** <note>Chapter 44:15.</note> **u)** <note>Verses 4 and 12.</note> The fact that the priests offer the Prince’s sacrifices here simply means they give thanks to God in the assembly for the offerings provided by the Prince and people. **x)** "and shall worship at the threshold of the gate" <note>Chapter 9:3; 47:1</note> and then depart. While in other times the King would enter the inner court to worship and sit there during the service, Ezekiel brings the Prince only to the threshold, where he stands while the sacrifice is offered. These are the words of the scholar **John Lightfoot** in his *Description of the Temple*. Lightfoot notes that Solomon had placed a bronze platform inside this gate where he prayed on his knees. In later times, kings entered through this gate and had their own place by the "royal pillar" <note>2 Chronicles 23:13</note>. His seat was placed inside this gate at one of the columns. **y)** <note>Compare Isaiah 60:11.</note>

**CHAPTER 46, v. 2. x)** "And he shall worship" with a *Metig* accent.

Chapter 44:11. m) The sacrifices of the people. Compare 1 Samuel 2:13, following. **CHAPTER XLVII, Verse 1.** n) Afterward (from the kitchens of the outer court toward the north, chapter 46:21, following), he brought me back. See v. 8, chapter 44:1. o) To the door of the House itself or the Temple (chapter 40:47, 48; 41:13; 43:16). This chapter can be divided either into five parts (according to Schmid) or even into two or three. For here are shown to the Prophet: I. Waters proceeding from the Temple of the Lord and growing into a deep river (v. 1–6), and Trees growing on both banks (v. 7). II. The course and use of the waters (v. 8–11) and the fruit of the trees (v. 12) are explained. III. The boundaries of the Holy Land to be divided (v. 13), toward the north (v. 15), east (v. 18), south (v. 19), and west (v. 21), are described, and foreigners or "sojourners" are also admitted into its inheritance (v. 22), so that there may be one flock and one universal Shepherd (chapter 34:23, 37:24, John 10:16). p) chapter 1:4, 40:3. q) Waters, mystical and entirely wonderful and healing (v. 8); namely, the Holy Spirit and His word and gifts, the Evangelical doctrine and saving knowledge of God, etc. See Isaiah 12:3 (and the Targum of Jonathan there), chapter 11:9, 44:3; compare Joel 4:18, Zechariah 14:8, which places the Jewish scholar Abarbanel himself compares to this passage. Add Psalm 23:2, John 4:10, chapter 7:38, 39, Revelation 7:17, and especially Revelation 22:1, following. For we should not understand here, as the scholar Grotius wished, natural waters which were led from the Etham spring <note>a historical spring near Jerusalem</note> through subterranean channels or pipes into the Temple, breaking out into the priests' court to wash the victims, purge the floor of blood, and cast out filth; even if the Holy Spirit perhaps alludes to that, as we shall soon hear from Lightfoot. Rather, these are entirely mystical and spiritual. See Calovius on this passage p. 583, and p. 584 on v. 12; also Meyer’s *Dissertation* p. 114 and 118, etc. Truly, says Abarbanel, the Prophet here speaks of intellectual <note>or spiritual</note> waters. *Commentary* folio 219a. r) They were going out. v. 12, on the highest mountain (chapter 40:2), as Isaiah also predicted in chapter 2:2. s) Below the threshold. Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan</note>: from the side of the threshold of the Temple (chapter 9:3, 10:4), from the throne of God and the Lamb (Revelation 22:1), who is the only door or entrance to God (John 14:6). t) Toward the east (chapter 45:7). u) For the face of the House (chapter 41:14). x) It was eastern or toward the east (v. 3). Cocceius: these things suggest to us that thought, that the Church of the New Testament, led from the east and established in the west, turns itself in its faith to Him who comes from the east, etc. y) And those waters were flowing down (v. 8). z) Below (Judges 7:8). a) From the side of the Temple (1 Kings 7:39). b) The right (2 Chronicles 4:10). c) From the southern side (chapter 40:2) of the Altar (chapter 43:13, 18). It alludes to the water flowing down into the Temple from the Etham spring, which for that reason was enclosed. For the pipes that brought water from there descended to the southern side of the Temple, to that place which was called the "descent of the water," etc. Lightfoot in his *Description of the Temple of Jerusalem*, p. 613. **Verse 2.** d) And he led me out. Compare chapter 42:1, 46:21. e) Through the North gate (chapter 40:35, 44:4, 46:9). f) And he led me around (1 Samuel 5:9, 10). g) Outside, by the exterior way. h) To the outer gate (chapter 44:1). i) By the way that looks toward the east (chapter 11:1, 46:1, 12). k) See v. 1. l) Vulgate: "overflowing waters were breaking out"; they were trickling (1) as if from a *lenticula* <note>a small flask or vessel</note>, a vessel with a narrow mouth, such as an oil vessel (1 Samuel 10:1, 2 Kings 9:1, 3). Or because the form is from *pachah* <note>to trickle</note>, rather compare the related *bachah* <note>to weep</note>, which is used no less of trickling waters than of tears (see Job 28:11 and 36:30). So in Arabic, *faki* means water or a tear flowed, from which comes the name *ayin* for both "fountain" and "eye." m) From the right side (v. 1). **Verse 3.** n) Therefore, when that man (described in chapter 40:3) went out with me (v. 2). o) Toward the east, as in v. 1. p) And he had a measuring line in his hand. See chapter 40:3. q) Jonathan: he measured a thousand cubits. So in v. 4, 5, namely proceeding toward the east. r) By the cubit measure (chapter 40:5). s) And he made me pass through the waters (v. 4, chapter 46:21). s) The waters of the ankles; the Vulgate: through the water up to the ankles (1).
