Hof. 6, 11, etc. **o)** verses 1, 2. **p)** On the bank of the river, verse 6. **q)** A tree, or collectively, there were trees, verse 12. Compare Genesis 1:11, 12; chapter 2:9. **r)** Very many. Verses 9, 10. **s)** Vulgate: "from each side." Verse 12, chapter 45:7. Cocceius: Revelation 22:1, 2 made this its own. It indicates that those speeches of the Church will not be fruitless, but through the grace of the Holy Spirit will be fertile for the germination of many righteous ones, who are like a tree planted by streams of water, Psalm 1:3.

**v. 8. t)** verse 6. He is about to declare more specifically those mystical waters (verse 1 and following) and then the trees (verses 7, 12). **u)** Those waters go out (verse 1). **x)** Toward Galilee. So the Septuagint, Jonathan, Syriac, Arabic, etc. See notes on Joshua 20:7, 1 Kings 9:11. Others, like the Syriac, say "to the border." Tigurine: "to the limit," etc., as in Joshua 13:2, but we prefer the former. **y)** Eastern (1). Septuagint, Jonathan, Syriac, and Arabic: "which is to the east." Others: "the forward [sea]." Compare Zechariah 14:8. **z)** And they shall descend (verse 1). **a)** Into the plain of the desert. See Isaiah 35:6 and compare Deuteronomy 4:49, Joshua 12:1, 3, 2 Kings 14:25. Septuagint and Arabic: "into Arabia." **b)** And they shall come to the sea, or they shall enter into the sea. Cocceius: Understand, he says, the Salt Sea or the Sea of Sodom. Commonly called the Dead Sea, or Lake Asphaltites. Regarding it, Tacitus <note>Roman historian, c. 56–120 AD</note> says in *Histories* Book V, chapter 6: "The lake is of immense circumference, in the appearance of a sea, in taste more corrupt, and by the weight of its odor pestilential to those living near it; it is neither stirred by wind, nor does it endure fish or birds accustomed to the water." This description beautifully fits this passage, and that lake provides an elegant symbol of the corrupt world or the whole human race, 1 John 5:19. See Calov <note>Abraham Calovius, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> on this passage and Hafenreffer, whom he cites. **c)** Into the sea, I say, they shall come; that is, those waters led out from the Sanctuary (verses 1, 12) shall flow in. Most here understand the Dead Sea. But Jonathan translates "into the Great Sea" (that is, the Mediterranean; see Numbers 34:5, Joshua 15:12, chapter 16:6, 8, chapter 17:9, chapter 19:26, 29) they shall be poured out. In this way, the healing waters flow toward all quarters of the world. See Abarbanel's commentary on this passage, folio 218d and 219b, compared with verse 9 and Zechariah 14:8. Thus Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa, 17th-century theologian</note> on Revelation 22, page 1219, says: The river that watered Paradise was divided into four channels, Genesis 2:10, just like Ezekiel's river flowing from the sanctuary; the same reasoning seems to have applied to the river of Revelation 22:1, 2, because it is established that both those passages are alluded to there. Truly, the image of that Dead Sea suffices to represent the matter, especially since in verse 10 the Great Sea is expressly distinguished from it. **d)** So that the waters may be healed and become sweet, and not retain those pestilential and harmful qualities. Verses 9, 11. Compare 2 Kings 2:21, 22 and Ephesians 2:1 following, 1 Corinthians 6:11, etc.

Compare chapter 1:12, 20. **h)** The double-river <note>original: "nahalayim"</note>. Flowing toward the east and the west. Verse 8, Zechariah 14:8. **i)** That shall live. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian</note>: It shall not perish, like those fish that are put into the Dead Sea. Compare again Ephesians 2:1 following. **k)** Cocceius: "and there shall be a generation of fish," or there shall be kinds of fish. Verse 10. **l)** Very many. Verses 7, 10. **m)** For when they have come there. Verse 8. **n)** These waters (verse 1). **o)** The sea waters shall be healed. Syriac: those waters shall be made sweet. So verse 8. **p)** So that it may live. Genesis 3:22, Numbers 21:8, 9, Deuteronomy 19:4, 5, John 3:16. **q)** Everything, namely, wherever the river comes.

Matthew 4:19, Luke 5:10. **u)** From En-gedi, a town of Judea, not far from the Dead Sea. See notes on Joshua 15:62, 1 Samuel 24:1, 2. **x)** To En-eglaim, which is called the "Spring of Calves" (1). For Jerome <note>4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note>, this town is at the beginning of the Dead Sea where the Jordan enters; while En-gedi is where it ends and is consumed. That is to say, from one end of the sea to the other: because, as Calvin <note>John Calvin, 16th-century Reformer</note> notes, fishermen will be active throughout the entire Dead Sea to enclose men in the dragnet of the Word, and draw them out to the harbor of the Church and eternal life. **y)** An expansion or spreading (1) of nets or dragnets. Compare Genesis 1:21. **b)** Their fish shall be. Vulgate: there shall be very many species of its fish, of the sea once dead; that is, various kinds of men shall be gathered to the life of God and the Church of Christ. Galatians 3:28, Colossians 3:11.

k) "In its going out" <note>Hebrew: *b’tzato*</note>—referring to those trees. Compare Ezekiel 33:16 and 58:11. x) "They go out from the Sanctuary." See verse 1.

Verse 11. f) "The miry places of the Dead Sea." (3) Job 8:11. Compare also Jeremiah 38:22. g) "And its marshes" or its pools. (2) Isaiah 30:14. Compare Isaiah 66:24, Zechariah 14:17, Revelation 20:8.
8. Cocceius: Such are those who arm themselves with their own wisdom against the truth and twist the scriptures everywhere with all cleverness. Such people are not easily led to the knowledge of truth. For they are mockers, and seem wise to themselves because they abound in talent for speaking against and making noise. But Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the prophets</note> says: for the profane, they will be as if destined for another and good use. Compare Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, the 15th-century Jewish philosopher</note>.

## 11 Its marshes <gloss>k</gloss> shall not be healed; they are given over to salt.
## 12 And by the river <gloss>l</gloss> there shall grow <gloss>m</gloss> upon its bank <gloss>n</gloss> on this side and on that all kinds of trees for food <gloss>o</gloss>; its leaf shall not wither <gloss>p</gloss> nor its fruit fail <gloss>q</gloss>; it shall bring forth fresh fruit <gloss>t</gloss> according to its months <gloss>s</gloss>, because its waters <gloss>u</gloss> flow out from the Sanctuary; and their fruit <gloss>v</gloss> shall be for food, and its leaf <gloss>w</gloss> for healing <gloss>a</gloss>.
## 13 Thus says the Lord <gloss>y</gloss> GOD: This <gloss>b</gloss> shall be the border by which you shall inherit the land for the twelve tribes of Israel; Joseph <gloss>f</gloss> shall have two portions.
## 14 And you shall inherit it, one as well as another, concerning which I lifted up my hand <gloss>g</gloss> to give it to your fathers; and this land shall fall to you as an inheritance.
## 15 And this shall be the border of the land on the north side <gloss>m</gloss>: from the Great Sea <gloss>o</gloss>, by the way of Hethlon <gloss>p</gloss>, as one goes <gloss>q</gloss> to Zedad <gloss>r</gloss>;
## 16 Hamath <gloss>s</gloss>, Berothah <gloss>t</gloss>, Sibraim <gloss>u</gloss>, which is between the border of Damascus <gloss>v</gloss> and the border of Hamath <gloss>w</gloss>; Hazar-hatticon <gloss>x</gloss>, which is on the border of Hauran <gloss>z</gloss>.

---

(1) It is clear that these things are truly mystical. There seems to be an allusion to the balsam shrub, which was native to Judea, as we noted above on chapter 27:17 from Pliny. Just as salvation is from Judea (John 4:22). Regarding the significance, Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> says that Oleander <note>Lucas Osiander, a 16th-century theologian</note> expressed it well: From the preaching of the Gospel and the administration of the sacraments, many Christians will be born everywhere, who are good and fruitful trees. And as various species of trees produce various good fruits, so they, according to the diversity of their gifts, serve their neighbor in various and diverse ways. Compare Isaiah 61:3, Matthew 13:52, Philippians 1:11, 1 Peter 3:1. But the Tree of Life, which (in imitation of this vision of Ezekiel) was seen by John in Revelation 22:2, bearing fruit on both sides of the river, signifies without any doubt Jesus Christ, who through His obedience and death became the cause of life and salvation for miserable sinners who would have perished without Him. For "in Him was life" (John 1:4). So Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa, a prominent 17th-century commentator on Revelation</note> in his Commentary on Revelation, page 1219. And it is necessary for us to be conformed to this Tree of Life, as fruitful trees, says Calovius on this passage, where more things deserve to be read. Nor does Cocceius write badly of the leaves of these trees in his Lexicon, page 826: The good works of the faithful, which otherwise even infidels do, smell of faith and charity, and thus are adapted for the conversion of the nations. * v. 13. b) c)

---

* v. 13. b) **GEH** <note>Hebrew term for "this"</note> and **LEVEN** in the written text (*Ktibh*), and **LEKHEN** in the read version (*Kri*). Jonathan, the Septuagint, Arabic, and Vulgate say: "this shall be the boundary." So Abarbanel. But for Cocceius it means an "elevation," and for Neumann <note>Caspar Neumann, a German scholar</note> it means the "bending or inclination of the border." (1). d) for which you shall receive the land as an inheritance. Numbers 33:54, Ezekiel 34:13, Isaiah 14:1-2. e) For the twelve tribes of Israel (v. 21, 22; c. 37:19). Not only does Abarbanel urge that all these tribes, according to the letter of this prophecy, must eventually be brought back to their homeland, but Meyer <note>Probably a reference to the scholar Sebastian Meyer</note> also undertook to prove this from Deuteronomy 30, Deuteronomy 32, Psalm 69, Isaiah 11, and Jeremiah 50. He suggests the return of the Israelites to their land is among those things that can happen; although the manner and circumstances remain a mystery. Cocceius agrees, yet notes that the "land of the nations" is also the inheritance of God (Jeremiah 3:19) and the Church will dwell on the heights of the earth. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch humanist and jurist</note> refers all this to the times of Ezra, writing: "This assignment would have taken place if the ten tribes had converted to God no less than Judah and Benjamin." But (as Calovius rightly says) here the possessions are simply assigned to all tribes. There is not the slightest trace of a condition or hypothesis here. Nor would there have been a need for an accurate designation of all borders if God had meant that those tribes would never return. Those not returning needed no possessions. It is in no way agreeable to think God, who foresees all from eternity, wished to determine these limits in vain. Therefore we have a clear argument here: these things cannot be understood literally about the land of Canaan and the twelve tribes of Israel, but must be understood of the *spiritual* Canaan, the Church of Christ, and the Israel according to the promise—the true faithful. The twelve tribes, therefore, are all the faithful. Meyer argues for a mystical meaning for these final chapters of Ezekiel, which even Abarbanel acknowledges elsewhere. It is useless for that same Jew to use a dilemma (that either everything is literal or everything is mystical) as an "invincible argument" against Christians. Whatever may be said about the return to Canaan, which we leave to divine providence: the things that occur regarding the House of the Lord and its ministry cannot be explained as a prophecy of a physical Temple and external worship, as such rites do not fit the state of the New Testament Church or other prophecies. f) Joseph shall have two "lines" <note>measuring cords</note>, i.e., as Jonathan has it: Joseph shall receive two portions (which used to be measured by cords). This was as of old, for the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, to complete the number of twelve tribes because the tribe of Levi received no part of the land inheritance. v. 14. g) And you shall inherit it. h) "A man" i.e., each one, just like his brother; meaning in equal parts through the twelve tribes; unlike what was done of old where a more numerous tribe was given more. i) "Because I lifted my hand" <note>a gesture of swearing an oath</note>. Jonathan: "Because I swore by my Word." k) Compare Genesis 12:7, 17:8. l) "And therefore it shall fall"—it shall be distributed to you as an inheritance by lot. v. 15. m) "This, I say, shall be the boundary." n) Toward the northern side. o) From the Great Sea (the Mediterranean). p) By the way of Hethlon, in Damascene Syria. r) Where one goes toward Zedad. v. 16. s) Hamath. t) Toward Berothah. u) And Sibraim. x) Which are towns. y) Between the border of Damascus and Hamath. z) Compare the notes on Isaiah 37:11 and Zechariah 9:1.

<column-break/>

* v. 12. k) Furthermore, next to the river. l) "It shall ascend," i.e., it shall grow (Isaiah 32:13). m) On its bank. n) On both sides. Abarbanel: i.e., on the side of the Israelites and of the nations. o) Trees of every kind (Genesis 2:9). p) Food, i.e., fruit-bearing. q) Whose leaves shall not fall or wither (Psalm 1:3), but shall always be green. r) Nor shall their fruit be finished. s) But in their individual months. The Vulgate and Jonathan: "through every month." The Syriac: "at every beginning of the months." t) They shall bring forth early or "precocious" fruits. u) Because (so that you may know the cause) its water; or because of the gathering...

---

* v. 11. **B'TZATO** <note>in its going out</note> with the reading variant *b'tzatav*. So also the Masoretic Erff. * v. 12. **LECHODASHAV** <note>for its months</note> spelled with Segol in various manuscripts. * v. 13. **GEH** with the reading variant *Gia*. v. 15. **LAVO** with Kametz.

<summary>This page describes the miraculous fertility of the river banks in Ezekiel's vision, where trees produce monthly fruit and healing leaves. It also begins the technical delineation of the borders for a restored Israel, sparking a scholarly debate between literal and spiritual interpretations of the twelve tribes' return.</summary>

**CHAPTER XLVIII. v. 1.**
a) These then are the names. Ex. 1:1. b) of the tribes. Concerning which he had spoken in general terms in ch. 47:13, 21, 22. But here all and each are recounted in a special order, some in a different place than they formerly occupied: a certain proof, without doubt, that old things have passed away and all things here are made new (2 Cor. 5:17). There are seven northern tribes (relative to the Sanctuary, which is placed in the middle v. 8-22): Dan, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, Reuben, and Judah (v. 1-7). There are five southern tribes: Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun, and Gad (v. 23-27). According to Schmidt, the parts of this chapter are three: I. the hereditary boundaries of the individual tribes are described v. 1-7 and v. 23-29. II. The *Terumah* <note>term: Terumah; the sacred portion of land set apart from the common land</note> or sacred portion of the land v. 8 and 20: for the priests and the sanctuary v. 10-12; for the Levites v. 13; for the city v. 15-16; for the suburbs v. 17; for the city workers v. 18-19; and for the Prince v. 21, 22. III. The exits and gates of the city v. 30-34, with its circumference and noble name v. 35. c) from the innermost extreme part. Tigurinus: in the extreme part. see note on ch. 33:2. Others, like Cocceius: from the northern boundary. d) to the north, toward the northern region ch. 47:15. e) next to the way, so to speak, "at hand," or at the side of the road. Compare Ex. 2:5, Num. 13:29, 1 Sam. 4:13, 18, 2 Sam. 15:2, ch. 18:4. f) see ch. 47:15. g) where one goes to Hamath ch. 47:20. h) Hazar-Enan. see ch. 47:17. i) the border of Damascus ch. 47:16. k) toward the north ch. 47:17. l) that is, next to Hamath, as just before. m) and they shall be to him, namely the tribe of Dan, at the end of the verse. n) Cocceius: the eastern side; or: from the eastern side. ch. 47:18. o) to the sea, that is, even to the western boundary ch. 47:20. and here in the following verses. <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἔσται αὐτῷ τὰ πρὸς ἀνατολὰς ἕως πρὸς θάλασσαν" - and the parts toward the east as far as the sea shall be his</note>.
So the Arabic. p) Dan one tribe, and the possessor and heir of one of the thirteen portions. See v. 2 and following.

l) to the waters of strife at Kadesh. (see the same place).
m) Scholarly note: "it shall be an inheritance." So the Septuagint, Jonathan, Syriac, Arabic, and Vulgate; but the Tigurine and Dutch versions: "to the river of Egypt, and as far as the Mediterranean Sea." (see note on ch. 47:19).
v. 29. n) This is the land (cf. Numbers 34:2, 12, 13; Deuteronomy 34:4).
o) which you shall divide by casting lots (see ch. 45:1).
p) from the inheritance. For the whole land is an inheritance; but not all of it is distributed by lot to the tribes: because the "Contribution" [the sacred portion] is within it; as Cocceius says.
q) to the individual tribes of Israel (v. 19, 31).
r) and these are the divisions or distributions of those tribes, or of those Israelites (cf. Joshua 11:23; 12:7; 18:10).
s) ch. 11:8; ch. 16:14.
v. 30. t) These indeed are the exits, that is, according to Menochius, the gates of the city (cf. ch. 42:11; Joshua 15:7; 16:3, 8).
u) from the northern side, as also the eastern (v. 32), southern (v. 33), and western (v. 34).
x) 4,500 reeds shall be the measure (v. 33), as was already said above in verse 16 (cf. Jeremiah 31:38, 39, 40).

<meta>This page marks the transition from the end of the Book of Ezekiel to the beginning of the "Book of the Twelve," commonly known as the Minor Prophets. # Preface to the Twelve Minor Prophets and Hosea

->§. 1.<-

<margin>The Twelve Prophets called "minor."</margin>
This sacred volume, which we now undertake to print by the favor of Christ the Lord, <note>original: "B. C. D.," likely abbreviating *Beante Christo Domino*.</note> encompasses the monuments of the Twelve Prophets. Because their works are shorter, and were thus collected into a single book long ago, they are usually called the *minor* prophets; as we already noted at the beginning of the Preface to Isaiah. For if you consider other factors, they do not yield to those we call "major" in the weight of their thoughts, the majesty of their words, or any other quality.

<margin>Sent before and after the captivity to the Israelites, Jews, and Gentiles.</margin>
§. 2. Most of these prophets flourished before the Assyrian and Babylonian captivities. Specifically, during the age of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, *Hosea* and *Amos* preached, primarily to the Ten Tribes (that is, the Kingdom of Israel). At roughly the same time, *Joel* and *Micah* preached to the Jews alongside *Isaiah*. Later, under Manasseh or Josiah, *Habakkuk* preached, and finally *Zephaniah* under that same Josiah. Regarding the Gentiles, *Jonah* prophesied to the Ninevites around the time of Uzziah; *Nahum* spoke against them during the age of Hezekiah or Manasseh. *Obadiah* prophesied against the Edomites, and *Habakkuk* against the Babylonians. However, after the Babylonian captivity was ended and the people returned, *Haggai* and *Zechariah* prophesied eighteen years after liberty was obtained, followed finally by *Malachi*, perhaps in the final years of Artaxerxes I (surnamed Longimanus). <note>See Vitringa, *Type of Prophetic Doctrine*, p. 42.</note> This followed the chronological sequence indicated partly by the titles and inscriptions of the books, <margin>Order and Age;</margin> and partly by the order in which they have succeeded one another in this volume since ancient times. This is true even though the age of some—especially Joel and Obadiah—is not yet so settled. Ancient Hebrew scholars think Joel was a contemporary <note>original Greek: <term>συγχρονον</term> (synchronon), meaning living at the same time.</note> of Elisha under Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, while others think he lived at the same time as Jeremiah. Most refer Obadiah to the times of Jeremiah; we shall discuss these in their proper place. a)

<margin>Characteristics and difficulties of Hosea.</margin>
§. 3. Each prophet, from Hosea to Malachi, has his own *characteristics*, which any skilled reader will easily observe (as Saint Jerome notes in his Preface to Hosea). Thus, frequent reading and repetition are necessary if one wishes to judge their style and meaning soundly. To come to Hosea—the first among these and a contemporary of Isaiah, Amos, and Micah—*he is extremely concise*, speaking as if through maxims or riddles. Therefore, he is profound in his meaning and often difficult in his expression due to brief allusions and frequent linguistic peculiarities. <margin>Helps: Prayer, History, Parallelism, Interpreters.</margin> *Hence Jerome writes in his prologue to Pammachius: "If in explaining all the prophets we need the coming of the Holy Spirit... by whose inspiration they were written... how much more must we pray to the Lord in explaining the prophet Hosea,"* and say with Peter: *"Explain this parable to us."* This is especially true since the author himself testifies to the obscurity of the volume at the end: *"Who is wise, and will understand these things? Understanding, and he will know them?"* <note>Hosea 14:9.</note> Yet Jerome rightly adds immediately: *"We should accept this not as something impossible, but as something difficult,"* etc. In obscure passages, light is provided by a deeper knowledge of the *history* of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, the state of their government and Church, and the *harmony* of the rest of Scripture and the other prophets of that time (which we diligently cite in our notes). Nor is there a lack of interpreters who have sought to unravel the sense of the prophecies more clearly. Aside from the Hebrew and ancient writers, the primary authors among our own people who have illustrated Hosea are *Luther* and *Brentz*, followed by *Tarnov* and *Schmid* (whom we will consult here above others). The work of Blessed Heinrich Ursinus on Hosea is brief and succinct, yet not to be deprived of its praise. A very clear and quite extensive commentary on Hosea was published in the English language by *Edward Pococke* at Oxford in 1685, though it is rarely found among us and has not been granted a Latin translation, unlike his commentary on Joel. However, the brevity of our own project does not permit us to present the opinions of many interpreters at length here. Nevertheless, where the connection of topics is difficult to find—as the learned Joannes Marckius thought it sometimes was, even in the Proverbs of Solomon—we have indicated it based on our own observations or those of others, confirming everything by the harmony or parallelism of Scripture.

<margin>Occasion: The security of the Israelites from prosperity, and impiety in worship and life:</margin>
§. 4. Furthermore, the *occasion* for these sermons by Hosea and the other prophets in Israel was this: under Jeroboam II, the affairs of the Israelites once again flourished greatly by divine mercy. Yet, they flattered themselves in their sins and considered God most gracious toward them, even though they had long ago cast aside the divine worship that God had prescribed through his servant Moses to exercise faith in the promised seed of Abraham. They had instituted new rites—indeed, worship strictly forbidden by the word of God. Thus, the more they enjoyed God's benefits, the worse they became; like beasts that become not more manageable, but more ferocious when fattened on delicate fodder. For they did not only wish to worship Jehovah under the foul symbol of calves (following the institution of Jeroboam I); but under the wicked King Ahab and the instinct of his most evil wife Jezebel, they publicly and solemnly received *Baal-worship*, killing those who dared to oppose the nefarious institution. Hence that slaughter of the prophets and servants of the Lord; hence the tears and complaining voices of Elijah, armed with divine zeal. And although that Baal-worship later seemed *extinguished* along with the family of Ahab by the new king Jehu, Jehu himself did not adhere sincerely to God. For "political interest" (as we usually say), he retained the worship of Jehovah under the calves (a truly detestable thing). Therefore, that other evil gradually broke out again, and through a horrific "syncretism" <note>A blending of different religions or beliefs.</note>, Baal and Moloch were worshipped alongside Jehovah, both privately and publicly. The history of the reformation undertaken by Hezekiah and the rebukes of the prophets everywhere testify to this. From this extinction of true worship and piety (which ought to be born from the doctrine of repentance and faith in Christ), there could not but follow wickedness and utterly corrupt morals in every part of life.

<margin>among the Kings</margin>
§. 5. For their *Kings* and *Princes*, having neglected God and His word, did not care for their own duty. Instead, they sinned against their poor subjects through injustice, impiety, the slaughter of innocents, and immoderate plundering. They did not consult the safety of the citizens; rather, they acted like thieves and robbers for their own treasury. Not even the very last king in Israel, *Hoshea*, was the worst of all, as we clearly read in the Book of Kings; yet superstition and stubbornness in retaining the worship of God corrupted by Jeroboam I had taken such deep root that no true, serious, or constant amendment ever occurred. This was despite the fact that they had been seriously warned not only by the prophets of God, but finally by Hezekiah through letters and messengers. Rather, they heaped sin upon sin through their very religious rites, until God finally rejected them from His face and overturned the kingdom through the Assyrians, never to be restored to them.

<margin>and the Priests</margin>
§. 6. For the *Priests*, who ought to have been the interpreters of the word and divine will, were not called or approved by God...

---

a) If their ages are taken into account, they should be arranged thus: Jonah, Joel, Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, Micah, Obadiah, Nahum, Jeremiah, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Daniel, Ezekiel, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. So says *Vitringa* in his *Type of Prophetic Doctrine*, p. 35. However, we do not think this is yet proven in all respects.

<summary>This preface introduces the Twelve Minor Prophets, explaining that "minor" refers to the length of their books rather than their importance. It focuses on Hosea, describing his difficult, enigmatic style and the corrupt historical context of the Northern Kingdom of Israel that necessitated his prophecies.</summary>
<keywords>Minor Prophets, Hosea, Chronology, Jeroboam II, Idolatry, Baal, Assyrian Captivity, Biblical Commentary, Jerome, Luther, Hezekiah</keywords>

--- Page 1161 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to the Minor Prophets, focusing specifically on the moral and spiritual decay of Israel and Judah during the time of Hosea. It transitions from the general history of the prophets to the specific structure and divine authority of the Book of Hosea.</meta>

They were approved <note>Hebrews 5:4</note> not by God, but by human will and under the direction of that impious Jeroboam <note>Jeroboam I, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel, who led the ten tribes into rebellion against the house of David.</note> <note>1 Kings 12:31</note> (whose memory is always condemned in Scripture; see 1 Kings 14:16; 15:26, 30; 16:26; 22:53; 2 Kings 3:3; 10:29, etc.). Having been introduced and maintained by his successors out of worldly wisdom, these priests likewise looked not to God or Christ, nor the salvation of souls, but only to their own bellies <note>Hosea 4:6, 8; 8:13</note>. Meanwhile, they were secure in their positions because they were supported by the favor and power of the Princes—whose ambitions they served <note>Hosea 7:3</note>. In disputes regarding true religion and the worship of God, they prevailed through the superstition and the vote of the multitude. They always cleverly used the name and worship of Jehovah (which they had not entirely abandoned) as a pretext for their impiety <note>Hosea 4:15; 5:2; 10:13; 8:3; cf. notes on 2:15, 18; 1 Kings 12:29, 32</note>. *) 6) In this way, it was not difficult for them to incite both the Princes and the common people against the teachers of true piety and to oppress them <note>Hosea 5:1, 2</note>. They would accuse them of being heretics or schismatics, or even seditious rebels, because the speech of those who preached of impending disasters was unpleasant—especially when everything still seemed to be going well for the impious. See a clear example of this in Amos 7:10 and following, and see the Preface to Hosea by our own Luther, as well as Hosea 4:4. For in every age, there have been those who traduced the pure word of God as a suspect doctrine or heresy <note>Hosea 8:12</note>. And as Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian and commentator.</note> observes on Hosea 4:4 (p. 147), the idolatrous hypocrisy of the Israelites had so demented them that they considered themselves righteous and religious; they did not recognize their own malice, but rather vigorously contradicted and falsely accused those who rebuked them. And on page 149, he says: "Thus, in the time of the prophet Jeremiah, the Jews argued with Jeremiah as if they had done rightly when they burned incense to the Queen of Heaven <note>original: "Melechet cælorum"</note> <note>Jeremiah 44</note>." And what wonder is this? Since the Jews, along with the hypocritical Pharisees, dared to contradict Christ himself and defend their hypocrisy; and likewise later the Apostles, and even today, they contradict true teachers.

<margin>As much as private ones.</margin>
§. 7. Private individuals, for their part, applied themselves chiefly to this study: by what arts and deceits they might scrape together some wealth and grow rich at the expense of others. See Hosea 4:2; 12:8, 9; Amos 2:6, etc. What shall we say of envy, prostitution, adultery, and other vices? <note>Hosea 4:11, 13, 14</note>. You would truly see a "Lerna" <note>A reference to the Lernaean Hydra, meaning a bottomless swamp or source of endless evils.</note> of all impieties and crimes in this people, as Brentius <note>Johannes Brenz, a German reformer.</note> writes in his preface to this book. See Hosea 4:1, 2; 6:10; 7:1. If any calamity befell them by divine judgment, such as famine or scarcity of grain <note>Hosea 7:14; 8:7</note>, or that horrible earthquake <note>Amos 1:1</note> which threatened the shaking of the kingdom (see notes on 2 Kings 14:25), or the violence of enemies, they did not sincerely turn to Jehovah their God <note>chapter 7:14-16</note>, as we have said. Instead, they fled now to the Assyrians, now to the Egyptians <note>Hosea 5:13; 7:11; 8:9, 13; 12:2</note>, and they mingled themselves with those nations <note>Hosea 7:8</note>. They mocked the teachers of piety <note>Hosea 7:16; see 2 Chronicles 30:10</note>, persisting against the express word of God as long as they had secured human protections for themselves <note>Hosea 5:14</note>. They did not believe this would be in vain <note>Hosea 7:9</note> until the outcome taught them that the threats of Jehovah were not empty <note>Hosea 6:14; 7:12, 13, 16; 8:3, 8</note>.

<margin>Also among the Jews.</margin>
§. 8. Matters were not much better among the Jews, as is known from the history of the times of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, etc. For although in political status under Uzziah and Jotham their affairs were stable enough, and neither Uzziah (at the beginning of his reign) nor Jotham handled sacred matters impiously or unsuccessfully; nevertheless, the zeal for piety grew cold during these favorable times, and under Ahaz, it degenerated into open idolatry. And when God, after the death of Ahaz, provided the Jews with a better prince in Hezekiah—who seriously cared for divine matters and under whose leadership some reform was made—the Princes, the Levites, the Priests, and the people did not burn with an equal zeal for piety. Thus, after the death of Hezekiah, under his degenerate son Manasseh, everything rushed toward the worse. This evil could not later be healed by Manasseh himself (though he eventually repented), nor even by the best King Josiah, who was second to none in piety toward God. When Josiah was extinguished by a lamentable death, at last, with the growing impiety to which his sons gave full rein, the divine judgments and the destruction of Jerusalem and the entire commonwealth were hastened; concerning which see the Preface to Jeremiah, §. 7 and 8.

<margin>The Purpose of the Prophetic Sermons.</margin>
§. 9. In the midst of such great corruption of both the Church and the State, so that all might not perish without warning, God, in His immense goodness, raised up not one, but many witnesses of the truth—an entire cohort of Prophets at that time. They were to seriously warn those who were erring and recall them to the right path, or at least render those stubborn minds inexcusable. They were also to encourage the small remnant of the godly with the promise of eternal salvation through Christ amid the imminent judgments, confirming them in hope and faith. Hence, these men of God not only courageously confront entire kingdoms and freely rebuke the errors and impiety of Kings, Princes, Priests, and people (even when everything seemed most prosperous); but they also, as we just said, wonderfully console the good and pious with frequently repeated promises concerning Christ; as has already been stated in the prefaces to Isaiah and Jeremiah.

<margin>The Argument of Hosea.</margin>
§. 10. Thus Hosea, with whom we are now primarily concerned, first through two symbolic acts <note>The marriage to Gomer and the symbolic naming of children.</note> and later in plain speech, portrays the most foul idolatry of Israel. Because their measure of sin was full, he precisely announces the imminent destruction for the whole kingdom: for Israel <note>Hosea 1:4</note> and for Judah <note>chapter 5:5</note>, and their rejection <note>1:9; 2:4; 5:6, 9, 12, etc.</note>. Yet, at the same time, while the impious multitude of his people perishes, he promises that a remnant will be saved and snatched as if from a general fire. He prophesies many things concerning the eternal divinity of Christ, His office, death, victory, and benefits <note>1:7; 2:20; 6:1</note>; the calling of the Gentiles <note>2:1</note>; the kingdom of Christ; and the conversion of Israel and Judah <note>1:7, 18, 22, 23; 2:5; 6:1; 11:10, 11; 14:3</note>. His style approaches the most elegant diction of Isaiah. See Heidegger’s *Biblical Handbook*, p. 308.

<margin>The Parts of the Book.</margin>
§. 11. Scholars generally agree that his book contains seven sermons: two symbolic ones and the rest plain. I. chapters 1 and 2. II. ch. 3. III. ch. 4. IV. ch. 5, 6, 7. V. ch. 8, 9, 10. VI. ch. 11. VII. ch. 12, 13, 14. See Calov’s *Illustrated Bible*, Gürtler’s *Prophetic Theology*, p. 106, and others. So also Heidegger in his *Handbook*, p. 310, except that he ends the fifth sermon with ch. 8 and begins the sixth with ch. 7. Schmidt, however, counts ten prophecies: I. ch. 1, 2. II. ch. 3. III. ch. 4. IV. ch. 5, 6. V. ch. 7. VI. ch. 8. VII. ch. 9, 10. VIII. ch. 11. IX. ch. 12, 13. X. ch. 14:2, etc. Others divide the whole book into "Legal Sermons" from ch. 1–10 and "Evangelical Sermons" concerning the love of God in Christ His son in ch. 11 and following—though they intend this to be understood not as an absolute exclusion, but preeminently <note>original: "κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν"</note> and by way of synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note>.

<margin>Of different times.</margin>
§. 12. That these prophecies of Hosea were published not at one time, but at different times, is evident both from the argument of each when closely inspected and from the fact that, according to the calculations of Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century Hebraist and clergyman.</note> in his *Chronology of the Old Testament* (p. 93) and others, Hosea himself performed the office of prophesying for at least 70 or, according to Heidegger, 80 years. He perhaps even saw the truth of his predictions fulfilled in the captive people of Israel, since the end of that kingdom fell in the sixth year of Hezekiah (whose beginnings Hosea survived, see Hosea 1:1) <note>2 Kings 18:10</note>. However, because neither the beginning nor the end of his prophetic office is precisely defined, it is uncertain whether (as others think) Hosea acted as a prophet for 90 years (See Ursinus in the *Prolegomena*, etc.). Lightfoot confesses (l.c.) that it is impossible to assign every prophecy or chapter of this book to the specific year it was delivered; it is not even possible to refer each one with certainty to the time of the individual Kings mentioned in the title of the book (ch. 1:1). Nevertheless, the first two chapters seem to have been brought forth at the very beginning of his preaching under Jeroboam and Uzziah, when the Prophet was still a young man and was thinking of marriage (cf. 1:2; Jeremiah 16:2; and the Preface to Jeremiah §. 20). The third and fourth chapters of Hosea also seem to have been published at the same time, because in 4:3 he mentions the plague of locusts and those events about which Joel and Amos spoke. Lightfoot (p. 102) reasonably judges that chapters five and six were published in the times of Ahaz; and the seventh and following chapters to the end of the book around the final times of Hosea <note>Referring to King Hoshea of Israel, not the prophet himself.</note>, the last King of the Israelites, or near the beginning of the reign of Hezekiah; as we will say in the appropriate places (see Lightfoot p. 105 and the note on 2 Kings 17:4).

<margin>Use and Divine Authority.</margin>
§. 13. Furthermore, his prophecies pertain not only to the Israelites, though he preached to them primarily, but in their own way to both the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, as is clear from the first chapter. Indeed, whatever was written in this and the other Prophets was written for our instruction, that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope <note>Romans 15:4</note>. Not only is the Word of God commended to us in the very title of the book (ch. 1:1), and therefore long ago included in the divine canon; but it is also frequently cited in the New Testament by Christ and the Apostles as a foundation of faith and a rule for what must be believed. Compare Matthew 2:15 with Hosea 11:1; Matthew 9:13 and 12:7 with Hosea 6:6; Luke 23:30 and Revelation 6:16 with Hosea 10:8; Romans 9:25 with Hosea 2:25; Romans 9:26 with Hosea 2:1; 1 Corinthians 15:54, 55 with Hosea 13:14; 1 Peter 2:10 with Hosea 1:9, 2:1, 5, 25; add Hebrews 13:15 compared with Hosea 14:3. Let it suffice to have warned of these things now. Blessed is he who reads and hears the words of the prophecy, and who observes those things written in it! <note>Revelation 1:3</note>.

...continue, etc. Compare Jeremiah 5:13, Mark 1:1. Furthermore, some (including Lightfoot in *Chronology*, page 93) conclude from these words that God made the beginning of prophetic predictions through Hosea, so that he is the first of all the prophets; but the chronology does not agree, nor do the words imply this. They are correctly rendered as referring to the first prophecy of Hosea by the Septuagint, the Chaldean paraphrase, etc., as Calovius says. **o)** "in Hosea" or "through Hosea." Compare 2 Samuel 23:2, Hebrews 1:1. **p)** An emphatic omission of conjunctions <note>original term: "asyndeton emphaticum"</note>. Compare chapter 3:1. **q)** "Take for yourself a wife" in lawful marriage (Genesis 24:3, 67; 34:4; Jeremiah 29:6). **r)** "A woman of whoredoms" (chapter 2:4; Genesis 38:24), that is, one who had been a prostitute but was to be reformed by repentance. The grammatical case indicates an attribute, like "a man of blood and deceit" (Psalm 5:7), etc. To pass over other views, Schmidt indeed thinks "a woman of whoredoms" here is nothing other than a concubine, taken without dowry or betrothal contracts (comparing Judges 11:1), but the simple sense has no difficulty if everything is considered correctly. For it was not illegal to marry a woman who had been a harlot, except for priests (Leviticus 21:7, 14). See Pfeiffer’s *Vexing Doubts* <note>original title: "Dubia Vexata"</note> on this passage and compare Joshua 2:1; 6:16, 24; Matthew 1:5; 21:31. Calovius says on this passage: The all-wise God had grave reasons for commanding this—both public ones, namely, to reproach the people more vehemently for their idolatry, and to remind them of His own kindness and long-suffering <note>original Greek: "μαקροθυμίαν"</note> in that He bears with them and bestows benefits even though they are fornicators; and private ones, to call that harlot away from her suitors and convert her through the Prophet. Nor was this contrary to the holiness of the Prophet, etc. "Children of whoredoms," that is, according to Pfeiffer and others, illegitimate children born to the mother through whoredom, but adopted by the Prophet along with her. Compare chapter 2:6. Such a strange symbolic act was necessary among the unbridled Israelites, to whom plain truth found no entry; this omen struck the minds of the careless more deeply and effectively. Compare Isaiah 20:2, 3; Jeremiah 27:2; Ezekiel 4:1, following. **According to Schmidt:** that is, "take a woman and father children from her." Thus, none other are understood than those born from the Prophet, whose birth and name are explained in what follows. **s)** Namely, spiritually (chapter 4:12, 15; Jeremiah 3:1, 6; Ezekiel 23:5; compare below chapter 3:1). **s)** "The land," a figure of speech <note>original term: "metonymy"</note> for the inhabitants of the land or the whole people. Compare chapter 4:1. This is what you shall represent to them through the character of your marriage. **x)** Compare 1 Kings 11:2; 2 Kings 17:21; Zephaniah 1:6. **Verse 3. v)** Thus the Prophet went and took her as a wife, not hesitating against the command of God (Galatians 1:16). **x)** "Gomer daughter of Diblaim." Nothing more is recorded of her or her parents in Scripture. Diblaim is a man's name, like Ephraim. Others, including Hiller, think she originated from the Diblaims, which might be the city of Diblah (Ezekiel 6:14) or Diblataim (Jeremiah 48:22), a city of the Moabites. Lightfoot (page 93) notes this signifies a "corruption of figs," comparing Jeremiah 24:3, but the simplest style of Scripture is for sons or daughters to be described by their fathers, as Schmidt says. **a)** Genesis 4:1; 16:4, 15; 21:2. **b)** Conceived by him (Genesis 30:5, 7, 17; 38:25). **Verse 4. c)** Since the name of this son of Hosea had to be symbolic of a hidden matter—the revelation or prediction of which belonged to the all-knowing God alone—it could not be given by anyone other than God Himself. **d)** Compare verses 6, 9; Isaiah 8:3. **e)** The same name as the royal city (1 Kings 21:1; 2 Kings 9:21). It means "God will scatter" or even "God will sow." For while it is used here in a negative sense, below in chapter 2:24 it is used in a positive sense, with very different and opposite meanings according to each interpretation. Jonah interprets it as "the dispersed." **f)** "In a little while." Isaiah 29:17; Haggai 2:6. In Greek: *eti mikron* <note>original: "ἔטי μικρόν"</note> (John 16:16). From this, interpreters conclude that this prophecy was published not long before the death of Jeroboam, after which the house of Jehu was visited. **g)** Chapter 2:13; 4:9; Exodus 20:5. **h)** "The blood of Jezreel," that is, the slaughters committed through unjust condemnations or other forms of cruelty by the Kings in Jezreel, and—following the example of the court—in the rest of the land. Compare Schmidt and below, chapter 4:1, 2; also Preface § 4, following. **i)** Whose kingdom nevertheless seemed to rest on the singular providence of God. See 2 Kings 10:30; 14:25. This prophecy was fulfilled in the murder of Zechariah, son of Jeroboam, by Shallum (2 Kings 15:10). See also the note on 1 Kings 16:7. **k)** "And thus I will finally cause it to cease entirely" (chapter 2:13; Isaiah 13:11). The prefix "And" <note>original: "Vau"</note> here does not connect things done at one continuous time, but rather things that followed each other after a long interval of about fifty years (Schmidt). **l)** 1 Samuel 15:28. **m)** Of the Ten Tribes. See 2 Kings 17:6; compare also below, chapter 2:5; Isaiah 17:4, following. **Verse 5. n)** Namely, of my wrath and vengeance (chapter 5:9; 9:7; Amos 5:18). **o)** "Then I will break the bow" and other weapons or defenses in which they trusted. Compare Leviticus 26:19; Jeremiah 49:35; Ezekiel 30:22; 39:3; Psalm 76:4; 78:9. **p)** "In the valley" or plain of Jezreel (Joshua 17:16; Judges 6:33), so that even Jezreel and Samaria are finally overcome by the Assyrians, and nothing is left to Israel. See Preface § 7, 10. **Verse 6. q)** Who, by her symbolic name just like the male offspring, must portend evil for the Israelites. To Schmidt, it specifically seems to refer to the pitiable nature of the sex. For the female sex usually obtains mercy more than the male; but here God did not wish to spare even her. **r)** See verse 3. **s)** "Lo-ruchama" (verse 8), which means "Not pitied" <note>original Latin: "Non-miferada"</note>. In Greek: *ouk eleēmenē* <note>original: "οὐκ ἠλεημένη"</note>. See 1 Peter 2:10 and below, chapter 3:25. **t)** "I will not add further" to have mercy. Compare similar constructions in Isaiah 47:1, 5; Proverbs 23:35.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening chapter of the Book of Hosea. Having established the symbolic marriage of the prophet to Gomer and the birth of their first two children, the text now transitions from the pronouncement of judgment upon the northern kingdom of Israel to a promise of mercy for the southern kingdom of Judah, ultimately pointing toward a future spiritual restoration.</meta>

<margin>
**u) Chapter 2, verse 6.** <note>original: "q. d." for "quasi dicat" — as if to say</note> I have shown mercy quite often: I adopted her when she was exposed in Egypt (Ezekiel 16:4 and following); I raised her up when she was prostrate under the Judges (Psalm 106:44 and following); I called her back when she was an adulteress under the kings (Jeremiah 3:1, etc.), as Ursinus notes. But **S.** <note>likely referring to the theologian Sebastian Schmidt</note> says: The sense is, you might ask, "Up to this point I have often shown mercy: will I yet show mercy to the house of Israel?" And indeed, I did so recently when I restored the borders of Israel through Jeroboam (2 Kings 14:25, 26). But after this, I shall not do so, but rather I will hand them over to total and perpetual devastation. For since this prophecy was issued, God has no longer shown mercy to the kingdom of Israel; instead, He allowed it to fall further into ruin until it finally collapsed so completely that they never returned to their land even from their captivity, nor did they ever again form a kingdom or a republic—at least not until they were invited and led to spiritual salvation under Christ.
**x)** For by taking away, I will take everything from them. Together with **S.**, we consider this the simplest interpretation, comparing it to Isaiah 8:4 and Jeremiah 49:29. See also Jeremiah 15:6.

See verse 4. **l)** *Lo-ammi*, that is, "not my people." The sense is partly about the present—that they are not now the people of God—and partly about the future—that they shall be "not-a-people" of God. Truly, under the Old Testament (for this is what must be looked at), the people of Israel were the people of God not only *spiritually* (in the way that the Church of Christ is the people of God under the New Testament), but also *politically*, regarding the unique government and providence of the republic in the land of Canaan with specific rituals of divine worship. Therefore, to be "not-a-people" of God is to be deprived of that unique providence of God and the hereditary land of Canaan itself, lacking the external form of a church and a definite republic. And so, it signifies the total overturning of the Church and the republic. **S.** **m)** For this is the reason and etymology of that mystical name. **n)** You. Doubtless addressing those with whom He has dealt so far, namely the ten tribes. **S.** Others refer this to both groups, the Jews (verse 7) and the Israelites (verse 6), because of the rejected Savior (verse 7) until the time of the <note>original Greek: "ἀποκατάστασεως" — restoration/reconstitution</note>, when the Israelites and Jews are to be reunited, gathered, and joined in the unity of faith, adhering to Christ, the Head and Bridegroom of the Church (chapter 1:21), so that a joyful catastrophe <note>meaning a dramatic turning point</note> appears, for which they should congratulate one another (chapter 2:3). So says Maius in *Economy of the Sacred*, pages 878 and following. Also Gunterus in *Prophetic Theology*, page 499: The Jewish nation, he says, which until now was the special possession of God, shall be repudiated and cast away; but the Lord will raise up from other peoples, long removed from His grace, innumerable "children of Israel," not indeed according to the flesh, but according to the spirit (compare Romans 9:25, 26, Matthew 21:41, 43, Isaiah 65:1, 7, etc.). **o)** I will not be your [God], for you are my people no longer, nor do you behave as such. Compare chapter 2:4. **p)** Therefore I also, by the most just law of retaliation. **q)** I will not be your God, nor will I acknowledge you as my people. Compare Genesis 17:7, 8, Exodus 19:5, 6, Leviticus 26:12, etc. According to Jonah <note>the Targum</note>: "Therefore my Word is not in your help." **CHAPTER II. Verse 1.** **r)** **S.** notes: Yet it shall be at some time, in the time of the Messiah (as even the Rabbis, Kimchi, Abarbanel, etc., accept it), in a spiritual state and kingdom. For here follows a mitigation of the preceding threat through a promise of the restoration of the church under the New Testament, the calling of the nations (Gentiles), and the conversion of Israel (verses 1, 2, 3). In what follows, Hosea draws out more specifically what has been indicated through certain symbols and explains more fully and clearly both the threats and the promises made above. **s)** A huge number (Numbers 23:10). **t)** Not only of the carnal [descendants], but—what holds more comfort—of the true and spiritual children of Israel, to be gathered both from the Israelites and from the Gentiles (Romans 9:5, 7, 24, 25, Isaiah 42:6, chapter 49:6, chapter 56:6, 7, chapter 60:3, etc.). For the Gentiles are called children of Israel along with the Israelites, because it was not that the Israelites came into the fellowship of the Gentiles, but the Gentiles came into the fellowship of the Israelites through Christ: as Paul brilliantly shows in Romans 11. Thus, the "children of Israel" are the Israelite descendants of the Patriarchs and all those Gentiles who belong to Israel and adhere to it. **S.** **u)** Compare Isaiah 10:22, Romans 9:27. **x)** Which shall not be measured by men (Jeremiah 33:22). **y)** Nor numbered (1 Kings 3:8). Nor shall it happen through your betrayal that the promises made to the Fathers by God should fail (Genesis 15:5, chapter 22:17, 18, chapter 26:24, chapter 32:13, etc.; compare Numbers 23:19, Romans 11:29, etc.). **z)** For it shall be. The reason is given why there will be such a great number of children of Israel: namely, because Christ will be preached to both Jews and Gentiles. **S.** **a)** According to Jonah <note>the Targum</note>: "in the place where they were led away among the Gentiles." The Septuagint <note>Greek translation</note> as in Romans 9:26. **b)** Where, according to this prophecy of mine, it shall be said. **c)** To the Israelites no less than the Gentiles. **d)** Chapter 1:9, 1 Peter 2:10. **e)** There (thus for the sake of clarity in Romans 9:26 and the Septuagint in the Alexandrian Manuscript, also the Syriac in this place) it shall be said to them (compare Isaiah 4:3, chapter 6:3, etc.). **f)** Children of the living God (Psalm 42:3, Psalm 84:3, 2 Corinthians 3:3, 1 Thessalonians 1:9). Specifically: "you are this through faith in Jesus Christ" (John 1:12, Galatians 3:26). Therefore, a kingdom or republic to be restored in the land of Canaan and the former external Mosaic worship is not promised to them, for being a child of God does not consist in those things. For to be a child of God is purely spiritual, says **S.** **Verse 2. h)** For those called shall be gathered, or shall gather themselves, to the Church of Christ. See Isaiah 11:12, chapter 49:18, chapter 60:4, Psalm 102:23. **i)** <note>original Greek: "Καὶ συνήχθησαν" — and they were gathered</note> (John 11:52). **j)** As many as shall be the children of God (verse 1), the true remnant (Isaiah 10:22, Romans 9:27). **k)** As many as are such by faith (Galatians 3:7, 9; compare Micah 2:12). **l)** Together, in the unity of faith. Compare Isaiah 11:13, Jeremiah 3:18, 19, Ezekiel 37:19, 22, Ephesians 2:14. **m)** They shall place or appoint for themselves (Deuteronomy 17:15), not by their own authority or election (John 15:16), but by faithful grasping and obedience (1 Corinthians 6:17; compare the word in Psalm 52:9, Psalm 91:9). **n)** One head, namely CHRIST, from the house of David, as Jonah <note>the Targum</note> adds; and Rabbi Solomon, Kimchi, and Abarbanel also rightly accept this as referring to the Messiah. Compare the phrasing in Numbers 14:4 and Micah 2:13. Christ is deservedly called "Head": under whom all the faithful are united into one mystical body; in which He most effectively exercises the office of Head as King and Priest, says **S.** (compare Ephesians 4:15, Colossians 1:18, chapter 2:19). **o)** From the whole earth they shall go up to the new city of God and the spiritual Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:17 and following, Hebrews 12:22; compare Isaiah 66:20, 22). The phrasing is poetic and taken from the Old Testament but is to be understood according to the nature of the New Testament. See Psalm 122:4. Others, like Luther, say: they shall ascend to the heavenly fatherland and a better life from this land of pilgrimage. Compare Philippians 3:20. But **S.** says: the Apostles and teachers of the Gospel shall go up from the land of Israel into the whole world, comparing Isaiah 2:3, Luke 24:47. In this way, the military significance of the word is retained but understood spiritually. **p)** They shall go out to attack the kingdom of the devil among the Gentiles, etc. (compare 1 Samuel 7:7, Isaiah 7:1, chapter 21:2, etc.).

**p)** For as he was previously known by signs, so now he will be great and illustrious by his benefits (compare Joel 2:11; Malachi 3:23). **q)** *The day of Jezreel*, meaning the day on which I will immensely increase my people, the true Israel (verse 1), and I will sow them again (verse 24), just as I had previously scattered them (Chapter 1:5; see also Isaiah 61:2 and 1 Kings 18:45). **Jonathan** <note>The Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Bible</note> says: because *great will be the day of their gathering*.

**v. 3. r)** *Say therefore*, whoever hears or reads this from me. The Imperative is used impersonally or absolutely, as in Isaiah 3:10, 35:4, 48:20, 53:11; Jeremiah 4:5, 31:10; Amos 3:9, etc. **s)** *to your brothers*, both the pious and the impious Israelites: to the latter, so they might repent; to the former, so they might sustain themselves with the promised hope of salvation (see Preface § 9, 10). **t)** *to my people*, those who are still my people. The Israelites are called this with respect to the time the prophecy was published, when the Ten Tribes still wished to be God's people, and God had not yet rejected them, but had only predicted that they *would* not be His people (Chapter 1:9, etc.; compare Chapter 4:6; Isaiah 1:3; Micah 6:3, 5). **u)** See Ezekiel 16:46. **x)** *those who have still obtained mercy* (see Chapter 1:6, and compare the word below in verse 23; Chapter 14:4; Isaiah 54:8). That the Israelites are considered as those whom God still pities is clear from verse 6, says **S.** But **Tremellio** <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a prominent 16th-century Hebraist</note>, who translates it thus: *Say to your brothers, O my people, and to your sisters, O obtained-mercy*; considers this an exhortation to the pious to call their brothers and the assembly of Israelites back to repentance. Interpreters disagree greatly both regarding the connection and sense of this verse, as well as the construction of the words; but many things—

***

—the Prophet, having been born, now exhorts the Israelites to perform penance and to avert the predicted punishments through it (says **S.**, p. 46). Nor do they agree on the time of this prophecy. For **S.** and many others refer it to the age of Hosea. Others, such as **Luther**, refer it to the New Testament. Likewise, **Gurtler** <note>Nicolaus Gürtler, a Dutch theologian</note> in his *Prophetic Theology* (p. 107) thinks that in the following verse 4, the struggle of the early Church with the Jews who were to be driven into exile by the Romans is commanded. We think those views should be subordinated; however, the Prophet immediately looked toward the Israelites of his own time (see notes on Isaiah 1:7; Chapter 2:1, 6:9, 58:1, etc.). **v. 4. y)** *Contend* (Chapter 4:1; Genesis 31:36; Jeremiah 2:9) *with your mother*, the synagogue of the Ten Tribes (verse 7; see Isaiah 50:1), namely through a bold reproach of crimes and constant admonition. **z)** The word is repeated to show that the matter is being handled seriously and urgently (**S.**). **a)** For she is of these morals (Chapter 1:2). <summary>This page provides a detailed scholarly commentary on Hosea 2:3-10, focusing on the metaphorical "divorce" between God and Israel due to the nation's idolatry. It interprets the "lovers" as false gods and explains the divine punishment—deprivation of basic needs like bread, wool, and water—as a disciplinary measure to lead the people back to their "first husband."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the prophetic discourse of Hosea Chapter 2. Having established the metaphor of an unfaithful wife, the text now details the specific punishments—stripping away the material wealth that the nation mistakenly attributed to false gods—before transitioning into a promise of future restoration in the wilderness.</meta>

g) see Ephesians 2:7. h) The scholar Gusset and others suggest: "what they made," meaning they transformed these gifts into an idol of Baal (comparing Numbers 11:8 and Jeremiah 37:15). However, **S.** <note>likely Sebastian Schmidt</note> suggests it means what they "worked upon" or "used for" Baal, encompassing all kinds of objects used in Baal worship, such as tools and ornaments (see below at 3:4 and Ezekiel 38:24). Other lesser gods are not excluded. Although King Jehu destroyed Baal worship for a time, it was undoubtedly restored by later kings or tolerated and practiced by the common people. e) <note>original Greek: "παύσω πᾶσαν τὰς πανηγύרεις αὐτῆς"</note> "I will cause all her festive assemblies to cease" (Hebrews 12:23). This refers to all joyful solemnities, whether established by God or by men. While God previously threatened to take away material goods relating to the state and household, here He explicitly mentions religious goods—feasts, Sabbaths, etc.—to emphasize the severity of the punishment, which includes the overturning of the religious order. **Martin Luther** interprets this as referring to New Testament times or the final destruction of Jerusalem and the cancellation of ceremonial law; however, we prefer, with others, to apply it to the Old Testament period leading up to Christ. **S.** <note>Schmidt</note> page 14. g) "And I will devastate" (Leviticus 26:31, 32; Ezekiel 30:11). h) see Joel 1:7, 12. i) Jeremiah 5:17. k) "Because" (Deuteronomy 3:24, 1 Samuel 2:23), or "concerning which" she spoke in verse 7. l) "A harlot’s pay" (1); compare the verb in 8:9, 10 and the related noun in 9:1 and Deuteronomy 23:19. m) "I will reduce them" (verse 7) and the whole land, so that she can hope for nothing more from it. n) see Isaiah 5:6, 7:21, 29:17, Micah 3:12. o) see Psalm 80:14, Isaiah 34:13, and the contrast in verse 20. **v. 15.** p) Hosea 1:4. The "days of the Baals" refers to the time of Baal-worship, to which they were devoted for a very long time (see note at verse 10; Judges 2:11, 13; 10:6; 1 Kings 16:31; also note on 1 Kings 12:32). It is as if God is saying He will send these punishments not for one or two years, but for many, so that they might fully pay for the days of Baal-idolatry and other false worship. This period lasts from the destruction of the Northern Kingdom by the Assyrians until the time of Christ. s) **v.** 4:13; see Ezekiel 6:13, 8:11, 16:18. s) "And earring, ornaments" (Ezekiel 16:10, Jeremiah 4:30, Ezekiel 16:13, 23:40). "Her earring"—most commentators agree here. Since this specific fashion is not common here, we will discuss it in more detail. It was a golden necklace or ornament (Genesis 24:22, 30; Exodus 35:22; Judges 8:24). It could be for the ears (Genesis 35:4, Exodus 32:2, 3) or for the forehead/nose. Eastern women typically did not only pierce their ears to hang rings or gems, but also decorated their foreheads or noses. Hence it is called a "nose ring" in Ezekiel 16:11, Proverbs 11:22, or "upon the nose" in Genesis 24:47. It hung by a thread tied to the forehead, as Ezra writes on Genesis 24:22. Similarly, **Jerome** in his commentary on Ezekiel 16:12 says: "To this day, among other ornaments of women, golden circles usually hang from the forehead and down over the nostrils." However, **Clericus** on Genesis 24:47 says: "I believe that in the past, as throughout the East today, rings were inserted into the nostrils; Solomon seems to allude to this in Proverbs 11:22." The traveler **Thevenot** (Travels to the Levant, Part II, book 2, ch. 9) confirms this custom still exists: "In Persia, as in the rest of the East, women pierce their noses for rings." w) "And her finery" (3) (Proverbs 25:12, Song of Solomon 7:2). The Arabic root has the same meaning (see 1 Peter 3:3, where the Greek says "the wearing of gold"). The Arabic root means "to adorn a woman with necklaces and her world/finery," and "the woman was adorned with her finery and was pleasing to the eyes." x) verse 7. Just as prostitutes seek out lovers if they do not come of their own accord. **S.** <note>Schmidt</note> y) Hosea 14:13 and 17:10, contrary to my warnings in Deuteronomy 8:14, etc. She left my worship. The Israelites thought they were not "forgetting" Jehovah, but rather worshiping Him through certain idols, like Jeroboam's golden calves (see Preface section 4 and the note on 1 Kings 12:29, 32). But God utterly rejects such worship. In truth, they were forgetting the Word of God (Hosea 4:6), in which He had prescribed His true worship. Therefore, whoever forgets the Word of God forgets God Himself. **S.** <note>Schmidt</note> see again the note on 1 Kings 12:32. **z) v. 18.** Isaiah 1:24. **v. 16. a)** "Therefore," because she is the most ungrateful of all and has forgotten me (verse 15). **S.** b) "Behold I," as I have already said I would do. c) "I will persuade her," no longer with benefits, but with the gravest chastisements and punishments (Jeremiah 2:7, Ezekiel 14:9), so that she might thereafter believe my words and obey. d) And therefore I will lead her by way of the Assyrians (Isaiah 42:16). e) "As if into a wilderness," as in the past when they were led out of Egypt (see Deuteronomy 8:2, Jeremiah 2:2, 6; and see Jeremiah 31:2, Ezekiel 19:13, Hosea 12:10, and verse 5 above). f) And finally, when she has become manageable and more attentive to me through the experience of her losses (verse 9, 3:5), I will speak to her heart "through the Gospel" (John). g) Through my servants the prophets, I will speak comforts to her heart. Note this highly emphatic phrase used in Genesis 34:3, 50:21, Judges 19:3, Ruth 2:13, 2 Chronicles 30:22, 32:6, and Isaiah 40:2; see also Zechariah 1:13, Matthew 11:28, Mark 8:2, 4. **v. 17. g)** Isaiah 61:8, Jeremiah 3:19. I will not only call her back with sweet words, but I will make that synagogue—indeed, that church—better through my benefits. **Tarnov.** <note>Johann Tarnow, 17th-century theologian</note> h) refers back to verse 14; see also Isaiah 17:3, 65:21, Jeremiah 31:5, Amos 9:14, Joel 2:18, 19. i) "From there," out of that most calamitous state or wilderness mentioned in verse 16. k) "The Valley of Achor," which means the valley of disturbance or despair (see Joshua 7:24, 26 and the note on Isaiah 65:10).

Verse 3. k) He adds the punishment for those crimes mentioned in verses 1 and 2. l) Having been devastated by enemies, drought, and locusts, the Israelite land mourns, and even more so, being utterly overturned, it groans. Jeremiah 4:28; 12:4. m) Isaiah 16:8; 19:8; Joel 1:10, 12. The emphasis of the word seems to be a failing and wasting away, as if the soul is struggling for breath until it finally exits miserably; this is a slow and most wretched death. **S.** n) with the beasts or among the beasts of the field. This further exaggerates the situation. **S.** q) compare Isaiah 19:5, 8. Just as now the waters of rivers and lakes are consumed by heat and drought. Compare notes on Joel 1:19, 20. r) they shall be taken away together. That is, they will be gathered into their own places so they appear no more. Compare Genesis 30:23; Isaiah 4:1; Psalm 85:4. For when the captivity of the Ten Tribes comes, the inhabitants are removed, and the beasts, birds, and fish will also fail; even the mute creatures will feel the Lord's wrath. He who does not believe this happened to the people of Israel should look at Thrace, Macedonia, and Pannonia, and all the land from the Propontis and Bosphorus to the Julian Alps; he will prove that along with humans, all living things have failed, which were provided by the Creator for human use. These are the words of Jerome <note>an early Christian scholar</note> on this passage.

Verse 4. s) but rather, 1 Samuel 15:6. We believe (from the second half of the verse) that God is speaking to the Prophet, who begins a new part of this prophecy here, addressing both priests and false prophets, and the whole idolatrous people; first he threatens the former, then the latter most severely. **S.** The Targum says: "Because they say: Let the scribe not teach, nor the prophet rebuke." t) everyone, as in 2:12. u) do not contend with them: namely, according to their own false persuasion of their piety, even if the causes of my contention are most just. Verse 1; compare 3:4. x) neither should anyone rebuke them. Amos 5:10; Proverbs 9:7, 8. For it will be in vain; they are incorrigible, and in persistent hypocrisy they consider themselves righteous. Thus the Septuagint <note>Greek translation</note> understands it: "as a priest who is spoken against." And the Syriac explicitly: "is like a priest contending," and the Arabic: "O my people, like a priest he quarrels." Truly, in the crime of contradiction, God equates all the children of Israel, priests and laity, except that the priests seduced the people. The letter *Kaph* <note>a Hebrew prefix meaning "like"</note> here is not simply for likeness, but for equalization—that the people are as bad as the priests; and *Cohen* (Priest) is used collectively for the order of priests, just as in the following verse 5, "Prophet" refers to all false prophets. **S.** But they are as guilty and stubborn as those who do not obey the Priest of God. Deuteronomy 17:13. Like Korah and his accomplices. Numbers 16:3. The Targum says they quarrel with their teachers, as in Jeremiah 15:10; 44:15, etc. Indeed, some refer this to 2 Chronicles 24:2, 22, but we retain **S.**'s opinion because of what follows.

Verse 5. a) Therefore you shall fall. Hosea 5:5; 14:2. Namely, the seductive priest himself, as implied by verse 4. Others say: "you impious nation." b) during the day. Nehemiah 4:16. c) Isaiah 31:3. d) The Targum says "false prophet." Compare Hosea 9:7, 8; Isaiah 3:3; 9:14; 28:7; Jeremiah 14:18, etc. e) in the night, or of the night. Job 27:20. There is a manifest opposition of day and night; yet one does not exclude the other, but rather explains it, showing that both apply to everyone. **S.** Compare Deuteronomy 28:66; Micah 3:6. f) and I will cut off. Verse 6; Hosea 10:7. g) The Targum says "your Synagogue." The people of the Ten Tribes. Verse 6; compare Hosea 2:4. h) they are cut off or to be cut off. Verse 5; Hosea 10:15. k) 2 Samuel 21:5; Isaiah 6:5; Obadiah verse 5. It is your fault, O impious priests and teachers, who did not imbue the people with the true knowledge of God, but rather with superstitions for which they must be cut off. **S.** i) He calls them "His people" because He had not yet utterly rejected them. **S.** Compare verse 12; 2:3. k) due to the lack of saving knowledge. Verse 1; Isaiah 5:13. While even the priests, who should have taught the people, turned away from the true knowledge of God, as follows. l) Because you, therefore, are a seductive priest (to be understood collectively, as in verse 4). **S.** m) the true knowledge of God. Verse 1. n) see 2 Kings 17:15; and compare Jeremiah 2:8; Amos 2:4; Hosea 7:10, 12, etc.; Zechariah 7:11, etc. o) therefore I also have rejected you. Compare 1 Samuel 15:23, 26. p) so that you shall not perform the priesthood for me. Compare 1 Kings 2:27; Malachi 2:7, 8. To understand this correctly, **S.** thinks it should be observed that although in 1 Kings 12:31 Jeroboam is said to have made priests from the common people, having driven out the true Priests and Levites of God (2 Chronicles 11:14), it should not be taken as if he removed all the Aaronic and Levitical priests by force; rather, when those who disagreed were sent into exile, many undoubtedly defected to his impure worship and were freely admitted by Israel. Compare Judges 17:12, 13. God did not immediately and absolutely reject them, just as He did not immediately reject the Ten Tribes themselves; but in His long-suffering He waited for them to repent, and by seeking and teaching the knowledge of the law, lead the Israelites to repentance. When they consistently despised and rejected that, God finally rejected them along with the people and abolished the priesthood. If He rejected the descendants of Aaron, much more so the priests made from the common people, who had no divine right to the priesthood. q) because you have maliciously forgotten and neglected the Scripture, indeed God Himself. Hosea 2:15; 8:14; 13:6; Deuteronomy 32:18; compare Psalm 119:61. r) who by right and in truth is your only God; not idols, or Jeroboam's calves alongside Him. Exodus 20:3. The Son speaks of God the Father, not exclusively, but inclusively. **S.** s) I will forget, and I will take no account of them. Compare Psalm 49:14; 77:10.

CHAPTER 4. verse 1. a) Listen with obedience to the word of the Lord, which He speaks through me. 2 Kings 20:16; Isaiah 1:10; 42:1; James 1:22. p) The Ten Tribes. As above in 1:4, etc.; 3:1. namely the priest, who is like the people; others say upon the priest and the people. i) Psalm 1:1; 2 Chronicles 6:30. k) chapter 5:4; 7:2; 9:15. l) chapter 12:3; Psalm 3:11; 66:15. **v. 10.** m) So that they eat. S. <note>Schmidt</note> understands this to be the Priests; others the whole people, as in verse 9. n) but they shall not be satisfied, on account of the scarcity of provisions and the divine curse. For this often happens in a famine, that men, however voracious, are never satisfied, because God "breaks the staff of bread," <note>A biblical idiom meaning to cut off the food supply.</note> that is, removes the power of nourishment from it, says Bochart in *Hieroz.* I, page 404. compare Leviticus 26:26; Micah 6:14; Haggai 1:6; add Joel 2:25. d) You pant for whoredoms and the sacrifices of my people, and desire to be filled from them, but I will send a curse upon you, so that though you eat, etc. But Schmidius says: the priests ate with the people and feasted to Bacchus; to the end that they might have him propitious and he might give them everything, always, and to satiety and abundance. God therefore threatens that he will nevertheless act so that they do not obtain their end, nor be satisfied with the goods they sought; but rather be pressed by hunger and thirst, both in their own land and in miserable captivity etc. o) The Priests make the people commit whoredom, or permit whoredoms to happen; through bigamy or polygamy, as Lightfoot thinks on Acts 15:20. others say by their own evil example, as in 1 Samuel 2:22. But Schmidius says: the Priests celebrated the rites of Venus by whoredom with the Israelites, to obtain from the immodest goddess an increase of offspring: for thus among the gentiles even sterile women prostituted their modesty to Venus to obtain offspring. God therefore threatens that he will act so that they do not obtain this end of theirs—that they might not be multiplied, but rather become sterile, or lose their children before they grow up. Compare the citations at verse 8 regarding that most impure cult of Venus. The word in the Hiphil <note>A Hebrew verb form usually indicating causative action.</note> (6) is not simply the same as in the Kal, "they shall play the harlot," as the Tigurine, Syriac, and others translate; but to make or permit to play the harlot, to prostitute or lead into whoredom. see below verse 18; chapter 5:3; Exodus 34:15, 16; Leviticus 19:29; 2 Chronicles 21:11, 13. p) yet they shall not break out with much offspring. Genesis 28:14; Job 1:10; 2 Chronicles 11:17. q) Isaiah 1:4; Jeremiah 2:13. r) to observing horrendous and impious institutes, plainly foreign to my precepts. compare Micah 6:16; and Genesis 18:19; Exodus 16:28; etc. Others: they deserted the Lord, namely from observing [him], so that they did not observe him. compare Zechariah 11:11.

**v. 11.** s) Whoredom. chapter 6:10; Jeremiah 3:9. t) chapter 7:14. u) S. <note>Schmidt</note> it has occupied the heart; others: it renders them mindless. Jeremiah 5:21. namely as elsewhere in Isaiah 5:11-12; chapter 28:7; Proverbs 25:1; 23:27, 33; Ephesians 5:18. then especially in those feasts of Bacchus and Venus, which carnal men so preferred! according to S. compare Amos 2:8; 2 Peter 2:13, 14. **v. 12.** x) My people verse 6; Exodus 19:5. Thus far it has dealt with the priests, now it deals with the people. s) their wood, which is certainly in their own power, and which they could use to feed a fire. S. see Isaiah 40:20; chapter 44:13 and following; Jeremiah 2:27; Habakkuk 2:19. y) he consults as a divine oracle. the same construction in Numbers 27:21; Judges 1:1; chapter 18:5. a) his rod or staff (Genesis 30:37; chapter 32:11; 1 Samuel 17:40, 43) shall give responses or divine signs, as in 1 Samuel 9:6; 1 Kings 10:3; chapter 14:3; 2 Kings 4:27; Isaiah 41:26; chapter 43:9; etc. Which kind of divination the Greeks call <term>rhabdomancy <note>original: ῥαβדוμαντείαν - divination by rods or wands.</note></term>, as Jerome writes on this passage. compare the notes on Deuteronomy 18:12; and Selden *On the Syrian Gods* I, chapter 2, page 101. Schmidius, however, thinks the Teraphim are noted here, chapter 3:4, and that they were human heads (either of corpses or artificial) erected upon staves and held as oracles. The phrase is taken, as Kimchi advises, from matrimonial matters: in which the wife is "under" her husband, as her lord, who has power over her and to whom she owes obedience. S. Compare Romans 7:2. **v. 13.** f) Jeremiah 3:6; Ezekiel 6:13; chapter 20:28. with extreme softness. g) Jeremiah 2:20. h) chapter 2:15. i) Genesis 35:8. k) Genesis 30:37. l) Genesis 35:4; Ezekiel 6:13. compare Isaiah 1:29; chapter 57:5. m) compare Deuteronomy 12:2, 13; chapter 16:21. n) therefore the most foul impiety spreads most widely: for from this it happens that all shame vanishes, and even daughters and daughters-in-law, who should and usually are kept most chastely at home, prostitute their modesty in these mountain and woodland rites with impunity and without shame. S. o) brides Isaiah 62:5, and your daughters-in-law Genesis 38:24. p) verse 14; chapter 3:1. **v. 14.** q) S. asks: Shall I not visit [punish]? as in Judges 21:22; 2 Samuel 23:5; 1 Kings 22:17; 2 Kings 5:26. q. d. Do they not deserve my most grave visitation of punishment because your daughters play the harlot and your daughters-in-law commit adultery, as was just said? For this is the force of the questions, to exaggerate the matter. see Jeremiah 5:9. Others, such as Gusset page 385 and Lundius book III, chapter 55, page 708, with the Talmudists and Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, the preeminent medieval commentator.</note>, interpret this regarding the waters of jealousy or testing in Numbers 5:27. As if God were threatening that he would no longer manifest suspected adulteresses through those waters, and that as a punishment for the husbands. But this interpretation is of no weight, says S., because the discourse is not only about wives but about daughters in general; and also because it is not only about hidden adulteries but manifest ones.

<header>### CHAPTER 4 & 5. HOSEA 4, 5</header>

Truly, as S. observes, it was *done* not without fraud and deceit, so that in places near Judah and Benjamin, idol worship was established; nor is it doubtful that many Jews, carried away by this scandal and invited by the Israelites, worshiped idols together with them in Gilgal and Bethel, and celebrated foul rites through drunkenness and harlotry. f) For Bethel was situated on a mountain, Joshua 16:1, 2 Kings 2:23. g) He says "House of Iniquity" <note>original: "Beth-aven"</note> instead of Bethel, that is, "House of God" (Genesis 28:17, 19) because of the idolatry established and practiced there.
