Compare Preface §. 4. i) 1 Samuel 20:3. The formula of the oath itself is not rebuked simply in itself, as it was commanded by God himself in Deuteronomy 6:13 and 10:20, but the abuse, when joined with horrific idolatry. Compare Isaiah 48:1, Jeremiah 4:2, 5:1, Ezekiel 20:39, Amos 8:14, Zephaniah 1:5 and 1 Samuel 28:10. For the Israelites pretended that through the worship of the calves they were not deserting the Lord <note>original: "Iehouam"</note>, but worshiping Him; which they said was evident from the fact that they *still* swore by the name of the Lord. S. Compare above, chapter 2:15, 18.
**v. 16, k)** Like a stubborn heifer, chapter 9:15, Deuteronomy 21:18. [Targum] Jonathan: like an ox that is fattened and *kicks back*. Compare Deuteronomy 32:15. Syriac: Like a heifer rebelling against the yoke. Compare Exodus 32:9, Zechariah 7:11, Nehemiah 9:29. l) Compare Isaiah 1:5. m) The Lord now feeds them, Zechariah 11:4, 7. n) Like a lamb destined for the slaughterhouse. Compare Jeremiah 11:19, 12:3, 2 Peter 2:12. But Kimchi: otherwise the Lord would now feed them like lambs. o) In a wide place, that is, a spacious place, Psalm 18:20, 31:9. It refers to that notable liberation by God, by which through Jeroboam II He asserted the Israelites into liberty and restored to them all that they had previously lost. Others take it in a bad sense: now the Lord will feed them in a spacious place, i.e., He will deport the captives into the vast regions of Media and Assyria, in which they may wander like a lamb that, torn from the flock and abandoned by its mother, fills everything with empty bleating and finally becomes prey for wolves. Thus Jerome, Cyril, Theodoret, Theophylact, and some of the Hebrews, as well as most of the moderns. But from the perpetual phrasing of Scripture, to "widen a place" for someone is to free him from distress and assert him into liberty, says Bochart in *Hieroz.* I. p. 412 following, compared with Isaiah 30:23, Psalm 4:2, etc.
**v. 17, p)** Associated (1) like spouses, Malachi 2:14, or confederates, Genesis 14:3, 2 Chronicles 20:35, 37. q) With idols, chapter 8:4, 13:2, 2 Samuel 5:21, Micah 1:7, Jeremiah 44:19. Compare 2 Corinthians 6:14, 16. r) The Ten Tribes, chapter 5:3. See note on Isaiah 7:5. s) He says, as it were, "allow him, concede to him his madness." 2 Samuel 16:11. S. "Let him go." Compare Exodus 32:10, 2 Kings 23:18. These words are either, according to S., the Prophet’s words to God, acknowledging His just judgment, as below in chapter 9:14, Jeremiah 17:18, etc., or according to others, God’s words to the Prophet, as above in verse 4, Isaiah 8:16, etc.
**v. 18, t)** Zurich version: "He has departed," and s. (understanding <term>wine</term> <note>original: "yayin"</note> as in 2 Kings 5:13, 6:27, Isaiah 7:21, chapter 10:4). If their wine or drink has departed (2) Isaiah 1:22. That is: If indeed it ever happens that their idolatrous drunkenness departs, so that they seem about to return to a sober and better mind (compare the phrase in 1 Samuel 1:14), yet soon all that hope vanishes, while they are immediately pulled back by their Kings and Princes into worse harlotry, even more than ever before; *therefore let them go*, as I said in verse 17. Moreover, they seemed about to return to a sober mind when the true Prophets rebuked them and terrified them with their threats and demonstrations. A clear example is in the history of Elijah. By his zeal, he finally brought it about that all exclaimed: *The Lord is God!* and they allowed the prophets of Baal to be killed and his altars overturned, 1 Kings 18:39 following. But soon they relapsed into worse things, and Elijah was forced to flee before Jezebel. So Jehu seemed about to restore the true worship of God; but he stuck in the worship of the calves, 2 Kings 10:16-29. Thus S. well notes. u) Yet they make them commit harlotry again, verse 10, chapter 5:3, 2 Chronicles 21:11, 13. x) They loved, Jeremiah 5:31, chapter 14:10. The past tenses include the present, because of the continuation of the deed, as above in chapter 2:7, Isaiah 1:34. y) S. adds (past tense from <term>to give</term> <note>original: "yahab"</note> or according to Cocceius' Lexicon 298, from <term>to give</term> of the form <term>to grow</term> <note>original: "gadal"</note> out of fear) comparing a similar lack of conjunction in 1 Samuel 2:3. But the Zurich version: "they rejoice (to say) Bring." And Gusset p. 860: "they loved 'give'." Compare Malachi 2:16. z) Ignominy and shameful idolatry. Compare verse 7, Jeremiah 13:26, Nahum 3:5. a) Her shields. By these, *Kings and Princes* are to be understood, or as some translate, "protectors of the people," which is beyond controversy, says S. Compare Psalm 47:10.
**v. 19. b)** He has bound or entangled her, the Israelite Synagogue <note>Meaning the assembly of the people.</note>; just as someone collects money to carry it with him. Compare chapter 13:12, Proverbs 7:20, Job 26:8. c) The wind. Isaiah 64:5. d) In its wings, which are everywhere attributed to the wind because of its speed, for example, Psalm 18:11, 104:3. Compare Psalm 139:9. Surely the wind, which in Hebrew is of common gender, is used first with a masculine verb, then with a feminine suffix. Schmidt, however, refers this suffix to the Israelite Synagogue itself: *that the wind is about to blow into the loose wings of Ephraim's garments* (compare Deuteronomy 22:12, Ezekiel 5:3) and thus bind her, so that she is carried far away with them: which can and usually does happen to a traveler walking with loose clothing. The Syriac favors this explanation: *the wind shall hiss in their wings*. e) Chapter 10:6, Isaiah 1:29. f) Compare verse 13, 14, chapter 9:4.

**CHAPTER V. v. 1. g)** Hear this—namely, what I am about to say in the following. Compare Micah 3:1, 9. For just as above in chapter 4:1 the Prophet began a new prophecy with these words, so here he begins a great threat, to be finished in the following chapter; and he severely demands attention from all to hear it. Here four things are to be observed: I. The summons or address to all ranks of the Israelite kingdom, v. 1. II. Rebuking of sins, ibid. following. III. Proclamation of punishments, through the whole chapter. IV. Hope of pardon or promise made to those who repent, v. 15, where there is a) mutual exhortation of the repentant, chapter 6:1 following. b) The Lord’s response, verse 4 following. Moreover, this prophecy seems to have been issued in the times of *Ahaz*: after not only Menahem, the tyrant of Israel, had become a tributary of the Assyrian (2 Kings 15:19), but also Ahaz had sought help from the Assyrian (2 Kings 16:7, 8, Isaiah 7:17, 2 Chronicles 28:16), as Lightfoot in his Chronology p. 102 and Schmidt’s Commentary on this place p. 205 conclude. h) Chapter 4:6, 8, chapter 9. i) 1 Samuel 15:22, Isaiah 43:18. k) The people of the Ten Tribes, chapter 1:6, 4:1, 12:1. l) Especially also the house of the King, or the Court: namely the King and the Princes and the royal Ministers. <note>marginal notes continued from bottom of source</note>
* "After vanities." See Acts 14:15. The Syrian translation says "after vanities." * v. 12. q) Therefore, I say, I will be like a moth. See Psalm 39:12, Job 4:19. This signifies that they will be gradually consumed by the hidden curse of God, just as clothes are consumed by the silent bite of a moth. Nor should it be feared that God's majesty is lowered by being compared to such a lowly creature. Properly speaking, God is not compared to the moth, but God's slow judgments are compared to the damage a moth does to a garment. It grows gradually, so that what previously seemed solid is eventually ruined by a silent bite. r) "And like rot." Others say "like a woodworm." See Proverbs 12:4, Job 13:28. * v. 13. t) When Ephraim noticed his sickness. u) The sickness of his republic. x) His festering wound. See Jeremiah 30:13, Obadiah verse 7. y) They went to Assyria, not to God. See 2 Chronicles 16:12, Jeremiah 17:5, 7. z) Menahem was led to trust in Assyria, in which they persisted to their own destruction. Hosea rebukes them for this repeatedly, predicting the Assyrian would be their king. a) Judah also sent messengers. See 2 Kings 16:7-8, Isaiah 7:17. b) To King Jareb. Some consider this a city in Assyria, but it is better explained as the "Adversary King" or, as Jerome and Symmachus have it, the "Avenging King." See 1 Samuel 24:16. d) He will not be able. Even if he wanted to. This phrase implies that by God's providence, he will not even be *able* to want to help. For when the King of Assyria came to help Ahaz, he soon turned and afflicted him. See 2 Chronicles 28:20. f) Nor will he care for or remove the wound from you. * v. 14. g) Because my Word is as in verse 12. This gives the reason why the King of Assyria cannot heal them: the implacable anger of God. h) Like a lion. See Hosea 13:7, Psalm 91:13. i) I will be this to Ephraim so that no one can heal him. m) I, even I, the almighty God. See Isaiah 43:25. n) I will tear and depart. o) I will carry away. See 1 Samuel 17:34. p) Deuteronomy 32:39, Micah 5:7. * v. 15. q) I will take away my Presence (Shekhinah), I will return to my holy dwelling in the heavens. See Ezekiel 11:23. r) This "place" is attributed to God figuratively, like a lion returning to its lair after the hunt; God will no longer care for Judah and Ephraim for a time. s) Not forever, but "until." t) Until they acknowledge they have sinned. u) To "seek the face" of someone is to humbly pray that they look upon you with a favorable countenance. x) Deuteronomy 4:30, Isaiah 26:16. y) This is a prediction and a promise of future repentance through the education of afflictions. They will seek me anxiously. The Greek version says "in their affliction they will rise early to me." CHAPTER 6. v. 1. z) "Go, and let us return," specifically through true repentance and certain trust. This is the beginning of the exhortation of the repentant Jews and Israelites, to which Christ's response is joined in the following verses. This refers to the times of the New Testament. a) The "LORD" (Jehovah) here refers to the Son of God, Christ, who revived us after two days, rising from the dead. b) The motive for repentance: He struck us so that we would return. c) He "tore" or wounded us like a lion's claws.

<summary>This page covers Hosea's prophecy regarding the internal decay of Israel and Judah, described as a slow rot or moth-eaten destruction, and their failed attempt to find healing through an alliance with Assyria. It concludes with God withdrawing His presence until the people truly repent, leading into the famous call to "return to the LORD" in Chapter 6.</summary>

---

<margin>
d) And he himself, not the Assyrian or anyone else [see chapter 5:13], will heal us [see 7:1, 14:5, and Deuteronomy 32:39], as he is our physician [Exodus 15:26]. e) He has struck us [Isaiah 57:17]. This should be understood with a "Vav-conversive" <note>a Hebrew grammatical feature where "and" changes the tense of a verb</note> [see chapter 8:12]. f) And he himself, like a surgeon, will bind us—that is, our wounds—up [Isaiah 1:6, Job 5:18]. The same sentiment is expressed twice for emphasis, using different words: the logical force is in the future tense—he *will* heal, he *will* bind, he *will* revive us. This tense expresses the Lord's will and contains a promise that those who repent can hold onto as hope for pardon when facing temptation. Sanctius <note>Gaspar Sanctius, a 16th-century Jesuit commentator</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
On the third day following. [See Matthew 16:21, Luke 18:33]. For the Jews interpret those "two days" as the Egyptian servitude and the Babylonian captivity, and the "third day" as the liberation from their present exile, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
Verse 2. g) "He will heal us" <note>Greek: hygiasei hēmas</note>. The Arabic version says: "You will restore health to us" [see Psalm 41:3]. But Sanctius says "he will revive us" not only spiritually [Ephesians 2:5] in the church, but also physically [1 Corinthians 15:22] at the end of the age [see Psalms 71:20, 80:19, 85:7, and Isaiah 26:19]. h) "After two days," as the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> has it, meaning after a short while [see Joshua 23:1], as most understand it here; the number two often signifies a small amount in Scripture [see 1 Kings 17:12, Isaiah 17:6, Jeremiah 3:14, and Noldius's Concordance]. But Sanctius argues the literal text should be kept where possible, as it fits the context: the penitent comfort themselves by the merit of Christ, by whose power he would revive them after the two days of his own death. i) See Genesis 22:4. Rising on the third day [Acts 13:32]. The "third day" following the two days is the third day of Christ, of Jehovah who gives life—specifically the third day after his death. Thus, it is not to be understood as occurring after *our* two days of suffering, but after *his* two days in the grave.
</margin>

v. 2. a) **He will revive us** <note>original Hebrew: yachayyênu</note> literally, "they will raise us up" [see 1 Samuel 2:8, 2 Samuel 12:17, Ezekiel 34:29, Amos 9:11]. b) "That we may live before him" [Genesis 17:18], meaning in this life in the kingdom of grace, holy and blameless; and afterward in the kingdom of glory, eternally blessed. Thus the immediate and ultimate goals are both included. Tarnovius <note>Johann Tarnow, a Lutheran theologian</note>. The Targum of Jonathan <note>an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note> says: "He will grant us life in the days of consolation that are to come; on the day of the resurrection of the dead, he will raise us up."

v. 3. m) **And let us know** <note>original: wênêde’āh</note> "Let us therefore acknowledge this." He connects this verse with what came before as a mutual encouragement among those repenting, just as in verse 1. n) And **let us press on** to this very thing, not after the wind or our own vain thoughts [chapter 12:2; see Deuteronomy 16:20, Isaiah 51:1, Psalm 34:15, Proverbs 21:21]. The lack of a conjunction here adds emphasis. o) See verse 6 and chapter 2:22 [compare 2:10, 4:1, 5:4]. p) For his going out is like the **dawn**, or like one who is "prepared as the dawn" [see Isaiah 8:20, 58:8, Romans 13:17, 2 Peter 1:19]. q) **Prepared** <note>original: nakhôn</note> [Exodus 34:2, Job 15:23], certain [Deuteronomy 13:15], and evident [Proverbs 4:18]. r) His "going out" from the Father [John 16:28; see Micah 5:1, Psalm 19:6, Malachi 3:20, Luke 1:78]. It is as if to say: his arrival is destined to be like the dawn for us, to bring us to life out of the darkness of our death. s) And **he will come**, or then he will come [Isaiah 35:4, 40:10]. t) As the **most healthful rain** [see chapter 14:6, Isaiah 44:3, 55:10]. u) To us, who acknowledge him with true faith, for our salvation [see Isaiah 9:5]. x) See Deuteronomy 11:14. y) Which **waters** (Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius, author of 'Philologia Sacra'</note> suggests it means "shooting toward" the earth) the ground and makes it fruitful [as in chapter 10:12; see also Jeremiah 5:24].

v. 4. z) **What shall I do to you**, O Ephraim? [See chapter 11:8, Isaiah 5:4]. This is the response of Jehovah—the Son of God—to the penitents. While showing their punishment is deserved, he promises to reform their hypocritical worship. According to Sanctius, this is the question of someone deliberating with himself [as in Genesis 27:37, Exodus 17:4, etc.] who eventually finds a good plan even when the situation seems hopeless [as in Luke 16:3]. It is as if he says: "What can I do to bring you to seek me seriously?" [chapter 5:15]. Certainly, the way you are currently going will not lead to true repentance, for your supposed "holiness," in which you trust, is worthless. I know what I will do: I will cut down your false prophets by my words and teach you that I want mercy, not sacrifice [Matthew 12:7]. s. a) "To you," meaning for your benefit and salvation. Sanctius. b) He questions Ephraim and Judah with an elegant figure of speech: not because they have the answer, but to force them to admit their own helplessness. Sanctius. c) See chapters 4:15, 5:5, 14. d) For **your love and holiness**, which you try to produce by your own will without true conversion [Isaiah 40:6], is too fleeting, vanishing, and useless [see 4:18, 7:16]; rather than standing up in judgment, it condemns you. e) Like a morning cloud that is dispersed by the sun without bringing rain; Wansleben <note>Johann Michael Wansleben, a 17th-century traveler</note> describes such clouds in his account of Upper Egypt [see Isaiah 44:22, Job 7:9, Jude 12]. f) Or like the **dew** [Isaiah 18:4]. g) The **morning** dew [chapter 13:3]. There are different types of dew; one falls in the morning, another at night ("drops of the night" in Song of Solomon 5:2). As Pliny writes in *Natural History*, morning dew is usually thinner and less lasting. h) Quickly vanishing into the air. The Targum says: "which quickly fails."

v. 5. i) **Therefore I have hewn them.** The Septuagint and Arabic say "I have harvested." But Sanctius, looking toward the New Testament, reads it as "I will cut off." The past tense here is "prophetic past," referring to the future [as in Isaiah 5:13, 9:2, Jeremiah 15:7]. This verse should be taken negatively, as it is followed by "I have slain them" [see Isaiah 10:15, 51:9, Psalm 29:7]. k) The **prophets**. Some read this as the object—meaning he has cut down the *false* prophets and teachers [chapter 4:5] like the Scribes and Pharisees. Others translate it as "I have hewn them *by* my prophets," meaning a corrective measure. l) **I have slain** them, namely the false prophets, or the rebellious Israelites [see chapter 9:13, Amos 4:10, 2 Kings 10:32]. m) By the **words of my mouth**, which are compared to arrows [Psalm 45:6] or a two-edged sword [Hebrews 4:12, Revelation 1:16] because of their divine power. n) And **your judgments**, which were obscured by false teachers [see Amos 5:24]. Some see these as "punishments," others as "laws to be observed." But for us, Sanctius says these "judgments" are the same as the **mercy** mentioned in verse 4, which is made light in Christ. In the New Testament, these are the "righteous requirements" (*dikaiōmata*)—firstly the righteousness of Christ by which we are justified [Romans 5:16], and secondly the righteous acts of a holy life [Luke 1:6] according to the Spirit [Romans 8:3-4]. o) "As the light," or according to Sanctius, "so that they *are* light," they shall go forth [Isaiah 62:1].

v. 6. p) The reason for the previous statements is given here. People often wrongly apply this only to the Old Testament. Christ himself cites this verse when discussing the end of the Sabbath and Levitical ceremonies to argue against the Pharisees. Sebastian Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> believes this refers to the abolition of Levitical worship in the New Testament. However, these views can be reconciled: while God does not want mere "shadows" and rituals in the New Testament, it is also true that even in the Old Testament, he always required true repentance and faith over external ritual [see chapter 14:3, Isaiah 1:11]. q) Not a fake love, but **true piety and holiness**, which does not judge its neighbor but loves sincerely [Matthew 9:13, Micah 6:8].

v. 3. **And let us know** <note>original: wênêde’āh</note>: The prefix "and" was erased in manuscript 5. A later hand in the Erfurt Masoretic text marks this as a **variant reading** <note>Aramaic: phêlugtā</note>.
v. 4. **To you** <note>original: lêkhā</note>: Written without certain vowel marks in various manuscripts. **And your love**: Written without the prefix "and" in manuscripts 1 and 2. **Like a cloud**: <gloss>so</gloss> it appears earlier on page 80. **Rising early**: <gloss>so</gloss> also in the phrase "and like the dew."

Commonly they make a comparison—but this opinion is hindered by the fact that it follows that sacrifice joined with mercy pleases God: which (while true in the Old Testament) is false concerning the New Testament, to which the Prophet's sentiment pertains. — For the prefix *min* <note>a Hebrew preposition meaning "from" or "more than"</note> simply denotes the choice of one over another, from a certain and just cause; as when good is loved over evil, and the tax collector was justified rather than the Pharisee (Luke 18:14). S. compare a similar prefix in Psalm 118:8, 9.

And this was done when the Gospel was first propagated to the Israelites, and then to all nations, through the Evangelists and Apostles who went out from Judea and Jerusalem. see Luke 24:47, Acts 13:46, and compare Ephesians 2:3, Matthew 10:5, 6, 15:24, John 4:22. d) when I *bring back the captives* of my people from spiritual captivity (Hebrews 2:14, 15); as was promised above (chapter 1:7). For this phrase is used in the Scriptures concerning the liberation through Christ. see Ephesians 52:8, Jeremiah 31:23, Zephaniah 3:20, Psalm 14:7, Psalm 126:1, etc. Thus not only Blessed Schmid, but also Diodati’s paraphrase in Pocock (p. 325) explains this very difficult verse with us. Others, however (like the Arabic Manuscript just cited and Rabbi Tanchum in Pocock), take "harvest" in a bad sense; in this manner: "Even Judah, consenting to your sins, has set [a harvest for judgment]..." We prefer to set aside several other inconsistent or straying commentaries of others.

<margin>
w. verse 7. *Adam*. "But they." namely, according to S., the false teachers (verse 5), according to others, Israel and Judah (verse 4). This is the second part of the reasoning begun in the preceding verse, by way of opposition. S. y) *as Adam in Paradise* (Genesis 3:6, Romans 5:12, 14) so most Hebrews understand it. Ionathas: "as the former or ancient generations." **CHAPTER VII.** verse 1. e) S. *When I healed Israel*; namely, when the boundaries of the kingdom were restored and recovered from the enemy (2 Kings 14:25 and following). Others: "Whenever I brought a remedy to Israel." compare chapter 5:13, 11:3, Jeremiah 17:14, 30:9. Some also compare chapter 6:1 above, which however deals with the healing of the Messiah under the New Testament. According to S., this Chapter VII (which others join to the preceding chapters V and VI, see Preface §11) contains a new, and indeed fifth, sermon of Hosea; in which God complains of the many and most grave sins of the Israelites, especially their persistent hypocrisy, and their flattery and seditions against their Kings and Princes. He threatens just punishments through four parts, in which Visinus wishes to observe four symbols or images of their most ruined state: (1) the despair of the field (verse 1 and following, compare Ephesians 1:5, 6); (2) the baker's oven or furnace (verse 3 and following); (3) bread baked in ashes or a corrupted cake (verse 8 and following); (4) a silly dove (verse 11 and following). Furthermore, Lightfoot (in his *Chronology*, p. 105) concludes that this and the following chapters, all the way to the end of the book, were published under the beginning of Hezekiah’s reign and the final times of King Hoshea. (1) he says, the common and perpetual speech which the Prophet has in these toward Ephraim shows that these were announced to the ten tribes before they were led away into captivity, which was now to happen within four years. (2) This was said after King Hoshea had made a friendship with Egypt, of which mention is made in 2 Kings 17:4. For observe how here in chapter 7:11 and 12:2 such a thing is hinted at. And (3) this was said after the first expedition of Shalmaneser (2 Kings 17:3) in which he destroyed Beth-Arbel (Hosea 10:14) and before his second expedition when he was about to destroy Samaria. compare also the notes on 2 Kings 17:4 and Schmid’s Commentary (p. 296 and following).

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Hosea chapter 7, following the transition from chapter 6 where the focus shifted from the corruption of the priests to the systemic iniquity of the entire kingdom of Israel, specifically naming the dominant tribe of Ephraim and the capital city, Samaria.</meta>

# HOSEA CHAPTER 7.

When I would have healed Israel, then the iniquity of **Ephraim** <note>Ephraim was the most powerful tribe of the Northern Kingdom of Israel, often used by the prophets as a name for the whole nation.</note> was uncovered, and the wickedness of **Samaria**; for they commit falsehood; the thief enters in, and the bandit troop raids outside. And they do not say to their hearts that I remember all their wickedness; now their own deeds have surrounded them; they are before my face. They make the king glad with their wickedness, and the princes with their lies. They are all adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker; he ceases from stirring <note>Or "from waking"</note> from the kneading of the dough until it is leavened. On the day of our king, the princes have made him sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with the scoffers. For they have applied their heart like an oven in their ambush; all night their baker sleeps; in the morning it burns like a flaming fire. They are all hot as an oven...

<meta>catchword: like an oven</meta>

<margin>
**f)** Then it betrayed itself even more; it was laid bare and detected. See Isaiah 22:14; Ezekiel 21:29. **g)** The impiety of Ephraim, as in chapter 13:12. This refers to the chief tribe (chapter 5:13). **h)** Chapter 14:1. This refers to the Royal Court: because the Israelites, puffed up by their successes, did not only relapse into their former vices but increased them with new and heavier ones (chapter 13:2). **i)** Explanatory: because or for they surely commit a lie. **k)** Compare Jeremiah 6:13; chapter 8:10; Proverbs 11:18; Revelation 21:27; 22:15. That is, according to Sebastian Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696) was a prominent Lutheran theologian and commentator</note>, they did not perform a true and serious repentance, nor did they work deeds worthy of repentance. And though they made a beginning of repentance by abstaining from idolatry and gross crimes, as can be gathered from 2 Kings 14:26-27 (for God would not otherwise have graciously looked upon them and intended to deliver them with such a notable liberation, by which all the borders of the kingdom were restored, if their repentance had been mere hypocrisy; compare the note on 1 Kings 21:29), nevertheless, they only behaved better externally in certain things, and they hid their crimes under an external appearance rather than avoiding them; as if God did not look upon or care for internal things, as is said shortly in verse 2. Their successes against enemies so blinded them that they thought God was surely appeased, or else He would not have helped or delivered them. Schmidt, pages 299 and 348. **l)** And, to proceed to specifics, he comes by stealth (Joel 2:9) and plunders the goods of others (Jeremiah 49:9), indeed he seizes the royal throne. See the note on 2 Kings 15:10. **m)** And spreads himself out (1 Samuel 37:8). **n)** A troop of seditious robbers (chapter 6:9). **o)** In the fields (Ezekiel 7:15), filling everything with thefts and robberies.
</margin>

<margin>
...they will be (chapter 10:2). **q)** Because all their malice (verse 1; chapter 9:15; 10:15). **r)** I am mindful (chapter 8:13; 9:9; Psalm 25:6). Not as if they denied all divine providence, like those in Malachi 3:14, but that what they themselves were preparing were not sins <note>The Hebrew text notes a "Milel" accentuation here, affecting the stress of the word.</note>...
</margin>

**v. 3.** **y)** Through their own malice. See verse 2. Namely, thefts, robberies, and other things which they perpetrated in wars, especially civil wars, for the sake of their own faction and to take revenge on the opposing side, according to Schmidt. **z)** They gladden, as a son who is thrifty gladdens his father (Proverbs 10:1). **a)** The King and the Princes of their own factions, who are pleased by this: that they fight so vigorously and eagerly for them. He says "the King" in the singular because although there were many successively, there was only one at a time. **b)** And with their lies, by which they deceive others. See chapter 10:13; Psalm 59:13. **c)** Compare verse 5 and chapter 4:18.

**v. 4.** **d)** All of them, namely the Ephraimites and the inhabitants of Samaria (verse 1), according to Schmidt. Others say: the King, the people, and the princes. Regarding the connection, Schmidt says: The sins which are rebuked through verse 7 inclusive are those committed by the whole people concerning the Kings and Princes, specifically two: (1) that they serve the Kings and Princes for a time with the foulest flatteries, whom (2) they nevertheless eventually, indeed shortly, kill, turning their flatteries into hatred and slaughter. He began to deal with flatteries in verse 3: "Through their malice they gladden the King," etc., which they did especially when they raised them to the throne and dignities, even with seditions, thefts, and robberies according to verse 1. Now in this verse 4 and verse 5, it is told how they continued those flatteries toward those raised to the throne: namely, by committing adultery for their sake and instituting sacred but idolatrous feasts on the "day of their King." **e)** Jeremiah 9:1; 23:10. Some take this simply as adultery properly so called; others as spiritual adultery, as above in chapter 2:4; Jeremiah 13:27; James 4:4. Schmidt, however, understands the adulteries committed in the rites of Bacchus and Venus on the King’s festival day, instituted in his honor (verse 5). Compare chapter 1:2; 4:11; 6:10. Unless you prefer that the crime of adultery here denotes the inconstancy and treachery of the people toward the Kings whom they themselves had previously adopted through sedition. **f)** As a furnace or oven (verses 6, 7; Genesis 15:17). We think the intensity of the heat is emphasized by this comparison, per Schmidt. **g)** Burning, that which glows. Masculine with a paragogic *He* <note>A grammatical feature in Hebrew where an extra letter is added to the end of a word for emphasis or style.</note>; compare Malachi 3:19. **h)** Kindled by the baker who bakes the bread (verse 6). **i)** He ceases, he rests (Genesis 2:2, 3; Exodus 16:30). **k)** Stirring up or the one who stirs. So Schmidt and Rabbi Tanchum <note>Tanchum ben Joseph of Jerusalem (c. 1220–1291), a Hebrew philologist and commentator.</note> in Pococke <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), an English Orientalist and biblical scholar.</note>, page 334. Compare Isaiah 41:2; Jeremiah 50:9; Zechariah 4:1. **l)** From kneading (Genesis 18:6). **m)** The dough (Exodus 12:34). **n)** Schmidt: "Until its fermentation." Compare Exodus 12:34, 39. That is, according to Schmidt, those who ought to stir them up from the sleep of adultery—the Priests and Prophets—cease from stirring and correcting them from the time the dough is kneaded (i.e., from the time the people begin to be molded) until the whole mass of the people is fermented, and thus all become adulterers. Compare 1 Corinthians 5:6.

**v. 5.** **o)** "The day is our King's"; either his birthday, or his inauguration, or a day solemn for whatever cause; namely, the priests say this (understanding the word "saying" before this verse, as in chapter 5:15; Psalm 2:3; Isaiah 14:8, etc.), according to Schmidt, solemnly proclaiming this day and the following feast in honor of the King. Others specifically look to 1 Kings 12:32. **p)** They make sick, namely the people; others say they corrupt themselves and the King. This is the Hiphil verb form from the root *chalah* (Isaiah 53:10; Micah 6:13; Proverbs 13:12). Others say "they begin," namely to drink together (as in Jonah) or "to be mad" (as in Syriac), but this is against the grammar. **q)** The impious Princes (verses 3, 16) bestowing wine upon the people. **r)** The "bottle" or "skin" (Habakkuk 2:15; compare Genesis 21:14, 15, 19). Others say "poison" prepared from wine, or a poison stronger than wine itself, or that which disturbs the mind more than wine; compare Psalm 58:4. So says Rabbi Tanchum in Pococke, page 337. **s)** "From wine" or a portion of wine. Compare chapter 4:11; Proverbs 20:1. A skin full of wine is a portion or "some" wine, says Schmidt. Regarding the prefix, see the notes on Leviticus 4:17; 1 Kings 12:9; Isaiah 47:13. Luther and others have best expressed the mode of corruption through the word "raging," so that it is a corruption of the mind through wine and a seduction in spiritual matters, especially through gifts of wine and flatteries, in which men do not hesitate to commit harlotry, adultery, and other evils. Schmidt. **t)** And the King himself also stretches out or puts forth and joins his hand; compare the verb in Amos 9:13; Psalm 149:12. That is, according to Schmidt, he flatters by giving his hand, and by this sign shows that their foul deeds please him. In this way, all the superiors of the people aid and foster their malice and adulteries: the priests proclaim the feast of Bacchus and Venus in honor of the King, the Princes give wine, and the King approves and courts the favor of the people. **u)** With scoffers, who are here men from the drunken populace who are not ashamed to mock God and men. Schmidt. Compare Isaiah 28:14, 22; Psalm 1:1; also Proverbs 20:1.

**v. 6.** **x)** But when they turn or apply (Isaiah 46:13). **y)** Like an oven (verses 4, 7). He takes up the comparison of the oven again to teach that there is the same impulse and fury in hatred and ambushes that was previously in love and flattery. Schmidt. **z)** In their ambush or in their lying in wait (the Infinitive, as in Jeremiah 9:7), so that they may devise secret plans against their King and Princes. It was said in the preceding verse how the people committed harlotry for the sake of the King and Princes; now he shows how mobile and inconstant they are, yet always evil, and soon they turn their minds away from the King and princes and apply them to lying in wait, consuming, and killing them, and that with the same heat and vehemence of hatred with which they were previously inflamed to perform the worst flatteries for them. Thus, the most inconstant and furious levity of the people is rebuked. Schmidt. **a)** All night, that is, during the whole time when an open sedition is still inconvenient. Compare Judges 16:2. **b)** He sleeps, that is, he conducts himself quietly and hides his plans: just as a baker, properly so called, goes to bed early toward nightfall and sleeps until the convenient time for heating the oven and baking bread, which is very early in the morning. Schmidt. Compare 1 Samuel 28:7. **c)** Their baker (verse 4). That is, the head of the sedition, for example Shallum, after he entered into a seditious covenant against Zechariah (2 Kings 15:10). **d)** But at dawn or in the morning, that is, when the opportune occasion for stirring up sedition arrives. Schmidt. Compare 1 Samuel 19:11; Micah 2:1. **e)** He, the leader of the sedition, burns (verse 4), and with open fury he and his accomplices rush upon their King and Princes in the presence of the people themselves (2 Kings 15:10). **f)** Like a fire of flame or a flaming fire, which consumes and destroys whatever it meets (Lamentations 2:3).

**v. 7.** **g)** And all of them along with the impious leader of the sedition. **h)** They grow hot with fury (Psalm 39:4).

They steal, plunder, and kill the innocent, as if they were doing everything by the right of war and justly. Nor is there any doubt that they behaved this way, especially because they adhered to and fought for those Kings of Israel who invaded the kingdom through violence and sedition, such as Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, Pekah (and King Hoshea himself). Schmidt. **5)** Chapter 5:7. **t)** Chapter 12:1; Psalm 17:11; Psalm 18:6. Like bailiffs. Tarnovius. Compare Proverbs 5:22. <summary>This page provides a detailed commentary on Hosea 7:1-7, using the metaphor of a heated oven to describe the volatile transition in Israel from flattering their kings to assassinating them. The text highlights the roles of the king, princes, and priests in national corruption, identifying specific historical figures like Shallum who led violent coups.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Hosea chapter 7. The previous page discussed the internal corruption of Israel's leadership, comparing their simmering conspiracies to a baker’s oven. This page continues that metaphor to describe the downfall of their kings and their foolish foreign alliances.</meta>

### CHAPTER 7. HOSEA 7.

<margin>
i) This is repeated from verse 4.
u) This is meant to emphasize the intensity of the heat: perhaps it also suggests a distinction between the baker and the oven. The baker is said to burn like a flaming fire in verse 6, while his people burn like an oven that is heated by that flaming fire. The author of the conspiracy or rebellion inflames the minds of all the others.
k) And thus, like a consuming fire (v. 6), they consume—that is, they destroy and kill. l) their judges. Some understand these to be good men who were beneficial to the state and the church; however, we take them to be those Princes spoken of in verse 5. m) Thus almost all their Kings fell: Zechariah (2 Kings 15:10), Shallum (v. 14), Pekahiah (v. 23), Pekah (v. 30). See also 1 Kings 15:27, 1 Samuel 1:12, and chapters 21, 22. n) They fell by their hands. Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> says they were "killed." See 2 Kings 15:10, 14, 23, 27, 30. o) Due to their extreme obstinacy and stupidity, there is not a single person among those rebels— p) who, under such great evils and shaking of the state, recognizes God's wrath and calls out to me in faith from true repentance. See verse 14, Isaiah 64:6, and Psalm 50:15.
</margin>

7) They are all hot <gloss>i</gloss> as an oven <gloss>u</gloss> and they have devoured <gloss>q</gloss> their judges <gloss>r</gloss>; all their kings <gloss>s</gloss> have fallen <gloss>t</gloss>; there is none among them who calls to me <gloss>u</gloss>.
8) **Ephraim** <gloss>x</gloss> <note>Ephraim is used here to represent the Northern Kingdom of Israel</note> among the nations <gloss>y</gloss> he mixes himself <gloss>z</gloss>; **Ephraim** <gloss>a</gloss> has become a cake not turned <gloss>b</gloss>.
9) Strangers have devoured <gloss>c</gloss> his strength <gloss>d</gloss> and he does not know it <gloss>e</gloss>; gray hair <gloss>f</gloss> is also sprinkled upon him <gloss>g</gloss> and he does not know it <gloss>h</gloss>.
10) And the pride of Israel <gloss>k</gloss> testifies <gloss>i</gloss> against his face <gloss>l</gloss>; and they do not return to the Lord their God, nor do they seek Him for all this <gloss>m</gloss>.
11) And Ephraim <gloss>n</gloss> has become like a dove <gloss>o</gloss>, simple <gloss>p</gloss>, without heart <gloss>q</gloss> <note>Meaning without understanding or common sense</note>; they call to Egypt <gloss>r</gloss>, they go to Assyria <gloss>s</gloss>.
12) When they go <gloss>t</gloss> I will spread my net <gloss>u</gloss> over them; I will bring them down like a bird <gloss>x</gloss> of the heavens <gloss>y</gloss>; I will chastise them <gloss>z</gloss> according to the report to their congregation <gloss>a</gloss>.
13) Woe to them <gloss>b</gloss> for they have strayed from me <gloss>c</gloss>; destruction to them <gloss>d</gloss> for they have transgressed against me <gloss>e</gloss>; though I would redeem them <gloss>f</gloss> yet they have spoken <gloss>g</gloss> [lies against me]

<margin>
Regarding verse 8 and 9: As it pertains to Ephraim and the kingdom of the ten tribes (see chapter 5:12). v) with the pagan nations, from whom God had separated them even in their dwelling place (Exodus 19:5, Leviticus 20:24, Numbers 22:9, Deuteronomy 4:34, 7:6, etc.). s) he mixes himself or is mixed. Others: "he will be confused" (Exodus 29:40). Most relate this to Israel's guilt—that they mixed themselves with them through destructive treaties or marriages, or rather polluted the true religion they outwardly professed with the profane superstitions of the Gentiles, as complained in Psalm 106:35. See Bochart, *Hierozoicon* <note>A famous 17th-century scholarly work on animals of the Bible by Samuel Bochart</note> I. 328. But Sebastian Schmid, along with Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, refers this to divine punishment or chastisement, so that for the most part, especially those across the Jordan, were led away among the nations, or were even confused and mixed with them in their own land, living among them (compare 2 Kings 13:3, 22; 15:29). It is as if God says: "I made it so that Ephraim...
</margin>

---

...would be mixed with the people by whom he was led away captive, in case he might be led to repentance in this way; but even this was in vain (v. 9, 10). z) Tenses are mixed, as often happens in prophecies (compare chapter 5:11).
u) bread baked under ashes, or a cake (Genesis 18:6). x) not turned while cooking (Judges 7:13, Lamentations 4:6). This refers to a type of cake baked over coals (see Rabbi Solomon on this passage and 1 Kings 19:6). If it is not turned in time, it is completely burned on the bottom before it cooks on the top. (As Bochart says in *Hierozoicon* I. 328-329: "Nor is bread baked under ashes perfectly cooked unless it is turned.") Ephraim is compared to such a cake—burnt on one side and providing little nourishment or flavor on the other—because his kingdom was most afflicted, largely overturned, and the remaining part was greatly weakened and without strength. Hence in chapter 5:11, Ephraim was called "oppressed and crushed."

**V. 9.** z) For they have consumed. Compare Jeremiah 10:25. The figurative language arises from the comparison to the cake in verse 8, which is also "eaten" by fire when it is burned. s. a) foreign enemies (chapter 8:7, Isaiah 1:7): the Syrians (2 Kings 13:7), the Philistines (Isaiah 9:11), and the Assyrians (2 Kings 15:19). b) his strength, with a large part of the kingdom torn away. See especially 2 Kings 15:29. c) yet he does not recognize it, in total security and stupidity; nor does he turn to God (verse 7, 10; Isaiah 42:25). d) even gray hair (Genesis 44:29, 31). A metaphor for a man growing old. e) it is sprinkled on him, or he sprinkles gray hairs on him (Exodus 9:10, Isaiah 28:24, Job 2:12). It is as if he has contracted old age and, with all strength exhausted, is near death. The Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic translations say: "gray hairs have sprouted on him." Compare chapter 11:1. f) This indicates persistent malice that does not yield even to clear evidence and external convictions, such as these great afflictions.

**V. 10.** g) Jonathan: "And the arrogance of Israel will be humbled while they watch." So say the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic. But Sebastian Schmid and others say better: *The pride of Israel answers in his face.* This signifies clear and irrefutable conviction, with his own conscience accusing and convicting him (chapter 5:5, Psalm 59:12, Wisdom 17:11). h) chapter 5:4, Amos 4:6, 11. i) chapter 5:15. k) throughout all this time in which these things were done to them (compare Isaiah 9:12, 16, 20). This highlights their extreme stubbornness—invincible not only through so many afflictions but also over such a long time.

**V. 11.** l) And Ephraim and Israel became (verse 8). m) like a simple dove, or one enticed (Deuteronomy 32:16, Proverbs 25:19; compare Proverbs 22:3). A dove has this praiseworthy quality: it harms no one. But it has this blameworthy quality: it does not watch out for itself, as the scholar Drusus writes. They say the simplicity of the dove is apparent in that it does not avoid nets or the snares prepared for it when it lands to eat. "Thus the Israelites did not foresee dangers and threw themselves into the power of their enemies." These are the words of Bochart (*Hierozoicon* II. 21, 22). Indeed, there is something worthy of praise in the simplicity of a dove if wisdom is added (Matthew 10:16, Romans 16:19); but there is something worthy of blame if it lacks wisdom. It is considered in the latter way here. A simple dove is mindless in its actions, needy, neither foreseeing nor anxious. Thus Ephraim went to Egypt and Assyria, not foreseeing that the whole matter would turn out unhappily without God. n) senseless (Jeremiah 5:21). Syriac and Arabic: "one who has no heart"—that is, unwise. This refers to the dove based on the Hebrew accent marks. o) now they call on the Egyptians for help, not me, their God and Lord (v. 7). See note on v. 1 and compare chapter 8:13, 12:2, 2 Kings 17:4. The Jews did the same (Isaiah 30:2, 31:1). p) now they go off to the Assyrians (chapter 5:13, 8:9, 12:2, 2 Kings 15:19).

**V. 12.** q) Zurich Bible: "But when they set out." Sebastian Schmid: "When they go." r) chapter 5:1, Ezekiel 12:13, 17:20, 19:8, 32:3. s) my net; so that by my providence they may be ensnared, and everything may turn out badly for them, nor can they escape my punishment (Psalm 9:16, Job 19:6, Lamentations 1:13). t) like birds of the sky, even if they have flown (Genesis 1:20). "Sky" is used here for its lower part. u) I will nonetheless cast them down to the earth so that they perish (Amos 9:2, Obadiah v. 4). For it sometimes happened that the Israelites seemed to themselves to have escaped all evil and even shaken off the yoke of their enemies; but suddenly the state of affairs changed, and they perished miserably, as happened to King Hoshea, whom Rivetus rightly cites here. x) I will chastise them. [Hiphil form] Jonathan: "I will bring correction upon them." See chapter 5:2. But Sebastian Schmid: "I will make them a lesson to others when they hear the fame of what happens to their assembly"—that is, I will punish them so severely that I make them an example of my wrath and punishment to others (Isaiah 23:5). y) according to the report or the word heard and announced (Habakkuk 3:1, Isaiah 53:1). z) often made to their assembly from the Law and the Prophets (Jeremiah 6:18; see above chapter 5:9, and Leviticus 26:14ff, Deuteronomy 27:15ff, 28:15ff, 2 Kings 17:13-25). Others: according to the fame and rumor regarding their assembly (Genesis 13:21).

**V. 13.** a) Woe, therefore, to them! because of those things which I said would come upon them from me (chapter 9:12, Lamentations 5:16; see note on Isaiah 1:4). b) they have wandered (chapter 9:17). This denotes the forsaking of God through foul idolatry. c) devastation is certainly determined and will come to them (chapter 10:14, Joel 1:15). d) chapter 8:1, Isaiah 1:2. Jonathan: "because they are rebels against my Word." e) For I not only liberated them from Egypt through Moses (Deuteronomy 7:8, 13:6, 21:8, Micah 6:4) and recently from the Syrians through Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25ff), but I am also going to redeem them eternally (chapter 13:14, Psalm 25:22, 130:5, 8). <note>original: "ἐγὼ δὲ ἐלוטרוסאמיין αὐτοὺς" — A mix of Greek and Hebrew meaning 'And I redeemed them.'</note> Titus 2:14, 1 Peter 1:18.

*. 9) The word "sprinkled" (*zarqah*) uses the Cholem vowel and a Bet in the text.

<summary>This page provides a detailed philological and theological commentary on Hosea 7:7-13, focusing on the metaphors of a "cake not turned" and a "silly dove" to illustrate Israel's political instability and foolish foreign policies. The author uses these images to describe the nation's spiritual decay and its impending judgment by God's "divine net."</summary>

f) But they have spoken lies against me, their God and Redeemer; according to Sebastian Schmidius <note>Sebastian Schmidius was a 17th-century Lutheran theologian and commentator</note> and others, they did this while promising repentance and better behavior (see note on verse 1), only to fall back into their previous or even worse sins (Psalm 78:36). They defended these sins with various excuses (2 Kings 17:9), imagining God to be nonetheless favorable to them (below, chapter 8:2), as if He were content with some external ritual and did not care for the internal heart (see above at verse 2). Or they acted as if idols or men could provide the same benefits (chapter 2:7, 14) or help (above verse 11) as God. Compare verse 15, chapter 12:1, Judges 16:10, Isaiah 28:15, 17, chapter 57:11, Ezekiel 13:19, Amos 2:4, Zephaniah 3:13; and the highest degree of this impiety in Matthew 26:59 and following, and chapter 27:12, 13, etc.

# CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>
1. ...contrite, as was also explained above regarding their exile;
</margin>

->1. Set the trumpet to your lips! Like an eagle over the house of the LORD, because they have transgressed my covenant and rebelled against my law.<-

<sig>Bbbb</sig>

<margin>
Verse 14: g) Compare verse 7 and chapter 8:2. h) Out of their own soul. Compare verse 3 and Isaiah 29:13. The coherence here is very easy for us, says Schmidius. For the deceptive and hypocritical repentance of the Israelites is further described—well begun, perhaps, but shamefully abandoned and corrupted by their temporary successes (see note on verse 1). Specifically, their prayers were hypocritical and did not come from a sincere heart. We understand the "cry of repentance" here; just as in the Book of Judges, the phrase "to cry out to God" is frequently used regarding the oppressed Israelites seeking deliverance through repentance. See Judges 3:9, 15, chapter 6:6, 7, chapter 10:10, 1 Samuel 12:8, 10, etc. i) Even when they wail (Isaiah 15:2, 3). k) Compare Micah 2:1, Psalm 4:5, and the opposite in Psalm 149:5. This circumstance aggravates the hypocrisy. For those who are truly sad cannot even find sleep in their bed, but wail miserably throughout the nights; especially those who are seriously contrite before God.
</margin>

...they did not do this in their heart, and it was without sincerity, as finally became clear. Schmidius: l) *over grain and much wine* (chapter 2:10, 11; chapter 4:11; chapter 8:7; chapter 9:2). m) *Schmidius: they gather themselves*, when idolatrous priests or princes invited them to the sacred rites of Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine and revelry</note> and Venus <note>The Roman goddess of love and beauty</note>, and promised an abundance of grain and wine. *Spanish:* (3) 1 Kings 17:10, Jeremiah 30:23, compare Psalm 56:7, Psalm 59:4, etc. As the *Syriac* version says, they are anxious about grain and wine; because the word גוּר <note>Hebrew: gur</note> also means *to fear* or to be afraid, as in Deuteronomy 1:17, Psalm 22:24, and below in chapter 10:5. n) *and they turn away against me.* Compare 2 Kings 13:6, Isaiah 30:11, Jeremiah 5:23, chapter 17:5, Psalm 14:3. Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan</note>: they rebelled against my Word. I would think the emphasis in this phrase is that they do not merely withdraw from the Lord, but even struggle against Him as He calls them back and wishes to retain them: which is to struggle against one's conscience, as we had above at verse 10. Schmidius: Verse 15: o) chapter 10:10. Schmidius here begins the conclusion of the entire chapter in this manner: *Because I have chastised them and soon strengthened their arms, they nonetheless devise evil against me; therefore their princes shall fall by the sword (verse 16).* Others think the vice of ingratitude is specifically rebuked here. *Jonathan: Indeed, as much as I brought chastisements upon them and added strength to their arms, so much they also think to add evils before me.* God excellently calls the previous afflictions a "chastisement," because He had not sent them for the purpose of destruction, as is expressly stated in 2 Kings 14:27. Compare Deuteronomy 8:5, Isaiah 28:26. p) Ezekiel 30:24, 25. Moreover, the Lord strengthened their arms in the wars of Joash (2 Kings 13:15–25) and especially of Jeroboam (2 Kings 14:25, 26), so that they repelled enemies and restored the borders of the kingdom. Schmidius: q) Compare verse 13, Nahum 1:9, 11. r) While hypocritically converted, having barely made a good beginning, they soon relapsed into their former evils and obstinately decided to persist in them. Thus, for example, the Kings of Israel, each and every one (even those who were otherwise praiseworthy, like Jehu in 2 Kings 10:31, Joash in chapter 13:3, Jeroboam II in chapter 14:24, and the last, Hoshea, in chapter 17:2) thought they should nonetheless retain the superstitions and idolatrous worship of God through the golden calves, despite so many warnings and God's most severe corrections (Hosea 8:5). They were moved by the same false political reasons that Jeroboam I (the man whose memory is condemned in Holy Scripture) had used to introduce it (1 Kings 12:26 and following). Verse 16: s) Schmidius interprets this assembly: *They return to their own vomit* (2 Peter 2:22). Compare Ezekiel 8:17, Nehemiah 9:28, etc. Therefore there will be no high one for them, that is, no King (comparing 2 Samuel 23:1). *They are false like a deceitful bow, therefore their princes shall fall, etc.* Others, like the Zurich Bible and many more: *They return or are converted, but not to the Most High*; comparing verse 10 and Jeremiah 4:1. Finally others, like Louis de Dieu and Gussetius (page 665), take עָל <note>Hebrew: al</note> as an adverb in this way: *They turn, but not upwards* <note>original: ὥς τις ἄνω (Greek)</note> (chapter 11:7) toward heavenly or divine things (Philippians 3:14), but as said above in verse 14, *mindful of earthly things, whose god is their belly* <note>original: τὰ ἐπίגεια φρονῶντες, ὧν ὁ θεὸς ἡ κοילία (Greek)</note> (Philippians 3:19). We omit more from others that are foreign to the text. t) Compare chapter 11:7, 2 Samuel 23:3, 15, Isaiah 19:18. u) A deceitful and perverse bow is one that strikes the person aiming it and wounds its own master, says *Jerome*. It is one that deceives the archer with a failing strike; or even when stretched, it breaks and gives way—that is, it goes slack and does not hit the mark when firing (Psalm 78:57), which fits excellently here. For the Israelites began to practice repentance, but soon relaxed and relapsed into their former impiety. s) x) Therefore they shall fall by the sword (verse 7, Jeremiah 44:12). y) The most implacable of them, about whom see verses 4, 5 and chapter 9:15. z) On account of indignation and impudence (Isaiah 30:27, Nahum 1:6). a) Compare verse 13, Jeremiah 9:2, chapter 43:2. b) This will be their mocking and the cause of the mockery with which others will in turn deride them (Psalm 123:4, Job 34:7). Compare Galatians 6:7. c) In the land, or because of the land of Egypt, in which they impiously placed their trust (see verse 11, etc.).

<margin>
CHAPTER 8. verse 1. d) *To your palate* (Job 6:30). e) Put or apply the trumpet or the horn. The Vulgate: *Let there be a trumpet in your palate.* Most think that God—perhaps the Son of God—addresses the Prophet to summon the enemy; others think He addresses the people, as in chapter 5:8. Schmidius, however, thinks He addresses the enemy himself. Compare Isaiah 58:1, where the metaphor is explained. Thus Jonathan: *Prophet, cry with your throat, like a trumpet. A new and sixth prophecy begins here against Israel, in whose communion of both guilt and punishment Judah also comes (verse 14). In this prophecy, I. most grave sins are severely rebuked, and II. the imminent punishment is certainly denounced for them.* Regarding the time, compare the note on chapter 7:1 and 2 Kings 17:4. f) Like an eagle, let the enemy be present or arrive quickly; for example, according to Schmidius's opinion: *To your palate, O enemy, put the trumpet, and come like an eagle.* Jonathan: *Behold, like an eagle that pours itself forth or flies, so shall the King ascend with his troops, and set up camp against the house of the Lord.* Compare Deuteronomy 28:49, Jeremiah 48:40, Habakkuk 1:8, Matthew 24:28, and the note on Ezekiel 17:3. g) That is, *over the people of Israel*, who are the house or church of God. Compare chapter 9:8, 15, Jeremiah 12:7. h) Numbers 20:12, Isaiah 29:13. i) Chapter 6:7, Isaiah 24:5. k) *And against my entire law*, prescribed for them by Moses. Compare verse 12, Jeremiah 6:19, chapter 9:12, chapter 16:11, Ezekiel 22:26. verse 2. l) And yet they cry out to me, or boldly address me, most impudent hypocrites (chapter 7:14, Isaiah 57:13, chapter 58:2). m) Distributively: *My God! they cry out, each one saying.* Compare chapter 2:18, 25. n) *We know you* indeed, truly and practically. Compare 1 Samuel 2:12, Titus 1:16. o) As if to say, your people Israel, whom you chose (Isaiah 1:3, chapter 44:1). Compare also chapter 29:13, chapter 48:2, and above chapter 4:15, etc. Jonathan: *As often as affliction comes upon them, they pray before me and say, "Now we acknowledge that there is no God for us besides you: deliver us, since we are your people Israel."* verse 3. p) Namely, Israel has rejected (verse 5, Zechariah 10:6). q) The good and true knowledge of Him from the word of God (verse 18, Amos 5:14). r) Therefore the enemy, whom He had summoned in verse 1 (compare Lamentations 2:3, 7, 17).

...recovered the kingdom <note>original: "regnum repetierit"</note> (see 2 Chronicles 13:5 and following; reread also the notes on 1 Kings 11 and 12). **u)** but *not from me*; although the hypocrites undoubtedly boasted of it, based on 1 Kings 11:29 and following. **x)** *they have made princes* (chapter 12:5, 21); they *removed* those kings (compare chapter 9:15), but the former interpretation is simpler. **y)** namely, *without consulting me*, as ought to have been done; to the point that, unless I knew of them through my omniscience, I (as far as they were concerned) would know nothing. I would think this refers to the seeking of divine oracles and Prophets. For God ought to be the primary cause in establishing every Israelite kingdom, so that nothing is done without the word of God and the responses of His prophets (according to Schmidius). **z)** *their silver*, or *from their silver and gold* (chapter 13:2; Isaiah 2:20). **a)** *they made for themselves* (chapter 2:10) **b)** *idols* (chapter 4:17). These terms undoubtedly refer to the simple outcome; the erection of these idols is joined here with the establishment of the kingdom, because they were the same kind of business and sin (Schmidius). Compare 1 Kings 12:26 and following. **c)** *so that it might be cut off*, referring to the commonwealth or each of them (Obadiah verse 9; Septuagint, Jonathan, Syriac, Arabic, Vulgate: *so that they might perish*). Here in verse 5, it does not mean the end intended by the idolaters, nor a simple event, but rather denotes the guilt and necessary outcomes (compare Jeremiah 44:8). The stupidity of men is noted here, who sin so grossly as if they desired with all their effort to be cut off. Compare Isaiah 1:5. **verse 5. d)** The Zurich Bible <note>original: "Tig." referring to the Tigurina version</note> translates: *God has repelled or rejected (others say "the enemy" from verse 3) your calf.* But Schmidius and others translate: *Your calf has withdrawn itself, or failed, or deserted you*, namely, being broken and led away, so that it no longer exists, nor can it help you, and nothing is left to you but destruction (verse 4; compare Psalm 74:1, Psalm 89:39, 53, and according to Kimchi, Lamentations 3:17). **e)** *your calf, O Samaria* (verse 6); for although the calves of Bethel and Dan are mentioned in 1 Kings 12:28-29, they are sometimes attributed by the Prophets to Samaria because it was the capital of the kingdom (compare chapter 10:5; Amos 8:14; Bochart, *Hierozoicon* volume 1, page 359). Schmidius, however, is uncertain whether both calves—one in Bethel and the other in Dan—remained until the overthrow of the kingdom; or whether (which seems more probable to him) in the final times, one was transferred to Samaria and worshipped there, and finally was captured and destroyed with Hoshea in Samaria. **f)** chapter 14:5; Isaiah 5:25. **g)** *for how long can they not at last be cleansed?* The question strongly affirms and reproaches the persistence of the hypocrites (compare Jeremiah 4, 14; chapter 12:4, chapter 23:26). **h)** *they cannot bear or admit* (Isaiah 1:13). **i)** *cleanliness or purity* (Genesis 20:5; Amos 4:6; compare Jeremiah 13:27). **verse 6. k)** *for*, to demonstrate the justice of my complaint and their madness. **l)** by Israel himself, who certainly cannot produce God (compare chapter 13:2, chapter 14:4). **m)** Isaiah 44:9 and following. m) even the calf itself exists, or has its origin, no less than other things which come from it, and by their own confession they cannot be gods (Schmidius). Compare chapter 4:12. **n)** because a craftsman or artisan made it (chapter 13:2; Isaiah 40:19-20, chapter 41:7, chapter 44:12). **o)** and therefore it is not God (compare Isaiah 37:19). **p)** *for it shall even become fragments*, that is, it will be broken into pieces. This meaning is proven by the Talmudic term **שבב** (*shabab*), meaning "he broke" (compare Bochart, *Hierozoicon* II, page 608, and the related word in Job 18:5). **q)** see verse 5. Just as long ago Aaron's calf was crushed into powder (Exodus 32:20; Deuteronomy 9:21) or the idols of the Babylonians were broken (Isaiah 46:1). **verse 7 r)** Because they therefore sow the wind in their most vain worship (compare chapter 12:2). **s)** therefore a whirlwind or a very great storm arising from the winds (compare Isaiah 17:13, 21:1, 29:6; Proverbs 1:27; Job 21:18). **t)** a grammatical form for emphasis <note>original: "parag. intensive signific." referring to the paragogic nun or similar intensification</note> as in Exodus 15:15-16; Psalm 63:8. **u)** they shall reap as the fruit or punishment of their idolatry and impiety (compare chapter 10:12; Proverbs 22:8; Romans 6:23; Galatians 6:7-8). **x)** standing grain (Exodus 22:5; Isaiah 17:5). **x)** *it shall not remain*, it will not be left to him, namely Israel; but everything shall be cast down. **y)** *sprout* or herb of the crop (Genesis 19:25; Ezekiel 16:7; Psalm 65:11). **z)** *it shall not yield meal*, or grains from which meal is made. Some take this literally (compare chapter 9:2; Amos 4:6); others, including Schmidius, take it figuratively, to denote all the goods, defenses, counsels, and actions that still remained for the Israelites or could be hoped for, which would be entirely useless to them. **a)** and if by chance it should yield or produce anything (Genesis 18:24, 28). **b)** nevertheless barbarians; foreign soldiers or enemies (chapter 7:9; Isaiah 1:7). **c)** compare Isaiah 28:4. **verse 8. d)** Israel is almost entirely devoured or swallowed up by its enemies (see note on chapter 7:8-9, and compare the verb in Isaiah 9:15). But to Schmidius, the past tense is a prophetic past used for the future; as if to say, to speak briefly and indicate its final outcome: Israel will eventually be swallowed up as if by a greedy and cruel beast (compare chapter 13:8). Thus he also takes the following verbs in the future sense. **e)** they have now become this out of my just anger and vengeance (Deuteronomy 28:25 and following) and by their own fault and treachery (compare the note above on chapter 4:2; 2 Kings 17:4). **f)** not in honor or value (as in Deuteronomy 4:6-7; 2 Samuel 7:9-10, etc.), but like some useless vessel of no value, in which there is no pleasure or desire, which no one cares for or loves (compare Jeremiah 22:28, chapter 48:38; Psalm 31:13; 2 Timothy 2:20). **verse 9. g)** For they themselves, to their own destruction and against my warnings (compare Jeremiah 2:18, 33, chapter 13:21). **h)** *they went up* (or *went away*, Jeremiah 37:9, chapter 34:21) to the Assyrians (see chapter 5:13, chapter 7:11; 2 Kings 15:19). But Schmidius thinks there is an objection here: "Far be it that Israel should be swallowed up and despised among the nations! (verse 8). They will go up to Assyria and be safe under the wings of the King of Assyria." To which it is answered: "On the contrary, when they go up to Assyria, this very thing will become the occasion for their destruction" (compare chapter 13:8).

<column-break/>

**s)** as the swiftest eagle [pursues] its prey (verse 1), he shall pursue him, so that he cannot escape (compare Deuteronomy 28:50; Joshua 7:5, etc.).

**verse 4. t)** And to trace the matter from its origin: They themselves had made kings <gloss>**השירו**</gloss> (see Judges 9:6; 1 Kings 12:20, chapter 16:16). The word *here* does not signify choosing a king so much as describing a certain way of reigning, says Schmidius. Some take this to refer to the election of King Saul, whom nevertheless, in response to their impious request (1 Samuel 8:5, 10:19, 12:17), **God himself gave** (1 Samuel 8:7, 9:16, 10:24, etc.). Others therefore take it to mean kings established through sedition, such as Zimri (1 Kings 16:9), Omri (verse 16), and Shallum (2 Kings 15:10). Most generally, however, commentators understand it as Jeroboam I, not excluding his illegitimate successors. For Jeroboam was elected seditiously by the people, and he seized the kingdom in such a way, not waiting for the manner and time that would please God (see the note on 1 Kings 11 and 12). Schmidius, however, believes here that the accusation is not so much against Jeroboam’s election by the people as against the impious confusion of the royal throne and the kingdom. For even after Jeroboam's election and the departure from Rehoboam, God discouraged the Jews from war and attributed it to Himself insofar as it was done in 1 Kings 12:24. But afterward, the ten tribes strengthened their kingdom and created various heresies; which God, through Ahijah, had expressly made temporary (1 Kings 11:39). They also transferred the kingdom outside the house of Jeroboam, to whom alone God had promised it—and even then not absolutely, but with the condition: "if he would do what was right in the eyes of the Lord," as Kimchi well observes (compare 1 Kings 11:32). And because of these other factors, the kingdom became illegitimate...

The commentary emphasizes the futility of Israel's foreign alliances and religious rituals, predicting their eventual "swallowing up" by Assyria.</summary>

death, and cause them to perish by famine and sword; compare chapter 4:3, 9:6. Or: "I will drive them, I will compel them into Samaria and other fortified cities, so that they may finally be captured and carried away into slavery by the enemy." So say Schmidius and others in Pocock, page 415. **s)** Certainly, many difficulties occur here, and the interpreters vary greatly in opinion. Some: *And they shall grieve, or they have grieved yet a little*, as in Isaiah 13:8, 23:5, etc. Others: *And they shall rest for a little while from the burden, or because of the burdens, which the Kings of Israel and their governors impose on them, such as paying money to the King of the Assyrians*, comparing 2 Kings 15:20, 17:3. Schmidius, however: *And a few shall remain from the burden of the King of Assyria and his Princes, with which he will burden and oppress them in captivity.* All these interpretations come from the root **חיל** (*ḥul*), which is related to the Arabic *ḥalal* (from which the grammatical marking here might be derived). Among other things, it means "to fall upon, to wait, to remain, to stay." See below chapter 11:6, Genesis 8:10, Jeremiah 23:19, Job 20:21, etc. However, because the future tense here is (1) converted to the past by the letter *Vau*, and (2) marked with a *Dagesh* <note>a grammatical dot emphasizing the letter</note>, and (3) as Ibn Ezra notes, from the root **חלל** (*ḥalal*) in Hebrew it rather means *and they began*, as in Judges 20:31, Ezekiel 9:6, etc. Therefore Tremellius and others take it this way: *for they began to be pressed or burdened for a little while* etc. Without omitting words, an Arabic manuscript in Pocock, page 418, rendered this text: *and they began, or they have already begun to be diminished* (as in Isaiah 21:17, Psalm 107:39, Proverbs 13:11, etc.) because of the burdens of the King and the princes. **V. 11. t)** For, let me further explain the causes of that punishment: the first is the multiplication of altars; the second is the contempt for the divine law, verse 12, which severely forbade such multiplication. Schmidius starts a new part of the prophecy here against Israel and Judah, such that the "result" <note>original: "apodosis"</note> to the causal particle *because* only follows in the last verse; in this way: *Because Ephraim multiplied altars... therefore I will send fire... v. 14.* However, we leave this undecided. **u)** verse 10. Especially since God had liberated them, chapter 10:1. **x)** The tribes of Israel verse 9, and also Judah verse 14, corrupted by them, chapter 4:15, Jeremiah 11:13. **y)** so that he himself might sin. Compare 1 Kings 12:30, 13:34, Amos 4:4. For God had prescribed one single place, Deuteronomy 12:5, which was a type <term>symbolic precursor</term> of the unique altar in the New Testament, Hebrews 13:10. See the notes on Leviticus 17:4, Deuteronomy 12:11. **z)** Vulgate: *altars were made for him for offense.* Syriac: *into a great sin or crime.* Schmidius: *they were to him altars in which the Jews sinned.* Compare chapter 4:15. **v. 12. a)** Syriac: *And I indeed prescribed for him the multitude of my laws, namely through Moses;* and thus most take it in the past tense. Compare chapter 6:1, 13:11. Others take it as: *I write, and I still prescribe for him through the Prophets.* Some take it in the future: *Even if I should prescribe for them again...* See Abarbanel. **b)** *multitudes*, or according to another reading, *multitude* (see Hiller on the *Keri* readings, pages 121 and 286), Job 11:2. That is, I wrote many and notable sections about this matter of sacrifice in my Law, in which I specifically commanded how sacrifices should be offered and that there should be only one altar. Others compare Deuteronomy 4:6, 8, 9 and understand it as the very extensive documents of the law. **c)** from which they stubbornly turned away, verse 1. **d)** but as something foreign, which does not belong to them; indeed, as Luther writes: *that is, a doctrine which would harm the state and extinguish religion among the people.* Compare Job 19:15, Numbers 11:20. **e)** *they are considered.* Isaiah 40:15, 19; Job 41:21. Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note> observes this regarding *those who do not practice Christianity sincerely.* Compare Isaiah 28:11, 42:20. We think, with Schmidius, that this is not saying what Israel *said* or claimed about the divine law, but rather God's judgment on the fact: that they did not consider their contempt of the law to be a sin, but the reality is here exposed. For as Luther rightly reminds us, they certainly did not build the altars with the intent to sin; rather, they thought this worship would be approved by God. Therefore, this is the judgment and sentence of the Holy Spirit, who says how things really are, and paints idolatry in its true colors. **v. 13. f)** *As for the sacrifices of my gifts* (1) which they think they are giving to me, and as it were, want to thrust upon me. Compare Isaiah 1:11 and following. **g)** *they indeed slaughter flesh for sacrifice.* Compare chapter 4:13, 14, 19; Psalm 50:13. **h)** *and they devour it.* chapter 4:8. **i)** But the Lord holds them as not at all pleasing or acceptable—neither such sacrifices nor such offerers—because they offer them illegitimately, against His word, and without repentance or faith. Compare chapter 9:4, Jeremiah 14:10. Moreover, the Son speaks of the Father. Compare verse 1, chapter 4:6, 5:2. **k)** rather, now (verse 10) He will remember their iniquity and visit their sins, because in their obstinate malice, they turn not to Him but to the Egyptians. Or: *For now, when He remembers and visits their sins, they themselves return to the Egyptians.* **l)** chapter 7:2, 9:9. **m)** compare chapter 4:14, 5:5, 9:7, Jeremiah 13:21. **n)** that is, to seek help from there. Compare verse 9, chapter 7:11, 9:3, 11:5. **v. 14. o)** And so Israel forgot [his Maker], and as he shared in the sins, so he finally comes to share in the punishment. Compare chapter 4:15, 5:5, 13, 14. **p)** See Isaiah chapter 2:15, 13:6, 51:13. **p)** to whom he ought to have turned and in whom he ought to have trusted. Compare Isaiah 17:7, 22:11. **q)** *and on the other hand he builds palaces*, Isaiah 13:22, in which he trusts. Others: temples, or as the Vulgate has it, "shrines"—namely for idols, as Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note> adds. **r)** 22:8, 9, 10. Trusting in stones more than in God. Compare the times of Uzziah, 2 Chronicles 26:15, 16, and Hezekiah, chapter 32:5. **s)** therefore through the Assyrians I will send fire, Amos 2:5, 1:4, 7, 10, etc. **r)** into the cities of Judah, see 2 Kings 18:13, 19:25, and compare Isaiah 8:8. **x)** the palaces of Israel, or Samaria, compare note on chapter 5:9. Or those of its individual cities, of both kingdoms. Compare Amos 1:4, 7, 2:2, 5; Jeremiah 17:27.

They will be snatched away, and eventually led into wretched slavery. Compare verse 3; chapter 10, 13; Joel 1, 11-12; Habakkuk 3, 17. Jonathan says: *it will not suffice them.* The wine will not please them. Acts 5, 3.
**v. 3. l)** For they shall not remain as they imagine. See Amos 5, 11; Zephaniah 1, 13. **m)** This is undoubtedly the *land of Canaan*, which the LORD chose for Himself to dwell in, and gave to the Israelites as His people. Yet they attributed its grain and wine to idols. See chapter 2, 7; Deuteronomy 11, 12; Jeremiah 2, 7; chapter 16, 18; Ezekiel 36, 18. **n)** And Ephraim will indeed return to Egypt seeking help, but in vain; for being carried away into captivity in Assyria, due to the lack of all things and a defect of food, they will be forced to eat unclean things from which human nature otherwise shrinks. So says Schmid. Others: Ephraim will return in part to Egypt as exiles, or eat unclean things in Assyria. Thus Gürtler in his *Prophetic Theology*, page 184. He says it is likely that many Israelites, as the Assyrians pressed in, fled to neighboring Egypt to escape the enemy's hand. **o)** See verse 6; chapter 8, 13. **p)** See verse 5, 13. **q)** See Ezekiel 4, 12-13; and compare 2 Maccabees 6, 18.

But some say: Because they do not pour libations, etc. The future tense, he says, stands for the present, noting what was already happening in Hosea's time, namely in the worship of the calves. **s)** Jonathan correctly says: *libations of wine.* See Leviticus 23, 13, 18. **t)** nor are their libations pleasing to Him. Jonathan: *like abominable bread.* **y)** See Leviticus 11, 7, 8, 27, 31. **z)** Ezekiel 44, 25. So far from their sacrifices being accepted, he says, everything is rather reckoned to them as sins by God. Compare Isaiah 1, 13. **a)** The reason they do not please the LORD is that they offer their bread to themselves, nor do they bring it to the house or Temple of the LORD, which was in Jerusalem, but rather to their calves. Schmid. **b)** *bread.* i.e., every sacrifice and gift of theirs according to the desire of their own soul. Citing Deuteronomy 12, 15, 20; chapter 14, 26; Psalm 78, 18. **d)** *it does not come*, or it is not brought, as in Joshua 6, 19. **e)** Ezekiel 2, 2; Joel 1, 14. Finally, such a sacrifice is regarded by God as sacrilege. See Leviticus 17, 3.
**v. 5. f)** Isaiah 10, 3; Jeremiah 5, 31. This is an emphatic address to the Israelites, by which the Prophet uses the outcome to prove that the festivals do not please God—those which they still celebrated solemnly in Hosea's time with the pretense of worshipping the LORD (as in Exodus 32, 5). Indeed, by the just indignation of God, all those things were soon to end along with the state itself. See above, chapter 2, 13; chapter 5, 7; Amos 5, 21; Lamentations 1, 4; 2, 6. **g)** See Numbers 10, 10, etc. Others: *as the Jewish and ancient Christian interpreters* say, on the day of vengeance or destruction, citing chapter 5, 13; Lamentations 2, 7. But we prefer the former based on the context, following Schmid and Pocock. **h)** As in Exodus 12, 14; chapter 13, 6; Leviticus 23, 39, 41; Judges 21, 19; etc.

It denotes the certainty of the prediction, as in Isaiah 3, 1; 17, 1; 19, 1; etc. **l)** those to whom he said in verse 5: "What will you do?" etc. they go or certainly will go (<term>Prophetic Past Tense</term> <note>A grammatical term for a future event described as if it has already happened because it is divinely certain</note>) into exile and captivity. Chapter 7, 13. **n)** *Egypt*, in which they seek help and refuge (verse 3). **o)** *he shall gather the dead.* Chapter 8, 10; Jeremiah 8, 2; Ezekiel 29, 5. **p)** *Moph.* Jonathan and the Syriac have *Maphes.* But the Septuagint and Arabic have *Memphis*, which comes from the Ethiopic *Manuph.* Among the Arabs today it is called *Misr*, from the Hebrew **מצרים** (Mizraim), commonly called Cairo. Compare Ludolf’s *New Ethiopic Lexicon*, columns 73 and 85. *Noph* was either the same or another city. p) Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a 16th-century Jewish-Italian convert and scholar.</note> and others take this as an infinitive, as in chapter 4:2, meaning "by swearing falsely," or "by making a covenant" while they are making it. However, S. <note>likely Sebastian Schmidius, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian.</note> takes it as a plural noun, as in Deuteronomy 29:20, etc. He joins it with the following phrase as the subject of the proposition in this manner: "To make a covenant is [to utter] empty curses," that is, vain, fraudulent, and deceitful oaths. See Jonah 2:9, Psalm 31:7, etc. The sense is: they do not only speak words of vanity in a trivial way to defraud others, but even in the most serious business of covenants, when they swear with signs and holy oaths, those curses are nothing other than lying curses which they do not care for, but recklessly and without shame transgress. S. adds that in this way no irregularity is admitted; the accents are not skipped over, and the sense is excellent, which history also proves. For more than once the Kings of Israel themselves treacherously and perjuriously broke covenants that were usually made with many curses. q) For this phrase, see Jeremiah 34:18. r) and it sprouted or broke out. See chapter 14:6, 8; Psalm 92:8. s) like hemlock. The common run of interpreters translate this as "gall," although it is properly a genus of bitter herb growing in cornfields; it is often joined with wormwood as being equally bitter. See Deuteronomy 29:17, Jeremiah 9:14, Lamentations 3:19, Amos 6:12. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* <note>A famous 17th-century study of biblical animals and plants by Samuel Bochart.</note>, Part 1, page 592. t) indeed, judgment is turned by you into the height of injustice. See Amos 5:7, 15; chapter 6:12; Habakkuk 1:4. u) upon the furrows (5) chapter 12:12; Psalm 65:11. x) the fields in which wheat—or of my fields in which wheat—ought to have grown, not hemlock.
