The feminine gender in this place is thought by some to pertain to the assembly. This "out-gendering" <note>original: ἐξωγενισμῷ</note> was very common among the Hebrews, who do not assign sex to gods—to make it all the more evident that they cannot be considered the true God, whose ten names are all masculine. Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, vol. I, page 355. z) i.e., of Bethel, and also of Dan, according to some; compare Amos 1:5 and below verses 8, 15, chapter 4:15. Others deny that the second calf in Dan still existed at this time, and they want there to be a shift <note>original: enallage</note> here, not only of gender but also of number (plural for singular); Schmidius thinks the prophet used this with respect to the name of God *Elohim*, for the sake of contempt and with a certain indignation. a) they will shortly be afraid. Deuteronomy 1:17. Construed with the one for whom there is fear, Job 19:29. b) every neighbor (Exodus 12:4, Isaiah 33:24) of Samaria, cf. chapter 8:5. S. says it is well noted by Rivetus that punishment is announced here to the Israelites. That punishment is the overthrow of the entire ecclesiastical worship (which they had established in the worship of calves) along with the republic; of which he speaks more distinctly in verse 8. c) for it shall soon mourn, Amos 8:8. A "prophetic perfect" tense used for certainty, as in Isaiah 5:13, chapter 9:2, etc. d) over it, namely, its calf. The construction refers back to the subject, not the grammatical form of the name; as in Genesis 49:6, 1 Samuel 25:27, etc. e) its people, that is, the worshippers of the calf. S. says the people of Beth-aven. f) and its sacrificial priests (3) Zephaniah 1:4, see 1 Kings 12:32. g) who still exult over it. An ellipsis of the relative pronoun, as in verse 1 and very often, e.g., Isaiah 28:16, etc. h) they shall mourn over its glory. Some refer the suffix to the calf, Schmidius to Beth-aven; we, with others, refer it to the people, as in chapter 4:7, 9:11, Isaiah 17:3; but in such a way that the calf is understood, just as the true God is elsewhere called the glory of Israel. See Jeremiah 2:11. i) because it has been cast away into exile or led away. See 1 Samuel 4:21, 22; Isaiah 24:11, 46:2; Jeremiah 48:7. **v. 6.** k) For also with the men and other spoils, see 2 Kings 18:9 and following. l) that very calf, see Numbers 26:25, Deuteronomy 20:8. m) into Assyria or to the Assyrian, i.e., to the King of Assyria. chapter 5:13, see Isaiah 2:4. n) it shall be carried away, chapter 12:2, Ezekiel 18:7, Psalm 76:12. o) as a gift. 1 Samuel 10:27. p) Vulgate: "to the avenging king." Jonah: "to the king who will come to punish them." See note on chapter 5:13. Thus the idols, which the Prophets could not overthrow with their sermons, were overthrown by other idolaters and carried elsewhere. See 2 Kings 18:34, 19:13; Isaiah 10:10, 21:9, 46:1, 2. q) then ignominious shame (r) shall take Ephraim. Compare Jeremiah 48:13. r) chapter 4:19, Isaiah 1:29. s) from his own counsel: which we, with Schmidius, take to mean not only the erection of the calves in 1 Kings 12:28, but their continual worship against the divine counsel so often revealed to them through the Prophets. See Deuteronomy 32:28, Isaiah 29:15, 30:1, Jeremiah 7:24, Micah 6:16, and Psalm 107:11, Proverbs 1:25, 30. **v. 7.** t) It shall be cut off, or it must be destroyed. Verse 15, Isaiah 6:5. u) Samaria. The name of the city with a masculine ending, as in 2 Kings 15:16, Isaiah 23:1. x) and her King in whom they placed their hope and trust, verse 3. A grammatical omission of conjunctions <note>original: Asyndeton</note>, as in Habakkuk 3:11. y) like foam or a bubble or boiling: elsewhere the word signifies the heat of anger, as in Isaiah 54:8. **v. 8.** z) And thus they shall be deleted, destroyed. Genesis 34:30, 1 Kings 15:27, Proverbs 14:11. See note on verse 6. a) all those High Places. 1 Kings 12:31, Amos 7:9. b) of idolatrous impiety. See verse 1, 2, chapter 8:11, Amos 3:14. g) and such great affliction will overwhelm them that in despair they will say even to the mountains, h) "Cover us." Numbers 16:33. That is, they will prefer death, even a miserable one, over life: so that, buried by mountains and hills and miserably crushed, they are not forced to see future evils, or see present ones any longer. S. For similar sentiments see Isaiah 2:10, 19; Luke 23:30; Revelation 6:15, 16. i) They will seek death indeed, but it will flee from them. Revelation 9:6, Jeremiah 8:3. **v. 9.** k) From the days of Gibeah. When the Benjamites in Gibeah plotted 그 that unspeakable crime against the Levite, and perpetrated it upon his concubine, and killed her so cruelly. See chapter 9:9, Judges 19:25 and following. l) and you in general have sinned, O Israel, you who have come into the fellowship of that sin; namely, as we shall soon hear from the opinion of Schmidius, that Israel did not seriously punish such an atrocious crime; others say that at the same time (Judges 19:17) they publicly and with impunity permitted the idolatry invented by Micah (Judges 17:3 ff) and established by the Danites in their city. See notes on Judges 18:30, 31 and chapter 20:1, 25, 29. m) for there they wept and hesitated; a contention having arisen among them concerning leadership. See note on Judges 20:18. The speech transitions from the 2nd person to the 3rd due to emotion, as in Judges 20:38; and the prophet, turning to the reader, explains what that sin of Israel was. n) war did not pursue or overtake them in Gibeah, nor did they experience vengeance before the punishment. (See the phrase in Deuteronomy 19:6, 28:15, etc.) until the Levite finally inflamed their minds in a horrible way, Judges 19:29. Nor did they take action against the idolaters. See note on Judges 19:22. o) war; which was finished with immense cruelty. Judges 20:48.

# CHAPTER 10. HOSEA

<margin>
(p) *on account of the sons of iniquity, that is, those nefarious rapists, the citizens of Gibeah. Compare 2 Samuel 3:34 and Judges 19:22, 20:13.* S. <note>Sebastian Schmidius</note> says it notes that the Israelites did not take the crime of the Gibeonites as seriously as they ought to have, or even vindicate it by war, but descended to it very reluctantly: not because they wished to spare blood, but because they themselves were impious and did not hate the deed to be punished from their hearts, and all but defended it along with the Benjaminites. They were therefore gathered together more in the spirit of such a crime than to voluntarily punish it; and what they did, they did as if forced. — Such sluggishness in punishing crimes, and the impunity of wicked men and idolaters, dominated in Israel from the days of Gibeah almost until King David. Compare Judges 17:6, 18:1, 19:1, 21:25.

(v. 10. q) *According to my desire, therefore, I will do, etc.* Deuteronomy 12:15, 20, 21; 18:6. 1 Samuel 23:10. Jeremiah 2:24. r) *that I might chastise them, so that they might return to fruitfulness, compare chapter 7:15, Jeremiah 31:18. s)* **when they are gathered** Isaiah 24:22. t) S. says *to them*; as in verse 12:11, Amos 3:9, etc. *and therefore they are gathered against them*; as in Micah 4:11, Psalm 55:15. Thus Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note>: *and I have gathered against them peoples who shall exercise dominion over them, just as when a pair of oxen is bound to their two furrows.* u) **peoples**, that is, according to S., neighbors: partly those made proselytes, or friends and confederates; partly subjects or tributaries, especially in the time of David and Solomon. x) **to bind** *them*, just like plowing oxen. 1 Samuel 6:7, 10. Jeremiah 46:4 and following. Genesis 49:11. y) S. says *to their two furrows.* (1) Thus Jonathan, Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish commentator</note>, etc. Compare Psalm 129:3. Others, less conveniently in this place, say *to their habitations*, as in Exodus 21:10. **To bind, however**
</margin>

10 In my desire I will chastise them; and the peoples shall be gathered against them, when they are bound to their two furrows.

11 Ephraim is a trained heifer that loves to thresh; but I passed over her fair neck; I will make Ephraim ride; Judah shall plow, and Jacob shall break the clods for himself.

12 Sow for yourselves for righteousness, reap according to mercy; break up your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the LORD, until He comes and rains righteousness upon you.

13 You have plowed wickedness, you have reaped iniquity; you have eaten the fruit of lies, because you trusted in your own way, in the multitude of your mighty men.

14 Therefore shall a tumult arise among your people, and all your fortresses shall be spoiled, as Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel...
**as Shalman**

---

**...we understand the union of all Israel into one kingdom under David and Solomon, says S.** (v. 11. pi) But Israel, or the ten tribes (chapter 4:17, Isaiah 7:5), especially Ephraim, was always an arrogant, contentious, and stubborn people. Compare Judges 8:1, 12:1, Psalm 78:9. a) *was like a heifer that was taught.* Isaiah 29:13, Jeremiah 31:18. Not taught to plow, but only to thresh, as follows: which work was far easier and more fruitful than plowing. For from this, being fat and becoming petulant, it not only declined labor and obedience but even kicked back (Deuteronomy 32:15) and defected from the house of David; indeed, it wished to dominate Judah itself. Compare 2 Chronicles 13:8, where God passed over its fierce neck so that, with 500,000 killed, they were more modest for a time. Later under Amaziah, although provoked, Joash, King of Israel, afflicted Judah significantly (2 Kings 14:12 following). And very recently in the time of our Prophet Hosea, Pekah the King of Israel, joined in a league with Rezin the King of Syria, had not only devastated Judea (2 Chronicles 28:6 following) but had also worked out impious plans with the same Rezin regarding the cutting off of the family of David and transferring the kingdom of Judah to another. Isaiah 7:1 following. Jonathan: *The assembly of Israel is like a heifer that they teach to plow, but it does not learn, but desires to walk according to the pleasure of its own soul.* b) *loving.* Compare Amos 4:1. A participle with a paragogic Yod, as in Jeremiah 51:13. c) *to thresh.* Oxen among the Israelites grew fattest especially when it was the time of threshing: because the law forbade muzzling the mouth of a threshing ox. Deuteronomy 25:4, Jeremiah 50:11, and see 1 Samuel 28:24; and regarding the various ways of threshing, Isaiah 28:27. Therefore Hosea, to teach that the Israelites declined labor and indulged their own inclinations, compares them with a heifer that is accustomed only to threshing. d) *therefore, as I did of old, I will pass over; that I might bind it and subdue it.* Compare the word in Exodus 12:12, Isaiah 8:8, Micah 5:7, Isaiah 51:23. e) Compare Deuteronomy 28:47. Since the neck of plowing oxen is worn down and ulcerated under the yoke, God praises the beauty of the neck in this heifer: because threshing oxen grew wonderfully fat, as we said. f) *for will I make Ephraim ride, and shall Judah plow? shall Jacob break the clods for him?* so that Ephraim may live sumptuously and splendidly (compare chapter 14:4, Deuteronomy 32:15, Isaiah 58:14) and Judah serve him? By no means will I do so, nor should you expect such a thing. We read these words as an interrogation with Schmidius; as in 1 Samuel 21:16, Isaiah 49:13; and this is an interrogation of one who is indignant and vehemently denying, as in Isaiah 58:5. g) *he shall plow:* verse 13. Just like oxen. Job 1:14. h) *shall he break the clods or break the furrows for Ephraim?* (3) Isaiah 28:24, Job 39:10. i) Jacob the patriarch, in his descendants. We understand this of Judah, who was born of Jacob no less than Ephraim, etc., says S. Compare Isaiah 42:24, 43:1, 22, 28. v. 12. k) *Sow rather, you Ephraimites, all and each of you.* On the occasion of the previous simile (*shall Judah plow? shall Jacob break clods?* verse 11), metaphorical expressions regarding performing repentance and doing good works are taken from the same rustic subject. Compare the word in chapter 8:7, Jeremiah 4, 3, Proverbs 11:18, 22:8. Jonathan: *House of Israel, do good works for yourselves, walk in the way of truth, establish for yourselves the doctrine of the law, etc.* l) **for yourselves.** This is not entirely redundant, but partly states the duty and partly the subsequent benefit; as if to say, *sow for yourselves*, that is, as it becomes you and will also be useful to yourselves. *For whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.* <note>original: "ὁ γὰר ἐὰν σπείרῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει" — Galatians 6:7</note> m) *according to righteousness.* Isaiah 32:1, Joel 2:23. The "Lamed" <note>the Hebrew letter 'L' used as a prefix</note> seems to us to be of the norm or rule: so that *to sow according to righteousness* is to do the seed of righteousness according to the doctrine and norm of righteousness contained in the Holy Scripture; so also *to reap according to mercy*, or rather piety, is to be understood regarding the norm and rule prescribed for piety in the Holy Scripture. S. n) Compare chapter 8:7. o) Exodus 15:21, Numbers 6:21. p) chapter 6:6. q) *renew for yourselves.* (2) Jeremiah 4:3. r) *fallow ground* (3) Proverbs 13:22. But the Syriac: *light a lamp for yourselves.* The Septuagint and Arabic: *Enlighten for yourselves the light of knowledge.* from another meaning, as in 1 Kings 11:36, 15:4. But the former is required by the context. s) *for it is time.* Genesis 29:7. t) through true repentance and faith. Isaiah 55:6. u) *and that until he himself comes* chapter 6:3. x) S. says *and teaches.* Others: instill or rain down, chapter 6:3, Isaiah 28:9, Joel 2:23, Psalm 25:8. y) Syriac: *his righteousness.* Compare Isaiah 45:8, Psalm 85:12, Daniel 9:24. v. 13. z) For you have plowed until now; or as S. connects it: But you, as often as I have exhorted you to repentance and piety, you have plowed impiety, and as many times as if starting anew, you have begun to be impious and worse than before. He proceeds in the trope taken from agriculture. Compare Job 4:8. a) Psalm 5:5. Namely, idolatry, fornication, rapacity, and other things about which the Prophets complained, joined with impenitence, and constantly continued. b) *and the greatest iniquity.* verse 9, Ezekiel 28:15, Psalm 25:3. That is, mature sins and crimes as it were. c) Compare verse 12, Job 4:8, Proverbs 22:8. d) S. says *of guilt;* as in chapter 4:8. Others *of punishment*, as in Proverbs 1:31, Isaiah 3:10. e) *fruit of lies* chapter 12:1. That is, according to Gussetius page 374 and others, *worthy of a lie;* or *deceptive*, and far different than you had hoped. Compare chapter 9:2, Psalm 7:15. But S., as we said, of guilt, so that the narrative of sins is continued; in which way it will be the fruit of a lie, not one which lies to men, but which lies to God; namely, not of truth and righteousness, but of the most foul hypocrisy: while they not only sowed and reaped malice and impiety, but also ate the fruit of a lie, always being the worst and even becoming worse daily. f) Compare Isaiah 42:17, Jeremiah 7:8, 13:25. g) Compare Isaiah 57:10, Jeremiah 2:23, 33. 1 Kings 15:26, 34. 2 Kings 16:3. With S., we refer this to religion, and the following clause to the state: because while it was still flourishing, the hypocrites imagined God was favorable to them, and that the worship of the calves and the rest of their idolatry was the true worship of Jehovah, whatever the true Prophets might teach to the contrary. Compare note on chapter 7:1 and Preface § 4. h) Compare chapter 1:5, 7. v. 14. i) *And therefore it shall arise.* Isaiah 31:2. It shall stand and endure. Numbers 30:5, 8. 1 Samuel 24:21. Jeremiah 51:29. k Jeremiah 25:31, Amos 2:2. l) *among your peoples* or *tribes.* Compare Leviticus 21:1, 4, 14, etc. m) *the whole.* Compare Isaiah 9:16. n) Jeremiah 5:7, Amos 5:9, Micah 5:10. o) *shall be devastated* chapter 7:13.

v. 11. **and Ephraim** <note>original: "ואפרים"</note> according to Rashi 6, 9, 20. thus future 5. v. 12. **and they reaped** <note>original: "וקצרו"</note> with the prefix Vau 6, 9. thus future 5. **he will teach** <note>original: "יורה"</note> accented on the penultimate syllable 1, 2, 3. both 5. v. 13. **you have plowed** <note>original: "חֲרַשְׁתֶּם"</note> through Merora accented on the last syllable 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 23. v. 14. **it shall be spoiled** <note>original: "יוּשַׁד"</note> through Patach 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, 21, 22. against the printed Masoretic text. <summary>This page provides a detailed philological and theological commentary on Hosea 10:10-14, using agricultural metaphors of plowing and threshing to describe Ephraim's shift from prosperity to rebellion and impending judgment. The text emphasizes the difference between the "easy" labor of threshing, which Israel enjoyed, and the "hard" labor of righteousness God now demands.</summary>

**CHAPTER XI.** v. 1. d) When. Ephesians 43:2. e) A boy, and as if he were still in his first and tender age: Israel. Indeed, just as humans do, so
</margin>

also do republics have their "ages," as *Drusius* says. See chapter 2:5, 17; Jeremiah 2:2; Ezekiel 16:4; and above, chapter 7:9. f) **And I loved him** Galatians 4:1, 3. The Israelite people are compared to a man in terms of their origin, progress, and duration; one who is a boy in his first age, and later grows up, etc. Thus Israel, in its first age in Egypt, grew from a few patriarchs into a people, yet they did not yet form a republic until they were finally led into the land of Canaan by God. g) f) By a free and clearly singular love I already loved him then, so that I preferred him above all peoples and brought him out of his servitude. See chapter 9:10, Deuteronomy 4:37, chapter 7:13, Ephesians 43:4, chapter 63:9, Jeremiah 31:3, Malachi 1:2, etc. With this new chapter, *Schmidius* begins a new prophecy or sermon, the eighth one. Its time is easily gathered from verses 5 and 6. See notes on chapter 7:1 and the Preface section 12. As in the preceding sections, so in this chapter God reproaches the ungrateful people for the greatest benefits bestowed upon them, and predicts the most just punishments for that reason in verse 4 and following. Finally, however, He also opens the treasures of His mercy to them, and promises the moderation of His most just anger, their conversion, and other goods under the New Testament through CHRIST in verse 8 and following. g) Also out of Egypt, where he would be forced to flee, Matthew 2:13. h) I called in my decree, or I will call back. See note on chapter 10:5. However, since Matthew has the past tense, he either retained the letter of the Prophet or accommodated the word to the time in which he himself wrote and the matter was fulfilled. S. i) **My son.** Some refer this to Israel as a "type" <note>a symbolic foreshadowing</note>, comparing Exodus 16:2, 22-23. Others refer it to both Israel and JESUS. For Jesus (these are the words of *Gartner* in *Prophetic Theology* page 380) came into Egypt in the loins of Perez, son of Judah, and returned from there in the loins of Nahshon. Matthew 1:3-4, Genesis 46:12, Numbers 1:7. But we subscribe to those who, with S., take this saying literally regarding Christ, according to Matthew 2:15. This is also required by the simplicity of Scripture, by which the *Son* is here distinguished from Israel. See Matthew 15:24, Romans 15:8. **v. 2. k)** *They called*, or (because of the following particle "so") *just as they called them*, namely to my worship and obedience, and to faith in the Savior promised to them (verse 1)—namely, Moses and the Prophets sent and raised up by me at every time. See Jeremiah 2:5, chapter 7:24, 11:8, Ezekiel 5:7, 20:13; and see, for example, Exodus 16:2, 28; 17:2-7; Deuteronomy 31:27, 29; Psalm 95:8-10; Hebrews 3:9-10. See 2 Kings 17:7-17. o) They sacrificed. Chapter 4:13-14, 12:12, Psalm 106:38. p) See Judges 17:3-4, 18:14, 30; Jeremiah 8:19, Psalm 78:58. q) Chapter 4:13. S. says: "We think our Prophet's discourse is about the times of the Judges, hence it is not surprising that he did not mention the calves of Jeroboam, which did not yet exist." **v. 3. r)** *I, however, nonetheless*, out of my clemency and mercy, did not cast them away, but still followed them with fatherly love (verse 1). s) He adapted my feet or my steps; r) S.: "I accustomed my going." But for others, the word is in the past tense, as in Ezekiel 17:5; the sense varies. Some say parenthetically: "rather, God took them up upon His arms." So says *Piscator*. Others, with Tremellius: "Ephraim took up those idols (verse 2) upon his arms, while God directed his feet." S. says better: "as if someone had taken them up upon his arms." It seems, he says, to be a comparative speech in which God compares Himself to a man who fatherly leads a boy who walks so poorly that he even takes him up upon his arms. x) See Deuteronomy 1:31, 32:11, and compare Isaiah 63:8-9. y) But they refused to acknowledge (Chapter 2:10, Isaiah 1:3, Jeremiah 4:22). x) That I healed them, that is, restored them to wholeness, both in the church and in the republic. Thus S. begins the divine threat here, and derives the word from the root *KWL* or *YKOL*, just as *ABIA* comes from *BOA*. Jeremiah 4:19 from the root *CHOL*. <header>CHAPTER XI. HOSEA 11</header>

<margin>
The Syriac clarity.

Now therefore

**Haftarah**
<note>Prophetic reading in the synagogue</note>
**Vayeitzei Yaakov**
<note>Hebrew: "And Jacob went out"—the name of the weekly Torah portion</note>

The Prophet prophesies what shall be after this destruction in captivity, until it is finished. Namely: (1) the people will persist in their turning away from God;
</margin>

<margin>
v. 5. k) No longer, as was recently done, shall Ephraim (the people of Israel, v. 3) return to the land of Egypt to seek help. l) see chapter 8:13 and 12:13. m) for Asshur (the Assyrian), to whom they had been tributaries since the time of Menahem (2 Kings 15:19), but recently, relying on Egyptian help, they had defected from him (2 Kings 17:4). n) he shall be his King: that is, he alone; so that they may not have their own King, nor an Egyptian ally. 5. For they were to be shut up by the Assyrian in a very tight siege in Samaria (so that they could not send to Egypt) and, destitute of all help and conquered, they were finally to be led away as captives into Assyrian lands (2 Kings 17:6 and above at chapter 5:13). o) because, as is clear from what was said in verse 4, they maliciously refused <note>original: "reuertuntur" (they return)</note> (Isaiah 1:20, Jeremiah 3:3). p) to return to me (chapter 5:4, Jeremiah 5:3, chapter 8:5).
</margin>

## 5 <gloss>k</gloss>He shall not <gloss>l</gloss>return to the land of <gloss>k</gloss>Egypt, <gloss>m</gloss>but the Assyrian <gloss>n</gloss>shall be his king, because <gloss>o</gloss>they refused <gloss>p</gloss>to return.
## 6 And the sword shall fall on his cities, and shall consume his branches, and devour them <gloss>q</gloss>because of their own counsels.
## 7 <gloss>a</gloss>And my people are bent <gloss>b</gloss>on backsliding from me: <gloss>c</gloss>though <gloss>d</gloss>they call them to the Most High, <gloss>e</gloss>none at all <gloss>f</gloss>would exalt him.
## 8 <gloss>g</gloss>How shall I give thee up, Ephraim? <gloss>h</gloss>how shall I deliver thee, Israel? how shall I make thee <gloss>i</gloss>as Admah? <gloss>k</gloss>how shall I set thee <gloss>l</gloss>as Zeboim? <gloss>m</gloss>mine heart is turned within me, <gloss>n</gloss>my repentings are kindled together.
## 9 <gloss>o</gloss>I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger, <gloss>p</gloss>I will not return to destroy Ephraim: <gloss>q</gloss>for I am God, <gloss>r</gloss>and not man; <gloss>s</gloss>the Holy One in the midst of thee.

---

whereupon (2) God could justly destroy them entirely like Admah and Zeboim (v. 8), which nevertheless (3) out of the stirring of His mercy He is not going to do, but will finally convert them through the Messiah (v. 8 seq.). a) S. <note>Schmidius</note> they are suspended, hanging and fixed they cling (Joshua 10:26, etc.); others: they are hanging, and verge toward ruin (Deuteronomy 28:66). b) S. to their turning away from me (compare chapter 9:10), so that the suffix is passive, as in Isaiah 53:11, chapter 56:7, Psalm 5:8, etc.; because of my turning away, by which I turned myself away from them (compare above chapter 5:6, 15; 9:12). In a negative sense this noun is always used, and signifies a turning away or perversion (cf. 14:7, Jeremiah 2:19, 3:22, 5:6, 8:5, 14:7, Proverbs 1:32). c) to the Most High, or to the things above and heavenly (chapter 7:16), like <term>מעל</term> <note>me'al</note> "from above" concerning heaven in Genesis 27:39. d) they do indeed call Him back (see v. 2). e) together, yet as one, or the whole people in general (Isaiah 22:3, Psalm 34:3). f) nothing exalts itself, or its God; so that, namely, it might prefer Him to human helps or its own counsels (v. 5, 6) and follow with due praises (Exodus 15:2, Psalm 66:17, Psalm 145:1).

g) How therefore? The interrogative particle <term>אֵיךְ</term> <note>eikh - "How"</note> is used not only for wondering and denying (as in Genesis 39:9, 44:34), likewise for deploring (Proverbs 5:12) and expostulating (Genesis 26:9, Judges 16:15, 2 Samuel 1:14), but also has the force of exaggerating and intensifying (see Jeremiah 9:18, Psalm 73:19). It therefore exaggerates in this place the numbness and stubbornness of Israel, and intensifies his most just punishments even to the highest degree, and this through the figure which rhetoricians call "communication"; as if to say: How then shall I treat you, O Ephraim? (for I appeal to your conscience and wish you yourself to be the judge: cf. Isaiah 5:3) shall I hand you over to the extreme punishment, O Israel? How, I say, shall I make you like Admah? shall I set you like Zeboim? which were burned from heaven with Sodom and Gomorrah in a horrible punishment, and perished utterly. Certainly such a punishment is not only deserved, but even seems to be demanded of me by that extreme obstinacy of yours, and my justice also required it. Yet my heart is turned within me, and at the same time all my bowels seethe, etc. Thus this verse says two things: (1) in the *Atnach* <note>a major musical/punctuation mark in the Hebrew text</note> phrase: What Israel has deserved by his stubbornness, namely extreme punishment and total destruction; (2) in the *Silluk* <note>the final punctuation mark</note> phrase, the most intense love and mercy of God in Christ, which alone prevents that which would otherwise be done according to the rigor of justice. h) "To give" to the Hebrews often means to place someone in a good or bad state, says S. (cf. Ezekiel 5:14, 26:21, and 35:9). i) cf. chapter 6:4. k) "just as Admah" in the Greek Septuagint; said to be from <term>מגן</term> <note>magen</note> "shield" from the root *ganan*; but more correctly S. and others: "shall I deliver thee?" Symmachus: "shall I give thee up?" Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note>: "I will exterminate thee." The *Mem* is radical (3) (Genesis 14:20, Proverbs 4:9). l) cf. Genesis 19:19, chapter 14:2. m) chapter 2:5, Jeremiah 6:8, Ezekiel 21:32. n) see Genesis 19:24 seq, Deuteronomy 29:22, Jeremiah 49:18. o) He describes a most vehement movement of mercy, by which the heart is completely turned within itself (see Lamentations 1:20 and cf. Jeremiah 31:20). p) it is not "against me," but "within me" or "upon me," namely when I think about cutting you off entirely. S. cf. Psalm 42:5, 6, 7. q) see v. 7. r) they seethe or are moved (4) (Genesis 43:30, 1 Kings 3:26, Lamentations 5:10; cf. Luke 6:36, 15:20, Romans 2:4). s) S. and others: "repentings," others: "my consolations" (3); see Isaiah 57:18, Zechariah 1:13. Guffetius <note>a Hebrew grammarian</note> page 506: "my consoling power is moved." v. 9. t) I will not therefore do it. The effect of that movement of divine mercy, about which v. 8 speaks, is added here (cf. Genesis 18:29, 30; also Amos 7:3, 6). u) the fury of my anger (Jeremiah 30:24, 49:37). x) I will not turn back, namely from showing mercy and my promises (cf. above chapter 2:11, 21); or, I will not turn away from the Israelites (compare Jeremiah 32:40). Jonathan: "my word shall not return." Others: "and I will not again destroy," comparing Genesis 26:18, 1 Kings 13:33, 2 Kings 4:35. y) for destroying; so that I may utterly blot out and extinguish, as formerly in the flood (Genesis 6:17, chapter 9:11, 15; compare Isaiah 54:9). z) because I am God, infinitely merciful, and not desiring the death of a sinner (Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11), and not knowing how to fail in promises given (e.g., Genesis 17:7, Leviticus 26:44, etc.). a) and not a man or a human, whose mercy is not so great, being finite; nor is his faith in promises certain (cf. Numbers 23:19, Malachi 3:6, Job 10:5, James 1:17). Jonathan: "because I am God. My word remains forever, nor are my works such as the works of the flesh (i.e., of men) which dwell on the earth." b) in the midst of thee (Isaiah 12:6). It denotes the place and the object in which and toward which He may exercise His holiness, and make it manifest and prove it, etc. S.

<column-break/>

Leviticus 26:25, 33, Isaiah 1:20). s) cf. chapter 8:14. t) and it shall finish (Jeremiah 14:12, Lamentations 2:22). u) bars (Exodus 25:13, 14); S. however and others with Jonathan understand "the strong ones" or "the nobles" or "his leaders" (see note on Isaiah 16:6). x) and it shall consume them (2 Samuel 12:8, Jeremiah 2:30, 46:10, 14). But the sword "eats" the city when it consumes its citizens. S. y) because of their counsels; both those against divine counsels and those against the Assyrians, conducted with the Egyptians (cf. # HOSEA. CHAPTERS 11 & 12

<margin>
**e)** *The Holy One of Israel.* 2 Kings 19:22; Isaiah 1:4. Holy in infinite mercy and divine truth. **d)** *and I will not enter the city.* So the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, the Vulgate <note>The Latin Bible</note>, the Syriac, Arabic, etc. See, regarding the construction, Deuteronomy 23:2 and following; 1 Samuel 23:7; Jeremiah 9:20, etc. But how this is to be understood is much debated by interpreters. Saint Jerome explains it thus: *I am not one of those who dwell in cities, who live by human laws, and think that cruelty is justice; so that it is the same as what was said before: "I am not a man."* The ancient Rabbis in Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish scholar</note>: *“And I will not grant you a way into the heavenly Jerusalem (cf. Hebrews 12:22; Galatians 4:26) having left you again, until I have restored the earthly Jerusalem,”* comparing Psalm 122:3, which we leave to its authors. Others say: *“And into no other city, besides Jerusalem, will I come.”* The Targum <note>The Aramaic translation of the Bible; original: "Ion." refers to Targum Jonathan</note>: *“nor will I stay any longer in Jerusalem as if it were another city.”* But there is nothing specifically about Jerusalem in this context. Others, according to Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>: *“and I will not come as an enemy”* (comparing the construction in Isaiah 40:10) *“or with an enemy,”* comparing 1 Samuel 28:16; however, there the noun is different because it has a very different form. Therefore, [Sebastian] Schmid prefers Jerome’s opinion, while at the same time making an opposition between the "midst of Israel" and "the city" in this manner: God is most holy in the midst of Israel, wherever it may be, even in the furthest exile; nor am I confined in one city like Jerusalem (or another) and the land joined to it (as the tutelary gods of the nations were bound to almost single locations, 2 Kings 19:12-13). For I am infinite, and hindered from saving in no place on earth. See 1 Kings 8:27; 2 Chronicles 6:18; and John 4:21; and regarding the construction, 2 Kings 24:10; Chapter 25:2, etc. To us, in this context, it seems simplest to take it as follows: that for now

**CHAPTER XII.**
5, 4, 9; Ch. 7:10; Ch. 8:3, 14; Ch. 9:7, 15, 17; Ch. 10:14, 15) is to be

abandoned, and it is said he must be permitted to the *Assyrian* enemies by God, yet the promise made to the Fathers concerning CHRIST remains safe. It is as if he said: even if I do not now enter the city of Samaria and the others, which are foully polluted with idolatry and other crimes and are no longer correctable but to be cut off by the sword. See v. 5, 6; Ch. 6:8; Ch. 7:1; Ch. 9:12, 15; Ch. 10:7, 8; Ch. 14:1. In this way, as Blessed Luther observes, the abolition of the Mosaic government and rituals is entirely included. Cf. Ch. 1:4; Ch. 3:4, etc.

**v. 10. e)** *For after the LORD* the Messiah, Isaiah 52:12. **f)** *at last they shall go*, and shall follow his leadership. Cf. Ch. 5:11; 1 Kings 14:8; and above Ch. 3:5; Jeremiah 3:17; Micah 4:2. This is the second part of the promise, which began in verse 9; and it is not merely a simple prediction, but also a promise that God will grant that they act so. **g)** who like a lion, having seized the prey, Amos 3:4. **h)** by the powerful and divine voice of the Gospel (Romans 1:16, 1 Thessalonians 2:13, Hebrews 4:12), *he shall roar*, and thus he will call not only them, but also all nations to the fellowship of eternal life and true happiness, just as a lion calls animals of its own kind, and especially its cubs, to the prey. Cf. Acts 2:39. The Targum: *His Word shall be like a roaring lion;* namely, the Word, which was in the beginning with God, John 1:1. **i)** *because* is explanatory: for he himself, the *Son of God* (Hebrews 1:2), *made flesh* (John 1:14), and the *Lion of the tribe of Judah* (Revelation 5:5). **k)** *he shall roar* with the voice of the Gospel, cf. Amos 1:2; Joel 4:16; Revelation 10:3, throughout the whole world. Romans 10:18. For to this he was sent and anointed by the Father, Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18. **l)** *and they shall run toward him with fear and reverence.* v. 11; 1 Samuel 16:4; Chapter 21:2; 2 Kings 4:13. It denotes a meeting or approach with the honor of the obedience of faith, says S. <note>Sebastian Schmidius</note>. Cf. above Ch. 3:5; Acts 2:37; Ch. 16:30; Philippians 2:12. **m)** *their sons and descendants;* not only (as the Targum adds) the exiled Israelites (Deuteronomy 14:1), but those whom the LORD by his grace will make such even from the nations. Cf. above Ch. 2:1; Romans 9:26; Isaiah 2:18; Psalm 45:17; John 1:12; Hebrews 2:10, 13; 1 Corinthians 4:15. **n)** *from the sea*, that is, from the West. Genesis 12:8. Cf. Isaiah 49:12; Matthew 8:11. The style is adapted to the layout of the land of Canaan: and mention is made of the quarters of the world because the Israelites were dispersed into all quarters of the world before Christ’s coming, and because the Gospel has gone out into all quarters of the world. S.

* **v. 11. o)** *They shall tremble*, i.e., they shall run trembling and with the greatest haste. v. 10. Not, however, a bodily movement from those lands, but a spiritual one to Christ is to be understood. S. **p)** *like a bird.* The Targum adds: which *comes openly (through the air).* Cf. Ch. 9:11. **q)** also from *Egypt* and from the South. Cf. note v. 10; and Isaiah 19:19 and following; Ch. 27:13. **r)** and *like a dove*, whose flight is very swift, see Psalm 55:7; and note Isaiah 60:8) gathered from the *North* and from everywhere. Cf. Zechariah 10:10; John 11:52; Ephesians 1:10. The Hebrews <note>The Jewish commentators</note> wrongly understand from these words the return of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity. For from v. 8 and 9 it is clear that it concerns the *Ephraimites*, whom Shalmaneser had led away. It does not appear that they, once led away, ever returned to Canaan. Therefore, since this prophecy was not fulfilled according to the letter, it must be understood mystically of the spiritual restoration and the calling of the nations, which took place through the preaching of the Gospel. Hence, that same roaring is signified of which Joel 4:16 speaks. Nor is the preaching of the Gospel unsuitably called a "roaring," since it is so clear and sonorous that it was heard throughout the whole world; nor did it strike only the ears, but also the minds of the listeners by its power, and made them anxious about obtaining their salvation with fear and trembling. Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, vol. i, p. 769. Cf. note Ezekiel 37:13. **t)** *here* in the Church, Matthew 16:18; 1 Timothy 3:15; Ephesians 2:19; and finally in heaven, John 14:2. According to S., this signifies the constancy of faith and finally its end, which is eternal life. The Targum adds: *“and my Word shall be for their help.”* Cf. Matthew 28:20. **x)** This is as it were the seal of the promise. Isaiah 1:14. Cf. Numbers 23:19; Psalm 33:4.

**CHAPTER XII. v. 1. y)** *They have surrounded me with lies* (Psalm 17:11). That is, wherever I look, they have practiced lying. So the Targum: *they have multiplied lies before me.* So Gussetius p. 376: *From every side they heap flattering lies upon me.* Comparing Job 31:28. The Son of God speaks, however, as S. and others observe, and he begins here a new and ninth sermon (to be continued in the following chapter and finished in Ch. 14:1), in which there are two parts, according to S.: **I.** against Judah. **II.** against Ephraim, v. 12 and following; indeed in such a way that in the first part, by an opposition made between the Jews and the Israelites, (1) he praises Judah for past constancy in faith and piety (v. 1-2), but (2) rebukes the same for present corruption (v. 3), and (3) by two reasons (the first from the most just retribution of God according to the good or bad works of each, v. 3, which is proven by the example of the Patriarch Jacob, v. 4-5; the other sought from the unity and immutability of God, v. 6) he calls them back to repentance (v. 7); (4) by the opposite example of the wicked and stubborn Ephraim (v. 8-9), who for that reason must now be forsaken, he teaches that he will be the God of Judah, especially under the New Testament (v. 10-11). From there at last he passes to the second part of this sermon, against Ephraim, v. 12 and following. Others, and most interpreters, refer the whole chapter to Ephraim in divided sections, who, compared with Judah, is worse (v. 1-2) and is even the author of corruption for him (v. 3), and so is completely degenerate from the piety of the patriarch Jacob (v. 4-5), whereas on the contrary, God on His part is always the same (v. 6), to whom therefore Ephraim is exhorted to return through repentance (v. 7); yet in vain because of his stubbornness in committing and defending crimes (v. 8-9). Wherefore GOD, always consistent with Himself (in the opinion of some interpreters), predicts exile for him; according to others, however, out of pure mercy, He confirms the promise of the restoration of the Israelite church under the New Testament (v. 10), as one who has not only not yet failed in his duty, having spoken through the Prophets in various ways, but will also abundantly give teachers of the Gospel and Prophets under the New Testament (v. 11), etc. Interpreters differ greatly, however, both on the coherence of the parts and on the meaning of the phrases and words, the more important of which we will touch upon briefly. **z)** *with lies*, i.e. according to S., false religion and idolatrous or hypocritical worship (5) Ch. 7:3, 13; Ch. 10:13. Cf. Isaiah 30:9; Ch. 44:20; Ch. 59:13; and John 8:44. Others compare above Ch. 10:4; others translate it as "denial," comparing Proverbs 30:9. **a)** *the Israelite* kingdom of the ten tribes, as in v. 2 and frequently in this book, Ch. 1:3, etc. **b)** *and with deceit.* Cf. Jeremiah 9:5, 7; Psalm 50:19. Cf. Ch. 1:4, 6, 7; Ch. 5:1. **d)** *and Judah*, and with him Benjamin, in opposition to Ephraim or the kingdom of Israel. Cf. Ch. 1:7. **e)** *still rules;* or while Judah was still ruling. So S. and others, comparing Jeremiah 2:31; but Ludovicus de Dieu and Cocceius, comparing the Arabic root, translate "desired"; and *Judah still observes himself with God, persevering with the saints.* Comparing likewise Jeremiah 2:31. The Targum: *But the Jews have been strong in worship;* namely while many among the Jews were still faithful, and the public worship of God flourished in the Temple at Jerusalem and was open to all. Cf. 2 Chronicles 12:12; Ch. 19:3. They almost all take this to be about the time of Hosea, cf. 2 Chronicles 30:1, 6; but it seems better, says S., that it be taken of the past, that Ephraim already then surrounded the Lord with lies when Judah was still ruling with God, that is, when the larger or more powerful part of Judah, which prevailed, still adhered to the true God and saw to it that the true worship of God remained. **f)** Ch. 2:1. The Son of God speaks of the Father, to indicate the mystery of the Holy Trinity, says S. Compare below at verse 5.

# CHAPTER 12. HOSEA 12

<margin>
...now they strike a covenant with the Assyrian. <note>original: "r) vid. c. 5, 13. c. 14, 4. 2 Reg. 15, 19. C. 17, 2."</note>
s) Chapter 10, 4. Concerning the phrase, compare Genesis 15: 9, 10, 18; Jeremiah 34: 18.
r) And soon with a treacherous mind [they carry] oil...
</margin>

<margin>
[Hebrew letters] nempe <note>namely</note>
</margin>

> 2. **Ephraim** <gloss>p</gloss> **feeds on** <gloss>k l</gloss> **the wind and pursues** <gloss>m n</gloss> **the east wind** <gloss>o</gloss> **all day long;** <gloss>s</gloss> **falsehood and destruction he multiplies, and a covenant with Assyria** <gloss>q</gloss> **they strike, and oil** <gloss>s</gloss> **is carried to Egypt.** <gloss>r</gloss>

---

...they carry a gift into Egypt. It is well-established that noble and abundant oil existed in the land of Canaan, as seen in Deuteronomy 8:8 and Ezekiel 27:17 (see the note on 1 Kings 5:25). **u)** Chapter 7:11; 11:5. **x)** They are forsaken <note>original: "desertur"</note>, Chapter 10:6; specifically for the purpose of obtaining help against the Assyrians (see Chapter 11:5 and 2 Kings 17:3). These things happened successively, says Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmid, a 17th-century theologian</note>; for after Jeroboam I, during the time of Ahab and other kings, the Israelites burned more and more with the madness of idolatry and persecuted the pious, as is well known regarding Jezebel. They multiplied foreign gods and idolatrous worship. Finally, they made treaties with the Assyrians and called the Egyptians for aid, until they utterly perished.

**Verse 3.** **y)** But now there is also a "dispute"—that is, the Lord must contend <note>original: "litigandum est Domino"</note> (Chapter 4:2; Micah 6:2). "The judgment is the Lord's" <note>original Greek: "ἡ κρίσις τῷ Κυρίῳ"</note>; compare John 3:19 and 12:31. **z)** With Judah and Benjamin (verse 1), while even these were being seduced by the Ephraimites (Chapter 4:15), especially in the latter times of the Prophet Hosea, they were greatly corrupted by the wicked King Ahaz (2 Kings 16:3, etc.). **a)** And this is so that He may punish Jacob. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation</note> and the Arabic version take this in a negative sense (as in Chapter 1:4; 2:15; 4:14; 8:13; Amos 3:2), as taking vengeance on Jacob; but Schmid takes it generally, as a "visitation" that could be either for good or for bad. **b)** Some take the name "Jacob" here to refer to the Ten Tribes, others to Judah, and others to both—as if to say He will visit all of Jacob (compare Chapter 10:11). But Schmid again takes it generally, to include the Patriarch Jacob with all his posterity; in this way, what follows pertains partly to the Patriarch and partly to his descendants, for whom he stands as an example. **c)** Compare Jeremiah 17:10; 32:19; Ezekiel 18:30; 33:20. **d)** Chapter 4:9. **e)** Verse 15; Genesis 50:15; Deuteronomy 32:43; 1 Samuel 26:23; 2 Samuel 22:21; Proverbs 12:14. It should be noted in this universal rule (which is also frequently repeated in the New Testament, e.g., Matthew 16:27; Romans 2:6; 1 Corinthians 3:13; 2 Corinthians 5:10; 1 Peter 1:17; Revelation 2:23; 20:12, 13; 22:12) that "ways" and "works" are taken generally to include faith, not specifically as being distinguished from faith, says Schmid. This seems opposed to the confidence and security of the Jews, who acted as if God would not punish them simply because they were the seed of Jacob (compare Matthew 3:9, 10).

**Verse 4.** **f)** *In the womb.* Jeremiah 1:5. For the sake of coherence, the explanatory particle "For" can be understood (as the Syriac version explicitly supplies it); as if to say: "For, to show by example how faith and its fruits please God, it proceeded with the Patriarch himself in such a way that already in the womb (just as John in Luke 1:15, 44), being stirred by the Holy Spirit, he held his brother by the heel." **g)** *He held the heel*—namely, Jacob (verse 3). For since the name of Jacob was used broadly there for the patriarch and his posterity, those things which are specific to the Patriarch are now rightly predicated of him without mentioning a new subject. These are added as an example of the previously mentioned rule, proving that the Lord visits Jacob according to his ways and works; for in this way the Lord repaid the Patriarch Jacob according to his faith and the works of faith (Schmid). Furthermore, this word (which in Arabic also means "he pressed the footsteps," "he came from behind at the heel," or "he followed in the tracks") is not very suitably rendered here as "they supplant." For neither this word itself, nor the name "Jacob" derived from it, implies blameable deceit or deception by itself; (though Esau, out of envy, dragged it to that meaning in Genesis 27:36, and the prophet alludes to the name of Jacob in that same sense in Jeremiah 9:3, because one might also attempt to seize another's heel with a deceitful mind to circumvent and supplant them). Rather, it denotes Jacob's praiseworthy zeal and victory here. For it says the same thing we clearly read in Genesis 25:26: "and Jacob's hand held Esau's heel." This certainly did not happen except by the singular virtue and providence of God, even from infancy, as recognized by Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra and Kimchi on this passage (compare also Genesis 25:22). The sense, therefore, according to Gussetius (p. 632), is that Jacob followed later in the order of birth, but by piety and the favor of God obtained through it, he anticipated his brother and secured the most noble dignity for himself, from which his grandson Ephraim now degenerates—the fall being all the more shameful because it is from such a high honor. The Targum puts it this way: "Prophet, tell them: Was it not predicted of Jacob before he was born that he would be greater than his brother?" (from Genesis 25:23). **h)** Namely, Esau; and here from his faith and the grace of God (Romans 9:11, 12) he also prepared the right of the firstborn for himself (Genesis 25:31 ff.). For without a doubt, the other story that follows praises the Patriarch’s faith (Schmid). **i)** The Targum, Syriac, Schmid, and others: *by his strength*; namely, not so much of the body (comparing 2 Kings 19:35) as of faith in the promises made to him (Genesis 28:13, 14, 15; 31:3; 32:13), through which, weeping and praying, he conquered. Gussetius (p. 21) explains this as a "vehement affection or desire" (compare verse 9; Genesis 35:12; 49:3; Deuteronomy 21:17; Psalm 105:36). **k)** He was superior in the struggle with God; or, he overcame God (Genesis 32:29). "Who was strengthened against God" <note>original Greek: "ὃς ἐνίσχυσε πρὸς τὸν Θεόν"</note>. The Targum and Syriac: "he bore himself as a great man or a prince"; others: "he wrestled powerfully with God" (specifically Genesis 32:25). **l)** See Genesis 32:29, 31. The Targum says "with an Angel," as in verse 5; namely, with the Son of God (see Genesis 16:9, 10, 13; 22:11, 12, 15, 16; 48:16; Malachi 3:1, etc.) who frequently appeared in the form of a man (Genesis 32:25; Joshua 5:13; Judges 13:3, 6). The sense, according to Schmid, is that he was not only filled with the Holy Spirit and faith in his mother's womb to conquer his brother, but even after many years, remaining constant in faith, he fought powerfully and most strongly in the strength of his faith—that is, he wrestled with God and conducted himself like a heroic spirit.

**Verse 5.** **m)** I say, he was superior. (Compare verse 4). **n)** This is a future tense in the Hebrew *Kal* stem from a related root. See Isaiah 32:1 and Proverbs 8:16; and the *Hiphil* stem above in Chapter 8:4. The connection here, using a common literary device, repeats what came before so that something new and fuller may be added to continue the story, says Schmid (compare 2 Samuel 3:7). **n)** Towards or against the Angel—that is, the Messenger or Ambassador of God the Father, through whom He performs all His works, yet who is also the supreme God. See the comments on verse 4 and, if you like, our dissertation on the Angel of God. **o)** And he prevailed (see Genesis 32:29; compare 30:8). Not by physical power or strength, but by tears, prayers, and faith in the divine promises (Genesis 28:13, 14, 15; 31:12, 13; 32:10), a force which is pleasing to God (compare Matthew 15:28; James 5:16; and Sirach 35:17). **p)** For *he* wept—not the Angel of God, as the Rabbis foolishly suggest (Mercer defending them in vain); rather, Jacob conquered him by weeping and praying (compare 1 Samuel 1:10). Indeed, the mode and medium by which Jacob prevailed is signified; this can be easily gathered and concluded from the words of the history in Genesis, and Hosea had this from divine inspiration (Schmid). **q)** And he supplicated him (Deuteronomy 3:23; 1 Kings 8:33, 47-59; Psalm 30:9; Esther 4:8; 8:3; see Genesis 32:27). **r)** *In Bethel.* See Genesis 28:17, 19—which has now, alas, become "Beth-aven" <note>House of Vanity/Idols</note> (Hosea 4:15).

->CHAPTER XII, v. 2. **Ephraim** through Ribia <note>a Hebrew accent mark</note> 3. 6. 9. 20. 33. and f. 1.<-

<column-break/>

**g)** *And with the holy ones*, by which some understand men, as in Psalm 16:3; others understand heavenly beings, as in Job 15:15. Schmid, however, along with Kimchi, understands it to be GOD Himself (compare Joshua 24:19), such that the particle "with" signifies not just any company, but help, strength, dominion, and the granting of faithfulness. (Compare Joshua 1:5; John 3:2). **h)** *He was faithful and constant.* This means that Judah was still faithful to God at that time and constantly held to His true worship (Schmid; compare Ecclesiastes 1:21; Psalm 78:8, 37).

**Verse 2.** **i)** See verses 1, 9, 15. **k)** *He feeds on the wind*, as if he were about to eat it: just as a starving beast greedily grazes on grass. (Compare Jeremiah 22:22; Psalm 37:3). **l)** *And pursues* (verse 6, 3) *the east wind.* (Chapter 13:15; Genesis 41:6; Ezekiel 19:12), which he will never catch. <note>original Greek: "καύσωנה" (the burning wind)</note>. So in Jonah 4:8; James 1:11; compare Proverbs 27:16; Ecclesiastes 5:15. The Targum: "They are like one who sows the wind and reaps the whirlwind," which we had above in Chapter 8:7. Rivetus thinks that in this way, vain confidence in human help is struck down (compare verse 7). Schmid, however, believes it describes not the punishment of Ephraim, but his increased and hardened malice, by which he promised himself much from his idolatrous worship, by which even Judah was seduced (verse 3). **m)** Isaiah 52:5. **n)** Ezekiel 28:15, 17. Rivetus and others think "lies and robbery" refer to human help, based on the outcome; but Schmid and Tarnovius believe it refers to idolatry and the false worship of gods and temples. Thus the Septuagint: "empty and vain things," for which the Arabic has "novelties and vanities." **o)** Chapter 7:13. "Falsehood" here, I would think, primarily notes the [moral] devastation of those who still loved and pursued the true worship of God, says Schmid. So compare 1 Kings 19:14 and 2 Chronicles 21:14. **p)** *Multiplies.* Chapter 8:4, 11; 10:1. **q)** *And now...*

<summary>This page analyzes Hosea 12:2-5, contrasting Ephraim's futile pursuit of political alliances and idols (likened to "feeding on the wind") with the ancestral legacy of Jacob. The commentary uses Jacob's wrestling with the Angel as an example of the true faith and persistent prayer that the current generation has abandoned.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Hosea 12, transitioning from the historical narrative of Jacob's struggle with the Angel to the theological implications of God's name and the current moral failures of the tribe of Ephraim.</meta>

<page-num>559</page-num>
<header>HOSEA. CHAPTER 12.</header>

<margin>
s) Jacob found Him. Deuteronomy 4:29, 1 Chronicles 28:9, Isaiah 55:6. This occurred when, warned by God in Genesis 35:1, he ascended to Bethel and fulfilled the vows he had made in Genesis 28:21-22. Others read: *The Angel found Jacob there*. Thus, according to Jonathan, God was revealed or appeared to Jacob in Bethel, as we read in Genesis 35:7-8.
t) There He spoke [with] Jacob. u) With us: namely, with the Triune God—Father and Son. Compare the note on verse 1, Genesis 1:26, 3:22, 11:7, John 14:23, and see Genesis 35:13-15. These are the words of the Angel of God, as Cocceius and Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, a preeminent medieval French commentator</note> believe. However, in his version, Castellio has: *with him*. So too the Syriac, along with Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion in the Greek scholia, as well as Rabbi Adonim and Rabbi Jonah in the *Michlal Yophi* <note>A Hebrew grammatical and exegetical work</note> citing Kimchi's Lexicon, and Rabbi Tanchum according to Pocock (p. 648). But this is contrary to the grammar. To Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval grammarian known as Radak</note> and others, these are the words of the Prophet: as if to say, God still speaks with us there—meaning with me, Amos, and the other prophets—to rebuke the idolatry now practiced by the Church, comparing it to Amos 5:4-5. But Piscator understands the Prophet to be speaking with the people. Thus Tarnovius: there God also spoke with us, who were yet in the loins of Jacob; a view Pocock (p. 649) ultimately prefers, comparing it to Psalm 66:6 and Hebrews 7:9-10. Others imply a relative sense: He spoke to Jacob of things which were done or happened *with us*. Drusius: "those things which pertained to us."
v. 6. x) Tremellius translates: "And yet" (or "Moreover," to add another argument for repentance) "Jehovah is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" (Gen 28:13, Ex 3:15), whom you have maliciously deserted (v. 2, 6, 7, 27, 35; Ch 11:2). He will be merciful to you if you repent (Ch 11:8-9); otherwise, He will punish you most severely...
</margin>

> 6. **And He found him, and there He spoke with us: the Lord is the God of hosts;**
> 7. **the Lord is His memorial. Therefore, by your God, return: keep mercy and justice,**
> 8. **and wait on your God continually. A merchant** <note>original: "Canaan"</note> **in whose hand are scales of deceit,**
> 9. **he loves to oppress. And Ephraim said: "Indeed, I have become rich, I have found wealth**
> 10. **for myself; in all my labors they shall find no iniquity in me that would be sin." But I am the Lord**
> **your God...**

<margin>
...He will punish you, and no one can prevent it (Ch 5:14, etc.). y) He is the God of Zebaoth (Amos 4:13, Ch 5:27, Romans 9:29, James 5:4), that is, of the hosts or of all things celestial and terrestrial (Genesis 2:1).
</margin>

...the one supreme and almighty God, for whom all creatures serve as soldiers and are ready at His nod (Compare Luke 7:8). These include the Angels (1 Kings 22:19, Psalm 103:21, Luke 2:13), the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19, Acts 7:42), the air, wind, fire, and hail (Psalm 148:8), men within the Church (Exodus 7:4, Ch 12:41) and His enemies (Isaiah 10:5 onward), even locusts (Joel 2:11), which have and acknowledge no king but Him (Proverbs 30:27). z) For ***JEHOVAH*** is that venerable and glorious name (Deuteronomy 28:55, 58) by which He wishes to be worshipped and distinguished from all fictitious deities (Isaiah 42:8, 1 Corinthians 8:5)—He who <term>is, who was, and who shall always be consistent with Himself</term> <note>original Greek: "ὁ ὤν ὁ ἦν κ. ὁ ἐρχ."</note> (Revelation 1:4). Regarding this passage, Vitringa says in his Commentary (p. 18): "It is clear that this name refers to the promises of the divine testaments, Old and New, the certain fulfillment or representation of which God promises to the Church by this sacramental name" (Exodus 6:3). a) This is His memorial (Exodus 3:15, Isaiah 26:8). It is not Baalim (Hosea 2:15, 18, 19; Ch 11:2), nor your calves (Hosea 8:5), nor other idols and carved images (Isaiah 42:8). Thus the name itself proves that He alone is the supreme and almighty God. So He lives in Christ (2 Timothy 3:12, Psalm 60:14) who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and as was said through Moses, His memorial shall be for all generations.

v. 7. b) Here we have the conclusion from the preceding arguments. As if to say: Since the matter stands as it does—that (1) Jehovah visits Jacob and repays him according to his works (v. 3), and (2) He is the God of hosts, always consistent in His promises and threats (v. 6)—therefore you, Israel, who are perverse and turned away from God (v. 1-2), and you, Judah (v. 3), finally come to your senses. c) <term>The One who is, the One who was, and the One who is coming</term> is in your very God. This means not only by His help and aid, as Ibn Ezra and Mercer rightly suggest (comparing Jeremiah 31:18), but also according to His guidance and prescription; namely, in true repentance and faith. Thus one lives in Christ (2 Timothy 3:12), who, with Christ’s help on the way, walks in the precepts of His word and in a manner pleasing to Him. (Compare Psalm 56:5, 11; Psalm 60:14). d) Return from your evil ways (Ch 14:2-3, Jeremiah 4:1). e) Keep <term>piety</term> <note>often translated as mercy or steadfast love</note> and <term>judgment</term> <note>justice</note>, and all the virtues of a godly life; that is, fruits worthy of true repentance (Ch 4:1, 6:4, 6, 10:12, Jeremiah 9:23, Micah 6:8). f) Observe them diligently and constantly (Compare Isaiah 56:1, Psalm 37:34, 37), and thus follow in the footsteps of your father Jacob (v. 4-5) (Romans 4:12, compared with Ch 9:8). g) And thus hope, or direct your hope and desire (Psalm 27:14, 37:34). 0. <term>Draw near to God</term> (James 4:8). h) To your God (Compare Deuteronomy 28:17-18, Psalm 144:15). i) 1 Chronicles 16:11 (Compare 1 Peter 1:13, Isaiah 26:4). This indicates perseverance to us, as if saying: do not fall away from Him so frequently. Others: "Thus you shall have your hope always placed in God," comparing the imperative in Genesis 42:18 and Proverbs 4:4. So Grotius: "For it will be that you should not despair of Him, provided you do your duty."

v. 8. k) **He is Canaan** or **He is a Merchant!** In this concise phrasing, born of indignant emotion, commentators struggle with both the meaning and the connection. To others (such as the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic), it is a proper name; as if to say: but he refers to Canaan (Genesis 8:25, Ch 9:18, 10:6) or a Canaanite. He refers to Ephraim, not the Jacob or Israel of Genesis 25:27, 32:28, 35:10, or John 1:48; for he imitates their impious customs and cursed worship (Leviticus 18:24, Deuteronomy 12:30-31). Thus the Targum: "The example of Jacob was set forth," it says in verses 4-5, "so that they might imitate his piety; but they instead reflect the character of the Canaanites." Compare Ezekiel 16:3, 29, Zephaniah 1:11, Zechariah 14:21, and the story of Susanna verse 56. Kimchi, however, makes a contrast between the preceding divine command in verse 7 regarding piety and justice, and the actual works of the Israelites. To others, such as Jonathan, Rashi, Kimchi, and others, the name is a common noun; as if to say: *He is a Merchant*. Such were the Canaanites or Phoenicians, who, as Grotius and other authors observe, were <term>lovers of money and foremost</term> <note>original Greek: "φιλοχρήματοί τε καὶ πρῶται"</note> as greedy deceivers. Compare Isaiah 23:8, Proverbs 31:24, Job 40:30, and Jeremiah 10:17. l) In his hand they are (Compare 1 Samuel 24:12, 26:18). This means that he holds them notoriously and indiscriminately, both in his power and in his practice, against the express prohibition of God (Leviticus 19:35, Deuteronomy 25:13-16). m) Amos 8:5, Micah 6:10-11, Proverbs 11:1. n) To defraud (Leviticus 5:21, 23, 19:13, Deuteronomy 24:14). Others translate the Greek <term>καταδυναστεύειν</term> as "to oppress," as in 1 Samuel 12:3-4 (Compare James 2:6). o) He loves—that is, he sins knowingly and willingly, indeed impudently and without fear. Compare Hosea 4:18, Amos 4:5; and see Amos 4:1, Micah 2:2. Jonathan applied this <term>correction</term> <note>original: "epanorthosin"</note> to the plunder, in this manner: "You have become like merchants in whose hands are deceitful balances."

v. 9. p) And yet, such is his impudent obstinacy, Ephraim said and still says (v. 1, 2, 15). q) As if to say: "Whatever the case may be, nevertheless..." (Compare note on 1 Samuel 16:6). r) I have become rich (Job 15:29), namely from the blessing of the Lord (Proverbs 10:22; Compare Zechariah 11:5, and above Ch 9:1, 10:1-2). Ephraim boasts of his wealth and prosperous successes as if they were an argument for divine approval (Gussetius, p. 249). s) Thus I have found and attained (Proverbs 1:13) t) desire (v. 4, Genesis 35:18), that is, the desired wealth (Job 20:10). Others translate it as strength (Genesis 49:3); to others, it is the same as <term>wealth</term>, multitude, or abundance (Proverbs 18:11, 30:15, comparing Deuteronomy 8:18). The Septuagint and Arabic (from the Arabic *aon*: convenience, rest, tranquility) have: <term>I have found relief for myself</term>, like the man in Luke 12:19. But the Vulgate has: *I have found an idol for myself*; with which compare Hosea 10:8, Numbers 23:21, 1 Samuel 15:23, and Ephesians 5:5, Colossians 3:5. u) As far as all my labors are concerned (Compare note on Ch 9:11) and the riches acquired by my labor and industry (Deuteronomy 28:33, Psalm 78:46, 128:2). x) They shall not find (or *it shall not be found*—impersonal, as in Esther 2:2, Nehemiah 2:7) namely, by those who consider the matter with an even mind (Psalm 17:3). y) Such iniquity or offense (Deuteronomy 19:15; Compare Hosea 8:13, 9:9, 13:12). z) Which would be so grave a sin that I would have knowingly and willingly wandered from the good, or that deserves to be so bitterly rebuked as happened in verse 8. (Compare Psalm 32:5). Cocceius in his Lexicon (226) says: "a depravity that would make me damnable and devoid of God's friendship," or "the act of a sinner, not a justified one." Compare 1 John 3:8-9. From this, it is easily apparent that I am not guilty of sin: for Nemesis <note>the goddess of retribution, here used metaphorically for divine justice</note> does not let those who are guilty go unpunished. (Junius & Tremellius).

v. 10. a) But I, whose most wholesome warnings (v. 7) you, Israel, shamelessly do not admit (v. 9). b) I am Jehovah; as was said in verse 6.

### CHAPTER 12. HOSEA 12

<margin>

</margin>

---

**of the time,** that is, according to Tremellius: as formerly for forty years (Numbers 14:33) they lived in the desert under tents (Leviticus 23:43). But again, others prefer another and specific meaning for the name *moed* <note>original: מועד, meaning "appointed time" or "festival"</note>. Cocceius in his Lexicon (p. 13) suggests: "as in the days of the assembly," not in the city (comparing Hosea 11:9 and Revelation 10:9). The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic versions read: "as in the days of the festival." Perhaps specifically the Festival of Tabernacles <note>Sukkot</note>, described in Leviticus 23:39, and compared with Revelation 21:3. Thus (in the words of Schmid), the blessed time of the New Testament is compared with the joyful feasts of the Old Testament, just as the "perpetual Sabbath" is mentioned elsewhere (Isaiah 66:23-24). **v. 11. g)** "Therefore I have spoken still." So it is in the past tense in Jonathan and the Vulgate. Others, like the Septuagint and Arabic (and Schmid regarding the New Testament), read it in the future: "And I will speak." We take this to mean not only clear and lucid words but also, with Schmid, a matter of supernatural speech and immediate revelation. Furthermore, just as each interpreter explained the preceding verse, they continue their sentiment here. The form of this and the following verb—or rather the accent, according to our Codices—is on the penultimate syllable, which requires a past tense meaning (as in Ecclesiastes 2:15); whereas the reversed meaning <note>the "waw consecutive" which flips past to future</note> takes the accent on the last syllable (as in Hosea 2:16, Exodus 25:22, Numbers 11:17, Jeremiah 1:17). Although some books noted in the variant readings have the accent on the end here, because a future tense follows at the end of the verse—which we, in this mixture of tenses, take as a continuous present (see notes on Chapter 7)—**h)** even these past tenses can be taken as prophetic and standing for the future, if the context requires it (see above, 10:5). **h)** Tremellius reads "by others" to the prophets (cf. 10:10); others read "together with the prophets" (cf. 10:14). But simply, the Vulgate says "upon the prophets," indicating the immediate descent of the Holy Spirit speaking through them, by which the word of God came upon them from heaven (these are Schmid’s words). So also Pocock (p. 683), comparing 2 Peter 1:21. **i)** "And I," lest you should perish. **k)** "prophetic visions" (1 Samuel 3:1, Psalm 89:20, Proverbs 29:18). This should be taken broadly, to include even visions in dreams (which Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century statesman and commentator</note> specifically understands here, comparing Numbers 12:6); for even the Apostles had their visions, says Schmid. **l)** "I multiplied" (see 2 Kings 17:13 and Amos 3:7). But others, as we said, read in the future: "I will multiply." This multiplication, says Schmid, is contrasted with the Old Testament, where prophets were much rarer than at the beginning of the New Testament (cf. Joel 3:1). **m)** That is, by the work and ministry of the Prophets (cf. Exodus 9:35, Isaiah 20:2). The prophets here, says Schmid, are the first teachers of the New Testament: the Apostles and the Prophets specifically so-called. **n)** "I propose similarities, examples, and parables." For example, when in Chapters 1 and 3 Israel was compared to a harlot or an adulteress; or as others prefer in the future, "I will propose parables" (cf. Psalm 78:2, Matthew 13:34-35). The word "word" is understood, as in Genesis 6:4 or Jeremiah 50:9 (compare our word in Lamentations 2:13, Isaiah 40:18, Jeremiah 6:2, Ezekiel 31:2, Song of Solomon 1:9). **v. 12. o)** "If" (4:15). Or "Whether?" or "Is it not?" (as in Isaiah 27:7, Amos 3:6). This is an interrogation of wonder for Schmid, but for Drusius, Noldius, and others, it is a vehement affirmation, as if to say: "As long as Gilead was vain and impious." Others, like the Targum and Castellio, prefer a conditional meaning but connect and understand the following words differently. In the midst of such perplexity among interpreters, we will briefly indicate what fits the words and their punctuation according to the accents, confirming it with parallelism, and leaving the rest. Regarding the coherence, see the notes on verse 1. For the Lord continues to contend with stubborn Ephraim (v. 9), teaching that he imitates the impious Gileadites rather than his pious father Jacob (v. 13), and thus brings God's wrath and destruction upon himself (v. 15). **p)** "Gilead," that is, the Gileadites or those across the Jordan (cf. 6:8, Numbers 26:29; and for the ancient holiness of that region or mountain, Genesis 31:21, 47). **q)** "wickedness and idolatry" (cf. v. 9, 10:8, Numbers 23:21, 1 Samuel 15:23, Isaiah 41:29). That is: if the Gileadites, devoted to wickedness and idolatry, were merely vain and frustrated, certainly the Ephraimites sacrifice bulls in Gilgal with similar madness. Indeed, they do not only do this there, but their idolatrous altars are almost innumerable and are seen everywhere like heaps of stones in all the fields. In Schmid's opinion, where "Aven" here is a proper name, it is the same as Bethel (as in 4:15, 5:8, 10:5, Amos 5:5). He reads it as a question: "Is Gilead also Aven/Bethel?" and the answer is: "Truly, Gilead and Aven/Bethel have become vanity." This can hardly stand due to the chronological factors noted in Chapter 7:1. For at the time when the destruction of Samaria and the end of the kingdom of Israel under King Hoshea were imminent, the Gileadites had already been carried away into miserable captivity by the Assyrians several years prior, under King Pekah (2 Kings 15:29, 1 Chronicles 5:26). **r)** "only" (Genesis 7:23, Exodus 10:17, Proverbs 14:23). Others, like Schmid, read "altogether" (Genesis 44:28, Jeremiah 2:15). **s)** "vanity," that is, they were vain and in vain (cf. Psalm 127:1-2). Schmid rightly says those who worship idols are vanity, just as the idols themselves are vanity (cf. Jeremiah 10:3, 15; 1 Corinthians 8:4). **t)** "in Gilgal," where there was both a shrine and a very famous altar (see 4:15, 9:15, Amos 5:5). Jonathan says: "in the temple of Gilgal they sacrifice calves to idols." **u)** "bulls." Plural (r) from the singular *Shor*; like *Shushan* (lily/thorn) in 1 Samuel 13:6 from the singular *Shush*. **x)** "with impious zeal and expense" (cf. 4:13). **y)** "yea, even" (Malachi 3:15). **z)** "their altars," which the Israelites built for their idols not only in the city but also in the fields (cf. 8:11, 10:11). **a)** "are like heaps." He alludes to the names Gilead (cf. Genesis 31:46-47) and Gilgal (Joshua 4:20, 5:9) and compares their altars—both for their worthlessness and their frequency—to the heaps of stones usually gathered by those clearing stony fields. Not to mention, to those looking from afar, the appearance is similar. (Bochart, *Hieroz.* I, p. 1091). Others say their altars will therefore be destroyed and become heaps (cf. Jeremiah 26:18), but we prefer the former due to the context and the following parallelism. **b)** Jonathan: "in the boundaries of the field." Schmid: "of my fields" (as in 10:4, cf. 9:3). **v. 13. c)** "But he fled," or "And when Jacob your Father (v. 4, 5) was devoted to God (Genesis 28:21) so that he might retain the blessing of Jehovah and the Messiah promised in it, being needy and poor (Genesis 32:11), he fled (Genesis 27:41, 43) and became a servant, and received a most generous compensation for his troubles in his descendants who were liberated from slavery and guarded (v. 14). On the contrary, Ephraim voluntarily provokes me to the most bitter anger, and therefore will undergo the most just punishments (v. 15)." Indeed, as Schmid holds, the preceding verse accused the Israelites of the foulest idolatry (as well as perfidy and hypocrisy in v. 1, dissension in v. 2, cf. 7:11; injustice and fraud in v. 8; and contempt for the divine word in v. 9, 11; cf. Jeremiah 7:2, 25:3-4, and Deuteronomy 8:6 onwards, from the observation of Rabbi Tanchum in Pocock). Now the punishment for it is added, as is clear from the last verse: namely, the punishment of *talion* <note>The law of retaliation, "an eye for an eye"</note>, by which his blood will be left upon him, and the Lord will return his reproach to him. This punishment of retaliation is illustrated by the contrast with the divine benevolence toward Jacob, the father of the Israelites. Furthermore, Schmid considers the *Vav* <note>The Hebrew letter 'and'</note> to be redundant here, except that histories usually begin with it (as in Joshua 1:1, 1 Samuel 1:1). Jonathan, however, to make a connection, prefixes: "The Prophet said to them: Did not Jacob your father go to the fields of Syria?" **d)** "into the field of Syria," that is, into Paddan Aram (Genesis 28:2, 5). The Septuagint reads: "into the plain of Syria," that is, into rural Syria or Mesopotamia. Thus Curtius (Book 3, c. 8) mentions the spacious plains of Mesopotamia; regarding which our Cellarius says: "Syria is mountainous; but across the Euphrates toward Babylonia, very spacious plains open up." Others read "into the field," meaning into the region or hereditary possession (2 Samuel 9:7). Aram, son of Shem (Genesis 10:22), from whom the whole nation and region took its name, not from that other son of Kemuel (Genesis 22:21; cf. Bochart, *Phal.* II, 5, p. 83). **e)** "And Jacob," or Israel as he was later called (Genesis 32:29), "served" (Genesis 29:18, 20; 31:41). **f)** "for a woman" of his kin; so that he would not have to marry a Canaanite and impious woman who would bring idolatry into the family (cf. Genesis 27:46, 28:1-2), from whose service he also diligently purified his household after his return (35:2).

<column-break/>

**k)** Your God, whom alone you were obliged to acknowledge and worship (13:4, Exodus 20:2-3, Deuteronomy 6:13). **c)** "from the land of Egypt" (2:17), from which slavery I liberated you, introduced you into this land, and adorned you with the greatest benefits, which you, most ungrateful, do not credit to me (cf. Deuteronomy 6:10, 8:7, Amos 3:10, 3:1, 9:7, Micah 6:4). **d)** "therefore again" (1:6, 3:1) I will lead you as if into the desert (2:16). Others read: "I still cause you to dwell in tents," that is, in your dwellings, and I still preserve you in them. So Pareus, Tarnovius, and Luther. **e)** "I will make you dwell in tents," just as your ancestors once did in the desert (cf. Leviticus 23:42-43), and as the Patriarchs also lived in tents (Genesis 12:8, 13:3, 18:1, 23:4; Hebrews 11:9), and later the Rechabites (Jeremiah 35:7). So Theodoret, Abarbanel, and Tremellius. These words contain a threat of exile, but for the end and hope of their correction, as above (2:16). Schmid, however, just as with verse 7, refers these verses to Judah (which Tirinus also wanted, in Pocock p. 679) and thinks great goods are thus promised to them. It is known, he says, that the anti-typical things of the New Testament are usually compared with the types of the Old Testament. Thus, in this place, the "dwelling in tents" is the dwelling in the spiritual tents of the Messiah (compare Isaiah 33:18, Acts 15:16, Revelation 13:6, 21:3). **f)** Schmid in his version: "according to the days of the appointed time" (cf. Exodus 9:5). That is, according to some, until the redemption through Christ (Galatians 4:4). According to others, like Abarbanel and Arias Montanus in Pocock, until the number of days defined for the present exile of the Israelites is completed (cf. Romans 11:25-26). But others take it comparatively to the measure of past time (as in 2:15, 17; Psalm 9:3, Psalm 90:15).

> 14 And by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved.
