### CHAPTER XIII.

> 1 When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he exalted himself in Israel; but when he offended in Baal, he died.
> 2 And now they sin more and more, and have made for them molten images of their silver...

---

The letter *Bet* <note>The Hebrew preposition meaning 'in' or 'with'</note> is understood: **in his bitternesses**; Castellio translates it "bitterly"; so that both the manner and the matter are signified, namely the most grave sins of the Israelites, especially idolatry and the idols themselves, by which they most bitterly provoked God to anger. (4) Jeremiah 6:25, chapter 31:15, 21. Others, such as Rabbi Tanchum and Abu'l-walid in Pococke page 709, explain it as: "with many rebellions," comparing Ezekiel 23:21 and Job 13:26. Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, medieval grammarian</note> truly relates it to statues or altars and high places, comparing Jeremiah 31:21 and Daniel 8:7, but this is without necessity and without just proof. s) **Therefore his blood-guilt he shall leave upon him**, and the Lord will not care for him (1 Samuel 19:2, chapter 12:22, etc.), nor will He avenge his blood shed by enemies: because Ephraim himself is the cause of his own death and destruction. Compare Leviticus 20:9, Joshua 2:10, 2 Samuel 1:16, etc., and the contrary in Psalm 9:13, Psalm 72:14, Genesis 9:5. t) **And his reproach**, with which he afflicted his GOD by deserting Him and going over to idols, compare Isaiah 65:7, Psalm 79:12, Daniel 11:18. u) **He shall return** <note>Hiphil verb form</note> verse 3, Nehemiah 3:36. This happened when GOD drove Israel into the utmost contempt of captivity and exile, and made them despised by all peoples. **S.** x) **His Lord**, to whom he most wickedly denied obedience. Compare verse 9, Malachi 1:6, and 1 Samuel 2:30.

->**CHAPTER XIII, VERSE 1.**<- y) **When Ephraim spoke.** Because it is shortly said that Ephraim "bore" [guilt] in Israel, and is thus distinguished from it; Ephraim is not taken here for the ten tribes as in chapter 12:1-2 and often elsewhere in this Prophet; yet the others are not excluded, but Ephraim is noted as the first and principal. For God proceeds to specifically argue against the sins of Ephraim and the Israelites, and to announce their punishments and the overthrow of the kingdom. It is as if He says: "For, to explain that provocation (chapter 12:15) and its punishments more distinctly: When Ephraim spoke, etc." z) **horror**, i.e., according to Luther and **S.**, **horrendous idolatry** through the calves of Jeroboam. (1) Compare the related word *retet* in Jeremiah 49:24, where the Syriac uses *r'ticha*: the root in both Chaldean and Syriac means "he feared, shuddered, trembled." The interpreters differ greatly here; we will refer only to those who do not manifestly conflict with the words and accents. Jonathan: "When one of the house of Ephraim spoke, trembling seized the peoples." Pococke, however, in his Commentary page 716, prefers this sense from the English version: "When Ephraim yet spoke with fear and trembling" (Philippians 2:12, just as his father Jacob humbly prayed to GOD, above in chapter 12:5) and did not speak against God stubbornly or proudly (chapter 12:9), **he exalted himself**, i.e., as Munster has it, "he was exalted in Israel." Pococke also refers the Syriac and Rashi to this, who explains *retet* as "with trembling" from Psalm 2:11, comparing also Isaiah 66:2. But **S.**, as we said, takes the abstract for the concrete, i.e., "horror" for a thing or "horrendous idolatry," which any pious person would rightly abhor and detest (compare Psalm 106:29, 20), and he understands this regarding the impious rites of Jeroboam I. For it cannot be believed (says **S.**) that mention of Baal is made here without something being premised about those calves, which are so hateful to our Prophet, see chapter 8:5, etc. Nor can it be taken for any other time than when Ephraim was divided from Judah, from whom he is usually distinguished in our Prophet. Therefore the sense is: "When Ephraim first spoke and established, in the time of Jeroboam I (who by that very act earned a permanent mark of ignominy; see above at chapter 7:15), that horrendous worship of God through calves (1 Kings 12:28), he brought back just punishments in Israel." a) **he himself bore**, namely that speaking of his, or that horrendous sin of his. Just as in the following clause the antecedent "and he became guilty" has its consequent evil, "then he died"; so we take these words with **S.** as the result or consequence of the preceding clause, and we take it in a bad sense; so that it is the same as what is elsewhere called "to bear one's iniquity or sin." See, for example, Leviticus 5:1, 17, chapter 17:16, chapter 19:8, chapter 20:17, chapter 24:15, etc. Sin or iniquity is "borne" when it is imputed and punished. And in truth, it was not unavenged, but the sin of the calves was most gravely punished, both in Jeroboam and his posterity who were deleted, and in the following Kings who did not depart from that sin. **S.** compare 1 Kings 13:34, chapter 14:10 and following. Others, such as Kimchi and Pagninus: "he lifted up," namely his head. Others: "he received," namely the kingdom. So Rabbi Tanchum in Pococke page 718: "he was raised to the dignity of the kingdom." Jonathan: "they were princes." Syriac and Tigurine: "he was made a prince." So Rashi, Ibn Ezra, and also Munster: "he was exalted"; but these interpretations have no less, but rather greater, difficulty in construction than the opinion of **S.** b) **in and with the rest of Israel**, who were seduced by Jeroboam to that detestable worship. Compare verse 9, also 1 Kings 14:15-16 and 2 Chronicles 13:15 and following. c) **and when he became guilty**, namely the same Ephraim with Israel (chapter 4:15, chapter 10:2, chapter 14:1, Isaiah 24:6). d) **not only in the calves** (which the successors of Jeroboam constantly retained out of false principles of political prudence) **but also in Baal** (chapter 2:10, 15, chapter 11:2). They rightly take this to refer to the times of Ahab, who at the instigation of his impious wife [Jezebel], reintroduced the worship of Baal. 1 Kings 16:31-32, chapter 18:18. From this, the people could afterwards be purged neither by the divine zeal of Elijah (1 Kings 18:40) nor by Jehu, the son of Nimshi (2 Kings 10:25 and following), such that the evil would not repeatedly flare up again. For what was once a sin in this matter under the Judges (see Judges 2:11, 13, chapter 6:25 and following, chapter 10:6, 1 Samuel 7:4, chapter 12:10) cannot be attributed to Ephraim above the other tribes, since the tribes of Judah and Benjamin were no less at fault; so says **S.** Others want the name of Baal to be used here as an insult for the calves, or for the whole flock of gods whom they joined to the Most High God. e) **then he died**; as in Numbers 25:1 and following; compare above chapter 9:10 and following. That is, he was so abandoned by God and pressed by enemies that he was as if gasping his last breath, or scarcely any corpse of a republic was left to him. "Lifeless, he began to rot, like a corpse." — Rittersbusius. Others: "he died spiritually and eternally," compare Genesis 2:17. So Rashi: "he died in this world and the world to come."

**V. 2.** f) **Nevertheless they were not even thus corrected**, but as if stupid and demented, now after those times of Ahab, and after the worship of Baal was overturned by Jehu (2 Kings 10:28), g) **they add to sin**, and heap sins upon sins. Compare chapter 7:1, Isaiah 1:5. For not only did they constantly retain Jeroboam's calves, as we said at verse 1, and relapsed into the worship of Baal, as we noted above at chapter 2:10; but they added, as if anew, manifold idolatry; for example, in Gilgal, in Beersheba (Amos 8:14). See 2 Kings 17:7-16, 21, 22. h) **and they made for themselves**, against my express prohibition (Exodus 20:4), i) **a molten image or cast images**; such as was the calf of Aaron (Exodus 32:4, 8). Here, however, we do not take this to be about the calves, nor about Baal, as the interpreters generally want with Kimchi; but about other various idols added on top, to which they also sometimes sacrificed humans, says **S.** The singular, as often, is collective; because the other accusative, which follows by apposition, namely **idols** <note>Hebrew: *atzabbim*</note>, is plural. Compare also chapter 10:1.

It uses metaphors of wild animals (lion, leopard, bear) to describe God's coming judgment upon a people who grew proud and forgot their Savior.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the verse-by-verse commentary on Hosea Chapter 13. The previous page concluded with the beginning of verse 8, describing God's judgment as a bear bereaved of her cubs. This page explores the anatomical specificities of a lion's attack, the theological implications of Israel's self-destruction, and the historical context of their demand for a king in the time of Samuel.</meta>

<page-num>561</page-num>
<header>HOSEA. CHAPTER 13.</header>

<margin>
c) *and I will tear apart, I will lacerate.* This is usually said of garments, as in Genesis 37:29, 34; 2 Samuel 13:19, etc. Compare also Joel 2:13, Psalm 35:15, and Matthew 7:6. d) *the enclosure* (2) Job 28:15 *of the heart*, that is, the pericardium or the diaphragm, namely their chest. Samuel Bochart <note>A 17th-century scholar famous for his work on biblical animals.</note> in *Hierozoicon* vol. 1, p. 740, warns that this should not be passed over lightly; for students of nature note that the lion especially seeks out the heart. But Munster <note>Sebastian Munster, a Hebraist and cartographer.</note> translates it: *I will tear their stubborn heart.* The Tigurine Bible: *I will pierce their heart.* So too Luther, and likewise the Jewish commentators Rashi, Kimchi. Abarbanel, however, compares it to Isaiah 6:10. e) See Jeremiah 50:17 and 51:34. f) *there*, specifically *on the way* in which I will watch them. Destruction is prepared for them there and from that place, even where they think they are most secure. See the note on chapter 8:9. g) See note on Psalm 5:9. h) *the wild beast of the field shall scatter them*, or *the wild beast shall tear them.* Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a prominent 17th-century theologian.</note> says the comparison should have continued: *like a beast of the field I will split them open.* Truly, to show that God would do all things through intermediaries—especially men, enemies, and cruel ones—he shifts the style and says, *the beast of the field shall split them*, meaning: I will cause the beasts of the field to split them open. Compare above, chapter 2:14. i) See chapter 14:1 and 2 Kings 2:24. These points pertain to our understanding of how terrifying the judgments of God are, and how fearful it is to fall into the hands of the living God (Hebrews 10:31). Here, due to His supreme direction, providence, and permission, even the actions of enemies are attributed to Him. These do not signify any ferocity in God (since that implies a vice), but rather a power that cannot be resisted.
</margin>

<margin>
*Suff.* Thus Rashi: "You have destroyed yourself, O Israel; because you have transgressed against me, you have rebelled against your help." So also Abarbanel; or as Schmidt in his Commentary, p. 581: "You have destroyed yourself,"
</margin>

<margin>The end is in him <note>Original Hebrew: קץ בו ק</note></margin>

<margin>
*. o. k) *He has destroyed you.* Some take this as a noun <note>Translating it as "your destruction" rather than a verb.</note> in the form of *Schillem* (Deut. 32:35), *Dibber* (Jer. 5:13), or *Kittur* (Jer. 44:21) with the suffix <term>ך</term>. That is: "This is your destruction." So the Vulgate, Cocceius, etc. Others take it as a verb in the 2nd person past *Piel* with a suffix.
</margin>

O Israel, when you destroyed yourself by acting against me, against your help. Otherwise, less unusually, the verb <term>shachat</term> <note>original: שחת</note> is in the 3rd person here: *This has destroyed you, O Israel, that you have transgressed against me, against your help.* So Kimchi and others. Indeed, this happened—as Schmidt excellently observed from the following verse 10—when they spurned Jehovah, their King and Lord, and demanded a king like the other nations from Samuel (1 Samuel 8:5 ff.). For this was the fountain of Israel's ruin; as their kings, ever becoming worse, deserted the true God and dragged the people with them into superstitions and idolatry. From this arose the causes and occasions of ruin, from which neither the King nor the Princes (in whom they trusted too much; see chapter 10:3) could deliver them. After God has hitherto reproached the Israelites for their manifold idolatry (v. 2) and their forgetting of Him (v. 6), and has announced the gravest punishments (v. 7, 8), He now descends to the beginning and source of all evil and destruction, namely: their distrust and desertion of Jehovah in requesting a king and princes (v. 10), as if without these Jehovah could not help, or as if these were more powerful than Jehovah. Schmidt notes the words of the verse are concise and difficult, though there is no great disagreement in the sense; except that Gussetius (p. 367) industriously tries a new interpretation: "He destroyed you because of me, in him who is your help," but this is forced, as anyone who reads and understands the words can easily see. l) *that against me*, namely, you have been or have rebelled. Cf. above chapter 7:13; Isaiah 1:2; Jeremiah 2:8, 3:13, etc. m) *against your help.* This refers back to Deuteronomy 33:26, 29; cf. Psalm 33:20.

**v. 10. n) Where is he?** So the Septuagint, Vulgate, Jonathan, Syriac, and others, as well as Abu al-Walid, Ibn Janah, and Rabbi Tanchum (cited by Pococke, p. 747). For <term>ehi</term> <note>original: אֱהִי</note> is written with a *He* in the middle; and it is more aspirated, and is the same as <term>ayyeh</term> <note>original: אַיֵּה</note> "Where?". Cf. below verse 14. o) *Your king*, in whom you trust (chapter 10:3) and whom you once thought would save you (1 Samuel 8:20). p) Schmidt and others translate: *now?* which in our opinion creates an excellent opposition between the present time and that past time when they sinned against Jehovah their help and requested a king. Schmidt says this particle is very emphatic and commonly used in questions (see Genesis 27:33, Judges 9:38, Isaiah 19:12). q) that is: "let him be present now and save you, if he can." It does not say that they had no king at all then, but that he would soon perish along with them, unable to save even himself, let alone others. r) *in all your cities*, which will soon have the greatest need of his help when the enemy comes to overturn them. Cf. Micah 5:13. s) *your judges* (Isaiah 3:2), namely, "where are they now?" Schmidt rightly understands these not as the supreme Judges given by God before the kings, but as those new Princes and Ministers who served under the kings. Cf. above chapter 9:7. Others understand the Kings themselves. t) *of whom you said* (1 Samuel 8:5 ff.). u) when you could have been content and happy with Me as your King and Prince (1 Samuel 8:9, chapter 10:19). x) Cf. chapter 8:4. Schmidt explains how Israel corrupted itself while sinning against Jehovah, its help (v. 9), and asking for a king. The sense is: "You destroyed yourself, O Israel, when you corrupted yourself against me, against your help, by asking for a king." This is now clearly shown by the outcome. For where is your king now, whom you thought would save you? Let him save you now! Is he not the immediate cause of your ruin?

**v. 11. y) Therefore I was giving** to you, to the Israel of the ten tribes, along with Judah and Benjamin. Grotius says: "I have given to you quite often," i.e., being angry at your sins, I allowed you to change kings at your whim through seditions and murders. So too Tarnovius: "I am accustomed to give," comparing 2 Kings 15 and 17, and Isaiah 3:4. But it is better that Schmidt and others refer this to Saul. The Hebrews often use the future tense in narratives for the past or imperfect. See Exodus 15:6, 7; Judges 2:1. z) *a king*, requested by you (1 Samuel 8:5, 19; 10:19), namely Saul, as we said. For they requested neither Jeroboam (though some take it so) nor any other specific king from God; rather, they requested a change in the constitution of the Republic through a king who would have perpetual successors (1 Samuel 12:17, 19). This does not conflict with 1 Samuel 9:15. For God was indeed angry that they had rejected Him from being King; nevertheless, He gave a king, but in such a way that (as Samuel warned them in 1 Samuel 12:14, 25) if they remained in God's ways, this sin would be forgiven; if not, He would avenge it, as He does here to Israel. b) *and now I will take him away* through the Assyrians. This does not refer back to Saul here, as others wish (comparing 1 Samuel 31:7), but generally to the King or the royal dignity of Israel. Cf. chapter 1:4, 3:4, and the verb in 2:11; Genesis 14:11. c) *in my fury*, concerning which see verses 7, 8 and above 2:5, 6, as was also predicted in 1 Samuel 12:14, 15. The Hebrew word usually denotes immense anger. See above chapter 5:10, which fits perfectly here: because this is an anger greater than that which existed when Saul was given.

**v. 12. d) For it is bound**, tied together, and as if kept in a bundle or a pouch (Proverbs 7:20). Cf. chapter 4:19; Proverbs 30:4. As Bochart writes: "Just as if something is tied in a bag, it is preserved and does not perish from the one who tied it; so all iniquity, because Ephraim sinned against God, is bound up with him and hidden, and reserved as if in a purse." See Job 14:17. e) Along with all other sins, even this iniquity of the impious and still unrepentant Ephraim, by which he requested a king (v. 10, 11). Bound sins are those which, not being forgiven, are retained for punishment, as Rivetus says, comparing Matthew 16:19. f) *his sin is hidden* (Job 21:19), namely in the divine memory and judgment. The Targum says: "all their sins are kept for vengeance." God has not forgotten them, though they had forgotten God (v. 6). Cf. Deuteronomy 32:34, 35; Jeremiah 17:1; Romans 2:5; Psalm 50:21. The Lord had said in verse 11 that He once gave them a king in His anger and would now take him away in His wrath. One might think—and perhaps every reader thinks—would God hold a sin committed several centuries ago against an unrepentant person for so long? God therefore answers: "Yes! For the iniquity of Ephraim is bound up, every bit of it, including that old sin, and he should not think I have forgotten."

**v. 13. g) Therefore the most grievous pains**, such as those of a woman in labor, shall come upon him. h) <term>chevel</term> <note>original: חבלי</note> as the Greek <term>odines</term> <note>original: ωδινες</note> (1 Thessalonians 5:3). The Targum says: "Anxiety and trembling shall come upon him, like pains upon a woman in childbirth." See Isaiah 26:17, Jeremiah 4:31, Micah 4:9, Psalm 48:6. This is the effect of that binding and hiding of sins in verse 12. h) *For he is a son* (cf. Isaiah 1:2, Jeremiah 31:20, Romans 9:4). Or: *for he is like an unwise son*, i.e., joyful in the womb, who wants to be born before the right time and maturity. i) *not wise* (chapter 14:10), but on the contrary most foolish and stupid, since by neglecting Me (v. 6), his King and Lord (v. 4, 5), he not only long ago requested another King (v. 9, 10), but now has even established several nefarious gods for himself to worship (v. 1, 2). Nor does he intervene with true repentance to avert that sad outcome or the punishments (v. 3, 7, 8), but still acts fiercely, nor allows himself to be contained by my laws (v. 15). Cf. Deuteronomy 32:6, 29 and below chapter 14:10.

The previous page discussed God's judgment using imagery of predatory animals and the historical failures of Israel's kingship. This page focuses on the famous promise of redemption from death (cited by the Apostle Paul) and the final destruction of Samaria.</meta>

<page-num>719</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER 13. 14. HOSEA 13, 14</header>

<column-break/>

<margin>
The difficulty in the words arises, says Sebastian Schmidt <note>S. refers to Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian and prolific commentator.</note>, regarding the price of the ransom; I will deliver them from the ransom or the price of redemption. See chapter 7:13 and Psalm 49:8, 9, 16.
</margin>

## 14 From the power of the grave I will ransom them; from death I will redeem them. O death, I will be your plagues; O grave, I will be your destruction! Repentance shall be hidden from my eyes. 15 Though he be fruitful among his brothers, an east wind shall come, the wind of the Lord coming up from the wilderness; and his spring shall become dry, and his fountain shall be dried up. He shall plunder the treasury of every precious vessel. 1 Samaria shall become guilty; for she has rebelled.

And note 1 Samuel 14:45; compare also Jeremiah 31:11, 1 Corinthians 6:20, 1 Peter 1:18–19, Hebrews 2:14. The suffix of the verbs is not exclusive but inclusive; that is, it refers not only to the Ephraimites, but also to all the children standing in the "womb" of the Old Testament, and indeed to all humanity. Compare Acts 13:46, 1 Timothy 2:4–6, Mark 15:15–16. **q)** *from death*, namely the second and eternal death described in Isaiah 28:15, Hebrews 2:15, and Revelation 2:11, 20:6, and 21:8. In this way, natural death—to which all are subject (Sirach 41:3, Job 13:24)—becomes a transition to a better and eternal life (John 11:25–26, 14:19; cf. 1 Corinthians 15:26, 2 Timothy 1:10, and the note on Isaiah 25:8). **r)** as a <term>Goel</term> <note>Hebrew: "Redeemer" or "Kinsman-Vindicator." In biblical law, a Goel was a relative responsible for redeeming a family member from debt or slavery, or avenging their blood.</note> (Job 19:25), that is, as their kinsman and vindicator (Leviticus 25:25–26, Numbers 5:8, 35:12, 19, Deuteronomy 19:6, 12, Ruth 3:9, 12). I will redeem and vindicate them. Compare notes on Isaiah 41:14, 43:1, and Hebrews 2:11, 13. These words, says Schmidt, are taken in their most proper sense, denoting redemption through a price; just as when a servant is redeemed with money, or a kinsman is redeemed by a kinsman from servitude, captivity, or death itself. Christ provided this redemption when he tasted death for all (Hebrews 2:9, 14–15) and paid the price of redemption (Matthew 20:28, 1 Timothy 2:6, 1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Thus, he became a plague to death and destruction to hell, as follows: **s)** *Where will they be then?* as in verse 10. So the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, Syriac, Arabic, and Tigurine versions. Also Rabbi Tanchum and Abu al-Walid. And so the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 15:55. Others translate it as *I will be*, which Schmidt says fits perfectly in our context. **1)** *your plague*, from the singular *debher* (Exodus 9:3). We take the plural to mean all kinds of plagues, says Schmidt, because Christ made satisfaction for all and abolished them all. Compare Isaiah 53:9. The Septuagint reads: <note>original Greek: "πῆ ἡ δίκη σου, θάνατε;"</note> "Where is your judgment, O Death?" **t)** from the singular *Dabhar*, meaning "word" or "cause" (Psalm 14:14). Paul, however, rendered it as <note>original Greek: "κέντρον"</note> "sting" or "goad," which is related to the Hebrew *darbhan* (1 Samuel 13:21, Ecclesiastes 12:11) and the Arabic *Dabbereh*. Some suggest it means a "bee" (*Debherah*) because a bee has a sting. See Mill’s *Onomasticon* and Pococke on this passage. **u)** Schmidt translates: "I will be your plague, O death!" This is an elegant dialogue, says Schmidt, where the situation is reversed. Before Christ, death killed humans eternally through pestilential diseases; but Christ lived so that he himself might become the plague of death and the eternal destruction of hell, since he himself was in death and in hell. **x)** *where?* or *I will be*, as said before. **y)** *utter destruction*. (1) Compare the related word in Isaiah 28:2, which in Psalm 91:6 is joined with pestilence.

<margin>
Paul in that passage.
</margin>

Paul in that passage says: <note>original Greek: "πῆ τὸ νῖκος"</note> "Where is the victory?" that is, the victory that brought eternal destruction to men. The Septuagint says "Where is your sting?" from an Arabic usage that the Apostle applied in the first instance. **z)** *O hell!* <note>original Latin: "inferne"</note>. An elegant <term>prosopopœia</term> <note>A rhetorical device where an abstract thing or deceased person is represented as speaking or being addressed.</note>, where the Redeemer challenges Death and Hell—the two antagonists and enemies of the human race (1 Corinthians 15:26)—and announces his victory obtained through his Priestly, Prophetic, and Kingly offices; as Ursinus notes. **a)** *repentance*, meaning that I will not repent of my promise of redemption. (1) Compare Psalm 110:4, Jeremiah 89:35–36. **b)** *it is removed and hidden from my eyes* (Genesis 41:2, 18), because this decree of redemption is sacrosanct, immutable, and unconditional. Compare Numbers 23:19, Romans 11:29. On how the ancient Jews understood this passage regarding the Messiah, redemption, and hell, see Raymond Martini in *Pugio Fidei*.

<margin>
CHAPTER XIV.
</margin>

# CHAPTER XIV.

**v. 15. c)** Schmidt: Because Ephraim himself (v. 12) is a foolish son; who does not stay in the womb of children but breaks out into idolatry (v. 13). **d)** *among brothers*. This refers to the tribes of Israel in general, and specifically to Judah and Benjamin, who were not yet as fierce. It seems to refer to the "sons" in verse 14 who were in the same Old Testament "womb" as he was, says Schmidt. Compare chapter 10:11. **e)** *he is fierce* or *acts fiercely*, like a wild beast or a wild donkey. (1) This word occurs only once in the sacred scriptures, and like our Schmidt, Abu al-Walid and Rabbi Tanchum interpret it correctly, comparing it to chapter 8:9. Add Genesis 16:12, Jeremiah 2:24, Job 11:11. **f)** The disagreements of interpreters have made this passage obscure; some missed the goal, others the grammatical logic. For example, the Tigurine Bible: "Because Christ himself will flourish among the wombs" (many Jews mistakenly derive this from a word meaning "meadow"). Others: "Because Ephraim still bears fruit among his Israelite brothers," an allusion to the name Ephraim (Genesis 41:52). Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a major Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> says: "Because he multiplied sins more than his brothers (Judah and Benjamin)." The Septuagint, Vulgate, and others, using an Arabic meaning, say: "Because he divides and has a kingdom divided from Judah." **f)** Therefore the <term>Eurus</term> <note>The East wind, often used as a metaphor for a destructive force from the desert.</note> shall come (chapter 12:1), a wind hostile to plants, parching them. See Ezekiel 19:12, Jonah 4:8. This *Eurus* is none other than the Assyrian enemy, compared to the East wind for his harshness, and to a wind rising from the desert for his great violence. **g)** *a wind sent by the Lord himself*, see Isaiah 27:8, 40:7, Psalm 48:8. Just as the Assyrian is elsewhere called the "axe of God" (Isaiah 10:5, 15). **h)** *turbulent and rapid*. **i)** *and with his shame he shall dry up*. **k)** *his spring* (Jeremiah 51:36). **l)** *and it shall be dried up* (Ezekiel 19:5). **m)** *his fountain*, so that their republic is utterly overturned. **n)** *he*, the enemy compared to the wind, *shall plunder* (Psalm 44:11). **o)** *the treasure*. **p)** *of all precious things* (Jeremiah 25:34).

**CHAPTER 14, v. 1. q)** Tigurine: "He has failed." Syriac: "She is guilty," namely of manifold idolatry (chapter 13:1, 2) and crimes, and will eventually be devastated. **r)** *Samaria* the city and its citizens, who rebelled against their God. This is the final and most cruel effect of the arriving Assyrian enemy. This verse is closely connected to the preceding ones. Later, this same Samaria was besieged for an entire year by Hyrcanus <note>John Hyrcanus, the Hasmonean leader (2nd century BCE).</note>, son of Simon Maccabaeus, and was finally captured and leveled to the ground. Josephus reports that he directed torrents through it until no trace of the city remained. Later, Herod rebuilt it and named it *Sebaste* in honor of Augustus. Its fall has been compared by some to the capture of Constantinople by the Turks. **s)** *because she was rebellious* (Deuteronomy 21:18). Others: "She provoked her God," but that strains the grammar.

<column-break/>

**k)** *which*. Others: *because*. What follows is interpreted in various ways. **(1)** Tigurine: Otherwise he would not have stayed in the "birth-place of sons," but through sincere repentance would have freed himself from his straits as soon as possible. **(2)** Louis de Dieu: So that he does not remain in the mouth of the womb, but repents early. **(3)** We, with Schmidt, say: he is foolish because he does not stay in the womb for the set time until his proper maturity, or the New Testament time, when I will deliver them from the power of hell (v. 14). **l)** *the right time* (Micah 5:2, Galatians 4:3–4). **m)** *he does not persist* or remain, waiting in true repentance, hope, and faith. **n)** *in the matrix*, or the womb of sons (2 Kings 19:3), in which the Church was kept under the shadows of the Old Testament until Christ (Galatians 3:23, 4:27).

**\* v. 14. o)** Namely, when I deliver them from the hand and power of hell (in the proper sense, as in Isaiah 28:15, Psalm 9:18) to which all men are subject because of sin. The Apostle cites this in 1 Corinthians 15:54 regarding Christ and his victory over hell and death. Thus, there is no doubt that a New Testament promise is found here. The sense is: "That son is not wise because he does not persist in the womb until the time when I shall free them from the hand of hell." This refers to the New Testament era which the Old Testament faithful were meant to wait for. Thus, our passage speaks properly and without distortion about the New Testament, until death itself is abolished, just as the Apostle applied it literally.

->CHAPTER 14, v. 1. . . . . . HOSEA 13:14–15. . . . 14:1<-

<vocab>Hosea, Samaria, Messia, Goel, Eurus, Assyria, Redemtor, Infernum, Prosopopœia, Hyrcano, Sebasten</vocab>

<summary>This page provides a Christological interpretation of Hosea 13:14, identifying the "plague of death" as Christ's victory over the grave, while also detailing the historical destruction of Samaria by the Assyrians and later by John Hyrcanus.</summary>

<keywords>Redemption, Christology, Goel, 1 Corinthians 15, Samaria, Assyrian invasion, John Hyrcanus, Sebaste, Biblical metaphors, Womb of the Old Testament</keywords>

--- Page 1193 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the final warnings of Hosea 13 into the concluding chapter of the book, Hosea 14. While the previous page focused on the inevitability of judgment and the "destruction" of the grave, this page begins with a graphic description of Samaria’s fall and immediately pivots to an earnest, final call for Israel's repentance and return to God.</meta>

<margin>
**verse 1. a)** Against Jehovah their God (referencing chapter 13:4). Jonah [translates this] "against the Word of God," since the rebellion was against His word, covenant, and warnings by turning to other gods. This was also the view in the Arabic Manuscript mentioned by Pococke <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), an English Orientalist and biblical scholar.</note> (p. 758), which translates it: "because they rebelled through idols" or "with idols." ***)** Namely, the citizens of Samaria and those who fled there for refuge (compare chapters 7:16 and 9:13). ***)** See chapter 10:14; 2 Kings 8:12; Psalm 137:9. **y)** And their pregnant women—specifically the women of the Samaritan people. The Hebrew term is masculine here, which has bothered some, but it also appears specifically in *Perishff.* <note>Reference to a specific grammatical or exegetical work.</note> 128:3 and in *Beshiah Thr.* 4:16. ***)** They shall be ripped open. See a similar description of barbarity and cruelty in 2 Kings 8:12; 15:16; Amos 1:13. **Partu** (by birth): Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt.</note> notes that the masculine verb includes the pregnant mothers. There is no doubt that all these threats from God were fulfilled through Shalmaneser [the King of Assyria], although in the very brief history of that event in 2 Kings 17:6, these specific cases are not listed. Or we might think that the Israelites finally repented during the calamity itself (since the siege lasted three years) and obtained a mitigation of their punishment (compare Jeremiah 18:7-8; Ezekiel 33:14; Joel 2:14; Jonah 3:9-10, etc.). **Toward** repentance, God certainly still seriously rouses them in verse 2 and following, making it clear through most gracious promises that this will not be in vain (verses 5–9). Here, the Prophet finally concludes his prophecy with a notable closing statement in verse 10.

**v. 2. a)** Return therefore, O Israel, to Jehovah your God (chapter 12:7; Zechariah 1:4, etc.). For you must necessarily do so (Hosea 2:9). **b)** If you desire to become a participant in the eternal salvation I have promised (chapter 1:7; 13:14) and the grace toward which I am most inclined (chapter 14:5 and following). According to Schmidt, a new section begins here: the Vth Sermon, and the final word of the prophet or of Jehovah Himself.
</margin>

...as the only way and remedy for salvation; joined with the sweetest Gospel promises, after the severe punishments for their rebellions and idolatries were announced in verse 1, and chapters 13:7, 8, 15, etc. Just as when Samaria perished—Israel, who was informed of their fall in their iniquities, should return to the Physician and receive health, or at least begin to, having fallen, etc., as Blessed Jerome writes. **b)** In opposition to Judah and Benjamin, the Kingdom of Israel (the ten tribes) is usually denoted in our Prophet (see chapters 1:4, 7; 4:15, etc.). Because its destruction was certainly predicted (chapters 13:1, 7, 11, 15; 14:1, etc.), Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi.</note> applies this to the Israelites remaining in the land of Judah, while others want these words addressed to the Jews themselves, so that they at least might learn from the example and punishment of the others. **Alternatively,** some say this is preached to the godly and the elect remaining among the people, though we think it pertains rather to everyone: the grace of God is seriously offered to all, provided they repent (Ezekiel 18:21, 22, 23, etc.). In the meantime, we prefer, following Schmidt, to refer this entire sermon to the New Testament and to Christ: a time when it would come to pass that even among the Israelites dispersed among the nations, this sermon of repentance would be sent, and many would be converted to Christ their God. — We take the Imperative as a Future; *Return* means *You shall return* at last under the Messiah, etc. For the Prophet (as you [Schmidt] continue after other remarks) elegantly places himself in the person of a New Testament preacher. But while we gladly acknowledge what was said about the conversion of Israel to Christ (from comparing chapter 2:1-2; 3:5; 11:10-11), such a change of person would be present from the very beginning of the speech. Thus, we think all these things should be subordinated, as above in chapter 2:1, 8, etc. For the Prophet certainly also said and wrote these things for the use of his present audience. And by this mitigation of punishments (as in chapter 2:1), not only were the stubborn made entirely inexcusable, but the few remnants of the godly were also to be sustained and lifted up against despair under those horrific calamities (compare Jeremiah 3:6, 8, 12 and following; 2 Chronicles 30:6–9). **c)** This is the same as the word "unto" according to Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (Radak), a medieval Jewish commentator.</note> (comparing Deuteronomy 4:30; 30:2; Joel 2:12). It indicates the limit of conversion most clearly: as if to say, "all the way to"; that is, not just occasionally, but perfectly convert, not stopping until one reaches God (compare the opposite in chapter 12:7). **d)** to Jehovah, who is your God not only by right and creation, but primarily by covenant, adoption, and the affection promised toward you, and so He will without doubt receive you into grace upon your repentance. (Schmidt, compare note on chapter 1:9 and 4:6). **e)** The moving reason for repentance, as in chapter 6:1. **f)** To be struck or to stumble, both spiritually and politically (chapter 4:5; see notes on 5:5 and 10:3, 8). **g)** Chapter 5:5; 9:7. No one else besides Jehovah can save or restore you: therefore, even now at last, seriously repent and return. **v. 3. h)** Take with you words. (Compare similar construction in Genesis 31:23; 43:1; Exodus 14:6; Joshua 8:1; 1 Kings 1:33; 11:18). This is in place of a gift or victims (Genesis 43:11; 1 and 2 Kings 8:8; compare Micah 6:6). **Alternatively,** receive them with an obedient mind and take my words with you, neither forgetting nor neglecting them (compare Proverbs 1:3; 2:1; 4:20; Job 22:22; and Luke 2:19, 51). But to Schmidt, "taking words with oneself" means to premeditate what is to be said, and to keep it in a ready memory, so that when it is time to speak, it may be brought forth without error. **i)** What those words are, or at least their essence, follows immediately: *and say, take away all iniquity*, etc., which Luther expressed well by supplying the demonstrative. Schmidt thinks a formula of prayer is being given to the penitent, as in Matthew 6:9; Luke 11:2; Numbers 6:23. **Jonah [Targum]:** Bring with you words of confession. The Lord does not demand from you in repentance (says Kimchi on this passage) silver and gold, nor burnt offerings (which the Israelites poured out for their idols at great expense, chapter 2:10, 15; 10:1; 12:12), but He wants good words, by which you confess your iniquities and return, as has already been said in verse 2, with the soul's preservation toward Jehovah with all your heart, and not just with your lips; as Kimchi again well says (compare chapter 2:9; 5:5; 6:1; Joel 2:12-13; see similar construction in Isaiah 48:20; Jeremiah 31:7; Psalm 66:3; 1 Chronicles 16:35). **m)** all; as in Psalm 51:17. For He would forgive a part in vain if one [sin] remained on account of which we stayed away from God (compare Psalm 103:3; 130:8; Galatians 3:10; James 2:10; Matthew 18:32; Colossians 2:13). **n)** take away our iniquity (verse 2), by which we are burdened as by a wall (Psalm 32:1; 38:5; Matthew 11:28). **o)** receive, give, and bring forth (Genesis 18:5; 1 Kings 17:10; Psalm 68:19; compare Ephesians 4:8) good: for certainly in us, He finds no other good than what He Himself has placed there. Thus God is asked to take of His own good to bestow upon us: Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar.</note> *Hierozoicon* I, 414. Tarnovius understands the righteousness of Christ as the "good" to be accepted for the penitent; we follow him in this sense: *and receive our good* (opposed to iniquity), the righteousness which we offer in faith for ourselves: not our own, but Christ's (compare above chapter 3:5). **p)** and we will render thanks for those benefits of yours (Psalm 50:14). **q)** Vulgate: calves, that is, young bulls (compare Psalm 51:21). The Septuagint (LXX), along with the Syriac and Arabic, translates: <term>original: καρπὸν χειλέων ἡμῶν; fruit of our lips</term>. So also Hebrews 13:15, in the same sense. For <term>original: καρπὸς; fruit</term> is taken for an offering, just as <term>original: κάρπωσις, κάרπωμα, ὁλοκάρπωσις & ὁλοκάרπωμα; fruit-offering, whole-offering</term> occur everywhere in the Greek version for sacrifice and burnt offering (Bochart, cited above). **r)** Vulgate and others: of our lips. As if to say, "we will render calves, namely [the calves] of our lips," an understood construction for the preceding absolute noun, as in Luke 12:14; Ezekiel 11:16; 40:15, etc. Others say, "instead of young bulls we will render our lips," that is, confession, praises, and thanksgivings, which you may hold in the place of sacrificed goods. Thus the Arabic Manuscript in Pococke (p. 775): "we will render in place of the offering of victims the sacrifices of our lips." That is, offerings suitable for the New Testament (compare Ephesians 5:1, 6; Psalm 51:22; 1 Peter 2:5). This kind of sacrifice was far more acceptable to God even under the economy of the Law than the sacrifices of oxen, says Bochart (comparing Psalm 50:8–14, 23; 51:17, 18; 69:31, 32). **Jonah [Targum]:** and let the words of your lips be accepted by you, as bulls for favor upon the altar (compare Psalm 141:2 and the note above on chapter 6:6). **v. 4. s)** The Syriac begins, *And say, the Assyrian*, etc., namely the King and the people in whom we have wrongly trusted (see chapter 5:13; 7:11; 8:9; 12:2). **Jonah [Targum]:** The King of Assyria shall not save us. **t)** The Prophet brings them to repent of what he often rebuked in the Israelites: when in their distress they made covenants with the Assyrians for help. But the Assyrians did not save them, but finally destroyed them. Schmidt (compare above chapter 5:13, 14; Jeremiah 3:23; Psalm 33:16, 17). **u)** upon horses, in which we took pride (compare chapter 1:7; Isaiah 2:7; Proverbs 21:31; Job 39:19 and following). **x)** we will not ride; we will place no confidence in our own strength nor in the help of others (compare chapter 10:11; Isaiah 30:16). **Jonah [Targum]:** and upon chariots or swift horses we will not trust (compare Psalm 20:8). **Alternatively,** and upon Egyptian horses we will not mount, nor will we implore their help as in chapter 7:11, because this defense is also vain (Isaiah 31:3). Thus Rashi, Abraham ibn Ezra, Abarbanel, Jerome, etc. (comparing Isaiah 30:1; 31:1). So Schmidt. It should be noted, he says, that Egypt abounded in horses (compare Deuteronomy 17:16; 1 Kings 10:18) and their horsemen fought (compare Exodus 14:6, 7, 9; 15:1, etc.). Thus the Israelites "rode upon horses" when they hired horsemen, chariots, and horses and called them to their aid by covenant.

<summary>This page contains the final call to repentance for Israel (Hosea 14:1-4), contrasting the horrific fate of Samaria with the offer of divine healing. The commentary explores the shift from physical animal sacrifices to the "calves of the lips"—spiritual sacrifices of confession and praise.</summary>
<keywords>Hosea 14, Samaria, repentance, Assyria, spiritual sacrifice, calves of the lips, Rashi, Kimchi, Sebastian Schmidt, biblical commentary, conversion, messianic prophecy</keywords>

--- Page 1194 ---
<meta>This page continues the conclusion of Hosea chapter 14. Having called for repentance in the previous verses, the text now details the specific renunciations the people must make and the lush, restorative promises God offers in response. The commentary focuses heavily on the transformation of Israel from a withered state to a flourishing garden, often interpreting these botanical metaphors through a Christian theological lens.</meta>

# HOSEA 14 CHAPTER 14.

<margin>
Without any merit of their own, as those who deservedly earned my anger and hatred, as seen above in chapter 9, verses 15 and 17. On this matter, compare also chapter 2, verses 16, 21, 22, and 25; and for the word, see Psalm 68:10 and Ezra. <note>original: "sine ullo merito ipsorum..."</note>
</margin>

<margin>
**y)** nor will we say anymore, as we foolishly did. Compare above chapter 2, verse 7. They promise perseverance in faith and the worship of the true God. **x)** <term>Our God</term><note>Hebrew: Eloheinu</note> that is, our divinities! Compare Ezekiel 43:17 and 44:17. **a)** Compare chapter 8:5, 13:2, and Isaiah 2:20. We shall recognize and detest that madness. **b)** Because. As in Deuteronomy 3:24, 1 Samuel 2:23, chapter 15:15, etc. **c)** In You, our Messiah and Savior alone, and no other; see chapter 1:7, Isaiah 45:17, 24, etc. **d)** He shall obtain mercy and be saved: This refers back to chapter 1:6, 8, and 2:3. Compare Isaiah 9:16, 54:8, and Proverbs 28:13. **e)** The orphan or the ward, who is destitute of all help. Compare above chapter 5:15, Psalm 10:14, 18, Psalm 68:6, Job 29:12, Lamentations 5:3, and Exodus 21:22, Deuteronomy 10:18.
</margin>

<gloss>y</gloss>And we will not say <gloss>x</gloss>anymore "Our God" <gloss>w</gloss>to the work of our hands, <gloss>v</gloss>for in You the orphan finds mercy. 4

<margin>
v. 5. **f)** I will indeed heal. Christ responds to the petition of the penitent in verse 3. He takes away all iniquity and explains that, and how, he is to receive the repenting Israelites. Therefore, this healing is spiritual, at least principally, as in chapter 6:1, Isaiah 6:10, Jeremiah 3:22, Malachi 3:20, Luke 1:77, 5:31, and 24:47. Compare also chapter 5:13, 7:1, and 9:16. Just as the Prophet predicted in chapter 3:5 that Israel would finally turn to Christ under the New Testament, so now he predicts that Christ will receive them mercifully and kindly and heal them. This is a remarkable promise, not conditional as many think, but one that declares a thing that will certainly happen. **g)** Their turning away and apostasy, that is, the idolatry and sins by which they turned away from me. Chapter 11:7, 10; Jeremiah 2:19. I will receive them in their conversion and forgive their sins. **h)** I will love them as they repent, as I did before in chapter 3:3, 11:1, and Malachi 1:2; constantly and with eternal love, Jeremiah 31:3. **i)** Truly, spontaneously and bountifully, with a kind and liberal mind, by free love and the proper movement of my grace. Ephesians 1:5, 9, 11; John 4:10. Just as a father has mercy on his children, Psalm 103:13; Luke 15:20.

->LIKE WINE<-

---

3, 5. and would be subject. <term>Rashi</term><note>A famous medieval Jewish commentator</note>: Spontaneously by My Spirit. Compare Psalm 51:14. This responds to that penitent plea in verse 3: "and receive and grant us good." **k)** because she has turned away, Jeremiah 2:35; namely, in their true repentance and faith. **l)** My anger, which had been kindled by their stubbornness, chapter 8:5. **m)** from him, namely Israel, my people; so that I will no longer remember their sins. Compare Micah 7:18 and following; Psalm 103:8 and following.

v. 6. **n)** I will be. <term>Jonathan</term><note>Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> says, as often, "My Word shall be." The consequences and effects of that healing and love of Christ in verse 5 are placed here. For Christ continues his discourse and promise, but clothes them in metaphors and similes throughout two verses. **o)** Like the dew, which, where rain is rare, falls abundantly and makes the earth fertile. It moistens, renews the buds, and makes them grow. Compare chapter 6:3, Deuteronomy 32:2, Psalm 72:6, 19, Psalm 133:3, and Proverbs 19:12. It signifies, as <term>Rivet</term><note>André Rivet, a 17th-century theologian</note> has it, the grace of justification, regeneration, and sanctification in Christ to be liberally communicated for a new life. Compare Micah 5:6. Its opposite is what was said above in chapter 13:15. **p)** truly and to the spiritual Israel. Romans 9:6, 7, 8; Galatians 6:16. **q)** from which, equipped with new strength, he may bloom; he will blossom in verse 8. Isaiah 27:6, 66:14; in the garden or Church of God, Psalm 92:13, 14. **r)** like the lily, Isaiah 35:1, 2; Song of Solomon 2:1, 2. Most beautifully (Matthew 6:28, 29 compared with Ephesians 5:27) and most abundantly. For nothing is more fertile than the lily, says Pliny, often sending out fifty bulbs from one root. *Natural History*, Book 21, chapter 5. **s)** and he shall strike; he will extend and thrust into the earth, i.e., he will fix and spread his roots: so that, with Christ dwelling in their hearts, they may always be rooted and grounded in him and in his love, Ephesians 3:17, 18; Colossians 2:7, nor can they be uprooted, Amos 9:15. See the appropriate passage above in chapter 9:15; compare also Isaiah 37:31. **t)** like Lebanon, that is, according to Jonathan and most others by <term>metonymy</term><note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it</note>, like the trees of Lebanon. Compare verses 7 and 8, Isaiah 35:2, 60:13, Psalm 92:13. Others say: he shall strike his roots like Lebanon, i.e., like Mount Lebanon, so that strengthened by divine help he himself shall stand unmoved and always flourishing, compared with Psalm 125:1 and Matthew 16:18.

v. 7. **u)** They shall go, or continuing in growth they shall proceed and advance further, they will expand and spread themselves. Jeremiah 12:2. "The branches go," says S., "when they become longer and more and more, in the way that they also extend themselves." Other effects of that celestial dew in verse 6 and its operations follow here. **x)** the branches or his young shoots, Isaiah 53:2, Ezekiel 17:22, Psalm 80:12, Job 8:16. Namely, of the Israel of God, or the Church in verse 6. Others say: of each of them. So S. and Jonathan: "His sons and daughters shall multiply," or his progeny, as <term>Grotius</term> has it; or <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> and <term>Abarbanel</term>, which we take in a spiritual sense, comparing Isaiah 49:21, 22; John 3:6; 1 Peter 1:23. But S. says, "To us, however, these branches will dig out something of those things which belong to the faithful themselves, and are found in them: namely, the increases of faith in the first place, and of charity, and of whatever Christian virtues; when the faithful proceed and strive toward a continually greater perfection," compare Philippians 3:12 and following; add Colossians 2:10, Galatians 5:22, and 2 Peter 1:5–8. **y)** and it shall be, i.e., so that it is like the olive or as an olive. Which, as the cypress has it, is ever-green and fruitful, always green and full of fruits. Compare Judges 9:9, Jeremiah 11:16, Psalm 52:10, Psalm 128:3; also Psalm 1:3. <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐלאία κατάκαרπος — "like a fruitful olive tree"</note>. So say the Arabic and Syriac: like an olive tree decorated with its fruits. But Jonathan wanders further from the text: "and their splendor shall be like the splendor of the sacred lampstand," undoubtedly from Leviticus 24:2; which compare with Philippians 2:15, Matthew 5:16, and Zechariah 4:11, 12. Glory, excellence, or his beauty. Job 40:10, Daniel 10:8. The more significant Glory of the olive is its many fruits, by which it is decorated and made beautiful, for which it is also praised, says S. Compare Philippians 1:11. **a)** and there shall be a fragrance to him; pleasing indeed to the pious, and acceptable to God: partly the works of the faithful and the variety of the table, partly their labors in the ministry of the word, and the zeal for converting others, as in 2 Corinthians 2:15. S. adds Philippians 4:18, Revelation 5:8. **b)** like Lebanon in verses 6 and 8, of whose most pleasing fragrance (both from the fragrant herbs and trees themselves, such as cedars, Pliny *Natural History*, Book 13, chapter 5, and from the flowers of trees and herbs) Scripture also makes mention elsewhere. See Song of Solomon 4:11, Sirach 39:14. But Jonathan says: "like the incense of aromatics"; perhaps for the reason that the Temple was sometimes called by the name of Lebanon, as some suggest in <term>Pococke</term><note>Edward Pococke, a 17th-century Orientalist</note>, page 794; compare Jeremiah 22:23, Habakkuk 2:17, Zechariah 11:1.

v. 8. **c)** The Vulgate: "They shall be converted, sitting in his shadow." That is, according to S., as if to say: "In addition to those things which I have promised up to now, this also will happen, that those converted from the Gentiles will return to the Church of Christ, dwelling..." etc. The Gentiles are said to return to the shadow of Israel because even in the Old Testament, proselytism was granted to them (compare Ruth 2:12). Thus, the most abundant conversion of the Gentiles to Christ under the New Testament is predicted here. This is S. But Pococke on page 796b thinks that the happiness of those who are members of the Israel of God, i.e., the Church of Christ, is described throughout this whole verse, as it was compared with a tree in the preceding verses. Jonathan: "They shall be gathered from the midst of their captivity," with which compare John 11:51, 52. **d)** Jonathan: "They shall dwell under the shadow of their Messiah or Christ; who is God himself in verses 2, 3, 4, and is the protector of his Church, even in afflictions." John 16:33, 2 Corinthians 4:11. Compare Job 7:2, Isaiah 4:6, 25:4, 5, 32:2, 37:35, Psalm 17:8, 36:8, 91:1, Song of Solomon 2:3, Lamentations 4:20. But it seems better, says S., that the relationship is not referred to the more remote subject, which is God, but to Israel. The shadow of Israel, however, is not what it makes, but what Christ makes for it in the New Testament; namely, the shadow of his grace and protection, etc. So <term>Brentius</term><note>Johannes Brenz, a Lutheran reformer</note>: "Why are many words needed? Israel will at last grow into such a tall, wide-spreading, and glorious tree that all who flee to its shadow will dwell under it confidently and securely." **e)** they shall also bring to life the grain, those who are converted from the Gentiles; namely, through the cultivation of their field and its sowing, as Rabbi Tanchum rightly has it in Pococke, page 799; which in a spiritual sense means: they will abound in all grace and the fruits of good works, compare Matthew 13:23. For the words, compare Genesis 19:32, Isaiah 62:8. **f)** and they shall blossom, verse 6. **g)** as the vine, compare Zechariah 8:12. By these two species, grain and wine, just as all other fruits of the earth are elsewhere signified, so here all kinds of fruits of faith are signified. S. For the Church, whether collected from Israelites or from Gentiles, will not be like an empty vine, as above in chapter 10:1, or bearing grapes of Sodom (Deuteronomy 32:32) and bad grapes (Isaiah 5:2), but like a fruitful branch, bearing the sweetest fruits on its vine, Christ Jesus, John 15:5, 8. Whence an honorable mention of it shall also be made, and it shall be extolled with praises by all men. See Brentius. **h)** The memory or mention of him, namely God or Christ, according to many interpreters, as above in chapter 12:6, compare Song of Solomon 1:2, 3. According to S., however, and <term>Tarnovius</term> and others, it is the memory of each of those dwelling in the shadow of Israel, even of the Gentiles converted to the Church. For these are no less a pleasing fragrance to God than the Israelites or Jews themselves in verse 7. S. Others say: "his fragrance." So Tremellius, Piscator, Abraham Ibn Ezra, Kimchi, Rabbi Tanchum, etc. Compare Leviticus 24:7, Numbers 5:26.

<meta>This page concludes the 14th chapter of Hosea. It follows the previous page’s discussion of repentance and God’s promise to heal Israel's faithlessness. This final section provides a dialogue between Ephraim (representing the people) and God, followed by a concluding wisdom statement on the "ways of the Lord."</meta>

<page-num>552</page-num>
<header>HOSEA. CHAPTER 14.</header>

-> **9** **Ephraim shall say: "What have I to do anymore with idols?" I have answered him and I will look upon him; I am like a green cypress tree; from Me is your fruit found.** <-
-> **10** **Who is wise, and he shall understand these things? Prudent, and he shall know them? For the ways of the LORD are right, and the just shall walk in them; but the transgressors shall fall therein.** <-

---

-> word <note>original: "dubar" - likely referring to the catchword "ver-" below</note> &emsp; Signature: Cccc 3 &emsp; 72 b 3 <note>Likely a reference to a specific manuscript or folio</note> <-

<margin>
He explains the words: Since Ephraim has said, "What more have I to do with idols?" then I will grant his desires; I will answer or look upon (compare Ecclesiastes 10:19) and I will watch over him. Thus say the Arabic Manuscript, Rashi <note>A famous 11th-century French rabbi</note>, Abraham Ibn Ezra, Kimchi, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
**i)** It will be so pleasant and sweet, just like the wine of Lebanon; which was not only celebrated by the ancients but is still praised today, compare Pliny’s *Natural History*, Book 14, Chapter 7. Schmidius also thinks this alludes to the sacrifices of the Old Testament in which wine was poured out to God, and they themselves were a pleasing memorial before God. Compare Exodus 29:40, 41 and the commentary on this place.
</margin>

<margin>
**k)** The Syriac version <note>An ancient Aramaic translation of the Bible</note> adds: "Ephraim shall say"; the Targum of Jonathan says "The Israelites shall say: 'What concern is it of ours to serve idols anymore?'" etc. So say Rabbi Solomon [Rashi], Ibn Ezra, Kimchi, and most interpreters. Tarnovius says: After God finished these very grand promises, now finally Ephraim repeats the pledge of obedience and faith made earlier (verses 3 and 4), and God in turn (in the latter half of the verse) promises His grace again, etc. But others, such as the Zurich Bible and Castalio, take "Ephraim" as a direct address, and these as the words of God Himself, in this manner: "O Ephraim, what have I to do anymore with idols?" as if to say, God says: "Do not join those things to Me anymore, for I alone am God, and all-sufficient for you": compare 2 Corinthians 6:15, 16. But Schmidius, who correctly explained the previous verse regarding converts from the Gentiles, also attributes these words to them, in this manner: "O Ephraim (you will say, having turned to the shadow of Israel): **l)** what business have I anymore with idols?" They thus renounce the worship of idols and trust in them. Compare Jeremiah 2:18, Joshua 22:24, Judges 11:12, 2 Samuel 15:10, 1 Kings 17:18, etc. and 2 Corinthians 6:16. **m)** Chapter 13:2. **n)** The readings are quite varied. The Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic read: "I have humbled him." The Zurich Bible: "I have afflicted, and again looked upon him"; as some read Psalm 18:36 and 1 Kings 8:35. Rabbi Tanchum says: "I, God, humbled Myself, and looked upon him," comparing Isaiah 57:15, etc. Some compare Psalm 119:67. You may also read it in this way.
</margin>

So says Castalio: "Having turned away from him, I shall look upon him." Truly, all attribute these words to God and explain them as His gracious providence; as if it were the opposite of what was said in Deuteronomy 31:17. Schmidius, however, as we have said, puts it thus: "I, the converted Gentile, have responded to the Lord graciously calling me." Compare above, chapter 2:17. **o)** "And I will diligently observe him," on the Lord’s part, compare Psalm 135:1, 2. Compare the word above in chapter 13:7, Numbers 23:9, 24:17. Or, as Schmidius prefers, "I will sing," that is, as the Syriac has it: "I will celebrate Him." Compare the word in the simple Hebrew form in Judges 5:1, Psalm 7:1, though this is usually constructed with a person in the dative case and the song in the accusative, for example Exodus 15:1, Psalm 21:14, Psalm 33:3, Psalm 59:17, Psalm 89:2, etc. **p)** "I," according to Pococke (page 807) and other interpreters, "I, God, will be to Israel like a green and thick tree; overshadowing, refreshing, and protecting them." Jonathan and Jerome, however, understand this as referring to Israel; and Schmidius thinks it is too harsh to interpret this as referring to God. In his opinion, the convert from the Gentiles here continues and says to Ephraim: "I am even now (and shall be) **q)** like a fir tree; others say like a cypress or a green juniper." Compare Isaiah 55:13. The comparison, says Schmidius, is made with the Fir because its greenness is excellent: especially if one considers not just the greenness of the leaves, but the moisture and health, or the strength of the tree. In this way, the faithful Gentile claims for himself the strength of the Spirit and constancy of faith. **r)** "From Me also," not as from a primary efficient cause, which is God and Christ (John 15:2, 5, 8), but as from a converted brother, who stands in the communion of faith and its fruits. **s)** "Your fruit is found in works of faith and charity." Compare Song of Solomon 7:14. Other interpreters say this of God: "From Me," that is, by My provision (John 15:5, 2 Corinthians 3:5, Philippians 2:13, Hebrews 13:21). "The fruit of good works is found in you, and most abundant ends will be supplied to you if you rest in Me," compare Romans 8:28, 32. For this must be understood not carnally but spiritually, as Rabbi Tanchum himself advises in Pococke, page 110, as seen in the following verse: *Who is wise, that you may understand these things?* verse 10. **t)** *Who is wise, that he may understand these things?* etc. There follows here an <term>epiphonema</term><note>A summary exclamation or concluding statement</note> or general conclusion of the entire prophecy; by which the Prophet not only deplores the lack of true wisdom in most of his hearers (compare chapter 13:13 and the note on Isaiah 53:1), but once more excites each and every person to a serious care for their salvation and a pious meditation on his sermons. Compare Isaiah 42:23, Jeremiah 9:11, Psalm 107:43. Furthermore, the Syriac takes the interrogative "Who" as a relative: "He who is wise shall understand these things, and he who is prudent shall know them." Compare Exodus 24:14, Judges 7:3, Isaiah 50:10, Proverbs 9:4, etc. So also Castalio and others. But Schmidius says: "Who is wise? and he will understand, or surely he will understand these things: who is prudent? and he will know them," so that these words provide a certain hope that those who meditate on these things out of a love for true wisdom will understand them. Compare Psalm 111:10. **u)** "Let him understand these things," or consider them. Compare Deuteronomy 32:29, Psalm 82:5, Proverbs 28:5, Daniel 12:10. The phrase indicates that everyone *could* understand if they only wished, through the grace of the Word and the Holy Spirit; for he exhorts that each person do what they can: then consequently he indicates that many are not going to do what they can through Christ. The demonstrative "these" and the following suffix "them" are referred by some to the whole book; however, they primarily look back to the immediately preceding promise, says Schmidius. **x)** Genesis 41:33, 39, Deuteronomy 4:6, Psalm 119:104. **y)** "And let him know them." Compare Ephesians 4:18, Psalm 92:7. This is not a bare understanding and knowledge, but one that results in action, work, and the fruit of work; so that one believes in them, is comforted by them, and works well by trusting them, because he knows that the ways of the Lord are right. **z)** Some translate: "that they are right." But others better translate it causally: "Because, or for they are right, level, and just," etc., thus giving the reason for the exhortation to know them. Compare Psalm 19:9, Proverbs 8:9, Nehemiah 9:13. **a)** "The ways of the Lord," proposed to you in my sermons. Compare 2 Samuel 22:22, 31, Isaiah 26:7, 57:14, Ezekiel 18:25, 29, Psalm 25:8, 10. **b)** "Therefore the righteous" (Psalm 1:5, 6, Proverbs 2:20, chapter 4:18) who are truly righteous through a purely gracious justification (Psalm 32:1 onward, Romans 4:6, 7, 8) through faith in Christ Jesus (Isaiah 53:12) and now serve righteousness (Romans 6:13, 1 John 2:29, 3:7, 8, etc.) **c)** according to their duty, by the power and spirit of Christ (Ephesians 4:31) they "gladly walk in them" (Ephesians 2:3, 1 John 1:7, 2:23, 3:3). Constantly and without stumbling (Psalm 119:33, 112, 165) with the Scripture shining before them (Psalm 119:105) and even under temptations (Matthew 24:13) they proceed in them from virtue to virtue (Psalm 84:8). The Targum says: "And the righteous who walk in it (the way of God) shall live in eternal life; but the impious shall be delivered to hell, because they did not walk in them." Compare Isaiah 66:24, Mark 16:16, James 1:25, etc. **d)** "But the transgressors" (chapter 7:13, 8:1, Psalm 1:2, 46:8) whose love, goal, and work it is to transgress—that is, to do things that are in truth nothing but transgressions, even if they profess to know God (Hosea 8:2), while in fact denying Him by their deeds (2 Timothy 3:4, 5, Titus 1:16) **e)** by their own negligence and fault "they stumble," and here by the just judgment of God they fall and are driven to ruin in them (verse 2, Isaiah 40:30, Proverbs 15:19). Compare Luke 2:34, 1 Corinthians 1:23, 24, 2 Corinthians 2:15, 16, 4:3, 4, 1 Peter 2:7, 8, Revelation 22:11, Sirach 39:24. Let us therefore follow the way of the Lord, and let us pray to Him that He may lead us by His Spirit and direct us in His ways: so that we may proceed straight to eternal happiness through our Lord Jesus Christ!

<meta>This page marks the transition from the Book of Hosea to the Book of Joel. The previous page concluded the prophecies of Hosea with a call to wisdom and a promise of healing for Israel. This page introduces the Prophet Joel, debating his historical context and providing the opening verses of his prophecy regarding a devastating plague of locusts.</meta>

# ON THE PROPHECY OF JOEL
->PREFACE.<-

<margin>
1. Joel's Name.
2. Family
3. Homeland
4. Age
</margin>
**JOEL**, (a name which means *THE LORD is God*, see Joel 2:27, Isaiah 9:5, Psalm 118:27-28, etc.) was not the son of the prophet Samuel mentioned in 1 Samuel 8:2, as the old Rabbis foolishly thought <note>original: "inepte putarunt"</note>; (see the Preface by Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> and Abendana’s notes); rather, he was the son of Pethuel. We have nothing more to say about his family from the sacred writings. Although some have handed down that he was from the tribe of Reuben and was born, died, and was buried in the territory of Beth-horon, we—along with the scholar Calovius—leave that as an uncertain matter. Nor is the time in which he flourished expressly recorded, either in the title of the book in chapter 1:1 or elsewhere in the Holy Scriptures; hence, learned men do not agree on his age. Some Jewish scholars think he rose to prominence before that seven-year famine under Joram, son of Ahab (2 Kings 8:1); others place him in the time of Manasseh and Hezekiah; others, such as Tarnovius, Calovius, and Heidegger, make him a contemporary of Josiah and Jeremiah because of the similarity of their topics (comparing Jeremiah 14:1 and following) and because Joel nowhere mentions the ten tribes of Israel, which they suppose had already been carried away into Assyrian captivity. 

We, along with Jerome <note>an early church father and Bible translator</note>, Abarbanel, Lightfoot, Vitringa, Majus, and Luther in his German Preface, believe he lived at the time of Hosea and Amos. We base this both on the order the book has held among the Twelve Prophets since ancient times, and on its subject matter. (Compare the notes on chapter 1:1 and 2:11). For Joel seems to have spoken to the people of Judah about the same plague of locusts, drought, and fire that Amos spoke of to the Israelites (see Joel 1:9, 14, 16; 2:1, 15, 17, 23; 4:1, 6, 8, 17, 19, 20). Out of the sense of present evil and the fear of future destruction by the Chaldeans <note>the Babylonians</note>—of which these calamities were like precursors—he aimed to stir them to repentance and faith in Christ, setting forth the sweetest comforts, partly earthly and temporary, and partly heavenly and eternal, to be fulfilled in Christ and the New Testament. 

Therefore: 
I. Joel predicts the imminent slaughter by locusts, drought, and famine—harbingers of destruction by the Chaldeans—with a mournful voice, repeatedly urging them to return to God (1:2-12 and 2:1-11). He gravely exhorts the Jews to repentance (1:13-20 and 2:12-20). 
II. To those who repent, he offers both physical and spiritual promises, especially concerning the *coming of Christ*, the teacher of righteousness (2:21 and following); the *outpouring of the Holy Spirit*; the signs preceding the death of Christ and the final destruction of Jerusalem; and the calling of the nations and the salvation of those who believe in the name of Christ (3:1 and following). 
III. He describes the punishment of the Church's enemies and the judgments upon hostile nations in chapter 4, looking through those events not only to his own time but also to the final fate of the Church and the eternal Jerusalem. 

Hence, the New Testament frequently looks back to our prophet. Compare, for example, Matthew 24:29 with Joel 3:4; Acts 2:17 and following and 10:45 with Joel 3:1 and following; also Romans 10:13 with Joel 3:5; and Revelation 9:7-9 with Joel 1:6 and 2:4-5. From this, not only is the divine authority of this prophecy confirmed (as asserted in 1:1), but it is also clear that it was written for our instruction, so that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures, we might have hope (Romans 15:4). For these are the last days, and the mystery of God will finally be fulfilled, just as He promised to His servants the prophets (Revelation 10:7).

<margin>
5. Jewish Audience
6. Purpose &
7. Argument
8. Parts
9. Canonical Authority
10. Use.
</margin>

---

# THE BOOK OF JOEL,
->Hebrew: *Yoel*<-

1. **The word of the LORD that came to Joel the son of Pethuel.**
2. **Hear this, you elders, and give ear, all inhabitants of the land! Has such a thing happened in your days, or even in the days of your fathers?**
3. **Tell your children about it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation.**
4. **What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten; what the swarming locust left, the hopping locust has eaten; and what the hopping locust left, the destroying locust has eaten.**

<column-break/>

<margin>
(continuing from previous points): ...in order (2:15, 16, 17). (4) He also promises more peaceful times in Judea with an abundance of all things (2:18, 19). (5) Amos (Chapter 1:2) demonstrates that the same imminent calamity of famine and barrenness which Joel predicted was already pressing upon the Israelites and would continue to press (4:6, 7). (6) Amos begins his prophecy with the same sentiment (1:2) with which Joel almost closes his (4:16).
</margin>

16. *The LORD will roar from Zion, etc.* Furthermore, after the title of the book, *the parts of this first chapter are threefold*: I. He prophesies a dire famine to be brought by a destructive army of locusts at the command of God the judge (verses 2-12). II. He exhorts the Jews to repentance, to be promoted by fasting and earnest prayers (verses 13-20). 

**Verse 2.** b) This is an "Apostrophe" or a waking-up call, as in Hosea 4:1, 5:1, Amos 3:1, 4:1, and Psalm 49:2. Jerome says: *By rhetorical art, he makes the listener attentive through the magnitude of the events.* c) *Elders* (v. 14, 2:16) refers to those who had seen and heard many benefits in their lifetime. Compare Job 37:7, Deuteronomy 32:7. d) Jerome notes: *Wherever these two phrases ("hear" and "give ear") are placed together, it must be understood that they pertain not only to the simple sound of the words, but to the hidden understanding of what is said;* compare Genesis 4:23, Isaiah 1:2. e) *All inhabitants of the land* refers to the Judean land (v. 14, 2:1). f) *Has this happened in your days?* g) *Indeed, has it happened in the memory of your fathers?* He proclaims that what he says is new and unheard of: namely, that the locusts brought such a slaughter, or that these cares were such as none could remember from any age; specifically in the land of Judah, just as once occurred in the land of Egypt (Exodus 10:6, 14). At the very least, this was more severe in terms of its duration. Compare below 2:2, 25. 

**Verse 3.** h) Regarding this, see 1 Kings 5:13. i) It is as if he says: this proof of divine severity is so immense and unheard of that it is worthy for you and your descendants to speak of it forever. Compare Exodus 10:2, Deuteronomy 4:9, 6:7, Psalm 44:2, 78:3. k) *To the later or following generation* (pp. 9, 13). Compare Psalm 102:19. Therefore, this prophecy also looks toward more remote times, as we hinted in the Preface (sections 8 and 10). 

**Verse 4.** l) *The residue* (Exodus 34:18). Jerome says that after the introduction, the narrative follows. m) The Vulgate and Septuagint translate this as "caterpillar," but according to Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar of biblical animals</note>, it is a type of locust (Joel 2:25, Amos 4:9) from an Ethiopic root meaning *to cut or cut off*, because it cuts off not only the grass but also the tender branches of trees. Leo Africanus says of locusts: *They eat the trees themselves along with the leaves and fruit.* n) *Has consumed* or *will consume*. See verse 15 and the note on verse 5. o) *The locust*, so named for its multitude. See Exodus 10:5, 15, Deuteronomy 28:38-39, Amos 7:1-2. p) *Has eaten.* The *Yelek* is another type of locust (Nahum 3:15-16) which, along with the previous ones, once afflicted the Egyptians (Psalm 105:34). According to some, the name comes from a root meaning "to be white," based on its color; but according to Ibn Ezra and Bochart, it is so called from "licking" and "consuming." Others understand it as a cankerworm, others as a "Bruchus" <note>a wingless locust or beetle</note>—that is, according to Hesychius, a "golden-cleanser" or a fruit-destroying beetle. Bochart rejects these because in the Scriptures it is numbered among the types of locusts. (Hieroz. II. p. 455).

<column-break/>

<margin>
**CHAPTER I. v. 1.** a) The Title and Inscription of the book. See Hosea 1:1 and our Preface to this book, number 9. We add here what Vitringa observed in his *Type of Prophetic Doctrine* (p. 350) regarding Joel's age. Our opinion, he says, is the same as Abarbanel's: that he lived at the same time as Amos, and a little before him published this prophetic sermon which bears his name. Our arguments are: (1) that among the enemies of the Jews, only Egyptians and Edomites appear (4:19), and there is so far no mention of Assyrians or Babylonians in this prophecy. For the passage in 2:20, like the earlier ones, pertains to the plague of locusts. (2) that he reproaches the Tyrians, Sidonians, and Edomites for exactly the same crimes as Amos did (they had carried away many captives from Judah of every sex and age, treated them harshly, sold them to foreigners, and invaded and occupied their fields); and he denounces a similar judgment upon them (4:2-7, compare Amos 1:9-11). (3) At the time Joel preached, the sacred rites were still standing among the Jews in their proper order...
</margin>

<meta>catchword: order</meta>

**CHAPTER I. v. 1. [Grammatical notes on Hebrew accents and Dagesh for verses 1, 3, 5, 15, 20, 21, 32.]**
