<meta>This page continues the introduction to the Book of Joel, specifically transitioning into the commentary on Chapter 1. The previous page discussed the various scholarly opinions on Joel’s historical era and family background. This page begins the actual text of the prophecy, focusing on the debate between literal and allegorical interpretations of the locust plague described in the opening verses.</meta>

# 660 JOEL. CHAPTER I. 1

<margin>
**q)** *Chasil:* <note>original: "S. bruchus"</note> A type of wingless locust or "cankerworm." Others, with the Septuagint and Vulgate, translate this as "rust" or "mildew," but incorrectly. According to Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar of biblical animals</note>, it is the fourth type of locust (6); see Isaiah 33:4 and among the Egyptian locusts in Psalm 78:46. The name is derived from its "consuming" nature; see the root **Ch-S-L** in Deuteronomy 28:38 and the Targum on Nahum 3:15. Therefore, this plague seems to have been prolonged over several years, so that as one swarm departed from a field, another succeeded it, consuming the remains of the previous one, until nothing was left in the field for humans or beasts to eat. See below where we will provide more details on this epidemic evil. Furthermore, a heavy question is debated: Should what is said here about locusts be explained literally, as Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi, Luther in his Commentary, and Bochart do? Or should it be understood, according to the mind of Jerome, Cyril, and others, that the "locusts" represent the enemies of the Jews and the Church—for example, the Babylonians, Persians, Greeks, and Romans—as Abarbanel contends? Likewise, if Chapter 1 is to be interpreted literally, should at least the descriptions in Chapter 1:6-7 and Chapter 2 be taken metaphorically as referring to the Assyrians (according to Grotius) or the Babylonians (according to Calovius and Gurtler)? Or should a "double sense" be applied to both chapters—a literal sense regarding locusts and a mystical sense regarding enemies? Just as the descriptions of real locusts in this context transition into the "mystical locusts" of the Holy Apocalypse? This was certainly the opinion of Vitringa on Revelation 9:3. He said: "Even if I do not deny that the passage speaks of locusts properly so-called in its primary sense, I am simultaneously persuaded that a higher and more sublime mystery lies beneath those words, and that under the image of four kinds of locusts, he depicts four numerous armies of fierce and distant nations who would devastate the people of God at various times." This is nearly the same opinion as Cyril and Theodoret. For the latter, after writing that some interpret these things tropically <note>figuratively</note>, says: "I believe these things are true; but I also think that what is understood literally actually occurred." Indeed, Jerome himself, as Bochart observed, seemed to waver between both opinions: "Unless I am mistaken," he says, "it seems to me the Prophet has reserved something here: the impiety of the enemies is narrated under the figure of locusts." And again, he speaks of the locusts as if they were being compared to enemies: *so that when you read 'locusts,' you think of enemies; and when you have thought of enemies, you return to the locusts.* Compare Amos 7:1-2 and the notes there.
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 5. a)** *Awaken:* 2 Kings 4:31, Proverbs 23:35. **b)** *Sober up:* <note>original: "Εκνήψατε"</note> see 1 Corinthians 15:34. **c)** *Weep:* to whom long drinking bouts usually bring sleep. See Ecclesiastes 11:13, Romans 13:11. **d)** *Those who drink wine to drunkenness:* see Isaiah 24:9, Amos 6:6. **e)** *Over the must* <note>new wine</note> (5) Joel 4:18, Song of Solomon 8:2, see Hosea 7:14. **f)** *Because it is cut off:* i.e., taken away (v. 13), as seen below in v. 9 and 16, namely by the locusts, the first species of which (v. 3) was named for its "cutting off." But here the Prophet prophesies unless they should repent. (v. 15). He speaks of future events in the past tense, in the manner of the prophets. See Isaiah 5, 13, Jeremiah 15:7, Ezekiel 7:12, etc. Although nothing prevents us from thinking these evils have already partially happened to the Jews, far more terrible ones were coming unless they repented. See Joel 2:24, 25. **v. 6. g)** *For:* to explain how the destruction of wine threatened in v. 5 will happen, *a nation shall ascend:* namely, of locusts. Not only do other writers and poets speak this way (see Bochart), but also Solomon regarding ants, etc. (Proverbs 30:25, 26). See below Joel 2:2, 5, 7, 11. **h)** If we take this as referring to God, as in v. 7, 4:2, and Hosea 9:3, others refer it to the Prophet. **i)** So numerous, copious. Joel 2:2, 5, 11, Numbers 32:1, Isaiah 60:22. **k)** So that there is no numbering it. See Judges 6:5, 7:12, Jeremiah 46:23. **e)** *Its teeth:* that is, of the nation of locusts. **d)** *Are the teeth of a lion:* which John transferred to the mystical locusts in Revelation 9:8. Pliny says of locusts: *gnawing everything with their bite, even the doors of houses.* **e)** *And the molars* (Proverbs 30:14) *of a lioness:* Isaiah 5:29. Their strength is truly astounding for such a small creature, so that Jerome rightly exclaims: *What is more innumerable and stronger than locusts, which human industry cannot resist?* **v. 7. f)** *That nation of locusts (v. 6) has laid my vine in desolation:* see v. 12, Hosea 2:14. **g)** For the mystical meaning of the vision, see Isaiah 5:1, Psalm 80:9. **h)** *And my fig tree:* the tree in v. 12, mystically see Matthew 21:19 and following. **h)** Bochart translates as *into a breaking, a stripping of bark.* <note>original: "εἰς κλασμόν"</note> Arabic root *broke under too much weight* and *a broken branch of a tree.* For locusts graze on the highest branches of trees, or break them by the sheer weight of their numbers sitting on them. Others, like the Septuagint with Ibn Ezra, translate *into foam*, i.e., into a thing of nothing. Compare Hosea 10:7. **i)** *It has stripped it bare:* Genesis 30:37, Psalm 29:9. **k)** *And cast it down* to the ground: Jeremiah 9:18. **l)** *They have turned white:* Isaiah 1:18. Either because the bark was pulled off, or because the bark itself rotted. **m)** *Its branches:* (3) Genesis 40:10, 12.
</margin>

<margin>
Furthermore, because this plague is rare in our lands by divine blessing, we will add only one testimony here from Thevenot's Collection, Part I, p. 12, so that the less experienced may understand how great a calamity this evil is. They can read more in Bochart and Ludolf's commentary on the *History of Ethiopia*. An anonymous author in Thevenot, describing the part of Scythia held by those called today the Cossacks, reports: "They are infested by locusts, which sometimes come to them, especially in exceedingly dry weather. They are driven by the east or southeast winds from Tartary, Circassia, and Mingrelia, which are almost never free of them. They are carried through the air like clouds in thick swarms; these clouds are fifteen or eighteen miles long and nine or twelve miles wide. They obscure the air so much that the clearest sky appears cloudy where they hover. Within two hours they harvest the crops: which increases the price of grain and sometimes creates a famine in those regions. These insects do not live longer than six months. In autumn they lay eggs, each laying three hundred, which hatch the following spring. If it happens to be dry, they multiply even more fiercely than the previous year. Heavy rains kill them and prevent the eggs from hatching. Pigs are very fond of these eggs and are used to clear the fields of them. The eggs are clustered like bunches, similar to the ears of Turkish wheat (maize), whose grains they resemble in color and shape. The Cossacks are freed from the locusts only if a north or northwest wind carries them into the Black Sea. When they are newly hatched and cannot yet fly, they enter houses, get into beds, and crawl into tables and food, so that food can hardly be eaten without some being swallowed. At night when they rest, the ground is covered with them to a depth of four fingers, or even more. If the wheel of a passing cart crushes them, such a foul odor arises that it can hardly be borne, especially when their carcasses begin to rot." Compare below Joel 2:2, 20. **v. 8. n)** *Lament* therefore; understand *my land* (v. 6). **v. 6.** *The virgin daughter of my people* (Jeremiah 14:17, Lamentations 1:15). The word is feminine (1) from the Chaldean and Syrian root *to mourn, weep, or lament*. See Jonathan on 2 Samuel 3:33. It agrees with *wail* above in v. 5. **o)** *Like a virgin:* Deuteronomy 22:19. Cocceius says: "He compares the people of Israel to a betrothed virgin not yet brought to the house. Such as Mary was betrothed to Joseph, who is called a betrothed woman. So was the people betrothed to Christ, who had not yet come to them, etc." **p)** *Girded with sackcloth:* or haircloth, the garment of mourning (Isaiah 3:24, 15:3, 22:12). **q)** Who mourns for her husband of her youth who is dead or taken from her; to whom she was recently betrothed and whom she still loves most tenderly. See Isaiah 54:6, Proverbs 2:17. **v. 9. r)** *It is cut off* by the locusts (v. 5) and ceased (Numbers 11:33). Jerome: "Because of the multitude of locusts or enemies, who are described under their appearance." See note v. 4. **s)** v. 13, Leviticus 2:1. **f)** Joel 7:14, Numbers 25:7. **x)** *From the house* or Temple of the Lord (v. 14, 16), which therefore still existed and had not yet been destroyed, as Abarbanel claims. See note at v. 1.
</margin>

An elegant Wordplay <note>The Hebrew words for "destruction" (shod) and "Almighty" (Shaddai) sound similar.</note>, as in Isaiah 13:6. **s)** However, the name of God does not sound like "Destroyer," but the "Omnipotent," as the Arabic verb is "to strengthen." compare note on Jeremiah 51:2, Hosea 13:15, Amos 3:5. **v. 16. t)** A question of one attesting, as in Genesis 4:7, Deuteronomy 31:17, 1 Samuel 12:17, Amos 5:20. **u)** before-one's-hands, as in Isaiah 38:6. **x)** with us looking on with the greatest sickness of heart. compare Psalm 23:5. Bochart. compare note on chapter 2:17. **y)** compare Isaiah 16:10, Jeremiah 48:33. Moreover, this joy ceases when the offerings are missing; and they were missing because the locusts left nothing untouched. Thus far in this chapter concerning the Locusts; there will now follow a lamentation regarding the drought, both preceding and accompanying and promoting the locusts, compare chapter 2:3 and note above at v. 7 and below at v. 19. **v. 17. z)** They have rotted, i.e., perished as dead or vanished, on account of the immoderate heat and drought v. 19, 20. (1) Arabic Root: "The filth dried up on the hand." Or it is the same as the Talmudic *ebash* "to rot," as below chapter 2:8. **yabash** <note>original: "יבש"</note> is the same as *ebash* according to Kimchi. **a)** scattered grains (1) compare the Syriac Matthew 13:31, John 12:24. **b)** under their clods. (2) Properly these are clods of a torrent (Job 21:33) then any clods. compare the root in Judges 5:21 which in Arabic signifies "to carry away"; and the names derived from it signify a flow of water carrying away the earth. However, the seed is corrupted under the clods not only when rains are excessive, but also from extreme drought: which, if we wish to speak properly, the seeds are said not so much to rot as to vanish. Pliny XVIII. 24: *“The reason why sowing is done more quickly in damp places is so that the seed does not rot from rain: in dry places later, so that rains may follow: lest lying for a long time and not conceiving, it vanishes.”* **c)** they are laid waste Amos 7:9.

# [Page 565] JOEL. CHAPTERS I. 2.

<margin>
**18. a)** storehouses (see 2 Chronicles 32:27). **c)** they are destroyed, they have collapsed (Proverbs 14:31). **f)** granaries? (compare Haggai 2:19). Jerome: <note>Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> "Because, if there were no grain and wine, it would be in vain to prepare storehouses and winepresses." **g)** see verse 10 and compare Amos 4:7-8; Haggai 1:11.
**18. h)** How the beasts groan! (Compare Jeremiah 14:7; Exodus 21:11), namely, for lack of fodder. **i)** and they are perplexed (3) (Exodus 14:3; Esther 3:15). The noun is in Ezekiel 22:5. **k)** herds of cattle (Genesis 29:10). **l)** compare Genesis 47:4; Psalm 18:5. Therefore they groan and low; otherwise than they are accustomed when necessities are not lacking (Job 6:5). **m)** also flocks of sheep and goats (Song of Solomon 1:7). **n)** they are desolated. Others: they are shamefully marred; namely, they are punished on account of the guilt of men (see Ephesians 24:6; Ezekiel 6:6; Hosea 14:1).
**19. o)** For I implore help, O Lord (Psalm 28:1). Here is a specific example of the Prophet’s own prayer. Cocceius. <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology."</note> **p)** for the fire of the Sun (chapter 1:2, 3) and immoderate heat (compare Amos 7:4; Ephesians 9:17, 18). **q)** it consumes the pastures or the green places of the desert (verse 20; chapter 2:22; Psalm 32:2). **r)** the flame burned; namely, in the grain (chapter 2:3; Malachi 3:19). Extreme drought is described. In a dry spring, the emergence of locusts is greater (Pliny the Elder, Natural History XI. 29).
**20. s)** Even the beasts of the field (verse 18; chapter 2:22; compare Jeremiah 14:5, 6; Hosea 4:3). **t)** they cry out to you (3) (Psalm 42:2; compare Jonah 3:7, 8). **u)** because they have withered, they are dried up (Genesis 8:14). **x)** channels of water (chapter 4:18; Psalm 42:2); indeed, the great abyss was swallowed up by the heat and part of it was consumed (Amos 7:4), so that even the fish perished (Hosea 4:3). **y)** verse 19; Jeremiah 23:10.

Amos 3:6. **f)** for the day of the Lord arrives (verse 11); namely, the day of vengeance and retribution. Specifically, that which is mentioned in chapter 1:15. **g)** because it is near (see chapter 1:15 and CHAPTER II).
Compare Amos 6:3. Bochart: <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a French Protestant scholar of biblical animals.</note> "The time when the beasts are to come is called the Day of the Lord; because then the Lord names a day for the guilty and will demand punishment from them." Others, with Jerome, understand the "day of the destruction of the Jews by the Babylonians" through the metaphor of locusts. So
</margin>

18 How the beasts groan! The herds of cattle are perplexed because they have no pasture; even the flocks of sheep suffer punishment.
19 To You, O LORD, I cry out; for fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and a flame has burned all the trees of the field.
20 The beasts of the field also cry out to You, for the water brooks are dried up, and fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness.

# כ CHAPTER II.

1 Blow a trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm on My holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of the LORD is coming; surely it is near.
2 A day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness. Like the dawn spread over the mountains, a people numerous and mighty; such as has never been from of old, nor will there be again after it for years of many generations.
3 Before them a fire devours, and behind them a flame burns. Like the garden of Eden is the land before them, and behind them a desolate wilderness; and indeed, nothing has escaped them.
4 Their appearance is like the appearance of horses; and like war-horses, so they run.

---

Cocceius in this place and Gürtlerus <note>Nicolaus Gürtler (1654–1711), a Swiss theologian.</note> (Prophetic Theology p. 123) say: "The Prophet predicts in this first chapter: I. the day of the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians (vv. 1–11). II. the return from Chaldea to Canaan, with preceding repentance and prayer (vv. 12–21). III. the coming of the Messiah, the Teacher of righteousness and author of all benefits, both earthly and heavenly (vv. 22–27)." However, Schmidius <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian.</note> more correctly says there are three parts to this chapter: I. Prediction and description of the plague of locusts (vv. 1–11). II. Exhortation to repentance and prayers (vv. 12–17). III. Promise of restoration (vv. 18–20) and then compensation (vv. 21 and following). Compare the note at chapter 1:4.

**v. 2. h)** *Day of darkness.* As light signifies prosperity, so darkness in the Scriptures denotes adversity (see Amos 5:18; Esther 8:16). Here also the literal sense of the word holds (compare Exodus 10:15). **i)** and *of gloom* (Isaiah 8:22; Zephaniah 1:15). **k)** *day of clouds* (Ezekiel 30:3) and *obscurity* (2 Samuel 22:10; Jeremiah 13:16; see the note above at chapter 1:7). **l)** as the dawn (Isaiah 58:8) **m)** spread over the mountains (Hosea 5:1; Psalm 105:39; Job 36:30). It signifies that this evil will be spread both widely and quickly. For both are characteristic of the dawn, whose light is scattered everywhere in an instant (Isaiah 58:8; Psalm 139:9). **n)** *a people numerous and mighty in arms* or powerful (vv. 5, 11); just as in chapter 1:6 he called the locusts a powerful and innumerable nation (so Proverbs 30:25, 26). **o)** *such as, or: the like of which* has not been before in Palestine (compare Exodus 9:18; chapter 10:14 and the note above at 1:2). **p)** compare note at Isaiah 44:7; chapter 46:9. **q)** nor will there be again. He means it will not be added to, i.e., happen again (compare Nahum 2:1). **r)** to the years of every age (Deuteronomy 32:7). **s)** *Before him*, the coming people of locusts, i.e., before his arrival. Thus regarding time (Amos 1:1; Nahum 3:5). **t)** *everything* almost is now consumed by fire and extreme drought (see chapter 1:19). **u)** and *after him*, i.e., after his departure (as Zechariah 7:14). **x)** *a flame shall burn the rest.* (chapter 1:19). **y)** *as the garden of Eden.* <note>original Greek: "as a paradise of delight"</note> (see Genesis 2:8). **z)** before the drought and the arrival of the locusts it was a pleasant land, which is compared to the garden of Eden, like Egypt and the field of Sodom before the disaster sent by God (Genesis 13:10; see also Ezekiel 36:35). **a)** but after his departure. **b)** chapter 4:19. **c)** and also that which escaped (chapter 3:5) will not be for the remnant of the locusts. For they will consume everything so that nothing remains of the land's produce. **d)** *Like the appearance of horses.* (compare Ezekiel 1:26). **e)** *his appearance.* (as Revelation 9:7). **f)** *as horsemen*: so they run (v. 9). Jerome: *Not that the Babylonians are compared to horsemen, but that the locusts, by a metaphorical transfer from enemies, are called horsemen running here and there. Compare note at chapter 1:16.* **g)** Like the noise of chariots. Jerome: so will be the sound of the locusts (compare Revelation 9:9). **h)** even over the peaks of the mountains (Ezekiel 6:13). **i)** they shall leap (Isaiah 13:21; Nahum 3:2).

**k)** like the noise of a fan of fire. Micah 29:6. <note>The "fan" refers to a winnowing tool that creates a rushing sound like wind or flame.</note>
**l)** consuming the stubble. Ecclesiastes 7:6. Bochart: <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a famous scholar of biblical animals.</note> This also perfectly fits the locusts, which fly with a great noise, fall upon the fields, and grind the crops with their teeth. Pliny the Elder writes (Book 11, Chapter 29): "With such a sound of flying wings that they are believed to be other birds."
**m)** verses 2 and 11. Bochart: It should be noted that this particular army is no longer called "a people," but "like a people." Therefore, when he called them a "nation" and a "people" above in verse 2, he was speaking metaphorically, calling those forces a "people" which in reality are not a people, but are like a people drawn up for battle. This is similar to what he adds in verse 7: they run like mighty soldiers, and like warriors they climb the wall; this is lest anyone should imagine actual soldiers and warriors here. But though they are not soldiers, they are rightly compared to them (1) by reason of their number and strength, and (2) by reason of the order they maintain in flight and in their march. Furthermore, to indicate a mystical sense, Revelation 9:11 also attributes a King to the locusts, which they otherwise lack according to Proverbs 30:27. **m)** prepared or ready (Jeremiah 6:23) for battle. Compare Revelation 9:9 and the notes above on verses 1 and 4.

We have translated very simply: "neither shall they change their paths." That is, they proceed like the most orderly soldiers; they do not wander outside their ranks. How aptly this is said of locusts, Jerome, an eyewitness, explains, writing thus in his Commentary on this passage: "This we recently saw in this province (Palestine). For when the swarms of locusts came and occupied the air between heaven and earth, they flew in such order by the disposition of God's command that, like the mosaic tiles that are fashioned on pavements by an artisan's hand, they kept their place, and did not decline to the other side even by a nail's breadth, so to speak." **w. 2. *)** Or one from another (Genesis 37:19; Exodus 10:23). **a)** the word "press" (2) Judges 2:18. **b)** but individuals, each one (Lamentations 3:39). M. I. says this is properly said of men, but here of locusts, because he compared them with men and mighty soldiers (verses 5 and 7). **c)** they shall go on their path or track (1 Samuel 6:12; Isaiah 59:7). Solomon also observes order in locusts (Proverbs 30:27), so that God rightly calls them "His great army" (below, verse 25). **d)** even rushing upon the sword (2 Chronicles 32:5; Job 33:18). **e)** they shall not be wounded (Amos 9:1; Job 6:9). This is the same, according to Kimchi and M. I., as the word for "wounded" in 1 Kings 10:37. **f)** *panah* and *panah* (face/turn); see also above on chapter 1:17. That is, according to M. I.: They will not be like human enemies, because you will not keep them out with swords or closed gates. For other animals, as Bochart notes in his *Hierozoicon* (II, p. 478), flee at the sight of a man; but these attack man of their own accord. Consequently, when a cloud of locusts attacks, everyone hides in their houses, lest they provoke them if they come out. **v. 9. f)** They shall walk through the city (Isaiah 33:4; Nahum 3:5). **g)** they shall run on the walls (verses 4, 7). **h)** they shall climb into houses, as Moses also foretold to Pharaoh (Exodus 10:6). **i)** through the windows themselves (compare Jeremiah 9:20). **k)** they shall enter like a thief (compare Matthew 24:43; John 10:1). Hence Jerome says: "Nothing is impassable to locusts, since they penetrate fields, crops, trees, cities, houses, and the secrets of bedchambers." Theodoret says: "For not only by flying, but by creeping up the walls, they penetrate into houses through the windows." See the note above on chapter 1:7. **v. 10. l)** Before him the earth trembles (verses 1, 6; Deuteronomy 2:25; 1 Samuel 14:15). **m)** and the heavens are moved (chapter 4:16; Judges 5:14). Jerome: Not that the locusts have such power that they can move the heavens and shake the earth; but that to those suffering adversity, the heaven seems to fall and the earth to fluctuate because of the magnitude of their terror. Pliny (11, 29): "That plague is understood as the wrath of the gods. For they are seen larger, and fly with such a sound of wings that they are believed to be other birds; and they overshadow the sun." See note on verse 5. **n)** sun and moon (chapter 3:4, 4:15). **o)** they are darkened; see similar instances from other causes in Jeremiah 4:28; Ezekiel 32:7; Micah 3:6; Isaiah 50:3, etc. **p)** they withdraw (Samuel 24:19) and take away from men (below chapter 4:15; Genesis 30:33; Psalm 85:4) their splendor (Proverbs 4:18). Jerome: "Before the multitude of locusts covering the sky, the sun and moon shall be turned into darkness, and the stars shall withdraw their light: while the cloud of locusts in the midst does not allow the light to reach the earth." **v. 11. q)** For the Lord, like a General, has given His voice (chapter 4:16; Psalm 18:14) **r)** before His army (see verse 25 and note on verse 3). **s)** which I rightly call so, for His camps are very great (or, so that His camps might be very great). Compare verse 2 and note on chapter 1:7. **t)** that he might be many (verse 5; Amos 5:12). **u)** who does or executes His word (Psalm 103:20, 148:8). And the magnitude of the Lord's power is demonstrated even in small living creatures, says Jerome. **x)** for he is great (Hosea 2:2; Zephaniah 1:14; Malachi 3:23; Jeremiah 30:7). **y)** see note on verses 1, 2 and chapter 1:15. **z)** and very terrible (verse 31; Habakkuk 1:7). **a)** and who can endure him? (Malachi 3:2). That is, the Lord by His word has conscripted many forces to exercise a heavy judgment upon sinners, which no one can endure. Here the threats end, followed by repeated exhortations to repentance and many promises in God's name. See note on verse 1. **v. 12. b)** Vulgate: "Now therefore." Tigurine: "But even now." Grotius: <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> He shows there is still some hope of escaping (Jeremiah 18:7-8). **c)** see note on Hosea 11:11. **d)** see Hosea 14:2 and Zechariah 1:4. **e)** Deuteronomy 6:5; 1 Samuel 7:3. That is, seriously and in good faith; without hesitation or hypocrisy (Jeremiah 3:10). **f)** chapter 1:14; Jeremiah 31:9. **g)** Grotius: to signify the sorrow conceived from sins. Jerome: The sense is: "Indicate repentance of the soul with all your heart, and with fasting, weeping, and mourning: so that you who are now fasting may later be satisfied; you who are now weeping may later laugh; you who are now mourning may later be comforted." Some believe Isaiah 22:12 refers to this passage. So Vitringa in his *Typology of Prophetic Doctrine* (p. 36): "That Isaiah saw this prophecy will be clear to the prudent from a comparison of both." Nor does it matter that no memory of the plague denounced by Joel exists in the history of that time, any more than the great earthquake under Uzziah was omitted in the same; of which there is very clear mention in Amos 1:1 and Zechariah 14:5. **v. 13. h)** but rend or tear your heart and [wickedness] has consumed. Jonah: "And take away the impiety of your heart." Compare Deuteronomy 10:16; Psalm 51:19; Romans 2:28-29; Colossians 2:11; and the note on Hosea 13:8. **i)** as they otherwise did in horrific events and mourning. See Joshua 7:6, etc.; then for an entreaty, as in Isaiah 58:35 and Matthew 26:65.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Joel 2, moving from the description of the locust plague (the "Day of the Lord") to a call for communal repentance and the promise of divine restoration. The previous page established the locusts as a metaphorical "army" or "nation" sent as judgment; here, the text focuses on the liturgical response required from the people and the priests to avert complete destruction.</meta>

# JOEL. CHAPTER 2.

<margin>
**k)** Jeremiah 4:1. Hosea 14:2, 3. Zechariah 1:3. Malachi 3:7. **Jerome** <note>Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was a priest and scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note>: "Because great sins will be deleted by great mercy." **l)** Exodus 34:6. Jonah 4:2. Psalms 103:8, 145:8. Numbers 14:18. Nehemiah 1:3. **Jonah**: It differs (it removes anger). **m)** Psalm 86:5. **Jonah**: And he multiplies benefits and truth. **n)** And when he repents of the evil which he threatened, namely, if the sinner sincerely returns to his senses. Exodus 32:14. Jeremiah 18:8. Jonah 4:2. **Jerome**: "So that if we have performed repentance for our sins, he himself may repent of his threat, and the evils which he threatened us, he may not bring upon us; and by our change of mind, he himself may be changed." **Jonah**: And he may recall his word from bringing on the evil. See notes on 1 Samuel 15:11, 2 Samuel 24:16, Amos 7:3; and compare Ezekiel 18:11. Regarding the manner of punishment, see Amos 3:6.
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 14. p)** "Who knows?" This is the expression of one who hopes well in a difficult matter. See Jonah 3:9, 2 Samuel 12:22, compared with verses 13 and 14 there; also Isaiah 37:4 and Zephaniah 2:3. Lest perhaps, as **Jerome** writes, they should despair because of the magnitude of their crimes, or the magnitude of divine mercy should make them negligent. **Luther** <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), leader of the Protestant Reformation.</note> beautifully says: "In our language, this phrase sounds like a denial, or rather a doubt: 'Who knows?' But it is the most fitting voice of a penitent. For it embraces both the sense of sin, which makes us realize that God is justly angry and punishing us, and the hope of liberation, since God is by nature kind and placable." Compare Matthew 8:2. Nor should we neglect what **Calvin** <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), influential French theologian.</note> advises: that the discussion here is not about the forgiveness of guilt, but about temporal affliction. **q)** God will return (see Isaiah 63:17, Micah 7:19, Psalm 90:13, etc.) and he will repent of the evil he threatened in verse 13. Others, but less correctly, the **Hebrew scholars** <note>Referring to medieval Jewish commentators like Kimhi or Rashi.</note> construct and interpret these words: "Whoever knows there are sins in himself, let him turn from them; then he will have mercy on him." For which **Abendana** <note>Jacob Abendana (1630–1685), a Sephardic rabbi and scholar in London.</note> prefers: "and let him repent."
</margin>

...so that, after He has given a blessing and forgiven our sins, we may be able to offer sacrifices to God. **Jerome.** **v. 15. x)** *Therefore sound the trumpet* to call the people together (verse 1; Numbers 10:7), a function now performed among us by church bells. **Jerome**: He still exhorts them to repentance before the enemy army arrives. Above, he says, I had said: "Blow the trumpet in Zion"—because the day of the Lord is coming—now because I am kind and merciful, I command again and say: "Sound the trumpet in Zion," and preach repentance among the people. **y) v. 16.** Chapter 4:9; see note on Chapter 1:14. **z) v. 16.** **a)** Chapter 1:14. **b) Jerome**: *sanctify the assembly*; so that no one in the assembly is unholy, lest perhaps your prayers be hindered, and a little leaven corrupt the whole mass. I.** Where she is hidden with her husband. Cf. Isaiah 4:5 and the word in Deuteronomy 33:12; and on this matter Psalm 22:13, Luke 14:20. **Grotius** compares Exodus 19:15 and 1 Corinthians 7:5, which we consider subordinate to our view. **v. 17. k)** *Between the porch of the Temple and the Altar* of burnt offerings (1 Kings 6:3, 2 Chronicles 8:12), that is, immediately in front of the Temple. Cf. note on Ezekiel 8:16. Therefore, these things must necessarily refer to the First Temple, when the Temple, Porch, and Altar were still safe and intact; not to the present exile of the Jews, as **Abarbanel** <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), Jewish commentator and statesman.</note> contends. Cf. notes on Chapter 1:1, 9, 16. **l)** Chapter 1:9, 13. **m)** Ezekiel 20:17, Nehemiah 13:22. **n)** Verse 18, 26; Chapter 4:2; Deuteronomy 9:26. **o)** The people who are Your special possession. Chapter 4:2, 1 Kings 8:51, Isaiah 63:17, etc. **p)** Verse 19, Psalm 44:14. **q)** Specifically *that they might rule over them*. So compare Deuteronomy 28:37, Job 17:6. But the Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic, and Vulgate read: *that the nations should rule in [among] them*. **Tigurinus** <note>The Zurich Bible.</note>: *that the nations should command them*. See Deuteronomy 15:6, Psalm 106:41, Lamentations 5:8. The sense is, according to **Petrus a Figuero** in **Pococke** <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), English Orientalist and biblical scholar.</note> page 184 following: *Spare Your people* by taking away this plague of locusts; for if it rages and spreads further, it will bring extreme famine, and thus Your people will be forced, to relieve the necessity of hunger, to flee to the regions of the nations, and serve them for bread, and endure their rule and reproaches, just as they once fled to Egypt and became slaves. **r)** Ezekiel 32:12, Psalm 79:10. **a) Grotius**: "Where is that God whom they boasted was known and worshiped only by them?" **Jerome**: "Whom they boasted was their leader and defender." Micah 7:10, Psalm 115:2. **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), Dutch theologian.</note>: In this reasoning is included the weight of hope and God's covenant, which He struck and which was received by faith. Cf. above, Chapter 1:14. **v. 18. b)** Specifically *Then surely the Lord will be jealous* (demonstrate His zeal). Ezekiel 39:23, Zechariah 1:14. The Prophet speaks of future things in the past tense, as in a vision. Cf. note above on Chapter 1:5. Likewise, future things are announced with past-tense words in 2 Chronicles 15:4. **c) Jerome**: *for his land*; which he previously despised as if it were foreign, and allowed the locusts to devastate with their common people. Cf. Numbers 11:29. **x)** Cf. Amos 7:2, 6. **v. 19. y)** *And he answered*, or *the Lord will answer*, and He will not be silent to the prayers of His people's festival. **Jerome**: And He spared the penitent to such an extent that He made them worthy of His response, and said: because the locust, the crawler, and the rust devastated all your crops, therefore I will give you grain, and the rest which the Prophet describes. **z)** Cf. Deuteronomy 28:12, Hosea 2:10. **a)** Cf. Hosea 2:11, 14, 17. **b)** In opposition to Chapter 1:10; mystically the Gospel, Isaiah 55:1, Zechariah 9:17. **c)** See verse 24. **d)** Verse 26, opposite of Chapter 1:16, 18. Similar construction in Proverbs 25:16. Spiritually cf. Isaiah 66:11, Psalm 22:27. **e)** From the north. So **Lightfoot**, *Chronology* page 94: "The locusts," he says, "had broken in from that part of the land which faces the north, where it looks toward Syria and Hamath, and proceeding like an organized battle line (verse 5), they devoured whatever was in their path, moving toward the southern part; but there, where they turned away, descending below the ends of the Dead Sea, the sterility of the region afflicted with hunger those very creatures which had afflicted the whole region with famine." **Vitringa**, *Prophetic Doctrine* page 35: "This passage," he says, "just like the ones above, pertains to the plague of locusts." But **Calovius** and others understand northern enemies. So **Jerome**: "And the Assyrian and Chaldean, who is from the north—often, under the metaphor of locusts, he describes the onset of the Chaldeans by which Judea was devastated. Thus he preserves the metaphor in the rest, and speaks according to the location of the province, as if he seems to refer not to enemies, but to locusts." But cf. notes on verse 1:5, 9, 11 and Chapter 1:4. **g)** Chapter 4:6. **h)** I will drive or propel him. 2 Samuel 15:14.

The commentary features extensive debates between scholars like Jerome, Luther, and Abarbanel on the nature of divine repentance and the historical context of the Temple.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Joel 2, transitioning from the description of the devastating locust plague to the promise of divine restoration. The previous page discussed the call for repentance; here, the text explains the physical and spiritual renewal promised to the land and the people.</meta>

# JOEL 2. CHAPTER 2.

<margin>
Isaiah 37:22. This view was rightly refuted by Calovius; we, along with Tarnovius and others, apply this to the army of locusts, even though Calovius (p. 777) considers this interpretation forced. How aptly all these details apply to locusts will become clear both from what we have noted so far and from the words of **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> himself.
</margin>

<margin>
**i)** into a land parching with drought. See Hosea 2:5, Psalm 63:2. **k)** of the wilderness, or "desolate," that is, into the Arabian Desert. Cf. Deuteronomy 8:15. **l)** its face, namely, the front part of the swarm, which is turned toward the East to face the rising sun. **m)** I will drive into the eastern sea, toward the east of Jerusalem. Jerome understands this to be the sea where Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim once stood, now called the "Dead Sea" because no living creatures survive there. See Ezekiel 47:18, Zechariah 14:8. **n)** its rear, that is, the western or final part of the marching column. **o)** into the western sea, that is, the Mediterranean. See Deuteronomy 11:24 and compare Exodus 10:19. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), Roman author and naturalist.</note> says of locusts in his *Natural History* (XI.29): "Having been lifted in swarms by the wind, they fall into seas or standing waters." This might seem to happen by chance, but it is by divine will. **Bochart** <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant scholar known for his work on biblical animals.</note> does not mention southern locusts because, since Jerusalem was at the southern edge of Canaan, the southern swarms were few compared to the City and were included under other headings. See *Hierozoicon* II, p. 479. **p)** its stench and foul smell would rise up. Isaiah 34:3, Amos 4:10. **q)** it shall ascend, I say, into the nostrils of those passing by. **r)** its foul odor. Cf. the **Targum** <note>The Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> on Ezekiel 23:20. The Syriac root means "impure," "stinking," or "contaminated." **s)** because, or "after." Compare Job 1:5. **t)** because it has done great things. The **Vulgate** <note>The standard 4th-century Latin Bible.</note> says "because it acted proudly"; the Syriac and Tigurine versions say "because it acted insolently." **Jonathan** <note>The Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel.</note> says "because it multiplied doing evil," meaning it brought numerous and massive losses upon you. See 2 Kings 21:6, Zephaniah 2:10, Daniel 8:4. In contrast, look at the following verse 21 and verse 26, where this can be understood of God: "because the Lord is great in His works." **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> refers this to the Assyrian king Sennacherib. See 2 Kings 19:22, Isaiah 37:23.
</margin>

->21. Fear not, <gloss>x</gloss> O land; <gloss>y</gloss> be glad and rejoice, <gloss>z</gloss> for the Lord has done great things <gloss>a</gloss> in His deeds.<-
->22. Be not afraid, <gloss>b</gloss> you beasts of the field, <gloss>c</gloss> for the pastures of the wilderness are green, <gloss>d</gloss> for the tree bears its fruit; <gloss>e</gloss> the fig tree and the vine yield their strength.<-
->23. And you children of Zion, be glad and rejoice in the Lord <gloss>f</gloss> your God, for He has given you the teacher of righteousness <gloss>g</gloss> and He will cause to come down for you <gloss>h</gloss> the rain, the early rain and the latter rain <gloss>i</gloss> in the first month.<-
->24. And the <gloss>k</gloss> threshing floors shall be full of grain, <gloss>l</gloss> and the vats shall overflow with new wine and oil.<-

Regarding this passage, **Jerome** says: "Even in our own times, we have seen swarms of locusts cover the land of Judea, which afterwards, by the mercy of the Lord—a wind arising—were cast into the first and the last seas (the Dead and the Mediterranean). When the shores of both seas were filled with heaps of dead locusts which the water had vomited up, their rot and stench were so harmful that they even corrupted the air, and a plague was birthed among both cattle and men." See notes on chapter 1, verse 7.

**v. 21.** **x)** Therefore, do not fear for yourself, O land! The Prophet concludes the omens of judgment with joyful promises of rain after the drought, and of blossoming trees and seasons after the locusts. Upon the occasion of this discourse regarding the restoration of temporal things, he rises to the promise of spiritual blessings in the days of Christ, such as the gift of tongues, and the prediction of miracles that would accompany Christ's death and precede the destruction of Jerusalem. **Lightfoot**, *Chronology*, p. 94. **Jerome**: "To all those whom he had previously threatened, he now promises the opposite." Cf. verses 1–11. **x)** rather exult and be glad (v. 23). Zephaniah 3:14. Cf. above chapter 1:10. **y)** because the Lord has magnified Himself by doing good for His people in you. This stands in direct opposition to the locusts in verse 20, which brought numerous and very heavy evils.

**v. 22.** **z)** Do not fear even you, beasts of the field (Isaiah 56:9). This is in opposition to chapter 1:18, 20. **a)** for they shall sprout, or turn green. <term>Kal</term> <note>A basic verb form in Hebrew.</note> (1) cf. the <term>Hiphil</term> <note>A causative verb form in Hebrew.</note> in Genesis 1:11. **b)** concerning which he had said in 1:19, 20, "fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness." **c)** for the tree; that is, collectively, trees of every kind, as in Genesis 1:11. **d)** they bear their apples or their fruit. Ezekiel 34:27, 36:8. **e)** see chapter 1:7, 12. **f)** they bring forth their strength or their various fruits. Cf. a similar expression in Genesis 4:12. Specifically, as we noted from Jerome on verse 21, the Prophet promises everything contrary to the threats that preceded: namely, that the desert pastures will grow green, trees will bring forth fruit, and the fig and vine will give their vigor; rain, both early and late, will be sent abundantly by God at the earliest time; and the threshing floors will be filled with grain, and the vats will overflow with wine and oil. Thus, the years—meaning the annual harvests—that the four species of locusts had consumed will be restored to the wretched Jews. **Bochart**, *Hierozoicon* II, p. 481 ff. These things, because they are promised by the Lord, we believe happened according to the letter, and the past sterility was compensated by new crops: so that whatever the locust, the hopper, the blight, and the caterpillar had consumed was filled in the following years. **Jerome**.

**v. 23.** **g)** The Tigurine version reads "But also you," or "Especially you, O children of Zion." **Jerome**: "He speaks specifically to the children of Zion, that they should exult and rejoice, not in any trivial thing, but in the Lord their God." **h)** verse 21, Isaiah 29:19. Other Prophets speak in the same way when they prophesy about Christ. See Isaiah 61:10, Zechariah 2:14, 9:9. **i)** Isaiah 40:9, Psalm 32:11, Psalm 97:12, Philippians 4:4. **k)** **Jerome**: because God the Father gave to you in His decree. Isaiah 9:5, John 3:16. **l)** A Master or Teacher. <note>The Hebrew word "Moreh" can mean both "early rain" and "teacher."</note> Isaiah 9:14, Job 36:22, Psalm 84:7. Thus interpreted by **Jonathan**, the **Vulgate**, **Rashi**, and **Abarbanel**. Certainly not Isaiah or another prophet, as **Grotius** perversely wished following Rashi, but that one long promised in Deuteronomy 18:18, 19, and vehemently desired by the pious in Psalm 14:7, Luke 10:24; the witness, leader, and instructor of nations in Isaiah 55:4, and that unique Master and Teacher in Matthew 23:8, 10—a name Christ rightly claims for Himself. Isaiah 63:1. So **Abarbanel** on this passage: <note>original: "והוא מלך המשיח"</note> "and he is the King Messiah," who will show the way (Matthew 21:16) in which they ought to walk, and the works they should do. Others, including the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, translate it as "timely rain," which is less ideal, though the Hebrew word signifies both, as seen later in this very verse. See the detailed discussion by **Cocceius** and **Calovius** (p. 780). **m)** for righteousness, namely, true and eternal righteousness (Daniel 9:24), which He will not only teach (Hosea 10:12) but acquire by His merits and bestow with the most abundant gifts of His grace upon all who call upon His name with true faith (chapter 3:5). Cf. Isaiah 53:11, Jeremiah 23:5, 6, 33:15, 16, Habakkuk 2:4. For He changes hearts through the Holy Spirit and pardons the vice within us, just as John beautifully says in John 1:17, and as **Blessed Luther** writes excellently on this passage. **n)** and He will send down rain for you (Ezekiel 34:26). **o)** the <term>early rain</term> <note>Hebrew: *Moreh*</note>, after the seed is sown, and the <term>latter rain</term> <note>Hebrew: *Malkosh*</note>, when the crop has grown into stalks and ears and the grains are swelling. **Jonathan** interprets: the first rain in its time, and the latter rain in the month of Nisan. According to the opinion of the Hebrews, the first rain descends in the month of Marcheshvan (October), and the latter rain in the month of Nisan. See notes on Deuteronomy 11:14 and Jeremiah 5:24, Hosea 6:3, Zechariah 10:1. The Greek reads: <note>original: "ὑετὸν πρόϊμον καὶ ὄψιμον"</note> "the early and the latter rain." See James 5:7. **p)** in the very first time, or "in the first month" (Ezekiel 29:17, 45:18), namely, when the early or late rain is needed. Cf. the note from Pliny at chapter 1:17. Others translate "as before." Compare Isaiah 60:9. Furthermore, some understand the early and latter rain spiritually: namely, that Christ will kindly refresh and irrigate the Church of the New Testament with the heavenly dew of His Spirit, Word, and Sacraments, both at the beginning of the sowing and later when it has grown into a mature harvest as the harvest of the final judgment approaches (discussed below in 4:13). So says **Gesner** in Calovius (p. 778) and others who take all the rest of this text allegorically regarding the benefits of the Gospel in opposition to the state of the Law. However, since the compensation for the years of drought in verse 25 refers back to what the Prophet said in the preceding chapter about the sterility brought by the locusts, there is no doubt that physical benefits are implied—that the Lord will kindly compensate for the previous lack in the fields and vineyards, as **Calovius** (p. 779) rightly judges. Cf. the note on verse 21 from Jerome.

**v. 24.** **q)** And the threshing floors shall be full (1 Samuel 23:1) **r)** of grain (Genesis 41:35, Amos 5:11). Cf. above 1:10, 17.

<meta>This page continues the transition in the Book of Joel from the physical restoration of the land (following the locust plague) to the spiritual outpouring promised for the future. # JOEL. CHAPTER 2. 3.

<margin>
q) *And they shall overflow* <note>original: "et redundabunt"</note>, as if to say, they shall cause to run about or flow out. Hiphil [verb form] (z) chapter 4, 18. Compare Psalm 65, 10. s) *the vats of the winepresses* <note>original: "lacus torcularium"</note>. Isaiah 16, 10. u) see verse 19. Compare Proverbs 3, 10.

verse 25. x) *And I will restore to you* <note>original: "Et compensabo vobis"</note>. Isaiah 57, 18. **Calvin**: The Prophet has confirmed the previous teaching and reasons from opposites: since it is no less easy for God to restore the abundant produce of the earth than it was previously easy to make the land barren by sending those corruptions. y) see note on verse 23. z) chapter 1, 4. a) see chapter 1, 4. Psalm 78, 46. b) chapter 1, 4. c) *that great army of mine* <note>original: "magnus fc. ille meus exercitus"</note>. See verses 2, 11. **Bochart**: God afflicted the Egyptians with such troops after they had despised frogs, flies, and lice. **Jerome**: The caterpillar (Locust) is called the "great power of the Lord"—because in a slow and small worm, the power of God and human fragility are demonstrated. d) *which I sent against you* <note>original: "quas misi contra vos"</note>. Compare Exodus 10, 4. Truly, the locusts, caterpillars, or beetles did not arise by chance; but God hired the labor of those soldiers, they were His troops and army to overwhelm them—The fact that He calls them a *great army* shows that God does not need mighty forces to scourge mankind. For when He arms locusts and tiny creatures that are of no significance, they snatch the food from people's mouths and leave them starving; even if no one draws a sword against them, they still waste away in their hunger. **Calvin**. But **Jonathan** and others interpret metaphorically: *and I will repay you with good years for the years in which the peoples, nations, and tongues, and commanders, and the kingdom of vengeance, my great army which I sent among you, plundered you*.

verse 26. e) Compare Hosea 4, 10. f) chapter 13, 6. Micah 6, 14. Haggai 1, 6. f) *in satisfying, you shall be satisfied* <note>original: "saturando sc. faturabimini"</note> verse 19. g) Isaiah 62, 9. Ecclesiastes 5, 18. Compare Deuteronomy.

Deuteronomy 8, 12 ff. chapter 32, 15. Proverbs 30, 9. h) *who has dealt with you*, by punishing in Zechariah 1, 6; by doing good to those who look to Him in Numbers 10, 32. i) *wondrously, even to a miracle*. Isaiah 29, 14. Psalm 31, 22.

->**CHAPTER III. verse 1. r)**<-

S. It shall also come to pass. For this chapter is connected with the previous one. (See note on chapter 2, 1, 21, 23.) And here God further promises and proclaims: I. The outpouring of the Holy Spirit (verse 1-2). II. The day of the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, with preceding signs (verse 3-4). And III. The rescue of believers in Zion, that is, the New Testament Church (verse 5). Afterwards. s) <term>in the latter days</term> <note>original: "באחרית הימים"</note> that is, as Peter says in Acts 2, 17, **in the last days** <note>original: "ἐν ταῖς ἐσחάταις ἡμέראις"</note>. Compare verse 2 following. **Calvin**: By which name is designated the final time, both regarding the Synagogue and the Jewish state, over which the end was looming, and regarding the final grace, etc. So **Kimchi**: It is the same, he says, as if you said <term>in the latter days</term> as in Isaiah 2, 2; namely, in the days of the Messiah (the time of the New Testament), collected from Isaiah 11, 9. **Abarbanel**: after those sad times mentioned in Psalm 74, 9. t) *I will pour out my Spirit.* **Jerome**: The word *outpouring* shows the abundance of the gift: that the gifts of the Holy Spirit would descend not upon a few Prophets, as used to happen in the Old Testament, but upon all who believe in the name of the Savior, the Spirit's gifts would descend, not just on this one or that one, but upon all flesh, etc. **Tarnovius**: The Old Testament differs from the New in that in the former these gifts only trickled down, as it were, while in the latter they flow out in great abundance, and are poured out **more fully** <note>original: "πλείως"</note> Titus 3, 6. In the former, there was only a taste of them in the Prophets; in the latter, there is an outpouring upon all flesh. See verse 2, Isaiah 32, 15, chapter 44, 3, Zechariah 12, 10, Acts 10, 45, Ephesians 4, 8, 1 Corinthians 12, 11. **M. I.** so that My Spirit may be copiously upon them. **Abarbanel**: it signifies that there will be abundant knowledge and notice of God, collected from Isaiah 11, 2, 9. u) **Jonathan**: My Holy Spirit. So in verse 2: the Spirit of grace and prayers, Zechariah 11, 10. The Spirit of knowledge and the fear of God, Isaiah 11, 2, with various gifts and spiritual graces, 1 Corinthians 12, 4 ff., chapter 14, 22. x) *upon all flesh*, that is, as the **Arabic version** has it: upon every human being endowed with flesh; that is, not upon Jews or Israelites alone (as **Abarbanel** and others rashly think, though Abarbanel himself refutes this impudence at this place, folio 242); but upon all people, of whatever nation, sex, or condition (verse 2), or time (Acts 2, 39), provided they believe in the name of the Savior (verse 5), and do not resist God, so that we may be taught by Him (Acts 6, 45). Compare the phrase in Genesis 6, 12, Isaiah 40, 5, chapter 49, 26, Zechariah 2, 17, Isaiah 65, 3, Romans 3, 20, chapter 10, 12, Galatians 3, 28, etc. Most certainly, says **Abarbanel** on this passage, this phrase encompasses all people, of whatever nation they may be: just as in Isaiah 66, 23, Psalm 145, 21, compared with Zephaniah 3, 8, 9. Therefore, "all flesh" is not to be understood only as those 120 in Acts 1, 15, who were gathered in the upper room in Jerusalem (Acts 2, 1). Although, therefore, on that feast of Pentecost, in the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit, the prophecy began to be fulfilled in an illustrious way; nevertheless, it does not pertain only to that solemn act; but concerns the entire state of the last times or the New Testament, in the manner of other universal promises; says **Calvin**, page 783. Compare, for example, Acts 10, 44 ff., chapter 11, 25, chapter 15, 8, chapter 19, 6, Galatians 3, 2. y) S. so that also your sons shall prophesy. Now, one is said to prophesy not only if he speaks mysteries and future things through extraordinary revelation (as in Acts 11, 28, chapter 20, 23, Revelation 1, 1, etc.), but also one who speaks divine things through ordinary revelation; whether with a singular approval of the Spirit or some use in good conscience: as **Cocceius** observes in his Lexicon, page 460. See 1 Corinthians 14, 1 ff. and compare the note on Numbers 11, 29. These promises thus indicate something partly extraordinary and partly ordinary. An example of the first kind is the daughters of Philip (Acts 21, 9) and many who spoke in tongues of the mighty works of God, though they had previously been **unlearned** <note>original: "ἀγράμματοι"</note> (Acts 4, 13) and elsewhere. But the extraordinary gift is a testimony and means for the ordinary gift, which is indicated in Isaiah 54, 13, Jeremiah 31, 33, 34, 1 Corinthians 14, 22. x) and your daughters. Compare Psalm 68, 12, 1 Corinthians 11, 5. **Cocceius**, Lexicon, page 460. After the word of the Gospel has been heard, and no further Prophet is expected to point out the word through which we may know God, and the Spirit of grace and adoption has been poured out: he who believes and speaks (2 Corinthians 4, 13) is in the same place where the Prophet once was; he learns from God through His words and the law set in public, with the Spirit inscribing it in his heart, and through those things he has learned, and through the words of the Spirit, he advances to wisdom and prudence and the knowledge of the mysteries of God. a) your old men. chapter 1, 2. As Paul says to Philemon, verse 9. **Cocceius**, Lexicon, page 23. Something ordinary is indicated: Old men, attending to the scripture of the Old Testament, will see what God is doing in the world, as once the Prophets did in dreams: and thus they will be warned by God to act prudently and be able to give prudent counsel. b) they shall dream divine dreams. Numbers 12, 6. which was customary in Job’s time, Job 33, 15, 16. Compare Genesis 37, 6, 9; 1 Samuel 28, 6; 1 Kings 3, 5; Daniel 1, 17, chapter 7, 1; Matthew 1, 20, chapter 2, 19, 12; and Grotler’s *Prophetic Theology*, page 16. c) your young men. Compare Amos 2, 11. d) they shall see visions by day or night. Compare Genesis 15, 12 ff., 1 Kings 22, 17, Isaiah 6:1, Jeremiah 1, 11, chapter 24, 3, Ezekiel 1, 4 ff., chapter 37, 2, Zechariah 1, 8, etc.; and from the New Testament: Acts 9, 10, chapter 10, 3, 17, chapter 16, 22, chapter 22, 5, 1 Corinthians 14, 19, 30, Revelation 1, 12, 13, etc. **Abarbanel**: He does not say *all* your old men or young men; but simply: so that you may understand those who were fit to receive the gift of Prophecy. **Calvin**, page 784. Not that the immediate revelations, which were made to the Patriarchs and Prophets, are to be granted to everyone—but that such things, which were once made known to certain selected persons through those extraordinary modes of revelation (prophecies, visions, and dreams), are to be made manifest to all through ordinary revelation: so that sons and daughters, old men and young men, servants and handmaids may now have divine knowledge, which was scarcely granted to Patriarchs, Prophets, and men of God in the past. For Scripture uses the phrases of the Old Testament to signify the blessings of the New Testament, as we see happening repeatedly in prophetic predictions. — For not even those in whom Peter (Acts 2, 16) testified this prediction was fulfilled had prophecy, or dreams, or visions; yet they were filled with the Holy Spirit and were able to bring forth **the mighty works** <note>original: "τὰ μεγαλεῖα"</note> of God in various tongues, **being carried along by the Holy Spirit** <note>original: "ὑπὸ τοῦ πνεύματος ἁγίου פֿערוֹמֶנוֹי"</note>, just as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance. See note on verse 2.

<meta>This page continues the exegesis of Joel, transitioning from the promise of physical restoration to the famous prophecy of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit and the "Day of the Lord." The commentary explores both the New Testament fulfillment (Acts 2) and historical interpretations regarding the destruction of Jerusalem.</meta>

### CHAPTER 3. JOEL 3 <note>In many English Bibles, this section is part of Chapter 2 (verses 28–32). The Hebrew and some older Latin versions begin Chapter 3 here.</note>

<margin>
...from Egypt. Deuteronomy 6:22; Jeremiah 32:21.
</margin>
**2** And also upon the **servants** and upon the **handmaids** in those days I will pour out my **spirit**.

<margin>
*Greek: wonders.* <note>original: "τέρατα"</note>
See Acts 2:19.
</margin>
**3** And I will show **wonders** in the heavens and in the earth: **blood**, and **fire**, and **pillars of smoke**.

<margin>
*Compare Joel 4:10 (Hebrew); Habakkuk 2:4; Mark 16:20. k) Jerome:*
Because the sun, when Christ was dying, was turned into darkness, and the moon into blood. See verse 4.
</margin>
**4** The **sun** shall be turned into **darkness**, and the **moon** into **blood**, before the great and terrible **day of the LORD** comes.

**5** And it shall come to pass, that **whosoever** shall call on the name of the **LORD** shall be delivered; for in **mount Zion** and in **Jerusalem** there shall be deliverance, as the LORD has said...

---

**4.** Others refer this to the Angel of the Lord and the heavenly hosts descending in Luke 2:9, 13; the Star appearing to the Magi in the sky in Matthew 2:2; and the events recorded by the Evangelists when Christ rose in Matthew 28:2 and following, and finally when He ascended into the heavens. We believe these should be understood more broadly as referring to all the prodigies and signs that appeared in the sky before that horrible day of the destruction of Jerusalem. **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch scholar</note> says: "comets, flaming swords, and other figures of this kind usually precede great revolutions of affairs." However, he very poorly refers this text to the arrival of the Babylonians. But compare the *words of Christ* in Luke 21:11, 25 and see **Josephus** <note>A 1st-century Jewish historian</note> in *The Jewish War*, Book 7, chapter 12 or 31.

*l)* Namely, as immediately follows: blood, fire, and smoke. **Jerome**: "Because the earth trembled with such violent and unusual motion that the tombs were opened and the rocks were split apart" (Matthew 27:51, 52). *m)* **blood and fire.** Jerome understands this as the blood of Christ (John 19:34, 35) and the fire of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:3; compare Luke 12:49). **Gussetius** (p. 947), however, interprets it as the blood of Christ’s martyrs (as does **Cocceius**, comparing 1 John 5:8) and the fire of the stakes <note>the burning of martyrs</note>, by whose power they struck the sound, willing and eager; while the "palms of smoke" refer to prayers ascending to heaven (compare Song of Solomon 3:6 and Revelation 8:3, 4). But **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot, a scholar of Hebrew traditions</note> in his *Hebrew Hours* on Acts 2:19 says: "These wonders in blood, fire, and smoke; I would understand as the slaughter and conflagrations committed among the Jewish people through seditions and internal war, amazing even to the point of being a prodigy. These were monsters rather than examples; and nothing could more prodigiously presage the ruin of the nation than that they so raged in mutual slaughter and devastation." Compare Ezekiel 38:22, Revelation 8:8, and Matthew 24:6, 7; Mark 13:7, 8, 19; Luke 21:9. *n)* **and palms** <note>symbolizing rising columns</note> (alpha) Song of Solomon 3:6 **of smoke**. The phrase elegantly depicts the ascent of smoke toward the sky, namely from the burning of cities and villages, according to the mind of Lightfoot, Cocceius, etc. And the *Greek* translates as "vapor of smoke," <note>original: "ατμίδα καπνοῦ"</note> as does the *Latin Vulgate*. So also in Acts 2:19. Hence **Luther** says: "I judge entirely that these signs which Joel cites are the same as those mentioned by the Evangelists as occurring during the passion of the Savior. There was a portentous eclipse of the sun on the very day of the full moon, which so involved everything in darkness that widely diffused smoke blocked the eyes from seeing things placed nearby." And the Prophet explains himself in this way when in verse 4 he adds about the darkened sun and the moon reflecting the appearance of blood, etc. **Jerome**: "Isaiah also speaks of this smoke in his great vision, in which the departure of the Jews was foretold." See Isaiah 6:4 and the notes there.

<margin>
*k) 4. o)* Some take this figuratively here as referring to the greatest afflictions, as in chapter 2:10 and chapter 4:15, when in the Jewish republic and church everything seemed to collapse, just as Christ had predicted in Matthew 24:29. But most truly this also happened when Christ was dying, as the Evangelists record in Matthew 27:45, Mark 15:33, and Luke 23:44, 45. "The sun also was turned into darkness, because it did not dare to see its Lord hanging, and the moon into blood," says Jerome. To **Abarbanel** <note>a medieval Jewish commentator</note>, the *Sun* in this place signifies the Edomites [Christians] and the *Moon* the Ishmaelites [Turks], to whom, along with Gog and Magog, the Prophet here predicts destruction, as in Ezekiel 38:22. But the genuine explanation of the Apostles and the Holy Spirit was irrefragably proved by the event itself among the Jews. If, however, anyone prefers a symbolic explanation of the Sun and Moon, **Vitringa** <note>Campegius Vitringa, a commentator on Revelation</note> provides a more fitting one on Revelation 6:12, where he has it thus: "It seems rightly interpreted elsewhere as the sudden death of King Agrippa (Acts 12:23), at which time he was shining in supreme majesty, and the mournful fall of Ananus the High Priest, who was throat-cut by the Idumeans and Zealots in the dead of night along with the most noble men of the sacred and civil order, as Josephus reports in *The Jewish War*, Book 4, chapter 17." See also the note at Micah 8:9. *p)* **before it comes.** 1 Samuel 9:15; 2 Samuel 3:35; Ezekiel 33:22. Let this teach that the moment or time of those preceding signs is one thing, and the true Day of Jehovah itself, and what accompanied or followed it, is another. *q)* Compare note on chapter 1:15 and 2:1. **Calovius**: "Here God the Father speaks concerning the day of Jehovah the Son of God, the Messiah and our Lord." See note on verse 5. *r)* **that great** (compare chapter 2:11). *s)* *Vulgate*: "and horrible, dreadful." Thus the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans is also described in Malachi 3:23, 24. Others understand the day of the Lord’s coming in the flesh; others the day of the passion, others the resurrection, and others (mostly the ancients) the day of the final judgment. **Jerome** (who more than once complains about the difficulty of this passage) says: "The day of the Lord, great and horrible, is to be believed as either the resurrection, or certainly much later the day of [the final] judgment, which truly is great and horrible. But because verse 5 follows: *And it shall be that every one who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved,* and the Apostle in Romans 10:13 refers this to the time of the Lord's passion, it is better understood as the day of the resurrection." So says the Blessed Father. But see the opinion of our scholars and others concerning the judgment of Christ upon the Jews in Matthew 24:27, 30; chapter 26:64; Mark 13:26; Luke 21:50, etc. *v. 5. s)* **It shall yet happen, as to everyone... that they may be snatched away**; that is, they will most certainly be snatched away. Compare note on Isaiah 65:24, chapter 66:23, and Ezekiel 30:16. *u)* **whoever calls on the name of the Lord.** Genesis 12:8; 13:4; 21:33; 1 Kings 18:24; Isaiah 41:25; 50:10. **Targum Jonathan**: "whoever prays in the name of the Lord." Luke 21:36. **Cocceius**: "Because this invocation is not possible except in Christ, and because Christ is taught to be adored and invoked, and because elsewhere the Prophets teach that the means of salvation is faith in Christ (Habakkuk 2:4; Isaiah 53:11), we conclude that this *Lord* is the *Son of God, the true Jehovah*; and the invocation of the Lord is placed as a sign of freedom from the yoke of ceremonies." John 16:21. Compare above note at verse 4. *x)* **shall be snatched away**, as if escaping from a hand. Genesis 19:17; Isaiah 49:25; Psalm 124:7; Daniel 12:1. *Greek: shall be saved.* *Vulgate: shall be safe.* The Apostles in Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13 teach that this should be understood not only of temporal preservation (concerning which see Matthew 24:16 and Eusebius' *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 3, chapter 5) but most especially of eternal salvation. *y)* **in mount Zion**, from whence the doctrine of the Gospel shall go forth (Isaiah 2:3), and in the Church of the New Testament. Compare Isaiah 10:22; 24:23; 27:13; Micah 4:7 and notes there. *z)* see ibid, and note on Isaiah 51:17. *a)* **there shall be a snatching away.** (**Targum** and **Syriac**: "liberation") or "escape": like one escaping from slaughter and persecution. Genesis 14:13. See Isaiah 4:2; 37:32; Obadiah verse 17. **Cocceius**: "From this verse it is to be seen that in the whole world, and even in the land itself or the Israelite people, there will be a great destruction because of the unbelief by which they do not receive the preached Christ; partly through bodily punishments, but especially through spiritual punishments (Romans 1, 18). There will be those, however, who escape spiritual punishments and the second death, being preserved; and also those who are not consumed by temporal afflictions."
</margin>

<column-break/>

*\* verse 2. beta) Vulgate* adds a conjunction: *But also* upon my servants. With the *Septuagint* and *Arabic*. So Peter in Acts 2:18. Compare *epsilon* in Philemon v. 10, 16. *f) gamma)* **upon the handmaids.** For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female: because we are all one in Christ. Galatians 3:28. Compare 1 Corinthians 7:22. *g)* **in those days of the New Testament** or times. Verse 10. *h)* **Targum Jonathan:** "I will pour out **my Holy Spirit**." See verse 1. **Abarbanel**: "The Spirit, namely of the **knowledge and fear of God**." Isaiah 11:2. It is not necessary (Abarbanel says the same here) to explain this spirit of God as the gift of prophecy, but as the notice and knowledge of God, as said in Isaiah 11:9. See the note on verse 1. **Jerome**: "Neither indeed will everyone who receives the Holy Spirit immediately have the (same) spiritual grace; but through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit they may obtain diverse graces: some prophecy, like the sons and daughters, who are of greater merit; others dreams, like the elders now of more advanced age; others visions, like the young men who have overcome the evil one (1 John 2:13, 14). But the servants and handmaids, who still have the spirit of fear and not of love (because perfect love casts out fear), will not have prophecies, nor dreams, nor visions, but content with the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, they will possess the grace of sound faith and salvation. And if they possess this grace, then what do they lack for expelling servile fear from the soul?" Therefore, this accommodation is to be taken more kindly. For <unclear>exis</unclear> (as our Blessed **Lightfoot** writes on this place), "I do not create new revelations for myself, but it simply signifies the gift of the Holy Spirit for the purification of the heart and excellent governance. This gift truly belongs to this time in the New Testament," etc. etc.
*v. 3. epsilon)* **And I will give wonders;** as formerly in the leading out of the Israelites...

\* verse 3. **pillars** [of smoke] written fully with the vowel markers according to the Masora <note>traditional Hebrew text notation</note> here and especially in Song of Solomon 3:6. The same have a composite vowel <unclear>Chateph-patach</unclear>. Others are defective and use a simple vowel. The Masora, however, has it thus in three places.
\* verse 3. beta) **And I will give wonders;** as formerly in the leading out of the Israelites...

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on the book of Joel. The previous page concluded the discussion of the "Day of the Lord" and the signs in the heavens. We now move into Chapter 4 of the Hebrew text (equivalent to Chapter 3 in most English Bibles), which focuses on the restoration of Judah and the judgment of the surrounding nations in the Valley of Jehoshaphat.</meta>

# JOEL. CHAPTER 4. <note>In Hebrew Bibles, this is Chapter 4; in English Bibles, this is Chapter 3.</note>

<margin>
**b)** "He knows," says the Lord. All those, namely, who are written for life (see Isaiah 4:3). **c)** Among the remnants or survivors (compare Joshua 10:20; Jeremiah 44:27). **Jerome** <note>A 4th-century scholar and Bible translator</note> says: We should understand the "remnants" to be those from the Jewish people who believed, of whom Isaiah speaks in chapter 1:9. However, **Calovius** <note>Abraham Calovius, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> (p. 786) says: "and among the remnants of the nations," that is, as **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius, a Dutch theologian</note> writes, in the fullness of the "seed" (compare Romans 4:12, 16, 27, 24). **d)** The Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> says "those whom the Lord shall call," specifically through His word (Acts 2:39).

**CHAPTER 4. verse 1. e)** For (lest it seem doubtful what He promised regarding the coming of the Messiah in 3:23, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit in 3:1, and the preservation of the faithful in 3:5), I confirm it will most certainly happen; so that I will not only bring back my captives but also take the most severe notice of their enemies and punish them (compare Jeremiah 30:3, 10; 31:8; Hosea 9:6). According to **Schmid**, the parts of this chapter are: **I.** The liberation of Israel from captivity and from enemies (v. 1). **II.** The conversion of the nations through judgment in the Valley of Jehoshaphat (v. 2), where we see (a) the summons to judgment (v. 2); (b) the process of judgment (v. 3); (c) the outcome (v. 17). But according to **Gurtler’s** *Prophetic Theology* (p. 223), God here predicts: **1.** Punishment of the enemies of the Church (v. 1-3), especially the Tyrians, Sidonians (v. 4-8), and other nations invading the lands of the Church (v. 9-15). **II.** The proclamation of the Gospel and the perpetual defense of the Church (v. 16-17) and the widest spreading of the truth (v. 18). **III.** The devastation of Egypt and Edom (v. 19). **IV.** Finally, the eternal peace of the Church (v. 20-21). Thus **Maius** in *Economy of the Old Testament* (p. 882) says: Here the fates of the Church under the Antichrist are more fully explained, regarding its oppression and affliction, and its full liberation—just as in Revelation chapters 11:2, 16:13-16, 21, and 22.
</margin>

<margin>
**CHAPTER 4.**
*Hebrew variant:* "I will restore" (אָשִׁיב)
22. Interpreters vary greatly in the explanation of this chapter, as can be seen in Calovius on this passage. We refer those things said here about the Tyrians, Sidonians, Philistines, Egyptians, and Edomites to the historical events before and after the Babylonian captivity...
</margin>

<column-break/>

...we do not doubt that this happened; so we refer the fullest fulfillment of this prophecy, through the context, to the final fates of the Church and the ultimate fulfillment of those events. **f)** In those last days (chapter 3:1-2). **g)** Namely, of the New Testament (see the word in Jeremiah 50:4, 20). **h)** When, or in which days they return (Jeremiah 32:44; 33:11). **i, k)** See Isaiah 66:18; Micah 4:12; Zephaniah 3:8. **l) Grotius:** Those nations, namely, who treated my people poorly, not because of the sins for which I permitted it, but out of hatred for me and the religion I handed down. **m)** And I will lead them down, as if to the place of judgment and punishment (Deuteronomy 21:4; Jeremiah 51:40). **n)** Into the Valley of Jehoshaphat, or rather, as Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> has it, "into the valley of divine judgment"; where God will judge and take vengeance on the enemies of His Church (see verses 12, 14). It is a mystical name, as even **Abarbanel** <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> acknowledges (fol. 243, col. 1). **Aben Ezra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century scholar</note> compares this to 2 Chronicles 20:16, 26, to which history the Prophet seems to allude here, just as Revelation 16:16 alludes to the mystical meaning of the name "Megiddo" (meaning "destruction"). **Luther** understands it as the Church, to which all nations are to be called and judged through the Word (compare John 16:8). **o)** Where I will enter into litigation with them (Isaiah 66:16; Jeremiah 25:31; Zephaniah 3:8). I will demand the reasons why they did this, and I will take vengeance on them (compare Isaiah 34:8; 35:4; Psalm 79:10; Psalm 94:1). **p)** See verse 3 and chapter 2:17. **q)** Chapter 2:17; Isaiah 19:25; 47:6; Galatians 6:16. **r)** Whom they scattered (Psalm 53:6; verse 3). **s)** Not only the Assyrians and Chaldeans (Jeremiah 50:17; Esther 3:8) but also certain closer neighboring peoples, relying on their help (Jeremiah 49:1). **t)** They divided (Joshua 13:7; Micah 2:4). * Verse 3. **u)** And over my people (verse 2). **x)** They cast lots, as was the custom regarding captives (see Nahum 3:10; Obadiah verse 11). **y)** Correctly rendered by Jonathan, the Syriac, and Abarbanel: "And they gave a boy as payment for harlots." For this is how the Hebrew should be interpreted, as indicated by the following part of the verse; and the sense is, as the Greek Septuagint and Arabic also have it: they gave Jewish boys to prostitutes in place of money (compare Nahum 3:4). The Vulgate reads differently: "and they placed the boy in a brothel," which the Jerusalem commentary explains as forcing them to change their masculine nature (compare Romans 1:26, 27). **z)** And the girl. The Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic read it as a collective "girls" (see Genesis 34:4; Zechariah 8:5). **a)** They sold for wine and at a cheap price (compare Amos 2:6). **b)** They drank with the lightest of hearts <note>original: "lenissimo animo," meaning they were unconcerned by the cruelty</note> (compare Psalm 14:4 and 2 Samuel 23:16, 17). * Verse 4. **c) Therefore also.** Note here the prophet’s digression or departure; while in the preceding verses he was undoubtedly dealing with New Testament times, he now suddenly turns to the people of his own or the coming age, so that from the subject of his prophecy he might warn, exhort, and convict them. Having done this, he resumes the thread of his prophecy in verse 9 and following. Indeed (as **Vitringa** observes), while the Prophet was describing the gravest judgments by which God will strike down the enemies of the Church, there came to his mind the injuries which the Jewish people—a part of the universal Church—were suffering in his time from neighboring nations: the Tyrians, Sidonians, and Philistines. He turns his speech to them in passing, announcing in God's name that they too will not go unpunished and that their sins must be avenged in that terrible slaughter of the Church's enemies according to the rule of divine justice. **d)** What are you to me, or what business do you have with me? (compare Joshua 22:24). **Grotius** says: "Why are you troublesome to me?" (compare Matthew 8:29). **e)** See on these Joshua 13:2, 8; 19:29; Isaiah 23:1; Ezekiel 26:1; Amos 1:10; Psalm 83:8. **f)** And all the borders (Joshua 13:2; 18:17). **g)** Vulgate: "of the Palestinians" (see 2 Chronicles 28:18 and their brief history in Isaiah 14:29). On the name, see notes on Exodus 15:14. **h)** "Is this such a retribution?" The Hebrew *He* is interrogative, as in Genesis 18:21. The name itself signifies a turning back or reflection; according to **Gussetius** (p. 171), it signifies a trade in merits, whether giving or receiving, both good and bad. **i)** Do you repay me, or gather against me? Do you harm my people without cause or provocation? (see 2 Chronicles 28:18). Christ speaks of his members as himself, as in Acts 9:4. **k)** But if you gather such things or commit them against me? (Psalm 7:5). The Septuagint renders this as "bearing a grudge" (as also in Genesis 50:15). **l)** Quickly and swiftly (Isaiah 5:26). **m)** I will repay your merit (Isaiah 65:15; Proverbs 12:14). **n)** Upon your head (verse 7; Obadiah v. 15). **Abarbanel** thinks this was done through Alexander the Great; **Gurtler** refers it to the destruction of Christian Tyre and Sidon by the Saracens at the beginning of the 13th century, though this is less solid. * Verse 5. **o)** Because (verse 19; Deuteronomy 3:24; Ezekiel 23:20). **p)** My precious things (1 Kings 20:6; Hosea 9:6; 13:15; Isaiah 64:10). **Grotius** says: God calls them this here, not the things of the temple that were carried to Babylon, but the things belonging to His people. As in verse 4, he says the injury done to the people was done to Himself. **q)** The best things (compare 1 Samuel 8:14, 16; 1 Kings 20:3). **r)** The Septuagint and Vulgate say "you brought into your shrines"; others say "into your palaces" (as in Isaiah 13:22; Amos 8:3; Proverbs 30:28).
