# JOEL CHAPTER 4. <note>In Hebrew Bibles, this is Chapter 4; in English Bibles, this is Chapter 3.</note>

<margin>
At that time, as Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch scholar</note> notes, when Gaza, Sidon, and Tyre were captured by Alexander the Great. **e)** Who will sell them to the Sabeans, **f)** that is, the Arabs. The Ionian <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase</note> says: the children or descendants of Sheba. (Genesis 10:7; compare 1 Kings 10:1; Jeremiah 6:20). The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek version of the Old Testament</note> and Arabic version say: <note>original Greek: εις αιχμαλωσίαν</note> "into captivity," which compares with Revelation 13:10. **d)** To be led away to a nation far removed from you. Compare the phrasing in Joshua 9:6, 9 and Deuteronomy 28:49. **e)** The Ionian says: because it has been so decreed through the Word of the Lord. And so...
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 6. s)** But you sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks: with whom the Phoenicians had great commerce from every age. See Ezekiel 27:13 and the notes on Deuteronomy 28:68. Compare also Genesis 10:2, 4; Daniel 8:21. Something like this seems to have happened under King Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:17, 18; compare Amos 1:6). The Greek version <note>The Septuagint</note> says "Greeks" <note>original: ελλήνων</note>. Because this term also denotes "Gentiles" in general in the New Testament (as in Romans 2:9, 10), Jerome <note>Early Christian scholar, d. 420 AD</note> interprets this here as referring to heretics: "The heretic," he says, "whomever he has deceived and made to worship his own idols, sells the children of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks (or Gentiles); he turns them from Christians into pagans." Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century theologian</note> argues this signifies that they handed over the children of the Church to be educated and imbued with Aristotelian doctrine rather than the Holy Spirit, so that they were moved far from their own boundary—that is, from the truth of the Christian religion. But it is also well known that many Latins, at the instinct of the Popes, set out for Palestine and perished by the frauds of the Greeks, as Gurtlerus says in his *Prophetic Theology* (p. 672). **t)** So that you might drive them far away. (chapter 2:20). **u)** From their own territory. (Joshua 18:5). Grotius: So that there would be less opportunity to ransom them.
</margin>

**6** The children also of Judah and the children of Jerusalem have ye sold unto the Greeks, that ye might remove them far from their border.
**7** Behold, I will raise them up out of the place whither ye have sold them, and will return your recompense upon your own head:
**8** And I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hand of the children of Judah, and they shall sell them to the Sabeans, to a people far off: for the Lord hath spoken it.
**9** Proclaim ye this among the Gentiles; Prepare war, wake up the mighty men, let all the men of war draw near; let them come up:
**10** Beat your plowshares into swords, and your pruninghooks into spears: let the weak say, I am strong.
**11** Assemble yourselves, and come, all ye heathen, and gather yourselves together round about: thither cause thy mighty ones to come down, O Lord.
**12** Let the heathen be wakened, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat: for there will I sit to judge all the heathen round about.
**13** Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great.
**14** Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision: for the day of the Lord is near...

**v. 14:** **r)** Vulgate: "Peoples, peoples." Tigurine: "Crowd, crowd." (S): "Heaps, heaps." Ionian: "Armies, armies"—very frequent ones. (compare Ezekiel 32:18; 33:12, 20; Genesis 17:4, 5, etc.). # JOEL. CHAPTER 4. <note>In Hebrew Bibles, this is Chapter 4; in English Bibles, this is Chapter 3:15-21.</note>

-> Dddd 1 <-

24, 25. **y)** The hills (Amos 9:3) will flow with the "milk of the Gospel" (Isaiah 55:1). Jonathan says: they shall flow with wine. See Ezekiel 3:8; Jeremiah 31:5; and 1 Timothy 4:8. **u)** and all the stream beds (chapter 1:20; 1 Samuel 23:16) **x)** of Judea, that is, of the Christian Church (verses 6, 20, 21). **y)** they shall flow with waters. See Isaiah 30:23, 25; 44:3, 4. **z)** a fountain, Psalm 87:7 (Isaiah 12:3; Psalm 36:10; 68:27; Revelation 7:17). **a)** Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, 15th-century Jewish statesman and commentator</note> on folio 242 says: "By this promise is included that which we read in Isaiah 2:3, that the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord to the whole world; which is figuratively signified by the fountain of the house of the Lord." He explains this at length on folio 243, column 3. See Ezekiel 47:1; Zechariah 14:8; Revelation 22:1, 2. **b)** visible, another [note] to Genesis 2:10. **c)** The valley (see 1 Kings 3:16, 17). The Vulgate and Tigurina versions say "the torrent." **d)** the river, which is the more common meaning. **d)** and others [say] Shittim. This was the name of the place where the last camp of the Israelites was in the desert (Numbers 25:1; Micah 6:5), named after the Arabic tree *Schitta* (Isaiah 41:19), which the Hebrews associate with cedars. Thus others translate it: the valley of most excellent cedars (comparing Psalm 92:13). But the Vulgate says: "the torrent of thorns." However, as Jerome writes on this passage, it is a type of tree in the desert, similar to white thorns in color and leaves, but not in size. Otherwise, they are such large trees that very wide planks are cut from them; the wood is very strong and of incredible lightness and beauty, so that from them even the vessels of winepresses, which they call *axonica* <note>original Greek: ἀξονικὰ — relating to axles</note> or *thelyca* <note>original Greek: θηλυκὰ — female or soft</note>, are made by the wealthiest and most diligent people. This wood is not found in cultivated places, nor on Roman soil, except in the Arabian desert. From this wood the Ark of the Covenant was made, and the other things we read of in the tabernacle of God (Exodus 25:10, etc.). **v. 19. e)** Egypt, spoken of here mystically. Isaiah 11:15; Revelation 11:8. Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius, 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> says: Under the name of Egypt and Edom, the enemies of the church are designated. **f)** Ezekiel 29:9; Micah 7:13. **g)** The Jews (Amos 1:11), the Antichristian kingdom. See Isaiah 11:14; 34:5, 6; 63:1. Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, 5th-century theologian</note> says: As far as the historical sense is concerned, Egypt was punished when Cambyses, son of Cyrus, conquered the kingdom. And Edom was reduced to a wasteland, as the facts themselves speak. However, the prophetic words seem to cover a hidden covenant, etc. Calovius: We do not deny the reference to ancient histories, but the times look toward the New Testament, and their fate is foreshadowed by the phrases and histories of the Old Testament. Gualter, *Prophetic Theology* page 719: "After the Roman war against the Jews," he says, "the Edomites ceased to be a distinct people (Obadiah 18). Therefore, since no Edomite people remains in these times of which Joel speaks, another similar to Edom must be understood." The Jews consistently explain this as referring to the Romans. The Edomites were from the same stock as the Israelites, their neighbors, but unmerciful enemies, thirsty for blood, predatory, proud; they slandered God, trusted in fortifications, and were finally destroyed. So too are the Antichristians. **h)** The Vulgate: "for that they have done wickedly against the children of Judah." And as Cyril has it, they harassed them intolerably. Truly, the genitive here is passive, as in Judges 9:24; Obadiah 10; Habakkuk 2:8, 17. **i)** verse 6. Cyril: that is, the saints, the children of confession. For Judah is translated as "confession." Thus Luther on this passage: Judah signifies the man who acknowledges, confesses, and praises God for His mercy shown to the human race. For all others, who do not admire and preach this benefit, blaspheme God. Compare Revelation 2:9; 3:9. **k)** Noldius page 106: "because of that," see verse 5. **l)** Psalm 79:3, 10. **m)** Isaiah 59:7; Psalm 10:8; 94:21. **n)** in their land or the land of them. See what Gurtler says, page 699. **v. 20. o)** But Judah, that is, the Church of Christ, verses 13, 19. Abarbanel: Judah with all the tribes, and Jerusalem with the other cities of Israel—as we understand it, it is used here with emphasis. Revelation 7:4; Galatians 3:28, 29; 6:16; Revelation 2:9, etc. **p)** shall remain or be inhabited forever (Isaiah 13:20). Compare above chapter 1:2; Isaiah 26:1; 60:21; Jeremiah 31:4; Ezekiel 37:25; 43:7, 9; Micah 4:7; Zechariah 2:8; Matthew 16:18; 28:20. **q)** that new and spiritual Jerusalem. See verse 16. Isaiah 52:1; Revelation 21:2, 3. **r)** verse 21. **s)** Isaiah 58:12; 60:15. **v. 21. s)** And I will cleanse, or I will acquit, or I will declare their blood innocent, which I had not declared innocent. This is a difficult verse, which interpreters construct and explain in various ways. But many do not follow the most immediate meaning of the word, nor the accents. The Vulgate is better: "And I will cleanse their blood, which I had not cleansed." Compare Ephesians 2:1, 2, 3; 10:7, 4. Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, 16th-century Hebraist</note> translates: "Where I will cleanse them whose blood I was not cleansing," and understands it as the Gentiles, comparing Ephesians 2. Others look at the connection of the accents as in Psalm 51:10. Thus the Tigurina version: "those whom I have not cleansed," namely on account of their own impenitence and unbelief (Jeremiah 3:31; Ezekiel 43:9; Hosea 12:15). Or, as others think, on account of the inability of the Law (Acts 13:39; 15:9, 10; compare Hebrews 9:26, 28; 10:1, 4). Schmid, however, with Pagnino: "Then I will indeed cleanse, but their blood I will not cleanse," that is, as we understand it, I will indeed cleanse the repentant (Psalm 19:13; Job 9:28; 10:14), but their blood (the blood of Christ's confessors, Luke 11:29) I will not cleanse, or allow to be shed with impunity by enemies. Compare the word in Exodus 20:7; 34:7; Numbers 14:18; 1 Kings 2:9; Jeremiah 30:11; Nahum 1:3. The simplest explanation seems to be the one we placed at the beginning; or this one from Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 17th-century Dutch theologian</note>: "And I will declare innocent those whose blood I did not treat as innocent, but whom I permitted to be slaughtered as if they were impious by the Antichristian nations (verse 19) because of their confession of the truth." Compare Revelation 6:10, etc. **t)** See Isaiah 72:14; Psalm 79:3, 10; Isaiah 26:21; Revelation 16:6; 17:6; 18:24. **u)** thus the Lord will be dwelling. See Revelation 7:15; 21:3. Not in a temple made with hands, but another, which was foreshadowed by it and built by Him. See Isaiah 66:1; Zechariah 6:13; Hebrews 3:3, 6. **x)** in His Church (verse 16; Isaiah 12:6; 24:24; Psalm 2:6; 87:1, etc.), from which He seemed to have withdrawn when the Antichrist sat in the temple of God (2 Thessalonians 2:4; Revelation 13:6). Compare Isaiah 60:19; 66:14; Ezekiel 37:26; 43:7, 9; 48:35; Revelation 21:3, 22; 22:3, 4. Many take this to refer to the Church Triumphant in heaven. But as spiritual promises can by no means exclude the benefits shown to the faithful in the kingdom of grace—the full enjoyment of which is expected in heaven in the kingdom of glory—so also this commemoration of the Lord's presence in Zion includes both a gracious and glorious presence: He is graciously present to Zion and His faithful on this earth, and He wishes to fill them with His glory in heaven. For there is one Zion, the Church militant and triumphant, which is cheered in this and the future age by the eternal presence and cohabitation of its head, Jesus Christ. So says Calovius on this passage.

# ON THE PROPHECY OF AMOS
## PREFACE.

<margin>
1. The Time of Amos.
2. His Condition.
3. His Homeland.
4. The Occasion of the prophecy.
5. The Goal.
6. The Audience.
7. The Subject Matter and Parts.
</margin>

**A**mos of Tekoa was a man contemporary with **Uzziah** and **Jeroboam II**, as well as **Isaiah** and **Hosea**; see chapter 1, verse 1. He was a simple man of humble condition, having previously been a shepherd of flocks; but after his divine calling, he became a grave and fearless Prophet. He was originally from Judah, but he prophesied among the people of Bethel in the Kingdom of Israel (chapter 1:1; chapter 7:11 and following). The occasion of his prophecy was the flourishing state of the Kingdom of Israel under Jeroboam (2 Kings 14:25ff.), and the resulting sense of security among the people (Amos 6:13), which was the mother of many great outrages (chapter 2:6ff.; 3:9, 10; 4:1, 4, 5; 5:7, 10, 18; 6:1, etc.). God sought to shake them from this state through the most serious threats delivered by Amos, to the end that they might repent (chapter 4:12; 5:4, 5, 6, 14, 15). He indeed prophesies against the Jews and neighboring nations, but mostly against the Israelites. The subject matter is **I. Threatening**, the summary of which he first sets forth in chapter 1:2, and then pursues in detail, dealing with (1) the judgment of God against the nations in chapter 1 and chapter 2:1-3; (2) the overthrow of the Judean kingdom by the Babylonians, and the Israeli kingdom by the Assyrians from verse 4 through chapter 9:10. This section includes sermons delivered plainly in chapters 2–6 and those represented by types and visions in chapters 7, 8, and 9:1-10. **II. Evangelical**, <note>In this context, "evangelical" refers to the "good news" of the coming Messiah rather than a specific modern denomination.</note> concerning the future auspicious reign of Christ over both Israelites and the nations in chapter 9:11–15.

---

->In Hebrew:<-
->Amos<-

#### CHAPTER 1. <note>The Hebrew letter Aleph (א) denotes the number 1.</note>
<margin>
CHAPTER 1. v. 1. a) i.e., the words divinely inspired to Amos; see Jeremiah 1:1, Ecclesiastes 1:1, and compare Haggai 1:12. b) among the sheep-masters, or concerning the sheep-masters; and here the term denotes a wealthy owner of livestock. Hence "lord of the flocks," and the translator Aquila <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note> uses the Greek terms *poimnotrophois* (sheep-breeders) or *ktenotrophois* (cattle-breeders). But the word <term>noqed</term> <note>Hebrew: נֹקֵד</note> signifies not just a hired shepherd, but also a master of a flock; for example, Genesis 4:2, 47:3. Conversely, <term>noqed</term> can also denote a hired worker: and it is very likely Amos was of this sort from chapter 7:14, 15, where he says he not only fed the flock but also worked at gathering sycamore figs—a very humble means of living. He was not, therefore, a great teacher among the Jews, nor distinguished by a famous lineage or office; yet, like the Galilean fishermen, he was illustrious in the school of the Lord. Compare Proverbs 30:2ff. c) A town in the tribe of Judah, with a nearby desert (2 Chronicles 11:6, 20:20, 2 Maccabees 9:33). Regarding this, Jerome <note>A 4th-century church father and translator</note> says in his Prologue to this Prophet: It is six miles to the south

which stretches all the way to the Red Sea. And because nothing in the way of crops grows on the arid and sandy ground, the area is full of shepherds, so that they might compensate for the barrenness of the land with a multitude of livestock. From this number of shepherds, Amos the Prophet also came. d) not with eyes of flesh, but with the insight of the mind, through the revelation of God; that is, the things which he prophesied (Isaiah 1:1). e) In its full breadth. Namely, after the prophecies against Damascus (v. 3-5), the Philistines (v. 6–8), the Tyrians (v. 9, 10), the Edomites (v. 11, 12), the Ammonites (v. 13–15), and the Moabites (ch. 2:1–3), he first prophesies by name against Judah (ch. 2:4, 5) and the tribes of the Israeli kingdom (v. 6ff.). Afterward, he prophesies primarily against the ten tribes, among whom he also lived (ch. 7:10ff.), though in such a way that he occasionally joins the Judean kingdom with them because of similar crimes, as in chapter 3:1, 6:1, etc. f) who was contemporary with the following king of Israel (2 Kings 15:1ff.). g) Jeroboam the Second, whom the added father's name distinguishes from Jeroboam the First, the son of Nebat (ch. 7:9, 10; 2 Kings 14:23ff.; Hosea 1:1). h) Two years before the earthquake. They say this happened at the time when Uzziah arrogantly took upon himself the priesthood which did not belong to him (compare Ephesians 6:4). But Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century scholar of Hebrew and the Bible</note> concludes in his *Chronicle* (p. 95, 99; compare 2 Kings 15:30, 33) that this is not the case; from that passage, he proves Uzziah died in the same year he was struck with leprosy. Furthermore, this was a horrific earthquake (Zechariah 14:5) and a prelude to greater evil, no less than the locusts (Joel 1:2ff; Amos 7:1), the fires sent from heaven (ch. 7:4), and the dryness of the earth and subsequent famine (ch. 4:6ff; Jeremiah 12:13 with notes). Compare Ephesians 5:25. As for those who think the Prophet spoke of the earthquake before it happened (ch. 3:15, 9:1; one might also add 4:11, 7:4), this is not sufficiently proven by the context of these passages, and it is also rejected by <term>Abarbanel</term> <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a famous 15th-century Jewish statesman and commentator</note> in his commentary on this place. i) From Zion—from Jerusalem, where the temple and the religion of God were: "to teach that God did not dwell in the cities of Israel, that is, in Bethel and in Dan, where the golden calves were, nor in the capital Samaria and Jezreel, but in the true religion." (Jerome). The meaning, therefore: Jehovah, that majestic God, whose presence has hitherto resided and been worshipped on the Throne in Jerusalem, just as a lion strikes terror into the flocks with his roar, so He will soon strike immense terror into the nations by the demonstration of His terrible wrath, which a most certain slaughter of both the regions and their inhabitants will follow, or rather accompany. k) He will roar like a lion, by whose terrible voice all living creatures are terrified (ch. 3:8). Jerome's opinion is that Amos, who was a shepherd from among shepherds, made use of the terms of his trade, calling the terrible and fearsome voice of the Lord the "roar and growl of lions," comparing the overthrow of the Israelite cities to the solitude of shepherds and the dryness of the mountains. But other Prophets also use the same phrasing when they describe the horrific judgment of devastation to be brought by Jehovah (compare Jeremiah 25:30, Joel 3:16). l) chapter 3:4; compare 2 Samuel 22:14. m) so that they mourn (ch. 9:5); that is, they take on a sad appearance because of the horrific desolation of themselves and the slaughter of the inhabitants (Jeremiah 12:11, Joel 1:10). n) the dwellings of shepherds, or those joyful pastures frequented by shepherds (Psalm 23:2). It refers to regions flourishing both in their fertility and in the multitude of their inhabitants (compare Jeremiah 33:12). o) let it dry up (compare Joel 1:12). p) the summit (ch. 9:3). q) Carmel itself, near Ptolemais, on the borders of Asher (Joshua 12:22, 19:26). It was otherwise a rich mountain, which once abounded in joyful pastures: hence it is placed here and elsewhere to represent any fertile and cultivated field (compare Jeremiah 4:26). Furthermore, this is the frontispiece of the whole prophecy, containing a kind of summary of the threat, not only against Israel, but also against the other nations to whom he denounces devastation. r) For thus He has said. The Prophet now explains that general oracle of verse 2 specifically and piece-by-piece, applying it to various nations.

### AMOS. CHAPTER 1. 1

<margin>
a) **For three transgressions of Damascus;** Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmid (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian and Bible commentator.</note> suggests this is spoken as a plea, namely regarding the events that follow in verses 4 and 5; however, these punishments could still have been averted if they had ceased their transgressions. It could also be conveniently connected with the word "I will send" in verse 4, assuming no missing words.
t) See the notes on Ecclesiastes 7:1; also Jeremiah 49:23 and Isaiah 8:4.
*) **For four, etc.** This means: "Even if I had forgiven the three sins of Damascus, though they deserved vengeance, because they added a fourth, they have completely filled the measure of their sins, and I cannot refrain from punishing them."
But Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar.</note> in his *Chronology*, page 95, says: **For three, etc.** specifically because of the fourth, comparing it to similar phrases in Proverbs 30:15, 18, 21. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> explains it this way: "If they had persecuted my people once or twice, I would grant pardon; but now that they have been cruel a third and fourth time, crushing the captive multitude with iron wagons, must I not punish them?" Compare verses 6, 9, 11, 13; chapter 2:1, 4, 6; and similar phrases like "two and three" in Job 33:29; "three and four" in Proverbs 30:15; "six and seven" in Proverbs 6:16 and Job 5:19; "seven and eight" in Ecclesiastes 11:2. Similarly in Homer, **thrice and four times**, and in Virgil and Seneca, *three and four times*. In these constructions, either the total number creates an exaggeration, or the final number is the one specifically intended.
x) **I will not turn it back;** <note>original: "aversum illud"</note> namely, what I have spoken or what follows in verses 4 and 5. I will most certainly carry out my decree. Compare Numbers 23:10. However, Lightfoot refers the pronoun back to "His voice" in verse 2.
y) **namely because they threshed** like grain, which Easterners beat out using iron threshing sledges. This was a severe form of punishment (Judges 8:7, 16; 2 Samuel 12:31).

**a)** That is, the Israelites across the Jordan: the Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Compare verse 13. Targum Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary.</note> says "the inhabitants of the land of Gilead."
**v. 4. b)** Therefore, I will send.
**i)** The prefixed letter is an emphatic addition, as in Genesis 39:15, 18, 21 and chapter 17:14. Its connection to the causal particle **for** in verse 3 is quite evident.
**c)** Compare verses 7, 10, 12, 14 and chapter 2:2, 5. This fate was carried out by the Assyrians under Tiglath-Pileser, when Rezin reigned in Damascus; compare 2 Kings 16:9. See also verse 5.
**d)** 2 Kings 8:7, 12.
**e)** which will consume the palaces (verses 7, 10, 12, 14; chapter 2:2, 5).
**f)** that is, the magnificent palaces of Damascus. So Jeremiah 49:27. This uses a part (the palaces) to represent the whole city. The palaces of Hazael and Ben-hadad are named specifically, not only as a reference to the guilt of these two kings who were so cruel to the Israelites (see note on verse 3; also 2 Kings 8:7 and 13:3, 24), but also because Damascus was especially enlarged and adorned with many works during their time, reaching what seemed to be its peak of prosperity.
**g)** **the gate bar**, the primary support for the doors in the gates, sometimes made of iron (Isaiah 45:2; Lamentations 2:9; Jeremiah 51:30). Targum Jonathan translates this as "strength." The meaning is: I will cause Damascus to be captured by enemies, even though it is heavily fortified.
**h)** **I will cut off the inhabitant.** See verse 8.
**i)** **from the Valley of Aven**, that is, Damascene Syria, situated between Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon, also called the **Valley of Lebanon** in Joshua 11:17. It is called **Coele-Syria** <note>original Greek: κοιλὴ συρία</note> or "the Hollow Plain" by Strabo, and **Aulon** (meaning a valley or channel) by Polybius, named for its location between mountains. See Bochart, *Sacred Geography*, Book II, chapters 6 and 8. Furthermore, **Aven** was interpreted as a proper name by the Targum, Syriac, and Septuagint; but the Vulgate translates it descriptively as **from the plain of the idol**, just as in Hosea 10:5 **Beth-aven** (House of Iniquity) is used for Bethel. Thus, the name of the region would also mark its guilt (as in Jeremiah 50:38).
**k)** **him who holds the scepter** (verse 8), that is, the princes and especially the King, who is called **scepter-bearing** <note>original Greek: σκηπτοῦχος</note> in Homer for the same reason. Compare Genesis 49:10 and its note. Targum Jonathan translates this as "him who exercises dominion." Others understand it to mean "an elder."
**l)** Bochart considers this a synonym for the Valley of Damascus, and thus a proper name. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> thinks it is the place in Syria that Ptolemy calls **Paradise**. Compare another place in Mesopotamia (2 Kings 19:12 and Genesis 2:8, 15). But the Vulgate translates it as **from the house of pleasure**.
**m)** **they shall go into exile**, as in 2 Kings 17:23 and 25:21.
**n)** **to Kir**, where the Syrians had long ago been newcomers (chapter 9:7). Regarding this region and the fulfillment of this prophecy, see 2 Kings 16:9 and compare Isaiah 22:6.
**o)** Verses 8, 13; chapter 2:3.
**p)** See note on verse 3.
**q)** Gaza, regarding which see the note on Joshua 10:41. It is placed here and in verse 7 to represent all the Philistines, as it held the leading position among their cities. Compare Isaiah 14:28; Jeremiah 47; Ezekiel 25:15; Zephaniah 2:4-5; Zechariah 9:5.
**r)** **turn it back.** See note on verse 3.
**s)** Namely (which is their fourth and primary transgression), that they led away captives from their homeland after occupying their settlements. This happened especially under Ahaz, in whose time the Philistines and Edomites invaded Judean cities (2 Chronicles 28:17-18) and severely afflicted them (Isaiah 9:11 and 14:29); although something similar could have happened earlier in the time of Jehoram, who was also involved in war with the Edomites (2 Kings 8:20; 2 Chronicles 21:16-17).
**t)** **an entire captivity** (that is, a whole crowd of Jewish captives) as in verse 9; meaning a great and full number. See Jeremiah 13:19 and compare Deuteronomy 28:15. But Grotius translates it as **peaceful**, meaning they sold the Jews—who had done them no harm—to the Edomites as if they were war captives. Compare Genesis 34:21.
**u)** **to deliver them up enclosed**, either for death or for slavery (chapter 6:8; Psalm 31:9; 1 Samuel 23:11-12). Just as the **Philistines** sold Jewish captives to the Greeks for a very small price (Joel 4:4, 6).
**x)** To the most bitter enemies of the Jews (compare verses 9 and 11; also notes on Isaiah 21:11).
**y)** See note on verse 4. We conclude this refers to the final destruction they suffered under Nebuchadnezzar, because a total destruction is predicted, even of the very remnants (verse 8). Compare Jeremiah 47:2; Ezekiel 25:15-17; and Isaiah 14:31.
**z)** Verse 10, 14; compare Jeremiah 49:27.
**a)** See the notes recorded just above for verse 6 and verse 8.
**b)** **I will cut off.** To ensure it doesn't seem the Prophet was only speaking of the sins of Gaza in verse 6, he now announces the destruction of each of the major Philistine cities in verses 7 and 8. However, he omits the fifth city (Gath, 1 Samuel 6:17). Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian.</note> gives the reason that Gath belonged to the Kings of Judah. Compare 2 Samuel 18:1; 1 Chronicles 18:1.
**c)** See note on Isaiah 20:1.
**d)** See note on verse 5.
**e)** Joshua 13:3; Judges 1, 18.
**f)** **and I will turn** (Isaiah 1:25; Zechariah 13:7). Cocceius translates it as "I will repeatedly bring upon." Rashi <note>Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: "I will strike with repeated blows." Compare note on Jeremiah 6:9.
**g)** Targum Jonathan says "the blow of my power."
**h)** Joshua 13:3.
**i)** Why he says "remnants" is explained in the note on Jeremiah 25:20. Compare Jeremiah 47:4; Ezekiel 25:16; also note on Isaiah 14:28 and 20:1.
**k)** **Tyre**, regarding which see the note on Isaiah 23:1 and Ezekiel 26:2. The Tyrians are joined with the Philistines in the threat of punishment as they were allies in crime and mutual assistants. So Jeremiah 47:4; Joel 4:4.

### CHAPTER 1. 2. AMOS 1, 2

<margin>
...and his blasphemous people <note>original Latin: "populum ipsius blasphemi"</note> in Ezekiel 35:13, contaminating the Temple with profane and impious comparisons in Obadiah verse 16. They were hostile, fierce allies and assistants in verse 11, 14, Psalm 137:7, bloodthirsty and cruel in Joel 4:19, Obadiah verse 10, and Jeremiah 49:11. They arrogated to themselves the land of both nations, Israel and Judah, with wicked presumption in Ezekiel 35:10.
</margin>

<margin>
k) See the note on verse 3. l) Because they had handed over the captives <note>original: "vinctam reddiderant"</note>, see verse 6 and Deuteronomy 23:16. Furthermore, sacred history does not explicitly mention this specific moment; however, it can hardly be doubted that the cruelty of the Tyrians toward the Jews should be referred to the same time as that of the Philistines. This is suggested not only by the order of the prophecy, in which the Tyrians immediately follow the Philistines, but also by the parallel in Joel 4:4, where a similar example of inhumanity is charged against both nations. Compare the note on verse 6. m) See note on verse 6. n) See the same. o) And so (others unnecessarily take this as a relative, "who," namely the Edomites) they did not remember. p) Of the covenant of brothers, or the brotherly covenant. He calls them brothers here as friends joined by necessity, because Hiram, the prince of Tyre, maintained friendships with David and Solomon. So Jerome notes. The Arabs also use the word **ach** <note>Hebrew/Arabic for 'brother'</note> to refer not only to a brother or relative, but to anyone joined by brotherly love. Compare 1 Samuel 5:11, 1 Kings 5:26, and also verse 15 and chapter 9:13, where Hiram explicitly calls Solomon "brother."

### CHAPTER 2 & 3. עמוס ב ג <note>Amos 2 and 3</note>

<margin>
**v. 15. k)** holding (skilled in handling) the bow, an archer. Jeremiah 46:9. **l)** he shall not stand, but shall either perish, Psalm 102:27 <note>original Latin: "non consistet, sed vel peribit"</note>, being unable to match the enemy, Daniel 11:6, 8, 25; or he shall immediately take flight, Jeremiah 46:21; Nahum 2:9. **m)** and he who is swift on his feet. see verse 14; 2 Samuel 2:18. **n)** namely, his life <note>original Latin: "animam suam"</note>, from verse 14 and the following part of this verse 15. **o)**
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 13. q)** Therefore, etc. He adds the punishment for such great ingratitude. Compare Isaiah 3:1; chapter 17:1. **r)** I am about to press down. **s)** **y)** from the root צוק <note>Tsuq - meaning to constrain or distress</note> in Chaldean and Syriac. **a)** constrained or narrowed, for the Hebrew צוק is the same. Something similar occurs in Hebrew where רבץ <note>to crouch</note> is used for רבץ, or רעע <note>to be evil/break</note> for רעע, and רצץ <note>to crush</note> for רצץ, which is frequent in Chaldaisms. Compare the nouns in Psalm 55:4; Psalm 66:11. **t)** This is taken here as a noun and almost as an abstract: "your inferiorities" <note>original Latin: "inferioritates vestras"</note>; that is, I will press you yourselves down, making you succumb beneath me, no differently than a wagon, well-loaded with sheaves of grain, presses down on whatever lies beneath it. So, אחרי <note>after</note> is used for the back part in 2 Samuel 2:23; בֵּין <note>between</note> for in the midst in Isaiah 44:4. Thus, it expresses the state of the one being acted upon, rather than the actor. Unless perhaps it is more pleasing to say that the particle with the suffix designates a turning toward the object, as if to say: "I will press, by bearing downward (as heavy things tend to do) upon you." But Jonathan <note>referring to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation</note>, understanding the pronoun "You," says: "I will bring upon you tribulation, which will press you in your place." Compare Exodus 16:29. **b)** he presses; but passively "they are pressed," and according to Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century theologian</note>, "is narrowed," though without necessity. **c)** a wagon. Isaiah 5:18; chapter 28:27. **d)** full for itself. A pleonasm <note>using more words than necessary for emphasis</note>, meaning "well-loaded." **e)** with a sheaf, used collectively for "sheaves." **(u)** Jeremiah 9:21; Micah 4:12.
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 15. n)** sitting upon a horse. Compare Psalm 33:17; Zechariah 10:5. **p)** Compare chapter 9:1.
**v. 16. q)** And he who is otherwise firm in his heart and unafraid. Compare Job 9:4, 19. **r)** Compare 1 Chronicles 12:1. **s)** having cast off his garment, which the enemy had grabbed, as in Genesis 39:12; just like that young man in Mark 14:52. But Jonathan <note>the Targum</note> adds: "without weapons." As if to say, you will throw away your weapons so that you may flee more quickly. **t)** verse 11. Compare the note on Ezekiel 11:8.
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 14. f)** And escape shall perish from the swift, verse 15. That is, there shall be none. Jeremiah 25:35; chapter 46:6; Job 11:20. After explaining the gravity of the imminent evil in verse 13, he now proceeds in verses 14, 15, and 16 to describe its inevitability; by which he anticipates any objection regarding speed, strength, bravery, equipment, or military skill. Compare Jeremiah 9:22; Ecclesiastes 9:11. **g)** he will not be able to apply his quality, or exert it—to resist. Proverbs 24:5. **h)** verse 16. Compare Jeremiah 9:22; chapter 46:6. **i)** you shall rescue your life <note>original Latin: "animam (vitam)"</note>.

**CHAPTER 3. v. 1. n)** This form of address is solemn for our prophet, exciting attention to hear a matter of great importance. See verse 13; chapter 4:1; 5:1; 8:4; and the note on Micah 1:2. **x). 2. y) o)** Children of Israel! He addresses all the tribes of both Judah and the Israelite kingdom (for he follows with an apposition and declaration: "against the whole family, which I brought out from the land of Egypt"). But a little later, setting aside the Jews, he turns specifically to the Israelite kingdom in verses 9, 12, 14. See note on 1.1.1. This chapter, as observed above, has three parts: I. The address and the Prophet's defense (v. 1–8). II. The malice and violence of Israel, which is worse than the pagans (v. 9–10). III. Their very heavy punishment (v. 11 ff.). **z)** chapter 2:10. **V. 2. a)** Only you. Job 1:15. As if to say: "I have done for no other nation as I have for you." Compare 2 Samuel 7:23; 1 Chronicles 17:21; also Psalm 147:20; Deuteronomy 4:8, 20. See the note on chapter 2:9 above. **b)** I have known, or graciously chosen. See note on Jeremiah 1:5. Jonathan: "In you was my pleasure." Psalm 1:6; Galatians 4:9. (Compare Hosea 9:10; chapter 13:5; Malachi 1:2). **c)** As a special possession from all, etc. Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 14:2; Psalm 135:4. **d)** Therefore, much more so even than other nations. This is a wondrous but most just conclusion. For from him who has received much, much is required; and the greater the measure of grace, the heavier the punishment for neglected or despised grace. Deuteronomy 28:63; Luke 12:48; Romans 1:9–10. Hence the Apostle warns in Hebrews 2:1–3. I will visit (revisit, remember) upon or against you, etc. I will be so mindful of your sins in my judgment that I will pour back their punishments upon your head. Verse 14; Exodus 20:5. **v. 3. f)** "For will two indeed go together," says the Prophet. They satisfy the Oriental style with the parabolic questions that follow; they are like Enthymemes <note>logical arguments with a hidden premise</note>, in which another proposition or conclusion always lies hidden. A brief application follows in verses 7 and 8. They seem to aim at this goal: to demonstrate (1) that he and other Prophets announce evils to the Israelites not by their own authority, but by divine command (v. 3, 8). (2) That this is not done rashly, but for very serious reasons, namely, because of the sins of the people (v. 4). (3) That these are not vain or empty omens, but will inevitably be fulfilled unless the people repent (v. 5). (4) Yet underneath this very announcement of wrath is the grace of God, who desires to consult his people so that they might prevent the predicted punishments through serious conversion (v. 6, 8, 9). **unless, except for** see verse 4; Judges 7:14. **h)** they have come together by agreement, or it was agreed upon by them, regarding a certain time and place where they are to go. Joshua 11:5; Job 2:11; Nehemiah 6:2, 10. The parable generally says that hardly anything happens by chance, rashly, or in vain, but by a fixed and certain end: this holds much more for the Prophets, who would never announce imminent signs unless they were divinely appointed to this office, having God present in everything they speak, not only as a companion but as the author. **v. 4. i)** Does a lion roar. verse 8. **k)** when prey (an animal to be torn) is not for him: In the roar of the lion, this is most terrifying: that by this growling, or this trumpet-call if you prefer, he declares war. And after the roar, slaughter and tearing immediately follow. For he is not accustomed to using that sharp and sustained roar unless he sees prey upon which he may immediately rush. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* Part I, 729. Compare Isaiah 5:29; chapter 31:4; Jeremiah 2:14; Ezekiel 22:25; Psalm 104:21. So too, God does not speak through the Prophets in vain, but threatens sinners with a horrible slaughter that will most certainly follow unless they are terrified by His voice and immediately repent. verse 8. **l)** a young lion; **m)** it is said when he begins to prey, Ezekiel 19:3; Judges 14:5. **m)** from his den. (Psalm 104:22; Song of Solomon 4:8; compare Nahum 2:12). For sometimes lions lay snares from their hiding places for other animals or men; Psalm 10:10; compare Jeremiah 5:29; Job 38:40; Lamentations 3:10. **n)** unless verse 3. **o)** he has caught something; or, unless he is about to catch something. It is a hunter's word, as in verse 5; Judges 15:14; Isaiah 24:18; Lamentations 4:20. And indeed, this latter clause is an explanation of the preceding one, or of the same sense as the first, with only the words changed. **v. 5. p)** Does it fall, i.e., is it accustomed to be snared? compare Proverbs 7:23. **q)** upon a snare stretched on the ground, or hidden. Psalm 124:7. **r)** **y)** where there is no trap for it. Though מוקשׁ and פַּח are synonyms, the latter here expresses the arrangement of the snare, which is so fitted by the fowler that it can bind small birds that fall into it; just as the former can signify a snare even when it is not actually set for catching. Compare Psalm 140:6 and 141:9. Thus the parabolic sense is: A snare does not catch a bird unless it is set by a fowler to catch. The goal of the parable here is that no evils happen by chance, but are intended by God against sinners unless they repent (v. 6), which He therefore reveals in advance to His servants, the Prophets. Thus Jeremiah 50:24; Hosea 7:12; Proverbs 5:22. **s)** Does it ascend, i.e., is the snare tripped? **t)** and catch nothing (nothing at all)? verse 4. So also God's designs, which He predicts through His servants, will not be in vain: but will certainly and heavily strike the unrepentant. **v. 6. u)** Is a trumpet blown. chapter 2:2; Joel 2:1. It seems to refer to a watchman stationed on a lookout, who, if he sees the enemy approaching, warns the people with a trumpet so that they may either escape immediately by fleeing or gather to resist the enemy. Ezekiel 33:2 ff.

<summary>This page concludes the judgment of Israel in Amos 2, emphasizing that neither speed nor strength will allow the wicked to escape God's "pressure." It begins Amos 3 by establishing the prophet's authority through a series of cause-and-effect parables, arguing that just as a lion roars only when it has prey, a prophet speaks only because God has acted.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the Book of Amos. Having concluded the charges against the nations and the initial warnings to Israel in chapter 2, the text moves into Chapter 3, which focuses on the "cause and effect" relationship between Israel's sin and God's inevitable judgment. The commentary focuses heavily on the nature of divine revelation and the role of the prophet as a messenger of impending "evil" (punishment).</meta>

### AMOS. CHAPTER 3.

<margin>
*) so that the people (the citizens and inhabitants of the city) do not tremble, or run together in fear and haste. See Hosea 11:10, 11; 1 Samuel 16:4. Now indeed the Prophets warn you of the imminent evils which they foresee through divine revelation; therefore, this warning is by no means to be despised by you, but rather you must fortunately provide for a serious conversion so that the imminent evil may be averted. Compare Ezekiel 3:17 and following; 33:2, 5, and following. y) If evil shall happen: this refers not to the evil of guilt <note>original: "non culpæ"</note>, as in Jeremiah 26:19, etc. (compare Psalm 5:5), but the evil of punishment <note>original: "pœnæ"</note>, as in Jeremiah 1:14; 18:8, etc. (compare Isaiah 45:7). z) which Jehovah has not done: if not always by immediate action, then by governing according to His secret wisdom and justice. Compare Isaiah 45:14, 6, 7; Lamentations 3:37. This is evident from the fact that He reveals evils to His Prophets before He brings them; He would by no means do this unless He Himself directed everything by His supreme will, compare verse 7. If indeed it is God who not only predicts evils but also inflicts them, then if He predicts any evil through the Prophets, it must be received by you with reverence, and not at all with murmuring or contempt.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 7. a) any evil on the earth (see verse 6). b) unless He has revealed, 1 Samuel 9:15. c) His secret or His counsel. Jeremiah 23:18, 22; Proverbs 3:32. Thus He revealed the flood to Noah, the destruction of Sodom to Abraham and Lot, and the ruin of Nineveh to Jonah, so that (to use the words of Jerome on this passage) those who heard the coming punishments might either perform penance and avoid the torments, or, by being contemptuous, be more justly punished. And note, (he says shortly after) that the merciful and kind God always foretells future things so that He is not forced to inflict punishments. And as for what the Heretics calumniate against the Creator—as if He were severe, grim, and cruel
</margin>

For He who foretells does not wish to punish the sinners. Compare Daniel 2:22; Revelation 1:1; and also Genesis 18:17.

<margin>
all things tremble, and the whole nature of living things is terrified. (Jerome). Nay, God Himself, who is in infinitely many ways more terrible than any lion, has threatened sinners with His wrath and horrendous judgments through me and other Prophets. (verse 7). See above at verse 4. For here he begins to apply to a more literal sense those things which he had spoken there figuratively and parabolically. e) <unclear>He who</unclear> in this place is understood not as an impossibility, but as a rarity. For he will not fear, and he will not prophesy, who out of his own hardness has contempt for hearing the Lord. (Jerome). Add that the word <term>Who</term> in this place is taken not so much regarding the fact, as regarding the right; compare Jeremiah 10:7. Indeed, the interrogation at the same time reproaches the madness and stupor of men, who are not even terrified at the voice of the terrible God, even though they know it is a fearful thing to fall into His hands (Hebrews 10:31). f) compare the note on Isaiah 19:7. g) He has spoken and commanded me to prophesy; see chapter 7:15. h) as if to say: We Prophets, therefore, cannot help but prophesy, even if you were to say to us a hundred times: "Do not prophesy" (chapter 2:12; 7:15, 16). Compare 1 Corinthians 9:16; Acts 4:20; 5:29. 
</margin> 

<margin> 
v. 9. i) Make your voice heard, i.e., proclaim (chapter 4:5). These are the words of God to His Prophets, compare verse 10. k) to the palaces in Ashdod (chapter 1:8). As if to say: call the neighboring peoples as witnesses, even though they are pagans and fascinated by superstition, so that observing the crimes of the Israelites, they may judge and testify against them. Compare Ezekiel 15:27; Micah 6:2. l) Ezekiel 39:17. m) chapter 4:1. n) great confusions; elsewhere it signifies punishment, as in 2 Chronicles 15:5; Isaiah 22:5, but in this place it signifies guilt—namely, open injuries which disturb everything and mix things upside down. Compare Ezekiel 22:5; Proverbs 15:16; and the related word in Jeremiah 51:34, to which below in chapter 4:1 the word <term>the oppressed</term> corresponds; regarding its difference from "to oppress," see our note there. o) and those oppressed by the powerful in its midst. See chapter 4:1; Jeremiah 50:33; Colossians 4:1. He commands them first to observe the crimes of Israel, so that they may then approve the just judgment of God over them.
</margin> 

<margin>
v. 10. p) For they do not know, or according to Schmid, "Yet they have not known." Isaiah 56:11; 82:5. q) right (4) 2 Samuel 15:3; Isaiah 59:14. It properly signifies that which is directly before the eyes (Proverbs 4:25; Isaiah 57:2), so that there is no need for the eyes to wander to the right or the left. Justice is of this kind: simple, flat, and foreign to twists—that is, to frauds and tricks. r) who treasure up, or collect and heap up as a treasure (5) 2 Kings 20:17; compare Romans 2:5. s) chapter 6:3; Genesis 6:11, 13. s) devastation, by the action through which they desolate the innocent. Jeremiah 6:7; 20:8. See above, chapter 2:6, 7 and chapter 5:11, 12.
</margin> 

<margin>
v. 11. *) Therefore. It refers back to verses 9 and 10. Namely, because of the horrendous injustice, detestable even to the Gentiles. x) there shall be distress, already in verse 2. Others: an enemy, namely, shall be present; compare Lamentations 4:12. y) and indeed in the circuit (perhaps the whole circumference, Lamentations 2:3) of the land. Thus the word for "adversary" <term>Tsar</term> is used for "distress" <term>Matsor</term> in Jeremiah 15:13; Ezekiel 13:7, 22. Which Cocceius in his Lexicon (p. 189) judges not unlike the Greek in Romans 9:23; Isaiah 1:26. z) He shall cast down, namely the Lord. But others say: he (the enemy) who shall tear down. Isaiah 63:6; Obadiah verse 3. a) your power. Exodus 26:11; chapter 30:6, 18. b) they shall be plundered. From the root "to plunder" in the Niphal form (3) Isaiah 24:3. c) your palaces, which for others are covered with luxury, verse 9; compare verse 10; chapter 6:8.
</margin> 

<margin>
v. 12. d) Chapter 1:3, 6; 2:1, 4, etc. The universality of the slaughter was described in verse 11; its magnitude is added here. e) he rescues, and indeed "scarcely" or "hardly." chapter 4:11; 1 Samuel 17:35; compare 2 Timothy 4:17. f) only the legs (9) Exodus 12:9. g) a lobe (1). The same is used for the mouth as is used for a person's "neck" in Exodus 29:20; it properly denotes a portion, from the root "to divide" in the Hiphil form; therefore the word is radical, not a prefix, although Kimchi follows the latter. Bochart, Hierozoicon Part I, pages 493, 494. h) thus only a few, and especially the weakest, while the greater and stronger part is consumed. Compare chapter 5:3; 9:8. i) they shall be rescued, they shall escape. Ezekiel 14:16, 18; Micah 4:10. k) those reclining here and there through the houses in the side or corner (Exodus 25:26; 26:18, 20) of a bed. He includes the sick or those weak with age to denote the most meager remains. For according to the accents, it depends not on the closer word "those dwelling," but the more remote "shall be rescued." Compare below, chapter 6:10. l) and in the corner or the support of a couch (1). To be explained by analogy with the preceding. It denotes some part of a bed or couch. Cocceius. But Neumann (Ex. L. S. p. 87) says: in a silken covering. Or it understands those hiding in the houses in the side of the dining rooms, compare Ezekiel 23:41; Esther 1:6; 7:8; or hiding in the corner of beds or behind the bed. Compare 2 Kings 11:2.
</margin>

Exodus 19:21. o) Ezekiel 11:8; 16:14. p) Observe here the full construction, as in chapter 5:14; 6:14. * Compare the note on Isaiah 1:24; Hosea 12:6.

<summary>This page analyzes Amos 3:6-14, emphasizing that God reveals His coming judgments to the Prophets as an act of mercy to allow for repentance. It includes detailed philological debates on the extent of the coming destruction, symbolized by a shepherd rescuing mere scraps of an animal from a lion.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general warnings of Chapter 3 to the specific destruction of the cultic altars at Beth-el and the luxurious homes of the elite. It then opens Chapter 4 with a scathing critique of the wealthy women (the "cows of Bashan") in Samaria and a satirical call to "worship" at the corrupt shrines of Beth-el and Gilgal, emphasizing that their religious rituals are merely for their own pleasure rather than God's honor.</meta>

<header>AMOS 3:14–4:5</header>

<margin>
z) In this visitation [punishment] mentioned in verse 2.
a) Referring to the calves wickedly constructed in 1 Kings 12:32 and 13:1–2; compare also Hosea 10:1–8.
x) Compare Chapter 4:4; Hosea 4:15 and 10:15.
y) That they may be cut down. See Isaiah 14:12 and Ezekiel 6:6.
z) The horns (projections, extending upward like horns; they are so named because they stand out) or based on their position at the four corners of the altars, as seen in Exodus 27:2. The Syriac word <note>original: "קרנא"</note> also means "corner," as in Acts 10:11, translating the Greek <note>original: "τεσσάρσιν γωνίαις"</note> [four corners].
a) Compare Chapter 7:9.
b) Compare Isaiah 21:9.
v. 15. c) And I will strike, as in Chapter 6:11. This refers to the time of the total destruction of the kingdom of Israel by the Assyrians, as noted above in verses 11–12. It does not refer to an earthquake here; compare the notes on Chapter 1:1 and 2 Kings 3:19.
d) The winter house, or house suited for spending the winter season. See Jeremiah 36:22.
e) Together with. Genesis 32:12.
f) The summer house. Genesis 8:22 and Zechariah 14:8. That is, both winter and summer residences, which kings and princes kept separate for their comfort. Compare Judges 3:20.
g) Houses of ivory, or houses shining with much ivory, or (according to Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the prophets.</note>) houses paneled with ivory. Chapter 6:4; 1 Kings 22:39; Psalm 45:9.
h) And they shall have an end. From the root <note>original: "סוף"</note>. Compare Isaiah 66:17 or Jeremiah 12:4.
i) Compare Chapter 6:11 and Isaiah 5:8. The Prophet seems to be looking at the state of the kingdom of Israel during the time of Jeroboam II (see Chapter 1:1) and later Pekah, under whose flourishing reigns the Israelites—especially the powerful—boasted in building many magnificent houses. Chapter 5:11; 6:11; and Isaiah 9:9.
</margin>

->### CHAPTER IV.<-

<margin>
Referring to those who are acting fiercely, like the well-fed cattle raised in the pastures of Bashan. Ezekiel 39:18; Psalm 22:13; Deuteronomy 32:14. This denotes an injurious insolence arising from an abundance of things. Jonathan <note>The Targum</note> explains it well: "those wealthy in resources." For he addresses the opulent and the great, though he later transitions to the whole people in verse 4.
</margin>

<margin>
CHAPTER IV, verse 1.
k) See the note on Chapter 3:1.
This Chapter 4 deals with:
I. A charge against the leaders of the kingdom of Israel (vv. 1–3).
II. A charge against all Israelites (vv. 4–11), reproaching the former for the oppression of the poor and luxury, and the latter for idolatry and persistence in sin, while threatening both with punishment.
III. An admonition to repentance (vv. 12–13).
l) O cows of Bashan, that is, the well-fed ones.
</margin>

Hosea 10:11. m) That is, in Samaria, the royal seat which was built upon the mountain. Chapter 3:9; compare 1 Kings 16:24. n) Ch. 3:9; Micah 2:2; Hosea 12:8. o) Ch. 2:7; 8:6. p) Crushing or bruising. The preceding word <note>original: "עשק"</note> is somewhat different; it is more general, denoting any injury or oppression, whether open or hidden by fraud. By contrast, <note>original: "רצץ"</note> means to inflict manifest violence (1 Samuel 12:3–4; Hosea 5:11; Judges 10:8). Literally, it means to crush something so thoroughly that it cannot stand upright (Isaiah 42:3). q) Ch. 2:6; 5:12. r) To their lords, that is, to the Kings who were equally evil. Although the singular could be translated as "Lord" (referring to their God, as in James 4:3), this noun with the third-person plural suffix is never used for God in the scriptures. See Genesis 40:1; Jeremiah 27:3; 2 Samuel 10:3, etc. s) Give here! or bring, so that we may drink. There is nothing to prevent this from being understood literally as the mutual gluttony of the princes and kings (whom he addresses in verse 1). Compare Ch. 7:4–8 and Hosea 7:5. However, Jonathan interprets it as a thirst for greed: "Give us the power that we may plunder." Compare Ch. 2:6–7. t) Therefore, He will not change His decree. Ch. 6:8; Psalm 110:4. u) By His holiness, which He can never deny. Psalm 89:8; 2 Timothy 2:13. x) Affirming, as in Ch. 2:10; Jeremiah 31:8. y) Compare Isaiah 7:17. z) That the Lord may carry you away. If interpreted as the Piel form, the vowel Kamets is used for Patach (as in 1 Kings 9:11). Or, in the Niphal form, "that you may be taken away" (as in 2 Kings 20:17), as if to say your very identity will be removed. See Numbers 26:47; Jeremiah 36:22. The grammatical genders are mixed here: Masculine for the literal sense, and Feminine continuing the metaphor of the "cows" from verse 1. a) With thorns or prickles. Proverbs 22:5. That is, with hooks. This corresponds to the following phrase "with fishing pots [hooks]," which shows that the points of thorns used in fishing were the original hooks. Compare Job 40:26, 31. Similarly, the word for hook <note>original: "חח"</note> in Ezekiel 29:4 comes from "thorns" in 2 Kings 14:9. Thus, two metaphors are mixed, and the sense is this: Jehovah will drag you from your cities and homes through the Assyrians, just as a fisherman pulls a fish from its element with a hook. See Jeremiah 16:16. b) And your last part, O Princes (from v. 1). That is, whatever remains or survives of you. See Ch. 9:1 and Ezekiel 23:25. Or, it could refer to your posterity or children. c) With thorns. Hosea 2:9. See what was just said above. d) Of fishing, meaning the fisherman's tool. (1) v. 14; compare Jeremiah 16:16. v. 3. e) And through the breaches of your torn-down cities. Ch. 9:11; 1 Kings 11:27. f) You shall go out, O cows (v. 1), into captivity. Ezekiel 36:20. g) Each cow [woman] straight ahead of her. That is, in every direction they look. The walls will be so torn apart by the enemy that exits will be everywhere, and they won't even need gates to leave. Compare Joshua 6:5, 20; Ezekiel 47:15; Jeremiah 49:5. h) This difficult word is explained differently by interpreters. Many versions take it as a passive, including the Septuagint and Vulgate: "you shall be cast out," treating the following word "Armonah" as a proper name. Others take it actively: "you shall cast away whatever you carried into the palace"; for your wealth, which you now gape at (Amos 3:10), will be of no use to you then. See Isaiah 2, 20; Ezekiel 7:19; Zechariah 11:13. i) To the palace. Ch. 2:14. Symmachus translates as "Armenia." Theodotion reads it as "Mount Mona." The Septuagint and Arabic versions have "Mount Remman." The Vulgate says "into Armon." Jonathan says "beyond the mountains of Armenia." Most treat it as a proper name, though some see it as a compound of "Har" (Mountain) and "Meni" (as in Jeremiah 51:27), referring to the Minyans, a part of Armenia. They were led into or beyond Armenia when taken captive by the Assyrians (2 Kings 17:23). Others take it as a common noun for "the palace" (Har-mon). v. 4. k) This is an ironic concession, like Jeremiah 7:21 and Ezekiel 20:39. As if to say: "Go ahead, do what you have always done; frequent the ungodly worship at Beth-el and Gilgal, but at your own peril. The more obstinate you are in maintaining that worship, the more severe I will be in inflicting punishment." l) See v. 5; Ch. 3:14; 5:5; Hosea 5:8. n) And Gilgal, where you instituted wicked worship just as at Beth-el and Dan. Although history is silent on this, the Prophets speak of it (Hosea 12:12). Indeed, Hosea 9:15 argues that the sum of Israel's wickedness was concentrated in this one place. The Ark of the Covenant had been here for a time, and it was where circumcision originally took place; these were perhaps used as a pretext for their religion. o) Transgress greatly. For whatever you did there was a transgression against God, whom you replaced with idols. p) In the morning, so there is no delay. Or rather, "every morning," taking the prefix "le" distributively. q) A hyperbole: and every three days (or every third day) bring your tithes; though the Mosaic law only required them every three years (Deuteronomy 14:28). Worship is vain—even harmful—when it is established against the mind of God, no matter how much "works of supererogation" or imagined merits are involved. Compare Micah 6:6–8.

r) And by burning [incense or sacrifices]. The word <note>original: "קטר"</note> means to burn not just for a pleasant smell, but for the fat-smoke of a sacrifice. s) From leavened bread. Exodus 12:15. This was a "chosen" worship, contrary to the divine law which commanded that all leaven be excluded from sacrifices (Leviticus 2:11). Or perhaps it is called leavened because, while technically unleavened, it is regarded by God as corrupted. Compare Isaiah 66:3; Jeremiah 7:21–22. t) Jonathan translates this as "from oppression" or cattle taken unjustly. t) A sacrifice of confession or praise. Leviticus 7:12.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the prophet Amos has just finished mocking the wealthy elite of Samaria for their performative and hollow religious rituals at Beth-el and Gilgal. He now transitions into a list of divine warnings—natural disasters and calamities—that God sent to the people to bring them to repentance, though they remained obstinate.</meta>

<margin>
**v. 5. a)** *and proclaim:* make it known publicly and with a solemn ritual. See Joel 2:15. Do this so that these things come to public notice and are preached. **x)** *voluntary offerings:* See Exodus 35:29, Leviticus 22:18, 21, and Deuteronomy 12:6. **y)** *hear, I say, and do:* make it known for the sake of ostentation, perhaps using trumpets or other musical instruments, much like the hypocritical Pharisees did in the time of Christ (Matthew 6:2, 5). It appears the meaning here is similar to a paraphrase: "and they bring it with music, saying: 'This is for God's pleasure.'" Compare a similar but innocent ritual in 1 Samuel 30:20. **z)** *you love to do so and have agreed to it;* but it is of little benefit or praise for you. This indicates a certain irony. See Jeremiah 7:31 and compare Ezekiel 66:3. **a)** See verse 3 and 6, and Chapter 3:10.

**v. 6. b)** This could be seen as a consequence, comparing the punishment with the guilt; as if to say, "therefore I also gave you, by most just reason, etc.," as in Ezekiel 31:2. However, in this passage, the prophet rather exaggerates the fault of their stubbornness and explains the cause of the decree to utterly abolish the kingdom of Israel (v. 2, 3)—namely, that they refused to be corrected by past punishments: famine, drought, blight, plague, and slaughter (v. 6–12). For this reason, in verses 12 and 13, he repeats and continues that decree. Thus we explain it: "For besides other kinds of punishments by which I intended to lead you to repentance, I also gave you—but you did not return." The repetition in verse 7 is emphatic. **c)** The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, the <term>Vulgate</term> <note>The Latin Bible translation.</note>, and other ancient versions translate this as "stupor," as if the meaning were drawn from a similar-sounding word in Jeremiah 31:29. However, it is better to stick to the constant use of the root word and translate it as *cleanness* or *emptiness*.

He lists here five types of punishments that lead up to the total and final judgment in verse 12.

13. Certain events were like preludes, namely: famine in verse 6; drought in verse 7; locusts and mildew in verse 9; pestilence in verse 10; and fire falling from heaven in verse 11. **e)** *yet you did not return*. Even though I intended, by punishing you, to give you an opportunity for repentance. See verses 8, 9, 10, and 11. Compare Ezekiel 9:12, Jeremiah 2:30, and 5:3. **f)** *to me*: This is emphatic. See notes on Lamentations 3:40 and compare Hosea 7:10. **v. 7.** **g)** *See the note on verse 6.* **h)** *I withheld* or *denied* to you. Genesis 30:2, Isaiah 31:3. **i)** See Joel 1:17, Jeremiah 14:1, and 1 Kings 17:1. **k)** *While there were still three months until harvest*; therefore, through an entire three-month period before the harvest, the crops could not help but wither completely. Jerome <note>The early church father and translator.</note> says this refers to the spring season at the end of April, from which there are three months left until the grain harvest: May, June, and July. **l)** *so that I caused it to rain on one city, but...* Genesis 2:5, Psalm 5:6. Thus the drought, even if not universal, was vast and scattered throughout the land (compare v. 8). From this you should have recognized that the drought was not accidental, but sent by God. **m)** *I caused it to rain or will cause it to rain*. It is clear that the future tense here and in following verbs stands in place of the past tense, because the consequence is always "yet you have not returned." This change of tense is for emphasis: just as future tenses can express continuous action, here they suggest the punishments were repeated. **n)** *and one part of the field*. 2 Samuel 14:30. **o)** *it was rained upon*, receiving rain. **(i p)** *it rains*: impersonal; or understand "the cloud" <note>original: "עָב"</note>, which is feminine in Hebrew (1 Kings 18:44). **q)** *it withered*. See Joel 1:12. **v. 8. r)** *They even wandered*, or *from where two or three cities wandered*. Chapter 8:12, Genesis 4:12. He withheld the rain so that they suffered not only a lack of bread (v. 7) but also the burning of thirst. Jerome notes: "In these places... except for small springs, all water comes from cisterns; and if the rains are suspended by divine wrath, the danger of thirst is greater than that of hunger." **s)** *But not even so did you return*. **v. 9. t)** *with blight, or* (as in Arabic) *a burning wind that scorches the crops so they dry up before maturity* (1 Kings 8:37). This is the destructive effect of the East Wind in the Orient. Genesis 41:6. **u)** *and with mildew*. This noun is usually joined with the previous one and marks a defect in the grain where it withers prematurely. Deuteronomy 28:2; compare the word for "yellow" in Leviticus 13:49. **x)** *the multitude*, meaning the majority of your gardens. Properly an infinitive, but used as a noun. **y)** *your fig trees, that is, the trees themselves*. Nahum 3:12. **z)** commonly *caterpillar* (Joel 1:3). Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar of biblical animals.</note> proves it is a type of locust, named for cutting or gnawing the branches of trees. In Arabic and the Talmud, the root means "to cut off." **v. 10. b)** Leviticus 26:25. **c)** *pestilence*; sent for a good purpose, namely that you might return (2 Chronicles 7:13). **d)** *in the way of Egypt*, meaning that part of your region that looks toward Egypt (Isaiah 10:24). This could refer to the kingdom of Israel (the inhabitants addressed in v. 1) or the whole land of Canaan, signifying southern Judea. Others say: "on the road to Egypt, when you went there seeking grain or help" (Hosea 7:11). Finally, others say: "after the manner of Egypt," like the plagues sent there (Exodus 9:3). **e)** Hosea 6:5. **f)** *young men in the flower of their youth, chosen for military service*. This occurred through the Syrian kings Hazael and Ben-hadad (2 Kings 8:12, 13:3) during the time of Joash, the grandfather of Jeroboam II, under whom Amos prophesied. **g)** *with captivity*, that is, while your horses were being captured. **h)** *captivity* usually denotes human captives, but it is also used for animals. **i)** *so that I caused the stench to rise*. Isaiah 34:3, Joel 2:20. **k)** *of your camps*, meaning the camps of the armies within the heart of the kingdom. **l)** *even into your nostrils*. See Numbers 11:20.

The commentary emphasizes the stubbornness of the people, who experienced these calamities but refused to return to their covenant with God.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER 4 & 5. AMOS 4 5</header>

<margin>
...earnestly, so that you may repent truly and without delay, lest you experience the most heavy wrath of Almighty God. For behold, he with whom you have business formed the mountains, etc., and so it is not to be doubted that he can bring about what he has threatened. 
**a)** the former of mountains. *Isaiah 43:5, 45:12, 18. Jeremiah 10:16.*
**b)** compare *Zechariah 12:1. Numbers 16:22, 27:16.* 
**c)** and as the omniscient God, he indicates to man and effectively convinces him that he...

<margin>
**verse 11. n)** I have overthrown among you, i.e., some of your cities and villages. The perfect tense signifies a part <note>The author explains that the Hebrew grammar implies a partial rather than total destruction at this stage.</note>, as in *Hosea 6:5, Psalm 78:31.* For this reason, he compares them to a firebrand snatched from the burning; because that destruction was not universal. 
**o)** according to the overthrow of God, wherewith he overthrew Sodom *Genesis 19:24, 25.* Drusius <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant Old Testament scholar.</note> thinks this hyperbolically signifies extreme devastation, as in *Isaiah 13:19* regarding Babylon, which is nowhere read to have been overthrown by a divine fire. But we prefer to explain it as a fire sent by God, by which several places in the Israelite kingdom were burned. Compare below *Amos 7:4 and notes on 1:1,* as was foretold by Moses in *Deuteronomy 29:22.* Something of this kind in the time of King Uzziah, under whom our prophet lived, is gathered from the contemporary *Isaiah 1:7-9.* 
**p)** like a firebrand (3) *Isaiah 7:4. Zechariah 3:2.* 
**q)** already scorched, yet still snatched away. *Chapter 3:12, Zechariah 3:2.* compare *Jude 1:23.* 
**r)** see note on verse 6.
</margin>

11 I have overthrown <gloss>n</gloss> among you <gloss>o</gloss> as the overthrow <gloss>p</gloss> of God <gloss>q</gloss> of Sodom and Gomorrah <gloss>r</gloss> and you were <gloss>s</gloss> like a firebrand <gloss>t</gloss> snatched from the burning <gloss>u</gloss> and you have not returned to me <gloss>w</gloss> says the Lord.
12 Therefore thus will I do to you <gloss>s</gloss> O Israel <gloss>t</gloss> because <gloss>u</gloss> I will do this to you <gloss>x</gloss> prepare to meet your God <gloss>y</gloss> O Israel.
13 For behold, he who forms the mountains <gloss>a</gloss> and creates the wind <gloss>b</gloss> and declares to man what is his thought <gloss>c</gloss> who makes the morning darkness <gloss>d, e, f</gloss> and treads upon the high places of the earth <gloss>g</gloss> the Lord, God of hosts, is his name <gloss>h</gloss>.

<margin>
**verse 12. s)** thus, as I threatened in verses 2 and 3. As if to say: I will affect you with a more severe discipline, you who have hitherto despised those preceding corrections. Compare *Ezekiel 7:27.* 
**t)** but because. That is: for this reason, because. *Numbers 14:24. 2 Samuel 12:10.* 
**u)** so I am about to do to you. 
**x)** and so prepare yourself, that even now you may still turn, and thus go to meet him, etc. *1 Samuel 7:3. Psalm 57:8.* 
**y)** to meet God, who is coming to inflict the most grievous punishment upon you *Amos 5:17,* so that you might turn away his wrath and imminent judgments through humble repentance and prayers before they break forth. For this is what it means to "meet God." Compare *1 Samuel 25:20, Jonah.* Adorn yourself to receive the teaching of the law of your God. Compare *Exodus 19:17.* But the Septuagint, Arabic, and Syriac versions say: prepare yourself to call upon your God.

**verse 13. z)** Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan, an early Aramaic translation and commentary.</note> adds: he will manifest himself. A moving argument taken from the omnipotence and majesty of God, as if to say: I strive with you vehemently...
</margin>

## CHAPTER V.

1 Hear <gloss>i</gloss> this word which I take up against you, a lamentation <gloss>k, l</gloss> O house of Israel <gloss>m</gloss>.
2 She has fallen <gloss>n</gloss> she shall no more rise, the virgin of Israel; she is forsaken <gloss>o, q</gloss> upon her land; there is none to raise her up <gloss>r</gloss>.
3 For thus says the Lord God <gloss>e</gloss> the city that went out by a thousand shall have a hundred left, and she that went out by a hundred shall have ten left, to the house of Israel <gloss>s, t, u</gloss>.
4 For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel <gloss>f</gloss> seek me and live <gloss>x, y, z</gloss>.
5 And do not seek <gloss>a</gloss> Beth-el, and Gilgal <gloss>b</gloss> you shall not enter, and Beersheba <gloss>c</gloss> you shall not cross over; for Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Beth-el shall become nothing <gloss>d, e</gloss>.

---

...to know what is happening, etc. He, therefore, who brings hidden things to light, will not be ignorant of your crimes, but will punish them severely and according to merit, unless you turn. A new argument from the omniscience of God. *Amos 5:12, Hosea 5:3. Compare Job 12:22.* **d)** his thought, namely, of man (1) from <term>shûach</term> <note>original: שׁוּחַ — to meditate or speak</note> *Psalm 77:4, 7, 13.* Others refer this to God: who out of supreme love for mankind <note>original: Φιλανθρωπια — philanthropy/divine love</note> indicates to man what his [man's] thought is, to warn him. Collated with *Amos 3:7.* **e)** making (in whose power it is to make or change) the dawn *Job 38:12.* It could mean the flourishing state of the kingdom, which he granted you under Jeroboam II *Amos 1:1, 2 Kings 14:25-27,* he can turn into the very gloom of evils, unless there is repentance. Compare below *Amos 5:8, Isaiah 21:12, 45:7.* **f)** into darkness (1) compare *Job 10:22.* Root <term>‘ûph</term> <note>original: עוף — to be dark or fly</note> *Job 11:17.* **g)** and he who treads upon the heights of the earth, subjecting everything to his power and dominion, even those things which seem highest. *Micah 1:3.* Compare *Deuteronomy 32:13, 33:29.* **h)** he, I say, whose name is Jehovah *Amos 5:27, Isaiah 48:2,* who therefore will most strictly keep what he has sworn and threatened you by his most holy name. Compare also below note on *Amos 3:13 and Hosea 12:6.* **CHAPTER V, verse 1. i)** Truly because I foresee your stubbornness, and consequently the magnitude of the evil judgments, therefore hear, etc. See note on *Amos 3:1.* **k)** which I am bringing forth [taking up]. *Numbers 23:7, Isaiah 14:4.* **l)** a lament. *Amos 8:10, Ezekiel 19:1.* **m)** Observe, moreover, that (1) he speaks to the Ten Tribes in *verses 1-17;* collated with *verses 5, 6, 15.* (2) to all, even to Judah and Benjamin, in *verses 18-27;* collated with notes on *21 and 27.* Otherwise compare *Amos 2:6, 3:1* and the notes there. **verse 2. n)** (1) she has fallen, alas! because of her sins. *Amos 8:14, Isaiah 24:20, Hosea 5:5.* He uses the Past tense in place of the Future emphatically in describing the fall, which he already perceived in spirit, and gazed upon as if present. Compare note on *Isaiah 5:13, Amos 9:2, etc.* **o)** nor will she continue (as she did several times before) to rise from the fall. *Isaiah 14:20.* The Israelites had fallen by the Syrians under Hazael and Ben-hadad, but they recovered themselves under Jeroboam II *2 Kings 14:25-27.* After his death, Pul the Assyrian was about to invade the Israelite kingdom, but would retreat after receiving silver *2 Kings 15:19-20.* He was followed by Tiglath-pileser, who indeed took the Trans-Jordanian tribes captive, yet the Cis-Jordanian ones remained *ibid. v. 29.* Finally, Shalmaneser deported these as well, and thus brought the Israelite kingdom to a complete end *Chapter 17:3ff.* And this is the fatal fall in question. Therefore, the rising of the Israelites is denied, not in every way, but insofar as they shall no longer have a kingdom and a Commonwealth, as they have had until now. For as to whether earlier times are referred to, the very repetition of the Word shows it. See *Hosea 1:6* and compare something analogous regarding Judah in *Jeremiah 19:11.* Meanwhile, from the fall into the judgment of reprobation, God testifies that he can and will revive them *Hosea 12:1, 2, etc. Romans 11:23, 26.* **p)** *Jeremiah 31:21.* **q)** S. she is cast down; but Cocceius says she is forsaken, so that she might fall forward into her land. **r)** compare *Amos 8:14, Deuteronomy 28:29.* **verse 3. s)** going out by thousands, i.e., that city which was able to lead out thousands, from which a thousand went out, as the Septuagint, Arabic, Jonathan, and Syriac have it. It is a metonymy <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it.</note>, by which that which belongs to the adjunct is attributed to the subject. Thus *Jeremiah 9:18:* "Let the eyes descend with tears," for "tears from the eyes"; *Joel 3:18:* "the hills shall go with milk," for "milk from the hills." Compare *Genesis 34:24.* **t)** she shall have only a hundred remaining, and those will be exiles, the rest being consumed by sword, plague, and famine. Compare *Amos 3:12.* **u)** compare *Amos 1:6, 13.* **verse 4. x)** For, if you desire to know the cause of such great evil, and the way of averting it. **y)** seek me with humble repentance and faith *verses 6 and 14.* **z)** and so live; emphatically for "you shall live" or "so that you may live." *verse 6, collated with verse 14.* Thus *Ezekiel 18:32, Proverbs 4:4, Amos 7:2.* See what we noted on such Imperatives in *Jeremiah 25:5.* He indirectly indicates that the cause of the announced evils is impenitence, and a stubborn perseverance in the worship of the calves <note>Referring to the golden calves set up by Jeroboam I as rival idols to the Temple in Jerusalem.</note> *verse 5.* **verse 5. a)** Nor, on the contrary (as you have done until now), should you seek Beth-el for the purpose of worshipping calves. *Amos 4:4.* **b)** and Gilgal, in the tribe of Ephraim, on the borders of the Benjaminites, near Jericho, where Joshua once remained with the Ark of the Covenant. *Joshua 4:20, 5:10.* See note above on *Amos 4:4.* This proximity of places also promoted the contagion of superstition in the Judean kingdom *Hosea 4:15.* **c)** and to Beersheba. It was a town of the tribe of Judah *Joshua 15:28, 1 Kings 19:3* assigned to Simeon *Joshua 19:2,* a seat of superstition, which the Jews themselves had also adopted from the Ten Tribes, below *Amos 8:14.* Behold then how great the power of mutual seduction is: the Jews, seduced by the Israelites *Hosea 4:15, Micah 1:13;* soon the seducers themselves seduce and corrupt more and more, so that these people, not content with calf-worship within the borders of their homeland, undertake pilgrimages for the sake of the same to the city of Beersheba in the Judean kingdom. They seem to have chosen this city because of the holiness and religion of the place, because Abraham *Genesis 21:31, 32* and Isaac *26:24* had lived there for some time, and because Jacob also had slaughtered sacrifices there to the God of Isaac *46:1,* just as today Christian sectaries shamefully abuse such holy places for superstition. **d)** do not cross over from your kingdom into the Judean kingdom. **e)** For, as you stand by the consequence, how much I loathe the wicked worship instituted in these very places.

**verse 12.** <term>ve-zot</term> <note>original: וזאת — and this</note> *compare Isaiah 1:3 and above 5.* **verse 13.** <term>ki</term> <note>original: כי — for/because</note> among *Pūm. 6. 9. 10. 20.* against *Maf. 2. and Eff. in this place and especially at the end f. 38. col. 7.* <term>u-vore</term> <note>original: וברא — and creates</note> for me *verses 3, 5, 22 and in the margin 6, 9, 10, 20, 21.* Thus with an otiose <note>A letter written but not pronounced.</note> yod *verse 12 according to Maf. 1. and Eff.* but except for the printed edition at *Isaiah 38:14.* Through *Makkaph 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 19, 20, 21* and with Munach together *22, 23:* Thus fe. 5. **CHAPTER 5, verse 5.** <term>la-El</term> <note>original: לאל — to God</note> without prefix T:auz. and in the margin *6, 9.*
