<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Amos Chapter 5. The previous page established the context of the lamentation for Israel; here, the commentator explores the linguistic nuances of the Hebrew text, focusing on the corruption of justice and the overwhelming power of God as Creator and Judge.</meta>

# AMOS CHAPTER 5

<margin>
**f)** "He shall surely go into exile" <note>original: "omnino migrabit in exilium"</note>, so that by omen and by name it becomes **Gilgal**, that is, "the place of migration." In the prophetic use of wordplay <note>term: Paronomasia (a play on words)</note>, etymological precision <note>original: "ἀκρίβεια"</note> is not required, but any kind of relationship in the radical sound is sufficient. Otherwise, Gilgal took its name from "rolling away" <note>original: "גלל"</note> in Joshua 5:9; compare the note on Jeremiah 51:2.

**g)** "It shall become" (Beth-Aven), or the "house of iniquity." See Hosea 4:15 and Habakkuk 3:7. Bethel (the House of God) will become Beth-Aven (the House of Vanity/Iniquity) in respect to its punishment, just as it has been so far in respect to its guilt. Schmidt <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian</note> on Hosea page 179 says it signifies that God will regard and treat it as a house of iniquity; that is, because of its crimes, especially its idolatry, He will destroy it with a horrific devastation. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase</note> translates it as "into nothing"; the Vulgate as "useless"; the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic as "into non-existent things" <note>original: "εἰς οὐק ὄντα"</note>. For the word **Aven** <note>original: "און"</note> denotes vanity in Isaiah 41:29, and is almost the same as **Ain** <note>original: "אין"</note>, meaning "nothing" or "none."

**verse 6. h)** Seek <term>the LORD</term> <note>original: "יהוה" (Yahweh). The commentator notes that while the Lord spoke in His own person in verse 4, the Prophet repeats it here to make the message his own for greater emphasis.</note>. **i)** "Lest He break through," or "lest the Lord invade." Judges 14:6, 2 Samuel 19:18. Jonathan: "Lest His wrath burn like fire in the house," etc. **k)** Deuteronomy 4:24, Isaiah 33:14. **l)** The kingdom of Israel, of which the royal and principal tribe was Ephraim; see verse 15, Obadiah verse 18, Zechariah 10:6. **m)** "And that fire devours." Lamentations 2:3. **n)** "So that there is none to quench the fire." Jeremiah 4:4, 21:12. **o)** see verse 5.

**verse 7. p)** "Especially those who turn" or "you who have turned." See the note on verse 12. This participle depends on the names "house of Joseph" and "Bethel" in verse 6; compare verse 8 and chapter 6:12. Here the Prophet turns his focus from the whole people (verse 4) specifically to the judges and leaders of the people (verses 10, 11, 12, 16). **q)** "Into wormwood." Chapter 6:12. Upright judgments and their own affairs among the people, once corrupted, are mere bitterness.
</margin>

6 <gloss>k</gloss> Seek the LORD and live, <gloss>l</gloss> lest He break out <gloss>m</gloss> like fire in the house of Joseph and devour it, <gloss>n</gloss> and there be none <gloss>o</gloss> to quench it for Bethel. <gloss>p</gloss>
7 You who turn <gloss>q</gloss> justice into wormwood <gloss>r</gloss> and cast down righteousness <gloss>s</gloss> to the earth. <gloss>t</gloss>
8 <gloss>v</gloss> He who made the Pleiades and Orion, <gloss>w</gloss> and turns the shadow of death <gloss>x</gloss> into the morning, <gloss>y</gloss> and darkens the day into night; <gloss>z</gloss> who calls <gloss>a</gloss> for the waters of the sea and pours them out <gloss>b</gloss> upon the face of the earth; <gloss>c</gloss> the LORD is His name. <gloss>d</gloss>
9 <gloss>e</gloss> Who strengthens destruction against the strong, <gloss>f</gloss> so that destruction comes <gloss>g</gloss> upon the fortress.
10 <gloss>h</gloss> They hate the one who rebukes in the gate, and they abhor <gloss>i</gloss> the one who speaks uprightly. <gloss>k</gloss>
11 <gloss>l</gloss> Therefore, because you trample <gloss>m</gloss> upon the poor and take from him <gloss>n</gloss> exactions of grain, you have built houses of hewn stone, <gloss>o</gloss> but you shall not dwell in them; <gloss>p</gloss> you have planted pleasant vineyards, but you shall not drink <gloss>q</gloss> their wine.
12 <gloss>r</gloss> For I know your many transgressions and your mighty <gloss>s</gloss> sins— <gloss>t</gloss> you who afflict the just, who take <gloss>v</gloss> a bribe, <gloss>w</gloss> and turn aside the needy in the gate. <gloss>x</gloss>
13 <gloss>y</gloss> Therefore the prudent shall keep silent in that time, for it is an evil time.

<margin>
ties. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian</note>. **v)** compare Isaiah 5:7, Ezekiel 5:6. **s)** "They cast down to the ground." Isaiah 28:2; compare Daniel 8:12.

**verse 8. v)** "The Maker." Connect this with the more distant object, Jehovah, in verse 6: "Seek, I say, the Lord, who made," etc. **w)** "The Pleiades" <note>original: "כימה" (Kimah)</note>. Job 9:9, 38:31. Mazius, in his notes on Cocceius (page 50), derives it from the Arabic root **kum**, meaning "to be great" or "to accumulate," as a great constellation and, as it were, a heap of many stars, which he thinks fits the Pleiades well.
</margin>

---

**x)** *Orion* <note>original: "כסיל" (Kesil)</note>. See the note on Isaiah 13:10. He names the stars here that are both the most well-known and those that stir up the storms which he threatens here; though they are contrary to each other: for the *Pleiades* release the cold, while *Orion* stirs up heavy disturbances. Poole in his *Synopsis*. **y)** "and who *turns*," that is, changes. Psalm 78:44, Psalm 114:8. Darkness into day, that is, the dawn. **z)** "and in turn darkens the day with night," that is, by making it dark He creates the night; which He does not only daily by directing the cycles of day and night, but He can likewise do so beyond the order of nature, as gathered from Exodus 10:23 and Psalm 105:28. Similarly, He exchanges sad things for joyful ones, and joyful things for sad ones, according to whether He intends to show His grace or establish His justice and vengeance; compare above chapter 4:13 and below 8:9, likewise Isaiah 45:7 and Jeremiah 13:16. **a)** "who *calls*," by an effective word and by His command. Chapter 7:4, 9:6. **b)** "and *pours* them out," through floods, as in chapter 9:5, or as of old in the flood of Genesis 6:17. **c)** "He, I say, whose name is *Jehovah*, and who always answers to the majesty of His name." Verse 27, Isaiah 42:8, Jeremiah 10:16, 31:35, 32:18, and also 33:2 (where you may see the note) and above chapter 4:13.

**verse 9. d)** "Who *recreates*" <note>original: "המבליג"</note>. Psalm 39:14, Job 9:27, 10:20; compare Jeremiah 8:18. Elsewhere it is used reflexively, but here transitively, joined to the object "destruction," that is, the one who is destroyed. The sense: "He who strengthens the weak, so that with recovered strength he rises against the strong one by whom he had previously been oppressed and devastated." Thus Jonathan translates: "Who increases strength for the weak against the strong." And the Syriac: "Who makes the weak to rule over the strong." Thus the word for "destruction" <note>original: "שֹׁד" (shod)</note> seems to be used concretely and in opposition to the following "fortress"; compare Isaiah 10:29, 30. But Cocceius (page 102) translates: "Who *makes easy* the devastation upon the robust"; who overthrows the strong with easy effort. This can be compared to the Arabic root: "He reached the proposed end," and in the fourth conjugation: "He made it arrive, he led it through," etc. **e)** Hosea 7:13. **f)** "the strong and well-fortified." Numbers 13:28. **g)** "so that devastation," etc. Compare Isaiah 1:31 and see Hosea 10:14. He describes God by His absolute power, according to which He sometimes exalts and strengthens whomever He wills, and sometimes humbles and breaks them (compare 1 Samuel 2:4-8); and He does this to the end that He might excite a holy fear among the Israelites toward the majesty of Him who is able both to save and to destroy.

**verse 10. h)** As if to say: "But why does He shudder at them? For they themselves have *hated*," etc., and they do not wish to endure those who advise better things; compare verse 13, Isaiah 66:5. **i)** "In the gate," the place of judgment (verse 12), where nevertheless the seat of truth and justice ought most especially to be (verse 15). Grotius does not render it badly: "*They hate those who are in the gate*," that is, the judges: "one who advises rightly." For the *phrase in the gate*, according to the accents, should be referred to the preceding "hated," not to the following "rebuker." **k)** "the rebuker." Isaiah 29:21, Hosea 4:4. **l)** "justly and perfectly," that is, the complete and noble truth; taking "perfect" <note>original: "תָּמִים" (tamim)</note> neutrally or substantively, as in Joshua 24:14, Judges 9:16. Or: "he who speaks as one who is upright," concretely, as becomes an upright man; compare Psalm 15:2, Proverbs 28:18; see Isaiah 33:15. **m)** "they detest." Micah 3:9, Job 19:19.

**verse 11. n)** "Therefore." As if to say: "Since therefore, as I said in verse 10, you will listen neither to Us nor to the warnings of others, therefore hear the sentence decreed against you." **o)** "Because you trample with your feet" <note>original: "בושסכם"</note>. This is either a variation for "trampling" <note>original: "בוססכם"</note>, a Piel infinitive from the root *bus* (Isaiah 63:18, Jeremiah 12:10), just as one word for "breastplate" is used for another; or it is a mixed form from two roots, "to trample" and "to be ashamed"; as if to say: "you trample the poor man with added ignominy." **p)** "upon the crushed." Chapter 2:7, 4:1. **q)** "and a gift, a tribute." It is said to be from "he lifted up" <note>original: "נשׂא"</note>, meaning whatever one offers to another or is bound to offer. Genesis 43:34, Ezekiel 20:40, 21:24. **r)** "of grain." Chapter 8:5, 6; Genesis 41:35, 49. **s)** "Therefore houses of hewn stone," that is, with stones cut into squares. 1 Kings 5:31, Isaiah 9:9. See what we noted above at chapter 3:15 concerning the luxury of the Israelites in their buildings; and compare Jeremiah 22:13, 14, 15. **t)** "though you have built them." This is used here like a future tense. Just as you have "planted," **u)** "but you shall not," etc. Zephaniah 1:13. **v)** "vineyards of desire," most desirable, most beautiful. Isaiah 32:12; compare Ezekiel 23:6. **y)** as was predicted in Deuteronomy 28:30, 39. The contrary is found below in chapter 9:14 and Isaiah 65:21.

**verse 12. x)** "For" (lest you think your crimes are hidden and therefore will go unpunished) "I know." Hosea 5:3; compare above chapter 4:13 and the note there. **a)** "that your transgressions are many." Compare chapter 4:4. One cannot translate "many" as a direct object because of the grammatical order, which requires the verb "to be" to be understood. Otherwise, the adjective would follow its noun, not precede it. **b)** "and that they are strong" or "numerous." Jeremiah 5:7, 10:14. Schmidt: "innumerable"; compare Joshua 3:5, Psalm 40:6, 13. **c)** "O you who distress the just!" bringing them into narrowness and affliction <note>original: "θλίψιν" (thlipsin)</note>. Schmidt: "who afflict." Psalm 7, 5, Psalm 143, 12. **d)** "taking a ransom" <note>original: "lytrum"</note> to the prejudice of a just cause. 1 Samuel 12:3, Proverbs 6:35. **e)** "and the poor." The pronoun "they" is understood, which often changes the second person into the third. Compare verse 7 and chapter 4:1. **f)** "they make to turn aside," that is, they pervert their cause. Proverbs 18:5. They thrust them away from the threshold of judgment (Isaiah 10:2), or from the way of justice into an inextricable difficulty <note>original: "ἀπορίαν" (aporian)</note> (Isaiah 29:21). Compare above chapter 2:6, 7; 5:10.

**verse 13. h)** "Therefore," in this state of affairs. This is resumed from verse 11; compare verse 16. **i)** "whoever shall be intelligent at that time," when the Lord takes vengeance on the crimes of His people (verse 11). Those are understood who groan over sins (Ezekiel 9:4), who watch for the judgments of God predicted by the Prophets, and who most humbly revere His justice (Psalm 6:10, Daniel 9:13); in opposition to the rest, who indeed experience the heavy hand of God, but without the recognition of sin and true humiliation of themselves before God (Isaiah 42:23, 24, 25). **k)** "he shall be silent," that is, he will revere the just judgments of God with a humble silence, nor will he murmur, but will patiently and suppliantly submit himself, and with silent sighs, his mouth lowered into the dust, he will long for the salvation of the Lord. Lamentations 3:28, 29, 30; Ezekiel 24:17; Leviticus 10:3; Psalm 4:5, 39:10. But Jonathan: "Therefore the teachers at that time fell silent because of the ungodly." **l)** "that shall be an especially evil time." Micah 2:3, Ephesians 5:16; which accordingly will also significantly humble pious and teachable minds. Or according to Rashi: a time destined for the execution of evil. Compare Jeremiah 2:28, 11:12, 14.

Manuscript 5 had done this but then deleted it. "And pours them out" [vayshpchem] thus in 1, 2, 10. verse 11. "Grain" [bar] with Qamets in 5. verse 13. # CHAPTER 5. AMOS 5

<margin>
**v. 14.** n) **so** <note>original: כֵּן</note> d) from the home, but also in all the open squares. Jeremiah 48:38. f) *with wailings* <note>original: planctibus</note> it will be in verse 17. g) *Alas, alas!* <note>original: heu heu!</note> Alas! b) 84, 847. Revelation 18:10. It agrees with **Woe** <note>original: הֹוי</note> in Jeremiah 22:18. i) **Woe** <note>original: הֹוי</note> Ezekiel 2:10. h) i) *they shall call* (those who wail publicly in the squares) *to mourning;* <note>original: vocabunt ad luctum</note> they shall command the farmers especially to mourn, because of the failure of the harvest: mourn, they say, especially, O wretched farmers. Jeremiah 14:4. Joel 1:11. i) & *wailing* they shall summon those skilled in lamentation; compare **he called** <note>original: קָרָא</note> with **to** <note>original: אֶל</note> Ezekiel 40:2. That is, to public wailing.

# 578 AMOS. CHAPTER 5.

u) with the instruments of the harps. <note>original Latin: "nabliorum instrumentis." Reference to Eli. q. 11.</note>
**v. 24.** x) On the contrary, **let it roll**, that is, let it exceed, flourish, and dominate, so that nothing at all stops its progress or force. The metaphor is taken from the waves of the sea, when mountains of water are rolled in the deep: hence <term>gal</term> <note>Hebrew: גַּל</note> for "wave" in Isaiah 48:18 and Zechariah 10:11. Or, it is taken from gushing waters, when they roll forth abundantly, bubbling up from their springs: hence <term>gullot</term> <note>Hebrew: גֻּלּוֹת</note> for "springs" in Joshua 15:19 and Judges 1:15; compare Proverbs 26:27. Furthermore, many scholars with us take this verse in a <term>paraenetic</term> <note>original Latin: "paraenetice," meaning as an exhortation or warning</note> sense, such as the Zurich Bible, Vatablus, Tarnovius, the Dutch version, and Cocceius. And so it stands in opposition to verses 7 and 12, compared with verse 15. But Blessed Luther and Calovius take it in a **prophetic** sense, specifically as an Evangelical promise of the righteousness of the New Testament. As if to say: "What are you? A time will eventually come when all these things shall cease, and righteousness shall be revealed most copiously." Compare Isaiah 48:18. y) compare Isaiah 11:9. z) compare Micah 6:8. a) like a river, Isaiah 30:2. b) **strong** <note>original: "fortis"</note> or **ever-flowing**. <note>original: "vadosi"</note> Psalm 74:15; compare Exodus 14:27.
**v. 25.** c) **Did you bring sacrifices and an offering** <note>Minchah</note> **to me, etc.** This is a difficult passage. For it is certain that sacrifices were offered to the Lord in the ratification of the covenant (Exodus 24:4ff), in the consecration of the altar and the tabernacle (Numbers 7), and likewise in the celebration of Passover in the second year after the departure from Egypt (Numbers 9:1ff). Rabbi Eliezer in the Babylonian Talmud <note>Chagigah f. 6. 2.</note> explained this passage as referring to the **daily sacrifice** <note>original: "sacrificio iugi"</note>, about which he thought that while the laws were given at Sinai, the sacrifice itself was not actually offered. Others extend this to sacrifices in general, but in such a way that they explain the "40 years" as a round number for those 38 and a half years remaining after the <unclear>scouting</unclear> and exploration of Canaan (compare Numbers 14:34), during the

<margin>
ceased in the meantime. Numbers 9:1; Joshua 5:6-10. But not without reason (says **Lightfoot** in his commentary on **Acts 7:42**) can it be suspected that the daily sacrifice was continued after that time; for there are coals on the Altar in **Numbers 17:11**, and the fire, burning perpetually on the altar, did not burn in vain. Therefore **Salomo van Til** (on **Deuteronomy 32:17, p. 63**) takes it **imputatively** or **interpretatively**, thinking that the sacrifices of the Israelites in the desert were considered as offered not to God, but to idols, because they did not think rightly of God, conceiving of Him without Christ and the Holy Spirit in no other way than the gentiles conceived of the deity they worshipped. Compare **Isaiah 66:3; 43:23**. But that sense of interpretation does not yet seem to settle the matter, comparing **Acts 7:42**, where the first martyr Stephen proves from this very passage the judgment of God, by which He gave them over (<unclear>handed them over</unclear>, compare **Romans 1:21, 24, 28**) to serve the stars and idols, just as He gave over the gentiles. Compare also **Deuteronomy 32:17**. We prefer, therefore, with Lightfoot, to take it as a complaint from God about **spontaneous sacrifices**, which were either not brought at all or rarely brought to the Tabernacle of God after that first year and a half from the departure from Egypt. Compare the notes on **Leviticus 17:4**. Truly it is not surprising that the Israelites offered those sacrifices, which were left more to their own will, to idols rather than to God, since they had already been accustomed to doing so even before the giving of the law (**Leviticus 17:7**), and Moses (**Deuteronomy 32:8**) rebukes them for having sacrificed in the desert according to their own pleasure and as it seemed good to them. Note here the connection with verses 22 and 23. For He had said that He did not want sacrifice out of a mere "work performed" <note>original: "ex mero opere operato," a theological term for ritual done without heart</note>. Now, therefore, appealing to the times of the desert, He hints that He can easily do without victims of this kind, just as He did of old; and that not so much sacrifices as obedience and justice are required by Him. Compare **Jeremiah 7:21, 22, 23**. d) compare **Chapter 2:10**.
</margin>

**v. 26.** e) **But you carried.** <note>original: "Atqui gestastis"</note> Compare regarding idols **Isaiah 46:1, 2; Jeremiah 10:5**; regarding the tabernacle of meeting **Numbers 1:50**. f) **Some say: Siccuth:** so that it is a proper name of an idol (1). Compare **Succoth Benoth, 2 Kings 17:30**. But more correctly the Septuagint <note>LXX</note> translates it as a common noun: <unclear>the tent of Moloch</unclear>, which compare with **Acts 7:43**. So the Syriac translates it "dwelling place" and the Vulgate "tabernacle." Compare below **chapter 9:11** and **Psalm 76:3**. It seems, therefore, to have been a portable shrine, modeled after the tent of Jehovah built in the desert. g) **of your King**, that is, of Moloch. See the note on **chapter 1:15**. "King" is among the names of God, signifying His supreme power and dominion over the universe (**Isaiah 6:5; Jeremiah 46:18; Chapter 48:15**), but by a most foul abuse it was attributed to the Ammonite idol; compare **Zephaniah 1:5**. It suffered the same fate as the name <term>Baal</term>. See Golius's Lexicon, column 2682. Moreover, **Samuel Petit** proves in his *Miscellanies* (Book 2, chapter 2) that the same was called *Cinn* in Plautus's *Poenulus*. They base this opinion on the fact that the Septuagint, and from them Saint Stephen in **Acts 7:43**, substitute another proper name (<unclear>Raiphan</unclear> or <unclear>Remphan</unclear>) for the Hebrew **Kiyyun** <note>Hebrew: כִּיּוּן</note>. However, the following plural **your images** <note>Hebrew: צַלְמֵיכֶם</note> is inconsistent with the preceding singular **Kiyyun**. From this we gather: 1) it is a common noun; 2) it is in the "construct state" or in "governance." That is, it relates to "your images" in the same way that "Sikkuth" relates to "your King." This is easily seen from the series and habit of the members: *the tabernacle of your King, and of your images, the star of your God.* The Greek **Remphan** was by no means expressed from the Hebrew **Kiyyun**, as is supposed. Anyone who accurately compares the Greek text with the Hebrew will notice that those two phrases—**Kiyyun your images** and **the star of your god**—suffered a transposition in the Greek; and only thus do the Greek and Hebrew agree: the Greek has <unclear>the star of your god Raiphan</unclear> for the Hebrew **the star of your god**; the Greek has <unclear>their types</unclear> <note>or "figures"</note> for the Hebrew **Kiyyun of your images**. From this comparison, we also observe that the pronoun "their" stands in place of the noun **your images**, while **Raiphan** was added to the Hebrew **your god** for the sake of explanation. From this, it is clear that those who think the Greeks read **Raiphan** instead of **Kiyyun** are guessing rashly. For besides what has been cited, 1) no such variation is observed in any Hebrew manuscripts; 2) even if they had read it so, they would have expressed it as *Rouan* with a "u" rather than with a "ph," which I do not know if it ever responds to the Hebrew <term>Qoph</term> in proper names. It is therefore a common noun, but with what meaning? Some say: **apparatus**, from the root *kun*, which in the Hiphil verb form means "to prepare"; others say, **a base or a pedestal** on which images are placed, comparing *ken* for "base" in **Exodus 30:18**. We agree with the Septuagint's <unclear>their types</unclear>, whom Luke follows in the speech of the First Martyr, and with the Vulgate's **image of your idols**, comparing the Hebrew *techunah*, which in **Ezekiel 43:11** is joined with *tsurah* (form or image). So in **Herodian, book 5**, <unclear>the type of the god</unclear> means the image of the god, and in **Josephus's Antiquities, book 1, chapter 19**, <unclear>types of the gods</unclear> is used several times for the Hebrew *teraphim* (images). i) **of your idols**, **Numbers 33:52; 2 Kings 11:18**. Joined to the preceding *Kiyyun*, it denotes fashioned idols or images. k) **and the star of the Gods**, or rather, according to the Septuagint and **Acts 7:43**, in the singular, <unclear>the star of your god Raiphan</unclear>; compare **Deuteronomy 4, 19; chapter 17:3**. Jerome understands this as Lucifer, whom he says the Saracens still worshipped in his time. But **Bochart** in *Phaleg* (book 1, chapter 15, p. 67), citing Kircher, proves that the Egyptian word **Rephan** is still in use among the Copts for **Saturn**. He believes the Septuagint used this word more willingly because they were writing in Egypt. It would therefore be superfluous to hunt for Hebrew etymologies in a foreign word, as some learned men do. l) not from divine institution and authority, but by private will and <unclear>self-chosen</unclear>. Furthermore, that it was possible, and indeed a fact, that the Israelite people worshipped idols in the desert, appears among other places from **Joshua 24:14** and **Leviticus 17:7**.
**v. 27.** m) **Therefore** (on account of your sins and those of your fathers) **I will cause you to migrate, I will deport you**, **Jeremiah 29:4, 7**, as I already threatened you in the desert; compare **Ezekiel 20:23**. n) **beyond Damascus**, which was terrifying to the Israelites from recent slaughter and vexation; **Chapter 1:3; 2 Kings 13:3, 7**. In place of this, **Stephen in Acts 7:43** says <unclear>beyond Babylon</unclear>. "And it must not be thought," says **Jerome** on this passage, "that the First Martyr erred." Rather, he provided the understanding rather than the literal word: because they were led through Damascus into Babylon, or beyond Babylon. And this must be observed in all the Scriptures, that the Apostles and Apostolic men, in citing testimonies from the Old Testament, do not consider the words, but the sense; nor do they follow the same tracks of speech, provided they do not depart from the meanings. Just as the invasion of the Chaldeans into Judea happened through Syria, so the deportation of the Jews to Babylon happened through the same. See **Jeremiah 1, 14** and the note there, and compare **2 Kings 25:6**. The particle **beyond** <note>original: "me-hal'ah"</note> denotes a more remote boundary, **Genesis 35:21; Jeremiah 22:19**, and thus in this passage it emphasizes the deportation by the distance of the place to which the Jews were to be deported. Compare **Jeremiah 8:19**. o) **Chapter 4:13**.

It was the capital of Chalonitis, as Pliny notes in Book 6, chapter 26. Bochartus approves this view in *Phaleg* Book 4, chapter 18, against others who interpret it as Callinicum in Osroene. b) Compare Jeremiah 2:10; 30:8. c) Hamath served as the northern border of the Israelite region, as seen in verse 14, Numbers 34:8, and Zechariah 9:2. Here at least Antioch is noted, as even Jerome admits, adding that it is called "the great" in this passage to distinguish it from the smaller Hamath, specifically Epiphania, which (following Josephus' *Antiquities* Book 1, ch. 7) he often asserts is still called Hemath today. See Bochart, *Phaleg* Book 4, ch. 36. d) **the great.** To Jerome, this is a distinctive title, as we just said. However, elsewhere cities are called "great" without comparison, much like the Roman "Augusta" titles; they were simply those that excelled in the size and magnificence of their buildings, such as "Great Sidon" in Joshua 11:8, and in the Syriac translation of the inscription of Luke, "Great Alexandria." e) Exodus 15:14; Joshua 11:22. f) **A difficult phrase.** Schmidt interprets it as: "Are they better than these... or is it not greater etc." The sense would be: "Learn from the example of these regions—which could not escape my judgment even though they were greater than yours—what I might decide regarding you and your land unless you repent." Compare Nahum 3:8 and Judges 11:25. Truly, the word **min** (from/than) after **ha-tovim** (the good) is an interrogative "is it?" We know of no place where it means "is it not?" unless the word **lo** (not) is added. Therefore, it should rather be translated: "Are the Chalonites, Hamathites, and Philistines better than these kingdoms (Judah and Israel, v. 1), or is their border larger than your border?" This is a reproach for God's blessings toward the ungrateful, similar to Jeremiah 2:5-7. The intended answer is negative: "These peoples were indeed quite happy and their borders wide; however, they were not happier than you, nor were their borders wider than yours, which you possess to this day by my favor. But because you have abused these blessings through extreme ingratitude for shameful security and luxury (v. 3-6), I will punish you by withdrawing these blessings (v. 7)." Compare Amos 9:7.

\* v. 3. g) **O you who put far off.** This vocative depends either on verse 2 or the particle **Woe** (Hoi) in verse 1. Woe to you who think the announcement of the "day of evil" by my servants is far off, so that it seems to you it will either never come (Amos 9:10; Micah 3:11; Isaiah 10:6) or will only arrive after many centuries (Ezekiel 12:22, 27; Joel 2:1). The root **nadah** (h) appears in Ezekiel 66:5, where it is <term>abomination</term> <note>original Greek: βδέλυγμα (bdelygma)</note> according to the Seventy (Septuagint); meaning to hold as detestable or to abominate. It fits with the noun **niddah** (filth) in Leviticus 20:21, which comes from the related root **nadad**, to withdraw or flee, specifically from a foul thing (Nahum 3:7). Thus, it could be understood here as "removal through detestation," while the following word **vataggishun** (you cause to come near) refers to bringing close what they love. That is: "You detest the Prophets' announcements of the day of evil, yet you love the assembly of injustice, from which the day of evil must necessarily follow." h) The letter *Lamed* serves the accusative case here, as in Jeremiah 40:2 and Job 5:2. Or understand it as: "setting a distant term for the day of evil." i) **and yet** or "on the contrary" you have caused it to be near; i.e., you act openly, continually, and from day to day. Compare Amos 5:10, 12. There is a certain opposition in this verb to the preceding **ha-menadim** (the ones putting far off). k) **the seat of violence**, that is, the kind of judgments in which a just cause fails, but force and injustice dominate. See verse 1 and compare Psalm 122:5; 74:20.

\* v. 4. l) (v. 2) **to those who lie down**, who recline. m) **upon couches** or dining couches, as Pliny calls them in Book 37, ch. 21. For the ancients, at more sumptuous banquets, they almost always took their food reclining at a table. Amos 2:8; Esther 1:6; Ezekiel 23:41. Luxury is therefore especially blamed here in the Princes. Compare Ecclesiastes 10:16. n) **of ivory**, i.e., made of ivory or adorned with ivory (Amos 3:15), which through their luxury were even made of gold in Esther 1:6. These were covered with spreads to provide a soft and magnificent place for the revelers to lie. o) **stretching themselves out**, to lie delicately and softly; or **acting wantonly**. The root **sarach** elsewhere means to abound or overflow, which is not far from this meaning. Compare Exodus 26:2. However, in the *Niphal* form it means to rot (Jeremiah 49:7). p) **on their frames or beds.** Psalm 132:3. q) **Lambs.** The word first denotes pastures (Isaiah 30:23; Psalm 65:14), and from that, secondly, "pasture-lambs," as here and in Deuteronomy 32:14, 1 Samuel 15:9, and 2 Kings 3:4. The Chaldean translator of Psalm 37:20 renders it with a word derived from the Greek <term>phagioi</term> <note>original: Φάגιοι</note>, meaning a lamb when it begins to be a yearling, at least four months old and already weaned. Bochart, *Hieroz.* Part I, p. 429. This passage teaches that especially sheep-kind—specifically delicate and sweet ones—are noted here. Compare the Ionic <term>kar</term>, <term>karnos</term>, <term>karx</term>, which Hesychius interprets as <term>sheep</term> or <term>grazing cattle</term>. But Schultens (in *Observations on the Old Testament*, p. 156) contends this word means nothing other than a ram. It is probable that **kari** among the ancient Hebrews meant something "leaping," from the root **karkar** (to dance/leap) in 2 Samuel 6:14 and **karkarah** (dromedaries) from their leaping. For whether a lamb or a ram, it is a leaping animal (Psalm 114:4). r) **fatlings** (Malachi 3:20; Jeremiah 46:21). See the notes on 1 Samuel 28:24 and more extensively Bochart, *Hieroz.* Part I, p. 301.

\* v. 5. s) **Who strum.** Compare Leviticus 19:10. Cocceius says: "those who twitter," singing delicately with broken tones and a quick rhythm. Gellius calls these "various repetitions" (Book 1, ch. 11). In Dutch: *die quinckelieren*. The Chaldean root means to do something piece by piece or individually. The Septuagint says "dominating" or (better in the Alexandrian Codex) <term>applauding</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπικροτοῦντες (epikrotountes)</note>. t) **to the harp**, or "over the mouth of the harp." That part of the instrument where the strings are drawn and which produces the sound would be called the "mouth." Compare Isaiah 5:12. u) David, who by divine instinct organized the music of the temple, even preparing instruments so that God might be praised with voice and string. Compare 1 Chronicles 7:6; 25:25, 27. You might think, seeing these people's banquet joys, that you were hearing a sacred concert like the one David instituted in the temple; but their music is far different, for it is established to foster luxury, revelry, and heavy drinking. Compare Isaiah 24:8, 9. x) **they have invented for themselves**, i.e., ingeniously adorned. Compare Exodus 26:1; 2 Chronicles 2:13. y) **musical instruments.** 1 Chronicles 16:42.

<column-break/>

**CHAPTER VI, v. 1. p)** **Woe!** See notes on Isaiah 1:4.
**q)** The Prophet continues in this chapter to prophesy against the Israelites and Jews, rebuking their various sins: namely, security (v. 1), luxury (v. 4), pride (v. 8), injustice (v. 12), and rash presumption (v. 13). He denounces just punishments for these in verses 1, 7, 8-11, and 14. **q)** **the tranquil** (Zechariah 1:13), i.e., the secure (Isaiah 32:9). For security is born from tranquility and a peaceful state of affairs. **r)** That is, in the kingdom of Judah, whose royal city is Zion. Compare Amos 2:4. **s)** **securely confident.** (Judges 18:7, 27). They are called secure and confident because they thought the "day of evil" foretold by the Prophets was as far away from them as possible (v. 3), meanwhile strenuously reveling and drinking, and not caring for the "shattering of Joseph" (v. 4, 5, 6). **t)** That is, in the kingdom of Israel (Amos 4:1). **u)** **named as the firstfruits** or "among the firstfruits of the nations," i.e., the princes of the people of Israel. Either "to be named" means generally to be famous (Numbers 1:16; Isaiah 14:20; Genesis 6:4), or it means the princes are specifically "chosen by name" from the people (Numbers 1:17; Ezra 8:20). **x)** This refers to the people of Israel, whom God had deigned to grant many eminent prerogatives above all nations. For "firstfruits" are those things which are excellent and distinguished in their kind. Compare verse 6, Jeremiah 49:35, and Micah 1:13. It is a different context when the Amalekites are called this in Numbers 24:20. **y)** **and to whom the house of Israel comes from everywhere**; the Jews to Jerusalem, and the other tribes to Samaria, where the highest tribunals of both kingdoms were. The preceding phrase is thus illustrated by <term>further explanation</term> <note>original Greek: επεξηγησιν (epexegetin)</note>. Compare Psalm 122:5, 4.
**\* v. 2. u)** They are commanded to "pass over" and "descend" not so much in physical location as in mind and understanding. Compare notes on Isaiah 66:24. "To pass over" means...

### AMOS. CHAPTER 6.

<margin>
v. 6. **Who drink wine from bowls or craters.** In fact (as the accents show) this is a grammatical shift of a construct form for an absolute <note>original: "enallage constructi pro absoluto"</note>, as in Psalms 71:19. Elsewhere these vessels are used for receiving and then sprinkling liquid, as in Numbers 7:13 and Zechariah 9:15, but here they are for drinking; (cf. the angel in a similar vision in Zechariah 13:2.) The Prophet rebukes them either for their extravagance—that they were made of silver, as Jonathan explained—or for their capacity—that they were quite large, designed more to overwhelm the mind than for moderate drinking. a) **and with the firstfruits of ointments**, that is, the most excellent. See note on verse 1 and cf. Exodus 30:23. b) which the Ancients were accustomed to use at banquets. cf. Psalms 23:5 and Proverbs 21:17. c) They anoint themselves and make the banquets festive. Guillet p. 433. They carry themselves like kings. cf. note on Isaiah 21:5. d) **nor (as they ought) are they moved by grief**, grieving, they do not sympathize, and in such a way that they would seriously and anxiously think about the remedies by which they might be healed. They do not care for the manifest judgments of God, but are secure and free from all anxiety (v. 1), feasting splendidly in the meantime. cf. 1 Samuel 22:8. e) **over the breaking**. Jeremiah 8:21. This refers to the evils already brought upon the Israelites, comparing chapter 5:15 above, and partly to those yet to be brought, which the Prophets had foretold. f) that is, of the kingdom of Israel. cf. note above on chapter 5:6. Here the Prophet begins (as he is accustomed to do), having addressed the Jews, to turn toward the separation of the 10 tribes. See below at verse 14.

v. 7. g) **Therefore**; namely, because of that security and wastefulness in verses 1 and 3–6. Cf. a similar connection of punishment with guilt in Isaiah 5:13, 14. h) **now**. that is, very soon, right now. Isaiah 43:19; Micah 7:10. Between the death of Jeroboam II, under whom Amos prophesies, and the deportation of the 10 tribes, 41 years intervened: which was certainly a short space in comparison
</margin>

<margin>

<term>Qamets Bo'q</term> <note>A technical grammatical note on vowel markings</note>

in dignity and wastefulness they led the way, so also they shall precede the common people in the portion of punishments. Deuteronomy 20:9; 1 Samuel 9:22; Micah 2:13. cf. 2 Kings 24:14. k) **in the assembly of the exiles**. see note on Jeremiah 31:7. k) they will indeed withdraw more slowly than they would have had they listened to the voices of God and the Prophets; while they are safe, they are unwilling to move. cf. Hosea 4:18. l) **feast**. So Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, who observes that in the Talmud it is used for banquets established in honor of gods. Likewise Cocceius, comparing Midrash Esther chapter 1:2, where it is held: **If the wicked man sits here, <term>and makes a mirzach</term> <note>original: וְעֹשֶׂה מִרְזֵחַ</note> and holds banquets.** Others: a song, joy; comparing the Arabic <term>razaha</term>, which Joseph Kimchi and the Casietes interpret as the lifting of the voice, whether for weeping or for joy. In this way, the contrary use of the word in Jeremiah 16:5, where it denotes mourning, could be reconciled. For it would agree with the Hebrew <term>ranan</term>, which means to cry out either in joy or in mourning. It could also be compared with <term>ruach</term>, to shout, through a substitution and transposition of the root letters. m) see verse 4.

**v. 8. n) Indeed, mortals are so stupid**, that they believe nothing less than that God is offended by their sins, cf. Jeremiah 2:35. Therefore, so that it may be understood that God seriously hates sinners, He swears most solemnly besides. see chapter 4:2. o) **That is, by His soul.** cf. note on Jeremiah 51:14. Or: by Himself; a well-known idiom discussed in the same place; cf. Hebrews 6:13. But Gussetius says "in His mind," as in Esther 4:13; 1 Samuel 2:35. However, the preposition <term>be</term> after a word of swearing almost always means "by." Thus the Lord swears by Himself in Genesis 22:16, Exodus 32:13; by the height or majesty of Jacob in Amos 8:7; by holiness in chapter 4:2 and Psalms 89:36; by His right hand in Isaiah 62:8; by His faithfulness in Psalms 89:50; by His great name in Jeremiah 44:26. Except for two places where <term>be</term> is used, Psalms 95:11 and 2 Chronicles 15:15, but with the sense clearly demanding this meaning. p) **I am abhorring**; Piel form (1) instead of <term>meta'eb</term>, with the letter *Ayin* changed to *Aleph* as they are letters from the same vocal organ. For **I hate** follows, with which "to abhor" is also joined elsewhere, as in Psalms 119:163. In the Kal form, it means to desire (2) Psalms 119:40, 174. cf. verse 20 there. Likewise <term>ga'al</term> in the Kal means to redeem; in the Piel to pollute, for <term>gi'el</term>, and in Job 21:24 **his pails are full of milk** just as in Chaldean; and <term>gama</term> and <term>gamats</term> is to swallow, and Arabic <term>ga</term> and <term>ga'i</term> to reveal, etc. Gussetius p. 893: "I who make to love, or generate love, I myself pursue pride with hatred," etc., but this is against the accents and the nature of Hebrew speech. q) **the pride of Jacob** Hosea 5:5; chapter 7:10; Jeremiah 13:9. Or metonymically: that which Jacob boasts of, in which he prides himself; such as the temple (Jonathan translates: the house of the sanctuary of the family of Jacob), palaces, cities, fortresses, and in general a flourishing state of affairs. For it is also used in a good sense, as the object of divine love, Psalms 47:5. Indeed, it even denotes God Himself below in chapter 8:7. r) cf. chapter 3:11 and 4:11. s) **and therefore I will shut up (deliver) to the enemies**, chapter 1:6, 9. t) that is, and whatever is in the city. cf. Isaiah 9:16.

**v. 9. u) If they were left in those calamities of war.** Genesis 44:21. x) **even ten**, that is, several men, Genesis 31:41; Leviticus 26:26; Zechariah 8:23, not yet cut off by the enemy's sword during the war. y) **yet they shall die** partly by famine, partly by plague, which will be joined with the calamity of war; and so much so, that only a tenth part will barely and with difficulty escape, comparing verse 10 to chapter 5:3 and Isaiah 6:13.

<column-break/>

**v. 10. z) And when he has taken him up**, the second to last to be carried out after the others have already met their fate. For this state of affairs is to be understood because of what follows, where only a single survivor is placed in the house. a) Gussetius p. 819: "his friend." We prefer: **his uncle**; a figure of speech <note>original: Synecdoche</note> for any surviving relative, whose duty it is because of kinship to perform this office for the dead. 1 Samuel 10:14, 15, 16. For although that word denotes a friend, it denotes one who is loved rather than one who loves, or it is more passive than active. Song of Solomon 1:13 etc. b) Some say: **and the same is his embalmer**, from the Samaritan root <term>saraf</term>, to anoint. This itself was also a solemn part of caring for funerals. Apuleius in *Florida* says: *Now all the limbs of that wretched man were sprinkled with spices, now his mouth was smeared with fragrant ointment, now having most diligently contemplated him after he was embalmed—* etc. But **his burner**, from the Chaldean <term>saraf</term> instead of <term>sharaf</term>, to burn, to consume by fire. Cocceius 581. He understands the funeral director, whose job it is to light incense at the funeral as a sign of honor. cf. 2 Chronicles 16:14, chapter 21:19; Jeremiah 34:5. But Gussetius p. 889 says: The circumstances of the matter, the cause of death, and the number of the dead, hardly allow for the burning of copious spices as was done otherwise; and it remains that it be explained as the burning of the corpse. On an unusual and urgent occasion, the corpses of Saul and Jonathan were burned, 1 Samuel 31:13. The occasion in Amos also urged the destruction by fire of the dire and lethal vapor of the crowded, piled-up corpses, infected with a malignant plague. c) **to carry out**, for the sake of burial, Luke 7:12. d) **bones**, or the corpse of the deceased. Exodus 13:19. e) **and shall say**. f) **to him who is in the sides** or inner corners, standing by, and who is likewise lying down so that he himself cannot bury his own dead. 1 Samuel 24:4; Psalms 128:3. g) **is there anyone still with you?**, namely, either living or to be buried. h) namely, lying down. i) **No one remains any longer**: all are now dead; I alone live. k) **then he shall say** the uncle or the burner. l) **hush! be silent** (8) that is, the present necessity of burial commands it be done through silence, without rites, and without hymns and prayers. Thus the burner would rouse himself to complete the burial of the corpse. cf. chapter 2:3; Habakkuk 2:20; Zephaniah 1:7; Zechariah 2:17. Or the address to the one lying down is continued, which pleases Gussetius p. 939. As if to say: Silence is appropriate for us here, on account of grief and shame, cf. Ezra 9:10; Daniel 9:7; and above, chapter 5:13. m) **there is no time** nor is it permitted now to commemorate words in the name of the Lord, namely by reciting prayers and songs, Psalms 20:8, which in Jewish burial, as it is today, so also then was perhaps solemn. See Buxtorf's *Jewish Synagogue* chapter 49. But Gussetius in the place cited: "because there is no business in which the name of Jehovah is celebrated," comparing by contrast Psalms 20:8. Indeed, His anger, desertion, hostile and just vengeance appears in it. For through the phrase "because of" <note>original: מִשּׁוּם</note>, by the negation of good, he hints at evil in the highest degree. Jonathan translates: "since, while they were among the living, they did not pour out prayers in the name of the Lord." The Syriac is similar.

### CHAPTER 6. 7. AMOS 6 & 7

<margin>
v. 12. <note>original: "Numquid currant in petra"</note> **u) Do horses run on the rock?** The sense here is negative: they cannot. It is phrased as a question to simultaneously strip away their false belief in their own strength and power.

**CHAPTER VII.** Because of this, they persuaded themselves that they would easily strike down any looming evils.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 11. **n) For**, to further explain the imminent judgments of God. It is explanatory, not causal; as in chapter 3, verse 14. **o)** cf. Isaiah 3:1. **p)** It is a command, and **he will strike.** Compare chapter 9:9 and the notes on chapter 9:1, Isaiah 10:6, 13:3, 48:5, etc. If He commands, how does He strike? If He strikes, how does He command? But in that He commands and orders His ministers, He is seen to be the one striking. <note>Jerome, following Psalm 33:9.</note> **q)** cf. chapter 3:15. **r) Great and small.** This is a distributive expression, signifying the universality of all types. However, Jerome interprets the "greater house" as the ten tribes <note>The Northern Kingdom of Israel</note> and the "smaller house" as the Kingdom of Judah; thus he sees in the **fragments** <note>original: "רסיסים"</note> an eternal captivity, and in the **fissures** <note>original: "בקעים"</note> the 70-year Babylonian captivity. **s) With ruptures** (1) from the root *rasas* (1) which in Ezekiel 46:14 means "to sprinkle"; hence this same word denotes a "drop" in Song of Solomon 5:2. Some reconcile this variety of meanings by suggesting that the rupture of houses follows the "dripping" or "sprinkling" of rain. But the etymology would then imply a slow and gradual rupture, whereas this passage seems to require a violent, swift, and massive one. It is more probable that the Hebrew root—as in the Chaldean—carries the force not only of sprinkling but also of rupture or breaking by accident: in which latter respect it would agree with the Hebrew *ratsats* (to which *ratat* in the Targumim <note>Aramaic translations/commentaries</note> corresponds), the Greek *rhēssō*, and the German *reissen* <note>to tear</note>, hence *rasas* is the same as *Riffi*. Also, in the Talmud, *rasis* means "broken" or "shattered." **z) With fissures.** cf. Isaiah 22:9. This seems to signify something less severe than "fragments": therefore it relates to the small house just as the small house relates to the great. And thus the proportion of the punishment is hinted at: for God affects the great with great punishment and the small with lesser punishment. cf. Wisdom 6:7, 9.
</margin>

11 <gloss>n</gloss>For <gloss>o</gloss>behold, <gloss>p</gloss>the Lord <gloss>q</gloss>commands, <gloss>r</gloss>and he will strike <gloss>s</gloss>the <gloss>t</gloss>great house <gloss>z</gloss>into fragments and the small house into fissures.

12 <gloss>u</gloss>Do <gloss>y</gloss>horses <gloss>x</gloss>run <gloss>x</gloss>upon the rock? <gloss>z</gloss>Or does one plow <gloss>a</gloss>there with oxen? For you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood.

13 <gloss>b</gloss>You who rejoice <gloss>c</gloss>in <gloss>d</gloss>nothing, <gloss>e</gloss>who say: “Have we not by our own strength taken <gloss>f</gloss>horns for ourselves?”

14 <gloss>g</gloss>For <gloss>h</gloss>behold, <gloss>i</gloss>I am raising up against you, O house of Israel, declares the Lord God of hosts, <gloss>k</gloss>a nation; and they shall oppress you from the entrance of <gloss>l</gloss>Hamath to the brook of <gloss>m</gloss>the Arabah. פ

1 <gloss>n</gloss>Thus <gloss>o</gloss>the Lord God <gloss>p</gloss>showed me: <gloss>q</gloss>and behold, <gloss>r</gloss>he was forming <gloss>s</gloss>locusts at the beginning of the shooting up of <gloss>t</gloss>the late crop; and behold, it was the late crop <gloss>u</gloss>after the king’s mowings.

2 <gloss>u</gloss>And it came to pass, <gloss>x</gloss>when <gloss>y</gloss>they had finished eating the...

<margin>
The connection with verse 11 here is: I have said that the great and small houses alike are to be devastated; you will be no more able to avert this devastation (though you presume otherwise) than horses, otherwise the strongest animals, can run on rough and rocky stone, or oxen, otherwise very robust, can plow the same. **x)** Or "will anyone plow in it (the rock) using oxen?" **y)** That is to say: This devastation will be inevitable because—others take this in a reproachful sense: because you have turned, etc. **z) You have turned into gall.** cf. chapter 5:7, 8; Deuteronomy 32:32; Hosea 10:4. Cf. Isaiah 5:20; Habakkuk 1:4. **a) Into wormwood.** chapter 5:7. **v. 13. b) O you who rejoice**, or you who are insolent because of your success in affairs. Habakkuk 1:15. The phrase **lo dabar** <note>literally "not a thing"</note> is an address to the second person, as in verse 3. **c) Over** (see a similar construction with **horns** in Proverbs 17:5) **a non-thing**, that is, a thing of nothing, namely over your presumed strength, which can be overthrown in a light moment. Cf. this kind of negative composition in Deuteronomy 32:17, 21; Hosea 1:25; Job 39:16. **d) Who say gloriously and through boasting.** This is an explanation of the preceding. **e)** That is: have we not prepared for ourselves plenty of strength to beat back any enemies? They sin in two ways in this speech: 1) because they glory in their strength as if it were their own, and thus to the prejudice of God the giver; cf. Deuteronomy 8:17. 2) against the decree and threat of God, against whom no boasting at all is valid; cf. Jeremiah 9:22. One must return here again to the history of Jeroboam II (chapter 1:1), whose flourishing and prosperous successes (2 Kings 14:25) gave the occasion for this boasting. **f) To strike our enemies.** A metaphor taken from beasts. cf. Deuteronomy 33:17; 1 Kings 22:11; Psalm 89:18. **v. 14. g)** This connects to verses 11 and 12. For it describes further how and by whom He is going to devastate the Israelites. **h)** Habakkuk 1:6. **i)** chapter 3:13. **k) Who will press**, or "so that they may press you." Judges 1:34; chapter 2:18. A plural verb is used for the sense, because "nation" is a collective noun. The Assyrians are meant here. **l) From where one comes to Hamath**, because it is the boundary of the Israelite land. cf. notes on verse 2 and 2 Kings 14:25. **m) To the river of the camp-plain.** This is not the river of Egypt, which constituted the southern boundary of all Palestine (2 Chronicles 7:8), but the Kidron, which flows into the northern bay of the Asphalt Lake <note>The Dead Sea</note> below Jericho, and there separates the Israelite kingdom from the Judaic. For Jericho—to whose vicinity this name (**ha-Arabah**) belongs as if it were its own (Joshua 11:16)—was on the border of both kingdoms (2 Chronicles 28:15) and belonged to the ten tribes (1 Kings 16:34). Thus in 2 Kings 14:25, Jeroboam II, under whom our Prophet prophesied, is said to have restored the boundaries of the Israelite kingdom (in opposition to the Judaic) "from the entrance of Hamath **to the sea of the Arabah**." This phrasing is equivalent to ours. Therefore, as we noted above at verse 6, the Prophet speaks separately and primarily here to the ten tribes.

**CHAPTER VII. v. 1. n)** Namely, in the spirit of prophecy. v. 4, 7; chapter 8:1; Jeremiah 24:1. This chapter embraces two parts: I. The Prophetic part, in which he explains the imminent judgments of God upon Israel, first begun under the symbol of α) locusts (v. 1) and β) fire (v. 4), then finally completed under the symbol of γ) a plumb line (v. 7). II. The actions taken with Amaziah the priest (or high priest) of the Israelites regarding this very prophecy (v. 13 ff.). **o) God was forming.** Genesis 2:7, 8, 19. The formation of locusts is attributed to God when they are unusually fertile and multiply immensely, because that does not happen without a special providence of God, who uses them to punish sins. <note>Bochart, Hierozoicon Part II, p. 486.</note> **p) Locusts (3)** Nahum 3:17. Arabic *gab* or *gabi* is the same, from the root "to emerge from the earth," which is characteristic of locusts. Aristotle (Book 5 of *History*, chapter 28) says when locusts have brought forth, there are worms in the appearance of eggs, which are surrounded by a very thin earth like a little membrane, from which they fly out. <note>Gaza's translation</note>. When this is dissected, the locusts emerge and fly out. <note>Bochart, p. 443.</note> But according to Gussetius (p. 159b), they are locusts endowed with a protruding back, relating to the word for "hunchback" or "vault." Furthermore, it is the Assyrians who are described under the image of locusts, about to pillage and graze upon the land of Israel under King Phul (2 Kings 15:19). Cf. Judges 7:12 and Revelation 9:3, and also Vitringa in his Commentary (p. 515) and Meius here. For although it cannot be denied that in Amos's time locusts also existed in a literal sense (cf. chapter 4:9), here at least they come as a symbol of another plague, just like the fire (v. 4) and the plumb line (v. 7). See note to Joel 1:3. **q) At the beginning of the shooting up of the crop**; when the grass had grown up or begun to sprout again after being cut back. **r)** Genesis 41:5. **s) (2)** here. It is called from the Chaldean *lakash* "late-ripening": whence also the Hebrew *malkosh*, the "late rain." Deuteronomy 11:14. Cf. the word in Job 24:6, "they harvest/gather the late fruits"; which in Syriac means "he was late" or "delayed." **t) After the hay-mowings (4)** Psalm 72:6. This provides the historical completion. For after the "mowing of the King"—or the slaughter brought upon Israel by Ben-Hadad, King of Syria (2 Kings 13:3, 7)—the state had begun to flourish again under Jeroboam (2 Kings 14). But Phul's army, flying into the kingdom of Israel like locusts, seemed about to devastate it entirely; yet by the prayers of Amos and other faithful ones, the devastation was averted, and Phul, pacified by money, departed (2 Kings 15:19). <note>Maimonides</note>. Cf. 1 Chronicles 5:26 and the notes above to chapter 1:3, 4. **v. 2. u) It happened therefore. x) When or after.** It is not only conditional but also temporal, as in Isaiah 24:13 and Genesis 38:9. **y) They had finished eating**, or "consumed," and were already about to proceed to the bushes, unless God, moved by His mercy and the prayers of the pious, had stopped this deadly plague (v. 3).
</margin>

v. 4. **h)** See verse 1. Namely, one plague was removed; but the sins of the people called for another. Cf. Isaiah 9:12. **II. i)** See note on chapter 5:8. Someone might ask here (as Jerome does on chapter 6:11): If He calls, how does He contend with fire? If He contends, how does He call?

</margin>

But see the response in our notes there. **k) To contend**, not with words, but with deeds. Isaiah 3:13. **l) By fire.** Lightfoot (Chronicle, p. 92) understands this as a great drought, mixed with certain terrible fiery flames falling from heaven, as in Egypt (Exodus 9:23, cf. Joel 1:19), from which even some cities were overturned like Sodom (Amos 4:11, Isaiah 1:9). The streams of water dried up (Joel 1:20); indeed (as it is said in this place) the "great deep" was absorbed by the heat and part of it consumed, with even the fish perishing (Hosea 4:3). However, the following vision of the plumb line (v. 7) favors a symbolic sense here, as we noted at verse 1. Therefore, the opinion of the celebrated Maius and others seems correct to us: that the fire is a figure for the fury of war, signifying Tiglath-Pileser, who invaded the Israelites with great heat and ferocity and carried away a huge multitude from both sides of the Jordan (2 Kings 15:29). He would have carried away the whole people if God, moved again by the prayers of the pious, had not restrained his heat (below, v. 5, 6). **m) i.e. like the sea.** Isaiah 51:10, Joel 1:20. See the notes previously cited from Lightfoot. He led away a large part of the Israelites. The "Deep" refers to a great force of water; "waters" signify "peoples." <note>Grotius</note>. **n)** so that it would consume. **o) its part.** Joshua 18:5, 6, 9. v. 5. **p) cease, I pray.** Job 7:16. **q)** see note on verse 2. **r)** ibid. verse 6. **s)** even that evil shall not happen—that is, it will not be continued to completion. v. 7. **t)** Finally, however, after He had delayed the total ruin once and then again (v. 3, 6), waiting in vain for the repentance of the people, **He made me see it thus.** v. 1, 4. **u) upon a wall of a plumb line**, that is, a wall built exactly to a plumb line, but now to be destroyed by that same standard. For just as the measuring line is used for building, so the plumb line in Scripture is double <note>used for both building and destruction</note>; compare Isaiah 34:11. **x) specifically of tin**, compare the Syriac on Ezekiel 22:18, 20. Or **of lead**, compare the Arabic on Job 19:24: indeed, in Arabic *anakh* <note>original: "אָנַךְ"</note> refers to both metals, whether black <note>lead</note> or white/purer <note>tin</note>; from the Arabic root meaning "it was thick." But here "tin" is taken for a level or plumb line (4) in verse 8, just as the "stones" in Isaiah 34:11. For either material is suitable for a plumb line due to its weight. Thus "a stone of tin" <note>original: "אֶבֶן הַבְּדִיל"</note> means a stone or weight of tin for a plumb line (German: *bleywaag* <note>lead-weight/level</note>), Zechariah 4:10. v. 8. **y)** chapter 8:2, Jeremiah 1:11, 13; chapter 24:3, where see the notes. **z) I am about to place or draw the level for destruction**, Isaiah 34:11. I.e., to forgive them. v. 9. **e) they shall therefore be devastated.** Ezekiel 6:3, 4. The beginning of the destruction was the overturning of the house or family of Jeroboam by the sword: for those who came after Zechariah snatched the kingdom like thieves (2 Kings 15:8–30). <note>Maius</note>. Cf. Hosea 1:4. Furthermore, the Prophet here prophesies nothing other than what had already been implicitly predicted long ago (2 Kings 10:30, cf. chapter 15:12), where the fulfillment of both that prophecy and this one is found in Zechariah, the son of Jeroboam. Cf. the note below on chapter 8:9. **m)** cf. chapter 9:1. v. 10. **n) He sent, therefore**, when this prophecy of Amos against Jeroboam and the whole kingdom of Israel became known. **o)** verse 12. He seems especially offended by the "boldness" <note>original: "παρρησία"</note> of Amos against the sanctuaries of Israel, of which he, as a priest, thought himself the rightful defender (v. 13). **p) undoubtedly the primary one.** Compare Hosea 4:6. **q)** verse 9. **r) he conspired.** 1 Samuel 22:8. The priest here uses a pseudo-theological strategy while acting to carve a political crime out of Amos's sermon, making the prophet himself a disturber of the State. Cf. 1 Kings 18:17. **s) He exaggerates the danger**, because the conspiracy is manifest and in the very "vitals" of the kingdom, where it is feared it may spread its contagion widely. **t) which is all the more intolerable** since he is himself a foreigner, a Judean (v. 12, chapter 1:1). Cf. Acts 16:20, 21.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the seventh chapter of Amos, specifically the confrontation between the prophet Amos and Amaziah, the priest of Bethel. It transitions from the previous discussion of visions to the historical narrative of the priest's attempts to silence the prophet.</meta>

### CHAPTER 7.

<margin>
**w)** To endure or sustain. Jeremiah 6:11, 8:11. **x)** [Amaziah's] accusation contains a charge of intolerable insolence. **y)** Some believe this actually happened; but the Prophet had not said exactly this in verse 9, nor does it fit the history in 2 Kings 14:29. Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> observes on this passage that the Prophet’s meaning was distorted by Amaziah in four ways: 1) He said, "Amos has said," as if Amos spoke from himself, whereas in all his speeches he always begins: "Thus says the Lord." 2) "He shall die by the sword," as if excluding the possibility of repentance; yet the Lord had said: "I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword," threatening punishment but not yet inflicting it. 3) "Jeroboam..." [himself], yet the prophet said, "against the house of Jeroboam"; indeed, Jeroboam did not die by the sword, but his son Zechariah did. 4) "Israel shall be led away captive from its land," without limit; whereas he should have added: "If they do not repent." Compare Jeremiah 16:3, 4, 12, 13, 14. **z)** verse 8, 17.
</margin>

<margin>
These words are not so much a suggestion as a command given with rebuke. **d)** In the land where you were born, where you may be heard freely. Jerome. Compare chapter 1:1. **e)** As if to say: "For we are not accustomed to nurturing such prophets, who only threaten misfortunes for our kingdom and our cult, as you do."
</margin>

11 **"For thus Amos has said: Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely go into captivity out of their own land."**

12 **"Then Amaziah said to Amos: 'O seer, go, flee away to the land of Judah; eat bread there, and prophesy there.'"**

13 <margin>
**v. 13. f)** verse 10. **g)** chapter 2:12, 5:2. **h)** Since it is the seat of religion and the sanctuary of the King, that is, established by royal authority and flourishing to this very day.
</margin>
**"But never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king’s sanctuary and the royal residence."**

<margin>
**v. 11. a)** It seems the court of Jeroboam was slower to agree with the Priest of Bethel against Amos, perhaps because they thought his prophecy was less dangerous than Amaziah had tried to persuade them. Therefore, Amaziah tries another way: while the royal mandate is delayed, he takes authority upon himself to command Amos to depart from the borders of the kingdom of Israel. **b)** "O prophet!" or "O Seer" <note>original: "חֹזֶה" (chozeh)</note>. 2 Samuel 24:11, 2 Kings 17:13. Compare 1 Samuel 9:9. He calls him this not sincerely, but hypothetically: "You, who call yourself a Prophet." **c)** "Flee," that is, be gone! As in Numbers 24:11. Some interpret this as if he were craftily suggesting flight, as the Pharisees did to Christ out of feigned love in Luke 13:31. Compare Matthew 10:23, Genesis 27:43. But from verses 13 and 16, it is easily understood...
</margin>

14 **"Then Amos answered and said to Amaziah: 'I was no prophet, nor was I a son of a prophet, but I was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore fruit.'"**

15 **"Then the Lord took me from following the flock, and the Lord said to me, 'Go, prophesy to My people Israel.'"**

16 **"Now therefore, hear the word of the Lord: You say, 'Do not prophesy against Israel, and do not spout words against the house of Isaac.'"**

17 **"Therefore thus says the Lord: 'Your wife shall be a harlot in the city; your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword; your land shall be divided by survey line; you shall die in a defiled land; and Israel shall surely go into captivity out of his land.'"**

---

**v. 13. i)** And the *house of the kingdom*, or the royal seat, as in 1 Samuel 27:5. Although the ordinary seat of the Israelite kings was Samaria, they seem to have had a house at Bethel as well, where they would stay whenever they came there for the sake of religion to worship the golden calf. He therefore orders the Prophet into exile from Bethel because his prophecies fit neither with the religion of the place nor with the royal court that frequently stayed there.

**v. 14. k)** Schmid [translates] in the past tense: *I was not a prophet*, that is, before this. For he had previously been among the herdsmen, as follows. Compare chapter 1:1. It is as if he said: "I myself thought of nothing less than becoming a Prophet; but meanwhile, since God expressly commanded me to prophesy, I had to obey, while you act impiously by forbidding it." Others suggest: "I am not a professional prophet, devoted to this one office alone, nor a regular teacher of the people, nor a student." Compare Proverbs 30:2, 3. **l)** Buxtorf <note>original: "Buxt. Lex. Talm."</note> observed something similar to this phrasing from the Talmud under the word *boker* <note>original: "בקר"</note>, where in *Avodah Zarah* f. 50. 2. they say: *I am not a craftsman, nor the son of a craftsman*. By contrast, Paul says in Acts 23:6: *I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee*. But perhaps it should be taken here as in 2 Kings 2:3, 5, 7, 15 and chapter 4:38, where *sons of the prophets* refers to their students and disciples; the sense being: "I was neither a prophet or teacher myself, nor did I ever study under any prophet as a disciple." **m)** For he was a herdsman or cattleman <term>boker: derived from the Hebrew word for cattle</term>. This is the view of most, as if the word were derived from *baqar* (cattle). However, we prefer the opinion of Gussetius (p. 145), who translates: *I was a seeker and examiner of figs*. Compare Leviticus 13:36, Ezekiel 34:11, 12. Thus this verb, like the next, refers to the Sycamore trees. For the meaning "herdsman" is unusual and contradicts verse 15, where he says he was a shepherd <note>original: "opilionem"</note>; these are very different parts of the pastoral art. **n)** Some say: "seeking, examining," connecting it to the Chaldean *balas* (to search). But Jerome says "nipping" or "plucking," from the Greek *knizon* <note>original: "κνίζων"</note> in the Septuagint version; which Hesychius explains as "stinging the fruit so that it becomes ripe." For Sycamores, says Jerome, produce wild figs which, if not nipped, become very bitter small figs and are ruined by gnats. And Dioscorides (Book I) says: "The fruit of the fig does not ripen unless it is nipped with a fingernail or iron." But Bochart <note>original: "Hieroz. P. I. p. 383"</note> says it is derived from the Arabic and Ethiopic *balis*, which means "fig," and in the Ethiopic version of Psalm 78:47 it even denotes sycamores. Thus *boles* <note>original: "בולס"</note> is correctly said of one who cultivates figs and sycamores; as from *kerem* (vineyard) comes *korem* (vinedresser). **o)** *Sycamines, Sycamores*: a wild genus of figs. Isaiah 9:9, 1 Chronicles 27:28. Dioscorides calls this fruit "un-nourishing" and "foul-tasting" <note>original: "ἄτροφος & κακόχυμος"</note>, and it easily rots. Therefore, it is not a thing of great value. It is the same as if Amos were saying he was a man of the lowest sort, born to a meager estate, sustaining life with a small and frugal diet. (Bochart).

**v. 15. p)** *The Lord took me*. 2 Samuel 7:8, Psalm 78:70. **q)** Therefore, I was led to prophesy neither by my own will nor the will of any man. Compare Galatians 1:1. **r)** *From behind the sheep*, following the sheep. 2 Samuel 7:8. **s)** A mandate I neither should nor could resist. Compare chapter 3:8, Jeremiah 26:12, Acts 4:19, 5:29, 26:19.

**v. 16. t)** Now therefore, because you deny me and resist the divine mandate, hear the word of the Lord, which is most certain. Compare 1 Kings 22:19, Jeremiah 28:7, 15. **u)** You oppose your command to God's command with the greatest impiety, as if you should be obeyed more than God. **x)** chapter 2:12. **y)** *And do not let [your words] drop*, that is, do not prophesy. Job 29:22, Ezekiel 21:2, 7, Micah 2:6, 11. Compare Deuteronomy 32:2. **z)** Compare verse 9.

**v. 17. a)** Because you were so shamelessly impious against God in verse 16. **b)** *In the city*, where a woman might save herself from attempted rape if she cried out (Deuteronomy 22:24), unlike in the open field (verse 25, 27). Nevertheless, this benefit will not save your wife; indeed, neither you nor anyone else will dare to utter a sound against such great violence from the enemy. **c)** *Shall be a harlot*, i.e., shall be violated and suffer ravishing by the enemies. Compare Job 31:10. **d)** *With a measuring line*. Zechariah 2:5, as in the division of lots or inheritance. Joshua 17:5, 14, Micah 2:5, Psalm 78:55. **e)** *Shall be divided*, destined to receive new cultivators and masters. For in place of the exiled Israel, the Assyrians brought in the Cutheans and other nations. 2 Kings 17:24. **f)** *Unclean* because of the idols and foul rites of the nations; in opposition to the Holy Land of Israel, which God had sanctified by the unique presence of His divinity. Joshua 22:19, Ezekiel 4:13, Hosea 9:3. **g)** Since you are to be led away as a captive there with the rest of Israel. **h)** See verse 11 and its fulfillment in 2 Kings 17:23.

### AMOS. CHAPTER 8.

<margin>
**CHAPTER VIII. v. 1.**
**a)** Compare chapter 7:1. Under the symbol <note>Latin: *typo*</note> of summer fruits, he intimates the end of the Israelite people and a famine of the divine word. **k)** Ezekiel 1:4. **l)** A basket or wicker hamper.
**(3) v. 2.** Elsewhere it signifies a cage, as in Jeremiah 5:27. So also the Greek *klobos* or *kloxos*, which is clearly formed from the Hebrew, denotes not only a cage, but in Hesychius is also a synonym for *kartala*, which he explains as "a woven vessel used in cooking," a textile container found in culinary books. See Bochart, *Hieroz.* Part I, page 662 and compare Jeremiah 24:1. Furthermore, this symbol has the same goal and meaning as that last vision of the lead plummet in chapter 7:7. For it is not unusual for the prophets to drive home the same point multiple times, changing only the words and figures. **m)** Summer fruits, especially figs. Micah 7:1. See the note on 2 Samuel 16:1.
**v. 2. n)** See chapter 7:8 and the note on Jeremiah 24:3. **o)** See the note on verse 1. **p)** "He said, therefore," namely, according to the explanation and application of that sign he had seen. **q)** The end. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation</note> renders it "the final vengeance." It alludes at the same time to the preceding word *kayits* <note>summer fruit</note>. As if to say: "So has my people ripened for the judgments of punishment, that now the end <note>Hebrew: *ketz*</note> is upon them, and they are to be led away captive, like fruit gathered into a basket." For a similar wordplay <note>Latin: *paronomasiam*</note>, see Jeremiah 1:11-12 and compare Ezekiel 7:2, 3, 6. **r)** See the note on chapter 7:8.
**v. 3. s)** "And they shall howl," that is, they shall be turned to howling and lamentation; compare verse 10 and Psalm 137:1 and following. **t)** Happy songs; see verse 10, chapter 5:23, and 6:5. **u)** Of the Temple, even the one in Jerusalem; compare 6:1. But Grotius and others translate: "songs of the palace," which used to resound in the royal residence. Proverbs 30:28; Isaiah 13:22; Joel 4:5; see 1 Kings 21:1 and Hosea 8:14. **x)** Ezekiel 11:8; chapter 16:14. **y)** Because there will be many dead bod—

**v. 4. b)** Namely, what I said in verses 2-3, or rather what I am about to say in verse 7 and following. Compare the note on chapter 3:1. **c)** Panting out of insatiable greed; or according to others, "crushing." ...so that you cause [them] to cease. Psalm 8:3. The wretched of the earth, Job 24:4. And by oppressing these, you alone may dwell in the land. Ephesians 5:8. **v. 5 f)**
*As if to say:* those who are so intent on their dishonest gain that they are impatient even for the delay of one day in which work must cease. *Compare* Proverbs 14:15. **g)** The New Moon. This day was a festival among the Jews, compare Numbers 10:10; 28:11; Psalm 81:4; so much so that it was unlawful to buy or sell anything on it. **h)** "That we may distribute" verse 6; Genesis 42:6. From *Shabar*, grain, by which hunger is broken <note>Latin: *frangitur*</note>, *ibid.* verse 19; compare Psalm 104:11. Whence *Shabar* in the *Kal* [verb stem] is a denominative verb, "to feed oneself," to buy grain, Genesis 41:57, and to sell, verse 56. **i)** Grain. Genesis 42:1 and following. **k)** "Let us open," that is, expose for sale: just as the Germans say "to open the beer" <note>German: *anstechen*</note>, Genesis 41:56. To "open the wheat" is said metonymically for opening the granaries. *Compare* Jeremiah 50:26. **l)** Wheat. verse 6; chapter 5:11; Psalm 72:16. **m)** "That we may diminish the Ephah"; that is, that we may measure out with a smaller Ephah <note>a unit of volume</note> to those buying. (4) Genesis 32:11; *compare* Deuteronomy 25:15, 14; 2 Samuel 7:19. **n)** "And increase the Shekel." Exodus 30:13. The shekels were weighed, Genesis 23:15, 22; they, however, made the other side of the scale heavier. Thus they profited twice, both in the merchandise and in the money, *Grotius*. **o)** "And that we may pervert" or deprave. Properly it signifies a bending, Ecclesiastes 7:13. Those things are said to be "bent" which depart from the rule of rectitude. *Compare* Job 8:3. **p)** Deceitful scales, such as they become after depravity. *Compare* Hosea 12:8; Micah 6:11. Although it is not probable that the greedy spoke this way out loud; they nevertheless had it in their minds, which God interprets. **v. 6. q)** "That we may buy" as if they were slaves. Exodus 21:2; Leviticus 25:39. **r)** For silver, chapter 2:6; Isaiah 43:24. **s)** Exhausted by our greed. chapter 4:1. **t)** And the poor, verse 4. **u)** See the note on chapter 2:6. **x)** Like the "fallings" of the grain, or the refuse, the dust and chaff mixed into the wheat. (2) Job 41:15. **y)** "Let us sell." verse 5. **v. 7. y)** After the address, in which he simultaneously reproached them for their crimes, he now adds the penal sentence of God Himself, for which he had summoned them to hear above in verse 4. "The Lord has sworn," he says, and thus everything he says, he says in earnest. *Compare note* above on chapter 6:8. **a)** By the excellency of Jacob. We discussed the various uses of this phrase above on chapter 5:8. Here it is the same as "by Himself," who made Himself most illustriously known through His works in Jacob. *Compare* Exodus 15:1. He swears by Himself because He has no one greater by whom to swear. Hebrews 6:13. **b)** "If (that is, I will not) I forget forever." Psalm 74:19. He says this in opposition to the opinion of the wicked, compare Psalm 10, 11. **v. 8. c)** "For on account of this," that is, such and so many horrendous crimes just recounted. An emphatic question by which the magnitude of the guilt is exaggerated, and the justice and necessity of the punishment is suggested to their consciences. *As if to say:* "If this has not merited that the earth should be moved etc., I certainly do not know what crime would seem to merit this punishment." *Compare* Isaiah 57:6; Jeremiah 5:9; Habakkuk 1:17. **d)** "Should not be moved," Joel 2:1; Psalm 18:8. *Compare* above, chapter 1:1. **e)** Chapter 9:5; Hosea 10:5. **f)** So that they rise up, that is, it swells up, and the whole is overwhelmed by the rising waves of divine judgments. chapter 9:5. For in Hebrew "to rise" <note>Hebrew: *alah*</note> is said not only of the thing that rises, but metonymically also of that in which something rises, as if by a river, namely, of Egypt, as follows immediately; that is, the Nile, which is accustomed to overflow every year and overwhelm Egypt with its waves. Jeremiah 46:7. It is therefore for "like the river" as the Ancient Versions have it and the parallelism below in chapter 9:5 clearly teaches. Thus *yabul* for *yakil* in Job 40:20 and *ha-asirim* for *ha-surim* in Ecclesiastes 4:14 etc. But Gusset, page 306, says "it rises" (it will burn, be reduced to smoke, compare Joshua 8:20, 21) as if by fire; as if to say: it will be devastated by fire and water. And this could hold, provided it were written with a *Shurek* [vowel mark], as in Isaiah 31:9 etc. But *or* [light] with a *Cholem* is "light," and never, as far as we remember, "fire." Furthermore, Jonathan translates: "And the King shall rise against her with his army, like the waters of a copious river, which shall cover her entirely." Compare with this Isaiah 8:7-8. **h)** "And be driven," or toss with waves, like a sea stirred by billows, Isaiah 57:20. Elsewhere it is "to be expelled," as in Jonah 2:5; but *compare the Targum*. There is a similar meaning of this word in this place. **i)** According to the *Keri* <note>The marginal reading of the Hebrew text</note>: "it shall be submerged," or sink down. (s) chapter 9:5; Jeremiah 51:64. But according to the *Cthib* <note>The written text</note>: "it shall be watered," or become irrigated. Niphal. (1) *compare* Genesis 2:6; chapter 13:10. **k)** Like the river of Egypt. Genesis 41:1, 17; Isaiah 7:18. **v. 9. l)** "Therefore it shall be." **m)** It signifies the "day of captivity," when both people shall be led away to the Assyrians and Chaldeans. Jerome on verse 2. **n)** verse 3. **o)** "I will cause the sun to set," that is, I will cause sorrow to suddenly rush in. Isaiah 13:10; Jeremiah 15:9; Micah 3:6. *Compare* Joel 3:4. **p)** In the very noon, that is, then, when the land will seem most to flourish, and to shine with the majesty of the kingdom and the restored magnitude of its ancient borders. Isaiah 59:10. History provides the certain fulfillment of this prophecy. For the times of Jeroboam II had been most auspicious and clear like the noon, 2 Kings 14:25; but six months after those times followed the murder of his son Zechariah, chapter 15:8, 10. After this, everything in the kingdom of Israel was thrown into confusion, both by internal movements and the incursions of foreign nations. *Compare the note above* to chapter 7:9. **q)** "And I will bring on darkness." chapter 5:8; Jeremiah 13:16. **r)** "On a clear day," when it is brightest. *Compare* Job 18:5-6; Isaiah 5:30.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Prophet Amos, moving from the conclusion of the vision of the summer fruit in Chapter 8 to the climactic vision of the Lord at the altar in Chapter 9. It focuses on the spiritual famine of Israel and the inescapable nature of divine judgment.</meta>
