<header>CHAPTERS 8, 9.</header>

<margin>
...for those blinded, in the same place <note>original: "ibid."</note> verses 10, 11, 12. This is the kind of famine that the wretched Jewish nation is oppressed by today.
\* 12. **i)** *And they shall wander,* they shall go astray, as in a time of drought or famine. Chapter 4:8; Jeremiah 14:10, compared with verse 3. See also below, chapter 9:9. **k)** Micah 7:12. **l)** *And they shall run to and fro.* Jeremiah 5:1; Daniel 12:4. **m)** Why? Because it is not from faith, but from rebellion, destruction, and stubbornness against God and Christ, whom they rejected. Outside of Him, whatever a man strives for is vain—it is rebellion. Compare Romans 9:31, 32.
</margin>

<margin>
\* v. 10. **s)** See above at verse 3 and compare Lamentations <note>original: "Thr." for Threnos</note> 5:15. **t)** Compare Hosea 2:13. **u)** Verse 3; Chapter 5:1. **x)** Isaiah <note>original: "Es." for Esaias</note> 15:3. **y)** Isaiah 15:2. **x)** *And I will make it* (I will do it). 1 Samuel 11:2. This refers to what I predicted about inflicting mourning upon you. **a)** *Like the mourning for an only son.* Jeremiah 6:25; Zechariah 12:9. **b)** *And its end or its latter parts.* I will cause it to end in such great mourning, as usually happens on a day bitter due to some fatal accident. Proverbs 5:4; Chapter 14:13. **c)** *As a day of bitterness,* or a bitter day. Compare Job 3:5.
**v. 11. d)** *For behold!* Those "latter parts" mentioned in verse 10 are now further explained by a notable example. **e)** *That I may send.* Ezekiel 14:13. **f)** *And indeed, not so much a famine of bread,* or for bread, such as he had already mentioned above in chapter 4:6 among other kinds of punishments. He removes this type of famine, not to exclude it, but to hint at a much worse famine, in respect to which that physical famine would not even be considered a famine at all. Compare Isaiah 8:21 and contrast Zechariah 10:2. Jerome and others apply this to the miserable lot of the Jews who, after the final destruction, were deprived of all comfort of the Word. But the following things—concerning the oath by the sin of Samaria, by the God of Dan and the way of Beersheba—teach that these matters concern the kingdom of the tribes of Israel. These instances of famine for the divine Word were punished in the Assyrian captivity, just as the Jews were in the Babylonian. Lamentations 2:9. **g)** *Nor a thirst for waters.* Verse 13. Compare Isaiah 65:13; Hosea 2:5. **h)** *But,* or though it be *for hearing,* namely, from their teachers, since they will have none before them. Lamentations 2:9 (see the note there); Ezekiel 7:26; Micah 3:7. Or certainly they will be futile teachers, who will only follow and find traditions. Isaiah 29:11... And although they will read Moses and the Prophets, they will be to them like a sealed book, by a just judgment...
</margin>

# CHAPTER IX.
->1. *v. 13. n)* Properly, they shall cover themselves or be covered, namely, with darkness from a fainting of the soul; that is, they shall fail or faint away. Genesis 38:14; Jonah 4:8. Compare Isaiah <note>original: "Ef." for Esaias</note> 51:20. This is an Oriental expression. So the Hebrew **עטף** <note>original: "ataph"</note> in Lamentations 2:11, 12, 19 and the Arabic **עטף** <note>original: "atafa"</note>, and likewise **עטי** <note>original: "ata"</note>, "to be covered," is very frequently used for a fainting of the soul. See Schultens’s *Observations on the Old Testament*, page 277 and following. *o)* *Because of thirst,* not so much in the proper sense as in the improper sense of verse 11. Isaiah 41:17. Compare Lamentations 4:4. *v. 14. p)* Those who formerly had sworn or now swear. Compare Deuteronomy 6:13; Joshua 23:7; Zephaniah 1:5; Psalm 63:12. *q)* *By the guilt.* 2 Chronicles <note>original: "2 Par."</note> 24:18. That is, by the calves of Samaria, which became the cause and occasion of guilt for them. Compare Deuteronomy 9:21; Ezekiel 14:3, 4, 6. *r)* *By the life* <note>original: "per vitam"</note>. Compare the note on 1 Samuel 20:3. *s)* 1 Kings 12:29, 30. *t)* *The way of Beersheba,* that is, of the Deity sought on that way. It is understood as an oath by God, as if He wished to have a sanctuary in Beersheba and Dan. Cocceius’s *Lexicon* 166. But Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> says: *The "way"* refers to how stable the laws (worship, religion) of Beersheba are; the name "way" is used as in Acts 19:23, 22:4. *u)* See the note on chapter 5:5. *x)* *And they shall fall so as not to rise again.* See the note on chapter 5:2 and compare Isaiah 43:17; Psalm 41:9.

**CHAPTER IX.** *v. 1. y)* *I saw;* not indeed with physical eyes, but with the mind and a prophetic spirit. Chapter 7:1, 4, 7; chapter 8:1; Isaiah 6:1. *z)* *The Lord himself,* and how great and powerful He is! Compare below, verses 5, 6. *a)* *Standing upon the altar,* which was now about to be destroyed along with the other parts of the temple. See chapter 7:7. But Jonathan: *I saw the glory of the Lord, which had departed from the Cherub (in the inner sanctuary of the temple); remaining upon the bronze altar in the upper court of the temple.* This was a symbol signifying that the temple was to be deserted by Jehovah. And the Paraphrast <note>Jonathan</note> seems to have looked to Ezekiel 9:3 and following, a prophecy which is parallel to this one in many circumstances. Compare also Ezekiel 10:18, 19 and the notes above at chapter 1:1. Furthermore, just as chapters 7 and 8 threatened the Israelites, so here, under the sign of the striking of the columns, he threatens the Jews especially with destruction, which the Prophet: I. amplifies in verses 1-8. II. restricts through the promise of restoration to wholeness under the kingdom of Christ in verses 8-15. *b)* The imperative is indefinite but emphatic. That is, He commands, and while He commands, the Lord Himself strikes; hence he immediately adds here, speaking of Himself in the first person: *the last of them I will slay with the sword.* Compare the note on chapter 6:11; also Zechariah 13:7 compared with Matthew 26:31. *c)* *Pomegranate.* Exodus 25:31, 33. That is, a capital or small capital, or collectively *capitals*, such as are placed at the top of columns for decoration. Zephaniah 2:14. *M. I.* <note>possibly a specific commentator</note> explains this as the priests and princes. And indeed, God was going to begin His judgments with these. Ezekiel 9:6, proceeding from there to the people, verse 7. We prefer, however, to take this and the shaking of the thresholds as a symbol of the destruction of the temple; the following words, *and cut them in pieces etc.*, then deal with the slaughter of the priests and the people, which is predicted in conjunction with the temple’s destruction. *d)* That they may tremble as they lean toward ruin. Isaiah 24:18. *e)* *The thresholds,* and thus the foundations and bottom parts of the temple. Compare Isaiah 6:4. *f)* *And cut them in pieces.* This agrees with the Arabic **בצע** <note>original: "batza"</note> "to cut into parts, to slice, to cleave." Compare Joel 2:8; Job 6:9, 27:8; and the Targum on Leviticus 2:5. The suffix can refer to the capitals, thresholds, and other structures of the temple. *g)* So that they fall upon the heads of all those who are in the temple, and especially in the inner court—namely the priests and Levites. That is, the people remaining after the priests have been killed. Chapter 4:2; Ezekiel 23:25. Note further that three distinct parts indicate 1) the ruin of the temple, 2) the slaughter of the priests, and 3) the slaughter of the people. Furthermore, Jonathan explains the first destruction by the Babylonians, stating: *Unless the people of the house of Israel turn to the law, the lampstand shall be extinguished; King Josiah shall be killed, and the temple shall be desolated, and the courts shall be scattered, and the vessels of the sanctuary shall go into captivity, and the remnant of them I will slay with the sword.* But Grotius in *Prophetic Theology*, page 506, and Maius in *Economy* 886, apply it to the second destruction by the Romans. *h)* Verses 4, 10. *i)* *Not one of them fleeing shall flee away.* Chapter 2:14, 15. *k)* Job 1:15. *m)* *An escaped one.* Genesis 14:13; Obadiah verse 14. *v. 2. n)* *If they dig,* that is, if they penetrate by digging. Ezekiel 8:8. The denial of escape, which he had threatened in verse 1, he now breaks down into parts to show that absolutely no escape will be available to them. Jonathan: *If they think they will be hidden as if in the underworld.* *o)* *Into Sheol* <note>original: "in infernum"</note>, or (to speak more generally with the Apostle in Ephesians 4:9) into the lower parts of the earth. For this name is widely used, signifying the abyss and the grave, both under the idea of depth. Isaiah 14:9; Proverbs 9:18, 15:24; Job 11:8. Compare Psalm 139:8; Job 14:13, 26:6. *p)* Jonathan: *From there, by my word, their enemies shall take them.* *q)* Psalm 139:8. Jonathan: *And if they ascend mountains as high as heaven.* *r)* *Yet from there I will pull them down.* Jeremiah 49:16; Hosea 7:12; Obadiah verses 3, 4. Jonathan: *From there they shall pull them down by my word.*

Compare verse 3. Leviticus 26:33; Exodus 5:2; 12:13, 14. **e)** verse 8; see note on Jeremiah 21:10. **f)** see note on Jeremiah 21:10; chapter 24:6.

For he is the Lord God of hosts, who touches the earth—how will you endure His wrath, when at His touch all nature is shaken and melts like wax? Compare notes on chapter 3:13 and 4:13. **h)** Compare Psalm 144:5. **i)** *so that it melts.* Jeremiah 2:9; Nahum 1:5; Psalm 46:7; 97:5. **k)** *and they shall mourn.* Chapter 1:2; 8:8; see note on 8:8. **m)** *it shall fail, it shall be submerged as if by a river.* Numbers 11:2; Jeremiah 51:64; see note above on chapter 8:8.

### 3 And if they hide themselves on the top of Carmel, from there I will search and take them; and if they be hid from my sight in the bottom of the sea, from there I will command the serpent, and he shall bite them. 4 And if they go into captivity before their enemies, from there I will command the sword, and it shall slay them: and I will set mine eyes upon them for evil, and not for good. 5 And the Lord God of hosts is he that toucheth the land, and it shall melt, and all that dwell therein shall mourn: and it shall rise up wholly like a flood; and shall be drowned, as by the flood of Egypt. 6 It is he that buildeth his stories in the heaven, and hath founded his troop in the earth; he that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The Lord is his name. 7 Are ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me, O children of Israel? saith the Lord. Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir? 8 Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from off the face of the earth; saving that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, saith the Lord. 9 For, lo, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth. 10 All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword.

...bound together by the one religion of the Lord. This last opinion is also held by Cocceius, and likewise the Targum Jonathan, which says: "He decorated His Church on the earth." **q)** Isaiah 23:13. **r)** see note on chapter 5:8. **s)** see note ibid. and chapter 4:13.

\* **verse 7. f)** He explains the cause of such a severe judgment, which is 1) the stubbornness of the Israelites in their sins, and 2) their supreme ingratitude toward the benefits of God. The connection, therefore, can be this: "Neither can you complain as if I were punishing you without cause; for are you not..." **s)** *as the children of the Cushites [Ethiopians],* who do not change their skin, just as you do not change your ways; Jeremiah 13:23. It is as if he said: "I have labored through all this time to lead you back to a better way and to command you away from sins, but in vain. For I have washed the Ethiopians, and they do not turn white." **x)** Truly a great benefit (chapter 2:10; 3:1), but you have not valued it or acknowledged it with gratitude any more than the barbarian nations—the Philistines and Syrians—of whom I led the former out of Caphtor and the latter out of Kir, just as I led you out of Egypt. **y)** Compare Genesis 10:14 and see note on Deuteronomy 2:23; Jeremiah 47:4. Behold, therefore, that for these nations too, their migrations and wars turned out successfully, not without the help and favor of the divine power. Compare concerning the Ammonites, Deuteronomy 2:19, 21; and the Edomites, verse 22, collected in verse 23. **z)** from where they were brought back by the Assyrians; chapter 1:5; 2 Kings 16:9. The Vulgate and Targum Jonathan read "Cyrene," not indeed that African one, which was never under the Assyrians, but a Mediterranean region of Media, by the River Mardus, called <term>Kyrne</term> <note>original: "Κύרנה"</note> by Ptolemy; unless one prefers to understand the region of Iberia by the River Cyrus. That it was near the Elymaeans is gathered from Isaiah 22:6. Compare Bochart, *Phaleg* book 4, chapter 32. This present passage teaches us that the Syrians were once newcomers in this region before Syria fell to them by divine favor.

\* **verse 8. a)** Behold, therefore, because you have been so stubborn and equally ungrateful toward me (verse 7). **b)** verse 4; compare Psalm 34:17. **c)** [My eyes] shall be against this sinful, wicked kingdom, characterized by the habit of sinning. He speaks of a certain and particular kingdom, namely that of his own people; compare verses 7, 10, which teaches this in this place. **d)** The demonstrative article is prefixed to both the noun and the adjective. **d)** Deuteronomy 6:15; Micah 5:13. [Compare Hosea 1:4. **e)**] *Except* <note>original: "Ephes"</note> which is the same as saying "Nevertheless." Numbers 13:28; Deuteronomy 15:4. **f)** *I will not utterly destroy.* Compare chapter 3:12; 5:3; Jeremiah 30:11; 18:7. "I will destroy the kingdom, not the people." — Grotius.

\* **verse 9. g)** see note on chapter 6:11. **h)** *and I will shake,* I will let them wander. Chapter 8:12; Numbers 32:13; 2 Samuel 15:20; Psalm 59:12. **i)** as if the house of Jacob were being shaken; or as something is shaken. <note>Hebrew grammar note: Niph.</note> Nahum 3:12. **k)** *in a sieve* — Celebrated scholar Maius in his Supplement, page 46, conjectures it is named from the multitude of holes, from the root *kavar* (to multiply), Job 35:16. From this also comes *mikbar* (a grate), for the same reason. Indeed, the Latin word *cribrum* (sieve) is from there by a transposition of letters. **l)** *and yet it shall not fall or be lost.* 1 Samuel 26:20. **m)** *any grain,* as if to say, the smallest particle of wheat. 2 Samuel 17:13; Proverbs 26:8. Clearly, only the chaff and the refuse shall fall, but the pure wheat (that is, the holy seed of Israel) shall remain. Compare especially Isaiah 6:13; Ezekiel 20:38; Luke 3:17; and Romans 11:2. "So also good men," says Grotius, "although partakers of the common evil, shall be preserved from destruction."

\* **verse 10. n)** *For they shall indeed die by the sword.* verse 1. **o)** *obstinate sinners* Isaiah 1:28; Psalm 1:1; see above at verse 8.

<header>CHAPTER 9. AMOS 9</header>

<margin>
Regarding the reign of Christ, the son of David (2 Samuel 7:12 ff; Luke 1:32, 33). **s)** The booth <note>original Latin: "tugurium"</note> (Isaiah 1:8) of David. Compare Isaiah 16:5. In the Targum of Jonathan: "the kingdom of the house of David." The meaning is: I will cause the kingdom of David, which has long since perished, to now rise up much more gloriously in the kingdom of Christ himself. Compare 2 Samuel 7:12 ff; Isaiah 49:6; Luke 1:32. Moreover, the Jews themselves apply these things to the Messiah.
</margin>

<gloss>verse 10, p</gloss> "My people who say <gloss>q</gloss> 'The evil shall not reach or overtake us.'" <gloss>verse 11</gloss> "In <gloss>r</gloss> that day I will raise up <gloss>s</gloss> the fallen booth of David, and I will wall up <gloss>x</gloss> its breaches, <gloss>y</gloss> and I will raise up its ruins, and I will build it <gloss>c</gloss> as in the days of old." <gloss>verse 12</gloss> "So that <gloss>d</gloss> they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations upon whom my name <gloss>g</gloss> is called, says the Lord who does this."
<gloss>verse 13</gloss> "Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, <gloss>i</gloss> when the plowman shall overtake the reaper, <gloss>l</gloss> and the treader <gloss>m</gloss> of grapes him who sows seed; and the mountains shall drip sweet wine, and all the hills <gloss>p</gloss> shall melt." <gloss>verse 14</gloss> "And I will restore the captivity of my people Israel, and they shall build <gloss>q</gloss> desolate cities and inhabit them, and plant vineyards and drink their wine, and make gardens and eat their fruit." <gloss>verse 15, w</gloss> "And I will plant them upon their land, and they shall <gloss>x</gloss> no more be plucked up from their land which I have given them, <gloss>c</gloss> says the Lord <gloss>d</gloss> your God."

<margin>Until here.</margin>

->VISION<-

The Jews refer this in the Talmud, tractate Sanhedrin chapter 11, folio 96, where it is said that **Rabbi Nachman** asked **Rav**: *"Have you heard when the 'Son of the Fallen' is coming?"* to which Rav replied, *"Whom do you mean by the 'Son of the Fallen'?"* He said, *"The Messiah."* Indeed, (continues **Rav**) you call him thus? Certainly, says **Rabbi Nachman**; for thus it is written: *On that day I will raise up the fallen booth of David.* **u)** *fallen*, because it fell. Chapter 5:2. **x)** *I will wall it up with a hedge.* Isaiah 58:12. **y)** *their breaches*, chapter 4:3; 1 Kings 11:27. Compare Isaiah 5:5; 58:12. The scholar **Maius** refers the plural suffix to both kingdoms [Israel and Judah], whose mention he thinks is deliberately made in the plural, lest anyone think it impossible to restore and unite the *Twelve Tribes* <note>original Greek: Δωδεκάφυλον</note>, so that they may seek God and eventually cling to the Messiah. Compare Ezekiel 37:17, 19; Hosea 2:2. But I would prefer to view the "booth of David" as a collective term, embracing all parts of the kingdom, or the cities. Such syntax is found in Jeremiah 51:43: "the land in which [plural]..." instead of "the land in whose cities no man shall dwell." Compare Judges 11:13. **z)** *its destroyed things* (i.e., David's; or the Davidic booth, by a change of gender), collecting Acts 15:16 <note>original Greek: αυτῆς</note>. Compare Isaiah 49:19. **a)** Compare chapter 7:2, 5; Hosea 6:2. **b)** Compare Jeremiah 33:7; 31:4. **c)** *As of old.* Micah 7:14; Isaiah 63:9; 51:9. Compare, for example, the most flourishing state of the kingdom under David (2 Samuel 8) and Solomon (1 Kings 4:20; 5:1-4). Therefore, this prophecy is much too illustrious to have been fulfilled in the time of **Hyrcanus**, as **Grotius** wrongly thought (Josephus 13:17).

**verse 12. d)** Therefore, so that they may receive as an inheritance those who were once foreigners, but are now to be adopted into the family of **Abraham** and the communion of the Church. Isaiah 14:2; 54:3; Jeremiah 49:2; Obadiah v. 17, 19. Furthermore, the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> (from which this text is quoted in Acts 15:17) reads quite differently: *so that the rest of men might seek* etc., reading **דרשו** <note>darshu - seek</note> instead of **יירשו** <note>yirshu - possess</note> and **אדם** <note>adam - man</note> instead of **אדום** <note>Edom</note>, omitting also the particle **את** and adding (in the Alexandrian Manuscript) *the Lord*. **Lightfoot** suspects on Acts 15:17 that this was done deliberately by those translators out of hatred and contempt for the Edomites, who were once the most bitter enemies of the Jewish people. Meanwhile, Luke, as he usually does, retains the Greek version all the more safely because it aptly proves the same point that the Hebrew text and **James** (who undoubtedly cited the original words) had intended to confirm from this passage. **e)** Obadiah v. 19, 21; compare Romans 11:5. Edom is specifically named as the most bitter enemy of Israel (see above, chapter 1:11), so that it might be understood that from the other nations, a holy remnant would much more likely be joined to the Church. **f)** i.e., those who shall be called by my name, *the people and sons of Jehovah*, Hosea 2:1, just as the Israelites were in Isaiah 63:19; Jeremiah 14:9. **g)** See note on Hosea 11:11. **h)** *doing this*: so that it does not remain a bare promise, but becomes truth in effect. Compare Isaiah 9:6 and note on Jeremiah 33:2.

**verse 13. i)** *the plowman shall reach the reaper.* So great and manifold will be the abundance of produce that in the autumn season, when the farmer usually plows and scatters the seed, he will have scarcely finished harvesting the crops. Reference is made to Leviticus 26:5, but under the type of earthly goods, the abundance of spiritual blessings in the New Testament is signified. Compare Isaiah 28:24; Proverbs 20:4. **k)** The harvest in Palestine begins in the month of Nisan, or our April. See note on Joshua 3:15. **l)** *treading grapes in the winepress.* Isaiah 63:2. **m)** *drawing the seed*, i.e., the sower, who pulls the seed from the cloth and scatters it in a trail on the ground. Compare Psalm 126:5. **n)** The meaning: The vintage (which in Palestine occurs in August or the beginning of September: see note on Numbers 13:20) will last until the sowing time. **o)** *the mountains shall drip.* Joel 4:18. This signifies the extreme fertility of the vine-bearing mountains; so that they flow white across the land with honey and milk from the abundance of livestock and bees, and the richness of all things. Exodus 3:8, etc. **o)** *new wine* <note>original Hebrew: עסיס - asis</note> Joel 1:5; 4:18; compare the root in Malachi 3:21. **p)** *they shall melt*, namely, from the abundance of wine and milk, i.e., everything will be full of wine and milk. <note>original: Hithpael form</note> Nahum 1:5; Psalm 107:26.

**verse 14. q)** Compare Jeremiah 30:18; Psalm 126:1. **r)** Compare Romans 11:26. **s)** Isaiah 58:12. **t)** See Isaiah 54:3. **u)** Isaiah 65:21, 22; compare the opposite above in chapter 5:11; Deuteronomy 28:30; Zephaniah 1:13. **x)** Jeremiah 31:5; Ezekiel 28:26; Hosea 2:17. **y)** Compare Isaiah 62:8 and the opposite above in chapter 5:11; Deuteronomy 28:30. **z)** Isaiah 65:21.

**verse 15. a)** *And I will plant them in their own places.* 2 Samuel 7:10; Jeremiah 24:6. **b)** *they shall be plucked up* through deportations and exiles. Compare Jeremiah 24:6; chapter 42:10; and the contrary in chapter 12:14, 15; chapter 48:4; 2 Chronicles 7:20. **c)** The seal of the promise, as in verse 12. Compare Numbers 23:19; Psalm 33:9; etc. **d)** *Their God* then, namely, O Israel! An address to the people.

\* **11. ruined-places** <note>original Hebrew: והריסותיו</note> *written fully in 1. 2. against the Masoretic text of Erfurt.*

<column-break/>

**p)** Zurich translation: *not approaching, nor removing evil from us.* But Schmidt: *do not bring, or cause evil to overtake us*, i.e., O God. Compare chapter 6:3. **q)** <note>Hiphil form</note> Job 41:2.

**verse 11. r)** Nevertheless on that day, after I have shaken them so that the sinners of my people have died (v. 9, 10). **t)** *booth* <note>original Greek: σκηνὴ</note> is translated in the citation of **James** in Acts 15:16. From which passage it is simultaneously clear that this refers to the day or time of the New Testament. But this is the question: is that promise already entirely fulfilled, or yet to be fulfilled? The former seemed provable from the cited Apostolic quotation. Nevertheless, the celebrated **Maius** prefers the latter in *Economy of the Old Testament* p. 886. He says it cannot be said to have happened under the Second Temple, as the restoration was once under David; hence it must still happen. For even if the Gentiles were called into the communion of the Church and have entered in part, yet the conversion and spiritual restoration of the Jews has not yet occurred. Indeed, Jehovah will perfect it as He promised, says Jehovah, doing this. Then it will be clear that all Israel shall be saved (Romans 11:26) together with the Edomites and all nations; when the Lord is one and His name one (Zechariah 14:9), one shepherd and one flock shall be (John 10:16; Acts 15:16, 17). **James** and the Apostles rightly conclude from this passage of **Amos** that God called the nations through the Gospel, according to the oracles of the prophets; but they do not say that all those things were then fully fulfilled: nor were the return from captivity of all Israel, or other spiritual goods most generously promised, then fulfilled. **s)** I restore, I will raise up from the fall, chapter 5:2; Jeremiah 50:32; Job 4:4; and ruin, Isaiah 44:25; chapter 61:4; and indeed in the kingdom.

<header>THE BOOK OF OBADIAH</header>

# THE BOOK
# OF OBADIAH,
## In Hebrew:
## עובדיה

The theme of this prophecy consists of: I. **A threat** against the Idumaeans <note>The descendants of Esau, also known as Edom</note>, to whom total destruction is predicted (verses 1–16) due to both their pride and the injuries they inflicted upon the people of Israel. II. **A Gospel message for Israel**, promising not only restoration but also the expansion of their inheritance and deliverance during the time of the New Testament. Its purpose is to comfort the Israelites and lift them toward the hope of future liberation, while calling the Idumaeans—if possible—back to repentance and a better mind. As <term>Jerome</term><note>A 4th-century scholar and Bible translator</note> says, he is a "Small Prophet" in the count of his verses, but not in the weight of his meanings. Indeed, under the type of *Israel* he figured the salvation of the Church, and under the type of *Edom* the destruction of the Antichrist.

---

<margin>
**Verse 1. a)** A prophetic *Vision* (as in Isaiah 1:1). This is the title and inscription of the prophecy. **b)** *Obadiah*, that is to say, "a worshiper of the Lord." Scripture is entirely silent regarding his homeland, his lineage, and his time; nor do we have any certainty. The <term>Talmudists</term><note>Jewish civil and ceremonial law scholars</note>, whom <term>Aben Ezra</term><note>A 12th-century Spanish rabbi and commentator</note> praises in his collection on the *Great Bible*, are of the opinion that this is the same Obadiah who was the palace supervisor in the court of King Ahab and who hid one hundred of God’s prophets against the wicked plots of Jezebel (1 Kings 18:3 and following). They add that he was an Idumaean who became a <term>proselyte</term><note>A convert to Judaism</note>: and in this way, he prophesied against his own nation. But if our prophet were that man, how would he have escaped Jezebel, who went about to wipe out the prophets of God? (ibid. v. 4). On the other hand, if one may conclude his age from the similarity of his subject and style, <term>Tarnovius</term><note>Paul Tarnow, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> and others are certainly to be approved, who make Obadiah a contemporary of Jeremiah. This is because both prophesy against the Idumaeans in almost the same words—only with a slightly changed order—and because Obadiah charges them with crimes that were committed at that time: for example, Obadiah v. 12 compared with Lamentations 4:21; as well as in verse 20 where he makes express mention of the captivity of Jerusalem.
</margin>

->The vision <gloss>a</gloss> of Obadiah <gloss>b</gloss> thus says <gloss>c</gloss> the Lord <gloss>d</gloss> GOD <gloss>e</gloss> concerning Edom <gloss>f</gloss> :<-
->A report <gloss>g</gloss> we have heard <gloss>h</gloss> from <gloss>i</gloss> the Lord <gloss>k</gloss> and a messenger <gloss>l</gloss> among the nations <gloss>m</gloss><-

->to the earth?" <gloss>l</gloss> : 4 Though you soar high <gloss>m</gloss> like the eagle, <gloss>n</gloss> and though between <gloss>o</gloss> the stars<-
->you set [your nest]<-

<sig>Eeee 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: as far as</meta>

---

**a)** *Parallel: 1 Chronicles 34:22.* **c)** And yet, he soon speaks in the plural in the name of himself and his people: *We have heard a report, etc.* Clearly, the Prophet teaches that whatever he says, he says not by human will, but inspired by the Spirit of God, whether he brings it forth under his own person, that of his people, or that of the Lord himself (cf. 2 Peter 1:21). **d)** Concerning the *Idumaeans*, please see the notes on Isaiah 21:11 and Amos 1:11. Furthermore, compare the parallel prophecies of Ezekiel 25:13 and following; and chapter 35; but especially Jeremiah 49:14 and following, with which our prophet harmonizes so closely, just as Micah 4:1 does with Isaiah 2:2; Jeremiah 48 with Isaiah 15 and 16; Jeremiah 48:46, 47 with Numbers 21:27 and following; and in the New Testament, the Epistle of Jude with the second [Epistle] of Peter. Therefore, this is a repetition and, in some places, an amplification of Jeremiah’s prophecy against the Idumaeans. **e)** *A report*, which is indeed joyful for us, but unlucky for the Idumaeans (Proverbs 15:30; Daniel 11:44). **f)** Instead of which is the singular *I have heard* in Jeremiah 49:14. Clearly, the Prophet speaks here, but in such a way that he introduces his people—for whose comfort he writes—or at least the rest of God’s Prophets who prophesied against Edom, speaking at the same time. Moreover, they *had heard* through divine revelation. **g)** and therefore it is no empty rumor that we have heard, but most true, because we have heard it *from the Lord* (cf. note on Isaiah 21:10). **h)** Namely, *a messenger*. The summary of that report follows: and so the **ו** <note>the Hebrew letter 'vav'</note> is explanatory. For the noun, compare Isaiah 18:2; Proverbs 13:17. The root in Arabic means *he went* or *set out* (cf. Joshua 9:4). **i)** *already sent to or among the nations* in divine providence, and in its own time it will most certainly be sent. This is a prophetic <term>hypotyposis</term><note>A vivid description that makes a future event seem present</note>, by which he presents a future matter as if already present, for the sake of noting its certainty. For one nation will send to another to enter into an alliance of war against the Idumaeans (cf. Proverbs 17:11). **k)** that is, *so that they may say to them* (understanding the word "saying," as in Isaiah 14:8, etc.) in the name of those sending: "Arise, and let us rise together," or, let us prepare ourselves (Judges 7:15; Jeremiah 6:5). **But** according to Schmidt: *that we may stand against*. See Amos 7:9; Psalm 27:3. **l)** *against her*, namely, Idumaea: to whom he soon speaks in the masculine in verse 2 and following, with respect to the people. **m)** *for war* to be brought upon her (Isaiah 7:1; Zechariah 14:1).

**v. 2.** **n)** Behold, he says, the Lord in His own person, whose report the Prophet had recounted in his own and the Jews' name in verse 1. **o)** *Amos 7:2, 5.* **p)** *Jerome* connects it with verse 3 in this way: *Since you are the least among all the surrounding nations, and small in number compared to other peoples, you are lifted up by pride beyond your strength.* See note on Jeremiah 49:15. Others, however, as we noted there, read it prophetically: *I will make you the smallest.* (cf. Ezekiel 35:3). **q)** *despised* (Jeremiah 49:15; Psalm 22:7).

**v. 3.** **r)** *But* or *Indeed the pride of your heart* (Jeremiah 49:16; 1 Samuel 17:28). **s)** deceived you, that is, it rashly inflated you and lifted you up to a vain presumption of strength (v. 7; Genesis 3:13). **But** the Septuagint and the Vulgate read: *it has extolled you*, as if they had read it with the letter *Sin*; however, it is found nowhere else in that form <note>the Hiphil stem</note>. **t)** *dwelling in the clefts*. The letter *Yod* is added at the end (as in Micah 7:14), for he is like an eagle staying in the crags of the rocks (cf. Job 39:28 and note on Jeremiah 49:16). **u)** *in the fissures* (3); see the note there. **x)** For the Idumaeans inhabited <term>Arabia Petraea</term><note>Stony Arabia, the region around the city of Petra</note> (cf. Isaiah 42:11). **y)** *in the height of his habitation*. In which he considers himself, because of the location's site, above all misfortune (Jeremiah 49:16; cf. Isaiah 33:16). Pertaining to this is what *Jerome* notes on verse 5: *Every southern region of the Idumaeans, from Eleutheropolis as far as Petra and Aila, has small dwellings in caves; and because of the excessive heat of the sun, since it is a southern province, it uses underground huts.* These they excavated in the highest rocks so that their hiding places would be safer. **z)** *who will force me to descend*, or throw me down to the earth. A question assuming the thing is impossible (cf. Isaiah 10:13).

**v. 4.** **a)** For it is permitted. *Amos 9:2, 3.* He now explains in what way it will come to pass that Edom feels himself shamefully deceived by his own opinion. **b)** *you have exalted*, that is, you have built in a high place, namely *your nest*, as soon follows; compare Jeremiah 49:16. **c)** cf. note on Jeremiah 49:16 and Job 39:27. **d)** cf. Isaiah 14:13. A hyperbole <note>an exaggeration for effect</note>.

<summary>This page introduces the Book of Obadiah, debating the prophet's historical identity and timing while providing a linguistic commentary on the first four verses regarding the certain destruction of Edom due to its pride.</summary>

Indeed these flow from the related word *damim* <note>original: "דמים", meaning bloods or kinship</note> in Psalm 4, 7. Others: "How would you have been compared?" from *damah* <note>original: "דמה"</note>, "he was like." **n)** The thieves—did they not take their sufficiency? See the note on Jeremiah 49, 9, and what we just gave from Jerome. **o)** Grape-gatherers. <term>Jonathan</term> <note>The Aramaic Paraphrase or Targum</note>: "robbers in the likeness of grape-gatherers." Ibid. **p)** (At least the small clusters of grapes, as in Judges 8, 2; Isaiah 17, 6; 24, 13; Micah 7, 1.) These clusters are called *sha'are qir* <note>original: "שערי קיר"</note>, whatever remains after the greatest part of goods or men has been plundered or killed.

<margin>
**q)** By placing, that is, you may place; which, however, you will never be able to do. A similar omission occurs in Numbers 23, 21. **s)** His nest. <term>Jonathan</term>: "your dwelling place." The metaphor of the eagle is continued. Cf. ibid. and Habakkuk 2, 9. **t)** And so I am about to touch what is possible, which indeed seemed impossible to you in verse 3. Cf. Amos 9, 2–3. **h)** See the note on Ezekiel 11, 8; Amos 3, 13.
**v. 5. i)** If. See the note on Jeremiah 49, 9. **k)** Job 21, 14. <term>Jerome</term>: "That is, if thieves and robbers, who are accustomed to dig through houses by night and seize what is in the houses, had entered unto you and, hidden by darkness, had gone around the corners of your house; they surely would have taken only what they thought sufficient for themselves, and would have left something in your buildings, either through being satisfied or through ignorance. If grape-gatherers had entered your vineyard... they would have left clusters hidden by the vines and leaves. But the enemies, who came to you at the Lord’s command (referring to the Babylonians and the army of Nebuchadnezzar), searched out everything," etc. See the note on Jeremiah 49, 9. **l)** Those who devastate, *bozezim* <note>original: "בֹּוֹזְזִים"</note>. Isaiah 15, 1. There is a mixture of literal and figurative language, as we observed in Jeremiah 49, 9 regarding the word *hashchitu* <note>to destroy</note>. **m)** A difficult phrase. It pleases us that this is a parenthetical exclamation ("O, how you are cut off!" or "O, how greatly you are destroyed!") Thus *eich* <note>how</note> exaggerates, as in verse 6. And the verb *damah* <note>original: "דָּמָה"</note> takes the meaning of being "cut off" from the related *dum* or *damam*, "to be silent," which often means "to be cut off," as in Hosea 10, 15 and 4, 6; for those who are cut off or perish are wrapped in perpetual silence (Psalm 94, 17; 115, 17). But the <term>Vulgate</term> <note>The common Latin Bible</note> has: "How would you have been silent?" The <term>Syriac</term>: "How have you been silent?" and <term>Jonathan</term>: "How did you sleep until they stole," etc.
</margin>

*v.* 6. **q)** But *how utterly they have been investigated*. So great was the diligence of the enemies in digging out the Idumaeans and their goods, that not even any clusters or remains were left to them. Verse 5. 1 Kings 20, 6; cf. Amos 9, 3. **v)** i.e., the Idumaeans, descendants of Esau. Jeremiah 49, 8, 10. **s)** *were searched out*. Isaiah 21, 12. **t)** *his hiding places*, to which they had fled. *Al.* hidden treasures. **r)** *of him*. But it marks the place rather than the thing, as the form of the noun teaches (which for the most part forms local nouns), and as seen in the parallelism of Jeremiah 49, 10, where it is *mistarav* <note>his secret places</note>. *v.* 7. **u)** *They escorted you even to the border*, as if with joined forces they were going to meet the enemy, yet from there they soon returned, and thus abandoned you to the enemies. Cf. Genesis 18, 16 and 12, 20, where the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> translates it as "they accompanied him." But <term>Jonathan</term>: "They made you migrate from your border." For *shilleach* also means to drive out, compared with Genesis 3, 23; Psalm 44, 3. That is, they were the moral cause of your migration, being advisers of an unhappy war and treacherous allies. <term>Jerome</term>: "When Nebuchadnezzar came, all who were previously allies of Edom... left him, and joined with the enemies, they stretched out snares." But it could perhaps also be understood effectively of the Babylonians themselves, of whom the Idumaeans were allies in the destruction of Jerusalem. **x)** *your allies*. Genesis 14, 13. **y)** verse 3. **z)** *prevailed over you*, namely by their counsels, which were either fraudulent or at least ill-fated. **a)** see Jeremiah 38, 22. **b)** *A difficult phrase. S. they will place your bread as a wound under you*; <term>Noldius</term> page 770: "ulcers in you." <term>Cocceius</term> thus: "They place their bread as foulness, which is under you," i.e., your excrement. That is, they force you to swallow your own excrement because of the extreme shortage of food in cities besieged by the enemy or in exile. Cf. 2 Kings 18, 27. But the accents do not favor this; according to them, it seems it should be translated: "instead of your bread they will place foulness under you, in which you will lie wounded or a captive." But the <term>Vulgate</term>: "those who eat with you." <term>Jonathan</term>: "those eating from your table," as if *ochelei* <note>eaters of</note> should be repeated from the preceding; with which the <term>Syriac</term> also (though against the accents) clearly connected it: "men of your peace and your bread," etc. Cf. Psalm 41, 10; Daniel 11, 26. **c)** *foulness* (**d**) Jeremiah 30, 13. *he'alah-mazor*, "to heal," from the Arabic *mazar*, "he loathed," whence it also denotes a purulent and foul wound (Hosea 5, 13) which causes nausea in those who see it. But the <term>Septuagint</term>, <term>Syriac</term>, <term>Arabic</term>, and <term>Vulgate</term>, looking not at the etymology but at the metaphor, have "snares" for "wound." And <term>Jonathan</term>: "a stumbling block." **d)** because if there had been in him such great insight and prudence as he boasts, he would hardly have allowed himself to be so greatly deceived. Verse 8. Deuteronomy 32, 28; cf. Proverbs 28, 30. **e) n)** namely in that state of the Edomites. Verse 6. *v.* 8. **f)** An emphatic question, as if to say: it would seem incredible to Edom that I have denied him wisdom, so that he might say perhaps: Where then and in what way has that famous wisdom of ours gone? Cf. Jeremiah 49, 7 and its note. But the answer: "Will it not..." **g)** verse 4. **h)** "even I will destroy." To others this is a change of state, not meaning, as in Genesis 3, 5; 27, 4. Or understand "it shall be" that I destroy. **i)** cf. Ezekiel 29, 14; Jeremiah 49, 7; 1 Corinthians 1, 19. **k)** <term>Jonathan</term>: "and every man in whom there is understanding." Verse 7. **l)** i.e., from Idumaea, which was a mountainous region. Verses 9, 19, 21. *v.* 9. **m)** *they shall be dismayed, they shall be broken*. Jeremiah 46, 5; 50, 36. **n)** Amos 1, 12; see note on Jeremiah 49, 7. **o)** *therefore*. "Because of which" is understood. It marks here not so much an end as an outcome. That is, from which dismay it will most certainly happen that he is cut off. Cf. Hosea 8, 4. **p)** <term>Jonathan</term> adds: "in whom there is strength." **q)** see note on verse 8. **r)** for the same, i.e., slaughter (**l**) with which your enemies will rage against you; or with which you raged against your brother Jacob (verse 10). Cf. Rad. 1, 13, 15. *v.* 10. **s)** *Because of the injury brought by you upon your brother* (Joel 4, 19). Now the Prophet begins to connect the punishment of the Idumaeans with its primary cause, which was their cruelty toward their kinsmen, the Israelites. See note on Isaiah 21, 11 and Amos 1, 11. **t)** see note on Amos 1, 11. "Jacob," just like "Esau" in verse 6, denotes his descendants rather than the individuals. He calls him "brother" to increase the magnitude of the impiety and crime committed against him. **n)** *shame shall cover (overwhelm) you* (**4**) Micah 7, 10; cf. Psalm 44, 16; 69, 8. Covering the face was a sign of shame and ignominy (Jeremiah 14, 3; Esther 6, 12); hence perhaps this phrase arose. **x)** and finally you shall be cut off. Verse 9. **y)** and not just for a short time, but forever. Jeremiah 49, 13; Malachi 1, 3. *v.* 11. **z)** Connects with the beginning of verse 10. That is, the injury I alleged, you brought upon Jacob on the day... **a)** when you stood at a distance, looking at the evil not without pleasure, so far from bringing help to your brother (2 Kings 4, 25); or "from the opposite side," i.e., against Jacob as a companion of the Chaldean cruelty. 2 Samuel 18, 13. **b)** on the day they took captive. Numbers 21, 1; Isaiah 14, 2. **c)** barbarian nations, the Babylonians. Isaiah 1, 7. **d)** *his army or his wealth*. Verse 13. **e)** and foreigners entered them. Lamentations 5, 2. **f)** conquered in war. Verse 13; Isaiah 13, 1; Psalm 79, 1. **g)** as if for dividing the spoil. Future Piel. For *yaddu* <note>they cast</note>. Joel 4, 3. **a)** Jeremiah 50, 14; a similar contraction occurs in Nahum 1, 4 and Lamentations 3, 33. **h)** although you were a brother (verse 10), you were like one of them. You were no better than the strangers. Cf. verse 13; Ezekiel 2, 12. Moreover, he speaks of a future thing as if it were already past. Cf. verse 12. *v.* 12. **i)** He adds a warning, which also explains the cause of the destruction he threatened against Edom. "Do not look," namely with joy, cf. Psalm 54, 9. That is, if you wished to avoid this punishment, you should not look, etc. Hence <term>Jonathan</term> repeats the threat from verse 10: "because you looked." So too in Jeremiah 49, 11, the cruelty and *epichairekakia* <note>original: "ἐπιχαιρεκακίא", joy over the misfortunes of others</note> of the Idumaeans is rebuked through the imperative mood. **k)** *the day of destruction*, as follows here and in verse 13. Cf. Psalm 137, 7. So "time" in Jeremiah 27, 7. **l)** see note on verse 10. **m)** *of his being made a stranger (1)* when God, because of his sins, had delivered him into foreign hands, and no longer wished to recognize him as His own or vindicate him from his enemies. Cf. 1 Samuel 23, 7; Job 31, 3; also Judges 2, 14; 3, 8. It is either a Noun or an Infinitive Kal. **n)** Ezekiel 25, 6; 35, 15; Micah 7, 18; Lamentations 4, 21. **o)** <term>Jonathan</term>: "and that you multiplied speaking grand things." The <term>Septuagint</term>: "and you should not have been high-minded." Cf. Ezekiel 35, 13; Zephaniah 2, 8; Daniel 7, 8, 20. **p)** verse 14; Psalm 20, 2.

**v. 17. u)** on the contrary, however, on Mount Zion—unlike on Mount Seir (verse 9) and the other nations, in which there is no escape (verse 16). **x)** escape, i.e., a multitude of those escaping. The masculine verb, by reason of syntax, regards the predicate that follows more than the subject, "escape" (deliverance), which is feminine. Or in place of the subject in the nominative case, "Mount Zion" should be repeated. The promise itself concerns the time of the New Testament. cf. A collective noun is joined by the Hebrews to a plural verb. **b)** *and they shall inherit in turn* — The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>Ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>: "those who had inherited them." Thus the <term>Vulgate</term>: "those who had possessed them." <term>Jonathan</term> paraphrases: "the wealth of the peoples who had possessed them." Surely after the captivity such a thing happened under the <term>Maccabees</term> <note>Jewish rebels who led a revolt against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BCE</note>, who subjugated Idumaea and the land of Ammon, comparing the note on Jeremiah 49:2, 20 and Ezekiel 21:11; Zephaniah 2:7, 9. But in such a way that this was only a shadow of a much greater and more illustrious fulfillment to come under the kingdom of Christ, in which the Israelite church was to receive all nations as an inheritance, cf. Isaiah 14:2, 23; Amos 9:12; Zechariah 2:13. However, because *morasheihem* <note>original: "מוֹרָשָׁיהֶם"</note> is, both by use and form, a place-name rather than the name of an actor (cf. Isaiah 14:23; Ezekiel 14:15), we prefer: *places or hereditary lands, formerly possessed by them, from which they had been driven by enemies.* But the amplitude and increase of this possession, especially in an <term>anagogical</term> <note>A spiritual or mystical interpretation of words</note> sense under the kingdom of Christ, is finally promised in verse 19 ff.

**v. 18. c)** which element consumes all materials it meets, especially dry ones. cf. Zechariah 12:6. **d)** Amos 5:6. By <term>synecdoche</term> <note>A part representing the whole</note> for all Israel, in which that primary tribe once was, and had a double portion; cf. Genesis 20:1; Psalm 81:6. Some from the ten tribes were indeed associated with the Jews returning from Babylon, but few: the fullness of them is nowhere read to be restored under the Old Testament. Therefore here also the primary respect is to the New Testament. cf. note on Jeremiah 39:4. **e)** flame, cf. Isaiah 10:17. **f)** on the other hand, the house of Esau, the Edomites and those like them, cf. verse 19 and Joel 4:19, on which place <term>William</term> <note>Likely William Lowth or another prophetic commentator</note> notes: "After the Roman war waged against the Jews, the Edomites ceased to be a distinct people." Therefore, since no Edomite people remains in these times, it is necessary that another be understood who is similar to the Edomite. <term>Major</term> <note>Georg Major</note> in his *Economy* p. 1033. He does not deny, says <term>Abarbanel</term> <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note>, that in the New Testament or in future times this is to be fully fulfilled—but in this he errs, that he calls all Christians the descendants of Edom and dreams of their total extirpation. If he had understood it regarding the Antichrist, of whom Esau was a type, he would have spoken more truly, and in agreement with the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, as we have often indicated: nor does it pertain here to explain every single word or comma. It ends in the kingdom of Christ, and the end of the prophecy declares its beginning and middle simultaneously. **g)** like stubble, which catches fire easily and is quickly consumed. **v. 19. l)** <term>Vulgate</term>: "those who are to the south"; <term>Septuagint</term>: "those in the Negev." Consequently, they translate what follows in the Accusative case: "the mount of Esau." And the same for the next part: "and those in the plains," etc. But is it wrong? Thus: "And they (the house of Jacob, v. 17) shall possess the southern parts of Judea with the bordering Idumaea or Mount of Esau." It is declared, clearly, what was said in verse 17 about recovering hereditary places by Israel; but at the same time, the amplification of the territories and cities of Jerusalem is promised (Jeremiah 31:38, 40). Regarding which, if the times of the Maccabees are considered, see <term>Josephus</term> Book 13, chapter 23. But if you look to the fulfillment in the kingdom of Christ; cf. Isaiah 26:15; 33:17; Psalm 22:28; also Zechariah 10:12 and Isaiah 49:20. Furthermore, "Negev" was used as a proper name for that part of Judea which turned toward Idumaea and the south. ### CHAPTER I. 1 OBADIAH

<margin>

And the lowland <note>the Shephelah</note> shall possess the Philistines: and they shall possess the fields of Ephraim, and the fields of Samaria: and Benjamin shall possess Gilead.
And this host of captives of the children of Israel, who are among the Canaanites, even unto Zarephath; and the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Sepharad, shall possess the cities of the south.
<margin>21</margin> And saviors shall come up on mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the LORD’S.

<margin>
*) And the sloping or lowland part of Judea, neighboring the Philistines, because it turned toward the west. Joshua 15:33. But the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> uses the nominative (see the notes already made at "the South"): *those in the Shephelah*. cf. 1 Maccabees 12:38. α) with the neighboring mountain range of the Philistines. cf. Zephaniah 2:7. Thus the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> at Jeremiah 30:10. The Ammonites in Ezekiel 25:5, 10 for the land of the Chaldeans and Ammonites. β) Benjamin (the land of the Benjaminites) with Gilead. Numbers 32:1; Zechariah 10:10. This last member of the sentence teaches how the prior parts should be explained: namely, "the South" and "the Shephelah" are in the accusative case, with the particle *et* <note>original: "את"</note> serving as a marker of association. For we nowhere read that the Benjaminites held Gilead.
</margin>

<margin>
Thus far indeed the Prophet in verse 19.
</margin>

->**And it shall be**<-

But here he repeats it for the sake of greater certainty, with a more abundant declaration of the subject. Hence the "h" <note>the Hebrew letter He</note> prefixed at the beginning of the verse is equivalent to our word *namely* or *I say*. Others translate it thus: *And the deported multitude of these Israelites shall possess what belonged to the Canaanites as far as Zarephath; and those deported from Jerusalem, that which is in Sepharad, shall possess along with the southern cities.* But these go against the accents. Now to the remaining words! r) The <term>Septuagint</term> translates: *and this is the beginning of the migration* <note>original Greek: "καὶ τῆς μετοικεσίας ἡ ἀρχὴ αὕτη"</note>. It treats *He-chel* <note>original: "ה חל"</note> as a noun for "beginning." But there is an obstacle, as the following word also requires a prefix. It is more correctly rendered as *this crowd* or *of the hosts*. Likewise in 2 Kings 18:17 and Isaiah 36:2, the word for "heavy army" <note>original: "חיל כבד"</note> is used. Though it sometimes means *rampart* or *outer wall* (2 Samuel 20:15), why shouldn't it also mean "troops"? Joined with the preceding word for "exile," it denotes the *deported host or multitude*. s) *of the children of Israel*. properly: *who are of the children of Israel*. t) *who are among the Canaanites*, namely the *exiles* or *dispersed*. These are the northern Canaanites, never subdued by the Israelites. u) *Zarephath* as far as, which in 1 Kings 17:9 and Luke 4:26 is attributed to Sidon, not for the sake of distinction, but for explanation. For the Jewish claim that this is a different place lacks foundation. Of this place <term>Josephus</term> <note>A 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> says, *it is a known town in the borders of the Canaanites, in the middle interval between Tyre and Sidon.* x) Jeremiah 40:1. y) The <term>Vulgate</term> <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> says *in Bosphorus*. But we nowhere read that the Jerusalemites were led there by Nebuchadnezzar. The <term>Syriac</term> says *in Spain*. And thus the common Jewish view following the <term>Chaldean</term> version, which has *in Aspamia*. Indeed, they promise themselves a Spanish and French kingdom under their Messiah based on a misunderstanding of this prophecy. The more prudent scholars take it as a part of the Babylonian Empire, though they have not defined it geographically. Recently, the <term>illustrious Hardt</term> <note>Hermann von der Hardt, a German orientalist</note> undertook to prove in a special book that it is *Sipphara*, a town of Mesopotamia near *Nearda*, where the Euphrates cuts into vast channels. This is the *Borsippa* of Strabo and Pliny, where the Talmudic writers lament the captive Jews. z) see verses 17, 19.

<margin>
v. 20. q) The deported, I say, Jeremiah 24:5. This verse has no small difficulty in terms of both words and sense. As to the latter, guided by the accents, we divide it into two parts; the first explains the Subject of the proposition, the latter the Predicate. The Subject is: *and this deported host of the children of Israel, who are dispersed among the Cana-*
</margin>

v. 21. a) *Saviors shall also ascend*. By these, some understand the Messiah and his associates. In the Old Testament, the judges were typical saviors (Judges 3:9). The Maccabees were also of this kind. Here, however, Christ is chiefly regarded, especially as the glorious King and conqueror of enemies, because it follows: *and the kingdom shall be the LORD’S*. b) by judgments of punishment and vengeance. c) v. 8, 9, 19. d) And *so shall the kingdom become the LORD’S*, to be manifested in glory after all enemies are defeated. Amen! Psalm 22:29; Daniel 7:27; Revelation 11:15.

### ON THE PROPHECY OF JONAH

->PREFACE<-

<margin>
*Jonah*
1. *age, homeland;*
</margin>

JONAH, (which is otherwise the name for a Dove among the Hebrews; cf. Matthew 10:16; Song of Solomon 6:9) was the son of Amittai (chapter 1:1). He was a contemporary of Isaiah, Hosea, Amos, and Micah—indeed, he was older than all the prophets we call "Minor." He originated from Gath-Hepher, a place in Galilee in the tribe of Zebulun (Joshua 19:13) between Tiberias and Sephovim, as Jerome witnesses. He is a *type <note>A person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of Christ</note> of that greatest Prophet, Jesus Christ*, who would come from a neighboring town in Galilee several centuries later (about 800 years) contrary to the opinion of the Pharisees (John 7:52; John 1:46, 47).

<margin>
2. *Prophecy against the Syrians,*
</margin>

He first prophesied to the Israelites under the beginning of the reign of Jeroboam II, or rather the end of the time of his father Joash. He foretold their joyful liberation from the power of the Syrians, as the fulfillment of that prophecy is recorded in 2 Kings 14:25. Later, as the sins of the Israelites grew and the Assyrians became too insolent under Pul or Tiglath-Pileser (2 Kings 15), he was sent by God to their royal city, Nineveh.

<margin>
*against the Assyrians or Ninevites;*
</margin>
<margin>
3. *Flight*
</margin>

However, our prophet declined that first call from God, choosing to flee into any other situation rather than undertake that most troublesome duty. This was partly out of love for his own nation, whom the Assyrians severely afflicted and finally destroyed, and partly from fear of danger—lest, by preaching the destruction of a great city to its enemies, he might be treated cruelly by them, or even be held as a liar by the Israelites if God should spare the repenting Ninevites and thus incur the hatred of his own people. See chapter 4:2 and compare the hesitation of Peter, the "son of Jonah," in Acts 10.

<margin>
4. *Punishment,*
</margin>
<margin>
5. *Prayers.*
</margin>

But after he was cast into the sea and miraculously preserved in the belly of a fish for three days and nights, and after ardent prayers (which he himself set forth in chapter 2), he returned alive to the land beyond all human hope. He thus became a most illustrious type and clear prefiguration of the death and resurrection of Christ, who would give and preach repentance to the nations (Matthew 12:40). Having returned, he was sent again by God and went to the Ninevites to preach their destruction (chapter 3:4).

<margin>
6. *Obedience etc.*
</margin>

They, however, obtained mercy by performing penance (chapter 3:10), though Jonah grieved heavily that his prediction was not fulfilled (chapter 4:1–3). But he was more correctly instructed by God, both by word and by the symbol of the plant, concerning the grace shown to the Ninevites (chapter 4:4 and following).

<margin>
7. *Parallel prophecy of Nahum.*
</margin>

A similar theme [was taken up] after forty...

<summary>This page concludes the commentary on Obadiah, debating the location of Sepharad and the identity of the "saviors" of Zion, before introducing Jonah as a historical figure and a prophetic "type" of Christ whose mission to Nineveh demonstrated God's mercy to the Gentiles.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the historical and theological introduction to the Book of Jonah, focusing on the timing of the prophecy in relation to the destruction of Nineveh and providing a summary of the book's structure. It then begins the verse-by-verse commentary on Chapter 1, exploring the etymology of Jonah's name, the location of Nineveh, and the possible reasons for his flight toward Tarshish.</meta>

...or even several years, yet not as a contemporary of our prophet, but <note>the author</note> treated the written prophecy of Nahum; which in the times of Josiah, as Jerome believes, or according to Abarbanel's calculation on Jonah chapter 3, page 259, and other reasons, had its fulfillment in the destruction of Nineveh during the beginnings of Nebuchadnezzar and the time of Zedekiah. From this we understand (these are the words of Jerome in the preface to this book) that at the first time, at Jonah's preaching, having performed penance, the Ninevites obtained pardon; but later, persisting in their former vices, they provoked God's sentence upon themselves.

<margin>8. Parts of the book, and 9. Use.</margin>
The parts of the book are two: I. The first calling of Jonah, which he refused; where we see the punishment of the reluctant prophet in chapter 1, and the revival of the supplicant in chapter 2. II. The second calling of Jonah, which he obeyed; where we see the preservation of the repentant Ninevites in chapter 3, and the conviction of the rashly indignant Jonah in chapter 4. Truly, what deserves to be noted most from this book is the supreme <term>philanthropia</term> <note>God's love for humanity</note> of God, and His providence regarding human affairs (Wisdom 14:3; compare Jeremiah 12:14–16; Romans 3:29; 1 Timothy 2:4). Note also in Chapter 4:10 how just He is in all His ways, and holy (or kind) in all His works (Psalm 145:17). Likewise, how in human weakness the strength of God is perfected in His servants (2 Corinthians 12:9). Thus Jonah, truly a wondrous man, is a sign and a portent in Israel and among the nations, alongside his <term>antitype</term> <note>a person or thing represented by an earlier symbol or "type"</note> and Lord (Isaiah 8:18; Luke 2:34). As a fugitive in the sea, shipwrecked and dead, he saves the tossing boat and saves the pagans—who were previously tossed about by the various opinions and errors of the world—as Jerome writes. But those who judge Jonah too arrogantly from a position of security, and think they stand, let them see to it that they do not also fall (1 Corinthians 10:12); let them serve the Lord in fear, and so rejoice with trembling. Blessed indeed are those who trust in Him (Psalm 2:11–12).

# THE BOOK
# OF JONAH,
### In Hebrew
# YONAH

<margin>
CHAPTER I. V. 1. a) Thus the Hebrews often begin their books. See 1 Samuel 1:1; Ruth 1:1; Esther 1:1; and the note on Ezekiel 1:1. b) Ezekiel 1:3; Zechariah 1:1. Jonah received the word of prophecy from the Lord. The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> renders this as in Luke 3:2. c) See the Preface. d) Amittai, as if to say "truth is of the Lord," or "the Lord is truth." Now, the Rabbis guess without any solid foundation or probability that Jonah’s father was rightly a Zebulunite (from 2 Kings 14:25 compared with Joshua 19:13), but that his mother was of the tribe of Asher and was that widow of Zarephath (of the Sidonians, Luke 4:25), and that Jonah himself was her son raised from the dead by Elijah (1 Kings 17:9 ff.). They further claim he was sent by Elisha to anoint Jehu (2 Kings 9:1), and from this beginning of his prophetic office, he lived two hundred years until the times of Zechariah, King of the Israelites (2 Kings 15:8). See <italic>Seder Olam</italic> chapter 18; Abarbanel on this passage, page 257 and 259, etc.
</margin>
<margin>
CHAPTER I.
<note>Haftarah for Yom Kippur Mincha</note>
</margin>
<gloss>a</gloss> And it came to pass <gloss>b</gloss> the word of the LORD <gloss>c</gloss> unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying: <gloss>d</gloss> Arise,
<gloss>e</gloss> go to Nineveh, that great city, <gloss>f</gloss> and cry out <gloss>g</gloss> against it; for <gloss>h</gloss> their wickedness has come up <gloss>i</gloss> before me. But Jonah rose up to flee <gloss>k</gloss> to Tarshish from the presence
of the LORD.

---

<margin>
V. 2. e) Arise and go without delay! (Chapter 3:2). An emphatic <term>asyndeton</term> <note>a figure of speech omitting conjunctions for speed/impact</note>, as in Hosea 1:2, etc. f) Nineveh, or Ninus, as the Greek and Roman writers call it; founded and named by Ninus on the eastern bank of the Tigris, as if to say:
</margin>
"The habitation of the son" (Genesis 10:11), or as Hiller prefers, "the dwelling of pleasantness" (<italic>Onomasticon Sacrum</italic>, p. 431). It was the metropolis and most ancient seat of the empire of the Assyrians, eventually overturned by the Medes and Chaldeans not long before the beginnings of Cyrus, when Zedekiah held the kingdom among the Jews and Nebuchadnezzar among the Babylonians. Thus, by the time of Lucian (around the end of the 2nd century AD), not even a trace of it remained, nor was its location certain: just as the Prophet Nahum clearly predicted (Chapter 1:8, 3:17). See more in Cellarius' <italic>Ancient Geography</italic>, Book III, chapter 17, p. 769, and Bochart’s <italic>Sacred Geography</italic>, Part I, p. 281–283. g) "That great city." For it was much larger than Babylon, according to Strabo, who in Book 16 defined the circuit of Babylon as 385 <term>stadia</term> <note>roughly 44 miles</note>, while according to Diodorus Siculus, Nineveh encompassed 480 stadia, which is 15 German miles in circumference. Cf. below Chapter 3:3, 4:11. Diodorus adds in Book 2, p. 65, that its founder Ninus proposed *to build a city of such magnitude that it would not only be the largest of the cities then existing in the whole world, but that no one afterward would easily attempt anything greater.* And a little later: *No one built such a city thereafter, neither in the size of its circuit nor the magnificence of its walls, etc.* h) Proclaim or preach against it, namely, that I have decreed its destruction unless it repents. Cf. Chapter 3:2, 4; Isaiah 58:1. i) "For it has ascended" (1 Samuel 5:12) "their malice" (Joel 4:13). The Septuagint and Arabic versions say "the cry of its wickedness," using a double origin or version for a single Hebrew word. Cf. below Chapter 2:10. That is to say: their sins and crimes are so great and open that they cry out to heaven and can no longer be tolerated. Cf. Genesis 4:10, 18:21, 19:13; Exodus 22:22–23; Deuteronomy 15:9; Ezra 9:6; Revelation 18:5. Certainly, in great cities, the greatest sins usually dominate. Grotius: *Luxury and robbery are accustomed to exceed all measure in royal cities. Scripture here does not descend into specific types of sins.* Cf. Nahum's prophecy concerning them.

V. 3. k) But Jonah arose, not to go where he was commanded in verse 2, but to flee. l) Chapter 4:2; Psalm 139:7. m) The Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic say "to Tarshish": by which Bochart and Pfeiffer (in <italic>Dubia Vexata</italic> on this passage) probably understand Tartessus in Hispanic Baetica (Spain); Josephus (<italic>Antiquities of the Jews</italic>, Book 9, chapter 11) understands Tarsus in Cilicia; the Jews an African city; Abarbanel says Tunis; others a place in India. Luther, Jonah, and others understand it as the sea or ocean in general, comparing Psalm 48:8; Isaiah 23:1. Cf. Genesis 10:4 and the note on 1 Kings 10:22; Ezekiel 27:12, etc. x) "From the presence of the Lord" (verse 10; Genesis 4:16). Jonah fled lest he should prophesy in the name of the Lord. That is, thinking he had escaped if he left Judea, or rather that God would abandon His call if he himself did something else and went as far away as possible. Jerome: *The Prophet knows, by the Holy Spirit suggesting it to him, that the repentance of the Gentiles is the ruin of the Jews; therefore, as a lover of his country, he does not so much envy the safety of Nineveh as he does not want his own people to perish.* — Furthermore, seeing his fellow prophets sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel to call the people to repentance, he grieves that he alone was chosen to be sent to the Assyrians, the enemies of Israel, and to the greatest city of the enemies, where there was idolatry and ignorance of God. And what is greater than these: he feared that by the occasion of his preaching, if they were converted to repentance, Israel would be utterly abandoned. Thus Maimonides says in <italic>Economy of the Old Testament</italic>, p. 895: "Jonah declined this legation (by which God signified the rejection and subversion of Israel and Judah, shown and foretold by Hosea, Amos, Joel, and Isaiah, was to be repaired by the calling of the Gentiles; and their judgment, if they would not repent and were worse than the Gentiles, was to be made heavier. Matthew 12:41, 21:41) out of love for his countrymen, being well aware that the entry of the Gentiles would be the abdication of the Jews." The Hebrews themselves do not deny this. For thus Rabbi Moses Isaac says Jonah shirked this mission because the nations of the world were closer to conversion, and he did not wish to further condemn the Israelites who did not obey the words of the Prophets. Cf. what we said in the Preface.

# JONAH 1 CHAPTER I.

<margin>
The Aramaic translation <note>Targum Jonathan</note> adds: "and when they saw that there was no use in them, they threw them out," etc.

i) they threw out (verse 4) the vessels, that is, the ship's gear, merchandise, and other things that were in the ship.

k) "they made a casting out of the gear" <note>original Greek: ἐκβολὴν ἐποιήσαντο τῶν σκευῶν</note>. They threw things overboard. Acts 27:18, 19. Jerome <note>an early Christian scholar</note> says: "They do not understand that the entire weight is the fugitive Prophet." k) so that they might lighten the load from themselves, if perhaps they could be relieved of those burdens.
</margin>

<margin>
o) and he went down to Joppa, a port of Judea in Palestine. See the note on Joshua 19:46 and compare Ezra 3:7, 2 Chronicles 2:15, and Acts 9:36. p) and he found a ship. Acts 21:2, chapter 27:6. q) going, that is, about to depart. Ruth 3:7. r) The Septuagint <note>ancient Greek translation</note>, the Vulgate <note>Latin translation</note>, etc. say "to Tarshish." Jonah <note>the Aramaic Targum</note> says "into the sea," as before. s) and so he gave its fare or passage money, as the Septuagint and Vulgate have it. t) Isaiah 41:10, Psalm 107:23. u) that he might go with them, namely the sailors. Compare the note on Ezekiel 5:1. x) to Tarshish. Jonah <note>the Aramaic Targum</note> says "through the sea," as already mentioned in this verse. y) The Syriac translation: "that he might flee from the sight of the Lord." Jonah <note>the Aramaic Targum</note>: "lest he should prophesy in the name of God," since he foreboded that the Assyrians were being preserved to be the punishment of Israel. Compare chapter 4:2.

Verse 4. z) But the Lord, powerful over all (verse 9), at whose nod the winds and tempests obey (Psalm 135:7, Psalm 148:8), and against whom nothing is secure. a) The Septuagint, Jonah <note>the Aramaic Targum</note>, and the Syriac: "He awakened." The Vulgate and Sanctius: "He sent." As if to say, He cast it in (verses 5, 12, 15; 1 Samuel 18:11, Ezekiel 32:4). b) a vehement wind (1 Kings 19:11, Job 1:19). Compare Luke 8:23, Acts 27:14. c) and a great storm arose in the previously calm sea, namely the Mediterranean (verse 12, Jeremiah 23:19). Compare Psalm 107:25, Matthew 8:24. d) "a great surge" <note>original Greek: κλύדων μέγας</note>. Luke 8:24. d) so that the ship "thought" <note>The Hebrew verb indicates the ship was personified as thinking</note> (Proverbs 24:8). e) to be broken; that is, through metaphor or metonymy, so that the sailors—in fact, all who were in the ship—thought the ship would be broken (Psalm 48:8). f) "it was in danger of being shattered" <note>original Greek: ἐκινδύνευε συντριβῆναι</note>. So the Vulgate. Compare Luke 8:23, 2 Corinthians 1:9.
</margin>

1 Kings 12:9, 10. q. "he fell asleep" <note>original Greek: ἑκοיμήθη</note>. Acts 27:38. Jerome says: "so that they might lighten the fleet from the greatness of the waves." r) Jonah, however, exhausted by cares and travel, and believing himself now secure in the ship, before the storm had descended. Others attribute this to sorrow, comparing Matthew 26:40, 43, 45. m) to the sides; the Vulgate says "to the inner parts." Jonah <note>the Aramaic Targum</note> says "to the bottom-most side." Compare Amos 6:10. n) ship. (1) This term is more commonly used among the Chaldeans <note>Aramaic speakers</note>, Syrians, and Arabs. o) he had reclined, that is, he had settled himself for sleep. Genesis 28:11. p) and he was lulled into a heavy and very deep sleep, sensing nothing yet of the raging storm. (7) verse 6, Judges 4:21, Psalm 76:7, Daniel 8:18, chapter 10:9. Compare Matthew 8:24. Jerome says: "The sleep of the prophet and the very heavy slumber signifies a man numbed by the sleep of error; to whom it had not occurred that he had fled from the face of God, unless his mind, overwhelmed by some folly, was ignorant of God's anger, and he slept as if secure, and his deep sleep sounded like a snore in the ship." The Greek versions say: "How did you sleep and snore?" <note>original Greek: πῶς ἐκάθεוδες καὶ ἔρεγχες</note>. verse 6. q) Matthew 8:25. r) Jonah <note>the Aramaic Targum</note> and Syriac: "the prince of the sailors," that is, the captain. The Greek version says: "bow-man" <note>original Greek: πρωρεύς</note>, the lookout. The Vulgate: "steersman." Compare Ezekiel 27:28, 29. s) why are you overwhelmed or lulled by sleep? verse 5, Proverbs 10:5. The Greek says: "Why do you snore?" <note>original Greek: τί σὺ ῥέγξεις</note>. Why do you snore in the greatest danger? The captain rebukes him for his improvident security, because while the others were in peril, he was snoring securely "on both ears." Compare Luke 22:46. t) compare verse 5. u) 2 Kings 19:4, Zephaniah 2:3. x) He will show himself serene and benevolent. (1) See the root in Jeremiah 5:28. Jonah <note>the Aramaic Targum</note>: "perhaps mercy will be shown from God upon us." The Syriac: "Perhaps God will save us." So also the Greek version: "if perhaps he may save us" <note>original Greek: εἴπως διασώση</note>. Acts 27:44, chapter 28:1. But the Vulgate: "if perhaps he might think of us." The Zurich Bible: "whether perhaps he is about to deliberate concerning us," following Aramaic usage. See Daniel 6:4 and a similar phrase in Psalm 40:18. y) verse 14, Chapter 3:9. Verse 7. z) Finally, when they had tried everything with them in vain, they said one to another. Genesis 11:3. a) come now, Genesis 37:20, 27. b) let us cast lots <note>Leviticus 16:8</note>. The Greek version says: "let us cast lots" <note>original Greek: βάλωμεν κλήρους</note>. Matthew 27:35. c) so that we may know. Judges 18:5. d) on account of whose guilt, or for whom. Thus rightly the Septuagint and Syriac. The Zurich Bible: "for whose sake," i.e., as Rashi <note>a famous 11th-century Jewish commentator</note> explains: "By whose deeds among us?" For what cause? Compare verses 8, 12. Jonah <note>the Aramaic Targum</note>: "Because of what?" Vulgate: "Wherefore?"—though this is less accurate. For they do not only ask about the situation, but also about the person. e) this evil, that is, this misfortune (Amos 3:6), so sudden and unexpected without any previous signs, and clearly supernatural. f) The Jews in the Pirke Eliezer, chapter 10, think this was said with emphasis: "upon *us*," meaning not upon others; because they saw other ships going and returning on both sides without harm, while only their ship was in danger. But Jerome says: "They knew the nature of the sea, and having sailed for so long, they knew the patterns of storms and winds. And certainly, if they had seen the usual waves arise, such as they had sometimes experienced, they would perhaps never have sought the cause of the shipwreck, nor sought to avoid a certain danger through an uncertain method." Compare 1 Samuel 14:38. g) when they therefore cast lots. 1 Samuel 14:42. Abarbanel <note>a 15th-century Jewish scholar</note> concludes from the plural number "lots," or rather from his own conjecture, that the lots were repeated several times or more types of lots were used, and they constantly pointed to Jonah. h) With God directing. Proverbs 16:33. Jerome says: "This fugitive is caught by lot, not by the power of the lots—especially the lots of the pagans—but by the will of Him who directed the uncertain lots." He also says: "Nor should we immediately trust in lots based on this example... since the privileges of individuals cannot create a general law." Verse 8. i) So that they might hold him as one guilty, confessed, and convicted. k) Compare Joshua 7:19. l) Vulgate: "for whose cause?" Kimchi <note>a 12th-century Hebrew scholar</note>: "on account of whom?" But Abarbanel says there are two questions here: 1. "Tell us, in what is the sin, and against whom is the sin committed?" Compare verses 7, 12. m) "What is your work?" that is, what is your business? Abarbanel understands this as the purpose of the journey. As if to say: surely you are not plotting some evil? Compare Exodus 20:9, Proverbs 24:27. n) Isaiah 39:3. o) what is your country? Genesis 30:25, chapter 31:3, 13.

Verse 5. f) They feared therefore and were terrified (verse 10)—the sailors. (4) Ezekiel 27:9, 27, 29. g) compare verse 14, Psalm 107:13. h) Jerome: "The sailors fear, and each one cries out to his god. Ignorant of the truth, they are not ignorant of providence; and under the error of religion, they know that something is to be venerated..."

<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on Jonah Chapter 1. Having established that Jonah was asleep in the ship's hold during a great storm, the narrative now turns to the sailors' interrogation of him and his confession of faith and flight.</meta>

# JONAH. CHAPTER I.

<column-break/>

<margin>p)</margin> From what people or nation are you? 1 Samuel 30:13. 2 Samuel 15:2. Jerome notes: "The brevity is to be noted, which we used to admire in Virgil." — His person, region, journey, and city are questioned, so that the cause of the danger might be known from these details.

Verse 9 <margin>q)</margin> I am a Hebrew. Genesis 14:13, chapter 39:14, chapter 40:15. Thus he expresses his homeland, people, and the place he came from. Compare 2 Corinthians 11:22, Philippians 3:5. Jonah <note>the Aramaic Targum</note>: "I am a worshiper of the Lord." This is in the style of his era.

The Septuagint: <note>original Greek: Ἆλος Κυρίου εἰμὶ ἐγώ</note> "I am a servant of the Lord." This arises from a visual error <note>misreading the Hebrew letters</note> or paraphrastic liberty. So also the Arabic version. <margin>r)</margin> Verse 4. Exodus 15:11. Deuteronomy 28:58.

<margin>s)</margin> Genesis 24:3, 7. Daniel 2:44. Nehemiah 1:4, 5. 2 Chronicles 36:23. Psalm 136:26. <margin>t)</margin> I fear, that is, I worship. The Septuagint: <note>original Greek: σέβομαι</note> "I worship." So also the Arabic. Compare Genesis 42:18, 2 Kings 4:1, Isaiah 29:23, Malachi 1:6. It is as if he says: "Not the gods whom you call upon and who cannot save, but the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land, etc." But Abarbanel <note>a 15th-century Jewish commentator</note> says: that is, I am afraid of or dread Jehovah (compare Genesis 32:12, Daniel 1:10), against whom alone I have sinned and from whom I fled, etc. However, Cocceius <note>a Dutch theologian</note> rightly advises: "I do not know if the fear of God is ever placed as a vice, although some fear is cast out by love, etc." 1 John 4:18, compared with Isaiah 66:2, 33:6. <margin>u)</margin> Genesis 2:4. <margin>x)</margin> That is, this entire universe. Genesis 1:1, 9:10. 2 Kings 19:15. Psalm 95:5. Acts 4:24. By this mark, the true God is usually distinguished from false ones. Compare Jeremiah 10:11, Psalm 96:5. The text adds nothing more here; however, from the following verse it is clear that Jonah, after recounting his nation and religion, added a clear narrative of his mission and his flight; for he frankly confessed everything as it was.
