For he had told them (verse 8), namely that he had sinned against the Lord and had fled from Him. Abarbanel. ->verse 11. d)<- Then they said to him (verse 8), when they had known that he was a Prophet. e) "What then shall we do to you, whom God demands for punishment?" f) "So that the sea may be silent," that is, be quiet (4) verse 12. Psalm 107:30. Which now testifies to the Creator's wrath by its swelling. Jerome. The Septuagint: <note>original Greek: καὶ κοπάσει</note> "and it will cease." Matthew 14:32. g) "from bothering us, from raging against us." Verse 12, 13. h) That is, for the sea was swelling more and more and was storming. Verse 13. Thus everywhere the increase of an action is signified by the verb "to go" among the Hebrews. See Genesis 8:5, 1 Samuel 17:41, 2 Samuel 3:1. ->verse 12. i)<- And he said to them. Not with a heart still hardened against God, as Abarbanel rashly judges—as if he preferred to be merged into the sea rather than follow God's commands—but repentant and acknowledging God's justice. k) "Lift me up." Verse 15. A similar imperative in John 2:19. Jerome: "For it is not our place to snatch death, but to willingly receive it when inflicted by others. Hence in persecutions it is not permitted to perish by one's own hand." l) "and throw me in as an offering to calm the storm." Verse 15. Compare 1 Corinthians 4:13. m) "and the sea will become tranquil." Verse 11. n) as if to say: "Do not doubt this, for by divine instinct I know that, etc." o) The Septuagint, Vulgate, etc.: "on my account." As if to say: "Because of what is in me, or what belongs to me, that is, because of my sin." Compare verse 7, 8. p) "Especially since this storm (verse 4) has come upon you." But what was to happen to him afterward, he seems to have been entirely ignorant of at that time, comparing chapter 2:4 ff. ->verse 13. q)<- However, the men rowed, that is, more vehemently, with all effort and struggle. As if to say: they dug in the sea with oars. For those rowing seem to dig in the water. Hence the expressions among the Latins: *to plow, to furrow, to cut the sea.* Ovid: *We have furrowed the vast water with fragile wood.* For the verb compare Amos 9:2, Job 24:16. The Septuagint: <note>original Greek: παρεβιάזοντο</note> "they used force." Luke 24:29. r) so that they might bring back the ship and Jonah, to avoid throwing him out. Jerome: "The Prophet had brought forth the sentence; but they, hearing he was a worshiper of God, did not dare to lay hands on him, etc." s) chapter 2:11, Genesis 1:9, 10. t) 2 Kings 3:26. Compare note on Exodus 8:14. 2) see verse 11. Compare Isaiah 54:11. ->verse 14. x)<- Therefore they cried out. Compare Psalm 107:28. They had become more religious in their danger. Grotius <note>a Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note>. z) "We pray, Lord!" Chapter 4:2, Isaiah 38:3, Psalm 116:4, 15. a) Genesis 18:8, chapter 18:3, 30, 32, chapter 19:18. b) verse 6, chapter 3:9. c) "for the life of this man," that is, because of the same thing we are about to commit against him. See 2 Samuel 14:7. But according to Jonah: "on account of the sin of this man's life." So compare Leviticus 4:27, Numbers 16:22. d) "and do not lay upon us," that is, do not impute to us (Syriac), Deuteronomy 21:8, or avenge it, Judges 9:24. e) "innocent blood." Deuteronomy 19:10, chapter 27:25. Who otherwise has done nothing wrong to us. Do not therefore punish us as killers of an innocent man. f) "For You, Jehovah, are God Almighty." Verse 9. g) "as You have willed and as You will." h) "so You have done and do." Others, such as the Syriac and Santagnolo <note>S.</note>, translate with two commas: *"For You are the Lord, and just as You will, so You do."* Jerome: as if to say: "We do not wish to kill Your Prophet; but Your wrath he himself has confessed, and the storm speaks. Your will is fulfilled by our hands. — Whatever we have undertaken, the fact that the whirlwind rises, the winds rage, the sea is stirred into waves, the fugitive is betrayed by lot, and he indicates what ought to be done—all this, O Lord, is of Your will: for You have done as You willed." Calovius <note>a Lutheran theologian</note>: "You, Jehovah, have directed this whole matter wonderfully; so that it is certainly necessary that either this man alone, or all of us together with him, perish, etc." Compare Psalm 115:3, Psalm 135:6, 2 Samuel 10:12. ->verse 15. i)<- Thus at last they lifted Jonah. Verse 12. k) and they threw him into the sea. Verse 5. Jerome: "not resisting, but offering his hands to their will." l) "and the sea stood," that is, it ceased or stopped. Verse 10. Compare Genesis 29:35, 2 Kings 4:6. m) from its boiling (Vulgate), from its heat. Isaiah 30:30, Proverbs 19:12. The Septuagint: <note>original Greek: ἐκ τοῦ σάλου αὐתῆς</note> "from its tossing." Luke 21:25. Jerome: "because it had found what it was seeking." Furthermore, the Rabbis in Pirke Eliezer chapter 10, and Abarbanel following them on this passage, tell or invent that the sailors made several more attempts; they first lowered Jonah into the water up to his knees or his navel, and since the sea then became quiet, they took him back; but when the sea rose again, Jonah was submerged up to his neck, and with the sea calmed, he was pulled back into the ship; but when the sea raged once more, Jonah was finally submerged entirely.

<meta>This page marks the transition from the end of Chapter 1, where the sailors offer sacrifices after the storm subsides, to the beginning of Chapter 2, featuring Jonah's famous prayer from the belly of the great fish. The commentary focuses heavily on the biological identity of the "great fish" and the miraculous nature of Jonah's survival.</meta>

# JONAH CAP. 2.

...that it might be able to swallow a man, they are attracted by the name "fish," though some prefer to understand a "cetacean" <note>original: "cetaceum"</note>—that is, a whale-like creature—which by reason of its massive size deserves to be reckoned among the whales. So says Bochart in his *Hierozoicon* <note>A famous 17th-century study of animals in the Bible</note>, part 1, page 52. However, he wishes it to be understood as a "sea-dog" <note>original: "canem marinum"</note>, which is called a *Carcharias* <note>The Great White Shark</note>.
**penultimate stress** <note>original Hebrew: מלעיל (mil'el), a grammatical note on the pronunciation of the word</note>

<column-break/>

16. And the men feared <gloss>a</gloss> the LORD with a great fear; and they offered a sacrifice <gloss>b</gloss> to the LORD and made vows <gloss>c</gloss>.
**CHAPTER II.** 1. And the LORD appointed <gloss>q</gloss> a great fish to swallow Jonah; and Jonah was in the belly of the fish for three days and three nights <gloss>s</gloss>.
2. And Jonah prayed <gloss>x</gloss> to the LORD his God <gloss>z</gloss> from the belly of the fish <gloss>a</gloss>.
3. And he said <gloss>b</gloss>: "I called out of my distress <gloss>d</gloss> to me <gloss>c</gloss> unto the LORD, and He answered me; from the belly of Sheol <note>The underworld or the grave</note> I cried, and You heard my voice <gloss>g</gloss>."
4. "For You cast me <gloss>i</gloss> into the deep, into the heart <gloss>k</gloss> of the seas, and the flood surrounded me; all Your breakers <gloss>n</gloss> and Your waves <gloss>o</gloss> passed over me <gloss>p</gloss>."
5. "And I said <gloss>q</gloss>: 'I am driven out <gloss>r</gloss> from before Your eyes <gloss>s</gloss>; yet <gloss>t</gloss> I will again look toward Your holy temple <gloss>y</gloss>.'"
6. "The waters encompassed me <gloss>x</gloss> even to the soul <gloss>a</gloss>; the deep surrounded me <gloss>b</gloss>; seaweed was wrapped around my head <gloss>e</gloss>."
7. "To the roots <gloss>f</gloss> of the mountains I went down; the earth with its bars <gloss>k</gloss> was around me forever..."

The name comes from the roughness and sharpness of its teeth; or it is called *Lamista* or *Lamna* **from having a great throat** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔχειν μέγαν λαιμὸν</note>, that is, an enormous gullet. Among these, as Aelian reports in his *History*, book 8, some are of such great size that they are rightly counted among the strongest whales. Rondelet writes that he saw a medium-sized one on the shore of Saintongue which did not exceed a thousand pounds in weight, yet had a gullet so wide that it could have taken in even a fat man. This adds credibility to Petrus Gillius, who reports that at Nice and Marseille, "lamias" <note>sharks</note> of 4,000 pounds were caught, in whose bellies whole armored men were found. These are the words of Bochart in the place cited. **s)** "to swallow Jonah." Compare Matthew 28:4. **s)** See verse 2, Ruth 1:11, Psalm 23:15. Just as Christ was in the tomb (Matthew 12:40), of whom Jonah bore a type <note>a prophetic symbol</note> (chapter 16:4; Luke 11:29, 30). Hence Augustine says in *The City of God*, book 18, chapter 30: "Jonah prophesied Christ not so much by his speech as by his peculiar suffering, certainly more clearly than if he had cried out His death and resurrection with his voice." etc. **t)** Interpreters observe several miracles here: 1) that the belly of the beast did not consume Jonah like other food, 2) that it allowed him to breathe, 3) that he was not killed by its stench and foulness, and 4) that it left him in possession not only of his life but of his mind. "I am not unaware," says Jerome, "that there will be some to whom it seems incredible that a man could be preserved for three days and nights in the belly of a whale, where shipwrecks are digested." These critics are either believers or unbelievers. If believers, they are compelled to believe much greater things: how the three boys sent into the furnace of raging fire were so unharmed that not even their clothes were touched by the flame (Daniel 3:27). How the sea receded and stood rigid like walls on either side to provide a way for the people crossing (Exodus 14:22). How, by human reasoning, the fury of the lions, despite their increased hunger, looked upon their prey with fear and did not touch it (Daniel 6:23), and many such things. Abarbanel <note>a Jewish commentator</note> advises almost the same, adding: "For behold, we see with our own eyes that a fetus or embryo subsists in the mother's womb for nine months without food or drink, without breathing or waste. Who could prevent God from doing the same for Jonah? For Divine power is above nature, and its force is greater than nature’s." **u)** Verse 2. **x)** "And Jonah prayed." **y)** Like the sailors in chapter 1:14. **z)** "His God," according to the covenant of grace and by faith. Jerome: "We understand that after he felt himself safe in the whale's belly, he did not despair of the Lord's mercy and turned entirely to prayer." Compare verse 7, chapter 1:9. **a)** "From the internal organs of that fish" (verse 1). "Every place serves as a temple," says Grotius. Compare the note on verse 8.

**Verse 3. b)** 5. "To have said." He also wrote later in this book the sighs or groans he uttered then in the belly of the fish to this effect. Hence he more often uses past tense verbs here. **c)** "He invaded the Lord" (Psalm 118:5), more in heart than with the mouth (Exodus 14:15). **d)** "Out of my distress," that is, which was upon me or pressed me from every side. Compare the cited place and Psalm 4:2, 120:1, 130:1. **e)** Psalm 3:5; compare Psalm 18:6, 31:4. **f)** Jerome: "I understand the 'belly of hell' <note>Sheol</note> to be the belly of the whale, which was to him like a tomb or the underworld." Verse 2; compare Psalm 18:6, 116:3, Job 7:9, 15, Amos 2:6, and the note on Ecclesiastes 38:10. Jonah speaks of the lowest abyss. **g)** Isaiah 58:9, Psalm 28:2. **h)** Psalm 31:23. Jonah: "And You granted my request." Abarbanel acts foolishly, thinking himself wiser than others, when he takes this to refer to the boy Jonah being raised by Elijah, as he supposes. Compare the note on chapter 1:1. **Verse 4. i)** That is, "You had indeed cast me" (through the sailors, chapter 1:15) into the deep (Exodus 15:5, Micah 7:19). **k)** "Into the heart," that is, the middle of the seas; into the high sea. Compare Exodus 15:8, 2 Samuel 18:14, Jeremiah 51:1, Ezekiel 27:4, 25, Psalm 46:3. **l)** "And the flow of the sea." Compare Psalm 93:3. It seems to refer to the course of the sea water, tending rapidly in a certain part. Onkelos <note>The Aramaic translator</note> page 498. **m)** "It was surrounding, encircling me on every side." Verse 6; compare Psalm 88:18. **n)** "All the floods," Vulgate: "all your whirlpools." Jonah: "all the storms of the sea and its waves." 2 Samuel 22:5, Psalm 88:8. **o)** "And your waves" (Isaiah 48:18), when mountains of water roll. **p)** Psalm 42:8, Isaiah 8:8. Jerome: "As far as the person of Jonah is concerned, the interpretation is not difficult. As far as the Lord Savior is concerned..." compare Psalm 69:2 and following, Psalm 89:39, etc. **Verse 5. q)** That is, "So much so that I said," or "I thought to myself." Compare Isaiah 38:11. **r)** Vulgate: "I am cast out" or "expelled." Syriac: "I am moved far away." Compare Exodus 34:11, Hosea 9:15. Greek: **rejected**, like a castaway. Romans 11:1, 2. **s)** "From the sight of Your eyes." Psalm 31:23, 33:18, 34:16. Jonah: "From the sight of Your face." Grotius: "Far from the land of Israel." Others more correctly: "From Your fatherly care, providence, and grace, so that I must perish forever." Compare 1 Samuel 26:20, Isaiah 1:16, Jeremiah 40:4, Psalm 31:8. **t)** Vulgate: "Nevertheless" or "But yet." The particle *ak* <note>Hebrew: אך</note> refers to the struggle of faith attacking and overcoming desperation. Compare Psalm 73:1, Hosea 12:9, Lamentations 2:16. **u)** That is, "I will add to look," i.e., I will do so again. Vulgate: "I shall see again." Compare Exodus 11:29, etc. **x)** "Toward." Similar construction in Exodus 3:6, Numbers 21:9, Psalm 34:6, etc. **y)** "Where I shall openly give You thanks." Compare verse 10, Isaiah 38:20, Psalm 5:8. **Verse 6. x)** "The waters surrounded me." **y)** 2 Samuel 22:5, Psalm 18:5. **a)** That is, to the ultimate crisis of life, as if about to shut in his spirit soon. Psalm 69:2, 3. Jonah: "Even unto death." **b)** "The abyss," and the huge vortex of the sea into which the fish snatched me. Genesis 1,:2, 7:11, Psalm 33:7. **c)** Vulgate: "It hedged me in," enclosed in a most troublesome prison. Verse 4; compare Ezekiel 15:5. **d)** "Seaweed" (Exodus 2:3, 5; Isaiah 19:6) swallowed by the fish. Grotius: "Which is plentiful in such deep places." And others: "It grows at the bottom of the sea or on the shores." From its abundance, even the "sea of weeds" <note>the Red Sea</note> is named. See Bochart, *Sacred Geography*, page 320. **e)** "It was bound" or "entangled with other filth" to my head. Exodus 29:9, Ezekiel 16:10. For seaweed is accustomed to be wrapped and bound around those swimming and submerged. But others think this happened in the belly of the fish. Others say the Prophet speaks metaphorically, that he was so submerged that he could not swim out: because there is no hope of emerging if one is entangled in weeds in the deep. Thus the Syriac: "and my head was enclosed in the bottom" or "the deep of the sea." **Verse 7. f)** "To the cuttings." Vulgate: "to the extremes." Syriac: "to the bottom." Jonah and the Masorah: "to the roots." That is, to the cuttings, namely the broken and abrupt roots, or to the cut-off peaks of the mountains. **g)** 1 Kings 6:25, 7:37. **g)** "Of the mountains," that is, of the rocks in the sea, among which are the deepest waters. Compare 2 Samuel 22:16. Grotius: "To the sea caves under the mountains: for much of the sea goes under the land." "Through hidden passages the sea is received and hidden," says Seneca. **h)** "I went down," or "I had descended," as the fish penetrated to the bottom with me. **i)** Vulgate: "the bars of the earth." Or: "as pertains to the earth." Just as we read in Exodus 15:12: "the earth swallowed them." Because the sea, which had swallowed the Egyptians and Jonah, is in the abysses of the earth. **k)** "Bars," bolts and obstacles to it (Jeremiah 51:30). **l)** "They were around me, they stood in my way." Vulgate: "they enclosed me." Genesis 7:16, 2 Kings 4:4.

---

Verse 16. **And they sacrificed** with the accent *Merca*... Verse 2. **Chapter II, verse 2**... **Chapter II** begins here in some versions... Verse 3. **My voice** with *Dagesh*...

<column-break/>

v. 16. **a)** They feared even more than in verse 10, and were confirmed in their recognition of the True God. Compare Matthew 8:27. **b)** Commonly: "and they sacrificed victims." These they certainly did not have literally in the midst of the waves; but because "the sacrifice of God is a broken spirit" (Psalm 51:19), as Jerome says, following Psalm 50:14 and Hosea 14:3. Others understand that they did so after they had left the ship. Osander: "after they had again reached the Holy Land." Jonah: "And they said they would perform a sacrifice before the Lord." Compare chapter 3:10, Psalm 107:23, and Psalm 50:23. **c)** And they made other vows. Compare Genesis 28:20, Psalm 76:12. Osander: "For while they were still sailing, they had vowed that they wished to show themselves grateful by the offering of victims in Jerusalem to the true God, the creator of heaven and earth, if they reached port safely."

---

**CHAPTER II, verse 1. q)** "He had provided" or "destined." Vulgate: "And He prepared." Chapter 4:6, 7, 8; Daniel 1:10; Job 7:3. Arabic: **He ordained**. Matthew 3:24, chapter 31:6. That is, as Jerome says, "He made it come next to the ship so that it might receive the falling Jonah into its embrace." And it should be noted that where destruction was expected, there was protection. There are three parts to this chapter: I. The swallowing of Jonah (v. 1), II. his prayers (v. 2–10), and III. his ejection onto dry land (v. 11). **r)** "A great fish." (The same fish is also indicated by the feminine ending in verse 2, compared with verse 11, contrary to Rabbi Solomon's dream.) So Jonah and the Syriac. But the Septuagint: **a great whale** <note>original Greek: κῆτος μεγάλο</note>, and soon **in the belly of the whale**, as in Matthew 12:40. Hence the more common opinion is that this fish was a whale or a "cete" properly speaking. See Pfeffer's *Vexed Doubts* on this passage. But since the throat passages of the immense "cete" or whale are too narrow for a whole man...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Book of Jonah, concluding the prayer of Jonah in the belly of the fish (Chapter 2) and beginning his second commission to the city of Nineveh (Chapter 3). The translator notes that the focus shifts from Jonah’s internal spiritual state to his external obedience and the sheer scale of Nineveh.</meta>

# JONAH. CHAPTERS 2 & 3. . . . .

m) forever. As if I were never to escape and return to the land of the living. compare Psalm 9:6. *) Syriac: "nevertheless You pulled me out," or "nonetheless You caused me to ascend," or "You brought me back." Vulgate: "and You will save." compare Psalm 40:3. o) from the pit. Syriac and S. <note>likely standing for the Spanish or another version</note>: "from the ditch." Vulgate: "from corruption." Likely a place where death was most imminently threatening, and I was, as it were, buried alive. compare Job 9:31, 17:14, 33:18, 22, 24, 28, 30. Regarding the prefigurement of Christ, see Psalm 16:10. p) my life. Psalm 103:4. Jerome: "Because he who was in the belly of the whale, according to the nature of bodies, ought to have decayed and become food for the beast, being diffused through its veins and limbs, yet he remained safe and whole." q) Jerome: "When he adds, 'O LORD my God' (or 'my God'), it is an expression of coaxing affection; though God is the God of all, by the greatness of the benefit Jonah felt Him to be his own, and specifically his God." compare the note on verse 2 and Romans 8:15.

note on verse 3. * . 9. y) Those who stubbornly observe and studiously worship. *Piel* <note>a Hebrew verb form indicating intensive action</note> (1) Jerome: "Those who have passed into the affection of the heart: who not only do, but so keep vanities as if they loved them, and think they have found a treasure." Kimchi <note>a medieval rabbi and grammarian</note> understands this of the sailors in chapter 1:16, who later relapsed into their impiety; Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> of the idolatrous nations; Abarbanel of the Ninevites, who would not long persevere in their repentance (compare note on chapter 3:8). But why not also of the impious Israelites, too addicted to idolatrous worship and the vanities of the world? compare Hosea 4:10, Micah 6:16, and the Preface to Hosea, section 4. z) vanities of nothingness, i.e., vain and empty idols. Syriac: "false deities." Hosea 10:4, Psalm 31:7. Septuagint: "vain and false things." compare Acts 14:15. a) their piety. Ephesians 4:6, Jeremiah 2:2, Hosea 6:4, Nehemiah 13:14. Or it refers to the grace and mercy shown to them by God; or as Jerome says, "We can understand God Himself, who is the fountain of kindness and all good things, from whom grace and benefits are bestowed." compare Psalm 144:2. Syriac, with a change of the suffix: "they abandon Your mercy." b) compare Genesis 24:27, Ruth 2:20, or Isaiah 1:4, Jeremiah 1:16, 16:17, Hosea 4:10. Jonah: Not like the idolatrous nations, who do not know from whence their benefit is conferred. Jerome: "This can be prophesied from the person of the Lord concerning the perfidy of the Jews, who, while they think they are keeping the precepts of men and the commands of the Pharisees, which are vanity and a lie, have forsaken God, who had always had mercy on them." verse 10. c) "But I, indeed," having been delivered from such great danger. d) "with a voice of praise," perhaps "of thanksgiving." Jonah: in the praise of confession. Psalm 26:7, 42:5, 50:14, 23. Septuagint uses a double expression: "But I, with a voice of praise and confession, will sacrifice to You." compare Hebrews 13:15 and above, chapter 1:2 note. e) "I will sacrifice," Vulgate: "I will immolate to You." Grotius: namely, victims owed for such a cause, according to the law in Leviticus 7:12, 13. compare above, chapter 1:16. But Abarbanel: "victims of praise and obedience." compare 1 Samuel 15:22; add Romans 12:1. f) Septuagint and Vulgate: "whatever I have vowed." Syriac: "and what I vowed." compare chapter 1:16. g) "I will return," or "pay in full." Abarbanel: "The obedience which I promised, I will perform; nor will I flee again." compare Psalm 76:12, 116:18. h) For salvation itself and in every form (of soul and body) belongs to Jehovah: who snatched me from such a death (2 Corinthians 1:10) and will save me eternally. Psalm 68:21, compare Psalm 3:9, Revelation 7:10, 19:1. The "He" suffix intensifies the meaning, as in Hosea 8:7, Psalm 44:27. verse 11. i) "He spoke," indeed; Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic: "He commanded" (from the meaning of the Arabic root) "the Lord commanded the fish." Abarbanel: i.e., He stirred it up so that it would go to the shore. For God is said to command even brute animals, as in Amos 9:3, 2 Chronicles 7:13; see note on 1 Kings 17:4 and compare Psalm 33:9. k) "And by the command of God, it vomited." Septuagint and Arabic: "it cast out." Syriac: "it set him out safe and unharmed." S.: "that it might spit out Jonah." Proverbs 23:8. l) "onto the dry land," chapter 1:13. But where, or on what shore he was set out, can only be said through conjectures. Sulpicius is mistaken in thinking he was cast out on the shores of the Ninevites; nor does Josephus deserve more trust, who in Book 9, chapter 11, relates that he was removed from the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>; as Bochart proved against him in *Hierozoicon* II, page 744 following. It is more credible, therefore, if we think him returned to the land of Palestine, or at least Phoenicia or Syria. compare chapter 3:2, 3. CHAPTER III, 1. m) S.: "Then it happened," etc. chapter 1:1. n) either in that place where he had been set out (chapter 2:11), when he had breathed a little from his labor; or when he had returned his vows in Jerusalem (chapter 2:10). o) "a second time," or "for the second occasion." Genesis 22:15. Because his first calling had become void to that extent; and Jonah could have doubted whether he still had to go to Nineveh. There are four parts to this chapter: I. The repeated calling of Jonah and the command of God, verses 1–2. II. Jonah’s obedience and his preaching in Nineveh, verses 3–4. III. The effect of this: the repentance of the Ninevites, verses 5–9. IV. The consequence: God’s indulgence and the preservation of the Ninevites, verse 10. verse 2. p) see chapter 1:2. q) see verse 3 and note on chapter 1:2. r) or "preach against it." chapter 1:2. s) Vulgate: "the preaching," or "sermon." Septuagint: "the proclamation" (the gospel) Matthew 12:41. t) Vulgate: "which I speak." Septuagint: "what I have spoken." Others: "what I am about to speak to you." namely, that their malice has ascended into My sight, and that accordingly, after 40 days, Nineveh is to be overturned. compare verse 4 and chapter 1:2. compare also Exodus 6:29, Jeremiah 1:7, 17. verse 3. u) as in chapter 1:2, but now with a different mind. x) Jeremiah 13:2. y) verse 1, chapter 1:2. z) "great to God." So S. Tig. Septuagint and Syriac, etc. which the Vulgate wrongly omitted. Jonah: "before the Lord." That is, truly the greatest, so that by God Himself—who sees all things and whose judgment cannot be deceived—this city, compared to others, was judged to be great, as one to which He Himself had given such great growth above others, and which was a care to God even because of the multitude of so many souls. compare below chapter 4:11 and Jeremiah 22:6. Similarly in Acts 7:20, a child is said to be "fair to God," who by the favor of God was such; as in 2 Corinthians 10:4, "weapons powerful to God," which He Himself made strong, etc. The Jews commonly refer this only to intensification, as if to say "a much greater city," compare Psalm 36:7, 80:11, etc. But Glassius in *Philologia Sacra*, pages 593 and 595, following Blessed Luther, correctly advised that in all those instances, the added name of God properly and formally denotes the efficient cause, and consequently only an intensive meaning. compare Bochart *Geographia Sacra* page 258 and 284; Gussetius *Lexicon* page 67; and Pfeiffer *Dubia Vexata* <note>Difficult Questions</note> on this passage and following. a) "of a journey," verse 4, Ezekiel 42:4, Nehemiah 2:6. b) Jerome: "It was of such a circumference that it could scarcely be circled in a three-day journey." Thus also Abraham ibn Ezra, Cyril, and Theodoret correctly explain this of the circumference, whereas Abarbanel wrongly contends on this passage that it should be understood of the diameter, or from gate to gate. But the size of a city is estimated especially from its circumference, not from its length alone; to say nothing of other points against Abarbanel’s opinion. compare the note above to chapter 1:2 and regarding these things, Pfeiffer *Dubia Vexata*. verse 4. c) "When, however, Jonah had begun to enter into the city." Genesis 9:20, 2 Chronicles 3:1, 2. d) Grotius: "walking through the city as much as was permitted in one day." compare verse 3.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Book of Jonah. Having survived the Great Fish, Jonah now fulfills his mission to Nineveh. The text explores the city's reaction, the king's decree of repentance, and the linguistic nuances between the Hebrew and Greek versions of the story.</meta>

# CHAPTER 3. JONAH 3.

<margin>
**must be turned:** compare 1 Samuel 10:6, Lamentations 1:20. <note>The Latin 'conuertenda' implies either a spiritual conversion or a physical overturning/destruction.</note> Or it is to be overthrown by divine judgment; but this is argued more with cleverness than with solid reasoning, and does not suit the simplicity of the Scripture: therefore we purposely omit more such clever arguments.

**v. 5. g)** The Ninevites immediately believed in God at that preaching of Jonah in verse 4. **Septuagint.** <note>The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>
</margin>

<gloss>e</gloss> 4 And he said: "Still <gloss>e : f : h</gloss> forty days, and Nineveh <gloss>f</gloss> shall be overthrown."
<gloss>g</gloss> 5 And the men of <gloss>h</gloss> Nineveh <gloss>i</gloss> believed in God; and they proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them <gloss>k</gloss> even to the least of them. <gloss>l</gloss> 6 For the word reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose <gloss>m</gloss> from his throne, <gloss>n</gloss> and he laid aside his robe from him, <gloss>o</gloss> and covered himself with sackcloth, <gloss>p</gloss> and sat in the ashes. <gloss>q</gloss> 7 And he caused it to be proclaimed <gloss>r</gloss> and published through Nineveh <gloss>s</gloss> by the decree of the king <gloss>t</gloss> and his nobles, saying: "Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, <gloss>u</gloss> taste anything; <gloss>x</gloss> let them not feed, <gloss>y</gloss> nor drink water. <gloss>z</gloss> 8 But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, <gloss>a</gloss> and cry mightily unto God; <gloss>b</gloss> let everyone turn from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands. <gloss>c</gloss> 9 Who knows <gloss>d</gloss> if God will turn <gloss>e</gloss> and repent, <gloss>f</gloss> and turn away?"

---

In God. Jonah in the Word of the Lord. Being conscious of their own heavy crimes, they applied faith to Jonah's words without hesitation, and without him needing to perform miracles. *Exodus 14:31, Psalm 106:12.* For behold, says *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a famous 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note>, a sign or wonder is not required from a Prophet if he only commands and warns concerning the observation of the law and the exercise of what is good and right; for we ought to hear such things from the mouth of any wise man. But if he commands the violation of some divine precept for some extraordinary act in the name of the Lord (idolatry excepted), then he must produce signs for the confirmation of his prophecy. compare the note on *Deuteronomy 18:22.* Jerome: "Nineveh believed, and Israel remains unbelieving; the uncircumcised believed, and the circumcision remains unfaithful." compare *Ezekiel 3:6, Matthew 12:41, chapter 21:43, Luke 11:31, Acts 13:45.* Moreover, they believed with a true and saving faith, which was the source and root of all the following good works. *Romans 14:23, Hebrews 11:6.* — **The Ninevites** (or perhaps others) at the command of Nineveh, narrated the deeds of Jonah; while we do not entirely deny this because of the passage in *Luke 11:30*, yet we do not concede that they would not have believed without that miracle, says *Pfeiffer* <note>August Pfeiffer, a 17th-century German theologian</note> on this passage. compare *Isaiah 55:11, Romans 1, 16, Hebrews 4, 12.* **h)** as a sign of their grief and penitence, the King and his nobles **v. 6. proclaimed a fast**, that is, they publicly announced it. *Joel 1:14, 1 Kings 21:9. i)* Vulgate: *and they were clothed in sackcloth v. 6. 8. 2 Samuel 3:31, 1 Kings 20:32, chapter 21:27, 2 Kings 19:1, Esther 4:1.* In this way, the luxury and ambition of the Assyrians were fittingly corrected; things by which they had also greatly offended God. **k)** that is, the great and the small: the highest and the lowest. *Jeremiah 6:13, chapter 31:34, Revelation 19:5, 18, etc.*

**v. 6. l)** For when that word had arrived, that is, the proclamation of Jonah in verse 4. compare *Judges 20:34, Esther 9:1, Daniel 9:21.* Grotius: "He gives the reason for the proclaimed fast and explains the manner." Pfeiffer: "It is possible that the report of this deadly prophecy was brought to the King, so that he might summon Jonah to hear him in person; even if this is not mentioned in this brief history." **m)** to the King of Nineveh. Probably *Phul (2 Kings 15:19, 1 Chronicles 5:26)* or others say *Sardanapalus.* **n)** he rose up from his throne. compare *Isaiah 47:1, 2 Samuel 13:31.* **o)** and he removed, he laid aside. Vulgate: *he cast it from him. 1 Kings 15:12, Ecclesiastes 11:10.* **p)** his royal robe *Joshua 7:21*, so that he might equal the others in mourning. Jonah: "instruments of his glory," or "garments." Syriac: *his diadem.* compare *Ezekiel 26:16.* **q)** Vulgate: *and was clothed with sackcloth.* And he drew on sackcloth, verses 3, 8. **r)** and sat in the ashes. compare *Isaiah 47:1, Ezekiel 26:16, Job 2:8, chapter 42:6, Esther 4:3.* <term>upon the ashes</term> <note>original Greek: epi spodo</note>. *Matthew 11:21.*

**v. 7. q)** And he ordered it to be proclaimed. compare *Joel 2:15.* **r)** and he announced through heralds in the whole city. <term>that which was both preached and spoken</term> <note>original Greek: ho kai ekerychthe kai errethe</note>. **u)** by the opinion, from the decree or command of the King. *Proverbs 26:16, Daniel 3:10, 29, Ezra 6:14.* **x)** and of the nobles, Vulgate: *and of the princes,* Abarbanel: *and of his counselors.* *2 Kings 10:11, Nahum 3:10. compare Esther 1:19, 21. that which was also from his great ones* <note>original Greek: ho kai para ton megistanon autou</note>. *Mark 6:21.* **y)** men, who had properly offended God with their crimes. **z)** and the beasts, which would also have perished in the destruction of the whole city *chapter 4, 11.* **a)** let them not taste anything *1 Samuel 14:24*, to testify to the heaviest mourning *2 Samuel 3:35.* **b)** let the beasts not be pastured, namely, the herds and flocks *Exodus 34:3.* **c)** and let neither men nor cattle drink water. *1 Kings 13:9. compare the note on 1 Samuel 7:6.* So that even by the sight and the cry of the mute animals (verse 8), men might be more moved to serious repentance and sorrow. Thus Virgil, concerning the bitter mourning for the death of Caesar, *Eclogue 5, verse 24 and following: In those days, Daphnis, no one drove the fed oxen to the cool rivers; no quadruped either sipped from the stream or touched a blade of grass. etc.*

**v. 8. d)** But let them be covered with sackcloth. *verses 5, 6, 2 Kings 19:1, 2, Joel 1:14.* These things still pertain to the King's command, as the Hebrew text and other versions show; but not to its execution, as the Septuagint rendered it: <term>and they clothed themselves and went up</term> <note>original Greek: kai periebalonto kai anebesan</note>. **e)** men and beasts. **v. 7.** Moreover, they seem to mean (as the Interpreters observe) horses, mules, and camels, which are usually adorned with precious coverings. These being pulled off, they imposed cheap ones: as today, just as in the past, according to Chrysostom, in the funerals of Nobles, the noble horses that the deceased used are dressed in black cloth, so that they may seem to mourn at the same time. **f)** and let both men and beasts cry out, the latter driven by hunger and thirst. compare *Joel 1:18, Psalm 147:9.* **g)** to God Jehovah, whose anger Jonah was denouncing. **h)** with vehemence or with all their strength. strongly. *Judges 8:1.* <term>earnestly</term> <note>original Greek: ektenos</note>. *Luke 22:44, Acts 12:5, 1 Peter 1:22.* Syriac: *with groaning.* M. I.: *with the whole heart.* S.: *with powerful devotion etc.* as if they were about to break through the clouds with the great force of their cry. *Sirach 35:17, Matthew 11:12, Luke 11:8.* **i)** Jerome: *and, having condemned their former vices, let them devote themselves entirely to repentance.* **k)** each one *Joel 2:7. l)* so that he may strip off the habit of sinning. *verse 10, Jeremiah 25:5, chapter 36:3, 7.* **m)** and the violence *Genesis 6:11, 13, Habakkuk 1:2, Psalm 58:3.* **n)** which is in their hands *Isaiah 59:6, Psalm 7, 4, Job 16:17. compare Isaiah 1, 15, 16.*

**v. 9. o)** Who knows, God will turn from his anger, if we turn from our sins. *Zechariah 1:3.* Septuagint, Vulgate, & Syriac: *Who knows if he will be turned; that is, before he himself changes his sentence and is reconciled to us.* compare *2 Samuel 12:22, Esther 4:14. Jonah (whom Abarbanel and others follow) here again, as in Joel 2:14 where see the note.* **p)** and let it repent God, that is, as the Vulgate has it, *and may God forgive.* **q)** (according to the Syriac) *let him have mercy on us. see verse 10, chapter 4, 2, Daniel 4, 24.* compare *Numbers 23:19 and the note on 1 Samuel 15:11, Jeremiah 18:8.*

<column-break/>

**e)** yet forty days, or after forty days yet. compare regarding the construction *Jeremiah 51:33, Hosea 1:4.* But the **Septuagint** wrongly changed this number of forty days into three days, writing thus: <term>yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown</term> <note>original Greek: eti treis hemerai, kai Nineue katastraphesesetai</note>, and they were followed by the Arabic version, Sulpicius Severus, and certain Fathers; as Bochart shows in *Hieroz. II. page 746.* However, Abarbanel, in his Commentary on this passage (folio 159, column 2 and 3), takes the particle **עוֹד** <note>Hebrew 'od', meaning 'yet' or 'still'</note> numerically for 80, and from these and the 40 days (which he considers as years, comparing *Leviticus 25:29*), he calculates 120 years until the destruction of Nineveh (for which he would have undertaken *A.I. Lib. IX. chapter 11. numbers 15 years*) according to the prophecy of Nahum and the *Seder Olam* <note>A 2nd-century Hebrew language chronology</note> in the first year of Nebuchadnezzar. **f)** Nineveh shall be overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah, because of similar crimes. *Genesis 19:21, 25, 29, Jeremiah 20:16, Amos 4:11.* Namely, if you continue to sin and do not extinguish the anger of God within this time by serious repentance and faith. compare *Jeremiah 18:8.*

**8. For such promises and threats, which are not absolute predictions, always involve this condition; although this condition was not expressed by the Prophet, or was even ignored.** compare *Genesis 20:3, 7, Ezekiel 18:1* and Gerlavi *Theol. Proph. page 12.* Cocceius: "The sense of this saying is: forty days are granted to the Ninevites for repentance." Thus the flood was denounced to the first world for 120 years. *Genesis 6:3.* He who went and preached to the first world in Noah *1 Peter 3:18, 19*, here preached through Jonah <term>in repentance</term> <note>original Greek: metanoia</note>.

**&c. Abarbanel wished to remove the apparent difficulty in another way, as if the Prophet had said: Nineveh must necessarily be changed within 40 days either through repentance or destruction.**

decreed by God to be spared, not because of their false religion or idolatry, but only because of the violence of their hands; from which, when they turned away, God also changed His mind; even though they did not cease from their [false] faith and perverse religion. But those who attribute true repentance to them feel more correctly altogether: even if, without a doubt, they did not persist in it for long, but relapsed into their former vices, security, and idolatry, they finally brought upon themselves the destruction which Nahum later prophesied. For they are said, as **Pfeiffer** observes on this location, to have believed in God (v. 5), whom the King also commanded to be called upon (v. 8). Therefore, they renounced idols, and had contrition for their sins, and faith in God, and produced worthy fruits of repentance. <note>Matthew 3:8.</note> Furthermore, the Savior expressly says they repented at the preaching of Jonah. <note>Matthew 12:41.</note> Unless they had received the grace of God known in Christ from this preaching, they could neither have believed in God for salvation, nor produced works pleasing to God. <note>Compare Jeremiah 5:3, Habakkuk 2:4, Romans 5:1, 14:23.</note> Nor are other examples lacking in the Scriptures where similarly true and serious repentance, though well-begun, was nevertheless not constant or continued. <note>See concerning Ahab, 1 Kings 21:27, 29; concerning Jehoash, 2 Kings 6:30; concerning Josiah, chapter 13, 14, etc.; concerning Jehu, 2 Kings 10:31.</note> Nevertheless, (says **Bochart** in the cited place) this fast, proclaimed by the Ninevites to turn away the anger of the Supreme Deity, the edict of Darius (Daniel 6:15, etc.), and another similar one by Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3:29), and others of this kind, were so many preparations for the conversion of the nations which followed the coming of Christ. For thus, little by little, and as if by degrees, the power and greatness of God became known even to those peoples who were strangers to the commonwealth of the Israelites, and who used to say with Pharaoh: "Who is the Lord, that we should obey him? We do not know the Lord." <note>Exodus 5:2.</note>

**CHAPTER IV. v. 1.** **a) But this was painful.** **Tigurine Bible:** It grieved Jonah. <note>Greek: ho lypē</note> as in Mark 10:22. **Abarbanel** thinks that in addition to the distress of his soul, Jonah even fell into a sickness or fever. But the Hebrew phrase signifies a mind badly affected, whether from just or unjust grief. <note>See Genesis 21:11, 12; 38:10; 2 Samuel 11:27; Nehemiah 13:8, etc.</note> **b) with greatest distress.** <note>Nehemiah 3:10.</note> **c) indeed, out of impatience and grief, anger also burned in him.** <note>v. 4, Genesis 4:5, 6; 30:2, 1 Samuel 15:11.</note> **Abarbanel:** Because he foresaw in his mind the evil that was to come upon the Israelites through the Assyrians. **Jerome:** Seeing a multitude of Gentiles entering in, and that verse being fulfilled <note>Deuteronomy 32:21</note>, he despairs for the safety of Israel, and is shaken with great grief, which breaks out into his voice, and he explains the causes of his sorrow, saying in a way: "Am I the only one chosen from such a number of Prophets to announce the ruin of my own people through the safety of others?" Therefore, he is not saddened, as some think, because the multitude of nations is saved, but because Israel perishes. **Pfeiffer:** Jonah is wrongly angry—not at God, for he would otherwise be extremely impious—but partly at the Ninevites because they were spared <note>compare v. 11</note>, and partly at himself, who had undertaken this mission. Jonah surely thought that God's decree concerning the temporal destruction of Nineveh was absolute, and would entirely follow, even if they performed the greatest repentance and were eternally saved. But when the defined time had passed and he saw Nineveh was not overturned, he was indignant that he had been the instrument of his own people's disgrace and loss, to whom he would now return hated and infamous, because he saved the Assyrians with his sermon—the very ones who would one day be armed against his people. <note>Compare Isaiah 10:5.</note> Nor did he fail to suspect that there would be those among his own who would translate him as a false prophet. <note>Compare Deuteronomy 18:22.</note> Truly, this chapter contains a twin dialogue between God and Jonah; and thus we must observe: I. Jonah’s indignation and complaint (v. 1-3) and God’s rebuke (v. 4). II. After Jonah’s exit from the city (v. 5), the birth and death of the plant (v. 6-7), hence Jonah’s impatience and wicked demand (v. 8), and God’s response and the conviction of Jonah (v. 9 onwards). **v. 2.** **d) Wherefore he prayed to the Lord** (chapter 2:2), but out of zeal, yet not according to knowledge; and not knowing what he asked. <note>Matthew 20:22.</note> **e) Vulgate:** I beseech thee, Lord! <note>chapter 1:14.</note> **f) Is this not my word, which I spoke and thought?** <note>Exodus 14:12.</note> **g) and now, and back to that time when I still was.** <note>Job 1:18.</note> **h) in my land and country.** <note>Compare chapter 1:8, Deuteronomy 12:19.</note> That is: My mind presaged this outcome of my sermon. **i) therefore I anticipated** <note>Psalm 119:147.</note> **k) Vulgate:** to flee to Tarshish <note>chapter 1:3.</note> **Syriac:** I hastened the flight. So that I might avoid this troublesome duty and its inconveniences. **l) Jerome:** For I knew you would do this. I was not ignorant that you are merciful, and for that reason I did not want to announce something severe and grim. **m)** See Exodus 34:6, Nehemiah 9:17. <note>Greek: eleēmōn kai oiktirmōn</note> **merciful and compassionate.** <note>Luke 6:36.</note> **n) long-suffering.** **Vulgate:** patient. <note>Numbers 14:18, Joel 2:13, Nahum 1:3.</note> <note>Greek: makrothymos</note>. <note>Compare Romans 9:22.</note> **o) great in grace.** **Vulgate:** and of much mercy. <note>Psalm 86:5.</note> <note>Greek: polyeleos</note>. <note>Compare 1 Peter 1:3.</note> **p)** Chapter 3:9, 10; Joel 2:13. **v. 3.** **q)** <note>Greek: Kai nyn despota Kyrie</note> **And now, Lord Master.** <note>Luke 2:29.</note> **Abarbanel:** That is: since you exercise clemency and long-suffering toward the Assyrians, so that they may come upon the land of Israel, my country, to devastate it. **r) is a circumlocution for death**, as in 1 Kings 19:4, but here it is the vow of an impatient soul. **s) Vulgate:** because death is better for me than life, v. 8. That is: It is better to die than to live like this. **Abarbanel:** That is: let me not see the evil that will find my people, and the destruction of my kindred (Esther 8:6) in the devastation of the tribes. **v. 4.** **t) But Jehovah said;** about to kindly lead back the one wandering too far. **u) Does anger burn well in you?** v. 9, etc. as **Symmachus** has it, "Have you burned justly?" So the **Vulgate**. That is: Surely you have no just cause why you should be so incensed. Others, like the **Septuagint, Jonah, Syriac, Arabic**: Are you thus greatly saddened? <note>Compare Deuteronomy 9:21, 13:15, 2 Kings 11:18.</note> But the question here is not about the fact, but about the right, and it is not of one ignorant or doubting, but of one protesting and informing. At this, **Abarbanel**, following **Rabbi Japhet** in **Abraham Ibn Ezra**, says: "Does it grieve you to do good?" That is: Is it because I (who am kind to all, Psalm 145:9) do good to the Ninevites, that you are angry? As in Matthew 20:15. But the Hebraism here is more correctly resolved as: "Is doing good [the cause], or do you do well, that you are so angry?" <note>Compare Deuteronomy 25:5, 18:17.</note> However, Jonah is silent here, undoubtedly covered in shame, having no sufficient cause to use as a pretext for his anger. **v. 5.** **x) For Jonah had gone out**, when he had finished his duty by preaching through the city; lest he himself be involved in the destruction which he still thought would most certainly follow. This verse is parenthetical, paving the way for what follows, whence we rightly take the words in the Pluperfect tense with **Pfeiffer** and others.

CHAPTER IV, v. 1. **And it was evil** So v. 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 10. And Genesis and hence Menachem 7, 8, 11-16, 19, 21, 22, 23. And through Mercer in place of Menachem 5, 17, 18, 34. Compare above 6, 2, 14.

<margin>
**y)** and he settled at the **eastern** side of the city. Ezekiel 11:23. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian</note> notes: from where there was the best view into the city.

**z)** **S. and he had made himself a booth there:** or rather a hut, a shelter made of twigs. Isaiah 1:8, chapter 4:6. It was meant to protect him from the harshness of the weather. Psalm 140:8, Job 40:22.

**a)** Ecclesiastes 2:3. <note>original Greek: ὁ ἕως ἂν ἴδῃ</note> **until he should see.** Philippians 2:23.

**b) what would happen when.** When the deadline had passed and he saw that no evil had befallen the city, he boiled over with anger.

**v. 6. c) S. And he had prepared.** others in the past tense with the Vulgate: **And the Lord God prepared.** verse 7, 8. Chapter 2:1.

**d)** **Septuagint:** <note>original: κικυῶν</note> **a gourd.** **Vulgate:** **ivy.** The Targum of Jonathan and the Syriac use **Kikayon.** So also in verses 7, 9, 10. Let us hear from St. Jerome <note>A 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> regarding what this might be: "In place of a gourd or ivy, we read **Kikaion** in Hebrew, which is also called **Elkeron** in the Syriac and Punic languages. It is a type of shrub or small tree, having broad leaves like a vine, providing a very dense shade, and supporting itself on its own trunk. It grows very frequently in Palestine, especially in sandy places; and in a marvelous way, if you cast the seed into the ground, it quickly rises into a tree, and within a few days, what you had seen as a sprout, you now look up at as a small tree." Jerome continues: "When we were translating the prophets, we wanted to express the Hebrew name itself, because the Latin language did not have a name for this species of tree; but we feared the Grammarians, lest they take the liberty of criticizing us, or imagine beasts of India or mountains of Boeotia, or fabricate portents." Samuel Bochart <note>A renowned 17th-century orientalist</note> proved at length that Jerome was correct. It is the same as our **Rikien**, the Talmudic **Kik**, and the Egyptian **Kiki**. Pliny <note>Roman naturalist</note> says this tree grows abundantly in Egypt and Spain; it is the height of an olive tree, with a stalk like a fennel, leaves like a vine, and a pale seed. Our people call it **RICINUS** <note>The Castor-oil plant</note> from its similarity to a tick.

**f) to deliver him.** <note>The text notes a specific grammatical accent here similar to 1 Samuel 21:30</note>. But it was so that the plant itself might provide shade.

**g) from his discomfort:** from the excessive heat.

God looks after even the beasts. Genesis 8:1, Matthew 10:29. Everything predicted about Nineveh came to pass 115 years later, according to Josephus.

<meta>This page transitions from the Book of Jonah to the Preface and opening of the Book of Micah. It establishes the historical context of Micah's ministry alongside contemporary prophets like Isaiah and Hosea, and begins a detailed philological analysis of the first two verses.</meta>

<page-num>586</page-num>
<header>PREFACE TO THE PROPHECY OF MICAH.</header>

<margin>
Micah's Homeland, Age, and Subject Matter.
</margin>

**M**icah, a Moreshethite by birth and a Jew by nation, prophesied at the same time as Isaiah and Hosea; in some places, he followed the words of the former [Isaiah] closely, as seen in chapter 4:1 and following, compared with Isaiah 2:2 and following. As a prophet, he is indeed terrifying and harsh because of his threats of judgment, but no less pleasant because of his Gospel promises. He threatens destruction to the Israelites and the Jews—to the former brought by the Assyrians, and to the latter by the Babylonians. He points to the cause of this evil as the sins of the people: idolatry, injustice, plunder, defiance, love of lies, complacency, ingratitude toward God, and finally, a supreme and universal impiety. He pursues these sins in such a way that he especially rebukes the capitals and the leaders, from whom crimes flowed to the provinces and the common people, as well as the prophets and priests who fostered a false sense of security. But lest the afflicted lose heart in the midst of such great evils, he also repeatedly and excellently depicts the restoration of Jerusalem and the flourishing state of the New Testament. And, to speak with Lightfoot in his *Chronicle*, page 100 <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was an English churchman and rabbinical scholar</note>, he announces illustrious things about Christ and His kingdom; he specifically designates the city where He was to be born; and he uses the very same words as Isaiah, who was then living, to describe the influx of those joining the kingdom of Christ under the Gospel, as well as His power and the peace that would exist under Him. By reason of this double argument, which is treated in turns, the whole prophecy is conveniently divided into three parts. I. He predicts the destruction of the kingdom and deportation to Assyria and Babylon for all the tribes, both Israel and Judah (chapters 1:1–2:11), and consoles them with the promise of a universal gathering and multiplication under Christ (chapter 2:12-13). II. He threatens the destruction of Jerusalem (chapter 3), to which he joins the comfort of the restoration of Zion under Christ (chapters 4 and 5). III. He introduces God contending with His people (chapter 6), but the Church lamenting her miseries (chapter 7:1-6), and raising herself up with the hope of better things (verse 7 to the end).

<margin>
Parts.
</margin>

---

# THE BOOK OF MICAH,
## Hebrew: מיכה <note>Michah</note>

<margin>
CHAPTER I. v. 1. a) Hosea 1:1, Joel 1:1, Jonah 1:1. b) **Micah**, which is to say: "Who is like the LORD?" <note>original Latin: "quis est sicut DOMINUS?"</note>. For it is written in Jeremiah 26:18 as *Michaiah*, whence the Greek *Michaias* and Latin *Michas*. And he who in 2 Chronicles 18:7 is called *Michaihu*, and in verse 8 *Mihahu*, is also called *Micha* in verse 14 of the same; this is formed from *Michahu* no less easily than *Yirmyah* from *Yirmyahu*, *Yeshayah* from *Yeshayahu*, *Amatzyah* from *Amatzyahu*, etc., by dropping the final *yod*. Cf. also Judges 4:1, 4, 5. Analogous to this among proper names is *Michael*, which is to say: "Who is like God?" <note>original Latin: "Quis sicut Deus?"</note>. Cf. below chapter 7:18, where our Prophet, as if mindful of his own name, proclaims the incomparability of God. An illustrious Prophet, whom we find cited not only in the New but also the Old Testament: Jeremiah 26:18, Matthew 2:5-6. There is another Micah, the son of Imlah, who lived in the time of Ahab and Jehoshaphat, and thus was prior to our prophet (1 Kings 22:8 and following). c) **Moreshethite**, that is, from Maresha (as Jonah has it), a town of the tribe of Judah near the borders of the Philistines (verse 15, Joshua 15:44). Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> testifies in his Prologue that in his own
</margin>

<margin>
CHAPTER I.
time it was still a small village near Eleutheropolis, a city of Palestine, which
</margin>

-> 1 <gloss>a</gloss> The word <gloss>b</gloss> of the LORD <gloss>c</gloss> which <gloss>d</gloss> came <gloss>e</gloss> to Micah <gloss>f</gloss> the Moreshethite <gloss>g</gloss> in the days of <gloss>h</gloss> Jotham, <gloss>i</gloss> Ahaz, <gloss>k</gloss> and Hezekiah, <gloss>l</gloss> kings of <gloss>m</gloss> Judah, <gloss>n</gloss> which <gloss>o</gloss> he saw <gloss>p</gloss> concerning Samaria <gloss>q</gloss> and Jerusalem. <-

-> 2 <gloss>l</gloss> Hear, <gloss>m</gloss> O peoples, <gloss>n</gloss> all of you; <gloss>o</gloss> listen <-

-> 75 b <-

<sig>Ffff 2</sig>

was formerly called Beth-shemesh (2 Kings 14:11, 13). We wonder, therefore, what came into the mind of Heidegger <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a Swiss Reformed theologian</note>, who in his *Biblical Handbook*, page 339, after appealing to this testimony of Jerome, said: "It was located, therefore, in the tribe of Ephraim." This is plainly contrary to Jerome; nor is it supported by any foundation, although among the Fathers, Epiphanius, Dorotheus, and Isidore also made Micah an Ephraimite. For that he was a Jew is also gathered by Abarbanel <note>Don Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and commentator</note> from the mention of the Kings of Judah. The vowel *Cholam* in *Maresha* <note>original: מרשה</note> comes from the first radical *Yod* in *Moresha* <note>original: מורשה</note>, which easily transitions into a *Vau*. But Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a Dutch theologian</note> in *Doctrine of the Prophets*, page 35, thinks it is named from Moresheth-gath (verse 14), a place, as it seems, bordering the Philistine city of Gath, on the boundaries of Judah and Benjamin, to the west of Jerusalem. d) At the same time, therefore, that Isaiah and Hosea prophesied, although they began a little earlier under Uzziah, the predecessor of Jotham (Isaiah 1:1, Hosea 1:1), in whose time Amos also prophesied (Amos 1:1). But the Prophet did not express specifically where each individual prophecy should be referred to in chronological order. And it is more easily understood (as Lightfoot says in his *Chronicle*, page 99) that the subject matter of the whole book exhibits the theme of prophecy held under each of these Kings, rather than determining which chapters were published during the specific times of each King. Perhaps, says Maim in *Economy*, page 898, he repeated the same prophecies at different times and under different Kings. See, however, what we have noted at chapter 3:1. e) Of whom [Jotham] the history may be seen in 2 Kings 15:32 and following; 2 Chronicles 27:1 and following. And compare the state of the people under the reign of these Kings as expressed by Varenius in the Appendix to our Preface to Isaiah. f) Concerning whom [Ahaz], see 2 Kings 16 and 2 Chronicles 28. g) Concerning whom [Hezekiah], see 2 Kings 18, 19, 20 and 2 Chronicles 29–32. h) which [was] the word of the LORD; or "who [was] Micah." i) **saw**, that is, prophesied. See the note on Amos 1:1. k) i.e., against the ten tribes, of which Samaria was the head, and Judah, of which Jerusalem was the head. He names the capitals specifically because vices especially ran wild there, and from there they poured out to all the provinces of both kingdoms (compare verses 5 and 6). He puts Samaria first here in verse 5 because its kingdom was not only larger than the Judean one, but was also devastated before it, just as it had led the way in crime and impiety. <term>v. 2. l)</term> He begins his addresses with a similar calling as Isaiah (chapter 1:2) and Moses (Deuteronomy 32:1), for the sake of arousal, so that they might listen attentively and reverently to things of the greatest weight, spoken not in his own name but in the name of Jehovah Himself. Cf. below chapter 3:1, 9; chapter 6:1, 2, 9; Isaiah 34:1; Jeremiah 6:18, 19; chapter 22:29; and the note on Amos 3:1. Because he sees a horrible devastation (says Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow (1562–1633), a Lutheran theologian</note>) certainly looming, he tries with great spirit and great vehemence to rouse men, who are as if asleep in their sins, to take up the care of amending their lives and averting punishment. It is notable, moreover, that our Prophet begins with the very same words with which the earlier Micah, son of Imlah, concluded his prophecy (1 Kings 22:28). Furthermore, this chapter predicts the overthrow of both kingdoms: I. Generally in verses 3 and 4, with the cause added in verse 5. II. Specifically: a) of Samaria in verses 6, 7, and 8; b) of Jerusalem and the kingdom of Judah, for nine of whose cities mourning, flight, and desolation are decreed under elegant wordplays (paronomasia) from verse 9 to the end. m) Lightfoot calls the syntax strange in his *Chronicle*, page 99: "you peoples, all of them!" But *kullam* <note>original Hebrew: כלם</note> is properly a substantive; as if to say, "yea, let the whole of them (the peoples) hear." It is not unusual among the Hebrews for a third-person suffix to follow or precede a vocative: such as what follows: "O earth, and the fullness thereof!" also Numbers 16:6, Job 17:10. By "peoples," however, he means the Israelite tribes and families, since our Micah, just like the previous Micah, addressed his words to them (Leviticus 19:16, chapter 21:1). Others understand the peoples of the whole world, whom they think are cited as witnesses against the Jews.

<summary>This page provides a scholarly introduction to the Book of Micah, identifying the prophet's historical era (the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah) and his geographical origins in Moresheth. It includes a linguistic breakdown of the prophet's name and a structural outline of the book's major themes: judgment for sin and the future hope of Christ's kingdom.</summary>

n) Works of either grace or (as in this place) justice.

<margin>
n) Listen. See Isaiah 10:30; Chapter 34:1. o) That is, and everything within it. Psalm 24:1. p) "And let the LORD be, etc." Do not despise or treat as worthless <note>original: "flocci pendere"</note> such a witness, who through me testifies his judgments and his will to you seriously and openly. The Prophet does this so that the people might receive the word to be announced by him, not as if from a man, but (as it truly is) as the word of God himself. 1 Thessalonians 2:13. q) Against you, your witness. 1 Samuel 12:5. God testifies through his servants, by seriously and gravely warning men of imminent evils unless they repent; so that they have no pretext of ignorance if they perish. Cf. 2 Kings 17:13; Psalm 50:7; Jeremiah 42:19. r) The LORD, I say, let him be a witness against you. An emphatic repetition, stressing the dignity of the one testifying. s) From the temple of his holiness. Whether the celestial temple is understood, as in Jonah 2:5; Habakkuk 2:20; Psalm 11:4; or the terrestrial one, in which his most holy Presence <term>Numen; the divine presence or will</term> resided, as in Psalm 79:1. Certainly, because both are the seat of holiness, only the most holy oracles can proceed from either of them, to be holily fulfilled; and they must be received no less holily by the listeners. Cf. Psalm 60:8.

2 **Hear,**<sup>n, p</sup> **all you peoples!**<sup>o</sup> **Hearken, O earth and all that is in it!**<sup>q</sup> **And let the Lord GOD**<sup>r, 1</sup> **be a witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple.**<sup>s, t</sup>

3) Descending. Let it be understood as he is about to reveal himself. Isaiah 26:21; Zechariah 14:3. Hence Ionathan <note>Referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note> says: he will make himself conspicuous, or manifest himself; from the place of the house of his majesty. Conversely, he is said to return to his place when he withdraws the operations of his grace, Hosea 5:15. x) And he shall descend, namely, from heaven, as if from his place.
</margin>
<margin>
v. 3. t) This is either introductory, as if to say: "Since, to begin explaining what Jehovah testifies to you through me..." Or it is causal, providing the motive for attention: "You have very strong reasons for listening, because behold, unless you listen, you will feel the most heavy wrath of God." u) He is about to go out from his place; marvelously from heaven. Psalm 115:3. He will manifest his wrath upon all impiety and injustice, Romans 1:18. God is said to "go out" or "descend," not as if he moves from a location—since he fills all things with his Divine Presence—but as he is about to make himself known.

Genesis 11:7. Regarding that passage, Blessed Luther says: *God descends, not in fact or substance, for he is everywhere; but he stops pretending not to see, he stops being long-suffering, and begins to reveal sin, to punish and to rebuke. Therefore, secure men, who previously thought him to be far away, now see that he is present, and they tremble.* Cf. below verse 12; and Psalm 144:5; Isaiah 63:19; chapter 64:1. y) *He will tread upon the heights of the earth*, as a demonstration of his power and wrath, to which even the highest things will be subjected. Cf. Amos 4:13 and the note there. z) A plural with a double termination, Masculine and Feminine, as in Isaiah 58:14; Job 9:8.

**Verse 4.** a) *And they shall be melted*; as if dissolved into waters they shall flow away, as those who can in no way endure the presence of an angry Avenger. Psalm 97:5. He describes the operations and effects of divine wrath figuratively, in the desolation of both kingdoms. Cf. Amos 9:5, 13; Isaiah 34:3; 63:19; 64:1; Psalm 97:5. b) *and the valleys.* c) *they shall split themselves*, they shall be split of their own accord, and they shall gape open with a huge concussion and movement. Numbers 16:31; Zechariah 14:4. d) *like wax* (4) Psalm 68:3. e) Cf. Isaiah 64:2. f) *poured out* verse 6; 2 Samuel 14:14. A Hophal participle from the root "to pour." g) *in a descent*, (4) Job 7:5. That is, in a sloping place, where water can in no way stay, but is carried downward in a headlong rush.

**Verse 5. h)** But if you wish to know the cause of these things, why God is going to act as he threatened in verses 3 and 4; the answer is: Because of the *transgression of Jacob or the Jacobites.* Chapter 3, 8. Cf. Amos 2:4, 6; Isaiah 1:2. i) *all this will happen.* It is an intensive expression, as in Isaiah 5:25; 9:20; Psalm 44:18. That is, a horrendous and immense evil, which brings many slaughters with it, so that it might more rightly be called an "Iliad of woes" <note>An ancient idiom referring to a long series of disasters</note> than a single one. k) But what is the cause of the transgression? So in verse 13, *the beginning of sin* is used metonymically <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it</note> for the first cause or occasion of sinning. He asks not about things, but about persons; therefore we have need of this version. Cf. note on Judges 13:17. l) *Is it not Samaria?* That is, its inhabitants, but especially the Kings, who are read everywhere to have been the authors of idolatry and sin for the people. 1 Kings 14:16; 15:26, 30; 16:13, 26, etc. Clearly, from the court into the royal city, and in turn from there into the provinces, impiety flowed. See note above on verse 1. m) *Who is the author or cause of the high places of Judah?* In which were the shrines and altars of gods. 2 Kings 23:8; Ezekiel 16:16; 20:28, 29. n) This is to be understood in the same way as the preceding name *Samaria.* Cf. regarding the Kings of Jerusalem 2 Kings 16:2, 21; 2 Chronicles 21:11; 28:25; regarding its prophets Jeremiah 23:15; and finally the whole city, insofar as it brought corruption to the entire Jewish kingdom. Chapter 32:35.

**Verse 6. o)** *Therefore I will place or make*, says the LORD, as in Jeremiah 19:8. He now transitions to explaining the destruction of Samaria specifically, as we noted at the beginning of verse 2 where we arranged the argument of this chapter. p) Cf. note on verse 1. q) *Into a heap of the field;* that is, I will so desolate it that nothing will remain except heaps of rubble and a field or open space. Chapter 3:12; Jeremiah 26:17; Psalm 79:1. Cf. Isaiah 17:1. *Into a hill that is plowed;* Grotius notes: *As it is in the Poet—and fields, where Troy once was.* r) *Into places of vineyard plantings*, so that vineyards may be planted, or can be planted, where the city of Samaria now stands. Ezekiel 17:7; 31:4. Reference is made to the site of Samaria, which was a mountainous city. 1 Kings 16:24; hence it is also called the mountain of Samaria in Amos 4:1; 6:1. *Ionathan says: into a desolate place for the planting of a vineyard.* s) *I will pour out*, I will make to flow down; that is, I will cast down and scatter, so that not one stone stays upon another. Matthew 24:2. Reference is made to the allegory drawn from water in verse 4. Cf. Jeremiah 18:21. t) *Into the valley below*, which in Isaiah 28:1, 4 is called the valley of the fat ones. u) *Its stones* and other materials from which it was constructed. Ezekiel 26:12; Psalm 102:15. x) *And I will uncover its foundations*, that is, I will make it so that the foundations appear bare without buildings: I will demolish the city to its base. Ezekiel 13:14; 2 Samuel 22:16. Cf. Psalm 137:7 and the note on Hosea 14:1.

**Verse 7. y)** *Its carved images*, whose worship it stubbornly refused to abandon. Isaiah 10:10. See note on Jeremiah 48:35. For this is not a simple prediction of evil, but at the same time a commemoration of the cause, as above in Amos 3:14. z) *They shall be crushed.* Isaiah 24:12; 2 Chronicles 34:7. a) *The wages of its harlotry*, the houses and wealth which it credited to its idols, impiously boasting of them as if they were the reward of idolatrous superstition. Compare Hosea 2:14; 9:1; also Isaiah 48:5. b) *Its idols*, with the idols. 1 Samuel 31:9. Cf. Hosea 4:17. *Ionathan: its idols.* c) Leviticus 26:33; Jeremiah 6:8. d) *From harlot's wages she collected;* i.e., whatever wealth she has collected until now was from harlot's wages, or those appearances, because she attributed and dedicated it all to the idols with whom she committed fornication. Jehovah had done nothing here, nor did the wicked nation wish to acknowledge my benefit. See the notes just made. e) This is said regarding the enjoyment of wealth in Proverbs 13:11; 28:8. f) *And so they shall return to—.* A proverbial expression. *Ill-gotten, ill-lost.* Or, as the Comic poet says in Cicero's 2nd Philippic: *Things badly acquired, badly slip away.* Harlot's gain is an abominable thing to the Lord (Deuteronomy 23:19); therefore he will not allow it to be stable. It is born from a foul thing, and it will perish foully and in the vilest way. Cf. here again Proverbs 13:11. In phrasing, there is something analogous to Genesis 3:19.

**Verse 8. g)** This can refer equally to what precedes as to what follows in verse 9 and following. h) *I will wail*, (cf. 2 Samuel 1:12) says the Prophet, to signify both the atrocity of the imminent evil and the pious will of God, who unwillingly and not without pain inflicts blows upon the stubbornness of men. Cf. similar laments of the prophets in Isaiah 16:9; Jeremiah 42:31; and throughout the Lamentations of Jeremiah.

Verse 5. **Is it not?** [Hebrew: Halo] defective in both, namely Masculine, as it seems; which however lies in error, as we noted at Amos 2:7.

a) **Stripped** <note>original: "Spoliatus"</note> by enemies of clothing; (so the following, וְעָרֹום, *naked*, would be the explanation.) or, as if stripped of mind, lacking counsel and spirit, as in *Job* 12:17, 19. b) *cf. Isaiah* 20:2. <note>The OCR "Ef." is likely a typographic error for "Es." (Esaias/Isaiah).</note> l) *lamentation verse* 11. *Amos* 5:16, 17. m) like jackals <note>original: "dracones" (dragons). In biblical contexts, this often refers to jackals or desert-dwelling creatures known for howling.</note>. So in the *Arabic harmonic* word חַנִּנִין, from the Greek Septuagint δρακοντων [*drakontōn*]. The name alludes to *shannoth*, which the most ancient interpreters explain as θρηνεῖן [*thrēnein*], "to wail," in *Judges* 11:40. Perhaps it refers to the horrific hissing of jackals with which the deserts ring. *Bochart. Part II.* c. 14. p. 437. Cf. "dragons" in similar material, like ostriches, as in this place, joined in *Job* 30:29. *In Ludolf's Historical Commentary on Ethiopia* p. 139, he prefers to understand it as crocodiles rather than jackals/dragons; because the latter indeed produce a vehement shriek and hiss, but not a wailing, while the ancients handed down that the former [crocodiles] weep and wail, hence the proverb about crocodile tears. So *cf. Ezekiel* 29:3. ch. 32:2. n) *and mourning Jeremiah* 6:26. o) *like female ostriches, Ezekiel* 13:22, which are very mournful and noisy, *Job* 30:28. See *Bochart* Part II. book IV. c. 14.

v. 9. p) *desperate, incurable cf. Jeremiah* 15:18. ch. 30:15. They have some affinity with אֱנֹושׁ [Enosh, meaning man or frailty], Niphal נִאֲשׁ [ni'ash] *to be desperate*: and it is held in the same way as חָלָה [*chalah*], "to be sick," which in the passive voice signifies the incurability of a disease in *Jeremiah* 10:19. Moreover, it is called incurable in this place because it could not be repaired by human aid, nor was it to be cured by God himself except after a very long time, collected in *Jeremiah* 30:13, 17. q) *each of its blows, which it received from the Assyrians Jeremiah* 30:12. ch. 19:8. r) *because it reached, or penetrated* v. 15. -dean kingdom. *cf. 2 Kings 17:18, 19, 20.* s) It indicates the order of divine judgment. For it had its beginnings in Samaria and the 10 tribes, carried away by the Assyrians; after 131 years passed (*comparing 2 Kings 18:10* with *ch. 25:2*) it pervaded to Jerusalem and the Judean kingdom. t) It reached, like a lethal strike, which killing the life by penetrating to the inner parts. *Jeremiah 4:10, 18.* Or: it touched, in a just order *Job 4:5.* u) what follows, *even to Jerusalem*, is an explanation. *v. 12. See note on Obadiah 13.* x) Tarnovius explains this regarding the Assyrian eruption into Judea under Sennacherib. *collecting 2 Kings 18:13, 17.* where, when Sennacherib had come even to Jerusalem, he is read to have been miraculously repelled by an Angel, after he had brought great calamity to the neighboring towns and the Jerusalem countryside. We prefer, however, to interpret it regarding the Babylonian invasion under Nebuchadnezzar, because of the mention of captivity or deportation in *v. 16 and following*, which is nowhere read to have been done by the Assyrians, just as it could not be done by them in such a headlong flight. Thus therefore עַד [*ad*, meaning "even to"] will be inclusive, just as it was just before "Judah" and *Job 4:5.* As if to say: not even Jerusalem will be immune from this evil. Meanwhile, if anyone wishes to include the invasion of Sennacherib, which was imminent at the time of this prophecy, as a prelude to the Babylonian one, he will by no means have us as opponents. *cf. Isaiah 10:28 ff.*

v. 10. y) A city of the Philistines, which had indeed been subdued by David *2 Chronicles 18:1.* but later restored to its own law, *collecting 1 Kings 2:39.* it kept a hostile mind against the Jews. z) lest the Philistines conceive a wicked joy from your destruction. It is like a parody of the Davidic threnody *2 Samuel 1:20.* the sense of which is: it would be desirable for you that the Philistines, if it were possible, should never know this, because they will rejoice so much in your misfortune. *cf. Lamentations 1:21. ch. 2:16.* a) that is, in the sight of the Philistines, or any enemies. b) in Beth-Aphra, as if to say: *in the house of dust*. Perhaps it is the Ophrah of the Benjaminites *Joshua 18:23, 21; 1 Samuel 13:17.* Another of the Manassites *Judges 6:11.* The prefixed ל, as in common nouns, so in this place in a proper name, serves to indicate the genitive case. For the rest, Hillerus suspects in *Onomasticon Sacrum* p. 950 that these names, which Micah uses, are not so much actual villages as they are paronomastic <note>puns or plays on words</note>. c) sprinkle yourself with dust. An elegant paronomasia [wordplay], of which many follow. For it is exactly as if a Latin speaker were to say: *You who are from Lutetia [Paris, from "Lutum," mud], wallow in the mud.* d) The textual *Kethib* to be pronounced in the past tense, and is by enallage [substitution of grammatical forms] for the future with a paragogic Yod: *you shall sprinkle yourself* (4) *Jeremiah 6:26; Ezekiel 27:30.*

v. 11. e) Pass on for yourselves, namely, into captivity, *collecting v. 16. Isaiah 47:2.* A strange syntax: which indeed is because the following יֹושֶׁבֶת [*yoshevet*, inhabitant] is a collective singular, signifying the whole assembly of inhabitants; and so it can be joined sometimes with the singular, because of the ending, and sometimes with the plural, because of the meaning. Therefore, the disparity of number is to be resolved thus: "Pass away for yourselves, O inhabitants." f) Shaphir, as if to say: *you who were once most beautiful.* *compare the root Sh-P-R, Psalm 16:6.* To Hillerus in *Onomasticon Sacrum* p. 950 it is Parah, likewise a town of the Benjaminite lot *Joshua 18:23.* for פָּרָה [Parah], which sounds like "adorned." g) in nakedness (6) and shame. An asyndeton <note>omission of conjunctions</note>. *Ezekiel 16:7, 22, 39. ch. 23:29. Habakkuk 3:9.* Or: stripped of shameful parts, with a naked body, as happens to those who are carried away into captivity after their clothes have been pulled off. Menochius *cf. Isaiah 47:23. Hosea 2:12.* h) she shall no longer go out, and lead out her troops joyfully *Amos 5:3.* or flocks. The inhabitants of Tsaanan shall not go out safe. i) The name is derived from צָאָה or יָצָא or a multitude of cattle going out under the shepherd's staff, as if to say "a town full of cattle." Hillerus in the place cited interprets it as Zenan of Judah *Joshua 15:37.* k) lamentation. Constructed from the absolute *misped* in verse 8. l) Proper name of a place, to whose literal meaning, without a doubt, as in the preceding and following, it is alluded. אָצֶל [*Atsel*] sounds like "vicinity" or "proximity" (next to, near); *See Ezekiel 43:6. Daniel 8:17. and Zechariah 14:5.* and so Beth-Etsel would be a place next to which those fleeing could safely stand (for compare the following עֶמְדָּתֹו [*standing place*]), or where the course of evils might stop. Unless perhaps it is alluded to the related sound צֵל [*tsel*], "shadow," as if to say *the house of shadow*, which seemed likely to offer shadow to those tired from flight, *collecting Jeremiah 48:45.* Hillerus in the place cited understands the Atselites from the tribe of Benjamin, whose city might be called Mozah, from the name of Mozah, who was the great-great-grandfather of Azel *Joshua 18:26. 1 Chronicles 8:37, 38.* m) it will take away from you its standing place. (i) Sense: Beth-haetsel, which itself will mourn, will provide no shadow for you fleeing in which you might stand, nor will it fix a limit for the evil to stop.

v. 12. n) It is explanatory rather than causal. As if to say: For to further explain the progress and magnitude of the evil. o) she grieved or will grieve *Jeremiah 5:3.* and that with the most bitter grief: for it alludes to the following Maroth, which sounds like bitterness. p) because of the good taken away. *cf. similar use of the prefix ל Isaiah 38:17.* q) Proper name of a place from *bitterness*, as said. *cf. Isaiah 33:7. Jeremiah 2:19.* Whether indeed that same place is Jarmuth, a town of Judah *Joshua 15:35.* we do not dare to define, although this pleased Hillerus in *Onomasticon Sacrum* p. 951. r) like rain, evil descended. *cf. above verse 3. Isaiah 55:10. Ezekiel 9:19.*

<summary>This page provides a detailed philological commentary on Micah 1:8-12, focusing on the Prophet's use of paronomasia (wordplay) to link the names of Judean cities—like Beth-Aphra (House of Dust) and Shaphir (Beautiful)—to their impending doom. The scholar explores the identification of various desert animals used as metaphors for mourning and debates the historical timing of these judgments between the Assyrian and Babylonian invasions.</summary>

### CHAPTER II.

**1** **Woe to those who devise iniquity and work evil on their beds; at the light of the morning they practice it, because it is in the power of their hand.** <gloss>a</gloss> <gloss>b</gloss> <gloss>c</gloss> <gloss>d</gloss> <gloss>e</gloss> <gloss>f</gloss> <gloss>g</gloss> <gloss>h</gloss>
