Many followed it later, for example, Beersheba in *Amos* 5:5. It is probable that this happened under the reign of Jehoram (cf. *2 Chronicles* 21:6, 13) and Ahaziah (ch. 22:3-4). Moreover, although the books of Kings and Chronicles are silent on this point, it is abundantly clear from this prophetic passage. Just as with the earthquake in the time of Uzziah, and other events of which the Prophets speak, the sacred historians are sometimes silent. **e)** Think of the idolatry that was spreading in the kingdom of Israel, see verse 5, *Amos* 3:14. *verse 14.* **f)** The causal particle refers either to the immediately preceding verse 13—namely, that the "daughter of Zion" <note>Jerusalem</note> imitated the Israelite idolatry following the example of the city of Lachish—or to the more remote verse 5. **g)** "You shall give," namely, O Lachish (v. 13), or rather by apostrophe <note>direct address</note>, O daughter of Zion, whom he seems to address below in verse 16. **h)** A difficult word in this place. (1) *Exodus* 18:2, *1 Kings* 9:16. In the former place, it signifies "sendings away" or "remissions"; in the latter, a "gift of marriage" (sending out from the paternal home) or a "dowry." Here some say: you will give gifts (to appease the enemy or redeem life) together with (as in *Exodus* 35:22) the town of Moresheth-Gath. But Cocceius <note>a 17th-century theologian</note> suggests: "a writ of divorce against Gath." Thus the sense would be: You will renounce your right over Gath, and by that very act permit it to others—at least you will be forced to permit it—as if you had given an instrument of cession (as is usually done in the sale of lands). Compare verse 15: "I am about to bring another heir to you." And chapter 2:4: "God changes the land of my people, giving it to other possessors," etc. So the word *shalach* <note>original: "שלח"</note> means to yield something or release it from one's power (*Deuteronomy* 15:12, ch. 21:14, *Job* 8:5, ch. 39:5). **i)** Moresheth-Gath, or in the vicinity of the city of Gath (v. 10), from which some derive the title "Morashtite" (v. 1), though it can also be from the following *Mareshah*. But Cocceius takes it appellatively <note>as a common noun</note>, as in *Deuteronomy* 33:4, "over the inheritance of Gath." That is to say: The lands which you have held until now near the city of Gath, you will lose in the future. **k)** Achzib, that is, of the "lying city," comparing the following *Achzab* <note>meaning deception or a dried-up brook</note>. This is also a town of Judah near Mareshah (*Joshua* 15:44); perhaps the same as Chezib (*Genesis* 38:5). There is another city of this name belonging to the tribe of Asher (*Joshua* 19:29, *Judges* 1:31), called *Ecdippa* by the Latins. **l)** "into frustration" (2) (*Jeremiah* 15:18) while they yield to the enemies, over whom the Israelite kings had promised themselves perpetual jurisdiction. **m)** To the Israelite kings, that is, the Judean kings. For these too are sometimes called thus when there is no opposition to the kings of the ten tribes (e.g., *2 Chronicles* 21:2, 4; ch. 28:19) because they ruled a part of the Israelite people, namely two tribes (cf. ibid ch. 11:3, ch. 12:1, 6). *verse 15.* **n)** Yet another heir, namely, the enemy. **o)** "I will bring." The letter *He* [ה] has dropped out by shortening, as in *1 Kings* 21:21. **p)** "inhabitant of Mareshah." A city in the tribe of Judah (*1 Chronicles* 2:42, *2 Chronicles* 11:8), the homeland of the prophet Eliezer who prophesied against Jehoshaphat (*2 Chronicles* 20:37) and of Micah himself (see above, v. 1). The same as *Mareshah* in *Joshua* 15:44. As a common noun, it sounds like "inheritance" <note>Hebrew: *Mareshah* sounds like *Yarash*, to inherit</note>. As if to say: "O people of Mareshah, you have possessed your city and surrounding lands until now by hereditary right; but soon I will bring one who, having driven out the old settlers, will succeed to that inheritance." **q)** which enemy will reach as far as Adullam, to occupy this and the remaining cities of Judah as if they were his inheritance (*Joshua* 15:35, *1 Samuel* 22:1, *2 Samuel* 23:13, *1 Chronicles* 11:15, *2 Chronicles* 11:7). There is a wordplay on the particle *AD* <note>meaning "until" or "to"</note>, which is contained in the beginning of the name Adullam. **r)** "indeed, he will come to the glory of Israel." Whatever glorious and excellent thing Israel has, he will pervade the whole and claim it for himself (*Isaiah* 17:3-4, cf. *Hosea* 4:7, ch. 9:11). Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow, a Lutheran theologian</note> explains it primarily regarding Jerusalem (cf. v. 9 and *Isaiah* 48:2; 32:13). *verse 16.* **s)** "make yourself bald" (*Leviticus* 21:5, cf. *Isaiah* 22:12, *Jeremiah* 16:6). **t)** "and cut off your hair," in the custom of those mourning deeply (*Jeremiah* 7:29, *Job* 1:20, cf. *Ezra* 9:3, and see *Curtius* Book 10, ch. 5). He addresses here not just one city, but the whole collection of Judean cities under the metaphor of a bereaved mother. **u)** "of your delights," those whom you held in delight (5) (ch. 2:9, *Proverbs* 19:10). **x)** "enlarge" (induce a very wide) baldness (*Isaiah* 3:24, cf. *Jeremiah* 16:6, *Ezekiel* 27:31). **y)** "like an eagle," which at the beginning of spring, like other birds of prey, is subject to the shedding of feathers (*Psalm* 103:5, cf. *Isaiah* 40:31). **z)** "your children shall migrate from you into exile" (cf. note on verse 9). **CHAPTER II. verse 1. a)** Woe! (*Isaiah* 1:4). Just as in the first chapter the Prophet rebuked the chief sin against the first table <note>the first half of the Ten Commandments</note>, idolatry, which turns into contempt for God; so in this second chapter he begins to argue against the vices against the second table, which turn to the harm of one's neighbor. Tarnovius. Add that here he rebukes the vices of the wealthy and the magnates especially, just as in chapter 1 he rebuked the whole people. There are two parts to this chapter: I. Reprehending or threatening, against the magnates and wealthy, because of robberies and contempt for the Prophetic word (v. 1–11). II. Evangelical, containing a universal promise about the regathering and multiplication of Israel, and the mission of Christ (v. 12-13). **b)** *Ezekiel* 11:2, *Psalm* 35:4. **c)** injustice (*Jeremiah* 4:14, *Psalm* 6:9). **d)** those striving or plotting. It is distinguished from the execution, which the next phrase describes; as in *Isaiah* 41:4. That is, it notes the operation of the heart rather than the effect of the external work (cf. *Psalm* 58:3). **e)** *Psalm* 36:5, *Hosea* 7:14. See the opposite in *Psalm* 4:5. **f)** i.e., as soon as the morning dawned (*1 Samuel* 14:36, ch. 25:34, 36; *Hosea* 7:6, cf. *Genesis* 44:3, *1 Samuel* 29:10). They do not long delay the execution of the crime they conceived at night. **g)** "they do," they execute. Certainly the power to do it is not lacking to them, if only they can and the strength is available. But since he addresses the magnates and princes throughout the chapter, who indeed do not lack strength; therefore we prefer it causally: **because**. Thus the sense here will be: They indulge their lust in everything; if they decide on something, they seize it without delay, held back neither by fear of the watching Deity nor by the laws of justice: this one thing is enough for them, that they are strong in power. But this is an abuse of power (cf. *Psalm* 12:5). **i)** "it is in the power of their hands" <note>i.e., powerful; cf. *El* (power/God) in *Genesis* 19:8, *1 Chronicles* 20:8; or rather proverbially: "their hand is for them a god," cf. *Habakkuk* 1:11 and that saying of Mezentius in Virgil's *Aeneid* X, line 773: *My right hand is my god, and the weapon which I poise to throw, now let them aid me.*</note> Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan</note>: "because power is in their hand." See *Genesis* 31:29, *Deuteronomy* 28:32. **verse 2. k)** And they covet wickedly, and bring into their minds to seize others' fields, against the 9th Commandment (*Exodus* 20:14, ch. 34:24, *Joshua* 7:21).

<column-break/>

**s)** as if from heaven <note>original: "e cælo"</note> (*Genesis* 19:24). This is added so that it may appear that this evil befell the Jews not by blind chance, but by the supreme governance of God, as a just judge (*Amos* 3:6, *Lamentations* 3:37, where you may see our notes). **t)** see verse 9.
*verse 13.* **u)** "Harness the chariot." (1) Arabic Root: "he bound, he tied around." Cf. *asar* <note>to bind</note> in *Genesis* 46:29. According to Bochart (*Hierozoicon* Part I, col. 100 <note>a famous 17th-century work on biblical animals</note>), *rethem* is properly to bind with a rope of Spanish broom, because *rethem* is Spanish broom or broom-plant (*1 Kings* 19:4, 5). This is a construction for the sense rather than for grammatical rules, where the masculine "harness" <note>rethem</note> is joined with the following feminine "inhabitant"; namely, because he understands the inhabitants under a collective feminine; so that "inhabitant" is just as if he had said: "whoever you are who inhabit." **x)** "to the swift horse" (4) (*1 Kings* 5:8), although by a futile attempt; namely, so that by fleeing with a swift escape you may avoid the impending evils. The root *rakash* is "to acquire," whence *rekush* is an "acquisition" or "possession," and our *Rechesh* <note>steed</note> is first any beast or beast of burden (like the Greek *ktēnos*); then the most noble of beasts of burden, the horse, and especially among horses, the most noble. Bochart (*Hierozoicon* Part I, col. 101). Moreover, the Prophet plays with the proximity of sounds between the proper name **Lachish** and the common noun **Rechesh**. **y)** A city in the plain of Judah, toward the west, at the borders of the Philistines (*Joshua* 15:39); besieged by Sennacherib (*2 Kings* 18:14, 17); afterwards overturned by the Babylonians with the remaining cities of Judah. **z)** He scatters here a very specific cause of this judgment. As if to say: Not undeservedly will the city of Lachish suffer that evil: for it stood as the **beginning**, i.e., the first cause of sin. See note on verse 5. So *Proverbs* 17:14, "the beginning of strife," for its first author and cause. **a)** emphasis by a change of person <note>enallage</note>, as in *Genesis* 49:4. **b)** i.e., to Jerusalem and the Judean kingdom (*Isaiah* 1:8). **c)** in you, the city of Lachish. **d)** "were found," i.e., first existed.

<margin>v. 15. *Ad* [Until/To] is marked with a *Revia* accent in 1:2, 5.</margin>

The commentary highlights the prophet's use of sophisticated wordplay (paronomasia) involving the names of Judean cities and their impending dooms.</summary>

<header>### MICAH CHAPTER 2</header>

<margin>
**l)** **And they seize what they crave**, contrary to the Seventh Precept <note>This refers to the commandment against theft or coveting, often numbered differently in historical traditions.</note>. As soon as someone craves the property of another, he seizes and occupies it. See Micah 3:2; Ezekiel 18:12, 16, 18; Psalm 35:10; compare 1 Kings 21:1. **m)** **And they covet houses**, and after coveting them, they take them away. See Numbers 16:15; compare Ephesians 5:8. **n)** **And they oppress by force** or seize (for there is no difference between the <term>גזל (gazal)</term> <note>violent robbery</note> and <term>עשק (ashak)</term> <note>oppression or fraud</note> except that the latter perhaps has a slightly broader meaning. See Leviticus 22:5, 21; compare Jeremiah 22:3. The one who suffers violence and the one who inflicts injury are correlated.) **a man and his house, etc.** namely, they subject men to slavery; compare Amos 8:6. **The houses and frauds** refer to unjust acquisition through usage. The word is used both for that which is unjustly taken (Malachi 3:5) and for the subject from whom it is taken (Leviticus 19:13; Amos 4:1; Proverbs 22:16). **o)** Compare 1 Kings 21:3, 15; Ezekiel 45:8.

**Verse 3. Therefore.** This refers back to the crimes described in verses 1 and 2. **q)** **I am planning evil**, that is, I am devising it, or I am acting to bring it about. Jeremiah 18:11; chapter 36:3; Lamentations 2:8. **r)** He uses this word either simply, as it denotes the opposite, or as a rhetorical play on words <note>original: "antanaclasi"</note> regarding the guilt, compare "those who devise" in verse 1. It is as if he says: Just as they devised the evil of guilt, so I in turn devise the evil of punishment, which the guilt deserves. **r)** **This family**, that is, this worst kind of people. Jeremiah 8:3. **s)** **Evil**, Amos 3:6. **Upon your necks** it will rest like a very heavy yoke. We add this because of what follows, in which this evil is proposed to be understood under the image of a yoke. **t)** From which you will either be **shaken**, that is, you will be drawn out or set free. Verse 4; Ephesians 22:25. **This yoke** you will not shake off as easily as untamed heifers are sometimes accustomed to do. **u)** **Your necks.** Jeremiah 27:12. **x)** **With pride.** (1) That is, loftily, or as the Syriac version has it, with an upright stature; as those who are proud or in good spirits are accustomed to be. Psalm 89:25. **Slavery and other**
</margin>

<margin>
**evils will weigh you down to the earth.** Compare the opposite in Leviticus 26:13. **y)** **A notably evil time**, or a time for executing evil. See the note on Amos 5:13.

**Verse 4. z)** **One shall utter**, with the word <term>איש (ish)</term> <note>a man/someone</note> understood. In English you would say: "It shall be uttered." Numbers 23:7; Ephesians 14:4; Amos 5:1. **t)** **A sad** or **mournful proverb**, which is shortly called by the more specific term **lamentation**. For such a thing is not

indeed false, nor uttered by enemies, but by the Israelite people themselves, who will deplore their own lot; this is shown by the following speech and the connection of the accents. **b)** **And he shall lament** (3) 1 Samuel 7:2; Ezekiel 32:18. Compare <term>הוי (hoy)</term> *Alas, alas!* Amos 5:16; <term>והי (vehi)</term> Ezekiel 21:10; and <term>הה (heah)</term> *Ah!* Ezekiel 30:2. These are the particles of those wailing, and they agree with our root here. **c)** **A lamentation of lamentation**, that is, something exceedingly lamentable. Jeremiah 9:17, 18, 19. **d)** It is said, clearly, wailing. **e)** **We are miserably devastated.** A passive form. (**f**) Jeremiah 4:20; chapter 10:20. **g)** **The portion** (that is, the estates or the land) **of my people.** Joshua 19:9. **g)** **God changes**, by transferring it to other masters, after his people have been driven out. Jeremiah 2:11; compare above chapter 1:15; and here verse 5. **h)** **How**, that is, by how great and how sad a reversal of things! Jeremiah 9:18; chapter 51:41. **i)** **He causes to depart** verse 3. That is, He takes away, or snatches from me! Understand the object either from the preceding *my portion*, or from the following *our fields*. Others: *how anything shall escape for me!* used intransitively, as in Exodus 13:22; Nahum 3:1; but this is more forced. **k)** **For so that he may cause to return from us** (that is, confer on others what was taken from us) **our fields, etc.** The word <term>שובב (shovev)</term> often signifies a repetition of movement *away from* a place rather than *toward* it. See the note on Jeremiah 40:5. So in this passage, the transitive "shovev" is said not in respect to the one to whom the fields return, but from whom they return. Others say: *that we may restore (yield unwillingly) our fields*, which were acquired through right and wrong; compare verse 2 and Job 29:10. **l)** **A new division of the land, as it were**, is described, in opposition to that ancient one made by Joshua. Joshua 13:7. Others: *the enemy divides the fields for himself*; compare Joel 4:2.

**Verse 5. m)** Taken up again from verse 3. **Therefore**, I say. And so it refers to verses 1 and 2 no less than that one does. **n)** **To you**, whoever you are that snatches the fields and houses of others (verses 1, 2). For he does not address the whole people here, but a certain part (as follows) *in the assembly of the Lord*; namely, the more powerful ones, for whom *their own hand* was their god (verse 1). **o)** **Casting a line in the lot**, for measuring out the hereditary estates distributed by lot, so that each might take what is his own. Compare Joshua 17:14; chapter 18:10; chapter 19:9; Amos 7:17. The meaning: You shall no longer enter into the inheritance of any estate in the land of the people of God. **p)** He hints that such men were, as it were, unworthy members in the assembly of the Lord, and so they would have no further rights or portion in it hereafter (Deuteronomy 23:2, 3, 4), even when the assembly of the Lord would return from captivity to their estates; for meanwhile they were to be utterly cut off. Ezekiel threatens something similar against the false prophets in chapter 13:9. Jeremiah says the same to the men of Anathoth in chapter 11:23, and to the Jews captured with Zedekiah in chapter 21:8 and following, in opposition to the Jews captured with Jeconiah in verses 5, 6, 7.

**Verse 6. q)** **Do not drip**, their false prophets *drip* <note>meaning: they keep repeating or preaching</note> to me and other true Prophets of God, preaching smooth things. This is **prophetic imitation** <note>original: "mimesis prophetica"</note>, such as in Isaiah 22:13; Hosea 4:4. By this, in addition to those already mentioned in verses 1 and 2, a new cause for divine judgments is brought forward: namely, the stubborn contempt for the true prophetic word. Compare Isaiah 30:10; Jeremiah 11:21; Amos 7:16; Job 21:14; 1 Kings 22:8. For **to drip** is **to prophesy**; compare below verse 11 and Ezekiel 21:2. The Arabic root in the first and fourth conjugations also signifies *to accuse of a fault* or *to charge*; which is what the prophets of the true God did among their impious listeners. **r)** **But unless they drip** (the true Prophets), and you admit them as they drip. The effect of the Prophetic sermons is excluded: namely, the conversion and repentance of the listeners. **s)** **According to these things.** We prefer to explain this regarding the manner and argument of the prophecy, rather than the personal object (to these). Compare a similar usage in Genesis 27:8. Clearly, they demanded smooth prophecies, such as those of the impostors (Isaiah 30:10), promising an abundance of wine and strong drink (compare below verse 11); they spurned true prophecies as being too hard and harsh (compare verse 7). **t)** **Nothing of the ignominies shall depart.** That is, *no one shall be removed from the shame.* Or, *nor shall the shame (which threatens the stubborn) depart or be turned away*; by a change of gender and number. From the root <term>נסג (nasag)</term> in the simple active form (i) Isaiah 59:13; compare below chapter 6:14 and Deuteronomy 27:17. He means to say: This would be the safest way of turning away the judgments of God, if you would obey the Prophets; but because you have refused to do this, that will not happen either.

**Verse 7. u)** **O said house of Jacob**, that is, O house of Jacob, you who are indeed called so, and love to be called so, though you have nothing of Jacob in you anymore. Compare Isaiah 45:1; John 8:39; and Romans 2:17. Micah addresses the entire house of Jacob, but especially the representative part, or certain ones who were most prominent in the house of Jacob—the powerful and the princes; compare verses 8 and 9. **x)** **Is the Spirit of the Lord shortened**, so that He is not allowed to prophesy whatever He wishes through His servants, unless He first obtains permission from you? Thus it would be a refutation of the impious inhibition of the Jews (verse 6). For it is the Spirit of the Lord who inspired the Prophets. 3:8. **Shortened** signifies impotence in Isaiah 50:2; chapter 59:1. But Cocceius (Lexicon 759) explains it: *has He become more powerless?* or *has He ceased to be long-suffering and forgiving?* For the phrase <term>מאריך אפים (ma'arik apim)</term> <note>slow to anger</note> marks a deficiency in Job 21:4; Proverbs 14:29. So the sense here would be: God has been made more than **long-suffering** <note>original: "μακρόθυμος"</note>, nor (as you indeed quibble) is He the kind of God who announces nothing but harsh and fatal things through the prophets. The last part of the verse seems to confirm this sentiment, saying the same thing from the opposite perspective. **y)** **Are these or such things**, or **are they of this kind?** So the singular <term>זה (zeh)</term> in Daniel 10:17; Song of Solomon 5:16. Meaning: God has never behaved in such a way, nor does He even now. Compare Lamentations 3:33-39. **z)** Psalm 77:12; Psalm 7:8, 7.

CHAPTER II. verse 3. <term>שדנו (shadunnu)</term> <note>we are destroyed</note> per Tischendorf 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 19, 20. **Verse 6.** <term>יסג (yasag)</term> <note>it shall depart</note> thus missing in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 22. In the Maffei 1, 2, 3 and Erfurt manuscripts. Likewise <term>יטיפו (yatifu)</term> <note>they preach</note> missing in 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 20, 22, 23. Others have them in full in both places.

He blames them most severely. **k)** To those passing by securely, suspecting no evil. See Proverbs 22:3 and 27:12. He explains what kind of people they were whom they stripped of their cloaks: namely, innocent people who never believed they would be punished by these wicked plunderers.

See chapter 7:2; Psalm 37:3; Psalm 15:2; and similar. For the syntax, see Job 31:26.

The connection is this: I said in verse 7 that my words abound in goodness toward whoever walks uprightly; but you are in no way such people, because <term>אֶתְמוּל (etmool)</term> <note>original: "heri," meaning "yesterday" or "recently"</note> recently, etc. See Isaiah 30:33. Compare Job 13:24. Others explain this differently. For it is distinguished from the following word <term>אֶדֶר (eder)</term> as being underneath. Otherwise, it signifies any garment. Exodus 22:8, etc. **h)** The looser and outer cloak, under which the inner <term>שַׂלְמָה (salmah)</term> lay. **(2)** Zechariah 11:13, where it denotes "glory" or "splendor," just as in this place, since the cloak is worn for the sake of glory. Compare 1 Kings 19:13. **i)** You drag away from others by force. Chapter 3:3; Genesis 37:23. If you saw someone dressed in a double garment, you immediately snatched the upper one, and nearly exhausted the people with such slanders. Here he critiques the tyranny of the magistrates toward the citizens.

To oppress such unsuspecting people is the highest sign of malice. Proverbs 3:29. **l)** Just like those who return from battle after the enemy has been routed and put to flight. For these, because they no longer have an enemy to fear, walk securely. Compare the similar syntax in Isaiah 59:10. **\* Verse 9. m)** Understand this as referring to widows, and compare Isaiah 10:2. **n)** You drive them out by seizing their homes. 2 Chronicles 20:11; compare Ezekiel 45:9. **o)** Each one from her "house of delights," or her dearest home **(5)** (chapter 1:16), in which she might have been able to soothe the sadness of her widowhood in some way. **p)** And from her little ones, the orphans of the unhappy widow. Nahum 3:10. **q)** You take away, by unjust and violent robbery. Genesis 27:36; Isaiah 49:25. **r)** My glory, that is, what was given to them by me; compare the similar suffix in Hosea 2:11, 10. Think of liberty and wealth, but especially the more decent clothing: which the preceding "from the front" (from above) also proves, as does the connection with verse 8 and the parallelism in Ezekiel 16:14 and Psalm 110:3. **s)** Forever. Exodus 21:6. So that all hope of recovery is cut off. This depends on the verb "you take away." It seems reference is made here to the law in Exodus 22:25, by which a garment taken as a pledge was ordered to be returned to the poor man before sunset: these people never returned them. **Verse 10. t)** Therefore, you in turn arise and depart from your seats, you who have expelled others (verse 9). He invites the penalty of retaliation <note>original: "talionis," the law of "an eye for an eye"</note>; for he who expels is expelled. Compare Revelation 13:10 and the words in 2 Samuel 17:21. **u)** For this will not be (as you presume) a perennial and firm rest. Ezekiel 21:31. The Targum says: this land is not the place of rest. Deuteronomy 12:9; Psalm 95:11; compare Hebrews 13:14. **x)** He again drives home the cause of such a severe sentence, lest they be ignorant: "because of your uncleanness," by which you have polluted the land. **(1)** See Leviticus 18:25, 28; Jeremiah 2:7; Ezekiel 36:18; Psalm 106:38. However, other manuscripts (see Variant Readings below) read it with a *Metheg* <note>a grammatical mark</note> on the third feminine: "because the land is polluted, and it destroys." **y)** It shall bring forth pain. Song of Solomon 8:5. That is, it will experience the heaviest sorrows (Isaiah 24:16)—the land, specifically the people of Israel, who are often presented by the prophets as a woman, hence the feminine words; as in Hosea 2:21; chapter 5:9; chapter 9:11. Others: because of impurity, which destroys or will destroy you. In Latin, you would call it "it will cut off." Ezekiel 13:5. **z)** And indeed, a pain. See Isaiah 66:7; Jeremiah 13:21; chapter 22:23; Hosea 13:13. Or: "and because of corruption." A noun from the preceding verb "to destroy." But the Targum says: that land is going to destroy you, and indeed with a sharp destruction, where all hope of restoration is plainly cut off. **a)** Powerful, vehement. 1 Kings 1:8. **\* Verse 11. b)** But if I or any other person were. It is not always an expression of a wish, but in some places simply a conditional statement. Ezekiel 14:15. **c)** A man who would walk (that is, follow after; compare Isaiah 33:15; Proverbs 6:12) the spirit (namely, his own or his own private spirit, even if he lies about it being the Divine Spirit, 2 Thessalonians 2:2; compare Ezekiel 13:3; Hosea 9:7). Scripture calls such people "Prophets out of their own heart" (Ezekiel 13:2), prophesying deception and the vision of their own heart (Jeremiah 14:14; chapter 23:16, 26). But according to Tarnovius, it is "one going with the wind," who is driven in a whirl by a wandering Spirit, which does not feed the souls of the listeners with solid consolation. Compare Hosea 12:1. **d)** And who would lie a lie (fictitious and empty prophecies). A false rebuke. The people were of such a reprobate judgment that they preferred to believe a lie rather than the truth; nor did anyone prophesy so absurdly that they would not trust him, provided he was a pleasant preacher and a helper of their impious security. Compare Ezekiel 13:19; 2 Thessalonians 2:10, 11; Isaiah 5:43; 2 Timothy 4:3, 4. **e)** If, I say, I were to "drip" or prophesy (verse 6). **f)** Concerning wine and strong drink, for the purpose of setting up drinking bouts, which this people loves. Leviticus 10:9; Psalm 5:12; chapter 32:13; Hosea 7:14; chapter 9:2. **g)** Then he would be that one, whoever he might be, whether me or another. **h)** The "dripper" (Prophet, verse 6) of this people, that is, such a one as this people desires and loves. But concerning such Prophets, compare Lamentations 2:14. Nor is something approved by God just because it is to the people's taste: divine judgment differs greatly from human judgment. Compare Luke 6:26. **Verse 12. i)** Nevertheless, such is my kindness, says Jehovah, in "gathering" (that is, completely and entirely) "I will gather." **a.** From sad things, he now passes to joyful ones. For the Prophets are accustomed to temper the harshest rebukes and threats with the sweetest comforts and promises; so that all may understand the severity of God and learn to value the riches of grace according to their merit. Similarly, chapter 4 connects with chapter 3. That this is a promise, rather than a threat about the violent confinement of the Israelites in fortified places for fear of enemies by whom they were to be besieged, is clear both from the words themselves, which are hardly ever placed in any sense other than that of blessing and grace; and from the connection with verse 13. However, the decision regarding the fulfillment of the promise is more difficult. Herman Witsius, in *The Ten Tribes of Israel* (chapter 6, pages 349 and 355), thinks it deals with the time preceding the revelation of the Messiah, comparing verse 13, and predicts the return of the captives to the land of Canaan—not only from there, but of the whole of Jacob, so that no tribe is missing; not that none of the tribes would remain in the lands of exile, but that he would give everyone the opportunity to return if they wished. He attempts to prove that the Israelites of the ten tribes also returned with the Jews when the Babylonian captivity was ended (though he admits himself they were few compared to the whole of their nations or the returnees from Judah) because in 2 Chronicles 36:23, Ezra 1:3, and Ezra 7:13, the power to return was given to the "whole people of God" or "Israelites"; in Ezra 2:2, 4:3, 7:7, and 1 Chronicles 9:2, the returnees are called "Israelites"; in Ezra 6:16, 17, and 8:35, victims were offered for "all Israel," according to the number of the tribes of Israel. But I do not know what is lacking in the arguments of that Distinguished Man to complete what was to be proved. For 1) 2 Chronicles 36:23, 22, 21 and Ezra 1:3, 1 deal with the return of the people after the seventy years of captivity, as Jeremiah predicted; this, however, was not of the Israelites, but of the Jews. **(2)** Nor does the mention of "Israel" in Ezra settle the matter. For even the Jews, considered separately from the ten tribes, can be understood as "Israel" (see the note above on chapter 1:15). Thus, a universal statement must be restricted to the subject matter: to Israel and the people of God insofar as they had been captivated by Babylon. **(3)** Certainly, there were some from the ten tribes among those returning from Babylon; but perhaps these were not those whom the Assyrians had originally captured, but those who had once joined the Kingdom of Judah and thus migrated with the Jews into the Babylonian exile. 2 Chronicles 11:13, 14, 16 and 15:9. **(4)** Even if some of the ten tribes captured by the Assyrians had returned with the Jews, this was not of such magnitude that the prophetic grandeur concerning the gathering of "all Israel" could be said to be fulfilled by it. Therefore, we prefer to place the outcome of this promise among those yet to come, along with Jansenius, who placed it "at the end." Nor is it an obstacle that the Messiah, of whom verse 13 speaks, has already come long ago. For similarly, Paul in Romans 11:26 connects the future conversion of all Israel with the coming of Christ that has already occurred, based on Isaiah 59:20. **k)** Jacob in his entirety, or "your whole collective." Isaiah 22:1; compare Ezekiel 36:10; Romans 11:12, 26, 32. **l)** Isaiah 40:11; Jeremiah 23:3. **m)** Chapter 5:6, 7; Hosea 10:20, etc.; Jeremiah 31:7.

**n)** *Equally*—that is, the whole, without distinction or exception. This is the force of the word used in Psalm 33:15 and Hosea 2:2. **o)** Genesis 21:13, 18; chapter 46:3. **p)** *Like the sheep of Bozrah.* By this emblem, the prophet elegantly signifies the expansion of Israel, both in sheer numbers and in the abundance of all things. See Jeremiah 33:12; Ezekiel 34:31, and 36:37. **q)** This was an Edomite city (Isaiah 63:1; Jeremiah 49:13) which was famous for its rich pastures and livestock. As a common noun, it signifies a "fortified city," such as the "City of God" in Isaiah 26:1. **r)** *Like a crowded flock.* Jeremiah 31:24. **s)** *In the midst of its fold.* **t)** Isaiah 5:17. **u)** *They shall make a noise.* The living Israelites will be like these folds; or rather, the Israelites themselves will multiply like sheep. The feminine ending in the Hebrew verb reflects the simile. This word comes from a root (Deuteronomy 7:23) signifying a commotion accompanied by sound and noise—the kind of sound a massive crowd of people makes. **w)** *Because of the multitude of men.* There will be so many people. The Targum <note>an ancient Aramaic translation</note> says "on account of the multitude of men." See Ezekiel 36:10, 37.

<margin>
**Verse 13. x)** *For the commander shall go up.* He will lead out the people who have been crushed by long captivity and servitude. This is a military term signifying an armed departure that enemies could not hope to stop. See Exodus 1:10; Hosea 2:2. **y)** *The breaker.* This is used with a definite article, meaning he is not speaking of some random person, but a specific one known by this <term>antonomasia</term> <note>a title used instead of a name</note>, who is soon called "their King" and "Jehovah"—namely, the Messiah. He will lead his people, and so...
</margin>

...the gate; like water when it breaks through a dam (2 Samuel 5:20). Some compare this to Ephesians 2:14. **z)** *Before them*—leading their front line, just as He did when He led the people out of Egypt (Exodus 13:21; Psalm 80:3; Isaiah 52:12). **a)** *Therefore they themselves will also break through.* All obstacles being shattered, they will follow Christ vigorously. The Leader's victory will not make them lazy; it will animate them. They will penetrate wherever they see the Leader has gone. Therefore, let us also "break through" the bonds of the flesh, the world, and Satan (Romans 8:6, 13) and lay a "glorious violence" upon the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 11:12), looking to Christ, the captain of our faith. **b)** *They shall pass through.* No one shall stop them. **c)** *They will break through the gate.* No gate will be so fortified that it can keep them out. **d)** *And they shall go out by it.* Just as they entered without resistance, they shall exit freely. Compare this to John 10:9: "He is the door... they shall go in and out." **e)** *For he shall pass.* **f)** This refers to the one whom the Israelites will seek "in the latter days" after long neglect (Hosea 3:5). **g)** *And Jehovah the Messiah.* **h)** *At their head*—or their first company; in French, *à leur tête*. This is the same as being "before them."

<column-break/>

**CHAPTER III.** **Verse 1. i)** While we are still far from those blessed times just promised, I spoke in the meantime to continue the prophetic <term>elenchus</term> <note>a logical cross-examination or rebuke</note> against the evil princes and teachers. This chapter is tightly linked to the last. The scholar Maius describes the argument thus: To the leaders of the state and church, the prophet denounces deserved punishments "in the power of the spirit" <note>original Greek: ἐν δυνάμει πνεύματος</note>. Specifically: I. To unjust judges who ignore the cries of the poor, God will deny His help (v. 1-5). II. To false prophets who "bite" and seek their own gain, God will take away their light (v. 5-8). III. To all of them together, for their shared crimes, the destruction of the State and Church (v. 9-12). **Chronologically**, there is no doubt this sermon belongs to the time of King Hezekiah. **l)** *Heads*—the leading men of Jacob. **m)** *And leaders.* See Ezekiel 22:6 and the whole of Psalm 82 regarding the rebuke of corrupt magistrates. **n)** This is an emphatic question that challenges the conscience of the princes. **o)** *It is for you*—it is your duty. The Syrian and Arabic translations read: "Was it not fitting for you?" **p)** *To know justice*—and to administer it. In Hebrew, "knowing" often implies care and affection; knowledge that does not lead to action is useless. **q)** *Justice*—regarding both the law courts (Isaiah 1:17) and moral law (worship due to God).

**Verse 2. r)** *Those who hate good.* The prophet compares their actions to the law. He is saying: "It is as I said, but if we look at your wicked practices, you have utterly renounced justice." Note that "good" and "evil" are treated here as abstract concepts. **t)** *Their skin*—that is, the skin of "my people," the innocent and poor. **u)** *From off them.* They are stripping the skin off by force. This refers to the crushing weight of taxes and burdens. This brings to mind the saying of the Emperor Tiberius (recorded by Suetonius), who told governors wanting to increase taxes that "a good shepherd shears his sheep, he doesn't flay them." The Targum says: "They are snatching the wealth of my people." **y)** *Their flesh from their bones.* They leave them as skeletons, exhausted by false accusations and heavy debts.

**Verse 3. x)** *Who devour.* He repeats the previous idea with new words to show how shameful it is. **a)** They flay them like butchers flaying cattle. **b)** *They break.* In one form of the verb, this means to burst into a shout of joy, but here it implies a "breaking" or "shattering." **c)** *And they divide.* They chop the people up like meat for a pot. The scholar Tarnovius says: "They plunder wealth and divide it for their own luxury and feasts... just as cooks slaughter miserable sheep and put them on the fire." He notes that God hates the excessive taxes of magistrates, no matter how they are excused. King David once refused to drink water brought at the risk of his men's lives; today, in some courts, it is considered a "virtue" to drink the blood (the substance) of the poor subjects. **d)** *Into the cauldron.* The word <term>qallachat</term> <note>cauldron</note> is related to the Greek word <term>chalkion</term> <note>bronze vessel</note>. It likely comes from a root meaning "to smooth with a hammer," referring to polished bronze.

<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on the Book of Micah, moving from the condemnation of the secular "princes" (the heads of the house of Jacob) in the first three verses of Chapter 3 to the divine silence they will face as punishment. It then introduces the second group of villains: the false prophets who exploit the people for profit.</meta>

# CHAPTER 3. MICAH 3.

<margin>
**v. 4. f)** *Then indeed.* This refers back (as we noted above at verse 1) to chapter 2, verse 3 and following. **g)** *But He will not answer them.* See Jeremiah 11:11, Hosea 5:6, Zechariah 7:13, Psalm 18:42, Proverbs 21:13, and Job 35:12. This does not take away from the truth of the divine promise that He hears all who call upon Him. For here, those are assumed who call upon God wickedly (James 4:3), not in truth (Psalm 145:18), but hypocritically, and only out of a sense of punishment (Proverbs 1:28, 24, and following), without conversion and faith (Isaiah 1:15, James 1:6). Johann Tarnovius <note>A 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> compares this kind of outcry to the tears of Esau in Genesis 27:34, 38 and Hebrews 12:17, and to the useless repentance of the damned in the Wisdom of Solomon 5:3. **h)** *And He will hide His face from them.* He will deem them worthy of no look of grace (Psalm 4:7), which is a sign of aversion and wrath (Isaiah 8:17, chapter 59:2; compare Isaiah 1:15). **i)** Some interpret this causally, "because," as the Greek Septuagint does with *anth' hon* <note>original Greek: ἀνθ’ ὧν, meaning "because of which"</note> as in Numbers 27:14, 1 Samuel 28:18, and Psalm 56:7. But the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> is more precise with "just as." Thus the causal meaning is included, but it more specifically suggests the justice of retaliation—the "law of the tooth"—in the relationship of the punishment to a similar fault. It is as if to say: those Princes who did not hear or respect the widows, orphans, and others oppressed by slander who cried out to them, shall now experience the same thing; what they have sown, they shall reap (Galatians 6:7; compare Proverbs 21:13, chapter 28:9, James 2:13). **k)** *They have done evil in their deeds.* 2 Samuel 12:25.
</margin>

<margin>
Compare chapter 28 and Ezekiel 13, etc. **m)** Those who lead people astray while promising a happy security (Isaiah 3:12, chapter 9:15, Ezekiel 13:10, Lamentations 2:14) and threatening ill-fortune against those who should not be threatened—both for the sake of their bellies (Ezekiel 13:19). **n)** *Biting.* Those who act like serpents (concerning their bite...

***

...that word is used properly, as seen in Genesis 49:17, Numbers 21:6, 8, 9, and Amos 5:19. They inflict poisonous and lethal strikes upon souls by teaching things that insinuate themselves like poison and cause harm. But Tarnovius argues that when they are given plenty to eat so they can tend to their stomachs, they then say pleasant things to the people; and thus, while "biting" pleasant food with their teeth, they proclaim peace. Similarly, Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note> describes those who, when offered banquets of meat, prophesy peace. These views are held because of the following opposing clause. However, the objection is that the Hebrew word <term>naschak</term> <note>original: נשך</note> never means "to chew food," but always "to inflict a harmful bite." **o)** *While they proclaim peace,* that is, prosperity of every kind (Jeremiah 6:14, chapter 8:11, Ezekiel 13:10). Observe, therefore, that there are some things that seem sweet and pleasant, but have a most harmful effect, like a poisonous bite (Proverbs 23:32; compare Proverbs 18:8). **p)** *And whoever does not put something in their mouths* for them to eat and feast upon (Genesis 25:28, Ecclesiastes 6:7). This argues that these prophets are far from being <term>anepachtheis</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνεπαχθεῖς, meaning "not burdensome" or "not greedy"</note> (1 Timothy 3:3, 8, Titus 1:7), serving their bellies and throats rather than God (Ezekiel 13:19, Romans 16:18). But Schmidt interprets: *whoever does not kiss their mouth* as a sign of flattery and veneration, perhaps from Genesis 41:40, but this is a bit forced. **q)** *They sanctify war against him,* that is, they stir up war with a solemn ritual. Regarding war, Gussetius <note>Jacques Gousset, a Hebrew scholar</note> says (page 733) it was a known custom, both in Israel and among other nations, to begin it with sacred ceremonies (Isaiah 13:4, Joel 4:9). Tarnovius extends the notion of "sanctification" here to mean they declare a "holy war" on account of injured religion. For such teachers dress up their own agendas with the beautiful title of religion, and seem to themselves and their followers to be great warriors of the Lord. (Compare the Preface to Hosea, section 6). **v. 6. r)** *Surely therefore,* because you are such as I described in verse 5. Note the connection: He had said "Thus says the Lord to the prophets," and to make it clear which prophets, He described them by their qualities. Now He explains what the Lord said, beginning immediately with the word "therefore," even though no direct speech has preceded yet; this implies we should repeat here what was said indirectly about the false prophets in verse 5. **s)** *Night and darkness* denote the black gloom of evils (Isaiah 21:11, Job 17:12; compare the note on Amos 5:18). **t)** We take this causally: *on account of the vision,* or as the Vulgate, Septuagint, and Syriac have rendered it, *from the vision.* As if to say: your prophecies, with which you deceived others, will become the cause and origin of immense evils for you. But Tarnovius **u)** takes it as privative, saying: *so that you are forced to cease from vision.* Thus Jonathan: "so that you do not prophesy anymore." And likewise the following *from divining* means "so that you do not divine henceforth" (Isaiah 1:1, Zechariah 13:4). **u)** *And darkness (v)* shall be. Or according to other books (on which see the Variant Readings below) "it shall become dark," used impersonally, meaning darkness will fall upon you. **x)** *Because of your divining* (verse 11, Ezekiel 22:28), or as a noun, *because of your divination,* following the <term>Segol</term> <note>a Hebrew vowel pattern</note> form like *isod*, etc. **y)** *For the sun will set,* and will leave the false prophets in a thick gloom of evils by which they will be suddenly overwhelmed. Jonathan: "and tribulation shall cover the false prophets like a mist" (Jeremiah 15:9, Amos 8:9). **z)** *And it shall become black,* like the sky when it is heavy with clouds gathered by a storm, bringing on a black gloom over the day (Joel 2:10, 1 Kings 18:45). Cocceius says: "All sad things will loom over them." **a)** This signifies that God's judgments will fall upon them unexpectedly, while it is still "full day" (Jeremiah 15:9) and "shining noon" (Amos 8:9)—at least as they thought, for they were imagining some fortunate and flourishing state for the people and persuading others to believe it. (Compare Preface to Hosea, section 4). **v. 7. b)** *And then indeed they shall be ashamed.* Past tense in the simple form, as in Isaiah 19:9. Their disgrace will be made public when everything turns out differently than they predicted (compare 2 Timothy 3:9). **c)** *The seers,* not in reality, but in their own and the people's opinion (Isaiah 28:15, Ezekiel 13:9). **d)** *And they shall be confounded* (Isaiah 1:29). **e)** *Vain diviners.* They are called this by their true nature, though they affected to be called seers (verses 6, 11; Deuteronomy 18:10, 14). **f)** *And they shall cover* (the Hebrew construction is "place a covering over") *the moustache*; like those who are ashamed, who do not want to be recognized, and who become unclean and detestable like lepers, mourning their miserable fate. For this was a ritual for lepers and mourners (Leviticus 13:45, 2 Samuel 19:25, Ezekiel 24:17, 22). Indeed, the shamed were also veiled (Song of Solomon 1:7, Psalm 89:46, Jeremiah 14:3, Esther 6:12, chapter 7:8). Jonathan adds: "like mourners." **g)** Using the part for the whole to mean the "mouth," as the Septuagint renders it in Leviticus 13:45. It is formed from <term>saphah</term> <note>original: שפה, meaning lip</note>, just as <term>pechah</term> (prince) in Nehemiah 5:14 is from <term>pechah</term>, and *Malkam* is from *Melek* (king), where the final letter is an addition. **h)** *Namely, because there is no answer from God.* But besides the fact that the Hebrew verb for "to answer" is rarely found in this specific form to mean simply "to respond" (even comparing Ecclesiastes 5:19), this form is in a construct state (see Variant Readings below) and thus is a noun rather than a participle. But even so, it is explained differently. Tarnovius says: "because there will be no hearing by God, since they refused to hear God until now" (verse 4; compare 1 Kings 18:26, 29). But the Vulgate: "because there is no answer of God," namely, *with* them, as they were boasting—for the outcome will make that clear. Jonathan also supports this: "the Spirit of prophecy from before the Lord is not in them." Thus it would be an explanatory phrase. As if to say: let no one wonder that I portend such things for the prophets, men whom God is believed to dignify with His speech: "because," etc. I would prefer to interpret the cause of mourning as the future withdrawal of the prophetic word, which Jeremiah also laments in the name of the captives (Lamentations 2:9) and Ezekiel predicts (chapter 7:26). As if to say: they feigned answers from God that I had not given; therefore, as punishment for this rashness, I will take away even the true answers, so that in the time of evil they shall have no one to tell them "how long" in the name of God, as the Psalmist says in Psalm 74:9. **v. 8. i)** *Nevertheless* (Genesis 48:19, 1 Kings 20:23). Although those who call themselves prophets not only fail to rebuke the sins of the Princes and the whole people but even approve of them (verse 5), there are still some, however few, who by divine power and an entirely fearless spirit rebuke the rebellion of Jacob; among whom, by the grace of God, I also am. **k)** In opposition to those evil prophets in verse 5. As if to say: I am not like those who rashly claim the prophetic name and office for themselves (compare 2 Corinthians 2:17, chapter 3:1). As Tarnovius observes, he proclaims the gifts granted to him by God not out of ambition, but out of necessity, just as Paul does in 2 Corinthians 10:11-13, Ephesians 3:4, and Philippians 3:4. **l)** *I am filled and full.* Therefore, whatever I speak is not out of some boldness of heart (Esther 7:5), but from the abundance of the divine Spirit (Jeremiah 6:11, Acts 6:3, 5, 8, chapter 7:55, chapter 11:24, 2 Corinthians 4:13).

<margin>
**v. 5. l)** Jonathan calls them "False Prophets." For they were such in truth, although they claimed the name of Prophet. They are those of whom he said in chapter 2:11 that they teach according to the palate concerning wine and strong drink. He joins these to the evil Princes because they both approved of their wickedness and were, along with them, the moral cause of the destruction of Jerusalem (verse 12). The "Beast" and the "False Prophet" usually go together and help each other (Revelation 19:20; compare Jeremiah 23:9 and following).
</margin>

->CHAPTER III. v. 6. *Night.* Marked with a <term>Rebhia</term> <note>a Hebrew accent mark</note> in versions 2, 6, 9, 20, and 23, against the Masoretic text 1 and 3, and the Erfurt edition. *And darkness* with a <term>Metheg</term> (see the notes to the text) in versions 7, 8, 22, 23, 24, and the Hebrew Concordance. v. 7. *Answer.* Here with a <term>Tsere</term> vowel in 2, 5, 6, 12, 19, 15, 20, 22, 23, and 24; so also in version 1 according to the Masoretes, version 2, and the Erfurt edition. Others use a <term>Segol</term> vowel.<-

**m)** with virtue or strength. See Matthew 7:29, Acts 1:8, 2:1, and 1 Corinthians 2:4. **n)** *with the Spirit of the Lord* (chapter 2:7). For where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is both strength and <term>boldness</term> <note>original Greek: παρρησία (parrhēsía), meaning "fearless confidence"</note>, and an intrepid mind. There are some who translate this as "from the Spirit," as if the Hebrew preposition used here was the same as *me'et* <note>original Hebrew: מאת, meaning "from"</note> in Genesis 49:25; but that meaning is neither certain enough, nor necessary here. According to our explanation, the first half of the verse encompasses two propositions: I. I am filled with the Spirit of the Lord; II. And along with the Spirit, I am also filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely 1. strength, 2. judgment, and 3. fortitude. See Job 32:8–9. **o)** *and judgment*, for the purpose of contending with my people and rebuking them for their impiety. See the note on Ezekiel 20:4. **p)** *and fortitude.* See Isaiah 11:2. **q)** *to declare* freely and without fear. This is contrasted with fearful and flattering concealment in Ezekiel 3:9 and Job 21:31. **r)** See chapter 1:5 and Isaiah 58:1.

**v. 9. s)** *And so that you may take a new trial of that divine strength of which I just spoke, listen, therefore, I pray.* See verse 1. **u)** *abhorring* (Amos 5:10). **x)** which was yours not only to know, but even to love and care for (verse 1). **y)** *and who—pervert.* Understanding the relative pronoun "who" <note>original Hebrew: אשר (asher)</note>, which in Hebrew tends to change from the first or second person into the third. **z)** *pervert all that is right.* They make crooked whatever is straight by entangling good causes. This is a metaphor transferred from a path to the process of law; compare Ephesians 5:8. It is contrasted with integrity in judging cases in Proverbs 10:9 and 28:18. A similar figure of speech is found in Amos 2:7; compare Ephesians 5:20.

**v. 10. a)** *Of which each one builds, forsooth!* This is an irony <note>original Latin: Ironia</note>—as if to say: "You certainly seem to yourselves to be building Zion splendidly, that is, to be deserving well of her and promoting her advantages; and indeed you ought to; but *how* are you building?"

He joins the Princes, Priests, and Prophets together as partners in wickedness, as in Ezekiel 22:25 and following, and Zephaniah 3:3–4. **e)** *for a gift*, not according to what the justice of the cause demands

But in the last days it shall come to pass, that the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established in the top of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills; and people shall flow unto it. **1**

therefore, but according to the gifts that are given. See Exodus 23:8, Deuteronomy 16:19, Ephesians 1:23, Ezekiel 22:12, 27, Zephaniah 3:4, Sirach 20:31, and below in chapter 7:3. **f)** regarding their duty in instructing the people in the law, see Leviticus 10:11, Deuteronomy 33:10, and Malachi 2:15. **g)** *they teach for a price*, not as if it were entirely unlawful for priests and teachers of the Word to receive a salary; (for the laborer is worthy of his food and his reward, Matthew 10:10, 1 Corinthians 9:7–14, Galatians 6:6, 1 Timothy 5:18; indeed in Malachi 3:8, 10 and Nehemiah 13:10–12, the Jewish people are rebuked because they had not paid the tithes for the support of the priests, and God himself had fixed salaries for the priests in Numbers 18:8 and following); but rather because they measured their doctrine by profit, and tempered it toward gain, teaching those things which would please the people and which they hoped would bring in some little bit of lucre. This <term>shameful greed</term> <note>original Greek: αἰσχροκέρדεια (aischrokerdeia), meaning "greedy for dishonest gain"</note> in the ministers of the Church is rightly condemned in 1 Timothy 3:3, 8, Titus 1:7, 11, and 1 Peter 5:2. **h)** Ezekiel 22:28. **i)** *for silver.* As each person pays out coins liberally, so they prophesy for him: they hold for sale the prophecies that each person likes. They love the wages of unrighteousness (2 Peter 2:15; compare Acts 8:20). **k)** *they divine* rather than prophesy <note>original Latin: divinant potius quam vaticinantur</note>. See the note on verse 7, namely as Balaam did in Joshua 13:22; see also 2 Kings 17:17, Isaiah 3:2, and Ezekiel 13:23. **l)** *and yet they lean upon Jehovah* (Isaiah 10:20), that is, they make a show of confidence in God, promising themselves all the best things from Him, as if they were the kind of nation that practiced righteousness and had not abandoned the law of its God (Isaiah 58:2). The Prophet marvels at the impudence of these men, that they promise themselves the grace of God while in their sins. Let us therefore also learn that trust in the merit of Christ is vain as long as one maliciously persists in sins. Compare Jeremiah 7:4–5 and following, and 1 John 3:7–8. **m)** A question full of emotion, as if it were impiety even to doubt the Lord’s favor; such was the stubbornness of their persuasion. **n)** *is* and will continue to be *among us*; namely, with His grace and favor (Leviticus 26:11–12, Numbers 14:42, Isaiah 58:2; compare Amos 5:14). Or the sense is: He is among us; He has His Temple among us, which He will not allow to be cut off (Exodus 25:8, 1 Kings 6:13). Therefore the evil that Micah and Isaiah threaten will not come upon us. And truly, confidence in the temple made the Jews feel secure (Jeremiah 7:4; compare Acts 6:13). **o)** See Jeremiah 5:12 and following, chapter 23:17, and Amos 6:3.

<column-break/>

**v. 12. p)** *on your account* (Deuteronomy 1:37, chapter 18:12)—meaning the princes, priests, and prophets of verse 11, since from them all corruption flowed into the Commonwealth and the Church; though the fault of the people is not excluded. He means to say: even if I were most inclined to spare Zion and Jerusalem, yet on your account I cannot spare them. **q)** *it shall be plowed as a field*, that is, it will be so overturned that hardly a trace of the city remains, as part turns into fields, part into ruins, and part into forest. (Tarnovius). Compare above, chapter 1:6. Furthermore, this entire verse is cited in Jeremiah 26:18, and from the same source (verse 19) it is evident that this sermon of Micah was not without remarkable fruit, for the King humbly besought God, and the punishment was delayed. **r)** Jeremiah 9:10. **s)** chapter 1:6, Psalm 79:1. **t)** see chapter 4:1–2. **u)** see Hosea 2:14. 

**CHAPTER IV, VERSE 1. x)** *Yet it shall happen.* This chapter is thus to be connected with Chapter III, and especially with its last verse, 12. For just as he had threatened destruction to Zion, Jerusalem, and the mountain of the house of the Lord because of the sins of the leaders in particular, so now, for the comfort of the afflicted Church, he offers a good omen to the same; and, so that this connection may immediately meet the eye, he designates the object of his prophecy by the same names as above: namely, the mountain of the house of the Lord (verses 1, 2) and Zion and Jerusalem (verse 2). We observe this modestly against the celebrated Maius (Oec. V. T. p. 941). Now, this passage deals with the kingdom of Christ, which is to be erected in place of the collapsed earthly one. The Prophet describes it at the beginning of the chapter in almost the same words as Isaiah (chapter 2:2 and following). And it is, as S. has well observed: I. A simple <term>prelude</term> <note>original Latin: Protasis, meaning the first part of a proposition</note> of the Evangelical promise concerning the kingdom of Christ under the New Testament and the conversion of the nations (verses 1–7). II. An application of the same to the afflicted and oppressed Church (verse 8 to the end). **y)** namely, in the time of the New Testament; see Hebrews 1:1 and the note on Isaiah 2:2. **z)** *the mountain of the house of the LORD* (Psalm 24:3, 2 Chronicles 33:15), that is, the New Testament Church, which is the house of God (1 Timothy 3:15, Hebrews 3:6) and His living temple (1 Corinthians 3:16, 2 Corinthians 6:16, 1 Peter 2:5), the eminence and dignity of which the prophet depicts here with typical and allegorical phrases. Compare Ezekiel 40:2. **a)** *firmly established*, so that it can never be cast down from its summit. The verb here is <term>pregnant</term> <note>meaning the word carries extra weight or implied meaning beyond the literal</note> in this place; it does not just mean "placed," but emphatically denotes the firmness of that placement. See the note on Isaiah 2:2. **b)** *at the summit of the mountains.* The Church of God will be placed in an illustrious location, so that all the nations of the world will subject themselves to it. This whole speech is allegorical, to be understood spiritually. For if Mount Moriah were understood literally, compared to other mountains it is only like a small hill. See Psalm 68:16 and following. **c)** *and they shall flow upon it.* This denotes a copious, spontaneous, and continuous flow, like that of a running river (Jeremiah 31:12). **d)** not Israelites alone, but all (verse 2; Isaiah 2:2). See Isaiah 60:5. **v. 2. e)** *For they shall go*, excited by the sound of the Gospel. A further exposition of the last clause of verse 1 (Isaiah 60:3, Jeremiah 16:19; see Hosea 11:10). **f)** according to the promise made to Abraham (Genesis 12:3), but most frequently confirmed by the Prophets. See Isaiah 11:10, chapter 42:6, Jeremiah 3:17, Zechariah 8:20–22. For the "middle wall" that has separated the nations and Israel until now will be broken down (Ephesians 2:14–15), and thus many more will frequent this temple than before, which had been made by hands.

But, says Tarnovius <note>Johann Tarnow, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note>, are there not wars among Christians? And is it lawful to wage war? He says it is indeed lawful against the wicked, which pertains to punitive justice. Nor should those who pursue war seek anything other than that life may be lived in peace. Yet this remains always true: if everyone lived according to the Gospel, there would be no wars, no discord, nor enmity among men. Thus far he speaks. Furthermore, Matthew 10:34 and Luke 12:51 (where Christ says He came not to bring peace but a sword) should not be opposed to this passage. For that happens incidentally through the malice of men; Christians do not stir up these troubles, but rather suffer them. For the rest, the full and final fulfillment of this prophecy may still remain for the very last period of the Church.

<margin>
**v. 4. c)** *And they shall sit*, namely, securely; this is the force of the word as used also in chapter 5:3. Compare Isaiah 32:18.
**d)** This was the state of things under the most flourishing reign of Solomon (1 Kings 5:5). A proverbial expression. The meaning: they will cultivate figs and vines securely, untroubled by any enemy invasions. Compare Zechariah 3:10; 22:6; Isaiah 65:21, 22.
**e)** So that there is no one to cause terror. Leviticus 26:6, Ezekiel 34:28, Zephaniah 3:13.
**f)** Which is most certain, because...
**g)** Since this promise might seem very difficult, it is confirmed by the person of the promiser, Jehovah, who cannot lie and for whom nothing is difficult, much less impossible <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατον (adynaton)</note>. Isaiah 14:27. Tarnovius. Compare Isaiah 1:20, 40:5, 58:14.
**h)** Isaiah 1:24, Hosea 12:6.
</margin>

Another very full confirmation of the promise, from a comparison of the true God with other false ones, and of the people who trust in Him and will endure forever, with others perishing in their superstition. Tarnovius. **k)** Inasmuch as they are separated from the true God and the fellowship of His Church (see above, verses 1, 2, 3) and are instead addicted to their most vain idols. Compare Isaiah 44:18 and following. **l)** They walk in the name of their gods, who are nevertheless not gods. Jeremiah 2:11; compare Jonah 1:5. Therefore, it is no wonder they are shamefully deceived by their hope, which they place in "little gods." **m)** *But we*; or, "Therefore we much more," who know and worship Jehovah, the true God. This is also an argument from the lesser to the greater. **n)** Just as "walking" for the Hebrews generally denotes the constant pattern and course of actions and pursuits (see verse 2), so to "walk in the name of Jehovah" is to acknowledge and profess Jehovah as the author, patron, and presiding head of all one's actions, and to refer everything faithfully to His will and His help. Zechariah 10:12, Psalm 20:6, 8, Colossians 3:17. **o)** So that nothing ever moves us from trust in His promises. Compare Matthew 16:18, Romans 8:38, 39, Psalm 62:7, 9.

For it follows immediately: "and her whom I have afflicted." Others interpret this as referring to guilt. Cocceius's Lexicon: "limping, not walking uprightly in the way of the Lord, falling to one side." So also Gousset, *Prophetic Theology*, page 708. Compare Isaiah 33:23, 24; 35:6; Psalm 35:15.
**t)** *and driven out* from the flock or fold. Deuteronomy 30:4, Ezekiel 34:16, Zephaniah 3:19.
**u)** Chapter 2:12, Isaiah 56:8.
**x)** *And whom I have in any way afflicted*, or treated poorly. Jonathan adds: "because of the sins of my people." Exodus 5:22, 23.

**b)** *dispersed far off.* The form of the participle is from *hal'ah* <note>original Hebrew: הלאה</note>, meaning "further," which denotes a remote limit. Amos 5:27.
**c)** *numerous*, with her children multiplied not only from her own race but from foreigners as well. See verse 3 and Isaiah 60:22.

Jeremiah 23:6. Compare above, chapter 2:13, also Isaiah 24:23, 33:17, 22, 52:7, Obadiah 21, Zechariah 14:9, Daniel 7:14, Luke 1:32. Jonathan: "and the kingdom of the Lord shall be revealed over them."
**e)** See verses 1, 2, and chapter 3:12.

<margin>
**f)** Not so much from the time of the prediction, as from the time of its fulfillment, or from "this day" which the Prophet mentioned in verse 6. The Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> seems to have had this in mind when it translates: *from this time forth*. Compare Isaiah 9:6. **g)** Compare Daniel 2:44.
**verse 8. h)** *As for you, then.* Here begins the second part of the chapter, according to the division we gave above at verse 1. **i)** A proper name of an obscure small village or farm in the vicinity of Ephrath or Bethlehem. Genesis 35:21; compare also verses 16 and 19. The name means "Tower of the Flock," perhaps because it was a place for gathering or protecting flocks. Jerome <note>An early Christian scholar and Bible translator</note> says in his *On Hebrew Places*: "Bethlehem, the city of David... and about a thousand paces away is the tower of Ader, which is interpreted as 'the tower of the flock,' signifying by a certain prophecy that the shepherds were the first to know of the Lord's birth." However, it is used here by way of a figure of speech <term>metalepsis: a rhetorical figure where one word is used to refer to a related concept</term> for the Bethlehemite line of Jesse, from which David once received the kingdom of Israel, and where the Messiah was later to be born and reign. This passage, therefore, concerns the eminence and dignity of the line of Jesse, and consequently of all Zion, which it was to achieve in its own time through Christ and His kingdom. See the notes on Genesis 35:21. For Abraham ibn Ezra <note>A celebrated Spanish Jewish scholar of the 12th century</note> correctly observes on this passage: "From here until the end, he speaks concerning the matter of the Messiah." So also Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase</note>: *"And you, King Messiah, who are hidden because of the sins of the congregation of Zion (though this suggests a Jewish error, unless you understand it more correctly from Isaiah 8:17, 59:2, 64:6, etc.), to you the kingdom shall come, and the first dominion shall come to the kingdom of the congregation of Jerusalem."* To be sure, there are some who think that a tower built in Jerusalem at the Sheep Gate or <term>probatike</term> <note>Greek for "pertaining to sheep," often referring to the Sheep Gate in Jerusalem</note> is meant; compare Nehemiah 3:1 and John 5:2. But no reason appears why this glory of which the Prophet speaks should peculiarly belong to that gate in Jerusalem.
</margin>

<column-break/>

### ^f ^g from now and forever.
### ^h And you, O Tower of the Flock, ^i the hill of the daughter of Zion, ^k to you it shall come; ^l the former dominion shall come, ^m the kingdom to the daughter of Jerusalem. 8
### ^n Now why do you cry out aloud? ^o Is there no king in you? Has your counselor perished? ^p For pain has seized you ^q like a woman in labor. 9
### ^r Writhe and groan, daughter of Zion, like a woman in labor; for now you shall go out ^s from the city and dwell in the field; ^t and you shall go to Babylon. ^u There you shall be delivered; ^x there the LORD will redeem you from the hand of your enemies. ^y ^z 10

### ^a ^b Arise and thresh, ^c daughter of Zion; for I will make your horn ^d iron. ^e 13

<column-break/>

<margin>
**k)** This is either a description of what preceded, meaning "you who are the hill of the daughter of Zion," that is, of the Judean kingdom; thus the site of the tower would be noted as being on higher ground. Or it is an <term>asyndeton</term> <note>a figure of speech where conjunctions are omitted</note> for "and the hill." In this way, it would be the "fertile hill," a part of the eastern side of Mount Zion, next to which was Mount Moriah. Nehemiah 3:26, 27; 2 Chronicles 27:3, 33:14.
</margin>

---

**l)** This can be translated simply as *to you* (Job 4:5; 32:11, 12), or emphatically as *all the way to you*; for this usually denotes an affection for a goal that is far distant. It is as if he were saying: You will wait for this kingdom for a long time and with anxiety, but at last it will reach the finish line and come to you. **m)** *It shall come.* Isaiah 21:12. Note here the emphasis of the <term>Athnach</term> <note>a Hebrew musical/grammatical mark indicating a major pause</note> in a sentence that is not yet complete. For what was to come is only explained in the following half-verse. Thus the pause holds the reader's mind in suspense for a while, to make them more attentive to what follows. **n)** *It shall come, I say.* Habakkuk 2:3. **o)** Dominion. 1 Kings 9:19. **p)** *The former,* such as it once was under David and Solomon in a physical and symbolic way. Compare Isaiah 1:26, Jeremiah 33:7, 11, and what we noted above at verse 4. **q)** *The kingdom, I say,* which belonged to or will belong to the daughter of Jerusalem.

**verse 9. r)** Since this is so, then *now*. This is a logical connector by which he applies that promise to the mourning Zion to soothe her pain. He says: Having such a certain promise of such an excellent kingdom, why do you not comfort yourself and moderate your excessive grief over the earthly kingdom being taken away? **s)** *You cry out with shouting* or *by vociferation* (Judges 7:21; Joel 2:1), that is, incessantly and excessively, as if it were completely and finally over for you. Isaiah 49:14. **t)** *Is there no King in you?* You have indeed lost an earthly king, you have lost your princely counselors, and you weep for this unrestrainedly; compare Lamentations 4:20. But do you therefore have no King and counselor at all anymore, not even God? The meaning is: You certainly do have one. Compare Isaiah 33:22. Therefore, restrain your grief. See also Hosea 10:3. **u)** *Is your counselor* [gone]? Isaiah 3:3, 9:5. **x)** Micah 7:2, Zechariah 9:5. **y)** *Because it has seized you.* Jeremiah 8:21. **z)** Jonathan: *"distress and trembling, like the pains of a woman giving birth."* Jeremiah 6:24, 50:43; compare Isaiah 13:8, Jeremiah 4:31, Hosea 13:13.

**verse 10. a)** *Be in labor.* Isaiah 66:8. This is the command of one offering comfort. He says: Only endure patiently and bravely what God inflicts upon you; for your pain will be followed by no less joy than that of a woman when she has given birth. Compare John 16:21. **b)** And *bring forth*. Judges 20:33, Ezekiel 32:2. The root <language>heb</language>גוח in general denotes motion with force; here, therefore, it specifically denotes the force of a woman in labor, with which she moves, turns, and strains so that the fetus may break out from the womb. Compare Psalm 22:10. It is close to the Arabic *gachach*, "to come out" or "send forth." **c)** Verse 9, Isaiah 42:14. **d)** *For*, so that you may not be ignorant of what fates hang over you. **e)** *Right now*, or *soon*. In this context, this "for" marks a third comparison of imminent evil with the corresponding comfort (namely, verse 10, verse 11 and following, and verse 14 and following). This observation is of some importance for demonstrating the very close connection of Chapter 5 with Chapter 4:14. He says "right now" or "soon" regarding something very close at hand, relative to the promised liberation. Compare 5:3, 7:4, 10; Isaiah 43:19. **f)** *You shall go out from the city* which you have inhabited until now. 1 Kings 1:41, 45. The Prophet is hinting at the Babylonian deportation. Compare 2 Kings 24:14, 25:11, 21. **h)** *And you shall dwell in the field*, namely, of the nations or the Babylonian empire, just as formerly after the exit from Egypt in the open fields of the desert. Jeremiah 17:6, Psalm 120:5, 6. See Ezekiel 20:35, 36 and Hosea 2:16. **i)** *But although you shall go.* We connect it this way because of the accents. **k)** *All the way to Babylon*, which is a remote region for you. Isaiah 39:3; see the note above on verse 8. **l)** *Nevertheless, there you shall be rescued.* That captivity too will have its end. Compare Amos 3:12, Psalm 34:18. **m)** *For there He will redeem you* or vindicate you as His special possession, which had been sold to enemies for no price because of sins (Isaiah 50:1, 52:3), and which the Lord will therefore reclaim from their unjust detention. Compare Leviticus 25:24 ff., Exodus 6:6, and the note on Isaiah 41:4. **n)** Judges 1:14.

**verse 11. o)** *And now*, or *even*, we have observed here a prophetic repetition. **p)** *They shall indeed gather themselves*, with the intention of wasting and utterly destroying. Hosea 10:10, Zechariah 12:3, Psalm 35:15. **q)** The Chaldeans <note>The people of Babylon</note> with their subject and allied nations, the Ammonites, Edomites, etc. Compare Lamentations 1:10. **r)** *Let her be defiled.* Psalm 106:38. So that she who was once called the holy city may be foul and profane in the future. **s)** *And let it see its pleasure—each of our eyes.* Micah 7:10, Obadiah 12, 13, Psalm 35:21. It denotes <term>epichairekakia</term> <note>Greek: joy at the misfortune of others</note> stemming from hatred. Compare Psalm 137:7, Lamentations 1:7, 2:16, 3:46, 4:21. **t)** Jonathan: *"against the assembly of Zion."*

**verse 12. u)** *But those* who come with a profane mind to waste you and presume almost to destroy you. **x)** Namely, His *secret* thoughts (Psalm 92:6) which are very different from their thoughts (Isaiah 55:8), tending toward your peace and good (Jeremiah 29:11) and toward inflicting the punishment of destruction on their enemies. **y)** *His counsel*, which is that you, having been corrected through them, should return to favor, while they finally perish miserably because of their cruelty. Compare Isaiah 10:7, 8, 46:10, 11, Zechariah 1:15 ff. **z)** *For*, to explain this counsel of God as it concerns the enemies. **a)** *He will gather them.* Past tense used for the future. **b)** *Like sheaves* of the harvest that has been cut and is now to be threshed. (d) Jeremiah 9:21, Amos 2:13. **c)** *To the threshing floor*, for the sake of tribulation. Compare verse 10 and Jeremiah 51:33. Just as crops are mowed and then ground on the threshing floor when they have ripened, so He will punish the enemies at the right time when, the measure of sin being full, they have ripened for His judgments. Compare Joel 4:13.

**verse 13. d)** *Arise then*, you who have been lying mourning in ashes and filth. Isaiah 52:2. A prophetic command. **e)** *And thresh the nations*, partly spiritually, by subjecting them to the kingdom of Christ through the Gospel; but also, and what our context most intends, punitively, by taking vengeance on your stubbornly wicked persecutors. Isaiah 41:15, Habakkuk 3:12. The Jews did nothing of this sort when they returned from captivity; therefore the fulfillment of this promise remains for the people of God in the New Testament. **f)** *For*, lest you perhaps plead your weakness. **g)** With which you will strike the enemies. Deuteronomy 33:17, 1 Samuel 2:10, Psalm 75:11. Because among the Jews the work of oxen was used to thresh grain (Deuteronomy 25:4, 1 Corinthians 9:9, 1 Timothy 5:18), she is compared to these; and in this respect horns and hooves are attributed to her. Compare the note on Isaiah 28:27. **h)** *I will make iron*, that is, of iron. Compare 1 Kings 22:11.

<summary>This page provides a detailed commentary on Micah 4:8-13, interpreting the "Tower of the Flock" as the Messianic lineage of David. It explains the prophecy of the Babylonian exile not as an end, but as a necessary labor pain leading to the ultimate redemption and the spiritual or literal "threshing" of the oppressive nations.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Micah chapter 4, which describes the judgment of Israel’s enemies and the suffering of its leaders, to the famous prophecy in Micah chapter 5 regarding the birth of the Messiah in Bethlehem. It reconciles the historical humiliation of the Davidic kings with the future glory of an eternal Ruler.</meta>

Rabshakeh <note>The chief messenger of the Assyrian King Sennacherib</note> was sent there with a select hand of troops to demand the surrender of the city, who is read to have returned immediately from there to Sennacherib in 2 Kings 18 and 19:8. **y)** Through shared
