</margin>

suffering, the Prophet speaks in the first person. <gloss>z)</gloss> "And they shall strike with a rod" *Isaiah 10:24.* Schmidt <note>Erasmus Schmidt, a 17th-century scholar</note> suggests a rod merely striking, as if it were a diminishing blow; but the following phrase "upon the cheek," as well as the personal object "the judge of Israel," seems rather to exaggerate the evil. It is as if to say: they shall treat the Judge of Israel himself in the most unworthy ways. <gloss>a)</gloss> *Upon the cheek*, which is the height of indignity. *Job 16:10, 1 Kings 22:24, Mark 14:65, John 19:3. b)* The Judge himself or (according to the Targum) the Judges of Israel. Compare *Hosea 13:11.* Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot, an English Hebraist</note> in his *Chronicle* page 108, whom the celebrated Maius follows on page 943, thinks Hezekiah is intended, against whom Sennacherib's reproaches are read like a shower of blows in *2 Kings 18:19 and Isaiah 36, 37.* Truly, however, from what precedes, and especially from verse 10, it is clear that the Prophet is not dealing here so much with the Assyrian invasion as with the Babylonian invasion of Nebuchadnezzar. Therefore, we might say Zedekiah is intended, who was captured by the Chaldeans in flight, and having been condemned by Nebuchadnezzar, the miserable man saw the slaughter not only of the princes but also of his own sons, and was himself later blinded and led away to Babylon. See *2 Kings 25:5 and following* and compare *Lamentations 4:20.* **CHAPTER V. verse 1. c)** The Syriac version says: *But you*; by way of contrast, as if to say: Although the city of Jerusalem shall be taken, and the King of Israel himself shall be treated most unworthily (as seen in *4:14*); yet Zion must not despair for that reason: for in His own time, He will give to Israel a Deliverer and a Ruler from Bethlehem, who will abundantly compensate for the loss of the kingdom and the Republic taken away by the Babylonians. As the birth of Christ from a virgin, says Lightfoot, was a sign to Ahaz, so His birth in Bethlehem is established as a sign in the days of Hezekiah. Compare what we noted at *4:10* concerning the connection of this chapter with the preceding one. In this chapter, therefore, the Prophet is entirely focused on proceeding to comfort afflicted Zion with promises of the Kingdom of Christ. According to Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow, a Lutheran theologian</note>, there are two parts, just as two persons speak here: I. A promise made by the Prophet, concerning the birth, Person, Church, and kingdom of Christ (verses 1-8). II. A confirmation added by Christ Himself (verses 9 and following), where three ways are set forth by which He would wonderfully save Zion, namely by removing 1) external protections (verses 9, 10), 2) idolatry (verses 11, 12, 13), and 3) the enemies of the Church (verse 14). Furthermore, the masculine gender used here and in the following words <term>mimmeka</term> <note>original: "from you"</note> and <term>tza'ir</term> <note>original: "little"</note> refers to the grammatical ending of the name *Bethlehem*, although otherwise, as the proper name of a city, it is feminine in its meaning. Compare notes on *2 Kings 15:16, Ezekiel 22:4, Hosea 10:7.* **d)** In the tribe of Judah *Matthew 2:6*, formerly the hometown of Jesse, and of the Davidic family that arose from him, *1 Samuel 17:12, Luke 2:4, 11, John 7:42.* **e)** Which is also called *Ephratah* in *Genesis 35:19, 48:7, 1 Chronicles 4:4.* The synonym is added to avoid ambiguity: for there was also another Bethlehem in the territory of Zebulun *Joshua 19:15.* **f)** You are indeed too small to be, and so forth. So say the Targum, the Syriac, and the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>. As if to say: you are indeed a small and lowly little town *Genesis 19:20, Judges 6:15, Psalm 119:141* and hardly worthy to be numbered among the thousands of Judah; (for it is called a "village" in *John 7:42*); yet from you shall come forth, etc., and by this means you shall by no means be the least. For so Matthew quotes it in *Matthew 2:6*. And the reconciliation between Micah and Matthew is easy. Micah calls it "small," looking at the town's outward state; Matthew calls it "not the least," looking at the birth of the Messiah, by which that town was wonderfully decorated and made illustrious. Others read it as a question, but more forced: "Would you be small among the thousands of Judah? And yet from you, etc." But Pococke <note>Edward Pococke, a 17th-century Orientalist</note> recognizes contrary meanings in this word, namely "small" and "Great"; and translates: *You shall be a Prince, i.e., primary.* And so Rabbi Tanchum and others cited by him, comparing *Jeremiah 48:4, Zechariah 13:7.* Truly, the syntax of the verb <term>lihyot</term> <note>original: "to be"</note> favors the first explanation more, nor should a <term>contradiction of meaning</term> <note>original: "ἐναντιότης" (opposition)</note> be invented at all, at least not without necessity. Finally, it could also be explained thus: *It is a small thing for you to be among the thousands of Judah, which dignity you have had until now; for in addition, from you shall come forth for me, etc., which dignity will far surpass that former one.* Thus compare *Isaiah 49:6.* But in the explanation of Scripture, the simpler something is, the more perfect it is. **g)** For the people of Israel were divided into their districts of thousands *Judges 6:15*, over each of which <term>leaders</term> <note>original: "ἡγεμόνες"</note> presided *Exodus 18:21, Numbers 1:16, Deuteronomy 33:17, Joshua 22:14, 1 Samuel 23:23*; hence in *Matthew 2:6* it is <term>among the leaders of Judah</term>, understanding the princes with their thousands. **h)** Yet, or nevertheless, from you, notwithstanding this smallness of yours. **i)** *For me*, says the Prophet in the name of his whole people, comparing the plural "against us" in *4:14*. Or it is a mixed speech: *for me*, namely the Lord, i.e., by my will and effect. **k)** *One shall come forth*, through birth from a virgin. The Targum supplies the subject *Messiah*. So say David Kimchi, Rashi, and Abendana. This is therefore the manifest meaning concerning the place of Christ's birth, which was also beyond doubt among the ancients, compare *Matthew 2:6 and John 7:42*; and so we do not dwell on the trifles of Abendana, who cavils that the Messiah was not to be born in Bethlehem, but only from the Bethlehemite family of David. **l)** That he may be the Ruler *Zechariah 6:13, Psalm 8:7, Psalm 22:29.* Compare *Judges 8:23, 2 Samuel 23:3, Isaiah 16:1, Jeremiah 30:21* also *Ezekiel 34:24.* **m)** Whose goings forth, however, are from eternity, through eternal generation from God the Father: for He is the Only Begotten of the Father *John 1:18.* The Firstborn of all creation *Colossians 1:15.* Who is before all things *verse 17, Proverbs 8:22, 23.* So that He did not then first begin to exist when He was born in Bethlehem; but was long before and from eternity. For just as the preceding "He shall come forth" indicates the birth of Christ according to the flesh, so these "goings forth" indicate His birth or generation according to the Divine nature. And the plural is indeed emphatic, either so that the excellence and magnitude of the matter may be signaled, or, as pleases most, so that a continuous act may be denoted, according to *Psalm 2:7, "Today I have begotten You."* Moreover, compare "goings out" used of birth or generation in *Genesis 17:6, Judges 8:30, Isaiah 39:7, Zechariah 4:7.* **n)** The Septuagint says <term>from the beginning</term> <note>original: "ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς"</note>, which compare with *John 1:1 and 1 John 1:1.* The Targum: "whose name was spoken from eternity or the beginnings of things." So the same on *Zechariah 4:7*, "before the world was founded," as they explain this passage in *Pirkei Eliezer* chapter 2. Used of God, it denotes eternity in *Deuteronomy 33:27, Habakkuk 1:12, Psalm 55:19, Proverbs 8:22, 23.* **o)** From the days of eternity *Isaiah 40:28, Proverbs 8:23.* These things seem indeed to be <term>incompatible</term> <note>original: "ἀσύστατα"</note>, days and eternity; but Scripture, says Tarnovius on this passage, speaks to us condescendingly <term>in human terms</term> <note>original: "ἀνθρωποπαθῶς"</note>. Just as we imagine there to be a place above the highest sphere, although in truth there is not, so also before time and in eternity we conceive of days and time as it were, because we cannot otherwise conceive how the Apostle sometimes calls eternity itself *eternal times*; not because they are such, if you take them physically, but because they seem so to us. Thus God is called the Ancient of Days in *Daniel 7:9.*

It is a noun, as in *Isaiah 45:2, Job 40:18.* **l)** and you shall crush, like chaff when the grain is threshed. *Isaiah 28:28, 41:15.* **m)** compare *5:7, 8, Zechariah 12:6.* **n)** and I will devote, I will entirely assign and consecrate *Leviticus 27:28, Joshua 6:18. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Micah chapter 5. The previous page ended with the prophecy of the ruler coming out of Bethlehem. This page explains the abandonment of Israel until the Messianic birth, the peaceful reign of the Shepherd-King, and the defense against "the Assyrian" (symbolizing the enemies of the Church). It draws on various commentators like Abendana and Tarnovius.</meta>

# MICAH CHAPTER 5

<margin>
**verse 2. p)** *Therefore.* <note>original Latin: "Propterea igitur"</note> Because this is God’s counsel: to first afflict Zion because of its sins, and only then to restore it through Christ, who is to be born in Bethlehem. Compare verse 1 with chapter 4:14 and the preceding verses. **q)** *He will indeed give them up.* <note>original Latin: "tradet quidem eos Dominus"</note> The Lord will give them up by leaving them to various enemies (2 Chronicles 36:17) and even to their own perverse character and habits (Acts 7:42; Romans 1:24, 26, 28); however, this is not forever, but only for a time. **r)** *Until the time she who is in labor has given birth.* <note>original Latin: "usque ad tempus parituræ, cum pepererit"</note> That is, when she who is to give birth in Bethlehem has brought forth (verse 1). This is a Prophetic Enigma regarding Mary, the Mother of God <note>original Latin: "Maria Deipara"</note>, who is called "She who is in labor" by way of excellence <note>term: antonomastically (using a title or description as a proper name)</note>, just as the same person is called "a woman who shall encompass a man" in Jeremiah 31:22; compare Isaiah 7:14. Others interpret this allegorically as the Israelite Church, though in different ways. **Abendana** <note>Solomon Abendana, a 17th-century Jewish scholar</note> in the *Spicilegium* says: "It means that in the time of salvation there will be great distress for Israel, such that it will be like a woman in labor," comparing it to Daniel 12:1, Jeremiah 30:6-7, and Hosea 13:13. But **Tarnovius** <note>Johann Tarnov, a Lutheran theologian</note> says: "Until the Gospel, brought forth from Zion (Micah 4:2), is preached to the whole world and the nations, and thus, like a fertile mother, she brings forth a numerous spiritual offspring." Compare Isaiah 49:21 and Psalm 87:4-6. Likewise **Wisinga** on Revelation 12:5 says: "This is a mystical speech. For it is supposed that the Jewish Church, according to the oracle of Isaiah 54:1-2, would produce a most fertile offspring through the preaching of the Gospel by Christ's ministers, so that the Tent of the Church would be spread throughout the whole world; this also implied the conversion of the Roman Empire and its rulers to Christ. During this time, the Prophet says the rebellious Jews are to be handed over to divine judgment until finally, after the times of the Gentiles have passed (Luke 21:24), God would have mercy on them." **s)** *for indeed the remnant...*
</margin>

<margin>
**verse 3.**
**p** *brothers, or the rest of his brothers.* **Abendana** understands this as the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, and by the "children of Israel," he understands the ten tribes. But I would prefer to interpret this as the Gentiles who are to be converted to Christ, comparing Isaiah 66:19 and following, and John 10:16. Indeed, the suffix (which Abendana also recognizes) must refer to...

**verse 3.** For as

<sup>3</sup> <gloss>u</gloss> And he shall stand and feed <gloss>x</gloss> in the strength of the LORD, <gloss>y</gloss> in the majesty of the name <gloss>z</gloss> of the LORD his God; and they shall dwell, <gloss>a</gloss> for now <gloss>b</gloss> shall he be great <gloss>c</gloss> to the ends of the earth.

**verse 3. n)** *He himself* (the Messiah) *shall stand.* Isaiah 11:10. This denotes diligence, circumspection, and pastoral care. For just as a shepherd stands upright to watch over and guard the flock more carefully, he is accustomed to stand and pay attention to them. Isaiah 61:5; compare Habakkuk 3:6. Similarly, "to sit" is used in another allegory of Christ in Malachi 3:3, signifying the application of study. **x)** verse 5, chapter 7:14, Psalm 23:1. **Jonathan** <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note>: "and he shall rule." **y)** That is, surrounded by his strength, majesty, and glory. Thus he will feed them, so that it may appear that he is equipped with divine strength and majesty. Compare 1 Samuel 2:10, Psalm 45:24. **z)** *in excellence or majesty.* Isaiah 24:14, Amos 8:3. **a)** That is, of Jehovah himself: for Jehovah and his name are one. Compare chapter 6:9, Psalm 5:12, Proverbs 18:10. And the Name of Jehovah is in Christ, Exodus 23:21 (see notes there) and Isaiah 30:27. **b)** *and so they shall dwell*, namely, securely. Chapter 4:4, Ezekiel 28:25; compare 2 Kings 4:13. The **Vulgate**: "and they shall be converted." So too **Jonathan** and the **Syriac**, as if they had read *Shebin* with a *Kibbuts* vowel. **c)** The foundation of secure dwelling comes from the greatness of the Messiah's kingdom. For since the whole earth will revere him as Lord, he will also contain everyone by his authority, or restrain them by his power, so that no one will infest his flock—at least not with success. Compare Ephesians 2:14. **d)** see note on chapter 4:10. **e)** Ezekiel 38:23, Malachi 1:11. **Jonathan**: "I will magnify his name." Compare 1 Chronicles 17:8. **f)** Psalm 2,8.

**verse 4. g)** *And this shall be peace.* The Messiah is "Peace," that is, the author of peace. **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish commentator</note>. Compare Ephesians 2:14. Namely, just as he is to produce peace with God, so he is to make peace for us from our enemies. Isaiah 8:10, chapter 27:5. **Jonathan** adds the dication "To Us." The Prophet says these things in opposition to the present or imminent state of his own time, where everything was full of disturbances and wars. **h)** *The Assyrian.* A figure of speech <note>term: synecdoche (where a part represents the whole)</note> for any enemy, or mystically for any final enemy of the Church, as in verse 5 and Zechariah 10:11, because when these things were written, the Assyrian was the most powerful and cruel enemy of the Israelite people. Compare the type in Isaiah 36 and following. The Hebrews explain this regarding Gog and Magog. There will certainly be such peoples who do not believe the Gospel of Christ (verse 14; Revelation 20:8). **i)** Therefore, what was said in verse 3 about the security of the Church does not exclude hostile attempts, but only their effect. **k)** *he shall tread*, he shall fix his foot in our palaces. Deuteronomy 11:24, Jeremiah 9:20, Psalm 122:7. **m)** *then we shall appoint* or *cause to rise up against him.* Judges 5:12. Saviors will not be lacking for us (Obadiah verse 21). **n)** *seven - eight.* If we explain it this way, as it certainly seems it should be explained, it is a figure of speech of a certain number for an uncertain one [meaning "many"], and the mystery of the number seven (which some seek here) falls away. Compare Proverbs 9:1, Ecclesiastes 1:14, Revelation 1:4, chapter 15:1. There is no doubt that this figure of speech is meant to exaggerate (meaning many) rather than diminish (meaning few) the number of princes. Compare Psalm 119:164, Ecclesiastes 11:2, Proverbs 24:16, chapter 26:25. **o)** **Jonathan**: "Kings." Verse 3; compare Jeremiah 23:4. However, Shepherds or Leaders are understood not alone, but with their flocks or troops. Jeremiah 6:3. **p)** *anointed ones* (נְסִיכֵי) *of men*, or from among men, i.e., princes of the people. Joshua 13:21, Ezekiel 32:30.

**verse 5. q)** *Who shall feed* [or waste] with the greatest severity and rigor. Revelation 2:27, chapter 19:15. Or "they shall graze down," comparing Jeremiah 2,16, chapter 6:3, Psalm 49,15. Others: "they shall break," from רעע, comparing Psalm 2:9. **r)** see note on verse 4. **s)** Not with a shepherd's staff, but with a sword. Compare Revelation 2:27, chapter 12:5, chapter 19:15. **t)** This is either Babylonia, where Nimrod began his kingdom (Genesis 10:10), or by further explanation <note>term: epexegetically</note> of the preceding, it is Assyria itself, where the same man later reigned after extending his dominion (Genesis 10:11-12). **u)** *within its gates*, that is, within the very cities of the Assyrians, which they shall enter through the gates. Chapter 7:5, Isaiah 13:2. As if to say: they will move the seat of war from our region into their own, so that while the Assyrians attacked us in our land, they themselves will be defeated within their own borders. **x)** And thus Christ will rescue us. Verse 1, 3; compare Isaiah 31:5. **y)** see note on verse 4 and note on Ezekiel 38:17.

**verse 6. z)** *And it shall be.* **a)** verse 7, chapter 2:12, chapter 4:7, chapter 7:18. **b)** *among many peoples*, specifically the teachable ones mentioned in chapter 4:1-3, from whom the anti-Christian and stubborn nations (mentioned here in verse 7 and 13) must be carefully distinguished. **c)** *like dew*, which refers to the multitude (Psalm 110:3) or rather to the effect: just as dew refreshes and fertilizes the fields, so the remnant of Jacob, converted to Christ, will sweetly affect and fertilize the peoples with the dew of the Gospel, so that they too may flourish and bear fruit for the Lord. Deuteronomy 32:2, Hosea 14:6, Psalm 133:3, Proverbs 19:12. **d)** *sent from the Lord.* According to the accents, this should be joined with the "dew." **e)** *and like copious rain.* Deuteronomy 32:2. **Jonathan**: "like the drops of the latter rain." But it is a more general name; compare Jeremiah 3:3. **f)** It is doubtful to which of the preceding nouns this should refer. The **Vulgate**: "which [the grass] does not wait for man." As if to say: it cannot be watered from anywhere else except from the Lord and the heavens. Compare Psalm 65:10-11, Job 38:28. Others: "[the rain and dew] which no one expects from man, but from God." Thus compare Jeremiah 14:22. Finally: Because Israel will not wait for man, nor trust in the son of man. And this is exactly what is said below in verses 9 and 10 about destroying trust in human protections. Compare Hosea 14:4. Moreover, it connects with the preceding roughly like this: I said that Israel among the nations would be like dew or rain; and this cannot happen in the present, so long as Israel looks to everything else rather than to God its helper. Yet it will certainly happen, because in the last times Israel will convert, having laid aside its trust in men.

->**1 Hear now what the LORD says: Arise, contend with the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice.**<-

->**2 Hear, O mountains, the LORD’s controversy, and you strong foundations of the earth; for the LORD has a controversy with His people, and He will contend with Israel.**<-

**CHAPTER VI. v. 1, 2)** From those longed-for times, which the Prophet had commanded the Church to hope for in chapters 4 and 5, he now returns to rebuking the state of his own time. There is, moreover, in this chapter a judicial dispute <note>original Latin: "disceptatio"</note> of God with His people, where **I. The Introduction** is very pathetic <note>term: pathetic (evoking pity or emotion)</note>, presenting partly the command of God regarding the instituting of the litigation (v. 1) and partly the *addressing of the listeners*, whether they be the guilty parties or the judges (v. 2). **II. The Dispute itself**, finished in three theses, of which 1) God brings to the memory of the ungrateful people His greatest benefits, to the end that the people may be convicted of their ingratitude toward so great and so kind a benefactor (v. 3, 4, 5). 2) He condemns the hypocritical atonements offered by the people (v. 6, 7), and in place of those requires rather the true duties of piety, shamefully omitted until now (v. 8). 3) He rebukes the sins which are diametrically opposed to these required duties (v. 9-12). **III. The Conclusion, or the passing of the judicial sentence**, consisting in the threat of punishments (v. 13 to the end). But according to Schmidius <note>Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> it is: **I. The Litigation of Jehovah** through the prophet with Israel over benefits (v. 1 ff). **II. The Method of True Repentance** prescribed (v. 6 ff). **III. Rebuke and Threat of Punishment** (v. 10 ff). **z)** The Prophet puts forward the command about instituting the litigation against the people so that he himself might be heard more attentively, since he is about to speak a cause not devised by himself, but commanded by the Lord Himself. Compare Isaiah 1:2. **a)** arise, that is, attack that work which I command you vigorously and with an intrepid mind. Judges 7:9; chapter 8:20. **b)** *litigate*, not indeed in your own name, but in mine (compare v. 2), where for that reason Jehovah Himself is introduced as the one litigating. The goal of this litigation is that both the kindness of God in the benefits displayed, and His justice in imposing punishments on the ungrateful people, may be made manifest (compare v. 5). **c)** *with the mountains*, namely those of Israel or of the land of Judah, as in Ezekiel 36:2, 4, 6. Furthermore, from this the *mountains* are presented as the ones to be accused; but in verse 2 they are addressed as witnesses. Therefore, either they are different mountains in verse 2, as we shall soon say; or it is merely a different perspective, so that here there is a substitution of the container for the thing contained <note>term: metonymy</note>, i.e., the region for the inhabitants, while there in verse 2 it is a personification <note>term: prosopopoeia</note> addressed to the mountains and hills, abstracting them from the inhabitants. Others explain the mountains and hills as the Princes and nobles, eminent among the Israelite people, comparing Isaiah 2:14. But this is inconsistent, because He contends not only with the princes, but with the whole people (v. 3). **v. 2. d)** *Hear therefore v. 1.* **e)** *O mountains*. If these are the same ones with whom the Prophet was commanded to initiate the suit in verse 1, they are addressed here with a slightly different respect, as we just noted; namely, they are summoned as witnesses against their own inhabitants, just as elsewhere heaven and earth are (compare Deuteronomy 32:1; Isaiah 1:2). So says Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow, a 17th-century theologian</note>: By personification, he says, he addresses the mountains and the hardest rocks rather than the Israelite people, to show that their sins and the equity of God the judge are so well known that not only men, but even other irrational creatures can abundantly testify to them. The *mountains* could indeed also be taken in exactly the same way here as above in verse 1, namely by metonymy for the inhabitants, so that Micah here would appeal to the judgment of those very ones who are the defendants as **self-condemned** <note>original Greek: "αὐτοκαταקρίτων"</note>, compare Isaiah 5:3, 4. But Vitringa in his *Commentary on Revelation* (17:9, p. 1035) says: *Princes are understood, Kings and the great men of other nations, to whose judgment the seer, about to plead God’s cause, appeals. This is the same use of this symbolic expression in Ezekiel.* So compare Amos 3:9; Ezekiel 16:27. **f)** see verse 1 and compare Hosea 4:1; chapter 12:3. **g)** *and the strong places of the earth, steep with high mountains and hills Genesis 49:24; Numbers 24:21. That it signifies mountainous regions is taught by the preceding word "mountains" and the associated "to ascend" in Jeremiah 49:19.* **h)** *foundations of the earth* Isaiah 24:18; Psalm 82:5. He understands mountains, standing firmly and immovably, which the Arabs call "firmaments." See the Quran, Surah 16:15 and 31:9. Compare Psalm 104:5. **i)** *since*, if you desire to know what that thing is which you ought to hear. Thus it would be explanatory. It could, however, also be causal: since you wish to know the cause of the demanded attention. And thus the argument would be drawn both from the one speaking and from the dignity of the object.

**v. 4. q)** That is to say: I not without merit ask this of you, since I led you out, etc., and thus I not only did not harm you, but I also adorned you with many and great benefits. Jonathan adds: *to make atonement for the people.* **z)** the sister of both, who was also herself a prophetess, and led her own sex in sacred music and hymns after the crossing of the Red Sea. Exodus 15:20. That she was of great authority among the people is also gathered from Numbers 12:1, 2, 15. Jonathan adds: *to instruct the women.* cf. Titus 2:3, 4. Nor does 1 Timothy 2:9 stand in the way. <note>The commentator argues that Miriam's leadership of women does not contradict the New Testament's restriction on women teaching in the general assembly.</note> **v. 5. a)** *My people!* By which name I do not hesitate to address you again, though you are undeserving: such is the strength of my affection for you. cf. verse 3 and the notes there. **b)** Deuteronomy 9:7; Isaiah 44:21. **c)** *what counsel he entered into, so as to destroy you*: which counsel I intercepted, forcing Balaam to bless, who had been hired to curse you. cf. Numbers 22:2. ff. **d)** *and what Balaam answered him.* This can be understood either as Balaam not answering as Balak wished and presumed (cf. Numbers 22:13, 18, and chapters 23 and 24 in full); or rather regarding that nefarious counsel by which he taught Balak to place the stumbling blocks of idolatry and fornication before the Israelites, so that, with the Lord provoked to anger, they might rush into destruction. Numbers 31:16; 25:1 ff. and 18; also Revelation 2:14. He wishes to say, therefore: Consider within yourself that pestilential counsel of Balaam; indeed, consider by how many various arts your enemies conspired for your destruction, and with what great faithfulness I always preserved you so that you would not perish. **e)** According to the accents, it is certain that this does not depend on the immediately preceding *what he answered him*, just as the subject matter itself does not allow it. Therefore Jonathan thought there was an ellipsis here, which he supplied thus: *Were not great deeds performed for you?* But the word *Remember* is quite conveniently repeated here from the beginning of the verse. That is: by remembering, return to your station in Shittim, and from there proceed even to Gilgal. Now Shittim was that very place in which the people began to commit fornication with the Moabite and Midianite women, ensnared by the counsel of Balaam. Numbers 25:1. **f)** where the people had their camp after entering the land of Canaan, until the greatest part of the land had been subdued. Joshua 4:20; 5:9, 10; 14:6. This term therefore includes the greatest benefits of God: namely, the defeat of Sihon and Og, the liberation from the deadly counsel of Balaam and the fornication with the Midianite women, the miraculous crossing of the Jordan, and the capture of Jericho and all of Canaan. Joshua also diligently impressed all these things upon the people in his final sermon. Joshua 24:8 ff. **g)** See the notes above at verse 1 on the word *lawsuit*. **h)** *the righteousnesses of the Lord.* Some understand this as "benefits"; while we by no means exclude that, both the etymology of the word and the present context suggest it be taken judicially, signifying the supreme and perfect justice of God, which he has now demonstrated from his benefits themselves. 1 Samuel 12:7. cf. Deuteronomy 32:4, 5. That is: I command you to consider these things for the purpose that you may recognize from the multitude of benefits how I have not failed you at all (as in verse 3), so that you may become liable to me. Psalm 51:6. **v. 6. i)** *By what*, i.e., equipped with what gift, or in what manner? 1 Samuel 6:2. These are the words of the people, who here and in what follows speak in turns, as happens in dialogues. Clearly, they do not dare to deny their guilt, yet they betray their hypocrisy by offering sacrifices and external rites, while being not at all concerned about conversion. **k)** *I shall come before the Lord*, or, shall I appear before him? Psalm 21:4; 88:14. **l)** *shall I bow myself?* in the manner of those worshiping. **Niphal (1)** <term>Niphal: a Hebrew passive or reflexive verb stem.</term> cf. Isaiah 58:5; Psalm 145:14. **m)** *to the high God.* Jonathan: *whose Presence is in the highest heavens.* Isaiah 33:5; Psalm 92:9. **n)** *with burnt offerings?* But see the response of God in verse 7. **o)** *and with calves of a year old*, such as God himself required for a burnt offering. Leviticus 9:3. **v. 7. p)** But I respond, says the Prophet: *Will the Lord be pleased*, etc. This is an interrogation not of the people, as others wish, but of the Prophet, as we have said, vehemently denying it. That is: He is by no means pleased with sacrifices; it would be absurd even to think such things of the Lord. And thus the offering of Israel is emphatically rejected. Now sacrifices are understood here not as they had been instituted by God himself, but insofar as the people under the Old Testament economy offered them without repentance and faith, and out of mere "work performed" (*ex opere operato*). cf. Isaiah 1:11; Jeremiah 6:20; 7:22; Hosea 6:6; 8:13; Amos 5:22; Psalm 40:7; 50:8 ff.; 51:18 ff.; Matthew 9:13; Hebrews 10:4. **q)** *with thousands of rams.* If I do not say you would slaughter one or two, but if you would sacrifice even thousands. An emphatic hyperbole, to remove the error of "work performed" from the people even more. **r)** *or with myriads.* Psalm 3:7. **s)** *of rivers.* This is said properly of flowing waters in Deuteronomy 8:7; but of other liquids hyperbolically, to signify a supreme and unusual abundance. Job 20:17. **t)** *of oil*, which was poured upon the grain offerings. Leviticus 2:1, 15. **u)** *Will I then*, says the people, *give my firstborn*, and thus one dear to me beyond not only my other goods, but my children also? That is: if animal offerings do not please, will human sacrifices perhaps please? Such as (horrendous to do) pagan superstition, and the Israelite people imitating it, sacrificed to idols. cf. Ezekiel 16:21; Hosea 13:2; 2 Chronicles 28:3; and Genesis 22:2.

**v. 8. a)** Here the Prophet responds again, and indeed *decisively* <note>Original Greek: *ἀποτόμως* (apotomos), meaning cuttingly or abruptly.</note>, by cutting off with one blow all their empty and hypocritical little questions. It is as if he says: "What do you seek, O man? As if the will of God were in the dark?" But he has sufficiently testified what pleases him. You could have known it in abundance, if only you wished; you certainly cannot pretend ignorance. *He has told you* etc. Deuteronomy 5:5, so that there is no need for long deliberation (chapter 30:11 and following). This word is opposed to pretending and hiding (2 Kings 4:27; Ephesians 3:9) and signifies to say something openly and to one's face (Job 21:31), to testify seriously and expressly (Deuteronomy 30:15). **b)** *whoever you are.* Ecclesiastes 12:13. **c)** *what is good*, that is, what is pleasing to God, and what would be prosperous and salvific for you. Deuteronomy 6:24; 10:13; 30:15; Jeremiah 6:16; Hosea 8:3. Cf. Matthew 11:29. **d)** *And what else?* He now explains the highest and most important points of the divine law, which Christ in Matthew 23:23 calls *the weightier matters of the law* <note>Original Greek: *τὰ βαρύτερα τοῦ νόμου* (ta barytera tou nomou)</note> in opposition to the merely instructional works of the law, which indeed ought to be done under the Old Testament economy, but in such a way that these weightier matters are not omitted. **e)** *God requires of you.* He looks back to Deuteronomy 10:12. **f)** *justice*, not only in the court but moral justice in general. It is called *judgment* <note>Original Greek: *κρίσις* (krisis)</note> in Matthew 23:23. Cf. 12:18. It signifies, therefore, the practical discernment of good and evil, truth and falsehood, so that we may bring a just judgment to every single thing. John 7:24. Cf. Ephesians 5:7; Hosea 12:7; Zephaniah 2:3. **g)** *and the love of mercy* or kindness toward one's neighbor. Hosea 6:6; 12:7; Matthew...

1 Peter 5:5, 6. **i)** *with or toward your God.* For the word *with* <note>Hebrew: *im*</note> is used objectively, comparing Deuteronomy 9:7, 24. The Jonathan Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Prophets.</note> says "in the fear of your God." Cf. Genesis 5:22. ***v. 9. k)*** Wherefore the voice of the LORD, through me again debating His case with the wicked people (v. 1). **l)** *calls to the city*, namely Jerusalem; whatever is said to it as the head is rightly believed to pertain to the other cities as well. It is a denunciation of punishment, which He proclaims to the city, having first reproached their crimes. **m)** *for reality* <note>Original Latin: *realitatem*</note>, the thing as it is. Schmid translates it as "integrity"; so compare Psalm 71:7. It is a more difficult noun, but emphatic (12). It must be formed from the unusual word *vashah*, from which comes *tushiyyah*, a substance truly existing. Proverbs 8:21. With the prefix *t* removed, it agrees in meaning and sound with the Greek *ousia* <note>Original Greek: *οὐσία*, meaning substance or essence.</note>. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek version of the Old Testament.</note> in Job 5:12 rendered it as *truth* <note>Original Greek: *ἀληθές* (alethes)</note>. Thus it is opposed to pretenses, pictures, and shadows; which is undoubtedly how it is used here, signifying the thing as it is, *the truth* <note>Original Greek: *ἀλήθειαν* (aletheian)</note> in Ephesians 4:21, in opposition to the images of divine worship or ritual works mentioned above in verses 6 and 7. Refer back to verse 8 and you will have what *tushiyyah* is. Cf. also Job 30:21. Elsewhere it denotes wisdom, namely that which is real and true. Proverbs 2:7; 3:21; 8:14; 18:1. etc. The accusative is placed here at the beginning of the clause before the nominative for the sake of emphasis, because the chief weight is in it, implying the removal of those things that the Lord does not regard. For the rest, it should be observed that this clause is parenthetical up to the punctuation mark *Athnach*, anticipating the false opinion that the Jews could have opposed to the truth of the announcement of judgments now to be instituted by the Prophet—taken, of course, from sacrifices and external worship (v. 6, 7). As if to say: "It will indeed seem incredible to the Jews what I am about to say, and all the more because they think they are performing their duty excellently as long as they offer sacrifices; but they think this in vain: for you indeed, O God! do not look at those ritual works, but at the reality and real worship." **n)** *sees*, that is, regards with favor, cares for, approves. Jeremiah 5:3; Habakkuk 1:13; Psalm 37:37; 66:18; Lamentations 3:35, 36; 1 Chronicles 17:17. Compare 1 Samuel 16:7; Job 10:4. **o)** *sees your Name*, that is, You see. For Jehovah and His Name are one, which we noted above at chapter 5:3. **p)** *Hear therefore, you Jews, and you inhabitants of Jerusalem especially.* Cf. note at 1:2. **q)** Tarnovius says: "the rod of God hanging over you," the prophecy about the rod—the prediction of the judgment by which you are to be lashed; compare Psalm 89:33. Thus also the Dutch Bible and others. Cf. Exodus 7:17; Isaiah 10:5, 15; Ezekiel 7:10. But Luther translates it as *O tribes*, namely the Israelite tribes, by a grammatical substitution of singular for plural. So Schmid: *Hear this, O tribe*. **r)** *and (at the same time notice or hear) who has appointed it*, namely that which I am about to say, or what is signified by the rod. Thus Tarnovius and Schmid translate it neutrally. For Grammar hardly allows the feminine suffix to refer to *matteh* (rod), which is masculine. In the plural, however, it is also feminine, comparing Numbers 17:22, 24. He commands that the author of the imminent judgments be especially noticed, so that when they come, they may not seem to have come by chance, but from God Himself, provoked by sins, as a just judge, inflicted at a set time and place. 2 Samuel 20:5; Jeremiah 47:7. Cf. Amos 3:6. ***v. 10. s)*** *For still*, namely after so many and so evident and serious warnings. Cf. verses 8 and 9. It coheres with verse 9 in such a way that the Prophet now explains the cause of the punishment or rod announced there. As if to say: "Do you want to know what draws this rod of God upon you? It is your crimes, in which you even now stubbornly persist, having been warned in vain by the Prophets to desist from them." **t)** Schmid: *Moreover: is it a man (Am I) of the house of the wicked, of the treasures of wickedness etc.* As if to say: "I am not one whom such things can please." Others: "Will it thus continue for the man (everyone) of the house of the wicked?" Gussetius on page 351, having tried first one thing and then another, finally suggests reading *ha-esh* as "Is it possible?" with the Septuagint and Arabic. Likewise the Vulgate and Syriac: *Still the fire*: meaning fornications and adulteries, which are causes of fire; compare Job 31:12; Proverbs 6:27, 28. But just as that first explanation does not entirely fit with the unusual spelling (for "man" is constantly written *ha-ish* with a *Yod*), so the latter one by Gussetius is not pleasing because it conflicts with the vowel points. Therefore the Jonathan Targum has: *are there?* So Rabbi Solomon and others, comparing 2 Samuel 14:19, where it is no less common for *esh* to be placed for *yesh* ("there is"): a similar thing is found in *Ishai* for *Yishai* (Jesse) in 1 Chronicles 2:13. It is therefore an affirmative question of one who is stunned and marvelling at their persistence. As if to say: "It is almost incredible that you cling so tooth and nail to your crimes; for the treasures of impiety and the deceitful measure ought to have long ago ceased in the house of the wicked: but this is exactly what draws my rod upon you" (v. 9). **u)** *in the house of the wicked.* The preposition *in* is understood, as in Genesis 24:23. **x)** *of impiety*, verse 11, that is, prepared impiously and by wrongdoing. Proverbs 10:2. **y)** *and the Ephah of leanness* <term>Ephah: a unit of measurement. "Leanness" implies it is undersized or fraudulent.</term> Psalm 106:15. A measure too thin, that is, smaller than is just, for defrauding others; or "emaciating," by which others are made thin and become poor. Cf. Leviticus 19:35, 36; Deuteronomy 25:15, 16; Amos 8:5. **z)** *detestable*, which the Lord detests, and has testified so many times and so seriously that He detests it. Proverbs 22:14; cf. 20:23 and Ezekiel 45:10. ***v. 11. a)*** Schmid: *For shall I justify the scales of wickedness?* Thus they would be the words of God Himself. But the verb in the simple form (*Kal*) is never used transitively for "to make just" or "to declare just," but intransitively, compare Psalm 51:6; Job 15:14. For this reason we translate it rather as: *For shall I be just with the scales of wickedness?* Namely, I myself or another, whoever it might be? Thus the Prophet speaks, forming the case in his own first person. (Cf. *Glassius, Sacred Philology*, page 898 and following). Such a speech is equivalent to a universal one, and in this place indeed a negative one, so that the sense is: Justice and wicked scales are so *incompatible* <note>Original Latin: *ἀσύστατα* (asystata)</note> that they cannot exist together in me or in any other. Hence the Jonathan Targum: "Shall they be just?" and the Syriac: "How shall they be justified?" in the plural. **b)** v. 10. cf. Ezekiel 45:10; Hosea 12:8; Amos 3:5; Proverbs 11:1. **c)** *and with the bag* (5) for storing weights. Deuteronomy 25:13; Proverbs 16:11. **d)** *of stones* (that is, of weights, for which stones were used in ancient times. See ibid.) *deceitful*. Jonathan Targum: *in which there are large and small weights: namely, large if for oneself; small if it is weighed out for others.* ***v. 12. e)*** *Because*, since. It is used causally, as in Deuteronomy 3:24. The Prophet therefore continues to explain the cause for which the rod of God is thus to be sent upon the Jews (v. 9). **f)** *its rich men*, of the city of Jerusalem (v. 9). So "its inhabitants" (v. 10). **g)** *are full of (abound in) violence*, namely in the active sense, which they inflict on others. See above 2:1, 2, 8, 9; 3:1, 2, 3; Amos 3:10; 6:3. **h)** Isaiah 59:3. **i)** *and their tongue is a tongue of fraud.* Or according to Schmid: *and as for their tongue, it is fraud etc.* Cf. Psalm 120:2, 3.

# MICAH CHAPTERS 6 & 7

**v. 13. k)** "And so, as a punishment for this persistence of yours, I also," says the Lord. He now begins to explain that rod [of punishment] to which he had previously commanded attention (v. 9). **l)** Schmid and Cocceius Lexicon 234: "I am weary," for **הֶחֱלֵיתִי** <note>Hebrew: hecheliti</note> "I have made myself weak"; which would be an *anthropopatheia* <note>original Latin: "ανθρωποπάθεια" — attributing human feelings or weaknesses to God</note>. But we prefer the active sense following Gussetius (p. 257): "I will make [you] sick by striking you," that is, I will strike you so as to make you weak. Cf. Isaiah 53:10, Deuteronomy 29:21, 1 Kings 22:34; compare also Psalm 33:3 "do well in playing" for "play well." Compare Isaiah 1:5 where both are said: the striking is attributed to God as the act, but the weakness or disease is attributed to the people as the effect. The Past tense is used here for the Future, as shown by the following future verbs and the context. For he is not so much narrating past plagues as threatening them for the future. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note>: "I have brought upon you a disease," or a plague, **m)** "by devastating," bringing desolation upon you. 1 Samuel 5:6, Isaiah 1:7. **n)** Cf. Jeremiah 30:14, 15.

**v. 14. o)** For, to explain this more distinctly to you: You indeed shall eat, **p)** yet you shall not be satisfied, because of the scarcity sent to you. Leviticus 26:26, Hosea 4:10, Haggai 1:6. **q)** "A depression," that is, your humiliation (to be formed from the unused root **שחח** <note>shachach</note>, which is related to **שחה** <note>shachah</note> "to bow to the ground"). Thus the sense would be: God will so humble you that you will no longer walk proudly (Chapter 2:3). Moreover, what follows, "in your midst," would signify that this humiliation will be manifest and almost palpable, so that it will be obvious to everyone’s eyes and cannot be concealed. Cf. Ezekiel 7:4, 9. As Gussetius (p. 351, 830) translates: "your corruption," as if to say, you carry a lethal wound, a disease by which you will perish, in your very bowels—namely, an inexpiable guilt by which you are certainly destined for destruction. Cf. Judges 6:3, Jeremiah 12:13, Haggai 1:6. **y)** You shall tread (pressing out by treading) olives. For winepresses were used for pressing oil from olives just as for must from grapes; compare Joel 2:24, Job 24:11. **z)** Nor shall you anoint yourself with oil. Deuteronomy 28:40, Ruth 3:3, Daniel 10:3. **a)** And you shall press out the new wine, **b)** but [not drink]. Cf. Amos 5:11. **v. 16. c)** For everyone has taken it upon themselves to observe, or diligently observes [these things]. Jonathan 2:9, Psalm 18:24. Cf. Hosea 4:10. Taym. <note>likely a reference to a specific commentator</note> connects it with the preceding thus: "And these things happen to my people—not only because they have sinned so nefariously against their neighbor, as was declared just before; but especially because they have perfidiously defected from me, their God, to idols, and will in no way allow themselves to be led away from this impiety." For also... **d)** "Idolatrous statutes." Leviticus 20:23, Jeremiah 10:3. **e)** Of the King of Israel [Omri], who was worse than all his predecessors and a notable establisher of foreign worship. 1 Kings 16:25, 26. **f)** Who [Ahab], not content with the golden calves, added the worship of Baal at the instigation of Jezebel. 1 Kings 16:30 and following. **g)** "In their counsels," that is, in the statutes and rituals of human invention and ordination. Jeremiah 7:24, Hosea 10:6, 11:6. **h)** With no other outcome than that I deliver you up. See the note on Amos 2:7. **i)** "Into a stupor," an object of horror, at whose terrible fall everyone will be stunned. Deuteronomy 28:37, 2 Kings 21:19. **k)** "And its inhabitants," namely, of the city; compare v. 9 and 12. A frequent change of person occurs in the Prophets. **l)** "Into a hissing." Cf. 1 Kings 9:8. **m)** So that you—each and every one—may bear the reproach of my people (with which I will affect my whole people). Isaiah 25:8, Jeremiah 31:19.

**CHAPTER VII, v. 1. n)** Woe is me! (Job 10:15). A particle of lamentation; it has a formal affinity with **אלל** and **ילל** and **יילל** <note>Hebrew roots for wailing/lamenting</note> (Joel 1:8), to wail, to lament. The Prophet speaks here, as Jonathan added in his paraphrase; yet he sometimes makes the whole Church speak with him, as is clear from v. 7 and following. First, he deplores the corrupt state of his people and the fewness of the good; then he leads the few good people who remain to patience in the hope of better things, especially in the kingdom of Christ, raising itself up from the divine promise, adding a doxology in which he admires and praises the mercy and truth of God to be shown to the Church. There are therefore two main parts to this chapter: I. Lamentation over present evils (v. 1–6). II. Consolation over future goods (v. 7–20). Schmid divides this into six parts: I. The complaint of the Church about the most corrupt state of her children (v. 1–6). II. Her solace from a better future state (v. 7–10). III. It is promised to her as being near (v. 11, 12). IV. The Church desires it with prayers (v. 14). V. The Messiah promises it (v. 15–17). VI. Finally, the Church gives thanks (v. 18–20). **o)** "Because I am like..." If it is the Prophet who says these things, the sense will be: "I see things to be thus in my people, and I find the state of affairs to be as one who seeks figs after the trees have been shaken, or grapes after the vintage and gleaning have already been done. For thus I seek the good, but find none." But if the Church speaks in the abstract, she mourns the fewness of her members and means to say: "Into such a state, alas, have I been reduced, as is that of figs and vines after the shaking and vintage; namely, I have no good fruit at all, or very little." Furthermore, Jonathan adds for the sake of explanation: "when the good are consumed, at the time when the holy perished from the earth." In this way, the Prophet himself explains the parabolic expressions in verse 2. **p)** "As after the collections" (Isaiah 32:10, 33:4). **q)** "Of summer fruits," especially figs; compare the note on 2 Samuel 16:1 and Jeremiah 40:10. **r)** "As in the gleanings" of the vintage or (as Jonathan rightly has it) *after* the vintage. Judges 8:2, Isaiah 17:6, 24:13. **s)** "There is no cluster." Genesis 40:10, Numbers 13:23, Deuteronomy 32:32. That is, according to Jonathan, there is no one in whom there are good works. Cf. Deuteronomy 32:32, Isaiah 5:2, 65:8, and the note on Jeremiah 8:13. **t)** "The early fig," that is, of the first time, as the Vulgate expressed it in Jeremiah 24:2 (see the note there). It signifies those ripening before summer (Isaiah 28:4), when there are not yet "bundles of figs" (Matthew 21:19, Mark 11:13), which are all the sweeter for eating because they are still rare for the season (Hosea 9:10). Such a time could be said in a certain respect to be under the Old Economy [the Old Testament], just as, by contrast, under the New Testament the full summer and the proper time for ripening arrived: meanwhile, however, not all fruit of piety had to be deferred to the harvest of the New Testament. Cf. Luke 13:7. Jonathan: "the good." **u)** "My soul desired," but in vain! Deuteronomy 12:20. **v. 2. x)** For to say what the matter is plainly and without tropes: The holy one has perished (Chapter 4:9). Namely, what had been said allegorically in v. 1 is now declared in literal words. Cf. Isaiah 57:1, Psalm 12:2 and following. **y)** Psalm 50:5. **z)** i.e., the Israelite [earth/land]. **a)** "Who is upright among men." Verse 4, chapter 2:7, Psalm 11:7. There is indeed an emphasis in the preposition, compare Genesis 6:9, 7:1. That is, the corruption is indeed immense where many are evil; but much worse, indeed the worst, when everyone has degenerated so that not one good person remains among them. Cf. the state of the pre-flood time (Genesis 6:5, 11, 12) and that of Sodom (Chapter 18:20 and following, compare Isaiah 1:9, 10). **b)** "No one" or "none," i.e., they are extremely rare. For just as "everyone" stands for "most," so "none" stands for "few." Jeremiah 5:1, 4, 5, 6; Psalm 14:1 and following; John 3:32. And so he means to say: "When I look upon the whole multitude of the Jewish people, I see everything so corrupt that it is difficult to find even one just and pious person in it." **c)** "They lie in wait for blood" (to shed it). Cf. above chapter 3:10, Isaiah 33:15, Psalm 37:32.

---

**v. 13. הֶחֱלֵיתִי** Thus detected without the *Vau* [letter] in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 22, 23, according to Masoretic note 2 and Erff. in this place; but on the contrary printed in Jeremiah 15:13. But without the *Iod* plural in 3, and so in 1, 2, 5 according to Masoretic note 2 and Erff. Thus also 6 and 9 in the margin. **v. 14. וְיֶשְׁחֲךָ** with a *Sin* instead of a *Samech* in 6 and 9 in the margin, against M. I. **v. 15. וְתִירֹשׁ** Iod without *Dagesh* in 1, 3, 5, 6, 9, 21, 22. **CHAPTER VII, v. 1. אַלְלַי** according to Masoretic note 2, 3. **לֶאֱכוֹל** thus clearly in 6, 9, 20, 21, 24 according to Masoretic note printed in Ezekiel 16:20. Others [are] defective.

# MICAH CHAPTER 7

<margin>
**Woe!** [Hebrew: *Hoy*]—In a <term>metonymic</term> sense (where one word stands for a related concept), this signifies wickedness or a lofty distress to be brought upon others. Psalm 5:10, 38:13, 55:12. **They weave it together** [Hebrew: *va-ye'abbetuha*]—cf. Psalm 6:13, 129:3. Like a leather strap or a rope woven from multiple threads; that is, they strengthen and firm it up, as in Ecclesiastes 4:12. Tarnovius. So it is here: **and they weave it.**
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 2. d)** *they hunt each other.* Genesis 27:3, 5. Like hunters who—in order to catch something—employ dogs, nets, and weapons (add also "throats," as noted on Ezekiel 19:4); so these wicked men invent strange arts, schemes, and deceits by which they may do harm. Tarnovius, Proverbs 6:26. **e)** *as with a net.* Habakkuk 1:15, 16, 17. Or, to the death, so that they might make him an *anathema* <note>original Latin: "anathema" — something devoted to total destruction</note>. Leviticus 27:28.

**v. 3. f)** *Besides doing evil*, or preserving that which they do badly. As if to say: "so that I may now pass over their other crimes." Jeremiah 4:22. **g)** *with both hands*, laboriously and with the greatest zeal. Proverbs 31:13. **h)** *to the point of doing well*, that is, excellently, and in such a way that nothing can be above it. This word, joined to others, is to be explained in an intensive and adverbial way, such as to move or break something "by doing well," that is, thoroughly and entirely. Deuteronomy 9:21, 2 Kings 11:18. But Schmid says: *When they do evil with both hands*, this is their "doing well." As if to say: the worse and more wicked a person is, the "better" he is in their eyes. Cf. Isaiah 3:9, 58:2, Jeremiah 9:5. Finally, Cocceius Lexicon 304: *Over evil are the hands to make it good*, that is, they fashion and mold evil so that it appears good. **i)** The prince asks for gifts, or a retribution, based on the following clause. **k)** and the judge judges for a reward; repeating the verb or participle. Cf. Micah 3:11, Isaiah 1:23, 5:23. **l)** and as for the great man, namely in wealth (1 Samuel 25:2) or in authority (2 Kings 5:1, Esther 9:4). **m)** Cocceius: wickedness; Schmid: the perversity of his soul—that is, what he has conceived in his mind, he speaks. As if to say: it is not enough for them to stir up wickedness in their hearts; having stirred it up, they also speak it shamelessly and most boldly. See above, Micah 2:1-2. It should be observed that **hu** <note>Hebrew pronoun "he/it"</note> as much as **hovah** <note>Hebrew: "ruin/mischief"</note> properly signifies distress (Proverbs 19:13), whether from the verb *havah* in place of *hayah* [to be], or from the participle *havah*.
</margin>

Cocceius Lexicon 598: *they thicken, like a cable, braiding many lies into one lie.* **v. 4. o)** *Their best*, comparatively the best among them; from which an inference may be made regarding the rest, who are worse. **p)** *is like a brier.* We translate this with a general term; but among the Arabs it is a specific name, *melongena* <note>The eggplant or nightshade family</note>, which is also called "scorpion's thorn" by the same, as taught by the Swedish botanist Celsus in his *Sacred Botany* from the Arab Abulfadli. Arabic root: **hadiq** *to surround and become a hedge*; from which **hadiq** means *an intricate thing* and **hadiqa** *a fenced garden*. Therefore, that kind of thorn is so named because it is both sharp and suited for living hedges. Cf. Proverbs 15:19, and here in the following phrase **thorn hedge**. (Cf. 2 Samuel 23:6, 7; Ezekiel 2:6; Psalm 58:10; Matthew 7:16). **q)** *their upright one, or the most upright of them.* v. 1, Micah 2:7. **r)** *is worse than a thorn hedge.* Proverbs 15:19, Isaiah 5, 5. Cf. the root **suk** *to fence with thorns*, Hosea 2:5, 8. In Arabic, **suk** with the letter *Shin* means *to prick* or *to be thorny*, and in the second conjugation *to fortify or hedge with thorns*. **s)** *therefore the day of your watchmen*, (he addresses the Jewish people) that is, the day of wrath and divine vengeance. Joel 1:15, 2:1, 2. Foreseen long ago by the Prophets as if from a watchtower, and faithfully announced to you. v. 7, Isaiah 21:6, 52:8; Ezekiel 3:17, 33:2, 7. **t)** *your visitation, I say*, that is, a punishing judgment, by which God will make it known that he has inspected and disapproved of your crimes. Isaiah 10:3, Ezekiel 9:1, Hosea 9:7. **u)** cf. Ezekiel 7:2, 5. **x)** even now. Cf. note on Micah 4:10. **y)** *their confusion shall happen.* Isaiah 21:5. The sense: The Jews will become so entangled by the variety and magnitude of evils that no plan for extricating themselves will be available to them. Cf. Esther 3:15; likewise the Arabic **buk** *to be confused and disturbed*, and in the seventh conjugation *to be of a disturbed mind and confused reasonings.* **v. 5. z)** *Do not trust a friend.* Jeremiah 9:3, 12:6; Proverbs 26:25; Matthew 10:21, 35, 36; Luke 12:52, 53. This is an indefinite imperative. For the aim here is not so much to establish rules of prudence as to depict the most corrupt state in every society and the universal treachery running rampant everywhere; as if to say: treachery has occupied everything to such an extent that trust is nowhere safe, and you must be most cautious, whoever you are, lest you be deceived by relatives, parents, children, spouse, or friends. Trust—as that common Latin proverb goes—*but see in whom.* **a)** *a close companion*—one to whom one is thoroughly accustomed. Proverbs 16:28, 17:9, where the **Septuagint** correctly rendered this as "Friend" [*Philon*]. It is from the root **alaph** *to become accustomed*, Proverbs 22:25. For familiarity comes from custom; indeed, custom is familiarity and friendship. Psalm 55:14. **b)** *from her who lies in your bosom*, or your most dear wife. Deuteronomy 13:7, 28:54. **c)** *guard, lest they rashly blab anything* that could create danger for you: for she is likely to betray you. **d)** *the doors of your mouth*, Micah 5:5. *He attributes doors to the mouth, because it either opens or closes the thoughts of the mind like a gate.* Cf. Psalm 141:3. **v. 6. e)** For, to continue describing the disturbed and most corrupt state of the people: **f)** *treats with contempt, affects the father with insults.* Deuteronomy 32:15, Jeremiah 14:21, Nahum 3:6. Cf. Isaiah 3:5, Mark 13:12; and Josephus' *Jewish War*, book 4, chapter 11. **g)** *rises up with a hostile mind.* Psalm 3:2. **h)** *and the daughter-in-law* (Leviticus 18:15) *against her mother-in-law* (Ruth 2:18). **i)** *his household members.* Genesis 17:27, 39:14. Everything is and will be filled with discord. Cf. Matthew 10:36. **v. 7. k)** But as for me. This creates an opposition to what came before. As if to say: "It is indeed so; everything is rushing toward the worse, and the just and terrible judgments of God are imminent and fall upon sinners; but how should I bear myself while things are in this state? In despair, or shall I murmur and impatiently speak against God? On the contrary, I..." Luther, observing this passage, notes two very remarkable things. First, he is not moved by the scandals of the impious multitude. But the second is greater: because even when in such behaviors the divine punishment and vengeance could not be far off, nevertheless he does not cast away all hope, but the Prophet casts his eyes back to God, certain that even if a universal punishment is about to run rampant like a flood, God still knows how to snatch away and preserve His own. **l)** Cocceius and others: *toward the Lord*, taking the Hebrew preposition **be** objectively, as in Psalm 66:7. It could also be translated thus: "relying upon the Lord and His divine promise, kindness, and faithfulness." Compare Psalm 119:49, or how it is used in 1 Samuel 17:45. **m)** *I will look*, that is, I will wait for the help of the Lord as if from a high watchtower, just as those who are besieged by enemies look out continuously from towers and wait for promised reinforcements. Hope leaning on the Lord looks forward into the future. Lamentations 4:17, Habakkuk 2:1, Isaiah 17:7, 25:9, 52:8, Psalm 121:1. **n)** Tarnovius: "nor shall I grow weary, even if help is delayed for a little while, but I will wait." Psalm 42:6. Cf. Lamentations 3:26 and the note there. **o)** The God of my salvation. The argument for hope is in the very name of God. As if to say: "He will certainly save me, because He has already been my salvation of old, and is called the God of my salvation." Isaiah 17:10, Habakkuk 3:18. **p)** *for He will hear me at last.* Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note>: "You will look upon my prayers." Therefore, continuous and unceasing prayers are assumed along with hope. **v. 8. q)** Do not therefore rejoice over me and my misfortune. He restrains their insolence and hostile <term>epichairekakia</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐπιχαιρεκακία" — malicious joy at the misfortune of others</note>. Cf. Isaiah 14:29, Obadiah v. 12, Psalm 13:5, Proverbs 24:17-18, Job 31:29, Lamentations 4:21-22, Sirach 3:12. **r)** *O my enemy*—v. 10. An <term>apostrophe</term> (speaking directly to an absent person or personified object). **s)** *for though I have fallen*, or although I might have fallen, yet I shall rise again from the fall. "Falling" in this place is understood as a punishment; "rising," therefore, is an emerging from evils. Cf. Psalm 37:24, 145:14, Proverbs 24:16; also Amos 5:2, 8:14. **t)** *though I sit in the darkness* of evils and calamities, as if in a dark prison. Isaiah 47:5, 49:9; Lamentations 3:2, 6. Cf. Psalm 23:4. **u)** *nevertheless Jehovah is and will be a light to me*, even in the midst of darkness. Psalm 27:1. Cf. Psalm 97:11, 112:4.

# MICAH CHAPTER 7

<margin>
**v. 9. a)** Indeed, he places the wrath or anger of the Lord first: (6) Isaiah 30:30; Proverbs 19:12; Jonah 1:15. Joshua. He speaks rightly, though it seems the Prophet spoke with this same person in the preceding verses, as we noted above at verse 1. However, he anticipates the reproach of the female enemy: why then does God, in whom she trusts, allow her to be so heavily afflicted? Cf. below verse 10. To which he responds: It is true that she suffers much; yet she bears those things humbly, first because she certainly deserved them by her sins, and second because she knows they will not be perpetual, but only for a time. **v.** *I will bear patiently and humbly, for I have deserved it, since...* etc. Cf. Leviticus 26:41, 43; Lamentations 3:27 and following; Luke 15:18; also Isaiah 26:20, 21; chapter 54:6 and following. **ζ)** *until.* This particle suggests two things: first, the unshaken patience of the Church; second, the end of the incumbent evils. Cf. Lamentations 3:25. **a)** *that he may plead my cause* against wicked adversaries. 1 Samuel 24:16; Psalm 43:1. **b)** Jonah: *and avenge my injury* (which I suffer), as a just judge. Psalm 9:5; cf. Jeremiah 50:7, 17 and following. **c)** *until he brings out*, or *he will bring me out*, namely from the darkness of verse 8 into the light. Cf. Hosea 6:6; Psalm 37:6. **d)** *that I may see*, and enjoy with great pleasure His righteousness, by which He saves His repentant people, but destroys the fierce and insolent adversaries. Verse 10; chapter 4:11; Psalm 54:9.

**v. 10. e)** *She shall see this*, therefore, not without grief. Psalm 112:10. **f)** verse 8; chapter 5:8. **g)** *shame shall cover her.* Cf. Ezekiel 7:18 and the note on Obadiah verse 10. But Tarnovius, as if it were the second person, says: *From every side ignominy and confusion shall surround her*, or *let those who look at her see nothing but infamy.* Cf. Psalm 89:46. **h)** That very woman who now impiously and proudly says to me: **i)** *Where is he, namely Jehovah your God?* A <term>pleonasm</term> <note>an intentional redundancy for emphasis</note> of the suffix, as in Exodus 2:6. Cf. Joel 2:17; Psalm 42:4, 11; Psalm 79:10; Psalm 115:2. **k)** **הן' כדנש** <note>Hebrew: "Behold, as for him"</note> Emphasis on the pronoun, as if to say: *about whom you were so boasting, and whom you called your God*, in opposition both to us and to our gods.
</margin>

**l)** *My eyes shall see.* This is more emphatic than if he had simply said, "I will see." See Job 19:27. **m)** *They shall see in her* the thing long hoped for. Jonah: *their ruin.* Verse 9; chapter 4:11. They rejoice not so much in the destruction of wicked enemies, but in the assertion of God’s glory, whose name those enemies had hitherto profaned by blasphemy and opposed as much as they could; and because they were unwilling to amend themselves, God's righteousness shining in their punishment is deservedly celebrated by the children of God. Tarnovius. Cf. Psalm 54:9; Psalm 112:8. However, the suffix could also refer—not inconveniently—to the righteousness of the Lord (mentioned in verse 10). In this way, it would be an emphatic repetition of the same matter. **n)** *Now, soon*, as in verse 4; Isaiah 43:13; Amos 6:7. **o)** *My enemy shall become a trampling*, that is, trampled down. Isaiah 5:5; chapter 26:6. **p)** 2 Samuel 22:43; Isaiah 10:6; Zechariah 10:5. **v. 11. q)** *There is, or shall be a day*, says God through the Prophet; a day, I say, most notable and illustrious, often promised by Me, and long desired by you. Verse 12. **r)** *to build the dry-stone walls or your walls.* He addresses the Church under the <term>type</term> <note>a historical person or event serving as a symbol of something later</note> of Jerusalem, and consoles her with these promises. It is indeed certain that the walls of Jerusalem were built after the Babylonian captivity, physically and typically, cf. Nehemiah 3:1 and following, and Daniel 9:25. However, the following parts and the parallelism teach that this prophecy looks further—that is, to the construction that is spiritual, solid, and perpetual through Christ under the New Testament, concerning which see Isaiah 49:16; chapter 60:10; Jeremiah 31:4 (where you may see the note); Amos 9:11; Psalm 51:20; Psalm 102:14-17. **s)** Isaiah 5:5; Psalm 89:13; cf. 2 Kings 12:12. **s)** Schmid: *this day, on which* (understanding *asher* <note>Hebrew relative pronoun "which"</note>), so in verse 12. But it can also be translated simply without an ellipsis: *on that day*, namely, the one I just mentioned. **u)** Interpreters go in various directions here. Tarnovius: *that decree shall go away into the distance*, concerning which see Psalm 2:7, 8, namely the doctrine of the Gospel. So Grotius, *Theologia Prophetica* page 705. *The statute shall be lengthened*, meaning the counsel of peace in Christ shall be announced far and wide, cf. Habakkuk 2:14; see also Isaiah 33:17. But Jonah says: *the decrees of the nations shall be abolished*, namely those who previously ruled over you tyrannically. Others: *the decree of God regarding the infliction of evils upon you shall be far away*; the Lord will cease to treat you badly, cf. Zephaniah 2:2. Finally, by "statute" could be understood the precepts of human authority and invention, superstitious and wicked, cf. above chapter 6:16. In such diversity and difficulty, we leave the choice to the reader's judgment; meanwhile, we are more inclined toward the middle interpretation. **v. 12. x)** Piscator: *On that day even unto you shall come that decree* (of verse 11), you who dwell as far as Assyria, etc. In this way, it would be a new <term>apostrophe</term> <note>a speech directed to an absent person or personified object</note> to the enemies, and the sense would be threatening. However, we are reluctant to change persons where it is not necessary. We prefer, therefore, with others, that these things are said to the people of God just as those in verse 11 were. Nor does the difference in gender here and in verse 11 stand in the way, for in verse 15 the masculine gender of the suffix must undoubtedly refer to the people of God. We agree with Schmid: *this is the day on which*; or more simply: *On that day, then (I say) they shall come unto you.* Namely, the *Vav* prefix is, for Schmid, in place of a relative pronoun, as in Genesis 11:4; chapter 49:25. For us, it is <term>pleonastic</term>, as in Genesis 3:5; chapter 22:4. We take the singular *shall come* here impersonally, for *they shall come* or *there shall be a coming*; we understand it as a submissive and humble coming, to embrace true worship in true communion with the people of God, having set aside errors, cf. Isaiah 45:24; also Isaiah 49:17 and following; chapter 56:6, 7; Zechariah 2:15, etc. **y)** *from Assyria*, which with the following Egypt comes here <term>synechdochically</term> <note>where a part stands for the whole</note> for any nations whatever that were once hostile to the people of God, but finally to be reconciled; as in Isaiah 19:23 and following, which place seems clearly identical to ours and sheds light upon it. Cf. below verse 17. **z)** Schmid: *and even to the cities of Egypt*, Isaiah 19:6. As a common noun, it means "fortification," cf. Psalm 31:22 and 60:11; 2 Chronicles 8:5. But additionally, because it agrees in sound with the proper name for Egypt, *Mitsraim*, the name is taken from the argument. For no region is safer in its natural situation than Egypt. Namely, from the west it has an inaccessible desert; from the south the cataracts of the Nile and the mountains of Ethiopia; from the east again a wasteland, and pits, and the Serbonian bog; from the north a sea almost without harbors. Bochart, *Phaleg* IV. chapter 24. **a)** *and on the other hand from Egypt to the river*, namely the one preeminently so called, the Euphrates, which the Assyrians dwell by. Jeremiah 2:18. **b)** *or rather to the sea from the sea; from one to the other.* Nations, placed between the most remote and entirely opposite seas and mountains, shall come to you. Tarnovius and others think that the Holy Land is designated here according to its borders: to the western or Great Sea from the other eastern or Dead Sea, and from Mount Lebanon to Mount Sinai, cf. Joshua 1:4; Joel 2:20; and Amos 8:12. But we prefer to leave the words here in their breadth, all the more because in the cited place of Amos 8:12, external regions (in which Israel and Judah were to live in exile) are described in a nearly similar way rather than the Israelite land, cf. what we noted there at verse 11, and Zechariah 9:10; Psalm 72:8 and following. **c)** *and from one mountain even to the opposite mountain.* The <term>ellipsis</term> of particles is to be supplied from the preceding. **v. 13. d)** Schmid: *Yet it shall be.* As if to say: *Before those magnificent promises are fulfilled regarding the restoration of Jerusalem (verse 11) and the bringing of various nations into her bosom; meanwhile, I say, first it shall happen...* etc. **e)** *this land*, namely the Israelite land, for it has the definite article *H*: and the text here seems to deal with a certain particular land. **f)** first through Nebuchadnezzar, then through Titus. Isaiah 5:7; Jeremiah 12:11. **g)** not as if it had to happen by some absolute decree, but *because of its inhabitants.* Cf. Isaiah 24:1, 5. **h)** *for the fruit of their deeds.* Cf. Isaiah 3:10 and the note on Jeremiah 32:19. Tarnovius: *that as they have sown, so they may reap.* **v. 14. i)** *Feed*, govern, rule, You who are the Good Shepherd. Chapter 5:3; Isaiah 40:11; Ezekiel 34:13; Zechariah 11:4, 7, 9; Psalm 23:1. By this word (says Tarnovius), whatever pertains to the preservation of the godly is summarized. He makes the connection of this with verse 13 as follows: *When these things happen to the wicked, this shall be the prayer of the Church believing the Gospel, and seeing that ruin of the Synagogue.* Cf. note on verse 1 and similar prayers in Habakkuk 3:2. **k)** *with Your staff.* Psalm 23:4. The staff not of Moses, or a rod of iron, but Your own—the leading of Your Spirit by the word of Your Gospel. Tarnovius: *By Your Word and Spirit*, for those are the instruments of the kingdom of God. A shepherd counts the sheep with a staff, and corrects, and leads them, showing where to go, where to head, from where to depart, and where they ought to graze. Cocceius, *Lexicon* 847. Cf. Leviticus 27:32; Ezekiel 20:37. **l)** *the flock, I say, of Your inheritance*, hereditary, or given to You as an inheritance. Psalm 95:7; cf. Psalm 2:8.

---

**v. 10.** *ve-tere* [and she shall see] with Tsere in manuscripts 1, 2, 5. But *ve-tere* with accent on the penultimate in 3, 6, 16, 19, 23, against the printed Masorah and David Kimchi in his Commentary on this place. Cf. a similar anomaly in Genesis 41:31 and Zechariah 9:5. For *Elohayich* [your God] manuscripts 6, 9, 14, 20 have *Elohayich* (with different vowels), so also in manuscript 5, against the printed Masorah in Jeremiah 2:19. *u-the-kasseha* [and it shall cover her] with the letter Nun missing in 1, 3, 7, 8, 21. Against the printed Masorah and the Great Masorah. *le-mirmas* [for a trampling] thus with Kamatz in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 23 according to Masorah 2 and Erfurt. The rest have it with Patach.

<summary>This page provides a philological and theological commentary on Micah 7:9–14, focusing on the themes of Jerusalem's patient endurance of divine wrath and the eventual promise of restoration. The commentator interprets the rebuilding of walls and the gathering of nations both as historical events and as spiritual types for the growth of the Christian Church.</summary>
