<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on the final chapter of the Book of Micah. While the previous page focused on the prophet's patient endurance amidst societal collapse, this page records a prayer for divine restoration and a concluding hymn of praise for God's incomparable mercy.</meta>

### CHAPTER 7. MICAH 7.

<margin>
**v. 14. p)** This is either a Subjunctive; *let them be fed*: or an optative; *make it so that they are fed*, or *let them have their pasture*. <note>original: "pascantur"</note> Cf. Isaiah 14:30; compare above chapter 5:3 and Ezekiel 34:23. **q)** in the region of Bashan, Jeremiah 50:19, a pasture region. Amos 4:1. **r)** cf. Obadiah v. 19. **s)** *as in the days of old.* <note>original: "sicut diebus priscis"</note> Amos 9:11; Malachi 3:4. For example, under David and Solomon, 1 Kings 5:5. These times were pre-figurations of the more illustrious happiness under the kingdom of Christ.
</margin>
<column-break/>
<margin>m</margin> dwelling alone <margin>n</margin> in the forest <margin>o</margin> in the midst of Carmel <margin>p</margin> let them feed in Bashan and Gilead as in the days of <margin>s</margin> old.
15 As in the days of your coming out of the land of Egypt, I will show him <margin>x</margin> wonders.
16 Nations shall see <margin>y</margin> and be ashamed of all <margin>a</margin> their might; they shall lay their hand <margin>b</margin> on their mouth, <margin>c</margin> their ears shall be deaf.
17 They shall lick <margin>d</margin> the dust like a snake, like crawling things of the earth; <margin>g</margin> they shall move trembling <margin>h</margin> out of their enclosures; <margin>k</margin> unto the Lord our God they shall fear, and they shall be afraid of You.
18 <margin>l</margin> Who is a God <margin>m</margin> like You, <margin>n</margin> pardoning iniquity <margin>o</margin> and passing over transgression <margin>p</margin> for the remnant of His inheritance? He does not retain His anger forever, <margin>r</margin> because He delights in mercy.
19 <margin>s</mentioned> He will again have compassion on us; <margin>t</margin> He will subdue our iniquities; <margin>u</margin> and You will cast <margin>x</margin> into the depths of the sea <margin>y</margin> all their sins.
20 <margin>z</margin> You will give <margin>a</margin> truth to Jacob and mercy to Abraham, <margin>c</margin> which You have sworn to our fathers <margin>d</margin> from days of old.

->THE BURDEN<-
<column-break/>
<margin>
**m)** *dwelling* <note>original: "habitantem"</note> (with a lengthening 'yod' at the end, as in Deuteronomy 33:16 and Obadiah v. 3) *apart*. This phrase is used in various ways in Scripture: 1) In opposition to community, as in Numbers 23:9; this is how the scholar Cocceius interprets this passage in his Lexicon. It means one who is separated from all men who do not share the same faith, speak the same Word of God, or walk in the same path. 2) To signify a state of mourning, as in Jeremiah 15:17 and Lamentations 1:1 (see the notes there) and chapter 3:28. 3) In the sense of desolation and desertion, as in Isaiah 27:10; this is how Tarnovius understands Micah here: "Care for that flock of yours all the more, which dwells alone, abandoned by men, living among beasts and enemies in great danger." 4) In the sense of peace, confidence, and security, as in Deuteronomy 33:28 and Jeremiah 49:31. For to "dwell alone" means to live in security without needing treaties or alliances with others (Judges 18:7). If the phrase is taken in this sense here, it provides an easy meaning that fits the text: Feed Your people so that they may *dwell apart*, that is, securely and tranquilly. The grammar here <note>the accusative case</note> marks not the object of the action, but the effect—much like the "desolate heaps" in Isaiah 37:26.
**n)** *the forest*, that is, *in* the forest. It depends on the verb "to dwell," which in Hebrew can be joined either with a direct object or with a preposition. 
**o)** This is either a list without conjunctions (*the forest and in the middle of Carmel*) or an ellipsis where the preposition "in" is omitted; as if to say, *in the middle of Carmel*. The sense is that they may live in woody and uncultivated places as safely and peacefully as in cultivated and fruitful fields, fearing no incursions from wild beasts or robbers. See Ezekiel 34:25 and Isaiah 11:6-7. Compare similar contrasts in Isaiah 10:18; 29:17; 32:15-16; 37:24. <term>Carmel</term> usually refers to a fruitful orchard or garden-land.
</margin>

***

**v. 15. s)** Indeed, as in the days when you formerly went out, with many and great miracles, which I performed for you in Egypt, in the desert, and finally in the occupation of Canaan. Cf. Isaiah 11:11; Ezekiel 20:35-36. This is the response of the Son of God to the preceding prayers of the Church; it is followed by the Church’s hymn of praise in verse 18, so that the context functions almost like a dialogue. <margin>**a)** *I will show him*, namely to my people (v. 14). The text shifts from the second person ("you") to the third person ("him"): we believe this change occurs because the speaker addresses the Church present in Micah's time (second person) but speaks of the Church as it will exist at the time of the final fulfillment (third person), as if of someone yet to arrive. **x)** cf. Psalm 106:22; also Isaiah 25:1; Psalm 98:1.</margin> 

**v. 16. y)** Namely, they shall see these wonders (v. 15). Cf. Isaiah 49:7; Psalm 40:4 and 126:2-3. **z)** with a saving and humble shame (v. 17). Cf. Ezekiel 16:63. **a)** *They shall be ashamed*, I say (for the emphasis of the accent requires the previous verb to be repeated), of all their own strength, however much they had imagined for themselves before; for they will feel that it cannot be compared to the wonders of Jehovah, and will be a source of blushing rather than glory. Ezekiel 32:30; cf. Isaiah 33:13; Jeremiah 10:6. Alternatively: "on account of all their power." Tarnovius says: "in the face of all their power," meaning the power of those who dwell in the bosom of the Church. Cf. Isaiah 28:6; Psalm 145:11-12. **b)** out of silent wonder, indicating they have no further grounds for boasting. Judges 18:19; Job 21:5; 40:4; cf. Isaiah 52:15. **c)** *they shall become deaf.* Psalm 38:1. Before the majesty of what they are about to hear. Tarnovius: for these things will strike their ears like a great and sudden thunderclap, which by its weight suspends the sense of hearing. Cf. 1 Samuel 3:11; Jeremiah 19:3; and regarding the matter, Isaiah 64:2-3.

**v. 17. d)** *They shall lick the dust*, as suppliants, with faces bowed to the ground; or (as Jonathan translates) they shall stretch themselves out on their faces on the earth. This denotes the greatest humility both toward God Himself (Psalm 72:9) and toward His people (Isaiah 49:23). **e)** cf. Genesis 3:14; Isaiah 65:25. **f)** *and like the crawling things of the earth*, reptiles that creep on the ground. Deuteronomy 32:24, where the Arabic Polyglot uses the same root with the same meaning. Cf. Bochart, *Hieroz.* Part I, p. 59. Furthermore, the second accent indicates this comparison should be joined not with the preceding verb, but with the following one. **g)** *they shall be moved*, they shall run trembling, they shall come out <unclear>disturbed</unclear>. Isaiah 14:9; 64:1. **h)** *from their enclosures*, that is, according to Jonathan, the fortresses in which they live shut up to be safe. 2 Samuel 22:46; Psalm 18:46. **i)** *they shall fear*, they shall run in terror, having laid aside their former ferocity. Hosea 3:5. **k)** namely, "O Jehovah, our God!" by a prophetic address. Cf. Jeremiah 10:7. Or, as we prefer: "O my people!" for then the speech flows more clearly. It implies the reverence not only owed to the Church but which will come to it. Cf. Deuteronomy 28:10.

**v. 18. l)** *Who is there then?* used as a question meaning "There is none." A hymn of praise <note>original: "doxologia"</note> full of holy wonder and amazement. The Church, whom Micah here introduces speaking again, is as if plunged into an abyss when she considers the riches of divine mercy and grace to be shown to her in the last days; much like Paul when he admires the wisdom of God in Romans 11:33. This is why "Who is a God" is phrased as a question. **m)** *like You* <note>original: "tui simile"</note>. Deuteronomy 3:24; Jeremiah 10:7; Psalm 89:9. There are some who think the prophet is alluding to his own name, **Micah** (which means "Who is like the Lord?"); we leave this as a possibility. See the notes at chapter 1:1. **n)** *taking away guilt*, not so that it does not exist (though we say this regarding its effect rather than its power), but so that it is not imputed; that is, forgiving. Ezekiel 34:7; Numbers 14:18; 1 John 1:9. **o)** *and passing over*, that is, letting go unpunished, transgression, behaving as if He did not see it at all. Amos 7:8; 8:2; Proverbs 19:11; cf. Jeremiah 31:34. **p)** *for the remnant of His inheritance*, His people, whom He holds as a special possession (v. 14) and acquired with precious blood (Titus 2:14), whom after so many and such great punishments, through so many centuries and crises, He has preserved for such grace in wonderful ways. Cf. above chapter 4:7; Isaiah 10:22. **q)** *neither did He retain* or keep His anger forever. Amos 1:11; cf. Psalm 30:6; 103:9-10; also Isaiah 12:1. **r)** *desiring mercy.* Here it denotes love, not that with which we have loved (though God elsewhere testifies He desires this, as in Hosea 6:6), but the mercy with which He Himself has loved us. 1 John 4:10; cf. Ephesians 1:5; 1 Thessalonians 1:11; 1 John 3:16.

**v. 19. s)** *He will return, therefore, and have mercy on us.* An idiom where the verb "to return" acts as the adverb "again," as in Deuteronomy 30:3; Malachi 1:4. It emphatically connotes a "turning back" of God's love, which had previously departed through anger. Zechariah 1:16; Psalm 71:20-21; 90:13; cf. Isaiah 14:1; 49:13; Joel 2:14. **t)** *He will subdue*, tread down, suppress. Jonathan adds: "through His mercy." There is great emphasis in this word; for sin and the guilt of sin are conceived as nothing other than a cruel tyrant, dragging us like slaves and prisoners to servitude and death, whose ferocity divine grace shall repress. Genesis 1:28; Jeremiah 31:11, 16; Zechariah 9:15; 2 Chronicles 28:10; cf. Romans 6:12, 14; Hebrews 2:5. Therefore, it is not a trivial or easy removal of sin, which rises against us in God's judgment, condemning us and demanding punishment; rather, it is a work of divine power. **u)** *and You will cast*, O God! as things we wish abolished and no longer value. Isaiah 30:17. **x)** *into the depths of the sea*; Exodus 15:5, 10. **y)** cf. Isaiah 43:25.

**v. 20. z)** *You will give* in actual effect, just as You once swore. Luke 1:73. **a)** *truth and mercy.* John 1:17. Cocceius says in his Lexicon (44) that when said of God, "mercy" denotes eternal love and the gifts of eternal love, as opposed to anger, enmity, and damnation; while "truth" denotes the display and fulfillment of promises. Psalm 69:14; cf. Luke 1:72 and Isaiah 55:3. **b)** *to Jacob... to Abraham*, namely, in their descendants. **c)** Luke 1:55. **d)** from the days of antiquity, that is, of old. 2 Kings 19:25; Lamentations 1:7.

***

**v. 16.** The word *their ears* <note>original: "ve-ozneihem"</note> appears with the prefix *vav* in several manuscripts. The word *shall be deaf* <note>original: "techirashnah"</note> appears with specific vowel markings in various editions. 
**v. 19.** The word *You will cast* <note>original: "ve-tashlich"</note> is written defectively <note>missing a vowel-letter</note> in certain sources.
The word *in the depths* <note>original: "bimtzulot"</note> is written defectively with a *Kibbutz* vowel in many codices. A marginal note mentions that while some codices may be in error, the scholars David Kimchi and others require a *Shureq* vowel here.

<summary>This concluding section of Micah features a prayer for God to shepherd His people in the fertile lands of Carmel and Bashan, followed by a celebratory hymn regarding God’s unique character in forgiving sin and fulfilling ancient promises to Abraham and Jacob.</summary>
<keywords>Micah 7, shepherding, Carmel, Bashan, divine mercy, forgiveness of sins, depths of the sea, Abrahamic covenant, Jacob, restoration of Israel</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as the formal introduction to the Book of Nahum, following the conclusion of the commentary on Micah. It transitions from the restoration of Israel to the specific judgment against its great oppressor, Nineveh.</meta>

THE BOOK OF NAHUM,

->Hebrew: *Nahum*<-

# ON THE PROPHECY OF NAHUM
## PREFACE.

<margin>
1. *Nahum's Homeland, name, order, etc.*
2. *His Age [Date], according to the opinion of:*
a) *the Hebrews and Grotius,*
b) *Vitringa,*
c) *others,*
d) *Bochart.*
</margin>
Nahum was an Elkoshite, or from Elkosh (though it is uncertain whether he was called this because of his tribe or his birthplace). As his name implies, he was *one of the comforters* <note>original: "vnus e consolatoribus"</note> of Jerusalem (referencing Isaiah 40:1) against the terror of the Assyrians. This is because the destruction of one's enemies provides consolation to the Church (comparing Tobit 14:15 and Proverbs 11:10). For this reason, in the ancient order of the Twelve Prophets, he was placed after Jonah by the Septuagint translators <note>The "LXX Interpp." refers to the scholars who produced the early Greek version of the Old Testament.</note>, because both of them wove a prophecy concerning Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrians, as Jerome observes in his prologue to this book (comparing Jonah 1:1). However, his *Age* [the time he lived] is not sufficiently certain or precisely clear; this creates more than one difficulty in explaining this prophecy, as we shall point out in the appropriate places. For the Hebrew scholars believe that both Nahum and Habakkuk wrote during the time of King *Manasseh* (cf. the notes on 2 Kings 21:10). Grotius says we are persuaded of this both by the ancient order—placing these prophets after those who lived in the time of Hezekiah—and by the actual events contained in their writings. Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a famous 15th-century Jewish statesman and commentator.</note> also holds this view in his commentary on this book (folio 268, column 1); and based on that hypothesis, he says in column 3 that, in his opinion, Nahum did not prophesy about the defeat of Sennacherib, because that event had already occurred. 

*Vitringa*, however, in his *Prophetic Doctrine* (p. 37), states that Nahum’s age must be fixed closely after *Isaiah* and *Micah*, and thus under King *Hezekiah*. He argues it was not only after the deportation of the ten tribes, but also after the defeat of Sennacherib (chapter 1:11, 12), from which the theme of the prophecy is drawn, seizing the opportunity to predict the total destruction of Nineveh and the Assyrian kingdom. Yet many others, such as Calovius in his *Prophetic Theology* (p. 122) and Maius in his *Economy of the Old Testament* (p. 8, 6), believe he lived in the time that passed between the deportation of the ten tribes to Assyria and the defeat of Sennacherib; they argue that the former event is mentioned by the prophet in chapter 1:12-13. This also seems very likely to Lightfoot in his *Chronology of the Old Testament* (p. 109), though he suggests Nahum began under Hezekiah and continued until the time of Manasseh, to which the Hebrews refer his age, as we just mentioned. But as for *Bochart’s* claim in *Phaleg* (p. 6)—that it is likely *Nahum wrote at the time when Diospolis <note>Diospolis is the Greek name for the Egyptian city of Thebes, called No-Amon in the Bible.</note> had been recently cut off by King Nebuchadnezzar, who, after capturing Jerusalem and Tyre, immediately invaded Egypt*—that seems very unlikely to us. For that great man did not prove (as his hypothesis requires) either that the Assyrian empire was overthrown by Nebuchadnezzar only in the final decade of his reign and after Egypt was laid waste; or that Nahum wrote outside his homeland among the exiles in Babylonia, at a time when the city and temple of Jerusalem had lain in ruins since the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar. Rather, it seems certain from chapter 2:1 that the public worship of God still flourished in Judah at that time, to say nothing of other points (cf. also the notes on chapter 3:7, 8).

<margin>
3. *Theme and object.*
4. *Occasion.*
</margin>
This is, therefore, a second and fatal prophecy against Nineveh (the capital) and the Assyrian empire. The Lord, the just judge and defender <note>original: "adsertor"</note> of His Church, was soon to take vengeance upon them through the Medes and Babylonians. For although the Assyrians had begun to repent at the preaching of Jonah, they did not persist in it for long. Instead, they returned to their former crimes, cruelty, robbery, and idolatry; indeed, they even broke out into blasphemies against Jehovah, especially under Sennacherib. Through Nahum, God declares that this will not go unpunished; He severely pronounces that their punishment is already prepared, and that He will compensate for the delay of the penalty with its great weight, so that even the location of that most vast and powerful city would be unknown to future generations. History has long since proven this true, as we noted at chapter 1:8.

<margin>
5. *Parallels.*
</margin>
From this, the agreement of our prophet is clear—both in subject matter and phrasing—with Isaiah (comparing Nahum 1:13 and 2:1 with Isaiah 10:27 and 52:7), with Micah (Nahum 2:2 and Micah 2:13), and with Zephaniah (Nahum 3:7 and Zephaniah 2:13, 14, 15). Furthermore, there is a clear connection here to the whole prophecy of Jonah and his complaints in Jonah 4:2 (comparing Nahum 1:2, 3, etc.).

<margin>
6. *Style.*
</margin>
We will say nothing here, for the sake of brevity, about his agreement with Moses and other divine writers. As for style and speech, this prophet’s diction is concise and grave, and is particularly difficult because of the frequent "change of persons" [shifting perspectives]. Jerome complains of this in his notes on chapter 2:2, saying: *“The speech is now turned toward Nineveh; and the prophets are especially obscure for this reason: that suddenly, while one thing is being discussed, the person addressed is changed.”* While it cannot be denied that the "change of persons" is common in Scripture—often required by intense emotion, imitation, or vivid description <note>original: "mimesis & hypotyposes"</note>—one must be careful not to make such claims without cause. In that very passage, the Blessed Father [Jerome] wrongly thought the speech turned to Nineveh, when it actually pertains to Judah (the Church), as we prove in our notes. (Compare also our remarks from Schmidt on Isaiah 52:14).

<margin>
7. *Parts of the book.*
</margin>
We have divided the book into three parts, following the number of chapters. After the title in 1:1, we have: I. God’s zeal, justice, power, and vengeance as punishment for the Assyrians (v. 2-11, 14), but as comfort for the Jews (v. 7), with a promise of better things and restoration under the New Testament (v. 12, 13). II. After that continued promise (2:1, 2, 3), the siege, capture, plundering, and destruction of Nineveh is depicted (2:4ff). III. The cause and manner of that destruction are described more fully and confirmed (3:1ff).

<margin>
8. *Use.*
</margin>
Moreover, whatever is now said against Nineveh, Jerome long ago rightly advised that it is also figuratively predicted of the "Antichristian city" or the world. Regarding the end of the world, he says, *“the prophecy is woven according to the spiritual meaning* <note>original: "secundum anagogen"</note> *for the consolation of the saints: so that whatever they see in the world, they may despise as passing and falling, and prepare themselves for the day of judgment, when the Lord is the avenger against the true Assyrians.”* (Cf. notes on chapter 2:1; Isaiah 13:4; 13:1; 30:25, 27, 31, 33; Micah 5:5, etc.).

Gg gg 4
<meta>catchword: until</meta>

<summary>This preface introduces the Book of Nahum, identifying the prophet as a "comforter" of Israel whose work predicts the total destruction of the Assyrian capital, Nineveh. The author debates the historical dating of the prophecy—placing it between the reigns of Hezekiah and Manasseh—and highlights the text's spiritual application as a comfort for the Church against worldly oppression.</summary>
<keywords>Nahum, Nineveh, Assyria, Elkoshite, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Sennacherib, Jerome, Grotius, Vitringa, prophetic interpretation, consolation, biblical chronology</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the general preface to the specific exegesis of Nahum Chapter 1. It focuses on the title, the prophet's identity, and the character of God as a judge, connecting the historical fall of Nineveh to theological principles.</meta>

<header>CHAPTER I. NAHUM 1</header>

# CHAPTER I. NAHUM 1

<margin>
It is believed that Nineveh was subverted under Astyages, king of the Medes. Others, however, think Nineveh was finally destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian and Cyaxares, King of the Medes.
</margin>

| **1** | The burden^a | of Nineveh^b | The book^c | of the vision^d | of Nahum^e | the Elkoshite^f. |
| **2** | God^g | is jealous^h | and an avenger^i | is the LORD^k | an avenger^l | is the LORD^m | and a master^l |
| | of wrath^l | an avenger^m | is the LORD^m | to His adversaries^n | and He reserves [wrath]^o | He | for His enemies^p. |

<margin>
**CHAPTER I. v. 1.** a) The Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> says "Burden." The Syriac and Arabic versions say "plague" or "Prophecy": namely, one that is heavy and denouncing misfortune. Compare Isaiah 13:1, 14:28, 15:1. Jerome <note>An early Christian scholar and Bible translator (c. 347–420 AD).</note> says: It is called this because it weighs down upon the one against whom it is seen, and does not allow them to lift their neck. See also the notes on Jeremiah 23:33 and Habakkuk 1:1. b) Concerning Nineveh, or against Nineveh. Compare chapter 2:9 and Jonah 1:2. It is one of the prophecies against the Gentiles [nations], as in Isaiah 13, 19, 21, and 22. This object must be carefully observed here, so that through the whole prophecy you may know against whom the prophetic word is chiefly directed. See for example 1:8, 11; 2:6, 8-14; 3:1, 8. Jonathan <note>Refers to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Prophets.</note> says: The burden of the cup of cursing, to be given to Nineveh to drink (see 3:11): against which Jonah, son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-Hepher, had prophesied previously, when she was spared from her sins; but when she continued to sin, Nahum of the family of Elkosh prophesied against her again, as written in this book. Truly Nineveh, at the preaching of Jonah, had been corrected by the repentance of its inhabitants and preserved by divine mercy (Jonah 3:4 and following). But soon relapsing into worse behavior, she finally brought upon herself divine vengeance and destruction. See the Preface, section 4. This prophecy was fulfilled not so much in the fall of Sennacherib (which some think is predicted in 1:12-13, though others, including Hebrew scholars, want it to have happened earlier), but in the actual overturning of Nineveh. This occurred in the sixteenth year of Josiah according to Ussher’s Annals <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), an Archbishop known for his biblical chronology.</note>, captured by the combined forces of Nabopolassar, father of Nebuchadnezzar, and Astyages the Mede. And in truth, Jerome says in his introduction to Jonah: as far as both Hebrew and Greek histories are concerned, especially Herodotus, we read that Nineveh was destroyed by Astyages
</margin>

king of the Medes, in the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, according to the Hebrew and Eusebian Chronicles <note>Eusebius was a 4th-century historian of the Christian Church.</note>, not long before the beginnings of Cyrus, when Zedekiah held the kingdom among the Jews. Compare notes on Jonah 1:2, the Preface to Jonah section 7, Tobit 14:15, Calovius, Gurtler, Vitringa’s Chronology, and especially Drusius <note>A group of 17th-century biblical commentators and chronologists.</note>. c) A book or writing, recorded for the use of the whole Church. Compare Isaiah 30:8, 34:16, Jeremiah 30:2. Others, like Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note>, say a "little book" sent in the manner of a letter to the Assyrians: which, as Tarnovius explains, is a special letter in which Nahum, in the name of his Supreme Commander Jehovah, declares war on the Assyrians, whom he immediately describes in verse 2, and records the reasons for His anger and the progress of the war. Indeed, the Hebrew name *sefer* <note>original: "סֵפֶר"</note> denotes not only a full volume or book, but also a small scroll, such as a genealogy (Genesis 5:1), a bill of divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1, 3), and a letter (2 Samuel 11:14, 2 Kings 5:5). d) A prophetic vision (Isaiah 1:1). e) See the Preface, section 1. f) Elkoshite, or as the Septuagint and Vulgate say, Elcesaeite. It is uncertain whether this name refers to his lineage or his birthplace. It is formed from *Elkosh*, meaning "late grass" or "late rain." Luther and others take it for the name of his homeland. Jerome says: "Some think Elkosh was Nahum's father... while today Elkosh is a small village in Galilee, barely showing traces of ancient buildings among its ruins, but still known to the Jews; and it was shown to me by my guide." Abarbanel, however, says: "Scripture provides no testimony that this is a place-name, nor do we have any certainty from the Scriptures or the monuments of our ancestors regarding the family or homeland of the Prophet." **v. 2.** g) A jealous God <note>original: "Deus Zelotes"</note>, the Vulgate says "emulator." Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> notes: one who cannot long look upon his oppressed friends or his flourishing enemies (Joshua 24:19; Exodus 20:5; and according to Abarbanel, Joel 2:18). h) An avenger (Psalm 94:1). i) Or "one who executes justice" (Revelation 6:10). i) Is the Lord. After the title or inscription of the whole book in verse 1, the Prophet begins his prophecy with a description of Jehovah as a severe avenger against enemies (v. 2-6), but very kind toward His own who repent (v. 8); he then follows with threats against the Ninevites (v. 8-11) and comfort for the Israelites, especially concerning the New Testament (v. 12 and following), as Sebastian Schmidt observed in his notes. k) Psalm 99:8. l) Vulgate: "and having fury." The Syriac: "and great is his anger," which he can very easily put into effect if he wishes. Compare Proverbs 22:24, 29:22, and Deuteronomy 4:24. m) The Lord, I say, is an avenger. The threefold repetition in this verse is not just for vehement emphasis, as Grotius thought, nor for the three deportations of the Israelites (which Abarbanel counts in 1 Chronicles 5:26, 2 Kings 15:29, and 17:6), but it seems to us to refer to the three persons of the Divinity <note>A reference to the Christian doctrine of the Trinity.</note>. Compare Isaiah 6:3. n) Vulgate: "avenging against his enemies." Jonathan: "The Lord is about to take vengeance on the enemies of his people." (Isaiah 59:18). o) "Against those who oppose him" (Hebrews 10:17). Abarbanel says: "For even if the Israelites deserved destruction and exile for their transgressions, the Assyrian was not moved to lay them waste by divine command, nor with the intention of serving God; rather, he came to waste the people of God moved by malice and arrogance, while God permitted it." Compare Isaiah 10:5, Zechariah 1:15. o) And he himself keeps anger for its proper time (Psalm 103:9). p) To his enemies (Isaiah 42:13, 59:18, 66:6, 14). Abarbanel says: "Do not think, therefore, that because He does not take vengeance immediately, He has forgotten them or forgiven all their injuries and crimes." See Preface, section 4. **v. 3.** q) Indeed, Jehovah is slow to anger. Vulgate: "patient." Jonathan: "he puts off his anger for a long time." Syriac: "long is the patience of the Lord." (Exodus 34:6, Joel 2:13), even more than Jonah wanted (Jonah 4:2). r) Vulgate: "and great in strength," namely to demonstrate his long-suffering and patience. Or: he is also great in strength, and therefore by no means etc. That is to say, that He delays punishment is an argument of His long-suffering, not His weakness. Compare Numbers 14:17. s) But nevertheless by no means... [will He] let the guilty go free, or allow the innocent to be unavenged—namely, His enemies. Jonathan says: "those who have not turned [repented]." And if He delays His anger, He will not forever allow His enemies to go unpunished for what they do; but He will eventually compensate for the slowness of the punishment with its severity. Compare Exodus 20:7, 34:7. Jerome says: "The sense is, He was indeed patient with the crime of the Assyrians for a long time... but because they despised the goodness of God and stored up wrath for themselves (Romans 2:5)... He will by no means let them go unavenged." t) Of the Lord, or as far as it pertains to the Lord. u) In the storm. Vulgate: "in the tempest." o) "In the completion" (Psalm 66:15, 83:16). x) And in the whirlwind (Job 9:17). y) Is His way, as He has demonstrated many times in the overturning of His enemies. Compare Isaiah 28:2, 29:6, Jeremiah 23:19, Zechariah 9:14. x) And the clouds. Vulgate: "and the mist." a) Are the dust (Exodus 9:9, Deuteronomy 28:24) of His feet. Grotius: He treads upon the clouds as men do upon dust; that is, He is the Lord of the clouds and uses them as He wills. Compare Exodus 14:20, 24, Isaiah 19:1, Psalm 18:10. **v. 4.** b) He rebukes the sea (Isaiah 50:2, Psalm 106:9). c) And makes it dry, as He did in Exodus 14:21. Similar contracted forms are found in 2:10, Obadiah 11, Lamentations 3:33. d) And as He once did to the Jordan (Joshua 3:17, Psalm 74:15), so He does to all rivers (Psalm 107:33) and to the Assyrian's Euphrates (Isaiah 8:7). e) He wastes, He dries up. Vulgate: "leading to a desert." (Isaiah 50:2, 51:10). Jerome: "The power of God is described, who will take vengeance for Israel... that it is not difficult for Him to destroy the Assyrians, He whose majesty can even change the elements." f) It languishes (Psalm 16:8) when God rebukes. g) Bashan and (Jonathan: Mathnan, Syriac: Mathnia) and Carmel, places most suitable for pasturing cattle: which are often joined for this reason, as in Isaiah 33:9, Jeremiah 2:7, 50:19, Amos 1:2, Micah 7:14. h) And the flower. The Septuagint and Arabic: "blooming things." Syriac: "and the sprout." Jonathan: "the trees of Lebanon languish and fall." Compare Isaiah 35:1-2, Hosea 14:6-8. Grotius: "After the pastures and fields, He even comes to the trees, to indicate that there is nothing that can last if God is unwilling." Examples of this saying are found in the times of Hezekiah (1 Kings 11:s), Joel (1:10), Jeremiah (14:1), etc. **v. 5.** i) The mountains; like Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:18). Jerome: "These are figures and are to be understood as the great and powerful." So also Rabbi Selomo [Rashi] on this passage. Abarbanel understands "mountains and hills" to mean kingdoms and provinces. Compare Isaiah 2:14, 65:19.

---

**Notes on Nahum 1, v. 1.** *Book of the vision.* Radak and Abarbanel say it should have a Kametz vowel, but this is against the evidence of the manuscripts and grammatical rules. *Nahum* is written with a Kametz in verses 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, 21, contrary to the printed Massorah. *The Elkoshite* is spelled fully according to the Erfurt Massorah. **v. 3.** *To clear* is written with a Tzere in various manuscripts (17, 18, 21, 24) and anomalous in the Berlin codex. *In the whirlwind*: The letter Samech is small here according to some printed Massorahs, but our manuscripts have no such thing.

<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on the first chapter of Nahum. It bridges the transition from God's terrifying power over nature to His specific judgment against Nineveh, while contrasting His wrath toward enemies with His goodness toward the faithful. It includes significant historical references to the fall of the Assyrian Empire.</meta>

<header>NAHUM. CHAPTER I. 1</header>

<margin>
k) Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin Bible.</note>: *they are moved by him* and *they shall tremble at the sight of him*. See 2 Samuel 22:8, Ezekiel 38:20. l) Isaiah 54:10. m) *they melt*, and are dissolved as if by their own accord. Hithpael <note>A Hebrew verb form indicating intensive or reflexive action.</note> (3) Amos 9:13; cf. Psalm 64:1, 2; a similar emphasis on this verb form is found in Micah 1:4. n) Syriac: and the earth *is shaken*; Vulgate: *it trembled*; Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase.</note>: *it is laid waste*; M. I. <note>Likely a reference to a specific commentator or manuscript, possibly "Manuscript of Isaac" or similar.</note>: *it burns or blazes*, comparing the word (but in the transitive sense) to 2 Samuel 5:21. So Schmid: *and it shall be burned*, and Gusset p. 535: *the earth shall be lifted up by a fire on high*, comparing verse 6 and the related noun in Judges 20:38, 40; Jeremiah 6:1; Ezekiel 17:9. Others more simply: *it lifts itself up*, or as if *lifting its voice*, comparing Numbers 14:1, Isaiah 42:2, 11; Habakkuk 1:3; Psalm 24:9. Tigurine Bible: *the earth lifts itself from his sight*. Abarbanel <note>Don Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a famous Jewish statesman and commentator.</note>: as if to say, even if the earth is naturally immobile and resting, it nonetheless lifts itself up from His sight and does not remain still. Thus, the world also lifts itself and those inhabiting it, so that it might remove and cast them out from His presence. All these things (continues Abarbanel) are said figuratively regarding Nebuchadnezzar, who comes like a rising whirlwind and a storm, with a darkening cloud, and makes the sea and rivers dry, which are symbols of the nations; see Isaiah 18:12; add Revelation 17:15. o) *the world* Isaiah 24:4, Chapter 34:1.
</margin>

## 5 The mountains quake before Him, and the hills melt; the earth heaves before Him, the world and all who dwell in it.
## 6 Who can stand before His indignation? And who can endure the heat of His anger? His wrath is poured out like fire, and the rocks are shattered by Him.

<margin>
who can resist God when He is angry and avenging His people? Compare 2 Thessalonians 1:6 and following; Revelation 6:17. s) Isaiah 13:9, Psalm 2:5. t) *heat*, Vulgate: *his indignation*. Deuteronomy 29:22, Esther 1:12. u) *it is poured out*, Syriac: *it burns like fire*. M. I.: *like things liquefied by fire*, for example, pitch or sulfur, and metals, etc.
</margin>

## 7 The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; and He knows those who take refuge in Him.
## 8 But with an overflowing flood He will make a complete end of its site, and will pursue His enemies into darkness.
## 9 What do you plot against the LORD? He will make a complete end; trouble will not rise up a second time.
## 10 For while they are folded together as thorns, and while they are drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry.

---

<margin>
v. 6. p) *Before his anger*. Isaiah 33:14, Psalm 76:8. q) *who shall stand*? 2 Samuel 6:20. r) and *who shall remain*? Amos 7:2, 5; Psalm 24:3. Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and Vulgate: *and who shall resist*? Jerome: *Symmachus <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Bible into Greek.</note> interpreted this more clearly: "and who shall sustain the wrath of his fury?"* So the Syriac: *and who shall bear the heat of his fury?* Jonathan: *When He appeared in mercy to give the Law to His people, the world was moved by His presence; how much more so when He shall be manifested in anger to take vengeance on those who hate His people? Before His retribution, who shall stand? And who shall endure the evil of His wrath?* Jerome: *Either you will be worn down, or no one will be found who—*
</margin>

Compare Exodus 9:33, Lamentations 2:3, 4; 2 Chronicles 34:21, 25; and Ezekiel 22:20, etc. x) and *the rocks themselves* Psalm 78:15, Job 14:18, to which men usually flee in the greatest danger; Revelation 6:15. y) *they are broken* (Septuagint and Vulgate: *they are dissolved*. Syriac and Arabic: *they melt*) *they are destroyed by him*. Jeremiah 4:26; cf. 1 Kings 19:11. Where, then, and how can anyone safely survive His presence? Jerome. Compare the opposition in the following verse 7. **v. 7. z)** Vulgate: *The Lord is good* <note>original Greek: "ho chrestos", as in 1 Peter 2:3</note>. Jonathan adds *to Israel*, from Psalm 73:1. <note>original Greek: "to the ones who wait for Him"</note>, James 5:11; cf. Psalm 25:8, Psalm 34:9, Psalm 86:5, Psalm 119:68.

68. Hitherto he has opposed the irresistible <note>original Greek: "anupostaton"</note> [power of God] to the ferocity of the Assyrians; now he briefly describes His goodness <note>original Greek: "chrestoteta"</note> for the comfort of His own people. a) *as a protection*. That is, so that He may be a rampart, namely, for the pious. Chapter 3:11; cf. Isaiah 25:2, Psalm 31:3, Psalm 46:2. b) See Jeremiah 16:19, Psalm 37:39, Psalm 91:15. c) The Lord, as the searcher of hearts, Psalm 7:10, *knows*, and recognizes with care and love, Psalm 31:8. So 2 Timothy 2:19. d) *those trusting or seeking refuge in him*. Psalm 2:12, Psalm 36:8. Jonathan: *who trust in His Word*. Cf. Romans 5:1 and following. The preposition *in* does not always hinder the construction, as above in verse 5, 2 Samuel 1:21, Psalm 5:12, Isaiah 28:9. **v. 8. Jerome:** *When he begins to be angry with the nations, and to lay waste once-powerful kingdoms, he will know those who are his: and he will not overwhelm the voyagers in a single storm.* **v. 8. e)** Whence (as I speak now regarding Nineveh in this hypothesis) *as if with an inundation*. Vulgate: *in a flood*. (The Syriac indicates) a consumption, see verse 9, Isaiah 10:23, Daniel 9:27, Chapter 11:22. f) *passing through*, that is, *overflowing*; i.e., an exceedingly impetuous flood, pervading all things. Consider not only the great army of the Medes and Babylonians who overthrew the Assyrian empire, but also the mass and force of all other evils. Cf. Chapter 2:1, Isaiah 8, Chapter 28:15, 18. g) *consumption* or *complete end*, verse 9, Isaiah 10:23, Jeremiah 30:11. h) *he will make its place*, namely, that of Nineveh; see Chapter 2:9. Tigurine Bible: *he will utterly destroy its place*. So that afterwards, you would not know where it had been. Cf. Daniel 2:35, Revelation 12:8, Chapter 20:11. This alludes either to the flood of the first world, or to the destruction of houses that usually happens when a great force of water carries away and prostrates everything in its path, Matthew 7:27. Or it may refer to that flood of the river by which the wall of Nineveh was thrown down for twenty stadia <note>A stadium was about 600 feet; twenty stadia is roughly 2.3 miles.</note>, and its capture was hastened under Sardanapalus, as Diodorus Siculus relates in *Library of History*, Book II, page 113. Thus, Nahum’s prophecy about the destruction of Nineveh had to be fulfilled, so that already in his own time, *Lucian* in the dialogue *The Overseers* (T. I. p. 292) expressly said: <note>original Greek: "Nineveh has already perished, and no trace of it remains, nor could you say where it once was."</note> And the most learned Bochartus confesses, after all his industry in *Phaleg* IV, c. 20, p. 284, that scholars tire themselves in vain precisely defining the location of Nineveh; and we know nothing certain in this regard except that Nineveh was on the Tigris toward the east, not far from the Lycus River. i) Vulgate: *and his enemies*, namely, consider the Assyrians. Abarbanel. k) *they shall pursue*. Thus most agree, as in Hosea 2:9, Proverbs 13:21. But M. I. takes it transitively: *God will cause darkness to pursue his enemies. Cf. Psalm 7:6.* l) *darkness and all things evil and sad*, both in this life and the future. Cf. Amos 5:18, 20; Job 5:14, Chapter 18:18, Chapter 20:26. Jonathan: *and his enemies he shall deliver into Gehenna <note>A place of spiritual punishment or hell.</note>.* **v. 9. m)** *What therefore*, you Assyrians, do you think or devise against the Lord, His power, and His decree? Do you think you will escape from His hand and resist His wrath? The interrogation exposes the foolishness of their thought. The Prophet anticipates the silent objections of the Assyrians, as if the Lord's threats would be empty or without effect, or as if any damage they suffered could be easily repaired. Cf. verse 6 above, Psalm 75:9, and the word in Hosea 7:15, Proverbs 16:9, Chapter 24:8, Daniel 11:24, 25. n) *But he himself will make a complete end, and send destruction upon you.* Verse 8, Chapter 2:1. o) *trouble will not rise twice* Psalm 27:3. Vulgate: *double tribulation shall not arise*. I.e., He will prostrate you not with repeated blows, but with one; compare 1 Samuel 26:8. Jerome: *Symmachus says more clearly: "they shall not sustain the onset of a second distress."* p) twice, Numbers 20:11. q) *distress* or *trouble*. Verse 7, Isaiah 8:22, Jeremiah 4:31, Chapter 6:24. Others: the enemy shall *not rise again*, or the city and empire of the Assyrians will not return; just as after that capture by Arbaces the Mede, of which Diodorus speaks (cited at v. 8); compare 1 Samuel 1:6, Jeremiah 51:64. **v. 10. r)** For. This is explanatory. For in this verse, he says how the total ruin or death of such a great city and empire could happen, based on a twofold cause or a threefold comparison: 1) *thorns*, which being entangled or packed together, are also burned together; 2) *drunkards*, who are easily overcome and slaughtered with none remaining; and 3) *dry stubble*, which is very easily consumed by fire. s) *even unto thorns*, i.e., to the point that they equal thorns in their entanglement. Cf. 1 Chronicles 4:27 and 2 Samuel 23:19. t) Isaiah 34:13, Psalm 58:10; cf. 2 Samuel 13:6. u) The Assyrians are entangled *by a multitude or by their own counsels*. (2) Job 8:17; cf. Genesis 22:13, and see Isaiah 10:34. The Vulgate makes the first part a premise and the following the conclusion: *For as thorns embrace one another, so is the banquet of those drinking together.* But Schmid, following the accents, takes these two parts as the cause, and the rest as the effect, in this way: *When they are entangled like thorns, and like their drunkards are drunken, they shall be eaten, etc.* we omit explanations foreign to the text. x) and *according to their drinking*. It is either a noun, as in Isaiah 1:22, Hosea 4:18, or rather an infinitive; cf. the future in Isaiah 56:12. y) having drunk, i.e., inebriated, or as if to say, they were swallowed up; compare Isaiah 28:7 and the Concordance Lexicon under the word "to swallow" col. 103. (1) Cf. the active form in Deuteronomy 21:20, Proverbs 23:20, 21. M. I.: *and like drunkards, lying on the ground, so that they cannot fight against the enemies.* Jerome: *Beautifully also he compared the multitude of the Assyrian army to a banquet of drunkards.* Perhaps not only a comparison with drunkards is intended here, but the actual revelry and drunkenness of the Assyrians are noted. Compare similar notes on the security of the Babylonians at Isaiah 21:4, 5, and what Diodorus related concerning Sardanapalus in the same place. *The King of Assyria,* he says, *ignorant of the revolt of the Bactrians, and elated by the kindness of his former fortune, turned himself to lazy leisure, and provided a great abundance of victims, wine, and other things for his soldiers to hold festive banquets. Therefore, while the whole army was indulging in feasts, Arbaces, informed by deserters of the negligence and drunkenness of the enemies, oppressed them suddenly by night.* See the whole history in Book 2, page 112 and following. z) Therefore they shall have been consumed, or shall be consumed, by the fire of divine wrath and warlike fury; Chapter 3:13, Nehemiah 2:3, 13. A prophetic past tense; see Amos 5:2. Cf. on this matter Isaiah 33:11, 12. a) *like dry stubble* Job 13:25, which suddenly catches flame and perishes, burned by a light heat. Cf. Isaiah 5:24, Chapter 47:14, Joel 2:5, Obadiah v. 18, Malachi 3:19.

# CHAPTER I. 2. NAHUM 1-2

<margin>11</margin> From you <gloss>c</gloss> came forth one who plots evil against the LORD, a wicked counselor. <gloss>d e</gloss>
<margin>12</margin> Full <gloss>b</gloss>: Thus <gloss>f</gloss> says the LORD: Though they are at full strength <gloss>g h</gloss> and many, even so they shall be sheared off <gloss>i</gloss> and pass away <gloss>k</gloss>; and though I have afflicted you <gloss>l</gloss>, I will afflict you no more. <gloss>m</gloss>
<margin>13</margin> And now I will break his yoke <gloss>o</gloss> from off you <gloss>p</gloss>, and your bonds <gloss>q</gloss> I will tear apart. <gloss>r</gloss>
<margin>14</margin> The LORD has given a command concerning you <gloss>s</gloss>: No more shall your name be sown; from the house of your gods I will cut off the carved image and the molded image; I will make your grave, for you are vile. <gloss>a</gloss>
<margin>15</margin> Behold, upon the mountains <gloss>c</gloss> the feet of him who brings good news, who proclaims

### CHAPTER II.
->PEACE<-

<margin>
b) full, in full number or in a heap. <note>original: "plena, pleno numero vel aceruo"</note> S. <note>Syriac version</note> fully. Compare Genesis 25:9, Isaiah 31:4, Jeremiah 12:6. To others, "full" refers to the stalk when it is mature. So say the Jewish commentators Rashi, Kimchi, M. J., and Abarbanel, collecting evidence from Exodus 22:18 and Jeremiah 6:11.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 11. c) S. Because from you went out, etc. Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note>: From you, O Nineveh, came forth a King who plotted evil against the people of God, who entered into a counsel of wickedness. Namely, Sennacherib, according to Abarbanel, and Rabshakeh, according to Grotius, comparing 2 Kings 18:13 and following, and Isaiah 36:1 and following. However, Calovius prefers this to be understood of any wicked counselors who thought evil against the Lord and His people. d) compare verse 9 and Ezekiel 38:10. e) S. a counselor of Belial, that is, wicked and diabolical. Compare chapter 2:1 and the note on Deuteronomy 13:14, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 12. f) Thus said the Lord. This is an assertion of divine truth, as is very frequent in the Prophets, made here for the consolation of the Church. Compare the note on verse 1. Furthermore, many difficulties arise in this verse if you compare the interpreters; most of whom take the following words up to the *Athnach* <note>a Hebrew accent mark indicating a pause</note> as referring to the Assyrians, while Schmidius takes them to refer to the Israelites. Some refer the section ending in *Silluki* <note>the final verse accent</note> to Nineveh, but others refer it to Jerusalem; nor do they agree in the explanation of individual words, as we will briefly indicate with one or two versions. S. "If you are perfect, you will likewise be many; and though they are so stretched out, it will now pass away: and though I have afflicted you, I will not afflict you further." The sense of this version, if I am not mistaken, is this: If you Jews have a heart whole toward God <note>1 Kings 8:61</note> like your King Hezekiah <note>2 Kings 18:3, 20:3</note>, you will also be multiplied more and more by divine blessing <note>Leviticus 26:9, Deuteronomy 30:16</note>, not only by offspring but by the addition of new citizens or allies <note>2 Chronicles 32:23</note>. And though the Jews and your brothers the Israelites are now completely subjected to that "hired razor" of the King of Assyria <note>Isaiah 7:20</note>, it will nevertheless pass away and cease.
</margin>

<margin>
CHAPTER II.
And that Assyrian enemy will no longer exist, taking flight after his army is struck down <note>2 Kings 19:35, Isaiah 31:9</note>. And though I have afflicted you, my church, because of sins, yet at last under the New Testament I will afflict you no more <note>Isaiah 28:1-6, 54:7-8</note>. But Jonathan translates: "Thus says the Lord: if the nations gathered to distress you, O Jerusalem, are perfect in counsel and many in number, and have crossed the Tigris and passed the Euphrates and come to afflict you; yet, those who subjected you shall subject you no more." Aben Ezra says the sense is: "Thus said the Lord to Jerusalem: If the camp of the Assyrians who come against you is at peace and fears no one, with all regions subjected, and thus they are many in the world; yet they shall be cut off, and all their army and power shall pass away" <note>2 Kings 19:35</note>. Jerome with the Vulgate: "If they are perfect and thus many, etc." He says, though the Assyrians are robust and their strength increases by the number of all nations, even so, as the Angel devastates them, they are "sheared." For just as a multitude of hairs does not resist sharp shears, so the number of God's adversaries will be removed with easy success. Again, the speech is directed to Jerusalem: "I have afflicted you, and I will not afflict you further." Not that he promises perpetual security, but only for that time and from those enemies by whom she was then besieged. Abarbanel, however: "This is said to Nineveh: I will not spare you, as in the days of Jonah; but I will pass over you once, and not repeat it" <note>compare verse 9 and 1 Samuel 26:8</note>. But truly the following verse is also more conveniently referred to the Church (explicitly addressed by the Prophet in chapter 2:1) than to Nineveh. We will now add a few things to the words of the text themselves. g) Vulgate, S., and C. <note>Commentators</note>: "If." Jerome: "Though," as in Deuteronomy 30:9, Judges 13:16, Isaiah 1:18, Jeremiah 15:1, etc. h) whole/perfect. Gusset page 252: unblemished and enjoying their whole strength. Most broadly it signifies "complete," such as a stone not cut or hewn <note>Deuteronomy 27:6</note>, a full weight <note>Deuteronomy 25:15</note>, a complete measure <note>Genesis 15:16</note>, a complete exile <note>Amos 1:6</note>, a finished building <note>2 Chronicles 8:16</note>, a man safe and sound in body <note>Genesis 38:13</note>, whole in soul without fraud or deceit toward men <note>Genesis 34:21</note> and toward God <note>1 Kings 8:61</note>. Hence the very diverse explanations of interpreters. i) yet so they shall be removed, sheared, cut down. <note>compare Genesis 38:13, Numbers 11:31, Amos 7:1, Psalm 90:10</note>. k) and it shall pass by, so that it ceases. l) and though I afflicted you through him <note>2 Kings 17:20, Psalm 90:15</note>. m) yet I will not afflict you further. <note>compare 1 Kings 11:39, Isaiah 54:11</note>. v. 13. n) S. But now shortly. o) I will break his yoke. Jerome: that is, by metaphor, the power of the Assyrian. p) from you, O Zion, or my Church. But Abarbanel says: "I will break the yoke of the King of Assyria from you, Nineveh; and your chains which you had placed on all kingdoms, I will break." But see Isaiah 10:27 and the note on the preceding verse 12. Jonathan: "For now I will break the yoke of the nations from your neck, and your chains I will tear away." q) Jeremiah 2:20, 5:5, 27:2; Psalm 2:3. r) Jeremiah 30:8, Psalm 107:14. v. 14. s) But over you, Assyrian, or King of Assyria (for we now understand from the masculine suffix) the Lord will command. Jerome: "so that what you are to suffer does not come by chance or without a judge, but you suffer by God’s decree." t) it shall not be sown; no one shall be sown or propagated from your name anymore. <note>compare the word in Numbers 5:28</note>. Jerome says: "immediately after Nineveh was overturned, Sennacherib was killed by his sons" <note>2 Kings 19:37</note>. However, since 1) others suppose the slaughter of Sennacherib had already occurred; 2) Sennacherib's son Esarhaddon succeeded him in the kingdom <note>Isaiah 37:38</note>; and 3) the things said here do not fit well with the slaughter of Sennacherib, we prefer the interpretation that the destruction predicted here is that of Saracus (or as others call him, Chinaladanus), the last King of the Assyrians, and the entire royal family and kingdom. u) from the house of your god or your gods; whom, having neglected me (even if you once began repentance), you worshipped again. x) in the destruction of the whole city I will cut off, I will destroy <note>Zechariah 13:2</note> specifically by the victorious Babylonians and Medes. y) a carved and molded <note>molten</note> idol. Just as the Assyrians themselves had done to the gods of other nations <note>2 Kings 19:18, Isaiah 37:19</note>. z) Syriac: "and I will turn it [the house of your god] into your grave." Jonathan: "and there I will place your grave." So that neither the place nor the gods can save you, but you shall fall and be buried among their ruins. a) for you are vile; Vulgate: "dishonored." Tigurine Bible: "ignominious." S. "because you have been made light" <note>Job 40:4; compare Daniel 5:27</note>. M. J.: "you shall be vile and despised, and that as a punishment because you despised me." Jonathan otherwise: "because this is easy before me," and Syriac: "quickly," as if the Hebrew word meant: "because it is light and of no weight before me." CHAPTER II. v. 1. b) Behold! I confirm what will most certainly happen. This chapter contains, as Schmidius rightly observed, I. a continuation of the consolation of Israel and Judah regarding the New Testament (v. 1, 2, 3) and II. a prophecy against Nineveh regarding its capture, plundering, and destruction (v. 4, etc.). And this is surely to be preferred to the opinion of Abarbanel and others who think the destruction of Jerusalem is described here. c) upon the mountains <note>Song of Songs 2:8</note>. Jonathan adds: "of the land of Israel." Regarding the coming of the Messiah, Moses Haddarsan also explained this. d) the feet are present <note>2 Kings 6:32</note> of the one bringing good news <note>literally: of those bringing good news, Isaiah 41:27</note>. Abarbanel says: The Prophet speaks thus because God hastens to effect these things. He thinks, however, with others, that nothing is promised here to the Jews except the news of the destruction of Nineveh and peace obtained from the Assyrians; which, however, Nebuchadnezzar soon disturbed with the most sad devastation of Jerusalem. Hence Nahum did not use the remaining words of Isaiah 52:7 here, because Isaiah speaks of liberation through the Messiah, but our prophet speaks only of liberation from the Assyrians. There are even some among Christians who feel this way. The opinion of Blessed Luther, Calovius, Schmidius, and others is better; they feel something more sublime is promised here no less than in Isaiah. Especially if the slaughter of Sennacherib had already occurred before this prophecy, and the destruction of Nineveh followed only many years later. Therefore the Prophet wishes to say: Far be it, brother Jews, that the Assyrian or any other truculent enemy could make your expectation, the hope of Israel, and the promised salvation in CHRIST <note>Genesis 49:10; Luke 2:25, etc.</note> doubtful or intercept it; rather, what Isaiah predicted <note>Isaiah 52:7</note>, I also confirm with the same words, and joyfully foresee the joy of the Gospel of Christ, to be announced and preached by His Apostles not only on the mountains of Judea, but finally through the entire world. Therefore, lift up your spirits with this hope, and now for the peace restored from the Assyrians, thankfully and joyfully pay your vows to God. For it is (in the words of Wigand) a message most pleasing to the Jews concerning Sennacherib slain by his own children; yet the Prophet looks further: since that protection and preservation happen primarily for the sake of the manifestation of the Messiah, because the Gospel, which brings peace of heart, would emanate from there into the whole world. e) Vulgate: "of the one announcing." Others: "of the one preaching," or of those proclaiming divine peace <note>Luke 2:14; Ephesians 2:14</note>.
</margin>

<column-break/>

v. 12. *sheared*. <note>Hebrew: נָגֹזּוּ</note>.
v. 13. *his yoke*. <note>Hebrew: מֹטֵהוּ</note>. Compare Isaiah 9:3.
And so Cocceius cites in his Lexicon. CHAPTER II, v. 1. Without the preceding space.

<summary>This page concludes the judgment on the Assyrian "wicked counselor" (likely Sennacherib or the final Assyrian king) and transitions to a message of comfort for Judah. It interprets the "good news" on the mountains as both the historical relief from Assyrian oppression and a prophetic foreshadowing of the Christian Gospel.</summary>
<keywords>Nahum, Assyria, Nineveh, Sennacherib, Hezekiah, Abarbanel, Jerome, Martin Luther, Gospel, Messiah, peace, biblical commentary, Hebrew exegesis</keywords>

--- Page 1265 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the proclamation of good news and peace for Judah at the end of chapter 1 (verse 15 in English Bibles) to the vivid description of the siege and destruction of Nineveh in chapter 2. The commentator focuses on the spiritual and historical restoration of the people of God, while debating whether the "scatterer" mentioned in verse 2 refers to a historical conqueror like Nebuchadnezzar or to a messianic figure.</meta>

# NAHUM. CHAPTER 2. SECTION 2.

<margin>
f) Keep your feast, therefore, celebrate. Exodus 23:14. <note>original Greek: "heortaze"</note>. 1 Corinthians 5:8. g) O Judah, with the Benjaminites and the rest gathered to you. 2 Chronicles 30:11; see also Note num. 2, 9 and Joel 4:18. h) Your feasts Exodus 45:11. i) Psalm 50:14; Psalm 76:12. Jerome: "O Judah, who reigns in Jerusalem, do not be anxious; your enemy has been killed in the temple of his own god. Behold, the messenger comes to you, running across the mountains and hills, and as if from a high watchtower, announces from afar that Sennacherib is dead. Repay the vows which you promised to God for the death of your enemy." But consider what we have just said. k) Chasjan says this refers to joy and festivity, because (as the Syriac has it) war will no longer be brought against you. l) He shall no more pass over you, as before in chapter 3:19; like a flood in 1:8; Isaiah 8:8; Daniel 11:10, 40; or a noxious wind in Psalm 103:16, etc. m) Vulgate: *Belial*, that is, a wicked or diabolic enemy. See note on 1:11. Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> uses the plural: "because the impious shall no longer pass through you." For what is said of the Assyrian is also to be understood of the other enemies of the Church according to the harmony of the Scriptures, to be finally so cast down that they cease to be a burden to the Church. See Isaiah 52:1; Joel 4:17; Micah 5:4, 5 and the notes there. n) Vulgate: he is entirely. 15. He has perished, he is cut off. Psalm 37:28. Jonathan: all are deleted. Jerome: both the king and the empire of the Assyrians have utterly fallen.
</margin>

<margin>
We firmly believe this comes from "he shall live" in Micah 2:13. q) Before your face, or before you. Genesis 32:22; 2 Samuel 15:18 and following. <note>original Greek: "archēgos kai teleiōtēs tēs pisteōs"</note>, the author and finisher of our faith. Hebrews 12:2; Ephesians.
</margin>

But compare also Jerome and Abarbanel. Isaiah 10:15 and following, and others at greater length, want Nebuchadnezzar to be understood here, but not correctly, as we firmly...

***

Isaiah 52:12; Hosea 2:2; removing obstacles. See Isaiah 45:2. We take these words as addressed to Judah, that is, the Church, through the context of verses 1 and 3, as do Jonathan, Rashi, Kimchi, and Abarbanel, though they explain the following parts differently and erroneously. Nor was Abraham ibn Ezra correct in thinking Nineveh is being addressed here, nor Saint Jerome, who says: *“Now the speech turns to Nineveh”*; and he suggests the Prophets are especially obscure because the person being addressed changes suddenly while another subject is underway. But 1) there is no need for a change of person here, as we noted in the Preface section 6; nor 2) as we already said regarding verse 1, does Nahum predict a siege here, which Abarbanel and others assume without context; nor 3) does he speak with Nineveh here according to the context, but with Judah or the Church, as is certain from verse 1. And 4) he does not threaten her with destruction here, but rather consoles her with a happier state of affairs and a most flourishing restoration under CHRIST, which is evident from verse 3. And thus finally he returns to his purpose *against Nineveh* (see verse 9 compared with 1:1) and describes its destroyers in verse 4 and following. r) *by guarding* i.e., most diligently, therefore, O Judah (v. 1), guard. Psalm 119:129; Proverbs 4:23; 13:3; 16:17. A similar omission of the finite verb after the Infinitive is found in Exodus 20:8; Ezekiel 24:5, etc. s) *the fortress*, a rampart. 2 Chronicles 14:5; 11:10. l) lest you fall from your station, but rather hold fast to that proposed hope. Hebrews 6:12, 18; 10:23; compare Habakkuk 2:1; 2 Peter 3:17. Abarbanel: *stand firm in the guard, that is, the fortress of the law*. Schmid refers this and all following words to Christ, translating: *For he has come up scattering before your face, to guard the fortress, to watch the road, to strengthen the loins, to fortify power mightily*. The Syriac can also be taken this way: *The author has come up before you, the guard of the guards, the watcher of the way, the sustainer of the loins, and his strength is most valid*; compared with 1 Peter 1:5, etc. However, our construction, which Kimchi also teaches, is common enough and seems simpler and clearer in this place. t) *by watching, namely, watch the road*; both the road you must walk (John 14:6; Galatians 1:16; Colossians 2:6; Hebrews 10:20) and the road by which the enemy might suddenly attack (1 Peter 5:8, 9). These phrases are born from warfare but are to be understood spiritually, as in Ephesians 6:10 and following. Abarbanel’s paraphrase is quite different: *Watch, O Jerusalem or Judah, the road by which you will go into Babylonian captivity; for you will not be rescued from this*. Compare Jeremiah 48:19; 1 Samuel 4:13; Isaiah 21:6; Micah 7:7; Psalm 5:4. u) *by strengthening* (namely, strengthen, or strengthen yourselves, as if from a tight belt, see Isaiah 22:21; 1 Peter 1:13. Or (with the gender changed after the *Atnach* <note>a Hebrew accent mark</note>, as Judah is regarded as a man or a people, no longer as a woman as in verse 1; compare note on Hosea 2:21; 5:9; Micah 2:10) *strengthen yourself* to endure all afflictions and calamities. x) *the loins, where the seat of strength lies*. See 1 Kings 12:10; Job 40:16; Ephesians 6:14. For the opposite, see below in verse 11; Deuteronomy 33:11; Ezekiel 21:11; Psalm 69:24. y) *by exerting strength*. Kimchi and M. J.: *strengthen your forces with good courage and confidence, so that you trust in the name of the Lord*. See Isaiah 35:3; Amos 2:14; Proverbs 24:5; Job 4:3, 4; Hebrews 12:12. <note>original Greek: "andrizasthe ischye sphodra"</note> "be brave and very strong." Arabic: *take courage with great fortitude*. See Ephesians 6:11.

v. 3. z) For, Jonathan: *Because the Lord has restored his strength to Jacob, his majesty to Israel*. This further explains and confirms what was said in verses 1 and 2. a) *he restored* i.e., prophetically, as stated above, *he will restore or is about to bring back* at last Jehovah, the Messiah, the author and giver of salvation. See Isaiah 52:8; Jeremiah 30:3, 18; Amos 9:14; Psalm 14:7. For Abarbanel wanders far from the mind of the Holy Spirit, contending—against the common opinion of other interpreters—that this is not a consolation but a threat about the capture of Jerusalem. He thinks the words should be understood as: *Because the Lord will lead Jerusalem and Judah into captivity by the Babylonians, as the glory of Jacob (Psalm 47:5), just as he led away the glory of Israel by the Assyrians (2 Kings 17)*. But the phrase of the Holy Spirit never signifies this. See besides the cited places Jeremiah 31:23; Hosea 6:11; Zephaniah 2:7; 3:20; Job 42:10. b) *the glory, or excellence of Jacob*, Psalm 47:5; Amos 6:8 (meaning Judah, with the other descendants of Jacob joined to her. Hosea 10:11; Isaiah 2:5, 6), *though it would be taken from them by the Babylonians and Romans because of their sins* (Jeremiah 13:9). c) *just as he will also restore the glory of Israel* (taken away by the Assyrians, Isaiah 17:3, 4). See Hosea 2:1; Isaiah 4:2; 60:15. and d) *for*, the reason why the Lord will do so is here, according to the Vulgate, *because the wasters have dissipated them*. Others, like Tarnovius: *although they have emptied them out*. e) *they emptied*, Jonathan: *they despoiled them* (the Jews and Israelites). Jeremiah 19:7; 51:3. f) *emptying*. Vulgate: *the wasters*. Abarbanel: namely, Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar; or the Assyrians and Babylonians, and others. See Isaiah 24:1, 3; Jeremiah 50:17. g) *and the branches*, Vulgate: *their shoots (1)* see seed, Numbers 13:23. Abarbanel: i.e., their peoples. Jonathan: the cities of their glory; the shoots of the vine or vineyard of the Lord. Isaiah 5:1-7; Psalm 80:9 and following. h) *they ruined or destroyed*. See Jeremiah 12:10.

v. 4. i) *The shield of his mighty men*. Abarbanel refers the suffix to Nebuchadnezzar. Schmid to *Belial* from verse 1. We refer it to the Lord, from verse 3, who used the Medes and Babylonians to punish the Assyrians. See a completely similar expression in Isaiah 13:3, concerning the Medes and Persians who were to capture Babylon. The connection with the preceding is this: The Lord will not lack instruments with which to execute his wrath on the enemies of his Church when he wishes, just as now the Medes and Babylonians are ready to overturn Nineveh. The Prophet graphically and elegantly describes their army in the following. k) *is red, or ruddy*, Exodus 25:5; from the color of the material, likely copper. Vulgate: *it is ignited*, perhaps from the flashing brass. But Abarbanel and Grotius: *it is all red from the blood of the slain*, see Deuteronomy 32:42 and Isaiah 63:2. l) Vulgate: *men of the army*. Jonathan: *those waging war, i.e., soldiers*. Judges 3:29; 2 Kings 24:15. Jerome: Describing the Babylonian army coming against Nineveh. m) i.e., *vermiculated*, meaning scarlet-clothed, according to Jonathan and M. J.: *they are dressed in scarlet garments*. (1) From *Tola* or *Tolaat*, a scarlet worm. Exodus 25:4; Isaiah 1:18; Lamentations 4:5. See Bochart, *Hierozoicon* II, p. 624. Grotius says we learn from Herodotus that the Eastern peoples used such military cloaks extensively. n) *with the fire of scythes*. (1) Most interpret this through a transposition of letters from verse 5 as "seats" or "faces." Abarbanel: "his chariots are sheared like fire." Grotius: *their chariots flash like lamps at the time of the expedition: namely, with sparking wheels*. So M. J. says that in swift motion, from the rubbing of iron-clad wheels, fire is struck from the stones. But because the Arabic root means "to cut into parts," and *Fulad* <term>Fulad: a high-quality Persian steel or steel-like iron</term> is the most excellent iron or steel; likewise *Mustad*, which is well-fortified with an edge and steel, like a sword; we preferred to conjecture that these are scythed chariots, to which he attributes fire not only from the striking but also because of their sharpness and brightness, as it is called in chapter 3:3: *the flame of the sword and the lightning of the spear*. o) *military chariots will be present*, Exodus 14:7; Isaiah 5:25. See the notes on these in Judges 4:13; 2 Samuel 10:18; and more in Curtius, Book IV, ch. 9 and 15, with Cellarius's notes. p) *the day of his preparation*, or when God prepares them for war. See 87:7, 14. q) *and the fir trees* i.e., metaphorically, according to Jonathan: *the Great ones*; according to Joseph Kimchi: *the strongest*; according to Abarbanel: *Kings and Princes*, see Isaiah 14:8; 37:24. Or by metonymy according to Kimchi and others: *weapons, spears, and lances*. Others, says Abarbanel, explain it by metonymy as spears made from the wood of fir trees and dipped in poison, as they still do today in Africa; see 2 Samuel 18:14. So also Grotius on this passage.

***

* z. Here at last they begin Chapter II, with a space provided beforehand... but against the printed Masoretic text.

<summary>This page analyzes Nahum 1:15–2:4, interpreting the prophecy as a message of consolation for Judah/the Church. It details the upcoming destruction of Nineveh by an army (the Medes and Babylonians) described with scarlet clothing and sparking, scythe-wheeled chariots.</summary>
