<meta>This page continues the exposition of the Prophet Nahum, moving from the proclamation of peace for Judah at the end of chapter 1 into the vivid, terrifying description of the siege and fall of Nineveh in chapter 2. The previous page concluded with the death of the "wicked counselor" (Sennacherib); this page details the military assault on the city and the panic of its inhabitants.</meta>

<margin>
Let us dismiss and change sentiments that are remote from the matter and the text.
</margin>

<margin>
Ezekiel 1: One might understand from verses 3 and 4: "The Lord will remember his mighty ones, and thus he so observes them that they fall," etc.
</margin>

<margin>
r) They are shaken. Joseph Kimchi <note>A renowned 12th-century Spanish-Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator.</note>: "They tremble; they quiver." Others: "They are horribly shaken." (1) Compare the noun in Isaiah 51:17 and Zechariah 12:2. The Chaldean and Syriac root is "to tremble" or "to falter" (see the Aramaic Targum on Isaiah 35:3 regarding knees), and in the *Aphel* form <note>An intensive verb form in Aramaic.</note>, "to shake." However, in Arabic, it means "to pierce with a spear forcefully and violently."
</margin>

# NAHUM 2

5 They were shaken <gloss>r</gloss>: in the streets <gloss>s</gloss> they shall rage <gloss>t</gloss>, the chariots <gloss>u</gloss> shall clash <gloss>w</gloss> in the broad ways <gloss>x</gloss>: their appearance <gloss>y</gloss> is like torches <gloss>z</gloss>, they shall run <gloss>b</gloss> like lightning <gloss>a</gloss>.
6 He shall remember <gloss>c</gloss> his nobles <gloss>d</gloss>; they shall stumble <gloss>e</gloss> in their walk <gloss>f</gloss>; they shall make haste <gloss>g</gloss> to her wall <gloss>h</gloss>, and the defense <gloss>k</gloss> shall be prepared <gloss>i</gloss>.
7 The gates <gloss>l</gloss> of the rivers <gloss>m</gloss> were opened <gloss>n</gloss>, and the palace <gloss>o</gloss> is dissolved <gloss>p</gloss>.
8 And it is decreed <gloss>q</gloss>: she is stripped <gloss>r</gloss>, she is carried away <gloss>s</gloss>, and her handmaids <gloss>t</gloss> lead her <gloss>u</gloss> as with the voice <gloss>w</gloss> of doves <gloss>x</gloss>, drumming <gloss>y</gloss> upon their hearts <gloss>z</gloss>.
9 And Nineveh <gloss>a</gloss> was like a pool of water <gloss>b</gloss> from her earliest days <gloss>c</gloss>; she <gloss>d</gloss> and they <gloss>e</gloss> flee <gloss>f</gloss>; "Stand! Stand!" <gloss>g</gloss> they cry <gloss>h</gloss>, and there is no one <gloss>i</gloss> who turns back <gloss>k</gloss>.

---

<margin>
s) Through the streets. Ezekiel 7:19; 26:11. t) They act like madmen, that is, the chariots rush into opposing sections with a swift course and the greatest force, as if driven by fury. See Jeremiah 46:9 and compare 2 Kings 9:20. u) They shall run to and fro. A four-letter Hebrew verb form (1) from *shakak*, as in Joel 2:9. w) Through the plazas. Compare Isaiah 15:3; Psalm 144:14. x) Their appearance (Jerome says this refers to the Babylonians). Ezekiel 1:5, 13. The feminine suffix is used either neutrally, or the word "chariot," otherwise masculine, is feminine here. y) It will be terrible, and the eyes so burning, like torches and lamps, that they terrify the adversaries by sight before they strike them down with a blade; as Jerome has it. Compare Daniel 10:6. a) Like lightning. Zechariah 9:14. b) They shall run most swiftly. An intensive verb (1) from *ruts*, "to run." Others derive it from *ratsats*: like lightning they shall break through and shatter everything. Compare Judges 10:8.
</margin>

Compare Jeremiah 14:10, Hosea 7:2, 8:13, and 1 Samuel 15:2. **d)** Chapter 3:18; Judges 5:13. **e)** Chapter 3:3; Psalm 9:4. **f)** In their marching. Habakkuk 3:6; Psalm 68:25. That is, having gone out to meet the enemies. **g)** In short, we say: these things can be understood as referring to either the Assyrians or the Babylonians. Regarding the former: Driven from the battle line, they will hasten to the repaired wall of Nineveh (see chapter 3:14), and there a *guard* will be stationed to defend the city against the enemies. Regarding the Babylonians, however, in this manner: Having slaughtered the Assyrian army outside the city, they will hasten to its wall either to climb it (as in Joel 2:7) or to undermine it (as in 2 Samuel 20:15). **i)** It shall be arranged, or made ready, protecting those attacking and undermining the wall against a breakout from the city, etc. **h)** And it shall be prepared, placed, or stationed. Zechariah 5:11; Proverbs 21:31. **i)** Protecting. The Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin Bible.</note> calls it a "canopy." Compare Ezekiel 28:14; Psalm 140:8. Jerome says: *The Assyrian will swiftly ascend the walls of Nineveh: and because of the very long siege, to ward off the heat, he will prepare sunshades.* Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note>, however, understands it in terms of the attackers as a "storming-cover" <note>original: "testudo"</note> or a sharp segment covered with skins under which soldiers lie hidden while attacking and undermining the wall. Thus Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note> says it is a *Testudo* (tortoise-shell formation) by which the walls are rightly undermined. Schmidt says: "When they hasten to its wall, the covering is already prepared."

**v. 7. k)** The gates of the rivers, i.e., emphatically of the Tigris, according to Tarnovius here and Geier on Psalm 74:15. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> and the Arabic version say: "The gates of the cities." Jonathan, however: "The bridges of the rivers are dissolved." Herodotus (Book 1, ch. 182) sheds considerable light on this place: "The river Halys receives Phrygia, where gates loom over it, through which it is absolutely necessary to pass and cross the river; there was a great fortification there." The Prophet seems to describe gates of this kind with a nearby fortification at the rivers of Assyria near Nineveh; so says Bochart in *Phaleg* (p. 276). Add these words of Diodorus Siculus (Book 2, p. 96) concerning Semiramis: "She also built two royal palaces on each side of the bridge at the river; from where she had a view of the whole city (Babylon), and as it were, keys to its most advantageous locations." Unless you prefer the Prophet to be looking back here metaphorically to that inundation of the Tigris (regarding which see the note on chapter 1:8). **l)** They were opened, or they shall be opened. Chapter 3:13; Genesis 7:11. **m)** And the Palace, of the kind we just described from Herodotus and Diodorus. Or the royal seat and palace itself. Isaiah 39:7. **n)** It is dissolved, or it shall be dissolved. Chapter 1:5; Exodus 15:15; Psalm 75:4.

**v. 8. o)** Ludovicus de Dieu and Schmidt: "For so it is established." As if to say, the sentence stands. Thus some also understand the verb in the passive (Niphal) in Psalm 39:6. Compare the Chaldean <unclear>atsir</unclear> in Daniel 2:45; 6:12. But Cocceius (Lexicon 328) establishes that it refers to the "vineyard" or the "tortoise-shell" formation from verse 6. Other Hebrews and some others take it as a proper name or synonym for the Queen, based on the slight reasoning that in Psalm 45:10 the queen is said <term>to stand</term> <note>original: "nitsavah"</note> at the King's right hand. The Vulgate has: "And the captive soldier was led away," doubtless because <term>a garrison</term> <note>original: "nitsav"</note> denotes a military guard in 1 Samuel 13:3-4 and 1 Chronicles 11:16. But the construction of the following words contradicts the gender, and the form of the word reveals it to be a verb, not a noun. Therefore, Schmidt's version is preferable, or it should be understood thus: although a protector <note>the *nitsav*</note> was established for the wall and city (v. 6), nevertheless, etc. **p)** De Dieu: "She shall be led away into captivity." (Pyal) But because this verb in the Psalms constantly means "to reveal," Kimchi and M.I. understand it better as "she was uncovered," or prophetically, "she shall be uncovered." Namely, so that she is revealed, i.e., Nineveh, which is presented as a shameful harlot in chapter 3:5. For the Prophet's discourse is about Nineveh, not Jerusalem, whatever Abarbanel may think to the contrary. **q)** She was led away, or prophetically, Nineveh shall be deported (v. 9). (Hophal) Used of a victim offered in Judges 6:28, and of those recorded in the book in 1 Chronicles 20:34. M.I.: "She was placed on a vehicle to be led away with the remaining captives." But because the causative form (Hiphil) sometimes means "to take away" or "remove" (Psalm 102:25), and the passive (Niphal) means "to be taken away" or "led off" (as in Numbers 16:24, 27; 2 Samuel 2:27), you will therefore rightly translate it here as: "she was led away" or "she shall be led away." Compare also the simple form (Kal) in Job 5:26. **r)** And her handmaids. Genesis 20:17; Exodus 2:5. Understand the handmaids metaphorically as the smaller cities, villages, and forts, as Jerome advised; and further, understand these metonymically as the people themselves who lived in them. Compare also the similar title of "Lady" or "Princess" used for Jerusalem in Lamentations 1:1, and for both the literal and mystical Babylon in Isaiah 47:5 and Revelation 17:18. **s)** They shall be leading her. Genesis 31:26; Deuteronomy 4:27. This verb seems to be used here of a choir of mourners, says Schmidt on 1 Samuel 30:20. Jonathan: "Led away after her, they go groaning." **t)** Namely, according to the voice of doves, with a mournful groaning. See Isaiah 38:14; 59:11. Jerome: "There will be such great terror that grief will not even break out into sobs and wailing, but they will groan silently within themselves, and swallow their tears with a dark murmur, in the manner of whispering doves." **u)** Namely, drumming, i.e., as Jonathan has it, "striking." (2) Psalm 68:26. **x)** Upon their hearts: beating their breasts with their palms. Kimchi: "In the manner of wailing and lamenting women." Compare Luke 18:13; 23:28, 48; and on this matter Ezekiel 27:30ff; Revelation 18:9ff; etc.

**v. 9. y)** For indeed Nineveh, of which I have spoken so far. Compare chapter 1:1. Namely, Nineveh. **z)** She was like a pool of waters. Ecclesiastes 2:6. Namely, populous and filled with many people, who flowed into her from all sides like water. For "many waters" are "many peoples" (Revelation 17:15). Compare the note on 1:5 above and Jonah 4:11. Nor is there any doubt that in such a large multitude, many gathered there from the most remote parts of the empire, attracted by the fame of the greatest city and mistress of nations. Compare chapter 3:15ff. **a)** From the days she was, i.e., for a long time now, from the ancient times in which she was founded. Genesis 10:11. Indeed, so that she might grow into that greatness, Ninus granted citizenship not only to Assyrians but also to all foreigners; whom it is likely the following kings imitated in this regard. See Diodorus Siculus (Book 2, p. 92) where he says, citing Ctesias: "Those to whom he gave the city to inhabit were mostly Assyrians, and the most powerful ones; but from other nations, whoever wished." **b)** But now those waters, i.e., those peoples, shall flee. Compare Jeremiah 48:45; 50:28; and below, chapter 3:16, 17. **c)** Supply with the Septuagint: "even if it is said or shouted to them." Abarbanel: "Even if the king and the leaders say to the soldiers: 'Stand, stand! to fight against the enemies.'" Compare the verb in Amos 2:15; Isaiah 47:12, 13. **d)** Yet there will not be anyone to look back at that cry. Jonathan: "No one who turns himself to resist." See Jeremiah 46:5; 47:3; 48:39. Jerome: "For Nineveh had peoples who would only flee, so that even as the 'mother' city cried out, 'Stand, stand! close the gates, ascend the walls, resist the enemies!' there would be no one to return, no one to look back at the mother, but all, turning their backs, would desert the city as prey for the enemies." Wherefore it is said to the Babylonians in v. 10: "Because they have fled, plunder the silver, and seize the wealth gathered over so much time in a sudden devastation." Compare what we advised concerning the shift in tense and speakers in the prophetic style in the Preface to this book (§ 6) and the Preface to Isaiah (§ 9).

<margin>
**v. 6.** c) Vulgate: "He will remember his strong ones." Namely, says Jerome, the Assyrian (noted by the name of Belial in the note on v. 1), will remember with grief his strong ones who fell while meeting the enemies; compare Lamentations 1:7 and the note there. Others, like Grotius: "The Babylonian king will remember his strongest men, whom he selects for the siege of Nineveh." Thus Abarbanel, but wrongly understanding his "strong ones" as Jews, based on a hypothesis refuted at v. 1 and 3. The Septuagint and Arabic versions, through a discrepancy in number, say: "Their Princes shall remember," with an incomplete sense. Hence Schmidt, with a double ellipsis but without removing all difficulty: "When each of his magnificent ones shall remember, stumbling in his march." As many others...
</margin>

---

**v. 6. בַּהֲלִיכוֹתָם** [in their march] — defective <note>Spelled without the vowel-letter 'vav'.</note> in editions 5 and 22, and the Erfurt Masorah. Furthermore, in the Variations of the Orientals and Occidentals, the spelling בַּהֲלִיכוֹתָם is attributed to the former, while בַּהֲלִיכוֹתָם [with different vowels] is given to the latter. But perhaps (as happens everywhere) the text is faulty. **v. 7. וְהַהֵיכָל** [and the palace] is an index mark. **חוֹמָתָהּ** [her wall], without a *Mappik* <note>A dot in the final letter 'He' indicating it should be pronounced as a consonant.</note> in 2, according to the Erfurt Masorah and a note in the margin. 1. **Thus Rashi and Jonathan interpreted the Targum: "the covering" (the *sochech*) is "soft" <note>Hebrew: *rafeh*, meaning the letter 'kaf' is pronounced as 'kh' rather than 'k'.</note>**. **v. 8. מְתֹפְפוֹת** [drumming/beating] — thus both are defective in 1, 2, 3, 22; and so in 5 according to the Masorah. **וְנִינְוֵה** [and Nineveh] v. 9 — marked with a *Zakeph Katon* and *Munach* instead of *Mehuppak* in 2. But marked with a *Tevir* followed by *Mercha* in 3 <note>These are technical notes on the musical/grammatical accents (cantillation marks) found in the Hebrew Bible.</note>.

<summary>This page provides a detailed philological and historical commentary on the siege of Nineveh as described in Nahum 2:5-9. It discusses the technical aspects of ancient warfare (the "testudo" or protective covering) and the geographical reality of the Tigris river gates being opened to destroy the city.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the Book of Nahum. While the previous page described the initial panic and the opening of the river gates, this section focuses on the systematic looting of Nineveh (chapter 2) and the prophet's denunciation of the city's inherent cruelty (chapter 3). The commentary continues to blend traditional Jewish exegesis (Abarbanel) with Christian patristic interpretations (Jerome).</meta>

# NAHUM. Chapters 2, 3.

<margin>
* verse 10. a) **Plunder silver therefore, etc.** <note>original: "Diripite itaque argentum &c."</note> See Ezekiel 38:13. Now the Prophet addresses the Babylonians as if the event were presently occurring. Similarly in Jeremiah 50:26, 27. f) **Because there is no end.** <note>original: "quia non est finis"</note> This is said because the store of wealth here is greatest and nearly infinite. Compare chapter 3:3, 9; Ezekiel 2:7. g) **To the preparation.** <note>original: "adparatui"</note> Jonah interprets this as "treasures." This refers to the riches and wealth which the Assyrians had gathered from every side. (3) Ezekiel 43:11; Job 23:3; see the word in 1 Chronicles 22:14; chapter 29:2, 3. h) **Abundance is present.** <note>original: "copia adest"</note> Chapter 3:3; Genesis 31:1; Esther 5:11. i) **Of every kind of precious thing,** as if to say, "from all vessels of desire." k) See Hosea 13:15.
</margin>

<margin>
Regarding Nineveh, as Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher known for his commentary on the prophets.</note> perceives; or, as we prefer, an insult against its presumed permanence and the invincible power of the Assyrians. Compare Isaiah 19:12; 33:18; 36:19; 37:13; and see the note above at chapter 1:8. x) **A dwelling place or den of lions.** <note>original: "habitaculum f. lustrum leonum"</note> verse 13; Ezekiel 19:2; Amos 3:4; Psalm 104:22.
</margin>

(1) Compare verse 3. m) Neumann: **Overthrown.** Syriac: **Cast down.** Others: **Pillaged** or **emptied.** (1) The repetition of the cognate words <note>The Hebrew text uses three words—bukah, mevukah, mevullakah—that sound similar to emphasize the total devastation.</note> intensifies the speech, as in Jeremiah 16:19. n) And **exhausted.** Neumann: **Shattered.** Syriac: **It shall be broken through.** Jonah: **The gate is opened to the enemy.** (1) See Isaiah 24:1. o) **Whence the heart shall melt.** No courage will remain for the Assyrians. Jonah: **Commotion.** Syriac: **Trembling.** Septuagint and Arabic: **Birth pains.** 1 Thessalonians 5:3. r) **It shall be in all loins.** Compare Deuteronomy 33:11; Ezekiel 21:11; and above verse 2. s) **And the faces of all,** as if wasting away from fear or deformed by paleness. <margin>
CHAPTER III. 1. Jonah: **Where are the dwellings of the kings?** As if to say: Where now is that royal Nineveh of the Assyrians,
</margin>

## 3

# CHAPTER 3. Nahum 3

<margin>
a) **of corpses, slain by enemies** <note>original: "cadaverum, ab hostibus interemtorum"</note> 1 Samuel 17:46; Amos 8:3. b) **indeed there will be no end.** <note>original: "immo finis non erit"</note> See verse 9; Chapter 2:10. c) **of prostrate bodies** <note>original: "stratorum corporum"</note> 1 Samuel 31:12; Psalm 110:6. d) **so that they stumble and fall upon the corpses of the slain.** <note>original: "ita ut impingant & corruant in cadaueribus interfectorum"</note> Chapter 2:6.

*v. 4.* e) **Because of the multitude of fornications.** <note>original: "Propter multitudinem scortationum"</note> Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> and others interpret this as referring to idolatrous cults, as in 2 Kings 9:22, Jeremiah 13:27, and Ezekiel 16:30. Others, like Abarbanel, interpret it as the treacherous treaties by which the Assyrians drew other nations to themselves and eventually subjected them. We accept both views. See 2 Kings 16:7, 10, 18; 2 Chronicles 28:20, 21; and Isaiah 23:17. For the Prophet returns to explaining the causes of Nineveh's destruction, as he began in verse 1. f) **of the harlot,** <note>original: "meretricis"</note> that is, according to the Targum Jonathan, the city which was a shameful (extravagant) harlot. Compare Revelation 17:2. g) **Specifically, a harlot of great grace,** <note>original: "S. scorti boni gratia"</note> that is, charming and beautiful in appearance, as the Aramaic and Syriac versions have it. **Abarbanel:** those who see her desire her, look upon her, and observe her eagerly, just as the Israelites had done, trusting in the Assyrians. Compare Genesis 6:2; 39:11; 1 Samuel 11:2; Proverbs 31:30. h) **skilled mistress.** <note>original: "magistra perita"</note> 1 Samuel 28:7. i) **of sorceries.** <note>original: "praestigiarum"</note> 2 Kings 9:22. k) **who sold nations,** <note>original: "quae gentes vendidit"</note> that is, stripped them of their liberty, reduced them to slavery, and took possession of them. Compare Joel 4:3; 1 Kings 21:20, 25. l) **and nations or the families of the world.** <note>original: "nationes f. familias orbis"</note> Compare Amos 3:2; Zechariah 14:7. m) **bewitched and deceived with her sorceries.** <note>original: "fascinauit & decepit praestigiis fuis"</note> Compare Isaiah 47:9, 12.

*v. 5.* n) **Specifically, "Therefore behold, I am against you."** <note>original: "S. Ideo ecce ego contra te ero"</note> **Abarbanel:** I will bring about your ruin through my providence. **Jerome:** <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate.</note> "Because you, O Nineveh, have sold nations in your fornications and families in your sorceries, and like a public brothel have spread your legs for everyone, therefore I myself will come to overthrow you." Targum Jonathan as in chapter 2:14. o) Exodus 7:8; 16:14. p) **and I will uncover and cast back your skirts and your lowest garment.** <note>original: "& retegam, reiiciam fimbrias & imam vestem tuam"</note>

Compare for the sake of honor in Esther 1:11. s) **your nakedness.** <note>original: "nuditatem tuam"</note> The Targum says "your shame," the Syriac says "your private parts." So says Abarbanel: for that, he says, would be extremely disgraceful for a woman. The sense is: I will not treat you like an honorable matron, but like a foul prostitute. (t) 2 Kings 7:36; compare Habakkuk 2:15. u) **and I will show the kingdoms your ignominy and foulness** <note>original: "& regnis ostendam ignominiam & turpitudinem tuam"</note> Hosea 4:7, 18. So that those who fornicated with you may themselves despise you, mock you, and treat you with insults, and you will be an example to all who see. "All these things," says Jerome, "are under the metaphor of an adulterous woman who, when caught, is brought into the public and stripped before the eyes of all." <margin>v. 6. x) And I will throw upon you, stripped (v. 5) and killed, things to cover you (2 Samuel 20:12) or as if to bury you. Compare Joshua 7:25, 26; 8:29; 10:27, etc. y) Vulgate: **abominations.** <note>original: "abominationes"</note> Syriac: **impurities.** filth, namely, and dung. Compare 2 Kings 10:27. Elsewhere, however, this word is used almost exclusively for idols, like *Gillulim* <note>term: Gillulim | A derogatory Hebrew term for idols, often associated with dung.</note>; see 2 Kings 23:13, 24; Ezekiel 7:20, etc. Therefore, also here compare above at chapter 1:4. y) Vulgate: **and I will treat you with insults, I will make you vile and most despised.** <note>original: "& contumeliis te afficiam, vilem & despectiſſimam te reddam"</note> Arabic: according to the degree of your obscenities. Deuteronomy 32:15; Jeremiah 14:21; Micah 7:6. z) Isaiah 25:2. a) **as a spectacle.** <note>original: "velut spectaculum"</note> So the Syriac and Arabic. The Greek (Septuagint) says: "for an example." Compare Matthew 1, 19. Vulgate: **as an example.** Compare Ezekiel 28:17. Targum: **and I will make you foul in the eyes of all who see you.** So Abarbanel, comparing Zephaniah 3:1.</margin> <margin>v. 7. b) Specifically: How it shall happen, which is most certain. Compare Isaiah 65:24. c) **everyone who sees you.** <note>original: "quicun te viderit"</note> Compare Isaiah 14:16. d) **shall flee away**, Vulgate: **shall leap back from you.** v. 17; Psalm 55:8. Just as from a *Nidda* <note>term: Nidda | A woman in a state of ritual impurity; here used to mean something loathsome.</note> or a foul thing: as the root among the Syrians means "to detest." Jerome: "He who sees the ruins of Nineveh, after I have made her an example to everyone, will be terrified and marvel." e) **wasted**, Targum: pillaged, plundered. Jeremiah 4:20; 49:3. f) **Nineveh**, which was the mistress and teacher of nations. Compare chapter 2:3, following; Zephaniah 2:13. g) **who will condole with her?** <note>original: "quis condolebit ei?"</note> The Greek asks: "who will groan for her?" So the Arabic, but with the person changed, as also the Vulgate: **who will shake his head over you?** and the Targum: **who will condole with you?** This is usually signified by a bowed head. Compare Jeremiah 22:10; Job 2:11. Jerome: "When it says 'who,' we should take it not so much as 'difficult' but as 'rare'." Compare Luke 12:42; Hosea 14:10; Psalm 24:3. h) **from where?** <note>original: "vnde?"</note> Genesis 29:4. i) **of which.** <note>original: "quarum"</note> See Ruth 3:1. k) **comforters.** <note>original: "consolatores"</note> 2 Samuel 10:3; Isaiah 51:19; Psalm 69:21. l) **for you.** <note>original: "tibi"</note> Grotius: as if to say, "I will find them nowhere, for you have offended all peoples during your prosperous times." See verse 19 and compare Jeremiah 15:5.</margin> <margin>v. 8. m) Vulgate: **Are you better?** <note>original: "Namquid melior es?"</note> Compare Judges 11:25; Esther 2:4, 9. n) Specifically: **than No-Amon**, that is, according to Bochart, <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century French Protestant biblical scholar and geographer.</note> than Thebes or Diospolis in Egypt; as if to say, "the habitation of Jupiter Ammon." However, to Hiller in his Sacred Onomasticon, it is Memphis, as if to say, "the habitation of him nourished there" (Lamentations 4:5), namely Apis or Osiris. Compare the Septuagint version of Ezekiel 30:15 and the testimonies of Authors, as we also briefly mentioned at Jeremiah 46:25 and Ezekiel 30:14. The Septuagint and Arabic stray from the text: "Prepare a part, fit a cord." And partly the Syriac: "Are you better than Javan of the Ammonites?" as if "Ammon" were written with an *Ayin* and a *Dagesh*. The Targum says: "than great Alexandria." and the Vulgate: **Alexandria of the peoples**; Jerome, Drusius, and others want this to be called so by prolepsis <note>term: prolepsis | The representation of a future act or development as if presently existing or accomplished.</note>, and Grotius thinks that *No* was located in Pharos near it. But Bochart correctly says that it is not likely that Ezekiel and Jeremiah announced the penalty of imminent destruction to a city that did not yet exist in the century they wrote. Or that Nahum addressed the city of Nineveh thus: "Are you better (i.e., more fortified) than Alexandria, which will one day be built by Alexander the Great?" Comparisons teach nothing unless they are taken from known things, and a city not yet founded could not be known. What of the fact that Ezekiel and Jeremiah, and even more Nahum (following verse 10), write that the inhabitants of the city of No-Amon had gone into captivity, and its little ones were dashed in pieces at the head of every street? And by that example (v. 11), he terrifies Nineveh, as if she would soon be punished with a similar penalty. Therefore, not only the construction but the destruction of the city of No-Amon preceded Nahum's writing. How, according to this opinion of Bochart, the age and writing of Nahum would be not only after the slaughter of Sennacherib, as the Hebrews want in *Seder Olam*, but even after the prophecies of Jeremiah and Ezekiel. But see what we warned in the Preface to this book. Those who think these were written before the slaughter of Sennacherib take the whole following verse 10 in the future tense, as if the Prophet says: "Yet that most fortified city of Egypt will also be captured by Nebuchadnezzar, and will go into captivity, and its little ones will be dashed," as the Prophet clearly says in the future tense with a mixed construction of times. Vitringa however says: "What the Prophet has here about the capture of Diospolis seems to refer to the times of Sabacon the Ethiopian (who according to Ussher and Marsham is the same as So, to whom Hoshea, the last king of the Israelites, sent legates, 2 Kings 17:4), not to Sennacherib." o) **where she dwells**, or was dwelling securely. Compare Judges 18:7; Isaiah 47:8; Ezekiel 27:3; Zephaniah 2:15; Zechariah 11:11. p) **among the streams**, and the rivers of the Nile, so that the waters were around her. Compare Exodus 7:19; 8:1; Isaiah 7:18; 19:6; Ezekiel 29:3 and the note on Genesis 41:1; Amos 8:8. q) Schmid, by natural construction: **which is the rampart of the sea, and in turn from the sea is its wall.** Compare Isaiah 23:4. But almost all others put the relative in the Genitive: Targum: **whose wall is the sea.** Syriac: **whose strength is the sea.** Vulgate: **whose riches are the sea.** Bochart: **whose outwork** (or the space between the wall and the outwork, including the trench) is the sea; from the sea its walls, that is, Diospolis being situated on the Nile, besides its seven branches, has the Red Sea and the Mediterranean as a natural rampart. Hiller however: **whose Memphis is the fortification, the sea** or a huge lake, made from Mende to Memphis toward the west and north; since it had the Nile from the east and south. r) It is said twice for the sake of confirmation. v. 9. s) Vulgate and others: **Ethiopia.** Bochart: **Chusean Arabia.** Compare Jeremiah 46:9; Ezekiel 29:10. t) **was her strength and protection.** Isaiah 40:29. u) Abarbanel: i.e., **the Ethiopians and Egyptians helped No-Amon**, to defend her from Sennacherib. Concerning that slaughter brought upon the Egyptians by the Assyrians, see the prophecy of Isaiah 20:3. x) **so that there was no end or number to the help.** Compare verse 3 and 2 Chronicles 12:3. y) Targum: **the Putai or Africans.** Vulgate: **Africa.** See Jeremiah 46:9; Ezekiel 30:5.
</margin>

CHAPTER III. v. 3. *Corpses and no* - Per Makk. 1. 2. For *they stumble* some have *they stumble* 6, 9, 20. But *they stumble* in 13, 19, 23 and in the margin 6, 9. Both are against the Masoretic impression. Hosea 1:1, 14:5. Space precedes *know*. 6-10, 20, 21, 22, 23. v. 7. *laid waste* with Kibbuts in 20, 21 and in the text of 6, 9. For *for her* some have *for her* 2. 3. Thus also 5. Against Masoretic 1 and Erff. v. 8. *Are you better* So also the Orientals read, though some write *Are you better*.

<summary>This page analyzes Nahum 3:3-9, interpreting Nineveh's fall through the metaphors of a shamed harlot and a broken empire. It features an extensive debate among scholars about the identity of No-Amon, concluding it is the Egyptian city of Thebes (Diospolis) and using its historical destruction as a precedent for Nineveh's coming doom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the detailed commentary on the third chapter of Nahum. The previous page discussed the "multitude of fornications" of the "charlot" Nineveh—referring to her deceptive political alliances and idolatry. Here, the focus shifts to a historical comparison with the fall of the Egyptian city No-Amon (Thebes) and the inevitable collapse of Nineveh’s own defenses despite her wealth and military numbers.</meta>

# NAHUM. CHAPTER 3.

z. **and Libyans.** <note>original: "Libyes"</note> See Daniel 11:43; 2 Chronicles 12:3 and 16:8. a) **were for your help.** <note>original: "fuerunt in auxilium tui"</note> See Isaiah 10:13; Psalm 35:3. The Syriac version suggests they were treacherous to her, namely to **No-Amon**, whom he mentioned in the preceding verse. By the rhetorical device of **apostrophe**, the Prophet turns here to address her directly. **Abarbanel**. v. 10. b) **Yet even she,** as powerful and strongly fortified as No-Amon was (see verses 8 and 9), c) **into deportation,** that is, **exile.** <note>original: "in deportationem f. exilium"</note> 2 Kings 24:15; Amos 1:15. d) **went among the captives.** <note>original: "abiit... inter captivos"</note> Deuteronomy 28:41; Isaiah 46:2. **Grotius**: Not only were her citizens made exiles, but also slaves, specifically by the Ethiopians whose King **Sabaco** <note>Pharaoh Shabaka of the 25th Dynasty</note> invaded Egypt and placed strong garrisons there before the time of Psammetichus, as witnessed by **Herodotus** in his second book, *Euterpe*. And here we note: this capture will also be carried out by the King of Babylon, who shall be the destroyer of both you and her. See note on verse 8. e) **even her little ones** <note>original: "parvuli eius"</note> 1 Samuel 15:3 f) **shall be dashed in pieces.** <note>original: "allidentur"</note> Isaiah 13:16; Hosea 10:14. Or rather, according to the **Vulgate** and **Samuel Bochart**, "they were dashed." In Hebrew narratives, the Future tense is often used for the Past or Imperfect. See, for example, Judges 2:1. g) **at the head,** that is, at the beginning or at the crossroads of all the streets. Isaiah 51:20. As usually happens in cities taken by force. See 2 Kings 8:12; Hosea 14:1; Psalm 137:9; Lamentations 2:19. h) **and for her honored ones,** those of No-Amon. See Isaiah 23:8–9; Psalm 149:8. i) **the victors** (the Chaldeans, according to Abarbanel; others say the Ethiopians) **cast lots.** <note>original: "miserunt fortem"</note> The Babylonians divided the most noble citizens among themselves as slaves by lot. <summary>This page analyzes the inevitable destruction of Nineveh by comparing it to the historical fall of No-Amon (Thebes). The prophet mocks Nineveh's preparations for siege and compares her vast numbers of leaders and merchants to locusts that vanish as soon as the sun rises.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the final verses of Nahum 3, focusing on the desertion of Nineveh's leaders and her incurable "fracture." It then transitions into the Book of Habakkuk, providing an introductory "Argumentum" (summary) of its historical context and theological structure. The catchword "mum" at the bottom of the previous page completes the word "momentum" or a similar phrase discussing the opportune moment for the city's allies to flee.</meta>

# NAHUM 3. CHAPTER 3.

<margin>
...as soon as the opportunity and hope for managing affairs better shines forth, they will desert you with such unanimous consent that not even the smallest trace of them will remain. <note>From Samuel Bochart’s *Hierozoicon* (a famous 17th-century study of animals in the Bible), Part II, p. 458.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
(Psalm 121:4; Isaiah 5:27) it refers to your governors and leaders, O King of Assyria. (cf. 2 Samuel 5:2; 7:7; Jeremiah 22:22). **t)** *they shall lie down,* resting in sleep (Isaiah 26:19; Psalm 16:9). Thus the Arabic root signifies nightly rest in the Quran, Surah 28:72 and Surah 40:63. The Tigurinus version says *they lie down*; the Syriac, *they settle.* Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and commentator</note> says *they shall remain in their place* (Psalm 55:7) and no longer go out to plunder (compare above, chapter 2:12-13). The Syriac has *they lived securely.* But the Source M.I. <note>Likely referring to a specific Hebrew manuscript or a minor commentator</note> signifies they are *dead* (compare Psalm 7:6; 94:17). The Vulgate says *they shall be buried,* etc. **x)** Vulgate: *princes*; Tigurinus: *heroes*; Syriac: *your magnificent ones.* (cf. b) Hence they are scattered like a flock without a shepherd; Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan, the Aramaic translation</note> and Syriac: *they are dispersed.* (4) Habakkuk 1:8. Both in sound and meaning, this agrees with the word for "scattered" in 2 Kings 25:5, etc. See also Schultens in his *Observations on the Old Testament*, p. 508 and following. **y)** Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, the Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note>: understand this as the common soldiers. **z)** cf. 1 Kings 22:17. **a)** and there is no one who gathers the dispersed back into a battle line. See Isaiah 13:14; Jeremiah 49:5. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note>: "With all the princes slain who could resist the adversaries, the rest of your weak and ignoble people are scattered on the mountains, and none of the leaders can be found who might gather them and force the collected group back into an army."
</margin>

<margin>
**(p)** *they flee, they depart.* Syriac: *everyone flies away.* (v. 7; Isaiah 16:2; Hosea 7:13). **q)** *nor is the place recognized,* <note>original: "nec agnoscitur locus"</note> even the place of each of them. (cf. Psalm 103:16). **r)** where they have been (Isaiah 19:12). Jerome: "For this is the nature of locusts, that they are sluggish when torpid in the cold, but fly about when warmed by the heat." The conclusion is easily understood: so your mercenary soldiers, leaders, and merchants will all flee in your hour of danger. It is as if he says: You are indeed a most populous city, and your inhabitants seem to you as numerous as locusts; many merchants and princes seek asylum in your hands, just as locusts hide in hedges when it is cold. But there is no reason for you to trust in such a large multitude, or to puff yourself up with the wealth of these merchants or the strength of your princes and leaders. For just as the locusts fly away when the sun rises and desert the hedge that had been their refuge in the cold, so the peoples, merchants, and princes—who had fled to your walls when your affairs were prosperous—will leave you.
</margin>

**v. 18. s)** *Your shepherds have slumbered; that is, they conducted themselves negligently.* Psalm 76:6. (and otherwise than...)

**v. 19. b)** The Septuagint <note>Greek translation</note> and Arabic: *There is no healing.* Syriac: *a scar.* Others: *a contraction.* Cocceius's Lexicon 362: *mitigation; literally a "dulling," so that it becomes less sharp and vehement.* cf. Leviticus 13:6, 21; Isaiah 42:3, etc. However, because this noun is also used for a "dull spirit," that is, a stricken and sad soul (Isaiah 61:3), just as the Arabic root means *he was weak, faint-hearted, and fearful*, and the Chaldean means *he grieved, or was affected by pain*; hence Jonathan and the Syriac have: *There is no one who grieves because of your breaking;* for everyone rejoices at your ruin, as Abarbanel adds. This is spoken to the King of Nineveh, as is clear from the masculine suffix. **c)** *your fracture [breaking].* cf. Ezekiel 32:9; Lamentations 2:13. **d)** *most sickly*; Vulgate: *worst*; Syriac: *your plague is desperate.* Isaiah 17:11; Jeremiah 10:19, 30:12. The Greek: *it was inflamed.* Grotius: *inflamed wounds are accustomed to bring about death.* It is as if to say: Since Nineveh is surrendered, the soldiers scattered, and the leaders sluggish, do you not see that your affairs have perished without remedy? **e)** *whoever shall have heard the report of your slaughter.* Isaiah 23:5. **f)** *they shall clap their hands over you;* certainly out of joy, as Jonathan and M.I. add. (Compare Psalm 47:2; 2 Kings 11:12; Isaiah 55:12). Jerome: "All who hear of Nineveh overthrown, the Assyrian kingdom conquered, and that most powerful city fallen, will either be stunned by the magnitude of the event and the unexpected news and press their hands together, or certainly out of the magnitude of their joy, insulting you, they will applaud with their hands and resound with a certain noise of joy." **g)** *for upon whom?* Job 25:3. **h)** *has not passed through, or pervaded.* Chapter 2:1. **i)** *your malice [wickedness].* 1 Kings 2:44; Isaiah 47:10, etc. Grotius: "To whom have your injuries not reached? To whom have you not been a nuisance?" **k)** *always; at all times.* cf. Isaiah 52:5; 65:3; Habakkuk 1:17. Hence, in turn, all have now become your enemies and rejoice at your destruction. The sense is the same as above in verse 7.

*v. 18. "They are scattered" (נָפֹ֧שׁוּ) — Note on the Hebrew letter Shin with a Dagesh.*

### BOOK OF
# HABAKKUK,
### Hebrew:
# CHAVAKUK

The **A**rgument <note>summary of the theme</note> of this prophecy fits most closely with the time of Manasseh, or rather Josiah (see chapter 1:5) and the following impious Kings. For **I.** he deplores that law and right have been overturned among the Jews (which, as Grotius notes, never happened more than under Manasseh; see 2 Kings 21:16), and therefore he earnestly longs for the coming of Christ (chapter 1:2–4). **II.** To these complaints, God severely predicts the destruction of the Jews by the Chaldeans (chapter 1:5–11). But **III.** the Prophet persists in prayer and raises doubts: how can that harsh judgment, which is to be executed through wicked enemies, be consistent with God’s wisdom, holiness, and justice? (v. 12–17). Nevertheless, **IV.** he withdraws into hope and silence, and awaits the divine response to his doubts (chapter 2:1). **V.** This response not only follows in chapter 2:2-3, promising the coming of Christ and exhorting to a faith that is not doubting but constant (v. 4), but also **VI.** prophesies against the enemies of the Church (v. 5–20). Finally, **VII.** the Prophet repeats all these things in a remarkable song [hymn] and commends them to God in prayer (chapter 3:1 and following). Furthermore, the style of this prophecy, especially in the second and third chapters, is concise and quite difficult, as any skilled reader will easily notice.

<summary>This page concludes the commentary on Nahum, describing the total collapse of Nineveh's leadership and the joy of her victims, before introducing the Book of Habakkuk as a response to injustice under the kings of Judah.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of the prophecy against Nineveh in Nahum to the beginning of the Book of Habakkuk. The commentary provides a detailed philological and historical introduction to Habakkuk’s oracle, identifying the prophet’s era and the theological structure of his dialogue with God.</meta>

# HABAKKUK. CHAPTER I.

<margin>
**Chapter I. verse 1. a)** Vulgate: *Burden.* Tigurinus: *Heavy prophecy.* <note>original Latin: "Onus. Tig. Gravis prophetia"</note> This refers to a prophetic weight or oracle, directed both against the Jews and against the Chaldeans. Compare Isaiah 13:1 and 14:28. But the Syriac simply says *The Prophet*, as in Nahum 1:1. The Source M.I. <note>likely a specific rabbinical manuscript</note> notes: It is called a prophecy because it is brought forth by the mouth of a man. Others, following the Greek Septuagint, interpret it as the "proclamation" or "presentation" of the divine word, for this term is used for teaching or promise. See Proverbs 31:1, Zechariah 12:1, Lamentations 2:14, and the word in Numbers 23:18, 24:3, Isaiah 14:4, and Job 27:1. **b)** Compare Numbers 12:6 and Isaiah 1:1. **c)** *Habakkuk*: this name signifies "embrace" or "the embracing of a son," based on 2 Kings 4:16. <note>From this passage, ancient Rabbis—found in Abarbanel’s commentary—foolishly concluded that our prophet was the son of the Shunammite woman.</note> Our Prophet expressed a most tender affection toward his people. See the final section of Luther’s Preface. Regarding his family, homeland, and age, nothing is recorded in the Scriptures. However, it is rightly inferred that he lived just before the Babylonian captivity, during the reign of Manasseh or more likely Josiah (as Calvin, Vitringa, and others correctly judge). This is because he testifies in verse 5 and following that the Chaldeans were being raised up against the Jewish people at that very time. Compare the contemporaneous prophecies of Zephaniah and Jeremiah, and the notes on 2 Kings 21:10. **d)** *The Prophet* and interpreter of the mysteries of God. Numbers 12:6, 1 Samuel 9:9. Compare Jeremiah 1:5, 20:2, 25:2, etc., and Isaiah 37:2, 38:1, 39:3. Our prophet follows in Isaiah's footsteps by announcing destruction to the Jews via the Chaldeans, which Isaiah had already predicted to Hezekiah in 2 Kings 20:17–18 and Isaiah 39:6–7. This chapter has four parts: I. The title or inscription (v. 1). II. A complaint about the impiety of the Jews (v. 2–4). III. A prediction of the
</margin>

<margin>
**CHAPTER I.** imminent coming of the Chaldeans to overthrow the Jews (v. 5–11). IV. The Prophet's doubts or prayers against the impious enemy (v. 12–17).
**v. 2. e)** *How long, O Lord!* Psalm 13:2. **f)** *I shall cry out to you* or *I shall implore you.* Psalm 18:8, 30:3. **g)** *Will you not hear me crying?* Psalm 22:3. **h)** *How long shall I cry*

<margin>
to you? Lamentations 3:8. **i)** *Force is used! I suffer violence; violence is practiced!* verses 3 and 9; Jeremiah 20:8; Ezekiel 8:17. **k)** *And yet you do not rescue or save us from evil:* not only temporal evil (as in 2 Samuel 14:4, 2 Kings 6:26), but especially spiritual evil. (Ephesians 25:9, 45:17, 21, 22, etc.; compare 1 Peter 1:10, 11) **so that** the long-awaited and promised Savior might finally arrive. Compare Genesis 49:18, Isaiah 35:4, etc. Regarding the structure: he first explains the guilt of the Jewish people (v. 2–4), then the punishment corresponding to that guilt (v. 5 onwards). He announces the guilt figuratively, addressing God himself, not just in his own name but in the name of every righteous person (compare v. 4), to show the state of his people, over which every good person groans (Ezekiel 9:4). It is as if he says: O God! In what times have you allowed us to fall, where one who lives innocently and justly is subject to the violence, strife, and snares of the impious multitude? **v. 3. l)** *Why?* He does not reproach God, but exposes the temptations he and other godly people face, seeking divine intervention. Cf. Jeremiah 12:1, Psalm 73:3, Job 21:7. **m)** *You make me see*, you show me, you make it appear in my time. Psalm 71:20. **n)** *Iniquity* mixed with pride. Psalm 55:11. In a way, labor and misery. Psalm 7:15, Job 5:6. **p)** *Will you watch and, as it were, tolerate it?* v. 13. Referencing Numbers 23:21. **q)** *So that it remains;* or, *How long will there be devastation?* chapter 2:17. **r)** v. 2. Genesis 6:11, Jeremiah 6:7. **s)** *Before me.* Numbers 22:32. **t)** *And there is a lawsuit* Genesis 13:7, Jeremiah 15:10. **u)** *And contention* Psalm 80:5, Proverbs 22:10. **x)** *by which the wicked man exalts himself.* Nahum 1:5, Psalm 24:9. He will easily prevail when everything is corrupt and the public courts of the nation are occupied by the wicked. Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note>: *Plunderers and robbers are before me, who prevail through contention and pride.* Others: *There is strife and contention because of what the wicked man brings forth.* See note on v. 1. So the Syriac: *whoever will there be, who will move strife and contention against me.* But this partly goes against the Hebrew accents. **v. 4. y)** *Therefore:* because you do not avenge the godly, nor yet fulfill our prayers by sending the promised Savior. Cf. Psalm 10:11 onwards, Ecclesiastes 8:11. **z)** *The law grows cold*, wavers, and loses its force. (Kal form) Genesis 45:26, Psalm 77:3; cf. Amos 5:12, 13. Under King Manasseh, the authentic book of the law had been so neglected that it was considered lost, until it was found under Josiah and brought back to public light. 2 Kings 21:2 onwards, 22:8. **a)** *Nor does it go forth* or be promulgated. Daniel 9:23, 25; Luke 2:1. **b)** *Forever.* That is, with the preceding negative, "never." Isaiah 13:20. Or: *it does not go forth to victory* so that the good cause wins; compare Isaiah 25:8 with 1 Corinthians 15:54. Schultens in his *Observations* p. 515: *to truth,* comparing Isaiah 42:3 and the Arabic word for truth—unsullied sincerity. See also 1 Samuel 15:29. **c)** *Just judgment.* cf. Genesis 18:25, Deuteronomy 32:4, 16:19, Isaiah 1:17, 28:17, 59:8, 9, 14. Grotius: *The matter remains undecided.* **d)** Syriac: *For the wicked circumvent*, surrounding and pressing from all sides like a crown. Judges 20:43, Psalm 22:13, 142:8, Proverbs 14:18. That is, <term>oppresses (original Greek: katadynasteuei)</term> James 2:6. **e)** *Therefore distorted judgment goes forth* or judgment twisted and perverted according to men's depraved lusts. Cf. Isaiah 5:23, 10:1. Grotius: *Often there is no judgment; often, what is worse, it is judged plainly against the law.* Thus far the complaint of the Prophet and the godly. Now follows in v. 5 the sentence pronounced by God the Judge against the impious Jews. **v. 5. f)** *Therefore see, O impious Jews, among the nations, and look around* at what I am preparing there: namely, your destruction and rejection. Or *look around* to see if any of them have endured as great a punishment as I have inflicted on you. Compare Lamentations 1:12. But the Syriac: *See, you bold or impudent ones*, and the Arabic (using the same word found below in 2:4): *O negligent ones.* With the Greek: <term>Behold, you despisers (original Greek: Idete hoi kataphronētai)</term>. Paul follows this version, as he often does, in Acts 13:41, because it was in people's hands and fits the context perfectly. There is no need for us to rashly suspect, with Capellus and Grotius, that <term>among the nations (original Hebrew: ba-goyim)</term> was once written differently in the Hebrew text. **g)** *And gaze* Isaiah 42:18. **h)** *And be amazed.* (Hitpael form) **i)** *Be astonished, I say.* Vulgate: *And be dumbfounded.* cf. Isaiah 29:9. **k)** *For I am working a work or about to work* Isaiah 41:4, Micah 2:1. **l)** *In these very days of yours.* See note on v. 1; 2 Kings 21:12 onwards, and Ezekiel 12:25. **m)** *Which you will not believe.* cf. Lamentations 4:12. **n)** *When it is told* if someone were to predict now that it would happen. cf. Isaiah 29:14, 52:15. **v. 6. o)** *For*, to explain what I am about to work in your days, *behold, I.* Isaiah 13:17. To show that I am not bound to endure your impiety and injuries, nor am I delighted by the Temple or external worship without repentance and faith in the Savior. cf. Isaiah 1:11 onwards. **p)** *I am about to raise up* 2 Samuel 12:11, Amos 6:14. **q)** See 2 Kings 24:2, etc. **r)** cf. Deuteronomy 28:49 onwards, Jeremiah 5:15. **s)** *Bitter*, harsh. 2 Samuel 17:8. That is, cruel and grim. cf. Jeremiah 50:42. **t)** *And swift* or ready. Isaiah 32:4; cf. 5:26. **u)** *Advancing and pervading everything into the breadths of the earth.* cf. Isaiah 8:8. <term>over the breadths of the earth (original Greek: epi ta platē tēs gēs)</term>. Revelation 20:9. **x)** *To occupy* Leviticus 20:24. **y)** *Habitations.* Jonathan: *Cities.* See Jeremiah 9:12. **z)** *Not his own* chapter 2:6. In the manner of tyrants. **v. 7. a)** *Terrible* Song of Solomon 6:4, 6. **b)** *And formidable.* Isaiah 18:2. **c)** *That nation is* v. 6. **d)** *From itself comes its judgment.* cf. 2 Kings 25:6. **e)** *And dignity (or uplifting).* Vulgate: burden; others: proclamation; Jonathan: its decree. cf. v. 1 and Job 13:11. They will not deal with you by treaties or fixed laws, but will rule absolutely according to their own whim. Jonathan: *From that very people (the Chaldeans) its own judgment and decree emanate.* **f)** It shall go forth, it shall flow out. See v. 4. **v. 8. g)** *And light*, i.e., they shall be swift. 2 Samuel 1, 23; Jeremiah 4:13. **h)** *More than leopards* (6) Ephesians 11:6, Jeremiah 5:6, Hosea 13:7, Song of Solomon 4:8. These animals have the greatest speed in running and leaping. See Bochart’s *Hierozoicon* I, p. 9 and 787 onwards. **i)** cf. Jeremiah 4:13.

HABAKKUK I, v. 3. *strife* (Hebrew: rib) written with Tethir in manuscripts 17, 18, 22, 23, against the Masoretic text 1, 2, and the Erfurt edition. Psalm 62, 12. others, as we said, regarding the Jews relatively: *he who had,* or *this one, whose it was.* as in Exodus 15:13, 16. **v. 12.** r) *But are you not from of old?* Facing that harsh decree of God, v. 5. seqq., the Prophet presses on with prayers in the name of the godly using various arguments: 1) from the nature and covenant of God graciously entered into with the Israelites, 2) from the divine counsel and purpose of the raised-up Nebuchadnezzar v. 12. 3) from the holiness and justice of God v. 13. 4) from the end of men and the special care of God for them v. 14. etc. with which that judgment of God seemed to conflict. s) Vulgate: *from the beginning* Psalm 143:5. or *from eternity* Psalm 74:12. Deuteronomy 33:27. Micah 5:1. t) *and you are Jehovah,* the faithful and immutable God. Exodus 6:2, 6, 7. u) *and from the covenant of grace also my God.* Genesis 17:7, 8. Psalm 71:22. Isaiah 41:10. Exodus 19:4. seqq. Leviticus 26:12. etc. x) Isaiah 1:4. ch. 12, 6. ch. 43, 3. *whom I hold most holy and worship.* Vatablus y) *therefore let us not die,* I and the rest who piously acknowledge you and holily worship you; which, under the impiety and tyranny of the Babylonians, seemed altogether to be feared: namely, that the Church would be utterly destroyed, or the promise made to the Fathers about the Savior to be born from the seed of Abraham would become void. This is not to be interpreted (says Schmidt on this passage) simply of corporal death, which no one can escape; but of the destruction of the people through extermination, and the delivering of the remnants into spiritual death: so that no one survives in whom the spiritual life might be active; compare Psalm 85, 7. Isaiah 23:13. namely Nebuchadnezzar; whom God therefore calls not only the hammer of the earth, but also His own hammer Jeremiah 50, 23. ch. 51, 20. seqq. **v. 13.** e) Schmidt: *O purer of eyes than that you should see or tolerate evil.* cf. similar construction of this adjective Proverbs 22:11. Job 17, 9. f) so that you cannot see and bear evil in your chosen people. Isaiah 33:15. cf. Psalm 5:5, 6. g) *and to look* with approval v. 3. Psalm 10, 14. Isaiah 22, 11. h) *you are not able.* Isaiah 1:13. i) *why then do you look,* or *would you look?* He does not accuse the ways of God, but rather hopes for the best, and desires to be instructed in his own and others' weakness. see v. 3. and he says this because of the narrowness of his mind, not knowing that gold is refined by fire, and that the three youths came out of the fiery furnace purer than they had entered. But we can also take this generally, that he speaks from the persona of human impatience, so that he breaks out in a complaining voice full of heat, saying: *Why do you look upon the despisers, and keep silence while the impious one tramples one more righteous than himself?* But he speaks this not knowing the unsearchable judgments of God, and the depth of the riches of His wisdom and knowledge, that God does not see as man sees etc. says Jerome in his Preface to this book. k) *the treacherous* and wicked Chaldeans Isaiah 21:2. ch. 24, 16. l) *why are you silent,* or *will you be silent and conceal it?* Numbers 30:5. Grotius: *The Jews were involved in great crimes; but nevertheless in that matter they were much surpassed by the Chaldeans.* **v. 14.** p) *Have you made and will you treat men,* created in your image Genesis 9, 6. whom you also cherish with special care, especially your chosen people. q) *as the fish of the sea,* which are often caught and killed in the greatest numbers by men. Genesis 9, 2. Numbers 11, 22. Job 12, 8. Genesis 9, 21. ch. 9, 2, 3. Psalm 104, 20. s) understood: *to whom there is no Lord or avenger.* cf. Genesis 34:2. ch. 43, 26. Isaiah 63, 19. since you are the guardian of men. <summary>This page analyzes Habakkuk 1:8-15, detailing the terrifying speed and ruthlessness of the Babylonian "evening wolves" and the prophet's agonizing question: why does a pure and holy God allow such wicked people to devour those more righteous than themselves?</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the Book of Habakkuk, transitioning from the description of the Babylonian "fishermen" who catch nations in their nets (Chapter 1) to the prophet’s patient wait for a divine response and the famous promise that the righteous shall live by faith (Chapter 2).</meta>

# HABAKKUK. CHAPTER I. 2.

y) he drags, bends, or snatches him away, or the whole group, that is, everyone mentioned from the beginning of the verse. From the root **גָּרַר** <note>original: *garar*</note> (to drag). See Proverbs 21:17; Jeremiah 32:23; Hosea 7:14. Bochart, however, in *Hierozoicon* I, page 714, suggests "he gathers," from the root **גָּרָה** <note>original: *garah*</note>, which usually means something else, comparing Psalm 56:7; Psalm 59:4; Psalm 140:3. From this, he thinks **גוּר** <note>original: *gur*, a cub</note> is so named because cubs or young animals gather around their mother. But Neumann in *Exodus*, page 190, considers this too far-fetched, believing the young of lions, bears, and dogs are so named because they wander about. z) with his net or his traps, v. 16, 17. Ezekiel 32:3; 26:5, 14; Ecclesiastes 7:26. a) and he collects there: v. 9; 2:5. b) in his dragnet, v. 16; Isaiah 19:8. c) whereby he impiously rejoices. See Proverbs 21:17. d) and in his crimes, because of his very fortunate successes, he exults. Psalm 13:5; compare Daniel 4:27.

v. 16. e) The Vulgate: *Therefore he will immolate to his net, and sacrifice to his dragnet*—as the superstitious Gentiles did. For from the origin of things, says Justin in Book 43, chapter 2: *The ancients worshipped spears as immortal gods; in memory of which religion, spears are still added to the images of the gods.* See more in Doughty's *Analecta* on this passage, page 295 ff. But Grotius says: that is, they attribute all victories to their own strength, as above in verse 11. f) because through those nets and traps his portion becomes fat. Genesis 49:20; Isaiah 30:23. g) his portion. Genesis 14:24; Psalm 17:14. h) his food and sustenance, Psalm 44:12. i) something fat, perhaps a fat fish. Zechariah 11:16.

v. 17. k) Shall he therefore? So that he attributes everything to himself and not to You, see verses 11, 16. Compare Amos 8:8. l) a full drawing up [of the net]. Genesis 42:35 and others. He will set free, he will lead out. Genesis 14:14; Leviticus 26:33; Psalm 35:3. m) his net, v. 15. n) and continually. Nahum 3:19. o) so that he slays whole nations, Ezekiel 13:13, and makes no end to the slaughters. p) will he not spare? Isaiah 30:14; 47:6; Jeremiah 21:7; Proverbs 6:33; Job 6:10.

<column-break/>

He drags them in his net and gathers them in his dragnet; therefore he rejoices and is glad.
<margin>16</margin> Therefore he sacrifices to his net and burns incense to his dragnet; for by them his portion is fat and his food is rich.
<margin>17</margin> Shall he therefore empty his net and continue to slay nations without pity?

## 20
### CHAPTER II.
I will stand at my watch and station myself upon the rampart, and I will keep watch to see what He will speak to me, and what I shall answer concerning my complaint.
<margin>2</margin> And the LORD answered me and said: "Write the vision and make it plain upon the tablets, so that he who reads it may run."
<margin>3</margin> For the vision is yet for an appointed time; it speaks of the end and will not lie. If it tarries, wait for it; for it will surely come, it will not delay.
<margin>4</margin> Behold, his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him; but the righteous shall live by his faith.

<sig>Hb hb 2</sig>

*The Lord answered me, verse 2. A metaphor from watchmen. Compare Isaiah 21:8; Ezekiel 3:17.* That is, after the Prophet poured out his complaints in Chapter 1, he now retreats into silence and hope. This second chapter contains, as Schmidt observed: I. *The expectation of a divine response to the earlier prayers, v. 1.* II. *The response itself; in which there is (1) a command to write, v. 2; (2) an exhortation to constant and undoubting faith, v. 3; (3) a prophecy against the proud enemy (v. 5), the greedy (v. 9), the violent (v. 12), the drunkard (v. 13), and the idolater (v. 18). All of these we understand in the literal and immediate sense to refer to the Chaldeans.* But according to *Guttler’s Prophetic Theology, p. 123* and others, following Cocceius, this chapter proclaims: I. The Coming of the Messiah, the true herald (v. 1-3). II. The division of the Jewish people at the presence of the Messiah, into those who are not upright and those who are just by faith (v. 4). III. The punishment of the Romans, both pagan and anti-Christian, who oppress the Church (v. 5-13). IV. The propagation of the Gospel (v. 14). V. The destruction of the Antichrist (v. 15-17). VI. The abolition of idolatrous images (v. 18, 19). VII. The peace of the Church (v. 20). Indeed, it is an easy descent from the type to the antitype, as Dr. Maius notes in *Economy of the Old Testament, p. 988.* r) *I would stand*, v. 1. 1 Samuel 17:16. s) *Upon my rampart. Nahum 2:2; compare 2 Peter 3:17.* t) *that I might keep watch. Psalm 5, 4.* u) *to see what Jehovah would speak in me. Abarbanel: namely, through the prophetic spirit or internal revelation. Compare Numbers 12:8; 2 Samuel 23:2; Zechariah 1:9; Hebrews 1:1.* x) *what I ought to answer. Exodus 19:8; Numbers 22:8.* y) *to my argumentation.* Schmidt: to that complaint of mine. Jonathan: to my prayer. Also translated well by Schmidt as <term>ἐπὶ τὸν ἔλεγχόν</term> <note>original Greek: *epi ton elenchon*, "upon the argument/rebuke"</note>. z) For the Prophet understands those reasons and arguments which he used in his prayers in 1:12 ff. against the Babylonians, and which he himself could not fully satisfy. Compare Job 23:4; Isaiah 1:18; and Psalm 73:2 ff. *v. 2.* a) *And so he answered me,* in His kindness, the Lord. Psalm 25:8; Amos 3:7. a) *write this vision* in a book, compare 1:1, so that it remains written for posterity. Compare Exodus 17:14; Jeremiah 30:2. b) *and explain it, write it clearly (3) Deuteronomy 2:5; 27:8.* c) *upon several tablets. Compare Isaiah 8:1; 30:8.* d) *so that anyone who reads it can run through it and grasp it quickly.* Compare a similar expression in Daniel 12:4. *v. 3.* e) *because certainly, etc. Daniel 12:7.* For this was the sum of the divine response to be written on public tablets. But the Vulgate, Schmidt, and others explain: *Because, as for the vision itself which is to be written, I will submit it immediately.* f) *there will yet be a vision:* i.e., the gift of prophecy will not entirely cease, nor will the Church, as you fear (1:12), utterly perish. But Schmidt: *Because the vision indeed (perhaps the thing promised in the prophetic vision) will yet be deferred until the appointed time. Compare Daniel 9:24; 10:14.* g) *until the fixed time. Psalm 102:14; compare Daniel 12:7, 9; Matthew 11:13; Galatians 4:4.* h) *Abarbanel: and this vision speaks not only of the overthrow of the Babylonian empire (v. 2), but reaching into a long time, even to the end of all the calamities of your people, and until the coming of the Messiah.* <term>ὅτι ἀנאτελεῖ εἰς πέראס</term> <note>original: "that it will rise toward the end"</note>. Vulgate: *and it will appear at the end.* Interpreters differ greatly concerning this phrase and the preceding word. *To Maius in "Economy of the Old Testament," also to Cocceius, Kimchi, and others, the name is:* <image-desc>No illustration present.</image-desc> that herald or witness <term>(the Word) John 1:1; the faithful witness Revelation 1:5; and the evangelist Isaiah 61:1-2.</term> At the end of that prescribed term he will be present or will come; from the root **פָּוּחַ** <note>original: *puach*, to breathe/speak</note>, compare Jeremiah 4:31 and Psalm 27:12. To others, it is the Hiphil form from the root **פָּוּחַ**, as if to say: and that vision will breathe or speak until the end, and will not deceive; compare Proverbs 6:19; 12:17; 14:5. Cocceius also referred these places to the category of a Name. *Abendana: as if to say: God, do not wonder that I delay the punishment of the Chaldeans for 70 years; for there is yet a vision pertaining to other and far remote times. We set aside many conjectures and explanations that either ignore the accents or do not render the sense.* i) *nor will it deceive*—that truthful Witness will not fail the hope of those expecting Him, nor will God allow His promises to become void. Numbers 23:19; see also Joshua 21:45; 1 Samuel 3:19; 1 Kings 8:56; Isaiah 31:16; 12:22; Zechariah 1:6. k) *if therefore it lingers, or seems to you to delay Genesis 19:16; see above 1:2.* l) *wait for it in silence and hope,* and do not let your soul despond. Isaiah 8:17; Zephaniah 3:8; Psalm 27:14; 33:20; see Isaiah 5:19; 28:16; and 2 Kings 6:33. No worship is better or more pleasing to God than the expectation of divine help in patience and obedience: because thus the honor of truth and omnipotence is attributed to God, says Brenz on Joshua 11:43. m) *because it will most certainly come* 1 Samuel 9:6; see Genesis 49:10; Ezekiel 21:32; Malachi 3:1. n) *and it will not be postponed,* it will not delay beyond the appointed time, nor come as if after it. Deuteronomy 7:10; Isaiah 46:13; 60:22. But in the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4) he will appear in the flesh, and provide help at all times to those truly believing in faith. <term>ὅτι ἐρχόμενος ἥξει, καὶ οὐ μὴ χρονίσῃ</term> <note>original Greek: "because coming he will come, and he will not delay," as quoted in Hebrews 10:37</note>. See also Hebrews 10:35 and 2 Peter 3:9. It is well that the Talmudists in Tractate *Sanhedrin*, chapter 11, folio 97b (as also Abarbanel and others) take this passage as referring to the coming of the Messiah; but they do poorly in thinking from this that his time can be delayed, and in saying that the calculation of the time should not be undertaken: not attending to the whole context, which says the opposite; nor to the intent of the passage, in which God only commands the soul to restrain its headlong desire. See many interpreters on this passage. *v. 4.* o) *Behold!* Psalm 52:9. Others, with the Septuagint, read it conditionally: *Behold, if, or But if, as in Leviticus 13:5, 8, 9.* p) *unattentive through zeal, or envious through zeal, and negligent through sloth.* (2) This meaning of the word is clear from the Arabic. See note on 1:5 and Numbers 14:44. Thus the same vice is noted here in the Jews as elsewhere, even in the New Testament: see Isaiah 6:9-10; 8:14 ff; Matthew 13:14; 22:3, 5; Hebrews 2:1, etc. However, our same word among the Arabs in the 6th conjugation also means *He hid or withdrew himself from someone*, whence the Septuagint and the Apostle (Hebrews 10:38) have <term>ἐὰן ὑποστείληται</term> <note>original Greek: "if he shrinks back"</note>. Whether he withdrew himself out of pride and trust in his own righteousness, or out of unbelief and neglect of the divine promise, or out of impatience and fear. See note on v. 1. q) *his soul is not upright or honest within him. Compare Deuteronomy 9:5; 1 Kings 9:4, 12.* r) in the man himself or the unbelieving people. Or: with God Himself and that faithful Witness (v. 3). *His soul is not upright,* and is not approved. <term>ὁ οὐκ εὐδοκεῖ ἡ ψυχή μου ἐν αὐטῷ</term> <note>original Greek: "in whom my soul is not well pleased"</note>. For souls ought to love God and the Savior above all things, Deuteronomy 5:5; Isaiah 26:8-9. But those who are perverse (Deuteronomy 31:5) and without faith cannot please God, Hebrews 11:6. *The soul is upright in the promised Witness, that is, in Christ, when it loves him. If it does not love him, it is crooked, says Cocceius in his Lexicon, page 228.*

others, following Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for federal theology</note>, think the Prophet is prophesying here about the enemies of Christ's Church after his coming. The Jewish scholar Isaac Abarbanel, on page 272, takes verses 5–11 as referring to Babylon, but verse 12 and following as referring to the Romans. He does this based on the hypothesis that verse 2 is the answer to the Prophet about Babylon, but verse 3 is about the coming of the Messiah; and also from verse 14, the truth of which (he argues) could not be demonstrated under the Second Temple, since the opposite was manifest (namely, he does not recognize Jesus, through whom the knowledge of salvation was made known to the nations); compare Isaiah 11:9, Jeremiah 31:34, and Zephaniah 3:9. We understand these things literally as referring to Babylon, but we think a mystical sense should be properly subordinated. See the note at verse 1. For just as that ancient Babel, long rich and powerful, was given over to luxury and idolatry, and oppressed the people of God and held them captive for a time, yet was eventually so devastated through various turns of fortune that today scarcely the ruins of that great city remain; so too does that "mystical Babylon" <note>The "Babylon" of the New Testament, often interpreted as Rome or an anti-Christian power</note> under the New Testament refer to it by a mystical name, and it is destined for the same judgments from God. **y) wine,** understand the preposition "by" <note>original Hebrew: ב (*be*)</note> as in Zechariah 10:7. Or "a man of wine," as in Psalm 109:4, 120:7, Ruth 3:2, and Daniel 9:23. Just as one is called "eloquent," "wordy," "beautiful," "bloody," or "warlike," meaning a man of words, of beauty, of blood, or of war. Or understand it as "one who drinks wine," comparing Proverbs 20:1. Abarbanel says Nebuchadnezzar is called this (and Rashi refers it to Belshazzar in Daniel 5) because he was a wine-bibber and often drunk, and therefore treacherous and not standing by his promises. Concerning the luxury of ancient Babylon, see also Curtius, Book V, chapter 1: *The Babylonians are especially given to wine and the things that follow drunkenness.* Compare also the notes on Isaiah 47:1. **z)** Isaiah 21:2. **a) an arrogant or proud man.** **b)** The Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin Bible translation</note>: *and he shall not be decorated.* Jacques Gusset (p. 20) suggests: *neither is he pleasing or desirable to God,* comparing Jeremiah 6:2. **c) neither shall he dwell securely,** namely, according to Abendana, in his own kingdom. Others say: *he does not dwell,* meaning he has no dwelling in the Church or in the heavens, being excluded from the fold of God and Christ. Compare Isaiah 15:2 and Psalm 68:13. **c)** Psalm 81:11. **d)** Isaiah 5:14, Proverbs 27:20, and 30:16. **e) and he is like death,** which spares no man. Compare Song of Solomon 8:6. **f) nor is he satisfied.** Compare Proverbs 30:16. **g)** Chapter 1:13. **h) so that he alone may rule,** just as Nebuchadnezzar did. **i)** Abarbanel says: *Do not think, therefore, as if the day of vengeance or punishment will not come. For shall not...* **k) all those oppressed.** **l)** See Isaiah 14:4, Jeremiah 24:9, Job 17:6. **m)** The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> uses "parable." Proverbs 1:6. **n) riddles.** 1 Kings 10:1. **o) concerning him,** Genesis 20:13. **p) so says any of the believers.** Vulgate: *and it shall be said.* Compare Isaiah 65:8, Micah 2:4. **q)** Verse 9, Isaiah 1:4. Compare Proverbs 3:33. **r) to the one multiplying** from 16, 17, 18. Proverbs 28:8. **s)** Vulgate: *things not his own.* Jonathan <note>The Targum or Aramaic translation</note>: *riches not his own.* Compare chapter 1:6. **t) for how long?** i.e., how long will he possess it? Compare Jeremiah 17:11. **u) and he loads upon himself.** Nehemiah 5:15. **x)** Vulgate: *thick clay.* <note>original: *densum lutum*</note> Compare Zephaniah 1:11 and 1 Timothy 6:9. Others say "debt," from the word *abtit* in Deuteronomy 15:6, 8, and 24:10. Jonathan: *How long will you weigh yourself down with the weight of sins?* **y) shall they not?** verses 6, 13. **z) suddenly,** Numbers 6:9. **a) they shall rise,** and rise up against you. Psalm 3:2. **b) biting like serpents,** Jeremiah 8:17, Micah 3:5. Or your creditors, seeking back their own from you with profit, comparing Deuteronomy 23:20. **c) and they shall awake,** Judges 16:14. **d) those who shake or disturb you.** Esther 5:9, Ecclesiastes 12:3. Compare the term in Jeremiah 15:4. **e) as a spoil,** 2 Kings 21:14, Isaiah 42:24, Zephaniah 1:13. **f) to those.** Isaiah 30:5. Abarbanel says he is speaking of the Medes and Persians. **g) For because you plundered, etc.** Isaiah 10:6, 33:1. **h) many nations.** See verse 5. **i) they shall plunder you in turn,** Ezekiel 39:10. Compare the law of retaliation in Judges 1:6-7. **k) all the rest of the peoples.** Jonathan: *all the remnants of the tribes.* Compare 2 Kings 25:11, Jeremiah 39:9, Zechariah 14:2. **l) because of the many slaughters of men,** verse 17, 2 Samuel 3:28. **m) and the violence done to the land,** verse 17, chapter 1:2-3, Joel 4:19, Obadiah 10. Jonathan: *and the violence exercised against the land of Israel, the city of Jerusalem, etc.* So says Rashi. **n) of the city,** i.e., the city of God, verse 17, Isaiah 26:1-2. Others, with Grotius, take it collectively: *on account of the plundering of lands and cities and all those dwelling in them.* Grotius adds: *You see that not everything done by nations under "law" is considered lawful by God; but the cause and the manner are scrutinized.* **o) Woe to the Babylonian,** verses 6, 12, 15, 19. **p) to the one making profit,** Psalm 10:3, Jeremiah 6:13. **q) evil gain,** Isaiah 56:11, Proverbs 1:19, 15:27. Jonathan: *Woe to him who violently seeks the riches of impiety for his house.* Till (p. 414) suggests this refers to carnal leaders in the Church and degenerate bishops. **r) for his house and family.** **s) to place his nest on high and in safety.** A metaphorical and proverbial expression taken from birds that nest in inaccessible rocks. Compare Numbers 24:21, Isaiah 22:18, Jeremiah 49:16, Obadiah 4, Job 29:18. **t) that he may be snatched away,** Isaiah 20:6. **u) from the hand of evil,** i.e., that he may be safe from the danger of enemies. Compare Psalm 106:41-42. Kimchi compares this to Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4:27. **x) For you have counseled, O impious Chaldean.** Compare Isaiah 7:5. **y) counsels which, by a contrary outcome, will turn to the shame and ignominy of your house.** 1 Samuel 20:30, Isaiah 30:3, 5, 42:17. *For not your counsels, but mine shall stand.* Isaiah 14:24. **z) by cutting off.** The Septuagint: *for you have counseled to cut off.* 2 Kings 10:32, Proverbs 14:6. **a)** verse 5, 8. **b)** Jonathan: *but you have sinned against your own soul.* So too: *you are sinning against your soul.* Compare verse 6. **c) For even the stone you build with** (verse 11) **cries out that you are unjust.** Jonathan: *For even the stone from the wall cries out that you are doing violence to it.* Compare Luke 19:40. **d)** Compare Deuteronomy 22:24.

<margin>
**s) But the righteous in his faith;** who, following the example of Abraham (Genesis 15:6), believed the promise of God and through that faith attained righteousness. **t) through his faith,** i.e., by faith in that Witness and Savior promised in Isaiah 53:11 ("He who is of my faith") and thus also according to the Vulgate: *the righteous by his faith,* by which he receives that gift of righteousness. Compare Jeremiah 5:1, 3; Psalm 2:12; Hosea 2:21, 27. **u) For the faith by which the righteous are established is both ours subjectively and Christ’s objectively,** as in Romans 3:22 and Galatians 2:20. It should be observed that according to the Hebrew accents, this belongs to the subject, not the predicate. Compare Romans 5:1, 10:30, 32. **v) shall live,** by the way of grace and glory (John 5:24), safe from spiritual and eternal death. Genesis 2:17; compare Leviticus 18:5, Ezekiel 18:23. **x)** Jonathan: *Behold, the impious say: all these things shall not happen; but the righteous shall remain in their truth.* How great the weight and value of this saying is can be seen from its triple citation by the Apostle: namely, Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11, where it concerns justification by faith, and Hebrews 10:38, where it concerns the continuation and perseverance of faith. These are not to be opposed, but subordinated to one another. It is also notable what the ancients hand down in the Talmud (Tractate Makkot, folio 23b and 24a): that into this one saying, **The righteous shall live by his faith,** Habakkuk reduced all 613 commandments that were formerly delivered by God to Moses on Mount Sinai.
</margin>
