So the most ample increase of divine science and knowledge, as the good of the end times, is promised elsewhere under the symbol of the water of light (Isaiah 30:26, 60:19, 20) and rising waters (Ezekiel 47:5, Joel 4:18). Others compare Daniel 3:29, 31; Ezra 1:1 and following; 2 Chronicles 36:23; Esther 8:16, 17.

<margin>v. 15. f) see v. 6, 9, 12. g)</margin> to one making his companion drink. Compare Genesis 19:32, 34; Numbers 5:24, 27; Amos 2:12. With many interpreters, I believe these things should be taken not literally but figuratively, as Van Til <note>Solomon van Til, a Dutch theologian</note> says on this passage; compare Revelation 17:2. **h)** to one adding or applying (Woe to you, I say) who studiously applies and offers the cup. **i)** 1 Samuel 2:36, Job 30:7. **k)** a skin-bottle, as in Genesis 21:14. Others: venom, or your poison; as in Deuteronomy 32:24, 33. Compare Hosea 7:5 and Revelation 18:3. **k)** and not without success, but even by making them drunk (Jeremiah 51:7). **l)** to look with wicked pleasure. Compare Psalm 22:18, 92:12. **m)** their stripped limbs or private parts. Participle *Pual*, from the root *‘ur*. Compare Isaiah 3:17, 32:11, Nahum 3:5, and Revelation 16:15. **Grotius:** By this allegory is understood the perfidy of the Chaldeans, who enticed peoples with treaties, whom they then treated most ignominiously.

<margin>v. 16. n)</margin> S: For you shall be satiated; others: you have satiated yourself. **Vulgate**: You are filled (Deuteronomy 8:11, 8:10, Psalm 88:4, 123:4). **o)** ignominy (Isaiah 22:18, Hosea 4:7; see above at v. 10). **p)** instead of glory; or: from that glory of yours. Compare Numbers 24:11, Philippians 3:19. Gürtler, in his *Prophetic Theology* (p. 712), understands this as referring to the Antichrist and compares Isaiah 11:4, Micah 7:10, Zephaniah 3:15, Psalm 5:7, 68:22. **q)** drink indeed, you also, from the cup of God's wrath, as the following explains. Compare Jeremiah 25:26, 28; Psalm 75:9; Revelation 14:8, 10; 18:6. **r)** and be uncircumcised, or you shall be held as such. (Z) Leviticus 19:23. S: so that your foreskin may be revealed. Compare Genesis 9:21. **Jonathan**: *‘ur*—to be made bare; so that you may be judged and treated as uncircumcised. **Grotius:** The sense is: you are to be stripped, just as you stripped others—that is, mocked. He was indeed literally uncircumcised, but he is ordered to suffer the judgment worthy of that state: he is not to be tolerated (cf. Deuteronomy 25:1). *Guffet. p. 641.* But **Van Til** on this passage (p. 460): show your foreskin; for those who desired to see the nakedness of others with pleasure (v. 15) would now be forced to show their own foreskin. Now, the foreskin was a mark of paganism (see 1 Samuel 17:36), just as circumcision was of Judaism. But since Scripture also speaks of the "foreskin of the heart" (Ezekiel 44:9), it is elegantly hinted that it will eventually be manifest that the lover, fornicating with a harlot, is not a true Christian, though he wished to seem so before; but an ethnic man, still having the foreskin of the heart, etc. **s)** for it shall eventually come around even to you (1 Samuel 5:8). **t)** Isaiah 51:17, Psalm 11:6, Lamentations 4:21. See also Matthew 20:22, 23. **u)** Deuteronomy 33:2, Jeremiah 25:15, 17; Psalm 75:9. **x)** **Vulgate**: and the vomit of ignominy. S: so that there may be ignominious vomiting. (y) Compare Isaiah 19:14 and Jeremiah 25:27.

<margin>v. 17. y)</margin> see v. 8. **z)** Lebanon—that is, according to **Abarbanel**, the land of Israel (cf. Deuteronomy 3:25). Others: the Sanctuary or the illustrious Temple; because it was largely built from the cedars of Lebanon (2 Chronicles 2:8, 15). Compare Ezekiel 17:3, Zechariah 11:1, and Isaiah 14:8. **Jonathan**: Because the robbery of the house of the sanctuary shall cover you, and the prey of its people shall crush you: because of the blood of men and the robbery of the land of Israel, the city of Jerusalem, and all inhabiting it. **a)** shall cover you (Obadiah v. 10, Micah 7:10). The metaphor seems to refer to an old custom where those condemned in judgment were covered with a veil, as if unworthy of the sight of men (cf. Esther 7:8). **b)** devastation (c. 1:3). **c)** *chathath*—hardship or misery (Romans 3:16). **c)** of cruel beasts. Compare Isaiah 56:9, Daniel 7:3, 7; Revelation 13:1, 11; 19:20. **d)** it shall preserve them; thus Rabbi Jonah in Kimchi. **e)** *chathath*—terror/dread. *Hiphil* future from the root *chathath* (Job 31:34). Others: "and because of the devastation of beasts which terrified them"—that is, according to **Abarbanel**, because of the devastation of the Jews (whom he here calls "animals" figuratively, since he had already called the land of Israel "Lebanon") by which the Roman enemy terrified them. e) see v. 8. f) compare Revelation 11:18, 18:24. **g)** of cities, and especially the city of God (v. 8).

<margin>v. 18. h)</margin> **Grotius:** The Jews will say this: what did the images of the gods profit the Chaldeans? But **Abarbanel**: Because the Roman Empire, which captured Jerusalem, was devoted to the idolatrous worship of sculptures and images, and even today, after accepting the faith of Jesus of Nazareth, they make sculptures of their God and all his saints with him, therefore he says against them: What does it profit, or what use has it ever provided? etc. (1 Samuel 12:21, Isaiah 44:9, 10, Jeremiah 16:19). Yet the impious Jew should not compare pagan Rome with Christians, nor can anyone today indiscriminately attribute "icon-worship" to all Christians. **i)** Exodus 20:4. Compare Isaiah 30:22. **k)** that he himself carved. (6) Exodus 34:1, 4; Deuteronomy 12:1, 3; 1 Kings 5:32. **l)** its molder. Compare Isaiah 44:9. **m)** what does a cast image profit? (Exodus 32:4, Isaiah 30:22). **n)** and he who stands by the sculpture, a teacher of lies, or teaching a lie? (Isaiah 9:14). **o)** because he trusts in insane superstition (Psalm 115:8).

-> 1 A prayer <gloss>k</gloss> of Habakkuk <gloss>l</gloss> the prophet <gloss>m</gloss> upon <gloss>n</gloss> Shigionoth <gloss>o</gloss>: <-

-> 2 O Lord, <gloss>p</gloss> I have heard <gloss>q</gloss> your report, <gloss>r</gloss> and I was afraid. <gloss>s</gloss> O Lord, <gloss>t</gloss> your work, <gloss>u</gloss> in the midst <gloss>x</gloss> of the years <gloss>y</gloss> preserve it alive! <gloss>z</gloss> In the midst <gloss>a</gloss> of the years <gloss>b</gloss> make it known; <gloss>c</gloss> in turmoil <gloss>d</gloss> remember <gloss>e</gloss> mercy. <-

h) Compare Isaiah 52:15, Psalm 107:42. i) Gurtler compares Isaiah 11:10, 32:17, 33:20; Titius compares Isaiah 60:11, Daniel 7:17-18, Revelation 11:15. **CHAPTER III.** v. 1. k) Prayer, or supplication (Isaiah 1:15, 37:4, Daniel 9:3). l) Of Habakkuk; or inspired by the Holy Spirit for Habakkuk. Compare Psalm 3:1, 4:1, and especially 17:1. m) See chapter 1:1. n) Upon Shigionoth <note>A musical term likely referring to a passionate song or rhythmic variation</note>. (2) Psalm 7:1. That is, according to the Septuagint <note>Greek Old Testament</note> and the Arabic version: in the manner of a song; or according to mixed odes, varying with different voices or choirs, carefully composed and entrusted to the master of sacred music for the public use of the entire Church (see v. 19). Indeed, he prays not only in his own name, but also in the name of his people (compare v. 14, 16, 19). This chapter therefore contains, as the title indicates, the prayer of Habakkuk, in which: I. The Church earnestly seeks preservation during those most sorrowful times (v. 2; compare v. 16-17). II. It conceives a hope of divine help based on the analogy of ancient times (v. 3–15). And thus III., after a brief summary of the imminent evils, it ends joyfully with confidence and hope in the promised Savior (v. 16 ff.). But according to the hypotheses of Cocceius <note>17th-century theologian</note>, Gurtler’s *Prophetic Theology* (p. 123), and others, this prophecy encompasses: I. The report of Christ's coming (v. 2). II. His resurrection from the dead (ibid). III. The light of the Gospel (v. 3–4). IV. The punishment of those who do not believe (v. 5–10). V. The light of the Church in the midst of Antichrist's darkness (v. 11). VI. The desertion of the Church by the Antichrist (v. 12–14). VII. The danger of her destruction by the Antichrist (v. 14–17). And finally VIII. The hope of the Church (v. 18–19). See these views, if you please, in Cocceius and Tillius on this passage. Compare also the Argument of this book and the note on 2:1. Furthermore, Gussetius (p. 52) correctly advised that the future tenses of this Song should not be converted into the past tense. Nevertheless, past events are interposed because the prophet looks back to them and confirms his hope from them, arguing for what is to come. v. 2. o) O God! He addresses the Father, whose glory it is to maintain faith with His own. So Tillius on this passage from a comparison of v. 13. p) Vulgate: I have heard your hearing, that is, your decree, or the prophecy heard by me (see 2:1-2). "Your report" <note>original Greek: Τὴν ἀκοὴν σου</note>, as in Isaiah 53:1, Romans 10:16; others: "your fame" (compare Numbers 14:15). q) and I was afraid, or I was struck with fear; because of the terrible judgments which you pronounced both against your people and against their enemies (compare v. 16, Isaiah 56:2, 5, Psalm 119:120). Thus the Prophet explains the occasion of this prayer: for he indicates that from that divine response given in chapter 2:1 ff., which he was anxiously expecting, he was affected by fear and reverence no less than when the sentence was pronounced above in chapter 1:5 ff. against the Jews. Abarbanel: as if to say, I heard what you revealed to me concerning the second exile and its long duration, and I feared how the Israelites would endure for so many centuries among their enemies. r) your work. Namely, the Church or your people. Compare Isaiah 45:11, 19:23, 60:21, Ephesians 2:10. This very title contains an argument for divine mercy (compare Isaiah 64:7-8). s) within those sorrowful years of punishment, concerning which see below v. 16-17 and 1:5 ff., until that defined time and end of evils (2:3), when all things are to be fulfilled which you signaled through your servants the Prophets (Revelation 10:7). Abarbanel: within the years of this long-lasting exile, during which Israel will be like the dead (compare Ezekiel 37:3, Romans 11:15). t) preserve it alive! (The suffix is emphatically redundant, as in Exodus 2:6, 1 Samuel 14, Isaiah 8:13, etc.) Namely, so that your people do not perish, or so that hope and faith do not die out in everyone (1:12; compare 2:4, 1 Peter 1:3, 5; see also Deuteronomy 33:6 and Psalm 118:17). Certainly, as Bochart (*Hieroz. I. p. 289*) and others believe, it had been predicted to the Jews held in the Babylonian captivity that after 70 years they would be restored to liberty (Jeremiah 25:11-12, etc.). Therefore Habakkuk asks God that in the meantime He might protect and save His captive people, whom he calls "the work of God." However, the fact that the prophet is not speaking exclusively of the Babylonian captivity is persuaded by both the preceding and following parts which speak of the coming of Christ; in this, the Hebrews commonly agree with other interpreters. For others, "preserve it alive" is a noun with a suffix, as in "lives" below in v. 10 and "his power" in Nahum 2:4, etc. As if to say: your work, or the operation of your grace, is its life—namely, the life of His people, or of every believer (compare 1:12, 2:4, Ephesians 2:1, 5, Isaiah 26:12). Thus Tillius, according to his and Cocceius's hypothesis: your work, or the operation of your power, is the resurrection and life of Jesus Christ, of whom 2:3 speaks (compare Psalm 21:5, Romans 6:4, Ephesians 1:19). We prefer the verbal sense. u) within those years, I say. x) may you make known your grace and power (Isaiah 63:1, Psalm 77:15), so that the way of life and salvation in Christ Jesus may be clear to us (Psalm 67:3, 103:7, Isaiah 53:1), and it may be revealed that you have not deserted your work and your people (Psalm 138:8). y) in turmoil. Or "in wrath" against the impious (2:4, Isaiah 14:4, Ezekiel 22:18, Job 3:17, 26). z) of mercy, or of having mercy on your own, may you remember (compare Genesis 8:1, Leviticus 26:42, 44, 45, 2 Samuel 24:14, Isaiah 54:8, 64:8, 11, Micah 7:18-19, Psalm 25:7, Luke 1:54, 72). Thus far is the summary of the Prophetic prayer: of whose success he hopes well in the following verses, based on the ancient miracles and benefits of God; based on the foundation that God is the same yesterday, today, and forever (Hebrews 13:8).

The Septuagint <note>The Greek version of the Old Testament</note> translates this as *Diapsalma* <note>original Greek: Διάψαλμα</note>, as if it denotes a change in musical melody, or according to others, a pause and relaxation of the voice. Kimchi <note>A prominent medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian</note>, however, on Psalm 3:3, derives it from *salal* or "lifting up," because there the singers would lift up their voices; compare Psalm 62:10. Thus Salomon van Til, on this passage, says: We think it is an imperative from the verb *salal*, (though not without anomaly, since the *Dagesh* mark is absent, etc.) by which the priest-trumpeters were moved, so that one of them would blow the trumpet and exalt its sound; which would serve as a kind of applause, and created a pause in the singing. To Cocceius, on this passage, *Selah* is an imperative from *salah*, as if to say: "Rouse your mind, reader, and weigh these things," compare Job 28:16, 19. To others, it is an expletive, a mark of different emotion, or an interjection. See Cocceius's *Lexicon* 57, and more extensively Forster’s *Dictionary* p. 548 following, Gussetius in the place cited above, and especially Noldius in his notes, 1877. g) when he covered the heavens. Ezekiel 32:7, Psalm 147:8. h) his majesty or glory. Psalm 8:2. Grotius <note>A famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note>: i.e., the air was full of lightning, compare Exodus 30:18, 11:16, 2:10. i) concerning his praise and glory, Isaiah 42:10. Or according to Kimchi: his splendor and light, compare Job 29:3, 31:26. k) the earth was filled, Isaiah 6:3, Psalm 48:11. Compare Exodus 15:14 following, Joshua 2:9 following. Abarbanel <note>A 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note>: This alludes to the divine glory, which appeared like fire on the summit of Mount Sinai, compare Exodus 19:18, 24:17. Others: Then also the majesty of Christ shall cover the Church, and his glory shall fill the earth, just as of old the bright cloud covered and filled the tabernacle. Exodus 40:34 following, Numbers 9:15, etc. v. 4. l) thus also splendor. 2 Samuel 23:4, Isaiah 60:3. m) That is, like light or the Sun. See Isaiah 18:4, Psalm 37:6, Job 21:18. Others in the genitive: as the Light, that is, the Sun of Righteousness, Isaiah 9:3, Hosea 6:3, Malachi 3:20, John 1:9, 14. n) shall be. So most scholars, by a change of gender. Cocceius, however, by an apostrophe: it shall be. o) That is, rays. Compare the note on Ezekiel 34:29, 30. The Septuagint and Vulgate, and others, say simply: horns, with which he strikes the enemies. Deuteronomy 33:17. Compare the "horn of the Messiah," 1 Samuel 2:10, and of the godly, Psalm 44:6, 75:11. p) from his omnipotent and avenging hand. Genesis 49:24, Isaiah 50:2. q) they shall be to him, the Light and Savior of his people. Compare Joshua 5:13, 14. r) and there, namely, it shall be made manifest. As if to supply: Joshua 5. s) a hiding. Others: there will be a hiding place (1) compare Isaiah 26:20. f) of his strength, by which he will provide refuge and help to his own against enemies. Compare Isaiah 4:5, 6, 45:4, Psalm 31:20, 21. v. 5. u) For before him. Joel 2:3, 10. x) there, the pestilence, Matthew 24:7, as once in Egypt, Exodus 9:3, or Israel, 2 Samuel 24:15, which takes away the ungodly, Leviticus 26:25, Deuteronomy 28:21, and strikes the land with a curse, Malachi 3:24. Abarbanel: Refers to Exodus 2:27. y) and as if to say: as of old, so also then shall go forth a flame; others say, a carbuncle or burning plague. See the note on Deuteronomy 32:24, and compare Psalm 76:4, 78:48, Job 5:7, Song of Solomon 8:6, also Psalm 18:13, 14, 2 Thessalonians 1:8. z) it shall go forth at his feet, i.e., follow him. See 1 Samuel 2:12, and compare Exodus 11:8, 2 Samuel 15:18. v. 6. a) Just as of old he acted against the enemies for his people, see Joshua 5:13, Daniel 12:1, and compare Micah 7:15. b) and he measured the land of Canaan, defining a portion for each tribe. Compare 2 Samuel 8:2, Psalm 60:8, and see Joshua 13:1 following. c) as once he saw with indignation the nations and their ungodliness, Genesis 6:5, 11:5, 15:16, 18:21, Zechariah 9:8, Psalm 10:11. d) and with an angry face he dissolved, or scattered. That is, according to Abarbanel, he cast the ungodly nations out of the land of Canaan. Isaiah 58:5. Arabic root: to scatter, disperse. Note: compare Psalm 44:2 following, and Psalm 2:9. e) so that they burst asunder, being scattered from one another. Reflexive <note>Hebrew Hitpael</note> (1) compare Jeremiah 23:29 and Psalm 68:2. f) mountains (Abarbanel: i.e., figuratively the kings or kingdoms of the Canaanites, Isaiah 41:15, Zechariah 4:7, Revelation 7:14) of eternity, Isaiah 9:5, which seemed insurmountable to themselves and the Israelites. Numbers 13:28–33. g) and just as of old they were cast down and humbled, Exodus 2:11, 17, Job 9:13. h) perpetual hills, Genesis 49:25, Isaiah 41:15, Psalm 114:4, 6. So also in his time they shall be made to give way. i) for his march or progress, Nahum 2:6, Psalm 68:25. Compare Zechariah 9:14. k) of eternity or of the age, and never to be interrupted while the world stands. 2 Kings 5:27. l) they are and will be, to disturb all the ungodly and antichristian nations. Compare Isaiah 41:2, 3. Abarbanel: the processes of the ages are all God's, that he may do in them as he pleases. v. 7. m) That is, under *Aven* [trouble]. Perhaps from comparison with Hosea 10:5, 8, Amos 5:5. Others: under vanity. Others: under mourning and pain, compare Proverbs 12:21. The Vulgate, however: For iniquity. Compare Habakkuk 1:3, Numbers 23:21, and 2 Samuel 19:22, Zephaniah 2:10. Thus Grotius: On account of that crime mentioned in Numbers 25:1 following, I saw the tents of the Ethiopians moved, i.e., the skins of the Midianites. Just as Bochart <note>A 17th-century French biblical scholar</note> in his *Phaleg* p. 235 considers Cushan and Midian as equivalent, compare Exodus 2:15, 21 and Numbers 12:1. But Calvin says: there is no reason why the Midianites should be confused with the Ethiopians here, or why this should be restricted to the history of Numbers 25. n) I saw in a prophetic spirit. Compare 1 Kings 22:17, Jeremiah 4:23 following. Others: I, the Jewish people, saw long ago as a punishment for sins. o) That is, the tents of Cushan: i.e., of some cruel tyrant and heavy persecutor of the Church, such as that king of the Syrians long ago, Judges 3:8, 10. But to the Septuagint, Vulgate, Luther, Hiller, and others, it is the same as Cush, the Ethiopians; and to Bochart, the Cushites or Midianites, as we just said. p) but they shall tremble before our avenger, verse 16. Exodus 15:14, Isaiah 64:1. q) curtains, Exodus 26:1, Jeremiah 49:29. r) the land of Midian, i.e., greedy nations and enemies of the Church, such as the Midianites were of old against Israel. Alludes to Judges 6:16, 21, as in Isaiah 9:3. v. 8. s) Was it against the rivers and the armies of the nations? Compare Isaiah 8:7, 18:2, 7. The question mark here indicates an affirmation, as in Jeremiah 31:20. Others take it negatively, as if we should not be moved by anger against nature, while God's providence stands for his people, in the case of the struck rivers. But Salomon van Til says poorly on this passage: Interpreters think of the Jordan; when here rivers are noted in the plural, and the chain of history does not allow the speech to leap back here, etc. He himself therefore understands the kingdoms of the peoples subjected from the Danube, just as Cocceius understands peoples afflicted with various plagues after the coming of Christ. But although we freely concede that the Prophet’s aim is not to narrate God’s ancient miracles historically here, but rather to prophesy about the future and confirm his readers; nevertheless, respect can be paid to the waters of the Nile turned into blood (Exodus 7:29) and the broken waters of the Jordan (Joshua 3:13–15), as our author progresses from literal to figurative, and from past to future. Compare also Psalm 74:15, Isaiah 11:13, 3, 5, Revelation 16:4. t) was kindled, O Lord, Zechariah 10:3, namely, your wrath, as follows in the next verse.

Alternatively: With rivers you split the earth of the enemies. Schmidius <note>Sebastian Schmidt, 17th-century theologian</note>: the earth splits rivers out of itself; he undoubtedly refers, as do Abarbanel and Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch jurist and theologian</note>, to Exodus 17:6, Numbers 20:11, Isaiah 58:15–16, Psalm 78:15–16, Psalm 105:41, etc.
**v. 10. m)** Just as they once saw you, so also in the future, when they see you and feel your power. Psalm 77:17, 114:3. **n)** they shall be in labor and tremble. Isaiah 13:8, 23:4. **o)** the mountains, that is, the kingdoms of the world. Moses ben Israel: the kings of the Canaanites. Verse 6, Psalm 114:6, compare Exodus 19:18. **Greek:** They saw you, and the peoples shall be in pain <note>original: "ὤφθηסάν σε, καὶ ὠδινήσουσι λαוί"</note>. So Abarbanel, citing Joshua 2:9–10. **p)** an inundation, Vulgate: a whirlpool of waters. Isaiah 25:4, 28:2. **q)** it passed and disappeared. Psalm 144:4, Song of Solomon 2:11, just as the sea once gave way. **r)** the abyss and the depth of the sea uttered its voice. Genesis 7:11, Isaiah 51:10. **s)** its sound and crashing. Psalm 93:3–4. Abarbanel: because those miracles were heard throughout the whole land of Canaan. **t)** the height also, or whatever was high. Compare Isaiah 2:11. Others: on high; with the preposition understood. **u)** its hands. A similar suffix is in Nahum 2:4. See the note on verse 2 above. **x)** lifted up. See Psalm 28:2, Lamentations 5:6. With the enemies of God conquered and subdued.

**v. 11. y)** Just as of old the Sun and Moon did. Joel 2:10, 4:15. **z)** it stood, or you stand still. Most interpreters not wrongly refer this to Joshua 10:11 and following; but others, like Cocceius, refer it to the darkness of Antichristianity, in which neither the Sun of Righteousness itself, nor the teachers (who like the Moon are illuminated by that Sun) shine in the Church. See note on verse 1. **a)** Vulgate: in its habitation. Schmidius: in its seat. 1 Kings 8:13, Psalm 49:15. **b)** at the light of your arrows. Deuteronomy 32:23, 42; Psalm 18:15, 45:6. Teachers of the Gospel, compare Isaiah 49:2, Psalm 127:4. **c)** they shall walk or proceed. Psalm 89:16. Just as the Israelites went against the enemies with lightning flashing before them. Joshua 10:8 and following. **d)** to the splendor. Verse 4. **e)** of your lightning spear. Deuteronomy 32:41, Nahum 3:3. According to Abarbanel and Moses ben Israel, this alludes to (thunder and lightning and) the hailstones which God sent upon the enemies of the Israelites in Joshua 10:11.

**v. 12. f)** In rigor and indignation. Lamentations 2:6. **g)** you shall march through the land. 2 Samuel 6:13, Psalm 68:8. **h)** in anger you shall thresh or crush. Judges 8:7, 16; Isaiah 41:15, Micah 4:13. **i)** the enemy nations, so that they may be subjected to Christ; just as you once subjected the Canaanites to Joshua, and other peoples to David.

**v. 13. k)** When you went out (as of old) for the salvation of your people. See Exodus 11:4, Judges 4:14, 2 Kings 19:35, Isaiah 37:36. **l)** **Greek:** to save your Anointed One <note>original: "ὁ σῶσαι τὸν Χριστόν σου"</note>. Schmidius: to save your anointed. As the noun acts as a verb, for example Deuteronomy 1:27, 19:11, Isaiah 13:19, etc. But Aquila <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note> (whom Jerome and Cocceius praise here) has: "with your Christ" <note>original: "σὺν Χριστῷ σου"</note>. The Vulgate: with your Christ. Just as the word **with** <note>Hebrew "et"</note> frequently means "with," for example Genesis 37:2. **m)** By this, some understand Moses, others (like Clericus on Hebrews 11:26) more incongruously the whole Israelite nation; some Saul, others more probably David, citing 2 Samuel 5:24. Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval rabbi and grammarian</note> however, with Moses ben Israel, Cocceius, and others, better understand the Messiah, the son of David. See Psalm 2:2, 6, 7; Psalm 45:8, Isaiah 61:1. For Kimchi reminds us that all these past tense verbs are "Prophetic Perfects"; (compare notes on Isaiah 5:13, 9:2, Jeremiah 15:7, 31:21, etc.) so that the sense is: Just as of old you went out for the salvation of your people, so then also you will go out for your people’s salvation with the Messiah or your anointed one. Compare Abarbanel fol. 273, col. 2. Raymundus’s *Dagger of Faith* <note>original: "Pugio Fidei"</note> p. 676, and regarding this or a similar going out of the Messiah, see Revelation 14:1 and following, 17:14, 19:11. **n)** as you once struck, so then you will strike or break the head. See Judges 5:26, Job 26:12, and Psalm 68:22, 110:5, 6. **o)** from the house, see chapter 2:9. **p)** see chapter 1:13 and Isaiah 11:4, 2 Thessalonians 2:3, 4. **q)** by overthrowing it. Psalm 137:7. **r)** from the foundation and up to the neck, flooding him. See Ezekiel 13:14, 30:4, Micah 1:6. **s)** see Isaiah 8:8, 30:28, Job 22:16. Grotius: you demolished the highest and lowest parts. **t)** indeed it shall be so. See verse 3.

**v. 14. u)** Schmidius: You pierced. Or prophetically, You will pierce. **Greek:** you cut through <note>original: "διέκοψας"</note>. So compare the verb in 2 Kings 12:10 and Job 40:24, 26. But Cocceius's *Lexicon* 528 and Van Til on this passage: You marked out, citing Genesis 30:28, Numbers 1:17, Isaiah 62:2. **x)** Schmidius: with his staffs, namely the Messiah’s or your people’s, verse 13. Compare the rod of Christ’s mouth, Isaiah 11:4. But Cocceius: You marked out among the tribes of Christ and His people. Compare verse 9 and Revelation 7:4 and following, 14:1 and following. Or: among his tribes, namely the wicked one's, you will pierce. **y)** The head of his villages, see Judges 5:7, Ezekiel 38:11, Esther 9:19. **z)** when the enemies rush in like a whirlwind or a stormy sea. Jonah 1:11, 13; see Isaiah 54:11 and Ezekiel 38:9. **a)** to me, your Church, to scatter. Ezekiel 20:23. Rashi <note>Shlomo Yitzchaki, the preeminent medieval French rabbi</note>: such as Sennacherib with his army, or according to Abarbanel: Pharaoh with all his troops pursuing the Israelites. Exodus 15:9. **b)** whose exultation and joy it is. Compare the verb in Psalm 25:2. **c)** as if to devour your poor, wretched people. Psalm 14:4, 27:2, Proverbs 30:14.

<summary>This page analyzes Habakkuk 3:8–14, interpreting the prophet's descriptions of cosmic upheaval—rivers splitting, mountains trembling, and the sun standing still—as both historical recollections of the Exodus and prophetic types of the Messiah's future victory over the "wicked." The commentary relies heavily on philological comparisons and the opinions of major 17th-century scholars like Cocceius and Schmidius, as well as medieval Jewish commentators like Abarbanel and Kimchi.</summary>

v. 16. i) All these things I have heard from you, as was said in v. 2. And I perceived how great the dangers are that threaten your Church. Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note>, following his own hypothesis, says: "I heard from the other prophets also the horrific judgment which you will one day execute through the Israelites," comparing Obadiah v. 18 and Micah 4:13. k) And my belly was moved; my whole body trembled. The Manual of Interpretation and Abarbanel suggest the "inner parts" or "heart," comparing similar phrases in Jeremiah 31:20 and Psalm 40:9. Cf. above v. 6. Deuteronomy 2:25. 2 Samuel 19:1. and Psalm 31:10, also Revelation 10:9-10. l) At that voice of yours which I heard. Cf. Ezekiel 27:28. Psalm 42:8. m) They tingled <note>original Latin: "tinnierunt"</note>; they trembled and palpitated so much that they almost rang or buzzed. Cf. 1 Samuel 3:11. n) It comes; or: as if rottenness had come (s) Proverbs 14:30. o) Into my bones, so that I cannot stand; as if my bones were eaten away by wasting or rot. Cf. Jeremiah 23:9. Psalm 6:3. Psalm 31:11. Psalm 51:10. Job 4:14. p) So that underneath me, or in my place. Cf. 2 Samuel 2:23. q) I should tremble all over, Isaiah 32:10. r) That, or according to Schmid, "because I shall rest." Cf. Deuteronomy 3:24. 1 Samuel 3:23. Others, however, who [rest]...
</margin>

3.) Of distress or affliction, Isaiah 37:3. Compare Isaiah 11:10, chapter 33:19, Revelation 3:10. Abarbanel: "That returning from Babylonia, I shall rest in my fatherland until another day of distress." u) For ascending, also Hosea 2:2. See Nahum 2:2. x) To the people; Schmid translates: "Against the people." Compare Judges 12:3. Ecclesiastes 3:21. But Abarbanel: "Because of the ascent of the people," perhaps because the people (the Romans, presumably) will ascend again to plunder us. y) Schmid: "Who will plunder him," the people of God, versus Genesis 49:19. Or according to Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Hebrew grammarian</note> and the Manual: "Who will plunder and devastate us in troops," as the grammar allows either translation. v. 17. z) For, that I am moved by terror did not happen from a rash or vain omen; but I most certainly foresee the sad signs of future times. a) The fig tree, as in Ecclesiasticus 34:4. Joel 1:7, 12. In the land of Canaan, otherwise fertile and frequent. Many take this literally regarding the famine which the Jews endured either before or after the Babylonian captivity, in a land then destitute of all goods. Jeremiah 14:1ff. Haggai 1:6, etc. Others, with Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century theologian</note>, take it figuratively and mystically regarding the calamity of the Church and the fewness of the pious under the tyranny of ungodly lords and the Antichrist. Compare the mystical meaning of the fig tree in Micah 7:1. Song of Solomon 2:13. Matthew 21:19. Luke 13:7. Abarbanel holds both: "The prophet speaks," he says, "of Israel, who is called fig, vine, olive, flock, and herd by the prophets," or these can all be taken literally. b) It shall not burst forth with early buds. Cf. Genesis 40:10. Numbers 17:20, 23. c) <term>Fruit-bearing</term> <note>original Greek: ϰαρποφόρος</note>. For the fig does not flower like other trees, but sends out small buds <note>original: "grossulos"</note>. c) Nor shall there be an increase or fruit. Leviticus 26:4. Judges 6:4. Haggai 1:10. d) In the vines. For a mystical interpretation, cf. Isaiah 5:2, chapter 27:2, 3. John 15:2, also Deuteronomy 32:32. e) It lies and fails expectation, Hosea 9:2, as the Latins say "the crop lied to our hope." f) Work, i.e., increase or fruit. Cf. Genesis 1:11, 12. g) Olive. The Vulgate: Olive. Cf. Judges 9:9-13. Psalm 52:10. Zechariah 4:3, 14. Romans 11:17ff. Revelation 11:4. h) Fields or cultivated lands, Isaiah 16:8. Cf. 1 Corinthians 3:6-9. i) They do not bring food or produce. Genesis 41:47. Cf. Joel 1:10. k) The enemy snatched away, or a lack of fodder, Joel 1:18. Others, intransitively: "It separated or snatched itself away." The Vulgate, impersonally: "The cattle shall be cut off." Isaiah 9:19, 12. Isaiah 37:11. l) From the sheepfold (3) Psalm 50:9. Psalm 78:70. m) Small cattle (sheep). Of men: Ezekiel 34:31. n) Nor shall the herd remain in the stalls (l), a word more common among the Talmudic writers. o) At the mangers <note>original Greek: ἐפὶ פάטנαις</note>. Luke 13:15. Abarbanel: "Take all these things figuratively regarding the fewness and weakness of the Israelites." v. 18. o) But I nevertheless, certain of divine liberation and help. p) Not in my own or human strengths, but in the Lord. Psalm 25:2. Psalm 33:3. Cf. Romans 5:2, 11. q) I will exult. Psalm 60:8. Zephaniah 3:14. Philippians 4:4. r) And I will dance for joy, Psalm 9:15. s) In the God of my salvation, i.e., in God my Savior. Isaiah 17:10. Micah 7:7. Psalm 18:47. Cf. Isaiah 12:2. Psalm 27:1. Abarbanel: "As if to say, all my hope and solace is not unless in my God," etc. Nor is the Vulgate bad: "In my God Jesus," Isaiah 49:18, 25:1. v. 19. t) Jehovah Elohim, i.e., the Lord God, Jeremiah 46:10. Ezekiel 28:2. u) The Lord (who is the cause and preserver of all) is my strength and protection. Cf. Psalm 27:1. Psalm 46:2. Isaiah 45:24, etc. x) *Shim* who will set my feet, Psalm 18:34. Van Till <note>Salomon van Till, a Dutch theologian</note> takes the feet as instruments of a journey, for the progress of the Apostles preaching the Gospel, who are not to be worn out, comparing Isaiah 40:31, chapter 52:7, Nahum 2:1. y) Like those of hinds/deer, so that they run diligently, eagerly, and without fatigue. The Manual of Interpretation: "To pursue my enemies." Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian</note>: "That I may escape that slaughter." Cf. Isaiah 35:6. 2 Samuel 22:34. Psalm 18:34. For after a hind has given birth, which mostly happens near roads trodden by men (because she fears wild beasts more than men, whom she despises in her confidence of speed), they say the fawns are immediately led by the mother into steep and rugged places with a single entrance, from which it is easy to ward off invaders. And these are those "high places" to which, like hinds, the prophets David (2 Samuel 22:34; Psalm 18:34) and Habakkuk here say they are led by God and placed in safety. Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century French Protestant biblical scholar</note>, *Hierozoicon*, vol. 1, p. 893. z) Upon my high places. Calovius, Tarnovius, and others take this as the return of the Jews to their fatherland from Babylonian captivity. But Salomon van Till says on this passage: "This phrase should be noted, which alludes to the occupation of the land of Canaan, taken from Deuteronomy 32:13, from where it is transferred here and in Deuteronomy 33:29, Isaiah 58:14, Psalm 18:34 to the future occupation and possession of the world; whose inheritance is analogous to the inheritance of the land of Canaan." Compare also Amos 4:13. Micah 1:3. a) He will lead, He will make me walk. Isaiah 42:16. b) To the Master of the sacred public symphony, i.e., to the Music Director; let this song be commended. See the note above at v. 1. The Hebrew *Menatzeach* generally means a "taskmaster," but here and in the Psalms, it undoubtedly denotes a Musical Director or Leader. Cf. Psalm 4:1, Psalm 5:1, etc. It is the Piel participle from the verb *natzaḥ*, which means to preside over a business, to press a work continuously and to the end. See 1 Chronicles 2:1, 17; chapter 34:12; Ezra 3:8, 9; and 1 Chronicles 15:21, where the verb itself is applied to musical matters. c) In my strikings/pulsations <note>referring to stringed instruments</note>, to be sung properly for the use and solace of the whole Church. See Psalm 4:1, Psalm 6:1, Isaiah 38:20.

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of the commentary on Habakkuk to the introduction and initial verses of the Book of Zephaniah. It provides historical context, placing the prophet in the reign of King Josiah, and outlines the structure of the prophecy, which ranges from the local destruction of Judah to the global judgment of the nations and the eventual restoration of the Church under Christ.</meta>

THE BOOK OF ZEPHANIAH, Hebrew: צְפַנְיָה

# ZEPHANIAH

ZEPHANIAH lived, as is clear from chapter 1, verses 1 and 14, and chapter 2, verse 13, etc., during the final years of King Josiah’s reign. He specifically predicts the same events that Habakkuk predicted and that Jeremiah reported in greater detail. Therefore, he should be carefully compared with both of them, and understood and explained in his more difficult passages by looking at their writings. See the note on chapter 1:1. Furthermore, after the title of the book in chapter 1:1:

I. He announces the Babylonian destruction and captivity to the Jews (chapter 1:2 and following).
II. He exhorts them to repentance (chapter 2:1-4).
III. He threatens destruction to the neighbors and enemies of Israel—to the west (verse 5), the east (verse 8), the south (verse 12), and the north (verse 13).
IV. He repeats threats against Jerusalem (both the historical type and the symbolic fulfillment) and again predicts its destruction by the Romans (chapter 3:1). He foretells the calling of the Nations (verse 9). To those Jews who repent, however, he promises better things (verse 12), and thus finally promises the glorious and eternal kingdom of Christ to the Church (verse 14 and following).

---

<margin>
**Chapter 1, verse 1. a)** Hosea 1:1, Joel 1:1. **The word of the Lord** <note>original Greek: λόγος Κυρίῳ</note>. Acts 8:25. **b)** 2 Kings 20:4. According to the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> as in Luke 3:2. **c)** To Zephaniah, which is as if to say *the Lord has hidden himself*, as Hiller shows in his Sacred Names <note>Hillerus in Onomasticon Sacrum</note> on page 312 by way of analogy. But according to the mind of Abarbanel <note>a famous 15th-century Jewish statesman and commentator</note> in his Preface to Ezekiel (folio 154a), he was so named because he revealed the hidden things and secrets of God, comparing Zephaniah 3:9. For Abarbanel noted in the same place (folio 153d) that names were given to such prophets not by the whim or will of parents, but by divine providence, so that they agreed with their actions and deeds. **d)** This linked series of Zephaniah's ancestors proves entirely that they were famous or well-known men, of whatever rank, place, or tribe they may have been. Abarbanel rightly denies that King Hezekiah is to be understood here, as Abraham ibn Ezra <note>a medieval Spanish biblical commentator</note> had thought. **e)** According to others, this occurred in the first years [of his ministry], among the nobles of Josiah, after the reformation of the Church (compare verses 4 and 8, and Lightfoot’s Chronology, p. 115). If his times, which are described in 2 Kings 22 and 23 and 2 Chronicles 34 and 35, are compared, the theme of the prophecy will be more evident. Our prophet was therefore contemporary with Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:1) and Huldah the prophetess (2 Kings 22:14), etc. Compare the note on 2 Kings 23:2 and the Preface to Jeremiah, sections 5 and following. **f)** 2 Kings 21:19.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Book of Zephaniah, transitioning from the introductory remarks into the first chapter's specific prophecies of judgment. The previous page established Zephaniah's historical context during the reign of King Josiah and outlined the four main themes of the book. This page focuses on the specific sins of the Judean leadership—their adoption of foreign customs, their social injustice, and their spiritual apathy—while describing the approaching "Day of the Lord" in vivid, terrifying detail.</meta>

# ZEPHANIAH. CHAPTER I. 1

<margin>
\* 8. o) regarding which see verse 7. q) see chapter 3, 3; and compare 2 Chronicles 24, 17; 23, 30. Also Jehoahaz in 2 Kings 23, 33, and Zedekiah in chapter 24, 17 and following; regarding whom see the Preface to Jeremiah §. 8 and following, and the notes to Jeremiah 22. Others think this refers to 2 Kings 25, 7. Namely (as Heidegger writes in his *Enchiridion*, page 353 and following) when King Josiah—second to none in piety and zeal for promoting the glory of God—had abolished false religion and renewed the true faith according to the law brought forward by Hilkiah, he found few supporters who were approved in that holy purpose, whether among the Princes, the people, or even his own sons. This is sufficiently proven by the response of Huldah in 2 Kings 22, 15 and following, the sermons of Jeremiah (see Preface to Jeremiah §. 7), and the events of subsequent times. For after Josiah's death, they soon returned openly to their former impiety and natural character. Compare the note on 2 Kings 23, 26. s) He rebukes the pride of the Jews and their vanity in the care of the body. Compare Ezekiel 23, 6, 12. "Perhaps," says Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher</note>, "this was said of the princes (collecting 1 Kings 20, 5) and the sons of the Kings, for whom it was a received custom—as it is today among Christians—not to delight in the clothing of their own region and nation, but to love the clothing of other foreign kings and peoples." Compare, for example, the image of Jehoiakim in Jeremiah 22, 13 and following, and the Preface to Jeremiah §. 9.
</margin>

<margin>
\* 9. t) I will also punish, see verse 8. u) against all those leaping over <note>original Latin: "transilientes"</note> (S) Psalm 18, 30. x) in memory of the fact that the idol Dagon had fallen face down on the ground before the Ark, with his head and hands broken against the threshold; the Philistines refrained from treading on the threshold of the temple, considering it a consecrated place for the idol, 1 Samuel 5, 5. This rite was promoted even through great wickedness for the sake of profit and gain, as follows. Thus, Junius and Tremellius <note>Franciscan and Reformed biblical scholars</note> understand this as a housebreaker, or an agent of violence, which the powerful used against the weak. Compare again the example of Jehoiakim in Jeremiah 22, 13 and following. y) of their lord, or their lords, 2 Samuel 10, 3. The Septuagint and others, translating it as "The Lord their God," understand this as referring to priests. But compare the note on Amos 4, 1. z) see Jeremiah 6, 7; Habakkuk 1, 2, 3. a) see Jeremiah 5, 27; Psalm 5, 7.
</margin>

<margin>
...that it lasted through many centuries can be gathered from these words of Zephaniah. Whence the Chaldean <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation</note> says: "And I will punish all those who walk in the laws of the Philistines." Thus Bochart in his *Hierozoicon*, part 1, page 365. Compare Isaiah 2, 6. Others, however, deny that this refers to the superstitious worship of Dagon, and instead refer it to the Jews who were unrepentant frequenters of the Temple. Thus Cocceius in his Lexicon, 697, referring to one who rashly approaches the house of God. Compare Isaiah 1, 12; Jeremiah 7, 2 and following; Ezekiel 9, 3; Ecclesiastes 4, 17. Abarbanel, however, refers it to the ministers of the Royal Princes, who [fill] their own and their masters'...
</margin>

\* **10. b)** in the day, that is, of the devastation mentioned in verses 7 and 8. **c)** verses 2, 3. **d)** Jeremiah 25, 36; chapter 48, 3. 5. 6. **e)** Nehemiah 3, 3; chapter 12, 39; 2 Chronicles 33, 14. **f)** wailing (4) Isaiah 15, 8; Zechariah 11, 3. **g)** see 2 Kings 22, 14. **h)** Jeremiah 4, 6; chapter 48, 3; chapter 50, 22. **i)** from the hills of Jerusalem, regarding which see <term>Josephus, The Jewish War</term>, book 6, chapter 13. For the city, although most strongly fortified, will be entirely occupied and devastated. Compare Jeremiah 4, 24.

\* **11. k)** Or: Therefore howl. Isaiah 13, 6; Zechariah 11, 2. **l)** "Lament" <note>original Greek: θρηνήσατε</note> John 16, 20. **l)** of charity. Judges 15, 19. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan</note>: "who dwell around the brook Kedron." S. and the Syriac: inhabitants of <term>Mactesh</term>, according to <term>Bochart, Hierozoicon</term>, part I, page 202; a place so named from its shape like a mortar, comparing Proverbs 27, 22. **m)** it shall be cut off, Isaiah 6, 5; chapter 15, 1. **n)** Jonathan: "whose works are like the works of the people of the land of <term>Canaan</term>." chapter 2, 5. <term>Abarbanel</term>: Because the people of Judah are similar to the Canaanites in sins, therefore they will also be similar in punishments to the Canaanites, who were torn away from the land when Israel entered it. Compare Ezekiel 16, 3. The Prophet plays with an ambiguity, and teaches his countrymen that they, by their most impure Canaanite customs, have acquired the same name for themselves and summoned the judgment of God. <term>Tremellius</term>. **o)** Isaiah 29, 20; Jeremiah 9, 20. **p)** laden (i) with silver. Jonathan: "rich in wealth." Compare Lamentations 3, 28 and Habakkuk 2, 6; 1 Timothy 6, 9.

\* **12. q)** I will search, Genesis 31, 35; chapter 44, 12. **r)** as if with lamps. Compare Proverbs 24, 27. Just as the Jews keep watch on the night before Passover, most scrupulously purging the leaven; or like the woman seeking the lost coin in Luke 15, 8. **s)** verses 8, 9. **t)** against those thickened, that is, coagulated; such as those who rest in tranquility, who are never stirred, like a coagulated thing. <term>Abarbanel</term> (3) Exodus 15, 8; Job 10, 10. **u)** on the lees. But <term>Gussetius</term> page 872: "in their casks." Like wine that is not poured out but settles on its dregs. (4) see Jeremiah 48, 11. Jonathan: "who are tranquil with tranquility in their riches." **x)** from the greatest impiety and security, Psalm 10, 6. **y)** "He does not do good," namely to the good. Compare Numbers 10, 32; Isaiah 41, 23; Psalm 119, 68. **z)** "nor does he do evil" to the wicked. For he does not care for human affairs. Compare Isaiah 5, 19; Malachi 2, 17; Lamentations 3, 35, 38.

\* **13. a)** their wealth, Isaiah 30, 6. **b)** 2 Kings 21, 14; Isaiah 42, 22; Habakkuk 1, 7. **c)** chapter 2, 4, 13. **d)** Amos 5, 11; compare Isaiah 65, 22. **e)** see Deuteronomy 28, 39. And by this very thing they shall know that God is a judge in the earth; and that sooner than they now believe in their security. Compare verse 14; Habakkuk 1, 5.

\* **14. f)** see verse 7. **g)** Jeremiah 30, 7; Joel 2, 11; Malachi 3, 23. **h)** and hastening greatly. Compare Isaiah 5, 19. "He will cry out" (2) Isaiah 42, 13. Compare above at verses etc. **m)** even the strongest warrior of the Jews, who now trust in their strength. Compare Ecclesiastes 3, 2; Jeremiah 9, 23; Chapter 46, 6, 12; Amos 2, 14; Psalm 33, 16. Jonathan: "there the strongest shall be killed."

\* **15. n)** verse 18. **o)** that day will be, verses 7, 14, as announced. **p)** Isaiah 37, 3; Proverbs 1, 27. **q)** Job 15, 24. **r)** of waste, Isaiah 10, 3; chapter 47, 11; Proverbs 1, 26. **s)** and of desolation (S) Job 30, 3; chapter 38, 27. **t)** Amos 5, 12. **u)** Joel 2, 2. **x)** Ezekiel 30, 3. **y)** Ezekiel 34, 12; Joel 2, 2.

\* **16. y)** the trumpet, the battle-signal of one sounding. Judges 7, 20. "Cities are accustomed to be captured at the sound of the trumpet," says <term>Grotius</term>. **a)** Joshua 6, 5, 20; Jeremiah 20, 16; Job 39, 25. **b)** Isaiah 36, 1; compare Isaiah 22, 10; Hosea 8, 14; Habakkuk 1, 10. **c)** corners, and towers, or bulwarks at the corners of the walls. See 2 Chronicles 26, 15; and compare <term>Josephus, The Jewish War</term>, book VI, chapter 13.

\* **17. d)** as if to say: I will make things narrow for men. That is, I will drive the Jews into straits. Jeremiah 10, 18; 2 Chronicles 28, 22; Nehemiah 9, 27. **e)** so that they see no more than the blind where they ought to turn. Compare Isaiah 8, 21, 22; chapter 59, 10.

It shifts from warnings against the Philistines to judgments against Moab, Ammon, Ethiopia, and Assyria, concluding with a reflection on the fall of Nineveh and a transition into the final woes against Jerusalem.</meta>

But Cocceius' Lexicon 132 best understands it as <term>ζῷα ἀγελαῖα</term> <note>Greek: zōa agelaia—gregarious animals</note>, not solitary ones, but animals in herds that form a "nation" or troop; which we noted regarding jackals at Judges 15, 4. Just as this very name <image-desc>ornamental dash</image-desc> and its synonym <image-desc>ornamental dash</image-desc> are read regarding locusts in Joel 1, 6. chapter 2, 2. also of ants and coneys in Proverbs 30, 25. 26. Thus Jonathan: "flocks of all the beasts of the field or wild animals." **a)** <term>also the pelican or the stellar heron (bittern)</term>. Leviticus 11, 18. The name is derived from vomiting: because the pelican revomits shells already swallowed after they have been opened by the heat of the stomach, so that it may pick the edible parts from them: which many also attribute to herons. They are aquatic birds, to whom a seat in desert places is assigned here without difficulty, as in Isaiah 34, 11. Psalm 102, 7. for not every desert is waterless, collection Exodus 15, 23. 27. Bochartus' *Hierozoicon* <note>A 17th-century study of biblical animals</note> II. page 292. following. **b)** <term>the hedgehog or porcupine</term> (3) Isaiah 14, 23. Bochartus proves from the ancients that it is contained under the same genus as the urchin or hedgehog: and it is an animal that seeks solitary places, <term>φιλέρημον</term> <note>Greek: philēremon—solitude-loving</note>; dwelling in the desolated cities of Babylonia, Bostra, and Nineveh; its quills also prevent it from the company of other animals, which no one may touch with impunity. -- Zephaniah gathers flocks, beasts, the pelican, and the hedgehog all into one bundle: which itself affects the reader more, when in the description of vastness those things that pertain to horror are proposed in such a confused order. See Bochartus' *Hierozoicon* I. book 3. chapter 36. page 1035. following. **e)** Namely, in its pomegranates <note>ornamental carvings</note>, surely broken down, and cast down from the summit of the houses or columns, in the destruction of the city. For a <term>caphtor</term> is not a tree, nor the fruit of a tree, but an ornament or globe, with which buildings and the summits of columns were accustomed to be crowned or wreathed, or even lampstands adorned. Compare 2 Kings 19, 21. Psalm 22, 8. Job 16, 4. **CHAPTER III. v. 1. x)** chapter 2, 5. Isaiah 1, 4. Nahum 3, 1. This chapter has two main parts: I. Prophecy against Jerusalem and the unrepentant Jews verses 1-8. II. A promise regarding conversion and restoration under the New Testament verses 9. following. And that, as Abarbanel observes, "the Interpreters wish to refer this to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians. But I feel otherwise (the same says in the Commentary on this place), namely that after the denunciation of the first destruction in chapter 1, and the visitation of the Second Temple in chapter 2, 7 (when they returned to Jerusalem, and the Lord took vengeance on the nations that had destroyed it and congratulated themselves on its ruin), then the Prophet in this section comes to signify what happened to the Jews under the Second Temple, until they fell into the second devastation (made by the Romans), etc." And certainly the Prophet also looked back to this at the same time, as the connection of the parts of this chapter in verses 9. following indicates clearly. Indeed, not only the final destruction of Jerusalem, but also under this type the judgment of the harlot and that mystical city, of which Revelation 11, 8. etc. is involved. Compare Isaiah 1, 21. chapter 57, 3. chapter 66, 6. and the note at Isaiah 6, 9. chapter 22, 1. chapter 24, 1. etc. also Maius' *Oeconomia Veteris Testamenti* page 999.

<summary>This page covers the judgment on Moab, Ammon, Ethiopia, and Nineveh, detailing their transformation into desolate haunts for wild animals. It also introduces Chapter 3, providing a historical and theological analysis that links these prophecies to the Second Temple period and the Roman destruction of Jerusalem.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the prophecy of Zephaniah, moving from the judgment of foreign nations in Chapter 2 to the specific accusations and woes against Jerusalem in Chapter 3. The previous page detailed the ruin of Nineveh; here, the focus shifts to the internal corruption of the holy city and God's persistent but unheeded calls for repentance.</meta>

# CHAPTER 3. ZEPHANIAH 3.

<margin>
y) Scholars differ greatly regarding the origin of this name. Some (rendered as "filthy" or "polluted") think it signifies impurity, comparing it to Leviticus 1:16. Thus Tremellius here translates it as "gluttony," but this is less probable, and therefore Abarbanel rejects it. Others, like the Vulgate, translate it as "provoker," or the Tigurine as "rebellious," as if from the root *marah* <note>original: מָרָה</note>; but this also goes against grammatical rules. Jonathan translates it as "hastening." The Syriac version uses a perverse reading or rather interpretation. But the Septuagint and Arabic translate it as "illustrious." Better yet is Cocceius (Lexicon 124 & 777), who translates it as "one to whom the opportunity of seeing was granted," that is, one to whom the Lord manifested himself, preaching liberty etc., from the Hophal of *naga* <note>original: נָגַא</note>, comparing Exodus 25:40 and 25:30; see also Ecclesiasticus 42:20 and, regarding the form, Judges 6:28. Finally, others derive it from the Pual of *naga* (Moraschet for Mmoraschet etc.) meaning "terrible," that is, according to Abarbanel, "formidable to her enemies" after the return from Babylon; or rather, according to Miller (*Onomasticon Sacrum* page 442 following), "frightened," or terrified by many punishments: because the Piel form signifies "to strike terror" in 1 Samuel 14:15, Nehemiah 6:9, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
...this [dove] pleased Abarbanel, suggesting that Jerusalem was like a dove; compare Song of Solomon 5:2.
</margin>

1 Woe <gloss>y</gloss> to the rebellious <gloss>z</gloss> and polluted, the city <gloss>a</gloss> the oppressor!

<margin>
z) Here too they disagree. The Tigurine version translates "and contaminated." S. "and polluted," etc., as in Isaiah 59:3 and Lamentations 4:14, where however a different form with a *Cholem* vowel argues for that meaning, as in Malachi 1:7, 12. Hence others, such as the Septuagint, Jonathan, Syriac, and Arabic, understand it as "redeemed"; because not only were they the "redeemed of the Lord" according to Abarbanel when they returned from the power of Babylon, but Jerusalem was also countered and redeemed by Christ, and the blood of the covenant was shed in her for the release from servitude. See Cocceius in the place cited and compare notes on Isaiah 41:14 and 52:3.

<margin>
d) Verse 7. Jeremiah 2:30. e) Jonathan: "In the Word of the Lord." f) Jeremiah 17:5, Psalm 78:22. But she trusted now in the Assyrians, now in the Egyptians, now in the Chaldeans, and often in their idols (Grotius). g) Compare Isaiah 48:16, James 4:8, Isaiah 29:13, 58:2, Matthew 15:8. Instead, she entered into alliances with the Romans and other nations (Abarbanel).
**v. 3. h)** Compare chapter 1:8, Jeremiah 25:38, Ezekiel 22:6, 27, Micah 3:11. It refers to the kings of the House of Herod and the tyrants who existed near the end of the Temple, who were its princes, etc. (Abarbanel). i) Because like lions they gaped for prey; compare Proverbs 28:15, Ezekiel 19:1 following, and the Septuagint with 1 Peter 5:8. k) Compare Jeremiah 5:28, Daniel 9:12, Psalm 141:6. l) They are evening or nocturnal wolves because of an innate madness or cruelty of character, which results in them thirsting for the blood of the people like wolves, and never being satisfied by it. See Habakkuk 1:2 and compare Jeremiah 5:6. m) Like the most voracious animals, they do not gnaw the bones until morning, but immediately consume the evening prey so completely that by morning nothing remains. This is the view of most ancients, along with Rabbi Solomon [Rashi], Kimchi, and Abarbanel. Nor is it an obstacle that Genesis 49:27 says the wolf eats prey in the morning. For Zephaniah deals with evening prey, and Moses with morning prey. I need not mention that a part of the prey is often left behind unwillingly because the narrowness of the stomach prevents consuming it all (Bochart, *Hierozoicon* I, page 822). But Neumann (*Exodus* page 294): they do not tear, scatter, or disperse (3), namely the sheep in this place, as with bones in Numbers 24:8 or shells in Ezekiel 23:24. n) Syriac and Jonathan: they do not wait for the day or the dawn; compare Exodus 34:25. But like those who flee from the light, they hide the works of darkness as best they can, and greedily tear and swallow everything immediately. See Neumann's *Genesis* page 64. 
**v. 4. o)** Jonathan: "The false prophets who are in her." See Jeremiah 2:8, 5:31, Ezekiel 22:28, Micah 3:11, Lamentations 4:13. p) They are worthless and very light men. (2) Judges 9:4. q) Men of transgressions (1), that is, deceivers and faithless. See note on Isaiah 24:16. r) Chapter 1:4. s) Leviticus 22:2, 15, Ezekiel 22:26, Malachi 1:12. t) S. "They violently twist the law"; they do violence to the law of Scripture and pervert it. See Jeremiah 2:8, Ezekiel 22:26. 
**v. 5. u)** Deuteronomy 32:4, Jeremiah 12:1, Psalm 11:7. v) Verse 3. Deuteronomy 6:15, 7:21. It is a rebuttal, as if to say: Jehovah is most just; the Messiah is our righteousness (Jeremiah 23:6). He is in the midst of the Jews (John 1:26), free from every vice, and daily pleads the cause of God against the wicked, publicly discoursing from Moses and the Prophets. Thus Gurtler in *Typico-Prophet.* page 119. This must be held against the blasphemous nonsense of Abarbanel, who nefariously twists the beginning and end of verse 4 against our most holy Savior and his disciples. y) Neither now nor in the past does he commit anything perverse. Verse 12, Deuteronomy 32:4, compare Isaiah 53:9, 1 Peter 2:22. z) Exodus 16:21, compare Isaiah 50:4, Jeremiah 7:13, 2 Chronicles 36:15. a) His justice and his word. Chapter 2:3, Psalm 147:19, Micah 6:8, compare Jeremiah 5:4, 5, 8:7. b) Isaiah 51:4, demonstrating and preaching his righteousness, both in the pardon of sin and in the judgment of false righteousness (Cocceius Lexicon 704). Compare Isaiah 48:17, Jeremiah 36:3, John 8:12. c) He is not lacking yet, nor will he ever be lacking in his duty. 1 Samuel 30:19, Isaiah 34:16. d) Jeremiah 8:12. e) The perverse and wicked Jew (5). Job 18:21, 29:17. f) Jeremiah 6:15, compare Jeremiah 3:3, Isaiah 26:10, Matthew 22:37, John 8:46. 
**v. 6. g)** I have cut off entire nations by a most just judgment and as a terror to the Jews (Habakkuk 1:17), specifically the ten tribes (2 Kings 17:7, 18, 20 etc., as I had threatened in 1 Kings 9:7). But S. says "Therefore I will cut off"; see above chapter 1:3, 4. Compare Ezekiel 21:8, 9. h) Ezekiel 33:8, Amos 7:9. i) All corners. Chapter 1:16. Tremellius: "their extremities," comparing Judges 20:2. S. "their princes." Compare Isaiah 19:13. k) Isaiah 37:18. l) Lamentations 4:5. m) Isaiah 34:10, Jeremiah 9:9, 11. n) They were captured by snares, or according to the Chaldean usage, made desolate. Niphal (1) from Kal "to hunt or lie in wait" (Exodus 21:13). o) Compare Jeremiah 5:6. p) Jeremiah 2:15. q) Chapter 2:5, Jeremiah 4:7. 
**v. 7. r)** I said, as if to say, I forced myself to think. Jonathan 3:5. s) Nevertheless, though you are most persistent, you should have been educated by the punishments of so many neighboring nations. Compare chapter 1:18, Psalm 139:11. t) Ezekiel 8:13, Jeremiah 5:21. u) Verse 2. Compare Isaiah 28:26. x) Schmid translates "so that it would not be cut off." Compare Isaiah 48:19, Hosea 8:4. y) "His habitation." Nahum 2:12, Jeremiah 9:10. Jonathan: "their habitations from the land of the house of my Shechina [Divine Presence]." Others specifically refer to the temple, comparing 2 Chronicles 36:15. z) Asyndeton: "and all" or "anything of them." a) Which I had already commanded (Jeremiah 15:3). b) Upon her, namely, so that it would not happen or (as S. supplies) return. Thus the accents require. Compare Genesis 27:13, Psalm 3:9. But Tremellius: "in all which I had noticed in her." The Tigurine: "according to all that I appointed over her," regardless of the accents. Jonathan and others take it in a good sense: "All the good things that I promised, I will bring to them." c) "But truly," Isaiah 49:4, 43:4. So far were they from mending their ways that they even became worse. See the Preface to Jeremiah § 6. d) Compare Isaiah 5:11, 26:10, and note on Jeremiah 5:8. This is opposed to divine grace, which calls them seriously and timely to repentance. See Jeremiah 7:13, 25, 11:7, 25:3, 4, etc.

# THE LAW: ZEPHANIAH. CHAPTER 3.

<margin>
e) Gen. 6:12; Deut. 31:29; Josh. 2:19; Ps. 14:1. f) v. 11; Ezek. 14:22; 20:43; 36:17.
* v. 8. g) Why do you wait for me? 1 Kings 9:3; Hos. 6:9; Hab. 2:3; Ps. 106:13; Jonah. Therefore wait for my Word. The question is: Whether this is a consolatory promise, or truly a denunciation of evils? Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note> responds to this place: This is not a bad denunciation, but he means to say, "After I carried you away into Babylon, and within a short space of time I visited you, so that you were liberated and returned to your land, and I did all that to the end that you might make your ways better, so that I might bring back all your brothers from captivity; but you were unwilling, and you corrupted all your actions; therefore I will not commit iniquity, because I am just, but I will bring my justice to light, specifically through the destruction of the second house (the Temple) and the captivity of the Jews by the Romans." But I will not visit you soon after a few days, as I did in the time of the Babylonian captivity, for you shall wait for me in your captivity until that day when I shall rise up into eternity, so that the resurrection becomes perpetual. For this is my judgment and my decree, to gather the nations and to assemble the kingdoms to the holy land and Jerusalem, so that I may pour out my wrath upon them there, etc. Indeed, he thinks it will happen thus when Christians in great numbers undertake the Crusades <note>original: "expeditiones cruciata"</note> to the holy land again, but are there to be slaughtered to the point of annihilation by the Turks and their allies; then truly the Turks and others will pass over to the side of the Jews, the Christians being excluded from this benefit as enemies of God and His word. Let it be enough to have only touched upon this madness of the Jews here: For another...
</margin>

# ON THE PROPHECY OF HAGGAI

## PREFACE.

<margin>1. The Age of Haggai.</margin>

**J**ust as all the preceding minor prophets prophesied before the Assyrian and Babylonian captivity, and Ezekiel and Daniel during the captivity itself: so Haggai and Zechariah prophesied to those who returned to Judea in the second year of Darius Hystaspis <note>Darius the Great (r. 522–486 BCE).</note>. The last, Malachi, prophesied in the final times of Artaxerxes Longimanus, as we shall show in its proper place. Both this prophecy of Haggai and that of Zechariah are what Ezra deals with in chapter 5. The occasion was this, as Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> well writes in this place: Cyrus, moved by God (who had foretold this through Isaiah, Isa. 44:28; c. 45:1, following), had granted in the first year of his reign the return of the Jews to their homeland, with the right of restoring the temple and the city. For thus Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 CE), Jewish historian.</note> in book 11, chapter 1, reports the edict of Cyrus from 2 Chronicles 36:23 and Ezra 1:1, following. Therefore, many from the tribes of Judah, Benjamin, and Levi had returned, and some also from other tribes to whom the worship of God was dear, Ezra 2:1, following, and they had laid the foundations of the temple, Ezra 3:10. But while Cyrus was occupied with wars, and Artaxerxes (or Cambyses) was circumvented, Ezra 4:5, 7, following, the neighboring Satraps, envying the Jews, had hindered the building of the temple for a long enough time. But when Darius Hystaspis obtained the Persian kingdom, God revealed to these prophets that He willed for the work begun to proceed: because He had surely decided to put thoughts favoring the Jews and promoting this work into the heart of King Darius. There were also those who believed Haggai, among whom Zerubbabel the Governor <note>original: *Ethnarcha*</note>, from the line of Da...

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of Zephaniah into the introductory commentary and first chapter of the Book of Haggai. It establishes the historical context of the post-exilic return to Jerusalem and debates the specific identity of King Darius.</meta>

...from the line of David, and **Joshua** <note>original: *Iesus*, the Latin form of the Hebrew name Yehoshua/Joshua</note>, son of Jehozadak, the high priest. However, many among the common people, fleeing from labor and expenses, preferred to believe whatever they wished rather than that which was troublesome to them. For they considered it enough to live in houses they had hastily built for themselves, well-roofed against the harms of the weather, and to enjoy the produce of the fields; yet this hope, by God's will, had deceived them. Therefore, Haggai, by divine command, rebukes this negligence of the Jews in building the temple and earnestly exhorts them that, having been warned by the evils with which they had been afflicted until now, they should seriously undertake the work of restoring the temple. If they did this, and turned themselves entirely to God and His worship, he promises that God would mercifully be present with His grace and protect them in this work; he further pledges that in due time, through the coming and presence of the Messiah, the future glory of this latter temple would be far greater than that of the former temple built by Solomon. It consists of four parts corresponding to as many sermons: I. On the 1st day of the sixth month, in the second year of Darius, he exhorts Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people to build the temple (chapter 1). II. On the 21st day of the seventh month, he promises that the Messiah will come into that temple (chapter 2:1–9). III. On the 24th day of the ninth month, he again reproves the Jews for the previously neglected temple structure, with a promise of future grace (v. 10–19). IV. On the same 24th day of the ninth month, he predicts the destruction of enemies and the perpetual preservation of Zerubbabel <note>here signifying the Messiah descending from him</note> and his kingdom (v. 20–23).

CHAPTER 1. v. 1. a) In the second year. Thus in 1 Kings 15:25, 2 Kings 1:17, chapter 14:1, etc. b) Of King Darius. The seventh Darius <note>original Greek: *ὁ ἑπτὰ Δαρείος*</note>. Thus in v. 15, chapter 2:10; as in Mark 2:26, Luke 3:2. Therefore after the captivity and in the same year that Zechariah prophesied. Zech. 1:1, 7:3, 5; Ezra 5:1. And which Darius? It is easily apparent that it was not that Mede mentioned in Daniel 6:1. For he, a contemporary of Cyrus, had long since passed away by the time of Haggai. See Lightfoot's *Chronology*, page 233. Some, therefore, such as Heidegger in his *Handbook*, page 339; Alsted in his *Chronological Tables*, page 38; Cocceius on this passage, and others, following the opinion of Scaliger, judge it to have been Darius H. or Nothus. This is made manifest from Ezra 4:7 compared with v. 24 and chapter 5:1, 6; also chapter 7:1, showing this Darius had a predecessor and successor both named Artaxerxes. This argument is granted to Darius Nothus if you observe with the learned that those successors of Cyrus—Cambyses the son and Smerdis the Magian, who was slain by the princes—had two names; or, as some believe, Ahasuerus or Artaxerxes and Darius were common sur-

Bessus, the murderer of his kin, according to Curtius (book 6, chapter 6), having taken the royal robe, ordered himself to be called *Artaxerxes*. See the notes by *Cellarius* and what we shall note on the book of Ezra. Furthermore, it follows that from this hypothesis, from the laying of the first foundations of the temple in Ezra 3:8–10 until the restoration of the work in chapter 5:2, more than a hundred years (at least 105) must be counted. Thus, Zerubbabel the Leader and Joshua the Pontiff would have to be at least 130 or 120 years old; and to others who had seen the splendor of the former temple (Haggai 2:2–3), nearly two hundred or even more years would have to be attributed. Therefore, the opinion of those who understand *Darius, son of Hystaspes* is preferred: specifically Josephus, Eusebius, and Jerome, who are followed by *Cappellus, Gertler, and Vitringa* in *Chronology*, p. 565 following; *Prophetic Doctrine*, p. 41 following; and in *Sacred Observations*, Book 6, p. 337. See also *Calovius* on this passage against the doubts of Cocceius. c) *In the sixth month v. 1.* Haggai, therefore, began to be enlightened by God with these visions two months before Zechariah; compare Zechariah 1:1. d) *On the first day.* Thus Genesis 1:5. Regarding the feast of the new moon, on which the people were accustomed to gather. See Numbers 28:11. e) *The word of prophecy from the Lord occurred.* Thus v. 3, chapter 2:1, 10; cf. Zephaniah 1:1, etc. f) *By the hand*, that is, through the ministry. Greek <note>original: *ὁ.*, referring to the Septuagint</note>: *by the hand*. Thus chapter 2:1, Galatians 3:19. For the hand of a man is the most fitting instrument or member for carrying out the business of the body. Hence that phrase is elegantly drawn by metaphor from its proper meaning into another; and he to whom someone can safely commit something that he wants correctly cared for is said by the Hebrews to have done it through his *hand*, even if the matter is brought to effect not by hands, but by mouth or other ways. So says *Reinbeck* on this passage; cf. notes on Exodus 9:35, Hosea 12:11. g) *Of Haggai.* This name suggests, as it were, that the festival of the Lord is to be celebrated again. Compare Nahum 2:1. *Abarbanel* says we do not know from which tribe he was. h) Ezra 5:1; see Habakkuk 1:1. i) *To Zerubbabel* chapter 2:2, 21; who was also called *Sheshbazzar* by the Chaldeans. Ezra 1:8. <note>where see the notes.</note> k) *The son, that is, the grandson of Shealtiel.* Matthew 1:12. For he himself was the son of *Pedaiah*, as Kimchi notes, comparing 1 Chronicles 3:17, 19. Abarbanel says: Perhaps his grandfather Shealtiel was more famous than his father Pedaiah; or he was raised by his grandfather Zerubbabel; cf. 2 Samuel 21:8 and chapter 6:23. l) *The Leader, that is, the Prince of the Jews.* v. 14, Ezra 1:8, 5:14, 2 Kings 25:27. m) *To Joshua* Zechariah 3:1 following; or Jesus Ezra 3:2, 3, chapter 5:2. n) *The son of Jehozadak*, who had been led into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, 1 Chronicles 5:40, 41. o) *The High Priest* v. 12, Leviticus 21:10, Numbers 35:25, 28. Namely, he addresses the leaders of the people, both sacred and political, and in them the whole people; compare v. 1, 12, chapter 2:2. In this chapter or first sermon of the Prophet, after the title in v. 1 and the noted circumstance of time, the following are to be observed: I. The command of God, reproaching in v. 2–4, calling to repentance in v. 5–6, commanding anew in v. 7–8, and describing past evils more fully in v. 9–11. II. The effect of the divine command, namely the obedience of the leaders and the people, v. 12–14. *p. 2) see* Nahum 1:12. q) Ephesians 1:24, Hosea 12:6. Greek: *Lord Almighty*. Thus v. 5, 7, 9, chapter 2:4, etc. Cf. 2 Corinthians 6:18, etc. r) *This people* of the Jews say. Grotius: that lazy and greedy common folk. See what we noted in the Preface regarding the occasion of this prophecy. s) *Not yet.* Genesis 2:5, Ezra 5:9, Job 22:16. t) *The right time* is Leviticus 15:25, Hosea 10:12. u) *Of coming.* That is, the time for coming has [not] come. Psalm 102:14. x) *Namely, the time of the house of the Lord or the Temple.*

**γ)** as an addition. Zechariah 8:9. The Vulgate <note>The Latin Bible translation</note> reads: "The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built." As if the Lord says: Although the time for building the temple is now right, specifically since Cambyses <note>A Persian King</note> is dead and the obstacles that stood in the way of building have been removed; nevertheless, that time does not yet seem convenient to the people, who measure the time for building only by their own convenience and private interests. See the Preface, section 2. Furthermore, the scholar Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> rightly says: "I have no doubt that this prophecy was issued before permission was given to the Jews by King Darius to restore the Temple." See Ezra 5:3 and following, up to chapter 6:14.
**v. 3. x)** And so it happened that the word of the Lord continued. Namely, because they spoke as in verse 2. Others begin a new prophecy here, thinking it was delivered on the 24th day of the sixth month (comparing verse 15). **a)** See the note on verse 1.
**v. 4. b)** Is it then time for you? See 2 Kings 5:26. **c)** O you lazy delayers? Or: "for you, I say." This is a repetition of the pronoun for emphasis, as in Genesis 27:34, 38; Psalm 9:7, etc. **d)** To dwell in your houses [verse 9]. **e)** paneled <note>original: *contabulatis*</note>. The Vulgate says: "ceiled" <note>original: *laqueatis*</note>. That is, constructed not just for necessity, but also for pleasure, and not without great expense and labor. The Targum of Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> says: "in houses that are covered with cedar panels." See 1 Kings 6:9; 7:3; Jeremiah 22:14. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note> remarks: "In your own affairs, no time is considered premature; in the affairs of God, you believe every time is premature." David was not so minded; his words in 2 Samuel 7:2 and Psalm 132:2 are referenced here. **f)** "And this house"—which (as a symbol of the incarnation and the gracious dwelling of the Son of God, see Malachi 3:1; John 1:14; Haggai 2:19, 21; Colossians 2:9; Hebrews 3:6; etc.) ought to have been restored before all else. **g)** "shall it be and remain desolate?" [verse 9; Jeremiah 33:14].
