...to say: if you notice the fates you have had up to now, you will easily understand, and almost feel with your hands, that God has punished your laziness in building the temple. **v. 6. m)** But in bringing back, you brought back little. The Vulgate: *you brought in little*, that is, you had small harvests [2 Samuel 9:10; see below verse 9, 10; chapter 2:16, 17; Deuteronomy 28:38; Micah 6:15; Isaiah 24:5]. **n)** *In eating* you have indeed eaten; but *not to satiety* [Isaiah 23:18; see Leviticus 26:26 and the note on Hosea 4:10]. **o)** *In drinking* you have indeed drunk wine or strong drink, *but you have not drunk until satisfied*. The same applies to drink as the previous word for "satiety" applied to food. See Genesis 43:34; Song of Solomon 5:1. **p)** *In clothing*, one puts on garments. The Greek Septuagint: <term>περιεβάλεσθε</term> <note>you clothed yourselves</note>. Matthew 6:29, 31. **q)** *And yet not to warmth* for himself, or so that it might be warm for him [1 Kings 1:1]. That is, the thin clothing was not enough to properly warm the body. See James 2:16. **r)** *And he who has earned wages for himself* or acquired them; others say: he who hired himself out for a wage so that he might bring it home. This Hebrew verb form <term>Hithpael</term> occurs only here. Compare the <term>Niphal</term> form in 1 Samuel 2:5. **s)** He earned it into *a purse* or small bag [1 Samuel 25:29; Proverbs 7:20]. **s)** *perforated*, or full of holes [2 Kings 12:10]. A proverbial expression for money that quickly slips away. The Targum Jonathan translates this as "to a curse." **v. 7. \*)** Wherefore the Lord says this again and again, etc. [verses 2, 5]. **v. 8. x)** Therefore, learn from these losses of yours, and *ascend into the mountain* of Lebanon. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century theologian</note>: He understands Lebanon, from which cedars were to be sought for building the house. Compare 1 Kings 5:20; Ezra 3:7. But the Targum Jonathan says "into the mountains." See Nehemiah 8:15. **y)** and from there *convey the wood*. **z)** *and build the house*, that is, the Temple [verses 2, 4]. **a)** *and I will take pleasure in it*, that is, it will be pleasing, and according to the Vulgate, "acceptable to me," as a symbol and pledge of my visitation [verse 4]; and though it does not shine with silver and gold as before, it shall shine now. See on the verb construction Micah 6:7; Proverbs 3:12; 1 Chronicles 29:3. The Targum Jonathan: *and I will take pleasure, that I may cause my Divine Presence (Shekhinah) to dwell in it with glory*. The Greek: *and I will be glorified in it*. See Colossians 1:19. **b)** *and I will be glorified* in it: even if external splendor is lacking. This is an argument from the glorious. See chapter 2:9; Isaiah 26:15. Furthermore, the Hebrews note that the letter "He" is missing from the written word <note>The Hebrew letter He (ה) has the numerical value of 5.</note> in this place to signify that five things were missing in the second temple: 1) the sacred fire fallen from heaven, 2) the Divine Presence (Shekhinah) or <term>σκήνωσιν</term> <note>dwelling/tabernacling</note>; regarding which see Exodus 29:42; 30:6; 40:34; Numbers 9:15; 1 Kings 8:10-12; 3) the Ark and the Cherubim, 4) the Urim and Thummim, 5) the Holy Spirit or the gift of prophecy. Others list even more in a slightly different order. See Abarbanel and the *Mishnah* on this passage. But since those were missing in the letter (as a shadow), it was necessary that they be given in truth and in the body. And this is signified by "I will be glorified," says Cocceius. Compare below, chapter 2:7, 9. **c)** See the note on verse 2. **v. 9. d)** Truly because you have neglected that which I commanded in verse 8 until now, and cared only for your own affairs, therefore *in looking, you indeed looked for much*, and expected abundant harvests [see verse 6]. **e)** but *behold, it went into scarcity*, it became little [2 Chronicles 29:34]. Jerome <note>Early Christian scholar and translator</note> says: "When the crops were already whitening and the time of harvest was pressing, and you thought you held the grain in your hands, you harvested empty stalks and gathered useless straw without the fruit of the ears. The threshing floors were full in expectation, but there was grief in the hands." **f)** and that tiny amount you *brought home* or into the granaries [verse 6]. **g)** yet on top of that *I blew* and scattered *it* [Ezekiel 22:20, 21]. A metaphor. See Isaiah 40:7. The Targum Jonathan: "I sent a curse upon it." **h)** *On account of what?* The Vulgate: "For what cause?" [Ezekiel 5:9]. **i)** verse 2; Ezekiel 11:8; 16:14. **k)** because it remains desolate [verse 4], even though its first foundations were laid back in the time of Cyrus [Ezra 3:10; see note below on chapter 2:18]. **l)** *but you run*. The Vulgate: "you hasten"; and you expend all your zeal and labor. See Proverbs 1:16. **m)** each one, individually [Isaiah 47:15; Jonah 3:8]. **n)** *to his own house* to adorn it and enrich it. *You are busy with your own remaining things; you do not care for God*; therefore he does not grant your desires. See verse 4; Philippians 1:21. **v. 10. o)** *Therefore, for your sake*. See Deuteronomy 28:23. The *Mishnah* and Abarbanel note: "while it rains upon other nations." See Amos 4:7 and Zechariah 8:11. The Targum Jonathan gives the cause: *because of your sins*. **p)** *they withheld the heavens*. Used impersonally, for "the heavens were withheld" or according to the Vulgate, "the heavens were prohibited." See Exodus 19:8; Hosea 12:9. Others, like the Septuagint and Arabic versions: "therefore the heavens abstained." The Targum Jonathan: "the heavens cease to send down rain." **q)** *from dew*; so that they gave neither dew nor rain. See the preface on the letter Mem used to indicate deprivation in Isaiah 23:1, and regarding the matter, 1 Kings 17:1. **r)** *and the earth withheld its fruit*. See verse 6; Habakkuk 3:17; Zechariah 8:12; Deuteronomy 11:17. Namely, because God was not answering them [Hosea 2:23, 24].

For what others want—that the beginning of building was only made on the 24th day of the month based on chapter 2:18—does not hold up with the beginning of the second chapter, where in verse 3 the elderly Jews do not yet see the new temple rising, but the Prophet addresses those already vigorously working in verse 4 on the 21st day of the seventh month (chapter 2:1). Their pious zeal, under God's guidance, was later also approved and aided by the decree of King Darius, so that they finished the whole building in the sixth year of Darius (Ezra 6:15).

**CHAPTER II. verse 1. b)** Compare chapter 1:1, 15. Three remaining sermons of our Prophet follow in this chapter. **I.** The excellence of the second Temple is promised, not in gold and silver, but in the coming of the Messiah (verses 1–9). **II.** A change from sterility to fertility is promised (verses 10–19). **III.** Zerubbabel is established as a type of Christ <term>type: a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a foreshadowing of something in the New Testament</term> for the time of the New Testament (verses 20–23). **verse 2. c)** Jeremiah 3:11; Ezekiel 17:12. **d)** Verse 21; chapter 1:1, 12. **e)** Verse 4; chapter 1:1, 12. **f)** Chapter 1:14. **g)** so that you may confirm them in faith and refute the silent objections that trouble their minds. For when the foundations of the Temple had been laid, and many of the elders, who had seen the previous Temple in its glory, judged that the present house was far surpassed by it, and were thus affected by great sadness and grew faint (verse 3), Haggai again and again stirs them all up to complete the work begun, proposing powerful reasons: (1) from the gracious presence and help of the entire Holy Trinity (verses 4, 5); (2) from the truth of the promises concerning the Messiah, who would certainly come to this very second temple and most abundantly supply what seemed to be missing (verses 6–10; compare Maius, *Economy of the Old Testament*, page 1076). **verse 3. h)** Who is among you? Isaiah 50:10. **i)** the survivors (Ezra 1:4). **k)** who saw this house in its former splendor? Indeed, there could still be very old men surviving who had seen Solomon’s Temple; just as 18 years prior, in the second year of Cyrus, there were still many such people, as Ezra 3:12 testifies. For from the destruction of the Temple until the present second year of Darius Hystaspis, there were 70 years (Zechariah 1:12), and until the first year of Cyrus, or the end of the captivity, 52. **l)** Compare Ezra 3:12 and below verses 7, 9. **m)** But how do you see it now? Compare Numbers 13:18. **n)** Is not its comparison—the suffix could refer either to the previous house: *is not this later one like nothing in comparison to that one?* or to the later one: *is not the comparison of this one like nothing in your eyes?* (Compare Genesis 44:18; Judges 8:12). **o)** Isaiah 40:17; Psalm 39:6. **p)** in your eyes and minds. The Syriac version says: "it is considered as nothing." Compare Numbers 13:33. **verse 4. q)** Yet now, nevertheless, even if these things are so. Exodus 10:17. **r)** be strong and of good courage. Joshua 1:6, 7, 9; Zechariah 8:13. **s)** Chapter 1:2, 13.

**v. 5. a)** "I am with you," says God the Father in verse 4, through that hypostatic <note>The "hypostatic" union refers to the union of divine and human natures in Christ.</note> Word. <term>Cocceius’s Lexicon</term> 150. It is noted that he of whom God speaks, and through whom He speaks, and who, when shown to men, speaks through the things themselves, is God. In 1 John 1:1, He is called "the Word of life," because the speech of the assembly is life concerning Him and from Him. See these points developed more broadly by the same author in his Commentary and by Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a prominent Lutheran theologian</note> on this passage, who also brilliantly defended this text against the distortions of the Jews. **b)** That which, or concerning which. From which it is clear that this is a great testimony regarding the Three Witnesses <note>A reference to the Trinity</note>, as Cocceius writes. </margin>

See note on verse 2. **i)** see chapter 1:12. **k)** *yet one, namely a time,* as in Exodus 30:10; 2 Kings 6:10; Psalm 68:18. Or, as Paul says in Hebrews 12:26–27: *yet once more* <note>original Greek: ἔτι ἄπαξ</note>, just as of old, when the Law was proclaimed from Mount Sinai with terrifying thunder and lightning, and all of nature was, as it were, shaken. Exodus 19:16 and following; Judges 5:4 and following. **l)** A parenthesis: and a brief one, namely, in a short time. Exodus 17:4; Isaiah 10:25. Specifically, a space of about 500 years from the construction of this Second Temple to the beginning of the New Testament. This is called "brief" by comparison, either in respect to the time already passed since the giving of the Law, as we said, or since the proclamation of the First Gospel <note>The "Protevangelium" or first promise of a savior in Genesis 3:15</note>, since which time the Messiah had been expected. This should also be noted here against the false hypothesis of the Jews, who think the Messiah was to appear not after the time of the Babylonian exile and the subsequent restoration of the city and commonwealth (as the Prophets Jeremiah 3:14–16, etc., state), nor while the Second Temple was still standing (Malachi 3:1), but after a new destruction of their commonwealth and a far more severe and lasting exile, such as the one in which they now live. Certainly, the gloss of Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a medieval Jewish commentator</note> on this passage is quite forced; he suggests God said: "besides that first house which the old men saw (v. 3), yet a second house shall be built, though it be small compared to the first; moreover, it shall be devastated again because *I will shake the heavens and the earth*, or the Romans shall come by sea and land and destroy it. *Nevertheless, after a very long time, I will also shake all nations*, so that they come into the holy land, and there I will take vengeance on them: and *then I will fill not this second, but a third* temple, to be built then, with my glory," etc. (verse 7). Compare Vitringa, *Prophetic Doctrine*, p. 140 and following. **m)** And I, the almighty God (verse 4). **n)** am powerfully *about to shake* (verse 7). The heavens and the earth, and I will bring about such a change of affairs among Jews and Gentiles that a new heaven and a new earth are produced. Isaiah 65:17; 66:22. *“The words ‘yet once more’ signify the removal of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain,”* says the Apostle in Hebrews 12:27. Compare also 2 Corinthians 3:11. For the Prophet indicates, according to the Apostle's interpretation, the institution of a new economy and the abolition of the old. **o)** even the heaven itself: of whose movement there is no mention in the history of the giving of the Law, as hinted in Hebrews 12:26; compare Exodus 19:18; Psalm 68:9. The shaking of a certain part of the earth where the Israelites then stayed signified the particular abolition of idolatry and a special institution of divine worship for that people, while the rest of the nations were still left to their own devices (Acts 14:16). However, the language concerning the shaking not only of the earth, sea, and dry land, but also of heaven itself, and thus of this whole universe, designates a universal abolition of the former piety among all nations, specifically through the Gospel, which was to be proclaimed while the Second Temple was still standing. By this prophecy, says Augustine in *The City of God*, book 18, chapter 35, "part is seen already fulfilled; part is hoped to be fulfilled at the end. For He moved the heaven by the testimony of angels and stars when Christ was incarnated. He moved the earth by the great miracle of the virgin birth. He moved the sea and dry land, as Christ is announced both in the islands and in the whole world. Thus we see all nations moved to the faith." See more in Calovius. **p)** <term>Metonymically</term> we understand this to refer to the inhabitants of the earth from verse 7; although the earth itself was also violently shaken at the time of Christ’s death, Matthew 27:51, which Gussetius prefers (p. 943). **q)** and the sea, namely, the islands of the sea and their inhabitants. See Isaiah 49:1, 6; 24:15; 42:4, 10, 12; 66:19; and the whole universality of sublunary things. Revelation 10:2. **r)** and the dry land, namely, the continent. Genesis 7:22; Exodus 14:21. Verse 7. **s)** For I will shake by the voice of the Gospel (verse 6) to repentance and faith. Compare Acts 17:6, 30; 21:28. **t)** all nations. Isaiah 66:19; Romans 10:18. **u)** and they shall come (Habakkuk 2:3; Zechariah 2:14; Malachi 3:1) the desire and delight (1 Samuel 9:20; 2 Chronicles 21:20) of all nations. The Vulgate: "and the one desired by all nations shall come." Namely, the Messiah, whom all nations (Isaiah 2:2; 52:10; 61:11; Psalm 22:28; 72:17; 67:4; 117:1, etc.) as the one and true delight of the whole human race (Song of Solomon 5:16) ought to desire and expect. See Genesis 49:10; Isaiah 42:4; 51:5; Luke 2:10, 32, etc. The construction is made according to the sense, as in Isaiah 15:4; 25:3; Job 29:10; 32:7. And Rabbi Akiba rightly explains this passage as referring to the days of the Messiah and his coming in the treatise *Sanhedrin*, chapter 11, folio 97b; although Rashi, in his gloss on that passage, rejects that explanation as absurd (based on his false principle that the Messiah has not yet come). Christian interpreters, and even Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian</note>, therefore rightly understand this passage as referring to Christ; as Calovius shows at length here. Others resolve the construction in this way: "and they shall come, namely, so that they come to the desire of all nations, that is, to Christ." For "to come" is also constructed absolutely with the accusative of the destination, without an intervening preposition. See, for example, Numbers 21:27; 1 Samuel 13:28; Jeremiah 32:24; Psalm 35:8; 36:12; 119:41, 77, etc. So Cocceius's Lexicon 85: "they shall approach," he says, "he who shall be given to the nations so that they love him... and so, aroused by the voice of the Gospel, the most desired—that is, the best and the elect of all nations—shall run together, allowing themselves to be brought into the order of salvation." Compare Isaiah 2:2–3; 11:10; 49:18, 22; 66:20; Matthew 2, 2, etc., and a similar construction in 2 Kings 19:23, etc. Thus, "the choice of all nations" <note>original Greek: τὰ ἐκλεκτὰ πάντων τῶν ἐθνῶν</note>. **x)** and then I will fill. Alludes to Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11. Compare Ezekiel 43:3; 44:4. **y)** this very house, which you think is not comparable to the first, not without sadness. See note on verses 2, 3. **z)** not with gold and silver, which I do not need (verse 8), but with the glory of my only-begotten Son, who shall appear in the flesh while this temple is standing, and shall perform miracles in it. Matthew 21:12–14. Grotius: "All Jews who lived before the destruction believed the Messiah would appear in the second temple. From that time they have devised new, violent, and various interpretations for these very clear passages..." <note>original Greek: χάριν σοφὰ φίγματα - "for the sake of clever inventions"</note>. Compare verses 3, 9.

*. 8. a) The silver is mine, and the gold is mine. Therefore, do not think that an abundance of gold or silver would make this house more pleasing to me. I will decorate it with another, and indeed much more precious, ornament, so that its future glory will nevertheless be greater than that of Solomon’s Temple, which sparkled with gold on all sides. *. 9. c) Greater shall be the glory of this latter House than the former: although many external ornaments that distinguished the previous Temple are missing in this one. See notes on verses 3, 7, and chapter 1:8. Thus, God taught that the privilege of this second Temple was none other than that Christ made it illustrious by his presence, teaching, and miracles. Otherwise, the second temple would not have approached the glory of the first in any part, nor would Haggai have said its glory would be greater. Regarding this argument, the Jews have nothing they can argue with any appearance of truth. For whatever they devise—whether regarding its more splendid restoration finally made by Herod, or its longer duration, or the offerings from the sacrifices of foreign kings, or finally even regarding some third Temple—it is of no weight and is only a sign of a bad case. Indeed, it is the Messiah who, as Lord, comes to that Temple of his (Malachi 3:1) and by his presence, teaching, and miracles, abundantly supplied the defects of the latter house, making it infinitely more illustrious than the former. For he brought fire from heaven—not material fire <note>See the note on chapter 1:8.</note> but the Holy Spirit himself, with which he baptizes his own (Matthew 3:11, Acts 2:3). He himself is the Ark of the Covenant, in whose middle (that is, his heart)

The Jewish interpreters raise complex questions here from the spirit of the Talmudists, which were rightly rejected by Abarbanel himself. Verse 13. e) Therefore Haggai said further. f) Syriac: *when the soul is unclean*. Namely, one who has touched a body abandoned by the soul, **polluted by a dead man**. See Leviticus 21:11, 22:4. g) Any or anything of those things, namely bread, wine, etc. (verse 12). h) Will it be polluted, namely the food or drink? i) They answered and said: "It will be contaminated," according to the law in Numbers 19:22. For that which is good is much more easily corrupted than that which is evil is mended. a) <note>original Greek: "μιανθήσεται" (will be defiled)</note>. Compare Titus 1:15. Verse 14. k) So also is this people, or has been until now. They were unclean themselves, and they made all things unclean (Titus 1:15). This is the application of the proposed case to the present purpose. That is to say, the Jews had already restored the Altar of burnt offerings before the Temple, and had offered their victims upon it in the time of Cyrus and Cambyses (Ezra 3:2, 3). But they had neglected the structure of the Temple begun in the second year of Cyrus, being terrified by their adversaries (Ezra 3:8 ff, 4:1-24), intent in their minds on **their own things** (Haggai 1:4), and rashly satisfied with their sacrifices. He therefore censures the error concerning sacrifices offered by the "work performed" <note>Theologians call this *ex opere operato*, the idea that a ritual works automatically regardless of the person's heart.</note>, and teaches that by an ungrateful heart, without true repentance and without faith in Christ, all things are contaminated by those who offer them; it is far from the case that those offerings make the ones offering them holy and approved by God. Compare Isaiah 1:11 ff., Amos 5:21 ff. l) So is this nation. The Jews are called "people" (populus) regarding their statecraft, and "nation" (gens) regarding their ethnicity. m) It was in my sight and judgment (Genesis 7:1, Jeremiah 2:16), even when they appeared before me with their sacrifices or prayers (Jeremiah 7:10, 15:1).

He strips its foundation, says Reinbeck <note>original: "illius fundum denudat"</note> in this place.

hail; compare Psalm 78:47, Psalm 148:8. o) See v. 14 and compare chapter 1:6, 10, 11. p) And yet none [turned]. 1 Samuel 14:26, chapter 26:12. q) Of you—as if you were to say barbarously: "of your selfhood" or "your society." Compare note on Ezekiel 31:4, chapter 47:17, Zechariah 7:7. r) "To me," i.e., turned himself. As it is said more fully in this same sense in Amos 4:9; compare Zechariah 1:3. Vulgate: "and there was no one among you who returned to me." Abarbanel: The sense is, he says, "and yet you did not turn to me," i.e., with your whole heart. s) v. 4, 8, 14, 23. v. 18. t) Therefore, pay attention. This is resumed from v. 15 so that what he warns may be observed most diligently. u) And "above," that is, backward to previous times. We take it in the same way here as in v. 15. Otherwise, it also notes subsequent time in 1 Samuel 16:13, etc., as was the custom of the Latins. So the Vulgate in this place: "and into the future." Schmid: "and thereafter." x) Namely, from this very twenty-fourth day, about which see v. 18. y) Returning in mind to that time which passed since the day... he wants to say: Consider only the time elapsed between this 24th day and the day of the first foundation of the temple. Compare the similar force of the particle *lamen* in Exodus 9:18, Deuteronomy 4:32, 2 Samuel 7:11, Jeremiah 7:7, 25. z) On which the temple was founded. He understands the first foundation of the temple, made in the second year of Cyrus, which was soon interrupted until the second year of King Darius. Ezra 3:10, 11; chapter 4:4 and following; compare Zechariah 8:9. *. 19. a) Is there yet seed, or has there been? i.e., none or very little remains. Compare Genesis 31:14, Ruth 1:11, when the granaries scarcely sufficed for sowing and extreme necessity; and that as a punishment for neglecting my worship and temple. b) In the granary. Schmid: in the storehouse. (1) Compare Joel 1:17. c) Even the vine. As if to say: "even unto the vine." Compare Genesis 6:7. d) And the fig tree. Habakkuk 3:17. e) And the pomegranate. Joel 1:12, Canticles 6:11. f) And the olive tree. Habakkuk 3:17. g) Has not borne its fruit. Ezekiel 17:8, Joel 2:22. h) But from this very day and time when you seriously undertook the building of the Temple. i) I will bless you with a great abundance of all these things. On the same day, see above v. 10, for the confirmation and illustration of those things which had already been said in v. 6 and 7.

*. 21. m) Speak (specifically to Zerubbabel, the Governor of Judah, v. 2, chapter 1:1). n) Saying for his consolation. Calovius p. 917: Not only so that he may certainly trust that what was said in v. 6, 7 about the glory of the second Temple would come to pass, but also specifically for that peculiar reason which pertained to the person of Zerubbabel himself, and not to the rest of the people: because by that shaking, the glory of this Zerubbabel was to be made more illustrious. Since he himself was the Leader from the royal line of David, from which the Messiah, the Desire of Nations, was to come. Therefore, God had chosen him so that the Messiah might be born from his seed, which is hinted at by this repetition. o) I will shake. Just as he had spoken before in v. 6, 7 about the shaking at the time of Christ's first coming; so now some think another shaking is predicted, to be expected at the time of the later coming or judgment. But Calovius says: It is no other shaking of heaven and earth designated by the Prophet here than that which was explained more at length before in v. 6. For he had already protested that there would be no other shaking: "yet once more," etc. So, as the same Calovius praises on p. 917, Calvin says: The Prophet affirms here that an admirable work of God is imminent, which will shake heaven and earth. This must therefore necessarily be referred to Christ, because it was like a new creation of the world, when Christ gathered those things which had been scattered in heaven and on earth, just as the Apostle says in Colossians 1:20, while He reconciled men to God and the Angels, while having conquered the devil He restored life to the dead, while He shone with His righteousness: then truly God shook heaven and earth, and even today He shakes, etc. Cocceius: He indicates the erection of that which is unshakable to be the end of the shaking. For those things which are shaken are removed, so that the unshakable things may be erected. From this, therefore, the Israelites were able to notice that this Temple, which they were to build, they ought not to count among permanent things (for they had seen it already shaken once, and it had been said of the princes of this world: "like other Princes you shall fall," Psalm 82:7) but they should expect something more stable and truly eternal, the spiritual kingdom of God in the faithful Messiah. p) Compare Isaiah 51:6, 65:17, 66:22, Hebrews 12:26, 27.

<summary>This page details the prophet Haggai's explanation of the hardships faced by the returning exiles—such as crop failure and blight—attributing them to their neglect of the Temple. It concludes with a promise of blessing and a Messianic prophecy regarding a divine "shaking" of the world through the line of Zerubbabel.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on Haggai 2, moving from the physical rebuilding of the Temple to the prophetic promises made to the governor Zerubbabel. It discusses the divine "shaking" of nations and the restoration of the Davidic line through a Messianic lens.</meta>

### HAGGAI. CHAPTER 2.

<margin>
**v. 22. q)** Overthrown successively, and finally, completely. <note>Compare Genesis 19:25; Judges 7:13; 2 Kings 21:13.</note> **r)** The chair or throne of all the kingdoms of the world which you fear. **s)** Schmid translates: and I will destroy <note>original: "perdam f. destruam"</note>. <note>See Amos 9:8; Zechariah 12:9.</note> **t)** Strength or power. <note>Compare Exodus 13:3, 14, 16.</note> **u)** See Daniel 2:44, 45; Psalm 2:8, 9. **x)** And the military chariots shall be overthrown. <note>Isaiah 66:14; Nahum 2:4; compare Zechariah 6:1 and following.</note> **y)** And those who are carried in them. <note>Jeremiah 17:25.</note> **z)** The Syriac version says: "and they shall fall." Jonathan's Targum says: "and the horses will be sufficient." <note>Compare the word in Deuteronomy 28:52; Ephesians 32:19; Lamentations 1:9.</note> **a)** and those sitting upon them, their horsemen. <note>Compare Exodus 15:1, 21; Ezekiel 38:15; Zechariah 10:5; Revelation 19:18.</note> **b)** By their mutual wars and slaughters. <note>Compare Judges 7:22; 1 Samuel 14:20; Ezekiel 38:21, 22.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
**22 Cocceius:** Meanwhile, while I overthrow the thrones. <note>Compare the notes on Ezekiel 24:26; chapter 29:21; and regarding the time of the New Testament, Isaiah 4:2; chapter 11:10, 11, etc.</note> **d)** This is the most certain saying or oracle of the Lord. <note>See verse 4.</note>
</margin>

->**And I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms, and I will destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the nations; and I will overthrow the chariot and those who ride in it; and the horses and their riders shall come down, every one by the sword of his brother.**<-

<margin>
**v. 23. c)** In that day, or at that time, concerning which see verses 21 and 22. Interpreters vary greatly regarding the sense of this verse. For those who take the preceding verse 21 to refer to the second or final coming of Christ understand the words of this verse as follows: "On that day of the last judgment (v. 21), I will take you, Zerubbabel, my servant, raised from the dead, and I will place you among the heavenly beings like a signet ring <note>a symbol of authority and deep personal value</note>, which men are accustomed to carry in their hands and before their eyes, and I will reward your faith and piety with the most abundant eternal glory: because I have chosen you." <note>Gathered from Romans 8:29, 30.</note> However, most scholars, because they judge the prophecy in verse 20 and following to be a repetition of the first coming of Christ from verses 6 and 7, understand by these words "in that day" the time of Christ or the entire New Testament era. Thus Calovius says: "The words *in that day* do not precisely designate a certain day, but a stretch of time within which Zerubbabel shall remain secure and safe under divine care and protection in the midst of disturbances and tumults." (page 918). Cocceius...
</margin>

->**On that day, declares the Lord of hosts, I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, declares the Lord, and I will make you like a signet ring; for I have chosen you, declares the Lord of hosts.**<-

---

->On the 4th day of the 11th month<-

8, 14, 17. **e)** He who can abundantly perform what He promises. <note>Chapter 1:2, etc.</note> **f)** I will take you into my faith and protection (Psalm 49:16), Zerubbabel: namely, in your posterity or <term>seed</term> <note>the family line</note>; according to the analogy of similar promises. <note>See Genesis 12:3; chapter 18:18; chapter 22:18; and the note on 2 Samuel 7:11.</note> **Calovius:** Even if that "taking" is said to concern Zerubbabel, it should not be believed to pertain only to him, or as his person is viewed alone—but in such a way that it extends itself to his preservation, not only regarding his life and reign, but regarding the propagation and blessing of his descendants. "I will take you" so that I may preserve and protect you, and propagate your lineage among those disturbances and overthrows of kingdoms (page 918). **Cocceius:** Surely all the godly are preserved during the commotions of the world and the very abolition of the world. Thus it is promised to Daniel in chapter 12:13. This is the consolation of all the faithful (Psalm 49:16), but we must penetrate deeper. Namely, Cocceius accepts these words both concerning Zerubbabel as a <term>type</term> <note>a historical person foreshadowing a future figure</note> and concerning Christ as the <term>antitype</term> <note>the fulfillment of the foreshadowing</note> (to whom all these predicates belong first and properly). Others understand it to be about Christ alone, who comes here under the name of Zerubbabel, just as elsewhere (e.g., Ezekiel 34:23, 24; Hosea 3:5) He is called "David," and in Psalm 72:1, "Solomon." This is both because Christ is from their seed, <term>the seed</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸ σπέρμα"</note>, and because they were distinguished "types" of Christ, as Zerubbabel was in the leading back of the people from captivity and in the building of the Temple. Thus **Abarbanel** <note>a famous 15th-century Jewish commentator</note> also comments on this place: Furthermore, he says, God indicated to Zerubbabel that the King who would reign in Israel at the time of their redemption would be the Messiah from the seed of Zerubbabel and the house of David. It seemed good to God, therefore, to indicate all these things to him to console and refresh his soul, as if He said: "Behold! It is indeed certain that you will not be King while the Second Temple stands, nor anyone from your seed. But at that time when God overthrows the kingdoms of the nations, and gathers His people Israel, and delivers them, then you shall rule over my people, because from your seed (the Messiah) shall be reigning in Israel at that time forever." Therefore He said: *I will take you Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, my servant, and I will set you as a signet ring; because I have chosen you.* For because the Messiah will be from his seed, He therefore says that he himself is accepted. And this expression is similar to that which is said in Ezekiel 37:23: *David my servant* (i.e., the Messiah, who is called the servant of God eminently in Isaiah 42:1; Ezekiel 34:23, 24; Zechariah 3:8) shall be their Prince forever. For the King Messiah is David himself, and he is Zerubbabel himself; because he will proceed from their stock (Isaiah 11:1). Thus far Abarbanel. **g)** The grandson of Shealtiel. <note>Chapter 1:1.</note> And thus the heir of the promise which was once made to David (2 Samuel 7:11 and following; Isaiah 55:3; Psalm 132:11). **h)** My servant. So called not without a sign of love; because he had faithfully executed the commands of God and had seriously promoted the worship of God by building the Temple of the Lord. <note>Compare 2 Samuel 3:18; chapter 7:5, etc.</note> It is worth noting (says Calovius, page 918) the observation of **Castrio**, which he handed down here: It was once celebrated by God, when He wished to reward the obedience of His servants, to promise Christ from their progeny, which they placed in the highest honor and favor, and by this hope alone they judged themselves most happy. Hence in Genesis 12:3, to reward Abraham because he had gone out from his land and his kindred, He promised him that Christ would be in his descendants. And in chapter 22:18, because of the obedience of the sacrificed son, it is said to him: "In your seed all nations shall be blessed," etc. And the same promise was given to Jacob in Genesis 28:14. To David also, to repay him because he had sworn (Psalm 132:2 and following), the Lord swore the truth: *of the fruit of your body I will set upon your throne* (verse 11). Because of this very thing, the ancient fathers so greedily desired sons, lest they be deprived of such a son, Christ. And for this reason, Hezekiah so anxiously mourned that he was being deprived of life (Isaiah 38:12). He fears, says **Jerome**, lest he be cut off like a weaver's thread in his very beginning, and by no means should Christ arise from his seed. Therefore, by the same reasoning that God promised David—because he had taken care to build a house for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob—that He would build him a house in which Christ would be King, of whose kingdom there shall be no end (Luke 1:32, 33); so to Zerubbabel, because he took care that the second house be built for God, God promises that He will illustrate him with Christ the Lord, who is to be born from him. And this is the reason why such a prophecy was made to Zerubbabel alone, that Christ would be born of his posterity. **i)** This confirmation is repeated here, and at the end of the verse, having been made before, not only for the sake of greater certainty but also because of the mystery of the Holy Trinity. <note>Compare the note on Nahum 1:2.</note> **k)** And so I will place you, Zerubbabel (Sirach 49:11), in your son as a signet ring, which men are accustomed to carry in their hand and before their eyes. <note>See Song of Solomon 8:6 and Jeremiah 22:24.</note> To that place where God testified the greatest loathing for Jeconiah, the grandfather of Zerubbabel, here on the opposite side it is alluded to for his consolation. This, others (says **Gualther**, cited by Calovius, page 920) explain as being about the highest favor and most diligent guardianship—whose opinion, while I do not entirely reject it, I think God is looking at something greater and more sublime, namely the promise of the Messiah, to which it is well known all the godly once looked. For because He was expected from the stock of David, the descendants of David were like a signet ring, with which God signed His promise as if visibly, when among so many disturbances and dangers, and the horrible ruins of the most illustrious families, He kept those unharmed from whom that promised Savior was to be born. In the same sense, the descendants of David are also called "lamps" (Psalm 132:17). God therefore promises that He acknowledges Zerubbabel as a genuine son of David, and that there will never be lacking from his posterity those who give faith to His promises. <note>Compare 1 Kings 12:12, 13, 36; and the note on 2 Kings 8:19; Isaiah 7:14, 16, etc.</note> **l)** For I have chosen you. As in Psalm 78:70; namely, that from you Christ may take His origin, who will erect His kingdom, and among so many changes and ruins of kingdoms will finally exert His head most powerfully (Daniel 2:44). **Calovius:** <term>Preeminently</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐξοχικῶς"</note> to be understood concerning the chief peak and summit of dignity and honor, to which Zerubbabel was chosen by the Lord. Without doubt, however, the chief thing is that he was chosen to be placed in the catalog of the ancestors of the Messiah; than which axiom the holy Patriarchs, Kings, and Leaders under the Old Testament held nothing more primary or more ancient. As on the contrary, Esau indicated a profane mind when he valued such great hope and prerogative so cheaply (Genesis 25:32 and following; Hebrews 12:16). Regarding the construction with the Hebrew letter <insert>Bet</insert> <note>a preposition usually meaning "in" or "with"</note> see the note on Isaiah 7:15. **m)** This is the signet of the promise. <note>See chapter 1:9; Hosea 11:11.</note> **Cocceius:** It was therefore impossible that Christ, the son of David, should not be given, and indeed in His own time. Nor is there anyone who may object to the sins of the people. For He does not say, "if the people obey" (which surely is the condition of participating in Christ proposed to the Jewish people in Zechariah 6:15; Psalm 95:7), but "because I have chosen you," and "the Lord has said." **n)** See the note on Isaiah 1:24; Hosea 12:6.

It emphasizes Zerubbabel's role as a "signet ring"—a chosen vessel and ancestor through whom the Davidic line and the future Messiah are secured.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the commentary on the Book of Zechariah. It provides a scholarly introduction (preface) to the prophet’s identity, his name's meaning, his priestly lineage, and the historical period of his ministry, while addressing the debate over whether he is the martyr mentioned in the New Testament.</meta>

# ON THE PROPHECY OF ZECHARIAH
## PREFACE.

<margin>Zechariah 1. Name.</margin>
**§. I.** Zechariah is the second to last in the collection of the Twelve Minor Prophets, and yet he is the greatest in terms of the size of his book. His name was common among the Hebrews; however, the literal meaning of the name fits our Prophet perfectly. Jerome explains it as "the memory of the Lord," Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnovius (1562–1633) was a German Lutheran theologian known for his commentaries.</note> as "one who remembers God" <note>original Greek: $\mu\nu\eta \sigma \acute{\iota} \vartheta \epsilon o \nu$</note>, and Hiller <note>Matthaeus Hiller (1646–1725) was a specialist in biblical languages and etymology.</note> as "*The Lord Remembers*," specifically referring to us or His covenant. Our Prophet was certainly such a man. For he himself remembered the Lord and stirred others to do the same, and he proclaimed that the Lord remains mindful of His covenant and His people.

<margin>2. Namesakes.</margin>
**§. II.** He shared this name with others, from whom he must be distinguished based on historical timing. One was Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, who was also moved by the Divine Spirit; however, because he rebuked the transgressions of the Jews and warned of God’s looming judgments, he was stoned by the people at the command of King Joash in the court of the temple (2 Chronicles 24:20 and following). Another Zechariah lived in the time of Uzziah, and he too, as the Holy Spirit testifies, was skillful in the visions of God (chapter 26:5). Finally, there was another Zechariah, son of Jeberechiah, or as the Septuagint and Vulgate express it, son of Barachiah (Isaiah 8:2), whom some—due to the timing—consider to be the father-in-law of Ahaz (for Isaiah prophesied during his reign; see the notes there). To identify him as our Prophet, however, is a forced interpretation.

<margin>3. Family.</margin>
**§. III.** Regarding the family of our Seer, he was (as he states himself in chapter 1:1, 7) the *son of Berechiah, the grandson of Iddo*. From this it is clear that the term "son" is used broadly, since in Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 he is simply called the *son of Iddo*, whereas strictly speaking he was his grandson. Nothing significant about his father is recorded in the Scriptures, but his grandfather Iddo is better known. <margin>Who was grandfather Iddo?</margin> Without doubt, this is the famous Iddo who, after the end of the captivity, was one of the chief priests who returned with Zerubbabel and Joshua from Babylonia to Judea (Nehemiah 12:1, 4, 7; compare verse 16). Yet Jerome, in his commentary on Zechariah 1:1, says: *It is not doubted, according to the book of Chronicles, that this is the same Iddo who was sent to Jeroboam son of Nebat, under whom the altar was split and the King’s hand withered.* The learned Father <note>referring to St. Jerome</note> seems to have looked to 2 Chronicles 12:15 and 13:22, where the commentaries of *Iddo the Prophet* are praised regarding the history of Rehoboam and Abijah; and especially to chapter 9:29, where the *prophecy of Iddo the Prophet against Jeroboam* is explicitly cited in the record of Solomon's deeds. Indeed, David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish rabbi and grammarian, also known as Radak.</note> says: *They say this is Iddo the Prophet; that is, the one from the passages we have already cited.* And in his commentary on 1 Kings 13:1, he confirms Jerome's opinion about Iddo being the one sent to Jeroboam, based on the calculation of the ancient Hebrews. But even if we grant that Iddo was that prophet who was sent to Jeroboam in 1 Kings 13:1 (though we preferred to "suspend judgment" <note>original Greek: $\acute{\epsilon} \pi \acute{\epsilon} \chi \epsilon \iota \nu$</note> alongside Blessed Schmidius in the notes there), Jerome and the Jewish teachers certainly confuse the timelines and mistake very different people for one another. To be sure, an Iddo lived in the time of Jeroboam I; but how could he be the grandfather of Zechariah, when more than three centuries passed between him and the start of Jeroboam's reign? Therefore, the Iddo mentioned in Chronicles must be distinguished from the Iddo who was Zechariah's grandfather, mentioned by Nehemiah.

<margin>4. Office.</margin>
**§. IV.** Furthermore, from what we have discussed regarding the Prophet's family and especially his grandfather, it is clear that he was a priest of the lineage of Aaron, just like Jeremiah and Ezekiel (see the Preface to Jeremiah, §. 2). Just as Iddo was among the chief priests or leaders of the priestly divisions during the high priesthood of Joshua (at the very time when Zechariah perhaps prophesied as a young man), so his grandson, when he was older, held the same position under the high priest Joiakim, son and successor of Joshua (compare Nehemiah 12:16, 4, 1). Thus our Prophet performed a dual office: the priestly office, which he obtained by birth through divine providence, and the prophetic office, which he received through an extraordinary calling from God.

<margin>5. Passion.</margin>
**§. V.** Though this Prophet presided over a most noble office in the Jewish Church, he is likely the one of whom Christ speaks in Matthew 23:35, saying he was *killed by the Jews between the Altar and the Temple*. Thus, like many Prophets, he sealed his teaching with his own blood, so that, as Balduinus <note>Friedrich Balduin (1575–1627), a Lutheran theologian.</note> reminds us on chapter 1, verse 1, *we have in this Prophet of ours not only a teacher, but also a martyr*. Indeed, we are not unaware that many interpreters believe the Zechariah mentioned by the Savior is instead the son of Jehoiada, whose murder in the temple court is narrated in 2 Chronicles 24:20 and following. They explain the discrepancy in various ways: some by suggesting a scribal error in Matthew, believing *Berechiah* was written instead of *Jehoiada*; others by suggesting Jehoiada had two names, as if he were also called Berechiah. But just as the former opinion is reckless and in no way to be approved, the latter is such that it should hardly be admitted unless a sufficient necessity forces it (which we do not yet see here). Therefore, we understand the Savior’s saying to refer to our Prophet, along with Vatablus, Sanchez, Ribera, Balduinus, Gualther, and others; however, we leave everyone the freedom to disagree on such a difficult question. Our reasons are: 1) He was the son of Berechiah, whom Christ says was killed by the Jews; the priest Jehoiada is never given that name in the Old Testament. 2) Our prophet is almost the last of the Prophets; if the saying were taken to refer to the son of Jehoiada, the question would arise why the Savior would mention him rather than the last one, who is, as it were, the completion of the others, after so many prophets had been killed. Nor does it matter that the murder of our Zechariah is "unwritten" <note>original Greek: $\acute{\alpha} \gamma \rho \alpha \varphi o \varsigma$</note> in the Old Testament. For the story of Jannes and Jambres (2 Timothy 3:8) is of the same nature. It is enough that the matter could have been known to the Jews through tradition. One might object that the Rabbinic records make no mention of this. But look at the Targum on Lamentations 2:20, where divine justice is brought in speaking this way: *Was it fitting to kill a priest-prophet, as you killed Zechariah the son (grandson) of Iddo* (this is our Prophet’s name, clearly referring to Ezra 5:1), *an excellent priest and faithful prophet, in the sanctuary of the Lord on the day of atonement, because he rebuked you so that you would not do evil before the Lord?* This passage, if it is authentic, is an illustrious testimony for establishing our opinion. For it is hardly credible that this Zechariah is anyone other than ours, who bears the name of both Berechiah and the son of Iddo—the latter from his grandfather, the former from his father. However, we do not wish to hide that the same saying in Lamentations 2:20, to whose Aramaic paraphrase we just appealed, is applied to the murdered Zechariah son of Jehoiada in the *Ekhah Rabbati* <note>A Midrashic commentary on the Book of Lamentations.</note> and the glosses of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> on *Sanhedrin* and *Yoma*, as well as in the *Spicilegium* of Abendana.

<margin>6. Time.</margin>
**§. VI.** Our Prophet prophesied after the Babylonian captivity, the second to last of all the Canonical Prophets. He began, as he himself records, in the eighth month of the second year of Darius (chapter 1:1), and thus he was only two months later than Haggai (compare Haggai 1:1). To determine Zechariah's age more precisely, one must ask which *Darius* among the Persian Kings is intended in the Prophet’s inscription. Scaliger and his followers identify him as *Darius Nothus*. But we prefer, with the ancients Josephus and Eusebius, and the most sharp-witted moderns, to identify him as *Darius Hystaspis*. The illustrious author of the *History of the Church of Gotha* weighs the arguments of both sides and decides for the latter. Leaving aside other arguments which you may see more fully deducted there: our Prophet certainly addresses those same leaders who, in the first year of Cyrus, had led the Jews back from Babylonia to their own land—namely, Zerubbabel and Joshua the High Priest. The times of Darius Nothus are too far removed from the first year of Cyrus for either the governorship of Zerubbabel or the high priesthood of Joshua to have extended that far. See also the notes on Haggai 1:1.

<meta>catchword: §. VII.</meta>

<summary>This preface introduces the Prophet Zechariah, explaining that his name means "The Lord Remembers" and identifying him as a priest of the line of Aaron who served after the Babylonian exile. It argues that Zechariah is the martyr mentioned by Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew and identifies the "Darius" of his era as Darius Hystaspis.</summary>
<keywords>Zechariah, Iddo, Berechiah, Darius Hystaspis, priesthood, martyrdom, Matthew 23:35, Minor Prophets, Babylonian Captivity, Zerubbabel</keywords>

--- Page 1295 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to the Book of Zechariah, moving from the identity of the prophet to the historical context of his ministry, his primary objectives, and the symbolic structure of his visions.</meta>

# PREFACE TO ZECHARIAH

<margin>The occasion for the prophecy.</margin> **§. VII.** The occasion for the prophecy was the restoration of the Temple in Jerusalem. Because this historical moment is crucial for understanding the Prophet, we must first explain it using the book of Ezra. Jehovah had moved the heart of Cyrus so that he would not only return the captive Jews in Babylon to their homeland, but also most graciously permit them to repair the Temple (Ezra 1). The leaders of the returning Jews—Zerubbabel, the political leader, and Joshua, the high priest—took advantage of this privilege. Before anything else, they rebuilt the altar of burnt offerings in the temple courtyard so they could perform sacred rites while the Temple itself was being restored (Ezra 3:1–6). They also prepared materials for the sacred building without delay (chapter 3:7), so that in the second year after their return, the foundations were laid (verse 8 and following). These events took place about 18 or 19 years before our Prophet and Haggai began their ministry. However, the work that was so fervent at the beginning was soon interrupted, or at least was not continued with the same diligence (chapter 5:16). The primary cause of this delay was the malice of their adversaries, especially those in Samaria; they made the Jews fearful and troubled them in their building efforts (Ezra 3:3) by hiring counselors in the Persian court to work against them and by poisoning the minds of Cyrus and Cambyses with slander (chapter 4:1–4 and following; compare Daniel 10:13, 20, 21; 11:1). Added to this was the apathy of the Jews themselves, whose devotion grew cold as they focused more on their own interests than on the things of God (Haggai 1:2, 4, 9). From this state of affairs, the Lord first stirred them through Haggai, who began prophesying *in the second year of Darius, on the first day of the sixth month* (Haggai 1:1). When the people, moved by Haggai’s sermons, returned to the restoration of the Temple on the *twenty-fourth day* of that same month (Haggai 1:14–15), the Lord sent Zechariah *in the same month of the same year* to vigorously support Haggai in urging the completion of the work. Thus, from the mouths of "two witnesses" (compare Deuteronomy 19:15; Matthew 18:16), the people were confirmed in God’s promised favor and help (Ezra 5:1–2).

<margin>The Aim.</margin> **§. VIII.** Therefore, the general aim of the Prophet is to call the people to repentance and to faith in Christ, to rouse the listless, to lift up the weak, to confirm the faithful, and to remind everyone of their duty. <margin>The Subject Matter.</margin> *Specifically*, however, his goal is to urge and promote the building of the Temple. Three main obstacles stood in the way of achieving this goal, which had to be removed:
I. *Sloth*: To shake them out of this, he presents to the minds of the Jews the losses they had suffered because the Temple had been neglected until now, and the benefits they would have if they continued piously with the building they had started (chapters 8, 9, etc.; compare Haggai 1:5 and following; 2:15 and following).
II. *Threatening difficulties* posed by enemies, which resulted in the people’s faint-heartedness and fear. To this, he opposes promises—for example, that God would intercept the enemy’s schemes and protect the Jewish people (chapter 1:14–15; 2:3 and following); that every obstacle, even those that seem insurmountable, would be removed (chapter 4:6, 7, 9); that an army of angelic chariots would be sent against the enemies of the Church (chapter 6:1–8); that he would do good to Jerusalem (chapter 8:4); that fasts held because the Temple was desolate would be changed into feast days and joy (chapters 7 and 8); and that the kingdom of Christ would eventually extend to those very nations that were then harassing the people of God (chapter 9, etc.).
III. *Grief over small beginnings* (Ezra 3:12–13). These beginnings, when compared to the splendor of the first Temple, seemed like nothing to the elders of the Jews (Haggai 2:3). To this, he opposes the promise that God would immensely enlarge and glorify these small things through the coming of the Messiah (chapter 4:10; 6:12 and following; 8:6, 20 and following; compare Haggai 2:7 and following).

<margin>Warning against mere ritualism.</margin> **§. IX.** Lest the Jews stop at external and Levitical worship—or "the work performed" <note>original: "opere operato," a theological term referring to performing a religious act as a mere ritual without inner faith</note>—he provides two safeguards: 
a) By requiring from them repentance and the worthy fruits of repentance (chapter 1:2 and following), emphasizing the moral law as the core of true worship that God primarily demands (chapter 7:9 and following; 8:16, 17, 19), and threatening a curse upon perjurers and thieves (chapter 5).
b) By leading them by the hand to Christ, whom all that Levitical preparation was meant to foreshadow. For Zechariah, more than almost any other prophet, speaks clearly and extensively about the coming of Christ, His person, His qualities, His office, His sufferings, His death, and His kingdom, as we will demonstrate with just a few examples in the following section.

<margin>Rising from the symbol to the truth and mysteries of the New Testament.</margin> **§. X.** It is worth noting that our Prophet frequently rises from the "figure" (the symbol) to the reality itself which the symbols foreshadow. He borrows words and phrasing from these symbols to paint the mysteries of the New Testament, teaching that even the Levitical worship was meant to be a schoolmaster <note>The author references Galatians 3:24, where the law is described as a "pedagogue" or tutor leading to Christ.</note> leading the people to Christ.
For example: On the occasion of the physical temple then being restored, he speaks of the construction of the House of God <term>not made with hands</term> <note>original Greek: "χειροποίητα" (cheiropoiēta); the author likely means the opposite, "not made with hands," referring to the spiritual church</note> through Christ (chapter 6:12–13). 
On the occasion of the temple foundation, where cornerstones were used, he speaks of Christ as the cornerstone (chapter 3:9; 4:7), which deserves comparison with Matthew 21:42, Acts 4:11, 1 Corinthians 3:16–17; 6:19, 2 Corinthians 6:16, Ephesians 2:20–22, and Revelation 3:12. 
On the occasion of the temple lampstands then being repaired, he speaks of the Lampstand of the Church (chapter 4:2 and following; compare with Revelation 1:12–13, 20; 2:1; 11:4). 
On the occasion of those who sent gold and silver from Babylon to adorn the temple, he speaks of the calling of the nations under the New Testament into the unity of the church (chapter 6:9 and following, and verse 15). 
On the occasion of the Aaronic priesthood being restored to divine favor, he speaks of the Melchizedekian priesthood of Christ (chapter 3:7 and following; verses 8–9; 6:13). 
On the occasion of the Divine Presence <note>original: "Numinis"</note> dwelling symbolically in the temple, he speaks of Christ's <term>advent</term> <note>original: "aduentu" (coming)</note> in the flesh (chapter 2:14–15; 8:3, etc.). The diligent reader will find many more examples of this kind of prophetic elevation.

<margin>Three general parts: 
1. Visionary, 
2. Didactic, 
3. Prophetic.</margin> **§. XI.** The parts of the entire book can be established as three (following Calovius, if you like): 
I. *Visionary* (or, if you prefer, *Emblematic*), which, after an introductory prophecy (chapter 1:1–6), is completed in nine visions or emblems: 
a) *The man riding a red horse*, standing among the myrtle trees, accompanied by red, sorrel, and white horses (1:7–end). 
b) *The four horns*, cast down by four blacksmiths (2:1–4). 
c) *The man with a measuring line in his hand* (2:5–end). 
d) *Joshua the High Priest* obtaining grace in God's judgment against the accusations of Satan (chapter 3). 
e) *The golden lampstand with two olive trees* (chapter 4). 
f) *The flying scroll of judgments* (5:1–4). 
g) *The ephah and the woman* sitting in it (5:5–end). 
h) *The four chariots* coming out from between two mountains of bronze (6:1–8). 
i) *The double crown* placed on the head of Joshua the High Priest (6:9–end). 
II. *Didactic*, concerning both ceremonial and certain moral matters (chapter 7). 
III. *Prophetic*, concerning Christ and His kingdom and blessings (chapter 8 to the end).

<margin>Obscurity.</margin> <margin>Arising not from a decline in prophetic ability after the captivity, but from the sublimity of the mysteries.</margin> **§. XII.** Furthermore, as Zechariah is more sublime in the matters he predicts, he is also more obscure and difficult in his words. Jerome, in his Prologue, calls it a "most obscure book." And Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note>, at the beginning of his commentary, acknowledges that Zechariah's prophecy is very hidden, and that his visions are like a dream given to an interpreter, whose interpretation no one can rely on as being firmly true until the TEACHER OF RIGHTEOUSNESS comes. He calls the Messiah by this name, drawing from Joel 2:23. We Christians accept this to the extent that we believe a large part of the prophecy is now more intelligible to us through the coming of Christ than it is to the Jews, who still erroneously wait for the Messiah (compare John 4:25). David Kimchi <note>A medieval rabbi and grammarian (1160–1235) known as Radak.</note> complains of the same obscurity; however, he alleges a cause that we find quite unsuitable: namely, that prophetic power supposedly decreased more and more after the captivity. He claims that for this reason, the words of the later prophets are not clear, and they themselves did not understand their visions as the prophets of earlier times did. We, on the other hand, look up with awe at the sublimity of the mysteries in this prophecy, and we acknowledge the dullness of our own intellect, saying with John in Revelation 13:18, *Here is wisdom; let him who has understanding calculate...* and also chapter 17:9, <term>Here is the mind that has wisdom</term> <note>original Greek: "Ὧδε ὁ νοῦς ὁ ἔχων σοφίαν"</note>. It is not without reason that we apply the words of Jerome from the Prologue of his second book of commentaries on Zechariah: "With Moses," he says, "we enter into the cloud and darkness. Deep calls to deep... and the spirit goes round and round, and returns to its circuits. We suffer through labyrinthine errors, and we guide our blind steps by the thread of Christ. Therefore... entreat the Lord that the veil of Zechariah, which was shown before the eyes of Moses, may be taken away from my face." Even the prophets themselves searched their own prophecies (1 Peter 1:11), so deep are the meanings they contain.

<meta>Catchword: §. XIII.</meta>

<summary>This page outlines the historical context of Zechariah’s prophecy—the rebuilding of the Temple after the Babylonian exile—and details the book's structure, including nine symbolic visions. It explains the prophet’s focus on moving beyond mere ritual toward moral repentance and the arrival of the Messiah, while acknowledging the text's profound difficulty.</summary>
<keywords>Zechariah, Temple of Jerusalem, Zerubbabel, Joshua the High Priest, Haggai, Cyrus, Darius, Messianic prophecy, typology, nine visions, Jerome, Rashi, Teacher of Righteousness, obscurity</keywords>

--- Page 1296 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the general preface into the specific commentary on Chapter 1. It establishes the author's humble hermeneutical approach—acknowledging that prophecy is only understood in part—before providing the historical and grammatical context for the opening verses of Zechariah, focusing on the call to repentance and the lineage of the prophet.</meta>

<margin>From our annotations.</margin>
§. 13. As for us, we have searched into this prophecy, though only according to our small measure. For in this endeavor, we have experienced exactly what Paul emphasizes in 1 Corinthians 13:8: <note>original: "Ἐκ μέρους γινώσκομεν, καὶ ἐκ μέρους προφητεύομεν"</note> *“We know in part, and we prophesy in part.”* We have indeed observed that many things which Zechariah foretold have already been fulfilled; however, we have observed no less clearly—following the lead of the **Blessed Tarnovius** <note>Johann Tarnow (1582–1629), a Lutheran theologian known for his commentaries on the Minor Prophets</note>, who in his Prolegomena to Zechariah (p. 1314) extends the fulfillment and consummation of these prophecies all the way to the end of the age—that some things are yet to be fulfilled and pertain to the final days of the Church. Thus, past events have already illuminated those parts; future events will likewise illuminate the rest. The Holy Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> also provides no small amount of light, and we therefore consult it diligently as a key to these prophecies. However, we do not presume to determine the specific manner or particular circumstances of the fulfillment in the final times, leaving those things to the wisdom of Him in whose hand are the times and <note>original: "καιροὶ"</note> *seasons*, and who, as the Poet says, “A wise [god] shrouds the outcome of future time in murky night.” We consider it better to wait patiently and humbly, as if from a watchtower, for the future outcomes of the prophecies, rather than to define them with over-curiosity. Yet we are certain that those things which are still obscure and closed for the present will finally be revealed in time, and will become clearer the closer they reach the boundary of their fulfillment (Daniel 12:4, 9). Meanwhile, if the reader receives any light from our modest work, let them attribute it to God; but if they notice that we have wandered or admitted flaws, let them forgive our human frailty! For we frankly acknowledge that in explaining such a sublime prophecy, we have done not as much as we ought, but as much as we were able.

# THE BOOK OF ZECHARIAH

# זכריה

<margin>
**The first vision** of a man riding a red horse, standing among the myrtle trees, and behind him red, sorrel, and white horses (v. 7 to the end).
</margin>

<margin>
**CHAPTER I. v. 1. a)** This occurred two months after Haggai's first sermon (Haggai 1:1), when the people, having returned from captivity and being encouraged by him, had shortly before returned to the restoration of the temple (ibid. v. 14, 15) and had already made some notable progress (c. 2:1, 10, 15, 18). Moreover, because the specific day is not added here, as is usually done elsewhere, it is probable that the eighth new moon or the first day of the eighth month is intended (compare notes on Jeremiah 40:1). New moons were festivals among the Hebrews (Numbers 10:10), so it is believable that Zechariah, serving the timing of the occasion, delivered this first sermon on the same day he received it: namely, during the sacred assembly of the new moon. **b)** in the second year (v. 7; cf. Haggai 1:1). **c)** of Darius (namely, Hystaspes) son of [Hystaspes] (v. 7, c. 7:1; see Preface §. 6 and notes on Haggai 1:1). **d)** The Jonathan Targum reads: "The word of prophecy from before the LORD." Likewise in v. 7, c. 4:8, c. 6:9, etc. (cf. Jonah 1:1). According to Gurtler in *Prophetic Theology* (p. 133), this chapter contains **I.** The first prophetic discourse, urging the Jews to repentance (v. 1–6). **II.** The second discourse [in the form of] an emblem.
</margin>

CHAPTER I. **א** 1 In the eighth<sup>a</sup> month, in the second<sup>b</sup> year of Darius<sup>c</sup>, the word of the LORD<sup>d</sup> came to Zechariah<sup>e</sup> son of Berechiah<sup>f</sup>, the son of Iddo<sup>g</sup>, the prophet<sup>h</sup>, saying<sup>i</sup>:

2 The LORD was angry<sup>k</sup> with your fathers<sup>l</sup> with [great] anger<sup>m</sup>.

3 Therefore say<sup>n</sup> to them, Thus says the LORD of Hosts<sup>o</sup>: Return to me<sup>p</sup>, declares<sup>q</sup> the LORD of Hosts, and I will return to you<sup>r</sup>, says the LORD of Hosts.

4 Do not be<sup>s</sup> like your fathers<sup>t</sup>...

---

**e)** See Preface §. 1, 2, 4, 5. **f)** See Preface §. 3. Greek: <note>original: "τὸν τοῦ Βαραχίου"</note> *the son of Barachias* (cf. Matthew 23:35). **g)** *of the son*, or rather, continuing the Accusative case following the accents, *the son*—that is, the grandson of Iddo (compare Ezra 5:1, c. 6:14 and the Greek <note>original: "υἱὸν Ἀδדὼ"</note> *son of Addo*). See Preface §. 3. **h)** The Septuagint and Vulgate read *the Prophet*; this is correct, as it is probable this title refers to Zechariah rather than Iddo (cf. Isaiah 38:1, Haggai 1:1). This is the reason we preferred to translate the preceding "son of Iddo" in the Accusative and interpret it broadly as "grandson," rather than strictly in the genitive as "son of [the prophet] Iddo," so as not to clash with the Hebrew accents. Rabbi Kimchi observes that Iddo is called a Prophet by the ancients in the Midrash; indeed, he suspects he is the same person called "Iddo the Seer" in 2 Chronicles 12:15, in which case it would be translated in the Genitive: "son of Iddo the prophet." But see this discussed in Preface §. 3. **i)** *saying*, namely to me (compare v. 3). For the Prophet addresses the whole people returned from captivity at once, of whom he was a member (cf. v. 2 ff.). Regarding the manner of address, cf. our notes on Jeremiah 40:3. **k)** *was angry* (Deuteronomy 9:19, Isaiah 47:6, 57:17, 64:4). **l)** *your fathers and ancestors*, those of the prophet and his people (cf. note on **saying** in v. 1). He primarily means those who lived at the time Jerusalem was captured by the Babylonians (v. 4, 5, 6). **m)** *was angry—with anger*, or most vehemently. The Septuagint: <note>original: "ὀργὴν μεγάλην"</note> *with great wrath*. This is an emphatic pleonasm (cf. v. 15, c. 7:12). The Targum of Jonathan adds the cause of such indignation paraphrastically: "because they provoked anger before Him, the Lord"—namely, by their evil ways and works (cf. v. 4, 6). This proposition is undoubtedly an enthymeme <note>term: enthymeme; a logical argument where one premise is implied rather than stated</note>, to be supplied thus: "What I did to your fathers, I can and will do to you, unless you seriously convert; therefore, learn wisdom from the example and losses of your fathers" (cf. v. 4). Furthermore, there are two main points this first prophetic sermon emphasizes: first, the wrath (v. 2), and then the mercies of God if they turn back (v. 3). **n)** *But you shall say to them*, O Zechariah (v. 1). **o)** The prophet (or rather Jehovah Himself) repeats this three times here, not as a tautology (which rhetoricians find fault with), but for the highest emphasis. For it is a matter being driven home and promised—a triple confirmation taken from the authority and faithfulness of the Triune God who speaks; so that the people do not hesitate to obey and believe, since this is the word not of a man, but of the Supreme Divinity. Thus elsewhere the Prophets, when they wish to win authority or trust for their words, repeat that "Jehovah" or "the mouth of Jehovah has spoken" (Isaiah 1:2, 20; 21:17; 22:25; 25:8; 40:5; 58:14; Joel 4:18; Obadiah 18; Micah 4:4; cf. notes on Nahum 1:2, Haggai 2:23). **p)** *Return to me* (v. 4). Jonathan: "to my worship." Indeed, in my mercy I have decreed to return to you, but only in this order: that you also turn. (Cf. Jeremiah 3:12, Malachi 3:7). The people had returned from Babylon to their fatherland; but it remained for them to return also to their God, whom their fathers had impiously deserted; for without this spiritual return, the physical return would benefit them little. **q)** v. 4, Haggai 2:2. **r)** *then I will return to you*, namely with mercies (v. 16), according to James 4:8: "Draw near to the Lord, and he will draw near to you." Jerome observes the contrary of this: *“You departed from me, and I departed from you”* (cf. Malachi 3:7, 2 Chronicles 30:6, 9; and the opposite below in c. 11:8). **s)** v. 4, 5, 6; cf. 2 Chronicles 30:7, 8; 36:15, 16. It is never safe to imitate ancestors except insofar as it is certain that they <note>original: "στοιχεῖν τῷ κανόνι"</note> *walk according to the rule*. Nor did even the Apostle Paul demand imitation of himself, except insofar as he proved himself an imitator of Christ (Cocceius on this passage).

18. Romans 5:12. The sense is: Even my servants the Prophets themselves, as far as their persons are concerned, have died; this must certainly be granted. Yet it is also true that there was a great distinction in their dying: for the wicked, death was a punishment, but for the pious, it was a gate to eternal rest and glory (Revelation 14:13). And this verse acts as a <note>original: "protaseos" — a preliminary statement or premise</note> to verse 6, where the eternal stability and duration of the prophetic word is opposed to the mortality of both the fathers and the prophets, serving as the <note>original: "apodoseos" — the concluding consequence or fulfillment</note>. Cf. Isaiah 40:8. <margin>v. d) verse 4. z) e) Where are they now? They are no longer among the living, but have long since died (as they were mortal men). Psalm 49:20; Psalm 103:16. f) the Prophets themselves. Jerome understands these as "False Prophets." For he says, "He would never say of the holy Prophets: 'Do they live forever?'" Therefore, both those who sinned and refused to turn to me, and those who deceived the sinners with false promises, have been laid low by death; but my words, which I spoke through my prophets, remain forever. See Jeremiah 37:19. But they are pious...</margin> *. 6. h) Truly, as if to say: There was a far different logic for my words, which the Prophets announced to your fathers; for they did not die out, but endured. i) My decrees, by which I had decreed that your fathers should die by the sword, famine, or plague, and the rest be carried away. See Kimchi <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a leading medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian</note>. k) verse 4; Jeremiah 7:25, 26:5. l) "Did they not overtake your fathers?" An emphatic word. From the perspective of the object, it suggests a flight (though a futile one); from the perspective of the subject, it suggests an act of pursuit. It is as if to say: They could in no way escape what the prophets threatened; it followed them step-for-step and caught them. Cf. Deuteronomy 28:15, 45; 2 Samuel 15:14; and conversely Deuteronomy 28:2. m) so that, feeling the punishment foretold by the Prophets, they finally returned and (that is, in a true change, and far differently than they had previously persuaded themselves) said... By this phrase of repetition (says Cocceius in his Lexicon 863), a turning to the contrary is noted—a contrary action. Deuteronomy 8:15, 30:3; Psalm 71:20. n) just as He thought, and predicted through the prophets what He was thinking. Chapter 8:14, 15; Jeremiah 4:28, 51:12. Cf. Amos 4:7. Thus, for example, Jeremiah in Lamentations 1:17 and Daniel in chapter 9:12 and following prayed in the name of the whole people. o) "According to our ways," I say. Verse 4. p) Observe here also (as above in verse 2) an <term>enthymema</term> <note>a logical argument where one premise is implied rather than stated</note>. For the speech to be complete, something must be supplied in this manner: "I finally wrung this confession from your fathers; beware, therefore, lest something similar happen to you." Compare verse 4. Furthermore, this discourse is rightly and deservedly the first, and occupies the frontispiece of the entire prophecy. For it places a true and genuine foundation in the minds of the listeners, from which the care for the Temple and public worship (the restoration of which Zechariah took up as his urgent task) should be derived, so that it does not degenerate into a mere mechanical ritual. Rather, it prepares the listeners and readers alike to accept those promises, which will follow through the whole book, in a pure and worthy manner. Verse 7. q) of the eleventh month. 1 Chronicles 27:14. Thus, nearly a three-month interval passed between the first and second prophetic discourse; see verse 1. r) Shevat. (1) Our January in part, and February in part. s) See the note on verse 1. t) See the same note there. x) by saying. As if to say: this is the word of the Lord which Zechariah later recited. For what follows in verse 8 and beyond are not the words of God, but of the reciting Prophet. Thus follows the second part of the prophetic discourse, which has been the first emblem until now; the scope of this is to encourage the Jews, so that they might not lose heart because of the tribulations and miseries which they had suffered until now, not only in captivity but also in their own land after the return from Babylon. Therefore, he depicts Christ sitting as an Envoy, standing among the myrtles, surrounded by angelic cohorts; so that they may understand that He will stand by them as a protector (v. 8; cf. 1:9). II. Sending out angels to scout and report on the state of the whole earth, and especially Judea; so that they may understand that they are His care and at His heart (v. 9-11). III. Interceding for Jerusalem and the cities of Judah (v. 12). And IV. bringing back the answer of God the Father, full of comfort, concerning the building of the city and Temple, and the multiplication of the Jewish people (v. 13 and following). All of these things lead to the goal that the people might proceed eagerly and vigorously in the building of the Temple they have begun. See Preface §. 8. Verse 8. x) "I saw this night"; the Vulgate says "through the night." A Prophetic Vision (Ephesians 6:1, 5). However, this vision is not to be counted among dreams, as Gurtler (Prophetic Theology, p. 15) concludes from the fact that the Prophet is represented as being awake, lifting his eyes (chapter 2:1), not sleeping. Otherwise, cf. Job 33:15. y) A Vision. Verse 10. Because He appeared under the assumed form of a Man. Cf. Ezekiel 1:26; Daniel 7:13. Note that this name also sometimes denotes masculine strength and virtue more than gender or sex (Isaiah 56:15; Jeremiah 5:23; Proverbs 8:4), which is why it is also attributed to the angel Gabriel in Daniel 9:21. Thus in this place, we interpret the "Man" as the "Angel of Jehovah" from verse 11—not, however, a created one, but the Son of God, who is the prince and Lord of angels, and who is both God and a most unconquerable hero. The ancient masters of the Hebrews in Kimchi appropriately say here: "He is not a Man (at least in the most eminent sense) but the Holy Blessed God," comparing Isaiah 13:3. Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Sephardic philosopher</note> proves on page 1078 that this is the Son of God: α) from divine inspiration or inner speaking (v. 9, 13, 14) which belongs to God alone (1 Peter 1:11). b) from the obedience and service which the ministering spirits perform for Him (v. 11, c. 2:7-8, c. 3:4). c) from His mediatorial, priestly office, because He intercedes for the people (v. 12); his prophetic office, while He instructs the Prophet with an internal breath; and his kingly office, while surrounded by angels, like a Lord in Zion, He shows Himself to be the omnipotent and merciful protector of the people (v. 8). Add d) that he is called "Jehovah" in the nominative case (c. 2:3, 12, c. 3:2). ε) that He forgives sins (c. 3:4; cf. Mark 2:7 and the note on Exodus 23:20). x) "sitting." He presents Himself as a rider, acting as a hero and a military commander. Cf. Psalm 45:5; Revelation 6:2, 19:11. a) "on a red horse." Why the horse was red, Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>12th-century Spanish rabbi and scholar</note> opines should not be sought after any more than why the bread in Judges 7:13 was barley and not wheat. Yet it can hardly be doubted that the color is a symbol of divine vengeance and wrath (cf. v. 15), portending blood and slaughter for the enemies of the Jews. Cf. 2 Kings 3:22; Isaiah 63:2; Revelation 19:11, 13. b) "He was standing," as a defender. c) "among the myrtles": (1) v. 10, 11; Ephesians 41:19. That is, those who are humble and pressed by various tribulations, yet who affect and detain Him with a sweet fragrance, as it were. So in Song of Solomon 2:16, Christ is said to graze among the lilies, and indeed among the "lilies of the depths" or "deep valleys" (cf. v. 1), which likewise seems to hint that He is most affected by the faithful when they are humble and pressed down by tribulations.
