<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on the first chapter of Zechariah, specifically focusing on the first vision of the horses among the myrtle trees. The previous page established the historical context of the second year of King Darius; here, the text moves into the symbolic interpretation of the heavenly messengers and the plea for Jerusalem's restoration after the seventy-year exile.</meta>

### CHAPTER I. ZECHARIAH 1.

of the sons, which the rider carries out, with respect to the Church. In the former way, it is taken from Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> 19:11, 14, where Christ, the victorious commander, and the Saints, who stand on those same sides, are shown as sitting upon white horses. This is appropriately referred there to Christ himself,

<column-break/>

8 I saw [in] the night, and behold, a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood between the myrtles which [were] <gloss>c</gloss> in the deep; and behind him were horses, <gloss>f</gloss> red, <gloss>f</gloss> sorrel <note>original: *seruqqim*; likely a reddish-yellow or speckled color</note>, and white.

9 Then I said, <gloss>h</gloss> “What are these, <gloss>i</gloss> my lord?” And <gloss>l</gloss> the angel <gloss>m</gloss> who talked with me said to me, <gloss>n</gloss> “I will show you what these are.”

10 <gloss>o</gloss> And <gloss>p</gloss> the man standing between the myrtles answered and said, “These are [those] <gloss>q</gloss> whom the Lord has sent <gloss>r</gloss> to walk to and fro through the earth.”

11 <gloss>s</gloss> And they answered the Angel of the Lord standing between the myrtles and said, “We have walked to and fro through the earth, and behold, all the earth sits still and is at rest.”

12 <gloss>t</gloss> Then <gloss>u</gloss> the Angel of the Lord answered and said, “O Lord of Hosts, <gloss>c</gloss> how long will You not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which <gloss>f</gloss> You have had indignation <gloss>g</gloss> these seventy years?”

***

and of his ministers: purity, holiness, splendor, and grace, of which the emblem is the color white.
In the latter way—in Zechariah, where the Angel, the Ruler of God's people, is shown sitting on a red horse. And other angels, who were present with him, on red, sorrel, and white horses: this clearly refers to the state of the Church and divine providence toward it, which divine providence these angels serve according to God's counsel. If God at this or that time or state (in which He has decreed wars and afflictions) governs the church; the angels are shown sitting on red horses; if peace, on white horses. If the sadness of the times, arising from whatever cause, on black horses. If times of a mixed kind and a varied state, on sorrel or chestnut horses.

f) A difficult word <note>original: *seruqqim*</note>. (1) The flow of the speech certainly requires it to be a name of a color; but what kind this may be, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> and David Kimchi confess they do not know. The Chaldean <note>Targum</note> has "pale," which Bochart in *Hieroz.* P. I. 107 conjectures signifies scarlet. Therefore, compare the Talmudic *saraq* and *saqar*, which means to color with red lead; likewise the name *seraq* or *seirikon* (red lead), or *Syricum*, which, according to Pliny 35. c. 6, is made of a mixture of sinopis and sandyx. The Vulgate has "various." Likewise the Septuagint <note>Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> "variegated." They also have, in addition, "dapple-gray," and seem to have expressed it with a double version. Indeed, a "dapple-gray" horse, as Bochart shows, is dark with notable spots, or perhaps ash-colored. But the Arabic interpreter, who composed his version from the Septuagint, expressed the Greek *psaroi* <note>dapple-gray</note> through *shaqar*, which, with the consonants transposed, seems to be entirely harmonious with the Hebrew. And *shaqar* among the Arabs is a bright and shining redness, especially in horses when the mane and tail are also of the same color. Meanwhile, Bochart in the cited place prefers to understand a color that suits flax, wine, and horses alike, collecting the term *seriqim*, which refers to vines in Isaiah 16:8, and *seriqot* flax, which in chapter 19:9 denotes Egyptian flax; namely, a reddish-yellow, close to yellow but more diluted, in German *falb* or *fahl*. So Gussit. 890 interpreted it as the color of the skin or film of the grapes of the Sorek valley; and Cocceius' Lexicon interprets it as crimson or chestnut. g) white. Ch. 6:3, Revelation 6:2.

h) 9. I said to the man sitting on the red horse in verse 8, who was showing me all these things and explaining what was shown. i) "What are these," that is, what do they mean? A question not of curiosity, but of attention, docility, and eagerness for that which God himself offered. Cf. 2:2, 4:4. k) Cocceius compares Psalm 110:1. l) The Angel, the same who was sitting on the red horse in verse 8. For this deals with a subject known from the preceding context, namely that one whom he had seen, and the vision concerning the ministers following him. The Prophet had asked. m) The one who was speaking in me. But the Septuagint, Arabic, Syriac, and Vulgate have "in me": which not only expresses the force and use of the Hebrew particle more strictly, but is also more emphatic, as it connotes an inner speech through the divine inspiration of the Holy Spirit (v. 13, 14; 2:1, 7; Numbers 12:6, 8; 1 Samuel 23:10, 21). n) Cf. 1 Peter 1:10. n) "I will cause you to see," that is, to understand by hearing and seeing. For the Angel satisfies the inquiring Prophet by instructing him both with words that struck the ears (v. 10) and by the deed that affected the sight—namely, the sending in the vision of those Angels to travel through the lands, from where Zechariah saw them return (v. 11). This word refers primarily to the manner of the prophetic vision, through which the Prophet saw and heard all these things (v. 8, v. 10).

o) Therefore he answered. Namely, since he had meanwhile ordered the Angels to travel the lands while the Prophet watched, as they departed, he began to speak anew to the Prophet, so that what he had already seen in action, he might now explain and confirm to him with words. p) The one from v. 8, the same as v. 9: the Angel of the Lord. For he who offers the promised response, saying, "I will make you see what these are," is undoubtedly the same one who is said here to have responded in act. q) Whom I sent, or the Lord God the Father sent, at my command and order. They are messengers and ministers of the Lord, sent for your sake and your good (Hebrews 1:14; Gen 16:7). and r) to travel through the whole earth, not only the land of Judah, but also this world (v. 11). Namely that, having surveyed all the affairs of the nations, they might report to God what they had seen and heard (cf. v. 11). For as Satan, by God's permission, so the good Angels by God's command, wander through the earth, though for very different purposes: the former to accuse the good, the latter to faithfully report what they have seen, so that He may punish the wicked and God may deliver the pious (Ch. 6:7; Job 1:6, 2:1, 2; Matthew 18:10; 1 Peter 5:8).

v. 11. s) Soon, or a little later, these horsemen responded, when they had returned after traveling the earth in the vision and had been asked by the Angel of the Lord—with the Prophet listening—in what state they had found their affairs. t) To the Angel of the Lord (v. 12), who is the man himself sitting on the red horse (v. 8) and the Angel speaking in the Prophet (v. 10). Think of Christ, who intercedes for his people (v. 12, ch. 3:1 ff; Hebrews 7:25) appearing for them before the face of God (Hebrews 9:24). u) To the Angel of His Presence himself (Isaiah 63:9) and his interpreter or mediator (Job 33:23 ff). See our Disputations on the Angel of God, and on the Interpreting Angel, and cf. Genesis 16:7 and the note on Exodus 23:20. x) See v. 8. x) "We have done as you commanded, we have traveled the earth" (v. 10). y) The whole earth, except Judah. This must be supplied from v. 12, where the Angel of the Lord therefore sends prayers to God for Jerusalem and Judah. The sense, then, is: all the neighboring nations flourish with prosperity, or at least their state is tolerable; Judah alone, which the people of God inhabit, is now in great evil and ruin (Nehemiah 1:2, 3; 2:3). z) "is inhabited and at rest" (Ch 7:7; Judges 18:27; 1 Chronicles 4:40). It is a *hendiadys* <note>a figure of speech using two words to express one idea</note> for: "it dwells quietly." Or "to inhabit" in this place should be taken with the adjunct: "dwelling in peace," as in 10:6 and Micah 5:3.

v. 12. a) Therefore he answered. (v. u): He refers to God the Father what the Angels had reported, and commends the cause of his people to Him. b) See note at v. 11. c) "How long." This is not the voice of one complaining, but of one praying urgently that God may make an end of the long-lasting evil. As if to say: You have been angry with your people long enough; therefore, return to them at last with your mercies (v. 16; Psalm 80:5; Psalm 90:13). d) Cf. v. 16; Psalm 102:14. It was because the Jewish people had been led back from exile into their own land, but they had many enemies from the neighboring peoples by whom the whole nation was vexed, subject to insults and contempt; Jerusalem was without walls, the Temple had lain in ruins until three months ago, and at this very time, danger was imminent from the Samaritan adversaries that they might again disturb the begun repair of the temple (cf. Ezra 3:3, 4:1, 4, 5 ff; 5:3; Nehemiah 1:2, 3; 2:3; and Daniel 9:25). Therefore, the Angel asks God to deliver His people from these evils too, just as from the captivity. e) Cf. Jeremiah 34:22. He makes a double object of his intercession: first the metropolis, then the provincial cities of Judah; God keeps the same order in responding. For He deals first with Jerusalem (v. 14, 15, 16) and then with the cities of Judah (v. 17). f) Against whom you have been angry severely and cuttingly, as if they were cursed. Cf. Numbers 23:7, 8; Malachi 1:4; Psalm 7:12. g) "these." This is not only a demonstrative of current or recently elapsed time, but also an exaggeration (as in Isaiah 7:3, 5). And there is an underlying argument from the long duration of the evil to move God's mercy (cf. Psalm 90:15). These are the years of captivity, about which Jeremiah spoke (25:12) and which had already expired in the first year of Cyrus (Ezra 1:1, 2; 2 Chronicles 36:21, 22); but they refer here to the desolation of the Temple and the city of Jerusalem (as in 7:3, 5), for the calculation of which see Haggai 1:1 and 2:3.

***

v. 8. *bametzulah* [in the deep]: Lamed without Dagesh <note>a grammatical mark</note>... [technical Masoretic notes regarding vowel points and accents in various manuscript versions like Erfurdt and Berlin].

<column-break/>

c) Vulgate: "in the deep"; where they happily come forth. Hence in Virgil's *Georgics* II v. 212: "the widest glade for myrtle-groves." Jonathan [the Targum] has: "in Babylon." And so the ancients according to Kimchi, comparing *tzulah* (deep) in Isaiah 44:27. But it seems rather to signify generally persecutions and the cross, under which the Church nevertheless grows, and specifically the humble and miserable state in which the Jewish people still were when Zechariah prophesied these things. Cf. 10:11.

d) And after him, as if after a leader and lord, they were following, ready to carry out his orders (v. 10, 11). Therefore these were ministering Spirits (Hebrews 1:14) and heavenly armies (Revelation 19:14).

e) Horses: as if with their angelic riders (Ch 6:2). Horses of various colors follow him; which is glorious for him, as Rabbi Solomon says. Furthermore, what the horses themselves and their colors denote in prophetic emblems, Vitringa explains brilliantly in his Commentary on the Apocalypse 6:2, p. 328 ff. "The horse," he says, "denotes: α) that the rider of the horse is a minister of divine counsel and providence; β) that he is equipped with the power to execute those counsels of God strongly and swiftly, and is excellently prepared for it." This is the reason why the Angels appeared to Zechariah sitting on horses. For since they are the executors of divine counsels, and administer this world under God, and care for human affairs; horses are given to them in the Emblem so that it may be declared that they are equipped with the necessary power to perform these duties swiftly, promptly, and eagerly. — The color of the horses, however, to which one must especially attend, can signify either the quality of the rider himself who executes the divine counsels, or the kind and quality of the divine counsels.

It provides a deep philological and symbolic analysis of the Hebrew text, interpreting the scene as a heavenly patrol reporting on the earth's state and interceding for the restoration of Jerusalem after seventy years of desolation.</summary>

v. 13. i) **But he answered**, whether the Prophet heard the voice of the one responding in the vision itself, or (which is perhaps more probable and pleases Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, a preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note>) he learned the response of God through the subsequent report of the Angel (v. 14). compare John 2:41. k) **good words**, that is, words full of grace and greatly desired. 1 Kings 12:7. This Accusative case depends not on the Particle "speaking," but on the more remote Verb **answered**, which the accents prove. l) **words**, I say, **of comfort** (3) Isaiah 57:18. This is emphasized by the adjectives. Indeed, this Name is either an adjective, as Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval biblical commentator and grammarian</note> proves; or it is a substitution of the absolute state for the constructed state in the preceding Name, resolved in this way: **words (words, I say) of comforts**. compare the index notes 18, 14; Moses 14:3; Ezekiel 11:16, etc.

v. 14. m) **For he said to me.** The Angel now explains that good response from v. 13 to the Prophet, so that he in turn may explain it to the people. z) see v. 9. o) **proclaim** with a high and sonorous voice, so that your people may hear this longed-for response of God and rejoice. v. 17. p) see the note on Nehemiah 1:12. q) **I have been jealous for Jerusalem**; at this very time, a burning zeal for my people has returned. For he who is jealous, says Jerome <note>Early Christian scholar and Bible translator</note>, shows that he loves (though he is jealous), comparing Ezekiel 16:42. This word, when constructed with a Dative, is taken in a good sense; with an Accusative or the prefix *ל* (to), it is taken in a bad sense, compare chapter 8:2; Joel 2:18. r) v. 17; chapter 9:9; see note on Isaiah 51:17. s) **with great jealousy**. For it affects me very badly that Jerusalem and Zion, which I love, have been harmed by enemies beyond measure and too cruelly, as seen in v. 15. compare chapter 8:2; Isaiah 9:6; 26:11.

v. 15. t) compare Isaiah 34:2. u) **over those nations at ease**. It is regarded, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> observed,

*tumultuous; as if from* שאן *they are noisy. compare 2 Kings 19:28. Such had been not only the Babylonians, but also the neighboring Edomites, Ammonites, Moabites, etc., after the destruction of the Babylonian Kingdom, finally resting securely under the Persian empire.* x) **because**. Isaiah 63:15. y) **I was angry with Jerusalem a little or moderately**, namely, compared to her guilt and to that which the cruelty of the enemies added. v. 2; Isaiah 47:6; compare 1 Chronicles 21:13. Otherwise, the wrath of the Lord was certainly great in itself, see below chapter 7:12. a) **they helped** (as if an accumulation were added) **toward evil** 2 Chronicles 20:23, namely, by excessive cruelty and continuous tribulation, beyond measure and without end. Isaiah 47:6; compare 2 Chronicles 28:9, 10. The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> says: *they joined in attacking for evil.* **Jerome:** *He is angry with the nations—because he himself delivered them (his people) to be corrected, but those nations raged against those delivered to them; just as if a father wanted a son to be amended by a tutor, but the tutor tried to kill and punish him as an enemy.* v. 16. b) **Therefore, or may you finally experience more joyful things in place of past calamity.** Jeremiah 30:16. c) v. 14; Nahum 1:12. d) **I have turned or returned to Jerusalem** chapter 8:3; Isaiah 63:17; Psalm 80:15; Psalm 90:13. e) **with mercies.** The plural is emphatic, to suggest the riches and greatness of divine mercy. Isaiah 54:7, 8. Reference is made here to the intercession of the Angel in v. 12, and thus it is signaled that although the wrath of God upon the Jews was long-lasting, it was not perpetual, as it was, for example, over the Edomites in Malachi 1:4. compare Isaiah 12:1; Psalm 60:3. f) **my house**, which lay in ruins until the first year of Cyrus, and from then on remained in its first foundations due to the malevolence of adversaries, will now be built. See the Preface § 7 and compare chapter 6:12; Jeremiah 30:18. g) see Haggai 2:1, 3. h) The Vulgate <note>The Latin Bible</note> says: **and the plumb line**. The Septuagint: **a measure**. Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note>: **a measuring cord shall be extended over Jerusalem** for measuring it and seeing how much its width and how much its length ought to be, chapter 2:5, 6; compared with 2 Kings 21:13; Isaiah 44:13; Job 38:5. This was done successively in type, especially by Nehemiah, who fortified the city with gates and a common wall. Nehemiah 2:17 and following. For the anti-type <note>The spiritual fulfillment</note> compare Jeremiah 31:38. v. 17. i) **Still** (besides those things which he already ordered to be proclaimed in v. 14 and following) **proclaim further.** *This suggests the abundance and excellence of the divine promise.* compare Job 36:2. k) That is: they have indeed endured many and by far the greatest evils until now, but this period will finally have an end, and another state, more longed for by them, will follow. compare Genesis 8:22. l) **they shall be spread out or shall spread themselves**. **Kimchi** explains it thus: *Because of the abundance of good and tranquility which they will have, they will be dispersed here and there, and the land will be inhabited everywhere.* compare 2 Samuel 20:22. Thus the explanation in this place could be what follows in chapter 2:8. But **Schultens** in his *Observations* page 330 and following, praises the Vulgate: **my cities shall flow with good things.** From the Arabic *fatsa*, to flow, to abound, to overflow, which he thinks is the primary notion of the root, while "to be dispersed" is secondary and arises from it; that is, to be poured out, spread out, compare Proverbs 5:16; Job 40:6. Thus Jonathan: *they shall be filled.* The Septuagint: *they shall be poured out.* **Abarbanel** <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a Portuguese Jewish statesman and philosopher</note>, however, wanders completely from the mark, contending that the captivity and devastation of the Second Temple is suggested by these words: *they shall be dispersed from good, that is, the inhabitants of the city shall be plucked away from all good and from the good land; but he will yet comfort, etc., namely, besides the consolation which the Jews, liberated from the Babylonian captivity, have now received.* m) He calls them **his cities**, meaning the Judean ones (v. 12), to show the affection of his love. n) **and he will further comfort**, as of old. Isaiah 12:1; chapter 66:13; compare Psalm 85:10. o) chapter 2:16; chapter 3:2; Isaiah 14:1; Psalm 132:13. **CHAPTER II, v. 1.** p) **Then I lifted up my eyes.** v. 5; chapter 6:1; Genesis 18:2; compare note on chapter 1:8. q) the same vision as in chapter 1:8; compare here v. 2 and 7, where the speaker is the same as in chapter 1. Therefore, in this chapter follows I. **The second emblem**, showing four horns to be cast down by four craftsmen, with the explanation added in verses 1–4. II. **The third emblem**, showing a man measuring the structure of the city, both a) in itself v. 5, 6, and b) with an explanation in v. 7 to the end. r) **4 horns.** Jonathan: **kingdoms.** So v. 2. *Horns in prophetic emblems signify nations and kingdoms ferocious in their strength*, compare Daniel 7:7, 8; chapter 8:3, 5–9; here, however, especially those hostile to Israel and Judah, compare v. 2. *The number four* (as we noted at Ezekiel 1:5) involves a reference to the four quarters of the world; compare below v. 10. In this place, it peculiarly denotes the nations attacking the Jewish people from everywhere and from the four quarters of the world: such as the Syrians, Assyrians, Babylonians from the North, and those who most recently troubled the Jews returning from exile, the Samaritans; the Ammonites and Moabites from the East; the Edomites and Egyptians from the South; and finally the Philistines from the West. compare Isaiah 9:11. Thus, among others, the celebrated **Maius (1678)** explains it. According to **Guitlavo (Prophetic Theology 133)**, *there are 4 supreme empires* under which the Jews subsequently had harsh fates: the Babylonian or Assyrian, the Persian, the Greek, and the Roman, destroyed by others and to be destroyed further. This is also the explanation of **D. Kimchi, Abarbanel**, etc., though it differs from others. In whatever way it is explained, the aim of this vision is at least sufficiently evident. For it comforts the Jews by showing that they should not lose heart, no matter how much they have been tossed by the storms of their enemies or are even now troubled: for God will not fail His Church but will send those who may restrain those enemies everywhere and at all times; so that, just as four horns attack the Jews, three [sic] <note>likely a typo for 'four'</note> craftsmen are opposed to them by God, or are to be opposed, to cast down those horns, so that they who intended devastation for the people of God may themselves be devastated. Let the Jews only proceed to convert themselves and build the temple as they had begun; they should commit the obstacles to God. v. 2. s) **And I said**, that is, praying, what this emblem meant for itself. chapter 1:9. t) This is the very one whom he had seen standing among the myrtles in chapter 1:8. u) chapter 8:9; 4:4; 6:4.

<margin>
*) This is a mixture of symbolic and literal speech, to be resolved thus: These horns are a symbol of those nations, etc. <term>Ien.</term> <note>Likely referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> These are the kingdoms (see verse 1, 4). y) **They scattered**, by driving them into captivity, or by continuous harassment, causing them to migrate to all regions of the world in voluntary exile. (see v. 4 compared with v. 10; also Jeremiah 40:12, 41:17, Ezekiel 5:10, 12). z) Therefore it also refers to the Assyrians, who took the ten tribes of Israel captive. Unless by the name "Israel" here are meant those of the ten tribes who joined the kingdom of Judah: which is proven by the fact that "Israel" in this place is not only placed after Judah, but is even placed in the middle between Judah and Jerusalem.

...prediction in Isaiah 13:5, Jeremiah 50:25. **v. 4. d)** *See verse 2.* **e)** *What are these (craftsmen) coming to do? To what end do they come?* **f)** *These things are repeated from verse 3, not only to be explained more clearly, but also so that the connection which the craftsmen have with those horns might become more conspicuous.* **g)** For <term>R. Solomon</term> <note>Rashi, a famous medieval commentator</note> this phrase is "pregnant," involving more than is expressed in words, to be described in this way: *they cast down Judah and humbled or depressed him, so that, etc.* For in this way the following member of the sentence fits together better. **h)** *according to.* And this Name notes the mode, reason, and proportion of a thing. Others: *they made him like a man or after the likeness of a man, who etc.* (compare Malachi 2:9). **i)** <term>Jon.</term> <note>Targum Jonathan</note> *nor did they allow a man to walk with an upright stature.* (compare Micah 2:3). The lifting of the face generally denotes joy and boldness (compare Psalm 3:4, Job 10:15, 11:15, 22:26, Luke 21:28); therefore its negation imports sadness, grief, and desperation or a "lack of way" in the soul. (compare Judges 8:28). **k)** *Therefore these craftsmen came.* (see verse 3). **l)** *to terrify those horns.* This verb involves some regard for the security of those nations, from the abuse of which they had insulted the people of God (compare 1:11, 15; Ezekiel 30:9). Truly a terror not in vain, but with a deadly effect: it is to be understood that the verb *to cast down* is added. **m)** *to cast down.* (Lamentations 3:52; compare Psalm 75:11). **z)** *of those lifting up a horn with a wicked and proud effort.* (compare 1 Kings 11:26, 27; Psalm 75:5, 6). A metaphor from fierce and butting animals. **o)** <term>Jon.</term> *to carry her away.* See note on verse 2. **v. 5. p)** *See verse 1.* Here begins the third symbol. **q)** (chapter 1:8). To <term>R. Solomon</term> he is the same as the Angel-interlocutor in verse 7; and rightly so, for he whom the prophet addressed as departing in verse 6, he describes as coming out in verse 7, and in such a way that he clearly identifies him as that Angel-interlocutor. (compare therefore 1:8 and 4:3). **r)** *a measuring line.* (Jeremiah 31:39, Ezekiel 40:3). Concerning the sense and fulfillment of this vision, it should be observed that, according to the time in which Zechariah prophesied, it most closely hints at the building of Jerusalem and the physical multiplication of the Jewish people, and the further departure from Babylon properly so called; these promises held no small comfort for the Jewish people, who were greatly afflicted until now. And so it also happened in reality not much later: for Nehemiah restored the walls of Jerusalem, as we noted above at 1:16; the people grew and were diffused through all of Canaan, occupying not only Judea, but also Galilee and the region across the Jordan, as even Gospel history teaches us; Ezra also later led a new colony of Jews from Babylon back into Judea (Ezra 7:1, 6, etc.). Meanwhile, the prophecy is certainly more grand than the mentioned events. From these, therefore, it proceeds by ascending to the final and chief fulfillment in the Messiah and his kingdom. This kind of prophetic "elevation" is frequent in our author (compare Preface § 10). Thus <term>D. Kimchi</term> <note>David Kimchi, medieval grammarian and commentator</note> says: "It is fitting that this vision looks to the days of the Messiah, just like the visions of Ezekiel 40 onwards, where the Angel measures the length and width of Jerusalem." **v. 6. s)** *Where are you going?* (chapter 5:10). **t)** *to measure.* (Ezekiel 40:5, Revelation 11:1). **u)** *to see*, that is, so that you and others may see; or according to <term>Schm.</term> <note>likely Sebastian Schmidt, a 17th-century theologian</note> *so that I may see.* He says, therefore, that he is about to build Jerusalem, and for that purpose he establishes the boundaries of width and length. **x)** *how great* (as if to say, according to what) *it ought to be.* (Genesis 47:8). The Greek says: "how great is its width and its length." (compare Revelation 21:16). **v. 7. y)** *But behold* (Ezekiel 1:4). The Angel, who spoke in me (verse 2), went out from his place (from the myrtles, 1:8) in verse 5 to measure Jerusalem, whom the Prophet had seen departing and had addressed in verse 6 for the sake of completing the work. Moreover, he goes out, not to desert the myrtles or his people by leaving, but so that he may be understood to be uniquely present for their unique necessity. It expresses the actual application of care in Christ, by which he actually approaches the building of Jerusalem, and signifies that it will be perfected soon (compare Isaiah 51:5, also Jeremiah 4:7). **x)** *another angel was going out from elsewhere to meet him* to receive and execute his commands, by whom he had been summoned (compare note on 1:8). **v. 8. a)** *The Angel-interlocutor said therefore to him, who had gone out to meet him.* And indeed he speaks with authority, so that it appears he is the Lord of Angels or Jehovah himself (verse 3; see again note on 1:8). **b)** *run.* go immediately and say (2 Kings 4:26). **c)** *to this young man,* (Judges 6:20), Zechariah, whom this title makes probable was still of a youthful age. Nor has God elsewhere despised that age in choosing Prophets. (See 1 Samuel 3:1 etc., Jeremiah 1:6, 7). Thus <term>A. Ezra</term> <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra</note>: "Three prophesied as boys or youths: Zechariah, Samuel, and Jeremiah." (compare 1 Timothy 4:12). The angel is sent to explain the symbol to the prophet, which he had seen while the Angel-interlocutor himself was measuring the city. (compare Daniel 8:16, Revelation 17:1, 21:9). **d)** *villages or country towns* (Esther 9:19) which do not have walls (Ezekiel 38:11). For they are distinguished from fortified cities in Deuteronomy 3:5, 1 Samuel 6:18. **e)** They explain this in different ways. The Vulgate: *without a wall* (as if to say, through the villages, in the manner of villages) *it shall be inhabited.* (compare 9:5, Joel 4:10). So R. Sal. <note>Rashi</note>. And Maius p. 1078 narrates the argument similarly: he says, "because of the very great abundance of men, it is to be inhabited without walls." But we prefer it thus: *Jerusalem shall inhabit villages,* by metonymy; that is, the multitude or people of Jerusalem. Which Kimchi explains thus: "Very many shall dwell outside the city, because the city will not contain them, even though it will be much longer and wider than it ever was; therefore many will dwell outside it in villages and country towns, without wall, gates, or bars, because they will dwell securely and without fear from any man, because they will have me as a wall of fire." (compare 1:17, Isaiah 49:19, 20).

<column-break/>

**v. 3. a)** *But on the contrary,* lest I should tremble while looking only at the horns with my tribes, he also showed me (verse 1; 3:1). **b)** *Jehovah,* in the direct case, who was just called the Angel of Jehovah and the Angel speaking in me (verse 1, 1:11, etc.). See what we noted above at 1:8. **c)** *four craftsmen* with their iron tools, to cast down those horns (verse 4). Craftsmen of destruction, surely (Ezekiel 21:36), whom God created for destroying, intending to use their work to blunt the enemies of the Church (Isaiah 54:16). Some Christians, as well as Hebrews, understand Zerubbabel, Joshua, Ezra, and Nehemiah. But although these four men deserved great praise from the Jews returning from exile, they do not seem to fit everywhere what the Lord predicates of the craftsmen in verse 4. For how did they terrify the nations? Or how did they cast them down? Rather, as we interpreted the four horns as enemies from...

f) *because of the multitude of men;* <note>original Latin: "prae copia hominum"</note> this was the situation at the time when Zechariah was prophesying, and during the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 7:4; cf. below 8:4, 5). 
g) *v. 9. I indeed,* <note>original Latin: "Ego vero"</note> lest anyone suspect that the city would be exposed to the incursions of enemies since I said in verse 8 that it would be inhabited without walls. *I will be &c.*
h) *a wall of fire,* <note>original Latin: "murus igneus"</note> which the enemies will neither be able to overcome nor attempt to cross with impunity (2 Kings 6:17; cf. below 8:9; Isaiah 26:1, 60:18; Proverbs 18:10; also Nehemiah 3:35 and 1 Samuel 25:16). 
i) *protecting it from all sides* <note>original Latin: "undique eam tutaturus"</note> (Psalm 34:8, 125:2).
k) *and I will be for glory,* <note>original Latin: "in gloriam ero"</note> that is, I will make my glory conspicuous; I will demonstrate myself to be the glorious God by protecting my own and prostrating the enemies, which will also be glorious for Jerusalem itself (v. 12; Isaiah 4:2, 11:10; Psalm 84:12, 85:10). *Kimchi* <note>Rabbi David Kimchi, a 12th-13th century Jewish scholar</note> restricts this primarily to the glorious protection of the Church (cf. Isaiah 4:5). *Jonathan* <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note> says: *I will make my Divine Presence or majesty dwell gloriously.* cf. Revelation 21:11. 
l) see v. 14, 15.
m) *v. 10. Ho! Ho!* <note>original Latin: "Heus! heus!"</note> v. 11; Isaiah 55:1. Jonathan introduces it with: *Cry out to the dispersed.* This is a heavenly summons or arousal of the people of God, drawn from the preceding verses and confirmed in the following ones (v. 12ff). It is as if he says: Since Jerusalem has such great and certain promises from God, it is your duty—whoever among you pants for the salvation of Jerusalem—to leave Babylon behind and betake yourselves immediately to its bosom, so that you may participate in its goods with her. Cf. Isaiah 66:10-14. *Kimchi* says these words are directed to those who had remained in Babylon and had not yet gone up from there in the first opportunity, who are now warned to leave and return to Jerusalem and build the Temple because the time has now arrived. *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century statesman and philosopher</note> refutes this opinion, however, as if it poorly fits the context, because it is said:

rather than to the exit from Babylon properly speaking (cf. especially Revelation 18:4), yet nothing prevents us from including that here, and all the more so because Zechariah's entire prophecy was prepared to excite and uplift the Jewish people of his own time, often ascending from present things to future ones, and conversely returning from future things to present ones, or finally connecting both skillfully. See note on Jeremiah 1:14. p) *according to, or, as if into the four cardinal winds*, that is, into all parts of the world (Ezekiel 37:9). q) *Sch. I will expand you.* <note>Sch. refers to a scholarly interpretation, likely suggesting a positive spreading out</note> Thus it would be a promise and would cohere with the first half of the verse, as an outcome of movement or flight, taking the sense that the Lord wishes to amplify and increase them if they go out. But because the verb is in the Perfect tense, we prefer to interpret it in a negative sense, *I have expanded, I have scattered you*; as in Ezekiel 17:21 and Psalm 68:15. The connection with the preceding member here will be: I commanded you to flee from the land of the north, in which you have been chiefly scattered and held captive, just as in other lands; do so therefore; for I desire that there finally be an end to the immense evil with which I afflicted you, because according to the four winds &c. Thus the sense is explanatory rather than causal. Indeed, how the Jews were scattered into the four winds, we have declared above at verse 1. *u v. 11. r) Ho! I say* (v. 10). Jonathan introduces: *Cry out to the assembly of Zion and say to her.* s) ch. 1:14, 17. t) rescue yourself by swift flight, lest you come into a share of the evils with Babylon (Genesis 19:17, 22; Jeremiah 51:6). x) *Vulgate: you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.* A similar expression is in Jeremiah 46:19; cf. note on Numbers 21:25, 26. & c. v. 12. x) Because, to further explain what the Lord is about to do for your sake and for your comfort. y) ch. 1:3, 4. z) Here the Speaking Person is especially to be noted: it is Jehovah of Hosts, God the Son, who leads the angelic armies (ch. 1:8), who has spoken in and with the Prophet thus far (v. 1, 7). By reason of essence, he is Jehovah with God the Father (v. 3, cf. v. 2); by reason of personality, he is distinct from him, seeing as he sent him (v. 13, 15). Here, therefore, speaking through a ministerial Angel (v. 7, 8), he explains the counsel of grace committed to him by God the Father. For what he says in verse 13, *I will be waving my hand over the nations, that they may become a spoil to those who served them,* and also in verse 15, *They shall be my people, and I will dwell in your midst, etc.,* the Prophet cannot say of himself, nor can a ministerial Angel. Yet what is immediately added there—*And you shall feel that Jehovah of Hosts has sent me to you*—does not fit God the Father. Thus, this is an excellent passage concerning the Deity of Christ and the mystery of the plurality of persons in the Godhead. a) *Jonathan: After the glory which was promised* to be brought upon you. Doubtless, reference is made to verse 9. As if to say: it is not enough for me to manifest my glory in Israel; I will moreover make my name illustrious among the nations themselves, giving them to you as a spoil, partly by converting them, partly by taking vengeance on them. Therefore, *after the glory* in this place is *above or beyond the glory*, signifying the addition of a huge heap to the glory (Isaiah 4:5). Thus in Isaiah 49:6, God the Father says to the Son: *It would be a light thing,* for the dignity of your person and office, *to be my servant only for raising up the tribes of Jacob... for I will also give you as a light to the nations &c. Kimchi* connects it thus: *It will not suffice for God to repay you with good in place of the evil you suffered in captivity; but he will also take vengeance on your enemies who plundered you.* b) v. 13, 15. cf. Isaiah 48:16 and the note there. Moreover, he is sent to those nations so that he may convert the penitent to the obedience of faith and take punishment from the impenitent, according to Psalm 2:8-end, etc. c) As if to say: because it is also for your sake, for. d) *touching, or, whoever touches you*, that is, harms you (Genesis 26:11; Jeremiah 12:14; Psalm 105:14, 15). Rightly *Jerome* says: *Take "touching" to mean vexation and injury.* e) *touches the apple <note>The Hebrew word refers to the "pupil" or "gate" of the eye</note> of his eye.* So David Kimchi, taking the pronoun reflexively. As if to say: effectively he harms himself most, for God will not allow you to be harmed with impunity. But to refer the evil to God: *the apple of His eye*, that is, of Jehovah of Hosts, for which the *Vulgate* has *my eye.* This indicates both God's supreme and most tender care in guarding his own, and the severity and certainty of vengeance if anyone harms them (cf. Deuteronomy 32:10; Psalm 17:8). God interprets that which is done to his people and servants as being done to Himself (cf. Matthew 25:40, 45; Acts 9:4). *v. 13. f) Because,* if you wish to know what I am about to do with those nations. g) *I am about to wave my hand*, which is a sign of one fiercely threatening or inflicting a blow (Isaiah 10:32, 19:16). h) It is said in... panting for the fault (v. 12). i) *Vulgate: to those who served them.* cf. Obadiah v. 17. k) *and then you will know from the outcome of this promise* (ch. 4:9, 9, 6:15; Ezekiel 5:13). *Kimchi: when this prophecy occurs, namely in the days of the Messiah.* l) v. 12, 15; ch. 4:9, 6:15; Isaiah 48:16. Here he says he was sent to predict; but above, namely in verse 12, to carry out what was to happen. *v. 14. m) Therefore shout and rejoice.* cf. ch. 9:9; Isaiah 12:6, 65:18; Zephaniah 3:14. Rightly *Kimchi* says: *It is most appropriate to explain this entire prophecy from verse 14 to the end as concerning the days of the Messiah, because verse 15 says "Many nations shall be joined."* In the meantime, although the matter of joy was yet to be in the future when Zechariah prophesied these things, the joy nevertheless pertained also to that very time, imparting relief to the afflicted Jews in their distress and strength of soul in their difficulties (cf. Nehemiah 8:10). n) *behold I* (the emphasis of the particle brings the future thing as if present, hinting at the certainty as well as the haste of the event) *am coming;* I, I say, whom the Father promised would come through so many ages past (ch. 9:9; Habakkuk 2:3; Psalm 40:8; cf. Matthew 11:3). Jonathan: *I will be revealed*. cf. Isaiah 40:5. o) *and I will dwell in your midst* as if in my temple, about to manifest myself to you by my coming in the flesh, by the operations and gifts of grace, and finally in glory (v. 15; ch. 8:3; Ezekiel 43:9; John 1:14; 2 Corinthians 6:18; Revelation 21:3). Reference is made to the shadow of the Tabernacle and the Levitical Temple (Leviticus 26:11, 12; Deuteronomy 12:5; Psalm 78:60). *Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> Lexicon 894: If a true dwelling <note>original Greek: σκήνωσις (skēnōsis)</note> had already preceded, he says, no mention would be made of another dwelling <note>original Greek: σκηνώσεως (skēnōseōs)</note> after that one. Yet the ark of the Lord was neither to be sought nor remembered (under the New Testament) (Jeremiah 3:16). When God is manifested in the flesh, then he truly dwells in us. God's house is not a tabernacle made by hands (Acts 7:48, 17:24).

# CHAPTER 2. 3. Zechariah 2, 3

<margin>
**v. 15. p)** They are joined, moreover, out of and with Israel to be united into one body <note>original Latin: "in unum corpus coalituri"</note> (Isaiah 14:1) to serve the Lord and to love the name of Jehovah, so that they may be His servants (chapter 56:3, 6). This connects with verse 14 in a similar way that verse 12 connects with the preceding ones. Namely, it attaches the conversions of the nations to the promise given to Israel, so that it appears the benefit of the Lord’s coming pertains not to the Jews alone, but to all peoples. **q)** Compare chapter 6:15; 8:22, 23; Isaiah 2:2, 3; 11:10; 52:15; 60:3; Jeremiah 16:19; Micah 4:2; Zephaniah 2:11; etc. **r)** *And they shall become,* those who join you, *my people.* Concerning the assumption of the Israelite people into the covenant of grace, it is said elsewhere: Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Deuteronomy 27:9. Compare below chapter 8:8; Ezekiel 11:20. **s)** *I will dwell,* I say. See verse 14 and the note there. **t)** See the notes for verses 12 and 14.
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 16. u)** *And He shall inherit,* He will possess Judah as an inheritance. Exodus 34:9; Psalm 32:8. **x)** *as His portion.* Deuteronomy 32:9. **y)** so that it is and remains the portion of Jehovah in the holy land, having been brought back there from the land of captivity. Compare Exodus 3:5 and the note on Isaiah 24:5. **z)** *and He will choose further,* those whom He had rejected for a time because of their sins, intending to confirm and continue the grace of election for them (chapter 1:17; 3:2).
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 17. a)** *Be silent, therefore,* <note>original Latin: "Sile itaque"</note> (8) Amos 6:8. This is a "majestic imperative," and also a prophetic one, as in Habakkuk 2:20 and Zephaniah 1:7. He effectively commands silence, and by the very act of commanding, he predicts the future: that all humanity <note>original Latin: "universa caro", literally "all flesh"</note> shall be made obedient to the Gospel of Christ, and will finally follow the Lord—whom they had impiously contradicted—with a worshipful silence. Compare Isaiah 45:23; 52:15. *I arrange.* <note>The word "Digero" appears to be a catchword or a note on the arrangement of the text.</note>

<gloss>c</gloss> *than* or *because He shall be roused;* like one who is stirred or wakes from sleep (chapter 4, verse 1; compared with Psalm 78:65). This is to say: enough time has passed during which God behaved as if sleeping, neglecting His people because of their own sins, and leaving the whole world to its errors. Now, finally, having shaken off that state as if in springtime, He will manifest Himself much more illustriously than of old, not only to the Jews but to all nations. Compare Isaiah 51:9; Psalm 44:24. *He shall be revealed.* <note>original Latin: "revelabitur"</note> **d)** *from the habitation of His holiness,* that is, from heaven. Deuteronomy 26:15; Jeremiah 25:30.

**CHAPTER III. v. 1. e)** Afterward, the interpreting Angel—the one who was sitting on the red horse in chapter 1:8 and 2:2ff—causes me to see. This chapter explains the **Fourth Vision**, in which he saw Joshua the High Priest accused by Satan (v. 1), acquitted by the Lord (v. 2–5), and stirred to diligent care of his office under the hope of angelic fellowship (v. 6, 7). Finally, it offers the promise of the Messiah’s coming to encourage him and his companions against any adversities (v. 8–10). The goal of the vision seems to be this: to show that until the true Priest should be manifested in the flesh—by whose unique sacrifice the iniquity of the land would be expiated—God would uphold the Levitical priesthood for the sake of the people's grace, even though the Devil worked to make its ministers hateful to God due to their various failings. If they would proceed vigorously in restoring the sacred worship, it would result in their good, despite Satan's vain opposition, and eventually the types and shadows would be succeeded by the "antitype" <note>the reality prefigured by the symbol</note> and the truth. **f)** *Joshua, the High Priest,* the head of his companions (v. 8) and the leader of sacred rites at that time (Haggai 1:1; Ezra 3:2, 8). He prefigured Jesus Christ, the true Priest, both in name (as the previous Joshua did; see notes on Joshua 1:1) and in his high-priestly office (Hebrews 4:14; 9:11; compare here v. 9). He is also represented below as both priest and king (chapter 6:11ff). Just as in this place, when he is led to judgment as a leader among his people (see Leviticus 21:4 and the note there) and is acquitted, it is credible that he stood as a clear "type" <note>a prophetic symbol</note> of our Savior. Compare Isaiah 53:8; 1 Timothy 3:16. **g)** whom God had nevertheless sanctified in a singular way (Leviticus 21:10ff). But if Satan accused the High Priest himself, who was the people's mediator before God (Hebrews 5:1), then he was attacking the entire people at once. **h)** *standing,* as a defendant (v. 3) and accused because of sins (v. 4). **i)** *before the Angel of Jehovah* as judge, who gives the sentence in his own name and the Father’s (v. 2ff). See note on chapter 1:11. Furthermore, *the Angel of Jehovah*, says Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa, a prominent 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> (on Revelation 12:7, p. 719), who could this be but the Son of God, a true participant in divinity? For is there any person in heaven so glorious besides the Son of God, to whom the Father commits judgment over men and Satan himself, as in this place, besides the Son of God? (John 5:22). Certainly, we are so persuaded that the "Angel Jehovah" named by this mystical title in Old Testament Scripture (Exodus 3:2; 23:20; Isaiah 63:9) is marked with such evident characteristics of true divinity that one must either say God shared His glory with a non-God, or the Church must recognize and adore in this Angel the true and proper Son of God. Scripture teaches He was not created, is superior to all heavenly power, is the Lord and judge of all nature, the prince of the army of God’s people, and their mediator and intercessor with God—characteristics which belong to Michael the Archangel (Daniel 12:1, etc.). **k)** *Satan* indeed, who bears his name from "opposing" and "accusing," because by accusing he stands in the way of the godly before God (v. 2; Job 1:6; 2:1; Revelation 12:9, 10). **l)** *was standing at his right hand.* Psalm 109:6. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Hebraist</note> (Lexicon 311) suggests this was a ritual in Oriental courts: the accuser, dragging the defendant to the judge, would be at his right hand. Compare Daniel 10:13; 1 Chronicles 21:1. Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow, a Lutheran theologian</note> notes: That Satan pretended to have a sufficiently grave cause for his accusation is indicated by that phrase, when he is said to have stood not at the left, but at the right of Joshua. For in Scripture, he is said to stand at the right and accuse who supports a good cause in judgment; at the left, one who supports a bad cause and is rightly accused. Or, as Gregory says, we speak of having something on the right when we consider it great, and on the left when we despise it. **m)** *to oppose him* (6); like an accuser against a defendant (Psalm 71:13 and 109:20, 29), so that Satan, named for his "opposing," might fulfill the measure of his name. Compare the noun in Ezra 4:6. **n)** As for the matter of the accusation, Scripture does not express it here. However, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> and Kimchi think it was because Joshua’s sons had married foreign women (Ezra 10:18) against divine law (Exodus 34:16; Deuteronomy 7:3). Thus, the Devil would have accused Joshua of the same "turning a blind eye" toward his sons of which Eli was guilty in ancient times (1 Samuel 3:13), with the goal that God would destroy him and his sons, just as he once accused Job (Job 1:2, 3). Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> also holds this; see below at verse 3. But even if we admit this, Joshua must be considered here not only in his own person or his sons', but as the head of his entire people (of whom the High Priest was the head, Leviticus 21:4). Therefore, he likely carried the sins of the people as a type of Jesus Christ, and was accused in divine judgment for that reason; Zechariah interpreted what he saw happening to the prince Joshua as happening to the whole people. Hence the Angel, delivering the sentence against the Devil, calls Jehovah the one "choosing Jerusalem" (v. 2), and below in verse 9, he promises that the iniquity of the whole land will be abolished.

The commentary interprets Joshua as a symbolic "type" of Christ, defending the priesthood against Satan's legalistic accusations through the mediation of the Angel of the Lord.</summary>

# THE TWELVE PROPHETS: ZECHARIAH CHAPTER 3

<column-break/>

**v. 2. n)** **And Jehovah said.** Kimchi correctly notes: "This is the Angel"; however, it is absurd when he adds that the Angel is called by his Master's name. For I do not believe it ever happens that anyone would call the legate of King Louis, or any other King, by the name of Louis or the King himself. But see what we noted at verse 1 from the celebrated Vitringa; and compare Jude verse 9. **o)** **May Jehovah [God the Father] rebuke you, Satan**, effectively restraining your insolence, by which you rise up against Joshua and my people in the judgment of God; or, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> has it: "so that it is not permitted for you to come before His face to accuse this righteous man." See Isaiah 17:13; Psalm 9:6; Psalm 68:31. Jerome says: "The Lord speaks concerning another Lord <note>original Latin: 'Dominus de altero Domino'; a reference to the Trinity, compare Genesis 19:24</note>, not because the Lord who speaks is unable to rebuke, but because out of the unity of nature, when the one has rebuked, He who speaks rebukes also." Thus says Jerome. But these words furthermore signify an admirable modesty (compare Jude verse 9) and present this Angel as a mediator, as above in chapter 1:12; compare Job 33:23. **p)** **Rebuke, I say.** An emphatic repetition. **q)** This depends on the name of Jehovah. Jonathan <note>The Targum</note> says: "to whom it was pleasing to place His Shekhinah <note>Divine Presence</note> in Jerusalem." This refers back to chapter 1:17 and chapter 2:16. It is as if to say: Jehovah, out of the riches of His love and mercies, has decreed to choose Jerusalem again; therefore, let Him rebuke you because you attempt to overturn that decree of grace with your accusations. Compare Romans 8:31, 33. **r)** **This man**, namely, Joshua with the whole people, whom he represents; compare the note on verse 1. **s)** **is like a burnt brand**, that is, half-burned. (3) Isaiah 7:4; Amos 4:11. **t)** Along with his people, he has only recently been snatched from the fire, and that by the gracious counsel of God, by which He chose Jerusalem again: you, therefore, wicked one, ought not to have demanded him back to the

back to the flame again, and thus further assist the evil which he has already suffered in great measure (chapter 1:15), and resist God when He has decreed to show His grace in him. Compare Jude verse 23.
**v. 3. u)** **In filthy garments** (2) verse 4. Compare Isaiah 4:4; Proverbs 30:12. Garments generally signify the state and condition 

---

and habit of a person: therefore, by "filthy," understand guilt and sins, according to verse 4, of which they are a symbol (Revelation 3:4). Conversely, "change of clothes" or "clean clothes" denote righteousness, as seen below in verses 4 and 5, and Revelation 3:18, 7:14, and 19:8. Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan</note> notes: As for Joshua, he had sons who had taken wives who were not worthy of the priesthood. See the note on verse 1. **x)** **And so he stood, etc.** See verse 1. **v. 4. y)** **Jehovah said to those standing before Him**, the Angels. See chapter 1:8. Jonathan: "to those ministering before Him." 1 Kings 10:8; compare Hebrews 1:7, 14. For that Angel, says Kimchi, was greater than the others and sent them. Indeed, he is as much greater as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs (Hebrews 1:4ff), since he is Jehovah Himself; compare verse 5 here. **z)** **Remove, etc.** Esther 4:4. Jonathan: "Tell him to cast out the wives who are not worthy of the priesthood from his house." See note on verse 1. The interpreters refer back to Ezra 10:18, 19. Truly, the removal of filthy garments rather denotes the non-imputation of sins (Romans 4:8; 2 Corinthians 5:19), just as the putting on of "change of clothes" denotes the imputation of righteousness in the divine judgment (Romans 4:6). Compare Isaiah 6:7; 27:9; 61:10. **a)** See verse 3. **b)** And, so that Joshua might understand what that symbolic act meant, He said to him: **c)** **See**, He says, so that Joshua might worthily consider the great benefit within himself, and not plunge back into voluntary sins. Compare John 5:14. **d)** Just as just now the filthy garments, so likewise **I have caused to pass (removed) from you**, etc. Not indeed so that sin does not exist, but so that it is not imputed. 2 Samuel 12:13; 24:10; Isaiah 6:7; compare 1 John 1:8, 9. **e)** **Your transgression**, of which the filthy garments were a symbol in verse 3; compare verse 9. For the typical High Priests also had their own sins (Hebrews 7:27). **f)** **And conversely, in clothing I have clothed you**, or I ordered you to be clothed (verse 5). Isaiah 61:10; Ezekiel 16:10. **g)** **With festive, or fine, or bright garments** <note>original Latin: 'nitidis vestibus'</note> (2) Isaiah 3:22; like those which are put off on workdays and kept at home. Compare the root in Deuteronomy 25:9; Titus 3:5. Unless you wish to interpret it as "given to you." Furthermore, just as here and in verse 3, he had compared guilt with filthy garments, so in this place he compares imputed righteousness with festive and bright ones. See note on verse 3 and compare Matthew 22:11. **v. 5. h)** Some think the speech of the Angel or Jehovah continues here: "I say also," or "Whence I say." But the end of the verse proves it is the prophet who is speaking. The Septuagint (LXX) omits the marker of speech, connecting the words with the preceding sentence: "And put a turban." The Vulgate and Syriac say: "And he said." Both, however, go against the grammar and the authentic reading of the Hebrew text. We therefore approve of Rashi's exposition: **And I said**, I, Zechariah, seeking mercy for him. For these are the words of one humbly vowing and desiring, rather than of one commanding with authority; this is recognized because he does not speak directly and imperatively, <term>Ponite</term> <note>original Latin: 'You (plural) place!'</note>, but indirectly and optatively, <term>Ponant</term> <note>original Latin: 'Let them place'</note>. Thus Kimchi: as if to say, "I said to the Angel: after you commanded that, having removed the filthy garments, they should clothe him in festive ones, command also that they place a pure turban on his head." **i)** **Let them put**: make, or command, the angels who minister to you to put it on (verse 4). **k)** The Syriac says: "a crown." Certainly, the word also denotes a royal diadem (Isaiah 62:3; Job 29:14; and thus compare 2 Timothy 4:8; Revelation 4:4). But since Joshua was the High Priest, we correctly understand the priestly mitre, otherwise called <term>Misnepheth</term>, which bore the sacred diadem or turban on the forehead. Compare Exodus 28:37; Leviticus 8:9. It is to us a symbol of the priesthood, especially to be administered in the future according to the good pleasure of God. Kimchi: "so that he might be high priest; for the high priest used to wear a mitre on his head." Thus Tarnovius regards the turban as the honor of public office, and the garments as symbols of private righteousness; he also praises Franciscus Junius, who notes: "Let Joshua be clothed here with all things necessary both for rightly performing the priesthood for the Church and for leading his own life holily in the Church." Likewise, Augustine, speaking of the Ministers of the Church: "They have," he says, "two things: one, that they are Christians; the other, that they are overseers. That they are Christians is for their own sake; that they are overseers is for the sake of the Church." **l)** **They put it on, therefore**, at my request and by Jehovah’s command. **m)** Kimchi: "they clothed him first," by way of chronological reversal <note>hysterology</note>. For the Angel had ordered him to be clothed before Zechariah asked for the turban to be placed (verses 3, 4). Jonathan: "and they commanded him to take a wife worthy of the priesthood." But this clothing is a benefit of grace rather than a requirement of office. See note on verse 3. **n)** **And the Angel of Jehovah** (verses 1, 6) **o)** **was standing by**, as the master commanding the rite, approving it, and adorning it with his presence. **v. 6. p)** **And he admonished or protested**, warning him gravely and seriously. Deuteronomy 4:26; 2 Kings 17:13; Jeremiah 11:6. Surely, after the filthy garments were removed and clean ones restored, the Lord warns him according to that which is written: "See, you are made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you" (John 5:14; compare Isaiah 38:15; Romans 6:1ff). **q)** See the note on verse 1. **v. 7. r)** God the Father, whose words the Angel, the Son of God, reports here; compare verses 8 and 9, where without doubt the Father is introduced preaching about the Messiah, the Son. See something similar above in chapter 1:14ff. **s)** Jonathan: "in the way which is right before me." Compare 1 Kings 3:14; Psalm 81:14.

**t)** **my charge**, that is, those things which I have commanded to be guarded, you shall guard. It expresses attention and care in observing God’s precepts, both negative and affirmative; see Genesis 26:3, 5; Leviticus 18:30, chapter 22:9; Malachi 3:14. **u)** **also you shall judge**, or rule, **my house**. Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> interprets this as "those who minister in the house of my sanctuary." He shall be the high priest and overseer of my house. See Jeremiah 19:1, and compare a similar promise in Jeremiah 15:19. However, Targum Jonathan understands "the house of the Lord" to mean the entire Church or the House of Israel; compare Numbers 12:7; Hebrews 3:2. **x)** **you shall keep**, namely with your associates and colleagues (v. 8); you shall shine with priestly dignity. **y)** **my courts**, both inner and outer; see Isaiah 1:12. **z)** **furthermore, I will give to you.** Those things which preceded in the first half of the verse are, in a way, earthly and temporal promises; but this one is **heavenly and eternal**. According to Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish scholar known as Radak</note>, the first half contains the **protasis** <note>the "if" part of a conditional sentence</note>, and this part is the **apodosis** <note>the "then" or concluding part</note>, in this manner: *If* you walk, *if* you keep, and *if* you judge; *then* I will give. But the former explanation is more pleasing because of the particle **וְגַם** (and also), which in these types of statements usually introduces the conclusion. **a)** **those walking**, or moving about. I will cause you and yours to walk. This is a participle in the *Piel* stem with transposed vowel points. If that is unpleasing, let us explain it as a noun: **I will give you walks**: (1) thus there is no "beastly" nature in them. The sense is: I will add the **Angels** as your companions and defenders, so that you are safe from Satan (v. 1); see Psalm 34:8, Psalm 91:11, Hebrews 1:14. Or rather: I will cause you to have communion with the servants—

*...[I will serve?] you, and I will give you feet walking among those Seraphim. Compare Revelation 3:4. **b)** **among these standing**, (v. 4) namely the **Seraphim and Angels** ministering before God, for whom there is no ceasing. Thus Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, the preeminent medieval commentator</note> and Midrash Tehillim; compare Isaiah 6:2. **v. 8. c)** **I pray** or "I would wish," he says, to instill a feeling of love, so that Joshua might take it well, and so that he might give his ears to one who wishes him well and exhorts him sincerely. Compare the note on chapter 1:4. **d)** **O High Priest** (v. 1). **e)** **you, I say, and your associates** or colleagues (namely, the rest of the priests). **f)** **sitting before you**, like disciples or listeners sitting before a teacher; see Ezekiel 23:18, 8:1; Acts 22:3; compare Matthew 23:2. It was therefore the duty of the High Priest to instruct the rest or the juniors. **g)** The Septuagint and Arabic versions translate: **men who shall see a miracle** or "seeing." Thus Jonathan: "the men are worthy that miracles be done for them." But this is a bit remote and only fits our context with force. Indeed, in Isaiah 8:18, **Christ and his disciples** are said to be "for signs and wonders"; and David in Psalm 71:7 complains that he is "as a wonder unto many." There, a "wonder" <term>prodigium: a sign that provokes awe or points to a future event</term> is said when someone has adversities so singular and unusual that he is an object of admiration and a spectacle to all like some omen (1 Corinthians 4:9). If he commanded this place to be taken in that way, the sense would be: "Hear, Joshua, with your associates, a promise of great comfort, which is necessary for you to lift the pain of present misery, because—as an argument for attention from your own state, in which you are surely in need of comfort—those men with you are **men of wonder**, i.e., of a wondrous or omen-like status; because, to explain the comfort itself, behold I, etc." And indeed, the status of the priests was certainly afflicted at that time; but the status of the people was not any better; so it is hardly believable that God wished to depict the misery of the priests specifically as "ominous" here. Therefore, the explanation of Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century federal theologian</note> pleases us more: "They are **men of sign** in whom something mild or unusual happens, by which men are excited to think about my promises." And in his Commentary on this place: "They are men of sign, that is, I have given them to the Israelite people as a sign and **manifestation** <note>Greek original: φανέρωσιν (phanerōsin)</note> of my counsel; they bear the figure of my Son. They foreshadow His priesthood." Compare Exodus 7:9, Ezekiel 12:6, 24:24, 27; Zechariah 12:24. In the following verses, he certainly describes the **antitypical priesthood of the Messiah**, especially in verse 9. Likewise, this Joshua in chapter 6:11 and following, with a double crown, is presented as a type and sign of Christ. **h)** **my servant**. For the Angel, or the Son of Jehovah, recites the Father's words concerning Himself; as we observed above at the start of verse 7; compare Psalm 2:7 and the note on Isaiah 42:1, 52:13, and Psalm 40:9. **i)** **That Branch**, Christ, for whom this is like a proper name among the Prophets (chapter 6:12; Isaiah 4:2; Jeremiah 23:5, 33:15), taken from the kingdom of vegetables or plants (Psalm 65:11). Just like the synonyms of Christ: "fruit of the earth" (Isaiah 4:2), "a branch from the trunk of Jesse" and "a shoot from his roots" (chapter 11:1), "a tender branch from the top of a cedar" (Ezekiel 17:23), and "the vine" (John 15:1). Jonathan correctly translates: "**Messiah**, who shall be revealed." Also Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century statesman and commentator</note> in his commentary on this place says: "The Branch is the **King Messiah**, who shall reign over Israel." And so say many Hebrew interpreters in Kimchi's works; however, having abandoned these, he himself, along with Rashi, wrongly interprets this as **Zerubbabel**, who (as he is forced to admit) had already come long ago, and was not "yet to be brought" as is proclaimed here. From the preceding and subsequent context, something must be supplied in this manner: "I am about to bring my servant the Branch, him for whom you shall meanwhile be a type and sign, and whom you ought to look upon for your comfort as the **cornerstone**." Compare verse 9. **v. 9. k)** We take this as explanatory. Because, so that it may further be clear what sort of person my Servant the Branch is (v. 8). **l)** It rouses one to attention, as in Isaiah 50:2. **m)** as for **this stone**, which I just now called the Branch. Gurtler, in *Prophetic Theology* page 423, says: "This stone is without doubt **Christ**," comparing Psalm 118:22, Matthew 21:42, Ephesians 2:16. So Jerome: "Christ is called the **cornerstone** because he joins both peoples together, and associates two walls into one house. Here, for those who do not believe, he is a stone of stumbling." Compare Isaiah 8:14 and Romans 9:32-33. Furthermore, that he calls Christ a stone seems to have been done primarily on the occasion of the founding and structure of the **Temple**, in which Joshua with Zerubbabel and the Jewish people was occupied at this very time. And thus below in chapter 4:7. See the Preface §10. **n)** whom, while I promised he would come (v. 8), I have by this very act **set before Joshua**, that is, I have proposed him to be continually looked upon as the foundation stone. Specifically, as Gurtler well says: "He is placed in the sight of Joshua the Jewish High Priest, so that he might be recognized by him and held as the **rock of salvation**." **o)** i.e., before you; compare verse 8. For in place of a pronoun, the name itself sometimes returns; compare Numbers 27:11. **p)** upon or **on this one stone** are, etc. Therefore, "**my eyes**" <note>original Hebrew: עֵינַי (einai)</note> will be the object, signifying the tendency of the seven eyes toward their object, or the stone. Others, as we shall soon see, take it subjectively: "upon or in this one stone there are..."*

# ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER 3. 4.

<margin>
**q)** Jerome explains these eyes as being positioned on the stone itself, mentioned below. According to his hypothesis, they are the ones Isaiah speaks of in chapter 11:2: *The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom*, etc. Thus, it would be helpful to compare Revelation 5:6, where the Lamb (Christ) is seen represented as having seven eyes, with this explanation: *which are the seven Spirits of God sent forth into all the earth*. And so the celebrated Maius says: Jesus Christ is revealed as the solid foundation of the Church or the stone upon which everything built can be safe, since he has seven eyes and can sufficiently provide for all. I do not know if we should also refer here to Jonas's note: *On the stone—are seven eyes seeing into the stone itself.* But most, as I said, regard the Stone not as the subject, but as the object of the seven eyes. And they are more correct, as it seems to us, **r)** because in the following half-verse, an objective care *toward* this stone is described, not a subjective care *of* the stone; 2) because of the parallelism in chapter 4:11, where the same Angel says these seven eyes belong to Jehovah the Father, and indeed are running through the whole earth, just as they are presented here as being most specifically directed upon the stone. However, interpreters differ in this: some attribute these seven eyes looking at the stone to the Church, others to God. The former pleases Cocceius in his Commentary, where he says: He promises that the seven eyes will turn toward that stone, that is, the faith of the Universal Church in seven periods <note>original: "perfus"</note> (see Revelation 1:4ff.) skillfully distinguished from the Old Testament prophecies. So also Gurtler in *Prophetic Theology* 423: *Upon one stone,* he says, *seven eyes.* The Church, passing through seven times after the arrival of the servant, the Branch (v. 8), will direct the eyes of faith toward the one Jesus Christ, and will look for no other Teacher or Savior.

<margin>
Kimchi supports the latter view, for whom the seven eyes are "observations" <term>שמירות</term> <note>Hebrew: *shemirot*, meaning watchful cares or observations</note>.

**CHAPTER IV.**
1. Many things from the Lord. 2. And finally, the celebrated Vitringa prefers this in his Commentary on Revelation 5:6.
</margin>

For these are the very eyes of Jehovah, which in chapter 4:10 are said to see the plumb line; and that it might be better understood to signify the Providence of God, it is added: *The eyes of the Lord run to and fro through the whole earth.* Surely eyes are a symbol of divine providence; compare below chapter 9:1, Deuteronomy 11:12, Ezekiel 1:18. Here [Zechariah] 5:5, which supposes Omniscience; Proverbs 5:21, chapter 15:3, chapter 20:13. The number seven is often used as a **synecdoche** <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole or a specific number represents perfection</note> for plurality and perfection; Leviticus 26:21, Proverbs 24:16. If, therefore, the Stone (that is, the Messiah) is considered here separately and outside His Church—the building of which He Himself supports as the cornerstone—the seven eyes will signify the most special Providence of God the Father, which followed Christ so that He might successfully complete all things (Isaiah 42:6). If, however, it is taken collectively with His body or Church, the same will signify the universal providence through all the intervals and states of the Church's time, as in Revelation 5:6 (on which see the celebrated Vitringa).

**v)** The Vulgate says: *I will engrave its sculpture*; just as engravers and sculptors carve stones to express various figures and ornaments on them (Exodus 28:9, chapter 31:5, chapter 36:1, 3). That is, I will cause that Stone to turn out most ornate; and He who was to the Jews a stone of stumbling and rejection shall soon become chosen and precious (1 Peter 2:4-7; cf. Vitringa on Isaiah 43:13). Isan says: *I will reveal its visions*, as if to say: I will make it so that in its own time He appears and is manifested; compare Jeremiah 31:4. **s)** The seal of the promise (Hosea 11:11, Haggai 2:23). **t)** Vulgate and Isan. **u)** **I will remove.** As if it were transitive in the *Kal* stem, which elsewhere is constantly neutral, meaning "to recede" (chapter 14:4, Joshua 1:8), just as <term>העביר</term> <note>Hebrew: *he'avir*</note> is to be removed or brought back. But the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> uses <term>ψηλαφήσω</term> <note>Greek: *pselapheso*, meaning "I will touch/grope"</note>, which the Arabic translator rendered as "I will search out." Compare the Arabic <term>משש</term> <note>mashash</note> for seeking the remains of grapes from a vine; and the Hebrew <term>משש</term> in Genesis 31:37. What the Septuagint translated as "you have searched" <note>Greek: *ereunesas*</note>, the Syriac expressed with the harmonious <term>משש</term>, which can be explained both as "I will feel" and "I will search thoroughly." The sense here is undoubtedly: *I will search out so that it is found no more; for I will take away every sin.* Compare Isaiah 41:12, Psalm 10:15. Cocceius (430), thinking the notion comes from the related <term>מוש</term> <note>mush</note>, explains it as "I will wipe away." This is more clearly illustrated by Schultens in *Observations on the Old Testament* (p. 532), noting that <term>מוש</term> for <term>משש</term> signifies to lead the hand over something by feeling, i.e., to delete; compare the Arabic <term>משח</term> <note>mashach</note> (with a soft *ch*) meaning "to delete" or "to wipe away." But however much the interpreters seem to differ, the explanations lead to the same point.

**x)** The type of this had been the iniquity removed from Joshua (v. 4); compare Daniel 9:24. **x)** **that land.** <term>אֶרֶץ הִיא</term> <note>Hebrew: *eretz hi*</note>. He seems to refer to the land of Israel, to whose inhabitants the promised redemption and salvation primarily belonged (Acts 3:26, chapter 13:46, Romans 1:16). Yet this cannot be understood exclusively; compare 1 John 2:2. **y)** **in one day**, that is, once and for all, namely through the single offering of Christ, to which it will not be necessary to add another hereafter; compare Hebrews 7:27, chapter 9:25–28, chapter 10:2, 14. It is Jewish darkness that Rashi <note>A famous medieval Jewish commentator</note> says he does not know what day is intended here. **v. 10. z)** **you shall call** (invite) each one. **a)** You shall dwell together quietly and securely as once under Solomon (1 Kings 5:5; cf. 2 Kings 18:31, and our notes on Micah 4:4).

**CHAPTER IV. v. 1. b) Afterward he returned.** Jerome raises a doubt: *Where had he gone, that he should return, especially he who was speaking in the Prophet, and could not be without him in whom he spoke?* But, he says, *whenever human frailty is left to its own weakness, the help of God and His angels must be believed to have departed from us.* Therefore, the Prophet, astonished by the stupor of the great vision, was numb in his whole mind and could not see the clear light of truth: whence he is stirred up from the past vision to another vision, as if waking from sleep, so that he may see what he did not see with closed eyes. Thus Jerome. Otherwise, this idiom of <term>שוב</term> <note>shuv</note> "he returned" [means he did it again]—and he waked me—meaning "he waked me again"; just as in chapter 5:1, "I returned and lifted my eyes" means "I lifted them again." **c) v. 4. 5.** see note on chapter 1:9. **d) and waked**, he roused me, as I was overwhelmed by the stupor and wonder of the previous vision like an ecstatic sleep (Song of Solomon 2:7, chapter 3:5, chapter 8; Daniel 8:18; and he is excited in chapter 2:17; Job 14:12). **f) from his sleep** (Genesis 28:16).

**v. 2. g)** The Angel asks Zechariah: *What do you see?* so that as he responds in ignorance and asks what he sees, saying, *What are these, my lord?* (v. 4), we may hear from him: *This is the word of the Lord,* etc. (v. 6). Jerome on Hosea 5:2, Jeremiah 1:11, 13, and the note on chapter 2:4, 3. **h) And I said.** Thus the *Keri* <note>The traditional reading of the Hebrew text</note> has it. But the *Cthib* <note>The written text of the Hebrew</note> reads and explains it as a passive in the *Niphal*, as if said impersonally: **and it was said** or answered by me; compare Genesis 42:14. Kimchi explains it as the Scripture narrating about the Prophet as a third person: "And Zechariah said" (chapter 2:1, 3). **h) A golden lampstand** in its entirety, that is, it was all made of gold (v. 11). This is the fifth emblem, and it seems to have been presented to the Prophet on the occasion of the golden lampstands being placed in the Temple, which had now begun to be restored (compare Preface §10; Exodus 25:31ff; 1 Chronicles 4:7; Hebrews 9:2). We must note regarding the emblem: I. Its parts and form, and II. Its sense. Neither is without obscurity.

We will explain, therefore, in the words of the celebrated Vitringa (Commentary on Revelation, p. 625ff): *To Zechariah,* he says, *were presented two olive trees through two tubes, into which their two larger branches were bent on both sides, supplying fresh oil—pressed out in those tubes as if by presses—in great abundance to the golden Lampstand of seven lamps, which was shown to him in the vision centered between the olive trees. Namely, two tubes, into which those two larger branches shook out the olives as if into presses, led into some larger vessel, which you may call a **Lecythus** or **Lenticula** <note>types of oil jars or flasks</note>, receiving the oil expressed in the tubes, which was above the Lampstand: from which vessel the oil flowed down through seven small pipes directly into each lamp of the Lampstand.*

The sense of this emblem is not obscure. The **Lampstand is the Church**. These **olive trees figure the Holy Spirit**, who was pleased to derive His grace into the Church; and then also all true and faithful teachers and rulers of the Church, whom the Holy Spirit uses in building or restoring His Church, who have the Spirit of Christ in them (Mark 9:50) and are led and moved by Him. The **two tubes** in this mystery signify those two instruments through which the teachings of the Ministers of God pass and are prepared for the common use of the Church: **oral preaching and scripture**. They pass, as I said, to the common use of the Church: which is sketched here by the bowl or larger vessel receiving the oil. For whatever is preached by mouth or published in writings is cast and flows as if into a common vessel—which descends through the smaller channels or tubes from the jar into the lamps. By these you may conveniently understand all the exercises, meditations, and labors of pious souls well-disposed toward God, through which, as through means, either individual believers or assemblies of believers (figured by the lamps of the Lampstand) transfer those common advancements of the Church and the learned into themselves for the nourishment of faith and the increase of their knowledge, by which they may conveniently shine before others in the darkness of this world. **i) Its Lecythus or jar.** A round vessel, sending down the oil it contained to the seven lamps through tubes (v. 3; cf. Ecclesiastes 12:6). Root <term>גול</term> <note>gul</note> "to roll": **for they are round and rolling.** The Syriac rendered it "dish," perhaps because it had the shape of a dish or a hollow lower hemisphere.

Before he explains the mystery of the vision, the angel responds to the prophet’s questioning with this inquiry, so that he might draw out an open and candid confession of ignorance (which follows immediately). <margin>
**q)** Two olive trees. See verse 11 and Revelation 11:4. Some details are omitted here in the history of the vision, which are explained more distinctly below in verse 12; namely, two olive branches or shoots full of olives, and likewise two *tsanterot* <note>original: צַנְתְּרוֹת</note> or larger tubes, through which the oil pressed from the olives of both branches flowed into the bowl.
