the explanation to make him more attentive. So also in verse 13 and Ezekiel 17:12. **verse 6. a)** Therefore, to help your ignorance and to interpret at your request what is an inexplicable mystery to you: *This is the word of Jehovah*, shadowed forth by this emblem. **b)** *to Zerubbabel*, the leader of the Jewish people, who was occupied in the restoration of the temple and especially in need of comfort due to the great difficulties he had to struggle against. See verses 9, 10; Haggai 1:1, 2:4-5. **c)** *Not by strength* (Ezekiel 17:17) and not by power (Isaiah 10:13), namely one's own power, which Zerubbabel and his people hardly possessed, whether you look at the magnitude and difficulty of the work undertaken or the power of their adversaries. See 1 Samuel 2:9; Psalm 147:10-11. There is a "sudden silence" <note>original: "Aposiopesis"; a rhetorical device where a sentence is left unfinished</note> here, to be filled in from verse 9 in this or a similar way: *the hands of Zerubbabel shall also finish this house which he founded*. **d)** *but by my Spirit*: namely, the Spirit assisting (Haggai 2:5), instructing (Isaiah 30:1), strengthening (chapter 12:1), and directing, promoting, and happily completing the whole business, even while enemies gnash their teeth (Isaiah 31:16; Job 32:8). *Rabbi Solomon (Rashi)*: I will put my Spirit upon Darius, so that he may command the building of the Temple for you, and help you with wheat, wine, oil, and wood, so that you do not need the help of men. Compare Ezra 6:4–9 and following. The application of the emblem according to *Tarnovius* is this: Just as you saw this lampstand with all its ornaments placed by divine power and supplied with necessary things, so know that the Church of God is sustained, defended, and ruled by His counsel and virtue alone, and now this work of building will be perfected under His leadership and auspices. The *purpose* of that emblem is indeed general—to show God's management of the Church through all periods of time; however, the immediate purpose, subordinated to this general one, is to show God's management of the Israelite Church at the time of the Temple's restoration, to give courage to Zerubbabel and the Jewish people. Compare Ezra 5:2. **e)** Confirmation from the authority of the one promising (Malachi 1:8). **verse 7. f)** *Who are you... before Zerubbabel?* He asks "who is he" to belittle him by the asking, and to despise him by the belittling. Compare Exodus 3:11; Judges 9:28, 38; 1 Samuel 17:26. It is as if to say: You seem very high, difficult, and almost insuperable; nevertheless, I will make it so that you become a *plain* before *Zerubbabel*, whom you opposed, and thus very easy to overcome. **g)** *Targum Jonathan:* What do you think you are, O foolish Kingdom, before Zerubbabel? Are you not like a plain? See also chapter 6:1; Isaiah 41:15; Jeremiah 51:25; Habakkuk 3:6; Psalm 68:17. He seems to be referring to the *Persian Kingdom*, whose nobles, corrupted by the Samaritans, prohibited the building of the temple for some time (Ezra 4:4-5 and following). *Rabbi Solomon (Rashi)* and *David Kimchi (Radak)* understand this as the prefects beyond the Euphrates, Tatnai and Shethar-bozenai with their colleagues, mentioned in Ezra 5:3. But just as things that are easy are called "level," so things that are arduous and difficult are called "very high." Therefore, a *great mountain* generally signifies a great difficulty placed before Zerubbabel in the building of the temple; and its change into a plain signifies the removal of that difficulty so that it no longer stands in the way. **h)** *Become a plain!* or be turned into one!—the voice of one commanding effectively. Hence the *Vulgate* translates with an exclamation: *into a plain!* See Isaiah 40:4; chapter 42:16. Compare 

<margin>
**v. 4. u)** verse 2 and following. **x)** What do these mean? As if to say: I have indeed seen all this, and I understand that a great mystery lies beneath it; but what it is, I confess I do not know: I desire therefore to be informed by you. See chapter 1:9, 2:2; Revelation 17:7.
</margin>

Matthew 49:11 <note>Likely a citation error for Isaiah 49:11</note>. **i)** *And Zerubbabel shall bring forth*—namely, through the birth of the Messiah—into the plain! (Isaiah 40:4; 42:16; compare Matthew 1:12 and following; Romans 1:3). He shall procreate him, matching the note on Micah 5:1. It is as if to say: Not only will he complete the restoration of the Temple, having overcome all difficulties, but he will be honored with another far more excellent honor from Me: that through his descendants, he shall finally present the Messiah himself from his own seed. He passes from the promise of a temporal good to the promise of a spiritual and eternal one. Compare the note on Haggai 2:23. **k)** *The primary stone*, literally the "head stone" (1) namely Christ, matching chapter 3:9 and the note there. **l)** *With shouts* (4) Isaiah 22:2; Job 36:29; chapter 39:7. **m)** of those saying: *grace! grace be to it! May God favor it! May men favor it!* The noun is doubled, following the solemn custom in acclamations (chapter 8:10; compare Luke 2:52) and that prayerful *Hosanna* in Matthew 21:9, 15 and Psalm 118:25.

# ZECHARIAH CHAPTER 4

<margin>8</margin> And the word of the LORD came to me, saying:
<margin>9</margin> "The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house, and his hands shall finish it; and you shall know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you.
<margin>10</margin> For who has despised the day of small things? And they shall rejoice and see the plummet stone <note>original: הָאֶ֧בֶן הַבְּדִ֛יל - literally "the stone of tin," referring to a weighted line used by builders to ensure walls are perfectly vertical</note> in the hand of Zerubbabel. These seven are the eyes of the LORD; they roam throughout the whole earth."
<margin>11</margin> Then I answered and said to him, "What are these two olive trees on the right of the lampstand and on its left?"
<margin>12</margin> And I answered a second time and said to him, "What are the two branches of the olive trees which are beside the two golden pipes <note>original: צַנְתְּרוֹת - technical term for tubes or channels</note> that empty the gold <note>referring to the golden-colored olive oil</note> from themselves?"
<margin>13</margin> And he spoke to me, saying...

<margin>
**v. 8, 9. x)** This section provides a confirmation and a more abundant declaration of the preceding verses. See chapter 1:1.
**v. 9. o)** See the note on verse 6. **p)** See chapter 2:9, Haggai 2:18, and Ezra 3:6, 10. **q)** "and his hands shall also finish," bringing the work to a happy conclusion as in Isaiah 10:12. The work he began would by no means be left unfinished, as the enemies presumed and as the weaker Jews feared. **r)** "And you shall know" by the very outcome, both you and your people, when all these things I have said about completing the Temple actually happen. You will experience that I have been a true messenger of the LORD. See chapter 2:13, 15 and 6:15. **s)** See the note on chapter 2:13. Observe here that the LORD himself speaks in verse 8, yet he is distinguished as one sent by the LORD who sends him. Clearly, this is the Son of God, who above in verses 1 and 5 was called the "Angel speaking in or with the Prophet." Compare Isaiah 48:16 and 61:1. The Targum of Jonathan adds: "to prophesy to you."
</margin>

<margin>
Would he not return (meaning one who had despised this day because of the smallness of the structure) and rejoice when he sees, etc. However, according to the Hebrew accents, the subject of this declaration is "these seven," located at the end of this first half-verse.
</margin>

The connection is thus: **"Who has despised... since these seven rejoice and see?"** Clearly, against the faint-heartedness and complaints regarding the smallness of the structure, the prophet opposes the grace of God and His all-encompassing providence regarding this building. It is as if he says: *“If the seven eyes of the LORD Himself, looking with favor, pleasure, and care, behold the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel, then none of you should be faint-hearted because of those small beginnings, nor should you despise them.”* Compare 1 Chronicles 29:9, 17 and 1 Samuel 19:5. **y) "that stone of tin"**, or *the tin weight*, compared with Deuteronomy 25:13, 15. This is a description of the plummet <note>a tool used to ensure a wall is straight</note>, compared with Isaiah 34:11 and the notes on Amos 7:7, 8. The **plummet**, which is of the greatest use in architecture, symbolically denotes all of Zerubbabel's zeal and application in building the Temple. For a similar construction, see Joshua 3:14. **z)** See verses 6, 7, 8, 9 and chapter 3:9. **a) Jonathan** <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> interprets this as: *“these seven eyes of the Lord [see] the stone like these,”* which is somewhat obscure. **Rabbi Solomon (Rashi)**, who cites the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> translation for support, explains that the layers of stones will be seven times greater than they were in the first foundation during the time of Cyrus; but this is a forced interpretation. **Sch.** suggests by apposition: *“these seven (namely, eyes).”* But it is more probable that the eyes here are said to *see subjectively* (the eyes are doing the seeing) rather than *be seen objectively*. **The Vulgate**, Septuagint, Arabic, and Syriac versions begin a new sentence here and connect it with the following: *“These seven are the eyes of the Lord,”* etc. However, these translations go against the Hebrew accents, which, as we observed above, indicate this subject belongs to the preceding verbs *“rejoice and see.”* Furthermore, the pronoun *“these”* with the number *“seven”* sends the reader back partly to the preceding text (chapter 3:9), where these seven were already designated, and partly to what immediately follows here, where he declares them further. For the sake of confirmation, we add the words of the **Celebrated Vitringa** <note>Campegius Vitringa, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> from his commentary on Revelation 5:6: "It is clearly alluded to here," he says, "in the passage of Zechariah 4:10, where mention is made of the seven eyes of the Lord, seeing and rejoicing that the plummet for building the house of God is in the hand of Zerubbabel. For that is the manifest meaning of that place, although I am not unaware that the **Illustrious Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Hebraist</note> interprets it otherwise and distinguishes the **Eyes** from the numerical notion of *seven*. Yet both that passage itself, read simply and compared with chapter 3:9, and this speech of John [in Revelation], which assumes our interpretation, stand in the way. There is no real difficulty in the matter. For Christ Jesus, who follows His Church with universal care and providence, supplies all necessary things to her." **b) "For the eyes of the LORD,"** which I point out through these seven. Understand this as the universal providence of God, by which He foresees and rules all things, and especially His Church. See chapter 9:1, 1 Chronicles 16:9, and Proverbs 15:3. **c) "are roaming through the entire earth."** Job 1:7, chapter 2:2, Daniel 12:4. To what purpose? The parallel passage in 2 Chronicles 16:9 explains: *“to help those whose heart is perfect toward Him.”* And in this place, it specifically hints that the eye will be upon Zerubbabel and the Jewish people, so that they may finish what they began and no longer be disturbed by enemies (Ezra 5:5). And so it happened. For although Tatnai and Shethar-boznai with the other Samaritans came upon the work and reproached the building begun without a new permit, they did not hinder the structure, but reported the whole matter by letter to Darius, who wrote back most mercifully for the Jews, stating that the building of the temple must not be prohibited, but rather promoted in every way (Ezra 5 and 6). The **Septuagint** translates: **οἱ ἐπιβλέποντες ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν** <note>those looking upon all the earth</note>. So too the Arabic and Syriac. But **Jonathan** translates: *“before the Lord the works of men are revealed in the whole earth.”* **v. 11. d) Regarding the olive trees** in verse 3, the prophet had indeed asked above in verse 4, and so far he had been instructed by the Angel about their mystery; here he repeats the question so that he might be informed specifically about their two branches, as appears from the following verse 11, in which the question is repeated and phrased more precisely. **e)** verse 3; compare Matthew 20:21, 23. **v. 12. f) "I answered again,"** both because of the burning desire with which I wished to know the mystery of each olive tree, and to express more specifically what I especially wanted explained to me regarding these two trees. Genesis 22:15. **ὁ κ᾽ ἐκ δευτέρου** <note>the one from the second [time]</note>, as in Matthew 26:42. **g) "two branches"** (**ear of grain** in Genesis 41:5) **of the olive trees.** He compares the branches of the olive trees with ears of grain because just as ears are full of grain, these were full of olives. **Kimchi.** See the notes above at verse 3. **h) "beside."** Deuteronomy 2:37, 2 Chronicles 21:16. **i) "of the tubes"** (x) regarding which see the note above on verse 3. It agrees with *tsinnor* <note>original: צִנּוֹר</note> **"canal"** (z) 2 Samuel 5:8, Psalm 42:8. But the **Vulgate** translates: *“golden beaks, in which are the pouring vessels of gold.”* The **Septuagint** has **μυξωτῆρες** <note>nozzles or lamp-wicks</note>, which Cocceius interprets in his Hebrew Lexicon as *“snuffers,”* that is, instruments for pressing the olives and expressing the oil. **Abarbanel**: *“instruments by which the oil is made.”* **k) "golden,"** referring either to the material of the tubes, as above in verse 2, or *“golden”* meaning the pure and shining liquid of the oil like gold, as at the end of the verse. **l) "pouring out,"** or in the nominative *“the ones pouring out,”* Malachi 3:10. This depends on the more distant *“branches of the olive trees,”* not only because of the accents, but also because of the grammar, by which this masculine participle is difficult to construct with the feminine noun *tsanterot* (tubes). If this is the case, perhaps the press by which the oil is expressed is omitted here, just as in verse 3 the branches themselves were also omitted. **m) "from (upon)"** see Micah 3:2, Leviticus 8:28.

<margin>
**v. 10. z)** "who has despised?"—a contracted form for *bazah*; the form *baz* nevertheless retains its meaning here from the related roots *buz* and *boz* / "to despise." Proverbs 1:7. The sense is: no one rightly or without absurdity despises it, or has a suitable cause for despising it. Compare a similar question in Isaiah 44:10. **\*) "the day"** (The word *baz* among the Hebrews is joined to the Dative case, as in Proverbs 6:30, 11:12, etc.) **"of small things,"** namely, of beginnings or foundations. Numbers 22:18. **Jonathan**: *“Who is this who has despised this day because of the structure, which is small?”* Compare the history in Ezra 3:12, where many of the elders, when they looked at the foundation of the second temple in relation to the first temple, are said to have wept; and in Haggai 2:3 the Prophet says: *“Is not the present house compared with the former one like nothing in your eyes?”* See the Preface, section 8. **x) "yet they rejoice,"** etc. **Jonathan**: *“Is it not...”*
</margin>

<header>CHAPTER 4 & 5. ZECHARIAH</header>

<margin>
**v. 6, 7** Regarding what Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for his work on federal theology and his Hebrew lexicon.</note> notes in his Lexicon, page 180: the whole people, who were brought near to the entrance of the kingdom of heaven through the offering of Christ, and even more through his resurrection, ascension, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, were unwilling to enter into it—and were thus subject to the curse.

**CHAPTER 5.**
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 13.** See the note on verse 5.
**v. 14.** "These are the two sons of oil" <note>original: שְׁנֵי בְנֵי־הַיִּצְהָר</note>; see Hosea 2:10 and Joel 1:10. These are individuals equipped with the oil and gifts of the Holy Spirit, whose work God uses to restore the true sanctuary in the Church. In this historical time, they were Zerubbabel and Joshua, who were restoring the temple (Haggai 1:1). In ancient times, they were Moses and Aaron in the Wilderness, and Elijah and Elisha during the apostasy of Baal worship. In the future, they are those two Martyrs mentioned in Revelation 11:3, 4 (on which see the work of Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note>). **p)** They are "standing" like ministers (see chapter 6:5; Genesis 18:8; Judges 3:19). **q)** "Beside the Lord of the whole earth" (chapter 6:5; Revelation 11:4; Exodus 23:17), which is appropriately called Jehovah, as discussed above in verse 10.
</margin>

## 14 And he said, "Do you not know what these are?" and I said, "No, my lord." Then he said, "These are the two sons of oil <note>meaning 'the anointed ones' or those who provide the oil</note> who stand by the Lord of the whole earth."

## CHAPTER 5: Then I turned and lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a flying scroll.

## 2 And he said to me, "What do you see?" and I answered, "I see a flying scroll; its length is twenty cubits and its width is ten cubits."

## 3 Then he said to me, "This is the curse that goes out over the face of the whole land; for every thief shall be purged away according to what is on one side, and every perjurer shall be purged away according to what is on the other side."

## 4 "I will send it out," says the LORD of hosts, "and it shall enter the house of the thief and the house of him who swears falsely by my name; and it shall remain in the midst of his house and consume it..."

---

<margin>
**CHAPTER 5, v. 1. r)** "Then I returned and lifted" (that is, once again I looked). See chapter 6:1 and the note on chapter 4:1. **s)** See verses 5 and 9. **t)** A "Scroll," specifically of judgment, such as Ezekiel saw in Ezekiel 2:9, 10; compare Revelation 10:2. That a book of judgment is understood is shown by the parallel passages cited, and by verses 3 and 4 below, where it is explained as a curse coming upon the whole land against thieves and perjurers. This is the sixth symbol, which Guillaume (in *Prophetic Theology*, page 134) places at the destruction of the Second Temple, interpreting the "land" mentioned in verse 3 as Judea. There are two parts to this chapter: I. The flying scroll (v. 1–4). II. The basket (Ephah) with a woman sitting in it (v. 5 onwards). **u)** "Flying" (v. 2), which signifies the swiftness of the coming judgment, as in Habakkuk 1:8.

**v. 1. x)** Then the uncreated Angel spoke, who was speaking with me or within me (chapter 1:9, 4:7). **y)** See note on chapter 4:2. **z)** verse 1. **a)** "Its length" (referring to the flying scroll) is twenty measurements in cubits—that is, cubit-lengths (Exodus 26:8, 27:9). It thus had the same measurements as the Porch of the Temple in length and width, as seen in 1 Kings 6:3.
</margin>

...to be cast down. For us, this generally signifies the magnitude of the curse and the judgment. **v. 3. b)** "This is the curse." Some understand this as a cursed and harmful doctrine that would occupy the whole land; others more correctly see it as the punishment of the curse or the wrath that awaits transgressors of the law. This is 1) because the Lord is said to send it out (v. 4), and 2) it is to consume the house of the wicked (v. 4). These points involve the notion of punishment rather than just guilt (compare Isaiah 24:6). However, the word *alah* <note>original: אָלָה - curse or oath</note> signifies not only the word by which a person is declared cursed for doing this or that (Ezekiel 16:59; compare 17:18), but the evil itself to which they are devoted, as in Isaiah 24:6 and Jeremiah 23:10, which is how it is primarily taken here. **c)** "Which goes out" (v. 5, 6) by the decree and permission of Jehovah (v. 4; Genesis 24:58; Ephesians 2:29), as if sent out from his tribunal and sanctuary to take vengeance on the wicked (1 Kings 22:22; Ezekiel 9:7; compare Numbers 17:11). **d)** "Over the face of the whole land," namely Judea in the immediate type (see note on v. 1), but the whole world in the ultimate antitype, when God shall hold the universal judgment. **e)** "Because," to make clearer what I said: that this scroll is or signifies the curse. **f)** "Everyone who steals," whoever he may be. Two types of sins are set forth: theft and perjury. The former is against the second table of the Decalogue (Exodus 20:13) and the latter against the first table (Exodus 20:7). By synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note>, these represent all sins against both tables: perjury for all irreverence toward the Divine, and theft for all injustice against one's neighbor. **g)** Some understand this regarding time, as if to say "from this time" <note>original: מִזֶּה</note>, but the word hardly ever has this meaning elsewhere. For others, it is local: "from here" or "from this place." "It shall be purged" <note>original: נִקָּה - niqqah</note>—meaning it shall be cleared out or removed (compare Genesis 37:17, 42:15). We will soon see how Rabbi Solomon explains this. But it should be noted that this particle is repeated in the following clause; in such cases, it usually signifies opposite sides, translated as "on this side and on that side" (see Exodus 17:12; Numbers 22:24; Ezekiel 47:7). Therefore, we prefer the opinion of Abraham Ibn Ezra, who holds that both sides of that Scroll were written upon, one against thieves and the other against perjurers, or (as he prefers) both against both. If we follow the first view, an analogy arises between the curse and the law. Just as the tables of the law were written on both sides, or "on this side and on that" (Exodus 32:15), so the curse striking the transgressors of both tables is likewise written "on this side and on that," so that every transgression receives a just <term>recompense <gloss>original Greek: μισθαποδοσίαν</gloss></term> (Hebrews 2:2). If the latter view is preferred, the magnitude and abundance of the curse are hinted at. Thus Ezekiel's scroll, which has a similar theme to ours, is said to have been written on the front and back, or on both sides, inside and out (Ezekiel 2:10). The ancients did not write on the back of a scroll unless the material was overflowing; hence Juvenal says in Satire I: "Orestes, written even on the back, and not yet finished." Therefore, we explain "according to it" in a way that understands the evil and curse coming upon the thief and perjurer according to that scroll, which was written on both sides. **h)** "According to it," as if to say, according to its tenor and argument; or as the Vulgate renders it: "just as it is written there." So also "according to my Gospel" (Romans 2:16) and "according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3, 4).

**i)** A difficult word, regarding which there are various erroneous opinions. Those who explain the "curse" as a cursed and perverse doctrine translate it as "he is pure," as if to say he is acquitted of the crime and judged to have committed no sin through this doctrine (compare Isaiah 5:20). Theodotio translates "you shall be beaten," as if it were from the root *nakah* (with a *Kaph*). The Septuagint and Arabic versions say "he shall be punished"; the Vulgate says "he shall be judged," perhaps by antiphrasis <note>The use of a word in a sense opposite to its proper meaning.</note>, for elsewhere it means to be immune from punishment (Ezekiel 20:19). Rabbi Solomon explains it this way: "Every thief until now has been immune from this punishment... because it was delayed until the measure of each was full." But now (v. 4), "I have made it go out." Cocceius (on Jeremiah 530) is closer to the truth: "he is emptied out," as if to say he is stripped of all good and deprived of it (compare Ephesians 3:26; Amos 4:6). The Arabic root *naqa* occurs with a similar usage in the History of Timur (page 162): "When Tamerlane," it says, "had purged <note>original Arabic gloss: אמתק - to the bone</note> Sebastia even to the flesh and marrow," that is, he had deprived it of all goods and despoiled it. **k)** "Swearing," namely by my name to a falsehood (v. 4), or perjuring, as in Psalm 24:4. **l)** Vulgate: "from this he shall likewise be judged." **v. 4. m)** For "I have made it go out" or "I will make it go out," namely the curse (v. 3; compare Malachi 2:2, 3:9). God had already previewed this in Haggai 1:6, 2:16. **n)** Compare Psalm 109:17. **o)** See the note on verse 3. **p)** Leviticus 19:12; Jeremiah 5:2. **q)** "And it shall spend the night," and perhaps not as a traveler turning aside from the road to lodge (Jeremiah 14:8), but to remain permanently (compare Psalm 25:13, 49:13; Job 17:2, 41:14). Vulgate: "it shall dwell." It is a feminine past tense with a *Segol* placed for a *Kametz*, as in Isaiah 59:5. **r)** It shall not stand at the doors, but shall penetrate to the very middle and interior of the house.

<header>402 ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER 5.</header>

<margin>
r) It consumes or devours that house along with its wood and stones, even those of the perjurer, like a most piercing fire such as in 1 Kings 18:38. Compare Hosea 11:6. s) See the note: not even a trace remains on the surface. Compare Habakkuk 2:11.
</margin>
<margin>
This is the measure by which those are punished whose eye is fixed on all the earth to seek out wealth, while making the Ephah basket small; and so they are measured with the same measure they used. But according to Cocceius's Lexicon 607: This is their eye—this is what people look at and seek. For the "eye" represents desire...
</margin>

**5** Then the angel who talked with me came forward and said to me, "Lift up your eyes now, and see what this is that is coming forth."

<margin>
v. 5. t) The angel went out, namely, from the myrtle grove (chapter 1:8) or, as Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A significant 12th-century Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> prefers, out from the rank of the other angels, so that he might show the vision more closely and clearly. Compare chapter 2:7 and the notes there. u) see chapter 1:9 and 4:1. x) see verse 1 and Ezekiel 8:3. y) What is this that comes out, appearing as if a curtain were being drawn back? The Targum Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and rabbinic paraphrase of the Prophets.</note> asks: "Who are these who appear?" See verses 3 and 6.
</margin>

**6** And I said, "What is it?" And he said, "This is an ephah <note>An ephah was a standard unit of dry volume, roughly equivalent to a modern bushel.</note> basket coming out." He said moreover, "This is their eye throughout all the earth."

**7** And behold, a lead cover was lifted up, and there was a certain woman sitting inside the ephah!

**8** And he said, "This is Wickedness." And he threw her back into the ephah, and threw the lead weight over its mouth.

<margin>
Here begins the seventh prophetic emblem, representing the Christian Church degenerating through the desire for and abundance of worldly goods. For just as the preceding emblem exposed the judgment of the degenerate Jewish Church (which reached its fullness in the final destruction of Jerusalem), so he now proceeds to depict what corruption would be brought into the Christian Church itself.
</margin>
<margin>
v. 6. z) What is that? I confess I do not know; I ask, therefore, that you instruct me (chapter 4:4, 12). a) This is the Ephah coming out. Targum Jonathan: "These are the people who took and gave false measures." Compare Amos 8:5 and Micah 6:10. Hugo Grotius <note>A famous 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> also understands this as Israelites and Jews using unjust measures, and for that reason being quickly led away into captivity by the Assyrians and Babylonians. However, in these Emblems, Zechariah is rightly believed to act as a prophet of the future rather than a historian. The Ephah is a measure of dry goods. It is placed here to represent the abundance of temporal goods greedily sought in a Church enjoying peace, according to Grotius and Marckius. b) Targum Jonathan: "Behold, these things are revealed before all the inhabitants of the earth." Rabbi Solomon (Rashi):
</margin>

**9** Then I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, two women were coming out, and the wind was in their wings. They had wings like the wings of a stork, and they lifted up the ephah between earth and heaven.

**10** Then I said to the angel who talked with me, "Where are they taking the ephah?"

**11** And he said to me, "To build a house for her in the land of Shinar <note>Shinar is the biblical name for the region of Babylon.</note>; and when it is ready, she will be set there on her own pedestal."

->Page 402<-

"Eye" signifies the intention of the mind, love, study, and affection (chapter 4:10, 9:1; Matthew 6:23; compare 2 Corinthians 4:18, 2 Peter 2:14). So says Gurtler in *Prophetic Theology* page 134 and *Typico-Prophetical Vocabulary* page 56: Christians enjoying peace fix their eyes on collecting wealth. The Ephah turns the eyes of everyone toward itself. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> reads: "This is their injustice," as if they had read the Hebrew word <term>עֲוֹנָם</term> <note>original: "awonam" (their iniquity) instead of "einam" (their eye)</note> with a *Vav*. Lambert Bos in his prolegomena to the Septuagint thinks this ancient reading is preferable to ours, though it is not strictly necessary. c) But this corruption, spread through the whole earth, finally found a fixed and principal seat in Rome—that is, in the land of Shinar—as seen in verse 11. **v. 7. d)** But behold! God does not allow Himself to be "without witness" <note>original: ἀμάרτυρον</note> against this luxury. e) A rounded mass, which in verse 8 is called a stone (1 Samuel 10:3, 2 Samuel 12:30). f) Of lead (Ezekiel 32:18). g) It was brought for this purpose: to be cast into the mouth of the wicked woman (verse 8). h) Construct it thus: "This one, who was sitting in the middle of that Ephah, was a certain woman." Just as above in verse 6, "This is the Ephah coming out" stands for "This thing which comes out is an Ephah." This woman is an image of a <unclear>destructive</unclear> <note>original: ὀλεθρίου</unclear></note> Hierarchy, rejoicing and glorying in an abundance of wealth; she is clearly the same as the Apocalyptic woman or harlot of Revelation 17:1–7, who in verse 18 is said to be that "great city which has dominion over the kings of the earth." Targum Jonathan, following its own hypothesis (from verse 6), continues to explain it this way: "Behold, swift peoples carry them away quickly, and other peoples come and dwell in their place, because they took and gave false measures." i) "Who was sitting." This is the character of the Apocalyptic woman in Revelation 17:1, 3, 9, 15, and 18:7. From this, that hierarchical <unclear>position</unclear> <note>original: στάσι</note> deserves its title, as it is commonly called the "Holy See" <note>original: sancta sedes</note>. k) "In the middle of that ephah," mentioned in verse 6. She is depicted this way to signify an abundance of wealth, as we noted there. **v. 8. l)** "This woman whom you saw sitting in the Ephah is Impurity" (Isaiah 9:17, Malachi 3:15, 19). That is, she is wicked and a teacher of wickedness (compare the use of <term>iniquity</term> <note>original: עֲוֹן</note> regarding Athaliah in 2 Chronicles 24:7), the "mother of harlots and abominations of the earth" (Revelation 17:5). She is like the wicked Jezebel (Revelation 2:20, 18:23, 19:2; compare the "mystery of iniquity" in 2 Thessalonians 2:7). m) And when this was done, he threw her, etc. Jerome <note>A 4th-century church father and translator of the Vulgate.</note> rightly says: "He seized the woman and sent her headlong into the middle of the jar; she who before was carried freely and sat upon the jar appearing to everyone." And Rabbi Solomon: "Until now she sat in the middle; but now he throws her and casts her down into its midst," signifying punishment. Thus in Revelation 2:22, the harlot is thrown into a bed with her adulterers as a punishment, just as she had previously committed adultery in a bed. I do not know if this refers to the sending of barbarian nations to devastate the Church—that is, the Roman Empire—by which that woman, luxuriating in an abundance of wealth, was cast down and <unclear>crushed</unclear>. Yet she did not repent (Revelation 2:21) but emerged from there and took up a fixed seat in the mystical land of Shinar, as seen below in verse 11, until she is finally entirely cut off. n) The stone or (as the Vulgate renders it) the leaden mass (verse 7). According to Gurtler (page 134), this leaden stone represents one or another people restraining the Antichrist; or according to Maius (page 1079), the witnesses of the truth who stop up the mouth of the lying beast. o) "Into its mouth." Jerome refers the "mouth" to the Ephah, saying: "Lest she should perhaps lift her head again, he sends a talent of lead in the manner of a very heavy stone into the mouth of the jar, so that he may oppress and shut up the wickedness in the middle, lest it should break out in any way." If one takes the Hebrew word <term>לוע</term>, "mouth" or "opening" signifies the open side from which something enters or exits (as in Genesis 29:2, Exodus 28:32). Most, however, refer it to the woman herself, who was the direct subject here. Rabbi Solomon says: "The leaden stone was cast into the woman's mouth so that she might no longer lift herself up, and so that her voice would not be heard bewailing the poor." Ibn Ezra cleverly compares this to Psalm 107:42. See further Job 5:16. **v. 9. p)** "Then I lifted up..." (see chapter 1, 6:1). The same woman is presented, but no longer cast down and restrained as in verse 8; rather, she is exalted, established, and after God's chastisement, returning to her harlotries even more furiously (compare Ezekiel 23:15–17). q) Gurtler (page 134) says the "other woman" is the civil power favoring the Antichrist. He perhaps interprets the second one as the ecclesiastical power. r) See note on verse 5. s) That is, they went out with such speed as if the wind were in their wings. "Wings" here is either found figuratively for the sails of ships which, being quite large, were inflated by the force of the wind to snatch those women into the air (compare Hosea 4:19), or, as is more credible, they are wings in the proper sense as a symbol of speed. The former involves a more passive and penal aspect which does not fit the context; the latter is confirmed by the following phrase. He means, therefore, that these women, driven by a favorable wind, flew swiftly on their own wings. t) Parenthesis: "For they were wings like the wings of a stork" (Leviticus 11:19, Psalm 104:17). Storks fly both swiftly and very high; in both respects, the women are compared to them, as they quickly promoted the dignity of the hierarchical woman and made it supreme. u) "And they lifted up," so that being led away they might find a fixed place (verses 10, 11). The Hebrew verb is <term>נָשָׂא</term> <note>to lift up/carry</note>, with the third radical letter dropped as in Jeremiah 2:31. As the Babylonian Harlot, says Maius, is "elevated by her parasites even to heaven," as if by wings, with both ecclesiastical and civil powers being granted and left to her. x) 2 Samuel 18:9. **v. 10. y)** See verse 5. z) "Where are these taking her?" (chapter 2:5, Numbers 11:11). a) This is taken collectively for the Ephah with the woman sitting in it (verse 7, compare verse 11). **v. 11. b)** There is a little more in the response than there was in the question. For he is not content to say where they are taking the Ephah; he explains another, no less necessary circumstance: the purpose for which they take it. It is credible that the Prophet desired to know this as well, even if he did not express it as clearly in words. He says, therefore, "To build a house for her," etc. It is as if he said: the woman, whom I just called "Wickedness" in verse 8, has wandered through various uncertain seats while corruption was spread throughout the Church; but now they are about to build a house for her, that is, a certain fixed and stable seat, which may be as it were a perpetual and prominent domicile of wickedness.

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Zechariah chapter 5 to the beginning of chapter 6. It concludes the vision of the woman in the Ephah basket (wickedness) being relocated to Shinar (Babylonia) and begins the vision of the four chariots coming from between two mountains of bronze. The commentary continues to debate whether these symbols refer to historical kingdoms or mystical spiritual realities.</meta>

### CHAPTER VI. ZECHARIAH 6. CHAPTER 6.

<margin>To be consecrated to God, received into grace, and saved. Vitringa, in his *Doctrine of Prophecy* page 55, refers this to those prophecies which generally describe the fates of the world</margin>
as they run their course in a certain order; compare Daniel 2:31-46; chapter 7:1-28; chapter 11:2 and following. And so that it may be clearer where this illustrious man is heading, he says on page 144: "The scope of the prophecy is to teach that after those four kingdoms mentioned—namely the Persian, Alexander’s, the Syro-Macedonian, and the Egyptian—had appeared on the globe by divine decree, one could expect Jesus Christ and his kingdom, heavenly and spiritual." However, the same illustrious man, in his *Commentary on the Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note> chapter 6, page 329, explains the four greater kingdoms shown under the emblem of the four chariots as the Babylonian, Persian, Alexander’s, and those of the Seleucids and Ptolemies. Gurtlerus, however, in his *Prophetic Theology* page 134, says: "The two mountains of bronze are the two kingdoms of Israel and Media; the four chariots with horses are the four kingdoms with their armies weighing upon Canaan. The black horses are the Medes and Persians, heavy and troublesome to the Jews, heading toward Babylonia and Assyria north of Palestine; the white are the Greeks under Alexander the Great, who favored the Jews; the various <note>dappled</note> are the Ptolemies and Seleucids, stirring up wars in Egypt; the red are the Romans, often invading Canaan and finally destroying the Jewish Republic." Truly, Tarnovius’s explanation relies <note>original: "πρὸς ἑρμηνεία", Greek for "upon the interpretation"</note> on verse 8 (as if the Angels are not said to go out on a raid, but to have quieted Babylonia, and it is not so much about subduing enemies in wrath as about calling them to the kingdom of Christ by grace) and it struggles with the difficulty of explaining the color of the horses, which is not only white, but also red, black, and varied—and thus suggests that those horses are the ministers of God’s punishing judgments in the mentioned lands. But neither the opinions of the celebrated Vitringa nor Gurtlerus prove themselves to us: for they confuse the chariots with the lands themselves or the empires to which the chariots are sent; compare Haggai 2:21, 22, 23. The easiest explanation seems to us to be that of the celebrated Maius in his *Economy of the Old Testament* page 1080, who establishes that by the type of the 4 chariots, divine judgments are indicated, to be executed by the holy Angels upon kingdoms adverse to the Kingdom of Christ; compare Haggai 2:22; Zechariah 1:14, 15; chapter 6:22; chapter 10, etc. For chariots and horses denote Angels in 2 Kings 2:11; chapter 6:17; Psalm 68:18, as swift executors of divine judgments in Isaiah 66:15; Habakkuk 3:8. And below in verse 5, the Angel himself explains the chariots as *Heavenly spirits going out from standing before the Lord of the whole earth*, sent out to patrol the earth in verse 7, which was also said of the Angels above in chapter 1:10. Moreover, what we have said becomes much clearer when one considers the connection of this emblem with the preceding one. Namely, it was said in chapter 5:11 that the woman, who in verse 8 was called "wickedness," had obtained a house in the land of Shinar. There, therefore, wickedness is now seen to be punished by the Prophet, just as in the remaining lands that had cherished it; compare chapter 5:6. This is especially true in the north country (which is the name for Babylonia; compare verse 10; Jeremiah 1:14, 15; chapter 6:22; chapter 10:22, etc.) as the chief seat and home of impiety; compare here below verse 6 and verse 8, where a repeated and more specific mention of the north country is made for that reason. Just as above (chapter 5:11) the land of Shinar was understood not literally, but mystically, so it is clear from this connection that the "north country" here is also mystical rather than literal, although the literal was a type of the mystical. For the rest, regarding the fourfold number of chariots, compare the note on chapter 2:1. k) "from between," that is, from the middle of two mountains. Psalm 104:12. l) "the mountains," which I mentioned, were "mountains of bronze." This denotes the strength of the mind and unshakable firmness; compare Jeremiah 1:18. Just as by the name of "mountain" itself something firm is signified; compare Psalm 36:7. According to Junius, these two mountains are signs of the most powerful and unsearchable providence of God, from whose hidden depths the firmest and inescapable counsels emerge. The celebrated Vitringa says much the same in his *Commentary on the Apocalypse* 6, page 327. Gurtlerus, as we have already noted, understands them as the two kingdoms of Israel and the Messiah. Wigandus thinks Jerusalem is hinted at, in which are the two mountains Zion and Moriah. Thus, the stability of the true Church, of which Jerusalem is the symbol, would be noted against the schemes of Satan and enemies. Nor is this explanation unsuitable. For when Angels are said to go out from Zion or Jerusalem, it is the same as if they were said to go out from the Lord, whose Presence dwells in the true church, who rules and protects the church; compare verse 5; cf. Joel 4:16, 17; Psalm 20:3. Jerome says: "of bronze," that is, insuperable and very strong, which cannot be consumed by any passage of time. verse 2. m) "red horses," portending slaughter and disaster; compare verse 8. See what we noted in chapter 1:8 about the colors of the horses and their significance. The illustrious Vitringa, in his *Commentary on the Apocalypse* 6, page 337, thinks they figure the Babylonians, sprinkled and dyed with the blood of the people of God, which we mentioned; we discussed this at verse 1. For the Babylonians, along with their like, are the *object* of these horses rather than the *subject* signified by the horses; compare verse 6 and 8, although in the added explanation, it is not explicitly said where the red ones specifically went. n) "black," omening unlucky and sad things, not to the Jews or the people of God as some explain, but to the northerners or Babylonians in verse 6, 8. Cf. Revelation 6:5. See what we noted above at verse 1 from the minds of Vitringa and Gurtlerus. verse 3. o) "white." Chapter 1:8. See below verse 6. p) The Septuagint, Jonathan, and the Vulgate: "various" <note>dappled</note>. They are called <note>original: "χαλαζωενοι", Greek for "hail-spotted"</note>, those who are sprinkled with white spots like hail, or "guttati" <note>spotted with drops</note>, <note>original: "λευκόסικτοι", Greek for "white-speckled"</note>; compare Genesis 31:10, 12. Bochart, *Hieroz.* Part I, page 109 and following. q) The Vulgate and others: "strong." Cf. Job 9:4. But to one reading the place attentively, it will be established that it is a name of a color. Jonathan: "ash-colored." More correctly the Syriac, Arabic, and certain Greek copies in Jerome say "reddish" or "red." (2) verse 7. It is the same as <note>original: "חָמוּץ", Hebrew for "sour" or "bright red"</note> red in Isaiah 63:1, with the guttural letters Aleph (א) and Het (ח) swapped: <note>original: "אָמֹץ"</note>, which among the Hebrews as well as the Arabs primarily means to become sharp or sour, <note>original: "ὀξύνειν", Greek for "to make sharp"</note>. Therefore, "hamits" or "amits" in colors is the same as the Greek <note>original: "ὀξύ", Greek for "sharp/bright"</note>, which is clear and vigorous and excited by much light; especially purple. Consequently, the horses are noted not indeed as purple—of which there are none—but those whose redness is <note>original: "ὀξύτερος", Greek for "sharper/more intense"</note> and more excited: by which they are distinguished from the horses of the first chariot in verse 2, which are simply called "red" <note>original: "אֲדֻמִּים"</note>. Bochart, *Hieroz.* Part I, page 111 and following.

<column-break/>

c) "in the land of Shinar," which it is certain was around Babylon; compare Genesis 10:10; chapter 11:2, 9; Daniel 1:2. Whence the Septuagint, Arabic, Syriac, and Jonathan in this place rendered it "in the land of the Babylonians"; and the same Septuagint, Arabic, and Jonathan in Isaiah 11:11 explained Shinar as Babylonia. Here, however, the same is not understood, but an analogical, mystical Babylon and spiritual one, of which Revelation 14:8; 16:19; 17:5; 18:2, 10, 21 speak. "A house in the land of Shinar," says Gurtlerus in *Prophetic Theology* page 134, "is the seat of the Antichrist in mystical Babylon."
d) "For a house is prepared for it." For this must be referred to the "house," which among the Hebrews is of the Masculine gender. Isaiah 30:33.
e) "And the Ephah will be placed there with the woman," so that it may remain in the house prepared for it. Isaiah 14:1. To be adored like a God or a Vice-God, 2 Kings 17:29; Isaiah 46:7; cf. 2 Thessalonians 2:4. By reason of grammar, this form is mixed from the Hophal and Hiphil <note>Hebrew verb patterns</note>.
f) "on its base" or in its habitation. As if to say, in its prepared place. (1) cf. 1 Kings 8:39, 43; Daniel 8:11.

The four chariots, where we have a) the vision itself in verses 1-3, and b) the explanation of the vision, partly general in verses 4-7, and partly special in verse 8. II. The twin Crowns placed on the head of the High Priest Joshua, where again is described a) the vision itself in verses 9-11, and b) the explanation of the vision from verse 12 to the end.

<margin>
**verse 4. r)** What are these, that is, what are they and what are they doing? Now follows the explanation of the Emblem, which the Prophet asks for in verse 4. The Angel grants it to the petitioner in verses 5 and 8. However, there follows a further report by the Prophet of the Emblem seen by him in verses 6 and 7. Compare chapter 3, 9; chapter 2, 2; chapter 4, 4.
**verse 5. s)** The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note>, Vulgate, and Arabic versions read "four winds," as the Hebrews are accustomed to designate not only the cardinal winds but also the four quarters of the world or the peoples dwelling in them; see chapter 2, 10; Jeremiah 49, 36; Daniel 7, 2; Revelation 7, 1. From this, Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan</note> says: "These are the four kingdoms, which are like the four winds of the heavens." But we prefer to interpret them as the four Spirits (or orders and troops of spirits) of heaven, that is, Angels going into the four quarters of the world, because they are said to go out from standing before the Lord, which is a duty specifically belonging to Angels, as we observed above at verse 1. Compare therefore Psalm 104, 4. **t)** "Going out," according to the command they received from the Lord, to be executed through all parts of the world. Compare chapter 1, 10. **u)** "From standing themselves," after they stood before the Lord to wait for and receive His orders, just as a servant appearing before a master watches for his nod and attends to what he must do; Job 1, 6; chapter 2, 1. Compare Exodus 34, 2; Numbers 11, 16; Zechariah 4, 14; Daniel 7, 10. **x)** "Before the Lord of all the earth," who rules the entire earth and each of its parts by His power and providence; chapter 4, 10, 14; chapter 9, 1; Joshua 3, 11, 13; Micah 4, 13; Psalm 24, 1.
**verse 6. y)** Furthermore, as for the chariot in which the black horses were: These words, as it seems, are no longer those of the Angel explaining the vision, but of the Prophet further reporting the thing seen, up

See the note on verse 5. **b)** "To the north country," or Babylonia (verse 8); yet it is mystical rather than properly so-called, see chapter 5, 11. See what we noted above at verse 1.

**c)** "The white indeed," from verse 3. This color is a symbol of victory and triumph; Revelation 6, 2; chapter 19, 11, 14. **d)** "After them," that is, they followed them to the same place. **e)** "The dappled indeed," see verse 3, and what we will say about the meaning of the mixed color at verse 7. **f)** "The south country," of which region Egypt was once the type, just as Assyria and later Babylonia were the type of the north; chapter 10, 11. Furthermore, these signs currently under discussion seem to be universal over the four parts of the world, which is not poorly gathered from the four-fold number of the chariots. But is there no mention here of the east and west? Perhaps, therefore, it should be said that the whole earth is here cut into two general parts, and thus north and south come synecdochically <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note> for all the quarters of the world, as in Isaiah 43, 6; Psalm 89, 13. **v. 7.** **g)** Namely to one. These are the same ones he had just called "spotted" or "dappled" in verse 6; compare verse 3. **h)** The Prophet therefore takes up again what he had already reported at the end of the previous verse regarding the exit of these horses, and does so for this purpose: to declare it more specifically. The Vulgate reads: <note>original: "Qui autem erant robustissimi"</note> *But those who were the strongest.* See note on verse 3. **h)** See note on verse 5. **i)** <note>original: "quæsiverunt ire"</note> *They sought to go.* Seeking, however, is not taken here for a mere attempt at acting that excludes the effect or the power to reach the effect; but it signifies the very turning of the mind and faculty toward acting, and is the same as if he said: by the very act they prepared themselves for going; compare chapter 12, 9; Daniel 9, 3. For it has already been stated that they went out. But Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow, 1562–1633, a Lutheran theologian</note>, for whom the southern land is Judea, says: "Of their own accord... they were asking from God, and requesting that this be entrusted to them, that they might walk to and fro... On account of that, moved by His mercy and the prayers of the holy angels, the Prince said: Go, walk through this land, and do what you were commanded and what you yourselves wished." **k)** <note>original: "ut obambularent"</note> *That they might walk to and fro* or traverse the land, partly to impose punishments on the wicked, and partly to defend the good, if any remain. For perhaps the variety of colors in these horses involves a varied operation according to the diversity of the objects: so that they are red and are instruments of vengeance in respect to the wicked; but white in respect to the good, to whom they bring peace and triumphs. See note on chapter 1, 10; and compare Job 1, 6, 7; chapter 2, 1, 2. **l)** "For he said" or "had said," for before the horses prepared themselves to go out, they received the command to go out; although in the report the former is mentioned first and the latter afterward. Unless perhaps Tarnovius's opinion, which we just gave, is more pleasing. **m)** <note>original: "Sic igitur obambularunt"</note> *Thus they walked to and fro.* The verb is feminine: therefore it cannot be referred to the horses if one stays within the metaphor, but it can be referred to the <term>merkavot</term> <note>original: "מרכבות"</note> or chariots, taken collectively along with the horses in verse 1. Or the Prophet speaks outside of the metaphor or figure, so that in his mind he had the celestial spirits (<term>ruachot</term> <note>original: "רוחות"</note>) themselves as the subject, which were shadowed by the figure of the horses in verse 5. **v. 8.** **n)** <note>original: "Inclamauit autem me"</note> *And he called out to me,* or roused me with a shout; Judges 4, 10, 13; as if to hear an especially notable message concerning the judgments of the north country or Babylonia, that one, namely, in which the Prophet had seen "wickedness" settled earlier in chapter 5, 11. **o)** "Behold!" especially those who went out etc. **p)** See note on verse 6. **q)** <note>original: "quiescere fecerunt spiritum meum"</note> *They have caused my spirit to rest.* These words, unless considered attentively, have some ambiguity. Tarnovius interprets it in a positive sense: "They calmed (especially the white ones) my spirit... Namely, by bringing many men lingering in Babylonia to repentance and piety through their ministry, and by keeping others in it whose piety had not yet entirely cooled, they brought it about that I do not yet entirely exclude all of them from my grace." But we explain it rather in a negative sense, so that it signifies the punishment imposed on the north, and that a most grave one. For we accept what Tarnovius also concedes, that the "spirit of the Lord" in this place is His wrath, just as it is taken in Ecclesiastes 10, 4; and the same was correctly explained by the Septuagint here and in Proverbs 29, 11; Job 15, 13, by the word *thymos* <note>original: "θυμὸϛ"</note> <note>Greek for wrath or passion</note>. When they are said to have "made the wrath of God rest" in the north country, the sense is that so much slaughter and so many evils were produced by them in this land that they did not cease until the entire force of divine wrath, its entire power, had as it were spent its rage and cooled down in that land, and God had been satisfied, taking vengeance on the wicked. Compare Ezekiel 5, 13; chapter 16, 42; chapter 21, 22; chapter 24, 13; and below Zechariah 9, 1. Nearly related to this phrasing is that where God threatens that He will consume His arrows or His wrath upon someone; Deuteronomy 32, 23; Ezekiel 6, 12; chapter 7, 8; chapter 13, 15; or that He wishes to comfort Himself by taking punishment from the wicked; chapter 5, 13. Jonathan says: "Tell them, 'Do my will in the north country'"; but this is wrong, as if he had read <term>hanichu</term> <note>original: "הניחו"</note> in the Hebrew text as an imperative. **r)** See chapter 5, 11; and what we noted here at verse 1.

\* **v. 6.** <term>ve-ha-amutzim</term> <note>original: "וְהָאֲמֻצִּים"</note> fully written 2. thus future 5. according to the printed Masorah on Ezekiel 14, 21.

A significant portion of the text debates whether "causing God's spirit to rest" in the north (Babylon) refers to bringing people to repentance or, more likely, the total satisfaction of divine wrath through judgment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Zechariah chapter 6. While the previous page focused on the vision of the four chariots representing divine judgment across the earth, this page transitions to a symbolic action: the crowning of the High Priest Joshua. This act serves as a "prophetic performance" or emblem, shifting the focus from the destruction of kingdoms to the arrival of a future King-Priest known as the "Branch."</meta>

# ZECHARIAH CHAP. 6.

->9. And the word of the LORD came to me, saying:<-
->10. Take from those of the captivity, from Heldai, from Tobijah, and from Jedaiah; and you, go on that same day, go to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who have come from Babylon.<-
->11. Take silver and gold and make crowns, and set them on the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest.<-
->12. And speak to him, saying: Thus says the LORD of hosts, saying: Behold, a man whose name is the Branch; and from his place he shall branch out...<-

---

<margin>...they shall bring gifts to Jerusalem, as the latter half of the verse teaches. Furthermore, it is believed that this Heldai had two names; for in verse 14 he is called Helem. **y) (you shall go, etc.)** A parenthesis [explanatory side-note] continuing to the end of the verse, instructing the Prophet where he might meet them and how he might receive the items from them. **x) on that day**, namely, the day on which he must perform what I now command. Perhaps God had determined a specific day in the vision, which the Prophet deemed less necessary to express in the description of the vision. If the same day on which the previous vision was presented and declared were intended—which the <term>Targum</term><note>An ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> prefers—the demonstrative pronoun for "this" would have been used: **y) on this very day**. **a) you shall go, I say.** The verb is repeated after the specific time is mentioned, so that its connection to the destination might strike the eye more readily. **b)** He is probably the same person called "Chen" in verse 14; for in both places he is called the son of <term>Zephaniah</term>. **c)** Perhaps the same person mentioned in 2 Kings 25:18. **d) which they entered**, or where they came, where they turned aside upon coming from Babylon; namely, the legates [representatives] whom the first half of the verse names. Others translate "who had come," but this goes against the Hebrew accents, according to which Josiah was the host of the action, and the others were the guests.</margin>

<margin>**verse 9. a)** See the note at Chapter 1:1. Now follows the final Emblem: the double Crown placed on the head of Joshua the High Priest, to prefigure both the priesthood and the kingship of Christ. Part II: The explanation and application of the Emblem. verses 12–15.</margin>

<margin>**verse 10. t) By taking**, that is, "take." **n) from the captivity**, that is, from the Jews still living in exile in Babylon; or, as Jonathan <note>The author of the Aramaic Targum.</note> translates, "the children of the migration," meaning the exiles. See Ezekiel 1:1, Ezra 1:11, chapter 4:1. For not all had returned to the fatherland immediately with Zerubbabel, even though King Cyrus had given the power to return to everyone; many returned only later with Ezra (Ezra 7:6, 7), and even then a large part remained in Babylonia and maintained frequent schools there as if in their own country. These "Babylonians" (for so we call them in contrast to the "Palestinians" who had already returned), when they heard about the resumed building of the Temple, soon sent gold and silver collected by them through the representatives named here, as a gift to adorn the temple. Zechariah is therefore commanded to receive from the exiles—that is, from the representatives of the exiled Jews—some part of that gold and silver, so that it may serve as an emblem to prefigure a most notable matter (compare verse 15 below). The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> uses a neutral term <term>receive</term> <note>original: ἀπολαβὲ</note> things from the captivity, or from those sent from the captivity; I believe because...</margin>

<margin>...they thought a word for "taking" was missing. But the Accusative [the object of the sentence], because of the parenthesis inserted in this verse, only follows in verse 11, and indeed after the verb is repeated: "Take, I say, the gold and silver." **x)** Namely from Heldai and the others, whom the Babylonians sent with gifts...</margin>

**verse 11. e) Take, I say.** Repeated from verse 10, so that the instruction, which the parenthesis had interrupted there, becomes complete and absolute. **f)** Compare Haggai 2:8, 9 and Isaiah 60:9. **g) and from it you shall make**, or cause to be made by a goldsmith. See Exodus 25:31, etc. **h) crowns** (verse 14, Job 31:36). The Syriac translates "crown," and Jonathan translates "a great crown"; both rendered it in the singular here and in verse 14, as if there were only one crown, but the plural noted its greatness; just as elsewhere "salvations" is used for a great salvation, or "sorrows" for grievous pain. However, it appears that two crowns are indicated here, one of gold and the other of silver, both from the plural ending (which we can hardly be persuaded to understand as singular without necessity) and from the double material which God commands to be requested from the Babylonians. Finally, it is clear from the application of the emblem itself in verse 13, where it is applied to a dual thing ("between them both"). Likewise, Rabbi David Kimchi interprets this as two crowns; however, he errs in presuming that one was to be placed on the head of Joshua and the other on the head of Zerubbabel. He is honest enough to admit that this explanation relies on opinion, not on the authority of the sacred text, as is his claim that Zerubbabel was greeted not as a prince but as a King after this crown was placed on him. The sacred page is entirely silent about Zerubbabel here; we will soon discuss what should be thought of his royal title at verse 12. Therefore, it is quite evident that both were placed on the head of Joshua. Furthermore, a crown is a sign of a person more venerable and sacred than others: in the Old Testament, it was worn not only by the King but also by the High Priest, though (as is believable) with a different design (Exodus 28:36, 37; chapter 29:6; compare 2 Samuel 1:10). Therefore the double crown, placed on the single head of Joshua, was intended to foreshadow a twin dignity, royal and priestly, joined in one subject; that is, the priesthood of <term>Melchizedek</term> (whom Joshua represented in this way), according to which he is both King and Priest of the Most High God (Genesis 14:18, Psalm 110:4, Hebrews 6:20, chapter 7:1 onwards). **i) and you shall place** one after the other. **k) Joshua** or (as the Septuagint and Vulgate express it) Jesus, who as above in chapter 3:1, was here by name and by omen a type of the Messiah (verse 11, here, and verses 12, 13). See Preface § 10.

**verse 12. l) You shall speak to him**, namely, in explanation of this symbolic act, so that he and other faithful people might know whom it regards and what this rite signifies. **m) Behold**, now he is excellently adorned by me with these crowns; but they are not placed on you for your own sake, but so that you may bear the figure and type of Christ the King and Priest. **Targum.** See note on Jeremiah 31:2. **n)** See note on chapter 1:8. **o) whose name is the BRANCH.** For which Jonathan rightly translates: "whose name shall be the MESSIAH." For the ancient Rabbis explained this place concerning the Messiah in *Eicha Rabbathi* and *Bemidbar Rabba*; hence Aben-Ezra, in his notes, setting aside the <term>nonsense</term> <note>original: φλυαρότητα</note> of some of his tribesmen, says: "It is more fitting that the discourse be about the Messiah, as the Chaldean Paraphrast [the Targum] explained." But Rashi, Kimchi, and Ibn Ezra wrongly want Zerubbabel to be understood, dreaming that he was afterwards greeted as King by the Jews, as we said at verse 11; but this is most improbable, since no trace of such a thing exists in the sacred writings. On the contrary, Nehemiah (a successor to Zerubbabel) when he was spitefully accused by the Samaritans of affecting royal honors and titles, rejected this as a lie and a calumny (Nehemiah 6:6-8). See further what we observed on this name at chapter 3:8, and our Discussion on the Names of Christ designating his human nature, § 8 onwards. Furthermore, the Vulgate translated it "the East/Rising" <note>original: Oriens</note>, the Septuagint and following it the Syriac and Arabic translated <term>the Rising/Branch</term> <note>original: ἀνατολὴν</note>. Since this suffers from a certain ambiguity, we learn from Jerome’s commentary on this passage: "The East," he says, "which in Hebrew is called *Tzemach*... that is, *anatole* [rising] or *anaphye* [growth] or *blastema* [shoot]—that is, a branch; because it would grow up suddenly from itself, and will sprout from its own root in the likeness of a branch." Less aptly, the Targum on Zechariah 3:9 says: "The Greeks," he says, "wrongly translated the Hebrew word *Tzemach* as *anatole* [rising], confusing it with *Zerach* or *Mizrach* [sunrise]." The verb itself <term>to rise/sprout</term> <note>original: ἀνατέλλειν</note> properly means <term>to bloom</term> <note>original: ἀνθίζειν</note> in a <term>metaphor of plants</term> <note>original: ἐν μεταφορᾷ βοτανῶν</note>. Compare Hebrews 7:14.

**p) who from beneath him**, for he shall sprout from his underlying place or ground in which he was sown, and is therefore rightly called the Branch. *Tzemach* [Branch] is placed like a Name, as below in chapter 12:8 and 16:29; Habakkuk 3:6. So also Aben-Ezra on Isaiah adds: "The Branch from himself." Cocceius proves this in his Lexicon, where he says: "It is noted that he is a being who receives his increase neither from kings nor priests as a predecessor, nor from any outside power." Likewise the celebrated Maimonides on the Old Testament: "from himself, to be sprouted by no human sowing." These things, as far as the matter itself is concerned, are well-stated: yet the emphasis of this particle seems to us to imply what we said at the beginning: that Christ would behave like a small plant, which rises slowly from its ground in which it was sown or planted, and in time grows to its proper size.

**v. 10.** *me-et* with prefix ¶ 1, 3, 5, 6, 9, 20, 23. **2. ha-golah** with final Sheva q. 3. 11. 14. 18. 24. and *Ber.* 'sh' by Mercha 1. 2. **v. 11. ve-asita** following the reading in M. I. **v. 12. Thus says the LORD of hosts** deleting the following "saying" [le-emor] sc. 2.

<meta>This page continues the detailed commentary on Zechariah 6, moving from the physical act of crowning the High Priest Joshua to the prophetic interpretation of that act. The focus is on the "Branch" (the Messiah), who will unite the roles of King and Priest—offices that were strictly separated in ancient Israel—to build a spiritual temple including all nations.</meta>

# ZECHARIAH. CHAP. 6. 1
<meta>catchword: you shall obey</meta>

<margin>
**p)** *Targum Jonathan: he shall be revealed*
**q)** *he shall be magnified. cf. Isaiah 1:1, 43:19. q) = he shall build. cf. note on Leviticus 3:4.* **r)** *the temple of the Lord v. 13, 14. This is distinct from the one which you, along with Zerubbabel, have now built, 1:16. Namely, that true spiritual one, not made with hands, whose building the pilgrims themselves will assist v. 15. Hebrews 8:2, 9:11, 23. Acts 7:48, 17:24. 2 Corinthians 5:1. This is the church of God, to be constructed not only from Jews, but also from the nations: 1 Corinthians 3:16, 17. 2 Corinthians 6:16. Ephesians 2:21, 22. If this had been the true temple of God which was already being built by Zerubbabel and Joshua, a place would by no means have been sought for another temple, for the building of which the Man whose name is* <note>original: צמח</note> *THE BRANCH <note>The Hebrew word 'Tzemach' refers to a sprout or shoot, a common Messianic title.</note> was finally to sprout or be born. cf. Hebrews 8:7, 8, 13. The structure of that typical temple was the occasion for this prediction concerning the antitype <note>An 'antitype' is the historical reality or person that fulfills a 'type' or symbolic foreshadowing.</note>, see Preface § 10.*
</margin>

<margin>
**A Qamets is in it [the word 'him']**
not of Aaron, but of Melchizedek cf. Psalm 110:4. I. 2. Hebrews 5:6, 10, 6:20, 7:11, 15, 17, 21. **a)** *upon this very throne of his, sitting upon which he shall rule as King.* **b)** *The Vulgate, Septuagint, and Arabic: between them*
</margin>

-> 13. And he shall build the temple of the LORD; and he shall bear the majesty, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both. <-

-> 14. And the crowns shall be for Helem, and for Tobijah, and for Jedaiah, and for Hen the son of Zephaniah, for a memorial in the temple of the LORD. <-

-> 15. And those who are far off shall come and build in the temple of the LORD, and you shall know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you. And this shall come to pass, if you will diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God. <-

...those two, namely the King and the Priest; as if the discussion here were about two people and their mutual conspiracy toward peace. But the structure of the emblem does not allow this explanation, according to which only one person, Joshua, shining with a double diadem, can figure as only one person—namely, the one whom he represented by this act. Nor does the nature of the promised thing itself allow it, because Christ himself is both King and Priest, carrying both offices in the unity of his person. Some indeed refer "between them both" to those who are near in Judea and those who are among the nations and still far from the church, comparing Ephesians 2:13 and following. Truly, no mention of these is made in the preceding parts of this final emblem, although in the following verse 15, the calling of the nations is finally treated. But Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian.</note> in his Lexicon, page 323, says *between both* refers to Jehovah and the *Man the Branch*; that is, a common will for granting peace, which Gousset <note>Jacques Gousset (1635–1704), a French Hebraist.</note> also approves on page 204. Truly, we prefer with Sch. the neutral sense, *between these two things*, comparing Ecclesiastes 11:6; namely, between the kingdom or royal dignity of Christ and his priesthood. These were discussed separately in the preceding lines: therefore, although these offices were always very diverse and separate in the Hebrew Republic, yet in the one person of Christ there will be a counsel of peace. That is, they will agree well; there will be a sweet harmony between the two, with no dissonance or discord, just as when in taking counsel there is one will and one opinion among the counselors. That we might prefer this explanation over others, we are prompted by the scope of the whole emblem and the prophetic prediction, which tends toward this: that under the scheme of a double crown placed on the head of one man, Joshua, a double dignity to be conferred by divine power on the one person of Christ might be figured. Therefore, the "two" mentioned here as harmonizing so sweetly must be explained in a way consistent with this given purpose.

<margin>
**v. 13. s)** *He, I say, shall build. This is taken up again from v. 12 through a pathetic anadiplosis <note>A rhetorical repetition of the last word of one clause at the beginning of the next for emphasis.</note>.* **t)** *See the same place.* **u)** *he shall receive (perfect passive) or shall wear the royal majesty like a cloak, compare Daniel 11:21, 1 Chronicles 29:25. See Psalm 8:2, Psalm 31:4 and 45:4.* **x)** *And he shall sit, namely upon his throne, which is added immediately; and it depends on this verb as much as on the following one; 1 Chronicles 29:23, Isaiah 16:5. At the right hand of God the Father, Psalm 110:1, Hebrews 8:3.* **y)** *and he shall rule, not only over Israel, Jeremiah 30:21, Micah 5:1, Luke 1:32, 33, but over the whole world, below in chapter 9:10. cf. Ezekiel 21:31.* **z)** *but he shall also be, or, the same shall simultaneously be a priest, and indeed a truly great one, Hebrews 3:1, 10:21. Such a one, clearly, who has sat down at the right hand of the throne of majesty in the heavens, chapter 8:1, made higher than the heavens themselves, chapter 7:26, who has a priesthood that is* <term>untransferable</term> <note>original: ἀπαράβατον; meaning a priesthood that does not pass to a successor because the priest lives forever.</note>
**v. 24.** *joined with royal splendor and majesty, according to the order...*
</margin>

**v. 14. c)** Meanwhile, until this promised royal Priest or Priest-King appears in the flesh and occupies both dignities, the crowns—that is, either of the crowns or both, the silver as well as the gold from verse 11—**d)** to the one who above in verse 10 was called Heldai. **e)** who above in verse 10 was Josiah, in whose house the Babylonians, bringing gifts for the building of the Temple, had turned aside. **f)** these shall be for them, I say, as a memorial, Exodus 13:9, or a monument of a matter indeed transacted in a type, but in truth still to be transacted. For whoever looks upon those crowns in the Temple will be reminded by the sight of them both of the piety of those men who either dedicated the gold and silver themselves, or of him who hospitably received those coming from remote regions to dedicate it; and also of this prophecy concerning the double dignity of the Messiah. Indeed, they will also be a memorial of another antitype: that just as the Babylonians came from a remote region to Jerusalem with silver and gold, and the Jerusalemite Josiah or Hen received them as they came; so likewise in the time of the New Testament, the nations, once most remote, will approach the Church, and be received by it readily and promptly, compare verse 15. **g)** publicly hung in the temple of the Lord. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105).</note> observes from the Talmudic Tractate *Middot* that those crowns were suspended from the windows of the Temple in its upper height. And they were without doubt among those <term>votive offerings</term> <note>original: ἀναθήματα; items dedicated to a god and displayed in a temple.</note> with which the temple is read to have been adorned in Luke 21:5, 2 Maccabees 9:16, 5:16. **v. 15. h)** And just as those of whom mention was made above in verse 10 and following came from Babylonia, a sufficiently remote land, Isaiah 39:3, bringing gifts with them to help and adorn the structure of the typical Temple, so in their own time those far off shall come, namely the nations, Ephesians 2:13, Isaiah 49:1, 57:19, to bring their glory into Jerusalem, Isaiah 35:1, 6:13, 66:12. cf. above 2:15 and below 8:22, also our Preface § 10. **i)** *and they shall build together* (or they shall have a part in the building, they shall build as one, they shall join themselves to the building), in the Temple of the Lord, as they are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens of the saints and members of the household of God, Ephesians 2:19, building themselves together with the people of God into a dwelling place and temple of the Lord in the spirit, v. 21, 22, 1 Peter 2:5. This is different from under the Old Testament, where gentiles and outsiders were barred from the communion of building the Temple, Ezra 4:2, 3. cf. Isaiah 60:10. Especially in this place, it signifies a part and partnership in the action, just as in Numbers 11:17, Ezekiel 12:20, Job 7:13. **k)** And then by the outcome of events and the prosperity of all, you shall know, Hier. See note on 2:13. **l)** See notes above on 2:13 and 4:9. **m)** Vulgate: *And this shall be*. Good, because it refers that back to the preceding, with the pronoun supplied; just as elsewhere the substantive verb should be referred to the place that preceded, for example Exodus 6:28, Numbers 25:12, Deuteronomy 2:16. Truly, for the sake of a more convenient connection, we prefer to translate it causally and declaratively, rather than adversatively: *For this shall happen*. For it declares in what way they will recognize that he was sent by the Lord, namely from the event, because what he predicted will most certainly come to pass. **n)** if only—you obey. The promise itself which preceded, concerning the Messiah, the spiritual temple, and the calling of the nations, is indeed absolute in itself, nor does it depend on the condition of either repentance or obedience; therefore the condition added here by no means suspends the actual completion of that promise, Romans 3:3, 11:29. Rather, it suggests only the caution and diligence to be applied by the Jewish people, lest they fall away from the enjoyment of the promised thing, to be fulfilled in its own time, by their own fault and stubbornness—just as happened later to a large part of the Jews when Christ had already come, Isaiah 50:1. He wishes to say, therefore: Just do what is yours to do; take care that you do not deprive yourselves of the enjoyment of such great goods through <term>disobedience</term> <note>original: ἀπείθειαν</term> and stubbornness; I, for my part, will faithfully perform what I promised you. cf. Psalm 95:7 and note on Haggai 2:23.

It interprets the participation of far-off nations as the inclusion of the Gentiles into the Church, while warning that the Jews must obey to share in these blessings.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the symbolic visions of the previous chapters to a teaching section. # ZECHARIAH | CHAP. 7. | ZECHARIAH

<margin>
**Chapter VII.**
Compare verse 5. *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was a prominent English Hebraist.</note> see in *Chronology of the Old Testament, p. 140.* He sent (Bethel) *the house or family of God*, that is, the congregation which was in Babylon. But such a naming of the captive people is unusual, and far from them
</margin>

<margin>
**CHAPTER VII. verse 1.**
**n)** After the first part of the prophecy, which was symbolic, there now follows its second part, which we can call teaching-focused, contained in two chapters, ch. VII and VIII, as we taught in the Preface § II. And in this chapter, the Prophet acts so that, on the occasion of a question proposed by the Jews—whether the fasts should now be continued, v. 1-3—he might instruct the people both concerning true and hypocritical fasts, v. 4-7. II. Concerning the fruits of conversion and repentance required by God rather than fasts, v. 8 to the end. **o)** *In the last year* of the four years, that is, *the fourth year*, specifically two years after the first beginning of the prophecy in ch. 1:1, 7. Since the Jews were still proceeding vigorously in the construction of the Temple, and now a joyful hope of soon putting the finishing touch to the work was shining, compare Ezra 6:15. **p)** Concerning which, see ch. 1:1 and in the Preface § 6. **q)** That word "and it was" which, after the parenthesis of v. 2, 3 is interposed, and the sign of the word is resumed in v. 4, will be explained in v. 5 and following, and throughout chapter 7. See note on ch. 1:1. **r)** *The fourth* day of the ninth month, or *November*. **s)** Specifically in the month of *Kislev* <note>original: כסלו</note> *Nehemiah 1:1.*
