doubt was the Prophet's response, who had sent the inquiry: but now the *people of the land* and the priests, to whom the response is directed in verse 5, were Palestinians, not Babylonians, as our notes there will show; therefore, with Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow (1562–1633), a Lutheran theologian.</note> and others, we establish that this delegation came from the returned people themselves living in Judea: the subject for this can be supplied from verse 5 here; *The people of the land had sent*; or the third person singular of the active verb can be translated impersonally or passively, *There had been sent* etc. **t)** Where to? *To the house of God*, that is, to the temple, where not only Jehovah himself dwelt, whom they are said to have been sent to pray to; but also the priests and Prophets, whom they were to consult, were gathered and ready at hand v. 3. ch. 8:9. Elsewhere indeed it is the proper name of the town *Bethel*, yet it arose from the fact that the house of God was there *Genesis 28:17, 19*. **u)** *Sharezer* (cf. another in *2 Kings 19:37*.) **x)** *Regem-melech*. Jehovah was certainly to be entreated, and the prophets and priests consulted, publicly and in the name of the whole people v. 5. But because (says Tarnovius) it was fitting for the sake of order and dignity that certain men of great name be delegated by a large assembly for taking counsel and managing affairs, they sent these men. **y)** and *men*, that is his companions, associates, and attendants, specifically either of Regem-melech especially, or of both. *2 Samuel 2:3. 2 Kings 25:23.* **z)** Why? And for what purpose? A twofold one: *α)* to entreat the face of the Lord, that is, to supplicate Him *ch. 8:21, 22. Exodus 32:11. 1 Samuel 13:12*. and **β)** after those prayers were offered, to speak etc. v. 3. For they were going to consult the Lord about the fasts; therefore, before all things, they strove to entreat the Lord with poured-out prayers, so that through His servants, the priests and prophets, He might deign to grant them some response, *Jeremiah 42:2, 3.* **v. 3. a)** *and so that they might say*. **b)** whom the people were accustomed to consult as regular teachers in causes pertaining to religion and sacred matters *Haggai 2:11. Malachi 2:7.* **c)** Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the prophets.</note> says: *who ministered in the house of the sanctuary of the Lord*. v. 2. **d)** who, as extraordinary and immediate interpreters of the divine will, no less than the priests, were accustomed to respond concerning the will of God. cf. *2 Kings 3:12 and following, ch. 22:13 and following. Jeremiah 18:18. ch. 42:1 and following. Ezekiel 7:26. ch. 8:1. ch. 14:1. ch. 20:1.* There is truly no doubt that Haggai and Zechariah are specifically indicated here by the name of Prophets: since they were at that time most known by this name among the Jews *Ezra 5:1.* although more seers could have been in Jerusalem at the same time than Haggai and Zechariah. See *Vitringa, Sacred Observations, book VI, p. 336. and cf. Nehemiah 6:7, 14.* **e)** *Shall I continue to weep?* The whole assembly, in whose name the response was sought from the priests and prophets, is introduced here speaking in the singular, as in *Numbers 20:18, 19. Joshua 9:7.* Truly, by "weeping" <term>synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole; here, "weeping" represents the entire ritual of fasting and mourning.</note>, public mourning and fasting joined with tears and wailing is understood, as Tarnovius rightly concludes both from parallels *Judges 20:26. 1 Samuel 1, 7. 2 Samuel 1, 12. Nehemiah 1, 4. etc.* and from the response in v. 5 and following, and finally from those things which immediately follow here (separating myself). **f)** In memory of the burning of the Temple and Jerusalem by the Babylonians in this month *2 Kings 25:8, 9, 10. Jeremiah 52:12, 13, 14.* For the Jews had instituted several such fasts on account of sorrowful events, compare here v. 5. and ch. 8:19. which truly could not be anything but burdensome and heavy to the Church: therefore when the people noticed that more joyful times had now come to them through the grace of God, when the temple and the city, which had formerly lain in ruins, were being vigorously restored, and the building of the Temple especially (see note v. 1) was succeeding prosperously; by a special delegation they consult whether they ought to continue this fast further, or (which seems to have been desirable to them) omit it? **g)** *by abstaining*, Leviticus 22:2. namely from food and drink, and other delights, in the manner of the Nazirites Numbers 6:2 and following. cf. Joel 2:15 and following. Jonathan: *shall I prohibit my soul from delights?* **h)** not without great trouble. **i)** here. see note ch. 1:12. **k)** *which years?* Genesis 47:8. that is, now for very many. For so they speak who wish to exaggerate a number or quantity. *Psalm 78:40.* They are, however, 70 years, compare here v. 5. concerning which see the note on ch. 1:12. and *Haggai 1:1. ch. 2:3.* **v. 4. l)** *It therefore came to pass*, I say. After the parenthesis of v. 2, 3 was completed, which opened the occasion of the following prophecy, this word is resumed from v. 1, so that the prophecy itself may now be added. **v. 5. m)** Say to the entire people of the land: and indeed *earnestly* <note>original Greek: ἐקτεנῶς</note> with the demonstrative *He* <note>Referring to the Hebrew definite article 'Ha', implying 'this very land'.</note>, as if "of this land"; so that the people who were in Judea, already returned from the Babylonian captivity, may be understood, just as in *Haggai 2:4.* but not those who were then still in Babylon, from whom if this delegation had been made, the Holy Spirit would have added that without doubt, just as above in ch. 6:10. see note v. 2. and cf. *2 Kings 11:14, 18, 19, 20. ch. 15:5.* **n)** and to the priests especially, both as they belong to the body of the whole people, with whom they themselves also fasted, and as they ought to instruct the people according to this response of God. The question indeed was brought to the assembly of prophets and the choir of priests, but the Spirit came upon Zechariah in that group, so that he might respond in the name of God both to the priests and to the people. cf. *2 Chronicles 20:14.* **o)** *Since you have fasted until now.* **p)** *and by mourning*, that is, you mourned. ch. 12:10, 12.

# ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER 7.

<column>
<margin>q) In the fifth month, verse 3; chapter 8, verse 19.</margin>
<margin>r) And (which is of equal account) in the seventh month, in memory of the slaughter of Gedaliah in this month, and of the scattered Jews whom he had with him. 2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41:1 and following.</margin>
<margin>s) And indeed during these 70 years. verse 3. see note on chapter 1:12.</margin>
<margin>t) "Did you fasting fast for me, even me?" The separate pronoun is used emphatically and <term>is redundant</term> <note>original Greek: πλεονάζει</note>, as in Genesis 27:34; Numbers 14:32; Psalm 9:7. The verbal suffix, which is most often explained through the Accusative case, here should be explained through the Dative, as in Judges 1:15; Job 15:21. The Dative here has the same force as **for my sake**, because of my command, or for my honor and benefit. For he wishes to say: I neither forced these fasts of yours upon you, nor commanded them, nor am I delighted by them; you yourselves instituted them, and you brought them upon yourselves by your own sins; no benefit resulted from them to me. Only repent now, and bear worthy fruits of conversion in the future; thus, through me, it will be permitted for you to cease those fasts of which you yourselves are the authors, nor will anything be lost to me by their omission. Compare Isaiah 43:23, 24, and according to some, Amos 5:25.</margin>
<margin>u) "But when you eat—is it not you yourselves who eat?" Not I. This is an example from the opposite side, which however follows a similar logic. In the same way, when you ate and drank, it was such that it neither contributed anything to me nor took anything away; so also you undertook your fasting. Both are indifferent to me, and neither will commend you to me by itself, nor make me indebted to you. The Vulgate expressed the latter half-verse not poorly: *Did you not eat for yourselves, and drink for yourselves?* The greatest weight of the</margin>

sentence is placed on the pronoun "You," compared with the opposition in verse 5. But some, who rendered the last words of verse 5 thus: "Did you fast for fasting and affliction (that is, truly and by which you afflicted your soul) before me?", then explained this verse as follows: *And that you ate and drank, was it not so that you might do good to yourselves that you drank?* It seems, therefore, that <term>eating and drinking</term> in the latter member refers to sumptuous and joyful banquets. Compare 1 Samuel 30:16; 1 Kings 1:25; chapter 4:20; Job 1:4. So the sense would be: You were so far from fasting truly and as is fitting, that you instead indulged your genius and pleasures by eating and drinking. Compare Isaiah 58:3, 4; James 4:3. But in this way, the force of the opposition between the pronouns "For me, for me" in verse 5 and "you yourselves, you yourselves" vanishes, or at least does not remain clear enough. Our explanation, however, almost agrees with Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnovius (1562–1633), a Lutheran theologian</note>, who observes that the Jews should conclude from this interrogation: Food does not commend us to God; for neither if we eat are we more in piety, nor if we do not eat are we less. 1 Corinthians 8:8. If, however, food does not commend us to God, neither will fasting by itself commend us, since both are <term>indifferent</term> <note>original Greek: ἀδιάφορον, a thing that is neither morally good nor bad</note>, and bodily exercise is profitable for little. 1 Timothy 4:8. And although if it is used rightly it may have some use, yet it is in no way to be compared with internal piety, which has the promise of the present and future life.

**verse 7. x)** *Do you not know the words:* Thus some by an omission of the verb governing the Accusative, as if it were a sudden silence. Others more correctly: *Is not this the very substance of the words*, or as the Septuagint rendered it, <term>Are these not the words?</term> <note>original Greek: οὐχ οὗτοι οἱ λόγοι</note>. The Vulgate: *Are they not true?* and the Syriac: *These are those words.* For the particle אֶת <note>et</note>, as the Hebrews observe, signifies <note>original Hebrew: כְּמוֹ עֶצֶם הַדָּבָר</note> *the "itself-ness" of some thing*, or the thing itself and <term>this very thing</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτὸ τοῦτο</note>, just as among the Rabbis אֹתוֹ <note>oto</note> is "he himself." See note on Joshua 22:17; Jeremiah 27:8; and compare further below, chapter 8:17; Haggai 2:17; Nehemiah 9:19, 32, 34. But Gussetius <note>Jacques Gousset (1635–1704), French Hebraist</note>, page 105: *Was there not with the words, which Jehovah proclaimed by the hand of the preceding Prophets—(verse 8) also the word of Jehovah to Zechariah*, saying etc. as if he were joining this prophecy promulgated through Zechariah with the prophecies of the ancients, whether he had already published it once or for the first time on this occasion. But, besides the fact that this interpretation is more forced, it also ignores the space interposed between verse 7 and 8, which indicates that a new paragraph begins with verse 8. Otherwise, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105)</note> makes the coherence with the preceding and following as follows: Who was the cause of fasting and lamentation for you? *Was it not the words of rebukes, which Jehovah proclaimed etc.?* Those (neglected words) devastated you: and therefore you fasted. These, however, are the words which he proclaimed: *Judge true judgment etc.* verse 9. But we connect it thus: God had said to the Jews that until now they had by no means offered true worship to him by their fasts. By this very thing, however, he had simultaneously hinted that there is another worship which he requires, and the neglect of which he severely punished; namely, that which consists in actual piety and justice according to the moral law of God, such as will shortly be described in verses 9 and 10. Compare Isaiah 1:12, 15 and following; chapter 58:3, 4; Jeremiah 5:3; Micah 6:6, 7, 8; Psalm 50:8; Romans 14:17. The Jews might have thought: *Oh! if only these things had been said to us long ago! For we would have obeyed, and thus avoided the penalty of the divine worship neglected by us, nor would we have had need of lamentation.* Lest they interpret what he had said as something new and unheard of, he adds that he had already long ago clearly and diligently drummed these things in through the former prophets; if the ancestors had obeyed them, that occasion of lamenting and fasting would never have been; no pretext of ignorance can be feigned here. **y)** which he proclaimed; chapter 1:14. **z)** by the hand, that is, by the ministry of the prophets. i.e., through the prophets. verse 12; Haggai 1:1. **a)** See verse 12 and note on chapter 1:4. **b)** *dwelling and tranquil*, i.e., dwelling tranquilly or inhabited. See note on chapter 1:11. **c)** 1 Chronicles 4:40. **d)** and when her cities (meaning provincial ones, which elsewhere are called "daughters") were around her. Before they were depopulated by enemies. **e)** and (as parts are also called daughters) when the southern part of Judea. See Numbers 13:17; Deuteronomy 34:3; Isaiah 30:6. **f)** and the sloping and western part of the same, Joshua 15:33; Jeremiah 17:26, which is read to have abounded in sycamores, 1 Kings 10:27. **g)** *dwelling*, i.e., inhabited. compare verse 5.

**verse 8. h)** Tarnovius demonstrates the connection thus: Lest the Jews should now ask, "What are those commands of God which we do not keep? What was that stubbornness of our ancestors? What was the punishment sent upon them?" all three are specifically added by the Prophet at the command of God: the precepts of God to be kept in verses 9 and 10; the obstinacy of the fathers not to be imitated in verses 11 and 12; and the punishment to be undergone in verses 13 and 14.

**verse 9. i)** If you desire to know what that is which I already long ago proclaimed through the former Prophets, thus he said etc. For it is clear from verse 11 and following that this Word is repeated from the past as having been spoken to the ancestors. **k)** True judgment and charity toward one's neighbor are placed in opposition to fasts and other types of chosen worship, as duties which God himself required and testified were pleasing to him, as in chapter 8:16; Isaiah 1:17, 23; Jeremiah 7:5; chapter 21:12; Ezekiel 18:8; Hosea 12:7. See Micah 6:8; also John 7:24. **l)** compare Hosea 6:6. **m)** Genesis 43:14; Psalm 105:4. compare Amos 1:11; Proverbs 12:10. ***)** *each with his brother*, i.e., toward his brother or neighbor. 2 Samuel 16:17.

<meta>catchword: que (because/and)</meta>

<summary>In this passage, the Prophet Zechariah challenges the sincerity of the ritual fasts established during the exile, explaining that God values moral justice and mercy over external rituals. He reminds the people that the former prophets had already delivered this same message before the destruction of Jerusalem, emphasizing that their ancestors' failure to listen led to their current state.</summary>

Just as in verse 9 he had stated what he desired in a positive sense, so now he explains what he does not want through negation <note>original: κατ' ἄρσιν; a Greek rhetorical term for defining something by what it is not</note>. p) Leviticus 5:21; 19:13. q) Do not oppress <note>original: μὴ καταדυναστεύετε</note>. cf. And this must be the established grammatical structure, because the word for "evil" <note>Hebrew: רעת</note> is in the construct state (linked to the following word). cf. 2 Kings 7:6; Isaiah 9:18. r) Do not think, or devise, chapter 8:17. For the rest, if evil is not even to be thought of, says Taym., how much less is it to be done. cf. Micah 2:1.

<meta>catchword: And it happened</meta>

p) However (as if these commands were a heavy yoke, Hosea 11:4; Psalm 2:3; Romans 6:20; compared with Matthew 11:30). s) To take up on their shoulders to carry, Nehemiah 9:29. Like a stubborn cow that withdraws itself from the yoke and resists. Hosea 4:16. x) And they made their ears "heavy," that is, they made themselves deaf and hard of hearing. Isaiah 6:10; 59:1. The Septuagint uses "burdened" <note>original: ἐβάρυναν</note>: compare this with Matthew 13:15; Acts 28:27; and Luke 21:34. "Heaviness" for the Hebrews refers to the inability or dullness of any sensation, Genesis 48:10; Exodus 9:7. Likewise, among the Arabs, "to make heavy" is to afflict with deafness (according to Golius' Arabic Lexicon, p. 2712), and "heaviness in the ears" for deafness or dullness of hearing occurs in the Al-Coran, Surah 17:48. y) *Lest* they hear, that is, so they would not hear or could not hear. v. 12. Isaiah 59:1. v. 12 z) They made it like adamant <note>a stone of extreme hardness, like diamond</note>, Vulgate: "as adamant" (Ezekiel 3:9), which does not yield easily to the hammer, just as their hearts did not yield to the word of God. Jeremiah 23:29. They made it adamant-like or hard as adamant, so that the power of the word would be in vain against them as they resisted obstinately. cf. Ezekiel 11:19; 36:26. Others suggest "emery stone" <note>original: smyritem</note>: but see the note on Jeremiah 17:1. a) cf. v. 11. b) By His Spirit, with which He inspired and animated the prophets to show Israel their transgression. Micah 3:8; cf. 2 Samuel 23:2; and 1 Peter 1:11. c) Through the prophets, or the ministerial cause (v. 7), just as the Spirit of God was the principal cause. d) See verse 7 and the note on chapter 1:4. e) From which arises wrath, as a punishment and consequence of disobedience. Chapter 1:2; Numbers 17:11. f) To which there is a "seeming contradiction" <note>original: ἐναντιοφανες</note> when God says in chapter 1:15 that He was only a little angry with Israel; but see the reconciliation of this in our notes there. v. 13. g) Just as the Lord had indeed called out, but they had not heard—rather He had called through the prophets in vain. v. 7; Isaiah 50:2; 65:12; 66:4; Jeremiah 25:4; Hosea 11:2. h) So in turn they later cried out in their troubles, and I did not hear; doing this to them in turn, according to the law of retaliation <note>original: ius talionis</note>. cf. Isaiah 1:15; 63:15; Jeremiah 11:11; 14:12; Ezekiel 8:18; Micah 3:4; Psalm 18:42; Proverbs 1:24, 28; Job 35:12. Furthermore, these "future" verbs in a historical narrative (as often elsewhere) should be translated as the imperfect past; this is clear from the end of verse 14, where the past tense "and they made" returns. Unless perhaps one prefers: "So they will call—the Lord of Hosts said to them in those times." v. 14. i) But I drove them out, or scattered them as with a whirlwind from their land. Job 27:21. Like chaff which the wind drives from the threshing floor. Hosea 13:3; Psalm 1:4. cf. Jeremiah 23:19; Amos 1:14. The Hebrew letter Aleph is specifically moved here by a Tsere vowel instead of a compound Shua, following Syriac grammar; similar to Isaiah 33:10, Exodus 18:23, or Daniel 3:22. k) To all (that is, all quarters of the world) nations, chapter 2:10; Daniel 9:7. Namely the Babylonians, also the Egyptians, and the surrounding Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, etc. Jeremiah 40:11, 12; 44:1 ff. l) Jeremiah 16:13; Deuteronomy 28:33. m) It was desolated, Jeremiah 12:11; Ezekiel 25:3. "After them," that is, after their fate and migration. Joel 2:3. n) So that there was no one passing through or returning through it. Chapter 9:8; Isaiah 33:8; Jeremiah 9:9, 12; Ezekiel 33:28; 35:7. o) "And they made," namely as the moral cause; in the same way that the burning of Jerusalem is attributed to Zedekiah in Jeremiah 38:23. God therefore devastated the land judicially, the Babylonians physically, and the Jews themselves morally. Jeremiah 6:8. p) The "land of desire," that is, the desirable, longed-for, most beautiful land. Jeremiah 3:19; Psalm 106:24; Daniel 11:16; Malachi 3:12.

# 8 ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER 8. 8

### CHAPTER VIII, verse 1.
<margin>
q) This continues the word of the Lord begun in the previous chapter. The occasion for this speech was the question the Jews asked about their ritual fasts in chapter 7, verse 2 (compared here with verse 19). Just as He had previously denied being pleased with their fasts and taught them that true fruits of piety and faith—which were required of their ancestors—had been neglected (the very cause of the evils they suffered and the mourning they practiced), so in this chapter He proceeds to answer that same question more directly. He explains His "Decree of Good Pleasure," by which He intends to do good to Zion and Jerusalem in the future beyond what they can conceive. He will change their fasts into joyful feast days, provided they cultivate true piety, which He exhorts them to do. Although there are several sections in this chapter (starting at verses 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 14, 18, 20, and 23), they can be divided into three general parts following the scholars <note>original: Sch.</note>. 
I. The promise of the restoration of Jerusalem, especially under the New Testament (verses 1–8). 
II. Encouragement for those building the temple through the further explanation of that promise (verses 9–17). 
III. The compensation for the fasts through the arrival of the promised times of the Messiah (verse 18 to the end). 
Regarding the fulfillment of this promise, there is certainly no doubt that its later parts, concerning the gathering of the Church from the nations and its union with the Jewish people (verse 20 onwards), reached their fulfillment only under the New Testament. But even the earlier parts, from the beginning of the chapter, (says the celebrated Marckius <note>Johannes Marckius (1656–1731), a Dutch theologian</note> on verse 1, page 1020) do not seem to have reached full completion in the city of Jerusalem as it was then rebuilt, which certainly <meta>catchword: cities</meta></margin>

could not be called the "City of Truth" and "Mountain of Holiness" (verse 3) when they resisted the Truth and Holiness itself appearing in the flesh <note>a reference to Jesus</note>. Verses 7 and 8 can be understood not as a physical return, but a spiritual one; nor verses 12 and 13.

1 <gloss>a</gloss> And the word of the Lord of Hosts came, saying:
2 Thus says the Lord of Hosts: <gloss>y</gloss> I was jealous <gloss>x</gloss> for Zion <gloss>z</gloss> with great jealousy, and I was jealous for her with great wrath.
3 <gloss>b</gloss> Thus says the Lord: <gloss>y</gloss> I have returned to Zion <gloss>t</gloss> and I will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem; and Jerusalem shall be called <gloss>z</gloss> the City of Truth, and the mountain of the Lord of Hosts, the Holy Mountain.
4 <gloss>a</gloss> Thus says the Lord of Hosts: <gloss>d</gloss> Old men and old women shall yet sit in the streets of Jerusalem, and each man with his staff <gloss>e</gloss> in his hand because of his great age.
5 <gloss>g</gloss> And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls <gloss>h</gloss> playing <gloss>i</gloss> in its streets.
6 Thus says the Lord of Hosts

**Verse 1.** Judah and Israel are joined here, though only Judah returned from the Babylonian captivity. David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish commentator, also known as the RaDak</note> says this is a promise for the future time of the Messiah. See also Cocceius on this passage and Johannes Meyer on the final parts of Ezekiel, page 96. Meanwhile, those things said in verse 2 about the Zeal of the Lord for Zion had already begun their fulfillment then (compare above, chapter 1:14). Similarly, what is said in verses 11 and 12 about increasing the yields of the fields by God’s blessing had already begun to be fulfilled (compare Haggai 2:16). We therefore conclude that this prophecy has a very broad scope, representing in a continuous series both the spiritual and physical blessings that God would perform for Jerusalem then and in the future. **v. 2. r)** This formula, placed at the start of each part of the prophecy, recurs repeatedly here (verses 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, etc.). It is not idle or redundant, but emphatic, used to mark the certainty of the promised thing, which might otherwise seem to exceed belief due to its magnitude (compare Hebrews 10:23 and Titus 1:2). **s)** "Although I inflicted just punishment on them because of the stubbornness of your ancestors, such is My goodness that I am now jealous again for Jerusalem with great zeal." This continues until you can be free from the burden of fasting and mourning in the future (compare verse 19). Abraham ibn Ezra <note>A significant medieval Spanish rabbi and scholar</note> notes: He consoles the messengers after reminding them of the desolation of the land. **t)** The "great wrath" refers to what I conceived against her enemies (compare chapter 1:15). **v. 3. u)** "Wherefore" (for this is an inference from what preceded). See the notes on verse 2. **x)** See chapter 1:16 and Malachi 3:7. Ibn Ezra supposes this promise is conditional; no doubt because he sensed the difficulty in reconciling what follows with the actual events under the Second Temple and the standing Jewish Republic. However, we seek the spiritual fulfillment of those things which are too glorious to fit the times of the Old Testament through Christ in the New Testament (see note on verse 1). We do not view this promise as suspended by a condition, but as given absolutely and simply according to the "good pleasure of God's will to the praise of His glorious grace" (Ephesians 1:5–9). **y)** This promise, taken in its breadth, can also refer to the symbol itself, meaning God would dwell in the Temple among the Jews (Deuteronomy 12:5; Haggai 1:8). Yet the primary focus here is the truth of the New Testament because of what follows. Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> says: "And I will make my Shekhinah <note>the Divine Presence</note> to dwell." **z)** "And it shall be called." This suggests that in the style of Scripture, "to be called" is "to be" (compare Isaiah 1:26, 61:6; Jeremiah 3:17). **a)** A city in which truth is loved and flourishes (verses 8 and 16). Namely, that truth which leads to godliness (Titus 1:1; compare Isaiah 1:27). The Targum <note>the Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> observes that this indirectly hints at why He previously left them and departed in anger: namely, because they had defiled themselves with lies and all kinds of injustice, and had foully profaned the holy city. **b)** Isaiah 11:9, 27:13; Jeremiah 31:23; Psalm 15:1. **v. 4. c)** See note on verse 2. **d)** Old men and women. Two things are promised here to the citizens of Jerusalem: longevity (verse 5) and a multitude of offspring. Both were among the physical promises under the Old Testament which God proposed as rewards for piety (Deuteronomy 4:40, 5:16, 30:20, etc.; compare 1 Timothy 4:8). Regarding the completion and fulfillment of this promise, we note from the Targum: although these things were fulfilled temporally or physically in some who lived at that time—Zerubbabel, Ezra, Nehemiah, Joshua, and others—and in those who lived later in the Church, surviving for many years, they are mostly to be understood as the spiritual grace that occurs in the kingdom of Christ. This is typical among the Prophets when they prophesy about the happiness of the New Testament; they foreshadow spiritual things under the type of physical things. See further Isaiah 65:20. **e)** "They shall sit in the streets," offering a beautiful sight with their very gray hair, while boys and girls play among them (verse 5). **f)** "As for each one, his staff shall be his"; or each shall have his own staff (Exodus 21:19). This protects them from the "multitude of days," meaning the troubles and weakness of old age. **g)** "Because of the multitude of days," or extreme old age (Job 32:7). **v. 5. h)** The same streets mentioned in verse 4. **i)** And girls (3) Genesis 34:4; Joel 4:3. **k)** Playing, as children do when a city is prosperous (Jeremiah 15:17). But some interpret this as "praising the Lord" with musical instruments, which this word can denote (2 Samuel 6:5; Jeremiah 30:19). **v. 6. l)** See note on verse 2.

z) as fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, Ephesians 2:19. a) Galatians 4:26; Revelation 21:2. b) See Jeremiah 30:22; Ezekiel 37:27; also above chapter 2, 15 and what we noted there. c) Genesis 17:7; Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 24:7; Chapter 31, 1, 33; Ezekiel 11:20; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Revelation 21:7. d) in truth and righteousness. According to the accents, these words apply equally to both preceding parts: namely, to the more remote "they shall be to me for a people," as well as to the nearer "I will be to them for a God." Furthermore, "truth" denotes sincerity, openness, and integrity of mind. 1 Kings 3:6; 2 Kings 20:3; chapter 61, 8; Jeremiah 2, 21; chapter 32, 41; cf. Deuteronomy 32, 20. e) Isaiah 1:27; Hosea 2:21; cf. 2 Timothy 2:19. v. 9. f) See note on verse 2. g) therefore let your hands be strong, verse 9. It properly signifies the strength of the hands and arms, but metonymically <note>where a symbol stands for a concept</note> it signifies the raising up of the spirit, in opposition to timidity and fear (Isaiah 35:3; Jeremiah 23:14), and the intensity of effort in opposition to sluggishness (2 Samuel 16:21). Just as, conversely, the "slacking of hands" signifies terror (Jeremiah 6:24; chapter 38, 4) and the stopping of work due to fear (2 Chronicles 15:7). He wishes to say: Continue now (as you have begun) with eagerness and vigor, finish the structure of the Temple, do what I have commanded you; and thus hope for the best things from my affection toward you. cf. Haggai 2:4; also Ephesians 5:2. Furthermore, that this exhortation has a connection with what follows is quite clear and is indicated by the causal particle "for" in verse 10. Yet the same undoubtedly looks back to the preceding things as well; as if to say: Since you have such glorious promises for the future (such as preceded in verses 3-8), it will certainly be your part to be of good courage and to continue tirelessly in what has been begun. 2 Corinthians 7:1. h) you, who have heard in these days verse 6. i) you, I say, who hear or have heard these words (for these must be repeated from the first half-verse, which has an emphatic *Atnach* <note>a Hebrew cantillation mark acting as a semicolon</note>) from the mouth of the prophets, who etc. namely from me and Haggai, chapter 7:3; Ephesians 5:1, 2. Thus Zechariah provides testimony for Haggai, as having spoken the same things at the same time and in the same spirit: he cites his colleague no less than himself and commands him to be heard, just as Peter does Paul in 2 Peter 3:15, 16. k) who were there on the day (time) when it was founded or begun, chapter 4:9; Haggai 2:18; Ezra 3:6, 10. l) namely the Temple. This is an explanation of the preceding word.

v. 10. m) This is the connection: I have said that those promises, which you heard from my mouth and Haggai’s, and especially those which I just set forth from verses 3-8, ought to be an encouragement to you to finish what remains eagerly and vigorously (verse 9). This is to be observed by you all the more because your previous laziness was more harmful to you, and because you have experienced a more brilliant blessing from God after you seriously began to restore the Temple. n) before those days in which the Temple began to be built by you, verse 9. o) the wage of man. Thus is called the profit or utility redounding from the labor of a man; just as soon "the wage of cattle" comes with a similar meaning. cf. Ecclesiastes 9:5; 2 Chronicles 15:7. And so the sense is: Whatever you labored at with your hands or your cattle was in vain and brought you either no fruit or certainly an unstable one, because of your negligence and disobedience. cf. Haggai 1:6, 9 and following; chapter 2, 16 and following. p) was not made by me for you. The Septuagint and Arabic versions add: "for benefit." q) and to the one going out and the one entering. When someone wanted to leave a city or enter another, the roads were infested everywhere by enemies and bandits, so that you could nowhere travel safely. Deuteronomy 28:19; 2 Chronicles 15:5. r) The Septuagint and Vulgate say "because of tribulation." But Jonathan says "because of the oppressor": which we prefer, compare Numbers 10:9; Lamentations 4:12; Esther 7:4. Such for example were the Samaritans, Ezra 4:1; and later in the time of Nehemiah, the Arabs, Ammonites, and Ashdodites, Nehemiah 4:1. s) indeed I sent, that is (as Jonathan rendered it), I stirred up or made them fight, Isaiah 10:6. By a just judgment I allowed them to consume themselves with internal discords. Cf. below chapter 11:6. Clearly the preceding phrase speaks of external enemies, this one of civil wars. t) cf. Isaiah 3:5; and Judges 7:22; 2 Chronicles 20:23. v. 11. u) But now, namely from that day when the Temple began to be built by you, and forward; compare verse 9 and Haggai 2:18, 19. x) I am not or will not be as in the former days. This is a contrast of time—where the opposition of the things themselves is to be noted: previously war, now peace; formerly the barrenness of the earth, now abundance; once everything was gathered in vain, nor could it be saved for long, but now they are possessed. Tarnovius. y) verse 6. z) verse 6. Isaiah 1:24; Hosea 11:11.

# ZECHARIAH CHAPTER 8

<margin>
* v. 12. a) **Because**, as I shall declare, what kind of person I will be toward them in the future, and what benefits I will give them. b) The Vulgate <note>The common 4th-century Latin translation</note> says: *But the seed of peace will be.* As if it were said of the people: They will be a seed that enjoys peace. Compare Ecclesiasticus 61:9, Isaiah 33:9, Haggai 2:9, and Psalm 72:3. But because the things that follow immediately pertain to the fertility of the earth, we likewise take this to refer to the sowing of the fields or the crop, as the Syriac <note>original: "Syr."</note> says: *the seed shall be in peace*; and the Targum of Jonathan <note>original: "Ion."</note> says: *the sowing shall be safe.* That is to say, there will be peace (well-being) in its very prosperity <note>original Latin: "vilitudinibus," likely a transcription error for "valetudinibus" meaning health or well-being</note>; as in 1 Samuel 25:6, 2 Samuel 20:9, Job 21:9. It will suffer no loss in the future due to drought, blight, locusts, or other accidents harmful to the crop. He says this in contrast to the previous barrenness of the trees and the plagues with which he had punished the Jews' laziness in sacred matters; compare above at verse 10 and Haggai 1:6, 9, 10; 2:15 and following. See Deuteronomy 28:38 and following, and Malachi 2:3. c) Haggai 2:19, Habakkuk 3:17. d) **It shall give its increase**, which it previously denied them (Haggai 1:10). Compare Leviticus 26:4 and following, 20; Deuteronomy 11:17; and Ezekiel 34:27; Psalm 67:7; Psalm 85:13. e) Jonathan: *they shall serve them with their dew.* Namely, to moisten and fertilize the earth (Genesis 27:28; Deuteronomy 33:13, 28; 1 Kings 17:1). They are said here to be about to give dew in opposition to Haggai 1:10; compare Hosea 2:23, 24. f) **And I will cause to inherit.** 1 Samuel 2:8; Proverbs 8:21. g) <term>κατακληρονομήσω - ταῦτα πάντα</term> <note>Greek: "I will grant as an inheritance all these things"</note>. Compare this with Revelation 21:7. g) See verse 6, note n; Zephaniah 2:9. h) Jonathan: *all these blessings.* This is the voice of one promising generously, or suggesting the abundance and greatness of the promised goods. Compare Matthew 4:9. Moreover, a certain difficulty arises here concerning the setting of the time for the fulfillment of this promise. to also contain a promise of physical good, and to have pertained to the times of the Prophet himself. We seem to gather this firmly enough from the parallelism with the contemporary Haggai, whom we have cited more than once. Meanwhile, that this temporal promise was conditional is shown to us by the later sermons of Malachi; compare Malachi 2:2, 3.

**v. 13. i)** *Indeed, it shall happen in its own time.* From physical goods, he rises to greater and spiritual things, from present or near-at-hand things to future things, as we noted at verse 12. However, nothing prevents this promise from also being physical and pertaining simultaneously to the very time it was issued, provided it is taken with the condition of obedience and piety. **k)** *a curse*, that is, in a state of being cursed (as the Septuagint rendered it), or an example and formula of a curse (2 Kings 22:19; Jeremiah 24:9). **l)** Psalm 44:15. **m)** See above, note on verse 1 and verse 12. **n)** *So, by the reverse turn and on the contrary.* Verse 15. **o)** *I will save* (verse 7, chapter 9:16, Isaiah 49:25). **p)** *that you may be or become a blessing*, that is, blessed, and a notable example of blessing no less than you were once an example of a curse (Genesis 12:9, Isaiah 19:24; compare Genesis 22:18, Isaiah 61:9, Ezekiel 34:26, Malachi 3:12). **q)** *therefore do not fear*; for I will faithfully fulfill these promises to you. You only do what is yours to do, and do not deprive yourselves of such great goods through negligence or stubbornness. Verse 15. The Gospel-like and sweetly consoling mood of prohibition (Genesis 50:19, 21; Isaiah 41:10, 13; 43:1, 5; 54:4; Jeremiah 30:10; 46:27, 28; Zephaniah 3:16; Haggai 2:5; compare Isaiah 12:2). The Septuagint uses <term>θαῤῥεῖτε</term> <note>Greek: "take courage"</note>. So in verse 15; compare Matthew 14:27, Luke 8:48, 47. **r)** *let your hands be made strong.* This is the same thing stated positively that he just said negatively and by opposition as "do not fear" (compare the contrary in Zephaniah 3:16). Yet this very freedom from distress and fear implies an alacrity in doing, and specifically here in continuing the restoration of divine worship; compare note above at verse 9 and Haggai 1:4. From this, Kimchi supplies: "at this time, because of those good comforts which you hear are coming to Israel."

**v. 14. s)** *Because, to proceed further in explaining the plan of my good pleasure, and thereby to add courage to you.* **t)** See note on verse 2. **u)** *I thought, I firmly proposed to myself.* Verse 15; chapter 1:6; Lamentations 2:17. **x)** Jeremiah 25:6, 29; 31:28; Micah 4:6. **y)** *when they made me boil over with their sins*; when they gave me cause for boiling over (chapter 1:2; Deuteronomy 9:7, 8, 22; Isaiah 54:9; 64:4). God adds the cause of so severe a decree here, lest anyone accuse him of decreeing evil upon men rashly, or of delighting in evil decrees. Compare Lamentations 3:33, 39 and following. **z)** Compare note on chapter 1:2. **a)** *and indeed in such a way that I did not repent of my decree, nor could I be led to change or abolish it* (Jeremiah 4:28, 20:16), surely because of their persistent lack of repentance (compare 15:6, 18:8, 26:3; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). The Septuagint uses <term>οὐ μετενόησα</term> <note>Greek: "I did not change my mind"</note>; compare Hebrews 12:17.

**v. 15. b)** *So.* See note on verse 13. **c)** *I have returned and thought*, that is, *I have thought to the contrary.* For "to return" joined with another verb occasionally signifies an action in the opposite direction; compare note on Malachi 3:18. Furthermore, to fill out the emphasis of the verb "to think," one can repeat here from verse 14: "and I will not repent." Compare Jeremiah 18:10, Psalm 110:4. **d)** Verses 9, 10, 11. **e)** Jeremiah 32:40, 41; Psalm 51:20; Joshua 24:20. See the contrary in Deuteronomy 28:63, Joshua 24:20. **f)** See note on verse 13.

**v. 16. g)** *But these are the words which, just as I urged upon your fathers long ago (see chapter 7:9 and following), so I now urge upon you also to do.* This "These" places the demonstration in opposition to the <term>αὐθαίρετα</term> <note>Greek: "voluntary" or "self-chosen"</note> fasts of the Jews (chapter 7:3, 5). *These things*, he says, *but by no means your fasts, which you may omit as far as I am concerned.* See note on chapter 7:9. To which this gloss by Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "A. Esra"</note> contributes: He responds these things to those asking whether they should continue to weep in the fifth month, they who were not keeping the law of God and yet were asking whether they should keep the paradoxes or traditions of the fathers. He responds therefore: You would have done better if you had obeyed the words of God and omitted the words of the fathers, rather than keeping the words of the fathers and omitting the words of God. Compare Matthew 15:2 and following. **h)** Verse 19. Each half of the verse commends truth, but in a different way: the first in general, as it should be between private individuals; the second specifically, as it ought to be cultivated especially in judgments. Compare Isaiah 33:15. The Septuagint is as in Ephesians 4:25. **i)** *Jerome says well: This is the judgment of peace, so that the judge may have the purpose of making peace between those in discord, according to that saying of the Gospel: Blessed are the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9).* **k)** Chapter 7:9. **l)** *in the gates*, that is, *in your judgments or forums.* Deuteronomy 21:19.

**v. 17. m)** See note on 7:10. **n)** *and an oath of falsehood*, that is, a false one. Compare chapter 5:4. **o)** *do not love, but rather detest.* Psalm 4:3, Proverbs 1:22. Kimchi thinks this word is used in opposition to the following "I have hated." As if to say: Do not go in a different direction and cherish a will contrary to mine, so that you love diametrically what I hate. **p)** All these things themselves. See what we noted above at chapter 7:7 concerning the particle <term>אֵת</term> <note>Hebrew direct object marker</note>. **q)** *This is an argument based on the detestability of the thing.* For what sane person loves, or how and by what right does he love, what God hates and detests? Compare Deuteronomy 12:31, 16:22; Jeremiah 44:4; Malachi 2:15; Proverbs 6:16.

* 18. v.) Now follows a specific answer to the question proposed above (chapter 7:3). For because, says Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnovius, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note>, the messengers had asked whether they should still fast, and the prophet had not then answered them openly, but had seized the opportunity to rebuke their fasts, he now expressly says that not only must those fasts which were undertaken for the sake of sorrow be abandoned and converted into splendid festivities and banquets, but he also demonstrates that other similar fasts, about which no inquiry had been made, are to be abolished.
v. 19. s) See the note on verse 2. s) The fast of the fourth <note>original: "ieiunium quarti"</note>, namely the month, in which Jerusalem was first conquered by the Chaldeans (Jeremiah 52:6, 7). u) Of the fifth month, in which the city along with the Temple was burned (chapter 7:3, 5; 2 Kings 25:8, 9). x) Of the seventh month, concerning which see chapter 7:5. y) Of the tenth month, in which the siege of Jerusalem by the Babylonians began (2 Kings 25:1; Jeremiah 52:4). These months, therefore, the Jews had distinguished in their calendars with fasts until now, in memory of those most sorrowful events. z) It shall become hereafter — into joy and gladness (Isaiah 35:10; 51:3, 11). For in place of past evils, I will hereafter heap upon the house of Judah many and great benefits (such as that which follows: the leading of the nations into the bosom of the Church under the New Testament, verse 20), so that mourning is to pass into joy, and gladness is to succeed in the place of former sorrow (Isaiah 61:3; Jeremiah 31:13). The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders this: "into joy and cheerfulness" <note>original: "εις χαραν & ευφροσυνην"</note>. The Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin Bible</note> says: "only truth." d) And peace, meaning concord with one's neighbor (verse 16; Psalm 34:15; see the opposite in Psalm 120:6). e) Love. ### AN ORACLE OF THE WORD OF THE LORD...

CHAPTER IX.
so that I may not be in evil. h) namely to the
</margin>

Temple and Church of God (verse 22; chapter 6:15, where you may see the note), stirred up by the Gospel being announced through all lands (Psalm 19:5; Romans 10:18). **v. 21. i)** They shall go indeed (Micah 4:2). This same propagation of the Church (concerning which see verse 20), says Tarnovius, is described by a remarkable vivid description <term>hypotyposis: a lifelike representation of a scene</term>, a most delightful personification <term>prosopopoeia: giving a voice to an abstract thing or groups</term>, and a most elegant imitation <term>mimesis</term>, so that it almost seems to be seen before one's eyes, and not merely read in the Prophet or seen as something spoken by him long ago. k) *The inhabitants of one city to the inhabitants of another.* (Ezekiel 36:10, 12). This is an expansion, showing that they will come not one after another, individually and separately, but in crowds in a great assembly (Tarnovius). l) *Let us go in going* <note>original: "Eamus eundo"</note>, that is, all together and with great zeal (verse 23; compare Isaiah 2:3; Jeremiah 31:6). m) *To entreat etc.* (verse 22; see the note on chapter 7:2). n) *And to seek the Lord*, whom they will find present to those seeking Him in the Church, as in a true Temple (verses 2, 22; compare Deuteronomy 4:29; Psalm 24:6; Psalm 27:8; 2 Chronicles 20:4). Josephus <note>likely referring to the commentator Jozo or similar</note> here and in verse 22: o) *to seek doctrine or instruction from the Lord:* in the same way Onkelos <note>The author of the famous Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> explained the same phrase in Exodus 33:7. Thus therefore compare Isaiah 2:3; Micah 4:2. The Septuagint: "an inquiry" <note>original: "ἐπερώτημα"</note>. Compare Acts 15:17; Romans 3:11; Hebrews 11:6. o) *"I will go also, etc."* one will say to another, as Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase</note> supplies. It is an imitation <term>mimesis</term>, representing the words of the nations so vividly as if we are not reading them reported, but hearing them ourselves with our own ears. The sense: they will run together individually in competition; no one will want to remain behind (compare Isaiah 44:5; Luke 16:16; Hebrews 4:1). **v. 22. p)** *And thus they shall come.* (verse 20). An outstanding passage concerning the calling of the nations. Rightly indeed Rabbi Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish commentator</note> says: "This will happen in the days of the Messiah" (compare chapter 2:15; 6:15; 14:16; Isaiah 2:2, 3; 49:18; 52:15; 60:4; 66:18, 20; Micah 4:3; Zephaniah 2:11; Haggai 2:7; and elsewhere). q) See the note on verse 21. r) The things promised here to Jerusalem, regarding their primary and final fulfillment, are promised to the New Testament Church; not only because the former was a type of the latter, but chiefly because the latter is its root and a notable part (compare Isaiah 2:3; John 4:22; Romans 11:16 and following; Tarnovius page 1449). s) *To entreat* (verse 21). **v. 23. t)** See note on verse 2. u) *And* See note on verse 6. x) It shall be that they take hold. The construction is almost the same as in verse 20, where we illustrated it. Tarnovius: "just as children are accustomed, or even others who desire to hold someone back, to cling to the cloaks or robes of their parents, which they grab while they either strive to go along with them, or at least hope they will stay with them, not easily allowing themselves to be pulled away." See 1 Samuel 15:27; Isaiah 4:1. y) *Ten*, that is, several, many; compare Genesis 31:7; Leviticus 26:26; Numbers 14:22. z) *Languages of the nations*, that is, nations differing in language or dialect (Genesis 10:20, 31; Isaiah 66:18). a) *They shall take hold, I say.* It is repeated from the first half of the verse. See something similar in chapter 6:11, compared with verse 10. b) *The hem of the garment.* (Isaiah 4:1; Haggai 2:12). The Septuagint: "of the tassel" <note>original: "κρασπέδου"</note> (Matthew 9:20). c) Compare Esther 8:17; Acts 16:9, 15. d) See verse 21. e) Compare Joshua 2:10; 9:9; and Romans 10:17. f) That God is with you, and has revealed Himself among you in an illustrious way, as *Immanu-El* <note>God-with-us</note> (Isaiah 7:14; 8:8, 10; Revelation 21:3). Jonathan: *"because the Word of the Lord is for your help."* Compare Genesis 26:3. **CHAPTER IX, v. 1. g)** Jonathan: *"The burden of the word of the Lord."* The Septuagint more broadly: "The intake/burden" <note>original: "λῆμμα"</note> etc., which the Arabic version rendered "revelation," and Suidas interprets as a prophecy or an aphorism. Likewise in chapter 12:1 and Malachi 1:1. We, with Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note>, translate it as "the utterance of the word of Jehovah," understanding the Word pronounced by Jehovah. For although the word *Massa* <note>original: "מַשָּׂא"</note> elsewhere signifies "a burden," yet in the titles of prophecies that word does not simply imply a "burden," but has a neutral meaning, comparing chapter 12:1 and Proverbs 31:1, from the root *nasa* <note>original: "נָשָׂא"</note>, which means not only "to carry" but also "to bring forth and pronounce" (Numbers 23:7, 18; 2 Kings 9:25; Job 27:1; 29:1). See the note on Jeremiah 23:33 and following. Schmidius: "The prophecy. The word of Jehovah is etc." which is indeed against the accents. Observe, however, that although elsewhere these words merely serve as an inscription and title, here they belong to the very substance of the prophecy, and constitute a prophetic announcement in this manner: *"The utterance is in or against the land of Hadrach etc."* For there follows a causal proportion, "because the Lord has an eye etc.," which would hardly fit if it were a mere introductory title. Furthermore, concerning the argument and scope of this chapter, Jerome rightly says: *"All this vision pertains to the calling of the nations and the building up of the Church."* Beautifully, therefore, it coheres with the end of the preceding chapter 8:20 and following, where the calling of the nations under the New Testament was discussed. And the parts of the chapter according to Schmidius are three: I. Prophecy against the land of Hadrach, Damascus, Tyre, Sidon, Philistia, and their future conversion to Christ (verses 1–8). II. The stirring up of Zion to joy on account of the coming and liberation of the King Messiah (verses 9–12). III. The promise of preaching the Gospel, even among the nations (verse 13 to the end).

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of Zechariah chapter 8, regarding the transformation of fasts into feasts, to the beginning of chapter 9, which contains a series of prophetic oracles against the nations surrounding Israel.</meta>

# ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER 9.

<margin>
h) *it shall be* or *it shall rest* (compared with its resting place) in the land of Hadrach. This is an obscure name in geography. Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan</note> rendered it "the south"; the Septuagint <note>Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> however rendered it as *Sedrach*, to which a Greek commentary adds: "it is a city of Arabia." Junius <note>Francis Junius, a Reformed theologian</note> says it refers to "the land surrounding Judea," from the Syriac <unclear>chad chad</unclear> meaning "to surround." He writes it is very likely the Prophet wished to use this word toward the Syrians (comparing Isaiah 14:4 etc.). We, following Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century polymath</note> in book II of *Phaleg* chapter 6, interpret it as a proper name for Damascene Syria, which the Prophet soon explains. Rabbi Jose, praised by Rashi and David Kimchi, says: "I call heaven and earth to witness that I am from Damascus, and there is found a place there whose name is Chadrach." The sense of this phrase and the following one is not very clear. M. I. explains it in a positive sense: "The prophecy of the Lord shall one day be in the land of Chadrach just as in the land of Israel, for it shall become part of the Israelite territory." And "Damascus shall be its rest," as if to say the "habitation of His glory." Thus say Rashi and David Kimchi, and likewise Jonathan, who rendered the latter part: "and Damascus shall be converted, so that it may become part of the land of the house of the Shekhinah" <note>the Divine Presence</note>. The illustrious Maius <note>John Henry Maius</note> says on page 1081: "He predicts the conversion of the neighboring kingdoms, because the word of the 'rest' of Damascus shall be in the future (verse 1) and in Hamath, which some think is Antioch." Certainly (the praised man continues) it is situated in those parts, and the first seats of the Christians are there (Acts 9:2, 19, 20; chapter 11:26). We add concerning Damascus Acts 9:2, 10, 19, 20; and concerning Tyre chapter 21:3, 4. Truly the closing of the second verse (which is very closely connected to this first one by the conjunction "and also") teaches that this verse portends something for the nations, and especially for Tyre and Sidon, which is...
</margin>

<margin>
...directly contrary to the presumption of wisdom that will occur: what that presumption is, and how God will counter it, is explained in the following...
</margin>

> <gloss>k</gloss>The burden of the word of <gloss>i</gloss>the LORD <gloss>h</gloss>in the land of Hadrach, <gloss>n</gloss>and Damascus <gloss>l</gloss>shall be its rest; <gloss>m</gloss>for <gloss>t</gloss>toward the LORD <gloss>q</gloss>is the eye of <gloss>r</gloss>man <gloss>s</gloss>and of all the tribes of Israel: 1
> <gloss>u</gloss>And Hamath also <gloss>w</gloss>shall border thereby; <gloss>y</gloss>Tyre <gloss>z</gloss>and Sidon, <gloss>a</gloss>though it be very wise: 2

---

...verses, that in verse 3 and this in verse 4. We prefer, therefore, with Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnovius, 17th-century theologian</note> to explain it as a threat. **The Burden** or *pronouncement* of the word of the Lord we take here in a pregnant and emphatic sense for a *word* which has substance beneath it; it is not empty or like "lightning from a basin" <note>an idiom for an empty threat</note>, but carries that which it says within itself in an indissoluble bond because it is *the Lord’s word*. Therefore, when it is said this will be *in the land of Hadrach*, the sense is that it will weigh upon it as a heavy burden, and in such a way that it cannot be averted or removed by human effort or wisdom. Just as in Isaiah 9:7-8 it is said: *The Lord sent a word* (into Jacob) *that it might be in Jacob, and it falls* (as heavy things usually do, not without damaging effect and impact) *into Israel; and all the people shall feel it* (they shall experience that it was not an empty word). For so Rashi and David Kimchi explain that passage. The conversion of these nations is only dealt with here in verse 7, surely following their overthrow, whether by Alexander the Great or by the Maccabees (verses 1–6). i) especially *Damascus* or the head of that region (Isaiah 7:8), concerning which see the note on Isaiah 17:1. k) *shall be the place of His rest*; that is: the word of Jehovah, which I just mentioned, shall rest in Damascus and weigh upon it like a <unclear>burden</unclear> (Isaiah 6:8; Ezekiel 5:13). Aben Ezra says: "for his word shall be fulfilled." Tarnovius: "Therefore it will not be an overflowing scourge passing quickly by, but here will be a stable and perpetual seat of judgment." Those who explain this in a positive sense should compare Isaiah 1:10 and Psalm 132:14. l) Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmid, Lutheran theologian</note> says: *For the eye shall be looking toward Jehovah*. Thus he would express the tendency of the eye toward its object; and the whole phrase would be taken in a better sense regarding the conversion of the nations to God in the time of the New Testament (cf. chapter 5:6; Isaiah 33:17; Psalm 145:15). But more correctly the Septuagint and the Arabic: *The Lord looks upon men*. The Syriac: *To the Lord men are manifest*. And Jonathan: "Before the Lord the works of the children of men are manifest." Indeed, Dathe says *the Lord is the subject, while the eye of man and of all the tribes of Israel is named as the object*, because He sees and inspects men in general and the Israelite tribes in particular (cf. above chapter 3:9 and 4:10, where Zechariah recorded things worthy of note regarding the eyes of the Lord being intent upon the Church and all men). Regarding the syntax, cf. Glassius' *Philologia Sacra*, page 636. The connection of the verse with the preceding is clear enough through the causal *for* (ki); as if to say: There is no reason why the Syrians and other nations, who are of a hostile mind toward the people of the Lord, should think they are hidden or promise themselves impunity from God. For how would He release unpunished those whom He surveys with His own eye, and whose crimes He sees? Or how would He not avenge injuries inflicted on His people, He who inspects and cares for the tribes of Israel? Cf. Jeremiah 32:19; Psalm 66:7; Psalm 94:9; Proverbs 5:21, 15:3, 20:12. m) and especially (cf. 1 Kings 11:1; Isaiah 1:1, etc.) *of all the tribes of Israel*, whom He so inspects that He does not allow them to be rashly harmed by anyone. Cf. Deuteronomy 11:12; Psalm 33:18; Isaiah 5:5; and Jeremiah 2:3. Jonathan says: "and he has good pleasure in all," etc. These things are seen, therefore, as spoken for the comfort of the Jews' then-afflicted state, whence Tarnovius orders it to be inferred thus: "Though the ferocity of your enemies has been intolerable to you until now, O Jews, nevertheless let it terrify you very little hereafter, because the burden of the divine decree is now reaching them, which you hear me proclaim against a most powerful King according to the mind of God, and first specifically against Damascus, a city known to you, and as your affairs now stand, more blessed than you." v. 2. n) See note on verse 7. o) *Hamath, the capital of Antiochian Syria*, concerning which see notes on Numbers 34:8 and Amos 6:2. p) Cocceius' Lexicon 125: *it shall have its limit* or *it shall place its borders in it, in the rest of the Lord*, that is, the land in which the Lord shall rest. Jonathan: "it shall be converted, that it may become part of the land of the house of His Shekhinah," in a positive sense, as above in verse 1. But Gussetius on page 160 explains it so that Hamath, a city of Syria, is included within the borders of that predicted burden, that is, the space in which the burden of the divine Word rested (verse 1), which has its boundary at that city, or which is bordered by Damascus (Exodus 19:12; Joshua 18:20). q) and also Tyre and Sidon, that is, Tyre with Sidon (comparing a similar construction in Deuteronomy 16:2, Isaiah 1:13, etc.). See Cocceius' Lexicon page 190. We explain it thus because of the following, where the discourse is at least primarily about Tyre alone. For the rest, concerning Tyre and Sidon, see the note on Isaiah 23:1, 4. r) They translate it as *although* (comparing Genesis 8:21, 34:9; Daniel 9:9) as if a silent objection were being met (cf. Proverbs 21:30). For the property of this little word, according to which it is causal, has its own emphasis: for the very opinion of one's own wisdom moves God, as it were, to decree something among men by which He may confound the wisdom they have presumed, by bringing evils upon them which no cunning can avert. s) *Tyre with neighboring Sidon is very wise*. The Vulgate translates it well: *For they have indeed taken to themselves great wisdom*. For it is not wisdom itself, but the presumption of it, the ostentation, and the vain confidence that is a vice, and this is especially reproached in the prince of the Tyrians in Ezekiel 28:3 and following. Cf. Isaiah 5:21, 19:11; Proverbs 3:7, 26:12, 28:11; Ecclesiastes 7:16; also Isaiah 29:14, 31:2, 44:23; Jeremiah 9:22; Obadiah verse 8; Job 5:13, 37:24. In what matters Tyre pleased itself because of its wisdom, the following verse explains (namely 1) in fortifications, 2) in building up riches), just as verse 4 explains how God is going to confound this wisdom of hers in both respects, by reducing her to poverty and casting her walls or wealth into the sea, and burning her up. v. 3. t) *For she built* and Tyre still builds. Having survived many great misfortunes under the Babylonian empire, she was reborn and flourished again after its fall; or, to speak with the Prophet, after 70 years she was visited by the LORD (though she acknowledges this very little) and returned to her harlot’s hire, that is, the commerce to which she had been devoted long ago (Isaiah 23:16, 17), and is now occupied in repairing her fortifications. u) *a stronghold, a fortification*. Isaiah 19:6; <note>original: "ὁχύרוμα"</note> *stronghold*. 2 Corinthians 10:4. x) for herself. A pleonasm <note>redundant use of words</note>, but an emphatic one, as if to say: And in building these fortifications she, as one exceedingly wise, is remarkably pleased with herself, and seems to provide so well for herself that she fears she will hardly have any need in the future. Diodorus Siculus, book 17, chapter 40, says: "She had the greatest confidence in the fortifications of the island and the prepared supplies of things." And in chapter 43: "Soon the Tyrians, in order to make the walls firmer, leaving a space of five cubits in the middle, built another wall ten cubits wide, and filled the empty space between both with stones and heaped-up earth." y) *and she heaps up* (va-titzbor) Genesis 41:35; Psalm 39:7; namely from the commerce which she conducts across the sea in every direction (cf. Isaiah 23:1 and following). z) *silver*, as dust (that is, soil, meaning a great quantity of silver). A hyperbolic and proverbial expression. Job 27:16; cf. Habakkuk 2:6; 2 Chronicles 9:27. a) *and gold* Proverbs 3:14, 8:10, 19. It is gold in general, like the Greek *chrysos* <note>original: "χρυσός"</note> or *chrysion* <note>original: "χρυσίον"</note>, which corresponds to the Hebrew in the Septuagint and is linguistically similar to it. We derive it from the Arabic *charatz*, "he desired greedily"; whence the Hebrew *charutz*, "diligent" or "greedy" (in a positive sense in Proverbs 10:4, etc.); just as *silver* is called *kesef* by the Hebrews from "desiring," because men are accustomed to greedily covet and desire it. Otherwise, it is derived from the Hebrew *charatz*, "to cut" or "to dig," so that it is called something dug or a fossil, because it is diligently sought and dug out before other metals. b) *as the mire of the streets*. c. 10:5. v. 4. c) Behold. The Prophet rouses the reader to perceive what the Lord is going to do against her, to confound the wisdom of Tyre, which he had reproached in verses 2 and 3; and while he rouses, he brings the matter as if into the present (because it was certainly to come to pass). See note on Jeremiah 31:8. d) THE LORD, whose eye surveys the whole of mankind (verse 1). e) Jonathan: "He will cast her out," namely from the city and her possessions, as if to say He will deprive her of her inheritance. Deuteronomy 11:23. And Schmid: "He will impoverish her," from the related root *yarash*, "to become poor" (Psalm 34:11). Altogether the first part of the phrase seems to be placed against her boasting in riches, just as the latter part is against the fortifications of Tyre (verse 3).

to which she [Ekron] repeatedly looked, along with the other Philistine provinces <note>original: *satrapiis*</note>, trusting in a treaty and alliance with a city [Tyre] so wealthy and powerful. Isaiah 20:5-6, cf. chapter 45:22. **q)** For, lest anyone think she grieves only for the misfortunes of others and not her own, she shall perish from Gaza; that is, no one shall be in her hereafter, because she is to be desolated and cut off. Cf. Jeremiah 49:38, Amos 1:8. **r)** *The King*, that is, the royal Governor, whom the Persians held there before Alexander. Curtius <note>Roman historian Quintus Curtius Rufus</note> in Book 4, Chapter 6, says: "Alexander was besieging the city of Gaza. It was commanded by Batis, a man of exceptional loyalty to his King." **s)** Zephaniah 2:4. This prophecy was fulfilled among the Philistines not only by Alexander, of whom we just cited Curtius, but also by the Maccabees later; see the notes on Zephaniah 2:4, 7 and 1 Maccabees 10:84, 12:43. Josephus <note>Jewish historian Flavius Josephus</note> *Antiquities*, Book 13, Chapter 8, 21. Regarding Gaza in particular, Strabo <note>Greek geographer</note> teaches in Book 16 that the city, once noble, was destroyed by Alexander and remained deserted; hence Acts 8:26: "this is a desert" <note>original: *αὐτή ἐστιν ἔρημος*</note>. **t)** *shall not be inhabited*, a figure of speech <note>term: *metonymy*</note> for "it shall be uninhabited," as the Septuagint, Arabic, Jonathan, and Vulgate translations have it. Thus also in Isaiah 13:20, Jeremiah 17:6, and 50:13, 39.

**V. 6. u)** Some say: *a bastard* <note>original: *spurius*</note> (z) Deuteronomy 23:2, namely one born of an uncertain father, according to Gousset <note>Jacques Gousset, Hebrew scholar</note> page 464. Not the proper and legitimate heir shall occupy the ancestral houses, gardens, and fields, but an infamous outsider, so that those of whom no one can point out the father say, "These things are mine; depart, old inhabitants," according to Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow, Lutheran theologian</note>. But we prefer to take the word here a little more generally, and with the Septuagint, Arabic, Syriac, and Jonathan, translate it as *foreigner* or *stranger*. For it comes from **זר** (stranger), with a double *Mem* prefix, just as **ממגור** (granary) is from **גור** (to dwell) in Joel 1:16. Jonathan declared what sort of foreigners are meant here: "The House of Israel, who were in it as foreigners." Thus also Rabbi Solomon [Rashi]. **x)** *the pride of the Philistines*, that is, the Philistines swelling with pride from their prosperity. However, there is an emphasis here: that God, when He punishes, intends more to cut off the evil itself than the evil people; which is apparent even from verse 7, where, after removing the blood and idols from the mouth of the Philistines, He says He will finally permit the remnants to be sacred to God. Isaiah 13:11, 16:6, Ezekiel 7:24.

**V. 7. y)** *And I will remove his blood from his mouth.* The Philistines, because of their savagery, which they had exercised especially against their neighbors the Israelites, are depicted as cruel beasts, thirsting for blood and greedily drinking it with their mouths. Ezekiel 39:17, 19. Cf. below v. 15 and Revelation 16:6. God therefore says that He wishes to purge that nation, just as from pride in v. 6, so here from cruelty and idolatry, so that it might become humble, gentle, and pious. Ezekiel 11:19. **z)** *and his detestations*, that is, his detestable idols (1 Kings 11:5, 7) or things sacrificed to idols (Isaiah 66:3). **a)** *I will remove from between his teeth*, for whom idolatry was like a most delicious food. For things that pleasantly affect or delight us are called "food" (John 4:34). Unless perhaps one prefers to understand "detestations" as things sacrificed to idols; in which case this phrase would apply properly and without a figure of speech. **b)** *and thus he shall be left for our God.* The remnants surviving from those evils, which I shall inflict upon them because of their sins, shall finally, under the New Testament, be assigned to God as a people and a special possession, to be converted through the Gospel of Christ. Jonathan: "and the proselytes who remain among them shall also be joined to the people of our God." And here God will indeed strike the nations, but He will also heal them again (Isaiah 19:22) and will preserve for Himself sacred remnants from them no less than from the Jews and Israelites (Isaiah 10:21-22, 11:11, 28:5, Romans 11:5). Having finished His "strange work" [of judgment], He will perform His own work among them, namely the work of grace and election into a people (Isaiah 28:21, Lamentations 3:31-33). There is thus here a wonderful transition from threat to promise, such as other prophecies against the nations also have (e.g., Isaiah 19:18, 23:15, Jeremiah 12:15-16, 46:26, 48:47, 49:6, 39, Ezekiel 16:55). **c)** *even the Philistine himself;* just like the land of Hadrach, Damascus, Hamath, Tyre, and Sidon in verses 1 and 2. For it is also a relative particle, which silently joins the Philistines with several nations of the same quality and fate, as in v. 3 and 11. While the Prophet deals directly with the Philistines to be converted to Christ, by this very link he implies indirectly, but not obscurely, that what he says of one is to be understood of all. Cf. "I also" in chapter 8:21. Furthermore, we saw this fulfilled among the Syrians above at verse 1. For Tyre and Sidon, cf. Isaiah 23:18, Psalm 45:13, Psalm 87:4, and the fulfillment in Acts 21:3-4, 27:3. For Philistia, whose famous towns were Ashdod <note>original: *Azotum*</note> and Joppa, cf. Acts 8:4, 9:36, 42-43 etc. See Gürtler, *Prophetic Theology*, page 471. **d)** *so that He who was until now our (the Jews') God, may hereafter become the God of those nations and of all the earth* (chapter 14:9, Isaiah 54:5). For Zechariah speaks here in his own name and that of his people, whom he seeks to lift up to joy and gladness by this very promise (cf. below v. 9). **e)** *as a chiliarch <note>term: a commander of a thousand</note> or leader in Judah* (chapter 12:5). The Jewish people were distributed into their thousands <note>original: *chiliadas*</note> (Judges 6:15), and those who presided over them were called *alluphi*, leaders or chiliarchs; see the note on Micah 5:1. However, "chiliarch" is understood here not alone, but with the "thousand" over which he presides (as in Matthew 2:6). Thus the sense is that the Philistine nation, once the middle wall of separation is removed by Christ, shall belong to the Church and the people of God just as if it were among the thousands of Judah. Cf. Ephesians 2:14.

<column-break/>

**f)** *Sch.* "and shall shake out." Cocceius: "and shall strike" (so that it falls) into the sea. This verb has the force of "to fix" or "to thrust in" (1 Samuel 23:14, 19:10, Hosea 14:6). But the Vulgate: "he shall strike her strength in the sea," as if to say, he will strike her even though she is very strong and situated in the sea itself. Cf. Psalm 28:4, Ezekiel 27:27, 32; and Curtius Book 4, Chapter 2, where Alexander says to the Tyrians: "You indeed, trusting in the location because you inhabit an island, despise this land army; but soon I will show that you are on the mainland." **g)** *Jonathan*, Syriac, *Schm.* and others: "her wealth," comparing chapter 14:14, Psalm 62:11. But Tarnovius: "her fortification," ramparts, walls, bulwarks, citadels. Cf. Psalm 48:14, Psalm 122:7, and specifically here 1 Kings 21:23. Indeed, whatever strong things she has. Isaiah 43:7. **h)** *and Tyre herself*, as to her buildings, shall be consumed by fire, becoming the food and material for flames. Amos 1:10. Curtius Book 4, Chapter 4 says: "Alexander, except for those who had fled into the temples, ordered everyone to be killed and fire to be set to the roofs."

**i)** *Ashkelon shall see this.* This was a Philistine province <note>original: *satrapia*</note>, as were the following ones: Gaza, Ekron, Ashdod (cf. Joshua 13:3, 1 Samuel 6:17). She shall experience, as it were, the pains of one in labor. Micah 4:9-10. **n)** *and Ekron, namely shall see, fear, writhe.* For these are to be repeated from what preceded. Joshua 15:33. **o)** Vulgate and Syriac intransitively: "because her hope was confounded." It interprets the subsequent "cleansing" of the Philistines as a prophecy of their future conversion and integration into the people of God.</summary>
