<meta>This page continues the commentary on Zechariah chapter 9. The previous page discussed the judgment falling upon the Philistine cities of Ashkelon, Gaza, and Ashdod. This page transitions to the promise of the Philistines' conversion and the subsequent protection of Jerusalem, leading into the famous prophecy of the Messiah’s humble entry.</meta>

# ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER 9.

# 8 And I will encamp around my house as a guard <note>original: מִצָּבָה (mizzabah)</note> against him who passes by and him who returns, and no oppressor shall pass over them anymore, for now I have seen with my eyes.

# 9 Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your king comes to you; he is righteous and saved <note>original: נוֹשָׁע (nosha), often translated as "having salvation"</note>; he is humble and riding on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

-> [Section Marker] <-

<margin>
f) And *Ekron*, which was a Philistine lordship (v. 5, Joshua 13:3), worshipped *Beelzebub* (2 Kings 1:2, 3, 6), and was therefore once excluded and <unclear>alienated</unclear> from the city of God in this world (Romans 2:12). g) *The Targum:* Jerusalem shall be filled with the house (families) of Israel. Therefore, I take this as the name of the city rather than a tribal name: *Ekron shall become like Jebus*, that is, like the city of the Jebusites, regarded as part of Israel. This occurs in Joshua 15:8 and 18:28. But as the preceding part, to which our text responds, undoubtedly indicates the <term>secret council</term> <note>original: סוֹד (sod)</note> of both nations, the Philistine and the Israelite; so here also <term>Jebusite</term> <note>original: כַּיְבוּסִי (ka-yevusi)</note> should be interpreted as a tribal name (which it properly is because of its ending): he shall become a Jebusite, or as the Jebusites, named after Jebus, which is the old name for Jerusalem (compare Judges 19:10, 11; 1 Chronicles 11:4). However, whether this refers to the ancient inhabitants of Jerusalem before the Jebusites were driven out, interpreters hold different views. Theodoretus, among others, follows this view, explaining it as: *The Jerusalem of Jacob shall become their own; for he calls them Jebusites, etc.* But the latter view pleases Hoeckius in his Commentary on this passage. Truly, the Jebusites dwelt in Jerusalem long ago, holding the fortress of Zion until the reign of David, while the Israelites occupied the lower part of the <unclear>city</unclear> (Joshua 15:63; 2 Samuel 5:6-9). Therefore, Hoeckius thinks this refers to that habitation, meaning: the Philistines will dwell among the people of God, just as the Jebusites once did among the Jews. And that can be admitted in its own way, except that this dual cohabitation was based on the very thing presently discussed. There, the Jebusites lived with the Jews against the will and command of God, who had ordered them to be wiped out, to the detriment of the tribe of Judah whose lot decreased because it was held by Jebusites; and finally, by foul idolatry...
</margin>

<margin>
h) Here, however, the communion of the Gentiles with the people
</margin>

of God is indicated, which they shall have by the favor and indulgence of God, and which shall be the future glory of the Israelite Church, assuming the conversion of the Gentiles. We believe, therefore, that this refers especially to the remnants of the Jebusites who remained in Jerusalem after Zion was captured by David, having embraced the religion of the true God. Such a man was *Araunah*, once a minor king of that nation, who not only remained in Jerusalem but also owned lands on Mount Moriah, upon which the temple was later built—not without mystery and prophetic guidance (2 Kings 24:18, 20 etc., where you may see our notes; compare Psalm 87:4-6; also Genesis 9:27). **Verse 8. h)** *And I will pitch camp around my house* (Psalm 34:8; compare above 2:9; and Genesis 32:2, 3; 2 Kings 6:17). i) Which is the Church (1 Timothy 3:15). *Tarnovius:* k) *Tarnovius:* because of the hostile army constantly breaking in, so that I may drive the enemy away, and because of those passing through, etc. Likewise *Kimchi:* so that it no longer needs to fear a besieging army, nor those passing through, etc. As if <term>mizzabah</term> <note>original: מִצָּבָה</note> were from <term>the army</term> <note>original: הַצָּבָה</note> used instead of <term>from the station</term> <note>original: מִצָּב</note> with an *Aleph*: neither of which is necessary. For we derive it from <term>to stand/station</term> <note>original: נָצַב (nazav)</note> with the prefix *Mem* and the servile *He*: I will encamp or surround my house with a *station or guard* (1) compared with <term>station</term> <note>original: מַצָּב (mazzav)</note> (1 Samuel 14:12) and <term>guard-post</term> <note>original: מַצָּבָה (mazzabah)</note> (Chapter 13:23) and <term>station</term> with the *Kibbutz* vowel (Isaiah 29:3) and the related <term>pillar/officer</term> <note>original: נְצִיב (neziv)</note> (1 Samuel 13:3, 4). These denote military stations or garrisons, <term>guards</term> <note>original: φρουράν (phrouran)</note> placed throughout the cities. The ancient translators held this etymology, except for the *Vulgate*, which followed it. Nor is there difficulty in the omission of the prefix *Kaph*, comparing Isaiah 29:3 where a similar effect occurs. l) I will make the majesty of my glory dwell in the house of my sanctuary; the strength of the arm of my power will surround it like a wall of fire. l) to provide security for it from the one passing through and returning, that is, foreigners traveling back and forth (Chapter 7:14; Ezekiel 35:7; compare Psalm 80:13; Psalm 89:42). m) nor shall he pass through anymore (Isaiah 28:15, 18), at least not with success and permanence. For compare below 12:2 etc.; 14:1 etc. n) the exactor, that is, the tyrant (Isaiah 9:3; Chapter 14:2). o) now I have seen what Jerusalem has suffered from enemies; and I have seen it in such a way that, having pitied her misery, I have now decided to help her, after I seemed for long enough to tolerate the enemies or be ignorant of what they were doing (compare Exodus 2:25; 3:7; Acts 7:34). *The Targum:* because now I have revealed my strength to do good to them. So says Tarnovius: You will easily see, he says, why He says He has "now seen," He who never fails to see; because He now makes it so that others experience that He has seen, just as He is said to "remember" when He manifests this to others through His works. **Verse 9. p)** Therefore exult greatly (Isaiah 12:19; Joel 2:23). God had promised that He would convert the nations themselves (v. 7) and protect His house from enemies (v. 8). This looked especially toward Zion, or the Jewish Church, which He intended to strengthen and lift up with these very promises. He now stirs her to joy, and not a simple or common joy, but one singular and extraordinary, which should break out into outward gestures and cheerful exultation, and indeed *greatly* (Hosea 9:1; Job 32:2; compare Psalm 24:7). So that this joy might be further promoted, He explains the cause and matter of it in what follows: namely, the coming of the Messiah, through whom those superior benefits would arrive, along with His qualities, kingdom, and spiritual goods—so much so that this is a confirmation of the preceding points. Furthermore, instead of *Exult greatly*, John, looking to the sense (12:15), has *Fear not*: because one who exults greatly does not fear. Matthew, however (21:5), in place of this, puts first, *Tell the daughter of Zion*, from the parallel in Isaiah 62:11. q) *The Targum: The Church, the daughter of Zion.* (Zephaniah 3:14). Daughter, says Cocceius in his Lexicon (106), when the name of a city or nation is added, denotes all the children of that city or nation. r) cry out and shout (Isaiah 44:23; Ezra 3:11). Thus, express your joy not only by gesture and the habit of the body, which is <term>exult</term> <note>original: גִּילִי (gili)</note>, but also by voice, which is the force of this word. The joyful shouts of *Hosanna* etc. look to this (Matthew 21:9, 15). s) Isaiah 37:22. t) Behold! This seems to be a demonstration, to place a long-hoped-for thing before the eyes as if it were present (Isaiah 35:4; 40:9; 62:11. See note above on v. 4). u) *Your King*. Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] ingenuously says: this cannot be explained except as referring to the MESSIAH, comparing v. 10; for we do not find that Israel had such a King as is described here during the Second Temple. So also others cited by Ibn Ezra, who however explained this text as referring to Judas Maccabeus no less wrongly than Rabbi Moses Haccohen did regarding Nehemiah. (Compare above 6:13; Isaiah 24:23; Hosea 3:5; Psalm 24:7, 8; Psalm 72:1). x) he shall come and will not delay his coming any longer (Chapter 2:14; Genesis 49:10; Isaiah 35:4; Habakkuk 2:3; Psalm 90:3). Correctly (says Tarnovius), Zechariah uses the Future *he shall come*, because he speaks of the Future; and correctly both Evangelists (Matthew 21:5; John 12:15) use the Present <term>he comes</term> <note>original: ερχεται (erchetai)</note>, because he was truly then approaching, whom the Prophets had promised would come. y) to you, for your consolation, benefit, and good. If therefore he comes to you, he is yours; it is yours to rejoice especially at his arrival. *The Targum:* within you, or in your midst. z) *righteous*, both in himself, because there is no wickedness in him, and effectively, because he is the mediator of righteousness (2 Samuel 23:3; Isaiah 45:24; 53:11; Jeremiah 23:5, 6; 1 Corinthians 1:30; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 John 2:1). The foundation of this interpretation also lies in the aforementioned pronoun "to you." a) <term>saved/having salvation</term> <note>original: נוֹשָׁע (nosha)</note>. The Septuagint, Arabic, Syriac, and Vulgate read *and savior*. From this, however, it does not follow that the word in the Hebrew codex was corrupted from <term>savior</term> <note>original: מוֹשִׁיעַ (moshia)</note>, but only that they took the participle <term>nosha</term> in an active or deponent sense. Perhaps as <term>nish'an</term> is to swear, or <term>nismakh</term> to desire. See Glassius, *Philologia Sacra*, p. 168. There are those who explain the <term>Niphal</term> <note>passive/reflexive verb form</note> as a reciprocal imminent action, *savior of himself*, i.e., saving himself by his own divine strength (compare Isaiah 59:16; 63:5; John 10:17), just as <term>nishmar</term> is "keeping oneself," etc. Pfeiffer, in *Dubia Vexata*, p. 550, says the participle should be explained as a noun, *salutary, endowed with salvation. Having salvation himself and giving it to others*. But we, while retaining the Hebrew reading and the constant passive meaning of this word in the Niphal, render it with others as *and saved* (compare Deuteronomy 33:29; Isaiah 45:17; Psalm 33:15, etc.). Rabbi Kimchi and M. I. explain: *saved* because of his righteousness, which compare with Acts 3:35 and 1 Timothy 3:16. Furthermore, the active "Savior" is not so much involved in the grammar as the thing itself, which follows as a consequence. For he is saved not for himself, but (as the Prophet had said, speaking entirely *to you*) for you. Namely, while Christ according to his human nature was himself truly saved from sufferings and death, he also became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him; so that they rejoice in his salvation, even the passive kind (Hebrews 5:7, 9; Psalm 20:2, 3, 6, 7; Psalm 69:30; Isaiah 53:8; Acts 2:24). And for this very reason the people of Christ, when he came to the city and fulfilled this prophecy of Zechariah, shouted that prayerful *Hosanna* (that is, "Save, O God, our Messiah") from Psalm 118:25 (Matthew 21:9, 15; John 12:13), because they knew their salvation depended on the salvation of their King and Messiah. Therefore, Rabbi Albo is said to have spoken beautifully: *Both yours and ours is the redemption, i.e., it shall be for salvation to you and to us*; and so that this might be better understood, Rabbi Barachias the priest adds: *Behold! what is written: Behold your King comes to you righteous and saved*. "Saving" is not written here, but "saved" or "to be saved." See these in *Yalkut Shimoni*, vol. II, folio 87a. b) *poor* <note>original: עָנִי (ani)</note>, that is, needy, not noble in any human splendor or power. For this is the constant and formal meaning of this form: which is clear from the fact that it is usually joined in Scripture with synonyms like pauper, grieving, expiring, or crushed (compare Deuteronomy 24:14; Isaiah 26:6; Zephaniah 3:12; Psalm 69:30; 88:16). Correctly, therefore, the Vulgate and Syriac say *poor* (Matthew 21:5; Luke 9:58; 2 Corinthians 8:9; Philippians 2:6, etc.). But the Targum, the Septuagint, and from them Matthew 21:5, read <term>meek/gentle</term> <note>original: πραϋς (praüs)</note>; and the Arabic, from the Greek, has *humbling himself or humble*. These can be perfectly reconciled, because such a needy misery is understood here, to which Christ lowered himself of his own accord, which consequently could not but have humility and meekness as companions (compare Matthew 11:29; Ephesians 4:2). Meanwhile, the notion of meekness properly belongs not to this form, but to the related form <term>meek</term> <note>original: עָנָו (anav)</note> in Numbers 12:3. Isinus, whom the Greek Scholia allege, gave it expressed in a double version: *meek and poor*. Furthermore, God carefully marked these characteristics of the Messiah here, and his poverty in particular, so that the Jews—perceiving what was to come—would not despise their Messiah for this very reason, that he was poor, humble, and needy.

<summary>This page provides an extensive commentary on Zechariah 9:8-9, discussing God's promise to protect Jerusalem and the prophecy of the Messiah's humble entry. It features a deep linguistic debate on whether the Messiah is described as "saving" or "being saved" and emphasizes his humility as a sign for the faithful.</summary>
<keywords>Zechariah 9, Messiah, Jerusalem, Jebusites, Ekron, David, Araunah, Hosanna, Niphal, humility, poverty, Kimchi, Ibn Ezra, Rashi, salvation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the detailed philological and theological commentary on Zechariah chapter 9. The previous page discussed the judgment of Philistine cities and their eventual inclusion into the people of God (becoming like a "Jebusite"). This page focuses on verses 10 and 11, detailing the peaceful nature of the Messiah's reign and the liberation of captives through the "blood of the covenant."</meta>

<header>ZECHARIAH 9. CHAPTER 9.</header>

<margin>
...which was following, the foal would approach. e) **Son of she-donkeys.** According to **Cocceius' Lexicon p. 105**, this refers to a young animal still seeking the company of the mothers, and thus one that has been unridden by anyone until now.
</margin>

<margin>
c) *Riding on a donkey*, not out of poverty or lack, as **Kimchi** suggests (for the whole world will be in his power), but out of humility. It is also to teach that **Israel** would have no need for horses and war-chariots, comparing verse 11. This is also the view of **Rabbi Solomon (Rashi)** and **M.I.** Compare *Hosea 14:4* and *Psalm 147:10*. In ancient times, even the most noble people did not consider it beneath them to be carried by a donkey (*Judges 10:4, 12:13, 2 Samuel 17:23, etc.*). Therefore *Christ*, in order to display a specimen of his kingdom to the *Jews*, used a donkey as his mount when he entered *Jerusalem*. This was a wondrous parade for a king, but for a king who was poor, and who was hidden under the garment of a servant. *See Bochart, Hierozoicon book 1, p. 184.* Furthermore, just as this passage deals with *Christ's* first and humble coming, so *Daniel 7:13* stands in contrast, dealing with the second and glorious coming in the clouds. d) **Ayir** <note>original: עיר</note> or this is, namely "upon a donkey" (8) **Aton** <note>original: אתון</note> should be taken as in *Job 30:6* and *Job 11:13*. This name among the *Hebrews* as well as the *Arabs* denotes a donkey without distinction of age; it comes from a root meaning "to set out," because the donkey is a convenient beast of burden for preparing journeys. The meaning is restricted to a "foal" or "young donkey" here only by the addition of *son of she-donkeys*; much like the word **Shor** <note>original: שור</note>, which means an ox in general, but when **Ben Bakar** <note>original: בן בקר (son of the herd)</note> is added, it specifically means a young bull. Moreover, from this passage and *Matthew 21:5*, the "and" is not additive but explanatory <note>meaning the donkey and the foal are the same animal in context</note>, as in *Genesis 13:15* and *1 Samuel 17:40*. For *Christ* sat only on the *foal*, according to *Mark 11:7, Luke 19:30, and John 12:14-15*. Nor does the plural <term>upon them</term> <note>original: ἐπάνω αὐτῶν (epano auton)</note> in *Matthew 21:7* pose an obstacle. For as *Tarnovius* notes, the plural is often used in *Scripture* when only one person or thing out of many is intended (compare *Genesis 8:4, Judges 12:7*). However, the disciples brought the she-donkey at the same time because they were yoked together, not for the *Lord* to ride her, but so that the foal might follow more easily with its mother...
</margin>

->**And I will cut off the chariot...**<-
->**And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off; and he shall speak**<-
->**peace to the nations, and his dominion shall be from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth.**<-
->**As for you also, by the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit where there is no water.**<-
->**Return...**<-

---

Compare *Mark 11:2* and the note on *Numbers 29:13*. **verse 10. f)** *For I will cut off the chariots.* This connects with the final part of the previous verse. It means: In ancient times, the people of *Ephraim* relied on chariots and those of *Jerusalem* on horses—both often trusting in the apparatus of war (*Isaiah 2:7, 31:1*). Lest the *Jews* should expect a *Messiah* with similar madness—one famous for war who would save his people with chariots and horses—I said that the *Messiah* will come to *Jerusalem* not as a glorious commander on a warhorse, but carried by a donkey; that is, as one humble and peaceful. I will instead destroy those warlike preparations and the vain trust in them; I will be far from using them for the liberation of my people, which will be spiritual. Compare *Hosea 14:4* and the notes on *Micah 5:9* and *Psalm 20:8*. **g)** *The battle bow*, used here as a figure of speech for every kind of weapon. **The Jonathan Targum** says: *and I will break the strength of those making war, the armies of the nations.* Rather: I will cause the use of "fleshly" weapons to cease in the *Church*, and the nations themselves, tamed by the word of the *Gospel*, shall cultivate peace with one another and with the people of *God*. Compare below the notes on *chapter 10:5, 1 Samuel 2:4, Ephesians 2:4, Hosea 2:20, Micah 4:3, and Psalm 46:10*. **h)** *Indeed* (if you ask how it will come to pass that chariots, horses, and bows cease) *that King of yours (v. 9) shall speak peace to the nations*, by reconciling them to one another and to you, so that they may agree sweetly, with enmity abolished (*Ephesians 2:15-17*). This is the fruit of the kingdom of *Christ*, who is the Prince of Peace (*Isaiah 9:5, 66:12, Micah 5:4, Psalm 72:3*). **i)** An emphatic phrase: *He shall speak peace*, and while he speaks, he will impose the law of peace upon those who are not rebellious. Worldly kings hardly obtain peace except through war and arms, but *Christ* achieves it through the *Gospel* and the Word, which conquers peoples and does not allow them to remain wild. Therefore, it is the effective word of divine power that is understood here, which carries its effect with it; such as the word used to "command" a blessing in *Leviticus 25:21* and *Isaiah 45:12*. **i)** *And his dominion shall be*, that is, he shall rule. *Daniel 11:4; compare above chapter 6:13, Psalm 22:29*. **k)** *From one sea even to the other*, that is, the opposite sea. *Psalm 72:8ff, Psalm 89:26*. **The Jonathan Targum:** *from the sea to the West*. See the note on *Micah 7:12*. **l) The Jonathan Targum:** *and from the Euphrates*. Thus the whole phrase is drawn from the descriptions of the boundaries of the Holy Land and the extent of the *Israelite* kingdom under *David* and *Solomon*, used as a "type" or symbol of a much greater reality. Compare *Exodus 23:31, Deuteronomy 11:24, Joshua 1, 1 Kings 5:1*. However, it should be understood as the magnitude of this promise in a much wider sense, meaning a universal and global kingdom over all nations. Thus the *Septuagint, Vulgate, and Arabic* translations are not wrong to say: *and from the rivers*, namely, whatever rivers they may be (compare *Psalm 89:26*). **m)** *even to the ends of the earth*, as far as the earth goes, that is, over the whole world. *Isaiah 45:22, Psalm 2:8, 59:14, 72:8; compare Isaiah 9:6*. **verse 11. n)** *Even you*, namely, O *Zion*! (compare verse 9). To this thread of prophecy, after describing the peaceful dominion of *Christ* over all nations, he now returns, so that he may apply and commend the coming of the promised King (which he said would be for the salvation of the nations) especially to her. A similar transition is found in *Isaiah 2:5* (compare verses 2-4). *Tarnovius* correctly makes the connection with the preceding verses: "When it was said that your king would rule far and wide, O *Jerusalem*, I want you to understand that the greatest benefits of this empire also belong to you. *For even you...*" On the emphasis of the word *even*, see verses 2, 7, and chapter 8:21. **o)** *Sch.* <note>likely a reference to the scholar Schultens</note> *Even as for you, through the blood of his covenant I will send out...* But the pronoun **At** <note>original: אַתְּ (you, feminine singular)</note>, which has a connecting accent, would then require a much larger pause. *Tarnovius* writes: "Even you shall have a part in this kingdom, indeed you shall reign through Christ (*Revelation 1:6, 1 Peter 2:9*) **through the blood of your covenant**." He believes this is a complete clause of the verse marked by the *Revia* accent, so that a new sentence begins after it regarding the release of prisoners from the pit. But one can gather that the sentence is not yet finished here, because there is only a minor pause accent here, while upon the word **Mibbor** <note>original: מבור (from the pit)</note> a "lord" accent <note>the Sakeph-katon</note> is placed, and even then the sense is not entirely complete. From this it appears that those accents do not separate distinct sentences, but rather the connected parts of a sentence. Thus we translate: *Even, as for you, in the blood of your covenant I have sent out etc.* **Rabbi Solomon (Rashi)** understands this as the merit of the blood of the covenant sprinkled upon the *Israelites* at *Sinai* (compare *Exodus 24:8*). So does the **Jonathan Targum**, who turns the prophetic text about the future into a purely historical one: *You also, with whom a covenant was made over blood (compare Psalm 50:5), you, I say, I redeemed from the slavery of the Egyptians; I gave you what was necessary in the desert, which was like a desolate, empty pit with no water.* But we, looking at the goal of this vision which the context shows to be prophetic, rather take it as referring to the *blood of the new covenant*, mentioned in *Isaiah 42:6* and *Jeremiah 31:31ff*; that is, the blood of *Jesus Christ*, who stands as the witness and guarantor of the new covenant through his blood. Compare *Matthew 26:28, Acts 20:28, Colossians 1:13-14, Hebrews 9:12-18, 10:29, 13:20*. **p)** *The Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic, and Vulgate* translate: *you sent out*. And so does **Blessed Luther**. This assumes the word is a past-tense form with an added letter "yod," a form found in the written text of *Jeremiah 3:5, 13:21, 31:31, Ezekiel 16:20, etc.* *Hiller* supports this in his work on the *Ketiv and Qere p. 381*, explaining the sense this way: *Even you, daughter of Zion and Jerusalem, the Church of Christ the Redeemer, because of the covenant blood shed by Christ, you have sent out your prisoners*, meaning you have had those previously bound by the chains of sin released. However, that grammatical form is quite rare and not used in the written text here. We therefore translate it as *I have sent out*; which is expressed as a past action in prophecy to represent the certainty of the future: *I will send out*. This is the opposite of <term>being guarded</term> <note>original: τῷ Φρουρουμένῳ (to phrouroumeno)</note>, meaning to be detained in chains, custody, or slavery (*Isaiah 45:13, 52:6, Jeremiah 34:9ff, 50:33, compare Galatians 3:23*). **q)** *your prisoners*, whom he will call "prisoners of hope" in verse 12 (compare *Isaiah 42:7, 61:1, 2 Timothy 2:26, Hebrews 2:14-15*). **r)** *out of the pit, in which there is no water. Genesis 37:24, Jeremiah 38:6ff.* A pit is a metaphor for a prison in *Exodus 12:29* and *Jeremiah 37:16*. **Rabbi Solomon (Rashi)** understands this as the Babylonian captivity. But **Cocceius (Lexicon p. 92)** says: The *Israelites* were enclosed under the Law as if in a prison, waiting for the appearance of *Christ* and the manifestation of eternal life. In that state, they bore an intolerable yoke, hungering and thirsting. But they were not yet allowed to see *Christ* and hear his words to be refreshed from their thirst. Compare *Galatians 3:23, Hebrews 2:15, Isaiah 55:1, 61:1, Jeremiah 31:14, 25*. **Gussetius** in his *Prophetic Theology* explains it similarly: I have liberated the faithful from the slavery of the Law, under which they did not hear the joyful teaching that sins are deleted by the shed blood of the *Messiah*. Compare *chapter 14:8, Isaiah 41:17, etc.* Others interpret the "pit" as the infernal lake, comparing *Isaiah 30:33*.

\* v. 10. **And I will cut off** <note>original: והכרתי</note> uses the Darga accent... while Piskma is used elsewhere... and **cities** <note>original: וערים</note> with the prefix Vav... \* v. 11. **Even you, by the blood of your covenant** <note>original: גם-את בדם-בריתך</note> as in the 3rd manuscript.

<summary>This page analyzes Zechariah 9:10-11, explaining the Messiah's role in ending physical warfare to establish a spiritual, universal kingdom. It identifies the "blood of the covenant" as the blood of Christ which liberates those "imprisoned" under the Old Testament Law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Zechariah chapter 9. The previous page discussed the humble entry of the Messiah into Jerusalem on a donkey, contrasting his peaceful reign with worldly empires. This page moves into verses 12 and 13, focusing on the call for the "prisoners of hope" to return and the prophecy of Zion's triumph over "Javan" (Greece).</meta>

# ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER 9. 9
<sig>Ll ll 4</sig> <sig>84</sig>

12 Return to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope; even today I declare that I will restore double to you.
13 For I have bent Judah for myself as a bow; I have filled the bow with Ephraim and stirred up your sons, O Zion, against your sons, O Javan <note>Greece</note>, and I have made you like a hero’s sword.
14 And the LORD shall be over them—

<margin>
12. The word [translated as "hope"] comes from the verb <term>קוה</term> <note>qavah</note> meaning "to be gathered," as in Jeremiah 3:17. Therefore, the Vulgate and others more correctly translate it as *prisoners of hope*: which Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note> explains as *prisoners who have hoped*.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 12. g) Jonathan: *Return so that you may become, that is, once again become a fortified city, after you have long been desolate regarding your cities.* In this view, the letter <term>ל</term> <note>Lamed, a prefix usually meaning "to"</note> would mark the goal of the change or the effect, and the whole phrase should be taken as in Isaiah 29:17. Most interpreters take it more simply: *Return to the fortification* or *citadel*, where <term>ל</term> signifies the destination of movement, a phrase that occurs frequently, e.g., Genesis 18:33, Ezekiel 18:55, Psalm 7:8. By *fortification*, Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish commentator</note> understands God himself, who is like a citadel and a strong tower (Psalm 61:4, Proverbs 18:10). Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century theologian</note> understands it as Christ, who is the citadel of salvation for all who flee to him (Psalm 2:12), which the Lexicon (p. 863) also declares: *having abandoned*, it says, *the citadel made by hands, seize the true citadel from which you have fallen away.* See also verse 9 above. We prefer to understand it as the City of God or Jerusalem—not the physical one, though it is called by the name "Stronghold" in Zechariah (compare chapter 2:2), but the mystical and spiritual one (Psalm 46:5, 8; Psalm 87:3), which Isaiah (chapter 26:1, 2) also praises as a strong city whose walls and ramparts are salvation, and whose gates the righteous nation that keeps faith shall enter. Thus Tarnovius says: *To the fortification*, he says, *that is, to the Church, betake yourselves, which God himself fortifies with his protection.* This is a parenthetical exhortation addressed to the children of Zion (compare 2 Peter 3:17). h) <term>the prisoner of the assembly</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ δέσμιος τῆς συναγωγῆς</note>. Thus the *Syriac* and *Arabic* versions. They are correct regarding the subject matter (for this address pertains primarily to the Jewish Synagogue), though less suitable regarding philology: for they assigned a new meaning to a word that elsewhere consistently means <term>expectation</term> or <term>hope</term>.
</margin>

*redemption.* Cocceius' Lexicon p. 740: *You who are held in custody, so that you may wait for the king who is to come to Zion* (compare the note on verse 11, also Isaiah 61:1, Psalm 14:7, Psalm 68:7, Psalm 107:0). Clearly, the Jews were enclosed under the law, as if in custody, so that they might wait for the appearing of Christ all the more eagerly (Galatians 3:23). i) **Even today**, (that is, in the day and time of the New Testament, when that promised King has come, see verse 9. For God speaks here not as if pointing out things far in the future, but as if he had already established the day that was to come as present). x) Cocceius' Lexicon p. 930: *another advocate* <note>original: ἀντὶ παρακλήτου; compare John 14:16</note> adding: *Once Christ has been taken up into glory, the Spirit of adoption is poured out.* Vitringa (on the Apocalypse, p. 561) agrees. But we disagree with them, both because the conjunction "even" here makes a clear relationship not between Christ himself and the Holy Spirit, but between "today" (the beginning of the New Testament) and the period of the Old Testament; and because <term>משנה</term> <note>mishneh - double/second</note>, as Gussetius observes (p. 875) regarding the nature of offices to be performed, does not denote a successor of equal rank or one appointed at the same time, but one of a lower rank (2 Kings 23:4, 25:18, Nehemiah 11:17, Esther 1:3), which cannot be comfortably applied to the Holy Spirit. Therefore, it is better understood this way: *Even today (and now indeed much more and more eminently than of old) I will restore to you one who announces—or let there be one who announces—double, or just as much good as the evil you have suffered*, namely, Christ himself with his Apostles and Evangelists. It is as if he said, *You had Prophets of old who comforted you by announcing the good things God would do for you; I will therefore bring it about that you now have those who disclose <term>the surpassing</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ ὑπερέχον</note> riches of my grace to you* (compare Isaiah 52:7, 8). *Double* stands for a large and superabundant compensation of good in place of evil (Isaiah 40:2, 61:7; compare Exodus 16:5, 22; Jeremiah 17:18, 16:18). Jonathan: *today also I will send to announce to you that I will bring to you the double blessings I promised you.* Jerome: *You have the Lord promising that, in exchange for the brief injury of captivity, you shall receive everything doubled; just as we read that Job also received* (compare Job 42:10). v. 13. y) **For**, [which is a reason] that ought to move you greatly to return to the fortification. In this sense, it would be a causal particle depending on the first half of verse 12. Or like this: *for*, as if to explain the nature of that "double good" with examples. In this case, it would clarify the second half of that same verse 12. However it is taken, the remaining part of this chapter is joined by the closest connection to what immediately precedes. Therefore, although some among the Hebrews (Rabbi Solomon) and among the Christians (Beatus Tarnovius and others) have explained these things as referring to the Hasmoneans <note>the Maccabees</note> against the Lagids of Egypt and Seleucids of Syria, David Kimchi more correctly judges that the prophecy of the Messiah continues here. In this way, the sequence of the entire prophecy will remain consistent, and there will be no need, as Vitringa does (Prophetic Doctrine, p. 206), to place <term>the latter</term> before <term>the former</term> <note>original Greek: ὕστερον... πρότερον</note>; which we admit reluctantly whenever we can do without it. z) **I have bent for myself** (supply "as a bow" from the following member) **Judah.** (Lamentations 2:4). That is, Judah will be to me <term>from a chosen arrow</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ ἰοῦ ἐκλογῆς</note> and like weapons which I will use to subdue the nations—and the Greeks in particular—to the kingdom of Christ. Regarding the figurative language of the prophecy, compare Isaiah 49:2, Psalm 45:4, 5, and Revelation 6:2. So says Cocceius in his Commentary: *Here*, he says, *primarily all the Apostles representing the tribes are indicated: then also the believers from all the tribes.* Thus also Gurtler (Prophetic Theology, p. 135) explains it as the bringing of the Greeks into the kingdom of Christ through the faithful from Zion. And Vitringa himself, whom we just cited as disagreeing, subscribes to this in his Commentary on the Apocalypse (p. 326) where he says: *Judah and Ephraim are the bow in a spiritual war, to be bent and filled by God himself.* And a little later: *Since the arrows denote the word of the Gospel itself, piercing more than any two-edged sword, the Bow from which those arrows are sent must signify the teachers and heralds from whose mouths these darts proceed, to be fixed deep in the minds of Christ's adversaries.* — Christ is said to tread or bend this bow when he equips, animates, and moves his ministers through his Spirit, etc. Jonathan: *I have strengthened for them my house of Judah.* a) **And as a bow.** This is understood also in the preceding member, which the word "tread" or "bend" implies; however, according to the accents, it must be referred to the following. <term>the bow</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ τόξον</note>, compare Revelation 6:2. Jonathan: *as a bow drawn in the armory or quiver*, comparing the Targum on Isaiah 49:2. But a bow, when it is bent, is not usually kept in a quiver, but is prepared for the use of shooting (compare Psalm 127:4). b) Jonathan: *I have filled* (that is, I will fill) *with strength.* Others supply "arrows." This, however, fits a quiver better than a bow (compare Psalm 127:5), for *to fill something with some thing* is said of a collection or abundance, but on a bow, single arrows are placed for single shots. Therefore, Cocceius' Lexicon (p. 436): *I have filled my hand with Ephraim as a bow.* But "I will fill" here seems to mean the same as "I will bend" in the preceding member. That is, since the word *to fill* can mean to stretch it (Jeremiah 4:5), why cannot *to fill the bow* be said instead of *to bend*? So the Arabs say *to fill the sight toward someone* instead of *to aim*, and what is more relevant, *to fill the tradition in the bow* <note>an Arabic idiom</note> for *stretching the bow strongly*, with the string pulled back powerfully for shooting. Thus 2 Kings 9:24: *he filled his hand with the bow* means he stretched the bow strongly with his hand. c) From this, David Kimchi concludes that this is a promise concerning the days of the Messiah. See below, chapter 10:6, 7; and compare the notes on chapter 8:11, 12; Jeremiah 30:4; Micah 2:12. Jonathan: *the house of Israel.* For Ephraim sometimes stands by synecdoche <note>a part representing the whole</note> for the ten tribes, as distinguished from the kingdom of Judah. See Jeremiah 31:9, 18, 20. d) **And I will stir up**, just as weapons are brandished against an enemy, e.g., a spear (2 Samuel 23:18), a bow (Habakkuk 3:9), a whip (Isaiah 10:26). Thus the allegory would be continued from the preceding verses, as in the following member. If this is not pleasing, it can also be translated *and I will stir up*, that is, I will lead them out and animate them to enter the war fearlessly (compare Jeremiah 6:22, Psalm 80:3). Jonathan: *and I will make them prevail, or I will make them strong*, as below in chapter 10:6. e) **Against your sons, O Javan.** This is a new address. He speaks to the sons of Zion and the sons of Greece as if he were addressing both in person. f) **Javan**, which without vowels is **Ionia**. It stands for all of **Greece**, from Thrace down to the Isthmus (compare Ezekiel 27:13, 19; Daniel 8:21; Joel 4:6). To this the Scholiast of Aristophanes in *The Acharnians* says: *The barbarians called all Greeks Iaones.* And there was once a column erected by Theseus on the isthmus itself with this inscription, the part facing Megara saying: *These are Peloponnesus, not Ionia.* See Bochart, *Phaleg* book III, chapter 3. It was named after Javan, son of Japheth, from whom the Peloponnesians also come, along with the Italians and other nations (Genesis 10:2, 4). Thus it is not obscure that "Greeks" here stands by synecdoche for the Gentiles and Europeans, especially those who live around the Mediterranean Sea. Hence Jonathan: *over the sons of the peoples.* And in the New Testament, the Greeks, as opposed to the Jews, are the Gentiles (Romans 1:16, 2:9, 10). This agrees with other prophecies suggesting the first expansion of Christ's kingdom among the descendants of Japheth and the islands of the sea (Genesis 9:28, Isaiah 42:4, 49:1, 51:5, 60:9, Psalm 72:10). g) **And I will make**, that is, I will cause you, Zion (Isaiah 41:15), h) **like a sword.** The effectiveness accompanying this ministry is expressed by the comparison to the power in a hero strongly brandishing a sword (compare Romans 1:15). Cocceius on this passage; compare Isaiah 49:2, Hebrews 4:12. i) Jonathan: *in the hand of a strong man or a vigorous warrior.* (Psalm 127:4). This is the Lord himself (Isaiah 9:5, Psalm 24:8, 45:4). The sons of Zion, however, are merely instruments which he will use for the expansion of his kingdom (compare however below, chapter 10:5, 6, 7 and Judges 7:20). k) **For Jehovah.** This is a confirmation and declaration of verse 13.

<footer>v. 14. k)</footer>

<summary>This page analyzes Zechariah 9:12-14, interpreting the "prisoners of hope" as those waiting for the Messiah's redemption and the "stronghold" as the spiritual City of God. The commentary frames the conflict between Zion and Javan (Greece) as a spiritual expansion of the Gospel through the Apostles, who are depicted as God's arrows and bow.</summary>

# CHAPTER 9. ZECHARIAH 9
<sig>15 140' b'q</sig>

<margin>
...[continuation from previous page] as in Isaiah 29:6, Jeremiah 23:19, and Nahum 1:3. If such things were meant to be understood here, the sense would be that God would powerfully avenge the neglect and disobedience toward His Gospel.
</margin>

-> 14. <gloss>l</gloss> over them <gloss>m</gloss> shall appear <gloss>n</gloss> and go forth like lightning <gloss>o</gloss> His arrow <gloss>p</gloss> and the Lord GOD <gloss>q</gloss> on the trumpet <gloss>r</gloss> shall blow <gloss>s</gloss> and shall go <gloss>t</gloss> in the whirlwinds <gloss>u</gloss> of the south: <-
-> 15. <gloss>t</gloss> The LORD of hosts <gloss>u</gloss> shall defend <gloss>x</gloss> them <gloss>y</gloss> and they shall devour and subdue <gloss>z</gloss> with slingstones <gloss>a</gloss> and they shall drink <gloss>b</gloss> and make a noise as with wine <gloss>c</gloss> and they shall be filled like a bowl <gloss>d</gloss> as the corners of the altar: <-
-> 16. <gloss>e</gloss> And He shall save them <gloss>f</gloss> the LORD their God in that day <gloss>g</gloss> as the flock of His people <gloss>h</gloss> for <gloss>i</gloss> the stones of a crown <gloss>k</gloss> shall be lifted up <gloss>l</gloss> upon His land: <-

---

...punishing the disobedience of the stubbornly wicked. This is what first the Jews, and then the Roman world, experienced, as history and the Holy Apocalypse testify. **v. 15. q)** See Hosea 12:6. **r)** He will protect them (chapter 12:8; Isaiah 31:5), acting as their shield <note>original: "clypeus"</note> (Genesis 15:1; Psalm 3:4; Psalm 18:31, 36), so that they remain unconquered through all persecutions; though they may be hard-pressed, they are not crushed (2 Corinthians 4:8-9). Indeed, they become more courageous through their sufferings to announce the word without fear (Acts 5:41; Philippians 1:14). **s)** So that they themselves may eat and peacefully enjoy their possessions and the spoils of their enemies (compare Deuteronomy 20:14). But Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 1603–1669, a Dutch theologian</note> on this passage says *They eat* (compare Psalm 22:30), meaning they receive the instruction of the Holy Spirit, so that they are solidified in the foundation and acquire strength in the Lord. Truly, just as "drinking" which follows refers to the blood of the conquered—as the latter half of the verse shows—so "eating" refers to their flesh. We therefore explain it as: *they shall eat and consume the peoples* (collectively; see chapter 12:6; Deuteronomy 7:16; and Numbers 14:9). They are depicted here as a spirited and fearless lion, whose food is what he attacks and whose drink is the blood of the slain (Numbers 23:24; Micah 5:7). This can likewise be referred to the spiritual victories of the Apostles over paganism: for they "ate" the nations and emboldened their spirits, and even "drank" of them, while they subjected them to the kingdom of Christ after idolatry was abolished. JONATHAN <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note>: *and they shall rule over the peoples and kill them.* **t)** and shall subject them, that is, prostrate them and subject them to the Lord (Numbers 32:22, 29; 2 Samuel 8:11; 1 Chronicles 22:18), so that they fall under Him (Psalm 45:5), becoming His footstool (Psalm 110:1; compare 2 Chronicles 9:18). **u)** *with slingstones*, cast from a sling (Job 21:19), just as David once prostrated Goliath (1 Samuel 17:49). But Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnov, 1562–1633, a Lutheran theologian</note> says: *after they have subdued or subjugated the slingstones*, that is, their enemies, among whom there were once many ranks of slingers, who were often considered the best soldiers (Judges 20:16). *Cocceius indeed in Lexicon 361 says: and they shall crush the slingstones*, making them fall in vain (compare Ephesians 6:16); they will resist the temptations of Satan. But our explanation, besides being easier, is also strengthened by the authority of the Septuagint <note>Ancient Greek translation</note>, the Arabic, and the Vulgate <note>Latin translation</note>. **x)** and they shall drink the blood of the wounded (Numbers 23:24; Isaiah 49:26; Ezekiel 39:17, 18, 19). For they drink blood who conquer, kill, and plunder enemies. JONATHAN: *and they shall plunder their wealth, and be satisfied by them as those who drink wine.* But Cocceius says they drink, meaning they draw consolation from the fountains of salvation, by which they are made eager, so that they exult and make noise as if from wine. **y)** and as if drunk with blood they shall make a sound, *they shall be in an uproar*, exulting with joy and emboldened by prosperous successes (compare chapter 10:7; Isaiah 22:2; Proverbs 20:1). Vulgate: *they shall be intoxicated* (compare Ephesians 5:18, 19, 20). **z)** as if from wine, which when drunk freely cheers the heart and draws out shouts of joy (chapter 10:7; Psalm 78:65). **a)** and they shall be filled, that is, they shall be wet with blood. The following comparison with the *bowl* <note>original: "pelui"</note>—in which the blood of victims was caught—and with the *corners of the altar*—at which the same blood was sprinkled from the bowl—teaches this. To be wet with blood belongs to the victors (compare Isaiah 63:1-2). But Cocceius comments on this place: Just as the bowls are always full, and as the corners of the altar are always wet with blood, so the power of the Holy Spirit is always fresh in them, lest they grow faint (Isaiah 40:29, 30, 31; John 4:14; 7:38). JONATHAN: *and their soul shall be full of delights, like a bowl which is full of fine flour and oil; and they shall shine like blood which shines on the wall of the altar.* **b)** like a bowl or crater (chapter 14:20; Numbers 7:13). **c)** and like corners (2) Psalm 144:12. Vulgate: *as the horns of the altar*, for so they are called elsewhere (compare Exodus 29:12; Leviticus 4:18, 25, etc.).

**v. 16 d)** And He will save them, not only in a negative sense by keeping them from all equally bad dangers, but also in a positive sense by heaping great goods upon them (compare verse 17; see chapter 8:7, 13; 10:6; 12:7). **e)** concerning which see verse 12. **f)** as sheep or the flock of His people. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the medieval French rabbi</note>: as sheep, which He led out of Egypt, that they might become a people for Him (compare Psalm 77:21). But it is rather a mixture of literal and figurative speech, in this sense: like <term>truth</term> <note>noting the particle used for comparison</note> (as <term>ὡς</term> <note>Greek: hōs</note> in John 1:14) His people, whom He leads, feeds, cares for, and defends like a shepherd his flock. Of this kind is *Sheep of men* (Ezekiel 36:37-38) or *Sheep of a man* (Genesis 16:12; compare Jeremiah 23:1; Ezekiel 34:10, 31; Micah 7:14; Psalm 79:13; Psalm 95:7; Psalm 100:3; and below chapter 10:2-3). **g)** Septuagint, Vulgate, and Arabic: <term>holy stones</term> <note>original: "lapides sancti"</note>. Clearly, just as <term>קדש</term> <note>qodesh</note> is to be separated and holy, so they attributed a similar meaning to <term>נזר</term> <note>nezer</note>: and there is indeed an analogy between the two. Others: <term>stones of a crown or coronation stones</term> (compare 2 Samuel 1:10; 2 Kings 11:12), which they explain in various ways. Tarnovius understands them as <term>trophies</term> <note>original: "tropæa"</note>, encircled above with crown-work and ribbons, so that they are monuments of liberation; Cocceius understands them as faithful people, whose light shines like gems before men (compare Ezekiel 28:14, 16; add Lamentations 4:1). JONATHAN: *He will choose them like the gems of the Ephod or the breastpiece.* This version, however, cannot stand unless it is reduced to the first exposition we gave: that they are considered the stones of the Ephod because they are peculiarly <term>holy</term>, for <term>נזר</term> <note>nezer</note> is never said of the Ephod, though it is used for the gold plate on the head of the High Priest (Exodus 29:6; Numbers 6:7). **h)** Vulgate: *they shall be lifted up*. In the Hebrew grammatical form [Hithpael] (2) Psalm 60:6. Gussetius <note>Jacques Gousset, 1635–1704, French Hebrew scholar</note> (page 519) well develops both the notion of the word and the common sense: "they present themselves to the eyes like some high signal" (compare <term>נזר</term> <note>nezer</note> in Isaiah 11:10) "to invite men." By those stones, he says, I think are understood the faithful, who invite others to participate in salvation with them, both by words and by the allurements of the graces granted to them. It is not merely passive, but a mix: as in Psalm 60:6, *You have given a banner to those who fear you* <term>להתנוסס</term> <note>le-hitnoses - to be displayed/lifted up</note>, which when raised strikes the eyes, and thus calls and regathers them to Himself to enjoy His protection (compare Isaiah 10:18; 59:19; and regarding the matter itself, concerning illustrious examples of faith or leaders, Jeremiah 50:8 with notes). **i)** *upon His land*, that is, the Lord's. For He has spoken of the people in the plural, but of the Lord in the third person singular until now in verses 14, 15, and 16; this is no less to be observed regarding verse 17.

<column-break/>

**1)** *over them (the sons of Zion)* He will be seen, that is, He will manifest Himself, as Jonathan translates. By the manifest successes which He will grant among the nations through the ministry of the sons of Zion, He will openly show that He is present with them (Isaiah 60:2; 66:5; Psalm 90:16). **m)** like lightning, with incredible speed and most penetrating efficacy (Nahum 2:5-6; <term>ὡς ἀστραπὴ</term> <note>Greek: hōs astrapē - "as lightning"</note> Matthew 24:27). **n)** *His arrow*, that is, His words, according to Jonathan. See what we noted at the beginning of verse 13 from Waringa, and compare Psalm 45:6. **o)** *the trumpet shall sound*, He Himself being the one to sound the signal, so that like a thundering commander He may embolden His own for battle (Judges 7:20; Job 39:24-25; compare Joel 2:11). **p)** and He shall march, to the aid of the sons of Zion, in the storms or tempests of the south, that is, by far the greatest. For the southern region is especially famous for horrendous storms (Isaiah 21:1; Job 37:9). Concerning the Ethiopians, Ludolf <note>Hiob Ludolf, 1624–1704, German orientalist</note> in his *History of Ethiopia* (Book 1, chapter 5) says: "When describing the thunders," he says, quoting Gregory, "those hearing them almost shudder; for having arisen together with rain storms, the sky is covered with black globes of clouds; soon continuous lightnings are everywhere, and very frequent and terrible thunderbolts strike even the minds of those who are firm and accustomed to such things," etc. Regarding the Arabs, Muhammad says throughout the Quran, e.g., Surah II, 18-19, where he describes thunders so horrendous that men put their fingers in their ears because of their crash, fearing death. He says the force of the lightning is so great that it is not far from taking away their lights and vision, etc. Therefore, the southern storms can be a symbol of divine majesty and omnipotence, by which the entire nations will be shaken, so that they hear the voice of the Gospel in no other way than if they were hearing thunders (compare Exodus 19:16; Haggai 2:6; Psalm 29:3 and following). Otherwise, storms are punitive judgments.

<margin>
**v. 17. k)** For, to explain that salvation of which I spoke in verse 16 for a stronger reason, and to teach that it should be valued worthily and according to its merits. **l)** "How," that is, "how great" it will be. The pronoun here is for emphasis <note>original: "exaggerationem"</note>, not simply a question, comparing Psalm 3:2 and Psalm 133:1. It is as if to say: His goodness will be so great that it cannot be explained in words; it will be inexpressible. Truly, the question suggests a holy wonder at the greatness of His goodness, as in Psalm 31:20 and Psalm 36:8. **m)** "His goodness" or "His good," namely, the Lord's, comparing verse 16. It signifies both the goodness itself and the good that flows from it as if from a fountain. See Jeremiah 31:14, Hosea 3:5, Psalm 31:20, Job 21:16, and Nehemiah 9:25. **n)** Indeed, what and how great will His beauty be? Just as the "good" of the Lord is understood as active, so also His "beauty" in this place is not that in which He Himself rejoices, but that with which He affects His people, so that the meaning is: how much good and how much beauty the Lord will provide for His people! Therefore, the suffix functions in the same way as in Ezekiel 16:13, chapter 23:41 ("my oil and my incense"), and Hosea 2:7 ("my bread, my drink," etc.). However, Cocceius and others refer the suffix to the people. **o)** Namely, grain (understand "He will make to grow" from the following part of the verse) for the young men; it will come forth in great abundance and liberally from the blessing of God, so that there is no lack of nourishment for children being raised to a flourishing age, so that they may become young men and virgins. See Psalm 62:8, Jeremiah 31:12-13, Ezekiel 36:29, Hosea 2:24, and Joel 2:18. This is the opposite of how it once was in the time of divine vengeance in Lamentations 2:11-12, Hosea 9:11, and Haggai 2:11. Furthermore, although it can be granted that this promise is also physical (comparing 1 Timothy 4:8), the mind should nevertheless be drawn to a much more sublime and excellent grain, namely, the heavenly and spiritual grain, the divine Word.
</margin>

<margin>
**CHAPTER X.**
as much substantial wine as that of the Gospel, Deuteronomy 8:3, Psalm 78:24, John 6:32 and following. This can be illustrated by the character of this whole prophecy, as well as by its opposite in Amos 8:11-12. **p)** "young men" (Psalm 148:12) prevailing in strength to overcome Satan (1 John 2:13-14, comparing Proverbs 20:29). **q)** and "the mournful" <note>This likely refers to those needing comfort, though the Latin text is slightly unclear here</note>, especially in a mystical and spiritual sense, or (as Cocceius says in his Lexicon, 343) the Word that nourishes, strengthens, and gladdens—doctrine and consolation (compare Psalm 4:8). **r)** Cocceius: "He makes to grow, He makes to flourish." **(q)** Psalm 62:11, Psalm 42:15. Properly used of plants and the fruits of the earth, comparing Deuteronomy 31:13. See therefore Isaiah 27:6, chapter 60:21. But Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] says: "He will make them fruitful," namely, with the product of labor and joy. Thus, compare Isaiah 57:19 and Proverbs 10:31. However, it is an obstacle that there is no additional word here denoting speech. **s)** "virgins," that is, the chaste, beautiful, and uncorrupted. For just as the young men are mentioned for their strength, so the virgins are mentioned for their "incorruptibility" <note>original Greek: "το αφθαρτον"</note> (1 Peter 3:4; compare Revelation 14:4).

as much substantial wine as that of the Gospel, Deuteronomy 8:3, Psalm 78:24, John 6:32 and following. This can be illustrated by the character of this whole prophecy, as well as by its opposite in Amos 8:11-12. **p)** "young men" (Psalm 148:12) prevailing in strength to overcome Satan (1 John 2:13-14, comparing Proverbs 20:29). **q)** and "the mournful," especially in a mystical and spiritual sense, or (as Cocceius says in his Lexicon, 343) the Word that nourishes, strengthens, and gladdens—doctrine and consolation (compare Psalm 4:8). **r)** Cocceius: "He makes to grow, He makes to flourish." **(q)** Psalm 62:11, Psalm 42:15. Properly used of plants and the fruits of the earth, comparing Deuteronomy 31:13. See therefore Isaiah 27:6, chapter 60:21. But Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] says: "He will make them fruitful," namely, with the product of labor and joy. Thus, compare Isaiah 57:19 and Proverbs 10:31. However, it is an obstacle that there is no additional word here denoting speech. **s)** "virgins," that is, the chaste, beautiful, and uncorrupted. For just as the young men are mentioned for their strength, so the virgins are mentioned for their "incorruptibility" <note>original Greek: "το αφθαρτον"</note> (1 Peter 3:4; compare Revelation 14:4).

**CHAPTER X, v. 1. t)** "Ask therefore." This connects especially with chapter 9:17. It is as if to say: Since you truly have such a good Lord, who will save you and heap all good things upon you, you can therefore, O children of Zion, ask from Him freely and with boldness <note>original: "parrhœsia"</note> whatever you want for your needs. This is an imperative not of burden, but of benefit, privilege, and legal right, with the hope of a certain hearing attached, as in Matthew 7:7 and John 16:24; compare 1 Kings 3:5, 2 Kings 2:9, Luke 11:9-10, John 15:7, 16, 1 John 3:22, and 5:14-15. It functions as a direct address <note>original: "apostrophes"</note> to the future believers of the New Testament, whom he calls to from afar to use their rights and privileges. This is evident because he soon slips back into the mode of prophesying about them in the third person: "He will give them showers of rain." Therefore, this chapter is a continuation, repetition, and confirmation of the previous prophecy in chapter 9 concerning Zion being made fruitful, visited, comforted, and gathered back from dispersion under the New Testament. **u)** namely, from the Messiah, who will save His people (chapter 9:16). **x)** "rain." This is parabolic and points to whatever is necessary for the life of faith and the growth of the Church (1 Corinthians 3:5, 7)—the pouring out of the Holy Spirit with His gifts, and the abundant and fruitful preaching of the divine Word. Compare Deuteronomy 32:2, 2 Samuel 23:4, Isaiah 5:6, chapter 35:10-11, Ezekiel 34:26, and Psalms 68:10 and 85:13. **y)** "in the time of the latter rain," when the latter rain is needed. This rain (according to the testimony of Jonah and Jerome on Deuteronomy 32:2) descends and waters the sprouts of the earth in the month of Nisan (around March), when the crop is in the ear and begins to ripen. See the note on Deuteronomy 11:14. The faithful are therefore commanded to hope for and ask from the divine goodness of the Messiah for whatever is salutary, specifically the "latter rain," so that the doctrine of the Gospel may grow and spread, and be instilled into souls so they produce joyful and abundant fruits, as the celebrated Maius observes in his *Economy of the Old Testament*, page 1032. However, the "first rain" (called <gloss>יורה - yoreh</gloss> in Jeremiah 5:24), that is, the first pouring out of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, is assumed to have already happened; and so the children of Zion are warned to ask for and expect that same gift of the Holy Spirit even afterward, and even in the last times of the New Testament, as He will give them the latter rain just like the first (Joel 2:23; compare Acts 2:39). **z)** For the Lord, having heard your prayers immediately, is going to do, etc. An argument from the certain hope of obtaining what was prayed for (Psalm 145:19). But Tarnovius, repeating the prefix *Mem*, connects it as an apposition with what came before: "from the Lord who brings the clouds." In this way, the added title simultaneously involves the reason why they ought to ask from the Lord and not from another. Cocceius also explains it in this sense: "because the Lord makes," etc., as if to say: no one can make lightnings, that is, gather clouds from which lightnings and rains break forth, except God. Thus, compare Jeremiah 5:24 and chapter 14:22. **a)** "lightnings" (<gloss>k</gloss>) Job 28:26, chapter 38:25, where <gloss>חזיז - chaziz</gloss> means the thunder of lightnings, that is, because it is the thunder itself, but is seen before. It is either from <gloss>חזה - chazah</gloss>, "to see" (just as <gloss>דגיג - dagig</gloss> is from <gloss>דג - dag</gloss>, so <gloss>חזיז - chaziz</gloss> is from <gloss>חזה - chazah</gloss>; compare <gloss>צליל - tzalil</gloss> from <gloss>צלל - tzalal</gloss>, <gloss>גליל - galil</gloss> from <gloss>גלל - galal</gloss>, and <gloss>פנינים - peninim</gloss> from <gloss>פנה - panah</gloss> in Lamentations 4:7); or from the Arabic <gloss>חז - hazz</gloss>, "he pierced or transfixed with a weapon," to which the Hebrew <gloss>חץ - chetz</gloss> (arrow) is related, whence Psalm 77:18 has <gloss>חצציך - chatzatzecha</gloss>, "arrows," for lightnings. This word has twisted the interpreters in a strange way. The Septuagint and Arabic say "fantasies" or "visions" <note>original Greek: "φαντασιας"</note>. The Vulgate says "snows," which Palestine hardly has in the time of the latter rain. Jonah says "winds." The Syriac says "showers." Finally, Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] says "clouds." We follow the etymology and the poetic parallelism. Lightnings are placed as the preceding things, and the focus is mostly on the rains joined with the lightnings, or following after the lightnings (compare Jeremiah 10:13 and Psalm 135:7). **b)** indeed, "rain of the shower," that is, copious and large (Job 37:6). This is an intensive construction of synonyms, such as "vanities of emptiness" for the highest vanities in Psalm 16:5, or "mud of the mire" for that which is thick and deep in Psalm 40:3, etc. Although <gloss>מטר - matar</gloss> and <gloss>גשם - geshem</gloss> are not entirely synonymous, since the latter denotes a shower and the former rain in general. Compare below chapter 14:17, Ezekiel 34:26, and Psalm 68:10. **c)** for the children of Zion (chapter 9:13 and following), whom he addressed by direct call in verse 1. **d)** and perhaps not only to these or those, or to many, but distributively "to a man," that is, to each one, to all and to individuals, whoever has only asked, He will give, etc. Therefore, this rain will not be partial, such as it was in the time of Amos, when God rained upon one city and not upon another, and one field was rained upon and another was not (Amos 4:7). No one will be excluded from this benefit, except he who excludes himself. Compare above chapter 8:11, 12. **e)** "grass in the field," a phrasing used instead of "grass of the field"; it is like "the beast in the forest" for "the forest beast" in Isaiah 56:9; compare Deuteronomy 11:15, chapter 29:21, and Psalm 72:16. **v. 2. f)** The connection here should be noted through the word "Because" <note>original: "Quia"</note>, whether causal or declarative. For he now illustrates by contrast what he had said about the faithful in verse 1. It is as if to say: the righteous, if they are the chosen and genuine children of Zion, may freely and trustfully ask from God whatever is necessary for them; I added that they would not ask in vain, for God would give to them abundantly. Because in this matter, the condition of those who are idolaters, whether from the Gentiles or the Israelites, will be far different. Compare Isaiah 65:13 and Malachi 3:18. **g)** "images" or "likenesses of gods" <note>referring to the Teraphim</note>, once worshiped by their cults among both Gentiles and Israelites, and giving oracles through their priests. Jonah says "cultivators of images." The Septuagint and Arabic say "those speaking oracles" <note>original Greek: "αποφθεγγομενοι"</note>. **h)** "spoke emptiness." The Vulgate says "useless." See the note on Amos 5:5. The sense: They speak such things with which they mock and deceive their worshipers, especially vain promises whose outcome is expected in vain. Compare Ephesians 4:19 with the note. **i)** "and the diviners" (Deuteronomy 18:10, Ezekiel 13:9; compare Ephesians 8:19, 20). **k)** Ezekiel 13:6 and following. **l)** "and dreams" — as the Vulgate rightly has it, "dreamers"; Jonah says "false prophets." For it is joined with a masculine verb, which is a construction according to the sense in Jeremiah 29:8. But the Septuagint, Arabic, and Syriac put it in the accusative case: "they spoke false dreams," contrary to the accents. **m)** "vanity" (that which is useless and in vain) they speak; and thus they shamefully deceive those trusting in them (Ezekiel 21:23, Job 15:31). **n)** "they comfort with vanity," that is, in their consolations there is nothing true or solid (Job 21:34; compare Ecclesiastes 5:6). Vanity and lies are to be taken in opposition to the reality and actual showing of good things which God provides; the idols with their diviners, though they promise, cannot provide. **o)** "therefore," because they fled to idols and diviners rather than to God Himself. Incidentally, he reveals here the source and causes of the evils which the Israelites once endured. **p)** "they set out," they went wandering miserably. Jonah says "they were dispersed." The Vulgate: "and they were led away." This verb is used generally for the leading or walking of sheep, even that which is for the sake of pastures (compare Jeremiah 31:21, Psalm 78:52); but here it implies walking without a shepherd, than which nothing is more miserable. Compare Jeremiah 50:6, 7. **q)** Jonah: "just as sheep are dispersed." Compare Numbers 27:17, Isaiah 53:6, Matthew 9:36, and the note on 1 Kings 22:17. **r)** "they were afflicted" (Isaiah 31:4 <note>Note: This may be a typo for Isaiah 3:1</note>, Psalm 116:10). **s)** "so good," comparing verse 3 and Matthew 9:36. He silently hints that the errors and so many evils of the people would not have been so great if they had happened to have better shepherds than those they had. And this is the reason that in verse 3 he promises he will punish the wicked shepherds, and in verse 4 he will give better ones.

---

\* v. 17. <gloss>בחוּרִים</gloss> (young men) fully written 1. 3. so 2. recent Masoretic printed editions of Psalm 148:12, but against the same in this place.
\* v. 2. <gloss>כִּי</gloss> (for) with a Maqqeph [hyphen] 6. 9. : 20. so edition 5.

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Zechariah chapter 10. Having previously discussed the vanity of idols and false shepherds in verses 1-2, the text now moves to God’s judgment against those leaders and His promise to transform His people into a victorious force.</meta>

<header>ZECHARIAH CAP. 10.</header>

<margin>
<note>original: "fui. h. e. facies eol fories..."</note>
He will be; that is, He will make them strong like a war-horse that rushes into battle without fear. See Jeremiah 8:6 and Job 39:19 and following. He will lead them as if by bridles to carry out His will; and just as proud kings boast of their horses, so will He hold them in the highest regard. He will adorn them with gifts, just as men are accustomed to decorate a horse with excellent trappings. Thus, this will be a preview of what is described in verse 6 and following. Compare Isaiah 63:13 and Song of Solomon 1:9. **d)** See verse 6 and 13. **e)** In war, specifically a "sacred" war, concerning which see verse 5 and following, as well as chapter 9:13.
</margin>

<margin>
**Verse 3. †)** Lest the people perish through the fault of the shepherds, or the evil shepherds escape punishment for their mistreatment of the flock, the Lord says: "Against the shepherds," who either ought to have fed the flock of my people or presumed to do so—whether they be princes, priests, or teachers. See chapter 11:5, 16, 17. Targum Jonathan translates this as "against the Kings." See the note on Jeremiah 23:1. **\*)** "My anger was kindled," because they neglected and ruined my flock. See Hosea 8:5. **x)** 
</margin>

3 Against the shepherds my anger was kindled, and against the goats <note>original: "attudim," referring to the leaders of the flock</note> I will bring punishment;<sup>† *</sup> for the LORD of Hosts has visited His flock, the house of Judah, and has made them<sup>a b c</sup> 4 like His majestic horse in battle.<sup>d e</sup> From him comes the cornerstone,<sup>g</sup> from him the tent peg,<sup>h</sup> from him the battle bow,<sup>i k</sup> from him shall come every ruler together.<sup>l</sup> 5 And they shall be like mighty men<sup>m</sup> treading down<sup>n</sup> the mud of the streets<sup>o</sup> in battle; and they shall fight<sup>p</sup> because the LORD is with them,<sup>q</sup> and they shall put to shame<sup>r</sup> those who ride on horses.<sup>s</sup> 6 And I will strengthen<sup>t</sup> the house of Judah, and the house of Joseph<sup>u x</sup> I will save;<sup>y</sup> and I will restore them<sup>z</sup> because I have had mercy on them;<sup>a</sup> and they shall be as though I had never rejected them,<sup>b</sup> for<sup>c</sup>

---

**Verse 4. f)** "From him," that is, from the Lord, it shall be or shall go forth. Thus the sense would be: The Lord Himself will give His people good and vigorous leaders. Compare Hosea 14:9. Or rather: "From him," meaning from Judah or my people. This is how *Ibn Ezra* explains it: No foreigner shall ever rule over them again. *Rashi* (Rabbi Solomon) says: From them shall be their kings, from them their princes, and finally from them those who carry out their wars. *Kimchi* adds: So that they will have no need for the help of another people, but their own hands shall suffice for them, as in Deuteronomy 33:7. See also Jeremiah 30:21, Micah 5:1, and Habakkuk 1:7, where this phrase expresses <term>autonomy</term> and independence. However, the sense here could also be: There will be those from among them whom I will use as leaders of my people and as weapons of war, as seen in chapter 9:13, 16. In this way, there would again be a reference to the Apostles and teachers of the Gospel, the majority of whom were Jews, and who reported distinguished victories over the pagan world.

**g)** "Cornerstone" or "corner stone." See Isaiah 28:16, Jeremiah 51:26, and Psalm 118:22. This term is used for a head or prince of the people in Judges 20:2 and Isaiah 19:13, because just as that stone supports a building, so the leader supports the people and the State. Thus, Jonathan translates this as "his King." According to the Paraphrast, this should be understood as referring to the Messiah, so that the following clause is an explanation, which he rendered as: "and from him His Messiah." See Ephesians 2:20.

**h)** "The nail" or "tent peg," meaning a minister of primary dignity in the State, such as Eliakim was in the kingdom of Judah (Isaiah 22:23). The reason for the name is clear, as added in verse 24: just as we hang household items from a peg, so the affairs of the State hang from such high ministers. See Ezekiel 15:3. Compare the Quran, Surah 38:11 and 89:9, where Muhammad uses the same word to call Pharaoh "the one endowed with pegs," meaning one possessing a multitude of nobles and magnates in his empire.

**i)** "The battle bow," which the Lord Himself will draw (chapter 9:13). **k)** Some explain it thus: "on the contrary, from him shall go away," meaning that in the future every oppressor or tyrant will be absent. See Isaiah 49:17 and 1 John 2:19. But we rightly take the phrase in the same way as the preceding half-verse: namely, that it denotes the origin from which the Lord will raise up these heroes.

**l)** "Every ruler together," that is, of whatever condition or kind he may be. This is a promised blessing. The word <note>Hebrew: "nogesh"</note>, which elsewhere signifies an extortioner or tyrant (chapter 9:8, Isaiah 9:3, chapter 14:2), here signifies a ruler and prince of the people in a positive sense, as in Isaiah 3:12 and 60:17. Similarly, in Ethiopic, the root *w-n-g-sh* means to rule or reign, from which *Nigus* means a King or the supreme ruler of a people. The Syriac version has "their princes," and Jonathan has "his governors."

**Verse 5. m)** "And the house of Judah shall be like strong men." See verse 7. The prefix *Caph* acts as a "particle of truth" (as in chapter 9:16), meaning they will conduct themselves as strong men, or as becomes strong men. Or it is a "particle of similarity," and thus it is silently hinted that they will not fight according to the flesh, but spiritually; their weapons of warfare will not be carnal, but powerful in God. See 2 Corinthians 10:3–6. In this sense, God said in chapter 9:10 that He would cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow would be abolished. And in this very verse: "Those who ride on horses shall be put to shame." Compare chapter 12:5, 6 and Isaiah 33:24.

**n)** "Treading down," namely their enemies. See Psalm 44:6. This is an anomalous form of the Kal participle <note>Hebrew: "bosim"</note>. Jonathan translates it as: "treading down the slain of the nations." **o)** "In the mud of the streets." See chapter 9:3. Compare Isaiah 5:25, 21:15, and Romans 16:20. **p)** They shall fight, and indeed with happy and prosperous success. See verse 3. **q)** For the Word of the Lord shall be for their help. Genesis 26:3, Joshua 1:5. **r)** On the contrary, they shall be confounded. All the ancient versions take this as intransitive. But *Cocceius* takes it actively: "and they shall put to shame the riders of horses," those protected by human power. See the note on chapter 9:5. **s)** To the Hebrews, these are the enemies who will come against Israel with cavalry. See chapter 12:4, Ezekiel 38:5, and Exodus 15:1. However, it could also be understood as the shaming of Israel's own trust in carnal weapons. See chapter 9:10.

**Verse 6. t)** "And I will strengthen," I will make them prevail. Piel form. See verse 12, Ecclesiastes 10:10. Compare Exodus 17:11, 2 Samuel 1:23. **u)** Up to this point, he has dealt with the house of Judah specifically (verses 3, 4, etc.), which can be referred to that first conversion at the beginning of the New Testament when a large part of the Jewish people obeyed the Gospel. Now, however, he speaks of the house of Judah and the house of Joseph together. Unless one wishes to refer this also to the beginning of the New Testament, when some from all the tribes were saved, it may look to a future time when the fullness of Israel will be converted (Romans 11:12, 26). See notes on Hosea 3:5 and Micah 2:12. **x)** Which in verse 7 and chapter 9:10, 13 is called Ephraim, signifying the ten tribes of the Israelite kingdom (Amos 5:6). **y)** Chapter 9:16, Zephaniah 3:17, 19. **z)** According to *Kimchi* and *Ibn Ezra*, this word is a mixture of "to return" and "to dwell." That is: I will bring them back and cause them to dwell. This implies a secure and tranquil dwelling (chapter 7:7, Jeremiah 32:37, Hosea 11:11, Psalm 107:36). **a)** The source of blessings is God's mercy. Deuteronomy 32:36, Isaiah 54:8, 10, Jeremiah 30:18, etc. **b)** "And they shall be as if I had never rejected them," that is, the abundance of present good will blot out the memory of past evil. Isaiah 43:18, 19, chapter 65:17, Job 11:16. For they shall be multiplied just as they were of old (see verse 8), and no traces of anger and rejection will remain. As for their former sins, I will wrap them in perpetual silence and oblivion, holding them as dear as if they had never sinned against me, or as if I had never decreed anything harsh against them. Isaiah 43:25, Jeremiah 31:34. **c)** Psalm 60:3, 12.

<column-break/>

<margin>
† "Against the he-goats," that is, the leaders of the sheep or goats. This is a general term for the goat and sheep kind. Compare Genesis 31:10, 12, where the Septuagint expressed it with two words: "the goats and the rams." *Cocceius Lexicon 654*. The leading men are noted here according to Jonathan, whom Scripture calls "rams" using a similar metaphor in Ezekiel 34:16 and Psalm 29:1, because just as he-goats and rams precede the flock, so these men precede the people. See Isaiah 14:9 and Jeremiah 50:8. But ecclesiastical leaders also seem to be included. **y)** "I will visit," that is, I will take notice of or punish. Isaiah 10:12. **z)** Because now at last He has visited graciously, by liberating them from evil aspects and gathering them from dispersion. Genesis 21:1, Zephaniah 2:7, Psalm 106:4. Thus the visitation of <term>total destruction</term> upon the shepherds and goats results from the decreed gracious visitation of the flock, according to which God no longer wishes to permit the flock to be under evil shepherds. He uses the past tense as if speaking at the very time of the visitation. See chapter 9:8. "Visited" <note>Hebrew: "Paqad"</note> is used significantly and most truly of the visitation in which God was manifested in the flesh, face to face, mouth to mouth, eye to eye. *Cocceius Lexicon 681*. **a)** "His flock." Isaiah 40:11, Jeremiah 31:10. In verse 6, "His flock, the house." See Acts 20:28, 29. **b)** Namely, the house of Judah. Hosea 1, 7. **c)** Like a horse of His glory.
</margin>

The commentary blends medieval Jewish scholarship with Christian Messianic interpretations, identifying figures like the "cornerstone" and "tent peg" as types of Christ or strong national leaders.</summary>

**d)** I am the LORD their God, just as they are my people, and this is according to the covenant of grace, chapter 2:8.

**7.** See above, chapter 9:15.
**h)** and their children, whom they then had safe with them, verse 9. **l)** they shall see this and rejoice. Psalm 107:42. **m)** indeed, they were not content with simple joy, but their heart shall exult. See the note on chapter 9:9 and compare Ephesians 5:18, 19; chapter 63:14; Psalm 13:6.

Isaiah 35:10, chapter 51:11. **r)** just as they were multiplied, namely, of old, or (as the Vulgate adds) "before," collecting Micah 7:14, Ezekiel 36:11. Compare for example Exodus 1:7, 1 Kings 4:20. Jonathan: "just as it was said they would be multiplied." He took the word literally from the promise: as if to say, according to that word of God, "They shall be multiplied"; according to the promise made to Abraham in Genesis 13:16, 17:2. But this explanation reeks of artifice.
