...not so that it perishes, but so that it bears fruit. Terretinus, who by reason of the outcome compares Acts 2:5, chapter 2:1, 4 (add chapter 18:19), James 1:1, 1 Peter 1:1, where after the ascension of Christ into heaven, believing Israelites are read to have been dispersed here and there for the great salvation of others.
</margin>

---

But *Maius* on page 1082 says: If anyone wishes to press the letter, the Prophet in verse 9 is speaking of the dispersion of the Jews among the nations after the return from the Babylonian captivity, and a new gathering from all peoples in verse 10, so that strengthened in the LORD they may walk in His name. And entirely, <term>זרע</term> <note>zara</note> seems here to denote the dispersion of exile, because at the end of the verse it says "they shall return," and in verse 10 they are to be brought back out of Egypt and Assyria into their own land. Indeed, it is the same here as the related word <term>ירה</term> <note>yara</note> in Jeremiah 15:7, Ezekiel 6:8, and 36:19; and just as the Greek <term>διαסποרὰ</term> <note>diaspora</note> is used in James 1:1 and 1 Peter 1:1. It is taken in a positive sense in Jeremiah 31:27 and Hosea 2:25, signifying fertility. **t)** nevertheless in the distant or most remote shores of the earth, to which I have dispersed them. Isaiah 8:9. **u)** they shall remember me; in their very dispersion they shall finally turn themselves, Ezekiel 6:9, Psalm 22:28 and 78:35, according to the prediction of Moses in Deuteronomy 4:27, 29-31, chapter 30:1 and following; compare Romans 11:26. **x)** and they shall live; in the course of so many years they shall by no means die out in exile, Deuteronomy 33:6, Habakkuk 3:2, Psalm 118:17. On the contrary, they shall receive life and Spirit from me when they turn themselves, Ezekiel 37:14. Jonathan: they shall prolong the years of life; compare Psalm 72:15. **y)** with their children, verse 7. **z)** and they shall return from their dispersion. Isaiah 35:10.

**v. 10. a)** For I will lead them back. A confirmation and declaration of the preceding verse 9. Compare Jeremiah 30:3. **b)** Egypt and Assyria, the former in the south, the latter in the north; these can be taken by synecdoche <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note> for any regions where God has dispersed His people. Isaiah 11:11, chapter 27:12, 13; Hosea 11:11. Compare the note on Micah 5:4. These are named especially because the Ten Tribes were formerly deported to Assyria (2 Kings 17:6) and before the Assyrian took them away, many of them had withdrawn to Egypt (Hosea 8:13, chapter 9:3, 6); indeed, because Egypt had long ago been a place of hard labor <note>original: "pistrinum" (mill/bakery)</note> for Israel (Exodus 1:11 and following), as seen here in verse 11. Gurtlerus, in his *Prophetic Theology* (pp. 135 and 707 and following), understands a mystical Egypt and Assyria, explaining this part of the prophecy as the conversion of many from among the false Christians, and with the Turks, many from the enemies of the Church. Compare Revelation 11:8. But we hold to the scope by which, throughout this whole chapter, special promises for the Israelite tribes are set forth. Compare verses 3, 6, 7, 9. **c)** see verse 8. **d)** to the land of Gilead and Lebanon. Thus are described parts not so much of the whole of Canaan, as it was once possessed by all the tribes, but specifically of Ephraim (compare verse 7), that is, the Israelite kingdom in particular. This was conveniently cut into two parts: the Trans-Jordanian part, which is called Gilead (compare note on Amos 1:3, 13), and the Cis-Jordanian part, which, because it was walled in by the mountains of Lebanon, is here called the land of Lebanon, as in Deuteronomy 3:25. Compare Obadiah verse 19, Micah 7:14. **e)** Zephaniah 3:20. **f)** Vulgate: "and no place shall be found for them," namely, one that can hold such a great multitude. He expressed the idiom, whereas Josephus and the Syriac expressed the sense: "it will not suffice for them," namely, that region which they inhabited of old. Joshua 17:16, Numbers 11:22. Whence expanded borders are promised in Isaiah 26:15, chapter 33:17, Obadiah verse 19, 20. Compare Isaiah 49:20, chapter 54:2, 3 and Galatians 4:27.

**v. 11. g)** Moreover, he shall pass, being led to the land of rest, verse 10. Compare Joshua 4:22, 23. **h)** The Septuagint and Arabic: "through a narrow sea"; this goes against the accents and results in an obscure and difficult sense. The Vulgate: "in the strait of the sea"; likewise inconveniently. According to the grammar of this place, <term>צָרָה</term> <note>tsarah</note> does not take the construct state, so that it could be translated as "sea of distress"; because the first noun has the prefix *He* hidden in the vowels. Nor is it a syntax of a substantive with an adjective, as the Septuagint and Arabic interpreted it; because <term>צַר</term> <note>tsar</note> is masculine, while <term>צָרָה</term> <note>tsarah</note> is feminine. Therefore, the latter is a declarative apposition: "through the sea, namely, distress." Thus, proper and allegorical meanings are mixed here. By "distress" are signified the calamities and hardships that will partly precede and partly accompany the conversion of Israel, through which the Lord will nevertheless prepare for His people a passage and a finally joyful exit. Isaiah 26:16 and following, Jeremiah 30:6, 7, Revelation 12:2 and following. Through the figurative "sea," the history of the Red Sea is alluded to, which, yielding at the command of the LORD, once gave free passage to the Israelites (Exodus 14:16); and thus a sweet harmony of the economy and works of God through all time is suggested. Compare a similar comparison in Isaiah 11:15, chapter 44:27, chapter 51:9, 10, Jeremiah 31:2, Hosea 2:16, 17. Jonathan: "and miracles and powers will be done for them, just as they were done for their fathers in the sea." **i)** for God will strike the waves in the sea, intending to restrain and settle them by divine power. Isaiah 11:15, Psalm 89:10, 11, Psalm 106:9, Psalm 114:3, 5, Matthew 8:26, 27. For the sake of illustration, compare the madness of Xerxes, King of the Persians, who, when a storm had dissolved the bridge joining the Hellespont, lowered chains into the sea and lashed the water, by an insane daring arrogating to himself what belonged to God. See Suidas under the word *Xerxes*. Jonathan: "and they saw the vengeance of their enemies, just as the powerful ones were once swept away by the waves of the sea." **k)** Isaiah 51:15. **l)** they shall be put to shame, being about to undergo a drying up which seemed impossible, verse 5. A personification, as in Jeremiah 48:1, Joel 1:10, 17. Others: "and they shall dry up," but it stands in the way that <term>יָבֵשׁ</term> <note>yabesh</note>, though it has the force of drying up, is never found elsewhere in the Hiphil <note>a Hebrew verb form indicating cause</note> as an intransitive. Compare Joshua 2:10, chapter 4:23, chapter 5:1, Psalm 74:15. **m)** depths. Exodus 15:5. Compare Isaiah 44:27. Jonathan: "all the Kings of the peoples." **n)** of the Nile. Genesis 41:1, Exodus 1:22. Just as once of the Jordan, Joshua 4:23, for making an exit for His people from the place of labor and the tribulations of Egypt. Compare Revelation 16:12.

# CHAPTER XI
# Open, O Lebanon 11 <note>original: "פתח לבנון יא"</note>

<margin>We do not refuse the opinion of *Abendana*, who in his *Spicilegium* <note>a "gleaning" or collection of notes</note> on M. I. regarding this passage says: This prophecy,</margin>
1 <gloss>it</gloss> **Open** <gloss>t</gloss> **O Lebanon** <gloss>b</gloss> **your doors** <gloss>at</gloss> **that the fire** <gloss>a</gloss> **may devour** **your cedars.** <note>original: "פְּתַח לְבָנוֹן דְּלָתֶךָ וְתֹאכַל אֵשׁ בַּאֲרָזֶיךָ"</note>
2 <gloss>c</gloss> **Howl** <gloss>d</gloss> **O cypress** <gloss>e</gloss> **for** <gloss>ayt</gloss> **the cedar** <gloss>f</gloss> **has fallen**
<gloss>g</gloss> **because** <gloss>h</gloss> **the glorious ones** <gloss>y</gloss> **are spoiled** <gloss>y</gloss> **howl** <gloss>k</gloss> **O oaks** **of Bashan** **for** **the forest** **of the fortified** <gloss>at</gloss> **has come down.** <note>original: "הֵילֵל בְּרוֹשׁ כִּי נָפַל אֶרֶז אֲשֶׁר אַדִּרִים שֻׁדָּדוּ הֵילִילוּ אַלּוֹנֵי בָשָׁן כִּי יָרַד יַעַר הַבָּצוּר"</note>

is difficult to understand, and its words are very obscure. Meanwhile, the Jews, wishing to interpret this, often wander blindly and twist this prophecy in strange ways. They would have a much plainer path in explaining it if they would recognize with us, from this chapter, Christ, who was sold for thirty pieces of silver. See *Preface* § 12. The first part of the prophecy is explained as a threat against the nations by *Jonathan* <note>the Targum/Aramaic translation</note>, whom *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Rashi</note> and *David Kimchi* approve. He puts it thus: *Open your gates, O peoples, and let the fire consume your fortifications* etc. But more correctly, regarding its goal, is *Jerome*: The Temple of the Jews is understood, which, having been restored or rather rebuilt by *Zerubbabel*, is prophesied to be overturned again by *Vespasian* and *Titus*. And they say the ancient Hebrews explained it this way, as *Rabbi Solomon* and *Abendana* mention, citing a notable passage (which exists in the Talmud, *Yoma* folio 39b): *Forty years before the destruction,* they say, *the doors of the temple opened of their own accord. Therefore Rabbi Jochanan son of Zakkai rebuked them and said: O Temple, Temple! why do you terrify yourself? I know that your end will be to be desolated.* For so Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied of you: *Open your doors, O Lebanon.* Thus the Temple would be called *Lebanon* because it was anciently constructed of the cedars of *Lebanon*, and newly restored by *Zerubbabel* (1 Kings 5:20; chapter 6:18, 36; Ezra 3:7; Haggai 1:8). In the same way, the armory of Solomon, which he had built in Jerusalem from cedar beams, was called the House of the Forest of *Lebanon* (1 Kings 7:2; 10:17). However, we prefer to interpret *Lebanon* as the whole of *Jerusalem*, so that the Temple, as the principal part, is included; for in this way what follows seems to fit better. It is called Lebanon both because of the quality of the buildings, many of which were of cedar (Jeremiah 22:23), and their abundance, for it abounded in houses as Lebanon does in trees (compare verse 2 here); and also because of the nobles and great men, whom Scripture is accustomed to compare to the cedars of *Lebanon*, dwelling in it (Ezekiel 17:3; compare Isaiah 2:13; 14:8; 10:34; Habakkuk 2:17). 2) *your doors.* A mixture of literal and figurative language: for doors belong to cities and especially to fortifications (Deuteronomy 3:5; 1 Samuel 23:7). Lebanon opens its doors (as Jerome says) so that the Roman army may enter and fire may devour its cedars; so that either everything is wasted by fire, or the leaders and princes are consumed by the hostile attack (compare Isaiah 45:1, 2). a) *that the fire may devour*, both literally, in relation to the buildings which the enemies will burn; and the fire of war, in relation to the princes of Jerusalem, whom they will consume with the sword (Jeremiah 17:27; 31:14; Hosea 8:14; Malachi 3:19). b) *your cedars*, or *among your cedars*; namely, just as fire blazes in wood and by blazing consumes it. Jerome says: Because he had called the Temple (we prefer Jerusalem) Lebanon <term>metaphorically</term> <note>original: "μεταפורικῶς"</note>, he maintains the translation in the rest, so that by cedars, firs, oaks of Bashan, and the thick forest, he signifies the princes, priests, and people of the Jews. We also understand here the actual cedar palaces themselves; but those things which follow in verse 2, we interpret as spoken to the provincial inhabitants, just as these in verse 1 are spoken especially to the metropolis.

V. 2. c) *Howl therefore*, not only for the sake of Lebanon and the cedars because they have fallen, but especially for your own sake: because if the cedars are not spared, then the firs and oaks, which are of less value than they, will be spared much less. The sense: O towns, and whoever excels in authority and power in the provinces, lament the fall of the metropolis and the princes she holds; but also weep for yourselves especially, for once the fall of the metropolis is set, yours is undoubtedly set as well (Ezekiel 23:6, 14; Jeremiah 48:20; 49:3). d) *firs.* Jerome interprets these as the priests and princes mutually mourning their devastation; so that what follows is in place of an explanation: *because the magnificent ones are wasted.* But observe that the *firs* are here distinguished from the *magnificent cedars*, and the *oaks of Bashan* from the *forest of the fortification*. By the firs and Bashanite oaks, therefore, we understand the provincial princes and towns; by the cedars, the metropolitan leaders; and by the *forest of the fortification*, Jerusalem itself (Isaiah 14:8; Ezekiel 31:8). *Jonathan*: *Howl, O Kings.* e) *the cedar has fallen*, and whatever was made of cedar or like cedar in Jerusalem (Ezekiel 1:23; 9:9). *Jonathan*: *because the princes are broken.* f) and because they were etc., or causally: *and because they are magnificent trees* (Ezekiel 17:8), that is, the great men of the people in the metropolis (Judges 5:13; 2 Chronicles 23:10). *Jonathan*: *those who were rich in wealth have been plundered.* Indeed, the magnificent palaces can also be included here (compare the noun in verse 3). g) v. 3. (Jeremiah 4:20). h) *oak of Bashan*, *Jonathan*: *the rulers of the provinces* (Isaiah 2:13). i) *has come down*, that is, cut down, or, as the Vulgate translates, *is felled* (Isaiah 32:19). k) Vulgate: *the fortified forest*; Septuagint: <term>thickly planted</term> <note>original: "σύνφυτος"</note>, that is, entangled, woody; or as the Arabic from them, but the Syriac from the Hebrew rendered it, *strong, mighty forest.* Namely, the written Hebrew form <term>Batzir</term> <note>original: "בָּצִיר"</note>, which is a passive participle, generally signifies whatever is difficult to reach (Jeremiah 33:3), or to do (Genesis 11:6; Job 42:2), or to overcome (Isaiah 20:15; 25:2): and therefore it notes a forest here, which because of its density and size seemed as if it could hardly be cut down; but with the figure resolved, it notes a city—great, populous, and fortified—which was presumed to be insurmountable, or at least that it would hardly ever be cut off to the point of destruction. Such was Jerusalem, which had grown with impregnable firmness, and was built by various kings and princes, and later by Herod, yet was destroyed by the Roman attacker. We include the Temple as the chief fortification of the city, but we interpret the "forest," because it signifies a collection and abundance of buildings, as the whole of Jerusalem. *Jonathan*: *because the region of your strength is wasted.* This can be explained as *forest of fortification*, i.e., difficult, fortified; as it is in the written text (compare Zechariah 9:12; Jeremiah 1:12); or *of cutting down*, i.e., to be cut down (Jeremiah 6:9; Psalm 76:13), as it might be called from its unhappy outcome. *Sch.*: *the forest of Batziri*; as if it were a proper name, and that allegorical from the fortifications, such as *Bozrah* (Isaiah 63:1). *Tarnovius*: *the forest of the vintage*, which, just as vines are stripped and spoiled in the vintage, so is it stripped of all its glory, honor, and riches (compare Leviticus 26:5). Finally, others: *the vintage or vineyard of cutting down* (compare Isaiah 5:1, 5, 6), though it would rather have been said **the forest of the vintage**, with the construction inverted.

CHAPTER 11, v. 1. Without a space preceding 6.–9. 12. 19. 20. & in the margin 22 according to the Masoretes 2 & the Essenes, but contrary to the printed edition.
v. 2. **the glorious ones** <note>original: "אַדִּרִים"</note> thus in 1, 3, 5, 6, 9, 20.

o) and the pride of *Assyria* shall be cast down, who acted proudly against my people (Isaiah 14:11; Psalm 56:5). *Jonathan*: the strength shall cease from *Assyria*. p) and the rod of *Egypt*, with which it struck Israel and enslaved them (Isaiah 9:3; 14:5). But *Jonathan*: and the dominion of the Egyptians shall be taken away: which exposition, although it seems founded on the parallelism of Genesis 49:10, cannot be admitted here, as *Gussetius* observes (p. 818), because here oppression and persecution are seen as being removed from the Israelites, nor is the word placed before the name **Egypt**, as it is there: "the scepter shall not depart from Judah." q) shall depart, namely, from Israel (compare Isaiah 10:27, 26; 14:25).

CHAPTER 11, v. 1. y) *But open, O Lebanon.* A prophetic imperative. The sense: it shall come to pass that you will be forced to open your gates to the enemies. From the promises of the New Testament concerning the coming of the Messiah, and the liberating, gathering, and strengthening of Judah and Israel through him, the Prophet returns to predicting the destruction of the Temple and the Jewish State: so that, just as there he depicted the grace of God toward believers, so now he depicts the <term>severity</term> <note>original: "ἀποτομίαν"</note> toward the stubborn and despisers of grace. We make three parts of this chapter with *Sch.*: I. The prophecy of the final destruction of Jerusalem and the devastation of Judea (v. 1-3). II. The explanation of the cause, which is disobedience toward the preaching of the Shepherd Messiah, and the shameful purchase of the Messiah for the same (v. 4-14). III. The prediction of the foolish shepherd (v. 15 to the end). For the rest, we acknowledge here indeed some <term>things hard to be understood</term> <note>original: "δυσνοητά"</note> (2 Peter 3:16); nor [is it] in every...

<summary>This page analyzes Zechariah 11 as a prophecy of Jerusalem's destruction by the Romans, metaphorically described as the burning of Lebanon's cedars. It synthesizes Rabbinic traditions (like the Temple doors opening on their own) with Christian interpretations of the "Messiah sold for thirty pieces of silver."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Zechariah, moving from the restoration of the people in chapter 10 to the somber prophecy of the "flock of slaughter" in chapter 11. The commentator focuses on identifying the "shepherds" and "lions" as the corrupt leaders of Judea and interprets the passage as a direct prophecy of the life of Christ and the subsequent Roman destruction of Jerusalem.</meta>

<header>ZECHARIAH. CAP. XI. 11</header>

<margin>
v. 3. **l)** This is a voice of wailing <note>original: "vox eiulatus"</note> (4) **Isaiah 15:8; Jeremiah 25:36.** That which was to come is depicted in a prophetic manner as if it were present and already striking the senses. Compare **Isaiah 13:4; 66:6; Jeremiah 25:36.** etc.
**m)** *of the shepherds*. See note on **chapter 10:3; Jeremiah 25:34; Ezekiel 34:2. following.** *Jerome* says: Those whom he had called cedars, firs, and oaks of *Bashan*, he now calls shepherds through another metaphor—that is, the princes and teachers, and those who were the leaders among the people.
**n)** *because*, or *that it is spoiled* v. 2.
**o)** *their magnificence/glory* (z) **Ezekiel 17:8.** Jerome explains this as the Temple, in which they gloried. Indeed, it can also be understood as the city itself, the splendid houses, the wealth, and whatever had been the material for their pride, comparing v. 2. **Ezekiel 24:21; chapter 33:28.** See note on **Amos 6:8.**
**p)** *roaring*, due to the loss of their lair and prey, compare note on **Jeremiah 51:38**; also **Psalm 38:9; Psalm 104:21.** That is, because of the desolated city and Temple, in which they had rested securely like lions and had gathered a great force of wealth as if it were prey.
**q)** *of the lions*—they are called this when they have begun to go out to hunt; likewise (to speak outside of the metaphor) those born to illustrious families when they are brought into the Republic, especially those who are of a fiercer nature and unmerciful. **Ezekiel 19:3, 5, 6; Nahum 2:11, 13; Zephaniah 3:3.** Jerome therefore rightly says: Those whom he called lofty trees, and again shepherds, he now calls lions.
**r)** *the pride of Jordan*, a wooded area abundant with lions who had their lairs there, compare note on **Jeremiah 12:5.** This refers to Jerusalem, specifically as the seat of the princes of the Jewish people. For the Prophet, as Jerome notes, because he had mentioned lions, maintains the metaphor. Otherwise, the whole prophecy was fulfilled in the destruction of Judea by the Romans. See page 416.
</margin>

<margin>
"The vintage" <note>original: "הבציר"</note> is the reading. <note>A Masoretic note regarding a specific spelling or reading in the Hebrew text.</note>
See the full account in Josephus’ *The Jewish War*.

v. 4. **s)** Now follows a detailed explanation <note>original: "exergasia"</note> of the preceding prophecy concerning the destruction of Jerusalem and Judea by the Romans. See below.
</margin>

> 3 The voice of the wailing of the shepherds; for their glory is spoiled: a voice of the roaring of young lions; for the pride of Jordan is spoiled.
> 4 Thus saith the LORD my God: Feed the flock of the slaughter;
> 5 Whose possessors slay them, and hold themselves not guilty: and they that sell them say, Blessed be the LORD; for I am rich: and their own shepherds pity them not.
> 6 For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land, saith the LORD: but, lo, I will deliver the men every one into his neighbor’s hand, and into the hand of his king: and they shall smite the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.

---

note v. 4. **t)** These are the words of the Son of God concerning the Father, as in **Isaiah 49:1. following; Psalm 2:7.** etc. For He is 1) the highest and most eminent shepherd of his flock (v. 7). 2) He takes punishment from the evil shepherds (v. 8). 3) He breaks his covenant, which he had entered into with all peoples (v. 10, 11). 4) He is the one whom the wretched sheep observe and look up to (v. 11). 5) He is the one whom the Jews valued at thirty pieces of silver, bought from a betrayer (v. 12, 13), as the Evangelist witnesses in **Matthew 27:9, 10.** All these things are so arranged that they do not fit Zechariah at all, but fit the Messiah perfectly. Therefore, the Son calls the Father "his God," because he was to be sent by Him in the form of a servant, to do His will by feeding the sheep, and through his obedience and death making atonement, having assumed human nature, according to which he was to be lesser than the Father **Isaiah 49:4, 5; Psalm 22:2, 3; also John 20:17; compare John 14:28 and Philippians 2:6.** following. **u)** *Feed you.* The duty of suffering is joined to Christ himself, and is taken away from the evil shepherds, who are mentioned in v. 5, 8 and above in **chapter 10:3**: such as in **Ezekiel 34:10. following** and under another figure in **Psalm 82:8.** compare v. 1. following. Moreover, Christ feeds the sheep by word and deed, by doctrine and example, seeking the lost, calling back the straying, healing the broken, comforting the weary, gathering the dispersed, and leading to the pastures and waters of the Gospel as many as heard his voice; and not only in his own person, but also through others whom he had sent in his name; and finally, by pouring out his life for the sheep. **Chapter 13:7; Jeremiah 23:4, 5; Ezekiel 34:11. following; Micah 7:14; Psalm 23:1; John 10:11. following; chapter 11:52; 21:16, 17; Hebrews 13:20.** The imperative command indicates the merciful will of God the Father toward the wretched sheep, according to which he did not want them to perish by hunger and thirst, and the errors and evils in which they were entangled. Compare **Matthew 18:11-14; Luke 15:4. following.** **x)** *sheep of slaughter* v. 7. *Tarnovius* explains this as those destined for butchery by their own evil shepherds, who until now—while exposed to the violence of their own shepherds who devour the flock **Psalm 14:4; Ezekiel 34:4; Jeremiah 23:1**—could expect nothing other than slaughter. Compare **Romans 8:36 and Psalm 44:23.** In general, it expresses that miserable state into which the Israelite people had fallen through the fault of their shepherds, which Christ found when coming in the flesh: and it is under this name of suffering that the Father's mercy was moved to send the Son, and the Son's mercy to feed the sheep. Compare **Matthew 9:36; chapter 10:6; 15:24; Mark 6:34.** See above **chapter 10:2.**

**v. 5. y)** *Whose owners.* He continues to depict the wretched state of the Jewish people at the time of Christ under the figure of sheep, and thus further explains the reason why he commends them to a better shepherd. By "owners," therefore, are to be understood both the evil princes and the ungodly teachers: the Hasmonean Kings, Herod, the High Priests, priests, scribes, Pharisees, etc., who did not feed the people as God's special possession, but <term>as lording it over the heritage</term> <note>original Greek: "ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κלήρων"</note>, **1 Peter 5:2, 3, 4.** **z)** *they kill them*, devouring those they ought to feed. It signifies that they serve their own bellies and do not spare the flock, nor care for the death of the sheep, provided they themselves have something to devour and with which to feed their own skin. **Ezekiel 34:2, 3, 4, 8, 10. following; Micah 3:3; Psalm 14:4.** **a)** *nor are they held guilty*; that is, they do this with impunity, nor do they even acknowledge any fault while they kill the sheep. **Jeremiah 2:3; chapter 50:7; Hosea 5:15.** Compare **Psalm 50:21; Ecclesiastes 8:11.** Jonathan the Paraphrast says: *sin shall not be imputed to us*. **b)** *and each of those selling them says.* The same ones who were just called owners are the sellers, insofar as they seek gain from the sheep, and in view of that, they hold the flock as if it were for sale, not hesitating to expose it to death, provided they obtain some small profit. **Amos 2:6.** **c)** They so far fail to acknowledge themselves as guilty that they bless themselves in their hearts, and praise God himself as the author of their unjustly acquired wealth. **Deuteronomy 29:18; Psalm 10:3; Psalm 49:19.** compare **Matthew 23:14.** **d)** *because* or *for I am enriched*, from those things sold off. **Hosea 12:9; Proverbs 21:17.** compare **1 Timothy 6:5.** **e)** *and any of those pasturing them* (a construction according to the sense, because he understands "men") or *these* (remaining in the allegory, through a change of gender) who take the name of shepherds, or ought to be such. **v. 3, 8, 17; chapter 10:3.** **f)** *hardly spares them*, v. 16. **Isaiah 9:18; chapter 30:14.** Having been touched upon, they are therefore fierce wolves rather than shepherds **Acts 20:29.** likewise thieves and robbers **John 10:8, 10, 13.**

**v. 6. g)** The causal particle, connected with the immediately preceding v. 5 (if one prefers), will suggest a coherence of this kind: The cause of such great misery is my anger and judgment because of the people's preceding sins, *because* etc. However, it also seems to depend on the command to feed in v. 4. As *Tarnovius* says: But there is another reason why there is need for Christ as another shepherd—namely, because the people are to be punished for the crimes of the shepherds, since they agree with them, and thus, while immense disasters are imminent, provision must be made for the remaining pious ones so they may be saved: for things have now reached the point that I have decreed not to delay the punishment any longer, etc. Evidently, God the Father, in the very threat of imminent evil, remembers his mercy, and commends to the Son that by feeding some at least, he might save them like a brand from the fire. **h)** *I will not spare anymore*, just as I have done until now and for a long time. **v. 7; Isaiah 30:14; Jeremiah 13:14; Ezekiel 5:11.** compare however **Luke 21:24; Romans 11:2.** **i)** *of the land*, not the whole world, but *of this* one, with the demonstrative "the," that is, Judea, of which he speaks. **k)** *I am about to deliver* (as if to say: I will cause them to be found or present in the hand of another) *men*. **Leviticus 9:12, 17; 2 Samuel 3:8.** **l)** *every one into the hand of another*, so that they themselves may rage against each other with internal discords **chapter 8:10**, which happened especially when Jerusalem was besieged by the Romans. Let us read Josephus, says Jerome, and the seven books of the Jewish captivity: and we shall see that this prophecy was fulfilled by the truth of history.

---

v. 3. **Wailing** <note>original: "יִלְלַת"</note> so in copies 6, 9, 14, 20, 22 according to *Michlal Yophi*. *Metheg* is also found in 8, 10, 13, 17, 18, 23, 24. — **And in the hand** <note>original: "וּבְיַד"</note> and the Berlin codex. **They slay** <note>original: "יַהֲרְגֻן"</note> others. v. 5. **And I am rich** <note>original: "וַאְעְשִׁר"</note> thus written deficiently in 1, 3, 7, 8, 15, 24. So in sc. 2, 5. So the Masorah i. 2. printed **וַאֲעְשִׁר** and Erfurt. Others write it fully. **They slay them** <note>original: "יַהֲרְגֻן"</note> with a feminine suffix in 1. and in the margin of 6, 9. v. 6. **In the hand** <note>original: "בְּיַד"</note> with a *Maqqeph* in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 16, 20.

# CHAPTER II. ZECHARIAH 11

<margin>It becomes clear that the entire Jewish people are described this way because of their wretched state under evil shepherds; and likewise from verse 9 and following, that Christ, as far as he was able, offered himself to everyone, not just those who would eventually believe and obey.</margin>

<margin>m) **into the hand of his King**, just as they were captured by the Hasmonean Kings <note>The Hasmoneans were the ruling dynasty of Judea from c. 140–37 BCE</note> (this undoubtedly refers to the brotherly discords of Hyrcanus and Aristobulus), and by Herod and his descendants, and finally by the Romans, compare: *We have no king but Caesar*, **John 19:12, 15.** n) **and they shall crush**, that is, they will miserably afflict and lay waste, both through internal collisions and external hostility. **Numbers 14:45; Deuteronomy 1:44; Isaiah 30:14; 2 Chronicles 15:6.** *) **nor will I deliver them or the land from their hand.** **Judges 6:9; 1 Samuel 10:18.**</margin>

->...his neighbor<sup>m</sup> and into the hand of his King<sup>n</sup>; and they shall crush the land, and I will not deliver<sup>o</sup> them from their hand.<-

->7 So I pastured<sup>p</sup> the flock of slaughter<sup>q</sup>; therefore<sup>r</sup>, O poor<sup>s</sup> of the flock! And I took for myself two<sup>t</sup> staffs: one I called Favor<sup>u</sup> and the other I called Bonds<sup>x</sup>; and I pastured the flock<sup>y</sup>.<-

->8 And I destroyed<sup>z</sup> the three shepherds<sup>a</sup> in one month<sup>b</sup>; and my soul was shortened toward them<sup>c</sup>, and also their soul loathed me<sup>d</sup>.<-

->9 And I said, I will not...<-

***

<margin>* 7. p) **I pastured therefore**, as the Father had commanded me in verse 4. For just as the command was given there, here is the execution of it, and in the words of the Son himself, as we noted at verse 4. Moreover, these things are prophetic regarding events that would certainly happen in the future. q) See the note on verse 4. r) **A difficult little word.** <note>Referring to the Hebrew word "laken"</note> It could very easily be explained as: "because of the wretched ones of the sheep," but we do not recall it being used as a preposition "because of" anywhere, but always as a causal adverb "therefore." The Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> has: "because of this, O poor of the flock," namely, because of the Father's command in verse 4. But according to the accents, the word *therefore* (לָכֵן) adheres more closely to the following vocative than to the preceding verb "I pastured"; and according to grammar, a causal adverb should have been placed at the beginning rather than the end of the clause. Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> says: "therefore, because they were the poor of the flock," following Noldius's *Concordance of Particles*, page 507, comparing **Isaiah 61:7; Jeremiah 2:33; and Job 34:25**, though from those places that meaning is hardly proven. Not to mention that Tarnovius supposes the "sheep of slaughter" to be those few sheep who recognize themselves as such and listen gladly to the shepherd's voice, whereas on the contrary, from verses 5 and 6...</margin>

Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian known for federal theology</note> resolves it such that it is either an Infinitive in the Hiphil <note>A Hebrew verb stem indicating causative action</note>, on account of **לָכֵן** in **Daniel 11:35**, meaning "to prepare the needy of the flock"; or a noun whose construct state is understood, meaning "on account of the right (I say right) of the needy of the flock," that is, because of that which is right among the needy of the flock, comparing verse 11 below, though the accents reject this explanation, and **Proverbs 11:19**, where it is not necessary. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the medieval French rabbi</note> and David Kimchi <note>A medieval biblical commentator and grammarian</note> say: "When I began to pasture... they were indeed the most wretched of the flock." This is how some explain the word **לָכֵן** in **Numbers 16:11 and Jeremiah 5:2.** Let the reader choose whatever he wishes. We, along with Schultens and others, translate: **for your sake, O wretched ones of the flock.** The suffix is irregularly formed with a *Tsere* instead of a *Segol* <note>Hebrew vowel markings</note>, as seen in **2 Samuel 24:3; Ecclesiastes 9:12; 1 Chronicles 21:3; 2 Chronicles 9:11.** There is a <gloss>tongue/usage</gloss> of this in **Genesis 19:19; 30:26; Leviticus 10:1; 11:21; Numbers 16:7**, etc. And the Masoretes <note>Scholars who standardized the Hebrew Bible text</note> understood it this way, adding a note that it is a feminine pronoun, as if to say: "Had I not known that I would have some obedient sheep in the Jewish people, though fewer and despised by the greater crowd, who would hear the shepherd's voice, the Father would not have sent me, nor would I have pastured them." But truly, I pastured the whole people so that from it I might save the wretched sheep, that is, the elect, who would not despise the pastoral care offered to all. s) **the wretched or poor of the flock.** The language mixes the proper term "wretched" in the masculine with the improper "flock." This refers to the remnant of the elect among the Jewish people who would believe in Christ (compare verse 11), because they were both despised by the majority and felt their own misery most acutely, needing the care of the Good Shepherd. **Isaiah 26:6; 66:2; Psalm 18:28; Matthew 5:3; 11:5; James 2:5.** These are the same as the "little sheep" in **Zechariah 13:7; Jeremiah 49:20; 50:45**, and the <note>original: "τὸ μικρὸν ποίμνιον"</note> <term>little flock (Luke 12:32)</term>, as opposed to the fat and strong ones in **Ezekiel 34:16, 20**, and the rich and satisfied in **Revelation 3:17**, to whom the office of Christ was worthless. t) **two staffs**, that is, two pastoral crooks, verses 10, 14; **1 Samuel 17:40, 43**; compare **Psalm 23:4.** He says he used two to suggest that the sheep were not pastured by him in only one way. u) **one I called Favor (Amenity)**, verse 10, by which he offered them the sweetness of the Lord to be tasted, so they might be sweetly enticed to faith and obedience. **Psalm 27:4; 90:17.** They understand this as the words of grace and sweetness with which Christ invited the Jewish people to the kingdom of God. **Psalm 141:6; Proverbs 16:24; Luke 4:22**; compare **Matthew 11:28, 29, 30; Titus 3:4.** x) Here the interpreters differ greatly: the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic rendered it "a cord" or "rope," but with obscure meaning and against the vowel points. Cocceius translates it as "sailors" or "pilots," comparing **Ezekiel 27:29 and Jonah 1:6**, understanding it (according to his hypothesis) as Bishops or Elders governing the Church like a ship by common counsel; when they disputed over the primacy of the seat, the brotherhood between the two parts of the Church (Ephraim and Judah) was abolished. But this concerns the care of Christ the Shepherd, not toward the universal Church of the New Testament, but primarily toward the lost sheep of the house of Israel, compare verses 4, 5, 6. To Gousset (page 237), **Bonds** (Choblim) is Christ’s human nature, which is most beautiful, while **Favor** (Noam) is the "sailor," the college of the Apostles. Christ broke those rods, he says, with respect to the Jews, both when he ceased to exercise grace and truth toward them (which is of his humanity) and by withdrawing the Apostles from them as a punishment for their unbelief, **Acts 13:46; Romans 11**, so that the fishers of men would no longer visit them in their travels across the world. But the mission of the Apostles to the Jews is undoubtedly part of the pastoral "favor"; it is hard to believe it should be distinguished as something different. Therefore, it can be translated as "those who destroy," whether the staff is named from the object (the staff with which those who act ruinously are struck, **Nehemiah 1:7**) or from the subject (the staff used by those who destroy and bring harm, **Ezekiel 32:7; Song of Solomon 2:15**), specifically because of an admitted fault, **Isaiah 54:16; Proverbs 13:13; Ecclesiastes 5:5.** Schultens and others say "of those who grieve," comparing **Isaiah 13:8 and Jeremiah 49:24**, which amounts to the same thing. This staff, since it is distinguished from the staff of "favor," can hardly be explained other than as the harsher discipline which Christ combined with the discipline of favor, so that by the latter he might gently invite, and by the former he might compel the stubborn to his fold, or punish those unwilling to be compelled. Indeed, the Lord used the staff of the grieving not only by threatening imminent destruction, but also by afflicting them with various evils, partly through the Romans, so that the people, stirred by this "pedagogy" <note>An educational or corrective discipline</note>, might repent—but for most, it was in vain! Compare **Isaiah 9:12; Jeremiah 2:30; 5:3; Matthew 11:17.** y) **and thus I pastured**, using both crooks, the flock. Verses 4, 9, 8. z) **And I destroyed**, verse 9; **Exodus 23:23**, specifically when they were unwilling to be ruled by the crook of favor, compare verse 10 here. a) **three shepherds** eminent among the Jewish people and distinguished by this very office, that is, these three orders of shepherds or rulers of the people. Lightfoot, in his *Hebrew Hours* on **John 10**, identifies them as the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes; Cocceius as priests, teachers (or prophets), and judges, comparing **Malachi 2:12.** Another in Jerome says priests, false prophets, and Kings of the Jews, all cut down at once after the passion of Christ, comparing **Jeremiah 2:26.** Tarnovius, finally, says the prophets (who ruled the people by divine revelations and oracles), the priests (by the explanation and teaching of the law), and the wise (by counsel), **Jeremiah 18:18.** The Gemarists <note>Commentators on the Jewish Mishnah</note> in *Taanith* folio 9a wrongly say Moses, Aaron, and Miriam; Rabbi Solomon says the house of Ahab, Ahaziah, and his brothers; Kimchi says the sons of Josiah: Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah. For this is not a history of past things, but a prophecy of future ones, compare verse 4 and following. Abarbanel understands the Maccabees: Judas, Jonathan, and Simon, who presided over affairs for 30 years and were removed by violent death. But Cocceius rightly says: "No coming of the shepherd preceded them," etc. Compare **Psalm 82:6.** b) **in one month**, **Job 7:3**; yet not a month of days, as in **Deuteronomy 21:13 or 2 Kings 15:13**, but of years, just as the weeks in **Daniel 9:24, 25**, as Abarbanel also feels here. Cocceius calculates them from the death of Christ until the overthrow of the Republic by the Jewish War. For this war broke out, as Calvin wishes, in 66 CE. Subtract 30 years, and you fall on the year 36. Now Christ is thought by Calvisius and Helvicus to have suffered in the year 33 of the common Christian era. Three years and some months remain. But Kimchi explains it as "a short time," by a prophetic synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note>. c) **for my soul was shortened in them**, namely, in bearing them longer; that is, I could no longer <note>original: "μακροθυμεῖν"</note> <term>exercise patience (suffer long)</term> toward them or defer punishment, due to loathing and just grief over their obstinacy. **Numbers 21:4; Judges 16:16; Job 21:4**; compare **Ezekiel 23:17, 18.** Jonah: "My Word detested them." d) **for their soul also had loathing (t) toward me.** We explain this in the pluperfect and causally with Jonah, who says: "because their soul had loathed my worship." For Christ did not loathe Israel until Israel had loathed him. Such is the word **loathed** (בָּעַל) <note>likely a reference to a specific Hebrew root</note>, as in "we have sinned," **Isaiah 64:4.** Compare the related **Jeremiah 3:14; 31:32**, and regarding this matter, see verse 12, 13 below; **Psalm 118:22; Matthew 21:42, 43; Luke 19:14; Acts 4:10, 11.**

<summary>This page analyzes Zechariah 11:7-9, interpreting the two staffs (Favor and Bonds) as Christ's dual approach of grace and discipline toward Israel. It also debates the identity of the "three shepherds" and the meaning of the "one month" timeframe for their destruction, linking it to the Roman-Jewish War.</summary>

# ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER XI. 11.

<margin>
v. 9. *e)* **I will no longer pasture you.** This signifies the rejection of the Jews and the transfer of the Gospel—which they had persistently spurned—from them to the Gentiles. See Matthew 21:43; Acts 13:46; Romans 11:1 and following. *f)* **What is dying, let it die**, whatever that may be; let it die, since it knowingly and prudently refused to live. Let it rush toward death and become subject to all evils; I will not care for it. Compare Jeremiah 15:2 and following, and the notes on chapter 34:17; Revelation 22:11. *g)* **which is cut off**, in Greek <term>ουκ αφανιζει</term> <note>original: "does not vanish" or "is not hidden"</note> (for this is the force of the word in Psalm 139:15), **let it be cut off**. See verses 8, 16; Exodus 9:15; Job 4:7. *h)* **the remaining ones, however, which survived these evils.** Ezekiel 6:12. *i)* **let each eat the flesh of another.** Jeremiah 9:19; Isaiah 1:19; so that you may perish partly through external evils and partly through internal ones. Compare verse 6 above and Isaiah 9:18–20. Josephus, in *The Jewish War* <note>Josephus was a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note>, Book 4, Chapter 1, writes: "Individual cities were agitated by tumult and internal war; and as much as they had a respite from the Romans, they turned their hands against themselves," etc. See Gurtler's *Prophetic Theology*, page 501 and following.
</margin>

<margin>
Either, therefore, this will be the sense: that I would break that ancient and universal covenant, which I had entered into not only with Israel but with all peoples (Genesis 12:3; 18:18; 22:18), in respect to the Jews, and I would exclude them from it.
</margin>

> 9 I will not <gloss>e</gloss> pasture you; <gloss>f</gloss> that which is dying, <gloss>h</gloss> let it die; <gloss>g</gloss> and that which is to be cut off, <gloss>i</gloss> let it be cut off;
> <gloss>k</gloss> and let the remaining ones eat every woman the flesh of her neighbor. 10 <gloss>l</gloss> And I took
> <gloss>m</gloss> my staff <term>Favor</term> <note>Hebrew: No'am, often translated as 'Beauty' or 'Pleasantness'</note> <gloss>n</gloss> and I cut it asunder, to break my covenant
> <gloss>p</gloss> which I had made with all the peoples. 11 <gloss>o</gloss> And it was broken in that day, and they knew

<margin>
v. 10. *k)* See verse 7. *l)* **and I cut it down**, so that by this staff of "pleasantness" I might be understood to no longer be about to rule the people. Verse 14. *m)* **that in this way I might abolish or break [it].** Verse 14; Judges 2:1. *n)* Some interpret this as the **covenant of grace**, taken away from the Jews through their rejection and <term>hardened state</term> <note>Greek: porōsin</note>. Therefore, they interpret "all peoples" as the twelve tribes of Israel. But although "peoples" is used for Israel (e.g., Genesis 28:3; 48:4), yet with the prefix of universality ("all"), it is not usually applied except to the nations as distinct from Israel. Compare chapter 12:2, 3, 6; 14:12, etc.
</margin>

---

Or, as we prefer, and as R. Sal. <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, or Rashi, the medieval commentator</note> and Cocc. <note>Johannes Cocceius, 17th-century theologian</note> approve here: I had hitherto restrained the nations, as if having entered into a covenant with them, so that they would not invade Judea—at least I ensured they did not completely overturn it (compare similar phrasing in Hosea 2:20; Job 5:23; also Ezekiel 34:25). But now, with this covenant removed, I have given power to the nations, and to the Romans especially, to rush upon the Jews, so that they might feel the staff of the suffering, they who refused to be ruled by the shepherd's crook of Favor. Compare Isaiah 5:26 and following; 56:9 and following; Daniel 9:26, 27; Matthew 23:37–39; 24:2, 15 and following; Luke 13:6–9. **v. 11. o)** *And thus the covenant entered into with the nations was broken or abolished.* Verse 10; Isaiah 8:10; Jeremiah 33:21. **p)** *And they acknowledged it as such, namely from the outcome of events, as I had predicted both in this very prophecy and elsewhere.* Compare chapter 2:15; 4:9; 6:15. **q)** *See note on verse 7.* **r)** *those observing me, who looked up to me as their shepherd, revered me, and held me in high value.* Hosea 4:10; Psalm 31:7; Psalm 59:10; compare Ezekiel 38:7. *The Targum Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> renders this: those doing my will.* **s)** *that it had not happened by chance or accident, but that it was the word of the Lord, and had occurred exactly as the Lord had long ago predicted.* Compare notes on Jeremiah 32:8. Cocceius says: "The effect in the upright among the poor of the flock is to recognize the truth of the word of the Lord, and not to be disturbed by the affliction of those days, as the Savior warned in Matthew 24:26." Eusebius, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 3, Chapter 7, says: "If anyone compares the words of our Savior with those recorded by the same writer (Josephus) regarding the whole (Jewish) war, he cannot help but admire the foreknowledge and prediction of our Savior, and confess it to be truly divine and stupendously beyond measure." Regarding how the Christians migrated from Jerusalem and Judea because of the imminent destruction they knew was coming, see the same Eusebius, Book 3, Chapter 5. **v. 12. t)** *And I said to them, namely the Jews and especially their leaders, before the shepherd's crook of Favor was cut down by me (v. 10) and the covenant with the nations was broken (v. 11).* Or, as it comes to the same thing according to Cocceius in the pluperfect: *And I had said.* For here he justifies his severity by narrating one particular, yet most signal and atrocious injury against himself—he who had come to feed them, only for them to kill him for the value of 30 shekels. **u)** *If it is good in your eyes, i.e., if it seems right to you, and if you judge it to be fair, that for so many benefits bestowed upon you (Acts 10:38), for so many labors undertaken for your sake and still to be undertaken (Isaiah 53:11), I should receive some reward from you.* He leaves it to their deliberation and judgment—not as if the matter itself were doubtful or required deliberation, or as if it were in man's power to give or deny the Lord his wage—but because he knew the Jews would be so ungrateful that they would not even consider him worthy of a sound wage, but would even drive him to the cross. Thus, the words are those of one silently reproaching ingratitude and expressing indignation that they do not observe even the common and most well-known principles of equity. **x)** *give my reward, which I have earned by the labor spent on you.* Genesis 30:18, 32, 33; Luke 10:7; 1 Timothy 5:18. *Abendana understands this as repentance and good works.* R. Salomo: *Keep my commandment; for this will be my reward for all the good I gave you, just as his own reward is given to a shepherd.* Targum Jonathan: *do my will.* Entirely, he seems to demand conversion, faith, and new obedience with the fruits of righteousness in place of a reward. It is as if he says: "Do this, O Jews, so that I have not labored in you in vain, and consumed my strength on your behalf without reward or fruit" (Isaiah 49:4; 5:2, 3). **y)** *but if not, leave it* (Jeremiah 40:4), <term>refuse</term> <note>Greek: apeipasthe</note>, *or reject it.* 2 Corinthians 4:2. It is as if he says: "But if, against all right, you deny me the reward due to me, and if it pleases you less to count it out, at least desist; I will not press my right further, but will commit it to God, since such a monstrous crime cries to heaven" (Deuteronomy 24:15; James 5:4). Tarnovius, compare notes on Ezekiel 3, 27. **z)** *But they, oh! unworthy deed! in place of the expected reward from me, they weighed out for my betrayer...* Genesis 23:16; Isaiah 46:6. <term>they set</term> <note>Greek: estēsan</note>. Matthew 26:15. **a)** *my reward—but a wicked and shameful reward, by which they would in no way remunerate my labors or fulfill their debt, but would impiously buy me for death.* Verse 13. Compare Deuteronomy 32:6. **b)** *namely, thirty shekels of silver. A vile price, which was paid to the master of a servant killed by a goring ox.* Exodus 21:32. Compare Matthew 26:15; 27:9, 10. Targum Jonathan: *And some living ones did my will.* But they wander from the goal. For if the remnants of the good were the reward, the Lord would by no means have ordered that reward to be cast away as unworthy (v. 13), nor would the shepherd have completely abdicated his office of pasturing (v. 14). Therefore, the Evangelist Matthew provides the torch for us in Matthew 26:15; 27:9, 10. See what we noted above at verse 1. **v. 13. c)** Tarnovius: *Then indeed, because of the unworthiness of the matter, the LORD God the Father spoke to me.* See note on verse 4.

<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on Zechariah 11, specifically focusing on the Shepherd’s final rejection of his role and the emergence of the "foolish shepherd." It bridges the narrative from the Shepherd receiving thirty pieces of silver to the prediction of a leader who will neglect the flock.</meta>

# CHAPTER II. ZECHARIAH 11.

<margin>
...you were valued; but if only indirectly, he says it should have been said that I should cast it away. 
*g)* by which I was or am considered precious. 1 Samuel 26:21. 
*i)* that is, *b)* from/with them, that is, from those in chapter 4:13. The particle "with" expresses the estimation in the mind, or how they valued Christ among themselves; "from" however is the declaration of the valuation in the work itself. 
But according to *Cocceius's Lexicon, page 334*: "by which I was deemed worthy to be taken away from those." 
*i)* **and I threw it**, that is, I directed the mind of Judas in such a way that the silver, which he had received but which otherwise would have been his, he himself, being repentant, threw into the temple. Matthew 27:3 and following.
</margin>

<margin>
*d)* Assign that price, as if it were a reward. Moreover, they "throw away" things that are useful but of no value, and things which we turn away from as unworthy. Exodus 22:30; Jeremiah 23:18; Chapter 52:3; Ezekiel 20:8. 
Furthermore, things are attributed to Christ here which are narrated as having been done respectively by the betrayer and the priests of the Jews. On this matter, Tarnovius <note>original: "Tarn." - Paul Tarnow (1562–1633), a Lutheran theologian</note> says: "It is only indicated," he says, "that by Christ’s providence all these things, though evil, were directed to this good end; while Judas desired to turn the money to his own use, and the priests to receive it back, nevertheless Christ—although standing in total humiliation before Pilate—compelled Judas by His omnipotence to return the reward of iniquity, and moved the hearts of the priests not to put it into the temple treasury, but to buy the potter's field." 
*e)* **to the potter**, that is, so that it might be given to the potter, or conferred upon the potter for the field he was about to sell. Matthew 27:5, 6, 7. 
*f)* namely, the magnificence <note>original: "magnificentiam (z)"</note>. Micah 2:8. 
**of the price**, that is, that magnificent and huge price. Proverbs 10:15. 
He calls it a "huge price" **ironically** <note>The author points out that 30 pieces of silver was actually a very low price, the cost of a common slave</note> because it was most cheap, so that he might more vividly suggest the unworthiness of the matter. As if to say: "I was of such great value to them, forsooth! that they judged me fit to be bought from a betrayer for cheap silver." There is a similar irony or antiphrasis <note>a figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its literal meaning</note> in Isaiah 57:12 and Mark 7:9. 
Moreover, these are no longer the words of God the Father speaking to Christ, but of Christ Himself, reporting and fulfilling the saying of His Father; this is proved by the accents as much as by the matter itself (compare verse 12). Therefore, this first half-verse is a mixture of direct and indirect speech.
</margin>

->13 "Throw it to the potter!"—the magnificent price at which I was valued by them. So I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the LORD, for the potter.<-

->14 Then I cut asunder my second staff, "Bands," to break the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.<-

->15 And the LORD said to me: "Take for yourself once more the implements of a foolish shepherd."<-

->16 "For behold, I am raising up a shepherd in the land who will not visit the vanishing ones, nor seek the young, nor heal the broken, nor sustain the standing, but will eat the flesh of the fat ones..."<-

<margin>
v. 14. *k)*
</margin>

But afterward (after I had cut the staff of "Favor," verse 10), I also cut [the second]. We cut things for which there is no further use. Clearly, this act is symbolic, signifying that Christ has rejected the Jews to such an extent that He no longer wishes to be angry with them or burn with zeal for them, but rather to leave them to their own character and misery until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered. *l)* verses 7, 10. *m)* see the note on verse 7. That is, Christ first performed His "proper work" among the Jews, for the sake of which He had come into this world: ruling them with the staff of "Favor," announcing the kingdom of God, inviting, urging, and consoling. But when the greater part of them had stubbornly rejected Him and offered no hope of reform, He then, having broken the staff of "Favor," performed His "alien work" (Isaiah 28:21), pasturing those "destined for pain" <note>original: "podolentium"</note> as a flock of which He Himself was the master and judge. Just as love departed when the staff of "Favor" was broken, so zeal for the Jews as His people departed from Christ when the staff of "Pain" was broken. This signifies their total rejection until they eventually acknowledge their guilt and seek the face of Christ. Compare Ezekiel 16:41; Hosea 5:15. *n)* **to abolish** (verse 10). *o)* **brotherhood** (1) An abstract noun from "brother," more common among the Arabs. *p)* This clearly alludes to the ancient division of the people into Judah and Israel made in the time of Rehoboam and Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:10). Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymo" - St. Jerome, 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> therefore likes this interpretation: "That I might dissolve the covenant and the kinship and the concord which had been between Judah and Israel, and separate the brothers from one each other; so that in the number of the Apostles and those who had repented, he might again be called 'Judah' and one who confesses his God; but those who remained in the hardness of their heart and said, 'We have no king but Caesar,' might be called 'Israel' and 'Ephraim' and 'Joseph'." Thus far Jerome. By the very fact that He denies that Israel will be recognized by Judah as a brother, He also denies that He will be the God of Israel (that is, of the Jewish synagogue), or that they will be His people. Compare Hosea 2:3–7.

<margin>
v. 15. *q)*
</margin>

Furthermore, the Lord spoke—no longer to the Messiah or God the Son, who had indeed spoken in verses 4–14—but to me, Zechariah. For the one whom the Lord addresses is commanded to take up the "schema" <note>the outward appearance or role</note> of a **foolish shepherd**, and thus to prophesy about him not only with words but with signs. This can apply to Zechariah, but not to Christ. Here begins the new and third part of this chapter (see note on verse 1). *r)* **Once more** <note>original: "Adhuc"</note>. This adverb refers to what came before: as if to say, "just as you already prophesied above in verses 3, 5 and 10:2–3 against the evil shepherds of the Jews, so to resume and continue this same argument, take up further or again..." etc. *s)* **vessel** <note>original: "vas"</note>, that is, the instruments or whatever constitutes a shepherd's equipment. 1 Samuel 17:40, 49; compare Deuteronomy 22:5. Jerome says: "We ought to understand the 'vessels' of the shepherd as his distinctive marks and dress: the pouch, the staff, the pipe, and the whistle." *t)* **a foolish shepherd** (1). Compare Job 5:2, 3. He is soon called in verse 16 by a related name, a "worthless shepherd" or "vain shepherd." Jeremiah 4:22; Hosea 9:7. Furthermore, Bochartus <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> says: "Since it does not seem a foolish shepherd can be distinguished from a good one by his dress, I think the Prophet, commanded by God, took the dress, pouch, and staff of a shepherd, but expressed his foolishness by his actions; namely, while he neglected the flock of sheep that appeared in the vision, neither binding the broken ones, etc., just as God had predicted that foolish shepherd would behave toward the mystical sheep, that is, the Church of God in verse 16." *Hieroz. P. I. p. 455.* The Septuagint <note>original: "LXX"</note> translates this as <term>ποιμὴν ἄπειρος</term> <note>original: "an unskilled/inexperienced shepherd"</note>.

<margin>
v. 16. *u)*
</margin>

**Because**, if you ask, or if others ask you, what this "schema" of yours means: "behold, I..." etc. For in this way you must represent the foolish shepherd who will arise in the Church of God. Compare similar symbols in Isaiah 20:3 and following; Jeremiah 18:6; Ezekiel 12:11. *x)* I will act with just judgment, or I will permit to arise. Amos 6:14; compare 2 Thessalonians 2:10, 11. *y)* **a shepherd of this kind, foolish** (verses 15, 17). This can be understood collectively of an entire class of shepherds, primarily the shepherds of the Jewish people, about whom he had already complained in 10:2, 3 and here in verses 3, 5; the word "once more" hinted that the discourse was continuing here. Compare Isaiah 56:11. However, the explanation of those who interpret this as the Antichrist (since the description is singular) can be subordinated here. Jerome, among others, says: "The foolish and unskilled shepherd is undoubtedly the Antichrist... who is prophesied under his own name in Daniel 9:27 and 2 Thessalonians 2:4 as the 'abomination of desolation' who will sit in the temple of the Lord and make himself out to be God." Compare 1 John 2:18. *z)* **who** (he is now described by the actions of a stupid shepherd) **the perishing**. See note on verse 9. *a)* **will not visit**, care for, or look for. Chapter 10:3; Jeremiah 23:2; compare Ezekiel 34:3 and following. *b)* Namely, the one tender in age, who because of weakness cannot go forward and is left behind in the field or woods. So Tarnovius. But Bochartus says: "A lamb is not often searched for, because it rarely wanders from the flock and usually follows its mother. Accordingly, in Matthew 18:12, it is not a lamb that is sought, but a sheep that has gone astray." Therefore, the Septuagint, Arabic, and Vulgate more correctly translate "the dispersed"; the Syriac "those who wander"; Jonathan <note>the Aramaic Targum</note> "the vagabonds" or "those who have moved away." From the Arabic root *na'ara* <note>original: "נער"</note>, it means to go here and there, to wander. Compare Buxtorf's *Talmudic Lexicon*, column 1363, where the following is cited from the Jerusalem Talmud: "He who leads a flock of sheep is prohibited from *lana'aro* <note>original: "לנערו"</note>; what does this mean? To lead from one place to another." *Hieroz. P. I. 445 & 446.* Furthermore, the word for "young" is also used as a feminine in the *Kethiv* <note>the written tradition of the Hebrew text</note> of Genesis 24:16. *c)* Ezekiel 34:4, unlike what the Good Shepherd does. Luke 15:4 and following. *d)* **the broken**, which has a broken or dislocated bone, he will not care for by binding it. Ezekiel 34:4, 16. *e)* **the standing**, that is, one staying still out of fatigue or disease. Thus among the Arabs *nasaba* <note>original: "נצב"</note> is to stand and be weary; and the noun *nasab* is fatigue from a journey, or laboring under disease. This certainly fits this passage, comparing Ezekiel 34:4, 16, where instead of this word it says "to strengthen the diseased." *f)* Jonathan: "he will not carry." Although this pleases Bochartus less (thinking that the root *k-l-k-l* <note>original: "כלכל"</note> never occurs in the sense of "carrying"), we do not hesitate to approve it, comparing Jeremiah 20:9, Malachi 3:2, Proverbs 18:14, and Isaiah 40:11. But the Syriac has: "he will not nourish the standing ones." The Vulgate: "that which stands he will not nourish." Thus a most learned man says: "he will not sustain," namely with food and nourishment. "Standing," he says, is here opposed to "lying down" or "bedridden from disease"; for just as the sick need medicine, so those standing and healthy need nourishment to preserve their good condition. *Hieroz. P. I. 446*; compare 1 Kings 17:9, 18:4, Nehemiah 9:21.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final verses of Zechariah 11 regarding the "worthless shepherd" and begins the exposition of Chapter 12. The previous page discussed the betrayal of the true shepherd for thirty pieces of silver; here, the text transitions to the judgment upon the corrupt leader who replaces him and the subsequent prophecy regarding Israel’s future restoration.</meta>

g) on the contrary, he will devour the fat flesh, as in Ezekiel 34:3. Compare Hosea 4:8, Micah 3:5, and Matthew 23:14. h) and their hooves, according to Deuteronomy 14:6. He shall tear them apart (8) as in 1 Kings 19:11, by driving them too much over steep rocks and cliffs. The Targum <note>The Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> suggests: Just as Greece will exhaust them, so that the hooves are broken. Compare Isaiah 5:28 and Genesis 33:14. But Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar.</note> prefers "he shall pull off their hooves." For hooves are pulled off rather than split; the Prophet signifies by this hyperbole that this shepherd—or more truly, a ravenous wolf—will turn everything entirely to his own advantage, not omitting even the most worthless parts, such as the hooves of the cattle. Compare Exodus 10:26. *Hierozoïcon* Part I, 446.

# Woe to the worthless shepherd who leaves the flock! The sword shall be upon his arm and upon his right eye; his arm shall completely wither, and his right eye shall be utterly blinded.

<margin>
Kimchi <note>original: "קמ' ב"ז'ק" - Likely referring to Rabbi David Kimchi (Radak).</note>

### CHAPTER XII.
# The burden of the word of the LORD concerning Israel, says the LORD, who stretches out the heavens, lays the foundation of the earth, and forms the spirit of man within him:

<margin>
Kimchi
</margin>

<margin>
...the prophets had seen, so much so that he called himself the son of God. Thus, the threat would contain an irony against his presumption of power and wisdom, clearly as in Ezekiel 28:7. The explanation of B. Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow (1562–1633), a Lutheran theologian.</note> can be joined to what follows: *His arm*, which he nefariously misuses to skin the sheep and treat them tyrannically, by withering it shall wither; and *his right eye*, with which he ought to have looked out for healthy pasture for the flock, since he misuses it, by darkening it shall be darkened, so that at once all strength, all help, and all counsel perish from him, and the wicked man finally dies a wicked death. We add that the blinding of the right eye is also a matter of foulness and reproach, compare 1 Samuel 11:2. o) so that it becomes juiceless and bloodless, and consequently weak and powerless, chapter 14:12, 1 Kings 13:4, Ezekiel 37:14, Psalm 22:16, Luke 8:6. p) by darkening it shall be darkened (7) Genesis 27:1, Deuteronomy 34:7, Job 17:18.
</margin>

CHAPTER XII. verse 1. q) *The Prophecy, the Word of Jehovah.* <note>original: "Prophetia, Verbum Iehova"</note> understood through apposition or asyndeton <note>A grammatical term for omitting conjunctions like "and".</note>. We prefer Cocceius’s view: *The proclamation of the word of Jehovah*, because of the accents; compare the note on chapter 9:1, also Malachi 1:1. Here begins the final discourse of the Prophet, which continues to the end of the book. r) See the note on Hosea 1:1. Here, the speaker is Jehovah God the Son, specifically the one who in verse 10 speaks of himself as having been once pierced by the Jews. s) *concerning or upon Israel; not, against Israel.* For the prophecy that follows is not threatening, but consolatory for Israel, at least in most parts and regarding its main purpose. Interpreters disagree about its fulfillment. Gürtler <note>Nicolaus Gürtler (1654–1711), a Swiss theologian.</note> in *Prophetic Theology*, page 135, followed by Cocceius, thinks the punishment of the Ptolemies and Seleucids <note>The Greek dynasties that ruled after Alexander the Great.</note> who harassed Judea is predicted here, and that verses 1–2 refer to the victories of the Maccabees; verse 3–5 to the subjugation of neighboring nations; verse 6 to the salvation of Judah through the Messiah appearing in a humble state; verses 7–8 to God’s judgment against the enemies of the Church; verse 9 to the pouring out of the Holy Spirit; verse 10 to the calamities and lamentations of Judea in verses 11–14. However, there are various things that seem to oppose this opinion. 1) The very series of the prophecy. The previous chapter dealt with the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans because the Messiah was despised, the judgment on the bad shepherds, and finally the rejection of the Jewish people; it is improbable that the Prophet would jump back from these to the Maccabean times, as long as another mode of explanation remains that continues the sequence of the prophecy. The circumstances of the prophecy are added, for 2) Jerusalem is said to be a burdensome stone, not only to the Egyptians and Syrians, but to *all peoples* in verse 3. 3) The tranquility of Jerusalem, mentioned in verse 6 (compare chapter 14:10–11), hardly fits the Maccabean times, which were undoubtedly included under the "troublous times" of Daniel 9:25. 4) The leaders of Israel are named here as the *House of David* in verses 7, 8, and 10. The Maccabees were from the priestly line of Levi. 5) The promise in verse 8 is too magnificent to have been fulfilled in the Maccabees, etc. All these things lead us to seek the fulfillment of the Prophecy in the times of the New Testament. Most understand "Israel" here as the *Israel of God*, that is, the Church united from Jews and Gentiles, which God promises to wonderfully defend against all enemies in those many afflictions, provided she runs to Christ in true faith, truly repenting of her sins. This is indeed a pious application, based on the analogy of similar cases. However, the prophecy itself seems to deal with the Jewish people rather than the universal New Testament Church. For it is inscribed *upon Israel* in verse 1; and in the treatment itself, it names not only Jerusalem, Judah, and the house of David as distinct parts of the people (verses 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10), but also specifically names individual Jewish families in verse 12 and following. Furthermore, it points to those who will look upon Him whom they themselves had once pierced or handed over to be pierced (verse 10). Likewise, the affliction and the deliverance from it seem to be specific, due to particular circumstances: for example, Judah fighting for a time against Jerusalem—unwillingly and driven by the violence of enemies (verse 2); the tents of Judah being saved before Jerusalem (verse 7); the enemies and their horses being struck with stupor and blindness (verse 4), etc. Furthermore, this does not deal indefinitely with days of affliction, but with a certain and defined *day* or *time* (verses 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11), which is the day of the New Testament era looking toward the very last period of the world, to which most things from here to the end of Zechariah should be referred. Compare chapter 14:1, 6, 7, 10. Meyer <note>Probably Sebastian Meyer (1465–1545), a Reformer.</note> in his commentary on the end of Ezekiel, page 97, says: "Nor can Zechariah chapter 11 be adapted to past times, but must be referred to the illustrious conversion of the whole Jewish nation dispersed throughout the whole world, etc." So also Hoecke in his Commentary explains the latter part of this chapter from verse 7 to the end. And we note that the famous Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian.</note> holds this same opinion in his *Sacred Observations*, book 2, chapter 9, page 172. And Maimonides <note>Though the text says Maim, it likely refers to a Christian commentator’s use of him or a similar source.</note> in *Economy of the Old Testament*, page 1083, says: "The series of the times of the Church is continued as far as Israel is concerned, etc." Altogether, the Prophet in chapter 11 had drawn the thread of his prophecy down to the rejected Jewish people. Therefore, lest the state of rejection be thought to last forever, there follows now a promise concerning Israel (the Jewish people): first, regarding their future liberation from enemies (verses 1–9), and second, regarding their conversion to Christ (verses 10–14). While we take this prophecy in this way, we nevertheless leave the manner of its fulfillment to divine wisdom, and we refer our reader to those cautions we gave in the Preface, § 13. We add at least that Rabbi Kimchi explains verses 1–9 as the wicked attempts and punishment of Gog and Magog, concerning which see Ezekiel 38 and 39 and Revelation 20:8 and following. t) After the inscription, which is completed in the first half-verse, the prophecy itself begins. Since it contains magnificent promises placed beyond the grasp of reason, it first of all premises a description of the Promiser, so that by this it may excite attention, confirm the certainty of the thing promised, and remove any doubt of impossibility. See chapter 3:9, 8:6, and Isaiah 1:24, Hosea 11:11, etc. u) *of the one stretching out* or *who stretches out* the heavens like a curtain. The Lord adds these titles to suggest that it is therefore in His hand both to destroy and pull down, and to build and plant. So Kimchi. Compare Isaiah 44:24, 45:12, 51:13, Psalm 104:2, and Jeremiah 32:17. x) *and of the one placing it*, so that it may be firm, as if it rests on a most solid foundation—which otherwise, strictly speaking, is fluid. As the Poet sings: "It hangs, and places its tracks on no bottom." And as another says succinctly: "The Earth is like a ball, resting on no support, the heavy work hangs in the air beneath." y) *and of the one forming the spirit*; hence God is called the God of the spirits of all flesh in Numbers 16:22 and 27:16. Otherwise, the word *forming* (root: *yatzar*) is used for the shaping of matter. Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a Spanish Jewish scholar.</note> therefore explains this as referring to the organs of the body that receive the faculty of the spirit, namely the heart and the brain. But just as the noun *spirit* (root: *ruach*) is used for thought, as an immaterial thing (Genesis 6:5, 8:21), why can the root not be taken similarly? Compare Isaiah 43:10, Psalm 33:15, and the note on Amos 4:13. According to Cocceius, it notes not only the breathing in of the soul, but also the distribution of the gifts of the mind. z) He adds *of men* by name, not only because man is the chief of creatures, for whom this universe was created, but to teach that all men are in His power: the godly to be saved, and the ungodly—such as the future enemies of Jerusalem—to be destroyed. Compare Isaiah 45:12.

<margin>
v. 17. i) Vah! or Woe! Isaiah 1:4. Therefore, because in verse 16 God permitted that foolish shepherd to rise, this is not to be understood as His consent and approval, but as the exercise of judgment; otherwise, you could not say "Woe" to him. k) to the worthless shepherd, literally "shepherd of nothingness" or "of vanity," that is, vain and foolish, as in verse 15 and Job 13:4. The *Yod* letter here is not a suffix (for the grammatical construction of the governing word hardly allows that) but is paragogic <note>An extra letter added to the end of a word for emphasis or style.</note>, as in Isaiah 38:12 and in the word *leaving* (*ozvi*) which follows. Compare Genesis 49:11, Exodus 15:6, etc. l) to the one deserting the flock, for whom he ought to have watched, cared for, and defended. John 10:12. m) the sword shall be, or shall come upon, etc. Jeremiah 50:35–38. n) compare 1 Samuel 2:31, Psalm 10:15. Jerome says: "Moreover, the sword of the Lord shall be upon his arm and upon his right eye, so that his strength and all the boasting of his power may be dried up with dryness, and the knowledge which he falsely promised himself under a false name may be obscured by eternal darkness." And the same: "By the arm (understand) strength, and by the right eye the cunning with which he boasted that he saw the sacraments of God acutely, and saw more...
</margin>

<summary>This page provides a detailed philological and theological commentary on the transition from the "worthless shepherd" in Zechariah 11 to the promise of Jerusalem's deliverance in Zechariah 12. It argues that these prophecies refer to the latter days and the eventual conversion of the Jewish people rather than historical Maccabean victories.</summary>
