<meta>This page continues the transition from the end of Zechariah 11, which dealt with the "worthless shepherd," into the prophecies of Chapter 12 concerning the divine protection of Jerusalem and the physical and spiritual restoration of Judah. It specifically focuses on the "cup of staggering" and the "stone of burden" metaphors.</meta>

<header>ZECHARIAH 12 CAP. 12.</header>

<margin>
**Targum Jonathan:** Because the nations will also bring the men of the house of Judah, compelled by force, to the siege against Jerusalem. Specifically [Hebrew: *ve-gam*], this is a mark of obligation, and in this place indeed a burdensome one: *But also upon Judah it shall be* (i) it shall also fall upon Judah, or, also for Judah.
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 2. a)** See note on chapter 9, verse 4. **b)** Elsewhere this word [Hebrew: *saf*] denotes a basin (Exodus 12:22; 1 Kings 7:50; 2 Kings 12:14), but here it means a cup; just as the *mizrak* <term>mizrak: a bowl or phial used for sprinkling sacrificial blood</term> is used for a drinking vessel in Amos 6:6. It corresponds somewhat with the Latin *simpulum*, a type of wooden vessel used in sacrifices, and also with *scyphus* [a drinking cup]. **Targum Jonathan:** a vessel full of drunkenness or an intoxicating drink. The **Vulgate** [Latin Bible] inappropriately translates this as "threshold" (*superliminare*); as do the **Septuagint** [Greek Bible] and **Arabic** versions <unclear>ve-ad safah</unclear> in verse 6. This does not fit with the following word *ra’al* [staggering/vertigo], which is usually paired with "cup and wine," making it clear that a drinking vessel is meant, not a threshold. **c) Vulgate:** "of drunkenness." **d)** cf. Isaiah 51:17, 22; Psalm 60:5. **Cocceius:** "of vertigo." It signifies a cup or drink that causes such mental disturbance that it drives the drunkard into vertigo, shaking them to and fro. cf. Nahum 2:4. It refers to the drink of divine wrath in Jeremiah 25:15. The meaning is: Peoples will flow from all sides toward Jerusalem with great heat, as if to quench their thirst by capturing and plundering it; but this drink they thirst for will turn out badly for them: it will so intoxicate them that they fall, seized by vertigo, and sleep the sleep of death (Jeremiah 51:39, 57). **d)** A difficult clause. **Tarnovius** renders it thus: *for each of them will also be against Judah in the siege against Jerusalem or the Church, wishing to oppress her.* But **Schultens** translates: *and also against Judah, whoever shall be in the siege against Jerusalem;* though the Hebrew accents seem to contradict this. **Vulgate:** *But Judah also shall be in the siege against Jerusalem,* neglecting the initial word *al* [upon/against], the sense of which **Targum Jonathan** explained.
</margin>

-> 2 Behold, I am making Jerusalem a cup of staggering <note>original: "saf-ra'al"</note> to all <-
> -> the surrounding peoples; and also upon Judah it shall be in the siege of Jerusalem. <-

-> 3 And it shall be in that day, I will make Jerusalem a stone of burden for all <-
> -> the peoples; all who lift it shall be severely lacerated, and all the nations <-

-> of the earth shall be gathered against it. 4 In that day, says the LORD, I will strike every horse with panic, <-
> -> and its rider with madness; but upon the house of Judah I will open My eyes, and every <-

-> horse of the peoples I will strike with blindness. 5 And the leaders of Judah shall say in their heart: <-
> -> Strength is mine <note>or "The inhabitants of Jerusalem are my strength"</note> in the LORD of hosts, their God. <-

[Judah] will be held or compelled to be in the siege, etc. Compare a similar use of the word in 1 Samuel 18:11; Ezekiel 45:17; Psalm 56:13; Nehemiah 13:13; and among the Arabs in the Quran (Surah 6:52): "There shall not be anything upon you regarding their account," meaning, you will not be forced to give any account for them. **Kimchi** <note>Rabbi David Kimchi (1160–1235), a major medieval Hebrew grammarian and commentator.</note> however, says: But also upon Judah shall be the cup of staggering when they are forced to come into the siege against Jerusalem; which will certainly be a great distress for them. Furthermore, that Judah is hinted at here as fighting against its own metropolis appears from chapter 14:14; but that in this very act they are to be understood as oppressed and coerced is shown here in verses 4, 5, and 7, where they are introduced as being saved. **e)** "in the siege" (Ezekiel 4, 3).

<margin>
**v. 3.**
</margin>
**f)** Namely, "it shall happen." Another allegory confirms what was said in verse 2. **g)** i.e., I will cause Jerusalem to become. cf. v. 2; Ezekiel 35:4. **h)** a stone of burden or heavy carrying. **(i)** **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), the translator of the Vulgate.</note> has notable remarks here: "It is a custom in the cities of Palestine," he says, "and even today throughout all Judea an old tradition is preserved, that in villages, towns, and forts, very heavy round stones are placed, which young men use for exercise, lifting them according to their strength—some to the knees, some to the navel, some to the shoulders and head, and some above the head with straight, joined hands, demonstrating the greatness of their strength. In the citadel of Athens, near the statue of Minerva, I saw a bronze sphere of very heavy weight; when I asked what it meant, I was told by the inhabitants that the strength of athletes was tested on that mass, and no one entered a contest until it was known by the lifting of the weight who should be matched against whom." The sense, therefore, is this: I will set Jerusalem before all nations like a very heavy stone to be lifted. They will indeed lift it and ravage it according to their strength; but it is necessary that, while it is lifted, the very exertion of lifting such a heavy stone will leave some cut or scrape on the bodies of those lifting it. **i)** v. 2, 4. **k)** all who lift it—whoever takes it up and places it upon themselves to carry, moving it from its place. Genesis 44:13; Nehemiah 13:15. **Targum Jonathan:** *whoever does violence to her.* **l) Vulgate:** *they shall be torn with laceration.* Thus, in lifting and carrying Jerusalem, they will not test their strength with impunity. (3) Leviticus 21:5; cf. chapter 19:28 and Luke 20:18. **Targum Jonathan:** *in wasting they shall be wasted.* **m)** an illustration of the first half of the verse. As if to say: I have not said without reason that Jerusalem will be a stone of burden to all peoples, for all the nations of the earth shall be gathered (though with a disastrous outcome for them). v. 2; Micah 4:11.

<margin>
**v. 4.**
</margin>
**n)** "In that day," i.e., at that time. v. 3. **o)** See note on verse 1. **p)** every horse of the enemy. cf. chapter 10:5. **q)** with panic (2) Deuteronomy 28:28, so that the horse, being insane and headlong, carries its rider with it into disaster. cf. Psalm 48:6. **r)** with madness (3) Ibid. I will take away all counsel and mind from them, so that they cast themselves headlong into the gravest destruction. **Tarnovius:** cf. Ezekiel 23:27; Judges 4:15; Psalm 76:6, 7. **s)** which just now had been forced to fight against Jerusalem (v. 6). They are therefore exempted from the fate of the hostile peoples by whom they had been driven to fight, because they fought unwillingly. **t)** I will indeed "open My eyes," namely, as **Rashi** <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, a premier medieval commentator.</note> and **Kimchi** explain: to guard them from the plague with which I strike the nations, even though they were among them; and so that their horses may be rescued from the plague. **Targum Jonathan:** *I will manifest my power to do good for them.* cf. Deuteronomy 11:12; 1 Kings 8:52; Psalm 32:8; 33:18; 34:16. **u)** "every" indeed. **x)** with blindness (2) Deuteronomy 28:28. There seems to be an antithesis here between the eyes of the Lord, with which He will watch over the house of Judah, and the eyes of the horses, of which He will deprive them. cf. 2 Kings 6:18.

<margin>
**v. 5.**
</margin>
**y)** Wherefore, when they see the enemies struck with madness and their horses with panic and blindness, and themselves rescued by the wonderful providence of God, they shall say. **z)** "the leaders of Judah," with their thousands (see note ch. 9, 7); namely, those very ones whom the enemies had forced to besiege Jerusalem with them. v. 2, 6. **a)** "in their heart," which will conceive a holy wonder at the miraculous help of God (Isaiah 49:21) and, once the distress that constricted it is loosened, it will be enlarged (ch. 60:5). It suggests that the joy will be such that it will be easier for them to perceive it in their heart than to express it with the mouth. Psalm 4:8; 106:2. For it is supposed they will also profess with their mouth later what they had conceived in their heart (Psalm 116:10). But **Jerome**, who explains the following laboriously, says: "They shall make vows in their hearts, because they do not dare to speak freely, that Jerusalem may win, so that Judah, though conquered with the enemies, may win with its own citizens." **b) Schultens:** "The inhabitants of Jerusalem are a confirmation [strength] to me," etc. It would be a Piel participle with the prefix Aleph dropped... As for the sense, it will be said below in verse 7 that the Lord will save the tents of Judah before Jerusalem, at least encouraging them to trust first in Jehovah their God. cf. 2 Kings 7:9 ff. The Greek translator **Aquila** uses the imperative: *be strengthened, O inhabitants,* etc. The **Vulgate** has: *let them be strengthened for me.* But it is rather a noun [Hebrew: *amzah*] of the same form as *ashpah* (quiver) in Isaiah 22:6... **Kimchi** therefore says: They will say—when they are among their enemies—"the inhabitants of Jerusalem will be a strength to me," since they will go out to fight by the help of the Lord their God; and thus we shall be rescued through them. **Targum Jonathan** however: *salvation was found for the inhabitants of Jerusalem in the Word of the Lord,* etc. as if he had read "for my salvation" [*lishi*] instead of "strength to me" [*li amzah*]. To us, among such a diversity of opinions, the explanation of **Tarnovius** is most pleasing: *Strength is to me and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, not in ourselves, but in Jehovah,* etc... formerly fearful, now we are full of confidence and divine strength. cf. v. 8; Isaiah 33:24; Joel 4:10. **c)** namely, in Christ. cf. Isaiah 45:24. **d)** Who, just as He is their God through the covenant of grace, so at this very time He demonstrates Himself as such to them openly, by defending the inhabitants of Jerusalem and rescuing us from the enemies. v. 8; ch. 8:8; 9:16; 10:6; Exodus 29:46; Ezekiel 34:30.

<header>ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER 12. 12</header>

<margin>
v. 6. e) See notes on verses 1 and 4. f) Compare with verse 2. That is to say, those very people who were recently forced by the enemy to fight against their own will now turn their weapons against the enemies and rule over their former oppressors, after they feel themselves in their hearts to be equipped with divine strength (v. 5). g) Like a basin <note>original: "fovea"</note> or pot, as in 1 Kings 7:38 where it refers to a laver; 1 Samuel 2:14 where it is a vessel for cooking meat; and 2 Chronicles 6:13 where it is a platform. The figure represents a rounded shape, derived from the Arabic <note>original: "fistuli forma"</note> meaning to wind around or roll in a circle. Similarly, the words for a pyre or hearth <note>original: "דּוּר & מְדוּרָה"</note> also come from the Arabic root meaning to go around, as if things are piled in a circle and set ablaze. This fits this passage perfectly, where the leaders of Judah are described through the allegory of fire as being about to consume the surrounding peoples. See also Leviticus 1:35. h) Among the wood which is consumed by fire (Jeremiah 5:14); thus the leaders of Judah will consume their enemies. See notes on Obadiah v. 18. i) Indeed, like a torch of fire (Genesis 15:17, Judges 15:4-5). k) In a sheaf or sheaves of harvested grain, which ignite much more easily than wood because of their dryness (Jeremiah 9:21). l) And they shall consume, as fire consumes its material. Let the allegory continue (Obadiah v. 18). Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum of Jonathan</note> says: "and they shall plunder all the wealth of the peoples." m) Toward the right and toward the left, that is, in every direction (Isaiah 9:19, 54:3, Job 23:9). This is shown by the following word "round about," added as an explanation. Jonathan says: "from the south and from the north." For to the Hebrews, the "right" is the south and the "left" is the north (Genesis 14:15). Here they are joined by a figure of speech <note>term: synecdoche (using a part to represent the whole)</note> to represent all quarters of the world, as in Psalm 89:13. n) With whom they had previously been forced to join (v. 2, 3, 4; cf. Psalm 41:15, Micah 4:13). o) The first half of the verse described the destruction of the enemies; this half, therefore, describes the resulting tranquility and peace of Jerusalem (Chapter 14:21, Jeremiah 17:25; cf. verse 3 above). q)
</margin>

<margin>
Chapter 3:10, Micah 4:4. When it is said that "Jerusalem shall dwell in Jerusalem," there are two different meanings: the first refers to the contents or the inhabitants <note>term: metonymy (the name of a place used for its people)</note>; the second refers to the container or the city itself. p) Furthermore, as in former times (Chapter 1:17, 2:16), contrary to what the enemies had thought...
</margin>

## 6 In that day I will make the leaders^e of Judah like a fire pot among wood^f and like a flaming torch among sheaves;^g and they shall consume^h all the surrounding peoples on the right^m and on the left,^n and Jerusalem^o shall yet dwell in her own place,^q even in Jerusalem.^p
## 7 And the LORD^r will save the tents^s of Judah first,^t so that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem may not be magnified over Judah.^u
## 8 In that day the LORD will defend^z the inhabitant of Jerusalem; and he that is feeble^a among them in that day shall be like David;^b and the house of David shall be like God,^d like the Angel^e of the LORD before them.^f
## 9 And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem.^g

<sig>Mm mm 2 81 2</sig>

---

e) v. 6. ...contrary to what those had thought who presumed they could utterly wipe out Jerusalem (cf. verse 3 above). q) "Under herself," that is, in her own place (Chapter 14:10, Exodus 10:23, Leviticus 13:23). She will be unshaken and immovable (Psalm 48:9, 87:1, 125:1). This is contrasted with the wicked attempt to lift or move her mentioned in verse 3. He adds: and she shall prosper. v. 7. r) Moreover, the Lord will save (Chapter 9:16, 10:6). s) The "tents of Judah," in contrast to the princes and the metropolitan citizens, or the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem mentioned in the second half of the verse. These are therefore the provincial people, who inhabit only villages, hamlets, or unwalled towns (v. 2). Jonathan translates: "the towns of the House of Judah" (1 Kings 12:16). t) "First," meaning before the capital city or Jerusalem itself; this connection is easily supplied from the following clause. This very point makes the explanation by Gousset <note>original: "Guffeti"</note> in his work *Typico-Prophetic* (p. 91) difficult to admit: he claims "The Messiah will save the Jews first, before other nations." For if "first" refers to the nations, the reason for priority which the Lord immediately adds would hardly fit. Unless one wishes to say that the "house of David" and "Jerusalem" represent the Church gathered from the Gentiles in opposition to the Church gathered from the Jews—but no other example of such a thing exists. Cocceius rightly says on this passage: "The inhabitants of Jerusalem must be taken literally here; both because they are contrasted with a specific part of Judah not living in Jerusalem, and because glory over Judah is attributed to them, and because both groups are understood as needing the Lord's salvation." Cocceius therefore explains it thus: This passage teaches that the beginning of the Gospel preaching had to occur outside Jerusalem, just as the Baptist preached at the Jordan in the wilderness (Isaiah 40:3) and Christ in Galilee (Isaiah 8:23, 9:1; add Matthew 4:13, 15, Luke 23:5, John 3:22). The reason for this choice is indicated by Christ in Matthew 11:25-26 and 1 Corinthians 1:19-28. Hence, the "builders" rejected this stone (Psalm 118:22); the rulers did not believe in Him, but the common people did (John 7:48-49), which became a "stumbling block" to those sitting in Jerusalem (Isaiah 8:14). See also his Lexicon (p. 13). However, even this explanation hardly satisfies the prophecy. For this is about a salvation where the Lord saves Judah and Jerusalem from the very distress described in verse 2, at the same time the enemies coming against Jerusalem are destroyed (v. 9). Christ came in the flesh long after the Maccabean afflictions, which is how Cocceius explains the preceding parts. We said above regarding verse 1 that this prophecy seems to us to look toward the end of the New Testament or the very last period of the world; therefore, we leave the manner of its fulfillment to God. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> illustrates the word "first" this way: "before the Jerusalemites come out of the city" (to fight the enemy). The sense would be that the glory of defeating the enemy will not belong to the Jerusalemites—who will exit the city after the enemy at the house is overcome—but to Judah, who in verse 6 was said to consume the enemies like fire; or rather to the Lord Himself, who strikes the enemies with madness (v. 4) and clothes Judah with strength to further defeat the already confused enemies (v. 5). u) So that there is no great boasting; that is, according to the Vulgate, "lest they should glorify themselves magnificently," as if the virtue of the princes or the fortifications of the capital had defeated the enemy (Daniel 8:9-10, Isaiah 10:12). Thus God prevents all human boasting so that (as Jerome says) they may know the victory in both cases belongs to the Lord. In this way, He keeps the glory for Himself, removing pride from the superiors and contempt from the inferiors. x) From which come the princes (cf. v. 12 and notes on Ezekiel 44:3, 46:16 ff). v. 8. y) See notes on v. 1. z) He will protect by equipping them with divine strength (Chapter 9:15, Isaiah 31:5). a) Used in an expansive sense: "one who has fallen," who after his fall is raised up by divine power—as can be seen in Peter. However, "the one stumbling" <note>original: "lapsans"</note> does not always mean someone who has actually fallen, but someone who is weak (the result put for the cause); cf. 1 Samuel 2:4, where those who stumble are contrasted with the mighty. Thus the Septuagint, Jonathan, Arabic, and Syriac versions use "the weak" (cf. Psalm 31:11). "Weak" is used here in comparison to others who are stronger; as if to say, God will so strengthen them that he who is called "weak" at that time will be like David of old. Similarly, in Isaiah 65:20, such longevity is promised that a person a hundred years old will be called a "youth." b) That most brave hero (cf. Isaiah 33:24, 40:31, 43:24, 60:22). c) But the house of David, or the leaders of the people (v. 7). Kimchi says: "The King Messiah." But see what follows. d) Jonathan says: "they shall be successful like heroes." The Septuagint and Arabic: "like the house of God." Gousset (p. 48) says more aptly: "Indeed, He promises the conformity of the faithful with Christ." The fact that someone is called both "God" <note>original: "Elohim"</note> and the "Angel of Jehovah" implies that there is one who is both God and the Angel of the Lord: and that is Christ, the very pattern to whose likeness the Church is called. Cocceius (Lexicon p. 99, 354) thinks the prefix "as" <note>term: Caph (the Hebrew letter 'K' used for comparison)</note> here is a "Caph of Truth," meaning: "And the house of David, that is, the Son of David, shall be before the inhabitants of Jerusalem in words and deeds as God, and as the Angel of God who is God, equal with God (Philippians 2:6, cf. John 1:14); He will show Himself to be such as He ought to show Himself." However, setting aside that "house of David" is a collective name, not an individual one (cf. v. 12), Christ Himself is introduced speaking in verse 10, promising that He will pour out the spirit of grace upon the house of David; we are hardly led to understand this about Christ Himself, who was anointed by the Father (Psalm 45:8). Furthermore, the prefix "as" here must be taken the same way as in the preceding clause: there it compared different things, so it should here as well. e) And like the uncreated Angel of the Lord, who is at once God Himself, as He was just called (cf. Genesis 16:7 with v. 13; and notes on Exodus 23:20). Moreover, the word "like" denotes conformity here, not equality, as in Matthew 5:48 (cf. 2 Samuel 14:17, 20). f) The Syriac says: "who was before them." The accents allow this; unless you decide that "before them" is also understood in the preceding clause. This seems to refer to the history of the Exodus from Egypt (Exodus 14:19, 23:20, 23), where the uncreated Angel of God preceded the Israelite camp as the leader of His people (cf. Philippians 4:13). v. 9. g) v. 8. See notes on v. 1.

* v. 6. "Among the wood" <note>original: "בְּעֵצִים"</note> with the vowel Kamatz in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5. "Among sheaves" <note>original: "בְּעָמִיר"</note> thus with Segol and Munach in 1, 2, 3. "And they shall consume" <note>original: "וְאָכְלוּ"</note> with Gerashayim in 1.
* v. 8. "The feeble" <note>original: "הַנִּכְשָׁל"</note> with Patach in 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 20, 22, against the analogy and the printed Masorah. For "like the Angel" <note>original: "כְּמַלְאַךְ"</note> some read "and the Angel," and thus in the margin of 6, 9.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Zechariah 12, specifically focusing on the divine promise to destroy the enemies of Jerusalem and the subsequent spiritual outpouring that leads the people to repentance and mourning over "the one they pierced."</meta>

<header>### ZECHARIAH 12. CHAPTER 12.</header>

<margin>
On adoption, chapter 8, 15. Galatians 4:5-6. Through whom, as a pledge, grace is sealed in hearts (2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13-14), driving out slavish fear (2 Timothy 1:7; compare John 1:17) and leading to supplication.
</margin>

<margin>
h) **They seek.** This denotes the effort to be applied to this matter and the direction of providence toward that end. As if to say: "Then I will apply effort so that they may be cut off." Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> compares this to notes on chapter 6:7. Or: "I will require," specifically the works and deeds of the nations, as a just judge (1 Samuel 20:16; Ezekiel 3:18, 20). i) **I will seek to destroy;** or, "I will require their destruction" (Haggai 2:22). k) Compare Isaiah 30:27, 60:12, and Jeremiah 30:11. From this it is clear that this prophecy was not to be fulfilled around the beginnings of the New Testament; for in those times God did not destroy the nations coming against Jerusalem, but rather destroyed Jerusalem itself along with the Jewish republic and Levitical worship through those nations. l) See verses 2, 3, 4, 6.
</margin>

->And it shall come to pass on that day, that I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem. And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn. In that day shall there be a great mourning in Jerusalem, as the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon.<-

*q) **Who shall instruct them,** so that with a supplicating voice they may seek the grace which they once despised, to be given and confirmed to them now (Jeremiah 31:9; Psalm 28:2; Daniel 9:3; compare Hosea 12:5; Romans 8:26-27). q) **They shall look to me.** Here follows the effect resulting from the outpouring of the Holy Spirit: namely, a look of trust toward Christ, accompanied by grief for former sins. This is not a wicked look, as in the past, or one joined with mockery (Psalm 2:18). For Cocceius rightly says on this passage: "To look" is the act of faith turning itself away from a vain hope toward the true <term>stronghold of salvation</term> <note>original: "salutis arce"</note> (chapter 9:12) and resting in it (compare Isaiah 45:22). Such a look is surely like that with which the Israelites of old, bitten by serpents, turned themselves to the bronze serpent erected by Moses as a type <note>A "type" is a biblical person or event seen as a precursor to something later, specifically Christ.</note> (Numbers 21:9; John 3:14-15). Gousset’s observation (p. 492) is worthy of being added here. He says that when he examined this word in Zechariah 12:10, he observed it implies a leaning of the soul, or at least the will, not a forced or unwilling sight; and not only that, but a look with approval and love (as in Psalm 102:20; Isaiah 66:2). And where a creature looks to God with desire and hope of finding a refuge in Him (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 51:1). Therefore, this passage (Zechariah 12:10) fits the conversion of a people who previously persecuted Christ. The Greek preposition *eis* (into/toward) in the citation of John 19:37 points to the same. But in the other citation in Revelation 1:7 concerning judgment, where the sight might be involuntary, the preposition *eis* is missing; it seems to be only an allusion rather than a strict citation. r) **To me.** Who is this? It is added, **"to him,"** namely the one they pierced, by way of clarification (as in Leviticus 22:15). The particle **את** <note>The Hebrew direct object marker</note> is governed less by the preceding verb "they shall look" than by the following "to pierce," with which it is joined by the accent marks. Cocceius indeed thinks the Father is speaking here—of Himself in the first person and the Son in the third: "to me, God the Father, him whom..." etc.

They pierced. But this is forced and stands against the citation in John 19:37: *They shall look on him whom they pierced* <note>original Greek: ὄψονται εἰς ὃν ἐξεקέντησαν</note>. Therefore, the words in their entirety are those of the Son of God or the <term>God-Man</term> <note>original: "Theanthropos"</note>. That it is God who speaks appears from the fact that He says He will pour out the Spirit of grace and supplications; yet that He is simultaneously man is shown by what follows, "whom they pierced," for God alone cannot be pierced. s) Nothing is more appropriately expressed than the crucifixion of Christ, in which He was pierced, struck through, and transfixed with nails and the soldier’s spear (compare Deuteronomy 32:15; Isaiah 13:4-5; Psalm 22:17 and 69:27). Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa, a noted commentator on prophecy</note> observes excellently (Sacred Observations Book II, ch. 9, p. 172) that many authors take John 19:37 as applying solely to the piercing of Christ’s side by the soldier’s spear. It should be held that John extends this testimony not to this act alone, but to all the preceding events. "These things were done," he says. Thus far Vitringa. It should be noted that this prophecy, regarding the confession of the Messiah, has already been fulfilled; but regarding the repentant look, which is the primary aim of the prophecy, it is still to be fulfilled. Moreover, the ancient Hebrews interpreted this as referring to the Messiah—though restricted to the "Messiah son of Joseph" whom Jewish legend says will fall in battle—in the Talmudic Tractate *Sukkah* (f. 52a), and also Abraham ibn Ezra and Abarbanel in their commentaries on this place. t) **And they shall mourn** in repentance (v. 12; chapter 7:15; Matthew 5:4) and out of the sorrow that is according to God (2 Corinthians 7:9-10). They will grieve for their sins committed throughout so many centuries (chapter 13:1; Isaiah 6:4, 34 ff.), especially that they and their ancestors not only rejected Christ their Savior but with a monstrous crime drove Him to the cross and pierced Him. They shall strike their grieving breasts (Isaiah 32:12) like the tax collector (Luke 18:13), to testify to their inward repentance and acknowledgment of their crimes (Jeremiah 31:19; Luke 23:48). There is another mourning of which Christ speaks in Matthew 24:30 and John in Revelation 1:7—namely, a mourning of punishment, by which the wicked will bewail their own unhappiness when they see Jesus Christ, whom they once rejected and whose death they approved, coming with great glory and majesty as an angry judge. This present mourning is considered a fruit of the Spirit of grace and prayer, while that other is the horrible offspring of an evil conscience. u) **For him** <note>original Hebrew: אֵלָיו</note>. Gousset (p. 605) takes this neutrally as "because of that," meaning because of the murder. He argues: 1) The pronoun would not agree with "to me"; 2) They do not mourn for Him, since they see Him alive, but they mourn the sin by which they had pierced Him. But we prefer to refer it to the person: "because of Him," because He was pierced by them. This fits the solemnity of the passage and the added comparison of mourning for an only son and a firstborn, where **עַל** <note>the preposition "over/for"</note> is usually placed before persons rather than things. The change in grammatical person does not hinder this, as Hebrews often change from the first or second person to the third after the relative "who" <note>Hebrew: "asher"</note> (as in Isaiah 18:16; Lamentations 3:1). x) Not a common mourning, but as if with a mourning etc. y) **For an only son,** whose death is usually the most sorrowful for parents. Mourning for an only son seems here to be taken simply for an immense and extraordinary grief (Jeremiah 6:26; Amos 8:10). Cocceius, however, thinks the mourning is magnified by the value of the person, who is the only-begotten Son of God (John 1:14, 18; 3:16, 18). z) **And shall be in bitterness,** that is, they shall weep bitterly (Isaiah 23:4). a) **For a firstborn,** who under the Old Testament had great dignity above the other brothers (Genesis 49:3; Deuteronomy 21:17). According to the explanation of Cocceius and Tarnovius, see Romans 8:29, Colossians 1:15, 18; Hebrews 1:3, 6; Revelation 1:5.

<column-break/>

v. 10. m) **Then indeed,** when the rebellious nations are cut off (v. 9), **I will pour.** This word shows the abundance of the gift (compare notes on Joel 3:1 and Isaiah 44:3-4; Ezekiel 39:29; Romans 5:5). The firstfruits of this outpouring occurred long ago upon the Apostles on the day of Pentecost, according to the prediction of Joel (Acts 2:16 ff.); but here it treats the outpouring of the same Spirit upon the Jews for the conversion of the entire nation, so that every single family might mourn for the crime once committed against Christ and turn themselves to the rock of salvation they once rejected. This outpouring, considering the scope of the prophecy, belongs not to the past, but to the future (Isaiah 32:15). n) These are the subjects receiving the Spirit. Although in verses 7 and 8 the divisions of the people were distinguished, here they are comprehended together by <term>synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note>, as is apparent from the effect of the outpouring throughout the whole land and every Jewish family in verse 12. o) **Spirit of grace** (Hebrews 10:29), through which the love and grace of God is poured into their hearts (Romans 5:5).

v. 11. b) See notes on verse 1. c) The same mourning is described as in verse 10; its magnitude and universality are illustrated by comparison with another great, public, and historic mourning. The text shows no sign of a change in subject or predicate. Therefore, Cocceius and others—who explain this as the mourning of judgment where those who did not mourn over the pierced one now mourn for another cause—do not persuade us. Rather, the theme of the gospel promise continues thereafter in chapter 13:1. d) See verses 7, 10. e) Tarnovius says most simply: **as the mourning of Hadadrimmon**, which is a place in the valley of Megiddo. The place which gave occasion for the mourning is described partly generally (Valley of Megiddo) and partly specifically (Hadadrimmon). Jerome says Hadadrimmon was a town in the valley of Megiddo, called Maximinianopolis in his time. Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> links it to the mourning for Ahab, son of Omri, and the mourning for Josiah, son of Amon, who was killed in the plain of Megiddo. Lightfoot (in *Chronicle of the Old Testament*, p. 46) thinks the prophet alludes to two great universal lamentations of Israel; the first at the Rock of Rimmon where a whole tribe was reduced to 600 men (Judges 20:47, 21:6, 13). But the objection is that that rock was simply called Rimmon, not Hadadrimmon.

# v. 10. For "the inhabitant" some versions have "the inhabitants." Similarly above in v. 7.

<summary>This page analyzes Zechariah 12:9-11, interpreting the "outpouring of the Spirit" and the "piercing" as a prophecy of the Jewish people's future conversion and repentance regarding the crucifixion of Christ. It includes scholarly debates on whether the mourning refers to historical figures like Josiah or symbolic lamentation for an only child.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Zechariah 12, specifically focusing on the universal mourning of the tribes of Israel, followed by the transition to Chapter 13, which promises a fountain for purification and the removal of idolatry.</meta>

<header>### ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER 12. 13.</header>

<margin>
f) A city of the Manassites with its surrounding field, located within the borders of the three tribes of Issachar (Joshua 12:21; 17:11; Judges 1:27; 5:19; 2 Kings 9:27). It was here that Josiah was killed by Pharaoh <note>Pharaoh Necho II, during the Battle of Megiddo</note>, inciting a great lamentation for him in Jerusalem and throughout all of Judah (2 Kings 23:29; 2 Chronicles 35:22, 24, 25).
</margin>

<margin>
g) **Moreover, the whole land shall mourn**, specifically the land of Judah or Israel, which was discussed in the preceding verses (see note on verse 10). The text continues describing the mourning of the Jewish people, which verses 10 and 11 had described as immense and bitter; now it is described as universal, reaching throughout the whole land and every single family. This makes it clear that the subject is such a conversion of the Jews that it will be both sincere and so illustrious that, as the Apostle says, "all Israel shall be saved" (Romans 11:26).
</margin>

<margin>
h) **And indeed, each family separately.** (Exodus 16:9). As Balduinus <note>Friedrich Balduin, a Lutheran theologian</note> advises, this mourning will not be partial or limited to a few, nor will it be feigned or hypocritical. Instead, all will mourn from the bottom of their hearts, as if they were mourning alone. That is to say: as many families as there are, so many will be the choirs of mourners; they shall all mourn collectively, and each one individually.
</margin>

<margin>
i) What he said in general in the preceding half-verse about the land and the individual families, he now breaks down into parts here and in verse 13. He then gathers these same parts back into a total sum in verse 14. He begins with the family of David as the royal line, to show that from the highest to the lowest, everyone will mourn (verse 7; chapter 13:1). Jerome says: "In David, the royal tribe is understood, that is, Judah; in Nathan, the prophetic order is described; Levi refers to the Priests, from whom the priesthood arose; in Shimei, the teachers are understood, for from this tribe the ranks of masters sprang forth."
</margin>

<margin>
k) This is said according to the custom of the Israelites, among whom the sexes lived not only separately (cf. Genesis 18:9; chapter
</margin>

->**CHAPTER XIII.**<-

1 In that day there shall be a fountain $^r$ opened $^s$ to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem for sin and for uncleanness. $^t$
2 And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord of hosts, that I will cut off the names of the idols $^u$ out of the land, $^x$ and they shall no more be remembered...

<margin>
CHAPTER XIII. verse 1. They were separated for the sake of modesty (cf. Exodus 15:20).
</margin>

---

l) **Jerome**, as we just mentioned, thinks the prophet **Nathan** is meant, and under him, the prophetic order. But **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rashi</note>, following the mind of others, thinks it refers to **Nathan**, the son of David (2 Samuel 5:14; 1 Chronicles 3:5; Luke 3:31). In the same way, he wants the **Shimeites**, who follow, to be a branch of the Davidic family. He says: "He mentions the house of David generally at first, then particularly and distributively." But the interposed family of the **Levites** stands in the way of this opinion. **verse 13. m)** **Of the Levites.** (Exodus 2:1). **n)** **Of the Shimeites** or **Simeonites**, that is, the tribe of **Simeon**. Others take it for the family of the **Gershonites** (cf. Numbers 3:21; Exodus 6:17). Finally, others (cited by Rabbi Solomon) take it for a branch of the Davidic family named after **Shammua**, the son of David (2 Samuel 5:14). However the matter stands, the goal of the prophecy remains clear enough. **verse 14. o)** Likewise, **all the remaining families**, of which to weave a catalog would be too long and laborious. That is to say: not only those families I have already mentioned will mourn, but also all the rest that I have not mentioned; indeed, to put it briefly, each and every one. Thus "the rest" stands for "the others" (Deuteronomy 19:20; 1 Chronicles 13:2). Others: "the remnant," that is, those surviving from the hardships of so many centuries (Isaiah 10:21, 22; chapter 11:11). **p)** **See verse 12.** **q)** This is a continuation of the prophecy from the preceding chapter concerning the Conversion of the Jews. This is apparent both from the notation of time, **"In that day"** (cf. chapter 12:3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11), and the designation of the subject, **"the house of David"** and the inhabitants of **Jerusalem** (cf. chapter 12:7, 8, 10). The sequence of the argument itself also teaches this, as will be said shortly. For there are two parts to this chapter. **I.** It completes the argument begun in the previous chapter. To those whom he had introduced in chapter 12:10ff. as mourning on account of their sins, he now promises the grace of: 1) the remission of sins through washing from the fountain of salvation opened (verse 1); 2) sanctification and renewal, so that idols are no longer worshipped by them, nor even named (verse 2). Likewise, the spirit of uncleanness is to be abolished (ibid.), and false prophets must either be killed by righteous zeal if they wish to prophesy falsely further, or they will acknowledge and set aside their falsehood (verses 3–6). **II. The fate** of the Jewish people from the beginning of the New Testament is repeated, as if to be compressed into a short system: where 1) the death of Christ (verse 7); 2) the collection of the "little sheep," namely the Apostles and disciples of Christ, and as many Jews as believed in Christ after his death (ibid.); 3) the judgment of destruction, to be brought by the Romans upon the stubborn Jews who refused to believe in the Gospel of Christ (verse 8); 4) the restriction of that same judgment, that at least the entire nation would not be cut off by the Romans, but a third part of it would survive the destruction (ibid.); 5) the testing of this third part in the fire and their conversion to Christ (ibid.). In this way, he shows the connection of this part of the chapter with the preceding ones, as he returns to the very things that were dealt with above. Now we come to the explanation of the individual points. **"In that day"**, when the immense and universal mourning of repentance will be among the Jews through the operation of the Holy Spirit (verse 12:10ff.). **verse 1) Fountain**, Christ himself as once slain (chapter 12:10), now to be exhibited to them through faith in the blood of the new covenant (chapter 9:11), poured out for the washing and remission of sin (Matthew 26:28; Romans 3:25; 5:9; Ephesians 1:7; Colossians 1:14; Hebrews 9:14; 1 Peter 1:2; 1 John 5:6). **Abarbanel** <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Portuguese Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> certainly explains this as the Messiah in this place and at Ezekiel 47, folio 218, though only in this respect: that he would be a fountain of pure and clear doctrine. Now, the use of water is twofold: first, for quenching thirst, as Christ elsewhere calls the thirsty to himself and satisfies them both with his doctrine and with the gifts of the Holy Spirit flowing abundantly from him (cf. Isaiah 12:3; 55:1; John 4:14; 7:37, 38; Revelation 21:6); second, for cleansing and washing, as Christ cleanses us by his blood and Spirit, primarily through baptism, no less from the dominion than from the guilt of sins (Ezekiel 36:25; Hebrews 10:23; 1 John 1, 7; Revelation 1:5). Regarding the first respect, **Jonathan** <note>Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation</note> translates: "the doctrine of the law, open like a spring of water" (cf. below chapter 14:8). But the end of the verse proves that the second respect applies here: **"against sin and uncleanness."** Therefore, it is called a "fountain" to suggest the abundance and perpetuity of the origins of grace in Christ (cf. Jeremiah 2:13; 17:13; Psalm 36:10; 68:27; and notes on 1 Kings 7:26). **s)** Nor is it perhaps a "closed" fountain (as is sometimes the custom in the East where water is rarer, Song of Solomon 4:12), but **"opened"**, that is, accessible to each and every person who truly mourns on account of sins, forbidden to no one (cf. Matthew 11:28). **t)** (See chapter 12:7, 8, 10). **u)** For the cleansing of sin and foulness or uncleanness, on account of which they shall mourn (chapter 12:10ff.; cf. Leviticus 12:2, 5; 15:19; and Isaiah 64:4, 5). **Jonathan** translates: "and their debts shall be forgiven," just as the waters of sprinkling commanded from the ashes of the heifer which is sacrificed for sin (cf. notes on Numbers 19:9, 13; also Psalm 51:9; Hebrews 1:3; 1 Peter 1:2). **x)** (See note on verse 1). **y)** (Cf. note on chapter 12:1). **z)** A somewhat proverbial expression, as if to say: I will so cut off idols and the worship of idols that they are not even to be named anymore (Isaiah 2:18, 20; Jeremiah 10:11; Hosea 2:19; Micah 5:11, 13; Nahum 1:14; Zephaniah 2:11; cf. Exodus 23:13; Deuteronomy 12:3; Psalm 16:4).

### CHAPTER 13. ZECHARIAH 13

<margin>
Poison or medicine <note>original: "Φαρμακον" (Pharmakon)</note>, compare Matthew 10:1; 12:43; Mark 1:26; Revelation 16:13, 14; also 1 Kings 22:21, 22; Hosea 4:12; 1 Timothy 4:1; 1 John 4:1. **f)** *I will cause to pass away*, that is, I will remove (Zechariah 3:4; 1 Kings 15:12; Psalm 119:37), so that it no longer rages through this land as it once did.
</margin>

<margin>
**a)** *Idols* (Hosea 14:9). That is, "sorrowful things," because the worship of idols holds nothing except sorrow and sickness (Psalm 127:2). Or rather, "anxiously crafted things," comparing Jeremiah 22:28 and Job 10:8. Idols seem to be placed here for any false and "self-chosen" <note>original: "electitio"</note> worship established against or beyond the Word of God; for it is hardly established that the Jews polluted themselves with crude idolatry, at least from the destruction of Jerusalem until these times. **b)** Some explain this as referring to the whole world, but we prefer, with others, the land of Israel, comparing verse 8 below, as well as chapter 12:12 and the notes on 7:5. **c)** So that they are not even mentioned anymore (Exodus 23:13; Hosea 2:19). **d)** But also the *prophets*, namely, the false ones: for they are joined here with the "spirit of uncleanness"; and below in verses 3 and 4, they are indicated as having spoken falsely. Furthermore, such a judgment is rightly conceived here as is allowed by its predicate—to be removed from the land—which implies something detestable and impure. Thus, Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel, an Aramaic paraphrase</note>, the Septuagint <note>Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, and the Arabic version understand "pseudoprophets." Compare Joel 3:1 and what we noted on Numbers 11:29 from Rabbi Bechai <note>Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish commentator</note>. Therefore, these two verses promise the elimination of two things: 1. False worship, in the first half-verse; 2. False doctrine, in the second half-verse. **e)** *And the spirit of uncleanness.* Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> understands this as original sin or the "evil inclination"; but because false prophecy is joined here, we prefer with Turnovius <note>Adrianus Turnebus, a 16th-century scholar</note> to interpret it as the Devil himself speaking through them in his manufactured oracles. He is called the spirit of uncleanness both because he is impure himself and because he defiles and seduces others through the impure doctrine which he inspires in these seers and his worshippers. The Septuagint: "and the unclean spirit."
</margin>

spread through the land. **V. 3. g)** And it shall come to pass, even if anyone should continue to prophesy—namely, speaking a lie in the name of the Lord, as follows—though this would not easily happen, comparing verse 2, since even false prophets would return to a better state <note>original: "ad frugem redituris"</note>, so that they repent of their impostures and madness (verses 4, 5, 6). He seems to speak hypothetically, setting up a case (compare Numbers 5:20), to show the mindset others would have toward false prophets if such a person were to exist thereafter. h) Immediately his father and mother will forget their parental role to maintain their service to God—Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century church father and translator of the Vulgate</note>. i) Those very ones who begat him, or his parents. That is, they will grant no more to natural affection than to zeal and piety toward God (Deuteronomy 33:9; compare Exodus 32:26 and following; Matthew 10:37; and on the contrary, verse 21). **k)** You shall not live, but, as you have deserved, you shall be killed (1 Kings 10:19). This refers to the Law of Moses, according to which it was a capital offense if anyone, claiming the name of a prophet, taught apostasy from the Lord, or truly spoke against the divine word, whether in the name of other gods or in the name of Jehovah himself (Deuteronomy 13:6). l) And thus they shall pierce him through (chapter 12:10). This signifies that the Church will be watchful so that such pests no longer exist; but if they should exist, the Church will have not only the gift of discernment to test the spirits, whether they are of God, but also the zeal to eliminate evil (1 John 4:1; 2 Corinthians 7:11; Deuteronomy 13:6). l) And thus they shall pierce him through (chapter 12:10). The minds of all toward God will be so pious, he says, that they will not wait for a public judgment, but those who are such will perish by the sentence of their relatives. Thus, whatever the case may be, it is hinted that there will be a "heroic zeal," just as Phinehas transfixed the Israelite with the Moabite woman in the brothel (Numbers 25:8). But it is not necessary to explain it as if the parents would transfix their son, the false prophet, only by private judgment. Rather, it is very probable that this refers to the law in Deuteronomy 13:7–11, according to which Israelites were bound, if enticed to idolatry even by a close relative, not only not to spare him, but to so detest his impiety that they would not spare him because of kinship, but would report him to the magistrate; and once condemned by the judges' sentence, they would be the first to lay hands on him to kill him, and only then the rest of the people. **m)** because he has prophesied in such a way. The prefix "because" <note>original: כ (ki)</note> is causal, as in 2 Chronicles 16:7 and 28:6. **V. 4. n)** In that day, when there will be such great light in the Church to discern spirits, and such zeal to eliminate the wicked (verse 3). **o)** they shall be put to shame; having the filthiness of the matter exposed and even acknowledged by themselves, they will return to a better state (Romans 6:21; compare Ephesians 44:9, 11). p) See the note on verse 2. **q)** Compare Micah 3:6. **r)** when he was prophesying, or when he formerly claimed the office of prophesying for himself (verse 3). **s)** nor shall they henceforth put on the robe or cloak of hair, that is, hairy or shaggy <note>original: "ὁ τειχίνην" (ho trichinen - Greek for "the hairy one")</note>, Genesis 25:25, made of goat's or camel's hair, which had formerly been the dress of Elijah and perhaps other Prophets of God (1 Kings 19:13, 19; 2 Kings 1:8; Matthew 3:4; Hebrews 11:37; Revelation 11:3). Even false teachers had imitated such Prophets in their clothing, so that they might commend themselves by an austere appearance of life (Matthew 7:15; Vulgate: "neither shall they be covered with a sackcloth mantle"; compare Isaiah 20:2; Revelation 6:12). **t)** to lie, under the pretense that they themselves were true prophets (1 Kings 13:18). **V. 5. u)** On the contrary, such a man will say, perhaps when asked if he is or was a prophet. **x)** He will be so ashamed of his former impiety and folly that he will pray against the name of "prophet," which he had once sought as an honor, as something shameful to himself; and, if it were possible, he would wish that he had never even sought this title, or that others did not remember it being sought by him. Compare Amos 7:14. **y)** cultivating the earth (Proverbs 12:11), a farmer (Genesis 4:2), more suited to the plow-handle and the plow than to teaching and prophesying. **z)** some man (Leviticus 1:2). **a)** He "sold me"; that is, he caused me to be bought <note>original: Hebrew Hiphil stem</note>. Others: "he compelled me to serve," from an Ethiopic usage, comparing the Ethiopic metaphrase of Revelation 9:20 and Psalm 2:11; see the note on Ezekiel 8:3. It seems to us it can be explained most simply: "he bought me," or "he had me as a slave or laborer for a price or wage" (Ecclesiastes 2:7; Nehemiah 5:8). For there are several words among the Hebrews whose meaning in the Kal and Hiphil conjugations hardly differs. **b)** from my youth (1 Samuel 12:2; Ezekiel 4:14).

**V. 6. c)** But if anyone, pressing further, should say to him. d) "Blows" or "wounds" here are the traces or scars of wounds. Kimchi <note>David Kimhi, a 12th-13th century Hebrew grammarian</note>: "If it is so, that you were not a prophet, then what are these wounds between your hands? For the wounds seem to betray that you dared to prophesy, and your parents struck and chastised you so that you would not prophesy." See the note above on verse 3. But Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch scholar</note> understands them as brands burned into the hands, by which people used to devote themselves to the gods of the Gentiles, by inscribing their sign, name, or number (Revelation 13:16, 17). We prefer this because of the following half-verse. Perhaps it also refers to the cutting of the hands common to the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:28), from which scars certainly remained. Compare, on the contrary, the "marks of Christ" (Galatians 6:17). **e)** between the hands, or in your hands. Thus Noldius <note>Christian Noldius, author of a work on Hebrew particles</note>, page 193, comparing Proverbs 26:13.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Zechariah 13. The previous page discussed the removal of idols and the end of false prophecy; this page focuses on the wounds of the false prophet and the pivotal command to "strike the shepherd" in verse 7, which the commentator links directly to the passion of Christ and the subsequent history of the Jewish people.</meta>

### ZACHARIAH CHAPTER 13

<margin>
Since the prophecy has now led to the final events of the New Testament—primarily the future conversion of the Jews in chapters 12 and 13—there are now introduced further points which generally pertain to the beginnings of the New Testament. Nor does this change in chronology present any defect.
</margin>

<margin>
**f)** "These are the wounds with which I was struck in the house of *my lovers*" <note>original: "amasiorum meorum"</note>, that is, of idols and demons, whom I—alas, the shame!—previously followed. This is a confession of former filth, not without a blush. As if to say: "Though I tried to hide it, you urge me with your questioning so that I must confess the truth, much as it shames me: these are not honorable marks that you have observed on my hands; they are surely signs of the idolatry and false prophecy to which I was once devoted." Thus he hints that the false prophets, though now converted, would still bear their disgrace, just as was predicted for the Levites and Priests from the family of Ithamar in Ezekiel 44:10–14. David Kimchi <note>A renowned 12th-century Jewish scholar</note> explains it this way: "They are not wounds inflicted because of prophecy, but those with which I was corrected in my youth by those who loved me, because I had been lazy in tilling the field." The Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase</note> says: "These are the wounds I brought upon myself voluntarily to deceive others, but with which I was struck against my will in the house of those who loved me, who brought me back from my evil way to the good through these harsh remedies when I refused to obey gentler ones." But against both these explanations is the fact that the participle *my lovers* <note>original: מְאַהֲבָי (me'ahavai)</note> is consistently used in a negative sense, signifying impure lovers with whom one commits adultery, whether physically or spiritually (Jeremiah 22:20, 22; Ezekiel 16:33, 36, 37; 23:5, 9, 22; Hosea 2:7, 9, 12, 14, 15; Lamentations 1:19).
</margin>

<margin>
**v. 7. 8)** To begin the explanation of the whole matter from the very start <note>original Latin: "ab ouo," literally "from the egg"</note>, I, God the Father, say this: "O sword," etc. This is surely a return <note>original Greek: "ἐπάנוδος" (epanodos)</note> to earlier themes (chapter 11:12, 13). For as we have...
</margin>

<sig>M m m m 4</sig> <meta>Catchword: פא ד</meta>

...for verse 9 returns to the final things, which the Lord saw fit to connect with the preceding ones through a brief recapitulation, so that they might become clearer and better explained in this way. (See above note on verse 1 and Vitringa, *Types of Prophetic Doctrine*, page 188). Now, it is a personification <note>original: "Prosopopœia"</note> when He calls to the sword as if it were a person (cf. Jeremiah 25:29). Furthermore, it should be noted that the sword here stands generally for an instrument of violence and death, so that although our Lord was not precisely killed by a sword, yet this prophecy fits His death well, because He was violently wounded even unto death (compare above 12:10; Isaiah 53:5; Daniel 9:26). But even swords were used by the Jews, at least during Christ's arrest (Matthew 26:47, 55). **h)** *awake*, that is, to be stirred up (compare notes on 9:13). The imperative is used for the future, as often: as if to say, "it shall be that it awakes or you stir it up." Yet it has this emphasis: to hint that Christ was killed by the decree and will of His Father; and thus the Jews, when they fixed Him to the cross, were the ignorant executors of the divine counsel (Isaiah 53:6, 10; Psalm 40:9; Acts 2:23). **i)** *against my shepherd*, not one who is such in title only, who was called foolish above in 11:15, 17; but him to whom I myself gave the sheep of the slaughter from the house of Israel to be pastured (11:4, 7), who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). Christ clearly teaches us who this is in Matthew 26:31 and Mark 14:27, where He applies this text to Himself. **k)** *and against the man*. This name denotes the divine strength and preeminence of Christ (compare notes on Jeremiah 31:22). **l)** *my fellow* <note>original: "proximum meum"</note>. This name, when joined to a human, denotes a sharer of the same nature, or (if we may so speak) a "co-human," of whatever race or region he might be (Leviticus 5:21; 18:20; 19:11, 15, 17; 24:19; 25:14, 15, 17). Therefore, he whom God calls *His fellow* must be "equal to God" <note>original Greek: "ἴσον Θεῷ" (ison Theo)</note> (Philippians 2:6) and "of one substance" <note>original Latin: "homoousion"</note> with the Father; such as, indeed, God the Son is (John 1, 18; Colossians 1, 15; Hebrews 1, 3). Thus, what *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Rashi</note> explains—"whom I have joined to myself to guard my sheep just as I do"—does not exhaust the emphasis of the word. *Jonathan* <note>The Targum</note>, however, wrongly shifted it into the third person: "and against his associate who is like him." **m)** chapter 3:9. **n)** *Strike*, that is, whoever you are who strikes. An indefinite or impersonal imperative, equivalent to the indicative: "the shepherd shall be struck," or (as the Evangelists have it in Matthew 26:31, Mark 14:27) "I will strike the shepherd." For the Lord, while He commands the strike, strikes Himself (compare notes on Amos 9:1 and chapter 6; also Isaiah 53:4; Psalm 69:27). **o)** so that, once the shepherd is captured and killed, *the sheep may be scattered* (1 Kings 22:17; Ezekiel 34:5), namely His disciples (John 16:32). **p)** *I will however turn* my hand, which I had withdrawn for a little while, leaving them to themselves (Targum). Thus the announcement of the dispersion is limited. As if to say: This dispersion will not be final, but momentary, for shortly after the resurrection of their Shepherd, I will gather those who wander back together (Isaiah 1:25). **q)** *against the little ones* or the small ones of the sheep, **r)** that is, to gather them together. The metaphor is continued, and thus those are indicated who had fled when the shepherd was struck: namely the Apostles, and others of the Jews already believing in Christ, and those who would later believe in Him through them. They are called *little ones* both because of their number (being outnumbered by the crowd of unbelievers) and because of the estimation in which they were held (being despised by many). Cf. 11:7, 11; Jeremiah 49:20; 50:45; and Luke 12:32. **v. 8. r)** *But as for* the stubborn and those unwilling to believe the Gospel of Christ, it shall come to pass, etc. **s)** *in all the land*, namely the Judean land (verse 2), which is customarily called such pointedly <note>original Greek: "δειϰτιϰῶς" (deiktikos)</note> and preeminently (compare notes on 7:5 and 12:12). For it explains what fates the Jewish people and land would have after the Shepherd was struck by them and His Gospel rejected. **t)** *a portion of two*, that is, double, twice as much. A phrase taken from the dividing of an inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17; 2 Kings 2:9). It signifies *two-thirds*, that is, the greater part of the inhabitants of the land; for it is placed in contrast with the third part which is promised to survive the destruction. **u)** *in it*, namely the Judean land. **x)** they shall be cut off by the Romans, under the Vespasians, Trajan, and Hadrian, and shall die (Genesis 7:21; Joshua 22:20). **y)** *but the third part at last*, that is, the smaller part (cf. Ezekiel 5:2 onwards). **z)** *shall be left*, that is, will remain as a survivor from the destruction *in it*, so that at least the entire nation is not cut off, but has a remnant to be saved in the last days, after they have first been brought through the fire (verse 9). Cf. 14:2; Isaiah 4:3; 37:31; Ezekiel 6:8, 9; 12:16; Zephaniah 3:12. **v. 9. a)** I will, however, bring also this third part, which survived the destruction under the Romans (verse 8). **b)** Jonathan: *into tribulation* as if into a furnace of fire. To this can be referred whatever evils the Jewish people felt through the entire time of their present dispersion, or will yet feel in the future. **d)** Kimchi especially explains this as the distress of the sufferings of the Messiah (as the Jews call them) and concerning the war of Gog and Magog (cf. Isaiah 6:13; Ezekiel 5:3, 4; 1 Corinthians 3:15). **e)** and thus I will melt them with the fire of tribulations, just as silver is melted, not so that it perishes entirely, but so that it is purged from dross (Isaiah 48:10; Ezekiel 22:22; Malachi 3:2, 3; Psalm 66:10; Proverbs 17:3). **d)** and finally I will test them or make them proven (Jeremiah 9:6; Psalm 66:10; 1 Peter 1:7).

-> *Just as yellow gold is seen in the fires,* <-
-> *So in hard times must faith be examined.* <-

**e)** Here finally, that is, the remaining people, melted and tested by fire. **f)** Isaiah 41:25; 65:24. **g)** chapter 10:6; Isaiah 58:9. **h)** I said, that is, I will say gladly and readily. **i)** cf. 2:15; 8:8; Isaiah 51:16; Hosea 1:9; 2:1, 3, 25. **k)** John 20:28; cf. Deuteronomy 26:17, 18.

**v. 7.** *Strike* <note>original: הך (Hakh)</note> so the Easterners read, but they write *his fellow* <note>original: עמיתו (amito)</note>. *And I will return* <note>original: והשבתי (v'hashivoti)</note> so in manuscripts 3, 7, 8, 15, 17, 18, 22 according to the Erfurt Masorah. But others have the different vowel point. **v. 8.** *And they shall die* <note>original: יגועו (yigva'u)</note> with the prefix *Vav* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3; so also in 5.

It interprets the "two portions" cut off as the Jews destroyed by the Romans and the "third part" as the refined remnant saved through tribulation.</summary>

### CHAPTER 14. Zechariah 14

->2 For I will gather^r all the nations^s against Jerusalem^t for war,^u and the city shall be captured,^x the houses plundered,^y and the women ravished;^z half^b of the city shall go^a into exile, but the residue^c of the people shall not be cut off^d from the city.<-

<margin>
**Day 1**
**of Sukkot**
<note>The Feast of Tabernacles</note>
Hesychius on this passage & among the Hebrews, David Kimchi, regarding the rescue of Jerusalem from the invasion of Gog and Magog.
</margin>

...we see that he has explained this as Gog <note>A symbolic enemy of God's people in biblical prophecy</note>. Cf. also *Meyer* on the end of *Ezekiel* p. 98 and following. What Zechariah has here regarding the glory of Jerusalem is rightly brought back no less to *Revelation* chapters 21 & 22. **n) *for the Lord.*** This is a Dative not only of the governing cause, but also of honor and glory. That is to say: a day which the Lord Himself will bring about by His wonderful governance, and which will exist as something exceedingly glorious for the Lord because of its illustrious outcome. *Isaiah 2:12; Ezekiel 30:3; 39:13.* **o) *that it may be divided***, or when it shall be divided by the enemies. *Psalm (3); Isaiah 33:23; Amos 7:17; cf. Genesis 49:27; Isaiah 53:12.* **p) *your spoil***, that is, what was taken from you, *Deuteronomy 13:17; Zechariah 20:14; Isaiah 33:4.* This is an apostrophe <note>A rhetorical figure where the speaker addresses an object or personified idea</note> to Jerusalem (collecting here verse 2), since he had already spoken of her above in chapter 12:2 and following; chapter 13:1 and following; or, if you prefer, to the land of Judah, concerning which chapter 13:8 etc. speaks in a favorable sense: *The house of Israel shall divide the wealth of the peoples in their own midst*, Jerusalem. But our exposition is confirmed by the following in verse 2 regarding the city being taken and the houses plundered, which contain the declaration of this verse. **q) *in your midst***, or within you, Jerusalem. This has its own distinct emphasis. For, as Jerome <note>A 4th-century scholar and translator of the Vulgate</note> says, it frequently happens that things plundered in a sudden rush on a city are divided outside in the field or in a solitary place, lest the enemies should suddenly come upon them: but here, the things plundered will be divided in the middle of the city, representing the security of the victory. **v. 2. r) *for I will gather***, doing this by a wondrous governance of affairs, so that they may come together, and that they may carry out—even unknowingly—the judgments which I have destined for my people by my holy counsel, and having carried them out, they in turn may perish in a horrible destruction. *Ezekiel 39:2; Zephaniah 3:8.* *Revelation 20:8* also seems to look back to this. **s)** cf. chapter 12:3 & *Ezekiel 38:4 and following.* **t) *against Jerusalem***, comparing the Hebrew preposition *el* <note>meaning "to" or "towards"</note> with *Joshua 10:6.* **u) *to war***, that is, for the purpose of fighting against her. *Isaiah 7:1; Obadiah verse 1.* **x)** Not only will the city be besieged, but it will also be captured. *1 Kings 16:18.* The efforts the enemies dare will not be mere attempts, but will have an effect; yet no greater than what I shall permit them, as the end of this verse shows. Thus, evils are first exaggerated as being great in the future, but then they are limited and moderated. **y) *and the houses shall be plundered. Isaiah 13:16; Psalm 89:42.*** **z) *and the women*** (so great will be the force and lust of the enemies that they do not even spare their bodies) ***shall be ravished*** (4) *Deuteronomy 28:30; Isaiah 13:16;* or what is the same, the *Keri* <note>The traditional reading of the Hebrew text</note> says: *shall suffer sexual intercourse.* **a) *and shall go out***, to be led away by the enemies—into captivity. *Jeremiah 29:16.* **b) *half part*** of the inhabitants of the city; to which the "residue of the people" is now opposed, as the other half part. **c) *but the residue of the people. 2 Kings 25:11; Zephaniah 2:9.*** It is hinted that as God has conscripted these nations like a general, so He will effectively command them, and by a wondrous governance of affairs will ensure that at least they do not lead everyone away as captives, but leave a half part of the people remaining in the city. Jerome attempts a reconciliation based on the layout of old Jerusalem. He asks how half the city could be captured while the rest of the people remained in the city—it is proven, he says, that the northern and lower part of the city was captured, but the mountain of the Temple and Zion, in which the citadel was, remained untouched. **d) *shall not be cut off from or out of the city***, that is, they shall remain in it. *Meyer* observes (on the end of *Ezekiel* p. 98) that these things cannot possibly refer to Jerusalem being conquered by the Romans, since all the Jews found in the city at that time were either killed or sold into slavery, and the city itself was utterly destroyed, so that no one remained as a survivor in it. **v. 3. e) *Then indeed***, when they have filled up the measure of divine judgments in the city of God, and have chastised her as much as is sufficient, He will go forth as a glorious general to fight now against those very enemies whom He had just gathered to fight against Jerusalem in verse 2. At last He will break the long-suffering with which He had hitherto winked at the enemies for the testing of His people. Or it can even be rendered causally, *For He will go forth*: so that the reason is given why the destruction of the city's inhabitants is denied to be universal. Furthermore, this is a military term, cf. *2 Samuel 5:24; 11:1; Isaiah 42:13; Habakkuk 3:13.* See note on *Micah 1:3 & cf. Revelation 19:11* and following; 20:9. **f) *and He will fight against those nations*** in verse 2, namely by an earthquake in verses 4 and 5; *Ezekiel 38:19, 20;* by sending a plague upon them, cf. here verse 12; by confusion in verse 13 and following; and, if one may judge from similar cases, also by pestilence, blood, rain, hail, fire and brimstone *Ezekiel 38:22; Isaiah 34:8, 9, 10; Psalm 11:6; Revelation 20:9.* Cf. *Isaiah 30:32.* **g) *as on the day of battle. 2 Samuel 17:11.*** Namely, against the Egyptians at the Red Sea, as Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> adds; and indeed at other times, whenever He Himself wonderfully helped His own and defeated the enemies from on high. Cf. *Exodus 14:14, 25; 15:3 etc.; Joshua 10:10, 11, 14; Judges 4:15; 5:20; 1 Samuel 7:10; 2 Samuel 5:24; 22:15; 2 Kings 19:35 etc.* We read of no such thing happening regarding the Romans, who attacked Jerusalem under Titus with impunity. **v. 4. h) *And His feet shall stand***, namely those of Jehovah, fighting against the enemies for His people in verse 3. We take this, just like the preceding "He will go out," as being said of the Lord <term>anthropopathically</term> <note>original: "$\alpha\nu\theta\rho\omega\pi o\pi\alpha\theta\hat{\omega}\varsigma$" — meaning: describing God in human terms or with human physical traits</note> along with the Chaldean <note>The Targum</note>, who puts it thus: *And He will manifest Himself in His strength.* Thus the Lord is read to have descended upon Mount Sinai, so that the whole mountain trembled on account of His majestic presence, *Exodus 19:18, 20; cf. Psalm 63:19; 64:1; 104:32; 144:5, 6.* And thus it is hinted that it will happen that the Lord will especially show His presence there, by striking the enemies and by preparing a refuge and escape for His own. **i) *day***, that is, in that time mentioned in verse 1. Cf. verses 6, 7, 8, 9, 13. **k) *upon the Mount of Olives. 2 Samuel 15:30.***

<column-break/>

**CHAPTER XIV. VERSE 1.**
**l) *But behold!*** A particle of arousal is placed first, because what follows is very notable, both regarding the signal affliction of the Church and regarding the illustrious help of God to be brought to the Church's afflicted affairs. **m) *some day is coming***, namely the same one about which he spoke above in chapter 12:2, 3 etc. by anticipating the action: for by this day Jerusalem is to be attacked by all those surrounding it in verses 2 and 12 (cf. 12:1, 2) and even by Judah itself in verse 14 (cf. 12:2). The Lord Himself will fight against those nations, verse 3 (cf. 12:9), a plague having been sent upon both men and beasts, along with panic and blindness, verses 12–15 (cf. 12:4). Jerusalem shall dwell in its own place below, verse 10 (cf. 12:6 etc.). So much so that it is a prolepsis <note>The representation of a future act as if it had already occurred</note>; whatever has already been said of this matter in chapter 12:1–9 is here further declared as if in its own proper place. *The coming of this day* is rightly believed to be still in the future, and the whole chapter is explained as being about the newest attempts of the enemies against the holy city, as well as the vengeance of God to be taken from the enemies, with the subsequent security and glory of Jerusalem following from then on. To this we are led both by the subject matter of the chapter itself, which we do not yet see fulfilled, and by its comparison with the New Testament and especially the Holy Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, which we shall provide throughout the notes. Nor does the illustrious Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> explain it poorly in his Commentary on the Apocalypse p. 1115, as being about the newest affliction of the Church, the type of which stood forth in the Epiphanic affliction <note>The persecution under Antiochus Epiphanes</note>; namely, that which falls into the time of the destruction of Antichristianism in Revelation 19:19; although others refer it to that affliction which will be the last brought upon the Church through Gog and Magog in Revelation 20:7, 8, 9 and Ezekiel 38 & 39.
