<meta>This page continues the commentary on Zechariah 14, specifically focusing on the miraculous splitting of the Mount of Olives and the nature of the "day of the Lord." It bridges the previous discussion of the siege of Jerusalem with the physical and spiritual changes accompanying the divine appearance.</meta>

### ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER 14. 14

<margin>
l) see Ezekiel 11:23. m) and the Mount of Olives shall be split (burst asunder). This will be the effect of the Lord’s feet standing upon the mountain. Moreover, this splitting of the mountain is sent through a future earthquake in v. 5. cf. Numbers 16:31. Psalm 78:13. Nehemiah 9:11. Furthermore, Tarnovius <note>original: "Tam."; likely referring to the theologian Paul Tarnovius</note> with others says: "This destiny is fulfilled partly on the day of the ascension, when the feet of Christ stood on this mountain, and He, before He ascended, gave instructions to the Apostles that they might spread the Gospel throughout the whole world; and partly after the day of Pentecost, when they were already equipped with the miraculous gifts of the Holy Spirit, and having left that land, they preached the word of the Gospel," comparing Mark 16:19–20, Luke 24:50–51, and Acts 1:12. Add Matthew 25:30 and Acts 1:12, comparing v. 9. For in this way, he says, spiritually that mountain of olives, at which the Apostles had been gathered, was divided into all corners of the world when they moved against the enemy, etc. We would also gladly interpret it this way; but both the thread and the argument of the prophecy lead us elsewhere. For in the preceding verses 1–3, the subject was the siege of Jerusalem—not by the Romans (which I think is noted from our own records), but a much different and later one, by the Antichrist, as far as we can grasp. Therefore, when the feet of the Lord are said to stand on the Mount of Olives on that same day, it easily appears that it must refer to the same period of time. If you look at the argument of the prophecy itself, the Lord is represented here not as one about to die or ascend to heaven (as in the cited passage where, with the Apostles watching, he was lifted by a cloud from the Mount of Olives), but as one about to descend from heaven onto that mountain, to strike the enemies and help His own people, comparing verses 3 and 5. Furthermore, this prophecy implies a violent splitting of the mountain...
</margin>

...which faces Jerusalem from the east; and the Mount of Olives shall be split across its middle, eastward and westward, forming a very great valley; and half of the mountain shall move northward and half of it southward.
5 And you shall flee to the valley of my mountains, for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azal; and you shall flee as you fled before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. And the Lord my God shall come, and all the holy ones with You.
6 And it shall come to pass in that day, that there shall not be light, but clarity and condensation <note>original: "yekarot ve-kippa'on"; a notoriously difficult Hebrew phrase often translated as "dwindling light" or "cold and frost"</note>.
7 And it shall be one day which [is known to the Lord]...

<margin>
...which will be terrible not only for the enemies but also for the faithful themselves, causing them to flee. As for other circumstances... 
7 *They shall congeal* <note>referring to the Hebrew "yikpa'on"</note>
</margin>

->Mm m m s<-

...this is only forcedly adapted to the ascension of Christ and the subsequent preaching of the Gospel. We believe, therefore, it is still to be fulfilled in a future time; however, regarding the manner of fulfillment, we confess the dimness of our own light and entrust it entirely to God. *n)* Vulgate: *from its middle part*. *o)* toward the rising and setting sun. Thus, when the mountain is split, a valley will emerge; its path and extension in length from west to east is described, with the northern part of the mountain receding toward the north, and the southern toward the south (as follows). *p)* into a valley. v. 5. so that between the parts of the mountain bursting asunder a great valley exists, or (as the Septuagint <note>LXX</note> expressed it using a harmonious term) a "great chaos" or gap. *q)* for it will recede (Numbers 4:4) from its place (Ezekiel 46:7) through the shaking of the earth (ch. 5:10). *r)* one half part of the mountain splits. v. 5. *s)* And you shall flee, my people (for he addressed them above in v. 1 using the feminine gender in respect to the city, which contains the people), certainly not without great terror and trembling because of that horrible shaking; however, it is for your salvation: since this flight will lead you to a refuge where you may be safe from enemies and my judgments about to rage against them. Cf. Numbers 16:34, ch. 35:25, and see below in the various readings. *t)* through the valley of my mountains, i.e., of the mountain split by me into two parts. v. 4. *u)* because this valley will reach, etc. (Ezekiel 8:8). The parenthesis continues until "Azol" <note>Atzal</note>, adding the movements of flight through this valley, opened by the Lord Himself for His people. *x)* Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> treats this as a common noun: "to that which He set aside" (Numbers 11:17), comparing a similar ellipsis of the pronoun in 1 Chronicles 15:12, "to that which I prepared for it," i.e., to the place prepared by me for the Ark. He says there is great consolation for the Church, because God has set aside something to which the pious (situated in that valley, where there is destruction of heights for the weary) can flee, having their souls as plunder, and finding necessary shelter and nourishment. But if the Lord (for it is clear from the phrase "valley of my mountains" in the first half of the verse that He is the one speaking) had meant this, He would have said in the first person, "I have set aside." The Vulgate says: *even to the next*; probably from *atsel* meaning "near" (Genesis 39:10), but with an obscure sense, or none at all. The simple flow of words suggests to the reader that this is a proper name of a place: *unto Atzal*. This is the view of Jonathan, Abraham Ibn Ezra, Sch., and others. And indeed, it is the name of a village in 1 Chronicles 8:37–38 and ch. 9:44; and a related place is Beth-ezel in Micah 1:11, where see the note. Furthermore, whether there was ever a place called *Atzal* near Jerusalem to the east, we do not dwell upon. For here there seems to be only an allusion to the symbolic or descriptive meaning of that name, which can be two-fold through different etymologies; both are good for the purpose of the prophecy. For if you derive it from *atsal* <note>to reserve/set aside</note>, it suggests a place *set aside* by the Lord to be a refuge for the pious, such as Zoar was for Lot (Genesis 19:20 ff.) and, around the time of the destruction of Jerusalem by Titus, Pella was for the Christians. But if derived from *tsel* <note>shadow</note> with a prefix: it suggests a place providing *shadow* and protection from evil. Whichever way you wish to form it, in general, it will signify an "asylum," a word which the Hebrew almost expresses by its very sound. *y)* "you shall flee," I say. After the inserted parenthesis, this verb is resumed from the beginning of the verse to complete the sentence. *z)* "just as you fled long ago," namely, in the loins of your ancestors, comparing Hebrews 7:9–10. Or it is a collective figure of speech as in Ezekiel 12:22, Hosea 10:3, etc. *a)* "because of the earthquake." It is assumed, therefore, that the Lord will come here against the enemies with an earthquake; just as it is explicitly stated in the prophecy against the Gogites (Ezekiel 38:19–20; cf. Isaiah 29:6; Revelation 6:12, 11:13, 19, 16:18). *b)* Concerning this shaking, the historians of the Old Testament are silent, but the contemporary prophet Amos speaks of it (Amos 1:1, see note). *c)* And thus He will come with and during the earthquake, as the avenger of His people. Others read it causally: "For He shall come... and be manifested" (cf. note on v. 3). Jerome notably and truly says: "It is clearly preached concerning the second coming of the Savior," comparing Revelation 1:7 and Matthew 24:30. *d)* "The Lord my God." Thus the Prophet speaks of God sometimes in his own name and sometimes in God's own name and words; in the former respect, he uses the third person for the Lord (as in v. 1, 3, 4), and in the latter, the first person (as in v. 2 and the start of v. 5). When, therefore, he calls the Lord *his God*, the Prophet by this very act testifies to his own desire, faith, and hope in this promised coming of the Lord. But Cocceius prefers these to be the words of Christ, indicating the foundation of our hope in this way: that God is the *God of Christ*, and has therefore promised us nothing, nor commanded us to ask or hope for anything, that He did not promise the Son from eternity. Compare ch. 11:4, Isaiah 49:4–5. But we hold the former opinion, because Christ Himself is undoubtedly the one whose coming and battle against the enemies is promised here (cf. Revelation 19:11 ff.). *e)* "and all the holy ones with you." An address to God. Hence the Septuagint, Arabic, Syriac, and Vulgate, keeping the speech plain, translated it "with Him." He changes the person (says Vitringa on Revelation 15:3, p. 917) in the speech, as elsewhere; and while speaking about God, he suddenly turns the speech to God, whose praise and glory it serves to have the holy ones with Him, both angels and men. Cf. Joel 4:11, Matthew 25:31, 27:51, 53, 1 Thessalonians 3:13, Jude v. 14, Revelation 15:3, 19:14. Abraham Ibn Ezra and others, however, refer the suffix pronoun to Jerusalem, comparing v. 1. But because "and He shall come" preceded it, the company of those coming with the Lord Himself is rightly understood here. v. 6. *f)* "And it shall be on that day," v. 1, 4. These seem to be a detailed explanation of what preceded. *g)* "there shall not be light," i.e., perfect and constant. In the name of "light" come the Church's salvation and rescue from enemies by God's help (Esther 8:16). *h)* "but by turns and mixedly clarities" or "splendors" (Job 31:26) and "thickness" or "density" (1) cf. Exodus 15:8. Vulgate: *but cold and frost*; of which the latter comes from "congealing" (cf. root in Job 10:10), and the former from "freezing" (cf. Genesis 8:22, Psalm 147:17), though as to the latter, it is against the grammar. Furthermore, it can be explained in the same sense we just gave: for the clarities (if any exist by turns) will be condensed and will soon pass into thick darkness. Cf. v. 7, Isaiah 21:12. v. 7. *i)* "For it will be one day," i.e., altogether unique, and which will hardly have an equal (cf. Job 23:13), both by reason of the rushing darkness of calamities and the divine light and help. In this way the Arabs call a year that is incomparable "one of the years." Compare Jeremiah 30:7. Others take the mark of unity as indefinite: "one day," i.e., a certain day (cf. 1 Samuel 27:1). But Cocceius says: "One day" means perhaps a short time, or something not to be repeated. It will happen once, not often.

---

v. 4. "Upon the face of" [al-pnei] according to Meren 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15-19, 21, 22, 23, but besides the printed Masorah at Genesis 30:36. [Yad] according to Par. 1, 2, second Masorah i. and 3. at Genesis 10:23. v. 5. Instead of "and you shall flee" [venastem], 3 have [venastem] and in the margin 6, 9, which reading is also attributed to other corrected books and the Oriental ones in M.I. ** Thus Jonathan read, while he rendered "and it shall be shut up" [vesatamhem], likewise the Septuagint "and it shall be blocked." [Venastem] thus 1, 3, so fz. 5. "Valley of my mountains" [ge-harai] with Aleph 2, 3, 10, 14, 15, 16, 20, so fz. 5 and in the margin 6, 9. Against the printed Masorah and Erfurt manuscript here, and printed Joshua 18:16. "Unto" [elai] with Kamatz 1, 2, 3, second Masorah i. 1, 2 and Erfurt, but besides the printed edition at Numbers 22:18. "And all" [ve-chol] with the prefix Vav fz. 1, 5. v. 6. "And condensation" [ve-kippa'on] thus in the text 3, and so fz. 5. And Rabbi Nachman observes a variation here for the second Masorah i. at this place and printed at Hosea 1:1.

However, concerning these things predicted here about the living waters coming forth from Jerusalem, Meyer <note>Sebastian Meyer, a 16th-century theologian</note> in his commentary on the final chapters of Ezekiel (page 101) argues for a mystical sense. It signifies the proclamation of the Gospel through

<margin>
**(k)** *is* known to the Lord. That is to say: This day will indeed be gloomy at the beginning, and unexpected darkness rushing in will throw the faithful into a certain stupor. But let them be of good heart; for although it is harsh, the day has been foreseen by the Lord, who knows its beginning and already knows its end. Compare 1 Corinthians 10:13. Or rather, the sense is this: That day of which I speak will most certainly exist, but at what precise moment of time it is to come, human calculation could hardly determine, since the Lord alone knows it and has reserved it for His own power and omniscience. Compare Matthew 24:36, Mark 13:32, Acts 1:7. **(l)** where there will neither be bright day nor total night, with more joyful things sometimes intervening or shining through the clouds of sadness. Compare verse 6. Jonah <note>The Targum</note> translates: "it will be neither like the light of day, nor like the darkness of night." **(m)** it will happen, however, around the time of evening. Genesis 8:11, chapter 24:11. When the darkness of night seems to break in with full force and draw a black gloom over the Church—that is (as Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish scholar</note> explains) at the time when distress will be at its greatest. Concerning this "evening" of the Church, compare Matthew 20:8. **(n)** at last there will be full light, a radiance shining without interruption; according to the saying, "when the bricks are doubled, Moses comes" <note>A traditional proverb meaning that divine help arrives when the oppression is at its peak</note>. Compare Isaiah 30:26, 60:1–3, 20; Psalm 112:4; Revelation 21:23, 25, 22:5; and the opposite in Isaiah 13:10.

**v. 8. o)** On that day, that is, in that stretch of time in which light is restored to the Church after the gloom (verse 7). **p)** living water (Genesis 26:19), that is, life-giving and refreshing because of its sweetness and healthfulness, which will mitigate the salt waters of the Mediterranean and Dead Seas with a sweet stream. This is a <term>metonymy</term> <note>a figure of speech where one thing is used to represent another</note>, just as if we called death a sluggish pasture for sheep, and the land...
</margin>

all nations, and the small stream of the gifts of grace flowing from there; compare Ezekiel 47:1 onwards, Joel 4:18, Revelation 7:17, 22:1 onwards. Just as Jerome <note>Early Christian scholar and translator of the Vulgate</note> says among the ancients: "The water which goes out from Jerusalem—that is, from the Church—indicates the doctrine of the Savior." Compare Isaiah 2:3, 11:9, John 4:14, 7:38. And among more recent writers, Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, 17th-century theologian</note> says: "The continuation and amplification of the grace of the interpretation of God's word is promised, and the demonstration of truth from it: so that it may continually go out from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem." **q)** Rabbi Bechai <note>Bahya ben Asher, 13th-century commentator</note> in his Commentary on the Law (folio 174d) explains this as the Jerusalem which is above, just as Paul speaks in Galatians 4:26. We can indeed admit this, provided that, according to the context of this passage, it is understood according to Revelation 21:2, 10. **r)** half, or one part of them. **s)** toward the anterior or eastern sea, that is, toward the Asphaltite Lake <note>The Dead Sea</note>, whose location is to the east of the earthly Jerusalem. Ezekiel 47:18, Joel 2:20. **t)** the posterior or western sea, that is, the Mediterranean, which is "behind" the inhabitants of Palestine when they face the East. See the notes on Deuteronomy 11:24, 34:2. Jerusalem is conceived as being situated in the middle, while the river flowing from it goes out into different and opposite regions. As for the meaning, Cocceius says: "Those to whom this grace will reach are compared with the Dead Sea and the Great Sea; we can understand the peoples who are to the east and the west of the Church." In the Prophets, "waters" and "seas" are peoples. **u)** but in summer and in winter this water will be and remain, so that it is neither broken by the frost of winter nor dried up by the excessive heat of summer, as Jerome explains. Genesis 8:22, Amos 3:15. This denotes the perennial nature of that benefit and the continuous course of the Gospel. Compare Isaiah 58:11. **v. 9. x)** The sense: The kingdom of Jehovah—which was both due to Him and which He has always held—He will now at last occupy openly, after His enemies have been gloriously conquered and placed as His footstool. Jonah <note>The Targum</note>: "and the kingdom of the Lord shall be revealed." Isaiah 52:7, Jeremiah 10:7, 23:5, Psalm 24:7ff, Psalm 45:2, 93:1, 97:1, 99:1, Hebrews 2:8, 10:13, Revelation 11:15, 12:10, 19:6, 20:4. **y)** over the whole earth, and thus even over the nations themselves (verses 16, 17). A truly Catholic <note>meaning universal</note> King and universal Monarch. Psalm 47:3, 8, 72:8–11, Daniel 2:35; compare Isaiah 54:5. **z)** the Lord shall be one, that is, all idols having been abolished, He alone will be everywhere acknowledged as God, preached, and called upon: just as He is one in Himself, so He will become one to all nations, so that they worship no God except Him. Deuteronomy 6:4, 5:7; compare above Zechariah 13:2, John 10:16, Romans 3:29–30, 1 Corinthians 8:5–6, Ephesians 4:5–6, 1 Timothy 2:5. For when the nations have abandoned their vanities (as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> says), it will become manifest that there is no other God with the Lord. Deuteronomy 32:39. Jonah <note>The Targum</note> translates this and the following clause thus: "Serving before the Lord with one shoulder" (a phrase taken from Isaiah 11:14, Zephaniah 3:9, implying that the peoples of the earth will no longer be "unequally yoked" <note>original Greek: ἑτεροζυγοῦντας (*heterozygountas*)</note>, 2 Corinthians 6:14): "because His name is true forever, and there is none besides Him." **a)** but also His name, by which He revealed Himself in His word, will be one, and there will be no more variety in acknowledging the Lord and His worship: schisms and disagreements concerning religion will be removed, and there will no longer be sects or heresies in the Church. Compare Jeremiah 32:39, Micah 4:5, John 4:23, 17:11, 21, 1 Corinthians 1:13.

**v. 10. b)** the whole of the land surrounding Jerusalem will be turned (Psalm 71:21), so that what had once been mountainous and rugged (Psalm 125:2) may now become level and like a plain. It is implied that all the mountains and hills round about—that is, everything high and proud—will be humbled, so that the holy Jerusalem may be uniquely exalted and conspicuous; compare what follows immediately, "she shall be exalted," and Isaiah 2:2, 12ff, 40:4. **c)** like a desert plain. This can be taken either indefinitely, referring only to the level site of the region; or definitely, regarding a specific plain, namely the Jordanic plain celebrated for its fertility (Deuteronomy 1:7, 3:17, 4:49), which would simultaneously imply the fertility of the surrounding soil. **d)** from Geba, a town of the tribe of Benjamin, and thus northern in relation to the city of Jerusalem (Joshua 21:17, 1 Samuel 13:3, 1 Kings 15:22, Isaiah 10:29), as far as Rimmon, a town of Judah in the southern part (Joshua 15:32, 21), formerly granted to Simeon (chapter 19:7). The boundaries described here are not of the plain itself, as some think, but of the land surrounding Jerusalem which is to be turned into a plain: as the [Hebrew] accents suggest. **e)** which (Rimmon) is to the south of Jerusalem. **f)** but she herself (namely Jerusalem) shall be exalted, while those things which are round about are humbled (Isaiah 2:2). Jonah <note>The Targum</note>: "she shall be magnified." It is from the root <unclear>רום</unclear> (*rum*), whose *Vav* sometimes changes into an *Aleph*, and that either silent (as in Hosea 10:14, Proverbs 24:7) or mobile (as here and in Psalm 22:17). **g)** and she shall dwell firmly beneath herself, no longer to be moved from her place. For this phrase implies the firmness and constancy of habitation (compare chapter 12:6); not precisely the same boundaries that had been there formerly, but rather that the holy city is to be extended beyond its ancient limits in length and breadth. Jeremiah 31:39–40. This itself seems to be implied here as well, when it is said she will dwell as far as the king's winepresses, which were probably formerly outside the city. **h)** from the gate of Benjamin, or the northern gate (Jeremiah 37:13, 38:7). **i)** to the first gate. It is uncertain why it is so called; perhaps it is the corner gate itself, or the same as the "old gate" in Nehemiah 3:6. **k)** the gate of the corners or the corner gate, perhaps so called because it was placed at the corner between the east and the north (2 Kings 14:13, 2 Chronicles 26:9). See the note on Jeremiah 31:38. **l)** and from the tower of Hananeel toward the east, from which the Sheep Gate is not far distant (Nehemiah 3:1, Jeremiah 31:38). **m)** as far as the king’s winepresses, which Cocceius guesses were near the royal gardens to the south. Jeremiah 48:33. Furthermore, John speaks more distinctly about the restoration of the New Jerusalem, and especially the gates, in Revelation 21:10ff.

**v. 11. n)** and they shall dwell in it, namely securely, as is said at the end of the verse. **o)** and the curse <note>original: *anathema* / *cherem*</note>, by which the land and the city were previously struck (Malachi 3:24), shall be no more (Revelation 22:3). It signifies that hereafter there will be no guilt in her which God would wish to avenge by extermination, such as existed either among the Jewish people or in the Christian Church. Cocceius, *Lexicon* 263. Compare Deuteronomy 7:26, Joshua 6:18, 7:12–13. Jonah <note>The Targum</note>: "slaughter." **p)** For the former things have passed away (Revelation 21:4, Job 11:16). **q)** see verse 10 and chapter 12:6. **r)** for security, that is, securely, so that she has no more enemies to fear; hence her gate shall never be closed (Revelation 21:25).

-># TORAH ZECHARIAH. CHAPTER 14.<-

<margin>
**v)** plague, verses 15, 18. **s)** those who served in the army, Ezekiel 29:7, 8. **t)** that new [plague], verses 2, 8, 10, 11. **u)** namely, by wasting away He will cause to waste away <note>original Latin: *contabescendo contabefaciet*</note>, Psalm 73:3, so that by drying up, one is deprived of all moisture and vigor and passes into corruption; compare above, chapter 11:17. **x)** his flesh or body, namely, of each of the enemies. **y)** while he (the man) is still standing on his feet; so that they shall be, as it were, living corpses. **v. 13. b)** Panic of the Lord, that is, to be sent upon them by the Lord, just as formerly in the Midianite camps, Judges 7:22, Isaiah 9:4, and the Philistines, 1 Samuel 14:20, when the enemies, confused by divine power, drew their weapons against one another. Compare Deuteronomy 7:23. It is a "Genitive of the efficient cause" <note>A grammatical term meaning the Lord is the one causing the panic</note>. **c)** so that each shall be seized, namely, by mistake, or as if they were enemies, or in some other way set against each other. Compare chapter 11:6, Isaiah 19:2, chapter 49:26, Ezekiel 38:21, 22. **d)** "and shall rise up," etc. This means they shall engage in hand-to-hand combat with one another. Genesis 26:12.

**v. 14. e)** "But even Judah shall fight against Jerusalem," namely, by compulsion, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> explains. Thus Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum</note>: "Even those who are of the house of Judah, the nations shall lead them, forced to fight, etc.," from which affliction and temptation, however, the Lord will deliver Judah. Compare the note on chapter 12:2. There are indeed some who explain that Judah would be found at Jerusalem not as one attacking the city, but as one defending it; but after the verb "to fight," the preposition "in/against" <note>Hebrew: ב (*be*)</note> placed before the names of cities is usually taken not as a location, but in an adversarial sense; compare Judges 9:45, 1 Samuel 23:1, 2 Samuel 12:27. Furthermore, it would not be strange for Judah to fight in or for Jerusalem, since as brothers they would be presumed to do this of their own accord, so that there would have been no need...
</margin>

<margin>
...no need at all to say, "But even Judah," etc., which implies something least expected—that is, that Judah was associated with the enemies themselves, although out of compulsion. **f)** see verse 12. **g)** it shall be gathered nonetheless as spoil, namely, by Judah (who had been forced into service) and by the Jerusalemites who were previously besieged but now delivered by the Lord's help, Isaiah 33:4; so that, with the enemies put to flight and slain, they...

12 <gloss>v</gloss> <gloss>s</gloss> <gloss>t</gloss> And this shall be the plague with which the Lord will strike all the nations that have fought against Jerusalem: <gloss>u</gloss> He will cause their flesh to rot while they stand on their feet, <gloss>x</gloss> <gloss>y</gloss> and their eyes shall rot <gloss>z</gloss> in their sockets, <gloss>a</gloss> and their tongue shall rot in their mouths. <gloss>b</gloss> 13 And it shall come to pass in that day that there shall be a great panic from the Lord <gloss>b</gloss> among them; and everyone will seize the hand <gloss>c</gloss> of his neighbor, and his hand will rise up against the hand of his neighbor. <gloss>d</gloss> 14 And even Judah shall fight <gloss>e</gloss> against Jerusalem; and the wealth of all the nations round about shall be gathered: gold, silver, and garments <gloss>f</gloss> <gloss>g</gloss> in great abundance. <gloss>h</gloss> 15 And such shall be the plague of the horse, the mule, the camel, and the donkey, and of all the livestock that shall be in those camps <gloss>i</gloss>—just like this plague. <gloss>k</gloss> 16 And it shall come to pass that everyone who is left of all the nations that came against Jerusalem <gloss>l</gloss> shall go up from year to year to worship <gloss>m</gloss> <gloss>n</gloss> <gloss>o</gloss> <gloss>p</gloss> <gloss>q</gloss> <gloss>r</gloss> the King, the Lord of hosts, and to keep the Feast of Tabernacles. <gloss>s</gloss> <gloss>t</gloss> <gloss>u</gloss> 17 And it shall be that whichever of the families of the earth does not go up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, upon them there shall be no rain.

...shall take rich spoils from their camps, just as formerly the people of Samaria did after the Syrians were put to flight by the Lord, 2 Kings 7:15, 16. **h)** wealth, for example: gold, silver, clothing, as is declared immediately. Isaiah 10:14, chapter 61:6, Micah 4:13. Compare Revelation 21:26. **i)** unto a multitude, that is, very many. 2 Chronicles 4:18.

**v. 15. k)** And so likewise. As if to say: Thus indeed God will not only strike the enemies themselves, but also their beasts of burden, which are instruments of war, partly for fighting and partly for carrying baggage and supplies. **l)** in those camps, namely, of the peoples attacking Jerusalem. Verse 12. **m)** namely, according to this plague, or the same one I just mentioned; so that their flesh, feet, and eyes waste away. Verse 12; compare above, chapter 12:4. **v. 16. n)** whoever shall be left, etc. 1 Kings 9:20. That is, whoever has not been destroyed will hereafter be converted and join the Church, and, mindful of the slaughter they received, will obey God. Isaiah 60:14. Thus it will be that the Lord reigns in the midst of His enemies, Psalm 110:2, and from those very ones who had attacked Jerusalem, He preserves a holy seed and holy remnants for Himself, to be reconciled to the Church. Proverbs 16:7; compare above, chapter 9:7. **o)** verses 2, 12. **p)** with changed minds they shall go up. Chapter 8:22, 23. Just as the Jews and Israelites formerly went up from the provinces to Jerusalem three times a year, Exodus 34:24, Psalm 122:4. Moreover, Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century theologian</note> well says: "Christians approach Jerusalem not bodily, but spiritually in the communion of saints. For how is it possible for men from the whole world to come to Jerusalem every year?" Isaiah chapter 66:23 brings this worship into every Sabbath and New Moon. **q)** yearly. 1 Samuel 7:16, 2 Chronicles 24:5. **r)** to prostrate oneself, which expresses the entire worship due to God, verse 17. Isaiah 66:23, Psalm 86:9, Revelation 15:4; compare Zephaniah 3:9, 10. **s)** Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra</note> says this is the Messiah; Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel</note> also approves of this, comparing Psalm 72:11. But lest they should be forced to recognize him as Jehovah, the Lord of Hosts, they devise a grammatical construction here as if it should be explained: "to the King of the Lord of Hosts," whom the Lord Himself appointed, comparing Psalm 2:6. But Jonathan is more correct, taking it absolutely: "to the King of the ages, the Lord," etc. So verse 17; compare above, verse 9, where Jehovah Himself was said to be King over all the earth. Therefore, the Lord of Hosts Himself is the King, and conversely, that King who is treated of here is the Lord of Hosts. Compare Isaiah 6:5, Psalm 24:8, 10. To Him, therefore, the nations shall prostrate themselves, as to the King of nations, manifest in glory, Jeremiah 10:7. **t)** to keep the <term>Feast of Tabernacles</term> <note>original: *festum tabernaculorum*</note>, verses 18, 19. <term>Skenopegia</term> <note>original Greek: σκῆנוπηγίας</note>, as in John 7:2. This feast was celebrated at the end of the year, after the harvest was completed, Deuteronomy 16:13, 16 (where it is also called the "Feast of Ingathering," Exodus 23:16), falling on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, Leviticus 23:34, when (as Jerome says) the moon is at its fullest at night, and all its darkness is dispelled by bright light. In it, the Jewish people renewed the memory of their dwelling in tents and their wandering journey through the desert, Leviticus 23:39–43, offering thanks together with joy that, after enduring the hardships of a tedious journey, the Lord had led them to a land of rest flowing with milk and honey, had given peace, and had filled the granaries with the abundant produce of the field at the end of each year's harvest; compare the whole of Psalm 81 (especially verse 4) and Psalm 107:4–9. That this joy might be more solemn, the Jews carried in their hands branches of palms, myrtles, and willows tied in a bundle; compare Maimonides in *Laws of the Sukkah and the Lulav* <note>original: *Hilchoth Succa Velulaph*</note> chapters 6 and 7, and Leviticus 23:40, Nehemiah 8:15 and following. They were also accustomed <note>original: *fusumque*</note> to sing the "Great Hallel" from Psalm 113 to Psalm 118, and from there (namely, from Psalm 118:25) to repeatedly sing the <term>Hosanna</term> song; compare Vitringa on Revelation, pages 410, 411. Finally, they poured a libation of water drawn from the fountain of Siloam, which is thought to be alluded to in John 7:37. This feast, therefore, the Church of the New Testament will one day celebrate, not indeed according to the Levitical law, but in spirit and truth, just like the feast of Passover and Pentecost, 1 Corinthians 5:7, 8. For a Sabbath truly remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9, after enduring the hardships of the desert—that is, of persecutions and troubles, Hosea 2:16, 17—at the close of the year of grace or the end of the world. When the Church, gathered from its dispersion, finds a city of habitation no less secure than tranquil, Isaiah 26:1, Psalm 107:3 and following, it will then have a most abundant harvest of the gifts of grace and the Holy Spirit, and of earthly goods themselves. These it will so enjoy that it celebrates a spiritual Feast of Tabernacles, joyfully drawing the water of consolation from the wells of salvation, chapter 12:3, Revelation 12:17, having palms in their hands, Revelation 7:9, and singing with a loud voice that great <term>Hosanna</term> and the great <term>Hallelujah</term>; on which passage see, if you please, Vitringa in his *Commentary on Revelation*, pages 410–413 and 421 and following.

**v. 12.** For "the peoples" <note>Hebrew: הָעַמִּים</note>, some have "the nations" <note>Hebrew: הַגּוֹיִם</note> in the margins of versions 6 and 9. It was thus in the text of 5. "He will cause to rot" <note>Hebrew: הָמֵק</note> is without a *Peshik* <note>a cantillation mark</note> in version 2. **v. 13.** "There shall be a panic" <note>Hebrew: תִּהְיֶה מְהוּמַת</note> thus in 1, 3, 5. "Hand" <note>Hebrew: יָד</note> with the prefix in 3, so in 2 and 5. Instead of "against the hand" <note>Hebrew: עַל־יַד</note>, the Oriental versions have "up to the hand" <note>Hebrew: עַד־יַד</note>. **v. 16.** Space is not placed before it in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 14, 15, 20. "And they shall go up" <note>Hebrew: וְעָלוּ</note> with a *Gaiah* <note>a secondary accent</note> in 1, according to its Masorah. "From year to year" <note>Hebrew: מִדֵּי</note> by *Pfikmun* in 1, 2, 3, 5. **v. 17.** "And it shall be" <note>Hebrew: וְהָיָה</note> with a *Gaiah* in 5, according to the Masorah of Erfurt 1.

Compare the related word in Nehemiah 12:27 and the root in 2 Kings 21:12. It is correctly explained as "bells." For pack horses, says Gusset (p. 715), especially in the East where many deserts are traversed with no worn paths, there was a need for some sounding instrument attached so that all companions might be warned, etc. Our own wagon-drivers keep the same custom, leading horses and carriages through the mountains, so that by the sound of bells, if any should approach from a distance, they are warned, lest they become stuck by colliding in the narrow ways. Furthermore, the phrasing here should be noted. For it does not say: *the bells shall be—holiness to the Lord*, but rather: *it shall be UPON the bells, etc.*, namely, by engraving or writing. This implies that "Holiness to the Lord" are the words to be taken materially here, just as in Exodus 28:36. However, it assumes that to be inscribed is to be truly holy. **m)** *holiness*, that is, they are holy things to the Lord. See verse 21. And thus they shall bear the same inscription which the gold plate bore on the forehead of the High Priest; compare Exodus 28:36. Symbolically, therefore, the horses are compared to the High Priest of the old economy in terms of holiness: to show that, the Levitical worship and distinction having been removed, all things in this final period of time will be holy, even the creature itself—since it is to be sanctified through the Word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:5)—and will be liberated from the service of vanity to which it was hitherto subjected, into the glorious liberty of the children of God (Romans 8:19 and following). In this way, a great prerogative of this time over the past is suggested, along with a much greater holiness, as stated above in chapter 12:8; Isaiah 60:22; and Ezekiel 43:12; compare the notes there, also Isaiah 60:21; Jeremiah 31:40; Psalm 93:5. **n)** the pots which are in the House of the Lord, for boiling the sacrificial meats which the people and priests would consume. Ezekiel 46:20; 2 Chronicles 35:13. According to the Levitical law, these were certainly of less value than the bowls used for the altar itself, to receive and sprinkle the blood, which was a most sacred thing in the sacrifices to the Lord, indeed by far the holiest. **o)** This is taken here in opposition to the *altar* which follows; and therefore only such pots are suggested here whose use was only in the courtyard, and whose holiness was lesser; compare Ezekiel 44:11–16. **p)** like the bowls. chapter 9:15; Exodus 27:3; 1 Kings 7:45. These things indicate the obsolescence of the Levitical worship. For whereas formerly in sacred matters (says Meyer on the end of the Psalms, p. 104 ff.) there were various degrees of holiness, and the pots in which the meat of the victims was boiled were of a far lower degree of holiness than the gold and silver phials used for offering fine flour and oil, for pouring the blood of victims around the altar, and for wine and incense—here, nevertheless, the pots and vessels of the lowest dignity are said to be like the gold and silver phials, the most precious and holy. **q)** verse 21. **q)** Indeed, every pot, or whatever pot, not only those in the house of the Lord (compare verse 20) but even those in Jerusalem and Judah. **r)** verse 20; Jeremiah 31:40; Ezra 8:28. **s)** as many as are about to sacrifice. **t)** and they shall take some of those pots. **u)** and shall boil the sacrificial meats in them, and that without any violation of religion. **x)** nor shall there be a Canaanite. One profane and impious, whether from the nations or from the circumcision. Isaiah 35:8; Ezekiel 16:3; chapter 44:7, 9; Joel 4:17; Revelation 21:27; chapter 22:15. This phrase is drawn from the antiquity of the Israelite people, to whom by the law of God the Canaanite nation was abominable, cursed, and impure due to their crimes, such that they were not to be tolerated in the land, much less in the temple. Otherwise, Canaanites as a nation are not excluded from the grace of the New Testament; compare above verses 16 ff; chapter 9:7; Psalm 45:12; Psalm 87:4; Matthew 15:22. But here it means a merchant <note>original Hebrew: *kena'ani* can mean merchant</note>; compare Ezekiel 23:8; Hosea 12:8; Proverbs 31:24; one to whose heart religion is not dear, nor holiness a concern; or those who think that godliness is a means of gain (1 Timothy 6:5). **y)** in the house of the Lord, that is, His Church, since it will then be, in an illustrious and glorious manner, the Congregation of Saints. Compare Isaiah 35:8; Joel 4:17; Revelation 21:27; chapter 22:15.

<header>ON THE PROPHECY OF MALACHI</header>

->§ ( 0 ) §<-

# ON THE PROPHECY OF MALACHI
->PREFACE.<-

->§. I.<-

<margin>The Name of Malachi.</margin> We now come to the last prophet of the Old Testament, *Malachi*. Following our established method, we shall offer a few remarks before unfolding the text itself. The name Malachi <note>original Hebrew: מלאכי</note>—in which the scholar Cocceius observes a "mention" <note>original Greek: μνημόσυνον</note> of the most significant prophecy of this book in chapter 3, verse 1—signifies the same as Malachiah <note>original Hebrew: מלאכיה</note>, that is, "Messenger of the Lord" <note>original Greek: ἄγγελος Κυρίου</note>, or "Envoy of the Lord." This was rightly taught by Hiller in his *Sacred Onomasticon* <note>a dictionary of proper names</note>. The Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation</note> and the Arabic version also translate it this way in chapter 1, verse 1: "by the hand of his messenger" <note>original Greek: ἐν χειρὶ ἀγγέλου αὐτοῦ</note>. Although this well describes the office of a prophet (compare chapter 2:7 and Haggai 1:13), we have no doubt—despite the hesitations of the very learned Vitringa—that this is the proper name of the divine seer, just like *Zechariah* and similar names. Indeed, the Syriac Translator and the Arabic inscription of this book accept it as a proper name, to say nothing of the Western versions. This position must be maintained against the opinion of the ancient Hebrews and some Church Fathers, specifically Jerome, who treated this name as a common title and believed that *Malachi* was actually *Ezra*. Similarly, Jonathan <note>the author of the Aramaic Targum</note> explicitly added after the name of Malachi in chapter 1, verse 1: "who elsewhere is called Ezra the Scribe" <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: דיתקרי שמיה עזרא ספרא</note>. We shall pass over other even less probable conjectures—such as those identifying him as *Haggai* or *Mordecai*—which were deservedly rejected by Abarbanel and others. For Ezra, although he was "divinely inspired" <note>original Greek: θεόπνευστος</note> and a sacred writer, is nowhere called a "Prophet" in the Scriptures, as Abarbanel and others noted at the beginning of this book.

### §. 2.

<margin>Order and Place</margin> §. 2. He was the very last of the prophets of the Old Testament era, as all Jewish and Christian interpreters admit, placing the "finishing touch" <note>original: colophonem</note> on the canonical prophecies of the Old Testament. For this reason, he is called by the Hebrews the "Seal of the Prophets" <note>original Hebrew: חותם הנביאים</note> and "the last among them" <note>original Hebrew: אחרון שבהם</note>. For although from his time until John the Baptist and the dawn of the New Testament there were some instances of extraordinary revelations of the divine will in the Jewish Church (as Vitringa has learnedly and extensively demonstrated), he is nonetheless the last of all the canonical writers of the Old Testament. He immediately preceded the times of Christ and pointed to His precursor, John, under the name of *Elijah* in chapter 3, verses 1 and 23. The *Apocryphal* books, which were written in that intervening time, lacked the dictate of that prophetic spirit, as Lightfoot noted following the confession of the Jews. Compare also 1 Maccabees 9:27 and Josephus's *Against Apion*.

### §. 3.

<margin>Age and Date</margin> §. 3. However, the precise age in which our prophet flourished is not so easily settled that everyone agrees. Some make him a contemporary of *Haggai* and *Zechariah*, but they are rightly refuted by Abarbanel, because Malachi says nothing about the building of the Temple. Instead, he corrects the sins committed in divine worship *after* it was built (chapter 1:10, 3:1, 10). Furthermore, Malachi is not praised alongside Haggai and Zechariah as one of the promoters of that construction in Ezra 5:1 or 6:14. Abarbanel himself, along with the author of the book *Kuzari*, believes Malachi lived not long after the temple was built and that the prophetic gift lasted nearly forty years under the Second Temple among the Jews returning from Babylon. Yet, Malachi’s age seems to belong even later. Gurtler places him near the age of Alexander the Great, but Calovius and Vitringa more correctly place him in the final years of Nehemiah. This is because while Malachi was prophesying, the Jews still had their own "civil governor" <note>original: Polytarchum</note>, as is certain from Malachi 1:8. History does not show any other civil prince over the Jews after Nehemiah; for after his death, the High Priests acted as national leaders <note>original: Ethnarchae</note>. Therefore, Vitringa concludes this prophecy was published after Nehemiah’s second return from Persia to Canaan, specifically after the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, when the High Priest was either *Eliashib* or his son *Joiada*. This is proven by comparing the prophecy of Malachi with the history of Nehemiah.

### §. 4.

<margin>Parallelism</margin> §. 4. Not only are the same crimes condemned in both records, but they are described in almost the same words. Here Vitringa bids us observe that the *Levites* and *Priests* are said to have broken the covenant of God by marrying "foreign women" <note>original Greek: ἀλλοφύλας</note> and by neglecting or divorcing the Hebrew wives to whom they were joined (compare Malachi 2:8, 11 with Ezra 9:1 and Nehemiah 13:23–29). Likewise, the Jews failed to pay tithes to the *Levites*, who consequently fled to their fields to seek the necessities of life (compare Malachi 3:8, 10 with Nehemiah 13:5, 12). There was also a neglect and corruption of divine worship, about which Malachi complains in 1:8 and 2:8, matching Nehemiah 13:15.

### §. 5.

<margin>Occasion</margin> §. 5. After the return from the Babylonian captivity under the leaders *Zerubbabel* the prince and *Joshua* the high priest, the Jews had not only established the commonwealth and laid the foundations of the Temple, but later—under the Persian King Darius Hystaspes—they finished the Temple and restored sacred worship. After the deaths of Zerubbabel and Joshua, under Artaxerxes Longimanus, *Ezra* the theologian and later *Nehemiah* the governor came to the aid of the Jewish affairs, which had collapsed again due to the negligence of the Priests and Prefects. They punished the vices of the people and ensured they were imbued with a solid knowledge of the divine law. The Levitical order was purged of crimes, and the study of sacred literature was cultivated with greater industry. However, despite all their zeal, these vices broke out again shortly after (while Ezra was dead and Nehemiah was absent). The priests, who should have guarded the dignity of their office, betrayed it with profane opinions and impure lives.

### §. 6.

<margin>Argument</margin> §. 6. Therefore, our prophet—intending to rouse the Jews to repentance and the recognition of God’s covenant in Christ—begins by rebuking the ungrateful mind and impiety of the whole people (with the exception of a few godly ones in 3:16). He specifically targets the negligence and profanity of the Priests. He notes that the people offered blemished or stolen sacrifices, while the priests brought the name of God into contempt through their profanity. They failed to correct others and instead led the common people astray by their bad example and teaching. He further rebukes illicit marriages with foreign women and the divorce of lawful wives. While before the Babylonian captivity the people were prone to idolatry, they now leaned toward "Epicureanism and atheism" <note>here meaning religious indifference or skepticism</note>, even among the priests and teachers of the law—acting as if God did not care for human affairs or as if the expectation of a Redeemer (under the "guardianship" <note>original: pædagogia</note> of the Mosaic Law) was in vain. Thus, God announces not only the coming of Christ...

<summary>This page introduces the Book of Malachi, identifying him as the final Old Testament prophet and the "Seal of the Prophets." It places his ministry in the late 5th century BCE, contemporary with Nehemiah's reforms, and highlights his focus on correcting priestly corruption and religious indifference.</summary>
<keywords>Malachi, Ezra, Nehemiah, Seal of the Prophets, Artaxerxes Longimanus, Levitical covenant, Second Temple, post-exilic history, prophecy, biblical chronology</keywords>

CHAPTER I. MALACHI 1 <note>original Hebrew: מַלְאָכִי א</note>

...and he surely promises the coming of the Forerunner <note>John the Baptist</note>, and through him the reformation of the Church in chapter 3, 1–4. But he also threatens those impious despisers of his covenant with the gravest punishments, both temporal and eternal, unless they repent (3:5–7). Having again rebuked the greed of the common people because they did not pay their tithes and firstfruits (3:8–12), and their thinking that it was in vain to serve God (3:12–15), he wonderfully consoles the remnant of the godly (3:16–21). And finally, regarding the future absence of <term>divinely inspired</term> <note>original Greek: θεοπנεύστοις</note> prophets under the old economy, he commends the pious observance of the Mosaic law—as a schoolmaster leading to Christ—against the emerging Epicureanism <note>the denial of divine providence</note> of the Sadducees and the superstition of the Pharisees. He also urges everyone to notice the announcement of Christ’s coming through his forerunner Elijah, that is, John the Baptist (3:22–24).

in v. 2–5. II. *Their ungrateful spirit*, manifest in the negligence of divine worship (v. 6). And III. he proves this especially against the quibbling of the Priests (v. 7–13), and IV. condemns it most gravely (v. 14). See the argument of the book in the Preface § 6. **v. 2. f)** *I have loved you*, without any merit of your own, with a unique love: I adopted you as my people long ago, and now I have even brought you back from captivity and restored the city and temple to you. Grotius: Namely, I loved you not just as humans, but more than other humans, and more than the other descendants of both Abraham and Isaac. Therefore, it was only right (as is implied here) that an extraordinary love be returned to me. Cf. Isaiah 43:4; 48:14; 63:9; Jeremiah 31:3; Hosea 11:1; Amos 3:2. **g)** v. 6; 3:8, 13. Abarbanel: God says, as it were: "Since I first acknowledged you, I have loved you with a constant love; and although you sinned before me so that I punished you, I still loved you constantly. Cf. Gen 15:8. They did not even want to acknowledge that extraordinary love of God toward them, far from being grateful. Perversely, Abarbanel [reads it as] "For what reason?" citing Deut 4:37, to emphasize the merit of the Patriarchs. **k)** *Was not Esau Jacob's brother?* i.e., according to Grotius: Do not the Edomites and you both draw your origin from Abraham and Isaac? Thus Esau and Jacob here, as in what follows, signify their descendants (of whose present and future state the Prophet speaks), just as Edom and Israel are used elsewhere. See Obadiah 10, 12. And in the same sense, the Edomite is called the brother of Israel in Deut 23:8. Others: Was not Esau the brother of Jacob? Meaning that both the ancestors themselves and all their posterity are signified, in this way: Although Esau and Jacob were twin brothers, I did not follow them and their descendants with equal love. For I adopted Jacob and his descendants and benefited them exceptionally; but I placed Esau and his descendants after them, and chastised them with the heaviest judgments according to their merit. Cf. Calovius on this passage. **l)** Cf. note on Ex 11:8; Hos 11:11; Hag 2:23. **m)** *Yet Jacob and his descendants* (of whom the preceding and following verses speak, as also Gen 25:23) *I loved more:* namely, with a love that is not common (like the love for all humans, Ps 145:9; Rom 11:32) but extraordinary and special, by leading him back even to his own borders (v. 5) and building him up after he was restored, in contrast to v. 3–4. This word is often understood comparatively elsewhere: e.g., Gen 29:31 compared with v. 30; Deut 21:15; 1 Sam 1:5; Luke 14:26 compared with Matt 10:37. **o)** *And I have made* Jer 6:8, as I had predicted in Ezek 35:4. **p)** *His mountains* Gen 36:8; Deut 2:4; Josh 24:4, etc. There is a silent contrast between the mountainous and rugged Edom and the land of Canaan, flowing with milk and honey (Ex 3:8). **q)** *A desolation*. Ex 23:29; Josh 8:28; Isaiah 1:16. For Edom was devastated after Judea by Nebuchadnezzar. See Jer 25:17, 21; 27:3; 49:7 onwards; Amos 1:11, 12; Obad 10; and especially Ezek 25:12 onwards. Cf. also the short history of the people at 2 Kings 21:11. **r)** For the <term>jackals</term> <note>original Latin: *draconibus* (dragons/serpents)</note> of the desert, and indeed in such a way that this state would last forever (v. 4). For jackals frequent solitudes; therefore the Prophets so often predict that populous cities will become dwellings for jackals, or be inhabited by jackals, when they threaten extreme desolation. Cf. Isaiah 13:22; 34:13; Jer 9:10; 51:37. But because <term>Tannoth</term> <note>Hebrew for jackals or dragons</note> is masculine elsewhere (e.g., Ex 7:12; Deut 32:33; Job 30:29, etc.), the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic versions substitute "dwellings of the desert," from the Arabic root <term>shakan</term> <note>original Hebrew: שכן</note> meaning "to stay, dwell, or inhabit." **v. 4. s)** *For:* or "indeed." Vulgate: *But if Edom shall say.* **t)** *We are impoverished:* reduced to poverty; also well rendered by the Vulgate as *destroyed*, i.e., we have now suffered the destruction of cities and houses. This is opposed to "building." (4) Cf. Jer 5:17; Ps 34:11; Prov 13:7. The Arabic root means "it weakened" or "rendered the loins weak by disease." **u)** Vulgate: *But returning, i.e., but now we will build again.* Jonathan [Targum]: *But now having become rich, we will build.* Which they did, as is clear from histories. Cf. a similar presumption in Isaiah 9:9.

The commentator uses historical and linguistic evidence to explain "loving" and "hating" as comparative terms regarding national destiny rather than individual salvation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first chapter of Malachi, moving from the comparison between Jacob and Esau to a sharp rebuke of the priesthood for their negligent and disrespectful sacrificial practices. It maintains the scholarly dialogue between Christian commentators like Jerome and Calovius and Jewish exegetes like Abarbanel and Ibn Ezra.</meta>

MALACHI. CHAPTER I.
תרמ <note>Hebrew page number: 440</note>

<margin>
x) ruins; things that were destroyed. Isaiah 5:17; 49:19. y) verse 6, 8. Nahum 1:12. z) Isaiah 1:24. Hosea 12:6. a) they shall build, but I will destroy. Or: if the children build, I will destroy. Cf. Jeremiah 45:4. Psalm 28:5. b) that is, they shall be called. This is used impersonally; see Ezekiel 39:11. Abarbanel: Because all men will recognize that I hate them and am opposed to their kingdom. c) the border of wickedness. Malachi 3:13; Zechariah 5:8. This refers to the region or territory of the impious, as Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Translation/Targum</note> has it; and for that reason, it is deservedly desolate. d) with whom the Lord is angry. Numbers 23:8; Isaiah 66:14. Jonathan: upon whom I will bring a curse. e) forever. Isaiah 34:10, 17. Jerome <note>original: Hieronymus</note>: "And my anger will be proved by their eternal devastation." This is to be taken in contrast to the Jewish people in verse 5; for although the Lord was angry with them for a long time (Zechariah 1:13), after seventy years had passed, he returned to them with grace and mercy (verses 16, 17). See notes on Zechariah 1:16. Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius, 17th-century theologian</note>: It is signified that Edom is to be punished with destruction, partly as a nation (except for a remnant, Amos 9:12) and partly as a name. This was fulfilled both because their captivity was never revoked by decree, unlike that of the Jews; and because the remnants who stayed in Idumea were mixed with other peoples, and being conquered by Hyrcanus, they were forced to accept circumcision and converted to Judaism. After the Roman devastation, they were so thoroughly wiped out that their name is no longer found on the earth. Cf. notes on Isaiah 21:11 and what we cited above for verse 3.

Jerome: "Imitating Cain, responding with proud voices against God, you question him whom hidden things do not deceive." Cf. Isaiah 45:9; chapter 58:2; Jeremiah 2:35. **t)** verse 7. Just as in verse 2 they did not want to acknowledge the love and benefits of God, so here they do not want to acknowledge their sins. ❈ **verse 7.** **u)** *You are offering. You offer*. chapter 2:13; 3:3; 1 Kings 5:1. This proves their ungrateful spirit. **x)** *polluted bread* verse 12; Job 3:5; Lamentations 4:14; Daniel 1:8. By which Grotius understands the <term>Mincha</term> <note>the grain offering</note> which was to be offered with the daily sacrifice (Exodus 29:40; Numbers 28:24); others more correctly understand even the victims and any offerings. Compare verse 8; also Leviticus 3:11; 21:6, 8, 17, 21, 22; 22:25; Numbers 28:2. Abarbanel: *unclean things*. Jonathan: *an impure or cursed offering*. These were sacrifices of contaminated men, unfit and not offered rightly, but without repentance and faith; by which the table of the Lord was polluted by those impure Priests both ceremonially and morally, neglecting the chief end of the offerings: the Messiah with his benefits, to be preached throughout the whole world, and the faith which ought to look solely to Christ. Compare Leviticus 22:25; Titus 1:15. **y)** see verse 2, 6. **z)** Vulgate: *in what have we polluted you?* <note>original Latin note: Piel (i)</note> **a)** Namely, *by this, that you say*. verse 12; chapter 2:17. **b)** *table*, that is, the altar of the Lord. So in verse 12. Because the sacrifice is like a banquet, in which (as Calovius has it in this place) God is the host, the altar is the table, the victim is the food, the libation is the drink, and the priest is the servant. Cf. Ezekiel 41:22; 44:16. Others compare Leviticus 24:6. **c)** *vile*, namely *contemptible*, Vulgate: *despised*. chapter 2:9; Isaiah 53:3; Jeremiah 49:15. And so it matters little what kind of victims or how we offer them: since all our worship is useless and the expectation of the Messiah, figured through it, is empty. Cf. verse 12; 2:17; and 3:14. Abarbanel: They said this because they offered fat and blood on the altar, which seemed to them to be contemptible things. But that is true of every part, even the most excellent part of the sacrifices, without respect and faith in Christ, from whom those shadows of the Old Testament had all their value. Compare Isaiah 61:11 onwards; Psalm 50:8 onwards. ❈ **verse 8. d)** Namely, *for if you offer*. That is, send such a thing *as a gift*. Judges 3:17; Psalm 72:10. **k)** *to your governor*. Jonathan adds: *who is over you*. Nehemiah 5:14, 15, 18; chapter 12:26. Cf. Preface § 3. **l)** *will he have you as accepted?* verse 10; Haggai 1:8. **m)** *or will he lift up your face?* verse 9. Will your arrival with such a gift be pleasing to him, so that he nods to your requests? Cf. Genesis 19:21; 32:21; 1 Samuel 25:35. **n)** divine worship, as in verses 2, 9, etc. ❈ **verse 9. o)** Now therefore. From a correction to an exhortation toward repentance, the Prophet transitions: teaching that there is still hope for pardon if they seriously repent; if not, they will by no means be unpunished. Cf. chapter 2:1. **p)** entreat humbly at last. 1 Samuel 13:12. **q)** *that he may have mercy on us*; or then he will have mercy on us. Amos 5:15; Psalm 67:2; Job 33:24. **r)** Namely, *for since this happens from your hand*. Specifically, the sin of the impure and unfit offering. verse 7, 8. see verses 10, 13; chapter 2:13; and cf. a similar expression in Isaiah 50:11. **s)** *will he accept faces from you*, so that you become accepted and pleasing to him? which the phrase signifies in the preceding verse 8. Others: that he might have regard for your office or person, and use <term>prosopolempsia</term> <note>original Greek: προσωποληψία; meaning partiality or favoritism</note> toward you? chapter 2:9. He will certainly not do so in any way, nor should you expect such a thing. Cf. Deuteronomy 10:17; 2 Chronicles 19:7; Romans 2:11; etc. **8)** see verse 2, 8.

<summary>This page analyzes Malachi's condemnation of the Judean priests for offering blemished sacrifices, contrasting Edom's permanent destruction with Israel's call to repentance. The commentary emphasizes that religious rituals are "contemptible" and "vile" when performed without sincerity or faith in the coming Messiah.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of the corrupt priesthood in the post-exilic period. While the previous page contrasted the fates of Jacob (Israel) and Esau (Edom), this page focuses on God’s rejection of the current Temple ritual and His prophecy that His name will eventually be honored by all nations, not just a negligent Judean priesthood.</meta>

v. 10. u) Who is there among you who would shut the doors for my benefit? So says the Syriac version. The sense is: I am so far from looking upon you with favor (v. 9) that I would rather the Temple be closed than have you worship me in vain with foolish sacrifices offered without true repentance and faith. Abarbanel: As if God says: "I wish someone would first stand up in your presence and shut the doors of the Temple, so that you would no longer offer such detestable offerings." Others think the greed of the Priests is being rebuked, and they draw the heavy meaning from the following clause: "Who among you would shut the doors for nothing?" They mean to say: *"The altar with the whole sanctuary, as if impure, has long since been rejected by God and overturned by enemies."* And although both were restored through Zerubbabel and Joshua, and the priesthood was also purified with great zeal by Ezra, nevertheless, neither the singular favor of God nor the Messiah promised by Haggai (2:6, 7, 19) appears to us. Because the poverty of the people (cf. below 3:10, 11) and that cheap food—by which we can scarcely sustain the dignity of the priesthood—prove that this worship is not dear to God’s heart, nor are we His concern. cf. 2:9. Clearly, these impious men did not feel that they were polluted by sins and were polluting everything; and having cast away hope and faith in Christ (the kernel and end of the Levitical ceremonies), they clung to the shell, prone toward apostasy, Epicureanism <note>a philosophy prioritizing physical comfort or indifference to the divine</note>, or hypocrisy, and then they openly rushed into it. cf. v. 7; 2:17; 3:13, 14; and Preface § 5, 6. **z)** *as for its return* or *its produce* (of the altar). ### CHAPTER II. v. 1. z)
"Now therefore." Compare chapter 1:9.
### a)
"To you especially," this pertains or belongs: lest you think that you do not need repentance. Compare Hosea 5:1.
### b)
"This commandment." verse 4. Namely, concerning repentance and a better administration of your office in the future. See chapter 1:9.
### c)
"O Priests!" chapter 1:6. Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish philosopher and commentator</note> says: that is, this fault or guilt pertains not so much to the common people, who lack wisdom and learning, as it does to you, who ought to have instructed the others. For God continues in this chapter to threaten and most gravely rebuke: I. The Priests for violating the covenant of God (1) through their disobedience and sluggishness (verse 2) in sacrifices and feasts (verse 3); (2) through corrupt doctrine (verses 4–7) and bad example (verse 8); (3) through wicked partiality toward persons (verses 9–10). II. Along with the priests, He also rebukes those of the people (1) who were unlawfully taking foreign wives (verses 11–12); (2) who were afflicting innocent wives (verses 13–16); and (3) who were impudently denying divine providence and the truth of the promises concerning Christ (verse 17).

<column-break/>

**i)** a curse. chapter 3:9. Compare Leviticus 26:14 and following; Deuteronomy 28:15 and following; Zechariah 5:3. **k)** "and I will curse." Genesis 12:3. **l)** "your blessings," namely material ones, gathered from verse 3 and Genesis 33:11. Jerome explains this as: those things which you now possess by my blessings. Genesis 49:25, 26. Abarbanel says: "I will turn the blessing, with which you have been blessed since the day the House of the Lord was founded (Haggai 2:19), into a curse." Compare below at chapter 3:10. Others say it refers to your priestly blessings. Compare Numbers 6:23 and following. **m)** as if to say: "again and again I say this to you, because you do not..." etc. Or "and I will also curse this." But the Tigurine version and Abarbanel use the past tense: "indeed, I have already cursed it (each of your blessings) from the moment you began to despise my name, and I saw that you would not take it to heart." **n)** compare 1 Samuel 2:30; Psalm 109:27 and following. **v. 3. o)** "Behold, I will rebuke and destroy for you." chapter 3:11; Psalm 9:6; Psalm 104:7. **p)** The Syriac says: "the seed of the earth." Jonathan's Targum says: "the produce of the crops or the nature of the crop," so that it does not sprout or bear fruit, or is even consumed by locusts while still a blade of grass. Compare chapter 3:10. r. Abarbanel: he mentions the "seed" in respect to the *Minchah* <note>the grain offering</note> and "dung" in respect to the offerings or victims of the Jews. **q)** "and I will scatter." Ezekiel 5:10 and 6:5. **r)** the dung from the entrails of the sacrificed victims. See Exodus 29:14. **s)** "upon your faces." Just as a Master who is disgusted by the gift of his servant throws it back in his face and scatters it. Abarbanel and Jonathan: "and I will reveal the filth of your crimes upon your faces." **t)** The Vulgate says: "of your solemnities," that is, of the festive victims. See Exodus 23:18; Isaiah 29:1; Psalm 118:27; and compare Amos 5:21. **u)** or "and it shall take you away to itself." Ezekiel 29:19. Jerome says: clearly the dung with which your faces are smeared shall occupy you entirely. Others take it impersonally: "and they shall take you away," or "you shall be taken away, along with it." So the Dutch version. Cocceius, however, applies this to the destruction of the city, Temple, and the Jewish state, in this manner: "and at last the people of a foreign Prince shall take you away to himself," referring to Daniel 9:26, which is a more remote interpretation.
### v. 4.
**x)** "And you shall know," having been taught by the experience of my threats. Compare Ezekiel 5:13. **y)** "that I have not sent this commandment to you through my Prophet in vain." verse 1. Compare Zechariah 2:13, 15. **z)** "to the end that," namely, so that it might be. The Tigurine version says: "that it might be," etc. But Abarbanel says: "for no other reason than that my covenant was with Levi and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord." Compare Numbers 17:23, 25. **a)** that is, with the Levites, as the Septuagint and Arabic versions have it. Compare Deuteronomy 33:8. Jerome says: through the patriarch Levi it reached his descendants Aaron, Eleazar, Phinehas, and the others who were born of his stock. **b)** see the note on chapter 1:8.
### v. 5.
**c)** My covenant or league—not just the common one I made with the whole people in Deuteronomy 29:9 and following—but one that is proper and peculiar. **d)** "it was with him," namely Levi or the Tribe of the Levites. See Exodus 32:29; Numbers 3:6, 12; chapter 8:14; chapter 18:19; Deuteronomy 10:8. Add for the Priests: Numbers 17:12 and following; Chapter 25:10 and following. **e)** "of life," namely. The Arabic says: "for life and peace." Compare Leviticus 18:5; Deuteronomy 30:15, 19; 1 Timothy 4:8. **f)** "and of peace." See regarding Phinehas in Numbers 25:12; and compare Numbers 6:26; Isaiah 54:10; Job 5:23, 25. **g)** "Which (namely life and peace; others say the Levitical precepts) I gave to him." **h)** "for fear," or "with fear," so that he might fear me, as follows. Compare chapter 1:6; Deuteronomy 31:12, 13; Ecclesiastes 66:2; Jeremiah 32:40; Psalm 130:4; and a similar construction of the word with a suffix and a following accusative in Psalm 74:14; Ecclesiastes 2:21. **i)** or "therefore, because of my name." As if to say: "from the face of" or "out of respect and fear of my name," which you impiously despise. chapter 1:6, 12. Compare Jeremiah 15:17; Nehemiah 5:15. **k)** or "he feared for himself." The Vulgate says: "he was terrified." Deuteronomy 1:21; Jeremiah 1:17; Ezekiel 2:6. Truly the religious diligence of the ancient priests and Levites is praised here and in verse 6; and how much the transgression of the priests of that time differs from their example and from the rule of the Priestly office (verse 7) is shown in verses 8 and 9.
### v. 6.
**l)** The Law or Doctrine of truth. Psalm 119:142. Compare Psalm 25:8. **m)** "was in his mouth." Compare Proverbs 10:11.

<header>MALACHI 2. CHAPTER 2.</header>

<margin>
The things that follow, which the Prophet adds, clearly indicate that he is teaching here not what the Priests are, but what they ought to be. Compare Deuteronomy 17:8 and following; 2 Chronicles 19:10; 2 Corinthians 5:20. Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> notes this is because the Priest is God's messenger between Himself and Israel; he adds the following reason from the Talmudic scholars: "If the priest is like an angel of the Lord of Hosts, they shall seek the law from his mouth; if he is not, they shall not depend on his mouth."
</margin>

<margin>
m) and perversity. Job 6:30; compare Leviticus 19:15. n) So that he might imitate his Lord. Compare Isaiah 53:9; 1 Peter 2:22. o) in peace (verse 5; Isaiah 27:5; Philippians 4:7; Hebrews 12:14) and in uprightness (Isaiah 11:4; Psalm 26:12). Abarbanel: with peace established among men, and with uprightness, in which he instructed everyone. p) he walked with me. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian</note>: that is, he retained my friendship by doing what was right. Compare Genesis 5:22; Micah 6:8; 1 John 1:6–7. q) and thus he turned many back from iniquity. Malachi 3:24; Jeremiah 23:22; Daniel 12:3; James 5:20. Thus Hillel commends the example of Aaron to his followers in Pirkei Avot <note>Ethics of the Fathers</note> chapter 1, verse 11, in these words: "Be," he says, "of the disciples of Aaron, who loved peace and pursued peace, loved mankind, and brought them close to the Law." Just as he had done. For also in chapter 1 verse 7 and chapter 2 verse 7. s) For the lips of the Priest. Proverbs 10:11, 32. s) The Vulgate says "they shall guard," that is, as in 1 Timothy 6:20. It means they have a duty to guard. See a similar use of the future tense in chapter 1:6, and compare 1 Timothy 6:20. For this is a Rule concerning the office of the Priests, with which the example of the ancients agreed, as we said at verse 5. t) knowledge and the understanding of divine matters, Hosea 4:1, drawn from Holy Scripture. Compare Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 31:9–12, 19; Ezra 7:10; 2 Chronicles 17:7–9; 2 Timothy 3:15; Titus 1:9. u) and the law, or as Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Targum of Jonathan</note> has it, the instruction or information taken from the Law of God and faithfully explaining it. Compare the note on Haggai 2:11. x) the unlearned shall seek it from his mouth. Verse 6: compare notes on Deuteronomy 33:10; Ezekiel 44:23; Nehemiah 8:3–4, 7–8; and the Hebrew word *bakash* <note>בָּקַשׁ - to seek or search for</note>. y) because he is an angel, that is, a messenger; Jonathan says "minister." Chapter 3:1; Isaiah 42:19; Haggai 1:13. z) "The messenger of the Almighty" in the Septuagint <note>original Greek: ὁ Άγγελος παντοκράτορός</note>. Exodus 1:24; Hosea 12:6. a) he is, or at least he ought to be, by virtue of his office. For what follows...
</margin>

**Verse 8.** *b) Abarbanel:* "But you," the priests of this age. See the note on verse 5. *c)* You yourselves have withdrawn from the way prescribed in the Word of God. *Abarbanel:* From the way in which I said those first Priests—Aaron, Eleazar, and Phinehas—walked in verse 6. Compare chapter 3:7; Deuteronomy 9:16, 11:28, 31:29; Jeremiah 8:8, 18:18; Daniel 9:5. *d) The Vulgate:* "and you have caused very many to be scandalized"; *Septuagint:* "you have made many strike against the law." Jeremiah 18:15; Matthew 18:6. *Abarbanel:* Namely, so that they withdrew from it and sinned against it; whereas those ancients converted many. This was by leading others astray through a wicked example and corrupt doctrine. See the practice of that time in Nehemiah 13:4 and following; and compare Isaiah 3:12; Jeremiah 18:18; Ezekiel 21:26, 44:11. *e)* You have ruined. *The Vulgate:* "you have made void." Ezekiel 32:7; Hosea 9:9. *f) Arabic:* "my Levitical covenant or pact," which I had made with the tribe of Levi. Compare Ezekiel 16:59; Hosea 6:7; also the note on Ezekiel 44:7; and almost the same words in Nehemiah 13:29. *g)* See note on chapter 1:13.

**Verse 9.** *h)* "Therefore I also," since I was despised by you in chapter 1:6–7, etc. This denotes a most just retribution <note>Latin: talionem</note>. Compare Ezekiel 16:43, 23:35. *i)* I have rendered you, Ezekiel 6:14, 25:7. *k)* looked down upon. Compare chapter 1:7; 1 Samuel 2:30. *l)* and humble or abject. Job 5:11. *m) Septuagint:* "to the whole people." Compare 1 Timothy 4:12; 2 Timothy 3:9. *n)* by the fact that. *The Vulgate:* "just as." Zechariah 2:4. *o)* you do not observe, as the ancients did in Deuteronomy 33:9. *p)* my ways; Jonathan: "the things that are right before me." See verse 8; Isaiah 2:3. Nor was your doctrine a law of truth, as was that of the men of old, about whom we spoke above in verse 6. *q)* but you have been "accepters of faces" <note>showing partiality</note> in the law or in handling the Word of God, having more regard for persons than for what is true and right. Chapter 1:9. You adapted your opinions to the most learned in order to win favor. Psalm 82:2. Contrary to Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 1:17, 8:7. Compare Isaiah 2:3; Proverbs 18:5; 1 Timothy 5:21; John 12:43, 5:44; James 2:1 and following.

**Verse 10.** *r) The Vulgate:* "Is there not one Father of us all?" Namely, God, as the following explanation clarifies; compare chapter 1:6; Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 64:7; John 8:41; Ephesians 3:15, 4:6. Thus the predicate could refer to all men (compare Isaiah 58:7), though others restrict it to the Jews in this way: "Are we not all descended from Abraham or Jacob?" Compare chapter 1:2; John 8:33, 37, 39. This is how *Grotius* was noted by Calovius. *s)* Did not one God create us? Compare Jeremiah 32:27; Job 34:19; Isaiah 43:1. *t)* Why then? Jeremiah 8:5, 19. *u)* we act faithlessly. Verse 11. See the note on this word *bagad* <note>בָּגַד - to act treacherously</note> in Judges 9:23 and Jeremiah 3:20. *x)* one against another? Leviticus 25:46; Nehemiah 5:7. That is, according to *Abarbanel*: a husband against a wife. This is incorrect, as it ignores the gender and phraseology of the text; he thought it should be connected with what follows, as Jerome also did. We refer it, along with Schmid's headings, to the "respect of persons" <note>partiality</note> mentioned in verse 9. *Grotius* truly cited Exodus 22:24; Leviticus 25:35; Deuteronomy 23:20. However, those are other words of the Law, and we do not find the word *bagad* used elsewhere for the oppression of the poor; therefore, it cannot be taken that way here, unless you consider the poor primarily in their role as "brothers," as he had said at the beginning of the verse. *y)* by profaning and violating. Verse 11; chapter 1:12. *z)* the covenant of our fathers. Compare Deuteronomy 29:13, 14, 24.

**Verse 11.** *a) Septuagint:* "He acted faithlessly." *Tiguro:* "Judah fell away," that is, the tribe or the Jewish church, which was betrothed to Christ as a mystical wife in a sacred covenant. Compare Isaiah 54:1; Jeremiah 3:1; Hosea 1:2, 2:4, etc. Regarding the construction with a feminine verb, see the note on Hosea 2:21, 5:9; Micah 2:10. Up to this point, he had dealt with the faithlessness and transgression of the Priests; now follows the rebuke of those who marry foreign women (verses 11–12) and those who afflict their innocent spouses (verse 13 and following). The transition is conveniently made through the word *bagad* <note>faithlessness/treachery</note> repeated from verse 10. *b)* and an abomination, or a detestable thing that should be loathed by all pious Jews. Deuteronomy 13:15. *c)* was committed in Israel, Benjamin, and the rest of the Israelites who had joined themselves to the returning Jews. See the note on chapter 1:1. Compare Genesis 34:7; 2 Samuel 13:12. *d)* even in Jerusalem itself, or especially in Jerusalem. Compare the note on Isaiah 1:1. *e)* explanatory, as in Hosea 11:10; Amos 3:14, 6:11. *f)* Judah has violated and prostituted. Verse 10; chapter 1:12; compare Leviticus 19:29. *g)* the holiness of the Lord and his own dignity; no small part of which, as *Grotius* writes, consisted in this: that Jews should not join in marriage with idol worshipers. Exodus 34:16; Deuteronomy 7:3. Regarding the phrase, see Exodus 22:30; Leviticus 11:44, 19:8, etc. *h)* which Jehovah loves. Compare Leviticus 19:2, 20:7; 1 Peter 1:15–16; Hebrews 12:14. *i) Septuagint:* "and he betrothed to himself." Namely, he called her his wife. Deuteronomy 21:13.
