Compare Chapter 1:13, Ephesians 1:15, Psalm 26:6. * v. 14. d) "Yet you say stubbornly." verse 17, chapter 1:2, 6. e) Vulgate: "For what cause?" Numbers 22:32, Jeremiah 9:11. That is: "Why can you not accept our gifts?" f) "For this reason, I say, because." Deuteronomy 31:17, Judges 3:12, Jeremiah 4:28. g) "Jehovah has testified." Genesis 31:49, 50. h) Vulgate: "and your wife you treat treacherously" (verses 11, 15, 16) while, having plucked the flower of her youth, you either divorce her or trample her by bringing in a foreign woman. Compare Matthew 19:3 and following. l) "though she is your companion" or your partner. Compare Ecclesiastes 4:10. m) Vulgate: "and the wife of your covenant," who was allied or joined to you by a matrimonial pact, and who has still performed what she owed on her part. Compare Obadiah verse 7, Ezekiel 16:60. * v. 15. n) This is an extremely difficult passage, interpreted very differently by commentators. Most, following Jonathan, Kimchi, etc., explain it in reference to Abraham, as we will briefly say. Kimchi: "Did not Abraham also do this?" the wicked asked. To whom the Prophet replied: "He by no means did so, because there were remnants of excellent and most outstanding virtue in his spirit." Others say: "Neither did the one Abraham, not yet increased with offspring (compare Isaiah 51:2, Ezekiel 33:24), whose example you try to use to defend your malice, act in this way when, by the persuasion and command of his wife, he admitted Hagar the servant into his bed (Genesis 16:1–4). For a remnant of the divine spirit (so our accents mark it) remained with him—quite different from you, who, not having the spirit of God (Jude verse 19), indulge your evil nature. For what did that one Abraham do when he took Hagar? Did he do it to the harm of his wife, so that she was distressed, while he himself satisfied his lust with a godless woman? Not at all. For he was seeking with great zeal and longing (chapter 3:1) a 'godly seed,' that is, the offspring or progency (Genesis 4:25) promised to him many times by God. See Genesis 12:2–3, 13:15–16, 15:4–5, 13–16, 18; compare 3:15. Because, as Calovius says, he had received the promise regarding the multiplication of his offspring, he sought it especially while he was still alone: and above all, that blessed seed, namely Christ. A promise had been given to him by God concerning the blessed seed, but it was not yet declared that he would receive it from Sarah's body; and therefore, by the counsel and consent of Sarah—indeed, Sarah herself wished to be 'built up' from the handmaid." etc. Jonathan: "Was not Abraham alone the one from whom the world was propagated? And what did that one seek, except that a progency might remain to him in the sight of the Lord?" That is, according to Abarbanel, children who would worship the venerable name of Jehovah; but certainly not so that he, like you, might indulge in lust. Others, however, think the Prophet is speaking of Adam. Rabbi Solomon [Rashi]: "Did not God make one pair of humans, Adam and Eve?" (referencing verse 14). Gussetius (pages 25, 781, and 814): "Did not God make two into one flesh?" Genesis 2:24. "And does not what remains of spirits—that is, the residual souls, just as the souls of that first pair—belong to God and fall under His power?" Compare Numbers 16:22, 27:16, Ezekiel 18:4. But because the context mentions neither Adam nor Abraham, Abarbanel says: "This text seems simply to be understood this way: 'Not even one among you has acted thus,' so that you might object with Moses, 'If one man sins, will you be angry with the whole congregation?' (Numbers 16:21)." See what follows. o) as pertains to the rest of the people of Judah (verse 11). p) "the spirit of God and His grace be present with him." Genesis 41:38, Numbers 14:24, 27:18, Job 32:8. q) "And how?" Job 9:2, 25:4. r) or a union of that kind, or every transgressor. s) "one who is seeking and can expect" (chapter 3:1). Ezekiel 10:11, Numbers 16:10, Nehemiah 5:18. t) "Godly seed," or children religiously worshiping God (Genesis 6:1, 4; Isaiah 6:13), if he prefers a mother who would lead the sons to idols? u) "Therefore guard yourselves." (verse 16). Deuteronomy 7:4. x) "in your spirit" or regarding your spirit. The Vulgate: "Therefore keep your spirit." Jerome: "lest you be led away by lust: lest you be conquered by the love of foreign women." The construction and sense are the same in Deuteronomy 24:8, 2 Samuel 20:10; compare 2 Corinthians 13:5. Calovius: "Thus he emphatically opposes the spirit of the Jews to the spirit of Abraham." But Schmidius translates "by your spirit." Jonathan: "your souls" or yourselves. To Gussetius (p. 781): "that is, under the peril of your spirits or souls, or as much as your soul is dear to you." Compare Jeremiah 17:21, Deuteronomy 4:15, Joshua 23:11. y) "and against the wife of your youth" (verse 14) O Judah (verse 11). Jerome: "who was first joined to you in virginal marriage."

e) see similar comparisons in Habakkuk 2:14, Ephesians 44:20, Nehemiah 3:37. f) see verse 15. g) nor should you violate the faith given in marriage. verse 11, 14. see the note on Judges 9:23, Jeremiah 3:20.

<margin>
r) to repudiate/divorce. Deuteronomy 22:19, 29. Symmachus omits this comma; but Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>12th-century Spanish-Jewish scholar</note> rightly explains it simply: "For God hates it if anyone dismisses his pure and innocent wife"; this is contrary to the common view of the Hebrews and Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase</note>. For [the other view suggests] if he hates her, let him dismiss her, as the Septuagint <note>LXX</note>, Vulgate, Arabic, and Portuguese versions have it, as if it were better to dismiss a wife than to keep her while hating her and treating her bitterly, comparing Deuteronomy 24:1. But because in the cited passage God did not command the dismissal of wives, nor even permit it except for what he tolerated due to the hardness of the Israelites' hearts (Matthew 19:7, 8; Mark 10:4, 5), Ibn Ezra’s explanation is to be preferred, which the Hebrew accents support, and our own scholars like Tarnovius and Calovius <note>17th-century Lutheran theologians</note> deservedly embrace. Even Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> admits that not all the Talmudists in the tractate Gittin <note>The section of the Talmud dealing with divorce</note> agree with the common explanation; and Abarbanel says there are those who interpret this place as: "If you hate your wife, dismiss her," comparing Deuteronomy 24:1, but there are also those who explain it as God pursuing with hatred the one who dismisses his wife. b) see verse 1, 8. c) Ephesians 17:6, Zephaniah 2:9. d) The Vulgate says "it covers," but "iniquity" and "violence covers" (or: *chamas* [violence] is his covering, or for the purpose of signaling—Exodus 21:10, chapter 22:26, Deuteronomy 22:12) his clothing: and the wicked divorcer of an innocent wife will put on <note>Deuteronomy 21:12</note> violence or the punishment for this violence (Habakkuk 2:17) upon his garment; as if a wrap over an undergarment, or an outer garment over an inner one. see Psalm 109:17, 18. Arabic: "and impiety shall cover his garment." e) see...
</margin>

<margin>
v. 17. h) You have fatigued the Lord. Jonathan: "You have caused trouble."
</margin>

...is before the Lord. <term>Hiphil</term> <note>The causative verb form in Hebrew</note> (3) Isaiah 43:23, 24. Abarbanel says the Scripture speaks <note>original: "ἀνθρωποπαθῶς"</note> <note>speaking in human-like terms to describe God</note> etc. i) with your words. compare chapter 3:13. Regarding the connection, Calovius says: "This is a new correction and accusation of the Jews, whom he rebukes for that extreme profanity into which they had gradually fallen from being accustomed to previous vices, so that they even slashed at God’s justice and truth with their impious words." Compare also the note above at verse 1 and the Preface § 6. k) yet you say, Syriac: "but if you should say." see verse 14, chapter 3:13. l) in what matter have we offended you? compare chapter 1:2, 7. m) through this, that you say. chapter 1:7. n) whoever works evil. chapter 3:15. compare above verses 11, 13, chapter 1:6, 7, 14. o) is approved and pleasing to the Lord. Numbers 24:1, 1 Samuel 29:9, 2 Samuel 3:36. compare Jeremiah 12:1, Job 21:7, and Psalm 73:2 and following, which psalm carries out this topic more fully and widely. p) Vulgate: "and such please him." compare chapter 1:10, Psalm 5:5, 9. Vulgate: "or certainly." They use a dilemma. r) where is he? Abarbanel: This particle is used for that which is not found, for example, Job 14:10. compare above chapter 1:6, 8, 13, 18. s. The God of (that) judgment, regarding which see verse 12, chapter 3:5. Jerome <note>Early Christian scholar and translator of the Vulgate</note>: that is, where is the truth of judgment? Compare below chapter 3:13, Psalm 50:21, Psalm 73:11. They wanted to say: "On the contrary, God often does not now avenge the sins of the most abandoned men (Ecclesiastes 8:11), nor does the Messiah, promised long ago for the restoration of the human race, hasten His arrival." compare 2 Peter 3:4, Isaiah 5:19, Jeremiah 17:15. To resolve this objection, God responds in the following Chapter III. CHAPTER III, verse 1. a) But indeed, behold I, that is, the Savior says, calling for attention, as in Isaiah 50:2, chapter 64:4, Zechariah 3:9. As if to say: "You blasphemously ask: where is the God of judgment? (chapter 2:17). But behold I, as the universal judge to whom the Father has given judgment (Psalm 72:1, Daniel 7:13, 14, John 5:27), who am about to announce judgment, or rather bring it forth to victory (Isaiah 42:1, 3, Matthew 12:18, 20), will most certainly be present at the time divinely appointed," etc. Nor are those in error who attribute these words to God the Father, as we shall soon see, comparing Matthew 11:10, Mark 1, 2, Luke 7:27, because the mission of John the Baptist, or the outward work of God, pertains to the entire Holy Trinity; compare also Luke 3:2, John 1:33. Furthermore, according to Schmidius, four parts are to be observed in this chapter: I. Prophecy regarding the coming of the messenger-precursor John the Baptist, and of Christ and his sermons (v. 1–6). II. Rebuking of the Jews for not giving tithes (v. 7–12). III. Those blaspheming Jehovah, as if he discerns nothing between the good and the bad (v. 13–18). IV. Their refutation through the arrival of Christ and his precursor Elijah (v. 19–24). b) Vulgate: "I send" or "I am about to send to you" (v. 23). *) "my messenger," that is, my news-bearer or legate, as in chapter 2:7, Haggai 1:13, Isaiah 42:19, John 1:6, 33. namely John the Baptist, the herald and precursor of Christ, as is most certainly established from the New Testament, comparing Isaiah 40:3, Matthew 3:3, chapter 11:10, Mark 1:2, Luke 7:27, etc. For illustration of the Greek wording <note>original: "dictionis"</note>, compare Luke 7:24, chapter 9:52, James 2:25, and the Septuagint Genesis 32:3, Numbers 20:14, chapter 24:12, Joshua 7:22, Judges 6:35, etc. The Jews fluctuate here and do not know which way to turn. Ibn Ezra imagines another Messiah, the son of Joseph, with his followers; Rashi imagines the angel of death; Abarbanel imagines our prophet Malachi; then truly on folio 300 b., along with Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, 12th-13th century grammarian</note>, he wrongly understands it as Elijah the Tishbite. d) Vulgate: "and he shall prepare," or "who shall prepare the way," by removing those things which are unpleasant or an impediment to one who is about to enter. compare Genesis 24:31, Isaiah 40:3, chapter 57:14, Psalm 80:10, and Psalm 24:7, 9. e) before me, as in Genesis 30:30, Jeremiah 28:8. For, according to Jerome and others, this is said from the person of Christ, for whom John the Baptist prepared the way (compare Luke 1:76), and who soon introduces the Father promising these things at the end of the verse. Others, like Kimchi (p. 279), say it is from the person of the Father, as if to say "before my face," that is, before Him in whom I shall offer myself to be seen, comparing Exodus 33:14, 15, Isaiah 63:9, and John 14:9. f) Vulgate: "and immediately." g) <note>original: "ἐξαίφνης"</note> suddenly, faster than your expectation (Luke 2:13), and very soon after his precursor (Matthew 4:12, 17, John 1:26, 27). compare Isaiah 30:13, chapter 43:19, Haggai 2:6. h) he will come in assumed flesh, and will publicly appear among you. Genesis 49:10, Habakkuk 2:3, Zechariah 1:14. c) to his temple, namely that second one; which through the arrival of the Messiah would be more glorious than the first temple, as Haggai had also predicted (chapter 2:7, 8, 9). And since God the Father here explicitly attributes the Temple to the Son, what wonder if Christ then twice claimed it for himself in John 2:15, 16 and Matthew 21:12, 13 (compare Isaiah 56:7). d) The Lord, Vulgate: the Ruler. That is, according to Kimchi and Abarbanel, the King Messiah; according to Ibn Ezra, the <term>Shechinah</term> <note>The Divine Presence</note>, which is itself the Angel of the covenant, and according to Abarbanel, the Lord of the whole earth (Zechariah 4:14). It should be noted that this name with the emphatic "He" [the Hebrew letter] always denotes GOD (see Exodus 23:17, chapter 34:23, Isaiah 1:24, chapter 3:1, 8, 10, 16, 33, chapter 19:4), and indeed God the Son (Daniel 9:17), whom David called his Lord (Psalm 110:1, compare Matthew 22:43, 44), and Moses called the Lord of lords (Deuteronomy 10:17, compare Revelation 19:16, and 1 Corinthians 2:6). "There is no doubt to anyone," says Jerome, "that this ruler is the Savior, who is the creator of all (see John 1:3, Colossians 1:17), and is called the angel of the testament and the angel of great counsel," namely in the Septuagint translation of Isaiah 9:6. e) whom you seek and ask for. Exodus 10:11, 2 Samuel 3:17. The pious with holy desire (Luke 2:25, chapter 10:24), the impious with a defiant desire (compare chapter 2:17, Isaiah 5:19, Amos 5:18, 2 Peter 3:4). The Hebrews observe that, besides the Ark, the Urim and Thummim, and the Celestial Fire which existed while Solomon's Temple stood, the second temple also lacked the <term>Shechinah</term> or the presence of the Divine Majesty, that is, the glory of the Son of God dwelling between the Cherubim. see the note on Exodus 25:22, 1 Samuel 4:4, Haggai 1:8, chapter 2:9, etc. Hence Abarbanel suggests with Ibn Ezra that this prophecy looks back to that very desire for the divine presence, by which they longed for the *Shechinah*; which God promises will return soon after the precursor. Compare for the fulfillment John 1:14, etc. f) and the Messenger or Angel, not some created being, but the Son of God, begotten from eternity. Psalm 2:7, Proverbs 8:22–31, Isaiah 48:16. elsewhere most eminently called the Angel or Legate of Jehovah (Genesis 16:7, chapter 22:11), the interpreter of the divine will (Job 33:23, compare John 1:18), the redeemer of Jacob (Genesis 48:16), who is the face of God (Exodus 33:14), as his true image (Colossians 1:15), and in whom is the name of God (Exodus 23:10, 11). who called Moses from the bush (Exodus 3:2, 4), appeared to Joshua (Joshua 5:13, 14), also to Gideon and Manoah (Judges 6:12, chapter 13:3, etc.), led the Israelites (Exodus 13:21, chapter 14:19, etc.), and gave the law to them (Exodus 20:1, where see the notes from Bechai, and compare him on many points in *The Law*, folio 98, columns 2 and 4).

# MALACHI. CHAPTER 3.

<sig>Nn nn 3</sig>

->THE PROPHETIC READING FOR THE GREAT SABBATH<-
<note>The "Great Sabbath" (Shabbat HaGadol) is the Saturday immediately preceding the festival of Passover. This section of Malachi is traditionally read in the synagogue on that day.</note>

1 Behold,<sup>i</sup> I am sending<sup>h</sup> my messenger,<sup>k</sup> and he shall prepare the way<sup>l</sup> before me; and suddenly the Lord, whom you seek, shall come to his temple; even the messenger of the covenant,<sup>g</sup> whom you delight in, behold, he comes,<sup>i</sup> says the Lord of Hosts.
2 But who<sup>m</sup> can endure the day of his coming?<sup>n</sup> And who shall stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s<sup>p</sup> fire, and like fullers’<sup>r</sup> soap.<sup>r</sup>
3 And he shall sit<sup>q</sup> as a refiner and purifier of silver; and he shall purify the sons of Levi,<sup>a</sup> and purge<sup>b</sup> them as gold<sup>c</sup> and silver, that they may be<sup>d</sup> to the Lord<sup>e</sup> those who offer<sup>f</sup> an offering<sup>g</sup> in righteousness.<sup>h</sup>
4 Then the offering<sup>k</sup> of Judah and Jerusalem<sup>l</sup> shall be pleasant<sup>i</sup> to the Lord, as in the days<sup>m</sup> of old, and as in ancient<sup>n</sup> years.
5 And I will come near<sup>o</sup> to you for judgment;<sup>p</sup> and I will be a swift witness<sup>r</sup> against the sorcerers,<sup>s</sup> and against the adulterers,<sup>t</sup> and against those who swear<sup>u</sup> falsely, and against those who oppress<sup>x</sup> the hireling in his wages, the widow,<sup>y</sup> and the fatherless,<sup>z</sup> and those who turn aside the stranger,<sup>a</sup> and do not<sup>b</sup> fear me,<sup>c</sup> says the Lord of Hosts.

---

<margin>
g) of the covenant, namely of grace and the New Testament, which God promised; see Jeremiah 31:33 and following. This refers to the man: regarding whom, in whom, and through whom the covenant is made, which God ever made with His own, and in whom He commanded all to believe in order to have a covenant with God. See Isaiah 42:6, chapter 49:6, and the note on Deuteronomy 33:16. h) verse 42. Behold, you in the day in which you delight. Which as often as the pious eaters and worshippers of my name [do]. See verse 16, compare 2 Samuel 23:5. i) "Behold," I say, and he is most certainly about to come. This is the style of the Prophets: to present future things as if present, even if separated by a long interval of time from the prophet’s own age. This is done not only because of the certainty of the matter, but especially with respect to the most rapid course of time; as Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> advises in his *Sacred Observations*, book 6, page 413. To these we may add the words of Zosimus, a pagan writer, who in his *History*, book 2, chapter 37, says: 
> "However, because these things that were predicted happened after only a few fates had intervened, those who investigate should not be disturbed, as if this prophecy (of the Sibyl) speaks of some other matter. For all time is short to God, who always exists and will be." 
<note>original Greek: Πᾶς γὰρ τῷ Θεῷ βραχὺς, אεὶ τῷ ὄντι. κ’ ἐσομένῳ.</note> Compare Revelation 3:11, Chapter 22:7, 12. k) see the note on chapter 1:8. l) Hosea 12:6. 
m) But who indeed among the evil and wicked will be able to stay, or rather, who will endure? Jeremiah 20:9, Joel 2:11. A question sometimes denotes difficulty, as in this place and Isaiah 53:1, Jonah 3:9; indeed, it implies a negative, unless they seriously repent. Compare the note on Hosea 14:10. n) the day of his coming, especially when he shall come to strike the earth, verses 17, 19, 23. Compare Joel 2:1, Amos 5:18. Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note>: *Who of the wicked shall stand before this teacher of the righteous judge (Joel 2:23)? Who of those who love darkness shall stand...*
</margin>

<margin>
*...stand before this sun?* John 3:20. o) and who will be standing? or who will consist? Psalm 130:3, Revelation 6:17. p) when he appears in his clarity like the Sun of Righteousness (verse 20). Judges 13:21, 1 Kings 18:2. The metaphor is taken from those whose eyes...
</margin>

...cannot rightly gaze upon or bear the splendor of the rising sun. Compare Isaiah 53:1, Matthew 2:3, chapter 3:12, and chapter 5:9. o) Jonathan <note>The Aramaic Translation or Targum Jonathan</note>: because his anger. It indicates that the power of the divine administration <note>original: οἰκονομίας</note> of the Lord’s coming will be intolerable to unbelievers, as Cyril says. p) he will be like a refiner's fire, which melts metals so that every impurity is cast out. Compare verse 3, Isaiah 1:25, chapter 4:4, chapter 48:10, Matthew 3:11, 12, Luke 12:49. Add, according to Jerome, Psalm 50:3. 5) and as lye, or herb, as Jerome, the Vulgate, etc. have it. (1) Jeremiah 2:22, where see the note. r) of the fullers, who wash out stains and make garments white. Mark 9:3, Isaiah 7:3. q) And just as a refiner sat to purge silver, so he himself is immaculate and pure (Hebrews 7:26). He will sit refining not lightly or cursorily, but with great zeal and exquisite labor. See Matthew 26:55. Jonathan: "And he will appear to refine and cleanse, like a man who refines and cleanses silver." x) see verse 2, Jeremiah 6:29, Zechariah 13:9. y) purging silver. Compare Matthew 5, 6, 7, and 23. z) especially he will purge them from the dross of false doctrine and a wicked life. Psalm 51:4. a) the sons of Levi, that is, the Levites, Priests, and pastors, whose vices he had criticized above in chapter 1:6, 2:1, etc. Compare Ezekiel 34:2 and following; and regarding their correction under the New Testament, Jeremiah 33:18, Acts 6:7. b) and he will liquefy. That is, he will purge them by melting (Psalm 12:7), the dross being cast away, about which he complains in Matthew 15:9, chapter 23:25, 28, Luke 18:31, where the Priests are specifically touched upon. c) like gold or silver. Compare Ezekiel 22:18, and another emblem in Matthew 3:11, 12. d) so that they may be. e) of the Lord, or for the Lord, and consecrated to his will. f) offering, or those who may offer. Chapter 1:7, 11. g) *Mincha*, that is, a gift. The Vulgate: "sacrifices." Namely, according to the character of the New Testament, a "rational worship" <note>original Greek: λογִκὴν λατρείαν</note> and "spiritual sacrifices" <note>original Greek: πνευματικὰς θυσίας</note>. See the note on chapter 1:11, Isaiah 66:20, Jeremiah 33:18, Romans 12:1, 1 Peter 2:5. h) in righteousness. Isaiah 1:27, chapter 61:10, Psalm 132:9. That is, justly, not as they do today, says Abarbanel. Jerome says: 
> "When the priests have been corrected and refined, then they will offer just sacrifices to the Lord." 
Verse 4. i) That is, then it will be sweet or pleasant and grateful. The Septuagint and Vulgate: "it will please the Lord." Jeremiah 6:20, Hosea 9:4, Proverbs 21:27, Hebrews 13:14, 1 Peter 2:5. Compare the opposite above in chapter 1:10, 13, 2:13, Isaiah 1:11 and following. k) an offering. See verse 3, etc. l) Compare Psalm 51:21, Acts 21:20, 26. m) as in former days. Amos 9:11, Micah 7:14. For example, the days of Abel (Genesis 4:4), Noah (Genesis 8:20, 21), Abraham (Genesis 22), Moses (Leviticus 9:21), Solomon (2 Chronicles 7:3), etc. n) and as in ancient years, or preceding years. Isaiah 43:18. Jerome: 
> "Just as in the beginning they pleased God, so after sin and repentance they may begin to please Him again, when they have been purged of all the filth of their sins." 
Compare Isaiah 1:16-18, Revelation 1:5, 6, etc.

Verse 5. o) That is, "Therefore I will come near to you." Isaiah 41:1. p) into judgment. Psalm 76:10. Jonathan: "And I will be revealed over you to execute judgment." Namely, not only a temporary one, but also an eternal one, regarding those who do not repent. God surely answers seriously to that saying above in chapter 2:17, "Where is the God of judgment?" "I will come," he says, "and I will be a swift judge and witness," etc. Abarbanel makes this connection: "Do not think," God says, "as if until that time (the coming of the Messiah), which is still far distant, the wicked will not suffer just punishment or loss: for I will come through death to punish you," etc. Because, of course, the Prophet urged the men of his own time to repentance (verse 7). Others, however, distinguish this prediction from the following exhortation, so that the former refers to the future times of the destruction of Jerusalem, and the latter to the times of the Prophet. See Calovius on this place. q) and I will be. Jonathan: "and my word will be against you." For God the Father is speaking, as seen by the connection of this verse with verse 1. r) a swift witness and an avenger. 1 Samuel 12:5, Genesis 41:32, Zephaniah 1:14. Compare the note on Jeremiah 29:23. "The swift witness." Compare Revelation 1:5, chapter 22:20. Jerome: 
> "How great a dread of judgment, when he himself is both the witness and the judge!" 
s) against the sorcerers. Exodus 7:11, chapter 22:17, Deuteronomy 18:10, Daniel 2:2, 2 Chronicles 33:6. "Against those who practice sorcery" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐπὶ τὰς φαρμακείας</note>. Revelation 21:8, chapter 22:15, Galatians 5:20. Compare for example Acts 8:9 and following, chapter 13:6 and following, chapter 19:13, 14. Also Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 20, chapter 6; and *The Jewish War*, book 2, chapter 12, 23. t) and against the adulterers. Jeremiah 9:1, Hosea 7:4, Psalm 50:18, Matthew 5:28, chapter 19:9. "Adulteresses" <note>original Greek: μοιχαλιδας</note> in Matthew 12:39; these crimes are committed in secret. u) and the perjurers. Those who swear falsely; the Septuagint and Arabic translations add "by my name." Leviticus 19:12, Jeremiah 5:2, Matthew 5:33, chapter 23:16 and following. x) and those who defraud, unjustly withdraw, and deny. Leviticus 5:21, 23. "And those who defraud" <note>original Greek: ὁ καὶ τοὺς ἀποστεרוῦντας</note>. James 5:4. y) Deuteronomy 24:14. z) Exodus 22:21, Deuteronomy 21:17, Matthew 23:14. a) and those who oppress the stranger. Amos 5:12, Proverbs 18:5. The Septuagint, Jonathan, and Arabic: "and those who pervert the right of the stranger." As in Deuteronomy 27:19, Exodus 23:6. Others say: "those who pervert the strangers," perhaps meaning proselytes, comparing Matthew 23:15, and the Hebrew word in Ezekiel 44:20, Proverbs 7:21. b) and those who do not fear me. Compare chapter 1:6, and below in verse 18. c) see verses 1, 6, 7, 8.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Malachi Chapter 3. # CHAPTER 3. MALACHI 3.

<margin>
to you. <note>referencing the Targum of Jonathan</note> then I will turn in my Word to do good to you. Zechariah 1:3. James 4:8. cf. Jeremiah 18:7. Chapter 25:5. Zechariah 8:3. p) chapter 1:8. q) you say impudently, as if you do not know the sin or iniquity from which you ought to turn. <note>referencing the commentator Isaac Abarbanel</note> Compare verses 8, 13; chapter 1:2, 6. r) in what shall we return? cf. Micah 6:6. Luke 15:7.
</margin>

6 : For I am the LORD, I do not change; therefore you, O sons of Jacob, are not consumed.
7 : Even from the days of your fathers you have turned away from my ordinances and have not kept them. Return to me, and I will return to you, says the LORD of Hosts. But you said, "In what way shall we return?"
8 : Will a man rob God? Yet you are robbing me. But you say, "In what way have we robbed you?" In tithes and offerings.
9 : You are cursed with a curse, for you are robbing me—the whole nation of you.
10 : Bring all the tithes into the storehouse, so that there may be food in my house, and test me now in this, says the LORD of Hosts, if I will not open for you the windows of heaven and pour out for you a blessing until there is no more need.
11 : And I will rebuke the devourer for your sake, so that he will not destroy the fruit of your ground for you; nor—

***

**v. 8. s)** Would a man then (to offer even a single example of your impiety) *spoil* or *defraud* God? (t) v. 9. Proverbs 22:23. <note>Abarbanel says: as if to say, do you not know that it is least fitting for a man to defraud and spoil his God?</note> Compare examples of divinely punished sacrilege in the cases of Antiochus (2 Maccabees 6:12 and following) and Heliodorus (2 Maccabees 3:23 and following). u) because you, with great consensus (v. 9. u), defraud and spoil me. cf. Romans 2:22. x) and you say most stubbornly (v. 7, 13). y) In what matter have we defrauded you? Obstinately denying the fault, as in chapter 2:17. z) In the tithes, truly, you defraud me (v. 10; Leviticus 27:30; Numbers 18:21). a) and in the **<term>Trumah</term>** <note>A Hebrew term for a "contribution" or "heave-offering" set apart for the priests.</note>. The Septuagint and the Vulgate translate this as *and in the first-fruits*. While you snatch these away from the Priests and Levites, you also snatch them from me, but to your own gravest loss. Grotius notes: *Trumah*, called *aphairema* <note>original Greek: ἀφαίρεμα, meaning "a thing taken away" or "portion"</note> by the Greeks in Leviticus 7:14, 32, was a portion not less than a sixtieth part of the grain, wine, oil, etc. cf. Deuteronomy 12:6; chapter 18:4; Nehemiah 10:38; chapter 13:5. And in truth, Jerome says regarding the historical order: because the people were not returning the tithes and first-fruits to the Levites, the Lord says he himself sustains the fraud, as his ministers, forced by hunger and penury, have deserted the Temple. (See Nehemiah 13:10, a passage which sufficiently shows that Malachi was looking at those times.) For if he is visited in prison through others, and received when sick, and receives food and drink when hungry and thirsty; why should he not himself receive the tithes in his ministers, and if they are not given, be himself deprived of his portion? **v. 9. b)** Therefore, indeed, through my curse (chapter 2:2) c) you are cursed. <note>A Hebrew grammatical form (Niphal) denoting the passive state of being cursed.</note> cf. Deuteronomy 28:15 and following. d) while you defraud me (v. 8). Jerome: Because you did not return to me the tithes and first-fruits, therefore you are cursed with hunger and penury. See v. 10, 11. e) the whole nation. Grotius: Because when the common people saw that the Levites were not being fed (because the Priests were drawing all the tithes to themselves, Nehemiah 13:10 and following, and yet were performing sacrifices perfunctorily, as we saw above in chapter 1:6 and following), they abstained from bringing the tithes. cf. chapter 2:9. **v. 10. f)** Abarbanel: But if you think this curse has happened to you by chance rather than for this cause, come now, let us test the matter thus: Bring every tithe. Deuteronomy 12:6. g) The Vulgate: *into the storehouse*. The Syriac: *into my storehouses*. Grotius: that is, under faithful guards, who may distribute their portions to the Priests and Levites. Furthermore, the *House of the Treasury* here is without doubt that chamber in which the collected tithes were to be brought, prepared by Eliashib the High Priest for the use of his kinsman Tobiah, concerning which see Nehemiah 13:5, 12, 13; compared with chapter 10:38, 39. h) so that there may be food. The Syriac: so that the tithes may be food. Proverbs 31:15; Psalm 111:5. i) that is, so that it may be provided for those ministering in my house, the Priests and Levites. k) then, I pray, prove me in this matter, or, as I most liberally grant this to you (cf. Isaiah 7:11; chapter 38:7, 22), make a sort of trial of me. cf. v. 15; Genesis 42:15; Psalm 95:9. l) if not. cf. Joshua 14:9; Jeremiah 22:6. m) I will open to you. Deuteronomy 28:12; Psalm 78:23. n) The Vulgate: *the floodgates of heaven* <note>original Latin: "catarractas caeli"</note> 2 Kings 7:2, 19; namely, to give rain to your land in its time. The opposite is a closed, brass, and iron heaven (Leviticus 26:19; Deuteronomy 11:17; chapter 28:23). o) and I will pour out for you. Genesis 42:35; Ecclesiastes 11:3. Jerome: The word for "pouring out" shows the name of abundance. cf. synonymous words in Isaiah 44:3; Joel 3:1; Zechariah 12:10. p) a blessing and a most copious abundance of goods. chapter 2:2; Genesis 33:11; Deuteronomy 28:8. cf. Ezekiel 44:30; Haggai 2:19. q) as if to say, until the failure (2 Kings 1:3; Isaiah 5:13) of measure or sufficiency (Esther 1:18); that is, according to the scholar Grosset, page 185: even to the point that there is never enough. According to Junius and the translator Danzius, page 156: so much so that you are not sufficient to enjoy or contain it. cf. for example Genesis 41:49; 2 Kings 4:3-6. Abarbanel: that is, not only so that it is enough, but so that it even overflows. The Vulgate: *even unto abundance*. Schmid: *until it shall not suffice*. That is, to supply the lack of sufficiency, etc. Grotius: He says this because they had already begun to suffer hunger. Nehemiah 5. **v. 11. r)** chapter 2:3. Jerome: But it can happen that, with rains irrigating the fields, there is indeed fertility, but either the locust or the caterpillar—destroy it, so that the labors of men perish; therefore he joins and says: And I will rebuke the devourer for you. s) Abarbanel: think of the locusts, which were consuming the crops. See notes on Joel 1:4 and following. t) Judges 6:4, 5. u) Genesis 4:3.

Grotius: **Kings are accustomed to make a record of those who are commended to them,** so that they might have special care for them, so that if any honors are vacant, they might promote them. From this, the comparison is taken. Our translation of Daniel 7:10. l) **for those fearing the Lord.** A dative of benefit, as often seen. m) Vulgate: **and to those thinking,** meaning those who seriously think about honoring his name, as Jonathan and the Zurich versions have it. cf. Deuteronomy 28:58. Ephesians 26:8. others who **value it most highly,** compare 1 Kings 10:21. Ephesians 53:3. Psalm 144:3. The Septuagint and Arabic: **those who show reverence.** etc.
n) v. 17. n) **For they shall be mine (says the Lord) for the day on which I am going to prepare a special possession.** So the accents suggest. cf. Ephesians 43:1, 4. o) Parenthesis. cf. note on chapter 1:8. p) **on the day or for that day prepared by my grace.** cf Exodus 19:11. Esther 3:14. chapter 8:13. Elsewhere it denotes distribution into individual days, as in Exodus 29:36, 38. 1 Chronicles 26:17. etc. By this "day," Tillius understands the **day of salvation** Ephesians 49:8 and **acceptance** Ephesians 61:1, 2, 3. others understand the **day of the final judgment:** so Jerome: on the day when the time of judgment shall arrive. Calovius, however, through the preceding and following verses, understands it as the day of the destruction of Jerusalem. We, because of the accents, understand it as the day of the New Testament, especially the pouring out of the Holy Spirit and the Church of Christ being separated from the impious assembly of the Jews (Ephesians 65:5, Luke 6:22, Acts 19:9), which was then followed by the day of vengeance against the impious (v. 19), in which, however, he promises his mercy to the pious, as the word *Silluq* teaches. q) v. 21. cf. Ephesians 60:21. Psalm 95:5. Ephesians 2, 10. r) Exodus 19:5. Deuteronomy 7:6. Psalm 135:4. <note>original Greek: "as the day which I make for a possession"</note> Titus 2:14. 1 Peter 2:9. s) **and my mercy toward them.** Vulgate: **and I will spare them** 1 Samuel 23:21. 2 Samuel 21:7. cf. Genesis 19:16. and regarding the matter Zechariah 11:7. Daniel 9:27. Jerome: He will spare them, because every man is under sin.

<meta>This page concludes the commentary and transcription of the Book of Malachi, specifically focusing on the final three verses (22–24 in the Hebrew, often designated as Chapter 4 in Christian Bibles). It continues the theme of judgment and the promise of a messenger before the "Day of the Lord."</meta>

# MALACHI. CHAPTER 3.

<margin>
**b)** **Jerome:** <note>original: "Hierov." - Saint Jerome, the 4th-century biblical translator</note> Abraham, comparing himself to divine majesty and feeling himself to be ash (**Genesis 18:27**), will see the Sun of Righteousness. **q)** But one who through pride said, *I will set my seat above the stars* (**Isaiah 14:13**) will be brought down to the earth and be like ash under the feet of the saints. **Calovius:** <note>Abraham Calovius, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> Total subjection and trampling is indicated when the wicked are said to become ash under the soles of the faithful; this implies solid peace and liberation from enemies **cf. Isaiah 60:21, Micah 4:13, etc.** **c)** **Vulgate:** <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> *the day in which I act* or am about to do these things. **v. 17.** **d)** see note on verses 1 and 8.

**v. 22. e)** **If** *remember* then, be mindful and observe. **1 Chronicles 16:11, 15. Abarbanel** <note>Don Isaac Abarbanel, a prominent 15th-century Jewish statesman and commentator</note> at the beginning of this book, folio 277b, says: *Because Malachi was the last of all the Prophets, and after his death the gift of prophecy ceased from Israel, therefore he warns and says: Remember, etc.* Indeed, it is the speech of God himself reminding the Israelites to persist in the diligent observation of the Mosaic law until the arrival of that unique servant of God, Elijah—that is, John the Baptist; for before that time, no new prophet of great authority would appear to the Nation. And he clearly declared that before the times of the new economy <note>The "new economy" refers to the era of the New Testament</note>, no such public or canonical prophet was to be expected further; as **Kirschgarten** noted in *Observations 3, book 4, page 413.* Compare the Preface to this book, section 2. **f)** *The Law of Moses,* for now, observe the doctrine of the entire Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note> more correctly than you have done until now, until better things shine forth through the arrival mentioned in verse 7. **cf. Galatians 3:23, 24; Hebrews 7:19, 9:10, 10:1, etc.** **g)** *which I commanded him in Horeb.* <note>Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai</note> **Exodus 3:1, 17:6; Deuteronomy 4:10, 15.** **h)** *to all Israel.* specifically regarding the whole people. **Deut. 29:13, 14.** **i)** *The Law* namely, containing *definitions.* **Vulgate:** *precepts.*
</margin>

22 **וְעַסֹּתֶם** <gloss>you shall trample</gloss> **רְשָׁעִים** <gloss>the wicked</gloss> **כִּי־יִהְיוּ** <gloss>for they shall be</gloss> **אֵפֶר** <gloss>ashes</gloss> **תַּחַת** <gloss>under</gloss> **כַּפּוֹת** <gloss>the soles</gloss> **רַגְלֵיכֶם** <gloss>of your feet</gloss> **בַּיּוֹם** <gloss>in the day</gloss> **אֲשֶׁר־אֲנִי** <gloss>which I</gloss> **עֹשֶׂה** <gloss>prepare</gloss> **אָמַר** <gloss>says</gloss> **יְהוָה** <gloss>the Lord</gloss> **צְבָאוֹת׃** <gloss>of hosts</gloss>

23 **זִכְרוּ** <gloss>remember</gloss> **תּוֹרַת** <gloss>the law of</gloss> **מֹשֶׁה** <gloss>Moses</gloss> **עַבְדִּי** <gloss>my servant</gloss> **אֲשֶׁר** <gloss>which</gloss> **צִוִּיתִי** <gloss>I commanded</gloss> **אוֹתוֹ** <gloss>him</gloss> **בְּחֹרֵב** <gloss>in Horeb</gloss> **עַל־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל** <gloss>concerning all Israel</gloss> **חֻקִּים** <gloss>statutes</gloss> **וּמִשְׁפָּטִים׃** <gloss>and judgments</gloss>

<margin>
**preface 3.** **-v- the law.** **cf. v. 7. Luke 5:14. k)** and judgments. **judgment.** <note>original: "δικαίωμα"</note> **Luke 1:6.** that is, as **Calovius** notes, the moral and ceremonial **Law**.
</margin>

## BEHOLD

The moral and ceremonial law. The former, so that they do not make themselves unworthy of the benefits of the Messiah; the latter, so that they might profit daily in the faith of the Messiah, of whom the Mosaic ceremonies were types, and that they might not despair entirely because of the delay of the Lord’s coming. For the end of the Law was **CHRIST** **Romans 10:4** and it served as a tutor toward him **Galatians 3:24.** Regarding the phrase, compare **Deuteronomy 4:5, 8, 14; Leviticus 26:46; Exodus 21:1; Psalm 147:19.** **Abarbanel** distinguishes these two as follows: *Chukkim* [statutes], he says, are those whose reason is unknown to us; *Mishpatim* [judgments] are those whose reason is known and manifest. But regarding these, see elsewhere.

**v. 23. l)** Behold! This was the first sign to which one's mind ought to attend, see note on v. 1. **m)** I am going to send to you. Surely while the second Temple still stood **v. 1, Haggai 2:7, 9.** After the most severe struggle with Antiochus **Daniel 3:9 ff.** and after the seventy weeks of years, passing from the time the edict was issued for restoring Jerusalem **Daniel 9:24, 27.** **n)** Elijah, not the Tishbite <note>Elijah of Tishbe, the historical prophet from the Book of Kings</note>, as the **Septuagint** and **Arabic** versions have it, as well as **Sirach 48:10** (according to the common opinion of the Jews, and indeed many of the Fathers, who thought—the former before the first coming of the Messiah, the latter before the end of the world and for the conversion of the Jewish nation—that Elijah the Tishbite must be restored to these lands. See **Matthew 17:11**; compare **Lightfoot** in the same place; **Augustine** *On the City of God* **book 20, chapter 29**, with the commentaries of **Juan Luis Vives** and **Leonhard Coquæus**: not to mention those who thought Elijah the Tishbite was indicated here and had already come because he appeared with Moses to the disciples on the mountain, speaking with Christ **Matthew 17:3; Mark 9:4; Luke 9:30.**) But as we said above regarding verse 1, it refers to John the Baptist, the messenger and precursor of the Lord (v. 1) who would represent Elijah in character, lifestyle, zeal, and many circumstances—or as the Angel says in **Luke 1:17**, "in the spirit and power of Elijah." See **Matthew 11:10–14, 17:10–13; Mark 9:11–13; Luke 1:16, 17, 76, 77.** For John himself denied that he was the Tishbite **John 1:21.** Scripture, however, as **Tilhis** writes on page 409, often applies the name of types to antitypes. Thus Christ came under the name of David **Jeremiah 30:9; Ezekiel 34:23, 37:24, 25** and Solomon **Song of Solomon 3:11, 8:11.** Jehu under the name of Zimri **2 Kings 9:31.** The leaders of Jerusalem as Sodom, and the people as Gomorrah **Isaiah 1:10.** So says **Paetus**: *And again a great Achilles shall be sent to Troy.* etc. **o)** A Prophet, and the first public teacher of the New Testament through immediate revelation from God **Luke 3:2; John 1:31–33.** John the Baptist was not only foretold as such by his father Zacharias **Luke 1:76**, and Christ testified that he was so **Matthew 11:9**, but the common people and the Jewish populace also recognized him as such **Matthew 14:5, 21:26.** Add **Josephus** in *Antiquities of the Jews* **book 18, chapter 7**, whose words, though from a Jewish man who either ignored or concealed the true sense and goal of the Baptist's teaching, deserve to be cited. Among the Jews, he says, there was an opinion that Herod’s army was destroyed by Aretas by a divine vision because of John, who was surnamed the Baptist (see **Matthew 3:1 etc.**). For the tetrarch killed him, an excellent man, urging the Jews to the study of virtues, especially toward piety and justice, and at the same time washing them for baptism: for he said this would finally be pleasing to God if they did not abstain from only one or two sins, but first purified their souls through righteousness, and then added the purity of the body, etc. **p)** before he comes. **Joel 3:4.** **q)** the day of the Lord, namely of Christ (v. 17), then of the gracious visitation of the Jews **Luke 19:44**, which John the Baptist's preaching immediately preceded, see above v. 1 and **Matthew 3:1 ff; Luke 3:1 ff.** **r)** then a day of wrath and vengeance, exercised against them through Titus. v. 24. **Acts 2:20** concerning which John also prophesied to them **Matthew 3:10, 12.** **s)** great, because of the greatness of the things to be executed at that time cf. **Hosea 3:2; Zephaniah 1:14; 1 Timothy 3:16. t) Vulgate:** and *terrible.* i.e., to be feared, because of the judgments to be executed on the wicked, and the destruction of the nation by the Romans **v. 19.** cf. **Joel 1:15, 2:1, 11, 3:4; Septuagint** as in **Acts 2:20.**

**v. 24. t) Vulgate:** *And he shall turn.* i.e., so that you turn, or he may bring back. cf. **26; Jeremiah 31:18; Luke 1:17.** **u)** the heart of the fathers cf. **1 Kings 12:27; Isaiah 6:10; 1 Samuel 7:3.** **x)** to the children. The verb "to turn" (shub) is rarely constructed with this particle, more frequently with *el*, *al*, or *ad*, see **Genesis 10:4; Psalm 11:1; Psalm 14:15; Ecclesiastes 12:7, 8; Chronicles 30:9; and Micah 5:2.** **y)** the heart of the children to their fathers. For this was the purpose of John the Baptist: that all Jews, greater and lesser, parents and children, without civil wars, without domestic discords, or distracted by different sects, might be prepared by his sermons and baptism (**Luke 1:17**) and with a harmonious mind and true faith believe in **CHRIST** **John 1:7, 12.** Even though the opposite happened among many, which Christ also predicted: **Matthew 10:21, 34 ff; Luke 12:51 ff, 21:16.** Interpreters vary greatly here, and it would be long to recount all their opinions. We will give a few of the better ones. According to **Jerome**, it means that Jews (from whom came the New Testament Patriarchs and Apostles) and Christians, who now differ, should agree with equal religion in Christ (before the final coming of the Lord). According to **Augustine**, in the place cited above for verse 23, the sense is that the children, i.e., the Jews, should (finally) understand the law just as the fathers, i.e., the Prophets and Moses himself, understood it, etc. But **Cocceius** understands the ancient Fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—to whose heart (meaning their sentiment, faith, and piety, i.e., the sense of the righteous as in **Luke 1:17**) the Jews, their descendants, are to be brought back through John the Baptist, so that Abraham and the others would not be ashamed of their children; compare **Isaiah 29:22, 23.** **z)** *lest.* This is consequential, as in **Leviticus 10:7; Psalm 2:12; etc.** It is not to be doubted as *lest perhaps,* as the **Vulgate** has it. **a)** *I come* with the judgment of the people and the destruction of the state. cf. **Psalm 50:3; Psalm 82:8; Matthew 25:64** and above v. 1, 2. **b)** *and I strike,* I shall smite. cf. **Numbers 14:12.** **c)** *the land* **Isaiah 15:4.** **d)** *with a curse* [anathema], that is, so that they do not all perish. cf. **Leviticus 27:29; Deuteronomy 2:34, 7:26, 10:6, 17:18, 11:11, 13, 20; Isaiah 43:23.** Compare also *Maran atha,* which means "Our Lord comes!" **1 Corinthians 16:22.** That is: lest I appear and find the whole land in its guilt or sins (cf. **1 John 5:19**) and strike it with extermination; that is, according to **Grotius**, lest when I come, it results in the eternal destruction of those imploring, through the ruin of the nation and Jerusalem, after they stubbornly neglected the time of their gracious visitation. **Luke 19:42, 44.** <note>original: "Ταῦτα δὲ πάντα τύποι συνέβαινον ἐκείνοις..."</note> *Now all these things happened to them as examples: and they were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.* **1 Corinthians 10:11.** May our Lord Jesus Christ grant, therefore, that with true repentance and faith we may approach him, by which we—having been thoroughly healed and cleansed from all defilements of flesh and spirit—may perfect our sanctification in the fear of God; and may our whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless until his coming! <note>original: "Εἴ τις οὐ φιλεῖ τὸν Κύριον..."</note> *If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema, Maran-atha. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you! Amen.*

**Hosea**: one hundred and ninety-seven: *“and my banner was not”*<gloss>f</gloss> *in righteousness* is the sign <note>The Hebrew word for "sign" (Siman) refers to a mnemonic device where a phrase's numerical value or keywords help scribes remember the verse count.</note>:

<meta>The previous page listed the books belonging to the Hagiographa (the third section of the Hebrew Bible), ending with the "Threni" (Lamentations). This page begins the formal introduction to that section and specifically the Book of Psalms.</meta>

->TO THE<-
# HAGIOGRAPHA AND THE BOOK
# OF PSALMS
## PREFACE.

->§. I.<-

<margin>Transition to the Hagiographa and the book of Psalms:</margin>
The third part of the Hebrew Bible, which we have now undertaken to print, contains the **Writings** <note>original Hebrew: *Ketuvim*</note> or *HAGIOGRAPHA* <note>A Greek term meaning "Holy Writings," used to describe the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, and among them first the *Book of Psalms*. It is because of this, or at least a similar tripartite division of the Hebrew Bible, that our excellent Savior in Luke 24:44 distributed the Old Testament into the *Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms*. In that passage, the Psalms—being first in the third order—stand in for the rest of the Hagiographa by synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part of something is used to represent the whole.</note>; just as in Matthew 27:9, *Jeremiah* stands for the entire volume of the Prophets, in which his book at one time held the first place. See our *Various Readings* on Jeremiah 1:1. To pass over briefly what learned men suggest or require regarding the relationship of individual books to this third class; <margin>Regarding their canonical authority and the difference from the Prophetic books, according to the mind of the Jews.</margin> *a)* the Jews admit and feel that all those books, no less than the books of the Law and the Prophets, were written **by the Holy Spirit** <note>original Hebrew: *Ruach HaKodesh*</note>; *b)* although regarding the manner of revelation, they would have these be slightly inferior to the prophetic books specifically so-called among them. However, they are led to this by arguments that are either non-existent, or quite weak and altogether unfit for demonstration. For David Kimchi <note>A famous 12th-13th century Jewish commentator and grammarian, often called the "Radak."</note>, a man of weightier judgment among the Jews, writes thus in his Preface to the Psalms: *Our ancestors say that this book was written by the Holy Spirit; therefore they also referred it to the Hagiographa, and not to the order of the Prophets. For its words were not dictated in the manner of prophecy, but by the Holy Spirit.* But Kimchi does not thus prove or explain the point in question; rather, he assumes what he is trying to prove and contrasts things that should not be contrasted. Nevertheless, so that the mind of the Jews may be clear, it must be held from them that they establish the gift of prophecy (after Moses, to whom they give first place in everything) as occurring when a person is **divinely inspired** <note>original Greek: *entheos*</note> and sees or hears divine revelation in an ecstasy. However, they call it a lower grade, or the gift of the Holy Spirit, if someone—remaining in possession of their mind and senses—brings forth things by the Spirit's breath or impulse which they could not know or recognize without it. But neither is that sufficient to establish such a distinction as they desire; nor can they demonstrate by any probable reason how the manner of the prophetic visions of Daniel (whom they referred to this class of Hagiographa) differs in kind from the visions of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the other Prophets; nor how a lower grade of the prophetic gift appears in the Psalms than in the historical books of Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings, which they number among the *Prophetic books* because of their prophetic authors. Hence elsewhere the Jews themselves also frequently praise David and Daniel in their writings by the name of *Prophet*, as is easily known to those skilled in Rabbinic literature. And to add just one thing here regarding the psalms, leaving aside the rest for now: If prophecy is the *prediction* of chances or contingent events of a future time, or the knowledge and interpretation of what cannot be known except by immediate revelation from God, then surely the title of "prophetic" must not be denied to these sacred songs. Many clear examples in them prove this, regardless of how the manner of revelation might have differed from others; on which point one may compare Numbers 12:6-7, as well as *Vitringa* <note>Campegius Vitringa, a noted Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note> in his *Type of Prophetic Doctrine*, chapter 2, and many others. It is enough for us, meanwhile, that the Jews recognize these books as written by the Holy Spirit and as **divinely inspired** <note>original Greek: *theopneustos*, literally "God-breathed."</note>; because of this, their divine authority and irrefragable certainty is established—about which there has never been doubt in the Church of Christ, especially regarding the Psalms. Compare 2 Samuel 23:1-2; 1 Peter 1:21; 2 Timothy 3:15 and following; and what we note in the following section from Aben Ezra and Kimchi.

->§. II.<-

<margin>The Name of the Psalms,</margin>
This first volume of the Hagiographa is called by the Hebrews **The Book of Praises** <note>original Hebrew: *Sefer Tehillim*</note> and in the New Testament **The Book of Psalms** in Luke 20:42 and Acts 1:20. The sacred songs themselves are called **Psalms** <note>original Hebrew: *Mizmorim*</note>, that is, *psalms* or *songs*, because they were sung to the beat of a harp or another musical instrument. *c)* cf. notes on Psalm 3:1. <margin>Collection,</margin> They are called **Hymns** <note>original Hebrew: *Tehillim*</note> (or more precisely *Tehillim*) from a later perspective, because most of them are **supplicatory** <note>original Greek: *exaitika*</note> and end in divine praises. Some, such as *Athanasius* <note>A 4th-century Church Father.</note> in his *Synopsis*, would have it that they were collected into this one volume by Ezra the Scribe or Theologian; *Clavius* says this is a common opinion in his Preface to this book; however, *Munster* <note>Sebastian Münster, a 16th-century Hebraist.</note> admits that nothing is found about this among Hebrew writers, and we also have found nothing as of yet. Rather, according to Kimchi’s Preface, David composed this book and wrote along with his own songs the songs of those musicians who are mentioned (in the titles of the psalms); and he gave his songs to them so that they might sing them publicly—just as is certain regarding Psalm 105, comparing 1 Chronicles 16:7. — And indeed, those psalms which are inscribed **by David** <note>original Hebrew: *L'David*</note>, David composed them, *d)* as well as those in which no other author’s name is mentioned. He even inserted into his book the Prayer of Moses, Psalm 90, <gloss>which was already written and held by tradition from Moses.</gloss> He also predicted future things in this book which only happened long after his death, for example, regarding the Babylonian captivity and the present exile, as well as many consolatory prophecies, etc. And *Aben Ezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a prominent medieval Spanish Jewish scholar.</note> says in his preface: *I do not know why it seems strange to interpreters that this book is not titled "The Prophecy of David." For there is no doubt among the Israelites that Moses wrote the book of Genesis; for so our holy ancestors were taught, even though we do not find written at its beginning: "And God spoke to Moses," etc.*

->§. III.<-

<margin>Authors:</margin>
However, it is called the Psalms of *David*, and indeed among the Ethiopians it is called simply *The David* *e)* likewise because of his prominence; although besides David, other secondary or instrumental authors also existed. *f)*

---

*a)* See Pfeiffer's *Sacred Criticism*, pages 11–18, etc. *b)* Thus Aben Ezra in his Preface to the Psalms: *I,* he says, *feel the same as the ancients, who establish that this entire book was written by the Holy Spirit. For behold, those who feel differently are offended by the name "Song" (as if a Song cannot be a prophecy). For behold, the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32) refutes their opinion. Likewise, since certain psalms (as Psalm 17:1) are titled "A Prayer": for the same is true of Habakkuk 3:1, who also in chapter 1:2 prophesies concerning the righteous in the manner of prayers. So also those prayers in Isaiah 63:17, etc.* *c)* They used to sing their songs to the beat of a harp or a lute both publicly and privately; loving musical harmony not with common pleasure (see Isaiah 5:12, Amos 6:5) but with a faithful pleasure, as *Augustine* speaks of David in Book 17 of *The City of God*, chapter 14. *d)* Kimchi himself, indeed, excepts the letter **L** <note>The Hebrew letter Lamed, used as a prefix meaning "to" or "for."</note> from this rule of his for Psalms 20 and 21, but he is mistaken due to Jewish prejudice: for we shall show in the proper place that those psalms were written by David not about himself, but about Christ. *e)* For example, when they want to say their Psalter is finished, they write at the end of it: *The David is finished.* *f)* For their principal author is the Holy Spirit himself, who dictated the psalms to David and others to be published in the Church, as the Jews admit. See above, Section I.

<summary>This preface introduces the Hagiographa (the third section of the Hebrew Bible), focusing on the Book of Psalms. It addresses the Jewish view that these books are divinely inspired by the Holy Spirit, though perhaps through a different mode of revelation than the primary Prophets, and discusses the roles of David and Ezra in their authorship and collection.</summary>
<keywords>Hagiographa, Ketuvim, Psalms, David Kimchi, Aben Ezra, Holy Spirit, Ruach HaKodesh, divine inspiration, theopneustos, Ezra the Scribe, biblical canon, Davidic authorship</keywords>

--- Page 1364 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface to the Book of Psalms, shifting from the general classification of the Hagiographa to a detailed discussion of the authorship and musical performance of the individual psalms.</meta>

# PREFACE.

<margin>David.</margin>
The collection is named for David in the same way we speak of "Luther’s *Songs*" or "Cicero’s *Letters*," which include songs or letters by other authors mixed in among them. David is indeed that "beloved of God"—which is what his name signifies (compare 1 Samuel 13:14 and 2 Samuel 12:25). He is the one called the **sweet singer of Israel** <note>original Hebrew: *ne’im zemirot Yisrael*</note> in 2 Samuel 23:1, through whose mouth God spoke (Acts 4:25), and upon whom the <term>Shekhinah</term> <note>The divine presence or indwelling of God.</note> of God rested so that he might bless Israel in this way (*Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary on the Psalms.</note> folio 2a). Indeed, no one before him received this gift: to write so many sweet sayings and elegant odes, exhibiting the full doctrine of piety for the perpetual use of the Church. Thus, the Syriac inscription of the Psalter is: *The Book of Psalms of David, King and Prophet*. 

In addition to David, however, <term>Kimchi</term> <note>David Kimchi (c. 1160–1235), a major medieval Jewish scholar known for his grammatical and literal approach to the Bible.</note> in his Preface—drawing from his predecessors—lists ten other authors of the psalms: 1. Adam, 2. Melchizedek, 3. Abraham, 4. Asaph, 5. Heman, 6. Jeduthun, 7. Moses, and 8, 9, 10. the three descendants of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent Jewish commentator on the Bible.</note> and the *Midrash Tehillim* (f. 3c) count them slightly differently: for them, the fourth is Moses, the fifth is David, the sixth is Solomon, the seventh is Asaph, and finally the three sons of Korah. Yet Rabbi Hunna in the *Midrash* (at the same place) asserts that all the psalms were written through David; others cited by Aben Ezra agree, as do Augustine in *The City of God* (Book 17, ch. 14) and many others cited by Luis Vives and Cocceius. 

Now, while those ancient Hebrew scholars perhaps overstate the number of authors, those who attribute every single psalm to David—even when unnecessary—diminish the count more than is right. Moses clearly displays his authority and name in Psalm 90. Heman and Ethan in Psalms 88 <margin>Moses, Heman, Ethan, Asaph.</margin> and 89. Asaph in Psalms 50 and 73–83. According to the opinion of others, Psalm 77 belongs to Jeduthun, and Psalms 42, 44–49, 84, 85, and 87 belong to the sons or descendants of Korah. Solomon is also named (even according to Jerome in his *Letter to Sophronius*) in Psalm 72 or 127. 

Admittedly, the attribution of these later psalms is less certain. As Aben Ezra admits in his preface, the phrase **for Solomon** <note>original Hebrew: *li-Shelomoh*</note> in Psalm 72:1 might refer *to* Solomon <note>i.e., David writing for his son.</note> because of the prefix used. Similarly, the psalm attributed to Jeduthun (one of the masters of sacred music in 1 Chronicles 16:41–42) in Psalm 77:1 likely belongs to Asaph, based on a similar grammatical construction in Psalm 62:1. Furthermore, the "sons of Korah" should perhaps be understood as singers rather than authors (compare Psalm 88:1), as it is unlikely that one and the same psalm was inspired by multiple people, unless one interprets it as "one of the sons" alongside others. However, even when there is doubt about Asaph's psalms—whether he wrote them or merely performed them—it seems more credible to us that **Asaph** indicates the author. Asaph himself was a Prophet (1 Chronicles 25:1) and is explicitly praised as an author of sacred songs alongside David (2 Chronicles 29:30), just as Heman and Ethan were famous for divine wisdom in their time (1 Kings 5:11) and are expressly called Prophets and Seers (1 Chronicles 25:1–5).

<margin>Unnamed psalms of David.</margin>
§. IV. There are many psalms—nearly a third of the collection—in which no author is mentioned. Of these, the Greek translators (the Septuagint) attribute Psalms 33, 43, 91, 95, 96, 98, 99, and 104 to David; Psalm 71 to the "sons of Jonadab and the first of the captivity"; Psalm 137 to Jeremiah; and Psalms 146, 147, and 148 to Haggai and Zechariah (not to mention the Eastern versions and their various inscriptions). Nevertheless, <term>Calovius</term>, <term>Heidegger</term>, and others most safely affirm that most were composed by David. Aben Ezra placed Psalm 105 beyond doubt as David’s work, and the same should be said of Psalms 106 and 136 (compare 1 Chronicles 16:34). It is certain to us that the unnamed <note>original Greek: *anepigraphoi*</note> Psalms 2 and 95 belong to David based on the testimony of Christ and the Holy Spirit in the New Testament (compare Acts 4:25 and Hebrews 4:7).

<margin>Prophecies in Psalms.</margin>
§. V. Furthermore, while we readily admit that Psalms 74, 79, and 80 sing of the calamity the people suffered under <term>Antiochus</term> <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king who persecuted the Jews in the 2nd century BCE.</note>, it is not at all necessary to assume they were added later by the Maccabees once religion was restored. The name of Asaph the Prophet is clearly prefixed to them. Even if we were to concede to Grotius that some psalms might have been added in later times by Ezra, he judged far too boldly in his preface that it is "foolish to doubt" that Psalm 137 was written during the Babylonian exile or Psalm 126 upon the return. Should we think the prophecies of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and others were written only after their fulfillment simply because they predict events with such detailed circumstances? <term>Porphyry</term> <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who famously attacked the authenticity of the Book of Daniel.</note> once argued this impudently regarding Daniel’s prophecies and was corrected by Methodius, Eusebius, and others. Therefore, following Aben Ezra, Schmid, and others, we regard those psalms as Davidic unless a name other than David's is prescribed.

<margin>To whom they were committed for public use.</margin>
§. VI. Those psalms which David wrote by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he handed over to **Asaph, Jeduthun**, and the other choir-masters of the Levites to be sung in the Tabernacle or Temple. This practice began with Psalm 105 when he brought the Ark of the Covenant to Mount Zion (1 Chronicles 16:7ff). Hence, the term **To the Choirmaster** <note>original Hebrew: *la-menatzeach*</note> is prefixed to many inscriptions (see the notes on Ps 4:1 and Hab 3:19). <margin>On the nature of music and instruments.</margin> Moreover, the instrument and musical style are often named for each psalm. Regarding these instruments and their names, <term>David Kimchi</term> honestly confesses that neither he nor other Jews are certain what they mean. The ancient music of those times has long since fallen into oblivion or disuse, and as Aben Ezra writes, there is no way to accurately identify those ancient instruments. Thus, what exactly were the <term>Neginoth</term> <note>Stringed instruments.</note> (Ps 4:1), <term>Nechiloth</term> <note>Flutes or wind instruments.</note> (Ps 5:1), <term>Sheminith</term> <note>An eight-stringed lyre or a low musical register.</note> (Ps 6:1), <term>Shiggaion</term> <note>A wild, emotional song or lament.</note> (Ps 7:1), or <term>Gittith</term> <note>A wine-press melody or a harp from the city of Gath.</note> (Ps 8:1), or what was <term>Muth-labben</term> <note>Literally "Death of the son"; possibly a tune name.</note> (Ps 9:1), is not yet fully explored or resolved—even if you follow the judgment of the great <term>Bochart</term> <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French biblical scholar.</note> (which Geier commended on Ps 5:1). 

Bochart suggests that just as the Hebrews name books by their first word (Genesis is *Bereshith*, Exodus is *Veeleh Shemoth*, Leviticus is *Vajjikra*), they also named songs this way in the titles of the psalms. For example, in the title of Psalm 22, the phrase **To the Choirmaster, upon "The Doe of the Dawn"** <note>original Hebrew: *Aijeleth haschchahar*</note> means it should be sung to the melody of a song that began with those words. Others are sung to the tune of "The Lilies" <note>original Hebrew: *Shoshannim*</note> (Ps 45:1, 69:1) or "The Lily of Testimony" (Ps 60:1). Others over "The Virgins" <note>original Hebrew: *Alamot*</note> (Ps 46:1). Others over "Sickness" <note>original Hebrew: *Machalat*</note> (Ps 53:1) or "The Sickness of Affliction" (Ps 88:1). Others over "The Silent Dove in the Distance" (Ps 56:1). These were the beginnings of various songs whose melodies were used for these psalms. I cannot understand why learned men reject this so disdainfully. They say it is beneath the dignity of the Church to use "popular tunes," but it is not necessary that these were lighthearted songs. The Jews could have had several sacred songs whose melodies David used for some of his psalms. These are Bochart's words. Whether they are satisfactory and preferable to other views, the reader shall judge by considering each title, where the most important opinions will be briefly...

The Syrian says: "A narrative of a sermon on good character, found in the canon of the nine beatitudes in Matthew chapter 5." The Arabic: "The beauty of piety and hope for the next world." And as Gregory the Great judged regarding the Book of Job: "When we know the matter itself, if we seek the writer, what are we doing but worrying about the pen while reading the letter?" m) Aben Ezra, following his peers, says: Psalms 137 and 79 are David’s prophecies of future events, like the one in 1 Kings 13:2. Augustine concludes the same in *The City of God*, Book 17, ch. 14.

<meta>This page continues the preface to the Psalter, moving from the list of traditional authors to the historical context, chronological order, and the structural division of the book into five sections mirroring the Torah.</meta>

# PREFACE.

We indicate this briefly. We remain silent here regarding the different system of accents in this and the following two books <note>The "three books" refers to Job, Proverbs, and Psalms, which use a unique poetic accentuation system in Hebrew.</note>, about which our own teachings and those of others can be compared.

<margin>On the different system of accents.</margin>
<margin>Time and occasion.</margin>
§. VII. Furthermore, in the titles or inscriptions of Psalms 3, 7, 18, 30, 34, 51, 52, 54, 56, 57, 59, 60, 63, and 142, the time and occasion of the psalm's writing is noted in advance. Along with these, the Davidic history in both books of Samuel and 1 Chronicles—from chapter 11 to the end of the book (compare also 2 Samuel 3:1, 6:16, 10:14)—must be diligently revisited and compared. For these historical circumstances are like a hidden key for more rightly understanding not only those psalms, but the others as well. In most psalms, we do not have such a clear testimony from the Holy Spirit regarding the occasion and time; hence, what interpreters supply or have wished to supply regarding these are often merely conjectures. Thus, while we pass over the Latin Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic versions in silence, the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> or certain Greek versions have attempted to reveal the occasions of some psalms to us: for instance, that Psalm 66 is a *psalm of resurrection*, Psalm 76 a *Song against the Assyrian*, Psalm 24 to be sung *on the first day of the Sabbath or week*, Psalm 48 *on the second day of the week*, Psalm 94 *on the fourth day*, Psalm 93 *for the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was inhabited*. Psalm 38 is *concerning the Sabbath*, Psalm 27 *before David was anointed*, Psalm 29 *concerning the end of the Tabernacle*, Psalm 143 *when his son pursued him*, and Psalm 144 written *against Goliath*. But how much weight should be given to all of these will only be established with more certainty from the actual argument and text of each Psalm. <term>Lightfoot</term> <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar.</note> performed a laudable service, as he sought to carefully investigate and distinctly describe the chronological order and occasion of the psalms (where known from their inscriptions) in his *Chronology of the Old Testament*. The celebrated <term>Dr. Maius</term> <note>Johann Heinrich Maius (1653–1719), a German theologian and Hebraist.</note> in his *Economy of the Old Testament* not only followed these meditations of that learned man, but occasionally supplemented and corrected them. However, that something has been left here for us and others as well, the treatment itself will show (see the notes to Psalm 3:1 and 11:1). And so that we may briefly dispatch the chronology of the psalms here: the Psalms of David were written by him either before or after his royal dignity, after he had been anointed by Samuel. Indeed, according to the mind of Lightfoot, in the *36th year of Samuel and Saul*, after Goliath was killed, Psalm 9 was written. In the *37th year of Samuel*, Psalms 59, 34, 56, and 142. In the *39th year of Samuel*, Psalm 58. However, in the 9th year of David’s reign, Psalms 68 and 132, as well as 96, 105, and 106. In David's 10th to 20th year, Psalms 60 and 108; in the 26th year, Psalms 51 through 50 <note>This likely refers to a grouping in the author's source.</note>; in the 35th year, Psalms 3, 7, 42, 43, 55; and after his return, Psalms 30 and 4. In the final years of his life and reign, David spoke and wrote Psalm 18, in which he looked toward the *Messiah*. Dr. Maius (page 797 and following) also referred several more psalms to Christ, likewise Psalm 39 concerning preparation for a blessed death (compare Psalm 90), and after the Levite worship was organized, Psalms 133–135, 147–150, and finally for the inauguration of Solomon, Psalms 72 and 117, as well as 119 and its summary in Psalm 1.

<margin>And the Chronology of the Psalms.</margin>
<margin>Masoretic division of the book,</margin>
§. VIII. Thus far concerning the time and occasion of the Psalms; we proceed now to their division, whether viewed according to the Hebrew or <term>Masoretic</term> <note>Referring to the Masoretes, Jewish scholars who preserved the traditional text and structure of the Hebrew Bible.</note> tradition, or by reason of their subject matter. As for the former, the Hebrews divided the whole volume into five books, as if it were a *second Pentateuch* <note>original Latin: "alterum Pentateuchum"</note> <note>n</note>). The first is from Psalm 1–41; the second Psalm 42–72; the third Psalm 73–89; the fourth 90–106—all of which end with the closing refrain "Amen and Amen" <note>original Hebrew: אָמֵן וְאָמֵן</note>; while the fifth, Psalm 107–150, ends with *Hallelujah*. Thus in the *Midrash Tehillim* (folio 2, column 1) they hand down the following: *Moses gave the Israelites five books of the Law, and so David also gave them the Psalter, in which there are also five books.* Likewise <term>David Kimchi</term> in his Preface, following the ancients: *Just as Moses divided the Law into five volumes, so also David divided his psalter into five volumes.* But just as that tradition about a Davidic division of the Psalter is not very solid—since individual Psalms are individual and, as it were, complete works of David—so too the Hebrew commentators reveal nothing certain to us regarding the reason for this division or the order the psalms obtained within it. <note>o</note>) For we do not have them arranged by the chronological order in which they were written, but perhaps as they were collected by holy men, or, according to Huetius, as they were later sung in the Temple. Nor is it likely that the collection of the entire psalter was made at one time, given the conclusion of Psalm 72:20, *where the prayers of David are said to be ended*, even though many psalms clearly inscribed with David’s name follow after. (See Psalms 86, 101, 103, 108, etc.) Something similar happened with the Proverbs of Solomon (compare Proverbs 25:1). And although some connection might be constructed from the present order of the psalms based on subject matter—so that, for example, Psalm 1 describes the kingdom of Christ and the order of salvation, which according to Psalm 2 his enemies, the Jews and Gentiles, oppose, and after them especially the Antichrist, just as the ancients in Kimchi explained Psalm 3 as being about Gog and Magog; against whom the Church in Psalm 4 retreats to God and meanwhile witnesses the truth to her enemies; and as they persist in their sins, she prays to God in Psalm 5, and sensing her own failings intimately, she prays for mercy in Psalm 6, etc.—nevertheless, it is more certain what *Kimchi* writes on Psalm 2: *Why*, he says, *this second Psalm follows the first, no reason for that is established among us. For the psalms do not follow each other in the order they were written. For example, the third, concerning Absalom, follows immediately after the second; though there are many that, by reason of history, should have been placed before it, such as Psalm 142.*

<margin>And the present order of the psalms.</margin>
<margin>Division of the Psalms by argument,</margin>
§. IX. More useful and certain, therefore, is the distribution taken from the matter or argument of the psalms, about which <term>Athanasius</term> <note>A 4th-century Church Father and Bishop of Alexandria.</note> writes succinctly in his *Letter to Marcellinus*: *Some are spoken in narrative, some in exhortation, some in prophecy, some as in prayer, some as in confession and thanksgiving.* <note>original Greek: οἱ μὲν ἐν διηγήματι λέγονται, οἱ δὲ ἐκ παραινέσεως, οἱ δὲ ἐκ προφητείας, οἱ δὲ ὡς ἐν εὐχῇ, οἱ δὲ ὡς ἐν ἐξομολογήσει.</note> That blessed man explains these types copiously through their various species, creating a proper treatise in that letter, which is rightly recommended to students of the Psalter. Above all, however, one should observe the warning of Gurtler in *Prophetic Theology* (page 98): *the greater part of the Psalms is prophetic*, and as many as do not explicitly indicate another subject at the beginning are to be explained either of Christ or of the Christian Church; this was formerly the opinion of Arnobius the Younger, and in the past century of Johann Bugenhagen and Conrad Heresbach, successful interpreters of the psalms. Thus also <term>Brentius</term> <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a German Reformer.</note> on 2 Samuel 23:2: *The Davidic Psalms*, he says, *were dictated by the Holy Spirit not only for this reason, that they are of certain truth, but because they look much further ahead than the letter shows at first glance. For David is accustomed to take up his own person in the Psalms, discussing his hosts, enemies, and adversities, so that you would think only David’s business was being handled. But if you look deeply within, he looks primarily to Jesus Christ, his son, whose wars, temptations, and victories he so described in the psalms that they can rightly be called Christ's songs of victory or triumphal hymns.* <note>original Greek: ἐπινίκια</note> For thus Christ also says in *Luke 24*: *It was necessary that everything be fulfilled which was written about me in the psalms.* This must be observed against the insane diligence of those who act as if by design to wrap in darkness the oracles of the Old Testament—which we have most clearly explained and demonstrated through Christ and the Apostles in the New Testament—and by their perverse study snatch away from us the spirit of prophecy, the testimonies concerning Christ, and the goal and kernel of the entire Scripture. Indeed, the Holy Spirit predicted Christ's human and divine natures, his eternal generation, his prophetic office, his priesthood and kingship, and especially his passions so clearly in this book that <term>Cassiodorus</term> <note>A 6th-century Roman statesman and scholar.</note> once judged that history, not prophecy, seemed to be written here. For even the words of him hanging on the cross, in which he complained of being deserted by God, and the final sigh of him returning his soul to the Father, were recorded in the psalms as if caught from his own mouth beneath the cross; the like of which is found in no other prophet. We pass over other articles of our entire faith and their most lucid testimonies here for the sake of brevity.

<margin>Prophetic.</margin>

***

*) Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures* §. V: *The Hebrews divided the Psalter into five books, so that it would be another Pentateuch.* <note>original Greek: τὸ ψαλτήριον διεῖλον εἰς πέντε βιβλία οἱ Ἑβραῖοι, ὥστε εἶναι καὶ αὐτὸ ἄλλην πεντάτευχον.</note> o) *I know*, says Jerome in his *Preface to the Psalms according to the Hebrew Truth* to Sophronius, *that some think the Psalter is divided into five books, so that wherever it is written in the Septuagint "so be it, so be it"* <note>original Greek: γένοιτο γένοιτο</note> *—that is, "fiat fiat"—it is the end of the books, for which "Amen, Amen" is read in the Hebrew. We, however, following the authority of the Hebrews, and especially of the Apostles, who always name the "book of psalms" in the New Testament, assert that there is one volume of psalms, etc.*

It emphasizes a Christological and prophetic interpretation, arguing that the Psalms primarily testify to the life, suffering, and victory of Jesus Christ.</summary>
