<meta>This page concludes the preface, focusing on the spiritual value of the Psalms as a "Little Bible," their frequent citation in the New Testament, the translator's methodology, and the variations in Psalm numbering between different biblical traditions.</meta>

# PREFACE.

<margin>The excellence, utility, and praises of the Psalter.</margin>
§. X. From this, it is easily apparent how great the dignity and excellence of this book is. It is rightly considered a manual of sacred prayers throughout the entire Christian world and serves as a compendium of the whole of Scripture. Our Blessed *Luther* was accustomed to calling it the *Little Bible* <note>original: "Parua Biblia"</note>, and he wonderfully extols its excellence and utility in his own Preface. Likewise, *Brentius* <note>Johann Brentz (1499–1570), a German Reformer.</note>, commenting on Psalm 1, says: *You would rightly and fittingly call the Psalter an epitome of the Bible.* By others, the *Psalter* is called a *Mirror* of God's grace and an absolute, complete anatomy of the whole man. In it are set forth every kind of teaching regarding the gracious promises and works of God toward His own people, His severity toward adversaries, and His faithfulness toward all. Likewise, it speaks of our faith in His promises, our obedience, our infirmities, and our patience, constancy, and deliverance in times of adversity; as well as the legitimate use of good things and the giving of thanks in times of prosperity. Finally, it treats our whole duty toward God and His faithfulness toward us in Christ, of whom most elegant and illustrious prophecies are found throughout for the consolation and confirmation of the Church. Whatever God has taught us in other books—how He speaks to us—in this book He teaches us what and how we ought to speak with Him in our prayers. And while in the rest of Scripture we have the Word of God, so to speak, in the abstract, here one may see it as if in practice (see, for example, Psalm 27:8). As *Athanasius* <note>A 4th-century Church Father.</note> writes in the passage cited above, though all Scripture is <term>divinely inspired</term> <note>original: "θεόπνευστος" (theopneustos)</note> and useful for doctrine, etc. (as Paul teaches in 2 Timothy 3:16), the Psalter nevertheless possesses certain things to be particularly observed by anyone who pays proper attention. For every book, as that holy man continues, treats and pursues its own specific argument—but the book of Psalms, like a Paradise containing the fruits of all the others, brings them forth in song, and moreover exhibits its own peculiar or proper fruits while one is singing. Similarly, Saint *Basil* <note>Basil the Great (c. 330–379), Bishop of Caesarea.</note> in his first Homily on the Psalms says: *But the book of Psalms includes what is beneficial from all. It prophesies what is to come, recalls history, gives laws for life, suggests things to be done; and in short, it is a common treasury of good teachings, finding for each person what is suitable for their care.*

<margin>The Psalms are cited frequently in the New Testament.</margin>
For this reason, its testimonies are very frequently cited in the New Testament, so that nearly a third of the Psalms are found quoted there. Even more frequently than one might think, the New Testament looks back to the phrasing of the Psalter. Thus (to show by only one or two examples what deserves to be observed in the other psalms as well), Paul refers to Psalm 1:2 in 1 Timothy 4:15, and to Psalm 1:6 in 2 Timothy 2:19. Compare Psalm 2:1-2 with Acts 4:25 and following; Psalm 2:7 with Acts 13:33, Hebrews 1:5, and 5:5; also Matthew 3:17 and 17:5. Regarding the words "I will give to you" in Psalm 2:8, compare Matthew 28:18, John 5:27, and Philippians 2:7-8. In the same place, regarding "your inheritance," compare Matthew 21:38 and Hebrews 1:2. Regarding the "ends of the earth," see Revelation 11:15-16. For Psalm 2:9, compare Revelation 2:27, 12:5, and 19:15. For Psalm 2:11, see Philippians 2:12. For Psalm 2:12, see Revelation 6:16-17, and so forth.

<margin>Regarding our annotations.</margin>
§. XI. As for our own annotations, we have wished at times to investigate the sense with great care and to explain it a little more fully, so as to show the way to students by example. (Often, however, we have only hinted with brief <term>scholia</term> <note>Short explanatory notes or comments.</note> at things that should have been said more at length, yet in such a way that the force and reasoning of what we have omitted may be easily understood, provided the reader brings a faithful mind that hungers for divine truth). Thus, even if we have not pointed it out everywhere, one must always observe in every reading of the Psalms the enmity and battle of the infernal Serpent and his impious seed against that blessed Seed of the Woman and His living members. This struggle has flourished perpetually and will flourish until the end of the conflict, just as the Lord foretold to us from the beginning for our hope and comfort in Genesis 3:15. For the rest, we recommend to all a diligent and pious meditation on every word, if one wishes to experience the sweetness of this heavenly food and taste it in the soul. For as the Blessed *Bernard* <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and mystic.</note> writes so well in his *Letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu*:

<margin>Saint Bernard's golden counsel.</margin>
> *Haphazard and varied reading, found as if by chance, does not build up but makes the mind unstable; and what is lightly admitted more lightly leaves the memory. But the mind must dwell upon and grow accustomed to certain great wits. For by whatever Spirit the Scriptures were made, by that same Spirit they desire to be read, and by Him they must be understood. You will never enter into the sense of Paul until, by the use of good intention in reading him and the study of constant meditation, you have drunk in his Spirit. You will never understand David until, by experience itself, you have put on the very affections of the Psalms. And so it is with the rest. In all Scripture, study differs as much from mere reading as friendship differs from being a guest, or a social affection from a chance greeting. But from daily reading, something should be lowered every day into the stomach of the memory, to be more faithfully digested and, when called back up, more frequently ruminated upon; something that suits the purpose, profits the intention, and holds the mind so that it does not care to think of foreign matters. One must often draw affections from the sequence of the reading and form a prayer that interrupts the reading; yet not so much hindering by interrupting as restoring the mind to a readier state for understanding the reading. Reading serves the intention. If you truly seek God in your reading, everything that you read works together for your good; it captures the sense of the reader and brings every understanding of the reading into captivity to the obedience of Christ. But if the reader's sense turns toward something else, it drags everything after itself, and finds nothing so holy or pious in the Scriptures that it does not apply to malice or vanity, whether through vainglory, a distorted sense, or a depraved understanding.*

Indeed, in reading all Scriptures, the beginning must be the fear of the Lord, so that the reader's intention may first be solidified in it, and from it the understanding and sense of the whole reading may be ordered and arise.

<margin>The numbering of the Psalms.</margin>
§. XII. It remains at last for us to mention something regarding the numbering of the Psalms. To the 150 canonical Psalms, the Greek <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and the Oriental Versions (Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic) add one apocryphal Psalm, making 151. However, they explicitly state that it is "extra-numerical" and does not belong with the preceding ones. Indeed, the Syriac version adds that some others have joined twelve more psalms, which they themselves do not need. Furthermore, the numerical order from Psalm 9 to Psalm 147 is different in the Hebrew than in the Greek and those that follow it, such as the Latin Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic codices. Specifically, these versions join Psalms 9 and 10 as one; conversely, they divide Psalm 147 into two, as we have noted at Psalm 10. We pass over the fact that some of the ancients in the Talmudic tractate *Berachoth* (folio 9 and following), as well as the Greeks (cited by Geier on Psalm 2), joined the second Psalm with the first because the second lacks a title. They added this clever reason: that David began every song pleasing to him with *Ashrei* ("Blessed") and also ended it with *Ashrei* (compare Psalm 1:1 and Psalm 2:12). However, Psalm 2 is explicitly cited as the "second" by Paul in Acts 13:33 according to almost all our codices and versions. Against the subtleties of his own people, *Kimchi* <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish commentator.</note> rightly notes in his commentary on Psalm 2 that in all approved books it is written as a new and second Psalm of David and should be considered a new song. *Schmidius* also proves this from the sufficiently diverse subject matter of these psalms in his *Commentary on the Psalms of Christ*. We add here only one observation from the comparison of codices: our Codex 5 (as well as the manuscript commentary of Rabbi Solomon) did not number the first psalm, treating it as a Preface to the whole book, but marked the second Psalm as number 1, the third as 2, and so on until Psalm 18, where the numbering ceased. But perhaps that scribe had similar subtleties in mind as the ones just cited, or like Rabbi Joshua ben Levi (mentioned by Lightfoot on Acts 13:33), about which there is neither need nor use for us to say more here.

<meta>The previous page discussed the general excellence of the Psalter as a "Little Bible" and a manual for prayer. This page begins the actual commentary on the first Psalm, focusing on the definition of true happiness and the character of the righteous person.</meta>

# THE BOOK OF PSALMS, Hebrew *Tehillim*

<margin>
Ps. I. v. 1. a) **Blessednesses**. <note>original: "Beatitudines"</note> This refers to right walking, happy progress, and prosperous success, as seen in the related name in Psalm 17:5 and the verb in Isaiah 1:17; 3:12; Psalm 41:3; Proverbs 4:14; etc. These are happinesses indeed, not only of this life, but also of the future life, toward which we all press as if toward a goal. See 1 Kings 10:8; Ecclesiastes 10:17; 1 Timothy 4:8. This name, says Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a prominent medieval Jewish biblical commentator.</note>, always occurs in the plural number (in the construct form, after the pattern of "tents" in 2 Kings 5:3); because a person is called "blessed" not because of one single good thing found in him, or because of one prosperous success that happens to him, but because of many good or happy things. See *Maimonides* <unclear>at the end of verse 1</unclear>, which compare with Matthew 5:3-11, where the subject of this proclamation was declared by our Savior himself in several ways, as the Syriac inscription of this Psalm reminds us. And just as Christ did there, so our poet here begins to explain the nature of true happiness, which Scripture alone—or the divine word in verse 2—shows in a clearly evangelical manner. We therefore understand here also what David says elsewhere in Psalm 32:1-2 and Paul in Romans 4:6-7, namely that the blessedness of man consists in God attributing righteousness to him without works; so that no entrance is given to others toward that true and eternal happiness except through the free remission of sins to be obtained from God in true repentance and faith because of Christ, as in Psalm 32:12; Luke 1:77; Acts 10:43; since outside of Christ every person is subject to divine judgment and <margin>damnation. Romans 3:19, 22. Furthermore, regarding the occasion,</margin>

or the time when this psalm was written by David, we have no indication, because it lacks a title; although one might not undeservedly call it a *compendium of Psalm 119* (which the aged David seems to have composed and recommended to Solomon; see the Preface to this book, § 7) or even an epitome of the entire Psalter or the whole of Holy Scripture, if one worthily meditates on the emphasis and weight of each word. Some (says Jerome, or whoever commented on this book under his name) say, *this psalm is like a preface of the Holy Spirit, and therefore has no title*. And Kimchi says: *This psalm is clearly excellent, and therefore David began his book with it*. For the whole Psalter, and indeed the entire Holy Scripture, works toward this end: to explain the happiness of the pious who are in Christ, and the unhappiness and eternal destruction of the wicked; which is the argument of this psalm. At the same time, it teaches what, of what kind, and where the true church of God is, and who are its living members in Christ—those among whom the study of the divine word and the practice of true piety flourish. Briefly, according to our Ethiopic version, this psalm is based on an antithesis: *A description of the righteous and the sinners*; compare Genesis 3:15. b) **Of that man** <note>original: "Illius viri"</note>—meaning any human being, of whatever sex or rank, age or dignity. For M. I. reminds us that both sexes are included here, comparing Leviticus 24:15, 17, 19, etc., and Galatians 3:28. c) **who does not walk**. This is to be understood not so much physically as morally. See Isaiah 65:2; Micah 6:16; Proverbs 1:10, 15. These past-tense verbs are to be taken as continuing into the present and future. Compare Ephesians 1:4; Hosea 4:18. d) **in the counsel and pleasures**. See Job 21:16; 22:18; 2 Chronicles 22:5. e) **of the wicked**, such as all those are who, left to themselves outside of Christ, live impiously and without God, as in Ephesians 5:12, 20; Romans 5:6, 8; and are therefore subject to death, misery, and eternal damnation. See below at verse 6; Jeremiah 5:26; Ezekiel 3:18; Psalm 109:7; Job 27:7. f) **in the way**. The Syriac says "in the sentiment or opinion." Kimchi: *The "way" is not understood literally, but refers to the customs, study, and occupation of a man*, as in Exodus 18:20; Ephesians 5:7; Job 17:9; add Genesis 6:12; Ephesians 5:6; Proverbs 13:26; Matthew 7:13; 2 Peter 2:2; and compare below verse 6 and Ecclesiastes 12:5. g) **of sinners**, specifically such people, and in opposition to the righteous in verse 5; namely, those who are not born again of God through repentance and faith in Christ, and who serve sin. John 8:34; Romans 3:23; 6:12, 16. Compare Numbers 32:14; Ecclesiastes 9:2; John 9:31; Matthew 5:17, 19; Galatians 2:15, 17; 1 John 3:4-9, etc. h) **does not persist, does not stay**; but having been called back by divine grace, he immediately departs, even if he has been carried away into error. Ezekiel 18:21, 27; Psalm 37:27; 1 John 2:1-2. Compare Genesis 19:17; Ecclesiastes 8:3. i) **and in the assembly or gathering**. Psalm 107:23; compare Psalm 94:20. k) **of scoffers** <note>original: "irrisorum"</note> of the truth and the divine word. Isaiah 28:14, 22; 29:20; Proverbs 1:22, 29, 30; 9:7, 8; 13:1; 21:24; Luke 16:14; 1 Corinthians 1:23; 2 Peter 3:3, etc. l) **does not sit**, to participate with the wicked in their counsels, words, and deeds. Psalm 26:4. There is a climax or gradation here: in the persons (the wicked in their heart and original vice, sinners in external acts, scoffers in their stubbornness); also in the counsel, way, and seat; and in the actions—if someone by *walking* consents and begins to sin, by *standing* persists in evil, and finally by *sitting* rests entirely in that impiety and evil life. On this see more in Kimchi, Calovius, and others. Verse 2. m) **But on the contrary** as in verse 4 and Isaiah 59:2; like those born again of God, John 1:12-13; 3:6; and the "new man" of 2 Corinthians 5:17. n) **in the law of the Lord**, by which is understood here not just the Pentateuch of Moses (as in Joshua 8:32, 34, etc.) or the Law in opposition to the Gospel, but all heavenly doctrine and truth revealed in the sacred writings: which alone can instruct us for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. 2 Timothy 3:15; Psalm 116:11; Romans 3:4; compare Psalm 19:8; Ephesians 1:10; 2:3; 8:16, 20, etc. o) **is his desire or delight**. Psalm 111:2. Just as a bridegroom delights in the bride whom he loves. Genesis 34:19; compare Psalm 40:9 and 119:35, 14, 47, 72; Romans 7:22. p) **he is occupied, he meditates** <note>original: "versatur, meditatur"</note> Joshua 1:8; Psalm 2:1; 63:7-8; <note>original Greek: μελετήσει - "he will meditate"</note> 1 Timothy 4:15. q) **with unwearied study**; so that even when the outward action ceases, the pious affection never ceases. See Deuteronomy 6:6-9; 11:18-20; Isaiah 26:9; Joshua 1:8; Psalm 42:4; 119:97; and compare Leviticus 8:35; 1 Chronicles 9:33; Luke 18:1, 7.

Ps. I. v. 1. *Ashrei* (אַשְׁרֵי): The first metrical word, which is also the most troubled regarding its accent. The Masoretes <note>Scholars who preserved the tradition of the Hebrew biblical text, including its vowels and accents.</note> have it as 16, 17, 18, 22 below, and *Ber.* has 34 above, both contrary to analogy. Regularly, a *Mahpach* <term>Mahpach: a Hebrew accent used to link words</term> would be required, which code 1 has. Codes 15, 16, and 24 have a *Merca* <term>Merca: a conjunctive accent</term> with us, which itself also serves *Rbhia* <term>Rbhia: a disjunctive accent indicating a pause</term>, not only when *Mercamahpachatum* immediately precedes it here, but also elsewhere when a "servant" accent falls on a difficult word. See for example, according to most codices, Psalm 71:3; 76:8; 85:14; Proverbs 29:10; 28:10. Others added no accent at all to the initial word, which was written in capital letters; except for code 5, which perhaps has a *Makkaph* <note>a hyphen-like mark connecting words</note>, as does code 1. Furthermore, the Masora <note>The body of notes on the traditions of the Hebrew text.</note> notes that this word is found four times with this accent: here and in Psalm 32:2; 40:5; Proverbs 8:34. This cannot be reconciled with the *Mahpach*, because in Psalm 45:5; 94:12; 127:5; 137:9, the same word likewise occurs with a *Mahpach*. Much less can it be reconciled with the *Zarka*, which the Masora foolishly—that is, against analogy and the evidence of the codices—demands. It must therefore be reconciled either to the *Merca*, which the better books have in the cited places, or to the euphonic accent *Metheg*, which code 22 has as a single mark (אַשְׁרֵי) and codes 1, 3, and 5 have as a double mark (אַשְׁרֵי), with the *Makkaph* either understood or expressed. *Asher* (אֲשֶׁר) without 'ל : Psalms 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 13. 'לו : 'לי - ' without *Pasek* <note>a vertical line between words used to prevent misreading</note> 1, 3, 5, 7, 8.

->Ps. II. v. 1. $\sigma$<- Why? as if to say: Why have the nations turned to madness so fruitlessly and impiously, without any cause or benefit to themselves? Thus God spoke through David in Acts 4:25. And so David himself, as a Prophet (others say the assembly of the Apostles and citizens of Christ’s kingdom in Acts 4:24), considers with wonder, and not without just complaint and indignation, the madness of worldly people opposing God and the Messiah. compare verse 4. Compare the force of reproach in this particle "Why" in Genesis 4:6; Exodus 5:4; and regarding useless action in Isaiah 55:2. etc. **$\tau$**) This psalm is "Antistrophic" <note>A term for a poetic structure where stanzas correspond.</note> among the Hebrews and Greeks, like the first and several others, about which we spoke in the preface §4. Hence the Eastern interpreters add a title from its subject matter. The Syriac has: "On the calling of the nations," implying a prophecy about the passion of Christ. The Arabic: "A prophecy about Christ the Lord, and the calling of the nations." So our Ethiopic version, from which the Roman, Collegium, and English Polyglot printed versions vary, as we noted in the Ethiopic Psalter. That this psalm is by David, the Ethiopic adds correctly, as we learn for certain from Acts 4:25. From which place also, no less than from the argument of this psalm, its true object is clear: namely, the Messiah (v. 2) who is the King in Zion appointed by the Lord (v. 6), namely JESUS CHRIST, our Lord and Savior, and his kingdom and adversaries, both the Gentiles and the Kings of the nations, as well as the nations and leaders of the Jews. Beware, for some think with the Jews that David himself should be understood, or David in the primary and literal sense and the Messiah in a mystical and hidden sense, as Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> thought, who was rightly refuted by Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a leading Lutheran theologian.</note>. Indeed, even the great Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant scholar.</note> wrongly wrote somewhere: "I refer the literal sense of the psalm to David with Musculus and other interpreters of great name." For that this psalm must be understood as referring to Christ in the first and immediate sense, the best and greatest interpreter of his own word, the Holy Spirit, has taught us through the Apostles in the New Testament. And certainly the subject of the psalm belongs so clearly to the Messiah alone that even the most stubborn of the Jews cannot deny it: because God calls him his son, appoints him Prophet, King, and Priest, attributes to him the inheritance of the whole world, assigns him omnipotence, and commands worship, reverence, fear, and finally faith in him from all nations. No one but a blasphemer can understand all these things of a mere man. As Rivetus writes. Indeed, almost every verse and every word of this psalm dictates that it must be understood of Christ; which Calovius proves with thirteen arguments: (1) from the naming of the Son v. 7, 12. cf. Acts 13:33. Heb 1:5. Matt 3:17; 17:5. (2) from the eternal generation v. 7. cf. Heb 5:5. (3) from the title of Messiah v. 2. cf. Is 61:1. Dan 9:25. etc. (4) from the breadth of his dominion v. 8. cf. Ps 72:8ff. Zech 9:10. (5) from the description of his rule v. 9. cf. Rev 19:15. (6) from the subjection of all Kings and Judges v. 10, 12. cf. Rev 19:16. (7) from religious veneration v. 11, 12. cf. John 5:23. (8) from divine threat v. 12. cf. John 3:18, 36. (9) from the honor of trust v. 12. cf. Jer 17:5. (10) from the promise of blessedness v. 12. cf. John 3:16. Acts 4:12; 10:43. (11) from the distinction of David's prophecies (Acts 4:25). (12) from the infallible explanation of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament. cf. Acts 4:25ff; 13:33. Heb 1:5; 5:5. Rev 19:15. etc. (13) the ancient [Jewish] opinions also agree on this, as even more recent ones admit: although these others, out of a desire to contradict, now prefer to take another path. Not to mention others whom Raymund Martini cited throughout his *Dagger of Faith*, and Calovius at p. 934, and Schmid at p. 10 in his *Psalms of Christ*, the Talmudic scholars in *Succah* fol. 52a interpret this psalm of the Messiah. So also in *Yalkut* part II, fol. 90b. *Bereshit Rabbah* at Gen 15:2, fol. 43b-c. *Midrash Tehillim* fol. 4b and fol. 63b. Likewise Alschech in his commentary at this place; and Aben Ezra, though doubtful, candidly admits at verse 1 that if the psalm is taken to be about the Messiah, everything is much clearer. Kimchi also writes at the end of his commentary: "There are those who explain this psalm of Gog and Magog, so that the Anointed One in verse 2 is the King Messiah. So also our ancient Doctors of blessed memory explained it. And the psalm is indeed clear in this way; yet it is more fitting that David said it of himself, as we have explained." Namely, because the persistent Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, according to his own manuscript codes for this passage, [wrote it] <term>to refute the heretics</term> <note>original Hebrew: "לחשוב המינים" — likely a transcription for "להשיב למינים" (to answer the heretics/Christians).</note> so that he might more easily respond to Christians and elude their arguments. For thus it is held in the parchment Erfurt Code of Rashi, which similarly Pococke <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), an English Orientalist and scholar.</note> observed in another manuscript; and which was deleted by Christian censors with great inconvenience, and is found neither in the Venice nor Basel editions. Furthermore, Kimchi thinks that this psalm was written by David at the beginning of his reign, when the nations gathered against him as we read in 2 Samuel 5:17ff; and Rivetus, Bosch, and others think that the occasion of this psalm was the same, as we hinted at in the note on 2 Samuel §25. However, because we read that the most illustrious promise concerning Christ given in 2 Samuel chapter 7 had not yet been made to David at that time, we prefer to [place] the occasion of this psalm at 2 Samuel 8 or 10...

# PSALM 2. II

...to refer back. For just as King David was most bitterly opposed by the impious nations surrounding him, and later even by his own son and the rebels of Israel, yet was constantly helped and preserved by God; so also, since he was a Prophet and knew that God had promised him by an oath that He would raise up the Messiah from "the fruit of his loins" <note>original: "fructu lumborum eius"</note> to be placed upon his throne, David foresaw all these things in the Spirit. He prophesied concerning the deliberations, pursuits, and endeavors of all anti-Christians against Christ, and concerning the kingdom of Christ, its magnitude, and its stability. <term>cf.</term> Acts 2:30, 31 and the work of Brentius <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a German Reformer and theologian.</note> <term>on this passage.</term> We have here, therefore, an irrefutable testimony of the Holy Spirit concerning CHRIST, the Son of God, from eternal generation, and concerning the salvation to be obtained through faith in Him; both of which the treacherous Jews <note>The author uses the phrase "perfidi Iudæi," reflecting the typical 17th-century religious polemic between Christianity and Judaism regarding the interpretation of the Messiah.</note> today condemn and reject. Furthermore, David foresaw and prophesied: **I.** that the world would raise a tumult against the kingdom of Christ <term>vv. 1-3,</term> but **II.** that God would most powerfully preserve and enlarge it <term>vv. 4-9,</term> so that **III.** even those Kings would either serve Him or perish <term>vv. 10-12,</term> as the headings in Schmidt's <note>Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696), a Lutheran theologian known for his biblical commentaries.</note> work have it. The style is mimetic <note>meaning it imitates the voices of different speakers</note>, and the psalm is written in the manner of a dialogue; yet, just as in the Song of Songs and elsewhere, the different persons speaking are not expressly named. On this, you may see more in Geier <note>Martin Geier (1614–1680), a prominent Hebraist and commentator.</note> and others <term>on this passage.</term> **a)** they have gathered together with tumult and noise. The Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible translation.</note> and the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible (LXX).</note> translate this as "they roared" <note>original: "fremuerunt"</note>, like horses. Others: "they were in a tumult." **(i)** This verb is more frequent in Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> and Syriac; see Daniel 6:6, 12, and the nouns in Psalm 55:15 and Psalm 64:3. In Arabic, it also signifies "it thundered," or when the heaven is shaken with a great crash, or when a camel bellows with a violent sound, etc. **a)** vain and impious nations. See Isaiah 40:17, Psalm 79:6, Ephesians 2:12, 4:17. Compare Luke 18:32, Acts 16:19, 21, 19:23, etc., concerning the historical persecution of the Church.

<margin>the [nations] of all ages.</margin>
<margin>**b)** The Vulgate: "and why the people" [f. stands for *fortasse*, meaning perhaps] "nations." Elsewhere it is used as broadly as the preceding term; here, however, it means nations, that is, families.</margin>
...and we understand the tribes of Israel, according to Acts 4:27. <term>cf.</term> Psalm 7:8, Genesis 25:23, Isaiah 34:1, etc. <margin>**c)** they will, what in the mind</margin> **c)** they will, they plot in their minds, as in Psalm 1:2, and bring forth with their mouth and tongue, Isaiah 59:3, Psalm 37:30, Proverbs 8:7—that which they have meditated upon and conceived in their hearts. <term>cf.</term> Luke 2:34, 35. <margin>**d)** vain things</margin> **d)** something empty, or vanity. Psalm 4:3, Psalm 73:13. Specifically, by fashioning vain suspicions for themselves, and vain and deceptive counsels, to see if they might in some way partly hinder and partly overturn the kingdom and church of Christ. <term>cf.</term> John 11:47-53, Matthew 26:3 ff., Acts 13:45, 23:12, etc.

**v. 2. e)** For they present themselves; or rather, repeating the question from v. 1: "Why have they risen up, why do they stand firm and oppose themselves?" Psalm 94:15, 1 Samuel 17:16. Alshech <note>Rabbi Moshe Alshich, a 16th-century Jewish commentator.</note> says: "This will happen when Gog comes." But experience has proven that it has already happened even then.

**f)** Not only the common people, but even the Kings of the earth; both of the Jews, such as Herod the Great in Matthew 2:3, 16, with his son Antipas in Luke 3:1, 22:11, 12, and his grandson Agrippa in Acts 12:1; and of the nations and Romans. <term>cf.</term> Psalm 48:5, Matthew 10:18, Luke 21:12, and Revelation 16:14, 17:2, 18, etc. **g)** and Princes, such as Pontius Pilate in Acts 4:27, and the Senators of the Jews, etc. Judges 5:3, Proverbs 14:28, 31:4. **h)** they have consulted, entering into a conspiracy and, as it were, "founded" themselves. For counsel is to action as a foundation is to a building, says Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian.</note>. <term>cf.</term> Psalm 31:14, Ephesians 1:3. **i)** together. The Septuagint, as in Acts 4:26, has "at the same" <note>original Greek: "ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό"</note>. In this they agree, as if with common vows, to be adversaries to Christ. <term>cf.</term> Luke 23:12, Matthew 22:34, etc. **k)** against Jehovah. v. 10. upon whom that harmony and obstinacy redounds. Luke 10:16, John 5:22, 1 John 2:23, Isaiah 50:10, etc. **l)** and against His Messiah [f. stands for *fortasse*, meaning perhaps] Christ, <term>that is,</term> the "Anointed One," so called in the highest eminence, as in Daniel 9:25. Namely, Christ Jesus, who according to his human nature was anointed with the Holy Spirit above his fellows: Isaiah 61:1, Psalm 45:8, John 3:34, Acts 10:38. He was anointed as King, <term>see below</term> v. 6; as Prophet, compared with 1 Kings 19:16; and as Priest, compared with Exodus 29:7, etc. The Targum says: "to rebel (before) the Lord, and to strive against His Messiah." <term>cf.</term> Matthew 21:15, 16, and also v. 38, 39, John 9:22, 11:57, etc.

**v. 3. m)** Saying, "Let us break," Judges 16:9, Jeremiah 2:20, 5:5, for the sake of protecting our liberty, compared with Romans 6:18, 21. Here a mimetic word "to say" <note>original Hebrew: "לֵאמֹר" (lemor)</note> is understood, as in Psalm 89:4, Isaiah 14:8, Ezekiel 27:32, Hosea 5:15, and very frequently. **n)** their bonds, (namely of Jehovah and His Christ, v. 2, compare John 14:24). Nahum 1:13, Psalm 107:14. These are instruments of subjection and symbols of servitude. Jeremiah 27:2, 6, 7. A metaphor taken from refractory horses or oxen. <term>cf.</term> Exodus 32:9, Psalm 32:9, Job 30:11, Matthew 11:29, Acts 7:51. **o)** and let us cast away from us. <term>cf.</term> Psalm 50:17. **p)** their cords, Judges 15:13, 14, 16:12, Isaiah 5, 18, Ezekiel 3, 25. For "we do not want this man to reign over us," Luke 19:14. <term>cf.</term> Job 21:14, 15, and Hosea 11:4, Matthew 11:30, 1 John 5:3. Without doubt, they call "bonds and cords" the Word, the precepts, and the obedience that must be shown to Christ and His word, says Schmidt (p. 18).

**v. 4. q)** But He who dwells or sits in the heavens, Psalm 123:1, as if on His throne, Isaiah 16:5, 66:1, Psalm 9:8. Thus He is in infinite ways greater and superior to all kings of the earth (v. 3). Job 4:19, see Isaiah 40:22, Psalm 113:5. **r)** He will not fear, but will despise and laugh at their threats. <term>cf.</term> Psalm 37:13, 59:9, Job 5:22, 39:7, 22. **s)** The Lord, the creator and preserver of all things. Isaiah 6:1, Daniel 9:17. Through whom and for whom all things exist. Romans 11:36, Colossians 1:16, 17, Hebrews 2:10. Thus, with the preceding *yod* combined with *Kametz* (see Hiller's *Onomasticon Sacrum* p. 257 ff.), it is from the most holy names of God, as the Masora notes everywhere, and as the note in our codices "unto" <note>original Hebrew: "עֳלֵי"</note> indicates at Genesis 18:3 and 19:18. The places where this occurs are poorly omitted for the most part in Hebrew Concordances, but Buxtorf exhibits them at the end. The Targum has "the Word of the Lord," Alshech has "the Shekhinah" <note>The divine presence of God.</note>, <term>that is,</term> the Messiah or the Son of God (v. 2, 7, 12), who is directly attacked by the impious, and who elsewhere is called *Haadon* ("The Lord") and the Lord of all the earth. See Zechariah 4:14, Malachi 3:1, etc. **t)** He will mock them, Psalm 59:9, Proverbs 1, 26, compared with 3:34. The Greek says "He will sneer at them" <note>original Greek: "ἐκמυκתיρίσει αὐτοὺς"</note>, a most just punishment of retaliation. Luke 16:14, 23:35, Galatians 6:7.

**v. 5. u)** Then, when they think the bonds have already been broken (v. 3). **x)** He will speak to them. The suffix is poetic, as in v. 3. **y)** in His anger (v. 12). He will announce and inflict upon them the gravest things, and finally eternal destruction, unless they repent. <term>cf. for example</term> Psalm 50:21, Isaiah 50:11, Matthew 3:7 ff., 23:13, 33, 38, Acts 7:51, 9:5, etc. **z)** and in His burning heat or fury. Psalm 69:25, 78:49. <term>cf.</term> Psalm 58:10. **aa)** He will terrify them or throw them into confusion, Psalm 48:6, 83:16, Ezra 4:4. So that they may either yield to holy warnings and sermons (below vv. 10, 11, 12), as happened in Acts 2:37, 5:38, etc.; or, being finally destitute of all hope, comfort, counsel, and help, they will plainly not know where to turn. Compare Nahum 1:6, 1 Samuel 28:21, Psalm 50:3, Isaiah 34:8 ff., Revelation 6:16, 17, Matthew 25:41.

**v. 6. b)** "But I," says the Lord God the Almighty Father (vv. 2, 4), in opposition to those Kings and Princes of dust (vv. 1, 2). **c)** that is, "I have anointed" as King, 1 Samuel 16:13, etc., from which also He was called the Messiah or "Anointed One" above in v. 2. So Symmachus: "I have anointed" <note>original Greek: "ἔχρισα"</note>. <term>cf.</term> Acts 4:27. Others, like the Syriac, "I have established." The Targum expressed both meanings: "I have anointed my King and established him." Namely, by my eternal, certain, and irrefutable counsel, so that neither can you hinder it, nor can the gates of hell overturn it. Compare Proverbs 8:23 and Acts 2:36. But the Septuagint, Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopic, against the grammar—lest the person speaking should change—read: "But I have been established as King by him over Zion his holy mountain, preaching his precept," etc. v. 8. <term>cf.</term> the Syriac in v. 7 and Psalm 3:3. **d)** My King, namely that anointed one (v. 2) and my son (v. 7). Psalm 45:1, 6-8. God calls Him "His King" whom He Himself established without the intervention of another, and whom He made altogether incomparable. Indeed, as Geier writes <term>on this passage</term>, that royal power is not something created or finite, but is the very divine glory itself, which the Son has in common with the Father. Hence other kings also fall before this King (v. 12). Compare Psalm 89:28, Daniel 7:14, 2:44, Luke 1, 32, 33. **e)** Over Zion; just as Saul is said to be anointed over Israel, 1 Samuel 15:17. <term>That is,</term> over the citizens of Zion or my Church, Isaiah 18:7, 49:14, 51:17, 52:1, Ezekiel 20:40, etc. Reference is made to the typical Kingdom of David and his seat on Mount Zion: 2 Samuel 5:6, 7, 1 Kings 8:1, 1 Chronicles 11:4, 7. Others: "I have inaugurated over Zion," <term>that is,</term> I have established Him after He was inaugurated or rather declared, through the pouring out of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:1-4), so that then the doctrine of the Gospel might go out from Zion. Compare Isaiah 2:3, Psalm 110:2. **f)** the mountain of my sanctuary. It is also called this in Psalm 15:1, 43:3, 48:2, etc., because the Ark of the Covenant was kept there (2 Samuel 6:12 ff., 1 Chronicles 15:1, 3, 12, 16:1, 2 Chronicles 8:11), and later the temple was built on the other contiguous ridge, Moriah (2 Chronicles 3:1). Whence Zion, both the typical and the anti-typical <note>referring to the literal mountain and the spiritual church</note>, is called the beloved mountain of God, <term>also</term> His habitation and seat. See Psalm 78:68, 87:2, 132:13, 17, etc. It is contrasted with Mount Sinai in Hebrews 12:22.

While the previous page established the historical context of David’s struggles and his prophetic foresight, this page dives into the theological heart of the Psalm: the eternal generation of the Messiah and his universal dominion. It heavily utilizes Church Fathers like Augustine and Reformers like Luther to explain the "Today" of God as an eternal present.</meta>

Acts 13:33. Hebrews 5:5. a) For I, God the Father (from verse 2), whom Agur also mentions in Proverbs 30:4. b) **Today**, that is, the "today of eternity" <note>original Greek: "ἡμέραν αἰῶνος", cf. 2 Peter 3:18 and verse 8</note>. According to Augustine in this passage, in this "today" nothing is past as if it ceased to be, and nothing is future as if it were not yet; it is only the present. For with God, there is never a tomorrow or a yesterday, but always a "today," as Augustine says in *On the Five Heresies*, chapter 4. For us (as the blessed Luther well advises on this passage), God speaks with us, but in a manner so high that it is outside of time for God. <note>Referencing Luther's *Works*, Jena Latin edition, Volume IV, folio 750, which contains many noteworthy points.</note> Thus in Proverbs 8:30, "day by day" <note>Hebrew: יוֹם יוֹם</note> is said regarding those things which were done in the divine eternity before the creation of the world; and in Micah 5:1, the "goings forth" of Christ are said to be from of old, "from the days of eternity" <note>Hebrew: מִימֵי עוֹלָם</note>. See the notes there. Cf. Isaiah 43:13. Hence Christ is also called the **firstborn of all creation**, <note>original Greek: "πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως", Colossians 1:15</note> meaning he was begotten before all things, as Basil has it in *Homily 4 against Eunomius*. Just as Orpheus, according to Lactantius (Book 1, chapter 5), calls the true and great God the **first-begotten** <note>original Greek: "θεογόνον"</note>, because before Him nothing was begotten, but from Him all things were generated. Cf. John 1:1, 2, 3. c) **I have begotten you**, wherefore I will always defend you eternally and most powerfully against all tumultuous enemies. God does not say "I have adopted you," but "I have begotten you"; this signifies the communication of the same divine essence and nature, yet in a way that is utterly inexpressible. Just as in human affairs, a father begetting a son makes him a sharer in his own human nature. Cf. the word concerning the father in Genesis 4:18, 6:10, 10:8, 13. Therefore Christ is and is called the **image of the invisible God** <note>original Greek: "εἰκὼν τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου", Colossians 1:15</note>, the **radiance of His glory and the exact representation of His being** <note>original Greek: "ἀπαύגασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτὴר τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ", Hebrews 1:3</note>. Furthermore, Raymundus Martini argues acutely in *The Dagger of Faith* <note>original: "Pug. fid." p. 526</note>: He does not say, "long ago I begot you," for then this generation would seem to have entirely passed and ceased; nor does He say, "today I beget you," for then it would seem to have newly begun. Most fittingly, therefore, He said, "today I have begotten you," to give it to be understood by "today" that this generation never passed nor ceased, and by "I have begotten," that it never started or newly commenced. Briefly, from the *Lexicon of the Councils* (p. 307): To him of whom it is said by God, "Today I have begotten you," his is an eternal proceeding from God. The Jews indeed object against this substantial generation using Deuteronomy 32:18, but there (1) it is not a "Father" but a "Rock" who is said to have begotten, and (2) he did not beget one person, but the whole people, whom he had taken into the kingdom of grace. Christ is essentially holy (Ephesians 1:4, 4:47, Daniel 9:24), just and innocent (Isaiah 53:9, 1 Peter 1:13, 19, Jeremiah 23:6), undefiled (Psalm 45:8), and separated from sinners (Hebrews 7:26), as the Jews also admit elsewhere.

v. 8. d) **Ask of me**, therefore; just request from me, in your capacity as man, whatever pertains to or is required for the majesty of your kingdom. See this performed in John 17:1ff. e) **And I will give to you** as a man, but in the unity of the person with the **Word** <note>Greek: "Λόγῳ"</note>, and as one exalted to my right hand in the heavens after your death. Psalm 110:1; cf. Psalm 21:3, Daniel 7:14, Matthew 28:18, John 5:22, 27. f) **not only the Jews and Israelites**, but also the Gentiles (Isaiah 49:6), who above in verse 1 were rebels, and under the Old Testament were "aliens from the commonwealth of Israel" (Ephesians 2:11, 12). g) **your heritage**, Psalm 33:12; cf. Psalm 16:5, 6, Psalm 47:5, Isaiah 53:12. For to no one but you, my Son, does that right of inheritance and universal dominion belong. See Psalm 82:8, Matthew 21:38, Hebrews 1:2. h) **and your possession**, Leviticus 14:34, Numbers 34:5, which no one will be able to snatch from you. John 10:28–30, Isaiah 45:23, Philippians 2:9ff. i) **the ends of the earth**, that is, the universal orb of the lands. Cf. Psalm 19:5, Psalm 22:28, Psalm 72:8, Isaiah 45:22, 52:10, Micah 5:3, Zechariah 9:10; and regarding the fulfillment after the seventh trumpet, Revelation 11:15.

v. 9. k) **You shall break them**; and thus the Targum: "you shall shatter them," meaning the rebels and enemies of verses 1 and 2, if they do not obey and submit to your kingdom, by the power handed to you as Judge; from the root *ra’a’* <note>Hebrew: רָעַע</note> (Proverbs 11:15, 25:19, Daniel 2:40). But the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic translate "You shall rule/shepherd them," from the root *ra’ah* <note>Hebrew: רָעָה</note>, as in Micah 5:3, 5. Hence Revelation 2:27, 12:5, 19:15. l) **a rod of iron** or "an iron scepter." Whether you understand this as a pastoral staff (as in Micah 7:14, Psalm 23:4) or a royal one, which we call a scepter (as in Psalm 45:7), it is prepared for the striking down of adversaries (Numbers 24:17, Isaiah 9:3, 14:5, 6, 30:31). The added name of the material—not gold, as in Esther 5:8, but iron, as the hardest metal (Daniel 2:40)—indicates a scepter of power (Psalm 110:2). This is "not a mortal instrument" <note>Greek: "ὄργανον οὐ θνητόν"</note> (Isaiah 11:4), but the "spirit of his lips" or the "sword of his mouth" (2 Thessalonians 2:8), that is, the word proceeding from his mouth (Revelation 1:16). Just as in the Gospel it is powerful for the salvation of everyone who believes (Romans 1:16), so in the final decree against the stubborn and the enemies, it is also terrible, and "sharper than any two-edged sword" (Hebrews 4:12, Revelation 19:15) for the destruction of all adversaries (2 Corinthians 10:4). Cf. Jeremiah 23:29, and for example John 18:6, Acts 9:4, 5. m) **like a potter’s vessel**, which is most easily broken and cannot be repaired. Isaiah 30:14, Jeremiah 19:10, 11. n) **you shall crush and scatter them** as if into fragments. Cf. Judges 7:19, Jeremiah 13:14, 48:12, 51:20ff, Psalm 137:9. This, as far as it concerns the Jews, was abundantly fulfilled through the destruction first by Titus, and then by Hadrian. For the fates of the remaining Antichristians, consult Church history and the Holy Apocalypse.

7. v. 7.) **I will tell** <note>Hebrew: אַסַּפְּרָה</note> therefore (says the King Messiah in verse 6, hence the Syriac version in the third person: "He shall be honored by my decree." Cf. verse 1 and 6). This refers to the undertaking of the prophetic office, both by himself and through my servants, exactly and as if by count, and with all boldness of speech (Acts 4:29), I announce to men the counsel of God concerning my office and kingdom and their salvation. Luke 7:30, John 1:18, Acts 20:27, Ephesians 1:11. Cf. Psalm 9, 2. 15, 22, 23, 40, 6. 10, 118, 17. s) **as a decree**, according to the prescription of the Father; I will say and do nothing of myself, but everything according to His mandate, comparing John 8:28, 12:49, 14:10. Equal to the Father (John 5:18, 23; 10:30, 33, Philippians 2:6) and altogether exceptionally beloved (Matthew 3:17, 17:5, 2 Peter 1:17, John 1:18). y) **you are**, whom I have installed as King (verse 6) and whom those rebels refuse to endure (verse 3). <summary>This page provides a dense theological and linguistic commentary on Psalm 2:7-9, interpreting the "Today" of the divine decree as an eternal, non-temporal generation of the Messiah. It contrasts the Messiah's role as a shepherd for the faithful with his role as a judge who shatters rebels with an "iron rod."</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the theological declaration of the Messiah’s sonship in the previous verses to a direct exhortation for earthly rulers. # PSALM 2 & 3

<sig>א</sig>

---

<margin>
v. 10. q) **Now** therefore. <note>original: "Nunc itaque"</note> See Ecclesiasticus 28:21. This is while the time of grace and the opportunity for pardon still remain, as in Psalm 95:7 and Galatians 6:10. Because all these things are arranged as stated, you must either yield and repent, or perish. This is a fatherly exhortation from David, or rather from the Holy Spirit (who is distinct from the Father and Son in verses 11 and 12). God does not desire the death of a sinner, but rather that they turn and live, as seen in Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11, and 2 Peter 3:9. Thus, Paul commands prayers for such kings and magistrates in 1 Timothy 2:2, 4. Compare also Peter’s exhortation in Acts 3:17, 19. r) O **Kings**, who with insane minds rose up with your nations against Christ in verse 2. q) Act **prudently**, and not according to your blind reason or ignorance, as in Psalm 14:2 and 94:8. For it is foolish to resist the one whose authority you cannot escape, and to fight back when eternal salvation is offered to you. The Septuagint and Vulgate translate this as **Understand** <note>original: "Intelligite"</note> these things spoken above. See Deuteronomy 3:29. r) **Be instructed** or **be corrected** through true and serious repentance, established according to the Word of God in Jeremiah 6:8. The Targum <note>an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> says **receive correction**; receive it verbally now through these words, so that you do not have to experience it physically, like a wicked slave who is only corrected by lashes, as in Proverbs 29:19 and Ezekiel 23:48. o) **Be disciplined** <note>original Greek: "παιδευθητε"</note> as in Titus 2:12. This refers back to verse 3, where the wicked said they would break the chains; here, they are told to accept the discipline of the divine word and the Gospel of Christ. s) **You Judges** and princes from verse 2. **Of the earth** or of the whole world. Such were the ancient Carthaginian **Suffetes**, <term>Suffetes: Carthaginian magistrates whose title is derived from the Hebrew word "shofetim" (judges).</term>
</margin>

v. 10. q) **Now** treat these matters. The Septuagint and Vulgate: *Be instructed*, specifically in true divine worship. See Psalm 119:2, Deuteronomy 28:47, Malachi 3:14, 18. n) Serve *Jehovah*, your Lord, whom you rose against in verse 2, though he is the God of gods and Lord of lords (Deuteronomy 10:17), to whom alone religious worship is due (Matthew 4:10). x) with holy fear and filial reverence, lest you offend him further; such fear is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7). y) and sensing how good and kind the Lord is (Psalm 34:9), rejoice! See Isaiah 9:2, Luke 2:10, Romans 14:17. z) with trembling (r) (Psalm 48:7) arising from the consideration of your own unworthiness and the supreme grace and salvation which God has granted you in Christ (Colossians 1:12). Geier notes: The joy of the spirit or faith is not overturned this way; rather, a bridle is adapted for the previous fury and tumult of verse 1, so that these true subjects of the Messiah tremble with pure awe whenever they see the temptations of their former rebellion sprouting again. Compare Philippians 2:12, which coincides with this passage.

v. 12. a) *Kiss*, namely with the kiss of reconciliation (Genesis 45:15), subjection (Genesis 41:40), and love (1 Samuel 10:1), or indeed religious worship (1 Kings 19:18, Hosea 13:2). b) *The Son*, meaning the Messiah from verse 2, whom Jehovah called His King and Son in verses 6 and 7, as your Savior and intercessor (Isaiah 53:11). Abraham ibn Ezra and the Syriac version correctly explain it this way with us. Kimchi fluctuates; however, the Targum, Septuagint, and Vulgate incorrectly have *Accept* or *Grasp discipline*. This specific word for *Son* <note>original: "Bar"</note> is rarer in Hebrew but more frequent in Aramaic and Syriac. See Proverbs 31:2, Daniel 3:25. c) lest he finally become angry in just vengeance. d) and you perish in soul and body (Matthew 10:28). e) in the way which you, as rebels against Jehovah and Christ, impiously entered. f) and you perish from the righteous way. The Syriac: *and you perish from his way*. g) because—the Targum and Syriac agree. h) it will kindle (Jeremiah 4:4) like an inextinguishable fire forever (Matthew 3:12). i) briefly, and sooner than you expect (Psalm 81:15). k) his wrath, like the smoke of the Judge of all (Psalm 110:5). He does not allow the riches of his goodness and patience to be despised with impunity (Romans 2:4). l) truly blessed are all, and it shall be eternally well with them. m) the Syriac: *who trust in him*. The Targum: *who hope in His Word*. Properly: those who have their refuge and retreat in Him, namely the Son of God, of whom this entire verse speaks. See Psalm 36:8, Isaiah 30:18, Romans 9:33. Furthermore, we add here what the Jews note in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>an ancient homiletic commentary on the Psalms</note>; although they wrongly apply it to the people of Israel, it truly belongs to Christ according to the Scriptures. They say, by way of a parable: If a King is angry with his subjects, and they go and plead with the King's son to reconcile the King to them, and he does so, then when they come to the King to sing a hymn of thanks, the King says: "Are you singing to me? Go and give thanks also to my son; for if it were not for him, I would have destroyed the whole province."

**Ps. III.** v. 1. m) *A Psalm*. A song for the use of the whole Church, to be sung then and now. The root in the simple form <note>the Hebrew 'Kal' stem</note> means to *prune* or *cut off* (Leviticus 25:3). In the intensive form <note>'Piel'</note> it means to *sing* or *play an instrument*, where the melody is "cut" into specific measures and numbers. Kimchi: They are called psalms not when they were written, but when they were sung in the Sanctuary. n) *By David* or *inspired for David*. o) when he fled. See 2 Samuel 15:14. We establish now that these prayers were not offered on the Mount of Olives, as Lightfoot thought, but after midnight or early in the morning when he received news of Ahithophel’s dangerous counsel, which the Lord had frustrated. p) from the face of, i.e., because of or out of fear of him. q) regarding whom see 2 Samuel 15. r) his son. This increases and exaggerates the calamity which God had predicted for him in 2 Samuel 12:11. Thus, this psalm is entirely about David and the afflictions prepared for him by his son’s arrogance. Yet, as Gürtler says, David here foreshadows Christ, and Absalom foreshadows the Jews or the Antichrist, or according to Arnobius, Judas the traitor. Schmidius rightly states these psalms are common to all the pious; for they are the prayers of a person surrounded by enemies, yet 2) trusting in God and 3) secure under His shield. Briefly, according to Geier, David presents: I. the multitude and cruelty of enemies (v. 2-3), II. God’s protection (v. 4-7), III. a prayer (v. 8-9).

v. 2. s) An address to God. t) How! or To what extent! It is used for emphasis, as in Psalm 8:2. u) they have multiplied! See 2 Samuel 15:12. x) my foes, pressing me from all sides. y) how many rise up against me!

v. 3. z) Many say. See Psalm 42:4.

# Psalms 3 and 4: Pages 3 and 4

<margin>
Similar to 2 Samuel 15:30. Lamentations 2:10. Compare also Psalm 9:14, Psalm 27:6, Psalm 83:3, Psalm 110:7.
**m)** Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, and others: *With my voice* <note>original: "Voce mea"</note>. The Hebrew preposition *be* <note>original: "ב"</note> is understood here, as in Psalm 2:18 and Genesis 39:14. Likewise Psalm 142:2. But Gussetius <note>a noted Hebrew grammarian</note> disagrees.

### Psalm IV.

Page 752. I sounded my clamor or my voice to the Lord.
</margin>

<margin>
**a)** *my soul*: Psalm 35:3, Isaiah 51:23; compare Psalm 69:21. **b)** Not, or so to speak, *nullity*; no salvation, absolutely no help. Genesis 20:11, Lamentations 2:30. **c)** Just as the Hebrew letter *He* added to the end of a word usually intensifies it, here—following the preceding negative—it denies all help or salvation to David. See Psalm 44:27, 63:8, 80:3, 102:1, and notes on Jonah 2:10 and 2 Samuel 12:3. **d)** *for him*: specifically, for David. The Syriac and Ethiopic versions, to avoid the change of gender and person, translate: "there is no salvation for thee (the soul) in thy God." Compare notes on Psalm 1:6, 7. **e)** *in God*: but because of his heavy sins, especially adultery and the murder of Uriah, he is now considered deserted and condemned by God. See the atrocious curses of Shimei against David in 2 Samuel 16:7, 8, and compare Psalm 10:11, 71:10-11, and 36:7. **f)** *Selah*: truly it is so. See verses 5 and 9, and the note on Habakkuk 3:3, 9.

**Verse 4. g)** *But You, O Jehovah*: whom he had already addressed in faith in verse 2. **h)** You are a *shield and buckler*: surrounding and protecting both soul and body from every side. The root *ganan* <note>original: "גננ"</note> means to hedge in or besiege. See Psalm 7:11, 18:3, 28:7, and 84:10, 12; also Genesis 15:1, Deuteronomy 33:29. **i)** *for me* or *around me*. Psalm 139:11, see note on Genesis 7:16. **Although** You were most gravely offended by my sins and separated from me (2 Samuel 11:27, Isaiah 59:2), yet because You did not only seek me out when I was perishing (Psalm 119:176, 2 Samuel 12:1), but also received me back into grace when I repented and desired to be cleansed in the blood of Christ (Psalm 51:8, 9; 2 Samuel 12:13, Ezekiel 18:21, Zechariah 7:3, James 4:8), I do not despair of Your goodness as my enemies wish; rather, I trust most humbly in You. See 2 Samuel 16:10. **k)** *my glory*: You are my glory even in the extreme disgrace I now suffer. Psalm 62:8, like my light and my salvation in Psalm 27:1. See Jeremiah 9:23. **l)** *and the lifter up of my head*: so that with my face and spirit restored, I may trust and be comforted, even though I am currently depressed by sadness and greatly humbled.

<term>π) answer me</term>: *my protector* in verse 4. <term>ρ) O God</term>: *I will cry*. The Targum says "I will pray." Psalm 4:4. <term>σ) my righteousness</term>: *for He heard me*. Others read this in the future tense. The Targum says "and He will accept my prayer." Geierus says: What God has done before, the psalmist hopes He will do again. Compare Psalm 10:17, 120:1, Isaiah 41:17. **q)** *from Zion*, His holy hill (Psalm 48:2), where the Ark and the mercy seat were located—a type of Christ toward which the praying people looked. Psalm 99:9, 1 Kings 8:48, Daniel 6:11, Romans 3:25. Compare note on Psalm 2:6. **r)** *Truly!* as in verse 3. Therefore, even if David confessed he was driven from the holy hill, he did not despair that God, who dwells there, would hear him. **s)** *I indeed*, although cast into flight, poorly fortified, and helped by few! See verse 3. In such great danger and the noise of enemies (2 Samuel 17:1, 2), I lay down alone. Genesis 28:11. **t)** *and I slept securely*. Psalm 4:9, Proverbs 3:24. See Psalm 127:2, Acts 12:6, 7. Here is the great emphatic division of this verse. **x)** *indeed, I even awoke safe and unharmed*. Psalm 17:15, Proverbs 6:22. This does not happen to everyone with equal success. See 1 Samuel 26:7–15. **y)** Because the Lord is my protector and shield, as in verse 4. **z)** *He sustains and supports me*, so that I do not succumb and perish. Psalm 37:17, 54:6. See 2 Samuel 17:14. Furthermore, based especially on this verse, Augustine, Rupertus, Tilius, and others conclude that this entire psalm should be understood as referring to Christ; it seems to sound more consistent with the passion and resurrection of the Lord than with the history of David’s flight from Absalom. This is especially because "lying down and sleeping" is elsewhere used for death (Psalm 41:9, Jeremiah 51:39, 57, Job 14:11-13), while "awakening" refers to the resurrection (Psalm 17:15, Jeremiah 31:26, compare Psalm 16:10). But for us, it is enough that these things are typically figured here in the person of David as a shadow of Christ. See note on verse 1.

**Verse 7. a)** *Therefore I will not fear*. Geierus says he perseveres in the wonderful efficacy of prayer, which not everyone experiences indiscriminately. See Psalm 27:1. **b)** *from myriads of people*. Numbers 10:36, Deuteronomy 33:17. See 2 Samuel 15:13, and 17:11, 12. **c)** *who from every side*. Job 18:11, 19:12. **d)** once they have pitched their camp, as in Isaiah 22:7, Psalm 49:15. Or transitively: "which myriads my enemies have placed all around me," as in Psalm 140:6. **e)** *against me*. See Jeremiah 50:29 and verse 2 above. **Verse 8. f)** *Arise now, O Lord!* You who seem to overlook or sleep through their insolence. See Psalm 7:7, 44:24, 26, 68:2. **g)** *save and rescue me* from these troubles. Psalm 7:2, 34:7. This looks back to the opposition of his faith in verse 3. **h)** *My God*. This possessive suffix is likewise animated by faith. Thus Psalm 5:3, 7:2, 84:4. See note on Habakkuk 1:12. **i)** *for as You have struck until now, so You will continue to strike* to their utter confusion and disgrace. Job 16:10. **k)** *all my enemies*. The Vulgate says "those opposing me." Psalm 6:11, 17:9. See also 1 Samuel 5:20. **l)** *on the cheekbone*, or *the cheekbone*. (The verb sometimes takes two accusatives, as in Deuteronomy 19:11, Psalm 51:15, etc.) See 1 Kings 22:24, Micah 4:14, 2 Chronicles 18:23. The Septuagint and Vulgate incorrectly translate this as "without cause." **m)** *teeth*. Psalm 57:5, 58:7, Micah 3:5. With these, they seemed ready to grind me like fierce beasts. Psalm 27:2. **n)** See Psalm 1:1. **o)** *You have broken* (Psalm 74:13) and restrained them so that they retreated to their own loss and shame. Psalm 6:11. See Job 4:10, 39:17. **Verse 9. p)** *To the Lord belongs this and every salvation!* Thus he closes with a doxology <note>a short hymn of praise</note> and a concluding summary, attributing all salvation and blessing over himself and the people of God to Him, in opposition to the claim in verse 3. **q)** This denotes the Author, fountain, and origin of this salvation, as in Jonah 2:10. See Psalm 42:6, 12, 43:5, 74:12, Isaiah 43:11, 45:21, Proverbs 21:31, 2 Chronicles 20:17, Revelation 7:10, 19:1. **r)** *upon Your people Israel* (Psalm 28:9, 85:3), who are uniquely set apart for You (Psalm 147:19, 20) and dedicated to You (Isaiah 64:8, Psalm 79:13). **r)** *Your blessing*: that is, let it be and remain, as in Genesis 27:13, Psalm 129:8; or "let it come," as in Proverbs 24:25. Thus Tarnovius and Geierus interpret it as a wish. This refers not only to temporal blessing (Deuteronomy 28:2), but especially to celestial and spiritual blessing in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 1:3), which was promised to Abraham (Galatians 3:14). See Genesis 24:35, Psalm 29:11. **s)** *it is so, so let it be!* Verses 3, 5; Habakkuk 3:3, 9.

**Psalm IV. Verse 1. t)** *To the Prefect of sacred music*. 1 Chronicles 15:21, 2 Chronicles 2:1, 34:12. See the Preface to this book, section 6, and the note on Habakkuk 3:19. The Septuagint (and with them the Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopic) wrongly translate this as "to the end," as if it were the same as the word in Psalm 44:24. But they are often less accurate in translating the Psalter; let it suffice to mention this once here. **u)** *on stringed instruments* (with instruments that were played with the fingers and touched). Psalm 6:1, Isaiah 38:20, Habakkuk 3:19. **x)** See Psalm 3:1. **y)** Ibid. Geierus notes here that it is not poorly conjectured that this psalm has the same theme as the third: namely, against the persecution of Absalom and the rebellious courtiers. So say Messius, Kimchi, Musculus, etc. Bochius, however, places it after the defeat of Absalom. But more probably, according to Lightfoot’s *Chronology of the Old Testament* (p. 67), David is reproaching the people for Sheba’s rebellion (2 Samuel 20) because they had despised him and his kingdom, attending vainly first to Absalom’s and now to Sheba’s reign; he warns Israel and Judah not to sin in their anger (2 Samuel 19:43). Dr. Maius nicely explained the argument and parts of this psalm in this way in his *Economy of the Old Testament* (p. 794). But Schmidius, being more concerned with the use than the occasion of this psalm, says in the introduction...

**Psalm III, Verse 3.** The word *salvation* <note>original: "ישועתה"</note> with the added mark <term>Pasek</term> 6. 9. 14. contrary to the Masorah of Erfurt. See notes on Psalm 12:3, 5. **2.** Truly (because they are affected by the <term>Silluk</term> accent, the <term>Munach</term> is substituted, but not affected) against the usual rule. **Verse 5.** *His holiness* <note>original: "קדשו"</note> thus in i. and fu. s. And *His holiness* 6. 8. 9. 10. 11. 12–18. 20. 21. 22. 23. Such a series of accents occurs in Psalm 46:8, 12 and 56:3. 3. 7. 24 agree with us. See a similar construction in Psalm 52:8, 61:5, etc. **Verse 6.** *And I slept* <note>original: "ואישנה"</note> thus s. 1. 3. and s. 5. These are more regular because the <term>Silluk</term> is not affected. However, see a similar sequence to ours in Psalm 5, 1, 14; Psalm 140:2. **Verse 7.** *From myriads* <note>original: "מרבבות"</note>. Correctly through <term>Munach</term> 2. 3. 5. and Berlin; also 24. Furthermore, for the <term>Sheva</term> vowel, 1. 22. 23. have a <term>Chateph Patach</term>. **Verse 8.** *Cheek* <note>original: "לחי"</note>. Without <term>Pasek</term> f. 7. 8. 11. 15. And thus very often the codices vary in placing or omitting the <term>Pasek</term> distinction; it should suffice to note this once or twice. **Verse 9.** *Selah* <note>original: "סלה"</note>. Thus with a <term>Dagesh</term> <note>a dot in the letter</note> 1. 2. 5. 17. 18. 24. and Berlin. The others omit it.

<column-break/>

**Psalm IV, Verse 1.** *With stringed instruments* <note>original: "בנגינות"</note>. Through the accent <term>Rebia Geresh</term> 14. and Berlin, perhaps by analogy, because it is the ordinary sub-distinctive of <term>Silluk</term>. But we have observed that the initial verses of the Psalms and chapters, and even middle ones (see note on Psalm 119:4), if they consist of only one prepositional phrase and need no other accent than <term>Silluk</term> with its sub-distinctives, almost all codices use a simple <term>Rebia</term> instead of a <term>Rebia Geresh</term>, except for two specific places—Psalm 40:1 and Psalm 70:1—where the printed Masorah specifically requires <term>Rebia Geresh</term> on the word "To the Chief Musician." Therefore, according to this Masorah, <term>Rebia Geresh</term> cannot stand at the beginning of the following Psalms: 13, 19, 21, 31, 41, 42, 51, 52, 64, and 140. In those cases, the codices correctly place a naked <term>Rebia</term>. There remain, however, Psalms 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 20, 21, 25, 39, 53, 54, 55, 58, 62, 65, 67, 68, 77, 89, and 92, where the cited Masorah cannot be adapted such that a naked <term>Rebia</term> is necessary, as in the more recent Psalms; yet in musical chanting, it holds that a naked <term>Rebia</term> could be admitted in such a case: that it *should* be admitted is suggested by the consensus of most (though not always all) codices.

# THE BIBLE: PSALM 4:4

Regarding the headings: These are the prayers, he says, of a righteous man against those who despise him in his affliction (v. 2), whom he encourages toward repentance and better things (v. 3–6). III. Against those who refuse, he trusts nevertheless that he will be secure in God (v. 7–9). The title, however, was observed quite artfully here by some who saw in it: I. Christ's complaint about the stubbornness of the Jews (v. 2, 3). II. The admonition of the Holy Spirit (v. 4, 5). III. The warning of a certain Apostle (v. 6, and following); but compare the notes on Psalm 3:1.

**Verse 2. a)** *In my crying out*, that is: *While I cry*. (v. 4. Psalm 50:15; Psalm 69:4; Psalm 141:1). The Targum <note>an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Bible</note> reads: *in the time of my prayer.* (Compare Exodus 14:15; 1 Samuel 1:13, 17). **a)** *answer me* or *hear me*. (Psalm 3:5; 1 Kings 18:37). Targum: *receive from me.* Contrary to the grammar, the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation</note> and the Vulgate <note>the Latin translation</note> etc., use the past tense: *he heard me.* See the note on verse 1. **b)** *God of my righteousness*, that is: You who give me righteousness or justify me (Isaiah 53:11; Jeremiah 23:6) and who vindicate and protect my just cause (Romans 8:33, 34; compare Psalm 24:5; Psalm 59:11; Psalm 144:2; also Psalm 18:21, 25). **c)** Targum: *in the time of distress, when I was reduced to desperate straits.* For the Hebrew word signifies both "narrow" (Numbers 22:26; Isaiah 49:10) and "distress," as well as "distressor" or "enemy." See Psalm 3:2 and Psalm 18:7. **d)** *you have made relief* or *latitude for me.* (Genesis 26:22; Psalm 18:20; Psalm 25:17; Proverbs 18:6). **e)** and so now *have mercy on me.* (Psalm 6:3; Psalm 51:3; Deuteronomy 7:2). He emphasizes God's grace and his own misery, not his own works or merit.

---

<margin>
**f)** Targum: *and receive my prayer* or *my supplication* (Psalm 54:4), namely, proceeding from a sincere soul and without deceit (Psalm 17:1ff; Psalm 32:2; Psalm 66:18, 19; John 9:31; 1 John 3:19–22).

**g)** Septuagint and Vulgate: *Sons of men.* Ethiopic: *Children of the offspring of the mother of the living*, that is, men of whatever rank or dignity, from Genesis 3:20; just as the Hebrews and Arabs elsewhere call men "sons of Adam." See the note on Isaiah 56:2. Others, however, through paraphrase, understand "Great men and princes," based on the opposition often made between these and the "sons of Adam" (Psalm 49:3; Psalm 62:10; compare Isaiah 2:9). **h)** *how long?* as if to say: will you not finally cease to act this way? (Compare Psalm 74:9; Psalm 79:5). **i)** *my glory, my honor.* (Psalm 7:6). **k)** *will it be in ignominy?* will it be exposed to your reproaches and shames? (Isaiah 30:3). From this phrase, the Septuagint made not only two words but two propositions, and from the preceding "my glory," they made "heavy-hearted" through a faulty reading: *how long are you heavy-hearted? why do you love...* etc. The Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopic follow them in this. See note on verse 1. **l)** *and you love* (Zechariah 8:17) **m)** *vanity?* (Psalm 2:1) **n)** *how long will you seek, will you search out against me?* (Compare Psalm 34:15; Zephaniah 2:3). **o)** *a lie* (Psalm 5:7; Psalm 62:5; Ephesians 28:15). **p)** see Psalm 5:3; Habakkuk 3:3.

**q)** *Indeed*, or *Rather recognize.* (Psalm 9:21; Psalm 46:11. Compare the prefix *van* in Isaiah 22:2; Habakkuk 1:8). **r)** Targum and Syriac: *that he has set apart*; Septuagint and Vulgate: *he has made wonderful*, that is, he has led in wondrous ways through prosperity and adversity. Truly, this word with a third <unclear>aleph</unclear> in the *Hiphil* <term>Hiphil: a Hebrew verb form indicating causative action</term> means "he made wonderful" (Isaiah 28:29); while with a third *He* it means "he separated, made excellent, distinguished" (see Exodus 8:18, 9:4, 33:16). As these forms agree, so also do their meanings, and they are sometimes interchanged. See Psalm 17:7.
</margin>

<margin>
**f)** 17:7; compare Psalm 31:22. **s)** Vulgate: *his holy one.* Or *his saint*; literally: *gracious to him.* Or according to Gellius (IX. c. 12), *Gracious* is that which applies grace, and that which admits it; thus חסיד <note>original: "Chesed"</note>, *Grace*, is he whom God embraces with grace and mercy.
</margin>

...God embraces with His mercy in Christ, and cherishes and loves him as His own client or beneficiary: and he who in turn, from the acknowledgment of the most abundant divine grace, presents himself as pious and holy toward God, and gracious and kind toward others (see Psalm 12:2; Psalm 18:26; Psalm 32:6; Psalm 132:9; regarding Christ Psalm 16:10; and concerning God Psalm 145:17; Jeremiah 3:12). The particle *לוֹ* <note>original: "lo" - for him/himself</note> we connect simply with the preceding, as others do by implying a relative pronoun, as in Psalm 18:6; Psalm 106:44. Others construct it with the verb, as if to say "he set apart for himself," but this goes against the accents. **s)** Therefore the same of the Lord, etc. (Compare John 5:14, 15). **u)** verse 2; Psalm 3:5. **Verse 5. x)** Or *Be moved.* Targum: *Tremble before him.* Thus also Aben Ezra, Kimchi, etc., regarding the fear of God (compare Psalm 77:19; Psalm 99:1; Isaiah 64:1). But the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic read: *Be angry*, and hence the Apostle in Ephesians 4:26. Which, as Bellarmine teaches in this place, means they should burn with a certain holy anger and resist evil desires, and in that way avoid sin. The imperative is conditional, standing for a potential future, as in Psalm 76:12; as if to say: *If you are angry, you must take care again and again lest you sin*; because the anger of man, unless it arises from a higher and divine principle, does not work the righteousness of God (James 1:20). If, therefore, it pleases you to be angry, let each be angry at his own sins (Lamentations 3:39) so as not to serve them as slaves (Romans 6:11, 12). The Hebrew verb in general, as Schmidt translates, is *to be moved* in body or soul, for example from one's place (2 Samuel 7:10; Psalm 18:8), or by sadness of soul, or by fear and dread (Exodus 15:14; Deuteronomy 2:25; 2 Samuel 18:33; Jeremiah 33:9; Joel 2:1), or by anger (Isaiah 28:21; Proverbs 29:9). **y)** This is a greater warning: he advises them not to sin while carried away by anger; but to piously meditate on the wondrous ways of God in their beds, at night, when the mind is usually more settled, and learn to sacrifice to God sacrifices of righteousness, and to trust. See note on verse 1. **z)** This, I say, speak or think within your mind (compare Psalm 10:6, 11, 13; Isaiah 14:1, 35:25; Deuteronomy 7:17; Matthew 24:48, etc.). Targum: *Say your prayer with your mouth, and your petition in your heart.* **a)** Compare 2 Kings 6:12; Hosea 7:14; Micah 2:1; Ecclesiastes 10:20. Targum: *and pray upon your bed.* Syriac: *say in your hearts, and meditate upon your beds.* **b)** *Be silent*, rest from that commotion and your tumultuous anger (compare Psalm 35:15; Psalm 37:7; Psalm 62:6; 1 Samuel 14:9; Jeremiah 47:6; Lamentations 2:18). Targum: *and remember the day of death.* **c)** verse 3; Habakkuk 2:3. **Verse 6. d)** *Sacrifice the sacrifices of righteousness* (Psalm 51:21; Deuteronomy 33:19); as if to say: what I said about ceasing from sin and anger in verse 5, you must necessarily do, unless you wish to be frustrated and unjust in all your worship and faith before God. For it is not enough to bring sacrifices, which perhaps you do; but they must be offered in such a way that they do not leave you alienated from righteousness, which God promised in Christ (Jeremiah 23:6; Genesis 15:6) and from the desire and fruit of it (Matthew 5:6; John 2:29). Sacrifice, therefore, the sacrifices of righteousness with a contrite and repentant heart (Psalm 51:19) and with humble and grateful faith (Psalm 50:14, 23), so that you may present yourselves as a living sacrifice to God, and your members as weapons of righteousness (Romans 6:13, 12:1); and thus with full confidence, trust in the Lord, even in your prayers (Psalm 41:2; compare Isaiah 56:7). Otherwise, if you continue as before, even the greatest apparatus of sacrifices will profit you nothing. (Compare 1 Samuel 15:22; Jeremiah 6:20; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21, 22; Micah 6:6ff; Psalm 50:8–13). **e)** Psalm 27:3; Psalm 62:9; Isaiah 12:2; Proverbs 28:1. **Verse 7. f)** Or: *But many are saying*, speaking insolently. As if to say: Truly, why do I exhort? For many may say, etc. For it is not the vow of the faithful and pious that follows here, as Geier and others feel (as if to say: "Would that someone would show us good, so that David might be restored to his kingdom!" compare Numbers 11:29; 2 Samuel 15:4, 23:15); rather, these are the words of the recalcitrant and the impious (compare v. 3; see Psalm 3:3; Jeremiah 17:15; and the note above on v. 1). **g)** *Who!* A haughty and stubborn contention, such as in Job 9:34 (compare Exodus 5:2; 1 Samuel 25:10). **h)** *will show us* or *cause us to see and experience* good, whether ecclesiastical, political, or economic. (Compare Psalm 37:13; Psalm 34:13; Psalm 85:8; Ecclesiastes 2:1, 3:13; and Jeremiah 5:12, 14:13). **i)** Or: *Lift up then over us.* (From the root *nasa* <note>original: "נשׂא"</note>; compare Numbers 5:26). The sibilant and light breath are changed into something harsher due to the vehemence of emotion and speech, as in Psalm 60:4; Job 4:2; Genesis 23:6; Jeremiah 19:11. And this is David's sigh opposed to the distrust and negation of those who refuse. **k)** *the light of his countenance, O Lord!* that is, look upon us with a gracious and kind face in Christ. (Compare Psalm 31:17; Psalm 89:16; Job 29:24). For all our salvation hangs upon the grace of the Son of God (Numbers 6:25; Psalm 67:2; Psalm 80:4; Psalm 3:12), who from ages past interceded with the Father and pledged for us, and according to the laws of that pledge, provided us with eternal redemption and remission of sins through His blood. Without that grace of Christ, sinners would perish. **l)** *O Lord!* who alone can make us possessors of our vow (v. 9), and you will certainly do so (compare Psalm 50:15; 1 John 5:15). **Verse 8. m)** Or: *For you give joy*, or, *For you have put gladness in my heart.* (Compare Ecclesiastes 2:26, 5:19; John 16:22; Romans 14:17; Philippians 4:4). **n)** *Great joy compared to the time*; others, *from the time.* But we rightly prefer the former as more significant. See the comparative *Mem* <term>Mem: a Hebrew letter used here to indicate "more than"</term> in Psalm 19:11; Psalm 130:6, etc.; and a similar ellipsis of the adjective before the comparative *Mem* in Isaiah 41:24; Micah 7:4; Psalm 62:10; Job 11:17, 35:2; Ecclesiastes 9:7. The sense is: You have put greater gladness in my heart than that which my enemies have in the time of harvest, when their grain and wine have most abundantly increased. (Compare Song of Solomon 1:2; and regarding that harvest joy, Leviticus 23:40; Deuteronomy 16:15; Isaiah 9:3; Jeremiah 48:33; Joel 1:12; Luke 12:19).
