<meta>This page concludes the analysis of Psalm 4 and begins the commentary on Psalm 5. The translator continues to synthesize various ancient versions—specifically the Targum (Aramaic), the Syriac, the Septuagint (Greek), and the Vulgate (Latin)—to provide a comprehensive theological and grammatical understanding of the text. There is a strong emphasis on interpreting the Psalms as prophetic of the Church and its struggles against "Antichristian" forces.</meta>

<margin>
o) Correctly interpreted by the Targum <note>an ancient Aramaic paraphrase</note> and the Syriac version together with the Hebrew, as in "grain etc." from Joel 1:10. There is a relative pronoun to be understood here, as is very frequent in places like Exodus 4:13, Ezekiel 20:25, and Genesis 39:4 (compared with verses 6 and 8). However, because of the accents, that pronoun should be supplied before the verb in this manner: *more than the time of their harvest and their new wine, when these things were multiplied.* p) Psalm 3:2; compare Genesis 27:28 and Deuteronomy 7:13.
</margin>

->**In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for You, O LORD, alone make me dwell in safety.**<-

<margin>
q) That is to say: *Go in peace and under the protection of the Lord.* Compare Numbers 6:26, Psalm 29:11, Psalm 55:19, Isaiah 26:3, Romans 5:1, chapter 14:17, and Philippians 4:7.
r) That is to say: *entirely* <note>original Greek: ὁλοκλήρως, "wholly" or "completely"</note> (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Likewise safe and unharmed in both soul and body with all my belongings.
s) For this word and its relatives usually indicate an association or joining of many things, as Geierus correctly observes regarding Psalm 141:10. Compare that passage and Genesis 13:6.
t) Deuteronomy 33:17, 1 Kings 3:18, Psalm 33:15, etc. s) *I will lie down and sleep* Psalm 3:6; compare Job 5:24 and 11:19. s) *In Jehovah*, the Guardian and defender of Israel, Psalm 121:3 and following.
u) *alone.* Deuteronomy 32:12. This is used emphatically, as in Psalm 5:13, as if to say: *I credit this benefit to You alone—that I can dwell confidently, securely, and without fear in the midst of tribulations.* x) *You will place me in security*, or *You make me dwell safely.* Leviticus 26:5, Jeremiah 49:31, Hosea 2:20. y) Jeremiah 32:37, Hosea 11:11, Deuteronomy 12:10. The Syriac adds: *with a good conscience*; without which, clearly, that divine peace cannot exist in our soul.
</margin>

# Psalm 5:1
<margin>
Regarding the subject matter of this Psalm, Bohlius writes—and Maiane in *Ecclesiastical Economy* page 794 and following—though they leave it undecided. However, most feel that this refers primarily to Daniel.
</margin>

**1 For the leader, upon the Nechiloth; a Psalm of David.**
**2 Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my meditation.**
**3 Hearken to the voice of my cry, my King and my God, for to You I pray.**
**4 LORD, in the morning You hear my voice; in the morning I set my prayer before You and watch.**
**5 For You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not dwell with You.**
**6 The boastful shall not stand before Your eyes; You hate all workers of iniquity.**
**7 You destroy those who speak lies; the LORD abhors the man of blood and deceit.**
**8 But I, in the abundance of Your mercy, will come into Your house; I will bow toward Your holy temple in fear of You.**

<margin>
Psalm 5, v. 1. a) *To the music director.* See Psalm 4:1. a) *Upon Nechiloth*; which is perhaps a type of song, or more likely a kind of musical instrument, like the *Machalat* in Psalm 53:1 and the *Neginoth* in Psalm 4:1. The Targum translates this as "to the pipes" or "flutes" <note>original Aramaic: משינייתא</note>. Compare the *chalil* <note>flute</note> in Psalm 5:12. b) See Psalm 3:1. Furthermore, it is explicitly stated that this psalm was composed regarding the same rebellion of Sheba (about which see the note on Psalm 4:1).
</margin>

For according to Schmid, these are the prayers of a faithful man concerning the condition of the one praying. The Syriac inscription makes it its own: *This Psalm is prophetic, and a Prayer in the person of the Church; which would visit the house of the Lord in the morning.* Thus, in the mind of Gurtler, the Church asks to be guarded from the teacher who is both deceitful and cruel; so that it applies to the times of "Antichrist-like" figures, as well as pagan and anti-Christian Rome. Compare the note on Psalm 3:1. **v. 2.** c) *My words* (Proverbs 1:1), specifically those of a supplicant regarding the subject of this psalm. d) The Vulgate: *Perceive with your ears.* Psalm 17:1, Psalm 39:13. e) *Perceive*, as if to say: *know distinctly.* Isaiah 28:9; compare Psalm 94:7–8, Daniel 9:23, chapter 10:1, and Romans 8:27. f) *My meditation*, that is, the desires of my soul, my groans and sighs. (a) Psalm 39:4; compare the word in Isaiah 38:14 and the note on Psalm 2:1. **v. 3.** g) *Attend, I pray*, Psalm 10:17, Psalm 31:3, Isaiah 21:7. h) *To the voice of my cry.* (i) Vulgate: *of my prayer.* Compare the word in Psalm 18:7, Psalm 30:3. i) He addresses the Son of God, yet not without the Father and Holy Spirit. Compare verse 7, Psalm 2:6, Psalm 45:2, 6, 7, Psalm 44:5, Psalm 34:4, Isaiah 40:9–10, chapter 52:7. k) *For to You*, the Judge, the protector and avenger of the godly. Isaiah 47:4. l) *I will pray* as a supplicant for my cause. 2 Kings 19:20, Isaiah 44:17; compare the Intensive form <note>Piel</note>, *he judged*, in 1 Samuel 2:25, Ezekiel 16:52, and *Peliim*, "judges," in Exodus 21:22 and Job 31:11. **v. 4.** m) *Therefore, O LORD.* v. 2, Psalm 3:3. n) *In the morning* Psalm 30:6, Psalm 90:14, Psalm 143:8; as if to say: *do not delay in hearing.* o) *You hear my voice* Psalm 17:7, Psalm 28:2, Psalm 64:2. p) *For in the morning*, and as if it were the first thing of all. Psalm 88:14, Psalm 92:3. q) Syriac: *I will prepare myself.* That is, *I will arrange myself and my cause.* See Job 33:5, 13:18, 23:4. Or, *I will arrange my voice and prayers*, just as the wood of the altar and the pieces of the morning sacrifice were arranged. Genesis 22:9, Leviticus 1:7, 12, 6:5, compared with Job 32:14. The Septuagint and Vulgate: *I will stand before You.* The Ethiopic: *I will stand in Your presence.* r) *I will watch*, expecting a favorable judgment and help from You (Habakkuk 2:1, Micah 7:7, Lamentations 4:17). Compare Psalm 121:1, Isaiah 26:9. **v. 5.** s) *Because.* He gives the reason why he surely promises himself help from God, taken from God's own justice, for He cannot help but extremely hate and turn away from the wicked and the stubbornly evil. t) *Desiring wickedness*, as the wicked also desire. Malachi 2:17. u) The subject of the statement is transposed for emphasis and with greater assertion, instead of: *You are not a God, etc.* The Syriac makes two propositions: *Because You are God, and You do not desire wickedness.* Compare Deuteronomy 31:4, Psalm 21:5–6, Psalm 45:8, John 9:31. x) The Septuagint, Vulgate, and other versions: *the evil man shall not remain, dwell, or stay with You.* Compare Psalm 15:1, 61:5, Genesis 32:5, Isaiah 11:6, and a similar construction in Job 31:18. y) Vulgate: *the malignant.* Compare Psalm 101:4. **v. 6.** *They shall not stand* 1 Samuel 12:7. Ethiopic: *Neither shall they endure.* Compare Psalm 2:9. a) *The foolish and the insanely boastful.* Psalm 73:3 and 75:5, Ecclesiastes 2:2, Romans 1:22, 32. Compare also Luke 12:19. Targum: *scorners.* Arabic: *those who contradict Your commands.* b) Compare Habakkuk 1:13, Psalm 34:17. c) Hosea 9:15, Zechariah 8:17, Proverbs 6:16. d) Psalm 6:9, Psalm 31:3, Matthew 7:23, Isaiah 3:4, 8, 9. Targum: *workers of falsehood or lies.* Compare with Revelation 22:15. **v. 7.** e) *You will destroy*, as the Egyptians in Deuteronomy 11:4, and the anti-Christians in Psalm 21:11, Psalm 9:6. f) Proverbs 1:32, 1 Kings 11:11. f) Psalm 4:3, John 8:43, 44. g) Syriac and Arabic: *a man who pours out blood.* Targum: *one who pours out the blood of the righteous.* Psalm 26:9, Psalm 55:24, Psalm 59:3. Compare Genesis 4:10, Exodus 1:15, Psalm 18:49. h) *And of fraud*, a fraudulent man. Psalm 17:1, 43:1, Genesis 34:13, 2 Kings 9:23. The Midrash Tehillim <note>a rabbinic commentary</note> specifically compares this place to 2 Thessalonians 2:3, 8, Isaiah 11:4, and 57:20–21. i) *He abhors*, and turns away from in the extreme. Psalm 119:163, Deuteronomy 7:26, Amos 5:10. Compare Matthew 5:23 and following. k) *God the Father.* For he has addressed the Son in the 2nd person until now. See the note on verse 3 and Zechariah 3:2. Others think there is a similar change of person here as in Genesis 49:4. **v. 8.** l) *But as for me*; in opposition to verses 5–7. Compare 1 John 3:21. m) *In the multitude and greatness of Your grace*, or *through Your great mercy.* Psalm 69:14, 17, Romans 5:17, Ephesians 1:7. n) *I will enter Your house* Psalm 66:13. The Tabernacle is called this in 1 Samuel 1:24, 3:15. Spiritually, the Church is called this in 1 Timothy 3:15. o) *I will bow* or *prostrate myself.* Exodus 20:5, Deuteronomy 26:10, Psalm 138:2. p) That is: *toward Your holy palace.* Psalm 45:9, 16, Isaiah 13:22. Namely, the interior part of the Tabernacle (for the Temple was not yet built) where the Ark of the Lord was, 1 Samuel 3:3, Hebrews 9:3–4. No one was allowed to enter there except the High Priest once a year, Hebrews 9:7–8, and it foreshadowed the most sacred seat of God in the heavens. Compare Psalm 11:4, Psalm 27:4, Jonah 2:5, 8.

<meta>This page continues the detailed philological and theological commentary on the Psalms. It concludes the analysis of Psalm 5 (focusing on verses 9–13) and introduces the penitential Psalm 6. The translator draws on classical sources like Jerome and modern (for the time) commentators like Geier and Schmid to explain the Hebrew grammar and the spiritual application of the text.</meta>

<margin>
**q)** *in your fear* <note>original: "in timere tu"</note> Psalm 2:11. In the Arabic version: "feeling fear of you." This stands in opposition to his adversaries mentioned in verse 5 and following; compare Psalm 10:4, Psalm 14:1, Psalm 36:2, etc.

**verse 9. r)** The Petitioner cries: *O Lord!* <note>original: "Jehova!"</note> verse 4. Understand it as if saying "saying," <note>original: "לאמר"</note> as in Psalm 2:2, 3, and 12. **s)** *lead me*—specifically, lead one who is barely aware of the path and easily prone to wandering. Compare Psalm 23:3, Psalm 31:4; by Your counsel, Psalm 32:8, Psalm 73:24; and by Your Spirit, Psalm 143:10. **t)** *in his righteousness*, perhaps "in the way of his righteousness" (Proverbs 8:20, chapter 12:28). This refers to that righteousness by which You justify a sinner out of pure grace, and thereafter teach them to live righteously. See Psalm 59:28, Isaiah 53:11, Jeremiah 23:6, Romans 8:16, chapter 3:21, 1 Corinthians 1:30, Matthew 5:10, etc. **u)** *because of those who pant after me*, my ambushers and observers, who seek to cast me down headlong; this is the correct reading in the Septuagint <note>Greek translation</note>, Vulgate <note>Latin translation</note>, Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, etc. The Targum <note>Aramaic paraphrase</note> wrongly renders this "because of my praise." See Psalm 27:11, Psalm 54:7, Psalm 59:11, Psalm 92:12. **x)** *direct*—meaning to gaze upon, observe, or lie in wait (Jeremiah 5:26, Hosea 13:7). **x)** *direct*, make level; make the way smooth and free of obstacles before me. Psalm 45:2, 13; Proverbs 3:6, chapter 4:25. **y)** *your way*, namely the one prescribed for me in Your word. Psalm 25:4, Psalm 86:11. This is so that I may run that path with an unstumbling foot, lest my fall stir up joy in my enemies; or lest I myself, out of distress, choose a wide path that leads to destruction (Psalm 139:24, Matthew 7:13). There was not enough reason for the Septuagint, Vulgate, and others to invert the suffixes to read "Direct my way in your sight." For as Jerome most excellently advises in his *Letter to Sunia and Fretela* (Volume III, p. 31), the Prophet asks that the Way of the Lord, which is straight in itself, may also become straight *for him*. This is according to what is said in the Lord's Prayer: "Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be Thy name!" It is not that it is hallowed because we pray for it—for it is holy in itself—but that we ask that what is holy by its own nature may be hallowed in us.
</margin>

-> **To the Chief Musician. With stringed instruments. On** <-

**verse 10. r)** According to the Vulgate and Abraham Ibn Ezra: *in their mouth*, meaning in the mouth of each of the adversaries. The Targum: *in the mouth of the wicked*. Compare Psalm 10:7. **s)** *right, firm, and certain*, that which agrees with the truth (Job 42:7, 8). **d)** *the innermost part, the interior*, that is, according to the Vulgate: *the heart, the soul, their desires and counsels.* Psalm 49:12; compare Matthew 12:35, chapter 15:18, 19, chapter 23:27; and the opposite in Psalm 103:1. **e)** *there are continual hardships and afflictions* which they devise against the godly. Psalm 38:13, 52:4, 9, 55:12, 94:20; Proverbs 19:13; Job 6:2. **f)** like an *open or gaping grave*. Jeremiah 5:16, Romans 3:13. **g)** *is their throat*. Isaiah 58:1, Psalm 115:7. Either because they gape to swallow others, or because they exhale nothing but a foul and pestilential stench (blasphemies, insults, deceits, etc.). Compare Matthew 23:27. **h)** *even when they make their tongue smooth.* Or, "even if they flatter with words." Psalm 36:3, 55:22, 140:4; Proverbs 2:16, chapter 28:23, chapter 29:5.

**verse 11. i)** Meaning: "Therefore, most just God, prosecute or pronounce them guilty; for they are guilty and have failed in many ways." This is the causative form <term>Hiphil</term> of the root. For the simple form <term>Kal</term>, see Psalm 34:22, Leviticus 5:5, 19, Ezekiel 21:4. **k)** *let them fall and collapse.* Vulgate: *let them fall away.* Psalm 36:13, Psalm 141:10. **l)** *from their wicked counsels.* Hosea 11:6. Others: *let them fail in their plans* and in their hope; compare Psalm 12:10. **m)** *because of the multitude of their transgressions.* Ezekiel 1:2, etc. Regarding the prefix, compare Genesis 18:28, Jeremiah 17:3, Jonah 1:7, 14. **n)** *disperse them*; Vulgate: *drive them out.* Deuteronomy 30:1, Ezekiel 13:14, Hosea 14:1. Compare Psalm 36:13. **o)** As if to say: "This I pray, not out of private or fleshly hatred, but out of a most just divine zeal." **p)** Deuteronomy 1:26, chapter 31:20, Isaiah 1:20. *Targum: because they are rebellious against Your Word.*

**verse 12. q)** *But let them be glad.* Others: *Then they shall be joyful in soul.* Psalm 4:8, 34:3, 107:42, 119:74. **r)** Targum: *those hoping in Your Word.* See the note on Psalm 2:12 and compare the similar construction in Psalm 24:1. **s)** Psalm 37:28, 73:26, 75:10, John 16:22, etc. **t)** *with the voice.* Psalm 29:6, 71:23, 84:3, Isaiah 35:10, chapter 65:14. **u)** *You will protect*; either because You will cover and protect them like wings (Psalm 91:4, 140:8) or like a shelter against the heat of the sun or rain (Isaiah 1:8, Jonah 4:5). See Isaiah 4:6, Revelation 7:15, 16, Psalm 121:5, 6, etc. From the root *skk* <note>meaning to cover or weave over</note>. **x)** Meaning: "so that they may exult," or rather, "they shall exult entirely." Synonyms are piled up here with a certain progression. 1 Samuel 2:1, Psalm 9:3, 25:2, 68:4, 5. **y)** *those loving Your name*, that is, You Yourself, as known from Your names and Your word. Psalm 69:37, Proverbs 18:10; compare synonyms in Psalm 40:17, 97:10, 119:132, 165.

**verse 13. r)** For You, O Lord, according to Your righteousness and mercy (verses 5–9). **a)** *will bless.* Others: "You are accustomed to bless," even when people curse (Psalm 109:28). Compare Psalm 3:9, 29:11, 115:12, 13. **b)** *Your people.* Targum and Syriac: *the righteous.* The singular number is often used in a distributive sense <note>meaning "each righteous person"</note>. For "the righteous," see verses 8 and 9 and the note on Psalm 1:5. **c)** *as if with a shield or buckler.* Psalm 91:4; see 1 Chronicles 9:15. **d)** *so Your grace and benevolence.* Deuteronomy 33:23, Psalm 145:16, Proverbs 8:35, chapter 12:2. **e)** *You will surround and protect him on every side.* Meaning: "You will encompass them, the righteous." If the suffix were changed, it would be "surround me." But the Septuagint, Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopic read: "You have crowned us." The simple form <term>Kal</term> means to surround (1 Samuel 23:26); the intensive form <term>Piel</term> means to crown (Psalm 8:5, 65:12, 103:4).

**Psalm VI, verse 1. f)** *To the overseer of sacred music with instruments*; see Psalm 4:1. **g)** Meaning: *upon the eighth.* Targum: *to the lyre of eight strings.* What this was precisely is uncertain. However, it seems to have been a type of song or a musical instrument; without doubt, as Geier advises, it was more suited to gravity than to lightheartedness. Compare Psalm 12:1, 1 Chronicles 15:21, and the preface to this book, section 6. **h)** The author of this psalm is therefore David; see note on Psalm 3:1. The Hebrews believe he composed it while he was ill, but Bohlius suggests—not improbably—that it was after the illness of his child (2 Samuel 12:15 and following). Or compare verses 3 and 4 of this psalm with 1 Chronicles 21:30. Others, following Cocceius, think it prophesies of Christ. Truly, as Luther long ago rightly advised, it applies to any Christian enduring these sufferings. Thus, according to Schmid, these are the "Prayers of a man placed in the distress of enemies and conscience," which Part I (verses 2–8) describes and prays against as being most grave. In Part II (verses 9–11), believing himself heard, he triumphs over his enemies.

**verse 2. i)** He repeats this address frequently (verses 3, 4, 5) just as he does the subject in verses 9 and 10, as the unique object of his prayers and faith, and his only helper. Compare Psalm 3:2. **k)** He does not pray against mere correction or fatherly chastisement, but against the wrath and rigor of divine justice. Compare Psalm 2:12, Isaiah 30:27, Jeremiah 10:24, Proverbs 3:11, 12. **l)** *rebuke me* (Genesis 21:25, 2 Samuel 7:14, 2 Kings 19:4, Psalm 38:2, Job 5:17). **m)** *nor in Your heat or fury* (Psalm 90:7), without grace or mercy; compare Psalm 79:6, 88:8.

---

**verse 10.** "For" <note>original: כִּי</note> with the added accent *Pâsk* 2. **verse 11.** "Pronounce them guilty" <note>original: הַאֲשִׁימֵם</note> with the accent *Rshia-mahpak* 1, 2; similarly in verse 5. "By their counsels" <note>original: מִמֹּעֲצוֹתֵיהֶם</note> thus written fully in 1, 2, 3, 5, according to the Masora 2 and Ess. but contrary to the printed version. "By their counsels" <note>original: מִמֹּעֲצֹתֵיהֶם</note> thus 1 with the accent *Sayka* 3. **verse 12.** "And they shall rejoice" <note>original: וְיִשְׂמְחוּ</note> with the accent *Rshia-mahpak* 3. "Those who trust" <note>original: חֹסֵי</note> thus with the accent *Rmahpak* 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 21, 23, 24, according to analogy because it is preceded by *Kadma*; compare Psalm 13:3 and 31:12. Others use *Ierach*. "And they shall exult" <note>original: וְיַעְלְצוּ</note> the letter *Ain* with the vowel *Patach* 1, 3, and in the margin 6, 9. Contrary to M. 1. **verse 13.** "You will surround him" <note>original: תַּעְטְרֶנּוּ</note> thus 8, 13, and in the margin 6, 9. Likewise 1 with a note that it was found thus in two books, but that our reading "You will surround him" <note>original: תַּעְטְרֶנּוּ</note> was confirmed by the Rabbis. **Psalm VI, verse 1.** "With stringed instruments" <note>original: בִּנְגִינֹת</note> Others use the regular accent *Rshia-resh*. But compare note on Psalm 4:1. **verse 2.** "O LORD, do not in Your anger" <note>original: יְהוָה אַל־בְּאַפְּךָ</note> thus 1, regularly indeed, but it is less emphatic.

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of Psalm 6 into the opening of Psalm 7. It focuses on the historical identity of "Cush the Benjaminite" and David’s plea for divine justice against slander and pursuit.</meta>

# PSALM 7.

<margin>
**q)** This is a song that David sang—using either his voice or a musical instrument—after he had overcome a period of great distress. It was intended for both his own use and the use of others. Compare 1 Chronicles 9:11; Judges 5:1; Proverbs 25:20; and Psalm 18:1. **r)** It was composed in honor of the Lord, from whom all blessing and salvation flow (Psalm 3:9). **s)** "Concerning the words": this refers either to slanderous words (see verse 4) or sarcastic remarks (as in Psalm 3:3), or other curses, such as those of Shimei (2 Samuel 16:5). It may also be a linguistic filler, as seen in Jeremiah 14:1. This song concerns "the Cushite." **t)** Cush. Many scholars, including the Targum <note>an ancient Aramaic translation</note>, Kimchi, Tarnovius, and Tilius, believe this refers to King Saul, the son of Kish (1 Samuel 10:1), using a wordplay <note>original: "paronomaisam"</note> on the name (compare Jeremiah 13:23 and Amos 9:7). They suggest Saul's name was withheld because one must not curse kings (Ecclesiastes 10:20). Others, such as Geier, believe this Cush was one of Saul’s generals or courtiers who slandered David (1 Samuel 24:10). Grotius suggests he was given the command to pursue David. Still others, including Bohl, Calovius, Pfeiffer, Lightfoot, and Mainz, take this to refer to Shimei the slanderer (2 Samuel 16:5), suggesting he either had two names or that David was mockingly alluding to the family of Kish. See Majus's *Economy*, page 789, where he suggests Psalm 11 has a similar theme, written when David was wandering without a fixed home, fleeing the cruel hands of the sons of Zeruiah (compare 2 Samuel 16:12). **u)** Meaning "the Benjaminite." The Targum identifies him as Saul, the son of Kish, who was from the tribe of Benjamin (see 1 Samuel 9:21; 22:7; 2 Samuel 16:11). According to the Scholars, this psalm contains David's prayers as an innocent man against his enemies and persecutors (verses 2–3), in which: I. He declares his innocence (verses 4–6). II. He asks for his restoration (verses 7–8). III. He appeals to God's justice (verses 9–10).
</margin>

<margin>
IV. David is certain that God’s justice will be favorable to him but most severe toward his enemies unless they repent (verses 11–17). V. Finally, he gives thanks (verse 18). **Chapter 2. x)** Verse 4: God is just, true, constant, and unchanging in His promises. Compare notes on Psalm 6:2; Exodus 6:2, 6, 8. **y)** Through the covenant of grace, He is "my God." See Psalm 3:8. **κ)** Psalm 5:12. Against Saul, or perhaps Absalom; deliver me from most present danger (verse 3). **d)** "Lest he tear" (Genesis 37:33) or "tear me apart" (Psalm 3:2). **(8)** Genesis 27:40. Deliver me (verse 2; 1 Samuel 17:35, 37; 2 Samuel 14:6; Psalm 5:29).
</margin>

**3, 8. κ)** Psalm 5:12; Isaiah 25:4. The Targum says: *In Your Word I have hoped,* as above in Psalm 2:12. **z)** Psalm 3:8. **b)** Perhaps Saul, or Absalom, and their followers. Compare verse 6; Genesis 14:14; Judges 4:16; Psalm 119:84. **c)** *Deliver* me from the most immediate danger to my life. Verse 3; Numbers 35:25; 1 Samuel 17:37; 2 Samuel 14:6; Psalm 18:1; Psalm 50:22.

**verse 3. d)** Lest the enemy seize or tear me like a wild beast. Or: Lest the enemies seize me. Compare verses 1, 2, 6, and the wording in Genesis 37:33 and Deuteronomy 33:20. **e)** Psalm 10:9; Psalm 17:12; Jeremiah 4:7. **f)** My soul and my life, or myself. Psalm 3:2; Numbers 23:10; chapter 35:11. **g)** Carrying away my soul, breaking me apart. The Targum says: *Let him tear.* **(8)** Genesis 27:40; Exodus 32:2; 1 Kings 19:11; Psalm 136:24. **h)** *Let there be no one* who rescues or frees me. Verse 2; 1 Samuel 17:35, 37; 2 Samuel 14:6; Psalm 5:29. **verse 4. i)** See verse 2. **k)** If I have done this—specifically what Shimei reproaches me for in 2 Samuel 16:7–8, or according to others, what Saul and his flatterers say in 1 Samuel 24:10 and chapter 25:10. David is testifying to his innocence in this matter; the consequence <note>original: "apodosis"</note> follows in verse 6. **l)** If there is such a crime, crookedness, or iniquity. Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 32:4; Ezekiel 3:20. **m)** In my hands. Genesis 20:5; Psalm 26:6; Psalm 71:4; Job 31:7. Hands are said to be "stained" when a crime is committed and "pure" when one is innocent. This is why people would wash their hands to testify to their innocence. **verse 5. n)** If I have repaid, shown, or done evil—if I have deserved this. The word can mean both to "retribute" and simply to "do good or evil." See Genesis 50:15, 17; 1 Samuel 24:18; Isaiah 3:9; chapter 63:7; Proverbs 31:12. **o)** Most manuscripts link these words with accents; so do the Septuagint <note>Greek translation</note>, Vulgate, Syriac, and Ethiopic: *To the one repaying me with evil.* However, the Targum uses a different distinction (see the variant readings below) and meaning: *If I have returned evil to the one at peace with me,* comparing Job 9:4; 22:21; and Psalm 55:21. **p)** Targum: *And I afflicted*; Syriac: *And I struck down*; others: *I plundered*, comparing 2 Samuel 2:21 and the Targum on 1 Samuel 31:8. **q)** For the one who was distressing me. Verse 7; Psalm 6:8; Numbers 25:17. "Without cause" means vainly and without any just reason. Psalm 25:3.

**verse 6. r)** *Let the enemy pursue,* implying that others may also pursue. The Hebrew form is a combination of two verb types <note>Kal and Piel</note>. Verse 2; Nahum 1:8. **s)** Myself, that is, my soul. Verse 3; Psalm 143:3. **t)** And let him catch or overtake me. Genesis 31:20; 44:4, 6; Exodus 15:9. **u)** And trample underfoot into the earth. Isaiah 28:3; 41:25; Nahum 3:14; Micah 5:7; Daniel 8:7. **x)** My life. Psalm 26:9; Psalm 64:2. **y)** And all my glory and reputation, acquired through Your favor. 2 Samuel 7:9; 8:13; Psalm 4:3; Job 19:9. **z)** Let him extinguish it and thrust it into the dust. Psalm 44:25; 119:25; Job 16:15. **a)** Vulgate: *Let him lead down.* This means "let him make me dwell or remain there," as if burying me. Psalm 94:17. **b)** "It is truly so!" I say this seriously and with a confident heart. The Greek <note>original: "διάψאלμα"</note> indicates a musical pause. The Targum says: *Forever.* See Psalm 3:5 and notes on Habakkuk 3:3. **verse 7. c)** Since my conscience completely clears me of these crimes: Arise, O Lord! Psalm 3:8; 9:20; 10:12. **d)** In Your anger (Psalm 6:2; 56:8; 90:7) against the fury of my enemies. **e)** Exalt Yourself, or lift Yourself up; as if ascending the highest throne of Your judgment. Isaiah 6:1; 33:10; Psalm 94:2. **f)** Because of (as in Psalm 5:11) or against the overflowing anger and furies. Hosea 5:10; Job 21:31. **g)** Of my enemies (verse 5). **h)** *And rouse Yourself by coming to me.* This is a "pregnant" verb <note>carrying extra meaning</note>: wake up as if from a sleep of abandonment or a failure to provide help. Psalm 44:24; 59:5–6. For otherwise, the Guardian of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4). **i)** That is: since You have commanded justice and judgment in Your Word, You cannot fail to administer justice to me Yourself. Compare Genesis 18:25; Exodus 23:6; Leviticus 19:15, 35; Deuteronomy 1:16–17; 10:18; 16:18–19; 27:19. The omission of the relative pronoun "which" is frequent; see verses 9 and 16, and Psalm 4:8. Others translate: "Because You have commanded for me the right or judgment of Your people," comparing 2 Samuel 6:21; 7:11. **verse 8. k)** For the assembly. The Septuagint and Vulgate say: *Synagogue.* Psalm 1:5; 22:17. **l)** Of the peoples of Israel. Psalm 2:1; Genesis 25:23. **m)** It surrounds or stands around You, the Judge, and awaits Your sentence. Psalm 26:6; compare 1 Kings 1:20. Others take this in a negative sense: they surround and attack not only me, but also You. Compare Psalm 17:11; 22:13, 17; Hosea 12:1. **n)** Therefore, to keep the assembly in their duty, or to show Yourself superior to Your adversaries: ascend Your most high judicial throne. Compare Psalm 11:4; 21:14; 93:4; and 1 Kings 10:19–20. **verse 9. p)** Targum: *The Word of the Lord, as the supreme, universal, and just Judge.* Verse 12; compare verse 2; Psalm 2:12; Genesis 18:25; Psalm 72:2; 82:8; John 5:27; Acts 17:31. **q)** He judges and will judge the nations. Psalm 9:9 and 110:6; 1 Samuel 2:10. **r)** Therefore, judge and vindicate me, O Lord! Psalm 26:1; 35:24; 43:1; Isaiah 1:17. **s)** According to my righteousness—that is, in this specific cause and dispute with my adversaries. Compare verses 4–5; Psalm 18:21 and 143:2. **t)** And according to my integrity or sincerity. Genesis 20:5–6; 2 Samuel 15:11; Psalm 25:21; 26:1, 11; 41:13. **u)** Which is "upon me" or "within me," in my soul. Psalm 16:6; 42:5; Hosea 11:8. But the Targum says: *Repay me*; meaning, let it be upon me or come to me, as in Psalm 3:9. **verse 10. x)** The Vulgate, Scholars, and others: *Let it be consumed, I pray.* Targum: *Let it be destroyed. Let it finally cease and reach its end.* Psalm 12:2; 57:3; 77:9; 138:8. **y)** The evil or malice. Vulgate: *wickedness.* Compare verse 5; Psalm 41:6.

**e)** *Every or all the day.* Psalm 38:10; 140:3; 145:2. This is contrary to what the wicked think (Psalm 10:11, 13), and thus He will punish them sooner than they expect. **v. 13. p)** *If or When.* Numbers 35:4. **q)** *If he does not turn back,* namely, my enemy (v. 6) and other wicked men (v. 10). Luther uses the impersonal: *If someone does not turn back.* The Septuagint, Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopic: *Unless you are converted.* This is what God prefers and what I pray for. Compare Ezekiel 18:21, 27, 32; 1 Timothy 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9. **q)** *He sharpens his sword for vengeance* (Genesis 4:22; 1 Samuel 13:20; Psalm 52:4). *His bow:* the judge stands ready. Compare Deuteronomy 32:41, 42; Isaiah 27:1; 34:5, 6; Ezekiel 21:14, 15. Most interpreters understand "God" as the subject here. But Geier and others take this whole section up to verse 17 as referring partly to the plots of the wicked man (v. 13, 14) and partly to their failure and opposite outcome (v. 15–17). In this view: *If my enemy does not turn back,* but continues to sharpen his sword, etc., behold, this will be the fruit: he will labor with iniquity. Compare Psalm 11:2; 37:13, 14. However, we prefer the first view due to the connection with verse 13. **\*)** *He bent his bow.* Habakkuk 3:9; Lamentations 2:4; 3:12. **t)** He made it firm or prepared it, and having placed the arrow, he aimed it. v. 10; Psalm 11:2; Isaiah 51:13. **v. 14. u)** Symmachus: "He prepared for himself," or rather, God prepared for the wicked man for the purpose of vengeance. Others say the wicked man prepared it for his own ruin. Zephaniah 1:7. Targum: "And because of the wicked man himself, God prepared [it]." **x)** *Instruments of death,* meaning lethal. The genitive denotes the effect, as in Ezekiel 21:30. But the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, and Ethiopic say: *for the burning ones,* meaning the enemies pursuing me with fervor. See Genesis 31:36; Obadiah v. 18; Psalm 10:2; Lamentations 4:19. Just as Saul was struck by the weapons of his enemies and finally killed by his own sword. 1 Samuel 31:3 ff; 1 Chronicles 10:3. **a)** prepared, brought about. **v. 16. p. 15. h)** *Behold therefore,* the wicked man conceives or labors. Compare Song of Solomon 8:5 and the term in Isaiah 66:7; Jeremiah 13:21. **c)** Vulgate: *injustice.* Symmachus: *iniquity.* Others: *vanity* or *vain efforts.* Psalm 5:6; 6:9; 10:7; 90:10; and notes on 1 Samuel 15:23. **d)** *But he shall be pregnant with labor,* or *he shall conceive excessive trouble,* to be inflicted on the innocent. v. 17; Isaiah 59:4. **e)** and you shall bring forth a lie; he will realize all his labor was in vain and he was deceived by his own work. Psalm 112:10; compare Psalm 33:17; Isaiah 26:18; 33:11; Job 15:33. **v. 16. f)** *He dug a pit* or prepared a snare. See Ezekiel 19:4, 8. **h)** *but he himself fell, or most certainly will fall.* Psalm 35:8. **i)** into the pit. Psalm 10:2; Proverbs 26:27. **k)** *which he made.* v. 14. An ellipsis of the relative pronoun as in v. 7, 9. Psalm 9:16. Regarding the matter, compare Ecclesiastes 10:8; Proverbs 26:8; 5:22. **v. 17. l)** For the wicked labor (or as the Syriac says, his iniquity) will return. v. 15. **m)** upon his own head; according to the saying: *Evil counsel is worst for the counselor.* Compare Psalm 140:10; 2 Samuel 3:29. **n)** and upon the top of his head. Psalm 18:21; Jeremiah 2:16. **o)** the force and violence intended for me. Genesis 6:10, 11; Habakkuk 1:2, 3, 9. **p)** like hail (Exodus 9:19; Deuteronomy 28:24) or a stone thrown at another (Ecclesiastes 10:9), it will descend by divine judgment. v. 13; Micah 1:12. *Because no law is more just than that the architects of death perish by their own art.* **v. 18. q)** I will therefore praise the Lord. Psalm 6:6. This word in the *Kal* stem means "He threw" or "He cast"; in the *Hiphil* stem, it is known to mean not only to confess (as in Psalm 32:5) but also to celebrate, to praise publicly, as if casting the praises of someone, as in this place and Psalm 9:2; 54:8; 108:4, etc. **r)** according to His righteousness clearly demonstrated. Compare v. 10, 12; 2 Thessalonians 1:6. **s)** and I will joyfully sing psalms with voice or instruments. Psalm 9:3; 27:6; 68:15, 50. Deuteronomy 28:58; compare Psalm 5:12; 113:1, 2. **u)** Of the Most High and supreme God and Arbiter of all. Psalm 9:3; 18:14; 47:3, etc. **PS. VIII, v. 1. x)** see notes on Psalm 4:1; Habakkuk 3:19. **y)** Symmachus: "upon Gittith"; which some take as a type of song or melody, and others as a type of musical instrument, but the specific kind is unknown to us. **(z)** Psalm 81:1 and 84:1. See the Preface to this book, section 6. Targum: *upon the lyre, which he brought from Gath:* whether that of the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:4; 27:3) or the Gath-Rimmon of the Levites (Joshua 21:25), from which they think Obed-Edom was called a Gittite (2 Samuel 6:10). The Septuagint, Vulgate, and Ethiopic incorrectly translate this as *for the winepresses* against the Hebrew text; although this could be explained regarding the passions and exaltation of Christ, following the analogy of Isaiah 63:1–3. **z)** see Psalm 3:1. Syriac: *A prophecy of David, that infants, children, and youths would speak praises to the Lord: Hosanna;* compare here v. 3 and Matthew 21:16. Symmachus: *A prophecy of David, in which the Church praises its God, because in the New Testament He made His name glorious through Christ and the Gospel, especially when He exalted CHRIST above all after a brief time of humiliation.* These views are surely better than Grotius and others who, following the Jews, foolishly apply this to the whole human race; or others who apply it to Adam in the state of innocence (who was neither "Enosh," a miserable and afflicted man, nor a "son of Adam," nor himself deserted by God, nor exalted above all things, even celestial ones). On the contrary, the ancient Jews recognize the Messiah is superior not only to Abraham and Moses, but even to the Angels; as we noted on Isaiah 52:13; compare Hebrews 1:4. Others incorrectly take this psalm to refer to restored man. For it deals, according to the infallible demonstration of Christ and the Apostle (Matthew 21:16; 1 Corinthians 15:27; Ephesians 1:20–22; Hebrews 2:5–9), with **CHRIST**, the man who, after His humiliation, was raised to the right hand of God. Thus, as Peter says in 1 Peter 1:11, the Holy Spirit through David, for the hope and solace of the Old Church and our own confirmation, here first testifies to the *sufferings of Christ and the glories that follow.* This wonderful mystery of godliness (1 Timothy 3:16), the holy poet celebrates in Psalm 8, verse 2.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary from the previous page, moving from the conclusion of Psalm 7 into a detailed Messianic analysis of Psalm 8. The translator notes that the author interprets the "glory" and "majesty" described by David not merely as a reflection of creation, but as a prophecy of Christ’s kingdom and the spread of the Gospel.</meta>

<margin>
g) A difficult phrase <note>original: "comma"</note> begins here; its words must be clarified before all else so that the meaning is established. Most interpret it relatively and in the first case <note>nominative</note>, such as the Targum and Syriac: "who hast given," that is, you have made your glory conspicuous and known, etc. The Septuagint <note>LXX</note>, however, and the Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopic versions read it substantively: "because it is elevated," as in Deuteronomy 3:24, 1 Samuel 2:23, Ezekiel 23:10, etc. But Sebastian Schmidt, reading it with the following suffix in the Genitive (as in Psalm 38:12, etc.), finds it a bit harsher: "for to give (your) glory is or should be," etc. h) who by giving, indeed, you gave, as the Targum and Syriac have it. For often after an infinitive, a finite verb is understood and must be supplied, as in Exodus 20:8, Psalm 37:19, 17:27, Ezekiel 24:5, Ecclesiastes 2:9, etc. The Septuagint, Vulgate, Arabic, Ethiopic, Luther, etc., read it impersonally and passively: "because your glory is exalted or lifted up"; this is not entirely unusual in Hebrew idiom (see Exodus 9:16, etc.). But to Schmidt, as we just hinted, the infinitive is absolute and acts as the subject: "to give whose praise or honor is or should be above the heavens," that is, whom even the Angels in the heavens confess and praise, comparing Isaiah 7:19, John 9:24; he adds Psalm 29:2, 3. i) who by giving gave your excellence, majesty, glory, and honor. Psalm 21:6, 145:5, 1 Chronicles 29:25. The Ethiopic: "how exalted is the magnitude of your praise." k) even above the heavens; Psalm 57:6, 12, 108:4, 148:13, so that the earth and heaven are filled with the praises of your name because of Christ—namely, the Church Militant <note>Christians on earth</note> and Triumphant <note>the saints in heaven</note>. Revelation 5:9, 12, 13, 12:10, 12. We prefer this sense with Schmidt, who says: "To us, the opinion is most pleasing which explains the honor of the Angels given to Jehovah above or in the heavens for the mysteries of the work of redemption through Christ." For even the Angels desire to look into these mysteries (1 Peter 1:12), and it is made known even to the principalities and powers...
</margin>

II. He explains verses 3–9, and III. confirms with a repetitive conclusion in verse 10.

[The Psalmist] addresses Christ the Redeemer in contradistinction to the incarnate God (see v. 5), yet without excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit. b) **Lord of us all**, or You who are our Lord and God. Psalm 2:4, 147:5, Nehemiah 10:30. Thus, in the view of Samuel Bohlius, the Messiah sings [this]; according to others, David and the Church of the Old Testament sing of the time of the New Testament; but according to Schmidt, it is the Church of the New Testament, whom David introduces here as speaking (as in Psalms 16 and 22 regarding the Messiah, etc.), because most words of the psalm are conceived as if the works of God being celebrated had already been accomplished. Everywhere the Prophet David foresaw the times of the New Testament in the Holy Spirit, and he commended this prophetic psalm to the Church of the Old Testament to confirm and console their faith and hope in the future Messiah, as we already said at verse 1. And Johannes Brenz rightly observed that David utters this verse just as if he saw the Apostles before his eyes, traveling among both Jews and Gentiles, and illuminating the glory of God's name revealed through Christ by their preaching; hence the Holy Spirit looks primarily to the time when the Apostles spread the gospel among all nations. **Our:** The pronoun "our" is added, which contains a protestation of faith and obedience, especially from an Israelite man. For although God is the Lord of all men, He specially declared Himself the Israelite Lord as of a people He had acquired, and they recognized Him as their Lord. c) **How!** This expresses intensity, as in Psalm 3:2. An exclamation proceeding from profound meditation and admiration of such great mystery and divine majesty. d) **Magnificent**, illustrious, and glorious. The Septuagint, Vulgate, and Arabic: *admirable*. The Ethiopic: "is greatly celebrated." So in verse 10; compare Psalm 76:5, Exodus 15:6, 10, 11, Jeremiah 14:3, etc. Schmidt: "namely, through your works, which are preached and celebrated in the Gospel." e) **Your name**, holy and venerable. Deuteronomy 28:58. Kimchi: that is, "how glorious You are," because <note>original: "כי שמו הוא והוא שמו"</note> "His name is He, and He is His name," for the Name of God signifies God Himself, and He is the one whom the name names. The magnificent Name of Jehovah, says Schmidt, is not the letters and syllables of the name, but God Himself, addressed and celebrated through His names; because nothing can be preached or praised concerning God without mentioning some name of His. And so, it is the same as if they said: "You, O God, whoever You are called by Your name Jehovah, O our Lord, are magnificent," etc. f) **Not as formerly in Egypt only**, or Judea, that is, the land of Canaan (Psalm 76:2, 147:19, 20), but in all the earth: so that throughout the whole world your grace, wisdom, power, and glory, wonderfully demonstrated in Christ, may be celebrated. 1 Timothy 3:16.

<margin>
...witnessing in the heavenly places the manifold wisdom of God. Ephesians 3:10.
</margin>

...so that on that account I may adore Christ also with God the Father. Psalm 97:7, Philippians 2:10, Hebrews 1:5, 6.

**v. 3.** l) *Out of the mouth of babes*, that is, infants, both by reason of years and age (as in Joshua 6:11, 9:20, Psalm 17:14, Lamentations 4:4) and by reason of character and infantile simplicity; compare Isaiah 28:9, 1 Corinthians 1:26, 27, 3:1. Namely, with praises sung to You and Your Christ from the mouth of infants (Matthew 21:15) and disciples (Luke 19:37-39), and the Gospel announced from the mouth of the Apostles, who were like little children in simplicity (Matthew 11:25, Mark 10:15), though later they were adults and perfect in mind (1 Corinthians 14:20). Namely, men of simple faith and infantile soul, with even the literal infant age not excluded, but rather singularly included here; because, in verse 2, the case for adults and infants in spiritual matters is the same; compare Matthew 18:3. That wonderful praise of Christ and preaching of the Gospel, by reason of its ministry, is celebrated here first by the Prophet. m) *and nursing infants* (Joel 2:16), whom Hebrew mothers nursed until a certain year (2 Maccabees 7:27, see Genesis 21:8, 1 Samuel 1:22-24, etc.). Thus, there is no need for great anxiety here as to whether nursing infants also shouted "Hosanna" to Christ? Since it undoubtedly happened, as Schmidt notes on page 44, that in such a great gathering of people (described in Matthew 21:8 and following, and Luke 19:37 and following) infants of both sexes, who were still sucking the breast and could hardly speak, were carried in arms and shown Jesus; and these, whether being carried or imitating the shouting boys, uttered that voice with an infantile mouth by divine movement. n) Targum: "you have founded." Syriac: "you have made firm." Others: "you have firmly established or decreed" (compare Esther 1:8, 1 Chronicles 9:21, Psalm 2:2) the power and strength of your kingdom (Psalm 29:1, 96:6, 7), which not even the gates of hell shall overcome (Matthew 21:18). Because the Gospel, by reason of its virtue, is the scepter of power (Psalm 110:2), that is, a strength founded and impregnable (Luke 21:15, Romans 1:16, 1 Corinthians 10:4). But the Septuagint, Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopic, as in Matthew 21:16, read "you have prepared or perfected praise," which meaning of "praise" some attribute to the Hebrew noun *oz* <note>strength</note> in 2 Chronicles 30:21, but without necessity. Hence Schmidt understands strength (*oz*), that is, a voice or praise uttered strongly, clearly, and fearlessly; as if to say: "You have so powerfully and wisely disposed and governed, and by Your Holy Spirit moved that mouth of babes and nursing infants, that with a robust, clear, and fearless voice of their mouth, psalming or shouting (Matthew 21:15), they sang praise to Your Christ." o) *Because of your enemies* (Psalm 6:8, 7:5, 7), namely those who opposed the word of the Gospel and the praises of Christ, whom Psalm 2 also distinctly describes. p) *To silence* <note>literally: to make cease</note> namely Ezekiel 30:10, Amos 8:4. Septuagint and Vulgate: "that you may destroy," and silence them and render them inexcusable, because they did not believe in such great light and virtue of Your word; by which light and virtue even boys and infants—such by age and simplicity—were illuminated and moved to Your praise. See Paul declaring this at length in 1 Corinthians 1:26–29. q) *The enemy* (Psalm 9:7) *and the avenger*, namely, one eager for vengeance (Psalm 44:17). By this, Bohlius, Calovius, and others understand the devil, who is the perpetual adversary of God and His Church, and who set himself as an avenger to the whole human race, and still sets the most ruinous snares; and he is called "the enemy" or "the foe" absolutely throughout the Scriptures (compare Zechariah 3:1, 2, Job 1:6, 7, 1 Chronicles 21:1, Matthew 13:39, Luke 10:19). But to Schmidt, both singular names are collective for the plural that preceded; he understands them according to the circumstances of this event in the New Testament: the High Priests, Pharisees, Scribes, and leaders of the Jews, so filled with enmity and desire for vengeance against Christ that they were already plotting the same. Matthew 21:23, 46, Mark 11:18, Luke 19:39, 48.

**v. 4.** r) Bohlius, according to his opinion which we briefly hinted at in verse 2, says: "Because I, the Messiah, exalted at your right hand, shall see," etc. The Targum, Septuagint, and Vulgate also read it causally: "Because I shall see"; but without a comfortable connection to what precedes or follows. Better, therefore, Schmidt and others read it adverbially: *When* or *Whenever* (Genesis 4:12, Exodus 7:9, Numbers 23:9, etc.) I behold and piously consider the heavens... Genesis 15:5, Job 35:5, etc. So that this verse coheres with verse 5, with only the word "I say" understood, or as I am compelled to say within myself, "What is man!" etc., comparing a similar ellipsis <note>omission of a word</note> in Song of Solomon 3:3. After the Church of Christ has first set forth divine magnificence, which He made admirable in the whole world (v. 2) while He disposed the strength of praise from the mouth of babes (v. 3), she now comes to the other, even more admirable thing, which is the ineffable exaltation of Christ, who was first emptied <note>humbled</note>. This is briefly proposed in verses 4 and 5, then in verses 6–9, through a certain opposition or comparison of the emptying and the exaltation, it is further explained. s) *that stupendous work and craftsmanship of your fingers* Psalm 102:26, Isaiah 40:12, 48:13. t) *the moon* Psalm 104:19, 148:3. u) *and the innumerable bright stars* Genesis 15:5. x) *which you prepared*, or, as Schmidt has it, *firmly established*, that is, without corruption, in a certain place, and in just order and wonderful motion in your heavens (Psalm 9:8, Deuteronomy 32:6). When I gaze upon these, I say, and at the same time think, that you have subjected not only other ignoble creatures, but even these most noble ones, to Your Christ, who as a man was exalted after a most humble emptying, I cannot help but exclaim (v. 5): *What is man!* etc. Furthermore, no mention is made here of the Sun, the most noble of all stars, because according to Calovius and others, this meditation was undertaken by David at night, when the Sun lay hidden below the horizon (compare Psalm 12:2, 119:62); according to Tilius, this hymn was sung through the night (compare Isaiah 30:29, Colossians 2:16, 17, Hebrews 8:5, 10:1, Psalm 66:23). But according to Schmidt, as the latter half of the verse speaks of nocturnal contemplation, the first half speaks of daytime contemplation of the sky, in this way: "When I look up at the heaven, first that lower part appears with its Sun; but at night, the Moon," etc.

<column-break/>

*v. 5. y)* What is man, <note>original: "אֱנוֹשׁ" (enosh)</note> miserable and full of sorrow. <note>Cross-referencing Genesis 4:26 and Job 7:1.</note> Abraham Calov <note>A 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> wonders: "What is that afflicted and sorrowful man, that you are mindful of him?" This admiration refers to the fact that he who was so afflicted in his "emptying" <note>The theological concept of *kenosis*, or Christ laying aside his divine attributes to become human</note> was later crowned with such glory and honor that all things are subjected under his feet, and he is placed as the supreme Lord over all. <note>See Hebrews 2:6.</note> Furthermore, these words in Psalm 144:3 do not speak of a specific individual man, but rather of human nature viewed in itself, which, when compared to God and His nature, is to be considered as nothing. Thus, it is no wonder that these words are used here for the "Son of Man" (the person of the Son of God assumed into humanity), but elsewhere for mere humans; for the nature is common to all. Martin Geier <note>A German Hebraist</note> correctly observed that the word for "man" here corresponds to "flesh" <note>Greek: <term>σαרξ</term> (sarx)</note> in John 1:14. **z)** that you, Jehovah the Father, are mindful of him, or remember him. <note>Comparing Genesis 8:1.</note> That is, you remembered him so much that you subjected even the heavens and all things to him. Geier notes that in Psalm 22:2, the "abandoned man" Christ asks God to remember him. **a)** the son of man, not just anyone (as in 1 Kings 8:39), but the same "Man Christ" is designated here by a common scriptural synonym; he who was born of Mary, bearing a human nature similar to the rest of the descendants of Adam. <note>original: "Adae"</note> Therefore, Christ is frequently called this in the New Testament. <note>See Matthew 8:20, 9:6, etc.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>
u, 19, etc. & see Daniel 7:13; Ezekiel 1:26. **h)** because he so graciously visits and exalts him. Sebastian Schmidt says this grace of ineffable exaltation is not by merit for himself, but by the right of sonship. See the word in Genesis 21:1.
</margin>

Exodus 4:31; Jeremiah 15:15; Psalm 106:4; Ruth 1:6. Others, such as Geier and van Till, think this indicates the most gracious coming of the Son of God into the flesh, and his most intimate union with that flesh, so that in it, as in his dwelling or temple, the fullness of the Godhead might dwell bodily. <note>Colossians 1:19, 2:9; Luke 1:68.</note> But Schmidt’s opinion is simpler and allows for an easier coherence of the entire text.

*v. 6. i)* Schmidt: You have indeed made him lack for a little while compared to the angels. Or, you willed him to be destitute for a little while from God; namely, in terms of the use and enjoyment of divine majesty and glory, of which he emptied himself. <note>Philippians 2:7.</note> Thus, according to the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, the Vulgate, and all other versions: **You have diminished**, or made him **lower** and **inferior** to the Angels. *d)* a little while. Not forever, but for the brief and small time of his "emptying," especially in his most bitter passion and death. <note>Philippians 2:8.</note> And although the state of Christ’s emptying lasted for thirty-three years, it is still a small time compared to the eternal glory which he immediately attained in his exaltation. *e)* Luther, Geier, and others: You made him destitute of God, as he himself complained on the cross in Psalm 22:2 and Matthew 27:46. But the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and the Apostle in Hebrews 2:7, 9 say: **you made him a little lower than the Angels or beneath the Angels**; because Christ in his sufferings not only lacked the company of Angels for a time, but was even made inferior to them so that their strength appeared greater than his. <note>See Matthew 26:53, Luke 22:43.</note> So too, these same versions express the name **Elohim** <note>original: "אלהים"</note> in Psalm 97:7 as the **Angels** of God, and Paul does the same in Hebrews 1:6, with the Jewish interpreters agreeing. Others, with Cocceius, think the word "Elohim" is used very broadly here to include the true God, and others called "gods" by analogy (whether in heaven or on earth, 1 Corinthians 8:5)—meaning angels and also the leaders of the Jews who gave him over to death. But soon, with the work of redemption finished, he was crowned with glory <note>Psalm 3:4</note> and honor <note>Psalm 21:6</note> (which he lacked in his state of emptying, Isaiah 53:2); that is, through emphatic synonyms, with infinite and divine glory and majesty. <note>See Daniel 7:14, Matthew 28:18, John 1:14.</note> *g)* The Vulgate and others: you have crowned. Others: you will crown him, exalted to the right hand of your glorious majesty. <note>Hebrews 1:3; 1 Timothy 3:16.</note> Like a conqueror, and King of Kings and Lord of Lords, so that the Angels also worship him. <note>Psalm 97:7; Hebrews 1:6.</note> The Hebrew verb here and in verse 7 implies the "conversive vav" <note>A grammatical feature in Hebrew that changes the tense of a verb</note>, as in Hosea 8:12.

*v. 7. h)* You, God the Father, will cause him to rule, or (implying the "conversive vav" from verse 6) you have made him rule. <note>Daniel 11:39; Acts 2:36.</note> Namely, by giving him supreme power and dominion over all things in heaven and on earth. <note>Matthew 28:18; John 5:26.</note> The verb in its basic form <note>Kal</note> means to command or rule (Genesis 3:16). From this comes the participle **Moschel** <note>original: "Moschel"</note>, meaning "Ruler" or "Governor," which is often among the titles of Christ. <note>See Isaiah 40:10; Micah 5:1.</note> **i)** over the works of your hands, without any exception: under which are contained not only the lowlier creatures in verses 8 and 9, but also the heavens and the Angels. **k)** for all things—heavenly, earthly, and those under the earth—whether willing or unwilling, faithful or enemies, good and bad Angels, even death and hell. For the Father excepted nothing that he did not subject to him (Hebrews 2:8). This will finally be fully evident to all, as Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 15:25. The Apostle so clearly testifies in Hebrews 2:5 that these things are to be understood regarding CHRIST, that it could not be taught more clearly. Therefore, those who explain this as being about anyone other than Christ contradict him directly, as Calvin rightly judges. **l)** you have placed. **m)** under his feet: so that all things venerate him either in humble subjection and obedience, or even unwillingly as enemies who cannot escape his power. <note>See Luke 10:19; Romans 16:20.</note> Consider also the table of Darius subjected to the feet of the victor Alexander in Curtius, Book 5, chapter 2.

*v. 8. n)* Even flocks of sheep and goats. **o)** and herds or oxen. <note>original: "אֲלָפִים"</note> The wealth of the ancients. **p)** all of them. Schmidt says: just as divine providence is ennobled and praised because it cares for even the lowliest creatures like sparrows and grass, so Christ's dominion is greatly extolled because it extends over even the lowliest creatures, such that nothing is excepted from him. **q)** The Vulgate: "moreover" or "even." **r)** beasts of the field or wild animals. For the earth and its fullness belong to Christ the Lord. <note>Psalm 24:1; 1 Corinthians 10:26.</note> Regarding the form of the name **Shaday** <note>original: "שדי" (field)</note>, see the note on Isaiah 56:9.

*v. 9. s)* Birds of the air. **t)** See the example of this dominion exercised by Christ over the fish in Matthew 17:27 and Luke 5:4.

It details his temporary humiliation below the angels and his ultimate exaltation as ruler over all creation, including animals, angels, and death itself.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Psalm 8 and begins a detailed analysis of Psalm 9. While Psalm 8 focused on the majesty of God and the dominion of the "Son of Man" over nature, the transition to Psalm 9 shifts toward a thanksgiving for victory over enemies, which the commentators interpret both historically (regarding David’s battles) and prophetically (regarding Christ's victory over the Antichrist and Satan).</meta>

# PSALM 8. 9. Psalm IX.

<margin>
x) Ethiopic: *and whatever walks.* Greek, etc.: *passing through*—whatever passes through the paths of the sea, perhaps wandering by swimming in the sea. See Isaiah 23:2. y) *paths* Job 6:18, 19; of the seas and all waves; Psalm 89:25; Genesis 1:10. Geier: <note>Martin Geier, a 17th-century Lutheran Hebraist</note> He mentions beasts, birds, and fish; so that there is a full distribution of living creatures according to the three elements they inhabit: earth, air, and water. This was also seen in the first inauguration of Adam (Genesis 1:28) and the blessing of Noah (Genesis 9:2). Calovius <note>Abraham Calov, a defender of Lutheran orthodoxy</note> adds: so that we may know that the dominion of Christ extends even to those who are outside the Church, and that the Messiah rules over them too—but in a far more eminent way than Adam ruled in his state of innocence—to restore to us, his members, the dominion we had lost; see Romans 14:8, 9, 11; 1 Corinthians 8:8; 10:26, 28. Others take all these in verses 8 and 9 figuratively: they understand the flock of sheep as the assemblies of the faithful, the oxen as the hardworking teachers of the Church, the beasts of the field as fierce men (Isaiah 11:6, 9), and the fish as Leviathan (Isaiah 27:1), etc. However, we believe the literal sense was intended by the Holy Spirit here and should be retained, though we do not reject a suitable figurative application.

* 10. z) Deservedly, therefore, we exclaim again and conclude: O Jehovah, our Lord, etc. See verse 2. a) See Zechariah 14:9.

Psalm IX, v. 1. b) See Psalm 4:1; Habakkuk 3:19. c) *Upon Muth-Labben* <note>original: "עַל־מוּת לַבֵּן"</note>—likely an instrument, as in Psalm 5:1 and 8:1; which Pfeifer <note>August Pfeiffer, a German Orientalist</note> and others see as a type of song or melody; see Psalm 57:1. Others interpret it as *concerning the death of* (Psalm 48:15; Genesis 25:31; Judges 8:18).
</margin>

<margin>
18.) *the son:* <note>original: "בֵּן" (ben)</note> namely, according to Bohlius’s conjecture, the death of Absalom, as well as Sheba and other adversaries, and even the defeat of the Ammonites; in this way, diverse events are joined. Others say: *concerning the death of that Son* mentioned in Psalms 2 and 8, namely Christ, and the victory gained through it. Others: *concerning the death for the son*—that is, on account of the Son of God; see Leviticus 19:28, 21:11; Numbers 6:7; Job 30:25. Thus Till <note>Salomon van Til</note> specifically interprets this as referring to the martyrs who die for the truth of the Gospel of Christ in the final distress or persecution of the Church; see verses 13 and 10 with Daniel 12:1. Indeed, Blessed Luther commonly explained this psalm as being about the martyrs of Christ. The Syriac inscription has: *Concerning Christ, receiving his throne and kingdom, and destroying the enemy* (see Revelation 11:17, 12:10). The Arabic: *Concerning the mysteries of the son:* on account of the glory of the Messiah and his resurrection and kingdom, and the destruction of all the rebellious. The first phrase comes from the Greek version: *concerning the secrets of the son*, which the Ethiopic also follows. But they wrongly took the Hebrew *Al-Muth* as a single word, as did those who interpret it as the "youth" of the son. We do not wish to delay the reader with the many uncertain conjectures of the Rabbis and others—for example, the death of Ben the Singer (1 Chronicles 15:18) or some barbarian king so named, or the death of Laban via anagram, which pleased Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch jurist and theologian</note>; for none of these fit the phrase and argument of this psalm. Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval rabbi and grammarian</note> offers a more elegant conjecture (supported by Tarnovius, Nobilius, Lightfoot, and others): that *Labben* is not "the son" but refers to the preposition or noun *bein* (between), and thus refers to the death of Goliath, who is called the "man of the space between" or the "Duelist," so to speak, in 1 Samuel 17:24. The Chaldean <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation</note> preceded him in this: *upon the death of the man who went out from between the armies*; see also verse 6. Yet, not everything in this psalm can refer to the circumstances of Goliath’s death, nor does verse 12 fit that time. For then the Lord, or the Ark of the Covenant, did not yet dwell specifically in the fortress of Zion. Whatever occasion David seized (says Maius), or whenever he wrote the psalm, it cannot be denied that Goliath is a type of Satan and the Antichrist. The matter itself and the emphasis of the words in verses 5, 6, and 7—which preeminently designate *the evil one, the adversary who exalts himself* (2 Thessalonians 2:3, 4, 8)—clearly show that Christ is introduced as the universal conqueror and judge of enemies, and the Church as celebrating the Lord’s victory far and wide. And Jerome says on this passage: "this entire psalm is sung by the Prophet in the person of the Church concerning the Antichrist." David had prophesied in Psalm 8 about the universal dominion of Christ. Lest anyone think no struggle remained for the New Testament Church, he describes here its struggle with adversaries, its tears and prayers, and finally its most joyful outcome. Thus, according to Schmid’s headings: I. He gives thanks to God for the turning away of his enemies (v. 2–7). II. He promises God's just judgment to the world and the godly (v. 8–11). III. For which the godly must confess (v. 12–15). IV. While the impious shall perish miserably (v. 16–21). Geier, however, establishes two parts: I. Thanksgiving (v. 2–13). II. Petition (v. 14–end). d) see Psalm 3:1, 4:1, etc.
</margin>

...pass through the paths of the seas. O Lord, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all **A** the earth!

**1** For the Chief Musician; upon the death of the son <note>Hebrew: *Muth-Labben*</note>. A Psalm of David. **2** I will give thanks to the Lord with all my heart; I will tell of all your wonders. **3** I will be glad and exult in you; I will sing praise to your name, O Most High. **4** When my enemies turn back, they stumble and perish before you. **5** For you have maintained my right and my cause; you sat on the throne judging righteously. **6** You have rebuked the nations, you have destroyed the wicked; their name you have **6** blotted out.

---

v. 2. e) Psalm 6:6; 7:18. f) Psalm 111:1; 119:10; 138:1. With a whole and sincere soul (Psalm 32:2) in spirit and truth (John 4:24); see Deuteronomy 6:5. g) *I will enumerate* Psalm 2:7; 66:16. That is, so that none of them is passed over without praise. h) *all your wonders* Psalm 26:7. He who is "Wonderful" (Isaiah 9:6) and alone does wonders (Psalm 72:18), both in the work of creation and in the redemption and preservation of your people. See Isaiah 55:8, 9; Romans 11:33; 1 Timothy 3:16. Though due to human weakness, they cannot all be counted (Psalm 40:6; Job 5:9).

v. 3. i) Psalm 4:8; 5:12; 31:8. k) In himself, as providing the matter for rejoicing, and through you. See Psalm 32:11; 33:1; Nehemiah 8:10; Philippians 4:4. Targum: *In your Word.* See 1 Corinthians 1:30, 31. l) Psalm 7:18; 61:9. m) Most High and Supreme God. Psalm 18:14; 47:3; 89:28; 91:2; etc.

v. 4. n) For when they turned back. Or: because they turned back and turned their backs out of fear struck by God (Psalm 6:11). Thus it notes the cause or rather the reason and motive for joy (as in 2 Chronicles 16:7, 28:6, etc.). Others use the adverb of time: *When they are turned back*, etc. (as in Psalm 3:1, 4:2; Joshua 6:5), because they take this whole psalm as a prophecy of the future; see Isaiah 12:1; Revelation 10:7. o) Psalm 3:8. p) Psalm 35:4; 40:15. q) *they shall stumble* further, or *so that they stumbled*. Use of the "conversive vav" <note>A Hebrew grammatical feature where the letter 'vav' changes the tense of a verb</note> as in Psalm 8:6, 9; Exodus 15:5; Judges 2:1. The word is used in Jeremiah 20:11; Proverbs 24:16; Daniel 11:19. r) Psalm 8:12; 21:11; 68:3. s) *From your face*—that is, from the sight of an angry and just avenger (v. 5). See v. 20; Psalm 21:10; 68:2; 2 Thessalonians 2:8.

v. 5. t) For you have done (1 Kings 8:32). u) *my right* or *my judgment* (Psalm 17:2; Micah 7:9). Targum: *my vengeance.* x) Vulgate: *and my cause* (Jeremiah 5:28; Psalm 76:9; 140:13). Arabic: *You judged for me, and you vindicated.* Thus through synonyms, both the just judgment and its execution are designated. Greek (LXX): see Luke 18:7, 8. y) Vulgate: *you sat upon the throne* or tribunal. See Isaiah 16:5; Psalm 47:9; Revelation 20:11. z) That is, a judge of justice or a just judge, as the Targum and Syriac have it. But as a participle in the Greek and Vulgate: *you who judge justice* (v. 8; Psalm 7:12; 50:6; Isaiah 11:3, 4).

v. 6. a) You rose up like a just and severe judge. Vulgate: *You rebuked and restrained the nations.* Targum: *the nations of the Philistines.* See note on verse 1 and the word in Isaiah 17:13. b) *you destroyed* Psalm 5:7; 119:95. c) Targum: *the wicked Goliath*, a type of the devil and the Antichrist (Isaiah 11:4). But Syriac uses the collective: *the wicked ones.* See verse 18; Psalm 1:6; 37:17, 20; 68:3; 104:35. Till says specifically the rebellious Jews. d) See Exodus 17:14; Deuteronomy 9:14; Isaiah 29:19; 2 Kings 21:13; and Exodus 32:33; Numbers 5:23; Deuteronomy 25:6; Psalm 109:13.

---

Psalm IX, v. 1. *Al-Muth*. They write *Almuth* as one word in various manuscripts. But as Ibn Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a medieval Spanish rabbi</note> and M. I. teach us on Psalm 48:15, the Masora <note>The tradition of the Hebrew biblical text</note> says otherwise. See the note above on text b).

* 3. *I will be glad and exult in you*—thus in manuscripts 1 and 3, and so in 5. * 4. *When my enemies turn back, they stumble and perish*—thus in 1, 2, 3, etc. Not bad.

d) Psalm 10:16; Micah 4:5; Daniel 12:3.
* verse 7. o) As far as the enemy is concerned. compare similar constructions in Psalm 15:4; 18:31; 2 Samuel 4:10; 2 Kings 15:22, etc. Others take this as a direct address (vocative), comparing 2 Kings 9:5. Tiberius and the Dutch scholars interpret it sarcastically and as a question: "O enemy, have the devastations been completed forever as you intended? Have you overturned the cities? Has the memory of them perished for all time?" But others more suitably refer this to God and His judgment against the enemies; see Geier on this passage. p) they are completed, they have now reached an end and ceased. Genesis 47:18; Deuteronomy 2:16; Job 31:40. q) desolations. Ezekiel 26:38; 4:10, 33; Malachi 1:4; Psalm 102:8. h) forever verse 19; Psalm 49:15; Isaiah 13:20; 25:8. i) You have uprooted the cities. The Vulgate <note>The common Latin translation of the Bible</note> says "their cities," meaning the enemies'. compare Isaiah 15:2; 18; Revelation 16:19. k) You, O just judge and avenger (verse 5), have destroyed—that is, uprooted them from the roots. For the word is properly used for plants. compare Jeremiah 1:10; 12:17; 42:10; 45:4; 2 Chronicles 7:20. l) the memory of those enemies has perished (verse 6). To others, "of those cities," and they themselves. Thus also the Syriac and Arabic versions have the feminine suffix. A total slaughter or destruction is signified, as in verse 6. compare Deuteronomy 32:26; Psalm 34:17; 41:6; 109:15; Job 18:17. m) and they themselves, or of them, I say. A similar emphasis of the pronoun occurs in Numbers 14:32; 1 Samuel 20:42; Ezekiel 34:11; Proverbs 22:19; and 23:15. The Greek Septuagint, Vulgate, and Arabic translate this as "with a noise," incorrectly deriving it from the root *hamah* (to roar) as in Psalm 46:4, 7. The Ethiopic version says "likewise all together."

divine judgment Psalm 1:5; Ecclesiastes 11:9; 12:14; Daniel 7:9, 10. v) The Vulgate says "His throne" or "His tribunal." Psalm 45:7; Lamentations 5:19. see Matthew 25:31; Revelation 20:11.
* verse 9. s) And He Himself in Christ, Acts 17:31; Psalm 72:1; John 5:22, 27. t) will judge the world. That is, according to the Targum, the people of the earth. compare Isaiah 13:11; Psalm 90:2; Genesis 18:25. The Greek Septuagint uses the same phrasing as Acts 17:31. u) that is, justly, as the following "in uprightness" suggests, meaning most accurately and correctly. compare Isaiah 11:4; Psalm 72:2; 96:13. x) Psalm 2:1; 7:8, 9; 1 Samuel 2:10. y) Psalm 17:2; 96:10; 98:13; Proverbs 1, 3.

Syriac: "house of refuge." Properly it means a high, fortified, and lofty place. Targum: "a fortress." Deuteronomy 2:36; Isaiah 33:16; Psalm 18:3. compare Psalm 37:39; Proverbs 18:10. c) for the crushed, or the oppressed. Psalm 10:18; 74:21. d) Greek and Vulgate, using a figurative turn: "helper." Arabic: "and his help." e) Greek and Vulgate: "in opportunities." At the opportune time, in distress. Targum and Syriac: "in times of distress." In the midst of tribulations. Psalm 10:1; Ecclesiastes 3:11; Isaiah 33:2; Psalm 138:7. f) Syriac: *antidikias* <note>original: "against the adversary"</note>. To which the Apostle refers in Hebrews 4:16. Others say regarding the sentence (mentioned in verse 1) in those times of extreme distress. compare Daniel 12:1; Deuteronomy 32:36; Isaiah 59:16, 17. Yet no time is to be excluded from this promise, compare 1 Corinthians 10:13; Matthew 28:20.
* verse 11. g) Syriac: "Whence they will trust." Vulgate: "And let them hope in You." Psalm 4:6. A very firm conclusion, as in Psalm 2:10; Malachi 3:6. g) Syriac: "all who know." Vulgate: "those who have known," namely, truly and in practice. Psalm 1:6; 36:11; 1 Samuel 2:12; Isaiah 51:7; Daniel 11:32, etc. h) Psalm 8:2; 91:14; Proverbs 18:10. i) For You have not abandoned, or do not yet abandon, but rather most mercifully hear and protect. compare Joshua 1:5; Isaiah 49:14-16. k) those who sincerely seek You with humble repentance and faith. Psalm 14:2; 34:6, 11; 69:33; 119:2; Isaiah 55:6, 7. Greek Septuagint as in Hebrews 11:6.
* verse 12. l) You therefore, who seek and have known God (verse 11), sing to the Lord, Psalm 7:18. A turning of pious affection (apostrophe), as in Psalm 30:5; 47:7, etc. m) Targum: "who caused His Shechinah <note>The Divine Presence</note> to dwell in Zion." Visibly as if present at the Ark of the Covenant, placed there in the tabernacle, 2 Samuel 6:17. compare Psalm 2:6; 74:2; 76:3, etc. n) declare, announce even among the peoples and nations of the world. Isaiah 12:4; Jeremiah 50:2. o) wondrous deeds or works; Arabic: "His miracles." Jeremiah 32:19; Psalm 66:5; 105:1.
* verse 13. p) Because. He states the cause for praising God; or it can be taken as the subject matter: "That namely..." etc. q) He is a seeker. For just as the pious seek God (verse 11), so He Himself seeks out and avenges their blood. Psalm 10:13; Genesis 9:5; 2 Chronicles 24:22. Greek Septuagint as in Luke 11:15. r) blood and slaughter, namely, as the Targum adds, of the righteous or the just ones. compare Genesis 4, 9; Deuteronomy 33:43; Psalm 72:14; 79:10; Revelation 6:9, 10. s) of the same, namely of blood or slaughters. So says Geier. But the Targum: "He was mindful or remembered the righteous." Psalm 8:5; Exodus 2:24. s) By this negation, the opposite antecedent is more strongly affirmed. compare Isaiah 49:14, 15; Psalm 10:11. t) compare Psalm 34:18; Genesis 4:10; Exodus 3:9; 2 Kings 5:3, 5, etc. x) Vulgate: "of the poor" or "the miserable." Others: "of the gentle." compare verse 19; Psalm 10:12, 17; Isaiah 61:1, etc. But here Schmidius supplies before the following verse, "Of those saying: Have mercy on me." compare verse 15; Psalm 8:2, 3; 5:8, 9, etc.
* verse 14. y) Have mercy on me therefore further, and deal with me not according to my merits, but according to Your grace and my misery. (1) in this form. compare Psalm 4:2; 25:16. z) with compassionate eyes, as in Psalm 25:18; 84:10; 1 Samuel 10:11. a) Greek: "from those who hate me." Syriac: "which is brought upon me by my enemies." Psalm 35:18; 18:18. Others, like Geier: "on account of those who hate me," comparing Psalm 5:9 and similar phrasing in Psalm 12:6, etc. b) You who lift me up, Psalm 18:49. compare Psalm 3:4. c) from the gates of death, and as if from the jaws of the underworld (Orcus). compare Isaiah 38:10; 107:18; Job 38:17.
* verse 15. d) That I may enumerate or announce, just as was proposed in verse 2. e) Psalm 73:28. e) Psalm 35:28; 51:17, etc. f) where formerly, as now in courts, the assemblies of people, judgments, and speeches were held. compare Genesis 23:10; Deuteronomy 22:19; Isaiah 29:21; Jeremiah 26:10; 38:7; Amos 5:10; Proverbs 31:31; Ruth 4:1. This must be connected with the following according to the accents. g) Targum: "in the congregation or Church of Zion." compare Galatians 4:26. Others: "Jerusalem." compare Zechariah 9:8; and by nature Numbers 21:25; Isaiah 1, 8; Micah 1, 18, etc. in opposition to the gates of death mentioned above in verse 14. h) that I may exult, Psalm 2:11; 13:5; Habakkuk 3:18.
