# Psalm 10

1 Why, O Lord, do You stand afar off? Why do You hide yourself in times of trouble?

---

...judgment, in which the wicked, whose souls are brought back from the underworld, will be forced to return there shortly after the resurrection of their bodies; as Gousset <note>Jacques Gousset, 17th-century Hebrew scholar</note> pointed out on page 834. **b)** see verses 6 and 17. **c)** to the lower regions, hell properly so-called, as in Numbers 16:30, 33; Isaiah 5:14, 28:15; Hosea 13:14. Compare Psalm 6:6, Proverbs 1:12, Isaiah 38:10. **d)** The Syriac and Vulgate versions say "and all nations," specifically the impious and incorrigible ones. See verses 16, 20, 21. Compare Revelation 11:18, 14:8, 19:15. **e)** The Vulgate reads: *those who forget God*, maliciously forgetting Him (ב) as in Isaiah 65:11. The Targum <note>The Aramaic translation/paraphrase</note> reads: *those who have forgotten the fear of the Lord*. Compare Psalm 50:22, Job 8:13, Romans 1:18-19, 2:14-15.

**v. 19. f)** *For not forever*, even if God delays His help for a while and the pious are oppressed. Verse 7; Psalm 74:19, 103:9. **g)** "Will be given to oblivion" by God (v. 13). This is an anthropomorphism <note>attributing human characteristics to God</note>, as in verse 13, Psalm 10:11, 13:2, Lamentations 5:20. Compare Isaiah 49:14-15. *He shall be forgotten*, as in Luke 12:6. **h)** *The helpless and afflicted*, anxiously desiring and expecting divine help. Psalm 72:4, 12-13, 113:7, 140:13, Isaiah 14:30. **i)** *Hope and expectation*. Psalm 40:2, 62:6, Job 5:16. **k)** Verse 13; Psalm 12:6, Isaiah 31:7. **l)** Correctly rendered by the Targum and Syriac as *shall not perish*, with the negation repeated from the preceding clause, as in Psalm 1:5 and Deuteronomy 33:6. Compare notes on Isaiah 23:4, 28:27, Ezekiel 11:11, etc. Regarding the phrase, see Psalm 112:10, Proverbs 10:28, Job 8:13, 14:19. **m)** *Unto eternity*. Verse 6; Psalm 21:6, 111:3, 10. Regarding the subject, see Psalm 25:3, Luke 18:7-8, Revelation 6:11, etc. **v. 20. n)** *Arise therefore, O Lord!* Psalm 7:7, 3:8, 10:12, etc. **o)** Lest he gain strength again or prevail. Psalm 18:18, 52:9, 76:2, Ezekiel 38:23, Psalm 68:29, Daniel 11:12. **p)** The Targum says *wicked man*. Til says *the Antichrist*. Compare verse 21; 2 Chronicles 14:10 and the note on Proverbs 3:23. **q)** Let them be judged and punished. Compare verse 5; Psalm 58:11-12, Ezekiel 36:19. **r)** see verses 6, 16, 18. **s)** For You shall exercise justice before Your face, or in Your sight. Compare verse 4; Psalm 34:17, Job 6:28. **v. 21. t)** *He has placed*, or because he established judgment for them as in Psalm 141:3. Gousset (p. 246) thinks it refers to a "war signal," as in Psalm 3:7, 140:6, Isaiah 15:9. **u)** *Terror*. This is the reading of the Masoretic traditional reading <note>original: Kri</note>, the Targum, Schmid, etc., as in Genesis 9:2, Deuteronomy 26:8, 34:12, Jeremiah 32:36. However, the written text <note>original: Cthibh</note>, as well as the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic versions read *Appoint a law* or *a legislator* for them, which Bohlius connects as *appoint for them a teacher for fear*, comparing Joel 2:23. Others derive it from the word for *razor*, as in Judges 13:5, 16:17, 1 Samuel 1:11, comparing Isaiah 7:20 and Ezekiel 5:1. But we rightly retain the former reading as simpler. **x)** *That they may know*, that the impious nations may recognize and feel it (v. 6, 20). **y)** That is, through their own machinations, as in Zechariah 8:23, so they may feel themselves to be wretched men. Compare verse 20 above, Psalm 8:5, 10:18, Isaiah 31:3, Psalm 7:4. **z)** they themselves are... **z)** they themselves are. Genesis 6:2, Ecclesiastes 1:9-10, 17, etc. **a)** verse 17; see note on Habakkuk 3:3.

**Psalm 10, v. 1. b)** *Why?* This is the voice of one reminding and supplicating, as in Psalm 22:2, 88:15, Job 3:11, 13:24, etc. Here, according to the Hebrews, Psalm 10 begins, which the difference in style also suggests. Among the Greeks, the Vulgate, and the Ethiopic versions, Psalm 9 is considered to continue because of the similarity of the subject matter. Therefore, in subsequent numbering, the titles of the Psalms are always one number lower until Psalm 147, from which they made two. Compare 7:25, Isaiah 8:15. This psalm contains, as Gürtler writes in *Prophetic Theology* (p. 99), *the prayers of the oppressed Church, asking for and hoping for liberation from an impious enemy who promises himself an eternal kingdom and speaks insulting words with a proud mouth*. By this enemy, Calovius, Geier, Til, and others understand the Antichrist. Compare the note on Psalm 9:1 and below at verses 16, 18, with Revelation 11:15. According to Schmid’s headings, these are the prayers of the Church against its impious persecutors. He describes: I. Their insolence, blasphemies, and frauds at length (v. 2-11). II. He invokes God against them (v. 12-15). III. He consoles himself and the wretched through the hearing of prayers and the destruction of the persecutors (v. 16-18). Til thinks the occasion for this psalm arose for David from reading Deuteronomy 32:36. Bohlius refers it to Absalom’s rebellion and Ahithophel’s treachery. **c)** *Calovius:* Christ is stirred up against the insolent wicked man; so also Til from verse 16, comparing Isaiah 33:22. **d)** Like a man who is not concerned with the cause: who does not wish to help the one in labor, or even cannot bring aid. Compare Psalm 38:12, 71:11, Jeremiah 14:8-9, Luke 10:31-32. **e)** *Why* (repeated from before) *do You hide*, hide Your face. The Targum says: *You hide yourself in the habitation of the holy*. The Syriac: *and You have turned away Your sight*. Compare v. 11, Psalm 10:1, 15, Lamentations 3:56. Others say *You turn a blind eye*, as in Ezekiel 22:26, Proverbs 28:27. **f)** see Psalm 9:10. **g)** In elation (Psalm 46:4), i.e., pride. Vulgate and Septuagint: *While the wicked is proud*. Compare Psalm 31:19, 73:6, Isaiah 13:11, etc. **h)** the wicked (v. 3); see note on Psalm 9:1, 6, 17, and on the pride and insolence of the Antichrist, here at verse 4 and following, 2 Thessalonians 2:4, compared with the type in Isaiah 14:13-14. **i)** *he pursues* (the wicked pursues the wretched, as in Genesis 31:36, 1 Samuel 17:53). Others, like Tigurinus and Cocceius, following the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Syriac, read: *the poor man burns* or is inflamed (with zeal and indignation against the wicked); compare Psalm 39:4, Jeremiah 20:9, Proverbs 29:2, 2 Corinthians 10:2, 2 Peter 2:8. This is less correct, for דלק (dalak) denotes an active burning, like that in fire, not a passive one. See also note on Psalm 7:14.

# PSALMS 10

<margin>
z) he does not seek, or he cares for nothing. See verse 13.
<term>Qere: His ways</term> <note>original: דרכיו קרי; the "Qere" is the traditional reading that differs from the written "Kethiv" text</note>.
14. Or, as the <term>Targum</term> <note>Aramaic paraphrase</note> and Ethiopian versions supply from what precedes and follows: he does not seek God, as in Psalm 14:2, 24:6, 78:34, and 2 Chronicles 16:12. a) all his thoughts are without God.

3) For the wicked boasts of his heart's<sup>p q r s</sup> desire; and the greedy<sup>t</sup> man blesses<sup>k</sup> and spurns<sup>u</sup> the Lord.
4) The wicked, through the pride<sup>x y</sup> of his countenance<sup>z</sup> <note>literally "his nose," a Hebrew idiom for anger or haughtiness</note>, will not seek<sup>a</sup> [God]; "There is no God" is in all his thoughts.<sup>b c d</sup>

->The poor<- <note>original: חַלְכָּאִים (Halkhaim); a very rare and difficult Hebrew term likely meaning "the wretched" or "unfortunate ones"</note>

---

just as "there is not" <note>original: אֶין</note> is placed in Exodus 21:11, Deuteronomy 32:4, Psalm 88:5, and Lamentations 5:3. Or all his thoughts are these: *there is no God*; one who, namely, would be about to punish his malice. For he acknowledges the existence of God below in verse 11; compare Psalm 14:1 and 36:2. **b)** The Syriac version reads: *in all his thoughts*. verse 2; Jeremiah 23:20. For he raises himself above all things, and demands to be revered in the place of God. 2 Thessalonians 2:4. **v. 5. e)** Geier <note>Martin Geier, 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> along with Luther translates: *His customs endure* or *persist*, compared with Job 20:21. But Schmid <note>Erasmus Schmid</note> says: *They bring forth pains*; the Zurich Bible: *They bring torment*; Cocceius: *His ways terrify*, as in Psalm 29:8. **d)** That is, his actions and established plans. Psalm 1, 1; Hosea 4:9; Proverbs 3:31. **e)** Proverbs 6:14. Because they always seek the slaughter and destruction of the good. Isaiah 59:7-8; Proverbs 1:16 and following. **f)** High, or a *sublime* thing; that is, they are extremely high and very far away from the mind of the wicked man. Compare 2 Kings 19:22; Psalm 56:3. **g)** Your *laws* and *judgments*. Psalm 36:7, 48:12, 119:20, 30, 39, etc. For just as the wicked man does not seek God Himself (verse 4), so he does not care for His judgments. **h)** From his sight. Compare the opposite in 2 Samuel 22:23, Psalm 18:23, and Psalm 51:5. **i)** As far as all his enemies are concerned. The Zurich Bible: *Against all his adversaries*. Psalm 6:8. **k)** Or, *he blows* upon them: he drives them away as if with a breath, and with threats he trusts that he will destroy them; or he blows and ignites the fire of war among them. Ezekiel 21:36; Proverbs 29:8. **v. 6. l)** Wherefore he speaks and thinks in his soul. Verse 11, 13; Psalm 14:1; Deuteronomy 8:17; Zephaniah 1:12. **m)** I shall not be moved, namely, from this happiness and my glory. See Revelation 18:7 and compare Psalm 30:7, Deuteronomy 32:35, Isaiah 41:7, etc. **n)** *unto generation and generation*, or in continuous generations, namely, I shall be; or it will be and succeed for me. Exodus 17:16; Isaiah 13:20; 60:15. **o)** *who may not be in evil*. Others, repeating from the preceding half-verse: *I shall not be moved for perpetual generations, because I shall not be in evil*. Verse 10; compare Deuteronomy 3:24, 1 Samuel 2:23, Ezekiel 39:29, 23:20, and the note on Zechariah 8:20. **p)** Compare Exodus 5:19, 2 Samuel 16:8, Psalm 41:2, Amos 6:3. **v. 7. q)** *By a curse*. The Zurich Bible: *By perjury*. Genesis 26:8, Leviticus 5:1, Numbers 5:27, Deuteronomy 29:18, 20. It indicates, Geier says, the blasphemy of the wicked tongue, by which through perjuries and profanation of sacred names they are injurious to God and neighbor—whom they either deceive by swearing falsely, or whom they curse and devote to destruction in extreme ways whenever they oppose them. van Til specifically understands this as anti-Christian excommunications <note>original: anathematismos</note> against dissenters. **r)** Romans 3:14; compare Psalm 5:10. **s)** *frauds*. Psalm 5:7. **t)** *deceits*. Psalm 55:12, 72:14. **u)** *under the tongue* and his speech they are, or are hidden. Psalm 140:4; Song of Solomon 4:11. *Under the tongue*, that is, in his mind and breast, compared with Psalm 66:18. But the metaphor is drawn from serpents, which keep saliva or venom in small sacs under the tongue and teeth, and pour it into the wound made by the teeth. **x)** Psalm 7:15. **y)** Psalm 5:6, 55:11. **v. 8. z)** *He sits in ambush*, as in Joshua 8:9, Judges 9:34, 35, 2 Chronicles 13:13. Compare here verse 9; Proverbs 1:11. **a)** *of the courts*. Ezekiel 40:19, Nehemiah 13:7. *Or of the villages and towns*. Leviticus 25:31, Joshua 19:8, Isaiah 42:11. That is, according to van Til, of the Churches; just as in Psalm 65:5, to dwell in the courts of God is to be a member of the Church. **b)** *in hiding places*. Psalm 17:12, 64:5. **c)** he slaughters, he kills. Compare Psalm 44:23. **d)** the innocent (Psalm 15:5) and the witnesses of truth. See 94:21. **e)** his eyes look out; or the wicked hide their eyes, looking out from hiding places. **f)** The Septuagint, Vulgate, and Arabic read: "against the poor," or one deprived of protection, as if against a slaughtered crowd or a crowd of strikers; because Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, medieval rabbi</note>, Bohl, and others think it is a compound word, which Geier also defends in this place. Others, from the Arabic root *ch-l-k* <unclear>ch-l-k</unclear> meaning he was dark, black, unlucky and wretched (whence *dark night*, an unlucky work, and a wretched or abject life are spoken of by them), understand it as those who are sad and mournful because of the corrupt morals of the Church. Thus van Til in this place. **(γ)** Verse 10, 14. So the Hebrew *halkhaim* for *troubles* or miseries, Psalm 74:20, 143:3. **g)** The Septuagint, Arabic, Vulgate, and Syriac read: they look back or are intent. Others: they hide themselves, lying in wait from their hiding places. Compare Psalm 56:7, Proverbs 1:11, 18, Psalm 37:32. **v. 9. h)** *He lies in wait*. Psalm 59:4; compare here verse 8. **i)** *in a hiding place*. Verse 8; Psalm 17:12; Habakkuk 3:14. **k)** like a predatory and ferocious lion. Psalm 7:3. **l)** *in his pit or den*. Jeremiah 25:38, Job 38:40. **m)** *I say, he lies in wait*. Deuteronomy 19:11. **n)** *that he may seize*: twice in this place and Judges 21:21. **o)** the oppressed and wretched, deprived of help. Verse 2. **p)** *he seizes* also, etc. **q)** when he draws him, like a fowler or a hunter, with his net. Psalm 9:16, 28:3. Compare a similar contrast with the instrument in Hosea 11:4, Job 24:22, 40:25. Others: when the wicked man pulls his net together. Thus compare Deuteronomy 21:3, Judges 5:14, 2 Kings 22:34. **v. 10. r)** In this way he is truly worn down, crushed. <term>Kal</term> and <term>Niphal</term> <note>Hebrew verb stems</note>. Psalm 38:9, 51:19. **s)** he is cast down, he is forced to humble himself. Isaiah 51:23, Psalm 44:26, Lamentations 3:20. **t)** and he falls through the powerful followers and helpers of the wicked, compared with Psalm 135:10. Or interpret: *and he falls into his strong teeth or claws*, just like those of the lion in verse 9, as a feminine noun; or to be explained by an ellipsis of the noun, as placed in Isaiah 41:21, and just as they are said to fall into hands or the sword, who have been caught by them. For example, Judges 15:18, 2 Chronicles 24:14, Jeremiah 20:4, etc. The Targum reads: *into the strength of his ambushes*.

<column-break/>

**k)** Verse 9; Psalm 14:6, 18:28. **l)** The Ethiopian version reads: and the wretched are caught, as the scholar supplies. The Septuagint, Vulgate, etc.: they are seized. **m)** 1 Samuel 23:26, Ezekiel 12:13, 19:4, 8. Others read it as a wish: Let the wicked therefore be caught, or let them be seized in their own craftiness, compared with Psalm 7:16, 9:16, Proverbs 5:22. But we prefer the former in this context. **m)** Or, through inventions; others, in machinations or wicked counsels. **v. 4.** Psalm 37:7, 139:20. Compare the verb in Deuteronomy 19:19. **n)** which [things]. Psalm 9:16, 12:8. **o)** Or, the wicked devise. Psalm 21:12, 140:3, 5; Jeremiah 11:19.

**v. 3. p)** Or, For the wicked glories, as in Psalm 44:9, 22:23. **q)** see verse 2. **r)** on account of the lust, the desire. Verse 10. **s)** his own soul: because all things succeed according to the wicked wish. Compare Psalm 27:12, Proverbs 21:10; and regarding the phrase, Ecclesiastes 26:8, Psalm 21:3. **t)** The Septuagint and Vulgate use the imperfect: and the greedy man. Isaiah 56:11, Jeremiah 6, 13, Habakkuk 2, 9, 2 Peter 2, 3. He is blessed by flatterers, Isaiah 66:3. Others: and the greedy man blesses, that is, he curses the Lord, compared with Job 1, 11... he blesses himself, Deuteronomy 29, 18. Others, as in Cocceius's Lexicon 118: the wicked man blesses the greedy man; that is, he praises and calls happy the one who seeks something other than the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and has prosperous success in that gain, etc. Compare Malachi 3:14, 15. **u)** Or, he despises. Others use the impersonal: the Lord is blasphemously scorned or provoked. Numbers 14, 11; 16, 30; Deuteronomy 32, 19.

**v. 4. x)** The wicked man. Verse 2, 3. **y)** for the height (Amos 2:9) and the pride (Ecclesiastes 7:8) of his nose. Compare Psalm 131:1. That is, according to the Targum, for the haughtiness of his spirit. Proverbs 16, 18. Note that among the Arabs and others, and even in our own vernacular, the phrase exists: "with a raised nose," that is, he was proud; and "high of nose," for haughty. But the Septuagint, Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopian versions read: "according to the multitude of his anger," as in Psalm 2:5.
<meta>catchword: z) non</meta>

---

**Psalm 10, v. 2.** The word *yidloqu* appears with a <term>Psik</term> <note>a vertical line in Hebrew punctuation used as a separator</note> in manuscripts 1, 5, 24, and in Berlin, according to analogy and the <term>Masorah</term> <note>the traditional body of notes on the Hebrew text</note>; compare the note on Psalm 13:3. Others omit it. **v. 3.** *Ubhotsea* is written fully in manuscript 1 and above in manuscript 5, according to Masorah 1. *Niets* is without a Psik in 1, 3, 11, 23, contrary to the index of Basel f. 61. b. **v. 4.** *Yidrosh* is written with a <term>Beth</term> instead of a <term>Caph</term> in 6 and 9 (which nevertheless have Caph in the margin) and 20. *Drosh* is written fully in 5; thus in manuscript 1 according to Masorah 1. **v. 10.** *Yidkeh* is written fully in 1, perhaps from its Masorah being badly applied; Erfurt manuscripts likewise, and the printed edition, rather looking to the last syllable, which is written here with a <term>He</term>, but elsewhere in the masculine suffix of the 2nd person singular it is without it. **v. 9.** *Lachatoph* is written thus with a <term>Chateph-Patach</term> <note>a Hebrew vowel sign</note> in 1, 3, 5, 21, 22, 23.

<summary>This page provides a scholarly analysis of Psalm 10:3–10, examining the character of the wicked through linguistic comparisons and the opinions of major theologians like Geier and van Til. It focuses on the wicked man's arrogance, his disregard for divine judgment, and his predatory behavior toward the poor and innocent.</summary>

# PSALMS 10 & 11
### PSALM 10:11–18 | PSALM 11:1

<margin>
u) **Kimchi**, as at verse 8: *divided, a crowd of the broken* or *crushed* <note>original: חיל כאים, from the root כאה</note>. Compare Isaiah 16:7, Psalm 109:16, Proverbs 15:13.
v) **The wicked says**, as in verses 6 and 13.
y) That is, **he will not avenge the oppressed** <note>verse 13, Psalm 9:13, 19</note>. He foolishly denies not so much the existence of God as His providence (care and oversight of the world). Compare the note above for verse 4.
z) **He turned away**, as if he **hid his face** from them, so that He would not wish to see them, nor wish Himself to be seen. See Psalms 27:9, 30:8, 44:25.
a) Ethiopic: **so that He does not see**.

<term>Qere</term> <note>The "read" tradition: עניים, "poor"</note>
Psalms 13:4, Habakkuk 1:3.
q) That you might render in its own time, and avenge the injuries inflicted upon the pious. Jeremiah 17:10, 32:19, 2 Thessalonians 1:6.
r) **With your avenging hand**. Verse 12. <term>Targum</term>: *that you may return a good reward to the righteous by your hand*.

11 He has said in his heart, "God has forgotten; He hides His face; He will never see it."
12 Arise, O Lord! O God, lift up Your hand; forget not the humble.
13 Why does the wicked spurn God? He has said in his heart, "You will not require an account."
14 You have seen it, for You observe trouble and grief, to repay it by Your hand; the hapless <note>original: חֵלֵכָה, a rare term for the poor or unfortunate</note> commits himself to You; You have been the helper of the fatherless.
15 Break the arm <note>symbol of power</note> of the wicked and the evil man; seek out his wickedness until You find none.
16 The Lord is King forever and ever; the nations have perished from His land.
17 Lord, You have heard the desire of the humble; You will strengthen their heart; You will cause Your ear to listen.
18 To judge the fatherless and the oppressed, so that man, who is of the earth, may no longer strike terror.

# PSALM 11
1 To the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David. In the Lord I take refuge.

-> Pppp 2 <note>Printer’s signature</note> <-

---

The <term>Septuagint</term> and <term>Vulgate</term> read: *that You might deliver them into Your hand* <note>original: vt tradas eos in manum tuam</note>, but we think the former reading is preferable. Compare Psalm 21:9. **s) in You**, verse 14, Psalm 64:6. *Or upon You*, Psalm 37:5. **t)** He yields, leaves, or casts himself and his whole cause [upon God]. Syriac: *he leaves himself*. Septuagint and Vulgate: *the poor is left to You*. Ethiopic: *he is cast upon You*. Targum: *he hopes in You*. Arabic: *he is comforted*. Compare Genesis 39:6. **u)** **the poor**. See verses 8, 10. **x)** Vulgate: **the orphan**, or *of the orphans*. **y)** You have been, You are, and You always will be. **z)** **the helper**. See John 14:8. 

**v. 15. a)** **Shatter** or *break*, that is, the power, strength, forces, and helpers. Psalms 44:4, Isaiah 33:2, Jeremiah 48:25, Ezekiel 30. **b)** Verses 2, 3, 4, 13. **c)** **as for the evil**, or *of the malicious*. **d)** Thus you shall search out. Verse 13, Psalm 9:13. **e)** Deuteronomy 9:17. **f)** **so that You may remove it from the midst, and find it no more.** Ethiopic: *so that it is not found*. Compare Ezekiel 23:48, Psalm 37:36, Job 20, Revelation 16:20, 18:21, 2 Thessalonians 2:8, Matthew 13:41, 42. For a similar connection of accents, see Psalm 17. 

**v. 16. g)** Jehovah the Son, with the Father and the Holy Spirit. See note on verse 1. **h)** **He is and shall be King.** Psalms 2:6, 21:2, 45:1, 146:10, Zechariah 14:9, Daniel 7:14, Revelation 11:15. **i)** **forever and ever**, that is, perpetual and eternal: just as the "covenant of the age" is perpetual. Genesis 9:16. Compare Psalm 9:6, 8, Psalm 21:5, 29:10, 45:7, Jeremiah 10:10, Lamentations 5:19, 1 Timothy 1:17. Moses had already proclaimed this in Exodus 15:18. **k)** **they perished** of old, and finally they shall perish utterly. Psalm 2:12, 9:4, 6. **l)** **the nations**, Psalm 9:6, 16. **m)** **from His land**, not only from Canaan—which He appropriated to Himself in Leviticus 25:23—but also from the entire world. Psalm 24:1, 21:11, 68:3. 

**v. 17. n)** **Desire**. See verse 3, Psalm 21:3, Proverbs 11. **o)** Verse 12, Psalm 9:13, 19. **p)** Isaiah 38:5, 65:24, Psalm 3:3, 5, 4:2, 6. **q)** **You confirm and make certain their heart.** See Psalm 51:12, 57:8, 78:8, 37, 1 Chronicles. Geierus: *both through the Word and frequent outward experience of help, and by the internal confirmation of the Holy Spirit.* See Romans 8:26, 1 John 3:19–22. **r)** Luther and Geierus: *that Your ear may attend, or that You might turn Your ear.* Psalm 5:3, Proverbs 2:2. Others read it as a wish: *May You confirm their heart, may You turn Your ear.* Or in the future tense: *You will prepare their heart, You will attend Your ear.* 

**v. 18. s)** **To judge**, so that You might judge, acquit, and avenge, as a just judge. Psalm 9:5, 7:9, Isaiah 1, 17. **t)** **the orphan** (verse 14) and **the crushed** (Psalm 9:10). Syriac: *the fatherless and the needy*. **u)** **so that he does not continue to exercise violence**, that is, *that he might not be terrible anymore.* **x)** Isaiah 2:19, 21, 47:12. **y)** **wretched and mortal man.** **z)** **of the earth**, that is, a descriptive way of saying *earthly*, both regarding origin (Genesis 3:19, John 3:31) and corruption (Philippians 3:19).

---

**Psalm 11:1. a)** See Psalm 4:1. **b)** Psalm 3:1. This psalm describes the trial of the pious man, both through the world's allurements (as some think from verse 1) and persecutions (verse 2, 3), but trust is placed in God (verse 1) while awaiting His just judgment (verse 4 onwards). According to May's *Economy of the Old Testament*, the theme of Psalm 11 is the same as Psalm 7; written when David wandered through the mountains with no fixed home to escape the cruel hands of his rebellious son, and seeing with a prophetic spirit the persecutions of the Christian Church by the Antichrist, whose destruction is clearly hinted at in verse 6. Certainly, here as elsewhere, the destruction of the wicked and the salvation of the pious are predicted. However, with Bohlius and others, we prefer to refer the occasion of the psalm to 1 Samuel 23:13. **c)** Targum: *in the word of the Lord*, etc. See Psalms 2:12, 36:8, 5:13, 55:23. Beneath this is an "enthymeme" <note>a logical argument with an unstated premise</note> which forms the foundation of the whole psalm: namely, that *hope trusting in God never returns confused.*

---

<margin>
**v. 13.** l) *Why [does the wicked]... [You will] prepare their heart, You will turn Your ear.* In the future: *You will dispose their heart, You will attend Your ear.* **v. 18.** i) See verse 4. u) k) Verses 6, 11. l) He will not search out or avenge his wickedness. Verses 4, 15. See verse 11 and Psalm 9:13.
**v. 14.** m) **You see** all things, whatever he might persuade himself to the contrary. Verses 11, 13, 2 Kings 9:26, Isaiah 38:5, Psalm 35:22, Lamentations 3:59. God's omniscience is expressed through the human metaphor of "seeing," says Geierus. Compare also Psalm 11:4, Job 11:11, etc. n) Trouble. Verse 7, Psalm 7:15, Habakkuk 1:3, 13. o) <unclear>distress</unclear>, regarding the sadness and indignation brought upon the pious. Proverbs 17:25, Ecclesiastes 7:3, 11:10. p) You perceive well, You gaze upon. Vulgate: *You consider*.
</margin>

**v. 10.** <term>Hal-ka'im</term> <note>the crushed ones</note>. Written thus with the letter *Lamed* without a <term>Schua</term> <note>a vowel point indicating a short "e" or no sound</note> in some manuscripts, correctly following the analogy of the **Qere** <note>the traditional reading</note>, to which the vowel points are perpetually adjusted. Others write it with a *Schua*. **v. 13.** The word for "what" <note>original: מָה</note> appears without a <term>Pesiq</term> <note>a vertical line serving as a musical or textual pause</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 7, and others, which follows the grammatical analogy. **v. 15.** The word for "seek" <note>original: תִּדְרוֹשׁ</note> is written fully in some versions according to their <term>Masorah</term> <note>tradition of textual preservation</note>. **v. 14.** "You have seen" <note>original: רָאִתָה</note> is written with an emphatic *Pesiq* in many manuscripts, similar to Job 24:14. "And grief" <note>original: וָכַעַס</note> uses the <term>Revia</term> accent <note>a diamond-shaped musical mark</note> in some versions, which creates an awkward sense. The word for "hapless" <note>original: חֵלֵכָה</note> is written with a *Segol* vowel in most sources, though others use a *Tsere*. **v. 15.** "Break the arm of the wicked" appears in sources 1 and 3. The word for "You will seek" <note>original: תִּדְרוֹשׁ</note> follows the tradition of **Ben Asher**, while **Ben Naphtali** writes it slightly differently. **v. 17.** Some write "humble" <note>original: עֲנָוִים</note> but read it as "poor" <note>original: עֲנִיִּים</note>. For our accent marks, compare Psalm 16:8 and Psalm 83:19.

# PSALM 11

<margin>
**Flee** <note>original Hebrew Qere: *Nudi*</note>
**of the wicked in verse 3** or "those who entice" in verse 4 and following. l) See Psalm 1:1. m) **They bend the bow**, as in Psalm 7:13. The Syriac version says "they have filled the bow," which compares with Zechariah 9:13. n) Psalm 7:13. o) **The arrow**, or "his arrows," one after another. p) **Upon the string**, or the cord, usually fitted to bows. Job 30:11; Judges 16:7-9. Compare Psalm 21:13, "he bends the bow." q) **To shoot**. u) **For the foundations** (z) Isaiah 1:10 <note>meaning: not only the pious and just people</note>. x) **Are destroyed**. Psalm 28:5; Psalm 58:7; Ezekiel 30:4. y) **The righteous man therefore**, Psalm 1:5. Was there such insolence? Job 11:8, 35:6. Others, following the Vulgate: **But what has the righteous man done** or attempted against the wicked? Compare Isaiah 4:1, 4; Micah 2:1.
</margin>

<margin>
d) **How then**. An expression of wonder, as in Psalm 73:19, and simultaneously of denial and reproach, as in Genesis 30:9, 44:34. e) **You say**, you adversaries, or even my companions and friends. See Geier <note>Martin Geier, a 17th-century Hebraist</note>. f) **Soul**, Psalm 3:3, 7:3, 105:18. g) **Flee, O soul**, Jeremiah 50:8; and "wander with uncertain dwellings," Genesis 4:12, 14. Or "flee, O companions of David." Or, according to his own opinion, or in a mixed speech—part direct and part indirect (like Song of Solomon 7:10)—**move yourself**, or **betake yourself**, or **betake yourselves**, to the mountain, namely, your mountain. See Psalm 34:16 and below in verse 4, "in the mountains." The Septuagint <note>Greek translation</note> for Psalm 11:14, 132:4, 102:139. The Greek says "to the mountain." The Ethiopic says "your mountain." i) **They intimately explore**. Vulgate: "Transmigrate?"
</margin>

<margin>
b) "To where shall I transmigrate?" d) The Oriental versions either omit this. The Targum: "Migrate to the mountains." The Syriac: "Migrate and dwell in the mountains." verse 5. l) "The Lord says." verse 4. Geier: To the divine omniscience (verse 4) he now joins justice, which cannot see crimes go unpunished, nor allow innocence to pass without defense or vindication. m) **The righteous**, verse 3. Targum: "the righteous ones" (plural), for it is a singular used distributively, as in Psalm 5:13. n) **He tests and explores**, verse 4. Psalm 17:3, 26:2; Job 23:10. And He "approves," which is clear from the following opposition. The Arabic: "He tempts"—namely, through various afflictions and trials, so that it may be clear who sincerely loves Him. See Psalm 66:10, Proverbs 3:12, Hebrews 12:5-6, Isaiah 48:10, Zechariah 13:9. o) **But the one loving [violence]**, and prone to it with every habit and inclination of his mind. Compare verse 7, Proverbs 17, Matthew 10:29. Targum uses the plural as before: "but those who love." p) **Violence**. See Psalm 7:17, Habakkuk 1:2-3. q) **His soul hates and intimately turns away from**. This is an anthropomorphism <note>speaking of God in human terms</note> to express more strongly God's deep-seated hatred toward sin: because God, through His internal and essential attributes, cannot help but hate the rebellious. Compare Psalm 5:5-6, Leviticus 24:2-3, 26:20, Isaiah 1:14. It is so far from the truth that the wicked can promise themselves God's favor because of their current prosperity (Psalm 10:3); rather, they will experience the horrible judgment of God unless true repentance follows His long-suffering. Romans 2:4, etc.

r) **For the Lord will rain down**, as He once did upon the overthrown Sodom and Gomorrha, Genesis 19:24. See Ezekiel 38:22. But Rabbi Judah in the *Yalkut* <note>a collection of Jewish legends/homilies</note> proves from here a "flood of fire," regarding which see also the note on Psalm 29:10. Targum: "He will send down the rains of vengeance." s) verse 2. t) Vulgate, etc.: **Snares**. Greek: *pagidas*. Luke 21:35. e) an upright and pious man, verse 2. Micah 7:2.
f) or used neutrally: *the right*, and as the Septuagint <note>ancient Greek translation</note>, Ethiopic, Syriac, and Vulgate <note>ancient Latin translation</note> have it, *equity*. Psalm 37:37. They refer back to verse 4 and Psalm 17:2.
g) The Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, and Ethiopic versions read: *his face or his countenance*; so also the commentators David Kimchi and Moses ben Isaac, who collect a similar suffix, as they think, in the singular in Job 22:2. But Gussetius (page 458) argues not poorly (as Rabbi Japhet also has in Abraham ben Ezra’s commentary on this passage, comparing Genesis 20:13) that it means: *their face*, namely, of the "Elohim," the triune God. Compare Gussetius’s further notes on Psalm 7:10. Regarding the present matter, see Psalm 1:6, 33:18, 34:16, Micah 6:9, Job 36:7, 1 Peter 3:12. Others translate: *the faces of the pious or of men will at last see what is right and equitable*; and in a reversed proposition the Targum <note>Aramaic paraphrase</note> says: *the righteous shall see the appearance of His face*. The Arabic version says: *and the upright shall see His face*, an explanation which Kimchi also brings forward, comparing Psalm 17:15, though with a double change in grammatical number. We set aside many other things brought forward by others which are more intricate.

<margin>
this may be said of those who incited Absalom against him, which is also Bohl's opinion regarding the occasion of this psalm. Compare the notes on Psalm 3:1, 9:1, etc.
v. 2. l) *Save*, grant salvation and help, O Lord! Psalm 3:8, 6:5, 20:10.
m) The Septuagint: *for he is consumed*; the Vulgate: *he has failed*. The Targum uses the plural: *the pious ones are consumed*. (s) see Psalm 7:10.
n) Psalm 4:4, 18:26. Compare 1 Kings 19:10, Romans 11:3, Isaiah 57:1, Micah 7:2, Revelation 3:4.
o) because they are diminished. The Septuagint: *they have failed, they have ceased*. (1) This connects with the root <term>אפס</term> <note>meaning to cease or come to an end</note>. Psalm 77:9, Genesis 47:15, 16. Just as these roots are related in Proverbs 16:26 and Job 33:7.
p) The Vulgate: *truths*. The Septuagint: fidelities. But the Targum: the truthful or the faithful. Compare Psalm 31:24. Thus Abraham ben Ezra says it is an adjective in this place, not a noun, as in Isaiah 26:2. It occurs in (8) Deuteronomy 32:20, 2 Samuel 20:19, Proverbs 13:17, etc. q) Psalm 11:4. Compare Jeremiah 7:28.

v. 3. r) On the contrary, they speak *Vanity and lies* (for the word denotes both). Kimchi: For they say with their mouths what they do not feel in their souls; that which is empty. See Exodus 20:7, 23:1, Isaiah 59:4, Ezekiel 13:8, Psalm 24:4, 41:7, 144:8, 11. s) *each one* Genesis 11:3, Ezekiel 1, 9. t) *with his neighbor* Exodus 11:2, Leviticus 19:18, Ephesians 4:25. u) *with a lip or lips*, that is, by the figure of metonymy, with speech. v. 4. Compare Psalm 31:19, 120:2, Proverbs 17:17. x) The Septuagint: *of flatteries or of flattering words*. v. 4. Compare Proverbs 6:24, and the verb in Psalm 55:22, Proverbs 2:16, 7:5. Kimchi says it is a noun or an adjective, with the word <term>אמרות</term> <note>original: "words"</note> understood. Abraham ben Ezra thinks the same regarding the adjective, comparing Genesis 42:7, 30: "he spoke harsh things." Compare Psalm 30:10. y) *with a heart and a heart*, that is, with a double mind; while they display friendship with words, they nevertheless cherish hatred in their breast. The repetition of the same word sometimes indicates diversity, whereas in contrast, 1 Chronicles 12:33, <term>בלא לב ולב</term> <note>original: "without a heart and a heart"</note> signifies a whole heart and a mind not at all deceitful; compare verse 38 there and Deuteronomy 25:13, 14. z) See Jeremiah 9:7.

v. 4. a) The Septuagint: *But the Lord shall cut off*; the Targum adds: *from the world*. The Ethiopic: *He will uproot*. Others, following the Septuagint, read it as a prayer: *May He cut off*. The former is a prophecy, the latter a petition. For the verb, see Isaiah 14:22, Malachi 2:12. b) lips of fraud. The Septuagint and Vulgate: *deceitful*. See verse 3. c) Isaiah 54:17, Psalm 52:6. d) *great things*, and speaking contemptuously of God and His holy ones. See Psalm 31:19, 1 Samuel 2:3, Job 5:9. Tilleman compares Daniel 17:8, 11, 25, Revelation 13:5, 6, 15, 2 Thessalonians 2:4–8, 2 Peter 2:18, Jude verse 16.

v. 5. e) *Those men*, who are equipped with those deceitful lips and tongues from verse 4, think or say. The Targum: *Those who, denying the foundation, say*. Compare Psalm 10:6, 11. f) *we will prepare strength and lordship for our tongue*, or *we will make our tongue prevail*. Aben Ezra: *on account of our tongue we shall be strong*. But the Targum, Rashi, and the Septuagint say: *by our tongue we shall prevail*. For the Hiphil <note>Hebrew causative verb form</note> see Daniel 9:27. On this matter, compare Psalm 73:9. g) *Our lips (verse 4) are with us* and in our power, Proverbs 3:28, *or are as a help to us*, and are ready, compare 2 Kings 9:32. For such men do not have the Spirit. Jude verse 19. h) *for who*? He denies it, as in Psalm 6:6, Ecclesiastes 8:1, comparing Exodus 5:2, Psalm 10:11, 13. i) *is Lord to us*, or is our Lord, who might hinder what pleases us and what has been decreed. Compare Psalm 73:9, Daniel 3:15, 11:36.

The prefix Mem denotes the impelling cause*, as in Judges 2:18, Obadiah verse 10. l) *of the oppressed and afflicted*. Psalm 9:13, 14. m) *because of the groaning* (4) Malachi 2:13, Psalm 79:11, 102:21. Compare the verb used for the groaning of a dying man in Ezekiel 26:15. n) Psalm 9:19, 69:34, Isaiah 41:17. o) *now*, after my hour has come. See Isaiah 42:14, etc. p) *I will break the delays of patience and rise up for vengeance*. See Psalm 3:8, 7:7, 44:27, Numbers 10:35, Isaiah 14:22, Jeremiah 31:26, Zephaniah 3:8. q) *says the Lord*. Isaiah 33:10. It is a prophecy, say Aben Ezra and Kimchi. r) *I will set* Isaiah 26:1, namely, those wretched and afflicted ones. s) *in safety*, just as was requested in verse 2, so that they cannot be moved by any storm. See Psalm 50:23. The Targum: *I will set salvation for my people*. See Isaiah 51:5, Habakkuk 3:13. t) The Septuagint: *him whom the wicked man puffs at*. Thus Gussetius (page 667): *against whom that one was blowing*, comparing Psalm 10:5. Kimchi: *him for whom he was setting snares*, comparing Proverbs 29:8. Others: *that he may breathe more for himself*, comparing Song of Solomon 2:16, Acts 3:19. The first explanation, however, is more certain.

### 13

# For the leader: a Psalm of David.

2 **How long,**<sup>r</sup> O Lord? Will You forget me<sup>s</sup> forever?<sup>t</sup> **How long**<sup>u</sup> will You hide<sup>x</sup> Your face<sup>y</sup> from me?<sup>z</sup>
<gloss>How long, O Lord, will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?</gloss>
3 **How long**<sup>a</sup> shall I take<sup>b</sup> counsels<sup>c</sup> in my soul,<sup>d</sup> with sorrow<sup>e</sup> in my heart<sup>f</sup> daily?<sup>g</sup> **How long**<sup>h</sup> shall my enemy<sup>k</sup> be exalted<sup>i</sup> over me?
4 **Look upon me;**<sup>l</sup> answer me,<sup>m</sup> O Lord my God! Lighten<sup>n</sup> my eyes, lest I sleep<sup>o</sup> the sleep of death;<sup>p</sup>
5 **Lest** my enemy **say,**<sup>q</sup> "I have prevailed over him";<sup>r</sup> lest my foes<sup>s</sup> rejoice because<sup>t</sup> I am moved.<sup>u</sup>
6 **But I**<sup>v</sup> have trusted<sup>y</sup> in Your mercy;<sup>x</sup> my heart shall rejoice<sup>z</sup> in Your salvation. I will sing<sup>a</sup> to the Lord, because<sup>b</sup> He has dealt bountifully<sup>c</sup> with me.

->For the leader<-

---

Luther, Volume II, Jena Latin edition, folios 139–141: Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> understands this as being about the entire people of Israel; but Kimchi understands it as being about the present exile of the Jews. Tillius understands it as the pious and witnesses of truth under the rule of the Antichrist, before the healing purification of the Church; he presents here, under one person, I. A Complaint in verses 2–3. II. A Prayer in verses 4–5. III. Consolation in verse 6. But Schmid, in the *Appendix to the Commentary on the Psalms*, page 4 and following, says this Psalm speaks of Christ, and contains I. The sufferings and temptations of Christ, verses 2–3, comparing Psalm 22:2 and Hebrews 5:7. II. A Prayer under temptation and suffering, verses 4–5. III. Consolation under suffering, verse 6. As for us, we can simply reject none of these, since all things ultimately redound to Christ—both those things moved by that infernal serpent <note>the devil</note> against Christ Himself, and against His members, whether individually or collectively in the Church (Genesis 3:15). Thus, Luther’s explanation pleases us most, which demonstrates that the words of this Psalm apply not only to David and, by his example, to every tempted person, but also to Christ Himself. Compare John 12:27 for verses 2–3, and Matthew 27:39 for verse 5.

**verse 2.** **r)** *How long?* Psalm 6:4, Job 8:2, Exodus 15:28, Numbers 14:11. **s)** *as if You forget me?* Psalm 9:13, 19; Psalm 42:10. **t)** *forever* Psalm 9:7, 19. Compare Psalm 79:5, Psalm 89:47. **u)** *Anaphora* <note>the repetition of the phrase "How long"</note>, arising from the most intense emotion of the one praying. **x)** *as if in anger You hide Your face.* The Targum: *the splendor of Your countenance.* Compare Psalm 10:11, Psalm 22:25, Psalm 27:9, Psalm 69:18, Deuteronomy 31:17, 18, Isaiah 59:2, Exodus 33:23, 24, 29; and the opposite in Psalm 4:7. **y)** *from me*, as if I were unworthy of Your sight. **z)** See verse 2.

**verse 3.** **a)** *shall I place, or arrange?* Psalm 12:6, Psalm 101:3. Namely, by night; Schmid notes that this is to be understood here in opposition to the "daily" that follows. **b)** *counsels* Isaiah 25:1, Proverbs 20:5. Namely, how I might finally escape from these hardships. It is an elegant phrase, he says, which denotes the turning over of thoughts: when now this, now that counsel must be taken, comparing many things together until a certain one is chosen. **c)** *and sadness or grief*, the Vulgate: *sorrow*. Jeremiah 20:18, Psalm 116:3. **d)** *in my heart and my soul*. Compare Proverbs 15:13, 30; chapter 17:22. **e)** *not only by night, but by day as well.* The Vulgate: *through the day.* Arabic and Ethiopic versions: *all day.* Psalm 1:2. **f)** *It is trivial* that the Rabbis conclude from this fourfold repetition (see note on verse 2) the four exiles of their nation: Babylonian, Persian, Greek, and Roman. See Rashi, Kimchi, and others. **g)** *shall exalt, shall lift himself up.* Vulgate: *shall be exalted* Psalm 12:9, Psalm 66:7. **h)** *my enemy.* Verse 5, Psalm 6:11. **i)** *over me*, so that I succumb and he rules.

**verse 4.** **k)** *Look, therefore,* with eyes of grace, and do not turn Your face from me any longer (verse 2). Compare Psalm 10:14, Isaiah 63:15, etc. **l)** Vulgate: *and hear me, answer me.* Targum: *and look upon my prayers*, and thus show that You have not forgotten me (verse 2). Compare Psalm 3:5, Psalm 4:2, Psalm 17:6. **m)** See notes on Psalm 3:8, Psalm 7:2. **n)** *illuminate* in these darknesses of miseries, which almost kill me, *my eyes*, namely with the light of Your grace and help. Compare Psalm 19:9, Psalm 118:27, Ecclesiastes 8:1, also Ezra 9:8, Isaiah 59:9, Psalm 97:11, etc. The Targum: *illuminate my eyes in Your law, lest I sin and sleep with those who are guilty of death.* Tillius, following his own opinion (see verse 1), says: so that I may discern truth from lies, and recognize Your most healthy counsel under these hard things, lest I perish in spiritual and eternal death. Compare Habakkuk 1:12. **o)** *lest I sleep.* In this way death is called *sleep* in Psalm 76:6, Job 3:13. **p)** *death*, or *the sleep of death*, as Rashi and Ibn Ezra note, comparing Jeremiah 51:39, 57; add Psalm 104:29.

**verse 5.** **q)** *Lest my enemy say* (verse 3), the devil the tempter, or his instruments. The Targum: *Evil desire.* **r)** *I have overcome him.* Vulgate: *I have prevailed against him.* Genesis 30:8, chapter 32:26, Psalm 129:2. **s)** *and lest they from every side*—my enemies who press me with distress—Psalm 3:2. **t)** *rejoice* (verse 6). Psalm 9:15, Habakkuk 1:15, Proverbs 24:17. **u)** Or *that I am moved*, or according to the Vulgate and Ethiopic *if I am moved*, Arabic *if I should slip.* The Targum: *if I should turn aside from Your ways.* Compare Psalm 10:6, Psalm 17:5, Psalm 125:1.

**verse 6.** **x)** Or *I, however*; whatever they might say (verse 5), or whatever most sad temptations might suggest to the mind (verses 3, 4). Compare Psalm 5:8. **y)** *in Your grace and mercy* Psalm 31:8, 17. Which is certain for all who observe Your covenant and testimonies (Psalm 25:10). Schmid, according to his own opinion (see verse 1): *in Your mercy toward the human race*, by which You will not abandon the work of their redemption. Compare Psalm 21:8. **z)** *I have confidence, I have trusted.* Psalm 4:6. **a)** *my heart rejoices and exults* Zechariah 10:7. Compare 1 Samuel 2:1. Kimchi: He says this in opposition to verse 5. **b)** Psalm 3:9, Psalm 9:15, Psalm 31:3. **c)** *indeed I will even sing to the Lord.* Compare Exodus 15:1, Judges 5:3, Psalm 27:6. **d)** *that.* Others, such as the Targum: *because.* **e)** Or *He has repaid me.* Vulgate: *who* (Targum: *because*) *He has given good things to me*, or has bestowed them upon me in the midst of all those miseries and evils. The Septuagint and Arabic: *who has done good to me.* Ethiopic: *who has helped me.* See note on Psalm 7:5 and compare Psalm 103:2, 10; Psalm 116:7, Psalm 119:17, Psalm 142:8, Proverbs 11:17, Isaiah 63:7, etc.

---

**verse 8.** **You, O Lord** <note>Hebrew: Atah Yehovah</note> so in manuscripts 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. But **And You, O Lord** in 1. Both readings are good for the sense; but the latter goes against the analogy of the composition: for the **substitute** <note>accent mark</note> does not take place unless the Atnach <note>a major pause accent</note> is struggling. **You will preserve him** without the Pfik <note>a vertical line accent</note> in 1, 2, 3. See the note on Psalm 13:3.
**verse 9.** **vileness** <note>Hebrew: zulluth</note> with a Cholem mark in the plural in 6, 9, 13, 20, 23. But 10 has neither Cholem nor Shurek.
**Psalm 13, verse 1. For the leader** <note>Hebrew: Lamnatzeach</note> so with a bare Rbhia accent in this place in all except the Berlin manuscript. See the note on Psalm 4:1. **verse 2. How long** <note>Hebrew: ad-anah</note> without a Pfik in 2, 3, 7, 8, 15, 16, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23. So in the future Berlin manuscripts except the Masoretic ones, which have it at verse 3. **verse 3. How long** with a Pfik in 14, 24. So in some Berlin manuscripts with a Yerach accent in 2, 3, 5, 10, 13, 14, 20—against the analogy, except for 2, where the preceding has a Mahpach with a Pfik in 2, 5, 24. This is according to the Berlin manuscripts against Masoretic 1 and the Erfurt manuscripts, which require the Shalsheleth accent in the poetic books eight times without a Pfik, specifically here, where it depends on the Silluk, and in Psalm 3:3, 34:8, 65:2, 68:15, 72:3, 137:9, Proverbs 1:9, and 6:27. In these places it depends on the substitutes for the Atnach and Rbhia-geresh, and therefore correctly lacks the distinctive Pfik according to the Masorah itself in its notes on Genesis 19:16.
**verse 6. to the Lord, because He has dealt bountifully** so in 2 and similarly in the future 5.

<header>PSALM 14. יד.</header>

<margin>
**Psalm 14, verse 1. f)** See Psalm 4:1. **g)** The Targum <note>The Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible</note> notes: through the Spirit of prophecy concerning David. See Psalm 3:1. **According to Kimchi’s view** <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish scholar also known as Radak</note>, this psalm, like Psalm 13, deals with the current exile of the Jews, and thus speaks not of their own impiety but of the impiety of the nations. However, the divine Apostle <note>Paul</note> teaches us otherwise in **Romans 3:9–19**. For in this Psalm, as *Schmid’s* headings have it, there is described: **I. The universal corruption of the entire human race** after the fall of Adam (verses 1-3). **II. The Jews and their impious leaders are heavily rebuked** because they would not acknowledge that corruption (verses 4-6). And thus **III. the desire of the pious and the expectation of Christ**, as the Syriac inscription has it, is explained (verse 7). Furthermore, **Brentius** <note>Johannes Brentz, a German Reformer</note> attributes the excellence of this psalm to the fact that it is repeated again later in **Psalm 53** with only a few words changed. *Schmid*, however, notes from the title of Psalm 53:1 that it was first sung with the usual musical instruments. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> in this place has "machalath" <note>original: μαχαלאθ, a musical term or instrument</note> adapted by David, and as **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch humanist and jurist</note> wished, the Apostle most firmly demonstrates in Romans 3:10 and following that all people, both Jews and Gentiles, are under sin and deprived of the glory of God, and cannot be saved except through the grace of God and the redemption of Christ. And **Calvin** writes well on this passage: "All of us, when we are born, bring from the womb this madness described by David and the stench of our whole life, and we remain such until God, by His secret grace, remakes us into new creatures." See **Calov** <note>Abraham Calovius, a Lutheran theologian</note> on this passage.
**h)** He says and thinks to himself. Psalm 10:6. Compare Ezekiel 8:12, Malachi 3:13. **i)** The fool. The Septuagint and Vulgate say: the unwise; not so much physically as theologically, and in spiritual matters, even if he seems to himself to be most wise, or is otherwise endowed with the best reason. For all people in the state of nature are such fools according to **Ezra** <note>likely referring to Abraham Ibn Ezra</note>, but not those in the state of grace, where they are called the people of God, the generation of the righteous, etc. (verses 4, 5): namely, those alienated from the life of God **Ephesians 4:18**, not born again, justified, or sanctified. Compare Deuteronomy 32:21, Isaiah 32:5-6, Psalm 74:22, Luke 12:20, Romans 1:21-23.
**k)** In his heart or soul. Psalm 10:6. Where the secret principles and seeds of this impiety lie hidden, even if they do not always break out into

See **Psalm 10:4.** For man is prone to atheism; and he is rightly accused of this crime who does not love God as God with his whole soul or heart **Deuteronomy 6:5, Romans 1:21**, but bears a hidden enmity against the Supreme Deity **Romans 8:6**, and lives as an atheist in the world **Ephesians 2:12, Titus 1:16.** **m)** Hence they corrupt themselves and their actions, as follows, and as the Targum supplies; or they act corruptly and wickedly. See **Genesis 6:11, 12; Exodus 32:7; Deuteronomy 31:29; Judges 2:19; Hosea 9:9; Zephaniah 3:7.** **n)** And they make them abominable or cursed. **1 Kings 21:26, Ezekiel 16:52.** **o)** Their actions and works: internal and external. **Verse 2. r)** For the omniscient Lord Himself, who searches the hearts and kidneys <note>original: "renes," a biblical metaphor for the seat of emotions and conscience</note> of men **Psalm 7:10.** **s)** Psalm 33:13, Isaiah 40:22. **t)** He has indeed looked forth, and always looks forth. Spoken anthropomorphically <note>describing God with human characteristics</note> as in **Exodus 14:24, Psalm 53:3, Psalm 102:20.** **u)** Upon the sons of Adam, **Psalm 11:4**, that is, upon the whole human race, as they are after the fall of Adam in their nature, and in opposition to the people of God **verse 4.** Compare **Genesis 6:1, 5; Job 34:21.** **x)** Compare **Genesis 11:5, chapter 18:21.** **y)** Whether there were any of them. **z)** Understanding, not a fool as in verse 1, who might have true understanding of divine things, or seriously care for his own salvation. **Amos 5:13, Psalm 2:10, Proverbs 10:5, 19; Job 34:27, 35.** **a)** Who would seek God with a sincere desire or study of the heart, to know and worship Him rightly. **Psalm 9:11, Psalm 10:4, Psalm 22:27.** **Calovius:** one who is either not corrupted in mind in perceiving spiritual things, or in will in embracing those things which are good. The Targum: *seeking doctrine or instruction from the Lord.*

**Verse 3. b)** But that entire group and that huge multitude of men, all and each, Jews and Gentiles, as to all subjects and times, are viewed in the state of their corrupted nature. See note on verses 1 and 2. **c)** He or they have turned aside from the right and good way, as **Abraham Ibn Ezra and Kimchi** supply; or from that understanding and study of seeking God in verse 2. Compare **1 Kings 15:5, chapter 22:43; 2 Kings 22:2; Ezekiel 6:9.** The Targum: *All have turned back, namely from the Lord; compare Isaiah 1:4.* **d)** All together **Psalm 19:10.** Jews and Gentiles alike **Romans 3:19.** **e)** They have become or were stinking in their souls and loathsome in their works before God. **Abraham Ibn Ezra:** corrupted; **Kimchi:** abominable, stinking and foul, rejected or reprobate. The Targum: *they have become remiss or negligent.* **(3)** Psalm 53:4. **Job 15:16.** The Arabic root in the 8th Conjugation means *it turned sour*, as when milk turns sour, etc. **The Septuagint** says "they have become useless" <note>original: ηχρειωθησαν</note>, as in **Romans 3:12.** But in **Job 15:16** "cursed," which pleases **Gussetius** <note>Jacques Gousset, a French Hebrew scholar</note> page 67 and following. **f)** *There was no one who did good* verse 1; namely, out of his own nature, which is only prone to evil **Genesis 6:5, chapter 8:21.** **g)** None, I say. The negation is repeated with emphasis. **h)** Even. He exaggerates, as in that passage **Proverbs 14:13, 20.** **i)** Not even one. Compare **Isaiah 59:16.** That this was by no means said hyperbolically, as **Grotius** wished, the Apostle most firmly demonstrates in **Romans 3:10** and following, proving from here that all men, both Jews and Gentiles, are under sin and deprived of the glory of God, and cannot be saved except through the grace of God and the redemption of Christ. And **Calvin** writes well on this passage: *"All of us, when we are born, bring from the womb this madness described by David and the stench of our whole life, and we remain such until God, by His secret grace, remakes us into new creatures."* See **Calov** on this passage.

**Verse 4. k)** Do they not know this? **h)** It is the question of one who is indignant and rebuking that malicious ignorance, as in **Ezekiel 13:7, Micah 3.** Compare **Ezekiel 8:12, Malachi 3:13, Psalm 82:5, and John 16:3.** **l)** The Targum: *all those performing a lie, especially the leaders of the people, etc.* **12. i)** The fool. The Septuagint **Psalm 5:6, Psalm 6:9**; and from the opposite **Psalm 15:2.** **m)** Devouring and consuming; even under the appearance of piety, justice, or zeal for divine worship; compare **John 16:2, Matthew 23:14.** **Schmid:** those who eat up the people of God not so much physically or civilly as spiritually, by tearing the souls of men with their false doctrines, like ravenous wolves **Matthew 7:15, Acts 20:29.** We, however, understand both the bad political and ecclesiastical leaders of the Jews, and their evil arts, doctrines, and oppressions of the good in any way. See **Micah 3:1–8, Habakkuk 3:14, Psalm 82:5.** The expression is figurative, as in **Numbers 14:9, Deuteronomy 7:16, Psalm 35:25, Lamentations 2:16, etc.** **n)** My people. The rabbis refer the suffix to David for other reasons; more rightly to God, as in **Joel 2:27.** **o)** They securely eat bread and take food **Exodus 18:22.** Indeed, they feast on the goods of the oppressed **Matthew 23:14.** Or, as **Abraham Ibn Ezra, Rashi, Kimchi, Geier, and Schmid** have it (understanding "as if" <note>Hebrew: כאשר</note>, as in **Proverbs 26:9**): just like those who eat bread; or as if they were devouring bread; compare **Numbers 14:9, Job 29:17, Proverbs 30:14.** **p)** The Lord, the observer of all and the avenger of his own **Psalm 10:14.**

<margin>verse 5. r) On the contrary, where the godly have nothing to fear (as seen in Psalm 53:6; and here also in the Septuagint, Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopic versions) but should rather rejoice (Luke 2:10), there the wicked fear or will fear. Compare Psalm 36:13, Job 35:12. Otherwise: There, or then, they shall fear when God, etc. Compare Psalm 132:17. **Abraham ben Ezra** <note>A renowned 12th-century Spanish rabbi and scholar</note>: "There," in the anxiety that will come upon them, so great that they will recognize God is an aid to the righteous. s) Conscious of their evil, they will tremble with dread and be greatly afraid; see Isaiah 33:14, Matthew 3:3, and John 11:48. t) because God. The **Targum** <note>The Aramaic translation</note> says: "because the Word of the Lord is [there]"; others say: "that God is," or "when God is present by His grace, glory, and salvation." u) In the generation of the righteous: that is, in the assembly of just men (Psalm 1:5). Compare the use of the first term in Psalms 24:6, 73:15, and 112:2.</margin>
—is hope and confidence in the Lord and His Christ, even if they see themselves destitute of all human protection. b) *The Lord is his refuge.* See Psalms 2:12, 46:2, 62:4; Isaiah 4:6, 25:4; Jeremiah 17:17; Joel 4:16. It is not a human arm (Jeremiah 17:5), nor carnal confidence, nor one's own righteousness, merit, or work. See Jeremiah 23:6; Philippians 3:4, 7–10; 1 Corinthians 1:30–31. **v. 7.** c) *Who will give at last?* The Targum says: *Who will hasten?* This is a formula expressing a wish, as in Exodus 16:3, Numbers 11:29, 2 Samuel 19:1, Psalm 55:6, etc. It is often expressed as a question with other words, as in 2 Samuel 23:15, Romans 7:24, etc. This is the prayer, indeed the desire of the Prophet and all the godly for the coming of the Messiah. **Schmid** <note>Sebastian Schmid, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> notes: *Who, except You, O Lord God, will give us the Messiah and His salvation?* d) *Out of Zion of David*, 2 Samuel 5:6, 9. From his family the Messiah was to be born (2 Samuel 7:12ff; 23:3ff), and from there He was to send His word into the whole world (Isaiah 2:3; see also Psalm 2:6, 20:3, 50:2, 110:2; Romans 11:26). *For salvation is from the Jews* (John 4:22). e) *salvation*, the Targum says *redemption*. Psalm 53:7 uses the plural: *salvations*, meaning salvation of every kind, to be found in Christ alone (Psalm 68:20; Acts 4:12; see Genesis 49:18, Psalm 3:9, 119:166; Isaiah 45:17–22, 46:13, 49:6, 52:7). "The Savior" [original: *ὁ τὸ σωτήριον*] in Luke 1:68–71, 2:30, Matthew 1:21, etc. f) See Romans 4:12. g) *For when the Lord restores.* The verb is transitive, as in Deuteronomy 30:3, Psalm 85:2, 5, 126:1. These provide the reason for the preceding wish. h) *the captivity* (of misery, Job 42:10; of ignorance and legal servitude, Zechariah 9:11–12, Galatians 3:23, Hebrews 2:13) of His people: so that the great and spiritual Jubilee year of liberty might be proclaimed through the Messiah (Isaiah 61:1–3; see also Isaiah 42:6–7, 49:9; Jeremiah 31:11; Amos 9:14; Psalm 102:21; Colossians 1:13). i) *then he shall exult.* Psalm 9:15, 13:6, 2:11. k) **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi, also known as Radak, a medieval grammarian</note>: meaning all twelve tribes descended from Jacob, as in Isaiah 40:27. Indeed, all who follow in the footsteps of his faith and that of Abraham (Romans 4:12, Psalm 24:6). l) The same is repeated with slightly changed words for the sake of affection and greater emphasis. See Psalm 5:12, and regarding this joy because of the Messiah, see Isaiah 9:2, 35:10; Joel 2:23; Zechariah 2:14, 9:9, etc. m) *The Israel of God* (Galatians 6:26) and those made according to the promise (Romans 9:6), such as Anna and Simeon, who were waiting with burning desire for that hope and consolation of Israel, and the better times of restoration (Hebrews 9:18, John 4:25), along with a few remnants of the true Israel at the time of Christ's birth (Luke 2:25–38), just as the Patriarch Jacob did long ago (Genesis 49:18).

**Psalm 15, verse 1.** n) See Psalm 3:1. The Syriac adds: *A perfect or sincere conversion to God.* For in this psalm, the genuine citizen of the kingdom of God is described, or the true member of the Church and heir of future celestial glory; such as no man is, unless truly converted to God through faith in Christ. And, as **Geier** <note>Martin Geier, a 17th-century Hebraist</note> observes, this psalm is not unfittingly joined to the preceding one, which expressed the common corruption of the entire human race. In this one, the chosen citizens of the Church are excellently described, whom the most holy Creator of men has destined for His own worship. According to Schmid, there are three parts: **I. The Question** (v. 1). **II. The Response** (v. 2–5). **III. The Conclusion** through a promise (v. 5). o) The Prophet asks God Himself, as does every man concerned for his salvation, so that the answer may be beyond all exception. See Luke 3:10, etc. p) *who shall abide?* The Targum: "Who is worthy to remain?" (Psalm 5:5). Others: "Who (as a stranger and pilgrim in this life) *shall sojourn?*" (Jeremiah 43:5, etc.; see Psalm 39:13, Genesis 47:9, Hebrews 11:13). q) *in Your tent.* As if Your household member or citizen; a partaker of grace here, and eventually of glory in the other life with the other saints (Ephesians 2:19, Psalm 61:5, 24:3; Isaiah 33:14ff). This refers either to the Tabernacle of Moses, which was then at Gibeon (1 Chronicles 16:39; 2 Chronicles 1:3, 5), or rather to that Tent which David had prepared for the Ark of the Covenant on Mount Zion (2 Samuel 6:17; 1 Chronicles 15:1, 16:1), where God testified to His presence in a singular way (Exodus 25:22, 1 Samuel 4:4); he had chosen Mount Zion and its adjacent ridge, Moriah, for His seat (Psalm 78:68, etc.). r) *who shall dwell, remain?* (Psalm 65:5, 102:29). s) See Psalm 2:6 and the things just mentioned. **Kimchi**: *By the tent and the holy mountain of God*, he says, *heaven is understood in this place*; see Isaiah 40:22, Psalm 11:4, 18:7. Which is true; however, the "heaven of grace," or the gracious kingdom of heaven in this life, is not excluded. **v. 2.** t) God, or the Holy Spirit, responds through the prophet: *He who walks*, and directs his whole way and life. See Psalm 1:1, etc. u) *blameless [integer].* Genesis 6:9, 17:1; Psalm 119:1, 80. The Targum and Ethiopic versions: *in integrity*; compare Judges 9:16, 19, 21; Psalm 84:12, etc. But **Abraham ben Ezra** says: *in a blameless way*, comparing Psalm 101:6. The reality or sense is the same: for the one truly converted to God is described, so that, having recognized the saving grace of God in Christ, he lives soberly, justly, and piously in this age (Titus 2:12; see Micah 2:7, Psalm 18:24; Proverbs 6:12, 28:18). x) *and who works or does righteousness.* Psalm 106:3; 1 John 2:29, 3:7; and by contrast, Psalm 14:4. y) *and who speaks truth.* Isaiah 33:15; Proverbs 16:13; Zechariah 4:16; Ephesians 4:25. z) *from the soul*, or *from the good treasure of his heart* (Matthew 12:35), so that he does not say one thing with his mouth and feel another in his heart. Compare Psalm 12:3. **v. 3.** a) He who does not act as a *spy* or *slanderer* (the word *ragal* is related to this). The Targum: *He who does not disparage.* The Syriac: *nor is he fraudulent.* The Septuagint, Vulgate, and Ethiopic: *He who did not act with guile or by guile.* See Genesis 42:9, 2 Samuel 19:28. b) *Upon.* The Vulgate: *on his tongue.* The preposition here designates the means or instrument, as in Genesis 27:40 and Deuteronomy 8:3; it restricts the use of the word from the feet to the tongue. For properly, it means to go about on one's feet to spy, to lay snares, and to disparage.

<margin>v. 6. x) Because you have despised the counsel of the needy and afflicted—by which he decided to trust in the Lord—and as much as is in you, you strive to confound it with your sarcasm, reproaches, and schemes. Compare Matthew 27:43. Contrast this with the counsel of the ungodly in Psalm 1:1, Job 10:3, etc. y) See Psalm 9:13, 10:10, 3; Zechariah 9:9. z) Ignominious, shameful, or foul to those despised. The Vulgate: *you have confounded.* This is an apostrophe <note>a direct address to an absent person or personified object</note> to those oppressors of the righteous and workers of iniquity in verse 4. Compare the word in Psalm 44:8, 53:6, and such mockery in Psalm 22:9. a) Because at the very least—</margin>

<note>The following are technical Masoretic notes regarding the accents and cantillation marks used for chanting the Hebrew text.</note>
Psalm 14, v. 5. **שָׁם** with *Merca* [accents 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20]. v. 6. **עֲצַת** with *Munach* [6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20]. **עָנִי** with *Merca*, *Dagesh* without a following one [11, 16, 21, 22, 23]. v. 7. **מִי־יִתֵּן** thus with *Maqqeph* [1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20, 24]. The rest with *Merca*, or as a *Sayka* minor sub-distinctive: a sequence you will hardly find, except once in Psalm 60:2. Compare the parallel Psalm 53:7. **יִתֵּן** with *Merca* [22 and 24] regularly: for it falls here on the *Dagesh*. But with *Munach* the others. See Psalm 53:7 and 116:16. Psalm XV, v. 1. **וּמִי־יִשְׁכּוֹן** with the prefix *Waw* [2 and in the margin 6, 9]. v. 2. **וּפֹעֵל** with *Munach* correctly [2, 3, 5, and 24]. But with *Merca* for most. v. 3. **לֹא־רָגַל** thus with *Mahpach* [1, 2, and 5].

# Michtam of David ^q 16

1 Keep me, O God ^r for I have taken refuge in You ^s :
2 You <note>feminine singular, addressed to the soul</note> said to the Lord ^t "You are my Lord" ^u
3 "My goodness is not for You" <note>meaning God does not benefit from it</note> : as for the saints who are in the earth ^x they [are] the excellent ones ^y all my delight is in them ^z :

-> [Signature Mark] Pppp 5 <-

---

<margin>
verse 4. h) **He is Despised.** <note>original: "Contemtus Est"</note> Isaiah 53:3. And rejected by God, Psalm 73:20. Deserving of contempt, Malachi 1:7, 12; compare 1 Samuel 2:30 and a similar participle in Psalm 18:4; Proverbs 21:20. Interpreters differ greatly in resolving the first part of this verse before the *Atnach* <note>a major musical/grammatical pause in Hebrew</note>. For some take the pious man himself as the subject, as in the Targum: *He who is despised and contemptible in his own eyes.* That is to say, one who is displeased with himself, not an admirer of his own virtue but of others; compare 1 Samuel 15:17; Romans 12:10; Philippians 2:3; and the contrary example of the Pharisee in Luke 18:9. So Guffetius, Ibn Ezra, and Kimchi, who says: "Furthermore, the text enumerates the virtues of the pious man, that although he is upright, doing justice and speaking truth, he does not lift himself up proudly, but rather seems vile and unworthy to himself when he considers in his mind that he does not perform even one in a thousand of the things he owes to the honor of his Creator." For others, however, the "despised" one is the subject—the impious man: *Despised in his eyes is the wicked or malignant person.* So the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, and Luther; this creates an excellent antithesis to the following phrase about honoring the pious.
</margin>

verse 4. e) *is worthy*, in the eyes of the righteous he is also a reprobate or one to be turned away from; not indeed (as *Geierus* notes here) as far as he possesses public authority, but insofar as he is impious, lest he be emboldened or become more insolent, etc. Compare Proverbs 26:1, 8; James 2:1, 9; and 2 Kings 3:14; Esther 3:2. i) coheres with the following by the accents, as we said. k) just as "reprobate silver" is rejected, Jeremiah 6:30. Compare Psalm 36:5; Psalm 53:5; etc. l) but those fearing the Lord, Psalm 25:12; Malachi 3:16. On the adversative use of *Vav* <note>the Hebrew letter 'and' used as 'but'</note>, compare Psalm 5:8; etc. m) he honors, Exodus 20:12; 1 Samuel 2:30; Malachi 1:6; Lamentations 1:8. *Geierus*: The sense is that the pious man makes nothing great except true piety; otherwise, whether wealth, honor, wisdom, or anything else splendid be present, it is little regarded by him. n) *he swears*. Kimchi suggests comparing Psalm 119:106 regarding a thing that is in itself honest and pious, so that he may be more strongly bound. Or understand the oath regarding an indifferent and lawful thing, with a conditional implied: *If he has sworn*; as in 2 Kings 5:13; Hosea 4:18; etc. o) Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, *Luther: to a neighbor*, comparing Proverbs 17:17. And by changing the vowel *Tsere* to *Patach*, as in Psalm 94:9; Psalm 136:6. Others, like *Pfeiffer* in *Difficulties Vexed*, say even to a wicked or impious man, regarding an indifferent and lawful matter, for example: *to a heretic, a Turk, etc. Others: to his own evil or loss or detriment.* Others, like Schmid, to the afflicting of himself. Targum: to the bringing of evil upon himself, namely, according to Rashi and Kimchi, through fasting; compare Numbers 30:14. But *Guffetius* (page 415) says: that he might suffer evil: because the infinitive after the letter *Lamed* sometimes implies passive suffering, as in Deuteronomy 31:17; 2 Samuel 14:25. *Guffetius* also takes this same word this way in Leviticus 5:4: if he has sworn that he will undergo certain evils or do certain good things; which he could not fulfill because of a physical or moral obstacle, etc. p) *yet he does not change it*, Leviticus 27:10, 33; out of reverence for the Supreme Deity, Exodus 20:7; and lest he seem to have sworn deceitfully, Psalm 24:4; and *he does not lie*.

<margin>
verse 5. q) Vulgate: Who [does not give] his money, silver or gold, etc. Leviticus 25:37. r) does not give on loan for usury, or grant for interest. Exodus 22:24; Deuteronomy 23:20; Ezekiel 18:8; Proverbs 28:8. s) a gift, bribes. Deuteronomy 16:19; Psalm 26:10; Proverbs 6:35. t) against the innocent, Psalm 10:8; Deuteronomy 27:25. u) he who does these things, namely through his life, as Kimchi notes. The Syriac adds: *is righteous*, perhaps from Ezekiel 18:9 or 1 John 2:29; chapter 3:7. x) shall not be moved from the mountain or tabernacle of the Lord (verse 1), or fall from the grace of God. Psalm 10:6; Psalm 13:5. y) forever. Kimchi: not even in death; but his soul shall remain in the place of glory after his death. Compare Psalm 30:7; Psalm 112:6; Psalm 125:1.

PS. XVI, verse 1. z) Or Michtam: which for others, such as Rashi and Ibn Ezra, etc., is the name of a song or melody; for others, it is better rendered as "Golden Jewel," "Treasure," or "Golden Song." (6) Psalms 56–60, 1. From the most excellent gold, Job 28:16, 19; Song of Solomon 5:11. For the Psalmist here represents to us Christ praying in his state of humiliation and passion: so that, according to Schmid, the headings to be observed here are: I. The prayer of Christ humbled and suffering (verse 1). II. His consolation, both from his consent to the divine purpose of human redemption (verses 2–4) and from the saving outcome of that humiliation and passion (verses 5, 6). III. The effects of that prayer and consolation (verses 7-11). a) Of David, or dictated to David by the Holy Spirit. See Psalm 3:1. However, the Apostles Peter (Acts 2:25–31) and Paul (Acts 13:35–37) explicitly argue that this psalm speaks not of David, but of the Messiah himself. They demonstrate this most firmly against the Jews, on the grounds that David had long since undergone corruption in the tomb. Therefore, since David was a prophet (these are Peter's words in Acts 2:30, 31) and knew that God had sworn to him with an oath that Christ would be raised up from the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, to sit upon his throne, he spoke with foreknowledge of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left among the dead, nor did his flesh see corruption. Compare also the pious meditations of Luther and Brentius on this passage, alongside Luke 22:41–44, though for the sake of brevity we omit other interpreters and versions that lack support here. b) Keep, Vulgate: Preserve me, Psalm 17:8. Preserve me, namely Your Son, the Messiah, in all parts of my humiliation and passion, until I perform and overcome all things that must be performed and overcome by me. Compare Matthew 26:37–39; John 12:27, 28; chapter 17:1 and following; Acts 2:25 and following. c) O Almighty God the Father. Psalm 5:5; Psalm 18:3; Psalm 22:2; Mark 14:36. d) He gives the reason for the petition, because of Christ's trust in His Father. e) In You alone I have trusted, and always will trust, You who are able both to preserve and to snatch me away, Hebrews 5:7. For the word, compare Psalm 2:12; Psalm 25:2, 3. verse 2. f) For you have said, O my soul, as the Targum, Rashi, David Kimchi, etc., supply; namely by a similar ellipsis and construction to 2 Samuel 13:38. So Jeremiah 4:19: *You have heard, O my soul*, instead of *I have heard*. Compare also Matthew 26:38. It is an elegant apostrophe <note>a speech addressed to an object or oneself</note> of Christ (says Schmid), turning his speech from God His Father to Himself or His soul, which He begins to console with the confidence that His prayers have been heard, and to lift up and strengthen against adversity; compare John 12:27. See also Psalm 42:6, 12. g) To Jehovah God the Father (verse 1), who is faithful in His promises, Psalm 7:2. h) You are the Creator, Preserver, and Lord of all things (see Psalm 2:4); but I, as a man, am Your servant, Isaiah 42:1; chapter 53:11, who willingly submits myself to Your will, Psalm 40:9; Matthew 26:39. i) Job 9:25; Ecclesiastes 5:17. A difficult verse. Guffetius (page 128): *You are my good or my happiness, and there is nothing above You*, compare Psalm 17:3. More correctly, in our judgment, Schmid says: *As far as my good or happiness is concerned, it is not mine on account of You:* because, to fulfill Your will, I emptied myself of it; compare 2 Corinthians 8:9; Philippians 2:4 and following; Hebrews 12:2. But the "good" or happiness is the blessedness belonging to the humble Christ, who is the Son of God (Psalm 2:7), of which He voluntarily emptied Himself. Others: *My good, that it may be well with me, that You may save me, which I prayed for in verse 1—this does not happen for Your sake <note>i.e., God does not need it</note>; yet it is a work and beneficial to the saints* (verse 3). k) And that for the saints; that is, for the benefit and salvation of the saints: such as are all those reborn through true faith in Christ and consecrated to God, Isaiah 4:3; Psalm 89:6, 8; Proverbs 9:10; Job 15:15; Daniel 8:24; John 17:19; 1 Corinthians 6:11; Ephesians 5:25, 26; Hebrews 2:11; chapter 12:14. Compare Luke 22:29. l) who are in the earth; not for the holy angels in heaven, or for the devils in hell. Hebrews 2:16. So that holy men are indeed in the world, but not of the world. Compare John 17:6, 11, 14 and following. m) they are. Compare Psalm 9:21. n) and for the excellent, illustrious, and glorious ones, Psalm 8:2, who are like leaders and prelates over the others. Jeremiah 14:3; chapter 25:34; chapter 30:21; Nehemiah 10:29; 2 Chronicles 23:20. Compare John 17:20. Or it preserves the order of the matter, compare Romans 8:30.
</margin>

---

<term>v. 4. נִבְזֶה (nivzeh - despised)</term> thus lacking [a letter] in manuscripts 5, 6, 7, 8, 15, 22, 23, 24; and thus in 2 according to the second Masora printed at Erfurt; and Masora 1, 4 printed at Erfurt at Leviticus 27:10.
<term>v. 5. לֹא־לָקָח (lo-lakach - he did not take)</term> with a *Makkaph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 22. Thus also *He did not give his money at interest and a bribe against the innocent he did not take, he who does these* with a *Patach* <note>a vowel mark</note> in 1, 2, 3, 7, 17, 18. Furthermore *he shall not be moved forever* thus in 6, 9, 10, 13, 20. To be compared with the similar *Siluk* <note>end-of-verse accent</note> diction in Psalm 46:8.

<term>PS. XVI. v. 1. שָׁמְרֵנִי (shomreni - keep me)</term> thus with a *Metheg* <note>a stress mark</note> in 2, 5, 7, 8, 17, 22 according to M. 1 and the Erfurt Museum here and Psalm 86:2. A similar *Metheg* is also in *my song* Psalm 30:4 and *to the generation* Psalm 38:21. The reading of *Qamets* as *Qamets-Chatuph* <note>a short 'o' sound</note> is no more an obstacle than the tonic accent in *all* Psalm 35:10; Proverbs 19:7.

<summary>This page concludes Psalm 15's list of ethical requirements for the godly and introduces Psalm 16 with a heavy emphasis on Christological interpretation. The commentary explores whether "despised" refers to the humble self-image of a believer or their rejection of the wicked, while interpreting Psalm 16 as the prayer of the suffering Messiah.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the detailed analysis of Psalm 16. The previous page (15) concluded Psalm 15's ethical requirements and began the opening of Psalm 16, identifying it as a "Michtam" (a golden poem or inscription) of David. This page focuses on verses 4 through 9, interpreting the text through a Christological lens—viewing the speaker as the Messiah—while providing heavy linguistic comparisons between the Hebrew, the Septuagint (Greek), and various Rabbinic commentaries.</meta>

<page-num>16</page-num>
<header>16. Psalm 16</header>

<margin>
3. The Septuagint <note>original: "LXX"</note> and other versions: *I will not remember, or record, or make mention of their names.*
κ) Just as the priests of old used to do when praying for those offering sacrifices: but as they deny me, I myself will also deny them.
</margin>

<margin>
n) *in whom is all my good pleasure and delight.* <note>original: "in quibus omne meum beneplacitum & delectatio est"</note> See Psalm 1:2; Isaiah 62:4; Luke 2:14, etc. For whom I sanctify myself by command, so that they also may be sanctified in truth. John 17:19.
V. 4. o) Schmidt <note>The abbreviation "S." likely refers to the commentator Sebastian Schmidt</note>: *On the contrary, they shall be multiplied.* Genesis 3:16; chapter 7:17; Job 9:17. p) *their sorrows and punishments,* both in this world and in the world to come. (4) Psalm 147:3; Proverbs 15:13; Job 9:28. Compare the words of Christ in Luke 23:28.
q) Schmidt: *those who hasten to another [god]* (Isaiah 28:16) and honor him as if providing a dowry for a groom. Exodus 22:15; compare the name in Genesis 34:12; 1 Samuel 18:25. That is, those who seek for themselves another Savior or another way of salvation, and refuse to receive righteousness, spirit, and life from me. Spiritually committing adultery or denying me. Compare Deuteronomy 32:16; Isaiah 42:8; Ezekiel 16:32–34; Leviticus 17:9; John 19:12–15; Acts 15:24; chapter 4:12.
r) *for I will not pour out libations,* <note>original: "non enim libabo"</note> as the true Priest and High Priest, established by the Father according to the order of Melchizedek. Psalm 110:4. For the word, see Genesis 35:14; Numbers 28:7. s) *their drink offerings and their entire worship* Numbers 29:39; chapter 15:4, 5. Even if they pour out their own blood (which some compare to 2 Timothy 4:6 and Philippians 2:17), it also regards Paul’s phrase regarding the abolition of the empty worship of ceremonies. Isaiah 66:3; Daniel 9:24–27; Matthew 23:38. t) *because of my wandering* and the blood of other godly people, compare Matthew 23:35; chapter 27:25; Ephesians 5:2. u) *thus indeed* I will proclaim their names. Exodus 20:7; Psalm 16:3.
