Matthew 10:33. Neither Priest, nor King, nor Judge shall be favorable to them. Compare John 17:9. **v. 5. y)** *Schmidt: Jehovah is the portion.* Others: *You, O Jehovah, are the portion,* by apostrophe; which, however, more correctly begins at the Silluk <note>a Hebrew accent marking the end of a verse</note>. **z)** *Schmidt: those who hasten to this [one]* (Isaiah 28:16) and honor him as if dowering a groom. Exodus 22:15; compare the name in Genesis 34:12; 1 Samuel 18:25. That is, those who seek for themselves another Savior or way of salvation, and refuse to receive righteousness, spirit, and life from me. Spiritually committing adultery or denying me. Compare Deuteronomy 32:16; Isaiah 42:8; Ezekiel 16:32–34; Leviticus 17:9; John 19:12–15; Acts 15:24; chapter 4:12. **a)** *my share,* or my part, with which I am content: for He acknowledges me as His son, and embraces me with the highest love. Isaiah 42:1; Matthew 3:17; chapter 17:5. Compare Psalm 17:14; Psalm 73:26; Lamentations 3:24. **b)** *of my cup.* Others in the Nominative: *and the cup is my portion* Psalm 11:6; Psalm 116:13. Best of all, Schmidt says, it seems to refer to the sacrificial banquets, in which the priests of the Old Testament were given their portions to eat and cups to drink, etc. Compare Exodus 29:26; Leviticus 7:33; chapter 8:29; Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 18:8. also 1 Samuel 1:5; etc. **c)** *You, O Jehovah,* the almighty Father. **d)** *are the sustainer.* The Targum <note>Aramaic paraphrase</note>: *You will sustain* and preserve. Psalm 17:5; Psalm 41:13. Namely, even to the end, lest it be snatched from me. John 10:29. The participle of the simple verb form <note>Kal</note> uses the *Chirek* vowel instead of *Tsere*; as in Isaiah 29:14; chapter 38:5. **e)** *my lot,* <unclear>λ. E.</unclear> the Church, and my elect within her in the true and holy faith, powerfully preserving them until the end of life and the world. Psalm 125:3. It refers to the distribution of the inheritance, which used to be done by lots, just as by the measuring lines, which follow immediately in verse 6, says Schmidt. Compare Joshua 17:14. But Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki</note> says: *You have directed and disposed my hand toward the best lot.* Thus Ezekiel 45:1. It means, he says, that a part and heritage was assigned to him by the will of God, so that his heritage might be certain, and not depend on the uncertainty of a lot, but as if God Himself placed the lots with His hand. But the former opinion is simpler. **v. 6. f)** *the lines of the inheritance to be divided* Amos 7:17. **g)** in the eternal decree of God they have fallen to me. This alludes to the division of the Promised Land. See Joshua 17:5, 14; Psalm 78:55; Psalm 105:11. **h)** *among the pleasant and delightful,* that is, according to Schmidt, among people most pleasing to me in faith, piety, and obedience. Others read it as neuter: *in pleasant things,* as in verse 11, or *among the pleasant*—the Jewish people, propagated among the nations to the ends of the earth. Psalm 2:8; Matthew 21:43. Namely, the Church; compare Deuteronomy 32:9. **k)** *it is beautiful.* (2) Job 26:13. **l)** *with me* Psalm 7:9. That is, as the Syriac version has it, *it was pleasing, or it is accepted and greatly pleases me.* See the phrasing in Daniel 3:32; 4:24; 6:2. Calovius: *For the Church, which is the kingdom of God, liberated from death, the power of the devil, and hell, and selected from the unclean world, is a very precious treasure <note>original: "κειμήλιον"</note> to Him,* compare Exodus 19:6; Deuteronomy 7:6; Titus 2:14; 1 Peter 2:9. Add above to verse 3. **v. 7. m)** Psalm 34:2; Psalm 145:1. Schmidt: *I will therefore bless Jehovah,* my Father, for this most merciful and wise counsel of His, which He proposed to Himself, and by which He gave to me my self-emptying and passion to be carried out, so that by active and passive satisfaction I might redeem the human race and lead them to eternal life and glory. Compare Matthew 11:25, 26. **n)** *who or which counseled me.* Exodus 18:19; Numbers 24:14; 1 Kings 1:12; Jeremiah 38:15. Compare the note on Isaiah 48:16. **o)** *indeed, not only during the day, but also in the nights.* Psalm 1:2; Psalm 92:3. Compare Mark 6:46; Luke 6:12. **p)** *they instruct and urge,* the Arabic version says: *they remind me.* Isaiah 8:12. The Greek <note>original: "παιδεύσαν με"</note>: *they disciplined me.* Titus 2:12. **q)** *the reins and my innermost senses,* all powers of mind and body. Compare Jeremiah 12:2; Psalm 7:10; Psalm 73:21; Psalm 139:13; Proverbs 23:16; Job 19:27. For Christ Himself, though He was the Son of God and subject to no sin (John 8:46; Hebrews 4:10; 7:26; 1 Peter 2:22), nevertheless learned obedience from the things He suffered; and having been made perfect, He became the cause of salvation for all who obey Him in true faith (as in Philippians 2:17); but from Hebrews 5:8, 9, Blessed Luther teaches this passage. Schmidt says: *To us, this chastisement of the reins seems to be nothing other than the holy movements in the soul of Christ, which the Holy Spirit (resting upon Him, Isaiah 11:2) excited in it, and animated Him to undergo and sustain all the most difficult things pertaining to the work of redemption,* compare Matthew 4:1; 26:39; John 12:27. Add Psalm 40:9; Isaiah 50:4, 5. **v. 8. r)** *For full of love and trust, I have placed or proposed Jehovah.* Psalm 21:6; Psalm 119:30. The Septuagint as in Acts 2:25. **s)** *before me* Isaiah 49:16; Psalm 18:23. Namely, looking back with the eyes of the mind at how truthful He is, and that the help He promised would be mine from them will never be denied. Compare John 11:42. **t)** <unclear>E</unclear>. 42:16. Even in the midst of my afflictions and temptations. Compare Matthew 27:43. **u)** Schmidt: *understand the word 'to say' <note>original: "לאמר"</note>,* as in Psalm 2:2, 3; 5:8, 9; 9:13. He thinks: *because He is at my right hand,* as my protection and defender. Compare Isaiah 42:1; Psalm 109:31; 110:5; John 8:16, 29; 16:32. But the Syriac: *and He is at my right hand.* The Targum: *for His Presence <note>Shechina</note> rests upon me.* Colossians 2:9. **x)** *therefore I shall not be moved* from my purpose, nor be conquered by enemies. Psalm 13:5; 17:5; 21:1, 15; chapter 59:3. Hosea 8. See Isaiah 50:7, 8, 9; Luke 9:51; etc. **v. 9. y)** *Furthermore, because God is my Father and helper, who will keep me unmoved.* **z)** *my heart is glad and prepared even for death itself.* Proverbs 23:15; Philippians 2:8. **a)** <unclear>B</unclear> *rejoiced* Psalm 9:15; 13:6. **b)** *my glory, i.e., my honor.* By which some understand the eternal Spirit of Christ (Hebrews 9:14); others, better with Kimchi, understand the *soul,* for it is opposed to the flesh or body: which those do not notice who, with the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Arabic versions, interpret it as the "tongue." Schmidt says both the soul and tongue of Christ. Compare Psalm 7:6; 30:13; 57:9; Genesis 49:6. **c)** *indeed, not only the soul, but also the body, verse 7.*

Thus Rashi: **because I am certain that you will not abandon, etc.** (verse 10). g) **Because**, even though I must die, so that I seem to be deserted by God in the judgment of all (Psalm 22:2), you will not truly abandon me, etc. Or as we said at verse 9: my flesh will lie down securely under the certain hope that you will not abandon, etc. h) **you will not desert** and completely leave behind (Psalm 38:22; compare Psalm 21:5; John 16:32). i) **my soul**; others say **me**, comparing Psalm 3:3, etc., but we prefer the former. k) **in hell** <note>original: "inferno"</note> (Psalm 6:6; Psalm 30:4; 1 Samuel 2:6), as if to say it would be detained there, as if swallowed up. This note refers to the soul, while "corruption" refers to the body. Thus Schmidt. Greek: <term>into Hades</term> <note>original: "εις αδου"</note> (Acts 2:27, 31). l) **nor will you so give** or permit. ### 1. A Prayer of David. <gloss>b</gloss> Hear, O Lord, <gloss>c</gloss> a just cause; <gloss>d</gloss> attend to <gloss>e</gloss> my cry; <gloss>f</gloss> give ear to <gloss>g</gloss> my prayer <gloss>h</gloss> from lips without deceit.

corruption or rotting (Psalm 49:10; Psalm 55:24). So the Septuagint and Acts 2:24, 27, 31; chapter 13:35. (Elsewhere it means a "pit," as in Psalm 9:16). But rather: on the third day you will raise me from the dead and gloriously bring me back alive from the tomb. (Compare Romans 6:4; Matthew 12:40; 16:21; 17:23; Luke 18:33; John 2:19-22). **v. 11. p)** **You will make known to me, O God the Father** (Psalm 51:8), through the resurrection from death. (Compare experimental knowledge in Isaiah 47:8; Ecclesiastes 8:5). **q)** **the way of eternal life** (compare Psalm 21:5; Isaiah 53:8, 10; Proverbs 5:6; 10:27; 15:24; Hebrews 10:20). **r)** **there will be satiety** <note>satisfaction/fullness</note>; **otherwise: you will make me experience satiety** (compare Psalm 17:15; 78:25; Isaiah 53:11; and Revelation 7:16, 17). **s)** **of joys** (Isaiah 51:11; Psalm 45:16). **t)** **with or before your face** (1 Kings 12:6; Psalm 21:7; 140:14; 1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 John 3:2). Syriac: **and I shall be satisfied with the pleasantness of your face.** **u)** **heavenly delights and those ineffable <note>too great for words</note> to men.** (1) Compare verse 6; Proverbs 24:4. **x)** **they shall be in your right hand**, which Abraham Ibn Ezra and others interpret to mean that God will give the most pleasant gifts with his right hand to those who love him (compare Proverbs 3:16). Others refer this to Christ’s sitting at the right hand of the Father and his exaltation (compare Psalm 110:1; Luke 22:69; Ephesians 1:20ff; Hebrews 2:9, etc.). And this is indeed, says Geier, to be glorified with that glory which Christ had before the world was (John 17:5). Cocceius (Lex. 525) combines both well: **You will make known to me the way of pleasant things which are in your right hand; which God has reserved in his hand for those who wait for him** (Isaiah 64:3; 1 Corinthians 2:9). These the Son of God, sitting at the right hand of the Father, receives to be given to the faithful even in this life (compare Acts 2:33; Psalm 110:1; and 68:19). **y)** **and that perpetually or forever** (Psalm 9:7; 13:2; Isaiah 25:8). Since Christ, raised from the dead, will not die again; nor will death ever rule over him (Romans 6:9, etc.). Thanks be to God, who has also given us the victory over death through our Lord Jesus Christ! (1 Corinthians 15:57).

**Psalm XVII.** **v. 1. a)** **Prayer or supplication** of David (Psalm 86:1; see notes on Psalm 3:1; 4:2; Habakkuk 3:1). The Arabic inscription sets forth the **Subject Matter** of the psalm thus: **A prayer in the person of a perfect or upright man, and of Christ himself, and of anyone redeemed by him.** Thus Brentius: **Let us feel,** he says, **that this psalm is the prayer which Christ used in his greatest afflictions, and especially on the Mount of Olives when he sweated drops of blood.** And Gurtlerus says: **It is indeed a prayer of David, but insofar as he was a type of Christ.** (Compare verse 3 and Psalm 16:7). To Rupert, the Head [Christ] himself here prays to God the Father for himself and his members, that they might not fail. Tillius, however, referred this psalm to the Apostolic Church, vexed by wicked Jews and pagan enemies (compare Acts 8:3; 12:1ff; James 1:2, 3; 1 Peter 1:6ff). We prefer the opinion of Schmidt, who states: **This psalm is the prayer of the Church militant at all times under Christ its head, to whom it is conformed against the kingdom of Satan (Genesis 3:15). I. For the preservation of herself and sound doctrine (vv. 1–8). II. For defense against false teachers and persecutors (vv. 9–14). III. In conclusion, she consoles herself against these with the living hope of eternal life (v. 15).** **b)** **Hear or listen,** O Jehovah (Psalm 4:2; 10:17; 39:13). **c)** **justice,** that is, my most just cause and complaint. Kimchi: **that is, prayers made justly because the mouth and soul agree.** Targum: **my prayer in justice, that is, a just prayer.** Ibn Ezra: **because I speak justice, because God does not hear vanity** (Job 35:13; compare John 9:31). The Septuagint, Vulgate, Arabic, and Ethiopic read: **my justice.** Some Catholic commentators concede that this should be understood as the justice of the cause, not the person. (Compare notes on Psalm 7:4, 9). Calovius and Tillius not inconveniently accept this as referring to Christ, our righteousness, interceding for us. (Compare Isaiah 53:11; Jeremiah 23:6; Daniel 9:24; 1 Corinthians 1, 30, 31; 1 John 2:1, 2; John 16:23, etc.). **d)** See Psalm 5:3. **e)** **my cry** (1 Kings 22:36), here a sad and suppliant one (compare 1 Kings 8:28; Jeremiah 7:16; Psalm 61:2), as elsewhere it is joyful (Psalm 30:6; 5:12, etc.). **f)** Psalm 5:2. **g)** Psalm 4:2. **h)** **without, or a prayer that is made without.** (1 Chronicles 12:37). The omission of the relative pronoun is frequent. **i)** **lips of fraud, deceit, or hypocrisy** (Psalm 5:7; 32:2); that is, not deceitful or hypocritical; without fraud or pretense. **v. 2. k)** **From your presence, or from you,** (Leviticus 9:24; Numbers 17:11; Esther 1:19) as the most just judge and avenger of the godly (Psalm 7:9). **l)** **the right and judicial sentence in my cause.** (Psalm 9:5). **m)** **let it go forth or be proclaimed.** See note on Habakkuk 1:4. Kimchi: so that you may avenge me of my enemies. **n)** Psalm 11:7. **o)** Psalm 9:9; Isaiah 33:15. **v. 3. p)** **For you have tested and examined my heart.** (Psalm 7:10; 11:5). **q)** **you have even visited it.** Syriac: **and you visited me.** (Compare Psalm 8:5; 1 Samuel 14:17; Job 7:18). **r)** **by night** (Psalm 16:7). Ibn Ezra: **when I was alone and remote from men.** (Compare Psalm 4:5). **s)** Septuagint and Vulgate: **you have examined me with fire.** (See Psalm 12:7). Tillius compares this to James 1:2, 3 and 1 Peter 1:6ff. **t)** **but nothing** (Psalm 16:2) **have you found** (Psalm 10:15) that would be a hindrance to my cause and integrity. (Compare Job 23:10, 11, 12; 1 John 3:19ff). For otherwise David would not have been unwilling to confess his defects and lapses before the divine judgment (e.g., Psalm 19:13; 143:2). **u)** **That is, for what I have thought as good, it shall not transgress.** Others simply: **for I have thought and purposed for myself.** (Compare Jeremiah 51:12; Lamentations 2:17). **x)** **so that it does not transgress, namely, your commands.** **y)** **also my mouth and tongue.** (Compare Psalm 39:2; James 3:2ff). **v. 4. z)** **As for the works of man or men.** (Compare Ezekiel 9:13). **a)** **By the word—others: according to the word—of your lips, namely, I have observed.** (Job 23:12; compare 1 Chronicles 21:19). The emphasis here is on David's constant and tireless study of the sacred words of God. Or more simply, understand the actions and efforts of men in mocking and perverting the word of God. (Psalm 11:3; 2 Peter 3:16).

**verse 7. p)** Septuagint and Vulgate: *Make wonderful*, that is, do [this]. **S.** *make marvelous*. Ethiopic: *Make it glorious*. <summary>This page contains the Hebrew text of Psalm 17:5-13 accompanied by an exhaustive Latin commentary and marginal notes comparing different ancient versions (Septuagint, Vulgate, Targum). It explores metaphors of divine protection, such as the "apple of the eye" and "shadow of wings," while identifying the psalmist's enemies and their worldly arrogance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the Psalms. The previous page concluded the discussion of Psalm 16, emphasizing the "Holy One" who would not see corruption. We now transition from the final verses of Psalm 17—contrasting the worldly portion of the wicked with the spiritual satisfaction of the righteous—into the monumental Psalm 18, a song of David’s deliverance which the commentators analyze both as a historical record and a prophecy of Christ.</meta>

Compare the construction of your glory, as in Job 4:21. **p)** *to their little ones.* Psalm 8:3. **v. 15. q)** *But as for me, I desire nothing*, see note at verse 13, except that I may eventually see your face in heavenly glory. **A. Ibn Ezra. r)** *in righteousness*; then the imputed and eternal righteousness of Christ (Jeremiah 23:6; Daniel 9:24; Philippians 3:9), then the inherent righteousness, begun here but then to be perfected. 1 Corinthians 13:10, 12; 2 Corinthians 3:17. The Ethiopic version: *in your righteousness*. Compare above at verse 5, and the note on the "Just Man" in Psalm 1:5. **s)** Psalm 16:11; Job 19:26, 27. And so, although no one is allowed to *see your face* on earth (Exodus 33:20), I shall nevertheless see it to my full satisfaction in the next life, just as it is in 1 John 3:2 and *face to face*, in that intuitive and blessed vision of Matthew 5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:12; compared with Ephesians 3:20. **t)** *I shall be satisfied by your face or image*; as those worldly people are by worldly things in verse 14. Compare Psalm 16:11; 17:22, 25; also 53:11; 65:13; Luke 6:25. **u)** *when* *I awake* from death. Compare Psalm 3:6; Isaiah 26:19; Jeremiah 31:26; 51:39, 57; Daniel 12:2. **x)** *I shall be satisfied, I say, by your form or image* Exodus 20:4; Numbers 12:8; Deuteronomy 4:16; Job 4:16. **Targum:** *by the image of your countenance*. It says the same as "face or countenance of God" in the preceding part and in Psalm 16:11, and the <term>accents</term> <note>the musical/grammatical marks in Hebrew text</note> suggest this. Others, like Luther and Calovius: *I shall be satisfied when I awake*; "I shall awake with your image," namely the original image, begun here but then fully restored and shining eternally in the saints. **Psalm XVIII, 1. y)** See Psalm 4:1. **z)** This notable title is also attributed to David in Psalm 36:1, because in his own time he served the decree of God (Acts 13:36). For, as Kimchi says here: "He who directs all his ways, intention, and actions to the honor of God is called a servant of God," etc. Compare the note on Deuteronomy 34:5. **a)** see Psalm 3:1. **b)** *who also spoke and wrote*. Compare 2 Samuel 22:1. **Targum** adds: *in prophecy or prophetically*. This is according to the mind of the Targumist regarding the future restoration of Israel, see verses 28, 29, 32, 49. According to the Syriac inscription: *concerning the ascension of Christ*; our countryman Brentius also thought this psalm should be understood literally and most closely of Christ alone, and only then applied to David and others reborn in Christ. On the other hand, the Jews and others commonly take it to refer to David alone, but poorly; some partly of Christ and partly of the Church; others more correctly take it *of David as a type, but of Christ as the Antitype*, that "Seed of David" in verse 51. Thus Schmidt says: "This psalm deals with David in such a way that he represents to us the Seed of David, Christ." However (the same Schmidt continues), that this psalm refers only to Christ and in no way to David also seems to us to say too much, since the psalm itself in verse 51 explicitly mentions David. To want to understand Christ by "David" and the Church by the "seed of David" would be clearly foreign to the simplicity of the style, etc. (Appendix p. 70). See also the final words of this verse. Thus Gurtlerus (*Prophetic Theology* p. 99) says: Similarly (as with XVII), Psalm XVIII *is the prayer of David, the servant of God*; but not only of the son of Jesse, but especially of the Messiah-David, the servant chosen by God. For Paul attributes the fragment of verse 3 to Christ in Hebrews 2:13, and verse 50 in Romans 15:9, to whom also the words of verses 5–8, 22–25, and 51 apply more fully than to David. Thus Saul is an image of the Jewish council demanding Christ's death. Compare also *Matthew's Economy of the Old Testament* p. 797. Regarding the unique analysis of this Psalm by Tillius (in which he thinks the resurrected Christ speaks in verses 3–20 before His ascension, and then one of the faithful or Apostles in 21–43, then Christ again in 44–46, and another in 47–51), we will not say much here. **It contains** and proclaims after the title in verse 1 according to its sections: I. The *answering* of the prayer not only of David but also of Christ (v. 2–7). II. His *deliverance* (v. 8–20). III. The *reward* for integrity (v. 21–32). IV. *Preservation* and defense in office (v. 33–46). V. *Thanksgiving and glorification* (v. 47–51), written in a very passionate and figurative style. Compare also the notes on 2 Samuel 22, where the meaning is the same, though syllables and words sometimes vary because both books were produced under divine inspiration by different authors. Compare Schmidt's *Appendix on Psalms concerning Christ* p. 71 and following, and the notes above on Psalm 14:1. **c)** *for the praise and honor of the Lord* Psalm 7:1. **d)** *the words themselves.* cf. Psalm 7:1; 137:3. **e)** *of this sacred prophetic song.* cf. Exodus 15:1; Numbers 21:17; Deuteronomy 31:19, 21, 30, etc. **f)** *in the day or time in which the Lord had delivered him* v. 18. An omission of the relative pronoun, as in Psalm 17:1, 14; Psalm 56:10, etc. **g)** 2 Samuel 19:10; Psalm 71:4. **h)** *who are many and various for both Christ and David*, as history teaches. cf. verses 4, 38, 41, 49. **i)** *especially* Proverbs 13:22. **k)** for the riches of your grace to lead them to repentance (Romans 2:4) and as if from the innermost depths you fill them in this age (Psalm 107:9; 144:13; Job 22:18; 3:15; 38:39; Acts 14:17). **l)** *their belly* Proverbs 18:20; Job 20:20; which is as if their god (Philippians 3:19). **m)** *even the children are satisfied*. Psalm 104:16; or as the Vulgate, Luther, and others have it: *they are also satisfied with children*, comparing Job 27:14; Psalm 144:12. **n)** *and they store up or leave behind...*

<column-break/>

**v. 14.** **From men** <note>original: "מִמְתִים"</note> thus with a *Chateph-patach* <note>a Hebrew vowel mark</note> twice here. Through a *Mahpach* accent in place of the latter Metheg. **Their portion** <note>original: "חֶלְקָם"</note> has a *Merca* accent, though irregularly. Our copies have it here and in Proverbs 8:34; but the *Masora* <note>the traditional system of notes on the biblical text</note> of Erfurt requires it. **Their babes** <note>original: "לְעוֹלְלֵיהֶם"</note> is spelled *defectively* according to the Western tradition.
**v. 15.** **When I awake** <note>original: "בְּהָקִ֗יץ"</note> according to the mind of Blessed Luther and others.
**Ps. XVIII, v. 1.** **To the Chief Musician** <note>original: "לַמְנַצֵּחַ"</note> Thus with a *Pasek* <note>a vertical line used as a musical/logical divider</note>. Others omit it. **The LORD** <note>original: "יְהוָה"</note> We give the accent as our codices showed it, though its health is doubtful. Let those who have the opportunity to examine the Masoretic books look further into it. Meanwhile, the sequence seems to us to be restored as **The LORD | him** <note>original: "יְהוָה ׀ אוֹתוֹ"</note> so that the *Zarka* is a companion, with a *Maqqeph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> either expressed or understood: plainly as in Psalm 31:22 and 66:20, which some have more correctly.
**v. 2.** **And he said** <note>original: "וַיֹּאמַר"</note> with a *Pasek-shal-shebeth* <note>a complex combination of Hebrew accents</note>.

The commentary extensively discusses whether Psalm 18 refers literally to David's deliverance from Saul or prophetically to Christ's victory over death.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the personal petitions of Psalm 17 into the grand, triumphal song of David in Psalm 18. Having previously discussed David's plea for protection from "men of the world," the commentator now focuses on this elaborate hymn of deliverance, which is interpreted as both a historical account of David's life and a prophetic shadow of the trials and victory of Christ.</meta>

For it is a description of one who is violently angry. See verse 16; Psalm 74:1; Deuteronomy 29:19; and the note on 2 Samuel 22:9. **l)** Psalm 97:3. **m)** *breaking out from the mouth of the angry God.* See Job 37:2; 41:11, 13. **n)** *it consumed the enemies.* Psalm 21:10; Psalm 50:3; Job 1:16. **o)** *burning coals*, that is, lightning and thunderbolts. <meta>This page continues the exposition of Psalm 18, moving from David’s plea for help into a vivid, "theophanic" description of God’s intervention. The text follows the sequence of natural wonders—darkness, clouds, hail, and lightning—that signal the arrival of the Divine Judge to rescue his servant from "many waters" and "strong enemies."</meta>

v. 27. <gloss>b</gloss>) **pure and clean** you exhibit yourself, so that it is certain from this that you love purity and sincerity of heart, and adorn it with your gifts. For the word, compare Daniel 11:35, 12:10. <gloss>c</gloss>) **but with the perverse, that is, the twisted and oblique**. Psalm 101:4. Proverbs 2:15, 28:18. <gloss>d</gloss>) Abraham ibn Ezra <note>a 12th-century Spanish rabbi</note>: **you wrestle**. That is, you contend with the perverse, and so overcome their cunning that not only does their evil not reach its goal, but they are punished as they deserve. Others: "With the morally perverse, you show yourself restrictive," that is, as Cocceius's Lexicon 697 says, "you distort yourself": so that he hopes in vain that he can deceive you. (4) Genesis 30:8. Proverbs 8:8. Job 5:13. Compare 2 Samuel 22:27 and Deuteronomy 32:5. For God renders to each according to his works. Job 34:11. Romans 2:6. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch jurist and theologian</note>: **With the candid you act candidly; with the one who walks crookedly, you walk crookedly**; out of divine reckoning, collected from Leviticus 26:23.

v. 28. <gloss>e</gloss>) **For, or Truly you: which the general experience of all times** teaches. The "e" is explanatory, as in verses 22, 23, Psalm 14, 6, etc. <gloss>f</gloss>) Psalm 10:2, 9. Compare Zechariah 9:9. <gloss>g</gloss>) Psalm 6:9. Matthew 1:21. etc. Compare Luke 1:52, 53. <gloss>h</gloss>) **but eyes that are high, that is, proud, or raised eyebrows**. Psalm 101:5, 131:2. Proverbs 6:17, 21:4, 30:13. <gloss>i</gloss>) **you are accustomed to humble and bring down**: as we have very often experienced even until now. Compare Isaiah 2:11, 22, 5:15. The Targum speaks of the future, as a prophecy: **"Since you will deliver the people of Israel, who are poor among the nations, and will bring down the strong nations that prevailed against them, just as in exile."** This is followed with confidence by the next verses 29, 32, 49. But we, with Schmid <note>Sebastian Schmid, a 17th-century theologian</note> and others, take it as general experience, which our Savior took upon himself, compare Psalm 119:52.

v. 29. <gloss>k</gloss>) Schmid: **Indeed, I can set myself as an example here**. For you, etc. Compare Isaiah 43:24. <gloss>l</gloss>) **you, I say, by your grace and providence, illuminate** Psalm 13:4, 118:27, 119:130. Proverbs 29:13. Ecclesiastes 8:1. Ezra 9:8. <gloss>m</gloss>) **my lamp**. Schmid: namely by supplying me with counsel and strength in narrow straits. Compare 1 Kings 11:36. Proverbs 20:27, 24:20. Job 21:17. <gloss>n</gloss>) Geier: **This is fixed by a singular and personal faith**. Compare verse 7 and the note on page 3. <gloss>o</gloss>) **by the splendor of his grace and help, he dispels the darkness and makes it shine**. (6) 2 Samuel 22:29. <gloss>p</gloss>) **all the darkness of my distress and adversities**. Compare Psalm 112:4. Job 29:3. Kimchi: **Distress is indicated by darkness, just as salvation and liberation from it are called light and splendor**. Compare Esther 8:16. Targum: **"For you will light the lamp of Israel, which was extinguished in exile; for you are the Lord of the light of Israel: the Lord my God will lead me from darkness into light; he will make me see the consolation of that world which is to come for his godly ones."** See the note on verse 28.

v. 30. <gloss>q</gloss>) **For by you and your help**. Compare Psalm 60:14. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>: through faith or trust in you. Compare Hebrews 11:32, 33. <gloss>r</gloss>) **I will run against the troops of the enemy, nor will I fear**. Thus the Syriac and Geier, from the root *r-u-ts* [to run], comparing Job 15:26, 16:14, Daniel 8:6. But Schmid and others: **So that with you I might crush them**. Kimchi: with your help **I will break** the troops of my enemies, from the root *r-ts-ts* [to crush], comparing the similar form in Proverbs 29:6, Psalm 91:6. Add Isaiah 42:3, 4. <gloss>s</gloss>) **a hostile troop**. Compare 1 Samuel 30:8, 15. <gloss>t</gloss>) **and with my God**. See verse 29. <gloss>u</gloss>) **I leap over** (5) 2 Samuel 22:30. Isaiah 35:6. Zephaniah 1:9. Song of Solomon 2:8. <gloss>x</gloss>) **a wall**, that is, I will conquer the most fortified cities of the enemy. Genesis 49:22. Rabbi Solomon compares 2 Samuel 5:6, 7. See also 2 Corinthians 10:4, 5.

v. 31. <gloss>y</gloss>) **For as it pertains to GOD**. Verse 33. <gloss>z</gloss>) **his way and his manner of acting with men is perfect**; without any error or fault. Verse 33, 2 Samuel 22:31. Proverbs 30:5. <gloss>b</gloss>) **it is as if purified and refined by fire, so that there is no deceit or falsehood in it**. Deuteronomy 32:4. <gloss>h</gloss>) **besides**. The *yod* [a Hebrew letter] is an extra grammatical addition, as in Deuteronomy 1:36. <gloss>i</gloss>) **our God**. Namely, Jehovah, the God of Israel. Exodus 3:14, 15. <meta>This page transitions from the general praise of God's law in Psalm 19 to three specific royal and prophetic psalms. Psalm 20 is a prayer for the king’s victory, Psalm 21 is a thanksgiving for that victory, and Psalm 22 begins the famous lament often interpreted as a prophecy of the suffering Messiah.</meta>

20. 21. 22.
# Psalms 20, 21, 22

<margin>Ps. XX.</margin>

1 **To the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David.**
2 May the Lord answer you <gloss>b</gloss> in the day of trouble; may the name <gloss>d</gloss> of the God of Jacob defend you <gloss>c</gloss>.
3 May He send your help from the sanctuary and support you from Zion.
4 May He remember all your offerings and accept <note>original: "make fat"</note> <gloss>e</gloss> your burnt sacrifice. Selah.
5 May He grant you according to your heart's desire and fulfill all your counsel.
6 We will rejoice <gloss>f</gloss> in your salvation, and in the name of our God we will set up our banners <gloss>g</gloss>; may the Lord fulfill all your petitions.
7 Now I know that the Lord saves His anointed; He will answer him from His holy heaven with the saving strength of His right hand.
8 Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we <gloss>h</gloss> will remember the name of the Lord our God.
9 They have bowed down and fallen, but we have risen and stand upright <gloss>i</gloss>.
10 Lord, save the King! Let Him answer us in the day we call.

<margin>Ps. XXI.</margin>
<margin>Accent on the penultimate syllable 3</margin>
<margin>And an extra letter?</margin>

1 **To the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David.**
3 The king shall joy in Your strength, O Lord <gloss>m</gloss>; and in Your salvation how greatly shall he rejoice!
4 You have given him his heart's desire, and have not withheld the request of his lips. Selah.
5 For You meet him <gloss>n</gloss> with the blessings of goodness; You set a crown of pure gold on his head.
6 He asked life from You, and You gave it to him—length of days forever and ever.
7 His glory is great in Your salvation; honor and majesty You have placed upon him.
8 For You have made him most blessed forever; You have made him exceedingly glad with Your presence.
9 For the king <gloss>r</gloss> trusts in the Lord, and through the mercy of the Most High he shall not be moved.
10 Your hand will find all Your enemies; Your right hand will find those who hate You.
11 You shall make them <gloss>p</gloss> as a fiery oven in the time of Your presence; the Lord shall swallow them up in His wrath, and the fire shall devour them.
12 Their offspring You shall destroy from the earth, and their seed from among the sons of men.
13 For they intended <gloss>v</gloss> evil against You; they devised a plot which they are not able to perform.
14 For You shall make them <gloss>d</gloss> turn their back; You shall aim Your arrows at their faces.
15 Be exalted, O Lord, in Your own strength! We will sing and praise Your power.

---

<margin>Ps. XXII.</margin>

1 **To the Chief Musician. Set to "The Deer of the Dawn." A Psalm of David.**
2 My God, my God, why <gloss>x</gloss> have You forsaken me? Why are You so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning?
3 O my God, I cry in the daytime, but You do not hear; and in the night season, and I have no rest.
4 But You are holy, enthroned in the praises of Israel.
5 Our fathers trusted in You; they trusted, and You delivered them.
6 They cried to You, and were delivered; they trusted in You, and were not ashamed.
7 But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people.
8 All those who see me ridicule me; they shoot out the lip, they shake the head.
9 He trusted in the Lord, let Him rescue him; let Him deliver him, since He delights in him.

<column-break/>

**Ps. XX. v. 1. a)** The prayer and congratulation of the faithful for a happy success in the work of redemption.
**v. 2. b)** *May Jehovah the Father hear You, His praying Son. c) May He exalt you. d) The Name of God, i.e., God of Jacob Himself.*
**v. 4. e)** May He regard it as fat, i.e., value it. The <term>Piel</term> <note>an intensive Hebrew verb form</note> is used here in a declarative sense. Similar to the <term>paragogic</term> <note>an added letter at the end of a word</note> in 1 Samuel 28:15.
**v. 6. f)** Then we shall shout for joy and sing. **g)** We shall mark our banners.
**v. 8. h)** We will renew the memory, or rather, we will boast and proclaim.
**v. 9. i)** And we remain standing upright.

**Ps. XXI. v. 1. k)** A prophecy concerning Christ: whose I. exaltation (v. 1–8), II. works as the exalted one (v. 9–13), and III. conclusion through a sigh or prayer (v. 14) are set forth.
**v. 2.** Targum <note>ancient Aramaic translation</note>: *The King Messiah or Christ.* **m)** How greatly he shall exult.
**v. 3. n)** and the request or petition (1).
**v. 4. o)** *Since You go before Him.*
**v. 6. p)** You shall bestow upon him.
**v. 7. q)** You shall make him glad, cheering him with joy.
**v. 8. r)** Targum: *Since the King Messiah, as in verse 2.*
**v. 9. s)** *Your invincible and almighty hand shall find them, O King Messiah. t) all your enemies.* So in Isaiah 10:10.
**v. 10. u)** You shall place or make them. **x)** at the time of Your angry countenance.
**v. 11. y)** fruit, i.e., offspring. Targum: *Their children.*
**v. 12. z)** They devised a wicked plan. **a)** which they will not be able to, namely, carry out.
**v. 13. b)** the shoulder, either to carry burdens or as the part you strike with your arrows. **c)** Rather, with your bowstrings or the cords of your bows. **d)** You shall aim your arrows.
**v. 14. e)** *O Jehovah, Messiah.*

**Ps. XXII. v. 1. f)** concerning the deer of the dawn. **g)** A prophetic psalm of David concerning CHRIST; where I. the complaints and sufferings of the suffering Christ (v. 2–19), II. prayers for deliverance (v. 20–22), and III. a promise of a grateful spirit (v. 23–32) are found.

**Ps. XX. v. 1.** *To the Chief Musician* with the accent <term>Revia Geresh</term>. Only in the Berlin manuscript. See notes on Psalms 4:1 and 19:1. **v. 3.** *May He send.* So in manuscripts 6, 9, 10, 13, 20. **v. 4.** *And your burnt sacrifice, may He accept.* So in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20, and above in 5. **v. 6.** *In your salvation.* The accent <term>Mahpakh</term> is omitted in 1, 3, 17, 18, and the Berlin manuscript. *And in the name of our God* thus in 1, 2, 3, 21–24. **v. 7.** *That.* So with <term>Mahpakh</term> in 2, 3, 5–23. But with <term>Maqqaf</term> in 1, with <term>Munach</term> in Berlin, and with <term>Merkha</term> in 24. *Saving strength* with <term>Merkha</term> in 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20, and together with the <term>Pesiq</term> mark in 17, 18; which the <term>Pesiq</term> also requires according to the Index Biblicus page 61b. Analogy proves our reading.

**Ps. XXI. v. 1.** *To the Chief Musician* with <term>Revia Geresh</term> in 2; and without <term>Pesiq</term> in 1, 2, 3, against the Masoretic note. Compare notes on Psalm 13:3. **v. 2.** *Milra* <note>accent on the last syllable</note> with <term>Teres</term> against the Great Masorah. **v. 3.** *And the request.* So in the Berlin edition, against the Great Masorah. Compare notes on Psalm 4:1. **v. 4.** *You shall make them.* **v. 13.** *For You shall make them.* Thus in 1, 2, 3.

**Ps. XXII. v. 1.** *The Dawn* with <term>Revia Geresh</term> in 7, 8, 14, 15, 17, 22, and Berlin. See note on Psalm 4:1. **v. 3.** *Silence/Rest* is written defectively in 22, so the printed Masorah for Psalm 62:6. **v. 6.** *They trusted* with <term>Tipcha</term> accent in 6, 9, 10, 13, 20. But *To You they cried* in 3, 5; so also *In You they trusted* in 3, 5, 7. **v. 9.** *He trusted* with <term>Tipcha</term> accent in 2, 6, 9, 10, 12, 13, 16, 17, 18, 20, 23, and Berlin. **v. 8.** *They ridicule*—lacking in 3, 6, 9, 22; so also in 1, 2, and the Great Masorah.

### Psalm 23.

1 **A Psalm of David.** The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. 2 He makes me lie down **in green pastures;**
He leads me **beside the still waters.** 3 He restores my soul; He leads me in the paths of righteousness
for His name’s sake. 4 Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil; for
You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me. 5 You prepare
a table before me in the presence of my enemies; You anoint my head with oil; my cup runs over.
6 Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life; and I will dwell in the house of the Lord
forever. <meta>catchword: to length (Hebrew: le-orekh)</meta>

---

**v. 9.** **"Since He delights"** thus in manuscripts 6. 9. 14. 20. **v. 10.** **"You"** with the accent *Tiphcha* 1. 3. more regularly; see however the note on Psalm 19. **v. 17.** **"Like a lion"** with the accent *Merka*, but besides the printed Masorah of Psalm 143:3 and the Erfurt manuscript of Psalm 117:2, **"Like a lion"** with the vowel *Patach* 3. against the Masorah 2 and printed editions. But **"Like a lion"** with the vowel *Shurek* on the letter *Yod*, with *Chiri-boasting.* g) *plainly, without a marginal note of the 'Kri' (the read version)*, 11-14. **Rabbi Chaiim in the Masorah Finalis** <gloss>testifies that he found in certain most correct copies written</gloss> **"Ka'ari"** (as in the soft *f.* manuscript witnessed by Gerard in Calovius at this place) with the *Kri* (marginal reading) **"Ka'aru"** (they pierced). And this *Cthib* (written text) was seemingly followed by the Septuagint: <note>original: "ὤρυξαν"</note> **"they dug,"** the Vulgate, Arabic, Syriac, and Ethiopic: **"they dug,"** likewise Jerome: **"they fixed,"** and Aquila: <note>original: "ἤסχυναν"</note> **"they put to shame."** The Masorah on Numbers 24:9 favors the same. <term>See what Guffet notes in his Commentary on the Hebrew Language p. 403.</term> **v. 24.** **"And fear"** So the Easterners read, although they write it differently. **v. 25.** **"Despised"** without the mark *Pfsik* 5-13. 15. 16. 17. 20-23. and *Ben Asher.* **v. 27.** **"The poor"** without *Pfsik* 6. 9-13. 20. 21. 23. **"Those who seek Him"** with the accent *Munach* in place of *Metheg* 6-16. 20-23. Otherwise they write and read **"Those who seek Him"** 1. 3. **Psalm 23, v. 6.** **"I will dwell"** with *Patach* 1. and in the Second Berlin edition of the Masorah, which however is more correctly referred to Psalm 27:4.

<insert>
Psalm 24:1. "Those who dwell in it" [veyoshevei] marked with a Maqqeph accent. v. 2. "Rivers" [neharot] with a Mercas accent. v. 3. "On the mountain of" [behar-]. As in "and who shall ascend the mountain of" with a final [jinalis] f. 1-a. d) in the verb "lifted up" [nasa] without a Pesiq. v. 4. "Unto vanity" [lashav] — the Masorah on Leviticus 1:1 commands the letter Vav to be written small; but this is undoubtedly an error and should have referred to the following word "my soul" [nafshi]. "My soul" [nafshi] is thus written with a Cholem vowel in the text, without the expected letter Yod. So too in verse 22, but here with a small Vav and a note: "It is given small because it must be so." This "read/written" [Keri/Kethib] variation regarding the Vav should be small according to the Great Masorah. There is no actual Keri/Kethib variation here. The Kadma accent is used analogically (which Rabbi Chajim wonders at in this place) according to the textual Great Masorah on Lev. 1:1. v. 6. "Those who seek him" [mevakshei] with several Mercas accents; but with Tisha and truth. g) "for those keeping the covenant and his testimonies." v. 8. "King" [melech] — here and in verse 10 it takes the Yerach accent. All others use Mahpach, though a Mercas-Mahpach is never used elsewhere. v. 10. "He" [hu] with a Maqqeph. Psalm 25:1. "Lord" [Yehovah] with a Rebia-Geresh accent. See the note on Psalm 4:1. v. 4. "Your paths" [orchotecha] is defective according to the Masorah of Erfurt, but contrary to the printed editions. Furthermore, the letter Aleph has a Qamets-Chatuf. Instead of a double accent, it only has a Mercas. v. 5. "In Your truth" [ba'amittecha] is accented on the last syllable [Milra] and with a Sheva. "You/I wait" [attah kivviti]...
</insert>

# 26
**1** Of David. Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my integrity; and I have trusted in the Lord, I shall not waver.
**2** Test me, O Lord, and try me; <gloss>refined</gloss> refine my kidneys and my heart.
**3** For Your lovingkindness is before my eyes, and I have walked in Your truth.
**4** I have not sat with vain men, nor will I go in with hypocrites <note>original Hebrew: *almim*, literally 'hidden ones'</note>.
**5** I hate the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the wicked.
**6** I will wash my hands in innocence, and I will go around Your altar, O Lord,
**7** To proclaim with the voice of thanksgiving, and to tell of all Your wonders.
**8** O Lord, I love the habitation of Your house, and the place where Your glory dwells.
**9** Do not gather my soul with sinners, nor my life with men of blood,
**10** In whose hands is a wicked scheme, and whose right hand is full of bribes.
**11** But as for me, I will walk in my integrity; redeem me and be gracious to me.
**12** My foot stands on level ground; in the congregations I will bless the Lord.

# 27
**1** Of David. The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
**2** When evildoers approached me to eat my flesh—my adversaries and my foes—they stumbled and fell.
**3** Though an army should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war should rise against me, in this I am confident.
**4** One thing I have asked of the Lord, that I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the Lord and to inquire in His temple.
**5** For He will hide me in His shelter in the day of trouble; He will conceal me in the secret place of His tent; He will lift me high upon a rock.
**6** And now my head shall be lifted up above my enemies all around me, and I will offer sacrifices of shouting in His tent; I will sing and make music to the Lord.
**7** Hear, O Lord, my voice when I cry; be gracious to me and answer me.
**8** To You, my heart has said, "Seek My face"; Your face, Lord, I will seek.
**9** Do not hide Your face from me; do not turn Your servant away in anger; You have been my help. Do not abandon me and do not forsake me, O God of my salvation.
**10** Though my father and my mother have forsaken me, the Lord will gather me in.
**11** Teach me Your way, O Lord, and lead me in a level path because of my watchful foes.
**12** Do not give me over to the will of my adversaries, for false witnesses have risen against me, and such as breathe out violence.
**13** Had I not believed that I would see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living! <note>The text contains dots over the word *lule* (had I not), a Masoretic feature indicating a textual point of interest or uncertainty.</note>
**14** Wait for the Lord; be strong and let your heart take courage; yes, wait for the Lord.

**Psalm 26, verse 1.** "Judge me" (*shofteini*) with a *Munach* accent <note>A musical/grammatical mark</note> as in the higher manuscript 3. This is more regular, unless the previous title of the psalm "Of David" (*le-David*) in this place should be taken separately from the rest of the sequence (as elsewhere). "For" (*ki*) with a *Maqqeph* <note>A Hebrew hyphen</note> in manuscripts 2 and 3. "I have walked" (*halakhti*) with a *Kamets* vowel in manuscripts 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, and 20; contrary to the Basel Index page 61 d. **v. 2.** "Lord" (*Yehovah*) with an anterior *Tipheha* accent in 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, and 20. **v. 4.** "I have not sat" (*lo yashavti*) with a *Munach* in 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20; similarly in manuscript 5. "And with" (*ve-im*) with a *Maqqeph* in 1, 3, 6, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 20; similarly in 5. **v. 6.** "And I will go around Your altar" (*va-asovevah et-mizbahakha*) thus in 2. **v. 10.** "In whose hands" (*asher biydeihem*) thus in 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. **Psalm 27, v. 2.** "They stumbled" (*hemmah kashlu*) in v. 2 with a *Munach* in 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20; similarly in 5. **v. 4.** "My life" (*hayyay*) with a *Kamets*. *Small letter* in "in his shelter" (*basukkoh*). **v. 2.** Printed and Erfurt editions and Basel Index f. 61 d. **v. 5.** *Basukkoh* with a small letter *Samech* for "shouting, eucharistic" as required by the final Masorah f. 1. a. and the textual scholar Levita at the end of book 1, though without the support of the codices. "And He will hide me" (*veyastireini*) thus lacking in 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 15; thus featured in 2 according to the second version. **v. 7.** "My voice" (*qoli*) according to the Masorah in 2, 3, printed and Erfurt editions. **v. 6.** "And now" (*ve-attah*) with a *Pesiq* mark in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. "Upon" (*al*) with a *Maqqeph* in 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20, 21. "I will sing and make music" (*ashirah va-azammerah*) thus in 1. **v. 8.** "Your face, O Lord" (*paniekha Yehovah*) in 1, 2, 3. **v. 10.** "Lord" (*Yehovah*) with a *Revia Geresh* accent in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. **v. 11.** "Teach me" (*horeini*) thus with a *Mercha* accent together with a minor *Mahpakh* sub-distinctive in 2, 5, 7, 8, 11, 15, 16, 21, 22; which is the sequence in Psalm 55:20. In manuscript 1 by *Mercha* alone. But the rest have *Mahpakh* alone, against analogy. **v. 12.** "For they have risen" (*ki-qamu*) thus in 1, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20.

<header>28. 29. 30. Psalms 28, 29, 30</header>

<margin>
PSALM XXVIII, v. 1.
a) lest, if You are silent, You depart from me as if mute. Understand the word "if" <note>original: im</note> as implied.
b) with those going down into the pit, who suddenly fall into the pit and into destruction.
</margin>
Lest You be silent to me, and I become like those who go down to the pit.
<margin>
v. 2. c) toward the inner sanctuary, called the "oracle" <note>original: oraculum</note>, because God would give answers from there.
</margin>
Hear the voice of my supplications when I cry to You, when I lift up my hands toward Your holy sanctuary.
<margin>
v. 3. d) Do not draw me away or snatch me away.
</margin>
Do not draw me away with the wicked and with the workers of iniquity, who speak peace with their neighbors, while evil is in their hearts.
<margin>
v. 4. e) Therefore give back to them, the stubbornly wicked. f) render to them their retribution or what they deserve.
</margin>
Give to them according to their deeds and according to the wickedness of their endeavors; according to the work of their hands give to them; return their recompense to them.
<margin>
v. 5. g) For indeed they do not pay attention. h) therefore He will overthrow and destroy them, and by no means rebuild them.
</margin>
Because they do not understand the works of the Lord and the deeds of His hands, He will destroy them and not build them up.

n) A Psalm of David concerning Christ <note>The commentator interprets the "anointed" or "sons of the mighty" through a Christian lens</note>, containing: I. An exhortation to hear the word of the Lord and give Him glory (v. 1-2).

<note>This final section contains technical scholarly notes on the Hebrew vowels and musical accents (cantillation), comparing various manuscripts and printed editions.</note>

**Psalm 28, v. 3.** *workers of iniquity* <note>original: po'alei aven</note>: Thus in manuscripts 2, 6, 7, 9-16, 20-24, according to the analogy. But others place a Mahpakh accent over the Aleph. **v. 4.** The first *give* <note>original: ten</note> is with a Tsere vowel in manuscript 22, contrary to the printed Masora and other editions. But the second *give* is with a Tsere and Munakh accent in 2, 3, 5, 22, which the already cited Masora seems to require, marking the first word with a note indicating it appears only once this way with a Segol vowel. **v. 5.** *not* <note>original: lo</note> is marked with a Yerakh accent in 3, 5, 6, 9, 14, 22, 23, 24. Others use a Mahpakh, contrary to the usual pattern. **v. 7.** *The Lord* <note>original: Yehovah</note> with a Sarka accent in 6, 9, 10, 13, 20. **PSALM XXIX, v. 3.** *God of glory* <note>original: el ha-kavod</note> thus in 1, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. **v. 4.** *voice of the Lord* thus in 1, but differently accented in 6, 9, 10, 13, 20. **v. 7.** *voice of the Lord* in 2. **v. 7.** *divides* <note>original: khotzev</note> with a simple Revia accent in 7, 8, 15, 22, 23, 24. See note on Psalm 4. **PSALM XXX, v. 4.** *You brought up* and *from my going down* with a Tsere vowel in 1 and in the margin of 6 and 9, contrary to the printed Masora at Exodus 33:1. *You have kept me alive* with a Kamatz vowel in 7, 10, 17, 18, contrary to the Masora. *From my going down*: the letter Yod is without a Meteg in 3, 21; the letter Daleth has a Tsere in various manuscripts. **v. 6.** *weeping* <note>original: bekhi</note> with an Atnach accent in many manuscripts. **v. 9.** *the Lord* <note>original: Adonai</note> thus in 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 20, 22 according to the Masora. Others have the name *Yehovah*.

Psalm XXXI, verse 1. The term *To the Chief Musician* <term>original: lamnatzeach</term> is marked with a simple *Rbhia* accent in this place by all our sources. See the note on Psalm 4, verse 1.
Regarding the *Dagesh* <note>A dot in a Hebrew letter indicating it is doubled or strengthened.</note> in verses 7, 8, and 15; and so it appears in the future tense in 2, 5, according to the Masoretic index. Verse 6: *You have redeemed* <term>original: paditah</term> is written without the letter *He* in sources 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, and 20.
Contrary to the Masoretic notes, verse 11: *with sighing* <term>original: be-anachah</term> appears in sources 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20, 21, 23, and 24.
The rest follow the analogy, except for source 1, which has *be-anachah* written as if the letter *He* were excluded. Others follow the contrary analogy of the word *with sorrow* in the preceding member of the verse. Verse 12: *my enemies* <term>original: tzorray</term> is written defectively in 1, 3, 6, 9, 21, and 23, and in the Psalter with the commentary of Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a major medieval Jewish commentator.</note>.
Contrary to the Masoretic index, verse 14: *I heard* is correctly marked with a *Pshik* in 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, etc., according to its own Masoretic tradition.
The *Mahpach* accent is irregular here. Verse 20: *in a pavilion* <term>original: be-sukkah</term> is joined by a *Maqqeph* <note>A Hebrew hyphen.</note> in 1, 3, and following 5; but with a *Merca* accent in 6, 9, 10, 13, and 20.
The word *be-sukkah* appears with a *Rbhia-geresh* in 1, 2, 5, 6, and 9, and in Kimchi’s Psalter. The rest use a simple accent.
Sources 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 23, and 24, as well as 5, show the word *He has shown* with a *Sarka* accent placed over the last letter.
Compare the notes on Psalm 18:1 and Psalm 66:20. However, it appears with a very simple *Merca* in 24.

<column-break/>

Verse 5: *my strength* is written in full.
Other sources omit it.
The word *against me* <term>original: alay</term> appears with a *Patach* vowel in source 1.
Others write it in full.
Verse 16: *deliver me* is marked with a *Merca* accent in 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, and 24. The rest use a different marking.
Verse 21: *to me* <term>original: li</term> is joined by a *Maqqeph* in 1 and 2.

# PSALMS 32 and 33

<margin>
PSALM XXXII.
a) An instructional song <note>original: "didascalicum carmen"</note> in which David: I. gives thanks for the forgiveness of sins (v. 1–3), through which II. a person is rendered blessed (v. 1, 2, 6), and III. God becomes a protector and guide (v. 7, 8), provided that IV. the person does not maliciously resist (v. 9, 10). Whence V. there is joy for those upright in heart (v. 11).
b) "forgiven" regarding the transgression.
c) "covered" regarding the sin.
verse 2. d) To whom the Lord does not calculate or reckon. e) fraud, deceit, and hypocrisy.
verse 3. f) For when I kept silent and did not wish to confess my sin frankly to You. g) they wasted away and were consumed as if by old age. h) because of my roaring and wailing.
verse 4. i) my moisture was turned and changed as if by the droughts of summer.
verse 5. k) But when I made known my sin and confessed to You. l) then You forgave.
verse 6. m) Because of this pardon of sins (v. 5). n) "in the time of finding," that is, an opportune time, while You may be found. o) certainly while the flood is imminent. p) it shall not reach the one praying piously.
verse 7. q) You are a hiding place and refuge for me. r) and You will guard me from the enemy and distress. s) You will surround me with shouts of deliverance. Note: Insert "to me" <note>original: "Lemoc"</note> before the next verse, according to the scholar Schmid, as in "saying to me."
verse 8. t) I will counsel for you (that is, to you) with my eye.
verse 9. u) Only do not be. x) who have no understanding. y) Whence with bit and bridle. z) his mouth (Psalm 103:5) must be muzzled. a) because otherwise they do not come near to You.
</margin>

1 A Psalm of David. A Maskil <gloss>a</gloss> <note>A "Maskil" is a contemplative or instructional poem.</note>. Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven <gloss>b</gloss>, whose sin is covered <gloss>c</gloss>.
2 Blessed is the <gloss>d</gloss> man to whom the Lord does not impute iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit <gloss>e</gloss>.
3 For when I kept silent <gloss>f</gloss>, my bones wasted away <gloss>g</gloss> through my groaning <gloss>h</gloss> all day long.
4 For day and night Your hand was heavy upon me; my moisture <gloss>i</gloss> was turned into the droughts of summer. Selah.
5 I acknowledged my sin to You <gloss>k</gloss>, and my iniquity I did not hide; I said, "I will confess my transgressions to the Lord," and You forgave <gloss>l</gloss> the iniquity of my sin. Selah.
6 For this <gloss>m</gloss> let every godly one pray to You at a time when You may be found <gloss>n</gloss>; surely in a flood <gloss>o</gloss> of great waters, they shall not reach him <gloss>p</gloss>.
7 You are a hiding place for me <gloss>q</gloss>; You will preserve me from trouble <gloss>r</gloss>; You will surround me with songs of deliverance <gloss>s</gloss>. Selah.
8 I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will guide you with My eye <gloss>t</gloss>.
9 Do not be <gloss>u</gloss> like the horse or like the mule, which have no understanding <gloss>x</gloss>, whose mouth <gloss>z</gloss> must be held in with bit and bridle <gloss>y</gloss>, else they will not come near <gloss>a</gloss> to you.
10 Many sorrows shall be to the wicked; but he who trusts in the Lord, mercy shall surround him.
11 Be glad in the Lord and rejoice, you righteous; and shout for joy, all you upright in heart!

<margin>
PSALM XXXIII.
b) I. The pious stir themselves to the praises of Jehovah (v. 1–3). II. They present the subject matter of praise (v. 4–19). III. They place their trust in God (v. 20–22).
c) it is beautiful and fitting; or, praise of God befits the upright.
verse 7. d) He gathers as if into a heap.

1 Rejoice <gloss>b</gloss> in the Lord, O you righteous! For praise is becoming to the upright <gloss>c</gloss>.
2 Give thanks to the Lord with the harp; sing praises to Him with a ten-stringed lute.
3 Sing to Him a new song; play skillfully with a shout of joy.
4 For the word of the Lord is right, and all His work is done in faithfulness.
5 He loves righteousness and justice; the earth is full of the goodness of the Lord.
6 By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and all the host of them by the breath of His mouth.
7 He gathers the waters of the sea as a heap <gloss>d</gloss>; He lays up the deeps in storehouses.
8 Let all the earth fear the Lord; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of Him.
9 For He spoke, and it was done; He commanded, and it stood fast.
10 The Lord brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; He frustrates <gloss>e</gloss> the plans of the peoples.
11 The counsel of the Lord stands forever, the plans of His heart to all generations.
12 Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people He has chosen as His own inheritance.
13 The Lord looks from heaven; He sees all the sons of men.
14 From the place of His dwelling He looks upon all the inhabitants of the earth;
15 He fashions their hearts alike; He considers all their works.
16 No king is saved by the multitude of an army; a mighty man is not delivered by great strength.
17 A horse is a vain hope for safety; neither shall it deliver any by its great strength.
18 Behold, the eye of the Lord is on those who fear Him, on those who hope in His mercy.

<note>
**Translator's Philological Note:**
Regarding Psalm 32, verse 2: The word *Ashrei* (Blessed) uses a <term>Pfik-mahpach</term> <note>A specific combination of musical accents in the Masoretic text</note>. While it is usually regular, the <term>Merca</term> accent (which is found in verses 1, 3, 5, etc.) requires the "printed Masorah" at this location and at Psalm 1:1. Others use a <term>Maqqeph</term> (hyphen). Furthermore, in verse 17, *Ashrei* appears with a <term>Gaiah</term> accent, and in verse 5 with a double *Ashrei*, showing remarkable variety. In verse 4, *nehpakh* (was turned) uses a <term>Mahpach</term>, which fits the grammatical analogy of "consecutive" forms. In verse 4, the word *be-harvonei* (in the droughts) follows the <term>Pfik</term> according to the Berlin codex. In verse 5, *hattati* (my sin) and *odiecha* (I acknowledge) in verse 8 use the <term>Yerach</term> accent in place of <term>Mahpach</term>, which is irregular; however, the <term>Metheg</term> accent is found in its place in other editions (Erfurt). In verse 5, the phrase "and You" (*ve-ata*) appears with *hattati* without a <term>Pfik</term> in some versions. In verse 7, *tesoveveni* (You surround me) carries a double accent in the Berlin codex, whereas others use only a <term>Munach</term>, contrary to standard rules. In verse 9, the words for "bit and bridle" are marked according to our local tradition where the second <term>Munach</term> is a substitute. In verse 9, *kerov* (to come near) is written deficiently (without the letter Vav) in several manuscripts and the printed Masorah. In verse 10, *makh’ovim* (sorrows) is also written deficiently, following the printed Masorah and the book of Lamentations 1:12.
</note>

XXXVII, v. 1. i) This is a Psalm of David, similar to Psalm 3:1 etc. It is an alphabetic acrostic—where verses begin with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet—similar to Psalms 25 and 34. I. <note>Translator's Note: The following section contains technical corrections regarding the Hebrew vowels and accents used in different manuscript traditions.</note>
v. 10. The word *ki* [for/because] is marked with a Makkaph <note>a joining horizontal stroke</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and others. In Psalm 37:4, the word *mish'alot* [desires] is spelled defectively <note>missing a vowel-letter</note> in manuscripts 3, 7, 8, and 15 according to the Masorah.
v. 12. *Ki* [for] is marked with a Mercha <note>a musical accent</note> in manuscripts 1, 3, 6, 9–16. Others write it fully. v. 13. *Adonai* [Lord] is marked with an ancient Tiphcha accent in 1, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20.
v. 15. In *charbam* [their sword], the letter Shin has a euphonic Dagesh in 5, 17, 18, 22, 24, and the Berlin manuscript according to the Masorah; others lack it. But the following Tau lacks a Dagesh in 2, 3, 17, 18, 24, and in the margin of 6 and 9; others include it.
The word *tishabarnah* [they shall be broken] here and in v. 17 uses a Qamets <note>a vowel marker</note> in 2 and 3 in both places, against manuscript 1 and the Index of Basil folio 61d. v. 16. *Tov* [better] uses a Munach accent in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 16, 20. But it uses a Makkaph in 3, 5, 7, 8. v. 19. *Lo* [not] uses a Makkaph in 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 22. v. 20. *Kalu* [they vanish] is stressed on the first syllable <note>Milel</note> because of the pause in 1, 3, 7, 8, 17, 18, 22, 24, according to A. Efram's notes on Psalm 137:7. Others stress the last syllable <note>Milra</note>. v. 24. *Ki yippol* [Though he fall] uses a Munach in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 16, 20, 27. *Yippol lo* appears thus in 2, 3, 5. Many others use a Mercha, but erroneously with the following word. Nevertheless, Munach is used in v. 27. *Me-ra* [from evil] uses a Qamets in 5, 14, 17, 23, 24, and the Berlin manuscript. Others use a Patach.
</insert>

### 38

<margin>PS. XXXVIII, v. 1. p) to bring to remembrance—namely, written for that purpose, or delivered to the chief of sacred music. This is a prayer of Christ or of a godly man heavily tempted because of his sins and his enemies; in which: I. He prays for relief from God's wrath (v. 2). II. He states the reasons for his prayer (v. 3–21). And III. He concludes with a sigh or a vow (v. 22–23).</margin>
1 A Psalm of David, <gloss>p</gloss> to bring to remembrance.

<margin>v. 3. q) They have come down, or were sent down and fixed into me.</margin>
2 O Lord, do not rebuke me in Your wrath, nor discipline me in Your hot displeasure.

<margin>v. 4. r) There is no integrity, nothing sound or whole.</margin>
3 For Your arrows <gloss>q</gloss> have sunk into me, and Your hand has come down upon me.

<margin>v. 6. s) They have rotted and stunk. t) and my scars or wounds have wasted away.</margin>
4 There is no <gloss>r</gloss> soundness in my flesh because of Your indignation; there is no health in my bones because of my sin.

5 For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me.

**v. 29. The righteous** punctuated with *Tipcha* in manuscripts 3 and 5. **v. 37. a future for the man** Both readings give the same distinction to the words—not the one most interpreters extract, but the one expressed by the Chaldean <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation.</note> besides the Dutch: *because the end of man is peace*; and more clearly by Campensis: *for the one who is such, perpetual peace remains*. Even Geier finally explains it in accordance with the accents: *And the latter end of (this) man*, adding an emphatic "he," just as "man" is taken demonstratively in verse 23. Perhaps, however, the *Tipheha* <note>a grammatical accent</note> is substituted here (referencing notes on Ps 38:18 and Ps 50:21). **v. 39. their stronghold** with the *Kibbutz* vowel in manuscripts 2, 3, 5, contrary to the Masora. **v. 40. and He saves them** the letter *Ain* has a *Patach* vowel in manuscript 1 and in the margins of 6 and 9.

**PS. XXXVIII, v. 3. they have sunk** with a *Maqqef* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 13, 14, 20, and together with a *Munach* accent in 3, 11, 12, 15, 16, 21, 23. **v. 4. Your indignation** with a *Chatef-patach* in 1, 2, 3, and 5. **v. 7. I am troubled** with a *Tipcha* in manuscript 3. **I am bowed down** written deficiently <note>spelled without a helper vowel letter</note> in 2, 3, 5, 22. Perhaps the *Tipheha* accent is substituted here; he notes this form appears twice, once deficiently (cf. Ps 35:14 where our codices have the full spelling).

**v. 14.** *For my help*: accented on the last syllable in manuscripts 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20, 21. **v. 15.** *To destroy it*: Thus with a Dagesh dot in 1, 2, 3, 5, 15, 22, 23, 24. Others omit it. **v. 16.** *Aha*: With the accent *Sarka* in 2, 5, 9, 12, 14, 15, 16, 22, 24. Others omit it. The *Peshik* mark is omitted by 1, 3. **v. 17.** *The Lord*: Most include the *Peshik* mark; omitted by 1, 2, 3, 5, 24, and the Berlin edition. Compare Psalm 35:13. **v. 18.** *The Lord (Adonai)*: Without the Dagesh dot in 1 and in the margin of 6, 9—contrary to grammatical rules. *And they said*: With the prefix "And" in 1, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20 and in the margin. **Psalm 41, v. 1.** *To the Chief Musician*: With the vowel *Kamatz* in 3, 16, 22; similarly in 2, 5 and the margins of 6, 9—contrary to the Masorah of 1, 2 and the Erfurt and Basel indexes. **v. 3.** *And keep him alive*: In manuscripts 1, 8, 17 and the Berlin edition, written with the accent *Revia-Geresh* according to the Masorah, though this is argued to be incorrect based on Psalm 40:1 and 70:1. **v. 3.** *The Lord (Jehovah)*: Manuscripts 6 and 9 have *Adonai* in the margin. **v. 5.** *I*: With a *Maqqeph* (hyphen) in 11, 12, 15, 16, 21, 22, 23. **v. 7.** *And iniquity*: Thus in 2, 3; a different division of the verse members. **v. 14.** *From everlasting and to everlasting*: Thus in 2, 3. Similarly in 1, 12, 14, 15, 22, 23, but without the *Peshik* mark in 1, 3, 21, 23. **Psalm 42, v. 1.** *To the Chief Musician*: With the accent *Revia-Geresh* in 17 and the Berlin edition. **v. 2.** *As the hart*: With a *Peshik* mark in 3, 6, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 20. **v. 3.** *God*: With the *Revia* accent in 1, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20.

v. 11. *Shasu* [they plundered]: Thus through Patach vowel in manuscripts 1 and 3; and thus the future tense in manuscript 5. v. 15. *Menod* [a shaking]: through the Mercha accent in manuscripts 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. Similarly the future tense in manuscript 5.
Otherwise, they write it defectively <note>Missing a letter, usually a vowel indicator like Vav or Yod.</note> in 2, 6, 9. Thus also in the second manuscript 5, and the future tense in 1 according to the Masora 2 and the Erfurt manuscript; but against Masora 1 and the printed edition.
Ps. 45, v. 1. *Yedidot* [loves]: Thus through the Kibbuts vowel (as if "a song of love") in manuscript 1. v. 4. *Chagor* [gird]: Thus through the Maqqeph [hyphen] in manuscript 24; and thus the feminine in the Berlin manuscript. But many use the Tiphecha accent on the tone syllable: cf. Variant readings for Proverbs 3, 2. v. 5. *Davar* [word/matter]: through the Munach accent in 2 and 3; thus also in the future manuscript 5. v. 8. *Elohim* [God]: without the Yerach accent in 2, 5-14, 20, 21, 22, 23. *Meshachakha* [he anointed you] in manuscript 2. *Elohim*! in manuscript 2, emphatically. Furthermore, our accents at first glance seem to favor the opinion of those who interpret *Elohim* not in the Vocative [O God], (as we do, comparing v. 7 and Hebrews 1:9), but in the Nominative [God...]: It should be observed, however, that the Munach accent under *Elohim* may not be a "servant" to the Atnach accent, but a substitute, so that the preceding *Passer* [Paser accent] depends on it, placed for a minor distinction in the domain that must be twice mediately sub-distinguished, as in Ps. 19, 15. *Eloheikha* [your God] through the ancient Tiphecha accent, less emphatically in 6, 9, 22, and 24. *Mechavereikha* [above your companions] written defectively in 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 22, according to Masora 2. But the printed and Erfurt editions write it differently. And though written defectively, it must nevertheless be understood as a plural, as M. I. advises in this place. Others write it fully with the Yod.

v. 21. <note>original: "Homo itaque in tali gloria..."</note> a) Therefore, a man who is in such glory, when he does not understand these things, b) is to be compared with the beasts, which live without reason and are cut off.

PSALM 50. v. 1. c) A prophetic Psalm of Asaph concerning the true worship of God and the abolition of the Old Testament sacrifices. Here, Part I: The Prophet’s Introduction to gain attention for the Messiah who is about to speak, v. 1–6. II: The address of Jehovah the Messiah to the godly concerning the abolishing of Old Testament sacrifices, v. 7–15. v. 18. f) "You agreed with him."

v. 20. g) "Infamy," or otherwise "a stumbling block."

v. 7. i) Behold, with adhering depravity—not just actual [deeds], but habitual [nature]. k) "I was conceived, I was formed." l) And with original sin and its guilt. m) "Conceived, warmed, or cherished me," referring to his mother. <note>original: "Praeteritum Piel"</note> <term>Piel: a Hebrew verb form usually indicating intensive action</term>.

LVI, v. 1. e) concerning the silent dove [or] becoming silent, of those far removed from their paternal home <note>original: "de columba obmutescentia f. obmutescente, longe remotorum a paterno domicilio"</note>. **2** Be merciful to me, O God, for man would swallow me up; fighting all day he oppresses me.
**3** My enemies would swallow me up all day long, for many are those who fight against me, O Most High.

**5** In God I will praise His word, in God I have put my trust; I will not fear. What can flesh do to me?

PS. LVII. v. 1. m) Do not destroy, or do not let me be destroyed <note>original: "Ne perdas aut perdi me sinas"</note>. n) Ps. 16, 1. o) into the cave <note>original: "in speluncam"</note>. 1 Samuel 24:4 etc. It has the same subject as the preceding psalm. **2** Be merciful to me, O God, be merciful to me! For my soul trusts in You; and in the shadow of Your wings I will make my refuge, until these calamities have passed by.
**3** I will cry out to God Most High, to God who performs all things for me.
**4** He shall send from heaven and save me; He reproaches him who would swallow me up. Selah. God shall send forth His mercy and His truth.
**5** My soul is among lions; I lie among those who are set on fire—the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.
**6** Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; let Your glory be above all the earth.
**7** They have prepared a net for my steps; my soul is bowed down; they have dug a pit before me; into the midst of it they themselves have fallen. Selah.
**8** My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast; I will sing and give praise.
**9** Awake, my glory! Awake, lute and harp! I will awaken the dawn.

**v. 22.** The word *mishamen* [than oil] appears with a *Rebia Geresh* <note>a specific musical accent</note> in codex 2 and the Berlin edition; similarly in edition 5. The rest use a simple *Rebia*. **v. 23.** The word *mot* [to be moved] has a *Rebia Geresh* in the Berlin edition. But most have a simple *Rebia*; "He will never permit the righteous to be moved." **v. 24.** The word *Ve’attah* [And You] has a postpositive *Zarqa* in verses 1, 2, 3, 5. Codex 2 and the Berlin edition omit the *Pesiq* <note>separating line</note> at *toredem* [You shall bring them down], which according to the logic of sequence can only stand if the following word *shachat* [pit] has a *Merkha Mahpak*, which only codex 14 has. Most have a *Rebia* over *shachat*, which specially functions in place of the *Merkha Mahpak* with its sub-distinction *Zarqa*. This idiom is not rare in our codices 1 and 2—where they use the leading *Rebia* instead of *Merkha Mahpak* (while still keeping its subordinate accents). Hence here also the letter *Bet* under *le-be’er* [into the pit] has a *Lerach*, though simultaneously with a *Maqqeph* [hyphen]. However, codices 6, 9, 20 place a *Zarqa* as a accompanying accent on the penultimate syllable, which here assumes two things: 1) that the last syllable has the servant accent *Mahpak*, as read by Ben Asher; 2) that the word *le-be’er* is joined by a hyphen, as it is in codex 12, or at least that a hyphen is understood. The full sequence would be *toredem le-be’er-shachat*. PS. LVI, v. 7. *Yaguru* [They gather] is without a *Pesiq* in codices 2, 3, 6, 8, 10, 13, 14, 20. Abraham Ibn Ezra in his Commentary cites *yaguru* and explains it from the root meaning a "troop." It seems (as Rabbi Chaim notes here) that he read it thus in his copy. **v. 10.** *Yashuvu* [They turn back] has an accompanying accent in codices 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 21, 22. The rest omit it. The word *zeh* [this] has a *Merkha* without a hyphen in codices 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. **v. 13.** *Alay* [upon me] with a *Munach* in 3, 7, 8; similarly in 5. **v. 14.** *Hitzalta* [You delivered] follows the analogy in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 16, 29, 23. Others use a *Mahpak*. *Halo raglay* [Have You not kept my feet] is regular in edition 5.

<margin>Psalm LVIII.</margin>

# 28

<margin>v. 1.</margin>
To the Chief Musician: "Do Not Destroy" <note>Hebrew: *Al-Tashchet*</note>. A Michtam <note>A term for a golden poem or an inscribed monument</note> of David.

<margin>v. 2. c) Do you then truly speak of the silencing of justice—that is, the suppression of innocence—with an unjust silence? The question here reproaches and accuses <note>original: "An ergo vere obmutescentiam iustitiæ f. innocentiam iniquo silentio suppressam loquimini? interrogatio arguit & accusat h. l."</note>.</margin>
**2** Do you indeed speak righteousness in silence? Do you judge uprightly, O sons of men?

<margin>v. 3. d) Rather, from the heart you commit iniquities <note>original: "Immo ex animo iniquitates committitis."</note>.</margin>
**3** Nay, in the heart you work wickedness; you weigh out the violence of your hands in the earth.

**4** The wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray from birth, speaking lies.

**5** Their poison is like the poison of a serpent; they are like the deaf cobra that stops its ear,

<margin>v. 6. e) Of the charmer casting spells, however expert he may be <note>original: "incantantis incantationes, licet peritissimi."</note>.</margin>
**6** Which will not heed the voice of charmers, or of the most skillful caster of spells.

**7** Break their teeth in their mouth, O God; break out the fangs of the young lions, O LORD!

<margin>v. 8. f) They shall be melted or rejected like water which is poured out on the ground. g) so that they may depart. h) when God aims His arrows at them. i) as if they were cut off <note>original Latin notes f-i detail the imagery of the wicked's disappearance</note>.</margin>
<margin>his arrows (Qere/marginal reading)</margin>
**8** Let them flow away as waters which run continually; when he bends his bow, let his arrows be as if cut in pieces.

<margin>v. 9. k) Just as a snail continues along in its melting and perishes. l) or like the stillborn child of a woman, they do not see the sun.</margin>
**9** Let them be like a snail which melts away as it goes, like a stillborn child of a woman, that they may not see the sun.

<margin>v. 10. m) Before men perceive—that is, sooner than expected. n) your thorns, O enemies and harmful men (compared to 2 Samuel 23:6–7), shall become a briar or buckthorn. o) which God will snatch away in a whirlwind by the breath of His fury.</margin>
**10** Before your pots can feel the burning thorns, He shall take them away as with a whirlwind, both in His living strength and in His burning wrath.

**11** The righteous shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance; he shall wash his feet in the blood of the wicked.

**12** So that men will say, "Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges in the earth."

<margin>Psalm LIX.</margin>

# 29

<margin>PSALM 59, v. 1. p) Psalm 57, 1. q) see 1 Samuel 19:1, 6, 10, 11 etc. These prayers are therefore against the snares of enemies: whose atrocity is presented to God, and deliverance from them is sought, with a promise of a grateful heart <note>original: "Preces igitur hic funt contra infidias hostium..."</note>.</margin>
**1** To the Chief Musician: "Do Not Destroy." A Michtam of David when Saul sent men, and they watched the house in order to kill him.

**2** Deliver me from my enemies, O my God; defend me from those who rise up against me.

**3** Deliver me from the workers of iniquity, and save me from bloodthirsty men.

**4** For look, they lie in wait for my life; the mighty gather against me, not for my transgression nor for my sin, O LORD.

**5** They run and prepare themselves through no fault of mine; awake to help me, and behold!

**6** You therefore, O LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel, awake to punish all the nations; do not be merciful to any wicked transgressors. Selah.

**7** At evening they return, they growl like a dog, and go all around the city.

<margin>Technical notes on vowel points [Qamets, etc.]</margin>
**8** Indeed, they belch with their mouth; swords are in their lips; for they say, "Who hears us?"

**9** But You, O LORD, shall laugh at them; You shall have all the nations in derision.

**10** Because of his strength, I will wait upon You; for God is my defense.

<margin>God of my mercy (Qere/marginal reading)</margin>
**11** My God of mercy shall come to meet me; God shall let me see my desire upon my enemies.

**12** Slay them not, lest my people forget; scatter them by Your power, and bring them down, O Lord our shield.

<margin>v. 13. r) They are caught therefore in their pride, and because of their curses <note>original: "Captantur igitur in superbia sua, & propter maledictiones."</note>.</margin>
**13** For the sin of their mouth and the words of their lips, let them even be taken in their pride, and for the cursing and lying which they speak.

**v. 14.** *ידעו* [they shall know] with a *Gaiah* accent... **v. 15.** *ככלב* [like a dog] with a *Revia Geresh* accent. Others use a simple accent as above in verse 1. **Psalm 60, v. 2.** The word *את* with a *Makkaph* [connector]... though a *Merca* accent with a *Segol* vowel is required by other traditions... **v. 3.** *תשובב* [restore] is accented on the penultimate syllable <note>Hebrew: *Milel*</note> in several manuscripts... but on the last syllable <note>Hebrew: *Milra*</note> in others. **v. 6.** *נס* [banner] the letter *Nun* has a dot <note>Dagesh</note> in some versions... **v. 12.** *אתה* [You] is accented with a *Munach*... others use a *Tiphcha*... **Psalm 61, v. 1.** *למנצח* [To the Chief Musician] is without a *Pesiq* mark in some versions... **v. 4.** *מחסה* [shelter] with a *Chateph-Patach* vowel... **v. 5.** *אחסה* [I will trust] with a simple *Sheva*...
