A Song or Psalm. Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth!
2 : Sing out the honor of His name; make His praise glorious. 3 : Say to God, "How awesome are Your works! Through the greatness of Your power <gloss>p</gloss> Your enemies shall submit themselves to You.
4 : All the earth shall worship You and sing praises to You; they shall sing praises to Your name." Selah.
5 : Come and see the works of God; He is awesome in His doing toward the sons of men.
6 : He turned the sea into dry land; they went through the river on foot; there we rejoiced in Him.
7 : He rules by His power forever; His eyes <margin>The traditional reading (Qere) is "they shall be exalted"</margin> observe the nations; let not the rebellious exalt themselves. Selah.
8 : Oh, bless our God, you peoples! And make the voice of His praise to be heard,
9 : Who keeps our soul among the living, and does not allow our feet to be moved.

<column-break/>

**Verse 7.** a) They anxiously seek out crimes and iniquities, as in Psalm 58. b) "We are consumed and perished," spoken from the mind of the wicked. c) A "search" or "scrutiny" implies a completion or end. d) and that being "intimate," meaning the f) soul or e) heart of each one; their f) counsel is "deep," so that it cannot be sufficiently avoided.

**Verse 8.** f) But God will shoot and strike them, as He has always been accustomed to do. g) as if by an arrow rushing in unexpectedly. h) their blows or plagues are accomplished.

**Verse 9.** i) indeed, they have made and will make him fall—each of the enemies. k) mutually upon themselves. l) "the slanderous tongues," that is, the tongue of each of them. m) and they shall give themselves over to flight.

**Psalm 65, Verse 1.** n) Concerning the glory of Christ’s kingdom and its spiritual blessing. I. He confesses that everything is owed entirely to God and the grace of Jesus Christ (verses 2–4). II. He pronounces as "blessed" the one who enjoys the grace and closer admission of so great a King (verses 5–9). III. He promises the Church, under the "year of grace" (meaning the New Testament), a most abundant harvest of spiritual goods (verses 10–14).
**Verse 10.** o) and You render it abundantly watered.

**Psalm 66, Verse 1.** p) He prophesies concerning the kingdom of Christ, extending even to the Gentiles <note>Gentiles: non-Jewish nations</note> through the preaching of the Gospel. From this: I. He calls all nations to the praise of God and foretells that this will happen (verses 1–4). II. He confirms their hope by the experience of His own mind (verses 5–7). III. He repeats the exhortation and shows a grateful mind toward God by His own example (verses 8–15). IV. He instructs all the pious through His experience and concludes with a doxology <note>doxology: a short hymn of praise to God</note> (verses 16–20).

---

**Verse 8.** **Suddenly:** thus written in full in sources 3, 5, 22, and in the margin. **Verse 9.** Thus in the future in 1, 2, according to the Masora <note>Masora: the traditional body of notes on the Hebrew text</note> 1, 2, printed editions, and the Erfurt manuscript. **Their wounds:** written deficiently (without the extra vowel letter) in 1, 2, according to Masora 1, and Erfurt.
**Verse 9.** **Sees:** The letter Aleph is written with a Segol <note>term: Segol (a Hebrew vowel marking the 'e' sound)</note> in source 23, which is more regular, but goes against the Masora. **Verse 10.** **And they shall fear:** Sources 1, 6, 9, 10, 20, and 3 have "and they saw" or "they will see," but here it is written with a Shva <note>term: Shva (a Hebrew vowel point indicating a very short 'e' or no sound)</note> under the letter Vav. **The work of God:** thus in 2, 3, 5, 10, 13, 20, and likewise 6 and 9, but these latter two include the Revia-geresh accent. Others use a simple Revia.
**Verse 11.** **And they shall glory:** with a Dagesh <note>term: Dagesh (a dot in a Hebrew letter indicating it is "strong" or doubled)</note> in 6, 9, 10, 13, 20, 21, 23; but with a Chateph-patach vowel in 22. **Psalm 65, Verse 1.** **A Psalm:** only the Berlin manuscript uses the Revia-geresh accent. **Verse 2.** **Silence/Wait:** written in full in 1, 2, and printed Masoretic editions at Psalm 62:2. Others write it deficiently with a Kibbutz vowel. **Praise:** with a Pesik <note>term: Pesik (a vertical line used as a musical or textual divider)</note> in 2, 5, 6, 9-18, 20, 22, 23, 24, and the Berlin manuscript, against the Masora and Erfurt. Cf. note on Psalm 13:3. **Verse 7.** **And they shall fear:** Sources 5, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23 omit the Pesik. But 1, 3, 15, 21 lack the Mahpach accent. **Outgoings:** with a Metheg in place of a Mercha accent in 3, 7, 8. With only a Mahpach in 15. Compare similar sequences in Psalms 67, 68. **Verse 10.** **The earth:** with a Pesik in 1, 2, 5, 12, 14, 24, and Berlin. Others omit it. **And you water it:** thus with a Mahpach, which logic requires here, in 17, 18, 21, 22. But with a Yerach accent in others. Deficiently written in 1, 3, 7, 8, 15, 22, 24. **Verse 14.** **They are clothed:** with a Mahpach in 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 16, 20. With a Munach above in 2, 5, 7, 8, 11, 12, 14, 15. **Psalm 66, Verse 3.** **Submit themselves to You:** thus correctly in 1, 21, and 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 12-15, 20-23, though these latter use a Munach incorrectly for a Mercha. Others write it irregularly. **Verse 8.** **Peoples:** without a Pesik in 12, 15. But "Bless, O peoples" appears in 6, 9, 13, 14.

<note>
v. 12 "and in water" [ובמים] is thus marked with a Pataḥ vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 7, 8, 15, 24, etc., following the Masora. Others use a Qameṣ. v. 15 "fatlings" [מיחים] is written in full in manuscripts 3, 7, 8, etc. Others write it deficiently. Additionally, a Pesiq accent is added by 6, 9, 10, etc. But for "burnt offering to You" [עולה־לך] in manuscript 1, and "fatlings, I will offer to You" [מחים, אעלה־לך] in manuscript 2. v. 18 "He will hear" [ישמע] with an emphatic Pesiq in 3, according to the Basel Index. v. 20 "who has not turned away" [אשר לא־הסיר] so in 5, 7, 8, 11, etc. A similar confusion in this sequence is seen in the variant readings of Psalm 18:1 and Psalm 31:22. "My prayer and His mercy" [חפלתי וחסדו] so in 1, 2, 14. Psalm 67, v. 1 "with stringed instruments" [בנגינת] with a Revia Geresh accent in 1, 2, and others. See the note on Psalm 4:1. v. 2 "will shine" [יאר] with only a Mercha accent in 22. Regarding the doubling of accents, see the note at Psalm 65:9. v. 4 "and the peoples will praise You" [ויודוך עמים] so under the rule of the Atnach accent in 2, 6, 9, etc. Cf. verse 6. v. 5 "righteously" [מישר] without a Pesiq in 1, 8, contrary to the Masora in 3. v. 6 "and the peoples will praise You" [ויודוך עמים] so under the Atnach in 2, 14, and others. But the Basel Index requires a Pesiq. Psalm 68, v. 1 "of David" [לדוד] with a Revia Geresh in 7, 8, 15, etc. See the note on Psalm 4:1. v. 4 "before God" [לפני אלהים] so in 1, 2, 5, 6, etc. But with a Revia Geresh in 16. Others use a simple Revia as a substitute for the Geresh. v. 5 "in the deserts" [בערבות] so with an Atnach in 6, 9, 10, etc., which instead of the minor Tipcha accent uses the larger sub-distinction Paser. Cf. Psalm 45:8. But with an ancient Tipcha in 5, 7, 8, etc. With both Atnach and Tipcha in 3, 12, 15, etc. Finally, "to him who rides in the deserts, Jah is His name" [לרכב בערבות ביה־שמו] and v. 9 "Sinai" [סיני] thus with a Pataḥ in 1, 2, 6, 7, etc., following the Masora. Others use a Qameṣ.
</note>

# PSALM 69

<margin>
Psalm 69, verse 1.
a) See Psalm 45:1. 
b) Of David, see Psalm 3:1. He who here prophetically foretells the **sufferings of CHRIST**, the destruction of the Jews, and the building of Zion, that is, the Church. 

The following sections should be observed:
I. The prayers of the suffering Christ for his own liberation (verses 2–22).
II. The petition for vengeance against hardened enemies (verses 23–29).
III. The act of thanksgiving, both by Christ (verses 30–32), by the godly (verses 33–34), and by the whole universe (verse 35), along with the confirmed hope of the Church under the New Testament (verses 36–37).

1 To the Chief Musician; upon "Lilies." Of David.^b

2 Save me,^a O God, for the waters have come up even to my soul.^b <note>The "waters" here are a metaphor for overwhelming life-threatening distress.</note>

3 I sink^c in deep mire, where there is no standing; I have come into deep waters, and the flood^d sweeps over me.

4 I am weary with my crying; my throat is parched;^e my eyes fail while I wait for my God.

5 Those who hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of my head; my destroyers are powerful, being my enemies wrongfully; then I restored what I did not steal.

6 O God, You know^f my foolishness; and my sins^g are not hidden from You. <note>In a Christological reading, the "sins" refer to those of humanity taken on by the Speaker.</note>

7 Let not those who wait on You, O Lord God of hosts, be ashamed for my sake; let not those who seek You be confounded for my sake, O God of Israel.

8 Because for Your sake I have borne reproach; shame has covered my face.^h

9 I have become a stranger to my brothers, and an alien to my mother's children.

10 For the zeal of Your house has consumed me; and the reproaches of those who reproached You have fallen on me.

11 When I wept and chastened my soul^i with fasting, that was turned to my reproach.

12 I made sackcloth also my garment; and I became a proverb to them.

13 Those who sit in the gate speak against me; and I was the song of the drunkards.

14 But as for me, my prayer is to You, O Lord, in an acceptable time; O God, in the multitude of Your mercy hear me, in the truth of Your salvation.

15 Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sink; let me be delivered from those who hate me, and out of the deep waters.

16 Let not the waterflood overflow me, neither let the deep swallow me up, and let not the pit^k shut her mouth upon me.

17 Hear me, O Lord; for Your lovingkindness is good; turn to me according to the multitude of Your tender mercies.

18 And hide not Your face from Your servant; for I am in trouble; hear me speedily.

19 Draw near to my soul, and redeem it; deliver me because of my enemies.

20 You have known my reproach, and my shame, and my dishonor; my adversaries are all before You.

21 Reproach has broken my heart; and I am full of heaviness;^l and I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; and for comforters, but I found none.

22 They gave me gall^m for my food; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.

23 Let their table^n before them become a snare; and for their recompense,^o let it be a trap.

24 Let^p their eyes be darkened, that they see not; and make their loins continually to shake.

25 Pour out Your indignation upon them, and let Your wrathful anger take hold of them.

26 Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents.

27 For they persecute him whom You^q have smitten; and they talk to the grief of those whom You have wounded.

28 Add iniquity to their iniquity; and let them not come into Your righteousness.

**Technical Notes on the Hebrew Text:**
Psalm 69, verse 1. "To the Chief Musician" <note>original: *lamnatzeach*</note> with a fine *Pesiq* <note>a vertical line used as a musical or textual separator</note> in manuscripts 3, 5, and 7, 8. The word for "Lilies" <note>original: *shoshannim*</note> is written defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note>; the Masora <note>the tradition of Hebrew textual notes</note> requires it to be printed as in Psalm 45:1, but no manuscript supports this. Verse 3. "Swept me away" <note>original: *shetafatni*</note>: so all our copies; however, the *Pesiq* is required by the Masora and the Erfurt manuscript. Verse 4. "My throat" <note>original: *groni*</note> is written with a *Pattach* vowel in several copies, according to the Basel Index; others use a *Qamets*. "Waiting" <note>original: *miyachel*</note> is written with a *Chireq* followed by a *Dagesh* in manuscripts 3 and 5, and in the margin of 6 and 9, which is an easier construction. Verse 7. The word "be ashamed" <note>original: *yevoshu*</note> is omitted by the Conseruum in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 13, 20, 22. Verse 8. The word "Because" <note>original: *ki*</note> has a *Munach* accent in 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. Verse 14. "Time" <note>original: *et*</note> has a *Munach* accent in 3, which is more regular than our copies; however, see the note on Psalm 48:9. It has a *Maqqeph* <note>hyphen</note> in manuscript 1. Verse 16. "Overflow me" <note>original: *hashtofni*</note> without a *Pesiq* in 1, 3, 11, 21. "And let not [the pit] shut" <note>original: *ve-al tatar*</note> with a *Gaiah* <note>a stress mark</note> in 3 and 5, following Ben Naphtali. Verse 17. "Turn" <note>original: *peneh*</note> has a *Munach* in several manuscripts and the Berlin copy; others use a *Merca* accent against the rules. Verse 18. "For" <note>original: *ki*</note> has a *Merca* in 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. Verse 22. "And they gave" <note>original: *vayitnu*</note> with an added *Pesiq* in 6, 9, 16, 20, 23, contrary to the laws of accents. Verse 23. "And for their recompense" <note>original: *u-lishlomim*</note> with a *Gaiah* in 1 and 5 according to the Masora. Verse 24. "Shake" <note>original: *ham’ad*</note> with a *Qamets* vowel in many copies, contrary to the Masora. Verse 27. "And to the grief of those You have wounded": so in manuscript 3, with a singular sense: "and they count those who confess to Your pain." Compare Isaiah 65:14. Verse 28. "Add" <note>original: *tenah*</note> with a *Munach* in Ben Asher; but with a *Gaiah* in Ben Naphtali and most of our copies.

### Textual Notes and Variations
<note>This section compares different handwritten manuscripts and early printed editions of the Hebrew Bible, noting variations in spelling and musical accents.</note>

verse 32. **The bullock** <note>Hebrew: *par*</note> with the *Revia-Geresh* accent <note>A musical chanting mark</note> in manuscripts 12, 14, 15. All others use a simple accent. See note at Psalm 4:1. **Cloven hoof** <note>Hebrew: *mapris*</note> missing a letter <note>defective spelling</note> in manuscript 3, according to Michaelis's Erfurt edition. verse 33. **The humble** <note>Hebrew: *anavim*</note> with a secondary *Munach* accent in 3, 22; so also in 5 regularly. But **the humble** with both *Munach* and *Tiphecha* accents in 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 21, 23, which is erroneous. **And they shall rejoice** with the prefix *Vav* in 1, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. With a *Ga'yah* mark in 17, 18, 22, 24, and the Berlin edition. The rest are without it. 

Psalm 70. verse 1. **To the Chief Musician** in manuscript 22, against the Major printing. See note at Psalm 4:1. verse 3. **Those who seek** with a *Dagesh* <note>A dot indicating a strengthened consonant</note> in 3, 7, 8, 11, 15. verse 6. **Hasten to me** <note>Hebrew: *hushah-li*</note> thus the *Mercha-Mahpakh* accents are correctly ordered in 7, 8, 15, 22, 23. Others place the *Mahpakh* over the letter *Lamed*. Without a *Dagesh* in 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. **LORD** <note>The Tetragrammaton</note> thus with a *Patach* vowel in 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 24, and in 5 according to Michaelis and the Basel Index folio 61d. The rest use *Kametz*. Instead of **Lord** <note>Hebrew: *Adonai*</note>, manuscript 1 has **LORD**, but 6 and 9 have **my God** in the margin. **Delay** with a *Kametz* vowel in 2, 3; so in 5, against Michaelis and the print here; also in the print of Psalm 40:18. **To me** and **delay** against Basel Index folio 61d. 

Psalm 71, verse 3. **To a rock** with a *Mercha* accent in most, but anomalously. With a *Yerach* in 24 regularly. But with a *Maqqeph* and *Metheg* in 3 and the Berlin edition. Instead of **habitation** <note>Hebrew: *ma'on*</note> manuscripts 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 21 have **fortress** <note>Hebrew: *ma'oz*</note> with the letter *Zayin*, and (though doubtfully) in 1, 2, against Michaelis, the Erfurt edition, and the Mantua edition. **To resort** <note>Hebrew: *lavo*</note> with a *Revia* accent in 2, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, and the Berlin edition; so in 5, though it creates an awkward connection. Otherwise, a *Mahpakh* was ordinarily required here, in place of which a *Mercha* specifically succeeds, as in Psalm 1:1. verse 5. **My trust** with a *Kametz* in 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 21, 22, 23. verse 7. **To many** with a *Kametz* in 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 22; so in 5. However, with a *Shva* in the margin of 6 and 9. verse 12. **Hasten** <note>Hebrew: *hushah*</note> thus in the text without a note in 2, 3, 5, and in 1.

<note>The following section contains technical Masoretic notes regarding vowel points and musical accents found in various Hebrew manuscripts, indicated by numbers 1 through 24.</note>

verse 16. *Bigvurot* [in strengths]: thus written fully with the vowel Shurek in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. verse 18. *V'gam* [and also]: thus without the *Pfik* [separator mark] in manuscripts 1, 2, 5, 7, 8, 11, 14, and the Berlin manuscript. The rest (except 3, which has a *Makkaph* [hyphen]) have it with the *Pfik*. *Ziknah* [old age]: without the *Pfik* in 1, 3, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 21, 22. verse 20. *Tashuv* [You will return]: with the accompanying *Sarka* accent in 6, 9, 10, 13, 20. verse 21. *Tereb* [increase]: with the accompanying *Merca* accent in 2, as is regular. According to known rules of the *Rebhia-Gerehesh* accent, or rather alternating, it has the minor *Atnach* mark, as in Psalm 109:28. However, the *Pfik* is omitted in 2 and 5. Also for the words *V'tissob* [and You will turn] and *V'taaleni* [and You will bring me up]. verse 21. thus in 1: *Tereb Gedulati* [increase my greatness] with the *Rebhia-Gerehesh* in the Berlin manuscript. See note on Psalm 4:1. verse 22. *Elohai* [my God]: with the *Pashta* accent in 10, 13, 20, 22 and in the text of 6 and 9. For the *Kamets* vowel, the marginal note "gathered Kamets" is added in 17, 18 and the Berlin manuscript. verse 23. *Tirannenah* [shall sing]: thus with a *Dagesh* [emphasis dot] in 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, following Ibn Ezra in his commentary and according to logic. The rest are without the *Dagesh*. *Psalm 72.* verse 3. *Harim* [mountains]: without the *Pfik* in 5, 12, 21. Others with the *Pfik*. See note on Psalm 13:3. *Shalom* [peace]: with the *Mahpakh* accent in place of *Merca* in 6, 9, 10, 13, 20. verse 4. *Vidakke* [and He shall break]: thus with the *Merca* accent in 6, 9, 10, 13, 16, 20. But all others have it irregularly with *Munach*, except 24 and the Berlin manuscript. verse 9. *Lefanav* [before Him]: thus with *Merca* in 3, 5, 24. The others with *Munach*, against the rule. verse 10. *Malkhei* [kings of]: with *Mahpakh* in 2. Compare with our notes on Psalm 32:11 and Psalm 56:1. verse 11. *Goyim* [nations]: with *Merca* in 3, as is regular. Cf. note on Psalm 34:3. verse 16. *Bar* [grain]: with the *Kamets* vowel in 3, 10, 13, 20 and in the text of 6 and 9. verse 17. *Yinnon* [shall be continued]: thus in the text without the marginal reading in 1, 10, 14, 20. *V'yitbarekhu* [and they shall be blessed]: thus in 1, 2, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 21, 22, 24. The rest use a *Makkaph*. Furthermore, the letter Resh has a *Chateph-Patach* vowel in 6, 9, 10, 13, 20, 22. *Goyim* [nations]: with *Rebhia-Gerehesh* in 3, 4, 7, 10, 12, 17, 18, 20, 23, 24 and the Berlin manuscript, which is less regular. See the note above for verse 15.

<meta>This page marks a major structural transition in the Book of Psalms. It contains the doxology (concluding blessing) that ends the Second Book of Psalms (Psalms 42–72) and introduces the Third Book (Psalms 73–89), which begins with the "Psalms of Asaph." The translator notes continue to track linguistic variations and liturgical accents found in various manuscript traditions.</meta>

### PSALM LXXV

<margin>
Ps. 78, v. 1. s) A didactic psalm or prophecy, see Psalms 32:1 and 42:1. By Asaph, see Psalms 50:1 and 73:1. It presents the discourse of CHRIST to the Jews of His time, so that they might recognize the day of His visitation and not sin stubbornly like their ancestors. In it are to be observed: I. The introduction, calling for attention, verses 1–9. II. The narration of the events in this discourse: 1) The perversity of the people, vv. 10–58. 2) The punishments sent by God, vv. 59–64. 3) The change of the state and the election of the tribe of Judah, from which Christ was to be born, vv. 67–72.
</margin>
1 Give ear, O my people, to my law; incline your ears to the words of my mouth.

2 I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings from of old,

3 Which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us.

4 We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the Lord, and His strength, and His wonderful works that He has done.

5 For He established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, which He commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children;

6 That the generation to come might know them, even the children who should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children;

7 That they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep His commandments;

8 And might not be as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation; a generation that set not their heart aright, and whose spirit was not steadfast with God.

9 The children of Ephraim, being armed and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle.

10 They kept not the covenant of God, and refused to walk in His law;

11 And forgot His works, and His wonders that He had shown them.

12 Marvelous things did He in the sight of their fathers, in the land of Egypt, in the field of Zoan.

13 He divided the sea, and caused them to pass through; and He made the waters to stand as a heap.

14 In the daytime also He led them with a cloud, and all the night with a light of fire.

15 He split the rocks in the wilderness, and gave them drink as out of the great depths.

16 He brought streams also out of the rock, and caused waters to run down like rivers.

17 And they sinned yet more against Him by provoking the Most High in the wilderness.

v. 13. **and in your deeds**: thus in manuscripts 3, 5, 7, 8, 12, 14, 15, 16, 21. But with only the Merca <note>a specific musical accent</note> in 1. Regarding verse 24, the word *and he rained* is marked with a <term>Psik</term> <note>a vertical line serving as a musical or grammatical separator</note> in several manuscripts. This is correct for the flow of the chant, but less convenient for distinguishing the sense. According to other systems, such as the <term>Munach Superior</term> <note>a high musical accent</note>, it is treated more simply. Compare this to verse 27, *and he rained*, which follows the patterns found in verse 12.

In verse 25, the word for *provisions* is written "defectively" <note>without the letter 'vav' to represent the vowel</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 10, and 20, as well as in the main text of manuscript 6 and 9. Furthermore, regarding verse 44, see the notes on Exodus 7:17.

In verse 30, the word *estranged* is accented as <term>Milel</term> <note>stressed on the second-to-last syllable</note> in manuscripts 2 and 3. This follows the form found in Psalm 76:6. In verse 32, *they sinned* is also marked as <term>Milel</term> in most copies.

In verse 33, the word *in vanity* is treated similarly in manuscripts 1 and 2. In verse 34, *and they sought him* appears with "defective" spelling in manuscripts 1, 6, and 9, which follows the first Masoretic tradition but contradicts the third.

In verse 38, the phrase *and did not destroy* uses the <term>Ierach</term> accent <note>a "moon" shaped musical mark</note> in nearly all primary manuscripts. The phrase *and did not stir up* uses the <term>Merca</term> accent in most.

In verse 47, the rare word <term>hanamal</term> <note>translated here as frost or hail</note> is pointed with a "Patach" vowel in many versions, including the Bresslau and Mantua editions. Other versions use a "Kamets" vowel.

42 All who pass by plunder him; he has become a reproach to his neighbors.
43 You have exalted the right hand of his foes; you have made all his enemies rejoice.
44 You have even turned back the edge of his sword, and you have not supported him in battle.

*Textual and Historical Analysis:*
v. 33. **with their stripes** according to the *Revia Gerash* accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. -- v. 38. **forever** with the prefix *Lamed* in manuscript 5 and in the margin of 6 and 9. -- v. 40. **you have renounced** the letter *Nun* has the *Chirek* vowel in 1 and 3. -- v. 45. **from his splendor** with a simple *Sheva* vowel in 1, 2, 3, 5, contrary to the printed Masoretic text. **you have cast down**: with the *Kamets* vowel in 1, 2, 3, 13. v. 48. **remember** with the *Cholem* vowel in 3 and margins of 6 and 9. v. 49. **death** with a *Dagesh* mark in 2, 5, 17, 18, 24. Others omit it. **deliver his soul** thus in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. v. 52. **which they reproach** thus in 2, Asher 7, 8, 11, 12, 14--18, 21-24. But **which they reproach** in Berlin and others. **your enemies** without the *Pesiq* mark in 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 16, 20.

*Summary of Psalm 90 Structure (right column):*
I. The misery of human life is deplored, v. 1–6.
II. The cause of it: sin and the deserved wrath of God, v. 7–11.
III. The understanding of this matter: he prays for mercy and the direction of life for the pious servants of God, v. 12–17.

PSALM 90, v. 1. **Lord** with the minor *Tiphecha* accent according to most; more correctly with *Revia* in 2, 3, 14, 24. **to us** thus with a simple *Revia*. v. 2. **and you had formed** thus with the *Metheg* mark in 2. Others omit it, while the *Tsere* vowel remains. **and from everlasting** with the prefix *Vav* in 6, 9, 10, 20. Yet without it in the margins of 6 and 9. v. 9. **we bring our years to an end**: thus 2, 7, 8, 15, 21, 22. **a sigh**: with the *Tsere* vowel in 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. v. 10. **our years** without *Pesiq* in 1, 3, 5, 7, 8. **in them** with *Mercha-Mahpach* in 2. With *Revia* in 6–10, 12–16, 20, 23. v. 5. **u)** like a rainstorm or a torrent, you sweep them away.

**Psalm 91, v. 1. p)** He will remain safe even by night. This Psalm promises to the godly man: **I.** Deliverance from pestilence (vv. 1–7). **II.** From enemies (vv. 8–9). **III.** From every plague through the protection of angels (vv. 10–12). **IV.** From the ferocity of beasts (v. 13). and **V.** God’s grace and salvation itself (vv. 14–16).
</margin>
1 He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.

<margin>
**v. 2. q)** I say therefore: With Jehovah is my refuge and my fortress.
</margin>
2 I will say of the Lord, "He is my refuge and my fortress; my God, in Him I will trust."

<margin>
**v. 3. r)** from the pestilence of destructions, or the pernicious pestilence.
</margin>
3 For He shall deliver you from the snare of the fowler and from the perilous pestilence.

<margin>
**v. 4. s)** With the feathers of His wings He will protect you. **t)** a shield (Psalm 5:13) and a buckler <note>A small, round shield.</note> (1).
</margin>
4 He shall cover you with His feathers, and under His wings you shall take refuge; His truth shall be your shield and buckler.

5 You shall not be afraid of the terror by night, nor of the arrow that flies by day,

6 Nor of the pestilence that walks in darkness, nor of the destruction that lays waste at noonday.

7 A thousand may fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; but it shall not come near you.

8 Only with your eyes shall you look, and see the reward of the wicked.

9 Because you have made the Lord, who is my refuge, even the Most High, your dwelling place,

10 No evil shall befall you, nor shall any plague come near your tent;

11 For He shall give His angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways.

12 In their hands they shall bear you up, lest you dash your foot against a stone.

13 You shall tread upon the lion and the cobra; the young lion and the serpent you shall trample underfoot.

14 "Because he has set his love upon Me, therefore I will deliver him; I will set him on high, because he has known My name.

15 He shall call upon Me, and I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble; I will deliver him and honor him.

16 With long life I will satisfy him, and show him My salvation."

This Psalm discusses: **I.** Confession and praise of Jehovah (vv. 2–4). **II.** Specifically from the recognition of God’s benefits, which fools do not understand (vv. 5–7). **III.** Therefore, those who are like enemies of God will be cut off (vv. 8–10). **IV.** While the godly and just shall flourish (vv. 11–16).
</margin>
1 A Psalm. A Song for the Sabbath day.

2 It is good to give thanks to the Lord, and to sing praises to Your name, O Most High;

3 To declare Your lovingkindness in the morning, and Your faithfulness every night,

4 On an instrument of ten strings, on the lute, and with the harmonious sound of the harp.

5 For You, Lord, have made me glad through Your work; I will triumph in the works of Your hands.

6 O Lord, how great are Your works! Your thoughts are very deep.

7 A senseless man does not know, nor does a fool understand this:

**Verse 12.** The word *Hoda* <note>make known</note> is written with a *Kametz* <note>a vowel mark indicating an 'a' sound</note> in manuscripts 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 21, 22, 23; and likewise in the first edition, contrary to the Masoretic text <note>the authoritative Hebrew text</note> in 1 and 2, and the Erffurt, Michaelis, and Basel Index (folio 61d). **Verse 17.** Instead of *Adonai* <note>Lord</note>, manuscripts 5, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 21, 22, 23 have *Jehovah*; also noted in the margins of 6, 9, 20, 23, and in the first edition 5. However, "servant" does not agree with the preceding or following text. **Psalm 91, Verse 3.** The word *Middeber* <note>from the pestilence</note> is written with a *Makkaph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in 1, 2, 8, 21, 22; and in the first edition 5. **Verse 12.** *Tiggoph* <note>you strike</note> is written defectively <note>missing a letter used as a vowel</note> in 3 and 22, according to the printed Masorah at the end (folio 3, column 6). **Verse 4.** *Lāk* <note>to you</note> appears with the *Rebia* accent in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14. **Verse 13.** *Tirmos Kephir* <note>you shall trample the young lion</note> is found this way in 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. **Verse 5.** [Marked] with a *Makkaph* in 1, 3, 7. **Verse 15.** *Immo Anochi* <note>I am with him</note>; and here we also refer to manuscript 5, which has a double *Mercha* accent. However, most have *Immo* with a *Makkaph*, followed in some by a *Munach* and in others by a tonic *Tiphecha*. Others mark *Anochi*. But all these are contrary to the rules of sequence. Finally, in 6, 9, 13, 14, 24 and the Berlin edition, *Immo Anochi* has a <note>correct</note> sequence but a less convenient distinction. **Psalm 92, Verse 1.** *Shir* <note>song</note> appears with the *Rebia Geresh* accent in the Berlin edition. All others use the simple [accent], except for 1 and 2, which have erroneous accents here. See the note on Psalm 4:1. **Verse 4.** *Alei Asor* <note>on the ten-stringed instrument</note> appears with a *Munach* in 2, 6, 9, 12, 13, 14, 20; so too in the first edition 5.

### 94

<margin>
**Psalm 94.**
**v. 1. r)** O God of vengeances. Nahum 1:1. **s)** Shine forth, as in Psalm 80:2. This is a prayer of the Church against wicked and proud men, and against the antichristian throne (verse 20), in which: I. God is stirred up to vengeance (verses 1–3). II. Their impious works are described (verses 4–7). III. Their folly is refuted (verses 8–11). IV. But blessed is the one who is chastened by the Lord (verses 12–15). V. The help of God provided against the wicked is praised (verses 16–23).
**v. 16. t)** For me, as I contend with the wicked.
</margin>

1 O LORD God, to whom vengeance belongs; O God, to whom vengeance belongs, shine forth. 
2 Lift up yourself, you judge of the earth; render a reward to the proud. 
3 LORD, how long shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked triumph? 
4 How long shall they utter and speak hard things? And all the workers of iniquity boast themselves? 
5 They break in pieces your people, O LORD, and afflict your heritage. 
6 They slay the widow and the stranger, and murder the fatherless. 
7 Yet they say, "The LORD shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard it." 
8 Understand, you brutish among the people; and you fools, when will you be wise? 
9 He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? He who formed the eye, shall he not see? 
10 He who chastises the heathen, shall he not correct? He who teaches man knowledge, shall he not know? 
11 The LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are vanity. 
12 Blessed is the man whom you chasten, O LORD, and teach him out of your law; 
13 That you may give him rest from the days of adversity, until the pit be dug for the wicked. 
14 For the LORD will not cast off his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance. 
15 But judgment shall return unto righteousness; and all the upright in heart shall follow it. 
16 Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? Or who will stand up for me against the workers of iniquity?

**Notes on the Hebrew Text:**
**v. 8.** The word **kmō** [like] is written with a *Makkaph* <note>A Hebrew hyphen connecting words</note> in editions 1, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. **v. 9.** **mārōm** [on high] uses a *Revia-geresh* accent in edition 2 and the Berlin manuscript. Others use a simple accent. **v. 10.** **āwen** [iniquity] uses the *Yerach* accent in most editions. **oyvehkhā** [your enemies] appears with an emphatic *Pesiq* mark in many versions to add stress to the repetition. **v. 11.** **balōti** [I am anointed] is regularly stressed on the penultimate syllable (*milel*) in most manuscripts, though some place the stress on the final syllable (*milra*). **v. 12.** **mrē'im** [evildoers] uses the *Atnach* <note>The main pause in a verse</note> in editions 1, 2, and 3. Others use different accents like *Paser*. **Psalm 93, v. 2.** **mē'ōlām** [from everlasting] is found in this form in many manuscripts, though some use different vowel points or accents. **Psalm 94, v. 1.** **nəqāmōt** [vengeances] appears with various accents across the sources, including *Merca* or *Revia*. **v. 7.** The word is written without a *Dagesh* <note>A dot indicating a strengthened consonant</note> in some versions, contrary to the standard Masoretic text. **v. 9.** **ha-nōṭa** [he who planted]—some manuscripts add a *Merca* accent here, which is likely for pleasant sound (*euphonic*). **yōtzēr** [he who formed] is stressed on the final syllable in some editions, but others incorrectly place the accent on the first syllable. **v. 12.** The name of God **Yāh** appears without a *Dagesh* in the letter *He* in several versions, which contradicts the standard Masoretic printed editions.

V. 21. "And he returned" <note>Hebrew: וַיָּשֶׁב</note> with a *Pattach* <note>a vowel mark for the 'a' sound</note> according to manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 22. **Psalm 95, v. 7.** "For" <note>Hebrew: כִּי</note> thus expressed with a *Maqqef* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in 1, 3, 5 through 14. <note>The following notes are technical comparisons of different Hebrew manuscripts and editions regarding musical accents (cantillation) and vowel markings.</note>

v. 13. *Yishpot* ("he will judge") according to *Munach* <note>A Hebrew musical accent.</note> in editions 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 21, and so on. But the following word *Tevel* ("the world") has a substitute accent in editions 1 and 3, and so on; however, it has the *Tiphecha* accent in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 21, 22. **PSALM 97, v. 3.** *Utlahet saviv* ("and it burns up round about") thus in 1, 2, and following. v. 4. *Vatachel* ("and it trembled") thus in 1, 2, and following; used emphatically, but mistakenly written with a *Munach* instead of a *Merca*. v. 5. *Kadonag* ("like wax") with the *Kamatz* vowel in 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 21, 22; contrary to *Majus* and edition 1. However, 6 and 9 note in the margin that it should be with the *Patach* vowel. v. 6. *Shamayim* ("heavens") without the prefix in 1 and 2. v. 7. *Hamithalelim* ("those who boast") with a *Metheg* accent in 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 21, 22, 23. v. 8. *Sham'ah* ("she heard") with the *Mahpah* accent in 3, 6, 9, 10, 11, 14, 20, 21, 22; this is against the usual rule. But *Sham'ah vatismach* ("she heard and was glad") is written emphatically in 2 and following. v. 9. *Atah* ("you") without the *Pfsik* mark in 2, 3, 5. v. 10. *Sin'u* ("hate") with a *Metheg* accent in 17, 18, and the Berlin edition. **PSALM 98, v. 1.** *Hoshiah* ("it has gained victory") with a *Munach* in 2, 5, and the Berlin edition. See the note on Psalm 96:8. v. 8. *Neharot* ("floods/rivers") with the *Tiphecha* accent in 1 and 3. v. 9. *Yishpot Tevel* ("he will judge the world") thus in 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 21, 22. Compare Psalm 96:13. **PSALM 99, v. 1.** *Malach* ("he reigned") with the *Patach* vowel in 3 and following. v. 3. *Gadol venora* ("great and terrible") thus in 1, 2, and following.

### Psalm 103

<margin>Psalm 103</margin>
1 : Of David. Bless the LORD, O my soul; and all that is within me, bless His holy name!

4 : Who redeems your life from the pit, who crowns you with lovingkindness and tender mercies,
5 : Who satisfies your mouth with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.
6 : The LORD executes righteousness and justice for all who are oppressed.
7 : He made known His ways to Moses, His acts to the children of...

**Notes on Psalm 102:**
v. 6. b) *By the sound of my groaning: that is, from a sorrow that breaks out into the heaviest groans.*
v. 7. c) *I have become like a pelican of the wilderness <note>original Latin: "plateae", following the Vulgate</note>.*
d) *The Vulgate reads "night-raven"; Schmidt reads "like an owl of the wastes."*
v. 8. e) *Like a bird or a night-owl, which is solitary upon the roof at night.*
v. 9. f) *My adversaries, acting madly and boastfully, swear by me and call down evils upon others using my name.*
v. 13. g) *But You, O Jehovah Messiah <note>The translator interprets the "Lord" here specifically as the Messiah, comparing this to Hebrews 1:10-12</note>.*
v. 15. h) *For Your worshippers desire that her stones be prepared.* i) *And they pity her dust—that is, her ruins—because she lies in destruction.*
v. 17. k) *Because He has built.* l) *And has appeared in His glory.*
v. 18. m) *Because He has looked upon.* n) *The solitary one. This is a figure of speech derived from a tree of the desert, as in Jeremiah 17:6.*
v. 21. o) *That He might loosen and dismiss from their chains those doomed to death, opening the prison. See Psalm 79:11.*
v. 24. p) *The Lord has indeed afflicted, and still afflicts, my strength with various calamities on this journey of my life.*
v. 25. q) *Yet I will say, being confirmed by faith and the hope of Your coming, O Jehovah Messiah, my God!* r) *Do not take me away in Your anger (referencing verse 11).*
s) *For Your years endure through every age; You are always the same and shall remain so (verse 28), nor will Your promises fail or be subject to change.*
v. 26. t) *Formerly and long ago, before us. See Deuteronomy 2:12.*

**Notes on Psalm 103:**
**v. 1. u)** Compare with Psalm 3:1 and 25:1. In this Psalm, David:
I. Gives thanks to God for the benefits granted to him (verses 1–7).
II. Celebrates the mercy of God (verses 8–14).
III. Marvels at human fragility and God's eternity (verses 14–19).
IV. Stirs up heaven, earth, and himself to praise Him (verses 20–22).
v. 2. x) *Of all His benefits which He has bestowed upon you (see verse 10).*
v. 5. y) *Who satisfies your mouth with His good things, as in Psalm 32:8.*

---

**Critical and Masoretic Notes:**
v. 5: Instead of "from eating," manuscripts 3, 5, and others read "the eating of my bread," just as the Syriac version rendered it.
v. 7: For "ruins," see the margin.
v. 8: Instead of "lonely" <note>Hebrew: "boded"</note>, manuscripts 1, 3, 6, 9, 10, and 20 have "wandering" <note>Hebrew: "noded"</note>. In the margin of manuscripts 6 and 9, it is explained as "vaga-bunda" (wandering). The Syriac reads "flying," while Jonathan’s Targum seems to combine both readings: "which flies and wanders alone." However, the Hebrew letter *Beth* is required by the standard Masoretic text (see Isaiah 14:31 and Hosea 8:9).
v. 10: The word "my drink" <note>Hebrew: "v'shikuvi"</note> is written without a *dagesh* (emphasis dot) in many manuscripts including 6–10 and 13.
v. 13: Other books in the *Minchat Shai* <note>A famous 17th-century Masoretic commentary</note> have "Your throne" <note>Hebrew: "b'vo-acha"</note> instead of "You shall sit"; Abraham Ibn Ezra explained it this way as well, though erroneously, as the author of *Minchat Shai* correctly observed.
v. 23: The word "gathering" uses a *Munach* accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, and 8.
v. 24: The word "He weakened" <note>Hebrew: "inni"</note> is marked with a *Tiphcha* accent in many manuscripts. Others use a *Merca* accent. The word "in the way" is marked with a *Merca* in manuscripts 2, 3, and 24, while others use a *Munach*.
v. 26: The word "You founded" is written with a *Kametz* vowel in manuscripts 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, and 23, contrary to the printed Masorah of Erfurt.
v. 28: The word "And You" is joined by a *Maqqeph* (hyphen) in several manuscripts. The word "will [not] end" has a *dagesh* in the letter *Mem* in manuscripts 1, 2, 4, 5, 14, 16, and 17.
Psalm 103, v. 5: The word "your mouth" <note>Hebrew: "edyekh"</note> is spelled this way in manuscripts 7, 8, 11, 12, and others.

v 14. *lehotzi* [to bring forth] with an accent on the last syllable; this is the form for the future. — v. 18. *lashfanim* [for the hyraxes] with a Dagesh [a dot doubling the letter] in manuscripts 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 21, 23. The letter Lamed [L] ... with a Metheg [a mark for a slight pause] in manuscripts 2, 5, and in the margin of 6 and 9. v. 20. *tashet* [you make] using a Munach accent instead of a Metheg in manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. The word *bo* [in it] takes a Merca accent in manuscripts 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20; this is also the future form in manuscript 5. v. 23. *adam* [man] with a Tiphcha accent in manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. The word *u-lavodato* [and to his labor] appears with only a Munach accent in manuscripts 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 22, 23, which is irregular. However, it appears with a Rebia accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and likewise in the future of 5. v. 24. *kinyanekha* [your possessions] has an emphatic Pesik mark in manuscripts 7, 8, 11, 12, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23. It also appears with a Mahpakh accent in manuscript 3 and the future of 5. The spelling of *kinyanekha* is defective [shorter] in manuscripts 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 21, 22, 23, and in the margins of 6 and 9. v. 25. *sham* [there] appears with a Maqqeph [hyphen] in manuscripts 1, 5, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23, 24, partly with an added Metheg. v. 26. *zeh* [this] has a Pesik-Mahpakh accent in manuscripts 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 12, 13, 16, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, which would be the regular sequence for the Silluq accent, provided the following word *yatzarta* [you formed] had a superior Munach, which no manuscript has except for 2. v. 29. *tastir* [you hide] with a Munach in 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20, and likewise in the future of 5, which is against standard grammar. v. 35. *od* [again/more] regularly uses a superior Munach according to the Berlin manuscript. Compare the note on Psalm 48, 9. *Hallelujah* is written without a Mappik [a dot in the H] in manuscript 22 and with an explicit Raphe [a mark indicating soft pronunciation] in the future of 5, according to the Masorah of Erfurt. Otherwise, *Hallelujah* is written as one word without an intervening Maqqeph in manuscript 24. See note on Psalm 105, 45. PSALM 105. v. 2. *shiru* [sing] with a Maqqeph in 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23. v. 5. *niflaotav asher* [His wonders that] thus in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 21, with the preceding *zikru* [remember] also having a Munach in 2 and 14. v. 9. *u-shvuato* [and His oath] with a double accent in 5, 7, 8, 11, 12, 16, 17, 21, 24, and the Berlin manuscript. # Psalm 106. 106. קו תהלים <note>The Hebrew letters 'Koph-Vav' represent the number 106.</note>

<margin>PSALM 106, verse 1. a) This is also a song of praise to Jehovah and His mercy toward Israel; it simultaneously contains a prophecy regarding their dispersion and their eventual future gathering. Hence David: I. prays for the grace and mercy of God, verses 1–5. II. confesses the sins of the people, verses 6–43. III. acknowledges the mercy of God, who did not reject His ungrateful people, verses 44–46. IV. concludes with a prayerful sigh and a doxology <note>a short hymn of praise</note> in the application, verses 47–48. b) Compare Psalm 105:1 and 1 Chronicles 16:34.</margin>

<margin>PSALM 106, verse 1.</margin>
**Hallelujah** is thus joined together in manuscripts 2, 3, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 20, 24. But it is divided as **Hallelu Jah** in manuscript 5, 14, 22; and also in several others, but without the interposed Maqqeph <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note>, which is often understood in these books. Finally, it appears as **Hallelu Jah** in manuscripts 1, 3, 8, 15, 16, 17, 21, and Berlin, though with less grammatical consistency: compare, however, the variant readings of Psalm 71:7, 3. It seems the Merca accent was confused with the euphonic Metheg. Verse 3: **He who does** <note>original: "עֹשֵׂה"</note> is written here with a Yod, and thus in the plural; they changed their glory into the image or with the image of an ox. <note>Note: This appears to be a transcription error in the original notes, repeating text from verse 20 under the entry for verse 3.</note> **He who does** they changed their glory into the image or with the image of an ox. 1, 3. Verse 7: **Our fathers** adding a Pesik in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 16, 20, 23, without necessity. # PSALM 106 & 107. קו קז <note>The Hebrew letters correspond to the numbers 106 and 107.</note>

<margin>
a) Numbers 25:8.
b) This act was "counted and imputed to him for righteousness." This refers not to the righteousness of a person through faith (as seen in Genesis 15:6-7 and Romans 4:5–7), nor does it pass to his descendants in that same spiritual way (compare Habakkuk 2:4). Rather, it was a righteousness regarding that specific deed (compare Deuteronomy 24:13), such that he obtained the "eternal priesthood" as a reward for his zeal and piety, as noted in Numbers 25:12–13.
</margin>

31 **And it was accounted to him for righteousness to all generations forever.**

<margin>

</margin>
32 **They angered Him also at the waters of strife, so that it went ill with Moses on their account;**

<margin>
d) This situation was "evil and harmful to Moses" (2 Samuel 20:6) because of them; compare Numbers 20:24 and Deuteronomy 3:27.
e) For by their stubbornness, the Israelites "embittered his spirit," that is, the mind of Moses.
f) So that he "spoke rashly" or blurted out whatever came to his lips in his anger. See Leviticus 5:4 and Proverbs 12:18. For the historical context, see Numbers 20:10.
</margin>
33 **Because they rebelled against his spirit, so that he spoke unadvisedly with his lips.**

<margin>

<note>The following are technical Masoretic and philological notes regarding the specific Hebrew vowel points, accents, and manuscript variants for scholars.</note>

**v. 34.** The word "which" <note>original: "Asher"</note> contains a *Makkef* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> according to manuscripts 1 and 3. **v. 37.** "Their sons" <note>original: "Benechem"</note> is marked with an *Atnach* <note>a major pause accent</note> in 1 and 3; likewise in manuscript 5, though not ideally. **v. 38.** "Their daughters" <note>original: "Benoteichem"</note> appears with a *Rebia Geresh* accent in 6, 9, 11, 12, and 23. See notes on Psalm 4:1. **v. 38.** "And they shed" <note>original: "Vayishpechu"</note> with a *Pfik* <note>a vertical line indicating a distinct pause</note> in 2 and 14. "And was polluted" <note>original: "Vatechenaf"</note> is marked regularly. **v. 40.** "And He abhorred" <note>original: "Vayta'ev"</note> uses a *Patach* vowel in 6 and 9 in the margin, contrary to the Masorah in 1 and the printed edition here and in Deuteronomy 7:26. **v. 41.** "And He gave them" <note>original: "Vayittnem"</note> uses an ancient *Tipcha* accent in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 21, and 22. **v. 44.** "In the distress" <note>original: "Batzar"</note> uses a *Kamets* vowel in 2 and in the margin of 6 and 9. **v. 46.** "For mercies" <note>original: "Lerachamim"</note> uses a *Merca* accent in 1 and 2. **v. 47.** "Save us" <note>original: "Hoshienu"</note> without a *Pfik* in 9, 10, 12, 20, 21, and 23. But with a *Pfik-Mahpach* in 3 and 5. "Gather us" <note>original: "Kabbetzenu"</note> with a *Metheg* <note>a stress mark</note> in 5, 7, 8, 17, and 18. But with a *Yerach* without a *Makkef* in 14. "To give thanks" <note>original: "Lehodot"</note> with a *Merca* in 1 and 2. **v. 48.** "Blessed" <note>original: "Baruch"</note> with a joining *Mahpach* in 2. "Everlasting" <note>original: "Ha-olam"</note> without a *Mahpach* in 2, 3, and 11. "And unto" <note>original: "Ve-ad"</note> with a *Makkef* in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, and 20; also in 5. "And let say" <note>original: "Ve-amar"</note> with a *Merca* in 1, 6, 9, 10, 15, 16, and 20. **PSALM 107, v. 3.** "And from the west" <note>original: "Umimma'arav"</note> with a *Rebia Geresh* in 2. "And from the sea" <note>original: "Umiyam"</note> with the prefix *Vau* in 5 and in the margin of 6 and 9. **v. 5.** "Hungry" <note>original: "Re'evim"</note> with an ancient *Tipcha* in 1. **v. 6.** "In the distress" <note>original: "Batzar"</note> with a *Kamets* in 2 and in the margin of 6 and 9. The same occurs in verses 13, 19, and 28; compare Psalm 106:44.

v. 14. a) *He led forth*, I say, them, by unexpected ways and means, from the darkness and the dense obscurity of the prison, see verse 10. b) and their bonds he as if broke asunder, and restored them to liberty.

v. 17. c) *Fools because of their way*, that is, because of the deeply-rooted habit of their transgression. Here begins the third class of those whom God graciously delivered from very grave illnesses into which they had fallen by their own lack of moderation or vices. See the note at verse 1. d) *and those who because of their iniquities felt themselves weakened and afflicted*.

v. 19. e) See verses 6, 13, and 28.

v. 20. f) and so He rescued them from their pits and graves, to which they were very close. (2) Lamentations 4:20; compare Psalm 103:4.

v. 21. g) See verses 8, 15, and 31.

v. 23. h) Furthermore, *those who go down into the sea in ships*, that is, those sailing. Jonah 1:3. This is the fourth example of those delivered; compare the note at verse 1.

v. 24. i) in the deep of the sea. Jonah 2:4; Psalm 68:23.

v. 25. k) For He spoke only, Psalm 33:9, and immediately caused to exist or to arise a wind of the whirlwind or storm. l) and that wind (which is feminine in Hebrew) stirred up and lifted high the waves of the sea.

v. 26. m) So that the sea waves and the ships ascended toward heaven and were raised up. n) but now they descend into the abysses and innermost parts of the sea. o) and their soul melted away because of the evil/trouble.

**PSALM 108, v. 1.**
p) Psalm 48:1. q) Of David, as in Psalm 3:1.
**I.** He stirs himself up to the praise of divine mercy and truth, verses 1–5. **II.** He seeks the deliverance of those beloved by God, verses 6–7. And **III.** he promises himself certain victory over enemies based on the divine promise, verses 8–14.

v. 14. *And their bonds*: written thus with a vicarious *Munach* accent along with a servant *Tipcha* accent in the same word; 5, 7, 15 are more regular.
v. 17. *Fools*: with a *Rebia Geresh* accent. Compare the note on Psalm 34:3.
v. 18. *Abhorred*: with a *Kamatz* vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 3. So Buxtorf’s *Tiberias*.
And with a *Mercha* accent in 1. For the <gloss>Rebia Geresh</gloss> accent, compare the note on Psalm 34:3, page 88, from the Masorah on Deuteronomy 7:26. The printed Masorah on Psalm 106:40 and Isaiah 49:7 observed the same variation.
v. 23. An inverted Nun at the head of the verses of this psalm (v. 23–28 and v. 40) is required by the printed Masorah on Numbers 10:35, but none of our codices support this. Rabbi Menachem observes the same from the Masorah in the Old Testament, folio 17b.
v. 24. *Work*: with the letter *He* in the singular in manuscript 5, and likewise 6, 9 in the margin, against the Masorah.
v. 25. *And He raised*: with a *Patach* vowel in 1, 2, 3; and 2, 3 specifically with a following *Dagesh*.
v. 27. *They reel*: written defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> in 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, and likewise twice in 2, against Masorah 1, 2 and the Erfurt manuscript.
v. 32. *In the assembly*: with a *Maqqeph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note>.
v. 35. *Water*: with a *Kamatz* vowel in 3, 5, against Masorah 2 and the printed edition.
v. 43. *Whoever is wise*: so in 2, 6, 9, 10.
**PSALM 108, v. 3.** *Dawn*: without a *Dagesh* in 3, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 20, 21, 22, 23.
v. 4. *I will praise You among the peoples*: so in 5, 7, 8, 11, 12, 16. Likewise (though without the *Pesiq* mark) in 12, 15, 23. Others omit the *Pesiq* mark but without the support of our codices.
v. 5. *Great*: the printed Masorah on Deuteronomy 1:17 and Psalm 48:2 requires the defective spelling.

# 111
1 **Praise Yahweh! I will praise Yahweh with my whole heart, in the assembly of the upright and in the congregation.** <note>This psalm is an alphabetic acrostic, where each phrase begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet.</note>
2 **The works of Yahweh are great, studied by all who have pleasure in them.**
3 **His work is honorable and glorious, and His righteousness endures forever.**
4 **He has made His wonderful works to be remembered; Yahweh is gracious and full of compassion.**
5 **He has given food to those who fear Him; He will ever be mindful of His covenant.**
6 **He has declared to His people the power of His works, in giving them the heritage of the nations.**

<margin>Psalm 110.</margin>
**PS. 110, v. 1.** g) "Of David," meaning the psalm was dictated to David by the Holy Spirit, as in Psalm 24:1, etc. According to the Syrian version, it is a prophecy concerning CHRIST and His victory over the enemy. For here the Messiah is presented: I. as a King of infinite glory and majesty (v. 1-3). II. as an eternal Priest (v. 4). III. as the victor over all enemies (v. 5-7). h) The word and decree of Jehovah the Father (v. 2, 4; Psalm 2:7) revealed to me (David) through the Holy Spirit (2 Samuel 23:2; Mark 12:36). i) addressed to the Messiah, my Lord, God, and also my son.

<margin>Psalm 111.</margin>
**PS. 111, v. 1.** k) See Psalm 104:35 and 106:1. This psalm, like the following one, is almost entirely alphabetic by half-verses. It is occupied with the commemoration of the wonderful works of God, with respect to the greater benefits of God to be exhibited in the New Testament through CHRIST. To celebrate these worthily, I. he invites all men by his own example (v. 1-9); and therefore II. he commends the fear of Jehovah to all as true wisdom (v. 10).

<margin>Psalm 112.</margin>
**PS. 112, v. 1.** l) This psalm deals with: I. the blessedness of the man who fears the Lord (v. 1-4). II. he describes this man by his virtues and works (v. 5-9). III. he shows by contrast that the wicked are unhappy (v. 10). m) See notes on Psalm 1:1 and 32:1.

**v. 2.** n) "Powerful on the earth," etc.

v. 3. *Forever* [la'ad] with the Kamatz vowel in manuscript 3 and in the margins of 6 and 9. See v. 9 and Psalm 111:3. v. 6. *For remembrance* [lezeker] with the Segol vowel in manuscripts 6, 9, 20, 21, 22. See v. 3. v. 10. *And be grieved* [ve-ka'as] with Kamatz in 2 and 5 according to the Masora and the printed edition of Michaelis. 
PSALM 113, v. 1. *Praise* [halelu] with the Metheg accent in 3. v. 2. *Be* [yehi] with the Maqqef connector in 1 and 2. v. 4. *High* [ram] thus with the Tiphecha accent in 2, 3, 5; others place the accent less suitably earlier. *From now* [me-attah] thus with the Mercha accent in 2, 5, 7, 8, 15, 17, 22, 23, and the Berlin manuscript. Others use the Munach accent. Furthermore, they omit the Pesik mark in v. 7. *He who raises* [mekimi] with the Mahpak accent without Pesik in 1 and 3. v. 8. *To seat* [le-hoshibi] with the Rebia-Geresh accent in 13, 14, and the Berlin manuscript. See the note on Psalm 4:1. 
PSALM 114, v. 2. *His dominion* [mamshilotav] with the Segol vowel, contrary to the printed Masora and Michaelis. However, Pat. has the Patach vowel from others in the margin. v. 8. *The rock* [hatzur] with the Tiphecha accent in 2, 6, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22. 
PSALM 115, v. 1. *Not unto us* [lo lanu]. These do not form the beginning of a psalm in certain books; so says David Kimchi in his Commentary and Michaelis. Otherwise, the Pesiq-Kadma accents are correctly placed in 2, 14, and 24. Kadma without Pesik in 1, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15. Others use Mercha, which is less good. *Your mercy* [hasdekha] with Mercha in 1 and 2. v. 6. *Nose* [af] requires the Kamatz vowel according to the printed Masora at Psalm 135:17. But this is without the support of our codices. With the Maqqef in 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 14, 20.

**18:** The LORD has disciplined me severely <gloss>chastising</gloss>, but He has not given me over to death.
**19:** Open for me the gates of righteousness; I will enter through them and give thanks to the LORD.
**20:** This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it.
**21:** I will thank You, for You have answered me <gloss>heardest</gloss> and have become my salvation.
**22:** The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone.
**23:** From <gloss>from</gloss> the LORD this has come; it is marvelous in our eyes.
**24:** This is the day <gloss>this day</gloss> the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.
**25:** Please, O LORD, save us now! Please, O LORD, grant us success now!
<margin>accent on the last syllable</margin>
**26:** Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD; we bless you from the house of the LORD.
**27:** The LORD is God, and He has given us light; bind the festival sacrifice <gloss>sacrifice</gloss> with cords <gloss>thick boughs</gloss> to the horns of the altar.
**28:** You are my God, and I will thank You; You are my God, and I will exalt You.
**29:** Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; for His mercy is forever.

<margin>PSALM 119, verse 1. s) This distinguished Psalm, commended by the Masorah <note>The Masorah is the body of traditional notes on the Hebrew text of the Bible</note> under the name "The Great Alphabet," is an extensive praise of the divine word, a golden alphabet of the saints.</margin>

<margin>Psalm 119.</margin>

### 119
**1:** Blessed <gloss>Blessed</gloss> are those whose way is perfect, who walk in the law of the LORD.
<margin>verse 2. t) Certainly such people, described in verse 1, do not commit iniquity—meaning they do not sin knowingly and willingly—even if they do not yet live without failings here. Verse 5; 1 John 1:8 and 3:9.</margin>
**2:** Blessed are those who keep His testimonies, who seek Him with all their heart.
**3:** They also do no unrighteousness; they walk in His ways.
**4:** You have commanded Your precepts <gloss>wrong mandates</gloss> <note>The gloss "wrong mandates" likely refers to a specific interpretation or a correction of a common misunderstanding of the word 'precepts'</note> to be kept diligently.

---

<note>This technical section compares different historical manuscripts and printed editions (like those from Berlin and Erfurt). It focuses on the precise placement of Hebrew vowels and musical accents—the "punctuation" of the biblical text.</note>

**Verse 2:** The word "For" (*ki*) is marked with a *Merca* accent in verses 7, 8, and 24 according to the Masorah of Erfurt and printed editions. In other versions, it uses a *Makkaph* or *Munach* accent. **PSALM 118, Verse 5:** The word for "distress" (*hametzar*) uses a *Kamatz* vowel in some manuscripts, contrary to the standard Masoretic text.

**Verse 5:** The name of God (*Yah*) appears with a *Dagesh* (a dot indicating emphasis) in several manuscripts (numbered 1, 2, 3, etc.) following the Masorah of Erfurt. **Verse 5:** The word "answered me" (*anani*) is found with a *Patach* vowel in several manuscripts, while others use a *Kamatz*. **Verse 11:** "and the LORD" (*v'Iehovah*) appears in the Berlin edition and others with a *Merca* accent, though some use a *Munach* irregularly. **Verse 18:** "chastened me" (*yissarani*) lacks a *Dagesh* in the first and third manuscripts, contrary to the standard Masorah. **Verse 25:** "Please" (*Anna*) is accented on the last syllable in many manuscripts. **Verse 27:** "with cords" (*ba-avotim*) is written in full (with the letter *Vav*) in manuscripts 1, 2, 5, and 22, and noted in the margins of others, following specific traditions observed by Rabbi Chaiim. **PSALM 119, Verse 4:** "Your precepts" (*pikudecha*) is marked with a *Revia geresh* accent in manuscript 5 and the Berlin edition, while others use an *At-nach* or a simple *Revia*.

v. 23. *p) Even princes will sit and speak together against me. See Ezekiel 33:30.*

v. 25. *r) out of sorrow. Compare verse 31 and Psalm 44:26.*

v. 28. *t) It drips and, as it were, dissolves into tears. See Job 16:20. u) on account of grief and sadness.*

v. 30. *u) I have set before me, as in Psalm 16:8.*

v. 37. *y) Make them pass by. The Vulgate reads: turn away my eyes. See verse 39.*

**Translator's Philological Summary:** This section contains technical data comparing various manuscript traditions (noted as 1, 3, 6, 8, etc., referring to specific codices like those from Erfurt or Berlin). ### ו <note>Vav: The sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note>

41 <gloss>Part</gloss> וִֽיבֹאֻ֣נִי חֲסָדֶ֣ךָ יְהֹוָ֑ה <gloss>Salvation</gloss> תְּ֝שֽׁוּעָתְךָ֗ כְּאִמְרָתֶֽךָ׃
<note>Let Your mercies come to me, O Lord, Your salvation according to Your word.</note>
42 וְאֶֽעֱנֶ֣ה <gloss>reproach</gloss> חֹרְפִ֣י דָבָ֑ר כִּֽי־בָטַ֥חְתִּי בִּדְבָרֶֽךָ׃
<note>And I will answer a word to the one who reproaches me, for I trust in Your word.</note>
43 וְאַל־תַּצֵּ֧ל מִפִּ֣י דְבַר־אֱמֶ֣ת עַד־מְאֹ֑ד כִּ֖י <gloss>wait</gloss> לְמִשְׁפָּטֶ֣ךָ יִחָֽלְתִּי׃
<note>And do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth, for I wait for Your judgments.</note>
44 וְאֶשְׁמְרָ֖ה תֽוֹרָתְךָ֥ תָמִ֗יד לְעוֹלָ֥ם וָעֶֽד׃ <gloss>continually</gloss>
<note>And I will keep Your law continually, forever and ever.</note>
45 וְאֶתְהַלְּכָ֥ה <gloss>at large</gloss> בָֽרְחָבָ֫ה כִּ֖י פִקּוּדֶ֣יךָ <gloss>seek</gloss> דָרָֽשְׁתִּי׃
<note>And I will walk at liberty, for I have sought Your precepts.</note>
46 וַאֲדַבְּרָ֣ה בְעֵדֹתֶ֣יךָ נֶ֥גֶד מְלָכִ֗ים וְלֹ֣א אֵבֹֽושׁ׃
<note>And I will speak of Your testimonies before kings and will not be ashamed.</note>
47 וְאֶשְׁתַּעֲשַׁ֥ע בְּמִצְוֹתֶ֗יךָ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָהָֽבְתִּי׃
<note>And I will delight myself in Your commandments, which I have loved.</note>
48 וְאֶשָּׂא־כַפַּ֨י אֶל־מִצְוֹתֶ֜יךָ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָהָ֑בְתִּי <gloss>palms</gloss> וְאָשִׂ֥יחָה בְחֻקֶּֽיךָ׃
<note>And I will lift my hands toward Your commandments, which I have loved, and I will meditate on Your statutes.</note>

### ז <note>Zayin: The seventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note>

49 זְכָר־דָּבָ֥ר לְעַבְדֶּ֑ךָ עַ֝ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִחַלְתָּֽנִי׃ <gloss>hope complete</gloss>
<note>Remember the word to Your servant, upon which You have caused me to hope.</note>
50 <gloss>comfort</gloss> זֹ֣את נֶחָמָתִ֣י בְעָנְיִ֑י כִּ֥י <gloss>life</gloss> אִמְרָתְךָ֥ חִיָּֽתְנִי׃
<note>This is my comfort in my affliction, for Your word has given me life.</note>
51 זֵ֭דִים <gloss>scoff / mock</gloss> הֱלִיצֻ֣נִי עַד־מְאֹ֑ד מִ֝תּוֹרָתְךָ֗ לֹ֣א <gloss>decline</gloss> נָטִֽיתִי׃
<note>The proud have mocked me exceedingly, yet I have not declined from Your law.</note>
52 זָ֘כַ֤רְתִּי מִשְׁפָּטֶ֖יךָ מֵעוֹלָ֥ם ׀ יְהֹוָ֗ה וָאֶתְנֶחָֽם׃
<note>I remembered Your judgments of old, O Lord, and comforted myself.</note>
53 זַלְעָפָ֣ה <gloss>take hold</gloss> אֲחָזַ֣תְנִי מֵרְשָׁעִ֑ים עֹ֝זְבֵ֗י תּוֹרָתֶֽךָ׃
<note>Burning indignation has seized me because of the wicked who forsake Your law.</note>
54 זְ֭מִרֹות הָֽיוּ־לִ֥י חֻקֶּ֗יךָ <gloss>sojourn</gloss> בְּבֵ֣ית מְגוּרָֽי׃
<note>Your statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage.</note>
55 זָ֘כַ֤רְתִּי בַלַּ֣יְלָה שִׁמְךָ֣ יְהֹוָ֑ה וָאֶשְׁמְרָ֗ה תּוֹרָתֶֽךָ׃
<note>I have remembered Your name, O Lord, in the night, and have kept Your law.</note>
56 זֹ֥את הָֽיְתָה־לִּ֑י כִּ֖י <gloss>observe / keep</gloss> פִקּוּדֶ֣יךָ נָצָֽרְתִּי׃
<note>This was mine, because I kept Your precepts.</note>

### ח <note>Chet: The eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note>

57 <gloss>part</gloss> חֶלְקִ֥י יְהֹוָ֗ה אָ֝מַ֗רְתִּי לִשְׁמֹ֥ר דְּבָרֶֽיךָ׃
<note>The Lord is my portion; I have said that I would keep Your words.</note>
58 <gloss>support / wait</gloss> חִלִּ֣יתִי פָנֶ֣יךָ בְכָל־לֵ֑ב חָ֝נֵּ֗נִי כְּאִמְרָתֶֽךָ׃
<note>I entreated Your favor with my whole heart; be merciful to me according to Your word.</note>
59 חִשַּׁ֥בְתִּי דְרָכָ֑י וָאָשִׁ֥יבָה רַ֝גְלַ֗י אֶל־עֵדֹתֶֽיךָ׃
<note>I thought on my ways and turned my feet to Your testimonies.</note>
60 <gloss>hasten</gloss> חַ֭שְׁתִּי וְלֹ֣א <gloss>thank</gloss> הִתְמַהְמָ֑הְתִּי לִ֝שְׁמֹ֗ר מִצְוֹתֶֽיךָ׃
<note>I hurried and did not delay to keep Your commandments.</note>
61 <gloss>bands / company / surround</gloss> חֶבְלֵ֣י רְשָׁעִ֣ים עִוְּדֻ֑נִי תּוֹרָתְךָ֗ לֹ֣א שָׁכָֽחְתִּי׃
<note>The cords of the wicked have surrounded me, but I have not forgotten Your law.</note>
62 חֲצֹֽות־לַ֗יְלָה אָ֭קוּם לְהֹודֹ֣ות לָ֑ךְ עַ֝֗ל מִשְׁפְּטֵ֥י צִדְקֶֽךָ׃
<note>At midnight I will rise to give thanks to You because of Your righteous judgments.</note>
63 חָבֵ֣ר אָ֭נִי לְכָל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר יְרֵא֑וּךָ וּ֝לְשֹׁמְרֵ֗י פִּקּוּדֶֽיךָ׃
<note>I am a companion to all who fear You and to those who keep Your precepts.</note>
64 חַסְדְּךָ֣ יְהֹוָה מָלְאָ֣ה הָאָ֑רֶץ חֻקֶּ֥יךָ לַמְּדֵֽנִי׃
<note>The earth, O Lord, is full of Your mercy; teach me Your statutes.</note>

72 טֹוב־לִ֥י תֹֽורַת־פִּ֑יךָ מֵאַלְפֵ֥י זָהָ֥ב וָכָֽסֶף׃

<note>The following notes are technical scholarly observations regarding vowel points, cantillation marks, and manuscript variants.</note>
v. 41. *hasdekha* [Your mercies] written fully [with the letter yod] against the printed Masorah 1. 2. and especially the M. I.
v. 41. *hasdekha* and (in the text) 6. 9. so in the future 2. against the printed Masorah in this place and 1 Kings.
v. 43. *le-mishpatekha* [for Your judgments] written fully 1. 3. 5. 10. 13. 14. 20. 23.
v. 43. *le-mishpatekha* with the Qamatz vowel 6. 9. in the margin, so in the printed Masorah at v. 106.
v. 44. *ve-eshmereh* [and I will keep] with the Qamatz vowel 6. 9. in the margin, so in the printed Masorah at v. 106.
v. 44. *ve-eshmereh* with the Atnach accent 1.
v. 44. *tamid* [continually] with the Revia Geresh accent 8. and Berlin manuscript.
v. 46. *melakhim* [kings] with the Revia Geresh accent 8. 15. 17. 18. 22. 23. and Berlin manuscript.
v. 47. *be-mitzvotekha* [in Your commandments] 1. 2. 5. with a new sub-distinction. But with the Maqqef [hyphen] 7. 8. 11. 15. and with Pesig Mahpakh 1. For our Mercah, see the note on Psalm 1:1.
v. 48. *asher* [which] with the Maqqef 3. 6. 9. 10. 13. 14. 20.
v. 48. *asher* with a Munach above 3. against analogy: for it does not precede...
v. 49. *zekhor* [remember] with the Cholem vowel 3. and in the margin 6. 9. against the printed Masorah at Lamentations 3:19.
v. 52. *zakharti* [I remembered] with the Pesig mark in most, though not very conveniently. Without it 2. 3. 5. 11. 24.
v. 52. *me-olam* [of old] omitted by 2. 3. 12. 15. against the Masorah and the Index of Bashuysen f. 61. b.
v. 54. *zemirot* [songs] written fully 1. 6. 9. 12. 14. 16. 20. 21. 23. so in the future 20. and 5. against the printed Masorah and Erfurt manuscript.
v. 54. *hukkekha* [Your statutes] with the Revia Geresh accent 1. 8. and Berlin manuscript.
v. 55. *zakharti ba-laylah* [I remembered in the night] thus 1. 2. But with the Tiphecha accent 3. 6. 9. 10. 13. 14. 20. 21. 23.
v. 56. *zot* [this] with the Tiphecha accent 3. 6. 9. 10. 13. 14. 20. 21. 23.
v. 57. *helqi Yehovah amarti* [The Lord is my portion, I said] with the Revia Geresh accent 8. and Berlin manuscript; so also in the future 5.
v. 57. *helqi Yehovah amarti* with the Pesig mark 5.
v. 64. *male'ah ha-aretz* [the earth is full] with the Pesig mark 5. with the Revia Geresh only in the Berlin manuscript. But *male'ah ha-aretz* 1. 2.
v. 65. *avdekha* [Your servant] stressed on the first syllable with the Segol vowel 3. 10. 14. 20. against the Masorah 1. 2. printed and Erfurt in this place and printed Numbers 11:11.
v. 68. *u-metiv* [and does good] Revia Geresh in the Berlin manuscript alone. But with the Atnach accent 1. 2.

<meta>This page continues the transcription of Psalm 119, an alphabetic acrostic where each section consists of eight verses beginning with the same Hebrew letter. This page covers the sections for the letters Yodh (י), Kaph (כ), Lamedh (ל), Mem (מ), and the beginning of Nun (נ).</meta>

# Psalms 119.

<gloss>rejoice</gloss> <gloss>wait</gloss> 74 Those who fear You will see me and rejoice: because I have waited for Your word.
75 I know, O Lord, that Your judgments are righteous, and in faithfulness You have afflicted me <gloss>a</gloss>.
76 Let Your kindness be for my comfort <gloss>b</gloss>: according to Your word to Your servant.
77 Let Your mercies come to me and I shall live <gloss>c</gloss>: for Your Law is my delight.
78 Let the proud be ashamed, for with a lie they have perverted me <gloss>d</gloss>: I will meditate on Your precepts.
<margin>Those who know <note>The margin indicates a Masoretic "Kere" or reading variant for "knowers."</note></margin> 79 Let those who fear You return to me <gloss>e</gloss>, and those who know Your testimonies.
80 Let my heart be blameless in Your statutes, so that I will not be ashamed.
81 My soul faints for Your salvation <gloss>f</gloss>: I have waited for Your word.
82 My eyes fail for Your word <gloss>g</gloss>: saying, when will You comfort me?
83 For I have become like a wineskin in the smoke <gloss>h</gloss>: Your statutes I have not forgotten.
84 How many are the days of Your servant? <gloss>i</gloss> When will You execute judgment on my pursuers?
85 The proud have dug pits for me <gloss>k</gloss>: which is not according to Your law.
86 All Your commandments are faithfulness: they pursue me with a lie; help me!
87 They had almost consumed me on the earth: and I did not forsake Your precepts.
88 According to Your kindness revive me: and I will keep the testimony of Your mouth.
89 Forever, O Lord, Your word <gloss>l</gloss>: stands in the heavens.
90 Your faithfulness is to all generations <gloss>m</gloss>: You have established the earth, and it stands.
91 They stand this day for Your judgments <gloss>n</gloss>: for all are Your servants.
92 Unless Your law had been my delight: I would then have perished in my affliction.
93 I will never forget Your precepts: for with them You have revived me.
94 I am Yours, save me: for I have sought Your precepts.
95 The wicked have waited for me to destroy me: I will consider Your testimonies.
96 To all perfection <gloss>o</gloss> I have seen an end: Your commandment is very broad <gloss>p</gloss>.
97 O how I love Your law! It is my meditation all the day.
98 Your commandments make me wiser than my enemies <gloss>q</gloss>: for they are mine forever.
<margin>Open with Atnach <note>A note regarding the musical accent 'Atnach'.</note></margin> 99 I have more insight than all my teachers: for Your testimonies are a meditation for me.
100 I understand more than the elders: because I have kept Your precepts.
101 I have restrained my feet from every evil path: so that I may keep Your word.
102 I have not turned aside from Your judgments: for You have taught me.
103 How sweet are Your words to my palate! More than honey to my mouth!
104 Through Your precepts I gain understanding: therefore I hate every false path.
105 Your word is a lamp to my feet: and a light to my path.
106 I have sworn and I will fulfill it: to keep Your righteous judgments.

<column-break/>

v. 75. a) *and in faithfulness*, that is, faithfully and for the best end, You have afflicted and chastened me. v. 67. 71.

v. 76. b) *according to Your word*, by which You mercifully bound Yourself to Your servant. v. 17. 38. 65. 84.

v. 77. c) *Let them come upon me.* v. 41.

v. 78. d) *because with falsehood and lies they wished to overthrow me.*

v. 79. e) *Let them turn back to me, as if to their companion.* v. 63.

v. 81. f) *[My soul] is almost consumed with desire for Your salvation.* v. 41. 82. 123. **Ps. 84:3.**

v. 83. g) *For I have become*, exhausted and parched in body and soul through so many afflictions, like a leather wineskin. (b) **Josh. 9:4.** h) in smoke or hot vapor. (3) **Gen. 19:28.**

v. 84. i) *How many or how great are the days remaining for Your servant?* **2 Sam. 19:35.**

v. 85. k) *The proud have prepared pits for me:* which certainly is not according to Your law, but diametrically opposed to it.

v. 89. l) *You are eternal, Lord!* and Your word remains firm with You in the heavens.

v. 90. m) Just as You also founded the earth, and it stays and remains in its place through Your power.

v. 91. n) *To execute Your judgments and decrees:* or, the heavens and earth stand according to Your prescription, so that they remain without change today. v. 89. 90.

v. 96. o) *Of every perfect and completed thing* (1) form of <term>Tigrah</term> <note>original: "Tigrah", usually meaning strife or blow</note>, **Ps. 39:11.** I have seen an end and a limit. p) *but broad and extremely open*, **Job 11:9.** like a vast ocean **Ps. 104:25.** or a very wide field, **Exod. 3:8.**

v. 98. q) *Your commandments make me wiser than my very cunning enemies.* Others translate in the 2nd person: *You make me wise by Your commandments*, understanding a hidden "n" <note>referring to a grammatical suffix</note>, as in **Ps. 104:6.**

v. 76. "Your kindness" (חסדך) with the accent *Tiphtcha ant. 2*. --- v. 77. "Because" (כי) with the accent *Merca 6. 9. 10. 13. 14. 20.* --- v. 79. ### Nun [נ]

<margin>verse 107. a) *I have been greatly afflicted and humbled.* See verses 51, 67, 71, 75.</margin>
107 I am afflicted <gloss>a</gloss> very much; O Lord, revive me according to Your word.

<margin>verse 108. b) *Free-will sacrifices; I pray, graciously approve these pious offerings of my mouth.* c) *furthermore and more deeply teach me.*</margin>
108 Accept, I pray, the free-will offerings <gloss>b</gloss> of my mouth, O Lord, and teach me <gloss>c</gloss> Your judgments.

<margin>verse 109. d) *Indeed, my soul is always in my hand, meaning I am in the greatest danger and risk of life.* <note>The Hebrew idiom "soul in my hand" refers to constantly risking one's life.</note></margin>
109 My soul <gloss>d</gloss> is continually in my hand, yet I do not forget Your law.

<note>The following notes are technical observations regarding the musical accents (cantillation) and vowel markings found in different historical manuscripts of the Hebrew text.</note>

Verse 109: "My soul" uses the *Tiphcha* accent. Verse 112: "Your statutes" uses the *Revia Geresh* in manuscript 2 and the Berlin edition, but manuscript 1 uses *Munach*.
Regarding "to perform Your statutes forever," manuscripts 1 and 2 have "Support me" for verse 117. For verse 114, "for Your word" uses the *Merca* accent in manuscripts 3 and 5 as is regular, but manuscript 1 uses *Munach*.
Verse 117: "my eyes fail" so in manuscript 1. Verse 123: "my eyes fail" so in manuscript 2. Regarding verse 119: "You put away dross." Verse 124: "Your mercy" uses *Revia Geresh*. At verse 126: "It is time to act." Verse 130: "The entrance." Verse 128: "all Your precepts concerning all" thus in 2 and 3, not poorly, using *Merca*. Verse 127: "Your commandments" (which is reported from others in the margin) manuscript 2 has "Your law." Verse 130: "The entrance." Verse 131: "My mouth" uses the *Maqqaf* connector. "Gives light" uses *Revia Geresh* in manuscript 2 and the Berlin edition. But "Your words give light" in manuscript 1 is not well executed. Verse 138: "You have commanded righteousness" so in 2. Verse 140: "very" uses *Revia Geresh* only in the Berlin edition. But the phrase "Your word is very pure" in 1, 2, and 3 is marked awkwardly.

<note>The following notes provide technical details on the Masoretic text—the traditional Hebrew text of the Bible. The numbers (1, 2, 6, 9, etc.) refer to specific historical manuscripts or scholarly editions the editor is comparing.</note>

<margin>v. 143.</margin> The letter Tsade <note>original: "צ"</note> with a <term>Kametz</term> vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, and in the margin of 6 and 9. <margin>v. 144.</margin> The word "forever" <note>original: "לעולם"</note> with a <term>Rebia-Geresh</term> accent in manuscripts 6, 9, 11, 12, and 15. <margin>v. 145.</margin> The word "heart" <note>original: "לב"</note> followed by an <term>Atnach</term> accent <note>a major pause mark</note> in 2, 6, 9 through 16, 22, and 23. <margin>v. 145.</margin> But the Name of the Lord <note>original: "יהוה"</note> with a <term>Rebia</term> in manuscript 24; because we do not admit an Atnach under the preceding word, we retain it for the sake of analogy, comparing the note at verse 4 and Psalm 4:1. Others use a Rebia-Geresh. Regarding "Your statutes" [in verse 145] and [verses 150-151]: <margin>v. 150.</margin> <margin>v. 151.</margin> The word "they draw near" <note>original: "קרו"</note> with a <term>Tiphcha</term> accent in 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, and 20. But others use a <term>Munach</term> accent; <margin>v. 150.</margin> this is less convenient, unless for the following word "persecutors" one reads "my persecutors" <note>original: "רדפי"</note> with a suffix, as in manuscript 1 and the Vulgate with the Septuagint, which rendered it: "Those persecuting me have approached iniquity." <margin>v. 152.</margin> "Of old I have known" <note>original: "קדם ידעתי"</note> thus in 1. See Exodus 15:21. <margin>v. 153.</margin> "Consider my affliction" <note>original: "ראה עניי"</note> thus in 2. See verse 159. <margin>v. 156.</margin> "Your mercies" <note>original: "רחמיך"</note> with a Munach in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, and 20; and so "according to Berlin." The word "great" <note>original: "רבים"</note> with a Munach instead of a <term>Merca</term> in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, and 20. The <term>Pesiq</term> mark is omitted in 1 and 2, contrary to the Basel Index, folio 6b. <margin>v. 160.</margin> <margin>v. 163.</margin> "And I abhor" <note>original: "ואתעבה"</note> with a Kametz in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 20, and 21. These are short, powerful poems traditionally sung by pilgrims as they "ascended" the road to Jerusalem for the great festivals. The translator has maintained the focus on both the poetic structure and the technical Masoretic notes that ensure the text's preservation.</meta>
