<margin>
PSALM 120, v. 1. a) A Song of Ascents <note>original: "Canticum graduum"</note>, by which David: I. Praises God for the liberation provided from a slanderous tongue (v. 1–2). II. Shows the greatness of that benefit by describing the deceitful tongue (v. 3–7).
v. 2. b) Therefore now also, O Jehovah, rescue my soul. c) From the lip of falsehood or the false-speaking [lip]. d) From the tongue, which is pure fraud and deceit.
v. 3. e) Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note>: "What indeed will he give to you, O slanderer, or what will he add to you, O detractor, you deceitful tongue?" Others [translate]: "How much, do you think, does a fraudulent tongue harm you?"
</margin>

# 120
## A Song of Ascents <margin>Psalm 120</margin>
**1** To the LORD in my distress I called, and He answered me.
**2** O LORD, deliver my soul from lying lips, from a deceitful tongue.
**3** What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you, O deceitful tongue?
**4** Sharp arrows of a warrior, with coals of broom wood <note>original: "retem," a desert shrub that produces intense, long-lasting heat when burned</note>.
**5** Woe is me, for I have sojourned in Meshech, I have dwelt among the tents of Kedar! <note>Meshech and Kedar represent distant, nomadic, and often hostile tribes—metaphors for living among people who do not share one's values</note>.
**6** Long enough has my soul dwelt with those who hate peace.
**7** I am for peace; but when I speak, they are for war.

---

<margin>
PSALM 121, v. 1. f) saying, "From where shall my help come?" David: I. Teaches that God's help alone is to be sought in prayers (v. 1–2). II. Gives the reason for this (v. 3–8).
</margin>

# 121
## A Song to the Ascents <margin>Psalm 121</margin>

**2** My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.
**3** He will not let your foot slip; He who guards you will not slumber.
**4** Behold, He who guards Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.
**5** The LORD is your guardian; the LORD is your shade at your right hand.
**6** By day the sun shall not strike you, nor the moon by night.
**7** The LORD will guard you from all evil; He will guard your soul.
**8** The LORD will guard your going out and your coming in, from now and forevermore.

PSALM 120, v. 3. **To you** <note>Hebrew: *lecha*</note> with the *Revia Geresh* accent <note>original: "Rbbiageresch"</note> according to the Berlin edition. But with the *Atnach* accent preceded by a double *Munach*. — v. 5. **To me** <note>Hebrew: *li*</note> without the *Daghesh* <note>a grammatical dot inside a letter</note> in manuscripts 3, 5, 16, 20, 21, 23.

PSALM 121, v. 4. **Guards** <note>Hebrew: *shomer*</note> thus written in full <note>original: "plene"</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 22, and according to the Masorah of manuscript 1 and 2 and the Erfurt Bible in this place, as well as the printed edition of 1 Samuel 17:22. PSALM 122, v. 2. **Standing** with the *Munach* accent in 2, 5, 15; and with the *Tiphcha* in 1. "The Church recounts," according to manuscripts 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 23. **They went up** with the *Yerach* accent in 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 21, 23; and in the Berlin edition, though less analogically.

PSALM 123, v. 1. **My eyes** with the *Qamets* vowel in 3, 14, 17, 18; but with the *Chireq* vowel only in the Berlin edition. Both would have been [the case], unless God etc., against the Masorah 1 and 2 and the Basel Index. v. 2. **Behold** with the *Pesiq* mark in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. **As the eyes of** with the *Yerach* accent in 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 23; and thus somewhat irregularly against the rule. v. 3. **Behold** with the *Munach*. II. The Church praises God [see below] irregularly in 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 17, 18, 20, 21, 23, and the Berlin edition. But with the *Mercha* accent in 14. For **Our soul**, see the *Mahpach* accent in 6, 7; and III. regarding His [help], see the note on Psalm 48:9. v. 4. **Of the proud** with the *Qere* <note>the traditional reading</note> as two words in 1, 7, 8, 13, 17, 22, 24, and the Berlin edition according to Masorah 1. Glories in help, printed and Erfurt editions in this place, also Rabbi David Kimchi in his Commentary, and finally the printed Masorah of 1 Chronicles 27:12. The others are without the *Qere*. Furthermore, manuscript 22 correctly does not interpose the *Maqqeph* <note>hyphen</note> which the others omit. But with the *Mercha* in place of *Mahpach* in 1, 5, 7, 8. With *Munach*, truly irregularly, in 6, 9, 10, 13, 20.

# Psalms 124, 125, 126, 127, 128

<margin>verse 2. a) If, I say, it were not Jehovah, who was—or according to the Syriac version, "who stood for us"—as stated in verse 1.</margin>
**2** "Let Israel now say: If it had not been the LORD who was on our side when men rose up against us,
<margin>b) when men rose up against us.</margin>

**Technical Philological Notes:**
Psalm 124, v. 4. **Nachlah** (stream), accented on the last syllable in manuscripts 1, 3, 7, 8, 15, 22, according to the *Masora of Erfurt* <note>a famous collection of traditional notes on the Hebrew Bible</note>; likewise in the printed editions compared with Numbers 34:5. v. 6. **She-lo** (who not) with a *Maqqaph* (hyphen) in manuscripts 1, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20. v. 7. **Nishbar** (broken) with a *Patach* vowel in manuscripts 1, 6, 9, 20, 23. Otherwise marked with a simple *Revia* accent in 24. But with an *Atnach* accent preceded by a *Munach* in manuscript 3. Psalm 125, v. 3. (the word **Lema'an**, "so that," appears only in manuscript 21) is found, besides the *Masora of Erfurt*, as we gave for Psalm 13:3. **Ve-yishlechu** (and they reach out) thus with a *Merca* accent in 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20. The *Peshito* version <note>the Syriac Bible</note> is also found elsewhere, as in Psalm 35:10, Proverbs 30:9, Job 34:37. Others have it with a *Tiphcha* accent. v. 5. **Ve-hamattim** (and those who turn aside) with a *Pesiq* mark in 1, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 23. Psalm 126, v. 4. **Shavitenu** (our captivity) in the text itself without the *Qere* <note>the traditional "read" correction in the margin</note> in 22; and so it appears in 3, 5, following the note in the margin of 22: "as it is written." However, our *Ketiv* (written form) and *Qere* (read form) are required by the *Masora of Erfurt* and David Kimchi <note>a famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and grammarian</note> in his commentary. **Ba-aphiqim** (in the streams) with a *Qamets* vowel in 17, 18, 24, and the *Berlin manuscript*. Otherwise, a *Merca* accent is found in 3, 5, and likewise the *Berlin manuscript*; but a *Munach* in 2, and a *Revia Geresh* in 1, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. Others have a *Tiphcha* accent, which is anomalous. v. 5. **Be-dim'ah** (in tears) with a *Revia Geresh* in 2, and likewise the *Berlin manuscript*. But with an *Atnach*, and the following word **be-rinnah** (with joy) with a *Revia Geresh* in 1. Others use a *Revia*. Psalm 127, v. 1. **Shaqad** (watched) with a *Merca* accent and the accompanying *Zarqa* in 6, 9, 10, 12–18, 20, 21, 22, 23, which is anomalous. v. 2. **Lakem** (for you) with a *Pesiq* in 1, 3, 5, 14, 24, and the *Berlin manuscript*, as well as Ben Asher <note>a famous 10th-century Masoretic scholar</note>. Others lack the *Pesiq*. **Mashkimei** (rising early) with a *Yerach* accent in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 23, and the *Berlin manuscript*, irregularly.

<header>Psalms 140, 141, 142</header>

<margin>
<note>Translator's note: The following are English translations of the Latin commentary provided for Psalm 140</note>
a) You, O Lord, have protected my head, or You have been a protector to my head in the day of weapons, that is, of battle. See Psalm 78:9.
v. 9. b) Therefore, do not even now grant the desires <note>original Latin: "desideria"</note> (1) c) do not allow his thought to break out, or be brought to its desired end. d) For they will exalt, or carry themselves high.
v. 10. e) As for the head of those surrounding me, let the labor and wickedness of their own lips overwhelm them. Compare Psalm 7:15.
v. 11. f) Let burning coals be moved or rolled over them: by the fire of lightning, or He shall cast them down into the infernal fire, into pits, or with great force, so that they cannot rise again.
v. 12. g) A man of an evil tongue shall not be established on the earth: as for the man of violence and evil, his own violence and malice shall hunt him to the point of downfall and destruction (1).
v. 13. h) For I know and am persuaded.
</margin>

9. Do not grant, O Lord, the desires of the wicked; <margin>b</margin> do not allow his plot to succeed, lest they exalt themselves. Selah.
10. As for the head of those who surround me, may the mischief of their own lips <margin>c, e</margin> cover them. <margin>The written text says "cover him," but the traditional reading is "cover them."</margin>
11. Let burning coals fall <margin>The written text says "let them be moved," but the traditional reading is "let them fall"</margin> <margin>f</margin> upon them; let them be cast into the fire, into deep pits, that they rise not up again.
12. Let not a slanderer be established in the earth; as for the man of violence, let evil <margin>g</margin> hunt him to overthrow him.
13. I know <margin>The written text says "you knew," but the traditional reading is "I know"</margin> <margin>h</margin> that the Lord will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the justice of the poor.
14. Surely the righteous shall give thanks to Your name; the upright shall dwell in Your presence.

<margin>Psalm 141</margin>
## 141

1. A Psalm of David. O Lord, I cry out to You; hasten to me! Give ear to my voice when I cry out to You. <margin>i</margin>
2. Let my prayer be set forth before You as incense, and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice. <margin>k</margin>
3. Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips. <margin>l, m, n</margin>
4. Incline not my heart to any evil thing, to practice wicked works <gloss>n</gloss> in wickedness with men who work iniquity; and let me not eat of their delicacies.
5. Let the righteous strike me in kindness and rebuke me; it shall be as oil for the head; let my head not refuse it. For my prayer is still against their evil deeds.
6. Their judges are thrown down by the sides of the rock, and they shall hear my words, for they are sweet.
7. As when one plows and breaks open the earth, our bones are scattered at the mouth of the grave.
8. For my eyes are toward You, O God the Lord; in You I take refuge; do not leave my soul defenseless.
9. Keep me from the jaws of the snare they have laid for me, and from the traps of the workers of iniquity.
10. Let the wicked fall into their own nets together, while I pass by safely.

PSALM 141, verse 1. i) See Psalm 3:1. A prayer of David, in which he seeks: I. That his prayers be heard (v. 1, 2). II. Protection from fellowship with the ungodly (v. 3, 4). III. Correction by the godly (v. 5, 6). IV. Deliverance from enemies (v. 7–10).
v. 2. k) Let my prayer be directed and carried straight, like the incense or the smoke of the morning sacrifice in Your sight: and may the lifting up of my hands be pleasing and acceptable to You like the evening offering.

<margin>Psalm 142</margin>
## 142

1. A Maskil <note>A contemplative poem or teaching psalm</note> of David; A Prayer when he was in the cave. <margin>o, p, q</margin>
2. With my voice I cry out to the Lord; with my voice I make supplication to the Lord.
3. I pour out my complaint before Him; I declare my trouble before Him.
4. When my spirit was overwhelmed within me, then You knew my path. In the way wherein I walked, they have secretly laid a snare for me. <margin>r</margin>
5. Look to the right and see, for there is no one who acknowledges me; refuge has failed me; no one cares for my soul.
6. I cried out to You, O Lord; I said, "You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living."
7. Attend to my cry, for I am brought very low; deliver me from my persecutors, for they are stronger than I. <margin>s</margin>
8. Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise Your name; the righteous shall surround me, for You shall deal bountifully with me.

PSALM 142, verse 1. o) See Psalm 32:1. p) See Psalm 57:1; 1 Samuel 22:1; chapter 24:1, 4 <note>These references link the Psalm to the historical accounts of David hiding from King Saul in the caves of Adullam and En Gedi</note>. q) David’s prayers against enemies: consisting of I. The Introduction (v. 2, 3). II. The Reasons (v. 4, 5, 6). III. The Petition (v. 7, 8).
v. 4. r) When it [the spirit] wraps itself up and truly fails within me. See Psalms 77:4, 107:6, and 143:4.
v. 7. s) because I have been made very thin or weakened.

<note>Scholarly critical footnotes discussing technical aspects of the Hebrew text</note>

v. 9. The word "desires" (*ma'awayei*) is written with a *Qamets* vowel without a following *Dagesh* [doubling mark]; this was required by Rabbi Jonah, relying on the Jerusalem Codex, in which David Kimchi found it written thus. v. 12. "He shall hunt him" (*yetsudennu*) with a *Merca* accent. v. 13. "You knew" (*yada'ta*) with a *Merca* accent. PSALM 141, v. 1. The name *Jehovah* appears in the text without the usual notes. v. 2. "Let it be set forth" (*tikkon*): let my prayers be arranged like incense burned before You. v. 3. "Keep watch" (*nitzrah*) without a *Dagesh* (which the *Minchat Shai* commentary calls euphonic). v. 4. "Wicked works" (*alilot*) without the *Pesiq* mark. Others use the *Levita* or *Mahpach* accent with an emphatic *Pesiq*. v. 8. "O Lord" (*Adonai*) with a preceding *Tiphecha* accent according to various manuscripts. v. 10. "Together I" (*yachad anochi*): written thus. PSALM 142, v. 4. "When overwhelmed" (*be-hit'atef*) has a regular *Munach* accent above it in the Berlin and Ben Israel editions, though some use a *Mahpach* accent against standard analogy. v. 5. "And no one cares" (*ve-ein doresh*) with the prefix *Vav* [and] according to the Masorah. v. 6. "My refuge" (*machsi*) with a *Chateph-Patach* vowel. v. 7. "From my persecutors" (*merodfai*) requires a *Patach* vowel according to the *Index Bashari*. v. 8. "For You shall deal bountifully" (*ki tigmol*): written thus.

v. 6. **עשה** [made] — found in manuscripts 2, 12, 14, 15. v. 8. **עורים** [blind] — with a Dagesh in manuscripts 1, 2, 15. v. 10. **ודר** [and generation] — using the "simple Rebbia" accent in manuscript 24, following the analogy mentioned at Psalm 4:1. The word **הללויה** [Hallelujah] is written as a single word in manuscripts 1, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20, 24.

**PSALM 147, v. 1. כי נעים** [for it is pleasant] — with the Merca accent in 2, 3, 6, 9. v. 5. **אדונינו** [our Lord] — written in full [plene] with the letter *Vav* in 1, 2, 3, 5 through 10, 15, 22, 24, according to the Masorah of the first and second printed editions. Others use the defective spelling. Furthermore, **כח** [power] uses the "ancient Tiphcha" accent in 2, 6, 9 through 11, 13, 20, 21, 22; and together with the Munach accent in 1, 12, 14 through 18, 23. v. 6. **משפיל רשעים** [He casts down the wicked] — thus in 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 16, 20, 21, 22, 24. Manuscripts 12, 17, 18, 23 have the Rebbia-Geresh accent. v. 10. **ולא בשוקי** [nor in the legs] — with the prefix *Vav* [and] in 3, 11, and similarly in 2, 5. v. 12. **חזק** [strengthened] — with the Metheg mark in 1, 3, 5. v. 14. **השם** [Who makes] — with the Metheg according to Ben Naphtali. v. 17. **קרחו** [His ice] — with the Qamets-Chatuf vowel in 6 through 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20 through 23. v. 19. **דבריו** [His words] — written thus in the text of manuscript 2, thus in 1, and thus in the margin of 5, contrary to the Masorah of the Erfurt and other printed editions. v. 20. **לכל גוי** [to any nation] — written as connected words in 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 24. **ידעום** [they knew them] — with a simple Rebbia in 7, 8. **הללויה** [Hallelujah] — written as one word in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 24.

**PSALM 148, v. 1. השמים** [the heavens] — with the Qamets vowel in 3, 5, 12, and in the margin of 6, contrary to the Masorah in 1, 2. v. 2. **הללוהו** [Praise Him] — with the ancient Tiphcha in 10, 13, 14, and with the Merca in 6, 9, 20. v. 3. **כוכבי** [stars of] — with a Maqqaph [hyphen] in 1, 3.

# THE BOOK OF PROVERBS

## Hebrew: *Mishlei*

->Contains the **all-excellent wisdom** <note>original: "πανάρετον σοφίαν" (panareton sophian)</note> of Solomon, or wisdom containing the precepts of all virtues, in five parts of the book: I. The *prologue*, which commends the love of true and divine wisdom, chapters 1–9. II. The miscellaneous maxims of Solomon, collected by the author himself, chapters 10–24. III. Maxims of the same Solomon, but gathered by the men of Hezekiah, chapters 25–29. IV. The sayings of *Agur*, chapter 30. V. The maternal instruction of *Bathsheba*, and the *praise of the capable woman*, chapter 31.<-

**MASORETIC AND CRITICAL NOTES**
PROVERBS 1, v. 1. *Mishlei*: The large *Mem* is found in manuscripts 11, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18 according to the Masora. Genesis 1:1, and the Berakhot <note>The Talmudic tractate</note> and many others have it. 1 Chronicles 1:1. Others have it regular. However, the note "Large Mem" and the entire word in large letters are in 24, Berakhot, and most in 17, 22, 24, and later in v. 3. *U-mesharim* (and equity) is written fully in 2, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 23, against the printed Masora in 3. And specifically in v. 4, *la-ptayim* (to the simple). v. 5. *ve-yoseph* (and he shall add) in 2, with the accompanying accent *Sarkea* (for which 3 has its own *Kadma*) in 2. v. 9. *Ki* (for) without the *Pesiq* in 2, 3 and printed Masora, against the printed Masora *chen* (grace) with *Pesiq* in 2 and Berakhot, against Masora 1 and Erfurt. See the note at Psalms 13:3. v. 8. *le-gargurotecha* (for your neck) is thus defective in 1, 3, 22. Others write it fully, including many others whom Rabbi Chayyim <note>Jacob ben Hayyim adonijah, a famous Masoretic scholar</note> testifies he inspected in the Masora for this place: but these are against the printed Masora. v. 10. *Bni* (my son) with the ancient *Tiphecha* in 2, but with *Revia* in 1; both are more regular. However, for *Paser*, compare Psalms 25:1 and 58:3. v. 17. *Mezorah* (spread) is defective in 1, 2, 3, 22 according to Masora 2 and Erfurt. v. 19. *Baza'* (gain) with only a *Munach* is wonderful in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, against Masora 1 and Erfurt, which requires *Milel* <note>accent on the penultimate syllable</note>. v. 21. *be-phtchei shearim* (at the openings of the gates) is thus in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, and so in 24, except that here it has *Mercha* more correctly instead of *Munach*. v. 22. *te'ehavu* (you will love) with *Yerach* in 2, 3, 14 and Berakhot. Others with *Metheg* and *Maqqaph*, either expressed or understood.

->SECTION 2<-
**1** My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments within you, <margin>CHAPTER II, v. 1. *g) An affectionate address, as in chapter 1:8, 10, 15. Solomon proceeds to invite men to the love of Wisdom: I. by desiring and requesting it (v. 1–2). II. by demonstrating the multiple benefits of studying wisdom (v. 3–22), namely: 1) the fear and knowledge of God (v. 5–8); 2) understanding what is just and good (v. 9); 3) the indwelling of wisdom, and thus delight and happiness (v. 10–11); 4) deliverance from the evil way, etc. (v. 12–15); 5) deliverance from the foreign woman (v. 16–19); and finally 7) walking in the way of the good (v. 20–22). h) O if only you would accept it! How good it will be if you receive it. See Psalm 139:19.*</margin>
**2** Making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding;
**3** Yes, if you cry out for insight and lift up your voice for understanding;
**4** If you seek her like silver and search for her as for hidden treasures;
**5** Then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God.
**6** For the LORD gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding.
<margin>
Read as: *Yitzpon* <note>The marginal *Keri* indicates the word should be read as "He stores up," though written differently in the main text</note>
</margin>

### Philological and Critical Notes
<note>This section compares various manuscripts (indicated by numbers) and explains specific Hebrew vowel points and accents.</note>

**v. 27.** **Storm:** marked with a *Pataḥ* vowel followed by a *Dagesh* <note>a dot indicating a doubled consonant</note> in manuscript 3, and similarly in the margins of 6 and 9. **v. 30.** **They despised:** marked with a *Chirek* vowel in 3, and in the margins of 6 and 9. **v. 31.** **And they shall eat:** marked with a *Pataḥ* and following *Dagesh* in 3, and in the margins of 6 and 9. **And from their schemes:** thus with a double accent rightly in 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 24, and the Berlin manuscript. Others use only the *Munach* accent, except 1 which has *Revia-Geresh*, and 3 which has *Mercha*. **v. 33.** **And at ease:** with a *Qametz* vowel in 1, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, 23; contrary to the *Mappiq* in 1, and printed versions of Jeremiah 30:10.

**CHAPTER II.** **v. 3.** **If for understanding:** manuscript 1 has the letter *Vav*, as the Chaldee <note>Aramaic</note> explained it: "and you shall call understanding a mother." Cf. Rabbi Chaiim in the margin of 7 and 8. **v. 4.** **You seek her:** with a *Dagesh* in 3, 10, 13, 19. **v. 5.** **Then:** with a *Munach* accent in 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20. **v. 7.** **For the upright:** manuscripts 2 and 3 have the *Tiphcha* accent correctly. Most have *Munach*; however, the word is marked by both in 6, 8, 9, 10, 13, 19, 20, 21, 22. **To those who walk:** marked with a *Maqqef* <note>hyphen</note> in 1 and 3. **v. 9.** **Then:** with a *Munach* accent in 1, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20. See above on v. 5. **v. 13.** **Those who forsake:** thus with a *Munach* instead of a *Meteg* in 8 and 22. In v. 12, 14–18, and in 2 and 23, only a *Munach* is used. Otherwise, the prefix *He* uses a *Pataḥ* in 1, 2, 7, 8, 15, 21. See v. 17. **v. 16.** **To deliver you:** with a *Meteg* instead of *Munach* in 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, 21. **v. 17.** **Who forsakes:** with a *Qametz* vowel in 1, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 23. **v. 19.** **And not:** with a *Maqqef* in 1, 2, 3, 7, 8. **v. 20.** **So that:** with a *Munach* in 3. **v. 21.** **And the upright:** with a *Tiphcha* accent in 1 and 2.

**CHAPTER III, v. 2.** Manuscript 1 includes a *Pesiq* mark.

### Critical Annotations

v. 2. **and they will add** <note>original: "ויוסיפו"</note> with the companion mark *Sarka* 2. and its own *Kadma* 3. <note>Technical names for Hebrew musical/accent marks used in chanting.</note> --- v. 3. **your throat** <note>original: "גרגרותיך"</note> thus written fully in manuscripts 7, 8, 15, 22.  
**write them** <note>original: "כתבם"</note> and so in manuscript 2 according to the Great [Masorah] 2, printed, and the Erfurt manuscript here and in printed version of chap. 1:9. --- v. 4. **favor and [good] understanding** <note>original: "חן ושכל"</note> thus in 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 16, 19, 20.  
But **and [good] understanding** <note>original: "ושכל"</note> erroneously in 1, II, 12, 15, 17, 18, 21, 22. --- v. 6. **your paths** <note>original: "ארחתיך"</note> thus with the *Kometschat* <note>A specific variant of the Kamets vowel.</note>.  
v. 8. **to your navel** <note>original: "לשרך"</note> without the *Dagesh* in 7, 10, 20. --- **and marrow** <note>original: "ושקוי"</note> contrary to Rabbi Chaiim at the end of the Masorah. The suffix *Kaph* with a *Dagesh* in 1, 3, 6, 9. --- II, 12, 13, 19, 20, 23. --- v. 12. **for whom [the Lord loves]** <note>original: "כי את־"</note> with a *Maqqef* [hyphen] in 1, 2, 3 and together with *Metheg* in 14 and Ben Naphtali, which is more according to analogy, but against Masorah I and the first printed version and the Erfurt manuscript here and in the printed version of Psalm 47:5, which requires a *Segol* without the *Maqqef*. Otherwise with a tonic *Tiphecha* in 7, 8, 10–13, 15, 16, 19, which compare with the variant readings of Psalm 45:4. --- **he loves** <note>original: "יאהב"</note> with a simple *Shua* in 8, 12, 15, 16, 23. --- v. 15. **not** <note>original: "לא"</note> with *Maqqef* in 1 with *Metheg* in 6, 9, 14, 17, 18, 20, 24. And **they compare** <note>original: "ישוו"</note> see chap. 8:11. --- v. 17. **her paths** <note>original: "נתיבותיה"</note> thus in 6, 9, II, 12, 16, 1, 20, 21, 24 according to analogy. --- But others only with *Munach*. --- v. 19. **founded with wisdom** <note>original: "בחכמה יסד־"</note> thus in 2, 7, 8, 21, 22.  
v. 21. **keep sound wisdom** <note>original: "נצר תושיה"</note> thus in 1. --- v. 24. **you lie down, [you will] not** <note>original: "תשכב לא"</note> thus in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, 24. *Tiphecha* also held in 23. --- and with *Munach* on the same word in 12. --- 17, 18. --- v. 27. **withhold good** <note>original: "תמנע טוב"</note> thus in 1, 2, 3.  
v. 28. **to your neighbor** <note>original: "לרעך"</note> thus in the text without note in 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 20, 23. And thus **say** <note>original: "אמר"</note> in 1, 2 contrary to Masorah 1, 2, printed, and Erfurt. --- v. 29. **and he dwells trustingly** <note>original: "והוא־יושב לבטח"</note> thus correctly in 2, 7, 8, II, 21, 22, 24. Others incorrectly.

# PROVERBS 3. 4. 5.

<margin>
<note>Hebrew marginal note for v. 34</note>
And to the humble—to be read <note>original: "ולענוים קרי"; indicates that while the text might be written one way, it should be read as "and to the humble."</note>
</margin>
34 In the house of the wicked, and the dwelling of the righteous He blesses: If to the mockers He mocks,
35 and to the humble He gives grace. Honor the wise shall inherit, but fools carry away shame <note>original: "קלון"; refers to ignominy or disgrace.</note>.

<margin>CHAPTER IV.</margin>
1 Hear, children, the discipline of a father, and attend to know understanding.
2 For a good lesson I have given to you; my teaching do not forsake.
3 For I was a son to my father, tender and an only child before my mother.
4 And he taught me and said to me: Let your heart hold fast my words; keep my commandments and live.
5 Acquire wisdom, acquire understanding; do not forget and do not turn away from the words of my mouth.
6 Do not forsake her, and she will guard you; love her, and she will preserve you.
7 The beginning of wisdom is: Acquire wisdom! And with all your acquisitions, acquire understanding.
8 Prize her highly, and she will exalt you; she will honor you when you embrace her.
9 She will give to your head a wreath of grace; a crown of glory she will grant you.
10 Hear, my son, and receive my sayings, and the years of your life will be many.
11 In the way of wisdom I have instructed you; I have guided you in the tracks of uprightness.
12 When you walk, your stride will not be narrowed; and if you run, you will not stumble.
13 Hold fast to discipline, do not let go; preserve her, for she is your life.
14 Into the path of the wicked do not enter, and do not walk in the way of the evil.
15 Avoid it, do not pass by it; turn away from it and pass on.
16 For they do not sleep unless they do evil, and their sleep is robbed if they do not make others stumble.
<margin>
<note>Hebrew marginal note for v. 16</note>
"They make stumble"—to be read <note>original: "יכשילו קרי"; the marginal reading for the verb "to stumble."</note>
</margin>
17 For they eat the bread of wickedness, and the wine of violence they drink.
18 But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, going on and brightening until the day is established.
19 The way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not know at what they stumble.
20 My son, to my words attend; to my sayings incline your ear.
21 Let them not depart from your eyes; guard them in the midst of your heart.
22 For they are life to those who find them, and to all his flesh, healing.
23 Above all guarding, guard your heart, for from it are the outgoings of life.
24 Remove from yourself crookedness of mouth, and deviousness of lips put far from you.
25 Let your eyes look straight ahead, and your eyelids be direct before you.
26 Level the track of your foot, and all your ways will be established.
27 Do not turn to the right or the left; remove your foot from evil.

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>
1 My son, to my wisdom attend; to my understanding incline your ear.
2 To observe discretion, and that your lips may guard knowledge.
3 For honey drips from the lips of a strange woman, and smoother than oil is her palate.

->AND ITS END<-

<column-break/>

v. 34. a) *When, otherwise.* Surely He will mock the mockers.

v. 35. b) *but each of the fools carries away and brings back shame.*

CHAPTER IV. v. 1. c) *Hear, sons, the instruction of a father.* Solomon commends wisdom and its precepts, as in the preceding chapters, 1:8, 2:1, and also 1 John 2:1, 12, 18. He uses a threefold exhortation with supporting reasons: I. from verses 1–9. II. from verses 10–19. III. from verses 20–27. d) *chap. 1:2, 24.*

v. 2. e) Arguments follow based 1. on dignity, 2. on Solomon's own example in verses 3–4, and the instruction itself in verse 5 and following. f) *chap. 1:5.* g) *chap. 3:1.*

v. 3. h) *For I also was a son exceedingly dear to my father.* i) *tender and as if an only child (Genesis 22:2, 12)* deeply beloved; compare 1 Chronicles 3:5. k) see *chap. 31:1.*

v. 4. l) *Moreover, my father taught me.* cf. 1 Kings 2:2 and following; 1 Chronicles 22:12 and following; chapter 28:9–10. m) *let your heart hold my words.*

v. 5. n) *Buy, that is, procure; make sure you possess (v. 7). o) nor turn aside (v. 27).*

v. 6. p) *love her (chap. 8:17, 21) like a chaste and beautiful bride (chap. 5:19), then she will keep you (chap. 2:8, 11).*

v. 7. q) *The beginning of wisdom is this: Procure wisdom (v. 5).*

v. 8. r) *Exalt and extol her, then she in turn will exalt you.*

v. 9. s) *chap. 1:9. t) a crown of ornament, that is, a beautiful one (chap. 16:31) — u) she will deliver to you (Genesis 14:20; Hosea 11:8).*

CHAPTER V, v. 1. x) *chap. 1:8, 4:1. y) of my wisdom, which I teach you. z) chap. 4:1, 10.* There are two parts to this chapter, each opposed to the other: I. *A warning against wisdom falsely so called, or folly, under the figure of an adulterous woman, verses 1–14.* II. *A commendation of true wisdom under the figure of a chaste and most sweet wife, verses 15–23.*

## CHAPTER VII.

<margin>CHAPTER VII, v. 1. x) So that, my son (ch. 1:8), you may be preserved from that evil woman (ch. 6:24ff), keep my words (v. 2; ch. 4:4). II. [and those] with flatteries (v. 13-22) & III. drawing them (v. 23-27) to death. v. 23. with repeated exhortation (v. 24-27).</margin>

2 <margin>v. 2. y) as with the letter *He* in v. 2. z) according to the Masoretic note <note>original: "sec. M. I."</note>, like the "blackness" (v. 9), that is, the pupil of your eyes (Deuteronomy 32:10; Psalm 17:8).</margin> Keep my commandments and live; and my teaching as the pupil of your eye.

### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>
CHAPTER 8, v. 1. s) Does not Wisdom [call out]? And indeed, she is a personal and substantial figure (v. 22; ch. 1:20), who is introduced here speaking as the best teacher for gaining wisdom (v. 1–3). In her speech, several parts can be observed: I. The Introduction (v. 4–9). II. The Proposition (v. 10). III. The Confirmation through many and most serious reasons (v. 11–31). IV. The Conclusion through a serious admonition (v. 32–36).
</margin>
1 Does not wisdom call out, and understanding raise her voice?

2 At the top of the heights along the way, where the paths meet, she takes her stand.

3 Beside the gates, at the entrance to the city, at the entry of the doors, she cries out:

4 "To you, O men, I call, and my voice is to the sons of man.

5 Understand prudence, O simple ones; and you fools, be of an understanding heart.

6 Listen, for I will speak noble things, and from the opening of my lips shall come right things.

7 For my palate shall speak truth; wickedness is an abomination to my lips.

8 All the words of my mouth are in righteousness; there is nothing twisted or crooked in them.

9 They are all straight to him who understands, and right to those who find knowledge.

10 Receive my instruction and not silver, and knowledge rather than choice gold.

11 For wisdom is better than pearls, and all desirable things cannot be compared to her.

<margin>
v. 2. t) In the "house of the paths," that is, at the crossroads, or as above in ch. 1:21, at the beginnings of the streets.
</margin>
12 I, wisdom, dwell with prudence, and I find knowledge and discretion.

13 The fear of the Lord is to hate evil; pride, arrogance, the way of evil, and a perverted mouth I hate."

v. 12. **Now outside, now** — thus in manuscripts 1, 2, and 14, following the regular pattern. v. 16. **Coverlets** — with a *metheg* <note>a small vertical stroke used as a secondary accent</note> in 2 and 3; perhaps because of the following weakened letter, as all our copies have. v. 18. **With love** — with a *chateph-patah* vowel in 1, 3, 6, 9, 10, and 20, contrary to the Masoretic notes of Ben Asher. v. 20. **Full moon** — with the *tsere* vowel in 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, and 19. **He goes** — so in 21, 22, 23; see Psalm 68:11, 21, 36 and Psalm 84:4, etc. for similar doubling. But with only a *mahpakh* accent below the line in 1, 2, 3; and together with a *paseq* and its companion *zarka* in 14. The rest have only a *mahpakh* accent on the penultimate syllable, which is anomalous. **And like a foot-chain** — in 9, contrary to the Masoretic notes in 1, 2, printed editions, and the Erfurt manuscript. v. 26. **Her slain** — spelled deficiently <note>missing a vowel-letter</note> in 3, 6, 9, 22, according to the Masorah, the Erfurt manuscript, and printed editions here and in Isaiah 26:21. Others spell it fully with the letter *Vav*. CHAPTER 8, v. 1. **They cry out** — the letter *Nun* is without a *dagesh* <note>a dot indicating doubling</note> in 1, 10, 14, 20, 21. v. 5. **Simple ones** — thus with a silent *Aleph* in 17, 22, 24, according to the Masoretic notes. Others spell it as *peta'iyim*. See ch. 7:7 and 9:6. v. 8. **In righteousness** — with the *tiphcha* accent in 1 and 3. v. 10. **Receive my instruction** — thus in 2. But elsewhere <note>likely referring to different vowel patterns</note> in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20. v. 11. **And all—** — with a *metheg* in 1, 2, 3, 8, 14, 16, 23. Furthermore, **to hate evil** is without a *yerach* accent, specifically the *mercha-mahpakh* and *sub-metheg* in 1, 2, 3, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 21, 22, 23. Most use an *atnach* accent <note>a major pause</note>, emphasizing the regular composition. But by a *tiphcha* accent in 2, 3, 21, 24, and the Berlin manuscript.

<margin>**CHAPTER IX.**</margin> **1** <gloss>u</gloss> Wisdom has built her house, she has hewn out her seven pillars:

**v. 13.** "And the mouth of perversity" <note>original: 'u-pi tahpukot'</note> so in manuscripts 1, 2, 3. **v. 16** In place of "earth" <note>original: 'aretz'</note> they have "justice" <note>original: 'tzedek'</note> in 1, 2, and other books in the Hebrew Concordance under "judge" <note>original: 'shafat'</note>: which is also how the Vulgate, Syriac, and Chaldee <margin>r</margin> interpreted it.
**v. 21.** "And their treasuries" <note>original: 'u-otzrotehem'</note> so in 6, 9, 24, and the Berlin edition. But with the Rebia Gerish accent in 1, 2. With Merka in 3. All others irregularly with only Munach. **v. 22.** "Possessed me" <note>original: 'kanani'</note> with Patah more regularly in 1, 3. **v. 23.** "From the beginning" <note>original: 'merosh'</note> with Rebia Gerish only in the Berlin edition. See note on Psalm 4:1. But with Etnahta and a preceding Munach in 1, 2. **v. 24.** "Depths" <note>original: 'tehomot'</note> written fully in 2, 3, 22 according to the Masorah in this place and in Exodus 15:5; but against Masorah 1 and the Erfurt manuscript, which variation <margin>Masorah</margin> Rabbi Chaiim also observed. **v. 27.** "In his decree" <note>original: 'be-hukko'</note> thus the Kaph is without a Dagesh <note>a grammatical dot</note> in 2, 6, 9, 22. I. which the printed Masorah also seems to hint. **v. 29.** "In his decree" thus lacking the dot in 1, 2, 3 according to Masorah 1 and Erfurt, but against the printed versions. **v. 33.** "And be wise" <note>original: 've-hachamu'</note> with Rebia Gerish only in Berlin. But "hear instruction and be wise" in 1 and 2. The <margin>Masorah</margin> note also appears in the Masorah as Merka in 2. **v. 34.** "Blessed is" in the Erfurt, which writes it with Metheg. **v. 35.** "He who finds me" <note>original: 'motz'i'</note> thus written with the added Keri in 6, 9, 10, Erfurt, or with a silent Aleph in 7, 8, 24. **CHAPTER IX, v. 6.** "Simple ones" <note>original: 'peta'im'</note> Most manuscripts, see ch. 8:5. **v. 7.** "And he who reproves" <note>original: 've-yoser'</note> manuscripts 2 and 3 add Metheg to the last syllable. Others use Merka.

# PROVERBS CHAPTERS 9 & 10

<margin>
a) and the knowledge of the holy ones <note>The Hebrew word is plural, likely referring to the Divine</note>, which makes one holy and is proper to those who are holy. (See Proverbs 30:3; Sirach 1:16; Wisdom of Solomon 7:27).
b) this is ultimately what true prudence is. (See Proverbs 1:2).
c) and they shall be added to you. This uses the imperfect verb form, as seen in Proverbs 6:30 and 3:2.
d) If you are wise, you are wise for yourself <note>meaning you reap the benefits of your own wisdom</note>. (Compare Job 35:3, 6-8).
e) If you indeed mock, or act as a mocker. Written in the "Kal" <term>simple active</term> verb stem.
f) Compare the name in verse 1. You alone shall bear it and pay the penalty. (Leviticus 19:8; Numbers 9:13).
</margin>

> **11** For by me your days shall be multiplied, and years of life shall be added to you. **12** If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; but if you scoff, you alone shall bear the consequences.

<margin>
g) On the contrary, the Woman of Folly is boisterous; according to the Vulgate <note>the 4th-century Latin Bible</note>, she is clamorous. (Proverbs 7:11).
h) She is the embodiment of fatuousness; or the "woman of folly," that is, a foolish woman.
i) She does not know anything (Job 13:13), specifically regarding true and saving knowledge.
</margin>

> **13** The woman of folly is boisterous, simple, and knows nothing. **14** And she sits at the door of her house, on a seat in the high places of the city,

<margin>
k) These are the same words used for true Wisdom in verse 4. This shows that the woman of folly also wishes to be regarded as a teacher of wisdom. (Compare 1 Timothy 6:20).
</margin>

> **15** to call to those who pass by, who go straight on their ways: **16** "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here"; and to him who lacks heart <note>a Hebrew idiom for "lacking understanding"</note>, she says: **17** "Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant."

<margin>
l) She allegorically commends the illicit allurements of the flesh and the fulfillment of lustful desires.
m) But the fool does not know the truth, having been enticed by her speech in verse 16. (Compare Chapter 7, verses 27 and following).
n) He does not know that the dead are there, and that he himself will be joined to them. (Proverbs 2:18).
o) Her invited guests and companions (verse 3) are in the lowest parts of hell <note>original: "inferni"</note>. (Proverbs 7:27).
</margin>

> **18** But he does not know that the departed spirits are there; her guests are in the depths of Sheol <note>the Hebrew underworld</note>.

### THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON
### CHAPTER 10

<margin>
CHAPTER 10, verse 1. p) These are the proverbs and miscellaneous maxims of Solomon. This marks the beginning of the second part of the book, which from here until Chapter 24 inclusive, contains the aphorisms of Solomon, collected by the author himself. (Compare the note at 1:7).
</margin>

> **1** A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is the grief of his mother. **2** Treasures of wickedness profit nothing, but righteousness delivers from death.

<margin>
v. 3 q) It is in vain (Proverbs 11:6; Psalm 52:4). God will drive away the desire of the impious from the just. (Job 18:18).
</margin>

> **3** The Lord will not let the soul of the righteous go hungry, but he thrusts away the craving of the wicked.

<margin>
v. 4 r) He becomes poor (Proverbs 14:20, 19:7; 2 Samuel 12:1) who works with a hand of deceit or a "treacherous hand" (Proverbs 12:24, 27; 19:15).
s) But the hand of the diligent and the industrious (Proverbs 12:24, 13:4) makes one rich through the blessing of God (verse 22).
</margin>

> **4** He becomes poor who works with a slack hand, but the hand of the diligent makes rich. **5** He who gathers in summer is a wise son; he who sleeps in harvest is a son who causes shame. **6** Blessings are upon the head of the righteous, but violence covers the mouth of the wicked. **7** The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked shall rot. **8** The wise in heart will receive commandments, but a babbling fool <note>literally: "a fool of lips"</note> shall fall. **9** He who walks in integrity walks securely, but he who perverts his ways shall be known. **10** He who winks with the eye causes sorrow, but a babbling fool shall fall. **11** The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but violence covers the mouth of the wicked. **12** Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all transgressions. **13** On the lips of him who has understanding, wisdom is found, but a rod is for the back of him who lacks heart. **14** Wise men lay up knowledge, but the mouth of the foolish is a near destruction. **15** The rich man’s wealth is his strong city; the destruction of the poor is their poverty. **16** The labor of the righteous leads to life, the increase of the wicked to sin. **17** He is in the way of life who keeps instruction, but he who refuses reproof goes astray. **18** He who hides hatred with lying lips, and he who utters a slander, is a fool. **19** In the multitude of words, transgression does not cease, but he who restrains his lips is wise. **20** The tongue of the just is as choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth.

<margin>
v. 21. u) To die through one who is senseless (verse 13; Proverbs 6:32, 7:7, 9:4).
</margin>

> **21** The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of heart. **22** The blessing of the Lord makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it.

**Verse 13:** "Boisterous" (הֹמִיָּה): Thus written defectively <note>missing a vowel-letter</note> in manuscripts 1, 6, 9, 22, 23, and the Erfurt Masorah. In Proverbs 7:11, it is noted by the Masorah. The printed Masorah for Isaiah 22:2 requires the full spelling, but the defective spelling is more correct there as well. "Know" (יֵדְעָה): with a *Merca* <term>musical accent</term> on the penultimate syllable in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 13, 19, 21, 22, and with a *Maqqeph* <term>hyphen</term> in 6, 9, 10, 20. **Verse 15:** "to those who pass by" (לְעֹבְרֵי): with a *Munach* accent on the penultimate syllable in 6–16 and 19–23; but on the final syllable in 1. "their ways" (אֹרְחוֹתָם): with a *Qamets-Chatuf* <term>short 'o' sound</term> in 1, 2, 3. **Verse 17:** "Stolen waters" (מַיִם גְּנּוּבִים): thus in 1, 6, 9, 10, 11, 14, 16, 20. But written slightly differently in 2, 3, 7, 8, 12, 14. **CHAPTER 10, verse 3:** "He thrusts away" (יֶהְדֹּף): with a *Patach* vowel in 1, 3, and several manuscripts in the Michaelis edition. **Verse 7:** "Memory" (זֵכֶר): with a *Tsere* vowel in 2, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 19, 22. **Verse 10:** "Winks" (קֹרֵץ): thus with a *Metheg* <term>stress mark</term> in 3, 22; others use a *Merca* accent. Some place the stress on the final syllable, others on the penultimate. **Verse 18:** "and he who utters" (וּמוֹצִיא): written defectively in 6, 9, 23, 24, following the printed Masorah for this passage and Numbers 14:37; however, most manuscripts use the full spelling.

# PROVERBS 10 & 11

<margin>
**a)** Nor does the Lord add or increase sorrow and anxious care with it. (Psalm 127:2).

**k)** (Verse 20; chapter 3:32).

**n)** But with the humble <note>Compare Micah 6:8</note>.

**o)** There is wisdom, by which they guard themselves from pride and shame.

**v. 9. r)** Aramaic Targum & Syriac: "By his mouth." (Chapter 6:12).

**s)** The impious man is a hypocrite and a profane simulator. (Psalm 35:16).

**t)** He wishes or seeks to destroy his neighbor. (Daniel 8:24, 25).

**u)** Targum: "But in his knowledge."

**v. 13. x)** One who walks in slander. (Chapter 20:19).

**y)** Reveals a secret. (Chapter 25:9).

**z)** But he who is faithful in spirit. (Chapter 14:29; chapter 25:13).

**a)** Conceals the matter; the Latin Vulgate says "the trust of a friend."

**v. 21. b)** Though hand joins hand <note>original: "Manus manui licet iungat"</note>, yet the evil man shall not go unpunished. (Chapter 16:5).

# Proverbs 10–11

...and He adds no sorrow with it. **23** Doing wickedness is like sport to a fool, but wisdom is for a man of understanding. **24** What the wicked man dreads will come upon him, and the desire of the righteous will be granted. **25** When the whirlwind passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is an everlasting foundation. **26** As vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who send him. **27** The fear of the Lord prolongs days, but the years of the wicked will be shortened. **28** The hope of the righteous is gladness, but the expectation of the wicked will perish. **29** The way of the Lord is a stronghold for the upright, but destruction for the workers of iniquity. **30** The righteous will never be moved, but the wicked will not inhabit the land. **31** The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but the perverse tongue will be cut off. **32** The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable, but the mouth of the wicked is perversity.

**11:1** Deceitful scales are an abomination to the Lord, but a just weight is His delight. **2** When pride comes, then comes shame; but with the humble is wisdom. **3** The integrity of the upright guides them, but the perversity of the treacherous destroys them. **4** Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death. **5** The righteousness of the blameless makes his way straight, but the wicked falls by his own wickedness. **6** The righteousness of the upright delivers them, but the treacherous are trapped by their own greed. **7** When a wicked man dies, his hope perishes, and the expectation of wealth comes to nothing. **8** The righteous is delivered from trouble, and the wicked comes in his stead. **9** With his mouth the hypocrite destroys his neighbor, but through knowledge the righteous are delivered. **10** When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices, and when the wicked perish, there is shouting. **11** By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted, but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked. **12** He who is devoid of heart despises his neighbor, but a man of understanding keeps silent. **13** A talebearer reveals secrets, but he who is of a faithful spirit conceals a matter. **14** Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in the multitude of counselors there is safety. **15** He who is surety for a stranger will surely suffer for it, but he who hates striking hands in a pledge is secure. **16** A gracious woman attains honor, and ruthless men attain riches. **17** The merciful man does good to his own soul, but he who is cruel troubles his own flesh. **18** The wicked man earns deceitful wages, but he who sows righteousness has a sure reward. **19** As righteousness leads to life, so he who pursues evil pursues it to his own death. **20** Those of a crooked heart are an abomination to the Lord, but those blameless in their way are His delight. **21** Though hand join hand, the wicked shall not go unpunished; but the offspring of the righteous will be delivered.

v. 27. "Shall add" <note>Hebrew: *toseef*</note> is written defectively <term>spelled without the vowel-letter 'vav'</term>. This requires a Masoretic note regarding Exodus 11:6, but none of our codices support this.
v. 27. "Shall be shortened" <note>Hebrew: *tiktsarnah*</note> is written with a Patach <term>short 'a' vowel</term>, but with a Kamatz <term>long 'a' vowel</term> in the margin.
v. 31. "Mouth" <note>Hebrew: *pi*</note> is marked with the Munach <term>a musical/accent mark</term> in various manuscript versions.
CHAPTER 11, v. 6. "And in the greed" <note>Hebrew: *u-ve-havvat*</note>—so it is in manuscript 2; not a bad reading.
v. 9. "They shall be delivered"—so in manuscript 2; likewise elsewhere.
v. 12. "Despises" <note>Hebrew: *baz*</term> with a Patach in the margins of versions 6 and 9, contrary to other Masoretic versions.
v. 13. "And faithful"—so in version 2 and in the Masorah of Jacob ben Chaiim.

v. 14. "Shall fall"—so it is defectively written <term>missing a vowel letter</term> in versions 1, 3, 6, 7, 10, and 21.
v. 15. "And he who hates"—thus written defectively in versions 1, 3, 6, 9, 20, 22, and likewise in Deuteronomy 19:4 and Isaiah 61:8. Others write it "plene" <term>fully, with the 'vav' vowel letter</term>.
v. 21. "Evil"—the Dagesh <term>a dot in the letter indicating doubling or hardening</term> is required here by the Masorah.

# PROVERBS CHAPTERS 11 & 12

<margin>
**verse 22. a)** *As a golden ring in a pig's snout, so is a woman who is beautiful indeed, but turning away from judgment—that is, foolish.*

**v. 23. b)** *Only that which is good is what they desire and also obtain.*
**c)** *Wrath, so that in place of the hoped-for good, they experience the anger of God.*

**v. 24. d)** *There is one who scatters and gives liberally. (Psalm 112:9).*
**e)** *And yet more is added to him. The Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> says: "and they become richer."* **f)** *And there is one who withholds his goods from what is right (chapter 14:2, 17:26).* **g)** *But it leads only to poverty, so that he becomes poorer.*

**v. 25. h)** *For a soul of actual blessing (Genesis 33:11, Ezekiel 44:30), meaning one who gives liberally, according to the preceding verse 24.* **i)** *Shall be made fat and have abundance (cf. chapter 22:9).*
**k)** *And he who waters others (Isaiah 55:10).* **l)** *He himself shall also be watered by God (Future Hophal <note>A Hebrew passive verb form</note>), so that he abounds in good things and is like a well-watered garden (Isaiah 58:11).*

**v. 27. m)** *He who seeks good (chapter 7:15, 8:17).*

**v. 30. n)** *The fruit of the righteous: everything said and done by him both wisely and piously.* **o)** *For the wise man captures souls with saving doctrine.*

**v. 31. p)** *On the earth, while he lives here; in contrast to the state of the righteous after death, where he will no longer suffer any chastisements for sins (1 Corinthians 11:32).* **q)** *Is recompensed, that is, he receives the retribution for his sins (chapter 13:13. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation</note> reads this as in 1 Peter 4:18).*

**CHAPTER 12. v. 1. r)** *He who loves discipline is the one who truly loves knowledge.* **s)** *He is dull-witted and, like a brute animal, is unteachable. (S) (chapter 30:2).*

**v. 11. t)** *But he who follows idle people (Judges 9:4).*

**v. 12. u)** *The wicked man desires the net of evil men, which serves as a snare for him toward evil.* **x)** *But God shall give a root to the righteous (as in verse 14, chapter 10:24), so that the righteous, being firmly rooted, are never captured by any movement, net, or snare.*

**v. 17. y)** *(chapter 6:19).*
</margin>

22 Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman who lacks discretion.
23 The desire of the righteous ends only in good, but the hope of the wicked ends in wrath.
<margin>Yesh</margin>
24 One person scatters, yet gains even more; another withholds what is right, only to come to poverty.
25 A generous soul will be made prosperous, and he who refreshes others will himself be refreshed.
<margin>Bar</margin>
26 The people curse him who withholds grain, but blessing is on the head of him who sells it.
27 He who diligently seeks good finds favor, but evil comes to him who searches for it.
28 He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf.

19 Truthful lips established forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment.
20 Deceit is in the heart of those who plot evil, but those who counsel peace have joy.

<margin>Chapter XIII.</margin>
**1** A wise son accepts his father’s discipline, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke.

**3** He who guards his mouth preserves his life, but he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin.
**4** The soul of the sluggard craves and has nothing, but the soul of the diligent is richly supplied.

**6** Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but wickedness overthrows the sinner.
**7** There is one who pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth.
**8** The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man does not hear rebuke.
**9** The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked goes out.
**10** Pride only breeds strife, but wisdom is found with those who take advice.
**11** Wealth gained from vanity will dwindle, but he who gathers little by little will increase it.
**12** Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.
**13** He who despises the word will be destroyed by it, but he who fears the commandment will be rewarded.
**14** The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, to turn away from the snares of death.
**15** Good understanding wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is hard.
**16** Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool displays his folly.
**17** A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.
**18** Poverty and shame come to him who neglects discipline, but he who regards reproof is honored.
**19** A desire realized is sweet to the soul, but it is an abomination to fools to turn away from evil.

**Verse 28.** In place of the word "not" <note>Hebrew: אל-</note>, certain manuscripts (3, 23, and the margins of 6, 9) have a variant that the ancients interpreted as follows: the Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin Bible</note> says, *but the devious path leads to death*; the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation</note> (and from it the Syriac and Arabic) say, *but the way of the wrathful leads to death*; the Chaldean says, *and the way of the perverse leads to death*. But these translators have distorted the noun for "pathway" <note>Hebrew: נתיבה</note>, which carries no meaning of deviousness, wrath, or perverseness. If the vowel <term>Segol</term> <note>A Hebrew vowel marking an 'e' sound</note> were to be maintained, the version could be expressed as: *But a path of the track (that is, a shortcut) is also given to death*; namely, if the work of injustice is pursued. However, most codices (7, 8, 15, 17, 18, 24, and the Berlin edition) read with a <term>Dagesh</term> <note>A dot indicating a strengthened consonant</note>.

**Chapter XIII, verse 1.** "Discipline" <note>Hebrew: מוֹסָר</note>. In verses 3 and 6, 9 (margin). **Verse 3.** The word "to him" <note>Hebrew: לוֹ</note> is without a Dagesh according to the Masora of Erfurt, which requires a <term>Patach</term> <note>A Hebrew vowel 'a'</note>. Others distinguish the phrase as: *Wealth is each man's ransom for his soul.* **Verse 8.** The word "soul" <note>Hebrew: נֶפֶשׁ</note> is marked with a <term>Tiphecha</term> <note>A Hebrew cantillation mark or accent</note> in old codices (2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 11, 14, 18, 21, 24). **Verse 10.** The word "and with" <note>Hebrew: וְאֶת</note> is marked with a <term>Makkeph</term> <note>A Hebrew hyphen</note> (1, 2, 23). **Verse 10.** "Those who take advice" <note>Hebrew: נוֹעָצִים</note> appears thus in 7, 8, 16, 18, 21, 24 and irregularly in Munster's edition. **Verse 11.** "Wealth" <note>Hebrew: הוֹן</note> with a Makkeph (11, 12, 23); this is an anomalous construction, but allows for easier distinction between words. **Verse 17.** "Messenger" <note>Hebrew: מַלְאָךְ</note> with a <term>Pashta</term> <note>A Hebrew accent</note> in the construct state (3, 6, 9); the Vulgate rendered this "the messenger of the impious," which is less accurate. **Verse 23.** "Much" <note>Hebrew: רָב-</note> with a Patach (3). With a <term>Kamatz</term> <note>A Hebrew 'a' vowel</note> and a <term>Metheg</term> <note>A vertical stress mark</note> in others (7, 8, 13, 14, 20). It means "Much in food," that is, fertile in crops is the fallow ground of the poor.

### Philological Notes

CHAPTER XIV, verse 6. *Bikesh* (seek) with the vowel *Tsere* and the accent *Mahpach* in manuscripts 6, 9, 10, 12—16, 19, 20, 23. However, it appears with *Segol* in the margins of 6 and 9. *Veda'at* (and knowledge) with the accent *Revia-geresh*. Verse 1 is best if followed by *Merca*. Verse 9: *Yalin* thus with *Chirek* in manuscript 2, according to the Masora in the first Jonah edition 4:10. As if to say: but the intelligence of the upright is favor, or acceptable to God and men. However, all the ancient translators <note>original: "metaphrastæ"</note> interpreted it with the vowel *Tsere*; and Rabbi Chaim confesses in the place cited that he found *Tsere* in all books. Verse 10: *Lev* (heart) thus with *Revia* in 3 and the Berlin manuscript, and together with *Munach* in 6, 7, 9. But in manuscript 1, with *Chirek* according to the first Masora on Psalm 142:8. Others are written <unclear>fully</unclear>. Verse 19: *Shachu* (they bow) occurs in 1, 2, 14. With *Kamatz* in 1, 2, 3 and in the margin of 6, 9. Verse 21: *Vechonen* (and shows favor) thus in 24 and Berlin. Also with *Maqqaf* (hyphen), but without *Metheg* in 2, 3, 6—16, 19—23; and in 7, 8 indeed with the added sign for "Note Well." But with *Munach* in 17, 18. Verse 23: *Etsev* (labor) with *Tsere* in 2, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, and in the text of 6, 9. But with *Cholem* in manuscript 1. Verse 25: *Veyafiach* (and breathes) is spelled defectively in 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 15, 22. And so in 1 according to the Masora. Others spell it fully. Verse 27: *Mimmokeshei* (from the snares) is defective in 3, 7, 8, 15, following the Masora on 2 Samuel 22:6. But most spell it fully. Verse 28: *Le'om* (people) is spelled fully in 1, 3, 17, according to the Masora and the Erfurt manuscript here and at Genesis 25:23. The others are defective.

# CHAPTER 14. 15. PROVERBS 14, 15

<margin>
a) a heart of health or a healing, that is, one healed from the excess of passions and diseases. b) but envy is the decay of the bones.
</margin>
A tranquil heart<gloss>a</gloss> is life for the body, but envy<gloss>b</gloss> is the rottenness of the bones.

<margin>
v. 31. c) He who oppresses the poor insults his Maker, namely God, who made the poor as well as the rich.
</margin>
He who oppresses<gloss>c</gloss> the poor insults his Maker, but he who is kind to the needy honors Him.

<margin>
v. 32. d) In his own wickedness, the impious person is pushed and cast down to his fall.
</margin>
The wicked is overthrown by his evildoing<gloss>d</gloss>, but the righteous finds refuge even in his death.

Wisdom rests in the heart of one who has understanding, but in the heart of fools it makes itself known. <note>The original Hebrew suggests that while wisdom is quiet in the wise, it "shouts" or makes a spectacle of itself when fools try to display what little they know.</note>

<margin>
v. 34. e) but a reproach to nations. Compare chapter 25, 10; Leviticus 20, 17; Job 6, 14.
</margin>
Righteousness exalts a nation<gloss>e</gloss>, but sin is a reproach to any people.

<margin>
v. 35. f) toward one who causes shame. See chapter 10, 5; chapter 12, 4.
</margin>
A king’s favor is toward a wise servant<gloss>f</gloss>, but his wrath is against him who causes shame.

CHAPTER XV.
The letter Hey is doubled (with a dagesh). <note>A technical note regarding the Hebrew grammar in the chapter title.</note>
</margin>
<margin>
CHAPTER XV, v. 1. g) A soft response turns away wrath; but a word of pain, harsh and painful, causes anger to rise and stirs it up.
</margin>
A soft answer<gloss>g</gloss> turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

<margin>
v. 2. h) makes good, that is, brings forth knowledge.
</margin>
The tongue of the wise commends<gloss>h</gloss> knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly.

The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good.

<margin>
v. 4. i) A healing of the tongue; a salutary speech proceeding from the tongue, intended to heal the soul.
</margin>
A healing tongue<gloss>i</gloss> is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit.

A fool despises his father’s instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is prudent.

<margin>
v. 6. k) In the house of the righteous there is much strength, or much wealth; but in the income or wealth of the wicked, there is something troubling.
</margin>
In the house of the righteous there is much treasure<gloss>k</gloss>, but trouble befalls the income of the wicked.

The lips of the wise spread knowledge, but the hearts of fools are not so.

The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is His delight.

The way of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but He loves him who pursues righteousness.

<margin>
v. 10. l) A bad and cruel discipline (Jeremiah 30, 14) will happen to the one who forsakes the way—specifically the right way shown by parents or teachers. See verses 5 and 7.
</margin>
There is severe discipline<gloss>l</gloss> for him who forsakes the way; whoever hates reproof will die.

Sheol and Abaddon <note>The underworld and the place of destruction</note> lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man!

A scoffer does not love one who reproves him; he will not go to the wise.

A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by sorrow of heart the spirit is broken.

Beautiful reading <note>original: "yefe keri" — a note on the traditional scribal reading.</note>
</margin>
The heart of him who has understanding seeks knowledge, but the mouths of fools feed on folly.

<margin>
v. 15. m) Truly all the days of the poor are evil or unhappy; but to be of a good heart (joy of heart) in the midst of hardships is like a continual feast.
</margin>
All the days of the afflicted<gloss>m</gloss> are evil, but the cheerful of heart has a continual feast.

<margin>
v. 17. n) Better is a bit of a meal of herbs.
</margin>

<note>The following section contains technical philological notes regarding the Masoretic Text—the authoritative Hebrew text of the Bible. It tracks minute details like accents (the musical notation for chanting) and vowel points across different ancient manuscripts.</note>

V. 31. *Oppressing* (עֹשֵׁק) appears without the Merca or Metheg marks in manuscript 2. But according to the meter, it uses only the Munach accent in manuscripts 1 and 3. CHAPTER XV, v. 1. *Soft* (רַּךְ) appears without the Dagesh (the doubling dot) in manuscripts 1, 3, 7, 10, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23, 24, and in the Berlin edition, contrary to the manuscript of Meir ha-Levi. v. 5. *Despises* (יִנְאַץ) is written with a Chateph-Patach vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, and 3. v. 7. *Spread* (יְזָרוּ) is thus accented on the penultimate syllable in 1, 3, 22, 24; others accent it on the last syllable or are ambiguous. v. 9. *Loves* (יֶאֱהָב) is written with a Chateph-Segol vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 16, and 19 through 23. v. 10. *Discipline* (מוּסָר) with a Patach vowel and accented on the penultimate syllable in 2, with its Masorah. *And whoever hates* (וְשֹׂונֵא) in the printed and Erfurt manuscripts here, and printed in 1 Samuel 20, 13. v. 13. *Makes cheerful* (יֵיטִֽיב) is spelled defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> in 1, 3, 7, 8, 15, 22, and perhaps 2; a note in the margin of the corrected books testifies to this spelling. Others spell it fully, contrary to Masorah 2 and 3, and the printed Erfurt versions here and in 1 Samuel 20, 13. v. 14. *And the mouth* (וּפִי) and similarly *and by the sorrow* (וּבְעַצְּבַת) are without the Dagesh in 1 and 3. v. 14. For *and the mouth* (וּפִי), manuscript 7 and Erfurt 8 have *and the faces* (וּפְנֵי), and so perhaps does 2. Against this, manuscript 3 writes and reads *and the mouth* (וּפִי). Both are against the printed Masorah in 2 Samuel 21, 6 and the Erfurt version here. v. 15. *And the good* (וְטוֹב) with a Vav, Makkaph, and Metheg in 3, 7, 8, 17, 18, 24, and the Berlin edition. v. 16. *Better* (טוֹב) with a Munach accent in 2 and 3. *Than treasure* (מֵאוֹצָר) with a Patach vowel in 2, 3, 7, 8, 11, 13, 15, 16, 19, 21, 22, which is less correct. *In it* (וּבוֹ) with a Dagesh in 17 and the Opitz edition. v. 17. *And love* (וְאַהֲבָה) with a Munach, accented on the penultimate syllable in 6 and 9 through 16, and 19 through 23. *In it* (בּוֹ) with a Dagesh in 2, 17, 23. v. 19. *As a hedge* (כִּמְשׂוּכַת) with a Beth instead of the prefixed Caph in 1, and in the margins of 6 and 9. v. 20. *Makes glad* (וְשִׂמַּח) with a Munach, accented on the last syllable in 3, 6, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16, 19, 20, and 23; and together with a Makkaph in 21. v. 25. *Tears down* (יִסַּח) thus with an emphatic Psik mark in 7, 8, 11, 15, and perhaps in the Berlin edition. Others omit it. Furthermore, instead of Munach, they have Merca in 7, 8, 11, 17, 18, which is incorrect, because here it is not a substitute for an Atnach accent, but a simple dependent mark.

# PROVERBS. CHAPTER 15. 16.

<margin>
a) pleasant words <note>original: "verba amoenitatis"</note>, or good and healthy speeches, harming no one.
v. 27. b) He who pursues greed disturbs his own house.
v. 30. c) & a good report makes the bones fat <note>original: "pinguafacit os," referring to health and vigor.</note>.
v. 32. d) see chapter 1, 25; chapter 13, 18.
CHAPTER XVI, v. I. e) To man belong the preparations of the heart, but from the Lord is and depends the answer of the tongue.
v. 2. f) All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, that is: whatever a man does and follows seems right to himself. g) but the one who weighs the spirits is Jehovah, who alone unfailingly knows what is right and what is profitable for man.
v. 4. h) The Lord has made and still makes all things for His own answer <note>original: "ad responsum suum"</note>, so that all things respond to His will and are humbly subjected. v. 1. chapter 29, 19. i) and thus even the wicked for the day of evil or punishment: as in Jeremiah 17:18 and Amos 6:3. Thus the wicked, because he does not respond to the grace of God (according to the first half of the verse), must nevertheless be subject to His justice and vengeance. cf. Job 21, 30; 2 Peter 2, 9.
v. 5. k) see chapter 11, 21.
v. 10. l) If divination and sagacity be on the lips of a king, so that by wise speech he can fish out what men strive to hide. This is taken in a positive sense, like the participle in Isaiah 3, 2.
v. 11. m) The scales and balances of justice <note>original: "iuris"</note> belong to the Lord, as their author and approver. n) and they are His work, which He himself commanded and finds pleasing. Just as the "sacrifices of God" in Psalm 51, 19; the "works of God" in John 6, 28; and the "righteousness of God" in Romans 3, 21-26. o) Stones of the pouch, meaning the weights usually kept in a pouch for commerce.
v. 21. p) He who is wise in heart is rightly called prudent; but sweetness of the lips—which knows how to bring forth the wisdom stored in the heart with sweet eloquence and share it with others—will increase learning in others, so that they too may be wise. See also v. 23.
</margin>

### Chapter XVI

**1** <margin>To man</margin> belong the arrangements of the heart, but from the Lord comes the answer of the tongue. **2** <margin>All the ways of a man</margin> are pure in his own eyes, but the Lord weighs the spirits. **3** <margin>Commit to the Lord</margin> your works, and your thoughts will be established. **4** <margin>Your thoughts:</margin> The Lord has made everything for His own purpose, even the wicked for the day of evil. **5** <margin>The day of evil:</margin> Everyone proud in heart is an abomination to the Lord; be sure of this <note>Literally, "hand to hand," an idiom for "certainly."</note>, he will not go unpunished. **6** <margin>By mercy</margin> and truth iniquity is atoned for, and by the fear of the Lord one turns away from evil. **7** <margin>When the ways</margin> of a man please the Lord, He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him. **8** <margin>Better</margin> is a little with righteousness than great revenues without justice. **9** <margin>A man's heart</margin> plans his way, but the Lord directs his steps. **10** <margin>A divine oracle</margin> is on the lips of a king; his mouth shall not transgress in judgment. **11** <margin>In judgment</margin> a just scale and balances belong to the Lord; all the weights of the bag are His work. **12** <margin>His work</margin> It is an abomination for kings to do wickedness, for the throne is established by righteousness. **13** <margin>For by righteousness</margin> Righteous lips are the delight of kings, and they love him who speaks what is right. **14** <margin>He shall love:</margin> The wrath of a king is as messengers of death, but a wise man will appease it. **15** <margin>He will appease it:</margin> In the light of a king's face is life, and his favor is like a cloud of the latter rain. **16** <margin>To get wisdom</margin> How much better it is to get wisdom than gold! ### PROVERBS CHAPTERS 18, 19.

<margin>CH. 18. 23</margin> <gloss>a</gloss> The poor man speaks with entreaties, but the rich man answers harshly.
<margin>24</margin> A man of <gloss>b</gloss> many friends may come to ruin, but there is a lover of a friend who <gloss>c</gloss> sticks closer than a brother.

---

<margin>CH. XIX. 1</margin> Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than one who is crooked in his lips and is a fool.
<margin>2</margin> Also, for a soul to be without knowledge is <gloss>d</gloss> not good, and he who hurries with his feet misses the way.
<margin>3</margin> The foolishness of a man subverts his way, and his heart frets against the Lord.
<margin>4</margin> Wealth adds many friends, but the poor man is separated from his neighbor.
<margin>5</margin> A false witness <gloss>e</gloss> shall not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies shall not escape.
<margin>6</margin> Many <gloss>f</gloss> will seek the favor of a prince, and every man is a friend <gloss>g</gloss> to a man who gives gifts.
<margin>7</margin> All the brothers of the poor man hate him; how much more do his neighbors go far from him? <gloss>h</gloss> He pursues them with words, <margin>marginal reading: to him</margin> but they are not there.
<margin>8</margin> He who acquires a heart <gloss>i</gloss> loves his own soul; he who keeps <gloss>k</gloss> understanding shall find good.
<margin>9</margin> A false witness shall not go unpunished, <gloss>l</gloss> and he who breathes out lies shall perish.
<margin>10</margin> <gloss>m</gloss> Luxury is not <gloss>n</gloss> fitting for a fool, much less for a servant to rule over princes.
<margin>11</margin> The discretion of a man <gloss>o</gloss> makes him slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook a transgression.
<margin>12</margin> <gloss>p</gloss> The king's wrath is like the roaring of a young lion, but his favor is like dew upon the grass.
<margin>13</margin> <gloss>q</gloss> A foolish son is a calamity to his father, and the <gloss>r</gloss> continual dropping of a leaky roof are the <gloss>s</gloss> contentions of a wife.
<margin>14</margin> House and wealth are the inheritance of fathers, but a prudent wife is from the Lord.
<margin>15</margin> Laziness brings on a deep sleep, and an idle soul shall suffer hunger.
<margin>16</margin> He who keeps the commandment keeps his soul, but he who despises his ways <margin>marginal reading: shall die</margin> shall be put to death.
<margin>17</margin> He who has pity on the poor lends to the Lord, and He will pay him back for his deed.
<margin>18</margin> Discipline your son while there is hope, and do not set your heart on <gloss>t</gloss> his destruction.
<margin>19</margin> <gloss>u</gloss> A man of great wrath <margin>marginal reading: great</margin> shall bear the punishment; for if <gloss>x</gloss> you deliver him, you will have to do it again.
<margin>20</margin> Listen to counsel and receive instruction, so that you may be wise in your latter end.
<margin>21</margin> There are many thoughts in a man's heart, but the counsel of the Lord shall stand.
<margin>22</margin> The desire of a man is his kindness, and a poor man is better than a man of lies.
<margin>23</margin> The fear of the Lord leads to life, and he who has it shall rest satisfied; he shall not be visited by evil.
<margin>24</margin> A lazy man buries his hand in the dish, and will not even bring it back to his mouth.
<margin>25</margin> Strike a scoffer and the simple will become wary; reprove one who has understanding, and he will understand knowledge.
<margin>26</margin> He who robs his father and drives away his mother is a son who causes shame and brings reproach.
<margin>27</margin> Cease, my son, to hear instruction if it causes you to stray from the words of knowledge.
<margin>28</margin> A worthless witness mocks at justice, and the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity.
<margin>29</margin> Judgments are prepared for scoffers, and beatings for the backs of fools.

<column-break/>

v. 23. a) <note>original: "Supplicationes loquitur pauper..."</note> *The poor man speaks entreaties; but the rich man answers with harsh, that is, haughty and troublesome words.*

v. 24. b) <note>original: "Vir amicorum..."</note> *A man of friends, who has faithfully and sacredly cultivated friendship with many, is worthy to be chosen as a friend. Compare ch. 22:24, Judges 14:20. c) for there is a friend more clinging and constant than a brother or relative.*

CHAPTER 19, v. 2. d) <note>original: "Etiam in non scientia..."</note> *Even in lack of knowledge, the thoughtlessness of the soul is not good: and the one who is hasty and headlong with his feet wanders from the true path. Judges 20:16, Job 5:24.*

v. 5. e) *& he who speaks lies. See verse 9, and chapter 6:19.*

v. 6. f) <note>original: "Orant, precibus infirmant..."</note> *They pray, or they weaken or soften the face of the prince with prayers. Psalm 45:13. g) and everyone is a friend to a man of gifts, who has the means to be generous. Compare ch. 17:8, ch. 18:16.*

v. 7. h) *Such a poor man pursues words which are nothing.*

v. 8. i) *Chapter 4:5, 15:32. k) by this outcome he will guard it, so that he finds good. A similar prefix is found below in verse 27.*

v. 9. l) *See verse 5.*

v. 10. m) *Chapter 17:7. n) pleasure, delight. Song of Solomon 7:7. Much less (v. 7) is it fitting for a foolish servant to rule over princes. Compare ch. 30:22.*

v. 11. o) <note>original: "Amos 7:8, Micah 7:18."</note>

v. 12. p) *A roaring, like that of a young lion, is the King's anger.*

v. 13. q) *Distress or calamity. Job 6:2. r) and like a dripping, that is, a continuous leaking of the roof. (2) Chapter 27:15.*
s) *are the quarrels of a woman. Compare chapter 25:24.*

v. 18. t) *but do not desire to kill him. Psalm 24:4.*

v. 19. u) *For a man great in anger carries the penalty. Or: For perhaps there is an outburst, so that one receives the penalty. x) because (to add a new argument), if you rescue him from immoderate beatings, then in the future you will add more and chastise him so that he is corrected.*

---

v. 23. **Supplications** <note>Hebrew: *tachanunim*</note> thus with the <term>Merca|A Hebrew cantillation mark or accent</term> in manuscripts 7, 8, 16, 21, 22. With the <term>Tipcha|A Hebrew accent indicating a minor pause</term> in 24 and Berlin. Others use the <term>Munach|A conjunctive accent</term>.
v. 24. **A man** <note>Hebrew: *ish*</note> deficiently, requires the <term>Maqqaf|A Hebrew hyphen</term>. Refer to 2 Samuel 14:19 and the Masorah in this place, meaning "friends who are truly friends." However, all our copies are full, as the Masorah in the Codices also testifies.
CHAPTER XIX, v. 7. **All** <note>Hebrew: *kol*</note> with a Maqqaf without accent or <term>Meteg|A vertical line used as a secondary accent</term> in 3, 6, 9-16, 20, 23, against the Masorah of Erfurt in this place, and also Rabbi Chaiim, which unanimously require a <term>Qamets|A vowel sign</term> with an accent. Further, **all-** in 7, 8 against the Masorah, here and Psalm 35:10, which orders the Maqqaf to be absent. But **all** with a <term>Mahpak|A pre-positive accent</term> in 1, against the Masorah and the first impression of Psalm 35:10, which requires Merca and Qamets, as in 17, 18, 22, 24. **Not** <note>Hebrew: *lo*</note> without a <term>Keri|A marginal reading</term> in 6, 9, 10, 14, 19, 20, 21. v. 16. **Despises** <note>Hebrew: *bozeh*</note> with the <term>Tsere|A vowel mark</term> in 2, 7, 8, 19 and in the margin of 6, 9, according to the Masorah. Others with a <term>Segol|A vowel mark of three dots</term>. v. 17. **Lends** <note>Hebrew: *malveh*</note> with a Segol in 2, 3. **Gracious** <note>Hebrew: *chonen*</note> instead of Merca, mistakenly has Tipcha in 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 19, 21, 22; more aptly with a Meteg in 23. But with Munach alone in 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. **And his deed** with a <term>Dagesh|A dot in a letter indicating emphasis</term> in 6, 9, 10, 13, 17, 18, 19, 20, 24, and Berlin. v. 19. **Great** <note>Hebrew: *gedol*</note> with the letter Daleth in the text of 1, 3, 10, against the Masorah of Erfurt. v. 25. **Become wary** <note>Hebrew: *ya'rim*</note> with a <term>Chatef Patah|A composite vowel</term> in 1, 3.
