<header>PROVERBS. CHAPTERS 20, 21.</header>

<margin>
a) Judgments <note>original: "Confusiones"</note> are prepared for the back of fools. <note>This refers to Proverbs 19:29.</note>

CHAPTER 20, verse 1. b) Wine is a mocker, and strong drink is a brawler: and whoever wanders in it, as if in an inextricable labyrinth, will not be wise nor become wise.

v. 2. c) Compare chapter 19:12. d) He who is provoked to anger against him. Compare chapter 26:17. e) He sins against his own soul and himself. Compare chapter 8:32, 8:36.

v. 3. f) To sit far away from, or to refrain from, a dispute. g) He is entangled in quarrels (3). Compare chapter 17:14; 18:1.

v. 4. h) Because of the winter and the wintry air, the sluggard does not plow his field. i) He will therefore ask from others for the harvest's produce. The Vulgate says: "he shall beg therefore, and it shall not be given to him."

v. 6. k) A multitude, or the common crowd of men, each proclaims his own kindness; but a man of faithfulness, who proves himself faithful by his very deeds, who can find? It implies rarity, as in chapter 31:10.

v. 9. l) Who can say with a clear and vain presumption, or who is able to say: "I have purified my heart; I am clean from my sin." See 1 Kings 8:46, etc.

v. 10. m) See verse 23; chapter 11:1; 16:11; Deuteronomy 25:13. n) Deuteronomy 25:14.

v. 11. o) He makes himself known; the Targum <note>an ancient Aramaic translation</note> and Syriac versions say "is known." p) Whether his work be pure and whether it be right.

v. 15. q) There is some gold and a multitude of pearls; but a vessel of value, that is, the most precious and much more noble, are the lips of knowledge, which teach true and solid knowledge.

v. 16. r) Take away his garment from the one who acts as a guarantor, as in chapter 27:13; since he has accepted a pledge for a stranger: and for others, or for a foreign debt, take a pledge from him. Compare chapter 6:1.

v. 17. s) With gravel or sand (2). Lamentations 3:16.

v. 23. t) See verse 10.

v. 25. u) It is a snare for a man if he inconsiderately vows something holy to God; and only after the vows does he inquire whether the vow can be retracted or limited.
</margin>

<center>
CHAPTER 20, v. 1. The word *Leitz* <note>mocker</note> appears without a Dagesh <note>a grammatical dot indicating emphasis or doubling</note> in sources 1, 2, 3, and in the margin of 6 and 9. v. 2. The word *Eimat* <note>terror</note> has the accent on the last syllable in sources 1 and 3.
v. 5. The word *Amukim* <note>deep</note> is spelled with a *Kuph* without a Dagesh in sources 2, 3, 12, 14, 23. v. 6. "And a man shall see"—this is the correct reading in 1 and 2. v. 19.
The word *Goleh* <note>revealer</note> appears with a Munach accent on the penultimate syllable in sources 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20. The word *Kod* <note>as in secret</note> appears without a Dagesh in the letter Dalet in sources 1, 3, 7, 10, 14, 21.
v. 22. The word *Tomar* <note>you shall say</note> with a Tipheha accent in source 2. The word *Ra* <note>evil</note> with the letter Resh having a Dagesh in sources 2, 6, 9. The word *Veyosha* <note>and He shall save</note> appears without a Merka accent in 1 and 2. Compare verse 25.
v. 24. The word *Me-Yod-He-Vav-He* <note>from the Lord</note> with a Tipheha accent in source 14. v. 25. The word *Yala* <note>devours/snares</note> appears thus with a Merka accent in 6, 9, 10, 14, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, as above in verse 22.
CHAPTER 21, v. 1. "The heart of the king"—this is the common reading. But "water, the heart" appears thus in 1. But "water, the heart of the king, in the hand" appears in 2.

verse 3. **chosen** <note>original: "nibchar"</note> with a Pathach <note>short "a" vowel</note> in the Past tense in sources 1, 2, 3. verse 3. **lamp** <note>original: "ner"</note> with a Tsere <note>long "e" vowel</note> in 10, 11, 21 and the Concordance. verse 26. **s)** chapter 11:24. Regarding this variety, see the note on Psalm 96:8. verse 10. **desires** <note>original: "avtah"</note> with a Munach in 3, 6, 9-16, 19, 20, 23. **CHAPTER 22, verse 1.** verse 11. **he receives** <note>original: "yikkach"</note> with a Makkaph <note>hyphen-like connector</note> in 2, 3, 7, 8, 11. verse 15. **to the workers of** <note>original: "le-poalei"</note> with a Makkaph in 1, 3. verse 17. **wine** <note>original: "yayin"</note> with a Makkaph in 2, 7, 8, 15, 21, 22. t) More excellent; the Vulgate: verse 18. **to the righteous** <note>original: "la-tzaddik"</note> with a Tiphecha in 2, 6, 9-13, 15, 19, 20, and together with a Munach in 7, 8, 14, 26. <meta>This page continues the scholarly edition and translation of the Book of Proverbs, moving into the middle of Chapter 22 and beginning Chapter 23. ### 714 PROVERBS. CHAPTERS 22, 23.

<margin>a) and favor is better than silver and gold, obtained through good character and understanding. See chapter 1, verse 9 and chapter 13, verse 15.</margin>
**A good name** is to be chosen rather than great riches; good favor rather than silver and gold.

<margin>b) The crafty and prudent (chapter 1, verse 4) sees imminent evil and therefore hides himself; but the imprudent pass on without circumspection and are therefore punished.</margin>
<margin>Hebrew: Written/Read variant</margin>
**The rich** and the poor meet together; the Lord is the maker of them all.
**A prudent man** sees evil and hides himself; but the simple pass on and are punished.

<margin>c) The reward of humility and the fear of the Lord are riches, etc. (chapter 3, verse 16).</margin>
**The reward** for humility and the fear of the Lord is riches, honor, and life.

<margin>d) Thorns (Job 5:5) and snares (Job 22:10) are, etc.</margin>
**Thorns** and snares are in the way of the perverse; he who guards his soul stays far from them.

<margin>e) Initiate a boy according to the requirements of his own way, namely, the matter he undertakes to handle; then even when he grows old, he will not depart from it.</margin>
**Train up** a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.

<margin>f) And the poor man who receives a loan becomes a servant to the man giving the loan, namely the creditor. Compare Isaiah 24:2 and Nehemiah 5:4–5.</margin>
**The rich** rule over the poor, and the borrower is a slave to the lender.

<margin>g) It will finally fail, namely, be consumed, so that in turn he who was tyrannically striking others may be struck.</margin>
<margin>Extra Vav</margin>
**He who sows** injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail.

<margin>h) Good-eyed—that is, according to the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note>, one who is prone to mercy; compare Ezekiel 16:5, and by contrast Proverbs 23:6 and Matthew 20:15.</margin>
<margin>Extra Yod</margin>
**He who has a bountiful eye** will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.
**Cast out** the scoffer, and strife will go out; yes, contention and reproach will cease.

<margin>i) Regarding him who loves the pure, namely, purity of heart: grace—that is, his lips will be gracious and accepted—and the king himself will be his friend.</margin>
<margin>Extra Vav</margin>
**He who loves** purity of heart, for the grace of his lips the king will be his friend.
**The eyes** of the Lord preserve knowledge, but He overthrows the words of the faithless.
**The sluggard** says, "There is a lion outside! I shall be slain in the streets!"

<margin>k) Thus far Solomon has presented scattered maxims <term>gnomas: short, pithy statements of truth</term>; but here, to stir the reader, he inserts a succinct recapitulation, as it were, of the subject he treated in chapters 1–9. It consists of: 1) an exhortation (verse 17), 2) the motive for the exhortation (verses 18, 20, 21), and 3) the subject and summary of the teaching (verse 19).</margin>
<margin>Extra Vav</margin>
**The mouth** of strange women is a deep pit; he who is abhorred by the Lord will fall into it.
**Folly** is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline will drive it far from him.
**He who oppresses** the poor to increase his wealth and he who gives to the rich will only come to poverty.
**Incline** your ear and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge.
**For it is pleasant** if you keep them within you, let them all be fixed upon your lips.

<margin>l) even you, I say. A similar pleonasm <term>pleonasm: the use of more words than are necessary to convey meaning, for emphasis</term> appears in chapter 23, verses 15 and 19.</margin>
**So that** your trust may be in the Lord, I have made them known to you today, even to you.

<margin>m) choice, excellent, so to speak, "ducal"—worthy even of leaders <note>original Latin: ducalia</note>; compare Exodus 14:7 and the synonym above in chapter 8, verse 6.</margin>
<margin>Read: "excellent things"</margin>
**Have I not** written to you excellent things of counsels and knowledge?
**To make you know** the certainty of the words of truth, that you may return words of truth to those who sent you?
**Do not rob** the poor because he is poor, nor crush the afflicted at the gate.
**For the Lord** will plead their cause and plunder the soul of those who plunder them.

<margin>n) and he will plunder, etc.</margin>
<margin>Read: "his ways"</margin>
**Make no friendship** with a man given to anger, and with a wrathful man you shall not go.

<margin>o) Do not associate with an angry man.</margin>
**Lest** you learn his ways and get a snare for your soul.
**Be not** one of those who strike hands in pledge, or among those who are sureties for debts.
**If you have nothing** with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?
**Do not remove** the ancient landmark which your fathers have set.

<margin>p) CHAPTER 23, verse 1. p) him who is before your face.</margin>
<margin>CHAPTER 23.</margin>
**Do you see** a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men.
**When you sit down** to eat with a ruler, consider carefully what is before you.
**And put** a knife to your throat if you are a man given to appetite.

CHAPTER 22, verse 2. **Maker** with a Segol [vowel mark] in manuscript 3. and in the margin of 6. and 9. Thus also in the previous chapter, verse 2, against the Masorah <note>the traditional Hebrew text</note> in this place and Exodus 15:3. For **and the simple**, manuscript 2 has it with an Aleph, and so do the margins of 6 and 7, against the printed Masorah and the Erfurt edition at chapter 1:22 and Psalm 119:130. Verse 5: **from them** with a Kametz [vowel mark] in manuscripts 1 and 3. Verse 9: **will be blessed** with a Munach accent in 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20. The printed Masorah at Psalm 112:2 requires a Patach, but all our copies have a Kametz. Verse 10: **And will cease**, indeed with a Segol instead of a Tsere in 3 and the margins of 6 and 9. Verse 11: **purity of heart** without the extra Vav in 1, 3, 10, 11, 12, 14, 21, 23. Verse 14: For **will fall there**, so 1 and the margins of 6 and 9. Verse 17: **the words of** with a Mahpah accent in 2 and 24; with a Maqqeph [hyphen] in 3 and Berlin. All others with a Merca. See the note at Psalm 1:1. Verse 19: **I have made known to you today**, thus in 2, 3, 7, 8, 15, 21, 22, 24. For our sequence, see the note at Psalm 34:3. Verse 20: **excellent things**, thus in the text without a note in 3, 10, 11, 23, against the Masorah and Erfurt. **with counsels**, thus in 2, 3, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 21, 24, and so also Berlin. But with a Rhingeresch accent in 1. Others irregularly with only a Munach. Verse 21: **to those who send you**, singular, without the Yod in 1, 7, 8, 13, 15, 19, 21, 22, and the Hebrew Concordance. This is also how the Syriac translates it. Verse 23: **for** with a Munach accent in 2, 6, 9, 13, 19, 20. Verse 25: **you learn** with a Chateph-segol in 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 20, 23. Verse 29: **kings** with a Merca accent in 12, 15, 16, 21, 22, 24, and so also Berlin. But with a Tiphecha accent in 3 and 14. CHAPTER 23, verse 1: **consider**, the printed Masorah requires it to be spelled defectively <note>missing a vowel-letter</note> in this place, which Rabbi Chaiim calls into suspicion of being an error; all our copies have it spelled fully.

-> Regarding Chapter 24, verse 4: The word "and they shall be filled" <note>Hebrew: וְיִמָּלְא֧וּ</note> is marked with a <term>Tsere</term> vowel and accented on the penultimate syllable <term>milel</term> according to sources 3, 6, and 9. However, the marginal note observes that many punctuators and the Babylonian Codex of Proverbs punctuated it with a <term>Shva</term> vowel. In verse 5, the word "with strength" <note>בְּע֧וֹז</note> is with a <term>Patach</term> vowel. In verse 6, the word "for you" <note>לָךְ</note> is without a <term>Dagesh</term>. In verse 10, "you falter in the day" is noted in sources 1 and 2, with "adversity" <note>צָרָ֥ה</note> having a specific accent <term>Revia Geresh</term>. In verse 14, "know!" <note>דְּ֘עֶ֤ה</note> is written with a <term>Segol</term> instead of the expected <term>Qamets</term> according to the Hillel Codex (noted by Kimchi). Other Masoretic notes regarding the positioning of accents like <term>Munach</term>, <term>Mahpach</term>, and <term>Pesiq</term> are detailed for verses 12, 14, 21, 23, 24, and 27, comparing various manuscripts like the Erffurt and Berlin codices. <-

# PROVERBS CHAPTER 24, 25

28 <gloss>a</gloss> **Do not be a witness against your neighbor without cause,** <gloss>b</gloss> **and do not deceive with your lips.**
29 **Do not say, "I will do to him just as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work."**
<margin>Open with an Atnach <note>a primary musical accent in the Hebrew text marking a pause</note></margin> 30 <gloss>c</gloss> **I passed by the field of a lazy man, and by the vineyard of a man lacking sense;**
31 **And behold,** <gloss>d</gloss> **it was all overgrown with thistles; its surface was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down.**
32 **Then I beheld, and I considered it well; I saw it and received instruction.**
33 **A little** <gloss>e</gloss> **sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest;**
34 **So shall your poverty come like a prowler, and your want like an armed man.**

---

<margin>CHAPTER XXV.</margin> 1 <gloss>f</gloss> **These also are the proverbs of Solomon, which** <gloss>g</gloss> **the men of** <gloss>h</gloss> **Hezekiah, king of Judah, transcribed.**
2 <gloss>i</gloss> **It is the glory of God to conceal a matter, but the glory of kings is to** <gloss>k</gloss> **search a matter out.**
3 **As the heavens for height and the earth for depth, so the heart of kings is unsearchable.**
4 **Take away the dross from the silver, and a vessel comes out for the refiner;**
5 **Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness.**
6 **Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence, and do not stand in the place of the great;**
7 **For it is better that it be said to you, "Come up here," than that you should be humbled before a noble whom your eyes have seen.**
8 <gloss>l</gloss> **Do not go out hastily to strive in court, for what will you do in the end when your neighbor puts you to shame?**
9 **Debate your cause with your neighbor himself, and do not disclose the secret of another;**
10 <gloss>m</gloss> **Lest he who hears it bring reproach upon you, and your ill-repute never pass away.**
11 <gloss>n</gloss> **Apples of gold in settings of silver is a word spoken in its proper time.**
12 **Like an earring of gold and an ornament of fine gold is a wise rebuker to a listening ear.**
13 <gloss>o</gloss> **Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a faithful messenger to those who send him, for he refreshes the soul of his masters.**
14 **Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a false gift.**
15 **By long forbearance a ruler is persuaded, and a soft tongue breaks the bone.**
16 **If you have found honey, eat only as much as you need, lest you be filled with it and vomit it up.**
17 **Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor’s house, lest he become weary of you and hate you.**
18 **A man who bears false witness against his neighbor is like a war club, a sword, and a sharp arrow.**
19 <gloss>p</gloss> **Like a** <gloss>q</gloss> **broken tooth and a** <gloss>r</gloss> **foot out of joint is confidence in a faithless man in time of trouble.**
20 <gloss>s</gloss> **Like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, or like vinegar upon soda, so is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.**
21 **If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink.**

<meta>catchword: For</meta>

<column-break/>

v. 28. a) <note>original Latin: "testis gratis"</note> *A witness for no reason*, that is, a false witness who testifies against another without cause or foundation of truth; see Chapter 1:11 and 26:2. b) <note>original Latin: "numquid enim persuadebis..."</note> *For will you indeed persuade the judge of a falsehood with your lips?* This would certainly be a most unworthy deed. Regarding the word choice, compare Chapter 1:10.
v. 30. c) This and the following verses graphically depict the folly of laziness. Compare Chapter 6:6, 9, and following.
v. 31. d) *It had entirely grown up*; see Isaiah 5:6. *With thistles* (1) and *the surface was covered or hidden by nettles.* See Zephaniah 2:9.
v. 33. e) See Chapter 6:10, 11.

CHAPTER XXV, v. 1. f) These also, just like the previous ones in Chapter 24:23, are maxims or proverbs of Solomon. See Chapter 1:1 and 10:1. This begins the third part of the book. Compare the note at 1:1. g) <note>original Latin: "quas vero non ipse..."</note> *Proverbs which Solomon himself did not arrange in this book, but which they perhaps transferred here from his other writings, or transcribed into this book.* See Genesis 12:8, Chapter 26:22, Job 14:18, and Chapter 18:4. h) Compare 2 Chronicles 29–31.
v. 2. i) *It is the glory of God to hide a matter.* See 1 Samuel 20:2.
v. 3. k) *Just as the heaven cannot be searched for its height, so also the heart of kings.*
v. 8. l) <note>original Latin: "ne quid facias..."</note> *Lest you do something at the end of that lawsuit that will be less than beneficial or honorable for you.* The interrogative word here becomes indefinite, as in Chapter 9:13 and Job 13:13.
v. 10. m) *Lest he affect you with shame.* (1) Compare Chapter 14:34.
v. 11. n) <note>original Latin: "Vulg. in tempore suo..."</note> *The Vulgate translation says: 'in its own time,' or 'in its opportunities.'* (1)
v. 13. o) <note>original Latin: "Sicut tentio nivis..."</note> *Like the keeping of snow, that is, snow covered in pits and underground vaults.* (1)

---

**Scribal and Grammatical Notes:**
v. 30. The word *passed* <note>original: עברתי</note> is marked with a Kametz <note>a vowel mark</note> in manuscripts 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 23, contrary to the standard Masoretic text here and the Basel Index.
v. 31. *Thistles* <note>original: קמשונים</note> appears without a Dagesh <note>an emphasis dot</note> in manuscripts 1, 3, 21. v. 32. *And I beheld* <note>original: ואחזה</note> uses the <term>Rbhia</term> accent in manuscripts 6, 9, 10, 12, 13, 16, 19, 20, 23; this is a different construction of the first-person pronoun.
CHAPTER XXV, v. 1. *These* <note>original: אלה</note> is marked thus in 7, 11, 21, instead of the <term>Munach</term> accent in 3, 12, 20, 23. v. 8. *Lest* <note>original: פן</note> is marked with a <term>Makkaph</term> <note>a hyphen-like connector</note> in 1, 2. v. 10. *Lest* <note>original: פן</note> uses a Patach <note>short 'a' vowel</note> in 3, 7, 8, 11–16.
The <term>Tiphcha</term> accent appears early in 3, 6, 9, 10, 23, 24, and in the Berlin edition. Others place it on the tone syllable or use a <term>Munach</term>, which is less convenient.
v. 6. *Do not put yourself forward* <note>original: אל־תתהדר</note> uses an early <term>Tiphcha</term> in 3. v. 7. *Better* <note>original: טוב</note> uses a <term>Pikkadm</term> accent in 2. v. 7. *Than that you should be humbled* <note>original: מהשפילך</note> in 19, 21, 22. v. 11. *Its proper time* <note>original: אפניו</note> is marked with a Cholem vowel in 2, 3. v. 16. *And you vomit it* <note>original: והקאתו</note> features a silent Aleph in 2, 3, 7, 11, 21. v. 19. *Broken* <note>original: רעה</note> has a stress mark on the penultimate syllable in 24, doubtless from the Small Masora <note>marginal scribal notes</note>, which is actually in error here and should be corrected from the Large Masora notes on this passage and Genesis 29:9, Isaiah 24:19. Although the <term>Tiphcha</term> accent is placed before the first syllable here, it should mentally refer to the tone syllable suggested by the logic of the reading.

<column-break/>

(1)
v. 19. p) Just like a broken tooth, from the root *ra'a'* <note>meaning to be broken</note>. q) and a wavering foot, from the root *ma'ad*. r) is the confidence of a traitor, or confidence placed in a treacherous friend.

### Textual Apparatus
<note>This section provides a technical comparison of different manuscript versions of the Hebrew text.</note>

**Verse 26.** The word "in the assembly" (*be-kahal*) appears with a *Patah* vowel followed by a *Dagesh* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and in the margins of 6 and 9, which goes against the printed Masorah. — **Verse 27.** "he will fall" (*yipol*) is the correct reading. — **Verse 27.** The phrase "it will return to him" is marked with a *Maqqef* (hyphen) and *Meteg* (stress mark) in manuscripts 3, 7, 8, and 22. The word "pit" (*shahat*) appears without a *Dagesh* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, up to 22.

**Verse 28.** The word "his victims" (*dakkav*) is written in full (*plene*) in 7, 8, 15, and 22. Others use the shorter spelling. Regarding **Chapter 27, Verse 17**, some interpret it as "one sharpens": a man sharpens the face of his friend.

**Chapter 27, Verse 1.** "For you do not know what [the day] may bring forth." The word "you know" (*teda*) regularly appears with a *Patah* vowel. **Verse 7.** "hungry" (*re-evah*) appears with a *Mahpakh* accent in 3, 7, 8, and others. **Verse 12.** "the simple" (*petayim*) is spelled with a silent *Aleph* in some traditions. **Verse 15.** "on a rainy day" appears without a *Keri* (alternate reading) in 2 and 19. **Verse 22.** Notes on the "pestle" (*be-eli*) and the "mortar" (*ba-makhtesh*). **Verse 25.** Regarding the removal of hay or winter grass.

**1 The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are as bold as a young lion.**

CHAPTER XXVIII, v. 2. **and with a man [u-ve-adam]** correctly with the *Merca* accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 22, 24, and *Berlin*; whereas others irregularly have the *Tiphcha* tone. v. 6. **Better [tov]** with *Munach* in 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 16, 19, 20. v. 8. **he shall gather it [yiqbetsennu]** thus in the *Piel* form in 1, 2, 3, 17, 18, 22, 24, *Berlin*, and *Ben Asher*, as the Great Masora records; all others with *Ben Naphtali* read it as **yiqbetsenu** in the *Kal* form, according to the *Erfurt Masora* at this place, and as printed in the *Erfurt* edition of Jeremiah 31:10. v. 10. **into his pit [be-shachuto]** with the *Tiphcha* accent in manuscript 14. *Masora sin. f.* 33. col. 8. v. 11. **understanding [mevin]** with *Rebia-Geresh* and the preceding *Merca* in 2, and with a preceding *Maqqeph* [hyphen]. v. 17. **man [adam]** with an ordinary *Daleth* and without a special mark in 2, 3, 10, 13, 14, 15, 16, 20, 21, 23, contrary to the *Erfurt Masora* here and the printed edition of Leviticus 1:1. **ל** deficient in 1, 7, 8, 22 and so similarly in 2, according to *Masora 1, 2* and *Erfurt* here, and *Masora 1, 3* and *Erfurt* at Exodus 21:33, but against *Masora 4* and the printed edition there. The *Orientals* also mark it as deficient, but the *Westerners* [Palestinian tradition] mark it as full. v. 22. **hastens [nevehal]** with *Pashta* in 1, 2, 3 and in the margin of 6, 9. The letter **Beth** has a *Chateph-Qamets* with a preceding *Metheg*.

<column-break/>

v. 15. **lion [ari]** with *Munach* in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20. Furthermore, one manuscript writes **be-shachuto** but reads it as **be-shuchato** [into his pit] in 22, following example and warning. v. 17. **man [adam]**—manuscripts 7, 8, 10, 13, 19, 21 have a *Metheg* in addition. **and not [ve-lo]** with *Merca* in 3, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12. v. 23. **after me [acharay]** with *Tsere* in 7, 8, 10, 11 and *Ben Israel*. But 1 reads from **achareyhu** [after him] similarly in 4, he stirs up a quarrel (chapter 15:18). **He who rebukes a man afterward [mochiach adam acharay]**, with the word *Maqqeph* understood as being for the sacrifice.

# PROVERBS 28, 29 CHAPTERS 28. 29.

<margin>CHAPTER XXIX.</margin> **28 When the wicked rise up, people hide themselves; but when they perish, the righteous increase.**

**1 A man <margin>a) A man of rebukes, who is indeed often and seriously rebuked. <note>original Latin: "Vir correptionum, qui sæpe quidem ac ferio corripitur."</note></margin> who remains stiff-necked <margin>b) Then a man of sorrows, who suffers pains (Isaiah 53:3); and yet hardening his neck. (Chapter 28:14; Exodus 32:9).</margin> after many rebukes will suddenly be broken, and there is no healing.**

**2 When the righteous increase, <margin>c) Chapter 11:10; Chapter 28:12, 28.</margin> the people rejoice; but when a wicked man rules, <margin>d) When indeed the wicked reigns. cf. Psalm 12:9.</margin> the people groan. <margin>e) The people groan. Exodus 2:23.</margin>**

**3 A man who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but he who keeps company with prostitutes <margin>f) But he who feeds on harlots (Chapter 28:7) wastes his wealth (Chapter 5:9, 10).</margin> wastes his wealth.**

**4 A king establishes the land by justice, but a man of "contributions" <note>The Hebrew term *terumot* refers to heavy taxes or someone who accepts bribes/gifts to pervert justice.</note> tears it down.**

**5 A man <margin>g) Using flatteries toward his companion (Chapter 2:16; Chapter 11:9).</margin> who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for <margin>h) He spreads a net against his feet.</margin> his steps.**

**6 In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare, <margin>i) In the transgression of an evil man is a snare by which he himself will be captured; but the righteous shouts for joy and rejoices, having been snatched from the snare. *Iarun* (he shouts) follows the form of *Iachid* in Psalm 91:6.</margin> but the righteous shouts for joy and is glad.**

**7 The righteous man knows the cause of the poor; the wicked does not understand such knowledge.**

**8 Mockers <margin>k) Men of mockery—that is, mockers—ensnare the city (Isaiah 42:22; Hosea 5:1), but the wise turn away the wrath of God from the city (Ezra 10:14).</margin> set a city aflame, but the wise turn away anger.**

**9 If a wise man goes to court <margin>l) Whether he is moved to anger or laughs, no rest is given so that the fool might acquiesce to the words of the wise.</margin> with a foolish man, there is raging and laughing, and no rest.**

**10 Bloodthirsty men hate the blameless, <margin>m) They love the upright, and therefore seek to protect and preserve his soul (Psalm 142:5; Luke 17:33).</margin> but the upright seek his soul.**

**11 A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man keeps it back and stills it.**

**12 If a ruler listens to lies, all his officials will be wicked.**

**13 The poor man and the oppressor meet; the Lord gives light to the eyes of both.**

**14 If a king judges the poor with truth, his throne will be established forever.**

**15 The rod and rebuke give wisdom, but a neglected <note>original: *meshullach*, meaning a child left to his own devices.</note> youth brings shame to his mother.**

**16 When the wicked increase, transgression increases; but the righteous will see their fall.**

**17 Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delights to your soul.**

**18 Where there is no vision, <margin>n) Where there is no vision—that is, prophecy. Where the prophetic word does not flourish, is not explained, urged, and observed. cf. 1 Samuel 3:1; Hosea 12:11.</margin> the people are unrestrained; <margin>o) They are stripped, or the people become lawless in sinning (Exodus 32:25).</margin> but happy is he who keeps the law.**

**19 By words alone a servant is not disciplined; <margin>p) For he understands, indeed, what you say, and yet gives no answer (Chapter 16:4).</note> though he understands, there is no response.**

**20 Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him.**

**21 He who pampers his servant from youth will have him as a son in the end.**

**22 An angry man stirs up strife, and a hot-tempered man abounds in transgression.**

**23 A man's pride will bring him low, but the lowly in spirit will retain honor.**

**24 Whoever partners with a thief hates his own soul; he hears the curse, but discloses nothing.**

**25 The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the Lord is set on high.**

**26 Many seek the face of a ruler, but a man's justice comes from the Lord.**

**27 An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, and he who is upright in his way is an abomination to the wicked.**

### CRITICAL NOTES

CHAPTER XXIX, v. 2. **Groans** (יאנח): thus in the *Kal* <note>The simple active verb form in Hebrew.</note> according to manuscripts 1 and 3. v. 4. **Contributions** (תרומות): the Masorah <note>The tradition of the biblical text's correct spelling and accents.</note> requires a "defective" spelling (missing a letter) as in 2 Samuel 1:21, but this goes against the Masorah of this passage and the evidence of all our codices. v. 6. **In the transgression of a man** (בפשע איש): thus in 1, 3, 6, 9, 10, 12–20, and 23. Another distinction: "in the treachery of a man, the evil one is a snare." **Shouts for joy** (ירון): with a *Cholem* vowel in 1, 2, and 3. v. 13. **Gives light** (מאיר): thus in 3 and the Berlin manuscript. v. 14. **Neglected** (משלח): thus with a *Patah* <note>A short 'a' vowel mark.</note> in 1, 3, 10, 14, 20, and in the text of 6 and 9. v. 15. **Neglected** (משלח): thus with a *Revia* <note>A specific diamond-shaped musical accent mark.</note> in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, and 20. But most have a *Mahpach* <note>A 'V' shaped accent mark.</note>, which is less appropriate. v. 17. **He will give you rest** (יניחך): without a *Dagesh* <note>A dot indicating a strengthened consonant.</note> in 1, 2, 3, 10, 13, 14, 19, 21, and 22. v. 19. **He is disciplined** (יוסר): *milra* <note>Accented on the last syllable.</note> with a *Tsere* vowel in 1, 2, 3, and in the margins of 6 and 9. CHAPTER XXX, v. 1. **To Ithiel** (לאיתיאאל): thus in 1, 3, and Berlin. Others have only a *Munach* accent, for which 3 has a *Tipheha*. **And Ucal** (ואכל): with a *Dagesh* in 14, 17, 18, 21, 22, 24, and Berlin.

### PROVERBS CHAPTER 30.

<margin>
a) [Refers to] the knowledge of the holy ones, which is proper to the holy ones (Chapter 9:10). <note>original: "at cognitionem sanctorum, quæ sanctis propria est"</note> He was therefore not indeed a philosopher, but rather God-taught <note>Greek: "Theodidaktos"</note> (John 6:45). The prefix "and" [v] is adversative here, as in Psalm 3:8, 15:4, 26:11, etc.
v. 4. b) A second aphorism. cf. Deuteronomy 30:12; John 3:13. c) cf. Exodus 3:13. d) cf. Genesis 32:30; Judges 13:18; Isaiah 9:5; Psalm 2:7; Matthew 11:27; Philippians 2:9; Revelation 19:12. e) Because you ought to know this, if you wished to be found false. John 17:3.
v. 5. f) A third aphorism. cf. 2 Samuel 22:31; Psalm 12:7; etc.
v. 6. g) Therefore, do not add anything. Deuteronomy 4:2; Chapter 13:1.
v. 7. h) A fourth saying. He asked for two things, etc.
v. 8. i) Poverty (Chapter 6:11; 10:15). k) "Feed me indeed with the bread of my portion." <note>original Latin: "ciba me vero pane demensi mei"</note>
v. 9. l) Lest I lie against God and deny Him in my soul or by my deeds. m) And lest I be impoverished (Chapter 20:13), a thief compelled by want (see Chapter 6:30). n) And I might handle and violate the inviolable name of my God by denying the theft. Exodus 20:7.
v. 10. o) Do not slander. Psalm 101:5. A fifth aphorism.
v. 11. p) A sixth aphorism, presenting four detestable types of men (verses 11–14).
v. 15. q) A seventh aphorism, concerning four insatiable things. Just as the Leech <note>original Latin: "Hirudo" or "Sanguisuga"</note> has two daughters, improperly so called—namely, "Give, give!"—so there are three things that are not [satisfied], etc.
v. 17. r) An eighth oracle. s) And despises obedience (l). Genesis 49:10.
v. 18. t) A ninth aphorism, concerning four inscrutable things.
v. 19. u) And especially the way of a man with an untouched virgin (l). Genesis 24:43; Exodus 2:8; Isaiah 7:14; cf. Jeremiah 31:22.
v. 20. x) A tenth saying!
v. 21. y) An eleventh saying, regarding four intolerable things.
</margin>

4 [Agur says:] I have not learned wisdom, nor do I have knowledge of the Holy One. <sup>a</sup> Who has ascended to heaven <sup>b</sup> and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? <sup>c</sup> Who has wrapped up the waters <sup>d</sup> in a garment? Who has established 
5 all the ends of the earth? What is his name, <sup>e</sup> and what is his son’s name, if you know? 
6 Every word <sup>f</sup> of God is pure; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him. Do not add <sup>g</sup> 
7 to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar. 
Two things <sup>h</sup> I have asked of you; do not deny them to me before I die. Vanity <sup>i</sup> 
8 and lying words keep far from me; give me neither poverty nor riches; 
9 feed me <sup>k</sup> with the bread of my portion. Lest I be full <sup>l</sup> and deny you and say, "Who is 
the Lord?" Or lest I be poor <sup>m</sup> and steal and profane the name of my God. <sup>n</sup> 
10 Do not slander <sup>o</sup> a servant to his master, lest he curse you 
11 and you be found guilty. There is a generation <sup>p</sup> that curses its father and does not bless its mother. There is a 
12 generation that is pure in its own eyes, yet is not washed from its filthiness. There is a generation—how lofty are its eyes 
13 and its eyelids are lifted up! There is a generation whose teeth are swords and whose jaw-teeth 
14 are knives, to devour the poor from off the earth and the needy from among men. 
15 The leech has two daughters: "Give! Give!" <sup>q</sup> There are three things 
16 that are never satisfied, four that never say, "Enough!" Sheol and the barren womb, 
17 the earth that is not satisfied with water, and the fire that never says, "Enough!" The eye <sup>r</sup> that mocks <sup>s</sup> 
a father and scorns to obey a mother, the ravens of the valley will pick it out and the young 
18 eagles will eat it. Three things are too wonderful <sup>t</sup> for me, <sup>u</sup> 
19 and four I do not understand: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent 
20 on a rock, the way of a ship in the heart of the sea, and the way of a man with a young woman. <sup>x</sup> Such 
is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, "I have 
21 done no wrong." Under three things <sup>y</sup> the earth trembles, and under 
22 four it cannot bear up: under a servant when he reigns, and a fool 
23 when he is filled with food; under an unloved woman when she gets a husband, and a maidservant when 
24 she displaces her mistress. Four things on earth are small, 
25 yet they are exceedingly wise: The ants are a people not strong, yet they provide 
26 their food in the summer; the rock badgers are a people not mighty, yet they make their home 
in the cliffs.

---

**Verse 4.** "Who has ascended" [mi-alah] appears thus in manuscript 2. "In his fists" [be-chofnav] with the *Revia* accent in manuscript 2, and noted in the margins of 6 and 9. Furthermore, a *Pesiq* mark is added in 7, 8, 9, 13, 16, 19, 20, 21, and 22. **Verse 6.** "Do not add" [tosef] with a *Dagesh* in 2, 3, 14, 19; and similarly in manuscript 1 according to the note in the *Masora*. According to all accurate copies, the letter *He* is doubled. **Verse 9.** "Lest" [pen] appears with a *Maqqeph* [hyphen] in 1, 2, 3, 24, as is regular. However, regarding the *Mercha* accent, see the note on Psalm 35:10. "And you be found a liar" [ve-nichzavta] with a *Qamets* vowel in 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 21, 23, against manuscripts 1, 2, and the Erffurt and Basel editions. **Verse 15.** "Slowly" [at] is correctly marked with a *Mercha* in 7, 8, 14, 15, 24, and the Berlin edition. Most use a *Munach* accent: "at" with a *Maqqeph* in 2, 3, without a *Pesiq* in 2, 3, 17, 18, 24, against the Basel edition. But with a *Maqqeph* in 1, and conjunctively in 5. Marked with a *Pesiq* erroneously in 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 19, 21, 23. Furthermore, *Qamets* instead of *Patach* appears in 2, 10, 20, 21, and in the margins of 6 and 9. **Verse 16.** "Water" [mayim] without a *Dagesh* in 1, 3, 6, 7, 9, 11, 14, 20, 21. With a *Qamets* in 3, 17, 18 and the Berlin edition; so too in manuscript 2, against 1, 2 and the printed editions here and in Deuteronomy 8:7 and Psalm 66:12. **Verse 17.** "To obey" [likhat] without a *Dagesh* in 1, 3, 8, 10, 14, 17, 18, against the Erffurt and Masoretic editions. But "likhat" with a preceding *Tifcha* in 17, 18, 24 and the Berlin edition; though incorrectly with a tonic accent in 23. "The ravens... will pick it out" [yiqruha] requires a *Patach* according to the Erffurt and Basel editions, but all our manuscripts use a *Qamets*. **Verse 18.** "And four" [ve-arba'ah] thus without a note in 3. "And four" without a note in 11, 12, 15, 16, 19, against the Erffurt and Masoretic editions. **Verse 19.** "In the sky, the way of a serpent" regularly in 2. **Verse 20.** "Her mouth" [piha] without a *Dagesh* in 2, 3, 7, 8, 11, 15–18, 21, 24, and the margins of 6 and 9.

<margin>
**CHAPTER XXXI, verse 1.**
**o)** The words of Lemuel. This name means "consecrated to God," and refers to Solomon, who is the author of the book as a whole and was a king, compare Ecclesiastes 1:1. Here begins the fifth and final part of the book, namely the maternal instruction of Lemuel (verses 2-9) and the praise of the virtuous and industrious woman (verses 10-31). # THE BOOK OF JOB

->Hebrew<-
->Job<-

The Book of Job (a work of most ancient wisdom and history, to be placed in time closest to the Book of Genesis) does not only intend to teach that the justice of the Supreme Deity is not to be measured according to the rules of human law and justice, or to show the great weakness of men under temptation (in whom the power of God is nevertheless perfected). It also serves—through the narration of the sufferings of a most afflicted man and their eventually joyful conclusion—as a living image of the sufferings of our most holy Savior and the glory that followed them; that is, to prefigure the mystery of the cross. See the Preface to our notes on this book.

<margin>
**CHAPTER 1, verse 1.** **a)** He was indeed a great and illustrious man who truly existed, as seen in Judges 13:2, chapter 17:1, 1 Samuel 1:1; compare Ezekiel 14:14, 20, James 5:11; and he lived before the time of Moses. **b)** *In the land of Uz*; named for the firstborn son of Nahor, Genesis 22:21. His brother was Buz, from whom came *Elihu the Buzite*, Job 32:2. According to the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and the Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note>, this was in the region of Ausitis, a part of desert Arabia toward the Euphrates, between the Chaldeans and Sabeans; see verses 15 and 17 below, and also Jeremiah 25:20, Lamentations 4:21. **c)** The name Job itself: as if to say, "The enemy of the devil and of vices," comparing Genesis 3:15; or from the Arabic, "One who is earnestly turned toward God." **d)** verse 8, chapter 2:3, etc. This first chapter describes: I. The piety of Job and his happy state, verses 1–3. II. His care in sanctifying his children, verses 4–5. III. Nevertheless, he is accused of hypocrisy by Satan, verses 6–11. IV. God permits Satan power over all that belongs to Job, verse 12. V. Consequently, Job loses his children, oxen, sheep, camels, and servants in a single day, verses 12–19. VI. Job, though mourning these adversities, does not sin through impatience, but even praises God, verses 20–22.

**v. 3. e)** verse 10, Genesis 4:20, chapter 13:2, 7. **f)** Furthermore, his household staff, male and female servants. (2) Genesis 26:14. **g)** Referring to the eastern inhabitants of Arabia, Judges 6:3, 1 Kings 5:10, Jeremiah 49:18.

**v. 4. h)** In the house of the man whose appointed day it was for the feast.

**v. 5. i)** When the days of the feast had gone their round. **k)** He himself, as the father of the family and in the manner of the Patriarchs. **l)** "And they blessed..." <note>The Hebrew verb "to bless" is often used here as a euphemism for "to curse" or "to renounce."</note> see verse 11, chapter 2:5, 9, Genesis 47:10, 1 Kings 21:10, 13.

**v. 6. m)** The angels. chapter 38:7, Daniel 3:25, 28. **n)** That they might present themselves according to their duty before Jehovah. **o)** Satan also came impudently among them to accuse Job, verse 8.

**v. 7. p)** 1 Peter 5:8, Matthew 12:43.

**v. 10. q)** verse 3, Genesis 28:14, chapter 30:30, 42, 43.

**v. 13. r)** verse 4. **s)** that is, the feasts were continuing. verse 4, 18, Genesis 27:25, Esther 5:6, chapter 7:2.
</margin>

<note>This final section contains technical academic notes on minor variations found in different Hebrew manuscript sources (labeled 1, 2, 3, etc.) regarding vowel points and musical accents.</note>

Verse 15: The word *and I escaped* <note>original: וָאֶמָּלְטָה</note>. In verses 16, 17, and 19, and in 2 Chronicles 17:8, various sources (1, 2, 3, 4, 22) use the Metheg accent instead of the Kadma accent. Verse 19: The word *came* <note>original: בָּאָה</note> has the accent on the last syllable <note>original: milra</note> in sources 3, 4, 6, 9, 14, 20, 21, 22, 23. Verse 20: *his robe*—source 2 notes this in the margin but deleted the particle 'et' from the main text. Verse 21: *blessed be the name*—this is the reading in sources 1, 2, 3, 4. CHAPTER 2, verse 1: *There was a day*—the full spelling appears in sources 2, 7, 8, 15, 22, 24. Verse 3: *on the earth*—so it appears in source 1. <margin>CHAPTER 4. verse 1. h) See chapter 2:11. Eliphaz, being the first in age and experience, was the first to deliver a speech to Job. Later, he received God's censure on behalf of all the friends in chapter 42:7. He responds in this and the next chapter with four goals: 1. To rebuke Job’s impatience (verses 2–6). 2. To correct Job's supposedly false opinion that he is just and God is unjust in punishing him (verse 17). He tries to prove that God afflicts only the guilty through: 1) historical evidence (verses 7–11), 2) a nocturnal vision (verses 12–21), 3) the consensus of holy men (chapter 5:1–2), and 4) his own experience (chapter 5:3–7). 3. He invites Job to hope in God's mercy rather than his own righteousness (chapter 5:8–15). 4. He promises liberation from evils if Job admits he sinned against God (chapter 5:16–27).</margin>

<meta>This section contains detailed scholarly notes on the Hebrew text, focusing on "vocalization" (vowel points) and "accents" (musical/grammatical marks) found in various historical manuscripts (represented by numbers like 3, 4, 7, etc.). The translator is comparing different traditions to establish the most accurate reading.</meta>

verse 16. <note>original: "ראו" (they saw)</note> Thus with the *Merkha* accent in manuscripts 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, 15, 16, 24, and the Berlin edition. Almost all others use the *Munach* accent, which is faulty.
verse 18. <note>original: "שאננו" (they are at rest)</note> with a *Qamets* vowel in 3, 7, 14, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, the Berlin edition, and (in the text) 6 and 9. 
verse 25. <note>original: "יבא" (it comes)</note> According to Mercator and the *Merkha* accent in 6, 9, 14, 20, 21, 22. 
verse 26. <note>original: "נחתי" (I was quiet)</note> according to the *Revia Geresh* accent in the Berlin edition alone. But according to Mercator, the *Merkha* and *Milra* (stress on the last syllable) in 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 22, 24, and Ben Asher. Others place the stress differently.
**CHAPTER IV.**
verse 1. <note>original: "התימני" (the Temanite)</note> Stress on the last syllable (*Milra*) in 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 24. Others use the *Geresh* accent. See the note on Psalm 4:1. 
<note>original: "ויאמר" (and he said)</note> Thus with the stress on the last syllable in 15, 17, 18, 22. See the note on chapter 3:1. Most use the final stress.
verse 2. <note>original: "יעצר" (he will withhold)</note> with the *Chateph Patach* vowel in 1, 3, 6, 9, 14, 20, 21, 23.
verse 7. <note>original: "מי" (who)</note> with a *Maqqeph* (hyphen) in 2, 3, 6, 9, 14, 20, 21, 22, and the Berlin edition. Others use the *Mahpakh* accent. 
<note>original: "הוא" (he)</note> with an earlier *Tifcha* accent.
<note>original: "ושרים" (and the upright)</note> with the companion accent in 3 and 4.

verse 16. <note>original: "דממה" (silence)</note> with the *Revia Geresh* accent. In truth, the *Merkha* accent should follow instead of *Munach*, which is found in 1 and 3. However, it is better for these two nouns to be joined because of the prefixing of the *Vav* conjunction. 
verse 17. <note>original: "יטהר" (he shall be pure)</note> with a *Maqqeph* in 2, 3, 4, 22.

**CHAPTER V, verse 1.** *a)* **Call forth** now, for a dispute or <term>testimony</term> of your cause, whomever you wish. See the **note at chapter 4, 1. b)** *to which of the holy ones will you turn*, whose example or testimony could you produce to the contrary? This is an <term>effective interrogation</term> implying a "no," as in 1 Samuel 6:20.

**v. 2. c)** For **wrath** kills the **foolish man** who contends against God; *the zeal of madness, or even God's own zeal, slays such an insane and fatuous person.*

**v. 5. d)** *The hungry shall consume the harvest of that fool, and even what he gathers from among the thorns, he will take away; and the robber shall greedily swallow up their wealth and resources.*

**v. 6. e)** *For it does not constantly or widely go forth,* etc.

**v. 7. f)** *Because man is born to labor and depravity after the Fall, just as the sons of a rapid throw—that is, arrows vibrated with force—fly high.* <note>The commentator interprets "sons of Reshef" as arrows rather than sparks.</note>

**v. 8. g)** *But truly indeed (chapter 8, 11). Here I will now send, and seeking, I will turn myself to God.* See also 8:19; 9:12; 11:10.

**v. 13. h)** See **1 Corinthians 3:19.** <note>This New Testament verse quotes Job 5:13: "He catches the wise in their craftiness."</note>

**v. 16. i)** *Therefore, hope in God the deliverer overflows for the wretched; provided that he is truly pious and does not murmur against God.* **k)** *But wicked iniquity, which stupidly accuses God himself,* is <term>contracted</term> as in Psalm 58:3 and 64:7, instead of <term>unrighteousness</term> <note>original: "Aulatha"</note> in Psalm 92:16. **l)** it *shuts* its mouth. Psalm 107:42.

**v. 17. m)** *Urging towards application.* See verse 27. **n)** Compare **Proverbs 3:11-12.**

**v. 18. o)** He afflicts with pain; the Vulgate says *he wounds and he heals.* See Hosea 6:1; Psalm 147:3. p) *they heal.* 1 Samuel 2:6; Jeremiah 31:9; compared with Lamentations 3:31–33.

**v. 26. q)** in extreme old age. <term>r)</term> c-

<meta>This page continues Job’s response to Eliphaz the Temanite in Chapter 6 and begins Chapter 7. On the previous page, Job began to justify his bitter complaint, comparing his suffering to a heavy weight that outweighs the sand of the sea. Here, he continues to describe his spiritual and physical agony before turning to a more general reflection on the misery of human existence.</meta>

a) they absorb or have absorbed, namely that sickness and calamity of mine from verse 2.

v. 14. m) To one who is wasting away, grace or charity is otherwise shown by his friend; but now he [the friend] omits the fear of God, while he exists toward the wretched man not as kind, but as injurious.
CHAPTER VII, v. 1. n) Is there not a hard service <note>original: "militia," often translated as "warfare" or "appointed time"</note> for wretched and troubled man? Here Job continues his response begun in Chapter VI, and begins to defend the sentiment of his first speech; first, under a persona in verses 1 and 2; and then openly in the first person in verses 3–6, he describes his most afflicted state; secondly (II), he proposes this to God in verses 7–10; and finally reproaches God with reasons that seem just to him in verse 11: 1) That he did not deserve such bitter things, verses 12–16. 2) even if he had deserved them, God should rather forgive, verses 17–21.

### Philological and Accentual Notes
<note>This section contains technical discussions about the Hebrew text's accents, vowels, and manuscript variants.</note>

v. 5. **הֲיִנְהַק** [does it bray?] according to the Maqqef [connecting line] in 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, 15. v. 8. **שֶׁאֱלָתִי** [my petition] thus with the *Tsere* vowel in 1, 4, and in the margin. v. 10. **וַאֲסַלְּדָה** [and I would harden] with the Rebia accent alone in 2, 4. v. 13. **וְתוּשִׁיָּה** [and wisdom] accented on the second to last syllable [milel] in 1, 2, 4. v. 14. **לַמָּס** [to the one wasting away] with the Marca accent on the last syllable [milra] in 6, 9 according to Masorah I and Erff. v. 23. a) *When the scourge, that is, a heavy plague sent by God (as in Isaiah 28:15), suddenly and without distinction kills both the godly and the ungodly, God—as if in mockery—seems to disregard the trials of the innocent.*

Ch. 10:20.

CHAPTER X, v. 1. m) *Now indeed, because that vow of mine is in vain (Ch. 9:34), my soul is weary of my life, which seems preserved only for my punishment and misery. Job certainly continues in this chapter his complaints begun in Chapter 9:25, and (I) asks God not to treat him as a wicked man (v. 1-2), and (II) gives the reasons for his petition: 1) that he is not wicked, which would make his treatment seem unjust (v. 3-6); indeed 3) cruel (v. 7-8); and 4) unmindful of past benefits (v. 9-13); and 5) more rigid than is fair (v. 14-19); and 6) this toward a man who is fragile (v. 9), miserable (v. 15, 18, 19), and of the shortest life (v. 20-21).*

### CHAPTER XI.

^1^ Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: ^2^ "Should a multitude of words go unanswered? And should a man full of talk be vindicated? ^3^ Should your empty babble make men keep silent? And when you mock, shall no one shame you? ^4^ For you have said, 'My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in your eyes.' ^5^ But oh, that God would speak, and open His lips against you; ^6^ and that He would show you the secrets of wisdom! For true wisdom has two sides. Know therefore that God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves. ^7^ Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty? ^8^ It is higher than heaven—what can you do? Deeper than Sheol <note>the underworld or place of the dead</note>—what can you know? ^9^ Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea. ^10^ If He passes by and imprisons, and calls to judgment, who can hinder Him? ^11^ For He knows worthless men; when He sees iniquity, will He not consider it? ^12^ But a stupid man will get understanding when a wild donkey’s colt is born a human. ^13^ If you prepare your heart, and stretch out your hands toward Him; ^14^ if iniquity is in your hand, put it far away, and let not injustice dwell in your tents. ^15^ Then surely you could lift up your face without spot; you would be steadfast and not fear. ^16^ For you would forget your misery, and remember it as waters that have passed away. ^17^ And your life would be brighter than the noonday; its darkness would be like the morning. ^18^ And you would be secure, because there is hope; you would look around and take your rest in safety. ^19^ You would lie down, and none would make you afraid; many would court your favor. ^20^ But the eyes of the wicked will fail, and they shall have no way to escape; and their hope shall be the breathing out of their last."

**CHAPTER XIII**, v. 1. *p)* Behold, my eye has seen all these things.
This chapter contains Part I: the second part of Job’s speech to Zophar, which is a rebuke of him and his associates. This includes: 1) The Introduction (v. 1–3); 2) The Arguments (v. 4–12); 3) The Conclusion (v. 13–16). Part II: the third part, which is Job’s colloquy with God. In this: 1) The introduction (v. 17); 2) The thesis (v. 18); 3) The confirmation by arguments: (Aleph ℵ) that he has no grave sins against his conscience (v. 19–23); (Bet ב) that he is being treated most severely for sins of infirmity, more harshly than is fair (v. 24–28).

**Critical Notes on the Text:**
v. 15. The word "Behold" (Hen) according to Munster editions 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 13, 19, 21. The word "not" (Lo) at the end according to the Keri in 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 16, 19, 20. But "not" (Lo) in the text without the note for "to him" (Vav). Both are against the Masora here and especially in Leviticus 11:21. The word "Only" (Ach) follows... explaining verses 1–3, Mercerus 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 19, 20. v. 21. The word "Keep far" (Harchak) with a Kamets vowel in 3, 4. But with a Tseri vowel in 2, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 23. against which 1) no one... Masora 1, 2, and Erfurt editions, also M.I. and the Basel Index. v. 21. "and your dread" (v'emat-cha) is deficient in 1, 3, 4, 22, 24 according to the Masora... and especially chapter 9:34. Others have it in full. "Make me afraid" (teva'atani) with a Kamets in 3, 4, 6, 9, 13, 19, 20, 23. But... without a Dagesh in 1, 11, 13, 19, 20. Both against the Masora and Erfurt. v. 24. "Why your face" (lamma panecha) thus in 1, 2, 3. Milra <note>accent on the last syllable</note> in 9, 10, 14, 15, 20, 23. CHAPTER XIV, v. 1. "and full of" (usva) according to Mercerus 1, 3. v. 2. "like a flower he comes forth" (ke-tsits yatsa). II. His speech... "for an enemy" (le-oyev) is deficient in 2, 3, 4, 6, 11, 13, 19, 20, 21, 22 according to the Masora, especially Erfurt; likewise "consumed it" (achalo) in verse 28. prayers to God, Masora 3 and printed versions. v. 3. "your eyes" (einecha) deficient in 3, 4, 6, 11, 13, 19, 20, 21, 22 according to the Masora and Erfurt. v. 12. "he shall plow" (?) ... "out of an unclean" (mitame) with the accent Rebia-Geresh in 4, 14 and Berlin edition of Deut 15:18. and their reasons concluding in v. 13-22. "nor awake" (ve-lo yuro) with a Makkef <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 11. v. 13. "you would appoint" (tashit) with a Mercas accent (instead of Metheg) in 6, 9, 10. v. 20. "you would appoint me a set time" (tashit li chok) thus regularly in 3. Moreover, Gerber and Rebia-Geresh accents are found in 1, 2.

### CRITICAL NOTES ON VARIANTS

V. 28. **He dwells**: according to several manuscripts (6, 9, 10, etc.). **Houses not inhabited**: defective in others (1, 3, 4). **Destined**: with a specialized accent mark (*Metheg*) in some, but defective in others. V. 30. **His shoots**: with *Metheg* in manuscripts 1, 17, 18. V. 31. **In vanity**: the *Keri* (marginal correction) reads "in vanity" in certain books. V. 32. **It shall be fulfilled**: marked with a specific grammatical sign (*Rubigaresch*).

CHAPTER XVI, v. 1. **Job answered**: uses an ancient accent (*Tiphcha*) in most manuscripts. **Job**: with *Metheg*. **And said**: pronounced with the stress on the penultimate syllable (*milel*) in several versions. v. 4. **I also**: nay, as if he were an enemy. v. 5. **I would strengthen you**: with *Metheg* in manuscripts 17, 18, 22. v. 8. **He has risen**: connected with a dash (*Makkaph*) in manuscripts 4, 6, 9, etc. **My leanness**: spelled with a short vowel (*Chateph-patach*) in many sources. v. 11. **To the ungodly**: marked with a specific musical note (*Munach*) in several codices. v. 14. **Breach**: written with a small letter *Tsade* according to the Masorah. v. 16. **Reddened**: spelled with a short vowel. v. 19. **Witness**: Job uses the word for "witness" twice, once in Hebrew (*Edi*) and once using an Aramaic form (*Sahadi*).

**[Critical Apparatus - Philological Notes]**

v. 21. **And he might plead for a man**: So in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4. **And a son of man**: with the *Merca* accent in 4, 7, 8, 11, 24 and Berlin. Others use *Rbhia-geresch*.
### CHAPTER XVII.
v. 1. **extinguished**: with a simple *Rbhia* accent in manuscript 24. See note on Psalm 41:1. But with an *Atnach* preceded by a *Munach* in 1.
v. 2. **mockers**: thus with a *Tiphecha* in 1 and 24, and with a *Munach* in 7, 8, 12, etc. Others have only a *Munach*, which is irregular. Furthermore, with a *Dagesh* (dot) in the letter Lamed in 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, etc. **their provocation**: without a *Dagesh* in 1, 2, 4, 6, etc., against the Masorah.
v. 7. **my members**: using the letter *Samech* instead of *Sin* in 6, 9, 10, 14, 20.
v. 9. **clean**: thus with a *Chateph-qametz* vowel in 2, 6, 9, 10, etc.
v. 10. **and come**: some have "they shall come," with the *Kri* (the traditional reading) being "and come" in 7, 8 and Eastern traditions.
v. 11. **my purposes**: written defectively (shorter spelling) in 1, 2, 3, 4, etc. Others use the full spelling.
### CHAPTER XVIII.
v. 1. **the Shuhite**: with the *Rbhia-geresch* accent. **and said**: with a simple *Rbhia*.
v. 4. **from its place**: shorter spelling in 3, 30, etc.
v. 11. **and drive him**: spelled fully in 1, 2, 4, 22. Most others use the shorter spelling.
v. 13. To the Eastern traditions is attributed the written form (*Cthib*) **his limbs**.
v. 14. **and it shall bring him**: shorter spelling in 1, 2, 3, 5, etc., according to the Masorah.

### CHAPTER XIX.

v. 1. *b) Job answers Bildad and his companions together: I. through a just reproach: in which there is 1) a complaint about the wrongs inflicted on him, as if he were a hypocrite (v. 2); 2) his complaint of justice (v. 3); and 3) a desired end to the wrongs (v. 2). II. through a solid refutation of their objection: where 1) the companions' objection (v. 4) and its 2) refutation is made 1) by arguing from concession and denying the consequence for various reasons (v. 4-22). II) By contradicting them, showing he has not erred: which he proves through his issued noble confession (v. 23-27). and so III) concludes with a grave warning (v. 28, 29).*
</margin>

**Scholarly Notes on Accents and Variants:**
v. 18. *and from the world* with the accent Rebia-Geresh in manuscripts 1, 2, 3 and in the margin of 6 and 9. But *and from the world* appears in 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, and 20. *They shall banish him* without the emphasis mark (Dagesh) in 7, 11, 12, 23. v. 20. *horror* spelled with the letter Shin in 7, 8, 10, 14, and 29. (Neither point used in 13, 19). v. 21. *and this is the place of him who does not know [God]* also in manuscript 2. The Tiphcha accent is also found in 4. But *place* is marked with Pesik-Mahpach in 3, 6, 9, 13, 14, 19, and 20; and by Mahpach alone in 10. Others use Munach. Similarly *does not know* uses the Mercat accent irregularly in all others including 5, and in the margin of 9, except for one Berlin manuscript which has a double Makkaph. CHAPTER XIX. v. 1. *Job* with Rebia-Geresh in 2, 4, 14, and Berlin. *and he said* (vomer) accented on the first syllable in 15, 17, 18, 22, 24... v. 2. *and you break me*—this spelling with a silent Aleph is required by the Erfurt and M. 1 manuscripts... the first Nun is doubled with a Dagesh in 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 16. v. 7. *I am answered* with Segol in 7, 8. v. 13. *he put far away* accented on the first syllable in 2, 3, 6, 9, 11-14, 16, 19, 21, 22. v. 14. *my kinsfolk*—the spelling is deficient in most manuscripts... v. 23. *they may be engraved* with a Dagesh in 3, 6, 9, 16, contrary to manuscript M. I.

CHAPTER XX. v. 1. e) In this second speech of Zophar, compared with chapter 11:1, we note: I. The introduction with reasons why he cannot remain silent (v. 2). II. The proposition (v. 3) which is somewhat obscured. III. The confirmation through various but very abundant reasons, as if Job were being punished as a hypocrite or a wicked man (v. 4–28). IV. v. 2. f) My thoughts (see chapter 4:13) bring me back or cause me to respond: and that is because of my haste, i.e., the urgent dictate of my conscience within me.

# JOB. CHAPTERS 20. 21.

<margin>
**CHAPTER XXI, verse 1.**
**a)** In this response by Job, the following points should be observed:
**I. The Opening**, designed to gain the listeners' attention, verses 2–6.
**II. The Thesis and its explanation**, arguing that God deals with the wicked in this life in two different ways: 1) some are dismissed here without punishment, verses 7–15; 2) others are indeed punished in this life, verses 16–22.
**III. Confirmation of both classes:** 1) concerning the former, verses 23–24; 2) concerning the latter, verses 25–26.
**IV. Handling an objection**, verses 27–33.
**V. Conclusion**, verse 34.

**v. 4. b)** Is my complaint <note>original: *meditatio & querela*</note> concerning man, according to human reason? See Chapter 23, 2.
**c)** Why then should my spirit not be shortened <note>meaning: impatient or exhausted</note>, while I am afflicted by God in such dreadful ways and provoked by you with such unworthy arguments?

**v. 5. d)** And be astonished at my fate—the fate of a righteous man. See Ezekiel 3, 15.

**v. 6. e)** For as often as I remember or recall to mind that terrible judgment of God, I am immediately troubled; and my flesh takes hold of horror. See Isaiah 21, 4.

**v. 10. f)** His ox breeds and does not fail; his cow calves and does not miscarry.

**v. 11. g)** With great fertility, they send out their little ones like a flock. See Chapter 19, 18.

**v. 12. h)** They lift up their voice and jubilation with the tambourine and lyre, and rejoice with a cheerful heart at the sound of the musical instrument—the pipes. See Chapter 30, 31.

**v. 19. i)** His iniquity. See Chapter 29, 10.

**v. 20. k)** His ruin and destruction.

**v. 23. l)** One dies in full strength—referring to those in verses 7–15. This is the division, compared with verse 25. See 1 Kings 21, 20.

**v. 25. m)** But another dies in bitterness of soul—referring to those in verses 16–22.

**v. 28. n)** As if to say: What difference then remains between the righteous and the wicked? To this doubt, he responds in verse 29.

**v. 31. o)** Who among his inner circle dares to declare his wicked way and his perverse character to his face?
</margin>

29 This is the portion of a wicked man from God, and the heritage appointed to him by God.

<meta>This page continues Job's response to Eliphaz the Temanite. In the previous chapter, Eliphaz accused Job of specific social sins and urged him to repent to find peace. Now, in Chapter 23, Job bypasses his friends entirely to address his longing for a direct trial before God’s throne, while Chapter 24 explores the disturbing reality of social injustice that seems to go unpunished.</meta>

# JOB CHAPTERS 23 & 24

<margin>
CHAPTER XXIII, verse 1.
a) In this response of Job, which will be finished in the following chapter 24, the following points are observed: I. The opening, regarding the unjust condemnation of himself and his speeches, verse 2. II. An appeal to the tribunal of God, verses 3–7. III. A refutation of the objection: "If Job is righteous, why then is he afflicted by God?" He responds: 1) that this very mystery is what he complains about, verses 8–9. Meanwhile, 2) he is certain of his innocence before God, verses 10–12. 3) This suffering pertains to the absolute freedom of God, verse 13, which he illustrates by his own example, verses 14–17.
</margin>

<margin>CHAPTER XXIII.</margin>
1. Then Job answered and said:
<margin>2</margin> Even today is my complaint bitter: <note>original: "mori"</note> my hand is heavy upon my groaning.
<margin>3</margin> Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat!
<margin>4</margin> I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments.
<margin>5</margin> I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say to me.
<margin>6</margin> Will he plead against me with his great power? No; but he would put strength in me.
<margin>7</margin> There the righteous might dispute with him; so should I be delivered for ever from my judge.
<margin>8</margin> Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him:
<margin>9</margin> On the left hand, where he works, but I cannot behold him: he hides himself on the right hand, that I cannot see him:
<margin>10</margin> But he knows the way that I take: when he has tried me, I shall come forth as gold. <margin>accented on the penultimate syllable</margin>
<margin>11</margin> My foot has held his steps, his way have I kept, and not declined.
<margin>12</margin> Neither have I gone back from the commandment of his lips; I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my necessary food.
<margin>13</margin> But he is in one mind, and who can turn him? and what his soul desires, even that he does.
<margin>14</margin> For he performs the thing that is appointed for me: and many such things are with him.
<margin>15</margin> Therefore am I troubled at his presence: when I consider, I am afraid of him.
<margin>16</margin> For God makes my heart soft, and the Almighty troubles me:
<margin>17</margin> Because I was not cut off before the darkness, neither has he covered the darkness from my face.

---

<margin>
v. 2. b) at his seat or his prepared throne (3) Ezekiel 43:11.
v. 6. c) For would he contend with me with a multitude of strength, or with his infinite power, to which I am by no means equal? I certainly do not think so. Or does he not himself put in me whatever strength or power is in me?
v. 13. d) But he himself is in one <note>meaning: truly one alone</note>, nor does he have an equal or superior to whom he is bound to give an account. Of truth, as in Proverbs 3:26, Isaiah 40:10, 18; see the notes there.
v. 17. e) so that he might have hidden the gloom from my face.
CHAPTER XXIV, verse 1. f) Why indeed are calamitous times not hidden from the Almighty, so that those who know him do not see and experience his sad days, which he brings upon men? Since Job in chapter 23:15–16 mentioned his troubled thoughts, he explains them here at greater length: I. Why does God send calamities to the pious, but allow the wicked to commit their crimes as if with impunity? verses 2–12. Yet these wicked people II. sin maliciously and against conscience, verses 13–17. While other wicked people are taken away by divine judgment, verses 18–24. From which III. a conclusion full of confidence is added, verse 25.
v. 6. g) They gather not only for the vintage, but are even forced to glean the leftover grapes. (1) see the name in Amos 7:1.
</margin>

<margin>CHAPTER XXIV.</margin>
1. Why, seeing times are not hidden from the Almighty, do they that know him not see his days? <margin>Note on the word "those who know him": the traditional reading is "his acquaintances"</margin>
<margin>2</margin> Some remove the landmarks; they violently take away flocks, and feed them.
<margin>3</margin> They drive away the donkey of the fatherless, they take the widow’s ox for a pledge.
<margin>4</margin> They turn the needy out of the way: the poor of the earth hide themselves together.
<margin>5</margin> Behold, as wild donkeys in the desert, they go forth to their work; rising early for prey: the wilderness yields food for them and for their children.
<margin>6</margin> They reap their fodder in the field: and they glean the vintage of the wicked. <margin>Note: the traditional reading is "they reap"</margin>
<margin>7</margin> They cause the naked to lodge without clothing, so that they have no covering in the cold.
<margin>8</margin> They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter.
<margin>9</margin> They pluck the fatherless from the breast, and take a pledge from the poor.
<margin>10</margin> They cause him to go naked without clothing, and they take away the sheaf from the hungry;
<margin>11</margin> Who make oil within their walls, and tread their winepresses, and yet suffer thirst.
<margin>12</margin> Men groan from out of the city, and the soul of the wounded cries out: yet God does not charge them with folly.
<margin>13</margin> They are of those that rebel against the light; they know not its ways, nor abide in its paths.
<margin>14</margin> The murderer rising with the light kills the poor and needy, and in the night is as a thief.
<margin>15</margin> The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, "No eye shall see me," and disguises his face.

->**Textual and Masoretic Notes**<-
<note>The following notes contain technical details regarding the Hebrew accents and spelling variants found in specific manuscripts, numbered 1 through 24.</note>

**CHAPTER XXIII**, verse 1. **Job** is written with the *Revia Mugrash* accent. 2. 3. 4. and the Berlin edition. **And he said** is accented on the penultimate syllable in manuscripts 15, 17, 18, 22, 24. verse 8. **Forward** is marked thus by the *Munach* accent in 2, 4, 7, 8, 15. Others awkwardly use the *Tipcha* accent. verse 9. **Left hand** is written defectively <note>without the letter 'Vav'</note> in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 14, 15, 16, 20, 23. verse 12. For **mouth**, manuscripts 1, 3, 4, 9 have **his mouth**; <note>Latin note</note>: "I have hidden the words of my mouth from my own decree; I have imposed a law of silence upon myself." verse 14. **And many such things** uses the *Revia Mugrash* accent with a following *Merca* accent in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20.

**CHAPTER XXIV**, verse 2. **Landmarks** <note>Hebrew: Gebulot</note> is written thus in 1, 2, 6, 9, 22. Some Masoretic notes for Psalm 74:17 mark this as "large letters," as the small version here would be considered a mistake. Most write it with the full spelling <note>Gebulot with a 'Vav'</note>. verse 4. **Needy** is written defectively in 1, 2, 7, 8, 15, 17, 18, 22, 24, as well as in the Erfurt manuscript and Psalm 140:13. Others use the full spelling. **And they know** is written this way in 1, 7, 8, 13, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 24 and the Berlin edition, contrary to the printed Masora for Amos 8:4. verse 8. **From the shower** uses the *Munach* accent in 2 and 4, which is more convenient than our version. verse 9. **They pluck** uses the *Tipcha* accent in a different construction in 2 and 3, which matches the Greek Septuagint and the Aramaic Targum: *they snatch the orphan from the breast*. verse 10. For **without**, manuscripts 2, 6, and 9 have **from without** in the margin. **They take away** is marked by the *Munach* accent in 2, 7, 8, 10, 14, 15, 21, 22 and the Berlin edition. Others use the *Makkaph* or *Merca* accent, which is considered incorrect. verse 14. **At the light** is written without the *Pesiq* mark in 1, 2, 3, 4, 15. verse 15. **Twilight** uses the *Munach* accent in 4, 7, 8, 15, 17, 18, 22, 23, 24. However, the Berlin edition and others use the *Revia* accent.

<summary>Job expresses a desperate desire to present his case before God's throne, confident of his innocence but terrified by God's absolute sovereignty. He then lists the various crimes of the wicked—oppressing the poor, the orphan, and the widow—and questions why God remains silent in the face of such blatant injustice.</summary>

In the previous chapters, Job struggled with God’s apparent silence; here, he reflects on the hiddenness of divine wisdom and contrasts his current misery with his former glory.</meta>

# JOB. CHAPTERS 29 & 30.

<margin>
a) *and as a turban or a diadem.* <note>original: "ac cidarim vel diadema"</note> See Isaiah 62:3, Zechariah 3:5.
verse 15. b) *I was eyes, or in the place of eyes* <note>original: "Oculi vel oculorum vice fui"</note> for the blind. See Numbers 10:31; regarding the blind, compare Leviticus 19:14, Deuteronomy 27:18.
verse 16. c) *and the dispute,* that is, *the cause of the one whom I did not know, I investigated.*
verse 18. d) *From where I also said and thought to myself.* <note>original: "Vnde etiam dixi & mecum cogitaui"</note> Psalm 30:7.
verse 20. e) *it flourished, and from time to time received new strength.* <note>original: "vigebat, & nouas subinde vires accipiebat"</note> Job 14:7, Isaiah 40:31.
verse 21. f) *They listened to me speaking, and awaited my opinion: and they were silent, as many were,* <note>original: "quasi multi"</note> *for my counsel.* See Exodus 15:16.
verse 22. g) *they did not repeat my words.* The Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> says: *They dared to add nothing to my words.*
verse 24. h) *they did not, or scarcely believed it, nor did they take confidence or audacity for themselves on that account.* See Genesis 45:26.
CHAPTER XXX, verse 1. i) *But now, with the turn of events completely changed, they mock me. After having described his former happiness in Chapter 29, he now deplores his present misery, and raises a complaint partly against men (verses 2-10) and partly against God (verses 11-23). II. He removes all blame from himself regarding:* 1) *lack of mercy toward the afflicted (verses 24 and following).* 2) *unchastity, etc. (Chapter 31:1 and following).*
verse 2. k) *Even the force and strength of their hands, of what use would it have been to me, since in those whose strength was lost, old age was ruined.*
verse 3. l) *Because of want and hunger, their old age was hard and miserable (verse 2), or each of them was solitary and miserable.* Job 3:7, 15:34. m) *they were forced to flee* (l) *into the arid wilderness.* Job 24:19. n) *where the passing night was always waste and desolation for them.* Job 38:27.
verse 4. o) *Where in extreme poverty they plucked salt-herbs,* others say *mallows, with the brushwood; and the root of broom-trees was their food.*
verse 5. p) *When they were expelled from among other men, they cried out against them as against a thief.*
</margin>

14 **I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; my justice was like a robe and a turban.** ^a
15 **I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame.** ^b
16 **I was a father to the needy, and the cause of the stranger I investigated.** ^c
17 **I broke the fangs of the unrighteous and plucked the prey from his teeth.**
18 **I thought, "I shall die in my nest, and multiply my days like the sand."** ^d <note>Some early commentators interpreted "sand" here as the "Phoenix," the mythical bird that renews itself.</note>
19 **My root reached to the waters, and the dew lay all night on my branch.**
20 **My glory was ever new with me, and my bow was renewed in my hand.** ^e
21 **Men listened to me and waited, and kept silence for my counsel.** ^f
22 **After my words they did not speak again, and my speech dropped upon them.** ^g
23 **They waited for me as for the rain, and opened their mouths as for the spring rain.**
24 **I smiled on them when they had no confidence, and the light of my face they did not cast down.** ^h
25 **I chose their way and sat as chief; I dwelt like a king among his troops, like one who comforts mourners.**

<margin>CHAPTER XXX.</margin>

1 **But now they mock me, men younger than I, whose fathers I would have disdained to put with the dogs of my flock.** ^i
2 **Indeed, of what use to me was the strength of their hands? Their vigor had perished.** ^k
3 **Gaunt with want and famine, they gnaw the dry ground in the gloom of waste and desolation.** ^l ^m ^n
4 **They pluck salt-herbs by the bushes, and the root of the broom-tree is their food.** ^o
5 **They are driven from human society; people shout after them as after a thief.** ^p
6 **In the gullies of the wadis they must dwell, in holes of the earth and the rocks.**
7 **Among the bushes they bray; under the nettles they huddle together.**
8 **A brood of fools, nameless people, they have been beaten out of the land.**

# JOB CHAPTERS 30 AND 31

<margin>verse 21. a) You have changed into a cruel one against me: and by the strength of your hand the enemy tears me away, or perhaps, you strike me out of hatred.</margin>
You have turned into a cruel one toward me; with the strength of your hand, you persecute me.
<margin>verse 22. b) You melt, or you dissolve me, as to my substance, or entirely.</margin>
You lift me up to the wind and make me ride it; you dissolve my very being.
<margin>*Tushiyah* <note>The Hebrew word for "substance" or "wisdom"</note> is the *Kere* <note>The traditional reading of the text, as opposed to how it is written</note>.</margin>
<margin>verse 23.</margin>
For I know that You will bring me to death, to the house appointed for all the living.
<margin>verse 24. c) Truly, let God stretch out His hand against me without my prayer of plea, if in His destruction of them, there was any cry against me by the merciful or the calamitous—be they men or women.</margin>
Surely He will not stretch out His hand against a ruinous heap, though they cry out in his destruction.
<margin>verse 25. d) grieved or felt pain (in Syriac and Chaldean/Aramaic).</margin>
Did I not weep for him who was in trouble? Was not my soul grieved for the poor?
<margin>verse 26.</margin>
But when I looked for good, evil came; and when I waited for light, darkness arrived.
<margin>verse 27. e) they were made to boil; compare Chapter 41:23 and Ezekiel 24:5.</margin>
My heart is in turmoil and does not rest; days of affliction have confronted me.
<margin>verse 28. f) without the burning sun; see Isaiah 24:23.</margin>
I go about blackened, but not by the sun; I stand up in the assembly and cry for help.
<margin>verse 29.</margin>
I have become a brother to jackals and a companion to ostriches.
<margin>verse 30.</margin>
My skin grows black and falls from me; my bones burn with fever.
<margin>verse 31. g) and my musical instrument; see Chapter 21:12.</margin>
My harp is turned to mourning, and my flute to the voice of those who weep.
