## CHAPTER 31
<margin>CHAPTER XXXI, verse 1. h) toward a virgin, to corrupt her in mind or deed; compare Matthew 5:28. Job begins in Chapter 30, verse 24 and following to remove all wickedness from himself, specifically: 1) lack of mercy toward the afflicted. He continues here what he began there, and clears himself of: 2) The crime of debauchery or a violated virgin (v. 1-4). 3) Deceit and fraud (v. 5-6). 4) Robbery or theft (v. 7-8). 5) Tyranny and cruelty toward servants (v. 13-15). 7) Harshness toward the wretched (v. 16-20). 8) Injustice in the court (v. 21-23). 9) Trust in gold and riches (v. 24-25). 10) The superstition of flattery or idolatry (v. 26-28). 11) *Epichairekakia* <note>A Greek term for "Schadenfreude" or rejoicing in the misfortune of others</note> (v. 29-31). 12) Inhospitality (v. 31). 13) Impudence or the hiding of sins (v. 33-34, regarding all of which he testifies his conscience is unstained, v. 35-37). 14) Tyrannical oppression of his citizens (v. 38-40).</margin>
I made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze upon a virgin?
For what is the portion of God from above, and the heritage of the Almighty from on high?
Is it not destruction for the wicked, and disaster for the workers of iniquity?
Does He not see my ways and count all my steps?
If I have walked with falsehood, or if my foot has hurried after deceit,
Let me be weighed in a just balance, that God may know my integrity.
If my step has turned from the way, or my heart has followed my eyes, or if any spot has stuck to my hands,
Then let me sow and another eat, and let my harvests be uprooted.
If my heart has been enticed by a woman, or if I have lurked at my neighbor’s door,
Then let my wife grind for another, and let others bow down over her.
<margin>*Yehu* <note>A scribal variant</note> is the *Kere*.</margin>
<margin>*Hi* <note>The Hebrew feminine pronoun "she"</note> is the *Kere*.</margin>
For that would be a wicked scheme; it would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges.
For it is a fire that consumes to the place of destruction, and would root out all my increase.
If I have despised the cause of my male or female servant when they complained against me,
What then shall I do when God rises up? When He punishes, what shall I answer Him?
Did not He who made me in the womb make him? And did not one God fashion us in the womb?
If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or caused the eyes of the widow to fail,
Or if I have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten from it—
But from my youth he grew up with me as with a father, and from my mother’s womb I guided her—
If I have seen any perish for lack of clothing, or the needy without a covering,
<margin>*Chalatzav* <note>Hebrew: "his loins"</note> is the *Kere*.</margin>
If his loins have not blessed me, and if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep,
If I have raised my hand against the fatherless because I saw my help in the gate,
Then let my shoulder fall from its blade, and my arm be broken from its socket.

### CHAPTER XXXIII. <margin>33</margin>

<margin>
CHAPTER XXXIII, v. 1. m) Furthermore, hear I pray you, Job, my speeches. In this chapter, after I. a special introduction to the speech directed to Job himself in v. 1-7, Elihu II. proposes Job’s thesis to be refuted in v. 8-11, and III. refutes it with arguments: first from the greatness (v. 12), the freedom (v. 13), and the majesty (v. 14) of God; and then from the revelations of God through a certain and irrevocable word in v. 14 and following...

<margin>
CHAPTER XXXIV. v. 1. m) This is Elihu's second discourse to Job, in which is noted: I. The Introduction, inviting them to hear (v. 2-4). II. The Proposition of the thesis to be refuted (v. 5-6, cf. ch 23:10, 27:2, etc.). III. The Refutation of that thesis through three primary reasons: 1) from the impiety of the thesis (v. 7-22), 2) from the goodness of God (v. 13-17), 3) from the blasphemous consequence (v. 18-31). IV. The Conclusion, where he declares himself ready to hear Job's exceptions (v. 32-33). He promises that all wise and sensible men will certainly agree with him (v. 34-37).
</margin>
# **CHAPTER XXXIV.**

## CHAPTER 36

<margin>
CHAPTER XXXVI. v. 1. i) The fourth, and also the final and consolatory speech of Elihu is contained in this and the following chapter; in which the following should be noted: I. The introduction to gain attention (v. 2-4). II. The proposition regarding the just Providence of God, especially concerning the salvation of men (v. 2, 3). III. The narration of God’s providence, both general toward all men (v. 5-7), special toward the afflicted (v. 8-15), and most special toward Job (v. 16 to Chapter 37:20). IV. The conclusion through a summary exposition of the true opinion (v. 2-21). Cf. note at Chapter 37, 1.
</margin>

### <gloss>i</gloss>Elihu also proceeded, and said:

<margin>
CHAPTER XXXVI.
</margin>
2 Bear with me a little, and I will show you that I have yet more to say on God's behalf.
3 I will fetch my knowledge from afar, and will ascribe righteousness to my Maker.
4 For truly my words shall not be false: he that is perfect in knowledge is with you.
5 Behold, God is mighty, and despises not any: He is mighty in strength and wisdom.
6 He preserves not the life of the wicked, but gives right to the poor.
7 He withdraws not His eyes from the righteous: but with kings are they on the throne; yea, He establishes them for ever, and they are exalted.
8 And if they be bound in fetters, and be held in cords of affliction;
9 Then He shows them their work, and their transgressions that they have exceeded.
10 He opens also their ear to discipline, and commands that they return from iniquity.
11 If they obey and serve Him, they shall spend their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasures.
12 But if they obey not, they shall perish by the sword, and they shall die without knowledge.
13 But the hypocrites in heart heap up wrath: they cry not when He binds them.
14 They die in youth, and their life is among the <term>unclean</term> <note>original: "qedeshim" - historically referring to those practicing cultic prostitution</note>.
15 He delivers the poor in his affliction, and opens their ears in oppression.
16 Even so would He have removed you out of the mouth of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness; and that which should be set on your table should be full of fatness.
17 But you have fulfilled the judgment of the wicked: judgment and justice take hold on you.
18 Because there is wrath, beware lest He take you away with His stroke: then a great ransom cannot deliver you.
19 Will He esteem your riches? No, not gold, nor all the forces of strength.
20 Desire not the night, when people are cut off in their place.
21 Take heed, regard not iniquity: for this you have chosen rather than affliction.
22 Behold, God exalts by His power: who teaches like Him?
23 Who has enjoined Him His way? Or who can say, "You have wrought iniquity"?
24 Remember that you magnify His work, which men behold.

<meta>This page marks the dramatic turning point of the Book of Job. After the lengthy debates between Job and his friends, and the concluding speech of Elihu on the previous page, God finally intervenes. The text transitions from human speculation about divine justice to a direct revelation of God's majesty through the wonders of the natural world.</meta>

# JOB CHAPTER 38

<margin>
**Chapter 38, verse 1.** a) Finally, Jehovah Himself answered Job (compare chapter 40, verses 1 and 7). b) See chapter 40, verse 6; compare chapter 36, verse 27 and following; chapter 37, verse 1 and following; also Genesis 3:8–9, Exodus 19:16, Deuteronomy 33:2, 1 Kings 19:11, and Nahum 1:3. c) Namely, when Job remained silent at these arguments of Elihu, God Himself finally intervened as judge and arbiter. He spoke from a stormy whirlwind or cloud in two discourses, so that Job, terrified by the divine majesty, might humble himself and revere the incomprehensible judgments of his God. Therefore, the first discourse of God to Job begins here and ends at chapter 40, verse 5. In it, several things should be noted: I. A brief introduction with a complex proposition: "You, Job, wrongly contend against Me regarding the troublesome order I have established for salvation" (verses 2–3; compare chapter 40, verses 2–3). II. A more extensive confirmation of this proposition, comparing Job with God in the works of divine wisdom and power, which Job can in no way grasp, let alone equal or surpass. This is shown through many examples of God's inimitable works from chapter 38, verse 4, to the end of chapter 39. III. The conclusion is made by emphasizing the foolishness of one who contends with God (chapter 40, verses 1–2). IV. Finally, Job's response to this discourse of God is added in chapter 40, verses 3–5.

**Verse 8.** d) And when God covered or enclosed the sea with doors (verse 7, chapter 3:23); when it burst forth as if it had issued from a womb.

**Verse 11.** e) "And here"—this refers to My statute or decree (verse 10)—"shall set for you" (namely, a barrier, limit, or boundary; verse 10, chapter 14:13).

**Verse 16.** f) To the "reefs" of the sea. <note>original: "ו" from the Arabic root *Nahach*, meaning 'to be high or exalted'</note>.

**Verse 27.** g) Even the most desolate places (chapter 30:3). h) The "output" or "growth" (Numbers 30:13) of grass (Genesis 1:11, 30).

**Verse 29.** i) Frost or ice (chapter 37:10). k) And the hoarfrost of heaven (Exodus 16:14).

**Verse 31.** l) See chapter 9:9.
</margin>

1 **Then Jehovah answered** Job out of the **whirlwind**, and said: <margin>CHAPTER XXXVIII.</margin>
2 **And He said**: "Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge? <margin>The margin notes a variant reading for 'from'</margin>
3 **Gird up** now your loins like a man; for I will demand of you, and you shall inform Me.
4 **Where were you** when I laid the foundations of the earth? Declare, if you have understanding.
5 **Who determined** its measurements, if you know? Or who stretched the line upon it?
6 Whereupon were its foundations fastened? Or who laid its corner stone,
7 When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?
8 **Or who shut up** the sea with doors, when it burst forth, as if it had issued out of the womb?
9 When I made the cloud its garment, and thick darkness its swaddling band,
10 And established My decree upon it, and set bars and doors,
11 And said: 'Thus far shall you come, but no further; and here shall your proud waves be stayed'?
12 **Have you** commanded the morning since your days began; <margin>The letter Aleph is used here instead of He; 'you have known the dawn' is the traditional reading</margin> and caused the dawn to know its place;
13 That it might take hold of the ends of the earth, and the wicked be shaken out of it? <margin>The letter 'Ayin' is suspended</margin>
14 It is turned as clay to the seal; and they stand forth as a garment. <margin>The letter 'Ayin' is suspended</margin>
15 And from the wicked their light is withheld, and the high arm shall be broken.
16 **Have you entered** into the springs of the sea? Or have you walked in the search of the depths?
17 Have the gates of death been opened to you? Or have you seen the doors of the shadow of death?
18 Have you perceived the breadth of the earth? Declare if you know it all.
19 **Where is the way** where light dwells? And as for darkness, where is its place,
20 That you should take it to its boundary, and that you should know the paths to its house?
21 You know it, for you were then born! And the number of your days is great!
22 **Have you entered** into the treasures of the snow? Or have you seen the treasures of the hail,
23 Which I have reserved against the time of trouble, against the day of battle and war?
24 **By what way** is the light parted, or the east wind scattered upon the earth?
25 **Who has divided** a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, or a way for the lightning of thunder;
26 To cause it to rain on the earth, where no man is; on the wilderness, where there is no human;
27 To satisfy the desolate and waste ground; and to cause the bud of the tender herb to spring forth?
28 **Does the rain have** a father? Or who has begotten the drops of dew?
29 Out of whose womb came the ice? And the hoary frost of heaven, who has fathered it?
30 The waters are hidden as with a stone, and the face of the deep is frozen.
31 **Can you bind** the sweet influences of the Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?
32 Can you bring forth the **Constellations** in their season?

<note>The following section contains highly technical scholarly notes regarding the Hebrew grammar, musical accents (cantillation), and specific scribal traditions found in the Masoretic text of Job 38.</note>

**Chapter 38, verse 1.** "And He answered" <note>Hebrew: *Vaya'an*</note> marked with the *Mahpach* accent. [Notes on verses 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20]. The "Pik" mark for the word "from" <note>Hebrew: *Min*</note> is omitted in some versions [17, 18, 24], contrary to the Index of Basel (folio 61b). However, according to the *Maqqeph* (hyphen-like connector) in various editions [1, 2, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15, 20, 21, 23]. Regarding the final *Nun* in the text without the *Keri* (marginal reading) [11, 14, 15, 23], which contradicts the Masorah and the Erfurt manuscript. In verse 22, the word for "whirlwind" <note>Hebrew: *Ha-se'arah*</note> is marked with the *Rebi'a-Geresh* accent. On the word "and He said" <note>Hebrew: *Vayo'mer*</note> and "from" <note>Hebrew: *Min*</note>, there is one written form but two traditional readings. See Hilderus on the *Keri*, page 138. 

**Verse 2.** "Who is this that darkens counsel?" [Verses 6, 9, 10, 13, 16, 19]. It means: who is obscuring [God's] plan with words, and that without knowledge? The word "with words" <note>Hebrew: *Be-millin*</note> is written simply, contrary to certain *Maqqeph* placements. 

**Verse 3.** "Man" <note>Hebrew: *Gever*</note> is written with a *Dagesh* (a dot indicating emphasis), as taught by Ben Naphtali in the work *M.I.* 

**Verse 13.** "The wicked" <note>Hebrew: *Resha'im*</note>. Note the "Suspended Ayin" <note>In the Hebrew scrolls, the letter 'Ayin' in 'wicked' is written smaller or higher than the other letters here and in verse 15, a mystical scribal tradition suggesting that the 'eye' (Ayin) of the wicked is blinded or that they will be removed from the earth.</note>. This is found here and in verse 15, though it contradicts some Masoretic indexes.

**Verse 19.** "Where is the way?" <note>Hebrew: *Ei-zeh*</note>. This is written as two words with a hyphen (*Maqqeph*) between them in most instances, though others join them into a single word. 

**Verse 31.** "Can you bind?" <note>Hebrew: *Ha-tikasher*</note>. Marked with the *Metheg* accent.

# JOB CHAPTERS 39 & 40

## CHAPTER XLII

<margin>
CHAPTER XLII, verse 1. o) In this last chapter are:
I. Job's response to God's second speech (verse 1), in which he:
1) acknowledges divine omnipotence (verse 2),
2) confesses his errors (verses 3, 5), and
3) repents (verse 6).
II. God's actions with Job's three friends, who are reconciled through him (verses 7-9).
III. Job's restored happiness, with the return of:
1) his authority (verses 10, 11),
2) his wealth (verse 12),
3) his children (verses 13-15),
4) long life and 5) descendants (verse 16), and
6) finally, a blessed death (verse 17).
</margin>

### Technical Notes on the Hebrew Text
Verse 29: **Will you play**—written thus with a <term>Methegh</term> <note>a small vertical line used as a secondary accent</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, etc. The Munster edition uses a <term>Makkaph</term> <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> with the accent on the penultimate syllable (<term>milel</term>). Others place the accent on the last syllable (<term>milra</term>) or use the <term>Tsere</term> vowel.
**And will you bind him**—so written in the intensive form (Piel).
Verse 32: **His hope**—written with the <term>Kametz</term> vowel in several manuscripts, contrary to the Masoretic tradition and the Erfurt edition.
Chapter 41, verse 1: **His hope**—missing the letter *vav* in several copies.
**Will he stir him up**—follows the Baghdad manuscript tradition.
Verse 2: Some manuscripts begin Chapter 41 here.
Verse 4: **Not**—written without the marginal correction (<term>Qere</term>) in many copies.
Verse 10: **Flash forth**—accented on the last syllable with a <term>Tsere</term> vowel in certain books.
Verse 18: **Spear**—written with a <term>Patach</term> vowel in the Erfurt edition, similar to 1 Kings 6:7.
Verse 26: **High**—written with a <term>Munach</term> accent in manuscripts 10-12.
Chapter 42, verse 1: **And he said**—marked with the <term>Rbhiagerefch</term> <note>a specific compound musical accent</note> in manuscript 15. See notes on chapter 3:2.

This transition shifts the focus from the wisdom literature of suffering and divine justice to the poetic and allegorical exploration of divine love.</meta>

# THE SONG OF SONGS, Hebrew: *Shir HaShirim*

->In this sacred and most excellent song, the article of faith concerning the mystical union of the church and of every godly soul with Christ, and its various states of weakness, temptation, abandonment, etc., as well as the properties, incentives, bond, and fruits of mutual love, are explained under a continuous allegory.<-

---

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>
<margin>Large *Shin* <note>The first letter of the Hebrew text is written larger than the others in many manuscripts, a tradition noted in the Masora.</note></margin>
1 **The Song**<sup>a</sup> **of Songs, which is Solomon's:**<sup>b</sup>

2 **Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your love is better than wine.**

3 Because of the fragrance of your good oils, your name is as oil poured forth; therefore the maidens love you.

4 Draw me after you; let us run. The king has brought me into his chambers; we will be glad and rejoice in you. We will remember your love more than wine; they love you uprightly.

5 I am black but comely, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.

6 Look not upon me because I am swarthy, because the sun has tanned me. My mother’s sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept.

7 Tell me, O you whom my soul loves, where do you feed? Where do you make your flock to rest at noon? For why should I be like one who veils herself by the flocks of your companions?

8 If you know not, O most beautiful among women, go forth by the footsteps of the flock, and feed your kids beside the shepherds' dwellings.

9 I have compared you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots.

10 Your cheeks are comely with rows of jewels, your neck with strings of beads.

11 We will make for you rows of gold with studs of silver.<sup>c</sup>

12 While the king is at his table, my spikenard <note>An expensive aromatic ointment</note> sends forth its fragrance.

13 A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; he shall lie between my breasts.

14 My beloved is to me a cluster of henna in the vineyards of En-Gedi.

15 Behold, you are beautiful, my love; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves.

16 Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, yes, pleasant; also our bed is green.

<margin>Our rafters (variant)</margin>
17 The beams of our houses are cedars, our rafters are cypresses.<sup>d</sup>

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>
1 I am the rose of Sharon, the lily of the valleys.

2 As a lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.

3 As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. In his shadow I delighted and sat down, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.

<margin>Qamets with Zaqeph Qaton <note>A grammatical note regarding a vowel and an accent mark.</note></margin>
4 He brought me to the house of wine, and his banner over me was love.

5 Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples, for I am sick with love.

->Love<-

<column-break/>

**CHAPTER I, verse 1. a)**
The Song of Songs, that is, most outstanding and most excellent. Just as "Holy of Holies" means most holy; "Ornament of Ornaments" means the most excellent (Ezekiel 16:7); "Prince of Princes," "King of Kings," and similar expressions. **b)** "which is Solomon's" in the sense of the secondary author <note>Implying God is the primary author</note>, as in Proverbs 1:1, 10:1, 25:1; compare Habakkuk 3:1, Psalm 3:1. After the canonical title of the book in **v. 1**, the ardent desire of the Bride and a triple vow are explained in this chapter: 1) for a kiss in v. 2-3; 2) for divine drawing in v. 4; 3) for finding rest in v. 7. Between these is placed the Bride's address to the daughters of Jerusalem in v. 5-6. **IV.** Christ’s response and the Bride’s instruction in v. 8, whom He praises and commends in v. 9-10, and to whom He promises more abundant grace in v. 11. **V.** The Bride's thanksgiving for the fruit of Christ’s benefits, through a double or triple simile in v. 12-14. **VI.** Praise of the Bride given by Christ in v. 15. But **VII.** this is returned to Him by her, with praise for her lot, in v. 16-17.

**verse 11. c)** "we will make and prepare." Namely, I <note>The speaker is interpreted as Christ/the Word</note> with the Father and the Holy Spirit, being one in essence, will, and operation. See Genesis 1:26, 3:22, 11:7, John 14:23, etc.

**CHAPTER II, verse 1. d)** I, the Bride, who spoke in the preceding verses (1:16-17), am the flower or rose (see Isaiah 35:1) in Sharon (Isaiah 33:9, 35:2). Here follows **I.** A brief dialogue between the Bride (v. 1) and the Bridegroom (v. 2). **II.** The Bride praises the Bridegroom (v. 3-4) and implores his help (v. 5) and proclaims it obtained (v. 6). **III.** The Bride's appeal to the daughters of Jerusalem (v. 7). **IV.** The Bride's exultation at the presence and voice of the Bridegroom, which she describes at length as most pleasing to her (v. 8-14). **V.** A new command from the Bridegroom (v. 15). **VI.** The Bride's boasting (v. 16) and **VII.** appeal (v. 17).

---

### Critical Apparatus <note>Notes on manuscript variations</note>

**CHAPTER I, v. 1. Song (שיר):** An ordinary *Schin* <note>The first Hebrew letter</note> is found in manuscripts 3, 10, 13, 14. However, manuscripts 1, 2, 4, 6–9, 12, 20, 21, 23 write the entire word in capital letters. But the *Masora* (2nd edition) and the Erfurt manuscript require only the *Schin* to be large here and in 1 Chronicles 1:1; likewise in the printed Genesis 1:1.
**v. 2. Your love (דּוֹדֶיךָ):** So in 1, 2, 4. **v. 3. Oil poured forth (שֶׁמֶן תּוּרַק):** So in 1, 2, 4. **v. 4. His chambers (חֲדָרָיו):** Thus in 1. **v. 5. Space:** Manuscripts 1, 2, 6 place a space before this. **v. 6. That [the sun] has tanned me (שֶׁשְּׁזָפַתְנִי):** 8, 9, 10, 20, 21.
**Full spelling:** *With Shurek* <note>A vowel mark</note> in 1, 3, 4, 6, 21; and thus almost in 2, according to Masora 1, 3 and Erfurt; but contrary to Masora 2 and printed editions.
**v. 9. To my mare (לְסֻסָתִי):** Full spelling. **v. 7. I have kept (נָטָרְתִּי). v. 16. Pleasant (נָעִים). v. 4. Let us rejoice (נָגִילָה):** Thus in 1. **v. 12. Until the king (עַד שֶׁהַמֶּלֶךְ):** Thus in 1.
*By Munach accent on the penult:* 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 14, 15, 16, 20; and together with a Maqqeph <note>hyphen</note> in 23.
1, 4. **But "Until the king":** Thus in 2. **v. 14. The henna (הַכֹּפֶר):** Thus with a *Pesiq* <note>vertical dividing line</note> in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 23, and almost in the Berlin edition according to the Basel Index. Others omit it. **v. 15. Space:** They place a space before this.
2, 4, 6–9, 20, 21. **v. 16:** They place a space before this. 6, 8, 9, 21. **Yes, pleasant (אַף־נָעִים):** with Maqqeph in 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 14, 20. **v. 17. Our rafters (רַהִיטֵנוּ):** with *Patach* vowel in 8, 15, 22. With a *Qoph* <note>The letter Q</note> in the text without *Keri* <note>marginal reading</note> in 2, 14; contrary to Masora and Erfurt.
**CHAPTER II, v. 4. He brought me to the house... and his banner over me:** Thus in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 14, 20.

# SONG OF SONGS, CHAPTERS 2–3

<margin>
**v. 7. a)** I adjure you, both men and women, daughters of Jerusalem, *by the gazelles or the does of the field*. <note>original: "per capreas aut per cervas agri"</note> **b)** *If*, that is, [meaning] "by no means," following the notes on Genesis 21:23 and 1 Samuel 24:22. **c)** *you stir up or cause to awaken*. This double form of the same verb (a doubling of the conjugation) expresses the great zeal of the one forbidding it, as also seen in 3:5 and 8:4. **d)** this love, this charity, this bride and my companion, greatly beloved by me, and also most loving of me. See 7:7.

**v. 9. e)** Truly my beloved is like a gazelle in his speed, or a young stag. **f)** emerging from the lattices or iron grates.

**v. 10. g)** He responds to my sent-forth sighs and silent prayers.

**v. 11. h)** winter (1) [The word used here, *setav*, is found in] Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic; more frequently in Hebrew the word is *Choreph*, as in Genesis 8:22 and elsewhere. **i)** it has passed. Tobit 4:15. This is a description of spring.

**v. 12. k)** Flowers (1) compare with the related words in Genesis 43:10 and Isaiah 18:5. **l)** the time of singing or the chirping of birds (2) Isaiah 25:5, has arrived. Ezekiel 7:12.

**v. 13. m)** The fig tree has ripened or "seasoned with honey" (4) Genesis 50:2, 3, 26, its early fruit (1). **n)** and the vines are blooming, they are in flower (3) verse 15, chapter 7:13.

**v. 15. o)** Foxes, with which Palestine has abounded in all times; see the notes on Judges 15:4, Psalm 63:11, Lamentations 5:18, and Nehemiah 3:35.

**CHAPTER III, v. 1. p)** I. Here follows a new narrative from the bride regarding the lost, long-sought, and finally found Groom (verses 1–4). II. The Groom's adjuration or plea to the women of Jerusalem (verse 5). III. Commendation of the bride (verse 6). and IV. A description of the Groom and his royal wedding preparations (verses 7–11).

**v. 2. q)** I said, "I will surely rise from my bed" (verse 1): this verb is to be understood both here and in verse 3, just as in Psalm 8:3 and other places where the context contains a clear imitation of speech.

<note>The following are technical Masoretic notes regarding vowel points and specific manuscript readings.</note>
v. 7. *te’iru* (stir up) ends with *Pasek* in manuscripts 3, 6, 9, 20, and so in the second future, against the Basel index page 61. v. 11. *ve-halakh* (and gone) with *Gaiah* marks in 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 22. v. 8. *Hineh* (behold) with a *Merca* accent in 1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 20; with a prefixed *Vav* in 3, 4, and so in the second future. v. 14. *u-mareikh* (and your appearance) the letter *Yod* is omitted in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, against the Masora 1 and especially Nahum 3:5. v. 15. A space is placed before in 2, 7, 8, 20, 21. *Semadar* (tender grapes) with a *Kames* vowel in 2, 3, 4, 10, 14, 17, 18, 20, 21, 24, and the Berlin edition. Thus in the first future, against Masora 1 and the Basel index. v. 17. *ve-nasu* (and flee away) thus accented on the penultimate syllable in 2, 4, 6–10, 13, 15, 16, 20, 22, 23, and 24. Others mark it differently. CHAPTER III, v. 2. *va-asovebah* (and I will go about) the Masora requires a defective spelling, especially in Ecclesiastes 1:6, but our books disagree. v. 6. Space before in 2, 3, 4, 7, 8. With a *Makkef* [hyphen] in 3, 4, 6, 9, 20. With a *Chatef-Patach* vowel in 2, 6, 9, 20, 22, 23 on the word *Timarot* (pillars).

<column-break/>

**v. 8. a)** **All** these are seized, that is, girded with a sword, or accustomed to seize and handle a sword. Compare the similar usage of the Participle in Judges 8:11. Consider it the sword of the divine word, as in Ephesians 6:17, Philippians 2:17, and Hebrews 4:12.

**v. 10. b)** **Septuagint and Vulgate** <note>original: "LXX. Vulg."</note> translate as *reclinatorium* [a place for reclining], but Alexander <note>original: "Av."</note> suggests *fulcrum* [a support] based on the verb in chapter 2:5. **c)** This is as if to say a *vehicle* or *seat* in which one sits, as in Leviticus 15:9 and 1 Kings 5:6. **d)** *It is paved*, as compared with the related noun in 2 Kings 16:17 and Ezekiel 40:17-18. It is paved with the *love of the Groom for the bride*.

**CHAPTER IV, v. 1. e)** *Behold, you are beautiful, my love or my companion!* Here we find (I) a longer speech by the Groom in verses 1–14 and (II) a shorter response from the Bride in verses 15–16. The Groom praises the Bride's beauty (verses 1–7), invites her to join him (verse 8), and urges her to do so because of the intensity of his love (verse 9) and her lovely grace (verses 10–14). The Bride then returns the praise to the Groom (verse 15) and concludes with a longing prayer (verse 16). **f)** *which descend to drink*, as in chapter 6:5.

**v. 12. g)** *A garden barred*, and closed to all except the Lord, similar to Judges 3:23-24. *You are, O my sister, my bride!* **h)** *river*, as in Isaiah 48:18. Others suggest a *heap* or *pile of fruits*, comparing Genesis 35:46; it is *closed and barred against the profane*.

**v. 13. i)** *Her shoots*, as if bound by a rope, like a "paradise" or a very grand garden, as in Ecclesiastes 2:5 and Nehemiah 2:8. *of pomegranate trees*. **k)** *of the most excellent fruits*, as in verse 16 and chapter 7:14; see also the note on Deuteronomy 33:13. **l)** *henna* as in chapter 1:14, appearing here with many spikenards of various kinds.

**v. 14. c.** see chapter 1:12.

**CHAPTER V, v. 1. m)** Here follows (I) the Groom's response to the Bride’s preceding prayer, which other commentators omit. He declares the duties the Bride has performed for him and, in verse 2, invites his friends in turn. (II) The Bride speaks of herself and the Groom. (III) A conversation between her and the daughters of Jerusalem regarding the Groom’s beauty (verses 9–16).

->Scholarly Textual Variants<-

Chapter 5, verse 1: The word "Beloveds" is written deficiently <note>missing a vowel letter</note> as the Masorah requires in Proverbs 7:18; but written fully in Masorah 1, 2, 4, and Erfurt manuscript. 
Verse 2: Space precedes it in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 - 10, 20, 21. The letter Resh is without Dagesh in 3, 4, 10, 20, 21.
"My locks" — the letter Tsade is without Dagesh in 1, 4, 6, 9, 10, 20, 23. Verse 4: For "upon him," manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20 have "upon me." Verse 5: "And my hands dropped," so in 6, 9, 14, 20. Verse 8: "The beloved" — so in Dagesh 1, 4, 6, 9 -- 12, 20. Verse 10: "My beloved is white" — thus in 1, 4. Verse 11: "His locks" — Tsade without Dagesh in 9, 20; contrary to Masorah 1 and Erfurt manuscript. Verse 14: "Bright" with the vowel Tsere in 1, 2, 3, 4. Verse 15: "As the cedars" with the vowel Patach in 3, 6, 21. Verse 5: "Turn away" thus with Patach with following Dagesh in 1, 2. However, with Qamets in 2 margin. "For they" thus in 7, 8, 24. "Thy hair" with Chateph-patach in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 -- 14, 16 -- 21, 23, 24. Chapter 6, verse 4: Space precedes in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 -- 9, 14, 20.

# CHAPTERS 6. 7. 8. SONG OF SONGS VI VII VIII

<margin>
v. 10. a) "Who is she?" the queens, concubines, and virgins from verse 8 ask in wonder.
v. 11. c) I went down into the garden of the nut or of nuts. After the Groom’s great praises of his Bride, he recounts his happy deed and destiny in verse 12. d) so that I might see with delight the green shoots (2) Job 8:12 of the valleys. e) so that I might see whether the vine had budded? chapter 2:13. Or if the pomegranates flourished? chapter 7:13; chapter 4:13.
v. 12. f) I did not know how my soul set me among the chariots of my willing people. <term>Anthropopathism</term> <note>Attributing human emotions or limitations to God or Christ</note>. Cocceius notes: Here Christ speaks in the manner of those who describe what they have done by an unforeseen opportunity, which they had not hoped for or thought they would do. For then we are accustomed to say, "I know not how," etc.
CHAPTER VII, v. 1. g) Here is: I. The conclusion of the preceding chapter, verse 1. II. The Groom commends the Bride again, and urges her to friendly enjoyment in verses 2–10. III. The Bride responds to the Groom, and repeating the testimony of her love, invites him into the field and vineyard, offering him all her things in verses 11–14.
CHAPTER VIII, v. 1. h) Who will give, or O if someone would give you! namely, according to the <term>Targum</term> <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note>, the King Messiah, my Groom and beloved, addressed just now in chapter 7:14. In this last chapter, note: I. The Bride's words, first of longing (verses 1, 2) then of celebration (verse 3). II. The Groom's charge to the daughters of Jerusalem (verse 4). III. The wonder of the spectators (verse 5). IV. The Bride's prayer (verse 6) and testimony (verse 7). V. The Bride's promise regarding the adorning of the little sister (verses 8–10). VI. Her promise regarding the fruits of the vineyard (verses 11, 12). VII. And finally, the mutual <unclear>address</unclear> <note>original Greek: προσφώνησις (prosphonesis)</note> of Christ (verse 13) and the Church (verse 14).

v. 10. a) "Who is she?" the queens, concubines, and virgins say in wonder in verse 8.
b) "who looks out and shows herself to be seen like the dawn? splendid as the pure light and shining like the sun itself," Isaiah 24:23. "And terrible, as an army set in order for battle with its banners!" verse 4.
v. 11. c) I went down into the garden of the nut or of nuts. The Groom, after the great praises of his Bride, recounts his happy deed and destiny in verse 12. d) so that with delight I might see the green shoots (2) Job 8:12 of the valleys. e) so that I might look whether the vine had budded? chapter 2:13. Or if the pomegranates flourished? chapter 7:13; chapter 4:13.
v. 12. f) I did not know how my soul set me among the chariots of my willing people. <term>Anthropopathism</term>. Cocceius: Christ speaks here in the manner of those who say they have done something due to an unforeseen opportunity, which they had not hoped for or thought they would do. For then we are accustomed to say, "I know not how," etc.
CHAPTER VII, v. 1. g) This is I. The conclusion of the preceding chapter, verse 1. II. The Groom commends the Bride again, and urges her to friendly enjoyment in verses 2–10. III. The Bride responds to the Groom, and repeating the testimony of her love, invites him into the field and vineyard, offering him all her things in verses 11–14.
CHAPTER VIII, v. 1. h) "Who will give," or "O if someone would give you!" namely, according to the Targum, the King Messiah, my Groom and beloved, addressed just now in 7:14. In this last chapter, note: 1. The Bride's words, first of longing (v. 1, 2) then of celebration (v. 3). II. The Groom's charge to the daughters of Jerusalem (v. 4). III. The wonder of the spectators (v. 5). IV. The Bride's prayer (v. 6) and testimony (v. 7). V. The Bride's promise regarding the adorning of the little sister (v. 8–10). VI. Her promise regarding the fruits of the vineyard (v. 11, 12). VII. And finally, the mutual address <note>original Greek: prosphonesis</note> of Christ (v. 13) and the Church (v. 14).

# THE BOOK OF RUTH,
In Hebrew:
### RUTH

<margin>*</margin>
This little book contains the history of Ruth the Moabite in its principal part. It was written around the time of David (chapter 4, 22) by Samuel or another divinely inspired man <note>original: "θεοπנευστῳ"</note>. It serves as the beginning of the books of Samuel and the entrance-hall to the history of David: it ensures that the genealogy and origin of David, and even of the Messiah himself, from Judah and Ruth the Moabite is established; compare 1 Chronicles 2, Matthew 1, and Luke 3. It presents first the sad history of Naomi and Ruth in chapter 1, and then the more joyful history in chapters 2, 3, and 4. Based on the timing of the events, it is referred to the time of Judges 3 and 4, or even to Judges chapter 6. Compare chapter 1, 1 with Judges 6, 1–6.

<margin>
*) Esther 7, 9. s) chapter 4, 14.
t) CHAPTER I, verse 1. 1. it happened. A similar beginning to books is found in Joshua 1, 1; Judges 1, 1; 1 Samuel 1, 1; Ezekiel 1, 1.
</margin>

<gloss>And it came to pass in the days when the judges ruled that there was a famine in the land. And a certain man of Bethlehemjudah went to sojourn in the country of Moab, he, and his wife</gloss>

1 Now Boaz went up to the gate and sat down there; and behold, the redeemer of whom Boaz had spoken was passing by. And Boaz said, "Turn aside, sit down here, my friend" <note>Hebrew: *Ploni Almoni*, a placeholder name like "Mr. So-and-so."</note>; and he turned aside and sat down.

<margin>
Grammatical Notes: Regarding the word "your garments" in verse 3, and "wash yourself" in verses 4, 6, 9, 10, 14, and 20. Some manuscripts read it one way but write it another according to the Erfurt Masorah. In verse 8, there is a space before the verse in some traditions. In verse 9, "your wings" is written fully in some Oriental manuscripts, contrary to other Masoretic traditions. In verse 13, the letter Lamed is written large in Oriental texts, while others use a large Nun. Regarding verse 15, the word "Bring" is noted as being among those derived from "to come" where the third radical letter Aleph is lost, though some grammarians dispute this and refer it to a different root. In verse 17, the Western traditions omit the particle *et*.

### CHAPTER 4. RUTH 4

<margin>accented on the last syllable</margin> 1 And Boaz said, "Turn aside, sit here, Mr. So-and-So" <note>original: "Peloni Almoni," a Hebrew idiom for an unnamed person, similar to "John Doe" or "a certain one."</note>; and he turned aside and sat down. 2 And he took ten men from the elders of the city and said, "Sit here," and they sat down. 3 And he said to the kinsman-redeemer, "The piece of land which belonged to our brother <note>meaning a close kinsman</note> Elimelech, Naomi—who has returned from the fields of Moab—is selling." 4 "And I thought, I will reveal it to your ear <note>meaning: I will inform you</note>, saying: Buy it in the presence of those sitting here and in the presence of the elders of my people. You are witnesses today." 11 And all the people who were at the gate and the elders said, "We are witnesses. May the Lord make the woman who is coming into your house like Rachel and Leah, the two of whom built the house of Israel; and may you do worthily in Ephrathah and be famous in Bethlehem. 12 And may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, from the offspring which the Lord will give you from this young woman." 13 So Boaz took Ruth and she became his wife; and when he went in to her, the Lord gave her conception, and she bore a son. 14 And the women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the Lord, who has not left you without a kinsman-redeemer today, and may his name be famous in Israel. 15 And he shall be to you a restorer of life and a nourisher of your [old age]..."

<column-break/>

a) *Turn aside for a little while* from the path, and come here. Compare Genesis 19:2, 3; Judges 4:18.
b) *Sit and wait* here. See verse 2.
c) *Schin. Peloni Almoni.* The Vulgate <note>The Latin Bible</note> translates this as *calling him by his name.* See 1 Samuel 21:3, 2 Kings 6:8, and the contracted form in Daniel 8:13. Compare the Greek expression *ho deina* in Matthew 26:18.
d) Judges 4:18; chapter 14:8.
v. 3. e) *The portion of the field*, see chapter 2:3 and 2 Samuel 14:30. *Which was of our brother, our kinsman, Elimelech*, as mentioned above in chapters 1, 2, and 3.
f) *She sold*, or *she has decided to sell*; the Vulgate says *is about to sell.* Naomi, as in chapter 1:6, 22.
v. 4. g) *I therefore said and determined within myself* Genesis 20:11. Schmidius suggests Boaz said this to Ruth, based on the wording in chapter 3:12.
h) *I will reveal your ear and advise you.* 1 Samuel 9:15; chapter 20:2.
i) *But if indeed he will not redeem it* (said by shifting the address to the elders standing by in verse 2) *the one who is the next kinsman, tell it to me, so that I may know and determine what I must do.*
v. 5. k) *Then also from Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of the deceased Mahlon* (chapter 1:5), *you acquire the field, on this condition, that you make to stand or preserve the name of the deceased* (verse 10; Deuteronomy 25:7) *upon his inheritance.* For Naomi did not intend to sell the field under any other condition.
v. 7. l) *Now this was the custom or habit of old* (Deuteronomy 2:10, 12) *in Israel in redemption or legal recovery (v. 6) and in exchange* (Leviticus 27:10, 33) *to establish* (Ezekiel 13:6) *every word* (Deuteronomy 19:15) *so that what was done in the contract would be valid and stable: the man who was ceding his right would loosen and draw off his shoe and hand it to the other. And this was the attestation of the initiated contract and the full cession* (Isaiah 8:16, 20) in Israel.
v. 11. m) *And perform strength; act valiantly.* Proverbs 31:29. n) *And call a name for yourself; that is, achieve fame and celebrity of name through sons and their successors, as in verse 14 and Genesis 48.*

v. 1. **פֹּה** (here) without a Dagesh <note>a grammatical dot in the letter</note> in manuscript 22. **וַיָּסַר** (and he turned aside) with a Qamets vowel in manuscripts 4, 6, 9, 14, and 20. v. 3. **מָכְרָה** (she sold) with a Pashta accent. v. 2, 4, 6–9, 14, 15, 20. **מִשְּׂדֵה** (from the field) written here *with the letter He* in manuscripts 1, 2, 4, 6–16, 20–24, according to the Maffaeianus codex 1, 2, 4 and the Erfurt codex; also in 2 Kings 1:21. Other manuscripts use the letter *Yod* as a plural. v. 4. **נֶגֶד** (before) has a Mercha servant accent before a Pashta here. This is required by the Maffaeianus and Erfurt codices here and in Exodus 6:6. However, all our books have a Munach accent. For **יִגְאַל** (he will redeem), manuscripts 3 have **וְיִגְאַל** (and he will redeem) with an added note. But manuscript 2 observes in the margin that according to Chananel, it might be read as **הֲגָאַל** in the second person. v. 7. **הַגְּאוּלָּה** (the redemption) thus with a Shurek vowel followed by a Dagesh in manuscript 1 and the Maffaeianus codex 1 and Erfurt codex. **הַמּוֹאֲבִיָּה** (the Moabitess) thus missing a letter in 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 22; and so in 4 according to Maffaeianus 1, 2, 4 and Erfurt here, as well as in chapter 1:4. v. 11. **חַיִל** (worthily/wealth) with a double Pashta accent in 1, 2, 3, 4.

# THE BOOK OF LAMENTATIONS,
### Hebrew
## אֵיכָה <note>pronounced "Eikhah," meaning "How"</note>

> These Lamentations <note>original: "Threni"</note>, which are alphabetical or acrostics <note>poems where each verse starts with a successive letter of the alphabet</note> through the first four chapters, are entirely different from those with which the author mourned the death of King Josiah in 2 Chronicles 35:25. For here he mourns the sorrowful state of the Jewish people, both during the siege and after the destruction of the city. He sees the causes of the evils and shows the means of obtaining divine grace—repentance, faith, and the amendment of life—through earnest prayers.

* * *

<margin>i) chapter 4:1. k) chapter 2:21. LAMENTATIONS CHAPTER 1, verse 1. l) "How?" The word of one in shock, as in chapter 2:1 and Isaiah 1:22. There are two speakers in this chapter: I. Jeremiah in verses 1-11, and II. Jerusalem herself (or the land of Judah) under the figure of a widow in verses 11-22. m) sits alone, or in solitude, in the manner of mourners; see chapter 3:28 and Jeremiah 15:17. n) full of people; see 1 Samuel 2:5 and Jeremiah 51:13. The letter "Yod" is an addition <note>term: paragogic Yod</note> here and in the following, as in Isaiah 1:21.</margin>
1 How^i ^k does the city sit solitary, that was full of people!^l She has become like a widow; she who was great among the nations and a princess among the provinces^m has become a forced laborer.^n
2 She weeps bitterly in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks; she has no comforter among all her lovers; all her friends have dealt treacherously with her; they have become her enemies.
3 Judah has gone into exile because of affliction and hard servitude; she dwells among the nations, she finds no rest; all her pursuers overtook her between the narrow straits.

<margin>Chapter II.</margin>
How the Lord has beclouded the daughter of Zion in his anger! He has cast down from heaven to earth the beauty of Israel, and has not remembered his footstool <note>A common biblical metaphor for the Temple or the Ark of the Covenant</note> in the day of his anger.

<margin>And did not [Keri/Ketiv note]</margin>
The Lord has swallowed up without pity all the dwellings of Jacob; he has thrown down in his wrath the strongholds of the daughter of Judah; he has brought them down to the ground; he has profaned the kingdom and its princes.

He has cut off in fierce anger every horn of Israel; he has drawn back his right hand from before the enemy, and he has burned in Jacob like a flaming fire that devours round about.

He has bent his bow like an enemy; his right hand stood like an adversary, and he has slain all that were pleasant to the eye in the tent of the daughter of Zion; he has poured out his fury like fire.

The Lord has become like an enemy; he has swallowed up Israel, he has swallowed up all her palaces; he has destroyed his strongholds, and he has increased mourning and lamentation in the daughter of Judah.

He has laid waste his booth like a garden; he has destroyed his place of assembly; the Lord has caused the appointed feasts and Sabbaths to be forgotten in Zion, and in his fierce indignation has spurned both king and priest.

The Lord has cast off his altar, he has disowned his sanctuary; he has delivered the walls of her palaces into the hand of the enemy; they have made a noise in the house of the Lord as in the day of a solemn feast.

The Lord purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out a line <note>A measuring line, here used for destruction rather than building</note>, he has not withdrawn his hand from destroying; therefore he made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together.

<margin>Small letter Mem</margin>
Her gates have sunk into the ground; he has destroyed and broken her bars; her king and her princes are among the Gentiles; the Law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the Lord.

The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground and keep silence; they have cast up dust upon their heads; they have girded themselves with sackcloth; the virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground.

My eyes fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my gall is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city.

<margin>I will testify [Keri]</margin>
They say to their mothers, "Where is grain and wine?" when they swoon as the wounded in the streets of the city, when their soul was poured out into their mothers' bosom.

What thing shall I take to witness for you? what thing shall I liken to you, O daughter of Jerusalem? what shall I equal to you, that I may comfort you, O virgin daughter of Zion? for your breach is great like the sea: who can heal you?

Your prophets have seen vain and foolish things for you:

**שְׁבוּתֵךְ** <note>original: "Your captivity"</note> — *Qere* <note>The "Qere" is a traditional reading that differs from the written text in the Hebrew Bible.</note> 

a) **Vain and foolish.** See Jeremiah 2:8 and Job 6:16. They did not reveal the covering of your iniquity that was placed upon you. See Chapter 4:22 and compare Isaiah 56:10.

s) **Those whom I dandled in my palms.** (2) Isaiah 48:13; compare verse 20 above.

t) **I have brought up.** (2) Ezekiel 18:2.

**CHAPTER III**, verse 1. u) **I am that man.** This refers to Jeremiah (compare verse 14), who throughout this chapter laments sometimes as a private person and sometimes in the name of the entire nation. He is the one who, more than other Prophets, saw and experienced affliction. This chapter contains: I. A complaint about extreme and nearly desperate misery (verses 1–18). II. A breath of relief through the remembrance of God's mercy (verses 19–25). III. An awakening to patience and waiting for God (verses 26–30). IV. The foundation of hope based on the nature of God (verses 31–38). V. An exhortation to repentance and confession of sins (verses 39–41). VI. Prayers to God for deliverance (verses 42–54). VII. An act of thanksgiving (verses 55–66).

### CHAPTER III.

1 I am the man who has seen affliction by the rod of His wrath.

2 He has led me and brought me into darkness, and not into light.

3 Surely against me He turns His hand again and again all the day long.

4 He has made my flesh and my skin old; He has broken my bones.

5 He has built against me, and surrounded me with gall and hardship.

6 He has set me in dark places, like those who have been long dead.

7 He has hedged me in, so that I cannot get out; He has made my chain heavy.

8 Even when I cry and shout, He shuts out my prayer.

9 He has enclosed my ways with hewn stone; He has made my paths crooked.

10 He is to me like a bear lying in wait, like a lion in secret places.

11 <margin>Note on the word "lion."</margin> He has turned aside my ways and pulled me in pieces; He has made me desolate.

12 He has bent His bow and set me as a target for the arrow.

13 He has caused the arrows of His quiver to enter into my kidneys <note>A Hebrew idiom for the innermost part of a person's being, often translated as "reins."</note>.

Verse 14. **Causes of banishment:** written deficiently <note>Without a vowel-marker letter.</note> in manuscripts 8 and 15 and Western copies. Others, following Eastern traditions, write it fully. 

Verse 18. Instead of **Lord** (*Adonai*), manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 have **the LORD** (*YHWH*), contrary to the Masorah. 

Verse 19. **Watches:** written fully in 1 and 4 according to the Masorah. However, it is written deficiently in 1... both according to Masoretic tradition. 

Verse 21. **And not:** with the prefix "And" (*Vav*) in manuscripts 2, 3, 6, 9, 20. 

**CHAPTER III**, verse 8. **Shuts out:** written with a *Patah* vowel in 2, 4, and the Berlin manuscript, contrary to the Masorah on Genesis 30:40. 

Verse 9. **My paths:** written deficiently in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12 according to the Masorah. Others write it fully. 

Verse 13. **Into my kidneys:** written with a *Patah* in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 29, contrary to the Masorah.

a) **to my people.** These are the words of the Prophet, as we said above regarding verse 1. Compare Jeremiah 9:1 and 15:10.

->### CHAPTER IV.<-

<margin>1</margin> How the gold has grown dim! How the fine gold has changed! The sacred stones are poured out at every street corner.
<margin>2</margin> The precious sons of Zion, once weighed against fine gold, how they are now regarded as earthen jars, the work of a potter's hands!
<margin>3</margin> <margin>Read: jackals</margin> Even the jackals <note>original: "tannin"</note> offer the breast and nurse their young; but the daughter of my people has become cruel, <margin>Read: like ostriches</margin> like ostriches in the wilderness.
<margin>4</margin> The tongue of the nursing infant clings to the roof of its mouth for thirst; the children beg for bread, but no one breaks it for them.
<margin>5</margin> Those who once ate delicacies are desolate in the streets; those brought up in scarlet <note>original: "tola," a dye derived from insects</note> embrace ash heaps.
<margin>6</margin> The iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than the sin of Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment, and no hands were laid on her.
<margin>7</margin> Her princes were purer than snow, whiter than milk; their bodies more ruddy than coral, their appearance like sapphire.
<margin>8</margin> Their appearance is blacker than soot; they are not recognized in the streets. <margin>According to our accents</margin> Their skin has shriveled on their bones; it has become as dry as wood.

<margin>10</margin> The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children; they became their food during the destruction of the daughter of my people.

<margin>12</margin> The kings of the earth did not believe, nor did any of the inhabitants of the world, that a foe or an enemy could enter the gates of Jerusalem.
<margin>13</margin> <margin>Read: all</margin> This happened because of the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, who shed the blood of the righteous in her midst.

**CHAPTER 4, v. 3.** The word **shadu** (breasts) appears with a Qamets vowel according to the manuscripts 2, 4, 6, 9, 20, 23. **Like ostriches**: Thus joined in the text, contrary to the Masorah <note>The traditional scribal notes on the Hebrew Bible</note> and the Erfurt manuscript. **v. 7. They were pure**: Thus accented on the last syllable in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9, 15, 17, 22, 23, 24. Others accent the penultimate syllable. **v. 10. They were white**: with a Qamets in 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20 & accented on the penultimate in 1, 4. **v. 9. For they**: with a Segol vowel in 1, 4, 17, 18 & the Berlin manuscript. Furthermore, the Munster edition omits verses 6, 9, 20–23, contrary to the printed Masorah. **v. 13. From the sin**: written fully <note>with the letter Vav</note> in manuscript 2 and 3, against the Masorah, manuscript 4, and the Erfurt manuscript; regarding this, consult what Rabbi Chaiim <note>Jacob ben Hayyim ibn Adonijah</note> notes here. **Her priests**: written fully with a Vav according to the Masorah and Erfurt, but without the support of our manuscripts. **v. 14. They could**: written deficiently <note>missing a letter</note> in the Oriental traditions, contrary to the Masoretic lexicon. **v. 15. Depart**: thus deficiently in the Masorah and printed editions; see Nehemiah 9:2.

**v. 57.** a) You were near at other times and ready to hear. Psalm 145:18. b) On the day I invoked You. Psalm 56:10 and 86:7. c) compare Jeremiah 1:18 and 39:10.
**v. 58.** d) You pleaded. Psalm 35:1. e) i.e., the causes that concerned my life and safety.
**v. 59.** f) You have seen now also, as of old (Psalm 10:4), the perversion of me (i), that is, the injuries and violence inflicted upon me. See verse 36 and Psalm 119:78. *The suffix is used passively, meaning "the evil which I suffer."* Psalm 35:4.
**v. 63.** g) Their sitting down and their rising up (i), that is, all their plans and efforts. Isaiah 37:28. h) Their melody/taunt (i). See verse 14.
**v. 65.** i) A stupor, or madness of the heart (i), from the Arabic and compared with Deuteronomy 28:28. k) May Your curse be upon them or fall upon them (i).
**CHAPTER 4, v. 1.** l) How (as in Chapter 1:1) is the gold covered and darkened? (i) Ezekiel 28:3 and 31:8. That is, the Jewish people, who once shone like gold in the sanctuary of God; compare verse 2. m) Poured out, like rubbish or filth. Leviticus 14:41 and Zephaniah 1:17. n) This alludes to the gems of the High Priest's garment, upon which the names of the twelve tribes of Israel were inscribed. Exodus 28:8–11. This chapter describes: I. the cruel famine of Jerusalem (v. 1–12); II. the cause, which is the gravest sins (v. 6, 13–20); III. the hope of restoration for Zion and the predicted destruction for the Edomites (v. 21, 22).
**v. 3.** o) Even the whales and immense sea-beasts extend or offer the breast. Job 3:12. p) She has become cruel. Job 30:21. Like the ostriches. Isaiah 13:22 and Micah 1:8.
**v. 5.** q) Formerly carried or nurtured. See Numbers 11:12 and Isaiah 60:4. r) Upon scarlet. Exodus 28:5 and Isaiah 1:18. s) They embraced. Job 24:8. Dunghills (i). See 1 Samuel 2:8 and Nehemiah 3:14.

<header>LAMENTATIONS. CHAPTER 4. 5.</header>

<margin>
a) <note>original: "clamauerunt ad eos"</note> "They cried to them." The meaning is that the Jews had become as abominable to the nations as lepers usually are. Compare *Leviticus 13:45.*
b) *Compare Isaiah 52:11.* 
c) *For they fled like* the Jews in *Jeremiah 48:9, and now they wander*, driven from their homes and fatherland. *Genesis 4:12, Jeremiah 14:10.* 
d) <note>original: "dicunt (i. e. Imperf. dicitur) inter gentes"</note> "It is said among the nations," the Jews shall no longer continue to stay or dwell in their own land. *Psalm 15:1 & 61:5.*
verse 17. e) *While we were still*, namely, in our land or our former state. *1 Kings 1:14.*
22. f) *Our eyes were consumed with longing.* *Psalm 69:4 & 119:82, 123.* 
g) *Looking for our help, which was a help of vanity:* that is, we waited in vain for assistance from the Egyptians. Compare *chapter 1:19, 2 Kings 24:7, Isaiah 30:7, Jeremiah 37:5-11.* 
h) *While with a watch (i)* we watched continually and earnestly for a nation that nevertheless could not save. *Isaiah 30:5, chapter 31:3.*
verse 20. i) <term>Breath of our nostrils</term> <note>original: "Spiraculum f. halitus narium nostrarum"</note>. *Genesis 7:22.* 
k) *Targum:* <note>The Aramaic translation of the Bible</note> He who was anointed with the oil of the Lord's unction, like Saul in *1 Samuel 24:6, 10.* Think of Zedekiah, who would have had a more peaceful state if he had kept faith with Nebuchadnezzar, from whom he received the kingdom. Compare *Ezekiel 17:13 and following, and the Preface to Jeremiah, section 11.* 
l) *He was captured in their pits (2)* *Psalm 102:20.* See the event in *2 Kings 25:6, Jeremiah 52:9, Ezekiel 19:4, 8.*
**CHAPTER V**, verse 1. m) *Remember, O Lord, what has been done, or happened to us. <margin>
(k) **CHAPTER III, v. 1.** To all things there is a season. Solomon continues in the removal of the false "highest good," the vanity of which he has proven since chapter 2:24 from the helplessness of man in attaining those things which his vain actions intend. This he supports with a new reason, taken from the freedom of divine governance, by which He appoints and defines a certain time for all things—even those contrary to each other. In accelerating or delaying these, human effort is useless. verses 1–11. II. He establishes the true "highest good" in verses 12–14. III. He addresses prejudices or obstacles against piety in verses 15–22.

v. 11. (a) God indeed made all things (Genesis 1:31) beautiful (verse 10; chapter 5:17) in their own time; so that in its own time everything He makes might be most fitting (Psalm 1:3 & 104:27). Wherefore man cannot, by all his reason and zeal, ward off adverse accidents from himself, but is finally compelled to commit himself and all his affairs to the providence and paternal care of God alone (cf. # CHAPTER 3 & 4. ECCLESIASTES

<margin>
verse 21. a) For how far <note>original: "Quousque enim," comparing to chapter 8:1 and Isaiah 42:23</note> does one know the *spirit* or *soul of the sons of man* <note>chapter 12:7, Psalm 31:6</note> and its massive distinction from the soul of the beasts? b) "which itself ascends." The prefix before the Participle acts as a relative pronoun ("which/who"), as in 2 Samuel 19:6 or Psalm 103:3; it is certainly not an interrogative, but uses the *Kamets* vowel because of the following guttural letter, as in Psalm 134:1. c) "upward," toward God the creator <note>Proverbs 15:24, chapter 12:7</note>. d) "and who knows the *spirit* or *soul of the beast*" <note>Psalm 104:29</note> which descends downward to the earth, and perishes and is abolished along with the body.
</margin>

...and all return to the dust. **Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of man goes** <sup>21</sup>
**upward, and whether the spirit of the beast goes downward to the earth?**
**And I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his works, for** <sup>22</sup>
<margin>The letter *Mem* has a *Segol* vowel</margin>**that is his portion; for who can bring him to see what shall be after him?**

**CHAPTER IV.** verse 1. e) *Furthermore, I turned myself* <note>verse 7, chapter 9:11</note> and *observed* or *saw* <note>verse 7, chapter 3:10, 16; Ezekiel 8:2</note> *all kinds of oppressed people* <note>Psalm 103:6 and 146:7</note> who are made such under the sun in this world <note>verse 3, 7; Chapter 1, 3; etc.</note>. Here the author removes a new "stumbling block" <note>original: "offendiculum"</note>—the idea that piety seems to offer no benefit to those who practice it. There are two parts to this chapter: I. Three remaining cases are presented which might deter a person from embracing the "Highest Good" and true piety: 1) the lack of comfort for the oppressed (verses 1-3); 2) the empty glory of men rising in this life through envy (verses 4-6); 3) perpetual singleness and the false hope of finding happiness in it (verses 7-16). II. The first precept of the fourth part of the book: regarding the worship of God from the soul (verse 17).
</margin>

<meta>catchword: there [Hebrew: shamah]</meta>

**Technical Notes on the Hebrew Text:**
In verse 21, the word **הַעֹלָה** ("which goes up") is written with a *Chateph-patach* vowel; some interpret this as a question ("Does it go up?"), as seen in Luther’s German version and ancient translations like the Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac, Chaldean, and Arabic. However, this contradicts grammatical rules, as a guttural letter would usually require a different vowel (*Patach*) for a question. Similarly, the word **הַיֹּרֶדֶת** ("which goes down") appears with a *Chateph-patach* in most versions, though some manuscripts (like the Erffurt codex) show a fuller spelling. In Chapter 4, verse 1, the word **הָעֲשֻׁקִים** ("the oppressed") is in the intensive form (*Piel*). There is a historical disagreement here between "Western" (Palestinian) scribes, who use a full spelling, and "Eastern" (Babylonian) scribes, who use a shortened spelling. Other notes track the use of the double-dot accent (*Dagesh*) in the word for "still" (**עֲדֶנָּה**) and specific vowel markers in the words for "travail" and "woe," comparing several scholarly manuscripts to maintain the most accurate traditional reading.

# ECCLESIASTES. CHAPTER 7.

<margin>
verse 7. a) Sebastian Schmid <note>A 17th-century Lutheran theologian known for his literal Bible translations and commentaries.</note> considers this a comparison <note>original: "similitudinis"</note> of a difficult nature, as in chapter 1, verse 1 and chapter 3, verse 18. For just as oppression <note>original: "impressio"</note>, mentioned in chapter 5, verse 7, so also this "laughter of fools" from verses 5 and 6 makes the wise man mad and corrupts him. It also destroys the heart, perhaps referring to a gift or bribe <note>original: "donum, f. munus"</note> accepted to the prejudice of a good cause; compare Exodus 23:8, Deuteronomy 16:19, and Proverbs 15:27. The masculine verb refers to the related masculine noun, using a grammatical shift <term>enallage</term> similar to that found below in verse 29 and in Genesis 4:7.

7 Surely oppression makes the wise man mad, and a bribe destroys the heart.

<margin>
verse 8. b) A good thing, or rather, the "end" or "outcome" of a thing is better than its beginning. Likewise, the "long-suffering" (literally: "long of spirit") is better—one who can restrain his spirit for a long time and is not headlong into anger and impatience; compare Proverbs 14:29 and 15:18. This is contrasted with the "high" or "proud of spirit" (Proverbs 16:5, 18, 32), who is immediately indignant and rushes into impatience; see also the note at verse 1.

8 Better is the end of a thing than its beginning; the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.

<note>The following notes are philological comparisons between different manuscripts and editions of the Hebrew text.</note>

verse 6. **Like the laughter** <note>Hebrew: _ke-schok_</note> Thus with the prefix *Vav* in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 4 (though here without the *Shva* vowel under the subject), also in 6, 9, 14, 20, 21, and 22. Here it includes a specific grammatical mark <note>original: "secund. Mas. impr. fin. f. 19. b."</note>. Others appear without it.
verse 7. **And destroys the heart** <note>Hebrew: _ve-yabed et lev_</note> Thus in 1, 2, and 3, but with a different construction and sense: "and it destroys" (meaning oppression or injustice) the heart, i.e., the man who receives a gift <note>original: "virum doni"</note>, specifically referring to bribes.
verse 11. **And an advantage** <note>Hebrew: _ve-yoter_</note> Written in full <term>plene</term> in editions 2 and 4. Others follow the shorter spelling in 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, and 21.
verse 18. **Your hand** <note>Hebrew: _et yadecha_</note> The particle **et** is omitted by manuscripts 2 and 3.
verse 20. **Good** <note>Hebrew: _tov_</note> Without the emphasis mark <term>Dagesh</term> in manuscripts 3 and 4.
verse 22. **You** <note>Hebrew: _atah_</note> Stressed on the first syllable <term>milel</term> in 1, 2, 6, 9, and 20. Others stress the final syllable <term>milra</term>.
verse 23. For **This** <note>Hebrew: _zoh_</note>, editions 6, 9, 20, and 21 have the variation **zoht**, against the Masoretic tradition of 1 and 2. However, the same editions note our reading in the margin. **I said** <note>Hebrew: _amarti_</note> with a double accent <term>Pashta gemin.</term> in 1, 3, 6, 9, 20, and 21.
verse 24. **And deep** <note>Hebrew: _ve-amok_</note> without the pause mark <term>Psik</term> in 6, 9, 20, and 21, against the Masoretic notes.
verse 26. **And I find** <note>Hebrew: _u-motze_</note> spelled with the vowel *Segol* in 1, 2, 4, 6–9, 15, and 23, according to Masoretic tradition. Others use the vowel *Tsere*.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Ecclesiastes (Kohelet) Chapter 7 and transitions into Chapter 8. The previous page discussed the value of patience and the dangers of anger and bribery. # ECCLESIASTES CHAPTER 7 & 8

<margin>
verse 28. a) *this—one from a thousand:* <note>original: "huius- nem, unum ex mille"</note> that is, one set apart from a huge multitude of people, sinners, and the defiled (compare Psalm 91:7). This is an enigmatic description <term>periphrasis</term> of CHRIST; see notes on Job 33:23, Song of Solomon 5:10, as well as Romans 5:14-19 and 1 Timothy 2:5. b) *I found* (verses 26, 29) through the illumination of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 11:27, 1 Corinthians 12:3). c) *and that woman* refers to evil desire <note>original: "pravam concupiscentiam"</note> (verse 26) existing in all those people, or in the entire remaining multitude of humanity (compare verse 20 and Romans 3:23). They are connected this way by the musical accents. d) *I did not find* (verse 27) namely, in that one man out of thousands. For He was free from all sin and set apart from sinners (Isaiah 53:9, 11; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15, 7:25).

verse 29. e) *Only, behold this alone, I found* (verses 27, 28) that God created man with his wife upright (Genesis 1:27, 31). f) *but they themselves, by the devil's suggestion, sought out what were* (verses 25, 28) *reasonings or inventions* <note>original: "ratiocinationes f. inventiones"</note> (2 Chronicles 26:15), many and infinite; or of many and great things; so that they might even equal the knowledge of God himself (Genesis 3:5). In this way, they brought sin and all evils upon themselves and their descendants. Therefore, in times of adversity, a person should not murmur impatiently (Lamentations 3:39).

CHAPTER 8, verse 1. g) Who is like the truly Wise one, who faithfully observes these warnings of mine? And who worthily recognizes the interpretation <note>original: "interpretationem"</note> of the matter I have given so far? Here Solomon passes to his eighth precept regarding the obedient observation of the mandate of the supreme King in heaven (verses 2–15). Then the ninth precept begins, concerning the abandonment of curious prying into divine governance (verses 16–17), which is completed in chapter 9:1–10.
</margin>

<margin>
CHAPTER 8.
An *Aleph* in place of a *He*.
</margin>

28 Which my soul still seeks but I have not found: one man among a thousand I have found, but a woman among all these I have not found.
29 See, this alone I have found: that God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes.

# CHAPTER 8

1 Who is like the wise? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A man’s wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.
2 I say: Keep the king’s command because of the oath of God.
3 Do not be hasty to leave his presence; do not take a stand in an evil matter, for he does whatever he pleases.
4 Where the word of a king is, there is power; and who may say to him, "What are you doing?"
5 Whoever keeps a command will know no evil thing; and a wise heart knows both time and judgment.
6 For every matter has a time and judgment, though the misery of man is heavy upon him.
7 For he does not know what will happen; for when it happens, who can tell him?
8 No man has power over the spirit to restrain the spirit, and no one has power over the day of death. There is no discharge in that war, and wickedness will not deliver those who are given to it.
9 All this I have seen, and applied my heart to every work that is done under the sun: there is a time in which man rules over man to his own hurt.
10 And so I saw the wicked buried, who had come and gone from the place of holiness, and they were forgotten in the city where they had so acted. This also is vanity.
11 Because the sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.
12 Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and his days are prolonged, yet I surely know that it will be well with those who fear God, who fear before Him.
13 But it will not be well with the wicked, nor will he prolong his days, which are as a shadow, because he does not fear before God.
14 There is a vanity which occurs on earth: there are righteous men to whom it happens according to the work of the wicked, and there are wicked men to whom it happens according to the work of the righteous. I said that this also is vanity.
15 So I commended enjoyment, because a man has nothing better under the sun than to eat, drink, and be merry; for this will remain with him in his labor all the days of his life which God gives him under the sun.

***

**VIII, verse 1.** The word for "schemes" <note>Hebrew: חִשְׁבֹנוֹת</note> appears without a *Dagesh* <note>A dot in a Hebrew letter indicating doubling or a harder sound</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 4, 12, and 16. **But** it is written as *chishbonot* <note>Hebrew: חִשְׁבֹּנֹות</note> in 6, 9, 20, and 21.
verse 29. The word "to know" <note>Hebrew: ידע</note> is written defectively <note>Missing a vowel letter</note> in manuscript 2; so also in some other sources, but printed differently in verse 7. The word for "interpretation" <note>Hebrew: פֵּשֶׁר</note> is written with a *Segol* vowel in 1, 3, 4, 6, 9, 20, and 21, contrary to the Masoretic notes from Erfurt.
verse 2. "And upon" <note>Hebrew: וְעַל</note> is written with a *Maqqaph* <note>A Hebrew hyphen</note> in 1, 3, and 4.
verse 3. "Do not be hasty" <note>Hebrew: תִּבָּהֵל</note> is written this way in 6 and 9 in the margin. **But** the same manuscripts, along with 3 and 20, use the *Piel* <note>intensive</note> verb form in the main text. Moreover, the phrase "be not hasty to go out of his sight" in 1 and 4 follows the construction used by the ancient translators.
verse 4. "In that" <note>Hebrew: בַּאֲשֶׁר</note> uses the *Merka* accent in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 20, 21, and 23.
verse 9. "Work" <note>Hebrew: מעשה</note> uses the *Munach* accent instead of *Metheg* in manuscript 1.
verse 10. "And from the place" <note>Hebrew: וממקום</note> uses the *Qamets* vowel in the absolute state in manuscript 4.
verse 12. "That so" <note>Hebrew: אשר כן</note> appears this way in 2, 4, 6, 9, 14, and 20.
verse 12. "Sinner" <note>Hebrew: חֹטֶא</note> uses the *Tsere* vowel in 2, 3, and 4, contrary to the Masoretic note for this location and chapter 7:26.
"Evil" <note>Hebrew: רע</note> uses the *Qamets* vowel in 1, 6, 9, 14, and 20, following the Masoretic list. Others use the *Patach* vowel.
verse 13. "God" <note>Hebrew: האלהים</note> includes the prefix *He* <note>The definite article "the"</note> in 2, 4, 6, 9, 14, 20, and 23; and so it was in manuscript 3.

# ECCLESIASTES CHAPTER 8 & 9

<margin>
verse 16. a) *After I gave/applied my heart and mind to know wisdom and to perceive the occupation etc.* Then I saw verse 17. Solomon transitions here to the ninth precept, by which the overly curious investigation of divine government is prohibited, as was already cautioned above at verse 1. b) *sleep he does not see/take* <note>original: "somnum non videt f. capit"</note> namely, my heart, or a person who is so insanely curious. Compare earlier in chapter 2:23 and Psalm 127:2.
</margin>

**16** When I applied my heart to know wisdom and to see the business that is done on earth—even though one sees no sleep in his eyes day or night—
**17** then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man may toil in seeking, he will not find it out; even if a wise man claims to know it, he cannot find it out.

<margin>
CHAPTER IX, verse 1. c) *For all this,* namely what I said in chapter 8:16–17 regarding the unsearchable depth of divine works, I laid to my heart, to accurately discuss or select and prove (Job 33:3). Specifically, that the righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand and direction of God, who approves, cares for, and protects them; nevertheless, no man knows either the love or the hatred of God from external events and things, whether prosperous or adverse. For both love and hatred from God are "before" the men themselves <note>meaning they are hidden from human sight or currently present in their experience without clear explanation</note>; since calamities sometimes happen to the pious, and on the contrary, the most happy successes often happen to the impious and those hated by God (compare verse 2). Ecclesiastes certainly confirms by his authority and continues his ninth precept about omitting insane curiosity regarding divine government (verses 1–6), and he finishes this by adding an exhortation to joyful and tranquil satisfaction (verses 7–10). Then he adds a tenth precept about wisdom being both greatly valued and pursued (verses 11–18 and chapter 10:1–15).
</margin>

### Chapter IX.

**1** For all this I laid to my heart, even to clear up all this: that the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God; whether it be love or hatred, man knows it not; all is before them.

**3** This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that there is one event unto all; yea, also the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.

**7** Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart; for God now accepts thy works.

# ECCLESIASTES CHAPTER 9 & 10

<meta>This page continues the transcription and commentary of Ecclesiastes, specifically covering the transition from Chapter 10 into the famous exhortations of Chapters 11 and 12. The previous page discussed the impact of wisdom and folly in the social sphere; here, the focus shifts to the exhaustion of fools, the proper conduct of rulers, and the call to lead a life of active charity and early piety before the onset of old age.</meta>

# ECCLESIASTES. CHAPTERS 10, 11, 12.

<margin>
verse 15. a) **The labor of fools**, spent in useless talk (verse 14), **will weary every one of them.** <note>The commentator notes the use of the Hebrew Piel verb form, suggesting intensive or repeated action; compare Joshua 7:3.</note> b) **because he knows not how to go to the city.** This is a proverbial and parabolic expression, meaning: He does not know the right or efficient way to conduct his business. Therefore, the author means to say, true wisdom must be sought above all else.

verse 17. c) **But your blessings are.** <note>original Latin: "Felicitates vero tuae sunt"</note> "Well is it for you!" or "Happy are you!" Compare 1 Kings 10:8 and Psalm 1:1. d) **son of nobles**, or of the freeborn and courageous; not by lineage alone, but especially in spirit, one of the valiant. Compare 1 Kings 21:8, 11 and Nehemiah 5:7. e) **for strength** (chapter 9:16) and not for heavy drinking. <note>The commentator notes the feminine form of the word in Esther 1:8 and compares the sentiment to Romans 13:14 in the New Testament. He also distinguishes this term for drinking (*sheti*) from the term for a "warp" or "stamen" in weaving found in Leviticus 13:52.</note>

verse 18. f) **Through the laziness of both hands** the rafters shall sink: and through the dropping of the hands, the house shall leak from the rain.

CHAPTER 11. verse 1. g) **Cast your bread upon the waters.** This expression seems to be taken from the context of maritime trade or navigation. It begins the 13th precept concerning the prompt and liberal giving of alms (verses 1–5), which is followed by the 14th and final precept concerning the study of piety, which should be started early in life (verses 6–10; chapter 12:1–7).

CHAPTER 12. verse 1. h) **First of all, remember your Creators**, that is, the Triune God who created you; compare Genesis 1:26, Isaiah 54:5, and Psalm 149:2. This final chapter (I) completes the 14th precept regarding the early study of piety, using the inconveniences and infirmities of old age as the primary reason (verses 1–7). (II) It concludes the entire book by repeating the opening theme (epanalepsis) from chapter 1:2, providing a brief recapitulation of the arguments: 1) The vanity of the world has been abundantly proven (verse 8). 2) Solomon’s authority, which has been emphasized throughout (verses 9–12). 3) The final conclusion and the sum of all doctrine (verses 13–14).
</margin>

**15** ...what will be; and what shall be after him, who can tell him? **16** The labor of the foolish wearies him, because he does not know how to go to the city. **17** Woe to you, O land, when your king is a child, and your princes eat in the morning! **18** Blessed are you, O land, when your king is the son of nobles, and your princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness! **19** By much slothfulness the building decays; and through idleness of the hands the house drops through. **20** A feast is made for laughter, and wine makes merry: but money answers all things. Curse not the king, no not in your thought; and curse not the rich in your bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which has wings shall tell the matter.

An extra *He* <note>A note on a specific Hebrew letter in the manuscript.</note>

All that comes is vanity.

**9** Rejoice, O young man, in your youth; and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth, and walk in the ways of your heart, and in the sight of your eyes: but know, that for all these things God will bring you into judgment. **10** Therefore remove sorrow from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh: for childhood and youth are vanity.

<margin>
verse 18. **yimmakh** [will sink] requires the stress on the penultimate syllable according to some grammatical authorities <note>original: "milel"</note>, but all our codices resist this.
verse 20. **gam** [also] marked with a *Maqqeph* [hyphen] in codices 1, 3, 6, 9, 14, 20, 21.
CHAPTER 11. verse 1. **ha-panim** [the face/surface] thus with a *Patach* vowel in codices 3, 6, 9, 10, 13, 19.
