# ECCLESIASTES 12. CHAPTER 12

[And the light of the sun and the moon] and the stars [be not darkened], and the clouds return after the rain^a ^b : In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves^c , and the grinders cease^d because they are few, and those that look out of the windows are darkened^e : And the doors shall be shut in the streets, when the sound of the grinding is low, and he shall rise up at the voice of the bird, and all the daughters of music shall be brought low: Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goes to his eternal home, and the mourners go about the streets:

<margin>The <term>Keri<note>A marginal reading in the Hebrew Bible indicating how a word should be pronounced, as opposed to how it is written in the text.</note></term> suggests "be removed."</margin>

Until^f the silver cord is not loosed, nor the golden bowl broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern: Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it. Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher; all is vanity.^g And moreover, because the Preacher was wise, he still taught the people knowledge; yes, he gave good heed, and sought out, and set in order many proverbs. The Preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth. The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd. And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.

<margin>A "Large Samech" <note>This refers to the scribal tradition of writing the first letter of the word 'Sof' (End) larger than the others to mark the conclusion.</note></margin>

->The end of the matter, all has been heard: Fear God, and keep His commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.<-

For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil.

<column-break/>

a) Verse 2 begins to describe, with figurative words, what was said with plain words in verse 1. It adorns the diseases and inconveniences of exhausted old age with the most elegant words, so that this tedious delay might not be burdensome to youth. According to the view of Gussetius <note>Referring to Jacques Gousset (1635–1704), a prominent French Hebraist.</note> on page 805, this allegorical description of old age consists of more than one kind of comparison. In verse 2, man is viewed as a world, from which light and serenity are snatched away by the storms of old age; in verse 3, as a fortress whose preservation is impossible due to a lack of means for defending, resisting, feeding, or keeping watch; in verse 4, as a worn-out and useless mill; in verse 5, as a new infancy; in verse 6, as a shattered well. See more in the more abundant notes to this book.

b) "And they return," that is, other dark and sad clouds succeed after the previous rain.

v. 3. c) "And they shall bow themselves" (as in chapter 1:15), the men of strength, that is, the robust members of the body.

d) "And the grinders shall cease," the teeth, when they have been diminished in strength and number. <note>The commentator notes the grammatical shift from the Piel to the Kal verb form.</note>

e) "And those seeing through the openings or windows shall be darkened." Compare Genesis 7:1, etc. On this matter, see also Genesis 27:1, chapter 48:10, 1 Samuel 3:2, and 1 Kings 14:4.

v. 6. f) Remember, I say, your Creator (verse 1) before (verse 1-2) the silver cord is removed—that is, the noble thread of life—and the golden phial of the heart is crushed, and the pitcher is broken at the fountain—that is, the veins at the right ventricle of the heart; and the wheel is broken at the cistern; the pulse being destroyed and the circulation of the blood abolished. <note>This interpretation reflects 17th-century medical interests following Harvey's discovery of blood circulation.</note>

v. 8. g) The epilogue or conclusion of the book; see the note at verse 10.

# THE BOOK OF ESTHER, Hebrew: אֶסְתֵּר

<margin>
CHAPTER I, verse 1. a) See the notes on Ezekiel 1:1 and Ruth 1:1. b) Ahasuerus; not to be confused with Astyages <note>mentioned in Daniel 9:1 and Tobit 14:15</note>, the father of Cyaxares and father-in-law of Darius the Mede <note>Daniel 6:1</note>, nor with Cambyses <note>Ezra 4:6</note>. He is identified here as Xerxes, the fourth king of the Persians <note>Daniel 11:2</note>. c) The name, derived from the Persian language, signifies a "venerable prince" or "mighty king." d) From India <note>chapter 8:9</note> as the eastern boundary, to Cush—which some identify as Ethiopia and others as Arabia bordering Egypt—serving as the western boundary <note>Genesis 10:6</note>.

This first chapter recounts: I. The extremely lavish banquet of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes), held for the sake of ostentation (verses 1-8). II. A similar banquet given by Queen Vashti for the women (verse 9). III. The Queen's refusal to appear when summoned by the king (verses 10-12). IV. The subsequent consultation with the kingdom’s nobles (verses 13-20). V. The king's repudiation of her and the public decree commanding all women throughout the empire to obey their husbands (verses 21-22).

v. 4. e) Since he wished to display the riches of his kingdom's wealth <note>Genesis 31:1</note>.
v. 6. f) White material or white hangings <note>chapter 8:15</note>. g) Fine cotton, seemingly green; and hangings of hyacinth or blue color <note>Exodus 25:4</note>. h) The Vulgate translation says they were supported or suspended by cords of fine linen or purple <note>Ezekiel 28:5</note>. i) Upon silver rings <note>1 Kings 6:34</note>. k) And upon columns of marble <note>Song of Solomon 5:15; 1 Chronicles 29:2</note>. l) Couches for reclining at meals <note>chapter 7:8; Ezekiel 23:41</note>. m) Upon a pavement <note>Ezekiel 4:17-18; 1 Kings 19:6</note> of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and precious stones.
v. 7. n) And they provided drink <note>comparing the construction to chapter 2:3 and 3:11</note>. o) The vessels were different from one another <note>chapter 3:8</note>.
</margin>

<column-break/>

Named after its principal subject and written by an author unknown to us, this book has nonetheless always been numbered among the divine or canonical scriptures. It is not only concerned with demonstrating the wonderful providence of God toward His church, but it also illustrates the history of the people from whom the Messiah was eventually to be born. It describes the events that befell the Jews under the Persian king Ahasuerus (Xerxes): primarily, I. Esther's elevation to royal dignity through her marriage to the king (chapters 1–2); II. The deliverance of the Jews from a plotted extermination, including the events leading up to it (chapters 3–4), the accompanying circumstances (chapters 5–9:16), and the consequences (chapters 9:17–10:3).

<margin>2</margin> In those days, when King Ahasuerus sat on the throne of his kingdom, which was in Shushan the citadel,
<margin>3</margin> In the third year<gloss>e</gloss> of his reign, he made a feast for all his princes and his servants; the power of Persia and Media, the nobles and princes of the provinces, being before him.
<margin>4</margin> When he showed the riches<gloss>f</gloss> of his glorious kingdom and the honor of his excellent majesty many days, even one hundred and eighty days.

CHAPTER I, verse 1. *Reigned*: This is marked with a single <term>Paschta<note>A Hebrew accent mark.</note></term>, and thus is <term>milra<note>accented on the last syllable</note></term> in verses 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 14, according to the grammatical rules and the <term>Masora<note>The tradition of notes on the text of the Hebrew Bible.</note></term>. # THE SCROLL OF ESTHER 1:13–2:3

<margin>
v. 13. a) Schmidt translates this as "those who understand the times." Compare with 1 Chronicles 12:32. b) For this was how the king's business was usually handled in the presence of all who were experts in law and judgment—that is, those skilled in the laws and customs of the fatherland. This is a parenthesis.

v. 14. c) "And those closest to him." The Vulgate <note>the 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> reads: "Indeed, they were the first and closest." v. 18. i) Indeed, today if the noblewomen—or the primary wives <note>referencing 2 Kings 11:3</note>—should speak of this matter, then there will be a "sufficiency" of contempt from the wives and an "excess" of wrath from the husbands. Compare with verses 12 and 17.

I. The King commands that all the most beautiful virgins be gathered to choose a queen from among them (verses 1–7).

III. Brought to the king, she is chosen as queen (verses 12–17). 
IV. A banquet is held (verse 18). 
V. Mordecai reveals a conspiracy formed against the king (verses 19–23).

v. 14. y) To the second harem, in which the king’s concubines were kept.
z) Specifically <note>Latin: *nominatim*</note>. Compare with chapter 4:11 and 6:4.

**Textual Notes on Verse 3:** The word "she shall change" is written with a <term>Segol</term> <note>vowel mark</note> in the Erfurt Masorah and other manuscripts (numbers 2, 7, 8, etc.), while others use a <term>Tsere</term> <note>a different vowel mark</note>.
**Verse 5:** A "Petuchah" <note>an open paragraph break in a Torah scroll</note> section is found in manuscripts 1 and 3. The letter Daleth is written with a <term>Chateph-Qamets</term> <note>a brief 'o' vowel</note> in several manuscripts (1, 2, 3, etc.). The editor of the T-Codex noted that in corrected copies, the name **Mordecai** is always written with this specific vowel under the Daleth.
**Verse 14:** Regarding the phrase "into the hand of," the Eastern <note>Babylonian</note> tradition uses a slightly different preposition.

When the turn came for Esther—the daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her as his daughter—to go in to the king, she requested nothing except what Hegai the king's eunuch, keeper of the women, advised. And Esther won favor in the eyes of everyone who saw her. So Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, into his royal palace, in the tenth month, which is the month of Tebeth <note>A month in the Hebrew calendar corresponding to December/January</note>, in the seventh year of his reign. And the king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won his favor and kindness more than all the other virgins; so he set the royal crown upon her head and made her queen in place of [Vashti]. Then the king gave a great feast for all his princes and servants—Esther’s feast. He also proclaimed a holiday for the provinces and distributed gifts with royal liberality. When the virgins were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. Esther had not yet revealed her family or her people, just as Mordecai had commanded her; for Esther continued to follow Mordecai's instructions just as she had when she was being brought up by him.

In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the threshold, became angry and plotted to assassinate King Ahasuerus. But the plot became known to Mordecai, and he told it to Queen Esther, and Esther informed the king in Mordecai's name. When the matter was investigated and found to be true, both men were hanged on a gallows <note>Hebrew literally: "on a tree"</note>; and it was recorded in the Book of the Chronicles in the presence of the king.

In this chapter: I. The King exalts Haman above all others and commands that he be honored (verses 1-2). II. Mordecai, however, does not do so, and Haman is informed (verses 2-4). III. ### Technical Philological Notes

*   **verse 10.** **Sitting:** written in the "full" form <note>refers to the inclusion of vowel-helping letters in the Hebrew spelling</note> in manuscripts 3, 15, 22, and 23, following the Masoretic tradition. Printed in Jeremiah 29:16 and the final Masorah 37b. Others use the "defective" <note>shortened</note> spelling.
*   **verse 11.** **Before him:** uses the *Rebbia* accent in manuscripts 6, 9, 20, 21. **And they said to him:** thus with a *Dagesh* <note>a grammatical dot emphasizing a letter</note> in 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 20, 24, according to the Masorah. Seen also in Genesis 19:2, Daniel 5:11, and Rabbi Chajim's notes. Others omit the *Dagesh*.
*   **CHAPTER VII, verse 2.** **And it shall be given:** the letter *Tau* uses the *Segol* vowel in 4, 8, 10, 13, 17, 18, 19, 22, 23, 24, and the Berlin manuscript. But it uses a *Merca* or *Metheg* accent in 10-16, 19, 20-24, and Berlin. Finally, it appears with a *Munach* accent in 3. **verse 4.** **Damage:** with a *Segol* in 1, 2, 3, 4, 6-9, 14, 15, 20, 21. **verse 5.** **Who:** uses a *Maqqaph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in 6, 9, 14, 20, 21. **And where:** written joined and without an intervening hyphen in 1, 2, 3, 4. **verse 7.** **And the king:** uses the *Rebbia* accent in 1 and 3. But uses the *Kadma* accent in 4, 11, 17, 18, 22, 24, and Berlin.

6. 9. v. 3. "the governors" [Hebrew: והפחות] with the Kametz vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 20, 21. v. 4. <header>THE BOOK OF DANIEL, in Hebrew דניאל (Daniel)</header>

In Daniel, the following are to be noted: I. **HISTORICAL MATTERS**, 1) concerning Daniel and his companions brought into the court of Nebuchadnezzar, and there instructed in Chaldean science and language (chapter 1). 2) Concerning Nebuchadnezzar's first dream, explained by Daniel (chapter 2). 3) Concerning the colossus <note>The "colossus" refers to the giant golden statue.</note> erected for worship by the order of Nebuchadnezzar (chapter 3). 4) Concerning the decree of Nebuchadnezzar, and the unique fates described therein (chapter 4). 5) Concerning the feast of Belshazzar (chapter 5). 6) Concerning Daniel rescued from the lions' den (chapter 6). II. **PROPHETIC MATTERS**, 1) concerning the four beasts, symbolic of as many kingdoms (chapter 7). 2) Concerning the ram and the goat, figures of the Persian and Macedonian kingdoms (chapter 8). 3) Concerning the seventy weeks decreed upon the Jewish people (chapter 9). 4) Concerning the troubles under the Persian and Macedonian reigns, and especially the storm caused by Epiphanes <note>referring to Antiochus IV Epiphanes</note> (chapters 10, 11, 12).

---

**CHAPTER 1, v. 1. a)** "Year of three," that is, the third. Compare chapter 2:1. This chapter describes Daniel and his companions: **I.** Deportation from Judea to Babylonia (verses 1–4). **II.** Education in the court of Nebuchadnezzar (verses 5–7). **III.** Piety toward God (verses 8–17). and **IV.** Divine wisdom (verses 18–21). **b)** Of the reign of Jehoiakim, restored and confirmed by Nebuchadnezzar. See 2 Kings 24:1. **c)** He came again. See 2 Kings 24:1.
**2.** See Jeremiah 25:9 and chapter 36:29.

CHAPTER II, v. 1. s) In the year of two, that is, the second year. Chapter 1:1. Here is recorded a notable dream concerning the principal shifts of the world's empires until Christ and his kingdom; this was presented to Nebuchadnezzar (v. 1), sought in vain from the Magi (v. 2–13), but revealed to Daniel (v. 14–30). The content of the dream is found in verses 31–36, and the interpretation in verses 37–45, followed by the outcome for both Nebuchadnezzar and Daniel in verses 46–49.

v. 13. The word for "delicacy" <note>original: "פת־בג"</note> is divided in various manuscripts (2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 20, 23), and likewise in verse 16. For the phrase "than all the youths," several manuscripts follow specific vocalization patterns. In verse 17, some manuscripts add a "and" before "gave." In verse 18, the name "Nebuchadnezzar" is written with a *Kametz* vowel in several sources. # DANIEL. Chapter 2.

<margin>
v. 8. a) *From the truth, that is, Certainly* <note>original: "Ex verse, i. e. Certe"</note>; see also verses 45, 6, 3, and 24. b) *The Vulgate* <note>The standard Latin Bible translation.</note> says: "you are buying time" <note>original: "tempus redimitis"</note>. That is, you are making excuses and weaving delays so that you may avoid the business I have demanded of you. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> compares this with Ephesians 5:16 and Colossians 4:5. c) *Since* <note>original: "quandoquidem"</note>; as if to say, "in every view of that which..." see verses 10 and 40. d) *Some say: the matter has gone from me, through forgetfulness.* Others say: *it has gone out*, and others: *it is established*, or *the word is firmly decreed by me*. See verse 5.

v. 9. e) *The Vulgate: there is but one sentence/verdict for you.* See verses 13 and 15. The suffix is not understood subjectively, but objectively, as in Genesis 16:5, "the wrong done to me [which I suffer]," and Isaiah 53:11, "by his knowledge [by which he is known]." f) *namely the word.* The prefix *Vau* <note>The Hebrew/Aramaic letter 'And'.</note> is used here to explain or clarify, as in chapter 4, verse 10. g) *lying and corrupt;* chapter 6, verse 5. You are prepared, or you have made. *The Written Text* <note>term: Ketiv; the traditional spelling in the scroll</note> says: "you have prepared yourselves to speak."

v. 11. h) *Compare Acts 14:11.*

v. 12. i) *he was angry.* Compare the Targum Jonathan <note>An Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible.</note> on Genesis 40:2 and Esther 2:21.

v. 13. k) *The law therefore went forth, that is, it was published with solemn ritual.* Chapter 9:25; Luke 2:1.

v. 14. l) *he returned counsel and reason/discretion; by inquiring into the cause of the edict, and by pointing out both its cruelty and a way in which the King could be satisfied.*

v. 15. m) *The Vulgate: so cruel.* In Aramaic: *harsh;* or *it is so urgent.*

v. 20. n) *be it.* Chapter 3:18. *The prefix Lamed added to Future verbs makes them into a wish or a command.*

v. 21. o) *He changes the appointed times* (chapter 7:25) *and the seasons.* Two synonyms are joined here to imply that the revolutions of all times depend on God’s will, regardless of what or of what kind they may be.
</margin>

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>
CHAPTER III, v. 1 m) "He made a golden colossus" <note>original: "Fecit colossum aureum"</note> [chapter 2:31 etc.]. This chapter presents a singular example of divine providence toward Daniel’s companions, by which He miraculously rescued them from manifest danger of death—to which they were liable because they refused divine worship to Nebuchadnezzar’s Colossus. Structure: I. The courageous confession of those three men [v. 1-23]. II. Their miraculous rescue [v. 24 to the end]. n) "its width" (2) [Ezra 6:3; compare Genesis 9:27]. o) Dura: a place name.
</margin>

King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue, whose height was sixty cubits <note>About 90 feet or 27 meters</note> and its width six cubits; he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.
Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent to gather the satraps <term>satrap: a high-ranking provincial governor in the Babylonian and Persian empires</term>, the prefects, and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates, and all the officials of the provinces to come to the dedication of the statue which King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

<margin>
v. 2. p) "to gather the satraps," overseers [Ezra 5:3, 14] and "the princes," judges of a higher order (2), "treasurers" (2) [compare Ezra 5:17], "those skilled in the law" (2), "legal experts" (2) [verse 3], and all the "governors of the provinces" [verse 3]. "That they might come" [infinitive form of the word 'to come'; chapter 7:22] to the "dedication of the colossus" [Esther 6:16; verse 3, 17; 2 Chronicles 7:9].
</margin>

Then the satraps, the prefects, and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates, and all the officials of the provinces were gathered together for the dedication of the statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up; and they stood before the statue that Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
Then a herald cried aloud, "To you it is commanded, O peoples, nations, and languages:
At the moment you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon <term>trigon: a three-cornered stringed instrument</term>, harp, bagpipe, and all kinds of music, you shall fall down and worship the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up;"

<margin>
v. 6. q) "into the middle of the furnace" <note>original: "in medium fornacis"</note> [verse 25] of "burning fire" [Ezra 6:7].
</margin>

"and whoever does not fall down and worship shall that very hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace."
Therefore, at that time, as soon as all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, and all kinds of music, all the peoples, nations, and languages fell down and worshipped the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

# DANIEL. CHAPTER 3.

<margin>
v. 8. a) The ancient translators rightly rendered this as: *they accused the Jews*. <note>original: "accusarunt Iudaeos"</note> The literal idiom is *they ate the pieces*, or *they made slanders against the Jews*; compare chapter 6, verse 25 and the Syriac version of Romans 1:30. The root **קרץ** <term>karatz: to pinch or nip</term> means "to cut off" for the Hebrews (Job 33:6). For the Arabs, it means "to sting" or "to bite," which fits the idea of slanders by which a person’s downfall is prepared and deadly bites are inflicted. The use of the word *eating* <note>original: "Comedendi"</note> expresses the "sweetness" or satisfaction that informers feel when they gain something from the betrayal and loss of others.
</margin>

v. 9. b) The customary greeting for Eastern Kings; see chapter 2, verse 4.

**Critical Notes on the Text:**
v. 8. **in it** (**בֵהּ**) follows the Munich manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 20. **and they ate** (**וַאֲכַלוּ**) uses the Kametz vowel in manuscripts 3, 6, 9, 10, 20. | v. 10. **you placed** (**שָׂמְתָּ**) uses the letter Sin with a Kametz in most versions; this seems to be from a misapplied Masoretic note which likely refers to the later syllable rather than the first. But it uses Patach in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20. **the pipe** (**מַשְׁרוֹקִיתָא**) is spelled defectively (missing a letter) in 7, 8, 15, 22. Most others spell it in full. **and the bagpipe** (**וְסִיפֹּנְיָה**) is defective in 2, 3, 22; compare verse 21. | v. 12. **Jews** (**יְהוּדָיִן**) is spelled with a silent Aleph and a mobile Yod in manuscript 8. **them** (**יָתְהוֹן**) uses a Patach in the Hebrew Concordance 11, 12, 15, 16, 19, 21, 22, 23; but uses a Makkaph in 2. The rest use an anomalous Munach accent; however, see a similar sequence in Jeremiah 30:11. **Nego** (**נְגוֹ**) uses a Patach in 3, 6, 8, 9, 11—16, 19, 22, 23, 24. Others use a Dagesh. **Nego** in verse 15 uses a Darga accent in 7 and 8, which also use a Tsere vowel. **Not** (**לָא**) lacks the final Aleph in 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 23; these same manuscripts do the same in verse 21 and almost always hereafter. | v. 16. **Nebuchadnezzar** spelled this way in 2. But in 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, it uses a Rebhia accent with a Munach. Finally, **we do not need** (**אֲנַחְנָא לָא־חַשְׁחִין**) is found in 1. **Nebuchadnezzar** uses a Kametz with a Metheg in 6, 9, 10, 14. | v. 18. **we are** (**אִיתַיְנָא**) with a Yod in 6, 9, 10, 14, 23, and follows the scribal note (Keri) to include an extra Yod.

# DANIEL 3. CHAPTER 3.

<margin>
v. 19. a) Sevenfold. As if to say "seven for one," or seven times more than once. Specifically, the number one, placed before other numerals, indicates a multiple; compare the Targum on Jeremiah 17:18: "one two," meaning double. <note>original Latin: "Septuplo... unum duo, i. e. duplum."</note> b) "Above that which," that is, more than what had been seen or decreed. To "see" is sometimes used to mean to judge or decree; compare the synonym in chapter 1, verse 13. c) "To heat it." An infinitive in the Peal stem from the root **אזה** <term>azah: to heat or kindle</term>.
</margin>

<margin>19</margin> [Nebuchadnezzar commanded] the furnace to be heated seven times<sup>a</sup> more than it was usually seen<sup>b</sup> to be heated<sup>c</sup>.

<margin>
v. 20. d) "To bind," or "so that they might bind."
</margin>

<margin>20</margin> And he commanded the mightiest men in his army to bind<sup>d</sup> Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and to cast them into the burning fiery furnace.

<margin>
v. 22.
v. 21. 23. 24. e) "For casting them from on high." See verse 6.
</margin>

<margin>
<gloss>Extra letter Aleph (א)</gloss>
</margin>

<margin>
v. 21. f) "They were bound" (as in verse 20) in their *sarabarae* or *sarabalae* <note>original Latin: "sarabaris, vel sarabalis"</note>; see verse 27. This signifies breeches or trousers that usually hang down to the feet. The root is **סרבל** <term>sarbel: to cover or wrap</term>. g) The Vulgate translates this as "tiaras," which were head-coverings used among the Persians. Perhaps they are like the *petasos* <note>a broad-brimmed hat</note> of the Latins and Greeks; from **פשט** <term>pashat: to extend</term>, as in Isaiah 23:13. h) The Greek version says "leggings," the Arabic "greaves," and the Vulgate "shoes." These are named from **כרבל** <term>karbal: to cover</term>, because they cover the feet; compare the root in 1 Chronicles 15:27.
</margin>

<margin>21</margin> Then these men were bound in their trousers<sup>f</sup>, their tunics<sup>g</sup>, and their turbans<sup>h</sup>, and their other clothes, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace.

Ezra 4:17. **g)** *This demand is by the word of the holy ones.* This is an explanation of the previous part. Therefore, in this place, *word* means the same as *decree*; the *holy ones* are the same as the *watchers* (compare **v. 10**); and the *demand* is the same as the *word*. It is called a *demand* or *petition* because the decree was made as if by a formal vote or request. **h)** *To the intent that*, or *to this end*, and *for this reason*, as in **v. 22**.

# DANIEL. CHAPTERS 4 and 5.

<margin>
**V. 24. a)** *Therefore let my counsel (1) cf. Nehemiah 5:7, be pleasing to you; that is, let it find favor with you, as in chapter 3:32.* **b)** *Namely (the "and" here is explanatory, as in verse 21) your sins (1) and especially your injustice.* **c)** *...through the opposite, which is righteousness, whether understood generally as a zeal for what is good and right, or specifically as giving each person their due. The Vulgate and others translate this as "alms," a meaning sometimes found in Syriac, Chaldee [Aramaic], Arabic, and Rabbinic writings; however, here it denotes righteousness because it is contrasted with sins, and it is most appropriate for a king, to whom this speech is directed, as it is a virtue proper to kings.* <note>original Latin: "Vulg. aliique eleemosynis... hic tamen iustitiam potiùs denotat"</note> **d)** *The Vulgate and others translate this as "redeem," following Chaldee and Syriac usage; but more correctly it is "break off" or "sever," as in Genesis 27:40 and Exodus 31. For nowhere in the Holy Scriptures are human sins said to be redeemed, but rather the humans themselves are said to be redeemed.* **e)** *...and your iniquities (1), especially those which sprouted from a lack of mercy and from cruelty, break them off by showing mercy to the poor, or through compassion toward the poor and miserable.* **f)** *(1) perhaps (chapter 2:3, 6, 9, cf. Acts 9:22). The Vulgate, Greek, and Arabic versions translate "perhaps" (cf. Amos 5:15, Joel 2:14, Jonah 3:9, Zephaniah 2:3).* **g)** *...it will be an extension (2, chapter 7:12) of your tranquility (1), so that just as you have been until now, you may continue to be safe and flourishing (verse 1).*

**v. 30. h)** *It is completed or fulfilled.* **i)** *...until his hair grew like the hair of eagles, and his nails (2, chapter 7:19) like the nails of birds.*

**CAP. V. v. 1. k)** *A banquet (1) cf. Isaiah 21:4-5. This chapter has four parts: I. The King's sacrilege (vv. 1-4). II. The subsequent omen (vv. 5-6). III. The interpretation of the omen, partly as impossible for the profane (vv. 7-9), partly as clear and easy for Daniel (vv. 10-29). IV. The fulfillment of the interpretation (v. 30).*
</margin>

...the tree [is] your kingdom, which shall be established for you from the time you acknowledge that the Heavens rule.

# DANIEL. CHAPTER 5.

<margin>
**verse 16. a)** *Interpretations, to interpret*, that is, to provide explanations. The Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> renders this as "to interpret obscure things."
**b)** *knots*, that is, things that are entangled and difficult, *to loosen*. See verse 12 and the note on verse 7.
**verse 17. c)** *Let them be yours*, that is, *let them remain, or, keep those things for yourself*. This uses a future tense with a prefixed *Lamed* functioning as an imperative, as seen in chapter 2:20. Daniel rejects the offered dignities and rewards so that the impious King may feel even more seriously that the matter at hand is grave. **d)** *and your rewards* (2) as in chapter 2:6. Others translate this as: *give them to another rather than to me*.
</margin>

...whose name was Belteshazzar. Now let Daniel be called, and he will show the interpretation. <margin>Extra letter *He*</margin>

**13** Then Daniel was brought in before the king. The king spoke and said to Daniel: "Are you that Daniel, who is one of the captives of Judah, whom the king my father brought from Judah?" <margin>Aramaic grammar note: *pel-eil*</margin>

**14** "And I have heard concerning you, that the spirit of the gods is in you, and that light and understanding and extraordinary wisdom have been found in you." <margin>Extra letter *Yod*</margin>

**15** "And now the wise men and the astrologers were brought in before me, that they might read this writing and make its interpretation known to me, but they were not able to show the interpretation of the matter." <margin>Extra letter *Yod*</margin>

**16** "And I have heard concerning you, that you are able to give interpretations and to loosen knots. Now if you are able to read the writing and make its interpretation known to me, you shall be clothed in purple and have a chain of gold around your neck, and you shall rule as third in the kingdom." <margin>Reading: "you are able"</margin> <margin>Reading: "you are able"</margin> <margin>Reading: "the chain"</margin>

<margin>
**verse 19. f)** *they trembled*, that is, they shook and were afraid, as in chapter 6:27. **g)** The Vulgate says *he struck*, from the root *macha* (to strike) as in chapter 2:34-35. But more correctly, *he allowed to live*, as the Syriac version has *he preserved*. This is a participle in the *Aphel* form <note>An Aramaic grammatical structure indicating causing an action</note> from the root *chaya* (to live), with the middle radical *vav* or *yod* removed; similar forms are found in the Targum <note>Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> for 1 Samuel 2:6. This interpretation is required by the contrast and the parallel structure of the sentences.
**verse 20. h)** *But after his heart was lifted up*. See Jeremiah 48:29, Ezekiel 28:2, 5, 17, Proverbs 16:18, and chapter 18:12. **i)** *and his spirit was hardened*, or *became strong*, like a tree that becomes so hard it can no longer be bent (chapter 4:8, 19), leading to pride.
**(1)** Compare the Hebrew in Nehemiah 9:10, 16, 29. *he was deposed*, by a disaster sent by God (chapter 4:22) from his throne.
**(3)** chapter 7:9. **8)** *they caused his honor to pass away*, used impersonally to mean "his honor was taken away from him." chapter 4:28.
</margin>

**17** Then Daniel answered and said before the king: "Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another; nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king and make the interpretation known to him." <margin>Extra letter *He*</margin>

**18** "O king, the Most High God gave to Nebuchadnezzar your father the kingdom, and greatness, and honor, and majesty." <margin>Reading: "Most High"</margin>

**19** "And because of the greatness that He gave him, all peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him. Whomever he wished, he killed; and whomever he wished, he kept alive; and whomever he wished, he raised up; and whomever he wished, he brought low." <margin>Reading: "trembled"</margin>

**20** "But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him." <margin>Reading: "they took away"</margin>

**21** "And he was driven from the sons of men, and his heart was made like the beasts, and his dwelling was with the wild donkeys. They fed him grass like oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, until he knew that the Most High God rules in the kingdom of men, and He sets over it whomever He wishes." <margin>Reading: "Most High"</margin> <margin>Extra letter *Yod*</margin> <margin>Extra letter *He*</margin>

<margin>
**verse 21. k)** *with the heart of a beast*, etc. The written text (*Ketiv*) says *it was made equal*, but according to the traditional reading (*Keri*) it is *they made equal*, used impersonally, which however is equivalent to a passive in the Aramaic idiom; just as the following *they fed* him is used instead of *he was fed*. See the note for chapter 4:22. According to those codices that have *shavvi* at the end of the *Keri*, it can be explained as "God placed or made equal" (verse 8), or, "Nebuchadnezzar placed his own heart with the wild beasts": however, both are a bit of a stretch.
</margin>

**22** "And you, Belshazzar his son, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this." <margin>Extra letter *Yod*</margin>

**verse 12.** *u-pish-dah* ("and its interpretation"): thus in manuscripts 1 and 2.
**verse 14.** *yatirah* ("extraordinary"): thus with a *He* in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 14, 17, 20, 23, 24 according to Masorah <note>The traditional system of notes on the Hebrew Bible text</note> 2. Others use the letter *Aleph*.
**verse 15.** *ha-alu* ("were brought"): thus with a *Dagesh* <note>A pronunciation dot in Hebrew/Aramaic</note> in 1, 6, 9, 10, 20, 23, following Masorah 1 and the Erfurt manuscript. Others lack the *Dagesh*.
The word *tukhal* ("you are able"): manuscripts 1, 2, 3 have *tu-khal* instead of *ti-ukhal* without a distinction between the written and read forms, against the Masorah and Erfurt.
**verse 16.** *pishar* ("interpretation"): thus with a *Kamets* vowel and without the *Mappiq* dot, following Masorah 1 and the Erfurt manuscript in this verse and verse 15.
**verse 17.** *u-ne-vaz-be-yata-kh* ("and your rewards"): thus with a double accent as required by the Masorah and the 1521 Venice edition.
However, some manuscripts either omit the *Merka* accent or place a *Metheg* there. Furthermore, the letter *Beth* appears with a *Kamets* or *Kamets-Chatuf* in manuscripts 8, 15, 17, Berlin, and perhaps more; but with a *Patach* in 1, 3, 22. Compare chapter 2:6. *qov* with a *Kamets* in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20.
**verse 20.** *ve-yiqarah* ("and his glory"): thus with the letter *He* in 1, 3, 7, 8, 15, 22, according to Masorah 1 and Erfurt here and in verse 15. Yet Masorah 2 requires an *Aleph*, which others have.
**verse 21.** *shavvi-u* ("they made equal"): with the *Keri* reading, which many omit; correctly in 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 22, following Masorah and Erfurt. *ve-yit-stab-ba* ("and it was wet") with a *Kamets* in 1 and 3, against Masorah 2 and Erfurt. *ale-hah* ("over it") with a *Kamets* in several manuscripts, against Masorah 2.
**verse 22.** *yada-ta* ("you knew"): with a *Kamets* in 3, 6, 9, 20, 23, against Masorah 1 and 2 and Erfurt.
**verse 23.** *shemayya* ("heaven") without the *Pesiq* mark in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, 21. *shatayin* ("drinking") without the plural *yod* in 1, 6, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 20, 23.

# DANIEL CHAPTER 5 & 6

<margin>
**verse 23. a)** Compare with Psalm 115:4 and following verses. 
**b)** In whose hand—that is, in whose power—your vital breath is; he can either preserve or destroy your life at his pleasure. See Genesis 2:7 and Isaiah 42:5. Also, "with whom are all your ways," referring to the direction and outcome of your life. See Jeremiah 10:23 and Proverbs 3:6.
**verse 24. c)** *was sent out*. The Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> translates this as "the knuckles of the hand." See verse 5.
**verse 25. d)** *Numbered* or *Defined*. Belshazzar's kingdom was defined by God, and that with a precise and strict limit. See verse 26. 
**e)** That is, *weighed*, a form of the word *Peres* in verse 28. 
**f)** "And they are the ones dividing it," meaning *divided*. Compare with verse 28.
**verse 26. g)** Regarding the first word *Mene*, which signifies "defined" or "numbered" in verse 25: He has defined it within its own terms and limits, so that it will not progress any further, much less be eternal. Compare with chapter 1:5, 10 and Isaiah 14:20. 
**h)** He has completed it; it is now at the point where He brings its fatal end. See Isaiah 38:12-13 and Job 23:14.
**verse 29. i)** *He ordered that they should clothe him*—though this likely was never fully realized, both because Daniel had previously refused this honor in verse 17, and because Belshazzar was killed that very night, changing the state of affairs entirely. See verse 30. 
**k)** *And they made a proclamation over him*. See chapter 3:4 and compare with Genesis 41:43 and Esther 6:11. This proclaimed that he would be the third ruler in the kingdom. See above at verse 7.
**verse 30. l)** That is, the last ruler of the Chaldean <note>Babylonian</note> nation; in contrast to Darius the Mede in chapter 6:1 and Cyrus the Persian in chapter 10:1.
**CHAPTER 6, verse 1. m)** In contrast, Darius the Mede, also known as Cyaxares, the son of Ahasuerus (Astyages the Mede). See chapter 9:1. He was the father-in-law and uncle of Cyrus. See the Preface to Ezra, section 10.
**verse 2. n)** Here at last a new subject begins concerning Daniel: I. His being cast into the lions' den because of his devotion to God (verses 2–19). II. His miraculous preservation and removal from the den (verses 20–29).
</margin>

**23** "...you have drunk from them, and you have praised the gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which do not see, nor hear, nor know. But the God in whose hand is your breath, and to whom all your ways belong, you have not honored."

**24** "Then from His presence was sent the palm of the hand, and this writing was inscribed."

**25** "And this is the writing that was inscribed: **MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and UPHARSIN**." <note>These are Aramaic terms for units of weight and currency: Minas, Shekels, and Half-shekels.</note>

**26** "This is the interpretation of the matter: **MENE**—God has numbered your kingdom and finished it."

**27** "**TEKEL**—you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting."

**28** "**PERES** <note>The singular form of *Pharsin*</note>—your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians."

**29** Then Belshazzar gave the command, and they clothed Daniel in purple <margin>the read version says: "and a chain"</margin> and placed a chain of gold around his neck, and they made a proclamation concerning him that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom.

**30** In that very night, Belshazzar, the Chaldean king, was killed.

## CHAPTER 6
<margin>The read version says: "appearance"</margin>

**1** And **Darius** the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.

**2** It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom one hundred and twenty satraps <note>term: satrap: a provincial governor in the ancient Persian empire</note> to be throughout the whole kingdom.

**3** And over them were three supervisors—of whom Daniel was one—so that these satraps might give an account to them, and the king should suffer no loss.

**4** Then this Daniel distinguished himself above the supervisors and the satraps because an extraordinary spirit was in him; and the king planned to set him over the entire realm.

**5** Then the supervisors and the satraps sought to find a ground for complaint against Daniel concerning the kingdom; but they could find no ground for complaint or corruption, because he was faithful, and no negligence or corruption was found in him.

**6** Then these men said, "We shall not find any ground for complaint against this Daniel unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God."

**7** Then these supervisors and satraps came by agreement to the king and spoke thus to him: "King Darius, live forever!"

# DANIEL CHAPTER 6

<margin>
**v. 8. a)** *They came together by agreement*; the Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin Bible translation</note> says "they entered into a council." Psalm 83:4. **b)** *The princes*. In verse 3 above, this term referred to the three supreme overseers of the kingdom, but here it is used more broadly, and the following names of ranks are included under it as specific types. **c)** Namely the overseers (Chapter 2, verse 48) and the Satraps (Chapter 3, verse 2), the leaders (Chapter 3, verse 24), and the governors (Chapter 2, verse 3). **d)** That the King might establish (firmly sanction) a statute. (Verse 9) and that he might strengthen (make valid) a bond—that is, a prohibition. See verses 9, 10, 13, 14, 19; compare with Numbers 30:3.

See verse 16; Chapter 3:28; Ezra 6:11; Esther 1:19 and 8:8. **f)** *Which shall not pass away*—meaning a perpetual and fundamental law. See Chapter 4:28; 7:14; Esther 1:19. **v. 11. g)** He entered his house from the court. See Chapter 3:24. **v. 14. n)** That is, "he had no regard for you." See Chapter 3:12. **o)** *He asks his petition*. Verses 16, 20, 23 omit this, but see verse 8. The word *ityatu* <note>meaning "they consulted"</note> is written with a *Qamets* vowel in versions 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20. The king is depicted as distressed and searching for a legal loophole to save Daniel, but he is ultimately bound by the unchangeable law of the Medes and Persians.</summary>

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>1</margin> In the first year of Belshazzar <sup>m</sup> king of Babylon, Daniel had a dream and visions of his head while on his bed. Then he wrote down the dream, telling the main <sup>n</sup> facts. <margin>2</margin> Daniel spoke and said, "I saw..."

<column-break/>

*verse 18. a) & he sealed it with his own ring, and with the rings (or ring) of his nobles; so that the will (i) <note>original: "voluntas"</note> might not be changed; or, so that nothing would be done to Daniel that opposed the King's will. Chapter 3, verse 28. Others, following Syrian usage, translate this as "anything."*

*verse 19. b) and he passed the night (i) <note>original: "pernoctavit"</note>. From this comes the Hebrew word 'bayit' for house. c) in a fasting state (1) <note>original: "in statu incœnato"</note>. The Latin Vulgate says "un-supped" <note>original: "incœnatus"</note>. The Arabic root 'tawa' refers to a deliberate effort to eat nothing. d) Some say "foods"; Rabbi Solomon <note>This refers to Rashi, the famous 11th-century French rabbi</note> says "tables," following Mishnaic usage; others suggest "Songs" or "musical instruments."*

*The word 'chada' means he rejoiced, because they cheer one up; or, by rearranging the letters from 'dacha,' it means they drive away sorrow. e) his sleep (1) fled from him. Vulgate: "from him." Compare Genesis 31:40 and Esther 6:1.*

*verse 20. f) just before dawn (1) <note>original: "sub auroram"</note>. Root 'shafar' meaning to be beautiful (verse 2). He rose with the first light. (1) Compare Proverbs 4:18.*

*verse 21. g) with a sad voice, full of grief (1). Compare 2 Samuel 19:3.*

*verse 23. h) & he shut the mouths of the lions by His wondrous power. Psalm 91:13, Acts 28:3 and following, Hebrews 11:33.*

*verse 24. i) as far as the King was concerned, it was very good, or he was cheered. Compare verse 15. k) Genesis 15:6. Hence Hebrews 11:33: "Through faith they shut the mouths of lions."*

*verse 29. l) he conducted matters successfully. Chapter 3, verse 30.*

*CHAPTER VII, verse 1. m) Here begins the second part of the book, which is Prophetic, following a specific chronological order. This Chapter explains a truly wonderful dream, which sets forth all the main turning points of the supreme Empires of the world, until the very end of the world. It has three parts: I. Introduction (v. 1-2). II. The dream itself, both as it was seen (v. 2-15) and as it was explained (v. 15-27). III. The conclusion (v. 28). n) & the head, that is, the entire sum. Psalm 119:160, Proverbs 8:26. Others say he told a brief summary of the matters or words.*

---

*verse 18. "With the signet rings" [Aramaic: ub-ezqata] written with a Kamatz vowel, thus plural... verse 21. "In his drawing near" [Aramaic: ub-miqrebeh] using the letter Beth... verse 24. "Who believed" [Aramaic: di heimin]... verse 26. "Darius" written with a Metheg mark, which others omit... CHAPTER VII, verse 1. For "to Belshazzar," which the accent mark [Maqqaf] requires, some manuscripts have a different spelling... "He said" [Aramaic: amar] written with a Kamatz vowel...*

> **v. 4.** *Made to stand* <note>original: הֳקִימַת</note> requires a *Chateph-seghol* <note>a specific vowel mark</note> according to the *Masorah* printed here. In regular forms indeed by *Chateph-qamets* 23. and the *Leiden Manuscript* with the note added "it is found twice in the Masorah," namely here and **verse 4** as Cocceius witnesses in the *Chaldean Lexicon* under the root *qum*. **v. 14.** *Everlasting* <note>Aramaic: "alam"</note> with a Chateph-Pathach vowel in manuscripts 1, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20. *Shall be destroyed* with a Kamatz vowel in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, 23, contrary to the Basel Index folio 61, column 8. **v. 15.** *Alarmed me* with a Kamatz in 3, 6, 9, 20, contrary to the Basel Index. **v. 16.** *I asked* written this way in 2, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 19, 21. **v. 17.** Of those horns. <margin>
**v. 13. a)** **But another certain Holy One said**, that is, an Angel (cf. 4:10), taking up the speech of the former by asking a question of that unnamed Holy One (†) (cf. 1 Sam. 21:3, 2 Kings 6:8, Ruth 4:1) who was speaking; likely Gabriel (cf. v. 16 and 10:21). **b) How long shall this vision last?** That is, the vision of the removal of the perpetual worship or daily sacrifice (v. 11). Here and the following genitives designate the object of the vision; the "vision" itself is used here to represent the things actually seen. It asks: How long will the removal of the daily sacrifice last, along with the other evils foreshadowed in this vision? **c) And the vision of the desolating transgression**—used transitively as in 12:11 (cf. 11:31)—that is, that which brings about desolation (cf. Ezek. 21:30, 34; 35:5). **d) Finally, that vision of giving**, that is, concerning the giving over of both the Sanctuary and the host—the people of God (cf. v. 10, 11, 14)—to be trampled <note>original: 'in conculcationem'</note>, like something thrown to the ground to be crushed underfoot (v. 10, 11; Micah 7:10).
</margin>

**...one holy one**<sup>a</sup> **speaking: "How long shall be the vision concerning the daily sacrifice**<sup>b</sup> **and the desolating transgression**<sup>c</sup> **to give over**<sup>d</sup> **both the sanctuary and the host to be trampled underfoot?"** **14** **And he said to me: "For two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings; then shall the sanctuary be vindicated."**

# DANIEL. CHAPTER 10.

<margin>
**v. 1. a)** *A great host* or *a great warfare*; used metonymically <note>a figure of speech where one thing is called by the name of something associated with it</note> to represent a *great sequence and series of future events*, or it deals with a *great and heavy warfare* in which the people of God will have to struggle against far more dangerous enemies. Compare Isaiah 40:1, Job 7:1, and 14:14.
**b)** The Vulgate <note>the 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> reads: *For understanding is needed in a vision.* But because the accent is on the *penultimate* syllable, as in Psalm 5:2, we prefer to explain it as an Imperative with the paragogic He <note>an additional letter at the end of a word for emphasis or grammatical mood</note>, meaning: *pay attention, I say, to that word;* compare similar syntax in Psalm 73:17. See also Matthew 24:15 and 2 Timothy 2:7. According to Geier <note>Martin Geier (1614–1680), a prominent Lutheran commentator</note>, this chapter serves as the Prologue to the following visions in chapters 11 and 12. Indeed, we find here I. *what* the Prophet saw, where we note 1) the *time of the vision* etc. v. 1; 2) the *occasion* v. 2, 3; 3) the *place* v. 4; 4) the *manner* v. 5; 5) the *person revealing* v. 5, 6; 6) the *disciple being instructed* v. 7, 8; 7) the *consequence*, both the *dread* and the *removal of that dread*, v. 8, 9, 10. II. *what he heard*, where one should attend to 1) the *opening* v. 11; 2) the *account of the prayer being heard*, both concerning the angelic mission v. 12 and the delay v. 13; 3) the *promise* of the revelation of future things v. 14; 4) the *strengthening* of the one who was terrified v. 15-19; 5) the *continuation of the message* v. 20, 21.

### Technical Notes on the Text
**verse 17.** The word **from now on** <note>Hebrew: me'attah</note> is accented on the final syllable according to manuscript 1. **verse 19.** The word **and as he spoke** uses the letter *Caph* instead of *Beth* in several manuscripts. **verse 20.** The word **why** <note>Hebrew: lammah</note> is accented with an *Ithib* mark in various manuscripts (6, 9, 10, etc.). **verse 21.** The phrase **what is inscribed in the writing** appears as such in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, etc. The word **in the writing** uses a *Patach* vowel in most sources.

**CHAPTER XI, verse 1.** The name **Darius** is written with a *Metheg* mark in manuscripts 1, 3, 17, and others, though some omit it. Instead of **the Mede**, the main text of some books reads **the King**. **verse 2.** The word **he shall enrich** uses the letter *Beth* instead of *Caph* in many versions. **verse 3.** Instead of **mighty**, some have **great**. The marginal reading for **dominion** uses a *Patach* vowel, contrary to the printed Masoretic text. **verse 4.** The word **and when he has arisen** uses *Beth* instead of *Caph* in several manuscripts. **verse 6.** The phrase **daughter of the king** is found in all major manuscripts. The word **agreement** <note>literally "upright things"</note> has a *Silluk* accent instead of *Atnach* in manuscript 3. The word **she shall not retain** follows the Eastern tradition against the Masoretic printed text. The word **and her father** <note>literally "the one who begot her"</note> is written without the *Mappik* dot in manuscripts 1 and 2.

### Technical Notes on the Hebrew Text
<note>This section translates the scholarly footnotes at the bottom of the page regarding variations in different ancient manuscripts and the Masoretic tradition.</note>

Verse 10: **And he shall be stirred up** <note>original: *veyitgareh*</note> appears in the text without the usual alternate readings (Kethiv and Qere) in several manuscripts, including those from Erfurt.
Verse 11: **And he shall go out** <note>original: *veyatza*</note> follows the Tebhir accent in various codices.
Verse 12: **And it was exalted** <note>original: *veram*</note> is written according to the Kethiv in many sources, while some prefer the reading **yirum** (will be exalted).
Verse 13: **And he shall set forth** <note>original: *ve-he’emid*</note> uses the Pashta accent in many major manuscripts.
Verse 16: **And he shall stand in the land** is consistent across most major codices (1, 6, 9, 10, etc.).
Verse 18: **And he shall turn** <note>original: *vayashev*</note> is marked with the Darga accent without the Pesik mark in several versions, though some indices suggest the Pesik should be there.
Verse 19: **Toward the forts** <note>original: *le-ma’uzei*</note> includes a Dagesh (emphasis dot) in many copies, while others omit it.
Verse 23: **The joining** <note>original: *hitchabrut*</note> is written with the full spelling in several versions.
Verse 24: **With a small** <note>original: *be-me’at*</note> uses the Merca accent.
Verse 25: **They shall devise** <note>original: *yachshivu*</note> appears in the Piel <note>intensive</note> verb form in several Erfurt manuscripts.

verse 31. **k)** And "arms"—meaning garrisoned soldiers (see verses 15, 22). **l)** The sanctuary, or that famous fortress. **m)** See chapter 8:11 and chapter 12:11. **n)** They shall place there the abomination of desolation (see chapter 9:27). Compare 1 Maccabees 1:54 or 57, chapter 3:45, and 2 Maccabees 6:2.

</margin>
**32** And such as do wickedly against the covenant shall he corrupt by flatteries;<sup><gloss>o</gloss></sup> but the people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits.<sup><gloss>p</gloss></sup>

**33** And they that understand among the people shall instruct<sup><gloss>q</gloss></sup> many; yet they shall fall by the sword, and by flame, by captivity, and by spoil, many days.

**34** Now when they shall fall, they shall be helped with a little help; but many shall cleave to them with flatteries.

**35** And some of them of understanding shall fall, to try them, and to purge, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for a time appointed.

**36** And the king shall do according to his will; and he shall exalt himself, and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak marvelous things against the God of gods, and shall prosper till the indignation be accomplished; for that which is determined shall be done.

**37** Neither shall he regard the God of his fathers, nor the desire of women, nor regard any god; for he shall magnify himself above all.

**38** But in his estate shall he honor the God of forces; and a god whom his fathers knew not shall he honor with gold, and silver, and with precious stones, and pleasant things.

<margin>The traditional reading is "he shall recognize."</margin>
**39** Thus shall he do in the most strongholds with a strange god, whom he shall acknowledge and increase with glory; and he shall cause them to rule over many, and shall divide the land for gain.

**40** And at the time of the end shall the king of the south push at him; and the king of the north shall come against him like a whirlwind, with chariots, and with horsemen, and with many ships; and he shall enter into the countries, and shall overflow and pass over.

<margin>The letter Kaf has a "patah" <note>short 'a' vowel</note>.</margin>

<margin>The letter Kaf has a "patah" <note>short 'a' vowel</note>.</margin>

**43** But he shall have power over the treasures of gold and of silver, and over all the precious things of Egypt; and the Libyans and the Ethiopians shall be at his steps.

<margin>The letter Aleph is used in place of the letter He.</margin>

<header>DANIEL. Chapters 11 and 12.</header>

<margin>
verse 45. **a)** *He shall plant* or rather *he shall fix* (compare Ecclesiastes 12:11) *the tents of his palace*, that is, covered with beautiful curtains (1) *between the seas*—referring to the Mediterranean, which is expressed in the plural here (it seems) due to its vastness compared to the smaller lakes of Palestine—*and the holy mountain of beauty* (see verses 16, 41).

CHAPTER 12, verse 1. **b)** *For at that time*, when that Tyrant <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes</note> shall rage most fiercely against the people and the Jewish worship. This chapter is connected with the previous one, and according to Geier <note>Martin Geier, 17th-century Lutheran commentator</note>, it contains: I. the defense of the godly in danger (v. 1); II. the resurrection of the dead (v. 2–3); III. Daniel's instruction, both regarding the sealing of these visions (v. 4) and the definition of a certain time limit (v. 5, 6, 7); then a fuller explanation of the same (v. 8–13); and finally the expected resurrection of the Prophet from the grave (v. 13).

**c)** See chapter 10:13, 21.
**d)** *everyone who is found written in the book*, perhaps the catalog of the faithful and even of the living, or those destined for life. See Isaiah 4:3; Ezekiel 13:9.

verse 2. **e)** *Many*, that is, an infinite multitude of men, namely as many as have died, whether godly or ungodly. Romans 5:15, 19; compare John 5:28. *From those sleeping in the earth of dust* (according to the accents, this refers not to the subject but to the predicate) *they shall awake*; that is, awaking from sleep, they shall become revived from the dead. Isaiah 26:19. **f)** *but others to reproaches, and to everlasting abhorrence*. Isaiah 66:24.

verse 4. **g)** chapter 8:26.
**h)** *Then they shall run to and fro*, that is, they will be promptly occupied in understanding those things. Amos 8:12; compare Habakkuk 2:2.

verse 6. **i)** chapter 8:13.
verse 10. **k)** chapter 11:35.
</margin>

### Chapter XII.

**1** And at that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time; and at that time your people shall be delivered, every one that shall be found written in the book.

**2** And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to reproaches and everlasting abhorrence.

**3** And those who are wise<sup><gloss>m</gloss></sup> shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.

**4** But you, Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end; many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased.

**5** Then I, Daniel, looked, and behold, there stood two others, the one on this side of the bank of the river, and the other on that side of the bank of the river.

**6** And one said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river: "How long shall it be to the end of these wonders?"

**7** And I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand unto heaven, and swore by Him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when the breaking of the power<sup><gloss>n</gloss></sup> of the holy people shall have been completed, all these things shall be finished.

**8** And I heard, but I understood not; then said I: "O my lord, what shall be the end of these things?"

**9** And he said: "Go your way, Daniel; for the words are shut up and sealed till the time of the end."

**10** Many shall purify themselves, and make themselves white, and be refined; but the wicked shall do wickedly; and none of the wicked shall understand; but those who are wise shall understand.

**11** And from the time that the continual burnt offering shall be taken away, and the abomination that makes desolate set up, there shall be a thousand two hundred and ninety days.

**12** Blessed is he who waits, and comes to the thousand three hundred and thirty-five days.

**13** But go your way till the end be; for you shall rest, and stand in your lot at the end of the days.

<header>THE BOOK OF EZRA</header>

->Hebrew<-

### Ezra

This little book is named after its author, **Ezra**, the son of **Seraiah the High Priest**, a priest of the primary rank and remarkably well-versed in the Scriptures (see Chapter 7:1 and following). It explains the deeds of 70 years:
I. The return of the Jews to their homeland granted by Cyrus under the leader Zerubbabel, and the beginning of the restoration of the state and sacred worship (Chapters 1–3).
II. However, this work was hindered under the reigns of Cyrus, Cambyses, and Smerdis <note>These are Persian kings who followed Cyrus; Smerdis is often identified as the "false Smerdis" or Bardiya</note> (Chapter 4).
III. Nevertheless, the work was continued (Chapter 5).
IV. And it was successfully completed under Darius Hystaspes (Chapter 6).
V. From there, when the affairs of the Jews had again collapsed, **Ezra** himself came to their aid in the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus; he corrected the vices of the leaders and the people and restored the legitimate order in the state and the religious assembly (Chapters 7–10).

---

<margin>
**CHAPTER 1, verse 1. a)** Now in the first year (see Chapter 5:13).
**b)** This phrase appears at the beginning of the book, which is either redundant in the Hebrew style; or, to continue the history of 2 Chronicles, it repeats the final words of that book here (see 2 Chronicles 36:22). Compare Joshua 1:1, Judges 1:1, and Ruth 1:1.
**b)** [referring to] Cyrus, king and emperor of the Persians, after the death of his uncle and father-in-law Cyaxares (the son of Darius the Mede, see Daniel 6:1). Compare below at verse 2, as well as Chapters 3:7 and 4:3. See also Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1–13.
**c)** That the word of the Lord might be fulfilled (2 Chronicles 29:34).
**d)** Given from the mouth of Jeremiah. See Jeremiah 25:12 and 29:10.
**e)** Jehovah stirred up (verse 5; Isaiah 41:2) *the spirit and mind of Cyrus* (Haggai 1:14; compared with Proverbs 21:1).
**f)** So that he ordered it to be proclaimed by the public voice of heralds (Chapter 10:7; Exodus 36:6).
**g)** And also by a writing, that is, an edict recorded in letters (Esther 1:21). Truly, in this first chapter:
**I.** Cyrus proclaims the return of the Jews to Jerusalem by voice and by writing (verses 1–4).
**II.** The leaders of the Jews arise to depart (verse 5).
**III.** Their hands are strengthened [by gifts] (verse 6).
**IV.** The *sacred vessels*, taken away by Nebuchadnezzar, are restored (verses 7–11).
**v. 2. h)** Thus in 2 Chronicles 36:23.
**i)** And the same was long ago [prophesied] through Isaiah (44:24–28, 45:1–13); perhaps also through Daniel (compare Daniel 1:21, 6:29, 8:2). "He has commanded me" (Numbers 4:27).
**v. 3. k)** 2 Chronicles 36:23.
**l)** Who is to be uniquely worshipped in Jerusalem.
**v. 4. m)** "Let them support him," I say (verse 6; Chapter 8:36), referring to his fellow citizens.
**v. 6. n)** They strengthened their hands, that is, they helped them by giving gifts.
**o)** And with precious things (4) (Genesis 24:53).
**p)** As if to say separately, besides all the rest who offered spontaneously for the restoration of the Temple (verse 4).
**v. 10. q)** Covered bowls (Chapter 8:27).
**r)** Secondary ones, or of the second rank (1 Chronicles 15:10, 18).
</margin>

<margin>CHAPTER 1.</margin>
**1** Now in the^a first year of Cyrus^b king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah^c might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation^f throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing,^g saying:

**2** "Thus says Cyrus^h king of Persia: The LORD God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he has charged me^i to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah.

**3** Who is there among you of all his people? May his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD God of Israel—he is the God^l—which is in Jerusalem.

**4** And whosoever remains in any place where he sojourns, let the men of his place help him^m with silver, and with gold, and with goods, and with beasts, beside the freewill offering for the house of God that is in Jerusalem."

**5** Then rose up the chief of the fathers of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests, and the Levites, with all them whose spirit God had stirred, to go up to build the house of the LORD which is in Jerusalem.

**6** And all those that were about them strengthened^n their hands with vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, and with beasts, and with precious things,^o beside^p all that was willingly offered.

**7** Also Cyrus the king brought forth the vessels of the house of the LORD, which Nebuchadnezzar had brought forth out of Jerusalem, and had put them in the house of his gods;

**8** Even those did Cyrus king of Persia bring forth by the hand of Mithredath^q the treasurer, and numbered them unto Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah.

<margin>A gap [in the text] as in Leviticus</margin>
**9** And this is the number of them: thirty chargers of gold, a thousand chargers of silver, nine and twenty knives,

**10** Thirty basins of gold, silver basins^r of a second sort four hundred and ten, and other vessels a thousand.

**11** All the vessels of gold and of silver were five thousand and four hundred. All these did Sheshbazzar bring up with them of the captivity that were brought up from Babylon unto Jerusalem.

---

**CHAPTER 1, verse 1.** *Persia* <note>original: פָּרַס</note> written with a *Kamatz* <note>a vowel mark indicating an 'a' sound</note> in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, 23. And so nearly the same in the following verses.
**v. 2.** *And he* <note>original: וְהוּא</note> with a *Kadma* <note>a type of musical/accent mark</note> in 1, 6, 9, 10, 12, 16, 20, and together with a *Makkaph* <note>a hyphen-like connector</note> in 21, 23.
**v. 4.** *And they shall lift him up* <note>original: וִיְנַשְׂא֫וּהוּ</note> thus written defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> in 1, 6, 9, 20, and so in 2 according to the Major Masorah 1, 2, and the Erfurt manuscript; but contrary to Major Masorah 3.
**v. 8.** *Mithredath* <note>original: מִתְרְדָת</note> with a *Patach* <note>a short 'a' vowel</note> in 1, 2, 3. *And he numbered them* <note>original: וַיִּסְפְּרֵם</note> with a *Munach* <note>a musical accent</note> in 1, 6, 9, 10, 12, 20. But with a *Zaqef Qatan* in 2. *To Sheshbazzar* <note>original: לְשֵׁשְׁבַּצַּר</note> with a *Segol* <note>an 'e' vowel</note> in 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 20, 23. Thus also in verse 11 and 14.
**v. 9.** A *preceding space* is found in manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 10, 12, 14, 19, 20, 21.

<margin>
a) Thus Zerubbabel was called in the Chaldean language <note>original: "Chaldaice"; referring to Aramaic, the administrative language of the Persian Empire</note>. Compare verse 8 and Daniel 1:7.
b) "With the bringing up," or "when they were being brought back up," utilizing the Niphal Infinitive <note>a Hebrew grammatical form indicating a passive or reflexive action</note>. See Exodus 40:36, 2 Samuel 2:27. This refers to the crowd of exiles. See chapter 2:1 and 2 Kings 24:15, 16.

->...Sheshbazzar, along with the bringing up<sup>b</sup> of the exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem.<-

<margin>
c) CHAPTER II, verse 1. Furthermore, these are the "children of the province," or the provincials, originating from the region of Judea broadly so named (comparing verse 25, chapter 5:8, and Nehemiah 1:3 and 11:3). Compare this phrasing below in verses 20, 21, and 24, as well as Matthew 8:12.
d) Those who went up or set out, see verse 59 and chapter 1:3, from the "captivity of the migration," meaning from among the captive exiles, chapter 1:11 and chapter 4:1. e) chapter 1:7, 2 Kings 24:14, and following.
This chapter provides an accounting of those who wished to return from captivity with Zerubbabel. I. The leaders and princes (verses 1–2). II. The people categorized by distinct families (verses 3–19); likewise by towns and cities, including the number of persons (verses 20–35). III. The Priests (verses 36–39) and the Levites (verses 40–42). IV. The Nethinim <note>Temple servants</note> (verses 43–54) and the descendants of Solomon’s servants (verses 55–58). V. The priests who were disqualified (verses 59–63). Then follows the total sum of all those recounted (verse 64). VI. It lists the servants, singers, and livestock (verses 65–67). VII. How they occupied their individual cities and fields after returning to Judea and performing sacred rites (verses 68–70). Nehemiah repeats this same catalog in his 7th chapter, though with many differences, concerning which you may consult the 11th section of our preface to the notes on this book.
f) With Zerubbabel, the prince of Judah (chapter 3:2, 8). He was called Sheshbazzar above in chapter 1:8, 11, and below in verse 63 he is also called by his official title, "Tirshatha," meaning a Judge or Royal Governor. g) Jeshua (or Joshua), the High Priest (chapter 3:2, Haggai 1:1, 12, 14).
h) Nehemiah (see Nehemiah 1:1 and following).
i) The sons of Gibbar, or the Gibeonites (comparing Nehemiah 7:25).
</margin>

# EZRA CHAPTERS 3, 4.

**7** They gave money to the masons and the carpenters, and food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and the Tyrians, to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea at Joppa, according to the grant <note>original: "concessionem"</note> that they had from Cyrus king of Persia.

**8** Now in the second year of their coming to the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and the rest of their brothers the priests and the Levites, and all those who had come out of the captivity to Jerusalem, began the work; and they appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to oversee the work of the house of the LORD.

**9** Then Jeshua stood with his sons and his brothers, Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together <note>original: "instar unius viri" - meaning with one mind or unanimous consent</note> to oversee the workers in the house of God; the sons of Henadad, with their sons and their brothers the Levites.

**10** And when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, they stationed the priests in their apparel <note>original: "vestibus suis" - referring to their sacred priestly vestments</note> with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the LORD according to the ordinance of David king of Israel.

**11** And they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, saying, "For He is good, for His mercy endures forever toward Israel." And all the people shouted with a great shout when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.

**12** But many of the priests and Levites and heads of the fathers' houses, the old men who had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy.

**13** So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people, for the people shouted with a loud shout, and the sound was heard from afar.

<margin>CHAPTER IV.</margin>
**1** Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the descendants of the captivity were building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel,

<margin>A variant reading in the Hebrew tradition</margin>
**2** They approached Zerubbabel and the heads of the fathers' houses, and said to them, "Let us build with you; for we seek your God, as you do; and we have been sacrificing to Him since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria, who brought us up here."

**3** But Zerubbabel and Jeshua and the rest of the heads of the fathers' houses of Israel said to them, "You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God; but we ourselves together will build to the LORD, the God of Israel, as...

<column-break/>

**Verse 7.** a) *to the sea or the bay of* Joppa, also known as Jaffa. <note>Joppa was the ancient port city closest to Jerusalem, modern-day Jaffa</note>. See 2 Chronicles 2:15 and notes on Joshua 19:46. b) *according to the grant or mandate.* c) *for or concerning them.* Ezekiel 27:5; Joel 1:3.

**Verse 9.** d) *Jeshua the High Priest was also present* (see v. 8), along with his sons and relatives. e) *likewise the sons of Judah, who are also called Hodaviah* in chapter 2:40. f) *like one man, that is, with unanimous consent and zeal, as in verse 1.*

**Verse 10.** g) *Therefore, while the builders (the masons) were laying the foundations of the temple* (v. 6), the leaders of the people and the High Priest ordered the priests (v. 5) to stand *clothed in their vestments* (ch. 2:69), with trumpets (Numbers 10:10), and the Levites (v. 8, 9), specifically the descendants of Asaph (ch. 2:41), *with sistrums or cymbals* (1 Chronicles 13:8; 15:16, 19), *to praise the LORD "at the hands of," that is, according to the institutions or ordinances* of David (Nehemiah 12:36; 2 Chronicles 29:27).

**Verse 12.** h) *Those who had seen the first temple on its foundation.* Barely 53 years had passed since Solomon's temple was destroyed. <note>The "first house" refers to the magnificent Temple built by King Solomon, destroyed by the Babylonians in 586 BCE</note>. Compare notes on Haggai 2:3. i) *While this house was in their eyes; as they saw these humble beginnings.* Compare Haggai 2:3, 9; Zechariah 4:10.

**CHAPTER IV, Verse 1.** k) *When the enemies heard this, they came to Zerubbabel.* These were the Cutheans or Samaritans. They I. offer common labor to restore the temple (v. 1-2), but II. are not admitted by the Jews (v. 3). Consequently, III. they impede them in every way (v. 4-5) and IV. write an accusation against them to Ahasuerus (Cambyses) (v. 6) and V. a long letter to Artaxerxes (Smerdis) (v. 7-16), from whom VI. they obtain a restraining order (v. 17-22). Hence VII. the restoration of the Temple ceased until the second year of Darius (v. 23-24).

---

**Verse 8.** The word "and they appointed" <note>Hebrew: ושאו</note> is noted with specific <term>accents</term> (Patah, Darga, Makkef) across various ancient manuscripts (numbered 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20). 
**Verse 9.** For the word "sons" <note>Hebrew: בני</note>, some manuscripts have "and the sons" with a specific vowel marking in the margin.
**Verse 13.** The word "from afar" is written in a "defective" <note>meaning a shorter spelling without certain vowel letters</note> form in manuscript 3 according to the printed Masorah.
**CHAPTER IV, Verse 2.** "Since the days of" <note>Hebrew: מימי</note> is marked with the <term>Paschta</term> accent in most manuscripts, but with <term>Graschaim</term> in one. The name **Esarhaddon** is written as one word in several manuscripts and in the margins. Other terms are noted as having full or defective spellings in the Erfurdt and Masoretic traditions.
**Verse 3.** "And the rest" <note>Hebrew: ושאר</note> is noted with the Patah vowel in several key manuscripts.

# CHAPTER 4 & 5. Ezra 4, 5.

<margin>
a) was destroyed. Ezekiel 26:2. 
b) "We therefore make it known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and the walls repaired" (verse 13), "therefore you will have no portion or possession in the region on this side of the Euphrates River" (verses 10, 11).

CHAPTER 5, verse 1. o) "Then he prophesied." Used without the conjunction "and," as in 1 Samuel 10:6, 13, and Jeremiah 26:9. p) chapter 6:14, Haggai 1:1. q) "Zechariah, son of Berechiah" (Zechariah 1:1, 7), "grandson of Iddo" (comparing the use of "Son" in chapter 3:2 and Nehemiah 12:23).
Here follows the more successful progress of the work. For at the urging of God’s prophets: I. The Jews set about finishing the temple (verses 1, 2). II. When the Persian governors intervene, they respond that they are building according to the decree of Cyrus (verses 3, 4). III. Regarding this matter, those governors write to King Darius (verses 5–17).
verse 4. s) "Then," as we shall say in verse 9 and as we said in chapter 4:8, "we spoke"—that is, I, Ezra, and the other leaders of the people.

v. 7 *they built*—so according to the Qamets vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, 23.
The rest place the accent on the penultimate syllable. *The whole* (kollā): accent on the last syllable in 15, 22, 23.
*The province*: with a Meteg mark in 17, 18, 22, 24. & Berlin.
v. 10 *their names*: thus in 23. Others write *their names* differently.
v. 11 *to say*: with a Qamets in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, 23.
v. 12 *he gave*: with a Patach in 2, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20.
v. 12 *and the people*: Thus without a Mappiq in the emphatic state (as the Greek and Syriac versions do). Masoretic editions print it this way. Many others, however, write it with a Mappiq, as do the Vulgate and Arabic versions, and some scholars argue it should be written with a masculine suffix because the word "house" in Aramaic is masculine.
v. 13 *for Cyrus the king*: thus in 2.
v. 14 *the gold*: thus with the letter He in 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 15, 17, 22, 23, 24 according to Masoretic sources 1, 2, 3 and the Erfurt edition. Likewise in Daniel 3:21. Others use the letter Aleph.
*to Sheshbazzar*: with a Segol vowel in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 22, 23.
v. 17 *to us*: with a Tsere vowel in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 22, 23.

v. 7 *peace*: thus with the accent on the last syllable in 1, 2, 3, 6—9, 11, 12.
v. 8 *which*: with a Munach accent in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 15, 16, 20—24.
*the province*: accent on the last syllable in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 21, 22.

*the Chaldean*: thus in the context of 2, 15, 16.
However, it seems less suitable for the "people of the house of God" to be called "the Jewish people" here; it should have been written with a masculine suffix because "house" is masculine in Aramaic.
