<meta>This page continues the narrative from Chapter 5, where the Persian governor Tattenai wrote to King Darius to verify the Jews' claim that King Cyrus had authorized the rebuilding of the Temple. Here, Darius orders a search of the royal archives, leading to the discovery of the original decree and his subsequent confirmation of it.</meta>

# CHAPTER 6. EZRA VI

1 Then King Darius issued a decree, and they searched <gloss>a</gloss> in the house of the archives <note>Literally "house of books," referring to the royal library or record office.</note> where the treasures were stored there in Babylon.
2 And there was found in Achmetha <gloss>b</gloss> <note>Also known as Ecbatana, the summer capital of the Persian Empire.</note>, in the fortress that is in the province of Media, a scroll, and within it this was written as a record <gloss>c</gloss>:
3 "In the first year of King Cyrus <gloss>d</gloss>, King Cyrus issued a decree concerning the house of God in Jerusalem: Let the house be rebuilt, the place <gloss>e</gloss> where they offer sacrifices, and let its foundations be firmly laid <gloss>f</gloss>. Its height shall be sixty cubits and its width sixty cubits;
4 With three layers <gloss>g</gloss> of large stones <gloss>h</gloss> and one layer of new timber. Let the expense be paid from the king’s house.
5 And also let the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple in Jerusalem and brought to Babylon, be restored <gloss>i</gloss> and returned to the temple in Jerusalem, each to its place; and you shall deposit <gloss>k</gloss> them in the house of God."
6 "Now therefore, Tattenai <gloss>l</gloss>, governor of the region beyond the River, Shethar-Bozenai <gloss>m</gloss>, and your colleagues, the officials of the region beyond the River, stay far away from there.
7 Leave <gloss>n</gloss> the work on this house of God alone. Let the governor of the Jews <gloss>o</gloss> and the elders <gloss>p</gloss> of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its site.
8 Moreover, I issue a decree regarding what you shall do for these elders of the Jews for the building of this house of God: From the king’s wealth, out of the taxes of the region beyond the River, the full cost is to be given to these men, so that they are not hindered.
9 And whatever is needed—young bulls, rams, and lambs for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, and oil, according to the word of the priests in Jerusalem—let it be given to them day by day without fail,
10 So that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons.
11 Also, I have issued a decree that if any man alters <gloss>q</gloss> this edict, a beam shall be pulled from his house and he shall be lifted up and impaled upon it; and his house shall be made a refuse heap for this crime.
12 And may the God who causes His name to dwell there overthrow any king or people who puts forth his hand to alter this, or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem. I, Darius, have issued the decree; let it be carried out diligently."

->**Then**<-

<column-break/>

**CHAPTER VI, v. 1.** a) Then therefore Darius, the king, commanded that they search in the record-office, where they were storing treasures there in Babylon. [Compare] chapter 5, 17. In this chapter: I. Darius finds the decree of Cyrus, verses 1–5. II. He confirms it and increases it with granted funds, verses 6–12. Therefore III. The restoration of the Temple is completed with no one hindering it, verses 13–15. IV. The temple is dedicated, verses 16–18. And V. The Passover is celebrated in Jerusalem, verses 19–22.

**v. 2.** b) And finally it was found, [compare] chapter 4, 19, in a chest; others, following the Vulgate and Arabic versions, say "in Ecbatana" (1) in the royal fortress or palace, [compare] Esther 1, 2, which is in the province of Media: where Cyrus happened to be staying at that time after the death of his father-in-law and uncle. c) A MEMORIAL or RECORD of the matter, thus committed to memory.

**v. 3.** d) chapter 1, 1; chapter 5, 13. e) that is, the place in which they shall sacrifice victims, chapter 4, 2. f) and its foundations are brought together; others translate as "let them be firm," great in mass and thickness, as in Psalm 144, 14.

**v. 4.** g) Rows; others translate as "Walls" (2) in this place. h) out of choice stones, chapter 5, 8.

**v. 5.** i) so that each of them may go away or return, chapter 5, 5; chapter 7, 13. k) and you, Sheshbazzar, shall replace them; or "make them go down" and they shall arrive in the house of God, verse 1, 3; chapter 5, 14, 15.

**v. 6.** l) verse 13; chapter 5, 3. m) chapter 5, 6.

**v. 7.** n) Allow the work to be done. Daniel 4, 12. o) The prefect of the Jews, Zerubbabel, chapter 1, 8; chapter 2, 2; chapter 5, 14. p) and the elders of the Jews, verses 8, 14; chapter 5, 5, 9.
**§** The mark of the Nominative case, as in 1 Chronicles 3, 2.

**v. 11.** q) whoever shall change (compare verse 12) this edict, [compare] chapter 4, 17, shall be plucked out, [compare] Deuteronomy 28, 63. A wooden beam (compare verse 4) from his house; r) being erected or suspended, let him be destroyed upon it—that is, let him be led to the cross <note>The Latin 'in crucem agatur' suggests crucifixion, but in the Persian context of the Aramaic 'zqif,' it refers to impalement.</note>—and his house shall become a dunghill or latrine.

---

**CHAPTER VI, v. 1. ובקרו** (and they searched) with the vowel *Pathach* in manuscripts 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15–19, 21–24. The others use *Qamets*. **v. 2. בבגוא** (within it) with *Qamets* in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, 21, 22, 23. **v. 3. בית** (house) with the accent *Munach* in 1, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. **v. 4. חדת** (new) with *Qamets* in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 26, 20, 23; contrary to the Index of Basel, folio 61, column 8. **v. 6. רחיקין** (far) with *Qamets* in 22. But with *Sheva* in 1, 2, 3, 23. **v. 8. מלכא** (the king) Thus with the accent *Revia* in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20; instead of which the others use *Hateph-Qamets*, which is less convenient. **די מדת** (of the tribute) thus with the accent *Telisha* in 2, 24, according to the Masorah 2. printed and Erfurt in this place; and printed Levi 5, 2. Others use *Mahpakh*. **v. 9. ובני** (and young [bulls]) with the hyphen *Maqqef* in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. **ואמרין** (and lambs) without the mark *Pesiq* in 2, 3, 21, against the Index of Basel, folio 61. But with the accent *Paser* in 6, 9, 20. **לעלון** (for burnt offerings) without *Pesiq* in 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, against the Index of Basel, line 6. **v. 12. די ישלח ודה** (who puts forth his hand) thus in 6, 9, 10, 14, 20; likewise in 1, except that here **די** uses *Maqqef*.

<note>The following section contains technical notes regarding the Hebrew and Aramaic vowel points and musical accents used by the Masoretes (early medieval Jewish scholars who standardized the biblical text).</note>

Verse 9. **He founded** [original: *yesud*] according to the *Merkha* accent in manuscripts 1, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. 
Verse 10. **And to do** [original: *vela'asot*] thus lacking the letter *Waw* in the text, but noted in the margin. 
**Commandments** [original: *mitzvot*] with the *Merkha* accent in various manuscripts and printed editions. 
Verse 11. **Commandments** [original: *mitzvot*] with the *Metheg* mark in manuscript 3; others are without it. 
Verse 13. **Volunteers** [original: *mitnaddav*] with the *Tsere* vowel in multiple manuscripts. 
**And his priests** [original: *vekohanohi*] with the *Qamets* vowel in manuscripts 6 and 20. Same for verse 16 and 24. 
Verse 15. **And gold** [original: *udehav*] with the *Patach* vowel in several manuscripts. 
Verse 17. **Bullocks** [original: *torin*] with the *Pesiq* mark in manuscripts 1, 22, 24, following the Masorah. Buxtorf in his *Clavis Masoretica* (p. 88) wrongly refers this to chapter 6:9, having suspected a random error. 
Verse 19. **And the vessels** [original: *umanya*] with the *Qamets* vowel. 
Verse 20. **To give** [original: *lemintan*] with the *Qamets* vowel in many sources; others use *Tsere* or *Segol*. The Masorah of Erfurt requires a *Patach* here. 
Verse 21. **I** [original: *anah*] with a *Patach* vowel in manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 20. The same applies to verse 23 and elsewhere.

### CRITICAL NOTES
**Ezra 8, v. 13.** *Jeiel*: thus in the text without the traditional reading (Keri) in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 19, 20, 22. Instead of "and with him" <note>Hebrew: v'imo</note>, manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 20, 21 have "and with them" <note>Hebrew: v'ima</note>. **v. 15.** Without a preceding space in manuscripts 6, 9, 12, 14, 19, 20, 23. **v. 17.** Instead of "And I sent" <note>Hebrew: v'otzah</note>, the written text (Kethiv) has "v'otziyah." But "v'atzviyah" with a Segol vowel is found in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, 23. **v. 20.** *The Nethinim*: thus in the text without the traditional reading (Keri) in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 11, 23. **v. 18.** *And Sherebiah*: with a Segol vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, 23. The same occurs in **v. 24**. **v. 22.** "His power and his wrath against—": thus in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. **v. 25.** *Those found*: the letter Yod appears with a Schwa vowel in manuscript 3 and another book in the Erfurt Massorah.

**Textual Notes:**
Verse 3: *And I plucked out* <note>original Hebrew: ואמרטה</note> is written thus with a <term>Rebia</term> <note>a Hebrew musical/syntactic accent</note> in manuscripts 6, 9, 10, 14, 17, 18, 20, 23, 24, and the Berlin edition. Others use the *Graphaim* accent, except for manuscript 22, which incorrectly has a *Zakef-Katon*. Verse 4: Manuscript 24 adds the name of the Lord. According to the <term>Masora</term> <note>traditional notes on the Hebrew biblical text</note> on Leviticus 5:2, the accent here is not a *Mahpak* but an *Ithib*. Verse 5: *My God* <note>original Hebrew: אלהי</note> appears thus in 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 20. Verse 6: *Sin* with a <term>euphonic Dagesh</term> <note>a dot in a letter to indicate doubling or distinct pronunciation for better sound</note> in 6, 9, 20 according to the Frankfurt edition. The word *Until* <note>original Hebrew: עד</note> is joined by a *Makkef* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, contrary to the Masora on Genesis 38:17. Verse 7: *Persia* with a *Kamets* vowel in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 20, 21, 22. Verse 10: *This* <note>original Hebrew: זאת</note> with a *Makkef* in 17, 18 and the Berlin edition. Verse 11: *By the hand of* with a *Makkef* in 2, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. The phrase *which filled it* has a *Mercha* accent in 2, 7, 8, 15, 24. Verse 12: *Their peace* thus in 6, 9, 10, 20. Verse 13: *From our iniquity* <note>original Hebrew: מעווננו</note> written in full spelling in 2, 4, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, 21, 22. Verse 14: *No remnant* thus in 17, 18 and the Berlin edition.

# THE BOOK OF NEHEMIAH,
->Hebrew:<-
# נחמיה

This book is titled *Second Ezra* by the Vulgate and the Arabic translator, and it is usually joined together with the preceding book into a single volume. Nehemiah, the leader and governor of the Jews, identifies himself as the author both at the beginning (chapter 1:1) and elsewhere throughout. He describes: I. The restoration of the city and walls of Jerusalem (chapters 1–3) despite the interference of enemies (chapter 3:33 – 4:17) and the complaints of the people (chapter 5), and the plots of Sanballat <note>A regional governor who opposed the Jewish restoration</note> and false brothers (chapter 6), continuing until completion; followed by the appointment of guards and the census of the returning inhabitants (chapter 7). II. The correction of the returning people and the reformation of the collapsed divine worship, both before his return to the Persian court (chapters 8:1 – 11:3, 5) and afterward (chapter 13:6–31). All these things were accomplished within a span of 12 or 13 years (comparing chapter 1:1; 2:1, 2, 6 with 13:6).

---

<margin>
NEHEMIAH
CHAPTER I, verse 1. b) *The words* (as in Jeremiah 1:1) or *the deeds* (as in 2 Samuel 11:18). Nehemiah (chapter 7:7), the prince and governor of Judea (chapter 5:14; 12:26), which is also what the title *Hattirshatha* <note>A Persian title for a local governor</note> means (chapter 8:9; 9:10). The same is said of Sheshbazzar in chapter 10:2. This Nehemiah is distinct from another Nehemiah, the son of Azbuk (chapter 3:16). This chapter narrates: I. How Nehemiah, while in Persia, learned of the miserable lot of the Jews in Judea (v. 1–3). II. How he turned to tears and prayers, fasted for several days, and prayed to God to make the heart of Artaxerxes, the King of the Persians, favorable to him (v. 4–11). c) Zechariah 7:1; Ezra 10:9; 1 Maccabees 4:52. d) *In the twentieth year*, namely of *Artaxerxes Longimanus* <note>Artaxerxes I, who ruled the Persian Empire from 465–424 BCE</note> (compare chapter 2:1; 5:14; Ezra 7:7). e) Esther 1:2; 2:3, 5; Daniel 8:2.
verse 2. f) *And I asked them about the Jews, the escape;* that is, according to the Vulgate, *those who remained or were left over from the slaughter and had returned from the Babylonian captivity* (Ezra 9:14–15). g) *And especially about Jerusalem* and its condition.
verse 3. h) *There in the province of Judea* (chapter 7:6; Ezra 2:1). i) *They are in great evil or affliction* (chapter 2:17; 13:18; Exodus 5:19). k) *Burned with fire* (chapter 2:3, 17; 2 Kings 25:10).
verse 4. l) *And I gave myself to mourning* (chapter 8:9; Daniel 10:2; Ezra 10:6) for some or many days (Genesis 40:4; Judges 11:4). m) *And I was fasting* (Esther 4:16; Ezra 8:21; 9:5).

<margin>
a) [Each builder] was girded at his loins [with his sword], see Psalm 45:4. Thus armed, they continued building; meanwhile, the one who sounded the trumpet, verse 14 d, was with me or beside me.

Or as Clericus [notes]: each one, verse 16, had his weapon and water, lest perhaps the post had to be deserted for the sake of drinking; compare 1 Samuel 26:12, 2 Chronicles 23:10.
CHAPTER V. v. 1. o) Indeed, there arose a cry and complaint of the poor people, Isaiah 5:7, Job 34:28, James 5:4, against their brothers or tribesmen, verses 5, 8, 10—the wealthier Jews. Specifically, the poor Jews brought heavy complaints to Nehemiah regarding the usury and plunder by the rich (verses 1–5). Nehemiah (II) severely rebuked and discouraged them (verses 6–11), and (III) bound them by an oath to restore to the poor what had been taken from them against law and right (verses 12–13). Finally, (IV) he explains with what restraint he served as governor of the Jews for twelve years (verses 14–19).

**v. 3.** "Great" [Hebrew: *gedolah*] is written "full" (plene) in some manuscripts but "lacking" (defective) in others.
**v. 5.** With a space preceding in various manuscripts. **v. 6.** "Gashmu" is written with a specific accent (Metheg) in some, but others use a Kamatz vowel. **v. 9.** "All of them" [Hebrew: *kullam*] is noted according to Rabbinic manuscripts. For the word "and you" [Hebrew: *ve-attah*] some have "and now" [Hebrew: *ve-ata*] in the margin. **v. 12.** "And behold" [Hebrew: *ve-hinneh*] follows specific accentuation in older copies. **v. 13.** Regarding "that I should fear," there are variations in the spelling across different editions.
**v. 16.** "And they were afraid" [Hebrew: *va-yiru*]: with a Metheg accent, this comes from the root for **fear** (as translated in the Latin Vulgate, Greek Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic). Without the accent, it would mean "and they saw." The version meaning "fear" is considered correct by most Masoretic scholars.

<note>The following notes are technical scholarly observations regarding vowel marks and manuscript variations in the Hebrew text.</note>

**v. 18.** The name **Arah** is written with a Kamets vowel according to various manuscripts. This differs from the Masoretic tradition in some editions.
**v. 19.** The word for **man** is noted in specific early printed editions.

### NEHEMIAH. CHAPTERS 9 & 10.

<margin>
a) Nehemiah 1:5, 6.
b) "Let not all this hardship and affliction be or seem small to You." Exodus 18:8; Numbers 20:14. The particle **את** <note>Hebrew: et</note> in this place is in the nominative case, as in verse 19 and 34, and Joshua 22:17.
c) "Which found us," or happened to us; Numbers 20:14; Judges 6:13. Specifically to our kings, princes, priests, prophets, and our fathers.
d) Those who began the deportation; 2 Kings 15:29; 17:6. e) Ezra 9:7.
v. 33. f) "And You indeed are righteous," verse 8; Deuteronomy 32:4; Daniel 9:14; Ezra 9:15; 2 Chronicles 12:6. "In all that has come," or rushed upon us like a storm; 1 Samuel 30:23; Ezra 9:13; 2 Chronicles 20:12. "Because You have acted in truth," and stood faithfully by Your promises, verse 13; Psalm 111:7. "But we have acted wickedly," Psalm 106:6; Daniel 9:5; 2 Chronicles 20:35; 22:3.
v. 35. g) "And when they," our kings and princes, etc. (verse 32) "in their kingdom," Daniel 8:23; "and in Your great and abundant goodness," verse 25; "and in the broad region," Exodus 3:8; Judges 18:10; "and fat," or fertile, verse 25; Ezekiel 34:6; "which You gave open before them," Jeremiah 9:12; 44:10. "They did not serve You," Deuteronomy 28:47; "nor did they turn from their wicked deeds," Judges 2:19; Zechariah 1:4.
CHAPTER X, v. 1. h) Schmidius: "Furthermore, after all this," or "in all these things," Jeremiah 3:10. "We were making," or we struck (as in 9:8) "a firm agreement," <note>Hebrew: amanah</note> that is, a firm and stable covenant of faithfulness (2) chapter 11:23. "And we also wrote it down," Jeremiah 32:12. "And on that sealed document," verse 2; Jeremiah 32:10, 11, 14. The witnesses of the sealed covenant were our princes (verses 2, 8, 15-28), likewise the Levites (verses 10-14), and the priests (verses 3-9). Nehemiah, along with the Levites and the leaders of the Jews, renew the covenant with God and confirm it with their signatures (verses 1-28). The people (II) then swear to the words of the covenant (verses 29-32) and promise what was owed to the Temple and the Priests (verses 33-39).
</margin>

# NEHEMIAH. CHAPTER 11.

<margin>
**CHAPTER XI.**
</margin>

<margin>
**CHAPTER XI, v. 1. a)** The leaders of the people lived, or settled <note>original Latin: "Habitauerunt autem vel consederunt"</note>, in Jerusalem (v. 3, 4). Those to be named (v. 4 and following) were in Jerusalem, but the rest of the people (v. 20; ch. 10:29) cast lots <note>original Latin: "fortes ierunt"</note> (ch. 10:35) to bring one out of ten to dwell in Jerusalem (v. 2; 1 Chronicles 9:3), the city of holiness or the holy city (v. 18; Isaiah 48:2; Joel 4:17; Matthew 4:5). This was so that a more frequently inhabited city could be better defended (compare above ch. 7:4, 5) and so that nine parts—or the result of the casting of lots <note>original Latin: "iactus fortis"</note> (Genesis 43:34; ch. 47:24; 2 Kings 11:7)—would remain in the other provincial cities (v. 3; ch. 7:73). In this chapter: **I.** Jerusalem, deserted of inhabitants, is furnished with volunteers and those chosen by lot (v. 1–3). Their leaders are listed: 1) from the tribe of Judah (v. 4–6); 2) from the tribe of Benjamin (v. 7–9); 3) from the Priests (v. 10–14); 4) from the Levites (v. 15–18); 5) from the Gatekeepers (v. 19). **II.** The cities of Judah and Benjamin that began to be inhabited are also recorded (v. 20–36).
</margin>

1. Now the leaders of the people lived in Jerusalem. And the rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of ten to live in Jerusalem, the holy city, while nine-tenths remained in the other towns.

<margin>
**v. 2. b)** And the people blessed—meaning they prayed for them with favorable praise (1 Kings 8:66)—**c)** those who willingly offered themselves (Judges 5:29; Ezra 7:13), in contrast to those who were somewhat compelled by being designated by lot.
</margin>

2. And the people blessed all the men who willingly offered to live in Jerusalem.

<margin>
**v. 3. d)** The province of Judea (ch. 1:3; Ezra 2:1). **e)** Everyone in his own hereditary possession (v. 20; 1 Chronicles 9:2), in their towns (above ch. 7:73). This included Israelites (1 Chronicles 9:3), Priests (v. 10–14), Levites (v. 15–18), Temple Servants <term>Nethinim: a group of temple assistants, literally "given ones"</term> (v. 21; ch. 10:29; Ezra 2:43), and the descendants of Solomon’s servants (ch. 7:57; Ezra 2:55–58; 1 Chronicles 9:2).
</margin>

3. These are the heads of the province who lived in Jerusalem; but in the towns of Judah everyone lived on his own property in their towns: Israel, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the descendants of Solomon's servants.

<margin>
**v. 4. f)** Specifically in Jerusalem (v. 1, 2) lived some from Judah and Benjamin (1 Chronicles 9:3, 7, 31). **g)** See v. 6; Genesis 46:12; Ruth 4:18; 1 Chronicles 2:4; Matthew 1:3.
</margin>

4. And in Jerusalem lived some of the people of Judah and of the people of Benjamin. Of the people of Judah: Athaiah son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, of the descendants of Perez;

<margin>
**v. 5. h)** A Shilonite (1 Chronicles 9:5).
</margin>

5. and Maaseiah son of Baruch, son of Col-hozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, son of the Shilonite.
6. All the sons of Perez who lived in Jerusalem were four hundred and sixty-eight valiant men.
7. And these are the sons of Benjamin: Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of Jeshaiah.
8. And after him Gabbai and Sallai, nine hundred and twenty-eight.
9. Joel son of Zichri was their overseer; and Judah son of Hassenuah was second over the city.

<margin>
**v. 10. i)** Those performing priestly duties (ch. 13:10) in the temple (ch. 3:8).
</margin>

10. Of the priests: Jedaiah son of Joiarib, Jachin;
11. Seraiah son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the officer of the house of God;
12. and their brothers who did the work of the house, eight hundred and twenty-two; and Adaiah son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah;
13. and his brothers, heads of ancestral houses, two hundred and forty-two; and Amashsai son of Azarel, son of Ahzai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer;

<margin>
<note>Technical note: A Dagesh (emphasis dot) follows the Shureq (u-vowel).</note>

15. And of the Levites: Shemaiah son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni;
16. and Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the leaders of the Levites, who were over the outside work of the house of God;
17. and Mattaniah son of Mica, son of Zabdi, son of Asaph, the leader who began the thanksgiving in prayer, and Bakbukiah, the second among his brothers; and Abda son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun.

<meta>This page marks the transition from the Book of Nehemiah to the First Book of Chronicles. The introductory text provides a scholarly overview of the book's authorship, title, and historical scope before beginning the genealogical lists of Chapter 1.</meta>

# THE FIRST BOOK
## OF CHRONICLES,

### Hebrew:
## Words of the Days
<note>Hebrew: Divrei HaYamim</note>

The final volume of the Hebrew Bible, written by Ezra or another divinely inspired <note>original: "θεοπנεύστῳ" (theopneustō), meaning God-breathed or divinely inspired</note> man after the release from the Babylonian captivity, and later divided into two books. It is titled in Hebrew **Words of the Days**, that is, **Daily Deeds** or **Annals of Times**. In Greek, it is titled **Things Passed Over** <note>original: "παραλειπόμεנה" (Paraleipomena), referring to details omitted in the Books of Kings</note>, which we may more significantly call, following Saint Jerome, the **Chronicle of the entire divine history**. It begins with Adam and the very start of things and concludes with the first year of Cyrus. Or, to speak only of this first book: Part I relates the **origin** and **spread of the Israelite people**, especially the tribe of Judah and the family of David (from whom the Messiah was to be born), through a series of generations from the world's beginning until the return of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity, reaching almost to the time of Christ (Chapters 1–9). Part II historically reviews the **Kingdom** and the **establishment of the state and Church** created by David, from the final days of Saul until the beginning of Solomon’s reign (Chapters 10–29).

---

<margin>
**CHAPTER 1, v. 1.** **a)** **Adam**, the first man, formed from the earth by GOD (Genesis 1:26, 27; 2:7). He died in the year of the world 930 (Genesis 5:5). **b)** **Seth**, so named because he was placed by God in **Abel's** place; he was the third son of Adam (Genesis 4:25; 5:3). No mention is made here of Abel or Cain because Abel died without offspring, and Cain’s entire lineage was wiped out by the Flood. No specific sign of generation is placed here because the order of birth is already well known from elsewhere (see also below, verses 17, 24-27, and Chapter 4:1). **c)** **Enosh** (Genesis 4:26; 5:6).
This first chapter contains: I. The genealogy of the Hebrew leaders up to Jacob (v. 1-34). II. That of the Edomites up to Iram (v. 35-54). More specifically: 1) The genealogy of the patriarchs from Adam to Noah (v. 1-4). 2) The descendants of Japheth (v. 5-8) and Ham (v. 9-16). 3) Shem and his sons to Abraham (v. 17-28). 4) The sons of Abraham: Ishmael (v. 29-31), Keturah (v. 32-33), and Isaac with his son Esau (v. 34) and his sons (v. 35-37) and relatives (v. 38-42). 5) Kings (v. 43-50) and Leaders or princes of the Edomites (v. 51-54).
**v. 2. d)** Genesis 5:9. **e)** Genesis 5:12. **f)** Genesis 5:15, 18.
**v. 3. g)** Genesis 5:18. He was the seventh from Adam and a prophet (Jude 1:14, 15), and was taken up alive by God to the blessed dwellings (Genesis 5:21-24; Hebrews 11:5). **h)** The longest-lived of all mortals; he lived until the year of the Flood (Genesis 5:21, 22).
**v. 4. i)** Noah (Genesis 5:29 ff.) and his son Shem (v. 27; Genesis 5:32). Shem was not the firstborn—that was Japheth (Genesis 10:21)—but the middle son (compare Genesis 7:6; 11:10). He is preferred here because he was to be the ancestor of Abraham and thus of **CHRIST**, just as were Isaac, Jacob, Judah, David, etc.
**v. 5. k)** See our more extensive notes below.
</margin>

### Our more extensive notes.

<margin>
**CHAPTER 1, v. 6.** *Riphath* spelled with a *Resh* in several manuscripts (10, 12, 21, 23) and in the margin of 16, which is the standard reading in Genesis 10:3, but it contrasts with some Masoretic printed editions and the Erfurt manuscript. **v. 7.** *Dodanim* spelled with a *Daleth* in many manuscripts (6, 9, 10, etc.), against some printed Masoretic texts and the Erfurt manuscript at this place. **v. 9.** *Raamah* ending in *He* in manuscripts 22 and 23, against the Erfurt and printed Genesis 10:7. **a)** who was later called Abraham, that is, "father of many nations" (Genesis 17:5; Romans 4:16, 17). 
**b)** According to the promise of God (Genesis 17:17; 18:12), he was born to a hundred-year-old father from a ninety-year-old mother (Genesis 21:3; Romans 9:8, 9; Galatians 4:23 and following). He is placed before Ishmael in this location not due to birth order, but due to his status, as seen above in verses 4 and 17.

**i)** verse 32. **j)** verse 33; Genesis 25:1.
**k)** A secondary wife; the Latin Vulgate calls her a "concubine" of the elderly Abraham (Genesis 25:6). According to the Old Testament scriptures, such a wife differed little from a legal wife except in social honor. **l)** She bore six sons to Abraham, who, though aged, was made vigorous after the birth of Isaac.
**m)** And Medan; from whom come the Medanites, easily confused with the Midianites in verse 46 (compare Genesis 37:28, 36).
**n)** From here comes Bildad, the friend of Job, a Shuhite (Job 2:11).

**q)** Genesis 25:4. From here comes the region of Ephah (Isaiah 60:6).

**Verse 28.** "The sons" appears this way in the Munster editions 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 21, and 22. But in verse 2, it is against the note in the margin of 22. The <term>Silluk</term> <note>a vertical line marking the strongest accent at the end of a verse</note> with the <term>Sophpasuk</term> <note>two dots marking the end of a verse</note> appears in 1, 3, 6, 9, 20, and 21.
**Verse 43.** "The kings" has a <term>Zakeph Katon</term> <note>a short pause accent</note> in 1, and so in the following in 5.
**Verse 45.** Instead of *Husham*, manuscripts 1, 6, 9, 10, 20, and 21 have *Husshamm* (with a double 's'); and *Husham* without the <term>Dagesh</term> <note>a dot in the middle of a letter indicating emphasis or doubling</note> in 3.
**Verse 46.** Thus in verse 46 also in 2 and 19. *Beded* with a <term>Kamatz</term> <note>the 'a' vowel sound</note> in 1, 2, 3, 5, 21, 22, and 23.
*Ayot*: 3, 7, 17, 18, 20, 22, 23, and 24 place the <term>Chirek</term> <note>the 'i' vowel sound</note> under the *Vau*. The others place it under the *Iod*, which is against the logic of the <term>Kethiv and Qere</term> <note>The Masoretic practice of writing one word in the text but reading another</note>.
**Verse 47.** "From Masrekah" with the letter *Shin* in 1, 6, 9, 13, 20, 22, and 23.
**Verse 49.** *Achbor*: written defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> according to the printed Masorah of Genesis 36:39, but written fully in the Erfurt Masorah in the same place.
**Verse 50.** *Hadad* with a *Kamatz* in 5, 6, 9, 12, and 20–23. But with a *Resh* at the end in 3, 6, 9, 20; and thus in verse 51, only in 3.
*Pai*: thus with a *Vau* instead of *Iod* in 2, and so in 1 and following in 5.

**Verse 42.** *Jaakan*.

**c)** This means "Tent of the High." Genesis 36:41. This was also used as a woman's name in Genesis 36:2, 25.
**d)** This means "Oak." From this name perhaps comes the city of Elath (or Eloth) and the Elanitic Gulf in the Red Sea <note>literally "the Edomite Sea"</note>. See Deuteronomy 2:8, 1 Kings 9:26, and 2 Kings 14:22.
**e)** The name Phunon, a station where the Israelites stopped in the wilderness, seems to be derived from this (Numbers 33:42, 43). This location in Edom was once very famous for its copper mines; it was also the place where the bronze serpent was set up by Moses, as discussed by Samuel Bochart in *Hierozoicon* (Volume II, page 427). **CHAPTER II, verse 1. g)** Arabic: "These are the sons of Jacob-Israel." Specifically, the patriarch Jacob, who was also called Israel (as seen in Chapter 1:34) because through prayers and tears he prevailed over the Angel—that is, the Son of God—during their struggle (Genesis 32:28, 29). He fathered twelve sons from two wives and their handmaids. In verse 1, the sons of Leah are listed; in verse 2, the sons of Rachel are listed along with the adopted Dan, followed by the sons of Bilhah and finally Zilpah. Compare this genealogy to Genesis 35:23 and following, and Chapter 46:8 and following. This chapter contains two main parts: I. The lineage of the fathers from Jacob down to David (verses 2–17), recorded because of CHRIST, who was to be born from David’s line. II. The lineage of Caleb (verses 18–23 and 42–55) and of Jerahmeel (verses 25–41) is described in detail; please see our more extensive notes on these.
</margin>

# CHAPTER 2. 1 CHRONICLES

<margin>
**v. 23. a)** Geshur and Aram—that is, the Geshurites and Arameans or Syrians, who were neighbors of the tribe of Manasseh to the north—captured the area by force. After they drove out the sons of Jair, they occupied their towns. Compare Joshua 12:5, 13:13, 2 Samuel 15:8, and 3:3; in the notes there, read Deuteronomy 3:14.
**b)** Numbers 32:41, Joshua 13:30, 1 Kings 4:13.
**c)** This was also called Nobah, according to Numbers 32:42.
**d)** Deuteronomy 3:4.
**e)** All these inhabitants of those towns were "sons" or descendants of Machir, who was the father of Gilead; they were born from his daughter, as mentioned in verse 21.

**v. 24. f)** After the death of Hezron (see verses 9, 21, 25) in the place called Caleb-Ephrathah. This was a village or town named after Caleb and his second wife, mentioned in verse 19.
**g)** Abijah was the third wife of Hezron; compare verses 9 and 21.
**h)** The word "father" here means the prince, leader, or founder (as in verses 45, 49, 50) of the town of Tekoa. See 2 Samuel 14:2 and Jeremiah 6:1. However, it is possible that Ashhur had a son of this name as well, similar to Gilead in verse 21.

**v. 25. i)** See verse 27. This was a different person than his uncle of the same name mentioned above in verse 9.

**v. 26. k)** His descendants are in verse 28. Another person of this name is found in Chapter 1, verse 40.

**v. 30. l)** See verse 28.
**m)** Meaning he died without children.

**v. 32. 34.** 2 Samuel 23:24. The Hebrew letter *He* <note>the definite article 'the'</note> is understood here, as in Job 8:11 and elsewhere.

**v. 31. n)** Regarding the sons of Appaim (verse 30), the most notable among them is Ishi, whose name means "Salvation is of the Lord." Compare others of this name in 4:20, 42, and 5:24. Note that the plural form "sons of" is used in this verse even though only one son is listed; for similar usage, see verse 7 and Chapter 3:22.

**v. 34. o)** To clarify, Sheshan (verse 31) had no sons. Ahlai, mentioned in verse 31, is likely the name of the daughter mentioned in verse 35. Alternatively, if Ahlai was a son, he died without children.

**v. 35. p)** Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha, his servant—specifically, a proselyte <note>a convert to the faith</note> whom he had granted freedom. The Hebrews did not shun Egyptians as strictly as they did Canaanites (see Deuteronomy 23:3, 8), and through this marriage, Jarha was counted among the people of Judah.
</margin>

# 1 CHRONICLES CHAPTERS 2 & 3
### Page 796 / 22

<margin>
(a) The daughter of Caleb (the son of Hezron, mentioned in verse 18, not to be confused with Caleb the son of Jephunneh in Chapter 4:15) was Achsah. Whether she was born to Maacah (verse 48) or another mother, her name suggests "little ornaments" or "anklets" <note>original: "Particclis," comparing Isaiah 3:18</note>. This is a different person from the daughter of the other Caleb mentioned in Joshua 15:16 and Judges 1:12.
(b) These following names were also the sons and descendants of Caleb (see verses 9 and 18). Caleb’s son was Hur (verses 19, 20), who was the firstborn of Ephrathah (verse 19). Hur’s son was Shobal (verse 52, Chapter 4:1), who was the "father"—meaning the restorer and founder (verses 21, 49)—of the city of Kiriath-Jearim (verse 52). This city sat on the border of the territory of Benjamin within the tribe of Judah (Joshua 9:17, 15:60, Judges 18:12).
(c) The son or brother of Shobal (verse 5) was Salma (verse 54). He is distinct from the Salma mentioned in verse 11 and Ruth 4:20. He was the founder (verse 50) of Bethlehem, the home of the Bethlehemite families (verse 54, Genesis 35:19, 1 Samuel 16:1, 4). As the scholar Grotius noted: "For from families come villages, and from villages come towns."
(d) Hareph was the father <note>founder</note> of the city of Beth-Gader, which is also called Gader (Joshua 12:13) and Gedera (Joshua 15:36). The name means "a sheepfold" or "walled enclosure." Compare below in Chapter 12:4 and 27:28.
</margin>

CHAPTER 3. v. 1. (e) Furthermore, these are the sons of David. They are carefully recorded here and later in Chapter 14:4–7, as well as in 2 Samuel 3:2–5 and 5:13–16. This record is vital because of the CHRIST <note>The Messiah</note>, who was to be born from David’s lineage (2 Samuel 7).

### Philological and Vowel Notes
Verse 24. **Anani**: accented on the last syllable <note>original: "milra"</note> in manuscripts 1, 6, 9, 20, 23. **CHAPTER IV**, verse 3. **Hazzelelponi**: likewise accented on the last syllable in manuscripts 1, 2, 5, 21, 22 according to the Masoretic text of Frankfurt. Others accent the second-to-last syllable <note>original: "milel"</note>. Furthermore, there is no doubling dot <note>Dagesh</note> in the letter *Tsade* in lines 15, 22, 23. Verse 4. **Father of Gedor**: accented on the last syllable in manuscripts 1, 2, 5, 21, 22, 23. Verse 7. **And Zohar**: Manuscript 7 has "And Izhar" instead of "Zohar." Verse 8. **And Coz fathered**: contrary to the Frankfurt Masorah in this place. Verse 9. **Jabez**: In verse 10, the names "Cush and Anub" appear as they do in the Septuagint (*kaì Sōbáb*), contrary to the Frankfurt Masorah. Verse 10. **And God brought that which**: written as one unit in manuscripts 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 15, 20, 23. Verse 9. **Harum**: written with the letter *Chet* instead of *He* in manuscripts 2 and 5, and in the margin of manuscript 6. Verse 13. **Hathath**: written with the vowel *Qamets* in most manuscripts. Verse 15. **And Kenaz**: written with *Qamets* in manuscripts 2, 6, 9, 13, 14, 19, 20.

# 1 CHRONICLES. CHAPTER 4.

**Hebrew page number: 797**

**a)** "she conceived and bore" <note>original Latin: "concepit autem & peperit"</note> (referencing Genesis 42:26 and Job 3:3). This refers to the wife of Mered, mentioned at the end of verse 18.
**b)** And the other wife of Mered was Jehudijah <note>or "the Jewess"</note>; compare the masculine form in Jeremiah 36:14 and Esther 9:29.
**c)** The father <note>meaning the founder or chief</note> of Gedor, a city in the tribe of Judah (compare verses 4 and 39; Joshua 15:58).
**d)** The father of Soco, a twin city in the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:35, 1 Samuel 17:1).
**e)** The father and restorer of Zanoah. There were also two cities of this name in the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:34, 56; Nehemiah 3:13).
**f)** These, I say, are the sons of Bithiah, the daughter of a certain Pharaoh, whom Mered had married (see verse 17).

**v. 19. g)** The sons of the wife of Hodiah; whose origin, as well as that of her brother <note>original Latin: "adanis," likely a typo for "adgnati" or "brother"</note> Naham, we are today unsure of. They were first the father and founder of Keilah in the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:44, 1 Samuel 23:1), the Garmite (descended from the family of Gerem), and the father of part of the inhabitants of Eshtemoa; also the Maacathite, likely descending from Maacah (compare 2:48).

**v. 20. h)** The sons of Ishi, the brother of Shimon, were Zocheth and Ben-Zocheth, his brother; I have not found more to be recorded concerning them.

**v. 21. i)** The sons—that is, the descendants—of Shelah, the son of Judah (2:3, Genesis 38:5), who have not been reviewed until now. **Kimchi** <note>a famous medieval Jewish commentator</note> remarks: "All the descendants of Judah enumerated so far were from the lines of Perez and Zerah; none were from the lineage of Shelah. He therefore adds these now to finish the genealogy of Judah."

**v. 24. k)** The sons and descendants of Simeon <note>the Simeonites</note>. He connects them here to the Judeans and places them before the Reubenites (Chapter 5) because the inheritance of Simeon was largely contained within the territory of the tribe of Judah.

**Textual Variants:**
Verse 33: **Pasach** written with a *Qamets* vowel in manuscripts 1, 5, 6, 9, 20. — v. 33: **Ashvath** with an *Aleph* in place of a *He* in manuscripts 1, 6, 9, 10, 20, 23. — v. 34: **Rohgah** appears without the extra *Vav* in manuscript 2; but the Erfurt Masora notes it with a *Qamets* as **Rahgah**. Other books have **Hubbah** spelled differently. — v. 34: **Hubbah** in the *Kethib* <note>the written text</note> is written one way, while the Masora notes another. — **Helem** in v. 35 is written with a *Segol* vowel in many manuscripts. — v. 35: **Shelesh** likewise with a *Segol* in 1, 2, 3, 5. — v. 36: **Imrah** and **Puspah** follow the *Oriental* tradition <note>Eastern/Babylonian tradition</note>. — v. 37: **Ithran** with an *Aleph* according to its Masora. — v. 38: **Ara** with a *Qamets* in 1, 2, 6, 9, 20. — v. 7: **Ahihud** written for **Abihud** in the Erfurt Masora. — v. 39: **Ishvael and Beri** found in manuscripts 7, 8, 14, 16. — CHAPTER 8, v. 1: **Aharah** with a *Qamets* in 1, 2, 6, 9, 20. — v. 7: **Ahihud** according to the Erfurt Masora; other books have **Achihud** in the margin. — v. 10: **Sakia** written with the letter *Kaph* in most manuscripts, a reading followed by the Latin Vulgate translator. Others use the letter *Beth* instead of *Kaph*, which is how the Greek Septuagint (LXX) read it. Furthermore, some write it with the letter *Sin*. — v. 12: **Shemed**—note!—is written with the letter *Resh* <note>making it 'Shemer'</note> in 1, 3, 17, 18, 21, 22, 24, and the Erfurt Masora. But the rest use the letter *Daleth*. The Vulgate followed the latter, while the Septuagint followed the former. — v. 13: **Gath** with a *Qamets* in most manuscripts. — v. 14: **Shashak** with a *Qamets* in many manuscripts. — v. 20: **Elienai** has various spellings in manuscript 1.

# 1 CHRONICLES CHAPTERS 10, 11

<header>I. CHRONICLES. CHAPTERS 10. 11.</header>

<margin>a) verse 8. 1 Samuel 28:4; chapter 31:1; 2 Samuel 1:6, 21. That mountain and the large village of the same name were located six miles from Scythopolis <note>A major city in the Jordan Valley, modern-day Beth Shean</note>, according to the historians Eusebius and Jerome.</margin>
**1** Now the Philistines fought against Israel; and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines, and fell down slain on Mount Gilboa<sup>a</sup>.
<margin>verse 2. b) The Philistines especially pursued Saul and his sons, as seen in Judges 18:22; 20:42; 1 Samuel 14:22; 31:2. c) chapter 8:33.</margin>
**2** And the Philistines followed hard<sup>b</sup> after Saul and after his sons; and the Philistines killed Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul<sup>c</sup>.
<margin>verse 3. d) chapter 5:22; Judges 20:34. e) see note on 1 Samuel 31:3. f) "those who shoot" 2 Samuel 11:20, 24. Those who shoot with the bow. g) The Syriac version <note>An ancient translation of the Bible</note> says: He was greatly terrified. Esther 4:4.</margin>
**3** And the battle went sore<sup>d</sup> against Saul, and the archers<sup>f</sup> found him<sup>e</sup>; and he was terrified<sup>g</sup> by the archers.
<margin>verse 4. h) See the note on 1 Samuel 31:4.</margin>
**4** Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw<sup>h</sup> your sword and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and abuse me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he was very afraid. So Saul took the sword and fell upon it.
<margin>verse 5. i) 1 Samuel 31:5.</margin>
**5** And when his armor-bearer saw<sup>i</sup> that Saul was dead, he also fell upon the sword and died.
<margin>verse 6. k) Thus Saul died, along with his three sons listed in verse 2. The fourth son, Eschbaal (also called Ish-bosheth in chapter 8:33), either escaped or was not at the battle, as compared to 2 Samuel 1:8. l) That is, as many of his household or relatives who were present at the battle were destroyed all together. 1 Samuel 31:6.</margin>
**6** So Saul died<sup>k</sup>, and his three sons; and all his house<sup>l</sup> died together.
<margin>verse 7. m) In the valley or plain of Jezreel, Judges 6:33; Hosea 1:5. n) However, they did not stay long, as seen in 2 Samuel 5:17 and following; chapter 7:10, etc.</margin>
**7** And when all the men of Israel who were in the valley<sup>m</sup> saw that they fled, and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities<sup>n</sup> and fled; and the Philistines came and lived in them.
<margin>verse 8. o) See 1 Samuel 31:8 and following.</margin>
**8** And it happened on the next day<sup>o</sup>, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, that they found Saul and his sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.
**9** And they stripped him, and took his head and his armor, and sent them into the land of the Philistines all around, to carry the news to their idols and to the people.
**10** And they put his armor in the house of their gods, and fastened his skull in the house of Dagon <note>The primary god of the Philistines, often associated with grain or fish</note>.
**11** And when all Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul,
**12** all the valiant men arose and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons, and brought them to Jabesh; and they buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh, and fasted seven days.
**13** So Saul died for his unfaithfulness which he committed against the Lord, because of the word of the Lord which he did not keep, and also for asking counsel of a medium <note>the "Witch of Endor"</note> to inquire of her,
<margin>verse 14. p) For he did not consult the Lord (verse 13) with integrity, in true repentance and faith; compare chapter 13:3; 15:13; 1 Samuel 13:8-14; 14:19, 24, 36, 37; 15:1, 9-26; 28:6. q) Therefore He killed him (chapter 2:3) and transferred the kingdom to David, the son of Jesse (chapter 2:15; 11:1; 12:23; 2 Samuel 2:3).</margin>
**14** and he did not inquire<sup>p</sup> of the Lord. Therefore He killed him<sup>q</sup> and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.

<margin>CHAPTER XI, verse 1. r) For finally all the Israelites were gathered. cf. 2 Samuel 5:1. This chapter deals with: I. The inauguration of David over all Israel (v. 1-3). II. The capture of the fortress of Zion (v. 4-9). III. His heroes or mighty men, who are listed in three orders (v. 10-20, v. 21-25, v. 26-47).</margin>
**1** Then all Israel gathered<sup>r</sup> to David at Hebron, saying, "Behold, we are your bone and your flesh.

**Textual Variations and Notes:**
CHAPTER 10, verse 3: *The archers* <note>original: "ha-morim"</note> so written in manuscripts 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 19, and similar to manuscript 5. verse 4: *Draw* <note>original: "shelof"</note> so marked with the accent *Merca* in 7, 8, 11-19, 23, 24 and manuscript 5. But with the accent *Darga* in 1, 3, 6, 9, 20, 21, 22 and manuscript 5. Finally, with *Makkaph* and *Ber*. Instead of *and they abuse [me]* <note>original: "ve-hitalelu"</note>, another book in the Erfurt Masorah <note>A traditional system of notes on the Hebrew biblical text</note> has *they shall abuse* <note>original: "ve-yitalelu"</note> with the letter Yod. verse 5: *And the armor-bearer saw* so in 22. verse 7: *And they abandoned* so in 2, 3, and manuscript 5. verse 8: *On the next day* with the accent *Metheg* instead of *Munach* in 1, 2, 3, 5, 14, 17, 18, 22, 23. *And they came*: with *Munach* without the following *kephk.* together with *Paschta* in 1, 24. verse 10: *His skull*: the letter Gimel with the vowel *Patach* in 6, 9, 20. verse 11: *And they heard* so according to Sa-cntra Masorah and Erfurt. verse 12: *Jabesh* written fully in 6, 9, 20, 22 according to the Erfurt Masorah. verse 12: *To Jabesh* <note>original: "Yabeshah"</note> written defectively in 1, 2, 3, omitting the word "et", if the printed index of these variations is correct. verse 14: *The kingdom* <note>original: "ha-mamlukah"</note>, but *the kingdom* <note>original: "ha-mamlukah" with different spelling</note> in the text of 6, 9, 20. CHAPTER 11, verse 1: For *and they gathered*. verse 2: *While Saul was*. verse 2: *While being* so in 6, 9, 20, and manuscript 5, but *also*.

**Verse 44.** The word "the Aroerite" <note>original Hebrew: "Ha-Ar-eri"</note> is written as "Ha-Ar-a-ri" in some versions, which is how the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> read it. **Verse 44.** The name "Jeuel" follows the "Oriental" <note>Babylonian tradition</note> manuscript tradition in the text. **Verse 2.** The word "left-handed" <note>original: "u-mashm'ilim"</note> is written with a mobile Aleph in several manuscripts. **Verse 3.** "Jeziel" follows the Oriental tradition without further notation. **Verse 4.** "The Thirty"—In this place, instead of the *Atnach* <note>a Hebrew musical/punctuation mark indicating a pause</note>, several manuscripts (1, 2, 3, etc.) use the *Silluk* and *Soph-pasuk* marks. **Verse 5.** For "Eluzai," some manuscripts read "the Haruphite." **Verse 6.** "Isshiah" is written thus in manuscripts 1, 3, and 5 and in the tradition of Ben Naphtali <note>a famous 10th-century Hebrew scholar</note>. **Verse 8.** For "Gedor," some read it with the vowel *Shurek* and the letter *Daleth*. **Verse 8.** For "spear," many manuscripts (16, 19, etc.) follow the reading found in the *Minchat Shai* <note>a famous 17th-century commentary on the Hebrew text</note>. **Verse 10.** "Mishmannah" is written with a *Patach* vowel in several codices and the Septuagint. "The fifth" is written without a *Dagesh* <note>a dot in a Hebrew letter indicating emphasis or doubling</note> in certain versions.

<column-break/>

**Chapter 12, Verse 1.** "To Ziklag"—This occurred when David was returning from the camp of the Philistines to Ziklag. The text continues with: III. Those from the tribe of Manasseh (verses 19–22). IV. Those from each tribe who, after the death of Saul and Ishbosheth, gathered at Hebron to make David king (verses 23–38). V. The public joy and festivities of the people (verses 39–40).

<meta>Technical textual variants regarding Hebrew grammar and manuscript discrepancies</meta>
Verse 17: **and judge** [Hebrew: *veyokach*] according to manuscripts Pat. 7, 8, 15, 22, 24, and the Basel Index folio 61d. Others read with a Kametz vowel. Verse 18: **clothed** [Hebrew: *labesh*] according to manuscripts He 2, 6, 9, etc., against the Masoretic Erff manuscript. But the letter Nun is used in Pat. 3, 5, etc. Verse 20: **Adnah** according to He 1, 3, 5. Verse 20: **upon him** without the *Pshik* accent in 2, 3, 6, 9, 20, 21. Verse 22: **to a camp** according to Tfers 2 and margin 6, 9. **Zillethai** has a Lamed without a *Dagesh* [dot] in 1, 3, 6, 9, etc. Verse 25: **Simeon** thus with the *Sakeph-katon* accent. Others use *Revia*, which is entirely irregular. See a similar anomaly in chapter 11:31. **Mighty men of valor** in verse 31. **From the half-tribe** in verse 38, chapter 11:1, and 2 Samuel 5:1. **For the army** so in manuscripts 1 and 5.

*Translator’s notes on the Hebrew markings:*
v. 7. The word "and they carried" (Wayyarkibu) uses a *Paschta* accent mark in source 1, and similarly in source 5.
v. 12. "The God" (Ha-Elohim) is marked with a *Munach* instead of a *Metheg* in sources 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14, and 19. Nevertheless, a *Kadma* remains on the preceding word irregularly.
CHAPTER 14, v. 1. "Hiram" is marked with a *Munach* in sources 1, 3, 6, and 9.
v. 14. The first instance of "Obed" is marked with a *Merca* accent in sources 1, 2, 3, 5, and 14. But the rest use a *Maqqeph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in the text without a note in sources 3, 6 through 10, 12 through 16, 19, 20, 21, and 23—this goes against the Masoretic tradition of Genesis 36:5, 12, 14, 20, 24. Others use a *Merca* following the Masoretic text of Erfurt.
v. 8. A space is placed before this verse in sources 1, 2, 3, 5 through 10, 19, 20, 21, 22, and 23.
v. 10. "Philistines" is written this way in the text without a note in sources 2, 11, 12, 13, 16, 21, and 23, against the Erfurt Masoretic text.
v. 11. "And they went up" (Wayya’alu) uses a *Merca* in sources 5 and 24, following the Masoretic text of Exodus 6:6. But the word "In Baal" (Be-Baal) is written with a *Maqqeph* and a *Segol* in sources 2, 3, and 5.

13 ᶜ) The Philistines raided yet again in the valley. 14 ᵈ) And David again consulted God, and God said to him, "Do not go up after them; turn away from them and come upon them from opposite the balsam trees. 15 ᶢ) And it shall be, when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then you shall go out to battle, for God has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines."
16 ʰ) David did as God commanded him, and they struck the camp of the Philistines from Gibeon even to Gezer. 17 ᵏ) And the fame of David went out into all lands, and the Lord put the fear of him upon all the nations.

<note>The following notes are technical observations by scholars regarding differences in spelling, vowel points, and musical accents across various ancient manuscripts (numbered 1 through 24).</note>

**v. 12.** The word *et* (the direct object marker) is written with a connecting line (Makkef) and a Segol vowel in manuscripts 2, 3, 6, 9, 20... **v. 13.** The word "at the first time" is written with a Merca accent in manuscripts 3, 5 through 11, 13... while others use a Meth accent. Furthermore, the first letter 'M' is written with a Chirek vowel in manuscripts 1 and 2. **v. 14.** "And the Levites" in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9... **v. 15.** Written with a Chateph-patach vowel in 1, 2, 22. "To the Levites" is accented on the last syllable in manuscript 5, but on the penult in 1 and 16. **v. 16.** "To raise" in manuscript 3... **v. 18.** "And Jehiel" is without a pause mark (Pfik) in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9... **v. 19.** "And Ethan" uses a Kibbutz vowel in manuscripts 1 and 3. **v. 21.** "And Azaziah" uses a Chateph-patach vowel in manuscripts 5, 6, 9, 20. **v. 24.** "And Shebaniah" uses the letter Caph instead of Beth in manuscripts 8 and 20. **v. 25.** "Obed" uses a Meth accent in 2, 3, 5. **v. 26.** "In helping" uses a Chateph-segol vowel in manuscripts 1, 7, 8, 11... others use a simple Schua. **v. 27.** "Clothed" uses a Patach vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 20.

<margin>Chapter XVII.</margin>
# CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>
CHAPTER XVII, v. 1. c) See the note on 2 Samuel 7:1.
d) 2 Samuel 7:2.
e) Exodus 26:1, 7. Compare above at chapter 15:1; 16:1; 28:2.
In this chapter: I. David piously considers and deliberates about building a Temple (v. 1–2), but is forbidden by God through Nathan (v. 4–6). II. However, after God recounts the benefits He has bestowed upon David (v. 7–10), He predicts that David’s son, whose kingdom would be eternal, would build it (v. 11–15). III. Therefore, David gives many thanks to God (v. 16–22) and humbly asks for the fulfillment of the divine promise (v. 23–27).
</margin>
1 <gloss>c</gloss>**And it came to pass**, when David dwelt in his house, that David said to <gloss>d</gloss>**Nathan** the prophet: "Behold, I dwell in a house of cedars, but the Ark of the Covenant of the LORD remains under <gloss>e</gloss>**curtains** <note>meaning the fabrics of the temporary Tabernacle tent</note>."

<margin>
v. 2. f) See the note on 2 Samuel 7:3.
</margin>
2 And <gloss>f</gloss>**Nathan** said to David: "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you."

<margin>
v. 3. g) Since he had deliberated with Nathan during the day. 2 Chronicles 1:7; Esther 6:1.
h) Compare note on 2 Samuel 7:4.
</margin>
3 <gloss>g</gloss>**And it happened** <gloss>h</gloss>**that night**, that the word of God came to Nathan, saying:

<margin>
v. 4. i) See 2 Samuel 7:5.
</margin>
4 "Go <gloss>i</gloss>**and tell** David My servant: Thus says the LORD: It is not you who shall build Me the house to dwell in.

<margin>
v. 5. k) Instead, I have been "walking" (as seen in v. 6 and 2 Samuel 7:6) from tent to tent, in places like Gilgal, then Shiloh, then Nob, then Gibeon. Compare note on Psalm 78:60.
l) Meaning from one tabernacle to another (Exodus 26:1). This signifies that the Church would migrate from one people to another.
</margin>
5 <gloss>k</gloss>**For** I have not dwelt in a house from the day that I brought up Israel until this day; <gloss>l</gloss>**but I have been** moving from tent to tent, and from one tabernacle to another.

<margin>
v. 6. m) 2 Samuel 7:7.
</margin>
6 <gloss>m</gloss>**In all** the places where I have walked with all Israel, did I ever speak a word to any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd My people, saying: Why have you not built Me a house of cedars?"

7 "And now, thus shall you say to My servant David: Thus says the LORD of Hosts: I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be a ruler over My people Israel.

8 And I have been with you in all that you have walked, and I have cut off all your enemies from before you, and I will make for you a name like the name of the great ones who are on the earth.

9 And I will appoint a place for My people Israel and will plant them, and they shall dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more; and the sons of wickedness shall no longer wear them down as they did at first,

10 and since the days that I commanded judges to be over My people Israel. And I will subdue all your enemies. Moreover, I tell you that the LORD will build a house <note>here meaning a 'dynasty' or 'lineage' rather than a building</note> for you.

11 And it shall come to pass, when your days are fulfilled to go with your fathers, that I will raise up your seed after you, who shall be of your sons, and I will establish his kingdom.

12 He shall build Me a house, and I will establish his throne forever.

13 I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to Me; and I will not take My mercy away from him, as I took it from the one who was before you <note>referring to King Saul</note>.

14 And I will settle him in My house and in My kingdom forever, and his throne shall be established forever."

<note>The following are technical Masoretic notes regarding the specific chanting accents and grammatical markings used in the Hebrew text of Chapter 17.</note>
CHAPTER XVII, v. 3. The word *Davar* (word) is marked with a *Makkaph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in versions 7, 8, 10, 13, 19. | v. 4. The word *Lo* (not) is marked with a *Mercha* accent in versions 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10–16, 19–24. The others use a *Makkaph*. However, in the phrase "not you" (*Lo Atah*), version 2 is different. | v. 5. The word *Israel* is preceded by "children of" in versions 6, 9, 20. v. 6. The word *Be-khol* (in all) is marked with *Mercha* in versions 1, 2, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 19, 24. This follows the printed Masorah of Exodus 6:6. Others use *Munach*. The phrase "my people" (*et-ammi*) appears in version 11. The Eastern scribal tradition (it seems) writes but does not read a specific variant for the word "why" (*lamah*) in version 2. v. 7. The phrase "thus you shall say" (*koh-tomar*) is marked this way in versions 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13–19. | v. 10. The word *Ve-aggid* (and I tell) appears without a *Dagesh* <note>a dot in a letter signaling a doubled or harder sound</note> in the letter Lamed in versions 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 14, 15, 20, 22. | v. 12. The word *Lo* (to him) is without a *Dagesh* in versions 3, 5, 7, 8.

v. 5. **Twenty**—with a *Meteg* <note>A small vertical line used as a stress or vowel-duration mark</note> in manuscripts 3, 5. **Twenty-two** thus in 1, 6, 9, 12, 20; and so in future 5.

v. 12. **And Abishai son of Zeruiah** thus in 3. But **Zeruiah** through *Sakeph Katan* <note>A specific musical/logical pause mark in Hebrew</note> in 20, 23, 24, and in Berlin. **Struck down Edom in the Valley of Salt** thus in 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 19. -># I. CHRONICLES CHAPTERS 22 & 23<-

Now, arise and build the sanctuary of the LORD God, to bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the holy vessels of God into the house built for the name of the LORD.

<margin>CHAPTER XXIII</margin>

### 23

When David was old and full of days, he made his son Solomon king over Israel.

He gathered all the princes of Israel, along with the priests and the Levites.

The Levites were numbered from thirty years old and upward; and their number by their head-count, man by man, was thirty-eight thousand.

"Of these," David said, "twenty-four thousand are to oversee the work of the house of the LORD, and six thousand are to be officers and judges.

Four thousand are to be gatekeepers, and four thousand are to praise the LORD with the instruments which I made for giving praise."

David divided them into divisions according to the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

Of the Gershonites: Laadan and Shimei.

The sons of Laadan: Jehiel the chief, Zetham, and Joel—three in total.

<margin>Shelomith (traditional reading)</margin>
The sons of Shimei: Shelomith, Haziel, and Haran—three. These were the heads of the fathers' houses of Laadan.

And the sons of Shimei: Jahath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah. These were the sons of Shimei—four.

Jahath was the chief and Zizah the second; but Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, so they were counted as one father's house for their census.

The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel—four.

The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses. Aaron was set apart to be sanctified as most holy, he and his sons forever, to burn incense before the LORD, to minister to Him, and to bless in His name forever.

As for Moses the man of God, his sons were named among the tribe of Levi.

The sons of Moses: Gershom and Eliezer.

The sons of Gershom: Shebuel the chief.

The sons of Eliezer were Rehabiah the chief. Eliezer had no other sons, but the sons of Rehabiah were very many.

The sons of Izhar: Shelomith the chief.

The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.

<meta>catchword: sons</meta>

<column-break/>

a) <note>original: "ut intromittatis"</note> *so that you may bring in*, see chapter 13:5 and 16:1. *The ark of the covenant of the LORD*, see 15:25. *And the remaining vessels, consecrated to God*, that is, belonging to the holiness of God, chapter 9:29 and Daniel 9:20. *Into the house to be built for the name of the LORD*, see verses 7, 8, and 10.

CHAPTER XXIII, verse 1.
b) <note>original: "Quum vero David consenuisset"</note> *When indeed David had grown old*, see Genesis 25:8 and 1 Kings 1:1, 15. *And was satisfied with days*, so that out of a desire for eternal life he did not wish for his mortal life to be prolonged, chapter 29:28, Genesis 25:8, 35:29, and Philippians 1:23. *He appointed his son Solomon as king, as his successor* designated for him by GOD Himself, chapter 22:9 and 28:5. *Over Israel*, 1 Kings 1:30–43 and 2 Chronicles 1:8, 9. This was done so that after his death, disturbances would not arise among his sons, such as the impiety of Absalom and the ambitious grasping of Adonijah had already shown, 1 Kings 1:5 and following.

In this chapter: I. David transfers the kingdom to his son Solomon, verse 1. II. He numbers the Priests and Levites and assigns them their sacred duties, verses 2–5. III. He distributes them through the three families of the Levites, verse 6: 1) *The Gershonites*, verses 7–11; 2) *The Kohathites*, verses 12–20; and 3) *The Merarites*, verses 21–24. IV. The reason for this new distribution is explained, verses 25–32.

verse 2. c) <note>original: "Congregavit etiam"</note> *He also gathered together*, chapter 15:4, all the leaders of Israel, chapter 22:17, and the Priests and Levites, chapter 9:2, 13:2, and 15:14.

verse 3. d) <note>original: "Et numerati sunt Levitæ"</note> *And the Levites were numbered*, who were not yet recorded in chapter 21:6; he did this so that, knowing their number, he could better distribute them into their orders. e) *As it had been prescribed of old* by Moses, Numbers 4:3, from which time they would perform their full ministry; compare the note on Numbers 8:24. There was, therefore, another census later in verse 24, instituted from the *twentieth* year of age, because once the temple was built, their labors were diminished; compare verse 27.

verse 4. f) <note>original: "Ex istis sunt"</note> *From these are*, David said (compare verse 5), those set to urge on the work and ministry of the house of the LORD, chapter 15:21 and 2 Chronicles 2:1.

---

**CHAPTER XXIII, verse 6.** <note>original: "וַיֶּחָלְקֵם"</note> *And he divided them*: thus it appears with the regular points in the <term>Piel|A Hebrew verb form usually indicating intensive action</term> in manuscript 3, and similarly in manuscript 5. But in the <term>Kal|The simple, active form of a Hebrew verb</term>, the word *vayechal-kem* appears with a <term>Qamets-hatuf|A Hebrew vowel mark indicating an 'o' sound</term> under the letter *Chet* in manuscripts 13 and 19, and similarly in manuscript 5; this is how the <note>original: "M. I."</note> <term>Manualis Isagoge|A common reference for Hebrew grammatical analysis</term> seems to resolve it (at least regarding the vowel <term>Segol</term> and the verb conjugation). Refer here to *vayechal-kem* in manuscripts 2 and 7. <note>The translator notes that these numbers refer to specific historical biblical manuscripts or codices used to compare textual variations.</note>

verse 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 21, 22. Compare chapter 24:3. For *the Gershonite* and *Kohath*, it appears this way in 6, 9, and 20. *Kohath* appears with a <term>Patach|A Hebrew vowel mark for 'a'</term> in 1 and 3, and in the margin of 6 and 9. verse 11: *And he was* (Vayehi) appears with the <term>Paschta|A specific musical/accent mark in Hebrew scripture</term> in 1, 2, 6, 9, and 20. Instead of *Vayehi* (singular), manuscript 1 has *Vayehiyu* (plural), which indeed agrees with verse 10. However, the letter <term>Aleph</term> at the end here is required by the <term>Masorah|The traditional system of notes on the Hebrew text</term> for Psalm 10:12. verse 12: appears with the <term>Rehia|An accent mark</term> in 3, and similarly in 5. verse 13: *holies* (kodashim) appears without the <term>Metheg|A small vertical line used as a pronunciation guide</term> in 2, 5, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 19, 21, and 22. verse 14: *his sons* (banav) appears with the <term>Merca|A musical accent mark</term> in 6, 9, and 20. verse 17: For *they increased* (rabu), manuscripts 6, 9, and 20 have a variant. verse 19: *Jahaziel* appears with the <term>Paschta</term> accent in 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14, 15, and 19.

It provides a genealogical breakdown of the Levite families and explains the administrative roles assigned to them to ensure the Temple's future operation.</summary>

<note>The following are technical notes regarding manuscript variations.</note>

**Verse 5.** Instead of **and among the sons** <note>original: "ובבני"</note>, some manuscripts [2, 3, etc.] and the margin of 6 and 9 have **and from the sons** <note>original: "ומבני"</note>.
**Verse 6.** Instead of **Zadok** <note>original: "וצדוק"</note>, others have **Zadik** <note>original: "וצדיק"</note>, compare 2 Samuel 8:13 and Ecclesiastes 11:2.
**Verse 15.** **Eighteen** <note>original: "שמונה"</note> is written in full here; and **Shelomoth** in **Verse 22** is written as such in several copies [2, 3, 5, 8], though without the vowel accents in others.
**Verse 23.** **Jeriah** <note>original: "יריהו"</note> appears thus in many copies [1, 2, 7, 8, etc.]; the missing words here are supplied from the Masoretic text and the Erfurt manuscript; but compare rather chapter 23:19 and 26:31.
**Verse 20.** Concerning the remaining Levites besides the Priests discussed above: the chief of the descendants of Amram [verse 21] was Shubael (or Shebuel) [chapter 23:13, 16; 26:24].
**Verse 27.** **The sons of Merari** <note>original: "בני מררי"</note> appears thus in manuscripts 2 and 3. In **Verse 28**, for **he had** <note>original: "היה"</note>, some copies [2, 3, 5, and margins of 6, 9] have a variant, contrary to the Masoretic printed editions and the Erfurt manuscript in this place and in chapter 23:22 and Genesis 41:48.

<summary>This page details the organization of the Jewish priesthood into twenty-four courses by casting lots to ensure impartiality, followed by a census of the remaining Levite families. It emphasizes that both high-ranking and lower-ranking families were treated equally in the distribution of duties.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the organization of the Levites, moving from the priests and general Levite families to the specific appointment of the Temple musicians and singers under the leadership of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun.</meta>

# I. CHRONICLES. CHAPTER 25.

**CHAPTER XXV, verse 1.**
**a)** Furthermore, David, along with the princes and commanders of the Israelite army [chapter 23:2; 26:26; 27:3], set apart for sacred service the descendants of Asaph [v. 2; 6:34], Heman [v. 4, 5; 6:18], and Jeduthun [v. 3; 9:16; 16:41-42]—who is also called Ethan [6:29; 15:17]. They were designated to "prophesy," <note>The Latin 'prophetarent' here implies a spiritual form of musical performance</note> that is, to sing prophetic hymns while playing musical instruments [v. 2, 3; 1 Samuel 10:5, 10; 19:20; 2 Kings 3:15]. **b)** The following was the number of these "men of work" <note>professional skilled laborers</note> who were appointed to fulfill this duty [9:33] for their service in the house of God [v. 6; 24:19], as detailed below in verse 7. This chapter is divided into two parts: I. The establishment of the singers from the families of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun (v. 1-7), and II. Their distribution by lot into 24 service divisions, each containing twelve members (v. 8-31).

**v. 2. c)** Regarding the sons of Asaph [v. 1]: Zaccur, who later received the third lot [v. 10]; Joseph, who was first by lot [v. 9]; Nethaniah, the fifth [v. 12]; and Asharelah (or Ischarela), perhaps the seventh [v. 14]. These four sons of Asaph were under the hand and direction of Asaph, who prophesied "at the hands and orders of the King," meaning he was supported by the king’s own authority. <note>See the more extensive notes for further detail.</note>

**v. 3. d)** Regarding Jeduthun [v. 1], his sons were Gedaliah, perhaps the second [v. 9]; Zeri, the fourth [v. 11]; Jeshaiah, the eighth [v. 15]; Hashabiah, the twelfth [v. 19]; and Mattithiah, the fourteenth [v. 21]. There were six in total, including Shimei, who presided over the tenth division [v. 17].

**v. 4. e)** Finally, regarding Heman [v. 1, 2], he had fourteen sons: Bukkiah, sixth in order [v. 13]; Mattaniah [v. 16]; Uzziel [v. 18]; Shebuel [v. 20]; Jerimoth [v. 22]; Hananiah [v. 23]; Hana... <unclear>nias</unclear> [v. 23], and so on.

Chapter XXV.
יהוי' י' <note>Abbreviations for the Divine Name and perhaps a liturgical marker</note>
</margin>
1 David and the commanders of the army set apart for the service the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, who prophesied with lyres, harps, and cymbals. The number of the men of work for their service was: **1**
2 Of the sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asharelah, the sons of Asaph, under the direction of Asaph, who prophesied under the direction of the king. **2**
3 Of Jeduthun: the sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah—six—under the direction of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre in giving thanks and praise to the Lord. **3**
4 Of Heman: the sons of Heman: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel, Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, and Mahazioth. <note>The names in the latter half of this verse are unusual and, when read together in Hebrew, form a poetic prayer: "I have magnified and exalted help; sitting in hardship, I have spoken of abundant visions."</note> **4**
5 All these were the sons of Heman, the king's seer <note>term: seer (Hebrew: chozeh); a prophet who receives divine visions</note> in the matters of God, to lift up the horn. <note>To "lift up the horn" is a Hebrew idiom meaning to increase power or dignity</note> And God gave Heman fourteen sons and three daughters. **5**
6 All these were under the direction of their father in the song of the House of the Lord, with cymbals, harps, and lyres, for the service of the House of God, under the direction of the king, Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman. **6**
7 The number of them, along with their brothers who were trained in song for the Lord—all who were skillful—was two hundred eighty-eight. **7**

### Technical and Grammatical Notes
**v. 2.** **Asharelah** is written with the letter *Sin* (שׂ) and so appears 5 times. Furthermore, the accent is *milra* <note>term: milra; a Hebrew grammar term meaning the stress is on the final syllable</note>.
**Mahazioth** <note>original: 'מַהוּיָאת'</note> is written defectively <note>missing a vowel letter</note> according to the Masorah <note>The tradition of scholars who preserved the Hebrew text</note>.
**v. 7.** **Trained** <note>original: 'מְלֻמְּדֵי'</note> is marked with the *Merca* accent.
**v. 9.** **He and his brothers** <note>original: 'הוּא וְאֶחָיו'</note> is marked with the *Thbir* accent, but preceded by a *Makkeph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note>.
**v. 11.** **The fourth** <note>original: 'הָרְבִיעִי'</note> is marked with the *Pashta* accent. This pattern continues for the following numbers.
**v. 18.** **Hashabiah** is written with a *Shurek* <note>a vowel representing 'u'</note> at the end in some manuscripts.

v. 11. The word "the third" is written defectively [missing a letter] in the first manuscript according to the Erfurt Masorah. v. 14. v. 32. **Strength** <note>original Hebrew: חיל</note> with the *Revia* accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 5–16, 19–23. The rest use *Zaqef Qaton*.
**CHAPTER XXVII, verse 1.**
With a space at the beginning in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5–19–23. **The fathers** <note>original Hebrew: הָאָבוֹת</note> thus with the *Pesiq* accent in 6–10, 13, 15, 17–22, 24. No, **the one** <note>original Hebrew: הָאַחַת</note>—the first *Tav* has a *Dagesh* in 6, 9, 17, 18. But in 24 it is *Milra* <note>accented on the final syllable</note> and in the Berlin edition. But the tone in this word is never found except on the last syllable.
v. 4. **And his division** <note>original Hebrew: וּמַחְלֻקְתּוֹ</note> with a *Metheg* instead of *Munach* in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 16, 20. v. 6. **His son** <note>original Hebrew: בְּנוֹ</note> thus in its place as in verse 2. **Warrior** <note>original Hebrew: גִבּוֹר - corrected from transcription error 'נְבוּר'</note> thus in its place in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 19, 20, and similarly in verse 5. v. 12. **The Anathothite** <note>original Hebrew: הָעַנְּתֹתִי</note> the *Nun* has a *Dagesh* in 8, 10–16, 19, and similarly in verse 5. The *Bet* has a *Tzere* in 7, 8, 11, 15, 16, 24 and the Berlin edition. The first *Nun* has an expressed *Shva* in 1, 2, 7, 8, 11, 15–18, 23, 24, and the Berlin edition, and in the margin of 6, 9; these are partly without and partly with a *Kere* <note>term: Kere — the traditional reading of the biblical text where it differs from the written word</note>. If the *Kere* is assumed, to which the vowel points must be accommodated, an expressed *Shva* cannot stand. Furthermore, **To the son of** <note>original Hebrew: לְבֶן</note> with a *Munach* in 3, 5, 24 and the Berlin edition, but with a *Mercha* in 22. This does not contradict the analogy of the accent connection; it seems necessary because, according to the indices of *Baal ha-Turim* (folio 61a), a *Pesiq* must be placed after the first part of the word **To the son of**, which assumes a preceding accent, as in a similar case of *Ketiv* <note>the written text</note> and *Kere* in Job 38:1. According to others, who have no accent under the *Bet*, the *Kere* should be understood as **To the Benjamite** <note>original Hebrew: לְבֶן־יְמִינִי</note> with a *Maqqaf* <note>hyphen</note> interposed.

<margin>CHAPTER XXVIII.</margin> **1** And David assembled <gloss>g</gloss> all the leaders of Israel: the leaders of the tribes <gloss>h</gloss>, the leaders of the divisions who served <gloss>i</gloss> the king, the commanders of thousands <gloss>k</gloss>, the commanders of hundreds <gloss>l</gloss>, and the overseers of all the property and livestock <gloss>m</gloss> of the king and his sons <gloss>n</gloss>, along with the officials <note>original: "sarisim," often translated as eunuchs, but here referring to court officials</note>, the mighty men, and every brave warrior, to Jerusalem.

**2** Then King David rose to his feet and said:
> “Hear me, my brothers and my people! I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the Ark of the Covenant of the LORD and for the footstool of our God, and I made preparations to build it.”

**3** But God said to me:
> “You shall not build a house for My name, for you are a man of war and have shed blood.”

**4** Yet the LORD, the God of Israel, chose me from all my father’s house to be king over Israel forever; for He chose Judah to be the leader, and in the house of Judah, my father’s house, and among my father’s sons, He was pleased with me to make me king over all Israel. **5** And of all my sons—for the LORD has given me many sons—He has chosen my son Solomon to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel.

**6** And He said to me:
> “Solomon your son is the one who shall build My house and My courts; for I have chosen him to be My son, and I will be his father. **7** I will establish his kingdom forever if he is steadfast in observing My commandments and My ordinances, as he is today.”

**8** Now therefore, in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of the LORD, and in the hearing of our God, observe and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, that you may possess this good land and leave it as an inheritance to your children after you forever. **9** And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve Him with a whole heart and a willing soul; for the LORD searches all hearts and understands every intent of the thoughts. If you seek Him, He will be found by you; but if you forsake Him, He will abandon you forever.

<column-break/>

**verse 31.** *a)* Over the smaller cattle <note>original: "minoribus pecudibus"</note> (referencing Job 1:3) presided Jaziz the Hagrite (in the Vulgate: Agareus), from Arabia (referencing chapters 5:10, 19, 20). *b)* All these were the "princes of substance," that is, those appointed over the king's resources (referencing chapter 28:1; Genesis 47:6; 1 Samuel 21:8).

**verse 32.** *c)* Jonathan, truly according to the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note>, was the paternal uncle, or according to Schmid, the cousin of David (referencing 2 Samuel 21:21). We prefer the former, even if this uncle of David is not mentioned elsewhere. *d)* He was a counselor (verse 33; chapter 26:14), for he was a prudent man (chapter 25:8; Proverbs 28:2) and a Scribe, which according to the Vulgate means "literate," and he was exceptionally well-learned in the Scriptures (chapter 2:55; Ezra 7:6).

**verse 33.** *e)* Ahithophel also was the king’s counselor (2 Samuel 15:12, 31; 16:23), and Hushai (2 Samuel 15:32, 37), the Archite from the town of Erech (Joshua 16:2), was the king's primary friend and intimate companion (2 Samuel 16:16; John 15:14, 15).

**verse 34.** *f)* After Ahithophel—either after his death or as next in rank (referencing verse 7)—was Jehoiada, the son of Benaiah (verses 5, 6). Likewise Abiathar (chapter 15:11). The leader and general of the royal army was Joab (verse 24; chapter 18:15; 2 Samuel 8:16).

**CHAPTER XXVIII, verse 1.** *g)* Finally, David convoked all the leaders of Israel (verse 21; chapter 13:5; 15:3). *h)* See chapter 27:16 and following. *i)* See chapter 27:1 and following. *k)* See chapter 12:20; 26:26. *l)* See chapter 13:1. *m)* And those appointed over all the wealth and private property (chapter 27:25–31). *n)* With the officials of the court (Genesis 37:36; 1 Samuel 8:15; 1 Kings 22:9). Surely, about to hand over the kingdom to his son Solomon, he:
**I.** Presents him to the assembled orders of the kingdom and exhorts all to the religious worship of God (verses 1–8).
**II.** Commands Solomon especially to fear God and build the temple (verses 9, 10).
**III.** Delivers to him the plan of the temple and all the preparations for it (verses 11–19), and again rouses him to readiness (verses 20, 21).
