<note>The following are technical notes regarding the Hebrew grammar and pronunciation found in specific manuscript copies.</note>

Verse 2: thus with the *Makkef* [connector] and *Kametz-Chatuf* [vowel] in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5. Verse 4: Instead of "talents of," manuscript 24:31 and 27:1 have "my talents" in the plural, and so in manuscript 5. Verse 9: "their willing offering" without the *Metheg* [stress mark] in manuscripts 1, 3, 6, 9–12, 15, 16, 20, 21. Verse 13: "and those praising" with the *Metheg* in manuscripts 1 and 3; the first letter *Lamed* has a *Chatef-Patach* vowel in manuscript 22. Verse 14: "we should be able," the letter *Ain* has a *Chatef-Patach* in manuscripts 1, 3, 7, 8, and manuscript 5. Verse 15: "like a shadow" without the *Paseq* [separator mark] in manuscripts 2, 3, 7, 8, 11, 14, 15, and 16, 21, 22, 23; this contradicts the Masoretic notes of Erfurt and the Basel Index. Verse 16: "to build" appears with a *Metheg* in manuscripts 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20, and R. Asher; others are without it.

**Technical Notes on the Hebrew Text:**
Verse 17: "To offer freely" <note>original: "להתנדב"</note> appears without the *Metheg* accent in several manuscripts (1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 11, 12, 15, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24). Verse 19: "And your testimonies" <note>original: "ועדותיך"</note> is written with the prefix *Vau* in the margin. In other manuscripts (3, 5), it is written with a "resting Vau," contrary to the Massorah of Erfurt. "To build the palace" <note>original: "ולבנות הבירה"</note> is found in manuscripts 7, 8, 11-14, 19, and 21-23. Verse 21: "To the Lord" <note>original: "ליהוה"</note> appears without the *Pasek* mark in several versions, contrary to the Index of Basel. Verse 23: "And he prospered" <note>original: "ויצלח"</note> is written with the *Qamets* vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, and 20. Verse 26: "Jesse" <note>original: "ישי"</note> and Verse 30: "With" <note>original: "עם"</note> also contain minor variations in accentuation across manuscripts.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Second Book of Chronicles. It follows the conclusion of David’s reign and the public installation of Solomon as king described at the end of 1 Chronicles. This page focuses on Solomon’s spiritual and political consolidation of power, specifically his famous request for wisdom at the high place of Gibeon.</note>

# THE SECOND BOOK OF CHRONICLES

<note>Hebrew: *Divrei HaYamim Bet*, meaning "The Words of the Days, Volume 2"</note>

-> THE SECOND BOOK OF CHRONICLES <-

This book deals both with the history of Solomon and with the events following the division of the kingdom, spanning 478 years until the liberation from the Babylonian captivity. It describes: I. The status of the kingdom as enviable and flourishing under Solomon, including his acts: 1) ecclesiastical (chapters 1–7), 2) political and economic (chapter 8), and 3) his glory and the fame of his reputation (chapter 9). II. The status of the divided kingdom under the remaining kings of Judah: (A) while it stood (chapters 10–32), and (B) as it weakened and fell (chapters 33–36), where finally, in chapter 36:22–23, mention is made of the release from captivity by Cyrus.

<margin>
**CHAPTER I.**

**Verse 1. a)** Solomon therefore established himself in his kingdom <note>original: "Confirmauit se ergo Salomo in regno suo"</note> against the plots of Adonijah and others (see 1 Kings 2:5; 2:12, 46; 1 Chronicles 29:23 and following). For the LORD his God was with him, as his father had desired (1 Chronicles 28:20), and made him great to the highest degree (1 Chronicles 29:25). This chapter describes Solomon’s beginnings and wealth. I. He sacrifices sumptuously to GOD at Gibeon (verses 1–6). II. God appears to him and grants the supreme wisdom he requests (verses 7–12). III. Having returned to Jerusalem, he reigns happily and gathers great wealth, especially for building the Temple (verses 13–18).

**Verse 2. b)** And Solomon spoke to all Israel <note>original: "Et edixit Salomo vniuerso Israeli"</note> (see Jonah 2:11 and 1 Chronicles 21:27), specifically so that they would go with him to Gibeon (from verse 3). **c)** See 1 Chronicles 28:1. **d)** Likewise to the judges (1 Chronicles 26:29) and to every prince or primary man of all Israel (chapter 5:6), the heads of the families (chapter 23:2; 1 Kings 8:1).

**Verse 3. e)** To the high place that was at Gibeon. Compare 1 Chronicles 16:39; 21:29; and the note on 1 Kings 3:4. **f)** Exodus 36:1 and following.

**Verse 4. g)** But the ark of God (chapter 19:3) David had brought up from Kiriath-Jearim (1 Samuel 7:1–2) into the place David had prepared for it (1 Chronicles 15:12). For he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:1, 29; 16:1; 2 Samuel 6:12, 17 notes).

**Verse 5. h)** Also the bronze altar <note>original: "Altare etiam æris"</note>, or the altar covered in bronze (verse 6; Exodus 27:1–2; 38:2), which Bezalel had made (Exodus 37:1; 38:1), was there at Gibeon. **i)** Therefore Solomon and the whole assembly sought it <note>original: "quæsivit ergo ipsum"</note>—that is, the altar (comparing Leviticus 17:3–4) or the LORD Himself (comparing chapter 15:2; 1 Chronicles 13:3; 15:13).
</margin>

**1** Solomon the son of David strengthened himself over his <sup>a</sup>kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him and magnified him exceedingly.
**2** And Solomon spoke to all Israel: <sup>b</sup>to the captains of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to every leader in all Israel, the heads of the fathers' houses.
**3** And Solomon and all the assembly with him went to the high place that was at Gibeon, for <sup>e</sup>there was the Tent of Meeting of God, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness.
**4** But <sup>g</sup>the ark of God David had brought up from Kiriath-Jearim to the place David had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.
**5** <sup>h</sup>The bronze altar which Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made was <sup>i</sup>there before the tabernacle of the LORD; and Solomon and the assembly sought it.
**6** And Solomon went up there to the bronze altar before the LORD, which was at the Tent of Meeting, and offered a thousand burnt offerings upon it.
**7** <sup>k</sup>In that night God appeared to Solomon and said to him, "Ask what I shall give you."
**8** And Solomon said to God, "You have shown great <sup>l</sup>lovingkindness to David my father, and have made me king in his place.
**9** Now, O LORD God, let Your word to David my father be confirmed, for You have made me king over a people as numerous as the dust of the earth.
**10** Now give me wisdom and knowledge, that I may go out and come in before this people; for who can judge this, Your great people?"
**11** And God said to Solomon, "Because this was in your heart, and you have not asked for riches, wealth, or honor, nor the life of those who hate you, nor have you asked for long life, but have asked for wisdom and knowledge for yourself, that you may judge My people over whom I have made you king:
**12** Wisdom and knowledge are granted to you; and I will give you riches, wealth, and honor, such as none of the kings who were before you have had, nor shall any after you have the like."

**CHAPTER I, verse 5.** Instead of *the bronze* <note>original: "הַנְּחֹשֶׁת" (ha-nechoshet)</note>, the Western traditions have *bronze* <note>original: "נחשת"</note> without the final *He*. The word "there" <note>original: "שם"</note> is written with a double dot [Shin] in manuscripts 2, 3, and 6. **verse 6. i)** See verses 9, 12, 14, 15, 16, 20, 23. Note how the Vulgate and Greek versions translate "there it was." But "there" <note>original: "שם"</note> appears with a double point in 18, and in the note on 1 Kings 3:4 it appears with no point in 7. **verse 6.** The phrase "offered upon it" <note>original: "ויעל עליו"</note> is thus in 3, 6, 9, 20, 23. **verse 7. k)** 1 Kings 3:5. **verse 9.** For the word "Your word" <note>original: "דברך"</note>, the Munach accent is used in manuscripts 3, 5 through 16, and 19 through 22. **verse 10.** For "the people" <note>original: "העם"</note>, thus in 1, 3, and 5. Others lack the Metheg accent. **verse 11.** "God" <note>original: "אֱלֹהִים"</note> appears with a Pesiq mark in 1, 3, 5, 6, 9. **verse 8. l)** 1 Kings 3:6, 20. The word "was" <note>original: "היתה"</note> has a strong Dagesh for euphony in the following letter in 1 and 2. The word "your heart" <note>original: "לבבך"</note> is thus in 1, 2, 3. The phrase "and not" <note>original: "ולא"</note> is joined by a Maqqeph in 1, 3. "And you asked" <note>original: "ותשאל"</note> appears with a Mahpach in 6, 9, 20. "And knowledge" <note>original: "ומדע"</note> appears with a Pashta in 1, 3, 6 through 23.

**Translator's Technical Notes on Variants and Vowels:**
Verse 17: **In six** [Beshesh] — noted with technical accents.
Chapter II: Sections beginning with verses 6, 9, 11, etc.
**Solomon** — marked with the *Rebia* accent in verses 1, 2, 3, and 5.
Verse 18: **To build** — spelled consistently in multiple cited manuscripts.

Following the former measurement used for the Mosaic Tabernacle, it was sixty cubits; 40 of these were designated for the Holy Place, and 20 for the inner sanctuary (the Holy of Holies), as seen in 1 Kings 6:17, 20. The width, from south to north, etc. See verse 4.
</margin>

<margin>
b) The vestibule (or porch), which was at the front—meaning at the facade of its length—and faced the eastern region, stood out like a very high tower (Chapter 29:7; 1 Kings 6:4). It stood before the width of the house and was twenty cubits wide. See verse 3.
</margin>

<margin>
g) The height, as referenced in Ezekiel 40:42, was one hundred and twenty cubits. Compare the notes on 1 Kings 6:2. He overlaid that veil, or entrance hall <note>original: "pronaon"</note> (Exodus 37:2) on the inside (Psalm 45:14; 1 Kings 6:19, 21) with pure gold. See verses 5 and 6, and Chapter 9:17.
</margin>

**[These are the foundations which Solomon laid for building] the house of God: the length in cubits according to the former measure was sixty cubits, and the width twenty cubits.**
**4 And the vestibule <term>Ulam</term> <note>The entrance hall or porch of the Temple</note> that was at the front of the length, across the width of the house, was twenty cubits, and the height was one hundred and twenty; and he overlaid it on the inside with pure gold.**
**5 And the larger house <note>The Holy Place, or Hekhal</note> he paneled with cypress wood, and overlaid it with fine gold, and carved on it palm trees and chains.**
**6 And he paved the house with precious stones for beauty; and the gold was gold of Parvaim.**
**7 He also overlaid the house—the beams, the thresholds, its walls, and its doors—with gold; and he carved Cherubim on the walls.**

<margin>
v. 5. c) The larger house, meaning the temple itself, he covered or overlaid (verses 7, 8, 9; 2 Kings 17:9) with cypress wood or fir planks (Chapter 2:7). Once paneled with wooden boards, he further overlaid it with the best gold. He caused to be "raised up" <note>original: "adscendere," referring to the application of the gold or the decorative motifs</note> on that gold or in that house (verse 14) figures of palm trees (1 Kings 6:29, 32, 35) and small chains (verse 16; 1 Kings 7:17).
</margin>

<margin>
v. 6. d) And he overlaid the house (verses 4, 10) with precious stones or gems (Chapter 9:1, 9, 10) to increase its splendor and ornament (Exodus 28:2, 40). The gold was gold of "Parvaim," perhaps meaning from Ophir, according to Bochart’s Sacred Geography (p. 769), coming from the island of Taprobane <note>Modern-day Sri Lanka</note>. See also Chapter 8:18; 1 Kings 9:28; Chapter 10:22.
</margin>

</margin>

**9 And the weight of the nails was fifty shekels of gold; and he overlaid the upper rooms with gold.**
**10 And in the Most Holy House he made two Cherubim of image-work <note>sculpted or carved figures</note>, and they overlaid them with gold.**
**11 And the wings of the Cherubim—their length was twenty cubits: the wing of the first was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house, and the other wing was five cubits, touching the wing of the other Cherub.**
**12 And the wing of the one Cherub was five cubits, reaching to the wall of the house, and the other wing was five cubits, joined to the wing of the first Cherub.**
**13 The wings of these Cherubim spread out twenty cubits; and they stood on their feet, and their faces were toward the house.**
**14 And he made the veil of blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen, and worked Cherubim on it.**
**15 And he made before the house two pillars thirty-five cubits long, and the capital that was on the top of each was five cubits.**

<margin>
a) The length and width of the bronze altar (Chapter 8:12, 1 Kings 8:64, Chapter 9:25) were as great as the width of the sacred temple (Chapter 3:3, 11). Its circumference was four times larger than the altar built by Moses (Chapter 1:5). Its height was 10 cubits (verse 2, Chapter 6:13). Consequently, the priests ascended to place wood and sacrificial victims upon it via a skillfully made ramp, as using steps was forbidden (Exodus 20:23/26). In this chapter are described: I. The bronze altar (verse 1). II. The bronze Sea and the basins (verses 2-6). III. The lampstands (verse 7). IV. Tables and bowls (verse 8). V. The priests’ court (verse 9), in which the bronze Sea was placed (verse 10). VI. The vessels and remaining furniture of the temple (verses 11-22).

### TEXTUAL AND PHILOLOGICAL NOTES

**CHAPTER V, verse 7.** The name *YHWH* is written with an added *Piska* <note>A space in the text often used to indicate a pause or division</note> 23. **v. 9.** "And it was there"—marked with a *Zakef Gadol* accent. **v. 3.** But elsewhere "And it was there until—". **v. 2.** and thus it was. **v. 5.** The letter *Tsade* is written with a *Kamatz* vowel. **v. 1, 6, 9, 20.** and thus it remains.
**v. 11.** "Those present"—the letter *Tsade* is written with a *Patach* vowel and followed by a *Dagesh* [a dot indicating doubling]. **v. 2, 3.** and thus in the margin. **v. 6, 9.**
**v. 12.** "And the singers"—written with a prefix *Vav*. **v. 5.** and thus in the margin. **v. 6, 9.** "And priests"—120. The Masoretic tradition requires it to be written with a double *Tsade* in sources 1, 2, 3, 5, according to the Masorah 1, 2, though the printed editions and the Frankfurt edition differ.
**CHAPTER VI, verse 1.** "To dwell"—written defectively <note>Missing a vowel letter</note>. **v. 2.** "Prayers to God"—written with the letter *Beth* instead of *Caph* in sources 1, 2, 13, 19, and in the margins of 6, 9. **v. 5.** "To be a leader over"—so in sources 3, 6, 9, 20, and thus in 5; however, this goes against the consensus of all our other manuscripts, both Biblical and Masoretic, in this place.

<note>Critical Apparatus / Masoretic Notes</note>

**v. 32.** **והתפללו** (*and they shall pray*) The letter <term>Pe</term> is marked with a <term>Metheg</term> <note>a vertical line indicating a secondary stress</note> in manuscripts 1, 6, 9, 10, 14, 20. The first <term>Lamed</term> has a <term>Chateph-patach</term> <note>a very short 'a' vowel</note> in 1, 6, 9, 20, but a <term>Dagesh forte</term> <note>a dot indicating a doubled consonant</note> in 3, 21, 22. Similarly in verses 34 and 38, these same sources repeat their reading. **v. 34.** **אשר־בחזת** (*which you chose*) marked with a <term>Maqqeph</term> <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in 2, 6, 9, 20. **v. 38.** **ושבו** (*and they return*) is <term>Milra</term> <note>accented on the last syllable</note> in 1, according to the Masorah. **v. 41.** **כהניך** (*your priests*) has a <term>Kadma</term> <note>an accent mark</note> in 6, 9, 17, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24; printed as in 1 Kings 8:48. **CHAPTER VII, v. 1.** Instead of **מהשמים** (*from the heavens*), some have **מן השמים** in the margin of 6, 9; here in 5.

**Technical Notes on the Hebrew Text:**
**v. 5.** **the sacrifice of oxen**: found thus in manuscripts 1, 3, and 5; a common distinction, but against the *Masora impressa* <note>The printed Masoretic traditional text</note>. **v. 6.** **trumpeting**: as found in the *Piel* <note>An intensive Hebrew verb form</note> grammatic form. **which David the king had made**: compare verse 7.5 and verse 7. **v. 7.** **was [not] able**: written *defectively* <note>A spelling style missing certain vowel-indicator letters</note> in manuscript 3. Although not listed among the full spellings in the *Masora* of manuscripts 3 and 5, or above in Numbers 13:30, it could be written fully in manuscripts 1 and 2 at this location. **v. 8.** **a great congregation**: so in manuscripts 2 and 3, and likewise in the feminine form in manuscript 5. **v. 13.** **I shut up**: Marked with a *Shua simplex* vowel. See also verses 12, 16, 17, 18, 24 and the *Kere* <note>The traditional reading of the text versus the written form</note>.

# II CHRONICLES. CHAPTER 9.

<margin>
**CHAPTER IX, verse 1. a)**
When the *Queen of Sheba* (located in Arabia Felix—"Fertile Arabia"—south of Jerusalem, see Luke 11:31, and the farthest part of Arabia, Matthew 12:42) *had heard the fame of Solomon* or *concerning Solomon* (Genesis 29:13; Psalm 97:8) brought to her, *she then came to Jerusalem to test* and *examine Solomon* (Chapter 32:31; Judges 2:22) with *riddles* <note>original: "aenigmatibus"</note>, that is, with weighty and sublime questions (Psalm 78:2; Judges 14:12). She came *with a very grand and numerous retinue* (1 Kings 10:2; compare 2 Kings 5:15) and *with camels* (2 Kings 8:9; Isaiah 60:6) *carrying spices* (verse 9, with which Fertile Arabia was abundant; cf. Ezekiel 27:22) and *gold* (Psalm 72:15) in great quantity (verse 9; Chapter 1:15), and *precious stones* or gems (verses 9, 10; Chapter 3:6). She came, I say, to Solomon, and *spoke with him about everything that was in her heart*, that is, whatever she had premeditated (Chapter 29:10; 1 Kings 10:2). 

In this chapter: 
I. *The Queen of the Sabaeans visits Solomon because of the fame of his supreme wisdom* (verses 1, 2). 
II. She greatly admires him and congratulates him (verses 3–8). 
III. *Having given and received gifts, she returns to her own country* (verses 9–12). 
IV. *Solomon's wealth and magnificence are described at length* (verses 13–28). 
V. *Upon his death, his son Rehoboam succeeds him* (verses 31–31).
</margin>

**1** When the Queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon <gloss>a</gloss>, she came to Jerusalem to test Solomon with riddles, with a very great retinue, and camels bearing spices and gold in abundance, and precious stones. When she came to Solomon, she spoke with him about all that was on her mind. **2** And Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was hidden from Solomon that he did not explain to her. **3** When the Queen of Sheba saw the wisdom of Solomon and the palace he had built, **4** the food of his table, the seating of his servants, the service of his attendants and their apparel, his cupbearers and their apparel, and his ascent <note>Some translations interpret this as the burnt offerings he offered, but the Hebrew suggests a physical walkway or staircase</note> by which he went up to the house of the Lord, there was no more spirit left in her. **5** She said to the king, “The report was true which I heard in my own land about your deeds and your wisdom. **6** I did not believe their reports until I came and my own eyes saw it. And behold, not even half of the greatness of your wisdom was told to me; you surpass the report that I heard. **7** Happy are your men, and happy are these your servants who stand before you continually and hear your wisdom! **8** Blessed be the Lord your God, who delighted in you to set you on His throne as king for the Lord your God! Because your God loved Israel, to establish them forever, He made you king over them to do justice and righteousness.” **9** Then she gave the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold, and a very great store of spices and precious stones; there was never such spice as that which the Queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.

v. 14. Instead of **"I made heavy"** <note>original: "ani hikbad"</note> they have **"I will make heavy"** <note>original: "akbid"</note> in the future tense, omitting the word "I"; and thus in 5 [manuscripts]. This is how David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian</note> read it, as is apparent from the Masoretic notes. In the same way, the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation</note> edited by the illustrious Beckius: *I will make your yoke heavy*. Abendana, in his notes, does not doubt this reading seen in two high-quality manuscripts and prefers it as the genuine reading, accusing the printed books of error for confusing the readings of Chronicles and Kings. 

v. 16. **"And all Israel"** with the accent <term>Rebia: a disjunctive Masoretic cantellation mark</term>, omitting the following verb **"saw"** in 7, 8, 11, 15, and 16 [manuscripts]; and so in 5. This was the reading not only of the aforementioned Chaldean Paraphrast, but also the Vulgate and the Septuagint. However, [scholars] Junius and Tremellius say in their notes: "In some copies 'seeing' is added, which perhaps crept in from 1 Kings 12:16, but our more approved copies lack it."

### II CHRONICLES CHAPTER 12

<margin>
**CHAPTER XII, verse 1.**
Indeed, it came to pass, when the kingdom of Rehoboam was established or strengthened (compare chapter 11:17; Isaiah 9:6) and when he had become powerful (compare chapter 26:16; Daniel 11:2, etc.), Rehoboam was delivered into the hands of Shishak, king of the Egyptians, by whom he was heavily fined, because he had neglected to observe the law of God (verses 1–12). However, he continued to reign (verses 13, 14), and upon his death, he left the kingdom to his son Abijah (verses 15, 16). b) and all Israel with him, with the exception of a few faithful ones (verse 12).
</margin>
And it happened, when the <note>original: "מלכות" (malkhut)</note> kingdom of Rehoboam was established and he became strong, he forsook the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him.

<margin>
**verse 2. c)** 1 Kings 14:25. Since God had scarcely tolerated their wickedness for more than a year (compare chapter 11:17), He was soon to lead them toward repentance.
</margin>
And it happened in the fifth year of King Rehoboam, that Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem, because they had transgressed against the Lord.

<margin>
**verse 3. d)** With twelve hundred chariots (compare chapter 1:14). e) The Libyans <note>original: "Lubie"</note>, or the Egyptian Libyans (chapter 16:8; Daniel 11:43; Nahum 3:9; and see notes on 1 Chronicles 1:11). f) The Vulgate calls them "Troglodytes" <note>original: "Troglodytæ"</note>, dwellers along the western shore of the Red Sea, named either from the huts or caves <note>original: "cauernis"</note> in which they lived (compare Psalm 10:9) or from the town of Succoth (also called Suchis) in the Troglodyte region. g) And the Ethiopians <note>original: "Chusiæ"</note> from Midian (chapter 14:8).
</margin>
With twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen; and there was no number to the people who came with him from Egypt: the Libyans, the Sukkiim, and the Ethiopians.

<margin>
**verse 4. h)** He therefore captured the fortified cities of Judah, which Rehoboam had built with great diligence (chapter 11:6 and following), and with a victorious army he came as far as Jerusalem (verses 1, 5, 9).
</margin>
And he took the fortified cities which belonged to Judah, and came as far as Jerusalem.

<margin>
**verse 5. i)** Then Shemaiah the prophet (verse 7; chapter 11:2) came.
</margin>
Then Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah, who were gathered at Jerusalem because of Shishak, and said to them: "Thus says the Lord: 'You have forsaken me, and therefore I also have left you in the hand of Shishak.'"

<margin>
**verse 6. k)** The leaders of Israel and the king himself humbled themselves (verse 7), acknowledging and confessing their sins and the justice of God (compare chapter 7:14; 13:18; 32:26; 33:12). l) Compare Deuteronomy 32:4; Jeremiah 12:1; Daniel 9:14; Ezekiel 9:15; Nehemiah 9:33.
</margin>
So the leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves; and they said, "The Lord is righteous." And when the Lord saw that they humbled themselves, the word of the Lord came to Shemaiah, saying, "They have humbled themselves; I will not destroy them, but I will grant them some measure of escape; and My wrath shall not be poured out on Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak.
For they shall be his servants, that they may know My service and the service of the kingdoms of the lands."
So Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem, and took away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the king's house; he took everything. He also carried off the gold shields which Solomon had made.
Then King Rehoboam made bronze shields in their place, and committed them to the hands of the captains of the guard <note>original: "הָרָצִים" (ha-ratzim), literally 'the runners'</note> who guarded the entrance to the king's house.

<margin>
**verse 11. m)** as often as the king entered (1 Samuel 1:7; 2 Kings 4:8). n) to the palace; the attendants or shield-bearers came (verse 10) and carried those shields, and afterward they returned them to the guardroom <note>original: "תָּא" (ta)</note> of the attendants (verse 10).
</margin>
And whenever the king entered the house of the Lord, the guard came and carried them, and brought them back into the guardroom.
When he humbled himself, the wrath of the Lord turned from him, so as not to destroy him completely; and things went well in Judah.
So King Rehoboam strengthened himself in Jerusalem and reigned. Now Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city which the Lord had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put His name there. His mother's name was Naamah, an Ammonitess.
And he did evil, because he did not prepare his heart to seek the Lord.

**Critical Notes:**

verse 15. Instead of "and Jeroboam," another book has "with Jeroboam" in the margin.
CHAPTER XIII, verse 1. Instead of "and he reigned," another book has "he reigned" in the margin.
verse 3. In the latter half of the verse, instead of "chosen men," two or three manuscripts have only "men," which is likely how the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and the Syriac <note>The Peshitta, or Syriac translation.</note> read it.
verse 6. "The servant of Solomon"—so it appears in six or nine manuscripts, and thus in the 5th edition.
verse 7. Written without a preceding space in manuscripts 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 12, 19, 20, 22, 23.
verse 11. The first "in the morning" is likewise marked with a *Munach* accent in manuscripts 1, 2, 6, 9, 20, and the 5th edition. "And in the evening" is thus marked with *Munach* in manuscripts 1, 2, 23, and the Berlin edition, and with an emphatic *Pashta* in 6, 9, 20. It appears with a *Makkaph* in manuscript 1, and a *Metheg* in 3 and 5. Others use a *Rehia* accent, as in the 5th edition, which is a most inconvenient distinction.

### II CHRONICLES. CHAPTER 16. 17

**CHAPTER XVI, verse 1.**
<margin>a)</margin> In the thirty-sixth year of the reign of Asa—that is, of Judah, 36 years since the division from Israel; specifically in the sixteenth year of Asa's actual reign, <note>original Latin: "coll. not. c. 15, 39" - referring to scholarly cross-references</note>—Baasha, king of Israel, went up with an army (see 12:2). Supported by the power and treaty of Ben-hadad of Syria (v. 3, 1 Kings 15:27 and following), he began to fortify Ramah, either the one in Benjamin (Joshua 18:25, Judges 19:12-13) or the one in Ephraim (Judges 4:5, 1 Samuel 1:19). This was done so that no one was permitted to go out or come in to Asa; in other words, to block the exit and entrance to Asa’s kingdom for the sake of those seeking the purer worship of God (see 15:5, 9). 

In this chapter: 
I. Asa, attacked by Baasha in war (v. 1), hires the king of Syria (v. 2-6). 
II. Rebuked for this by a prophet, he casts the prophet into prison (v. 7-11). 
III. Asa himself falls into a disease and finally dies (v. 12-14).

**v. 2.** <margin>b)</margin> From which Asa brought out—or produced (see Genesis 24:53, Ezra 1:7)—silver and gold (see 15:18). These were from the treasures of the house of the Lord and the royal palace (see 12:9). And he sent them to Ben-hadad, etc. (see 1 Kings 15:18).

**v. 4.** <margin>c)</margin> Therefore Ben-hadad obeyed King Asa (see 10:15, 1 Kings 15:20). <margin>d)</margin> and [attacked] all the store-cities <note>original: "penuaria"</note> (see 8:4, 17:12, 32:28, Exodus 1:11).

**v. 6.** <margin>e)</margin> and [built] Geba and Mizpah, on the borders of Benjamin and Judah (Joshua 15:38, 18:24, 26, 21:17), so that they might be a bulwark for the kingdom of Judah against the kingdom of Israel.

**v. 7.** <margin>f)</margin> At that very time, when Asa's affairs seemed to be going best, at God's command there came (see 12:5, 18:14, 25:7) Hanani the Seer—that is, the prophet (see 19:2, 1 Samuel 9:9). <margin>g)</margin> "Because of your reliance," that is, according to the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note>, "Because you had confidence" (v. 8, 13:10). <margin>h)</margin> See the notes on 1 Kings 15:19 and the more extensive notes on this location.

**v. 9.** <margin>i)</margin> For as concerns Jehovah [the Lord] (Psalm 11:4), His eyes survey—that is, they range—through the entire earth (2 Samuel 14:2, 8, Zechariah 4:10, etc.).

<note>The following section contains technical notes on variations between different ancient Hebrew manuscripts and the Masoretic text.</note>

v. 11. *and all the prophets*: The Paschta accent is placed over the letter He in manuscripts 5 and 2. &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; v. 12. *good*: without the Daghesh <note>A grammatical point in Hebrew indicating emphasis or doubling.</note> in manuscripts 1, 3, 7, 8, 10 through 16, and 19 through 22.
v. 13. *it*: The word "et" <note>the Hebrew direct object marker</note> is omitted in this text in manuscripts 6, 9, and 20; however, it is present in the margins of 1, 6, and 9.
v. 16. *scattered*: written with the Shurek vowel in manuscript 3 (feminine) and 5 (feminine). &emsp;&emsp; Instead of *to them* <note>Hebrew "lahen"</note>, manuscripts 3, 6, 9, 10, 14, and 20 have an alternative reading.
v. 19. *at Ramoth*: thus in manuscript 2, against the Masoretic note in 1 and 2 (printed editions) and the Erfurt manuscript in this place, and the printed Ezekiel 25:36. &emsp; v. 20. *the Lord*: Other versions are defective. *And he said*: written in full in 1, 6, 9, and 20 according to the Masoretic note 1 and the Erfurt manuscript here and the printed chapter 22:5 and Proverbs 6:17. &emsp; v. 22. *the Lord*: In manuscripts 4, 6, 10, *the Lord* is marked with the Sakeph Gadol accent in 2 and 3.

<margin>a) <note>original: "audite me"</note> Listen to me (see also chapter 15:4 and 1 Chronicles 28:2), O Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem! (see verse 15, 18). Believe in the Lord—that is, strengthen your trust in the Lord your God (Deuteronomy 1:32, Isaiah 28:16). For then you will be established (Isaiah 7:9). Believe His prophets (Exodus 14:31, 1 Samuel 27:12, Psalm 106:12) and you will prosper. The Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> rightly says: "and all things shall turn out prosperous." For this is an "imperative of promise," where a command implies a guaranteed result (as in Psalm 37:27 and Proverbs 3:4).</margin>
20 “Listen to me, O Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem! Believe in the LORD your God and you shall be established; believe His prophets and you shall prosper.” **21** And when he had consulted with the people,
<margin>b) v. 21. The king therefore took counsel with the people and their leaders (compare chapter 10:6, 8; 25:17). These sacred musicians went out at the very front of the army, before the armed men (chapter 17:18, Numbers 32:25, 29), and said: "Praise the LORD, etc." (chapter 5:13, 7:3, 6, Psalm 136:1 and following).</margin>
he appointed singers for the LORD and those who should praise in the beauty of holiness as they went out before the army and said, “Give thanks to the LORD, for His mercy endures forever.”

**Textual Notes:**
CHAPTER XXII, v. 6. The word *asher* <note>which</note> is marked with a Maqqeph <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in manuscript 2 and following. However, for *asher*, the word *ki* <note>because/that</note> is found in the margin of manuscript 2.
v. 8. For the word *bihishapet* <note>when judging</note>, manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, and the margins of 6 and 9 use the letter *Kaph* instead of *Beth* (making it *kihishapet*).
v. 9. The word *mit-chabe* <note>hiding</note> appears with an added *Pesiq* <note>a vertical line serving as a musical or structural pause</note> and followed by a *Dagesh* <note>an emphasis dot</note> in manuscript 22. The words "they slew him and they buried him" appear this way in manuscripts 2 and 3 and following. For the word *la’atzor* <note>to restrain/hold</note>, the letter *Ayin* is written with a simple *Shuva* without a preceding *Metheg* <note>a stress mark</note> in manuscripts 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 15.
v. 11. "And she stole him" appears this way in manuscripts 7, 8, 10, 13, 15–19, 20–24, and the Berlin manuscript.
CHAPTER XXIII, v. 1. The name "Azariahu" is written without the letter *Shurek* at the end of the word in manuscripts 7, 8, 11, 17, 18, 21, 22, 24, and the Berlin manuscript.

v. 6. **valor**: written with the vowel *Patach* in manuscripts 3, 21, 22, contrary to the first printed Masoretic text and the Frankfurt editions.
v. 15. In place of the latter word **to him**, manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5 have a shorter form.

Others are without it. **We made you**: so the letter *Tav* with a *Kamatz* vowel without a following *Dagesh* [dot], and thus in the first person perfect in 1, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19, 20, 23. This is quite suitable, because **they strike you** soon follows (meaning "they will strike you," for "you will be struck"), by which analogy it would here be said "they have appointed you," for "you are appointed." But this is against the printed Masorah. **Stop**: with the *Mercha* accent in 1, 2, 6, 9, 20; and thus also in 5.

<column-break/>

v. 8. **To help**: the letter *Ayin* is written with the *Chatef-Patach* vowel in manuscripts 1 and 3.
v. 9. **For the hundred**: written thus without the silent letter *Vau* in 1, 3, 5, 6, 9, 20, 21, 22, and the Major Erfurt manuscripts.
v. 16. Written thus with the *Revia* accent in 3, 5, 7, 8, 15, 22, 23, 24; also in 2, but there with a preceding *Munach* accent.
v. 17. **And he said, "I know"**: thus in manuscript 2. Others have **And he said, "I know"** with a *Zakef-Katon* accent, which is incorrect.

## II CHRONICLES CHAPTERS 25 & 26

<margin>
a) *Through a parable, according to the custom of the Eastern peoples (compare Judges 9:7 and following), he testified to his contempt for the king of Judah.*

b) *The Vulgate translation uses "thistle" (see Isaiah 34:13), which grows in Lebanon (Nahum 1:4). He sent word to the "cedar," the most noble of trees found in Lebanon (see 2 Chronicles 2:8 and 1 Kings 5:13). See also the notes on 2 Kings 14:9.*

c) *Verse 19. You have said, or you think to yourself: "Look, you have struck Edom"—referring to your defeat of the Edomites, a warlike and strong people (verses 3, 11, 13; 2 Kings 14:10)—and because of this, your heart lifts you up to boast. Compare 2 Chronicles 26:16.*

d) *Therefore, stay now in your own house and keep within the borders of your own kingdom. Why should you meddle with trouble? (See Daniel 11:10, 25 and notes on Deuteronomy 2:5).*

e) *Verse 20. This happened because of God, who justly permitted it (compare verse 16; 2 Chronicles 22:7; 1 Chronicles 5:22), so that He might deliver them into the hands of the Israelites because they had sought after the gods of Edom and abandoned the true God (verses 14, 15).*

f) *Verse 21. And they saw one another face to face; that is, both sides brought forth their troops and fought (verse 17; 2 Kings 14:8; 23:29). This occurred near Beth-Shemesh (2 Chronicles 28:18), a Levitical city in the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:10; 21:16), which is to be distinguished from another city of the same name in the tribes of Issachar and Naphtali (Joshua 19:22, 38; Judges 1:33).*

g) *Verse 23. Son of Jehoahaz, who is also called Ahaziah (2 Chronicles 21:17; 22:1).* h) *Joash captured him (2 Kings 14:13; 2 Chronicles 25:6).* i) *As far as the Corner Gate, which faces the angle (2 Chronicles 26:9; 2 Kings 14:13; Jeremiah 31:38; Zechariah 14:10).*

k) *Verse 24. In the possession of Obed-Edom the Levite or Priest (compare another man of this name in 1 Chronicles 13:13; 2 Chronicles 26:15).* l) *And the "sons of the pledges," meaning the hostages (2 Kings 14:14).*

m) *CHAPTER 26, verse 1; 2 Kings 14:21. Described here is Uzziah: I. Pious and formidable during the life of Zechariah the prophet (verses 1–15). II. Proud and impious, and consequently struck with leprosy until his death (verses 16–23).*

<note>Critical Apparatus explaining textual variations across manuscripts</note>

Verse 5: **To seek** <note>original: "לִדְרֹשׁ"</note> is written thus "defectively" (missing the letter vav) in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5 through 9, 15, 20, 22, 23, 24, according to the Masorah of manuscripts 1 and 2, and the Erfurt editions; others write it "plene" (fully). **To see** <note>original: "לִרְאֹת"</note> is written fully in 15 and 23, against the Masorah here. But **In seeing** <note>original: "בִּרְאֹת"</note> with a Metheg under the Beth in manuscript 22, as if it were a contraction of **In the fear of** <note>original: "בְּיִרְאַת"</note>, which is how Junius and Tremellius translated it from the Heidelberg manuscript as "in the fears of God," meaning things pertaining to the fear of God. However, "In seeing" appears in manuscripts 2 and 3, and thus in 5; this matches the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic translations as "in the fear of the Lord." See more in Glassius, *Philologia Sacra*, book V, page 575. Our reading is confirmed by the Masorah here. Verse 6: **Wall of Gath** <note>original: "חוֹמַת גַּת"</note> is thus accented on the last syllable in 1, 2, 3, 11, 12. Verse 7: **And He helped him** <note>original: "וַיַּעְזְרֵהוּ"</note> with the vowel *Patach* under the letter Ain in 1, 5, 6, 9, 14, 20, 21; but with *Qametz* in 1, 5, 7, 8 according to the Masorah of 1 and the Erfurt editions. Verse 9: **Upon** <note>original: "עַל"</note> has a marginal note **Until** <note>original: "עַד"</note> in manuscript 22. Verse 11: **Making** <note>original: "עֹשֵׂה"</note> with the vowel *Segol* in 1, 2, 3, 11, 21, and in the margins of 6 and 9. But **Makers of** <note>original: "עֹשֵׂי"</note> in the plural with the letter Iod in 6 through 10, 13, 14, 15, 19, 20, 22, 23. **Hand** <note>original: "יַד"</note> with a *Munach* accent in 3 and 2. Verse 15: **And he made** <note>original: "וַיַּעַשׂ"</note> without the *Pesiq* mark in 1, 2, 21, but with a *Tiphcha* in 2 and 5. The Masorah requires a *Pesiq* here. **In Jerusalem** <note>original: "בִּירוּשָׁלִַם"</note> with an added *Pesiq* in 6, 9, 10, 13, 19, 20. Verse 16: **And as his strength** <note>original: "וּכְחֶזְקָתוֹ"</note> using the letter Beth instead of Caph in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 20.

**Textual Notes:**

Verse 13: *rabbah ashamah* ("great guilt") — so in manuscripts 1 and 2.
Verse 13: *rabbah* — written fully <note>original: "plene"</note> according to the Masorah and Erfurt manuscripts.
Verse 14: With a preceding space in manuscripts 1, 2, 5–10, 12, 19.
Verse 15: *bachamorim* ("on donkeys") — written fully according to the Masorah and Erfurt manuscripts.
Verse 18: After *Timnah*, manuscripts 7, 8, 10–19, 21, 23, 24 have "and its villages" instead of "and Gimzo and its villages."
Verse 15: *Yericho* — the letter *Resh* is marked with the vowel *Chirek* in manuscripts 2 and 3, and in the margin.
Verse 15: These are written fully with the letter *Yod*.
Verse 20: *Tiglath* — the *Gimel* is without a *dagesh* <note>a grammatical dot</note>, correctly in 7, 8, 15, 22. Others include it.
Verse 20: Marked with a *Makkaph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in manuscript 22.
Verse 23: *vayiomer* ("and he said") — marked with a *Grafshaim* accent in 3, 5, and with a *Kadma* accent in 1.
Genesis 36:6. Our reading of "and its daughters/villages" (*ve-et-benoteiha*) was confirmed by the editor of Codex 22, with the note: "so it must be according to the Masorah."
Verse 19: Marked with a *Patach* vowel in manuscript 1, similar to the Vulgate and Septuagint reading "Gamzo."
Verse 19: *ba’avur Achaz melech* ("because of Ahaz the king") — so in 1, 3.
*melech* ("king") — marked with *Makkaph* and *Metheg* in 6, 9, 12, 17, 18, 24, and the Berlin edition.
*vayatsar* ("and he besieged/oppressed") — the letter *Tsade* is with a *Segol* in 5 and the margin of 6 and 7.

### II Chronicles Chapters 29 & 30

<header>II CHRONICLES 29:27–30:5</header>

### 2 CHRONICLES CHAPTERS 30 & 31

<header>2 CHRONICLES CHAPTERS 30 & 31</header>

<margin>
a) *The LORD, who is good (Psalm 25:8), will make atonement for them.* <note>original Latin: "Iehoua, qui bonus est, Ps. 25, 8. expiabit pro iis."</note> This is how the word "God" <note>אלוה - Eloah</note> is understood here, according to Abraham ibn Ezra <note>A prominent 12th-century Spanish biblical commentator.</note> on Psalm 73:15. David Kimchi <note>A 12th-13th century grammarian and commentator known as the Radak.</note> also suggests this in his commentary on this passage. This interpretation allows the following verse to refer back to Hezekiah. However, Kimchi, the Septuagint, the Vulgate, Schmid, and others connect this phrase with the following verse, despite the interruption of the *Silluk* <note>A Hebrew punctuation mark indicating the end of a verse.</note>—which adds emphasis to the construction—in this manner: *The Lord will make atonement for them: specifically for everyone who has directed [his heart], etc.* Compare this phrasing to Exodus 30:10; 32:30; and Psalm 78:38; and regarding the *Silluk* punctuation, see Leviticus 17:8, 9; Numbers 31:22; and Judges 10:11, 12.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 19. b) Schmid: *Specifically for everyone who has prepared his heart,* as in chapter 12:14 and Job 11:13, *to seek the LORD,* as in chapter 19:3, *even if not according to the purification of the sanctuary,* or that purity which the Levitical laws otherwise required (1 Chronicles 23:28).
</margin>

<gloss>b</gloss> —who has set his heart to seek God, the LORD, the God of his fathers, even though he is not cleansed according to the purification of the sanctuary.

<margin>
v. 20. c) *And the Lord heard Hezekiah,* (cf. chapter 33:13) and *healed the people;* that is, He forgave them so that they might recover from the guilt of sin as if from a disease, and not be punished with death. Compare Leviticus 15:31; Psalms 41:5 and 103:3; Isaiah 6:10; Mark 4:12; and 1 Corinthians 11:30.
</margin>

And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.

### CRITICAL NOTES ON MANUSCRIPTS

v. 18. **בעד** <note>for/on behalf of</note> The letter *Ayin* has a *Kametz* vowel in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 20, 23. This is also the case in edition 5.
v. 19. **האלהים** <note>The God</note> Thus it appears in manuscript 1.
A *Psik* <note>A vertical line acting as a musical or logical separator.</note> appears in 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 15, 22, 23, 24 according to the Basel Index, page 61b. Others omit it.
**כטהרת** <note>according to the purification</note> The letter *Tet* has a *Patach* vowel in 3 and in the margin of 6 and 9, followed by a *Chatef-Patach*.
v. 21. **ישראל** <note>Israel</note> Marked with a *Tifcha* accent in manuscript 1.
**הנמצאים** <note>who were present</note> The letter *Tsade* has a *Kametz* vowel in 6, 9, 20.
**בכלי** <note>with instruments of</note> The letter *Lamed* has a *Chirek* vowel uniquely in 2 and in the margin of 6 and 9. It is joined by a *Maqqef* <note>A Hebrew hyphen.</note> in 1 and 2, and so in edition 5.
v. 22. <unclear>A space</unclear> <unclear>is placed before</unclear> this in 1, 2, 3, 5 through 10, 19, 20, 23.
v. 23. Accompanied by a preceding space in 5, 6, 9, 10, 19, 20, 22.
**ויעשו שבעת-** <note>And they kept seven [days]</note> Thus in 1, 2, 3, 5.
**שמחה** <note>joy</note> With the prefix **ב** <note>with/in</note> in 6, 9, 13, 19, 20, and so in edition 1.
v. 24. **פרים** <note>bulls</note> Joined by a *Maqqef* in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 20.
v. 27. Instead of **לשמים** <note>to the heavens</note> (which manuscript 22 records in the margin), manuscripts 3 and 22 have **בשמים** <note>in the heavens</note>.
CHAPTER 31, v. 1. The first mention of **ישראל** <note>Israel</note> has a *Merca* accent in 7, 8, 15, 22, 23, contrary to the major printed editions.
**הנמצאים** <note>who were present</note> The letter *Tsade* has a *Kametz* vowel in 1, 10, and in the margin of 6 and 9; so too in 5.
v. 2. Accompanied by a preceding space in 1, 3, 5 through 10, 20, 21, 22, 23.
v. 3. Accompanied by a preceding space in 5 through 10, 20, 21, 23.
**ומנת** <note>And the portion</note> Written with a *Patach* in 2, 3, 23, against the Massorah of the first printed edition and the Erfurt manuscript in this place, as well as the Massorah on Exodus 36:5 and Rabbi Chaiim’s notes on the final printed Massorah, page 13d. Compare with verse 4.

<margin>
CHAPTER XXXII, v. 1. c) After these things were done, which are described in chapters 29, 30, and 31, and after that faithfulness of the king shown in restoring divine worship (chapter 31:20), in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah (Isaiah 36:1), Sennacherib <note>original Latin: "Sancherib"</note> king of Assyria came. This chapter details: I. The fierce war he prepares against Hezekiah (verse 1). II. Hezekiah, with a brave and pious spirit toward God, prepares himself and his citizens for the defense of Jerusalem (verses 2–8). III. Sennacherib’s ministers attempt to incite the people of Jerusalem to defect with arrogant and blasphemous words against God (verses 9–19). IV. For this reason, the Assyrian army is destroyed by the Angel of the LORD, and the king is slain at home (verses 20–23). V. Hezekiah falls ill and is healed by God (verse 24); however, he provokes God's anger through pride, but repentance delays the punishment, and he finally dies a peaceful death (verses 25–33).
</margin>

**Critical Notes on the Text:**
*Verse 22:* Instead of the phrase "and who," manuscript .3 has "and the wife of" [Hebrew: *ve-ishet*], agreeing with the *Qere* <note>marginal reading</note> "and the wife."
*Verse 25:* "and it shall be poured out" [Hebrew: *va-tittach*]; this follows the standard vocalization with a *Shua* in editions 1, 17, 18, and the Berlin edition. Thus, "LORD" appears in edition 5 according to the printed Masorah and Prefaces. Others use a *Patach* followed by a *Dagesh*.
*Verse 26:* A *Piska* <note>a liturgical pause or space in the text</note> occurs in the middle of the verse in edition 5 according to the printed Masorah and Prefaces.
*Verse 27:* "Utterance" [Hebrew: *neum*]; verse 22 uses a *Makkef* <note>a Hebrew hyphen</note> in manuscripts 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14, 19, and so in edition 5.
*Verse 28:* Instead of "to your fathers," manuscript .3 reads "upon your fathers," as does edition 5. "Your eyes" is marked with a *Rebia* <note>an accent mark</note> in manuscripts 2, 5, 6, 9, 14, 20.
*Verse 31:* "and his testimonies"; here it is written with a "resting Vav" in manuscripts 2, 3, 8, and edition 5, contrary to the printed Masorah and Prefaces.

**36** <margin>CHAPTER 36, verse 1. f) Then the people of the land took (chapter 33:25; 2 Kings 23:30) Jehoahaz, who is also called Shallum in Jeremiah 22:11 (see the note there). This chapter describes the four final kings of the Judean kingdom and its eventual overthrow: I. The people appoint Jehoahaz to succeed his father Josiah, verses 1–2. II. Necho of Egypt removes him from the throne and replaces him with his older brother Jehoiakim, verses 3–5. III. In his place, having been taken to Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar appoints his son Jehoiachin to reign, verses 6–9. IV. However, Nebuchadnezzar soon gives the throne to his uncle Zedekiah, verses 10–12. V. Because he rebelled, Jerusalem was captured and he was blinded, verses 13–19, and the people were led away into captivity, verses 20–21. VI. This captivity is finally ended by Cyrus, verses 22–23.</margin> The people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah and made him king in place of his father in Jerusalem.
**2** Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem.
**3** Then the king of Egypt deposed him in Jerusalem and laid a tribute on the land of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold.
**4** The king of Egypt made his brother Eliakim king over Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim; but Necho <note>Pharaoh Necho II of Egypt</note> took his brother Jehoahaz and carried him to Egypt.
**5** Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD his God.
**6** Against him King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon came up, and bound him in bronze shackles to take him to Babylon.
**7** Nebuchadnezzar also carried some of the vessels of the house of the LORD to Babylon and put them in his palace <note>or temple</note> in Babylon.
**8** Now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and the abominations that he did, and what was found against him, are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah; and his son Jehoiachin succeeded him.
**9** Jehoiachin was eight <note>Some manuscripts say eighteen</note> years old when he began to reign; he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.
**10** In the spring of the year King Nebuchadnezzar sent and brought him to Babylon, along with the precious vessels of the house of the LORD, and made his brother <note>relative/uncle</note> Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem.
**11** Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.
**12** He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD his God. He did not humble himself before the prophet Jeremiah who spoke from the mouth of the LORD.
**13** He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar...

<meta>This page concludes the Second Book of Chronicles. Following the death of Josiah described on the previous page, the narrative rapidly covers the decline of the final kings of Judah—Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and finally Zedekiah—leading to the destruction of Jerusalem and the Babylonian exile, before ending with the hopeful decree of Cyrus the Great.</meta>

<header>2 CHRONICLES 36</header>

<margin>Qamatz in Zaqef <note>A Hebrew grammatical note regarding the vowel 'Qamatz' under the 'Resh' in the word 'rebelled' when it appears with a specific musical accent called 'Zaqef Qaton'.</note></margin> **13** He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, [a] who had made him swear by God. He stiffened his neck [b] and hardened his heart [c] against turning to the Lord, the God of Israel.
<margin>Extra Vav <note>A scribal note indicating an additional letter 'Vav' in the Hebrew spelling.</note></margin> **14** Furthermore, all the leaders of the priests [b] and the people multiplied their unfaithful deeds, following all the abominations of the nations; and they defiled [c] the house of the Lord which He had sanctified in Jerusalem. **15** The Lord, the God of their fathers, sent word to them by the hand of His messengers, [d] sending them early and often, because He had compassion on His people and on His dwelling place.
**16** But they mocked the messengers of God, despised His words, and scoffed at His prophets, until the wrath of the Lord rose against His people, until there was no remedy. **17** Therefore He brought up against them the king of the Chaldeans, [e] who killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary, and had no compassion on young man or virgin, old man or the aged; He gave them all into his hand.
**18** All the vessels of the house of God, great and small, [f] and the treasures of the house of the Lord, and the treasures of the king and of his leaders, all these he brought to Babylon. **19** Then they burned the house of God [g] and broke down the wall of Jerusalem, burned all its palaces with fire, and destroyed all its precious vessels. **20** Those who escaped from the sword he carried away to Babylon, where they became servants to him and his sons until the reign of the kingdom of Persia.
**21** This was to fulfill the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. As long as it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years. **22** Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, <margin>Extra Vav</margin> that the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and also put it in writing, saying: **23** "Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: All the kingdoms of the earth the Lord, the God of heaven, has given me. And He has commanded me to build Him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever is among you of all His people, may the Lord his God be with him, and let him go up!" [h]

<column-break/>

a) <note>original: "Insuper etiam contra regem Nebucadnetsarem rebellavit."</note> Moreover, he also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar. See the Preface to Jeremiah, § 11. Although he had made him swear by the God of Israel. See Ezekiel 17:13 and following. b) <note>original: "obduravit cervicem suam"</note> *He stiffened his neck*, as in Exodus 32:9 and 2 Kings 17:14. c) <note>original: "cor f. animum suum obfirmavit"</note> *He hardened his heart or his spirit*, as in Deuteronomy 2:30, so that he would not return to the Lord, the God of Israel. See Hosea 11:5.

v. 14. b) <note>original: "Sed & omnes principes f. antistites sacerdotum"</note> *But also all the leaders or chief priests*, who were from the high-priestly family, see 1 Chronicles 24:5. c) See chapter 28:19 and chapter 33:6, 23.

v. 15. d) <note>original: "per nuntios suos, prophetas"</note> *Through His messengers, the prophets*, verse 15. *Rising early and sending*, that is, calling them back to a better mind early enough and continuously. See Jeremiah 11:7; 25:4; 26:5; 35:14; and Ezekiel 12:8. *Because He wished to spare His people and His dwelling place*, namely the city and the temple; compare chapter 30:27, Zephaniah 3:7, and Psalm 26:8.

v. 17. e) <note>original: "Adscendere enim tandem iussit contra eos..."</note> *For at last He ordered the king of the Chaldeans to go up against them with a large army*, verses 6, 10. *Who killed their young men with the sword*, see 2 Kings 8:12 and Amos 4:10. *In the very house of their sanctuary*, which they themselves had polluted with crimes, verse 14 and chapter 33:4, 7. *Nor did he spare young man or virgin*, Jeremiah 15:8 and Ezekiel 9:6. *The old man or the decrepit*, Job 12:12. *For God delivered them all into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar*, Jeremiah 27:6 and 32:3-4.

v. 18. f) See verses 7, 10; 2 Kings 24:13; Jeremiah 52:18 and following; and Ezra 1:7, 11.

v. 19. g) 2 Kings 25:9; Jeremiah 34:22; 39:8; and 52:13.

** h) See after 2 Kings 25:30. i) <note>original: "typographus ne ledatur"</note> *May the printer not be harmed* <note>A traditional scribal prayer for the safety of the work and the worker.</note>. k) The total number of verses in both books of Chronicles is 1656. The mnemonic for this number is found in the words **את הארון** <note>original: "Eth Ha-Aron" meaning "the Ark"</note> from 1 Samuel 6:13. The middle verse is 1 Chronicles 27:25. There are 25 Masoretic sections, the sign for which is found in the word **לך** <note>original: "Lekh" meaning "Go"</note> from Joshua 17:14.

---

# Be strong and let us be strengthened; may the scribe not be harmed

-> The total number of verses for the whole of Chronicles is one thousand six hundred and fifty-six. The sign is: *And they saw the Ark and rejoiced to see it*. The middle point is: *And over the king's treasuries was Azmaveth the son of Adiel*. It has twenty-five sections; the sign is: *Until now the Lord has blessed me*. <-

---

v. 13. *Rebelled*: 'Resh' with Patach in manuscripts 1, 3, 7, and 8. But others have the opposite note, Qamatz, which the Erfurt Masorah confirms.
v. 15. *By the hand*: With the accent 'Merca' in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14, 15, 19, 20.
v. 16. *And scoffed*: Thus the letter 'Mem' with a Shva in manuscripts 1, 6, 9, 20. *At His prophets*: Thus defective <note>Spelled without the vowel-letter 'Yod'</note> in 1, 3, 6, 9, 20.
v. 17. *Young man*: With a Patach in 6, 9, 20.
*Until the rise*: Thus in 1 and others. But 'until the rise' in verse 16 is found in 2 according to the Masorah, and in 3 and Erfurt. Others spell it fully.
v. 21. *To fulfill*: Thus defective without the 'Vav' in 1 according to its Masorah.
*Desolate*: The prefix 'He' with Chateph-patach in 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 19, 20.
But with a Patach in 11, 13, 21.

<column-break/>

*And they broke down*: Thus with the accent 'Pashta' in manuscript 1.
v. 19. *Wall*: [note on manuscript 2].
Furthermore, the letter 'Shin' is without a Dagesh in 1, 3, 6, 9, 20.
v. 22. *Persia*: Occurs twice in this passage with a Qamatz in 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 20. The same in verse 23.
Instead of 'to fulfill' <note>original: "Lichloth"</note>, manuscripts 1 and 3 have 'to finish'.
v. 23. *And He*: With the accent 'Kadma' in 3, 6, 9, 20, and similarly in 5.
*His people*: With the accent 'Zaqef Qaton' in 1 and 10.
